title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental programming syntax elements from Python through structured flashcard review and peer testing activities. This foundational activity helps students build automatic recognition of essential code components before moving to problem-solving tasks.
learning_objectives: Students will identify common Python syntax elements (variables, loops, conditionals, functions) by correctly matching code snippets to their descriptions
Students will recall basic Python keywords and operators through rapid-fire flashcard exercises with 80% accuracy
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 essential Python syntax elements including: variable assignment (=), comparison operators (==, !=, <, >), conditional statements (if, elif, else), loop structures (for, while), function definitions (def), and common built-in functions (print, input, len). Each flashcard shows a code snippet on one side and its description/purpose on the reverse.

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to review all flashcards, reading each code snippet aloud and checking the description. Instruct them to separate cards into 'confident' and 'needs practice' piles.

Phase 2 (15 minutes): Pair students randomly. Partner A shows code snippets from the 'needs practice' pile while Partner B identifies the syntax element and explains its purpose. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes, cycling through all challenging cards twice.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Conduct a whole-class rapid-fire review. Display syntax examples on the projector for 5 seconds each. Students write the syntax element name on mini whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Keep score of correct responses per student.

Phase 4 (5 minutes): Final individual assessment where students complete a matching worksheet connecting 10 code snippets to their correct descriptions without referring to flashcards. Collect worksheets immediately upon completion.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (20 cards per student covering Python basics)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Projector and computer for displaying code snippets
Printed matching worksheets for final assessment
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade the final matching worksheet using a 10-point scale (1 point per correct match). Success criteria: 8/10 correct matches demonstrates mastery. During rapid-fire review, track individual response accuracy - students should achieve 70% correct responses. Observe peer interactions to ensure students can verbally explain syntax purposes to partners.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference sheet with syntax definitions during practice phases, pair with stronger students, and allow extra review time with flashcards. For advanced learners: include bonus flashcards with more complex syntax (list comprehensions, lambda functions), challenge them to create original code examples using each syntax element, or have them assist struggling classmates as peer tutors.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Challenge: Practical Workshop
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements including keywords, operators, and basic command structures. This activity uses structured repetition and peer assessment to build foundational coding vocabulary that students can instantly recognize and reproduce.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recall 25 essential Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, etc.) by matching them to their correct syntax usage within 30 seconds per keyword

Students will memorize the correct syntax for 15 basic Python operations (variable assignment, print statements, input functions, basic arithmetic operators) through repetitive flashcard drills and peer quizzing
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to pairs of students (5 minutes setup). Each set contains 40 cards: 25 Python keyword cards and 15 syntax operation cards. One side shows the programming concept (e.g., 'conditional statement'), the other shows the Python syntax (e.g., 'if condition:'). 

Round 1 (15 minutes): Student A holds cards showing only the concept side to Student B, who must verbally state the exact Python syntax. Student B gets 30 seconds per card. Mark correct answers with a checkmark. Switch roles after 20 cards.

Round 2 (15 minutes): Repeat the process but now show the syntax side, requiring students to identify what programming concept it represents.

Round 3 (10 minutes): Speed challenge - students work through their missed cards from rounds 1-2, aiming for 15-second response times.

Conclusion (10 minutes): Each pair reports their top 5 most challenging syntax elements to the class. Instructor addresses common misconceptions and demonstrates correct usage on the whiteboard. Students must write down any corrections in their notebooks for future reference.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (40 cards per pair) with Python keywords and syntax
Timer or stopwatch for each pair
Pencils for marking correct answers
Individual student notebooks
Whiteboard and markers for instructor demonstrations
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (32 out of 40 cards correct) across both concept-to-syntax and syntax-to-concept rounds. Track progress using peer-marked scoresheets. Final assessment includes a 10-question written quiz where students write the exact Python syntax for given programming concepts, with no reference materials allowed.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce card set to 20 most essential items and increase response time to 45 seconds. Provide a reference sheet with syntax examples during initial rounds. For advanced learners: Add 15 additional cards with more complex syntax (list comprehensions, lambda functions, exception handling) and challenge them to explain when each syntax element would be most appropriately used.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Challenge: Practical Workshop
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements through structured flashcard activities and verbal recitation exercises. This activity focuses on building automatic recognition of basic programming constructs without requiring code execution.
learning_objectives: Students will identify Python keywords, operators, and data type declarations by matching them to their correct syntax format within 3 seconds per item
Students will recall the exact spelling and capitalization of 20 essential Python commands through repetitive flashcard practice and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 Python syntax elements (front: concept name, back: exact syntax). Spend 5 minutes having students silently review all cards individually, reading both sides aloud quietly. Next, organize students into pairs for 10 minutes of mutual quizzing - Partner A shows concept names while Partner B recites exact syntax, then switch roles after 5 minutes. During this phase, circulate to ensure students are pronouncing syntax correctly and spelling accurately. Follow with a 10-minute whole-class rapid-fire session where you display concept names on screen for 5 seconds each while students write exact syntax on individual whiteboards, then hold up answers simultaneously for immediate feedback. Conclude with 5 minutes of individual silent review where students identify their 3 weakest items and practice those specifically. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact spelling, proper capitalization (e.g., 'True' not 'true'), and complete syntax including colons, parentheses, and brackets where required.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (one per student) with 20 Python syntax items
Individual mini-whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Digital projector or screen for displaying concept names
Timer for managing activity segments
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by achieving 90% accuracy (18/20 correct) on the final whiteboard rapid-fire round. Record individual scores based on exact syntax matching including proper capitalization, spelling, and punctuation. Provide immediate verbal feedback during pair work and note students who struggle with specific syntax categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce flashcard set to 10 items and provide reference sheet with common patterns. Allow extra review time and pair with stronger students during partner work. For advanced learners, include more complex syntax like list comprehensions and lambda functions, or challenge them to explain when each syntax element would be used in actual programs.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Challenge: Visual Analysis
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements through a structured flashcard matching activity. This activity focuses on recognizing basic programming constructs, operators, and keywords without requiring code execution or analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will identify Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, return) by matching them to their correct definitions within 30 seconds per card
Students will recall Python operators (+, -, *, /, ==, !=, <, >, and, or, not) through visual recognition exercises with 80% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to pairs of students, with each set containing 20 cards split into syntax elements and definitions. Students work in pairs for 25 minutes total. First, give students 5 minutes to review all cards individually, reading each syntax element and its corresponding definition. Next, have Student A hold the syntax element cards while Student B holds the definition cards. Student A shows a syntax card (e.g., 'def'), and Student B must find and show the matching definition card ('keyword used to define a function') within 30 seconds. If correct, they keep the pair; if incorrect, cards go to a 'retry' pile. After 8 minutes, students switch roles. Continue alternating every 4 minutes until all cards are matched or time expires. In the final 5 minutes, both students work together to review any cards from their 'retry' pile, saying each syntax element aloud followed by its definition three times. Circulate during the activity to ensure students are pronouncing syntax elements correctly and understanding definitions rather than just memorizing card positions. Record which pairs each team successfully matches for assessment purposes.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (20 cards each): 10 Python syntax element cards and 10 definition cards per pair
Timer or stopwatch
Assessment checklist for instructor tracking
Optional: laminated cards for durability
assessment_method: Observe and record each pair's successful matches during the activity using a checklist. Success criteria: students must correctly match at least 16 out of 20 syntax-definition pairs (80% accuracy) and demonstrate proper pronunciation of syntax elements. Conduct a quick verbal spot-check with 3-4 random pairs, asking them to state definitions for 3 randomly selected syntax elements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce card set to 10 pairs focusing only on basic keywords (if, else, for, while, def) and provide a reference sheet with visual examples. Allow extra review time and permit students to use cards in 'hint mode' where they can see partial definitions. For advanced learners: add challenge cards with more complex syntax (try/except, lambda, list comprehensions) or have them create their own flashcard sets for concepts like data types or built-in functions.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Challenge: Practical Workshop
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental syntax elements from Python programming language through structured flashcard drilling and peer quizzing. This activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for writing basic code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 essential Python syntax elements (keywords, operators, symbols) by matching them to their correct names and purposes
Students will recall the exact spelling and capitalization of Python keywords through repeated practice and peer assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 Python syntax elements (print, if, else, while, for, def, return, ==, !=, <=, >=, +, -, *, /, %, (, ), [, ], :). Each flashcard shows the syntax symbol/keyword on one side and its name plus one-sentence description on the other. Students work individually for 10 minutes studying their flashcards, focusing on exact spelling and capitalization. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 8 minutes - Partner A shows syntax symbols while Partner B recalls names and basic purposes, then switch roles. During the final 7 minutes, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire quiz where you display syntax elements on the projector and students write down the correct names on their answer sheets. Call on random students to verify answers aloud. For the last 5 minutes, have students self-assess by checking their answer sheets against the correct answers displayed on screen, counting their correct responses.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (one per student) with 20 Python syntax elements
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-20
Computer/projector for displaying syntax elements
Answer key slide for self-assessment
assessment_method: Students achieve success by correctly identifying 15 out of 20 syntax elements (75% accuracy) on the final quiz. Evaluate through: (1) completed answer sheets showing written responses, (2) self-reported accuracy scores, and (3) instructor observation of peer quizzing engagement and correct verbal responses during whole-class segments.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a reference sheet with the 20 elements listed alphabetically, allowing them to match rather than recall from memory. Extend advanced learners by adding 10 additional syntax elements (import, class, try, except, and, or, not, True, False, None) or having them create example code snippets using each syntax element.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Customer Data
description: Students analyze visualized customer purchase data to distinguish between normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions. They will explain how different distribution patterns reveal specific business insights and customer behavior patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will classify distribution types (normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, bimodal) by examining histograms and box plots of customer transaction data
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through written interpretations connecting statistical concepts to real-world scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing printed histogram and box plot pairs showing customer data (purchase amounts, session duration, items per order) to teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives 6 different distribution visualizations without labels. Step 1 (10 minutes): Teams examine each visualization and classify it as normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, or bimodal using provided reference cards showing distribution characteristics. Step 2 (15 minutes): For each classified distribution, teams write a 2-3 sentence explanation of what this pattern suggests about customer behavior, using a structured template: 'This [distribution type] suggests that most customers [behavior pattern] because [statistical reasoning].' Step 3 (10 minutes): Teams compare their classifications with answer key and discuss discrepancies. Step 4 (15 minutes): Instructor presents three new unlabeled distributions on screen. Each team submits classifications and business interpretations on index cards. Step 5 (10 minutes): Debrief by having teams share one interesting insight they discovered about how distribution shape connects to business understanding. Emphasize key concepts: right-skew often indicates outliers, bimodal suggests distinct customer segments, normal distributions are rare in real business data.
materials_needed: 6 printed histogram/box plot pairs per team (18 total unique visualizations)
Distribution classification reference cards with visual examples
Interpretation template worksheets
Answer key for initial 6 distributions
Index cards for final assessment
Projector/screen for displaying challenge distributions
assessment_method: Evaluate using 3-point rubric: Classification accuracy (correctly identifies 5-6 distributions = 3 points, 3-4 = 2 points, 1-2 = 1 point), Business interpretation quality (demonstrates clear connection between distribution shape and customer behavior with statistical reasoning), Participation in team discussions (observed engagement and contribution to group analysis)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional reference examples showing extreme cases of each distribution type and sentence starters for interpretations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify specific statistical measures (median vs. mean positions, standard deviation implications) and suggest data collection methods that might create each distribution pattern.

title: Optimization in Action: Designing a Solar Panel Array for Maximum Energy Output
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem by determining the optimal configuration of solar panels to maximize energy output given physical and budgetary constraints. This activity integrates partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization to address a practical renewable energy challenge.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to optimize solar panel array configurations by solving constrained optimization problems with real-world parameters
Students will implement multivariable calculus concepts through systematic analysis of cost-benefit trade-offs in renewable energy system design
instructions: Begin by distributing the solar panel optimization worksheet containing a specific scenario: a company has $50,000 to install solar panels on a rectangular roof measuring 40m × 25m, with panels costing $200 each and generating power based on P(x,y,θ) = 150xy cos(θ) - 0.5x²y - 0.3xy² watts, where x and y represent panel dimensions and θ represents tilt angle. Students work in pairs for the first 20 minutes to set up the optimization problem, identifying the objective function (maximize power output) and constraints (budget: 200n ≤ 50,000, roof space: nx·ny ≤ 1000, where n is number of panels). Next, spend 30 minutes having students apply Lagrange multiplier methods to find critical points, computing ∇P = λ∇g where g represents the combined constraints. During this phase, circulate to check that students correctly calculate partial derivatives: ∂P/∂x = 150y cos(θ) - xy - 0.3y², ∂P/∂y = 150x cos(θ) - 0.5x² - 0.6xy, ∂P/∂θ = -150xy sin(θ). For the following 25 minutes, students solve the resulting system of equations using computational tools, then verify their solution using the second derivative test to confirm they've found a maximum. Finally, allocate 15 minutes for pairs to present their optimal configuration (number of panels, dimensions, tilt angle) and calculate the total expected power output and cost utilization, comparing results across different solution approaches.
materials_needed: Solar panel optimization worksheet with specific scenario parameters
Graphing calculators or computer access with CAS software (Mathematica, Maple, or GeoGebra)
Graph paper for sketching constraint regions
Scientific calculators for verification calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly sets up Lagrange multiplier equations, solves system accurately, and provides optimal solution with justification; (3) Minor computational errors but demonstrates understanding of optimization process; (2) Sets up problem correctly but makes significant solving errors; (1) Shows partial understanding but major conceptual gaps. Students must submit their constraint equations, critical point calculations, second derivative test verification, and final optimal configuration with power output prediction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed Lagrange multiplier setup showing the first constraint equation as a model. Offer a step-by-step derivative calculation guide for the power function. For advanced learners, add a second scenario with non-rectangular roof geometry requiring more complex constraint handling, or introduce seasonal variation by making the tilt angle θ time-dependent, requiring optimization over a time interval.

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive security analysis of a provided e-commerce web application's architecture diagram and codebase. They will systematically identify potential attack vectors, evaluate the effectiveness of existing security measures, and determine the root causes of vulnerabilities across database, application, and presentation tiers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-tier web application architectures by identifying and categorizing security vulnerabilities across database, application logic, and presentation layers
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of implemented security controls through systematic threat modeling and attack vector mapping
instructions:
Begin by distributing the ShopSecure e-commerce application materials: architecture diagram, database schema, and code samples (PHP backend, JavaScript frontend, MySQL queries). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Database Security Analyst, Application Logic Analyst, Frontend Security Analyst, and Integration Analyst. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each specialist analyzes their assigned tier using the provided security checklist. Database analysts examine SQL injection vulnerabilities, privilege escalation risks, and data encryption gaps. Application analysts focus on authentication flaws, session management issues, and input validation weaknesses. Frontend analysts identify XSS vulnerabilities, CSRF risks, and client-side data exposure. Integration analysts map data flow between tiers and identify trust boundary violations.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams reconvene to create a comprehensive vulnerability matrix, plotting each identified issue against CIA triad impacts (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) and OWASP Top 10 categories. Students must provide specific code line references and explain the technical mechanism enabling each vulnerability.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams develop attack scenario flowcharts showing how identified vulnerabilities could be chained together for maximum impact. They must demonstrate understanding of how a single entry point (e.g., XSS) could escalate to full system compromise through privilege escalation and lateral movement.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Present findings using the standardized vulnerability report template, including severity ratings based on CVSS scoring methodology and specific remediation recommendations with implementation priority rankings.
materials_needed: ShopSecure application package (architecture diagram, PHP/JavaScript source code, MySQL schema)
OWASP Top 10 reference sheets
Security analysis checklists for each tier
Vulnerability matrix templates
CVSS calculator access
Presentation computers with network access
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (4) Comprehensive identification of 15+ vulnerabilities with accurate technical explanations and valid attack chains; (3) Good identification of 10-14 vulnerabilities with mostly accurate explanations; (2) Adequate identification of 6-9 vulnerabilities with basic explanations; (1) Limited identification of fewer than 6 vulnerabilities. Additional points for creative attack scenarios, proper CVSS scoring, and actionable remediation strategies. Deduct points for incorrect vulnerability classifications or technically impossible attack chains.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vulnerability hint cards for each tier and pre-populated attack vector examples. Offer guided code walkthrough sessions focusing on common patterns. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify zero-day potential vulnerabilities not covered in standard checklists, develop proof-of-concept exploits, or design automated scanning tools. Provide access to additional real-world CVE databases for comparison analysis.

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze a complex three-tier web application's architecture to identify security vulnerabilities, examining attack vectors across presentation, application logic, and data tiers. They will deconstruct the system's security weaknesses and evaluate the effectiveness of existing countermeasures against specific threat models.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-tier web application architectures by systematically identifying security vulnerabilities across presentation, business logic, and data access layers
Students will evaluate existing security countermeasures through threat modeling techniques and attack vector analysis
instructions:
**Phase 1: Architecture Decomposition (20 minutes)**
Provide teams of 3-4 students with the detailed system architecture document for 'EduPortal' - a university management system. Students first map the three tiers: React frontend, Node.js/Express API layer, and PostgreSQL database. Each team creates a visual diagram identifying all components, data flows, authentication points, and external integrations (payment gateway, email service, file storage).

**Phase 2: Vulnerability Identification Matrix (30 minutes)**
Using the OWASP Top 10 as a framework, teams systematically examine each architectural component. They complete a vulnerability matrix documenting: specific vulnerable components, potential attack vectors, impact severity (1-5 scale), and likelihood of exploitation. Focus areas include SQL injection points, XSS vulnerabilities in React components, API endpoint security, authentication bypass possibilities, and insecure direct object references.

**Phase 3: Attack Path Analysis (25 minutes)**
Teams select their three highest-risk vulnerabilities and map detailed attack paths. For each vulnerability, they document: entry points, required attacker capabilities, step-by-step exploitation sequence, potential data exposure, and cascading effects across system tiers. Teams use attack trees to visualize complex multi-step attacks.

**Phase 4: Countermeasure Evaluation (20 minutes)**
Examine existing security measures documented in the architecture (input validation, parameterized queries, JWT tokens, HTTPS, rate limiting). Teams assess each countermeasure's effectiveness against identified vulnerabilities, noting gaps and potential bypasses. They rank countermeasures by implementation quality and coverage.

**Phase 5: Presentation and Peer Review (15 minutes)**
Each team presents their most critical finding to the class (3 minutes each), followed by structured peer questioning. Other teams challenge assumptions and suggest additional attack vectors or overlooked vulnerabilities.
materials_needed: Detailed EduPortal system architecture documentation (15 pages including database schema, API specifications, and deployment diagrams)
OWASP Top 10 reference cards
Vulnerability assessment matrix templates (Excel/Google Sheets)
Attack tree diagramming software (draw.io or Lucidchart access)
Laptops with internet access for research
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Architectural understanding (20 points - accuracy of component identification and data flow mapping), Vulnerability identification depth (30 points - number and accuracy of vulnerabilities found, use of OWASP framework), Attack path analysis quality (25 points - logical attack sequences, realistic attacker capabilities, cascading impact assessment), Countermeasure evaluation (15 points - thorough assessment of existing controls, identification of gaps), and Professional presentation (10 points - clear communication, peer engagement). Minimum passing score: 70/100.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled vulnerability matrix templates with example entries, offer guided questions for each analysis phase, and pair with stronger technical students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify zero-day attack possibilities, analyze advanced persistent threat scenarios, or propose novel countermeasures. Provide additional real-world CVE databases for deeper vulnerability research and encourage exploration of emerging attack techniques like supply chain vulnerabilities.
original_title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture: Exercise 2
description: Students will dissect a complex e-commerce web application's architecture to identify security vulnerabilities across presentation, application, and data tiers. They will analyze attack vectors, evaluate security controls, and determine the cascading impact of identified vulnerabilities on the entire system.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the security posture of a multi-tier web application by systematically examining each architectural layer and identifying potential attack vectors
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of existing security controls through threat modeling and vulnerability impact assessment techniques
instructions: Begin by providing students with a detailed architectural diagram and codebase of a fictional e-commerce application called 'SecureShop' containing intentional security flaws. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a specific analysis focus area. Start with a 15-minute briefing explaining the application's business logic: user authentication, payment processing, inventory management, and admin functions. Each team receives access to the application's source code repository, database schema, network configuration files, and deployment documentation. Students spend 45 minutes conducting initial reconnaissance, mapping data flows between tiers, and documenting system components. Next, teams perform a 60-minute systematic vulnerability analysis using provided OWASP Top 10 checklist and CWE database. They must identify at least 5 vulnerabilities across different tiers, documenting each with CVSS scoring, affected components, and potential business impact. Teams then spend 30 minutes creating attack scenario flowcharts showing how vulnerabilities could be chained together for maximum damage. During the final 30-minute phase, teams prepare executive summary reports ranking vulnerabilities by risk level and proposing specific mitigation strategies with implementation timelines and resource requirements. Conclude with 10-minute team presentations where each group presents their most critical finding to simulate briefing senior management.
materials_needed: SecureShop application codebase with intentional vulnerabilities (PHP/MySQL/JavaScript)
Network architecture diagrams and infrastructure documentation
OWASP Top 10 vulnerability checklist and CWE database access
Vulnerability scanning tools (Burp Suite Community, OWASP ZAP)
Threat modeling templates and CVSS calculator
Laptops with Docker containers running the vulnerable application
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Vulnerability identification accuracy (25 points), technical analysis depth (25 points), risk assessment quality using CVSS methodology (20 points), attack scenario feasibility and creativity (15 points), and mitigation strategy practicality (15 points). Students must submit written reports documenting findings with evidence screenshots, risk matrices, and remediation roadmaps. Assess presentation quality based on technical accuracy and executive communication clarity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide vulnerability hunting worksheets with guided questions and pre-configured scanning tool profiles. Offer intermediate checkpoints every 30 minutes with instructor feedback. For advanced learners, challenge them to develop custom exploit code demonstrating identified vulnerabilities or design automated testing frameworks. Provide additional complex scenarios like API security analysis or cloud infrastructure assessment for extended learning.

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture: Exercise 3
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive security analysis of a provided e-commerce web application's architecture diagram and codebase. They will systematically identify potential attack vectors across all tiers and evaluate the effectiveness of existing security measures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-tier web application architectures by identifying security vulnerabilities across presentation, business logic, and data tiers
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of implemented security controls through systematic threat modeling and risk assessment techniques
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with identical packets containing: architecture diagrams of 'ShopSecure' e-commerce application, sample code snippets from each tier, and current security implementation documentation. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students individually examine the three-tier architecture, documenting potential vulnerabilities using the STRIDE threat model (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege). They must identify at least 2 vulnerabilities per tier. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), teams collaborate to consolidate findings, prioritize vulnerabilities using CVSS scoring criteria, and create a vulnerability matrix mapping threats to specific architectural components. During Phase 3 (25 minutes), each team analyzes the existing security controls (input validation, authentication mechanisms, encryption protocols, access controls) and evaluates their effectiveness against identified threats. Teams must determine which vulnerabilities remain unmitigated. In Phase 4 (20 minutes), teams prepare a technical briefing slide deck presenting their top 5 critical vulnerabilities, including: affected components, potential impact, likelihood assessment, and recommended countermeasures. Conclude with 5-minute team presentations followed by peer evaluation using provided rubric.
materials_needed: ShopSecure application architecture diagrams (3-tier: web server, application server, database)
Code samples in Java/Python showing authentication, session management, and database queries
STRIDE threat modeling worksheets
CVSS vulnerability scoring reference sheets
Laptops with network analysis tools (Wireshark, OWASP ZAP)
assessment_method: Teams scored using 100-point rubric: Vulnerability identification accuracy (25 points), STRIDE methodology application (20 points), security control evaluation depth (25 points), risk prioritization justification (15 points), technical presentation clarity (15 points). Individual accountability ensured through random questioning during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing vulnerability checklist templates and example STRIDE analyses. For advanced learners, introduce additional attack vectors like side-channel attacks or supply chain vulnerabilities, and require them to propose specific remediation architectures with cost-benefit analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Performance Analysis
description: Students will critically evaluate three different visualizations of the same student academic performance dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key insights. They will assess each visualization against established data visualization principles and justify their final recommendation with evidence-based reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying established design principles and identifying strengths and weaknesses
Students will justify their visualization recommendations through structured comparison and evidence-based argumentation
instructions: Begin by distributing the evaluation worksheet and displaying three visualizations of student grade data: a pie chart showing grade distribution, a bar chart comparing average grades by subject, and a scatter plot showing study hours vs. final grades. Give students 5 minutes to examine all three visualizations silently. Next, introduce the evaluation criteria: clarity (Is the message immediately clear?), accuracy (Does it represent data truthfully?), and purpose alignment (Does it serve the intended analytical goal of identifying factors affecting student performance?). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes to complete the evaluation matrix, rating each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and writing 2-3 sentence justifications. During the next 10 minutes, pairs should discuss and select their top-ranked visualization, preparing a 1-minute verbal justification. Conduct a gallery walk where each pair presents their choice and reasoning to the class (15 minutes total, allowing brief questions). Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing different perspectives and identifying common evaluation themes. Students must submit their completed evaluation matrix and a final paragraph explaining their reasoning, addressing potential counterarguments to their choice.
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations of student academic performance dataset
Evaluation matrix worksheet with criteria and rating scales
Timer for time management
Whiteboard or flip chart for recording class insights
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of criterion application (4 points - correctly identifies visualization strengths/weaknesses using all three criteria), (2) Quality of justification (4 points - provides specific evidence and logical reasoning), (3) Consideration of alternatives (2 points - acknowledges other valid perspectives or limitations of chosen visualization). Total: 10 points. Success threshold: 7/10 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'A weakness I notice is...'. Create a checklist of questions for each criterion. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific improvements to the weaker visualizations or consider how audience (teachers vs. students vs. parents) might change their evaluation.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Performance Analysis: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same student performance dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to justify their recommendations for presenting data to school administrators.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific assessment criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique data presentation choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning to recommend optimal visualization strategies
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the Student Performance Dataset (containing 200 records with variables: student_id, math_score, reading_score, study_hours, attendance_rate, grade_level) and three pre-created visualizations: Visualization A (clustered bar chart), Visualization B (scatter plot matrix), and Visualization C (dashboard with multiple chart types). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine the dataset to understand variables and identify 2-3 key insights that should be communicated to school administrators. Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the provided Visualization Evaluation Rubric, groups systematically assess each visualization across four criteria: Data Accuracy (Are calculations correct?), Visual Clarity (Is information easy to understand?), Audience Appropriateness (Suitable for administrators?), and Insight Communication (Does it highlight key findings?). Groups score each visualization 1-4 on each criterion. Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups calculate total scores and identify strengths/weaknesses for each visualization. Step 4 (10 minutes): Groups prepare 2-minute presentations defending their choice of most effective visualization, citing specific evidence from their evaluation. Step 5 (15 minutes): Each group presents their recommendation and reasoning. Step 6 (10 minutes): Class discusses patterns in evaluations and votes on most convincing argument.
materials_needed: Student Performance Dataset (CSV file with 200 records)
Three pre-created visualizations (printed copies or digital files)
Visualization Evaluation Rubric (4 criteria, 4-point scale)
Calculators or computers for scoring
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: Systematic Use of Criteria (5 points - consistently applied all four evaluation criteria), Evidence-Based Reasoning (5 points - cited specific examples from visualizations), Quality of Recommendation (5 points - clear, justified choice), Presentation Effectiveness (5 points - clear communication within time limit). Success criteria: Students score 16/20 or higher, demonstrating ability to systematically evaluate data visualizations using multiple criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example evaluation of a fourth visualization, highlight key phrases for justification ('This visualization is effective because...'), assign specific roles within groups (timekeeper, scorer, presenter). title: Design Your Dream House: Area and Perimeter Optimization Challenge
description: Students will design a floor plan for their dream house using geometric shapes while working within specific area and perimeter constraints. They will create both a scaled blueprint and a mathematical justification report explaining their design choices and calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original house floor plan by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, squares, and composite shapes within given constraints
Students will construct a mathematical justification document through detailed calculations showing how their design meets the specified requirements
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: Students are architects designing a dream house with a maximum area of 2,400 square feet and must include at least 6 rooms. Distribute constraint cards showing required rooms (living room 300-400 sq ft, kitchen 200-250 sq ft, master bedroom 250-300 sq ft, two additional bedrooms 150-200 sq ft each, and one bathroom 80-100 sq ft). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to brainstorm room arrangements and relationships. Next, provide graph paper (1 square = 10 sq ft) and have students sketch their initial floor plan for 25 minutes, ensuring all rooms fit within a reasonable perimeter that maximizes interior space while minimizing exterior walls. Students then spend 20 minutes calculating the exact area of each room and the total house perimeter using appropriate geometric formulas. For the next 30 minutes, students create a clean, scaled blueprint on fresh graph paper, including measurements and room labels. Finally, students spend 25 minutes writing a one-page mathematical report explaining their design decisions, showing all area and perimeter calculations, and justifying how their design optimizes space usage. Conclude with 15-minute pair presentations where teams explain their design rationale and respond to questions about their mathematical reasoning.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1/4 inch grid, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers and measuring tools
Colored pencils or markers
Constraint requirement cards (printed)
Calculators
Design planning worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations (25%), (2) Creative and practical floor plan design meeting all constraints (25%), (3) Quality of mathematical justification report with clear explanations (25%), and (4) Professional presentation of blueprint with proper scaling and labeling (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category with all calculations within 5% accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing area/perimeter formula reference sheets and pre-drawn room templates they can arrange. Offer calculation check-sheets for step-by-step verification. For advanced learners, add challenges like irregular room shapes, multiple floor levels, or cost optimization using price-per-square-foot constraints. Consider allowing advanced students to explore triangular or circular room elements.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Memory Palace Construction
description: Students will memorize the seven-layer OSI model and four-layer TCP/IP protocol stack by creating detailed visual memory palaces. They will then recall specific protocols, headers, and data units at each layer without reference materials.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize all seven OSI layers and four TCP/IP layers with their specific functions by constructing personalized memory palaces
Students will recall at least 15 specific protocols and their corresponding layers through systematic memory rehearsal techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the protocol reference sheet and explaining the memory palace technique (5 minutes). Students select a familiar physical location (their home, school building, or favorite store) as their memory palace foundation. They must identify 7 distinct rooms/areas for OSI layers, mapping Physical→Application layers to specific locations in logical order (10 minutes). For each location, students create vivid mental images linking layer functions to room characteristics (e.g., Physical layer = basement with ethernet cables as pipes, Data Link layer = garage with MAC address license plates). Provide 25 minutes for students to build these associations, writing brief descriptive notes for each room. Next, students memorize specific protocols: TCP/UDP at Transport layer, IP/ICMP at Network layer, HTTP/FTP at Application layer, etc. They create character personas for each protocol living in appropriate rooms (15 minutes). Students practice walking through their memory palace mentally, reciting layers bottom-to-top, then top-to-bottom (10 minutes). Pair students for reciprocal testing—partners quiz each other on random layers, protocols, and functions (15 minutes). Conclude with individual silent rehearsal where students mentally traverse their palace three complete times, strengthening neural pathways (10 minutes). Students must achieve fluent recall without hesitation before proceeding to protocol header field memorization in subsequent lessons.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet with layer details
Memory Palace Template worksheet
Protocol-to-Layer mapping chart
Timer for practice intervals
Blank paper for memory palace sketches
assessment_method: Students complete a timed recall assessment where they must list all OSI/TCP-IP layers in order (both directions) within 60 seconds, identify the correct layer for 15 given protocols with 90% accuracy, and explain the primary function of each layer without reference materials. Pass threshold: 13/15 protocols correctly placed and all layers recalled in proper sequence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with only 4 TCP/IP layers before adding OSI complexity, provide pre-drawn memory palace templates of common locations, use acronyms (Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away). For advanced learners: Include specific port numbers, header field details, and protocol interaction patterns between layers. Create memory palaces for multiple protocol suites (IPX/SPX, AppleTalk).

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Ensemble Methods
description: Students will analyze cross-validation results from multiple ensemble algorithms to understand how bias-variance tradeoffs manifest in real model performance metrics. They will interpret learning curves, validation curves, and decomposition plots to explain why certain ensemble methods perform differently under various data conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing the mathematical relationship between model complexity and generalization error in ensemble methods
Students will explain cross-validation performance patterns through systematic comparison of Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and AdaBoost learning curves
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-generated dataset containing cross-validation results from three ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost) trained on both high-noise and low-noise versions of a regression problem. Each student receives identical Jupyter notebooks containing validation curves, learning curves, and bias-variance decomposition plots. In Phase 1 (15 minutes), students individually examine the validation curves showing model performance versus hyperparameter values (n_estimators for RF, learning_rate for GB, n_estimators for AdaBoost). They must identify optimal complexity points and document where overfitting begins. In Phase 2 (20 minutes), students analyze learning curves plotting training/validation scores versus sample size, identifying which algorithms show high bias versus high variance characteristics. They must calculate the gap between training and validation scores at different sample sizes. In Phase 3 (20 minutes), students examine bias-variance decomposition plots showing how prediction error splits into bias², variance, and noise components across different train set sizes. They must interpret why Random Forest shows different bias-variance characteristics compared to boosting methods. In Phase 4 (15 minutes), pairs discuss their interpretations and create written explanations for why each algorithm behaves differently under high-noise versus low-noise conditions. Students must connect mathematical concepts (bias-variance tradeoff) to practical model selection decisions. Final phase (10 minutes) involves whole-class discussion where pairs share insights about when to choose each ensemble method based on bias-variance analysis.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-computed cross-validation results and plots
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Printed bias-variance decomposition reference sheet with formulas
Dataset documentation explaining noise characteristics
assessment_method: Evaluate written explanations using rubric: (1) Correct identification of bias vs variance dominance in each algorithm (25 points), (2) Accurate interpretation of learning curve patterns and mathematical relationships (25 points), (3) Clear explanation of how noise level affects ensemble method selection (25 points), (4) Logical connection between decomposition plots and practical model choice recommendations (25 points). Students must submit annotated plots with written justifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example analysis of one algorithm's results with step-by-step interpretation guide. Offer templates for describing mathematical relationships between bias, variance, and model complexity. For advanced learners: Include additional bagging vs boosting comparison tasks, or provide raw data to compute their own bias-variance decompositions using mlxtend library. Consider adding analysis of how feature dimensionality affects the bias-variance tradeoff.

title: Grocery Store Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to real-world grocery shopping scenarios by calculating discounts, sales tax, and tips. They will create shopping lists within specific budgets while navigating various percentage-based pricing situations.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages, discounts, and sales tax by solving realistic grocery shopping problems within given budget constraints
Students will apply percentage formulas through hands-on manipulation of prices, quantities, and budget allocations in a simulated shopping environment
instructions:
Begin by distributing grocery store flyers and price lists to each student pair (5 minutes). Assign each pair a specific budget ($50, $75, or $100) and a shopping scenario (family of 4 weekly groceries, party planning, or monthly staples). Students must create a shopping list that stays within budget while accounting for: 15% off produce, 10% off canned goods, 7.5% sales tax on non-food items, and a 3% credit card processing fee on totals over $60. 

First, students identify needed items and record original prices (10 minutes). Next, they calculate applicable discounts item by item, showing work for each percentage calculation (15 minutes). Then, they determine which items qualify for sales tax and calculate the 7.5% addition (10 minutes). Students must then calculate their subtotal and determine if the 3% credit card fee applies (5 minutes). 

If their total exceeds budget, they must adjust quantities or substitute items, recalculating percentages for their new selections (10 minutes). Finally, each pair presents their final shopping list, total cost breakdown, and explains one percentage calculation to the class (10 minutes). Throughout the activity, circulate to check calculation methods and provide guidance on percentage formula application.
materials_needed: Grocery store flyers or printed price lists (1 per pair)
Budget scenario cards with different spending limits
Calculators (1 per student)
Percentage calculation reference sheet
Recording worksheets with itemized budget tracking sections
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct application of percentage formulas for discounts and taxes, (2) Accurate final budget calculations within assigned limits, (3) Clear documentation of calculation steps, (4) Appropriate adjustments when over-budget. Students must achieve 3/4 rubric points and stay within $2 of their budget limit to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing percentage calculation templates and working through the first discount calculation together. For advanced learners, add compound scenarios like 'buy 2, get 1 at 50% off' deals or loyalty program discounts that require multi-step percentage applications. Consider pairing stronger math students with those who need support.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Sorting Implementations
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms by examining provided code implementations and tracing through execution patterns. They will identify bottlenecks, compare efficiency trade-offs, and predict performance on different dataset sizes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and worst-case scenarios
Students will evaluate space complexity patterns through systematic examination of memory allocation in recursive versus iterative implementations
instructions: Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4 and distribute the three algorithm implementation handouts (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) along with the analysis worksheet. Each group receives the same code samples written in Python. In the first 15 minutes, students work individually to trace through each algorithm using the provided dataset [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] and count the number of comparisons and swaps. Next, spend 20 minutes in group discussion where students compare their traces and identify patterns in the number of operations relative to input size n. Groups must complete the complexity analysis table, categorizing each algorithm's best, average, and worst-case time complexity using Big O notation. During the following 15 minutes, introduce three additional scenarios: a nearly-sorted array, a reverse-sorted array, and a large random dataset of 1000 elements. Groups predict which algorithm would perform best for each scenario and justify their reasoning. In the final 20 minutes, groups present their analysis to the class, specifically explaining one algorithm's complexity derivation and defending their scenario predictions. Each presentation must include a visual diagram showing how the algorithm's operations scale with input size.
materials_needed: Three algorithm implementation handouts (Python code for bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort)
Algorithm complexity analysis worksheet with comparison table template
Sample datasets printed on paper: [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90] and scenario descriptions
Whiteboard markers and large paper for presentation diagrams
Stopwatch or timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O notation identification for each algorithm (25%), (2) Correctness of execution traces and operation counts (25%), (3) Quality of scenario predictions with valid justifications (25%), (4) Clarity of group presentation including visual complexity diagram (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed trace example for bubble sort and offer guiding questions like 'How many times does the outer loop run?' For advanced learners, challenge them to analyze the space complexity of iterative versus recursive implementations, or consider hybrid algorithms like Timsort that combine multiple approaches.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Fraud Detection
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) applied to healthcare fraud detection, evaluating their effectiveness across multiple metrics and real-world constraints. Students will justify their recommendation for deployment based on comprehensive analysis of performance, interpretability, and ethical considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and computational efficiency metrics
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic assessment of business constraints, ethical implications, and interpretability requirements in healthcare contexts
instructions: **Phase 1 (30 min):** Provide student teams of 3-4 with identical healthcare claims datasets and pre-trained models (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) with their respective performance outputs. Each team receives: model accuracy scores, confusion matrices, ROC/AUC values, precision-recall curves, feature importance rankings, prediction times, and false positive/negative cost analyses. **Phase 2 (45 min):** Teams systematically evaluate each model using the provided evaluation framework worksheet. They must calculate cost-benefit ratios using given false positive costs ($500/claim) and false negative costs ($5000/claim), assess interpretability scores using the provided rubric (1-5 scale), and analyze fairness metrics across demographic groups. Students document findings in structured comparison tables. **Phase 3 (30 min):** Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their model recommendation. They must address: quantitative performance justification, ethical considerations (bias, fairness), interpretability requirements for healthcare auditors, computational constraints for real-time processing, and regulatory compliance implications. **Phase 4 (45 min):** Each team presents while others complete peer evaluation forms scoring the recommendation quality, evidence use, and consideration of trade-offs. Instructor facilitates discussion of conflicting recommendations, highlighting how different priorities (accuracy vs interpretability vs speed) lead to different optimal choices.
materials_needed: Healthcare fraud detection dataset (10,000 claims with labels)
Pre-trained model outputs (accuracy, confusion matrices, ROC curves for 3 models)
Model Evaluation Framework worksheet with cost-benefit calculation templates
Interpretability Assessment Rubric (1-5 scale with criteria)
Peer evaluation forms with scoring criteria
Python/R environment with scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
Presentation timer and scoring sheets
assessment_method: Students assessed via rubric (100 points total): Quantitative Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation of metrics and cost-benefit ratios; Critical Reasoning Quality (25 points) - depth of trade-off analysis and constraint consideration; Recommendation Justification (25 points) - evidence-based defense of model choice with acknowledgment of limitations; Peer Evaluation Participation (15 points) - quality of feedback provided to other teams; Professional Presentation (10 points) - clear communication within time limits. Success threshold: 80+ points indicates mastery of evaluation-level thinking.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide completed example evaluation for a different algorithm pair, offer calculation check-ins during Phase 2, assign specific roles within teams (metrics calculator, ethics analyst, presenter). **For advanced learners:** Add ensemble method evaluation, require statistical significance testing of performance differences, include analysis of model robustness under adversarial attacks, or incorporate recent research papers critiquing current fraud detection approaches for additional context.

title: Design and Construct an Optimization Algorithm for Multi-Variable Real-World Problems
description: Students will create an original optimization algorithm that solves complex multi-variable problems with constraints, then implement and validate their solution using programming tools. They will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and computational mathematics to address authentic business or engineering scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a novel optimization algorithm by combining Lagrange multipliers, gradient descent methods, and constraint handling techniques to solve multi-variable optimization problems
Students will design a comprehensive validation framework through computational implementation, sensitivity analysis, and real-world application testing
instructions: Step 1 (30 minutes): Present students with three complex scenarios: supply chain cost minimization with 8 variables and 12 constraints, satellite trajectory optimization with fuel/time trade-offs, or renewable energy grid optimization with variable demand. Students select one scenario and identify all variables, constraints, and objective functions. Step 2 (45 minutes): Students design their optimization approach by selecting and justifying mathematical techniques (gradient descent variants, penalty methods, or genetic algorithms). They must create detailed pseudocode showing how their algorithm handles constraints, convergence criteria, and edge cases. Step 3 (60 minutes): Using Python/MATLAB, students implement their algorithm from scratch (no optimization libraries allowed). Code must include input validation, iterative solver, constraint checking, and convergence tracking. Step 4 (30 minutes): Students generate test cases with known solutions to validate accuracy, then apply their algorithm to the original problem. They document computational complexity and sensitivity to initial conditions. Step 5 (45 minutes): Students prepare a technical presentation including algorithm flowchart, mathematical justification, implementation results, and comparison with standard optimization methods. They must propose two potential improvements and identify limitations. Step 6 (30 minutes): Peer review session where students test each other's algorithms with different parameter sets and provide feedback on mathematical rigor and computational efficiency.

Presentation equipment for final demonstrations

title: Basic Programming Terminology Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 fundamental programming terms and their definitions through structured flashcard practice. They will demonstrate their ability to identify key programming vocabulary through matching exercises and verbal recall activities.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 basic programming terms (variable, function, loop, array, string, integer, boolean, parameter, argument, method, class, object, algorithm, syntax, debugging, compile, execute, input, output, comment) by matching terms to correct definitions
Students will recall programming vocabulary definitions through verbal quizzing and written identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student (20 cards with terms on front, definitions on back). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, taking turns reading terms aloud while their partner provides definitions from memory. Next, conduct a whole-class 'definition auction' where you read a definition and students bid on which term matches by raising hands and stating the term. Award points for correct matches. Follow with individual silent study time (8 minutes) where students review their flashcards independently, focusing on terms they missed. Create four stations around the room: Station 1 has term-definition matching worksheets, Station 2 has digital quizzes on tablets/computers, Station 3 has peer quizzing in pairs, and Station 4 has instructor-led rapid-fire verbal assessment. Students rotate through stations spending 5 minutes at each. Conclude with a final whole-class assessment where you display terms on the board and students write definitions on paper. Collect papers immediately and provide verbal feedback by reading correct definitions aloud while students self-check their work.

Timer for station rotations

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Purchase Data Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real-world e-commerce dataset to distinguish between correlation and causation relationships. They will interpret statistical outputs and explain why certain variable relationships cannot establish causal claims despite showing strong correlations.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing correlation matrices and scatter plots from customer purchase data
Students will interpret statistical relationships through guided examination of confounding variables and spurious correlations in business scenarios
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the pre-loaded dataset containing 1000 customer records with variables: age, income, website_visits, email_opens, social_media_follows, purchase_amount, and season. Display the correlation heatmap on the main screen.

**Phase 1 - Initial Observations (15 minutes):** In pairs, students examine the correlation matrix and identify the three strongest positive correlations (r > 0.7). They record these relationships and write initial hypotheses about which ones might represent causation. Circulate to ensure students are reading the matrix correctly.

**Phase 2 - Guided Analysis (20 minutes):** Present three specific correlation pairs: (1) ice_cream_sales vs drowning_incidents (r=0.95), (2) website_visits vs purchase_amount (r=0.78), and (3) email_opens vs social_media_follows (r=0.82). For each pair, students complete a structured worksheet asking: What third variable might explain this relationship? What experiment would test causation? What business decision would be risky based on this correlation alone?

**Phase 3 - Application (15 minutes):** Students select one correlation from their dataset and create a 2-minute explanation addressing: the correlation strength, potential confounding variables, why correlation doesn't prove causation, and what additional data would help establish causation. They present findings to another pair for peer feedback.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Class discussion on common misconceptions and real-world implications of confusing correlation with causation in data-driven business decisions.
materials_needed: Pre-loaded customer dataset (CSV file with 1000 records)
Jupyter notebooks or Excel with correlation analysis capabilities
Correlation vs Causation analysis worksheet (printed)
Access to computers/tablets for pairs
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of strong correlations from matrix, (2) Clear explanation of why correlation doesn't imply causation with specific examples, (3) Identification of plausible confounding variables, (4) Appropriate suggestions for establishing causation. Students must score 3/4 points on each criterion. Collect worksheets and observe pair discussions for formative assessment.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a correlation interpretation guide showing how to read decimal values and signs. Offer sentence starters like 'This correlation might be explained by...' and 'To test causation, we would need to...' **For advanced students:** Challenge them to calculate partial correlations controlling for confounding variables, or research real examples of Simpson's Paradox in their chosen industry.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Supply Chain Network Design
description: Students will apply calculus-based optimization techniques to solve a real-world supply chain problem involving multiple distribution centers, variable costs, and capacity constraints. They will use Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization to minimize total operational costs while meeting demand requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier optimization methods to minimize multi-variable cost functions by solving a complex supply chain distribution problem
Students will implement constraint optimization techniques through systematic analysis of production capacity limitations and demand fulfillment requirements
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet describing MegaCorp's three-facility supply chain network (Facility A: capacity 500 units/day, $12/unit; Facility B: capacity 800 units/day, $15/unit; Facility C: capacity 600 units/day, $10/unit) serving four regional markets with specific demands (Northeast: 400 units, Southeast: 350 units, Midwest: 450 units, West: 300 units). Students work in teams of 3-4 for 90 minutes. Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams define variables (x₁₁, x₁₂, etc. representing shipments from facility i to market j) and formulate the objective function incorporating both production costs and transportation costs ($0.50 per unit per 100 miles using provided distance matrix). Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams establish constraint equations for capacity limitations (∑xᵢⱼ ≤ capacity for each facility) and demand requirements (∑xᵢⱼ = demand for each market). Step 3 (35 minutes): Apply Lagrange multiplier method by constructing L(x,λ,μ) = f(x) + λᵢ(capacity constraints) + μⱼ(demand constraints), then solve the system of partial derivative equations ∇L = 0. Teams must show all algebraic steps and verify second-order conditions. Step 4 (15 minutes): Calculate optimal shipment quantities, minimum total cost, and shadow prices from Lagrange multipliers, interpreting economic meaning of each shadow price for management decision-making.
materials_needed: Supply chain scenario packet with facility data and distance matrix
Scientific calculators or computer algebra system (Mathematica/Maple)
Graph paper and colored pens for network diagram visualization
Constraint optimization reference sheet with Lagrange multiplier formulas
assessment_method: Teams submit complete solution packets including: (1) properly formulated objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) correct application of Lagrange multiplier methodology with all algebraic work shown (35 points), (3) accurate final numerical results for optimal shipments and minimum cost (25 points), (4) interpretation of shadow prices with business recommendations (15 points). Solutions must demonstrate systematic problem-solving approach and mathematical rigor.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint matrices and guided practice with 2-variable Lagrange problems first. Offer algebraic manipulation checkpoints every 10 minutes. For advanced learners: Add integer constraints requiring discrete shipment quantities, incorporate additional factors like delivery time windows, or extend to dynamic multi-period optimization with inventory carrying costs.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 AWS S3 Outage
description: Students will analyze the root causes, cascading effects, and architectural vulnerabilities that led to the 2017 AWS S3 outage in the US-East-1 region. They will examine system logs, architecture diagrams, and post-incident reports to identify failure patterns and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real incident data, system logs, and architectural dependencies from the AWS S3 outage case study
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of fault tolerance mechanisms through systematic comparison of pre-incident and post-incident system designs
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4, providing each team with the complete AWS S3 incident report, system architecture diagrams, and anonymized log excerpts (15 minutes setup). Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze the provided materials using the failure analysis framework worksheet, identifying: (1) the initial trigger event and human error, (2) cascading failure sequence across dependent services, (3) architectural single points of failure, and (4) monitoring blind spots that delayed detection. Students must create a visual timeline mapping the failure propagation across services like Lambda, EC2, and CloudFormation. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams examine the post-incident architectural changes, comparing the original distributed consensus protocol with the implemented improvements. They must identify which changes address each root cause and categorize improvements as preventive, detective, or corrective controls. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Each team presents their analysis using the provided template, focusing on one specific aspect: Team 1 analyzes human factors and operational procedures, Team 2 examines technical architecture failures, Team 3 evaluates monitoring and alerting gaps, and Team 4 assesses the recovery process effectiveness. During presentations, other teams use the peer evaluation rubric to score the analysis depth and accuracy. Conclude with a 15-minute synthesis discussion where teams identify common patterns applicable to other distributed systems and propose additional preventive measures not implemented by AWS.
