AWS architecture diagrams showing S3 service dependencies pre and post-incident
Sanitized log excerpts showing error propagation patterns
Failure analysis framework worksheet with structured analysis questions
Digital presentation template with required analysis sections
Peer evaluation rubric for assessing analysis quality
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of root cause identification (25%), (2) Quality of failure propagation analysis with supporting evidence (25%), (3) Depth of architectural vulnerability assessment (25%), and (4) Effectiveness evaluation of implemented solutions with justification (25%). Teams must submit their completed analysis worksheet and deliver a 10-minute presentation demonstrating their findings with specific references to the provided evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each analysis phase and a sample failure analysis of a simpler system outage as reference. Create checkpoint discussions every 20 minutes to ensure teams stay on track. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research and compare this incident with similar outages from other cloud providers, propose alternative architectural solutions, or model the economic impact of the outage using availability calculations.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 AWS S3 Outage: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze the root cause, cascading effects, and systemic vulnerabilities of the 2017 AWS S3 outage by examining real incident reports, dependency maps, and failure patterns. They will decompose the complex failure into contributing factors and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented countermeasures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between distributed system components by mapping service relationships and identifying single points of failure in the AWS S3 infrastructure
Students will evaluate the cascade failure patterns through systematic examination of error propagation across multiple service layers and geographic regions
instructions:
**Phase 1: Initial Analysis (45 minutes)**

Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with the official AWS post-mortem report, timeline data, and service dependency diagrams. Teams spend 15 minutes individually reading materials, then 30 minutes collaboratively creating a failure timeline with root causes.

**Phase 2: Dependency Mapping (60 minutes)**

Using Lucidchart or draw.io, teams construct detailed dependency graphs showing: (1) affected AWS services, (2) external services impacted, (3) geographic propagation patterns. Each connection must be labeled with failure type (timeout, authentication, data unavailability). Teams identify and highlight all single points of failure with red annotations.

**Phase 3: Failure Pattern Classification (45 minutes)**

Teams categorize each identified failure into Deutsch's Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing framework. For each fallacy violated, they document: specific evidence from the incident, impact severity (1-5 scale), and recovery time. Create a matrix mapping fallacies to specific AWS services affected.

**Phase 4: Countermeasure Evaluation (30 minutes)**

Analyze AWS's implemented fixes against each identified root cause. Teams score effectiveness (1-10) and provide evidence-based justification. Identify gaps where additional countermeasures should be implemented.

**Phase 5: Presentation and Peer Review (45 minutes)**

Each team presents their dependency map and failure analysis for 8 minutes, followed by 2 minutes of peer questions. Other teams score presentations using provided rubric focusing on analysis depth and technical accuracy.
materials_needed: AWS S3 outage post-mortem report (February 28, 2017)
AWS service architecture diagrams and dependency documentation
Access to Lucidchart or draw.io for dependency mapping
Deutsch's Eight Fallacies reference sheet
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Peer evaluation rubric forms
assessment_method: Teams submit: (1) Annotated dependency diagram with failure points marked (40 points), (2) Failure classification matrix mapping incidents to distributed computing fallacies with evidence (35 points), (3) Countermeasure effectiveness analysis with scoring rationale (25 points). Rubric evaluates technical accuracy, depth of analysis, use of evidence, and clarity of failure causation chains.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide pre-made partial dependency diagrams with major AWS services already mapped. Offer guided questions for each analysis phase and allow extended time for Phase 2. **Advanced extension:** Challenge advanced learners to design alternative architectures that would prevent similar cascading failures, or analyze a second major outage (GitHub 2018) for comparison patterns.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Performance Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and judge the effectiveness of three different data visualizations created from the same sales dataset. They will evaluate each visualization's ability to communicate key insights about quarterly sales performance, identify strengths and weaknesses, and rank them based on established data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data visualizations by applying standard design principles including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique multiple visualization approaches through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a fictional quarterly sales dataset (50 rows) containing columns for Month, Product Category, Sales Amount, and Region. Display three pre-created visualizations of this data: a cluttered pie chart with 12+ segments, a clear bar chart showing monthly trends, and a poorly formatted scatter plot with overlapping points. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization for 3 minutes, taking initial notes on what story each tells about the sales data.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation criteria sheet with four categories: Data Accuracy (Does it represent data correctly?), Visual Clarity (Is it easy to read and understand?), Insight Communication (Does it reveal meaningful patterns?), and Design Quality (Are colors, labels, and layout appropriate?). Students score each visualization 1-5 in each category.

Step 3 (15 minutes): In pairs, students compare their individual scores and discuss differences in their evaluations. They must reach consensus on rankings and identify the top 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses for each visualization.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair writes a 100-word recommendation memo stating which visualization they would present to a sales manager and why, referencing specific evaluation criteria. They must also suggest one concrete improvement for their chosen visualization.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Three pairs present their recommendations to the class, explaining their reasoning and defending their choice when questioned by peers.
materials_needed: Fictional quarterly sales dataset (Excel/CSV file with 50 data points)
Three pre-created visualizations (pie chart, bar chart, scatter plot) as printed handouts or digital images
Evaluation criteria rubric sheets (one per student)
Computers or tablets for viewing visualizations if digital
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 20-point rubric: Systematic use of evaluation criteria (5 points), Quality of reasoning in pair discussions and consensus-building (5 points), Clarity and justification in written recommendation memo (5 points), Ability to defend their choice and respond to peer questions during presentation (5 points). Success requires scoring 16+ points with evidence of applying at least 3 of the 4 evaluation criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a simple bar chart before the activity, and offer sentence starters for the recommendation memo ('This visualization is most effective because...'). For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific tool recommendations (Excel, Tableau, Python libraries) for creating improved versions, or have them sketch an alternative visualization approach that addresses identified weaknesses.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Performance Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations of the same sales dataset to determine which chart type most effectively communicates key insights to a business stakeholder. They will apply evaluation criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness to justify their selection.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts by applying specific visualization criteria to a sales dataset
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by providing each student with three printed visualizations of quarterly sales data: a stacked bar chart showing sales by region and product category, a multi-line graph showing sales trends over 12 months by region, and a pie chart showing market share by product category. Give students 5 minutes to examine all three visualizations silently. Next, introduce the evaluation framework using the acronym CLEAR: Clarity (Can the main message be understood in 10 seconds?), Legibility (Are labels, axes, and legends readable?), Effectiveness (Does the chart type match the data story?), Accuracy (Are proportions and scales truthful?), and Relevance (Does it answer the business question?). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes to score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each CLEAR criterion, writing specific justifications for their scores. Then conduct a 10-minute whole-class discussion where pairs share their lowest and highest-scoring visualizations with reasoning. Finally, give students 10 minutes to individually write a recommendation memo (100-150 words) to a fictional sales manager, identifying which visualization they would recommend and why, addressing at least three CLEAR criteria in their justification. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students share one insight about what makes data visualizations effective for business communication.
materials_needed: Three printed versions of the same sales dataset visualized as bar chart, line graph, and pie chart
CLEAR evaluation framework handout with scoring rubric
Blank recommendation memo template
Pens or pencils for scoring and writing
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (3) Sophisticated evaluation - uses all CLEAR criteria with specific evidence, clear recommendation with strong business justification; (2) Proficient evaluation - uses most criteria with adequate evidence, reasonable recommendation with basic justification; (1) Developing evaluation - uses few criteria with minimal evidence, weak or unclear recommendation. Assess both the paired scoring sheets and individual recommendation memos.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth chart type and highlight specific language for critiquing visualizations. For advanced learners, ask them to create an improved version of the lowest-scoring visualization or evaluate an additional complex visualization like a dashboard with multiple chart types.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Performance Analysis: Exercise 2
description: Students will critically assess three different visualization approaches used to present the same sales dataset, determining which visualization best communicates key insights to business stakeholders. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization method.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different visualization types by applying specific criteria for clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison and justify their recommendations with evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with the same sales dataset (CSV file with 200 records containing: date, region, product category, sales amount, salesperson) and three pre-created visualizations of this data: a basic bar chart showing total sales by region, a complex dashboard with multiple charts and filters, and a simple line graph showing sales trends over time. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Have students individually examine each visualization and complete the provided evaluation matrix, rating each visualization (1-5 scale) on: data accuracy, visual clarity, ease of interpretation, appropriateness for business audience, and overall effectiveness. Students must provide written justification for each rating.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Within groups, students compare their individual ratings and discuss differences. They must reach consensus on which visualization is most effective and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their choice. Groups should identify specific strengths and weaknesses of each option, referencing visualization best practices covered in previous lessons.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Each group presents their evaluation and recommendation to the class. Other groups ask clarifying questions and challenge reasoning where appropriate.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Conclude with a class discussion comparing different groups' conclusions. Students reflect on how evaluation criteria influenced their decisions and what they learned about effective data visualization principles.
materials_needed: Sample sales dataset (CSV file with 200 records)
Three pre-created visualizations of the same dataset
Evaluation matrix handout with rating criteria
Computers with spreadsheet software or basic visualization tools
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Grade using rubric with four components: (1) Completed evaluation matrix with clear justifications (25%), (2) Quality of group discussion and consensus-building (25%), (3) Presentation clarity and evidence-based reasoning (30%), (4) Participation in Q&A and final reflection (20%). Success requires students to demonstrate systematic evaluation using multiple criteria and provide specific evidence for their judgments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of specific elements to look for in each visualization (axis labels, legend clarity, data completeness). Offer sentence starters for justifications. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest improvements for the weakest visualization or consider how different stakeholder audiences might prefer different approaches. Encourage them to reference additional visualization principles beyond the basic criteria.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Performance Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same sales dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key business insights. learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying Nielsen's usability heuristics and data visualization best practices to assess clarity, accuracy, and insight communication

instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the evaluation worksheet and three printed visualizations (bar chart, pie chart, and line graph) showing identical Q1-Q4 sales data across five product categories. **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each visualization independently, completing the provided evaluation matrix. They rate each visualization (1-5 scale) on: data accuracy representation, visual clarity, insight accessibility, and professional appearance. **Group Presentation Preparation (15 minutes):** Each pair joins another pair (groups of 4) to prepare a 2-minute presentation defending their choice of 'most effective' visualization. title: Design and Build a Miniature City Water Distribution System Using Algebraic Functions
description: Students will create an original mathematical model for a water distribution system serving a miniature city with three districts. They will design linear and quadratic functions to represent water flow rates, calculate optimal pipe dimensions, and present their system with visual diagrams and mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will construct original linear and quadratic functions to model water flow rates and pressure relationships by analyzing real-world constraints and district population data
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts including systems of equations, optimization, and function graphing through designing a comprehensive infrastructure solution
instructions:
Begin by distributing city planning packets containing population data for three districts (residential: 2,400 people, commercial: 800 businesses, industrial: 150 facilities). Students work in pairs to first establish their water demand equations. Have them create linear functions where y = mx + b represents daily water usage (y in gallons) based on population size (x). Provide the constraint that residential usage averages 80 gallons per person daily, commercial needs 200 gallons per business, and industrial requires 1,500 gallons per facility.

Next, students design the pipe network system. They must create quadratic functions modeling water pressure loss over distance, using the formula P(d) = -0.5d² + 40d + 100, where P is pressure (PSI) and d is distance (hundreds of feet) from the main pump. Students calculate optimal pipe placement by finding maximum pressure points and determining where pressure drops below the minimum 30 PSI threshold.

For the distribution network, students solve systems of equations to balance water flow between districts while maintaining adequate pressure. They must create at least two constraint equations and find intersection points representing optimal distribution points.

Students then construct a scaled physical model (1 inch = 100 feet) using provided materials, marking pipe locations, pump stations, and service areas. Finally, they prepare a 5-minute presentation including their mathematical models, calculations showing total daily capacity needed, pressure analysis graphs, and rationale for their design choices. Each pair presents to another pair for peer feedback before final submission.
materials_needed: City planning data packets with population statistics
Graph paper (1/4 inch grid)
Colored pencils or markers for district coding
Cardboard base (12x16 inches per pair)
Pipe cleaners or straws for physical pipe representation
Small labels for marking pump stations
Calculators or graphing calculator access
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of functions and calculations (25%), (2) Creativity and feasibility of system design (25%), (3) Quality of physical model and visual presentation (25%), (4) Clarity of mathematical reasoning and presentation delivery (25%). Students must demonstrate correct function creation, accurate solution of systems of equations, logical optimization decisions, and clear communication of their problem-solving process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide function templates with partially completed equations and offer step-by-step calculation guides. Consider pairing stronger math students with those needing support. For advanced learners, add complexity by introducing exponential decay functions for water quality over distance, or require cost-optimization equations incorporating pipe material expenses. Provide extension challenges like designing backup systems or calculating environmental impact variables.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Specifications Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units for each layer of the TCP/IP protocol stack through structured flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network architecture essentials that advanced computer science students must know automatically.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact names, order, and primary functions of all four TCP/IP protocol stack layers by completing timed written assessments
Students will identify specific protocols and data unit names for each TCP/IP layer through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet containing the four layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) with their associated protocols (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SMTP, TCP/UDP, IP/ICMP/ARP, Ethernet/WiFi) and data units (Data/Message, Segment/Datagram, Packet, Frame). Students work individually for 15 minutes studying the reference sheet, using any memorization technique they prefer. Remove all reference materials. Conduct Round 1 (5 minutes): Students write the four layer names in correct order from top to bottom. Collect papers and provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers. Round 2 (8 minutes): Students list two specific protocols for each layer without looking at previous answers. Round 3 (10 minutes): Students write the data unit name for each layer and provide one-sentence function descriptions. Between each round, allow 2 minutes for students to review missed items using their reference sheets. Conclude with a final 5-minute rapid-fire verbal quiz where you randomly call on students to state specific protocols, data units, or layer functions. Students who answer incorrectly immediately receive the correct answer and must repeat it back. Record all responses for assessment purposes. Maintain brisk pacing throughout to reinforce automatic recall rather than analytical thinking.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet (one per student)
Blank paper for written responses (4 sheets per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor reference
Pencils or pens
assessment_method: Grade each round using a point system: Round 1 (4 points - 1 per correct layer name and order), Round 2 (8 points - 1 per correct protocol), Round 3 (8 points - 1 per correct data unit name and function). Verbal quiz responses earn 1 point each for correct answers. Total possible: 20+ points. Success criteria: 85% accuracy (17/20 points) demonstrates mastery of recall objectives. Document individual student weaknesses for follow-up practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (like 'All The Internet Needs' for layer names) and allow color-coding on reference sheets during study time. Create additional practice sessions focusing on their specific missed items. For advanced learners: Add OSI model correlation questions, require them to state port numbers for specific protocols (HTTP:80, HTTPS:443, FTP:21), or include IPv4 vs IPv6 distinctions in their responses.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves
description: Students will analyze pre-computed learning curves from polynomial regression models with varying complexity to understand how bias and variance manifest in real model performance. They will interpret the relationship between model complexity, training set size, and generalization error patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between bias-dominated and variance-dominated model behaviors by analyzing cross-validation learning curve patterns
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and bias-variance trade-off through systematic comparison of polynomial regression results
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with learning curve datasets for polynomial regression models (degrees 1, 5, 10, 15) trained on a synthetic dataset with 1000 samples. Each dataset contains training and validation scores across different training set sizes (50, 100, 200, 400, 800 samples). Students first spend 15 minutes individually examining the curves and noting observations. Then teams collaborate for 25 minutes to create comparative visualizations using provided plotting templates. They must identify: (1) which models show high bias vs high variance, (2) at what training set sizes convergence occurs, (3) optimal complexity for the given dataset size. Teams then analyze additional complexity metrics: final gap between training and validation curves, slope of validation curve improvement, and minimum validation error achieved. In the final 20 minutes, teams prepare a 5-slide presentation explaining their findings, including specific numerical evidence from the curves. Each slide must address: model ranking by final performance, identification of underfitting/overfitting regions, training set size recommendations, and complexity selection rationale. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where other teams score interpretations using provided rubric.
materials_needed: Pre-computed learning curve datasets (CSV format) for 4 polynomial degrees
Jupyter notebooks with plotting templates and data loading code
Bias-variance interpretation guide with key indicators
Presentation template with required slide structure
Peer evaluation rubrics (printed copies)
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct identification of bias vs variance dominance for each model complexity (4 points), (2) Accurate interpretation of convergence patterns and training set size effects (3 points), (3) Justified model selection with numerical evidence from curves (3 points). Students must achieve 7/10 points demonstrating clear understanding of bias-variance manifestations in learning curves.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated example curves showing clear bias/variance patterns and highlight key numerical thresholds (gap > 0.1 indicates variance, plateau indicates bias). For advanced learners: Include regularization parameter learning curves and ask them to predict optimal lambda values based on bias-variance analysis, or analyze curves from different algorithms (SVM, Random Forest) on the same dataset.

title: Budget Builder: Applying Percentage Calculations to Create a Personal Monthly Budget
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional college student by calculating percentages for different expense categories. They will apply percentage calculations to determine actual dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and entertainment based on a given monthly income.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine specific budget amounts by converting percentages to dollar values within realistic spending scenarios
Students will calculate percentage distributions across multiple budget categories through hands-on budget creation and verification exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Budget Worksheet and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card contains a different monthly income amount ($1,200, $1,500, $1,800, or $2,000) representing part-time work earnings. Explain that students will create a monthly budget using specific percentage guidelines: 40% housing, 25% food, 15% transportation, 10% entertainment, and 10% savings. 

Have students work individually to calculate each category amount using their assigned income (15 minutes). They must show their work for each calculation (example: $1,500 × 0.40 = $600 for housing). Next, students research actual costs in your local area using provided websites or apps to verify if their calculated amounts are realistic (10 minutes). They should find at least one example for each major category (apartment rent, grocery costs, gas prices).

Form groups of 3-4 students with different income scenarios (10 minutes). Each student presents their budget to their group, explaining their calculations and comparing their percentages to real-world costs. Groups identify which categories might need adjustment and calculate new percentages if needed. Finally, each group selects their most realistic budget to present to the class (15 minutes). During presentations, other students verify the math calculations using calculators and provide feedback on the budget's practicality. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students write one insight about how percentages help in financial planning.
materials_needed: Budget Worksheet template with income scenarios
Calculators (one per student)
Computers/tablets with internet access for cost research
Local housing/grocery cost reference sheets
Poster paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Budget Worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, realistic cost research documented, clear presentation of final budget; (3) Minor calculation errors, adequate research, good presentation; (2) Some calculation errors, minimal research, unclear presentation; (1) Major calculation errors, insufficient work shown, poor presentation. Students must achieve level 3 or higher to demonstrate mastery of applying percentage calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing the formula (Income × Percentage = Amount) and work through one example together. Offer a calculator with percentage function and pair them with stronger math students during group work. For advanced learners: Challenge them to create budgets for different life scenarios (family of four, single professional) or calculate the impact of percentage changes on their budget totals. Have them explore compound percentage calculations for savings growth.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations
description: Students will analyze and compare the performance characteristics of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining provided implementations and testing them with different dataset sizes. They will identify bottlenecks, predict performance patterns, and justify their findings with evidence from code structure and execution results.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithm complexity by examining code structure and identifying performance bottlenecks in three different search implementations
Students will compare algorithmic efficiency through systematic testing and data collection across varying input sizes
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-written search algorithm implementations (linear search, binary search, hash table lookup) in the chosen programming language, along with a dataset generator that creates sorted arrays of sizes 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 integers. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Students examine each algorithm's code without running it, documenting their predictions about relative performance and identifying key structural differences (loops, conditionals, data access patterns). Next 30 minutes: Pairs run timing tests on each algorithm using all four dataset sizes, recording execution times in a provided spreadsheet template. They perform 5 trials per algorithm-size combination to account for variability. Following 30 minutes: Students create visual representations (graphs/charts) of their timing results and analyze patterns. They must identify which algorithm performs best at each data size and explain why performance changes as input size increases. Final 15 minutes: Each pair presents one key finding to the class, specifically focusing on either the most surprising result or the clearest example of how code structure impacts performance. Throughout the activity, students document their analysis in a structured worksheet that prompts them to connect code features to performance outcomes.
materials_needed: Three pre-written search algorithm implementations (provided as code files)
Dataset generator script that creates integer arrays of specified sizes
Timing measurement code template or built-in timing functions
Spreadsheet template for recording execution times
Algorithm analysis worksheet with guided questions
Computers with programming environment installed (Python, Java, or C++)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all major algorithmic differences, accurately predicts and explains performance patterns with specific code evidence; (3) Identifies most key differences, explains most performance patterns with general reasoning; (2) Identifies some differences, explains basic performance trends; (1) Limited identification of differences, minimal explanation of results. Also assess the quality of one verbal presentation per pair focusing on clarity of explanation and use of evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a code annotation guide highlighting key structural elements to examine (nested loops, conditional statements, array access patterns). Offer sentence starters for analysis explanations like 'This algorithm is slower because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict Big O notation for each algorithm and verify their predictions, or have them modify one algorithm to improve its performance and test their optimization.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations: Comparative Study
description: Students analyze three different search algorithm implementations (linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup) by examining their code structure, tracing execution paths, and evaluating time complexity trade-offs. They will decompose each algorithm's logic and compare performance characteristics across different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the structural differences between linear search, binary search, and hash table implementations by examining code snippets and identifying key algorithmic patterns
Students will evaluate time complexity trade-offs through systematic comparison of algorithm performance across varying data sizes and organization states
instructions: Begin by providing students with three code implementations: a linear search function, a binary search function, and a hash table lookup function, each written in the same programming language (Python recommended). Divide students into groups of 3-4. In Phase 1 (15 minutes), each group receives printed code snippets and traces through each algorithm using a provided dataset of 16 sorted integers [2, 5, 8, 12, 15, 18, 23, 27, 31, 35, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60]. Students manually trace the search for target value '27' in each implementation, documenting the number of comparisons and steps taken. In Phase 2 (20 minutes), groups analyze the code structure by identifying: loop types used, conditional statements, data structure requirements, and preprocessing needs. They complete a provided comparison matrix with these findings. In Phase 3 (15 minutes), students predict performance for different scenarios: searching in datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 elements, considering best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios. Groups document their analysis on a structured worksheet. In Phase 4 (10 minutes), each group presents one key insight about algorithmic trade-offs they discovered, focusing on when each search method would be most appropriate. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting student observations to Big O notation concepts.
materials_needed: Printed code snippets for three search algorithms (one set per group)
Algorithm comparison matrix worksheet
Sample dataset cards with 16 sorted integers
Performance prediction worksheet
Stopwatch or timer for pacing
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices (40%), accuracy of algorithm traces (30%), and quality of performance predictions with justifications (30%). Success criteria: correctly identify at least 4 structural differences, accurate trace execution showing proper step counting, and logical performance predictions that demonstrate understanding of algorithm efficiency concepts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed trace tables and highlight the first few steps of each algorithm. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to the search space after each iteration?' For advanced learners: extend activity by having them analyze space complexity, consider cache performance implications, or implement hybrid approaches combining multiple search strategies.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze and compare the performance characteristics of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining code implementations, predicting theoretical complexity, and interpreting empirical timing data. learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of three search algorithms by examining their code structure and identifying key operations that affect performance

instructions: Begin by providing students with three code implementations (linear search, binary search, hash table lookup) in their familiar programming language, along with a spreadsheet containing timing data for each algorithm tested on datasets of sizes 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 elements (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group one algorithm to focus on initially. title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze and compare the performance characteristics of linear search versus binary search algorithms by examining code implementations, predicting time complexity, and evaluating actual runtime data. title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Predicting Customer Churn Using Industry-Standard Metrics
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare the performance of three different machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Logistic Regression) trained on a telecom customer churn dataset. learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative performance of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and business impact metrics

instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Provide students with pre-trained models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression) and a holdout test dataset of 2,000 telecom customers with features including monthly charges, contract type, tenure, and demographics. title: Design and Justify a Custom Cryptographic Hash Function for Digital Identity Verification
description: Students will create an original cryptographic hash function by combining advanced mathematical concepts including modular arithmetic, prime number theory, and linear algebra. They will then mathematically prove key properties of their function and present a security analysis comparing it to existing industry standards like SHA-256.
estimated_duration: 5.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize modular arithmetic, prime number theory, and matrix operations to construct an original cryptographic hash function with specified collision-resistance properties
Students will formulate mathematical proofs demonstrating their hash function's one-way property and avalanche effect through rigorous analytical methods
instructions: Begin with 15-minute individual brainstorming where students review provided research papers on hash function vulnerabilities and identify 3-4 mathematical weaknesses in existing functions. Form teams of 3-4 students, ensuring each team has members with complementary strengths in number theory, linear algebra, and computational complexity. Teams spend 45 minutes designing their hash function architecture, selecting: (1) a prime modulus p > 10^9, (2) a 4x4 invertible matrix over GF(p), (3) a polynomial mixing function of degree ≥ 3, and (4) compression ratio (input block size to output size). Next, 60 minutes for implementation where teams code their function in Python, creating test cases with 1000+ random inputs to verify basic functionality. Following this, teams spend 90 minutes on mathematical analysis: proving their function satisfies the avalanche criterion (changing one input bit affects ≥50% of output bits), demonstrating computational infeasibility of finding collisions using birthday attack analysis, and calculating theoretical security margins. Teams then spend 45 minutes preparing presentations including: function specification, mathematical proofs, experimental results showing avalanche effect measurements, complexity analysis comparing their function to SHA-256, and identified limitations. Final 60 minutes consists of team presentations (12 minutes each) followed by peer review where other teams attempt to identify vulnerabilities and suggest cryptanalytic attacks. Conclude with 20-minute reflection where teams document lessons learned and propose refinements based on peer feedback.
materials_needed: Research papers on cryptographic hash function vulnerabilities (MD5, SHA-1 attacks)
Python 3.9+ with NumPy, matplotlib, and hashlib libraries installed
Digital whiteboards or large paper sheets for algorithm design sketching
Calculators capable of modular arithmetic with large integers
Access to mathematical reference materials on finite fields and group theory
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor of hash function design (25 points - correct use of modular arithmetic, appropriate prime selection, valid matrix operations), Proof quality (25 points - logical structure, mathematical notation, completeness of avalanche effect and collision resistance proofs), Implementation accuracy (20 points - functional code, comprehensive testing, proper handling of edge cases), Security analysis depth (20 points - realistic threat assessment, comparison with industry standards, identification of potential vulnerabilities), Presentation clarity (10 points - clear explanation of technical concepts, effective visual aids, professional delivery). Deliverables include: complete Python implementation, 8-page technical report with mathematical proofs, 12-slide presentation, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide template code structure with key functions outlined, offer guided worksheets breaking down modular arithmetic steps, assign peer mentors strong in relevant mathematical areas. For advanced learners: challenge them to implement additional security features like salt handling, explore quantum-resistant modifications, or analyze their function against advanced cryptanalytic techniques like differential analysis. Provide optional extension to submit their work to undergraduate research symposiums.

title: Binary Number System Memory Card Match
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0-15 through a structured flashcard matching activity. This foundational exercise builds automatic recognition of basic binary-to-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 through 1111 by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8) through visual pattern recognition activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary flashcard sets to each student pair. Each set contains 16 cards with 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on one side and blank on the reverse. First, conduct a 10-minute guided introduction where students follow along as you demonstrate converting 0000 to 15 using the place value method (8-4-2-1 positions). Have students write the decimal equivalent on each card's blank side as you work through all 16 numbers together. Next, students work in pairs for 15 minutes practicing with one partner showing the binary side while the other recalls the decimal equivalent, then switching roles every 3 minutes. Follow with a 10-minute individual memorization phase where students study their complete set silently, using any personal memory techniques. Conduct three timed recall rounds (3 minutes each): Round 1 - students arrange all 16 cards in ascending decimal order (0-15) starting from the binary representations; Round 2 - instructor calls out decimal numbers randomly while students hold up corresponding binary cards; Round 3 - students complete a written quiz matching 10 randomly selected binary numbers to their decimal equivalents. Between rounds, allow 2-minute review periods. Conclude with students self-checking answers using an answer key and recording their accuracy scores for each round.
materials_needed: Pre-printed binary flashcard sets (16 cards per student showing 0000-1111)
Answer key sheets with binary-decimal conversion chart
Stopwatch or timer
Pencils for students to write decimal equivalents
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (13/16 correct) on the final written quiz and successfully complete the timed card arrangement in under 3 minutes. Track progress through three scoring checkpoints: card arrangement speed, verbal recall accuracy during partner practice, and final quiz score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a place value reference chart (8-4-2-1) and start with just 8 cards (0000-0111). For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (00000-11111) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider allowing struggling students extra review time or reducing the final quiz to 8 questions.

title: Binary Number System Memory Card Match: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through a structured flashcard matching activity. This foundational exercise builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by matching physical cards without calculation
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through repeated exposure and memory exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing one complete set of 32 cards (16 decimal cards showing 0-15, 16 binary cards showing 0000-1111) to each pair of students. Have students work in pairs with one deck between them. 

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students lay out all 32 cards face-up in a 4x8 grid. Partner A selects any decimal card and reads it aloud. Partner B must find and point to the matching binary card within 10 seconds. If correct, they keep the pair. If incorrect or time expires, cards return to grid. Partners switch roles after each attempt. Continue until all 16 pairs are matched.

Phase 2 (10 minutes): Shuffle all cards and place face-down in same 4x8 grid. Students play traditional memory/concentration game, flipping two cards per turn seeking decimal-binary matches. When players find a match, they must state both values aloud (e.g., 'Seven and zero-one-one-one'). Mismatched cards flip back face-down. Player with most pairs wins.

Phase 3 (5 minutes): One partner holds decimal cards, other holds binary cards. Decimal holder shows card for 3 seconds, then hides it. Binary holder must produce matching binary card from their hand within 5 seconds. Switch roles every 8 cards.

Conclude with whole-class rapid-fire recall: instructor calls out random decimal numbers 0-15, students write binary equivalents on individual whiteboards and hold up simultaneously for immediate feedback.
materials_needed: 16 decimal number cards (0-15) per pair of students
16 binary number cards (0000-1111) per pair of students
Individual small whiteboards and dry erase markers
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key chart for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly matching at least 14 out of 16 decimal-binary pairs during Phase 1 within time limits, and achieving 80% accuracy (13/16 correct) on the final whiteboard rapid-fire assessment. Instructor observes and records individual student performance during partner activities using a simple checklist.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide reference chart showing binary place values (8-4-2-1) and allow longer response times initially. Focus on patterns like powers of 2 first (1,2,4,8). For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (16-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to complete Phase 2 memory game in under 8 minutes.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance outputs from a pre-trained Random Forest model used for customer churn prediction. Through guided analysis of importance scores and visualizations, students will demonstrate understanding of how different customer attributes contribute to churn predictions and explain the business implications of these relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance scores from Random Forest models by analyzing numerical rankings and explaining the relative contribution of each feature to prediction accuracy
Students will explain the business significance of feature relationships through structured analysis of customer churn prediction results
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided Jupyter notebook containing a pre-trained Random Forest model with feature importance data for a telecommunications customer dataset (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to complete the analysis worksheet. First, have students examine the feature importance visualization showing the top 10 features ranked by importance score (10 minutes). They must identify the three most important features and write one sentence explaining what each feature measures in business terms. Next, students analyze the feature importance table containing all 20 features with numerical scores (15 minutes). They calculate what percentage of total importance the top 5 features represent and identify any surprising low-importance features. In the third phase, students examine partial dependence plots for the top 3 features (15 minutes), describing in writing how changes in each feature value affect churn probability. Students then complete a structured comparison exercise (10 minutes) where they contrast the Random Forest feature importance with provided correlation coefficients between individual features and churn, noting at least two significant differences and explaining why these differences might occur. Finally, pairs prepare a 2-minute presentation (10 minutes preparation) where they recommend three specific business actions based on their feature importance analysis, justifying each recommendation with specific importance scores. Conclude with pair presentations and class discussion about the practical limitations of feature importance interpretation (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-trained Random Forest model and telecommunications customer churn dataset
Printed analysis worksheet with structured questions and tables
Feature importance visualization (bar chart) showing top 10 features
Partial dependence plots for top 3 features
Data dictionary explaining all 20 customer features
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification and business explanation of top features (25%), (2) Accurate calculations of importance percentages and identification of surprising results (25%), (3) Appropriate interpretation of partial dependence plots with directional relationships (25%), (4) Justified business recommendations linked to specific importance scores (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example analysis for one feature and highlight key phrases like 'most important,' 'contributes X% to predictions.' Offer sentence starters for business explanations. For advanced learners, provide additional datasets (credit approval, employee turnover) to compare feature importance patterns across domains, or challenge them to identify potential issues with feature importance interpretation such as correlated features or data leakage.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus of Variations
description: Students will apply principles of calculus of variations and optimization theory to determine the optimal positioning and configuration of a residential solar panel array. They will work with real-world constraints including roof dimensions, shading patterns, and energy efficiency calculations to maximize power output.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques by solving a constrained optimization problem involving solar panel positioning to maximize energy output
Students will implement the calculus of variations through systematic analysis of panel angle, spacing, and orientation variables in a realistic engineering scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the Solar Panel Optimization Worksheet containing a standardized house blueprint with roof dimensions (40ft x 25ft), monthly sun angle data, and shading obstacle measurements. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to identify decision variables: panel tilt angle (θ), azimuth angle (φ), inter-panel spacing (d), and number of panels (n). Next, have students spend 25 minutes setting up the objective function P(θ,φ,d,n) representing total annual power output using the provided solar irradiance formula: P = ηA∑[I(θ,φ,t)cos(α(t))] where η is panel efficiency, A is panel area, I is irradiance, and α is the angle between sun and panel normal. Students must incorporate constraints: roof area limitation (∑Ad ≤ 1000 sq ft), minimum spacing requirement (d ≥ 2ft), tilt angle bounds (0° ≤ θ ≤ 60°), and shading restrictions from chimney and trees. During the next 30 minutes, students apply Lagrange multiplier method to solve the constrained optimization problem, calculating partial derivatives ∂P/∂θ, ∂P/∂φ, ∂P/∂d, and ∂P/∂n, then setting up and solving the system of equations. In the final 15 minutes, pairs use provided Excel template to verify their analytical solution numerically and create a visual diagram showing optimal panel layout. Each pair presents their final configuration with calculated maximum annual energy output in kWh.

Solar irradiance data tables for local geographic coordinates
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Excel template with solar calculation formulas pre-programmed

assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification and setup of objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier method with proper partial derivatives (30 points), (3) Mathematically sound solution with numerical verification (25 points), (4) Clear presentation of optimal configuration with energy output calculation (20 points). Students must achieve minimum 70 points and demonstrate computational accuracy within 5% error margin.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide worked example with 2-variable optimization problem first, offer constraint identification checklist, and supply partial derivative calculation templates. For advanced learners: Add economic optimization component by including panel cost and payback period calculations, introduce seasonal variation analysis, or explore impact of battery storage systems on optimal configuration.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Analysis: Big-O Performance Breakdown of Sorting Algorithm Implementations
description: Students will dissect and analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms by examining their actual implementations, identifying key operations, and comparing theoretical vs. empirical performance data. They will decompose each algorithm's behavior across different input scenarios to determine optimal use cases.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by identifying dominant operations and counting primitive steps in worst, average, and best-case scenarios

Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through systematic examination of recursive call stacks, temporary array allocations, and in-place operations across the three sorting implementations
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) in Python, each containing detailed comments marking key operations. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (30 minutes): Each pair receives a worksheet with three columns (one per algorithm) and rows for 'Basic Operations,' 'Loop Structure Analysis,' 'Recursive Calls,' and 'Memory Usage.' Students trace through each algorithm with a 10-element array, counting comparison operations, swaps, and recursive calls. They must identify the dominant operation in each algorithm's inner loop. Phase 2 (45 minutes): Provide empirical timing data from running each algorithm on arrays of sizes 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 elements under three conditions: sorted, reverse-sorted, and random data. Students plot this data and compare it to their theoretical predictions. They must identify which scenarios produce best/worst-case performance for each algorithm. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students complete a comparative analysis table ranking the algorithms by time complexity, space complexity, and stability, providing justification for each ranking based on their code analysis and empirical evidence.
materials_needed: Pre-coded Python implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort with annotated key operations
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with structured comparison tables
Empirical performance data spreadsheet with timing results across different input sizes and types
Graph paper or digital plotting tools for visualizing complexity curves
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all dominant operations, accurate complexity classifications, and provides clear justification linking code structure to theoretical complexity; (3) Minor errors in operation counting or complexity classification; (2) Demonstrates understanding of concept but with significant analytical gaps; (1) Incomplete analysis or fundamental misunderstanding of complexity relationships. Students must also submit their comparative ranking table with evidence-based justifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed trace-through example showing how to count operations in the first few iterations. Highlight specific lines of code that contribute to complexity. For advanced learners, challenge them to modify one algorithm to improve its space complexity or analyze how the algorithms perform with nearly-sorted data, requiring them to predict and explain performance variations.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Satisfaction Analysis

instructions:

Students will identify key implementation characteristics and optimal use cases for complex data structures through systematic information retrieval
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-formatted reference sheet templates and providing students with the list of 15 data structures/algorithms: Red-Black Trees, AVL Trees, B-Trees, Fibonacci Heaps, Disjoint Set Union, Segment Trees, Fenwick Trees, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Bellman-Ford Algorithm, Floyd-Warshall Algorithm, Kruskal's Algorithm, Prim's Algorithm, Rabin-Karp String Matching, KMP Algorithm, and Suffix Arrays. Students work individually for 90 minutes to complete their reference sheets from memory only - no textbooks, notes, or internet access permitted. For each data structure/algorithm, students must recall and document: (1) Best, average, and worst-case time complexities for all major operations, (2) Space complexity, (3) Three specific real-world use cases, (4) Key implementation considerations or constraints, and (5) One advantage and one disadvantage compared to similar structures. Students must use proper Big O notation and be specific about which operations they're describing (insert, delete, search, etc.). After 90 minutes, conduct a 15-minute verification phase where students can check one item per data structure using approved resources and mark any corrections in red ink. Conclude with a 15-minute peer review where students exchange sheets and verify the accuracy of three randomly selected entries using the provided answer key.
materials_needed: Pre-formatted reference sheet templates (3 pages per student)
List of 15 specified data structures and algorithms printed on cardstock
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor verification
Red ink pens for corrections
Approved textbooks for verification phase only
assessment_method: Grade based on accuracy and completeness: 75 total points (5 points per data structure/algorithm). Each entry scored as: 2 points for correct complexity notations, 1 point for accurate use cases, 1 point for implementation details, 1 point for advantages/disadvantages. Deduct 0.5 points for incomplete entries. Minimum passing score: 60/75 points (80%). Bonus points awarded for exceptional detail or notation precision.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide complexity notation reference chart and allow completion of 10 items instead of 15. For advanced learners: require additional analysis of when to choose each structure over alternatives, or include amortized complexity analysis. Consider allowing struggling students to work in pairs for the peer review portion while maintaining individual accountability for their own sheets.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves
description: Students will analyze learning curves generated from cross-validation experiments to understand how model complexity affects bias and variance components of prediction error. They will interpret mathematical relationships between training set size, model complexity, and generalization performance across different algorithmic families.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition patterns by analyzing cross-validation learning curves for polynomial regression models of varying complexity
Students will explain the mathematical relationship between model complexity, training set size, and generalization gap through systematic comparison of learning curve behaviors
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-generated learning curve plots for polynomial regression models (degrees 1, 5, 10, 15) trained on a synthetic dataset with known ground truth function. Provide each student group with four sets of plots: training accuracy vs. training set size, validation accuracy vs. training set size, training time vs. model complexity, and prediction variance across 10-fold CV runs. In pairs, students spend 15 minutes examining the curves and identifying three key patterns: where training and validation curves converge/diverge, how the gap changes with training set size, and how variance changes across complexity levels. Next, provide the mathematical framework: bias = (E[f̂(x)] - f(x))², variance = E[(f̂(x) - E[f̂(x)])²], and irreducible error. Students spend 20 minutes mapping observed curve behaviors to these mathematical components, specifically identifying which complexity levels exhibit high bias (underfitting) versus high variance (overfitting). Distribute a structured worksheet requiring students to predict learning curve shapes for: Support Vector Machines with different kernel complexities, Random Forest with varying tree depths, and Neural Networks with different hidden layer sizes. Students must justify predictions using bias-variance principles and specify optimal complexity selection strategies. Conclude with 10 minutes of pair discussions comparing predictions, followed by instructor-led verification using actual learning curves. Students submit completed worksheets showing mathematical reasoning connecting curve interpretations to bias-variance theory.
materials_needed: Pre-generated learning curve plots for 4 polynomial regression complexities (printed sets)
Bias-variance decomposition formula reference sheet
Structured prediction worksheet with 3 algorithm families
Actual learning curves for verification (digital slides)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of bias vs. variance patterns in given curves (25%), (2) Accurate mathematical reasoning connecting curve behaviors to decomposition formulas (35%), (3) Logical predictions for new algorithm families with justified complexity recommendations (25%), (4) Clear explanation of optimal model selection strategy using learning curve analysis (15%)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide annotated example showing one complete bias-variance pattern analysis with explicit formula connections. Offer visual aids highlighting curve convergence points and mathematical equation color-coding. For advanced learners, extend activity with ensemble methods learning curves and challenge them to derive optimal training set size recommendations using statistical significance testing of performance gaps.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze cross-validation learning curves from multiple machine learning models to understand how training set size affects the bias-variance tradeoff. They will interpret visual patterns in learning curves to distinguish between high-bias and high-variance scenarios and explain the underlying mathematical relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret learning curve patterns by analyzing the gap between training and validation scores to identify bias-variance characteristics
Students will explain the mathematical relationship between model complexity, dataset size, and generalization error through systematic comparison of polynomial regression models
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-generated learning curves from polynomial regression models of degrees 1, 5, and 15 trained on the same dataset with varying training sizes (50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 samples). Organize students into groups of 3-4. Each group receives printed learning curve plots showing both training and validation scores versus training set size for all three models. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine the degree-1 model curves first. They must identify: (a) the gap between training and validation scores, (b) whether scores converge as training size increases, and (c) the final performance plateau level. Students document observations using the provided analysis worksheet.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups analyze the degree-15 model curves, comparing patterns to the degree-1 results. They must explain why the training score starts high but decreases, why the validation score starts low but increases, and interpret the persistent gap between curves even with large training sets.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups examine the degree-5 model as the 'optimal complexity' case, noting how both curves converge to similar performance levels with sufficient data.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each group creates a written explanation connecting their observations to bias-variance theory. They must define high-bias (underfitting) and high-variance (overfitting) scenarios using evidence from their curve analysis. Groups must also predict how each model would perform with 2000 training samples and justify their predictions.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Groups present their findings to the class, focusing on one specific model complexity and its bias-variance characteristics.
materials_needed: Pre-generated learning curve plots for polynomial regression (degrees 1, 5, 15)
Learning curve analysis worksheet with observation prompts
Colored pens/highlighters for marking curve features
Large poster paper for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of bias-variance patterns in each model (25%), (2) Accurate explanation of mathematical relationships between complexity and generalization (25%), (3) Appropriate use of technical vocabulary (bias, variance, overfitting, underfitting) (25%), (4) Quality of predictions and justifications for model behavior with larger datasets (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a bias-variance identification flowchart and sentence starters for explanations. Offer one-on-one curve reading practice focusing on identifying which line represents training vs. validation scores. For advanced learners, provide additional learning curves from different algorithms (SVM, Random Forest) and challenge them to compare bias-variance characteristics across algorithm families, or ask them to design experiments that would generate specific bias-variance patterns.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Learning Curves: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze and interpret learning curves generated from polynomial regression models with varying complexity to understand how bias and variance manifest in real model performance. They will examine cross-validation results to identify underfitting, overfitting, and optimal model complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance tradeoff patterns by analyzing training and validation learning curves across different polynomial degrees
Students will distinguish between underfitting and overfitting scenarios through systematic examination of cross-validation performance metrics
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-generated dataset containing learning curves for polynomial regression models (degrees 1-15) trained on a synthetic dataset with 1000 samples. Each student receives identical plots showing training RMSE, validation RMSE, and standard deviation bands across sample sizes from 50 to 800. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine the learning curves and identify three distinct regions: low complexity (degrees 1-3), medium complexity (degrees 4-7), and high complexity (degrees 8-15). They annotate each region on their plots.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students analyze the gap between training and validation curves for each complexity region. They calculate the average gap for degrees 2, 5, and 12, recording values in a provided worksheet. Students must explain what these gaps indicate about model variance.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students examine the absolute validation error levels across all polynomial degrees. They identify which degrees show high validation error despite small training-validation gaps (indicating high bias) and which show large gaps with potentially lower validation error (indicating high variance).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair selects the optimal polynomial degree by identifying the point where validation error is minimized while maintaining reasonable training-validation gap. They must justify their choice using bias-variance terminology.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present their optimal degree choice and reasoning to another pair, defending their interpretation of the bias-variance tradeoff visible in their selected model.
materials_needed: Pre-generated learning curve plots for polynomial degrees 1-15
Bias-variance analysis worksheet with calculation tables
Colored pens/highlighters for plot annotation
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all three complexity regions and accurately calculates training-validation gaps with proper bias-variance explanations; (3) Identifies regions with minor errors and mostly accurate gap calculations; (2) Shows partial understanding with some incorrect interpretations; (1) Demonstrates minimal comprehension of bias-variance concepts. Additionally, observe pair discussions for accurate use of terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using degree 1 and degree 15 as extreme cases to illustrate clear bias vs. variance scenarios. Offer guiding questions: 'What does a large gap suggest about model consistency?' For advanced learners, provide additional complexity by asking them to predict how learning curves would change with different noise levels or sample sizes, and to connect their observations to regularization techniques.

title: Pizza Party Fraction Calculator: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios
description: Students will apply their knowledge of adding, subtracting, and comparing fractions to solve real-world problems involving pizza ordering for a class party. They will calculate total amounts needed, determine leftovers, and make recommendations using proper fraction operations and equivalent fractions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction addition and subtraction operations by solving multi-step word problems involving food portions for a party scenario
Students will demonstrate fraction comparison and conversion skills through calculating and comparing different pizza quantity combinations using common denominators
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' to each student (15 minutes setup). Present the scenario: 'Our class of 24 students is having a pizza party. Each student typically eats 3/4 of a pizza, but we also invited 8 parents who each eat 1/2 pizza. We need to order whole pizzas only.' Students work in pairs to solve four sequential problems: (1) Calculate total pizza consumption needed by adding 24 × 3/4 + 8 × 1/2, showing all work with common denominators; (2) Determine how many whole pizzas to order by converting their answer to a mixed number and rounding up; (3) Calculate leftovers by subtracting actual consumption from pizzas ordered; (4) Compare three different ordering strategies (20 pizzas vs. 22 pizzas vs. 24 pizzas) and determine which leaves closest to 1/4 pizza per person as leftovers. During work time (25 minutes), circulate to check fraction operations, ensure students are finding common denominators correctly, and verify conversion between improper fractions and mixed numbers. Have pairs record their final recommendations on chart paper with complete calculations shown. Conclude with a 10-minute gallery walk where pairs post their solutions and compare strategies, followed by whole-class discussion of the most efficient ordering approach and verification of calculations.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Sheet (one per student)
Chart paper (one per pair)
Colored markers or pencils
Calculator (for verification only, after hand calculations)
Fraction strips or circles (for visual support)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly applies all fraction operations with proper common denominators, shows complete work, and provides logical recommendation; (3) Correctly applies most fraction operations with minor computational errors; (2) Shows understanding of process but makes significant errors in operations or common denominators; (1) Attempts problems but shows limited understanding of fraction operations. Check for proper conversion between improper fractions and mixed numbers, accurate addition/subtraction with unlike denominators, and reasonable final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide fraction strips or visual models, pre-calculate the common denominators (4 and 2 become 4), and break problem into smaller steps with checkpoints. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including different pizza sizes (small = 2/3 consumption, large = 4/3 consumption), calculate costs per strategy, or determine optimal ordering for different class sizes using algebraic thinking.

title: Pizza Party Fraction Calculator: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply their knowledge of adding, subtracting, and comparing fractions to solve a multi-step real-world problem about planning a class pizza party. learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction addition and subtraction skills by calculating total pizza amounts needed and consumed in a party planning scenario
Students will demonstrate fraction comparison abilities through evaluating different pizza ordering options and determining the most efficient choices
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' to each student (15 minutes setup). Present the scenario: 'Your class of 24 students is planning a pizza party. Each student will eat 2/3 of a pizza on average. You need to determine how many pizzas to order, calculate costs, and plan for leftovers.' 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to calculate total pizza needed by multiplying 24 × 2/3. Have them show their work using visual fraction models or cross-multiplication.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Present three pizza package options: Package A (15 pizzas for $180), Package B (18 pizzas for $198), Package C (20 pizzas for $220). Students calculate leftover amounts for each package by subtracting 16 (total needed) from each package size, then determine cost per pizza.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students compare fractions to determine which package offers the best value by calculating leftover pizza fractions and cost efficiency ratios.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pair students to compare answers and justify their reasoning. Each pair must agree on one recommendation with written justification showing all fraction calculations.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Three volunteer pairs present their solutions to the class, explaining their fraction work on the board. Class votes on most convincing argument.

Closure (5 minutes): Students reflect on how fraction operations helped them make real-world decisions and identify one fraction skill they used most effectively.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Sheet (one per student)
Fraction calculation worksheets with visual models
Calculators (optional for checking work)
Whiteboard markers and erasers
Chart paper for pair presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly performs all fraction operations with clear work shown, makes logical recommendations with complete justification; (3) Performs most fraction operations correctly with minor errors, provides reasonable justification; (2) Shows understanding of fraction operations but makes computational errors, basic justification provided; (1) Attempts fraction operations with significant errors, minimal or unclear justification. Collect individual worksheets and observe pair discussions for participation points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide fraction strips or circle models for visualization, allow use of calculators after showing manual work, pair with stronger math partners.
