title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance Analysis
description: Students will analyze real model performance data from multiple ensemble algorithms to interpret how bias-variance tradeoffs manifest in different scenarios. They will examine decomposition outputs and explain the underlying mathematical relationships driving model behavior patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing quantitative outputs from ridge regression, random forest, and gradient boosting models across varying complexity parameters

Students will explain the mathematical relationship between ensemble size, individual learner complexity, and resulting bias-variance components through comparative analysis of decomposition visualizations
instructions: Begin by providing each student team with three pre-computed bias-variance decomposition datasets from scikit-learn's regression models trained on Boston housing data with different hyperparameters (15 minutes setup). Teams receive: Ridge regression (alpha: 0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0), Random Forest (n_estimators: 10, 50, 100, 500), and Gradient Boosting (learning_rate: 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, max_depth: 3, 6, 12). Students first examine the numerical decomposition tables showing bias², variance, and irreducible error for each configuration (20 minutes). Next, they create interpretation matrices mapping hyperparameter changes to bias-variance shifts, identifying three key patterns per algorithm (25 minutes). Teams then analyze the provided scatter plots showing prediction distributions across 100 bootstrap samples, interpreting how visual clustering patterns reflect numerical decomposition values (30 minutes). Students write detailed explanations for why Random Forest variance decreases with more trees while bias remains stable, why Ridge regression bias increases with higher alpha values, and why Gradient Boosting shows complex bias-variance interactions with learning rate and depth combinations (40 minutes). Finally, teams present one counterintuitive finding from their analysis, explaining the underlying mathematical mechanism using decomposition formulas provided in reference sheets (20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition CSV files for three algorithms with multiple hyperparameter settings
Jupyter notebooks with mlxtend bias_variance_decomp output visualizations
Reference sheet containing bias-variance decomposition mathematical formulas
Large format printouts of prediction distribution scatter plots for visual analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate interpretation matrices for accuracy of bias-variance trend identification (40 points), written explanations demonstrating understanding of mathematical relationships between hyperparameters and decomposition components (40 points), and presentation quality showing ability to explain counterintuitive findings using quantitative evidence (20 points). Success requires correctly identifying at least 8/9 major bias-variance patterns and providing mathematically sound explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided interpretation templates with sentence starters like 'When alpha increases in Ridge regression, bias increases because...' and highlight specific numerical ranges to focus analysis. For advanced learners, add cross-algorithm comparison tasks requiring explanation of why ensemble methods show different bias-variance profiles than regularized linear models, and include analysis of noise level effects on decomposition stability.

title: Personal Budget Planning: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Expenses
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional college student by calculating percentages for different expense categories. They will apply percentage calculations to determine how much money should be allocated to housing, food, transportation, and entertainment from a given monthly income.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages of a whole number by applying the percentage formula to budget categories within a realistic monthly income scenario
Students will solve percentage problems through hands-on budget creation using recommended spending guidelines
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Worksheet' and explaining that students will create a monthly budget for 'Alex,' a college student with $1,800 monthly income. Display the recommended budget percentages on the board: Housing 30%, Food 20%, Transportation 15%, School Supplies 10%, Entertainment 10%, Savings 10%, Miscellaneous 5%. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to calculate the dollar amount for each category using the formula: (Percentage ÷ 100) × Total Income. For example: Housing = (30 ÷ 100) × $1,800 = $540.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Pair students to compare calculations and resolve any differences. Circulate to check work and provide guidance on calculation errors.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Present students with three 'real-world scenarios': Alex finds a cheaper apartment ($450/month), Alex's car breaks down (needs $200 repair), or Alex gets a part-time job (+$300/month). Each pair selects one scenario.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs recalculate their budget based on their chosen scenario, determining new percentages or maintaining original percentages with adjusted totals. They must show all calculation work.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Each pair shares their scenario and one calculation with the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning.

Conclusion (5 minutes): Discuss how percentage calculations help in making informed financial decisions and preview how these skills apply to tips, discounts, and interest rates.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Calculator for each student
Whiteboard markers and eraser
Real-world scenario cards (3 different scenarios)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with clear work shown, (3) Minor calculation errors with work shown, (2) Some correct calculations with partial work, (1) Major errors or incomplete work. Additionally, observe pair discussions for mathematical reasoning and problem-solving approach. Students must achieve at least 6/8 correct calculations to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference card and work through the first calculation together. Pair struggling students with stronger peers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research actual local housing/food costs and compare with their calculated amounts, or have them create a budget for different income levels ($1,200 or $2,400) and analyze how percentages change their spending power.

title: Personal Budget Planning: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Expenses: Comparative Study
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional teenager using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage formulas to determine exact dollar amounts for savings, entertainment, transportation, and other realistic expenses.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate specific dollar amounts from percentages by applying percentage formulas to budget categories
Students will determine what percentage each expense represents through systematic calculation and verification methods
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Teen Budget Scenario' worksheet showing monthly income of $800 from a part-time job (15 minutes setup). Explain that students must allocate this income using given percentage guidelines: 20% savings, 15% transportation, 25% entertainment, 10% clothing, 20% food, 10% miscellaneous. Students work individually to calculate exact dollar amounts for each category using the formula: (Percentage ÷ 100) × Total Income. They must show all work step-by-step on the worksheet. Next, have students verify their calculations by adding all dollar amounts to ensure they equal $800 total (10 minutes). Then introduce the extension challenge: students receive 5 actual expense receipts totaling $180 and must calculate what percentage each receipt represents of their $200 entertainment budget. They apply the reverse formula: (Individual Amount ÷ Total Amount) × 100. Students complete calculations on the worksheet, showing work for each receipt. During the final 10 minutes, students exchange worksheets with a partner for peer checking using provided answer keys. Partners initial each correct calculation and identify any errors for revision. Teacher circulates throughout, checking calculation methods and providing individual guidance. Conclude by having 3-4 students share one calculation aloud, explaining their step-by-step process to reinforce proper percentage application techniques.
materials_needed: Teen Budget Scenario worksheet (one per student)
Calculator for each student
5 sample receipt images printed on paper
Answer key for teacher and peer checking
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Students must correctly calculate all 6 budget category dollar amounts (10 points each) and 5 receipt percentages (8 points each) with proper work shown. Success criteria: 80% accuracy on calculations with clear step-by-step work demonstrated. Peer checking sheet must show verification of partner's work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example calculation and percentage formula reference card. Offer a calculator tutorial if needed. For advanced learners: add a comparison activity calculating percentage differences between their budget and a provided 'recommended teen budget' using percentage change formulas.
original_title: Personal Budget Planning: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Expenses

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Big O Notation Comparison Lab
description: Students analyze and compare the time complexity of different sorting algorithms by examining pseudocode, tracing execution paths, and categorizing algorithms by their Big O classifications. They will dissect algorithm performance patterns and justify their complexity classifications through systematic analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort algorithms by examining their nested loop structures and recursive calls
Students will compare algorithm efficiency patterns through systematic step-counting and complexity classification using Big O notation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the algorithm analysis worksheet containing pseudocode for bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (10 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group one algorithm to analyze first (5 minutes). 

Step 1: Students trace through their assigned algorithm using a sample array of 8 elements, counting the number of comparisons and swaps at each step (15 minutes). They document this in the provided tracking table.

Step 2: Groups analyze the nested loop structure or recursive calls in their algorithm's pseudocode, identifying which operations contribute to time complexity (10 minutes). They highlight key lines and annotate decision points.

Step 3: Each group determines their algorithm's worst-case, average-case, and best-case time complexity using Big O notation, showing mathematical reasoning (15 minutes). They complete the complexity analysis chart.

Step 4: Groups rotate and repeat the analysis process for the remaining two algorithms (30 minutes total, 15 minutes each).

Step 5: Teams create a comparative matrix showing all three algorithms' complexities across different scenarios (10 minutes).

Step 6: Each group presents their findings for one algorithm, explaining their reasoning and defending their Big O classification to the class (15 minutes total, 5 minutes per presentation). Other students ask clarifying questions and challenge conclusions.

Conclude with a class discussion comparing all three algorithms and identifying patterns in algorithmic complexity analysis (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with pseudocode for bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort
Step-counting tracking tables (printed copies)
Big O complexity reference chart
Sample data arrays (8-element integer arrays)
Colored pens/highlighters for code annotation
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of step-counting and tracing (25%), (2) Correct Big O classification for all three complexity cases (35%), (3) Quality of mathematical reasoning and justification (25%), (4) Participation in group presentation and peer questioning (15%). Students must correctly identify at least 2 out of 3 algorithms' worst-case complexities and provide valid mathematical justification to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed tracking tables and step-by-step Big O calculation examples. Pair them with stronger peers and offer individual guidance during tracing activities. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity, consider hybrid algorithms like Timsort, or extend analysis to additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in a High-Stakes Healthcare Prediction Scenario
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models trained to predict patient readmission risk using real hospital data. They will evaluate model performance, identify potential biases, assess ethical implications, and make evidence-based recommendations for deployment in a clinical setting.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of logistic regression, random forest, and neural network models by analyzing performance metrics, statistical significance, and clinical relevance in healthcare prediction

Students will critique potential algorithmic bias and ethical concerns through systematic analysis of model predictions across different demographic groups and assessment of real-world deployment risks
instructions:
**Setup (15 minutes):** Provide teams of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models (logistic regression, random forest, neural network) and a holdout test dataset containing 2,000 patient records with features including age, gender, race, insurance type, diagnosis codes, and length of stay. Each team receives identical model outputs, confusion matrices, ROC curves, and demographic breakdowns of predictions.

**Phase 1 - Technical Evaluation (45 minutes):** Students calculate and compare accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC for each model. They must identify which metrics are most critical for hospital readmission prediction and justify their reasoning. Teams create comparative visualizations and perform statistical significance tests between model performances.

**Phase 2 - Bias Analysis (30 minutes):** Students examine prediction accuracy across demographic subgroups (age brackets, gender, race, insurance type) to identify potential algorithmic bias. They calculate fairness metrics including equalized odds and demographic parity, documenting disparities in false positive/negative rates across groups.

**Phase 3 - Ethical and Clinical Assessment (45 minutes):** Teams evaluate each model's suitability for clinical deployment by considering: interpretability requirements for medical staff, potential impact of false positives/negatives on patient care, regulatory compliance needs, and resource allocation implications. They must identify specific risks and mitigation strategies.

**Final Recommendation (25 minutes):** Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation recommending one model for deployment, including: quantitative justification based on performance metrics, analysis of bias concerns and proposed solutions, implementation timeline with risk mitigation steps, and monitoring protocols for ongoing evaluation.
materials_needed: Pre-trained ML models (saved as pickle files): logistic regression, random forest, neural network
Holdout test dataset with 2,000 patient records (CSV format with anonymized healthcare data)
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
Model evaluation template spreadsheet with performance metric calculations
Demographic fairness analysis worksheet
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using rubric (100 points total): Technical analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation and interpretation of performance metrics; Bias identification (25 points) - thorough demographic analysis with specific examples; Ethical reasoning (25 points) - comprehensive consideration of clinical implications and risks; Recommendation quality (25 points) - evidence-based decision with clear justification and implementation plan. Final presentations assessed for clarity, use of data visualization, and response to instructor questions about methodology choices.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide performance metric calculation templates, offer mini-lectures on fairness metrics during activity, assign stronger technical students as peer mentors within teams. **Extensions for advanced learners:** Challenge them to implement additional fairness constraints, perform sensitivity analysis on decision thresholds, or design A/B testing protocols for model comparison in clinical settings. Provide access to additional demographic variables for more nuanced bias analysis.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Probability Distribution Model for Real-World Phenomena
description: Students will construct an original probability distribution function to model a complex real-world scenario of their choice, then rigorously validate their model through mathematical proof and statistical analysis. This capstone activity synthesizes advanced probability theory, calculus, and statistical inference into an original mathematical contribution.
estimated_duration: 480 minutes (5 class periods of 90-120 minutes each, plus independent work time)
learning_objectives: Students will create an original continuous probability distribution function by integrating advanced calculus concepts with probability axioms to model a specific real-world phenomenon
Students will validate their constructed distribution through rigorous mathematical proof of probability properties and empirical testing using computational simulation
instructions:
**Phase 1: Model Selection and Justification (Day 1, 90 minutes)**
Students select a complex real-world phenomenon that existing standard distributions (normal, exponential, Weibull, etc.) cannot adequately model. Examples: arrival patterns at emergency rooms during natural disasters, stock price movements during market volatility, or failure rates of emerging technologies. Students must justify their choice with preliminary research and data analysis showing why standard models are insufficient.

**Phase 2: Distribution Construction (Days 2-3, 180 minutes)**
Using calculus and probability theory, students construct their probability density function f(x). They must: (1) Define the sample space and parameter constraints, (2) Construct f(x) ensuring it integrates to 1 over the domain, (3) Derive the cumulative distribution function F(x), (4) Calculate theoretical moments (mean, variance, skewness), and (5) Determine parameter estimation methods. Students document all mathematical derivations with complete proofs.

**Phase 3: Computational Implementation (Day 4, 120 minutes)**
Students implement their distribution in Python/R, creating functions for: PDF evaluation, CDF calculation, random number generation, and parameter estimation. They generate 10,000 random samples and create visualization plots comparing their distribution to real data.

**Phase 4: Validation and Presentation (Day 5, 90 minutes)**
Students perform goodness-of-fit tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling) comparing their model to real data. They prepare a 15-minute presentation including: problem motivation, mathematical derivation, computational implementation, validation results, and potential applications. Presentations must include formal mathematical notation and statistical evidence supporting their model's validity.
materials_needed: Access to statistical software (Python with SciPy/NumPy or R with specialized packages)
Real-world datasets relevant to chosen phenomena (provided via online databases)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Maple)
Presentation software with LaTeX equation support
Access to statistical reference tables and probability theory textbooks
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points): Mathematical rigor and correctness of PDF construction (25 points), proof of probability axioms satisfaction (20 points), quality of computational implementation and documentation (20 points), statistical validation using appropriate tests (20 points), presentation clarity and mathematical communication (15 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery, with partial credit requiring revision and resubmission of deficient components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided templates for PDF construction starting with modifications of existing distributions, offer pre-selected datasets with clear modeling gaps, and provide checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive asymptotic properties, explore multivariate extensions, or connect their distribution to existing mathematical literature through formal comparison studies. Consider pairing students with complementary strengths in theory versus computation.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers from 0000 to 1111 (0-15) through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of 4-bit binary patterns essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) by achieving 90% accuracy on flashcard drills
Students will identify binary number patterns through repeated exposure and memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary flashcards to each student (16 cards total, showing binary numbers 0000 through 1111 on one side, decimal equivalents 0-15 on the other). Students work in pairs for the first 15 minutes: Partner A shows binary side, Partner B states decimal equivalent, then Partner A reveals answer. Partners switch roles after attempting all 16 cards once. During the second 10 minutes, students work individually to sort their flashcards into two piles: 'confident' (can recall immediately) and 'need practice' (took more than 3 seconds or incorrect). Students spend the next 10 minutes focusing only on their 'need practice' pile, using the look-cover-recall method: look at binary number, cover decimal answer, state answer aloud, check accuracy. In the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class speed round where you display binary numbers on the board for 5 seconds each, and students write decimal equivalents on paper. Complete all 16 numbers twice, randomizing order each time. Students self-check answers against the answer key you provide after each round.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards with 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on front, decimal equivalents (0-15) on back
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces 1-16
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projector for displaying binary numbers
Answer key handouts for self-checking
assessment_method: Success is measured by achieving 14/16 (87.5%) correct answers on the final speed round. Record individual scores from both rounds. Students who score below 12/16 (75%) should receive the flashcards for additional home practice. Observe during partner work to identify students struggling with specific binary patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a powers-of-two reference chart (8-4-2-1) and highlight the place value pattern. Start with simpler 2-bit or 3-bit numbers if needed. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit or 6-bit binary numbers, or introduce hexadecimal equivalents of the same binary patterns. Create competition element by tracking class-wide improvement scores.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and verbal recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal value of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire verbal recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (decimal on one side, binary on reverse). Spend 5 minutes explaining that students should focus on memorizing, not calculating. Have students work in pairs for 10 minutes, with Partner A showing decimal numbers while Partner B states the binary equivalent, then switch roles. Next, conduct a whole-class 'popcorn' activity for 8 minutes where you display decimal numbers on the board and students rapidly call out binary answers. Follow with individual silent study time for 7 minutes where students quiz themselves using their flashcards, sorting correctly answered cards from those needing more practice. Conclude with a 5-minute speed round where students work through their entire deck, timing themselves and recording how many they complete correctly in 2 minutes. Have students repeat the speed round twice, aiming to improve their score each time. Throughout the activity, emphasize that the goal is instant recall without counting or calculating.
materials_needed: 16 flashcards per student (decimal 0-15 on front, binary on back)
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard and markers
Score tracking sheets for students
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) on their final speed round within 2 minutes. Observe students during pair work to ensure they're recalling rather than calculating. Collect score tracking sheets showing improvement across the three timed rounds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with just numbers 0-7, provide a reference chart during initial practice, pair with stronger students. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), challenge them to recall in under 1 second per conversion, or have them create their own flashcards for hexadecimal conversions.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill: Exercise 2
description: Students memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and verbal recitation. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-to-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 through 1111 by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recall binary-to-decimal conversions for 4-bit numbers through verbal recitation exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on one side and decimal equivalents (0-15) on the reverse. Demonstrate proper card handling: show binary side first, state answer aloud, then flip to verify. Have students work in pairs for 10 minutes, with Partner A showing cards to Partner B, who must state the decimal equivalent within 3 seconds before checking the answer. Partners switch roles after 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire round lasting 8 minutes: call out binary numbers randomly while students write decimal answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate feedback. Create competitive energy by tracking correct responses. Follow with individual silent practice for 7 minutes where each student cycles through their personal flashcard set three complete times, separating cards into 'mastered' and 'needs practice' piles. Conclude with a 5-minute verbal assessment where students stand and recite the complete sequence from 0000=0 through 1111=15 in unison, then individually volunteer to demonstrate mastery by converting 5 random binary numbers called out by the instructor.
materials_needed: 16 flashcards per student with 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on front and decimal equivalents (0-15) on back
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (1 per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Pre-written list of random binary numbers for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly converting at least 14 out of 16 binary numbers (0000-1111) to decimal within 3 seconds each during individual assessment. Track performance using a simple checklist with student names and checkmarks for each correct rapid response. Success criteria: 87.5% accuracy rate (14/16 correct) within time limit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: start with just 0000-0111 (0-7) before adding 1000-1111 (8-15), provide visual place value charts showing 8-4-2-1 positions, and allow 5-second response time initially. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (00000-11111 = 0-31), challenge them to convert decimal-to-binary direction, or have them create their own flashcards for 6-bit numbers.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice and peer testing. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization exercises and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for 20 minutes, with Partner A showing decimal numbers while Partner B recalls the binary representation, then switching roles after 10 minutes. During practice, students should say answers aloud and immediately check the back of the card for correctness. After paired practice, conduct a whole-class memory drill where you display decimal numbers on the board for 5 seconds each, and students write binary answers on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for quick assessment. Follow with a reverse drill showing binary numbers for students to convert to decimal. Conclude with a 5-minute individual quiz where students complete a worksheet containing 10 randomly selected decimal-to-binary conversions and 10 binary-to-decimal conversions. Emphasize that this is pure memorization - no calculation methods should be used during the activity. Students who finish early can create their own flashcards for numbers 16-31. Monitor student progress by walking around during pair work, noting which number pairs cause the most difficulty for future review sessions.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Individual dry-erase whiteboards and markers for each student
Printed quiz worksheet with 20 conversion problems
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final individual quiz to demonstrate successful memorization. During the whiteboard drill, record which students consistently show correct answers for formative assessment. Use a simple checklist to track each student's performance on both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with just numbers 0-7 and provide a visual chart showing the place values (8-4-2-1). Allow these students additional practice time with a peer tutor. For advanced learners, extend the activity to include 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider providing mnemonic devices for difficult numbers like 6=0110 or 9=1001.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill

title: Interpreting Correlation Matrices and Identifying Data Relationships in Customer Behavior Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-constructed correlation matrix from an e-commerce customer dataset to identify patterns, interpret relationship strengths, and explain the business implications of different variable correlations. This activity focuses on understanding correlation coefficients and their practical meaning in business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficient values between -1 and 1 by categorizing relationship strengths and directions using a provided customer behavior dataset
Students will explain the business significance of identified correlations through structured analysis of customer purchasing patterns
instructions:
Begin by distributing printed correlation matrices showing relationships between 8 customer variables: age, income, time_on_site, pages_viewed, items_in_cart, previous_purchases, review_scores, and total_spent (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and provide the interpretation guide showing correlation strength categories: weak (0.0-0.3), moderate (0.3-0.7), strong (0.7-1.0). 

Step 1: Students spend 20 minutes identifying and highlighting correlations in each strength category using colored pens (weak=yellow, moderate=orange, strong=red). They must find at least 3 examples of each strength level.

Step 2: For 25 minutes, pairs complete the structured analysis worksheet, focusing on 5 specific correlations: age vs. total_spent, time_on_site vs. items_in_cart, previous_purchases vs. review_scores, income vs. pages_viewed, and items_in_cart vs. total_spent. For each correlation, students write: the coefficient value, strength category, direction (positive/negative), and a 2-sentence business interpretation.

Step 3: During the final 15 minutes, each pair presents one correlation finding to the class, explaining why this relationship makes business sense or identifying potential causation concerns. Instructor facilitates discussion about correlation vs. causation and asks follow-up questions about marketing implications.

Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students correctly identify coefficient directions and can articulate the difference between correlation strength and business importance.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix (28x28 grid) for customer behavior dataset
Correlation strength interpretation guide handout
Structured analysis worksheet with 5 correlation scenarios
Colored highlighters or pens (3 colors per pair)
Calculator for verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of correlation strengths and directions (25 points), (2) Quality of business interpretations showing understanding of practical implications (25 points), (3) Correct completion of all 5 required correlation analyses (25 points), (4) Clear verbal explanation during presentation demonstrating understanding of correlation concepts (25 points). Students must score 70% or higher to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example analysis for one correlation pair and create reference cards showing positive vs. negative correlation examples. For advanced learners: Include additional questions about multicollinearity concerns, ask them to identify potentially spurious correlations, or have them suggest additional variables that might influence the relationships they've identified.

title: Optimizing Production Costs Using Linear Programming with Real Manufacturing Constraints
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex multi-variable optimization problem involving production scheduling, resource allocation, and profit maximization for a furniture manufacturing company. They will use graphical methods and the simplex algorithm to find optimal solutions while interpreting real-world constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-constraint business optimization problem into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex algorithm through systematic calculations to determine optimal production quantities that maximize profit while satisfying resource limitations
instructions: Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario: 'Artisan Furniture Co. produces chairs ($60 profit) and tables ($80 profit). Each chair requires 3 hours assembly, 1 hour finishing, 4 board-feet lumber. Each table requires 2 hours assembly, 3 hours finishing, 6 board-feet lumber. Weekly constraints: 120 assembly hours, 90 finishing hours, 300 board-feet lumber, minimum 10 chairs for standing orders.' Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to identify decision variables (x = chairs, y = tables), write the objective function (maximize Z = 60x + 80y), and formulate constraints as inequalities. Step 2 (20 minutes): Students graph the feasible region on provided coordinate paper, plotting each constraint line and shading the feasible area. They must identify and label all corner points. Step 3 (25 minutes): Using the corner point method, students evaluate the objective function at each vertex to find the optimal solution graphically. Step 4 (30 minutes): Students apply the simplex algorithm using provided templates, setting up the initial tableau with slack variables and performing pivot operations until reaching optimality. Step 5 (15 minutes): Students interpret their solution in business context, calculating maximum weekly profit and explaining resource utilization. Each pair submits completed worksheets showing all mathematical work, graphical representation, and a one-paragraph business recommendation explaining their optimal production plan.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario handouts with detailed constraints
Graph paper with pre-drawn coordinate axes (scale 0-50)
Simplex algorithm calculation templates
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils for constraint line graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation including objective function and all constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphical solution with properly identified feasible region and corner points (25%), (3) Correct simplex algorithm implementation with accurate pivot operations (30%), (4) Appropriate business interpretation and recommendation based on mathematical results (20%). Students must achieve 75% overall to demonstrate proficiency in applying linear programming techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed constraint formulations and pre-plotted constraint lines. Offer a simplex algorithm reference card with pivot selection rules. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how solutions change if lumber costs increase by 20% or if a third product (desks) is added with specified resource requirements and profit margins.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices: Which Chart Tells the Best Story?
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key insights. They will justify their choice using established data visualization principles and identify specific strengths and weaknesses of each option.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying visualization design principles and assessing clarity of communication
Students will critique data presentation choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by displaying three different visualizations of a simple sales dataset (bar chart, line graph, and pie chart showing quarterly revenue by product category). Provide students with the 'Visualization Evaluation Framework' handout covering five criteria: clarity, accuracy, audience appropriateness, visual hierarchy, and insight communication. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization for 3 minutes, taking notes on initial impressions and what story each chart tells.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the evaluation framework, students score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for all five criteria, writing 1-2 sentences justifying each score.

Step 3 (10 minutes): In pairs, students compare their evaluations and discuss differences in scoring, reaching consensus on the most effective visualization.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair presents their choice to the class in 2 minutes, stating their selection and top two reasons. Instructor facilitates brief Q&A after each presentation.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Class votes on the most convincing argument (not just most popular chart) and instructor reveals which visualization actual business analysts chose for a board presentation, explaining their reasoning.

Conclude with 5-minute reflection where students write one insight about visualization evaluation and one question for further exploration.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of quarterly sales data (one per chart type)
Visualization Evaluation Framework handout with 5 criteria and 1-5 scale
Student evaluation sheets with scoring grids
Timer for time management
Projector/screen for displaying visualizations to full class
assessment_method: Grade evaluation sheets using rubric: Thorough application of all 5 framework criteria (40%), quality of written justifications showing reasoning (30%), active participation in pair and class discussions (20%), and final reflection demonstrating learning (10%). Success = 80% of students score 3/4 or higher overall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This chart is effective because...' and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest improvements to the weakest visualization or identify additional criteria not covered in the framework. Consider providing a fourth, poorly designed visualization for extra comparison.

title: Design Your Dream Amusement Park: Applying Geometric Principles and Statistical Analysis
description: Students will create an original amusement park layout using geometric transformations, calculate optimal ride placement using coordinate geometry, and design a pricing strategy based on statistical data analysis. This project synthesizes multiple mathematical concepts into a comprehensive real-world application.
estimated_duration: 6 class periods (45 minutes each) over 2 weeks
learning_objectives: Students will construct an amusement park layout by applying geometric transformations, coordinate geometry, and area calculations to optimize space usage and visitor flow
Students will develop a data-driven pricing strategy through statistical analysis of demographic surveys and probability calculations for different visitor scenarios
instructions:
**Phase 1: Planning and Data Collection (Days 1-2, 90 minutes total)**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives a 20x20 coordinate grid representing 400 square units of park space. Teams first conduct a survey of 20 people (peers, family, teachers) asking: age, preferred ride types, maximum spending amount, and visit frequency. They compile this data in a spreadsheet and calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for spending amounts.

**Phase 2: Park Design (Days 3-4, 90 minutes total)**
Using their coordinate grid, teams design 8-12 attractions. Each ride type has specific space requirements: roller coasters (6 units, rectangular), carousels (4 units, circular), water rides (8 units, L-shaped), food courts (3 units, square). Students must use at least three geometric transformations (rotation, reflection, translation) to position rides efficiently. They calculate total area used, remaining space for walkways, and create scaled technical drawings showing exact coordinates for each attraction corner.

**Phase 3: Business Strategy (Day 5, 45 minutes)**
Teams analyze their survey data to determine optimal ticket pricing using statistical insights. They create probability trees for different visitor types (child, teen, adult, senior) and calculate expected revenue per visitor. Teams must justify their pricing strategy with specific statistical evidence from their data collection.

**Phase 4: Presentation (Day 6, 45 minutes)**
Teams present their park design using a poster showing the coordinate layout, a 3D model or digital visualization, and a business proposal including statistical analysis. Each presentation lasts 8 minutes with 2 minutes for peer questions.
materials_needed: 20x20 coordinate grid paper (4 sheets per team)
Colored pencils/markers for coding different ride types
Calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Survey template worksheets
Protractors and rulers for geometric measurements
Large poster board (24x36 inches) for final presentation
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Mathematical accuracy of geometric calculations and coordinate plotting (25 points), appropriate use of statistical measures and data interpretation (25 points), creativity and feasibility of park design with proper space utilization (25 points), clarity of presentation with evidence-based reasoning (25 points). Students must show all mathematical work and cite specific data points in their business justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated ride dimensions and coordinate plotting templates. Offer guided practice with geometric transformations using manipulatives before the main activity. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate trigonometric calculations for ride angles, create multiple pricing scenarios with break-even analysis, or design rides with complex geometric shapes requiring advanced area formulas.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Challenge
description: Students memorize and accurately recall the formal definitions, mathematical notations, and canonical examples of 15 advanced algorithm complexity classes including polynomial hierarchy levels, exponential variants, and space complexity bounds. This rapid-fire recall activity builds foundational knowledge for advanced computational complexity theory.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize and recite the formal Big-O notation definitions for 15 advanced complexity classes including P, NP, PSPACE, EXPTIME, and polynomial hierarchy levels by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recall specific canonical algorithm examples for each complexity class through structured memorization exercises and verbal recitation sessions
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute study period where students review the provided complexity class reference sheet containing 15 classes: P, NP, co-NP, NP-complete, PSPACE, PSPACE-complete, EXPTIME, NEXPTIME, Σₚᵏ and Πₚᵏ (k=1,2,3), LOGSPACE, and NL. Each entry includes formal definition, mathematical notation, and 2-3 canonical problem examples. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs using digital flashcards, with one partner showing the complexity class name while the other recites the complete formal definition and time/space bounds. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Individual silent memorization using the reference sheet, focusing on problem examples like 3-SAT (NP-complete), TQBF (PSPACE-complete), and Chess (EXPTIME). Phase 3 (15 minutes): Rapid-fire group recall session where instructor calls out complexity classes randomly and students must immediately state: (1) formal definition, (2) mathematical notation, (3) one canonical example. Students raise hands to volunteer answers. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Written recall quiz where students must fill in a chart with all 15 complexity classes, their definitions, and examples from memory without references. Maintain brisk pace throughout - emphasize speed and accuracy of recall rather than deep understanding.
materials_needed: Complexity class reference sheet with 15 advanced classes and formal definitions
Digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet) pre-loaded with complexity class deck
Printed quiz template with blank complexity class comparison chart
Timer or stopwatch for pacing activities
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on the final written recall quiz, correctly providing formal definitions and canonical examples for at least 12 of 15 complexity classes. Verbal participation during group recall is assessed using a 3-point scale: 3 points for immediate correct response with complete definition and example, 2 points for correct but slow response, 1 point for partial correctness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices and allow them to focus on mastering 8-10 core classes before attempting all 15. Create acronyms like 'PNP-SPACE-EXP' for major categories. For advanced learners, add 5 additional classes like BPP, RP, ZPP from probabilistic complexity theory, or include multiple canonical examples per class and historical context of when each class was defined.

title: Algorithm Complexity Visualization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity classifications for 30 advanced algorithms across sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and string matching categories. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge essential for algorithm analysis and selection in complex programming scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity notations for 30 advanced algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions and written assessments
Students will identify space complexity classifications for dynamic programming and graph algorithms through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet containing 30 algorithms organized into 6 categories (5 algorithms each): Advanced Sorting (Timsort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort, Counting Sort, Shell Sort), Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's), Dynamic Programming (Longest Common Subsequence, Knapsack variants, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Optimal Binary Search Tree), String Matching (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick, Suffix Array), Tree Operations (AVL rotations, Red-Black insertions, B-tree operations, Splay tree operations, Trie insertions), and Advanced Search (A*, Bidirectional BFS, Jump Search, Exponential Search, Interpolation Search). Students spend 15 minutes studying the sheet, focusing on memorizing both worst-case time complexity and space complexity for each algorithm. Remove reference sheets and conduct Phase 1: Category-based recall where students work in pairs, with one student naming an algorithm category and the other reciting all 5 algorithms with their complexities (10 minutes total, switching roles halfway). Phase 2 involves individual written recall where each student receives a worksheet listing the 30 algorithm names in randomized order and must write the corresponding time and space complexity notations without references (15 minutes). Phase 3 consists of rapid-fire verbal assessment where the instructor randomly calls out algorithm names and students must immediately state the complexity, eliminating those who answer incorrectly until 3 winners remain (10 minutes). Conclude with peer verification where students exchange worksheets and grade using the answer key, identifying algorithms requiring additional memorization work.
materials_needed: Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet with 30 algorithms and their Big O notations
Individual recall worksheets with randomized algorithm names
Answer key for peer grading
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard markers for tracking elimination rounds
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (24/30 correct) on the written recall worksheet to demonstrate mastery. Additional assessment through verbal rapid-fire round participation, where students must respond within 5 seconds per algorithm. Track individual progress using a checklist marking algorithms correctly recalled versus those requiring additional study.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices for complexity patterns (e.g., 'Most graph algorithms are O(V+E) or O(V²)'). Allow color-coding during study phase to group similar complexities. For advanced learners, extend the activity by including average-case complexities, asking them to explain why certain algorithms have their specific complexity, or having them create complexity justification flashcards for teaching others.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results and Model Generalization Patterns in Ensemble Methods
description: Students will analyze and interpret cross-validation performance metrics across different ensemble algorithms to understand model generalization behavior. instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared Jupyter notebook containing cross-validation results from three ensemble methods (Random Forest, XGBoost, AdaBoost) applied to both a high-dimensional dataset (genomics) and a structured dataset (financial). First 20 minutes: Students examine the provided box plots, violin plots, and statistical summary tables showing mean, median, standard deviation, and confidence intervals for each model's cross-validation scores. They must identify which model shows highest mean performance, lowest variance, and most consistent results across folds. Next 25 minutes: Students analyze correlation matrices between fold performances and examine learning curves showing training vs. validation scores across different sample sizes. They document patterns in overfitting behavior and convergence characteristics. Following 25 minutes: Students interpret feature importance rankings and partial dependence plots to understand how each ensemble method captures different aspects of the data relationships. Final 20 minutes: Students synthesize findings by creating written interpretations explaining why XGBoost shows lower variance on structured data while Random Forest generalizes better on high-dimensional data, connecting observations to theoretical understanding of bagging vs. boosting mechanisms.

title: Budget Planning for a Class Pizza Party
description: Students will apply basic arithmetic operations and percentage calculations to create a realistic budget for organizing a class pizza party. learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication and division skills to calculate cost per person and determine quantities needed by analyzing real pizza menu prices and class size

instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a Pizza Palace menu, calculator, and budget worksheet. Post the scenario on the board: 'Plan a pizza party for 24 students with a $150 budget. Sales tax is 8.25%.' **Step 1 (10 minutes):** Students individually examine the menu and identify pizza sizes, prices, and estimated servings per pizza. Have them calculate how many pizzas are needed (assuming each student eats 2-3 slices, with 8 slices per large pizza). **Step 2 (15 minutes):** Students select pizza combinations and calculate subtotals. They must show work for: total pizza cost, tax amount (subtotal × 0.0825), and final total including tax. **Step 3 (10 minutes):** Students determine if their plan fits the budget. If over budget, they must revise selections and recalculate. **Step 4 (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare solutions and verify each other's calculations. Partners check arithmetic and discuss different pizza combinations that work within budget. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Select 3-4 student pairs to present their budget plans to the class, explaining their reasoning for pizza selections and showing their tax calculations on the board.
materials_needed: Laminated Pizza Palace menu with prices for each student
Budget planning worksheet with calculation spaces
Basic calculators (one per student)
Whiteboard markers for student presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (3) All calculations correct, budget adhered to, work clearly shown; (2) Minor calculation errors, budget considerations evident, most work shown; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Additionally, observe student explanations during pair sharing for understanding of percentage calculations and problem-solving reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template with labeled spaces for each step and allow use of multiplication tables. Start them with simpler combinations (all same pizza type). For advanced learners: Add complexity by including drinks and sides in the budget, or challenge them to find the combination that feeds the most people within budget while maintaining variety.

They explore at least 3 different combinations and record costs. **Step 3 (10 minutes):** Students apply a 20% student discount to their pizza totals using percentage calculations. title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithm Performance

instructions: Begin by providing students with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (15 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group the same three algorithms. They must document each step on the analysis worksheet, creating execution trees for merge sort and recording pivot selections for quick sort. In Phase 2 (20 minutes), groups analyze patterns by testing algorithms with pre-sorted data [11, 12, 22, 25, 34, 64, 90] and reverse-sorted data [90, 64, 34, 25, 22, 12, 11], documenting operation counts for each scenario. Phase 3 (25 minutes) requires students to complete the comparison matrix, identifying Big O notation for time/space complexity, and determining best-case/worst-case scenarios for each algorithm. Students must justify their complexity analysis with specific evidence from their traces. In Phase 4 (15 minutes), groups prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining which algorithm they would recommend for: (a) sorting 10 elements, (b) sorting 10,000 elements with limited memory, and (c) sorting data that's already mostly organized. title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithm Performance: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their implementations and testing their performance with datasets of varying sizes. learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by tracing through their execution steps and identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and data access patterns

Students will compare algorithm efficiency through empirical testing with datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 elements, measuring execution time and memory usage to validate theoretical complexity analysis
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python (15 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, with each team receiving the same three algorithm files and a data generation script that creates random integer arrays. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Students examine each algorithm's code structure, identifying and documenting: number of nested loops, recursive function calls, array access patterns, and temporary variable usage. They create a visual flowchart for each algorithm showing decision points and iteration patterns.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Teams run performance tests using the provided timing module. They execute each algorithm on datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 randomly generated integers, recording execution time in milliseconds and peak memory usage. Students repeat each test 5 times and calculate average performance metrics.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students plot their empirical results on provided graph templates, creating time vs. dataset size curves for each algorithm. They compare their experimental data against theoretical Big O complexity charts (O(n²) for bubble sort, O(n log n) for merge sort and average-case quicksort).

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams analyze discrepancies between theoretical and experimental results, considering factors like system overhead, compiler optimizations, and worst-case vs. average-case scenarios. They document three real-world scenarios where each algorithm would be the optimal choice, justifying their decisions based on dataset characteristics, memory constraints, and performance requirements.

Conclude with team presentations (15 minutes) where each group shares one key insight about algorithm trade-offs.
materials_needed: Pre-written Python files containing bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort implementations
Data generation script for creating random integer arrays
Graph paper templates or digital graphing tool access
Computers with Python 3.x and time/memory profiling modules installed
Big O complexity reference chart handout
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of code structure analysis and complexity identification (25%), (2) Completeness and accuracy of empirical testing data collection (25%), (3) Quality of comparison between theoretical and experimental results with clear explanations of discrepancies (30%), (4) Appropriateness of real-world application scenarios with justified algorithm selections (20%). Students submit completed analysis worksheets, performance data tables, and scenario recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed analysis templates with guided questions and highlight key code sections to examine. Offer algorithm complexity cheat sheets and pair weaker students with stronger peers. For advanced learners, introduce additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or have them analyze best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios separately. Challenge them to modify algorithms and predict performance impacts.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Customer Churn Prediction

They will assess model performance using multiple metrics, justify their recommendations, and present a comprehensive business case for model deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning algorithms by systematically comparing performance metrics, interpretability, and computational efficiency
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive analysis of business constraints, data characteristics, and stakeholder requirements
instructions: Begin by providing students with a preprocessed telecommunications customer churn dataset (10,000 records) and pre-trained models saved as pickle files. In the first 30 minutes, students work individually to load and examine each model's performance using sklearn.metrics, calculating accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC for all three models. Next, spend 45 minutes having students analyze feature importance plots, confusion matrices, and ROC curves for each model, documenting strengths and weaknesses in a structured comparison matrix. During the following 60 minutes, students work in pairs to evaluate business-specific criteria: model interpretability (can business users understand predictions?), prediction speed (can it handle real-time scoring?), maintenance complexity, and alignment with company risk tolerance. Students must then spend 30 minutes creating a decision framework weighing technical performance (40%), business interpretability (30%), operational feasibility (20%), and cost considerations (10%). In the final 45 minutes, each pair prepares a 5-minute presentation defending their model recommendation to a simulated executive committee, addressing potential counterarguments and implementation challenges. title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Transportation Networks

They will develop their own algorithm, validate it with real data, and present implementation recommendations to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize differential equations, network theory, and optimization techniques by constructing an original mathematical model for urban traffic flow optimization
Students will design and validate a novel algorithmic solution through computational implementation and real-world data analysis
instructions:
Phase 1 (60 minutes): Students form teams of 3-4 and select a real metropolitan area (provided dataset options include NYC, London, Tokyo traffic networks). Each team analyzes the provided traffic flow data, road capacity matrices, and timing constraint parameters. Teams identify 2-3 specific optimization objectives (minimize travel time, maximize throughput, reduce emissions) and document mathematical assumptions.

Phase 2 (90 minutes): Teams construct their mathematical model by defining state variables, establishing constraint equations using graph theory principles, and formulating the objective function. Teams document their mathematical derivations and justify each modeling decision.
