Students must identify at least 3 data quality issues and provide specific examples when critiquing each approach to earn full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of common data quality issues to look for and sentence starters for evaluation comments. Highlight specific sections in each report that demonstrate key methodological differences. For advanced learners, ask them to propose a third hybrid approach combining the best elements of both methods and justify their data cleaning pipeline choices with statistical reasoning.

title: Design Your Own Amusement Park: Creating a Coordinate Geometry Adventure
description: Students will design an original amusement park layout using coordinate geometry principles, incorporating linear and quadratic functions to represent ride paths, calculating distances and areas, and presenting their park with mathematical justifications. This project synthesizes multiple geometry and algebra concepts into a creative, real-world application.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original amusement park design by applying coordinate geometry, linear functions, and quadratic functions to represent ride layouts and pathways
Students will synthesize distance formulas, slope calculations, and area computations through designing and justifying their park's mathematical features
instructions:
**Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Distribute coordinate grid paper (20x20 units) and project requirements handout. Explain that students will design a 5-ride amusement park where each ride must incorporate specific mathematical elements. Review the requirements: 2 rides following linear paths, 2 rides following parabolic/curved paths, 1 entrance pathway, food court placement using distance optimization, and fencing calculations for the perimeter.

**Phase 2 (40 minutes):** Students begin sketching their park layout on grid paper. They must plot and label coordinates for all major features, write equations for each ride path (linear rides need slope-intercept form, curved rides need vertex form quadratic equations), and calculate the distance between the entrance and food court using the distance formula. Circulate to provide guidance on equation writing and coordinate plotting.

**Phase 3 (30 minutes):** Students calculate the total fencing needed by finding the perimeter of their irregularly shaped park, determine the area of their food court (must be rectangular or triangular), and create a legend showing all mathematical work. They must also write a 2-paragraph explanation justifying their design choices using mathematical reasoning.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Students prepare a 3-minute presentation of their park, highlighting one linear ride equation, one quadratic ride equation, and their optimization reasoning for food court placement. Set up gallery walk stations where students post their designs and rotate to view others' work, using provided peer feedback forms to evaluate mathematical accuracy and creativity.
materials_needed: 20x20 coordinate grid paper (2 sheets per student)
Colored pencils or markers
Graphing calculators or Desmos graphing software access
Project requirements handout with mathematical specifications
Peer feedback forms for gallery walk
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct equations, calculations, and coordinate usage (25%), (2) Design Creativity - originality and logical park layout (20%), (3) Mathematical Justification - clear explanations connecting math to design choices (25%), (4) Communication - presentation clarity and professional appearance (15%), (5) Peer Feedback Quality - constructive comments during gallery walk (15%). Students must demonstrate mastery by earning at least 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy and justification categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-plotted coordinate templates with suggested ride locations, offer equation format cards showing slope-intercept and vertex form templates, and pair with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate trigonometric functions for circular rides, optimize multiple variables (cost, safety, efficiency), or create 3D coordinate representations using technology tools. Provide additional support by posting anchor charts with distance formula, slope formula, and area formulas visible throughout the activity.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Speed Test
description: Students will rapidly identify and recall the time and space complexity classifications of 40 advanced algorithms across various domains including graph theory, dynamic programming, and advanced data structures. This high-speed recognition activity reinforces memorization of crucial algorithmic complexity facts that form the foundation for algorithm selection and optimization decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big-O time complexity notation for 40 advanced algorithms including A*, Floyd-Warshall, and FFT by matching algorithm names to complexity expressions within 3 seconds per item
Students will identify the space complexity requirements of advanced sorting, graph, and string processing algorithms through rapid-fire classification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet containing 40 algorithms with their complexities for 5-minute study period. Students work individually to memorize entries. After study time, collect reference sheets. Launch the digital flashcard system displaying algorithm names for 3 seconds each. Students must write the time complexity (Big-O notation) on their answer sheet before the next algorithm appears. Present algorithms in randomized order: Dijkstra's Algorithm, Merge Sort, Quick Sort (average), Quick Sort (worst), Heap Sort, Radix Sort, Counting Sort, Binary Search, Linear Search, DFS, BFS, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, A* Search, Prim's Algorithm, Kruskal's Algorithm, Topological Sort, FFT, Matrix Multiplication (standard), Strassen's Algorithm, KMP String Matching, Rabin-Karp, Suffix Array Construction, LCS Dynamic Programming, Knapsack (0/1), Fibonacci (naive recursion), Fibonacci (dynamic programming), Hash Table Insert/Search (average), Hash Table (worst case), AVL Tree operations, Red-Black Tree operations, B-Tree operations, Trie Insert/Search, Union-Find with Path Compression, Convex Hull (Graham Scan), Closest Pair of Points, Maximum Flow (Ford-Fulkerson), Minimum Spanning Tree verification, Primality Testing (Miller-Rabin), and Integer Factorization (trial division). After completing time complexity round, repeat process for space complexity identification. Conclude with immediate answer review where correct complexities are displayed for each algorithm.
materials_needed: Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet (printed copy per student)
Digital presentation system with timer capability
Pre-programmed flashcard sequence with 40 advanced algorithms
Answer sheets with numbered lines 1-40 for time and space complexity
Stopwatch or timer application
assessment_method: Students receive 1 point for each correctly recalled complexity notation (exact Big-O format required). Success criteria: 32/40 correct for time complexity (80%) and 28/40 correct for space complexity (70%). Partial credit not awarded - notation must be precisely correct including proper Big-O format (e.g., O(V²), O(n log n)). Final scores calculated as percentage of total possible points (80 points maximum).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet connecting algorithm types to complexity patterns, allow 5-second response time instead of 3 seconds, or focus on subset of 25 most common algorithms. For advanced learners: Include average vs. worst-case distinctions, add amortized complexity analysis, or extend to parallel algorithm complexities. Consider grouping algorithms by complexity class for pattern recognition.

title: Interpreting Deep Learning Model Architecture Trade-offs through Comparative Loss Function Analysis
description: Students analyze and interpret how different neural network architectures (CNN vs. Transformer vs. LSTM) perform on the same time-series forecasting task by examining their loss curves, convergence patterns, and computational efficiency metrics. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining the underlying reasons for performance differences and predicting optimal use cases for each architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between neural network architecture choices and training dynamics by analyzing loss curves, gradient flow patterns, and convergence behavior across three different model types
Students will explain the computational and performance trade-offs between CNN, Transformer, and LSTM architectures through systematic comparison of training metrics and resource utilization data
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-trained models (CNN, Transformer, LSTM) trained on the same cryptocurrency price prediction dataset, along with their complete training logs, loss curves, and performance metrics. In teams of 3-4, students spend 20 minutes examining the provided TensorBoard visualizations, training logs, and model summaries. Each team member focuses initially on one architecture. Students then rotate every 15 minutes to examine each model's: (1) loss convergence patterns and training stability, (2) computational requirements (memory usage, training time, parameter count), (3) validation performance across different time horizons, and (4) attention/feature visualization outputs where applicable. After individual analysis (45 minutes total), teams reconvene for 30 minutes to create a comparative analysis matrix documenting: convergence speed differences, overfitting tendencies, computational efficiency ratios, and performance stability across validation sets. Teams then spend 25 minutes developing hypotheses about why each architecture exhibits its observed behavior, connecting architectural features (attention mechanisms, recurrent connections, convolutional filters) to performance patterns. Finally, each team presents a 10-minute analysis explaining which architecture they would recommend for: (1) real-time trading applications, (2) long-term forecasting with limited computational resources, and (3) research applications requiring interpretability. Presentations must include specific evidence from the metrics and clear reasoning linking architectural choices to observed performance characteristics.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded model training histories and metrics for CNN, Transformer, and LSTM models
TensorBoard visualization files for all three model architectures
Standardized cryptocurrency dataset (Bitcoin hourly prices, 2-year period)
Comparative analysis matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Model architecture diagrams and parameter summaries for each network type
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of metric interpretation (25%) - correctly identifies convergence patterns, computational differences, and performance variations, (2) Quality of architectural reasoning (35%) - demonstrates clear understanding of how architectural features influence observed behaviors, (3) Appropriateness of use-case recommendations (25%) - provides well-justified architecture selections based on specific application requirements, (4) Integration of evidence (15%) - effectively uses quantitative data from training logs and visualizations to support conclusions. Students must score 3+ on all categories to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each architecture analysis (e.g., 'How does the validation loss compare to training loss after epoch 50?') and a partially completed comparison matrix with key metrics pre-identified. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity by providing models with different hyperparameter settings for the same architecture, or challenge them to propose hybrid architectures that combine beneficial elements from multiple approaches and justify their design choices.

title: Real-World Budget Planning with Percentages and Decimals
description: Students will apply percentage calculations and decimal operations to create a realistic monthly budget for a college student scenario. They will use given income data to allocate funds across different expense categories while meeting specific financial constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting percentages to decimals and multiplying with total income
Students will demonstrate decimal operations through calculating remaining funds and adjusting budget categories to meet spending limits
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Challenge' worksheet and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card contains a different monthly income amount ($800, $1000, or $1200). Explain that students must create a budget following these rules: housing cannot exceed 40% of income, food must be 15-20% of income, transportation 10-15%, entertainment maximum 10%, and they must save at least 5%. 

Have students work individually for the first 15 minutes to calculate their maximum amounts for each category using their scenario's income. They should convert percentages to decimals (40% = 0.40) and multiply by total income. For example, with $1000 income: housing maximum = 0.40 × $1000 = $400. 

Next, students spend 20 minutes researching realistic costs using provided local housing/food cost sheets or approved websites. They must find actual apartment rents, grocery costs, and transportation options, then adjust their theoretical maximums to realistic amounts while staying within constraints. 

For the final 15 minutes, students calculate their total expenses using decimal addition, determine remaining funds by subtracting total expenses from income, and verify all percentage requirements are met by dividing each category by total income and converting back to percentages. 

Conclude with a 10-minute partner share where students compare budgets and discuss which calculations were most challenging. Partners should verify each other's percentage calculations and check that all constraints were satisfied.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Challenge worksheet (one per student)
Scenario cards with different income amounts ($800, $1000, $1200)
Local cost reference sheets (housing, food, transportation)
Calculators
Access to approved cost-research websites
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage-to-decimal conversions correct, all budget constraints met, arithmetic accurate; (3) Minor calculation errors but constraints mostly met; (2) Some percentage calculations incorrect or 1-2 constraints violated; (1) Multiple calculation errors or several constraints not met. Also observe problem-solving process during work time.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example with $900 income showing step-by-step percentage calculations. Offer percentage-to-decimal conversion charts and encourage use of estimation to check reasonableness. For advanced learners, add complexity by including variable income scenarios, irregular expenses, or requiring them to calculate how income changes would affect their budget percentages.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis Through Runtime Comparison
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code structure, predicting time complexity, and comparing actual runtime performance on datasets of varying sizes. They will identify the relationship between theoretical complexity and real-world performance to determine optimal algorithm selection criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithm efficiency by examining code structure and identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and data operations to determine Big O notation
Students will compare theoretical time complexity predictions with empirical runtime data through systematic testing and graphical analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python (15 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group all three algorithms. In Phase 1 (20 minutes), students examine each algorithm's code without running it, identifying key structural elements: nested loops, recursive calls, and data manipulation operations. They document their findings on the provided analysis worksheet, predicting time complexity for each algorithm. In Phase 2 (25 minutes), groups run each algorithm on provided datasets of sizes 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements, recording execution times in milliseconds. Students use the timing module to measure performance and log results in a shared spreadsheet template. During Phase 3 (15 minutes), students create graphs plotting dataset size versus execution time for each algorithm using provided graphing software. In Phase 4 (20 minutes), groups analyze their graphs against their initial predictions, identifying which algorithms scale linearly, quadratically, or logarithmically. They complete a comparison matrix identifying best-case scenarios for each algorithm. Finally (10 minutes), each group presents one key finding about the relationship between code structure and performance, supported by their data visualization.
materials_needed: Python development environment (IDLE or VS Code)
Pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (bubble, merge, quick)
Algorithm analysis worksheet template
Test datasets (random integers) in sizes 100, 1000, 5000, 10000
Graphing software (matplotlib or Excel)
Shared spreadsheet template for data collection
Comparison matrix handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of initial complexity predictions based on code analysis (25%), (2) Completeness and accuracy of runtime data collection (25%), (3) Quality of data visualization and correct identification of complexity patterns from graphs (30%), (4) Justification of algorithm selection recommendations with supporting evidence (20%). Students must submit completed analysis worksheet, runtime data tables, graphs, and written recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide code annotation guides highlighting loop structures and recursive patterns, offer simplified datasets (sizes 10, 100, 500), and pair with stronger coding partners. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), challenge them to test with different data types (strings, objects), or have them implement their own timing framework with statistical analysis including multiple runs and standard deviation calculations.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn Using Multiple Performance Metrics
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting) trained on a customer churn dataset. They will evaluate model performance using multiple metrics, identify potential biases, and make justified recommendations for production deployment considering business constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of three machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and feature importance to determine optimal model selection
Students will critique model limitations and biases through systematic analysis of prediction errors, class imbalance effects, and business impact considerations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup and Initial Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a preprocessed customer churn dataset (10,000 records) and three pre-trained models with their predictions. Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team calculates comprehensive performance metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and precision-recall curves for each model. Students must document their calculations in Jupyter notebooks, creating visualizations for each metric.

**Phase 2: Deep Dive Evaluation (60 minutes)**
Teams analyze confusion matrices to identify which customer segments each model struggles with most. They examine feature importance rankings and assess whether models rely on potentially problematic features (e.g., demographic variables that could indicate bias). Students create error analysis plots showing false positive and false negative patterns across different customer characteristics (tenure, monthly charges, contract type).

**Phase 3: Business Context Integration (45 minutes)**
Provide business constraints: false positives cost $50 in retention offers, false negatives cost $200 in lost revenue. Teams recalculate model value using these costs and evaluate which model provides best ROI. They assess model interpretability requirements for regulatory compliance and customer service team usage.

**Phase 4: Recommendation and Justification (30 minutes)**
Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation recommending one model for deployment. They must justify their choice using quantitative evidence, address potential risks, and propose monitoring strategies. Teams present to class, defending their recommendations against peer questions and instructor challenges about edge cases and ethical considerations.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn
Preprocessed telecom customer churn dataset (CSV format)
Three trained model files (.pkl format) with prediction outputs
Business cost matrix specification document
Model evaluation template notebook with starter code
assessment_method: Students evaluated using detailed rubric (100 points total): Technical accuracy of metric calculations (25 points), depth of error analysis and bias identification (25 points), quality of business impact assessment (25 points), and strength of final recommendation with supporting evidence (25 points). Deliverables include completed Jupyter notebook with all analyses and 10-minute team presentation with Q&A defense.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates for complex metrics and guided questions for error analysis. Offer office hours for technical troubleshooting. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional evaluation techniques like LIME explanations, cross-validation stability analysis, or fairness metrics across demographic groups. Encourage exploration of ensemble methods combining multiple models.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Real Estate Investment Portfolio Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical framework combining probability theory, calculus optimization, and linear algebra to solve a complex real estate investment problem. They will develop their own mathematical model from scratch, incorporating multiple constraints and variables to maximize portfolio returns while managing risk.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts from probability, calculus, and linear algebra to construct an original optimization model for real-world investment scenarios

Students will design and implement a comprehensive mathematical framework that incorporates stochastic processes, constraint optimization, and sensitivity analysis to solve multi-variable investment problems
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a realistic scenario: They have $5 million to invest across 8 different real estate markets with varying risk profiles, expected returns, and market correlations. Step 1 (45 minutes): Students individually research and define their mathematical variables, including return rates (R_i), risk coefficients (σ_i), correlation matrices (ρ_ij), and constraint parameters. They must establish at least 6 mathematical constraints including budget limits, risk tolerance thresholds, and diversification requirements. Step 2 (60 minutes): Working in pairs, students construct their objective function using advanced calculus concepts, incorporating both expected return maximization and risk minimization through utility theory. They must derive their own utility function U(x) = E(R) - λσ² where λ represents their chosen risk aversion parameter. Step 3 (75 minutes): Students apply Lagrange multipliers to solve their constrained optimization problem, showing all mathematical derivations. They must also incorporate Monte Carlo simulation techniques to model uncertainty in market returns using probability distributions they define and justify. Step 4 (90 minutes): Teams implement their mathematical model using computational tools, running sensitivity analyses on key parameters and creating visual representations of their optimization surfaces. Step 5 (60 minutes): Students present their complete mathematical framework to the class, defending their modeling choices and demonstrating how their solution adapts to changing market conditions through dynamic programming approaches they design.
materials_needed: Advanced graphing calculators or mathematical software (Mathematica, MATLAB, or Python with NumPy/SciPy)
Real estate market data sets with 10-year historical performance metrics
Large format paper or digital presentation tools for model visualization
Access to statistical reference tables and probability distribution resources
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of derivations (30 points), originality and sophistication of modeling approach (25 points), proper integration of multiple mathematical domains (20 points), computational implementation and accuracy (15 points), and clarity of presentation and defense of modeling choices (10 points). Students must submit written documentation of all mathematical work plus a functional computational model.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide templates for basic optimization setups and guide them toward simpler utility functions. Offer pre-calculated correlation matrices and suggest using linear programming before advancing to nonlinear optimization. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate behavioral economics factors, implement machine learning prediction components, or extend to dynamic portfolio rebalancing using stochastic optimal control theory.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard activities and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid recognition exercises within 3 seconds per conversion
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student, with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for the first 15 minutes, taking turns showing decimal sides while partners recall binary representations aloud. Partners should provide immediate feedback and help with corrections. Next, reverse roles for another 15 minutes, showing binary sides for decimal recall. After pair practice, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire session where you display either decimal or binary numbers on screen for 5 seconds each, and students write answers on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for quick assessment. Create three rounds: Round 1 shows decimal numbers for binary recall, Round 2 shows binary for decimal recall, and Round 3 mixes both directions randomly. Between rounds, have students self-check answers against the answer key and mark their scores. Conclude with a 5-minute individual silent review where students identify their three most challenging conversions and practice them using their flashcards. Throughout the activity, circulate to observe student responses and provide immediate correction for errors.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (16 cards each showing 0-15 decimal with 4-bit binary equivalents)
Individual mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each student
Digital presentation slides with decimal and binary numbers
Printed answer key sheets for self-checking
Timer or stopwatch for pacing activities
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14 out of 16 correct) on the final mixed round of rapid recognition. Track individual whiteboard responses during whole-class rounds, recording correct/incorrect for each student. Provide immediate feedback checklist showing which specific conversions each student missed for targeted follow-up practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a binary place-value chart (8-4-2-1) as reference and start with smaller ranges (0-7). For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing more support during partner practice phases.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by correctly identifying at least 12 out of 16 conversions within 30 seconds
Students will recognize decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire identification exercises with 80% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (15 minutes setup). Each card shows a decimal number (0-15) on one side and its 4-bit binary equivalent on the other. Students work in pairs for the first 20 minutes: Partner A shows decimal numbers while Partner B states the binary equivalent, then they switch roles after 10 minutes. Emphasize that students should aim for immediate recall without calculation. Next, conduct a whole-class 'Binary Bingo' activity (15 minutes): Create a 4x4 grid on the board with random decimal numbers 0-15. Call out binary numbers (e.g., '1010') and students identify the decimal equivalent (10). Students mark correct answers on their personal bingo sheets. For the final 10 minutes, implement individual timed challenges: each student receives a worksheet with 16 binary-to-decimal and 16 decimal-to-binary problems. They have 2 minutes per section to complete as many as possible. Circulate during all activities to observe student recall speed and accuracy. Record students who struggle with specific number patterns for follow-up practice. Conclude with a brief whole-class recitation where students chorally state binary equivalents for numbers 0-15 in sequence.
materials_needed: 16 laminated flashcards per student pair (decimal 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents)
Binary Bingo sheets (4x4 grids with random decimal numbers 0-15)
Individual assessment worksheets with 32 conversion problems
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard markers for tracking class progress
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (13/16 correct) on the final timed worksheet for both binary-to-decimal and decimal-to-binary sections. Observe and record fluency during pair practice - students should demonstrate recall (not calculation) for at least 12/16 numbers. Award full credit for meeting both accuracy and fluency benchmarks, partial credit for meeting one criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide reference charts showing place values (8-4-2-1) and allow extra practice time with numbers 0-7 before progressing to 8-15. Create mnemonic devices for challenging numbers (e.g., 'lucky 7 = 0111'). For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to teach struggling peers using their own explanation strategies.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge: Exercise 2
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science fundamentals.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises within 3 seconds per conversion
instructions: **Setup Phase (5 minutes):** Distribute pre-made binary-decimal conversion charts showing numbers 0-15 in both decimal and 4-bit binary format (0000-1111). Have students sit in pairs. Provide each pair with a set of 32 flashcards: 16 showing decimal numbers (0-15) and 16 showing corresponding binary numbers (0000-1111). **Study Phase (10 minutes):** Students spend 5 minutes individually studying the conversion chart, then 5 minutes testing each other using the reference chart. Partner A shows a decimal card, Partner B states the binary equivalent, then they check the chart together. Switch roles every 2 minutes. **Drill Phase 1 (8 minutes):** Remove reference charts. Partner A holds decimal cards, shows one card for 3 seconds. Partner B must state the 4-bit binary equivalent from memory. Record correct answers on tracking sheet. Complete all 16 decimal numbers, then switch roles. Each partner attempts all 16 conversions. **Drill Phase 2 (8 minutes):** Repeat the process with binary-to-decimal conversions. Partner A shows binary cards (like '1010'), Partner B states decimal equivalent ('10'). Track results on the same sheet. **Challenge Round (4 minutes):** Combine both card sets. title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a provided real estate dataset to distinguish between correlational and causal relationships among variables like square footage, location, price, and amenities. They will create visual interpretations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of why correlation does not imply causation.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing specific variable relationships in a real estate dataset and identifying confounding variables
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots through guided analysis to explain why strong correlations may not indicate causal relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided real estate dataset (CSV file with 500 properties including variables: price, square_feet, bedrooms, bathrooms, age, distance_to_downtown, school_rating, crime_rate). Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to load the dataset in Excel/Google Sheets and create scatter plots for three assigned variable pairs: (price vs. square_feet), (price vs. school_rating), and (crime_rate vs. distance_to_downtown). Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the CORR function, students calculate correlation coefficients for each pair and record results on the provided worksheet. They must categorize each correlation as weak (-0.3 to 0.3), moderate (0.3 to 0.7), or strong (>0.7). Step 3 (25 minutes): Present students with three scenario cards describing potential causal claims: 'Larger homes cause higher prices,' 'Good schools cause low crime rates,' and 'Distance from downtown causes lower crime.' For each scenario, pairs must identify at least two confounding variables that could explain the correlation without causation (e.g., neighborhood wealth affecting both school quality and crime rates). Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair completes a structured comparison chart listing evidence supporting correlation vs. evidence needed to establish causation for one assigned scenario. Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present their findings to another pair, explaining why their assigned correlation does not prove causation and what additional data/methods would be needed to establish causal relationships.

Correlation analysis worksheet template (digital or printed)
Three scenario cards describing causal claims
Structured comparison chart template
Access to Excel, Google Sheets, or similar spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct correlation coefficient calculations and categorizations (25%), (2) Accurate identification of at least 2 relevant confounding variables per scenario (35%), (3) Clear written explanations distinguishing correlation from causation with specific examples from dataset (25%), (4) Appropriate suggestions for establishing causation through experimental design or additional data collection (15%). Students must score 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation coefficient interpretation guide and example confounding variable for first scenario. Pre-highlight key variables in dataset and offer sentence starters for explanations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate partial correlations controlling for identified confounding variables, or research Simpson's Paradox examples in the dataset by examining subgroups (e.g., properties by neighborhood).

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Resource Allocation
description: Students will apply calculus-based optimization techniques to solve a complex business scenario involving manufacturing constraints, profit maximization, and resource limitations. They will use partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint analysis to determine optimal production quantities for a multi-product manufacturing company.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to identify optimal solutions in multi-variable constrained optimization problems by solving a realistic manufacturing scenario
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to handle equality constraints through systematic mathematical modeling and computational verification
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the scenario packet describing AcmeTech Manufacturing, which produces smartphones and tablets with specific profit margins ($180 per smartphone, $220 per tablet), labor constraints (3.5 hours smartphone labor, 4.2 hours tablet labor, maximum 8,400 hours available), material costs ($45,000 budget limit with $85 smartphone materials, $105 tablet materials), and storage limitations (maximum 2,200 total units). Form groups of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Problem Modeling (15 minutes):** Students define variables (x = smartphones, y = tablets), write the objective function P(x,y) = 180x + 220y, and establish constraint equations: 3.5x + 4.2y ≤ 8,400 (labor), 85x + 105y ≤ 45,000 (materials), x + y ≤ 2,200 (storage), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negativity).

**Phase 2 - Unconstrained Analysis (20 minutes):** Students find partial derivatives ∂P/∂x = 180, ∂P/∂y = 220, noting the linear objective function has no critical points in the interior, requiring boundary analysis.

**Phase 3 - Constraint Implementation (25 minutes):** Using Lagrange multipliers, students solve the system: ∇P = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ + λ₃∇g₃ where g₁, g₂, g₃ represent active constraints. They systematically test corner points of the feasible region using substitution methods.

**Phase 4 - Solution Verification (10 minutes):** Students use graphing calculators or computer algebra systems to verify their analytical solutions, checking that their optimal point (approximately x = 353, y = 1,847) satisfies all constraints and produces maximum profit of approximately $470,000.

**Presentation (15 minutes):** Each group presents their solution methodology and final recommendation, explaining the economic interpretation of their Lagrange multipliers as shadow prices for each constraint.
materials_needed: AcmeTech Manufacturing scenario packets (one per group)
Graphing calculators or laptops with computer algebra software (Mathematica, Maple, or GeoGebra)
Graph paper and colored pencils for constraint visualization
Lagrange multiplier reference sheets with method summary
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct mathematical model setup (25 points), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier technique (30 points), (3) Accurate computational solution with constraint verification (25 points), (4) Clear interpretation of results including economic meaning of multipliers (20 points). Students submit written solutions showing all work plus brief presentation explaining their optimization strategy and business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint graphing templates and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier worksheets. Offer intermediate checkpoints after each phase. For advanced learners: Add inequality constraints requiring Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, introduce sensitivity analysis for parameter changes, or extend to three-product scenarios with additional complexity.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage
description: Students will analyze the architecture, failure cascade, and recovery strategies of the 2017 Amazon S3 US-East-1 outage by examining system logs, dependency graphs, and post-incident reports. They will decompose the complex distributed system failure into its constituent components and identify critical design weaknesses that amplified the initial human error.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by mapping service dependencies and identifying single points of failure in cloud infrastructure
Students will examine failure propagation patterns through detailed timeline reconstruction and root cause analysis of cascading system failures
instructions: Begin with 15-minute individual review of provided materials: AWS post-incident report, simplified S3 architecture diagram, and sample error logs. Form teams of 3-4 students for 90-minute analysis phase. Each team receives different colored sticky notes and large poster paper. Step 1 (25 minutes): Create a visual dependency map of S3 services, identifying upstream/downstream relationships. Use blue notes for core services, yellow for dependent AWS services, red for external services affected. Step 2 (30 minutes): Construct a detailed failure timeline using the provided log excerpts and incident report. Plot on horizontal axis with timestamps, vertical axis showing affected service layers. Use different colors to show failure propagation paths. Step 3 (35 minutes): Identify and categorize failure types: initial trigger (human error), primary failures (direct service impacts), secondary failures (cascade effects), and tertiary failures (external service impacts). Create a matrix showing failure type vs. recovery time. Teams then present 5-minute findings focusing on: most critical architectural weakness, fastest spreading failure type, and one specific design change to prevent recurrence. Conclude with 20-minute structured discussion comparing team findings and identifying common patterns across distributed system failures.
materials_needed: AWS S3 Post-Incident Report (February 28, 2017)
Simplified S3 architecture diagram with service dependencies
Curated log excerpts showing error messages and timestamps
Large poster paper (24x36 inches) per team
Colored sticky notes (4 colors per team)
Markers and pens
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 4-point rubric: (1) Dependency mapping accuracy and completeness (25 points), (2) Timeline precision and failure categorization (25 points), (3) Root cause analysis depth and technical accuracy (25 points), (4) Design recommendation feasibility and justification (25 points). Additional 10 points for presentation clarity and peer question responses. Minimum 70 points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students: Provide pre-labeled service categories and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer simplified dependency map template with major services already placed. Advanced learners: Include additional failure scenarios (Netflix Chaos Engineering examples) for comparison analysis, or challenge them to propose specific implementation details for their design recommendations using actual AWS services and configurations.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices: Ice Cream Sales Analysis Critique
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same ice cream sales dataset to determine which best communicates the business insights. They will justify their evaluation using established data visualization principles and recommend improvements.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, line graph, pie chart) by applying data visualization best practices criteria
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison of clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Ice Cream Sales Dataset (temperature, sales volume, flavor preferences over 12 months) and three pre-made visualizations: Visualization A (clustered bar chart), Visualization B (multi-line graph), and Visualization C (series of pie charts). Give students 5 minutes to examine all materials individually.

Form groups of 3-4 students. Provide each group with the Visualization Evaluation Rubric covering five criteria: data accuracy, visual clarity, appropriate chart type, design aesthetics, and business insight communication. Spend 10 minutes explaining each criterion with examples.

Groups spend 25 minutes systematically evaluating each visualization against all five criteria, scoring each on a 1-4 scale and writing specific justifications. They must identify at least two strengths and two weaknesses per visualization.

Next, groups spend 15 minutes ranking the three visualizations from best to worst, creating a one-page written recommendation memo explaining their choice for a ice cream shop owner audience. The memo must include specific improvement suggestions for their top-ranked visualization.

Conclude with 10-minute group presentations where each team presents their ranking and justification. Other groups can challenge decisions, requiring presenters to defend their evaluation using evidence from the rubric criteria.

Instructor facilitates discussion on common evaluation patterns and reinforces key principles of effective data visualization critique.
materials_needed: Ice Cream Sales Dataset (CSV file with 12 months of data)
Three pre-made visualizations (printed color copies)
Visualization Evaluation Rubric handout
Memo template worksheet
Laptops/tablets for digital memo creation
assessment_method: Grade completed evaluation rubrics (40%), written recommendation memo quality and justification strength (40%), and presentation defense of evaluation decisions (20%). Success criteria: Students score visualizations within 1 point of instructor expert ratings, provide specific evidence-based justifications, and demonstrate understanding of visualization principles in recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation justifications and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. Highlight specific rubric examples during explanation phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest alternative visualization types not provided and create quick sketches of improved designs. Have them lead peer discussions during presentations.

title: Design Your Dream Playground: Area and Perimeter Optimization Challenge
description: Students will design an original playground layout using geometric shapes while working within budget and space constraints. They must calculate areas, perimeters, and costs to create a feasible design that maximizes play value within given parameters.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original playground layout by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, circles, and triangles to optimize space usage
Students will construct mathematical models through cost-benefit analysis using real-world constraints and geometric calculations
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute grid paper, calculators, and constraint sheets. Post the playground equipment cost chart on the board showing: rectangular sandbox ($8/sq ft), circular merry-go-round ($12/sq ft), triangular climbing structure ($15/sq ft), and rectangular basketball court ($6/sq ft). Each student receives a constraint sheet specifying: total budget of $2,400, maximum perimeter of 200 feet for the entire playground, and minimum area requirements (sandbox: 64 sq ft, merry-go-round: 50 sq ft).

**Design Phase (25 minutes):** Students sketch their playground layout on grid paper (1 square = 2 feet). They must include all four equipment types and can add multiple units if budget allows. Students calculate the area and perimeter of each shape, showing all work with proper formulas. They create a budget table listing each piece of equipment with dimensions, area calculations, and costs.

**Optimization Round (15 minutes):** Students review their initial design and modify it to either maximize total play area or minimize cost while meeting all constraints. They must justify their optimization strategy in writing and recalculate all measurements.

**Presentation Preparation (10 minutes):** Students prepare a 2-minute presentation including their final design sketch, total cost breakdown, total perimeter calculation, and their optimization reasoning. They must explain how they used geometric formulas to solve real-world constraints.

**Gallery Walk and Presentations (15 minutes):** Students post designs around the room and present to small groups of 3-4 peers, receiving feedback on mathematical accuracy and design creativity.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1/4 inch squares)
Scientific calculators
Constraint specification sheets (pre-printed)
Rulers and colored pencils
Playground equipment cost chart (posted reference)
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Mathematical accuracy (40 points) - correct area/perimeter formulas and calculations; Design feasibility (30 points) - meets all constraints and budget requirements; Optimization reasoning (20 points) - clear justification for design choices; Presentation clarity (10 points) - effective communication of mathematical thinking. Students must show all calculations and submit both initial and optimized designs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide area/perimeter formula reference cards and pre-drawn shape templates. Start with simpler rectangular shapes only. For advanced learners: Add irregular polygon shapes, introduce efficiency ratios (play area per dollar), or require multiple design alternatives with comparative analysis. Consider adding landscape features with curved boundaries.

title: Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Recall Challenge
description: Students will create and use a structured memory palace technique to memorize and instantly recall 50 specific time and space complexities for advanced algorithms and data structures. This activity focuses on building rapid, accurate recall of Big O notations for complex computational scenarios that are essential for technical interviews and system design.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize and recall the exact time and space complexity notations for 50 advanced algorithms including graph algorithms, dynamic programming solutions, and advanced tree operations

Students will identify and recite the specific complexity characteristics of advanced data structures including B-trees, skip lists, Fibonacci heaps, and suffix arrays through systematic memorization techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the curated list of 50 algorithm/data structure complexity pairs, organized into 5 categories of 10 items each: Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, Tarjan's, etc.), Advanced Tree Operations (AVL rotations, Red-Black insertions, B-tree operations), Dynamic Programming Solutions (Knapsack variants, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain), Sorting/Searching Variants (Radix sort, Interpolation search), and Advanced Data Structures (Skip list operations, Fibonacci heap operations). Students have 15 minutes to study the list, noting patterns and groupings. Next, introduce the memory palace technique: students must mentally map each category to a specific room in a familiar building (home, school, etc.) and assign each algorithm/complexity pair to a specific object or location within that room, creating vivid mental associations. Spend 25 minutes having students build their palaces, walking through each room mentally and rehearsing the associations. Conduct the first recall test: call out random algorithm names, students must write down the exact time and space complexity within 10 seconds per item. Record scores and identify weak areas. Provide 10 minutes for palace reinforcement, focusing on missed items. Repeat the testing process twice more with different random orderings of the same 50 items. Between tests, allow 5-minute palace maintenance sessions where students mentally walk through their weakest rooms. Conclude with a rapid-fire oral round where students must respond verbally within 5 seconds to demonstrate fluency.
materials_needed: Printed reference sheet with 50 algorithm/data structure complexity pairs organized by category
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-50
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard for tracking class performance statistics
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (45/50 correct) on the final written test with proper Big O notation formatting. Oral responses must be delivered within the 5-second time limit with correct pronunciation of complexity terms. Track improvement across the three testing rounds - students must show measurable progress between first and final attempts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce the initial set to 30 items focusing on more common algorithms, and allow 15 seconds per recall item instead of 10. Provide memory association examples and help them choose more familiar buildings for their palaces. For advanced learners, add 25 additional items including amortized analysis complexities, worst-case vs. average-case distinctions, and require them to also memorize the specific conditions that trigger worst-case scenarios for each algorithm.

title: Interpreting Statistical Power Analysis Results for A/B Testing in E-commerce
description: Students will analyze pre-computed statistical power analysis results from three different A/B testing scenarios in e-commerce contexts. They will interpret power curves, effect sizes, and sample size requirements to make strategic recommendations about test design and resource allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical power analysis outputs by explaining the relationship between effect size, sample size, and detection probability in A/B testing contexts
Students will distinguish between Type I and Type II error implications through analysis of power calculation scenarios with varying business constraints
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-prepared datasets containing power analysis results for: (1) email click-through rate optimization (baseline 2.3%, minimum detectable effect 0.3%), (2) checkout conversion rate improvement (baseline 12.1%, minimum detectable effect 1.5%), and (3) average order value increase (baseline $47.82, minimum detectable effect $3.50). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Students examine power curves showing statistical power (y-axis) versus sample size per variant (x-axis) for each scenario, identifying the sample sizes needed to achieve 80%, 85%, and 90% power. Next 25 minutes: Students analyze effect size sensitivity tables showing how minimum detectable effects change with fixed sample sizes of 1,000, 5,000, and 10,000 per variant. They calculate the percentage change these effects represent relative to baseline metrics. Following 25 minutes: Students review cost-benefit matrices showing estimated testing costs ($2.50 per participant for email tests, $8.00 for checkout tests, $12.00 for order value tests) against potential revenue impacts of detecting true effects. Next 15 minutes: Students synthesize findings to recommend optimal sample sizes and testing durations for each scenario, considering statistical rigor versus business practicality. Final 5 minutes: Pairs present one key insight about power-sample size trade-offs to the class.
materials_needed: Three pre-computed power analysis datasets (Excel or CSV format)
Power curve visualization graphs for each scenario
Cost-benefit analysis templates
Statistical power reference tables (α=0.05, β=0.20)
Access to spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets, or R/Python)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate interpretation of power curves and sample size requirements (25%), (2) Correct explanation of effect size implications and business relevance (25%), (3) Justified recommendations balancing statistical rigor with practical constraints (25%), (4) Clear articulation of Type I/II error trade-offs in business context (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided interpretation worksheets with specific questions about each power curve section and offer one-on-one clarification of statistical power concepts. For advanced learners, include additional scenarios with unequal sample sizes between variants, sequential testing considerations, or multiple comparison corrections. Consider providing business context about typical effect sizes in different industries.

title: Grocery Store Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real Shopping Scenarios
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to solve realistic grocery shopping problems involving discounts, sales tax, and budget constraints. They will use real grocery store flyers and calculators to determine the best purchasing decisions within a given budget while calculating total costs including tax and savings from discounts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discount amounts, sales tax, and final costs by working through authentic grocery shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate percentage skills through comparing prices, calculating savings, and making budget-conscious purchasing decisions using real-world data
instructions:
Begin by distributing grocery store flyers and the Budget Challenge worksheet to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student has a $50 budget to purchase items for a family dinner for 4 people, including appetizer, main course, side dishes, and dessert. Students must select at least 8 items total.

In the first phase (15 minutes), students browse the flyers and select potential items, writing down original prices. They should identify items with percentage discounts (e.g., '20% off', '15% savings', 'Buy 2 Get 1 50% off').

During phase two (20 minutes), students calculate the discounted price for each sale item using the formula: Discounted Price = Original Price - (Original Price × Discount Percentage). They must show all work on their worksheet, including converting percentages to decimals.

In phase three (15 minutes), students calculate the subtotal of their selected items, then apply 8.5% sales tax using the formula: Tax Amount = Subtotal × 0.085. They determine the final total and verify it stays within the $50 budget.

For the final phase (10 minutes), students complete a reflection section calculating their total savings from discounts and determining what percentage of their budget they used. They must write one sentence explaining their best purchase decision and why.

Circulate throughout to check calculations and provide guidance on percentage conversion. Remind students to round monetary amounts to the nearest cent.
materials_needed: Current grocery store flyers or advertisements (1 per student)
Budget Challenge worksheet with calculation spaces and reflection questions
Basic calculators (1 per student)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, stays within budget, complete reflection; (3) Minor calculation errors, within budget, adequate reflection; (2) Some calculation errors, budget issues addressed, basic reflection; (1) Multiple errors, incomplete work. Check specifically for correct percentage-to-decimal conversion, proper discount calculations, accurate tax computation, and realistic item selections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage conversion chart (10% = 0.10, 20% = 0.20, etc.) and work through the first discount calculation together. Highlight sale items in the flyer beforehand. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including unit price comparisons, coupon stacking scenarios, or calculating the percentage saved on their total purchase compared to buying everything at full price. Allow them to create shopping lists for different family sizes.

title: Analyzing Database Query Performance: Execution Plan Investigation
description: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans to identify performance bottlenecks and compare the efficiency of different query approaches. They will examine index usage, join operations, and resource consumption patterns to determine optimization strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by examining join algorithms, index scans, and cost estimates to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will compare multiple query implementations through systematic evaluation of execution statistics and resource utilization patterns
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a sample e-commerce database containing tables: customers (50,000 records), orders (200,000 records), and products (10,000 records). Each student receives three functionally equivalent SQL queries that retrieve customer order history with product details using different approaches: nested loops, hash joins, and indexed lookups.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (25 minutes):** Students execute each query while capturing execution plans using EXPLAIN ANALYZE or equivalent database tools. They document: execution time, rows examined vs. returned, index usage, join algorithms employed, and memory consumption. Students create a comparison matrix showing these metrics for all three queries.

**Phase 2 - Deep Dive Investigation (20 minutes):** Students select the worst-performing query and systematically analyze its execution plan tree. They identify each operation node, trace data flow from leaf to root, and calculate the cost contribution of each step. Students annotate the execution plan diagram, highlighting expensive operations and documenting why certain algorithms were chosen by the query optimizer.

**Phase 3 - Comparative Analysis (15 minutes):** Working in pairs, students present their findings to each other, explaining which query performed best and why. They must justify their conclusions using specific metrics from execution plans, not just execution times. Pairs collaborate to identify patterns: when do hash joins outperform nested loops? How does index selectivity affect query plans?

**Synthesis (10 minutes):** Each pair writes a brief optimization report recommending the best query approach and suggesting two specific database modifications (indexes, table restructuring) that would improve performance further. Reports must reference specific execution plan elements as evidence.
materials_needed: Sample e-commerce database with populated tables (customers, orders, products)
Database management system with query execution analysis tools (PostgreSQL with EXPLAIN ANALYZE or MySQL with EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON)
Three pre-written SQL queries performing identical operations using different approaches
Execution plan comparison worksheet template
Access to database query interface (command line or GUI tool)
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25%) - correctly identifies join types, index usage, and operation costs; (2) Quality of comparative analysis (35%) - systematically compares queries using appropriate metrics and draws valid conclusions; (3) Depth of bottleneck identification (25%) - pinpoints specific expensive operations and explains their impact; (4) Optimization recommendations (15%) - suggests realistic improvements supported by execution plan evidence. Students submit annotated execution plans, comparison matrix, and optimization report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan reading guides with common operation symbols explained, offer simplified queries with fewer joins initially, and pair with stronger students during Phase 3. For advanced learners: Challenge them to modify queries and predict execution plan changes, investigate query hint effects on optimizer decisions, or analyze how data distribution affects join algorithm selection. Consider providing additional tables with different indexing strategies for extended analysis.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow
description: Students will create an original mathematical model combining differential equations, graph theory, and optimization techniques to solve real-world urban traffic congestion problems. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then present their solution to address a specific city's traffic challenges.
estimated_duration: 8 class periods over 2-3 weeks (approximately 14-16 hours total)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory by constructing an original mathematical model for traffic flow optimization
Students will design a comprehensive solution framework through integration of theoretical analysis, computational methods, and real-world data interpretation
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with real traffic data from three different city intersections (provide 48-hour traffic count data, peak hour patterns, and accident frequency reports). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team selects one intersection scenario. 

Phase 1 (Day 1-2, 180 minutes): Teams research existing traffic flow models (assign readings on fundamental diagrams, queuing theory, and network flow models). Students must identify limitations in current approaches and formulate their improvement hypothesis. Teams create a mathematical framework document outlining their chosen variables, constraints, and objective function.

Phase 2 (Day 3-5, 300 minutes): Students develop their mathematical model by: (1) Writing differential equations governing traffic density and flow rates, (2) Constructing weighted directed graphs representing intersection topology, (3) Formulating optimization constraints including safety buffer times, pedestrian crossing requirements, and emergency vehicle priority protocols, (4) Creating algorithms for signal timing optimization.

Phase 3 (Day 6-7, 240 minutes): Teams implement their model computationally using provided programming environment. They must code their algorithms, run simulations with provided traffic data, and generate comparative analysis showing improvement metrics versus baseline scenarios.

Phase 4 (Day 8, 120 minutes): Each team presents 15-minute solutions to a panel including instructor and two guest evaluators (ideally traffic engineers or city planners). Presentations must include: mathematical model derivation, computational results, sensitivity analysis, implementation feasibility assessment, and cost-benefit projections. Conclude with peer evaluation session where teams provide constructive feedback on alternative approaches.
materials_needed: Real traffic count datasets from 3 urban intersections (48-hour data files)
Access to mathematical software (MATLAB, Mathematica, or Python with NumPy/SciPy)
Graph theory visualization tools (NetworkX or similar)
Large format paper and markers for model diagramming
Digital presentation capabilities with projection system
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and originality (25 points), Integration of multiple mathematical domains (20 points), Computational implementation accuracy (20 points), Real-world applicability and feasibility analysis (20 points), Presentation clarity and peer engagement (15 points). Success requires minimum 80 points with no category below 15 points. Students must demonstrate novel synthesis beyond textbook examples and show measurable improvement over baseline traffic scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for basic traffic flow equations and offer guided tutorials on graph theory applications. Create checkpoint meetings after each phase for progress review. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements for unpredictable events, multi-objective optimization for environmental factors, or machine learning integration for adaptive signal control. Encourage exploration of game theory for multi-intersection coordination.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an original mathematical model using calculus, graph theory, and optimization techniques to solve a real-world traffic congestion problem. They will design their own intersection layout, develop corresponding equations, and present a comprehensive solution with visual simulations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory by constructing an original mathematical model for traffic optimization
Students will design and validate a comprehensive solution through mathematical proof, computational simulation, and visual presentation
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a fictional city district experiencing traffic congestion (provide map with 4-6 intersections). Students work in teams of 3-4 over three phases. Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the traffic pattern data provided, identify key variables (flow rates, signal timing, pedestrian crossings), and select their mathematical approach (options include queuing theory, network flow optimization, or differential equation modeling). Each team must justify their chosen method and define at least 8 variables with units. Phase 2 (120 minutes): Teams construct their mathematical model by writing the governing equations, establishing constraints, and determining optimization criteria. They must create at least 3 differential equations or 5 linear constraints, depending on their approach. Teams also design a modified intersection layout as their proposed solution. Phase 3 (90 minutes): Using graphing software or programming tools, teams simulate their model with the original data and their proposed changes. They create visualizations showing traffic flow improvements and prepare a 15-minute presentation including: problem analysis, mathematical model derivation, solution methodology, simulation results, and real-world implementation considerations. Conclude with team presentations where other students ask technical questions and evaluate feasibility.
materials_needed: Traffic flow dataset with hourly counts for each intersection
City district map with current signal timing data
Graphing calculators or computer access
MATLAB, Python, or Desmos graphing software
Large poster paper and markers for model visualization
Presentation timer and evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness (30 points) - equations must be dimensionally consistent and logically derived; Creative problem-solving approach (25 points) - novel methods or innovative intersection designs; Simulation accuracy and interpretation (20 points) - results must align with mathematical predictions; Presentation clarity and technical communication (15 points); Peer evaluation of feasibility and questioning responses (10 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by explaining their mathematical reasoning and defending their optimization choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide equation templates and guide variable identification through structured worksheets. Offer simplified scenarios with 2-3 intersections only. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, consider multi-objective optimization (emissions + flow), or create dynamic models with time-varying parameters. Provide access to real traffic engineering standards and encourage consultation with actual traffic data from local municipality.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban traffic congestion problems. They will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear programming, graph theory, and statistical analysis to develop a comprehensive solution with implementation recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original multi-variable optimization model by integrating calculus-based functions, linear programming constraints, and graph theory applications to address urban traffic flow efficiency

Students will synthesize statistical data analysis, mathematical modeling techniques, and computational algorithms through designing a complete traffic management system with quantifiable performance metrics
instructions: Begin by providing student teams (3-4 members) with authentic traffic data from a real city intersection or corridor, including hourly vehicle counts, accident statistics, and current signal timing data (15 minutes setup). Students first spend 45 minutes analyzing the dataset to identify key variables, constraints, and optimization opportunities. Next, teams dedicate 90 minutes to constructing their mathematical model, which must include: (1) objective function using calculus to minimize travel time or maximize throughput, (2) at least 5 realistic constraints expressed as linear inequalities, (3) graph theory representation of the traffic network, and (4) statistical probability functions for predicting peak hours and accident likelihood. During the 60-minute development phase, students create their optimization algorithms, test multiple scenarios, and calculate expected improvements over current conditions. Teams then spend 45 minutes preparing a comprehensive presentation that includes their mathematical model, computational results, sensitivity analysis, and practical implementation recommendations. Each presentation (15 minutes per team) must demonstrate the model using specific numerical examples, show graphical representations of their solutions, and defend their mathematical choices. Conclude with a 30-minute peer evaluation session where teams critique each other's models using provided mathematical criteria and suggest improvements.
materials_needed: Real urban traffic datasets (vehicle counts, signal timing, accident data)
Graphing calculators or computer access with Excel/Python/MATLAB
Large poster paper and markers for model visualization
Mathematical optimization reference sheets
Presentation equipment (projector, screen)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy and complexity (30 points), Creative integration of multiple mathematical concepts (25 points), Practical feasibility of solution (20 points), Quality of presentation and defense (15 points), Peer evaluation scores (10 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving at least 80% accuracy in mathematical calculations and presenting a model that shows measurable improvement over baseline conditions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template frameworks for objective functions and constraint formation, offering mini-tutorials on optimization software, and pairing them with stronger mathematical partners. Extend advanced learners by challenging them to incorporate dynamic programming elements, consider multi-objective optimization (time vs. environmental impact), or develop mobile apps that implement their algorithms.
