title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical model using calculus, linear programming, and graph theory to optimize traffic flow in a simulated urban intersection. They will validate their model through computational analysis and present actionable recommendations for traffic management.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize calculus optimization techniques, linear programming, and graph theory to construct a novel mathematical model addressing real-world traffic flow challenges
Students will design and implement computational algorithms to validate their traffic optimization model through iterative testing and refinement
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Provide each team with the urban intersection dataset containing traffic count data, signal timing patterns, and peak hour statistics for a 4-way intersection over 30 days. Teams must first analyze the data to identify patterns and constraints (45 minutes). Next, students design their mathematical model by selecting appropriate optimization variables (traffic light duration, pedestrian crossing times, turn lane priorities), defining objective functions (minimize average wait time, maximize throughput), and establishing constraints (safety regulations, minimum crossing times, maximum queue lengths). This model construction phase requires 90 minutes with instructor check-ins every 30 minutes. Students then implement their model using Python or MATLAB, creating algorithms to process the traffic data and generate optimal timing solutions (75 minutes). Teams must test at least three different traffic scenarios: morning rush hour, evening rush hour, and weekend patterns. During the validation phase (45 minutes), students run simulations comparing their optimized model against the current traffic system, documenting improvements in average wait times, queue lengths, and overall intersection efficiency. Finally, teams prepare a 15-minute presentation including their mathematical formulation, computational implementation, validation results, and specific recommendations for traffic engineers. Each presentation should include visual models, performance graphs, and cost-benefit analysis of implementing their solution.
materials_needed: Urban intersection traffic dataset (CSV files with 30 days of traffic data)
Computers with Python/MATLAB and optimization libraries (scipy.optimize, PuLP)
Graph paper and colored pens for model sketching
Digital presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Traffic engineering constraint reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model sophistication and accuracy (25 points), computational implementation and code quality (25 points), validation methodology and results interpretation (25 points), presentation clarity and practical recommendations (25 points). Students must demonstrate measurable improvement over baseline traffic patterns and show mathematical rigor in their optimization approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-defined objective function templates and guide them toward simpler two-variable optimization problems. Offer coding scaffolds with partially completed algorithms. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or machine learning prediction components. Provide additional datasets from multiple intersections for network-wide optimization.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze correlation matrices and heatmaps from a customer churn dataset to identify relationships between variables and explain how these patterns inform feature selection decisions. This activity focuses on understanding correlation patterns rather than calculating them, developing critical interpretation skills for data exploration.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients in heatmaps by identifying strong, moderate, and weak relationships between customer behavior variables
Students will explain the implications of multicollinearity through systematic analysis of feature correlation patterns in business context
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-generated correlation heatmap showing 12 customer features (monthly_charges, tenure, total_charges, contract_length, tech_support_calls, internet_service_type, etc.) with correlation coefficients displayed. Students work in pairs for 25 minutes. First, have students spend 10 minutes creating a three-column table: 'Strong Correlations (|r| > 0.7)', 'Moderate Correlations (0.3 < |r| < 0.7)', and 'Weak Correlations (|r| < 0.3)'. They should list variable pairs and exact correlation values in each category. Next, students spend 10 minutes writing explanations for why three specific strong correlations make business sense (e.g., tenure vs. total_charges correlation of 0.83). title: Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex multi-constraint manufacturing optimization problem. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal production quantities that maximize profit while meeting real-world limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a complex manufacturing scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will execute both graphical and simplex methods to solve optimization problems and interpret results within the business context
instructions:
Begin by presenting the manufacturing scenario: ABC Electronics produces two products (smartphones and tablets) with limited resources. Provide specific data: smartphones yield $150 profit each, tablets $200 each; assembly line capacity is 480 hours/week; smartphones require 3 hours assembly, tablets require 4 hours; quality control has 240 hours/week capacity; smartphones need 2 QC hours, tablets need 3 QC hours; material budget is $50,000/week with smartphones costing $120 materials, tablets $180; minimum production requirements are 40 smartphones and 30 tablets weekly. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students work in pairs to define variables (x = smartphones, y = tablets) and formulate the mathematical model. They must write the objective function (maximize Z = 150x + 200y) and all constraints including assembly time (3x + 4y ≤ 480), quality control (2x + 3y ≤ 240), material budget (120x + 180y ≤ 50,000), and minimum production (x ≥ 40, y ≥ 30).

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using graph paper, students plot constraint lines and identify the feasible region. They must clearly mark intersection points and shade the feasible area.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Students calculate corner points algebraically by solving systems of equations at constraint intersections. They evaluate the objective function at each corner point to determine the optimal solution.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Using provided simplex tableau templates, students verify their graphical solution through the simplex method, completing at least two iterations.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Students interpret results in business terms, calculating maximum weekly profit, optimal production quantities, and identifying binding constraints. They must also perform sensitivity analysis by determining shadow prices for each constraint.
materials_needed: Graph paper with 1mm grid spacing
Scientific calculators
Pre-designed simplex tableau templates
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint graphing
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets access for verification
assessment_method: Students submit a complete solution packet including: (1) Correctly formulated mathematical model (20 points), (2) Accurate graphical representation with properly identified feasible region (25 points), (3) Correct calculation of all corner points and optimal solution (30 points), (4) Complete simplex tableau showing all iterations (20 points), (5) Business interpretation with sensitivity analysis (25 points). Total: 120 points. Partial credit awarded for methodology even with computational errors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint inequality templates and pre-plotted axes with scale markings. Offer checkpoint verification after each step. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints requiring whole unit production, or introduce a third product with additional constraints. Provide access to optimization software (like Solver in Excel) to verify manual calculations and explore 'what-if' scenarios.

Constraints include: tablets require 2 labor hours, $180 materials, laptops need 4 hours, $400 materials, smartphones need 1.5 hours, $250 materials. Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to define variables (x₁=tablets, x₂=laptops, x₃=smartphones) and write the objective function P = 150x₁ + 300x₂ + 200x₃. Step 2 (20 min): Formulate constraint inequalities from the given data: 2x₁ + 4x₂ + 1.5x₃ ≤ 480 (labor), 180x₁ + 400x₂ + 250x₃ ≤ 50,000 (materials), x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≤ 200 (assembly), plus non-negativity constraints. Step 3 (25 min): Using graphing software or manual calculation, students identify the feasible region and corner points. Step 4 (20 min): Apply the corner point method, evaluating the objective function at each vertex to find the maximum profit point. Step 5 (15 min): Interpret results in business context, calculating total profit and resource utilization. Students must show complete mathematical work and provide a written business recommendation with justification.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario handout with specific numerical constraints
Graphing calculators or computer access with linear programming software (Excel Solver or GeoGebra)
Graph paper and rulers for manual plotting
Linear programming reference sheet with simplex method steps
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate identification of feasible region and corner points (30%), (3) Proper application of optimization method with clear mathematical work (30%), (4) Business interpretation and recommendation quality (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and guided practice with two-variable problems first. Offer step-by-step worksheets breaking down the simplex method. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how results change with 10% variations in constraints, or add integer programming requirements for realistic production quantities.
original_title: Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming

title: Reverse Engineering and Analyzing Malware Static Analysis Patterns in Compiled Binaries
description: Students will perform static analysis on provided compiled malware samples to identify behavioral patterns, attack vectors, and code structures. They will decompose the binary files using disassemblers and hex editors to analyze assembly code, identify suspicious function calls, and categorize malware families based on their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze malware binary structures by examining assembly code, PE headers, and string artifacts to identify malicious behaviors and attack methodologies
Students will differentiate between malware families through systematic comparison of static analysis findings including API calls, code patterns, and embedded resources
instructions: Begin by distributing three different malware samples (safely contained in VMs) to teams of 2-3 students. Students must work in isolated virtual environments with internet disabled. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each team uses IDA Pro or Ghidra to load their assigned binary and generate initial disassembly. Students document PE header information, entry points, imported libraries, and exported functions in provided analysis worksheets. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams examine the disassembled code to identify key functions, focusing on system calls, network operations, file I/O, and registry modifications. Students create flowcharts mapping program execution paths and highlight suspicious API sequences. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Using hex editors, students search for embedded strings, URLs, IP addresses, and file signatures that indicate malware capabilities. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams compare their findings with the other two malware samples, creating comparison matrices that categorize similarities and differences in code structure, behavioral patterns, and potential attack vectors. Students must identify which samples belong to the same malware family and justify their conclusions. Final phase (30 minutes): Each team presents their analysis findings, explaining their methodology and defending their malware family classifications to the class.
materials_needed: Three distinct malware samples (trojans, ransomware, spyware) in isolated VM environments
IDA Pro or Ghidra disassembler software
HxD or similar hex editor applications
Structured analysis worksheets with sections for PE analysis, API mapping, and comparison matrices
Isolated virtual machines with Windows/Linux environments
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Accurate PE header analysis (20 points), identification of malicious API calls and functions (25 points), quality of execution flow documentation (20 points), correct malware family classification with supporting evidence (25 points), and clarity of final presentation defending conclusions (10 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of static analysis techniques and provide concrete evidence for all classifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted sections of assembly code and guided questions about specific API calls. Offer reference sheets with common malicious APIs and their purposes. For advanced learners, introduce dynamic analysis correlation challenges where they must predict runtime behaviors based on static findings, or provide packed/obfuscated samples requiring unpacking techniques before analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness: A Comparative Analysis of Sales Dashboard Designs
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different dashboard designs showing the same sales dataset, evaluating their effectiveness in communicating key insights. Students will use established visualization principles to judge which dashboard best serves its intended audience and purpose.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization approaches by applying established design principles (clarity, accuracy, efficiency) to assess dashboard quality
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison of how well each dashboard communicates key business insights to its target audience
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with three printed dashboard mockups (Dashboard A: cluttered bar charts with 3D effects, Dashboard B: clean line graphs with consistent colors, Dashboard C: mixed chart types with poor color choices) showing identical Q4 sales data for a fictional company. Include a one-page scenario describing the audience (executive team) and key decisions needed (budget allocation for next quarter).

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students complete an evaluation matrix, rating each dashboard (1-5 scale) on: visual clarity, data accuracy representation, ease of finding key insights, appropriate chart type selection, and color/design effectiveness. They must provide written justification for each rating.

**Peer Comparison (10 minutes):** Students pair up to discuss their ratings and justifications, identifying areas of agreement and disagreement. Each pair must reach consensus on which dashboard is most effective overall.

**Class Discussion (15 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion where pairs share their conclusions. Create a class tally of dashboard preferences on the board. Ask students to defend their choices using specific visualization principles.

**Final Reflection (10 minutes):** Students individually write a 150-word recommendation memo to the fictional company, specifying which dashboard to implement and listing three specific improvements for the chosen dashboard. They must reference at least two data visualization principles learned in previous lessons.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Collect evaluation matrices and recommendation memos. Briefly review key evaluation criteria that emerged from discussion.
materials_needed: Three printed dashboard mockups (one page each) showing identical sales data
Business scenario handout describing context and audience
Evaluation matrix template with 5-point rating scales
Blank paper for recommendation memos
Whiteboard/flipchart for class tally
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Evaluation matrix completeness and justification quality (40%), peer discussion participation observation (20%), final recommendation memo clarity and use of visualization principles (40%). Success criteria: Students provide specific evidence-based justifications for ratings, demonstrate understanding of audience needs, and reference appropriate design principles in their recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of specific questions to ask about each dashboard (Can you find the highest sales month in under 10 seconds? Are the colors distinguishable?). For advanced learners: Ask them to sketch one additional improvement for each dashboard or consider how the evaluation might change for different audiences (sales team vs. executives).

title: Design Your Dream City: Quadratic Functions in Urban Planning
description: Students will design a city layout by creating quadratic function models for parabolic structures like bridges and water fountains. They will develop original mathematical models, justify their design choices, and present their city plans with supporting quadratic equations and graphs.
learning_objectives: Students will construct original quadratic functions by designing parabolic architectural elements and determining appropriate coefficients based on real-world constraints
Students will synthesize mathematical modeling skills through creating a comprehensive city plan that integrates multiple quadratic functions with written justifications
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and explaining they are urban planners tasked with designing a city district (30 minutes total setup). Distribute city planning templates showing a 20x20 coordinate grid representing a 2km x 2km area. Each team must include exactly 3 parabolic structures: one suspension bridge, one decorative fountain, and one architectural arch. 

For each structure, students must: 1) Determine the vertex location based on practical considerations (bridge height for ship clearance, fountain spray pattern, arch doorway dimensions), 2) Write the quadratic function in vertex form, 3) Convert to standard form, 4) Graph the parabola on their city grid, and 5) Explain why their chosen parameters make sense for the structure's purpose.

Provide specific constraints: bridges must span at least 200m with minimum 40m clearance, fountains must have maximum heights between 5-15m, and arches must be 3-8m tall. Students spend 45 minutes on mathematical calculations and graphing, then 30 minutes preparing a presentation poster showing their city map, all three functions, and written justifications for their design choices.

Circulate during work time to ensure students are correctly applying vertex form f(x) = a(x-h)² + k and can explain how 'a' affects the parabola's width and direction. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where each group explains one structure's mathematical model and design rationale. Other teams provide feedback using peer evaluation forms focusing on mathematical accuracy and real-world feasibility of the quadratic models.
materials_needed: 20x20 coordinate grid templates (1 per team)
Colored pencils or markers
Graphing calculators or Desmos access
Large poster paper for presentations
Peer evaluation rubrics
Reference sheet with parabola formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: Mathematical Accuracy (correct quadratic functions and graphs, 25%), Real-world Application (appropriate parameter choices with clear justifications, 25%), Creativity and Design (innovative city layout meeting all constraints, 25%), and Communication (clear presentation and written explanations, 25%). Students must earn at least 3/4 points in Mathematical Accuracy to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vertex form templates with partially completed examples and offer one-on-one guidance during parameter selection. Create reference cards showing how 'a', 'h', and 'k' values affect parabola shape and position. For advanced learners: Challenge them to add a fourth parabolic structure, incorporate piecewise functions for complex designs, or calculate actual construction costs based on their mathematical models. Encourage use of transformation compositions for more sophisticated designs.

title: Personal Budget Creation Using Percentage Calculations
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional young adult using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage formulas to determine exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, savings, and discretionary spending based on given income scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate specific dollar amounts from percentages by applying the percentage formula (part = whole × percent) to allocate a monthly income across budget categories
Students will solve real-world percentage problems through creating and justifying a complete personal budget using recommended financial guidelines
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Budget Challenge' worksheet and scenario cards (10 minutes setup). Each student receives a different monthly income scenario ($2,400, $2,800, $3,200, or $3,600). Display the recommended budget percentages on the board: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 12%, Savings 10%, Insurance 8%, Personal/Entertainment 15%, Miscellaneous 10%. Students work individually for 25 minutes to calculate exact dollar amounts for each category using their assigned income. They must show all calculations using the formula: Dollar Amount = Monthly Income × (Percentage ÷ 100). For example, if income is $2,400 and housing is 30%, then Housing = $2,400 × 0.30 = $720. After calculations, students must verify their work by adding all categories to ensure they equal 100% of income. Next, students spend 15 minutes researching actual costs in your local area using provided tablets/computers to check if their calculated amounts are realistic for rent, groceries, and car payments. They adjust percentages if needed while maintaining the total at 100%. In the final 10 minutes, students pair up with someone who had a different income level to compare budgets and discuss how percentage allocations change the actual dollar amounts available for each category. They complete a reflection question: 'How does earning $400 more per month change your lifestyle options?'
materials_needed: Young Adult Budget Challenge worksheets (one per student with different income scenarios)
Calculators or smartphones with calculator apps
Tablets or computers with internet access for price research
Local housing/grocery cost reference sheets
Whiteboard markers and projection screen
assessment_method: Grade completed budget worksheets using a 20-point rubric: Correct percentage to dollar calculations (8 points), All categories sum to 100% of income (4 points), Realistic adjustments based on local research (4 points), Clear mathematical work shown (2 points), Thoughtful reflection response (2 points). Students must achieve 16/20 points to demonstrate proficiency in applying percentage calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example budget with the first two calculations done, offer percentage-to-decimal conversion charts, and allow calculator use throughout. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including tax calculations (reduce gross income by 22%), require comparison of budgets across three different cities, or have them create budgets for different life stages (single, married, with children).

title: Personal Budget Creation Using Percentage Calculations: Comparative Study
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional character using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage formulas to determine exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and savings based on recommended financial guidelines.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate specific dollar amounts from percentages by applying the percentage formula (P = W × R) to allocate a monthly income across budget categories
Students will solve multi-step percentage problems through creating a balanced personal budget that totals 100% of available income
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Character Profile Cards' - each student receives a card with a fictional person's monthly after-tax income (ranging from $2,400 to $4,800). Display the '50-30-20 Budget Rule' poster showing: 50% needs (housing, utilities, groceries), 30% wants (entertainment, dining out), 20% savings and debt payment. 

Step 1 (8 minutes): Students calculate their character's budget allocations using the percentage formula. They must show work: multiply income by 0.50 for needs, 0.30 for wants, and 0.20 for savings. 

Step 2 (12 minutes): Within each major category, students apply additional percentages. For the 'needs' amount, they allocate: 60% housing, 25% groceries, 15% utilities/phone. For 'wants': 40% entertainment, 35% dining out, 25% hobbies. Students calculate exact dollar amounts for each subcategory.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Using the provided 'Budget Worksheet,' students create a complete monthly budget showing all calculations. They must verify their total equals 100% of income by adding all dollar amounts.

Step 4 (5 minutes): Students swap worksheets with a partner to check calculations using calculators. Partners verify that percentages were applied correctly and totals match the original income amount.

Circulate during work time to check calculation methods and provide individual support. Remind students to round to the nearest cent and show all multiplication steps.
materials_needed: Character Profile Cards with monthly income amounts ($2,400-$4,800 range)
50-30-20 Budget Rule reference poster
Budget Worksheet templates (one per student)
Calculators (one per student)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Grade completed Budget Worksheets using rubric: 4 points for correct application of percentage formula with work shown, 3 points for accurate calculation of all subcategory amounts, 2 points for budget totaling exactly 100% of income, 1 point for neat organization and proper labeling. Maximum 10 points. Students must achieve 8/10 to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage-to-decimal conversion chart (50% = 0.50) and work through first calculation together. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including irregular expenses (annual car insurance divided by 12 months) or calculating how budget changes with a 15% salary increase.

description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional young adult by applying percentage calculations to determine spending categories. Students will demonstrate understanding of percentages through practical money management decisions and mathematical computations
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Profile Cards' to each student, containing fictional characters with different monthly incomes ($2,500, $3,200, $4,000, or $4,800). Display the recommended budget percentages on the board: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 12%, Savings 10%, Utilities 8%, Entertainment 10%, Clothing 5%, Miscellaneous 10%. After calculations, students create a visual budget chart on poster paper, drawing pie charts or bar graphs to represent their allocations. In the next 20 minutes, pair students with different income levels to compare budgets and discuss how income affects spending choices. For the final 10 minutes, conduct a gallery walk where students post their budgets and view others' work. description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional college student by applying percentage calculations to determine spending categories. They will use given income amounts and percentage guidelines to calculate exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and other expenses.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to convert percentage allocations into specific dollar amounts within a budget context
Students will demonstrate percentage concepts through creating and justifying a balanced personal budget
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Scenario' worksheet to each student (10 minutes setup). Each worksheet contains a fictional student profile with monthly income of $2,400 and recommended spending percentages: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 10%, Savings 10%, Entertainment 8%, Personal Care 5%, Miscellaneous 7%, Emergency Fund 15%. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to calculate exact dollar amounts for each category using the formula: (percentage ÷ 100) × total income. Colored pencils or markers for optional pie charts
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with work shown, budget totals exactly $2,400, thoughtful justification provided; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget within $10 of target, adequate justification; (2) Some calculation errors, budget within $50 of target, basic justification; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. title: Personal Budget Creation Using Percentage Calculations: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to create and analyze a realistic monthly budget for a hypothetical young adult scenario. They will calculate percentages for different expense categories and make budget adjustments based on percentage constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages of total income for various budget categories by using decimal multiplication and division methods
Students will apply percentage increase and decrease concepts through budget modification scenarios and constraint problems
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Young Adult Budget Scenario' worksheet containing a fictional monthly income of $2,400 and a list of 8 expense categories (rent, food, transportation, utilities, entertainment, savings, clothing, miscellaneous). Provide calculators and percentage reference sheets.

**Phase 1 - Initial Budget Creation (15 minutes):** Students work individually to allocate dollar amounts to each category, ensuring the total equals exactly $2,400. They must then calculate what percentage each category represents of their total income using the formula: (Category Amount ÷ Total Income) × 100. Students record both dollar amounts and percentages on their worksheet.

**Phase 2 - Budget Analysis (10 minutes):** Students compare their percentages to provided 'recommended budget guidelines' (e.g., housing should be 25-30% of income, savings should be at least 10%). They identify which categories exceed or fall short of recommendations.

**Phase 3 - Budget Adjustment (15 minutes):** Present constraint scenarios: 'Rent increases by 15%' and 'You want to increase savings to exactly 15% of income.' Students must recalculate affected amounts, determine the new dollar values using percentage calculations, and adjust other categories to maintain the $2,400 total. They show all calculation work using the formulas: New Amount = Original Amount × (1 + percentage change) and Target Amount = Total Income × Target Percentage.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students pair-share their final budgets, explaining one percentage calculation they performed and one adjustment strategy they used.
materials_needed: Young Adult Budget Scenario worksheet (one per student)
Calculators (one per student)
Percentage calculation reference sheet
Recommended budget guidelines handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of percentage calculations - all 8 categories correctly calculated, (2) Proper use of percentage formulas - work shown for at least 4 calculations, (3) Successful budget adjustments - both constraint scenarios completed with correct new amounts, (4) Mathematical reasoning - written explanation of one adjustment strategy demonstrates understanding of percentage relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made percentage calculation templates and allow use of percentage calculators or decimal conversion charts. For advanced learners: Add complexity by introducing compound scenarios (e.g., 'What if income increases by 8% and you want to maintain the same percentage breakdown?') or have them create budget recommendations for different income levels using proportional reasoning.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Time Complexity Decomposition
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code structures, identifying nested loops and recursive calls, and categorizing their best/worst-case scenarios. They will create detailed complexity breakdowns and justify their Big O classifications through systematic code examination.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by systematically identifying and categorizing loop structures, recursive calls, and conditional branches within provided code implementations
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through detailed examination of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios using mathematical reasoning and code trace analysis
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (15 minutes setup). In Phase 1 (30 minutes), students examine bubble sort code line-by-line, identifying all loops and counting maximum iterations. They document findings on the analysis worksheet, noting that nested loops create O(n²) complexity. In Phase 2 (35 minutes), groups analyze merge sort, tracing through the recursive division process and merge operations. Students must identify the log(n) levels of recursion and n comparisons per level, concluding O(n log n) complexity. Phase 3 (35 minutes) focuses on quicksort analysis, where students examine both best-case (balanced partitions) and worst-case (already sorted) scenarios. They trace through partition operations and recursive calls to determine O(n log n) average and O(n²) worst-case complexities. In Phase 4 (25 minutes), groups complete a comparative analysis table showing time complexities, space requirements, and stability characteristics. Each group presents one algorithm analysis (10 minutes total). Students must justify their complexity classifications using specific code evidence, explain why certain operations dominate runtime, and provide concrete examples of input scenarios that trigger best/worst-case performance.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (one set per group)
Algorithm analysis worksheets with complexity comparison tables
Calculators for mathematical computations
Whiteboard markers and chart paper for group presentations
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of Big O classification for each algorithm (40%), (2) Quality of code analysis with specific line references and loop identification (30%), (3) Correctness of best/worst-case scenario explanations with concrete examples (20%), (4) Clarity of comparative analysis and mathematical justification (10%). Students must achieve 75% accuracy in complexity classifications and provide at least two specific code references per algorithm to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted code sections showing loop boundaries, offer a step-by-step complexity calculation guide, and assign simpler bubble sort analysis first. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), ask them to analyze space complexity, or have them modify algorithms and predict complexity changes. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during code examination phases.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Real-World Business Impact
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning approaches (random forest, gradient boosting, neural network) applied to a customer churn prediction dataset, assessing not only technical performance but also business viability, ethical implications, and implementation feasibility. They will present justified recommendations to a simulated executive committee.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, computational costs, and interpretability trade-offs within a business context
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive assessment of technical limitations, ethical considerations, and organizational implementation challenges
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup and Initial Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the preprocessed telecom customer churn dataset and three pre-trained models (random forest, XGBoost, neural network) along with their training code and performance outputs. Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team receiving identical datasets but different business constraint scenarios (startup with limited resources, established enterprise, regulated industry). Each team member initially focuses on one model, spending 20 minutes analyzing performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), computational requirements, and training time. Teams then spend 25 minutes sharing findings and identifying initial strengths/weaknesses of each approach.

**Phase 2: Deep Evaluation Analysis (60 minutes)**
Teams conduct systematic evaluation using the provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: predictive performance, interpretability, computational efficiency, scalability, robustness to data drift, and alignment with business constraints. Students must identify at least three significant limitations per model, assess feature importance consistency across models, analyze prediction confidence intervals, and evaluate potential bias in predictions across customer demographics. They document findings in the structured evaluation matrix, noting specific evidence and quantitative support for each assessment.

**Phase 3: Executive Recommendation (45 minutes)**
Teams prepare 8-minute presentations for simulated executives (instructor and peer evaluators), including model ranking with detailed justification, implementation roadmap with timeline and resource requirements, risk assessment with mitigation strategies, and success metrics for deployment monitoring. Presentations must address the specific business scenario constraints and include at least two alternative deployment strategies. Following presentations, teams engage in 7-minute Q&A sessions where they defend their recommendations against challenging business questions.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Real-World Business Impact: Business Application
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning approaches applied to a complex business problem, evaluating their trade-offs in accuracy, interpretability, computational cost, and ethical implications. instructions: Begin by providing students with a realistic business case study (e.g., loan approval system) and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, Neural Network, and Logistic Regression, each with different performance characteristics. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 45 minutes analyzing model outputs, confusion matrices, feature importance plots, and fairness metrics across demographic groups. They must complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing: (1) predictive accuracy using precision, recall, F1-score, (2) interpretability using SHAP values and feature importance rankings, (3) computational requirements including training time and inference speed, (4) fairness metrics including demographic parity and equalized odds, and (5) business implementation costs. Students then synthesize findings into a 15-minute stakeholder presentation recommending one model while explicitly addressing trade-offs and risks. Presentations must include: executive summary with clear recommendation, comparative analysis table, risk assessment with mitigation strategies, and implementation timeline with resource requirements. title: Design a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Calculus and Graph Theory
description: Students will create an original mathematical model that combines differential calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory to solve a real-world traffic optimization problem. They will design algorithms, validate their model with simulated data, and present their solution as a comprehensive research proposal.
estimated_duration: 3 weeks (approximately 45 hours total: 15 hours class time, 30 hours independent/team work)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory by constructing an original mathematical model for traffic flow optimization
Students will design and validate a novel algorithmic solution through computational implementation and statistical analysis of performance metrics
instructions:
Begin with a 15-minute presentation of the challenge: students must model traffic flow for a city intersection system with 4-6 interconnected nodes, considering variables like traffic density, signal timing, and flow rates. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a unique intersection layout with specific constraints (rush hour patterns, construction zones, emergency vehicle priorities). 

Week 1 (Days 1-3): Teams research existing traffic models and identify mathematical frameworks. They must select and justify their approach using calculus for optimization (minimizing wait times), linear algebra for system states, and graph theory for network representation. Teams submit a 2-page mathematical framework proposal.

Week 2 (Days 4-7): Students develop their complete model, creating mathematical equations for traffic flow dynamics, optimization functions for signal timing, and adjacency matrices for intersection relationships. They must derive at least three key equations from first principles and prove convergence of their optimization algorithm.

Week 3 (Days 8-10): Implementation phase using Python or MATLAB. Students code their model, generate synthetic traffic data, and run simulations. They must create visualizations showing traffic flow before/after optimization and statistical analysis proving their model's effectiveness.

Final presentations (Day 11): Each team presents their complete solution in 15 minutes, demonstrating mathematical rigor, computational results, and real-world applicability. Presentations must include problem formulation, mathematical derivation, algorithm design, validation results, and limitations analysis. Peer teams provide technical feedback using provided evaluation rubrics.

Scientific calculators

assessment_method: Students evaluated on four components: (1) Mathematical rigor and originality of model (25%) - equations must be derived, not copied, with proper justification; (2) Computational implementation (25%) - working code with clear documentation and error handling; (3) Validation and analysis (25%) - statistical proof of model effectiveness with confidence intervals; (4) Presentation and communication (25%) - clear explanation of technical concepts to expert audience. Final deliverable includes 10-page technical report, commented source code, and presentation slides.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for basic traffic models and step-by-step guides for Python implementation. Challenge them to consider real-time adaptive algorithms or integration with smart city IoT systems.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 to 1111 (0-15) through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-to-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8) through repeated practice and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary flashcards to each student pair. Each card shows a 4-bit binary number on one side (e.g., 1010) and its decimal equivalent on the other (e.g., 10). Start with a 5-minute instructor demonstration using the first four cards (0000, 0001, 0010, 0011), explicitly showing the place value method: rightmost bit = 1, next = 2, next = 4, leftmost = 8. Have students chant the place values together three times. Next, students work in pairs for 15 minutes with one partner holding cards showing only binary numbers while the other states the decimal equivalent. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes. During practice, circulate and ensure students are using place value addition rather than just memorizing. After pair practice, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire round where you display binary numbers on the board and students write decimal answers on mini whiteboards. Show each binary number for exactly 5 seconds. Complete three rounds of 8 different numbers each. For the final 5 minutes, students individually complete a written quiz with all 16 binary numbers (0000-1111) presented in random order. They must write the correct decimal equivalent next to each binary number. Collect quizzes immediately upon completion for assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards with 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) and decimal equivalents - one set per student pair
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers - one per student
Printed quiz sheets with binary numbers 0000-1111 in random order
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade individual quizzes using this rubric: 16/16 correct = Mastered (A), 14-15 correct = Proficient (B), 12-13 correct = Developing (C), below 12 = Needs Support. Additionally, observe during pair practice and note students who consistently answer within 3 seconds versus those requiring longer thinking time. Record observations for differentiation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a place value chart (8-4-2-1) they can reference during practice, start with just 0000-0111 before adding 1000-1111, and pair them with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to convert 8-bit numbers (00000000-11111111), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or have them create their own quiz questions for classmates.
