original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured repetition and peer quizzing. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through peer-based quiz activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (decimal 0-15 on one side, binary on reverse). Spend 5 minutes explaining that students will see either a decimal number (like 7) or binary (like 1011) and must state the conversion aloud. Start with individual study: students flip through their complete set 3 times, spending 30 seconds per card, saying both numbers aloud each time (15 minutes total). Next, pair students and conduct structured peer quizzing: Partner A shows the decimal side, Partner B states the binary equivalent, then they check the answer together. Switch roles after 8 cards. Complete one full cycle (32 total questions per pair) in 10 minutes. For round two, Partner A shows binary side, Partner B states decimal equivalent, following the same process for another 10 minutes. Conclude with individual speed testing: students work alone through their deck, timing how long it takes to correctly convert all 16 numbers (both directions = 32 conversions total). Record their time and accuracy. Students who finish early help struggling peers by holding flashcards and providing encouragement. End with a brief whole-class recap where volunteers demonstrate 2-3 conversions at the board.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 (one side) and corresponding 4-bit binary (reverse side) - one set per student
Stopwatch or timer (smartphone apps acceptable)
Whiteboard and markers for demonstration
Student recording sheet for tracking time and accuracy scores
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (maximum 3 errors out of 32 total conversions) during the final individual speed test. Record completion time and accuracy on individual tracking sheets. Observe peer quizzing sessions to ensure students are correctly stating conversions aloud. Success criteria: 14/16 correct for decimal-to-binary AND 14/16 correct for binary-to-decimal within 8 minutes total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1 column headers) and allow finger-counting methods during initial practice. Pair them with patient, supportive partners. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or challenge them to convert without looking at cards. Have them create additional flashcards for numbers 16-31 as enrichment.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge: Written Report
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential number system recognition skills needed for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire verbal or written responses
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend the first 10 minutes having students work in pairs, with one partner showing the decimal side while the other attempts to recall the binary representation, then switching roles every 2 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers on the board for 3 seconds each, and students write the binary equivalent on their whiteboards, holding them up for immediate feedback. Follow with the reverse exercise, showing binary numbers for students to convert to decimal. For the final 15 minutes, implement a progressive elimination game: all students stand, you call out either a decimal or binary number, students have 5 seconds to write the conversion on their mini-whiteboards and hold them up. Students with incorrect answers sit down, continuing until one winner remains or time expires. Throughout the activity, emphasize the pattern recognition aspect: how each binary digit position represents a power of 2 (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s place values). Conclude with students completing a individual 16-question quiz covering all decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions for numbers 0-15, allowing 30 seconds per question.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Individual mini-whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Stopwatch or timer
Binary conversion reference chart for instructor
Printed quiz sheets with 16 conversion problems
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) on the final individual quiz covering all decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions for numbers 0-15. Additionally, observe during pair work and whole-class activities to identify students who consistently struggle with specific number patterns for follow-up instruction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1) and allow them to use finger counting initially. Start with smaller ranges (0-7) before progressing to full 0-15 range. For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need additional support during partner work.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge

title: Interpreting Statistical Bias in Real-World Survey Data Collection Methods
description: Students analyze three different survey methodologies used to collect demographic data and identify how each method introduces specific types of statistical bias. They will categorize bias types and explain how each affects data validity and representativeness.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between selection bias, response bias, and sampling bias by analyzing concrete survey collection scenarios
Students will explain how different data collection methods compromise sample representativeness through structured comparison exercises
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute three survey scenario cards: (1) Online survey about internet usage habits shared only on social media platforms, (2) Phone survey about political preferences conducted only during weekday business hours, (3) Mall intercept survey about shopping behaviors conducted only at high-end shopping centers. Each group receives a bias identification worksheet with definitions of selection bias, response bias, and sampling bias. 

First 15 minutes: Groups read scenarios and individually identify potential biases in each method. Next 20 minutes: Groups collaborate to categorize each identified bias using the provided definitions, recording their reasoning on the worksheet. They must explain specifically how each bias manifests and which population segments are likely excluded or overrepresented. 

Minutes 35-45: Groups create a comparison matrix showing how each survey method fails to represent the target population. They identify 2-3 specific demographic groups that would be systematically excluded from each method. Final 10 minutes: Each group presents one scenario to the class, explaining the primary bias type and its impact on data validity. Instructor facilitates discussion on how these biases compound when multiple methods contain similar flaws. 

Groups must provide specific examples of how their identified biases would skew results (e.g., 'phone surveys during business hours exclude working professionals, potentially underrepresenting middle-income perspectives').
materials_needed: Three printed survey scenario cards per group
Bias identification worksheets with definitions
Comparison matrix templates
Whiteboard or projection for group presentations
assessment_method: Groups submit completed worksheets showing: (1) Correct identification of at least 2 bias types per scenario, (2) Accurate explanations of how each bias affects sample representativeness, (3) Specific examples of excluded populations. Rubric awards 4 points for correct bias categorization, 4 points for clear explanations of impact, 2 points for specific demographic examples.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students receive bias definition cards with examples from different contexts. Advanced learners design improved survey methods that minimize identified biases and calculate potential impact on effect sizes. Provide sentence starters like 'This method introduces [bias type] because it systematically excludes...' for students needing structure.

title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world warehouse optimization problem involving multiple constraints and objective functions. They will formulate mathematical models, solve using the simplex method or graphical analysis, and interpret results to make data-driven business recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-constraint warehouse optimization scenario into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method or graphical solution approach to solve complex optimization problems and interpret solutions within business contexts
instructions:
**Phase 1: Problem Introduction (15 minutes)**
Present students with AcmeCorp's warehouse scenario: They need to determine optimal quantities of Product A (profit $40/unit, requires 2 sq ft storage, 1 labor hour) and Product B (profit $30/unit, requires 1 sq ft storage, 2 labor hours). Constraints: maximum 100 sq ft storage space, 80 labor hours available, minimum 10 units of Product A required for contracts.

**Phase 2: Model Formulation (20 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to:
1. Define decision variables (x = units of Product A, y = units of Product B)
2. Write the objective function (Maximize Z = 40x + 30y)
3. Formulate all constraint inequalities:
   - Storage: 2x + y ≤ 100
   - Labor: x + 2y ≤ 80
   - Contract: x ≥ 10
   - Non-negativity: x, y ≥ 0

**Phase 3: Solution Implementation (25 minutes)**
Pairs choose either graphical method (plot constraints, identify feasible region, find corner points) or simplex tableau method. Provide graph paper for graphical approach or simplex tableau templates for algebraic approach. Students must show all calculation steps and identify the optimal solution point.

**Phase 4: Analysis and Recommendation (10 minutes)**
Each pair calculates maximum profit, optimal production quantities, and writes a 2-paragraph business recommendation explaining their solution's practical implications, including resource utilization rates and sensitivity considerations.
materials_needed: Graph paper (at least 4 sheets per student)
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint plotting
Calculators (scientific or graphing)
Simplex tableau templates (printed handouts)
AcmeCorp warehouse scenario handout with complete problem data
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct mathematical formulation of objective function and all constraints (25%), (2) Accurate solution methodology with clear work shown (35%), (3) Correct identification of optimal solution values (25%), (4) Quality of business interpretation and recommendations (15%). Students must achieve 70% to demonstrate proficiency in applying linear programming techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint formulation templates and guide them through the first constraint setup. For advanced learners: Add sensitivity analysis component asking them to determine how profit changes if storage space increases to 120 sq ft, or introduce integer programming constraints requiring whole-unit production.

title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world warehouse optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the simplex method to determine optimal storage allocation for maximizing profit while minimizing operational costs.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a complex warehouse optimization scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic calculations to determine optimal resource allocation solutions
instructions: Begin by presenting students with the scenario: MegaStore Warehouse has 10,000 sq ft of storage space and must decide how to allocate space between three product categories: Electronics (E), Clothing (C), and Home Goods (H). Provide the constraint data: Electronics require 8 sq ft per unit with $15 profit; Clothing requires 3 sq ft per unit with $8 profit; Home Goods require 5 sq ft per unit with $12 profit. Additional constraints include: minimum 200 Electronics units, maximum 800 Clothing units, and Home Goods cannot exceed 40% of total units stored. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to formulate the problem by defining variables (E, C, H), writing the objective function (Maximize 15E + 8C + 12H), and listing all constraints including space limitation (8E + 3C + 5H ≤ 10,000), minimum/maximum requirements, and non-negativity constraints. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students convert constraints to standard form by introducing slack variables and create the initial simplex tableau. They must identify the basic feasible solution and calculate the Z-row values. Step 3 (30 minutes): Students perform simplex iterations by identifying entering and leaving variables, conducting pivot operations, and updating the tableau until reaching optimality. They must show all calculations and justify each pivot choice. Step 4 (15 minutes): Students interpret their final solution, calculating optimal quantities for each product type, maximum profit achieved, and unused resources. They must verify their solution satisfies all original constraints and present findings with business recommendations.
materials_needed: Warehouse optimization problem handout with all constraint data
Simplex tableau templates (printed or digital)
Graphing calculators or Excel/Google Sheets access
Graph paper for constraint visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Problem formulation accuracy (25%) - correct objective function and all constraints identified; Simplex method execution (40%) - proper tableau setup, accurate pivot calculations, and correct iteration process; Solution interpretation (25%) - valid optimal values, constraint verification, and business context understanding; Mathematical communication (10%) - clear notation, organized work, and logical presentation of steps.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed initial tableau and guide them through the first pivot operation step-by-step. Offer a constraint checklist template to ensure all requirements are captured. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking them to determine how profit margins could change before the optimal solution shifts, or add integer programming constraints requiring whole units only.
original_title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming

title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world warehouse optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the simplex method to determine optimal storage configurations that minimize costs while maximizing efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will apply the simplex method to solve multi-variable linear programming problems by setting up tableau iterations and interpreting optimal solutions
Students will construct mathematical models from real-world scenarios through constraint identification and objective function formulation
instructions: Begin by distributing the warehouse scenario packets to teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). Each packet contains floor plans, storage requirements for 5 product types, labor costs, space limitations, and accessibility constraints. Students first spend 20 minutes analyzing the scenario to identify decision variables (x₁ = pallets of Product A in Zone 1, x₂ = pallets of Product A in Zone 2, etc.). Next, teams formulate the linear programming model (25 minutes): objective function minimizing total cost C = 12x₁ + 15x₂ + 18x₃ + 10x₄ + 14x₅, subject to constraints including storage capacity (x₁ + x₂ ≤ 500), demand requirements (x₃ + x₄ ≥ 300), and non-negativity conditions. Using graphing calculators or Excel Solver, students solve the system using the simplex method (30 minutes), creating initial tableaux, performing pivot operations, and iterating until reaching optimality. Teams document each iteration step, identifying entering/leaving variables and calculating z-values. Finally, students interpret their solutions (15 minutes), determining optimal storage quantities, minimum cost, and shadow prices for constraints. Each team presents their solution strategy and results to another team for peer verification, explaining how their mathematical solution translates to practical warehouse operations. Conclude with teams submitting complete solution packets including problem formulation, tableau iterations, and business interpretation.
materials_needed: Warehouse scenario packets (5 different layouts per class)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent) or laptops with Excel
Linear programming tableau worksheets
Graph paper for constraint visualization
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Problem Formulation (25%) - correct identification of variables and constraints; Mathematical Execution (35%) - accurate simplex method application with complete tableau iterations; Solution Interpretation (25%) - correct analysis of optimal values and shadow prices; Communication (15%) - clear presentation of methodology and business implications. Require submission of complete work showing all pivot operations and final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint identification template and first tableau setup. Offer simplified 2-variable version focusing on graphical method before advancing to simplex. For advanced learners: Include integer programming constraints requiring rounding analysis, sensitivity analysis of constraint changes, or dual problem formulation. Provide additional scenarios with transportation or assignment problem variations.
original_title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis in Real-World Web Application Code
description: Students will examine actual vulnerable code snippets from open-source web applications to identify security flaws, trace attack vectors, and evaluate the potential impact of each vulnerability. They will analyze the relationship between different vulnerabilities and assess the effectiveness of proposed mitigation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze real-world code samples by identifying specific security vulnerabilities and mapping their potential exploitation paths
Students will evaluate the interconnected nature of security flaws through systematic vulnerability assessment and impact analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the curated code packet containing 8 vulnerable code snippets from different categories: SQL injection, XSS, authentication bypass, and buffer overflow examples (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team 4 different code samples to ensure coverage across vulnerability types. Students first spend 30 minutes individually examining their assigned code samples, using the provided vulnerability checklist to identify potential security flaws. They must document: the specific line numbers where vulnerabilities exist, the type of vulnerability, the attack vector an adversary might use, and the potential data/system impact. Next, teams reconvene for 45 minutes to share findings and create a comprehensive vulnerability matrix mapping relationships between different flaws (e.g., how an XSS vulnerability might be chained with authentication bypass). During this phase, teams use the threat modeling template to trace complete attack scenarios from initial exploitation to potential system compromise. In the final 30 minutes, teams analyze three provided mitigation strategies for each vulnerability type, evaluating effectiveness using the security assessment rubric. They must identify which mitigations address root causes versus symptoms, and determine if proposed fixes introduce new vulnerabilities. Teams document their analysis in a structured report template, including vulnerability classifications, attack chain diagrams, and mitigation effectiveness ratings with justifications.
materials_needed: Curated packet of 8 vulnerable code snippets with line numbers
Security vulnerability checklist and classification guide
Threat modeling canvas templates
Proposed mitigation strategies document for each vulnerability type
Digital collaboration tools (Miro or equivalent for attack chain mapping)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of vulnerability identification (25 points), (2) Completeness of attack vector analysis (25 points), (3) Quality of vulnerability relationship mapping (25 points), (4) Depth of mitigation strategy evaluation with clear justifications (25 points). Students must achieve 80+ points demonstrating expert-level analysis skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide vulnerability hint cards with leading questions and common vulnerability patterns reference sheet. For advanced learners: add advanced persistent threat (APT) scenario where they must analyze how identified vulnerabilities could be exploited in sophisticated, multi-stage attacks, and evaluate zero-day vulnerability potential.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Chart Critique Workshop
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different data visualizations of the same dataset to determine which most effectively communicates insights. They will apply established visualization principles to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each chart type.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying data visualization best practices and design principles
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by displaying three versions of the same sales data: a cluttered 3D pie chart, a clear bar chart, and a misleading truncated y-axis line graph (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and provide each group with the 'Visualization Evaluation Checklist' containing criteria: clarity of message, appropriate chart type, accurate representation, visual design quality, and audience suitability. Each group examines all three visualizations for 20 minutes, rating each on a 1-5 scale for every criterion and documenting specific strengths and weaknesses. Groups then spend 15 minutes ranking the visualizations from best to worst, providing written justification for their rankings. During the 20-minute sharing phase, each group presents their top-ranked visualization and explains their reasoning while other groups can challenge or support their conclusions. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where students identify common evaluation patterns and discuss how visualization choices impact data interpretation. Throughout the activity, circulate among groups to probe deeper with questions like 'What specific design element makes this misleading?' and 'How would your target audience affect this ranking?'
materials_needed: Three printed copies of each visualization per group (9 total per group)
Visualization Evaluation Checklist handout
Timer or stopwatch
Projector for displaying visualizations to whole class
Flipchart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate application of visualization principles (4 points), (2) Quality of written justifications with specific evidence (4 points), (3) Logical ranking rationale (3 points), and (4) Constructive participation in group discussions (4 points). Students must identify at least 3 specific issues per visualization and provide clear reasoning for their final ranking to demonstrate successful evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional examples of good vs. poor visualizations before the activity and offer sentence starters like 'This chart is ineffective because...' For advanced learners, challenge them to suggest specific improvements for each visualization and consider how different stakeholder perspectives might change the rankings.

title: Design a Mathematical Board Game for Teaching Fraction Operations
description: Students will create an original board game that teaches addition and subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators. They will design game mechanics, create visual materials, and develop instruction sets that demonstrate their understanding of fraction operations while making the concept accessible to younger students.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original board game by integrating fraction addition and subtraction rules into engaging gameplay mechanics
Students will synthesize their understanding of least common denominators and equivalent fractions through the creation of game scenarios and challenge cards
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Each team receives their materials and reviews the fraction operation requirements: their game must include at least 15 scenarios requiring addition or subtraction of fractions with unlike denominators. Teams first brainstorm game themes and mechanics (20 minutes), then create a rough prototype using cardboard and markers (40 minutes). Students must design a game board with 20-30 spaces, incorporating fraction problems naturally into gameplay (landing on spaces, drawing cards, or completing challenges). Next, teams create 20 challenge cards featuring fraction problems with step-by-step solution guides on the back (30 minutes). Each card must show the process: finding LCD, creating equivalent fractions, and simplifying answers. Teams then write comprehensive game rules (20 minutes) including setup instructions, turn sequence, winning conditions, and how fraction problems integrate into play. During the final phase (30 minutes), teams create an instruction sheet with three sample problems worked out completely, demonstrating proper mathematical notation and reasoning. Conclude with a 15-minute reflection where each team presents their game concept to the class, explaining one sample fraction problem and how their game mechanics reinforce mathematical learning. Teams should be prepared to justify their design choices and explain how their game makes fraction operations more engaging and understandable.
materials_needed: Large cardboard sheets (11x17 inches)
Colored markers and pencils
Index cards (3x5 inches, 25 per team)
Rulers and compasses
Dice and game pieces (buttons, coins)
Glue sticks and scissors
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy - all fraction problems correctly solved with proper LCD identification (25%), (2) Game design creativity - original mechanics that meaningfully integrate fraction concepts (25%), (3) Instructional clarity - rules and examples are clear and complete (25%), (4) Educational value - game effectively teaches fraction operations to target audience (25%). Students must demonstrate mastery by successfully solving at least 12 of 15 fraction problems and creating playable, coherent game mechanics.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made fraction problem templates and offer a simplified game board template with fewer spaces. Pair stronger math students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate mixed numbers, fraction multiplication/division, or create digital versions using basic programming tools. Provide extension problems involving fraction word problems or real-world applications within their game scenarios.

title: Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure Implementation Details Recall
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific implementation details, time complexities, and space complexities of 12 advanced data structures using the memory palace mnemonic technique. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge that students can later apply in algorithm design and system optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time and space complexities for insertion, deletion, search, and traversal operations of red-black trees, B-trees, suffix arrays, segment trees, Fenwick trees, and skip lists by constructing a detailed memory palace

Students will identify and recite the specific implementation requirements, invariants, and structural properties of tries, heaps, hash tables with different collision resolution methods, and graph representations through systematic memorization drills
instructions:
Begin by distributing the comprehensive data structure reference sheet containing 12 advanced structures: Red-Black Trees, B+ Trees, Suffix Arrays, Segment Trees, Fenwick Trees, Skip Lists, Radix Tries, Fibonacci Heaps, Cuckoo Hash Tables, Adjacency Lists, Disjoint Set Union, and Bloom Filters. Each entry includes exact Big-O notations, invariant rules, and implementation pseudocode snippets.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students select a familiar physical location (their home, campus building, or imaginary castle) as their memory palace. They must identify exactly 12 distinct, memorable locations within this space and write them down in a specific walking order.

Step 2 (25 minutes): For each data structure, students create vivid mental associations linking the structure's properties to their chosen location. For example, a Red-Black Tree might be visualized as their front door with red and black paint following specific color rules. Students must write down their associations and include mnemonic devices for remembering complexity values (e.g., 'Red-Black operations are all O(log n) like counting stairs to the second floor').

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students practice their complete memory palace walk three times, verbally reciting all details without looking at notes. Partners can verify accuracy using the reference sheet.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Individual assessment where students write down all memorized information from memory, then immediately self-check against the reference sheet, marking errors in red for focused review.
materials_needed: Advanced Data Structures Reference Sheet with 12 structures, their operations' time/space complexities, and key implementation details
Memory Palace Location Worksheet with numbered spaces for 12 locations
Red pens for self-assessment marking
Timer or stopwatch for timed practice sessions
assessment_method: Students receive points based on accuracy: 5 points per data structure for perfect recall of all time complexities (60 points total), 3 points per structure for correct identification of key invariants/properties (36 points total), and 2 points per structure for accurate implementation details (24 points total). Passing threshold is 96/120 points (80%). Students must demonstrate recall within 90 seconds per data structure during oral spot-checks.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce to 6 data structures initially, provide pre-made visual associations, or allow reference to location notes during first attempts. Pair with strong memorizers for peer coaching. For advanced learners: Add variant implementations (e.g., left-leaning vs standard red-black trees), include amortized analysis details, or extend to 16 structures including advanced topics like persistent data structures and lock-free implementations.

title: Design and Implement a Custom Encryption Algorithm Using Modular Arithmetic and Linear Algebra
description: Students will create an original encryption system by combining advanced mathematical concepts including modular arithmetic, matrix operations, and number theory. They will develop a working algorithm, prove its mathematical validity, and demonstrate its cryptographic properties through practical implementation.
estimated_duration: 300 minutes (5 hours) across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize modular arithmetic principles with linear algebra concepts by designing a novel matrix-based encryption algorithm
Students will construct mathematical proofs demonstrating the decryption process validity through rigorous algebraic verification
Students will evaluate cryptographic strength by analyzing their algorithm's resistance to common attack methods using statistical and computational approaches
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 2-3. Provide each team with the mathematical framework requirements: their encryption algorithm must use modular arithmetic (mod p where p is prime ≥ 101), incorporate invertible matrices of minimum size 3×3, and include a key generation process. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams research existing encryption methods (Caesar cipher, Hill cipher, RSA basics) to identify mathematical foundations. They must document three mathematical properties their algorithm will improve upon.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Students design their algorithm architecture. They must define: the mathematical operations sequence, key generation method using prime number selection, matrix construction rules ensuring invertibility, and the modular arithmetic implementation. Teams create detailed mathematical notation describing each step.

Step 3 (75 minutes): Implementation phase using Python or mathematical software. Students code their encryption and decryption functions, incorporating error-checking for invalid keys and input validation. They must include comments explaining each mathematical operation's purpose.

Step 4 (45 minutes): Mathematical proof construction. Teams write formal proofs demonstrating that decryption correctly reverses encryption, showing algebraic steps including matrix inverse calculations and modular arithmetic properties.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Security analysis. Students test their algorithm against frequency analysis attacks using provided sample texts, calculate key space size, and identify potential vulnerabilities.

Step 6 (45 minutes): Presentation preparation. Teams create demonstrations showing encryption/decryption of sample messages, present their mathematical proofs, and compare their approach to classical methods. Each presentation must include live coding demonstration and mathematical derivation explanation.
materials_needed: Computers with Python 3.8+ or Mathematica/MATLAB access
Prime number reference tables (primes 101-997)
Linear algebra reference sheets with matrix inverse formulas
Sample plaintext files (various languages and lengths) for testing
Whiteboard or digital presentation tools for proof demonstrations
Cryptographic attack simulation datasets
assessment_method: Evaluate using four-tier rubric: Algorithm Design (25 points) - mathematical correctness, innovation, complexity; Implementation Quality (25 points) - code functionality, efficiency, documentation; Mathematical Rigor (25 points) - proof validity, notation precision, theoretical analysis; Communication (25 points) - presentation clarity, demonstration effectiveness, peer comprehension. Students must achieve 80+ points with minimum 18/25 in Mathematical Rigor to demonstrate expert-level creation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide matrix invertibility checking algorithms, offer pre-selected prime numbers, and give proof templates with fill-in sections. For advanced learners: challenge them to incorporate elliptic curve concepts, implement padding schemes, or analyze computational complexity using Big-O notation. Provide additional support through peer tutoring sessions and optional mini-lectures on advanced number theory topics.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 through 1111 (0-15) using digital flashcards and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-to-decimal conversions through repetitive practice and self-assessment.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) with 90% accuracy within 3 seconds per conversion
Students will recall the positional values of binary digits (1, 2, 4, 8) through structured memorization practice
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary conversion reference sheet showing binary numbers 0000-1111 with their decimal equivalents (0-15). Give students 10 minutes to study this reference, encouraging them to identify patterns and use mnemonic devices. Next, demonstrate the Anki digital flashcard software, showing how cards display a binary number on front and decimal equivalent on back. Have students create their own Anki deck with 16 cards (0000-1111), typing each binary number as the question and decimal equivalent as the answer. Students spend 15 minutes practicing with their digital deck, clicking 'Again,' 'Hard,' 'Good,' or 'Easy' based on recall difficulty. After initial practice, conduct three timed recall rounds: Round 1 (10 minutes) - students work through their deck focusing on accuracy; Round 2 (8 minutes) - emphasis on speed while maintaining accuracy; Round 3 (5 minutes) - final speed challenge. Between rounds, provide 2-minute breaks for students to review missed conversions. Conclude with a partner quiz where students take turns showing binary numbers and timing responses. Record individual accuracy rates and response times on the provided tracking sheet. Students who achieve 90% accuracy proceed to the extension activity (5-bit numbers), while others continue practicing the core 16 conversions.
materials_needed: Binary-to-decimal reference sheet (0000-1111)
Anki flashcard software or alternative digital flashcard app
Individual computers or tablets
Stopwatch or timer app
Student progress tracking sheets
Printed binary number cards for partner quiz
assessment_method: Students must correctly convert 14 out of 16 binary numbers (0000-1111) to decimal within 3 seconds each during the final timed assessment. Track accuracy percentage and average response time on individual score sheets. Success criteria: 87.5% accuracy (14/16 correct) with average response time under 3 seconds per conversion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional visual aids showing place value breakdown (8+4+2+1), allow use of finger counting method initially, and extend practice time. For advanced learners: introduce 5-bit numbers (16-31), challenge with decimal-to-binary reverse conversions, or explore hexadecimal connections. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during partner quiz activities.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recall Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student, with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary representations on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend 5 minutes explaining proper flashcard technique: look at decimal number, state binary equivalent aloud, flip to check, separate correct/incorrect piles. Students work individually for 15 minutes practicing decimal-to-binary conversion, cycling through cards until they can complete the full set without errors. Next, students flip their approach for 10 minutes, viewing binary numbers first and stating decimal equivalents. Partner students for 10 minutes of mutual testing: Partner A shows decimal numbers while Partner B responds with binary, then roles reverse. Conduct a whole-class rapid-fire session where you display numbers on screen for 3 seconds each - students write answers on individual whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Include both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions randomly. Conclude with a 5-minute individual quiz where students complete 16 conversions (8 each direction) within the time limit. Emphasize that this is pure recall - no calculating or counting methods should be used during final assessment phases.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (16 cards each showing 0-15 and binary equivalents)
Individual small whiteboards and dry erase markers
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying numbers during group exercise
Printed quiz sheets with 16 conversion problems
assessment_method: Students must achieve 14/16 correct answers (87.5%) on the final timed quiz covering both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions. Additional formative assessment through observation during partner testing phase, noting students who consistently respond within 2-second intervals during rapid-fire exercises.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide visual pattern recognition aids showing how binary place values (8-4-2-1) relate to common numbers, allow extra practice time with numbers 0-7 before advancing to full range. For advanced learners: extend activity to include 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents alongside binary representations.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recall Challenge: Exercise 2
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, taking turns showing decimal numbers and having their partner state the binary equivalent, then switching roles. During this phase, encourage students to use the provided binary conversion reference chart when needed. Next, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers on the projector for 5 seconds each, and students write the binary equivalent on their answer sheets. Complete all 16 numbers twice in random order. Following the drill, have students self-assess using the answer key provided. For the final 10 minutes, run a 'Binary Bingo' game where you call out decimal numbers and students mark the corresponding binary representation on their bingo cards. title: Interpreting Statistical Relationships in Customer Churn Data Through Correlation Analysis
description: Students will analyze a telecommunications customer dataset to understand and interpret correlation patterns between customer characteristics and churn behavior. They will distinguish between different types of correlations and explain their practical business implications.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and their significance by analyzing relationships between customer features and churn rates in a telecommunications dataset
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through guided analysis of customer behavior patterns and discussion of confounding variables
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 1000 records, 12 features including tenure, monthly charges, contract type, and churn status). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. First 15 minutes: Students load the dataset using provided Python notebook template and generate a correlation matrix using pandas.corr() and seaborn.heatmap(). They identify the three strongest positive and negative correlations with the churn variable. Next 15 minutes: Students calculate specific correlation coefficients manually for two selected variable pairs to reinforce understanding of the mathematical relationship. They use the provided correlation formula worksheet. Following 15 minutes: Pairs analyze and interpret their findings by completing a structured interpretation worksheet that asks them to explain what each correlation means in business terms, identify potential confounding variables, and distinguish correlation from causation. For example, if tenure negatively correlates with churn (-0.65), students explain this means longer-tenured customers are less likely to churn, but discuss whether tenure causes loyalty or if other factors influence both. Final phase: Each pair presents one key finding to the class in 2 minutes, explaining the correlation strength, direction, business meaning, and one potential confounding variable. Instructor facilitates discussion about common misinterpretations and real-world implications for customer retention strategies.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 1000 records)
Python Jupyter notebook template with pandas and seaborn pre-imported
Correlation formula reference worksheet
Structured interpretation worksheet with guided questions
Laptops/computers with Python environment
assessment_method: Evaluate completed interpretation worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of correlation strengths and directions, (2) Accurate business interpretation of relationships, (3) Clear distinction between correlation and causation with specific examples, (4) Identification of at least one plausible confounding variable per correlation analyzed. Students must score 3/4 to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated correlation values and focus on interpretation rather than calculation. Offer sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests that...' and 'However, this doesn't mean that X causes Y because...'. For advanced learners: Include partial correlation analysis to control for confounding variables, or extend to multiple regression interpretation. Provide additional datasets from different industries to compare correlation patterns.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques and linear programming to solve a real-world problem of maximizing energy output from a solar panel installation. They will work with constrained optimization involving budget limitations, space restrictions, and varying sun exposure angles to determine the optimal panel configuration for a given location.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to optimize solar panel placement by incorporating multiple real-world constraints including budget, space, and sun angle variables
Students will construct and solve linear programming models through graphical and analytical methods to determine maximum energy output configurations
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing a fictional commercial building's specifications: 10,000 sq ft rooftop, $75,000 budget, three panel types with different costs ($200, $350, $500) and efficiency ratings (15%, 20%, 25%). Students work in teams of 3-4. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the constraint equations, identifying variables (number of each panel type: x₁, x₂, x₃) and writing the objective function for total energy output: E = 150x₁ + 200x₂ + 250x₃. Step 2 (25 minutes): Establish constraint inequalities for budget (200x₁ + 350x₂ + 500x₃ ≤ 75,000), space (4x₁ + 4x₂ + 4x₃ ≤ 2,500 panels max), and minimum requirements (x₁ ≥ 100, x₂ ≥ 50). Step 3 (35 minutes): Apply graphical method for 2-variable simplified version, then use Lagrange multipliers for full 3-variable optimization. Calculate partial derivatives: ∇E = λ∇g₁ + μ∇g₂. Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams use Excel Solver or Python optimization libraries to verify hand calculations and test sensitivity analysis by adjusting budget constraints by ±$10,000. Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their optimal configuration, explaining mathematical reasoning and real-world feasibility. Instructor facilitates comparison of different approaches and discusses corner point solutions versus interior critical points.
materials_needed: Solar panel scenario packets with building specifications and panel data sheets
Graphing calculators or laptops with Excel/Python installed
Large grid paper for constraint graphing
Scientific calculators for Lagrange multiplier calculations
assessment_method: Teams submit complete solution showing: (1) Correctly formulated objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate mathematical calculations using both graphical and analytical methods (35 points), (3) Technology verification with sensitivity analysis (20 points), (4) Clear presentation explaining optimization strategy and real-world implications (20 points). Rubric deducts points for computational errors, incomplete constraint identification, or failure to verify solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier template. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-variable version first. For advanced learners: Add weather variability factors requiring stochastic optimization, or include panel degradation over time requiring dynamic programming approaches. Consider adding integer constraints to make problem more realistic.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Linear Programming: Visual Analysis
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to determine the optimal configuration of solar panels for a specific geographic location and energy demand scenario. learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus techniques to optimize solar panel tilt angles and spacing by calculating partial derivatives and using the gradient method
Students will implement linear programming constraints through systematic analysis of budget limitations, space restrictions, and energy requirements
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing: Phoenix, AZ location data, $50,000 budget, 2000 sq ft available roof space, and target of 15,000 kWh annual output. Students work in teams of 3-4. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze the solar irradiance function I(θ,φ,t) where θ is panel tilt, φ is azimuth angle, and t is time of year. Students calculate ∂I/∂θ and ∂I/∂φ to find optimal angles, then verify using the gradient ∇I = 0 condition. Provide calculus reference sheets and scientific calculators. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams formulate the linear programming problem. Define variables: x₁ = number of 300W panels, x₂ = number of 400W panels. Establish constraints: 300x₁ + 450x₂ ≤ 50,000 (budget), 15x₁ + 20x₂ ≤ 2000 (space), 300x₁ + 400x₂ ≥ 15,000 (energy requirement). Students graph the feasible region and identify corner points. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Using Excel Solver or MATLAB, teams input their optimization model and generate solutions. They must test at least three different objective functions: minimize cost, maximize energy output, and maximize efficiency ratio. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical work, optimal configuration, and justification for their recommended solution including sensitivity analysis for ±20% budget variations.
materials_needed: Solar irradiance data sheets for Phoenix, AZ with mathematical functions
Scientific calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Laptops with Excel and Solver add-in installed
Graph paper and rulers for constraint plotting
Solar panel specification sheets (300W and 400W models with dimensions and costs)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of derivative calculations (25 points), correct formulation of linear programming constraints (25 points), proper use of optimization software with documented steps (20 points), presentation clarity and mathematical justification (20 points), sensitivity analysis completeness (10 points). Students must submit Excel workbooks showing all calculations and a 2-page written summary of their methodology and results.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed partial derivative examples for similar functions and pre-formatted Excel templates with constraint equations started. Offer graphing assistance with constraint boundaries. title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Linear Programming: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques and linear programming to determine the optimal configuration of solar panels for a given roof space, maximizing energy output while adhering to real-world constraints. This activity integrates multiple mathematical concepts to solve an authentic engineering problem.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to maximize solar energy output by analyzing the relationship between panel angle, spacing, and shadowing effects
Students will implement linear programming techniques through constraint modeling to determine optimal panel placement within budget and space limitations
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a real rooftop scenario: a 40m × 20m rectangular roof with a 15° south-facing slope, $50,000 budget, and requirement for 80% energy coverage of a 15,000 kWh annual household consumption. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Each team receives blueprints, solar irradiance data, and panel specifications. Step 1 (30 minutes): Teams establish variables and constraints. Variables include: number of panels (n), tilt angle (θ), row spacing (d), and panel type selection. Constraints include: roof dimensions, budget limits, building codes requiring 3-foot perimeter clearance, and shadow-length calculations. Step 2 (45 minutes): Students apply calculus to model energy output function E(θ,d) = n × P × η × cos(θ-15°) × (1-S(d,θ)), where P is panel power rating, η is efficiency factor, and S represents shading losses. Teams use partial derivatives to find critical points and determine optimal tilt angle and spacing. Step 3 (40 minutes): Implement linear programming using Excel Solver or Python to optimize panel selection and placement. Objective function maximizes total energy output subject to budget constraint: Σ(n_i × cost_i) ≤ 50,000, space constraints, and minimum energy requirement. Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams validate solutions by calculating annual energy production, payback period, and cost per kWh. Present findings with visual layout diagrams and mathematical justification for chosen configuration.
materials_needed: Roof blueprint templates with dimensions and specifications
Solar panel specification sheets (3 different types with varying costs, efficiency, dimensions)
Solar irradiance data tables for local geographic location
Computers with Excel or Python programming environment
Calculators with trigonometric functions
Graph paper and rulers for manual layout sketching
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical modeling accuracy - correct setup of optimization functions and constraints (25 points), (2) Calculus application - proper use of partial derivatives and critical point analysis (25 points), (3) Linear programming implementation - accurate constraint formulation and solution interpretation (25 points), (4) Solution validation and presentation - energy calculations, cost analysis, and clear communication of results (25 points). Deliverable includes written report with mathematical work, Excel/Python files, and visual roof layout diagram.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written energy function templates and guided worksheets breaking down each optimization step. title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Linear Programming: Practical Workshop

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns Through Multi-Layered Architecture Decomposition
description: Students will dissect a complex distributed system failure scenario by examining system logs, network traces, and architectural diagrams to identify cascading failure patterns. They will break down the multi-tier architecture into component interactions and trace the propagation of failures across microservices, databases, and load balancers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure propagation by examining log files, network traces, and system metrics to identify root causes and cascading effects
Students will decompose complex multi-tier architectures through systematic component isolation and dependency mapping to understand failure points
instructions: **Phase 1: Setup (15 minutes)** - Distribute the case study packet containing: system architecture diagram of a failed e-commerce platform, timestamped log files from 6 different services (web server, API gateway, user service, payment service, inventory database, Redis cache), network latency metrics, and error rate dashboards. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Architecture Analyst, Log Investigator, Network Analyst, and Timeline Coordinator. **Phase 2: Individual Analysis (45 minutes)** - Each role holder analyzes their assigned data type independently. Architecture Analysts map service dependencies and identify potential bottlenecks. Log Investigators parse error messages chronologically across all services. Network Analysts examine latency spikes and connection failures. Timeline Coordinators create a master timeline of all events. **Phase 3: Synthesis (30 minutes)** - Teams collaborate to overlay their findings, identifying correlation patterns between network issues, service failures, and cascading effects. They must trace the failure from initial trigger through final system collapse. **Phase 4: Pattern Documentation (20 minutes)** - Teams create a visual failure pattern diagram showing: root cause identification, dependency chain analysis, failure propagation sequence, and system recovery bottlenecks. **Phase 5: Cross-team Analysis (25 minutes)** - Teams present their failure pattern diagrams to another team for peer review, defending their analysis methodology and conclusions through technical questioning.

6 sets of timestamped log files in JSON format

Students will construct a mathematical model through scale factor applications and create cost projections based on area calculations
instructions: Begin by organizing students into pairs and distributing coordinate grid paper (20x20 units minimum). Explain that each pair will design a playground for their local community with a budget constraint of $50,000 and a maximum area of 10,000 square feet. In the first 15 minutes, students brainstorm playground features (swing sets, slides, sandbox, basketball court, etc.) and research typical costs per square foot for each element. Next, students spend 30 minutes creating their initial design on coordinate paper, where each unit represents 10 feet. They must include at least 6 different geometric shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles, trapezoids) representing various playground equipment and safety zones. During the following 25 minutes, students calculate the area of each playground element using appropriate formulas, showing all work on a separate calculation sheet. They then apply the scale factor to convert coordinate units to real-world square footage. In the next 20 minutes, pairs determine total costs by multiplying areas by researched cost-per-square-foot values for each element, ensuring they stay within budget constraints. Students spend 15 minutes creating a final presentation poster that includes their coordinate design, area calculations, scale conversions, cost breakdown, and a brief written justification explaining why their spatial arrangement is optimal for safety and functionality. Finally, dedicate 25 minutes for pair presentations (3 minutes each) where students explain their design choices, mathematical processes, and how they balanced budget constraints with playground functionality.
materials_needed: 20x20 coordinate grid paper (2 sheets per student)
Rulers and compasses for precise measurements
Calculators
Chart paper for final presentation posters
Colored pencils or markers
Access to internet/tablets for cost research
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Design Creativity (original layout with logical spatial relationships), Mathematical Accuracy (correct area calculations for all shapes, accurate scale conversions), Budget Management (stays within $50,000 constraint with realistic cost estimates), and Presentation Quality (clear explanation of design choices with mathematical reasoning). Each category worth 25 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide area formula reference sheets and pre-researched cost estimates. Consider allowing simpler shapes initially. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include irregular shapes requiring decomposition, add landscaping elements, or create multiple design options with comparative cost analyses.

title: Advanced Data Structure Method Signature Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the exact method signatures, parameters, and return types for 25 advanced data structure operations across trees, graphs, and hash tables. This activity reinforces foundational knowledge essential for advanced algorithm implementation and technical interviews.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact method signatures for binary search tree, AVL tree, and red-black tree operations including insert, delete, search, and rotation methods

Students will memorize the precise parameter lists and return types for graph algorithms including Dijkstra's shortest path, depth-first search, breadth-first search, and minimum spanning tree implementations
instructions: Begin by distributing the reference sheet containing 25 advanced data structure method signatures divided into five categories: Binary Trees (5 methods), Balanced Trees (5 methods), Graph Algorithms (5 methods), Hash Tables (5 methods), and Heap Operations (5 methods). Allow students 15 minutes to study the sheet, emphasizing they should focus on exact spelling, parameter order, and data types. Remove all reference materials and begin the recall session. Display category names on the board one at a time. For each category, call on individual students to recite complete method signatures from memory. Require students to state the full signature including access modifiers, return types, method names, parameter types, parameter names, and any throws clauses. Record correct responses on the board for verification. If a student provides an incomplete or incorrect signature, move to the next student without providing corrections initially. After completing all five categories, reveal the reference sheet again and have students identify discrepancies between their recalled versions and the correct signatures. Conduct a second round where students who missed signatures in round one get priority to demonstrate improved recall. Conclude with students writing down the three signatures they found most challenging to remember and explaining why these specific method signatures are important in algorithm implementation. Document each student's accuracy rate for individual feedback.
materials_needed: Reference sheet with 25 advanced data structure method signatures
Whiteboard or projection system for displaying categories and recording responses
Individual student tracking sheets for accuracy recording
Timer for study and recall phases
assessment_method: Grade based on percentage of method signatures correctly recalled: 90-100% (A), 80-89% (B), 70-79% (C), 60-69% (D), below 60% (F). Award full points only for complete signatures including correct spelling, parameter order, data types, and syntax. Partial credit given for signatures missing only minor elements like parameter names while maintaining correct types and order.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide category-specific study cards and allow practice with a partner before the formal assessment. Advanced learners should be challenged to also recall time and space complexity for each method and explain when each data structure method would be preferred over alternatives. Consider providing memory palace or mnemonic techniques for students who struggle with rote memorization.

title: Deconstructing Algorithmic Bias in Predictive Models: A Comparative Analysis of Fairness Metrics
description: Students will analyze three different predictive models (COMPAS recidivism, hiring algorithm, and medical diagnosis) to understand how various fairness metrics reveal different types of algorithmic bias. Through systematic comparison of demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration metrics, students will grasp the complex trade-offs inherent in bias mitigation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration by calculating and comparing these metrics across three real-world biased datasets
Students will interpret the mathematical relationships between fairness constraints through guided analysis of confusion matrices stratified by protected attributes
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-processed datasets with calculated prediction outcomes and protected attributes (race, gender, age). In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students work in groups of 3-4 to calculate demographic parity for each dataset using the formula: P(Ŷ=1|A=0) = P(Ŷ=1|A=1), where A is the protected attribute. They document results in provided worksheets, noting which models satisfy this constraint. Phase 2 (60 minutes) focuses on equalized odds calculations: P(Ŷ=1|A=0,Y=y) = P(Ŷ=1|A=1,Y=y) for y∈{0,1}. Students create stratified confusion matrices and calculate true positive rates and false positive rates by group. Phase 3 (45 minutes) addresses calibration: P(Y=1|Ŷ=1,A=a) across different values of a. Students plot calibration curves using provided Python scripts. Phase 4 (30 minutes) involves cross-group presentations where each team explains their findings for one dataset, highlighting which fairness metrics are satisfied/violated. Instructor facilitates discussion on the impossibility theorem showing these metrics cannot be simultaneously satisfied when base rates differ between groups. Students complete individual reflection sheets connecting mathematical findings to ethical implications.
materials_needed: Three pre-processed CSV datasets (COMPAS recidivism data, synthetic hiring data, MIMIC-III diagnostic predictions)
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded confusion matrix and calibration plotting functions
Printed calculation worksheets with fairness metric formulas
Individual reflection sheets with guided questions
Access to Python environment with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, and scikit-learn
assessment_method: Evaluate completed calculation worksheets for mathematical accuracy (40%), assess group presentations for clarity in explaining metric violations and their implications (35%), and review individual reflection sheets for depth of understanding regarding fairness trade-offs and ethical considerations (25%). Success criteria include correctly calculating all three metrics with <5% error, identifying at least two metric conflicts per dataset, and articulating why simultaneous fairness satisfaction is mathematically impossible.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with partially completed confusion matrices and step-by-step calculation templates. Offer advanced learners additional datasets from different domains (finance, criminal justice, healthcare) to explore domain-specific bias patterns. Consider pairing students with strong mathematical backgrounds with those having domain expertise in ethics or social sciences to enhance cross-disciplinary understanding.

title: Budget Planning for a School Event: Applying Percentage Calculations and Basic Operations
description: Students will create a realistic budget for a school dance by applying percentage calculations to determine costs for decorations, food, and entertainment. They will use real-world constraints and mathematical operations to make informed financial decisions within a given total budget.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine individual category budgets by allocating portions of a total event budget
Students will execute multi-step problem solving through calculating costs, taxes, and remaining funds for a realistic scenario
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'School Dance Budget Worksheet' and explaining that each student group will plan a dance for 100 students with a $500 total budget. (5 minutes)

Step 1: Present the budget categories on the board: Decorations (25%), Food/Drinks (45%), Entertainment (20%), and Contingency (10%). Have students calculate the dollar amount for each category using percentage calculations. Monitor and assist as needed. (10 minutes)

Step 2: Provide the 'Vendor Price List' handout with realistic costs: balloon packages ($15-30), streamers ($5-12), DJ services ($75-120), snack platters ($25-45), etc. Students must select items within each category budget, calculating subtotals and applying 8% sales tax where applicable. (15 minutes)

Step 3: Students create their final budget summary, showing calculations for each purchase, tax amounts, category totals, and remaining contingency funds. They must justify any budget adjustments between categories (maximum 5% transfer allowed). (10 minutes)

Step 4: Each group presents their budget plan to another group, explaining their mathematical reasoning for major purchases and demonstrating their percentage and tax calculations. Groups provide peer feedback on mathematical accuracy and budget feasibility. (10 minutes)

Conclude by having 2-3 groups share one challenging calculation with the class, showing their problem-solving process on the board. Collect completed worksheets for assessment. (5 minutes)
materials_needed: School Dance Budget Worksheet (1 per student)
Vendor Price List handout with 15-20 realistic items and costs
Calculators (1 per student)
Chart paper and markers for budget summaries
assessment_method: Grade completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, appropriate item selections within budget, accurate tax calculations, clear justification for decisions; (3) Minor calculation errors, mostly appropriate selections; (2) Some calculation errors, budget categories exceeded; (1) Major errors in calculations or budget planning. Observe group discussions for mathematical reasoning and peer feedback quality.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference chart and pre-calculated category amounts. Pair with stronger math students for peer support. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including venue rental costs, requiring comparison shopping between multiple vendors, or calculating cost per student ratios. Challenge them to create alternative budget scenarios with different percentage allocations.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Big O Notation Comparison Through Code Performance Testing
description: Students will analyze different sorting algorithms by examining their code implementations, predicting their time complexities using Big O notation, and validating their predictions through empirical testing with datasets of varying sizes. This activity bridges theoretical analysis with practical performance measurement.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by examining their nested loop structures and recursive calls
Students will compare theoretical Big O predictions with actual runtime performance through systematic testing of different input sizes
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) in the same programming language. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each pair examines the code without running it, identifying loop structures, recursive calls, and decision points. They complete an analysis worksheet predicting Big O notation for each algorithm, justifying their reasoning by highlighting specific code sections. Phase 2 (35 minutes): Using provided timing code templates, students modify each algorithm to measure execution time. They test each algorithm with arrays of sizes 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements, recording results in a data table. Ensure students use the same randomized data sets for fair comparison. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Students create graphs plotting input size vs. execution time for all three algorithms, using spreadsheet software or graphing tools. They should use different colors/markers for each algorithm. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Pairs compare their theoretical predictions from Phase 1 with their empirical results from Phase 3, identifying matches and discrepancies. They write a brief analysis explaining why quicksort might sometimes perform worse than expected, or why merge sort shows consistent performance. Instructor circulates throughout, asking probing questions about specific code sections and encouraging students to explain their reasoning.
materials_needed: Three pre-written sorting algorithm files (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort)
Code timing template with system time functions
Algorithm analysis worksheet with Big O prediction tables
Spreadsheet software or graphing calculator access
Computers with programming environment (Python, Java, or C++)
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of Big O predictions with proper justification from code analysis (25%), (2) Correct implementation of timing measurements and data collection (25%), (3) Quality of graphs showing clear trends and proper labeling (25%), (4) Written analysis comparing theoretical vs. empirical results with explanations for discrepancies (25%). Students must submit their completed worksheet, timing data table, graphs, and written analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a code annotation guide highlighting where to look for loops and recursive calls. Offer a partially completed timing template with comments. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, insertion sort) or investigate best-case vs. worst-case scenarios by testing with sorted, reverse-sorted, and random data. Encourage exploration of space complexity analysis alongside time complexity.

title: Design and Construct an Optimization Algorithm for Multi-Variable Resource Allocation
description: Students will create an original mathematical algorithm to solve a complex real-world optimization problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will develop, test, and present a complete mathematical model with computational implementation and theoretical justification.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be spread across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design an original optimization algorithm by integrating calculus, linear programming, and computational methods to solve multi-variable resource allocation problems
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical model through systematic analysis of constraints, objective functions, and feasibility conditions with full theoretical documentation
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a complex scenario: A renewable energy company must optimize the placement of 50 wind turbines across a 100km² region, considering wind patterns, environmental restrictions, transmission costs, and maintenance accessibility. Students work in teams of 3-4. Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams analyze the problem, identify all variables (turbine coordinates, power output, cost functions), and define constraints (environmental zones, minimum distances, budget limits). They must create mathematical expressions for each constraint and the objective function. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Students design their optimization approach, choosing between methods like gradient descent, linear programming, genetic algorithms, or hybrid approaches. They must justify their choice mathematically and create pseudocode for their algorithm. Phase 3 (120 minutes): Teams implement their algorithm using computational tools, creating working code that produces numerical solutions. They must test multiple scenarios and validate results against simplified analytical solutions. Phase 4 (60 minutes): Students document their complete mathematical framework, including convergence proofs, complexity analysis, and sensitivity studies. Phase 5 (45 minutes): Teams present their solutions, defending their mathematical choices and demonstrating algorithm performance with live computational examples.
materials_needed: Laptops with Python/MATLAB/Mathematica installed
Access to optimization libraries (SciPy, CVX, or similar)
Large format paper for mathematical derivations
Graphing calculators
Wind pattern data sets and environmental constraint maps
Presentation software and projection capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of model formulation (25 points), algorithm design creativity and theoretical justification (25 points), computational implementation functionality and efficiency (20 points), validation and sensitivity analysis completeness (15 points), presentation clarity and defense of mathematical choices (15 points). Students must submit working code, complete mathematical documentation, and performance analysis data.
