scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template constraint matrices and simplified 2-variable versions of the problem to build confidence. Offer pre-written code modules for basic optimization routines. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or real-time constraint updating. Encourage development of novel hybrid algorithms combining multiple optimization techniques.

title: Memory Palace: Identifying and Matching Programming Language Keywords
description: Students will memorize and identify 20 essential Python keywords through flashcard drilling and matching activities. This foundational exercise builds vocabulary recognition necessary for reading and writing basic Python code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 core Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, return, try, except, and, or, not, True, False, None, break, continue, pass, elif) by sight with 90% accuracy
Students will recall the correct spelling of Python keywords through written matching exercises without reference materials
instructions: Begin by distributing the Python keyword reference sheet and having students spend 5 minutes silently reading through all 20 keywords. Next, demonstrate the digital flashcard system using the first 5 keywords, showing students how to click 'Easy,' 'Good,' or 'Again' based on their recognition speed. Have students work individually for 15 minutes using the digital flashcards, cycling through all 20 keywords until each keyword appears at least 3 times. After flashcard practice, distribute the printed matching worksheet with 20 keyword definitions in Column A and 20 keywords scrambled in Column B. Students have 10 minutes to draw lines connecting each definition to its corresponding keyword without using reference materials. For the final assessment, display keywords one at a time on the projector for 3 seconds each. Students write each keyword on their answer sheet as it appears. Complete this rapid-fire identification test twice - once in alphabetical order, once randomized. Collect answer sheets immediately after the second round. During independent work time, circulate to ensure students are actively engaging with flashcards and not simply clicking through without reading. Remind students that the goal is recognition speed and spelling accuracy.
materials_needed: Python keyword reference sheet (printed, one per student)
Anki or Quizlet digital flashcard deck with 20 Python keywords
Matching worksheet (printed, one per student)
Answer sheets for identification test (printed, one per student)
Projector or smart board for displaying keywords
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade the rapid-fire identification test answer sheets using a 20-point scale (1 point per correctly spelled keyword). Success criteria: 18/20 (90%) correct on final identification test. Additionally, check matching worksheets for completion and award participation points. Record individual student struggles with specific keywords for follow-up review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce keyword set to 10 most common words (if, else, for, while, def, True, False, and, or, not) and provide additional 5 minutes of flashcard time. For advanced learners: Add 10 additional keywords (lambda, yield, with, as, global, nonlocal, assert, del, from, in) and challenge them to categorize keywords by function type (control flow, boolean, etc.).

title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Returns Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real estate investment optimization problem involving multiple properties, budget constraints, and return objectives. They will use the simplex method to determine optimal investment allocations across different property types while considering realistic market constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to model a multi-variable real estate investment problem with at least 5 constraints and 4 decision variables
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic tableau operations to determine optimal investment strategies that maximize expected returns
instructions: Begin by distributing the Real Estate Investment Scenario packet containing market data for 4 property types: residential apartments, commercial offices, retail spaces, and industrial warehouses. Each property type has different expected annual returns (8%, 12%, 15%, 10% respectively), minimum investment requirements ($50K, $100K, $75K, $200K), and risk ratings. Present the investor constraints: $2M total budget, maximum 40% in any single property type, minimum $200K in low-risk properties (residential/industrial), and at least 3 property types must be selected. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify decision variables (x1, x2, x3, x4 representing investment amounts) and formulate the objective function to maximize annual return: 0.08x1 + 0.12x2 + 0.15x3 + 0.10x4. Next, have pairs spend 20 minutes writing all constraint inequalities including budget, diversification, risk management, and minimum investment requirements, plus non-negativity constraints. Provide constraint verification checklist for self-assessment. Then demonstrate setting up the initial simplex tableau on the board, showing slack variables and basic solution setup. Students spend 35 minutes performing simplex iterations using provided tableau worksheets, with partners checking each pivot operation. Circulate to verify pivot element selection and arithmetic accuracy. In the final 25 minutes, students interpret their optimal solution by calculating total investment per property type, expected annual return, and unused budget capacity. They must write a 2-paragraph business recommendation explaining their optimal portfolio allocation and justifying why this solution maximizes returns while satisfying all constraints. Conclude with pairs presenting one key insight about their optimal solution to the class.
materials_needed: Real Estate Investment Scenario packet with property data tables
Simplex tableau worksheets (5-6 blank tableaus per student pair)
Graphing calculators or Excel with Solver add-in
Constraint verification checklist handout
assessment_method: Grade based on: Correct problem formulation (25 points) - accurate objective function and all constraints properly written; Simplex method execution (35 points) - correct tableau setup, proper pivot operations, and accurate arithmetic throughout iterations; Solution interpretation (25 points) - correct optimal values, feasibility check, and clear business recommendation; Mathematical communication (15 points) - organized work, proper notation, and logical presentation of findings. Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint templates and a simplex method reference card with pivot rules. Pair weaker students with stronger mathematical partners. For advanced learners: Add sensitivity analysis requirements - have them determine how changes in property returns affect optimal allocation, or introduce integer programming constraints requiring whole multiples of $25K investments.

title: Distributed System Failure Pattern Analysis: Dissecting a Real-World Microservices Architecture Breakdown
description: Students will analyze a complex multi-component distributed system failure scenario from a real e-commerce platform, identifying failure cascades, bottlenecks, and architectural vulnerabilities. They will decompose system logs, trace inter-service dependencies, and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented resilience patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real production logs, service dependency graphs, and performance metrics to identify root causes and failure propagation paths
Students will evaluate architectural design decisions through systematic comparison of implemented resilience patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, timeouts) against industry best practices
instructions:
Begin by distributing the case study packet containing: production logs from a 6-service e-commerce system during a 45-minute outage, service dependency diagram, and monitoring dashboard screenshots. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one primary service to focus on (User Service, Product Catalog, Payment Gateway, Inventory Management, Order Processing, or Notification Service). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Each team examines their assigned service's logs to identify error patterns, response time anomalies, and failure timestamps. Students create a timeline of events specific to their service using the provided timeline template. 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the service dependency diagram to trace how their service's failures affected downstream services. They must identify at least three failure propagation paths and document the cascade effects using the dependency analysis worksheet. 

Step 3 (30 minutes): Students examine the monitoring data to identify performance bottlenecks, resource exhaustion points, and SLA violations. They calculate actual vs. expected throughput rates and response times, documenting findings in the metrics analysis template. 

Step 4 (35 minutes): Teams evaluate the existing resilience patterns implemented in the system by comparing log evidence against pattern definitions provided in the reference sheet. They assess effectiveness of circuit breakers, retry mechanisms, and timeout configurations. 

Step 5 (30 minutes): Each team presents their analysis findings to the class, focusing on their service's role in the overall failure. Other teams ask probing questions about alternative failure scenarios and architectural improvements. 

Conclude with teams submitting their completed analysis worksheets and a 2-page technical report detailing root causes, failure patterns identified, and recommended architectural modifications.
materials_needed: Real production log files from 6-service e-commerce system (anonymized, 500+ log entries per service)
Service dependency diagram with 47 inter-service connections
Monitoring dashboard screenshots showing CPU, memory, network, and response time metrics
Timeline analysis template with 15-minute interval slots
Dependency analysis worksheet with failure propagation tracking tables
Metrics analysis template with calculation formulas pre-populated
Resilience patterns reference sheet defining 8 common patterns with implementation examples
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Timeline accuracy and completeness (20 points), failure propagation path identification with correct causality relationships (25 points), metrics analysis with accurate calculations and bottleneck identification (25 points), resilience pattern evaluation with evidence-based effectiveness assessment (20 points), and quality of architectural improvement recommendations (10 points). Minimum passing score is 75 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions for each analysis step and a sample failure path analysis from a simpler 2-service system. Offer one-on-one log reading tutorials focusing on timestamp correlation and error code interpretation. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by providing network partition scenarios and asking them to model alternative failure modes using chaos engineering principles. Challenge them to design automated detection rules for the identified failure patterns.

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Methods for Customer Survey Dataset
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different approaches to cleaning a messy customer satisfaction dataset with missing values, outliers, and inconsistent formatting. They will justify which cleaning method produces the most reliable results for subsequent analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data cleaning approaches by comparing their impact on data quality metrics and downstream analysis results
Students will critique data cleaning decisions through systematic comparison of before/after dataset characteristics and justification of chosen methods
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared customer survey dataset containing 500 responses with intentional data quality issues (15% missing values, outliers in age/income, inconsistent text formatting). Form pairs and assign each pair one of three cleaning approaches: Method A (delete all rows with missing data), Method B (fill missing values with means/modes), or Method C (use advanced imputation with median for numerical and most frequent for categorical data). Give pairs 20 minutes to apply their assigned method using provided Python scripts in Jupyter notebooks. Next, have each pair document their results by recording: original dataset size, final dataset size, summary statistics before/after cleaning, and one sample visualization. Then rotate pairs through stations to examine all three cleaned datasets (15 minutes total). Each pair completes an evaluation worksheet comparing all methods across four criteria: data retention rate, statistical validity, representation of original population, and suitability for analysis goals. Pairs must rank the three methods from best to worst with written justification (10 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where pairs present their rankings and defend their choices, focusing on trade-offs between data completeness and accuracy. Instructor facilitates discussion of real-world implications and context-dependent decision making.
materials_needed: Pre-created customer survey CSV file with 500 rows and intentional data quality issues
Three Python cleaning scripts (one for each method) in Jupyter notebook format
Evaluation worksheet template with comparison criteria and ranking sections
Computers with Python, pandas, and Jupyter notebook installed
assessment_method: Grade completed evaluation worksheets using rubric: accurate documentation of cleaning results (25%), systematic comparison across all criteria (30%), clear ranking with logical justification (30%), participation in class discussion with evidence-based arguments (15%). Success requires demonstrating understanding that different cleaning methods have trade-offs and the 'best' choice depends on analysis context.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions on the evaluation worksheet and offer sentence starters for justifications. Pair weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners, add a fourth cleaning method involving predictive imputation or ask them to propose hybrid approaches combining multiple methods. Encourage advanced students to consider ethical implications of different cleaning choices.

title: Design and Build a Scaled Model City with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design and construct a scaled model city neighborhood using geometric principles, proportional reasoning, and linear programming to optimize land use within a fixed budget. They will create mathematical models to justify their design decisions and present cost-benefit analyses of their urban planning choices.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric concepts, scale factors, and area calculations by designing a proportionally accurate model city layout
Students will construct mathematical optimization models through linear programming to maximize city functionality within budget constraints
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the City Planning Packet containing a 24×18 inch base grid (1 square = 10×10 feet), budget allocation sheet ($500,000 virtual budget), and building cost chart with 8 structure types (residential: $50/sq ft, commercial: $75/sq ft, parks: $25/sq ft, roads: $30/sq ft, schools: $100/sq ft, hospitals: $120/sq ft, fire stations: $90/sq ft, police stations: $85/sq ft). 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams research real city layouts and identify 5 essential urban elements. They must calculate the actual square footage represented by their grid (57,600 sq ft total) and determine minimum requirements: 30% residential, 15% commercial, 10% green space, 20% roads, and 25% public services. Students create preliminary sketches showing building placement and calculate initial costs.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams construct their 3D models using cardboard, measuring each building to maintain 1:120 scale accuracy. They must create at least 12 structures with varying heights (1-4 stories) and document all measurements. Simultaneously, they develop linear programming equations to optimize land use: maximize population served while minimizing costs, subject to zoning constraints.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students prepare presentations including: scaled technical drawings, cost breakdown spreadsheets, optimization equations with solutions, and 3-minute pitch explaining design rationale. Each team presents their model, demonstrating mathematical reasoning behind placement decisions and budget allocation strategies.

Conclude with peer evaluation where teams assess others' mathematical accuracy, creative problem-solving, and practical feasibility using provided rubric sheets.
materials_needed: 24×18 inch grid paper base boards (1 per team)
Cardboard sheets, rulers, protractors, calculators
City Planning Packet with budget sheets and building cost charts
Colored markers, scissors, glue sticks
Laptops/tablets with spreadsheet software
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five categories: Mathematical Accuracy (correct scale calculations, area computations, budget math - 25%), Creative Design (innovative solutions, aesthetic appeal, functionality - 20%), Optimization Model (proper linear programming setup, constraint identification, solution justification - 25%), Presentation Quality (clear communication, visual aids, time management - 15%), and Peer Collaboration (teamwork, constructive feedback, respectful interaction - 15%). Students must achieve 3.0 average to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-calculated area templates, simplified budget worksheets with guided formulas, and partner them with stronger math peers. Offer building placement suggestions and basic linear programming examples. For advanced learners: introduce additional constraints like environmental impact factors, population density calculations, or multi-objective optimization including traffic flow modeling. Challenge them to incorporate advanced geometric concepts like trigonometry for building angles or calculus for cost minimization curves.

title: Computer Architecture Components and Memory Hierarchy Recall Challenge
description: Students will systematically recall and identify specific components of CPU architecture, cache hierarchies, and instruction set classifications through a structured memorization and verification exercise. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of advanced computer systems concepts that must be automatically recalled for higher-level analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the complete memory hierarchy from CPU registers to secondary storage with specific latency values and capacity ranges by completing timed identification exercises
Students will memorize and recite the five stages of the classic RISC pipeline and their specific functions through structured repetition activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the Computer Architecture Reference Sheet containing 50 key terms, values, and components across four categories: CPU Components (register types, ALU functions, control unit elements), Memory Hierarchy (L1/L2/L3 cache specifications, typical latencies, capacity ranges), Instruction Set Architecture (RISC vs CISC characteristics, addressing modes, instruction formats), and Pipeline Stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback details). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to study the reference sheet, using active recall techniques - cover sections and attempt to recite from memory, then verify accuracy. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement spaced repetition using flashcard method - students create physical or digital flashcards for each item, cycling through them with increasing intervals between reviews. Focus on exact specifications: L1 cache typically 32KB with 1-2 cycle latency, L2 cache 256KB-1MB with 10-20 cycle latency, main memory 4-32GB with 200-300 cycle latency. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Rapid-fire recall testing in pairs - one student reads category prompts while partner recites complete information without reference materials. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual written verification - complete the comprehensive recall worksheet covering all 50 items without references. Students must achieve 80% accuracy on exact specifications and component relationships.
materials_needed: Computer Architecture Reference Sheet with 50 specific terms and values
Blank flashcards or access to digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet)
Recall Verification Worksheet with prompts for all 50 items
Timer for spaced repetition intervals
assessment_method: Students complete a 50-item recall worksheet requiring exact specifications (cache sizes, latencies, pipeline stage functions, instruction format details). Success criteria: 40/50 items (80%) answered with complete accuracy including numerical values and technical specifications. Partial credit not awarded - responses must be precisely correct to demonstrate reliable recall foundation needed for advanced analysis tasks.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial set to 25 core items, provide mnemonic devices for numerical values (L1-L2-L3 cache progression), and allow additional 10-minute study period. For advanced learners: Add 25 supplementary items covering advanced topics like branch prediction accuracy rates, out-of-order execution specifics, and modern CPU architectural features (speculative execution, hyperthreading parameters). Encourage creation of memory palaces for complex numerical sequences.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Hyperparameter Optimization
description: Students will analyze cross-validation performance curves across different hyperparameter values to understand how model complexity affects bias-variance tradeoff. They will interpret validation curves and learning curves to explain the underlying mathematical relationships between model capacity, training data size, and generalization performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition patterns by analyzing validation curves across hyperparameter ranges for ridge regression and random forest models
Students will explain the mathematical relationship between model complexity and generalization error through systematic examination of cross-validation performance metrics
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed dataset (California housing) and two model types: Ridge Regression and Random Forest. Step 1 (15 min): Students examine provided validation curves showing training and validation scores across different alpha values (Ridge: 0.001-100) and max_depth values (RF: 1-20). They must identify the bias-dominated region (high training/validation error gap) and variance-dominated region (low training error, high validation error). Step 2 (20 min): Using provided learning curves (training set sizes from 100-8000 samples), students analyze how bias and variance components change with data size. They document observations in a structured template: for each hyperparameter value, record training score, validation score, gap magnitude, and classify as underfitting/overfitting/optimal. Step 3 (15 min): Students calculate and plot the bias-variance decomposition using 50 bootstrap samples at three specific hyperparameter settings (low/medium/high complexity). They must explain why bias decreases and variance increases with model complexity. Step 4 (10 min): Students synthesize findings by writing explanations for: why validation error exhibits U-shaped curve, how cross-validation prevents overfitting in hyperparameter selection, and why optimal complexity depends on dataset size. Provide sentence starters: 'The bias component dominates when...', 'Variance increases with model complexity because...', 'The optimal hyperparameter balances...'.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-computed validation curves and learning curves
California housing dataset (preprocessed)
Analysis template with structured observation tables
Scikit-learn validation_curve and learning_curve outputs
Bootstrap sampling results for bias-variance calculation
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric: (1) Correct identification of bias/variance regions in validation curves (25 points), (2) Accurate interpretation of learning curve trends (25 points), (3) Mathematical explanation of bias-variance tradeoff relationship (30 points), (4) Clear articulation of optimal hyperparameter selection rationale (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining three specific examples of how complexity changes affect both components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated example curves with bias/variance regions pre-labeled, offer guided questions like 'What happens to the gap between training and validation scores as alpha decreases?' For advanced learners: Include additional model types (SVM, Neural Networks), ask them to derive expected validation curve shapes theoretically, or analyze how noise level in data affects optimal complexity.

title: Personal Budget Planning with Linear Equations
description: Students will apply linear equations to create and analyze a personal monthly budget for a hypothetical teenager. They will use equations to calculate savings goals and determine how many hours they need to work at a part-time job to meet their financial objectives.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear equation solving techniques to determine work hours needed for specific savings goals within a personal budget context
Students will construct and interpret linear equations through real-world budget scenarios involving income, expenses, and savings targets
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Teen Budget Scenario' worksheet containing a realistic monthly expense breakdown ($150 phone bill, $80 entertainment, $40 transportation, $60 miscellaneous expenses, totaling $330). Explain that students are planning for a hypothetical part-time job paying $12/hour and want to save $200 monthly for a car. Have students work in pairs for 5 minutes to identify what they need to calculate. Next, guide them through setting up the linear equation: Total Income = Fixed Expenses + Savings Goal, which becomes 12h = 330 + 200, where h represents hours worked per month. Students should solve this equation step-by-step, showing 12h = 530, then h = 530/12 = 44.17 hours. Have them convert this to weekly hours (44.17/4 = 11 hours per week). In the extension phase, students modify variables: change hourly wage to $10 and $15, then recalculate required hours. They should create a simple table showing the relationship between wage and hours needed. Finally, students add a new scenario where they want to increase savings to $300 monthly and determine the new work requirements. Each pair presents one calculation to the class, explaining their equation setup and solution process. Conclude with a brief discussion on how linear equations help in financial planning decisions.
materials_needed: Teen Budget Scenario worksheet (one per student)
Calculators
Graph paper or lined paper
Whiteboard markers for student presentations
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheet showing correct equation setup (2 points), accurate algebraic solving steps (3 points), and proper interpretation of results in context (2 points). Observe pair discussions for mathematical reasoning (3 points). Total: 10 points. Success criteria: Students correctly set up linear equations from word problems and solve for unknown variables while interpreting solutions meaningfully.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide equation template '___h = ___ + ___' and highlight key numbers in the word problem. Offer calculator support for division. For advanced learners: Add variables like tax deductions (8% of income) or percentage-based expense increases, requiring multi-step equation solving.

title: Personal Budget Planning with Linear Equations: Technical Implementation
description: Students will apply their knowledge of linear equations to create and analyze a realistic monthly personal budget scenario. They will use linear functions to model income and expenses, then solve for break-even points and savings goals.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear equation concepts by creating mathematical models for monthly income and expense scenarios
Students will solve linear equations through real-world budget calculations to determine savings potential and financial goals
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Budget Scenario' worksheets containing realistic income and expense data for a recent high school graduate. Give students 5 minutes to review their assigned scenario (each student receives different values for part-time job wages, hours worked, and fixed expenses). Next, guide students through setting up their first linear equation: y = mx + b, where y represents total monthly income, m is hourly wage, x is hours worked, and b is any fixed income sources. Students should write this equation using their specific scenario numbers (10 minutes). Then, have students create a second linear equation for total monthly expenses, incorporating both fixed costs (rent, phone bill) and variable costs (entertainment budget per week). Students will write: E = F + vw, where E is total expenses, F is fixed costs, v is variable cost per week, and w is number of weeks (10 minutes). For the application phase, students must solve three specific problems: 1) Calculate their monthly surplus or deficit by solving Income - Expenses = Net amount, 2) Determine how many extra hours they must work to save $200 monthly by solving the equation Income + (wage × extra hours) - Expenses = 200, and 3) Find their break-even point if they want to increase entertainment spending by creating and solving Income = New Expense Total (15 minutes). Students should show all algebraic steps and check their solutions by substituting back into original equations. Conclude with students presenting one calculation to a partner and explaining their problem-solving process (5 minutes).
materials_needed: Young Adult Budget Scenario worksheets (pre-made with varying income/expense data)
Calculator or smartphone calculator app
Graph paper or lined worksheet for showing algebraic work
Colored pens or pencils for highlighting different equation components
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly sets up both linear equations with proper variables and solves all three application problems with complete algebraic work shown; (3) Sets up equations correctly and solves 2-3 problems with minor computational errors; (2) Shows understanding of linear equation setup but makes significant errors in solving or shows incomplete work; (1) Attempts to create equations but demonstrates limited understanding of linear relationships or problem-solving process. Collect worksheets and check for proper equation setup, accurate substitution of scenario values, complete algebraic steps, and reasonable final answers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example using different numbers, offer a template with equation structures already written (y = ___ × ___ + ___), and allow pair work for the problem-solving phase. Create a reference sheet showing the steps for solving linear equations. For advanced learners: Add a fourth problem involving graphing their income and expense functions to find intersection points, or challenge them to create a system of equations involving multiple income sources and determine optimal work hour distribution between different jobs.
original_title: Personal Budget Planning with Linear Equations

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Transaction Systems
description: Students analyze SQL query execution plans and database performance metrics from a simulated e-commerce platform to identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks. They will decompose complex queries, examine index usage, and compare alternative query structures to determine optimal database operations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining join operations, index scans, and resource consumption metrics to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will decompose complex database queries through systematic breakdown of subqueries, joins, and filtering operations to understand computational complexity
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 students) with the pre-configured database containing 50,000 customer records, 100,000 product entries, and 250,000 transaction records. Students access the database through provided SQL client software with query execution plan visualization enabled. In the first 15 minutes, teams examine three progressively complex queries: a simple customer lookup, a monthly sales report with joins across three tables, and a complex inventory analysis with nested subqueries. For each query, students must document execution time, number of rows examined, and memory usage from the performance metrics panel. Next, teams spend 25 minutes using the EXPLAIN PLAN command to generate execution plans for each query, identifying specific operations like table scans, nested loops, and hash joins. They create visual diagrams showing the query execution flow and mark operations consuming over 30% of total execution time. In the following 20 minutes, students analyze the relationship between query structure and performance by modifying one query at a time - adding indexes, rewriting subqueries as joins, or changing WHERE clause order. They document performance changes and hypothesize causes. Finally, teams spend 15 minutes preparing a structured analysis report comparing the three queries, ranking them by efficiency, and proposing specific optimization strategies. Each team presents their findings to another team for peer review, defending their analysis with specific evidence from execution plans and performance metrics.
materials_needed: Pre-populated MySQL database with e-commerce schema (customers, products, transactions tables)
MySQL Workbench or similar SQL client with execution plan visualization
Performance analysis worksheet template with metrics tracking tables
Query optimization reference guide with common bottleneck patterns
assessment_method: Students submit analysis reports containing: (1) Execution plan diagrams with bottlenecks clearly marked (25 points), (2) Performance metrics comparison table with specific measurements (25 points), (3) Written analysis explaining relationship between query structure and performance with evidence (30 points), (4) Three concrete optimization recommendations with justification (20 points). Peer review feedback forms also contribute to assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan reading guide with common symbols explained, offer pre-filled performance metrics template with column headers, and pair with stronger SQL students. For advanced learners: Add concurrent user simulation to analyze lock contention, introduce query optimization cost models, or have them create additional test queries to validate their optimization hypotheses.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection
description: Students will critically assess three pre-built machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) designed to detect healthcare insurance fraud, evaluating their effectiveness across multiple dimensions including performance metrics, ethical implications, and business constraints. They will justify which model should be deployed in production by synthesizing technical, ethical, and practical considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative effectiveness of machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and feature importance across different evaluation frameworks
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive assessment of bias, fairness, interpretability, and real-world deployment constraints in healthcare contexts
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with three Jupyter notebooks containing pre-trained models on the same healthcare fraud dataset (10,000 claims with 15 features including patient demographics, procedure codes, and claim amounts). Each notebook includes model training code, performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), confusion matrices, feature importance plots, and computational time logs. **Individual Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Students first complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing models across six dimensions: 1) Performance metrics analysis, 2) False positive/negative impact assessment, 3) Model interpretability for healthcare auditors, 4) Training/inference computational costs, 5) Potential demographic bias identification, 6) Regulatory compliance considerations. **Collaborative Discussion (30 minutes):** Form groups of 3-4 students to debate their individual findings. Each group must reach consensus on ranking the three models and identify the top two critical trade-offs that influenced their decision. **Final Recommendation (30 minutes):** Students individually write a 500-word executive summary recommending one model for deployment, addressing stakeholder concerns (hospital administrators, auditors, patients), implementation timeline, monitoring strategies, and potential risks. They must explicitly justify why their chosen model is superior despite any identified limitations and propose mitigation strategies for the model's weaknesses.
materials_needed: Three pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with trained ML models on healthcare fraud dataset
Structured evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Healthcare fraud detection case study background document
Access to Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Technical analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct interpretation of metrics and model outputs; Critical thinking depth (25 points) - identification of non-obvious trade-offs and limitations; Ethical considerations integration (20 points) - meaningful discussion of bias, fairness, and stakeholder impact; Business justification quality (20 points) - realistic implementation considerations and risk mitigation; Communication clarity (10 points) - professional writing and logical argument structure. Students must score 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide interpretation guides for confusion matrices and ROC curves, offer guiding questions for each evaluation dimension, allow peer consultation during individual analysis phase. **Advanced extensions:** Challenge high-performing students to propose ensemble methods combining the three models, calculate statistical significance tests between model performances, or design A/B testing frameworks for production deployment. Encourage analysis of edge cases and corner scenarios not well-represented in the training data.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network) applied to healthcare fraud detection, analyzing their performance metrics, interpretability, ethical implications, and business viability. They will provide evidence-based recommendations for model deployment in a real-world healthcare insurance context.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple ML models by systematically analyzing performance metrics, feature importance, and prediction reliability across different fraud detection scenarios
Students will critique the ethical and business implications of each modeling approach through comprehensive cost-benefit analysis and bias assessment frameworks
instructions:
**Setup (15 min):** Provide teams of 3-4 students with identical healthcare claims datasets (50,000 records) and pre-trained models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) with documented hyperparameters and training logs. Each team receives standardized evaluation templates and access to model outputs.

**Phase 1 - Technical Evaluation (45 min):** Teams systematically evaluate each model using provided confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and SHAP values. Students calculate and compare precision, recall, F1-scores, and AUC for each model, then analyze feature importance rankings and prediction confidence distributions. They document findings in evaluation matrices, noting performance variations across demographic subgroups.

**Phase 2 - Contextual Analysis (30 min):** Students assess each model's business impact by calculating false positive/negative costs ($500 per false positive investigation, $5,000 average fraud loss per false negative). They evaluate model interpretability requirements for regulatory compliance, computational costs for real-time deployment, and potential algorithmic bias against protected demographics using provided fairness metrics.

**Phase 3 - Critical Comparison (20 min):** Teams create comprehensive comparison frameworks weighing technical performance against business constraints, ethical considerations, and implementation feasibility. They identify each model's strengths, limitations, and appropriate use cases.

**Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (25 min):** Students formulate evidence-based deployment recommendations, including preferred model selection, risk mitigation strategies, monitoring protocols, and implementation timeline. They prepare 5-minute presentations with supporting data visualizations.

**Phase 5 - Peer Evaluation (25 min):** Teams present recommendations to peers who challenge assumptions, question methodology, and evaluate reasoning quality using provided peer assessment rubrics.
materials_needed: Healthcare fraud dataset (CSV format, 50,000 records with 15 features)
Three pre-trained models with saved outputs and performance metrics
Jupyter notebooks with SHAP analysis and fairness metrics code
Model evaluation templates and comparison frameworks (Excel/Google Sheets)
Cost-benefit analysis worksheets with healthcare industry benchmarks
Peer assessment rubrics for presentation evaluation
assessment_method: Students submit comprehensive evaluation reports (70% of grade) including technical analysis tables, cost-benefit calculations, bias assessment results, and justified recommendations with supporting evidence. Presentations are peer-evaluated (20%) using rubrics assessing argument quality, evidence use, and response to challenges. Participation in peer questioning and methodology critique accounts for remaining 10%. Success criteria: demonstrates systematic evaluation methodology, provides quantitative justification for recommendations, identifies at least 3 model limitations with proposed mitigation strategies, and shows awareness of ethical implications in deployment decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example evaluation for one model as a template, offer guided worksheets for cost calculations, and assign specific roles within teams (technical analyst, business analyst, ethics reviewer). For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional evaluation metrics (calibration plots, prediction intervals), research regulatory requirements for AI in healthcare, or propose ensemble model solutions that combine strengths of individual approaches. Consider providing access to additional demographic data for more sophisticated bias analysis.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network) for detecting healthcare insurance fraud using real-world Medicare data. They will evaluate model performance, interpretability, implementation feasibility, and ethical implications to recommend the optimal solution for a healthcare organization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of three ML models by comparing performance metrics, computational requirements, and business applicability in a healthcare fraud detection context
Students will critique the strengths and limitations of each modeling approach through systematic analysis of bias, interpretability, and regulatory compliance considerations
instructions:
Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with a standardized Medicare fraud dataset (CMS-1500 claims data with 50,000 records, 23 features). Each team receives pre-trained models: Random Forest (scikit-learn), XGBoost, and a 3-layer Neural Network (TensorFlow), along with their training logs and hyperparameter configurations.

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct comprehensive model evaluation using provided test set. Students calculate precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices. They document computational time, memory usage, and training stability metrics from provided logs.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Students perform interpretability analysis using SHAP values for tree-based models and LIME for the neural network. They identify top 5 most influential features per model and assess feature importance consistency across approaches.

Step 3 (75 minutes): Teams evaluate models against healthcare-specific criteria: regulatory compliance (HIPAA), explainability requirements for auditors, integration complexity with existing EMR systems, and potential bias against demographic groups. Students analyze false positive/negative distributions across patient age, gender, and procedure types.

Step 4 (90 minutes): Each team prepares a comprehensive evaluation report including: quantitative performance comparison table, interpretability assessment matrix, implementation feasibility analysis, ethical risk evaluation, and final recommendation with detailed justification. Teams must address trade-offs between accuracy and explainability, computational costs vs. performance gains, and regulatory constraints.

Step 5 (60 minutes): Teams present 15-minute recommendations to simulated healthcare executives (instructor + guest expert), followed by 5-minute Q&A defending their choice and addressing implementation challenges.
materials_needed: CMS Medicare fraud dataset (50,000 preprocessed claims records)
Three pre-trained models with training logs and hyperparameter documentation
Jupyter notebooks with evaluation framework and SHAP/LIME libraries
Healthcare regulatory compliance checklist and EMR integration requirements document
Presentation template for executive summary and recommendation report
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical accuracy of performance evaluation and metrics interpretation (25%), (2) Depth of interpretability analysis and feature importance assessment (20%), (3) Quality of business and regulatory considerations analysis (25%), (4) Soundness of final recommendation and trade-off justification (20%), (5) Professional presentation and response to questions (10%). Teams must score 3+ in all categories to demonstrate mastery-level evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with guided worksheets for each evaluation step and example interpretability plots. Offer mid-activity check-ins to validate metric calculations. For advanced learners, introduce additional evaluation dimensions like adversarial robustness testing, cost-sensitive analysis with different false positive/negative penalties, and consideration of model drift in production healthcare environments.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Fraud Detection

title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Urban Transit Systems
description: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and operations research concepts to create an original mathematical model that optimizes bus route efficiency in a fictional city. They will develop both the theoretical framework and implement a computational solution using real-world constraints and data patterns.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across 2-3 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive multi-variable optimization model by integrating partial derivatives, matrix operations, and constraint programming to solve complex urban planning problems
Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts through designing, testing, and presenting an original algorithmic solution with documented assumptions and limitations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with the fictional Riverside City transit brief containing: population density heat map, current 8 bus routes, ridership data, and budget constraints of $2.3M annually. Students must first analyze the existing system using calculus-based methods to identify inefficiencies (45 minutes). Next, teams formulate their optimization problem by defining decision variables (route lengths, frequency, stops), objective function (minimize cost while maximizing coverage), and constraints (budget, fleet size of 12 buses, minimum service standards). This requires establishing mathematical relationships using partial derivatives for cost functions and linear programming for resource allocation (90 minutes). Teams then implement their model using provided Python optimization libraries, creating code that can process the city data and output recommended route modifications (120 minutes). Each solution must include sensitivity analysis showing how results change with ±10% budget variations. Teams document their approach in a technical report (30 minutes) and prepare 15-minute presentations demonstrating their model, showing before/after route maps, and defending mathematical choices. Conclude with team presentations where other groups provide peer feedback using provided evaluation criteria (75 minutes total).
materials_needed: Riverside City transit dataset (Excel file with 5 years ridership data)
Population density heat map (high-resolution PDF)
Python 3.8+ with SciPy, NumPy, and PuLP optimization libraries installed
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Large format paper (A2) for route visualization
Technical report template (LaTeX or Word format)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: Mathematical Rigor (25% - correct application of optimization theory, appropriate use of calculus and linear algebra), Model Innovation (20% - creative problem formulation, novel constraint handling), Implementation Quality (20% - functional code, accurate computations, proper sensitivity analysis), Communication Clarity (20% - technical report completeness, presentation effectiveness), and Practical Viability (15% - realistic assumptions, acknowledgment of limitations, actionable recommendations). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 points in Mathematical Rigor and Implementation Quality to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide optimization problem template with pre-defined variable structures and guide them through one sample constraint formulation. Offer simplified city dataset with only 4 existing routes. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements (weather impact on ridership), add environmental objectives (emissions minimization), or extend to multi-modal transportation including bike shares. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling teams during implementation phase.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Matching Activity
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and matching exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify matching binary-decimal number pairs through physical card matching activities within specified time limits
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student, with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary representations on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students spend 10 minutes in individual study, flipping through cards and saying answers aloud before checking. Next, conduct a 5-minute rapid-fire drill where you call out decimal numbers and students must write binary answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for quick assessment. For the matching activity, distribute two sets of laminated cards per pair of students: one set with decimal numbers 0-15, another with binary equivalents. Students work in pairs to match cards as quickly as possible, with one student timing and the other matching. Switch roles and repeat. Conclude with a 3-minute individual quiz where students fill in a chart converting 8 randomly selected numbers from decimal to binary. Throughout the activity, emphasize memorization rather than calculation - students should recognize patterns like powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8) and common combinations. Monitor student progress by walking around during pair work and noting which number pairs cause hesitation. End with a brief review of any commonly missed conversions.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (decimal 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back) - one set per student
Laminated matching card sets (decimal and binary separate) - one set per student pair
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers - one per student
Timer or stopwatch
Binary-decimal conversion quiz sheets - one per student
assessment_method: Success measured by: (1) 90% accuracy on final individual quiz (7/8 correct conversions), (2) completion of matching activity within 3 minutes during pair work, (3) consistent correct responses during whiteboard drill (observable participation). Use provided answer key to quickly grade quizzes and record completion times for matching activity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide reference sheet showing place values (8-4-2-1) and highlight patterns like 'powers of 2 have only one 1-bit.' Allow extra study time with flashcards. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or include hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to help struggling peers explain patterns they notice.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices for Customer Segmentation
description: Students will analyze and interpret correlation matrices from a customer dataset to understand relationships between demographic and behavioral features. They will explain how these correlations inform feature selection decisions for a customer segmentation machine learning model.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing strength, direction, and statistical significance of relationships
Students will explain the implications of multicollinearity through examining correlation patterns and their impact on model performance
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-calculated correlation matrix from an e-commerce customer dataset containing 12 features (age, income, purchase_frequency, avg_order_value, time_on_site, pages_viewed, email_opens, social_media_engagement, loyalty_years, returns_count, support_tickets, satisfaction_score). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. First 15 minutes: Each pair examines the correlation matrix heatmap and identifies the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording specific coefficient values. Next 15 minutes: Students categorize all correlations as weak (|r| < 0.3), moderate (0.3 ≤ |r| < 0.7), or strong (|r| ≥ 0.7), creating a summary table. Following 10 minutes: Pairs identify potential multicollinearity issues by finding feature pairs with |r| > 0.8 and explain why these might cause problems in clustering algorithms. Final 5 minutes: Students write a brief recommendation memo (150 words) suggesting which features to remove or combine based on their correlation analysis, justifying decisions with specific coefficient values and business logic.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix heatmap (color-coded) for customer dataset
Digital spreadsheet file with exact correlation coefficients
Correlation interpretation reference sheet with coefficient ranges
Memo template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation identification and categorization (25%), (2) Correct interpretation of correlation strength and direction using appropriate terminology (25%), (3) Logical identification of multicollinearity issues with |r| > 0.8 (25%), (4) Quality of feature selection recommendations with business justification (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation coefficient interpretation anchor chart and highlight one example of each correlation strength category. For advanced learners: Include additional task of calculating variance inflation factors (VIF) for highly correlated features and researching domain-specific correlation benchmarks for customer analytics.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Placement Using Multivariable Calculus
description: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel efficiency. They will determine optimal tilt angles and spacing for a solar array to maximize energy output while working within budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives to model solar energy output as a function of panel angle, spacing, and seasonal sun position
Students will implement Lagrange multipliers to optimize energy production while maintaining cost constraints through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario: Students represent engineering consultants designing a 50-panel solar array for a community center with a $75,000 budget. Provide the energy output function E(θ,d,t) = 1000cos(θ-45+15sin(2πt/365))×(1-0.1×shadow_factor(d))×A where θ=tilt angle, d=panel spacing, t=day of year, A=panel area. The constraint is cost: C(d,A) = 500A + 100d ≤ 75,000. 

Step 1 (20 min): Working in pairs, students analyze the shadow factor function shadow_factor(d) = max(0, (2-d)/2) and graph E vs θ for different d values to understand the physical relationships.

Step 2 (30 min): Students set up the Lagrangian L(θ,d,A,λ) = E(θ,d,A) - λ(C(d,A) - 75,000) and compute all partial derivatives: ∂L/∂θ, ∂L/∂d, ∂L/∂A, ∂L/∂λ.

Step 3 (40 min): Teams solve the system of equations ∇L = 0 using numerical methods or graphing calculators. Students must find critical points and verify they represent maxima using the second derivative test.

Step 4 (25 min): Students calculate the annual energy output using their optimized parameters and compare results across teams. They must justify their solution by showing that constraint conditions are satisfied and interpreting the Lagrange multiplier λ as the marginal increase in energy per dollar of budget increase.

Step 5 (15 min): Each pair presents their optimal configuration (θ*, d*, A*) with calculated annual kWh output and explains how seasonal variation affects their design choice.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Printed scenario sheets with energy function and constraints
Graph paper and rulers
Access to numerical solver software (Desmos, Wolfram Alpha, or MATLAB)
Presentation slides template for final solutions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct setup of Lagrangian and partial derivatives (25%), (2) Accurate solution of optimization system showing all algebraic steps (30%), (3) Physical interpretation of results including constraint satisfaction and λ meaning (25%), (4) Clear presentation of final design with energy output calculations (20%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-computed partial derivatives and focus on interpreting/solving the system. Offer step-by-step algebraic templates. For advanced learners: Add weather variability constraints or extend to 3D panel orientation optimization. Challenge them to incorporate economic factors like electricity pricing or equipment degradation over time.

title: Distributed System Performance Bottleneck Analysis Using Real-World Case Studies
description: Students will analyze performance metrics and system architecture diagrams from three real distributed systems (Netflix, Uber, Discord) to identify bottlenecks, evaluate design trade-offs, and propose optimization strategies. This activity requires students to synthesize multiple data sources and apply distributed systems principles to diagnose complex performance issues.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by examining load balancing patterns, data partitioning strategies, and communication protocols to identify potential performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate system design trade-offs through comparative analysis of CAP theorem implementations, consistency models, and fault tolerance mechanisms across different platforms
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute three case study packets: Netflix's content delivery optimization (2019-2023), Uber's real-time matching system architecture, and Discord's message delivery scaling challenges. Each packet contains: system architecture diagrams, performance metrics (latency, throughput, error rates), database schemas, API response times, and user growth data. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze each system individually, identifying components, data flow paths, and potential bottlenecks using provided analysis templates. Students must document their findings using distributed systems vocabulary (sharding, replication, eventual consistency, etc.). Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create comparative matrices evaluating how each system handles: data consistency, partition tolerance, availability, and scalability. They must identify specific trade-offs made in each architecture. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Based on their analysis, teams propose three concrete optimization strategies for each system, justifying their recommendations with performance metrics and architectural principles. Teams must consider cost implications, implementation complexity, and potential negative side effects. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams present their most critical finding and one optimization recommendation to the class, defending their analysis with evidence from the case studies.
materials_needed: Three comprehensive case study packets with architecture diagrams and performance data
Analysis template worksheets with guided questions
Laptops/tablets for research and documentation
Distributed systems reference sheets (CAP theorem, consistency models, partitioning strategies)
Digital presentation tools (slides, whiteboard software)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of trade-offs (25%), (3) Feasibility and justification of proposed optimizations (25%), (4) Use of appropriate distributed systems terminology and concepts (25%). Deliverables include completed analysis templates, comparative matrices, and team presentation. Observe during group work for collaborative problem-solving and technical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide glossary of distributed systems terms, offer structured templates with more specific guiding questions, and allow access to additional reference materials. Create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify potential performance improvements, research additional real-world examples, or propose novel architectural patterns. Encourage them to consider emerging technologies (edge computing, serverless) in their optimization strategies.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for House Price Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualization approaches used to display a housing price dataset and determine which visualization best communicates key insights to a real estate stakeholder. They will justify their choice using data visualization principles and audience needs.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying fundamental design principles and stakeholder requirements
Students will judge the appropriateness of visualization choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by distributing the housing dataset (containing 200 records with price, bedrooms, square footage, and neighborhood) and three pre-created visualizations: a scatter plot matrix, a grouped bar chart, and a heat map showing average prices by neighborhood and bedroom count. Give students 10 minutes to examine each visualization individually, taking notes on what information each conveys. Next, provide the evaluation framework worksheet with criteria: clarity (can patterns be easily identified?), completeness (does it show relevant relationships?), and audience appropriateness (suitable for real estate agents?). Students spend 15 minutes scoring each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, writing specific justifications. In pairs, students discuss their scores for 10 minutes, then individually write a 200-word recommendation memo selecting the best visualization. The memo must identify the chosen visualization, provide three specific reasons why it's superior, cite two weaknesses of the rejected options, and suggest one improvement for the selected chart. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where volunteers share their choices and reasoning. Emphasize that different valid conclusions are possible with proper justification.
materials_needed: Housing dataset CSV file (price, bedrooms, sqft, neighborhood for 200 properties)
Three pre-made visualizations (scatter plot matrix, grouped bar chart, neighborhood heat map)
Evaluation framework worksheet with scoring rubric
Computers with spreadsheet software or printed copies of visualizations
assessment_method: Grade the recommendation memo using a 4-point rubric: clear choice identification (1 point), three well-supported reasons with specific evidence (3 points), identification of two weaknesses in rejected options (2 points), and one realistic improvement suggestion (1 point). Total: 7 points. Look for use of visualization vocabulary and connection to stakeholder needs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'A real estate agent would find this confusing because...'. For advanced learners, add a requirement to sketch their own improved version or evaluate how the visualizations might perform with different stakeholder audiences (home buyers vs. investors).

title: Design a Community Garden Layout Using Geometric Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical model to design an efficient community garden layout by applying area, perimeter, and proportion concepts. They will develop their own system of constraints and optimization criteria to maximize growing space while meeting practical gardening requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize area, perimeter, and ratio concepts by designing an original community garden layout that optimizes space utilization within given constraints
Students will construct mathematical justifications through creating detailed calculations and visual representations that demonstrate their optimization decisions
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a scenario: They are landscape designers hired to create a community garden on a rectangular plot measuring 40m × 30m. Provide each student with grid paper and calculators. In the first 15 minutes, students individually brainstorm essential garden features (vegetable plots, pathways, compost area, tool shed, water source) and research typical dimensions online or from provided reference sheets. Next, spend 20 minutes having students establish their own mathematical constraints: minimum pathway widths for wheelchair accessibility (1.2m), maximum plot sizes for easy maintenance (3m × 4m), required percentage of total area for pathways (15-20%), and spacing requirements between plots (0.5m). During the 45-minute design phase, students create scaled drawings on grid paper where 1 square = 1m², calculating areas and perimeters for each section. They must include at least 12 individual plots, communal spaces, and infrastructure while maximizing growing area. Students then spend 25 minutes creating a detailed mathematical report showing: total growing area calculations, percentage breakdowns of land use, justification for their layout choices using mathematical reasoning, and comparison of at least two alternative arrangements they considered. Finally, allow 15 minutes for students to present their designs to small groups of 3-4 peers, explaining their mathematical decision-making process and receiving feedback on their optimization strategies.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, minimum 2 sheets per student)
Rulers and measuring tools
Calculators
Colored pencils or markers for design visualization
Reference sheet with standard garden dimensions
Computers/tablets for research (optional)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area and perimeter calculations, (2) Creativity and practicality of design solutions, (3) Quality of mathematical justification for optimization choices, and (4) Clear visual representation with proper scaling. Students must demonstrate calculations for at least 85% accuracy, include minimum required elements, and provide written explanations connecting mathematical concepts to design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated examples of 2-3 plot arrangements and guide them through area calculations step-by-step. Offer templates with partially completed layouts to build confidence. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints like irrigation system design requiring geometric calculations, budget limitations requiring cost-per-square-meter analysis, or seasonal rotation planning using algebraic patterns. Challenge them to create multiple design variations and compare efficiency ratios.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions and Header Fields Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific functions of each TCP/IP protocol stack layer and identify key header fields for TCP, IP, and Ethernet protocols. This activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and timed recall exercises to build foundational knowledge of network protocol fundamentals.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the seven specific functions of each TCP/IP protocol stack layer (Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical) by completing timed flashcard sessions with 90% accuracy
Students will identify and recite the purpose of 15 key header fields across TCP, IPv4, and Ethernet protocols through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made protocol reference sheets containing TCP/IP layer functions and header field definitions. Students have 20 minutes to study these materials individually, using highlighting to mark unfamiliar terms. Next, organize students into pairs for 15 minutes of mutual quizzing using the provided flashcard sets - one student reads the protocol layer or header field name while the partner recites its function from memory. Rotate roles every 5 minutes. Following peer practice, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session where you display layer names or header field terms on screen for 10 seconds each - students write down the function or purpose on their answer sheets. Include 25 terms total: 5 layer functions plus 20 header fields (8 TCP fields like sequence number and window size, 7 IPv4 fields like TTL and protocol type, 5 Ethernet fields like destination MAC and EtherType). After the recall test, immediately provide correct answers for self-checking. Students mark their incorrect responses and create a personalized study list of missed items. Conclude with 10 minutes of individual review using spaced repetition app Anki or physical flashcards, focusing on previously missed terms. Students must demonstrate their knowledge by verbally reciting any 5 randomly selected protocol functions to you before leaving class.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Reference Sheets (one per student)
Pre-made flashcard sets with 25 protocol terms and definitions
Digital timer or stopwatch
Presentation slides with protocol terms for rapid-fire session
Anki flashcard app or physical index cards
Answer sheets for timed recall exercise
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (23/25 correct) on the timed recall exercise and successfully recite 5 randomly selected protocol functions verbally. Track individual performance using a checklist containing all 25 terms, marking correct/incorrect responses for each student. Provide immediate feedback and require students scoring below 80% to complete additional memorization homework using provided flashcard sets.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices for layer functions (e.g., 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical) and reduce initial memorization load to 15 most critical terms. Advanced learners should additionally memorize IPv6 header fields and compare protocol evolution differences between IPv4 and IPv6 implementations.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection
description: Students will analyze cross-validation results from three different machine learning models (linear regression, random forest, and neural network) applied to a housing price prediction dataset. They will interpret the bias-variance tradeoff patterns to explain why each model performs differently and make justified recommendations for model selection based on the decomposition analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition components by analyzing cross-validation score distributions and identifying systematic patterns of underfitting and overfitting
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and bias-variance tradeoff through comparative analysis of three distinct algorithm types on the same dataset
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared Jupyter notebook containing cross-validation results from 10-fold CV applied to three models predicting house prices: Linear Regression (degree 1 and 3 polynomial features), Random Forest (10, 100, 500 trees), and Neural Network (1, 2, 4 hidden layers). Each student receives identical datasets with 20 bootstrap samples showing training scores, validation scores, and prediction variances across different train-test splits. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the provided box plots showing score distributions and calculate the mean squared error decomposition: Bias² = (mean_prediction - true_value)², Variance = variance_of_predictions, and Noise = irreducible_error. Step 2 (20 minutes): Working in pairs, students complete a structured analysis worksheet identifying which models show high bias (consistent underfitting), high variance (overfitting with high score variability), or balanced performance. They must cite specific numerical evidence from the CV results. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students create a 2x3 comparison matrix plotting bias vs. variance for each model complexity level, annotating with explanations of why simpler models trend toward high bias/low variance while complex models show low bias/high variance. Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair presents one key insight about how the bias-variance tradeoff explains their observed CV patterns, connecting model complexity to generalization performance.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-loaded CV results and bias-variance calculations
Structured analysis worksheet with bias-variance decomposition formulas
Housing price dataset with 1000 samples and 8 features
Python environment with sklearn, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn installed
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of bias² and variance components from CV data, (2) Accurate identification of high-bias vs. high-variance models with numerical evidence, (3) Clear explanation of how model complexity relates to bias-variance patterns, (4) Justified model selection recommendation based on decomposition analysis. Students must achieve 3/4 points on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using a simple linear vs. quadratic model comparison, highlight the key formulas on a reference card, and offer guided questions like 'Which model has the most consistent validation scores?' For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them implement bias-variance decomposition from scratch using bootstrap sampling, or analyze how different dataset sizes affect the bias-variance tradeoff patterns.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection: Written Report
description: Students will analyze pre-computed cross-validation results from multiple machine learning models to interpret bias-variance trade-offs and model complexity relationships. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining how different sources of error contribute to overall model performance and making justified model selection recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition components by analyzing cross-validation score distributions across models of varying complexity
