Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and generalization error through systematic comparison of training vs. validation performance metrics
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing cross-validation results for 5 models: Ridge Regression (α=100, 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01) trained on a polynomial regression problem. Each student receives: CV scores table, training scores table, and bias-variance decomposition calculations. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine the CV results table, identifying patterns in mean scores, standard deviations, and score ranges across the 5 alpha values. They must calculate the coefficient of variation for each model and rank models by stability.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students create visualizations plotting: (a) training vs. validation scores against alpha values, (b) bias² vs. variance vs. noise components for each model. They must identify the bias-variance trade-off inflection point and annotate regions of underfitting/overfitting.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students analyze the decomposition table, calculating the percentage contribution of bias², variance, and irreducible error to total MSE for each model. They must identify which error source dominates at high/low complexity.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Working in groups of 3, students write a technical report section (300 words) explaining: why α=1.0 shows optimal bias-variance balance, how variance changes with regularization strength, and what the CV standard deviation reveals about model stability. Each group presents their key finding in 2 minutes.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students predict how results would change with: doubled dataset size, added polynomial features, or different CV folds.
materials_needed: Pre-computed CV results spreadsheet with 5 Ridge regression models
Bias-variance decomposition calculation table (Excel/CSV format)
Graph paper or digital plotting tools (Python/R notebooks)
Technical writing template with report structure
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of bias-variance trade-off point (25%), (2) Accurate calculation and interpretation of error component percentages (25%), (3) Quality of written explanation linking regularization to variance reduction (25%), (4) Justified model selection with supporting evidence from CV metrics (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example for first alpha value, offer bias-variance definition cards, and allow partnership for calculations. For advanced learners: Add bootstrap resampling analysis, compare with learning curves, or extend to classification metrics like precision-recall trade-offs. Consider providing coding templates for automated analysis.
original_title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze cross-validation results from multiple machine learning models to identify patterns indicating high bias vs. high variance scenarios. They will interpret performance metrics across different model complexities to understand the bias-variance tradeoff and its implications for model selection.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation performance patterns by analyzing the gap between training and validation scores across model complexities
Students will distinguish between bias-dominated and variance-dominated model behaviors through systematic examination of learning curves and performance distributions
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a dataset containing cross-validation results for 5 different algorithms (linear regression, polynomial regression degrees 2-15, random forest with varying max_depth, SVM with different C values, and neural networks with varying hidden layers) trained on the same regression problem. Each dataset includes training scores, validation scores, and their standard deviations across 10-fold CV.

Step 1 (15 mins): Students work in pairs to create visualizations showing training vs validation performance for each algorithm family. They plot mean scores with error bars representing standard deviation.

Step 2 (20 mins): Students analyze three specific scenarios: (a) linear regression results showing consistently low training and validation scores, (b) high-degree polynomial results showing large gaps between training/validation with high validation variance, and (c) optimally tuned random forest showing balanced performance.

Step 3 (15 mins): For each scenario, students complete a structured analysis template identifying: bias level (high/low), variance level (high/low), primary evidence supporting their conclusion, and recommended next steps for model improvement.

Step 4 (20 mins): Students examine validation score distributions using box plots to understand uncertainty in model selection. They identify which models show consistent performance vs. those with high variability across folds.

Step 5 (15 mins): Pairs present one bias-dominated and one variance-dominated example to the class, explaining their reasoning using specific numerical evidence from the cross-validation results.

Throughout the activity, emphasize connecting mathematical concepts (bias = systematic error, variance = sensitivity to training data) to practical patterns visible in the validation results.
materials_needed: Pre-computed cross-validation results dataset (CSV format) with training/validation scores and standard deviations
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
Bias-variance analysis template worksheet (PDF)
Box plot examples showing performance distributions across CV folds
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis templates using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies bias/variance levels with specific numerical evidence and accurate explanations, (3) Identifies bias/variance correctly with some supporting evidence, (2) Partially correct identification with limited evidence, (1) Incorrect identification or minimal evidence. Also assess presentation quality where students clearly explain their reasoning using cross-validation metrics.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional guidance on interpreting the gap between training and validation scores as a key indicator. Offer sentence starters like 'The large gap between training (X%) and validation (Y%) scores suggests...' For advanced learners, extend by having them calculate bias-variance decomposition mathematically or explore how different data sizes affect the bias-variance patterns in the results.
original_title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection

title: Pizza Party Planning: Applying Fractions to Real-World Scenarios
description: Students will plan a class pizza party by applying fraction operations to determine how many pizzas to order, calculate costs, and distribute slices fairly among classmates. This hands-on activity connects mathematical concepts to authentic problem-solving situations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction addition and subtraction to calculate total pizza quantities needed by analyzing individual consumption preferences
Students will demonstrate fraction multiplication and division through determining costs per person and pizza slice distributions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Worksheet' and organizing students into groups of 3-4. Explain that each group will plan a pizza party for the entire class using real pizza restaurant menus and prices. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Groups conduct a class survey asking each student how much pizza they typically eat (options: 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, or 1 whole pizza). Record responses on the data collection sheet.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using calculators, groups add all individual fractions to determine total pizzas needed. They must show their work using common denominators and proper fraction addition techniques. For example: if 5 students want 1/2 pizza each, calculate 5 × 1/2 = 5/2 = 2 1/2 pizzas.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Groups examine provided pizza restaurant menus with actual prices. They calculate total costs by multiplying number of pizzas needed by price per pizza, expressing costs as mixed numbers when applicable.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students determine cost per person by dividing total cost by number of class members, practicing fraction division. They must convert improper fractions to mixed numbers for final answers.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Groups create a visual poster showing their calculations, including fraction operations used, total pizzas needed, total cost, and cost per student. Each group presents their solution to the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning.

Conclude by having groups compare results and discuss any differences in their calculations, identifying where fraction operations were most challenging.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Worksheets (one per group)
Real pizza restaurant menus with prices
Calculators (one per student)
Poster paper and markers
Rulers for fraction models
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of fraction calculations (40 points), (2) Proper use of mathematical procedures and showing work (30 points), (3) Clear presentation of results on poster (20 points), (4) Explanation of mathematical reasoning during presentation (10 points). Students must achieve 70% (70/100 points) to demonstrate proficiency in applying fraction operations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing fraction strips or visual models for addition/subtraction operations. Offer step-by-step calculation templates showing where to place numerators and denominators. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them calculate different pizza sizes (small, medium, large) with varying prices, or factor in tax and tip calculations using decimal operations.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Complexity
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort) by examining their code implementations, tracing through execution steps, and comparing their time complexities. They will create a comprehensive analysis report that breaks down the best, average, and worst-case scenarios for each algorithm.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by tracing through their execution steps and identifying the relationship between input size and operations performed
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through comparative analysis of Big O notation, space complexity, and practical performance implications
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three code files containing implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort in their preferred programming language. Distribute the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet template and sample datasets of sizes 10, 100, and 1000 elements.

**Phase 1 - Code Examination (20 minutes):** Students work in pairs to examine each algorithm's code structure. They must identify nested loops, recursive calls, and key operations, documenting their findings in the provided worksheet. For each algorithm, they should highlight the lines of code that contribute most significantly to time complexity.

**Phase 2 - Execution Tracing (25 minutes):** Using the dataset of 10 elements, students manually trace through 3-4 iterations of each sorting algorithm. They count the number of comparisons and swaps/moves performed, recording these metrics in their analysis worksheet. Students should create visual diagrams showing array states at key steps.

**Phase 3 - Complexity Analysis (30 minutes):** Students determine the Big O notation for each algorithm's best, average, and worst cases. They must justify their conclusions by connecting their execution traces to mathematical analysis. Using provided timing data from larger datasets, they verify their theoretical analysis against practical performance.

**Phase 4 - Comparative Report (20 minutes):** Students complete a structured comparison chart ranking the algorithms by efficiency in different scenarios (small datasets, nearly sorted data, random data, reverse-sorted data). They must provide specific recommendations for when to use each algorithm, supported by their analysis findings.
materials_needed: Three code files with bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort implementations
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet template with comparison charts
Sample datasets of varying sizes (10, 100, 1000 elements)
Timing data spreadsheet showing execution times for different input sizes
Graph paper or digital graphing tool for visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O analysis for all three algorithms (25%), (2) Quality of execution tracing with correct operation counts (25%), (3) Depth of comparative analysis with justified recommendations (30%), (4) Clear connection between theoretical analysis and practical implications (20%). Students must submit completed worksheets, execution diagrams, and final comparison report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled execution traces for the first 2 steps of each algorithm and offer a Big O reference sheet with common patterns. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity, implement hybrid sorting approaches, or extend analysis to additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort. Provide real-world datasets with different characteristics (partially sorted, duplicate values) for additional complexity analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Business Decision-Making
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning approaches (logistic regression, random forest, and neural network) applied to a customer churn prediction problem. They will evaluate model performance, business impact, and implementation feasibility to make a justified recommendation for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, interpretability, and computational requirements in a business context
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of trade-offs between accuracy, explainability, and operational constraints
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained model suite containing three customer churn prediction models trained on the Telco Customer Churn dataset, along with validation results and business context documents. Form teams of 3-4 students for 90 minutes of analysis. Each team receives identical model outputs including confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance rankings, training times, and prediction latencies. Students first spend 30 minutes individually examining each model's technical performance using provided Jupyter notebooks containing model evaluation code. Next, teams collaborate for 45 minutes to complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing models across six dimensions: predictive accuracy (F1-score, AUC), interpretability (feature transparency, business user comprehension), computational efficiency (training time, inference speed), robustness (performance across customer segments), implementation complexity (integration requirements, maintenance needs), and regulatory compliance (explainability requirements). Teams must justify ratings using quantitative evidence from model outputs and qualitative assessment of business requirements. Finally, teams spend 15 minutes preparing a 5-minute presentation defending their recommended model choice, addressing anticipated stakeholder concerns, and proposing monitoring strategies. Each presentation must include specific performance metrics, implementation timeline, resource requirements, and risk mitigation strategies. Instructors circulate during analysis phases to probe reasoning and challenge assumptions through Socratic questioning.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset with three pre-trained models (logistic regression, random forest, neural network)
Jupyter notebooks with model evaluation code and performance visualizations
Business context document including budget constraints, regulatory requirements, and stakeholder priorities
Evaluation matrix template with six assessment dimensions
Access to Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries
assessment_method: Students evaluated using rubric with four criteria: Technical Analysis (25% - accuracy of performance metric interpretation, depth of computational analysis), Critical Reasoning (35% - quality of trade-off evaluation, justification of model selection), Business Application (25% - relevance to stakeholder needs, feasibility of implementation plan), and Communication (15% - clarity of recommendation, defense against challenges). Each criterion scored on 4-point scale: Exemplary (4), Proficient (3), Developing (2), Inadequate (1). Peer evaluation component where teams score each other's presentations adds 10% weight to final assessment.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing performance metric interpretation guides and decision framework templates. Offer one-on-one guidance during individual analysis phase. For advanced learners, introduce additional evaluation criteria like model fairness across demographic groups, A/B testing design considerations, or cost-benefit analysis incorporating false positive/negative business impacts. Challenge high-performers to consider ensemble approaches or propose hybrid solutions combining multiple models.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Business Decision-Making: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning approaches (linear regression, random forest, and neural network) applied to a customer churn prediction problem. They will evaluate model performance, business impact, and implementation feasibility to make a justified recommendation for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will critically evaluate multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, interpretability, and business constraints to determine optimal deployment strategy
Students will judge the validity and reliability of model outputs through comprehensive bias analysis, cross-validation assessment, and stakeholder impact evaluation
instructions: Begin with a 15-minute briefing presenting students with a realistic business scenario: a telecommunications company experiencing 15% annual customer churn seeks to implement predictive modeling. Provide datasets containing 50,000 customer records with demographics, usage patterns, and churn outcomes. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 180 minutes to implement and evaluate three pre-specified models using provided starter code. Each team must train models using identical train/validation/test splits, then spend 60 minutes conducting systematic evaluation across five dimensions: statistical performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score), model interpretability (feature importance, SHAP values), computational efficiency (training time, inference speed), business impact (cost-benefit analysis using provided churn intervention costs), and ethical considerations (demographic bias analysis). Teams document findings in a structured evaluation matrix, identifying strengths and limitations of each approach. The final 45 minutes involves teams presenting 8-minute recommendations to simulated business stakeholders (instructor and peer evaluators), defending their chosen model while addressing challenges from the audience. Teams must justify why their selected model best balances technical performance with business requirements, demonstrating critical thinking about real-world deployment considerations including maintenance costs, regulatory compliance, and scalability constraints.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with Python 3.8+, pandas, scikit-learn, tensorflow, and SHAP libraries installed
Telecommunications customer dataset (50,000 records) with engineered features
Pre-written model implementation starter code for all three algorithms
Business cost structure document (customer acquisition costs, intervention expenses)
Evaluation matrix template spreadsheet
Presentation timer and scoring rubrics
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis (30 points - correct implementation of evaluation metrics, statistical significance testing), Critical Reasoning (25 points - depth of comparative analysis, identification of trade-offs), Business Application (25 points - realistic cost-benefit analysis, stakeholder consideration), Presentation Quality (20 points - clear communication, effective defense of recommendations). Peer evaluation contributes 15% of total score through structured feedback forms.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing evaluation checklist templates and step-by-step metric calculation guides. Offer advanced learners additional challenges: ensemble method comparison, hyperparameter optimization impact analysis, or A/B testing design for model deployment. Circulate during work time to guide teams toward balanced technical and business perspectives rather than purely algorithmic focus.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Business Decision-Making

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Multi-Variable Optimization in Real-World Systems
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model addressing a complex real-world problem with multiple constraints and variables. They will design the mathematical framework, implement computational solutions, and present their findings with rigorous mathematical justification.
estimated_duration: 6 weeks (approximately 8-10 hours total active learning time)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive multi-variable optimization model by identifying constraints, defining objective functions, and selecting appropriate mathematical techniques for a self-chosen real-world scenario
Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and computational methods through the creation of both analytical and numerical solution approaches
instructions: **Phase 1 (Week 1-2): Problem Selection and Model Design (120 minutes)** Students individually select a complex optimization problem from domains like logistics, economics, engineering, or environmental science. Examples include supply chain optimization, portfolio management, or resource allocation. They must identify at least 5 decision variables and 8 constraints. Students create a mathematical problem statement, define all variables with proper notation, and establish the objective function(s). **Phase 2 (Week 3-4): Mathematical Framework Development (180 minutes)** Students develop the complete mathematical model using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers, linear programming, or nonlinear optimization methods. They must create both exact analytical approaches (where possible) and numerical approximation methods. Students document all mathematical derivations, prove feasibility conditions, and establish bounds on solutions. **Phase 3 (Week 5): Computational Implementation (120 minutes)** Using Python, MATLAB, or R, students implement their optimization model. They must write original code that includes constraint checking, multiple solution algorithms, sensitivity analysis, and visualization of results. Code must include comprehensive comments explaining mathematical reasoning. **Phase 4 (Week 6): Validation and Presentation (90 minutes)** Students validate their model using test cases, perform sensitivity analysis on key parameters, and create a professional presentation including problem motivation, mathematical development, computational results, and practical implications. Final deliverable includes a 15-minute presentation and comprehensive written report.
materials_needed: Access to computational software (Python with scipy.optimize, MATLAB Optimization Toolbox, or R with optimization packages)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Academic databases for researching real-world optimization problems
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Students evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Rigor (25 points - completeness of constraints, objective function formulation, mathematical notation), Solution Method Innovation (25 points - creativity and appropriateness of analytical/numerical approaches), Computational Implementation (20 points - code functionality, efficiency, documentation), Problem Complexity (15 points - realistic constraints, multiple variables), and Professional Communication (15 points - clarity of presentation, mathematical exposition quality). Peer review component includes students evaluating two classmates' models for mathematical soundness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected problem scenarios with partially defined constraints, offer template code frameworks, and schedule mandatory progress check-ins every week. Create study groups for collaborative mathematical development. For advanced learners: Encourage multi-objective optimization, stochastic elements, or machine learning integration. Challenge them to compare multiple solution methodologies or extend to integer programming. Provide access to advanced optimization literature and encourage conference-style presentations.

title: Python Data Types Memory Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) and their defining characteristics through a structured flashcard activity. This foundational knowledge-building exercise uses spaced repetition and peer testing to ensure accurate recall of essential programming concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) and provide accurate definitions for each type within 30 seconds per item
Students will identify the correct syntax examples for each Python data type through verbal recitation and written matching exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards with data type names on one side and definitions/examples on the reverse (5 minutes setup). Have students work in pairs, with Partner A holding cards showing only the data type names while Partner B attempts to recite the definition and provide a syntax example (10 minutes). Partners switch roles and repeat the process (10 minutes). Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session where you call out a data type and students must immediately state its definition and give an example - use a 10-second timer for each response (8 minutes). Follow with a written matching exercise where students connect data types to their correct syntax examples without reference materials (7 minutes). title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze a correlation heatmap of customer data features to identify relationships between variables and explain how these correlations inform feature selection decisions for a churn prediction model. Through guided interpretation, students will distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while understanding their implications for model performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients in a heatmap by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3) and explaining their business meaning
Students will explain feature multicollinearity issues through identifying highly correlated variable pairs and describing their impact on model interpretability
instructions: Begin by distributing the customer churn dataset correlation heatmap (provided as both color-coded visual and numerical matrix). In pairs, students spend 5 minutes examining the heatmap to identify the darkest and lightest colored cells. Next, provide the interpretation guide showing correlation strength categories. Students then complete Part 1 (15 minutes): systematically examine each correlation coefficient, marking strong correlations in red, moderate in yellow, and weak in green on their printed heatmap. For Part 2 (20 minutes), students select three strong positive correlations and three strong negative correlations, writing 2-3 sentences explaining what each relationship means in business terms (e.g., 'Monthly charges and total charges show 0.85 correlation, indicating customers with higher monthly fees tend to have higher lifetime value'). In Part 3 (15 minutes), students identify problematic multicollinearity by finding variable pairs with correlations above 0.8, then recommend which variables to remove and justify their choices. Finally, conduct a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share their most interesting findings and multicollinearity solutions. Circulate during pair work to ensure students are correctly reading correlation values and making logical business interpretations.
materials_needed: Printed customer churn correlation heatmap (11x11 feature matrix)
Correlation coefficient interpretation guide handout
Colored markers or highlighters (red, yellow, green)
Customer feature definitions glossary
Jupyter notebook with seaborn heatmap code (optional for extension)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed heatmaps for correct correlation strength categorization (40%), quality of business interpretation explanations using domain vocabulary (35%), and logical multicollinearity identification with justified removal recommendations (25%). Success criteria: 80% accurate correlation classifications, clear explanations connecting statistical relationships to business context, identification of at least 2 multicollinearity issues with reasonable solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example interpretations for the first two correlations and highlight specific heatmap cells to examine. Include a correlation strength reference card. For advanced learners: Extend with calculating VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) values or creating their own heatmap subset focusing on specific feature categories. Challenge them to research domain-specific correlation benchmarks for telecom churn analysis.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Churn Prediction: Business Application
description: Students analyze correlation heatmaps from a customer dataset to identify relationships between features and explain how these correlations impact churn prediction model performance. They will interpret correlation coefficients and justify feature selection decisions based on multicollinearity concerns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients in heatmaps by explaining the strength and direction of relationships between customer features
Students will distinguish between useful and problematic correlations through analysis of multicollinearity patterns in churn prediction contexts
instructions:
Begin by providing each student group (3-4 students) with a pre-generated correlation heatmap from a telecom customer churn dataset containing 15 features (monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, contract_length, etc.). Display the heatmap on computers using matplotlib/seaborn with correlation values visible. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine the heatmap and identify the 5 strongest positive correlations and 5 strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values and feature pairs.

Step 2 (15 minutes): In groups, students categorize correlations into three buckets: 'Strong' (|r| > 0.7), 'Moderate' (0.3 < |r| < 0.7), and 'Weak' (|r| < 0.3). They must explain what each correlation means in business context (e.g., 'customers with longer tenure tend to have higher total charges').

Step 3 (20 minutes): Groups identify potential multicollinearity problems by flagging feature pairs with |r| > 0.8. They must explain why including both features in a churn prediction model could be problematic and propose which feature to remove and why.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each group presents one 'interesting' correlation finding to the class, explaining the business implication and whether it supports or contradicts their intuition about customer behavior.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Students individually write a brief summary explaining how they would use this correlation analysis to inform their feature selection strategy for building a churn prediction model.
materials_needed: Pre-generated correlation heatmap (matplotlib/seaborn visualization) of telecom churn dataset
Laptops/computers with Python environment or printed high-resolution heatmap copies
Correlation coefficient reference sheet with interpretation guidelines
Customer churn dataset documentation with feature descriptions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation coefficient identification and categorization (25%), (2) Quality of business context explanations for correlations (25%), (3) Correct identification of multicollinearity issues and reasonable solutions (25%), (4) Clear articulation of feature selection strategy based on correlation analysis (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by providing specific examples and justifications rather than generic statements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation interpretation guide with examples (e.g., r=0.8 means 'strong positive relationship'). Offer sentence starters like 'The correlation between X and Y suggests that...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify non-linear relationships that correlation might miss, or ask them to research Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) as an alternative multicollinearity detection method. Provide additional datasets for comparison.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Trigonometric Functions
description: Students will apply trigonometric functions, optimization principles, and geometric relationships to determine the optimal solar panel tilt angle and spacing configuration for maximum energy output at their specific latitude. This activity integrates real-world renewable energy engineering with advanced mathematical concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent) to calculate optimal solar panel tilt angles by analyzing sun elevation angles throughout the year

instructions: Begin by providing each team with their assigned latitude coordinate and solar irradiance data table. In the first 15 minutes, students research their location's solar noon sun angles for winter solstice, spring/fall equinox, and summer solstice using the formula: Sun Elevation = 90° - |Latitude - Solar Declination|. Next, teams spend 25 minutes calculating optimal panel tilt angles using trigonometric relationships. They apply the formula: Optimal Tilt = Latitude ± 15° (subtract 15° for summer optimization, add 15° for winter). Students then calculate energy collection efficiency using: Efficiency = cos(Panel Tilt - Sun Elevation) × Solar Irradiance. For the following 30 minutes, teams determine minimum row spacing to prevent shading using shadow length calculations: Shadow Length = Panel Height ÷ tan(Sun Elevation). They must ensure 90% of panels remain unshaded during peak hours (10 AM - 2 PM). Students create a comprehensive data table showing monthly energy output predictions and calculate annual totals. In the final 20 minutes, teams prepare a technical presentation including their mathematical work, optimal configuration diagram, and energy production forecast. Each presentation must demonstrate clear application of trigonometric functions, show all calculations with proper units, and justify their final recommendations based on mathematical analysis rather than intuition.
