title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Trigonometric Functions: Visual Analysis
description: Students apply trigonometric functions and optimization principles to design an efficient solar panel array for a specific geographic location. They will calculate optimal tilt angles, spacing between panels to minimize shading, and total energy output based on seasonal sun path variations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent) to calculate optimal solar panel tilt angles by analyzing sun elevation angles throughout the year
Students will implement optimization techniques through systematic calculation of panel spacing and energy output scenarios using real geographic and solar irradiance data
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a specific city's latitude, monthly sun elevation data, and average solar irradiance values (15 minutes setup). Students first calculate the optimal tilt angle using the formula: Tilt = 3.7 + (0.69 × |Latitude|), then verify by computing seasonal energy collection using E = I × A × cos(θ) where θ is the angle between panel surface and sun rays (20 minutes). Next, teams determine minimum spacing between panel rows using shadow length calculations: Shadow Length = Panel Height × cot(sun elevation angle). They must calculate this for the winter solstice when shadows are longest (25 minutes). Using grid paper scaled 1:100, students draw their array layout showing 20 panels arranged in optimal configuration, ensuring no shading occurs between 10 AM and 2 PM on December 21st (30 minutes). Teams then compute total annual energy output by calculating monthly energy production using E = Number of panels × Panel wattage × Peak sun hours × cos(incident angle) × System efficiency (0.85), summing across all months (25 minutes). Finally, students prepare a technical report including: calculated optimal tilt angle with justification, scaled array diagram with dimensions, shadow analysis calculations, monthly and annual energy projections, and cost-benefit analysis comparing their design to a standard flat installation (35 minutes). Each team presents their findings in a 5-minute presentation showing their calculations and defending their design decisions (25 minutes total for all presentations).
materials_needed: Solar irradiance data sheets for 8 different cities with varying latitudes
Grid paper (1/4 inch squares, 2 sheets per student)
Scientific calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Rulers and protractors
Solar panel specification sheets (dimensions: 1.65m × 1m, 300W rating)
Sun path angle tables for winter and summer solstice dates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accurate tilt angle calculation (20 points), correct shadow length computations with appropriate spacing (25 points), properly scaled and labeled array diagram (20 points), accurate energy output calculations showing work (25 points), and clear technical report with justified design decisions (10 points). Deduct points for computational errors, missing units, or unrealistic design constraints.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed sample calculations for one month as a template, offer trigonometric function reference cards, and pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add variables like ground albedo reflection, temperature coefficients affecting panel efficiency, or economic analysis including installation costs and payback period calculations. Consider having them optimize for both summer and winter performance simultaneously.
original_title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Trigonometric Functions

title: Reverse Engineering and Analyzing Malicious Code Patterns in Network Traffic
description: Students will analyze captured network packet data containing simulated malware communications to identify attack vectors, decode obfuscated payloads, and determine the underlying command-and-control architecture. This expert-level activity combines network security analysis, reverse engineering techniques, and threat intelligence gathering.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze network packet captures to identify malicious communication patterns by examining protocol anomalies, payload structures, and traffic timing
Students will decompose obfuscated malware payloads through static and dynamic analysis techniques to determine attack methodology and system impact
instructions: Begin by distributing three PCAP files containing different malware families (Zeus banking trojan, Cobalt Strike beacon, and ransomware C2 traffic) to teams of 2-3 students. Students first use Wireshark to examine overall traffic patterns, documenting unusual ports, protocols, and communication frequencies in a structured analysis worksheet. Next, they filter and extract suspicious payloads, particularly focusing on HTTP POST requests, DNS queries with unusual characteristics, and encrypted traffic patterns. Using hex editors and Python scripts, students decode base64-encoded payloads and analyze XOR-encrypted strings commonly found in malware communications. They then correlate findings with MITRE ATT&CK framework techniques, mapping observed behaviors to specific tactics and techniques. Students use Ghidra or IDA Free to perform static analysis on extracted executables, identifying imported functions, string references, and control flow patterns. For dynamic analysis, they set up isolated virtual machines using VMware/VirtualBox to execute samples while monitoring system calls, registry modifications, and network connections using Process Monitor and TCPView. Finally, teams create comprehensive threat intelligence reports documenting indicators of compromise (IoCs), attack timelines, and defensive recommendations. The activity concludes with team presentations where groups defend their analysis methodology and findings to simulate real-world threat intelligence briefings.
materials_needed: Three malware PCAP files (sanitized/simulated samples)
Wireshark network protocol analyzer
Python 3.x with scapy and base64 libraries
Hex editor (HxD or similar)
Ghidra or IDA Free disassembler
Isolated virtual machines with Windows/Linux
Process Monitor and TCPView utilities
MITRE ATT&CK framework reference materials
assessment_method: Students submit detailed technical reports (15 pages minimum) including: network traffic analysis summary with visual diagrams (25 points), decoded payload analysis with methodology explanation (25 points), MITRE ATT&CK technique mapping with justifications (20 points), static/dynamic analysis findings with screenshots (20 points), and actionable defensive recommendations (10 points). Presentations evaluated on technical accuracy, analytical depth, and professional delivery quality.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-configured Wireshark filters and sample Python decoding scripts as starting points. Create step-by-step guides for virtual machine setup and tool configuration. For advanced learners, introduce additional challenges like analyzing packed executables, identifying zero-day indicators, or developing custom detection signatures. Consider pairing less experienced students with those having prior security experience.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Online Shopping Behavior
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations showing the same online shopping dataset, determining which visualization best communicates customer behavior patterns. They will justify their choice using established data visualization principles and identify specific strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization approaches by applying data visualization principles to assess clarity, accuracy, and insight generation
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three visualization sheets showing identical e-commerce data: Sheet A (bar chart of purchases by age group), Sheet B (scatter plot of purchase amount vs. time spent browsing), and Sheet C (pie chart of payment methods). Each student receives all three sheets plus an evaluation matrix template.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each visualization using the provided checklist covering: data accuracy representation, visual clarity, appropriate chart type selection, and insight accessibility. They complete the evaluation matrix, rating each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and writing 2-3 sentence justifications.

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their ratings and discuss discrepancies. They must provide specific evidence from the visualizations to support their positions (e.g., 'The pie chart fails because percentages don't sum to 100%' or 'The scatter plot reveals the correlation that other charts miss').

**Final Evaluation (10 minutes):** Each student writes a one-paragraph recommendation memo identifying which visualization is most effective for helping an online retailer understand customer behavior. The memo must include: their top choice with three specific reasons, one major weakness of their chosen visualization, and one improvement suggestion.

**Debrief (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion where 3-4 students share their recommendations, highlighting different evaluation criteria that led to different conclusions.
materials_needed: Three printed visualization sheets per student (A4 size, color preferred)
Evaluation matrix template with 4 criteria rows and 3 visualization columns
Sample e-commerce dataset description (one page)
Data visualization principles reference sheet
assessment_method: Grade the evaluation matrix (40%) for completeness and reasoning quality, and the recommendation memo (60%) using rubric: excellent justification with 3+ specific evidence points (A), adequate justification with 2 evidence points (B), minimal justification with 1 evidence point (C), opinion without evidence (D). Look for use of technical vocabulary and recognition of visualization trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'The main weakness I notice is...'. Highlight specific elements to examine (axis labels, data points, legends). For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest alternative visualization types or identify the target audience that would benefit most from each approach. Encourage discussion of cultural or accessibility considerations.

title: Design a Mini Golf Course Using Geometric Transformations
description: Students will create an original 6-hole mini golf course by applying geometric transformations (translations, rotations, reflections) to design challenging obstacles and pathways. They will calculate angles, distances, and predict ball trajectories using mathematical reasoning to justify their design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original mini golf course by systematically applying geometric transformations to create at least 6 unique holes with mathematical justification
Students will construct detailed blueprints through precise geometric calculations, angle measurements, and coordinate geometry principles
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and providing each team with grid paper, rulers, protractors, and colored pencils. Introduce the challenge: design a 6-hole mini golf course where each hole demonstrates a different geometric transformation concept. Start with a 15-minute planning phase where teams brainstorm themes and sketch rough ideas. Next, spend 45 minutes on the design phase. Students must create detailed blueprints on grid paper, with each hole occupying a 10x10 grid square. Hole 1 must use translation (straight pathway with obstacles), Hole 2 requires rotation (curved paths around a central point), Hole 3 incorporates reflection (using barriers to bounce balls), Hole 4 combines two transformations, Hole 5 uses scale factor changes (varying pathway widths), and Hole 6 is student's choice combining any concepts. For each hole, students must calculate the optimal angle for the initial putt, measure all distances using coordinate geometry, and write a 2-sentence mathematical explanation justifying their design. During construction, circulate to ensure students are using precise measurements and proper geometric vocabulary. Conclude with a 20-minute gallery walk where each team presents one hole, explaining the mathematical concepts used and demonstrating the predicted ball path using a pencil as a tracer. Teams must also estimate par (number of strokes) for each hole based on geometric complexity.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers with metric measurements
Protractors
Colored pencils or markers (6 different colors)
Calculator
Mini golf course design template handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Geometric accuracy - correct application of transformations with precise measurements, (2) Mathematical justification - clear explanations using proper terminology for each hole design, (3) Creativity and complexity - innovative obstacle placement and thoughtful integration of multiple concepts, (4) Blueprint quality - neat, labeled diagrams with accurate scale and coordinate references. Students must also complete a reflection sheet explaining how they used coordinate geometry and which transformation was most challenging to implement.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn basic hole templates they can modify, offer transformation reference cards with examples, and allow use of online graphing tools for visualization. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate trigonometry for calculating optimal angles, design holes using composite transformations, or create a mathematical formula for predicting par scores based on geometric complexity and pathway length.

title: Memory Palace: Advanced Computer Architecture Component Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific names, functions, and interconnections of 50+ components within a modern CPU microarchitecture diagram. This high-stakes recall activity tests retention of complex processor design elements including execution units, cache hierarchies, and pipeline stages.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact names and primary functions of all major CPU microarchitecture components (ALUs, branch predictors, decode units, cache controllers) by completing timed identification exercises
Students will recite the specific data flow paths and control signal sequences between processor components through structured verbal presentations
instructions: Begin by distributing unlabeled microarchitecture diagrams of Intel Core i7 Skylake processor (30 minutes study time). Students receive a master reference sheet showing all 52 components labeled with names and 2-sentence function descriptions. During study phase, students must create personal memory aids - no notes allowed during testing. After study period, collect all reference materials. Present students with identical blank diagrams and component word bank containing 75 terms (23 are distractors). Students have 25 minutes to: (1) Label all components using correct terminology from word bank, (2) Draw and label 8 major data pathways with arrows, (3) Write one-sentence function description for each of 12 specified critical components (highlighted in yellow on test diagram). Proctor must enforce strict silence and monitor for any reference material use. In final 10 minutes, randomly select 8 students to verbally present one complete instruction execution path from fetch to retirement, naming each component the instruction touches. Selected students stand and trace path on wall-mounted master diagram while reciting component names and handoff processes. Record accuracy scores for both written and verbal portions. Conclude with immediate feedback session where students identify their weakest recall areas using provided self-assessment checklist of all tested components.
materials_needed: Intel Core i7 Skylake microarchitecture diagrams (labeled master copies and blank test versions)
Component word bank sheets with 75 technical terms
Yellow highlighters for marking critical components
Wall-mounted large-format processor diagram for presentations
Timer for study and testing phases
Self-assessment checklists with component categories
assessment_method: Written portion: 1 point per correctly labeled component (max 52), 2 points per accurate data pathway (max 16), 3 points per correct function description (max 36). Verbal presentation: 5 points per correctly named component in execution sequence, 3 points for accurate pathway tracing. Total possible: 140 points. Success threshold: 112 points (80%). Immediate scoring using answer key with exact terminology matching required.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students: Provide mnemonic device examples during study phase, allow creation of acronyms for component clusters, offer option to focus on 30 core components instead of full 52. Advanced learners: Challenge them to include timing specifications (clock cycles) in their descriptions, add comparative elements from ARM or RISC-V architectures, require explanation of performance implications for each pathway they trace.

title: Comparative Analysis of Bias-Variance Tradeoff Across Ensemble Methods Using Bootstrap Sampling Distributions
description: Students will analyze and interpret how different ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagging) manage the bias-variance tradeoff by examining bootstrap sampling distributions of prediction errors across multiple model complexities. They will synthesize theoretical understanding with empirical evidence to explain why certain ensemble approaches excel in different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between model complexity and bias-variance decomposition by analyzing bootstrap sampling distributions of prediction errors across three ensemble methods

Students will synthesize empirical evidence from bootstrap experiments to explain why Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Bagging demonstrate different bias-variance characteristics through comparative visualization analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed dataset (Boston Housing or Wine Quality) and three pre-configured ensemble model templates with varying complexity parameters. In pairs, students first execute 100 bootstrap samples (30 minutes) using provided Python scripts, collecting prediction errors for each ensemble method at three complexity levels: low (max_depth=3, n_estimators=10), medium (max_depth=6, n_estimators=50), and high (max_depth=12, n_estimators=200). Students then calculate bias-squared, variance, and irreducible error components for each method-complexity combination using the bias-variance decomposition formula provided. Next, they create comparative visualizations (45 minutes): box plots showing error distributions, line plots tracking bias-variance components across complexity levels, and heatmaps displaying method performance matrices. During analysis phase (30 minutes), students identify patterns by comparing how each ensemble method's bias and variance change with complexity, noting inflection points where total error begins increasing. They must explain these patterns using ensemble theory: Random Forest's decorrelated trees reducing variance, Gradient Boosting's sequential learning reducing bias but potentially increasing variance, and Bagging's bootstrap aggregation primarily targeting variance reduction. Students conclude by synthesizing findings into a structured comparison matrix, documenting which method performs best under high-bias vs. high-variance scenarios, and justifying their interpretations using both empirical results and theoretical ensemble principles. Instructor circulates to guide interpretation discussions and ensure students connect mathematical decomposition results to conceptual understanding.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with scikit-learn, numpy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Pre-processed dataset (Boston Housing or Wine Quality) with train/test splits
Python template scripts for bootstrap sampling and bias-variance decomposition calculations
Ensemble model configuration files (RandomForestRegressor, GradientBoostingRegressor, BaggingRegressor)
Comparison matrix template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate calculation and interpretation of bias-variance components for all method-complexity combinations, (2) Correct identification of patterns and inflection points in visualizations, (3) Theoretically sound explanations connecting empirical results to ensemble principles, (4) Clear synthesis of when each method excels based on bias-variance characteristics. Students must demonstrate understanding by accurately explaining at least 2 key differences between methods and providing evidence-based recommendations for method selection.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated example calculations for one method-complexity pair and guided questions for pattern identification ('What happens to Random Forest variance as n_estimators increases?'). For advanced learners: Extend analysis to include cross-validation stability, computational complexity tradeoffs, or additional ensemble methods like XGBoost. Consider adding hyperparameter sensitivity analysis or feature importance correlation with bias-variance patterns.

title: Budget Planning for a School Fundraiser: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create and analyze a realistic budget for organizing a school bake sale fundraiser. They will calculate expenses, profit margins, and price adjustments while working with real-world scenarios that require multiple percentage operations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine pricing, expenses, and profit margins by creating a comprehensive fundraiser budget
Students will calculate percentage increases and decreases through analyzing various budget scenarios and making pricing adjustments
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Budget Planning Worksheet and scenario cards to each pair of students. Display the sample cost breakdown on the board: ingredients ($50), supplies ($15), advertising ($10). **Introduction (10 minutes):** Explain that students are planning a bake sale to raise money for new playground equipment costing $500. Each pair receives a scenario card with their assigned bake sale items (brownies, cookies, cupcakes, or muffins). **Activity Phase 1 (15 minutes):** Students calculate their total expenses using the base costs, then add a 20% contingency buffer for unexpected costs. They must show their work: Base cost + (Base cost × 0.20) = Total budget needed. **Activity Phase 2 (15 minutes):** Students determine selling prices by calculating a 150% markup on ingredient costs per item. If ingredients cost $2.00 per dozen cookies, students calculate: $2.00 × 2.50 = $5.00 selling price per dozen. **Activity Phase 3 (10 minutes):** Students calculate how many items they need to sell to reach their portion of the $500 goal (each pair needs to raise $125). They divide their target amount by profit per item. **Challenge Round (10 minutes):** Present a scenario where costs increase by 15% due to supply shortages. Students recalculate budgets and determine new selling prices or sales targets. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Each pair presents one key calculation to the class, explaining their percentage application and reasoning.
materials_needed: Budget Planning Worksheet (printed copies)
Scenario cards with different bake sale items
Calculators
Chart paper for final presentations
Markers or colored pencils
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly applies all percentage calculations with proper formulas and achieves realistic budget goals; (3) Applies most percentage calculations correctly with minor computational errors; (2) Shows understanding of percentage concepts but makes calculation mistakes; (1) Attempts percentage calculations but shows fundamental misunderstandings. Check worksheets for proper formula usage, accurate calculations, and logical reasoning in scenario responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage conversion charts (50% = 0.5, 150% = 1.5) and calculator keystroke guides for percentage calculations. Break down multi-step problems into smaller chunks with checkpoints. For advanced learners: Add variables like sales tax (8.5%) on purchases, bulk discount calculations (buy 10+ items, save 12%), or profit-sharing percentages among team members. Challenge them to create break-even analysis charts.

title: Budget Planning for a School Fundraiser: Applying Percentage Calculations: Exercise 1
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic budget for organizing a school bake sale fundraiser. They will calculate costs, profits, discounts, and tax to determine if their fundraising goal can be met.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine ingredient costs, selling prices, and profit margins by creating a detailed fundraiser budget
Students will calculate tax amounts and discount scenarios through real-world problem-solving situations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Bake Sale Budget Worksheet' and explaining that each student group (2-3 students) will plan a fundraiser with a $500 goal. Provide the ingredient price list showing flour ($3.50/5lb bag), sugar ($2.80/4lb bag), eggs ($3.00/dozen), butter ($4.20/lb), etc. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Groups select 3 baked goods to sell and research typical recipes to determine ingredient quantities needed for 50 items of each type. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students calculate total ingredient costs by applying unit pricing. They must show work: if cookies need 2 cups flour and there are 18 cups per bag, they calculate 2÷18 = 0.11 bags needed, then 0.11 × $3.50 = $0.39 flour cost per batch.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Calculate selling prices by applying a 250% markup to ingredient costs (multiply by 2.5). Round to nearest quarter.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Apply 8.5% sales tax to determine final customer prices. Students calculate: selling price × 1.085.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Calculate total revenue if all items sell, then subtract ingredient costs to find net profit. Compare to $500 goal.

Step 6 (5 minutes): Apply discount scenarios - calculate new profit if 25% of items sell at 20% discount for end-of-day sales.

Groups present their budgets showing all percentage calculations with proper mathematical notation and explain whether their fundraiser would succeed.
materials_needed: Bake Sale Budget Worksheet (printed copies)
Ingredient price list handout
Calculators
Recipe resource sheets or internet access
Poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown, realistic pricing, accurate profit projections; (3) Minor calculation errors, mostly correct methodology; (2) Some calculation errors, unclear work shown; (1) Major errors in percentage applications or incomplete work. Observe group discussions for understanding of percentage concepts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed examples of markup and tax calculations, offer percentage calculation reference cards (e.g., 'to find 8.5% tax: multiply by 0.085'), pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including overhead costs (table rental, advertising), calculate break-even points, or analyze profit margins for different markup percentages (200%, 300%, 350%).
original_title: Budget Planning for a School Fundraiser: Applying Percentage Calculations

title: Budget Planning for a School Fundraiser: Applying Percentage Calculations: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic budget for a school fundraiser event. They will calculate costs, profits, and allocate funds across different expense categories using real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine profit margins, tax amounts, and budget allocations by creating a complete fundraiser budget
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage operations through solving authentic financial planning problems
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Fundraiser Planning Packet' containing scenario details: the school needs to raise $2,000 for new playground equipment through a bake sale and carnival games. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes.

Step 1 (10 minutes): Review the scenario and explain that students must calculate various percentages. Each pair receives a budget template with categories: ingredients/supplies (40% of expected revenue), volunteer incentives (15%), advertising (10%), equipment rental (20%), and profit goal (remaining percentage).

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students calculate dollar amounts for each category based on a projected revenue of $3,500. They must show work for each calculation: $3,500 × 0.40 = $1,400 for supplies, etc. Students then calculate the profit percentage and determine if it meets the $2,000 goal.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Present a 'challenge scenario': due to weather, revenue drops to $2,800. Students recalculate all categories using the same percentages and determine new profit amount.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students create a brief presentation slide showing original budget, revised budget, and whether the fundraising goal was met. They must explain their calculations and suggest one alternative solution if the goal wasn't reached.

Circulate continuously to check calculations and provide hints. Remind students to convert percentages to decimals before multiplying and to round to nearest cent for realistic monetary values.
materials_needed: Fundraiser Planning Packet (printed scenario with revenue projections)
Budget calculation template worksheets
Calculators
Presentation slides template (digital or paper)
Colored pens/pencils for budget categories
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown, realistic budget created, challenge scenario completed accurately; (3) Most calculations correct with minor errors, budget mostly realistic; (2) Some calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of percentage application; (1) Significant errors in calculations or incomplete work. Check final presentations for accurate profit calculations and logical alternative solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a conversion chart showing common percentages as decimals (40% = 0.40), and offer a step-by-step calculation guide. Consider pairing with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including sales tax calculations (8.5% on supplies), multi-day events with varying daily revenues, or compound percentage scenarios like 'early bird' discounts that affect overall revenue projections.
original_title: Budget Planning for a School Fundraiser: Applying Percentage Calculations

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Breakdown
description: Students will analyze and compare the time and space complexity of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code structure, identifying key operations, and evaluating performance trade-offs. They will create detailed complexity breakdowns and justify which algorithm is most appropriate for specific scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and key operations within each algorithm's implementation
Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through systematic examination of memory allocation patterns and auxiliary space requirements in different sorting approaches
instructions: Begin by providing students with implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in their preferred programming language (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning each team one algorithm to focus on initially. Each team spends 25 minutes creating a line-by-line analysis document that identifies: (1) all loops and their iteration counts, (2) recursive function calls and their depth, (3) comparison and swap operations, and (4) additional memory allocations. Teams must create a visual flowchart showing the algorithm's execution path and mark each section with its contribution to overall complexity. Next, teams rotate and spend 20 minutes reviewing another team's algorithm using the same analysis framework, comparing their findings with the original team's work. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents a 5-minute comparative analysis where they demonstrate: the Big O notation for both time and space complexity, best/average/worst case scenarios with specific input examples, and provide a recommendation matrix showing which algorithm to use for different data characteristics (small datasets, nearly sorted data, memory-constrained environments, etc.). Teams must support their recommendations with specific evidence from their complexity analysis.
materials_needed: Code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort
Large sheets of paper or digital whiteboard access for flowcharts
Complexity analysis worksheet template
Timer for rotation activities
Computers with programming environment or code viewing capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of complexity identification - correctly identifies all loops, recursions, and operations (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis - demonstrates clear understanding of trade-offs between algorithms (30%), (3) Justification of recommendations - provides evidence-based reasoning for algorithm selection in different scenarios (30%), (4) Presentation clarity - effectively communicates findings with proper use of Big O notation (15%). Students must submit their analysis documents and recommendation matrix.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed analysis template with some complexity components already identified, and offer guiding questions like 'How many times does this loop execute?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional factors like cache performance, parallel processing potential, or implement hybrid approaches that combine multiple algorithms based on input characteristics.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Breakdown: Comparative Study
description: Students will systematically analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort) by examining their code structures, tracing execution patterns, and comparing time/space complexities. They will identify performance bottlenecks and justify which algorithm is most efficient for specific data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort by examining their algorithmic structures and counting operations
Students will compare algorithm performance characteristics through systematic code tracing and complexity calculation exercises
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet containing pseudocode for all three sorting algorithms and three test datasets: small array (10 elements), large sorted array (1000 elements), and large reverse-sorted array (1000 elements). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Each group examines the bubble sort algorithm first. Students trace through the algorithm using the small dataset, counting the number of comparisons and swaps. They record their findings in the provided table and identify the nested loop structure that determines complexity.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Groups repeat the analysis process for merge sort, focusing on the divide-and-conquer approach. Students draw the recursion tree for the small dataset and calculate operations at each level. They identify how the algorithm breaks down the problem and merges results.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students analyze quick sort, paying special attention to partition operations and pivot selection. They trace execution for both best-case (balanced partitions) and worst-case (unbalanced partitions) scenarios using different datasets.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Groups complete the comparison matrix, filling in Big-O notation for time complexity (best, average, worst cases) and space complexity for each algorithm. They must provide mathematical justification for each entry.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Students write recommendations for when to use each algorithm based on their analysis. They consider factors like input size, data ordering, and memory constraints. Each group presents one key finding to the class for discussion.
materials_needed: Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with pseudocode and data tables
Three test datasets (small, large sorted, large reverse-sorted)
Calculators or computers for complexity calculations
Whiteboard markers for group work
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all complexity measures with mathematical justification and provides accurate algorithm recommendations; (3) Correctly identifies most complexity measures with minor calculation errors; (2) Identifies basic complexity patterns but lacks detailed justification; (1) Shows minimal understanding of algorithmic analysis concepts. Also assess group presentation quality and peer discussion contributions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed trace examples for the first few iterations of each algorithm and offer a complexity calculation reference sheet. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or consider real-world implementation factors like cache performance and parallelization potential. Encourage them to research hybrid sorting approaches used in production systems.
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Breakdown

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness and ethical implications of three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, Neural Network, and Logistic Regression) used to predict patient readmission risks. They will assess model performance metrics, identify potential biases, and make evidence-based recommendations for clinical implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and feature importance across different patient demographics
Students will critique the ethical implications and potential biases of healthcare prediction models through systematic bias detection and fairness metric analysis
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Model Performance Analysis**
Provide student teams of 3-4 with the healthcare dataset containing 10,000 patient records and three pre-trained models. Each team receives identical performance reports showing accuracy, precision, recall, F1-scores, and AUC-ROC curves for all three models across different demographic groups (age, gender, ethnicity, insurance type). Students must first individually analyze the numerical metrics, then collaborate to identify which model performs best overall and for specific subgroups.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Bias Detection and Ethical Assessment**
Teams use the provided bias detection framework to examine each model's predictions across protected classes. They calculate equalized odds, demographic parity, and individual fairness metrics using the supplied Python notebooks. Students must document instances where models show discriminatory patterns and assess the severity of these biases in healthcare contexts.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Evidence-Based Recommendation Development**
Teams synthesize their technical analysis with ethical considerations to develop implementation recommendations. They must justify their choice of preferred model, propose bias mitigation strategies, and outline monitoring protocols for clinical deployment. Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation with specific evidence supporting their recommendations.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Peer Evaluation and Critique**
Teams present their recommendations while other teams use structured evaluation forms to assess the quality of evidence, logical reasoning, and completeness of ethical considerations. Presenters must defend their choices against peer challenges and incorporate valid criticisms into final written recommendations.
materials_needed: De-identified hospital readmission dataset (10,000 records) with demographic variables
Three pre-trained ML models (Random Forest, Neural Network, Logistic Regression) with performance reports
Jupyter notebooks with bias detection algorithms and fairness metrics calculations
Structured peer evaluation rubrics for presentations
Access to Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, and fairlearn libraries
assessment_method: Students submit a 1500-word written report (60%) containing: quantitative comparison table of model performance (15%), bias analysis with specific examples and metrics (20%), implementation recommendation with justification (15%), and ethical considerations discussion (10%). Presentation quality and peer defense accounts for 25%. Peer evaluation participation worth 15%. Success requires demonstrating critical thinking beyond surface-level metrics, identifying at least 3 specific bias instances, and providing actionable recommendations supported by evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide model performance interpretation guide, bias detection checklist, and recommendation template with sentence starters. Assign stronger technical students as 'consultants' for statistical interpretation. For advanced learners: challenge them to propose novel fairness metrics, design A/B testing protocols for model comparison, or develop cost-benefit analyses incorporating false positive/negative impacts in healthcare settings. Provide additional datasets from different hospitals for cross-validation analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) trained on a heart disease prediction dataset. They will evaluate model performance using multiple metrics, identify potential biases, and make evidence-based recommendations for clinical deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and ROC curves within a healthcare prediction context
Students will critique model limitations and biases through systematic analysis of feature importance, demographic performance disparities, and clinical applicability
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-trained models on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset, each with validation results saved as pickle files. In the first 30 minutes, students individually examine model outputs including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices for each algorithm. They must calculate and compare specificity, sensitivity, and positive/negative predictive values. Next, spend 45 minutes having students work in pairs to conduct bias analysis by examining model performance across demographic subgroups (age brackets: <45, 45-65, >65; gender; chest pain types). Students must identify performance disparities and research clinical implications of false positives vs. false negatives in cardiac diagnosis. In the following 60 minutes, pairs analyze feature importance plots for each model, evaluating which clinical indicators drive predictions and assessing medical validity through literature research. Students must identify potentially problematic features that could introduce bias or lack clinical support. For the final 45 minutes, each pair creates a detailed evaluation report ranking the three models with specific recommendations for clinical deployment, including patient populations where each model performs best/worst, implementation considerations, and required monitoring protocols. Pairs present 8-minute recommendations to the class, defending their choices against peer questioning.
materials_needed: Cleveland Heart Disease dataset with 303 patient records
Three pre-trained model files (RandomForest.pkl, XGBoost.pkl, NeuralNet.pkl) with validation predictions
Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn
Access to PubMed or medical literature database
Model performance visualization templates (ROC curve, feature importance plots)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Model Performance Analysis (25 points - accurate calculation and interpretation of all metrics), Bias Assessment (25 points - thorough demographic analysis with specific examples), Clinical Validity Evaluation (25 points - evidence-based critique of feature importance with literature support), Final Recommendation (25 points - clear ranking with justified reasoning for deployment decisions). Students must demonstrate critical thinking by identifying at least 3 specific limitations per model and providing concrete implementation recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide metric calculation templates and guided questions for each analysis section. Offer a checklist of bias types to investigate (selection, measurement, algorithmic). For advanced learners, require additional analysis of model calibration, cost-benefit analysis of false positive/negative rates in clinical settings, and consideration of regulatory requirements (FDA approval pathways). Encourage exploration of fairness metrics like demographic parity and equalized odds.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Real Estate Market Dynamics
description: Students will develop an original mathematical model that predicts housing price fluctuations in a specific metropolitan area using multivariable calculus, statistical regression, and economic theory. They will then validate their model against historical data and present policy recommendations based on their findings.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multivariable calculus, linear algebra, and statistical methods by constructing an original predictive model for complex real-world economic data
Students will formulate mathematical relationships between economic variables through rigorous data analysis and theoretical justification of model parameters
instructions: Begin by having students select a specific metropolitan area and gather 5-7 years of housing data from sources like Zillow Research, Census Bureau, and Federal Reserve Economic Data (20 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to identify 6-8 independent variables (interest rates, unemployment, population growth, construction permits, etc.) and justify their theoretical relationships to housing prices using economic principles (45 minutes research and discussion). Next, students construct their mathematical model by: (1) defining functional relationships between variables using calculus concepts like partial derivatives to show rate of change effects, (2) applying multiple regression analysis to determine coefficients, and (3) incorporating time-lag effects using difference equations (90 minutes model construction). Students must then validate their model by splitting their dataset chronologically, training on earlier data and testing predictions against the most recent 18 months (30 minutes validation). Have students calculate R-squared values, mean absolute percentage error, and conduct residual analysis to assess model accuracy (20 minutes statistical analysis). Students create a comprehensive presentation including: mathematical derivation of their model, graphical representations of relationships, validation results, sensitivity analysis showing how changes in key variables affect predictions, and three specific policy recommendations for city planners or investors (60 minutes presentation preparation). Conclude with 8-minute presentations per team followed by peer questioning sessions where other teams challenge model assumptions and methodology (40 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Statistical software (R, Python with pandas/scikit-learn, or Stata)
Access to economic databases (FRED, Census Bureau, Zillow Research)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Presentation software with mathematical equation support
Historical housing and economic data spreadsheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correct application of calculus/statistics concepts (25 points), Model originality and theoretical justification (20 points), Validation methodology and statistical analysis quality (20 points), Accuracy of predictions when tested against holdout data (15 points), Quality of policy recommendations with mathematical support (10 points), Presentation clarity and ability to defend model during peer questioning (10 points). Success requires scoring 80+ points with no category below 60% proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template equations for common economic relationships, offer guided practice with simpler single-variable models first, and allow use of Excel instead of advanced statistical software. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate non-linear relationships, multiple metropolitan areas for comparison, or machine learning techniques like neural networks; encourage exploration of spatial econometrics or time series analysis methods like ARIMA models.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall basic syntax elements from Python programming language through structured flashcard drilling and peer testing. This activity focuses on building foundational recall of essential Python keywords, operators, and syntax symbols.
learning_objectives: Students will identify Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, return) by matching them to their correct definitions within 3 seconds per card
Students will recall Python operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) through verbal recitation with 90% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 Python syntax elements (10 keywords, 10 operators) with definitions/examples on reverse sides. Give students 15 minutes for individual study time to review all cards, reading both sides and practicing recall. Next, pair students and have them take turns testing each other for 10 minutes - one partner shows the syntax element, the other must provide the definition/usage within 3 seconds. Partners should keep track of correct responses on the provided scoring sheet. After paired practice, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire round where you display syntax elements on screen for 3 seconds each while students write answers on individual whiteboards. Hold up boards simultaneously for immediate visual assessment. Follow with a second round using definitions/examples where students must recall the corresponding syntax element. Conclude with students sorting their original flashcards into three piles: 'mastered' (recalled correctly both times), 'needs practice' (recalled once), and 'must study' (recalled incorrectly both times). Have students record their pile counts and identify their top 5 syntax elements requiring additional study for homework review.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (20 cards per student) with Python syntax elements
Individual mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers
Scoring sheets for partner testing
Timer or stopwatch
Computer/projector for whole-class rapid-fire round
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly identifying 16/20 syntax elements (80%) during the rapid-fire rounds. Use whiteboard responses for immediate formative assessment, recording individual scores on class roster. Success criteria: accurate spelling of syntax elements, correct matching of keywords/operators to definitions, completion of self-assessment sorting activity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide cards with first letter hints, allow 5-second response time, or pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: include additional syntax elements (try/except, lambda, list comprehension symbols), require students to provide code examples rather than just definitions, or have them create new flashcards for other students.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Data Analysis
description: Students will analyze a curated real estate dataset to distinguish between correlational and causal relationships among variables like home price, square footage, school ratings, and crime rates. They will interpret correlation matrices and scatter plots to explain why strong correlations don't necessarily imply causation.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing correlation coefficients and identifying potential confounding variables in real estate data
Students will interpret correlation matrices and scatter plots through systematic examination of statistical relationships and their underlying mechanisms
instructions:
Begin by providing each group of 3-4 students with the pre-loaded real estate dataset containing 500 properties with variables: price, square footage, bedrooms, school rating, crime index, distance to downtown, and year built. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the correlation matrix showing relationships between all variables. Have them identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording the correlation coefficients.

Step 2 (20 minutes): For each identified correlation, students create scatter plots and discuss whether the relationship suggests causation or mere correlation. Provide guiding questions: 'Could Variable A directly cause changes in Variable B?' and 'What other factors might influence both variables?'

Step 3 (25 minutes): Present three specific scenarios: (a) School rating vs. home price (r=0.78), (b) Square footage vs. number of bedrooms (r=0.65), and (c) Crime index vs. distance to downtown (r=-0.43). Students must categorize each as 'likely causal,' 'likely correlational only,' or 'unclear' and provide written justification.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Groups identify potential confounding variables for each correlational relationship. For example, neighborhood socioeconomic status might influence both school ratings and home prices.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each group presents one example where they initially thought correlation implied causation but reconsidered after identifying confounding variables. Facilitate class discussion on why this distinction matters in data-driven decision making.

Conclude with students completing individual reflection worksheets summarizing key differences between correlation and causation with specific examples from their analysis.
materials_needed: Real estate dataset (CSV file with 500 properties and 7 variables)
Jupyter notebooks or Excel with data analysis capabilities
Pre-generated correlation matrix handout
Scatter plot template worksheets
Individual reflection worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of correlation coefficients and their strength, (2) Correct categorization of relationships as causal vs. correlational with sound reasoning, (3) Identification of at least 2 plausible confounding variables per scenario, (4) Clear written explanations demonstrating understanding of why correlation doesn't imply causation. Students must score 3/4 on each criterion to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide (0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong) and sentence starters like 'This correlation might be explained by...' For advanced learners, introduce concepts of partial correlation or have them research additional variables that might strengthen causal arguments, such as temporal data or natural experiments in housing markets.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Data Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real estate dataset to identify correlations between variables and distinguish between correlation and causation. They will create visualizations and provide written explanations demonstrating their understanding of when correlations may or may not imply causal relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing relationships in housing price data and identifying confounding variables
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots through guided analysis of at least five variable pairs in real estate data
instructions: Begin by providing students with a cleaned real estate dataset containing 1000+ records with variables: house price, square footage, number of bedrooms, age of house, distance to city center, crime rate, and school rating. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to calculate correlation coefficients between house price and each other variable using provided correlation matrix templates. Step 2 (20 minutes): Each pair creates scatter plots for the three strongest correlations they identified, adding trend lines and noting the correlation strength. Step 3 (25 minutes): Present students with three specific scenarios: 'Houses with more bedrooms cost more,' 'Houses farther from city center cost less,' and 'Older houses have lower school ratings nearby.' For each scenario, students must determine whether the correlation suggests causation and identify potential confounding variables. They complete a structured worksheet with sections for correlation strength, potential causal relationship (yes/no), alternative explanations, and confounding variables. Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs present one scenario to another pair, explaining their reasoning and receiving feedback. Step 5 (10 minutes): Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion highlighting common misconceptions and reinforcing that correlation does not equal causation, using student examples from their analysis.
materials_needed: Real estate dataset (CSV file with 1000+ records)
Correlation matrix calculation template (Excel or Google Sheets)
Scatter plot creation tool (Excel, Google Sheets, or Python/matplotlib)
Correlation vs. Causation analysis worksheet (printed or digital)
Calculator or computer with spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strength, accurately distinguishes correlation from causation, provides multiple relevant confounding variables; (3) Mostly accurate correlation identification, generally distinguishes correlation/causation with minor errors; (2) Some accuracy in correlation identification, attempts to distinguish correlation/causation; (1) Limited accuracy in correlation identification, minimal understanding of correlation vs. causation. Additionally, assess scatter plots for accurate representation of data and appropriate trend lines.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation coefficient interpretation guide (0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong) and offer sentence starters like 'This correlation might not show causation because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to research additional variables that might affect house prices, calculate partial correlations controlling for one variable, or explore non-linear relationships in the data. Provide examples of Simpson's Paradox if students show strong understanding.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Data Analysis

title: Optimization Design Challenge: Maximizing Solar Panel Efficiency Through Calculus Applications
description: Students apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving solar panel placement and angle calculations. They will use derivative applications, constraint optimization, and trigonometric functions to determine optimal configurations for maximum energy output given specific geographical and structural limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply first and second derivative tests to optimize solar panel angle and spacing by analyzing energy output functions with respect to seasonal sun position data
Students will implement Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems through calculating maximum solar energy capture within given roof space and budget limitations
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a scenario packet containing: roof dimensions (40ft x 60ft), location coordinates (Chicago, IL), seasonal sun angle data, panel specifications, and a $50,000 budget constraint. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a different season to focus on initially (15 minutes setup). 

Students first model the solar energy function E(θ,s) where θ represents panel tilt angle and s represents panel spacing. They must incorporate the given sun angle data, panel efficiency ratings, and shading effects between panels. Provide the base energy formula and have students modify it for their specific constraints (45 minutes). 

Next, teams apply calculus optimization techniques: find critical points using partial derivatives, apply second derivative tests for maxima/minima, and use Lagrange multipliers to handle the budget and space constraints. Students must show all mathematical work including derivative calculations and constraint equations (60 minutes). 

Teams then use graphing software (Desmos 3D or GeoGebra) to visualize their optimization functions and verify their analytical solutions. They must create 3D surface plots showing energy output versus angle and spacing variables (30 minutes). 

Finally, each team presents their optimal configuration with mathematical justification, comparing their season-specific results with other teams. They must address how their solution changes across seasons and propose a year-round optimization strategy using weighted averages of seasonal data (45 minutes presentations and discussion).
materials_needed: Solar panel specification sheets with efficiency curves and dimensions
Chicago solar irradiance data by month with sun angle tables
Roof layout templates (40ft x 60ft) with obstacle markings
Graphing calculators or computers with Desmos 3D/GeoGebra access
Cost breakdown sheets for panels, inverters, and installation materials
Large poster paper and markers for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of optimization calculations (40 points) - correct partial derivatives, critical point identification, and Lagrange multiplier application; Problem setup and constraint modeling (25 points) - appropriate energy function formulation and constraint equations; Technology integration (15 points) - accurate 3D visualizations that support analytical work; Communication and justification (20 points) - clear presentation of methodology and results with proper mathematical notation. Students must submit all calculation work, computer visualizations, and a 2-page technical summary of their optimal solution.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed energy function templates and step-by-step derivative calculation guides. Offer one-on-one support during the mathematical optimization phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables such as panel degradation over time, varying weather patterns, or optimization across multiple roof orientations. Encourage investigation of dynamic optimization where panel angles adjust seasonally versus fixed installations.

title: Database Query Optimization Analysis: Deconstructing Performance Bottlenecks in E-commerce Systems
description: Students will analyze a complex e-commerce database with multiple performance issues, systematically identifying bottlenecks through query execution plans and performance metrics. They will deconstruct the relationships between schema design, indexing strategies, and query performance to determine root causes of inefficiencies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database query execution plans by interpreting cost metrics, join operations, and index usage patterns to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will deconstruct the relationships between table structures, indexing strategies, and query performance through systematic performance profiling and schema examination
instructions: Begin by providing students with a PostgreSQL database containing an e-commerce schema (customers, orders, products, order_items tables) with 100,000+ records and intentionally poor optimization. In pairs, students first spend 15 minutes exploring the schema using \d commands to understand table relationships and existing indexes. Next, provide 8 pre-written queries of varying complexity (simple selects, multi-table joins, aggregate functions with GROUP BY, subqueries) that exhibit different performance issues. Students execute each query while timing execution and capturing query plans using EXPLAIN ANALYZE. For 45 minutes, they systematically document execution times, scan types (sequential vs. index), join algorithms used, and memory usage for each query. Students then analyze patterns by categorizing bottlenecks into schema design issues (missing foreign keys, poor normalization), indexing problems (missing indexes, unused indexes, wrong index types), and query structure issues (inefficient joins, unnecessary subqueries). In the final 30 minutes, pairs create a prioritized remediation plan, ranking issues by performance impact and implementation difficulty. They must justify their analysis using specific metrics from execution plans and propose concrete solutions (specific index creations, query rewrites, or schema modifications). Each pair presents their top 3 findings with supporting evidence from their performance analysis.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database server with sample e-commerce dataset (100K+ records)
Database client software (pgAdmin, DBeaver, or command-line psql)
Pre-written SQL query set with performance issues
Performance analysis worksheet template
Stopwatch or timing functionality
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification using execution plan metrics (25%), (2) Quality of root cause analysis linking schema/indexing to performance issues (30%), (3) Justification of remediation priorities using quantitative evidence (25%), (4) Technical precision in interpreting query execution plans and database concepts (20%). Students must submit documented analysis with execution times, screenshots of query plans, and written justifications for their conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a query plan interpretation guide with common patterns and a structured analysis template. Offer pre-filled examples for the first 2 queries. For advanced learners, include additional complex queries with CTEs, window functions, or provide a second database system (MySQL) for comparative analysis. Consider adding memory usage analysis and buffer hit ratios for deeper investigation.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which chart type most effectively communicates key business insights. They will use established data visualization principles to justify their evaluation and provide specific recommendations for improvement.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, pie chart, line graph) by applying data visualization best practices criteria
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Customer Sales by Region' dataset (15 data points showing quarterly sales across 5 regions) along with three pre-made visualizations of this data: a horizontal bar chart, a pie chart, and a line graph (10 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4 people. Provide each group with the 'Visualization Evaluation Checklist' containing 6 criteria: clarity of message, appropriate chart type for data, readability of labels/legends, use of color, accuracy of representation, and actionability for business decisions. Each criterion uses a 1-5 scale with specific descriptors. Groups spend 25 minutes systematically evaluating each visualization against all criteria, documenting scores and written justifications. Students must identify the target audience (sales managers making quarterly decisions) and business question (which regions need attention). Next, groups rank the three visualizations from most to least effective (10 minutes), providing evidence-based reasoning. Each group creates a 5-minute presentation defending their ranking and suggesting two specific improvements for the lowest-ranked visualization (15 minutes preparation). During presentations (20 minutes total), other groups can challenge rankings using evidence from the checklist. Conclude with a brief class discussion comparing group conclusions and identifying common evaluation themes (10 minutes). Provide worksheet templates for systematic documentation throughout the activity.
materials_needed: Customer Sales by Region dataset (printed handouts)
Three pre-made visualizations of the same data (bar chart, pie chart, line graph)
Visualization Evaluation Checklist with 1-5 scoring rubric
Presentation planning worksheets
Computers or tablets for presentation creation (optional)
assessment_method: Grade based on completed evaluation checklist (40% - accuracy of criteria application), quality of written justifications (30% - use of specific evidence), ranking defense presentation (20% - logical reasoning and evidence use), and improvement suggestions (10% - feasibility and specificity). Success criteria: Students score 3+ on all checklist items, provide evidence-based justifications, and offer actionable improvement recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example evaluation of a fourth visualization as a model, highlight key criteria definitions, and pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Add evaluation of color accessibility, request alternative visualization suggestions, or have them create their own improved version using tools like Google Sheets. Consider providing sentence starters for justifications: 'This visualization is effective/ineffective because...' and 'The evidence for this is...'

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making: Business Application
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same sales dataset to determine which is most effective for business decision-making. They will apply evaluation criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness to make evidence-based judgments about visualization quality.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying established criteria for clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will justify their choice of best visualization through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by displaying three different visualizations of the same monthly sales data: a cluttered 3D pie chart with 12+ categories, a clean horizontal bar chart with top 5 categories, and a line graph showing trends over time. Provide students with the evaluation criteria sheet listing: clarity (can viewers quickly understand the main message?), accuracy (does the visualization represent data truthfully without distortion?), and audience appropriateness (suitable for business executives making quarterly decisions?). 

Step 1 (10 min): Students individually examine each visualization and rate them 1-5 on each criterion, writing brief justifications. 

Step 2 (15 min): Form groups of 3-4 students to discuss their individual ratings and reach consensus on which visualization is most effective overall. Groups must document their reasoning using specific evidence from the visualizations.

Step 3 (10 min): Each group presents their choice and top two reasons to the class in 90 seconds or less.

Step 4 (10 min): Facilitate class discussion comparing group decisions and reasoning. Highlight how different evaluation priorities (quick overview vs. trend analysis) might lead to different 'best' choices.

Step 5 (5 min): Students individually write a final reflection identifying which criterion they found most important and why, connecting to real-world data science applications.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of identical sales data (one per student)
Evaluation criteria reference sheet with 3-point rubric for each criterion
Blank evaluation worksheets for individual ratings
Flipchart paper and markers for group work
assessment_method: Evaluate students on: (1) Individual evaluation worksheet showing ratings and justifications for each visualization (40%), (2) Quality of group reasoning and evidence used in presentation (40%), (3) Final reflection demonstrating understanding of evaluation criteria and real-world application (20%). Success criteria: Students provide specific evidence for ratings, connect evaluation to business context, and demonstrate understanding that 'best' depends on purpose and audience.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is clear because...' and highlight specific elements to examine in each chart. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest improvements for the weakest visualization or consider how different stakeholders (sales team vs. executives) might evaluate differently. Provide additional visualization types for comparison if groups finish early.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making: Exercise 2
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations of the same sales dataset, evaluating their effectiveness for specific business audiences. They will justify their rankings using established visualization principles and recommend improvements for the weakest visualization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data visualizations by applying design principles and assessing audience appropriateness
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for improvement
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with three printed visualizations of monthly sales data: a cluttered pie chart with 12+ segments, a clean bar chart with proper labeling, and a line chart with inconsistent scaling (15 minutes setup). Distribute the 'Visualization Evaluation Worksheet' containing evaluation criteria: clarity, accuracy, audience appropriateness, and visual design principles. 

Students work individually for 25 minutes to complete Part 1: ranking the three visualizations from most to least effective for a business executive audience, using the provided criteria checklist. They must provide specific evidence for each ranking decision, citing elements like color usage, label clarity, data-ink ratio, and cognitive load.

For Part 2 (20 minutes), students select the lowest-ranked visualization and write detailed improvement recommendations, addressing at least three specific weaknesses with concrete solutions (e.g., 'reduce pie chart segments from 15 to 5 by grouping smallest categories into 'Other').

Conduct a structured peer review session (15 minutes) where students pair up to compare rankings and discuss one improvement recommendation. Partners must identify one strength and one area for refinement in each other's evaluations.

Conclude with a brief whole-class discussion (10 minutes) where 3-4 students share their top-ranked visualization choice and primary reasoning, allowing the instructor to highlight key evaluation principles and common assessment patterns.
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations per student (pie chart, bar chart, line chart of same dataset)
Visualization Evaluation Worksheet with criteria checklist
Sample business context scenario handout
Colored pens or highlighters for marking visualizations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate ranking with 3+ specific evidence points per visualization, (2) Clear justification using visualization principles terminology, (3) Three concrete improvement recommendations with implementation details, (4) Quality of peer feedback exchange. scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth visualization and reference sheet of key visualization principles. For advanced learners: Add requirement to redesign the worst visualization using free online tools like Canva or Google Sheets, or evaluate for multiple audience types (executives vs. analysts).
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making: Business Application
description: Students will critically assess and rank three different visualizations of the same sales dataset based on clarity, accuracy, and business relevance. They will provide justified recommendations for which visualization best supports a specific business decision about product performance.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying established design principles and business context criteria

Next, present the business scenario: 'TechCorp needs to decide which product category to prioritize for increased marketing investment next quarter.' Evaluation criteria sheet with 4 assessment dimensions
Recommendation worksheet template
Business scenario handout
