title: Cryptographic Protocol Vulnerability Analysis: Dissecting a Man-in-the-Middle Attack on TLS Handshake
description: Students will systematically analyze a simulated TLS handshake communication flow to identify specific vulnerabilities that enable man-in-the-middle attacks. They will examine packet captures, certificate validation failures, and cipher suite negotiations to determine attack vectors and assess the effectiveness of different exploitation techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze TLS handshake packet sequences by examining certificate chains, cipher negotiations, and key exchange mechanisms to identify protocol weaknesses
Students will evaluate man-in-the-middle attack effectiveness through comparative analysis of successful versus failed exploitation attempts across different TLS configurations
instructions: Begin by distributing three Wireshark packet capture files: (1) normal TLS handshake, (2) successful MITM attack, and (3) failed MITM attempt with certificate pinning. Students work in pairs with one analyzing packets while the other documents findings. First 20 minutes: Students examine the normal handshake capture, mapping each packet to TLS handshake steps and identifying security mechanisms (certificate validation, cipher suite selection, key exchange). Next 30 minutes: Analyze the successful MITM capture, comparing it packet-by-packet with the normal flow. Students must identify: forged certificates, modified cipher suites, intercepted key exchanges, and timing anomalies. Provide the SSL Kill Switch tool configuration used in this attack. Following 25 minutes: Examine the failed MITM attempt, focusing on certificate pinning implementation and how it prevented the attack. Students trace the exact point of failure and analyze error messages. Final 25 minutes: Teams create a vulnerability matrix comparing the three scenarios, ranking attack feasibility (1-10 scale) across five categories: certificate validation bypass, cipher downgrade success, key extraction difficulty, detection probability, and mitigation effectiveness. Each team presents their analysis to another pair, defending their vulnerability rankings with specific packet evidence. Conclude with teams proposing three concrete countermeasures based on their analysis.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared Wireshark capture files (normal_tls.pcap, mitm_success.pcap, mitm_failed.pcap)
Wireshark network analyzer software installed on student computers
SSL Kill Switch tool documentation and configuration files
TLS handshake reference diagram poster
Vulnerability analysis matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Packet analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct identification of handshake steps and security mechanisms; Vulnerability identification (30 points) - precise pinpointing of attack vectors with packet evidence; Comparative analysis quality (25 points) - thorough comparison across three scenarios with justified rankings; Countermeasure proposals (20 points) - feasible, specific recommendations linked to identified vulnerabilities. Students must submit completed vulnerability matrix plus 2-page technical report with packet screenshots supporting their analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated packet examples showing key fields to examine, offer TLS handshake flowchart with packet mapping, pair with stronger partners for peer support. For advanced learners: Add fourth capture file with TLS 1.3 comparison, challenge them to identify zero-day attack possibilities, require analysis of cryptographic key strength variations, ask them to simulate additional attack scenarios using provided tools.

title: Evaluating Data Quality and Visualization Effectiveness in Real-World Datasets
description: Students will critically assess the quality of a provided dataset and evaluate the effectiveness of three different data visualizations created from that dataset. They will make judgments about data reliability, completeness, and which visualization best communicates key insights to specific audiences.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data quality by systematically assessing completeness, accuracy, and consistency using a structured checklist and criteria framework
Students will critique the effectiveness of different data visualizations through comparative analysis against established design principles and audience appropriateness
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Coffee Shop Sales' dataset (CSV file with 500 rows containing date, product, price, quantity, customer_age, location columns with intentional data quality issues). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the dataset using Excel or Google Sheets, completing the provided 'Data Quality Assessment Checklist' that covers missing values, duplicate entries, inconsistent formatting, outliers, and logical errors. They must document specific examples and calculate percentages for each issue type. Step 2 (20 minutes): Present three pre-created visualizations of the same data: a cluttered bar chart with poor color choices, a clear line graph showing sales trends, and a pie chart with too many categories. Students use the 'Visualization Evaluation Rubric' to score each visualization (1-5 scale) on clarity, accuracy, design principles, and audience appropriateness. They must provide written justification for each score. Step 3 (10 minutes): Each pair completes a 'Final Recommendation Sheet' where they rank the visualizations from most to least effective, identify the top 3 data quality issues that must be addressed before analysis, and recommend which visualization they would present to a coffee shop manager and why. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share their top-ranked visualization choice and defend their decision using specific criteria from the rubric.
materials_needed: Coffee Shop Sales dataset (CSV file with intentional data quality issues)
Data Quality Assessment Checklist (printable worksheet)
Three pre-created visualizations (printed or displayed digitally)
Visualization Evaluation Rubric (scoring sheet)
Final Recommendation Sheet (template)
Access to Excel, Google Sheets, or similar spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Data Quality Assessment (40 points) - accuracy of issue identification and documentation; Visualization Evaluation (40 points) - appropriateness of scores given with clear justifications; Final Recommendations (20 points) - logical reasoning and evidence-based conclusions. Success criteria: Students must identify at least 4 out of 6 intentional data quality issues, provide specific examples for each visualization critique, and demonstrate understanding of audience-appropriate design choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example of the data quality checklist and highlight specific rows/columns to examine first. Offer sentence starters for justification statements like 'This visualization is effective because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific improvements for each visualization and calculate the potential impact of data quality issues on business decisions using quantitative estimates.

title: Design a Mathematical Model for a Community Garden Water Distribution System
description: Students will create an original mathematical model to optimize water distribution for different sections of a community garden, incorporating variables like plant water needs, rainfall patterns, and budget constraints. They will develop equations, create visual representations, and present their complete irrigation solution with mathematical justification.
estimated_duration: 85 minutes (single block period or two 45-minute sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-variable mathematical model by integrating linear equations, inequalities, and graphical analysis to solve a real-world optimization problem
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts including systems of equations, graphing, and data analysis through designing an original water distribution solution
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the Community Garden Data Sheet containing: 6 garden sections with different square footage (vegetables: 400 sq ft, herbs: 150 sq ft, flowers: 300 sq ft, fruit trees: 250 sq ft, greenhouse: 200 sq ft, composting area: 100 sq ft), water requirements per square foot for each section, monthly rainfall data for the past year, and a $500 monthly water budget with cost per gallon. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Analysis (15 minutes):** Teams analyze the provided data to identify key variables and constraints. Students must define variables (W = weekly water needed, R = rainfall adjustment, C = cost function) and identify relationships between garden sections, water needs, and budget limitations.

**Phase 2 - Model Development (25 minutes):** Each team creates their mathematical model including: (1) equations representing water needs for each section, (2) inequality constraints for budget limitations, (3) functions that account for seasonal rainfall variations, and (4) optimization equations to minimize cost while meeting plant needs. Students must show all mathematical work and create at least one graph visualizing their system.

**Phase 3 - Solution Design (20 minutes):** Teams develop their complete irrigation system design, calculating specific water allocations, seasonal adjustments, and total costs. They must create a visual diagram of their system and prepare mathematical justification for their choices.

**Phase 4 - Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents their model using their equations, graphs, and system design. Other teams evaluate presentations using the provided peer assessment rubric focusing on mathematical accuracy, creativity, and real-world applicability.
materials_needed: Community Garden Data Sheet (printed for each team)
Graph paper (4 sheets per student)
Colored pencils or markers for diagrams
Calculators or tablets with graphing capability
Large poster paper for final presentations
Peer Assessment Rubric (one per student)
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Accuracy (30 points) - correct equations, proper variable definition, accurate calculations; Problem-Solving Process (25 points) - logical approach, appropriate constraints identified, optimization strategy; Visual Representation (20 points) - clear graphs, effective diagrams, professional presentation; Real-World Application (15 points) - practical feasibility, consideration of actual constraints; Collaboration and Communication (10 points) - effective teamwork, clear explanation of mathematical reasoning during presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template with partially completed equations and guided questions like 'What happens to water needs when rainfall increases?' For advanced learners: Add complexity by including variables for seasonal plant growth rates, different irrigation efficiency methods, or environmental impact calculations. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling teams during Phase 2.

title: Design a Mathematical Model for a Community Garden Water Distribution System: Visual Analysis
description: Students will design and construct a mathematical model using linear programming to optimize water distribution for different crop sections in a community garden. They will create visual representations, write constraint equations, and present their optimization solution with justifications for real-world implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a linear programming model by defining variables, writing constraint inequalities, and formulating an objective function for a water distribution scenario
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts through creating visual graphs, calculating optimal solutions, and designing a presentation that justifies their model's real-world applicability
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup and Context (15 minutes)**
Distribute the Community Garden Scenario handout describing a 1000 square meter garden with 4 crop sections: tomatoes (needs 5L/m²/day), lettuce (3L/m²/day), peppers (4L/m²/day), and herbs (2L/m²/day). Present the constraints: maximum 2800L water daily, tomatoes need at least 100m², lettuce maximum 300m², peppers at least 150m². Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 2: Model Construction (25 minutes)**
Students define variables (x₁=tomato area, x₂=lettuce area, etc.) and write the objective function to maximize total garden area or minimize water waste. They must create at least 6 constraint inequalities including water limits, space requirements, and non-negativity constraints. Each team records their complete mathematical model on large poster paper with clear variable definitions.

**Phase 3: Visual Representation (20 minutes)**
Using graphing calculators or Desmos, students plot their constraint lines and identify the feasible region. They must create a hand-drawn coordinate plane showing intersection points and shade the feasible region. Students calculate at least 4 corner point coordinates and evaluate their objective function at each point.

**Phase 4: Solution and Design (25 minutes)**
Teams determine their optimal solution and create a scaled garden layout diagram showing exact dimensions for each crop section. They must include water usage calculations, total area utilized, and unused space. Students prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their model, showing their visual representations, and justifying why their solution works for real gardeners.

**Phase 5: Presentations and Reflection (15 minutes)**
Each team presents their garden design and mathematical justification. Other teams ask one clarifying question per presentation. Activity concludes with individual reflection writing about model limitations and potential improvements.
materials_needed: Community Garden Scenario handouts (1 per student)
Large poster paper (1 sheet per team)
Colored markers and rulers
Graphing calculators or devices with Desmos access
Grid paper for garden layout diagrams
Timer for presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical Model Accuracy - correct variables, constraints, and objective function (25%), (2) Visual Representation Quality - accurate graphs with labeled feasible region and corner points (25%), (3) Solution Justification - correct calculations and logical reasoning for optimal choice (25%), (4) Design Presentation - clear communication of garden layout with supporting mathematics (25%). Students must score 3/4 in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide constraint equation templates and work through the first constraint together. Offer simplified scenarios with 2 variables only. For advanced learners: add additional constraints like crop rotation requirements, seasonal water variations, or profit maximization. Challenge them to create sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with different water availability levels.
original_title: Design a Mathematical Model for a Community Garden Water Distribution System

title: Advanced Data Structure Memory Palace: Recalling Complex Algorithm Time Complexities and Implementation Details
description: Students will memorize and recall specific time and space complexities for 20 advanced data structures and algorithms, along with their key implementation characteristics. This activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and verbal recitation to solidify foundational knowledge required for advanced algorithmic problem-solving.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexities (best, average, worst case) for 20 advanced data structures including B-trees, Red-Black trees, Skip Lists, and Fibonacci heaps by completing timed flashcard sessions

Students will identify specific implementation details and invariants for advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, and various graph traversal methods through structured verbal recitation exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made flashcard deck containing 60 cards (20 data structures × 3 complexity aspects each). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Individual silent review - each student examines all cards, focusing on memorizing exact Big-O notations, space requirements, and key invariants (e.g., Red-Black tree properties: root is black, red nodes have black children, etc.). Next 20 minutes: Paired drilling - Partner A shows the data structure name, Partner B must recite: insertion time complexity, deletion time complexity, search time complexity, space complexity, and one key implementation detail. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Use the provided timer app set to 30-second intervals per card. Final 10 minutes: Speed round assessment - instructor calls out data structure names randomly, students write answers on provided answer sheets within 15 seconds per question. Cover advanced structures: B+ trees, AVL trees, Splay trees, Treaps, Fibonacci heaps, Skip lists, Disjoint sets with union-find, Segment trees, Fenwick trees, Suffix arrays, KMP algorithm, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Prim's, Kruskal's, Tarjan's SCC, and Topological sort. Students must achieve 90% accuracy on time complexities and 80% on implementation details to demonstrate mastery.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard deck (60 cards) with data structures and algorithms
Digital timer application or physical stopwatch
Individual answer sheets with 20 numbered blanks for each complexity type
Reference answer key for instructor verification
Pencils or pens for written responses
assessment_method: Students complete a timed written assessment where they must recall exact time complexities (O-notation) and space complexities for randomly selected data structures. Success criteria: 18/20 correct time complexities (90%) and 16/20 correct implementation details (80%). Partial credit given only for correct Big-O notation with minor notation errors (e.g., missing parentheses). Track individual progress using provided scoring rubric: 4 points per complete correct answer (time + space + detail), 2 points for time complexity only, 1 point for recognizing the data structure category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet (e.g., 'Red-Black trees: Red Roses Need Black Soil' for the four key properties) and allow extended review time. Create visual association cards linking data structures to real-world analogies. For advanced learners: Include additional cards with amortized analysis complexities and challenge them to explain why certain bounds exist. Provide advanced implementation variants (e.g., left-leaning Red-Black trees vs. standard implementation).

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance
description: Students will analyze the mathematical decomposition of prediction error into bias, variance, and irreducible error components using ensemble bootstrap sampling results. They will interpret how different model complexities affect each component and explain the fundamental bias-variance tradeoff through quantitative analysis of real model outputs.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between bias, variance, and irreducible error by analyzing bootstrap ensemble predictions across different model complexities
Students will explain how regularization parameters affect bias-variance decomposition through comparative analysis of ridge regression models with varying alpha values
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with a dataset containing 1000 bootstrap predictions from 5 different ridge regression models (alpha = 0.001, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0) trained on the Boston housing dataset. Each model has predictions for 50 test samples, with true target values provided. **Step 1 (20 minutes):** Students calculate bias² for each model-sample combination using the formula: bias² = (mean_prediction - true_value)². They compute this across all 50 test samples for each alpha value, creating a 5x50 bias matrix. **Step 2 (25 minutes):** Students calculate variance for each model-sample combination using: variance = mean((predictions - mean_prediction)²). Using the 1000 bootstrap predictions per sample, they compute variance across bootstrap samples for each test point and alpha value. **Step 3 (20 minutes):** Students plot three graphs: (1) mean bias² vs alpha, (2) mean variance vs alpha, (3) total error (bias² + variance + noise) vs alpha. They identify the optimal alpha where total error is minimized. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Students write a 200-word interpretation explaining: why bias increases with higher alpha values, why variance decreases with higher alpha, and how the optimal alpha balances these components. They must reference specific numerical values from their calculations. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Pairs compare their optimal alpha values and discuss why their bias-variance curves show the characteristic U-shape for total error.
materials_needed: Pre-computed bootstrap prediction dataset (CSV file with 250,000 predictions)
Python environment with pandas, numpy, matplotlib
Jupyter notebook template with data loading code
Bias-variance decomposition formula reference sheet
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Correct calculation of bias² and variance matrices (40 points), (2) Accurate plotting of three required graphs with proper axis labels (30 points), (3) Written interpretation that correctly explains the mathematical relationship between regularization and bias-variance components with specific numerical evidence (30 points). Success criteria: Students must identify alpha value within 0.1 of optimal value and explain why bias increases monotonically while variance decreases monotonically with regularization strength.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed calculations for alpha=0.1 as an example and offer a step-by-step calculation worksheet. For advanced learners: Extend activity by having them derive the analytical bias-variance decomposition for linear regression and compare theoretical predictions with empirical results. Provide additional datasets (polynomial regression, classification) to test generalizability of their understanding.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance: Written Report
description: Students analyze real cross-validation results from multiple machine learning models to understand how bias-variance tradeoff manifests in practice. They will interpret learning curves, validation curves, and performance metrics to explain the underlying mathematical relationship between model complexity, bias, variance, and irreducible error.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing cross-validation performance patterns across models of varying complexity
Students will explain the relationship between underfitting/overfitting and bias-variance components through systematic examination of learning curves and validation metrics
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a dataset containing cross-validation results for polynomial regression models (degrees 1-15) trained on a synthetic dataset with known noise level. Include: training/validation RMSE scores across 10 folds, learning curves (performance vs training set size), and validation curves (performance vs polynomial degree). Each student receives identical datasets in CSV format.

**Phase 1 - Pattern Recognition (20 minutes):** Students work individually to create visualizations of: (1) training vs validation RMSE by model complexity, (2) learning curves for degrees 2, 8, and 12, (3) box plots of cross-validation score distributions. They identify inflection points, convergence patterns, and variance in scores.

**Phase 2 - Mathematical Interpretation (25 minutes):** In pairs, students calculate and interpret: expected validation error, bias estimates (difference between average prediction and true function), variance estimates (variability of predictions across folds), and model complexity sweet spots. They use provided bias-variance decomposition formulas to connect observed patterns to theoretical concepts.

**Phase 3 - Synthesis (15 minutes):** Students write a technical interpretation explaining: which models exhibit high bias vs high variance, how training set size affects the bias-variance tradeoff, and optimal model selection strategy. They must reference specific numerical evidence from their analysis and connect findings to regularization techniques.
materials_needed: Cross-validation results dataset (CSV file with RMSE scores for 10 folds × 15 polynomial degrees)
Learning curve data (training set sizes: 50, 100, 200, 400, 800 samples)
Python/R environment with matplotlib/ggplot2, pandas/dplyr, numpy/base R
Bias-variance decomposition formula reference sheet
Graph paper or digital plotting tools
assessment_method: Evaluate students' written technical interpretation using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of high-bias vs high-variance models with numerical evidence, (2) Accurate explanation of learning curve patterns and their relationship to bias-variance components, (3) Appropriate mathematical reasoning connecting cross-validation variance to model complexity, (4) Sound model selection recommendation with justification. Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining counterintuitive results (e.g., why validation error sometimes increases with more training data).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide labeled example plots showing clear high-bias and high-variance cases, offer guided questions about specific data points, and give templates for calculation steps. For advanced learners: Include bootstrap sampling results for bias-variance estimation, ask them to predict how different noise levels would affect the patterns, or have them derive the mathematical relationship between cross-validation variance and model stability.

description: Students will analyze and interpret bias-variance trade-offs in machine learning models by examining cross-validation results across multiple algorithms on the same dataset. learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing cross-validation score distributions across different model complexities

Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance: Written Report
description: Students will analyze the mathematical decomposition of prediction error into bias, variance, and irreducible error components using simulated datasets with known ground truth functions. They will interpret how different model complexities affect each component and explain the implications for model selection in real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between bias, variance, and total error by analyzing decomposition results across multiple model complexities
Students will explain the trade-off mechanisms between bias and variance through comparison of parametric and non-parametric models on controlled datasets
instructions: Begin by providing students with a Jupyter notebook containing three pre-generated datasets: (1) linear relationship with Gaussian noise, (2) polynomial relationship with heteroscedastic noise, and (3) sinusoidal relationship with outliers. Each dataset contains 1000 training samples and known ground truth functions. Students work in pairs to execute the bias-variance decomposition analysis. First, they implement 100 bootstrap samples from each dataset and train five different models on each sample: linear regression, polynomial regression (degree 3, 6, 10), and k-nearest neighbors (k=5). For each model-dataset combination, students calculate predictions on a fixed test set of 200 points, then compute the bias-variance decomposition using the provided formulas: Bias² = E[(f̂(x) - f(x))²], Variance = E[(f̂(x) - E[f̂(x)])²], and Total Error = Bias² + Variance + σ². Students create visualization matrices showing bias, variance, and total error for each model-dataset pair, then write analytical interpretations addressing three key questions: (1) Which models exhibit high bias vs. high variance on each dataset type? (2) How does the optimal model complexity change based on the underlying data generating process? (3) What are the practical implications for model selection when ground truth is unknown? Finally, students present their findings in a structured 10-minute presentation to another pair, focusing on explaining the trade-off mechanisms rather than just reporting numerical results.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-coded datasets and bias-variance decomposition framework
Python environment with scikit-learn, numpy, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Presentation template with structured sections for bias-variance analysis
Access to computational resources capable of running 1500 model training iterations
assessment_method: Students submit a completed notebook with accurate calculations (40%), three interpretation paragraphs demonstrating understanding of bias-variance mechanisms (40%), and peer evaluation of presentation clarity in explaining trade-offs (20%). Success criteria include correctly identifying which models are high-bias vs. high-variance, accurately explaining why model complexity affects each component differently, and providing actionable insights for model selection in practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional guided questions about specific model-dataset combinations and offer pre-calculated examples for one dataset. For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them implement regularization techniques (Ridge, Lasso) and analyze how regularization strength affects the bias-variance decomposition, or apply the same analysis framework to ensemble methods like Random Forest.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance: Visual Analysis
description: Students analyze pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results across different machine learning algorithms and cross-validation scenarios to understand the fundamental trade-off. They will interpret how model complexity, training set size, and algorithm choice affect the bias-variance components and overall generalization error.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing numerical outputs and visualizations across three different algorithms (linear regression, random forest, neural network)
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and bias-variance trade-off through systematic comparison of decomposition metrics
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-computed bias-variance decomposition dataset containing results for three algorithms tested on synthetic regression problems with varying noise levels and training set sizes (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to first examine the data structure: bias², variance, noise, and total error columns for each algorithm-complexity combination. 

Next, students create three comparative visualizations using provided Python templates: (1) bias vs variance scatter plots for each algorithm, (2) bias-variance components as training set size increases, and (3) total error decomposition as model complexity varies (25 minutes). Instructor demonstrates the first plot as an example.

Students then analyze patterns by answering guided questions: 'Which algorithm shows highest bias at low complexity?' 'At what training set size does variance stabilize for random forests?' 'How does irreducible error compare across scenarios?' They document findings in a structured analysis worksheet (20 minutes).

Pairs present one key insight to the class, specifically explaining how their chosen algorithm's bias-variance profile affects model selection decisions (15 minutes presentations). Instructor facilitates discussion connecting observations to real-world model deployment scenarios.

Conclude with individual reflection where students explain, in writing, why understanding bias-variance decomposition matters for model evaluation beyond simple accuracy metrics, using specific examples from their analysis (10 minutes). Collect worksheets and reflection responses for assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition dataset (CSV format) with 150 algorithm-scenario combinations
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Structured analysis worksheet with 8 specific interpretation questions
Visualization code templates (3 different plot types)
Individual reflection prompt handout
assessment_method: Grade analysis worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly interprets all bias-variance patterns with detailed explanations, (3) Correctly interprets most patterns with adequate explanations, (2) Some correct interpretations but lacks depth, (1) Minimal correct interpretation. Reflection responses assessed for accurate explanation of bias-variance trade-off implications and specific examples from analysis. scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example analysis for one algorithm to serve as template. Offer simplified question set focusing on basic pattern recognition. Challenge them to propose optimal complexity selection strategy based on decomposition analysis.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze and interpret bias-variance trade-offs across multiple machine learning algorithms using cross-validation results from a synthetic regression dataset. They will explain how different model complexities affect generalization performance and identify optimal hyperparameter ranges based on decomposition analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing cross-validation curves and explaining the relationship between model complexity and generalization error
Students will distinguish between overfitting and underfitting phenomena through systematic comparison of training versus validation performance across multiple algorithms
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-generated dataset containing cross-validation results for polynomial regression (degrees 1-15), Random Forest (n_estimators: 10-500), and SVM (C values: 0.001-1000) on a synthetic dataset with known ground truth. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Students examine the provided CSV files containing mean training scores, validation scores, and standard deviations across 10-fold CV for each hyperparameter setting. They create three separate plots showing training/validation curves for each algorithm. Next 30 minutes: Using the bias-variance decomposition formulas provided, students calculate and plot bias², variance, and irreducible error components for each model configuration. They identify the point where bias and variance curves intersect for each algorithm. assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correctness of bias-variance calculations and plots (40 points), (2) Accuracy of pattern identification and algorithm comparison (30 points), (3) Quality of written explanations connecting mathematical concepts to practical implications (30 points). title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance: Technical Implementation
description: Students will analyze multiple machine learning models' performance across different cross-validation folds to understand the bias-variance trade-off. They will interpret visualizations and numerical decompositions to explain why certain models generalize better than others in specific contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing the mathematical components and their relationship to model complexity
Students will explain the trade-off between underfitting and overfitting through examination of cross-validation performance patterns across different algorithms
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared dataset containing cross-validation results for 5 different models (linear regression, polynomial regression degrees 2, 5, 10, and random forest) trained on a synthetic regression problem with known ground truth. Each student receives: (1) CV performance matrices showing MSE for each fold, (2) bias-variance decomposition calculations, and (3) learning curve plots.

Step 1 (15 min): Students individually examine the numerical bias-variance decomposition table, identifying which models have high bias vs. high variance. They must calculate the total error for each model using the formula: Total Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible Error.

Step 2 (20 min): In pairs, students analyze the learning curves and cross-validation score distributions. They identify patterns: Does the polynomial degree 10 model show high variance across folds? Does linear regression show consistently poor performance (high bias)? Partners must document three specific observations with supporting numerical evidence.

Step 3 (15 min): Students interpret the practical implications by writing explanations for two scenarios: (a) Why might the random forest perform well on this dataset? (b) Under what conditions would the high-degree polynomial be preferred despite its variance?

Step 4 (10 min): Class discussion where pairs share one key insight about model selection based on bias-variance analysis. Instructor guides discussion toward real-world model selection principles and when to prioritize bias reduction vs. variance reduction.

title: Planning a School Garden: Applying Area and Perimeter Calculations
description: Students will apply their knowledge of area and perimeter formulas to design rectangular garden plots for their school. They will calculate dimensions, determine fencing needs, and optimize space usage within given constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply area and perimeter formulas for rectangles by designing garden plots that meet specific size requirements
Students will demonstrate understanding of rectangular measurements through real-world problem-solving scenarios involving space optimization
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'School Garden Planning Worksheet' and explaining that students are landscape designers hired to create vegetable garden plots. Each student receives a scenario card specifying: available budget ($200), cost of fencing ($3 per foot), and minimum garden area needed (48 square feet). 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to brainstorm 3 different rectangular designs for their garden plot. They must sketch each rectangle on grid paper where each square represents 1 square foot, labeling length and width.

Step 2 (15 minutes): For each design, students calculate the area using A = length × width and perimeter using P = 2(length + width). They record calculations in the provided table, showing all work.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students determine fencing costs by multiplying perimeter by $3, then check if the cost stays within the $200 budget while meeting the 48 square foot minimum area requirement.

Step 4 (15 minutes): In pairs, students compare their viable designs and discuss which option provides the most garden space for the budget. They must justify their choice using mathematical evidence from their calculations.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each pair presents their optimal garden design to the class, explaining dimensions, total area, perimeter, cost, and reasoning. Other students verify calculations using calculators and ask clarifying questions about the design choices.
materials_needed: School Garden Planning Worksheet (1 per student)
Scenario cards with budget and space constraints
Grid paper (1/4 inch squares, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers and pencils
Basic calculators for verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct application of area formula (A = l×w), (2) Correct application of perimeter formula (P = 2(l+w)), (3) Accurate cost calculations and budget analysis, (4) Clear mathematical justification for final design choice. Students must demonstrate all calculation steps and explain reasoning to earn full points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide formula reference cards and pre-drawn rectangle templates with dimensions partially filled in. Use smaller numbers (like 24 sq ft minimum, $2 per foot fencing). For advanced learners: Add constraints like 'garden must fit in a 12×8 foot available space' or introduce irregular shapes requiring area addition of multiple rectangles.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Performance Profiling
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms by implementing them, measuring their performance with varying data sets, and identifying the relationships between theoretical complexity and real-world execution times. This activity bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical programming analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity differences between bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by comparing their performance across datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 elements
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through systematic performance measurement and identify factors that cause deviations from theoretical Big O predictions
instructions: Begin by providing students with skeleton code containing three sorting functions (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) with timing instrumentation already embedded. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Students complete the missing logic in each sorting algorithm, ensuring they understand each approach. Next 30 minutes: Students run performance tests using three pre-prepared datasets - random integers (sizes 100, 1000, 10000), already sorted arrays, and reverse-sorted arrays. They record execution times in a provided data collection spreadsheet. Following 25 minutes: Students create performance graphs plotting execution time vs. input size for each algorithm, identifying linear, quadratic, and logarithmic patterns. They annotate graphs with theoretical Big O notation predictions. Final 15 minutes: Students write a comparative analysis identifying which scenarios favor each algorithm, explaining why bubble sort performs worse on larger datasets, why quicksort struggles with already-sorted data, and when merge sort's consistent performance justifies its memory overhead. Students must support conclusions with specific data points from their measurements and connect observations to theoretical complexity classes.
materials_needed: Python development environment (IDLE, PyCharm, or VS Code)
Skeleton code template with timing functions
Pre-generated test datasets (CSV files with 100, 1000, 10000 elements)
Data collection spreadsheet template
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed algorithms for correctness (25 points), accuracy of performance measurements recorded in spreadsheet (25 points), quality of performance graphs showing clear trends with proper Big O annotations (25 points), and depth of written analysis connecting empirical results to theoretical complexity with specific examples (25 points). Success requires identifying at least 3 specific performance patterns and explaining 2 cases where real-world results deviate from theoretical predictions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pseudocode hints for incomplete algorithms and guide them to focus on one clear trend in their analysis rather than comprehensive comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement hybrid sorting approaches, analyze memory usage patterns, or test with different data types (strings, objects) to explore how data characteristics affect performance beyond just size.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Performance for Healthcare Diagnosis: A Comparative Critical Analysis
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance, ethical implications, and business viability of three different machine learning models (Random Forest, Neural Network, and Logistic Regression) trained to predict diabetes diagnosis. They will analyze multiple evaluation metrics, assess model bias, and make evidence-based recommendations for deployment in a clinical setting.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and fairness metrics across demographic groups
Students will critique model deployment readiness through systematic assessment of performance trade-offs, ethical considerations, and stakeholder impact in healthcare contexts
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup and Data Analysis (30 minutes)**
Provide students with three pre-trained models on the Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset, including model outputs, prediction probabilities, and demographic breakdowns. Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives identical model performance files (CSV format) containing predictions, actual labels, confidence scores, and demographic attributes (age groups, BMI categories). Teams begin by loading data into Python/R and generating basic performance statistics.

**Phase 2: Comprehensive Model Evaluation (45 minutes)**
Students calculate and compare: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR for each model. They must create visualizations showing ROC curves and precision-recall curves side-by-side. Additionally, students perform bias analysis by computing performance metrics stratified by age group and BMI category, identifying potential fairness issues. They document findings in a structured evaluation matrix comparing all three models across technical performance and fairness dimensions.

**Phase 3: Critical Analysis and Recommendation (45 minutes)**
Teams evaluate each model's suitability for clinical deployment by considering: false positive/negative costs in healthcare, interpretability requirements for medical professionals, computational efficiency for real-time diagnosis, and ethical implications of demographic bias. Students must weigh trade-offs between sensitivity (catching all diabetes cases) versus specificity (avoiding false alarms). They prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their choice of one model for deployment, addressing anticipated counterarguments and proposing mitigation strategies for identified weaknesses.

**Phase 4: Peer Review and Defense (30 minutes)**
Teams present recommendations to the class. Other teams serve as a review panel, asking probing questions about methodology, assumptions, and conclusions. Presenting teams must defend their analysis and acknowledge limitations in their evaluation approach.
materials_needed: Three pre-trained ML model outputs on Pima Indians Diabetes Dataset (CSV files)
Python/R environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
Model evaluation template spreadsheet
Healthcare context briefing document with stakeholder requirements
Presentation slides template with evaluation criteria checklist
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical accuracy of performance calculations and bias analysis (25%), (2) Quality and clarity of data visualizations (20%), (3) Depth of critical analysis considering healthcare context and stakeholder needs (25%), (4) Soundness of final recommendation with evidence-based justification (20%), (5) Response quality during peer questioning and ability to acknowledge limitations (10%). Deliverables include completed evaluation matrix, visualizations, recommendation report (2 pages), and presentation performance.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide performance metric calculation templates and interpretation guides. Offer prompting questions like 'What happens if this model incorrectly diagnoses a patient?' **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to propose additional evaluation metrics (e.g., calibration plots, SHAP values for interpretability), consider regulatory compliance requirements (FDA approval process), or design A/B testing frameworks for model comparison in clinical trials. Encourage exploration of ensemble methods combining multiple models.

title: Design and Implement a Mathematical Model for Pandemic Spread with Policy Interventions
description: Students will create an original mathematical model combining differential equations, probability theory, and optimization to simulate disease transmission dynamics. They will design policy intervention scenarios and evaluate their effectiveness through mathematical analysis and computational implementation.
estimated_duration: 14 days (70 hours total: 35 hours class time, 35 hours independent work)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from differential equations, probability distributions, and optimization theory by constructing a comprehensive epidemiological model with at least three intervention variables
Students will design and validate mathematical policy scenarios through computational modeling and statistical analysis of outcomes
instructions: **Phase 1 (Days 1-2): Model Architecture Design** Students work in teams of 3-4 to research and select their mathematical framework. Each team must choose between SEIR differential equation models, stochastic compartmental models, or network-based transmission models. Teams complete a mathematical specification document outlining their chosen equations, parameter definitions, and assumptions. **Phase 2 (Days 3-5): Core Model Development** Teams implement their base model using Python, MATLAB, or R. The model must include: population dynamics equations, transmission rate functions, and recovery/mortality parameters. Students must derive their equations from first principles and document all mathematical derivations. **Phase 3 (Days 6-8): Policy Intervention Integration** Teams design three distinct intervention scenarios (e.g., vaccination campaigns, social distancing measures, contact tracing). Each intervention must be mathematically represented through parameter modifications or additional constraint equations. Students must formulate optimization problems to determine optimal policy timing and intensity. **Phase 4 (Days 9-11): Computational Implementation and Analysis** Teams run simulations across multiple parameter sets and intervention combinations. They must perform sensitivity analysis on key parameters and validate results through comparison with real-world data or established models. **Phase 5 (Days 12-14): Evaluation and Presentation** Teams prepare technical reports (15-20 pages) and present their models to a panel including instructor and guest experts. Presentations must include live demonstrations of their computational models with real-time parameter adjustments.
materials_needed: Python/MATLAB/R programming environment with numerical libraries (NumPy, SciPy, ggplot2)
Access to epidemiological datasets (WHO, CDC, or Johns Hopkins COVID-19 data)
Mathematical software for symbolic computation (Mathematica, Maple, or SymPy)
Presentation software with LaTeX equation support
Digital whiteboard or collaborative platform (Miro, Jamboard)
assessment_method: Students evaluated using comprehensive rubric: Mathematical rigor and accuracy of model formulation (25%), Innovation and sophistication of intervention design (25%), Quality of computational implementation and validation (25%), Technical communication and presentation clarity (25%). Each component scored on 4-point scale with specific criteria for parameter selection justification, equation derivation completeness, code efficiency and documentation, and professional presentation delivery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation structures and guided parameter estimation worksheets. Offer daily check-in sessions for mathematical concept clarification. Create peer mentoring pairs with stronger mathematical background students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate spatial heterogeneity, age-structured populations, or economic impact modeling. Encourage exploration of machine learning integration for parameter optimization or consideration of uncertainty quantification methods.

title: Programming Fundamentals Vocabulary Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 essential programming vocabulary terms through digital flashcard creation and peer testing. This activity builds foundational knowledge for beginning programmers by establishing core terminology that will be used throughout the course.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and define 20 fundamental programming terms including variable, function, loop, array, and conditional statement through flashcard study
Students will recall programming vocabulary definitions with 85% accuracy through timed peer quizzing activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made list of 20 programming terms: variable, function, loop, array, conditional statement, algorithm, debugging, syntax, compiler, interpreter, integer, string, boolean, parameter, argument, method, object, class, iteration, and recursion. Students have 5 minutes to review the terms and identify any they already know. Next, students create digital flashcards using Quizlet, spending 15 minutes entering each term on one side and its definition on the other (definitions provided on handout). After creation, students spend 10 minutes using Quizlet's study mode to practice their flashcards individually. Then pair students and have them quiz each other for 8 minutes using the flashcard app, with each student taking turns as questioner and responder for 4-minute intervals. During peer quizzing, the questioner shows only the term and waits for the complete definition. Finally, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire review where you display terms on the projector and students write definitions on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously. Award points for correct definitions and provide immediate feedback for incorrect responses. Conclude with students rating their confidence level (1-5 scale) for each term on their tracking sheet.
materials_needed: Pre-printed handout with 20 programming terms and definitions
Individual devices with internet access for Quizlet
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Projector for whole-class review
Student confidence tracking sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (17/20 correct) during the final whole-class whiteboard quiz. Assessment includes observing peer quizzing sessions for engagement and accuracy, reviewing completed Quizlet flashcard sets for proper term-definition matching, and evaluating final whiteboard responses for correct definitions using provided answer key.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide simplified definitions, allow use of visual aids or examples, and pair with stronger partners during peer quiz. For advanced learners: challenge them to create additional flashcards with more complex terms like polymorphism or encapsulation, or have them write example code snippets that demonstrate each term in context.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Marketing Campaign Data
description: Students analyze a provided marketing campaign dataset containing customer demographics, spending patterns, and campaign responses to distinguish between correlational relationships and potential causal claims. They will create visual explanations demonstrating why certain data patterns cannot support causal conclusions.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing marketing campaign data and identifying confounding variables
Students will explain why specific correlational findings cannot support causal claims through written justifications and visual representations
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute overview explaining the activity using the provided marketing dataset (15 minutes total setup). Distribute the 'MarketingCampaign.csv' file containing 2,000 customer records with variables: age, income, education_level, campaign_response, purchase_amount, social_media_usage, and geographic_region. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students work in pairs to explore the dataset using provided correlation matrices and scatter plots. They identify the three strongest correlations and document their findings on the analysis worksheet.

Step 2 (25 minutes): For each strong correlation identified, pairs must brainstorm and list at least two potential confounding variables that could explain the relationship. They use the 'Confounding Variables Template' to structure their thinking systematically.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students create simple visual explanations (hand-drawn diagrams or digital tools) showing why one selected correlation cannot prove causation. They must include arrows showing alternative causal pathways and label confounding variables.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs present their chosen correlation example to another pair, explaining their reasoning for why the relationship is correlational rather than causal. Listening pairs provide feedback using the peer evaluation checklist.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class debrief where 2-3 pairs share their most compelling examples. Instructor highlights common misconceptions and reinforces key concepts through student examples.
materials_needed: MarketingCampaign.csv dataset file (provided via LMS or USB)
Printed correlation matrix and scatter plot packet for each pair
Analysis worksheet templates
Confounding Variables Template handout
Peer evaluation checklist
Computers/tablets with Excel or basic data viewing software
assessment_method: Students submit their analysis worksheet and visual explanation diagram. Grading rubric awards points for: correctly identifying correlations (25%), listing plausible confounding variables (35%), creating clear visual explanations (25%), and providing logical written justification for why causation cannot be claimed (15%). Peer feedback forms provide additional formative assessment data.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a partially completed example analysis and a list of common confounding variable categories (demographic, behavioral, environmental). For advanced learners: challenge them to research and propose experimental designs that could test causal relationships, or analyze additional variables for interaction effects and non-linear relationships.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Marketing Campaign Data: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed dataset of marketing campaign metrics to distinguish between correlational and causal relationships. They will examine scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and contextual factors to explain why certain variable relationships indicate correlation without causation.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing marketing campaign data and identifying confounding variables
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots through guided examination of customer engagement metrics
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'E-commerce Marketing Campaign Dataset' containing 500 rows with variables: ad_spend, email_frequency, social_media_posts, website_visits, conversion_rate, and season. Have students work in pairs for 45 minutes.

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students examine the correlation matrix provided and identify the three highest correlation coefficients. They record these values and the variable pairs in their worksheet.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the pre-generated scatter plots for each high-correlation pair, students describe the visual relationship patterns. They must write 2-3 sentences explaining what they observe about the data distribution and trend direction.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Present three scenario cards describing potential causal mechanisms for each correlation pair. Students evaluate each scenario and mark whether they believe the relationship is 'likely causal,' 'likely correlational only,' or 'unclear.' They must provide written justification citing potential confounding variables like seasonality, market conditions, or customer behavior patterns.

Step 4 (5 minutes): Students complete a reflection comparing their strongest correlation (highest coefficient) with their most likely causal relationship, explaining any differences and what additional data they would need to establish causation. Conclude with a 5-minute class discussion where 2-3 pairs share their most surprising finding about a correlation that seemed causal but likely wasn't.
materials_needed: Pre-processed CSV file: 'E-commerce Marketing Campaign Dataset' (500 rows x 6 variables)
Correlation matrix printout for each pair
Set of 6 scatter plot visualizations per pair
Scenario evaluation cards (3 cards per correlation pair)
Student worksheet with structured response sections
assessment_method: Grade student worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of correlation coefficients and visual pattern descriptions, (2) Accurate classification of causal vs. correlational relationships with valid justification, (3) Identification of at least two relevant confounding variables per scenario, (4) Quality of reflection comparing correlation strength to causal likelihood. Each component worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a 'Confounding Variable Reference Sheet' with examples like seasonal trends, economic factors, and customer demographics. Offer sentence starters for justifications. For advanced learners, include additional variables like customer_age and geographic_region, and challenge them to propose experimental designs that could test causation.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Marketing Campaign Data

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Business Functions with Lagrange Multipliers
description: Students will apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve real-world constrained optimization problems involving production costs, resource allocation, and profit maximization. They will work through complex multi-variable scenarios where businesses must optimize outcomes while operating under specific constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems by setting up and solving systems of partial differential equations in business contexts
Students will interpret economic meaning of Lagrange multipliers through analysis of shadow prices and marginal rates of substitution in resource allocation scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct business scenarios: manufacturing optimization (minimize cost C(x,y) = 2x² + 3y² + xy subject to production constraint 4x + 5y = 200), advertising budget allocation (maximize reach R(x,y,z) = 15√x + 20√y + 12√z subject to budget constraint x + y + z = 10000), and packaging optimization (minimize surface area while maintaining volume). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning one scenario per team initially (20 minutes setup). Each team must first identify the objective function and constraint(s), then set up the Lagrangian L = f(x,y) + λg(x,y). Teams calculate partial derivatives ∂L/∂x, ∂L/∂y, and ∂L/∂λ, then solve the resulting system of equations (45 minutes). Circulate to check mathematical setup and computational accuracy. Teams must verify their solutions using the bordered Hessian determinant test for constrained extrema (15 minutes). Next, teams interpret their λ value economically – what does it represent for their specific business context? (20 minutes discussion). Finally, teams rotate scenarios, spending 30 minutes applying their method to a new problem, comparing solution approaches and economic interpretations. Conclude with teams presenting one complete solution to the class, emphasizing both mathematical rigor and business interpretation (20 minutes presentations). Throughout, emphasize checking feasibility of solutions and boundary condition analysis.
materials_needed: Three printed business scenario handouts with specific functions and constraints
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos/Wolfram Alpha
Large poster paper and markers for solution presentations
Bordered Hessian reference sheet
assessment_method: Grade based on: Mathematical setup accuracy (25% - correct Lagrangian formation and partial derivatives), Solution accuracy (25% - correct algebraic manipulation and final values), Economic interpretation (25% - meaningful explanation of λ value and business implications), Presentation quality (25% - clear communication of process and results). Use rubric with 4-point scale for each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with Lagrangian setup partially completed and step-by-step derivative calculation guides. Pair with stronger mathematical peers. For advanced learners: Introduce inequality constraints using KKT conditions, or extend to three-variable problems with multiple constraints. Challenge them to create their own business scenarios with non-standard constraint types.

title: Analyzing Algorithm Complexity Trade-offs in Real-World Database Query Optimization
description: Students will dissect and compare three different database indexing strategies (B-tree, Hash, and Bitmap indexes) by analyzing their performance characteristics across varying query types and data distributions. They will break down the algorithmic components, identify performance bottlenecks, and determine optimal use cases for each indexing method.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity relationships of B-tree, Hash, and Bitmap indexing algorithms by decomposing their core operations and mathematical properties
Students will evaluate trade-offs between different indexing strategies through systematic performance analysis using provided dataset scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing three pre-configured database scenarios: e-commerce transactions (1M records), user demographics (500K records), and IoT sensor data (2M records). Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team receiving identical MySQL database instances loaded with all three datasets. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams execute provided query suites against each dataset using different index types. They record execution times, memory usage, and disk I/O statistics using MySQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE command and Performance Schema.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Students decompose each indexing algorithm by mapping out the data structures, analyzing insertion/deletion operations, and calculating theoretical complexity bounds. They create visual diagrams showing tree traversal paths, hash collision handling, and bitmap operations.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze performance patterns by plotting execution times against data size, query selectivity, and update frequency. They identify algorithmic bottlenecks by correlating theoretical complexity with observed performance metrics.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Students synthesize findings into decision matrices, categorizing scenarios where each index type excels or fails. They must justify recommendations using specific complexity analysis and empirical evidence.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams present one critical insight about algorithm behavior that wasn't immediately obvious from theoretical analysis alone, supported by their experimental data.
materials_needed: MySQL Server 8.0 with three pre-loaded databases (e-commerce, demographics, IoT)
Standardized query suite with 15 SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE operations per scenario
Performance monitoring tools (MySQL Workbench or equivalent)
Graph paper or digital graphing tools for complexity visualization
Stopwatches for manual timing verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis - correct identification of O-notation and algorithmic bottlenecks (25%), (2) Quality of empirical analysis - systematic data collection and pattern recognition (25%), (3) Trade-off evaluation - logical reasoning connecting theory to practical scenarios (30%), (4) Synthesis - novel insights demonstrating deep algorithmic understanding (20%). Students submit annotated performance graphs, decision matrices, and one-page insight summaries.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity analysis templates with partially completed Big-O calculations and guided questions about each algorithm step. Offer pre-made performance graphing templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to design hybrid indexing strategies or analyze additional factors like concurrent access patterns and index maintenance overhead during bulk operations.

title: Comparative Algorithm Complexity Analysis
description: Students will dissect and compare the performance characteristics of different database query execution plans for a complex multi-table join scenario. They will analyze time/space complexity trade-offs and evaluate the decision-making process of query optimizers under varying data conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the computational complexity of nested loop, hash join, and merge join algorithms by examining execution plans and performance metrics across different data distributions
Students will evaluate query optimizer decision trees through systematic comparison of execution strategies under varying memory constraints and data cardinality scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a PostgreSQL database containing three tables: customers (1M records), orders (5M records), and products (100K records). Teams will analyze a complex query joining all three tables with WHERE clauses and aggregations. Step 1 (20 min): Have students execute EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the provided query and document the chosen execution plan, noting join algorithms, estimated vs. actual row counts, and execution times. Step 2 (25 min): Students modify database statistics using ALTER TABLE SET STATISTICS and pg_stat_statements to simulate different data distributions (uniform, skewed, clustered). Re-run the query and document how the optimizer's plan changes. Step 3 (30 min): Teams force specific join algorithms using pg_hint_plan extension, creating three versions: force nested loop joins, force hash joins, and force merge joins. For each version, measure execution time, memory usage, and I/O operations under three scenarios: limited work_mem (4MB), moderate work_mem (64MB), and high work_mem (256MB). Step 4 (25 min): Students create a detailed comparison matrix analyzing why each algorithm performs differently under each memory constraint. They must identify the mathematical relationship between input size and performance, explain the optimizer's cost model decisions, and determine optimal scenarios for each approach. Step 5 (20 min): Teams present their findings, focusing on the trade-offs between time complexity, space complexity, and practical performance considerations in production environments.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL 14+ with pg_hint_plan extension installed
Pre-populated database with customers, orders, and products tables
Complex multi-table join query template
Performance monitoring script for memory and I/O tracking
Comparison matrix worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis and Big-O notation identification, (2) Depth of optimizer decision tree evaluation with specific cost model references, (3) Quality of trade-off analysis including mathematical justification, (4) Clarity of presentation explaining why performance varies across scenarios. Each criterion weighted equally, with successful completion requiring demonstration of all four query optimization strategies and quantitative performance comparison.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled templates for the comparison matrix and guided questions about each join algorithm's characteristics. Offer simplified queries with fewer tables initially. For advanced learners, challenge them to analyze additional factors like parallel query execution, index usage optimization, and the impact of different storage engines. Have them explore custom cost parameters and write their own hint-based optimization strategies.
original_title: Analyzing Algorithm Complexity Trade-offs in Real-World Database Query Optimization

title: Evaluating Data Quality and Analysis Methods in Real Estate Price Predictions
description: Students will critically assess the quality of a housing dataset and evaluate two different analytical approaches used to predict home prices. They will judge which method is more reliable and justify their decision using specific data quality criteria and analytical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data quality issues in a real estate dataset by applying standard data assessment criteria (completeness, accuracy, consistency, and relevance)
Students will critique two different analytical approaches for predicting house prices through systematic comparison of methodology, assumptions, and results validity
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Housing_Analysis_Packet.csv' containing 200 Boston housing records with intentional quality issues (missing values, outliers, inconsistent formats) and two pre-completed analysis reports (Method A: Simple Linear Regression using only square footage; Method B: Multiple regression using square footage, bedrooms, and neighborhood). **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Students examine the dataset using provided Data Quality Checklist, identifying specific issues in each category: completeness (count missing values in each column), accuracy (spot obvious errors like negative square footage), consistency (find formatting inconsistencies in categorical variables), and relevance (assess if variables actually relate to house prices). **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Students read both analysis reports and complete the 'Method Evaluation Matrix' comparing: data preparation steps taken, variables included/excluded, assumptions made, statistical validity measures (R-squared, p-values), and practical applicability. **Step 3 (10 minutes):** Students write a 150-word recommendation memo stating which analytical method they would trust more for real estate investment decisions, citing specific evidence from their data quality assessment and method comparison. **Step 4 (10 minutes):** Pairs share recommendations and discuss reasoning, focusing on how data quality issues affected their method preference.
materials_needed: Housing_Analysis_Packet.csv file (200 records with intentional quality issues)
Two pre-written analysis reports (Method A and Method B)
Data Quality Checklist worksheet
Method Evaluation Matrix template
Computers with Excel or Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Data Quality Assessment (25% - correctly identifies 80%+ of planted issues), Method Comparison (35% - systematically compares all matrix elements with evidence), Recommendation Justification (30% - clearly links data quality findings to method preference with logical reasoning), Professional Communication (10% - memo format and clarity). Success = 3.0+ average across categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example for first 3 rows of data quality assessment and highlight key sections in analysis reports. For advanced learners: Add challenge question asking them to propose a third analytical method that would better handle the identified data quality issues, or provide additional dataset with more complex quality problems.

title: Evaluating Data Quality and Analysis Methods in Real Estate Price Predictions: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically assess two different approaches to predicting house prices using provided datasets with varying quality issues. They will evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of each method and justify which approach produces more reliable results for decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the reliability of two different data analysis approaches by comparing their methodologies, assumptions, and results accuracy
Students will critique data quality issues through systematic assessment of completeness, accuracy, and relevance in real estate datasets
instructions:
Begin by distributing Dataset A (clean, 500 house records with complete price, size, location data) and Dataset B (messy, 800 house records with 15% missing values, inconsistent formats, outliers) along with two analysis reports. Each report uses different methods: Report 1 uses simple linear regression on Dataset A, Report 2 uses multiple regression with data cleaning on Dataset B. 

Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to examine both datasets using Excel/Google Sheets, documenting data quality issues using the provided checklist (missing values, duplicates, outliers, inconsistent formats).

Step 2 (20 min): Pairs review both analysis reports, noting methodology differences, assumptions made, and how each handled data quality issues. They complete a comparison matrix rating each approach on: data preparation thoroughness, method appropriateness, result reliability, and practical usability.

Step 3 (15 min): Students calculate basic accuracy metrics provided in appendix (mean absolute error, R-squared) for both approaches using the given formulas and test results.

Step 4 (25 min): Each pair creates a written evaluation (300-400 words) answering: Which approach would you recommend to a real estate agency and why? They must justify their choice by weighing trade-offs between dataset size, data quality, analytical complexity, and prediction accuracy. Include at least three specific evidence points from their analysis.

Step 5 (10 min): Pairs share recommendations with another pair, discussing differences in their evaluations and reasoning.
materials_needed: Dataset A: Clean real estate data (CSV file, 500 records)
Dataset B: Messy real estate data (CSV file, 800 records)
Two sample analysis reports (PDF format)
Data quality assessment checklist (printed worksheet)
Comparison matrix template (printed worksheet)
Excel or Google Sheets access for each pair
assessment_method: Evaluate written recommendations using rubric: Data quality assessment accuracy (25%), methodology comparison depth (25%), evidence-based reasoning (30%), and practical recommendation justification (20%). Success requires identifying at least 5 data quality issues, comparing 4 methodological differences, and providing clear recommendation with supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each step and example phrases for evaluation language. For advanced learners, add extension questions about bias sources, ethical considerations in data selection, or alternative methods they would recommend.
