Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support.
original_title: Evaluating Data Quality and Analysis Methods in Real Estate Price Predictions

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Flash Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and instantly recall 25 advanced Big O notation expressions, their formal mathematical definitions, and corresponding algorithm examples. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge for advanced algorithm analysis through structured repetition and peer verification.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact mathematical definitions of 25 advanced complexity notations including O(log log n), O(n log* n), and O(2^√(log n)) by completing timed memory exercises
Students will identify specific algorithms that exhibit each complexity class through rapid-fire matching activities with 95% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing the Advanced Complexity Reference Sheet containing 25 complexity notations from O(1) to O(n!) including uncommon ones like O(log* n), O(n^(1/3)), and O(2^√(log n)). Students have 20 minutes to study the sheet, focusing on memorizing both the notation and one example algorithm for each complexity class. Remove all reference materials. Round 1 (10 minutes): Display complexity notations one at a time on screen for 15 seconds each. Students write the formal mathematical definition and one example algorithm. Round 2 (8 minutes): Reverse format - show algorithm names, students write the complexity notation. Round 3 (7 minutes): Lightning round - show complexity notation for 8 seconds, students write example algorithm only. Between rounds, allow 2 minutes for students to review their answers with the reference sheet. For peer verification, pair students and have them quiz each other for 10 minutes using the reference sheet, alternating questioner roles every 2 minutes. Conclude with individual written assessment where students must recall 20 randomly selected complexity notations with definitions and examples within 15 minutes. Record completion percentages and accuracy rates for each student.
materials_needed: Advanced Complexity Reference Sheet with 25 notation definitions
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying prompts
Individual answer sheets (4 pages per student)
Red pens for peer checking
assessment_method: Success measured by accuracy percentage on final written recall test: 90-100% = mastery, 80-89% = proficient, 70-79% = developing, below 70% = needs remediation. Students must correctly provide both mathematical definition AND example algorithm for each notation to receive credit. Track response time for lightning rounds - target under 8 seconds per response.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet and allow highlighting of 5 most challenging notations for extra study time. Create visual complexity hierarchy chart showing relationships between notations. For advanced learners: Add amortized analysis notations and require multiple algorithm examples per complexity class. Challenge them to create their own memory palace techniques and teach struggling peers.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Ensemble Model Outputs for High-Dimensional Healthcare Data
description: Students will analyze feature importance outputs from multiple ensemble algorithms (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) applied to a complex healthcare dataset to understand how different models prioritize features differently. They will interpret the statistical and practical significance of feature rankings and explain the underlying mathematical reasons for discrepancies between models.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings from three different ensemble algorithms by analyzing mathematical properties and model assumptions
Students will explain discrepancies in feature importance across models through examination of algorithm-specific calculation methods and data characteristics
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed healthcare dataset containing 50+ features (demographics, lab values, vital signs, medical history) and target variable (30-day readmission). Students work in pairs using Jupyter notebooks with pre-fitted Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost models already trained on the dataset. Step 1 (20 minutes): Each pair extracts feature importance values from all three models using .feature_importances_ attributes and creates comparative visualizations showing top 15 features for each model. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students calculate Spearman rank correlations between the three importance rankings and identify features that show high variance in rankings across models. Step 3 (30 minutes): For the top 5 most discrepant features, students research and document the mathematical basis for importance calculation in each algorithm (Gini impurity reduction vs. gradient-based importance vs. gain-based metrics). Step 4 (25 minutes): Students examine partial dependence plots for the most discrepant features to understand non-linear relationships and interaction effects that might explain ranking differences. Step 5 (20 minutes): Pairs write a technical memo explaining which model's feature importance they would trust most for clinical decision-making, justifying their choice based on algorithm properties, data characteristics, and domain knowledge. Conclude with 10-minute pair presentations of their recommendations.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, xgboost, matplotlib, seaborn
MIMIC-III derived dataset with 50+ healthcare features (anonymized)
Pre-fitted ensemble models saved as pickle files
Algorithm reference sheets explaining importance calculation methods
Technical memo template with specific sections for analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate technical memos using rubric: (1) Accuracy of mathematical explanations for importance calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of statistical analysis comparing rankings (25 points), (3) Depth of interpretation connecting algorithm properties to observed differences (25 points), (4) Soundness of final recommendation with domain-appropriate justification (25 points). Students must correctly identify at least 3 mathematical reasons for discrepancies and provide statistically supported arguments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm flowcharts showing where importance calculations occur and pre-written code snippets for correlation analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement permutation importance as a fourth comparison method and analyze computational complexity trade-offs. Provide additional ensemble methods (AdaBoost, Extra Trees) for extended analysis. Include discussion of SHAP values as an alternative interpretation framework.

title: Budget Your Dream Pizza Party: Applying Multiplication and Addition to Real-World Planning
description: Students will apply basic multiplication and addition skills to calculate costs and quantities for planning a class pizza party within a given budget. This activity connects mathematical operations to practical decision-making scenarios that students can relate to their daily lives.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication skills to calculate total costs for multiple items by using real pizza menu prices and quantities
Students will apply addition and subtraction to determine if their party plan fits within the given budget through hands-on budget planning
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pizza party planning worksheet and fake pizza menu to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student has a $100 budget to plan a pizza party for 24 classmates. Students must calculate how many pizzas, drinks, and desserts they can afford while staying within budget. 

First, have students work individually to read the menu and identify prices (5 minutes). Next, guide them through calculating how many pizzas are needed (24 students ÷ 3 students per pizza = 8 pizzas minimum). Students then apply multiplication to find costs: if large pizzas cost $12 each, 8 pizzas = 8 × $12 = $96 (10 minutes).

Students continue by calculating drink costs (24 sodas × $1.50 each = $36) and dessert options (24 cookies × $0.75 each = $18). They apply addition to find total costs and subtraction to check remaining budget (15 minutes).

In pairs, students compare their party plans and verify each other's calculations (10 minutes). Partners check multiplication and addition work, identifying any errors. Finally, have 3-4 student pairs share their complete party plans with the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning and budget decisions (10 minutes). Conclude by discussing how they applied math operations to make real-world decisions and what they learned about budgeting.
materials_needed: Pizza party planning worksheet (1 per student)
Fake pizza restaurant menu with prices (1 per student)
Calculators (optional, 1 per student)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (3) All calculations correct with clear work shown, budget maintained; (2) Minor calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of operations; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Observe student explanations during pair sharing for evidence of applying mathematical reasoning to practical decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing 'quantity × price = total' format, allow calculator use, and pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add constraints like 'must include vegetarian options' or 'calculate tax and tip,' or have them create their own menu with different pricing scenarios.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big-O Decomposition
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by breaking down their code structures, identifying key operations, and determining their time complexity classifications. They will create detailed comparison charts showing how each algorithm's performance scales with input size.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the step-by-step execution patterns of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by tracing through their recursive and iterative structures
Students will differentiate between O(n²), O(n log n), and average-case complexities through systematic comparison of algorithmic components and nested loop structures
instructions: Begin by distributing three code samples (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) to student pairs. Each pair receives a worksheet with analysis tables pre-formatted for their findings. In Phase 1 (15 minutes), students examine bubble sort code, identifying nested loops and counting comparison operations for arrays of size 4, 8, and 16. They record actual operation counts in their table. Phase 2 (20 minutes) focuses on merge sort analysis. Students trace through the recursive divide phase, counting how many times the array splits (log n levels), then analyze the merge operations at each level (n operations per level). They calculate total operations as n × log n. Phase 3 (20 minutes) covers quicksort analysis. Students identify the partitioning process, analyze best-case (balanced partitions) versus worst-case (unbalanced partitions) scenarios, and determine why average case is O(n log n) but worst case is O(n²). In Phase 4 (15 minutes), pairs complete a comparison matrix showing algorithm name, best case, average case, worst case, and space complexity. They must justify each classification with specific code references. Phase 5 (10 minutes) involves creating a visual graph plotting performance curves for n=100, n=1000, n=10000 data points. Finally (5 minutes), pairs present one key insight about when to choose each algorithm based on their analysis.
materials_needed: Pre-written code samples for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in chosen programming language
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with comparison tables and graph templates
Calculators or computers for operation counting
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of Big-O classifications for all three algorithms, (2) Quality of step-by-step operation counting with correct mathematical reasoning, (3) Completeness of comparison matrix with justified algorithm selection criteria, (4) Clarity of visual representation showing relative performance differences. Students must achieve 3/4 points on each criterion to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed trace tables and highlight specific lines of code to analyze first. Offer a Big-O reference sheet with common complexity patterns. For advanced learners: Include analysis of space complexity, challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or have them optimize one of the provided algorithms and re-analyze its complexity.

title: Design a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Urban Traffic Flow Management
description: Students will create an original mathematical model using calculus, linear programming, and statistical analysis to optimize traffic light timing across a city intersection network. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then validate their model using real traffic data and present actionable recommendations to city planners.
estimated_duration: 6 class periods (630 minutes total) plus independent work time
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multi-variable calculus, linear programming, and probability theory by designing an original traffic optimization algorithm that minimizes average wait times across multiple intersections
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical model through integration of constraint optimization, statistical validation, and computational simulation techniques
instructions:
**Phase 1: Model Development (Days 1-2, 180 minutes total)**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Provide each team with traffic count data from 4 interconnected intersections during peak hours. Teams must first identify decision variables (light cycle times, green/red ratios per direction), constraints (minimum pedestrian crossing times, maximum cycle lengths, traffic flow continuity), and objective function (minimize total system wait time). Using Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization, teams derive the theoretical optimal solution.

**Phase 2: Computational Implementation (Days 3-4, 240 minutes total)**
Teams translate their mathematical model into Python code using NumPy and SciPy optimization libraries. They must implement: (1) constraint matrix representing traffic flow physics, (2) objective function incorporating stochastic arrival rates, (3) Monte Carlo simulation to test model robustness under varying conditions. Teams run 1000+ simulations with different traffic patterns and document convergence behavior.

**Phase 3: Validation and Refinement (Day 5, 120 minutes)**
Using provided historical traffic data, teams validate their model predictions against actual outcomes. They calculate root-mean-square error, analyze residuals, and identify model limitations. Teams must modify their original equations based on validation results and justify all mathematical adjustments.

**Phase 4: Professional Presentation (Day 6, 90 minutes)**
Teams prepare 15-minute presentations for mock city planning committee. Must include: mathematical derivation summary, computational results visualization, cost-benefit analysis of implementation, and specific policy recommendations with confidence intervals.
materials_needed: Real traffic count datasets from 4-intersection network (provided as CSV files)
Python programming environment with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, and Pandas libraries
Historical traffic light timing data for validation
Large format paper and markers for mathematical derivations
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Rubric evaluates: (1) Mathematical rigor - correct application of optimization theory, constraint handling, and statistical validation (40 points), (2) Computational implementation - working code with proper documentation and error handling (30 points), (3) Model validation - appropriate statistical tests and honest assessment of limitations (20 points), (4) Professional communication - clear presentation of technical concepts to non-mathematical audience (10 points). Minimum 75/100 points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template constraint matrices and guided worksheets for Lagrange multiplier setup. Offer office hours focused on translating mathematical concepts to code. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables like weather effects, emergency vehicle priority, or multi-objective optimization including environmental factors. Encourage exploration of machine learning integration for dynamic traffic prediction.

title: Programming Language Syntax Components Memory Match Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify fundamental syntax elements from Python programming language through a structured flashcard and matching activity. This foundational exercise helps students build automatic recall of basic programming constructs before writing code.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the correct syntax for 15 basic Python programming constructs (variables, loops, conditionals, functions) by matching code examples to their descriptions
Students will identify Python keywords, operators, and punctuation marks through visual recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 30 cards: 15 Python code syntax examples and 15 corresponding description cards. Display the master list of syntax elements on the board: variable assignment (=), if statements (if:), for loops (for x in:), while loops (while:), function definition (def name():), print statements (print()), comments (#), indentation (4 spaces), string quotes (''), list brackets ([]), dictionary braces ({}), comparison operators (==, !=, <, >), logical operators (and, or, not), import statements (import), and return statements (return). Students work individually for 10 minutes to study the flashcards, reading each code example aloud and matching it mentally to its description. Next, have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, taking turns showing their partner a code example card while the partner states its purpose and usage rule from memory. Partners provide immediate correction and reinforcement. For the final 15 minutes, conduct a whole-class matching game: post the 15 description cards randomly on the board, then call individual students forward to place the corresponding syntax example card next to its match while explaining the pairing to the class. Record each student's accuracy on a tracking sheet. Conclude with a 5-minute rapid-fire review where you display syntax examples on screen and students write the corresponding term or description on paper.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (30 cards per student pair)
Master syntax reference sheet for projection/board display
Magnetic strips or tape for board posting
Individual tracking sheets for instructor assessment
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must correctly match at least 12 out of 15 syntax-description pairs during the board activity and score 80% or higher on the final rapid-fire written quiz. Track individual performance using a checklist rubric: 3 points for perfect recall (15/15), 2 points for strong recall (12-14/15), 1 point for developing recall (8-11/15), 0 points for insufficient recall (below 8/15).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference sheet with syntax examples during study time, allow extended practice with flashcards, and pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: include additional complex syntax elements like list comprehensions, lambda functions, or exception handling; challenge them to create their own flashcards for advanced concepts and teach struggling peers.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Datasets
description: Students will analyze correlation matrices and heatmaps from a telecommunications customer churn dataset to identify relationships between customer characteristics and churn behavior. Through guided exploration, students will explain how different features correlate with each other and with the target variable.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between numerical features by analyzing correlation matrices and explaining the strength and direction of relationships
Students will explain the implications of feature correlations through systematic examination of correlation heatmaps and written analysis
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the prepared Telco Customer Churn dataset and correlation analysis worksheet (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to load the dataset in their chosen analysis tool and generate a correlation matrix for all numerical variables including tenure, monthly_charges, total_charges, and churn. Next, have students create a correlation heatmap with a diverging color scheme where values range from -1 to +1 (20 minutes). Guide students through examining the correlation matrix systematically: first identify the three strongest positive correlations (excluding perfect self-correlations), then the three strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values and variable pairs. Students should then focus specifically on correlations with the churn variable, ranking all features by their correlation strength with churn from highest to lowest absolute value (25 minutes). In the analysis phase, students write interpretations for each significant correlation (|r| > 0.3), explaining what the relationship means in business terms. For example, if monthly_charges correlates 0.19 with churn, students explain that higher monthly charges are associated with slightly higher churn rates. Students must also identify potential multicollinearity issues by flagging feature pairs with correlations above 0.7 and explaining why this might be problematic for predictive modeling (30 minutes). Conclude with pairs presenting one surprising correlation finding to the class, explaining both the statistical relationship and its potential business implications (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (CSV file with 7,043 records)
Correlation analysis worksheet template
Python/R environment with pandas/seaborn or equivalent statistical software
Access to correlation heatmap visualization tools
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all significant correlations with accurate coefficient values and provides insightful business interpretations; (3) Identifies most correlations correctly with good interpretations; (2) Identifies some correlations with basic interpretations; (1) Shows minimal understanding of correlation patterns. Check for accurate calculation/reading of correlation values, appropriate identification of multicollinearity concerns, and clear explanations of business implications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide with examples (e.g., 0.7 = strong positive, -0.3 = moderate negative) and sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests that as X increases, Y tends to...' Advanced learners can investigate partial correlations, create correlation matrices for different customer segments, or research how correlation analysis informs feature selection in machine learning pipelines.

title: Engineering a Sustainable City Water Distribution System Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to design an optimal water distribution network for a growing metropolitan area. They will use real-world constraints including budget limitations, environmental regulations, and population demands to create a mathematically sound solution that minimizes cost while meeting all service requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve a multi-variable optimization problem by formulating objective functions and constraint inequalities within a real-world engineering context
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis techniques through systematic problem-solving to determine optimal resource allocation for municipal infrastructure
instructions:
Begin by distributing the City Planning Data Packets containing population projections, terrain maps, and budget specifications for the fictional city of Riverside (15 minutes setup). Organize students into teams of 3-4 municipal engineering consultants. Each team receives identical base data: current population of 250,000, projected 40% growth over 10 years, $50M infrastructure budget, and environmental constraints limiting pipeline routes through protected wetlands.

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams identify decision variables (pipeline routes, pump station locations, reservoir capacities) and formulate the linear programming problem. They must define their objective function (minimize total system cost) and establish at least 6 realistic constraints including: minimum water pressure requirements (40 PSI), environmental protection zones, maximum pipeline lengths, budget limitations, and capacity requirements for different city districts.

Step 2 (35 minutes): Using graphing calculators or Excel Solver, teams apply the simplex method to solve their optimization problem. They must document each pivot operation and interpret shadow prices for resource constraints. Students create a detailed cost breakdown showing pipeline installation ($200/meter), pump stations ($500K each), and reservoir construction ($1M per million gallon capacity).

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams prepare technical presentations including: optimal solution coordinates, total system cost, sensitivity analysis for budget variations, and visual network diagrams showing pipeline routes and facility locations. Each presentation must demonstrate mathematical rigor while addressing practical engineering considerations.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams present 5-minute solutions to the 'City Council' (other teams) who evaluate feasibility and cost-effectiveness. Conclude with reflection on how mathematical optimization influences real infrastructure decisions.
materials_needed: City Planning Data Packets with population demographics and terrain maps
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent) or computers with Excel
Large format graph paper (11x17 inches)
Colored pencils for network diagram creation
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint or Google Slides)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem Formulation (25 points) - correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints; Mathematical Application (30 points) - accurate simplex method implementation and solution verification; Engineering Analysis (25 points) - realistic cost calculations and feasibility assessment; Communication (20 points) - clear presentation with visual aids and technical justification. Success requires achieving 80+ points with demonstrated mastery in applying linear programming to solve complex, multi-constraint optimization problems.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint formulation templates and step-by-step simplex method reference cards. Offer simplified scenarios with fewer variables for students needing additional practice. For advanced learners, introduce integer programming constraints (whole number pump stations) or multi-objective optimization including environmental impact minimization alongside cost reduction. Provide extension challenges involving stochastic demand variations or network reliability analysis.

title: Analyzing Memory Management Vulnerabilities in C++ Code Through Static Analysis and Exploitation Vectors
description: Students analyze real-world C++ code samples to identify memory management vulnerabilities, trace execution paths that lead to security exploits, and evaluate the effectiveness of different mitigation strategies. This expert-level activity requires students to decompose complex code interactions and assess risk severity.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze C++ source code to identify buffer overflows, use-after-free, and memory leak vulnerabilities by tracing variable lifetimes and pointer operations
Students will evaluate the exploitability of discovered vulnerabilities through systematic assessment of attack vectors and potential impact scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three C++ code samples (150-200 lines each) containing realistic memory management vulnerabilities from different domains: network server code, image processing library, and database connector. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes to perform initial code review using provided vulnerability checklists. Next, students spend 60 minutes using Valgrind and AddressSanitizer tools to validate their manual findings, documenting memory access patterns and heap/stack interactions. In the third phase (45 minutes), pairs create detailed vulnerability reports categorizing each issue by CWE classification, assigning CVSS scores, and mapping potential exploitation scenarios. Students then spend 30 minutes cross-reviewing another pair's analysis, providing peer feedback on missed vulnerabilities or incorrect risk assessments. Finally, conduct a 30-minute class discussion where each pair presents their most critical finding, explaining the root cause analysis and proposing specific code fixes. Throughout the activity, students must document their analytical reasoning process, showing how they traced data flow, identified unsafe operations, and connected vulnerabilities to real-world attack patterns. Instructors should circulate during analysis phases, asking probing questions about edge cases and encouraging deeper investigation of complex pointer arithmetic and memory allocation patterns.
materials_needed: Three C++ source code files with embedded memory vulnerabilities
Vulnerability assessment checklist with CWE categories
Linux environment with Valgrind and GCC AddressSanitizer installed
CVSS calculator tool or reference chart
Vulnerability report template document
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of vulnerability identification (25%) - correctly identifies 80%+ of planted vulnerabilities, (2) Quality of root cause analysis (25%) - demonstrates clear understanding of memory management principles and execution flow, (3) Risk assessment precision (25%) - appropriately categorizes severity and provides realistic exploitation scenarios, (4) Technical communication (25%) - vulnerability reports are clear, technically accurate, and include actionable remediation steps. Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional guided questions about specific code sections, offer simplified code samples with fewer nested pointers, and pair with stronger technical partners. For advanced learners: introduce race condition analysis in multithreaded code sections, challenge them to develop proof-of-concept exploits, or ask them to evaluate automated static analysis tool effectiveness by comparing tool outputs with manual findings.

title: Evaluating Data Quality Issues in Customer Survey Dataset
description: Students will critically assess a real customer satisfaction survey dataset to identify data quality problems, judge the severity of each issue, and recommend specific data cleaning strategies. They will justify their recommendations by weighing the trade-offs between different data handling approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the completeness, accuracy, and consistency of survey data by systematically analyzing missing values, outliers, and inconsistent responses
Students will critique different data cleaning approaches through structured comparison of their advantages, disadvantages, and impact on analysis results
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'CustomerSurvey_Raw.csv' dataset containing 500 customer responses with intentionally introduced quality issues. Give students 15 minutes to explore the dataset using basic functions (head(), info(), describe(), isnull().sum()). Next, distribute the 'Data Quality Evaluation Worksheet' and have students spend 20 minutes systematically documenting issues they find in each column, categorizing problems as missing data, outliers, inconsistent formatting, or logical inconsistencies. For the evaluation phase (25 minutes), students must rate each identified issue's severity on a 1-5 scale, considering factors like percentage of affected records, potential impact on analysis, and feasibility of correction. They should then research and propose three specific solutions for the two most severe issues, documenting the pros and cons of each approach. In the final 15 minutes, pair students to peer-review each other's evaluations using the provided checklist, focusing on whether the severity ratings are justified and if proposed solutions are realistic. Students must provide written feedback on their partner's reasoning and suggest improvements. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where 2-3 pairs share their most interesting findings and the rationale behind their recommendations.
materials_needed: CustomerSurvey_Raw.csv dataset (pre-loaded with quality issues)
Data Quality Evaluation Worksheet (structured template)
Peer Review Checklist
Computers with Python/Pandas or Excel installed
Access to internet for researching data cleaning techniques
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Completeness of issue identification (25%), (2) Appropriateness of severity ratings with clear justification (30%), (3) Feasibility and specificity of proposed solutions (25%), (4) Quality of peer feedback and constructive criticism (20%). Students must submit their completed worksheet and a 1-page summary defending their top two severity ratings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a sample analysis of the first three columns and a severity rating example with detailed reasoning. Offer a checklist of common data quality issues to guide their exploration. For advanced learners, challenge them to calculate the potential statistical impact of each issue (e.g., how outliers affect mean vs. median) and research industry-standard data quality frameworks like DAMA-DMBOK principles.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating Mathematical Models for Urban Planning
description: Students will create a comprehensive mathematical model for a city district by integrating geometric principles, statistical analysis, and algebraic functions. They will design layouts, calculate resource needs, and present justifications using multiple mathematical concepts in a real-world context.
estimated_duration: 145 minutes (2.5 hours, can be split across 2 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric area calculations, proportional reasoning, and statistical analysis by designing an optimal city district layout within given constraints
Students will construct mathematical models using linear and quadratic functions through analyzing population growth, resource allocation, and budget planning for their urban design
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute introduction explaining the scenario: students are urban planners designing a 2-square-kilometer district for 15,000 residents with a $50 million budget. Distribute city planning packets containing grid paper, constraint cards, and resource tables. In the first 30 minutes, students work individually to sketch their initial district layout on grid paper (1 cm = 50 meters), including residential areas (60% minimum), commercial zones (15-25%), parks (minimum 10%), and infrastructure (roads, utilities). During the next 45 minutes, students calculate specific requirements: total building areas using geometric formulas, population density per zone using ratios and proportions, and create linear functions modeling utility costs based on district size. Students then spend 30 minutes developing mathematical models for three scenarios: population growth over 10 years (exponential/linear functions), monthly budget allocation (pie charts and percentages), and traffic flow optimization (creating coordinate systems and calculating optimal road placement using distance formulas). In the final 25 minutes, students prepare a presentation board including their scaled district map, mathematical calculations with work shown, function graphs, and written justification explaining how their design meets all constraints while optimizing livability. Conclude with 5-minute peer gallery walks where students examine others' solutions and identify different mathematical approaches used.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
City Planning Constraint Cards with budget/zoning requirements
Resource calculation tables (utility costs, construction prices)
Colored pencils or markers for zone coding
Calculators
Rulers and protractors
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and function creation (25%), (2) Appropriate use of multiple math concepts (geometry, algebra, statistics) with correct notation (25%), (3) Creative integration of mathematical solutions within real-world constraints (25%), (4) Clear mathematical communication through written explanations and visual representations (25%). Students must demonstrate at least 3 different mathematical concepts and show all calculation work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated building templates with areas marked, offer function equation starters, and allow partnership for calculation checking. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including environmental impact calculations using rates, optimize designs using systems of equations, or create 3D models incorporating volume calculations and trigonometry for building heights.

title: Memory Palace: Recalling Complex Algorithm Time Complexities and Space Trade-offs
description: Students will systematically memorize and recall the time and space complexities of 20 advanced algorithms across sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and string matching categories. They will use spaced repetition flashcards and verbal recitation to demonstrate precise recall of Big O notations, best/worst case scenarios, and memory requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity (Big O notation) for 20 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, KMP string matching, and advanced sorting algorithms within 5 seconds per algorithm
Students will identify and recite the space complexity trade-offs and auxiliary memory requirements for each algorithm through structured verbal assessment
instructions: **Phase 1 - Information Encoding (15 minutes):** Distribute the algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 20 algorithms organized in 4 categories (5 algorithms each): Advanced Sorting (Radix, Bucket, Counting, Heap, Quick), Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A*, Kruskal's), Dynamic Programming (Longest Common Subsequence, Knapsack variants, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Optimal Binary Search Tree), and String Matching (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick, Suffix Array). Students spend 3 minutes per category silently reading and creating mental associations. **Phase 2 - Active Memorization (20 minutes):** Students create physical flashcards with algorithm name on front, complete complexity profile on back (time complexity best/average/worst case, space complexity, auxiliary space requirements). They practice in pairs using spaced repetition - 1st round: 30 seconds per card, 2nd round: 15 seconds, 3rd round: 10 seconds, final round: 5 seconds. Partners track accuracy on provided scoring sheets. **Phase 3 - Rapid Recall Assessment (10 minutes):** Instructor calls out algorithm names randomly. Students write down complete complexity profile within 5 seconds. No reference materials allowed. **Phase 4 - Verbal Verification (10 minutes):** Students pair up for oral quiz. Partner A states algorithm name, Partner B has 5 seconds to verbally provide all complexity information. Switch roles after 10 algorithms. Record accuracy scores.
materials_needed: Algorithm complexity reference sheets (printed, one per student)
Blank index cards (20 per student)
Scoring sheets with algorithm names and accuracy tracking grid
Timer/stopwatch
Pencils/pens for writing responses
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (17/20 correct) on the rapid recall written assessment. Each algorithm response must include: correct time complexity notation, identification of best/worst case scenarios, and space complexity. Verbal assessment requires 80% accuracy (16/20) with responses delivered within 5-second time limit. Partial credit given for incomplete but accurate partial responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet with pre-created memory aids (e.g., 'Dijkstra Drinks V-log-V cocktails' for V log V complexity). Allow additional 5 minutes for initial memorization phase. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity factors such as cache performance, parallelization potential, and implementation-specific optimizations. Challenge them to recall specific constant factors and explain why certain algorithms have the same Big O but different practical performance.

title: Memory Palace: Recalling Complex Algorithm Time Complexities and Space Trade-offs: Practical Workshop
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity characteristics of 15 advanced algorithms including their best, average, and worst-case scenarios. This activity uses spaced repetition and mnemonic techniques to ensure long-term retention of critical algorithm performance metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the time complexity (best, average, worst case) for 15 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's, A*, QuickSort variants, and tree traversal methods within 30 seconds per algorithm
Students will memorize and recite the space complexity requirements and key implementation constraints for each algorithm through structured flashcard repetition and peer testing
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made algorithm complexity reference sheets containing 15 algorithms: Dijkstra's shortest path, A* search, QuickSort (3-way partitioning), Merge Sort, Heap Sort, AVL tree operations, Red-Black tree insertion, Binary search variants, DFS/BFS traversals, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, Kruskal's MST, Prim's MST, Radix Sort, and Counting Sort. Each sheet includes algorithm name, time complexity notation for all cases, space complexity, and one key implementation note. Students spend 20 minutes creating personalized mnemonic devices or memory associations for each algorithm's complexity profile. Provide example: 'Dijkstra is Dense - O(V²) with dense graphs, but Elegant with heaps - O((V+E)logV)'. Next, students create digital flashcards using Anki or physical cards with algorithm name on front, complete complexity analysis on back. Conduct three 10-minute spaced repetition rounds: immediate review, 15-minute delay, then 30-minute delay. During each round, students work in pairs taking turns as questioner and responder. Questioner shows algorithm name, responder must state all complexity information within 30 seconds. Incorrect responses require immediate correction and re-drilling. For final assessment, conduct rapid-fire individual testing where instructor calls out random algorithm names and students write complete complexity profiles on provided answer sheets. Track accuracy rates and identify algorithms requiring additional memorization work.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm complexity reference sheets (15 algorithms per student)
Blank flashcard templates or access to Anki flashcard software
Individual answer sheets for final assessment
Timer for spaced repetition intervals
Red/green cards for peer feedback signaling
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/15 correct) on final rapid-fire recall test where they write complete time/space complexity information for randomly called algorithms within 30-second time limits. Grade based on: correct Big O notation (2 points), accurate best/average/worst case distinctions (2 points), correct space complexity (1 point) per algorithm. Maximum 75 points total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with only 8 algorithms, focus on pattern recognition (divide-and-conquer vs greedy vs dynamic programming), provide pre-made mnemonics, allow 45-second response time initially. For advanced learners: Add 5 additional algorithms (suffix arrays, segment trees, fenwick trees), require explanation of why complexity differs between implementations, challenge them to create memory techniques for the class to use.
original_title: Memory Palace: Recalling Complex Algorithm Time Complexities and Space Trade-offs

title: Interpreting Dimensionality Reduction Trade-offs in High-Dimensional Genomic Data
description: Students will analyze the mathematical relationships and practical implications of different dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP) applied to a 20,000-gene expression dataset. They will interpret how parameter choices affect biological signal preservation versus computational efficiency trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the mathematical foundations and assumptions underlying PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP by comparing their loss functions and optimization objectives
Students will interpret how hyperparameter modifications (perplexity, n_neighbors, min_dist) affect cluster preservation and biological interpretability through systematic parameter analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with a preprocessed single-cell RNA sequencing dataset (10,000 cells × 2,000 highly variable genes) and three Jupyter notebooks containing pre-configured dimensionality reduction pipelines. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students work in pairs to execute each algorithm with default parameters, documenting runtime, memory usage, and initial 2D visualizations. They must annotate each plot with cell type clusters and calculate silhouette scores for cluster separation quality. In Phase 2 (60 minutes), students systematically modify key hyperparameters: PCA (n_components: 10, 50, 200), t-SNE (perplexity: 5, 30, 100), and UMAP (n_neighbors: 5, 15, 50; min_dist: 0.1, 0.5, 0.8). For each configuration, they record computational metrics and assess how biological signal preservation changes using provided marker gene expression overlays. Phase 3 (45 minutes) involves creating a comparative analysis matrix where students categorize each method's strengths/weaknesses across five dimensions: computational scalability, local structure preservation, global structure preservation, parameter sensitivity, and biological interpretability. Students must justify their categorizations using specific evidence from their parameter sweeps, citing quantitative metrics (silhouette scores, trustworthiness indices) and qualitative observations about cluster boundaries and marker gene expression patterns. Finally, they prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining which method they would recommend for three different research scenarios: exploratory data analysis, publication-quality visualization, and downstream machine learning preprocessing.
materials_needed: Preprocessed single-cell RNA-seq dataset (10,000 cells × 2,000 genes, .h5ad format)
Three pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with scikit-learn, scanpy, and umap-learn installations
List of 20 cell-type-specific marker genes with expected expression patterns
Computational resources with minimum 16GB RAM per student pair
assessment_method: Students submit their completed analysis matrix (40 points) evaluated on accuracy of mathematical explanations, appropriate use of quantitative metrics, and quality of biological interpretations. Their 5-minute presentations (30 points) are assessed on clarity of trade-off explanations and appropriateness of method recommendations for given scenarios. Bonus points (10 points) awarded for identifying non-obvious parameter interactions or suggesting novel evaluation metrics.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a decision tree flowchart linking parameter changes to expected outcomes, and offer pre-calculated trustworthiness indices for reference. Advanced learners can explore batch effect correction integration, implement custom distance metrics, or investigate how different preprocessing steps (log-normalization vs. z-scoring) interact with dimensionality reduction assumptions. Provide access to additional datasets with known ground truth for validation exercises.

title: Personal Budget Planning: Applying Percentages to Monthly Income
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a young adult by applying percentage calculations to a given income scenario. They will allocate funds across different expense categories using the 50/30/20 budgeting rule and calculate exact dollar amounts for each category.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting percentages to dollar amounts within a realistic income scenario
Students will demonstrate percentage problem-solving skills through creating and justifying a complete monthly budget plan
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Income Scenarios' worksheet containing three different monthly income amounts: $2,400, $3,200, and $4,000. Explain the 50/30/20 budgeting rule: 50% for needs (rent, groceries, utilities), 30% for wants (entertainment, dining out), and 20% for savings/debt repayment. Students work in pairs and each pair selects one income scenario. First, students calculate the dollar amount for each category by multiplying the monthly income by each percentage (0.50, 0.30, 0.20). Next, they create detailed subcategories within each main category. For 'needs,' they might allocate specific amounts for rent ($800), groceries ($300), phone ($50), etc., ensuring the total equals their calculated 50% amount. They repeat this process for 'wants' and 'savings' categories. Students then create a visual budget chart showing both percentages and dollar amounts for each category and subcategory. In the final 15 minutes, pairs present their budget to another pair, explaining their allocation reasoning and demonstrating their percentage calculations. The presenting pair must show their work for at least three percentage-to-dollar conversions and justify why their subcategory allocations are realistic for their chosen income level. Conclude with a brief class discussion comparing different approaches to the same income scenario.
materials_needed: Young Adult Income Scenarios worksheet (printed for each student)
Calculators or smartphones with calculator apps
Graph paper or budget template sheets
Colored pencils or markers for visual charts
Whiteboard and markers for demonstrations
assessment_method: Students earn points based on: (1) Accurate percentage calculations showing correct conversion from percentages to dollar amounts (40 points), (2) Realistic budget allocations that total correctly within each category (30 points), (3) Clear visual presentation of budget with both percentages and dollar amounts displayed (20 points), (4) Verbal explanation demonstrating understanding of calculation process during pair presentation (10 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example using a $1,000 income to model the process, offer percentage-to-decimal conversion charts, and allow calculator use for all calculations. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including irregular expenses (annual car insurance, quarterly payments), require them to adjust percentages based on different life situations (student loans, dependents), or have them create budgets for multiple income scenarios and compare the lifestyle differences.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big-O Performance
description: Students will analyze and compare the time and space complexity of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining code implementations and performance data. They will break down each algorithm's operations to determine Big-O notation and identify the relationships between algorithm design choices and computational efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by counting operations and deriving Big-O notation for best, average, and worst-case scenarios
Students will examine the relationship between algorithm design patterns and performance characteristics through systematic comparison of recursive versus iterative approaches
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes setup). Provide each team with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort, along with performance data tables showing execution times for arrays of sizes 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 elements. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze each algorithm's code structure. Students trace through each algorithm with a sample 8-element array, counting the number of comparisons and swaps/moves for each step. They document their findings in the provided analysis worksheet, noting loop structures, recursive calls, and memory usage patterns.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the performance data tables, teams create graphs plotting array size versus execution time for each algorithm. Students identify growth patterns and match them to theoretical complexity curves (linear, logarithmic, quadratic, etc.).

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams complete a comparative analysis matrix, determining Big-O notation for time and space complexity for each algorithm's best, average, and worst cases. They must justify their conclusions by referencing specific code segments and data patterns observed in Steps 1-2.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each team presents one algorithm analysis to the class (8 minutes presentation, 2 minutes Q&A). Presenting teams must explain their Big-O derivation process and defend their complexity classifications using evidence from their code tracing and performance graphs.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Conduct whole-class discussion comparing all three algorithms, identifying when each would be most appropriate based on data size, memory constraints, and performance requirements. Students complete individual reflection questions connecting algorithm choice to real-world applications.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (one set per team)
Performance data tables with execution times for different array sizes
Algorithm analysis worksheets with comparison matrices
Graph paper or graphing software access
Calculators
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate operation counting and code tracing (25 points), (2) Correct Big-O notation derivation with justification (30 points), (3) Accurate graph creation and pattern identification (20 points), (4) Quality of comparative analysis and real-world application connections (25 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed tracing tables and highlight key code sections to focus analysis. Offer simplified 4-element array examples for initial practice. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or challenge them to analyze space-time tradeoffs and hybrid algorithm approaches. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling teams during analysis phases.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Pandemic Spread with Policy Interventions
description: Students will create an original compartmental epidemiological model (extending beyond basic SIR) that incorporates real-world policy interventions and demographic factors. They will develop the differential equation system, implement it computationally, and present policy recommendations based on their mathematical findings.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a novel epidemiological model by extending traditional compartmental models to include at least three policy intervention parameters and two demographic stratifications
Students will synthesize mathematical modeling techniques, differential equations, and computational analysis to generate evidence-based public health policy recommendations
instructions: Begin with a 20-minute research phase where students select a specific infectious disease and geographic region, gathering real epidemiological parameters from peer-reviewed sources. Students work individually for 90 minutes designing their compartmental model structure, determining which compartments (S, E, I, R, D, V, etc.) to include and defining transition rates. They must incorporate at least three policy interventions (e.g., vaccination rates, social distancing compliance, quarantine effectiveness) and stratify by two demographic factors (age groups, socioeconomic status, etc.). Next, students spend 60 minutes deriving their system of differential equations, clearly defining each parameter and initial condition. Using Python/MATLAB/R, students implement their model computationally (45 minutes), creating functions for different policy scenarios. They run simulations comparing baseline scenarios with various intervention strategies, generating graphs showing disease progression over time. Students then analyze results for 30 minutes, identifying optimal policy combinations and noting model limitations. Finally, students prepare a 15-minute presentation including: model architecture diagram, mathematical equations, simulation results, policy recommendations, and critical evaluation of assumptions. During presentations, peers ask technical questions about mathematical choices and model validation approaches.
materials_needed: Access to epidemiological databases (CDC, WHO, PubMed)
Python with NumPy/SciPy/Matplotlib or equivalent (MATLAB/R)
Jupyter notebooks or similar coding environment
Scientific calculators
Presentation software with equation editor
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of differential equations (25 points), Innovation in model design and realistic parameter incorporation (25 points), Computational implementation accuracy and code quality (20 points), Quality of analysis and policy recommendations (20 points), Presentation clarity and response to peer questions (10 points). Students must demonstrate mathematical reasoning behind each modeling choice and provide sensitivity analysis for key parameters.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with a template showing basic SIR model structure and sample policy intervention examples. Offer intermediate students guidance on demographic stratification techniques. Challenge advanced learners to incorporate stochastic elements, spatial dynamics, or economic cost-benefit analysis. Provide debugging support for computational implementation and encourage peer collaboration during coding phases.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real customer churn dataset to identify correlations between variables and explain why these correlations do not necessarily imply causation. They will practice distinguishing between statistical relationships and causal relationships by examining confounding variables and proposing alternative explanations.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing customer churn data patterns and identifying at least three confounding variables that could explain observed correlations
Students will explain the limitations of correlation analysis through written justifications for why specific variable relationships cannot establish causal claims
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (3-4 people) with the Telco Customer Churn dataset containing 20 variables including monthly charges, contract type, tenure, and churn status. Give groups 15 minutes to explore the data using provided correlation matrices and scatter plots. Next, present three pre-calculated correlation findings: (1) Monthly charges correlate positively with churn (r=0.35), (2) Month-to-month contracts correlate with churn (r=0.40), and (3) Senior citizens correlate with churn (r=0.23). Have students spend 20 minutes discussing these correlations within their groups, then assign each group one correlation to analyze in depth. Groups must create a visual diagram showing: the two correlated variables, at least two potential confounding variables, and alternative causal explanations. For example, for monthly charges and churn, students might identify service quality, customer satisfaction, or income level as confounding variables. After 25 minutes of group work, each team presents their 3-minute analysis to the class, explaining why their assigned correlation does not prove causation. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where students identify common patterns across all three correlations and establish criteria for when correlation might suggest (but not prove) causation versus when it clearly cannot.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (CSV file with 7,043 records)
Pre-calculated correlation matrix handout
Scatter plot visualizations for three key variable pairs
Large paper sheets for creating causal diagrams
Colored markers or pens
Laptops with Excel or Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of confounding variables (2 points), (2) Clear explanation of alternative causal pathways (2 points), (3) Correct use of correlation vs. causation terminology (1 point), and (4) Quality of visual diagram showing relationships (1 point). Success requires scoring at least 5/6 points and demonstrating understanding that correlation alone cannot establish causation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a template diagram showing the relationship structure and offer examples of confounding variables from other domains (ice cream sales and drowning rates). For advanced learners, challenge them to design a controlled experiment that could test causation for their assigned correlation, or have them identify additional datasets where similar correlation-causation fallacies might occur in business decision-making.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Churn Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a customer churn dataset to distinguish between correlation and causation by examining statistical relationships and evaluating potential confounding variables. learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing customer churn patterns in a telecommunications dataset

instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the telecommunications customer churn dataset (provided CSV file) and ensure each student has access to Python/Jupyter notebooks or Excel. Display the activity worksheet on screen.

**Phase 1 - Initial Exploration (15 minutes):** Students load the dataset and examine variables including monthly_charges, total_charges, contract_length, customer_tenure, and churn_status. They calculate basic descriptive statistics and identify the churn rate (percentage of customers who left).

**Phase 2 - Correlation Analysis (20 minutes):** Students create a correlation matrix for numerical variables and generate scatter plots for: (1) monthly_charges vs churn_rate, (2) contract_length vs churn_rate, and (3) customer_tenure vs churn_rate. **Phase 3 - Causation Investigation (25 minutes):** Present three scenarios to students: 'High monthly charges cause churn,' 'Long contracts prevent churn,' and 'Tenure increases loyalty.' For each scenario, students must: identify potential confounding variables (e.g., service quality, customer satisfaction, promotional pricing), create segmented visualizations breaking down relationships by customer demographics, and write 2-3 sentences explaining whether correlation likely indicates causation.

**Phase 4 - Synthesis (15 minutes):** Students complete a structured worksheet ranking the three relationships from most likely to least likely causal, providing evidence from their analysis. They must cite specific statistical evidence and explain their reasoning for each ranking.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief discussion where 2-3 students share their top-ranked causal relationship and reasoning.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Arrays Using Calculus and Trigonometry
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and trigonometric principles to determine optimal solar panel placement for maximum energy efficiency in a real-world city planning scenario. They will calculate angles, shadow effects, and energy output variations throughout seasons.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative optimization techniques to determine maximum solar panel efficiency by calculating optimal tilt angles and spacing ratios
Students will implement trigonometric functions and solar geometry principles through analysis of seasonal sun path variations and shadow casting effects
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the scenario packet detailing a 50m × 30m rooftop in Denver, Colorado (latitude 39.7°N) where students must design an optimal solar array. Each team receives building specifications, seasonal sun angle data, and energy requirement targets. Teams first spend 20 minutes analyzing the given solar irradiance formula: I = I₀ × cos(θ) × cos(α - β), where θ is the angle between sun and panel normal, α is solar elevation, and β is panel tilt angle. Students then calculate optimal tilt angles for four seasonal positions using derivative optimization (25 minutes), setting dI/dβ = 0 and solving for β. Next, teams apply trigonometric shadow calculations using the formula: Shadow Length = Panel Height × cot(elevation angle) to determine minimum spacing between panel rows (20 minutes). They must ensure no shading occurs during peak hours (10 AM - 2 PM) during winter solstice. Teams use provided spreadsheet templates to model energy output variations across 12 months, applying their calculated angles and spacing (30 minutes). Finally, students prepare a 10-minute presentation showing their optimized design, mathematical justifications, total energy output predictions, and cost-benefit analysis comparing their solution to standard installations (35 minutes for all presentations). Throughout the activity, circulate to verify mathematical accuracy and push teams to justify their optimization choices with calculus-based reasoning.

Students must show all calculation steps and achieve within 5% of theoretical optimal values.

Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to cos(α - β) when α equals β?' For advanced learners, introduce additional variables like panel temperature effects using T-coefficient calculations, or challenge them to optimize for both summer and winter simultaneously using Lagrange multipliers.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: CAP Theorem Trade-offs in Real-World Architectures
description: Students will analyze actual distributed system architectures from major tech companies to identify how each system navigates CAP theorem trade-offs during failure scenarios. They will decompose complex system designs and evaluate the consistency, availability, and partition tolerance decisions made under different failure conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by examining how Netflix, Amazon DynamoDB, and Google Spanner handle CAP theorem trade-offs during network partitions and node failures
Students will evaluate the relationship between system design decisions and business requirements through comparative analysis of consistency models and failure handling strategies
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with detailed architecture diagrams and failure scenario case studies for three systems: Netflix's microservices architecture, Amazon DynamoDB, and Google Spanner. Each team analyzes all three systems but focuses primarily on one assigned system.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine their primary system's architecture documentation, identifying: (1) data replication strategies, (2) consensus mechanisms, (3) failure detection methods, and (4) partition handling protocols. Students must map specific components to CAP theorem elements and document trade-offs in a provided analysis template.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Present teams with three escalating failure scenarios: single node failure, network partition affecting 30% of nodes, and cascading datacenter outage. Teams trace through their system's response to each scenario, identifying which CAP properties are prioritized and which are sacrificed. They must provide specific evidence from system documentation.

Phase 3 (35 minutes): Teams create comparative analysis matrices examining all three systems' approaches to the same failure scenarios. They must identify patterns, trade-offs, and justify why different business contexts (streaming media, e-commerce, financial transactions) drive different architectural decisions.

Phase 4 (25 minutes): Each team presents their analysis of one critical failure scenario across all three systems, defending their conclusions about CAP trade-offs with specific architectural evidence. Other teams challenge findings and propose alternative interpretations.
materials_needed: Netflix microservices architecture documentation and Hystrix circuit breaker specifications
Amazon DynamoDB technical papers including eventual consistency model details
Google Spanner academic papers and TrueTime synchronization documentation
CAP theorem analysis templates with failure scenario worksheets
Digital whiteboarding tool (Miro or equivalent) for collaborative diagramming
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric across three dimensions: (1) Accuracy of CAP theorem application to real systems (25 points), (2) Depth of failure scenario analysis with specific architectural evidence (35 points), (3) Quality of comparative analysis identifying patterns and business justifications (40 points). Deliverables include completed analysis matrices, failure scenario trace documents, and peer evaluation of presentation defenses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted sections of key documentation and CAP theorem decision trees. Offer guided questions for each analysis phase. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by including Byzantine fault tolerance considerations or asking them to propose architectural improvements that better balance CAP trade-offs for specific business scenarios.

title: Evaluating Data Visualizations: Chart Detective Challenge
description: Students will critically assess and compare different data visualizations of the same dataset to determine which charts best communicate key insights. They will justify their evaluations using data visualization principles and recommend improvements for poorly designed charts.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types by applying data visualization best practices and principles of visual communication

instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a packet containing 6 different visualizations of the same sales dataset (bar chart, pie chart, line graph, scatter plot, poorly formatted table, and misleading 3D chart). Include a one-page data visualization evaluation checklist covering: chart type appropriateness, visual clarity, accurate representation, clear labeling, and audience suitability.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students work independently to examine each visualization using the checklist. They rate each chart on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and write 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning. Students must identify the main message each chart attempts to communicate and note any misleading elements.

**Ranking and Justification (15 minutes):** Students rank all six visualizations from most effective to least effective. For their top choice, they write a paragraph explaining why it best serves the intended purpose. For their bottom choice, they list three specific improvements needed.

**Peer Review Phase (15 minutes):** Pair students to compare their rankings and justifications. Partners must reach consensus on the top two and bottom two visualizations, documenting where they agreed/disagreed and why.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Poll the class on their top choices and facilitate discussion about common evaluation criteria. Have 2-3 pairs share their most significant disagreements and how they resolved them.

**Final Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write a brief reflection on which evaluation criterion they found most important and why, connecting to real-world scenarios where they might need to assess data visualizations.

Projector for class discussion polling

Collect ranking worksheets and reflection paragraphs as evidence of critical thinking.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Bias in Gradient Boosting Algorithms

Next 25 minutes: Students generate SHAP summary plots and waterfall plots for 10 randomly selected samples from each demographic group (gender, race, age brackets). They calculate and record the mean SHAP values for 'education' and 'hours-per-week' features across groups. Following 20 minutes: Students create partial dependence plots for the 'age' feature, stratified by gender and race, noting inflection points and slope differences. title: Personal Budget Application Using Percentage Calculations
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to create and analyze a realistic monthly budget for a college student. They will use percentages to allocate income across different expense categories and make budget adjustments based on percentage changes.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages and percentage changes by creating expense allocations for a monthly budget scenario
Students will apply percentage concepts through real-world budget analysis and adjustment problems
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Template' worksheet and calculators to each student (10 minutes setup). Present the scenario: students are college freshmen with a monthly income of $1,200 from part-time work and family support. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students calculate dollar amounts for each budget category using given percentages: Housing 35%, Food 20%, Transportation 10%, Entertainment 15%, Savings 10%, Miscellaneous 10%. They must show their percentage calculations (e.g., 35% of $1,200 = 0.35 × $1,200 = $420).

Step 2 (20 minutes): Present three budget adjustment scenarios. Scenario A: Income increases to $1,320 (10% increase) - students recalculate all categories maintaining the same percentages. Scenario B: Housing costs increase by 15% - students determine the new housing amount and what percentage of total budget this represents. Scenario C: Students want to increase savings to 15% - they must determine which categories to reduce and by how much.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students compare their original budget to their adjusted budgets, calculating the percentage change for each modified category using the formula: ((New Amount - Original Amount) / Original Amount) × 100.

Step 4 (10 minutes): In pairs, students peer-review calculations and discuss which budget scenario seems most realistic. Conclude with whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their findings and calculation strategies.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Template worksheet (one per student)
Basic calculator (one per student)
Pencils and erasers
Budget scenario handout with three adjustment problems
