Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of validation results, bias-variance tradeoffs, and real-world deployment constraints
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with a pre-processed telecommunications customer dataset (10,000+ records) containing features like monthly charges, contract length, service usage, and churn labels. Each team receives three pre-trained models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) with their training code and hyperparameter configurations. Students first spend 30 minutes analyzing each model's architecture and training approach, documenting assumptions and limitations. Next, teams conduct comprehensive evaluation over 60 minutes: calculate and compare accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC; generate confusion matrices; analyze feature importance/SHAP values; assess prediction confidence distributions; and evaluate computational efficiency (training time, inference speed, memory usage). Following evaluation, teams spend 45 minutes researching deployment considerations including model interpretability requirements for regulatory compliance, scalability needs for real-time predictions, maintenance complexity, and integration challenges with existing systems. Teams then analyze business impact by calculating potential revenue retention, false positive costs (unnecessary retention efforts), and false negative costs (lost customers). Finally, teams prepare 15-minute presentations defending their model recommendation, addressing anticipated counterarguments and discussing implementation roadmap. Each presentation includes quantitative performance comparison tables, visualizations of model behavior, cost-benefit analysis, and risk assessment matrix.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV format, 15+ features)
Three pre-trained models with training scripts (Python/scikit-learn/TensorFlow)
Jupyter Notebook environment with required libraries (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, SHAP)
Business context document with cost assumptions and regulatory requirements
Evaluation rubric templates for systematic model comparison
assessment_method: Grade presentations using rubric covering: quantitative analysis depth (25% - comprehensive metric calculation and statistical significance testing), critical evaluation quality (25% - identification of model limitations, bias assessment, generalization concerns), business justification strength (25% - cost-benefit analysis, implementation feasibility, risk mitigation strategies), and recommendation defense (25% - addressing counterarguments, evidence-based reasoning, alternative scenario consideration). Require written executive summary with recommendation matrix comparing all three models across technical and business dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing model evaluation checklists, guided worksheets for metric interpretation, and example business impact calculations. Offer intermediate checkpoints for metric validation and interpretation clarification. For advanced learners, introduce ensemble method evaluation, cross-validation strategy assessment, A/B testing design considerations, or model fairness auditing across customer demographic segments. Encourage exploration of advanced interpretability techniques like LIME or adversarial example generation.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Emergency Response Networks
description: Students will develop an original mathematical optimization model to determine optimal placement of emergency response stations in a simulated urban environment. They will integrate graph theory, linear programming, and statistical analysis to create a comprehensive solution that minimizes average response time while considering budget constraints and population density variations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from graph theory, optimization theory, and statistical modeling by designing a multi-variable mathematical model that addresses real-world emergency response logistics
Students will construct and validate an original algorithmic solution through iterative testing, mathematical proof, and computational implementation using professional-grade software tools
instructions: Begin with 30 minutes of individual research where students analyze provided urban demographic data, existing emergency response statistics, and geographical constraints for a fictional city of 500,000 residents. Provide each student with identical datasets including population density heat maps, historical emergency call locations, current station positions, and budget parameters. Students then spend 90 minutes formulating their mathematical model by defining decision variables (station locations, resource allocation), objective functions (minimize weighted average response time), and constraints (budget limits, coverage requirements, staffing ratios). They must document their mathematical reasoning using formal notation and create at least three different optimization approaches. Next, dedicate 60 minutes to computational implementation where students code their model using provided optimization software (MATLAB, Python with SciPy, or similar), running multiple scenarios with different parameter values. Students must validate their solutions by proving mathematical feasibility and testing edge cases. In the final 45 minutes, each student presents their unique model to a panel of 3-4 peers who act as city planning commissioners, defending their mathematical choices and demonstrating how their solution outperforms existing systems. Presentations must include visual representations of their network design, mathematical proofs of optimality, and quantitative comparisons showing improvement metrics. Conclude with 15 minutes of peer evaluation where students provide written feedback on the mathematical rigor and practical applicability of presented solutions.
materials_needed: Urban demographic dataset (population density, emergency call history, geographical boundaries)
MATLAB, Python with SciPy/NumPy, or equivalent optimization software with network analysis capabilities
Graph theory reference materials and optimization algorithm documentation
Large format paper or digital presentation tools for network visualization
Calculators or computational devices for complex mathematical operations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Design (35 points - originality, mathematical rigor, appropriate variable selection, constraint formulation), Implementation Quality (25 points - code functionality, algorithm efficiency, validation testing), Solution Effectiveness (25 points - quantitative improvement over baseline, practical feasibility, optimization proof), and Communication (15 points - clear mathematical explanation, professional presentation, effective visual aids). Students must achieve minimum 80% in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template frameworks showing basic optimization model structure and offer guided practice with simpler 2-station placement problems before attempting the full network. Supply reference sheets with common optimization formulas and graph theory notation. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints such as multi-type emergency vehicles, dynamic traffic patterns, or stochastic demand modeling. Challenge them to compare multiple optimization algorithms (simplex, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing) and analyze computational complexity.

title: Programming Language Syntax Elements Memory Cards Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements including keywords, operators, and data types through structured flashcard activities. This foundational exercise builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for beginning programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 core Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, etc.) by matching them to their correct definitions within 90% accuracy
Students will recall the correct syntax symbols for arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, **) and comparison operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) through timed recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 35 Python syntax elements to each student (15 minutes setup). Each card shows a syntax element on one side and its definition/purpose on the reverse. Students work in pairs for the first 20 minutes, taking turns showing cards and testing each other's recall. Partner A shows the syntax element side while Partner B states the definition from memory, then they switch roles after going through all cards once. During the next 15 minutes, conduct individual silent study where students sort cards into 'know well,' 'somewhat familiar,' and 'need practice' piles, focusing extra attention on their weak areas. Follow with a 10-minute speed recognition round where you display syntax elements on the board for 5 seconds each while students write the definition on their answer sheets. Conclude with a 10-minute partner quiz where students create 5 original questions using the syntax elements to test their partner's understanding. Throughout the activity, circulate to observe student progress and provide immediate feedback on incorrect responses.
materials_needed: 35 pre-made flashcards per student covering Python keywords, operators, and data types
Answer sheets with numbered lines 1-20
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projector for speed recognition round
Pencils or pens for students
assessment_method: Grade the 20-question speed recognition answer sheets using a point system (5 points per correct answer, 100 points total). Success criteria: 80+ points demonstrates mastery, 60-79 points shows developing understanding, below 60 points indicates need for remediation. Additionally, conduct spot-checks during partner work, awarding participation points for active engagement and correct verbal responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce flashcard set to 20 most essential elements and provide definition word banks during speed recognition. Pair weaker students with stronger partners during collaborative phases. For advanced learners, include additional syntax elements like lambda, yield, and exception handling keywords, or challenge them to create example code snippets demonstrating each syntax element's usage.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Science Scenarios
description: Students analyze three authentic business datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation, explaining the implications of each relationship type for data-driven decision making. They will create visual interpretations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of when correlation suggests causation versus when it represents spurious relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from real business datasets
Students will explain the practical implications of correlation vs. causation through written interpretations of data relationships in marketing, healthcare, and e-commerce contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-prepared datasets: Dataset A (ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents), Dataset B (marketing spend vs. revenue with seasonal trends), and Dataset C (exercise frequency vs. mental health scores). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Each pair calculates correlation coefficients using provided Excel templates or Python scripts, then creates scatter plots for all three datasets. Second 15 minutes: Pairs examine each relationship and discuss whether the correlation likely represents causation, spurious correlation, or potential causation requiring further investigation. They must identify confounding variables for each scenario. Final 15 minutes: Each pair completes a structured worksheet categorizing each dataset relationship and providing 2-3 sentence explanations for their reasoning. Students must specifically address: (1) the strength and direction of correlation, (2) whether causation is plausible based on logical reasoning, (3) what additional data or experiments would be needed to establish causation, and (4) potential business decisions that might be incorrectly made if correlation were assumed to be causation. Circulate during work time to ensure students are engaging with the statistical concepts rather than just the computational aspects.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with correlation scenarios
Correlation analysis worksheet template
Excel with Data Analysis ToolPak or Python/Jupyter notebooks
Graph paper or digital graphing tools
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all three relationship types with sophisticated explanations of confounding variables and business implications, (3) Correctly identifies relationship types with adequate explanations, (2) Identifies most relationships correctly but explanations lack depth or contain minor errors, (1) Shows basic understanding but significant misconceptions remain. Look for specific mention of confounding variables and practical decision-making implications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a relationship decision tree flowchart and sentence starters for explanations. Offer simplified datasets with more obvious distinctions. For advanced learners, add a fourth dataset with partial correlation requiring statistical control variables, or ask them to design an experiment that could establish causation for one of the correlation scenarios.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Science Scenarios: Written Report
description: Students analyze three different datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation, explaining why certain relationships exist and identifying confounding variables. They will create visual interpretations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of this fundamental data science concept.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing three different real-world datasets and identifying potential confounding variables
Students will explain the reasoning behind statistical relationships through written justifications and visual annotations of correlation matrices
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three pre-selected datasets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents by month, (2) Number of firefighters vs. property damage in fire incidents, and (3) Hours of TV watching vs. childhood obesity rates. First 15 minutes: Groups use Python/R or Excel to create scatter plots and calculate correlation coefficients for each dataset. Next 20 minutes: For each dataset, students must identify whether the relationship is correlational or causal, writing a 2-3 sentence explanation. They should identify at least one potential confounding variable per dataset. Minutes 35-50: Groups create annotated visualizations showing their correlation matrices, highlighting in red relationships they believe are purely correlational and in green those that might be causal. They must add text boxes explaining their reasoning. Final 10 minutes: Each group presents one dataset analysis to the class, defending their correlation vs. causation determination. Instructor facilitates discussion on why Dataset 1 (temperature as confounding variable), Dataset 2 (fire severity as confounding variable), and Dataset 3 (socioeconomic factors as confounding variables) demonstrate correlation without direct causation.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with the specified variables
Computers with Python (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn) or R (ggplot2) or Excel
Printed handout with correlation coefficient interpretation guide (-1 to +1 scale)
Digital presentation tool for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct calculation of correlation coefficients (20 points), (2) Accurate identification of correlation vs. causation for each dataset with proper justification (40 points), (3) Identification of realistic confounding variables (20 points), (4) Clear visual presentation with appropriate annotations (20 points). Students must score 70+ points to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a decision tree flowchart asking 'Does changing X directly cause Y to change?' and 'What other factors might influence both X and Y?' For advanced learners: Add a fourth dataset requiring them to suggest experimental design to test causation, or have them research Bradford Hill criteria for establishing causation.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Science Scenarios

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Science Scenarios: Visual Analysis
description: Students analyze three authentic business datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation patterns. They examine statistical relationships, identify confounding variables, and explain why certain correlations cannot imply causal relationships using data visualization and statistical evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing statistical relationships in business datasets and identifying potential confounding variables
Students will explain the limitations of correlational analysis through examining scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and alternative explanations for observed patterns
instructions:
Begin with a 5-minute warm-up where students review correlation coefficient ranges (-1 to +1). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students. Distribute three pre-loaded datasets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents, (2) Education spending vs. student performance by state, (3) Social media usage vs. depression scores. Each group receives printed scatter plots and correlation coefficients for all three datasets.

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine Dataset 1 (ice cream/drowning, r=0.67). Students calculate basic statistics using provided formulas and identify the strong positive correlation. They brainstorm why this correlation exists without implying ice cream causes drowning.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Groups analyze Dataset 2 (education/performance, r=0.34). Using guided questions, they identify potential confounding variables (socioeconomic status, teacher quality, class size) that might explain the moderate correlation. Students create a list of alternative explanations and rank them by likelihood.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Groups examine Dataset 3 (social media/depression, r=-0.28). They discuss whether increased social media directly causes depression or if other factors explain this relationship. Students identify the difference between observational and experimental data.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Each group presents one dataset analysis to the class, explaining: (a) the correlation strength, (b) why correlation doesn't equal causation, (c) two potential confounding variables, (d) what type of study would be needed to establish causation.

Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students write three key differences between correlation and causation studies in their data science journals.
materials_needed: Three printed datasets with scatter plots and correlation coefficients
Calculators or laptops with Excel/Google Sheets access
Guided analysis worksheet with prompting questions
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
Data science journals or notebooks for individual reflection
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct interpretation of correlation coefficients (25%), (2) Identification of at least two plausible confounding variables per dataset (35%), (3) Clear explanation of why correlation doesn't imply causation with specific examples (25%), (4) Quality of group presentation including statistical reasoning (15%). Success criteria: Students score 3/4 or higher on each rubric component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation interpretation cheat sheet and sentence starters like 'This correlation might exist because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to design experimental studies that could test causation or research Simpson's Paradox examples in the datasets. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during group work.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Science Scenarios

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance and Trade-offs in Real-World Data Scenarios
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of five sorting algorithms (QuickSort, MergeSort, HeapSort, RadixSort, and TimSort) across different data distributions and constraints. They will decompose empirical results to identify optimal algorithm selection criteria for specific use cases.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity trade-offs of five sorting algorithms by examining empirical performance data across varied dataset characteristics
Students will differentiate between theoretical and practical algorithm performance through systematic comparison of benchmark results under memory and stability constraints
instructions:
**Phase 1 - Setup (20 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a workstation with pre-installed performance testing framework and five datasets: (1) Random integers (100K elements), (2) Nearly sorted array (95% sorted), (3) Reverse sorted array, (4) Array with many duplicates (10 unique values), (5) Small arrays (100 elements each, 1000 trials). Teams also receive implementations of all five sorting algorithms with built-in timing and memory measurement capabilities.

**Phase 2 - Data Collection (45 minutes):** Teams execute each sorting algorithm on all five datasets, recording: execution time (milliseconds), memory usage (MB), number of comparisons, and number of swaps. Each test runs 10 times for statistical validity. Students document results in provided spreadsheet template with columns for algorithm, dataset type, trial number, and all metrics.

**Phase 3 - Analysis Framework (30 minutes):** Using guided analysis worksheet, teams calculate mean, median, and standard deviation for each metric. They create performance ranking matrices showing best-to-worst algorithm performance per dataset type. Teams identify outliers and investigate causes using algorithm implementation code provided.

**Phase 4 - Trade-off Analysis (35 minutes):** Teams complete comparative analysis charts examining: (1) Stability requirements vs. performance, (2) Memory constraints vs. speed, (3) Dataset size impact on algorithm choice, (4) Data distribution effects on performance variance. Students must justify algorithm selection for three given real-world scenarios: mobile app sorting user lists, database index maintenance, and embedded system data processing.

**Phase 5 - Findings Presentation (30 minutes):** Each team presents 5-minute analysis of their most significant finding, including evidence from their data and recommendation for specific use case.
materials_needed: Computers with Python 3.8+ and performance profiling libraries (time, memory_profiler, matplotlib)
Pre-implemented sorting algorithms with instrumentation code
Five standardized test datasets in CSV format
Analysis worksheet template with guided questions
Performance measurement spreadsheet template
Real-world scenario descriptions handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric (100 points total): Data collection accuracy and completeness (25 points), mathematical analysis of performance metrics (25 points), quality of trade-off identification and reasoning (30 points), and appropriateness of algorithm recommendations for given scenarios with supporting evidence (20 points). Students submit completed analysis worksheets, raw performance data, and written justification for scenario-based recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated sample data for one algorithm-dataset combination as example, offer guided questions worksheet with specific prompts for each analysis step. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (IntroSort, CountingSort), add cache performance metrics, or require students to modify algorithm parameters and analyze impact on performance characteristics.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Dashboard Design
description: Students will critically assess three different sales dashboard prototypes using established visualization principles and business requirements. They will evaluate each dashboard's effectiveness in communicating key metrics and recommend the best solution with detailed justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization approaches by applying visualization principles (clarity, accuracy, efficiency) to assess dashboard designs
Students will critique dashboard designs through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework and business context requirements
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Divide students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with printed copies of three sales dashboard mockups (Dashboard A: bar charts with data tables, Dashboard B: interactive pie charts and line graphs, Dashboard C: minimal design with key KPIs and sparklines) and the business scenario document describing FreshMart grocery chain's need to track weekly sales, top products, and regional performance for store managers. **Evaluation Phase (25 minutes):** Each group receives the Dashboard Evaluation Framework handout containing four criteria: Data Clarity (Is information easy to understand?), Visual Hierarchy (Are most important metrics prominent?), Actionability (Can managers make decisions from this?), and Cognitive Load (How much mental effort required?). Groups spend 20 minutes systematically evaluating each dashboard using the 1-5 scale provided for each criterion, documenting specific observations and evidence. Students must identify at least two strengths and two weaknesses per dashboard, citing specific design elements. **Decision Phase (15 minutes):** Groups calculate total scores and discuss trade-offs between dashboards. They must reach consensus on their recommended dashboard choice and prepare a 2-minute pitch explaining their decision. **Presentation Phase (15 minutes):** Each group presents their recommendation to the class, explaining their reasoning and responding to one question from another group. **Reflection (10 minutes):** Individual students complete a brief reflection form comparing their initial gut reaction to their evidence-based final recommendation.
materials_needed: Three printed sales dashboard mockups (A, B, C) - one set per group
Business scenario handout describing FreshMart grocery chain context
Dashboard Evaluation Framework rubric with 1-5 scoring scale
Individual reflection worksheets
Timer for activity phases
assessment_method: Students are assessed using a 3-point rubric evaluating: (1) Systematic Application of Criteria - evidence that all four evaluation criteria were used with specific examples cited, (2) Quality of Reasoning - logical connections between dashboard features and business needs with clear justifications, (3) Critical Analysis Depth - identification of trade-offs and consideration of multiple perspectives beyond surface-level observations. Each group submits their completed evaluation framework sheets and individual reflection forms are collected for participation credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This dashboard is effective for data clarity because...' and 'The main weakness I observe is... which could impact managers by...'. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to consider additional factors like accessibility, mobile responsiveness, or scalability. Ask them to propose specific design improvements rather than just identifying weaknesses.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Dashboard Design: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different sales dashboard designs by applying data visualization principles and user experience criteria. They will justify their evaluations using specific evidence and recommend the most effective dashboard for a fictional retail company.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three sales dashboard designs by applying fundamental data visualization principles (clarity, accuracy, efficiency) and provide evidence-based judgments
Students will critique dashboard effectiveness through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework and business context requirements
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with printed copies of three different sales dashboard mockups (Dashboard A: cluttered with 12+ metrics, Dashboard B: clean with 6 key metrics, Dashboard C: visually appealing but missing key data). Include a one-page fictional company profile (GreenLeaf Retail: 50 stores, focus on quarterly sales trends, used by store managers). **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each dashboard using the provided evaluation checklist covering: visual clarity (can you find key information in under 10 seconds?), data accuracy representation (are chart types appropriate for data?), business relevance (does it answer: which stores need attention?), and cognitive load (how many mental steps to understand?). Students rate each criterion 1-5 and write 2-3 sentence justifications. **Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their initial ratings and discuss differences in judgment. Encourage them to challenge each other's reasoning with questions like 'What evidence supports that rating?' **Final Evaluation (15 minutes):** Students individually complete a structured comparison matrix, ranking dashboards 1-3 for overall effectiveness. They must write a 150-word recommendation memo to GreenLeaf's CEO explaining which dashboard to implement and why, addressing at least three specific design elements. **Debrief (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief whole-class discussion on evaluation criteria that proved most challenging to assess.
materials_needed: Three printed sales dashboard mockups (A4 size, color preferred)
GreenLeaf Retail company profile handout
Dashboard evaluation checklist with 1-5 rating scale
Comparison matrix template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate students' final recommendation memos using rubric: Evidence-based reasoning (25 points - uses specific examples from dashboards), Application of visualization principles (25 points - correctly identifies design strengths/weaknesses), Business context integration (25 points - considers user needs and company goals), Clear justification (25 points - logical argument structure). Success threshold: 70+ points indicating ability to systematically evaluate data visualizations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for justifications ('This dashboard is effective because...', 'The weakness I notice is...'). Highlight one clear example of good/poor design in each dashboard. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific design improvements for their lowest-rated dashboard or consider how evaluation criteria might change for different user roles (CEO vs. store manager).
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Dashboard Design

title: Design a Community Garden Layout Using Area, Perimeter, and Scale
description: Students will design an original community garden layout by applying geometric concepts including area calculations, perimeter constraints, and scale drawings. They will create a detailed proposal that balances mathematical requirements with practical gardening considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original garden layout by calculating areas of composite shapes and applying perimeter constraints within given parameters
Students will create a scaled mathematical model through precise measurements and proportional reasoning to represent their garden design
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: students are landscape designers creating a community garden for a local neighborhood with a rectangular plot measuring 40m × 25m. Distribute the project packets containing grid paper, measuring tools, and requirement sheets. (10 minutes)

Step 1: Students individually brainstorm garden sections (vegetable plots, pathways, compost area, tool shed, gathering space) and sketch initial ideas. They must include at least 6 different sections with varying geometric shapes. (15 minutes)

Step 2: Provide specific constraints: pathways must total at least 150m in length but not exceed 200m, individual vegetable plots must be between 12-30 square meters each, the tool shed must be exactly 16 square meters, and 15% of total space must remain as gathering/rest areas. Students calculate these requirements and adjust their designs accordingly. (20 minutes)

Step 3: Students create their scaled drawing (1:50 scale) on grid paper, clearly labeling dimensions and calculating the area of each section. They must show all mathematical work for area calculations of rectangles, triangles, and composite shapes. (25 minutes)

Step 4: Students prepare a written proposal including: total area breakdown, perimeter calculations for fencing needs, justification for their design choices, and a materials cost estimate using provided price lists. (20 minutes)

Step 5: Peer review session where students present their designs in pairs, checking each other's calculations and providing feedback on both mathematical accuracy and design practicality. (15 minutes)

Conclude with a gallery walk where students display their completed garden designs and vote on the most mathematically sound and creative solutions.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares)
Rulers and measuring tape
Calculators
Colored pencils or markers
Project requirement sheets with constraints
Sample materials price list
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area and perimeter calculations (25%), (2) Adherence to all given constraints (25%), (3) Quality and precision of scaled drawing (25%), (4) Creativity and practicality of overall design with clear justification (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide area formula reference sheets, pre-drawn basic shapes to modify, and calculator support for complex calculations. For advanced learners: add constraints requiring circular or triangular garden beds, include irrigation system design with additional geometric calculations, or require cost optimization within a specific budget limit.

title: Design a Community Garden Layout Using Area, Perimeter, and Scale: Exercise 1
description: Students will design an original community garden layout by applying geometric concepts of area, perimeter, and scale. They will create a detailed blueprint that addresses real-world constraints while demonstrating mathematical reasoning and problem-solving skills.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original garden layout by calculating areas and perimeters of geometric shapes within given constraints
Students will create a scaled blueprint through applying proportional reasoning and unit conversions
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: students are landscape designers tasked with creating a community garden on a rectangular plot measuring 40m × 25m. Distribute graph paper (1 square = 1 square meter) and provide the constraint list: minimum 8 rectangular vegetable plots (each 15-30 sq meters), 2 circular flower beds (minimum 3m diameter each), 1 tool shed (rectangular, exactly 12 sq meters), pathways at least 1.5m wide connecting all areas, and a composting area (minimum 20 sq meters). Students work individually for 15 minutes sketching initial ideas, then form pairs to refine designs for 25 minutes. Each pair must calculate total area used, remaining space, and perimeter of each garden section. They create a final scaled blueprint on new graph paper where 1 square represents 0.25 square meters, requiring them to convert their original measurements. Pairs then prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their design choices and showing calculations. During presentations, other students evaluate designs using provided criteria sheets. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where pairs identify one mathematical concept they found challenging and how they overcame it.
materials_needed: Graph paper (2 sheets per student, 1cm grid)
Rulers and measuring tools
Colored pencils or markers
Scientific calculators
Design constraint handout
Peer evaluation criteria sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations (25%), appropriate use of scale and proportions (25%), creative design meeting all constraints (25%), clear presentation of mathematical reasoning (25%). Students must show all calculation work and explain how they resolved constraint conflicts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-drawn geometric shapes to trace and area formula reference cards. Pair them with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: add constraints requiring irregular polygons or introduce concepts like optimization (maximizing growing space while minimizing pathway area). Encourage them to research actual garden spacing requirements.
original_title: Design a Community Garden Layout Using Area, Perimeter, and Scale

title: Advanced Data Structure Implementation Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate recall of complex data structure implementations by reproducing exact code syntax, time complexities, and algorithmic steps from memory. This activity focuses on memorizing and accurately reciting advanced concepts including B-trees, Red-Black trees, and graph traversal algorithms without reference materials.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific implementation details of advanced data structures (B-trees, Red-Black trees, Dijkstra's algorithm) by writing complete code segments from memory
Students will identify exact time and space complexities for 15 advanced algorithms through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing blank coding sheets and setting up a distraction-free environment. Announce that this is a closed-book recall exercise lasting 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (30 minutes): Present students with 10 data structure names (B-tree insertion, Red-Black tree rotation, AVL tree balancing, Dijkstra's shortest path, A* search, Bellman-Ford algorithm, Floyd-Warshall algorithm, Kruskal's MST, Prim's MST, and Topological sort). Students must write the complete pseudocode or actual implementation code for each from memory, including all edge cases and error handling. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Display 15 algorithm names on screen for exactly 30 seconds each. Students must immediately write down the exact Big-O time complexity, space complexity, and best/average/worst case scenarios for each algorithm. No partial credit for approximations. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Provide 8 complex tree/graph diagrams. Students must trace through specific algorithms step-by-step, showing exact intermediate states, variable values, and data structure modifications at each step. They must recall and apply the precise algorithmic steps without deviation. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Students must list from memory the exact syntax for implementing these structures in two different programming languages (e.g., C++ and Python), including all necessary header files, import statements, and class definitions with correct method signatures.
materials_needed: Blank coding paper (5 sheets per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Pre-prepared algorithm name cards
8 printed complex tree/graph diagrams
Projector for displaying algorithm names
Answer keys with exact implementations for grading
assessment_method: Grade using exact-match rubric: Full points (5) only for 100% accurate recall including correct syntax, variable names, and algorithmic steps. Partial points (3) for 80-99% accuracy. Minimal points (1) for 60-79% accuracy. Zero points for below 60% or any conceptual errors. Total possible: 165 points (10 implementations × 10 points + 15 complexities × 5 points + 8 traces × 7 points + 2 syntax implementations × 10 points). Success threshold: 132/165 points (80%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide memory palace technique training one week prior, create acronym sheets for algorithm steps, and allow color-coding during recall. For advanced learners: Add bonus section requiring recall of proof sketches for algorithm correctness, implementation variants, and optimization techniques. Consider adding concurrent/parallel versions of algorithms for extra challenge.

title: Deconstructing Bias Patterns in Machine Learning Model Predictions Through Multi-Dimensional Analysis
description: Students will examine a pre-trained hiring algorithm's decision patterns across multiple demographic dimensions to identify systemic biases. They will interpret statistical measures of algorithmic fairness and explain how different bias definitions lead to conflicting conclusions about model equity.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration metrics by analyzing their mathematical relationships and real-world implications in hiring decisions
Students will explain the trade-offs between different fairness definitions through systematic comparison of bias detection results across protected attributes
instructions: Begin by providing students with a synthetic hiring dataset containing 5,000 candidates with features including education, experience, gender, race, and age, plus corresponding algorithmic hiring recommendations. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives identical Jupyter notebooks pre-loaded with the dataset and visualization libraries. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams calculate baseline demographic statistics, computing hiring recommendation rates across each protected attribute using pandas groupby functions. They create bar charts showing recommendation disparities. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students implement three fairness metrics - demographic parity (equal positive prediction rates), equalized odds (equal true positive rates across groups), and calibration (equal positive predictive values). They calculate these metrics using provided code templates, filling in missing statistical formulas. Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams generate confusion matrices for each demographic group and compute fairness metric violations, identifying which groups experience the largest disparities. Step 4 (20 minutes): Using a provided bias mitigation algorithm, students apply post-processing threshold adjustments to improve demographic parity. They recalculate all three fairness metrics to observe the trade-offs created. Step 5 (25 minutes): Teams create a comprehensive bias audit report documenting their findings, explaining why optimizing for one fairness definition worsened others, and interpreting the practical implications for hiring decisions. Each team presents their key findings in a 5-minute summary highlighting the most significant bias patterns discovered.
materials_needed: Synthetic hiring dataset (CSV file with 5,000 records)
Pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn
Bias audit report template (Word document)
Fairness metrics reference sheet with mathematical definitions
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate calculation of all three fairness metrics with correct statistical interpretation, (2) Clear identification of specific bias patterns with supporting numerical evidence, (3) Coherent explanation of fairness metric trade-offs using concrete examples, (4) Professional bias audit report with actionable recommendations. Each criterion weighted equally for final score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed examples of demographic parity calculations and pre-written code snippets for confusion matrix generation. Offer guiding questions like 'Which demographic group has the lowest hiring recommendation rate?' Advanced learners can explore intersectional bias by analyzing combinations of protected attributes (e.g., race + gender) and research additional fairness metrics like individual fairness or counterfactual fairness.

title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional college student by calculating percentages for different expense categories. They will apply percentage calculations to determine how much money should be allocated to housing, food, transportation, and other expenses based on a given monthly income.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages of a total income by converting percentage guidelines into dollar amounts for budget categories
Students will apply percentage increase and decrease calculations through adjusting budget allocations to meet spending constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Scenario' worksheet to each student (10 minutes setup). Each worksheet contains a fictional student profile with monthly income ($1,200-$2,000 range varies by worksheet) and recommended percentage guidelines: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 10%, Entertainment 8%, Savings 10%, Miscellaneous 12%, Emergency Fund 5%, School Supplies 10%. Students work individually for the first 25 minutes calculating dollar amounts for each category using their assigned income. They must show all percentage calculations (Income × Percentage ÷ 100 = Category Amount). Next, introduce a 'budget challenge' where students discover their housing costs will increase by 15% (10 minutes). Students must recalculate their housing expense and adjust other categories to stay within their total income, showing all work for percentage changes. For the final 15 minutes, students pair up to compare their budgets and identify which categories they adjusted and why. Each pair presents one key insight about percentage trade-offs in budgeting to the class. Students complete a reflection question: 'If your income decreased by 20%, which two categories would you reduce and by what percentage?' They must calculate the new amounts and explain their reasoning. Circulate throughout to check calculations and provide guidance on percentage formula application.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Scenario worksheets (different income levels)
Calculators (one per student)
Budget Planning template sheets
Percentage reference chart (Income × % ÷ 100 = Amount)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, realistic adjustments made, clear explanation of changes; (3) Most calculations correct, appropriate adjustments with minor errors; (2) Some calculation errors, adjustments attempted but incomplete reasoning; (1) Multiple calculation errors, unrealistic or missing adjustments. Check for proper percentage formula usage, accurate dollar amounts, and logical responses to budget constraints.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference card and pre-worked example with $1,000 income. Allow use of percentage calculator apps. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including variable income (part-time job hours change monthly) and ask them to create percentage ranges for flexible budgeting. Introduce compound percentage changes (housing increases 15%, then food costs decrease 8%).

title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create and analyze a realistic monthly budget for a young adult scenario. They will use percentage formulas to determine spending allocations across different budget categories and evaluate whether their budget meets financial guidelines.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine spending amounts for each budget category by using the formula: (percentage × total income) ÷ 100
Students will apply the 50/30/20 budgeting rule through creating a balanced personal budget that allocates percentages to needs, wants, and savings
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Profile Cards' - each student receives a different scenario with monthly income, age, and living situation (15 minutes). Students work individually to create their budget using the provided worksheet. First, they calculate 50% for needs (rent, groceries, utilities), showing work: income × 0.50. Next, calculate 30% for wants (entertainment, dining out, hobbies) using income × 0.30. Then calculate 20% for savings/debt using income × 0.20. Students must then break down each category into specific line items (rent = 30% of income, groceries = 12%, etc.) and calculate dollar amounts for each item. After completing calculations (20 minutes), students use colored pencils to create a pie chart showing their budget breakdown with percentages labeled on each section (10 minutes). In pairs, students present their budgets to each other, explaining their reasoning for specific allocations and checking each other's percentage calculations (10 minutes). Finally, students complete a reflection comparing their budget to the 50/30/20 rule and identify one adjustment they would make, calculating the new percentage and dollar amount (10 minutes). Teacher circulates throughout, checking calculations and providing guidance on realistic expense amounts.
materials_needed: Young Adult Profile Cards (15 different scenarios with varying incomes $2000-$4000)
Personal Budget Worksheet with percentage calculation spaces
Calculators
Colored pencils or markers
Compass or string for drawing pie charts
assessment_method: Students earn points using this rubric: Accurate percentage calculations (25 points) - all three main categories calculated correctly; Detailed breakdown (25 points) - at least 8 specific line items with correct dollar amounts; Visual representation (20 points) - pie chart accurately reflects percentages; Mathematical work shown (20 points) - formulas and steps visible; Reflection quality (10 points) - thoughtful analysis of budget decisions. Success requires 80+ points total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a calculator reference sheet showing percentage-to-decimal conversions (50% = 0.50) and offer pre-calculated examples. Give budget templates with some categories pre-filled. For advanced learners: add complexity by including taxes, irregular expenses, or have them create budgets for different life stages. Challenge them to research actual costs in their area and adjust percentages accordingly.
original_title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages

title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic monthly budget based on a given income scenario. They will allocate funds across different expense categories using percentage-based budgeting rules and calculate actual dollar amounts for each category.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting percentages to dollar amounts across multiple expense categories
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage concepts through creating and justifying a balanced personal budget scenario
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Monthly Income Scenarios' worksheet where each student receives a different monthly income amount between $2,000-$4,000. Display the recommended budget percentage guidelines on the board: Housing 30%, Transportation 15%, Food 12%, Utilities 8%, Savings 10%, Entertainment 10%, Clothing 5%, Miscellaneous 10%. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students calculate the dollar amount for each category by multiplying their income by each percentage. For example, with $3,000 income: Housing = $3,000 × 0.30 = $900. Have students show their work for all calculations.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students complete their budget worksheet, ensuring all categories total 100% and equal their given income amount. They must verify their calculations by adding all dollar amounts.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Present students with three 'budget challenge' scenarios: 1) Income decreases by 20%, 2) Housing costs increase by $200, 3) They want to save an additional 5% for vacation. Students must recalculate their budgets, adjusting percentages and amounts accordingly.

Step 4 (10 minutes): In pairs, students compare their original budgets and challenge solutions, checking each other's percentage calculations and discussing their adjustment strategies. Each pair identifies one calculation to share with the class.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Conduct a brief whole-class share where 3-4 pairs present one calculation, explaining their process and reasoning for budget adjustments.
materials_needed: Monthly Income Scenarios worksheet (one per student with different income amounts)
Budget Planning worksheet with category columns
Budget Challenge scenario cards
Calculators
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, budget totals 100%, challenge scenarios solved accurately; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget balances, most challenge scenarios correct; (2) Some calculation errors, budget approximately balances, partial challenge completion; (1) Multiple errors, budget doesn't balance, limited challenge work. Observe pair discussions for mathematical reasoning and problem-solving approaches.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage-to-decimal conversion chart and calculator practice with simple examples before starting. Consider pairing them with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including irregular expenses (annual insurance payments), multiple income sources, or asking them to create budget scenarios for different life stages (student, family, retirement).
original_title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages

title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic monthly budget based on a given income scenario. They will allocate funds across different expense categories and justify their choices using mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine appropriate budget allocations by converting percentages to dollar amounts and vice versa
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage concepts through creating and defending a balanced monthly budget scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Monthly Income Scenarios' worksheet containing different job roles and corresponding monthly incomes ($2,000-$4,000). Have students work in pairs and assign each pair one scenario (15 minutes setup). Explain that students must allocate their given income across six mandatory categories: Housing (25-35%), Food (10-15%), Transportation (10-20%), Savings (10-20%), Entertainment (5-10%), and Miscellaneous (5-15%). Students first calculate the dollar range for each category by applying the percentage ranges to their assigned income. For example, with $3,000 income, housing budget ranges from $750 (25%) to $1,050 (35%). Next, students research actual costs in your local area using provided websites or handouts showing apartment rents, grocery costs, and transportation expenses. They must then create their specific budget, choosing exact dollar amounts within each range and ensuring the total equals exactly 100% of income. Students complete the 'Budget Justification Sheet' explaining their percentage choices with mathematical reasoning (e.g., 'We chose 30% for housing ($900) because local one-bedroom apartments average $850-950'). Finally, pairs present their budget to another pair, showing all percentage calculations and defending their allocation choices. The receiving pair checks all mathematical calculations using calculators and provides feedback on reasonableness of choices.
materials_needed: Monthly Income Scenarios worksheet (6 different job scenarios)
Local cost-of-living reference sheets or internet access
Budget Justification Sheet template
Calculators
Percentage-to-decimal conversion reference chart
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of percentage calculations (25 points), (2) Budget allocations fall within required ranges (25 points), (3) Total budget equals exactly 100% of income (25 points), and (4) Written justifications demonstrate understanding of percentage relationships (25 points). Students must achieve 80% (80/100 points) for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a percentage calculation template showing the formula (Income × Percentage = Dollar Amount) and worked examples. Offer a calculator tutorial for percentage conversions. For advanced learners, add complexity by including irregular expenses (annual insurance divided by 12 months) or having them create budgets for different life scenarios (single vs. family of four) and compare percentage allocations.
