title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis Through Big O Complexity Comparison
description: Students will examine three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort) by analyzing their code implementations, identifying key operations, and comparing their time complexities. They will create visual complexity charts and justify which algorithm performs best under different data conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze sorting algorithm implementations by identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and pivot operations to determine Big O time complexity
Students will compare algorithm performance characteristics through systematic evaluation of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (15 minutes setup). In Phase 1 (25 minutes), students examine each algorithm individually, counting nested loops, identifying recursive patterns, and marking key operations on their code printouts. They should create a data collection sheet listing: algorithm name, number of nested loops, presence of recursion, and identified pivot points. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), groups use their analysis to determine Big O complexity for each algorithm's best, average, and worst cases, consulting the provided Big O reference chart. They must document their reasoning with specific code line references. In Phase 3 (20 minutes), students create a comparison matrix showing all three algorithms across the three performance scenarios, then graph the complexity curves on logarithmic paper. Finally, in Phase 4 (15 minutes), each group presents one algorithm analysis to the class, explaining their complexity determination process and showing their visual representation. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are examining actual code structure rather than memorizing known complexities. Encourage groups to trace through small examples (arrays of 4-8 elements) to verify their theoretical analysis.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (one set per group)
Big O complexity reference chart
Logarithmic graph paper
Algorithm analysis worksheet template
Colored pencils for graph creation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O complexity identification for all three scenarios per algorithm (40%), (2) Quality of code analysis documentation with specific line references (30%), (3) Correctness of visual complexity comparison charts (20%), and (4) Clarity of reasoning in group presentation (10%). Success requires correctly identifying at least 7 of 9 complexity scenarios and providing valid code-based justifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a guided analysis template highlighting where to look for loops and recursion, and offer a completed example using selection sort. For advanced learners, add space complexity analysis and introduce amortized analysis concepts for quick sort, or challenge them to analyze more complex algorithms like heap sort or radix sort.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in High-Stakes Healthcare Decision Making
description: Students will critically assess the validity, reliability, and ethical implications of three different machine learning models designed to predict patient readmission risk. They will evaluate model performance metrics, identify potential biases, and make justified recommendations for clinical implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of competing ML models by analyzing performance metrics, statistical significance, and clinical relevance within healthcare contexts
Students will critique model limitations and biases through systematic examination of training data, feature selection, and validation methodologies
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost) along with their training datasets, validation results, and documentation (15 minutes setup). Each team receives identical materials including confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and demographic breakdowns of predictions. Students first spend 45 minutes independently analyzing each model's performance metrics, calculating additional statistics (specificity, NPV, F1-scores for subgroups), and identifying potential sources of bias in training data composition. Next, teams collaborate for 60 minutes to systematically compare models using a provided evaluation framework covering: statistical performance, clinical interpretability, computational requirements, and ethical considerations. Teams must document their analysis in a structured evaluation matrix, noting strengths, weaknesses, and red flags for each model. In the final 45 minutes, each team prepares a 10-minute presentation recommending ONE model for implementation, explicitly addressing: which performance metrics are most critical for this use case, how identified biases could impact patient care, what additional validation steps are needed, and what monitoring protocols should be established post-deployment. Presentations include a risk assessment and mitigation strategy for their chosen model.
materials_needed: Three pre-trained models with saved weights and prediction outputs
Hospital readmission dataset with 10,000+ patient records
Model documentation including hyperparameters and training procedures
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded visualization libraries (matplotlib, seaborn, sklearn.metrics)
Evaluation framework template with assessment criteria
Access to statistical computing environment (Python/R)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Accuracy of statistical analysis and metric calculations (25%), (2) Depth of bias identification and impact assessment (25%), (3) Quality of model comparison methodology and reasoning (20%), (4) Justification strength for final recommendation including risk mitigation (20%), (5) Professional presentation of findings with clear communication (10%). Students must demonstrate mastery by correctly identifying at least 3 sources of potential bias, accurately calculating performance metrics for demographic subgroups, and providing evidence-based reasoning for model selection.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates for common metrics and a bias detection checklist focusing on demographic parity and equalized odds. Offer guiding questions for model comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized opportunity), conduct statistical significance tests between model performances, or propose novel validation approaches for the healthcare domain.

title: Binary Number Recognition and Recall Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard activities. This foundational exercise builds automatic recognition of basic binary patterns essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the 4-bit binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, with one partner showing the decimal side while the other recalls the binary representation aloud. Partners switch roles every 2 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class 'around the room' activity for 8 minutes where each student must correctly state one binary-to-decimal or decimal-to-binary conversion before sitting down. Create two columns on the board labeled 'Decimal' and 'Binary' and have students take turns filling in matching pairs. For the final 12 minutes, students work individually with their flashcard set, sorting cards into 'know immediately' and 'need practice' piles. They focus intensive study on their 'need practice' pile, using the look-cover-check method: look at the decimal number, cover it, write the binary equivalent, then check their answer. End with a 5-minute speed round where students attempt to correctly convert as many numbers as possible from a randomized list you call out, recording their answers on paper.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and corresponding 4-bit binary representations
Whiteboard or blackboard with markers/chalk
Individual paper sheets for students' final speed round answers
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Evaluate students based on their final speed round performance: 13-16 correct conversions = excellent recall, 10-12 = proficient recall, 7-9 = developing recall, below 7 = needs additional practice. Also observe during pair work for immediate feedback on accuracy and fluency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with numbers 0-7 (3-bit) before progressing to full 4-bit representations, and provide a conversion reference chart they can gradually wean off. For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents alongside binary representations.

title: Understanding Data Preprocessing Pipeline Through Real Estate Dataset Analysis
description: Students will examine a messy real estate dataset to identify common data quality issues and explain the rationale behind different preprocessing steps. They will analyze the impact of missing values, outliers, and inconsistent formatting on data analysis outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and categorize data quality issues (missing values, outliers, inconsistent formats) by examining a real estate dataset with 15+ deliberate quality problems
Students will explain the rationale behind specific preprocessing techniques through written justifications for handling each identified data quality issue
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'messy_housing_data.csv' file containing 500 property records with intentional data quality issues including: missing bedrooms/bathrooms, price outliers ($50 and $50M listings), inconsistent city names ('NYC', 'New York City', 'new york'), mixed date formats, and special characters in numeric fields.

**Phase 1 - Data Exploration (15 minutes):** Students work in pairs to open the dataset in Excel/Google Sheets and create a 'Data Quality Issues Log' with three columns: Issue Type, Specific Examples, and Potential Impact. They must identify at least 8 different quality problems, documenting specific row numbers and describing how each issue could affect analysis (e.g., 'Missing bathroom data in rows 47, 83, 156 would reduce sample size for correlation analysis').

**Phase 2 - Preprocessing Strategy Development (20 minutes):** Each pair selects 5 issues from their log and writes detailed explanations for how to handle each one. For missing values, they must choose between deletion, mean imputation, or other methods and justify why. For outliers, they must explain detection methods and treatment rationale. For inconsistent formatting, they must specify standardization rules.

**Phase 3 - Impact Analysis (10 minutes):** Students compare original vs. cleaned data by calculating basic statistics (mean price, property count by city) before and after applying their preprocessing decisions. They document these changes in a summary table showing how their choices affected the dataset's characteristics.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Pairs share one surprising finding about how preprocessing affected their data insights.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared 'messy_housing_data.csv' file with 500+ records and 15+ quality issues
Data Quality Issues Log template (digital or printed)
Access to Excel, Google Sheets, or similar spreadsheet software
Calculator or basic statistical functions
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Data Quality Issues Log completeness - identified 8+ issues with specific examples and impact descriptions (25 points), (2) Preprocessing strategy explanations - clear rationale for handling 5 selected issues with appropriate method choices (35 points), (3) Impact analysis accuracy - correct before/after calculations with meaningful interpretation (25 points), (4) Professional documentation - organized presentation of findings (15 points). Minimum 70/100 for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a starter list of 3 data quality issue types to look for, offer sentence starters for explanations ('I chose this method because...'), and pair them with stronger partners. **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to research advanced preprocessing techniques (z-score outlier detection, multiple imputation methods), or analyze how different preprocessing choices might bias results toward certain conclusions. Provide additional datasets from different domains for comparison.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Arrays Using Quadratic Functions and Constraints
description: Students will apply quadratic optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving solar panel placement. They will use calculus-based optimization methods to maximize energy output while working within physical and budgetary constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply quadratic function optimization to determine maximum energy output by finding critical points using derivative calculus
Students will implement constraint-based optimization techniques through systematic analysis of multi-variable cost-benefit scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Solar Array Design Packet containing site specifications (50m × 30m rooftop), budget constraints ($45,000), and energy requirements (minimum 25kW output). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Engineer, Cost Analyst, Energy Calculator, and Presenter. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze the given quadratic function E(x) = -0.2x² + 12x + 85, where E represents daily energy output in kWh and x represents the number of panel rows. Students must identify the vertex form and determine the theoretical maximum energy output using calculus (finding E'(x) = 0).

Step 2 (20 minutes): Introduce real-world constraints. Panel cost function C(x) = 850x + 2400 represents total installation cost. Students must solve the system of inequalities: C(x) ≤ 45,000 and E(x) ≥ 25. They apply algebraic manipulation to find the feasible domain for x.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Using graphing software, teams plot both functions and identify the optimization region. They must calculate the optimal number of panels that maximizes energy output within budget constraints, applying the constraint optimization formula: maximize E(x) subject to C(x) ≤ budget.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams calculate ROI using the formula ROI = (Annual Savings - Installation Cost)/Installation Cost, where annual savings = E(optimal) × 365 × $0.12 per kWh. Students must justify their solution using mathematical reasoning and present their final recommendation with supporting calculations.
materials_needed: Solar Array Design Packet with site specifications and cost data
Graphing calculators or Desmos/GeoGebra access
Graph paper and rulers
Scientific calculators
Presentation templates for final recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification and calculation of quadratic maximum using derivatives (25 points), (2) Accurate application of constraint inequalities and feasible region identification (25 points), (3) Proper use of optimization techniques to find constrained maximum (25 points), (4) Mathematical justification and practical interpretation of results (25 points). Students must submit calculation worksheets and deliver 3-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated derivative templates and constraint inequality starter problems. Offer graphical checkpoints every 10 minutes. For advanced learners: Introduce additional variables like panel angle optimization (θ) with trigonometric efficiency functions, or add weather variability using probability distributions. Consider multi-objective optimization with environmental impact factors.

title: Analyzing Time and Space Complexity Trade-offs in Dynamic Programming Solutions
description: Students will dissect and compare multiple dynamic programming implementations of the same algorithmic problem to identify optimization strategies and complexity trade-offs. They will analyze how memoization, tabulation, and space optimization techniques affect performance characteristics and determine the most suitable approach for different constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity relationships between top-down memoized, bottom-up tabulated, and space-optimized dynamic programming solutions by examining execution traces and memory usage patterns
Students will evaluate the suitability of different DP implementations through systematic comparison of performance metrics under varying input constraints and resource limitations
instructions: Begin by providing students with three implementations of the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) problem: recursive with memoization, iterative tabulation, and space-optimized tabulation. Divide students into teams of 3-4 members (20 minutes setup). Each team receives identical test datasets: small (strings of length 10), medium (length 100), large (length 1000), and memory-constrained scenarios. Students must instrument each implementation with timing code and memory profiling tools. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams execute all three implementations on each dataset, recording execution time, memory usage, and cache hit/miss ratios for memoized version. They create execution trace diagrams showing the order of subproblem solving for small inputs. Phase 2 (40 minutes): Students analyze the collected data to identify patterns. They must graph time/space complexity curves, calculate the actual Big-O performance, and identify break-even points where one implementation becomes superior. Teams document how input characteristics (string similarity, length ratios) affect performance differently across implementations. Phase 3 (35 minutes): Each team presents their analysis focusing on one critical insight: when would they choose each implementation in a real system? They must justify their recommendations with specific evidence from their analysis, considering factors like available memory, input size predictions, and execution frequency. Conclude with a class discussion comparing findings and identifying optimization principles applicable to other DP problems.
materials_needed: Python environment with time and memory_profiler modules installed
Three pre-written LCS implementations (memoized, tabulated, space-optimized)
Standardized test datasets in CSV format with string pairs of varying lengths
Jupyter notebooks with timing and profiling code templates
Graphing tools (matplotlib or similar) for visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis and empirical measurements (25%), (2) Quality of performance comparison and pattern identification (25%), (3) Justification of implementation choice recommendations with evidence (25%), (4) Clarity of execution trace diagrams and visual presentations (25%). Teams must submit annotated graphs, performance data tables, and a 2-page technical analysis report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed timing code and guided questions for interpreting results. Include reference Big-O complexity charts for comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement and analyze additional optimizations like rolling arrays or parallelization, or extend analysis to other DP problems like edit distance or knapsack variants.

title: Design Your Dream Park: A Geometry and Budgeting Project
description: Students create an original amusement park layout using geometric shapes and area calculations while staying within a specified budget. They must design attractions, pathways, and facilities while justifying their mathematical decisions through detailed cost-benefit analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original park design by applying area formulas for rectangles, circles, triangles, and composite shapes to optimize space usage
Students will construct a comprehensive budget proposal through multi-step calculations involving percentages, ratios, and unit rates
instructions: Begin by distributing the park design brief: students receive a 20cm × 30cm grid paper representing a 200m × 300m plot of land and a $2.5 million budget. In the first 20 minutes, students brainstorm and sketch at least 5 different attractions, determining which geometric shapes best represent each (roller coaster = composite rectangles, Ferris wheel = circle, food courts = rectangles). Next, spend 40 minutes having students calculate exact areas for each attraction using appropriate formulas, with minimum requirements: one circular attraction (minimum 15m radius), two rectangular buildings (minimum 400 sq meters each), one triangular structure, and pathways connecting all attractions (2m wide). Students then research realistic construction costs online for 30 minutes, creating unit rates (cost per square meter) for different attraction types. During the following 45 minutes, students develop their complete budget breakdown, ensuring total costs don't exceed $2.5 million while including 15% contingency funds. Students must create scale drawings with precise measurements and include a written justification (200 words minimum) explaining their geometric choices and budget decisions. In the final 25 minutes, students present their designs to small groups of 3-4 peers, defending their mathematical reasoning and responding to questions about area calculations and cost efficiency.
materials_needed: 20cm × 30cm grid paper (1cm squares)
Rulers and compasses
Calculators
Internet access for cost research
Colored pencils or markers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and budget computations (25%), (2) Creative and logical design layout incorporating all required geometric shapes (25%), (3) Realistic cost research and budget justification staying within constraints (25%), (4) Clear presentation of mathematical reasoning and response to peer questions (25%). Students must show all calculation work and achieve 80% accuracy on computations to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated unit costs and area formula reference sheets, allow partnerships for calculations, or reduce the number of required attractions to 3. For advanced learners, add constraints like environmental impact calculations, introduce irregular polygon attractions, or require optimization problems (maximum visitors per dollar spent).

title: Database Normalization Forms Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the definitions, rules, and characteristics of the six database normalization forms (1NF through 6NF) through intensive flashcard drilling and rapid-fire identification exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge essential for advanced database design.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the precise definitions and requirements for each normalization form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF, 4NF, 5NF, 6NF) by completing timed recall exercises with 95% accuracy
Students will identify the specific violations and dependency types associated with each normalization form through rapid classification tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made normalization reference sheets containing formal definitions for all six normalization forms. Students have 15 minutes to study these definitions silently, focusing on memorizing key terms like 'atomic values,' 'partial dependency,' 'transitive dependency,' 'multivalued dependency,' and 'join dependency.' Next, collect all reference materials and initiate the first recall round: display normalization form names (1NF, 2NF, etc.) on screen for 30 seconds each while students write complete definitions from memory on provided answer sheets. After completing all six forms, redistribute reference sheets for 5-minute verification and correction phase where students mark their errors in red ink. Conduct second recall round focusing specifically on dependency types: call out scenarios like 'non-prime attribute depends on part of candidate key' and students must identify which normal form this violates (answer: 2NF violation). Continue with 15 different dependency scenarios, allowing 20 seconds response time each. Third phase involves rapid-fire violation identification: present 20 table schemas on slides, each violating specific normalization rules. Students identify the highest normal form each table satisfies and list specific violations present. Conclude with peer verification where students exchange papers and grade using provided answer key, discussing discrepancies with instructor mediation.
materials_needed: Pre-printed normalization reference sheets (one per student)
Blank answer sheets with numbered sections 1-6
Red pens for self-correction
PowerPoint slides with 20 sample database schemas
Digital timer or stopwatch
Answer key sheets for peer grading
assessment_method: Students must achieve 95% accuracy on definition recall (17/18 key components correct across all normalization forms) and correctly identify 16/20 normalization violations in the schema recognition phase. Grade based on final answer sheets: definitions (60 points), dependency identification (20 points), schema analysis (20 points). Document completion time for each student to track recall fluency development.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices ('First Normal Form = Atomic values First') and allow color-coded reference cards during first two rounds. Advanced learners can create additional violation examples for classmates and research newer normalization forms like Domain-Key Normal Form (DKNF). Consider pairing strong students with those needing support during peer grading phase.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Patterns in Cross-Validation Learning Curves
description: Students will analyze and interpret complex learning curves from cross-validation experiments to identify bias-variance trade-off patterns across different model complexities. They will demonstrate deep understanding by explaining the underlying mathematical relationships between training/validation error patterns and generalization performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition patterns by analyzing the convergence behavior of training and validation errors across varying model complexities
Students will explain the relationship between learning curve characteristics and generalization performance through systematic analysis of underfitting and overfitting indicators
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 people) with three pre-generated learning curve datasets from polynomial regression models with degrees 1, 5, and 15 trained on identical datasets with varying sample sizes (50 to 2000 samples). Each dataset contains training RMSE, validation RMSE, and training time metrics. Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams examine the raw numerical data and create visualization plots showing training/validation error curves as functions of sample size for each polynomial degree. Step 2 (20 minutes): Students identify and annotate specific curve characteristics including: convergence points, gap magnitudes between training/validation errors, slope changes, and asymptotic behavior. Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the bias-variance implications by mapping observed patterns to theoretical concepts - high bias indicators (both curves plateau at high error), high variance indicators (large gaps that persist), and optimal complexity zones (minimal validation error with reasonable gap). Step 4 (15 minutes): Students predict generalization performance on unseen data by extrapolating curve trends and justifying their reasoning using bias-variance framework principles. Step 5 (10 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about how sample size interacts with model complexity to affect the bias-variance trade-off, supported by specific numerical evidence from their analysis.
materials_needed: Three CSV files containing learning curve data (polynomial_degree_1_curves.csv, polynomial_degree_5_curves.csv, polynomial_degree_15_curves.csv)
Python environment with matplotlib, pandas, and numpy installed
Whiteboard or digital annotation tools for curve marking
Reference sheet with bias-variance trade-off definitions and mathematical formulations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of pattern identification in learning curves (25 points - correctly identifies convergence, gaps, slopes), (2) Quality of bias-variance mapping (25 points - accurately connects curve characteristics to bias/variance concepts with mathematical reasoning), (3) Validity of generalization predictions (25 points - logical extrapolation supported by evidence), (4) Clarity of explanation during presentation (25 points - uses precise terminology and demonstrates causal understanding)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated example learning curves showing labeled bias/variance indicators and guided questions like 'What does it mean when training error is much lower than validation error?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify the bias-variance components numerically using bootstrap sampling techniques or to compare learning curves across different algorithm families (linear vs. tree-based models)

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Patterns in Cross-Validation Learning Curves: Written Report
description: Students will analyze pre-generated learning curves from multiple machine learning models to identify and explain bias-variance trade-off patterns. They will differentiate between underfitting, overfitting, and optimal complexity scenarios by interpreting training and validation error convergence patterns across different dataset sizes.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance trade-off manifestations by analyzing training and validation error curves across varying model complexities
Students will differentiate between underfitting, overfitting, and optimal model complexity through systematic examination of learning curve patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared dataset containing 12 learning curve plots (4 sets of 3 models each: linear regression, polynomial regression with degree 5, and polynomial regression with degree 15) trained on different synthetic datasets. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Each pair examines the first set of three learning curves without model labels. They identify which curve represents underfitting, optimal fit, and overfitting by analyzing gap patterns between training and validation errors, final error levels, and curve convergence behavior. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Pairs complete a structured analysis worksheet documenting specific evidence from curves including: training error plateau levels, validation error trends, gap magnitude between curves, and sample size sensitivity. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Reveal model identities and have pairs explain why each model complexity produced its observed pattern. They must connect polynomial degree to bias-variance components. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Pairs analyze remaining three curve sets, predicting model complexity ranking before verification. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Class discussion where pairs present one counterintuitive finding and explain the underlying bias-variance mechanism. Throughout, emphasize interpreting curve shapes rather than memorizing patterns - students should explain why low-complexity models show high training error (high bias) while high-complexity models show large training-validation gaps (high variance).
materials_needed: Pre-generated learning curve dataset with 12 plots (3 complexity levels × 4 different synthetic datasets)
Structured analysis worksheets with bias-variance interpretation framework
Model complexity reveal sheets for verification
Python/R environment with plotting capabilities for instructors
assessment_method: Grade completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of underfitting/overfitting patterns (25%), (2) Accurate explanation of bias-variance mechanisms causing each pattern (35%), (3) Proper interpretation of training-validation error gap significance (25%), (4) Quality of counterintuitive finding presentation with mechanistic explanation (15%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in pattern identification and provide mechanistically sound explanations to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide bias-variance definition reference cards and guide them to focus on two key indicators - training error level (bias) and training-validation gap (variance). For advanced learners: Include learning curves from regularized models (Ridge/Lasso) and challenge them to explain how regularization parameter affects the bias-variance trade-off patterns. Consider adding ensemble method curves for complexity.
original_title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Patterns in Cross-Validation Learning Curves

title: Budget Planning for a School Event Using Linear Equations
description: Students will apply their knowledge of linear equations to create a realistic budget for organizing a school dance. They will use linear relationships to calculate costs, determine ticket prices, and analyze break-even points.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear equation concepts by calculating total costs based on variable attendance numbers
Students will determine appropriate ticket pricing through solving linear equations for break-even scenarios
instructions: Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4 and distributing the event planning worksheet and calculators. Start with a 10-minute whole-class discussion about school dance expenses (venue, DJ, decorations, refreshments). Present the scenario: 'Your group is planning a school dance with a $800 fixed cost and $12 per-person variable cost for food and drinks.' Step 1 (15 minutes): Students create the linear equation C = 800 + 12n, where C is total cost and n is number of attendees. Have them calculate total costs for 50, 100, 150, and 200 attendees. Step 2 (15 minutes): Students create a revenue equation R = tn, where t is ticket price and n is attendance. They calculate revenue for different ticket prices ($15, $18, $20, $25) at each attendance level. Step 3 (20 minutes): Students find break-even points by setting C = R and solving for n at each ticket price. They must show algebraic work: 800 + 12n = tn, then solve for n = 800/(t-12). Step 4 (15 minutes): Groups create a recommendation memo stating their chosen ticket price, expected attendance, and profit margin, justifying their decision with calculations. Conclude with 10-minute group presentations of their recommendations. Circulate during work time to check equation setup and algebraic manipulation. Ensure students are showing all steps in their calculations and connecting mathematical results to real-world decision-making.
materials_needed: Event Planning Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Scientific calculators (one per student)
Graph paper for plotting cost/revenue functions
Presentation rubric handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct setup of linear equations (25%), (2) Accurate algebraic solutions for break-even points (25%), (3) Appropriate calculations for different scenarios (25%), (4) Clear justification of final recommendation with mathematical reasoning (25%). Students must submit completed worksheet and present 2-minute group recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide equation templates with blanks to fill in, use smaller numbers initially, and offer step-by-step algebra review sheets. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including multiple venue options, consider profit maximization problems, or introduce quadratic cost functions for bulk discounts.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Performance
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code implementations, tracing through execution steps, and evaluating their Big O notation performance. They will break down each algorithm's structure to identify nested loops, recursive calls, and decision points that contribute to overall efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by identifying and counting nested operations, loops, and recursive calls
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of Big O notation and performance characteristics under different input conditions
instructions: Begin by distributing three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) and input datasets of sizes 10, 100, and 1000 elements. In pairs, students first spend 15 minutes examining each algorithm's structure, identifying loops, conditionals, and recursive calls. They create a visual flowchart for each algorithm showing decision points and iteration patterns. Next, students trace through each algorithm using the size-10 dataset, counting the number of comparisons and swaps performed, recording results in a provided analysis table. For the larger datasets, students calculate theoretical operation counts using their identified patterns rather than manual tracing. Students then plot their findings on provided graphs showing input size (x-axis) versus operations performed (y-axis) for each algorithm. In the final 20 minutes, pairs analyze their graphs to determine Big O classifications, identifying which algorithms show linear, quadratic, or logarithmic growth patterns. Students complete a comparison matrix evaluating best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for each algorithm, noting when each would be most appropriate. They conclude by writing a 2-paragraph analysis explaining which algorithm they would choose for different scenarios (small datasets, large datasets, partially sorted data) with specific justifications based on their findings.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in chosen programming language
Three sample datasets (10, 100, 1000 integer elements) provided as text files
Algorithm analysis worksheet with comparison tables and graph templates
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
Calculators for operation counting
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all algorithm components and accurately calculates Big O notation with detailed justification; (3) Identifies most components with minor calculation errors but reaches correct conclusions; (2) Shows understanding of concepts but makes significant errors in analysis or classification; (1) Demonstrates minimal understanding with major gaps in analysis. Check visual flowcharts for accuracy and completeness of algorithm representation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-marked code with loop levels highlighted and operation counting templates with partially completed examples. Offer guiding questions like 'How many times does this inner loop run for each outer loop iteration?' For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or challenge them to analyze space complexity alongside time complexity. Have them research and compare their findings with published algorithm performance benchmarks.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Performance: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code implementations and measuring their performance with datasets of varying sizes. They will decompose each algorithm's structure to identify efficiency bottlenecks and compare their theoretical Big O notations with empirical runtime data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by tracing through their execution patterns and identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and data access patterns
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic testing with datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 elements to validate theoretical Big O predictions
instructions: Begin by providing students with pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python (15 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one primary algorithm to focus on initially. In Phase 1 (25 minutes), students trace through their assigned algorithm using a small dataset of 8 numbers, documenting each step and counting operations. They should identify: nested loops, recursive calls, array accesses, and comparisons. Using this analysis, groups predict the Big O time complexity. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), groups implement timing code using Python's time.time() function to measure actual runtime performance. They test each of the three algorithms with randomly generated arrays of 100, 1000, and 10000 integers, running each test 5 times and calculating average runtime. Students record results in a provided data table. In Phase 3 (20 minutes), groups analyze their empirical data by creating simple graphs (hand-drawn or using spreadsheet software) plotting array size vs. runtime for all three algorithms. They compare these graphs with their predicted Big O curves (linear, n log n, quadratic). Finally (15 minutes), each group presents their findings, explaining discrepancies between theoretical and actual performance, discussing factors like best/worst case scenarios, and identifying which algorithm performs best for different dataset sizes. Students submit their completed analysis worksheet, timing data table, and performance graphs.
materials_needed: Pre-written Python code files for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with tracing tables and Big O prediction sections
Data recording table template for timing results
Computers with Python installed and text editor/IDE access
Graph paper or access to spreadsheet software for plotting results
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of algorithm components and Big O predictions (25%), (2) Accurate timing methodology and data collection (25%), (3) Appropriate analysis of empirical vs. theoretical results (25%), (4) Clear explanation of performance differences and algorithm suitability for different contexts (25%). Students must submit completed worksheets, timing data, graphs, and participate in group presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm flowcharts and step-by-step tracing examples for the first few iterations. Offer pre-formatted timing code templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity in addition to time complexity, implement additional sorting algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or investigate best/average/worst-case scenarios with specific input patterns (already sorted, reverse sorted, random data).
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Performance

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Diagnosis
description: Students will critically assess and compare three pre-trained machine learning models for medical image classification, evaluating their suitability for real-world clinical deployment. They will analyze performance metrics, identify potential biases, and make evidence-based recommendations for implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different machine learning models by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, and clinical impact metrics
Students will critique model limitations and biases through systematic analysis of demographic performance disparities and edge cases
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three pre-trained models (CNN, Random Forest, SVM) trained on chest X-ray datasets for pneumonia detection, along with test datasets containing 500 images with known diagnoses and demographic information. Teams spend 20 minutes familiarizing themselves with model outputs and documentation. Next, teams conduct systematic evaluation over 90 minutes: (1) Calculate and compare sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and F1-scores for each model (20 min); (2) Generate and analyze ROC curves, identifying optimal thresholds for clinical use (25 min); (3) Perform demographic bias analysis by examining performance across age groups, gender, and image quality subsets (25 min); (4) Conduct error analysis on false positives/negatives to identify systematic failures (20 min). Teams then spend 30 minutes preparing recommendations addressing: Which model to deploy and why? What are the key limitations and risks? What additional validation is needed? How should the model be integrated into clinical workflow? Finally, conduct 40-minute presentations where each team presents 8-minute recommendations followed by 2-minute peer questioning. Other teams use provided evaluation sheets to assess the rigor of analysis, quality of evidence, and feasibility of recommendations. Conclude with 10-minute instructor debrief highlighting key evaluation principles and real-world considerations.
materials_needed: Pre-trained ML models with standardized API access
Chest X-ray test dataset (500 images) with ground truth labels and metadata
Python environment with scikit-learn, matplotlib, pandas pre-installed
Model evaluation template spreadsheet
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Technical accuracy of metric calculations and interpretations (25%), (2) Depth of bias and error analysis with specific examples (30%), (3) Quality of evidence-based reasoning in recommendations (25%), (4) Critical assessment of clinical implementation challenges (20%). Require written executive summary (2 pages) and presentation slides as deliverables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation templates and interpretation guides. Assign specific roles (metrics calculator, bias analyst, presenter). For advanced learners: Add cost-effectiveness analysis, regulatory compliance considerations, or comparison with radiologist performance benchmarks. Encourage exploration of model interpretability techniques like LIME or SHAP.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Encryption Algorithm Using Modular Arithmetic
description: Students will create an original symmetric encryption algorithm incorporating advanced modular arithmetic concepts, then rigorously test its security properties and computational efficiency. This capstone activity synthesizes number theory, abstract algebra, and cryptographic principles while requiring students to defend their design choices through mathematical proof.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original encryption algorithm by integrating modular arithmetic operations, prime factorization, and group theory concepts within a secure cryptographic framework
Students will evaluate and validate their algorithm's security through mathematical proof techniques, complexity analysis, and systematic vulnerability testing
instructions:
**Phase 1: Algorithm Design (90 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to design their encryption algorithm. Begin by having each pair select a mathematical foundation: either elliptic curves over finite fields, polynomial rings modulo prime ideals, or multiplicative groups of integers modulo composite numbers. Provide each pair with a specification sheet requiring: key generation method, encryption function, decryption function, and security parameter selection. Students must mathematically justify why their chosen operations preserve invertibility and demonstrate the algorithm through hand calculations on sample plaintexts.

**Phase 2: Implementation and Testing (120 minutes)**
Pairs implement their algorithm in Python, creating functions for key generation, encryption, decryption, and basic cryptanalysis resistance testing. Distribute the provided template code containing input validation and timing functions. Students must successfully encrypt/decrypt messages of varying lengths and document computational complexity. Each pair then attempts to cryptanalyze another pair's algorithm, documenting attack vectors and success/failure results.

**Phase 3: Formal Validation (90 minutes)**
Students prepare a mathematical proof addressing three security properties: semantic security, resistance to chosen-plaintext attacks, and computational hardness assumptions. They must present formal definitions, state their security theorem, and provide either a complete proof or proof sketch with clearly identified gaps. Conclude with 10-minute peer presentations where pairs defend their algorithm against questions about implementation choices, security assumptions, and practical applicability.
materials_needed: Python 3.9+ with NumPy and SymPy libraries installed
Algorithm specification template sheets
Pre-generated test vectors and sample plaintexts
Digital whiteboards or presentation software
Cryptanalysis worksheet with common attack methodologies
assessment_method: Evaluate using four-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical rigor of algorithm design and justification of modular arithmetic operations, (2) Correctness and efficiency of implementation with proper error handling, (3) Thoroughness of security analysis including formal definitions and proof attempts, (4) Quality of cryptanalytic testing on peer algorithms with documented methodology, (5) Clarity of presentation and defense of design decisions. Each dimension scored 0-4 points (total 20 points). Require submission of complete code, mathematical writeup, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm design flowchart templates and step-by-step modular arithmetic reference sheets. Offer pre-coded helper functions for basic operations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate zero-knowledge proof elements or design algorithms resistant to quantum attacks. Provide research papers on post-quantum cryptography for additional complexity. Consider allowing advanced students to work with lattice-based or code-based cryptographic primitives.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze and interpret three different statistical distributions (normal, exponential, and Poisson) within the context of e-commerce customer behavior data. They will identify distribution characteristics, explain their business implications, and compare how different customer segments exhibit different statistical patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the shape, center, and spread parameters of normal, exponential, and Poisson distributions by analyzing pre-processed customer purchase datasets
Students will explain the business significance of different distribution patterns through structured comparison of customer behavior metrics across three market segments
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three CSV datasets labeled 'Premium_Customers.csv', 'Regular_Customers.csv', and 'Bargain_Customers.csv' containing purchase amounts, time between purchases, and monthly purchase counts respectively. Students work in pairs, with each pair receiving identical datasets and a structured analysis worksheet.

**Phase 1 - Distribution Identification (15 minutes):** Each pair loads datasets into their preferred tool and creates histograms for: purchase amounts (Premium customers), time between purchases in days (Regular customers), and number of monthly purchases (Bargain customers). Students identify which theoretical distribution (normal, exponential, or Poisson) best matches each histogram pattern using provided distribution characteristic cards.

**Phase 2 - Parameter Interpretation (20 minutes):** Using built-in statistical functions, pairs calculate key parameters: mean and standard deviation for the normal distribution, lambda for the exponential distribution, and lambda for the Poisson distribution. Students complete interpretation statements: 'The mean purchase amount of $X indicates...', 'The exponential decay parameter of Y suggests customers typically...', 'The Poisson parameter of Z means customers average...'.

**Phase 3 - Business Implications Discussion (15 minutes):** Pairs complete a comparison matrix examining what each distribution reveals about customer behavior patterns. They discuss questions like: 'Why might premium customer spending follow a normal distribution?' and 'What does exponential distribution of purchase timing suggest about customer retention strategies?'

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Three volunteer pairs share one key insight about how distribution shape connects to business strategy, with instructor facilitating connections between mathematical properties and real-world implications.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with realistic e-commerce data (500-1000 records each)
Distribution characteristic reference cards showing normal, exponential, and Poisson curve shapes
Structured analysis worksheet with parameter calculation tables and interpretation prompts
Python/R/Excel or similar data analysis software with statistical functions
Comparison matrix template for business implications analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correct distribution identification and parameter calculations, (2) Accurate interpretation of statistical parameters in business context, (3) Logical connections drawn between distribution characteristics and customer behavior implications. Each pair submits their completed worksheet and comparison matrix. Success criteria: 80% of pairs correctly identify all three distributions and provide reasonable business interpretations for at least 2 out of 3 scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide distribution identification flowchart ('Is the data symmetric? → Normal; Does it decay rapidly? → Exponential; Is it count data? → Poisson') and sentence starters for interpretations. **Extension for advanced learners:** Challenge them to propose specific marketing strategies based on each distribution pattern and calculate confidence intervals or perform goodness-of-fit tests to validate their distribution choices.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Customer Purchase Data: Written Report
description: Students will analyze a real e-commerce customer dataset to identify and explain patterns in three different statistical distributions. They will interpret histograms, calculate descriptive statistics, and explain what each distribution reveals about customer behavior using domain-specific vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing customer purchase frequency, order values, and session duration histograms
Students will explain the business implications of distribution patterns through written interpretations connecting statistical measures to customer behavior insights
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the pre-loaded dataset containing 1,000 customer records with purchase frequency, order values, and session duration (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to create three histograms using provided Python code templates, adjusting bin sizes to reveal distribution shapes clearly. For each histogram, pairs calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation, then record these values in the provided worksheet template. Next, students identify each distribution type (normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, or bimodal) by comparing mean/median relationships and examining histogram shapes. They must write a 3-sentence interpretation for each distribution explaining: (1) the distribution type and key statistical measures, (2) what this pattern reveals about customer behavior, and (3) one business decision this insight could inform. Pairs then compare findings with another pair, discussing any differences in their interpretations and refining their explanations. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their most interesting finding, focusing on how distribution shape connects to business meaning. Instructor facilitates by asking follow-up questions about why certain distributions might occur in customer data.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with 1,000 records)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Distribution analysis worksheet template (PDF)
Pre-written Python code snippets for histogram generation
Statistical measures reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of all three distribution types, (2) Accurate calculation of statistical measures, (3) Clear written explanations connecting distribution patterns to customer behavior, (4) Appropriate use of statistical vocabulary. Students submit completed worksheets with histograms and written interpretations. Look for evidence they can distinguish distribution shapes and explain business relevance rather than just identify statistical properties.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a distribution identification flowchart and sentence starters for interpretations like 'This right-skewed distribution suggests that most customers...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential causes of observed patterns and suggest additional variables that might explain distribution shapes. Consider having them research industry benchmarks to contextualize their findings.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Customer Purchase Data: Written Report
description: Students will analyze pre-processed customer purchase datasets to identify and interpret different statistical distributions (normal, skewed, bimodal). learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of normal, right-skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing customer purchase amount histograms and explaining what each pattern reveals about customer behavior
