title: Optimization in Architecture: Designing Cost-Effective Solar Panel Arrays
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to solve a real-world architectural problem involving optimal placement and sizing of solar panel arrays on building rooftops. They will work with constraints including budget limitations, roof geometry, shadow effects, and energy requirements to maximize energy output while minimizing costs.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization methods to determine optimal solar panel configurations given multiple real-world constraints
Students will implement linear programming techniques through systematic problem formulation to solve complex resource allocation problems in renewable energy design
instructions: Begin by distributing the building specifications packet containing three different commercial building blueprints with detailed roof dimensions, orientations, and obstacle locations (30 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team one building type: warehouse (flat roof), office complex (multi-level), or retail center (irregular roof shape). Each team receives identical constraint parameters: $50,000 budget, panel specifications (dimensions, cost per unit, energy output), local solar irradiance data, and minimum energy targets. Students first spend 45 minutes mapping their assigned roof space using provided graph paper, identifying usable areas while accounting for HVAC equipment, structural elements, and required maintenance walkways. Next, teams formulate their optimization problem by defining decision variables (number of panels, placement coordinates), objective function (maximize energy output or minimize cost per kWh), and constraint equations (budget, space, shading effects between panel rows). Using graphing calculators or provided spreadsheet templates, students apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to find critical points, then verify solutions using boundary analysis techniques. Teams must document their mathematical process, showing partial derivatives, constraint equations, and verification that their solution satisfies Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents their optimal configuration using a scaled roof diagram showing exact panel placement, total system cost, projected annual energy output, and mathematical justification for their solution. Other teams evaluate presentations using peer assessment sheets, checking mathematical accuracy and constraint satisfaction.
materials_needed: Building specification packets with detailed roof blueprints (3 different building types)
Graph paper and architectural scales/rulers
Scientific calculators with graphing capabilities or laptop access to spreadsheet software
Solar panel specification sheets with dimensions, costs, and performance data
Local solar irradiance charts and shading calculation worksheets
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 100-point rubric: mathematical formulation accuracy (25 points), correct application of optimization techniques (30 points), constraint satisfaction verification (20 points), presentation clarity and visual design quality (15 points), and peer evaluation scores (10 points). Successful completion requires demonstrating all constraint equations, showing complete Lagrange multiplier calculations, and producing a feasible solution within budget and space limitations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint equation templates and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier worksheets with partially completed examples. Offer simplified building layouts with rectangular roofs only. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as time-varying energy pricing, seasonal solar angle adjustments, or multi-objective optimization balancing cost and environmental impact. Encourage exploration of integer programming methods for discrete panel placement decisions.

title: Analyzing Cryptographic Hash Function Vulnerabilities Through Collision Attack Simulation
description: Students will decompose and analyze the structural weaknesses in simplified MD5 and SHA-1 hash functions by implementing collision attacks and evaluating the security implications. They will examine real-world vulnerability patterns and differentiate between theoretical and practical attack vectors.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze cryptographic hash function vulnerabilities by implementing differential cryptanalysis techniques on simplified MD5 algorithms
Students will evaluate the relationship between hash function design choices and security weaknesses through systematic collision attack simulation
instructions: **Phase 1: Setup (15 minutes)** - Distribute three hash function implementations: a simplified 32-bit MD5 variant, a truncated SHA-1 (80-bit output), and a secure SHA-256 baseline. Students work in pairs with one acting as 'attacker' and one as 'defender.' **Phase 2: Vulnerability Mapping (30 minutes)** - Students analyze the source code of each implementation, identifying specific structural differences: round function complexity, message scheduling algorithms, and collision resistance mechanisms. They document findings in a vulnerability matrix comparing bit-level operations, noting where simplifications create attack surfaces. **Phase 3: Collision Attack Implementation (45 minutes)** - Using provided Python frameworks, students implement birthday attacks against the simplified functions. They must: (1) Generate message pairs with identical hash outputs, (2) Measure computational complexity in terms of hash operations required, (3) Document successful collision examples with hex dumps. **Phase 4: Security Analysis (30 minutes)** - Students analyze their attack results, calculating theoretical vs. actual collision probabilities, identifying which design elements made attacks feasible, and comparing attack complexity across the three implementations. **Phase 5: Defense Evaluation (20 minutes)** - Teams propose specific code modifications to increase collision resistance, implementing one change and re-testing their attacks to measure effectiveness. Final deliverable includes a technical report with attack vectors, collision examples, and security recommendations.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with hashlib and cryptography libraries installed
Simplified hash function implementations (MD5-32bit.py, SHA1-truncated.py, SHA256-baseline.py)
Collision attack framework template files
Vulnerability analysis worksheet with hash comparison matrices
Access to computational resources capable of 10^6 hash operations
assessment_method: Technical report (60 points) must include: successful collision examples with proof-of-work (20 pts), quantitative analysis of attack complexity with statistical validation (20 pts), and specific security recommendations with implementation rationale (20 pts). Live demonstration (40 points) requires students to execute their collision attack in real-time and explain the underlying mathematical principles to instructor.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written collision detection functions and focus analysis on interpreting results rather than implementation details. Offer simplified vulnerability checklists. For advanced learners: Challenge them to develop novel attack optimizations, implement rainbow table approaches, or analyze timing-based side-channel vulnerabilities. Provide access to research papers on advanced cryptanalytic techniques.

title: Design Your Dream Park: A Geometric Area and Perimeter Project
description: Students will design and create a detailed blueprint for a community park using geometric shapes, calculating areas and perimeters while applying real-world constraints. They will present their design with mathematical justifications for their choices, demonstrating mastery of area and perimeter concepts through creative problem-solving.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original park design by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and circles to maximize space efficiency
Students will synthesize mathematical calculations with creative design elements through developing a comprehensive blueprint with cost analysis
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: The city council has allocated a 10,000 square meter plot of land for a new community park with a $50,000 budget. Students work individually for the first 30 minutes to brainstorm park features (playground, walking paths, gardens, sports courts, pond). Provide each student with the constraint sheet showing costs per square meter for different features (grass: $5/m², concrete paths: $15/m², playground equipment area: $25/m², sports courts: $30/m²). 

For the next 60 minutes, students create their blueprint on grid paper (1 square = 10m²) using rulers and compasses. They must include at least one rectangular area, one circular feature, and one triangular space. Students calculate the area and perimeter of each section, showing all work on a separate calculation sheet. They must also track their running budget total.

During the final 45 minutes, students prepare a 3-minute presentation of their design. They must justify their mathematical choices (why they chose specific dimensions), explain how they stayed within budget, and describe how their calculations influenced their design decisions. Set up a gallery walk where students post blueprints and calculation sheets, then present to small groups of 4-5 peers who rotate every 5 minutes.

Circulate throughout to ask probing questions: 'How did you decide on these dimensions?' 'What would happen if you increased this area by 20%?' 'How does the perimeter of your walking path affect the user experience?' Encourage students to make real-time adjustments if they discover calculation errors during peer feedback.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, minimum 20x20 grid per student)
Rulers and compasses
Colored pencils or markers
Park feature cost constraint sheets (pre-printed)
Calculators
Presentation timer
Sticky notes for peer feedback
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area/perimeter calculations with shown work), Creative Design (innovative use of space and thoughtful feature placement), Budget Management (stays within $50,000 with accurate cost calculations), and Communication (clear presentation with mathematical justification). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in Mathematical Accuracy to demonstrate mastery. Collect calculation sheets, blueprints, and use peer feedback forms for comprehensive evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made templates with basic shapes outlined and formula reference cards. Start with simpler polygons and allow calculator use for all calculations. For advanced learners: Add constraints like accessibility requirements (wheelchair ramp angles), introduce composite shapes, or include irregular plot boundaries. Challenge them to optimize for maximum green space or create multi-level designs with volume calculations.

title: Advanced Concurrency Control Mechanisms Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific implementation details, algorithms, and characteristics of advanced database concurrency control mechanisms. This activity focuses on precise recall of Two-Phase Locking variants, Multiversion Concurrency Control, and Optimistic Concurrency Control protocols.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact steps and phases of Strict Two-Phase Locking, Conservative Two-Phase Locking, and Rigorous Two-Phase Locking protocols by completing timed identification exercises
Students will memorize the specific data structures, timestamp ordering rules, and conflict resolution mechanisms used in MVCC and OCC through structured flashcard sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the 150 pre-prepared flashcards covering concurrency control mechanisms (50 cards each for 2PL variants, MVCC, and OCC). Students work individually for the first 15 minutes, sorting cards into 'know immediately', 'need review', and 'don't know' piles. Next, form pairs where students quiz each other using the 'need review' pile for 20 minutes, focusing on exact algorithm steps, lock compatibility matrices, and timestamp comparison rules. During minute 35-45, conduct rapid-fire whole-class recall sessions where instructor displays protocol names and students must immediately state: lock types used, when locks are acquired/released, deadlock prevention methods, and rollback conditions. For minutes 45-55, students complete individual written recall sheets listing the complete steps for each protocol without references. In the final 10 minutes, students self-check answers against provided solution keys and identify remaining knowledge gaps. Throughout the activity, emphasize memorizing exact terminology: 'shared locks', 'exclusive locks', 'read timestamps', 'write timestamps', 'validation phase', 'write phase', etc. Students must recall precise conditions like 'TS(Ti) < W-timestamp(Q)' for timestamp ordering conflicts.
materials_needed: 150 pre-made flashcards with concurrency control protocol details
Printed recall worksheets with protocol completion exercises
Solution keys for self-checking
Timer for rapid-fire sessions
Lock compatibility matrix reference charts
assessment_method: Students complete a 20-question recall quiz requiring exact reproduction of algorithm steps, lock compatibility rules, and timestamp comparison conditions. Success criteria: 90% accuracy on protocol step sequences, 85% accuracy on technical terminology usage, and ability to recall complete algorithms within 2-minute time limits per protocol. Use checklist rubric marking correctness of each algorithm phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices for protocol phases (e.g., 'Growing-Shrinking' for 2PL phases) and color-coded cards grouping related concepts. Advanced learners can extend by memorizing additional protocols like Graph-Based protocols or Thomas Write Rule variations. Create visual flowcharts for complex timestamp ordering rules to support visual learners.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results and Model Selection Trade-offs in Hyperparameter Tuning
description: Students will analyze complex cross-validation outputs from multiple machine learning algorithms with different hyperparameter configurations. They will interpret performance metrics, bias-variance trade-offs, and computational costs to make informed model selection decisions for a multi-class classification problem.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation results by analyzing mean scores, standard deviations, and learning curves across different hyperparameter configurations
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity, generalization performance, and computational efficiency through comparative analysis of grid search outputs
instructions: Step 1 (10 min): Distribute the prepared dataset containing cross-validation results from scikit-learn's GridSearchCV for three algorithms (Random Forest, SVM, XGBoost) on a customer churn dataset. Each student receives identical CSV files with columns: algorithm, hyperparameters, cv_fold, accuracy, precision, recall, f1_score, fit_time, score_time. Step 2 (20 min): Students work individually to create summary statistics tables showing mean and standard deviation for each performance metric across the 5 CV folds for each hyperparameter combination. They must identify the top 3 configurations per algorithm based on F1-score. Step 3 (25 min): In pairs, students create comparative visualizations showing the trade-off between model complexity and performance. They plot hyperparameter values against CV scores, highlighting regions of overfitting vs. underfitting. Students must annotate plots with observations about variance in performance across folds. Step 4 (20 min): Teams of 4 students (2 pairs combined) engage in structured discussions using provided question prompts: 'What does high standard deviation across CV folds indicate?', 'How do you balance computational cost with marginal performance gains?', 'Which algorithm shows most stable performance?' Step 5 (15 min): Each team presents their final model recommendation with three supporting arguments based on their analysis. Presentations must address business context (customer retention), computational constraints (real-time scoring), and performance requirements (minimizing false negatives).
materials_needed: Pre-generated GridSearchCV results CSV file with 450 rows (3 algorithms × 30 hyperparameter combinations × 5 CV folds)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Structured discussion prompt cards with 8 specific questions
Model comparison template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of statistical summaries and identification of top performers (25%), (2) Quality of visualizations showing complexity-performance trade-offs with proper annotations (25%), (3) Depth of explanations regarding cross-validation variance and its implications (25%), (4) Justification quality in final model recommendation addressing all three constraints (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly interpreting CV standard deviations and articulating when high-performing models might not be optimal choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code for generating summary statistics and basic plotting functions. Include guided questions worksheet with specific metrics to calculate first. For advanced learners: Extend activity by having them implement custom scoring functions, analyze learning curves with varying training set sizes, or incorporate cost-sensitive evaluation metrics. Provide additional datasets with different characteristics (imbalanced classes, high dimensionality) for comparative analysis.

title: Budget Your Dream Vacation: Applying Decimal Operations and Percentages
description: Students will create a realistic vacation budget by applying decimal addition, subtraction, and percentage calculations to real-world travel costs. They will use actual prices from travel websites to plan a 3-day trip while staying within a given budget constraint.
learning_objectives: Students will apply decimal addition and subtraction by calculating total vacation costs from itemized expenses
Students will apply percentage calculations through computing taxes, tips, and discounts on travel purchases
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Dream Vacation Budget Worksheet' and assign each student a budget of $800 for a 3-day vacation. Provide access to computers/tablets with internet access. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Students choose a destination city and research actual prices using provided travel websites (Expedia, Hotels.com, restaurant review sites). They must find: round-trip flight cost, hotel cost per night, three restaurant meals with menu prices, and two activities with admission fees. **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Students calculate their base costs by adding all decimal amounts using proper decimal alignment. They record each calculation showing their work: Flight + (Hotel × 3 nights) + Meal costs + Activity costs = Base Total. **Step 3 (15 minutes):** Students apply percentage calculations for additional costs: add 8.5% sales tax to hotel and activities, add 18% tip to restaurant bills, and subtract any available discounts (provide 10% student discount cards for one activity). **Step 4 (10 minutes):** Students compare their final total to the $800 budget. If over budget, they must revise choices and recalculate until within limit. If under budget, they calculate remaining amount and suggest additional purchases. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Students present their final budget to a partner, explaining their calculations and defending their choices within the budget constraint.
materials_needed: Dream Vacation Budget Worksheet (pre-printed with calculation spaces)
Computers or tablets with internet access
Calculators
List of approved travel websites for price research
10% student discount cards (printed props)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All decimal calculations accurate with proper alignment, percentage calculations correct, stays within budget; (3) Minor calculation errors, mostly accurate percentages, budget constraint met; (2) Some calculation errors, basic percentage understanding shown, budget approximately met; (1) Multiple errors, incomplete calculations, budget significantly exceeded. Observe student explanations to partner for understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculator reference sheet showing decimal alignment examples and percentage calculation steps (multiply by 0.085 for 8.5% tax). Offer pre-selected destinations with simplified pricing. For advanced learners: Add currency conversion calculations for international destinations, include compound discounts, or require comparison of budget versus actual spending tracking with daily allowances.

title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Policy Interventions
description: Students will construct an original compartmental epidemiological model (beyond basic SIR) incorporating real-world policy interventions, then validate their model against historical data and present recommendations to a simulated public health board. This activity integrates differential equations, parameter estimation, and statistical validation techniques.
estimated_duration: 270 minutes (4.5 hours) - can be split across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will construct a novel compartmental epidemiological model by incorporating at least three policy intervention variables (vaccination rates, social distancing measures, quarantine protocols) using systems of differential equations

Students will synthesize mathematical modeling, statistical analysis, and data validation techniques through the creation of a comprehensive policy recommendation framework supported by quantitative evidence
instructions: **Phase 1: Model Design (90 minutes)** - Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a different historical epidemic scenario (1918 flu, 2003 SARS, 2009 H1N1, COVID-19 regional outbreaks). Teams must first research their assigned epidemic's basic parameters (R₀, incubation period, recovery time) and identify 2-3 policy interventions implemented. Using differential equation software, teams design a compartmental model extending beyond SIR to include: exposed populations (E), quarantined individuals (Q), vaccinated populations (V), and policy intervention parameters (β reduction factors, quarantine rates, vaccination schedules). Students must justify each compartment and parameter mathematically. **Phase 2: Parameter Estimation and Validation (75 minutes)** - Teams access provided historical datasets and use least-squares fitting or maximum likelihood estimation to calibrate their model parameters. They must demonstrate goodness-of-fit using R² values, residual analysis, and chi-square tests. Teams calculate confidence intervals for key parameters and perform sensitivity analysis on intervention variables. **Phase 3: Policy Scenario Testing (60 minutes)** - Using calibrated models, teams test three counterfactual scenarios: earlier intervention timing, different intervention intensity levels, and combined intervention strategies. They must quantify outcomes using metrics like total infections prevented, peak infection reduction, and economic cost-effectiveness ratios. **Phase 4: Presentation and Peer Review (45 minutes)** - Each team presents 12-minute formal recommendations to simulated public health board (other teams), defending model assumptions, validation results, and policy recommendations. Peer teams provide structured feedback using provided evaluation criteria and challenge model limitations.
materials_needed: Laptops with MATLAB, R, or Python (SciPy/NumPy) installed
Historical epidemic datasets (provided CSV files with daily case counts, policy implementation dates)
Scientific calculators for backup calculations
Large format paper (A3) for model diagram sketching
Access to academic databases for parameter research
Policy recommendation template (provided Word document)
Peer evaluation rubrics (printed copies)
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical sophistication - model complexity, appropriate use of differential equations, parameter justification (25 points); (2) Statistical validation - fitting procedures, goodness-of-fit analysis, uncertainty quantification (25 points); (3) Policy analysis - scenario testing rigor, quantitative comparisons, realistic constraints (20 points); (4) Communication - clarity of presentation, defense of assumptions, response to peer questions (20 points); (5) Peer collaboration - quality of feedback given to other teams, constructive criticism (10 points). Deliverables include: annotated model code, validation report with statistical analysis, policy brief with recommendations, and presentation slides. Success threshold: 70/100 points minimum, with all teams required to demonstrate functional model with statistical validation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation structures and guided parameter estimation worksheets. Offer simplified datasets with pre-cleaned data and basic MATLAB/Python tutorial handouts. Pair struggling students with stronger mathematical modelers within teams. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, spatial heterogeneity, or economic optimization constraints. Encourage exploration of advanced fitting techniques like Bayesian parameter estimation or machine learning approaches. Provide access to more complex, multi-regional datasets requiring data preprocessing skills.

title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Policy Interventions: Technical Implementation
description: Students will construct an original compartmental epidemiological model (extending beyond basic SIR) that incorporates multiple intervention strategies, then validate their model against real-world data and present policy recommendations. This activity integrates differential equations, parameter estimation, and mathematical modeling principles.
estimated_duration: 7 class periods (approximately 14-16 hours total, including homework time for research and coding)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize differential equation theory, statistical analysis, and real-world constraints to construct an original epidemiological model with at least 5 compartments and 3 intervention parameters
Students will evaluate and justify their model's validity through systematic comparison with historical epidemic data and create evidence-based policy recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1 (Days 1-2, 180 minutes):** Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team selects a specific epidemic (COVID-19, H1N1, Ebola, etc.) and geographic region. Teams must research and identify at least 3 distinct intervention strategies used (lockdowns, vaccination campaigns, contact tracing, etc.). Using whiteboards or digital modeling software, teams sketch their initial compartmental model, extending basic SIR to include: exposed populations, intervention compliance rates, reinfection possibilities, or age stratification. Teams must justify each compartment and transition rate with mathematical reasoning.

**Phase 2 (Days 3-4, 240 minutes):** Teams formalize their model into a system of differential equations, defining all parameters explicitly. Using programming environments (Python/MATLAB), students implement their model numerically. Teams must incorporate at least 3 adjustable policy parameters (e.g., lockdown intensity α ∈ [0,1], vaccination rate v(t), contact reduction factor β). Students run preliminary simulations to ensure model stability and biological feasibility (non-negative populations, realistic time scales).

**Phase 3 (Days 5-6, 180 minutes):** Teams obtain real epidemic data from public health databases (CDC, WHO, regional health departments). Using least-squares fitting or maximum likelihood estimation, students calibrate their model parameters to match observed data for the first 60% of their chosen epidemic timeline. Teams must document their parameter estimation methodology and assess goodness-of-fit using correlation coefficients and residual analysis.

**Phase 4 (Day 7, 120 minutes):** Teams validate their calibrated model by predicting the remaining 40% of epidemic data, calculating prediction accuracy. Based on their model, teams generate 3 specific policy scenarios, run comparative simulations, and prepare evidence-based recommendations with uncertainty quantification.
materials_needed: Programming environment (Python with NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB with ODE solvers)
Access to epidemiological databases (CDC, WHO, Johns Hopkins CSSE)
Graphing software or programming plotting libraries
Whiteboard or digital collaboration platform (Miro, Jamboard)
Laptops/computers with internet access
Research databases for intervention strategy documentation
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Mathematical rigor of model construction (25 points) - correct differential equation formulation, parameter justification, biological feasibility; Implementation quality (20 points) - functional code, appropriate numerical methods, stability analysis; Data analysis and validation (25 points) - systematic parameter estimation, goodness-of-fit assessment, prediction accuracy calculation; Policy recommendations (20 points) - evidence-based conclusions, uncertainty quantification, practical feasibility; Presentation clarity (10 points) - clear mathematical communication, effective visualizations. Success threshold: 80+ points demonstrates expert-level mathematical modeling competency.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide template differential equation structures for common compartmental models; offer guided parameter estimation worksheets with step-by-step curve-fitting procedures; create debugging checklists for common programming errors; provide simplified datasets with pre-cleaned data. **For advanced learners:** Challenge students to incorporate spatial dynamics (partial differential equations), stochastic elements, or economic cost-benefit analysis; encourage exploration of advanced parameter estimation techniques (Bayesian methods, Monte Carlo); suggest investigation of model sensitivity analysis and uncertainty propagation through Latin hypercube sampling.
original_title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Policy Interventions

title: Binary Number System Flash Card Drill
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flash card exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flash card exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal value of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization practice and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash cards to each student (15 minutes setup). Each card shows a decimal number (0-15) on one side and its 4-bit binary equivalent on the other. Demonstrate proper card usage: show decimal side, state binary answer aloud, flip to verify, sort into 'known' and 'practice needed' piles. Students work individually for 10 minutes practicing their 'practice needed' pile, repeating incorrectly recalled numbers until accurate. Next, pair students for 15 minutes of mutual quizzing: Partner A shows decimal numbers randomly, Partner B responds with binary, roles switch after 7 minutes. Conduct whole-class rapid-fire round (10 minutes): instructor calls out decimal numbers, students write 4-bit binary answers on mini whiteboards, hold up simultaneously for immediate feedback. For final 5 minutes, students complete individual written quiz covering all 16 conversions. Throughout activity, emphasize that students must respond within 3 seconds to demonstrate memorization rather than calculation. Circulate continuously to correct errors immediately and ensure proper 4-bit format (e.g., '5' becomes '0101', not '101'). Maintain energetic pace to sustain engagement and build automaticity.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flash cards showing decimal 0-15 with corresponding 4-bit binary (one set per student)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Written quiz sheets with decimal numbers 0-15 for final assessment
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) on final written quiz completed independently. Award full credit for correct 4-bit binary format, partial credit for correct digits in wrong format, no credit for calculation errors. Document individual student progress by noting which specific numbers require additional practice during circulation observations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide memory aids like '8-4-2-1 place value' reference cards and allow extra practice time with cards 0-7 before progressing to 8-15. For advanced learners: extend activity to include 5-bit numbers (16-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider allowing advanced students to tutor struggling peers during partner work phase.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed customer churn dataset to identify and explain correlation patterns between different features. They will create visual correlation matrices and provide written explanations of the relationships they discover, demonstrating their understanding of how variables interact in predictive modeling contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between multiple features by analyzing correlation matrices and identifying strong positive, negative, and weak relationships
Students will explain the business implications of feature correlations through written analysis connecting statistical patterns to real-world customer behavior scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the preprocessed telecom customer churn dataset (provided CSV file) and the analysis template. Students work individually for the first 25 minutes. Step 1 (10 minutes): Students load the dataset using pandas and examine the first 10 rows, identifying numerical features (monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, etc.) and categorical features that have been encoded. Step 2 (15 minutes): Using matplotlib and seaborn, students create a correlation heatmap of all numerical features, ensuring proper color scaling and feature labels. They must identify the top 3 strongest positive correlations and top 3 strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values. Step 3 (20 minutes): Students analyze their heatmap by writing 2-3 sentence explanations for each identified correlation, addressing: what the relationship means mathematically, why this relationship might exist from a business perspective, and how it could impact churn prediction. Step 4 (15 minutes): In pairs, students compare their interpretations and discuss any differences in their business explanations. Step 5 (10 minutes): Three volunteer pairs present one surprising correlation finding to the class, explaining both the statistical relationship and business reasoning. Instructor facilitates brief discussion on how correlation understanding guides feature selection in machine learning models.
materials_needed: Preprocessed telecom customer churn dataset (CSV file with 1000+ records)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, and numpy installed
Analysis template worksheet with sections for correlation values and interpretations
Projector for student presentations
assessment_method: Students submit completed analysis templates containing: (1) accurate correlation heatmap visualization (20 points), (2) correct identification of strongest 6 correlations with exact coefficient values (30 points), (3) business explanations for each correlation demonstrating understanding of variable relationships (40 points), (4) participation in pair discussion and class presentation (10 points). Success criteria: correlation values accurate to 2 decimal places, explanations connect statistical patterns to logical business scenarios, visualizations are properly labeled and readable.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide code snippets for creating correlation matrices and offer a list of potential business explanations to choose from. Pair them with stronger partners during discussion phase. For advanced learners: challenge them to identify potential confounding variables, discuss correlation vs. causation implications, or explore partial correlations between specific feature subsets. Provide additional datasets from different industries for comparison analysis.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed customer dataset to identify and interpret correlation patterns between different features and customer churn behavior. They will create correlation matrices, interpret coefficient values, and explain the practical business implications of their findings through structured analysis worksheets.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features and churn rates by analyzing numerical relationships and explaining their practical significance
Students will distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations through systematic examination of correlation matrices and feature pair comparisons
instructions:
Begin by distributing the telecommunications customer dataset (3,000 records with 12 features including monthly charges, contract length, customer service calls, etc.) and correlation analysis worksheet to each student. Spend 5 minutes explaining that students will work individually for 25 minutes, then share findings in pairs for 15 minutes. 

Direct students to first load the dataset in their spreadsheet software and create a correlation matrix using built-in functions, focusing on relationships between numerical features and the binary churn variable (0=stayed, 1=churned). Have them record correlation coefficients in the provided table on their worksheet.

Next, instruct students to categorize each correlation as strong (|r| > 0.7), moderate (0.3 < |r| < 0.7), or weak (|r| < 0.3) and highlight the three strongest positive and negative correlations with churn. Students should then write 2-3 sentence interpretations for each of these six relationships, explaining what the correlation means in business terms.

For the analysis phase, have students complete guided questions about why certain features might correlate strongly (e.g., 'monthly charges' vs 'total charges'), identify potential confounding variables, and distinguish correlation from causation. Students must provide specific examples using actual coefficient values from their matrices.

During pair sharing, partners compare their strongest correlations, discuss any differences in interpretation, and collaborate to identify one surprising correlation pattern they found. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where pairs share their most interesting finding and explain its potential business impact.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 3,000 records)
Correlation analysis worksheet with guided questions and coefficient recording table
Spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets, or equivalent) with correlation function capability
Correlation strength reference chart (strong/moderate/weak categories)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate calculation and recording of correlation coefficients, (2) Correct categorization of correlation strength, (3) Clear business interpretation of top 6 correlations using specific coefficient values, (4) Thoughtful responses to guided analysis questions distinguishing correlation patterns and business implications. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example showing correlation calculation for one feature pair and sample business interpretation. Offer a correlation coefficient interpretation guide with sentence starters like 'This moderate positive correlation (r=0.45) suggests that...' For advanced learners, include additional questions about partial correlations, non-linear relationships, and multiple correlation analysis between feature clusters.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis: Written Report
description: Students analyze a correlation matrix from a telecommunications customer churn dataset to identify meaningful patterns between features and explain how these relationships inform predictive modeling decisions. They will demonstrate understanding by creating annotated visualizations and written explanations of correlation insights.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing a pre-computed correlation matrix and identifying strong, moderate, and weak relationships
Students will explain the implications of feature correlations through written analysis connecting statistical patterns to business context and modeling considerations
instructions: Begin by distributing the telecommunications churn dataset correlation matrix (15x15 features including monthly_charges, tenure, contract_type, etc.) and correlation interpretation reference sheet. In pairs, students spend 10 minutes examining the matrix to identify the three strongest positive correlations, three strongest negative correlations, and three near-zero correlations, recording coefficient values and feature names. Next, each pair creates a visual annotation of their correlation heatmap using colored markers to highlight significant relationships (red for strong negative r < -0.5, blue for strong positive r > 0.5, yellow for moderate 0.3 < |r| < 0.5). During the 20-minute analysis phase, students write explanations for each identified correlation, addressing: (1) what the relationship means in business terms, (2) why this correlation might exist logically, and (3) how it could impact churn prediction model performance. For example, if monthly_charges and total_charges show r = 0.85, students explain this indicates customers with higher monthly bills accumulate higher total charges, which makes business sense, but creates multicollinearity concerns for regression models. Students then spend 15 minutes preparing a 3-minute presentation of their most interesting correlation finding. Conclude with pair presentations where each team shares one correlation insight, explaining the coefficient value, business interpretation, and modeling implications while displaying their annotated heatmap.
materials_needed: Pre-computed correlation matrix for telecommunications churn dataset (printed, one per pair)
Correlation coefficient interpretation reference sheet
Colored markers (red, blue, yellow) for heatmap annotation
Blank paper for written analysis
Timer for activity phases
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation identification (correctly identifies coefficient values and strength categories), (2) Quality of business interpretation (logically connects statistical relationships to real-world customer behavior), (3) Understanding of modeling implications (explains multicollinearity, feature selection, or prediction challenges), (4) Clear communication in presentation (uses precise statistical language and supports claims with evidence)
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing correlation strength categories chart (weak: |r| < 0.3, moderate: 0.3-0.7, strong: > 0.7) and sentence starters like 'The correlation of X suggests that customers who...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional features that might strengthen weak correlations, and consider partial correlation analysis to isolate direct relationships.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students analyze a pre-processed customer dataset to identify and explain correlation patterns between features like monthly charges, contract length, and customer tenure. They will interpret correlation matrices and scatter plots to understand which customer characteristics are most strongly associated with churn behavior.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and their statistical significance by analyzing customer churn data patterns
Students will explain the relationship between multiple features through guided correlation matrix analysis and visualization interpretation
instructions: Begin by distributing the Telco Customer Churn dataset (provided as CSV) and correlation analysis worksheet to each student. In the first 10 minutes, students examine the dataset structure and identify the target variable (churn) and key features (tenure, monthly_charges, total_charges, contract_type). Next, guide students through generating a correlation matrix using provided Python code in Jupyter notebooks, focusing on correlations above 0.3 or below -0.3. For 20 minutes, students work in pairs to complete the interpretation worksheet, identifying the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations with churn. materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn CSV dataset (7043 records)
Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib installed
Correlation Analysis Worksheet (PDF with guided questions)
Pre-written Python code snippets for correlation matrix generation
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all correlation strengths and provides accurate business interpretations, (3) Identifies most correlations with minor interpretation errors, (2) Identifies correlations but explanations lack business context, (1) Struggles to identify or interpret correlation patterns. Check that students distinguish between correlation strength and direction, and penalize confusion between correlation and causation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation reference chart showing ranges (0.7-1.0 strong, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.0-0.3 weak) and sentence starters like 'As [feature] increases, [target variable] tends to...' For advanced learners, ask them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional features that might strengthen the analysis. Consider providing a second dataset for comparison analysis.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis: Business Application
description: Students will analyze a correlation matrix from a customer churn dataset to identify meaningful relationships between variables and explain how these patterns inform business decisions. instructions: Begin by providing each student with a pre-generated correlation matrix heatmap from a telecommunications customer churn dataset containing 12 variables (monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure_months, contract_type_encoded, tech_support, online_security, streaming_services, payment_method_encoded, senior_citizen, partner, dependents, churn). Next, individually (15 minutes), each student completes a structured analysis worksheet with three sections: (1) Classification - categorize each of the six identified correlations as strong, moderate, or weak using the provided thresholds; (2) Business Interpretation - write 2-3 sentences explaining what each correlation means in plain business terms (e.g., 'The 0.83 correlation between monthly_charges and total_charges suggests customers with higher monthly bills tend to have spent more money overall with the company'); (3) Causation Analysis - select two correlations and explain whether the relationship implies causation or just association. Conclude with small group discussions (10 minutes) where 3-4 students compare their interpretations and identify any disagreements. Finally, conduct a whole-class debrief (10 minutes) where groups share one surprising correlation finding and one example where correlation doesn't imply causation. Instructor should clarify common misconceptions about correlation strength thresholds and emphasize that domain knowledge is crucial for interpreting statistical relationships.

Step 1 (25 minutes): Students work in pairs to define variables (x = standard deliveries, y = express deliveries), formulate the objective function (maximize profit: P = 8x + 12y), and write constraint inequalities from the given parameters. They must identify at least 5 realistic constraints including vehicle capacity, time limits, fuel budget ($200/day), and service requirements.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using graph paper and graphing calculators, students plot constraint lines, shade feasible regions, and identify corner points. They must clearly label axes, show intersection calculations, and verify which points satisfy all constraints.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students apply the corner point method, substituting each feasible corner point into the objective function to determine the optimal solution. They must show complete algebraic work for each calculation.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Using provided Excel templates or online linear programming solvers, students verify their manual calculations and explore sensitivity analysis by adjusting one constraint (e.g., increasing fuel budget by $50) to observe solution changes.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Pairs prepare a 3-minute presentation summarizing their optimal solution, expected daily profit, and one business recommendation based on their sensitivity analysis. Include visual displays of their feasible region graph and final calculations.
materials_needed: QuickBite Delivery Company scenario packets (pre-printed with maps and data)
Graph paper (at least 20x20 grid)
Graphing calculators or computer access
Excel templates with linear programming solver add-in
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint line graphing
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation (25 points - correct objective function and constraints), Graphical method execution (30 points - accurate plotting, feasible region identification, corner point calculations), Optimal solution determination (25 points - correct corner point method application), Technology verification (10 points - proper use of solver tools), Business communication (10 points - clear presentation with justified recommendations). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in mathematical procedures and demonstrate understanding through verbal explanations during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates with sentence starters ('The vehicle capacity constraint can be written as...') and offer simplified scenarios with only 3 constraints. Check their variable definitions and first constraint before proceeding. For advanced learners: Introduce integer programming constraints (whole number deliveries only), add a third variable (premium deliveries), or explore multi-objective optimization considering both profit and customer satisfaction scores. Encourage investigation of real delivery company logistics strategies.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort) by examining their behavior under varying memory constraints and data distributions. They will decompose algorithm efficiency metrics, compare trade-offs between time and space complexity, and evaluate which algorithm performs optimally under specific system limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between memory allocation patterns and algorithm performance by profiling sorting algorithms with different heap size limitations
Students will compare and contrast the performance trade-offs of three sorting algorithms through systematic benchmarking and statistical analysis of execution metrics
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 min):** Distribute pre-written implementations of QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort in Java. Students work in teams of 2-3. Each team receives datasets: random integers (100K, 500K, 1M), nearly-sorted arrays, and reverse-sorted arrays. **Phase 2 (40 min):** Teams configure JVM with three memory constraints: -Xmx64m, -Xmx128m, -Xmx256m. For each algorithm-dataset-memory combination, students collect: execution time, memory usage peaks, garbage collection frequency, and any OutOfMemoryExceptions. Use JProfiler or VisualVM for memory profiling. Students create a data collection spreadsheet with 27 test scenarios per algorithm (81 total). **Phase 3 (30 min):** Teams analyze collected data by calculating performance ratios, identifying performance degradation patterns, and mapping memory allocation behaviors. Students create comparative charts showing time complexity vs. space complexity trade-offs. **Phase 4 (25 min):** Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation analyzing which algorithm performs best under: (1) severe memory constraints, (2) large dataset processing, (3) nearly-sorted data. Teams must justify recommendations using quantitative evidence and explain the underlying algorithmic reasons for observed performance patterns.
materials_needed: Pre-written Java implementations of QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort
JProfiler or VisualVM memory profiling software
Pre-generated datasets (random, nearly-sorted, reverse-sorted integer arrays)
Computers with Java 11+ and configurable JVM settings
Data collection spreadsheet template with performance metrics columns
assessment_method: Teams submit: (1) Complete performance data spreadsheet with all 81 measurements, (2) Comparative analysis report (2-3 pages) identifying performance patterns and algorithmic explanations, (3) Algorithm recommendation matrix for different constraint scenarios. Rubric: Data accuracy and completeness (30%), depth of comparative analysis (40%), quality of algorithmic reasoning (30%). Presentations evaluated on evidence-based conclusions and technical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided data collection templates with sample calculations and interpretation hints. Offer pre-configured JVM command scripts. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (TimSort, RadixSort) or investigate cache miss rates and CPU profiling metrics. Provide access to larger datasets (10M+ elements) for extended analysis.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments: Exercise 1
description: Students will systematically analyze the performance characteristics of quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort algorithms when operating under varying memory constraints. They will decompose each algorithm's memory usage patterns, examine space-time trade-offs, and evaluate algorithmic efficiency in resource-limited scenarios through empirical testing and theoretical analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the space complexity and memory allocation patterns of three sorting algorithms by implementing and profiling their performance under controlled memory constraints
Students will evaluate algorithmic trade-offs through systematic comparison of execution time, memory consumption, and cache efficiency across different dataset sizes and memory limits
instructions: Begin by providing students with skeleton implementations of quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort in C++ or Java (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, with each team receiving identical hardware specifications and memory profiling tools (Valgrind for Linux or Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools for Windows). Phase 1 (60 minutes): Students complete the algorithm implementations and instrument them with memory tracking code to monitor heap allocation, stack depth, and cache misses. They must test each algorithm with three dataset sizes: 10,000, 100,000, and 1,000,000 integers. Phase 2 (45 minutes): Teams artificially constrain available memory using system limits (ulimit on Unix systems) to simulate embedded environment conditions: 16MB, 8MB, and 4MB memory ceilings. Students record algorithm behavior including execution time, memory peak usage, swap file activity, and failure points. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students analyze collected data to identify patterns in space-time complexity, determine which algorithms degrade gracefully under memory pressure, and examine why certain algorithms fail at specific memory thresholds. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams create comparative visualizations showing performance curves and write technical analysis reports identifying the optimal algorithm choice for different memory-constrained scenarios, supported by empirical evidence and theoretical complexity analysis.
materials_needed: C++ or Java development environment with memory profiling capabilities
Valgrind memory profiler (Linux) or Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools (Windows)
Pre-generated integer datasets of 10K, 100K, and 1M elements
System administration access to set memory limits (ulimit or equivalent)
Graphing software or libraries (matplotlib, Excel, or similar)
Template code with skeleton algorithm implementations
assessment_method: Evaluate technical reports (40%) using rubric covering: algorithm complexity analysis accuracy, empirical data quality and interpretation, identification of memory bottlenecks, and justified algorithm selection recommendations. Assess implementation quality (35%) based on correct instrumentation, proper memory tracking, and handling of memory constraints. Grade data visualizations (25%) for clarity, accuracy, and effectiveness in demonstrating performance relationships. Success criteria: Students must demonstrate understanding of space-time trade-offs, accurately measure and interpret performance metrics, and provide evidence-based recommendations for algorithm selection in constrained environments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed memory tracking code examples and guided worksheets for data interpretation. Offer intermediate checkpoints to verify correct implementation before proceeding to testing phases. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional sorting algorithms (radix sort, counting sort), analyze cache-oblivious algorithms, or extend analysis to parallel sorting implementations. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling peers during implementation phases.
original_title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices: Customer Sales Dashboard Critique
description: Students will critically assess three different dashboard designs for a coffee shop's monthly sales data, evaluating the effectiveness of visualization choices and recommending the most appropriate solution. This activity develops judgment skills in selecting appropriate charts and identifying misleading visual elements.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar charts, pie charts, line graphs) by analyzing how well each represents coffee shop sales data patterns
Students will critique dashboard designs through systematic assessment using data visualization principles and recommend improvements based on audience needs
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and distribute the three pre-prepared dashboard mockups showing the same coffee shop sales data (monthly revenue, product categories, customer demographics) presented differently: Dashboard A uses multiple pie charts, Dashboard B uses bar charts and tables, Dashboard C uses line graphs and heat maps. Provide each group with the evaluation criteria checklist covering clarity, accuracy, appropriateness, and audience suitability. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine each dashboard individually, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses using the criteria checklist. They should identify specific issues like misleading scales, inappropriate chart types, or unclear labeling.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups complete the structured evaluation matrix, rating each dashboard (1-5 scale) on four criteria: data accuracy representation, visual clarity, appropriateness for business audience, and overall effectiveness. They must provide written justification for each rating.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups select the best dashboard and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their choice. They must identify at least two specific improvements for their chosen dashboard and explain why they rejected the other options.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents their evaluation and recommendation. Other groups ask clarifying questions about the reasoning behind ratings and suggestions.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conduct class discussion comparing group choices and reasoning, highlighting common evaluation criteria that emerged across groups.
materials_needed: Three pre-designed dashboard mockups (printed color copies, one set per group)
Coffee shop sales dataset summary (1 page per student)
Evaluation criteria checklist handout
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Completeness of evaluation matrix with justified ratings for all criteria, (2) Quality of written justifications showing understanding of visualization principles, (3) Appropriateness of dashboard selection based on evidence provided, (4) Clarity and persuasiveness of oral presentation defending their choice. Each component worth 25 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing sentence starters for justifications ('This chart is effective because...', 'The main problem with this visualization is...'). For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge to redesign one problematic element from any dashboard and explain their design choices using specific visualization principles. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those who need support during group work.

title: Design Your Own City: A Proportional Scale Mathematics Project
description: Students will create an original city layout using proportional scaling, geometric principles, and area calculations. They will design buildings, roads, and public spaces while applying mathematical concepts to solve real-world urban planning challenges.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a scaled city map by applying proportional reasoning and geometric relationships to create realistic spatial layouts
Students will synthesize area calculations, perimeter measurements, and scale factor concepts through designing functional urban infrastructure
instructions: **Phase 1: Planning (15 minutes)** - Divide students into pairs. Provide each pair with the project packet containing city requirements: minimum 12 buildings, 4 types of roads, 3 public spaces, and 1 water feature. Explain the scale constraint: 1 inch = 50 feet. Students brainstorm their city theme and sketch initial ideas on scratch paper. **Phase 2: Mathematical Foundation (20 minutes)** - Students calculate the actual dimensions their 18x24 inch poster board represents (900x1200 feet). They must determine realistic building sizes by researching actual building dimensions and converting using their scale. Provide building dimension reference sheets. Students create a mathematical planning sheet listing each structure's real-world dimensions and corresponding scaled measurements. **Phase 3: Design Creation (35 minutes)** - Using rulers, protractors, and colored materials, students draw their city to scale on poster board. They must maintain proportional accuracy within 5% tolerance. Students calculate and label the area of each building, total road length, and percentage of land use for different purposes. **Phase 4: Problem Integration (15 minutes)** - Present students with three mathematical challenges: calculate population density if each building houses specific numbers of people, determine total construction costs using provided per-square-foot rates, and optimize traffic flow by calculating shortest routes between key locations. **Phase 5: Presentation (10 minutes)** - Each pair presents their city design, explaining three key mathematical decisions and demonstrating one calculation process to the class.
materials_needed: 18x24 inch poster board (1 per pair)
Rulers, protractors, and measuring tools
Colored pencils, markers, or crayons
Building dimension reference sheets
Mathematical planning worksheets
Calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (calculations within 5% tolerance, correct scale application), Creative Design (original layout, functional city elements), Problem Solving (successful completion of three mathematical challenges), and Communication (clear explanation of mathematical reasoning during presentation). Students must submit their planning worksheet showing all calculations and their final city poster with labeled measurements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated building dimension options and step-by-step scale conversion templates. Pair with stronger math partners and offer measuring guides with common conversions marked. For advanced learners: Add constraints like budget limitations, environmental factors, or geometric requirements (buildings must include specific shapes). Challenge them to incorporate coordinate geometry by creating a grid system for their city addresses.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the precise time complexity classifications of 50 advanced algorithms across multiple domains including graph theory, dynamic programming, and computational geometry. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge for algorithm analysis and selection in complex systems design.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity notation for 50 advanced algorithms by completing timed classification exercises
Students will identify specific algorithm names and their corresponding space complexity through rapid-fire memory retrieval tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared algorithm reference sheets containing 50 algorithms from categories: graph algorithms (Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, Tarjan's SCC), sorting variants (Timsort, Radix sort variants), tree algorithms (Red-Black operations, B-tree operations), string algorithms (KMP, Rabin-Karp, suffix arrays), and computational geometry (convex hull, line intersection). Students have 15 minutes to study the complete list with complexities shown. Remove reference sheets and project algorithm names one at a time using the slideshow template. Students write the time complexity on individual whiteboards, holding up answers simultaneously after each 10-second timer. Record correct/incorrect responses on the tracking sheet. For round two, reverse the process: project time complexities (e.g., O(V²), O(n log n), O(nm)) and students recall 2-3 algorithms matching that complexity. Conduct three complete cycles through all 50 algorithms, tracking improvement. Between rounds, allow 3-minute review periods where students can discuss missed items with partners. Conclude with individual written assessment where students complete the algorithm-complexity matching worksheet without references. Instructor provides immediate feedback by displaying correct answers and explaining any algorithms where class accuracy fell below 70%.
materials_needed: 50-algorithm reference sheet with time/space complexities
Pre-made slideshow with algorithm names and complexity notations
Individual student whiteboards and dry erase markers
Digital timer/stopwatch
Student response tracking sheet
Final assessment matching worksheet (printed copies)
assessment_method: Success measured by final worksheet completion with 80% accuracy (40/50 correct matches). Track individual student progress across three rounds using response sheets. Students must demonstrate recall speed of under 8 seconds per algorithm by round three. Provide numerical scores and identify specific algorithm categories requiring additional memorization work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide algorithm category hints (graph/sorting/string) and allow partnerships during review periods. Create shortened 25-algorithm version focusing on most common algorithms. For advanced learners: include average-case vs worst-case complexity distinctions, add space complexity requirements, or extend to amortized analysis cases for data structures like dynamic arrays.

title: Interpreting Advanced Feature Engineering Transformations in High-Dimensional Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze and interpret complex feature engineering techniques applied to a real-world telecommunications customer churn dataset with 150+ features. They will examine the mathematical rationale and business implications of advanced transformations including target encoding, polynomial interactions, and dimensionality reduction techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical mechanisms behind target encoding, polynomial feature generation, and PCA transformations by analyzing their effects on feature distributions and predictive power

Students will explain the business rationale for specific feature engineering choices through detailed analysis of correlation matrices, variance explained ratios, and domain-specific customer behavior patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing the preprocessed telecommunications churn dataset containing 150 features across 50,000 customers, along with three versions: raw data, engineered features, and PCA-transformed data. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to examine the documentation file explaining each transformation type. Next, each pair receives three Jupyter notebooks with pre-written code showing: (1) target encoding implementation for categorical variables like 'contract_type' and 'payment_method', (2) polynomial interaction features between tenure and monthly_charges, and (3) PCA transformation reducing 150 features to 50 components. For 45 minutes, students execute each notebook section-by-section, documenting in a shared template: the mathematical formula used, the before/after feature distributions (using provided histograms), and the correlation changes with the target variable. Students then spend 25 minutes analyzing the business implications by matching each transformation to specific customer retention strategies. For example, they examine why target encoding 'contract_type' reveals month-to-month customers have 0.73 churn probability versus 0.12 for two-year contracts. Finally, pairs spend 20 minutes comparing model performance metrics (AUC, precision, recall) across the three dataset versions, interpreting why certain transformations improve prediction accuracy. Each pair submits a completed analysis template with mathematical explanations, business interpretations, and performance comparisons.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV, 50,000 rows × 150 features)
Three pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with feature engineering code
Feature transformation documentation file with mathematical formulas
Analysis template spreadsheet with sections for each transformation type
Access to Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib libraries
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis templates using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of transformation explanations (25 points), correct interpretation of distribution changes and correlations (25 points), relevant business justifications linking transformations to customer behavior (25 points), accurate comparison of model performance metrics across dataset versions (25 points). Students must correctly explain at least 3 of 4 transformation types and provide business rationale for 2 techniques to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional visual aids showing step-by-step mathematical calculations and highlight key sections in the code. Offer simplified business scenarios connecting transformations to customer retention strategies. For advanced learners, challenge them to propose additional feature engineering techniques, critique the chosen transformations' limitations, or suggest alternative dimensionality reduction methods like t-SNE or UMAP for comparison.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Expenses
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional young adult using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply their understanding of percentages to make realistic financial decisions and justify their choices using mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by computing exact dollar amounts for each expense category
Students will demonstrate percentage concepts through creating and defending a realistic monthly budget scenario
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario cards and budget worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Present the scenario: 'You are 22 years old, just graduated, and earn $3,200 per month after taxes. You must allocate your income using these guidelines: Housing 25-35%, Food 10-15%, Transportation 10-20%, Savings 10-20%, Entertainment 5-10%, Other expenses 10-15%.' 

Students work individually for 20 minutes to calculate exact dollar amounts for each category using their chosen percentages within the given ranges. They must show all percentage calculations (e.g., if choosing 30% for housing: $3,200 × 0.30 = $960). Ensure percentages total exactly 100%.

Next, students pair up for 10 minutes to compare their budgets and explain their mathematical choices. They should discuss why they selected specific percentages and verify each other's calculations.

For the final 15 minutes, facilitate a whole-class discussion where 4-5 pairs share one interesting difference in their budget allocations. Students must explain their percentage choices and demonstrate their calculations on the board. Conclude by having students reflect on how percentage calculations helped them make informed financial decisions.

Circulate throughout to check calculations, ensure proper percentage conversion (decimal or fraction method), and prompt students to justify their mathematical reasoning. Remind students that their percentages must be realistic and mathematically accurate.
materials_needed: Scenario cards with monthly income ($3,200) and percentage ranges for each category
Budget worksheet template with calculation spaces
Calculators (one per student)
Whiteboard markers for student presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using this rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (40 points) - all percentage calculations correct and total 100%; Application of Constraints (30 points) - percentages fall within given ranges; Problem-solving Process (20 points) - shows clear calculation steps; Justification (10 points) - provides logical reasoning for choices. Students must score 70+ points to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example showing percentage-to-decimal conversion and one sample calculation. Create reference cards with percentage calculation formulas. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including variable expenses, tax considerations, or comparing budgets across different income levels. Challenge them to create visual representations of their budget allocations.

title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Real-World Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve a complex real-world problem, then validate their model using multiple mathematical techniques and present their solution with full mathematical justification. This expert-level activity requires synthesis of calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and mathematical modeling concepts.
estimated_duration: 240 minutes (4 hours) across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original multi-variable optimization model by identifying constraints, defining objective functions, and selecting appropriate mathematical frameworks for a self-chosen real-world scenario
Students will validate their mathematical model through analytical solution methods, computational verification, and sensitivity analysis while documenting all mathematical reasoning
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Problem Identification and Model Design**
Students work individually to select a complex optimization problem from provided categories (supply chain logistics, portfolio optimization, resource allocation, or engineering design). They must define at least 4 decision variables, 6+ constraints, and 1 multi-term objective function. Using provided research databases, students gather real data to parameterize their model. They document their mathematical formulation using LaTeX notation in a shared template, clearly stating assumptions and variable definitions.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Model Implementation and Solution**
Students implement their model using both analytical methods (Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions, or simplex method) and computational tools (MATLAB Optimization Toolbox or Python scipy.optimize). They must solve their model using at least two different approaches and compare results. Students create visualization plots showing feasible regions, objective function contours, and optimal solutions. All code and mathematical derivations are documented in a structured notebook format.

**Phase 3 (60 minutes): Validation and Sensitivity Analysis**
Students perform comprehensive model validation by conducting sensitivity analysis on key parameters, testing boundary conditions, and comparing their solution to published benchmarks or industry standards. They must identify model limitations, assess robustness of their solution, and propose model improvements. Students prepare a technical presentation including problem motivation, mathematical formulation, solution methodology, results interpretation, and model validation findings.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Peer Review and Presentation**
