Students present their complete mathematical model in 8-minute technical presentations, followed by 4-minute peer questioning sessions. Audience members complete structured peer evaluation forms assessing mathematical rigor, model creativity, and solution validity.
materials_needed: MATLAB with Optimization Toolbox or Python with scipy/numpy libraries
LaTeX editor (Overleaf accounts or local installation)
Access to real-world datasets (provided economic, engineering, or scientific databases)
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint/Beamer)
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across 5 dimensions: (1) Mathematical Formulation Quality (correct variable definition, appropriate constraints, realistic objective function), (2) Solution Methodology Rigor (correct analytical techniques, proper computational implementation, solution verification), (3) Model Validation Completeness (sensitivity analysis depth, limitation identification, benchmark comparison), (4) Mathematical Communication (clear notation, logical presentation, accurate interpretation), (5) Innovation and Complexity (problem originality, model sophistication, creative solution approaches). Final deliverable includes technical report (60% weight) and presentation performance (40% weight). Minimum passing requires 3/4 points in mathematical formulation and solution methodology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected problem templates with partially completed formulations, offer guided worksheets for constraint identification, schedule individual consultations for analytical solution methods, and allow pair programming for computational implementation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, develop multi-objective optimization models, implement custom algorithms, or extend their model to dynamic/time-dependent scenarios. Provide access to graduate-level optimization textbooks and research papers for additional theoretical depth.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Visual Recognition
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and visual pattern recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary number patterns through visual recognition drills using pre-made binary number cards
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary-decimal conversion chart to each student and allow 5 minutes for silent study. Students should examine the patterns in the 4-bit binary representations (0000 through 1111). Next, organize students into pairs and provide each pair with a set of 32 flashcards (16 showing decimal numbers, 16 showing corresponding binary numbers). Partner A holds decimal cards while Partner B holds binary cards. For the first 10-minute round, Partner A shows a decimal number card, and Partner B must quickly locate and show the matching binary card. Switch roles for the second 10-minute round. After partner practice, conduct individual assessment rounds. Each student receives a shuffled deck of decimal number cards (0-15) and must write the corresponding binary representation on their answer sheet within 3 minutes. Provide immediate feedback by displaying the conversion chart on the board. For visual pattern recognition, show binary number cards in sequence (0000, 0001, 0010, 0011...) and have students chant the decimal equivalents aloud. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal quiz where you call out decimal numbers and students respond with binary representations in unison, then individually spot-check 5 random students with 3 conversions each.
materials_needed: Binary-decimal conversion chart (0-15) printed for each student
32 flashcards per pair: 16 decimal number cards (0-15), 16 binary number cards (0000-1111)
Answer sheets with numbered lines 1-16
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projector for displaying answer key
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) on the 3-minute written conversion test and respond correctly to 2/3 verbal spot-check questions. Record individual scores on a checklist and note students who need additional practice. Success criteria: correct 4-bit binary format, no leading digit errors, and completion within time limits.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1) and allow them to work through the place value method initially. Create a smaller subset focusing on numbers 0-7 first. For advanced learners: extend to 16-31 (5-bit numbers) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider adding reverse conversion (binary to decimal) or simple binary arithmetic problems.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Data Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three authentic datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation, explaining why certain relationships exist and identifying potential confounding variables. They will create visual interpretations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of when correlation implies causation versus when it indicates spurious relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from real datasets
Students will explain the presence of confounding variables through guided examination of multivariate relationships in authentic data scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing three pre-prepared datasets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents by month, (2) Education level vs. income across demographics, and (3) Social media usage vs. depression scores with age groups. Form groups of 3-4 students and assign each group one primary dataset plus access to all three for comparison.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students load their assigned dataset into provided spreadsheet software and create a scatter plot. They calculate the correlation coefficient using built-in functions and record the numerical value.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups examine their correlation coefficient and discuss: 'What does this number tell us about the relationship?' They must write one paragraph explaining the strength and direction of correlation without making causal claims.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Introduce the key question: 'Does this correlation indicate that Variable A causes Variable B?' Groups brainstorm alternative explanations using the provided 'Third Variable Checklist' worksheet. They identify at least two potential confounding variables and explain how each might influence both original variables.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents their dataset's correlation coefficient, describes the relationship strength, and explains why correlation does/doesn't equal causation in their specific case. Other groups ask clarifying questions.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Facilitate whole-class discussion comparing all three scenarios, highlighting how context determines whether correlation suggests causation (education-income) versus spurious relationships (ice cream-drowning).
materials_needed: Three pre-cleaned CSV datasets with 50-100 data points each
Spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets, or similar) with chart functions
Third Variable Checklist worksheet template
Correlation coefficient calculation guide handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate correlation coefficient calculation and interpretation, (2) Clear distinction between correlation and causation with specific examples, (3) Identification of at least two plausible confounding variables with logical explanations, (4) Quality of group presentation demonstrating understanding through peer questions answered correctly.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'The correlation coefficient shows...' and 'This relationship might exist because...' Advanced learners can explore partial correlation analysis by controlling for one confounding variable using additional spreadsheet functions, or research the Bradford Hill criteria for establishing causation in their chosen scenario.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Data Scenarios: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze three real-world datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation patterns. They will identify confounding variables and explain why correlation does not imply causation using specific data examples and statistical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from three different real-world datasets
Students will identify potential confounding variables through guided examination of dataset contexts and statistical relationships
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with printed handouts containing three datasets: ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths (monthly data), education level vs. income (survey data), and hours of TV watching vs. obesity rates (demographic data). Each dataset includes scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and contextual information.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine Dataset A (ice cream/drowning) and calculate the correlation coefficient using the provided formula sheet. Students record their findings on the analysis worksheet, noting the strength and direction of correlation.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups brainstorm and list at least three possible explanations for the correlation they observed. Facilitate discussion by asking: 'What other factors might influence both variables?' Groups should identify temperature/season as a confounding variable.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Repeat the process with Datasets B and C. For education/income, students should consider family background, geographic location, and economic opportunities as confounding variables. For TV/obesity, they should identify lifestyle factors, socioeconomic status, and activity levels.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group creates a visual diagram showing the relationship between their assigned dataset's variables, including the confounding variable they identified as most significant.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Groups present their findings to the class, explaining why their correlation does not prove causation. Other groups ask clarifying questions and suggest additional confounding variables.

Conclude with a class discussion summarizing the key principles: correlation measures association strength, causation requires experimental evidence or longitudinal studies, and confounding variables often explain spurious correlations.
materials_needed: Three printed dataset handouts with scatter plots and raw data (one per group)
Correlation coefficient calculation formula sheets
Analysis worksheets with guided questions
Chart paper and markers for visual diagrams
Calculators or laptops with Excel/Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Evaluate groups using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients, (2) Identification of at least two relevant confounding variables per dataset, (3) Clear explanation of why correlation doesn't prove causation with specific examples, (4) Quality of visual diagram showing variable relationships. Students must score 3/4 on each criterion to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide correlation coefficient ranges (0.7+ strong, 0.3-0.7 moderate, <0.3 weak) and sentence starters like 'This correlation might exist because...' For advanced learners, introduce concepts of spurious correlation and challenge them to research additional real-world examples or design experiments that could test causation.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Data Scenarios

title: Optimizing Hospital Emergency Department Staffing Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real-world hospital staffing optimization problem. They will formulate constraint equations, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal staffing levels to minimize costs while meeting patient care requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate a multi-variable optimization problem by translating real-world constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal solutions through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the hospital scenario handout detailing Springfield General Hospital's emergency department staffing needs (15 minutes). Students work in pairs to analyze the problem: minimum 8 nurses needed during day shifts, 5 during night shifts; at least 12 doctors required during peak hours (8am-8pm), 6 during off-peak; union contract requires minimum 40% of staff be full-time; budget constraint of $180,000 monthly for staffing. Have students identify decision variables: x₁ = full-time nurses, x₂ = part-time nurses, x₃ = full-time doctors, x₄ = part-time doctors (20 minutes). Next, students formulate the objective function to minimize total cost: Z = 6500x₁ + 3200x₂ + 12000x₃ + 7500x₄, and write constraint inequalities including staffing minimums, budget limits, and contract requirements (25 minutes). Using graphing software or grid paper, students plot the feasible region for a simplified 2-variable version focusing on nurse staffing optimization (30 minutes). Students then apply the corner point method to test vertices of the feasible region, calculating objective function values at each point (20 minutes). For the complete 4-variable problem, students use provided simplex tableau templates to implement the simplex algorithm, performing pivot operations to reach optimal solution (40 minutes). Finally, students interpret their mathematical solution in the hospital context, writing a 2-paragraph recommendation memo explaining optimal staffing levels and projected monthly costs (15 minutes). Conclude with pairs presenting their solutions and justifications to the class (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Hospital staffing scenario handouts with detailed constraints and cost data
Graphing paper or digital graphing software (Desmos, GeoGebra)
Scientific calculators
Pre-formatted simplex tableau worksheets
Computers with spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate application of graphical method and simplex algorithm with shown work (35 points), (3) Correct identification and verification of optimal solution (25 points), (4) Quality of business interpretation and recommendation memo (15 points). Students must achieve minimum 70% for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates and guided practice with simpler 2-variable problems first. Offer step-by-step simplex algorithm reference cards. For advanced learners: Include sensitivity analysis requirements, asking students to determine how solution changes if budget increases by 10% or if minimum staffing requirements change. Challenge them to model additional constraints like staff scheduling preferences or overtime costs.

title: Analyzing Security Vulnerabilities in Authentication System Architecture
description: Students will dissect a multi-tier web application's authentication system to identify potential security vulnerabilities and attack vectors. They will examine code snippets, database schemas, and network communication patterns to categorize threats and evaluate the effectiveness of existing security measures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze authentication system components by examining source code, database design, and API endpoints to identify specific security vulnerabilities
Students will evaluate the relationship between different security measures through systematic threat modeling and risk assessment techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided case study materials: a simulated e-commerce application with login system code (PHP/MySQL), API documentation, and network traffic logs (45 minutes total setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to systematically analyze the system. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams examine the login.php file, user database schema, and session management code to map the authentication flow and identify components. Step 2 (30 minutes): Using the OWASP Top 10 as a framework, teams analyze each component for vulnerabilities - specifically checking for SQL injection points, password storage methods, session hijacking possibilities, and input validation gaps. Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams review the provided network packet captures using Wireshark to analyze data transmission security, looking for unencrypted credentials, session tokens in URLs, or insecure cookie configurations. Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams create a vulnerability matrix categorizing found issues by severity (Critical/High/Medium/Low) and exploitability, then propose specific countermeasures for each identified vulnerability. Step 5 (20 minutes): Each team presents their top 3 critical findings to the class, explaining the attack vector, potential impact, and recommended remediation. Instructor facilitates discussion comparing different teams' analyses and highlighting missed vulnerabilities.
materials_needed: Pre-built vulnerable web application code package (PHP, HTML, SQL files)
Sample database with user records and schema documentation
Wireshark network capture files (.pcap format)
OWASP Top 10 reference sheets
Vulnerability assessment template spreadsheet
Laptops with text editors and Wireshark installed
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric across: 1) Completeness of vulnerability identification (25 points - must find at least 6 of 8 planted vulnerabilities), 2) Accuracy of threat categorization and risk assessment (25 points), 3) Quality of countermeasure recommendations with technical specificity (25 points), 4) Demonstration of systematic analysis methodology (25 points). Teams submit vulnerability matrix and present findings for combined assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with specific line numbers to examine in code files and pre-highlighted sections in packet captures. Offer vulnerability checklists for each OWASP category. For advanced learners: Include additional challenges like analyzing encrypted traffic, examining client-side JavaScript for vulnerabilities, or researching zero-day exploits relevant to the technology stack. Provide access to additional penetration testing tools like Burp Suite.

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Purchase Dataset
description: Students will critically assess two different data cleaning strategies applied to a messy customer purchase dataset containing missing values, duplicates, and outliers. They will judge the effectiveness of each approach and recommend the superior method based on specific evaluation criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of two data cleaning approaches by comparing their impact on data quality metrics and analytical outcomes
Students will critique data preprocessing decisions through systematic analysis of missing data handling, outlier treatment, and duplicate removal strategies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and providing each pair with the same raw customer purchase dataset (500 rows, 8 columns) containing 15% missing values, 8% duplicates, and obvious outliers. Give each pair two pre-processed versions of this dataset: Version A uses median imputation for missing values, removes all outliers beyond 2 standard deviations, and drops exact duplicates; Version B uses forward-fill imputation, caps outliers at 95th/5th percentiles, and removes duplicates based on customer ID only. Students spend 15 minutes exploring both cleaned datasets using provided Python code snippets to generate summary statistics, visualizations, and data quality reports. Next, students complete a structured evaluation worksheet comparing the two approaches across four criteria: data retention rate, distribution preservation, business logic alignment, and impact on correlation patterns. They must calculate specific metrics (percentage of data retained, skewness before/after, correlation coefficient changes) and provide written justifications. Students then spend 20 minutes creating a recommendation report stating which cleaning approach they would choose and why, including at least three specific pieces of evidence from their analysis. Finally, pairs present their 2-minute recommendations to another pair, defending their choice when challenged. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share their decisions and reasoning, allowing instructor to highlight key evaluation principles.
materials_needed: Customer purchase dataset CSV file (raw version)
Two pre-cleaned versions of the dataset (Version A and Version B)
Evaluation worksheet template with comparison criteria
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries
Data quality analysis code snippets document
assessment_method: Grade students using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of calculated metrics and data quality measures (25%), (2) Quality of evidence-based reasoning in written justifications (35%), (3) Appropriateness of final recommendation considering business context (25%), (4) Effectiveness of verbal defense during peer presentations (15%). Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas to demonstrate evaluation-level thinking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional guided questions on the evaluation worksheet and offer one-on-one support during metric calculations. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners, challenge them to propose a third cleaning approach that addresses weaknesses they identified in both provided versions, or ask them to consider how their evaluation might change for different types of analyses (regression vs. classification).

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Purchase Dataset: Business Application
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different data cleaning strategies applied to a messy customer purchase dataset. They will judge the effectiveness of each approach based on data quality metrics and business impact, then defend their choice of the best method.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three data cleaning approaches by analyzing completeness, accuracy, and consistency metrics for each method
Students will critique the business impact of different data cleaning decisions through cost-benefit analysis and recommendation justification
instructions: Begin by providing each student with three pre-processed versions of the same raw customer purchase dataset (500 rows, 8 columns including customer_id, purchase_date, product_name, price, quantity, customer_email, phone_number, address). Each version represents a different cleaning approach: Method A (removes all incomplete records), Method B (fills missing values with averages/modes), and Method C (uses sophisticated imputation techniques). Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to examine each dataset using provided Python scripts that calculate data quality metrics (completeness percentage, duplicate count, outlier detection). Next, students spend 15 minutes researching the business context using a provided scenario: an e-commerce company needs clean data for customer segmentation and sales forecasting. In pairs (10 minutes), students discuss their initial findings and concerns about each method. Students then work individually for 25 minutes to complete an evaluation matrix comparing all three methods across five criteria: data completeness (%), processing time, information preservation, accuracy for business use, and implementation cost. Finally, students spend 15 minutes writing a one-page recommendation memo to a fictional data science manager, stating which cleaning method they would choose and providing three evidence-based justifications. The memo must include specific metrics from their analysis and address potential counterarguments. Conclude with 10 minutes of peer review where students exchange memos and provide feedback using a provided checklist.
materials_needed: Three versions of customer purchase dataset (CSV files)
Python environment with pandas and numpy libraries
Data quality analysis scripts (pre-written Python code)
Business scenario handout
Evaluation matrix template (Excel or Google Sheets)
Memo template with required sections
Peer review checklist
assessment_method: Grade the recommendation memo using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accurate use of data quality metrics with specific numbers, (2) Clear justification linking cleaning method to business needs, (3) Acknowledgment and addressing of method limitations, (4) Professional communication and logical argument structure. Additionally, assess the completed evaluation matrix for thoroughness and accuracy of comparisons.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed evaluation matrix with sample entries and highlight key metrics to focus on. Offer sentence starters for the recommendation memo. For advanced learners, challenge them to propose a hybrid cleaning approach or consider additional factors like data governance compliance. Provide extra datasets with different data quality issues for extended practice.
original_title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Purchase Dataset

title: Design Your Own Board Game Using Probability and Statistics
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates specific probability concepts and statistical elements. They will design game mechanics, calculate probabilities for different outcomes, and create visual representations of their statistical analysis to demonstrate how mathematics makes games engaging and fair.
estimated_duration: 150 minutes (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will design an original game system by integrating probability calculations, expected value computations, and statistical analysis of player outcomes
Students will construct mathematical models through game mechanics that demonstrate understanding of independent events, conditional probability, and data visualization
instructions: **Phase 1: Planning (20 minutes)** - Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives the game design template and probability reference sheet. Teams brainstorm their game theme and core mechanic (racing, collection, strategy, etc.). They must identify at least 3 probability elements their game will include from the provided list: dice rolls, card draws, spinner outcomes, or random events. **Phase 2: Mathematical Design (40 minutes)** - Teams calculate the theoretical probabilities for their chosen game elements. For example, if using two dice, they create a probability distribution table showing all possible sums and their likelihoods. They determine expected values for point scoring systems and design balanced risk-reward scenarios. Students must create at least one visual representation (tree diagram, histogram, or probability table) showing their calculations. **Phase 3: Game Creation (60 minutes)** - Using poster board and art supplies, teams construct their physical game board, pieces, and cards. They write detailed rules that explicitly reference their probability calculations (e.g., 'Players have a 16.7% chance of landing on bonus spaces'). Teams create a 'Designer's Mathematical Analysis' document explaining how probability affects game balance and player experience. **Phase 4: Testing and Revision (30 minutes)** - Teams play-test another team's game for 15 minutes, collecting actual outcome data. They compare observed results to theoretical probabilities and suggest mathematical improvements. Original designers use feedback to make final adjustments to their game mechanics or probability calculations.
materials_needed: 11x17 poster board (1 per team)
Colored markers, pencils, and rulers
Standard six-sided dice (6 per team)
Blank playing cards (20 per team)
Game design template worksheet
Probability reference sheet with formulas
Calculators
Small game pieces (buttons, coins, or tokens)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct probability calculations and expected value computations (25%), (2) Creative Integration - innovative use of mathematical concepts within game mechanics (25%), (3) Visual Communication - clear, accurate graphs, tables, or diagrams explaining probability elements (25%), (4) Game Functionality - playable game with balanced mechanics that demonstrate mathematical principles (25%). Students submit their physical game, mathematical analysis document, and reflection on how testing data compared to theoretical predictions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated probability tables for common dice combinations and offer simplified game templates focusing on single probability concepts. Pair struggling students with mathematically stronger teammates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate compound probability scenarios, create games with conditional probability elements, or design statistical tracking systems that analyze player performance over multiple games. Encourage use of technology tools for complex calculations.

title: Design Your Own Board Game Using Probability and Statistics: Exercise 1
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates specific probability concepts and statistical analysis. They will develop game mechanics, calculate theoretical probabilities, and test their game to collect and analyze empirical data.
estimated_duration: 180 minutes (4 class periods of 45 minutes each)
learning_objectives: Students will design an original board game by integrating probability concepts such as expected value, compound events, and conditional probability into game mechanics
Students will construct statistical analyses through collecting empirical data from game testing and comparing it to theoretical predictions
instructions:
**Day 1 (45 minutes): Game Design Phase**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a design template and must create a board game incorporating at least three probability concepts: simple probability, compound events, and expected value. Students sketch their game board, write rules, and identify all probability elements. They must calculate theoretical probabilities for key game events (dice rolls, card draws, spinner outcomes). Require teams to include at least one decision point where players must choose between options with different expected values.

**Day 2 (45 minutes): Prototype Creation**
Teams build physical prototypes using provided materials. They create game boards on poster paper, design cards or tokens, and prepare data collection sheets for testing. Teams must finalize their probability calculations and create a 'designer's guide' explaining the mathematical concepts embedded in their game.

**Day 3 (45 minutes): Testing and Data Collection**
Teams rotate between stations, spending 10 minutes playing each other's games while recording data on outcomes. They track frequency of events, player choices, and game results. Each game must be played at least 20 times across all rotations to generate sufficient data.

**Day 4 (45 minutes): Analysis and Presentation**
Teams analyze their collected data using provided statistical tools (calculators or spreadsheet software). They calculate experimental probabilities, compare to theoretical values, and identify patterns. Teams create a final presentation including game overview, mathematical concepts used, data analysis, and reflection on how experimental results compared to predictions.
materials_needed: Poster paper (11x17 inches minimum)
Colored markers and pencils
Standard dice (6-sided and 10-sided)
Index cards for game pieces/cards
Rulers and protractors
Calculators or access to spreadsheet software (Excel/Google Sheets)
Game design template worksheet
Data collection sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy of probability calculations (25 points), (2) Creative integration of probability concepts into game mechanics (25 points), (3) Quality of data collection and statistical analysis (25 points), (4) Clarity of presentation and reflection on theoretical vs. experimental results (25 points). Students must submit their game prototype, designer's guide with calculations, completed data analysis, and deliver a 5-minute team presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide probability calculation templates, offer pre-made spinner templates with marked sections, and allow use of simple dice-based mechanics. Create partnerships with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate normal distributions, regression analysis, or game theory concepts like Nash equilibrium. Encourage use of technology for Monte Carlo simulations to test theoretical predictions.
original_title: Design Your Own Board Game Using Probability and Statistics

title: Advanced Data Structure Memory Palace: Recall Complex Implementation Details
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall specific implementation details, time complexities, and property definitions for 12 advanced data structures including B-trees, skip lists, and Fibonacci heaps. This intensive recall activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and timed recitation to build foundational knowledge for advanced algorithms courses.
learning_objectives: Students will recall exact time complexities (average and worst-case) for all operations on 12 advanced data structures by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will recite precise definitions and key properties of complex data structures through structured verbal presentations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared flashcard deck containing 144 cards (12 cards per data structure) covering B-trees, B+ trees, Red-Black trees, AVL trees, Skip lists, Fibonacci heaps, Binomial heaps, Treaps, Splay trees, Segment trees, Fenwick trees, and Disjoint Set Union structures. Each set includes cards for: insertion/deletion/search time complexities, space complexity, key structural properties, balancing mechanisms, and use cases.

Phase 1 (20 minutes): Students work individually through the entire deck using the Leitner spaced repetition method. Cards answered correctly move to the next box, incorrect cards return to box 1. Students must achieve 90% accuracy on initial pass.

Phase 2 (15 minutes): Pair students for rapid-fire recall sessions. Partner A draws random cards and times Partner B's responses (maximum 10 seconds per card). Partners alternate every 3 minutes. Record accuracy scores on provided tracking sheets.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Conduct structured group recitation. Divide class into 4 groups, assign 3 data structures per group. Each student must verbally present one complete data structure profile (all 12 elements) to their group within 2 minutes. Group members verify accuracy using answer keys and provide immediate corrections.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual written assessment. Students complete a 24-question rapid-recall quiz covering randomized questions from all data structures. No reference materials permitted. Questions include fill-in-the-blank time complexities, true/false property statements, and short identification prompts.
materials_needed: 144 pre-prepared flashcards with advanced data structure details and answer keys
Leitner box organizers (4-compartment boxes, one per student)
Digital timers or stopwatch apps
Accuracy tracking sheets with partner recording grids
24-question written assessment with answer key
Printed reference sheets for group verification
assessment_method: Success measured through three criteria: (1) 90% accuracy on individual flashcard pass in Phase 1, (2) Average response time under 8 seconds with 85% accuracy in paired recall sessions, and (3) Score of 20/24 (83%) on final written assessment. Track progress using provided scoring rubric with specific point allocations: flashcard mastery (40 points), partner session performance (30 points), group recitation completeness (20 points), written assessment (10 points). Students achieving 85+ total points demonstrate mastery-level recall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide abbreviated starter cards focusing on 6 core data structures initially, allow 15 seconds per response instead of 10, and offer pneumonic device reference sheet. Create study buddy partnerships pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Add supplementary cards with implementation code snippets, variant analysis questions, and comparative trade-off scenarios. Challenge them to create original mnemonics for complex properties and teach mini-lessons to struggling peers.

title: Family Budget Planning: Applying Percentages to Real-World Expenses
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional family using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage formulas to determine exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and savings while staying within the family's total monthly income.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate specific dollar amounts by applying percentage formulas to a given monthly income total
Students will demonstrate percentage application skills through creating a balanced family budget that totals 100% of available income
instructions: Begin by distributing the Family Profile Cards, each describing a different family situation with monthly income ranging from $3,000-$6,000 (10 minutes). Post the Budget Category Guidelines on the board: Housing 25-35%, Food 10-15%, Transportation 10-20%, Utilities 5-10%, Savings 10-20%, Entertainment 5-10%, Miscellaneous 5-15%. Students work individually to select one family profile and create a budget using these percentage ranges (15 minutes). They must first decide on a specific percentage for each category within the given ranges, ensuring all percentages total exactly 100%. Next, students apply percentage calculations (Income × Percentage ÷ 100 = Category Amount) to determine dollar amounts for each budget category (10 minutes). Provide calculation worksheets with the formula clearly displayed and space for showing work. Students then complete their budget by filling in a provided budget template showing both percentages and dollar amounts (5 minutes). Finally, students pair up to check each other's calculations and verify that their partner's percentages total 100% and dollar amounts are mathematically correct (5 minutes). Conclude with students presenting one interesting budget decision to the class, explaining their percentage choice and calculated amount (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Family Profile Cards (8-10 different family scenarios with varying incomes)
Budget Category Guidelines handout
Percentage calculation worksheets with formula reference
Budget template worksheets
Calculators (one per student)
Whiteboard markers and poster paper for guidelines
assessment_method: Grade completed budgets using a 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (percentages total 100%, calculations correct), Application of Formulas (proper use of percentage formula with work shown), Realistic Choices (percentages fall within provided ranges), and Presentation Quality (clear organization and explanation of one budget decision). Students must achieve 3/4 points in Mathematical Accuracy to demonstrate successful percentage application.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a completed example budget and highlighting the percentage formula on individual reference cards. Pair them with mathematically stronger partners during the checking phase. For advanced learners, add complexity by including irregular income scenarios, requiring them to calculate annual budgets, or having them create emergency fund calculations using compound percentage applications.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Performance Through Big O Evaluation
description: Students analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code implementations, predicting theoretical time complexity, and comparing actual runtime performance data. They will identify the relationship between theoretical Big O notation and real-world performance characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithm complexity by examining code structure and identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and data access patterns to determine Big O notation
Students will compare sorting algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of runtime data across different input sizes and data arrangements
instructions: Begin by distributing code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort to student pairs (15 minutes setup). Students first examine each algorithm's structure independently, counting nested loops, identifying recursive patterns, and documenting their observations on the analysis worksheet. Next, have students predict the Big O time complexity for each algorithm's best, average, and worst cases, justifying their predictions with specific code references (20 minutes). Provide students with performance data tables showing actual runtimes for each algorithm across input sizes of 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements, tested on random, sorted, and reverse-sorted arrays. Students plot this data on provided logarithmic graph paper, creating separate curves for each algorithm-input combination (15 minutes). In pairs, students analyze discrepancies between their theoretical predictions and actual performance data, identifying factors like implementation details, system overhead, and input characteristics that explain variations (20 minutes). Students then complete a comparative analysis matrix, ranking algorithms by efficiency for different scenarios and explaining when each algorithm would be most appropriate. Conclude with pair presentations where each team explains one significant finding about algorithm performance that surprised them, supported by specific data evidence (15 minutes presentations, 5 minutes feedback).
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (3 pages per student pair)
Algorithm analysis worksheet with observation tables and prediction sections
Performance data tables showing runtime results across different input sizes and arrangements
Logarithmic graph paper (2 sheets per student)
Comparative analysis matrix template
Calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O predictions with proper justification (25%), (2) Correct interpretation of performance data and graph construction (25%), (3) Quality of analysis identifying factors affecting real-world performance vs theoretical predictions (30%), (4) Effectiveness of algorithm comparison and scenario-based recommendations (20%). Students submit completed worksheets, graphs, and analysis matrices. Presentations assessed on clarity of explanation and use of data evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a Big O reference sheet with common patterns and examples, offer guided questions for code analysis (e.g., 'How many times does this inner loop execute?'), and pair them with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort, ask them to research and explain cache performance impacts, or have them modify one algorithm and predict how changes affect complexity. Consider providing actual code profiling tools for hands-on runtime measurement.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Selection for Real-World Business Impact: A Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis
description: Students critically evaluate competing machine learning models by analyzing their performance metrics, business constraints, and ethical implications to make justified recommendations for deployment. They will assess trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, computational cost, and fairness across different stakeholder perspectives.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative merit of three different machine learning approaches by systematically analyzing performance metrics, business constraints, and ethical considerations within a realistic deployment scenario
Students will critique model selection decisions through structured peer review and defend their recommendations using evidence-based arguments that balance technical and business requirements
instructions:
**Phase 1: Case Study Setup (20 minutes)**
Provide students with a loan approval dataset and business scenario from a mid-sized bank. Present three pre-trained models: Random Forest (highest accuracy), Logistic Regression (most interpretable), and Gradient Boosting (best precision). Each student receives identical performance metrics, confusion matrices, feature importance plots, and business constraints document outlining regulatory requirements, computational limitations ($500/month cloud budget), and fairness requirements.

**Phase 2: Individual Model Evaluation (45 minutes)**
Students complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing all three models across seven criteria: accuracy, precision, recall, interpretability, computational cost, training time, and bias metrics across protected classes. They must calculate business impact metrics (revenue loss from false positives/negatives at $50K average loan) and assign weighted importance scores to each criterion based on stakeholder priorities. Students document their analysis in a decision matrix with quantitative scores and qualitative justifications.

**Phase 3: Recommendation Development (25 minutes)**
Using their evaluation matrix, students write a 300-word executive recommendation memo selecting one model for deployment. The memo must address three stakeholder perspectives (technical team, business executives, compliance officers), acknowledge trade-offs, and provide specific implementation recommendations including monitoring strategies and performance thresholds for model retraining.

**Phase 4: Peer Review and Defense (30 minutes)**
Students exchange memos with partners and conduct structured peer evaluations using provided rubric. They identify strengths, weaknesses, and gaps in reasoning. Original authors then defend their recommendations in 5-minute presentations, responding to peer challenges and explaining how they weighted competing priorities.
materials_needed: Pre-processed loan approval dataset with 10,000 records
Three trained model outputs with performance metrics and predictions
Business constraints document with regulatory and budget requirements
Model evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Peer review rubric with evaluation criteria
Sample confusion matrices and bias fairness reports for each model
assessment_method: Students assessed on: (1) Evaluation matrix completeness and accuracy of calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of reasoning in balancing trade-offs between technical and business requirements (30 points), (3) Executive memo clarity and stakeholder consideration (25 points), (4) Peer review quality and presentation defense (20 points). Success requires scoring 75+ points with demonstrated ability to justify model selection using quantitative evidence while acknowledging limitations and ethical considerations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example row in evaluation matrix, offer template phrases for memo writing, and allow use of calculators for business impact computations. For advanced learners: Add ensemble method consideration, require cost-benefit analysis with ROI calculations, or include A/B testing design for model comparison. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger peers during review phase.

title: Design and Implement a Novel Cryptographic Algorithm for Secure Digital Communication
description: Students will synthesize concepts from number theory, modular arithmetic, and computational complexity to create an original encryption algorithm. They will construct mathematical proofs of their algorithm's security properties and develop a working implementation with efficiency analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original cryptographic algorithm by integrating prime factorization, modular exponentiation, and discrete logarithm principles
Students will synthesize mathematical proofs through formal verification of algorithm security properties including computational hardness and resistance to known attacks
instructions: Begin with 30 minutes of individual research where students review RSA, Elliptic Curve, and Diffie-Hellman algorithms to identify mathematical foundations. Students then spend 45 minutes designing their algorithm architecture, choosing a mathematical hard problem (e.g., integer factorization variant, discrete logarithm in custom groups, or lattice-based problem). Next, allocate 60 minutes for students to formally define their key generation, encryption, and decryption processes using precise mathematical notation. Students must specify: domain and codomain of each function, exact algorithmic steps with complexity analysis, and parameter constraints. Following this, students spend 45 minutes constructing formal proofs addressing: correctness (decryption recovers original plaintext), security reduction to their chosen hard problem, and resistance to at least two specific attack methods. Students then implement their algorithm in Python or MATLAB during a 90-minute coding session, including functions for key generation, encryption/decryption, and performance testing with various input sizes. Finally, students conduct 30 minutes of empirical analysis measuring encryption speed, key generation time, and memory usage, comparing results against theoretical complexity predictions. Each student presents their algorithm in a 10-minute technical presentation demonstrating encryption of a sample message, explaining security proofs, and discussing computational efficiency trade-offs.
materials_needed: Access to Python 3.8+ or MATLAB R2020a+ with symbolic math toolbox
Number theory reference materials (Rosen's Elementary Number Theory or equivalent)
Digital presentation software with LaTeX support for mathematical notation
Computational devices capable of handling large integer arithmetic
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Algorithm originality and mathematical rigor (25 points), correctness and completeness of security proofs (25 points), implementation functionality and code quality (25 points), empirical analysis accuracy and theoretical comparison (15 points), presentation clarity and technical communication (10 points). Students must demonstrate successful encryption/decryption of a 256-character message and provide formal proof documents.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing algorithm design templates focusing on variations of existing methods rather than entirely novel approaches. Offer pre-written code frameworks for implementation structure. For advanced learners, challenge them to address additional security properties like forward secrecy or resistance to quantum attacks, or to optimize their algorithm for specific hardware constraints like embedded systems.

title: Python Data Type Memory Challenge: Flash Card Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list) and their characteristics through structured flash card practice. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary knowledge needed for Python programming.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the names of Python's five basic data types (int, float, str, bool, list) with 100% accuracy within 30 seconds
Students will identify the correct data type for given Python values through visual recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash cards to each student (5 minutes). Each set contains 20 cards: 5 cards showing data type names (int, float, str, bool, list), 5 cards with definitions, and 10 cards with example values. Demonstrate the activity by showing the 'int' card and explaining it stores whole numbers like 42 or -7. Have students arrange their cards in five groups, matching each data type name with its definition and two example cards (10 minutes). Walk around to verify correct groupings before proceeding. Next, collect definition and example cards, leaving only the five data type name cards. Call out definitions randomly ('stores decimal numbers') and have students hold up the correct card ('float'). Repeat 15 times, tracking correct responses (10 minutes). For the final challenge, display Python values on the board one at a time (examples: 'Hello', 3.14, True, [1,2,3], 42) and have students write the corresponding data type on their whiteboards. Show each value for 10 seconds, then have students reveal answers simultaneously. Complete 15 examples, ensuring each data type appears at least twice (15 minutes). Conclude by having students recite all five data types from memory in alphabetical order three times as a class.
materials_needed: Pre-made flash card sets (20 cards per student: 5 type names, 5 definitions, 10 examples)
Individual whiteboards and dry erase markers
Timer or stopwatch
Projector or whiteboard for displaying Python values
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on the visual identification exercise (12/15 correct responses) and successfully recite all five data types in order without prompting. Use a checklist to track individual student performance during the flash card holding activity and whiteboard responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with data type names and allow them to use it during the first half of activities. Pair them with stronger students during card sorting. For advanced learners, add complexity by including data type methods (e.g., .append() for lists) or introduce additional types like tuple and dict as bonus challenges.

title: Interpreting Statistical Bias in Real-World Healthcare Datasets
description: Students will analyze pre-processed healthcare datasets to identify and explain different types of statistical bias. instructions: Begin by organizing students into pairs and distributing the three prepared datasets: Hospital A (urban, high-income area), Hospital B (rural, mixed-income), and Hospital C (emergency-only admissions). Each pair receives one primary dataset and access to the other two for comparison. In the first 15 minutes, students examine their assigned dataset using the provided data profiling checklist, noting demographic distributions, missing value patterns, and outcome variables. During minutes 15-30, pairs rotate through stations to view summary statistics from all three datasets displayed on poster boards. In minutes 30-45, each pair selects one identified bias and prepares a 3-minute explanation using the structured template: bias type, evidence from data, potential impact on ML models, and one mitigation strategy. For minutes 45-60, pairs present their findings to another pair, with listeners using the peer evaluation form to assess explanation clarity and accuracy. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where each group shares one key insight about how their identified bias could affect real healthcare decisions. title: Distributed System Architecture Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive technical analysis of the 2017 Amazon S3 outage by examining system architecture diagrams, failure cascades, and engineering decisions. They will decompose the incident into its constituent technical components, identify critical failure points, and evaluate the systemic vulnerabilities that amplified the initial human error into a widespread service disruption.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by dissecting the technical architecture and identifying single points of failure in Amazon's S3 infrastructure
Students will evaluate engineering trade-offs and design decisions through systematic examination of how architectural choices contributed to failure propagation and recovery time
instructions: Begin by distributing the Amazon S3 incident report, system architecture diagrams, and timeline data (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team a specific technical focus: Team A analyzes the billing subsystem dependencies, Team B examines the index subsystem architecture, Team C evaluates the restart/bootstrap procedures, and Team D focuses on monitoring and alerting systems. Each team spends 45 minutes creating a detailed failure flow diagram, identifying: (1) the initial trigger event, (2) dependent system connections, (3) cascading failure points, (4) recovery bottlenecks, and (5) architectural vulnerabilities. Teams must map out the technical relationships between subsystems using provided AWS architecture templates, annotating each connection with failure propagation timelines from the incident data. During the next 30 minutes, teams rotate through other teams' work stations, spending 7 minutes at each, adding sticky notes with questions and observations about others' analyses. Finally, conduct a 45-minute whole-class synthesis where each team presents their subsystem analysis for 8 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of technical questioning from other teams. The instructor facilitates identification of cross-cutting architectural patterns and leads discussion on how different subsystem failures compounded each other. Conclude with teams submitting annotated architecture diagrams and a 2-page technical analysis identifying the top 5 architectural design decisions that amplified the incident's impact.
materials_needed: AWS S3 incident post-mortem report (February 28, 2017)
AWS S3 system architecture diagrams (pre-incident and current)
Incident timeline spreadsheet with service impact data
Large format paper (A2/A1) for architecture diagrams

Digital collaboration tool (Miro or Lucidchart) access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical accuracy of failure analysis (30 points), depth of architectural vulnerability identification (25 points), quality of system interdependency mapping (20 points), evidence-based reasoning using incident data (15 points), and clarity of technical communication during presentations (10 points). Deliverable includes annotated architecture diagram and written analysis identifying specific design decisions, code-level issues, and systemic patterns that contributed to failure propagation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided analysis templates with pre-identified system components and prompt questions like 'What happens when this service becomes unavailable?' Advanced learners should be challenged to propose alternative architectural patterns (microservices vs. monolithic components) and calculate theoretical recovery time improvements based on their design modifications. Provide additional AWS architecture case studies for extended analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different data cleaning strategies applied to a messy customer satisfaction survey dataset. They will justify which approach produces the most reliable results for business decision-making by examining data quality metrics and potential biases introduced by each method.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data cleaning strategies by comparing data quality metrics and analyzing their impact on survey conclusions
Students will critique data cleaning decisions through systematic assessment of trade-offs between data completeness and accuracy
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a deliberately messy customer satisfaction dataset containing 500 responses with missing values (15%), duplicate entries (8%), inconsistent formatting, and obvious outliers. Divide the class into groups of 3-4 students. Each group receives the same raw dataset and three pre-applied cleaning approaches: Approach A (removes all incomplete responses), Approach B (uses mean imputation for missing numerical values and mode for categorical), and Approach C (uses advanced imputation methods and outlier capping). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Groups examine each cleaned dataset and document the cleaning decisions made, calculating basic statistics like final sample size, mean satisfaction scores, and data completeness percentages. 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students analyze the business implications by comparing key findings from each approach. They should identify how different cleaning methods affect conclusions about customer satisfaction patterns, demographic trends, and actionable insights. 

Step 3 (30 minutes): Groups create evaluation matrices scoring each approach on five criteria: data completeness (%), statistical reliability, business interpretability, potential bias introduction, and computational efficiency. Each criterion is scored 1-5 with written justifications. 

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their choice of best cleaning approach, explicitly addressing why they rejected the other two methods and what limitations their chosen approach still contains. 

Step 5 (15 minutes): Class discussion where groups challenge each other's decisions and instructor facilitates debate about trade-offs in real-world data cleaning scenarios.
materials_needed: Customer satisfaction survey dataset (CSV file with 500 responses containing intentional quality issues)
Three pre-cleaned versions of the dataset showing different cleaning approaches
Data analysis software (Excel, Google Sheets, or Python/Pandas environment)
Evaluation matrix template with scoring criteria
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Grade based on completed evaluation matrix with justified scores (40%), quality of written justification for chosen approach addressing specific trade-offs (35%), and participation in presentation and peer critique discussions (25%). Success criteria: matrices show clear understanding of each cleaning method's strengths/weaknesses, justifications reference specific data quality metrics, and students can articulate at least two limitations of their chosen approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions about what to look for in each dataset and a partially completed evaluation matrix example. Offer vocabulary support for data quality terminology. For advanced learners, challenge them to propose a fourth cleaning approach combining elements from the given methods, or to consider how their evaluation might change for different business contexts (e.g., regulatory compliance vs. marketing insights).

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Test Results with Multiple Testing Corrections
description: Students will analyze real A/B test datasets from e-commerce experiments to understand how p-hacking and multiple comparisons affect statistical validity. They will interpret results using Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg corrections to distinguish between statistically significant and practically meaningful findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the impact of multiple testing corrections on p-values by comparing uncorrected results with Bonferroni and FDR-corrected outcomes across 15 simultaneous A/B tests

Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through analysis of effect sizes, confidence intervals, and business impact metrics in conversion rate experiments
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a CSV dataset containing results from 15 simultaneous A/B tests run by an e-commerce company testing different website features (button colors, checkout flows, product recommendations, etc.). Each test includes: test_name, control_conversions, control_visitors, treatment_conversions, treatment_visitors, revenue_per_conversion. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Students work individually to calculate conversion rates, effect sizes (Cohen's h), and uncorrected p-values using two-proportion z-tests for all 15 experiments. They identify which tests appear 'significant' at α=0.05. **Step 2 (20 minutes):** In pairs, students apply Bonferroni correction (α/15 = 0.0033) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction (α=0.05, FDR=0.1) to their p-values. They document how many tests remain significant under each correction method and discuss why results differ. **Step 3 (25 minutes):** Students calculate 95% confidence intervals for conversion rate differences and estimate annual revenue impact using: (treatment_rate - control_rate) × monthly_visitors × 12 × revenue_per_conversion. They create a summary table ranking experiments by: (a) statistical significance, (b) effect size magnitude, (c) estimated business impact. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Pairs present their top 3 recommended experiments to implement, justifying selections based on statistical validity AND business value. **Debrief (10 minutes):** Class discusses how multiple testing corrections prevent false discoveries and why statistical significance alone is insufficient for business decisions.

Python/R environment with scipy.stats, statsmodels packages installed
Jupyter notebook template with data loading code and correction formulas

assessment_method: Grade final summary table (40 points): correct p-values (10), proper application of corrections (15), accurate business impact calculations (10), justified recommendations (5). Deduct points for recommending tests that lose significance after proper corrections without acknowledging limitations.

Create calculation template with first experiment completed as example. Pair weaker students with stronger partners. **Extend advanced learners:** Challenge them to implement permutation tests for p-value validation, calculate statistical power for each experiment, or design optimal sample size calculations for future tests. Ask them to research and apply alternative correction methods (Holm-Bonferroni, Storey's q-value).

title: Budget Planning for a School Field Trip
description: Students will apply addition, subtraction, and multiplication skills to create a realistic budget for a class field trip to a local science museum. They will work with real-world constraints including transportation costs, admission fees, and meal allowances to determine if their trip is financially feasible within a given budget limit.
learning_objectives: Students will apply addition and multiplication operations to calculate total costs for transportation, admission, and meals by working with real price data
Students will apply subtraction skills to determine remaining budget amounts and make financial decisions through budget comparison activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the Field Trip Budget Worksheet and price information sheets to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student has a $25 per person budget to plan a field trip for their class of 24 students, giving them a total budget of $600. Present three cost categories: transportation ($8 per person by bus or $12 per person by chartered van), museum admission ($6 per child, $8 per adult, with 2 adults required), and lunch options ($4 for packed lunch, $7 for cafeteria meal, or $9 for restaurant meal). Have students work individually for 20 minutes to calculate costs for each category using multiplication (cost per person × number of people). They must then add all category totals to find their complete trip cost and subtract this from $600 to determine if they're over or under budget. If over budget, students must recalculate using different options until they create a feasible plan. During the final 10 minutes, have students pair up to compare their budget solutions and verify each other's calculations. Each student must complete their worksheet showing all multiplication and addition work, circle their final choices, and write one sentence explaining why their plan works within the budget constraints.
materials_needed: Field Trip Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Price Information Reference Sheet with transportation, admission, and meal costs
Calculators (optional for verification)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: 4 points for accurate calculations in all three categories with correct final budget total, 3 points for mostly accurate calculations with minor errors, 2 points for correct process shown but multiple calculation errors, 1 point for attempted calculations but incorrect method or major errors. Students must also provide a written explanation of their final plan to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed example showing the multiplication setup for one category (e.g., 24 students × $6 admission = $144). Consider allowing calculator use for verification after hand calculations. For advanced learners, add complexity by including a 6% sales tax on meals or asking them to create budget plans for two different class sizes (18 and 30 students) to compare cost efficiency.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Implementations
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms by examining their code implementations, predicting their behavior with different input types, and interpreting actual runtime data. This activity develops critical thinking skills for evaluating algorithmic trade-offs in real-world programming scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by examining their code structure and identifying key performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate algorithm performance through systematic comparison of empirical runtime data across different input scenarios (sorted, reverse-sorted, and random arrays)
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the algorithm analysis worksheet and three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) written in Python. Each group receives datasets of 1000, 5000, and 10000 integers in three configurations: already sorted, reverse-sorted, and randomized.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine each algorithm's code without running it. They complete a prediction table estimating relative performance rankings for each algorithm-dataset combination, justifying their reasoning based on code structure analysis.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups run each algorithm on all nine dataset combinations (3 algorithms × 3 data types × 3 sizes) using the provided timing script. Students record actual execution times in milliseconds and note any patterns or unexpected results.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students create comparison charts plotting execution time vs. input size for each algorithm, using different colors for each data type (sorted/reverse/random). They identify which algorithms show linear, quadratic, or logarithmic growth patterns.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups analyze discrepancies between their predictions and actual results. They write a brief report explaining why certain algorithms performed better or worse than expected with specific input types, referencing code structure to support their conclusions.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each group presents one surprising finding to the class, explaining the algorithmic reason behind the unexpected performance behavior they discovered.
materials_needed: Pre-written Python files: bubble_sort.py, merge_sort.py, quicksort.py
Dataset files: sorted_1000.txt, reverse_1000.txt, random_1000.txt (and 5000, 10000 versions)
Algorithm analysis worksheet with prediction tables
Python environment with time module installed
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis based on code examination (25%), (2) Quality of performance predictions with logical justification (25%), (3) Correct interpretation of empirical data patterns and graphical representation (25%), (4) Depth of analysis in explaining prediction vs. actual result discrepancies with specific algorithmic reasoning (25%). Students must submit their prediction table, timing data, graphs, and written analysis report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a code annotation guide highlighting loop structures and recursive calls that impact performance. Offer sentence starters for analysis explanations. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or challenge them to predict performance on partially sorted data. Consider having them modify one algorithm to improve its worst-case performance.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Implementations: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code implementations, predicting time complexities, and comparing actual runtime performance on datasets of varying sizes. They will decompose each algorithm's structure and evaluate trade-offs between different approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithmic complexity by examining code structure and predicting Big O notation for time and space requirements
Students will evaluate algorithm performance trade-offs through empirical testing and comparative analysis of runtime data
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Divide students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three code files containing bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort implementations in Python. Each file should include timing functions and data generation methods. **Phase 1 - Static Code Analysis (25 minutes):** Students examine each algorithm's code without running it. For each algorithm, they must: (1) identify the main loop structures and recursive calls, (2) trace through the algorithm with a small dataset (5 elements), (3) predict the worst-case and best-case time complexity using Big O notation, and (4) estimate space complexity requirements. Groups document their predictions in a provided analysis worksheet. **Phase 2 - Empirical Testing (30 minutes):** Students run each algorithm on datasets of 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 randomly generated integers. They record execution times in milliseconds for each test, running each test 3 times and calculating averages. Results are logged in a data collection spreadsheet. **Phase 3 - Comparative Analysis (20 minutes):** Using their empirical data, students create graphs plotting dataset size vs. execution time for each algorithm. They compare their initial predictions with actual performance results. **Phase 4 - Report Generation (15 minutes):** Each group writes a brief analysis report identifying which algorithm performs best for different dataset sizes, explaining discrepancies between predicted and actual performance, and recommending optimal use cases for each sorting method.
materials_needed: Three Python files with bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort implementations
Algorithm analysis worksheet template
Data collection spreadsheet (Excel/Google Sheets)
Computers with Python 3.7+ and matplotlib library installed
Timer/stopwatch functionality in code
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of Big O predictions (25%), (2) Completeness of empirical data collection (25%), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between predicted vs actual results (25%), (4) Appropriateness of algorithm recommendations for different use cases (25%). Students must submit completed worksheets, data spreadsheets, performance graphs, and final analysis reports.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide Big O notation reference sheet and algorithm tracing examples. Consider pairing with stronger peers for code analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional factors like memory usage, implement hybrid sorting approaches, or test with different data distributions (sorted, reverse-sorted, partially sorted arrays).
