title: Evaluating and Defending Model Selection for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will critically evaluate three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression) trained on a customer churn dataset, justify their selection of the optimal model considering business constraints, and defend their choice against peer critiques. This activity requires students to synthesize technical performance metrics with real-world business implications.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, feature importance, and business impact to justify optimal model selection
Students will critique peer model selections through structured debate sessions, defending their choices using evidence-based reasoning and addressing counterarguments
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Individual Model Analysis**
Provide each student with the pre-trained models and validation results on the telecom churn dataset. Students must complete a comprehensive evaluation matrix comparing: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, training time, inference speed, interpretability score (1-10), and implementation complexity. They calculate business impact metrics including potential revenue saved, false positive costs ($50 per customer), and false negative costs ($200 lost revenue per churned customer).

**Phase 2 (30 minutes): Model Selection and Justification**
Students write a 500-word technical memo to a fictional VP of Customer Retention, recommending one model. The memo must include: quantitative performance comparison, business impact analysis with specific dollar figures, implementation timeline and resource requirements, model interpretability assessment for regulatory compliance, and risk analysis of false positives/negatives.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Peer Evaluation and Defense**
Divide class into groups of 4. Each student presents their recommendation (5 minutes), followed by structured critique sessions where peers challenge assumptions, question methodology, and propose alternative interpretations. The presenter must defend their choice with evidence. Rotate until all students present and receive feedback.

**Phase 4 (20 minutes): Synthesis and Reflection**
Students revise their original recommendation based on peer feedback, documenting what critiques they accepted/rejected and why. Submit final recommendation with a 200-word reflection on how peer evaluation changed their analysis.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-trained Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression models
Telecom customer churn validation dataset (5,000 records) with ground truth labels
Model performance results spreadsheet template with business cost parameters
Technical memo template with required sections
Peer evaluation rubric with specific criteria for critique quality
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Evaluation matrix completeness and accuracy (25%), (2) Quality of business justification with quantitative support (30%), (3) Effectiveness of peer critiques using specific evidence and technical reasoning (25%), (4) Defense quality including addressing counterarguments with data (20%). Use provided rubric with 4-point scale for each criterion. Minimum passing: demonstrates clear model comparison methodology, provides business-grounded recommendation, offers substantive peer feedback, and responds to critiques with evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed evaluation matrices and sentence starters for business impact analysis. Offer one-on-one consultation during Phase 1. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional evaluation metrics (fairness, robustness), consider ensemble methods, or analyze cross-validation stability. Encourage them to lead peer discussions and mentor struggling classmates during group sessions.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flash Card Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall basic syntax elements from three common programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) through structured flashcard activities and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential syntax recognition skills needed for coding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall basic syntax symbols and keywords for Python, Java, and JavaScript by correctly identifying them in flashcard exercises with 80% accuracy
Students will memorize fundamental programming constructs (variables, loops, functions) through repeated exposure and timed recall activities
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made syntax flashcards covering 30 essential elements: 10 Python syntax items (def, if, elif, else, for, while, print(), input(), #, :), 10 Java syntax items (public, static, void, class, int, String, System.out.println(), Scanner, //, {}), and 10 JavaScript syntax items (let, const, var, function, console.log(), if, else, for, while, //). 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs, taking turns showing flashcards to their partner. The card holder shows the front (syntax description like 'Python function definition keyword') and the partner must recall the exact syntax ('def'). Partners alternate roles every 5 minutes, cycling through all 30 cards twice.

Phase 2 (10 minutes): Conduct individual timed recall sessions. Display syntax descriptions on the projector for 10 seconds each. Students write answers on provided answer sheets. Cover all 30 items once, spending exactly 10 seconds per item with 5-second transitions.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Immediate self-assessment using answer keys. Students check their responses, count correct answers, and identify which language's syntax they recalled best and worst. They must write down three specific syntax elements they need to review further.

Phase 4 (5 minutes): Quick verbal review where volunteers share one syntax element they found challenging and one they remembered easily, reinforcing learning through peer discussion.
materials_needed: 30 pre-made flashcards with syntax descriptions and answers
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-30
Answer keys for self-assessment
Projector or large display for timed recall phase
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students achieve success by scoring 24/30 (80%) or higher on the timed recall exercise. Grade based on: correct syntax recall (80% of grade), completion of self-reflection identifying strengths/weaknesses (20% of grade). Observe during pair work to note participation and peer teaching behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce to 20 cards focusing on one language, provide syntax reference sheets during pair work, allow 15 seconds per item instead of 10. For advanced learners: Add 10 additional cards with more complex syntax (classes, exceptions, arrow functions), challenge them to explain syntax usage context, or have them create additional flashcards for bonus points.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Customer Purchase Behavior
description: Students will analyze pre-prepared histograms, box plots, and summary statistics from an e-commerce dataset to identify and explain different distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal). They will connect statistical concepts to real business scenarios by interpreting what these patterns reveal about customer purchasing behaviors.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, and bimodal distributions by examining visual plots and statistical measures from customer transaction data
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through structured analysis of customer purchase amount data
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared dataset containing customer purchase amounts from three different product categories (electronics, clothing, books) along with pre-generated visualizations. In the first 10 minutes, have students work individually to examine Dataset A (electronics purchases) - they should identify the distribution shape using the histogram, note the relationship between mean and median, and observe the box plot for outliers. Next, organize students into pairs for 15 minutes to analyze Dataset B (clothing purchases) together, having them complete a structured worksheet that asks them to: (1) describe the distribution shape, (2) identify which tail is longer, (3) explain why the mean differs from the median, and (4) hypothesize what this pattern suggests about customer behavior. For the final 20 minutes, conduct a whole-class analysis of Dataset C (books purchases) which shows a bimodal distribution. Guide students through recognizing the two peaks, discussing what customer segments this might represent (casual readers vs. heavy readers), and comparing all three datasets. Have students complete exit tickets explaining which distribution pattern would be most concerning for inventory management and why. Throughout the activity, emphasize connecting statistical observations to business meaning rather than just identifying shapes.
materials_needed: Three prepared datasets with customer purchase data (CSV files)
Pre-generated histograms and box plots for each dataset
Structured analysis worksheets with guided questions
Summary statistics tables (mean, median, mode, standard deviation) for each dataset
Exit ticket templates
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric for each dataset analysis: (3) correctly identifies distribution type AND provides accurate business interpretation, (2) correctly identifies distribution type with basic business connection, (1) identifies distribution type but lacks business context. Additionally, assess exit ticket responses for understanding of practical implications, requiring students to demonstrate they can connect statistical patterns to real-world decision-making scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide distribution identification flowcharts and sentence starters like 'This distribution is ___ because the mean is ___ than the median and...' For advanced learners, include additional datasets with more complex patterns (uniform, exponential) and ask them to calculate skewness coefficients to quantify their observations. Consider providing business context cards that explain different customer behavior scenarios to help students make connections.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Customer Purchase Behavior: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze real e-commerce customer data to identify and explain different distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal) in purchase amounts, frequency, and seasonal trends. They will create visual interpretations and write explanations connecting distribution shapes to underlying business phenomena.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of different distribution shapes (normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, bimodal) by analyzing customer purchase data and explaining what each pattern reveals about customer behavior
Students will distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate conclusions from distribution visualizations through guided analysis of histogram and box plot comparisons
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded dataset containing 1000 customer records with purchase_amount, purchase_frequency, customer_age, and month_purchased columns. Form pairs and provide each team with the analysis worksheet. Step 1 (10 min): Students load the dataset in Python/R and create histograms for purchase_amount, purchase_frequency, and customer_age using 20 bins each. They must save these plots and note the general shape. Step 2 (15 min): Using the provided distribution identification guide, pairs categorize each histogram as normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, or bimodal, writing one sentence explaining their reasoning for each classification. Step 3 (20 min): Students create box plots for the same three variables and compare them to their histograms, identifying outliers and quartile positions. They must write explanations for any discrepancies between what the histogram and box plot suggest about the data. Step 4 (15 min): Pairs examine purchase patterns by month, creating a bar chart of average purchase amounts per month, then write a 3-sentence interpretation of seasonal trends they observe. Step 5 (10 min): Each pair completes the worksheet by selecting which distribution pattern (from their three histograms) best represents typical customer behavior and justifying their choice with specific reference to business implications. Conclude with 2-3 pairs presenting their key findings to demonstrate different interpretations of the same data patterns.
materials_needed: Pre-cleaned CSV dataset with 1000 customer purchase records
Distribution identification reference guide with visual examples
Python/R environment with matplotlib/ggplot2 installed
Analysis worksheet with guided questions
Projector for student presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (3) Correctly identifies all distribution types with accurate business explanations, (2) Identifies most distributions correctly with mostly appropriate explanations, (1) Shows basic understanding but with significant errors in identification or interpretation. Check that visualizations display appropriate titles, axis labels, and clear distribution shapes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using a different variable (customer_age) and highlight key phrases for describing distributions. Offer sentence starters like 'This right-skewed distribution suggests that most customers...' For advanced learners, add tasks to calculate and interpret specific statistics (skewness coefficients, kurtosis) or compare distributions across customer segments using faceted plots.

title: Optimization in Real Estate Development: Maximizing Profit Through Calculus
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and constraint optimization techniques to solve a realistic real estate development problem. They will determine optimal building dimensions and unit configurations to maximize profit while adhering to zoning regulations and budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus techniques to optimize profit functions by setting up and solving systems of partial derivative equations
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to handle constraint optimization through systematic mathematical modeling of real-world limitations
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet: students represent developers planning a 50-unit apartment complex on a rectangular lot (200m × 150m). Present three constraints: total construction budget of $8 million, maximum building height of 6 stories per zoning laws, and minimum 40% green space requirement. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to identify variables: building footprint dimensions (x, y), number of stories (n), and unit types (studio vs. 2-bedroom ratio). Next, guide students through establishing the profit function P(x,y,n,r) where r represents the studio-to-2BR ratio. Provide construction costs ($120,000 per studio, $180,000 per 2BR) and monthly rent data ($1,800 studio, $2,800 2BR). Teams spend 30 minutes deriving the constraint equations: budget constraint g₁(x,y,n,r) = 0, zoning constraint g₂(n) ≤ 6, and green space constraint g₃(x,y) ≤ 0.6(30,000). Students then apply Lagrange multipliers for 40 minutes, setting up ∇P = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ + λ₃∇g₃ and solving the resulting system. Provide graphing calculators or Mathematica for computational support. Teams spend final 25 minutes interpreting results: optimal building dimensions, story count, unit mix, and projected 10-year profit. Each team presents their solution with economic justification for 5 minutes, explaining how mathematical optimization informed their development strategy.
materials_needed: Real estate development scenario packets with cost/revenue data
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Mathematica or MATLAB software access
Large grid paper for constraint visualization
Financial calculator for NPV calculations
assessment_method: Teams submit a 3-page technical report containing: (1) Complete mathematical setup with properly defined variables and constraints (25 points), (2) Correct application of Lagrange multiplier method with all partial derivatives shown (35 points), (3) Accurate solution with numerical results (25 points), and (4) Business interpretation explaining economic significance of mathematical results (15 points). Oral presentation assessed on mathematical accuracy and real-world application clarity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and offer one-on-one guidance during Lagrange setup. Create visual aids showing geometric interpretation of constraints. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including variable interest rates, construction timeline constraints, or market demand elasticity. Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements or sensitivity analysis for key parameters.

title: Optimization in Real Estate Development: Maximizing Profit Through Calculus: Visual Analysis

instructions: Begin by distributing the Real Estate Development Portfolio packets containing lot specifications, zoning restrictions, and market data (10 minutes). Organize students into development teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Project Manager (coordinates timeline), Financial Analyst (handles calculations), Compliance Officer (tracks constraints), and Market Researcher (analyzes demand data). Present the scenario: Teams have purchased a 12,000 sq ft rectangular lot in downtown Portland and must design a mixed-use building with retail ground floor and residential units above. Provide specific constraints: maximum building height 8 stories, minimum 30% green space, parking ratio 1.5 spaces per unit, construction budget $2.8M, and variable costs based on unit types (studio: $45k, 1BR: $65k, 2BR: $85k). Teams spend 15 minutes analyzing provided market data showing rental rates and occupancy statistics. Next, students formulate the optimization problem by defining variables (x₁=studios, x₂=1BR units, x₃=2BR units), establishing the objective function P(x₁,x₂,x₃) = revenue - costs, and listing all constraints as inequalities (25 minutes). Using graphing calculators or Desmos, teams plot constraint boundaries and identify feasible regions (20 minutes). Students then apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to find critical points, calculating partial derivatives ∂P/∂x₁, ∂P/∂x₂, ∂P/∂x₃ and setting up the system λ∇g₁ + μ∇g₂ + ... = ∇P (30 minutes). Teams verify solutions using the corner-point method, testing vertices of the feasible region (15 minutes). Finally, each team prepares a 5-minute presentation showing their optimal solution, mathematical justification, and projected 5-year ROI analysis (15 minutes preparation, 20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Real Estate Development Portfolio packets with lot specifications, zoning maps, and market data spreadsheets
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent) or laptop access to Desmos Graphing Calculator
Large grid paper (11x17 inches) for constraint plotting
Financial calculator or Excel access for ROI calculations
Presentation materials (poster board or digital presentation capability)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Setup (25 points - correct objective function and constraint formulation), Calculus Application (30 points - proper use of partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers with accurate calculations), Constraint Analysis (20 points - correct identification of feasible region and corner points), Solution Verification (15 points - checking answer reasonableness and testing boundary conditions), and Professional Presentation (10 points - clear communication of methodology and business rationale). Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and a final recommendation memo.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates and guided practice with single-variable optimization before attempting multivariable problems. Offer calculator tutorials for plotting functions and finding intersections. For advanced learners: Include additional constraints like environmental impact costs, variable interest rates over time, or seasonal demand fluctuations. Challenge them to incorporate sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with constraint modifications.
original_title: Optimization in Real Estate Development: Maximizing Profit Through Calculus

title: Analyzing Memory Management Performance in Multi-threaded Applications Through Buffer Overflow Vulnerability Assessment
description: Students will dissect a vulnerable C++ multi-threaded application to identify memory leaks, race conditions, and buffer overflow exploits. They will analyze the relationship between memory allocation patterns, thread synchronization mechanisms, and security vulnerabilities using static analysis tools and runtime profilers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze memory allocation patterns and identify critical vulnerabilities by examining multi-threaded C++ source code using Valgrind and AddressSanitizer
Students will differentiate between various memory management flaws through systematic evaluation of heap corruption, stack overflow scenarios, and race condition impacts
instructions: **Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the vulnerable banking simulation program 'ThreadedBankApp.cpp' containing intentional memory leaks, buffer overflows, and race conditions across 3 threads managing account transactions. Students work in pairs using Linux VMs with Valgrind, GDB, and AddressSanitizer pre-installed. **Phase 1 - Static Code Analysis (25 minutes):** Students examine the source code line-by-line, documenting suspected vulnerabilities in a structured analysis worksheet. They must identify: unsafe string operations (strcpy, sprintf), missing mutex locks around shared variables, and dynamic allocation without corresponding deallocation. Each pair creates a vulnerability matrix categorizing findings by severity (Critical/High/Medium). **Phase 2 - Dynamic Analysis (30 minutes):** Compile the program with AddressSanitizer flags (-fsanitize=address -g). Execute the program with concurrent transaction loads while monitoring with Valgrind's memcheck tool. Students capture and interpret tool outputs, correlating runtime errors with their static analysis predictions. They must trace specific memory addresses through allocation/deallocation cycles and identify which thread caused each detected violation. **Phase 3 - Impact Assessment (15 minutes):** Using GDB, students craft specific input sequences to trigger buffer overflows and demonstrate heap corruption. They analyze stack traces to understand exploitation pathways and document the relationship between memory layout and vulnerability exploitation. **Synthesis Phase (10 minutes):** Pairs present one critical vulnerability to the class, explaining the detection method, potential impact, and proposed remediation strategy.
materials_needed: ThreadedBankApp.cpp source code with embedded vulnerabilities
Linux virtual machines with GCC, Valgrind, GDB, AddressSanitizer installed
Vulnerability analysis worksheet template
Sample malicious input files for exploitation testing
assessment_method: Students submit a comprehensive vulnerability report containing: (1) Static analysis matrix with 8+ identified vulnerabilities categorized by type and severity (25 points), (2) Dynamic analysis results showing correlation between predicted and detected issues with tool outputs (30 points), (3) Exploitation demonstration with documented input sequences and stack traces (25 points), (4) Technical recommendations for each critical vulnerability with specific code fixes (20 points). Success requires identifying all 3 critical buffer overflows, 2 race conditions, and 4 memory leaks with accurate technical explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vulnerability identification checklist focusing on common C++ pitfalls, offer pre-configured Valgrind command templates, and assign stronger students as technical mentors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to develop automated exploitation scripts, analyze assembly code output, or propose custom static analysis rules. Consider providing additional vulnerable modules (file handling, network communications) for extended analysis.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City with Mathematical Constraints
description: Students will create an original scale model city layout that meets specific population, area, and geometric requirements. They will integrate concepts of scale, area, perimeter, proportional reasoning, and geometric properties to design a functional city plan with buildings, roads, and public spaces.
estimated_duration: 135 minutes (3 class periods of 45 minutes each)
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city layout by applying scale factor calculations and area/perimeter formulas to meet specified population and space constraints
Students will construct a mathematical model through creating detailed floor plans and 3D representations that demonstrate proportional relationships and geometric principles
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 students) with the city requirements sheet and base materials. Explain that they have 3 class periods to complete their city design. Day 1 (45 minutes): Teams review requirements (population 10,000-15,000, total area 500 square units on grid paper, minimum 20% green space, residential/commercial/industrial zones). Students calculate building dimensions using their chosen scale (1 unit = 50-100 people) and sketch initial layouts on graph paper. They must show all mathematical work for population density calculations and area measurements. Day 2 (45 minutes): Teams finalize their mathematical calculations, create detailed building floor plans showing exact dimensions, and begin constructing 3D models using cardboard and craft materials. Each building must be labeled with its function, capacity, and scale measurements. Day 3 (45 minutes): Students complete construction, prepare a presentation board showing all calculations, scale conversions, and area/perimeter measurements for each zone. Teams present their cities in 5-minute presentations, explaining their mathematical reasoning for design choices, how they met population requirements, and demonstrating understanding of scale relationships. Throughout the activity, circulate to check calculations and provide guidance on mathematical accuracy.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm grid, 3 sheets per team)
Cardboard pieces (various sizes)
Rulers and measuring tape
Calculators
City Requirements handout with population and zoning constraints
Colored pencils and markers
Glue sticks and scissors
Presentation boards (poster size)
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - all scale calculations, area/perimeter measurements, and population density calculations are correct; Design Requirements (25%) - city meets all specified constraints for population, area, and zoning; Mathematical Reasoning (25%) - clear explanation of mathematical choices and problem-solving process; Presentation Quality (25%) - organized display of work and clear communication of mathematical concepts. Students submit calculation worksheets, design plans, physical model, and reflection essay explaining their mathematical decision-making process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated scale factor options (1 unit = 75 people or 1 unit = 100 people) and area calculation templates. Offer checkpoint meetings after each day to review calculations. For advanced learners: Add constraints such as budget limitations requiring cost per square unit calculations, or elevation changes requiring volume calculations for multi-story buildings. Challenge them to optimize their design for maximum green space while meeting population requirements.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City with Mathematical Constraints: Exercise 1
description: Students will create an original scale model city layout that incorporates geometric shapes, area calculations, and proportional reasoning. They must design buildings, roads, and parks while meeting specific mathematical requirements and budget constraints using area and perimeter formulas.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a scale model city by applying area and perimeter formulas to design buildings and spaces within given constraints
Students will synthesize proportional reasoning and geometric principles through creating an original urban planning solution
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and provide each team with a 24×18 inch poster board representing their city plot (scale: 1 inch = 50 feet). Distribute the City Planning Packet containing requirements: minimum 8 buildings of different geometric shapes, at least 3 parks with combined area of 200,000 square feet, road system connecting all buildings with total length between 3,000-4,000 feet, and a $2.5 million construction budget. Students spend 15 minutes reviewing requirements and sketching initial ideas individually. Next, teams collaborate for 20 minutes to combine ideas and create a unified design plan, calculating areas and costs as they plan. Provide construction materials (colored paper, rulers, protractors, calculators) and have teams spend 45 minutes building their 3D model city, with buildings having actual height proportional to their base area (1 square inch base = 2 inches height). During construction, students must maintain a budget spreadsheet showing building costs ($50 per square foot for commercial, $30 for residential, $10 for parks) and area calculations for each structure. In the final 25 minutes, each team presents their city for 4 minutes, explaining their design choices, demonstrating mathematical calculations used, and justifying how they met all constraints. Other teams use evaluation sheets to assess mathematical accuracy and design creativity. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students identify the most challenging mathematical concepts and how they solved spatial reasoning problems.
materials_needed: 24×18 inch poster boards (1 per team)
City Planning Packet with requirements and budget constraints
Colored construction paper (various colors)
Rulers, protractors, and calculators
Glue sticks and scissors
Budget tracking spreadsheets
Peer evaluation sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct area/perimeter calculations and scale conversions (25%), (2) Constraint Adherence - meeting all city requirements and budget limits (25%), (3) Design Innovation - creative use of geometric shapes and spatial organization (25%), (4) Presentation Quality - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning and design choices (25%). Students must submit calculation worksheets and budget spreadsheets alongside their physical model.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide area/perimeter formula reference cards and pre-calculated examples of simple shapes. Offer templates for budget spreadsheets and encourage starting with rectangular buildings before attempting complex shapes. For advanced learners, add challenges such as incorporating curved roads (requiring arc length calculations), multi-story buildings with varying floor areas, or environmental constraints requiring specific building orientations and shadow calculations.
original_title: Design and Build a Scale Model City with Mathematical Constraints

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City with Mathematical Constraints: Exercise 2
description: Students will create an original scale model city layout that incorporates geometric shapes, area calculations, and proportional reasoning. They must design buildings, roads, and public spaces while adhering to specific mathematical constraints and real-world urban planning principles.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original scale model city by applying geometric principles, area calculations, and proportional reasoning to create buildings and infrastructure
Students will formulate mathematical justifications for their design choices through written explanations that demonstrate understanding of scale, perimeter, area, and spatial relationships
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with a 24x18 inch poster board as their city base. Explain that they must create a city with exactly 8 buildings, 4 parks, and a road system, all drawn to a scale of 1 inch = 50 feet. Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams brainstorm their city concept and assign roles - architect (building design), urban planner (layout), mathematician (calculations), and presenter. Step 2 (30 minutes): Students calculate the actual dimensions their scaled buildings and spaces will represent, then determine appropriate sizes for their poster. Each building must be a different geometric shape (rectangle, square, triangle, trapezoid, etc.) and teams must calculate both perimeter and area for each structure. Step 3 (45 minutes): Using rulers, protractors, and colored materials, students construct their city layout. They must ensure total building area doesn't exceed 40% of the poster board and parks comprise at least 15% of total space. Roads must connect all buildings and follow geometric principles (parallel, perpendicular, or at specific angles). Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams create a mathematical report documenting all calculations, including total areas, scale conversions, and geometric properties of their shapes. Step 5 (30 minutes): Each team presents their city design, explaining their mathematical reasoning and demonstrating how they met all constraints. Other teams evaluate presentations using provided rubrics.
materials_needed: 24x18 inch poster board (one per team)
Rulers, protractors, and measuring tools
Colored pencils, markers, or construction paper
Calculators
Graph paper for planning sketches
City planning constraint worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of calculations and scale conversions, (2) Creative design that meets all geometric constraints, (3) Clear documentation in mathematical report showing work and reasoning, (4) Effective presentation explaining mathematical choices. Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy and demonstrate correct area/perimeter calculations for 7/8 buildings to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated examples of scale conversions and area formulas reference sheet. Offer building templates with dimensions already marked. For advanced learners: Add constraints requiring specific angle measurements for roads, incorporate volume calculations for 3D building models, or challenge them to optimize city layout for maximum efficiency using mathematical reasoning.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Sprint
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the time complexity classifications (Big O notation) of 40 advanced algorithms across data structures, graph theory, string processing, and dynamic programming domains. This high-speed recall activity reinforces foundational knowledge essential for technical interviews and algorithm selection.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the exact time complexity (Big O notation) for 40 advanced algorithms by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recall algorithm complexity classifications within 3 seconds per algorithm through structured repetition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 40 algorithms organized into 4 categories: Advanced Data Structures (10 algorithms including Red-Black Tree insertion, B-Tree search, Fibonacci Heap operations), Graph Algorithms (10 algorithms including Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, Tarjan's SCC), String Algorithms (10 algorithms including KMP, Rabin-Karp, Suffix Array construction), and Dynamic Programming (10 algorithms including Longest Common Subsequence, Knapsack variants, Matrix Chain Multiplication). Allow students 15 minutes to study the reference sheet silently. Next, implement a three-round drilling system: Round 1 (20 minutes) - Project algorithm names one at a time using slides, students write down the time complexity on provided answer sheets, 30 seconds per algorithm. Round 2 (15 minutes) - Rapid-fire verbal quiz where students must verbally state the complexity when you call out algorithm names, 10 seconds per response, rotate through all students. Round 3 (10 minutes) - Partner drill where Student A reads algorithm names from randomized cards while Student B provides complexity, then switch roles after 5 minutes. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class verification session where you display correct answers and students self-assess their accuracy. Record individual scores for each round to track memorization progress.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared algorithm complexity reference sheet (40 algorithms with Big O notations)
Randomized algorithm name flashcards (40 cards)
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-40
Projection system for displaying algorithm names
Timer/stopwatch for each drilling round
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery by correctly recalling 85% (34/40) of algorithm complexities across all three rounds. Track individual performance using a scoring rubric: Expert level (38-40 correct), Proficient level (34-37 correct), Developing level (28-33 correct), Beginning level (below 28 correct). Assess based on written responses in Round 1, verbal accuracy in Round 2, and peer verification during Round 3 partner work.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing mnemonic devices for common complexity patterns (e.g., 'Divide and conquer usually gives O(n log n)'). Create color-coded reference cards grouping algorithms by complexity class. For advanced learners, add 10 bonus algorithms including amortized analysis examples (Dynamic Array resize, Disjoint Set with path compression) and challenge them to explain why certain algorithms have their specific complexities.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Cross-Validated Model Performance Metrics
description: Students will analyze and interpret the bias-variance tradeoff in machine learning models by examining decomposed error components across different regularization parameters in ridge regression. They will explain how changes in model complexity affect generalization performance through systematic analysis of cross-validation results.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between bias, variance, and irreducible error components by analyzing decomposed MSE results from ridge regression models with varying regularization strengths
Students will explain the implications of bias-variance tradeoff patterns through detailed examination of cross-validation performance curves and their underlying mathematical components
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared dataset containing bias-variance decomposition results for ridge regression models trained on a synthetic regression problem with known ground truth (15 minutes setup). The dataset should include 50 different alpha values (regularization parameters) ranging from 0.001 to 1000, with corresponding bias², variance, and irreducible error measurements obtained through 100 bootstrap samples. Organize students into pairs and distribute the analysis worksheet containing guided questions. Students first examine the numerical results table, identifying patterns in how bias² increases and variance decreases as regularization strength increases (20 minutes). Next, they create three separate line plots showing bias², variance, and total error versus log(alpha), using provided plotting templates in Excel or Python (25 minutes). Students then analyze the intersection point where bias² and variance curves meet, calculating the optimal alpha value that minimizes total error (15 minutes). Following this quantitative analysis, pairs collaborate to write detailed explanations for five scenario-based questions: Why does variance approach zero at high regularization? How does bias² relate to model underfitting? What causes the U-shaped total error curve? When would you choose a slightly suboptimal alpha in practice? How would results differ with a more complex base model? (30 minutes). Finally, each pair presents one scenario explanation to the class, defending their interpretation using specific numerical evidence from their analysis (15 minutes total for all presentations).
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition dataset (CSV file with 50 alpha values and corresponding error components)
Analysis worksheet with guided questions and plotting templates
Computer access with Excel or Python/Jupyter notebook environment
Scientific calculators for manual optimization calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate based on four criteria using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of pattern identification in numerical data (plots correctly show inverse relationship between bias² and variance), (2) Mathematical precision in optimal alpha calculation (within 5% of true minimum), (3) Conceptual depth in scenario explanations (demonstrates understanding of underfitting/overfitting mechanisms), (4) Use of quantitative evidence in justifications (cites specific values from dataset to support claims). Each criterion worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example plots for a simpler dataset and highlight key numerical patterns before analysis. Offer sentence starters for explanations like 'When alpha increases, variance decreases because...' For advanced learners: Extend activity by asking them to predict how bias-variance patterns would change with different loss functions (absolute error vs. squared error) or compare results to LASSO regularization decomposition.

title: Grocery Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Shopping
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to solve realistic grocery shopping scenarios involving discounts, tax, and budget constraints. They will use their knowledge of percentages to make purchasing decisions and calculate final costs within given budget limits.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, sales tax, and final prices by working through realistic grocery shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate their understanding of percentage concepts through creating and justifying budget-conscious shopping decisions
instructions: Begin by distributing the Grocery Store Flyer worksheet and Budget Scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each card contains a family budget ($150-200) and specific shopping requirements (feed family of 4 for one week, must include proteins, vegetables, and grains). Students examine the flyer showing 15 grocery items with original prices and various discounts (10% off produce, buy-one-get-one-free deals, $2 off coupons). Next, students work individually to select items that meet their family's needs while staying within budget (15 minutes). They must calculate the discounted price for each selected item, showing their work step-by-step using the percentage formula (discount amount = original price × discount percentage). After calculating discounts, students add 8.5% sales tax to their subtotal and determine if they're within budget (10 minutes). If over budget, they must revise their selections and recalculate. Students then create a final shopping list showing: original prices, discount calculations, discounted prices, subtotal, tax amount, and final total (10 minutes). Finally, students pair up to compare their solutions and explain their mathematical reasoning for item selections, discussing how percentage calculations influenced their decisions (10 minutes). Conclude with 2-3 student pairs presenting their shopping strategies to the class, emphasizing the percentage calculations that led to successful budget management.
materials_needed: Grocery Store Flyer worksheet with 15 items and various discount offers
Budget Scenario cards (6 different family situations)
Calculator for each student
Blank shopping list template
Pencil and paper for calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed shopping lists using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, stays within budget, shows complete work; (3) Minor calculation errors, stays within budget, shows most work; (2) Some calculation errors, may exceed budget slightly, shows some work; (1) Multiple errors, exceeds budget significantly, minimal work shown. Also assess verbal explanations during pair sharing for mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference sheet and pre-calculated examples. Allow use of calculators and consider pairing with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including compound discounts (additional 5% off already discounted items) or requiring them to calculate unit prices to determine best value purchases.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Big-O Evaluation
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining their implementations, tracing execution paths, and determining Big-O notation. They will create a comparative analysis report identifying the strengths and weaknesses of each algorithm in different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of three search algorithms by tracing their execution steps and calculating Big-O notation
Students will evaluate algorithm performance through systematic comparison of worst-case, best-case, and average-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three code implementations (linear search, binary search, hash table lookup) and a dataset of 1000 integers to each student pair (15 minutes setup). Students first trace through each algorithm using a target value of 847, documenting the number of operations required at each step on the provided worksheet (20 minutes). Next, have students calculate theoretical time complexities: they must identify the input size variable, determine how operations scale with input size, and express this as Big-O notation for each algorithm (25 minutes). Students then complete a structured comparison chart analyzing: prerequisite conditions (sorted vs unsorted data), memory requirements, best/worst/average case scenarios, and practical use cases for datasets of sizes 10, 1000, and 1,000,000 elements (30 minutes). For the final phase, student pairs write a 2-page analysis report recommending which algorithm to use for three given scenarios: searching a small unsorted contact list, finding records in a large sorted database, and implementing a spell-checker dictionary. Each recommendation must include specific Big-O justification and consideration of real-world constraints like memory usage and data preprocessing requirements (40 minutes). Conclude with pair presentations of one scenario analysis to the class (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Three algorithm implementations in Python or Java (linear search, binary search, hash table)
Dataset of 1000 integers in text file format
Algorithm tracing worksheet with step-by-step tables
Comparison chart template with complexity categories
Computers with IDE or code execution environment
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct Big-O notation calculation with proper mathematical reasoning (25%), (2) Accurate algorithm tracing showing step-by-step operations (25%), (3) Comprehensive comparison analysis addressing all required scenarios and constraints (30%), (4) Quality of written recommendations with clear justifications linking theory to practical applications (20%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example trace for bubble sort, offer a Big-O reference sheet with common patterns, and allow use of online Big-O calculators for verification. For advanced learners: Add analysis of space complexity, introduce amortized analysis for hash tables, or have them implement and analyze a fourth algorithm like interpolation search or Fibonacci search.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Model Architectures for Real-World Business Impact
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning approaches (traditional ML, deep learning, and ensemble methods) applied to a real business dataset, evaluating their performance, interpretability, computational efficiency, and business viability. They will synthesize their analysis into executive-level recommendations with detailed justifications for model selection in production environments.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative strengths and limitations of different ML architectures by systematically comparing performance metrics, interpretability scores, and resource requirements across identical datasets
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive cost-benefit analysis that weighs technical performance against business constraints and stakeholder requirements
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Dataset Analysis & Model Training**
Provide teams of 3-4 students with the Telco Customer Churn dataset and three pre-configured model templates: Random Forest (traditional ML), Neural Network (deep learning), and XGBoost + Voting Classifier (ensemble). Each team member takes ownership of one approach while collaborating on data preprocessing. Students must train all three models using identical 80/20 train-test splits with fixed random seeds, documenting hyperparameter tuning decisions and training times.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Multi-Dimensional Evaluation**
Teams create comprehensive evaluation matrices comparing models across six dimensions: predictive accuracy (precision, recall, F1), model interpretability (SHAP values, feature importance), computational efficiency (training time, inference speed, memory usage), robustness (cross-validation stability, outlier sensitivity), scalability (performance with dataset size variations), and business applicability (implementation complexity, maintenance requirements). Students must generate quantitative scores and qualitative assessments for each dimension.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Stakeholder Impact Analysis**
Teams assume roles of different business stakeholders (IT operations, marketing team, C-suite executives) and evaluate how each model choice impacts their specific needs. They must identify potential conflicts between stakeholder priorities and propose resolution strategies.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Executive Recommendation Synthesis**
Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation with final model recommendation, including decision matrix, risk assessment, implementation roadmap, and alternative scenarios. Teams must defend their choices against peer questioning and instructor challenges about overlooked considerations or alternative interpretations.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (CSV format)
Jupyter Notebook environment with scikit-learn, TensorFlow, XGBoost, SHAP libraries pre-installed
Model template notebooks for Random Forest, Neural Network, and Ensemble approaches
Business context document with stakeholder personas and constraints
Evaluation matrix template spreadsheet
Presentation template with required sections
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Technical Rigor - accuracy and depth of model comparison analysis (25%), (2) Critical Thinking - identification of trade-offs and limitations not explicitly stated (25%), (3) Business Judgment - realistic assessment of implementation challenges and stakeholder needs (20%), (4) Evidence Quality - appropriate use of quantitative metrics and qualitative reasoning (20%), (5) Recommendation Defense - ability to justify decisions under questioning and consider alternative perspectives (10%). Deliverables include completed evaluation matrices, stakeholder impact analysis documents, and presentation with Q&A performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide decision trees showing which metrics to prioritize under different business scenarios, and offer templates with partially completed evaluation criteria. For advanced learners: Add constraints such as regulatory compliance requirements (GDPR, fairness metrics), budget limitations, or time-to-market pressures. Challenge them to incorporate A/B testing design considerations and model monitoring strategies into their recommendations.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimal Resource Distribution in Emergency Scenarios
description: Students will create an original multi-variable optimization model to solve a complex emergency resource allocation problem, incorporating real-world constraints and uncertainty factors. They will develop both the mathematical framework and a computational implementation to validate their solution.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize linear programming, probability theory, and graph theory concepts by constructing an original optimization model for emergency resource distribution
Students will design and implement a computational algorithm through coding that solves their mathematical model and generates actionable recommendations
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a complex scenario: A natural disaster has struck a region with 15 population centers of varying sizes, connected by a damaged transportation network. Students have 120 minutes to work in pairs. First 20 minutes: Each pair selects their specific disaster type (earthquake, hurricane, wildfire) and defines 8-10 variable parameters including population densities, resource types (medical supplies, food, water, personnel), transportation costs, time constraints, and supply limitations. Minutes 21-40: Students must formulate their mathematical model using at least three optimization techniques—linear programming for resource allocation, graph theory for transportation routing, and probability distributions for demand uncertainty. They should define objective functions, constraint equations, and decision variables clearly on provided worksheets. Minutes 41-80: Using Python, MATLAB, or Excel Solver, students code their model, input realistic data values, and run simulations. They must test at least 3 different scenarios (best case, worst case, most likely case) and document results in a structured data table. Minutes 81-100: Students create a visual presentation showing their model structure, computational results, and practical recommendations for emergency coordinators. Final 20 minutes: Each pair presents their solution to another pair for peer evaluation, explaining their mathematical reasoning and defending their modeling choices through structured questioning.
materials_needed: Laptops with Python/MATLAB/Excel Solver installed
Structured worksheet templates for model formulation
Real demographic and infrastructure data packets for 15 fictional cities
Graph paper and mathematical reference sheets
Digital presentation software access
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Mathematical rigor - proper use of optimization techniques and constraint formulation, (2) Model originality - creative integration of multiple mathematical concepts, (3) Computational accuracy - correct implementation and realistic results, (4) Real-world applicability - practical feasibility of recommendations, (5) Communication clarity - ability to explain complex mathematical reasoning. Each criterion worth 20 points for 100-point total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint equation templates and step-by-step coding tutorials. Offer simplified 5-city scenarios with guided parameter selection. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate machine learning predictions for dynamic demand forecasting, add multi-objective optimization considering both cost and response time, or extend to multi-period models with evolving disaster conditions.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall binary number representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and verbal recitation. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the correct binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by matching flashcards with 100% accuracy
Students will recite from memory the binary equivalents of decimal numbers 0-15 through timed verbal recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student pair - one set with decimal numbers 0-15 on white cards, another set with corresponding 4-bit binary numbers on blue cards (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Give students 5 minutes to examine both sets and notice patterns. Next, conduct guided practice: hold up decimal cards while students chorus the binary equivalent, starting with 0-7, then 8-15. Repeat this 3 times with increasing speed. For independent practice (15 minutes), students work in pairs taking turns: one student shows a decimal card, partner states binary equivalent, then they check using the blue cards. Switch roles every 5 cards. Follow with a memory consolidation round where students close their eyes and partner calls out decimal numbers for verbal binary responses. Conclude with a whole-class rapid-fire challenge: teacher calls random decimal numbers, students write binary answers on mini whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Record individual accuracy rates for assessment. End by having students create their own memory tricks for challenging numbers (like 'decimal 10 is binary 1010 - one zero one zero').
materials_needed: 16 white index cards labeled with decimal numbers 0-15
16 blue index cards labeled with 4-bit binary equivalents (0000-1111)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Timer or stopwatch
Assessment checklist for tracking individual student accuracy
assessment_method: Use a checklist to record each student's accuracy during the final rapid-fire round. Success criteria: 80% accuracy (13/16 correct) on decimal-to-binary conversions within 3-second response time per number. Document specific numbers students struggle with for follow-up practice. Observe pair work for participation and peer teaching behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: start with numbers 0-7 only, provide printed binary place value chart (8-4-2-1), allow finger counting on place values. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (16-31), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, challenge them to create conversion tricks for teaching peers. Consider grouping strong students with those needing support.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recognition Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid recognition exercises within 3 seconds per conversion
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary-decimal conversion flashcards to each student (16 cards total, covering 0000-1111 binary to 0-15 decimal). Start with a 5-minute individual study period where students examine both sides of each card, saying the conversions aloud quietly. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 10 minutes: Partner A shows the decimal side, Partner B states the binary equivalent, then they switch. Circulate to ensure correct pronunciation of binary digits. After partner practice, conduct a whole-class 'popcorn' review where you randomly call out either a decimal or binary number, and students respond with the conversion. For the main assessment, students work individually through a timed recognition worksheet with 20 mixed conversion problems (both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal). Allow exactly 60 seconds for completion. Conclude with a quick group recitation where the class chants the complete conversion sequence from 0000 (zero) through 1111 (fifteen) in unison. Throughout the activity, emphasize that students should visualize the number patterns and use repetition rather than calculation methods. Remind students that this is pure memorization work - they should not be computing conversions but rather developing automatic recall of these fundamental relationships.
materials_needed: 16 double-sided flashcards per student (binary on one side, decimal on other)
Timed recognition worksheet with 20 conversion problems
Stopwatch or timer
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Grade the 60-second timed worksheet for accuracy: 18-20 correct = Mastery (90-100%), 16-17 correct = Proficient (80-89%), 14-15 correct = Developing (70-79%), below 14 = Needs Retry. Record completion time for students achieving mastery. Observe during partner work for correct verbal responses and note students requiring additional practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a visual pattern chart showing binary place values (8-4-2-1) and allow extra study time with the flashcards. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider having fast finishers help tutor classmates or create additional practice problems.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Recognition Challenge

title: Optimization in Agricultural Resource Allocation: A Multi-Variable Calculus Application
description: Students will apply advanced calculus techniques including partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization to solve a real-world agricultural resource allocation problem. They will determine optimal crop distributions and resource investments to maximize profit while working within realistic constraints such as land area, water availability, and labor capacity.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing a multi-variable profit function for agricultural production
Students will implement gradient vector calculations and interpret economic marginal rates of substitution through systematic mathematical modeling of resource allocation scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario worksheet featuring 'GreenField Farms' - a 500-acre operation growing corn, soybeans, and wheat with specific profit margins ($180/acre corn, $150/acre soybeans, $120/acre wheat). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to set up the problem framework, identifying variables (x₁=corn acres, x₂=soybean acres, x₃=wheat acres) and constraints (land: x₁+x₂+x₃≤500; water: 25x₁+20x₂+15x₃≤10,000 gallons; labor: 8x₁+6x₂+4x₃≤3,200 hours). Next, spend 25 minutes having students construct the Lagrangian function L(x₁,x₂,x₃,λ₁,λ₂,λ₃) = 180x₁+150x₂+120x₃-λ₁(x₁+x₂+x₃-500)-λ₂(25x₁+20x₂+15x₃-10,000)-λ₃(8x₁+6x₂+4x₃-3,200). Students then calculate all partial derivatives and set them equal to zero, creating a system of six equations. Allow 35 minutes for systematic equation solving using substitution and elimination methods, with instructor circulating to verify intermediate steps. Students must solve for optimal acreage allocation and calculate the maximum profit. In the final 15 minutes, pairs present their solutions, explaining the economic interpretation of their Lagrange multipliers (shadow prices) and discussing how constraint changes would affect optimal allocation. Students must verify their solution satisfies all constraints and represents a maximum using the bordered Hessian determinant test.
materials_needed: GreenField Farms scenario worksheet with profit margins and constraint data
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Mathematica, Maple, or Python with SciPy)
Large grid paper for systematic equation organization
Constraint verification checklist template
assessment_method: Students submit a complete solution portfolio including: (1) Properly constructed Lagrangian function (25 points), (2) Correct calculation of all six partial derivative equations (30 points), (3) Accurate solution of the system yielding optimal allocation (25 points), (4) Economic interpretation of Lagrange multipliers and constraint analysis (15 points), (5) Mathematical verification using second-order conditions (5 points). Solutions must show all algebraic steps and include constraint verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed Lagrangian setup and guide them through the first two partial derivatives as examples. Offer a step-by-step equation solving template. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by having them calculate how the optimal solution changes with ±10% variations in each constraint, or extend to include risk analysis using variance in crop prices.

title: Dissecting Cache Performance: Analyzing Memory Hierarchy Trade-offs in Real-World Applications
description: Students analyze actual cache performance data from three different processor architectures running identical algorithms to identify bottlenecks and evaluate design decisions. They examine cache miss rates, access patterns, and performance counters to determine optimal cache configurations for specific computational workloads.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze cache performance metrics by comparing miss rates, hit ratios, and access patterns across three different processor architectures
Students will evaluate memory hierarchy design trade-offs through systematic examination of performance data and architectural specifications
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student group with three datasets containing cache performance metrics from Intel Core i9 (complex OoO), ARM Cortex-A78 (mobile-optimized), and AMD Zen 3 (high-throughput) processors. Each dataset includes: L1/L2/L3 cache specifications, performance counter data for matrix multiplication, linked list traversal, and hash table operations, plus memory access trace files. **Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students create comparison tables documenting cache sizes, associativity, replacement policies, and miss penalties for each architecture. They calculate miss rates per cache level for each workload and identify patterns in the memory access traces using provided visualization tools. **Phase 2 - Bottleneck Analysis (30 minutes):** Groups analyze where performance degradation occurs by examining: cache capacity misses vs. conflict misses, prefetcher effectiveness, and memory bandwidth utilization. They graph performance scaling as working set sizes increase beyond cache capacities. **Phase 3 - Design Evaluation (25 minutes):** Students determine which architectural choices (cache size, associativity, prefetching strategies) best serve each workload type. They must justify their analysis using quantitative evidence from the performance data. **Synthesis (15 minutes):** Each group presents one key insight about cache design trade-offs, supported by specific metrics from their analysis.
materials_needed: Three pre-generated cache performance datasets (Intel, ARM, AMD architectures)
Memory access trace visualization software (Cachegrind or custom Python scripts)
Performance counter analysis templates in spreadsheet format
Architectural specification reference sheets for each processor
assessment_method: Students submit analysis reports containing: (1) Accurate calculation and comparison of cache metrics (25 points), (2) Identification of at least 3 specific bottlenecks with supporting evidence (30 points), (3) Justified recommendations for cache optimization based on workload characteristics (25 points), (4) Quality of synthesis connecting performance data to architectural design decisions (20 points). Groups also deliver 3-minute presentations demonstrating one key analytical insight.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide worked examples of cache miss rate calculations and highlight key metrics to focus on first. Offer guided questions like 'What happens to miss rate when working set exceeds L2 cache size?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict performance on hybrid workloads, analyze power consumption trade-offs, or model the impact of different replacement policies using the provided trace data.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and judge the effectiveness of different data visualizations created from a customer satisfaction survey dataset. They will compare multiple chart types, evaluate their appropriateness for the data and audience, and make evidence-based recommendations for the most effective visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and histograms by analyzing their clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness for categorical survey data
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using established data visualization principles
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with a printed customer satisfaction survey dataset (50 responses, 5 questions with ratings 1-5) and three different visualizations of the same 'Overall Satisfaction' question: a horizontal bar chart, a pie chart, and a histogram. Give students 10 minutes to individually examine all three visualizations and the raw data.

Next, distribute the 'Visualization Evaluation Framework' handout containing four criteria: clarity (can audience understand quickly?), accuracy (does it represent data truthfully?), appropriateness (matches data type and audience needs?), and visual appeal (professional and engaging?). Students spend 15 minutes scoring each visualization on a 1-4 scale for each criterion, writing specific evidence for their scores.

Form groups of 3-4 students for 20 minutes of structured discussion. Each group member presents their evaluation of one visualization, sharing scores and evidence. Groups must reach consensus on ranking the three visualizations from most to least effective, documenting their reasoning.

Conclude with a 15-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents their ranking and top two reasons. Record group rankings on the whiteboard to identify patterns and facilitate debate about differing evaluations.

Finally, students individually complete a 10-minute written reflection answering: 'Which visualization would you recommend to the company's CEO and why?' and 'What would you change about your top-ranked visualization to make it even more effective?'
materials_needed: Printed customer satisfaction dataset (1 per student)
Three different visualizations of the same data (bar chart, pie chart, histogram) - 1 set per student
Visualization Evaluation Framework handout with 4-point rubric
Whiteboard and markers
Individual reflection worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (1) Quality of evidence used to support visualization scores (specific examples from charts), (2) Depth of reasoning in group consensus process (documented justifications), and (3) Sophistication of final recommendation (considers audience needs, data type, and design principles). Success requires scoring 2/3 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters for evaluation criteria and pair them with stronger analytical thinkers during group work. Offer a completed example evaluation of a different chart type. For advanced learners, provide additional visualization types (scatter plots, box plots) to evaluate or ask them to sketch improvements to existing visualizations with specific design modifications.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations created from the same customer satisfaction survey dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization type.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and scatter plots by applying specific visualization criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for optimal data presentation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Customer Satisfaction Dataset (100 responses with ratings 1-5 for service, price, and quality) and three pre-made visualizations: a horizontal bar chart showing average ratings by category, a pie chart showing distribution of overall satisfaction levels, and a scatter plot comparing service vs. price ratings. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization and the raw dataset. They should identify what story each visualization tells and note initial impressions.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation framework using the provided rubric covering four criteria: Visual Clarity (is it easy to read?), Data Accuracy (does it correctly represent the data?), Message Effectiveness (does it clearly communicate insights?), and Audience Appropriateness (suitable for business executives?).

Step 3 (20 minutes): In pairs, students systematically evaluate each visualization using the rubric, scoring each criterion on a 1-4 scale and providing specific evidence. They should identify strengths and weaknesses, noting details like color choices, label clarity, and scale appropriateness.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Pairs complete an evaluation matrix comparing all three visualizations side-by-side, then write a 3-sentence recommendation stating which visualization is most effective and why, supported by their rubric scores.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conduct a class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their recommendations and reasoning. Focus on how different criteria might lead to different conclusions and the importance of considering audience needs in visualization selection.
materials_needed: Customer Satisfaction Dataset (Excel file with 100 survey responses)
Three pre-made visualizations (bar chart, pie chart, scatter plot) as PDF handouts
Visualization Evaluation Rubric (4 criteria, 4-point scale)
Evaluation Matrix worksheet template
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation matrices with rubric scores and evidence for each visualization, plus their final recommendation paragraph. Grade using a 20-point scale: accurate rubric application (8 points), quality of evidence provided (6 points), clear recommendation with justification (4 points), and professional presentation (2 points).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters for evidence statements and highlight specific elements to look for in each visualization. For advanced learners, ask them to suggest specific improvements for the weakest visualization or consider how different stakeholder audiences might prefer different visualization types.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer satisfaction dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and scatter plots by applying specific data visualization criteria to customer satisfaction data
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison and justify their recommendations using evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by distributing three printed visualizations of identical customer satisfaction survey data (100 responses, 5-point scale across 4 categories: product quality, customer service, pricing, delivery). Visualization A shows a grouped bar chart, Visualization B shows four pie charts, and Visualization C shows a scatter plot matrix. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to examine each visualization and complete the 'First Impressions' worksheet, noting what story each chart tells and any immediate concerns.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation framework using the provided criteria sheet: Clarity (can insights be quickly understood?), Accuracy (does the chart type match the data?), Completeness (are all important patterns visible?), and Audience Appropriateness (suitable for business executives?).

Step 3 (20 minutes): In pairs, students systematically evaluate each visualization using the scoring rubric (1-4 scale per criterion). They must document specific evidence for each score and identify strengths/weaknesses.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair completes a recommendation memo (template provided) selecting the most effective visualization and explaining their reasoning with specific examples from their evaluation.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Three pairs present their recommendations to the class (2 minutes each), followed by a brief discussion comparing different conclusions and reasoning approaches.

Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students individually write one key insight about effective data visualization evaluation.
materials_needed: Three printed customer satisfaction visualizations (one set per student)
Evaluation criteria reference sheet with 4-point rubric
First Impressions worksheet template
Business memo recommendation template
Timer for time management
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Systematic application of evaluation criteria with specific evidence (40%), (2) Quality of reasoning in recommendation memo including clear justification (35%), (3) Identification of specific strengths and weaknesses in each visualization (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ in each category and demonstrating evidence-based decision making rather than personal preference.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation comments and highlight 2-3 specific elements to focus on per visualization.
