For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to redesign the weakest visualization and explain their design choices, or evaluate how different stakeholder audiences might prefer different approaches.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis: Exercise 3
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer satisfaction dataset to determine which best communicates key insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique visualization choices through structured comparison and justify their recommendations with evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three different visualizations of a customer satisfaction dataset (bar chart, pie chart, and scatter plot showing the same 5-question survey results from 100 customers). Distribute the evaluation worksheet with criteria: clarity (can insights be understood quickly?), accuracy (does the chart represent data truthfully?), and appropriateness (does the chart type match the data and message?). 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses using the three criteria. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students complete the evaluation matrix, rating each visualization 1-5 on each criterion and writing specific justifications for their scores. They must identify at least one strength and one weakness per visualization.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Pairs rank the three visualizations from most to least effective, writing a 3-sentence recommendation explaining their top choice with specific evidence from their evaluation.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Conduct gallery walk where pairs post their rankings and justifications. Students place dots next to evaluations they agree with and write questions on sticky notes for evaluations they disagree with.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Debrief as a class, discussing common evaluation patterns and addressing disagreements. Focus on how different evaluation criteria might lead to different conclusions about visualization effectiveness.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of customer satisfaction data (one per student)
Evaluation worksheet with criteria matrix
Sticky notes and dot stickers
Large poster paper for gallery walk display
assessment_method: Grade evaluation matrices using rubric: 4 points for complete criterion application with specific evidence, 3 points for clear justifications with some evidence, 2 points for basic evaluation with minimal support, 1 point for incomplete evaluation. Additionally assess final recommendation for logical reasoning and use of evaluation evidence (5-point scale).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is clear because...' and 'The accuracy is questionable due to...' For advanced learners, add a fourth criterion about visual design principles or ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-ranked visualization.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Analysis

title: Advanced Algorithms Flashcard Mastery Challenge: Complexity Classification and Properties
description: Students will memorize and recall key properties, time/space complexities, and implementation characteristics of 25 advanced algorithms across graph theory, dynamic programming, and string processing domains. This intensive recall activity uses spaced repetition techniques to build foundational algorithmic knowledge required for advanced computer science coursework.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall time and space complexity notations for 25 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, KMP, and A* by completing timed flashcard sessions

Students will identify specific algorithmic properties and constraints (such as negative edge handling, optimal substructure requirements, and worst-case scenarios) through systematic memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared algorithm reference sheets containing 25 algorithms organized into three categories: Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's, Topological Sort, A*, DFS/BFS variants), Dynamic Programming (Knapsack variants, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Coin Change), and String Processing (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Suffix Arrays, Aho-Corasick). Students work individually for the first 15 minutes, creating physical flashcards with algorithm names on front and comprehensive details on back including: Big O time/space complexity, key properties, input constraints, and one real-world application. Next, implement a structured spaced repetition protocol: Round 1 (10 minutes) - students review all 25 cards, separating into 'confident' and 'needs review' piles. Round 2 (8 minutes) - focus only on 'needs review' cards, again sorting by confidence level. Round 3 (5 minutes) - final review of remaining difficult cards. After individual study, pair students for peer testing: Partner A selects random cards and asks specific questions ('What is the time complexity of Floyd-Warshall?', 'Which algorithms handle negative edges?', 'What property must problems have for dynamic programming?'). Partners alternate every 5 minutes for total 20 minutes of peer assessment. Conclude with rapid-fire whole-class quiz where instructor calls out algorithm names and students must immediately state time complexity and one key property within 10 seconds per response.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm reference sheets (25 algorithms with complete specifications)
Blank index cards (minimum 25 per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Randomized question bank for peer testing phase
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (23/25 correct) on final rapid-fire quiz covering algorithm complexities and properties. Award points as follows: correct time complexity (2 points), correct space complexity (1 point), accurate key property identification (2 points) per algorithm. Track individual performance during peer testing phase using observation checklist. Provide immediate feedback and require re-study of missed items.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-made acronyms and memory devices (e.g., 'BED' for Bellman-ford handles Negative Edges and Detects negative cycles), allow additional 5-minute study periods between rounds, and pair with stronger students during peer testing. For advanced learners: include additional algorithms (Red-Black tree operations, FFT, Network Flow algorithms), require recall of specific implementation details or prove complexity bounds, and challenge them to create memory devices for classmates.

title: Interpreting Advanced Cross-Validation Results for Model Selection in High-Dimensional Data
description: Students will analyze and interpret complex cross-validation outputs from multiple machine learning algorithms applied to high-dimensional datasets. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining variance-bias tradeoffs, overfitting indicators, and model selection rationale across different CV strategies including nested CV, time series CV, and group CV.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation performance metrics and variance patterns by analyzing CV output tables and learning curves from at least 5 different algorithms on high-dimensional data
Students will explain the implications of different cross-validation strategies through written analysis comparing nested CV, time-series CV, and stratified group CV results
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 min):** Distribute three pre-computed cross-validation result datasets: (1) 10-fold CV on genomics data (p=50,000, n=500) with Random Forest, SVM, Elastic Net, XGBoost, and Neural Network; (2) Time-series CV on financial data with same algorithms; (3) Nested CV results showing inner/outer loop performance. Each dataset includes mean scores, standard deviations, feature importance rankings, and learning curves. **Phase 2 (25 min):** Students work in pairs to create comparison matrices identifying: highest mean performance, lowest variance, evidence of overfitting (training vs validation gaps), algorithm stability across folds, and computational complexity indicators. **Phase 3 (30 min):** Each pair writes a 500-word technical memo explaining: why certain algorithms show high variance in high-dimensional settings, how time-series CV results differ from standard CV and why, what the nested CV outer loop reveals about true generalization, and which model they would select for each scenario with specific justification. **Phase 4 (15 min):** Pairs present their model selection decisions to another pair, defending their interpretations and discussing alternative viewpoints. Instructor circulates to probe understanding with questions like 'Why might Random Forest show lower variance than SVM here?' and 'What would happen if we had more samples than features?'
materials_needed: Three pre-computed CV result datasets (CSV format with performance metrics, standard deviations, and learning curve data)
Cross-validation interpretation guide with key indicators of overfitting and underfitting
Technical memo template with specific sections for each analysis component
Laptops with Excel/Google Sheets or Python/R for data visualization
assessment_method: Grade technical memos using rubric: (1) Correct identification of overfitting indicators (25 points), (2) Accurate explanation of CV strategy differences (25 points), (3) Justified model selection with consideration of variance-bias tradeoff (30 points), (4) Proper interpretation of high-dimensional data challenges (20 points). Students must achieve 80% to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide interpretation flowchart with decision trees for common CV patterns and sample phrases for technical writing. For advanced learners: Include additional scenarios with class imbalance, missing data patterns, or conflicting metrics (precision vs recall) requiring more nuanced interpretation and discussion of business context impact on model selection.

title: Planning a Class Pizza Party: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios
description: Students will apply their knowledge of fraction addition, subtraction, and multiplication to solve authentic problems related to planning food portions for a class party. They will calculate pizza quantities, determine leftover amounts, and adjust recipes using mixed numbers and improper fractions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication) to solve real-world problems involving food planning and portion calculations
Students will demonstrate understanding of mixed numbers and improper fractions through practical scenario-based computations with step-by-step justification
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: 'Our class of 24 students is planning a pizza party, and you're the food coordinator.' Distribute the Pizza Party Planning worksheet to each student (15 minutes total setup). 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to solve Problem 1 - 'Each student eats 2¼ slices on average. If each pizza has 8 slices, how many pizzas do we need?' Students must show conversion of mixed numbers to improper fractions (2¼ = 9/4), multiply by 24 students, then divide by 8 slices per pizza.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Pair students to tackle Problem 2 - 'We ordered 7 pizzas but only 5⅜ pizzas were eaten. How much pizza is left?' Students practice subtracting mixed numbers, requiring them to borrow when necessary (7 - 5⅜ = 1⅝ pizzas remaining).

Step 3 (15 minutes): In groups of 3-4, students solve Problem 3 - 'The leftover pizza will be divided equally among 5 teachers. How much does each teacher get?' This requires dividing 1⅝ by 5, reinforcing division of fractions.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students complete Problem 4 - 'If we want to make fruit punch using a recipe that serves 8 people but need to serve 24, and the recipe calls for 2¾ cups of juice concentrate, how much concentrate do we need?' Students apply fraction multiplication in scaling recipes.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Whole-class discussion where 3-4 students present their solutions on the board, explaining their fraction operations and real-world reasoning. Teacher facilitates peer feedback and addresses common misconceptions.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning worksheet (one per student)
Calculator (optional, for checking work)
Whiteboard markers and erasers
Fraction strips or visual aids for struggling students
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheets showing all mathematical steps and conversions. Grading rubric: 4 points per problem (1 point for correct setup, 2 points for accurate fraction operations, 1 point for reasonable final answer). Observe group discussions for mathematical reasoning and peer collaboration. Minimum 12/16 points indicates proficiency in applying fraction operations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide fraction strips, allow use of visual pizza models, and pair with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: Add extension problems involving decimal conversions, percentage calculations for food costs, or creating their own multi-step party planning scenarios with fraction operations. Consider allowing advanced students to create problems for classmates.

title: Analyzing Algorithm Efficiency: Big O Notation Performance Breakdown
description: Students will analyze the time complexity of different sorting algorithms by examining their code implementations and comparing their performance characteristics. They will break down each algorithm's operations to determine Big O notation and evaluate which algorithm is most efficient for different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort algorithms by examining their nested loops and recursive calls to determine accurate Big O notation
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency trade-offs through systematic comparison of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for each sorting method
instructions: Begin by providing students with printed code implementations of three sorting algorithms: bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (10 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one algorithm initially. Each group spends 15 minutes identifying and marking all loops, recursive calls, and operations in their assigned algorithm, using colored highlighters to distinguish between different operation types. Groups then create a step-by-step operation count analysis, tracking how operations scale with input size n. After initial analysis, groups rotate algorithms every 10 minutes until each group has analyzed all three algorithms (30 minutes total rotation). Next, groups use provided datasets of different sizes (100, 1000, 10000 elements) to predict performance differences and fill out a comparison matrix showing time complexity for best/average/worst cases (15 minutes). Groups then test their predictions using provided timing code snippets to measure actual execution times on the different datasets (15 minutes). Finally, each group presents their findings for one algorithm to the class, explaining their Big O analysis methodology and comparing predicted vs. actual performance results (15 minutes presentations). Conclude with a class discussion comparing all three algorithms and determining optimal use cases for each based on the analysis (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort (one set per group)
Colored highlighters (3 colors per group)
Algorithm comparison matrix worksheets
Pre-generated datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 integer elements
Computer access with Python/Java environment and timing measurement code templates
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices for accurate Big O notation identification (40 points), quality of step-by-step operation analysis with clear reasoning (30 points), accuracy of performance predictions vs. actual results (20 points), and group presentation clarity explaining analytical methodology (10 points). Success criteria: 80% accuracy in Big O identification, clear documentation of analysis steps, and demonstration of understanding efficiency trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide operation counting templates with partially completed examples and focus on analyzing simpler bubble sort first. Offer visual flowcharts showing algorithm execution steps. For advanced learners: Include analysis of space complexity, challenge them to analyze additional algorithms like heap sort, or have them optimize one algorithm's implementation and re-analyze the improved version.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Model Performance Across Demographic Segments
description: Students will critically assess the fairness, reliability, and business impact of three competing machine learning models for loan approval by analyzing performance disparities across different demographic groups. They will synthesize quantitative metrics with ethical considerations to make evidence-based recommendations for model deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML models by systematically analyzing bias metrics, predictive accuracy, and fairness indicators across demographic segments
Students will critique model deployment decisions through synthesis of technical performance data, ethical implications, and business constraints to formulate justified recommendations
instructions: **Phase 1 - Data Exploration (45 minutes):** Distribute the loan dataset containing 10,000 records with features including credit score, income, age, gender, race, and loan outcomes. Students work in teams of 3-4 to load three pre-trained models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) and generate predictions on the test set. Each team calculates baseline accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores for each model using provided Python scripts. **Phase 2 - Bias Analysis (60 minutes):** Teams compute demographic parity, equalized odds, and calibration metrics across gender and racial groups using the fairness-indicators library. Students create comparative visualizations showing performance disparities and document instances where models exhibit differential treatment. They must identify at least 3 specific bias patterns and quantify their magnitude. **Phase 3 - Business Impact Assessment (45 minutes):** Teams receive business context documents outlining regulatory requirements (Equal Credit Opportunity Act), cost matrices (false positive = $500 loss, false negative = $2000 loss), and deployment constraints. Students calculate expected monetary impact for each model and assess regulatory compliance risk. **Phase 4 - Critical Evaluation & Recommendation (60 minutes):** Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation defending their model recommendation. They must address trade-offs between accuracy and fairness, justify their weighting of different stakeholder concerns, and propose specific mitigation strategies for identified biases. Teams present to other groups who serve as a review board, asking probing questions about methodology and assumptions.
materials_needed: Loan approval dataset (CSV file with 10,000 records)
Three pre-trained models (pkl files: logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost)
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, fairness-indicators, matplotlib
Business context packet including regulatory guidelines and cost matrices
Evaluation rubric handouts for peer assessment
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical accuracy of bias calculations and model metrics, (2) Depth of fairness analysis with specific quantified examples, (3) Integration of business constraints and regulatory considerations, (4) Quality of evidence-based argumentation in recommendations, (5) Critical questioning during peer presentations. Final deliverable includes team presentation and individual 2-page reflection analyzing limitations of their chosen approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide code templates for bias calculations and interpretation guides for fairness metrics. Create checkpoint sheets for each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose novel fairness constraints, implement additional bias detection techniques, or design A/B testing frameworks for deployment. Encourage exploration of intersectional bias analysis across multiple demographic dimensions simultaneously.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Urban Traffic Flow Optimization
description: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, statistics, and linear programming to create an original mathematical model that predicts optimal traffic light timing for a simulated urban intersection. They will validate their model using real traffic data and present implementation recommendations to a mock city planning committee.
estimated_duration: 315 minutes (5.25 hours) spread across 2-3 class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multivariable calculus, statistical regression, and optimization theory by constructing an original traffic flow prediction model
Students will evaluate model effectiveness through statistical validation and create actionable policy recommendations for urban planners
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Modeler, Data Analyst, Validation Specialist, and Policy Advisor. Provide each team with the intersection dataset containing 6 months of hourly traffic counts, current signal timing, and accident reports. 

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the raw data to identify patterns, seasonal trends, and peak flow periods. Students must create at least three preliminary mathematical relationships using regression analysis, incorporating variables such as time of day, day of week, weather conditions, and special events. Each team documents their data exploration process and justifies their variable selection using statistical significance tests.

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Students construct their optimization model by defining objective functions (minimize wait time, maximize throughput, minimize accidents) and constraints (minimum pedestrian crossing time, maximum cycle length, coordination with adjacent intersections). Teams must incorporate calculus-based rate of change analysis for dynamic timing adjustments and use linear programming techniques to solve their optimization problem. Students program their model using Python or MATLAB, creating functions that accept real-time inputs.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Teams validate their models by testing against reserved validation dataset (20% of original data) and calculating prediction accuracy metrics including R-squared values, mean absolute error, and confidence intervals. Students must achieve minimum 75% prediction accuracy to proceed to presentation phase.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents their model to simulated city planning committee (instructor and guest experts), delivering 10-minute presentations including mathematical derivation, validation results, implementation costs, and expected traffic improvement percentages. Teams must defend their model choices during 5-minute Q&A sessions.
materials_needed: Urban intersection traffic dataset (CSV format with 6 months hourly data)
Computers with Python/MATLAB software installed
Graphing calculators or statistical software packages
Large format paper and markers for model visualization
Access to online traffic engineering resources and databases
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and model complexity (25 points), statistical validation and accuracy metrics (25 points), programming implementation and documentation (20 points), presentation clarity and policy recommendations (20 points), team collaboration and peer feedback (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery level.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling teams with template optimization frameworks and guided worksheets for variable identification. Advanced learners can incorporate machine learning algorithms, consider multi-intersection coordination, or add environmental impact factors. Offer mid-activity check-ins where teams present progress for instructor feedback and peer suggestions.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Urban Traffic Flow Optimization: Visual Analysis
description: Students will develop an original mathematical model combining differential equations, graph theory, and optimization techniques to solve real-world urban traffic congestion problems. They will create both theoretical frameworks and computational implementations, then validate their models against actual traffic data.
estimated_duration: 6-7 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions or intensive workshop format)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize differential equations, network theory, and linear programming to construct an original traffic flow optimization model by integrating multiple mathematical domains
Students will design computational algorithms and create visual simulations through programming to demonstrate their model's effectiveness in solving urban planning challenges
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with authentic traffic data from a major city intersection (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Modeler (differential equations), Network Analyst (graph theory), Optimization Specialist (linear programming), and Data Validator (statistical analysis). 

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze provided traffic count data, identify key variables (traffic density, flow rates, signal timing, pedestrian crossings), and research existing models. Each specialist researches their domain's application to traffic systems, then teams reconvene to brainstorm integration approaches.

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Teams construct their mathematical model. Lead Modelers develop differential equations for traffic flow dynamics, Network Analysts create graph representations of intersection topology, Optimization Specialists formulate objective functions for minimizing wait times, and Data Validators establish statistical measures for model accuracy. Teams must document all mathematical reasoning and assumptions.

Phase 3 (90 minutes): Implementation phase where teams translate their mathematical model into computational code using Python or MATLAB. They create visual simulations showing traffic flow under current conditions versus their optimized solution. Teams must demonstrate their model works with the provided dataset.

Phase 4 (60 minutes): Validation and presentation. Teams test their models against reserved validation data, calculate prediction accuracy, and prepare 10-minute presentations explaining their approach, mathematical reasoning, computational results, and real-world applicability. Include limitations and potential improvements.

Conclude with peer evaluation where teams critically assess other models' mathematical rigor, creativity, and practical feasibility (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Real traffic count datasets from municipal transportation departments (3-4 different intersections)
Computers with Python/MATLAB and mathematical plotting libraries installed
Graph paper and mathematical reference materials
Digital presentation tools (projector, laptops)
Printed traffic engineering standards and flow theory resources
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness (30 points), Creative integration of multiple mathematical domains (25 points), Computational implementation and visualization quality (20 points), Model validation and accuracy against test data (15 points), Presentation clarity and real-world applicability discussion (10 points). Success requires minimum 80% accuracy on validation dataset and demonstration of novel mathematical approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for each mathematical component and guided worksheets for model integration steps. Offer additional office hours for technical programming support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like weather conditions, emergency vehicle priority, or multi-objective optimization. Encourage exploration of machine learning integration or dynamic real-time model adaptation.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Urban Traffic Flow Optimization

title: Analyzing Network Protocol Vulnerabilities in Captured TCP Traffic
description: Students will examine real network packet captures to identify security vulnerabilities and protocol weaknesses in TCP communications. They will dissect packet structures, trace connection patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of different attack vectors against network protocols.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze TCP packet structures and communication patterns by examining authentic network captures to identify protocol-level vulnerabilities
Students will evaluate the security implications of different TCP flag combinations and sequence behaviors through systematic packet inspection and threat modeling
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 students) with three pre-selected PCAP files containing different network scenarios: normal HTTP traffic, a TCP SYN flood attack, and a session hijacking attempt. Students first spend 20 minutes individually examining the packet captures using Wireshark, documenting initial observations about packet counts, protocols used, and any anomalies noticed. Next, teams collaborate for 45 minutes to perform deep packet analysis: filtering traffic by protocol, examining TCP header fields (sequence numbers, flags, window sizes), identifying connection establishment and teardown patterns, and mapping communication flows between hosts. Students then spend 30 minutes creating a vulnerability assessment matrix, categorizing each identified weakness by severity (critical, high, medium, low) and attack vector type (DoS, data interception, session manipulation). Teams document their analysis methodology, including specific Wireshark filters used, statistical observations, and technical reasoning for vulnerability classifications. In the final 25 minutes, each team presents one critical finding to the class, explaining the technical mechanism of the vulnerability, potential impact, and recommended mitigation strategies. Throughout the activity, students maintain detailed logs of their analysis process, including screenshots of relevant packets, filter commands used, and reasoning for their security assessments.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared PCAP files with different attack scenarios
Wireshark network protocol analyzer software
Vulnerability assessment matrix template
Individual workstations with network analysis capabilities
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 100-point rubric: technical accuracy of packet analysis (30 points), depth of vulnerability identification (25 points), quality of security impact assessment (20 points), clarity of methodology documentation (15 points), and effectiveness of presentation (10 points). Review submitted analysis reports, vulnerability matrices, and peer evaluations of presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured Wireshark filter templates and a guided analysis checklist focusing on specific TCP header fields. Advanced learners can be challenged to write custom scripts for automated vulnerability detection or analyze more complex multi-protocol attacks involving application-layer exploits.

title: Design and Build a Data-Driven Community Park Layout
description: Students will create an optimal park layout for their community by collecting real demographic data, applying geometric principles, and using proportional reasoning. They will present a scaled blueprint with mathematical justifications for their design choices based on population needs and spatial constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original park layout by integrating area calculations, proportional reasoning, and geometric transformations within a 500m × 300m rectangular plot
Students will construct mathematical arguments through data analysis of local demographics to justify facility sizing and placement decisions
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Collection (20 minutes)** Students work in teams of 3-4. Provide each team with fictional community demographic sheets showing population by age group (0-12: 15%, 13-17: 8%, 18-64: 62%, 65+: 15%) and activity preferences survey results. Teams calculate actual numbers of people in each category for a community of 25,000 residents. **Phase 2: Constraint Analysis (15 minutes)** Present the rectangular plot dimensions (500m × 300m = 150,000 m²). Teams must allocate space following requirements: playgrounds need 15 m² per child aged 0-12, sports courts require specific dimensions (basketball: 28m × 15m, tennis: 23.77m × 10.97m), walking paths must be minimum 3m wide, parking needs 12 m² per 100 residents, and 20% must remain green space. **Phase 3: Design Creation (40 minutes)** Using graph paper (1 square = 10m), teams sketch their park layout to scale. They must calculate areas for each facility, show geometric relationships, and ensure all constraints are met. Teams create a data table showing facility dimensions, areas, and population served. **Phase 4: Presentation Preparation (15 minutes)** Teams prepare 3-minute presentations explaining their mathematical reasoning, constraint solutions, and design trade-offs. **Phase 5: Gallery Walk and Presentations (20 minutes)** Teams post designs around room, conduct gallery walk for 10 minutes, then present solutions with mathematical justifications.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers and measuring tools
Calculators
Community demographic data sheets (fictional)
Facility requirement specification handouts
Colored pencils or markers
Large poster paper for final designs
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area calculations, proportional reasoning, constraint adherence), Design Innovation (creative solutions, efficient space use, aesthetic considerations), Mathematical Communication (clear justifications, proper use of geometric vocabulary, data presentation), and Collaboration (equal participation, respectful discussion, shared decision-making). Final deliverable includes scaled blueprint, calculation worksheet, and presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide area calculation templates, offer pre-made facility dimension cards, and suggest starting with largest facilities first. For advanced learners: Add budget constraints requiring cost-benefit analysis, introduce irregular plot shapes, or challenge them to optimize for accessibility compliance with specific pathway requirements and maximum distances between facilities.

title: Operating System Process State Transition Memorization and Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the seven standard process states in modern operating systems and their specific transition conditions. This activity uses spaced repetition and active recall techniques to ensure students can instantly identify process states, triggering events, and valid state transitions without reference materials.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all seven process states (New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, Terminated, Suspended Ready, Suspended Waiting) and their definitions within 30 seconds
Students will identify the specific system events that trigger each of the 12 possible state transitions through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Process State Reference Sheet containing definitions of New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, Terminated, Suspended Ready, and Suspended Waiting states, plus the 12 transition triggers (process creation, scheduler dispatch, time quantum expiration, I/O request, I/O completion, process termination, memory shortage leading to suspension, memory availability for unsuspension, etc.). Students study individually for 10 minutes, using highlighting and margin notes. Next, collect all reference materials. Conduct Round 1: Display process state names one at a time using slides. Students write definitions from memory (3 minutes per state, 21 minutes total). Round 2: Show transition scenarios (e.g., 'Process requests file read operation') and students identify the before/after states and triggering event (2 minutes per scenario, 12 scenarios, 24 minutes total). Round 3: Present state transition diagrams with missing labels. Students fill in state names and transition conditions (15 minutes). Between rounds, allow 2-minute peer discussion periods where students can compare answers but not consult materials. Conclude with immediate feedback session where correct answers are revealed and students self-assess their accuracy. Record individual scores for each round. Students who score below 80% in any round receive additional practice sheets for homework. Advanced students who achieve 95%+ accuracy proceed to create their own scenario questions for next class.
materials_needed: Process State Reference Sheet (laminated, collected after study period)
Individual answer sheets with numbered blanks for each round
PowerPoint slides with state transition scenarios
Blank state transition diagrams (printed copies)
Timer or stopwatch for time management
assessment_method: Students earn points based on accuracy in three rounds: Round 1 (35 points - 5 points per correct state definition), Round 2 (24 points - 2 points per correct transition identification), Round 3 (15 points - varies by diagram complexity). Success criteria: 80% overall accuracy (59/74 points) demonstrates successful memorization. Track common errors to identify concepts needing reinforcement. Provide individual score sheets with specific feedback on missed items.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (e.g., 'New Roads Run While Trucks Stay Stopped' for state sequence) and allow an extra 30 seconds per question. Create simplified diagrams focusing on the five basic states before introducing suspended states. For advanced learners: Challenge them to recall additional details like typical duration of each state, CPU scheduling algorithms that affect transitions, or real-world examples from specific operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS).

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code structure, identifying performance bottlenecks, and comparing their time complexity characteristics using both theoretical analysis and empirical testing. This activity develops critical thinking skills for algorithm evaluation and optimization decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by decomposing their recursive and iterative structures into constituent operations
Students will evaluate algorithm performance trade-offs through systematic comparison of theoretical complexity and empirical runtime data
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python. Give groups 10 minutes to examine the code structure without running it. Next, guide students through a 15-minute analysis phase where they identify and mark: (1) nested loops, (2) recursive calls, (3) comparison operations, and (4) data movement operations in each algorithm. Have groups create a visual breakdown chart showing the hierarchical structure of operations for each algorithm. In the third phase (20 minutes), students will instrument the provided code with counter variables to track actual comparisons and swaps, then run tests on pre-prepared datasets of sizes 100, 500, 1000, and 2000 elements. Students must record execution times and operation counts in a provided data table. During the final 15-minute synthesis phase, groups will plot their empirical data against theoretical complexity curves (provided as reference) and identify which algorithm performs best under different conditions. Each group will prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining one key insight about when to choose each algorithm. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing findings across groups and addressing any discrepancies between theoretical and observed performance.
materials_needed: Printed Python code for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (one set per group)
Pre-generated random integer datasets in CSV format (sizes: 100, 500, 1000, 2000)
Data recording worksheets with tables for timing and operation counts
Computers with Python 3.x and matplotlib installed
Reference graphs showing O(n²), O(n log n) complexity curves
assessment_method: Evaluate groups using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of code structure analysis and operation identification (25%), (2) Correct implementation of instrumentation code and data collection (25%), (3) Quality of empirical analysis and comparison with theoretical predictions (25%), (4) Clarity and insight demonstrated in final presentation (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in at least three categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated code examples highlighting loop structures and offer step-by-step guides for adding counter variables. Create simplified data collection templates with pre-filled headers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity, implement additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or explore worst-case vs. average-case scenarios with different input patterns (sorted, reverse-sorted, random data).

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their time complexity, space complexity, and practical runtime behavior. They will decompose each algorithm's structure to identify efficiency bottlenecks and compare performance across different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of sorting algorithms by examining their recursive structures, loop patterns, and memory usage
Students will evaluate algorithm performance trade-offs through systematic testing with varied data sets and identifying optimal use cases
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet containing implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python. Each group receives three data sets: sorted array (best case), reverse-sorted array (worst case), and random array (average case), each with 1000 elements.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine each algorithm's code structure, identifying loops, recursive calls, and memory allocations. They complete a code analysis table marking: number of nested loops, recursive depth, and auxiliary space requirements.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups run timing tests using the provided Python timer module, executing each algorithm on all three data sets. Students record execution times in milliseconds and calculate averages across 5 runs per combination.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students analyze their timing data, creating performance comparison charts and identifying patterns. They examine why certain algorithms perform better with specific data arrangements by tracing through algorithm steps.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Groups complete the analysis matrix, categorizing each algorithm's Big O notation for time/space complexity and determining optimal use cases. They identify specific code segments responsible for performance bottlenecks.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each group presents one key finding about algorithm trade-offs, explaining their reasoning using evidence from code structure and timing data. Conclude with class discussion comparing results across groups.
materials_needed: Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with pre-written sorting algorithm implementations
Python development environment (IDLE or online compiler)
Timer module code snippet for performance measurement
Three pre-generated data sets (sorted, reverse-sorted, random arrays)
Performance comparison chart template
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Algorithm Analysis Worksheet (40 points): code structure analysis accuracy (15 points), timing data collection and calculations (10 points), Big O complexity identification (10 points), and use case recommendations with justification (5 points). Assess group presentations on clarity of trade-off explanations supported by evidence (10 points).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide Big O notation reference sheet and highlight specific code lines to examine (loop beginnings, recursive calls). Offer guided questions like 'How many times does this loop execute?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict performance before testing, analyze memory usage patterns, or implement hybrid sorting approaches combining multiple algorithms.
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition: Practical Workshop
description: Students analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) by examining their code structure, identifying performance bottlenecks, and comparing time complexity through hands-on testing. They will break down each algorithm's components to understand how implementation choices affect computational efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the structural components of sorting algorithms by identifying loops, recursive calls, and data access patterns that contribute to time complexity
Students will compare algorithm performance through systematic testing and data analysis to determine optimal use cases for each sorting method
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) in their preferred programming language. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the code structure of each algorithm, identifying and documenting key components including nested loops, recursive calls, array access patterns, and conditional statements. They should create a visual breakdown showing the logical flow of each algorithm. Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups implement timing tests using arrays of different sizes (100, 1000, 10000 elements) with random data. Students record execution times for each algorithm-size combination, running each test 5 times and calculating averages. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students analyze their timing data by creating graphs showing performance trends and identifying which algorithms scale better with larger datasets. They should correlate their empirical results with the theoretical time complexities (O(n²), O(n log n)). Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups examine edge cases by testing with already-sorted arrays, reverse-sorted arrays, and arrays with duplicate values. Students document how each algorithm's performance changes and identify why certain algorithms handle specific data patterns better. Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams prepare a comparative analysis report identifying the strengths, weaknesses, and optimal use cases for each algorithm based on their structural analysis and performance testing. Conclude with group presentations of key findings and recommendations.
materials_needed: Computer with programming environment (Python, Java, or C++)
Pre-written sorting algorithm code files for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort
Spreadsheet software or graphing calculator for data analysis
Timer library or built-in timing functions documentation
Analysis worksheet template with sections for code structure, timing data, and conclusions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a rubric with four components: (1) Code Structure Analysis (25 points) - accurate identification of algorithmic components and complexity drivers, (2) Experimental Design (25 points) - proper implementation of timing tests and data collection, (3) Data Analysis (25 points) - correct interpretation of results and correlation with theoretical complexity, (4) Comparative Conclusions (25 points) - well-reasoned recommendations for algorithm selection based on use cases. Students submit their analysis worksheet, timing data, and a one-page summary of findings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide code annotation templates highlighting where to look for loops and recursive calls. Offer pre-made timing test templates and step-by-step guides for data collection. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or investigate space complexity alongside time complexity. Encourage exploration of hybrid algorithms or optimization techniques within existing implementations.
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition: Exercise 3
description: Students analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) by examining their time complexity, space usage, and behavior with different input datasets. They will break down each algorithm's components and synthesize findings into a comprehensive comparison report.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of sorting algorithms by tracing execution patterns and measuring performance metrics across varied input sizes
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency trade-offs through systematic comparison of computational resources and implementation complexity
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations and six test datasets: sorted array (1000 elements), reverse-sorted array (1000 elements), random array (1000 elements), nearly-sorted array (1000 elements), and two larger random datasets (5000 and 10000 elements). Students first spend 30 minutes individually examining the code structure of each algorithm, identifying key operations (comparisons, swaps, memory allocations) and documenting their observations in provided analysis worksheets. Next, teams collaboratively run performance tests (45 minutes), recording execution times and memory usage for each algorithm-dataset combination using the built-in profiling tools. Students must trace through at least 10 iterations manually for the smallest dataset to understand step-by-step execution patterns. Following data collection, teams analyze results by creating performance graphs, calculating growth rates between input sizes, and identifying best-case/worst-case scenarios for each algorithm (40 minutes). Finally, teams synthesize their findings into a structured comparison matrix examining: theoretical vs. actual performance, stability of sorting, adaptability to input patterns, and memory overhead. Each team presents their analysis conclusions in a 5-minute presentation, defending their recommendations for specific use cases. The instructor facilitates discussion comparing team findings and addresses discrepancies in results or interpretations.
materials_needed: Pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python/Java
Six prepared test datasets as CSV files with specified characteristics
Performance profiling software (Python's cProfile or Java's JProfiler)
Algorithm analysis worksheet templates with comparison matrices
Computers with programming environment and timing libraries installed
assessment_method: Students submit a completed analysis worksheet (40 points) including performance data, complexity calculations, and algorithm trace diagrams. Team comparison matrix with justified recommendations (30 points). Peer evaluation of team presentation clarity and technical accuracy (20 points). Instructor observation of analytical reasoning during algorithm tracing activities (10 points). Success criteria: accurate identification of time complexities, correct performance trend analysis, and logical recommendations based on evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide algorithm pseudocode with line-by-line complexity annotations, offer guided questions for tracing activities, and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: challenge them to modify algorithms for optimization, analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or implement hybrid approaches combining multiple sorting strategies.
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition

title: Design and Justify a Novel Cryptographic System Using Modular Arithmetic
description: Students will create an original encryption algorithm by combining multiple mathematical concepts including modular arithmetic, matrix operations, and prime number theory. They will then test their system's security and present a mathematical proof of its effectiveness to peers for validation.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original cryptographic encryption system by integrating modular arithmetic, linear algebra, and number theory concepts
Students will construct mathematical proofs demonstrating their system's security properties through formal logical arguments and computational complexity analysis
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 2-3 (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a packet containing: sample plaintext messages, basic encryption algorithms (Caesar cipher, Vigenère cipher), and mathematical reference sheets. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze weaknesses in provided classical ciphers by performing frequency analysis and brute force attacks. They document vulnerabilities using provided attack templates. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Teams design their novel encryption system by combining at least three mathematical elements: modular arithmetic operations, matrix transformations, and prime number properties. They must create: (a) detailed algorithm steps with mathematical notation, (b) worked examples showing encryption/decryption of a 20-character message, (c) key generation procedure with mathematical justification. Phase 3 (60 minutes): Teams develop security proofs by calculating computational complexity, analyzing key space size, and identifying potential attack vectors. They complete a formal proof template demonstrating why their system resists common attacks. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents their system to two other teams who attempt to break it within 15 minutes per presentation. Presenting teams defend their design using mathematical arguments. Phase 5 (30 minutes): Teams revise their systems based on peer feedback and submit final documentation including: complete algorithm specification, security analysis, implementation code or pseudocode, and reflection on mathematical concepts utilized.
materials_needed: Classical cipher reference sheets with Caesar and Vigenère examples
Graphing calculators or computer access for modular arithmetic computations
Prime number tables up to 1000
Matrix operation reference guides
Attack template worksheets for frequency analysis and brute force documentation
Formal proof template with logical argument structure
Sample plaintext messages of varying lengths
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of algorithm design (25 points), Integration of multiple mathematical concepts (20 points), Quality and rigor of security proof (25 points), Successful defense against peer attacks (15 points), Clear documentation and presentation (15 points). Students must demonstrate their system works correctly, resists at least two different attack methods, and incorporates sophisticated mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step templates for algorithm development and offer simplified mathematical operations (smaller modulus values, 2x2 matrices only). Create checkpoint meetings every 30 minutes during design phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate elliptic curve mathematics, implement their system in actual code, or analyze computational complexity using Big O notation. Encourage exploration of digital signature capabilities.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 to 1111 (0-15) through systematic flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalent of any 4-bit binary number (0000-1111) within 3 seconds by using memorized conversion patterns
Students will identify binary place values (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s) through structured repetition and visual reinforcement
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing binary numbers 0000-1111 on one side and decimal equivalents 0-15 on the reverse. Students work in pairs for 25 minutes total. First 10 minutes: Student A shows binary side to Student B, who states the decimal equivalent before checking the answer. Switch roles after 5 minutes. Encourage students to say place values aloud (e.g., '1010 = 8 plus 2 equals 10'). Next 10 minutes: Repeat the process but with decimal-to-binary conversion, showing decimal numbers and requiring binary responses. Final 5 minutes: Conduct individual timed challenge where each student receives 16 random cards and must correctly identify 12+ within 2 minutes. Record individual scores on provided tracking sheet. Throughout the activity, remind students that 1 in the 8s place = 8, 4s place = 4, 2s place = 2, 1s place = 1, and they should mentally add these values. Circulate to ensure students are verbalizing the place value addition process rather than just guessing. For incorrect answers, have students write out the place value calculation on scratch paper before continuing.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards (16 cards per student pair) with 4-bit binary numbers 0000-1111
Individual score tracking sheets
Stopwatch or timer
Scratch paper for calculations
Pencils for recording scores
assessment_method: Students must correctly recall 12 out of 16 binary-decimal conversions (75% accuracy) within the 2-minute timed challenge. Track both speed and accuracy on individual score sheets. Observe during pair work to ensure students verbalize place value calculations rather than guessing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a place value reference chart (8-4-2-1) and allow them to point to positions while calculating. Start with easier patterns like 0001, 0010, 0100, 1000. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit or 6-bit binary numbers, or introduce hexadecimal equivalents for the same numbers.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire quiz activities within 3 seconds per conversion
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend 5 minutes having students examine all cards simultaneously to notice patterns. Next, conduct Round 1 (10 minutes): students work in pairs, with one partner showing decimal numbers while the other states the binary equivalent, then switch roles after going through all 16 cards twice. For Round 2 (10 minutes), reverse the process - show binary numbers and state decimal equivalents. During Round 3 (8 minutes), students work individually, sorting cards into 'confident' and 'need practice' piles, spending extra time on difficult conversions. Conclude with Round 4 (7 minutes): individual timed practice where students flip through their entire deck, stating answers aloud and setting aside any cards they cannot answer within 3 seconds. End with a whole-class verification session where you call out random numbers and students respond chorally, allowing self-correction of any remaining errors.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards (16 cards per student) with decimal 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back
Timer or stopwatch for timed rounds
Binary conversion reference chart posted visibly in classroom
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) during final individual timed round. Record student performance using checklist noting which specific conversions each student struggles with. Success criteria: correctly recall binary equivalent within 3 seconds for at least 14 decimal numbers, and correctly identify decimal equivalent within 3 seconds for at least 14 binary numbers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide visual aids showing place values (8-4-2-1 positions) and allow them to use finger counting initially. Create smaller sets focusing on 0-7 first. For advanced learners: extend to 8-bit numbers (0-255), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or challenge them to find patterns in binary sequences.

description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice and rapid-fire recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary patterns essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal values from 4-bit binary numbers through visual recognition exercises without calculation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary representations on the reverse (00000 through 1111). Have students work in pairs, with one partner showing decimal cards while the other recites binary equivalents. After 10 minutes, switch roles. Next, expand to include numbers 8-15 for another 10 minutes of practice. In the third phase, mix all cards 0-15 randomly for 15 minutes. Individual score tracking sheets

Track progress using individual score sheets showing number of correct responses and time taken.
