learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by interpreting query costs, join operations, and index usage patterns to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will compare different query structures through systematic performance testing to determine optimal approaches for complex data retrieval scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student with access to a pre-populated MySQL database containing three tables: customers (10,000 records), orders (50,000 records), and products (1,000 records). Students work individually for the first 40 minutes, then pair up for comparison discussions. First, students execute and analyze three provided queries of increasing complexity: a simple SELECT with WHERE clause, a JOIN between two tables, and a complex query with subqueries and multiple JOINs. For each query, they must capture the execution plan using EXPLAIN ANALYZE, record execution time, and document resource usage. Next, students identify specific performance issues by examining table scan operations, missing index usage, and inefficient join strategies in the execution plans. They then modify each original query using at least two different optimization techniques (adding indexes, rewriting subqueries as JOINs, using LIMIT clauses, or restructuring WHERE conditions). After implementing optimizations, students re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and document performance improvements, calculating percentage improvements in execution time and analyzing changes in the execution plan structure. Finally, students create a comparative analysis document explaining why specific optimizations worked, which query patterns caused the most significant performance issues, and ranking the three original queries from most to least efficient with detailed justification based on their analysis findings.
materials_needed: MySQL database server with sample e-commerce database pre-installed
Database management tool (MySQL Workbench or phpMyAdmin)
Spreadsheet software for recording performance metrics
Query analysis worksheet template with execution plan interpretation guide
assessment_method: Evaluate students based on: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25 points) - correctly identifying table scans, index usage, and join types; (2) Quality of optimization strategies (30 points) - implementing appropriate techniques and achieving measurable improvements; (3) Depth of performance analysis (25 points) - providing detailed explanations of why optimizations worked; (4) Comparative reasoning (20 points) - logical ranking and justification of query efficiency based on evidence
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a glossary of execution plan terminology and highlight key metrics to focus on (rows examined, execution time, index usage). Offer pre-written optimization hints for each query type. For advanced learners: Challenge them to create their own complex queries with intentional inefficiencies, then optimize them, or investigate advanced techniques like query caching, partitioning effects, or analyzing the impact of different storage engines on performance.

title: Design and Implement a Dynamic Portfolio Optimization Algorithm Using Multi-Objective Programming
description: Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts including linear programming, calculus of variations, and stochastic processes to create an original portfolio optimization algorithm. They will develop a complete mathematical framework that balances risk minimization with return maximization while incorporating real-world constraints and market volatility.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multi-objective optimization theory, stochastic calculus, and constraint programming to construct an original portfolio allocation algorithm that addresses at least three competing financial objectives simultaneously
Students will design and validate a comprehensive mathematical model through rigorous proof techniques, sensitivity analysis, and computational implementation using real market data
instructions: Begin by having students form teams of 2-3 (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a dataset of 50 stocks with 5 years of daily returns, volatility measures, and correlation matrices. Teams must first formulate their optimization problem by defining: (1) objective functions for risk, return, and liquidity; (2) constraint sets including budget, sector diversification, and regulatory limits; (3) stochastic components modeling market uncertainty. Next, students spend 90 minutes developing their mathematical framework, choosing between approaches like Markowitz mean-variance optimization, Black-Litterman models, or novel hybrid approaches. They must derive all mathematical relationships from first principles, including Lagrangian formulations for constrained optimization and proof of convergence properties. Following framework development, teams implement their algorithm computationally (60 minutes), coding in Python/MATLAB to handle matrix operations, numerical optimization, and Monte Carlo simulations for risk assessment. Students then validate their model using backtesting on reserved data (30 minutes), calculating Sharpe ratios, maximum drawdown, and comparing performance against benchmark portfolios. Finally, teams prepare 15-minute presentations demonstrating: mathematical rigor of their approach, computational results, sensitivity analysis showing how parameters affect outcomes, and critical evaluation of model limitations. Each presentation includes live demonstration of their algorithm processing new data inputs.
materials_needed: Historical stock price dataset (CSV format) with 50 securities over 5-year period
Python/MATLAB software with optimization toolboxes (scipy.optimize, cvxpy, or Optimization Toolbox)
Jupyter notebooks or MATLAB Live Scripts for documentation
Access to financial databases (Yahoo Finance API or Bloomberg Terminal)
Graphing calculators for preliminary calculations
Whiteboard/flipchart paper for mathematical derivations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical Rigor - correctness of derivations, proof techniques, and theoretical foundation (25%); (2) Innovation - originality of approach, creative constraint handling, novel objective functions (25%); (3) Implementation Quality - code efficiency, numerical stability, proper handling of edge cases (20%); (4) Validation & Analysis - appropriate backtesting methodology, statistical significance of results, honest assessment of limitations (20%); (5) Communication - clarity of mathematical exposition, effective visualization of results, professional presentation (10%). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 in mathematical rigor to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide template code structure, offer guided derivation worksheets for basic Markowitz optimization, and allow focus on 2-objective rather than 3-objective optimization. Create study groups pairing stronger and weaker students. For advanced learners: challenge them to incorporate behavioral finance factors, develop real-time updating mechanisms, or extend to international markets with currency risk. Provide access to advanced texts like Luenberger's 'Investment Science' for theoretical depth.

title: Interpreting Distribution Patterns in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze three different histograms representing customer purchase amounts from different retail sectors to identify distribution types, outliers, and business implications. They will demonstrate understanding by categorizing distributions and explaining the underlying business patterns that create these data shapes.
learning_objectives: Students will classify distribution types (normal, skewed, bimodal) by examining histogram characteristics and calculating summary statistics
Students will explain the relationship between distribution patterns and real-world business scenarios through guided analysis of customer purchase data
instructions: Begin by displaying three unlabeled histograms on screen: luxury goods (right-skewed), grocery purchases (normal), and subscription services (bimodal). Give students 5 minutes to individually examine each histogram and write initial observations about shape, spread, and any unusual patterns. Form groups of 3-4 students and distribute the analysis worksheet with summary statistics for each dataset (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles). Have groups spend 15 minutes completing Part A: identifying distribution type for each histogram using both visual cues and statistical measures. Provide the distribution identification reference sheet listing characteristics of normal (mean≈median, symmetric), right-skewed (mean>median, tail extends right), and bimodal (two distinct peaks) distributions. For Part B (10 minutes), reveal the business context labels and have groups match each distribution to its most likely business scenario, explaining their reasoning. In Part C (15 minutes), groups identify potential outliers using the IQR method and discuss what these might represent in business terms. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents one distribution analysis, focusing on how the data pattern reflects customer behavior. Circulate during group work to check understanding and guide students toward recognizing the connection between statistical patterns and business reality.
materials_needed: Three printed histograms (luxury goods, grocery, subscription data)
Analysis worksheet with summary statistics table
Distribution identification reference sheet
Calculators or laptops with basic statistical functions
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using rubric: Distribution identification (4 points - correct classification with supporting evidence), Business reasoning (4 points - logical connection between data patterns and business context), Outlier analysis (2 points - correct IQR calculation and business interpretation). Observe group discussions for accurate use of statistical terminology and understanding of distribution characteristics.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using a fourth, simpler dataset and highlight key vocabulary terms. Offer sentence starters like 'This distribution is __ because the mean is __ compared to the median.' For advanced learners, include additional questions about sampling bias, data collection methods, and how seasonal factors might affect these distributions.

title: Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming Applications
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex multi-constraint manufacturing optimization problem. They will formulate objective functions, establish constraint systems, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal production schedules that maximize profit while meeting resource limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a real-world manufacturing scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement graphical and simplex method solutions to determine optimal production quantities through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario handout featuring TechCorp Electronics, which produces smartphones and tablets with specific material, labor, and storage constraints (10 minutes). Students work in pairs to read the scenario: TechCorp has 480 hours of assembly time, 360 hours of testing time, and storage for 200 units weekly. Smartphones require 3 assembly hours, 2 testing hours, 1 storage unit, and yield $150 profit. Tablets need 2 assembly hours, 3 testing hours, 1.5 storage units, and yield $200 profit. Next, guide students through constraint formulation (15 minutes): let x = smartphones produced, y = tablets produced. Students must write the objective function (Maximize P = 150x + 200y) and all constraints (3x + 2y ≤ 480, 2x + 3y ≤ 360, x + 1.5y ≤ 200, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0). Then, students graph the feasible region on provided coordinate paper (20 minutes), identifying intersection points by solving constraint equation systems algebraically. Students must find vertices: (0,0), (0,133.33), (60,120), (120,60), (160,0). Finally, students evaluate the objective function at each vertex (10 minutes) and determine the optimal solution. They must show that producing 60 smartphones and 120 tablets yields maximum profit of $33,000. Students complete a summary report showing all mathematical work, justifying their solution, and explaining the business implications of their optimization results.
materials_needed: TechCorp Electronics manufacturing scenario handouts
Graph paper with coordinate grids (minimum 200x200 scale)
Scientific calculators
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint line graphing
Linear programming solution template worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: Problem formulation (5 points) - correct objective function and all constraints identified; Mathematical execution (8 points) - accurate graphical representation, correct vertex calculations, and proper algebraic work shown; Solution interpretation (4 points) - optimal point identified with correct profit calculation; Communication (3 points) - clear mathematical notation and logical business justification. Students must submit completed graphs with labeled constraints, vertex coordinate calculations, and written analysis explaining why their solution is mathematically and practically optimal.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint equation templates and vertex calculation guides with step-by-step algebraic solving methods. Offer graphing assistance by pre-marking axis scales and providing intersection point hints. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how profit changes with constraint modifications, or extend to three-variable problems requiring simplex tableau methods. Consider providing graphing calculator tutorials for students unfamiliar with linear programming applications.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing a Multi-Node Database Outage
description: Students analyze a realistic distributed database system failure scenario by examining system logs, performance metrics, and architecture diagrams to identify root causes, failure propagation patterns, and system design weaknesses. They will deconstruct the cascading failure events and evaluate the effectiveness of existing fault tolerance mechanisms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the causal relationships between component failures in a distributed system by examining timestamped logs and performance metrics to construct a failure timeline
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of fault tolerance mechanisms through systematic examination of system behavior under failure conditions
instructions: Distribute the provided case study packet containing: system architecture diagram of a 3-tier web application with load balancers, application servers, and sharded MongoDB cluster; 2 hours of timestamped logs from all system components; performance monitoring dashboards showing CPU, memory, network, and database metrics; and incident timeline with user-reported issues. Students work in teams of 3-4. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the architecture diagram and identify all failure points and dependencies. They create a dependency map showing how components interact. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students analyze logs chronologically, identifying the first failure event and tracking how it propagated through the system. They must correlate log entries across different components using timestamps and trace IDs. Teams create a detailed failure timeline with exact timestamps and affected components. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Using performance metrics, students analyze system behavior before, during, and after the failure. They identify which monitoring alerts should have triggered and when. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate existing fault tolerance mechanisms (connection pooling, circuit breakers, retries, failover procedures) and determine why they failed to prevent the outage. They categorize failures as: design flaws, implementation bugs, operational errors, or capacity issues. Deliverable: Teams present a 10-minute analysis including the root cause, failure propagation diagram, timeline of events, and three specific architectural improvements to prevent similar failures.
materials_needed: Distributed system case study packet with architecture diagrams
Realistic system logs from web servers, application servers, load balancers, and database nodes (provided as text files)
Performance monitoring dashboard screenshots (Grafana/DataDog style)
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool (Miro, Lucidchart) for creating failure diagrams
assessment_method: Rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of root cause identification (25 points), (2) Completeness of failure timeline with correct causal relationships (25 points), (3) Quality of dependency analysis and failure propagation mapping (25 points), (4) Depth of fault tolerance mechanism evaluation with specific examples (25 points). Teams must correctly identify at least 80% of the failure events and their sequence to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed failure timeline template and highlight key log entries that indicate failures. Offer a glossary of common error codes and their meanings. For advanced learners: Include additional logs from monitoring systems (Prometheus, New Relic) and challenge them to calculate the exact impact on system availability using SLA metrics. Provide optional extension: design a chaos engineering experiment to test their proposed improvements.

title: Design Your Dream Community: A Linear Programming Optimization Project
description: Students will create a mathematical model for optimizing land use in a fictional community development project. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and design visual presentations of their optimal solutions using real-world considerations like budget, environmental impact, and community needs.
estimated_duration: 140 minutes (2.5 hours) - can be split across 2-3 class periods
learning_objectives: Students will construct a linear programming model with at least 4 variables and 6 constraints by analyzing community development scenarios
Students will design and present an optimal land allocation plan through graphical analysis and mathematical justification of their solution
instructions: **Phase 1 - Setup (15 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the 'Community Development Brief' handout containing a 500-acre plot with $50 million budget. Each team receives different community profiles (suburban family area, college town, retirement community, or mixed-use district). **Phase 2 - Model Creation (45 minutes):** Teams identify 4-5 land use variables (residential units, commercial space, parks, schools, etc.) and create at least 6 realistic constraints including budget limitations, zoning requirements, environmental regulations, and community service ratios. Students must research actual costs and requirements using provided reference materials. **Phase 3 - Mathematical Solution (30 minutes):** Using graphing calculators or GeoGebra, teams graph their constraint system, identify the feasible region, and determine the optimal solution using their chosen objective function (maximize profit, minimize environmental impact, or maximize community satisfaction). **Phase 4 - Design Presentation (20 minutes):** Teams create a visual presentation including: constraint equations with real-world justifications, graphical solution with clearly marked optimal point, scaled community map showing land allocation, and 3-minute pitch explaining why their design best serves their community type. **Phase 5 - Community Council Meeting (30 minutes):** Teams present to a mock city council (other students and instructor) who ask questions and vote on the most viable proposal.
materials_needed: Community Development Brief handouts (4 different scenarios)
Reference sheets with construction costs, zoning laws, and environmental regulations
Graphing calculators or computers with GeoGebra software
Graph paper and colored pencils
Large poster paper for presentations
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Mathematical Model (25 points) - accuracy of constraints and objective function; Solution Process (25 points) - correct graphical analysis and optimization; Real-world Application (25 points) - realistic constraints and practical feasibility; Presentation (25 points) - clear communication and visual design. Teams must submit written mathematical work, final presentation poster, and reflection on how changing constraints would affect their solution.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint equation templates and simplified 2-variable scenarios first. Pair with stronger math students and offer pre-calculated cost sheets. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints (whole building requirements), consider multi-objective optimization, or incorporate probability elements like market uncertainty and population growth projections.

title: Advanced Operating Systems Kernel Components Memory Palace
description: Students will memorize and recall specific kernel subsystem components, their memory addresses, and interaction sequences for Linux kernel version 5.15. This activity uses spatial memory techniques to help students internalize complex kernel architecture details that form the foundation for advanced systems programming.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact names and memory address ranges of 15 core Linux kernel subsystems by constructing a visual memory palace
Students will identify specific kernel data structures (task_struct, mm_struct, vma_struct) and their byte offsets through systematic memorization drills
instructions: Begin by projecting the Linux kernel memory map diagram showing kernel space (0xC0000000-0xFFFFFFFF for 32-bit x86). Distribute the kernel component reference sheets containing 15 subsystems: Process Scheduler (0xC0100000), Memory Manager (0xC0200000), VFS Layer (0xC0300000), Network Stack (0xC0400000), Device Drivers (0xC0500000), Interrupt Handlers (0xC0600000), System Call Interface (0xC0700000), File Systems (0xC0800000), Block Layer (0xC0900000), Character Devices (0xC0A00000), TTY Subsystem (0xC0B00000), Crypto API (0xC0C00000), Security Framework (0xC0D00000), Power Management (0xC0E00000), and Debugging Interface (0xC0F00000). Students work individually for 20 minutes to create their memory palace by associating each subsystem with a specific room in their house or familiar building. They must write down: room name, subsystem name, starting address, and one key data structure. Next, conduct three 5-minute recall sessions with 3-minute breaks between each. During recalls, students close their reference sheets and write from memory on provided templates. After each session, allow 2 minutes for self-checking against reference sheets. For the final 15 minutes, pair students to quiz each other using the kernel component flashcards, focusing on subsystem names, addresses, and primary functions. Monitor pairs to ensure accurate information exchange and provide immediate corrections for any errors.
materials_needed: Linux kernel 5.15 memory map poster (minimum 24x36 inches)
Kernel subsystem reference sheets (15 components with addresses and data structures)
Memory palace template worksheets
Recall session answer sheets (3 sets per student)
Kernel component flashcards (45 cards total)
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/15 correct) on final recall test covering subsystem names and memory addresses. Grade based on: subsystem identification (60%), correct memory address recall (25%), and data structure naming (15%). Use provided rubric with specific point deductions: -2 points per incorrect subsystem name, -1 point per wrong address, -1 point per missing data structure.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-drawn memory palace templates with familiar locations (school layout) and allow use of mnemonic devices like acronyms. Pair them with stronger memorizers during quiz sessions. For advanced learners: add kernel function names (schedule(), alloc_pages(), sys_open()) and require recall of interrupt vector numbers. Challenge them to memorize task_struct field offsets and sizes.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Curve Analysis
description: Students will analyze cross-validation learning curves from three different machine learning models (linear regression, polynomial regression, and random forest) to understand how bias-variance tradeoff manifests in real model performance. They will interpret validation curves to identify underfitting, overfitting, and optimal model complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance tradeoff concepts by analyzing cross-validation learning curves from multiple model complexities
Students will distinguish between underfitting and overfitting scenarios through systematic examination of training and validation error patterns
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-generated datasets: a simple linear relationship with noise, a polynomial relationship, and a complex non-linear pattern. Distribute validation curve plots for each dataset showing training and validation scores across different model complexities (polynomial degrees 1-15, random forest n_estimators 10-500, ridge regression alpha values 0.001-100). In pairs, students first spend 15 minutes examining the linear dataset curves, identifying where training and validation errors converge, diverge, and reach minimum validation error. They should annotate plots marking high bias (underfitting) and high variance (overfitting) regions. Next, allocate 20 minutes for analyzing the polynomial dataset curves, comparing how the optimal complexity differs from the linear case. Students document why certain model types perform better on specific data patterns. For the final 20 minutes, groups examine the complex dataset results, identifying which models handle the complexity best and explaining the bias-variance implications. Students create a summary table categorizing each model-dataset combination as high bias, high variance, or balanced, with written justifications. Conclude with 10 minutes where pairs present one key insight about how data complexity affects optimal model selection. Throughout the activity, emphasize connecting visual curve patterns to underlying bias-variance theory rather than just memorizing definitions.
materials_needed: Pre-generated validation curve plots for 9 model-dataset combinations (printed or digital)
Three synthetic datasets with known complexity patterns
Summary table templates for bias-variance classification
Colored pens for plot annotation
Python/R code snippets showing how curves were generated (reference only)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed summary tables using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies bias-variance category for all 9 combinations with accurate theoretical justifications, (3) Correctly identifies 7-8 combinations with mostly sound reasoning, (2) Correctly identifies 5-6 combinations with basic explanations, (1) Fewer than 5 correct with limited understanding demonstrated. Also assess plot annotations for accurate identification of underfitting/overfitting regions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet defining high bias (training and validation errors both high) and high variance (large gap between training and validation errors). Offer guided questions like 'Where is the validation error minimized?' and 'What happens to the gap between curves as complexity increases?' For advanced learners, provide additional curves with regularization parameters and ask them to explain how regularization affects the bias-variance balance.

title: Personal Budget Calculator: Applying Percentages and Decimals to Real Monthly Expenses
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional 22-year-old using actual local pricing data, applying percentage calculations to determine spending categories and using decimal operations for precise financial planning. They will solve real-world problems involving salary deductions, savings goals, and expense allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by calculating 20% for savings, 30% for housing, and other category percentages from a given monthly salary
Students will solve multi-step decimal problems through real-world expense calculations including tax deductions, tip calculations, and price comparisons
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Young Adult Profile' worksheet showing a fictional character earning $3,200 monthly gross income. Provide local pricing research sheets with actual costs for rent, groceries, transportation, and utilities in your area. **Step 1 (10 minutes):** Students calculate net income by applying tax deductions (subtract 22% for federal, state, and social security taxes from gross salary using decimal multiplication). **Step 2 (15 minutes):** Using the 50/30/20 budgeting rule, students apply percentages to allocate net income: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings. They must show percentage-to-decimal conversion work (30% = 0.30) and multiplication steps. **Step 3 (20 minutes):** Within the 'needs' category, students research and assign actual local costs for housing (applying percentage calculations to determine maximum affordable rent at 30% of gross income), groceries, utilities, and transportation. They must use decimal addition and subtraction to ensure totals don't exceed their calculated 'needs' allocation. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Students apply percentage calculations to determine how much they can spend on dining out (calculating tips using percentages), entertainment subscriptions, and shopping within their 'wants' category. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Calculate specific savings goals by applying compound interest formulas to determine monthly savings needed for a $5,000 emergency fund within 18 months. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students verify their budget balances using decimal addition, ensuring total expenses equal net income with zero remainder.
materials_needed: Young Adult Profile worksheet with salary and demographic information
Local pricing research sheet with actual rent, grocery, and utility costs
Calculators or computer access
Budget template worksheet with designated percentage categories
Compound interest formula reference sheet
assessment_method: Grade completed budget sheets using rubric: Correct tax calculation with shown work (25 points), accurate percentage-to-decimal conversions for all categories (25 points), realistic expense allocations within calculated limits (25 points), balanced final budget with proper decimal addition verification (25 points). Students must show all mathematical work including percentage calculations and decimal operations to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage-to-decimal conversion charts and step-by-step calculation templates. Pair with stronger math partners for peer support. For advanced learners: Add investment portfolio calculations, compare different budgeting methods (70/20/10 rule), or calculate long-term financial goals like mortgage payments using compound interest and amortization formulas.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Comparing Index Strategies
description: Students will analyze the performance impact of different database indexing strategies on SQL queries by examining execution plans and timing results. They will compare non-indexed queries versus single-column and composite indexes to determine optimal database design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between database index types and query performance by examining execution plans and timing data
Students will evaluate the trade-offs between different indexing strategies through systematic performance comparison and cost-benefit analysis
instructions:
Begin by providing each student team (2-3 members) with access to a pre-populated MySQL database containing a 'sales_transactions' table with 50,000 records including columns: transaction_id, customer_id, product_category, sale_date, and amount. Start with a 10-minute briefing explaining the scenario: they are database administrators tasked with optimizing query performance for a retail analytics system.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students execute three baseline queries without any indexes: (a) SELECT * FROM sales_transactions WHERE customer_id = 12345, (b) SELECT * FROM sales_transactions WHERE product_category = 'Electronics' AND sale_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31', and (c) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_transactions WHERE amount > 1000. They record execution times using MySQL's EXPLAIN ANALYZE command and document the query execution plans.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams create single-column indexes on customer_id, product_category, sale_date, and amount columns separately. They re-execute all three queries, recording new execution times and analyzing the EXPLAIN ANALYZE output to identify changes in query strategies (table scans vs. index seeks).

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students create composite indexes: one on (product_category, sale_date) and another on (customer_id, amount). They test queries again and compare performance improvements across different index configurations.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams analyze their collected data to determine which indexing strategy provides optimal performance for each query type. They create a comparative analysis chart showing execution times, I/O operations, and memory usage for each scenario. Finally, they prepare a 5-minute presentation recommending the best indexing strategy with supporting evidence.
materials_needed: MySQL database server with pre-loaded sales_transactions table (50,000 records)
Database client software (MySQL Workbench or phpMyAdmin)
Performance monitoring worksheet template
Computers with database access for each team
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of performance data collection and execution plan interpretation (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing clear understanding of index impact (30%), (3) Logical reasoning in final recommendations with supporting evidence (25%), and (4) Clear presentation of findings with appropriate technical terminology (20%). Success requires scoring at least 3/4 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using a smaller dataset and guide them through interpreting their first EXPLAIN ANALYZE output. Offer a structured data collection template with pre-formatted tables. For advanced learners, challenge them to analyze query plan costs, explore covering indexes, or investigate the impact of different data distribution patterns on index effectiveness.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Comparing Index Strategies: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze the performance impact of different indexing strategies on database queries by examining execution plans and timing results. They will break down complex queries to identify bottlenecks and evaluate the effectiveness of various optimization techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database query execution plans by comparing performance metrics before and after applying different indexing strategies
Students will evaluate the trade-offs between query optimization techniques through systematic performance testing and data interpretation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-populated sample database containing 50,000 customer records and 200,000 order records (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair a workstation with database management software installed. Present the scenario: an e-commerce company experiencing slow query performance during peak hours. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students execute the provided set of 5 baseline queries without any indexes, recording execution times and analyzing the generated execution plans. They must document which operations (table scans, joins, sorts) consume the most resources using the query analyzer tools.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students implement different indexing strategies on assigned tables: clustered indexes on primary keys, non-clustered indexes on frequently queried columns, and composite indexes on multiple columns used in WHERE clauses. They re-execute the same queries and record new performance metrics.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students analyze the before/after data by calculating percentage improvements, identifying which queries benefited most from indexing, and examining how index choices affected different query patterns. They must create a comparison chart showing execution time changes and explain why certain indexes were more effective.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair presents one key finding to the class, focusing on a specific query where they identified the most significant performance bottleneck and explaining their analysis process. Conclude with a brief discussion on when indexing might negatively impact performance (insert/update operations).
materials_needed: Pre-populated SQL database file with customer and order tables (50K+ records)
Database management software (MySQL Workbench, SQL Server Management Studio, or PostgreSQL)
Query performance analysis worksheet with data recording tables
Set of 5 standardized test queries of varying complexity
Computers with database software installed and configured
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25%), (2) Correctness of performance data collection and calculations (25%), (3) Quality of analysis explaining why certain indexes improved specific queries (30%), and (4) Ability to identify query bottlenecks and propose appropriate solutions (20%). Students must submit their completed worksheet with documented findings and present their most significant discovery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided template for interpreting execution plans with key terms highlighted, and offer simplified queries to analyze first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to investigate query hints, analyze memory usage patterns, or explore the impact of database statistics on query optimization. Consider providing additional complex queries involving subqueries or multiple table joins for extended analysis.
original_title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Comparing Index Strategies

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Deployment Strategies for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning model deployment architectures for a customer churn prediction system. They will analyze trade-offs between batch processing, real-time API, and edge deployment strategies using actual performance metrics and business constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML deployment architectures by analyzing performance metrics, cost implications, and scalability constraints
Students will critique model deployment decisions through systematic comparison of latency, throughput, maintenance complexity, and business alignment factors
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members. Provide each team with the customer churn dataset (telecommunications company with 50,000 records) and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network. Each team receives deployment scenario documentation including: batch processing pipeline (daily predictions), REST API service (real-time predictions), and edge deployment (mobile app integration). Teams spend 45 minutes examining provided performance benchmarks: latency measurements, memory usage, prediction accuracy across different data volumes, and infrastructure costs. Next, teams analyze business requirements document specifying: maximum acceptable prediction latency (500ms), daily prediction volume (10,000 customers), budget constraints ($2000/month), and accuracy threshold (85% precision). For 60 minutes, teams systematically evaluate each deployment option against criteria using provided evaluation matrix template. They must assess technical feasibility, cost-effectiveness, scalability potential, and maintenance complexity. Teams then spend 30 minutes preparing recommendations, identifying the optimal deployment strategy and explaining trade-offs of rejected options. Each team presents 10-minute findings to the class, defending their chosen architecture and addressing questions about alternative scenarios. During presentations, other teams complete peer evaluation forms rating the thoroughness of analysis, quality of evidence used, and consideration of business constraints. Conclude with 15-minute class discussion comparing different team conclusions and identifying common evaluation patterns across teams.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV file with 50,000 telecommunications records)
Three pre-trained model files (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network in pickle format)
Deployment performance benchmark spreadsheet with latency, memory, and cost data
Business requirements document template
Evaluation criteria matrix template
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Jupyter notebooks or Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Completeness of technical analysis - examines all deployment options thoroughly, (2) Quality of evidence - uses quantitative metrics and references specific performance data, (3) Business alignment - demonstrates clear connection between technical choices and business requirements, (4) Critical thinking - identifies limitations, assumptions, and trade-offs in reasoning, (5) Communication effectiveness - presents findings clearly with logical flow. Each dimension scored as Exemplary (4), Proficient (3), Developing (2), or Inadequate (1). Minimum passing score: 12/20 points. Deliverables include completed evaluation matrix, written recommendation report (2 pages), and oral presentation with Q&A responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation criteria checklist with specific questions to guide analysis (e.g., 'Does latency meet business requirements?'). Offer simplified cost calculation templates. For advanced learners: Include additional deployment scenarios (hybrid cloud, serverless, containerized options). Provide real-world case studies from companies like Netflix or Uber for comparison. Encourage consideration of A/B testing strategies and model versioning complexities. Consider adding regulatory compliance requirements (GDPR, data residency) as additional evaluation criteria.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Food Distribution Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban food distribution challenges. They will synthesize concepts from linear programming, graph theory, and statistical analysis to develop a comprehensive solution that minimizes cost while maximizing accessibility and nutritional equity across different socioeconomic neighborhoods.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-objective optimization model incorporating linear programming constraints and graph theory algorithms to solve complex urban food distribution problems
Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts through the creation of an original computational model that addresses real-world socioeconomic equity issues
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, each assigned specific roles: Data Analyst, Model Architect, Algorithm Developer, and Equity Specialist. Distribute the Urban Food Desert Dataset containing demographics, existing store locations, transportation networks, and nutritional access scores for a fictional city of 500,000 residents across 20 neighborhoods. Teams spend 45 minutes analyzing the data to identify key variables and constraints. Next, teams must formulate their optimization problem by defining: objective functions (minimize total distribution cost while maximizing nutritional access equity), decision variables (number and location of distribution centers, delivery routes, inventory levels), and constraints (budget limitations, capacity restrictions, demographic requirements). Teams then construct their mathematical model using either MATLAB, Python with optimization libraries, or Excel Solver, spending 90 minutes developing algorithms that integrate shortest-path calculations for delivery routes, linear programming for resource allocation, and statistical weighting for equity measures. Each team must validate their model using provided test scenarios and create visualizations showing optimized distribution networks overlaid on city maps. Teams conclude by preparing a 15-minute presentation explaining their model architecture, mathematical justification for chosen approaches, computational results, and how their solution addresses food equity. During presentations, other teams serve as peer reviewers using provided evaluation criteria. The final 30 minutes involve teams iterating on their models based on peer feedback and instructor guidance.
materials_needed: Urban Food Desert Dataset (CSV files with demographic and geographic data)
Computers with MATLAB, Python (SciPy, NumPy, PuLP libraries), or Excel with Solver add-in
Digital city maps (GIS format or high-resolution images)
Graphing calculators as backup computational tools
Large format paper and colored markers for model visualization
Peer evaluation rubrics (printed copies)
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a comprehensive rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Model Construction (40 points) - correctness of objective functions, completeness of constraints, appropriate variable selection; (2) Algorithm Implementation (30 points) - computational accuracy, code efficiency, proper use of optimization techniques; (3) Real-world Application (20 points) - consideration of equity factors, feasibility of solutions, validation of results; (4) Communication and Justification (10 points) - clarity of mathematical explanations, quality of visualizations, response to peer questions. Success criteria include producing a working computational model that generates quantifiable improvements over baseline scenarios and demonstrating mathematical reasoning that connects abstract optimization concepts to concrete social outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code with partial implementations, offer simplified datasets with fewer variables, and allow use of Excel Solver instead of programming languages. Create reference sheets with common optimization formulations and constraint types. For advanced learners: Introduce stochastic elements (demand uncertainty), multi-period optimization, or integration with machine learning for demand forecasting. Challenge them to incorporate additional mathematical concepts like network flows, integer programming, or game theory for competitive market scenarios.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Food Distribution Networks: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban food distribution challenges using linear programming, graph theory, and statistical analysis. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then present their solution to address food accessibility issues in a specific metropolitan area.
estimated_duration: 420 minutes (7 hours) across four sessions plus independent work time
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize linear programming, graph theory, and statistical modeling techniques by designing an original optimization model for urban food distribution networks
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical solution through developing algorithms, validating models with real data, and creating implementation protocols for city planners
instructions: Begin by assigning students to teams of 3-4 members, with each team selecting a specific metropolitan area (population 500K+) for their focus. Provide each team with access to demographic data, existing food retailer locations, transportation networks, and census information for their chosen city. In the first session (90 minutes), teams must analyze their city's current food distribution gaps using statistical methods, identifying underserved areas through correlation analysis and regression modeling. They should create visual representations using GIS mapping tools and calculate food accessibility indices. During the second session (120 minutes), students design their optimization model framework. They must define decision variables (warehouse locations, delivery routes, inventory levels), establish objective functions (minimize cost, maximize coverage, minimize delivery time), and create constraint equations (budget limitations, vehicle capacity, demand requirements). Teams should formulate their problem as a mixed-integer linear program and justify their mathematical choices. The third session (120 minutes) focuses on computational implementation. Students code their optimization model using Python with PuLP or Gurobi libraries, incorporating real transportation networks as weighted graphs. They must validate their model using historical data and perform sensitivity analysis on key parameters. The fourth session (90 minutes) involves solution refinement and presentation preparation. Teams analyze their optimal solutions, compare multiple scenarios, and calculate potential improvements over current systems. They prepare executive summaries with mathematical justifications, implementation timelines, and cost-benefit analyses. Final presentations (30 minutes per team) should include live demonstrations of their optimization software, mathematical proofs of solution optimality, and responses to technical questions from peers acting as city planning committees.
materials_needed: Census demographic datasets and GIS shapefiles for major metropolitan areas
Python programming environment with PuLP, NetworkX, and Matplotlib libraries installed
Access to Google Maps API or OpenStreetMap for transportation network data
Scientific calculators and graphing software (GeoGebra or Desmos)
Large format paper and markers for mathematical modeling diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model formulation and correctness (25 points), computational implementation and code quality (25 points), real-data validation and sensitivity analysis (20 points), presentation clarity and technical depth (20 points), innovation and feasibility of proposed solution (10 points). Students must submit their complete mathematical derivations, working Python code, validation datasets, and a 10-page technical report. Peer evaluation forms assess presentation quality and technical question responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template optimization model structures and guided worksheets breaking down constraint formulation. Offer office hours focused on linear programming review and Python coding support. For advanced learners, encourage incorporation of stochastic elements (demand uncertainty), multi-objective optimization techniques, or machine learning predictions for demand forecasting. Challenge them to consider dynamic routing algorithms or seasonal variation models.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Food Distribution Networks

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Food Distribution Networks: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban food distribution challenges, incorporating multiple variables, constraints, and objective functions. They will present their model with complete mathematical justification and computational implementation to address food desert problems in a specified metropolitan area.
learning_objectives: Students will formulate an original multi-variable optimization model by integrating linear programming, graph theory, and statistical analysis to address urban food distribution inequities
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts from calculus, operations research, and discrete mathematics through designing a comprehensive solution framework with computational validation
instructions:
**Phase 1: Problem Analysis (45 minutes)** Provide students with real demographic and geographic data from a metropolitan area with documented food deserts (e.g., Detroit census tracts, existing grocery store locations, transportation networks). Working in teams of 3-4, students analyze the data to identify key variables: population density, income levels, transportation accessibility, existing food retailers, and potential distribution sites. Each team selects one specific neighborhood cluster (3-5 census tracts) as their focus area.

**Phase 2: Mathematical Model Construction (90 minutes)** Teams develop their optimization model by: (1) Defining decision variables (number and location of distribution points, delivery routes, inventory levels), (2) Formulating objective function(s) to minimize cost while maximizing accessibility, (3) Establishing constraints including budget limitations, capacity restrictions, demographic requirements, and transportation networks, (4) Creating mathematical equations using linear/integer programming techniques, incorporating at least one element from graph theory (shortest path, network flow) and one statistical component (demand forecasting, population modeling).

**Phase 3: Implementation and Testing (75 minutes)** Using MATLAB, Python, or Excel Solver, teams program their model with the provided dataset. They run multiple scenarios, testing sensitivity to parameter changes (budget variations, population growth, new competitors). Teams document their computational process, including code snippets, convergence analysis, and solution validation through at least three different test cases.

**Phase 4: Presentation and Defense (30 minutes per team)** Each team presents their model using visual aids showing: mathematical formulation on whiteboard, computational results via projected displays, and practical implementation recommendations. Other teams and instructor pose questions challenging assumptions, mathematical validity, and real-world applicability. Presenting teams must defend their mathematical choices and demonstrate model robustness.
materials_needed: Census demographic dataset for selected metropolitan area (CSV format)
GIS mapping data showing transportation networks and existing food retailers
Laptops/computers with MATLAB, Python (with SciPy/PuLP), or Excel with Solver add-in
Whiteboards and colored markers for mathematical notation
Projectors for computational demonstrations
Graph paper and scientific calculators for preliminary work
assessment_method: Evaluation using 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Formulation (25 points - correctness of variables, constraints, objective functions), Integration of Mathematical Concepts (20 points - appropriate use of optimization, graph theory, statistics), Computational Implementation (20 points - working code, accurate results, sensitivity analysis), Problem-Solving Innovation (15 points - creative approaches, handling of real-world complexities), Presentation and Defense (20 points - clear mathematical communication, response to challenges). Deliverables include written model documentation, computational code with comments, and 15-minute presentation with Q&A defense.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks showing basic linear programming setup, offer simplified datasets with fewer variables, allow use of graphical methods for small-scale problems before computational implementation. For advanced learners: Encourage incorporation of stochastic elements (uncertain demand), multi-objective optimization techniques, dynamic programming for time-dependent factors, or machine learning integration for demand prediction. Provide additional datasets for comparative analysis across different metropolitan areas.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Food Distribution Networks

title: Binary Number System Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing memory drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by displaying a reference chart showing decimal numbers 0-15 with their 4-bit binary equivalents (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.) for 3 minutes while students study silently. Remove the chart and distribute pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers on one side and binary on the reverse. Have students work in pairs for 10 minutes, taking turns showing decimal numbers and asking partners to state the binary equivalent, then checking answers. Switch roles after 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class memory drill: display decimal numbers on screen for 5 seconds each while students write binary equivalents on individual whiteboards, then hold up answers simultaneously for immediate feedback. Cover all 16 numbers twice in random order. Follow with a reverse drill showing binary numbers for students to convert to decimal. Conclude with a 5-minute individual quiz where students complete a worksheet with 20 mixed decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions without references. Collect worksheets and provide immediate verbal feedback on common errors. End with students creating personal memory aids or patterns they noticed (like powers of 2) in their notebooks.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 (one side) and binary equivalents (reverse side)
Individual mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Binary-decimal reference chart for initial study phase
Digital timer or stopwatch
Printed quiz worksheets with 20 conversion problems
Projector or smartboard for displaying numbers during drills
assessment_method: Grade the final quiz worksheet using a 20-point scale (1 point per correct conversion). Success criteria: 18/20 correct (90% accuracy) demonstrates mastery. During whiteboard drills, note students who consistently struggle with specific numbers for additional practice. Use checklist to track participation during pair work and note-taking during reflection.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a powers-of-2 reference sheet (1, 2, 4, 8) and teach the addition method for conversion. Start with numbers 0-7 only, then expand. For advanced learners, extend to 8-bit numbers (0-255) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Allow struggling students extra study time with the reference chart before removing it.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices in Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real customer churn dataset's correlation matrix to identify relationships between features and explain how these relationships influence predictive modeling decisions. They will distinguish between different types of correlations and their implications for feature selection.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by categorizing relationships as weak, moderate, or strong and explaining their business significance
Students will explain multicollinearity issues through identifying highly correlated feature pairs and describing their impact on machine learning model performance
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a customer churn dataset (telecommunications company with 3,000 records, 15 features including monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, contract_type, etc.) and a generated correlation heatmap using seaborn. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine the correlation matrix and identify all feature pairs with correlation coefficients above 0.7 or below -0.7, recording these in a provided worksheet template.

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students categorize correlations as positive/negative and strong/moderate/weak using the scale: |r| > 0.7 (strong), 0.3-0.7 (moderate), < 0.3 (weak). They must provide business explanations for why specific correlations make logical sense (e.g., tenure vs. total_charges).

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students complete a guided analysis worksheet where they identify the top 3 most problematic feature pairs for multicollinearity and explain why including both features in a linear regression model would be problematic. They must reference specific correlation values and describe the variance inflation effect.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair presents one correlation finding to the class, explaining the coefficient value, business logic, and modeling implications in 2 minutes. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting findings to feature engineering decisions.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Individual reflection where students complete exit ticket explaining when they would remove highly correlated features versus keeping them, citing specific examples from the activity.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib pre-installed
Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 3,000 records)
Correlation analysis worksheet template (PDF)
Exit ticket form (digital or paper)
assessment_method: Grade completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strength, provides accurate business explanation, and clearly explains multicollinearity impact; (3) Minor errors in interpretation or explanation; (2) Identifies correlations but explanations lack depth; (1) Significant misunderstandings of correlation meaning. Participation in pair discussions and presentations assessed via observation checklist.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation interpretation reference card with coefficient ranges and sample business explanations. Pair them with stronger partners and offer one-on-one guidance during Step 3. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate partial correlations for selected feature triplets and explain how controlling for a third variable changes relationships. Ask them to research variance inflation factor (VIF) calculations.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices in Customer Churn Analysis: Business Application
description: Students will analyze a real customer churn dataset by examining correlation matrices to understand relationships between customer features. They will interpret correlation coefficients and identify patterns that influence customer retention decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing numerical values and visual heatmaps to determine relationship strength and direction
Students will explain the business implications of feature correlations through structured analysis of how customer behaviors interconnect in churn prediction
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the Telco Customer Churn dataset and a pre-built Jupyter notebook template. In the first 10 minutes, have students load the dataset and examine the first 10 rows to familiarize themselves with features like monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, and contract_type. Next, guide students through generating a correlation matrix using pandas corr() function for numerical features (15 minutes). Students should create both the numerical matrix and a seaborn heatmap visualization. In pairs, students spend 20 minutes analyzing specific correlations: Have them identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, writing down the exact coefficient values. They must then interpret what each correlation means in business terms. For example, if monthly_charges and total_charges show r=0.65, students should explain this indicates customers with higher monthly bills tend to have higher lifetime spending. Next, students individually complete a structured analysis worksheet (25 minutes) where they categorize correlations as strong (|r|>0.7), moderate (0.3<|r|<0.7), or weak (|r|<0.3) and explain which customer behaviors are most interconnected. Finally, conduct a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share one surprising correlation they discovered and hypothesize why this relationship exists in customer behavior.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (CSV file)
Jupyter notebook template with pandas and seaborn imports
Structured analysis worksheet with correlation interpretation prompts
Computers with Python environment installed
assessment_method: Evaluate student worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strengths, provides accurate business interpretations, and demonstrates clear understanding of positive/negative relationships; (3) Minor errors in interpretation but shows good understanding; (2) Some correct identifications but weak business explanations; (1) Significant misunderstandings of correlation meaning or values.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with correlation strength guidelines and example business interpretations. Highlight the diagonal of 1.0 values to reinforce that variables perfectly correlate with themselves. For advanced learners, have them explore partial correlations or investigate why certain expected correlations might be weaker than anticipated, considering confounding variables.
original_title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices in Customer Churn Analysis

title: Multi-Stage Optimization: Maximizing Profit in a Manufacturing Supply Chain
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex three-stage manufacturing optimization problem involving raw material procurement, production scheduling, and distribution logistics. They will use real-world constraints and multiple objective functions to determine optimal resource allocation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems by formulating objective functions and constraint systems from complex business scenarios
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis techniques through systematic problem-solving procedures to find optimal solutions
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario handout describing MegaCorp Manufacturing's three-facility operation with specific production capacities, raw material costs, and distribution requirements (10 minutes). Students work in pairs to analyze the given data: Facility A produces 150 units/day max, Facility B produces 200 units/day max, raw material X costs $12/unit with 500 units available daily, material Y costs $8/unit with 400 units available daily. Each product unit requires 2 units of X and 1 unit of Y, with profit margins of $25/unit from Facility A and $30/unit from Facility B. Students must formulate the linear programming problem by defining variables (x₁ = units from Facility A, x₂ = units from Facility B), writing the objective function (Maximize P = 25x₁ + 30x₂), and establishing constraints (facility capacity, material availability, non-negativity) (20 minutes). Next, students apply the graphical method by plotting constraint lines on provided coordinate grids, identifying the feasible region, and locating corner points (25 minutes). They then evaluate the objective function at each corner point to determine the optimal solution and calculate maximum profit (15 minutes). Finally, students prepare a written recommendation including the optimal production schedule, resource utilization rates, maximum profit achievable, and analysis of binding constraints (20 minutes). Instructor circulates to verify constraint formulations and provide guidance on graphical interpretation techniques.
materials_needed: MegaCorp Manufacturing scenario handout with data tables
Graph paper with pre-drawn coordinate axes (scale 0-300)
Colored pencils or markers for constraint line differentiation
Scientific calculators
Linear programming solution template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation (25 points - correct variables, objective function, and all constraints), Graphical solution (30 points - accurate plotting, feasible region identification, corner point determination), Mathematical calculations (25 points - correct corner point evaluations and optimal solution identification), Business recommendation (20 points - clear interpretation of results with practical implications and constraint analysis)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates with partial completion and offer individual guidance on graphical plotting techniques. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking them to determine how changes in profit margins or material costs affect the optimal solution, or extend to integer programming constraints requiring whole unit production.

title: Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in Multi-threaded Hash Table Implementations
description: Students will dissect and compare three different concurrent hash table implementations (lock-based, lock-free, and wait-free) by examining their source code, profiling their performance under various workloads, and identifying specific bottlenecks. They will analyze thread contention patterns, memory access patterns, and scalability characteristics to determine optimal use cases for each approach.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between synchronization mechanisms and performance bottlenecks by profiling three concurrent hash table implementations under different thread loads and operation ratios
Students will decompose complex multi-threaded code to identify critical sections, race conditions, and scalability limitations through systematic code inspection and performance measurement
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-compiled hash table implementations: ChainedHashMap (coarse-grained locking), LockFreeHashMap (compare-and-swap based), and WaitFreeHashMap (helping mechanism). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes on initial analysis, then individually for the remaining time. First, students examine the source code for 20 minutes, creating a comparison matrix documenting synchronization primitives used, critical section sizes, and potential contention points for each implementation. Next, they spend 25 minutes setting up performance tests using the provided benchmark harness, configuring tests for 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 threads with 80/20, 50/50, and 20/80 read/write ratios. Students then execute benchmarks for 30 minutes, collecting throughput and latency data while monitoring CPU utilization and cache miss rates using the integrated profiler. During the 35-minute analysis phase, students create performance graphs, identify inflection points where implementations' relative performance changes, and correlate code features with observed bottlenecks. They must pinpoint specific lines of code causing performance degradation and explain the underlying mechanisms (false sharing, lock convoy effects, ABA problems, etc.). Finally, students spend 20 minutes documenting their findings in a structured analysis report, including workload-specific recommendations and justifications for their conclusions. The instructor circulates during benchmark execution to ensure proper profiler usage and data collection.
materials_needed: Three concurrent hash table implementations with source code (provided as Maven/Gradle project)
JProfiler or Intel VTune performance profiling software
Multi-core development machines (minimum 8 cores recommended)
Benchmark harness with configurable thread counts and operation ratios
Analysis report template with performance comparison matrices
assessment_method: Evaluate submitted analysis reports using a 100-point rubric: Code analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct identification of synchronization mechanisms and critical sections; Performance data quality (20 points) - comprehensive benchmark execution with proper profiler integration; Bottleneck identification (30 points) - precise correlation between code features and performance issues with technical explanations; Recommendations (25 points) - justified workload-specific implementation choices supported by evidence. Students must achieve 80+ points and correctly identify at least 4 specific bottleneck types across the implementations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated code snippets highlighting key synchronization points and a bottleneck identification checklist (lock contention, memory barriers, cache coherence issues). Offer pre-configured profiler templates and interpretation guides for common performance metrics. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement micro-optimizations for identified bottlenecks, analyze assembly output for critical paths, or extend analysis to NUMA-aware performance characteristics. Provide additional lock-free algorithms (skip lists, queues) for comparative analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Dashboard Critique and Recommendation Workshop
description: Students will critically assess three pre-selected business dashboards with intentionally different quality levels, identifying strengths and weaknesses in data presentation choices. They will then provide specific, evidence-based recommendations for improvement using established visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data visualization choices by applying design principles and identifying specific strengths and weaknesses in real business dashboards
Students will critique data presentation methods through systematic analysis using a structured evaluation framework and provide actionable improvement recommendations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Dashboard Evaluation Worksheet and displaying three business dashboards on screen: Dashboard A (sales performance with cluttered charts and poor color choices), Dashboard B (customer analytics with clear design but missing context), and Dashboard C (financial metrics with excellent design principles). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to examine Dashboard A, using the provided evaluation criteria checklist covering clarity, accuracy, relevance, and visual appeal. They document specific observations about chart types, color usage, data-to-ink ratio, and readability.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Repeat the evaluation process for Dashboards B and C, noting comparative strengths and weaknesses. Students must identify at least three specific issues and three positive elements for each dashboard.

Step 3 (20 minutes): In pairs, students compare their individual assessments and create a collaborative ranking of the three dashboards from most to least effective. They must justify their ranking with specific evidence from their evaluations.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each pair selects the lowest-ranked dashboard and develops three concrete improvement recommendations. Recommendations must specify exact changes (e.g., 'Replace pie chart with horizontal bar chart for better comparison of sales categories') and explain the reasoning using visualization principles.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Pairs present their dashboard ranking and top improvement recommendation to the class in 90-second presentations. Other students provide feedback using the peer evaluation form.

Conclude with a class discussion identifying common evaluation criteria and improvement themes that emerged across all groups.
materials_needed: Three sample business dashboards (provided as printed handouts and digital display)
Dashboard Evaluation Worksheet with criteria checklist
Peer evaluation feedback forms
Projector or large monitor for dashboard display
Timer for activity pacing
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Completeness of individual dashboard analysis (25%), (2) Quality of evidence used to support evaluations (25%), (3) Specificity and feasibility of improvement recommendations (25%), (4) Clear justification linking recommendations to visualization principles (25%). Students must demonstrate evaluation skills by providing at least 6 specific observations per dashboard and 3 actionable recommendations with principle-based reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guiding questions on the evaluation worksheet and create mixed-ability pairs. Offer a reference sheet with common visualization problems and solutions. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify subtle usability issues, suggest alternative chart types, or consider accessibility improvements. Encourage them to reference specific design frameworks like Tufte's principles or Nielsen's heuristics.

title: Design Your Dream City: A Geometric Urban Planning Project
description: Students will design and construct a scale model city layout using geometric shapes, calculating areas and perimeters while applying mathematical concepts to real-world urban planning challenges. They will create a comprehensive city plan that optimizes space usage and incorporates mathematical justifications for their design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city layout by applying area and perimeter calculations to optimize land use within given constraints
Students will construct a mathematical model through geometric shape combinations while justifying design decisions with quantitative reasoning
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with a 12x18 inch poster board representing 12 square kilometers of land. Explain that they must design a city for 50,000 residents with specific zones: residential (40% of total area), commercial (25%), industrial (15%), parks/recreation (15%), and transportation (5%). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups calculate the exact area needed for each zone using the given percentages and record calculations on their planning sheet. They must show all mathematical work.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using geometric shapes (rectangles, squares, circles, triangles), students sketch their initial city design on graph paper, ensuring each zone meets the area requirements. They must calculate the area of each geometric shape used and verify totals match their zone requirements.
