Step 3 (25 minutes): Groups refine their design by calculating perimeters of each zone to determine infrastructure costs (roads, utilities). They must minimize total perimeter while maintaining required areas, documenting their optimization strategy.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Students construct their final city model on the poster board using colored paper geometric shapes cut to scale. Each shape must be labeled with its dimensions and calculated area.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Groups create a mathematical summary report showing: total calculations for each zone, optimization strategies used, and cost analysis based on perimeter calculations (assume $10,000 per kilometer of perimeter for infrastructure).

Conclude with 5-minute group presentations where students explain their design choices and mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: 12x18 inch poster board (one per group)
Graph paper and rulers
Colored construction paper in 5 different colors
Scissors and glue sticks
Calculators
Planning worksheet templates
Measuring tape or meter sticks
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area and perimeter calculations (25 points), (2) Creative and logical city design that meets all constraints (25 points), (3) Quality of mathematical justification and optimization strategy (25 points), (4) Physical model accuracy and presentation clarity (25 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate clear mathematical reasoning in their design choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated area formulas reference sheet and consider pairing with stronger math students. Offer simplified shapes (rectangles and squares only) initially. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate irregular shapes, calculate population density per zone, or add budget constraints that require cost-benefit analysis of different geometric configurations.

title: Design Your Dream City: A Geometric Urban Planning Project: Written Report
description: Students will design and construct a scale model city layout using geometric principles, incorporating area calculations, proportional reasoning, and spatial optimization. They will create an original city plan that balances residential, commercial, and recreational spaces while meeting specific mathematical constraints.
estimated_duration: 110 minutes (can be split across two class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original city layout by applying area calculations, perimeter measurements, and scale factor conversions to design functional urban spaces
Students will synthesize geometric principles through creating a detailed mathematical justification report that explains their spatial decisions and resource allocations
instructions: **Phase 1: Planning (20 minutes)** Distribute city planning packets containing a 12x18 inch grid paper (each square = 1 city block), colored pencils, calculators, and rulers. Present the city requirements: total area of 200 square blocks, minimum 40% residential (green), 25% commercial (blue), 15% recreational (yellow), 10% industrial (red), and 10% transportation/roads (black). Students work in pairs to brainstorm their city vision and sketch initial layouts. **Phase 2: Mathematical Design (40 minutes)** Students calculate exact areas for each zone using the percentage requirements, then design their city layout on grid paper using the color-coding system. They must show all area calculations on a separate worksheet, ensuring each zone meets the minimum requirements while maintaining logical spatial relationships (e.g., industrial areas separated from residential). Students create a scale where 1 grid square = 2 city blocks, requiring them to convert their measurements accordingly. **Phase 3: 3D Construction (30 minutes)** Using building blocks or cardboard pieces, students construct key buildings in their city, maintaining proportional heights and spacing based on their 2D plan. Each building's footprint must match their grid design exactly. **Phase 4: Mathematical Justification (20 minutes)** Students complete a written report explaining their design choices, showing all area calculations, scale conversions, and geometric reasoning for building placement and transportation routes. They must include at least three mathematical justifications for their spatial decisions.
materials_needed: 12x18 inch grid paper (1 sheet per pair)
Colored pencils or markers (5 colors minimum)
Rulers and calculators
Small building blocks or cardboard squares (30-40 pieces per pair)
City Planning Requirements handout
Mathematical Justification worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and scale conversions (25%), (2) Design creativity and functionality meeting all zone requirements (25%), (3) Quality of mathematical justifications in written report (25%), and (4) Collaboration and presentation of final city model (25%). Students must achieve minimum 80% accuracy in calculations and include at least 3 geometric principles in their justification report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated area templates and allow use of area formulas reference sheet. Offer visual fraction circles to help with percentage calculations. For advanced learners: Add constraints like budget limitations requiring cost-per-square-block calculations, or incorporate geometric shapes beyond rectangles (triangular parks, circular plazas) requiring more complex area formulas.
original_title: Design Your Dream City: A Geometric Urban Planning Project

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity classifications for 25 advanced algorithms across sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and tree operations. This rapid-fire recall activity tests foundational knowledge essential for algorithm analysis and technical interviews.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity (best, average, worst case) for 25 advanced algorithms within 3 minutes by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify the space complexity and auxiliary space requirements for advanced data structure operations through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared algorithm complexity reference sheets containing 25 algorithms: Heap Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Radix Sort, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A* Search, Breadth-First Search, Depth-First Search, Kruskal's MST, Prim's MST, Binary Search Tree operations, AVL Tree rotations, Red-Black Tree operations, Hash Table operations, Trie operations, Knapsack DP, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Convex Hull (Graham Scan), Fast Fourier Transform, KMP String Matching, and Rabin-Karp Algorithm. Give students 10 minutes to study the complexity notations intensively using active recall techniques - covering answers and testing themselves repeatedly. Next, conduct Round 1 (8 minutes): Project algorithm names one at a time using slides. Students write time complexity (best/average/worst) and space complexity on answer sheets within 15 seconds per algorithm. Cover all 25 algorithms systematically. After Round 1, provide 3 minutes for students to review missed items using reference sheets. Conduct Round 2 (5 minutes): Rapid-fire the same 25 algorithms in randomized order, allowing only 10 seconds per response. Students must write complete complexity analysis. Conclude with immediate peer checking using provided answer keys, where students exchange papers and grade using the detailed rubric. Record individual scores and identify algorithms requiring additional study.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm complexity reference sheets (1 per student)
Answer sheets with algorithm names and complexity columns
Timer/stopwatch for timed rounds
Projector/slides with algorithm names
Detailed answer key with complete complexity analysis
Grading rubric sheets for peer assessment
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 algorithms correct) on Round 2 rapid recall. Each algorithm scores 4 points: 1 point each for best-case time complexity, average-case time complexity, worst-case time complexity, and space complexity. Partial credit given for partially correct responses. Peer graders use provided rubric to mark each complexity component, with instructor spot-checking 25% of papers for accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce initial set to 15 core algorithms and extend study time to 15 minutes. Provide mnemonic devices sheet for common complexity patterns. For advanced learners, include amortized analysis requirements and ask them to explain why specific complexities occur. Create study partnerships pairing stronger recall students with those needing support during review periods.

title: Shopping Cart Percentage Calculations: Applying Discounts and Tax
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to real-world shopping scenarios by computing discounts, sales tax, and final prices. They will work through multiple purchase scenarios using different percentage rates to reinforce their understanding of percentage applications.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate discounts and sales tax on purchases by applying percentage formulas to given shopping scenarios
Students will determine final purchase prices through multi-step percentage calculations involving both discounts and tax rates
instructions: Begin by distributing the Shopping Cart Worksheet containing 8 different purchase scenarios (15 minutes setup). Each scenario includes an original price, discount percentage, and local sales tax rate. Model the first example on the board: Original price $80, 25% discount, 8.5% sales tax. Demonstrate: Step 1 - Calculate discount amount ($80 × 0.25 = $20), Step 2 - Subtract discount from original price ($80 - $20 = $60), Step 3 - Calculate tax on discounted price ($60 × 0.085 = $5.10), Step 4 - Add tax to get final price ($60 + $5.10 = $65.10). Have students work in pairs for 20 minutes to complete scenarios 2-5, checking their work with partners before moving forward. Circulate to provide individual support and verify calculations. For scenarios 6-8, students work independently for 15 minutes. These scenarios include additional complexity such as multiple items and varying discount rates. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class review where volunteer pairs present their solutions for scenarios 6-8, explaining their calculation process step-by-step. Record correct answers on the board and address any common computational errors. Students must show all four calculation steps for each scenario to receive full credit.
materials_needed: Shopping Cart Worksheet with 8 purchase scenarios
Calculators (one per student)
Whiteboard and markers
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheets showing all calculation steps. Grade using 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct final answer with all steps shown clearly, 3 points for correct process with minor computational errors, 2 points for correct setup with significant calculation mistakes, 1 point for attempting the problem with major conceptual errors. Minimum 75% accuracy (6 out of 8 scenarios correct) indicates mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a calculation template showing the four steps with blanks to fill in, offer a reference sheet with percentage-to-decimal conversions (25% = 0.25), and allow use of the first modeled example as a guide. For advanced learners: add compound discount scenarios (e.g., 20% off sale price already marked down 30%), include tip calculations on restaurant bills, or create their own shopping scenarios with multiple items and varying tax rates for classmates to solve.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Multi-Class Medical Diagnosis
description: Students will critically assess three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, SVM, and Neural Network) applied to a multi-class medical diagnosis dataset, evaluating their appropriateness, limitations, and real-world implementation feasibility. They will synthesize findings into evidence-based recommendations for clinical deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of three ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, computational requirements, and interpretability trade-offs within a medical diagnosis context
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of validation results, bias detection, and clinical implementation constraints
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-processed medical dataset (e.g., dermatology conditions with 34 features, 6 diagnostic classes) and three pre-trained models with their training logs, validation results, and prediction outputs. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team the same dataset but different random seeds for model training results. 

Step 1 (45 min): Teams analyze each model's performance using provided confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and feature importance plots. Students calculate additional metrics not provided (F1-macro, balanced accuracy, Cohen's kappa) and document computational training times and memory usage.

Step 2 (30 min): Teams evaluate model interpretability by examining feature importance rankings, SHAP values (provided), and prediction confidence intervals. They assess which model provides most clinically meaningful explanations.

Step 3 (45 min): Students research and document real-world constraints: FDA approval requirements for medical ML, hospital IT infrastructure limitations, clinician workflow integration, and patient data privacy considerations. They evaluate how each model addresses these constraints.

Step 4 (60 min): Teams create evidence-based recommendation reports (max 2 pages) ranking the three models with detailed justifications. Reports must address: performance trade-offs, implementation feasibility, ethical considerations, and potential failure modes.

Step 5 (30 min): Each team presents 5-minute recommendations to the class, followed by peer questioning and instructor-facilitated discussion comparing different teams' conclusions and reasoning processes.
materials_needed: Dermatology diagnosis dataset (CSV format with 366 samples, 34 features)
Three pre-trained model files (.pkl format) with training/validation results
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded visualizations (confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP plots)
Medical ML deployment research packet with FDA guidelines and case studies
Model performance summary templates (Excel/Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical analysis accuracy of model performance metrics and interpretability assessment, (2) Critical reasoning quality in identifying trade-offs and limitations, (3) Evidence integration of technical results with real-world constraints, (4) Recommendation justification with clear, logical argumentation, (5) Peer evaluation during Q&A demonstrating deep understanding. Students must score 'Proficient' (3/4) or higher in at least 4/5 dimensions for successful completion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation templates and guided questions for each evaluation step. Offer one-on-one check-ins during Step 2 to ensure interpretability analysis is on track. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose ensemble methods or conduct additional bias analysis across demographic subgroups. Encourage investigation of model uncertainty quantification and its clinical implications.

title: Programming Keywords Memory Card Matching Game
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental programming keywords from Python, Java, and C++ through a structured card matching activity. This activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for reading and writing code in multiple programming languages.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recall 20 fundamental programming keywords (if, else, while, for, class, function, return, etc.) by matching term cards with definition cards
Students will recognize programming keywords across Python, Java, and C++ syntax through repeated exposure and verbal recitation exercises
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Prepare 40 index cards - write one programming keyword on 20 cards (if, else, while, for, class, def/function, return, import, try, catch, int, string, boolean, array, list, loop, break, continue, public, private) and corresponding definitions on the remaining 20 cards. Shuffle all cards together. **Round 1 (15 minutes):** Place all 40 cards face-down in an 8x5 grid on desks. Students work in pairs, taking turns flipping two cards to find keyword-definition matches. When a match is found, the student must verbally state the keyword and its definition before keeping the pair. If incorrect match, cards are flipped back face-down. **Round 2 (10 minutes):** Remove cards from play area. Give each pair a complete set of 20 keyword cards face-up. Call out definitions randomly - students race to identify and hold up the correct keyword card. Award one point per correct identification. **Round 3 (15 minutes):** Display keyword cards on board. Students work individually to write definitions from memory on paper, then compare with official definition cards. **Closing (5 minutes):** Students verbally recite all 20 keywords in alphabetical order as a class, with instructor prompting definitions for random selections.
materials_needed: 80 blank index cards (40 per pair of students)
Black markers for writing cards
Timer or stopwatch
Prepared list of 20 programming keywords and definitions
Paper and pencils for Round 3
Whiteboard or projector for displaying cards
assessment_method: Students must correctly match 16/20 keyword-definition pairs during Round 1, identify 15/20 keywords correctly when definitions are called in Round 2, and write accurate definitions for 14/20 keywords from memory in Round 3. Record individual scores for each round using a simple checklist rubric.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with 5-7 most common keywords highlighted and allow consultation during Round 1. For advanced learners: Include additional keywords specific to object-oriented programming (inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation) or ask them to provide example code snippets using each keyword during the final recitation.

title: Understanding Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Dataset
description: Students will analyze correlation matrices and scatter plots to identify relationships between customer features and churn behavior. They will interpret correlation coefficients and explain how different variables influence customer retention patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing a correlation heatmap and identifying strong, moderate, and weak relationships
Students will explain the practical implications of feature correlations through written analysis connecting statistical patterns to business scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (3-4 people) with the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a telecommunications customer churn dataset with 15 features including monthly charges, contract length, internet service type, and churn status. In the first 15 minutes, students individually examine the correlation matrix heatmap and identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations with the churn variable, recording correlation coefficients in their analysis worksheet. Next, spend 20 minutes in groups where students create scatter plots for the top 4 correlated features against churn, discussing what they observe about data distribution patterns. During minutes 35-50, groups analyze multi-collinearity issues by identifying feature pairs with correlations above 0.7 and discussing why this matters for predictive modeling. In the final 25 minutes, each group writes a 200-word business interpretation explaining: (1) which customer characteristics most strongly predict churn, (2) which features might be redundant due to high correlation, and (3) two actionable business recommendations based on their correlation analysis. Groups present their key findings in 2-minute summaries to the class. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are correctly interpreting correlation values and distinguishing between correlation strength and causation.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib pre-installed
Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 15 features, 2000+ rows)
Correlation analysis worksheet template
Access to computers/laptops for each student group
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of correlation coefficients and their strength categories (25%), (2) Correct interpretation of scatter plot patterns and outliers (25%), (3) Appropriate identification of multi-collinearity issues (25%), (4) Quality of business recommendations connecting statistical findings to actionable insights (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide showing coefficient ranges (-1 to -0.7 strong negative, -0.7 to -0.3 moderate negative, etc.) and pre-highlighted examples in the heatmap. For advanced learners, introduce partial correlation analysis and ask them to calculate correlation significance tests using scipy.stats, or have them explore non-linear relationships using mutual information scores.

title: Critical Analysis of Database Query Optimization Strategies in Real-World Systems
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics and trade-offs of different query optimization techniques by examining execution plans, identifying bottlenecks, and evaluating the effectiveness of various indexing strategies on a complex e-commerce database. This expert-level activity requires students to deconstruct optimization decisions and justify alternative approaches based on data patterns and system constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze query execution plans by dissecting cost estimations, join algorithms, and index utilization patterns to identify performance bottlenecks in complex multi-table queries
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different optimization strategies through systematic comparison of execution statistics, resource consumption metrics, and scalability implications
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 2-3 students with access to a pre-loaded PostgreSQL database containing 500,000+ records across 8 interconnected tables (users, orders, products, categories, reviews, inventory, shipping, payments). Students receive five deliberately inefficient queries that simulate real-world e-commerce scenarios: customer lifetime value calculation, inventory turnover analysis, geographic sales patterns, product recommendation correlation, and seasonal trend analysis. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams execute each query using EXPLAIN ANALYZE, documenting baseline performance metrics including execution time, buffer hits/misses, and cost estimates. They must identify specific bottlenecks by analyzing sequential scans, nested loops, and sort operations in the execution plans.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students systematically test three optimization approaches per query: index creation (B-tree, partial, composite), query restructuring (subquery elimination, join reordering, CTE usage), and materialized view implementation. For each approach, they document the rationale, implementation steps, and resulting performance changes.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams analyze trade-offs by examining storage overhead, maintenance costs, and query pattern compatibility. They must justify which optimization strategy provides the best balance for each scenario, considering factors like update frequency, concurrent user load, and memory constraints.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Each team presents their most surprising finding, explaining the underlying database concepts that caused unexpected results and proposing additional testing methodologies to validate their conclusions.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database server with pgAdmin or DBeaver access
Pre-populated e-commerce database schema with realistic data volumes
Five complex SQL queries designed with intentional inefficiencies
Performance monitoring worksheet template
Database optimization reference guide with index syntax examples
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical accuracy of execution plan interpretation (30 points), quality of optimization strategy selection and implementation (25 points), depth of trade-off analysis with specific metrics and reasoning (25 points), clarity of bottleneck identification and solution justification (20 points). Students must submit annotated execution plans, performance comparison tables, and written analysis defending their optimization choices with quantitative evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide execution plan reading guides with annotated examples and a decision tree for selecting appropriate index types. Offer intermediate checkpoints where students can verify their analysis before proceeding. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints such as limited memory budgets, specific SLA requirements, or concurrent workload scenarios that require more sophisticated optimization strategies and cost-benefit calculations.

title: Design a Mini-Golf Course Using Quadratic Functions
description: Students will design and construct a 3-hole mini-golf course where each hole's path is modeled by a different quadratic function. They will create physical models, write corresponding equations, and justify their mathematical choices through peer presentations.
learning_objectives: Students will construct quadratic function models by designing realistic mini-golf hole trajectories that demonstrate vertex form, standard form, and factored form applications
Students will synthesize their understanding of quadratic properties through creating physical representations and defending mathematical design choices to peers
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with construction materials. Explain that they have 90 minutes to design a complete 3-hole mini-golf course with specific mathematical requirements.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams brainstorm and sketch three different hole designs on graph paper. Each hole must demonstrate: Hole 1 - a parabolic path opening upward (ball goes up and over an obstacle), Hole 2 - a parabolic path opening downward (ball follows a valley or depression), and Hole 3 - a parabolic path with two x-intercepts (ball must pass through two specific points).

Step 2 (45 minutes): Teams construct their physical models using cardboard as the base (18" x 24" per hole), pipe cleaners or wire to show the parabolic paths, and small objects as obstacles. Simultaneously, they must write the quadratic equation for each hole's trajectory, showing work in vertex form, standard form, and factored form where applicable.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams create a 'Course Guide' poster showing all three equations, explaining the domain and range for each hole, identifying key features (vertex, y-intercept, axis of symmetry), and justifying why each mathematical choice makes sense for their physical design.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Set up a gallery walk where teams display their courses and mathematical work around the classroom, preparing 2-minute presentations explaining their design choices and mathematical reasoning.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1 sheet per student)
Cardboard pieces (18" x 24", 3 pieces per team)
Colored pipe cleaners or bendable wire
Small wooden blocks or plastic cups for obstacles
Golf balls or ping pong balls for testing
Rulers and protractors
Poster paper for Course Guide
Colored markers or pencils
Graphing calculators or Desmos access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (equations correctly represent physical models, all three forms shown with correct work), Physical Design Quality (models clearly demonstrate parabolic paths, creative and realistic obstacles), Mathematical Reasoning (Course Guide clearly explains vertex, intercepts, domain/range with proper justification), and Communication (clear 2-minute presentation defending design choices). Each category worth 25 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-made coordinate grids on cardboard bases and equation templates showing vertex form structure. Offer midpoint check-ins at 30 and 60 minutes. Extend advanced learners by requiring them to include quadratic inequalities showing 'safe zones' where balls won't go out of bounds, or by having them calculate optimal launch angles and velocities using physics applications of their quadratic models.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units for each layer of the TCP/IP protocol stack through a structured flashcard and timed recall exercise. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network protocol architecture that students must have memorized for advanced networking courses.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the four TCP/IP protocol stack layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) and their specific functions by completing timed memory exercises
Students will identify the primary protocols and data units associated with each TCP/IP layer through systematic memorization and verification activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet containing 16 specific protocol functions, 12 key protocols, and 4 data unit types across the four layers. Give students 15 minutes to study the materials using any memorization technique they prefer. Next, collect all reference materials and distribute blank TCP/IP Layer Template worksheets. Students have 8 minutes to complete Section A: writing all four layer names in correct order from top to bottom. Then allow 12 minutes for Section B: listing three specific functions for each layer (12 total functions required). For Section C, give students 10 minutes to write the primary protocols for each layer (minimum 2 per layer, maximum 4 per layer). Finally, allocate 5 minutes for Section D: identifying the correct data unit name for each layer (packet, frame, segment, message). After completion, redistribute reference sheets for immediate self-checking. Students mark their own papers using the provided answer key, circling incorrect or missing answers. Conduct a brief whole-class review where volunteers share memorization strategies that worked best. Close by having students create a personal study plan for any areas where they scored below 80% accuracy, identifying specific protocols or functions they need to re-memorize before the next class session.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet (one per student)
Blank TCP/IP Layer Template worksheets (one per student)
Answer key for self-checking
Timer or stopwatch
Red pens for self-marking
assessment_method: Students self-assess using provided answer key. Success criteria: 100% accuracy on layer names and order, 80% accuracy on protocol functions (minimum 10/12 correct), 75% accuracy on protocol identification (minimum 6/8 protocols correct), 100% accuracy on data unit identification (4/4 correct). Instructor spot-checks 25% of completed worksheets for verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pneumonic devices for layer order (e.g., 'All Teachers In Night-school') and allow an additional 5 minutes study time. Create simplified reference sheets with only essential protocols. For advanced learners: Add Layer 5 challenge requiring recall of specific port numbers for common protocols, or include OSI model comparison section requiring recall of all 7 OSI layers and their mapping to TCP/IP layers.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units of each layer in the TCP/IP protocol stack. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network architecture through systematic memorization and retrieval practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the four layers of the TCP/IP model and their specific functions by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will identify the primary protocols operating at each TCP/IP layer through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP reference sheets containing all layer information (15 minutes for initial study). Students work individually to review: Application Layer (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS), Transport Layer (TCP, UDP, port numbers), Internet Layer (IP, ICMP, ARP routing), and Network Access Layer (Ethernet, WiFi, MAC addresses). After study time, collect all materials. Conduct Round 1: Display layer names on screen, students write down 3 key functions per layer (8 minutes). Round 2: Show protocol acronyms (HTTP, TCP, IP, ARP), students identify correct layer and write full protocol name (5 minutes). Round 3: Present network scenarios ('sending email,' 'web browsing'), students list all four layers' roles in sequence (10 minutes). Between rounds, allow 2-minute review periods where students can re-examine their reference materials. For final assessment, students complete a comprehensive recall sheet listing all protocols, their layers, primary functions, and data unit names (segments, packets, frames) without any references (12 minutes). Use timer prominently displayed for all phases. Collect completed sheets immediately when time expires.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheets (one per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Assessment recall worksheets
Projector for displaying prompts
Answer key with complete protocol information
assessment_method: Grade recall worksheets using point system: 4 points per layer correctly named, 3 points per protocol correctly placed in appropriate layer, 2 points per accurate function description, 1 point per correct data unit identification. Total possible: 100 points. Mastery threshold: 85+ points indicates successful memorization of TCP/IP fundamentals.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonics like 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for layer sequence, allow color-coding of materials during study phase. For advanced learners: add OSI model comparison requirements, include specific port numbers for protocols, require identification of protocol headers and their fields.
original_title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Challenge

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance
description: Students will analyze the time complexity of different searching and sorting algorithms by examining code implementations, tracing execution paths, and comparing theoretical Big O notation with empirical runtime data. They will decompose algorithms into component operations and evaluate trade-offs between different algorithmic approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort algorithms by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and operation counts
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of Big O notation against measured runtime performance on datasets of varying sizes
instructions: Begin by providing students with four code implementations: linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort in their familiar programming language (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair two algorithms to analyze. Students first trace through each algorithm with a sample dataset of 8 elements, counting the number of comparison operations performed and documenting decision points where the algorithm branches (20 minutes). Next, students identify nested loops, recursive calls, and repetitive operations, then determine the theoretical Big O time complexity for best, average, and worst-case scenarios (25 minutes). Provide students with a timing framework and datasets of sizes 100, 1000, and 10000 elements. Students run each algorithm multiple times, record execution times, and create graphs showing runtime growth patterns (30 minutes). Students then create a comparison matrix analyzing: operation counts, memory usage patterns, input sensitivity (sorted vs. unsorted data impact), and scalability predictions for datasets of 100,000 elements (20 minutes). Conclude with pair presentations where each team explains their complexity analysis, shows their runtime graphs, and justifies which algorithm they would choose for specific scenarios: small datasets, large datasets, memory-constrained environments, and frequently searched data (15 minutes per presentation). Instructor facilitates discussion comparing theoretical predictions with empirical results and addressing discrepancies.
materials_needed: Code implementations of linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort
Computers with programming environment (Python, Java, or C++)
Pre-generated datasets (100, 1000, 10000 elements) in CSV format
Timing measurement code template
Algorithm analysis worksheet with comparison matrix template
Graphing software or spreadsheet application
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O complexity identification (25 points), (2) Correct operation counting and tracing documentation (20 points), (3) Quality of empirical data collection and graphing (20 points), (4) Depth of algorithm comparison analysis including trade-offs discussion (25 points), (5) Presentation clarity and justification of algorithm selection for given scenarios (10 points). Students submit traced examples, completed comparison matrices, runtime graphs, and scenario recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed tracing examples and Big O reference sheet with common patterns. Offer pre-made timing code and step-by-step complexity analysis checklist. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms like quicksort or heap sort, challenge them to analyze space complexity alongside time complexity, or have them implement optimizations and measure improvement impacts.

title: Algorithm Complexity Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of different search and sorting algorithms by examining code implementations and empirically testing performance with varying dataset sizes. They will decompose algorithmic structures to identify efficiency patterns and evaluate trade-offs between different approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort algorithms by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and data access patterns
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency trade-offs through systematic performance testing and complexity classification using Big O notation
instructions: Begin by providing students with four pre-written algorithm implementations (linear search, binary search, bubble sort, merge sort) in their chosen programming language. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical code files and a data analysis worksheet. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams examine each algorithm's code structure, counting nested loops, identifying recursive patterns, and documenting their observations on the worksheet. They must trace through each algorithm with a small dataset (10 elements) to understand execution flow. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students run performance tests using provided datasets of sizes 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements. They record execution times and memory usage for each algorithm-dataset combination in a structured table. Emphasize consistent testing conditions. Step 3 (15 minutes): Teams graph their timing results with dataset size on x-axis and execution time on y-axis, creating separate plots for search and sort algorithms. Step 4 (20 minutes): Students analyze their graphs to identify complexity patterns, matching observed performance curves to theoretical Big O classifications (O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(log n)). They must justify their classifications with specific evidence from code structure and performance data. Step 5 (10 minutes): Teams present one algorithm analysis to class, explaining the relationship between code structure and observed performance, highlighting specific bottlenecks or efficiency gains.
materials_needed: Pre-written algorithm implementations in Python/Java/C++ (4 algorithms per student)
Performance testing datasets (CSV files with 100, 1000, 5000, 10000 integer elements)
Algorithm analysis worksheet with tables for observations and measurements
Graphing software or graph paper for plotting results
Computers with programming environment and timing libraries installed
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of algorithm complexity patterns from code analysis, (2) Accurate performance data collection and graphing, (3) Proper Big O classification with supporting evidence, (4) Clear explanation of structure-performance relationships. Students must achieve 3/4 points on each criterion. Additionally, assess team presentations for accurate complexity justification and identification of specific code elements causing performance differences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm flowcharts and highlight key structural elements (nested loops, recursive calls) before analysis begins. Offer guided questions like 'How many times does this inner loop execute?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity in addition to time complexity, or have them modify algorithms to improve efficiency and test their optimizations. Provide additional algorithms like quicksort or hash table implementations for extended analysis.
original_title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance

title: Model Performance Audit: Evaluating Bias and Fairness in Healthcare AI Systems
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three pre-trained machine learning models designed for medical diagnosis prediction, critically assessing their performance across different demographic groups and making evidence-based recommendations for model selection in a clinical setting. This activity requires students to synthesize technical performance metrics with ethical considerations and real-world implementation constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the fairness and bias of machine learning models by analyzing performance disparities across demographic subgroups using statistical parity and equalized odds metrics
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of multiple evaluation criteria including accuracy, interpretability, computational efficiency, and ethical implications
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data and Model Setup (30 minutes)**
Provide students with a synthetic healthcare dataset containing 10,000 patient records with features including age, gender, race, insurance type, and medical history, along with three pre-trained models: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Neural Network. Students work in teams of 3-4 and receive identical datasets but different model performance reports.

**Phase 2: Technical Performance Analysis (45 minutes)**
Teams calculate and compare standard metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC) for each model on the overall test set. Then, students segment the data by demographic groups (gender, race, age brackets) and recalculate these metrics for each subgroup. They must identify performance gaps exceeding 5% between groups and document findings in a structured comparison matrix.

**Phase 3: Bias and Fairness Assessment (60 minutes)**
Using provided Python code templates, students calculate fairness metrics including demographic parity (equal positive prediction rates), equalized opportunity (equal true positive rates), and calibration across groups. Teams must determine which model exhibits the least bias using at least three different fairness definitions and justify why different fairness metrics may conflict.

**Phase 4: Contextual Evaluation and Recommendation (45 minutes)**
Teams receive a hospital implementation scenario with specific constraints: limited computational resources, requirement for model interpretability, diverse patient population, and regulatory compliance needs. Students must weigh technical performance against fairness concerns and practical constraints to recommend one model, providing a detailed justification addressing all stakeholder perspectives including clinicians, hospital administrators, and patient advocacy groups.
materials_needed: Synthetic healthcare dataset (CSV format) with demographic variables and health outcomes
Three pre-trained model files (.pkl format) with different architectures
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, and fairlearn libraries
Model evaluation template spreadsheet with pre-formatted metric calculations
Hospital implementation scenario document with specific constraints and requirements
assessment_method: Teams submit a 4-page technical report with: (1) Quantitative comparison table showing all performance and fairness metrics across models and demographic groups (25 points), (2) Critical analysis section identifying trade-offs between accuracy and fairness with specific examples (25 points), (3) Evidence-based recommendation with detailed justification addressing technical, ethical, and practical considerations (30 points), (4) Risk assessment discussing potential consequences of their chosen model in clinical practice (20 points). Rubric includes technical accuracy, depth of analysis, quality of reasoning, and consideration of multiple stakeholder perspectives.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed examples of metric calculations for one demographic group and model, offer guided questions for each analysis phase, and allow extended time for Phase 3. For advanced learners: Include additional fairness metrics (counterfactual fairness, individual fairness), require analysis of feature importance and model interpretability, or add a cost-benefit analysis incorporating potential legal and reputational risks. Consider pairing stronger technical students with those better at ethical reasoning.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Differential Equations and Graph Theory
description: Students will synthesize differential equations, graph theory, and optimization techniques to create an original mathematical model that addresses real-world urban traffic congestion. They will design their own traffic network scenario, develop governing equations, and propose implementable solutions with quantitative justification.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical model combining differential equations and graph theory by analyzing traffic flow dynamics in a self-designed urban network scenario
Students will synthesize optimization techniques and real-world constraints through developing implementable traffic management solutions with complete mathematical justification
instructions:
**Phase 1 (40 minutes): Network Design and Problem Formulation**
Students work in pairs to design a fictional urban intersection network with 4-6 roads, specifying: road capacities (vehicles/minute), typical traffic volumes, traffic light timing, and peak/off-peak patterns. They must identify a specific traffic problem (bottlenecks, inefficient light timing, or emergency vehicle access). Using graph theory, students represent their network as a directed graph with weighted edges representing traffic flow rates.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Mathematical Model Development**
Students formulate differential equations governing traffic flow using conservation principles (∂ρ/∂t + ∂q/∂x = 0 where ρ is density, q is flow). They must incorporate: fundamental traffic flow relationships (q = ρv, where v is velocity), capacity constraints, and traffic light controls as piecewise functions. Students define state variables, parameters, and boundary conditions specific to their network design.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Optimization Strategy Creation**
Using calculus of variations or linear programming, students formulate an optimization problem to minimize total travel time or maximize throughput. They must define objective functions, constraint equations, and decision variables (light timing, lane configurations, or speed limits). Students solve simplified versions analytically and propose computational approaches for complex scenarios.

**Phase 4 (35 minutes): Solution Implementation and Validation**
Students present their complete model including: network diagram, governing equations, optimization formulation, proposed solutions, and quantitative predictions of improvement (% reduction in wait time, increased throughput). They must address model limitations, sensitivity to parameters, and real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Graphing software (GeoGebra, Desmos, or MATLAB)
Large format paper for network diagrams
Scientific calculators
Access to optimization solver (Excel Solver or Python scipy.optimize)
Traffic flow data sheets with realistic parameter ranges
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four criteria (25 points each): 1) Mathematical rigor and correctness of differential equations and graph representation, 2) Creativity and feasibility of network design and problem identification, 3) Completeness and validity of optimization formulation and solution approach, 4) Quality of mathematical communication and justification of results. Students must submit written model documentation and deliver 10-minute presentations with peer Q&A.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing traffic flow equation templates and simplified 2-road intersection examples. Offer parameter value ranges and dimensionality checking guides. For advanced learners, introduce stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or dynamic programming approaches. Provide extension challenges involving pedestrian flows, autonomous vehicles, or environmental impact optimization.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Differential Equations and Graph Theory: Exercise 1
description: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, graph theory, and operations research to create an original mathematical model that optimizes traffic flow in a real urban intersection. They will develop custom differential equations, validate their model with real data, and present implementation recommendations to city planners.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical model incorporating differential equations and graph theory by analyzing real traffic flow data and urban infrastructure constraints
Students will design a comprehensive optimization solution through integration of multiple mathematical domains and validation against empirical evidence
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Research and Data Collection**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team selects a specific urban intersection using Google Earth/Maps and gathers traffic count data from city transportation departments or estimates based on observation videos. Teams identify key variables: vehicle arrival rates, signal timing, road capacity, pedestrian crossings, and turning restrictions. They photograph/screenshot intersection layouts and measure approximate distances and angles.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Model Development**
Teams formulate their intersection as a directed graph where nodes represent decision points and edges represent traffic lanes with capacity constraints. They develop a system of differential equations modeling vehicle density ρ(x,t) using conservation laws: ∂ρ/∂t + ∂(ρv)/∂x = S(x,t) where v is velocity and S represents sources/sinks (traffic lights, merging). Students incorporate optimization constraints using Lagrange multipliers to minimize total wait time while maximizing throughput. They must justify each mathematical choice with real-world reasoning.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Computational Implementation**
Using Python/MATLAB, teams program their model with actual parameters. They run simulations comparing current traffic light timing versus their optimized solution. Students generate visualizations showing traffic density heat maps, average wait times, and throughput metrics. They perform sensitivity analysis by varying key parameters (±20% traffic volume, different signal timings).

**Phase 4 (60 minutes): Validation and Presentation**
Teams prepare 15-minute presentations as if presenting to city traffic engineers. They must defend mathematical assumptions, demonstrate model accuracy against known data, and provide specific implementation recommendations with cost-benefit analysis. Include limitations, assumptions, and suggestions for model refinement.
materials_needed: Laptops with Python/MATLAB installed
Access to real traffic data (city databases or video footage)
Graph paper and measuring tools
Digital presentation software
Calculator with matrix capabilities
Printed city intersection maps
assessment_method: Evaluation based on 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical Rigor - correct application of differential equations and graph theory with appropriate complexity (25%), (2) Model Innovation - originality and sophistication of approach beyond standard textbook methods (25%), (3) Empirical Validation - effective use of real data and meaningful sensitivity analysis (25%), (4) Professional Communication - clear presentation of technical concepts to non-mathematical audience with actionable recommendations (25%). Students submit written technical report and deliver oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation forms and guide them to modify coefficients rather than derive from scratch. Offer simplified intersections (2-way stops vs complex roundabouts). For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multiple intersection networks, or machine learning optimization. Provide access to advanced simulation software like SUMO traffic simulator for validation.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Differential Equations and Graph Theory

title: Computer Hardware Component Matching Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify essential computer hardware components through a structured flashcard activity and matching game. This foundational activity helps students build vocabulary and visual recognition skills for internal computer parts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the names and basic functions of 10 essential computer hardware components by completing flashcard exercises
Students will identify computer hardware components through visual recognition activities using labeled diagrams and physical matching tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the hardware component flashcard set to each student (15 minutes for individual study). Students should review cards showing images of: CPU, RAM, motherboard, hard drive, power supply, graphics card, cooling fan, optical drive, network card, and sound card. Each card shows the component image on one side and name plus one-sentence function on the reverse. After individual review, pair students and have them quiz each other for 10 minutes, taking turns showing images and asking for component names. Next, display the large poster showing a computer's internal layout without labels. Call out component names randomly and have students point to the correct location on the poster - award one point per correct identification. For the final matching challenge (20 minutes), spread physical component cards face-up on tables. Read aloud component functions (e.g., 'This component stores data permanently even when power is off') and have students race to touch the correct component card. Students must state the component name aloud when touching the card. Keep score and provide immediate feedback for incorrect answers. Conclude with a quick verbal review where students recite all 10 component names from memory while looking at the unlabeled poster.
materials_needed: Laminated flashcard set with 10 computer hardware components (one set per student)
Large poster showing computer internal layout without component labels
Physical component identification cards for matching game
Whiteboard markers for scoring
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify 8 out of 10 components during the poster pointing activity and score at least 7 points during the matching challenge. Final success requires verbally naming all 10 components while viewing the unlabeled diagram within 60 seconds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with component names during the matching game and allow them to work with a partner. For advanced learners, add 5 additional specialized components (SSD, heat sink, BIOS chip, expansion slots, cables) and require them to explain component functions in their own words rather than just identifying names.

title: Optimizing Hospital Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex hospital resource allocation problem involving staff scheduling, equipment distribution, and budget constraints. This activity requires students to translate real-world constraints into mathematical inequalities and use the simplex method to find optimal solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to formulate a multi-variable optimization problem by converting real-world hospital constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method to solve complex resource allocation problems through systematic mathematical computation and interpretation of results
instructions:
Begin by distributing the hospital scenario packet to each group of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Present the problem: Memorial Hospital needs to optimize allocation of 120 nurses, 80 doctors, and $2.4M monthly budget across four departments (Emergency, Surgery, ICU, General). Each department has minimum staffing requirements and maximum capacity constraints. Students must maximize patient care effectiveness score while meeting all constraints.

Step 1 (30 minutes): Groups identify decision variables (staff allocation per department), write objective function (maximize care effectiveness: 85x₁ + 92x₂ + 78x₃ + 71x₄), and formulate constraint inequalities for staffing limits, budget restrictions, and minimum care requirements.

Step 2 (45 minutes): Using provided simplex method worksheets and calculators, students set up initial tableau, identify pivot elements, and perform row operations. Monitor groups closely during pivot calculations as errors compound quickly.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students interpret final tableau results, determining optimal staff allocation numbers and maximum effectiveness score. They must verify solutions satisfy all original constraints by substitution.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents their optimal allocation strategy to the class, explaining trade-offs between departments and justifying their mathematical approach. Conclude with comparison of different groups' solutions and discussion of sensitivity analysis implications.
materials_needed: Hospital scenario packets with detailed constraint data
Simplex method calculation worksheets
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for constraint plotting
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate simplex method calculations with proper pivot selection (35%), (3) Valid interpretation of results with constraint verification (25%), (4) Clear presentation explaining optimization rationale (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in calculation accuracy to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates and pivot selection flowchart. Offer one-on-one calculation checks after each tableau iteration. For advanced learners: Include sensitivity analysis questions about parameter changes and introduce dual problem formulation. Consider adding integer programming constraints for more realistic modeling.

title: Optimizing Hospital Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming: Technical Implementation
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex healthcare resource optimization problem involving nurse scheduling, bed allocation, and budget constraints. This real-world scenario requires students to formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and interpret solutions within a practical context.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to formulate and solve a multi-variable optimization problem by defining objective functions and constraint inequalities
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the hospital scenario handout describing Metro General Hospital's staffing crisis (5 minutes). Present the problem: optimize nurse scheduling across 3 shifts while minimizing costs and meeting patient care requirements. Students work in pairs to identify decision variables: x₁ (day shift nurses), x₂ (evening shift nurses), x₃ (night shift nurses). Guide them to formulate the objective function: Minimize C = 480x₁ + 400x₂ + 520x₃ (hourly wages × 8-hour shifts). Next, have students identify constraints from the scenario data: patient care minimums (x₁ ≥ 12, x₂ ≥ 8, x₃ ≥ 6), union requirements (x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≤ 45), and budget limits (480x₁ + 400x₂ + 520x₃ ≤ 18,000). Using graphing calculators or Excel Solver, students plot constraint boundaries and identify the feasible region (25 minutes). They then apply the corner point method to evaluate the objective function at each vertex of the feasible region. Students calculate costs at points (12,8,6), (12,8,25), (12,25,8), and (27,8,6), determining the optimal solution. Finally, pairs present their solutions, explaining why their combination minimizes costs while meeting all constraints. Conclude with interpretation: students must explain what their mathematical solution means for hospital operations, including trade-offs and real-world implementation challenges (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Metro General Hospital scenario handout with detailed constraint data
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent) or laptops with Excel
Graph paper for manual plotting verification
Linear programming solution worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of graphical/simplex method (35%), (3) Correct identification and verification of optimal solution (25%), (4) Clear interpretation of results in healthcare context (15%). Students must submit completed worksheets and present 3-minute solution explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint formulation templates and guide them through the first constraint identification. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how the solution changes if nurse wages increase by 10% or patient care minimums rise. Consider adding integer programming constraints requiring whole numbers of nurses.
original_title: Optimizing Hospital Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming

title: Optimizing Hospital Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming: Visual Analysis
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world hospital resource allocation problem involving nurse scheduling, bed assignments, and budget constraints. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will construct linear programming models by translating complex multi-variable hospital resource scenarios into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis to determine optimal resource allocation solutions while interpreting results in healthcare management context
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the 'Metro General Hospital Case Study' packet containing: staffing costs ($45/RN per hour, $28/LPN per hour), patient-to-staff ratios (ICU: 1:2 RN minimum, General: 1:4 RN/LPN flexible), bed capacity (20 ICU, 80 General), and daily budget constraints ($15,000 staffing limit). Form teams of 3-4 students. **Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (25 minutes):** Teams identify decision variables (x₁ = ICU RN hours, x₂ = ICU LPN hours, x₃ = General ward RN hours, x₄ = General ward LPN hours), write the objective function (minimize cost or maximize patient capacity), and establish constraints including regulatory requirements (RN certification mandates), budget limits, and minimum staffing levels. Each team documents their mathematical model on provided templates. **Phase 2 - Solution Implementation (35 minutes):** Using graphing calculators and provided LP software templates, teams solve their formulated problems using both graphical method (for 2-variable simplified versions) and simplex method (for full 4-variable problems). Students must show all pivot operations and constraint boundary calculations. **Phase 3 - Validation and Interpretation (15 minutes):** Teams verify solutions by substituting back into original constraints, calculate total costs/capacity achieved, and prepare 2-minute presentations explaining their optimal staffing recommendations. **Debrief (10 minutes):** Class discusses variations in approaches and real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Metro General Hospital Case Study packets (printed scenarios with specific numerical data)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Linear Programming Excel template with Solver add-in activated
LP solution documentation worksheets
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical formulation accuracy - correct identification of variables, constraints, and objective function (25 points), (2) Solution methodology - proper application of simplex method with shown work (30 points), (3) Answer verification - substitution check and feasibility confirmation (20 points), (4) Professional interpretation - realistic healthcare management recommendations with cost-benefit analysis (25 points). Teams submit written solutions and deliver oral presentations.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide constraint-writing templates with sentence starters ('The total cost cannot exceed...', 'The number of RN hours must be at least...'). Offer simplified 2-variable versions focusing only on RN vs LPN allocation. Create checkpoint sheets for each phase. **For advanced learners:** Introduce integer programming constraints (whole-person shifts only), add complexity with multiple hospital departments, or incorporate sensitivity analysis to determine how solution changes with budget modifications. Challenge them to consider multi-objective optimization balancing cost and patient satisfaction scores.
original_title: Optimizing Hospital Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming

title: Analyzing Cache Performance Trade-offs in Multi-level Memory Hierarchy Systems
description: Students will examine real-world cache performance data from different processor architectures to identify bottlenecks and analyze the relationships between cache parameters, memory access patterns, and overall system performance. They will deconstruct how cache design decisions impact different computational workloads and propose optimization strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze cache miss patterns and performance metrics by examining profiling data from three different memory-intensive applications across varying cache configurations

Students will deconstruct the relationships between cache size, associativity, block size, and replacement policies through systematic comparison of benchmark results and identification of performance trade-offs
instructions: Begin by providing students with three datasets containing cache performance metrics (hit rates, miss penalties, execution times) from matrix multiplication, database query processing, and image filtering applications running on processors with different L1/L2/L3 cache configurations. Form teams of 2-3 students and assign each team one primary application to focus on. In the first 30 minutes, teams examine their assigned dataset using provided Excel templates, identifying cache miss patterns across different input sizes and calculating cache utilization ratios. Students must plot miss rate curves and identify inflection points where performance degrades significantly. During minutes 30-60, teams analyze how changing cache parameters (doubling L1 size vs. increasing associativity vs. larger block sizes) affects their application's performance, using the provided calculator tool to model theoretical improvements. They must identify at least three specific cache design trade-offs and quantify their impact. In minutes 60-90, teams rotate to examine the other two applications' datasets, comparing how different memory access patterns (sequential vs. random vs. spatial locality) respond to the same cache modifications. Finally, in the last 30 minutes, each team presents a 5-minute analysis identifying the most critical cache bottleneck for each application type and defending their recommendation for optimal cache configuration given a fixed transistor budget. Teams must support conclusions with specific numerical evidence from their analysis and explain why their recommended configuration balances the competing demands of the three workload types.
materials_needed: Three cache performance datasets (CSV files with miss rates, execution times, cache statistics)
Excel template with pre-configured charts and calculation formulas
Cache performance modeling calculator (web-based tool or spreadsheet)
Laptops/computers with data analysis software
Large format paper for creating comparison charts
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of cache bottleneck identification with supporting quantitative evidence (25%), (2) Quality of trade-off analysis showing understanding of competing cache design factors (25%), (3) Appropriateness of optimization recommendations with clear rationale connecting cache parameters to application characteristics (25%), (4) Presentation clarity and use of data visualizations to support conclusions (25%). Teams must demonstrate analysis depth by citing specific numerical thresholds and explaining causal relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided analysis worksheets with specific questions about interpreting miss rate graphs and highlight key data points to examine first. Offer pre-calculated examples showing how to compute cache utilization ratios. For advanced learners, introduce additional variables like cache coherency overhead in multi-core scenarios or challenge them to model the impact of prefetching strategies on their performance analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Quality: Netflix Movie Dataset Analysis
description: Students will critically assess the quality and reliability of a Netflix movie dataset by identifying data issues and judging the appropriateness of different cleaning methods. They will then defend their data quality assessment using specific evidence from the dataset.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of a real-world dataset by systematically identifying completeness, accuracy, and consistency issues using pandas profiling techniques
Students will judge the effectiveness of different data cleaning approaches through comparative analysis and defend their recommendations with evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with the Netflix Movies and TV Shows dataset (available on Kaggle) and load it into Jupyter notebooks. Display the evaluation criteria on screen: completeness (missing values), accuracy (logical inconsistencies), consistency (format variations), and relevance (useful for analysis goals).

**Individual Analysis Phase (25 minutes):** Students use pandas functions (.info(), .describe(), .isnull().sum(), .value_counts()) to examine the dataset. They document specific issues found: missing ratings, inconsistent date formats, duplicate entries, and unrealistic duration values. Students create a data quality scorecard rating each criterion (1-5 scale) with written justification.

**Comparison Phase (20 minutes):** Present students with three pre-prepared data cleaning approaches: Method A (drop all rows with missing values), Method B (fill missing values with mode/median), Method C (selective cleaning based on column importance). Students calculate the impact of each method on dataset size and analyze sample outputs to evaluate which preserves data integrity best.

**Evaluation and Defense (20 minutes):** Students write a 200-word recommendation memo stating which cleaning method is most appropriate for a movie recommendation system project. They must cite specific evidence from their analysis, address potential limitations of their chosen method, and explain why they rejected other approaches.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange memos with partners and provide feedback using the evaluation rubric, checking for evidence-based reasoning and consideration of trade-offs.
materials_needed: Netflix Movies and TV Shows CSV dataset from Kaggle
Jupyter Notebook with pandas pre-installed
Data Quality Scorecard template (Excel or Google Sheets)
Three pre-prepared cleaning method examples
Evaluation rubric handout
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Data Quality Assessment - identifies 4+ specific issues with accurate pandas code (25 points), (2) Method Comparison - correctly analyzes impact of each cleaning approach with quantitative evidence (25 points), (3) Recommendation Defense - provides clear reasoning with dataset-specific evidence and addresses limitations (30 points), (4) Critical Thinking - demonstrates understanding of trade-offs and context considerations (20 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of pandas functions to try and examples of what data quality issues look like. Offer sentence starters for the recommendation memo. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose a fourth cleaning method, calculate statistical significance of data loss, or consider how different analysis goals might change their recommendations.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Playground Using Geometric Principles
description: Students will create an original playground design by applying geometric transformations, calculating areas and perimeters, and constructing a proportional scale model. They will justify their design choices using mathematical reasoning and present their project to simulate a city planning proposal.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize knowledge of geometric transformations, area calculations, and scale ratios by designing an original playground layout that meets specific spatial constraints
Students will construct a physical scale model and mathematical documentation through hands-on building and detailed calculations
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: students are junior architects tasked with designing a playground for a rectangular lot measuring 120 feet by 80 feet, with a budget allowing for 2,400 square feet of equipment coverage. Divide students into teams of 3-4. In the first 20 minutes, teams brainstorm playground elements and research real playground dimensions online. Next, spend 30 minutes having students sketch their initial design on coordinate plane paper (1 unit = 10 feet), ensuring they include at least 5 different geometric shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles, trapezoids, etc.) representing playground equipment. Students must apply at least two geometric transformations (rotation, reflection, translation) to create symmetrical or repeated elements in their design. During the following 40 minutes, teams calculate the area of each playground element, verify their total area stays within the 2,400 square foot limit, and determine the perimeter of the entire playground for fencing purposes. For the construction phase (50 minutes), students build a 3D scale model using a 1:240 scale ratio (1 inch = 20 feet) on poster board bases. They cut geometric shapes from colored paper and cardboard to represent equipment, creating height using layered materials. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents their playground design, explaining their mathematical calculations, geometric choices, and how their transformations created visual appeal or functional benefits.
materials_needed: Coordinate plane paper (1/4 inch grid)
Colored cardstock and construction paper
Poster board (11x17 inches minimum)
Rulers, protractors, and compasses
Calculators
Glue sticks and scissors
Access to computers/tablets for research
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations and scale conversions, (2) Correct application of geometric transformations with clear identification, (3) Creative and functional playground design that meets all constraints, (4) Quality of scale model construction and presentation clarity. Students must submit calculation worksheets showing all mathematical work and a written reflection explaining their design rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-made templates of basic playground equipment with dimensions, and offer area calculation worksheets with partially completed examples. Advanced learners can incorporate more complex geometric shapes (hexagons, composite figures), calculate material costs using unit pricing, or design accessible playground features requiring additional spatial considerations and ADA compliance measurements.

title: Personal Budget Creation Using Percentages and Basic Operations
description: Students will apply percentage calculations and basic arithmetic operations to create a realistic monthly budget based on a given income scenario.
