They will allocate funds across different expense categories using percentage guidelines and calculate exact dollar amounts for each budget category.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting percentages to dollar amounts using a given monthly income
Students will demonstrate addition and subtraction skills through creating a balanced budget that accounts for all income and expenses
instructions: Begin by distributing the budget scenario worksheets and providing each student with a calculator. Present the scenario: 'You have a monthly take-home income of $3,200. Create a monthly budget following the 50/30/20 rule: 50% for needs, 30% for wants, 20% for savings.' Step 1 (10 minutes): Students calculate the dollar amount for each main category by finding 50% of $3,200 ($1,600 for needs), 30% of $3,200 ($960 for wants), and 20% of $3,200 ($640 for savings). Step 2 (15 minutes): Within the 'needs' category ($1,600), students allocate percentages to subcategories: housing (65% of needs budget), food (20% of needs budget), transportation (10% of needs budget), and utilities (5% of needs budget). They calculate exact dollar amounts for each. Step 3 (15 minutes): For the 'wants' category ($960), students choose their own subcategories (entertainment, dining out, hobbies, etc.) and assign percentages that total 100%, then calculate dollar amounts. Step 4 (10 minutes): Students verify their budget by adding all expenses and confirming the total equals $3,200. They complete a budget summary table showing categories, percentages, and dollar amounts. Circulate during work time to check calculations and provide guidance on realistic expense categories.
materials_needed: Budget scenario worksheet with income amount and category guidelines
Scientific or basic calculators (one per student)
Budget summary table template
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations are correct, budget totals exactly $3,200, realistic expense categories chosen; (3) Minor calculation errors (1-2), budget within $50 of target, appropriate categories; (2) Some calculation errors (3-4), budget within $100 of target, mostly appropriate categories; (1) Multiple errors, budget significantly off target, or unrealistic allocations. Students must show work for all calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference sheet and pre-filled examples for the first two subcategories. Allow use of percentage calculators or conversion charts. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including irregular expenses (quarterly insurance, annual fees) that must be converted to monthly amounts, or have them create budgets for different income levels and compare allocation strategies.

title: Personal Budget Creation Using Percentages and Basic Operations: Exercise 1
description: Students will apply percentage calculations and basic arithmetic to create a realistic monthly budget for a hypothetical entry-level job scenario. They will use given salary information to calculate expenses, savings, and discretionary spending while ensuring their budget balances to 100%.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentage-based budget allocations by applying percentage formulas to a given monthly salary
Students will demonstrate accurate use of addition, subtraction, and percentage calculations through creating a balanced personal budget worksheet
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Monthly Salary Cards' - each student receives a card showing a different entry-level job with monthly take-home pay ranging from $2,200-$3,000. Present the budget categories on the board: Housing (30%), Transportation (15%), Food (12%), Utilities (8%), Savings (10%), Insurance (5%), Entertainment (10%), Miscellaneous (10%). Students first calculate each category amount by multiplying their salary by the percentage (converted to decimal). For example, with $2,500 salary: Housing = $2,500 × 0.30 = $750. Have students work for 15 minutes calculating all categories, showing their work clearly. Next, students add all calculated amounts to verify they equal their original salary, demonstrating budget balance. In the final 15 minutes, students adjust one category up or down by $50 and recalculate the affected percentage, then adjust another category to maintain balance. Students must show: original calculations, verification sum, adjustment calculations, and new percentages. Circulate to check work and provide individual guidance on calculation errors. Students complete their work on the provided budget worksheet template with clearly labeled sections for each step.
materials_needed: Monthly Salary Job Cards (pre-made with 8-10 different jobs/salaries)
Personal Budget Worksheet template (printed copies)
Calculator (basic four-function)
Pencil and eraser
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, budget balances, adjustment calculations accurate; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget approximately balances; (2) Some calculation errors, demonstrates understanding of process; (1) Multiple errors, incomplete work. Check for clearly shown work, correct percentage-to-decimal conversion, and accurate final verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a step-by-step calculation guide showing percentage-to-decimal conversion examples, allow use of multiplication tables, pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: challenge them to research actual costs in your local area and compare to calculated amounts, or create a budget for a family of four with additional categories like childcare and education expenses.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Order System
description: Students analyze the performance characteristics of different SQL queries on a simulated e-commerce database, identifying inefficient operations and explaining the relationship between query structure, indexing, and execution time. They will decompose complex queries to understand how different components impact overall system performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by examining index usage, join operations, and scan types to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate the relationship between database schema design and query efficiency through systematic comparison of execution metrics
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a pre-populated MySQL database containing three tables: customers (50,000 records), orders (200,000 records), and order_items (500,000 records). Students work in pairs and access the database through MySQL Workbench or similar tool. **Phase 1 (25 minutes):** Students execute five provided queries of increasing complexity, recording execution time and examining the EXPLAIN output for each. Query 1: Simple SELECT with WHERE clause on non-indexed column. Query 2: Same SELECT with indexed column. Query 3: JOIN between two tables without proper indexing. Query 4: Complex query with multiple JOINs and subqueries. Query 5: Optimized version of Query 4. For each query, students document: execution time, rows examined, join type, and whether indexes were used. **Phase 2 (20 minutes):** Students analyze patterns in their data, identifying which query characteristics correlate with poor performance. They create a comparison table showing before/after metrics when indexes are added or query structure is modified. **Phase 3 (15 minutes):** Each pair writes a brief analysis explaining why certain queries performed poorly, which specific elements caused bottlenecks, and how the database engine's execution strategy differed between efficient and inefficient queries. Students must reference specific metrics from their EXPLAIN analysis to support conclusions.
materials_needed: MySQL database with pre-loaded e-commerce dataset (customers, orders, order_items tables)
MySQL Workbench or equivalent database client software
Prepared SQL query file with 5 test queries
Data collection worksheet template
Access to computers with database connectivity
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed data collection table with execution metrics for all 5 queries, (2) Written analysis (300-400 words) identifying at least 3 specific performance bottlenecks with supporting evidence from EXPLAIN output, (3) Correctly identifying which query optimizations had the greatest impact on performance. Rubric awards points for accurate data collection (30%), correct identification of bottlenecks (40%), and quality of analysis linking query structure to performance metrics (30%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed data collection template and guiding questions about what to look for in EXPLAIN output (e.g., 'Does this query use an index? How many rows were examined?'). For advanced learners: Challenge them to write their own optimized versions of the slow queries and predict performance improvements before testing, or analyze additional metrics like buffer pool usage and temporary table creation.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Order System: Exercise 1
description: Students analyze SQL query execution plans and performance metrics from a simulated e-commerce database to identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks. They will examine actual vs. estimated costs, index usage, and join operations to determine why certain queries perform poorly and propose optimization strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining operator costs, row estimates, and index seeks to identify performance bottlenecks in database queries
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient query patterns through systematic comparison of execution statistics and resource utilization metrics
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a pre-populated PostgreSQL database containing 50,000 customer records, 200,000 orders, and 500,000 order items. Include both optimized and deliberately inefficient queries for comparison.

**Phase 1 - Baseline Analysis (15 minutes):** Students execute five provided queries of varying complexity against the e-commerce database using pgAdmin or similar tool. They must record execution time, rows examined, and memory usage for each query using EXPLAIN ANALYZE commands. Students create a comparison table documenting these baseline metrics.

**Phase 2 - Execution Plan Deep Dive (20 minutes):** For the two slowest queries, students generate detailed execution plans using EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON). They identify specific operations consuming the most resources by examining node costs, actual vs. estimated rows, and buffer hit ratios. Students annotate printed execution plans, highlighting sequential scans, nested loops, and missing index usage.

**Phase 3 - Pattern Recognition (15 minutes):** Students compare execution plans between fast and slow queries, categorizing performance issues into four types: missing indexes, inefficient joins, unnecessary data retrieval, or poor query structure. They complete a structured analysis worksheet identifying which category each bottleneck represents.

**Phase 4 - Optimization Proposal (15 minutes):** For each identified bottleneck, students propose specific solutions (create index statements, query rewrites, or schema modifications) and predict expected performance improvements. They must justify recommendations using execution plan evidence and estimate potential speed improvements based on cost reductions observed in the plans.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database with pre-loaded e-commerce sample data (customers, orders, order_items tables)
Five test queries of varying performance characteristics saved as .sql files
Performance analysis worksheet template with comparison tables
pgAdmin or DBeaver database client software
Execution plan annotation handout with key terminology
assessment_method: Students submit completed analysis worksheet showing baseline metrics, annotated execution plans for two queries, categorized bottleneck identification, and specific optimization proposals with justifications. Rubric awards 25% for accurate metric collection, 35% for correct bottleneck identification using execution plans, 25% for appropriate optimization recommendations, and 15% for clear justification of proposed solutions using performance data.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan reading guide with visual examples of common patterns, offer simplified queries initially, and give partially completed analysis worksheets. For advanced learners: Include queries with subqueries and window functions, challenge them to write their own inefficient queries for peer analysis, or have them research advanced optimization techniques like query hints and partitioning strategies.
original_title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Order System

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Order System: Exercise 2
description: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans and database performance metrics from a simulated e-commerce order management system. They will identify performance bottlenecks, examine indexing strategies, and differentiate between efficient and inefficient query patterns to propose optimization solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining query costs, join operations, and scan types to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient database design patterns through comparative analysis of query performance metrics
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 members) with the provided database schema and sample dataset containing 50,000 orders, 10,000 customers, and 1,000 products (15 minutes setup). Teams will execute five pre-written queries of varying complexity against the database using the query analyzer tool, recording execution times and examining the generated execution plans (20 minutes). For each query, students must document: actual execution time, estimated vs. actual row counts, index usage patterns, and join operation types. Next, teams will analyze the execution plans by identifying expensive operations (>30% of query cost), noting table scan operations vs. index seeks, and documenting any missing index warnings (25 minutes). Students will then compare Query A (unoptimized with no indexes) against Query B (same logic with proper indexing) to analyze performance differences, calculating percentage improvements and explaining why specific indexes improved performance (20 minutes). Teams will examine the database schema design, identifying potential normalization issues, missing foreign key relationships, and inappropriate data types that could impact performance (15 minutes). Finally, each team creates a written analysis report documenting their findings: top 3 performance bottlenecks identified, specific optimization recommendations with justification, and predicted performance improvements with evidence from their testing (25 minutes). Conclude with team presentations of their most significant finding (15 minutes).
materials_needed: MySQL or PostgreSQL database with sample e-commerce dataset (orders, customers, products tables)
Database query analyzer tool (MySQL Workbench or pgAdmin)
Pre-written SQL queries document with 5 test queries of varying complexity
Database schema diagram showing table relationships
Performance analysis worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric: Query execution plan interpretation accuracy (25 points), correct identification of performance bottlenecks (25 points), quality of optimization recommendations with technical justification (25 points), and analysis report completeness including quantitative performance comparisons (25 points). Students must achieve 18/25 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a sample execution plan analysis for the first query, offering a checklist of common performance indicators to look for (table scans, high-cost operations), and pairing them with stronger database students. Extend advanced learners by having them write additional test queries, research advanced indexing strategies (composite indexes, partial indexes), or analyze query performance across different database engines.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn: A Multi-Algorithm Comparative Analysis
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare the performance, reliability, and business viability of three different machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost) applied to a customer churn prediction problem. They will assess model performance using multiple metrics, identify potential biases and limitations, and provide justified recommendations for production deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple machine learning algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, bias detection, and interpretability trade-offs within a business context
Students will critique model reliability and generalizability through systematic assessment of validation techniques, feature importance analysis, and edge case performance
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with a pre-processed customer churn dataset (10,000 records) and three pre-trained models with their training code. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. **Phase 1 - Model Performance Analysis (45 minutes):** Each team evaluates all three models using confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and calculates accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC. Students must identify which metrics are most relevant for the business problem and justify their choices. **Phase 2 - Bias and Limitation Assessment (30 minutes):** Teams analyze feature importance rankings, test for demographic bias using fairness metrics (equalized odds, demographic parity), and examine prediction confidence distributions. They identify potential data leakage, overfitting indicators, and model interpretability limitations. **Phase 3 - Business Viability Evaluation (25 minutes):** Students calculate cost-benefit analysis considering false positive/negative costs, assess computational requirements for real-time deployment, and evaluate model maintenance complexity. **Phase 4 - Synthesis and Recommendation (25 minutes):** Teams prepare a 2-page executive summary ranking the models with detailed justifications, identifying risks and mitigation strategies, and providing implementation recommendations. Include specific confidence intervals for performance estimates and timeline for model retraining.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV format, 10,000 records with 20 features)
Three pre-trained model files (.pkl format) with training scripts
Jupyter Notebook template with evaluation framework
Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, fairlearn libraries
Business context document with cost assumptions and deployment constraints
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Technical accuracy of performance metrics calculation and interpretation (25%), (2) Depth and validity of bias/limitation analysis with supporting evidence (30%), (3) Quality of business reasoning and cost-benefit analysis with realistic assumptions (25%), (4) Clarity and justification of final recommendations with risk assessment (20%). Students must demonstrate critical thinking by identifying at least 3 specific limitations per model and providing quantitative evidence for their final ranking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation templates and guided questions for each evaluation phase. Offer a decision matrix template for systematic comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional fairness metrics, conduct statistical significance tests for performance differences, or design A/B testing frameworks for model deployment. Encourage exploration of ensemble methods or hybrid approaches combining multiple algorithms.

title: Binary Number System Flash Card Memory Challenge
description: Students memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0-31 using systematic flashcard practice. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-to-decimal conversions through structured repetition and self-assessment.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 00000 through 11111 (0-31) by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the positional values of each bit position (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary flashcards to each student (5-bit binary numbers 00000-11111 on front, decimal equivalents 0-31 on back). Spend 5 minutes reviewing the positional value system: rightmost bit = 1, next = 2, then 4, 8, 16. Have students write these values on a reference card. Divide class into pairs for 15 minutes of partner practice: Student A shows binary side, Student B states decimal equivalent, then checks answer. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes. After partner practice, conduct individual self-testing phase (10 minutes): students go through entire deck alone, creating two piles - 'know immediately' and 'need more practice.' Students focus remaining time on their 'need practice' pile, using the reference card to calculate conversions. Conclude with a 5-minute speed challenge: students attempt to correctly convert as many cards as possible from their original 'difficult' pile. Record their improvement count. Throughout activity, emphasize that students should aim for instant recall without calculation for numbers 0-15, and quick mental math for 16-31.
materials_needed: 32 flashcards per student with 5-bit binary numbers (00000-11111) on front and decimal equivalents (0-31) on back
Reference cards showing positional values (16-8-4-2-1)
Timer or stopwatch
Student tracking sheets for recording progress
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: 3 points = correctly recalls 29-32 conversions (90%+), 2 points = correctly recalls 25-28 conversions (78-87%), 1 point = correctly recalls 20-24 conversions (63-77%). Assess through final individual quiz where instructor shows binary cards and students write decimal equivalents within 3 seconds per card.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with 3-bit numbers (000-111) covering only 0-7, provide calculation worksheets showing step-by-step conversion process, and allow extended time with reference cards. For advanced learners: Extend to 6-bit or 8-bit numbers, introduce hexadecimal equivalents on card backs, or challenge them to convert decimal back to binary for reverse practice.

title: Binary Number System Flash Card Memory Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will create and use flash cards to memorize the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15. Through repetitive practice with physical cards, students will commit these fundamental binary-decimal conversions to memory for instant recall.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by correctly stating the 4-bit binary equivalent within 3 seconds
Students will identify decimal values of 4-bit binary numbers through flash card practice with 90% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing 16 index cards to each student and displaying the binary conversion chart (0000=0 through 1111=15) on the board. Have students spend 10 minutes creating their flash cards: write the decimal number (0-15) on one side in large, clear numbers, and the corresponding 4-bit binary code on the reverse side (ensure leading zeros are included, e.g., 0101 for 5). Once cards are complete, demonstrate the self-testing technique: hold card with decimal side facing you, state the binary equivalent aloud, then flip to check accuracy. Students practice independently for 15 minutes, sorting cards into 'know immediately' and 'need practice' piles. Next, pair students for 10 minutes of partner testing: Partner A shows decimal side to Partner B, who has 3 seconds to respond with binary equivalent. Partners switch roles after testing all 16 cards. Conclude with a whole-class rapid-fire assessment: display random decimal numbers on screen for 5 seconds each while students write binary answers on paper. Repeat process showing binary numbers for decimal conversion. Finally, have students complete a 5-minute individual written quiz featuring 10 random decimal-to-binary and 10 binary-to-decimal conversions without reference materials.
materials_needed: 16 blank index cards per student
Black markers or pens
Printed binary conversion reference chart (0-15)
Projector or interactive whiteboard
Timer or stopwatch
Quiz worksheets (pre-prepared with 20 conversion problems)
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (18/20 correct) on the final written quiz covering both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions. During partner testing, observe and record students who consistently respond within the 3-second time limit. Flash cards will be collected and checked for accuracy and completeness (all 16 cards present with correct conversions).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce the initial set to numbers 0-7 (3-bit binary) and provide a multiplication chart showing powers of 2. Create visual aids with place value columns labeled 8-4-2-1. For advanced learners, extend the activity to include 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Provide additional challenge problems involving simple binary arithmetic.
original_title: Binary Number System Flash Card Memory Challenge

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Design Using Trigonometric Functions and Constraint Analysis
description: Students will apply advanced trigonometric functions, optimization techniques, and geometric principles to design an efficient solar panel array layout for a real building rooftop. They will calculate optimal panel angles, spacing, and configuration while considering shadow interference, seasonal sun variations, and physical constraints.
estimated_duration: 195 minutes (3.25 hours) - can be split across 2-3 class periods
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent) and inverse trigonometric ratios to determine optimal solar panel tilt angles and spacing by analyzing sun elevation angles throughout the year
Students will implement optimization strategies and constraint analysis through mathematical modeling to maximize energy output while respecting physical limitations of rooftop installations
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a specific building scenario packet containing: rooftop dimensions, geographical coordinates, local sun path data, and budget constraints (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to tackle this multi-stage problem. Stage 1 (45 minutes): Teams calculate the optimal tilt angle for their location using the formula: Optimal Tilt = 3.7 + 0.69 × Latitude, then verify using trigonometric analysis of seasonal sun angles. They must create shadow-length calculations using L = h × cot(θ), where h is panel height and θ is sun elevation angle. Stage 2 (60 minutes): Students apply spacing formulas to prevent row-to-row shading: d = h × sin(tilt) / tan(sun elevation). They must calculate this for winter solstice conditions (worst case) and create scaled technical drawings. Stage 3 (45 minutes): Teams optimize the array layout by applying mathematical constraints: total roof area, weight limits (using load calculations), electrical connectivity requirements, and budget restrictions. They use systems of inequalities to define feasible regions and apply calculus-based optimization or linear programming concepts. Stage 4 (30 minutes): Each team presents their final design with mathematical justifications, comparing energy output calculations using trigonometric models of seasonal performance. Instructor facilitates peer review using provided evaluation criteria focusing on mathematical accuracy and practical feasibility.
materials_needed: Building scenario packets with specific rooftop dimensions and geographical data
Scientific calculators or computer access with spreadsheet software
Graph paper and engineering rulers for scaled drawings
Solar path diagrams and sun angle reference tables
Digital protractors or angle measurement tools
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of trigonometric calculations for angles and spacing (25 points), (2) Correct application of optimization techniques with mathematical justification (25 points), (3) Quality and precision of technical drawings with proper scaling (20 points), (4) Feasibility analysis considering all constraints (20 points), (5) Clear presentation of mathematical reasoning and results (10 points). Students must submit calculation worksheets, technical drawings, and a 2-page mathematical summary report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated sun angle tables, offer templates for calculation worksheets, and assign specific roles within teams (calculator, drawer, presenter). Create checkpoint reviews after each stage. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like panel efficiency curves, temperature coefficients, or economic payback calculations using compound interest formulas. Encourage exploration of calculus-based optimization methods or computer modeling approaches.

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis in Multi-Layered Web Application Architecture
description: Students analyze a complex e-commerce web application's architecture to identify security vulnerabilities across multiple layers (presentation, business logic, data access, and infrastructure). They will decompose the system into components, trace attack vectors, and evaluate the effectiveness of existing security controls.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-tier web application architectures by systematically examining each layer's security implementation and identifying potential attack vectors
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of security controls through structured vulnerability assessment and risk prioritization matrices
instructions: Begin by providing student teams of 3-4 with the ShopSecure case study materials (architecture diagrams, code snippets, configuration files, and security documentation). In the first 30 minutes, teams examine the provided system architecture diagram showing the React frontend, Node.js API gateway, microservices (user management, payment processing, inventory), PostgreSQL database, and AWS infrastructure components. Each team member takes responsibility for one layer: presentation (React app), API layer (Node.js gateway), business logic (microservices), or data/infrastructure layer. During minutes 31-90, students individually analyze their assigned layer using the provided vulnerability checklist, documenting findings in the shared analysis template. They identify specific vulnerabilities such as XSS potential in React components, authentication flaws in API endpoints, SQL injection risks in database queries, and misconfigurations in cloud security groups. In minutes 91-150, teams reconvene to map cross-layer attack scenarios using the attack chain methodology. They trace how a vulnerability in one layer could be exploited to compromise other layers, creating visual attack flow diagrams. Teams then prioritize vulnerabilities using the CVSS scoring system and business impact assessment provided. In the final 60 minutes, teams prepare their comprehensive security analysis report, including executive summary, detailed vulnerability findings by layer, attack scenario mappings, risk prioritization matrix, and recommended remediation strategies with implementation timelines. Each team presents their top 3 critical vulnerabilities and proposed fixes to the class in 8-minute presentations.
materials_needed: ShopSecure case study packet (architecture diagrams, code samples, configuration files)
Vulnerability assessment checklist templates for each architectural layer
CVSS calculator and risk assessment matrix worksheets
Attack chain mapping templates and diagramming tools (Lucidchart or draw.io access)
Security analysis report template with sections for each deliverable component
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Completeness of layer-specific vulnerability identification (25 points), accuracy of technical analysis and attack vector mapping (25 points), quality of cross-layer attack scenario development (20 points), appropriate use of CVSS scoring and risk prioritization (15 points), and clarity/professionalism of final report and presentation (15 points). Teams must identify at least 8 legitimate vulnerabilities across all layers, correctly map 2 complete attack chains, and provide technically sound remediation recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled examples of vulnerability analysis for one component and offer guided questions for each analysis step. Advanced learners can be challenged to research zero-day vulnerabilities specific to the technologies used, propose additional security testing methodologies, or design automated security scanning integration into the CI/CD pipeline. Consider pairing weaker technical students with stronger ones within teams, and provide reference materials for common vulnerability patterns (OWASP Top 10, CWE database).

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Ice Cream Sales Dashboard Assessment
description: Students will critically assess three different dashboard designs displaying ice cream sales data using established visualization principles. They will compare the effectiveness of each design and recommend the best option for a business owner, justifying their evaluation with specific criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization approaches by applying design principles and identifying strengths and weaknesses
Students will critique data presentation methods through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by distributing three different dashboard mockups showing the same ice cream sales dataset (monthly sales by flavor, temperature correlation, and customer demographics). Spend 5 minutes explaining the business context: a small ice cream shop owner needs to understand sales patterns to make inventory decisions. Provide students with the evaluation criteria checklist covering clarity, accuracy, visual hierarchy, and actionability. In pairs (10 minutes), have students examine Dashboard A, rating each criterion on a 1-5 scale and noting specific observations. Rotate pairs to Dashboard B (10 minutes), then Dashboard C (10 minutes), using the same evaluation process. Students should document what works well and what doesn't for each design. Next, pairs spend 15 minutes completing a comparison matrix, ranking dashboards from best to worst for each criterion. They must provide written justification for rankings, citing specific visual elements (colors, chart types, layout choices). Finally, each pair presents their 2-minute recommendation to the class (20 minutes total), stating which dashboard they would recommend to the ice cream shop owner and why. During presentations, other students can ask clarifying questions about the evaluation reasoning. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing different pair conclusions and identifying common evaluation themes.
materials_needed: Three printed dashboard mockups (A, B, C) showing ice cream sales data with different design approaches
Evaluation criteria checklist handout with 1-5 rating scale
Comparison matrix worksheet template
Timer for rotations
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Completed evaluation sheets showing thorough analysis of each dashboard (40%), (2) Comparison matrix with clear rankings and specific written justifications citing visual elements (40%), (3) Quality of oral recommendation including evidence-based reasoning (20%). Students must demonstrate critical thinking by identifying specific design flaws and strengths rather than general preferences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This dashboard is effective because...' and 'The main weakness is...' For advanced learners, ask them to sketch improvements for the lowest-ranked dashboard or consider how different stakeholders (owner vs. employee vs. supplier) might evaluate the same dashboards differently.

title: Design Your Dream Theme Park: Optimizing Layout Using Area, Perimeter, and Scale
description: Students will create an original theme park blueprint using geometric principles, scaling, and area optimization. They must design attractions within specific constraints while maximizing visitor capacity and minimizing walking distances between popular rides.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original theme park layout by applying area and perimeter calculations to optimize space utilization within given constraints
Students will construct accurate scale drawings and mathematical justifications through systematic measurement and proportional reasoning
instructions: **Phase 1 (15 minutes):** Distribute materials and explain the scenario: Students are theme park designers with a rectangular plot of land measuring 800m × 600m. They must include exactly 8 attractions with specified minimum areas: 2 roller coasters (3000 m² each), 3 family rides (1500 m² each), 2 food courts (800 m² each), and 1 water attraction (4000 m²). **Phase 2 (25 minutes):** Students calculate total required area and remaining space for pathways. Using grid paper (1 square = 400 m²), they sketch their initial layout at 1:400 scale. They must ensure all attractions fit within the boundary and calculate actual dimensions for each attraction on their grid. **Phase 3 (35 minutes):** Students refine their designs by creating pathways connecting all attractions, calculating pathway areas, and determining walking distances between the two most popular attractions (roller coasters). They must minimize this distance while maintaining adequate pathway width (minimum 8m in real scale). **Phase 4 (20 minutes):** Students create a final blueprint on clean grid paper with labels, a scale indicator, and a data table showing: attraction names, scaled dimensions, actual dimensions, individual areas, total park area used, and shortest distance between roller coasters. **Phase 5 (15 minutes):** Present designs to neighboring pairs, explaining optimization choices and mathematical reasoning behind layout decisions.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers marked in centimeters
Colored pencils or markers (at least 8 colors)
Calculators
Theme park constraint handout with attraction requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and scaling (25%), (2) Adherence to all design constraints (25%), (3) Optimization justification with clear mathematical reasoning (25%), (4) Blueprint quality with proper labeling, scale notation, and data table completion (25%). Students must demonstrate all calculations on a separate work sheet.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated area conversion table and templates for data tables. Consider pairing with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add constraints such as irregular plot shapes, elevation changes requiring Pythagorean theorem for pathway distances, or budget limitations requiring cost per square meter calculations for different attraction types.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Flash Card Drill and Verification
description: Students will memorize and instantly recall the precise time complexity notations for 25 advanced algorithms across different domains (graph algorithms, dynamic programming, advanced sorting, string algorithms). They will demonstrate perfect recall through rapid-fire identification and verification exercises using standardized algorithm descriptions.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations for 25 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, KMP string matching, and advanced tree traversal methods
Students will identify time complexity classifications instantly when presented with algorithm names or pseudocode snippets through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the standardized algorithm reference sheet containing 25 algorithms with their formal names, brief descriptions, and complexity notations (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to create physical flash cards: algorithm name/description on front, complete complexity analysis (best, average, worst case) on back. Provide exactly 30 minutes for card creation using the template format provided. Conduct three progressive recall phases: Phase 1 (10 minutes) - Students self-test using their cards, cycling through all 25 algorithms twice. Phase 2 (15 minutes) - Partner students for reciprocal testing where Partner A shows algorithm name, Partner B must state all three complexity notations within 5 seconds, then switch roles. Track accuracy on provided scoring sheet. Phase 3 (20 minutes) - Instructor-led rapid-fire session where algorithm names are projected for 8 seconds each. All students write answers simultaneously on response sheets. Include 5 challenge rounds with pseudocode snippets instead of names. Conclude with immediate verification where students check answers against master key, highlighting any gaps in recall for remediation homework assignment.
materials_needed: Standardized Algorithm Reference Sheet (25 algorithms with Dijkstra's, A*, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, KMP, Rabin-Karp, QuickSelect, Heap operations, Red-Black tree operations, etc.)
Blank index cards (50 per student)
Flash card template with sections for Best/Average/Worst case complexity
Partner scoring sheets with algorithm checklist
Individual response sheets for rapid-fire session
Master answer key for verification
Projector for displaying algorithm names and pseudocode snippets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (23/25 correct) on the final rapid-fire verification round to demonstrate mastery. Assessment includes: perfect notation format (correct Big O/Theta/Omega symbols), accurate complexity expressions (e.g., O(V²) not just 'quadratic'), and completion within time limits. Partner testing phase scores are recorded but used for practice feedback. Students failing to reach 90% receive specific remediation assignments targeting missed algorithms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made flash cards for 10 most common algorithms, allow extra 10 minutes for memorization, and permit use of complexity cheat sheet during partner phase. Group struggling students with strong peers during partner phase. For advanced learners: Include 5 additional rare algorithms (like Aho-Corasick, Manacher's algorithm), require them to explain why each complexity bound exists, and have them create challenge questions with space complexity requirements for extra credit.

title: Interpreting Statistical Power Analysis in A/B Testing Scenarios for Business Decision Making
description: Students will analyze pre-computed statistical power calculations from three real-world A/B testing scenarios to determine optimal sample sizes and interpret the trade-offs between Type I and Type II errors. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining how power analysis results influence business decisions and experimental design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical power curves and sample size calculations by analyzing the relationship between effect size, significance level, and power across different business scenarios
Students will explain the practical implications of Type I and Type II error rates through detailed written justifications of A/B testing design decisions
instructions: Begin by distributing three case study packets, each containing power analysis outputs from different business scenarios: (1) e-commerce conversion rate optimization, (2) mobile app retention testing, and (3) email marketing campaign effectiveness. Each packet includes power curves, sample size tables, and cost-benefit matrices. Form groups of 3-4 students and assign each group all three scenarios (45 minutes total). Students first spend 15 minutes individually reviewing the materials and completing a guided worksheet that asks them to identify: minimum detectable effect sizes, required sample sizes for 80% and 90% power, and associated testing duration/costs. Next, groups spend 20 minutes collaborating to complete scenario-specific analysis sheets where they must: interpret why different power levels were chosen for each business context, explain how practical constraints (budget, time, traffic) influenced the experimental design, and justify whether the proposed sample sizes are appropriate given the business impact of false positives versus false negatives. In the final 10 minutes, each group presents one scenario to the class, focusing on how they would communicate the power analysis results to non-technical stakeholders. Groups must explain their reasoning for recommending either proceeding with the test as designed, modifying parameters, or abandoning the test entirely based on the power analysis outputs.
materials_needed: Three printed case study packets with power analysis outputs (R or Python generated plots and tables)
Individual guided analysis worksheets with structured questions
Group collaboration sheets for each scenario
Cost-benefit matrices showing business impact calculations
Access to calculators for verification calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of power analysis interpretation (25%) - correctly identifying key parameters and relationships, (2) Quality of business reasoning (35%) - logical connections between statistical concepts and practical decisions, (3) Communication clarity (25%) - effective explanation to non-technical audience, (4) Group collaboration evidence (15%) - demonstrated integration of multiple perspectives in final recommendations. Students must achieve proficiency (3/4) in categories 1 and 2 to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a power analysis reference sheet with key formulas and definitions, and offer guided questions during group work focusing on one scenario at a time. For advanced learners, include additional complexity by having them critique the assumptions underlying each power analysis and propose alternative experimental designs (sequential testing, Bayesian approaches) that might be more appropriate given the business constraints.

title: Budget Planning for a School Event: Applied Percentage Calculations
description: Students will create a realistic budget for organizing a school movie night by applying percentage calculations to determine costs, discounts, and tax amounts. They will use real-world scenarios to practice calculating percentages, percentage increases, and percentage decreases in a practical context.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages, percentage increases, and decreases by creating itemized budgets for a school event scenario
Students will apply percentage concepts to solve multi-step real-world problems through budget planning and cost analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Movie Night Budget Worksheet' and explaining that each student will plan a movie night for 50 students with a $500 total budget (10 minutes). Provide students with the vendor price list showing: pizza ($12 per large pizza, feeds 8 people), drinks ($0.75 per bottle), popcorn ($8 per large bag, feeds 10 people), and decorations ($45 total). Students first calculate base quantities needed and costs (15 minutes). Next, introduce real-world complications: the pizza vendor offers a 15% discount for orders over $100, drinks have a 20% price increase due to demand, and all purchases require 8.5% sales tax (except pizza, which is tax-exempt). Students must recalculate their budgets incorporating these percentage changes (20 minutes). Have students work in pairs to check each other's calculations and discuss their reasoning (10 minutes). Finally, students present their final budgets to a small group, explaining how they applied percentage calculations and stayed within budget constraints. If over budget, they must justify their choices or make adjustments using percentage reasoning (15 minutes). Circulate during work time to provide guidance and check mathematical accuracy.
materials_needed: Movie Night Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Vendor Price List handout
Calculators (one per student)
Percentage calculation reference sheet
assessment_method: Students will be assessed using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of percentage calculations (25%), (2) Correct application of discounts and tax rates (25%), (3) Logical budget decisions and staying within constraints (25%), and (4) Clear explanation of mathematical reasoning during presentations (25%). Full credit requires all calculations correct within 2%, proper sequencing of percentage operations, and coherent budget justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation template showing 'part/whole × 100' and 'percentage × original amount' formulas. Break the problem into smaller chunks, completing base costs before introducing percentage changes. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including bulk pricing tiers (additional discounts at higher quantities), comparison shopping between vendors, or calculating cost per person and exploring how percentage costs change with different attendance numbers.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Examining Index Impact on SELECT Operations
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of SQL queries with and without database indexes, examining execution plans and timing results. They will break down complex queries into components and evaluate how different indexing strategies affect query efficiency and resource utilization.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by comparing indexed versus non-indexed table operations to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate the trade-offs between different indexing strategies through systematic performance testing and data interpretation
instructions: Begin by providing each student pair with a pre-populated MySQL database containing a 'customers' table (50,000 records) and 'orders' table (200,000 records) with no indexes except primary keys. Students work in pairs for 75 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Students execute three provided SELECT queries of increasing complexity: (1) simple WHERE clause on customer name, (2) JOIN between customers and orders with date range filter, (3) complex query with GROUP BY and HAVING clauses. They record execution times using MySQL's profiling feature and capture execution plans using EXPLAIN. Next 20 minutes: Students create appropriate indexes (single-column on customer name, composite index on order_date and customer_id, covering index for the GROUP BY query) and re-execute the same queries, documenting new execution times and plans. Following 25 minutes: Students analyze the 'before and after' execution plans, identifying specific changes in query processing methods (table scans vs index seeks, join algorithms, sorting operations). They create a comparison table showing execution time improvements, rows examined, and temporary table usage. Final 15 minutes: Students write a technical analysis report explaining which indexes provided the most significant improvements, why certain queries benefited more than others, and what trade-offs exist (storage space, insert/update performance). They must support conclusions with specific metrics from their testing and demonstrate understanding of underlying database optimization principles.
materials_needed: MySQL Server 8.0 or higher installed on student computers
Pre-populated database file (customers_orders.sql) with sample data
Performance analysis worksheet template (digital or printed)
MySQL Workbench or command-line client access
assessment_method: Evaluate students on: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25 points) - correctly identifying scan types, join methods, and key usage, (2) Quality of performance comparison analysis (30 points) - comprehensive data collection and meaningful insights about performance improvements, (3) Technical report clarity (25 points) - clear explanations of why certain indexes were effective with supporting evidence, (4) Understanding of trade-offs (20 points) - demonstrates knowledge of indexing costs and appropriate use cases. Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided worksheet with specific questions about each execution plan element and pre-written SQL commands for creating indexes. Offer additional explanation of execution plan symbols and terminology. For advanced learners: Challenge them to design their own complex queries, experiment with different index types (partial, functional), or analyze the impact on INSERT/UPDATE operations. Provide access to larger datasets or additional tables for more sophisticated analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost) for predicting customer churn using a telecommunications dataset. They will evaluate model performance, business impact, and implementation feasibility to make justified recommendations for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will critically evaluate multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, interpretability, and business constraints to determine optimal deployment strategy
Students will assess the reliability and validity of model predictions through comprehensive bias analysis, feature importance evaluation, and cross-validation techniques
instructions: Begin by providing students with a telecommunications customer dataset (10,000+ records) containing features like contract type, monthly charges, tenure, and churn status. Students work in pairs to implement three pre-specified models using provided starter code templates. First 60 minutes: Students train all three models using identical train/test splits and record performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC). They must document training time, memory usage, and any convergence issues. Next 45 minutes: Students conduct bias analysis by examining model performance across customer segments (age groups, contract types, service categories) and identify potential fairness issues. They evaluate feature importance rankings and assess model interpretability using SHAP values for business stakeholder communication. Following 45 minutes: Students analyze business context by calculating potential revenue impact of false positives/negatives, considering implementation costs, and evaluating model maintenance requirements. They must factor in regulatory compliance needs and data privacy constraints. Final 60 minutes: Each pair prepares a comprehensive evaluation report with explicit recommendations. They present 8-minute findings to class, defending their chosen model against peer questioning. Reports must include quantitative performance comparisons, qualitative trade-off analysis, implementation roadmap with timeline, and risk assessment with mitigation strategies.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV format, 15+ features)
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, XGBoost, SHAP libraries
Jupyter Notebook templates with model skeleton code
Business context document with cost/benefit parameters
Model evaluation rubric and reporting template
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical accuracy of model implementation and metrics calculation (25%), (2) Depth of bias and fairness analysis with supporting evidence (20%), (3) Quality of business impact assessment and cost-benefit analysis (20%), (4) Justification strength and logical reasoning in final recommendation (25%), (5) Professional presentation and response to peer challenges (10%). Deliverables include completed Jupyter notebook, written evaluation report (1500 words), and peer presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional code comments, offer simplified feature engineering options, and give guiding questions for each evaluation dimension. Create checkpoint reviews at 60 and 120-minute marks. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement ensemble methods, conduct advanced statistical significance testing, or incorporate time-series analysis for temporal churn patterns. Encourage exploration of additional evaluation frameworks like MLOps readiness assessment.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn Analysis: Exercise 1
description: Students evaluate and critique three different machine learning models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Neural Network) trained on a telecommunications customer churn dataset. They assess model performance, identify biases, validate assumptions, and defend their choice of the optimal model for production deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by comparing performance metrics, identifying limitations, and assessing real-world applicability
Students will critique model assumptions and potential biases through systematic analysis of feature importance, prediction patterns, and ethical implications
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-processed telecommunications churn dataset and three trained models with their outputs (30 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives: model performance reports, confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance plots, and prediction samples for 1000 test customers.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams systematically evaluate each model using the provided evaluation framework worksheet. They analyze accuracy, precision, recall, F1-scores, and AUC values, then examine prediction patterns across different customer segments (age groups, contract types, payment methods). Students identify potential biases by checking if models perform differently across demographic groups.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams investigate model interpretability and business viability. They analyze feature importance rankings, assess whether key features align with business logic, and evaluate computational costs. Students examine false positive/negative cases to understand failure patterns and calculate potential revenue impact using provided cost matrices ($50 retention cost per customer, $200 lost revenue per churned customer).

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation defending their model selection. They must address: overall performance comparison, bias assessment results, interpretability concerns, implementation feasibility, and projected business impact. Teams anticipate counterarguments and prepare evidence-based responses.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams present their evaluations while others provide peer feedback using structured critique forms. Instructor facilitates discussion on evaluation criteria weightings and real-world deployment considerations.
materials_needed: Telecommunications churn dataset (CSV file with 10,000 customer records)
Three trained model outputs and performance reports (Python pickle files or detailed spreadsheets)
Model evaluation framework worksheets
Business cost matrix handout
Peer evaluation rubrics
Jupyter notebooks or Excel for analysis
Presentation software
assessment_method: Grade based on evaluation depth (25%), evidence quality (25%), critical reasoning (25%), and presentation defense (25%). Students must identify at least 3 model strengths/weaknesses each, demonstrate bias analysis across 2+ demographic segments, justify model selection with quantitative evidence, and effectively respond to peer challenges during presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide evaluation checklist templates, offer guided questions for bias detection, and allow additional time for metric interpretation. For advanced learners: introduce ensemble method evaluation, require cost-benefit sensitivity analysis, or add adversarial testing scenarios with data drift considerations.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Customer Churn Analysis

title: Programming Terminology Memory Card Match
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 fundamental programming terms through a physical card matching game. This activity focuses on building foundational vocabulary recognition that beginners need before writing their first programs.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 basic programming terms (variable, function, loop, array, string, integer, boolean, algorithm, syntax, debug, compile, execute, input, output, parameter, argument, condition, iteration, sequence, assignment) by matching term cards to definition cards
Students will recall the exact definitions of fundamental programming concepts through timed recognition exercises
instructions:
Preparation (5 minutes): Print and cut 40 cards - 20 with programming terms, 20 with corresponding definitions. Shuffle each set separately. Arrange students in pairs at tables with clear workspace. 

Round 1 - Learning Phase (10 minutes): Give each pair one complete set of 40 cards face-up. Students work together to match all 20 terms with definitions. Instructor circulates, providing immediate feedback and clarification. Students must read each match aloud to their partner before moving to the next pair.

Round 2 - Speed Practice (10 minutes): Collect cards, reshuffle, and redistribute face-down in two separate piles (terms and definitions). Students take turns flipping one card from each pile. If cards match, they keep the pair and explain the connection. If no match, cards go to bottom of respective piles. Continue until all pairs are matched.

Round 3 - Individual Assessment (10 minutes): Give each student a worksheet with 20 terms listed. Students write definitions from memory without looking at cards. Allow 30 seconds per term.

Wrap-up (5 minutes): Review any commonly missed terms as a class. Students create personal 'difficult terms' list for future study.
materials_needed: 40 printed cards per pair (20 term cards, 20 definition cards) on cardstock
Individual assessment worksheets with 20 blank definition spaces
Timer or stopwatch
Pencils for each student
assessment_method: Success measured by individual worksheet completion: 18-20 correct definitions = Excellent recall, 15-17 = Good recall (review 3-5 missed terms), 12-14 = Needs improvement (additional practice required), Below 12 = Requires remediation. Observe pair work for engagement and accurate verbal explanations during card matching.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students: Reduce to 10 most essential terms (variable, function, loop, array, string, input, output, algorithm, syntax, debug). Provide definition word bank during individual assessment. Advanced learners: Add 10 intermediate terms (class, object, method, inheritance, recursion, data structure, pointer, constructor, exception, interface) or challenge them to create example code snippets demonstrating each term.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Design Using Calculus and Trigonometry
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus, trigonometry, and optimization techniques to design an efficient solar panel array layout for a given geographic location and energy requirement. They will calculate optimal tilt angles, spacing between panels to minimize shadowing, and total array area needed while considering seasonal sun angle variations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply optimization techniques from multivariable calculus to determine optimal solar panel tilt angles and spacing by analyzing shadow-casting functions and energy output equations
Students will apply trigonometric identities and solar geometry principles to calculate seasonal energy variations through mathematical modeling of sun position throughout the year
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a specific scenario: a location (latitude/longitude), monthly energy requirement (kWh), and plot dimensions. Students have 90 minutes to complete their design.

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students research their assigned location's solar data and establish coordinate systems. They must identify the latitude, calculate solar declination angles for each month using δ = 23.45° × sin(360° × (284 + n)/365°), and determine solar noon angles.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using trigonometry, students calculate optimal tilt angles by applying the formula: Tilt = Latitude ± 15° (+ for winter optimization, - for summer). They must then model the shadow length cast by panels using L = H × cot(solar elevation angle), where H is panel height.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Students apply calculus optimization to minimize shading while maximizing energy output. They set up the constraint equation for panel spacing (d ≥ L/tan(minimum sun angle)) and the objective function for total energy output: E = ∑(monthly solar irradiance × panel area × cos(incidence angle) × efficiency).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams calculate total array area needed, number of panels required, and create a scaled technical drawing showing panel placement, dimensions, and shadow projections for winter solstice (worst-case scenario).

Students must show all mathematical work, including derivatives for optimization, trigonometric calculations for sun angles, and justification for design decisions. Each team presents their solution with mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: Solar irradiance data tables for assigned geographic locations
Scientific calculators or computer algebra systems (CAS)
Graph paper and rulers for technical drawings
Solar panel specification sheets (dimensions, efficiency ratings)
Protractors and compass for geometric constructions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of calculations (40 points), proper application of optimization techniques (25 points), correct use of trigonometric relationships (20 points), quality of technical drawing and design justification (15 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in mathematical computations and demonstrate clear understanding of optimization constraints to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated solar declination tables and step-by-step formula sheets for shadow calculations. Offer guided practice with simpler single-panel optimization before attempting array design. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables such as temperature effects on panel efficiency, ground reflection coefficients, or economic optimization including panel costs and energy prices.

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns in Microservices Architecture
description: Students will dissect a failed e-commerce transaction scenario involving multiple microservices to identify cascading failure patterns, analyze system bottlenecks, and evaluate the effectiveness of different resilience patterns. This activity requires students to trace execution flows, examine monitoring data, and determine root causes of distributed system failures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure propagation by examining service dependency graphs and identifying critical failure points in microservices architecture
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of circuit breaker, bulkhead, and timeout patterns through systematic comparison of system behavior under different failure scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the complete case study packet containing: system architecture diagram of 8 microservices (User Service, Order Service, Payment Service, Inventory Service, Notification Service, API Gateway, Database clusters, and Message Queue), timestamped log files from all services during a 30-minute failure window, and monitoring dashboards showing CPU, memory, network, and response time metrics. Students spend the first 45 minutes individually reviewing all materials and creating a timeline of events. Next, teams collaborate for 90 minutes to map the failure cascade: they must identify the initial failure point, trace how it propagated through dependent services, and document which services failed due to timeout, resource exhaustion, or dependency unavailability. Teams then spend 60 minutes analyzing three different resilience patterns implemented in the system - examining log entries showing circuit breaker state changes, bulkhead partition behavior, and timeout configurations. For each pattern, they evaluate effectiveness by calculating failure rates, recovery times, and user impact metrics from the provided data. Teams conclude by spending 45 minutes creating a visual failure analysis diagram showing: the complete failure timeline, service dependency relationships, points where resilience patterns activated or failed, and proposed architectural improvements. Each team presents their 10-minute analysis to the class, defending their root cause identification and pattern effectiveness evaluations with specific evidence from the logs and metrics.
materials_needed: Microservices architecture diagram with 8 services and dependencies
Timestamped log files from all services (JSON format, 500+ entries per service)
Grafana-style monitoring dashboard screenshots with metrics data
Case study packet with business context and SLA requirements
Laptops with log analysis tools (grep, jq, or ELK stack access)
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool for timeline creation
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of failure timeline and root cause identification (25 points), (2) Quality of failure propagation analysis with supporting evidence from logs (25 points), (3) Depth of resilience pattern effectiveness evaluation with quantitative metrics (30 points), (4) Clarity and technical accuracy of final presentation and visual diagram (20 points). Students must cite specific log entries, timestamps, and metric values to support conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a template timeline with some initial events filled in, and offer guided questions like 'Which service shows the first error timestamp?' and 'What happens to response times in dependent services?' For advanced learners, provide additional complexity by including distributed tracing data, asking them to calculate system availability percentages, or having them design alternative architectural patterns to prevent the identified failure modes.

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns in Microservices Architecture: Exercise 1
description: Students will dissect a complex distributed system failure scenario involving multiple microservices to identify cascading failure patterns, bottlenecks, and architectural vulnerabilities. They will analyze system logs, performance metrics, and dependency graphs to determine root causes and evaluate the effectiveness of existing resilience mechanisms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining multi-service log traces, performance metrics, and dependency relationships to identify root causes and cascading effects
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of circuit breakers, retry mechanisms, and load balancing strategies through systematic examination of system behavior under failure conditions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the comprehensive failure scenario package containing: system architecture diagram (15 microservices), 2-hour log dump from 8 services, Grafana dashboard screenshots showing CPU/memory/network metrics, and service dependency map. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (coordinates analysis), Log Detective (focuses on log correlation), Metrics Specialist (analyzes performance data), and Architecture Reviewer (examines system design). 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the initial failure trigger at 14:23:15 when the payment service began responding slowly. Students must timeline the failure propagation using provided logs, identifying which services failed first and mapping the cascade pattern. They should use log correlation techniques to trace request IDs across services and identify timeout patterns.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students analyze the system's resilience mechanisms. They examine circuit breaker logs to determine if breakers activated appropriately, evaluate retry attempt patterns in service logs, and assess load balancer behavior during service degradation. Teams must identify which protective mechanisms worked, failed, or were absent.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams synthesize findings into a failure analysis report identifying: primary root cause, secondary contributing factors, failure propagation timeline, effectiveness of each resilience mechanism, and three specific architectural improvements. Each team presents their 8-minute analysis to the class, defending their conclusions with specific evidence from logs and metrics.

Provide teams with analysis templates including timeline grids, cause-effect matrices, and evidence tracking sheets to structure their investigation systematically.
materials_needed: Distributed system failure scenario package (architecture diagrams, log files, metrics dashboards)
Log analysis tools (ELK Stack or similar)
Spreadsheet software for timeline correlation
Digital whiteboard tool for collaborative diagramming
Analysis templates (timeline grids, cause-effect matrices)
Presentation software for final reports
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accuracy of root cause identification (25 points), quality of failure timeline construction with supporting evidence (25 points), depth of resilience mechanism analysis (25 points), and clarity of architectural improvement recommendations with justification (25 points). Teams must demonstrate their analysis process and defend conclusions during presentations. Provide peer evaluation forms where teams assess each other's evidence quality and reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled timeline templates with some key events marked, offer guided questions for log analysis ('What happens 30 seconds after the payment service slows?'), and assign peer mentors from advanced students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify the business impact using provided transaction volume data, research and propose specific resilience patterns (bulkhead, saga) that could prevent similar failures, or analyze the scenario from a chaos engineering perspective to identify additional failure injection points.
original_title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns in Microservices Architecture

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns in Microservices Architecture: Exercise 2
description: Students will examine real-world distributed system failure scenarios to identify cascading failure patterns, analyze root causes, and evaluate the effectiveness of different fault tolerance mechanisms. This expert-level activity requires students to dissect complex system interactions and propose architectural improvements.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure cascades by examining service dependency graphs and identifying single points of failure in microservices architectures
Students will evaluate fault tolerance strategies through comparative analysis of circuit breaker patterns, bulkhead isolation, and timeout configurations in failed system scenarios
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three real failure case studies: Netflix's 2008 database corruption incident, GitHub's 2018 service degradation, and Slack's 2020 connectivity issues. Each case study includes system architecture diagrams, monitoring logs, timeline of events, and implemented solutions. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze their assigned case study using the provided failure analysis framework. They must map the failure propagation path, identify contributing factors (network partitions, resource exhaustion, dependency failures), and categorize the failure type (Byzantine, fail-stop, or fail-slow). Students document findings in a structured analysis template.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using the system architecture diagrams, teams identify architectural vulnerabilities and rank them by criticality. They must explain how each vulnerability contributed to the failure cascade and estimate the blast radius of each failure point.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Teams evaluate the implemented solutions against alternative approaches. They analyze trade-offs between consistency and availability, assess the effectiveness of implemented patterns (circuit breakers, retries, timeouts), and propose three architectural improvements with justification.

Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams present their analysis to another team for peer review. The reviewing team challenges assumptions, questions the analysis methodology, and suggests alternative interpretations. Both teams document the discussion points and refine their analysis based on feedback received.
materials_needed: Three curated failure case studies with architecture diagrams and log files
Failure analysis framework template (digital document)
System monitoring dashboards (screenshots/simulated data)
Laptops with network analysis tools (Wireshark, tcpdump)
Distributed systems reference architecture patterns documentation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of failure cascade mapping (25 points), (2) Depth of root cause analysis with supporting evidence (25 points), (3) Quality of architectural vulnerability assessment (25 points), (4) Justification of proposed solutions with trade-off analysis (25 points). Successful completion requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated ability to trace complex failure interactions and provide evidence-based recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled dependency mapping templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer reference materials on common failure patterns and CAP theorem implications. For advanced learners, include additional chaos engineering scenarios and require formal verification of their proposed solutions using TLA+ specifications or similar formal methods.
