original_title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns in Microservices Architecture

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for Customer Sales Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different data visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key business insights. They will justify their evaluation using established data visualization principles and provide recommendations for improvement.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, line graph, pie chart) by applying data visualization best practices criteria
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for improvement
instructions:
Step 1 (5 min): Provide each student with three printed visualizations of monthly sales data by product category: Version A (stacked bar chart), Version B (multiple line graph), and Version C (series of pie charts). Include the raw dataset showing 6 months of sales data for 4 product categories.

Step 2 (15 min): Students individually examine each visualization using the provided evaluation checklist covering: data accuracy, clarity of message, appropriate chart type selection, visual design principles (color, labels, scales), and ease of interpretation. They rate each criterion on a 1-4 scale with written justification.

Step 3 (10 min): Students identify the primary business question each visualization attempts to answer (trend analysis, proportion comparison, or categorical comparison) and assess whether the chosen chart type effectively addresses that question.

Step 4 (15 min): Students rank the three visualizations from most to least effective, writing a 200-word justification that references specific evaluation criteria. They must cite at least three concrete examples from the visualizations to support their ranking.

Step 5 (10 min): Students create a written recommendation list of three specific improvements for the lowest-ranked visualization, explaining how each change would better serve the intended audience (sales managers making quarterly planning decisions).

Step 6 (5 min): Students submit their completed evaluation forms, rankings, and improvement recommendations for assessment.
materials_needed: Three printed copies of different visualizations of the same sales dataset (one per student)
Raw dataset printout showing monthly sales figures by product category
Structured evaluation checklist with 1-4 rating scales
Evaluation criteria reference sheet defining visualization best practices
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Thoroughness of evaluation checklist completion with specific evidence cited, (2) Logical reasoning in visualization ranking with clear justification, (3) Quality of improvement recommendations that address identified weaknesses, (4) Appropriate use of data visualization terminology and principles. Students must score 3/4 in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for justifications ('This visualization is effective because...', 'The main weakness is...'). Highlight key evaluation criteria to focus on first. For advanced learners: Ask them to redesign the weakest visualization and explain their design choices, or evaluate how well each visualization serves different stakeholder needs (executives vs. sales staff).

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for Customer Sales Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key business insights. They will justify their evaluation using established visualization principles and business context.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, pie chart, line graph) by applying data visualization best practices and business communication needs
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by displaying three visualizations of monthly sales data by product category on the projector: (1) a 3D pie chart with 8 categories, (2) a clustered bar chart showing the same data, and (3) a line graph tracking each category over 12 months. Distribute the evaluation worksheet containing the business scenario: 'You are presenting quarterly results to executives who need to quickly identify top-performing product categories and make budget decisions for next quarter.' 

Students work individually for 15 minutes to complete the evaluation matrix, rating each visualization (1-5 scale) on: clarity of main message, ease of data comparison, visual appeal, and appropriateness for executive audience. They must provide written justification for each rating.

Next, organize students into groups of 3-4 for 20 minutes to compare their individual evaluations and reach group consensus on which visualization is most effective. Groups must document three specific reasons supporting their choice and two major weaknesses of the rejected options.

Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where each group presents their recommendation in 2 minutes, followed by instructor-led analysis of visualization principles demonstrated. Focus on why pie charts struggle with many categories, how bar charts enable comparison, and when line graphs show trends effectively. Students submit individual worksheets and group recommendation sheets.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of the same sales dataset (one per student)
Evaluation worksheet with rating matrix and business scenario
Projector/screen for displaying visualizations
Sample dataset: 12 months of sales data across 8 product categories
assessment_method: Grade individual evaluation worksheets using rubric: appropriate ratings with clear justifications (40%), accurate identification of visualization strengths/weaknesses (40%), quality of written explanations (20%). Group recommendations assessed on logical reasoning and use of visualization principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of visualization evaluation criteria (readability, accuracy, efficiency). For advanced learners, add a fourth visualization option or ask them to suggest improvements to existing charts. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during group work.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for Customer Sales Analysis

title: Design Your Dream School: A Multi-Step Algebraic Modeling Project
description: Students will design a comprehensive plan for their ideal school campus by creating and solving systems of linear equations and inequalities. They will incorporate real-world constraints like budget limitations, space requirements, and enrollment projections to develop mathematical models that optimize their school design.
estimated_duration: 190 minutes (3.2 hours) - can be split across 2-3 class periods
learning_objectives: Students will create original systems of linear equations and inequalities by modeling real-world constraints in school design scenarios
Students will construct mathematical optimization models through integrating multiple variables including budget, space, and population requirements
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the School Design Challenge packet containing sample floor plans, budget guidelines ($2-5 million range), and enrollment targets (200-800 students). Each team selects their target enrollment and receives corresponding budget constraints.

Step 1: Planning Phase (30 minutes) - Teams brainstorm their ideal school features and research real costs for construction, technology, and facilities. They must identify at least 6 variables (e.g., number of classrooms, cafeteria capacity, gymnasium size, library square footage, parking spaces, outdoor areas).

Step 2: Mathematical Modeling (45 minutes) - Students create their system of equations and inequalities. They must include: budget constraint equation, space limitation inequalities (total campus area ≤ available land), capacity constraints (facilities must accommodate chosen enrollment), and at least two optimization objectives (minimize cost while maximizing student amenities).

Step 3: Problem Solving (40 minutes) - Teams solve their systems using graphing calculators or Desmos, finding feasible solutions that satisfy all constraints. They test multiple scenarios and document their mathematical reasoning.

Step 4: Design Presentation Creation (35 minutes) - Students prepare a 5-minute presentation including their mathematical models, solutions, campus layout sketch, and justification for design choices. They must explain how their equations represent real-world constraints and demonstrate their solution process.

Step 5: Gallery Walk and Peer Feedback (30 minutes) - Teams present their designs while others evaluate using provided rubric, focusing on mathematical accuracy, real-world applicability, and creative problem-solving approaches.
materials_needed: School Design Challenge packet with budget guidelines and enrollment options
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos Graphing Calculator
Grid paper and rulers for sketching campus layouts
Research handout with typical school construction costs per square foot
Poster boards or presentation slides template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct formation and solution of systems with at least 4 equations/inequalities (25 points), (2) Real-World Application - realistic constraints and feasible solutions (25 points), (3) Creative Design - innovative school features that maintain mathematical validity (25 points), (4) Communication - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning and design rationale (25 points). Students must submit their written mathematical models, solution work, and design sketches alongside their presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates they can modify, offer simplified scenarios with 3-4 variables instead of 6, and pair with stronger math students. Create checkpoint sheets for each phase to ensure progress. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include non-linear constraints (quadratic relationships for efficiency), add statistical elements like probability of enrollment fluctuation, or incorporate calculus-based optimization for multiple objectives simultaneously.

title: x86-64 Assembly Instruction Set Recall Championship
description: Students will recall and match specific x86-64 assembly instructions with their exact syntax, operand types, and functional descriptions. This rapid-fire memory activity reinforces foundational knowledge of processor instruction sets through competitive recall exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall 50+ x86-64 assembly instructions with their precise mnemonic codes, operand requirements, and flags affected by completing timed matching exercises
Students will identify specific addressing modes, register names, and instruction categories through structured memorization challenges
instructions: Begin by distributing laminated instruction reference cards containing 60 x86-64 instructions across 8 categories: arithmetic (ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, etc.), logical (AND, OR, XOR, NOT), data movement (MOV, LEA, PUSH, POP), control flow (JMP, JE, JNE, CALL, RET), string operations (MOVS, CMPS, SCAS), bit manipulation (SHL, SHR, ROL, ROR), floating-point (FADD, FMUL, FLD, FST), and SIMD (ADDPS, MULPS, MOVAPS). Each card shows instruction mnemonic, operand syntax, description, and affected flags. Students work in pairs, with one partner holding answer cards face-down while the other attempts recall. Round 1 (15 minutes): Partner A reads instruction mnemonic, Partner B recalls complete syntax and function. Switch roles after 30 instructions. Round 2 (10 minutes): Partner A describes instruction function, Partner B recalls mnemonic and operand types. Round 3 (10 minutes): Speed challenge - Partner A shows random mnemonics, Partner B has 10 seconds per instruction to state operand requirements and primary function. Track correct answers on provided score sheets. Round 4 (15 minutes): Category sorting - present mixed instruction cards, students sort into 8 predefined categories within time limit. Conclude with whole-class verification where instructor randomly selects 20 instructions for group recall, ensuring accuracy of memorized information through immediate feedback and correction.
materials_needed: 60 laminated x86-64 instruction reference cards (4x6 inches each)
Printed score tracking sheets for each student pair
Digital timer/stopwatch for timed rounds
Category label cards for sorting activity
x86-64 instruction set reference poster for verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (48/60 instructions) across all four rounds combined. Assess through: (1) Partner score sheets documenting correct recalls per round, (2) Category sorting accuracy (7/8 categories correctly sorted), (3) Speed challenge performance (minimum 15/20 instructions recalled within time limits), (4) Final verification round participation with accurate responses to instructor prompts
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing mnemonic devices (MOV = move, LEA = load effective address) and allowing reference to instruction category groupings during initial rounds. For advanced learners, add complexity by requiring recall of specific CPU flags affected (carry, zero, sign, overflow) and common addressing modes (immediate, register, memory displacement) for each instruction type.

title: Interpreting Multicollinearity Diagnostics in High-Dimensional Regression Models
description: Students will analyze a complex healthcare dataset to identify and interpret multicollinearity issues using advanced diagnostic techniques. They will examine correlation matrices, variance inflation factors, and eigenvalue decomposition to understand how feature interdependencies affect model performance and statistical inference.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret VIF values, condition indices, and eigenvalue decompositions by analyzing their mathematical relationships and thresholds in the context of feature selection
Students will distinguish between different types of multicollinearity through systematic examination of correlation structures and their impact on regression coefficient stability
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a healthcare dataset with 15,000 patient records and 47 predictor variables for predicting hospital readmission risk. In pairs, students first execute provided code to generate a correlation heatmap and identify variable clusters with correlations >0.7 (15 minutes). Next, they calculate Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) for all variables using statsmodels, documenting which variables exceed the threshold of 10 and explaining why these values indicate problematic multicollinearity (20 minutes). Students then perform eigenvalue decomposition on the correlation matrix, identifying eigenvalues <0.01 and their corresponding eigenvectors to pinpoint the specific linear combinations causing collinearity issues (25 minutes). Following this, pairs compare regression coefficients and standard errors from models with and without highly collinear variables, documenting how coefficient signs change and confidence intervals widen (20 minutes). Students create a structured analysis report interpreting: (1) which clinical measurements are inherently correlated and why, (2) how removing different combinations of collinear variables affects model interpretability versus predictive accuracy, and (3) recommendations for variable retention based on clinical relevance and statistical diagnostics (30 minutes). Conclude with pair presentations of their most surprising finding about multicollinearity patterns in the healthcare context (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Pre-loaded healthcare dataset (MIMIC-III derived with 47 variables)
Required Python packages: pandas, numpy, seaborn, matplotlib, statsmodels, sklearn
Multicollinearity diagnostic template worksheet
Access to statistical reference tables for VIF and condition index thresholds
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate calculation and interpretation of VIF values with correct threshold application (25%), (2) Proper identification of problematic eigenvalues and explanation of corresponding variable combinations (25%), (3) Clear articulation of how multicollinearity affects coefficient stability and statistical inference (25%), (4) Justified recommendations balancing statistical diagnostics with domain knowledge (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly explaining why specific variables are collinear and predicting the directional impact on model performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example using 5 variables before the full analysis, offer a decision tree flowchart for interpreting VIF thresholds, and give sentence starters for explaining multicollinearity impacts. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement ridge regression as a multicollinearity solution, explore partial correlation analysis, or investigate multicollinearity detection in polynomial and interaction terms using the same dataset.

title: Shopping Cart Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students will create a realistic grocery shopping list with a $50 budget, then apply percentage calculations to determine sales tax, discounts, and tips. They will use real grocery store prices to practice calculating percentages in authentic contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine sales tax, discounts, and tips by working with real-world shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage operations through creating and analyzing itemized grocery receipts
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a grocery store flyer and calculator (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to select 8-12 grocery items totaling close to $45, writing item names and prices on their shopping worksheet. Next, students calculate a 15% discount on their total, showing all work step-by-step using the formula: discount = original price × 0.15, then subtract from original total (10 minutes). Following this, students add 8.5% sales tax to their discounted total using: tax = discounted total × 0.085, then add to get final grocery cost (10 minutes). Students then calculate an 18% tip for grocery delivery using: tip = final total × 0.18 (5 minutes). In pairs, students compare their calculations and check each other's work, identifying any errors and discussing solution strategies (10 minutes). Finally, each student presents one calculation to the class, explaining their process and final totals. The teacher circulates throughout, providing guidance on decimal-to-percentage conversions and helping students organize their multi-step calculations clearly.
materials_needed: Current grocery store flyers or printed price lists (one per student)
Basic calculators
Shopping Cart Budget Worksheet with spaces for items, calculations, and final totals
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Grade completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown; (3) Minor calculation errors but correct process demonstrated; (2) Some correct calculations with incomplete work shown; (1) Major errors in percentage calculation process. Students must achieve level 3 or higher to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage calculation reference cards showing formulas and example problems. Allow use of percentage calculator functions after demonstrating manual calculations. For advanced learners: Add compound scenarios like calculating percentage savings compared to regular prices, or determining what percentage of monthly allowance the shopping trip represents.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Sorting Algorithm Performance Decomposition
description: Students will analyze and compare the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms by examining their code structure, identifying key operations, and evaluating performance characteristics. They will break down each algorithm's efficiency patterns and justify which algorithm performs best under specific data conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and dominant operations
Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through systematic examination of memory allocation patterns in each sorting implementation
instructions:
Begin by distributing three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) with line numbers and complexity analysis worksheets (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3, assigning each member one algorithm initially. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each student individually examines their assigned algorithm, counting nested loops, identifying recursive structures, and marking lines where new memory is allocated. They complete Section A of the worksheet, documenting: loop depth at each level, number of comparisons per iteration, and memory allocation points.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Students rotate algorithms within their group, now analyzing their second algorithm using the same systematic approach. They complete Section B, comparing patterns observed between their first and second algorithms.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students analyze their third algorithm and complete Section C with full comparison matrix.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Groups collaborate to create a comprehensive analysis chart showing: Best/Average/Worst case time complexity for each algorithm, space complexity analysis, and data condition recommendations (when to use each algorithm). Groups must provide specific justifications citing code structure evidence.

Phase 5 (15 minutes): Each group presents one key finding to the class, specifically explaining how code structure directly impacts complexity classification. Instructor facilitates discussion on trade-offs between time and space efficiency.
materials_needed: Three printed code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) with line numbers
Algorithm complexity analysis worksheets with sections A, B, C
Big-O notation reference chart
Stopwatch or timer for phase management
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all complexity factors with detailed code citations, (3) Identifies most complexity factors with adequate justification, (2) Identifies basic patterns with minimal explanation, (1) Incomplete analysis with errors. Check group comparison charts for accuracy of Big-O classifications and appropriateness of algorithm recommendations for different data scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted code versions marking loop beginnings/ends and include a completed example using selection sort. For advanced learners: Add analysis of hybrid algorithms (like Timsort) or challenge them to propose optimizations for worst-case scenarios. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during rotation phases.

title: Machine Learning Model Selection and Validation Critique
description: Students will critically evaluate three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) applied to a customer churn prediction problem, assessing model appropriateness, validation methodology, and business impact. They will make evidence-based recommendations for model deployment while identifying potential biases and limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the appropriateness of different machine learning algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, computational complexity, and interpretability trade-offs within a business context
Students will critique cross-validation strategies and bias detection methods through systematic analysis of model validation reports and fairness metrics
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with three pre-built model reports for a telecom customer churn dataset (10,000+ customers, 20 features). Each report contains: model architecture, hyperparameter choices, training methodology, performance metrics (AUC, precision, recall, F1), validation strategy, feature importance, computational costs, and bias analysis across demographic groups. Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze each model report individually, documenting strengths and weaknesses using the provided evaluation framework covering: statistical performance, business relevance, interpretability, scalability, fairness, and validation rigor. Step 2 (30 minutes): Teams complete a comparative analysis matrix, ranking models across six evaluation criteria and identifying critical concerns (overfitting, data leakage, sampling bias, etc.). Step 3 (45 minutes): Each team prepares a 10-minute stakeholder presentation recommending one model for deployment, including: risk assessment, implementation timeline, monitoring strategy, and mitigation plans for identified limitations. Step 4 (60 minutes): Teams present to simulated stakeholders (instructor + guest industry professional if possible), followed by 5-minute Q&A sessions where presenters defend their recommendations against challenges about bias, generalizability, and business impact. Step 5 (20 minutes): Peer evaluation round where teams score other presentations using provided rubric, followed by class discussion on evaluation criteria disagreements and real-world deployment considerations.
materials_needed: Three detailed ML model reports (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) with performance metrics and validation results
Customer churn dataset documentation with feature descriptions and business context
Model evaluation framework template with scoring criteria
Comparative analysis matrix worksheet
Presentation rubric for peer assessment
Access to Python/R with scikit-learn, pandas for optional analysis verification
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Completed evaluation framework showing depth of analysis (25%), (2) Comparative matrix with justified rankings and risk identification (25%), (3) Stakeholder presentation quality including recommendation defense and Q&A responses (35%), (4) Peer evaluation participation and constructive feedback quality (15%). Use 4-point rubric for each component focusing on evidence-based reasoning, consideration of multiple perspectives, and practical implementation awareness.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guiding questions for each evaluation criterion and example bias detection scenarios. For advanced learners, include additional complexity: ensemble method evaluation, A/B testing design for model comparison, or regulatory compliance considerations (GDPR, fair lending). Provide optional supplementary papers on ML interpretability and algorithmic fairness for deeper analysis.

title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Urban Traffic Flow Management
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban traffic congestion problems using multi-variable calculus, linear programming, and statistical analysis. Teams will develop both theoretical frameworks and computational solutions, then present their models to simulate city planning scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced calculus concepts (partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers) with linear programming techniques by designing an original traffic optimization algorithm
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical model through integration of real traffic data, constraint analysis, and multi-objective optimization functions
instructions: Begin with 15-minute team formation (3-4 students per group) and distribute traffic datasets from three different metropolitan areas. Each team selects one city and spends 30 minutes analyzing baseline data including traffic volume, intersection capacity, peak hour patterns, and accident frequency. Teams then spend 45 minutes defining their optimization problem by identifying decision variables (signal timing, lane allocation, route recommendations), establishing objective functions (minimize travel time, reduce emissions, maximize throughput), and listing constraints (budget limitations, infrastructure capacity, safety requirements). During the next 60 minutes, teams develop their mathematical model by writing the complete system of equations, incorporating at least two optimization techniques (linear programming for resource allocation and calculus-based methods for continuous variables), and creating constraint matrices. Teams spend 45 minutes implementing their solution using provided software, running simulations with different parameter values, and documenting results including convergence analysis and sensitivity testing. The final 30 minutes involve preparing presentations that include problem statement, mathematical formulation, solution methodology, computational results, and practical implementation recommendations. Each team presents for 8 minutes followed by 4 minutes of peer questioning, with other teams evaluating the mathematical rigor and practical feasibility using provided rubrics.
materials_needed: Real traffic datasets from 3 metropolitan areas (CSV format with hourly flow data)
Optimization software access (MATLAB with Optimization Toolbox or Python with SciPy)
Large format paper and markers for model visualization
Laptops or desktop computers with spreadsheet software
Digital presentation tools and projector setup
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - correct formulation of objective functions and constraints; Innovation (25%) - originality of approach and creative problem-solving; Technical Implementation (25%) - successful computational execution and result interpretation; Communication (25%) - clarity of presentation and defense of methodology. Peer evaluation forms assess each team's mathematical reasoning and practical applicability.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template constraint matrices and example objective function formats. Offer intermediate check-points at 45 and 90 minutes for instructor feedback. Extend advanced learners by challenging them to incorporate stochastic elements, multi-period optimization, or machine learning prediction components. Provide optional complexity additions like environmental impact factors or economic cost modeling.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Visual Patterns
description: Students will memorize the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-31 through repetitive practice with physical flashcards and pattern recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-31 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the binary equivalents of powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) through visual pattern matching exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (decimal on front, binary on back for numbers 0-31). Spend 5 minutes having students examine the cards and notice patterns, particularly how powers of 2 appear in binary (1, 10, 100, 1000, etc.). Next, conduct a 10-minute guided group practice where you hold up decimal numbers and students call out binary equivalents in unison, starting with powers of 2, then multiples of powers of 2. For the main activity (20 minutes), pair students and have them alternate roles: one partner shows the decimal side while the other states the binary equivalent, then they check the answer together. Partners should go through the entire deck twice, removing cards they both answer correctly on first attempt. Have pairs focus remaining time on challenging cards. In the final 10 minutes, conduct individual timed quizzes where each student writes binary equivalents for 15 randomly selected decimal numbers (0-31) within 3 minutes. Collect these for assessment. Throughout the activity, emphasize the visual patterns: how adding 1 in decimal affects the rightmost binary digits, how powers of 2 create clean patterns, and how binary place values double from right to left (1, 2, 4, 8, 16).
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-31 on front, binary equivalents on back (one set per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Individual quiz sheets with 15 decimal numbers for binary conversion
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Grade individual timed quizzes using binary conversion accuracy (1 point per correct answer, 15 points total). Success criteria: 13/15 correct answers (87%) demonstrates adequate memorization. Observe pair work for participation and peer teaching effectiveness. Track which specific numbers students struggle with most for future remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with smaller sets (0-15), provide binary place value charts (128|64|32|16|8|4|2|1), and allow extra practice time with powers of 2 only. For advanced learners: Extend to decimal numbers 32-63, introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or have them create their own memory devices and teach struggling classmates.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Test Results for E-commerce Conversion Rates
description: Students will analyze real A/B test data from an e-commerce website to understand statistical significance concepts and interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes. They will explain what the statistical results mean for business decision-making and identify potential limitations in the experimental design.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes by analyzing provided A/B test results and explaining their practical business implications
Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through comparison of multiple A/B test scenarios with varying sample sizes and effect magnitudes
instructions: Begin by providing students with three A/B test datasets (15 minutes setup). Dataset A: 10,000 visitors per variant, 2.1% vs 2.3% conversion rates, p-value=0.03. Dataset B: 1,000 visitors per variant, 2.1% vs 2.8% conversion rates, p-value=0.08. Dataset C: 50,000 visitors per variant, 2.10% vs 2.13% conversion rates, p-value=0.001. Students work in pairs to complete a structured analysis worksheet (25 minutes). First, they calculate the absolute and relative differences in conversion rates for each test. Next, they interpret what each p-value means in plain English and determine which tests are statistically significant at α=0.05. Then, they examine the provided 95% confidence intervals and explain what these ranges tell us about the true effect size. Students must also calculate the potential revenue impact assuming $50 average order value and 100,000 monthly visitors. Finally, they rank the three tests by business importance and justify their reasoning. Conclude with pair presentations (15 minutes) where each team explains their interpretation of one dataset to the class, focusing on the distinction between statistical and practical significance. Instructor facilitates discussion about sample size effects and business context importance.
materials_needed: Three prepared A/B test datasets with statistical results (CSV files or printed sheets)
Structured analysis worksheet with calculation templates
Calculators or laptops with Excel/Google Sheets access
Statistical significance reference chart (p-values and confidence intervals)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation of conversion rate differences and revenue impact, (2) Accurate interpretation of p-values and statistical significance, (3) Clear explanation of confidence interval meaning, (4) Logical ranking of business importance with justification. Students must score 3/4 to demonstrate understanding. Additionally, assess verbal explanations during presentations for clarity and use of appropriate statistical terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a p-value interpretation guide with example phrases ('p=0.03 means there's a 3% chance...'). Offer calculation templates with partially completed examples. For advanced learners, add questions about Type I/II errors, power analysis, or multiple testing corrections. Provide additional datasets with more complex scenarios like multi-arm tests or segmented results. Consider discussing minimum detectable effect and sample size planning for extension activities.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Test Results for E-commerce Conversion Rates: Business Application
description: Students will analyze pre-collected A/B test data from an e-commerce website's checkout button experiment. They will interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes to determine whether observed differences in conversion rates are statistically meaningful and practically significant for business decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical significance measures (p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes) by analyzing A/B test results and explaining their business implications
Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through guided analysis of conversion rate data with varying sample sizes and effect magnitudes
instructions: Begin by distributing the A/B test scenario: an e-commerce site tested two checkout button colors (Control: blue, Treatment: green) over 4 weeks. Provide students with three different result datasets showing varying levels of statistical significance. In pairs (10 minutes), have students examine Dataset 1 (p=0.03, CI: 0.2%-2.1% difference, n=5000 per group). Students should identify the p-value, confidence interval bounds, and sample sizes, then discuss what each number means in plain English. Reconvene as a class (8 minutes) to clarify interpretations and address misconceptions about p-values. Next, distribute Dataset 2 (p=0.45, CI: -0.8%-1.2% difference, n=1200 per group) and Dataset 3 (p<0.001, CI: 0.05%-0.15% difference, n=50000 per group). Working in the same pairs (15 minutes), students complete a structured worksheet comparing all three datasets. They must answer: Which results are statistically significant? Which represent practically meaningful improvements? What business recommendation would you make for each scenario? Provide sentence starters like 'The p-value of ___ indicates that...' and 'Although statistically significant, this result suggests...' During pair work, circulate to check understanding and provide hints. Conclude with a gallery walk (10 minutes) where pairs post their recommendations and vote on the most compelling business case, followed by instructor synthesis of key concepts and common interpretation errors.
materials_needed: Three printed datasets showing A/B test results with different statistical outcomes
Structured interpretation worksheet with guided questions and sentence starters
E-commerce A/B test scenario handout with business context
Chart paper and markers for gallery walk recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (3) Correctly interprets all statistical measures and provides appropriate business recommendations with clear reasoning, (2) Interprets most measures correctly with minor errors in business application, (1) Shows basic understanding but contains significant misconceptions about p-values or confidence intervals. Additionally, assess participation in pair discussions and quality of posted business recommendations during gallery walk.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference card defining p-values and confidence intervals in simple terms, and offer one-on-one clarification during pair work. Use colored highlighting to help students locate key numbers in datasets. For advanced learners: Include additional questions about Type I/II errors, power analysis, and multiple testing corrections. Challenge them to calculate needed sample sizes for detecting smaller effect sizes or to critique the experimental design's potential limitations.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Test Results for E-commerce Conversion Rates: Business Application
description: Students will analyze pre-collected A/B test data from an e-commerce website's checkout button experiment to determine statistical significance and interpret business implications. This activity focuses on understanding p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes rather than calculating them from scratch.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical significance by analyzing p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes from A/B test outputs
Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through examination of real e-commerce conversion data
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing A/B test results for two checkout button designs (Control: blue button, Treatment: green button) with 10,000 visitors each. Provide students with summary statistics showing Control conversion rate: 3.2%, Treatment conversion rate: 3.8%, p-value: 0.042, 95% CI for difference: [0.02%, 1.18%], and effect size: 0.6 percentage points. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Have students work individually to examine the statistical outputs and write initial interpretations of each metric. Step 2 (15 minutes): Form pairs to compare interpretations and discuss what each statistic means in business context. Step 3 (10 minutes): Present three scenarios with different p-values (0.001, 0.08, 0.45) and conversion rate differences (0.1%, 2.3%, 0.05%) for students to categorize as 'statistically significant,' 'practically significant,' 'both,' or 'neither.' Step 4 (10 minutes): Pairs create a one-paragraph business recommendation memo explaining whether to implement the green button, addressing both statistical and practical considerations. Step 5 (10 minutes): Three pairs share their memos with the class, followed by instructor-led discussion highlighting common interpretation errors and the importance of considering business context alongside statistical results.
materials_needed: Printed A/B test summary statistics handout (one per student)
Three additional scenario worksheets with different statistical outcomes
Calculators or laptops for basic arithmetic
Whiteboard or projector for displaying scenarios
assessment_method: Evaluate students' business recommendation memos using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correct interpretation of p-value and confidence interval, (2) Accurate distinction between statistical and practical significance, (3) Clear business recommendation with supporting rationale. Additionally, observe pair discussions for evidence of understanding statistical concepts in context.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet defining p-values ('probability of seeing this difference by chance') and confidence intervals ('range of likely true differences'). For advanced learners, introduce additional considerations like sample size planning, multiple testing corrections, or segmentation analysis of the same dataset by user demographics.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Test Results for E-commerce Conversion Rates: Business Application
description: Students will analyze real A/B test data from an e-commerce website to determine statistical significance and interpret confidence intervals. They will compare two webpage designs' conversion rates and explain what the statistical results mean for business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret p-values and confidence intervals by analyzing A/B test conversion rate data and explaining their statistical meaning
Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through comparison of effect sizes and business impact metrics
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided dataset containing 30 days of A/B test results for two webpage designs (Control: 15,247 visitors, 1,219 conversions; Treatment: 14,982 visitors, 1,344 conversions). Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work in pairs to calculate basic conversion rates for both groups using calculators or Excel. Step 2 (15 minutes): Provide pre-calculated statistical test results showing p-value = 0.023, 95% CI for difference = [0.002, 0.018], and effect size = 0.012. Students must interpret each statistic by writing one sentence explaining what each number means in plain English. Step 3 (15 minutes): Present three business scenarios with different contexts (startup vs. established company, high vs. low traffic costs, seasonal vs. year-round campaign). Students discuss how statistical significance interpretation might change across scenarios. Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair presents their interpretation of one statistic to the class, explaining both the mathematical meaning and business implications. Step 5 (10 minutes): Instructor facilitates discussion on common misinterpretations of p-values and when statistical significance doesn't guarantee business value. Students complete reflection worksheet identifying key differences between statistical and practical significance.
materials_needed: A/B test dataset spreadsheet with visitor and conversion counts
Pre-calculated statistical test results handout
Three business scenario description cards
Statistical interpretation reflection worksheet
Calculators or laptop access to Excel/Google Sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of conversion rate calculations, (2) Correct interpretation of p-value meaning, (3) Appropriate explanation of confidence interval, (4) Clear distinction between statistical and practical significance in business context. Students must score 3/4 on each criterion to demonstrate understanding. Collect reflection worksheets for individual assessment of concept comprehension.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'The p-value of 0.023 means...' and visual aids showing confidence interval on number line. Offer additional practice with simpler examples. For advanced learners: Introduce Type I/II error concepts, discuss multiple testing corrections, or explore power analysis calculations. Provide supplementary reading on effect size interpretation in business contexts.

title: Optimizing Warehouse Layout Using Linear Programming and Calculus
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques and multivariable calculus to solve a real-world warehouse optimization problem. They will determine optimal storage allocation, minimize transportation costs, and maximize efficiency while working with realistic constraints including budget, space, and labor limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to optimize warehouse storage allocation by formulating objective functions and constraint equations from real-world scenarios
Students will implement multivariable calculus techniques to minimize cost functions through systematic problem-solving procedures and mathematical modeling
instructions: Begin by distributing the warehouse scenario packet containing floor plans, cost data, and operational constraints (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze 'MegaStore Distribution Center' which needs to optimize storage for 5 product categories across 3 warehouse zones. Each team receives: current inventory data, transportation costs per zone, storage capacity limits, and monthly budget constraints of $2.3M. Teams first identify decision variables (storage quantities x₁, x₂, x₃ for each zone) and formulate the objective function to minimize total costs C = 45x₁ + 38x₂ + 52x₃ + 0.02x₁² + 0.015x₂² (includes linear transportation costs plus quadratic congestion penalties). Next, teams establish constraint inequalities: storage capacity (x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≤ 850,000 units), budget (45x₁ + 38x₂ + 52x₃ ≤ 2,300,000), and minimum service levels (x₁ ≥ 125,000, x₂ ≥ 200,000, x₃ ≥ 180,000). Using graphing calculators and Excel Solver, teams plot feasible regions and identify corner points for linear constraints, then apply partial derivatives ∂C/∂x₁, ∂C/∂x₂, ∂C/∂x₃ to find critical points for the quadratic components. Teams calculate optimal allocation values, verify solutions satisfy all constraints, and compute minimum total cost. Finally, each team prepares a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical approach, optimal solution (expected: x₁ ≈ 267,000, x₂ ≈ 324,000, x₃ ≈ 259,000 with minimum cost ≈ $1,847,000), and practical implementation recommendations for warehouse management.
materials_needed: Warehouse scenario packet with floor plans and data tables
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Laptops with Microsoft Excel and Solver add-in installed
Graph paper and colored pencils for constraint plotting
Digital presentation platform access
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Setup (25% - correct objective function and constraints), Solution Process (35% - proper application of linear programming and calculus techniques), Accuracy (25% - solution within 5% of optimal values), Communication (15% - clear presentation of methodology and results). Students must submit Excel workbooks showing calculations and deliver team presentations demonstrating understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed constraint templates and step-by-step calculus derivative worksheets. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-variable problems first. For advanced learners: introduce integer programming constraints (storage units must be whole pallets), add time-dependent demand variations requiring dynamic optimization, or include probabilistic elements with uncertain demand forecasts requiring robust optimization techniques.

title: Design Your Dream Playground: Area and Perimeter Budget Challenge
description: Students will design an original playground layout using geometric shapes while working within budget constraints based on area and perimeter calculations. They will create detailed blueprints, calculate costs, and present their design with mathematical justifications for their choices.
estimated_duration: 100 minutes (can be split across 2 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will create an original playground design by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and circles within specified constraints
Students will construct a mathematical budget proposal through multi-step calculations involving unit rates and optimization decisions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario packet: students have been hired as playground designers with a $25,000 budget and must create a design for a rectangular lot measuring 60m × 40m. Provide the pricing sheet: safety surfacing costs $15 per square meter, fencing costs $8 per linear meter, and equipment costs vary by footprint area ($50-200 per square meter depending on complexity). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students sketch their initial playground vision on graph paper, including at least 5 different zones (play equipment, sports court, garden area, seating, pathways). Each zone must use different geometric shapes.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students calculate the area and perimeter for each zone using appropriate formulas. They must show all work on their calculation sheets, including proper units and labeling.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Using the pricing guide, students calculate costs for each zone (surface area × surface cost + perimeter × fencing cost + equipment costs). They create a detailed budget breakdown and adjust their design if over budget.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students create their final blueprint on poster paper with color coding, dimensions clearly labeled, and a cost summary table.

Step 5 (25 minutes): Each student presents their 3-minute pitch to the 'city council' (classmates), explaining their design choices and demonstrating their mathematical calculations. Listeners use evaluation forms to assess mathematical accuracy and design creativity.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm grid, 2 sheets per student)
11×17 inch poster paper
Colored pencils or markers
Scientific calculators
Rulers and measuring tools
Scenario packets with pricing guides
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area/perimeter calculations with shown work, accurate budget totals), Design Creativity (innovative use of space, variety of geometric shapes), Budget Management (stays within constraints, shows cost-conscious decisions), and Communication (clear presentation, mathematical reasoning explained). Final deliverables include the blueprint poster, calculation worksheet, and presentation performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide formula reference sheets, pre-drawn shape templates, and partner them with stronger math students during calculation phases. Offer simplified pricing (round numbers). For advanced learners: Add constraints like accessibility requirements, introduce irregular shapes requiring decomposition, or challenge them to minimize waste/maximize usable space through optimization techniques.

title: TCP/IP Stack Layer Function Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units of each TCP/IP stack layer through structured flashcard drilling and rapid-fire recall sessions. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network architecture components that advanced computer science students must know fluently.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the specific protocols operating at each TCP/IP stack layer (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) by completing timed identification exercises
Students will memorize the data unit names, encapsulation processes, and primary functions of each layer through systematic repetition and peer testing
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP reference sheets and giving students 10 minutes to review. Next, introduce the memorization structure: Layer 4 (Application) - protocols HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, data unit is 'data'; Layer 3 (Transport) - protocols TCP/UDP, data unit is 'segment/datagram'; Layer 2 (Internet) - protocol IP, data unit is 'packet'; Layer 1 (Network Access) - protocols Ethernet/WiFi, data unit is 'frame'. Have students create flashcards with layer numbers on front, complete information on back (15 minutes). Conduct three progressive recall rounds: Round 1 - students self-quiz using flashcards for 8 minutes, checking accuracy against reference sheet. Round 2 - pair students for peer testing, one reads layer number/protocol name, partner must state remaining details (10 minutes, then switch). Round 3 - rapid-fire whole class drill where instructor calls out layer numbers and students must immediately state all protocols and data units for that layer within 5 seconds (12 minutes). Conclude with individual written quiz where students fill in a blank TCP/IP stack diagram with all protocols, functions, and data units from memory (10 minutes). Emphasize that this is pure memorization - no explanation or analysis required, just accurate recall of technical specifications.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Stack Reference Sheet (one per student)
Blank index cards for flashcards (8 per student)
Stopwatch or timer
Blank TCP/IP stack diagram worksheets for final assessment
assessment_method: Grade the final written diagram completion quiz using a 20-point rubric: 4 points per layer for correctly listing all protocols (12 total protocols), 4 points for correctly naming all data units, 4 points for accurate layer numbering/naming. Students must achieve 16/20 points (80%) to demonstrate successful memorization. Track participation during peer testing rounds for engagement points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide acronym memory aids (e.g., 'All The Internet Needs' for layer order) and allow color-coding of flashcards by layer. Advanced learners can memorize additional details like port numbers for Application layer protocols (HTTP:80, HTTPS:443, FTP:21, SMTP:25) and practice reverse recall (given protocol, state the layer and data unit).

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Model Complexity Analysis
description: Students will analyze polynomial regression models of varying complexity on a noisy dataset to understand how bias and variance components change with model complexity. They will interpret visual decompositions of prediction error and explain the mathematical relationship between model flexibility and generalization performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition plots by analyzing how prediction error components change across different polynomial degrees
Students will explain the mathematical relationship between model complexity and the bias-variance tradeoff through examination of overfitting and underfitting scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-generated dataset containing 100 training samples from a cubic function with Gaussian noise (σ=0.3). Distribute the analysis worksheet containing bias-variance decomposition plots for polynomial models of degrees 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 15. In the first 20 minutes, students work individually to examine the six plots, each showing: (1) true function, (2) individual model predictions across 50 bootstrap samples, (3) mean prediction, (4) bias², (5) variance, and (6) total error decomposition. Students must identify which degree corresponds to minimum total error and mark the transition points where bias dominates to where variance dominates. Next, form pairs for 25 minutes to complete interpretation questions: explain why degree-1 shows high bias but low variance, describe what causes the variance spike in degree-15 models, and predict optimal complexity for datasets with different noise levels. Each pair must annotate the plots with arrows and labels indicating 'underfitting zone,' 'sweet spot,' and 'overfitting zone.' In the final 15 minutes, conduct structured discussions where pairs present their interpretations of one specific model degree, explaining the mathematical intuition behind their observations. Students must use precise terminology: irreducible error, model flexibility, generalization gap, and expected prediction error. Conclude by having each pair write a 3-sentence summary explaining why neither the simplest nor most complex model performs optimally.
materials_needed: Pre-generated noisy cubic dataset (100 training points)
Six bias-variance decomposition plots (one per polynomial degree)
Analysis worksheet with interpretation questions
Colored pens for plot annotation
assessment_method: Evaluate annotated plots for correct identification of bias/variance dominant regions (25 points), accuracy of written explanations for mathematical relationships (35 points), appropriate use of technical terminology in discussions (25 points), and quality of final summary demonstrating understanding of optimal complexity selection (15 points). Success requires scoring 75+ points with demonstrated ability to connect visual patterns to underlying mathematical concepts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a glossary of bias-variance terms and highlight one example plot with pre-marked annotations. Offer guiding questions: 'What happens to the spread of predictions as degree increases?' Advanced learners should analyze additional regularization scenarios or extend analysis to cross-validation curves, connecting bias-variance concepts to learning curves and validation strategies.

title: Shopping Cart Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to determine discounts, tax amounts, and final costs for items in simulated shopping scenarios. They will use basic percentage formulas to solve authentic problems involving sales, tips, and budget planning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculation formulas to determine discount amounts, tax calculations, and tips by working through realistic shopping scenarios
Students will calculate final costs and budget remaining amounts through hands-on problem-solving with mock purchase receipts
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made shopping scenario cards to pairs of students (5 minutes). Each card contains 3-4 items with original prices, discount percentages (10%, 15%, 25%), local sales tax rate (8.25%), and a budget limit ($150). Students must calculate: 1) discount amount for each item, 2) sale price after discount, 3) subtotal of all items, 4) tax amount on subtotal, 5) final total, and 6) remaining budget. Provide the formula reference sheet: Discount = Original Price × Discount%, Sale Price = Original Price - Discount, Tax = Subtotal × Tax Rate, Final Total = Subtotal + Tax. Have students work in pairs for 20 minutes, showing all calculations step-by-step on the provided worksheet. Circulate to check work and provide guidance. After calculations, each pair presents one item's complete calculation process to the class (10 minutes total for all presentations). Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify which step was most challenging and share one real-world situation where they might use these skills. Students must show all work clearly, use proper mathematical notation, and round monetary amounts to the nearest cent throughout the activity.
materials_needed: Shopping scenario cards (one per pair, 6 different scenarios)
Percentage calculation formula reference sheet
Structured calculation worksheets with spaces for each step
Calculators (basic four-function)
Whiteboard markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with clear step-by-step work shown, proper rounding applied; (3) Minor calculation errors but correct process and formulas used; (2) Correct formulas identified but multiple calculation errors or unclear work; (1) Incorrect formulas or processes used, major errors throughout. Check final answers against answer key and observe pair collaboration during work time.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculators and highlight which formula to use for each step, work through the first item together as a guided example. For advanced learners: Add compound scenarios with multiple discounts (clearance + coupon), include tip calculations for restaurant scenarios, or have them create their own shopping scenarios for classmates to solve.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementation Performance
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity and space complexity of linear search versus binary search algorithms by examining code implementations and performance data. They will decompose the algorithms to identify efficiency bottlenecks and justify which algorithm is more appropriate for different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of linear and binary search algorithms by examining their code structure and identifying key operations
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of performance metrics and data structure requirements
instructions: Begin by providing students with working implementations of both linear search and binary search algorithms in their chosen programming language (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and distribute the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet containing datasets of varying sizes (100, 1000, 10000, 100000 elements). Each pair runs both algorithms on identical unsorted and sorted datasets, recording execution times and memory usage using built-in profiling tools. Students then examine the source code line-by-line, counting comparison operations and identifying loops to determine Big O notation (30 minutes). Next, students create a comparison matrix analyzing: worst-case scenarios, best-case scenarios, average performance, memory requirements, and prerequisite conditions (sorted vs unsorted data). They must identify the specific lines of code that contribute most to time complexity and explain why binary search requires sorted data while linear search does not (25 minutes). Students then receive three real-world scenarios: searching a phone directory, finding a student ID in an unsorted class roster, and locating a product in an inventory system. For each scenario, they must justify which algorithm is more appropriate by referencing their complexity analysis and practical constraints (15 minutes). Finally, pairs present one scenario analysis to another pair, defending their algorithm choice and explaining the trade-offs they identified (10 minutes). Throughout the activity, students document their findings in the provided analysis template, showing calculations for Big O notation and citing specific evidence from their performance testing.
materials_needed: Pre-written linear search and binary search code implementations
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with structured comparison matrices
Computers with programming environment and profiling tools installed
Test datasets in CSV format (100, 1000, 10000, 100000 integer elements)
Real-world scenario descriptions handout
Big O notation reference chart
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Algorithm Analysis Worksheets using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate Big O notation identification with mathematical justification, (2) Correct interpretation of performance data with specific evidence, (3) Appropriate algorithm selection for each scenario with detailed reasoning, (4) Clear identification of code segments affecting complexity. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category, with partial credit for showing work and reasoning even if conclusions are incorrect.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step Big O calculation examples and highlight the specific loop structures to analyze first. Offer a partially completed comparison matrix template. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (interpolation search, exponential search) or modify the existing algorithms to improve efficiency. Have them research and explain why binary search performs better on arrays versus linked lists.

title: Evaluating and Critiquing Predictive Models for Real Estate Price Forecasting
description: Students will critically assess three different machine learning models (linear regression, random forest, and neural network) trained on real estate data by analyzing their performance metrics, assumptions, and business applicability. They will provide justified recommendations for model selection based on comprehensive evaluation criteria including accuracy, interpretability, computational efficiency, and stakeholder needs.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, residual patterns, and model assumptions within a real estate pricing context
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and business constraints
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the Boston Housing dataset with three pre-trained models (linear regression with R²=0.67, random forest with R²=0.85, neural network with R²=0.88) along with performance outputs, residual plots, and feature importance charts. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (45 minutes):** Each student independently examines all three models using the provided evaluation framework: (1) Statistical performance (RMSE, MAE, R²), (2) Residual analysis for bias patterns, (3) Feature importance and interpretability, (4) Computational requirements, (5) Overfitting indicators via cross-validation scores. Students complete standardized evaluation sheets with numerical scores and qualitative observations.

**Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (30 minutes):** Teams consolidate individual analyses, identifying areas of agreement and disagreement. They must reach consensus on ranking the models across five dimensions: predictive accuracy, interpretability, robustness, computational efficiency, and business value.

**Phase 3 - Stakeholder Scenarios (25 minutes):** Teams receive three different stakeholder scenarios: (A) Real estate investment firm needing explainable decisions, (B) High-frequency trading platform requiring fast predictions, (C) Consumer app prioritizing user trust. For each scenario, teams must justify which model best serves that stakeholder's needs.

**Phase 4 - Presentation and Defense (30 minutes):** Each team presents their model recommendations for one assigned scenario, followed by Q&A where other teams challenge their reasoning. Presentations must include specific evidence from their analysis and address potential counterarguments.
materials_needed: Boston Housing dataset with 506 observations and 13 features
Pre-trained model outputs (predictions, residuals, performance metrics) in CSV format
Model evaluation framework worksheets with scoring rubrics
Three stakeholder scenario descriptions with specific business constraints
Python/R environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib libraries
Presentation software or collaborative whiteboard platform
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Evaluation Framework Application (25 points) - accuracy and thoroughness in applying statistical and business criteria to assess each model, (2) Critical Analysis Quality (30 points) - depth of insights about model trade-offs, limitations, and appropriate use cases, (3) Stakeholder-Specific Reasoning (25 points) - alignment between model recommendations and specific business constraints/needs, (4) Evidence-Based Argumentation (20 points) - use of quantitative data and logical reasoning to support conclusions during presentations and peer challenges.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide model evaluation checklists with specific questions to guide analysis, offer mini-tutorials on interpreting residual plots and cross-validation scores, and assign roles within teams (statistician, business analyst, presenter). For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional evaluation criteria not in the framework, have them propose model ensemble strategies, or ask them to design experiments for testing model performance on different market conditions or geographic regions.

title: Design and Validate a Custom Cryptographic Hash Function
description: Students will design an original cryptographic hash function from scratch, implementing it computationally, and then conduct rigorous mathematical analysis to evaluate its security properties. This culminating activity integrates number theory, modular arithmetic, probability theory, and computational complexity analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original cryptographic hash function by synthesizing principles of modular arithmetic, bit manipulation, and collision resistance theory
Students will construct formal mathematical proofs through security analysis demonstrating their function's resistance to known attack vectors
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 2-3 members. Each team receives a specification sheet requiring their hash function to map arbitrary-length inputs to 256-bit outputs with specific security requirements. 

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams design their hash function architecture. They must choose: (1) a compression function using modular arithmetic operations, (2) a padding scheme for variable-length inputs, (3) initialization vectors, and (4) round constants. Students document design rationales using number theory principles, referencing prime number properties, discrete logarithm hardness, or polynomial irreducibility.

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Implementation phase using Python or Mathematica. Teams code their hash function, ensuring it handles edge cases (empty strings, single bits, maximum length inputs). They must create test suites demonstrating correctness and generate hash outputs for provided test vectors.

Phase 3 (150 minutes): Security analysis phase. Teams mathematically analyze their function's collision resistance by calculating birthday attack complexity, demonstrate preimage resistance through computational impossibility arguments, and test avalanche effect by measuring bit-change propagation. They must construct formal proofs showing their function satisfies one-wayness under reasonable computational assumptions.

Phase 4 (60 minutes): Peer evaluation phase. Teams attempt to break other teams' hash functions by finding collisions, preimages, or demonstrating statistical weaknesses. They document attack strategies and present findings.

Final presentations (45 minutes): Each team presents their hash function design, implementation, security analysis, and defense against peer attacks. Presentations must include complexity analysis, security proofs, and comparative evaluation against established hash functions like SHA-256.
materials_needed: Computer workstations with Python 3.x and mathematical libraries (NumPy, SymPy)
Access to Mathematica or equivalent symbolic computation software
Cryptographic reference materials (NIST standards, academic papers)
Large whiteboards for mathematical proof development
Digital presentation tools for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor of design rationale (25 points), correctness and efficiency of implementation (25 points), depth and validity of security analysis including formal proofs (30 points), effectiveness of peer attacks and defense strategies (10 points), clarity and technical accuracy of final presentation (10 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by successfully defending their design choices under questioning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template functions for basic operations, offer guided worksheets for proof construction, and allow consultation of additional cryptographic resources. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement quantum-resistant features, analyze their function against specific attack models (differential, linear cryptanalysis), or extend their work to create a full cryptographic suite including key derivation functions.

title: Design and Validate a Custom Cryptographic Hash Function: Exercise 1
description: Students will design their own cryptographic hash function by combining advanced mathematical concepts including modular arithmetic, matrix operations, and number theory. They will then validate their function's security properties through rigorous mathematical analysis and create a comprehensive security proof.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original cryptographic hash function by integrating modular arithmetic, linear algebra, and prime number theory within a 512-bit output specification
Students will formulate mathematical proofs demonstrating collision resistance and preimage resistance through probability theory and computational complexity analysis
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Students work in pairs to design their hash function architecture. Provide each pair with the constraint template: input messages of arbitrary length must produce exactly 512-bit outputs. Students must incorporate: (1) A compression function using modular arithmetic with a prime modulus >2^256, (2) Matrix multiplication over finite fields GF(2^8), (3) At least two rounds of non-linear transformations. Students document their design using mathematical notation, specifying all constants, operations, and bit-wise manipulations. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Implementation and testing phase. Using provided Python environment, students code their hash function and test it against a dataset of 1000 pre-generated test vectors. They must demonstrate their function passes basic requirements: deterministic output, avalanche effect (>50% bit change for 1-bit input change), and uniform distribution across output space. **Phase 3 (75 minutes):** Security analysis and proof construction. Students analyze their function for collision resistance by calculating the birthday paradox probability bounds, analyze preimage resistance using one-way function theory, and construct a formal mathematical argument for why their design resists known attacks (length extension, differential cryptanalysis). They create a 3-page mathematical proof document with formal notation. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Peer validation where pairs exchange proofs and attempt to find theoretical or practical weaknesses in the other team's design, providing written feedback on mathematical rigor and potential vulnerabilities.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with NumPy and hashlib libraries installed
Scientific calculators capable of modular arithmetic
Pre-generated test vector dataset (1000 input/output pairs)
Constraint specification template with required parameters
Access to mathematical reference materials on finite fields and cryptographic primitives
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Design Innovation (25 points) - originality and mathematical sophistication of hash function architecture, (2) Implementation Accuracy (25 points) - code functionality and test vector performance, (3) Mathematical Rigor (35 points) - quality of security proofs, correct use of probability theory and complexity analysis, (4) Peer Analysis Quality (15 points) - depth of critique provided to other teams. Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm templates with partial implementations and guided proof frameworks. Offer reference implementations of simpler hash functions (MD5 structure) as starting points. For advanced learners: Challenge them to prove security against specific advanced attacks (chosen-prefix collisions, quantum cryptanalysis using Grover's algorithm), or to optimize their function for hardware implementation with gate count analysis.
original_title: Design and Validate a Custom Cryptographic Hash Function

title: Python Basic Syntax Identification Flash Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements including keywords, operators, and data types through structured flash card activities. This activity focuses on building foundational vocabulary recognition essential for beginning programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 core Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, etc.) by matching them to their correct definitions
