Students will recall the proper syntax for Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) through visual recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash card sets to pairs of students (10 minutes setup). Each set contains 30 cards: 15 with Python syntax elements on the front and definitions/examples on the back, plus 15 matching cards with code snippets. Start with Round 1 (15 minutes): Student A shows syntax cards to Student B, who must state the definition and provide a simple example. Award 1 point per correct response. Switch roles after going through all cards once. Round 2 (15 minutes): Mix syntax cards face-up on desk. Student A reads a definition aloud; Student B must quickly identify and grab the correct syntax card. Award 2 points for immediate correct answers, 1 point if correct within 5 seconds. Switch roles halfway through. Round 3 (10 minutes): Challenge round using code snippet cards. Students work together to identify all syntax elements present in each code example, writing them on provided answer sheets. Final phase (5 minutes): Each pair reports their total points and demonstrates mastery by having each student correctly identify 5 random syntax elements drawn from the instructor's master deck. Record individual scores for assessment purposes.
materials_needed: Pre-printed Python syntax flash cards (30 cards per pair)
Code snippet cards with basic Python examples
Answer sheets for Round 3
Timer or stopwatch
Scoring sheets for each pair
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 4 out of 5 randomly selected Python syntax elements in the final demonstration to show mastery. Track individual performance using a checklist rubric: 5/5 correct = Exceeds (A), 4/5 correct = Meets (B), 3/5 correct = Approaching (C), below 3/5 = Needs Support.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide syntax reference sheets during activities and allow them to use cards in groups of 3 instead of pairs for additional support. For advanced learners: Include additional cards with more complex syntax (lambda functions, list comprehensions, exception handling) and challenge them to create their own code examples using the identified syntax elements.

title: Optimization Models for Real-World Business Scenarios Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve complex multi-constraint optimization problems in realistic business contexts. They will formulate mathematical models, implement solutions using graphical and algebraic methods, and interpret results to make data-driven recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert real-world business constraints into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical solutions to optimize multi-variable problems through systematic mathematical procedures
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct business scenarios: a manufacturing company optimizing production mix, a transportation company minimizing shipping costs, and an investment firm maximizing portfolio returns (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, with each team selecting one scenario. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), teams must identify decision variables, formulate the objective function, and translate all given constraints into mathematical inequalities. They should clearly define what each variable represents and ensure units are consistent. In Phase 2 (60 minutes), teams solve their problem using both graphical method (for 2-variable problems) and simplex tableau method (for problems with 3+ variables). Students must show all algebraic steps, identify feasible regions, and determine optimal solutions with exact values. During Phase 3 (30 minutes), teams prepare a business report interpreting their mathematical solution: What does the optimal solution mean in business terms? What is the maximum profit/minimum cost? Which constraints are binding? What happens if constraints change by ±10%? In Phase 4 (20 minutes), each team presents their scenario, mathematical model, solution process, and business recommendations to the class. Other teams must verify calculations and challenge interpretations. Instructor circulates throughout, checking mathematical accuracy and pushing teams to justify their constraint formulations.
materials_needed: Three detailed business scenario handouts with numerical data
Graph paper and rulers for graphical solutions
Scientific calculators
Simplex tableau worksheets
Microsoft Excel or online linear programming solver (optional verification tool)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Correct identification and definition of decision variables (20%), (2) Accurate formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (3) Proper execution of solution method with clear mathematical steps (25%), (4) Correct interpretation of optimal solution in business context (20%), (5) Quality of presentation and ability to defend solution (10%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy criteria to demonstrate successful application of linear programming techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates and encourage starting with simpler 2-variable versions. Offer guided practice with identifying key phrases that translate to mathematical inequalities. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis, shadow prices, or integer programming constraints. Challenge them to modify scenarios by adding complexity like minimum production requirements or discrete decision variables.

title: Analyzing Database Query Performance Bottlenecks Through Execution Plan Decomposition
description: Students will dissect and analyze SQL query execution plans to identify performance bottlenecks in complex database operations. They will examine real-world database scenarios with multiple table joins, subqueries, and indexing strategies to determine optimization opportunities and predict performance impacts.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by systematically examining operator costs, row estimates, and index usage patterns to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient query strategies through comparative analysis of multiple execution plan alternatives
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 2-3 students with three SQL queries of increasing complexity: a simple SELECT with WHERE clause, a multi-table JOIN with aggregation, and a query with nested subqueries. Using PostgreSQL with the EXPLAIN ANALYZE command, students first generate execution plans for each query on a provided sample database (minimum 100,000 records per table). In the first 20 minutes, teams document baseline metrics including total execution time, sequential scan costs, and memory usage. Next, students systematically analyze each node in the execution tree, identifying the most expensive operations by examining the cost values, actual time spent, and rows processed versus estimated. They must create a visual breakdown showing data flow through each operator (Hash Join, Nested Loop, Index Scan, etc.). During minutes 30-50, teams modify queries by adding/removing indexes, rewriting subqueries as CTEs, and changing join order. For each modification, they regenerate execution plans and compare performance metrics. Students must identify at least three specific bottlenecks (e.g., missing indexes causing sequential scans, inefficient join algorithms, or poor selectivity estimates) and propose concrete solutions. In the final 25 minutes, teams prepare a technical analysis report documenting their findings, including before/after execution plans, quantified performance improvements, and reasoning behind each optimization decision. Each team presents their most significant optimization discovery in a 3-minute explanation to the class.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database server with pgAdmin or command-line access
Pre-loaded sample database with customer, orders, and products tables (100K+ records each)
Three prepared SQL query files of varying complexity
Execution plan analysis worksheet template
Laptops with database client software installed
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification with specific cost/time evidence, (2) Quality of optimization solutions with measurable performance improvements, (3) Depth of execution plan analysis showing understanding of database operations, (4) Clear documentation of methodology and reasoning. Successful completion requires identifying at least 3 bottlenecks with 20%+ performance improvements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide execution plan reading guides highlighting key metrics to examine first (total cost, actual time, rows). Offer simplified queries focusing on single bottleneck types. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity with window functions, materialized views, or parallel query execution analysis. Provide access to database performance monitoring tools like pg_stat_statements for extended analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Results
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer satisfaction dataset, ranking their effectiveness based on clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness. They will identify strengths, weaknesses, and potential misrepresentations in each visualization to determine which best communicates the data insights.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by analyzing clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness for business decision-making
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison using established design principles
instructions: Begin by distributing three printed visualizations of customer satisfaction survey data: a pie chart showing overall satisfaction ratings, a bar chart comparing satisfaction across product categories, and a misleading 3D chart with truncated y-axis. Provide students with the raw dataset (100 customer responses, 5-point satisfaction scale, 4 product categories). Form pairs and give each pair the evaluation worksheet with assessment criteria. Students spend 10 minutes individually examining each visualization, noting observations on their worksheet. Next, pairs discuss their individual observations for 15 minutes, focusing on: data accuracy representation, visual clarity and readability, appropriate chart type selection, potential for misinterpretation, and suitability for presenting to company executives. Each pair then ranks the three visualizations from most to least effective, writing a 2-3 sentence justification for their ranking. During the final 15 minutes, conduct a whole-class discussion where pairs share their rankings and reasoning. Facilitate debate when pairs disagree, encouraging students to defend their evaluations with specific evidence. Record class consensus on the board, highlighting key evaluation criteria that emerged from discussions.
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations (one per student)
Raw customer survey dataset printout
Evaluation worksheet with assessment criteria checklist
Calculators for data verification
assessment_method: Grade based on completed evaluation worksheet (40%), quality of pair justification for ranking (30%), and participation in class discussion with evidence-based reasoning (30%). Success criteria: identifies at least 2 specific strengths/weaknesses per visualization, provides clear ranking rationale, and demonstrates understanding of visualization principles through discussion contributions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guiding questions like 'Can you easily read all labels?' and 'Does this chart type match the data type?' For advanced learners: ask them to sketch an improved version of the least effective visualization or consider how different audiences (executives vs. analysts) might evaluate these differently.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Results: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer satisfaction dataset to determine which best communicates key insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge visualization quality and defend their recommendations with specific evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying clarity, accuracy, and insight communication criteria
Students will justify their visualization preferences through structured comparison using a decision matrix framework
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with printed copies of three visualizations showing identical customer satisfaction survey data: a pie chart showing overall satisfaction ratings, a horizontal bar chart comparing satisfaction by product category, and a scatter plot showing satisfaction vs. purchase frequency. Also distribute the evaluation rubric and decision matrix template.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each visualization independently, rating them on five criteria using a 1-5 scale: clarity of message, visual appeal, data accuracy representation, ease of interpretation, and actionability of insights. They complete the decision matrix by scoring each visualization and adding brief justification notes.

**Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discussing disagreements and refining their reasoning. Partners must reach consensus on which visualization ranks highest and identify at least two specific strengths and one weakness for each chart.

**Written Recommendation (15 minutes):** Each student writes a 200-word recommendation memo to a hypothetical marketing manager, clearly stating which visualization they recommend and why. The memo must reference specific visual elements, cite potential user needs, and acknowledge limitations of their chosen visualization.

**Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates discussion about common evaluation patterns, highlighting how different business contexts might change visualization preferences. Students share one surprising insight from their analysis process.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of customer satisfaction data (one per student)
Evaluation rubric with 5 criteria and 1-5 rating scale
Decision matrix template worksheet
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Completeness of decision matrix with justified ratings, (2) Quality of reasoning in written recommendation with specific evidence cited, (3) Clear identification of strengths/weaknesses for each visualization, (4) Professional tone and structure in memo format. Students must score 3/4 or higher on all criteria to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for the recommendation memo and highlight 2-3 specific visual elements to focus on during evaluation. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-rated visualization and consider how different stakeholder audiences might evaluate the charts differently.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Survey Results

title: Network Protocol Stack Memory Challenge: OSI Layer Component Recall
description: Students memorize and accurately recall the seven OSI model layers, their specific functions, and associated protocols through structured repetition and retrieval practice. This advanced memory exercise focuses on precise technical terminology and protocol-to-layer mappings essential for network engineering.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all seven OSI model layers in correct sequential order by completing timed verbal recitation exercises
Students will identify specific protocols and their corresponding OSI layers through rapid-fire flashcard drilling sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the OSI reference sheets and protocol mapping charts to each student (5 minutes). Have students work in pairs to create physical flashcards: one side shows the layer number and name (e.g., 'Layer 4 - Transport'), the reverse shows three key protocols and two primary functions (15 minutes). Conduct the first memorization phase where students spend 10 minutes silently studying their cards using the spacing method - review each card, set aside correct ones for 2 minutes, incorrect ones for 30 seconds. Next, implement partner drilling: Student A holds cards and quizzes Student B for 5 minutes, then switch roles (10 minutes total). Execute the recall assessment phase: students must write all seven layers from memory in 2 minutes, then list three protocols per layer in 5 minutes - no references allowed. Follow with the rapid identification round where you display 20 protocol names on slides (2 seconds each) and students write the corresponding layer number. Conclude with peer verification where partners check each other's work against the answer key and record accuracy scores. Students scoring below 85% repeat the drilling cycle once more before final submission.
materials_needed: OSI model reference sheets (one per student)
Protocol-to-layer mapping charts
Blank index cards (14 per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Pre-prepared protocol identification slides
Answer keys for peer verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on layer sequencing (7/7 correct), 80% accuracy on protocol identification (16/20 correct), and demonstrate fluent recall speed (complete layer listing in under 2 minutes). Use provided scoring rubric: Layer Recall (35 points), Protocol Mapping (40 points), Speed Component (25 points). Document individual scores and identify students needing remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices ('All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for layers 7-1), allow color-coded cards by layer category, and extend drilling time by 50%. For advanced learners: add sub-layer distinctions (LLC/MAC for Data Link), include less common protocols (SCTP, MPLS), and require them to explain protocol interactions between adjacent layers.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Production Environment
description: Students will critically assess the real-world performance of deployed machine learning models by analyzing production metrics, identifying model drift, and making evidence-based recommendations for model improvement or replacement. They will evaluate multiple models across different business contexts and defend their recommendations through comprehensive analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate machine learning model performance by analyzing production metrics, confusion matrices, and business impact data across multiple deployment scenarios
Students will critique model reliability and fairness through systematic assessment of bias, drift detection, and stakeholder impact analysis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with three distinct production ML model scenarios: a credit scoring model, a recommendation system, and a predictive maintenance model. Each scenario includes 6 months of production data, original training metrics, current performance dashboards, and business context documentation.

Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams conduct individual model assessments. For each model, students must: (1) Calculate performance degradation using provided metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC), (2) Identify statistical evidence of concept drift using population stability index and characteristic stability index calculations, (3) Analyze fairness metrics across demographic groups using equalized odds and demographic parity measures, (4) Quantify business impact using provided ROI data and error cost matrices.

Phase 2 (45 minutes): Teams create comparative evaluation matrices ranking the three models across dimensions: technical performance, business value, fairness, and operational stability. Students must weight each dimension based on stakeholder priorities and document their reasoning.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Each team presents their critical evaluation to the class, defending their ranking methodology and providing specific, actionable recommendations for each model (retrain, replace, or maintain). Teams must address potential counterarguments and justify resource allocation priorities.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Peer evaluation session where teams critique each other's evaluation frameworks and challenge assumptions. Instructor facilitates discussion on evaluation trade-offs and industry best practices.
materials_needed: Three production ML model datasets with 6-month performance histories (CSV format)
Business context documentation packets for each model scenario
Python/R environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
Model evaluation template spreadsheet with pre-built metric calculations
Stakeholder priority weighting worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis Quality (30 points) - accuracy of drift detection, bias calculations, and performance metric interpretation; Evaluation Framework Rigor (25 points) - logical weighting system, comprehensive criteria consideration, and methodology transparency; Recommendation Quality (25 points) - actionability, evidence-based reasoning, and business alignment; Presentation and Defense (20 points) - clarity of argument, response to challenges, and peer critique quality. Students must achieve 80+ points and successfully defend at least two recommendations against peer challenges.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates for complex metrics like PSI and CSI, offer guided worksheets for bias detection, and assign peer mentors for technical support. For advanced learners: Introduce additional evaluation dimensions like model interpretability and computational efficiency, require cost-benefit analysis with uncertainty quantification, and challenge them to develop novel fairness metrics relevant to specific use cases.

title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Real-World Resource Allocation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve a complex resource allocation problem involving multiple variables and constraints. They will develop their own objective function, identify realistic constraints, and implement a solution method while justifying their mathematical choices throughout the process.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original multi-variable optimization model by formulating objective functions and constraint systems for a self-selected real-world scenario

Students will synthesize multiple mathematical techniques including linear programming, calculus-based optimization, and statistical analysis through developing and validating their complete solution methodology
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Problem Identification and Model Framework**
Students work individually to select a real-world optimization scenario (e.g., supply chain logistics, portfolio investment, environmental resource management, or healthcare staffing). They must identify at least 4 decision variables and 6 constraints. Students document their problem statement, define all variables with units, and create a preliminary mathematical framework on provided template sheets.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Mathematical Model Construction**
Using graphing calculators and optimization software, students formulate their complete mathematical model. They must: (1) Write the objective function with justified coefficients based on research or reasonable assumptions, (2) Express all constraints as mathematical inequalities or equations, (3) Define the feasible region, and (4) Select and justify their solution method (simplex method, Lagrange multipliers, or gradient descent). Students document each step with mathematical notation and written explanations.

**Phase 3 (75 minutes): Implementation and Validation**
Students implement their solution using Excel Solver or Python optimization libraries. They must solve their model, interpret results in context, perform sensitivity analysis on at least two parameters, and validate their solution's reasonableness. Students create a comprehensive solution report including: mathematical model, computational results, sensitivity analysis graphs, and practical interpretation of findings.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Peer Review and Revision**
Students exchange models with partners for peer review using provided evaluation criteria. They identify potential improvements in mathematical formulation, constraint completeness, and solution methodology. Students incorporate feedback and finalize their optimization model with documented revisions.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Laptops with Excel and Solver add-in installed
Python environment with SciPy optimization package (optional advanced option)
Mathematical model template worksheets
Access to online databases for parameter research
Peer review evaluation rubric sheets
assessment_method: Comprehensive portfolio assessment using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Mathematical Model Quality (25%) - correctness of objective function and constraints, appropriate variable selection; (2) Solution Implementation (25%) - proper use of optimization techniques, computational accuracy; (3) Analysis and Interpretation (25%) - sensitivity analysis depth, practical relevance of conclusions; (4) Mathematical Communication (25%) - clarity of notation, thoroughness of explanations, professional presentation. Students must achieve proficient (3/4) or higher in all categories for successful completion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected problem scenarios with guided variable identification worksheets, offer simplified 2-variable models initially, and provide step-by-step optimization software tutorials. For advanced learners: Encourage non-linear optimization problems, multi-objective optimization with Pareto analysis, or stochastic optimization incorporating uncertainty. Provide access to advanced optimization software like MATLAB or specialized OR tools for complex implementations.

title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Real-World Resource Allocation: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model addressing a complex real-world resource allocation problem, then develop and implement solution algorithms. They will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and statistics to construct both the mathematical framework and computational solution method.
estimated_duration: 270 minutes (4.5 hours) across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-variable optimization model with realistic constraints by identifying key variables, objective functions, and limitation parameters from a self-selected real-world scenario
Students will design and implement an original solution algorithm through combining analytical calculus methods with computational approaches to solve their constructed optimization problem
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Identification (45 minutes)** Students individually research and select a real-world resource allocation problem from provided domains: urban planning, supply chain management, renewable energy distribution, or healthcare resource allocation. They must identify at least 4 decision variables, 6 constraints, and 1 multi-objective function. Students document their chosen scenario in a 2-page proposal including stakeholders, measurable outcomes, and available data sources. **Phase 2: Mathematical Model Construction (90 minutes)** Working in pairs, students formulate their optimization problem mathematically. They define decision variables using proper notation, construct objective function(s) incorporating multiple competing goals, and establish constraint equations/inequalities. Students must justify each mathematical choice with real-world reasoning and create a comprehensive variable definition table. They sketch the feasible region when possible and identify the mathematical classification of their problem (linear, quadratic, etc.). **Phase 3: Solution Algorithm Design (75 minutes)** Students design a hybrid solution approach combining analytical methods (Lagrange multipliers, KKT conditions) with computational algorithms (gradient descent, simplex method, or genetic algorithms). They must create detailed pseudocode, identify potential convergence issues, and establish stopping criteria. Students implement their algorithm using Python or MATLAB, including error handling and result validation procedures. **Phase 4: Analysis and Presentation (60 minutes)** Students test their model with realistic parameter values, perform sensitivity analysis on key variables, and interpret results within the original real-world context. They prepare a 15-minute presentation demonstrating their model, solution process, and practical recommendations for stakeholders.
materials_needed: Python or MATLAB software access with optimization libraries
Real-world datasets from selected problem domains
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Research access to academic databases
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Students evaluated using detailed rubric (100 points total): Mathematical model accuracy and completeness (25 points), algorithm design creativity and correctness (25 points), implementation functionality and documentation (20 points), real-world applicability and interpretation (20 points), presentation clarity and mathematical communication (10 points). Final deliverable includes written report, working code with comments, and oral presentation with Q&A session.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing problem template frameworks and guided algorithm selection flowcharts. Offer mid-process check-ins with instructor feedback on mathematical formulation before implementation phase. For advanced learners, encourage incorporation of stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization techniques, or machine learning integration. Provide extension challenges involving uncertainty quantification or robust optimization methods.
original_title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Real-World Resource Allocation

title: Optimizing Production Lines Using Linear Programming in Manufacturing Scenarios
description: Students will apply the simplex method to solve complex multi-constraint optimization problems based on real manufacturing scenarios. They will construct mathematical models from business contexts and implement solution algorithms to determine optimal resource allocation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve multi-variable optimization problems with at least 4 constraints by constructing and solving simplex tableaux
Students will implement the simplex algorithm systematically through manual calculations and technology verification to determine optimal production strategies
instructions: Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario handouts featuring three different companies (electronics, furniture, textile) with varying production constraints (15 minutes). Students work in pairs to select one scenario and identify decision variables, objective function, and all constraints. Have them write the standard form linear programming model on provided templates. Next, students construct their initial simplex tableau, ensuring proper slack variable incorporation and coefficient accuracy (25 minutes). Guide them through the first pivot operation together, demonstrating ratio calculations and pivot element selection. Students then continue independently, performing successive pivot operations until reaching optimality, documenting each iteration on separate tableau sheets (40 minutes). Require students to verify their solutions using graphing calculator or Excel Solver, comparing manual results with technology outputs (15 minutes). Have pairs present their optimal solution interpretation, including maximum profit/minimum cost values and resource utilization analysis to another pair for peer verification (20 minutes). Conclude with students completing reflection sheets analyzing the business implications of their solutions, discussing what happens if constraints change by ±20%, and identifying which constraints are binding versus non-binding. Throughout the activity, circulate to check tableau setup, pivot calculations, and solution interpretation accuracy.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario handout packets (3 different companies)
Simplex tableau template sheets (minimum 6 per student pair)
Graphing calculators with linear programming capabilities or computer access to Excel
Solution verification worksheets
Peer evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Correct mathematical model formulation from business context (25 points), (2) Accurate simplex tableau construction and pivot operations with all work shown (35 points), (3) Correct final optimal solution with proper interpretation (25 points), (4) Technology verification matching manual solution within acceptable tolerance (15 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in tableau calculations and provide economically meaningful solution interpretation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint identification guides with sentence stems like 'The limitation on [resource] means that...' and pre-filled tableau headers. Offer checkpoint sheets after each pivot to verify calculations before proceeding. For advanced learners: Include scenarios with degeneracy or unbounded solutions, require sensitivity analysis calculations, or challenge them to solve using dual simplex method for comparison.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing Multi-Node Database Crash Scenarios
description: Students analyze a complex multi-node distributed database system failure by examining system logs, network traces, and performance metrics to identify root causes and cascading failure patterns. They will decompose the failure into component-level issues and evaluate the effectiveness of existing fault tolerance mechanisms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining multi-source diagnostic data to identify primary and secondary failure causes
Students will decompose complex system crashes through systematic evaluation of component interactions, timing dependencies, and network partition scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing the failure scenario packet containing: system architecture diagram of a 5-node MongoDB replica set, 48 hours of aggregated logs from all nodes, network latency measurements, and CPU/memory utilization graphs. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (coordinates investigation), Network Specialist (focuses on communication failures), and Database Specialist (examines data consistency issues). 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the timeline leading to system failure, creating a chronological map of events across all nodes. Students must identify the initial trigger event and trace how it propagated through the system. They should mark critical timestamps where node states diverged and network partitions occurred.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students analyze component interactions by mapping data flow between nodes during the failure window. They must identify which consensus mechanisms failed, how leader election was affected, and where data replication broke down. Teams create dependency graphs showing how individual component failures cascaded through the system.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students evaluate the existing fault tolerance mechanisms (heartbeat protocols, automatic failover, read/write concern settings) by analyzing why they were insufficient. They must identify specific configuration weaknesses and timing issues that allowed the failure to propagate.

Phase 4 (25 minutes): Teams present their analysis using a structured format: root cause identification, failure propagation timeline, component interaction breakdown, and fault tolerance evaluation. Each team has 8 minutes to present findings with 2 minutes for peer questions.
materials_needed: Distributed system failure scenario packet with 5-node MongoDB logs
Network trace files in Wireshark format
System monitoring graphs (CPU, memory, disk I/O) for 48-hour window
MongoDB cluster architecture diagram with configuration details
Digital timeline creation tool (Lucidchart or similar)
Large format paper for dependency mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Root cause identification accuracy (25 points), failure propagation timeline completeness (25 points), component interaction analysis depth (25 points), fault tolerance mechanism evaluation (15 points), and presentation clarity (10 points). Success requires correctly identifying the primary failure trigger, mapping at least 80% of the cascading failures, and proposing specific configuration improvements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided analysis worksheets with specific log entry examples and pre-formatted timeline templates. Offer intermediate checkpoints every 30 minutes with instructor feedback. For advanced learners, include additional network partition scenarios and ask them to propose alternative architectural patterns that would prevent similar failures. Consider providing access to actual MongoDB profiling tools for deeper analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Sales Insights
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which best communicates key business insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge visualization quality and provide justified recommendations for business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying established design principles and clarity criteria
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison of how well each chart type communicates business insights to stakeholders
instructions:
Begin by distributing three visualization examples (bar chart, pie chart, and line graph) showing quarterly sales data by product category for a fictional retail company. Each chart displays identical data but uses different visual approaches. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization and complete an initial reaction worksheet noting what insights they can quickly identify from each chart.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation framework covering five criteria: clarity of message, appropriate chart type for data, visual design quality, ease of interpretation, and business relevance. Provide a scoring rubric (1-4 scale) for each criterion.

Step 3 (20 minutes): In pairs, students systematically evaluate each visualization using the framework, documenting scores and specific evidence for their ratings. They must identify at least two strengths and two weaknesses per visualization.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair creates a recommendation memo (one paragraph) stating which visualization they would present to company executives and why, including specific improvements for the other two charts.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Three pairs present their evaluations to the class, defending their choice with evidence from their scoring rubric. Other students can challenge their reasoning through structured questioning.

Conclude with instructor-led discussion connecting evaluation decisions to real-world data science scenarios where visualization choice impacts business outcomes.
materials_needed: Three printed visualization examples of quarterly sales data (one per student)
Evaluation framework handout with 5-criteria scoring rubric
Initial reaction worksheet template
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed rubric scorecards (40%), quality of written recommendation memo with specific justifications (40%), and participation in peer questioning during presentations (20%). Success requires systematic application of all five criteria with specific evidence supporting scores.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation comments and pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add a fourth visualization type or ask them to redesign the weakest chart with specific improvement suggestions and create their own evaluation criteria.

title: Design and Present a Mathematical Model for a Community Problem
description: Students will identify a real problem in their local community and create an original mathematical model using functions, equations, or statistical analysis to propose solutions. They will present their model and justify their mathematical reasoning to classmates acting as community stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical model by selecting appropriate functions, equations, or statistical methods to represent a real-world community problem
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts through creating visual representations, calculations, and evidence-based recommendations for their chosen problem
instructions: **Phase 1 - Problem Selection (20 minutes):** Provide students with a list of 8-10 community issues (traffic flow, water usage, population growth, budget allocation, energy consumption, recycling rates, etc.). Students work in pairs to select one problem and complete a 'Problem Analysis Worksheet' identifying key variables, constraints, and available data sources. **Phase 2 - Model Development (40 minutes):** Students research their chosen problem using provided data sets or collect simple data through surveys/observation. They must create a mathematical model using at least two of: linear/quadratic functions, systems of equations, statistical regression, or optimization techniques. Students document their work on a 'Model Building Template' showing variable definitions, equations/functions, sample calculations, and assumptions. **Phase 3 - Solution Creation (25 minutes):** Using their mathematical model, students generate three specific, quantified recommendations for addressing their community problem. They create visual representations (graphs, charts, diagrams) and prepare a cost-benefit analysis or impact prediction using their model. **Phase 4 - Stakeholder Presentation (30 minutes):** Each pair presents their 5-minute pitch to the class, with remaining students role-playing as city council members, community leaders, or affected citizens. Presenters must explain their mathematical reasoning, defend their model choices, and respond to questions about feasibility and accuracy.
materials_needed: Community problem scenario cards (8-10 different issues)
Problem Analysis Worksheet template
Model Building Template with guided sections
Access to graphing calculators or Desmos online calculator
Chart paper and colored markers for visual displays
Sample data sets for each community problem
Stakeholder role cards for audience members
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy and appropriate model selection (25%), (2) Clear variable identification and realistic assumptions (20%), (3) Quality and clarity of visual representations (20%), (4) Logical connection between model results and recommendations (20%), (5) Effective communication during presentation and response to questions (15%). Students must demonstrate mathematical work, provide written justification for model choices, and deliver a coherent presentation to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected data sets, offer template equations with blanks to fill in, and allow use of simplified linear models only. Create partnership groups mixing ability levels. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate multiple mathematical concepts (statistics AND functions), require sensitivity analysis showing how changing variables affects outcomes, or have them create digital interactive models using spreadsheet tools.

title: Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Challenge
description: Students memorize and recall specific time and space complexity classifications for 40 fundamental algorithms across sorting, searching, graph traversal, and dynamic programming categories. This intensive memorization activity builds foundational knowledge essential for technical interviews and advanced algorithm analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity (best, average, worst case) for 40 standard algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify space complexity classifications for fundamental algorithms through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the standardized algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 40 algorithms organized into four categories: sorting (10), searching (10), graph algorithms (10), and dynamic programming (10). Each entry includes algorithm name, best/average/worst case time complexity, and space complexity. Give students 15 minutes to study the sheet silently, encouraging them to use mnemonic devices and pattern recognition. Next, implement spaced repetition using digital flashcards. Students work individually through three 10-minute rounds: Round 1 focuses on sorting and searching algorithms, Round 2 covers graph algorithms, and Round 3 addresses dynamic programming. Each flashcard shows the algorithm name; students must verbally state all complexity values before revealing answers. After each round, provide 3-minute review periods where students can re-examine missed items. Conclude with a comprehensive 15-minute assessment where students complete a fill-in-the-blank worksheet listing all 40 algorithms with empty complexity fields. No reference materials allowed during assessment. Students must achieve 85% accuracy (34/40 correct) across all complexity categories to demonstrate mastery. Provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers on screen, allowing students to identify specific gaps in their memorization.
materials_needed: Standardized algorithm complexity reference sheet (40 algorithms)
Digital flashcard platform (Anki or Quizlet with pre-loaded deck)
Printed assessment worksheet with 40 algorithm entries
Timer/stopwatch for each study phase
Answer key projection capability
assessment_method: Students complete a 40-item fill-in-the-blank assessment requiring exact Big O notation for time complexity (best, average, worst) and space complexity. Success criteria: 85% accuracy minimum (34/40 correct responses). Partial credit given only for complete time complexity triplets (all three cases correct). Space complexity must match exactly. Immediate scoring using answer key overlay.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded reference sheet grouping algorithms by complexity patterns (O(n log n) sorting algorithms in blue, O(1) space algorithms in green). Allow additional 5-minute study period focusing on most commonly missed algorithms from practice rounds. For advanced learners: Include 10 additional algorithms from specialized domains (string matching, computational geometry) and require explanation of why certain algorithms have specific complexity characteristics.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Model Performance Scenarios
description: Students analyze four different machine learning model performance scenarios to understand how bias-variance decomposition explains prediction errors. They will interpret diagnostic plots and model behavior patterns to categorize problems and recommend appropriate solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance trade-off patterns by analyzing learning curves, validation curves, and residual plots across multiple model scenarios
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity, training data size, and prediction error components through systematic diagnostic analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with four pre-prepared model scenario packets, each containing: learning curves (training vs validation error), validation curves (model complexity vs error), residual plots, and model performance metrics. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one primary scenario to analyze deeply (15 minutes). Each scenario represents a distinct bias-variance problem: Scenario A (high bias, low variance - underfitting), Scenario B (low bias, high variance - overfitting), Scenario C (high bias, high variance - poor model choice), and Scenario D (low bias, low variance - well-tuned model). Students examine their assigned scenario's diagnostic plots, identifying key patterns: gap between training and validation curves, curve shapes and convergence behavior, residual distribution patterns, and performance metric trends. They must document three specific observations about bias-variance characteristics and propose two concrete remediation strategies. Groups then rotate through remaining scenarios (10 minutes each), comparing patterns and noting differences in diagnostic signatures. During rotation, students complete a structured comparison matrix, categorizing each scenario's bias-variance profile and ranking remediation strategies by effectiveness. Conclude with groups presenting their primary scenario analysis (5 minutes per group), explaining how specific plot features indicate bias vs variance problems. Facilitate class discussion connecting theoretical bias-variance concepts to observed diagnostic patterns, emphasizing how practitioners use these tools for model improvement decisions.
materials_needed: Four scenario packets with learning curves, validation curves, and residual plots
Bias-variance diagnostic checklist handout
Scenario comparison matrix worksheet
Colored pens/highlighters for plot annotation
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of bias-variance patterns from diagnostic plots (25%), (2) Correct explanation of relationship between plot features and underlying model behavior (30%), (3) Appropriate remediation strategy selection with justification (25%), (4) Quality of comparative analysis across scenarios showing understanding of diagnostic signatures (20%). Students submit completed comparison matrices and scenario analysis summaries.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide bias-variance reference cards with common plot patterns and corresponding interpretations. Offer guided questions: 'What does the gap between curves tell you?' and 'How does curve shape relate to model flexibility?' For advanced learners, include scenarios with noise levels, ensemble methods, or regularization effects. Challenge them to predict how specific hyperparameter changes would alter the diagnostic plots.

title: Budget Planning for a School Pizza Party
description: Students will apply their knowledge of multiplication, addition, and money calculations to create a realistic budget for a class pizza party. They will work with real-world constraints including student count, dietary restrictions, and spending limits to make mathematical decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication and addition operations to calculate total costs for food items by working with realistic quantities and prices
Students will apply mathematical reasoning to make budget decisions through comparing options and staying within spending limits
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Budget Worksheet' and informing students they have a $150 budget for a class of 24 students, with 3 vegetarian students. Display the price menu on the board: large pizzas $12 each (feeds 4 people), drinks $8 per 12-pack (12 servings), paper plates $3 per pack (20 plates), napkins $2 per pack (100 napkins). Students work in pairs for 25 minutes to complete calculations. Step 1: Calculate how many pizzas needed (24 ÷ 4 = 6 pizzas minimum). Step 2: Determine pizza types (students must calculate costs for different combinations ensuring vegetarian options). Step 3: Calculate drink needs (24 ÷ 12 = 2 packs minimum, round up). Step 4: Determine supply needs for plates and napkins. Step 5: Add all costs and compare to $150 budget. Step 6: If over budget, students must adjust quantities and recalculate. Circulate during work time to check calculations and guide problem-solving. In the final 10 minutes, have 3-4 pairs share their budget plans with the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning. Record different solutions on the board to show multiple valid approaches. Conclude by discussing how mathematics helps in real-world decision making.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Budget Worksheet (one per pair)
Calculators (optional, encourage mental math first)
Whiteboard/projector to display price menu
Sample budget template drawn on board
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct, budget within limit, work clearly shown; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget close to limit, most work shown; (2) Some calculation errors, budget somewhat over/under, some work shown; (1) Multiple errors, unrealistic budget, minimal work shown. Also observe pair discussions for mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed worksheet with the first calculation done as an example, offer calculators, and suggest breaking down multi-step problems into smaller parts. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including tax calculations (8% sales tax), require them to create two different budget scenarios, or challenge them to find the maximum number of students they could serve with the same budget.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Scenarios
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of different SQL queries against a simulated e-commerce database by examining execution plans, identifying inefficiencies, and categorizing performance bottlenecks. They will decompose complex queries to understand how different components affect overall performance and make evidence-based recommendations for optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by identifying table scans, join types, and index usage patterns to determine performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between various query optimization strategies through systematic comparison of execution times and resource utilization metrics
instructions:
Begin by providing each student team (2-3 students) with access to a pre-populated MySQL database containing 50,000 product records, 100,000 customer records, and 500,000 order records representing an e-commerce system. Distribute the 'Query Analysis Worksheet' containing 8 different SQL queries of varying complexity (simple SELECT, JOINs, subqueries, and aggregate functions). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams execute each query using MySQL Workbench and record execution times using the built-in profiler. Students must run each query 3 times and calculate average execution time.

Step 2 (20 minutes): For each query, students generate and examine the execution plan using EXPLAIN command. They document the scan types (full table scan, index scan, etc.), number of rows examined, and join algorithms used.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students categorize each query's performance issues using provided classification framework: Index-related (missing/unused indexes), Join-related (inefficient join order/type), or Logic-related (unnecessary subqueries/redundant conditions). They must provide specific evidence from execution plans.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams create a prioritized list ranking queries from most to least problematic, justifying rankings using quantitative data (execution time, rows examined) and qualitative analysis (scalability concerns).

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each team presents their top 2 most problematic queries to the class, explaining their analysis methodology and findings. Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing different team approaches and introducing advanced optimization concepts.
materials_needed: Pre-configured MySQL database with sample e-commerce data (products, customers, orders tables)
MySQL Workbench installed on student computers
Query Analysis Worksheet with 8 test queries of varying complexity
Performance Classification Framework handout
Stopwatch or timing tool for manual verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25 points) - correctly identifies scan types, join methods, and index usage, (2) Quality of bottleneck categorization (25 points) - appropriately classifies issues with supporting evidence, (3) Logical reasoning in query ranking (25 points) - uses both quantitative and qualitative factors in prioritization, (4) Presentation clarity (25 points) - effectively communicates findings with specific examples. Students submit completed worksheets and present findings for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan reading guide with visual examples of common patterns, allow use of simpler 3-query subset initially, pair with stronger students for peer support. For advanced learners: Include additional queries with window functions and CTEs, challenge them to propose specific optimization solutions (index creation, query rewriting), have them analyze queries on larger dataset with 1M+ records to observe scalability patterns.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Scenarios: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans and performance metrics from a simulated e-commerce database to identify inefficiencies and bottlenecks. They will examine multiple query variations, compare execution times, and determine which indexing strategies and query structures produce optimal performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining query costs, join operations, and table scans to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate the relationship between database design choices and query performance through systematic comparison of execution metrics
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-populated MySQL database containing three tables: customers (50,000 records), orders (200,000 records), and products (5,000 records). Distribute the 'E-commerce Query Analysis Worksheet' containing six different SQL queries of varying complexity. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes. First 15 minutes: Students execute each query using EXPLAIN ANALYZE command and record execution times in provided data table. Next 30 minutes: For each query, students examine the execution plan output, identifying table scans, join types, and estimated vs. actual row counts. They categorize each query as 'efficient' or 'inefficient' based on execution time thresholds provided (>500ms = inefficient). Following 30 minutes: Students analyze three specific problem queries by testing alternative versions with different WHERE clause orders, JOIN syntax, and subquery approaches. They document performance differences in milliseconds and explain why certain approaches perform better. Final 15 minutes: Each pair creates a ranked list of the six queries from most to least efficient, providing specific evidence from execution plans. They must identify at least two concrete optimization strategies (such as 'add index on customer_id' or 'replace correlated subquery with JOIN') for the three slowest queries. Instructor circulates to verify students are correctly interpreting execution plan symbols and timing measurements.
materials_needed: MySQL database with pre-populated e-commerce tables (customers, orders, products)
E-commerce Query Analysis Worksheet with 6 SQL queries and data recording tables
Database management tool (MySQL Workbench or phpMyAdmin)
Computers with MySQL access for each pair
assessment_method: Grade completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: Query categorization accuracy (25% - correct identification of efficient/inefficient queries), execution plan interpretation (35% - accurate identification of scans, joins, row counts), optimization recommendations (25% - specific, actionable suggestions with technical justification), performance comparison analysis (15% - correct ranking with supporting evidence from timing data).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan symbol reference sheet and highlight key metrics to focus on (actual rows, execution time, scan types). Offer pre-written alternative query versions for comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to write their own optimized versions of the inefficient queries, test with different dataset sizes, or analyze the impact of various index combinations on query performance.
original_title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Scenarios

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Multiple Deployment Scenarios
description: Students will critically assess the real-world viability of three different machine learning models by evaluating their performance across multiple business contexts, ethical considerations, and technical constraints. They will synthesize findings to make evidence-based recommendations for model selection and deployment strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, bias indicators, and business impact across different deployment scenarios
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive assessment of technical limitations, ethical implications, and stakeholder requirements
instructions: **Phase 1: Setup (30 minutes)** - Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with identical datasets containing results from three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Neural Network, Gradient Boosting) tested on a customer churn prediction problem. Include performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), fairness metrics across demographic groups, computational requirements, and interpretability scores. **Phase 2: Multi-Criteria Evaluation (90 minutes)** - Teams analyze each model across four evaluation dimensions: (1) Technical Performance - compare statistical metrics and identify trade-offs, (2) Business Impact - calculate potential revenue impact using provided cost-benefit matrices, (3) Ethical Assessment - evaluate bias metrics and fairness across protected attributes, (4) Operational Feasibility - assess deployment complexity, inference time, and maintenance requirements. Students must document evidence supporting their analysis using provided evaluation templates. **Phase 3: Scenario Testing (60 minutes)** - Each team receives three different deployment scenarios: high-volume real-time predictions, batch processing with explainability requirements, and resource-constrained edge deployment. Teams re-evaluate their model rankings for each scenario, justifying how context changes their recommendations. **Phase 4: Synthesis and Recommendation (45 minutes)** - Teams prepare executive summaries presenting their model recommendation with supporting evidence, addressing limitations and risks, and proposing monitoring strategies post-deployment.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared dataset with model performance results (CSV format)
Model evaluation templates (Excel/Google Sheets)
Business impact calculation worksheets
Fairness metrics reference guide
Three deployment scenario briefing documents
Access to Python/R with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
assessment_method: Teams submit written executive summaries (2-3 pages) evaluated on: (1) Depth of technical analysis - thorough comparison of performance metrics and statistical significance testing (25%), (2) Quality of ethical evaluation - comprehensive bias assessment with proposed mitigation strategies (25%), (3) Business context integration - realistic cost-benefit analysis and stakeholder consideration (25%), (4) Evidence-based reasoning - clear justification for recommendations with acknowledgment of limitations (25%). Rubric includes ratings from 1-4 for each criterion with specific descriptors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide decision matrix templates with weighted criteria and step-by-step calculation guides. Offer mini-lectures on interpreting confusion matrices and ROC curves. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as model ensemble evaluation, A/B testing design considerations, or regulatory compliance requirements (GDPR, fair lending). Encourage exploration of advanced fairness metrics like equalized odds or demographic parity.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Resource Allocation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization algorithm to solve a complex real-world resource allocation problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will develop their own computational model, implement it using programming tools, and validate their solution through mathematical proof and practical testing.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize knowledge of linear programming, calculus of variations, and constraint optimization to construct an original algorithm for multi-variable resource allocation problems
Students will create a comprehensive mathematical model that integrates theoretical foundations with computational implementation and real-world validation testing
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a complex scenario: a renewable energy company must optimize the placement of 50 solar panels, 30 wind turbines, and 20 battery storage units across 5 geographic regions, considering variables including weather patterns, energy demand fluctuations, installation costs, maintenance accessibility, and environmental impact scores. Students work in teams of 3-4 over three phases. Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the problem constraints, identify all variables and their relationships, then design their unique optimization approach by choosing and justifying their mathematical framework (linear programming, genetic algorithms, gradient descent, etc.). They must create original objective functions and constraint equations, documenting their mathematical reasoning. Phase 2 (120 minutes): Students implement their algorithm using Python, MATLAB, or R, creating code that accepts variable inputs and outputs optimal resource allocation. They must include error handling, convergence testing, and solution validation methods. Teams also develop a mathematical proof demonstrating their algorithm's theoretical soundness under specified conditions. Phase 3 (60 minutes): Students test their algorithms using provided datasets, compare results against established optimization methods, and prepare a technical presentation defending their approach. They must demonstrate how their solution handles edge cases and explain computational complexity. Throughout all phases, students document their decision-making process, mathematical derivations, and algorithm modifications. Final deliverable includes working code, mathematical proof, test results comparison, and a technical report explaining their creative approach and its advantages over existing methods.
materials_needed: Computers with Python/MATLAB/R programming environment
Multi-variable dataset with energy demand, weather, and cost parameters
Whiteboard or digital collaboration space for mathematical notation
Access to optimization libraries (SciPy, MATLAB Optimization Toolbox, or similar)
Scientific calculators for verification calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Algorithm originality and mathematical soundness (25 points), successful implementation with proper error handling (25 points), mathematical proof of convergence/optimality (20 points), validation testing and comparison analysis (15 points), technical presentation clarity and defense of design choices (15 points). Students must demonstrate their algorithm produces feasible solutions, converges within reasonable iterations, and shows measurable improvement over baseline methods.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide template code structure, offer simplified constraint sets, and allow collaboration with advanced peers during implementation phase. Provide reference materials on optimization theory and example proofs. For advanced learners: introduce additional complexity such as dynamic constraints, multi-objective optimization, or uncertainty modeling. Challenge them to prove algorithm optimality bounds or develop hybrid approaches combining multiple optimization techniques.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Resource Allocation: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization algorithm to solve a complex resource allocation problem involving at least 4 variables and 6 constraints. They will develop the mathematical framework, implement the algorithm computationally, and validate their solution through sensitivity analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and optimization theory concepts by designing an original multi-variable optimization algorithm for a real-world scenario
Students will construct and validate a complete mathematical solution through computational implementation and comprehensive sensitivity analysis
instructions: Step 1 (30 min): Present students with three complex scenarios: hospital staffing optimization with budget/skill/time constraints, renewable energy grid allocation with weather/demand/storage variables, or supply chain distribution with cost/capacity/sustainability factors. Students select one scenario and define their specific problem parameters, identifying minimum 4 decision variables and 6 constraint equations. Step 2 (45 min): Students formulate their optimization problem mathematically, establishing the objective function using appropriate techniques (Lagrange multipliers, linear programming, or nonlinear optimization). They must justify their mathematical approach and document all assumptions. Step 3 (60 min): Using Python, MATLAB, or similar software, students implement their algorithm from scratch (no pre-built optimization libraries). They must code the mathematical logic, constraint handling, and convergence criteria. Step 4 (45 min): Students test their algorithm with at least three different parameter sets, documenting convergence behavior and solution quality. They perform sensitivity analysis by systematically varying constraint bounds and objective function coefficients. Step 5 (30 min): Students create a comprehensive technical report including problem formulation, mathematical derivation, algorithm pseudocode, computational results, sensitivity analysis graphs, and recommendations for implementation. Step 6 (30 min): Present solutions in 8-minute technical presentations, defending mathematical choices and demonstrating algorithm performance to peers acting as stakeholder review committee.
materials_needed: Computers with Python/MATLAB/Mathematica installed
Access to numerical computing libraries (NumPy, SciPy for Python)
Graphing capabilities for sensitivity analysis visualization
Technical report template with required sections
Real-world scenario datasets with authentic constraints
assessment_method: Evaluation based on 4-point rubric: Mathematical Rigor (25% - correct formulation, appropriate optimization method, valid constraints), Algorithm Innovation (25% - original implementation, efficient convergence, proper constraint handling), Technical Validation (25% - comprehensive testing, meaningful sensitivity analysis, result interpretation), Professional Communication (25% - clear technical writing, effective presentation, stakeholder-appropriate recommendations). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm flowchart templates, offer choice of simpler 3-variable problems, allow use of optimization toolboxes with requirement to explain underlying mathematics. For advanced learners: Challenge with stochastic constraints, multi-objective optimization, or comparison of multiple algorithmic approaches. Provide just-in-time coding support through peer programming partnerships.
original_title: Design and Implement a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Resource Allocation

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Resource Allocation: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization algorithm to solve a complex resource allocation problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then validate their solution against industry benchmarks.
estimated_duration: 255 minutes (4.25 hours) - can be split across multiple sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and optimization theory to construct an original multi-variable optimization algorithm for constrained resource allocation problems
Students will evaluate and refine their mathematical model through iterative testing and comparison with established optimization methods like simplex or genetic algorithms
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Definition (30 minutes)** Present students with a complex scenario: A renewable energy company must optimize placement of 50 wind turbines across a 100km² area, considering wind patterns, environmental restrictions, transmission costs, and local regulations. Students work in teams of 3-4 to define decision variables, objective functions, and constraints mathematically. **Phase 2: Algorithm Development (90 minutes)** Each team creates their original optimization approach, choosing from methods like gradient descent variations, evolutionary algorithms, or hybrid approaches. They must derive mathematical foundations, including convergence proofs and complexity analysis. Students document their algorithm using formal mathematical notation and create pseudocode. **Phase 3: Implementation (60 minutes)** Teams code their algorithm using Python/MATLAB, incorporating provided wind data and constraint parameters. They must handle numerical stability, convergence criteria, and computational efficiency. **Phase 4: Validation and Refinement (45 minutes)** Students test their algorithm against three benchmark solutions and real industry data. They analyze performance metrics (solution quality, computation time, convergence rate) and iterate on their design. **Phase 5: Presentation (30 minutes)** Teams present their algorithm's mathematical foundation, implementation decisions, and comparative performance analysis to simulate a technical review meeting.
materials_needed: Python/MATLAB software with optimization libraries (scipy, cvxpy)
Dataset: Wind speed measurements across 100km² grid (provided CSV files)
Environmental constraint maps (GIS shapefiles)
Benchmark optimization solutions for comparison
High-performance computing access or cloud computing credits
Technical presentation templates with mathematical notation support
assessment_method: Rubric evaluating: (1) Mathematical rigor of algorithm derivation (25 points) - correctness of objective function, constraint formulation, and theoretical analysis; (2) Implementation quality (20 points) - code functionality, efficiency, and numerical stability; (3) Innovation and creativity (20 points) - originality of approach and problem-solving techniques; (4) Performance analysis (20 points) - thorough comparison with benchmarks and interpretation of results; (5) Technical communication (15 points) - clarity of mathematical presentation and professional documentation. Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm templates with key components outlined, offer intermediate checkpoints with instructor feedback, and pair with stronger mathematical peers. Supply additional resources on numerical optimization methods. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements (uncertain wind patterns), multi-objective optimization (cost vs. environmental impact), or dynamic constraints. Encourage exploration of cutting-edge techniques like reinforcement learning or quantum-inspired algorithms.
original_title: Design and Implement a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Resource Allocation

title: Binary Number System Identification and Recall Quiz
description: Students will memorize and identify the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 to 1111 (0-15 in decimal). Through flashcard practice and timed recall exercises, students will build foundational knowledge of binary-to-decimal conversion patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) from memory within 3 seconds per number
Students will identify correct binary-to-decimal conversions through visual recognition of number patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing binary numbers 0000-1111 on one side and decimal equivalents 0-15 on the reverse. Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, with one student showing binary numbers while their partner recalls decimal equivalents aloud. Partners switch roles after 7-8 minutes. Next, display the binary-decimal conversion chart on the projector for 5 minutes, instructing students to study silently while covering/uncovering sections with paper. Conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session where you display each binary number on screen for 10 seconds maximum - students write decimal answers on individual whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Record which numbers cause hesitation. Follow with a second round focusing only on problematic numbers. Conclude with a 10-question written quiz where students have 30 seconds per question to write decimal equivalents of displayed binary numbers. Emphasize that this is pure memorization - no calculation methods should be used during recall phases. Remind students that 1000 always equals 8, 1100 always equals 12, etc. Encourage students to notice patterns like how 1111 is always 15, and 1010 is always 10.
materials_needed: 16 flashcards per student pair (binary 0000-1111 with decimal equivalents)
Individual student whiteboards and dry-erase markers
Printed binary-decimal reference chart (one per student)
Digital projector or smartboard
10-question quiz sheets
