Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students pass by correctly recalling 14 out of 16 binary-to-decimal conversions (87.5%) within the 3-second time limit during the final quiz. Award full points for immediate recall (0-3 seconds), partial credit for delayed recall (4-6 seconds), and no points for calculations or incorrect answers. Track individual progress using a checklist of all 16 binary numbers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with binary numbers 0000-0111 (0-7) only, then gradually add 1000-1111. Create visual memory aids using dot patterns or finger counting. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or include hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to recall in reverse (decimal-to-binary) or identify patterns in binary counting sequences.

title: Interpreting Correlation Patterns in Real-World Marketing Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a provided marketing campaign dataset to identify and explain correlation patterns between customer demographics, spending behaviors, and campaign response rates. Through guided exploration using correlation matrices and visualization tools, students will distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while explaining the practical business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3) and explaining what each relationship means in business context
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through analysis of customer behavior patterns and guided reflection questions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the provided marketing dataset (marketing_campaign.csv) containing 2,240 customer records with variables including age, income, education, marital status, number of children, spending on different product categories, and campaign response rates. Students work in pairs using Jupyter notebooks or Google Colab. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students load the dataset and examine the first 10 rows, identifying which variables are numerical and suitable for correlation analysis. They document 5 variables they predict will be highly correlated.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Guide students to create a correlation matrix using pandas .corr() function and visualize it using seaborn heatmap with annotations. Students must adjust the figure size to 12x10 and use the 'coolwarm' colormap for clarity.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations from their matrix, recording the exact coefficient values. For each correlation, they write a 2-sentence business interpretation explaining what the relationship means for marketing strategy.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Present students with the scenario: 'Income and wine purchases show a correlation of 0.79. A manager concludes that giving customers more income will increase wine sales.' Students must explain why this reasoning is flawed and provide two alternative explanations for this correlation.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Students create scatter plots for their two most interesting correlations using matplotlib, adding trend lines and appropriate titles. They conclude by writing a 3-sentence summary of insights a marketing team could use from their analysis.
materials_needed: Marketing campaign dataset (marketing_campaign.csv) with 2,240 customer records
Jupyter Notebook or Google Colab access for each student pair
Python libraries: pandas, seaborn, matplotlib, numpy
Correlation interpretation reference sheet with coefficient ranges
Digital worksheet template for recording findings and interpretations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification and categorization of correlation strengths (25 points), (2) Accurate business interpretations of at least 4 correlations (25 points), (3) Clear explanation of correlation vs. causation with valid alternative explanations (25 points), (4) Properly formatted visualizations with appropriate titles and insights summary (25 points). Students submit completed Jupyter notebook and filled worksheet template.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation strength reference card (0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7+ strong) and sentence starters for business interpretations ('This correlation suggests that customers who... tend to...'). For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential confounding variables, calculate partial correlations, or explore non-linear relationships using additional statistical measures. Provide business case studies where correlation insights led to successful marketing strategies.

title: Analyzing Network Security Vulnerabilities in Distributed System Architecture
description: Students will examine a multi-tier distributed system architecture diagram and network traffic logs to identify security vulnerabilities, analyze attack vectors, and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented security measures. This expert-level activity requires students to break down complex system interactions and assess security implications across multiple layers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by identifying potential security vulnerabilities at each tier (presentation, application, data) and evaluating the impact of each weakness on overall system security
Students will examine network traffic patterns and system logs through forensic analysis techniques to determine attack vectors and assess the effectiveness of current security countermeasures
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a detailed network architecture diagram showing a three-tier web application (load balancer, web servers, application servers, database cluster) and corresponding network traffic logs from a 48-hour period. Students have 45 minutes to individually examine the materials and identify potential vulnerabilities using the STRIDE threat modeling framework (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege). Next, teams spend 60 minutes collaboratively mapping identified vulnerabilities to specific components, analyzing interdependencies between system layers, and evaluating how each vulnerability could be exploited in combination with others. Teams must create a vulnerability matrix categorizing threats by severity, likelihood, and affected components. During the final 30 minutes, each team presents their analysis to the class, defending their risk assessments and proposing mitigation strategies. Instructors should circulate during team work, asking probing questions about threat vectors and challenging students to consider edge cases and less obvious attack scenarios. Provide additional network segments or traffic samples to teams that finish early to extend their analysis scope.
materials_needed: Detailed network architecture diagrams (one per team) showing specific IP ranges, ports, and service configurations
Sanitized network traffic logs in PCAP format from real or simulated environments
STRIDE threat modeling reference sheets
Wireshark or similar network analysis software
Vulnerability assessment templates/matrices
Presentation computers with projection capability
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Vulnerability identification accuracy (25 points), threat modeling framework application (20 points), interdependency analysis quality (20 points), risk assessment justification (20 points), and presentation clarity/defense of findings (15 points). Students must identify at least 8 distinct vulnerabilities across different system tiers, correctly apply STRIDE categories, and provide evidence-based risk ratings with clear technical justification.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions about specific protocol behaviors and offering simplified attack scenario examples. Create reference cards with common vulnerability patterns for each system tier. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as containerized microservices, API gateways, or cloud-native security considerations. Provide access to CVE databases and encourage students to research recent exploits relevant to identified vulnerabilities.

title: Evaluating Data Quality and Visualization Effectiveness in Student Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess the quality of a messy student lifestyle survey dataset and evaluate the effectiveness of three different data visualizations created from the cleaned data. They will make judgments about data reliability and recommend the most appropriate visualization for decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data quality issues by identifying specific problems in a real survey dataset and rating their impact on analysis reliability
Students will critique multiple data visualizations through systematic comparison using established design principles and effectiveness criteria
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'Student Lifestyle Survey' dataset containing 200 responses with intentionally planted issues (missing values, duplicate entries, inconsistent formatting, outliers). Give students 15 minutes to examine the dataset using Excel or Google Sheets, creating a data quality checklist where they identify and categorize problems as 'Critical,' 'Moderate,' or 'Minor' based on potential impact on analysis. Next, present three pre-created visualizations of the cleaned data: a cluttered bar chart with too many categories, a clear pie chart showing study hours distribution, and a misleading line graph suggesting causation. Form groups of 3-4 students and assign 20 minutes for groups to evaluate each visualization using the provided 'Visualization Effectiveness Rubric' covering clarity, accuracy, relevance, and design principles. Each group must complete evaluation matrices scoring each visualization 1-5 on specified criteria. In the final 15 minutes, groups present their 2-minute recommendations identifying which visualization best supports the research question 'How do study habits relate to student wellness?' They must justify their choice using specific evidence from their evaluations and explain why rejected options were inadequate. Conclude with groups submitting written evaluation summaries and recommendations.
materials_needed: Student Lifestyle Survey dataset (CSV file with 200 responses)
Data Quality Assessment Checklist template
Three pre-created visualizations (bar chart, pie chart, line graph)
Visualization Effectiveness Rubric handout
Evaluation matrix worksheets
Computers with Excel or Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Data Quality Assessment - accuracy in identifying issues and appropriate severity ratings (25%), (2) Visualization Critique - thorough application of evaluation criteria with specific examples (35%), (3) Recommendation Justification - logical reasoning connecting evaluation evidence to final choice (25%), (4) Presentation Quality - clear communication and use of data science terminology (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in categories 1-3 to demonstrate proficiency in evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of data quality assessment for the first 10 rows, offer sentence starters for evaluation criteria ('This visualization is effective/ineffective because...'). For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose specific improvements for rejected visualizations, or have them create their own visualization and defend why it's superior to the provided options.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Scale Model Urban Plan with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design and construct a scaled urban city layout using geometric principles, area calculations, and algebraic budgeting. They must balance mathematical constraints with creative city planning to produce a feasible municipal design.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original city layout by applying scale factor calculations, area formulas, and coordinate geometry to design functional urban spaces
Students will construct a mathematical budget model through algebraic equations and inequalities to justify their city planning decisions within financial constraints
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with a 24"x18" poster board representing 12 square miles of land (scale: 1 inch = 0.5 miles). Teams receive a $500 million budget breakdown sheet with costs per square mile: residential zones ($15M), commercial zones ($25M), parks ($5M), industrial zones ($20M), roads ($10M per mile), and public buildings ($30M each). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams sketch their initial city design on graph paper, calculating the area of each zone using geometric formulas. They must include at least 4 zone types and demonstrate understanding that total area cannot exceed 12 square miles.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students create algebraic equations representing their budget: 15R + 25C + 5P + 20I + 10L + 30B ≤ 500, where variables represent square miles of each zone type. They must solve for feasible combinations and adjust their design accordingly.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams transfer their final design to the poster board using coordinate geometry to precisely place buildings and zones. They draw to scale using rulers and protractors, ensuring accurate measurements.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students create a mathematical justification report showing all area calculations, budget equations, and scale factor work. They must prove their design is both geometrically accurate and financially viable.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Teams present their cities, explaining one geometric calculation and one algebraic budget decision to the class.
materials_needed: 24"x18" poster boards (one per team)
Graph paper sheets
Rulers and protractors
Colored pencils or markers
Budget constraint worksheets with cost breakdowns
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct area calculations, scale conversions, and algebraic budget equations; (2) Design Feasibility - city layout meets all constraints and requirements; (3) Creative Problem-Solving - innovative solutions to balance budget and space limitations; (4) Mathematical Communication - clear justification report with proper mathematical notation and reasoning. Each category worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made templates with partial calculations completed and zone suggestion cards. Offer frequent check-ins during Steps 1-2. For advanced learners: Add additional constraints like population density requirements, environmental impact factors, or traffic flow optimization using more complex mathematical models.

title: Interpreting Statistical Power and Effect Size Trade-offs in A/B Testing Scenarios
description: Students will analyze complex A/B testing scenarios to understand the mathematical relationships between statistical power, effect size, sample size, and significance level. They will interpret how changes in these parameters affect business decision-making in real-world contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the interdependent relationships between statistical power, effect size, sample size, and alpha level by analyzing pre-calculated A/B test scenarios
Students will interpret the business implications of statistical power trade-offs through structured case study analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the Statistical Power Analysis Worksheet containing 8 A/B testing scenarios from different industries (e-commerce, healthcare, fintech). Each scenario presents identical base parameters: α=0.05, β=0.20, baseline conversion rate=15%. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes. First 30 minutes: Students analyze Scenarios 1-4 where sample sizes vary (1000, 5000, 10000, 50000 users per variant) while effect sizes remain constant (2% absolute lift). They calculate statistical power using provided lookup tables and interpret how sample size changes affect detectability. Next 30 minutes: Students examine Scenarios 5-8 where effect sizes vary (0.5%, 1%, 3%, 5% absolute lift) while sample sizes remain constant at 10000 per variant. They determine minimum detectable effects and explain practical significance versus statistical significance. Final 30 minutes: Each pair completes interpretation matrices showing how power curves shift under different business constraints (budget limitations, time constraints, competitive pressure). Students must explain three key trade-offs: cost vs. sensitivity, speed vs. accuracy, and business risk vs. statistical rigor. Conclude with 5-minute pair presentations of one scenario analysis to the class.
materials_needed: Statistical Power Analysis Worksheet with 8 pre-calculated A/B testing scenarios
Statistical power lookup tables (printed reference sheets)
Power curve interpretation matrices (blank templates)
Calculators or laptops with basic calculation software
assessment_method: Grade completed interpretation matrices using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly explains all parameter relationships with accurate business context, (3) Explains most relationships with minor gaps in business application, (2) Shows basic understanding but struggles with complex trade-offs, (1) Demonstrates minimal comprehension of statistical concepts. Success requires scoring 3+ on at least 6 of 8 scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide worked example of Scenario 1 with step-by-step power calculation and business interpretation. Offer additional lookup tables with highlighted relevant sections. For advanced learners: Include bonus scenarios with unequal sample sizes, multiple testing corrections, and sequential testing considerations. Challenge them to propose alternative experimental designs.

title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to solve realistic shopping scenarios involving discounts, sales tax, and tips. They will work through three different shopping situations where they must calculate final costs and determine if purchases fit within given budgets.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, sales tax, and tips by solving authentic shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate budget management skills through calculating total costs and comparing them to spending limits
instructions: Begin by distributing the Shopping Scenario Worksheets and calculators to each student (5 minutes). Explain that they will work individually for 15 minutes, then share solutions in pairs. Present the three scenarios: (1) Buying a $85 jacket with a 20% discount plus 8.5% sales tax within a $75 budget, (2) Restaurant bill of $42.30 with 18% tip needed within a $52 budget, and (3) Online purchase of $120 headphones with 15% discount, $8 shipping, and 6% sales tax within a $110 budget. Students must show all calculation steps: original price × discount percentage = discount amount, original price - discount = sale price, sale price × tax rate = tax amount, sale price + tax = final cost. For each scenario, they determine if the purchase fits the budget and by how much they're over or under. During individual work time, circulate to check calculation methods and provide hints without giving answers. After 15 minutes, have students pair up to compare their solutions and resolve any discrepancies (8 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where volunteers share one scenario's solution on the board, explaining their step-by-step process (7 minutes). Emphasize the real-world importance of calculating total costs before making purchases.
materials_needed: Shopping Scenario Worksheets (3 scenarios per student)
Basic calculators (1 per student)
Whiteboard and markers for demonstrations
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct final answers with clear calculation steps shown, 3 points for correct process with minor computational errors, 2 points for correct process but significant calculation mistakes, 1 point for attempted work with major conceptual errors. Students must correctly identify whether each purchase fits within budget to demonstrate full mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a calculation template showing the order of operations (discount first, then tax, then compare to budget) and allow use of the percentage-decimal conversion chart. For advanced learners, add a fourth scenario involving compound discounts (20% off, then additional 10% off the sale price) or have them create their own shopping scenario with multiple items and mixed discounts.

title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to determine discounts, sales tax, and tips while planning purchases within a given budget. They will use real store advertisements and calculate actual costs to make informed buying decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentage discounts, sales tax, and tips by solving multi-step real-world shopping scenarios
Students will apply percentage formulas through hands-on budget planning activities using authentic store data
instructions: Begin by distributing store advertisements, calculators, and budget worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Assign each student a specific scenario: planning a birthday party with $150, buying school supplies with $75, or purchasing ingredients for a family dinner with $100. Students must select items from the provided advertisements totaling close to their budget limit. Next, have students calculate the discount price for each sale item using the percentage formula: Original Price × (1 - Discount Rate) = Sale Price (15 minutes). For example, a $40 backpack with 25% off becomes $40 × 0.75 = $30. Then students add 8.5% sales tax to their subtotal using: Subtotal × 1.085 = Total with Tax (10 minutes). If their scenario includes a restaurant meal or service, they must calculate an 18% tip on the pre-tax amount (5 minutes). Students record all calculations showing their work step-by-step on the worksheet. Finally, students compare their final total to their budget and adjust purchases if they exceed the limit (10 minutes). They must document which items they removed or substituted and recalculate. Students present one calculation example to the class, explaining their process and reasoning for item selection (10 minutes). Conclude by having students reflect on how percentage calculations affect real purchasing power.
materials_needed: Current store advertisements or flyers (grocery, electronics, clothing)
Budget scenario worksheets with specific spending limits
Basic calculators
Local sales tax rate reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown, budget maintained; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget mostly maintained; (2) Some calculation errors, basic process understood; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Check for proper use of percentage formulas and logical purchase decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide percentage calculation reference cards with step-by-step formulas and allow use of percentage calculators initially. Offer pre-calculated examples for the first item. For advanced learners, add compound discounts (sale price + additional coupon), comparison shopping between stores, or calculating annual interest on credit card purchases.
original_title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases

title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases: Business Application
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to plan a realistic shopping trip within a given budget. They will calculate discounts, sales tax, and tips while making purchasing decisions for a specific scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, sales tax, and final costs by working through authentic shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate budget management skills through systematic calculation of multiple percentage-based adjustments to item prices
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario cards and calculator worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Present the challenge: 'You have $150 to buy items for a back-to-school shopping trip. You must purchase at least one item from each category: clothing, school supplies, and food/snacks.' Display the store price list on the board, showing original prices, discount percentages (10%-40% off various items), and note that 8.5% sales tax applies to all purchases except food. 

Have students work individually for 20 minutes to select items and calculate costs. They must: 1) Choose items from each required category, 2) Calculate the discounted price for each item (original price × discount percentage), 3) Subtract discounts from original prices, 4) Calculate 8.5% sales tax on non-food items, 5) Add tax to get final prices, 6) Sum all final prices to ensure they stay within the $150 budget. 

Provide the calculation worksheet with clearly labeled sections for each step. Students must show all work, including the percentage calculations (e.g., $25.00 × 0.20 = $5.00 discount; $25.00 - $5.00 = $20.00 sale price). 

After individual work, pair students for 10 minutes to compare their shopping lists and verify each other's calculations. Finally, conduct a 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 students share their final shopping lists, total costs, and explain one challenging calculation they completed. Address any common calculation errors observed during the activity.
materials_needed: Pre-made store price list with 15-20 items showing original prices and discount percentages
Scenario cards with the shopping challenge and budget limit
Calculation worksheets with organized sections for discounts, tax, and totals
Basic calculators (one per student)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, stays within budget, includes all required categories; (3) Minor calculation errors, meets budget and category requirements; (2) Some calculation errors or missing categories, budget awareness evident; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Observe student explanations during pair work and class discussion for understanding of percentage calculation process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation reference card showing percentage formulas and one worked example. Consider pairing them with stronger math students during verification time. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including a 15% tip calculation for a restaurant meal option, or challenge them to find the combination that maximizes their purchases while staying closest to the $150 limit without going over.
original_title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Purchases

title: Design a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Urban Transportation Network
description: Students will construct an original mathematical model to optimize traffic flow in a city intersection network using multi-variable calculus, linear programming, and graph theory. They will create both the theoretical framework and implement a computational solution to minimize travel time while maximizing throughput.
estimated_duration: 4 hours (can be split across 2 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory to design an original optimization model for real-world traffic flow problems
Students will construct a complete mathematical framework including objective functions, constraint systems, and algorithmic solutions through iterative model development and testing
instructions:
Begin by providing students with real traffic data from a 4-intersection urban grid (15 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Lead Modeler, Computational Analyst, Constraint Specialist, and Validation Engineer. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze the traffic data to identify key variables (vehicle flow rates, signal timing, pedestrian crossings, emergency vehicle priority). Students must define their optimization objective - whether minimizing average wait time, maximizing total throughput, or balancing both. Each team creates their unique objective function using multi-variable calculus.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams develop constraint systems incorporating: traffic light timing constraints (30-120 second cycles), maximum vehicle capacity per lane, pedestrian crossing requirements, and emergency vehicle preemption protocols. Students must justify each constraint mathematically and explain real-world implications.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Using Python with SciPy optimization libraries, teams implement their model computationally. They must code their objective function, constraint matrix, and run optimization algorithms (linear programming or gradient descent). Students test multiple scenarios: rush hour, accident conditions, and special events.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams validate their models by comparing outputs to actual traffic flow data, calculating percentage improvements in their chosen metrics. They must identify model limitations and propose refinements.

Final Phase (45 minutes): Each team presents their complete model including mathematical derivation, computational implementation, validation results, and real-world applicability. Other teams provide peer feedback using structured evaluation forms focusing on mathematical rigor, computational accuracy, and practical feasibility.
materials_needed: Real traffic flow dataset from local transportation department (4-intersection grid with hourly data)
Computers with Python, SciPy, NumPy, and Matplotlib installed
Graph paper and calculators for initial model sketching
Access to online linear programming visualization tools (optional)
Presentation software for final model showcase
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Design (25 points - originality, correctness of objective function and constraints), Computational Implementation (25 points - code functionality, algorithm selection, debugging), Validation and Analysis (25 points - comparison with real data, limitation identification, improvement suggestions), Presentation and Communication (25 points - clarity of mathematical explanation, professional delivery, peer interaction). Success requires scoring 80+ points with no category below 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template objective functions and constraint examples from simpler 2-intersection problems; offer guided worksheets for setting up optimization matrices; pair with stronger computational partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements (random arrival patterns), add multiple intersection types (roundabouts, highway on-ramps), or extend to city-wide network optimization; encourage exploration of machine learning integration for dynamic traffic prediction.

title: Python Data Types Memory Challenge: Flashcard Creation and Recall
description: Students will create digital flashcards for the six fundamental Python data types and their characteristics, then participate in a structured recall exercise to memorize key properties and syntax examples. This activity builds foundational knowledge essential for Python programming through active repetition and peer interaction.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) by creating accurate flashcards with definitions and examples
Students will recall specific syntax and characteristics of each Python data type through structured peer-testing activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the Python data type reference sheet to each student (5 minutes). Have students work individually to create 12 digital flashcards using Quizlet or index cards: one card per data type with the type name on front, and one card per data type with a code example on front. The back should contain the definition, key characteristics, and sample code snippet. Give students 15 minutes for card creation, circulating to ensure accuracy. Next, arrange students in pairs for the recall phase (2 minutes setup). Partner A tests Partner B using the definition cards for 5 minutes, then they switch roles for another 5 minutes. Follow with the code example round: Partner A shows code examples, Partner B must identify the data type (5 minutes), then switch (5 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class rapid-fire review where you display code snippets on the projector and students raise hands to identify data types. Record participation and accuracy on your checklist. End by having students review any missed items with their flashcards for final reinforcement (3 minutes).
materials_needed: Python Data Types Reference Sheet (printed, one per student)
Computer/tablet access for Quizlet.com or physical index cards
Projector for displaying code snippets
Teacher checklist for tracking student responses
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify 5 out of 6 data types during peer testing and 4 out of 6 code examples during the final rapid-fire round. Assess flashcard quality using a 3-point rubric: complete and accurate definition (1 point), proper code example with correct syntax (1 point), clear formatting and legibility (1 point). Observe peer interactions for active participation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed flashcard template with fill-in-the-blank sections and pair them with stronger partners during testing. For advanced learners, challenge them to include more complex examples (nested lists, formatted strings) and have them assist peers who finish early. Consider allowing audio recordings on digital flashcards for auditory learners.

title: Optimization in Business: Designing a Packaging System Using Calculus
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve a real-world business optimization problem involving packaging design. They will determine dimensions that minimize material costs while meeting specific volume constraints for a product distribution company.
learning_objectives: Students will apply first and second derivative tests to find optimal dimensions for cylindrical packaging by analyzing cost functions and volume constraints
Students will implement Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical modeling of business scenarios
instructions: Begin by presenting students with this scenario: 'EcoShip Company needs cylindrical containers with exactly 1000 cubic inches of volume. Material costs $0.15 per square inch for the sides and $0.25 per square inch for the top and bottom.' Form teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). Each team receives the problem packet containing detailed specifications and cost breakdowns. Students first establish variables (r = radius, h = height) and write the volume constraint equation V = πr²h = 1000 (15 minutes). Next, they derive the cost function C(r,h) = 2πr²(0.25) + 2πrh(0.15), representing bottom/top and side costs respectively (20 minutes). Using the constraint, students eliminate h to create C(r) = 0.5πr² + 300/r (15 minutes). Teams then find dC/dr and set equal to zero: πr - 300/r² = 0, solving for r = ∛(300/π) ≈ 4.37 inches (20 minutes). Students verify this is a minimum using the second derivative test: d²C/dr² = π + 600/r³ > 0 (10 minutes). They calculate the corresponding height h = 1000/(πr²) ≈ 16.7 inches and minimum cost C ≈ $98.47 (15 minutes). Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical work, including graphs of the cost function, and justify why this solution minimizes expenses while meeting volume requirements (20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Problem scenario packets with company specifications and cost data
Graphing calculators or Desmos access for function visualization
Grid paper for sketching cost function graphs
Presentation materials (whiteboards, markers, or digital presentation tools)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct mathematical setup including constraint and objective function formulation, (2) Accurate application of differentiation techniques and critical point identification, (3) Proper verification using second derivative test or alternative methods, (4) Clear communication of solution with business context interpretation. Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and deliver a coherent team presentation explaining their optimization process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint equations and guide them through the substitution process step-by-step. Offer derivative reference sheets and encourage use of graphing tools to visualize the optimization. For advanced learners: Extend to rectangular boxes with square bases, introduce multiple constraints (weight limits, shipping dimensions), or have them compare costs across different geometric shapes to determine the globally optimal container design.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Theme Park with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design an original theme park layout using coordinate geometry, scale factors, and area calculations while working within a specified budget. They will create both a mathematical blueprint and a physical 3D model, then present their design with justifications for all mathematical decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original theme park layout by applying coordinate geometry, scale factors, and area optimization within given constraints
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical model through integration of geometry, proportional reasoning, and algebraic problem-solving
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with identical constraint packets: $2 million budget, 500m × 300m rectangular lot, and attraction cost sheet (roller coaster $800K, water ride $600K, food court $200K, etc.). Students spend 15 minutes reviewing constraints and brainstorming initial ideas. Next, students create their coordinate system on graph paper, establishing scale (suggested 1 cm = 10m) and plotting the park boundary. Over 45 minutes, teams design their layout by calculating area requirements for each attraction, determining optimal placement using coordinate geometry, and continuously checking budget constraints through area-based cost calculations. Students must include minimum 5 attractions, 2 food areas, parking for 1000 cars (3m × 6m per space), and pathways connecting all areas. During the 30-minute construction phase, teams build 3D models using provided materials, maintaining their established scale and accurately representing their mathematical blueprint. Each structure must match calculated dimensions when measured. Finally, teams prepare 8-minute presentations explaining their coordinate system, scale factor applications, area calculations, budget breakdown, and design rationale. During presentations, other teams complete peer evaluation forms assessing mathematical accuracy and design creativity. Conclude with 15 minutes of whole-class reflection on problem-solving strategies and real-world applications of coordinate geometry.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm grid, 2 sheets per student)
Cardboard pieces, foam blocks, craft sticks for 3D construction
Rulers, protractors, calculators
Attraction cost reference sheets with area requirements
Colored pencils or markers for blueprints
Digital presentation tools or poster paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of scale, coordinates, and area calculations, (2) Creative design that meets all constraints, (3) Clear justification of mathematical decisions in presentation, (4) Physical model accuracy compared to blueprint measurements. Students must achieve proficient (3/4) in mathematical accuracy and demonstrate integration of at least 3 mathematical concepts to meet success criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn coordinate grids, offer attraction placement templates, and allow partnership with stronger math students for calculations. For advanced learners: Add constraints like environmental impact calculations, profit optimization using linear programming concepts, or incorporation of geometric transformations for ride designs. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling teams during construction phase.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Theme Park with Budget Constraints: Exercise 1
description: Students will create an original theme park layout using geometric principles, coordinate systems, and linear programming to maximize attractions within a fixed budget. They will design blueprints, calculate areas and perimeters, and present their mathematical reasoning for design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original theme park layout by applying coordinate geometry, area calculations, and scale factor conversions
Students will construct mathematical models through budget optimization using linear inequalities and constraint analysis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with a 'Theme Park Challenge Packet' containing: budget of $2.5 million, price list for 12 different attractions (ranging from $50,000 carnival games to $400,000 roller coasters), and a coordinate grid representing a 500m × 300m plot of land. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the constraint requirements - minimum 8 attractions, at least one major ride, maximum 60% of land can be used for attractions, remaining space for pathways/amenities. Students create a constraint inequality system.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using graph paper with 1cm = 10m scale, teams sketch their park layout on coordinate grids. They must plot each attraction as geometric shapes with accurate dimensions (provided in packet), calculate total area used, and verify scale calculations.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams solve their linear programming problem to maximize either total attractions or visitor capacity while staying within budget and space constraints. They must show algebraic work for optimization.

Step 4 (35 minutes): Groups create a final blueprint with: coordinate locations of each attraction, area calculations with work shown, budget breakdown with running totals, and mathematical justification for layout choices (traffic flow using slope calculations between attractions).

Step 5 (20 minutes): Each team presents their park design for 3-4 minutes, explaining their mathematical reasoning and constraint solutions. Other teams evaluate designs using provided peer assessment rubric.

Teachers circulate during work time, checking mathematical accuracy and pushing teams to justify decisions quantitatively rather than aesthetically.
materials_needed: Theme Park Challenge Packets (attraction prices, dimensions, constraints)
Graph paper (1cm grid, minimum 30cm × 20cm sheets)
Rulers and protractors
Calculators
Colored pencils or markers
Poster paper for final blueprints
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (constraint equations, area calculations, scale conversions - 25%), Design Creativity and Feasibility (layout logic, attraction variety - 25%), Problem-Solving Process (shown work, optimization strategy - 30%), and Presentation Quality (clear explanation of mathematical reasoning - 20%). Students must achieve level 3+ in Mathematical Accuracy to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made constraint templates and area calculation worksheets, pair with stronger math students, offer simplified attraction list with round numbers. For advanced learners: Add profit maximization component using visitor capacity data, include trigonometry for curved pathway calculations, or incorporate 3D volume calculations for multi-level attractions.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Speed Drill
description: Students will rapidly identify and classify the time and space complexity of 30 advanced algorithms and data structure operations using Big O notation. This high-intensity recall activity tests memorization of complexity formulas for sophisticated algorithms including graph traversals, dynamic programming solutions, and advanced sorting methods.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity of 25+ advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, and various tree operations by completing timed classification exercises
Students will identify space complexity requirements for advanced data structures and recursive algorithms through rapid-fire recognition drills
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared complexity cards face-down to each student (30 cards total). Set up a digital timer visible to all students and prepare the answer key spreadsheet on the projector. Students work individually for the first 15 minutes.

Round 1 (15 minutes): Students flip cards one at a time, writing the algorithm name, time complexity, and space complexity on their answer sheet. Cards include: Bellman-Ford algorithm, A* search, red-black tree insertion, heap sort, quick select, merge sort for linked lists, binary heap operations, AVL tree rotations, breadth-first search on adjacency matrix, depth-first search recursive implementation, Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching, Rabin-Karp algorithm, and others. Students must complete all 30 within the time limit.

Round 2 (10 minutes): Display the answer key and have students self-grade using the provided rubric. Each correct time complexity = 2 points, each correct space complexity = 1 point (90 points total). Students mark incorrect answers in red.

Round 3 (10 minutes): Redistribute cards randomly for a second attempt, focusing on previously missed items. Students attempt only the algorithms they got wrong in Round 1.

Closing (5 minutes): Collect answer sheets and have students verbally share which complexity classifications they found most challenging. Record common misconceptions on the whiteboard for future review sessions.
materials_needed: 30 laminated algorithm cards with algorithm names and brief descriptions
Pre-printed answer sheets with numbered lines for responses
Digital timer or stopwatch
Answer key spreadsheet for projection
Red pens for self-grading
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (72/90 points) to demonstrate mastery. Grade breakdown: Time complexity identification (60 points maximum), Space complexity identification (30 points maximum). Track individual student performance on specific algorithm categories (graph algorithms, sorting, tree operations, string algorithms) to identify knowledge gaps requiring remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with common complexity patterns (O(n), O(log n), O(n²)) and allow extra time during Round 3. Advanced learners can be challenged with additional cards featuring amortized analysis problems or asked to explain why certain algorithms have their specific complexities. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger ones for the verbal sharing portion.

title: Hands-on Algorithm Complexity Testing
description: Students will rapidly identify and classify the time and space complexity of 40 advanced algorithmic code snippets across multiple programming paradigms. This high-intensity recall activity reinforces memorization of complexity patterns in nested loops, recursive functions, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and advanced data structures.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the Big O time complexity of advanced algorithmic patterns including nested iterations, recursive calls, and divide-and-conquer approaches by analyzing code snippets under time pressure

Students will identify space complexity classifications for algorithms involving recursive call stacks, dynamic programming tables, and auxiliary data structures through rapid pattern recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the complexity reference sheet and giving students 2 minutes to review. Project the first code snippet on screen for exactly 45 seconds while students individually write their answers on the response sheet, marking both time and space complexity using Big O notation. After 45 seconds, immediately advance to the next snippet without discussion. Continue this pattern through all 40 snippets, maintaining strict timing. Include snippets featuring: quicksort partitioning, binary tree traversals, matrix multiplication algorithms, hash table operations with chaining, fibonacci with memoization, merge sort implementations, graph traversal algorithms, and nested loop patterns with varying dependencies. At the 15-snippet mark, provide a 2-minute stretch break. After completing all 40 snippets, display the answer key on screen. Students self-score their responses, marking correct answers in green and incorrect in red. Have students tally their correct responses and write their score at the top of their sheet. Collect response sheets for grade recording. Conclude by having students identify which algorithm categories they missed most frequently by reviewing their incorrect responses and categorizing them into algorithm types (recursive, iterative, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, graph-based). This reflection helps identify specific complexity patterns requiring additional memorization work.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared slideshow with 40 advanced code snippets
Printed complexity reference sheet (one per student)
Response sheets with numbered blanks for time/space complexity answers
Timer or stopwatch for precise 45-second intervals
Answer key slideshow for immediate feedback
Green and red pens for self-scoring
assessment_method: Students receive 1 point for each correctly identified time complexity and 1 point for each correctly identified space complexity (80 points total). Success criteria: 70+ points demonstrates strong recall of advanced complexity patterns. Track common error patterns across the class to identify algorithmic concepts requiring remediation. Grade based on accuracy of Big O notation usage and correct complexity classification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional reference materials highlighting visual patterns in code that indicate specific complexities (e.g., nested loops = quadratic, recursive calls = potential exponential). For advanced learners: Include amortized analysis examples and ask them to identify best/average/worst case scenarios for algorithms with variable performance. Consider providing bonus snippets involving advanced topics like segment trees or suffix arrays.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Business Contexts
description: Students will critically assess and compare the effectiveness of three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) applied to a customer churn prediction problem, evaluating not only technical metrics but also business impact, ethical implications, and implementation feasibility. They will defend their model recommendation through a comprehensive evaluation framework.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML models by analyzing technical performance metrics, business constraints, and ethical considerations within a real-world customer churn scenario

Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic application of a multi-criteria evaluation framework that weighs accuracy, interpretability, computational cost, and business impact
instructions:
**Phase 1: Dataset and Model Setup (30 minutes)**
Provide students with a pre-processed customer churn dataset (10,000 records, 20 features) and three pre-trained models with their predictions and probability scores. Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives identical model outputs but different business context scenarios (B2B SaaS, retail subscription, telecommunications).

**Phase 2: Technical Performance Analysis (45 minutes)**
Students calculate and compare: precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices for each model. They must identify which metrics are most critical for their assigned business context and justify their reasoning. Teams create visualizations showing model performance differences and analyze prediction confidence distributions.

**Phase 3: Multi-Criteria Evaluation Framework (60 minutes)**
Teams apply a structured evaluation matrix assessing: (1) Predictive accuracy, (2) Model interpretability, (3) Computational requirements, (4) Implementation complexity, (5) Ethical considerations (fairness across demographic groups), (6) Business impact potential. Students assign weights to each criterion based on their business context and score each model on a 1-10 scale with detailed justifications.

**Phase 4: Critical Analysis and Recommendation (45 minutes)**
Teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their model recommendation. They must address potential counterarguments, discuss limitations of their chosen model, and propose monitoring strategies. Include specific implementation timeline and success metrics.

**Phase 5: Peer Evaluation and Discussion (30 minutes)**
Teams present to peers representing different business contexts. Audience members challenge recommendations using their own business constraints, fostering critical discussion about context-dependent model selection.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV format with 10,000 records, 20 features)
Pre-trained model outputs (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network predictions with probability scores)
Business context scenario descriptions (3 different industries)
Multi-criteria evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
assessment_method: Rubric-based assessment (100 points total): Technical accuracy of performance calculations (25 points), depth of multi-criteria analysis with justified weightings (25 points), quality of model recommendation defense addressing limitations and counterarguments (25 points), effectiveness of peer critique and response to challenges (15 points), clarity of presentation and visualizations (10 points). Success requires demonstrating critical thinking beyond surface-level metrics comparison.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates for performance metrics and guided questions for each evaluation criterion. Offer example business impact scenarios and sample justifications. For advanced learners: Introduce additional complexity such as cost-sensitive learning, model ensemble evaluation, or A/B testing design considerations. Challenge them to propose custom evaluation metrics specific to their business context.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Business Contexts: Business Application
description: Students will critically assess three pre-trained machine learning models designed for customer churn prediction by evaluating their performance metrics, business applicability, and ethical implications across different industry contexts. They will justify their recommendation for model selection based on comprehensive evaluation criteria beyond accuracy alone.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple ML models by analyzing performance metrics, bias indicators, and business constraints within specific industry contexts
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of trade-offs between technical performance, interpretability, fairness, and business requirements
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Context Analysis and Criteria Development**

Provide students with three industry scenarios: healthcare insurance, telecommunications, and e-commerce subscription service. Each scenario includes specific business constraints (regulatory requirements, cost of false positives/negatives, interpretability needs). Students work in teams of 3-4 to develop weighted evaluation criteria for each context, considering accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, model interpretability, computational cost, bias metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds), and regulatory compliance.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Model Performance Analysis**

Distribute performance reports for three models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression, each trained on the same customer dataset but with different hyperparameters. Reports include confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance rankings, prediction confidence distributions, training time, inference speed, and bias audit results across demographic groups. Teams analyze each model's strengths and weaknesses using statistical significance tests and effect size calculations.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Critical Evaluation and Recommendation**

Teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their model choice for each business context. They must address potential counterarguments, acknowledge limitations, and justify why their selected model optimizes the weighted criteria. Include discussion of monitoring strategies and model lifecycle considerations.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Peer Review and Synthesis**

Teams present findings while others complete structured peer evaluation forms. Conclude with class discussion on how evaluation criteria should adapt to different stakeholder priorities and regulatory environments.
materials_needed: Three detailed business scenario documents with specific constraints and requirements
Model performance reports with comprehensive metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, bias metrics)
Statistical analysis software access (Python/R with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib)
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Presentation software and projection capability
assessment_method: Teams submit a 3-page written recommendation report (40 points) with quantitative justification, trade-off analysis, and limitation acknowledgment. Presentation delivery and defense of recommendations (30 points). Peer evaluation participation and quality of feedback (20 points). Individual reflection essay on lessons learned about evaluation complexity (10 points). Rubric emphasizes depth of analysis, consideration of multiple stakeholder perspectives, statistical rigor, and acknowledgment of uncertainty.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation criteria templates and guided questions for metric interpretation. Offer mini-tutorials on statistical significance testing. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as cost-sensitive learning evaluation, ensemble method comparison, or A/B testing design considerations. Encourage exploration of emerging fairness metrics and their mathematical foundations.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Business Contexts

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Business Contexts: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance and business viability of three different machine learning models applied to a customer churn prediction scenario. They will assess model metrics, interpret trade-offs, and make justified recommendations for model deployment considering real-world constraints and stakeholder needs.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple ML models by analyzing performance metrics, business impact, and implementation feasibility within a realistic business context
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of accuracy, interpretability, computational cost, and ethical considerations
instructions: Begin by providing students with a realistic customer churn dataset from a telecommunications company and three pre-trained models: Random Forest (85% accuracy, high interpretability), XGBoost (89% accuracy, medium interpretability), and Neural Network (91% accuracy, low interpretability). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, with each team receiving identical model outputs, confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance rankings, and computational cost data. In the first 45 minutes, teams analyze each model's performance using provided metrics, calculate business-relevant measures (cost of false positives vs. false negatives based on customer lifetime value data), and evaluate model interpretability requirements for regulatory compliance. During the next 60 minutes, teams complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing models across six dimensions: predictive accuracy, precision/recall trade-offs, computational efficiency, interpretability for business stakeholders, implementation complexity, and potential bias concerns. Teams must identify the most critical business constraints from provided stakeholder personas (C-suite executive, compliance officer, ML engineer, customer service manager) and weight their evaluation criteria accordingly. In the final 45 minutes, each team presents their model recommendation to the class, defending their choice with quantitative evidence and addressing potential counterarguments. Other teams act as stakeholders, challenging recommendations with specific questions about model limitations, deployment risks, and long-term maintenance considerations. Conclude with teams submitting a one-page executive summary justifying their final recommendation.

assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Depth of quantitative analysis (25%) - thorough use of multiple metrics and business calculations, (2) Quality of critical reasoning (30%) - identification of key trade-offs and limitations, (3) Justification strength (25%) - evidence-based arguments connecting analysis to recommendation, (4) Stakeholder consideration (20%) - demonstration of understanding different business perspectives and constraints. scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each evaluation dimension and a sample partial analysis of one model.
