title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Transit Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban transit challenges by integrating graph theory, linear programming, and statistical analysis. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation to minimize travel time while maximizing coverage for a given city's population distribution.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory, linear programming, and statistical modeling concepts by designing a comprehensive transit optimization algorithm that addresses real urban planning constraints
Students will construct and validate an original mathematical model through computational implementation and present defendable solutions to authentic transportation engineering problems
instructions:
**Phase 1 (Days 1-2): Problem Definition and Research (4 hours)**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Assign each team a different mid-sized city (50,000-500,000 population) with publicly available demographic and geographic data. Teams must define their specific optimization problem: minimize average commute time, maximize population coverage within walking distance, or minimize infrastructure costs. They research existing transit systems, population density maps, and identify 15-20 key locations (employment centers, hospitals, universities) that must be connected.

**Phase 2 (Days 3-5): Mathematical Model Development (6 hours)**
Teams construct their optimization model using three integrated components: (1) Graph theory representation where nodes represent transit stops and edges represent routes with weighted costs (time, distance, construction cost), (2) Linear programming constraints including budget limitations, maximum route lengths, minimum service frequency, and population coverage requirements, (3) Statistical analysis incorporating population density heat maps and travel pattern predictions. Students must write formal mathematical notation for their objective function and constraint system.

**Phase 3 (Days 6-7): Computational Implementation (4 hours)**
Using Python with NetworkX, SciPy, and optimization libraries, teams code their model. They input real geographic coordinates, population data, and run optimization algorithms. Students must handle computational challenges like local optima and constraint infeasibility. They generate visual network maps, performance metrics, and sensitivity analyses showing how solutions change with different parameter values.

**Phase 4 (Day 8): Validation and Presentation (2 hours)**
Teams prepare 15-minute presentations including model assumptions, mathematical framework, computational results, and real-world feasibility analysis. They must defend design choices and demonstrate how their solution addresses the original optimization criteria.
materials_needed: Python programming environment with NetworkX, SciPy, Matplotlib, and PuLP libraries installed
Access to census data and geographic information systems (GIS) databases
Laptops or computers with internet connectivity
Large format paper or digital presentation tools for network visualization
Real urban demographic datasets from assigned cities
assessment_method: Rubric evaluation (100 points total): Mathematical model sophistication and correctness (25 points), computational implementation functionality and efficiency (25 points), real-world applicability and constraint handling (20 points), presentation clarity and defense of design decisions (20 points), innovation and creative problem-solving approach (10 points). Final deliverables include documented Python code, mathematical model specification, visual network solution, and written analysis comparing their solution to existing transit systems.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structures, pre-selected datasets, and simplified constraint examples. Offer daily check-ins to review mathematical notation and computational debugging. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate dynamic programming for temporal optimization, multi-objective optimization techniques, or machine learning predictions for ridership patterns. Encourage exploration of stochastic models accounting for uncertainty in travel demand.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Customer Purchase Behavior Datasets
description: Students will analyze pre-processed e-commerce customer data to identify and explain patterns in purchasing behavior through statistical distribution analysis. They will interpret histograms, box plots, and summary statistics to understand customer segmentation patterns and explain business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical distributions in customer data by analyzing histograms, box plots, and summary statistics to identify purchasing behavior patterns
Students will explain the business significance of distribution characteristics through written analysis connecting statistical findings to real-world customer segmentation strategies
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the provided customer purchase dataset (CSV file with 1000 records including customer_id, age, annual_income, purchase_amount, days_since_last_purchase). Students work in pairs and open the dataset in their preferred analysis tool. **Phase 1 - Initial Exploration (15 minutes):** Students generate basic summary statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles) for purchase_amount and annual_income variables. They create histograms for both variables using 15-20 bins and note initial observations about shape, central tendency, and spread. **Phase 2 - Distribution Analysis (20 minutes):** Students create box plots for the same variables and identify outliers, skewness, and potential customer segments. They compare histogram shapes to theoretical distributions (normal, uniform, skewed) and document which distribution type best describes each variable. **Phase 3 - Pattern Interpretation (15 minutes):** Working in pairs, students analyze the relationship between age groups (18-30, 31-50, 51+) and purchase patterns by creating side-by-side box plots. They identify which age group shows highest variability in spending and explain potential reasons. **Phase 4 - Business Application (10 minutes):** Each pair writes a 150-word business memo explaining what the distribution patterns reveal about customer segments and recommends two specific marketing strategies based on their statistical findings. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Three pairs share their key insights with the class, focusing on how distribution characteristics translate to actionable business intelligence.
materials_needed: Customer purchase dataset (CSV file with 1000 records)
Statistical analysis software (R, Python with pandas/matplotlib, or Excel)
Computers/laptops with internet access
Business memo template worksheet
Distribution reference sheet with normal, skewed, and uniform examples
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of statistical calculations and visualizations (30 points) - correct summary statistics and properly formatted plots, (2) Quality of distribution interpretation (40 points) - correctly identifies distribution types, outliers, and skewness with appropriate statistical terminology, (3) Business application relevance (30 points) - business memo demonstrates clear connection between statistical findings and practical marketing recommendations with logical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a completed example using a different variable (days_since_last_purchase) showing proper interpretation language and business connections. Offer sentence starters for business memo such as 'The right-skewed distribution suggests...' **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to perform Shapiro-Wilk normality tests, create probability density plots, or analyze multivariate distributions by examining purchase_amount vs. annual_income scatter plots with distribution overlays. Have them research industry benchmarks to contextualize their findings.

title: Cryptographic Protocol Vulnerability Analysis: Examining SSL/TLS Handshake Security Flaws
description: Students will dissect and analyze real-world SSL/TLS protocol implementations to identify specific vulnerability patterns and attack vectors. They will examine packet captures, protocol specifications, and exploit demonstrations to understand how design decisions create security weaknesses.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SSL/TLS handshake sequences by examining packet-level communications to identify protocol vulnerabilities and implementation weaknesses
Students will deconstruct cryptographic attack vectors through systematic examination of real exploit scenarios and their underlying protocol design flaws
instructions: Begin by providing students with three distinct datasets: (1) Wireshark packet captures of normal SSL/TLS handshakes, (2) captures showing the POODLE attack against SSL 3.0, and (3) captures demonstrating the Heartbleed vulnerability exploitation. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes examining the normal handshake capture using Wireshark, documenting each message type, cipher suite negotiation, and certificate exchange process in a provided analysis template. Next, distribute the RFC 6101 SSL 3.0 specification excerpt focusing on padding validation. Students spend 25 minutes mapping the specification requirements against the POODLE attack capture, identifying where the protocol specification allows the vulnerability to exist. They must trace the exact sequence: client hello, cipher suite downgrade, CBC padding oracle setup, and data extraction process. For the final 30-minute phase, students examine the Heartbleed OpenSSL implementation code snippet alongside the exploit packet capture. They must identify the bounds-checking failure in the heartbeat extension implementation and trace how the memory disclosure occurs. Students document their findings using a structured vulnerability analysis framework: attack vector classification, affected protocol layers, exploitation prerequisites, impact assessment, and mitigation strategies. Each pair presents a 5-minute analysis of one vulnerability to the class, explaining the protocol design decision that enabled the attack and proposing specific specification changes that would prevent it. Conclude with a 10-minute discussion comparing how different layers of the protocol stack contribute to overall security posture.
materials_needed: Wireshark packet capture files (normal SSL/TLS, POODLE attack, Heartbleed exploit)
RFC 6101 SSL 3.0 specification excerpt (padding validation section)
OpenSSL heartbeat extension source code snippet with vulnerability
Vulnerability analysis template worksheet
Wireshark software installed on student computers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed vulnerability analysis templates using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate protocol message sequence identification (25%), (2) Correct mapping of specification requirements to vulnerability (25%), (3) Precise explanation of exploitation mechanism (25%), (4) Viable mitigation strategies with technical justification (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying at least 2 specific protocol design decisions that enabled each vulnerability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted packet captures with key messages marked and a glossary of SSL/TLS terminology. Offer a vulnerability analysis example using a simpler protocol flaw. For advanced learners, include additional attack scenarios like BEAST or Lucky13, and challenge them to identify potential countermeasures' own security implications or implementation challenges.

title: Design a Community Garden: Area and Perimeter Optimization Challenge
description: Students will design an original community garden layout by creating geometric plots with specific area and perimeter constraints. They must justify their design choices using mathematical reasoning and present their solution to address real-world gardening needs.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original garden design by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and circles within given constraints
Students will construct mathematical justifications for their design choices through written explanations and visual presentations
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: The city has allocated a 100m × 60m rectangular plot for a community garden, and students must design efficient layouts for different crop sections. Distribute the design brief requiring: 1 rectangular section (minimum 800m²), 1 triangular herb section (maximum perimeter 40m), and 1 circular flower section (area between 150-200m²). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to brainstorm initial sketches on grid paper. Next, spend 45 minutes having students calculate exact dimensions using area and perimeter formulas, ensuring all sections fit within the total plot without overlap. Students must show all mathematical work on calculation sheets. During the final 30 minutes, each pair creates a visual presentation on poster paper showing their scaled garden layout (1:100 scale), labeled dimensions, area/perimeter calculations, and a written justification (minimum 150 words) explaining why their design maximizes growing space while meeting community needs. Circulate during work time to check calculations and provide guidance. Conclude with 3-minute presentations where pairs explain their design rationale and mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
Calculators
Rulers and compasses
Poster paper (1 sheet per pair)
Colored pencils or markers
Design brief handouts with constraints
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations (25%), creativity and feasibility of garden design (25%), quality of written justification demonstrating understanding of optimization (25%), and clarity of visual presentation with proper scaling and labeling (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide formula reference sheets and pre-drawn coordinate grids with plot boundaries marked. Offer calculation templates with partially completed examples. For advanced learners: Add constraints requiring irregular polygon sections or challenge them to minimize total fencing needed while maximizing planting area. Encourage exploration of multiple design iterations with comparative analysis.

title: Pizza Party Planning: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios
description: Students will plan a pizza party for their class by applying fraction addition, subtraction, and multiplication to calculate how many pizzas to order based on individual preferences and dietary restrictions. This activity connects mathematical concepts to authentic decision-making situations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction addition and subtraction by combining different pizza preference data to determine total quantities needed
Students will demonstrate fraction multiplication through calculating partial pizza portions for students with varying appetites and dietary needs
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' and explaining that students are event planners tasked with ordering pizzas for a class celebration (5 minutes). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and provide each group with a scenario card containing data about 20 hypothetical party guests, including how much pizza each person wants (expressed in fractions like 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 pizza) and their topping preferences (10 minutes setup). Students must first calculate the total amount of cheese pizza needed by adding all cheese pizza fractions, then repeat for pepperoni and vegetarian options. They should show all work using common denominators and proper fraction notation (15 minutes). Next, students apply their fraction skills to determine how many whole pizzas to order, rounding up appropriately since partial pizzas cannot be purchased. They must also calculate the cost by multiplying the number of pizzas by the given price per pizza (15 minutes). Groups then create a summary report showing their calculations and final pizza order recommendation, including total cost and justification for their choices (10 minutes). Conclude with each group presenting their solution to the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning and defending their pizza quantity decisions (10 minutes presentations). Circulate during work time to ensure proper fraction operations and provide guidance on complex additions requiring multiple common denominators.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Sheet (1 per student)
Scenario cards with guest data (1 per group)
Calculators (optional for checking work)
Chart paper for final presentations
Colored pencils or markers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of fraction addition/subtraction calculations (25 points), (2) Correct application of fraction multiplication for cost calculations (25 points), (3) Appropriate rounding and real-world reasoning for final pizza quantities (25 points), (4) Clear presentation of mathematical work and logical justification of decisions (25 points). Students must achieve 70% or higher to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide fraction strips or visual models, pre-calculate some common denominators, and pair with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including discount calculations for bulk orders, comparing costs across different pizza restaurants, or incorporating sales tax calculations into the final pricing.

title: Pizza Party Planning: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios: Exercise 1
description: Students apply fraction addition, subtraction, and multiplication skills to plan a class pizza party by calculating portions, costs, and ingredient amounts. They work through authentic scenarios requiring fraction operations to determine how much pizza to order and budget allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction addition and subtraction operations by calculating combined pizza portions and remaining amounts in a party planning context
Students will apply fraction multiplication through determining ingredient quantities and cost calculations for multiple pizza orders
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: 'Our class of 24 students is planning a pizza party. Each student will eat 3/4 of a personal pizza, teachers will eat 1 1/2 pizzas total, and we want 1/4 extra for unexpected guests.' Distribute the Pizza Party Planning worksheet and have students work in pairs (10 minutes setup). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students calculate total pizza needed by adding fractions: 24 × 3/4 + 1 1/2 + 1/4. They must show all conversion to common denominators and simplification steps. Circulate to check work and provide hints on finding least common multiples.

Step 2 (10 minutes): Present pizza pricing: Small (serves 1) = $8, Medium (serves 2 1/2) = $15, Large (serves 3 3/4) = $20. Students determine the most cost-effective combination by calculating cost per serving for each size using division of fractions.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Give students a budget constraint of $180. They must apply their calculations to determine optimal pizza orders, showing how much budget remains or is exceeded. Students calculate differences using fraction subtraction.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Extension challenge - if 1/3 of students want vegetarian pizza and 2/5 want pepperoni, with remainder wanting cheese, calculate specific quantities needed for each type while maintaining the same total amount.

Conclude with pairs presenting one calculation to the class, explaining their fraction operations and reasoning (15 minutes). Emphasize real-world applications and common error checking strategies.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning worksheet (one per pair)
Calculators for verification only
Chart paper for final presentations
Fraction strips or circle models for visual support
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly applies all fraction operations with proper notation and gets accurate final answers; (3) Minor computational errors but demonstrates understanding of operations; (2) Shows partial understanding with some incorrect applications; (1) Minimal evidence of applying fraction concepts. Also assess verbal explanations during presentations for mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling learners: Provide fraction strips and encourage drawing visual models. Start with simpler numbers (half portions instead of 3/4). For advanced learners: Add complexity with tax calculations (8.5% sales tax), discount scenarios (15% off orders over $150), or multiple topping price variations. Consider having them create their own similar problem.
original_title: Pizza Party Planning: Applying Fraction Operations to Real-World Scenarios

title: Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Real-World Business Decision Making
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model incorporating at least three variables and four constraints to solve a complex business problem. They will develop the mathematical framework, implement it using linear programming techniques, and present their solution with justification for all modeling decisions.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive multi-variable optimization model by translating real-world business constraints into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will synthesize linear programming theory, graphical analysis, and computational methods through the creation of a complete optimization solution with sensitivity analysis
instructions: Begin by presenting students with three complex business scenarios: manufacturing resource allocation, investment portfolio optimization, or supply chain logistics (15 minutes). Students work in pairs to select one scenario and spend 20 minutes researching additional constraints and variables specific to their chosen industry. Next, students formulate their mathematical model by defining decision variables (x₁, x₂, x₃, etc.), writing the objective function to maximize profit or minimize cost, and establishing at least four realistic constraints including non-negativity constraints (45 minutes). Using graphing software, students create visual representations of their feasible region and identify corner points (30 minutes). Students then solve their model using both graphical methods (for 2-variable projections) and the simplex method or software solver, documenting each step and explaining why their solution is optimal (60 minutes). Following solution, students conduct sensitivity analysis by systematically varying constraint parameters by ±20% and analyzing how changes affect the optimal solution (30 minutes). Finally, students prepare a professional presentation including problem statement, mathematical model, solution process, optimal solution interpretation, and sensitivity analysis results (40 minutes). Each pair presents their model to the class for 8 minutes, followed by 2 minutes of peer questions focusing on mathematical rigor and real-world applicability. Conclude with a reflection where students identify potential model limitations and suggest improvements (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Graphing software (Desmos, GeoGebra, or similar)
Linear programming solver (Excel Solver, Python scipy.optimize, or online LP calculator)
Business scenario handouts with industry-specific data
Large format paper or digital presentation tools
Calculators for manual simplex method calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct formulation of objective function and constraints, proper variable definition (25%); (2) Solution Process - appropriate use of optimization techniques, clear documentation of steps (25%); (3) Analysis Quality - thorough sensitivity analysis, realistic interpretation of results (25%); (4) Professional Communication - clear presentation, effective visual aids, confident response to questions (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint templates and guide them through one complete example before independent work. Offer step-by-step graphical method worksheets. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate integer programming constraints, multiple objective functions using goal programming, or nonlinear elements. Encourage exploration of more sophisticated software like MATLAB or specialized optimization packages.

title: Binary Number System Identification and Recall Activity
description: Students will memorize and identify the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through flashcard drills and verbal recitation. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for understanding how computers represent data internally.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through verbal recitation and written quizzes
instructions: Begin with a 5-minute introduction showing students a completed binary-decimal conversion chart for numbers 0-15 (0000=0, 0001=1, 0010=2, etc.). Have students spend 10 minutes copying this chart into their notebooks, emphasizing the pattern of place values (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s). Next, distribute pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers on one side and binary on the reverse. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes, alternating roles as questioner and responder, drilling through the flashcards twice. The questioner shows the decimal number, the responder states the binary equivalent, then they check the answer and record incorrect responses. Switch roles after 7.5 minutes. Follow with 8 minutes of individual silent study where students review their recorded mistakes and re-memorize problem numbers using the reference chart. Conclude with a 7-minute whole-class verbal quiz: call out decimal numbers randomly, students write binary answers on mini whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Record accuracy for each student. End with 5 minutes of cleanup and reflection where students identify which numbers they found most difficult to remember.
materials_needed: Pre-printed binary-decimal conversion chart (numbers 0-15)
Laminated flashcards with decimal on front, 4-bit binary on back (one set per pair)
Individual notebooks or worksheets
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Score the final whiteboard quiz out of 10 points (call 10 random numbers). Award 1 point for each correct binary representation. Students must achieve 8/10 (80%) to demonstrate successful recall. Additionally, observe pair work and note students who struggle during flashcard drills for follow-up support.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a place-value template (8-4-2-1 boxes) and allow them to use finger counting during initial practice. Create additional practice sheets for homework. For advanced learners: extend the activity to include 16-31 (5-bit numbers) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to find patterns in binary sequences.

title: Optimizing Production Costs Using Linear Programming with Graphical Solutions
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving multiple constraints. They will formulate objective functions, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal production quantities to maximize profit while adhering to resource limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to formulate and solve a multi-constraint optimization problem by translating business scenarios into mathematical models
Students will determine optimal solutions through graphical analysis of feasible regions and systematic evaluation of corner points
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'GreenTech Solar Panel Manufacturing' scenario handout (15 minutes for reading and initial setup). Students work in pairs to analyze a company producing two solar panel types with constraints on labor hours, raw materials, and storage space. Each pair receives: production data sheets, constraint summary cards, and graphing materials. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students identify decision variables (x = standard panels, y = premium panels) and formulate the objective function for profit maximization. They must write inequality constraints for: 40 labor hours weekly limit, $12,000 material budget, and 200-unit storage capacity. Circulate to verify correct mathematical translation of business constraints.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using graph paper or graphing software, students plot constraint lines and shade feasible regions. They must clearly identify boundary lines, determine intersection points algebraically, and verify which corner points lie within the feasible region. Require students to show all calculation work for intersection coordinates.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students evaluate the objective function at each corner point of the feasible region, including origin and axis intercepts. They must create a comparison table showing coordinates and corresponding profit values, then identify the optimal production combination.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair prepares a brief presentation slide showing their optimal solution, expected weekly profit, and resource utilization percentages. Include sensitivity analysis: 'What happens if labor hours increase by 10%?' Conclude with 3-minute pair presentations and peer verification of solutions using provided answer key.
materials_needed: GreenTech Solar Panel Manufacturing scenario handouts (one per pair)
Graph paper (4 sheets per student) and colored pencils/markers
Graphing calculators or Desmos graphing software access
Production data reference sheets with cost/profit margins
Digital presentation slides template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation and constraint identification (25%), (2) Accurate graphical representation and feasible region determination (30%), (3) Proper corner point evaluation and optimal solution identification (30%), (4) Clear presentation and business interpretation of results (15%). Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas to demonstrate mastery of linear programming application.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint identification worksheet with sentence starters like 'The labor constraint can be written as...' and offer pre-drawn coordinate grids with scales. For advanced learners: Introduce shadow price concepts and ask them to solve an additional problem with three variables using algebraic methods, or explore what happens when constraints become non-linear.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory Constraints
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort under varying memory limitations by implementing each algorithm with instrumented memory tracking. They will decompose the trade-offs between time complexity, space complexity, and cache efficiency to determine optimal algorithm selection for resource-constrained environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the performance trade-offs between QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort by implementing memory-instrumented versions and comparing empirical results across different memory constraints
Students will examine the relationship between theoretical complexity analysis and real-world performance through systematic benchmarking and cache behavior analysis
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Implementation Setup**
Students work in pairs to implement three sorting algorithms with memory instrumentation. Provide starter code templates containing memory tracking functions (malloc_count, cache_miss_counter). Each pair implements one algorithm with detailed memory allocation logging. Students must instrument their code to track: heap allocations, stack depth, cache misses, and memory access patterns.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Systematic Testing**
Teams create test datasets: small arrays (100 elements), medium arrays (10,000 elements), large arrays (1,000,000 elements), and pathological cases (already sorted, reverse sorted, many duplicates). Run each algorithm on all datasets under three memory constraint scenarios: unlimited memory, limited heap (50% of optimal), and severely constrained (20% of optimal). Record execution time, memory usage peaks, cache miss rates, and algorithm completion status.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Comparative Analysis**
Students create performance matrices comparing all three algorithms across all test conditions. They must identify break-even points where one algorithm becomes superior to others, analyze why certain algorithms fail under memory constraints, and correlate theoretical Big-O predictions with empirical results. Teams prepare visual graphs showing performance degradation curves and memory usage patterns.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Synthesis and Recommendations**
Each pair presents their analysis to another team, defending their algorithm selection recommendations for three specific scenarios: embedded systems programming, large-scale data processing, and real-time applications. Teams must justify their recommendations using quantitative evidence from their testing.
materials_needed: C++ or Java development environment with profiling tools
Memory profiler (Valgrind, Visual Studio Diagnostic Tools, or JProfiler)
Performance monitoring library (custom malloc wrapper provided)
Graphing software or libraries (matplotlib, Excel, or similar)
Test data generation scripts (provided template)
Benchmark timing utilities
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Implementation quality and instrumentation accuracy (25 points), systematic testing methodology and data collection completeness (25 points), depth of comparative analysis including identification of performance crossover points (30 points), quality of algorithm selection justification with quantitative support (20 points). Deliverable: technical report with performance graphs, raw data tables, and recommendation matrix for different use cases.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide detailed pseudocode templates and pre-written memory tracking functions. Offer guided worksheets for data analysis with partially completed comparison tables. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include additional algorithms (TimSort, RadixSort), analyze multi-threaded performance, or implement custom memory allocators to simulate specific hardware constraints. Provide optional extension to analyze algorithm behavior on different CPU architectures.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory Constraints: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort algorithms by examining their behavior under different memory allocation scenarios. They will deconstruct each algorithm's memory usage patterns and evaluate trade-offs between time complexity and space efficiency in resource-constrained environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the space-time complexity relationships of three sorting algorithms by implementing memory-profiled versions and comparing performance metrics
Students will evaluate algorithmic trade-offs through systematic decomposition of memory allocation patterns and execution benchmarks
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3, assigning each member one sorting algorithm (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort). Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each student implements their assigned algorithm in Python with memory profiling using the 'memory_profiler' library, adding @profile decorators to track memory usage line-by-line. Students test algorithms on identical datasets: 1K, 10K, and 100K randomly generated integers. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams reconvene to share implementation code and initial profiling results. Each member explains their algorithm's memory allocation strategy to teammates. Phase 3 (60 minutes): Teams collaboratively create comparative analysis documents examining: peak memory usage at each dataset size, memory allocation patterns (stack vs heap usage), performance degradation under simulated memory constraints (limit available RAM to 50MB using resource.setrlimit), and identification of memory bottlenecks through profiling data. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams simulate memory-constrained environments by artificially limiting system memory and re-running benchmarks. They analyze how each algorithm degrades under pressure, documenting which algorithm maintains best performance ratios. Final phase (30 minutes): Teams present findings to class, defending their analysis of which algorithm performs best under different memory scenarios and explaining the underlying reasons for performance differences based on algorithmic design principles.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with memory_profiler library installed
Jupyter notebooks or PyCharm IDE
Pre-generated test datasets (1K, 10K, 100K integers)
Performance monitoring template spreadsheet
Algorithm implementation starter code templates
assessment_method: Teams submit a 4-page technical analysis report containing: algorithm complexity analysis (25%), memory profiling data with visualizations (25%), comparative performance tables under different memory constraints (25%), and justified recommendations for algorithm selection based on resource scenarios (25%). Presentations evaluated on technical accuracy and depth of analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed algorithm implementations with memory profiling already set up, and offer guided questions for analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement hybrid approaches or analyze additional algorithms like radix sort, and consider cache performance impacts using tools like Cachegrind.
original_title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory Constraints

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for a Customer Survey Dataset
description: Students will critically assess three different data cleaning strategies applied to a messy customer satisfaction survey dataset. They will analyze the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and justify which method produces the most reliable results for business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data cleaning techniques by comparing their impact on data quality metrics and analysis outcomes
Students will critique data preprocessing decisions through systematic assessment of missing data handling, outlier treatment, and data transformation choices
instructions: Begin by providing students with a customer satisfaction dataset (200 rows) containing missing values, duplicate entries, inconsistent formatting, and potential outliers in rating scores. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Present three pre-processed versions of the same dataset: Version A uses deletion methods (removes all incomplete records), Version B uses mean imputation for missing values and removes outliers, and Version C uses forward-fill imputation and keeps all data points. Each group receives all three versions plus documentation of the cleaning steps used. Students spend 30 minutes exploring each dataset using basic descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation, data completeness percentages). They calculate and compare key metrics: data retention rate, distribution of satisfaction scores, and identify potential biases introduced by each method. Next, students spend 25 minutes creating a comparison matrix evaluating each approach across four criteria: data completeness, representativeness of original population, potential for bias introduction, and suitability for business insights. They must provide specific evidence from their analysis to support each evaluation. Groups then prepare 5-minute presentations defending their choice of the best cleaning approach, citing specific statistical evidence and discussing trade-offs. Conclude with 15 minutes of peer feedback where groups challenge each other's reasoning and discuss alternative perspectives on data quality priorities.
materials_needed: Customer satisfaction CSV dataset with intentionally introduced data quality issues
Three pre-cleaned versions of the dataset with documented cleaning procedures
Jupyter Notebooks or Excel for data exploration
Comparison matrix template worksheet
Access to basic statistical functions (mean, median, count, etc.)
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Evidence-based evaluation (30% - uses specific data to support claims), Critical analysis (25% - identifies strengths/weaknesses of each approach), Justification quality (25% - logical reasoning for final recommendation), Peer interaction (20% - thoughtful questions and responses during presentations). Students submit comparison matrix and 2-paragraph written justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions like 'What percentage of data was lost in each method?' and 'How do the mean satisfaction scores compare?' For advanced learners, introduce concepts of sampling bias and statistical power, or have them research additional cleaning techniques like multiple imputation and evaluate why they weren't used.

title: Design Your Dream Theme Park: Creating a Mathematical Model with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design an original theme park by creating mathematical models that incorporate area calculations, budget optimization, and statistical analysis of visitor capacity. They will synthesize geometric principles, algebraic expressions, and data analysis to produce a comprehensive business proposal with mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original theme park layout by applying area formulas, coordinate geometry, and scale factor calculations to design efficient spatial arrangements
Students will construct mathematical models through algebraic expressions and inequalities to optimize budget allocation and maximize visitor satisfaction within given constraints
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with grid paper, calculators, and the scenario packet containing a $2.5 million budget, 50-acre plot dimensions (1100×1980 feet), and attraction cost data. Explain they are theme park designers competing for a contract.

**Phase 1 - Planning (25 minutes):** Students sketch their park layout on grid paper using 1 square = 100 sq ft scale. They must include: 5 major rides, 3 food venues, 2 gift shops, parking area, and walkways. Have them calculate the area of each section using appropriate geometric formulas (rectangles, circles, triangles). They create a data table listing each attraction's dimensions, area, and estimated construction cost.

**Phase 2 - Mathematical Modeling (30 minutes):** Students develop algebraic expressions for total cost: C = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ + R₄ + R₅ + F₁ + F₂ + F₃ + G₁ + G₂ + P + W, where each variable represents individual attraction costs. They must create inequalities ensuring their total cost ≤ $2,500,000 and total area ≤ 2,178,000 sq ft. Students then model visitor capacity using linear equations based on ride throughput data provided.

**Phase 3 - Optimization and Justification (25 minutes):** Students adjust their designs to maximize projected daily revenue while staying within constraints. They create graphs showing the relationship between investment in each attraction type and expected visitor satisfaction scores. Finally, they prepare a 3-minute presentation including their scale drawing, mathematical calculations, constraint verification, and revenue projections with supporting data tables and graphs.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1/4 inch squares)
Scientific calculators
Scenario packet with attraction costs and specifications
Colored pencils or markers
Rulers and compasses
Spreadsheet software (optional for advanced students)
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and algebraic models (25 points), creative and realistic design layout (20 points), proper constraint satisfaction and optimization reasoning (25 points), clear presentation with appropriate mathematical vocabulary (15 points), and use of multiple mathematical concepts integration (15 points). Students submit their scaled drawings, calculation worksheets, and mathematical justification document.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made templates with some attractions already placed and area formulas reference sheet. Offer partnership opportunities for calculation checking. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include profit margin analysis, compound interest calculations for loan scenarios, or statistical probability models for weather impact on attendance. Encourage use of spreadsheet software for complex calculations.

title: Memory Palace: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classes Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete hierarchy of computational complexity classes (P, NP, PSPACE, EXPTIME, etc.) along with their formal definitions, key problem examples, and containment relationships. This intensive memorization activity uses spaced repetition and visual association techniques to ensure precise recall of advanced theoretical computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the complete formal definitions of 12 major complexity classes (P, NP, co-NP, NP-complete, NP-hard, PSPACE, PSPACE-complete, EXPTIME, EXPSPACE, BPP, RP, ZPP) by creating and rehearsing structured memory associations
Students will recall the exact containment relationships between complexity classes and identify 3-4 canonical complete problems for each class through systematic drill exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the standardized complexity class reference sheet containing formal definitions, notation, and examples. Students have 5 minutes to review the material silently. Next, introduce the memory palace technique: students mentally map each complexity class to a specific location in a familiar building (their home, school, etc.). Spend 10 minutes having students create their mental maps and practice walking through them. Implement Phase 1 (15 minutes): Display each complexity class name for 30 seconds while students recite the formal definition aloud, then move to their assigned mental location. Cover all 12 classes twice. Phase 2 (15 minutes): Show problem examples (3-SAT, Traveling Salesman, etc.) for 20 seconds each. Students must immediately state which complexity class contains this problem and justify with the formal definition. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Present containment relationship diagrams with missing elements. Students fill in blanks from memory, stating relationships like 'P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE ⊆ EXPTIME.' Conclude with rapid-fire recall (10 minutes): instructor calls out complexity classes randomly, students respond with complete definitions within 15 seconds. Record accuracy rates for each student. Repeat the entire sequence twice with 5-minute breaks between iterations to reinforce memory consolidation through spaced repetition.
materials_needed: Laminated complexity class reference sheets (one per student)
Digital timer with audible alerts
Whiteboard markers and large whiteboard
Pre-made PowerPoint slides with complexity class names and problem examples
Individual scoring sheets for tracking recall accuracy
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on a final recall quiz containing: (1) providing formal definitions for 8 randomly selected complexity classes within 20 seconds each, (2) correctly identifying the complexity class for 10 given problems, and (3) drawing the complete containment hierarchy diagram with all 12 classes positioned correctly. Each component weighted equally (30 points total).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym helpers (P = 'Polynomial-time,' NP = 'Nondeterministic Polynomial') and allow use of visual cue cards during first two practice rounds. For advanced learners: include additional classes like #P, PP, or quantum complexity classes (BQP, QMA), and require memorization of specific reduction types (Karp vs Cook reductions) used to establish completeness.

title: Budget Planning for a School Dance: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic budget for a school dance event. They will calculate discounts, tax rates, and budget allocations while working with real-world pricing scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine actual costs after discounts and taxes by solving authentic budget scenarios
Students will demonstrate percentage problem-solving skills through creating and justifying a complete event budget within given constraints
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'School Dance Budget Challenge' worksheet and price list to each student (5 minutes). Explain that they have a $800 total budget and must plan decorations, food, music, and supplies. Present the scenario: 'The student council has allocated $800 for the spring dance. You must create a complete budget using the provided vendor price list, accounting for all discounts and taxes.' 

Have students work individually for the first 15 minutes to review the price list and calculate base costs. The price list should include: DJ services ($200 with 10% student discount), decorations ($150 with 15% bulk discount), snacks ($120 with 8% tax), drinks ($80 with 8% tax), and miscellaneous supplies ($100 with 5% tax).

Next, guide students through calculating their first item together (10 minutes). Model finding the DJ cost: $200 × 0.10 = $20 discount, so $200 - $20 = $180 final cost. Have students complete remaining calculations independently (20 minutes).

Students then allocate their calculated costs and determine if they're within budget. If over budget, they must adjust quantities and recalculate percentages. Finally, students complete a budget summary sheet showing: original prices, discount/tax amounts, final costs, and total budget usage.

Conclude with students presenting one budget line item calculation to a partner, explaining their percentage work step-by-step (10 minutes). Circulate to observe explanations and provide feedback on calculation accuracy and reasoning.
materials_needed: School Dance Budget Challenge worksheet (one per student)
Vendor price list with discount/tax information
Calculators
Budget summary template sheet
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown, budget stays within $800, explanations are mathematically accurate; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget within range, explanations mostly correct; (2) Some calculation errors, budget somewhat realistic, explanations partially correct; (1) Major errors, unrealistic budget, unclear explanations. Students must submit completed worksheet with all calculations shown.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a percentage calculation reference sheet and allow them to work with a partner during independent work time. Consider pre-calculating one additional example beyond the guided practice. For advanced learners: add complexity by including multiple discount tiers (e.g., 'additional 5% discount if total decoration order exceeds $120') or have them create a comparison budget for two different event scenarios.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Big O Notation Comparison Lab
description: Students will analyze the time complexity of four different sorting algorithms by examining their code implementations, tracing through execution patterns, and categorizing their Big O classifications. They will then create a comparative analysis report justifying their efficiency rankings with specific evidence from code structure and performance characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, selection sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and conditional statements to determine Big O notation
Students will compare algorithm efficiency patterns through systematic code tracing and create evidence-based rankings of algorithmic performance
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and distributing the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet containing four sorting algorithm implementations (bubble sort, selection sort, merge sort, quicksort) written in pseudocode. Each group receives laptops with the provided code files and timing visualization tool. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Each group member takes one algorithm and individually traces through the execution using a sample array of 8 elements, counting the number of operations (comparisons and swaps) performed. Students document their findings on the worksheet's operation count table.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups reconvene to analyze the code structure of each algorithm. Students identify nested loops, recursive patterns, and decision points, marking these directly on printed code sheets with colored highlighters (yellow for outer loops, green for inner loops, blue for recursive calls). They complete the 'Code Pattern Analysis' section noting the relationship between input size and operation patterns.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Using the timing visualization tool, groups run each algorithm with datasets of sizes 100, 1000, and 10000 elements, recording execution times in the provided data table. Students create simple graphs plotting input size vs. execution time for visual comparison.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups synthesize their findings to determine Big O classification for each algorithm, referencing their operation counts, code pattern analysis, and timing data. They complete a comparison matrix ranking algorithms from most to least efficient, providing three pieces of evidence for each ranking decision.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each group presents one algorithm's analysis to the class, explaining their Big O determination and supporting evidence. Other groups provide feedback using the peer evaluation checklist.
materials_needed: Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with four sorting algorithm implementations
Laptops with algorithm timing visualization tool installed
Printed code sheets for annotation (one set per group)
Colored highlighters (yellow, green, blue) - one set per group
Graph paper for plotting execution times
Peer evaluation checklist forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of Big O classifications (4 points each algorithm), (2) Quality of evidence provided in comparison matrix (3 points per ranking justification), (3) Correct identification of code patterns through highlighting and annotations (2 points per algorithm), (4) Mathematical reasoning connecting operation counts to Big O notation (4 points). Total possible: 40 points. Success criteria: Students must correctly identify at least 3/4 Big O classifications and provide valid evidence-based reasoning for algorithm rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a Big O reference chart with common patterns (single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²), divide-and-conquer = O(n log n)). Include sentence starters for evidence justifications. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze best-case vs. worst-case scenarios for quicksort, or extend analysis to space complexity. Provide additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort for bonus analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students critically analyze and evaluate three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) applied to a real customer churn dataset, assessing their performance, interpretability, and business applicability. They will judge the most appropriate model considering multiple evaluation criteria and provide evidence-based recommendations to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, computational requirements, and interpretability trade-offs within a business context
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of bias-variance trade-offs, feature importance analysis, and deployment feasibility considerations
instructions: **Phase 1 (30 minutes): Dataset Analysis and Context Setting** - Provide students with a telecommunications customer churn dataset (10,000 records, 20 features) and three pre-trained models with their outputs. Students work in teams of 3-4 to examine the dataset characteristics, missing values, class imbalance (70/30 split), and business context documentation. Each team receives model performance reports showing accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, training time, and prediction latency for all three models. **Phase 2 (45 minutes): Multi-Criteria Model Evaluation** - Teams systematically evaluate each model using provided evaluation framework: (1) Performance Analysis - compare confusion matrices, ROC curves, and cross-validation results; (2) Business Impact Assessment - calculate potential revenue impact using provided cost matrix (false negatives cost $200, false positives cost $50); (3) Interpretability Analysis - examine SHAP values, feature importance plots, and model complexity; (4) Deployment Considerations - assess memory requirements, prediction speed, and maintenance complexity using provided infrastructure specifications. **Phase 3 (30 minutes): Stakeholder Recommendation Development** - Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their model choice, addressing three stakeholder perspectives: technical team (accuracy/performance), business team (ROI/interpretability), and operations team (deployment/maintenance). **Phase 4 (45 minutes): Peer Evaluation and Critique** - Each team presents while others evaluate using structured critique forms, challenging assumptions and questioning trade-off decisions. Instructor facilitates discussion on evaluation criteria conflicts and real-world constraints.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV format, 10,000 records)
Three pre-trained model outputs with performance metrics and visualizations
Business context documentation with cost matrices and infrastructure specifications
SHAP analysis plots and feature importance visualizations for each model
Evaluation framework template with scoring rubrics
Jupyter notebooks with Python (pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn)
Presentation template for stakeholder recommendations
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Quality of multi-criteria analysis (25%) - depth of performance metric interpretation, business impact calculations, and trade-off identification; (2) Evidence-based reasoning (30%) - use of quantitative data to support arguments, acknowledgment of limitations, and consideration of alternative perspectives; (3) Stakeholder communication (25%) - clarity of recommendation, addressing different stakeholder needs, and handling of critique questions; (4) Peer evaluation quality (20%) - constructiveness of critiques, identification of overlooked factors, and quality of questions posed to presenting teams. Rubric includes specific indicators for each criterion with 4-point scale (inadequate, developing, proficient, exemplary).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide model evaluation checklist with specific questions for each criterion, offer simplified business impact calculation templates, and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as fairness metrics across customer segments, A/B testing design considerations, or ensemble method evaluation. Provide access to additional datasets for comparative analysis and encourage exploration of advanced evaluation techniques like learning curves or calibration plots.

title: Portfolio Risk Assessment Using Matrix Operations and Monte Carlo Simulation
description: Students will apply advanced linear algebra concepts to analyze a diversified investment portfolio's risk and return characteristics. They will use matrix multiplication for portfolio calculations and implement Monte Carlo methods to simulate potential future outcomes under market uncertainty.
learning_objectives: Students will apply matrix operations to calculate portfolio weights, expected returns, and variance-covariance relationships by manipulating real financial data matrices
Students will implement Monte Carlo simulation techniques through iterative probability calculations to model portfolio performance under 10,000 market scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with historical return data for 8 assets (stocks, bonds, commodities) in Excel format covering 5 years of monthly returns. Students first create the variance-covariance matrix (8x8) by calculating pairwise correlations and standard deviations. Next, they define three portfolio allocation vectors: conservative (60% bonds, 40% stocks), balanced (50% bonds, 50% stocks), and aggressive (20% bonds, 80% stocks). Using matrix multiplication, students calculate expected annual returns for each portfolio by multiplying the allocation vector by the mean returns vector. They then compute portfolio variance using the formula w^T * Σ * w, where w is the weight vector and Σ is the covariance matrix. For the Monte Carlo simulation phase, students generate 10,000 random scenarios using normal distribution functions with parameters derived from their historical analysis. Each simulation run calculates one-year portfolio value assuming $100,000 initial investment. Students track outcomes in arrays and calculate key statistics: mean return, standard deviation, Value at Risk (5th percentile), and probability of loss. Finally, they create histograms showing return distributions for all three portfolios and prepare a 10-minute presentation comparing risk-return profiles. Instructors circulate to verify matrix calculations and provide debugging assistance for simulation code. Teams present findings with recommendations for different investor risk tolerances.
materials_needed: Excel spreadsheet with 5 years of monthly return data for 8 financial assets
Scientific calculators or computers with Excel/Python/R access
Portfolio analysis worksheet template with matrix calculation guides
Presentation software (PowerPoint or Google Slides)
Random number generation tables (backup for non-computer users)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Matrix calculations accuracy - correct covariance matrix and portfolio variance computations (25 points), (2) Monte Carlo implementation - proper random sampling and 10,000+ iterations completed (25 points), (3) Statistical analysis - accurate calculation of VaR, probability metrics, and summary statistics (25 points), (4) Business application - clear portfolio recommendations supported by quantitative findings (25 points). Submit Excel files showing all calculations plus presentation slides.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step matrix multiplication examples and pre-built Excel templates with formula hints. Offer simplified 3-asset portfolios and 1,000 simulation runs. For advanced learners: Include options pricing using Black-Scholes formula, multi-period portfolio rebalancing scenarios, or optimization using Solver to find efficient frontier. Encourage exploration of different probability distributions (t-distribution, skewed distributions) beyond normal assumptions.

title: Analyzing Security Vulnerabilities in Real-World Web Application Architecture
description: Students will dissect a complex multi-tier web application's security architecture to identify vulnerability patterns and attack vectors. They will decompose the system's authentication, data flow, and access control mechanisms to evaluate security weaknesses and their potential exploitation paths.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between architectural components and security vulnerabilities by examining authentication flows, database interactions, and API endpoints in a simulated e-commerce application
Students will differentiate between various attack vectors through systematic vulnerability assessment using penetration testing tools and static code analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided e-commerce application codebase (Node.js/Express backend, React frontend, PostgreSQL database) and architectural diagrams to teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Students first spend 45 minutes examining the system architecture, creating a component interaction map that identifies all data flow paths, authentication mechanisms, and external integrations. Next, assign each team a specific attack vector category: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, authentication bypass, or privilege escalation (10 minutes). Teams spend 60 minutes using static analysis tools (SonarQube, ESLint security plugins) and dynamic testing tools (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite Community) to identify vulnerabilities within their assigned category. Students must document each vulnerability with: exact code location, input vectors, potential impact severity, and proposed exploitation scenario. In the analysis phase (45 minutes), teams create vulnerability dependency maps showing how individual weaknesses could be chained together for complex attacks. Teams then present their findings (8 minutes per team) using a standardized vulnerability report template, explaining the technical mechanics of each vulnerability and demonstrating proof-of-concept exploits in the sandboxed environment. Conclude with a 30-minute cross-team analysis session where teams evaluate each other's findings, identify overlapping vulnerabilities, and prioritize remediation based on exploitability and business impact. Students submit individual reflection papers (500 words) analyzing how architectural decisions influenced the vulnerability landscape and proposing systematic security improvements.
materials_needed: Pre-configured vulnerable web application codebase with documentation
Virtual machines with penetration testing tools (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite Community)
Static code analysis tools (SonarQube, ESLint security plugins)
System architecture diagrams and data flow documentation
Vulnerability report templates and assessment rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical accuracy of vulnerability identification (30 points), depth of architectural analysis and component relationship mapping (25 points), quality of exploitation scenarios and attack chain documentation (25 points), effectiveness of cross-team collaboration and peer evaluation (10 points), and clarity of individual reflection on architecture-security relationships (10 points). Students must identify at least 5 vulnerabilities with accurate technical descriptions and demonstrate understanding of attack vector relationships.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with guided vulnerability checklists and code annotation examples. Offer advanced learners additional challenges like analyzing mobile API endpoints or implementing automated scanning scripts. Create mixed-ability teams pairing security-experienced students with those new to penetration testing. Provide reference materials on common vulnerability patterns and OWASP Top 10 mappings.

title: Evaluating Data Visualizations for Business Decision Making
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations presenting the same sales dataset to determine which visualization best supports a specific business decision. They will justify their evaluation using established data visualization principles and make a recommendation with supporting rationale.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization types by applying visualization design principles and assessing clarity of communication
Students will critique data presentation choices through systematic comparison of strengths, weaknesses, and appropriateness for decision-making contexts
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with three printed visualizations of the same quarterly sales data: a pie chart showing regional sales percentages, a bar chart comparing sales by region and quarter, and a line graph showing sales trends over time by region. Also provide the business scenario: 'The marketing director needs to decide which region should receive additional advertising budget next quarter.' 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization and complete a structured evaluation worksheet with sections for: data clarity, visual design effectiveness, and relevance to the business decision. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students discuss their individual evaluations and identify points of agreement and disagreement. They must reference specific visualization elements (axes, colors, scales, labels) in their discussions.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Each pair selects the most effective visualization for the given business scenario and prepares a 2-minute oral justification addressing three criteria: how easily stakeholders can extract relevant information, whether the visualization highlights the most important patterns, and if any elements might mislead decision-makers.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs present their recommendations to the class. After each presentation, the instructor facilitates a brief Q&A where other students can challenge the recommendation or ask for clarification on evaluation criteria.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conclude with a class discussion on common evaluation themes and introduce the concept that visualization effectiveness depends heavily on audience and purpose context.
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations per student (pie chart, bar chart, line graph of same dataset)
Business scenario handout describing decision context
Structured evaluation worksheet with criteria sections
Timer for presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric for: (1) Identification of specific strengths/weaknesses in each visualization, (2) Application of visualization principles in their critique, and (3) Quality of justification linking chosen visualization to business decision needs. Students must demonstrate understanding that different visualizations serve different purposes and that context matters in evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of specific elements to examine (title clarity, axis labels, color usage, data completeness). For advanced learners, introduce additional evaluation criteria such as accessibility considerations, cognitive load, or cultural factors that might influence interpretation. Consider providing examples of poorly designed visualizations for additional practice.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall specific time and space complexity notations for 25 advanced algorithms across sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and string matching categories. This high-intensity recall activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and timed retrieval exercises to build algorithmic complexity fluency.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations for 25 advanced algorithms within 3 seconds per algorithm by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify precise space complexity notations for recursive and iterative algorithm implementations through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 25 algorithms: QuickSort (average/worst case), MergeSort, HeapSort, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A* Search, Breadth-First Search, Depth-First Search, Kruskal's Algorithm, Prim's Algorithm, Knuth-Morris-Pratt String Matching, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Knapsack Problem, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Convex Hull (Graham Scan), Binary Search, AVL Tree operations, Red-Black Tree operations, Trie insertion/search, Radix Sort, and Counting Sort. Students spend 15 minutes studying the sheet, focusing on exact notation (O, Θ, Ω) for both time and space complexity. Next, implement spaced repetition using Anki digital flashcards or physical cards. Each card shows algorithm name on front, complete complexity analysis on back (time complexity best/average/worst case, space complexity, and key constraint notes). Students complete three 10-minute drill rounds with 2-minute breaks between rounds. In Round 1, students self-pace through all 25 cards, marking incorrect recalls. Round 2 focuses only on previously missed cards plus 5 random review cards. Round 3 involves instructor-led rapid-fire questioning where students must respond within 3 seconds. During rapid-fire, instructor randomly calls algorithm names and specifies whether asking for time or space complexity. Students write answers on individual whiteboards and display simultaneously. Track accuracy rates for each student on provided scoring sheet. Conclude with 5-minute reflection where students identify their weakest algorithm categories and plan additional study focus areas.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm complexity reference sheet (25 algorithms with complete Big O/Theta/Omega notations)
Individual student whiteboards and dry erase markers
Digital timer or stopwatch
Anki flashcard software installed on student devices OR 25 physical flashcard sets
Instructor scoring sheet with student names and 25 algorithm checkboxes
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (23/25 correct) on final rapid-fire round to demonstrate mastery. Track three metrics: (1) Accuracy percentage in each round, (2) Response time consistency (staying under 3-second limit), (3) Improvement rate between Round 1 and Round 3. Award full points for 90%+ final accuracy, partial credit for 80-89%, and require remediation for below 80%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce initial set to 15 most common algorithms and extend study time to 20 minutes. Provide mnemonic device cards for complex algorithms like Floyd-Warshall (W³ = O(V³)). For advanced learners, add 10 additional specialized algorithms (suffix arrays, segment trees, Fenwick trees) and require explanation of why specific complexity bounds exist. Consider pairing strong students with those needing support during study phase.

title: Algorithm Complexity Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall specific Big O notation formulas, time complexities, and space complexities for 25 advanced algorithms and data structures. This intensive recall activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and timed recall sessions to build foundational knowledge essential for algorithm analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity notation for 25 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, Ford-Fulkerson, and advanced sorting algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions

Students will identify and state from memory the space complexity requirements and key algorithmic steps for advanced data structures including B-trees, Red-Black trees, and Fibonacci heaps through structured recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 25 advanced algorithms with their time/space complexities (5 minutes setup). Students work individually to study the reference sheet for 15 minutes, focusing on memorizing exact Big O notations and key characteristics. Remove reference sheets and introduce the digital flashcard system (Anki or Quizlet) loaded with algorithm names on front, complexities on back. Students complete three rounds of flashcard review (10 minutes each round) with 2-minute breaks between rounds. Conduct first timed recall test: display algorithm names on projector for 30 seconds each while students write time complexity, space complexity, and one key characteristic on answer sheets (15 minutes total). Provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers after each algorithm. Allow 5-minute review period for missed items. Execute second timed recall session using different algorithm order, reducing display time to 20 seconds per algorithm (12 minutes). Students self-check using provided answer key and record their accuracy scores. Conclude with rapid-fire verbal recall where instructor calls out algorithm names and students respond chorally with time complexity (8 minutes). Document individual student scores throughout all three assessment phases for progress tracking.
materials_needed: Pre-made reference sheet with 25 advanced algorithms and their Big O complexities
Digital flashcard platform (Anki or Quizlet) with algorithm deck loaded
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces for 25 algorithms
Projector/screen for displaying algorithm names during timed tests
Timer/stopwatch for precise timing control
Answer key sheets for self-checking
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on time complexity recall and 75% accuracy (19/25 correct) on space complexity identification during the final timed session. Assessment rubric: 4 points for exact notation match, 3 points for correct complexity class with minor notation errors, 2 points for approximately correct complexity, 1 point for reasonable attempt, 0 points for incorrect/blank responses. Track improvement between first and second timed sessions as secondary success metric.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for common complexity patterns (O(n log n) = 'divide and conquer sorting'), allow use of reference sheet during first recall attempt, pair with stronger students for peer coaching during review periods. For advanced learners: add average vs worst-case complexity distinctions, include amortized analysis complexities, challenge them to recall specific constant factors or explain why certain complexities occur.
