title: Algorithm Complexity Visualization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 specific time and space complexity notations for advanced algorithms and data structures. This intensive recall activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations for complex algorithmic operations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity notation for 15 advanced sorting, graph, and dynamic programming algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify the precise space complexity notation for 10 advanced data structures through rapid-fire verbal quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared complexity reference sheets containing 25 algorithm-complexity pairs (e.g., 'Dijkstra's Algorithm: O(V²) or O(E + V log V)', 'AVL Tree Insertion: O(log n)', 'Floyd-Warshall: O(V³)'). Students have 15 minutes to study these pairs silently, using any memorization technique. After study time, collect all reference materials. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students. Round 2: Show data structure names for 8 seconds each. Students write space complexity notations. Cover 10 data structures in 3 minutes. Between rounds, allow 2-minute discussion periods where groups can quietly compare answers. End with individual verification: each student must privately write all 25 complexity notations from memory within 10 minutes. Individual answer sheets with numbered blanks

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Bias in COMPAS Recidivism Risk Assessment
description: Students will analyze the controversial COMPAS algorithm used in criminal justice to understand how feature importance metrics can reveal algorithmic bias. They will interpret SHAP values, permutation importance, and demographic parity metrics to comprehend the relationship between model performance and fairness.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and permutation importance scores by analyzing their mathematical relationship to model predictions in the COMPAS dataset
Students will distinguish between different types of algorithmic bias through comparative analysis of demographic parity, equalized odds, and individual fairness metrics
instructions:
Begin by providing students with the preprocessed COMPAS dataset containing 6,000 defendant records with features including age, race, gender, prior convictions, and risk scores (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members. Each team receives a Jupyter notebook template with pre-trained Random Forest and Logistic Regression models already fitted to the data. 

In Phase 1 (45 minutes), teams calculate and interpret SHAP values for 10 randomly selected high-risk and 10 low-risk predictions. Students must identify the top 3 contributing features for each prediction and explain how positive/negative SHAP values relate to increased/decreased recidivism probability. They document their findings in a structured template comparing feature contributions across demographic groups.

Phase 2 (40 minutes) focuses on permutation importance analysis. Teams systematically shuffle each feature and measure the resulting drop in model accuracy. They rank features by importance and compare these rankings to their SHAP analysis, noting discrepancies and explaining why global importance differs from local explanations.

In Phase 3 (35 minutes), students calculate fairness metrics by demographic groups. They compute demographic parity (difference in positive prediction rates), equalized odds (difference in true positive rates), and calibration metrics across racial groups. Using provided formulas, they determine which fairness criteria the model violates and by what margin.

Finally (25 minutes), teams synthesize their findings into a bias assessment report, explicitly connecting feature importance patterns to fairness violations and recommending which features should be excluded to improve algorithmic fairness while maintaining predictive performance.
materials_needed: COMPAS dataset (CSV file with 6,000 preprocessed records)
Jupyter notebook template with pre-trained models and SHAP library
Python environment with scikit-learn, SHAP, pandas, numpy, matplotlib
Bias assessment report template (Word document)
Feature importance comparison worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: SHAP interpretation accuracy (25 points - must correctly identify feature contribution direction and magnitude), permutation importance analysis (25 points - accurate ranking and comparison to SHAP), fairness metrics calculation (25 points - correct demographic parity and equalized odds computations), and bias synthesis report (25 points - clear connection between feature importance and fairness violations with actionable recommendations). Students must achieve 80+ points to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed examples of SHAP interpretation for 2-3 sample predictions and a fairness metrics calculation walkthrough. Offer a simplified template focusing on just demographic parity. For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them implement counterfactual fairness analysis or optimize the model using fairness-aware machine learning techniques like adversarial debiasing. Provide additional datasets (credit scoring, hiring) for comparative bias analysis.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Monthly Expense Calculator
description: Students will apply basic arithmetic operations and percentage calculations to create a realistic monthly budget for a young adult scenario. They will use addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division to allocate income across different expense categories and determine if their budget is balanced.
learning_objectives: Students will apply addition and subtraction operations to calculate total income and expenses within a monthly budget scenario
Students will apply percentage calculations to determine appropriate spending allocations for housing, food, transportation, and savings categories
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Young Adult Budget Scenario' worksheet to each student (5 minutes). Each worksheet contains a different monthly income amount between $2,500-$3,500 and specific circumstances (student loans, car payment, etc.). Explain that students must create a balanced budget where expenses do not exceed income. 

Step 1: Students calculate their after-tax income by subtracting 22% for taxes from their gross monthly salary using multiplication and subtraction (10 minutes). 

Step 2: Using the provided expense category guidelines, students apply percentage calculations to determine maximum amounts for each category: Housing (30% of after-tax income), Transportation (15%), Food (12%), Utilities (8%), Entertainment (5%), and Savings (10%). Students must show all calculation work (15 minutes).

Step 3: Students research actual costs in your local area using provided websites or apps, then apply addition to find total monthly expenses. They must make adjustments if over budget by subtracting amounts from flexible categories (15 minutes).

Step 4: Students apply subtraction to determine their final budget balance (income minus total expenses) and create a summary showing whether their budget has a surplus or deficit (10 minutes).

Conclude with students presenting one budget category calculation to a partner, explaining their mathematical reasoning and real-world choices (5 minutes).
materials_needed: Young Adult Budget Scenario worksheets (one per student with varying incomes)
Calculators or smartphones
Access to apartment rental websites (Zillow, Apartments.com)
Local grocery store flyers or apps
Budget template worksheet with expense categories
assessment_method: Students submit completed budget worksheets showing all mathematical calculations with 80% accuracy. Evaluate: (1) Correct tax calculation using 22% deduction, (2) Accurate percentage calculations for each spending category, (3) Proper addition of total expenses, (4) Correct final balance calculation, (5) Budget adjustments that demonstrate mathematical problem-solving when initial totals exceed income.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example budget and calculator reference sheet with percentage-to-decimal conversions. Allow pair work for research phase. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including irregular expenses (quarterly insurance), investment calculations with compound interest, or comparing budgets across different salary scenarios using ratio analysis.

title: Dissecting a Social Media Algorithm: Analyzing Content Recommendation Systems
description: Students will analyze the algorithmic patterns behind social media content recommendation systems by examining real user data scenarios and identifying the underlying decision-making logic. They will break down complex algorithmic behaviors into component parts and evaluate how different factors influence content visibility and user engagement.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the component factors of recommendation algorithms by deconstructing provided user interaction datasets and identifying weighted decision patterns
Students will evaluate algorithmic bias and effectiveness through systematic comparison of content delivery outcomes across different user profiles
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the 'Social Media Data Packet' containing three anonymized user profiles with 50 posts each, including engagement metrics (likes, shares, comments, time spent), user demographics, and posting timestamps. Each group receives different user profiles (fitness enthusiast, news consumer, entertainment seeker). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine their assigned user profile data and create a preliminary hypothesis about what content gets prioritized. They should identify 5-7 potential ranking factors (recency, engagement rate, user similarity, content type, etc.).

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the provided 'Algorithm Analysis Worksheet,' students systematically test their hypotheses by categorizing the top 20 most-shown posts versus bottom 20 least-shown posts. They create comparison charts identifying patterns in timing, engagement ratios, content categories, and user interaction history.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Groups use the 'Algorithmic Weight Calculator' spreadsheet template to assign numerical weights to each factor they identified, attempting to recreate the ranking system. They test their algorithm against 10 holdout posts to verify accuracy.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents their findings using the provided slide template, explaining their identified factors, assigned weights, and prediction accuracy. Other groups challenge their reasoning and suggest alternative interpretations.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Facilitate a class discussion comparing findings across different user types, highlighting how the same algorithm produces different outcomes for different users and discussing implications for information bubbles and algorithmic bias.
materials_needed: Social Media Data Packet (3 different user profile datasets with post metrics)
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet (structured template for pattern identification)
Algorithmic Weight Calculator spreadsheet template
Presentation slide template with required analysis sections

assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of factor identification (25%) - correctly identifies at least 5 relevant algorithmic factors, (2) Quality of analysis (35%) - systematically compares data patterns with supporting evidence, (3) Algorithm recreation (25%) - creates testable weighted model with >60% prediction accuracy on holdout data, (4) Critical evaluation (15%) - identifies potential biases and discusses broader implications. Students submit their completed worksheets, algorithm models, and a 2-page reflection analyzing their findings.

title: Model Performance Audit: Evaluating Machine Learning Solutions for Healthcare Readmission Prediction
description: Students critically assess competing machine learning models designed to predict patient hospital readmissions by analyzing performance metrics, identifying biases, and recommending implementation strategies. They will evaluate real-world constraints including interpretability, fairness, and clinical workflow integration to determine which solution should be deployed in a healthcare setting.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by systematically comparing performance metrics, bias indicators, and interpretability measures within a healthcare context
Students will critique model deployment readiness through comprehensive assessment of technical limitations, ethical considerations, and stakeholder requirements
instructions:
**Phase 1: Individual Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide each student with the Healthcare Readmission Dataset containing three pre-trained models: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Neural Network. Students receive model outputs, confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP values, and demographic performance breakdowns. Each student individually analyzes: (1) Overall performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC), (2) Fairness metrics across age, gender, and ethnicity groups using demographic parity and equalized odds, (3) Model interpretability using SHAP value distributions and feature importance rankings, (4) Computational requirements and inference speed benchmarks.

**Phase 2: Collaborative Evaluation (60 minutes)**
Form teams of 3-4 students. Teams create a comprehensive evaluation matrix scoring each model across six criteria: predictive performance (25%), fairness across demographics (20%), interpretability for clinicians (20%), computational efficiency (15%), robustness to missing data (10%), and regulatory compliance potential (10%). Teams must justify their scoring methodology and weight assignments based on healthcare stakeholder priorities.

**Phase 3: Recommendation Development (45 minutes)**
Teams prepare deployment recommendations addressing: (1) Primary model selection with detailed justification, (2) Implementation timeline with risk mitigation strategies, (3) Monitoring framework for post-deployment performance tracking, (4) Stakeholder communication plan for model limitations and appropriate use cases. Each team creates a 10-slide executive summary for hospital administrators.

**Phase 4: Peer Review and Defense (30 minutes)**
Teams present their recommendations to two other teams who serve as critical evaluators, challenging assumptions, questioning methodology, and identifying overlooked risks. Presenting teams must defend their choices and incorporate feedback into final recommendations.
materials_needed: Healthcare Readmission Dataset with 50,000 patient records
Three pre-trained model outputs with performance metrics
SHAP value visualizations and feature importance data
Demographic bias analysis spreadsheets
Model evaluation rubric template
Jupyter Notebooks with Python libraries (pandas, scikit-learn, shap)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis Quality (30 points - accuracy of metric interpretation, depth of bias analysis), Evaluation Framework (25 points - appropriateness of criteria, justified weightings), Recommendation Soundness (25 points - logical conclusions, risk consideration), and Critical Thinking (20 points - addressing limitations, stakeholder awareness). Students must score 80+ points and successfully defend their methodology during peer challenges to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing metric interpretation guides and bias detection checklists during Phase 1. Offer example evaluation criteria and stakeholder priority frameworks. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as cost-benefit analysis, A/B testing design for model comparison, or regulatory submission requirements. Provide access to domain expert videos explaining healthcare ML deployment challenges.

title: Design and Build a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Water Distribution Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve a complex urban water distribution problem using graph theory, linear programming, and calculus concepts. They will design both the theoretical framework and implement a computational solution, then present their model to municipal engineering stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 7 class periods (approximately 11 hours total over 2-3 weeks)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory, optimization techniques, and differential equations to construct an original mathematical model for water flow optimization by integrating multiple mathematical domains
Students will design and implement a computational algorithm that solves their optimization model through programming and mathematical software applications
instructions: Begin by presenting students with authentic municipal water distribution data from a mid-sized city (population 100,000-300,000). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Day 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the provided network maps, flow rate data, pressure requirements, and cost constraints. Students must identify key variables, constraints, and optimization objectives. They create preliminary sketches of their mathematical approach. Day 2-3 (180 minutes total): Students develop their complete mathematical model. This includes: defining the network as a weighted directed graph, establishing flow conservation equations using Kirchhoff's laws, creating objective functions for cost minimization or efficiency maximization, and incorporating real-world constraints (pipe capacity, pressure limits, pump station locations). Day 4-5 (180 minutes): Implementation phase where teams code their solution using Python/MATLAB or similar tools. They must create algorithms that can handle their mathematical model, generate test cases, and validate results against known solutions. Day 6 (90 minutes): Teams prepare technical presentations including: problem statement, mathematical formulation with proofs of key theorems used, computational implementation details, results analysis with sensitivity testing, and recommendations for municipal engineers. Day 7 (90 minutes): Final presentations to panel including instructor and invited engineering professionals. Each team presents for 15 minutes followed by 5-minute technical Q&A session.
materials_needed: Real municipal water distribution network dataset with GIS coordinates
Python or MATLAB software with optimization toolboxes
Graph theory and linear programming reference materials
Large format paper for network diagrams and mathematical notation
Access to computational resources (computers with sufficient processing power)
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Mathematical model completeness and accuracy (25 points), innovative integration of multiple mathematical concepts (20 points), computational implementation functionality (20 points), technical presentation clarity and professional quality (15 points), ability to defend model during Q&A with engineering professionals (10 points), team collaboration and individual contribution documentation (10 points)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-structured templates for mathematical notation, offer simplified network examples for initial practice, schedule mandatory check-ins after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements (demand uncertainty), add multi-objective optimization (cost vs. reliability), or extend to dynamic optimization over time periods. Consider allowing advanced students to mentor struggling teams.

title: Python Data Type Identification and Classification Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) through a structured flashcard activity. They will identify data types from code examples and classify values into their correct categories.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) by correctly naming them from memory within 30 seconds
Students will identify specific data types from Python code examples through visual recognition exercises with 90% accuracy
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Print 48 flashcards - 24 showing Python values (e.g., '42', '3.14', '"Hello"', 'True', '[1,2,3]', '{"name": "John"}') and 24 showing data type names. Arrange students in pairs and distribute one complete set per pair. **Round 1 - Memorization (10 minutes):** Students take turns showing their partner data type name cards while the partner recites the definition and provides one example. Switch roles every 2 minutes. **Round 2 - Speed Recognition (15 minutes):** Partner A holds up value cards one at a time. Partner B must immediately state the data type. Track correct answers on provided score sheet. After 25 cards, switch roles. **Round 3 - Matching Game (15 minutes):** Spread all 48 cards face down on desk. Students take turns flipping two cards, trying to match Python values with their corresponding data types. When a match is found, student must verbally confirm the data type name and provide one additional example of that type before keeping the pair. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Each pair sorts their collected matches by data type category and instructor spot-checks by randomly selecting cards for students to identify aloud.
materials_needed: 48 printed flashcards per pair (24 value cards, 24 data type cards)
Score tracking sheets (1 per student)
Pencils for scoring
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students pass by correctly identifying 22/25 data types during Round 2 speed recognition (88% accuracy). Instructor observes and records performance on provided checklist. Final verification through random spot-checking where students must name the data type and provide an additional example not shown on cards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with data type definitions and reduce speed requirements to 3 seconds per identification. For advanced learners: Include complex nested examples like lists containing dictionaries, or introduce additional types like tuples and sets. Consider adding syntax examples showing variable declarations.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Statistical Visualizations
description: Students will analyze three different datasets with varying distribution patterns (normal, skewed, and bimodal) to understand how statistical measures and visualizations reveal data characteristics. They will interpret boxplots, histograms, and summary statistics to explain what each distribution pattern indicates about the underlying data.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between distribution shape and statistical measures by analyzing mean, median, and standard deviation across three different dataset types
Students will explain the practical implications of data distribution patterns through written analysis of real-world scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-prepared datasets: customer ages (normal distribution), household income (right-skewed), and daily website traffic (bimodal). Each dataset should contain 500-1000 data points. In pairs, students first examine Dataset 1 (15 minutes): create a histogram with 20 bins, generate a boxplot, and calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation using provided software. They record observations about shape, center, and spread on the analysis worksheet. Repeat this process for Dataset 2 (15 minutes) and Dataset 3 (15 minutes). After analyzing all three datasets individually, students compare patterns (10 minutes): they identify which dataset is normally distributed, right-skewed, and bimodal by examining the relationship between mean and median, histogram shape, and boxplot symmetry. For the interpretation phase (20 minutes), students write a 150-word explanation for each dataset describing: what the distribution shape suggests about the real-world phenomenon, why this pattern makes logical sense, and what decisions a data scientist might make based on this distribution. Conclude with pair presentations (15 minutes) where each pair explains one dataset's distribution pattern and its practical implications to the class. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting distribution types to appropriate statistical tests and modeling approaches.
materials_needed: Three CSV datasets with known distribution patterns (normal, right-skewed, bimodal)
Statistical analysis software (R, Python with pandas/matplotlib, or Excel)
Distribution Analysis Worksheet template
Computers or tablets for each pair of students
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of distribution types based on statistical evidence, (2) Accurate interpretation of mean-median relationships and their significance, (3) Logical real-world explanations connecting distribution patterns to underlying phenomena, (4) Clear communication during pair presentations. Students must correctly identify 2/3 distribution types and provide coherent explanations for each to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference chart showing distribution shapes with corresponding mean-median relationships, and offer sentence starters for written explanations. For advanced learners: introduce concepts of kurtosis and provide additional datasets with outliers to analyze their impact on distribution interpretation, or have them research when each distribution type commonly occurs in different fields.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel placement on irregularly shaped rooftops. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal configurations that maximize energy output while respecting budget and structural limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a complex real-world solar energy optimization scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems through systematic calculation and interpretation of feasible regions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Solar Panel Optimization Scenario packet containing three different rooftop layouts (L-shaped residential, rectangular commercial, triangular industrial) with specific dimensions, weight limits, and budget constraints. Each student team of 3-4 receives one unique scenario. (5 minutes setup)

Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (25 minutes): Teams identify decision variables (number of Type A panels at $400 each producing 300W, Type B panels at $600 each producing 450W), formulate the objective function (maximize total wattage), and establish constraints (budget ≤ $12,000, weight ≤ roof capacity, area ≤ available space, non-negativity). Students must document their mathematical model on the provided worksheet template.

Phase 2 - Graphical Solution (30 minutes): For scenarios with 2 variables, teams plot constraints on coordinate planes using graphing software or grid paper, identify the feasible region, locate corner points, and evaluate the objective function at each vertex. They must show all intersection calculations and clearly mark the optimal solution.

Phase 3 - Simplex Method Application (35 minutes): Teams convert their problem to standard form, set up initial simplex tableau, and perform iterations until reaching optimality. Provide the Simplex Algorithm Reference Sheet with pivot rules and stopping criteria. Students document each tableau transformation.

Phase 4 - Solution Interpretation and Presentation (15 minutes): Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their optimal solution, including total panels of each type, maximum wattage achieved, remaining budget, and practical implementation considerations. Each team presents to the class with their final rooftop configuration diagram.
materials_needed: Solar Panel Optimization Scenario packets (3 different building types)
Graphing paper or digital graphing tool (GeoGebra/Desmos)
Scientific calculators
Simplex Algorithm Reference Sheet with pivot rules
Linear Programming Worksheet Templates
Presentation materials (whiteboard/projector access)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct problem formulation with appropriate variables and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of solution methods with proper calculations (35%), (3) Correct interpretation of optimal solution with practical considerations (25%), and (4) Clear presentation of methodology and results (15%). Students must submit completed worksheets showing all mathematical work and deliver their team presentation to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide constraint identification templates and worked examples of simpler 2-variable problems. Offer calculation checkpoints after each simplex iteration. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis questions: 'How would the solution change if budget increased by $2000?' or extend to integer programming constraints requiring whole numbers of panels. Provide additional scenarios with 3+ variables for extra challenge.

title: Critical Analysis of Database Normalization Trade-offs in E-commerce System Design
description: Students will analyze the normalization decisions in a real e-commerce database schema by examining performance bottlenecks, storage efficiency, and maintainability trade-offs. They will deconstruct the design choices and evaluate alternative normalization strategies using actual query execution plans and performance metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between normalization levels and query performance by examining execution plans and identifying specific bottlenecks in denormalized versus normalized schemas
Students will evaluate trade-offs between storage efficiency and query complexity through systematic comparison of alternative database designs using quantitative metrics
instructions: Begin by providing students with a partially denormalized e-commerce database schema containing tables for customers, orders, products, and order_items with deliberate redundancy (90 minutes total). Step 1 (20 minutes): Students examine the provided schema and identify all normalization violations, documenting each instance of data redundancy and categorizing violations by normal form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF). Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the provided dataset of 100,000 records, students execute a set of 10 predetermined queries against the denormalized schema, recording execution times and analyzing the generated query execution plans using EXPLAIN ANALYZE commands. Step 3 (25 minutes): Students redesign the schema to achieve 3NF, creating normalized tables and establishing proper foreign key relationships. They must document their decomposition decisions and justify why they stopped at 3NF rather than BCNF. Step 4 (20 minutes): Students execute the same 10 queries against their normalized schema, comparing execution times, storage requirements, and plan complexity with the original denormalized version. They create a detailed comparison matrix showing trade-offs for each query type (simple selects, complex joins, aggregations, updates). Final deliverable: Students produce a 2-page technical analysis report recommending optimal normalization strategy for different use cases, supported by their empirical findings and specific performance metrics.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database server with sample e-commerce dataset (100,000+ records)
Database modeling tool (ERDPlus or MySQL Workbench)
SQL query execution environment with EXPLAIN ANALYZE capability
Predefined set of 10 benchmark queries covering various complexity levels
Template for performance comparison matrix
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Schema analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct identification of all normalization violations; Normalization design (25 points) - proper 3NF implementation with justified design decisions; Performance analysis (30 points) - accurate execution time measurements, correct interpretation of query plans, and valid trade-off identification; Technical report (20 points) - clear recommendations supported by empirical evidence and professional presentation. Students must demonstrate quantitative analysis skills and provide specific performance metrics to support their conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist for identifying each normal form violation and offer simplified queries focused on basic joins. Supply a template for the comparison matrix with example entries. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement and analyze BCNF and 4NF versions, explore indexing strategies' impact on their findings, or analyze the schema under different workload patterns (OLTP vs OLAP). Consider having advanced students present alternative designs using NoSQL approaches for comparison.

title: Design and Build a Mathematical Game Board for Linear Functions
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates linear function concepts, requiring players to solve slope, y-intercept, and graphing challenges to advance. This activity synthesizes multiple linear function skills into an engaging, playable format that demonstrates deep understanding of mathematical relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original game board by integrating slope calculations, y-intercepts, and linear equations into playable game mechanics
Students will construct comprehensive game rules through systematic application of linear function properties and real-world problem scenarios
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and provide each team with design materials and the Linear Function Game Requirements handout. (10 minutes)

Phase 1 - Concept Integration (20 minutes): Teams brainstorm how to incorporate at least three linear function concepts (slope calculation, finding y-intercepts, writing equations from graphs, parallel/perpendicular lines) into game mechanics. Students must create a concept map showing how each mathematical element will function within their game structure.

Phase 2 - Game Design (30 minutes): Teams sketch their board layout on large poster paper, including start/finish positions, challenge spaces, and special zones. Each team creates 30 question cards across three difficulty levels (10 easy, 15 medium, 5 challenging) featuring original linear function problems with complete solutions on the back.

Phase 3 - Rule Creation (15 minutes): Students write detailed, typed game rules including setup instructions, turn sequence, winning conditions, and how mathematical challenges integrate with game progression. Rules must specify how incorrect answers affect gameplay.

Phase 4 - Prototype Construction (25 minutes): Teams assemble their physical game using poster board, markers, and provided game pieces. They create player tokens, dice modifications if needed, and organize question cards by difficulty color-coding.

Phase 5 - Peer Testing (30 minutes): Each team plays another team's game for 15 minutes, then provides written feedback on mathematical accuracy, game flow, and engagement level. Original creators observe and take notes for potential improvements.

Conclude with teams presenting one unique mathematical challenge from their game to the class, explaining the linear function concept involved and demonstrating the solution process. (15 minutes)
materials_needed: 22x28 inch poster board (1 per team)
Colored markers and pencils
Index cards (40 per team) in three different colors
Game pieces/tokens (buttons, small objects)
Standard dice
Glue sticks and scissors
Graphing paper sheets
Calculators
Linear Function Game Requirements handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25% - all problems solved correctly with clear work shown), Concept Integration (25% - at least 3 linear function topics meaningfully incorporated), Game Functionality (25% - rules are clear, game flows smoothly during peer testing), and Creative Design (25% - original layout, engaging mechanics, professional presentation). Students submit their game boards, question cards with solutions, written rules, and a reflection explaining their mathematical choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template board layout and 10 sample question cards to modify rather than create from scratch. Pair with stronger math students and allow use of graphing calculators throughout. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate piecewise functions, systems of linear equations, or real-world data analysis. Require them to include at least one 'challenge zone' with college-level linear function applications.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Reference Chart Creation
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 15 specific Big O complexity notations, their mathematical definitions, and corresponding algorithm examples. This activity focuses on building a comprehensive mental reference system for time and space complexity analysis through systematic recall practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact mathematical notation and definition for 15 different Big O complexity classes including O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(n³), O(2ⁿ), O(n!), O(√n), O(log log n), O(n log² n), O(n^k), O(k^n), O(n^n), and O(c^n) by completing a timed reference chart
Students will identify specific algorithm examples for each complexity class through a structured memorization and recall exercise
instructions: Begin by distributing the blank complexity reference template containing 15 rows with columns for notation, mathematical definition, growth rate description, and algorithm example. Students have 5 minutes to review their notes and textbooks. Remove all reference materials and explain that students will complete the chart from memory in three phases. Phase 1 (8 minutes): Students fill in only the Big O notation symbols (O(1), O(log n), etc.) in order from most efficient to least efficient. Phase 2 (12 minutes): Students add the mathematical definitions and growth rate descriptions for each notation. For example, O(log n) should include 'logarithmic growth, doubles input size adds constant operations.' Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students provide specific algorithm examples for each complexity class, such as 'binary search' for O(log n) or 'quicksort average case' for O(n log n). During each phase, students work individually without consultation. After completion, conduct a systematic review where students self-check their answers against the provided answer key. Students mark incorrect responses in red and correct ones in green. Conclude with a 5-minute discussion identifying the most commonly missed complexity classes and their characteristics. Students must achieve 80% accuracy across all categories to demonstrate successful recall mastery.
materials_needed: Blank Big O complexity reference template (15 rows x 4 columns)
Complete answer key with accepted algorithm examples
Red and green colored pens for self-assessment
Timer or stopwatch for phase management
assessment_method: Students submit completed reference charts showing 12 of 15 complexity notations correctly recalled (80% accuracy threshold). Grading rubric: Notation symbols (30 points - 2 points each), Mathematical definitions (45 points - 3 points each), Algorithm examples (45 points - 3 points each). Partial credit given for incomplete but accurate responses. Charts scoring below 80% require remediation and retesting.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed template with the most common notations (O(1), O(n), O(n²)) pre-filled as anchors. Allow advanced learners to include additional complexity classes like amortized analysis notations or provide multiple algorithm examples per complexity class. Consider extending with space complexity analysis for high achievers.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance Techniques in Complex Machine Learning Pipelines
description: Students will analyze and compare three different feature importance methods (SHAP, permutation importance, and LIME) applied to the same gradient boosting model trained on tabular data. They will interpret the underlying mathematical principles and explain why different methods yield varying importance rankings for the same features.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical foundations of SHAP values, permutation importance, and LIME by analyzing their computational approaches and underlying assumptions
Students will distinguish between global and local feature importance interpretations through comparative analysis of method outputs on identical model predictions
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a pre-trained XGBoost model on the UCI Adult Income dataset and three sets of feature importance outputs (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to examine Dataset A: SHAP summary plots and waterfall charts, Dataset B: permutation importance rankings with confidence intervals, and Dataset C: LIME explanations for 5 specific predictions. In Phase 1 (30 minutes), students document the top 5 most important features according to each method, noting numerical importance scores and ranking differences. They must identify which features show the largest ranking discrepancies between methods. In Phase 2 (45 minutes), students research and summarize the mathematical approach each method uses: SHAP's game-theoretic Shapley values, permutation importance's model performance degradation measurement, and LIME's local linear approximation technique. They create a comparison matrix showing method type (global vs local), computational complexity, and interpretability trade-offs. In Phase 3 (40 minutes), students select three features that ranked differently across methods and write detailed explanations for why these discrepancies occur, referencing the mathematical foundations. They must connect method assumptions to observed differences (e.g., SHAP considers feature interactions while permutation importance may not capture complex dependencies). Students conclude by writing a 300-word technical memo recommending which method to use for different stakeholder audiences (technical teams vs business executives), justifying their recommendations with specific mathematical and interpretability reasoning.
materials_needed: Pre-trained XGBoost model file (.pkl format) with UCI Adult Income dataset
Three CSV files containing SHAP values, permutation importance scores, and LIME explanations
Jupyter notebook template with data loading code and visualization functions
Python environment with shap, scikit-learn, and lime libraries installed
Comparison matrix template (Excel or Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Accuracy of mathematical explanations for each method (30 points) - must correctly describe Shapley values, permutation testing, and local approximation; (2) Quality of discrepancy analysis (25 points) - identifies valid reasons for ranking differences with specific examples; (3) Appropriateness of stakeholder recommendations (25 points) - matches method characteristics to audience needs; (4) Technical memo clarity and precision (20 points) - uses correct terminology and logical reasoning
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions about each method's core concept and offer simplified explanations of Shapley values using game theory analogies. Include reference sheets with method definitions. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement simplified versions of each algorithm from scratch, or analyze additional methods like Integrated Gradients or TreeExplainer optimizations. Encourage exploration of computational complexity trade-offs in production environments.

title: Building a Dream Playground: Area and Perimeter Application
description: Students will design a rectangular playground by applying area and perimeter formulas to meet specific budget and space constraints. They will calculate dimensions, determine costs, and justify their design choices using mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply area formulas to calculate the space needed for playground equipment by solving real-world constraint problems
Students will apply perimeter formulas to determine fencing costs through hands-on design scenarios
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the playground design worksheet and measuring tools. Post the constraint requirements on the board: playground must have area between 200-400 square meters, budget of $2,000 for fencing at $5 per meter, and must fit on a lot that is 25 meters wide maximum.

**Individual Planning (10 minutes):** Students sketch their initial playground design on grid paper (1 square = 1 square meter). They must label dimensions and show where swings, slides, and benches will go within their rectangle.

**Calculations Phase (15 minutes):** Students calculate the area of their proposed rectangle using length × width. Then calculate perimeter using 2(length + width). Next, they multiply perimeter by $5 to find fencing cost. If over budget, they must redesign.

**Partner Review (10 minutes):** Students pair up to check each other's calculations using calculators. Partners verify that all constraints are met and calculations are correct.

**Presentation Preparation (5 minutes):** Each student prepares a 1-minute presentation explaining their final design, showing their calculations, and stating why their playground meets all requirements.

**Gallery Walk (10 minutes):** Students post their designs around the room and walk around to view others' solutions, noting different approaches on sticky notes.

**Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write a brief paragraph explaining which constraint was most challenging to meet and how they adjusted their design.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
Rulers and measuring tape
Calculators
Colored pencils or markers
Playground design worksheet template
Sticky notes for feedback
assessment_method: Students will be assessed using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct area calculation, (2) Correct perimeter calculation, (3) Design meets all three constraints, (4) Clear explanation of design choices. Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher. Observe during partner work to assess problem-solving process and mathematical communication.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template with dimensions already started (e.g., 'If length is 15m, width could be ___'). For advanced learners: Add a third constraint requiring the playground to have specific equipment zones with their own area requirements, or introduce irregular shapes requiring composite area calculations.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Performance Under Different Data Conditions
description: Students will systematically analyze and compare the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their execution times and operation counts under various data conditions. They will identify patterns in algorithm behavior and determine optimal use cases for each algorithm based on empirical evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity behavior of sorting algorithms by measuring execution times across different input sizes and data distributions
Students will evaluate algorithm performance trade-offs through systematic comparison of operation counts and memory usage patterns
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Divide students into groups of 3-4. Each group receives the provided Python template containing implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort with built-in counters for comparisons and swaps. Students should verify all algorithms work correctly with the sample dataset provided.

**Data Preparation (15 minutes):** Each group generates four test datasets for each size category (100, 500, 1000, 5000 elements): (1) randomly shuffled integers, (2) already sorted integers, (3) reverse-sorted integers, and (4) datasets with many duplicate values. Students should use the random.seed(42) function to ensure reproducible results.

**Execution Phase (25 minutes):** Groups systematically run each algorithm on every dataset combination, recording: execution time (using time.perf_counter()), number of comparisons performed, number of swaps/moves executed, and qualitative observations about performance patterns. Students must run each test three times and calculate average values to account for system variations.

**Analysis Phase (30 minutes):** Students create comparative charts showing performance trends across input sizes and data types. They identify which algorithm performs best under specific conditions and document unexpected results. Groups should calculate the growth rate ratios between different input sizes to verify theoretical complexity predictions.

**Synthesis Phase (15 minutes):** Each group prepares a summary table ranking algorithms by performance category and writes recommendations for when to use each algorithm based on their empirical findings.
materials_needed: Python 3.x environment with matplotlib library installed
Provided algorithm template file (sorting_analysis.py)
Spreadsheet software or graph paper for data recording
Timer/stopwatch functionality (built into Python template)
Sample datasets generator script
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) completed data table with all timing and operation count measurements, (2) three comparative graphs showing performance trends, (3) written analysis (250 words) explaining which algorithm performs best under different conditions with specific evidence from their data, and (4) algorithm recommendation matrix matching use cases to optimal algorithms. Rubric awards points for data accuracy (25%), graph clarity (25%), evidence-based conclusions (30%), and practical recommendations (20%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-generated datasets and focus on analyzing provided results rather than generating data. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to bubble sort time when data is already sorted?' For advanced learners: Include analysis of hybrid algorithms, investigate memory usage patterns, or implement additional algorithms like heap sort. Consider having advanced students analyze space complexity alongside time complexity.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Emergency Response Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to minimize emergency response times across a city network, then develop algorithms to solve their model and present implementation strategies. This activity integrates graph theory, calculus optimization, and linear programming to address real-world emergency services allocation.
estimated_duration: 5.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical optimization model incorporating multiple variables and constraints by analyzing emergency response network requirements and applying advanced mathematical techniques
Students will design custom algorithms and solution methods through systematic mathematical reasoning and computational implementation to solve their created optimization problem
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with a city map dataset containing 50+ locations, population densities, and current emergency station positions. Teams must first analyze the problem constraints: response time targets (<8 minutes), budget limitations ($2M), staffing requirements, and coverage mandates (Phase 1: 45 minutes). Next, students formulate their mathematical model by defining decision variables (station locations, resource allocation), creating objective functions (minimize average response time or maximize coverage), and establishing mathematical constraints using inequalities and equations (Phase 2: 60 minutes). Teams then develop solution algorithms, choosing from linear programming, genetic algorithms, or custom heuristic methods, documenting mathematical justification for their approach (Phase 3: 75 minutes). Students implement their algorithms using provided computational tools, test multiple scenarios, and validate results against real-world feasibility (Phase 4: 90 minutes). Finally, teams create comprehensive presentations including mathematical model formulation, algorithm design rationale, computational results with visualizations, sensitivity analysis, and implementation recommendations for city planners (Phase 5: 60 minutes). Throughout the activity, instructors circulate to provide mathematical guidance, verify model validity, and ensure rigorous mathematical reasoning. Teams present their solutions in 15-minute sessions, with peer evaluation and expert feedback on mathematical sophistication and practical applicability.
materials_needed: City geographical datasets with coordinate systems and demographic data
MATLAB, Python with optimization libraries, or Mathematica software access
Graph theory reference materials and optimization textbooks
Large format paper and mathematical drawing tools for model visualization
Laptops or workstations with mathematical computing capabilities
assessment_method: Evaluate using a detailed rubric scoring: Mathematical model formulation and constraint accuracy (25 points), algorithm design creativity and mathematical rigor (25 points), computational implementation and results validation (20 points), presentation clarity and real-world applicability (20 points), peer collaboration and mathematical communication (10 points). Final deliverables include written mathematical model documentation, working algorithm code, results analysis report, and oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for model formulation, offer simplified constraint examples, and pair with stronger mathematical peers. Supply additional resources on optimization theory basics. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or dynamic programming approaches. Encourage exploration of machine learning integration or real-time adaptive algorithms. Provide access to advanced mathematical literature and professional optimization software.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Emergency Response Networks: Practical Workshop
description: Students will synthesize multiple mathematical concepts including graph theory, optimization techniques, and probability distributions to create an original mathematical model that optimizes emergency response dispatch systems for a city. They will present their model with complete mathematical justification and computational implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical optimization model by integrating graph theory, linear programming, and stochastic processes to solve a real-world emergency response problem
Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts through developing algorithmic solutions and defending their modeling choices with rigorous mathematical proof
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Present students with authentic city emergency response data including: historical call volumes by district, response time requirements, ambulance/fire truck locations, and traffic pattern data. Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the mathematical relationships and identify optimization opportunities. **Phase 2 (90 minutes):** Teams construct their mathematical model by: (1) Defining decision variables and constraints using linear/integer programming notation, (2) Formulating objective functions that balance response time minimization with resource allocation efficiency, (3) Incorporating probabilistic elements for call prediction using Poisson distributions or similar stochastic models, (4) Creating graph-theoretic representations of the road network with weighted edges for travel times. **Phase 3 (60 minutes):** Teams implement their model computationally using optimization software (CPLEX, Gurobi, or Python with PuLP library). They must run sensitivity analyses testing different scenarios (rush hour traffic, multiple simultaneous emergencies, equipment failures). **Phase 4 (45 minutes):** Each team presents their complete solution including: mathematical formulation with all equations clearly stated, computational results with performance metrics, theoretical justification for modeling choices, and comparison with current city response systems. Teams must defend their approach during a 10-minute Q&A session with mathematical rigor.
materials_needed: Real emergency response dataset (6 months of call data, response times, locations)
City road network graph data with traffic patterns
Optimization software access (CPLEX, Gurobi, or Python with PuLP/SciPy)
Graphing calculators or mathematical software (MATLAB, Mathematica)
Large format paper for mathematical notation and model visualization
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Mathematical rigor and correctness of model formulation (30 points), Innovation and sophistication of approach integrating multiple mathematical domains (25 points), Computational implementation accuracy and efficiency analysis (20 points), Quality of mathematical presentation and defense of methodology (15 points), Practical applicability and improvement over baseline systems (10 points). Final deliverable includes written mathematical report with complete proofs and executable code.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students: Provide template frameworks for linear programming formulation and sample graph theory applications. Offer guided practice with smaller optimization problems first. Advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate machine learning prediction models, multi-objective optimization with Pareto frontiers, or dynamic programming for real-time updates. Encourage exploration of network flow algorithms and advanced stochastic modeling techniques.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Emergency Response Networks

title: Binary Number System Digit Cards Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the decimal equivalents of single-digit binary numbers (0000-1111) through repetitive flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential number system recognition skills needed for all computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) by completing timed flashcard sessions with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8) through structured memorization drills and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary flashcards to each student (16 cards total: 0000=0 through 1111=15). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, with Partner A showing the binary side while Partner B states the decimal equivalent, then switching roles after 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class place value chant: students stand and recite '8-4-2-1' while pointing to each finger position three times. For minutes 15-25, students work individually through their complete card stack three times, sorting cards into 'know immediately' and 'need practice' piles. During minutes 25-30, conduct Round 1 assessment: call out binary numbers randomly while students write decimal answers on whiteboards, holding up answers simultaneously. Record students who answer correctly within 3 seconds. For minutes 30-35, have struggling students practice with their 'need practice' pile while proficient students help peers. Conclude with Round 2 assessment (minutes 35-40): repeat the whiteboard exercise with different binary numbers, aiming for improved accuracy and speed. End with students completing a self-reflection checklist rating their confidence level (1-5) for each binary number.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards showing 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on one side and decimal equivalents (0-15) on reverse
Individual dry-erase whiteboards and markers for each student
Timer or stopwatch
Self-reflection checklist worksheet
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 14 out of 16 binary-to-decimal conversions within 3 seconds each during the final timed assessment round. Track accuracy using a checklist with student names and binary numbers (0000-1111). Success criteria: 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) with response time under 3 seconds per conversion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a place value chart (8-4-2-1) reference sheet and focus on patterns (all numbers ending in 1 are odd, numbers starting with 1 are 8 or higher). For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (10000-11111) or challenge them to convert decimal back to binary. Consider pairing strong students with those needing support during partner practice.

title: Deconstructing Algorithm Efficiency: Big O Analysis of Real-World Code Implementations
description: Students will analyze multiple implementations of the same algorithmic problem to identify performance bottlenecks and compare time/space complexity trade-offs. They will decompose complex nested algorithms, examine recursive patterns, and evaluate which implementation performs best under different data constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of nested loop structures and recursive functions by systematically breaking down each operation and identifying dominant terms
Students will compare multiple algorithm implementations through detailed complexity analysis and empirical performance testing
instructions: Begin by providing students with 4 different implementations of a graph shortest-path algorithm (brute force, Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, and A*). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Each pair examines the code structure, identifying loops, recursive calls, and data structure operations without running the code. They create a visual breakdown showing nested operations and dependency relationships. Next 25 minutes: Students mathematically derive the Big O notation for each implementation, documenting their reasoning step-by-step. They must identify the worst-case scenario for each algorithm and explain why. Following 25 minutes: Pairs run each algorithm on three different graph datasets (small dense graph with 50 nodes, large sparse graph with 1000 nodes, and medium complete graph with 200 nodes), recording actual execution times and memory usage. Final 20 minutes: Students create a comparison matrix analyzing when each algorithm performs best, identifying the breakeven points where one algorithm becomes more efficient than another. They must connect their theoretical Big O analysis to the empirical results, explaining any discrepancies between predicted and actual performance.
materials_needed: Four pre-written graph algorithm implementations in Python or Java
Three graph datasets of varying sizes and densities (provided as adjacency matrices)
Performance profiling tools (Python's cProfile or Java's JProfiler)
Computers with development environment installed
Algorithm complexity reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate based on 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of Big O derivations with complete mathematical justification, (2) Quality of visual algorithm breakdown showing understanding of nested operations, (3) Correctness of performance predictions and actual testing methodology, (4) Depth of analysis connecting theoretical complexity to empirical results, including explanation of discrepancies and identification of optimal use cases for each algorithm
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template showing how to count operations in simple nested loops before tackling complex algorithms. Offer a step-by-step Big O calculation example. For advanced learners: Challenge them to modify one algorithm to improve its complexity, or analyze how different data structures (heaps vs arrays) affect the same algorithm's performance. Provide additional algorithms like Bellman-Ford for extended comparison.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Chart Type Selection Critique
description: Students critically assess the appropriateness of different chart types for given datasets and research questions. They will evaluate pre-made visualizations, identify strengths and weaknesses, and justify their recommendations for improvement based on data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types by analyzing their appropriateness for specific data types and research questions
Students will critique data visualizations through systematic assessment using established visualization principles and best practices
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with the 'Visualization Evaluation Worksheet' containing 6 different charts (bar chart, pie chart, scatter plot, line graph, histogram, and box plot) created from the same ice cream sales dataset. Each chart attempts to answer the question 'Which ice cream flavor sells best during summer months?' 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization and complete the initial assessment section, rating each chart's clarity (1-5 scale) and noting first impressions.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation criteria checklist covering: data type appropriateness, visual clarity, accurate representation, ease of interpretation, and relevance to research question. Students re-examine each chart using these specific criteria.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students rank the 6 visualizations from most to least effective, writing 2-3 sentence justifications for their top and bottom choices.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pair students to compare rankings and discuss discrepancies. Each pair must reach consensus on the top 2 and bottom 2 visualizations.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class discussion where pairs share their conclusions. Record common themes on the board.

Step 6 (15 minutes): Students individually complete reflection questions: 'What makes a visualization effective for this research question?' and 'How would you improve the least effective chart?' Provide specific improvement suggestions with rationale.

Conclude by having 3-4 students share one key insight about chart selection they discovered during the evaluation process.
materials_needed: Visualization Evaluation Worksheet with 6 pre-made charts from ice cream sales dataset
Evaluation Criteria Checklist handout
Sample ice cream sales dataset (Excel/CSV file with flavor, month, sales volume columns)
Computers or tablets for viewing digital charts
Whiteboard or flipchart for class discussion notes
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of chart type evaluation (25 points) - correctly identifies strengths/weaknesses of each visualization type; (2) Quality of justification (25 points) - provides clear, evidence-based reasoning for rankings; (3) Use of evaluation criteria (25 points) - systematically applies provided criteria framework; (4) Improvement suggestions (25 points) - offers specific, actionable recommendations for enhancing poor visualizations. Students must score 70+ points to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of one chart before the activity begins, and offer guiding questions like 'Does this chart type match the data type?' For advanced learners: Include additional challenge charts with misleading scales or inappropriate chart types, and ask them to create their own improved version of the worst-performing visualization using spreadsheet software.

title: Design Your Dream Playground: Area, Perimeter, and Budget Optimization Project
description: Students will design an original playground layout by creating geometric shapes, calculating areas and perimeters, and working within a realistic budget constraint. They will present their design with mathematical justifications for their choices and optimize their layout based on cost-effectiveness.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original playground layout by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and circles within specified constraints
Students will construct mathematical arguments through cost-benefit analysis and geometric optimization while presenting their design rationale
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute grid paper, calculators, and project packets containing: playground equipment catalog with prices, safety spacing requirements, and lot specifications (rectangular lot: 120ft × 80ft, budget: $45,000). Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Design Phase (40 minutes):** Teams sketch their playground layout on grid paper using 1 square = 4ft². They must include at least 6 pieces of equipment, calculating the area each occupies plus required safety zones (circles/rectangles around each item). Students create a data table showing: equipment name, dimensions, area calculation with formula, safety zone area, and cost.

**Optimization Phase (25 minutes):** Teams calculate total playground area, remaining green space, and total cost. If over budget, they must redesign by removing/replacing items or adjusting layout. They calculate the cost per square foot of play area to determine efficiency.

**Presentation Preparation (15 minutes):** Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation including: final design sketch, area calculations table, budget breakdown, and one mathematical justification for their layout choice (e.g., "We positioned the swing set in a corner because its 20ft safety radius creates a semicircle against the fence, saving 314 square feet compared to a full circle").

**Presentations (30 minutes):** Each team presents while others use provided feedback forms to evaluate mathematical accuracy and design creativity. Teacher records area calculations and budget totals for assessment.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1 sheet per student)
Playground equipment catalog with dimensions and prices
Scientific calculators
Rulers and colored pencils
Project specification sheets with lot dimensions and budget
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Mathematical accuracy (40%) - correct area/perimeter formulas and calculations; Design creativity (25%) - innovative layout and equipment selection; Budget management (20%) - staying within constraints and showing optimization; Presentation clarity (15%) - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning. Successful projects score 3+ on all rubric categories with accurate calculations and realistic designs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide area formula reference sheet and pre-calculated safety zone templates. For advanced learners: add irregular shapes like hexagonal climbing structures, include landscaping costs with irregular areas, or optimize for maximum play area rather than staying under budget. Consider pairing stronger math students with those needing support.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Speed Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate rapid recall of Big O notation definitions, common algorithm complexities, and mathematical properties through timed identification exercises. This activity reinforces memorization of fundamental complexity theory concepts essential for advanced algorithmic analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the precise mathematical definitions of Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations within 30 seconds per definition
Students will instantly identify the time complexity classifications for 25 common algorithms through rapid-fire recognition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the algorithm complexity reference sheet face-down to each student. Explain that this is a timed recall exercise with three phases. Phase 1 (10 minutes): Display asymptotic notation symbols (O, Θ, Ω) one at a time on the projector for 30 seconds each. Students must write the complete mathematical definition including limit notation and inequality relationships. Collect responses immediately after each symbol. Phase 2 (15 minutes): Present algorithm names on flashcards in rapid succession (15 seconds per card). Include: QuickSort average case, QuickSort worst case, MergeSort, HeapSort, Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, Binary Search, Linear Search, Hash table insertion, Red-Black tree insertion, BFS, DFS, Matrix multiplication (naive), Strassen's algorithm, FFT, KMP string matching, Rabin-Karp, Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, Counting Sort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort, Prim's algorithm, and Kruskal's algorithm. Students write only the Big O complexity. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Show complexity expressions (e.g., '2n² + 3n + 1', 'log(n!) + n²', '4^log₂(n)') and students must identify the simplified Big O form within 20 seconds per expression. Use a timer visible to all students. Ring a bell between each item to maintain pace. Students may not reference materials during the exercise but can use the reference sheet during a 2-minute review period before starting.
materials_needed: Algorithm complexity reference sheet (1 per student)
Digital timer with audible alerts
Projector for displaying problems
Pre-prepared flashcards with 25 algorithm names
Answer collection sheets numbered 1-40
Bell or chime for transitions
assessment_method: Grade using a point system: Phase 1 (30 points) - 10 points per correct mathematical definition including proper limit notation; Phase 2 (25 points) - 1 point per correct algorithm complexity; Phase 3 (15 points) - 1.5 points per correct simplified expression. Total possible: 70 points. Success criteria: 80% accuracy (56+ points) demonstrates mastery of complexity theory recall. Partial credit given for definitions with minor notation errors but correct conceptual understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a practice session 24 hours prior using half the material at slower pace. Allow them to create personal mnemonics during review time. For advanced learners: Add Phase 4 with space complexity recall for the same algorithms, or include amortized analysis complexities for advanced data structures like dynamic arrays and splay trees. Consider bonus questions on average vs. worst-case distinctions.

title: Interpreting Deep Learning Model Interpretability Through SHAP Value Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values from a pre-trained neural network to understand feature importance and model decision-making processes. They will examine how different feature contributions lead to specific predictions in complex black-box models.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP value distributions and feature importance rankings by analyzing waterfall plots, summary plots, and partial dependence plots from a pre-trained deep learning model
Students will explain the relationship between local and global model interpretability through systematic examination of individual prediction explanations and aggregate feature impact patterns
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-trained neural network model (TensorFlow/Keras) trained on the California Housing dataset and corresponding SHAP explainer object (15 minutes setup). Distribute the standardized Jupyter notebook template containing the model, test dataset (500 samples), and SHAP values pre-computed to save processing time. 

Students work in pairs to complete four analysis phases: First, examine global feature importance using SHAP summary plots, identifying the top 5 most influential features and documenting their average impact magnitude (20 minutes). Second, select 3 specific predictions with different price ranges (low, medium, high) and generate SHAP waterfall plots for each, documenting how individual features push predictions above or below the expected value (25 minutes). Third, create partial dependence plots for the top 2 features, analyzing how feature value changes affect model output while holding other features constant (20 minutes). Fourth, compare local explanations (individual predictions) with global patterns, identifying instances where local feature importance deviates significantly from global trends (15 minutes).

Students document findings in a structured analysis template, recording specific SHAP values, feature importance rankings, and written interpretations of model behavior. Each pair presents one key insight about feature interactions or unexpected model behavior to the class (20 minutes). Conclude with instructor-led discussion connecting SHAP interpretations to real-world model deployment considerations, ethical AI, and stakeholder communication strategies (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Pre-trained neural network model file (.h5 format) trained on California Housing dataset
SHAP library (v0.41+) and explainer object pre-computed
Structured analysis template worksheet (digital PDF)
California Housing test dataset (500 samples, CSV format)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of SHAP value interpretations and feature importance rankings, (2) Quality of explanations connecting local predictions to global patterns, (3) Identification of meaningful insights about model behavior and feature interactions, (4) Clear communication of findings with appropriate technical vocabulary. Students submit completed analysis template plus one-paragraph reflection on implications for model transparency in real-world applications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions for each analysis phase and pre-highlighted examples of strong vs. weak feature contributions. Offer simplified interpretation frameworks focusing on positive/negative impacts before magnitude analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential model biases through SHAP analysis, compare SHAP explanations with LIME interpretations, or explore clustering of similar explanation patterns across predictions.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Scenarios
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional college student using given income data, then apply percentage calculations to allocate funds across different expense categories. They will calculate what percentage of income goes to each category and determine if adjustments are needed to stay within budget limits.
