learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting dollar amounts to percentages of total income
Students will implement mathematical problem-solving strategies through real-world budget scenarios requiring percentage-based decisions
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'College Student Profile' worksheet containing a fictional student's monthly income of $1,200 from part-time work and family support (5 minutes). Organize students into pairs and provide each pair with expense category cards showing typical costs: Housing ($480), Food ($240), Transportation ($120), Entertainment ($96), Savings ($144), and Miscellaneous ($120). Students first calculate what percentage each expense represents of the total $1,200 income using the formula (expense ÷ income) × 100 (15 minutes). Next, present a scenario where the student's income drops to $1,000. Pairs must recalculate percentages and decide which categories to adjust, ensuring expenses don't exceed income (20 minutes). Students then create a visual pie chart showing their final budget allocation with both dollar amounts and percentages labeled clearly (10 minutes). Have each pair present one category adjustment they made and explain their mathematical reasoning using percentage language (e.g., 'We reduced entertainment from 8% to 6% of total income') (15 minutes). Conclude with students completing individual reflection questions about when percentage calculations are useful in financial decisions (10 minutes). Circulate continuously to check calculations and guide students toward correct percentage formulas. Emphasize that percentages must total 100% and expenses cannot exceed 100% of income.
materials_needed: College Student Profile worksheets (one per pair)
Expense category cards with dollar amounts
Calculators
Blank pie chart templates
Colored pencils or markers
Individual reflection question sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets for accurate percentage calculations (40 points: 5 points per calculation with work shown). Assess pie charts for correct visual representation with properly labeled percentages totaling 100% (30 points). Grade oral presentations on clear explanation of mathematical reasoning using percentage terminology (20 points). Review reflection responses for understanding of real-world percentage applications (10 points). Success criteria: 80% accuracy on calculations, visual charts match numerical work, and explanations demonstrate understanding of percentage relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage calculation reference cards showing the formula step-by-step, offer pre-drawn pie chart sections to reduce cognitive load, and pair them with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including variable income scenarios, introduce compound percentage changes (e.g., 'income increases 15% but rent increases 8%'), or have them create budget comparison charts showing percentage changes over multiple months.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional character using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply their knowledge of percentages to solve practical financial planning problems while justifying their budget decisions based on mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by computing exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and savings categories
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage relationships through creating and defending a balanced monthly budget scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the character profile cards (10 minutes). Each student receives a different fictional character with specific monthly income, age, location, and family situation. Explain that students must create a realistic monthly budget using the 50/30/20 rule as a starting framework: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings. Provide the budget worksheet template and demonstrate one calculation example on the board. Students work individually for 25 minutes calculating exact dollar amounts for each category. They must show all percentage calculations (income × percentage = dollar amount) and ensure totals equal 100% of income. After completing calculations, students must justify why they allocated specific percentages within each major category (for example, explaining why they chose 15% for food versus 12% for transportation within the 'needs' category). In the final 15 minutes, pair students to present their budgets to each other, comparing allocation strategies and identifying mathematical reasoning behind decisions. Partners check each other's calculations for accuracy and provide feedback on whether percentages add up correctly. Conclude with whole-class discussion about how percentage applications help in real-world decision making, highlighting different valid approaches students discovered.
materials_needed: Character profile cards (20 different scenarios with varying incomes from $2,500-$5,000)
Budget worksheet templates with percentage calculation spaces
Calculators (one per student)
Colored pencils or highlighters for categorizing expenses
assessment_method: Grade completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Calculation accuracy - all percentages correctly converted to dollar amounts, totals sum to 100% (2) Mathematical work shown - clear percentage calculations displayed (3) Realistic allocations - budget categories appropriate for character profile (4) Written justification - explanations demonstrate understanding of percentage relationships in decision-making
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a partially completed example budget and offer percentage calculation reference cards showing the formula (whole × percent ÷ 100 = part). For advanced learners: include additional complexity by adding irregular expenses like annual insurance payments that must be converted to monthly percentages, or challenge them to create budgets for multiple family members with different income sources.
original_title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Scenarios

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional college student using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage increase/decrease concepts to adjust their budget based on changing circumstances.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by calculating percentages of total income for housing, food, transportation, and entertainment expenses
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage change by adjusting budget categories when income increases or decreases by given percentages
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Scenario' worksheet to each student (5 minutes). Students receive a fictional monthly income of $1,800 and must allocate funds using these percentage guidelines: housing (35%), food (20%), transportation (15%), entertainment (10%), savings (10%), miscellaneous (10%). Have students work individually to calculate dollar amounts for each category using the formula: (percentage ÷ 100) × total income. Students should show all work and round to the nearest dollar (15 minutes). Next, present three budget adjustment scenarios on the board: Scenario A - income increases by 15% due to a promotion, Scenario B - income decreases by 20% due to reduced work hours, Scenario C - housing costs increase by 25% while income stays the same. Students select one scenario and recalculate their entire budget, maintaining the same percentage allocations where possible (20 minutes). For Scenario C, students must decide which categories to reduce to accommodate the housing increase. Students then pair up to compare their calculations and discuss their decision-making process for Scenario C adjustments (10 minutes). Finally, each pair presents one calculation example to the class, explaining their method and reasoning (15 minutes). Throughout the activity, circulate to check calculations and provide guidance on percentage formulas.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Scenario worksheets (one per student)
Calculators
Whiteboard or projector for displaying scenarios
Pencils and scratch paper
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with clear work shown, appropriate scenario adjustments with logical reasoning; (3) Most calculations correct with minor errors, reasonable scenario adjustments; (2) Some calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of percentage concepts; (1) Multiple errors indicating incomplete understanding. Also observe peer discussions for evidence of explaining mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a percentage calculation reference sheet and work through the first budget category together. Consider pairing them with stronger math students during pair work. For advanced learners: add a fourth scenario requiring them to calculate what percentage income increase would be needed to afford a $200 rent increase while maintaining all other allocations, or have them create compound scenarios (e.g., income increases 10% AND housing costs increase 15%).
original_title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Scenarios

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Population Dynamics in an Ecological System
description: Students will create an original mathematical model using differential equations to predict population changes in a predator-prey ecosystem. They will validate their model against real data, present their findings, and propose management strategies based on their mathematical predictions.
estimated_duration: 405 minutes (6.75 hours, typically spread across 2-3 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a system of coupled differential equations by analyzing ecological relationships and population feedback mechanisms
Students will synthesize mathematical modeling techniques, parameter estimation methods, and data validation to create a comprehensive predictive tool for ecosystem management
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team a different predator-prey system (wolves-deer, lynx-snowshoe hare, sharks-fish, etc.). In the first 90 minutes, teams research their assigned ecosystem and identify key variables affecting population dynamics. Students must establish at least 4 mathematical relationships including birth rates, death rates, predation rates, and carrying capacity. Next, teams spend 120 minutes constructing their differential equation system using the Lotka-Volterra model as a foundation, but modifying it to include realistic factors like environmental carrying capacity, seasonal variations, and human interference. Students should use symbolic math software to set up their equations and define parameters. During the following 90 minutes, teams obtain real population data from ecological databases (provide specific datasets for each ecosystem) and use numerical methods to estimate parameters for their model. They must validate their model by comparing predictions to actual population trends over a 20-year period. In the final 60 minutes, each team creates a presentation showing their mathematical model, parameter justification, validation results, and three specific management recommendations based on their model's predictions. Teams must also propose one extension to their model that addresses climate change impacts. Conclude with 45 minutes of presentations where each team has 8 minutes to present plus 2 minutes for peer questions. Require teams to defend their mathematical choices and parameter selections during the Q&A period.
materials_needed: Access to mathematical software (Mathematica, MATLAB, or Python with SciPy)
Ecological population datasets from GBIF or similar databases
Graphing calculators or tablets for parameter estimation
Presentation software and projector
Printed research articles on assigned predator-prey systems
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model construction and justification (35 points), parameter estimation and validation accuracy (25 points), presentation quality and defense of mathematical choices (20 points), creativity in model extensions and management recommendations (15 points), peer evaluation of questions asked during presentations (5 points). Success requires demonstrating mathematical rigor, ecological understanding, and clear communication of complex quantitative relationships.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template differential equation structures and guiding questions for parameter identification. Offer intermediate checkpoints every 60 minutes for instructor feedback. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, spatial distribution factors, or multiple predator species. Provide reference sheets with common ecological parameters and units to prevent computational errors.

title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Portfolios Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real estate investment optimization problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will use the simplex method and graphical analysis to determine optimal property allocations while maximizing return on investment within budget and risk parameters.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to transform a multi-variable real estate investment scenario into a mathematical model with objective functions and constraints
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis to solve optimization problems through systematic computational procedures
instructions: Begin by distributing the Real Estate Investment Scenario packet containing data on 5 different property types (residential, commercial, industrial, retail, mixed-use) with specific ROI percentages, initial costs, maintenance requirements, and risk factors. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify decision variables, constraints, and the objective function. Each pair must define variables (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄, x₅ representing investment amounts in each property type), establish constraints (budget limit of $2.5M, maximum 40% in high-risk properties, minimum 15% in residential, maintenance costs under $150K annually), and formulate the objective function to maximize total ROI. Next, spend 25 minutes having pairs set up the initial simplex tableau on provided grid paper, clearly labeling all columns and rows. Students then execute 3-4 iterations of the simplex method, showing all pivot operations and calculations. For verification, pairs use graphing calculators or Desmos to create a graphical representation of the feasible region (limited to 2-3 variables for visualization). During the final 20 minutes, each pair prepares a one-page investment recommendation report stating their optimal solution, maximum expected return, and justification for the allocation. Circulate continuously to verify mathematical accuracy and provide hints on pivot selection. Conclude with 3-4 pairs presenting their solutions, comparing different optimal allocations and discussing sensitivity analysis implications.
materials_needed: Real Estate Investment Scenario data packets (1 per pair)
Large grid paper sheets for simplex tableaux
Graphing calculators or laptop access to Desmos
Investment recommendation report template
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation accuracy (25 points) - correct variables, constraints, and objective function; Simplex method execution (35 points) - proper tableau setup, accurate pivot operations, correct final solution; Graphical verification (20 points) - feasible region identification and optimal point marking; Professional recommendation report (20 points) - clear communication of results and business justification
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed first simplex tableau and constraint inequality examples. Offer a step-by-step simplex method reference card. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking them to determine how changes in ROI rates affect the optimal solution, or add integer programming constraints requiring whole property purchases.

title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Portfolios Using Linear Programming: Visual Analysis
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real estate investment optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal investment strategies for maximizing profit while managing risk and budget limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert real-world investment scenarios into mathematical constraint systems
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis to determine optimal investment allocations through systematic problem-solving procedures
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Real Estate Investment Scenario packet containing data on 5 property types (residential, commercial, industrial, retail, mixed-use) with their respective ROI rates, risk factors, and minimum investment requirements. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a different investor profile with unique budget constraints and risk tolerance levels. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze their investor profile and identify decision variables (x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄, x₅ representing investment amounts in each property type). They must formulate the objective function to maximize expected annual return while incorporating risk penalties.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students establish constraint equations including: budget limitations (total investment ≤ available capital), diversification requirements (no single property type > 40% of portfolio), minimum investment thresholds per property type, and risk tolerance limits (weighted risk score ≤ investor's maximum acceptable risk).

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams apply the graphical method for simplified 2-variable versions of their problem, plotting constraint lines and identifying the feasible region. They locate corner points and evaluate the objective function at each vertex.

Step 4 (35 minutes): Using provided simplex method worksheets, students solve their complete 5-variable optimization problem. They set up initial tableau, perform pivot operations, and iterate until reaching the optimal solution.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation showing their optimal investment allocation, expected annual return, risk assessment, and justification for their mathematical approach. Each presentation must include visual displays of their constraint graphs and final simplex tableau.
materials_needed: Real Estate Investment Scenario packets (one per team with different investor profiles)
Graph paper and rulers for plotting constraint lines
Scientific calculators
Simplex method worksheet templates
Presentation boards or poster paper
Excel or GeoGebra software access (optional for verification)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation accuracy (25 points - correct objective function and all constraints identified), Mathematical execution (35 points - proper application of graphical and simplex methods), Solution validity (25 points - optimal solution satisfies all constraints and maximizes objective function), Presentation clarity (15 points - clear explanation of methodology and results). Teams must submit their complete work showing all mathematical steps and receive peer evaluations during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates with partially completed examples, offer guided practice with simpler 2-variable problems first, and create checkpoint moments for instructor feedback. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis to examine how changes in ROI rates affect optimal solutions, explore integer programming constraints for whole-property purchases only, or incorporate stochastic elements with probability distributions for uncertain returns.
original_title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Portfolios Using Linear Programming

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Diagnosing Performance Bottlenecks in a Microservices Architecture
description: Students analyze real-world distributed system failure scenarios by examining system logs, performance metrics, and architectural diagrams to identify root causes of cascading failures. They will dissect the relationships between service dependencies, resource constraints, and failure propagation patterns in a complex e-commerce microservices ecosystem.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining multi-service log traces, performance metrics, and dependency graphs to identify root causes and failure propagation paths
Students will evaluate system architecture trade-offs through systematic decomposition of service interactions, resource utilization patterns, and bottleneck identification techniques
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the complete failure scenario package: system architecture diagram showing 12 microservices (user service, inventory, payment, shipping, notification, etc.), 2 hours of aggregated logs from all services during a Black Friday traffic spike, performance metrics dashboard screenshots, and service dependency matrix. Students have 45 minutes to individually examine the materials and identify potential failure points. Next, teams spend 60 minutes collaboratively mapping the timeline of failures using provided analysis templates. They must trace specific transaction flows through the system, correlating timestamps across services to identify where delays compound. Teams then spend 45 minutes conducting root cause analysis using the 5-Whys technique, documenting their reasoning in structured worksheets. They must differentiate between symptoms (slow response times) and causes (database connection pool exhaustion). In the final 30 minutes, teams prepare detailed failure analysis reports including: failure timeline visualization, identified bottlenecks with supporting evidence, cascade failure explanation, and proposed architectural improvements. Each team presents their findings to another team for peer review using provided evaluation criteria. Throughout the activity, teams must justify their conclusions with specific log entries, metric data points, and architectural reasoning.
materials_needed: Distributed system architecture diagram (12-service e-commerce platform)
Multi-service log files (JSON format, 2-hour window, 50MB total)
Performance metrics dashboard screenshots (CPU, memory, latency, throughput)
Service dependency matrix spreadsheet
Failure analysis worksheet templates
Access to log analysis tools (ELK Stack or similar)
Timeline visualization software (Lucidchart or draw.io)
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a detailed rubric: Accuracy of root cause identification (25 points - must identify correct primary bottleneck with supporting evidence), Quality of failure timeline reconstruction (20 points - chronological accuracy and service correlation), Depth of architectural analysis (20 points - understanding of distributed system concepts), Use of evidence (15 points - specific log entries and metrics cited), Proposed solutions feasibility (10 points - realistic architectural improvements), Presentation clarity (10 points - clear communication of technical findings). Success requires scoring 70+ points and correctly identifying the primary bottleneck (database connection pool exhaustion in the inventory service).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted critical log entries, offer guided questions for each analysis phase, and supply service interaction flowchart templates. For advanced learners: Include additional failure scenarios with multiple concurrent root causes, challenge them to propose monitoring strategies, or ask them to design circuit breaker implementations. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during the collaborative analysis phase.

title: Design a Mathematical Model for Community Garden Resource Allocation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world resource allocation problems for a community garden. They will integrate linear programming, graphing, and constraint analysis to develop a comprehensive solution that maximizes garden productivity while respecting budget and space limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize linear programming concepts, graphing techniques, and constraint analysis by designing an original optimization model for resource allocation
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical presentation through visual displays, algebraic justification, and practical recommendations
instructions: Begin by presenting students with the scenario: A community garden has $2,000 budget, 500 square feet of space, and wants to maximize either profit or food production. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). Each team receives a unique constraint set including: specific crop options with different space requirements (tomatoes: 4 sq ft, lettuce: 1 sq ft, peppers: 3 sq ft), costs per plant ($2-8 range), and yields/profits. Teams spend 15 minutes analyzing their constraints and defining variables (x = number of tomatoes, y = number of lettuce, etc.). Next, students formulate their linear programming problem by writing the objective function and all constraints as inequalities (20 minutes). They must identify at least 4 constraints including budget, space, and two additional realistic limitations they create (minimum variety requirements, labor constraints, etc.). Students then solve graphically by plotting constraint lines on coordinate planes, identifying the feasible region, and testing corner points to find optimal solutions (25 minutes). Provide graph paper and colored pencils for clear visualization. Teams create a professional presentation board including: their mathematical model, graph with labeled feasible region, optimal solution with justification, and practical recommendations for garden implementation (20 minutes). Conclude with 3-minute team presentations where each group explains their model, defends their constraints, and shares their optimal planting strategy (15 minutes). Encourage questions between teams to compare different approaches and constraint interpretations.
materials_needed: Graph paper (2 sheets per student)
Colored pencils or markers (4 colors minimum)
Calculators
Large poster paper (1 per team)
Rulers and straightedges
Constraint scenario cards (pre-prepared for each team)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of linear programming formulation and graphical solution (25%), (2) Creativity and realism of additional constraints developed (25%), (3) Quality of visual presentation including clear graphs and professional layout (25%), (4) Oral presentation clarity and ability to justify mathematical reasoning (25%). Students must demonstrate correct identification of feasible regions, accurate calculation of corner points, and logical connection between mathematical solution and practical recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint equation templates and step-by-step graphing guides. Offer pre-drawn coordinate grids with scales marked. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate non-linear constraints, consider multi-objective optimization, or add integer programming requirements (whole plants only). Provide extension problems involving sensitivity analysis or seasonal planning across multiple time periods.

title: Interpreting Complex Machine Learning Model Performance Through Multi-Metric Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret the performance of a pre-trained ensemble model (Random Forest + XGBoost) on an imbalanced customer churn dataset using multiple evaluation metrics. They will explain the trade-offs between different metrics and justify which metrics are most appropriate for the business context.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR by analyzing confusion matrices and performance curves from multiple machine learning models
Students will explain the implications of class imbalance on model evaluation through comparative analysis of metric performance across different decision thresholds
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a Jupyter notebook containing: (1) a pre-trained Random Forest and XGBoost model on the Telco Customer Churn dataset, (2) test set predictions with probability scores, (3) pre-generated confusion matrices at default 0.5 threshold, and (4) ROC and PR curves. **Individual Analysis Phase (25 minutes):** Students examine the provided confusion matrices and calculate precision, recall, and F1-score manually for both models at the 0.5 threshold. They then analyze the ROC curves (AUC = 0.847 RF, 0.863 XGB) and PR curves (AUC = 0.521 RF, 0.548 XGB) to identify optimal thresholds for different business objectives. **Threshold Investigation (20 minutes):** Using provided probability predictions, students calculate metrics at three different thresholds (0.3, 0.5, 0.7) and document how precision/recall trade-offs change. They create a summary table showing how each metric responds to threshold adjustments. **Business Context Analysis (15 minutes):** Students write a 200-word explanation addressing: Why AUC-PR is lower than AUC-ROC for this dataset, which threshold they would recommend for a business that prioritizes customer retention (minimizing false negatives), and which model performs better when considering the 10:1 cost ratio of losing a customer versus retention campaign costs. **Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange their analyses with a partner and provide feedback on the business justification and metric interpretation accuracy.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-trained models and predictions
Telco Customer Churn dataset with test/train split
Pre-generated ROC and PR curves as PNG files
Confusion matrix templates in Excel/Google Sheets
Business scenario document with cost assumptions
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) completed metric calculation table with correct values at three thresholds (40 points), (2) written business analysis explaining metric trade-offs and threshold selection with clear reasoning (40 points), (3) accurate interpretation of why PR-AUC differs from ROC-AUC in imbalanced contexts (20 points). Success criteria: 85%+ accuracy on calculations, clear explanation of precision-recall trade-offs, and appropriate threshold recommendation with business justification.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a metric calculation template with formulas partially filled in, offer a glossary of terms (Type I/II errors, sensitivity, specificity), and include guided questions for each analysis section. **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to calculate cost-sensitive metrics using the provided business costs, analyze feature importance differences between models, or investigate how metrics change across different customer segments using demographic splits.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations in Real-Life Scenarios
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional teenager by calculating percentages of income for different expense categories. They will apply percentage calculation skills to determine exact dollar amounts for savings, entertainment, and essential expenses.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages of a given income amount by applying the percentage formula to create budget categories
Students will solve real-world percentage problems through hands-on budget planning and verification activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Teen Budget Challenge' worksheet and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card shows a different teen's monthly income ($400, $600, or $800 from part-time jobs). Explain that students must allocate their teen's income using these percentage requirements: 30% savings, 25% entertainment, 20% clothing, 15% food/snacks, 10% miscellaneous. Have students work individually for 15 minutes to calculate the exact dollar amount for each category using the formula: (percentage ÷ 100) × total income. Students must show their work for each calculation and verify that all categories sum to 100% and equal their total income. After calculations, students spend 10 minutes creating a visual budget pie chart using the provided circle template, labeling each section with both the percentage and dollar amount. For the final 15 minutes, pair students with different income scenarios to compare their budgets. Partners must explain their calculations to each other and identify which budget categories have the largest dollar differences despite using identical percentages. Conclude with a 5-minute whole-class discussion where 2-3 pairs share one interesting discovery about how percentages translate differently across various income levels. Students submit their completed worksheet showing all calculations, the labeled pie chart, and written responses to reflection questions about percentage applications in budgeting.
materials_needed: Teen Budget Challenge worksheet (one per student)
Scenario cards with different monthly incomes
Circle template for pie charts
Colored pencils or markers
Calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, pie chart accurately labeled, reflects meaningfully on percentage applications; (3) Most calculations correct, minor errors in chart or explanations; (2) Some calculation errors, chart present but incomplete; (1) Major calculation errors, missing components. Check that dollar amounts sum correctly and percentages total 100%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing the first example worked out, offer percentage-to-decimal conversion chart, allow calculator use throughout. For advanced learners: Add a bonus challenge to adjust percentages while keeping the same total, or calculate how income changes would affect their ability to maintain the same dollar amounts in each category.

title: Analyzing Database Query Performance: Identifying Bottlenecks in JOIN Operations
description: Students will examine execution plans and performance metrics of database queries containing multiple JOIN operations to identify inefficiencies and propose optimization strategies. They will analyze real query scenarios to understand the relationship between query structure, indexing, and performance outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database query execution plans by examining JOIN operation costs, row estimates, and index usage patterns
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient query structures through systematic comparison of execution metrics and resource consumption
instructions: Begin by providing each student group with a pre-configured database containing 50,000 customer records, 200,000 order records, and 500,000 order detail records (15 minutes setup). Distribute three SQL queries of varying complexity: Query A (2-table inner join), Query B (3-table join with WHERE clause), and Query C (4-table join with subquery). Students first execute each query using SQL Server Management Studio or MySQL Workbench, recording execution time and rows returned (10 minutes). Next, students generate and save execution plans for each query, identifying the graphical representation of JOIN types, estimated costs, and index scans versus seeks (20 minutes). In pairs, students create a comparison matrix documenting: JOIN method used (nested loop, hash, merge), estimated vs. actual row counts, index usage (clustered/non-clustered/table scan), and total query cost (25 minutes). Students then analyze patterns by answering guided questions: Which query shows the highest cost operations? Where do estimated and actual row counts differ significantly? Which tables lack proper indexing? (15 minutes). Finally, each pair proposes three specific optimization strategies (add indexes, rewrite JOIN order, modify WHERE clauses) and predicts expected performance improvements with justification based on their execution plan analysis (20 minutes). Groups present one key finding and proposed solution to the class (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-populated sample database (Customer, Orders, OrderDetails tables)
SQL Server Management Studio or MySQL Workbench
Three prepared SQL queries with varying JOIN complexity
Execution plan analysis worksheet template
Comparison matrix template (digital or printed)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices for accuracy of execution plan interpretation (40 points), quality of pattern identification showing understanding of performance bottlenecks (30 points), and feasibility of proposed optimization strategies with clear justification linking to execution plan evidence (30 points). Students must correctly identify at least 2 performance issues and propose logical solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example of execution plan analysis for a simple 2-table join, highlighting key elements to examine. Offer sentence starters for optimization proposals. For advanced learners, provide additional queries with window functions or CTEs, and challenge them to create their own performance test scenarios or write alternative query versions to compare efficiency.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in High-Stakes Healthcare Prediction
description: Students critically evaluate three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) trained to predict patient readmission risk, assessing their real-world applicability, ethical implications, and business value. They must justify which model should be deployed in a hospital system by weighing multiple evaluation criteria beyond accuracy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the appropriateness of different ML models for healthcare deployment by analyzing performance metrics, interpretability, and ethical considerations
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive assessment of business constraints, regulatory requirements, and stakeholder needs
instructions: Step 1 (15 min): Provide teams of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models and their outputs: confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP values, feature importance plots, prediction probabilities for 100 test patients, and model training logs. Include dataset documentation showing 50,000 patient records with demographic, clinical, and socioeconomic features. Step 2 (45 min): Teams analyze each model using provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: statistical performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC), interpretability (SHAP consistency, feature importance alignment with medical knowledge), bias assessment (performance across demographic groups, fairness metrics), computational requirements (inference time, memory usage, retraining frequency), regulatory compliance (model transparency requirements, audit trail capability), and clinical workflow integration (alert fatigue potential, physician trust factors). Step 3 (30 min): Teams complete detailed comparison matrix scoring each model 1-5 on all six dimensions with written justifications. Step 4 (20 min): Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their recommended model choice, addressing potential counterarguments and implementation risks. Step 5 (40 min): Presentations followed by peer questioning, where other teams challenge recommendations using provided 'devil's advocate' prompt cards covering scenarios like model drift, false positive costs, and physician resistance. Step 6 (10 min): Individual reflection where each student identifies the strongest and weakest aspects of their team's evaluation process and writes recommendations for improving model evaluation methodology.
materials_needed: Three pre-trained models with complete performance documentation (confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP outputs)
Synthetic patient dataset with 100 test cases including demographics and outcomes
Evaluation framework rubric with six assessment dimensions
Devil's advocate prompt cards with 15 challenging scenarios
Hospital context briefing document including regulatory constraints and workflow requirements
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Comparison matrix completeness and justification quality (40%), (2) Presentation defense and counterargument handling (35%), (3) Peer evaluation of critical questioning during others' presentations (15%), (4) Individual reflection depth and methodology improvement suggestions (10%). Use provided rubric with specific criteria for each component including evidence usage, logical reasoning, stakeholder consideration, and professional communication.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation dimension templates with guiding questions and example justifications from a different domain. Assign specific roles within teams (statistical analyst, ethics reviewer, business analyst). For advanced learners: Include additional complexity with model ensemble options, cost-benefit analysis requirements, and regulatory submission documentation. Provide access to recent research papers on ML bias in healthcare for deeper analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in High-Stakes Healthcare Prediction: Comparative Study
description: Students critically assess and compare three different machine learning models trained to predict patient readmission risk, evaluating their appropriateness for clinical deployment. They must consider statistical performance, ethical implications, interpretability requirements, and regulatory compliance to make evidence-based recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will critically evaluate machine learning model performance by analyzing multiple performance metrics, bias indicators, and clinical interpretability requirements within a healthcare context
Students will judge the suitability of predictive models through systematic comparison of statistical accuracy, ethical considerations, and practical deployment constraints
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with identical datasets containing performance metrics for three models: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Neural Network, all predicting 30-day hospital readmission. Each model's results include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, confusion matrices, and demographic bias analysis across age, gender, and racial groups. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze statistical performance using provided Jupyter notebooks, calculating additional metrics like specificity, positive predictive value, and examining calibration plots. They identify which model performs best overall and within specific demographic subgroups.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Students research regulatory requirements for healthcare AI (FDA guidelines, HIPAA considerations) and clinical interpretability needs using provided medical literature excerpts about model explainability in healthcare decisions.

Step 3 (60 minutes): Teams complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing all three models across six criteria: overall accuracy, demographic fairness, interpretability, computational efficiency, regulatory compliance readiness, and clinical workflow integration. Each criterion is scored 1-5 with detailed justification required.

Step 4 (45 minutes): Teams prepare 10-minute presentations defending their model selection choice, addressing potential counterarguments and explaining their reasoning hierarchy. They must explicitly state which factors they prioritized and why, demonstrating critical thinking about trade-offs between statistical performance and practical deployment considerations.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Class discussion where teams present conflicting recommendations, fostering debate about evaluation priorities in high-stakes applications.
materials_needed: Pre-computed model performance datasets in CSV format with demographic breakdowns
Jupyter notebook templates with partially completed analysis code
FDA guidance documents on AI/ML-based medical devices (excerpts)
Clinical literature on model interpretability requirements (3-4 research papers)
Evaluation matrix template with weighted scoring framework
Access to Python with pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib libraries
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation matrices (40 points) with detailed justifications for each scoring decision, plus a 2-page written recommendation memo (40 points) defending their chosen model for clinical deployment. Presentation delivery and response to questions accounts for 20 points. Rubric evaluates: depth of statistical analysis, consideration of ethical implications, quality of evidence cited, logical consistency of arguments, and ability to address counterarguments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions for each evaluation criterion and simplified statistical interpretation guides. Offer one-on-one check-ins during Step 1 to ensure understanding of performance metrics. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by including cost-benefit analysis, asking them to research specific hospital implementation cases, or requiring them to propose monitoring strategies for deployed models.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in High-Stakes Healthcare Prediction

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Sustainable Urban Water Distribution
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve a complex urban water distribution problem, incorporating multiple real-world constraints and variables. They will design their own objective function, constraint system, and solution methodology while justifying their mathematical choices through theoretical analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from linear programming, graph theory, and calculus to design an original optimization model for water distribution by integrating multiple mathematical domains
Students will construct a novel solution algorithm and validate their mathematical model through computational implementation and theoretical proof of optimality conditions
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a fictional city dataset including population density maps, elevation data, existing infrastructure, and water demand projections (15 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives different city parameters to ensure unique solutions.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze their city data and formulate the problem mathematically. Students must identify decision variables (pipe diameters, flow rates, pump locations), create an objective function (minimize cost while maximizing reliability), and establish constraints (pressure requirements, flow conservation, budget limits). Teams document their mathematical reasoning using formal notation.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students design their optimization approach by selecting and justifying solution methods (linear programming, nonlinear optimization, or hybrid approaches). They must prove feasibility of their constraint system and demonstrate understanding of optimality conditions through mathematical analysis. Teams create algorithmic pseudocode for their solution approach.

Phase 3 (75 minutes): Using provided computational tools, teams implement their model and generate solutions. Students must validate results through sensitivity analysis, testing how solutions change with parameter variations. They identify critical constraints and prove mathematical properties of their optimal solutions.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams prepare technical presentations defending their mathematical choices. Each presentation must include: problem formulation with rigorous mathematical notation, theoretical justification of solution methodology, computational results with interpretation, and proof sketches of key mathematical properties. Conclude with peer evaluation where teams critique others' mathematical approaches using provided evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: City infrastructure datasets (population, elevation, existing pipes, demand projections) - unique for each team
MATLAB, Python with SciPy/NumPy, or Mathematica software access
Digital graphing tools (GeoGebra or similar)
Large format paper for mathematical notation and proof sketches
Scientific calculators
Access to optimization solver libraries (CVX, Gurobi, or similar)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical rigor of problem formulation including proper notation and constraint completeness, (2) Theoretical justification of solution methodology with proof elements, (3) Implementation accuracy and computational validation, (4) Originality and creativity in mathematical approach, (5) Quality of mathematical communication in presentation. Students must score 3+ in all categories, with written peer evaluations contributing 20% of final score. Deliverables include mathematical model documentation, computational code, solution analysis report, and live presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for constraint formulation and offer guided questions for systematic problem decomposition. Supply reference materials on optimization theory and worked examples of similar problems. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements (uncertain demand), multi-objective optimization, or develop novel solution algorithms. Encourage exploration of mathematical connections to network flow theory, game theory, or robust optimization.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Healthcare Data Visualization
description: Students will analyze pre-created scatter plots and correlation matrices from a healthcare dataset to distinguish between correlational relationships and potential causal claims. They will categorize findings and explain the reasoning behind different types of relationships they observe.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing healthcare data visualizations and explaining why strong correlations may not indicate causal relationships
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plot patterns through systematic analysis of patient outcome data
instructions: Begin by distributing the healthcare dataset summary sheet containing 8 pre-created visualizations showing relationships between variables like BMI vs. blood pressure, exercise hours vs. cholesterol, age vs. medication count, and income vs. health outcomes (10 minutes setup). Form pairs and assign each pair 4 visualizations to analyze. Students first examine each scatter plot and record the correlation coefficient, visual pattern strength, and direction in their analysis worksheet (15 minutes). Next, pairs categorize each relationship into one of four categories: 'Likely Causal,' 'Possibly Causal,' 'Correlational Only,' or 'Spurious Correlation,' providing written justification for each classification (20 minutes). During the classification phase, students must identify potential confounding variables and alternative explanations for observed patterns. Pairs then rotate to review another pair's classifications and provide feedback using the peer review checklist (10 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where each pair presents one 'tricky' example they found most challenging to classify, explaining their reasoning and responding to questions from other students (15 minutes). Throughout the activity, emphasize that students should consider biological plausibility, temporal relationships, and potential third variables when making their determinations.
materials_needed: Healthcare dataset visualization packet (8 scatter plots with correlation coefficients)
Student analysis worksheet with classification categories
Peer review checklist
Projection system for class discussion
assessment_method: Grade completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accurate interpretation of correlation strength and direction, (2) Appropriate categorization of relationship types with clear reasoning, (3) Identification of potential confounding variables, (4) Quality of peer feedback provided. Success criteria: Students correctly classify at least 6/8 relationships and provide scientifically sound explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with correlation coefficient interpretation ranges and guiding questions for each relationship type. For advanced learners: Include additional variables to consider (genetic factors, socioeconomic status) and ask them to propose study designs that could help establish causation for 'possibly causal' relationships.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Manufacturing Cost Reduction
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem involving material costs, production constraints, and profit maximization. They will use partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to determine optimal production levels for a company manufacturing two complementary products.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to optimize a multi-variable profit function within given manufacturing constraints
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical modeling of business scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario worksheet describing TechCorp's production of smartphones and tablet cases with specific cost functions, material constraints, and market demand limits (10 minutes). Organize students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Mathematician (coordinates calculations), Business Analyst (interprets results), Quality Controller (verifies calculations), and Presenter (prepares final recommendations). Present the problem: TechCorp's profit function P(x,y) = -2x² - 3y² + 120x + 150y - xy - 5000, where x = smartphones (hundreds) and y = tablet cases (hundreds), subject to material constraint x + 2y ≤ 60 and non-negativity constraints. Teams first identify the unconstrained critical points by computing ∂P/∂x = 0 and ∂P/∂y = 0, then verify these are maxima using the second derivative test (25 minutes). Next, teams apply Lagrange multipliers to handle the material constraint, setting up the system: ∇P = λ∇g where g(x,y) = x + 2y - 60 = 0. They solve the resulting system of equations systematically, checking boundary conditions along x = 0, y = 0, and the constraint line (35 minutes). Teams then evaluate profit at all critical points and boundary intersections to determine the global maximum, calculating actual profit values and production quantities (20 minutes). Finally, each team presents their optimal solution with business justification, explaining why their production levels maximize profit while satisfying all constraints (15 minutes). Conclude with instructor-led verification of solutions and discussion of how optimization techniques apply across various industries.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario worksheets with TechCorp profit function and constraints
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Desmos, Wolfram Alpha, or similar)
Graph paper and rulers for constraint visualization
Role assignment cards for team organization
Presentation templates for final recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification and solution of critical points (25%), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier method (25%), (3) Accurate evaluation of boundary conditions and global optimization (25%), (4) Clear business interpretation and presentation of results (25%). Students must submit written calculations showing all work and deliver a 3-minute team presentation with specific production recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step Lagrange multiplier template with blanks to fill in, offer visual constraint graphing aids, and allow use of computer algebra systems for computational verification. For advanced learners: Extend to three-variable problems with additional constraints, introduce sensitivity analysis to examine how constraint changes affect optimal solutions, or challenge them to model uncertainty using probability distributions in the profit function.

title: Comparative Analysis of Cache Replacement Algorithms Through Memory Trace Simulation
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three cache replacement algorithms (LRU, FIFO, Random) by examining their behavior on real memory access traces. They will decompose algorithm trade-offs and evaluate cache hit/miss patterns to determine optimal use cases for each algorithm.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze cache replacement algorithm performance by comparing hit rates, temporal locality exploitation, and implementation complexity across LRU, FIFO, and Random policies
Students will examine memory access patterns through trace simulation to identify algorithmic strengths and weaknesses in different workload scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 2-3 students with three different memory trace files: sequential_access.txt (simulates array traversal), random_access.txt (simulates hash table operations), and mixed_locality.txt (simulates typical program execution). Each team receives a cache simulator framework with placeholder functions for each replacement algorithm. Step 1 (20 minutes): Students implement the three cache replacement algorithms in the provided simulator framework, ensuring proper data structure management for LRU ordering, FIFO queuing, and random selection. Step 2 (30 minutes): Run simulations on each memory trace with cache sizes of 64, 128, and 256 entries, recording hit rates, miss penalties, and algorithm overhead metrics. Students must document cache state transitions for the first 50 memory accesses to understand behavioral differences. Step 3 (25 minutes): Create comparative analysis matrices examining: algorithm complexity (time/space), hit rate performance across workloads, and sensitivity to cache size changes. Students must identify which algorithm performs best for each trace type and explain why based on locality patterns. Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams prepare 5-minute presentations analyzing one critical finding, such as 'Why LRU fails in sequential scans' or 'Random algorithm's surprising effectiveness in certain scenarios.' Step 5 (15 minutes): Class discussion where teams present findings and challenge each other's conclusions with evidence from their simulations. Instructor facilitates analysis of conflicting results and guides students to recognize that optimal algorithm choice depends on workload characteristics and implementation constraints.
materials_needed: Cache simulator framework code (Python/Java) with skeleton functions
Three memory trace files: sequential_access.txt, random_access.txt, mixed_locality.txt
Performance monitoring template spreadsheet
Presentation timer and projection system
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct algorithm implementations verified through code review and simulation output validation (40 points), (2) Depth of comparative analysis demonstrated in written matrices and identification of algorithm-workload relationships (35 points), (3) Quality of evidence-based conclusions in presentations, including ability to defend findings during peer questioning (25 points). Success requires identifying at least 3 specific performance trade-offs and correctly predicting algorithm performance on unseen workload patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm pseudocode templates and pre-filled cache state examples for first 10 memory accesses. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens when LRU cache is full and needs replacement?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement write-back policies, analyze cache coherency implications, or design hybrid algorithms combining multiple replacement strategies. Provide additional complex traces with nested loop structures.

title: Design and Build a Geometric Garden: Creating Optimization Solutions for Real-World Constraints
description: Students will create an original mathematical model to design a community garden layout that maximizes growing area while satisfying multiple geometric and budgetary constraints. They will develop their own optimization problem, solve it using multiple mathematical approaches, and present a comprehensive proposal with visual models and mathematical justification.
estimated_duration: 150 minutes (2.5 hours) or two 75-minute class periods
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric principles, algebraic modeling, and optimization techniques by designing an original garden layout problem with realistic constraints

Students will construct multiple mathematical representations (algebraic, geometric, and graphical) through creating comprehensive solutions that demonstrate deep understanding of mathematical relationships
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Provide each team with the base scenario: designing a community garden on a rectangular lot measuring 50m × 30m with a $2,000 budget. Teams must first create their own unique set of constraints by selecting 4-5 from provided options (pathway requirements, water access points, composting areas, tool storage, accessibility features) and adding 2 original constraints (15 minutes). 

Next, teams develop their mathematical model by defining variables, writing constraint equations, and formulating an objective function to maximize planting area (25 minutes). Distribute graphing materials and technology access for teams to solve their problem using at least three different approaches: algebraic manipulation, geometric construction, and graphical analysis using coordinate geometry (45 minutes).

Teams then create their garden proposal including: a scale drawing with precise measurements, algebraic work showing optimization calculations, a cost breakdown spreadsheet, and a written explanation connecting mathematical solutions to practical design choices (35 minutes). 

Conclude with team presentations where each group explains their unique constraints, demonstrates their mathematical approaches, and defends their optimal solution. Other teams ask clarifying questions about mathematical reasoning (20 minutes). Provide presentation rubrics beforehand and ensure each team member has a specific role: mathematical modeler, visual designer, cost analyst, and presenter.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm grid, 5 sheets per team)
Graphing calculators or laptops with Desmos/GeoGebra access
Colored pencils and rulers
Constraint option cards with realistic garden requirements
Sample cost list for garden materials (fencing, pathways, plants)
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Creativity - originality of constraints and problem formulation (25%), (2) Mathematical Accuracy - correct application of optimization and geometric principles (30%), (3) Multiple Representations - effective use of algebraic, geometric, and graphical approaches (25%), (4) Real-world Connections - practical feasibility and clear explanation of mathematical reasoning (20%). Students submit both individual reflection worksheets and team proposals.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint templates and guiding questions for each mathematical approach. Offer simplified scenarios with fewer variables. Extend advanced learners by challenging them to include non-linear constraints (curved pathways), incorporate trigonometry for irrigation coverage, or add time-based optimization considering seasonal planting schedules. Provide additional constraint cards for students who finish early.

title: Advanced Data Structure Terminology and Classification Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall precise definitions and classifications of 50 advanced data structures and their associated algorithmic complexities. This activity focuses on building foundational vocabulary essential for advanced computer science coursework through systematic memorization techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions of 50 advanced data structures including B-trees, skip lists, treaps, and suffix arrays by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify time and space complexity notations for fundamental operations on each data structure through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared flashcard deck containing 50 advanced data structures, each with definition, visual representation, and complexity information on reverse side. Students work individually for 15 minutes reviewing cards using the 'look-cover-write-check' method: examine front term, cover it, write definition from memory, then check accuracy against back of card. Next, organize students into pairs for 10 minutes of reciprocal testing where Partner A shows term while Partner B provides definition, then roles reverse. Implement the 'three pile system': correctly recalled cards go to 'mastered' pile, partially correct to 'review' pile, and incorrect to 'study more' pile. Conduct whole-class rapid-fire round where instructor displays data structure names on projector for 30 seconds each while students write definitions on response sheets. Follow with classification exercise where students categorize all 50 structures into provided taxonomy chart (linear vs. non-linear, static vs. dynamic, etc.) within 20 minutes. Conclude with individual self-assessment where students identify their weakest areas and create personalized study plan for structures scoring below 80% accuracy. Throughout activity, emphasize exact terminology and precise complexity notation rather than conceptual understanding.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard deck with 50 advanced data structures (Red-Black trees, AVL trees, B+ trees, Fibonacci heaps, etc.)
Blank response sheets for definitions
Data structure taxonomy classification chart handouts
Projector for displaying terms
Timer for timed exercises
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on final written recall test covering all 50 data structures. Grade based on: exact definition accuracy (60 points), correct complexity notation (30 points), proper classification (10 points). Partial credit given only for definitions containing all essential components. Track individual progress through pile sorting results and self-assessment completion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic device examples and reduce initial set to 25 core structures, focusing on most fundamental ones first. Create visual association cards linking structure names to memorable images. For advanced learners: add implementation pseudocode requirements and challenge them to recall variant types (e.g., different B-tree orders, various heap implementations). Provide additional structures like van Emde Boas trees or persistent data structures.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Bias in Gradient Boosting for Healthcare Prediction
description: Students will analyze SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and feature importance outputs from a pre-trained XGBoost model predicting hospital readmission risk. They will interpret how different patient demographics and clinical features contribute to model predictions and identify potential algorithmic bias patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP waterfall plots and summary plots by explaining how individual features contribute to specific patient predictions in quantitative terms
Students will distinguish between global feature importance and local explanations through comparative analysis of model outputs across different patient subgroups
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared Jupyter notebook containing a pre-trained XGBoost model with 1,000 synthetic patient records and pre-calculated SHAP values (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to first examine the global feature importance plot, ranking the top 5 most influential features and writing 2-3 sentences explaining what each feature's importance score means in clinical context. Next, students select 3 specific patient cases with different demographic profiles (provided case IDs: high-risk elderly patient, young patient with comorbidities, middle-aged patient with normal vitals). For each case, they interpret the SHAP waterfall plot by: (1) identifying which features pushed the prediction above/below the baseline risk score, (2) quantifying the magnitude of each feature's contribution in probability units, and (3) explaining the clinical reasoning behind why each feature might logically increase or decrease readmission risk. Students then compare SHAP summary plots across three demographic subgroups (age <40, 40-65, >65) to identify potential bias patterns. They document instances where the same clinical feature (e.g., blood pressure, previous admissions) has different importance rankings across age groups. Finally, students complete a structured worksheet analyzing whether the model shows evidence of age bias by comparing average SHAP values for identical clinical presentations across different age cohorts. Conclude with pairs presenting one significant bias finding to the class (10 minutes total presentations).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-trained XGBoost model and calculated SHAP values
Synthetic healthcare dataset (1,000 patient records with demographics and clinical features)
SHAP interpretation worksheet template with guided questions
Python environment with shap, xgboost, pandas, and matplotlib libraries installed
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of SHAP value interpretation (25 points) - correctly identifies positive/negative contributions and quantifies magnitude, (2) Quality of clinical reasoning (25 points) - provides logical explanations connecting features to readmission risk, (3) Bias identification (25 points) - correctly identifies at least 2 instances of differential feature importance across subgroups, (4) Presentation clarity (25 points) - clearly communicates one bias finding with supporting evidence
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional examples of SHAP waterfall interpretation with color-coded annotations showing positive (red) and negative (blue) contributions. Create a reference sheet with clinical context for each feature. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate fairness metrics (equalized odds, demographic parity) using the SHAP values, or to propose specific mitigation strategies for identified biases such as feature engineering or threshold adjustment techniques.

title: Apply Percentage Calculations to Real Shopping Scenarios
description: Students will solve authentic shopping problems by calculating discounts, sales tax, and tips using percentage formulas. They will work with realistic store scenarios to determine final costs and savings amounts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discount amounts, sales tax, and final prices by solving real-world shopping scenarios
Students will calculate tips and compare savings through hands-on practice with authentic store receipts and price tags
instructions: Begin by distributing shopping scenario cards and calculators to pairs of students (5 minutes). Each card contains a realistic shopping situation with original prices, discount percentages, tax rates, and tip scenarios. Demonstrate the first problem on the board: 'A $80 jacket is 25% off. Sales tax is 8.5%. What is the final price?' Show students the three-step process: (1) Calculate discount amount ($80 × 0.25 = $20), (2) Find discounted price ($80 - $20 = $60), (3) Add sales tax ($60 × 1.085 = $65.10). Have student pairs work through their assigned scenarios using this method (15 minutes). Each pair must show all calculation steps on their worksheet and write the final answer in a complete sentence. Circulate to check work and provide guidance. After completion, have each pair present one problem solution to the class, explaining their calculation steps aloud (10 minutes). Create a class chart comparing the savings amounts from different scenarios. For the final 5 minutes, students complete an exit ticket with one new percentage problem to solve independently, demonstrating they can apply the process without support.
materials_needed: Shopping scenario cards (6 different scenarios per pair)
Basic calculators (one per student)
Student worksheet with calculation spaces
Whiteboard markers and eraser
Exit ticket handouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly calculates all three steps with proper formulas, (3) Correctly calculates two steps with minor errors, (2) Shows understanding of process but makes calculation errors, (1) Attempts calculation but shows minimal understanding. Observe pair discussions for problem-solving approach and check exit tickets for individual mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a formula reference card and start with simpler scenarios involving only one calculation step. Use visual fraction circles to represent percentages. For advanced learners: Include compound discounts (additional 10% off clearance items) and have them create their own shopping scenarios with multiple percentage calculations for classmates to solve.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Big O Complexity Comparison Lab
description: Students analyze the time complexity of three different sorting algorithms by examining their code implementations, predicting their Big O notation, and validating predictions through empirical testing with datasets of varying sizes. They will systematically break down each algorithm's structure to identify nested loops, recursive calls, and operations that contribute to overall complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort algorithms by examining their nested loop structures and recursive patterns to determine Big O notation
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through systematic comparison of theoretical predictions against empirical runtime data collected from multiple dataset sizes
instructions:
**Phase 1: Code Analysis (20 minutes)**
Provide student pairs with printed implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort in Python. Students examine each algorithm line-by-line, identifying and highlighting: (1) outer loops in red, (2) inner loops in blue, (3) recursive calls in green, and (4) basic operations in yellow. They create a structural analysis table documenting loop nesting depth and operation counts for each algorithm.

**Phase 2: Complexity Prediction (15 minutes)**
Using their code analysis, students predict Big O time complexity for each algorithm. They must justify predictions by explaining how nested structures contribute to complexity (e.g., 'bubble sort has nested loops where outer runs n times and inner runs n-1, n-2... times = O(n²)'). Record predictions on the provided worksheet.

**Phase 3: Empirical Testing (25 minutes)**
Students run provided Python test scripts measuring execution time for each algorithm on datasets of 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000 random integers. They record runtimes in milliseconds and plot results on provided graph paper, creating separate line graphs for each algorithm with dataset size (x-axis) vs. runtime (y-axis).

**Phase 4: Analysis Validation (15 minutes)**
Compare theoretical predictions with empirical results. Students identify which graphs show linear growth (O(n)), quadratic growth (O(n²)), or logarithmic growth (O(n log n)). They write a concluding paragraph explaining whether their predictions matched results and identify any discrepancies.
materials_needed: Printed algorithm implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quick sort in Python)
Algorithm analysis worksheet with prediction tables
Computers with Python 3.8+ installed
Pre-written timing test scripts (timing_test.py)
Graph paper and colored highlighters (red, blue, green, yellow)
Calculators
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Code Analysis Accuracy - correct identification of loops/recursion (25%), (2) Big O Predictions - accurate complexity notation with valid justification (30%), (3) Data Collection - complete runtime measurements and accurate graphs (25%), (4) Analysis Synthesis - logical comparison of theoretical vs empirical results with supported conclusions (20%). Students submit completed worksheets, graphs, and written analysis paragraph.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide algorithm flowcharts alongside code, offer pre-highlighted sample code showing loop identification, give partially completed analysis tables. Create mixed-ability pairs. **Advanced extension:** Challenge students to analyze space complexity, implement their own timing functions, or research and analyze additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort. Have them investigate best-case vs worst-case scenarios using sorted and reverse-sorted datasets.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Proposal
description: Students will design and present a comprehensive urban planning proposal for a new city district using area, perimeter, scale, proportions, and budget calculations. They will integrate geometric concepts with real-world constraints to create an original city layout with detailed mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original city district layout by applying geometric principles of area, perimeter, and scale to design buildings, parks, and infrastructure within specified constraints
Students will construct detailed budget calculations and proportional reasoning through systematic cost analysis and resource allocation for their urban planning proposal
instructions:
