**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute grid paper, rulers, calculators, and city planning packets containing: lot size requirements (residential: 0.25 acres, commercial: 0.5 acres, parks: minimum 2 acres), building height restrictions, and cost per square foot data ($150 residential, $300 commercial, $75 parkland). Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Design Phase (25 minutes):** Teams receive a 50-acre rectangular plot (scale: 1 cm = 10 meters) and must design a district containing: minimum 60% residential area, 25% commercial area, 15% green space, plus roads (6-meter width). Students sketch their layout on grid paper, calculating actual dimensions and areas for each zone. They must show all mathematical work for area calculations and ensure proportional requirements are met.

**Phase 2 - Budget Creation (20 minutes):** Using their area calculations, teams create detailed budgets including: land development costs, infrastructure expenses (roads at $200/linear meter), and total project costs. Students must justify their allocation decisions mathematically and identify cost-saving strategies while maintaining required proportions.

**Phase 3 - Proposal Presentation (25 minutes):** Each team presents their 3-minute city proposal including: visual layout display, mathematical justification for all measurements and proportions, complete budget breakdown with calculations shown, and explanation of design decisions. Other teams evaluate proposals using provided rubric focusing on mathematical accuracy and creative problem-solving.

**Wrap-up (10 minutes):** Class discussion comparing different approaches, identifying most cost-effective designs, and reflecting on how mathematical concepts apply to real-world urban planning challenges.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1 cm squares)
Rulers and measuring tools
Scientific calculators
City Planning Data Packet with cost information and zoning requirements
Colored pencils or markers for zone coding
Presentation rubric handouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct area, perimeter, and proportion calculations with work shown, (2) Design Creativity - innovative layout solutions meeting all constraints, (3) Budget Completeness - detailed cost analysis with justified allocation decisions, (4) Presentation Quality - clear communication of mathematical reasoning and design rationale. Students must score 3/4 on mathematical accuracy to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing area calculation templates and breaking budget creation into smaller steps with guided practice problems. For advanced learners, add complexity by including population density calculations, transportation efficiency metrics, or environmental impact assessments requiring additional mathematical modeling and analysis.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Proposal: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original city layout using geometric principles, algebraic relationships, and statistical planning methods. They will synthesize multiple mathematical concepts to design a functional urban environment that meets specific population and infrastructure requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city layout by applying geometric transformations, area calculations, and proportional reasoning to create functional districts
Students will develop mathematical models through algebraic equations and statistical analysis to justify population distribution and resource allocation decisions
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 (10 minutes). Distribute city planning packets containing: population data (50,000 residents), zoning requirements (30% residential, 20% commercial, 15% industrial, 10% parks, 25% infrastructure), and budget constraints ($500 million). Each team receives graph paper and colored pencils.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams design their city layout on a 20x20 grid where each square represents 0.25 square miles. Students must calculate total area needed for each zone using proportional reasoning, then apply geometric principles to create efficient shapes and arrangements. They use transformations (rotations, reflections, translations) to optimize space usage and create aesthetically pleasing patterns.

Phase 2 (40 minutes): Students create mathematical models for their city. They write linear equations relating population density to housing units, calculate traffic flow using ratios and rates, and use statistical methods to distribute services (schools, hospitals, fire stations) based on population clusters. Teams must show all calculations and justify decisions mathematically.

Phase 3 (35 minutes): Students create a comprehensive presentation including: scaled city map with labeled coordinates, mathematical justification document showing all calculations, budget breakdown using percentages and unit rates, and population distribution analysis using measures of central tendency.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams present 5-minute proposals to the class, acting as the 'city council.' Presentations must highlight three key mathematical decisions and explain how geometric and algebraic principles influenced their design choices.
materials_needed: Graph paper (20x20 grid, 1 sheet per student)
Colored pencils or markers (6 colors minimum per team)
City Planning Data Packets (population statistics, zoning laws, budget constraints)
Calculators
Rulers and protractors
Presentation poster board (1 per team)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct area calculations, proportional reasoning, and algebraic models (25%), (2) Creative Integration - original use of geometric transformations and innovative problem-solving approaches (25%), (3) Justification Quality - clear mathematical reasoning and evidence-based decision making (25%), (4) Presentation Effectiveness - clear communication of mathematical concepts and professional delivery (25%). Students submit calculation worksheets, final city design, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing area calculation templates, offering pre-made algebraic equation formats, and pairing them with stronger mathematical peers. Challenge advanced learners by adding constraints like environmental impact calculations, requiring trigonometric applications for road angles, or incorporating exponential growth models for future city expansion planning.
original_title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Proposal

title: Pizza Party Budget Planning: Applying Percentage Calculations and Unit Rates
description: Students will plan a realistic pizza party for their class by applying percentage calculations to determine tips and tax, calculating unit rates to compare pizza deals, and working within a fixed budget. This hands-on activity connects mathematical concepts to real-world decision-making scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine tax and tip amounts by analyzing real pizza restaurant pricing scenarios
Students will calculate and compare unit rates through evaluating different pizza size and pricing options to make cost-effective decisions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' and announcing that each group has a $150 budget for a class party of 25 students. Divide students into groups of 3-4 and provide each group with printed menus from 3 different pizza restaurants (create realistic menus with various sizes: personal 8", medium 12", large 16", extra-large 20" with corresponding prices). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups calculate the cost per square inch for each pizza size at each restaurant using the formula: Price ÷ (π × radius²). Students must show all calculations on their worksheet.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups determine how many pizzas they need assuming each person eats 2 slices and pizzas are cut into standard portions (personal=4, medium=6, large=8, extra-large=10 slices). They select the most cost-effective combination while considering variety.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students apply percentage calculations to add 8.5% sales tax and calculate a 15% tip on the pre-tax amount. They must verify their total stays within the $150 budget.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Groups present their final order to the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning for pizza selection and showing their percentage calculations. Each presentation must include: total cost breakdown, cost per person, and justification for their choices.

Circulate continuously, checking calculations and guiding groups who struggle with the area formula or percentage applications. Encourage students to use calculators for complex arithmetic but require them to show the setup for each calculation.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning worksheets (1 per student)
3 different realistic pizza restaurant menus (printed, 1 set per group)
Calculators (1 per student)
Chart paper for final presentations
Markers or colored pencils
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly calculates all unit rates and percentages with proper formulas shown, stays within budget, provides clear mathematical justification; (3) Minor calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of processes; (2) Shows partial understanding with some correct applications; (1) Significant errors in applying formulas or concepts. Collect worksheets showing all work and observe group presentations for mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide the area formula written out (A = π × r²) and a step-by-step percentage calculation template. Pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add constraints like 'must order from 2 different restaurants' or include additional costs like drinks and plates, requiring more complex budget management and multi-step percentage problems.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Big O Performance Comparison
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of different sorting algorithms by examining code implementations, tracing execution paths, and comparing performance characteristics. They will deconstruct each algorithm's operations to determine Big O notation and justify their conclusions with evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort algorithms by counting operations and identifying dominant terms
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic examination of best-case, worst-case, and average-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing students with clean implementations of three sorting algorithms: bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort in their preferred programming language (20 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one algorithm initially. Phase 1 (30 minutes): Teams trace through their assigned algorithm using a sample array of 8 elements, counting primitive operations (comparisons, swaps, assignments) at each step. They create a detailed execution trace showing how operations scale. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Teams analyze their algorithm's behavior with different input scenarios - already sorted array, reverse sorted array, and random array. They identify the mathematical relationship between input size n and operation count. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams determine Big O notation for both time and space complexity, documenting their reasoning with specific evidence from their traces. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Rotate teams so each group analyzes all three algorithms, building comparison charts. Phase 5 (15 minutes): Teams present findings, defending their Big O classifications and explaining which algorithm performs best under different conditions. Conclude with class discussion comparing theoretical analysis to practical performance considerations.
materials_needed: Pre-written code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort
Sample datasets of varying sizes (8, 16, 32 elements)
Algorithm tracing worksheets with operation counting tables
Graphing paper or digital graphing tools
Computers with code execution environment
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of operation counting and algorithm traces (25%), (2) Correct identification of Big O time/space complexity with mathematical justification (35%), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between algorithms showing understanding of trade-offs (25%), (4) Clear presentation of findings with evidence-based reasoning (15%). Students submit completed tracing worksheets, Big O analysis reports, and comparison charts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed tracing templates with first few steps shown, offer operation counting hints, and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Include analysis of additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), examine space-time trade-offs in detail, or analyze recursive call stack behavior. Consider providing real performance timing data to compare with theoretical analysis.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Transit Network Efficiency
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban transit challenges by integrating concepts from graph theory, linear programming, and statistical analysis. They will develop their own objective functions, constraints, and solution algorithms while justifying their mathematical choices through rigorous analysis.
estimated_duration: 330 minutes (5.5 hours) across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory, optimization theory, and statistical modeling to construct an original mathematical framework for transit network analysis
Students will design and implement a novel optimization algorithm through computational programming and validate their model using real transit data
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Problem Definition and Model Architecture**
Provide students with transit data from 3 different cities (NYC, Tokyo, London). Students work in teams of 2-3 to identify a specific optimization problem (minimize travel time, maximize coverage, optimize cost-efficiency). They must define their own objective function using mathematical notation and justify variable selection.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Mathematical Framework Construction**
Students construct their mathematical model by: (1) Creating a weighted graph representation of their chosen transit system with at least 50 nodes, (2) Formulating constraint equations based on real-world limitations (budget, time, capacity), (3) Developing their optimization function using calculus of variations or linear programming techniques, (4) Proving mathematical validity through formal proofs or counterexample testing.

**Phase 3 (120 minutes): Algorithm Development and Implementation**
Using Python or MATLAB, students code their optimization algorithm from scratch. They must implement error-checking, convergence criteria, and performance metrics. Students test their algorithm on provided datasets and document computational complexity using Big O notation.

**Phase 4 (60 minutes): Model Validation and Presentation**
Teams validate their models using statistical significance tests, create visualizations of their solutions, and prepare 10-minute presentations defending their mathematical choices. They must address potential criticisms and propose model improvements.
materials_needed: Real transit network datasets (NYC MTA, Tokyo Metro, London Underground) in CSV format
Python/MATLAB software with optimization libraries (SciPy, MATLAB Optimization Toolbox)
Graph visualization software (NetworkX, Gephi)
Statistical analysis software (R or Python pandas)
Presentation software with LaTeX equation support
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and originality of model (25 points), correctness of algorithm implementation (25 points), validation methodology and statistical analysis (20 points), presentation clarity and defense of mathematical choices (20 points), documentation quality and reproducibility (10 points). Students must submit complete code, mathematical proofs, validation results, and a 5-page technical report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structures and pre-defined constraint examples; offer guided practice with smaller 10-node networks first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or machine learning components; require comparison with existing published algorithms and formal complexity analysis proofs.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a curated dataset containing variables that show correlation but not causation (ice cream sales and drowning incidents) to distinguish between these concepts. They will create visual representations and write explanations demonstrating their understanding of when correlation does and does not imply causation.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from three different variable pairs
Students will explain the concept of confounding variables through identification of lurking factors in correlation examples
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing three datasets: (1) ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents by month, (2) number of firefighters vs. property damage from fires, and (3) hours studied vs. test scores. Divide students into groups of 2-3. In the first 15 minutes, have each group calculate Pearson correlation coefficients for all three datasets using pandas .corr() function and create scatter plots using matplotlib. Next, spend 20 minutes having students interpret their visualizations by answering guided questions: 'What is the correlation strength?', 'Does the correlation make logical sense?', and 'What other variables might influence this relationship?'. For the ice cream/drowning example, guide them to identify temperature/season as the confounding variable. For firefighters/damage, help them recognize that larger fires require more firefighters AND cause more damage. During the final 20 minutes, each group creates a two-column comparison chart listing 'Evidence of Correlation' vs 'Evidence Against Causation' for each dataset pair. Groups then present their findings for one dataset to the class, explaining why correlation exists but causation does not (except for study hours/test scores). Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion on real-world implications of misinterpreting correlation as causation.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas and matplotlib installed
Pre-loaded CSV files: ice_cream_drowning.csv, firefighters_damage.csv, study_scores.csv
Guided analysis worksheet with correlation interpretation questions
Computers or tablets for each student group
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients, (2) Accurate identification of confounding variables for at least 2/3 datasets, (3) Clear explanation of why correlation ≠ causation in their comparison charts, (4) Effective verbal presentation demonstrating understanding. Students must score 3/4 points to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation coefficient interpretation guide (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong) and sentence starters for explanations. Offer pre-written code snippets for correlation calculations. For advanced learners, introduce additional datasets with more complex relationships, ask them to research the Bradford Hill criteria for causation, or have them create their own examples of spurious correlations.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Dataset Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-selected healthcare dataset to identify correlations between variables and distinguish between correlation and causation. They will interpret correlation coefficients and explain why certain relationships cannot imply causation through structured data exploration.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing real healthcare data and identifying confounding variables
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots through guided dataset exploration to explain relationship strength and direction
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Health Outcomes Dataset' containing 1000 patient records with variables: age, exercise_hours_weekly, sleep_hours_nightly, stress_level (1-10), income, and health_score (1-100). Students work in pairs for 60 minutes total.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students load the dataset in Excel/Google Sheets and create scatter plots for three specific pairs: (exercise_hours, health_score), (income, health_score), and (age, stress_level). They calculate correlation coefficients using built-in functions.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Provide interpretation framework: r > 0.7 = strong positive, 0.3-0.7 = moderate positive, etc. Students categorize their three correlations and write one sentence describing each relationship's strength and direction.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Present causation analysis worksheet with guided questions: 'Could exercise hours directly cause higher health scores? What other factors might influence both variables?' Students identify potential confounding variables for each correlation pair.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Class discussion where pairs share one 'strong correlation' they found and explain why it may not indicate causation. Record responses on whiteboard, highlighting common confounding variables like socioeconomic status, age, or lifestyle factors.

Conclude with students completing exit ticket: 'State one correlation you found and explain two reasons why correlation does not equal causation using your example.' Emphasize that correlation is necessary but not sufficient for establishing causal relationships in data science.
materials_needed: Health Outcomes Dataset (CSV file with 1000 patient records)
Computers with Excel, Google Sheets, or similar spreadsheet software
Correlation interpretation reference sheet
Causation analysis worksheet with guided questions
Exit ticket template
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients (25 points), (2) Accurate categorization of relationship strength using provided framework (25 points), (3) Identification of at least two relevant confounding variables per correlation pair (30 points), (4) Clear explanation on exit ticket distinguishing correlation from causation with specific example (20 points). Success criteria: 70% or higher demonstrates understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated correlation coefficients and focus on interpretation rather than calculation. Offer sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests..., but it doesn't prove causation because...'. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research actual studies related to their correlations and identify experimental designs that could test causation, or introduce partial correlation concepts to control for confounding variables.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Dataset Analysis

title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Returns Using Calculus Applications
description: Students will apply differential calculus and optimization techniques to solve a realistic real estate investment problem. They will analyze rental property scenarios, determine optimal purchase prices, and calculate maximum profit margins using mathematical modeling.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques to optimize profit functions in real estate investment scenarios by finding critical points and determining maximum values
Students will construct and solve mathematical models for rental property investments through multi-variable analysis and constraint optimization
instructions:
Begin by distributing the real estate investment packet containing three property scenarios with different rental rates, maintenance costs, and appreciation models (10 minutes). Organize students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (calculates derivatives), Financial Modeler (sets up equations), Market Researcher (interprets constraints), and Project Manager (coordinates and presents). Each team receives a different neighborhood scenario with varying market conditions.

Students first establish profit functions P(x) where x represents months of ownership, incorporating rental income R(x) = ax + b, maintenance costs M(x) = cx² + dx + e, and property appreciation A(x) = fx^(3/2) + gx (20 minutes). Teams must identify realistic constraints such as minimum ownership periods, maximum investment capital ($500,000), and local zoning restrictions affecting rental rates.

Next, students apply calculus techniques to find optimal solutions. They calculate P'(x) using power rule, product rule, and chain rule as needed, then solve P'(x) = 0 to find critical points (25 minutes). Using the second derivative test P''(x), teams determine whether critical points represent maximum profit scenarios. Students must also evaluate boundary conditions and constraint violations.

Teams then create detailed financial projections using their optimized values, calculating total ROI, monthly cash flow, and break-even timelines (15 minutes). Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation with mathematical justification for their investment recommendation, including graphs of profit functions and clear identification of optimal points. Conclude with team presentations where other students evaluate the mathematical accuracy and business viability of each proposal (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Real estate investment scenario packets (3 different neighborhoods with market data)
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos/GeoGebra
Large grid paper for function sketching
Financial projection templates
Presentation materials (poster paper, markers, or digital presentation tools)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Correct derivative calculations and critical point identification (30 points), appropriate application of optimization techniques including second derivative test (25 points), accurate financial modeling with realistic constraints (25 points), clear mathematical reasoning in presentation with proper notation (20 points). Students must show complete work for all calculus procedures and justify business decisions with mathematical evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written profit function templates with blanks to fill in coefficients, and offer derivative formula reference sheets. Create checkpoint moments at 15-minute intervals for instructor feedback. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints like tax implications, property management fees, or multi-property portfolio optimization requiring Lagrange multipliers. Provide extension problems involving piecewise functions for different market phases.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Ice Cream Sales Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different visualizations of the same ice cream sales dataset to determine which chart best communicates key business insights. They will justify their choice using established data visualization principles and identify specific strengths and weaknesses of each option.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types by applying data visualization best practices to assess clarity, accuracy, and insight communication
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with the 'Sweet Treats Ice Cream Shop' dataset containing 3 months of daily sales data (temperature, flavor, sales volume, day of week). Present three pre-made visualizations of this data: (1) a cluttered pie chart showing all 12 flavors with percentages, (2) a clear line graph showing sales trends over time with temperature overlay, and (3) a confusing 3D bar chart comparing weekend vs weekday sales by flavor. Give groups 10 minutes to examine all three charts without discussion. Next, distribute the 'Visualization Evaluation Checklist' covering: clarity of message, appropriate chart type, visual design principles, and actionable insights. Have each group spend 15 minutes systematically evaluating each chart using the checklist, scoring each criterion from 1-5 with written justifications. Groups then spend 10 minutes discussing their findings and reaching consensus on which visualization is most effective and why. Each group creates a 2-minute presentation defending their choice, specifically addressing: (1) what business question each chart answers best, (2) which design elements help or hinder understanding, and (3) their recommended improvements for the weakest chart. Conclude with group presentations followed by class discussion comparing different groups' reasoning and evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: Sweet Treats Ice Cream Shop dataset (CSV file with 90 days of sales data)
Three pre-made visualizations (printed copies or digital display)
Visualization Evaluation Checklist worksheet
Presentation timer
Flip chart paper and markers for notes
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: systematic use of evaluation checklist (5 points), quality of written justifications for each chart (6 points), logical reasoning in final recommendation (5 points), and clear communication during presentation (4 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of visualization principles by citing specific design elements and connecting chart effectiveness to business decision-making needs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions like 'What story does this chart tell?' and 'Who is the intended audience?' Advanced learners can create an improved version of the weakest chart and explain their design choices, or evaluate additional visualization types like heat maps or scatter plots using the same dataset.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Ice Cream Sales Analysis: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically assess three different data visualizations of the same ice cream sales dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key business insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge effectiveness and justify their recommendations with specific evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization types by applying established visualization principles and criteria
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Ice Cream Sales Evaluation Packet' containing three visualizations of monthly ice cream sales data: a pie chart showing flavor preferences, a line graph showing seasonal trends, and a bar chart comparing regional sales. Each visualization addresses the business question: 'Which region should receive additional marketing budget?'

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each visualization using the provided evaluation checklist covering: data accuracy representation, visual clarity, appropriate chart type selection, and ability to answer the business question. They score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and write 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning.

**Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their individual evaluations, discussing differences in scoring and identifying specific visual elements that influenced their judgments. Pairs must reach consensus on which visualization is most effective.

**Class Presentation (15 minutes):** Each pair presents their chosen visualization to the class, providing three specific reasons why it best answers the business question. They must cite evidence from their evaluation criteria and explain why the other two visualizations were less effective.

**Reflection Writing (10 minutes):** Students individually write a brief reflection identifying what makes a data visualization effective for business decision-making, using examples from the activity. They conclude by suggesting one improvement for their chosen visualization.
materials_needed: Ice Cream Sales Evaluation Packet (3 printed visualizations per student)
Visualization Evaluation Checklist handout
Scoring sheets with 1-5 rating scales
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of evaluation criteria application (25%), (2) Quality of evidence-based reasoning in justifications (25%), (3) Effectiveness of pair presentation with specific examples (25%), and (4) Depth of reflection on visualization principles (25%). Students must demonstrate critical thinking by identifying both strengths and weaknesses in each visualization.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation comments and a completed example evaluation of a fourth visualization. For advanced learners: Challenge them to redesign the least effective visualization and explain their design choices, or have them create additional evaluation criteria beyond the provided checklist.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Ice Cream Sales Analysis

title: Design and Build a Mathematical Board Game Using Quadratic Functions
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates quadratic functions as the core gameplay mechanic. They will design game rules, create visual elements, and develop mathematical challenges that require players to work with quadratic equations, parabolas, and real-world applications.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize their understanding of quadratic functions by designing an interactive board game that demonstrates vertex form, factored form, and standard form applications
Students will construct mathematical problems and solutions through game mechanics that require players to interpret parabolic graphs, solve quadratic equations, and apply optimization concepts
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Explain that each team will create a board game where quadratic functions drive the gameplay mechanics. Distribute materials and introduce the project requirements: games must include at least 15 quadratic function problems across three difficulty levels, incorporate visual parabolic elements, and include real-world scenarios. 

Day 1 (50 minutes): Teams brainstorm game concepts and create detailed design documents specifying game objectives, rules, and how quadratic functions will be integrated. They must sketch the board layout and identify where mathematical challenges will appear. Each team submits a one-page proposal with their game concept, target mathematical skills, and preliminary rules.

Day 2-3 (100 minutes total): Students construct their physical game boards using poster board and art supplies. They create game pieces, cards, and mathematical challenge components. Simultaneously, they develop their question bank of quadratic function problems, ensuring variety in formats (word problems, graphing challenges, equation solving, vertex identification). All mathematical content must be verified for accuracy before integration.

Day 4 (50 minutes): Teams finalize their games, write comprehensive instruction manuals, and create answer keys. They prepare 5-minute presentations explaining their game mechanics and demonstrating how quadratic functions are utilized. Each team must also prepare to teach their game to other students.

Day 5 (50 minutes): Game showcase and testing session. Each team presents their game (5 minutes), then facilitates gameplay with another team (15 minutes). Teams rotate through at least three different games, providing feedback on mathematical accuracy, engagement, and clarity of instructions. Conclude with reflection discussions on how creating games enhanced their understanding of quadratic functions.
materials_needed: 22" x 28" poster board (1 per team)
Colored markers, pencils, and art supplies
Graph paper and rulers
Index cards for game questions/challenges
Dice, game pieces, and small manipulatives
Graphing calculators
Laminating sheets (optional for durability)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy and variety of quadratic function applications (40 points), creativity and functionality of game design (25 points), clarity of instructions and playability (20 points), team presentation and demonstration (15 points). Students must also submit individual reflection essays explaining how their game incorporates specific quadratic function concepts and what they learned through the creation process.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing quadratic function reference sheets and pre-written problem templates they can modify. Offer advanced learners extension challenges like incorporating quadratic inequalities, systems of equations, or optimization problems. Consider pairing stronger math students with creative students to balance teams. Provide checkpoints on Days 2 and 3 to review mathematical content accuracy before final construction.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Notation Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the mathematical definitions, formal notations, and standard complexity classes for Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notations. This activity focuses on exact recall of formal definitions and their mathematical representations used in algorithm analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the precise mathematical definitions of Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notations using formal limit notation and inequality expressions
Students will identify and recite the standard time complexity classes (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ), O(n!)) with their formal mathematical expressions
instructions: Begin by distributing the complexity notation reference sheet containing formal mathematical definitions. Students have 15 minutes to study the definitions silently, focusing on memorizing the exact mathematical notation for each complexity class. After study time, collect all materials. Conduct Phase 1 (20 minutes): Display algorithm names one at a time on the projector (Binary Search, Merge Sort, Bubble Sort, Linear Search, Matrix Multiplication). Students must write the exact Big O notation and formal mathematical definition on their answer sheets within 2 minutes per algorithm. Phase 2 (15 minutes): Present mathematical expressions (e.g., 'f(n) = 3n² + 2n + 1') and students must identify the complexity class and write the formal Big O definition. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Quick-fire verbal recall where students stand and recite definitions when called upon - incorrect answers require the student to sit down. Conclude with a 5-minute review where students check their written answers against the reference sheet and calculate their accuracy percentage. Record individual scores for assessment purposes.
materials_needed: Printed reference sheets with formal mathematical definitions of Big O, Omega, and Theta notations
Individual answer sheets with numbered sections for each phase
Projector and laptop for displaying algorithm names and mathematical expressions
Timer or stopwatch for phase management
Red and green colored pens for self-assessment marking
assessment_method: Grade answer sheets using a 100-point rubric: Phase 1 - 50 points (10 points per correct algorithm complexity with proper mathematical notation), Phase 2 - 30 points (6 points per correct expression analysis), Phase 3 - 20 points (participation and accuracy in verbal recitation). Students must achieve 80% accuracy to demonstrate mastery of complexity notation recall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for common complexities (e.g., 'Constant, Log, Linear, Linearithmic, Quadratic, Exponential, Factorial') and allow them to use color-coded reference cards during Phase 1. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity classes like O(n³), O(√n), and amortized analysis definitions, plus require them to provide mathematical proofs for their answers.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Complex ML Models Through Error Analysis
description: Students will analyze pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results from three different machine learning models (linear regression, random forest, and neural network) applied to the same dataset. They will interpret how model complexity affects the bias-variance tradeoff and explain the implications for model selection and generalization performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition components by analyzing numerical results and visualizations from models of varying complexity
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and bias-variance tradeoff through comparative analysis of error breakdowns
instructions:
Begin by distributing the bias-variance analysis worksheet containing pre-computed results for three models trained on a housing price dataset: Model A (linear regression), Model B (random forest with 100 trees), and Model C (deep neural network with 3 hidden layers). Each student receives identical datasets showing: total error, bias², variance, and irreducible error values, plus learning curves and residual plots. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine the numerical decomposition table and identify which model corresponds to which complexity level based solely on the bias-variance values. They must justify their reasoning in writing.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Form groups of 3-4 students to compare interpretations. Groups analyze the learning curves showing training/validation error vs. training set size for each model, discussing how these curves relate to the bias-variance values.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups examine residual plots and error distribution histograms for each model, identifying patterns that indicate high bias (systematic errors) versus high variance (inconsistent predictions across different training sets).

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each group creates a comprehensive explanation document addressing: (a) which model suffers from high bias vs. high variance, (b) how they determined this from the data, (c) practical implications for model deployment, and (d) recommendations for addressing identified issues.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Groups present their key findings to the class, focusing on one specific insight about how bias-variance tradeoff manifests in the real-world scenario. Instructor facilitates discussion on conflicting interpretations and guides students toward consensus on complex cases.
materials_needed: Bias-variance decomposition worksheet with pre-computed results for 3 models
Learning curve plots (training/validation error vs. sample size)
Residual plots and error distribution histograms for each model
Digital copies of all materials for projection/screen sharing
assessment_method: Evaluate group explanation documents using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of high-bias vs. high-variance models with supporting evidence, (2) Accurate interpretation of learning curves in relation to bias-variance values, (3) Clear explanation of practical implications for model selection, (4) Quality of reasoning and use of statistical evidence. Minimum passing requires 3/4 points with particular emphasis on criterion 1.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a bias-variance reference sheet with key indicators (high bias = consistent but inaccurate predictions, high variance = accurate on average but inconsistent). Create simplified comparison tables highlighting the most obvious differences first. For advanced learners: Include bootstrap sampling results showing prediction distributions, challenge them to propose specific hyperparameter adjustments, or analyze how different train/test splits affect the decomposition values.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Runtime Complexity
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms by examining their time complexity patterns with varying dataset sizes. They will break down each algorithm's operations, identify efficiency bottlenecks, and compare their practical performance against theoretical predictions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by tracing through their recursive calls and loop structures
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through systematic comparison of empirical runtime data against Big O theoretical predictions
instructions:
Begin by providing students with implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in their preferred programming language (15 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives datasets of sizes 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 randomly generated integers. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams run each sorting algorithm on all four datasets, recording actual execution times in milliseconds. Students create a data table with algorithms as rows and dataset sizes as columns.

Step 2 (20 minutes): For each algorithm, students manually trace through the first few iterations using a sample of 8 numbers, counting the number of comparisons and swaps. They document the step-by-step breakdown in flowchart format.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Students graph their runtime results, plotting dataset size (x-axis) versus execution time (y-axis) with separate lines for each algorithm. They identify patterns and inflection points where one algorithm outperforms others.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams research the theoretical Big O complexity for each algorithm and overlay predicted performance curves on their empirical graphs. They analyze discrepancies between theory and practice.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about when to choose each algorithm, supporting their recommendation with specific data points from their analysis. Class votes on most compelling analysis.
materials_needed: Pre-written sorting algorithm implementations in Python/Java/C++
Random number generator datasets (100, 1000, 5000, 10000 integers)
Stopwatch/timing functions built into code
Graph paper or digital graphing tool (Excel/Google Sheets)
Big O complexity reference chart
assessment_method: Evaluate completed data tables (25%), accuracy of manual algorithm traces (25%), quality of performance graphs with correct trend identification (30%), and analysis of theory vs. practice discrepancies with specific examples (20%). Students must identify at least two factors causing real-world performance variations from theoretical predictions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed trace tables and highlight specific lines of code to focus on during manual tracing. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios, or introduce additional algorithms like heap sort for broader comparison.

title: Optimizing Emergency Vehicle Routes Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world emergency services optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the graphical method to determine optimal ambulance deployment strategies for a city district during peak hours.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert real-world emergency response scenarios into mathematical constraint systems with objective functions
Students will implement the graphical method to solve multi-variable optimization problems and interpret solutions within practical emergency services contexts
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the Emergency Services Scenario packet containing a city district map with 6 hospital locations, population density data, and current ambulance response times. Form teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives graphing paper, colored pencils, and calculators.

**Problem Formulation (25 minutes):** Teams analyze the scenario where the city must optimally position ambulances at two strategic locations (A and B) to minimize total response time. Students identify decision variables (x = ambulances at location A, y = ambulances at location B), formulate constraints based on: minimum coverage requirements (2x + 3y ≥ 18), maximum available ambulances (x + y ≤ 12), budget limitations (4000x + 6000y ≤ 40000), and non-negativity constraints. Teams establish the objective function to minimize total weighted response time: Z = 8x + 5y.

**Solution Implementation (30 minutes):** Students graph all constraint inequalities on coordinate planes, identifying the feasible region using different colors for each constraint. They locate corner points of the feasible region algebraically by solving systems of equations at intersections. Teams evaluate the objective function at each corner point: (0,0), (0,6), (3,6), (7,4), and (9,0).

**Solution Analysis (15 minutes):** Students determine the optimal solution by comparing objective function values, identifying (0,6) as optimal with Z = 30. Teams interpret this solution: deploy 6 ambulances at location B, none at location A, achieving minimum response time of 30 minutes. They verify their solution satisfies all constraints and discuss practical implications including cost savings and coverage effectiveness.
materials_needed: Emergency Services Scenario packets with city district maps and data tables
Graphing paper (1/4 inch grid)
Colored pencils or markers (4 different colors per team)
Scientific calculators
Rulers for precise line drawing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly formulates all constraints and objective function, accurately graphs feasible region, identifies optimal solution, and provides comprehensive practical interpretation; (3) Minor errors in formulation or graphing but reaches correct optimal solution; (2) Correct setup but significant computational or graphical errors affecting final answer; (1) Incomplete formulation or major conceptual misunderstandings. Submit final solution report including constraint equations, labeled graph, corner point calculations, and written recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates with partially completed inequalities, offer corner point calculation worksheets with step-by-step algebraic solution formats, and assign peer mentors within teams. For advanced learners: Extend to three-variable problems requiring simplex method, introduce sensitivity analysis by varying constraint parameters, or add integer programming requirements where ambulance numbers must be whole units.

title: Distributed System Architecture Failure Analysis: Decomposing the 2017 AWS S3 Outage
description: Students will systematically analyze the 2017 AWS S3 outage by examining architectural components, failure cascades, and system dependencies. They will identify root causes, trace failure propagation patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of recovery strategies used in this real-world distributed system failure.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between system architecture components and failure propagation by deconstructing the AWS S3 outage's technical timeline
Students will differentiate between immediate causes and underlying systemic vulnerabilities through comparative examination of pre-failure and post-failure system states
instructions: Begin by distributing the AWS S3 outage post-mortem document and system architecture diagrams (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a specific analysis framework: Component Interaction Analysis, Failure Timeline Reconstruction, Dependency Mapping, or Recovery Strategy Evaluation. Each team receives identical base materials but focuses on their assigned analytical lens. Teams spend 45 minutes creating detailed analytical diagrams using draw.io or Lucidchart, mapping their assigned perspective. Component teams identify all system elements and their normal interactions. Timeline teams create chronological failure cascades with timestamps. Dependency teams trace how failures propagated through interconnected services. Recovery teams analyze mitigation steps and their effectiveness timing. After initial analysis, teams rotate stations (20 minutes per rotation) to examine other teams' work and add insights using different colored annotations. This cross-pollination reveals how different analytical approaches reveal different aspects of the same failure. Teams then synthesize findings into comprehensive failure analysis reports (40 minutes) that integrate all four analytical perspectives. Each report must include: root cause identification with supporting evidence, failure propagation pathway diagrams, critical dependency vulnerability points, and ranked effectiveness assessment of recovery actions. Conclude with team presentations (8 minutes each) where teams present their integrated analysis and field questions about their reasoning process and evidence interpretation.
materials_needed: AWS S3 outage post-mortem documentation (official AWS report)
AWS architecture diagrams showing S3, EC2, and dependent services
Laptops with draw.io or Lucidchart access
Colored pens/markers for annotation activities
Large format paper for collaborative diagram creation
Timer for rotation management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of component relationship identification and failure pathway tracing, (2) Quality of evidence-based reasoning connecting architectural decisions to failure outcomes, (3) Depth of analysis in distinguishing primary causes from secondary effects, (4) Integration effectiveness of multiple analytical perspectives in final synthesis. Students must demonstrate expert-level analysis by identifying at least 3 architectural vulnerabilities not explicitly stated in the post-mortem and providing technical justification for their assessments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided analysis templates with partially completed component maps and specific guiding questions for each analysis step. Offer vocabulary support sheets with distributed systems terminology. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by providing supplementary technical documentation about AWS internal architecture and challenge them to propose alternative architectural designs that could have prevented the cascade failure. Encourage advanced students to research similar outages (GitHub 2018, Cloudflare 2019) for comparative analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness: Chart Type Selection Critique
description: Students will critically assess and compare different data visualization approaches for the same dataset. They will evaluate the effectiveness of various chart types in communicating specific insights and make evidence-based recommendations for optimal visualization choices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types by analyzing their ability to communicate specific data insights accurately
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison using established design principles
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a dataset containing monthly sales data for 4 product categories over 12 months, plus 6 different visualizations of this same data: bar chart, line graph, pie chart, stacked area chart, scatter plot, and heat map. **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each visualization and complete an evaluation matrix, rating each chart (1-5 scale) on: clarity of trends, ease of comparison between categories, visual appeal, and accuracy of data representation. They must write 2-3 sentences justifying each rating. **Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discussing discrepancies and defending their ratings with specific evidence from the visualizations. **Scenario Application (15 minutes):** Present three different audience scenarios: (1) executive summary for quarterly board meeting, (2) detailed analysis for marketing team, (3) public infographic for customers. Students rank the top 3 visualizations for each scenario and write a 1-paragraph justification for their first choice, explaining why it best serves that specific audience and purpose. **Class Synthesis (10 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion where volunteers share their recommendations for one scenario, focusing on the reasoning behind their evaluation. Record common evaluation criteria on the board.
materials_needed: Sample dataset: Monthly sales data for 4 product categories (Excel or CSV format)
6 pre-created visualizations of the same dataset in different chart types
Evaluation matrix worksheet with rating scales
Scenario description handouts
Computer or tablet access for viewing digital visualizations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed evaluation matrices for thoughtful justifications (40%), scenario-specific recommendations with clear reasoning (40%), and quality of evidence-based arguments during pair and class discussions (20%). Success criteria: ratings show understanding of visualization strengths/weaknesses, written justifications reference specific visual elements, scenario recommendations demonstrate audience awareness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of visualization evaluation criteria (Can you easily see trends? Are categories comparable? Is the message clear?). For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to redesign the weakest visualization and explain their improvements, or evaluate accessibility considerations for colorblind users.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness: Chart Type Selection Critique: Visual Analysis
description: Students will critically assess the appropriateness of different chart types for specific datasets and research questions. They will judge the effectiveness of existing visualizations and justify alternative approaches using data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the appropriateness of bar charts, line graphs, and pie charts by analyzing three different datasets and their corresponding research questions
Students will critique existing data visualizations through systematic assessment using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by displaying three datasets on the board: monthly sales data (12 months, 4 product categories), student grade distributions (5 grade ranges, percentages), and city population growth (10 cities, 5-year trend). Distribute the evaluation worksheet containing three poorly matched chart examples: a pie chart showing the population growth trends, a line graph displaying grade distributions, and a bar chart comparing monthly sales across categories but formatted as separate bars rather than grouped/stacked. 

Divide students into pairs and provide 15 minutes for them to examine each visualization-dataset pairing. Students must complete the evaluation matrix, rating each chart on a 1-4 scale across four criteria: data type appropriateness, clarity of message, visual accuracy, and audience accessibility. For each criterion, they must write a 2-3 sentence justification.

After individual evaluation, pairs spend 10 minutes discussing their ratings and reaching consensus. Each pair then selects their lowest-rated visualization and designs an alternative chart type, sketching it on paper with labels and brief explanation of why their choice better serves the research question.

Conduct a 15-minute whole-class discussion where three pairs present their worst-rated visualization and proposed alternative. Other students vote on whether they agree with the assessment using colored cards (green=agree, red=disagree), and briefly justify their position. Conclude by having students individually complete a reflection form rating their confidence in chart selection and identifying two key principles they'll use for future visualization decisions.
materials_needed: Three printed datasets (monthly sales, grade distributions, population growth)
Evaluation worksheet with 4-criteria matrix and rating scales
Three example visualizations (printed or digital display)
Colored voting cards (green and red) for each student
Blank paper for sketching alternative charts
Individual reflection forms
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Evaluation Matrix completion (40% - must provide justified ratings for all criteria), Alternative Chart Design (35% - appropriate chart type selection with clear rationale), Class Participation (25% - meaningful contribution to discussion and peer voting). Success criteria: Students score 3/4 or higher on evaluation accuracy, propose contextually appropriate alternative charts, and demonstrate understanding through peer critique participation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with chart type guidelines (when to use bar, line, pie charts) and sentence starters for justifications. Pair stronger analytical thinkers with peers who need support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to consider additional factors like color accessibility, cultural considerations, or mobile device compatibility in their evaluations, and ask them to sketch two alternative solutions with trade-off analysis.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness: Chart Type Selection Critique

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Function Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units of each layer in the TCP/IP protocol stack through structured repetition and peer testing. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network architecture that students must have instant recall of for advanced networking concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the four TCP/IP layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) and their specific functions by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will identify the correct protocols and data units for each TCP/IP layer through structured peer assessment activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made protocol stack reference sheets to each student (5 minutes). Have students spend 15 minutes silently studying the TCP/IP layer information, focusing on layer names, primary functions, key protocols (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP/SMTP for Application; TCP/UDP for Transport; IP/ICMP/ARP for Internet; Ethernet/WiFi for Network Access), and data units (messages, segments, packets, frames). Next, collect all reference materials and divide the class into pairs (3 minutes). Conduct Round 1: Partner A quizzes Partner B for 8 minutes using the provided question prompts ('What layer handles end-to-end communication?', 'Which protocols operate at the Application layer?', 'What is the data unit at the Transport layer?'). Partners switch roles for Round 2 (8 minutes). Redistribute reference sheets for a 5-minute review period where students can check answers and clarify misconceptions. Remove materials again and conduct Round 3: rapid-fire individual assessment where you call out layer names and students must write down three key facts within 30 seconds per layer (8 minutes total). Conclude with a whole-class verbal review where volunteers state one function or protocol for each layer while others verify accuracy (8 minutes). Throughout the activity, emphasize exact terminology - 'segments' not 'packets' for Transport layer, 'frames' not 'packets' for Network Access layer.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Stack reference sheets (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Peer assessment question prompt sheets
Blank paper for final assessment
Whiteboard/projector for whole-class review
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on the final rapid-fire written assessment, correctly identifying 3 out of 4 key elements (primary function, main protocols, data unit) for each TCP/IP layer. Award 1 point per correct layer function, 1 point per correct protocol identification, 1 point per correct data unit term (maximum 12 points total). During peer assessment rounds, observe and note students who consistently provide accurate answers to award participation credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory devices (ATNI for layer order), allow them to review materials an additional 5 minutes, and pair them with stronger peers during practice rounds. For advanced learners: challenge them to also recall port numbers for common protocols (HTTP:80, HTTPS:443, FTP:21) and explain encapsulation/decapsulation processes, or have them create additional quiz questions for classmates incorporating OSI model comparisons.

title: Decoding Feature Engineering Strategies in Production ML Pipeline Failures
description: Students analyze three real-world machine learning pipeline failure scenarios to identify how improper feature engineering decisions led to model degradation. They will examine feature selection, transformation, and scaling choices to understand their cascading effects on model performance and business outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate feature engineering techniques by analyzing production ML pipeline failure case studies
Students will explain the relationship between feature preprocessing decisions and downstream model performance through systematic evaluation of pipeline components
instructions: Begin by distributing three anonymized case study packets, each containing: original dataset schema, feature engineering code, model performance metrics over time, and business impact reports (15 minutes setup). Divide students into expert groups of 3-4, assigning each group one case study. Students spend 45 minutes examining their assigned case, identifying: (1) specific feature engineering decisions made, (2) technical symptoms of pipeline degradation, (3) root cause analysis of why features caused failures, and (4) alternative approaches that could have prevented issues. Each group creates a diagnostic framework mapping feature engineering choices to observed outcomes. Next, reorganize into jigsaw groups with one expert from each case study (20 minutes). Experts teach their case to new group members, focusing on the feature engineering lessons learned. Groups then collaborate to develop a unified 'Feature Engineering Risk Assessment Checklist' incorporating insights from all three cases (25 minutes). Conclude with groups presenting their checklists to the class, explaining how different feature engineering anti-patterns manifest across domains (15 minutes). Instructor facilitates discussion connecting student insights to broader principles of feature engineering best practices, data leakage prevention, and production ML system design.
materials_needed: Three detailed ML pipeline failure case studies with real datasets and code
Performance monitoring dashboards (screenshots or interactive)
Business impact reports showing financial/operational consequences
Jupyter notebooks with feature engineering code examples
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool for framework development
assessment_method: Evaluate students on: (1) Accuracy of root cause identification in case analysis (40%), (2) Quality of explanations linking feature engineering decisions to outcomes during jigsaw teaching (30%), (3) Comprehensiveness and practicality of final risk assessment checklist (30%). Use rubric measuring technical accuracy, depth of understanding causal relationships, and ability to generalize principles across different ML contexts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for case analysis focusing on specific code blocks and metrics. Include glossary of feature engineering terms. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including distributed systems considerations, real-time feature serving challenges, or regulatory compliance requirements. Encourage them to propose novel monitoring approaches for early detection of feature-related issues.

title: Analyzing Algorithm Efficiency: Comparing Sorting Performance Through Trace Analysis
description: Students analyze and compare the performance characteristics of bubble sort and quicksort algorithms by examining execution traces, identifying patterns in their time complexity, and evaluating their suitability for different data scenarios. This activity develops critical thinking about algorithmic trade-offs and performance optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the step-by-step execution patterns of bubble sort and quicksort algorithms by examining detailed trace outputs and counting operations
Students will evaluate the relative efficiency of different sorting algorithms through systematic comparison of operation counts and identification of best/worst-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student with three datasets: a sorted array [1,2,3,4,5], a reverse-sorted array [5,4,3,2,1], and a random array [3,1,4,2,5]. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to manually trace both bubble sort and quicksort on the sorted dataset, recording each comparison and swap operation on provided worksheets. Next, have students form pairs (25 minutes) to trace the algorithms on the remaining two datasets, with one partner focusing on bubble sort and the other on quicksort. Partners must verify each other's traces and resolve discrepancies. In the analysis phase (30 minutes), pairs create a comparison matrix documenting: total comparisons, total swaps, and execution patterns for each algorithm-dataset combination. Students then identify which algorithm performs better under each condition and hypothesize why. During the final synthesis phase (20 minutes), pairs join to form groups of four to discuss their findings and prepare a brief presentation highlighting the most significant performance differences they discovered. Each group presents their key finding to the class (15 minutes total). Throughout the activity, circulate to check trace accuracy and guide students toward recognizing patterns like bubble sort's consistent O(n²) behavior versus quicksort's dataset-dependent performance.
materials_needed: Algorithm trace worksheets with operation counting tables
Three pre-prepared datasets printed on cards
Stopwatches or timers
Whiteboard markers and poster paper for group presentations
Reference sheets with bubble sort and quicksort pseudocode
assessment_method: Evaluate trace accuracy (40% - correct identification of comparisons and swaps), analysis quality (35% - accurate operation counts and pattern recognition), and synthesis depth (25% - insightful conclusions about algorithmic trade-offs). Use a 4-point rubric where 4=comprehensive analysis with clear reasoning, 3=mostly accurate with minor gaps, 2=basic understanding with some errors, 1=incomplete or inaccurate analysis.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed traces and highlighting the first few steps. Offer visual aids showing array state changes. For advanced learners, introduce additional datasets (nearly sorted, many duplicates) or challenge them to predict performance on larger datasets and verify with actual runtime measurements using provided code implementations.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Multiple Business Scenarios
description: Students will critically assess three different machine learning models (logistic regression, random forest, and neural network) applied to a customer churn prediction problem, evaluating their performance using multiple metrics and business constraints. They will justify which model should be deployed in production by weighing technical performance against real-world business considerations including interpretability, computational costs, and regulatory requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of three machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and ROC curves within specific business contexts
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic assessment of trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, computational efficiency, and regulatory compliance requirements
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with the pre-trained model results dataset containing performance metrics for three models predicting customer churn for a fictional telecommunications company. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the provided performance summary containing accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, training time, prediction time, and feature importance rankings for each model. Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the business scenario document, teams evaluate each model against five specific criteria: prediction accuracy requirements (minimize false negatives), interpretability needs (regulatory requirement for explainable decisions), computational constraints (real-time prediction under 100ms), model maintenance complexity, and data drift sensitivity. Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams complete the structured evaluation matrix, scoring each model (1-5 scale) on each criterion and calculating weighted scores based on provided business priority weights. Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their model recommendation, addressing potential counterarguments and explaining why their chosen model outperforms alternatives given the specific business context. Step 5 (45 minutes): Each team presents their recommendation while other teams provide peer feedback using the provided critique framework. Step 6 (15 minutes): Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion comparing different team conclusions and reasoning approaches, highlighting how business context influences model selection decisions beyond pure technical performance metrics.
materials_needed: Pre-generated model performance results dataset (CSV format with metrics for 3 models)
Business scenario document detailing company context and constraints
Structured evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Peer critique framework rubric
Access to Python/R with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn for data visualization
Presentation slides template
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 4-level rubric (exemplary/proficient/developing/inadequate) across four dimensions: (1) Technical Analysis - accurate interpretation of performance metrics and statistical significance of differences between models, (2) Business Integration - thoughtful consideration of real-world constraints and stakeholder needs, (3) Critical Reasoning - systematic evaluation process with clear justification for weighting decisions and trade-offs, (4) Communication - clear presentation of recommendations with evidence-based arguments addressing counterpoints. Final deliverable includes completed evaluation matrix with justifications and 5-minute recorded presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each evaluation criterion, offer examples of how to interpret confusion matrices, and give sentence starters for justification responses. Include a glossary of technical terms and business concepts. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring cost-benefit analysis with specific dollar amounts for false positives/negatives, consideration of model ensemble approaches, or evaluation of additional models like XGBoost. Challenge them to propose A/B testing frameworks for model deployment validation.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-selected dataset containing variables with strong correlations to distinguish between correlation and causation relationships. They will interpret correlation coefficients, create visualizations, and explain why correlation does not imply causation using concrete examples from the data.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and their statistical significance by analyzing relationships between variables in a healthcare dataset
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through guided analysis of confounding variables and alternative explanations
instructions: Begin by providing students with the 'Health and Lifestyle Dataset' containing variables: exercise hours/week, ice cream consumption, drowning incidents, temperature, and life satisfaction scores (dataset available via provided CSV file). Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to load the dataset using provided Python/R template code and generate a correlation matrix using .corr() function. They identify the three strongest correlations (>0.7 or <-0.7). Step 2 (20 min): Each pair creates scatter plots for their identified correlations using matplotlib/ggplot, adding trend lines and correlation coefficients as annotations. Step 3 (25 min): Provide students with 'Correlation Analysis Worksheet' containing guided questions: 'What does a correlation of 0.85 between ice cream sales and drowning incidents tell us?' and 'List three possible explanations for this relationship that don't involve ice cream causing drownings.' Students must identify at least two confounding variables (temperature, season) for each correlation. Step 4 (15 min): Students complete a 'Causation Evidence Checklist' evaluating each correlation against criteria: temporal precedence, mechanism plausibility, alternative explanations ruled out, and experimental evidence. Step 5 (10 min): Pairs present one correlation example, explaining why it represents correlation without causation. Instructor facilitates discussion highlighting common misconceptions and real-world implications of misinterpreting correlations.
materials_needed: Health and Lifestyle Dataset (CSV file with 500 rows, 8 variables)
Python/R template code with data loading and basic analysis functions
Correlation Analysis Worksheet (printed or digital)
Causation Evidence Checklist handout
Computers with Python/Jupyter or R/RStudio installed
assessment_method: Grade students using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients (25%), (2) Accurate identification of confounding variables with explanations (35%), (3) Clear distinction between correlation and causation with specific examples (25%), and (4) Quality of reasoning in Causation Evidence Checklist responses (15%). Students must score 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
