scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed correlation matrix and pre-made visualizations, focus on interpreting existing results rather than generating them. Offer sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests...' and 'However, this doesn't mean causation because...'. For advanced learners: Include additional variables for multiple regression analysis, introduce concepts of partial correlation, or have them research and present real-world examples of correlation-causation confusion in media or research studies.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a provided dataset containing ice cream sales and drowning incidents to distinguish between correlation and causation. They will create visualizations, calculate correlation coefficients, and explain why correlation does not imply causation through guided analysis and peer discussion.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from a real-world dataset
Students will explain the concept of confounding variables through identification of lurking factors in data relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing monthly data for ice cream sales, drowning incidents, and temperature across 24 months (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to complete Part 1: Create a scatter plot of ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents using matplotlib, then calculate Pearson correlation coefficient using pandas.corr() function. They record their findings on the provided worksheet, noting the correlation strength (20 minutes). In Part 2, students create a second scatter plot showing temperature vs. ice cream sales, and a third showing temperature vs. drowning incidents. They calculate correlation coefficients for both relationships and compare all three correlations side-by-side (25 minutes). For Part 3, pairs discuss and write explanations for: Why ice cream sales and drowning incidents are correlated, what confounding variable explains this relationship, and why we cannot conclude that ice cream sales cause drowning incidents. They must provide at least two additional examples of correlation without causation from their own experience (20 minutes). Conclude with a gallery walk where pairs post their explanations and visit three other pairs' work, adding sticky note questions or comments. Facilitate a 10-minute whole-class debrief focusing on identifying confounding variables and real-world implications of mistaking correlation for causation in business or research decisions.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-loaded dataset (ice_cream_drowning_data.csv)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Printed analysis worksheet with correlation recording tables
Sticky notes for gallery walk feedback
Computers/tablets with internet access for each pair
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients, (2) Accurate creation of three required scatter plots, (3) Clear explanation of why correlation doesn't imply causation with temperature identified as confounding variable, (4) Two relevant real-world examples of correlation vs. causation. Students must score 3/4 points to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation coefficient interpretation guide (0.7-1.0 = strong, 0.3-0.7 = moderate, 0-0.3 = weak) and sentence starters for explanations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research and propose statistical methods that could help establish causation (randomized controlled trials, instrumental variables) and identify additional potential confounding variables beyond temperature.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze pre-selected datasets containing strong correlations to distinguish between correlation and causation relationships. They will identify confounding variables and explain why correlation does not imply causation through guided analysis of three different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing real-world datasets and identifying potential confounding variables
Students will explain the limitations of correlation analysis through written justifications of why observed relationships may not be causal
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and distribute the three prepared datasets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths by month, (2) Number of firefighters vs. property damage in fires, and (3) Chocolate consumption vs. Nobel Prize winners by country. Provide each group with printed correlation coefficients and scatter plots for all three datasets (10 minutes setup). 

In Phase 1 (15 minutes), groups examine Dataset 1 and complete a structured worksheet asking: What is the correlation coefficient? What does this suggest about the relationship? What alternative explanations could account for this pattern? Groups must identify at least two potential confounding variables and explain their reasoning.

Phase 2 (20 minutes) involves rotating datasets so each group analyzes all three scenarios. For each dataset, students must: calculate or verify the correlation strength, propose a causal hypothesis that the correlation might suggest, identify at least one confounding variable, and write a 2-3 sentence explanation of why the correlation likely does not indicate causation.

In Phase 3 (15 minutes), groups present one dataset analysis to the class, focusing on their identified confounding variables and alternative explanations. Other groups can challenge or add to the explanations.

Conclude with a whole-class discussion (10 minutes) where students create a checklist of questions to ask when encountering correlations in future data analysis work.
materials_needed: Three printed datasets with correlation coefficients and scatter plots
Structured analysis worksheets (one per student)
Calculators or laptops with basic statistical software
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strength AND provides 2+ valid confounding variables AND clearly explains why correlation≠causation; (3) Identifies correlation AND provides 1-2 confounding variables AND attempts explanation; (2) Identifies correlation AND provides 1 confounding variable; (1) Identifies correlation only or shows misconceptions about causation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a list of potential confounding variable categories (time-based, geographic, demographic) and sentence starters like 'Another factor that might explain both variables is...' For advanced learners, challenge them to design a study that could test for actual causation or research additional examples of spurious correlations online.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a provided healthcare dataset to distinguish between correlational relationships and potential causal relationships. They will examine scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and contextual factors to explain why strong correlations may not indicate causation.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots by identifying the strength and direction of relationships between variables in a healthcare dataset
Students will differentiate between correlation and causation through systematic analysis of confounding variables and logical reasoning
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Heart Disease Risk Factors' dataset containing 500 patient records with variables: age, exercise_hours_weekly, cholesterol_level, heart_disease_present, income_level, and education_years. Have students work in pairs for 45 minutes.

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students load the dataset in their analysis tool and create scatter plots for three variable pairs: (exercise_hours vs heart_disease), (income_level vs exercise_hours), and (education_years vs cholesterol_level). They calculate Pearson correlation coefficients for each pair.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students identify which correlations are strongest (above 0.5 or below -0.5) and describe the relationship direction. They record their findings in the provided worksheet, noting correlation strength as weak (<0.3), moderate (0.3-0.7), or strong (>0.7).

Step 3 (20 minutes): For each strong correlation found, students brainstorm and list at least three potential confounding variables that might explain the relationship without direct causation. They consider factors like socioeconomic status, geographic location, or lifestyle patterns that could influence both variables simultaneously.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students write a 200-word explanation for their strongest correlation, explicitly stating why correlation does not equal causation in this case. They must reference specific confounding variables and explain how controlled experiments would be needed to establish causality.

Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share their most surprising correlation finding and their reasoning about causation limitations.
materials_needed: Heart Disease Risk Factors dataset (CSV file with 500 records)
Statistical analysis software (R, Python with pandas, or Excel)
Correlation Analysis Worksheet template
Computers with internet access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate correlation coefficient calculations and interpretations, (2) Correct identification of relationship strength and direction, (3) Quality of confounding variable identification (minimum 3 per strong correlation), (4) Written explanation demonstrates clear understanding of correlation vs. causation with specific examples from their analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation interpretation guide with examples of weak/moderate/strong relationships. Pre-calculate one correlation as an example. For advanced learners: Have them explore partial correlations to control for one confounding variable, or research the Bradford Hill criteria for establishing causation in epidemiological studies.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Analysis

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Trigonometric Functions and Calculus
description: Students will apply advanced trigonometric functions and differential calculus to determine the optimal angle and spacing for solar panels in a realistic energy efficiency scenario. They will analyze real solar irradiance data and calculate maximum energy output configurations for different geographic locations and seasonal conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions and their derivatives to model solar panel efficiency by calculating optimal tilt angles based on latitude and seasonal sun position data
Students will implement optimization techniques through differential calculus to determine maximum energy output configurations while accounting for shadow interference between panel rows
instructions: Begin by providing each team with solar irradiance data sheets for three different cities (Phoenix, Seattle, Miami) containing monthly sun angle measurements and average daily sunshine hours. Students work in groups of 3-4 for 20 minutes to analyze the data patterns. Next, introduce the energy output formula: E(θ) = I₀ × A × cos(θ - α) × η × t, where θ is panel tilt angle, α is sun elevation angle, I₀ is solar irradiance, A is panel area, η is efficiency coefficient, and t is time. Students spend 30 minutes setting up their trigonometric models using graphing calculators or Desmos, inputting real values: A = 2m², η = 0.20, I₀ = 1000 W/m². For the next 40 minutes, students apply calculus optimization by taking derivatives of their energy functions with respect to tilt angle θ, setting equal to zero, and solving for optimal angles. They must calculate this for each city and compare results. During the final 25 minutes, students incorporate shadow analysis using the spacing formula: d = L × sin(θ)/tan(β), where d is minimum spacing, L is panel length, θ is tilt angle, and β is minimum sun elevation angle. Teams present their optimized configurations, showing mathematical work and justifying their solutions with calculated energy outputs. Each group must defend why their configuration maximizes annual energy production while minimizing land use.
materials_needed: Solar irradiance data sheets for Phoenix, Seattle, and Miami with monthly measurements
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent) or computer access to Desmos graphing calculator
Solar panel specification sheets showing dimensions and efficiency ratings
Latitude and longitude reference charts for the three cities
Graph paper and rulers for sketching panel layouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct application of trigonometric functions in energy model setup (25%), (2) Accurate use of differential calculus to find optimal angles with proper derivative calculations (35%), (3) Integration of shadow spacing constraints with geometric reasoning (25%), and (4) Quality of mathematical justification in final presentation with clear explanation of optimization process (15%). Students must submit calculation worksheets and deliver 5-minute group presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated sun angle values and guide them through the first derivative step-by-step. Offer simplified energy formulas initially. For advanced learners, introduce additional variables like seasonal adjustment mechanisms, economic cost analysis, or multi-objective optimization considering both energy output and installation costs. Encourage exploration of battery storage optimization as an extension.

title: Distributed System Architecture Analysis: Microservices vs. Monolithic Performance Bottleneck Investigation
description: Students will analyze the architectural decisions and performance bottlenecks in two equivalent e-commerce systems (one microservices-based, one monolithic) by examining system traces, database query patterns, and network communication logs. They will identify failure points, scalability limitations, and propose architectural improvements based on their systematic analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by comparing performance metrics, communication patterns, and failure modes between microservices and monolithic implementations
Students will dissect system bottlenecks through systematic examination of application logs, database queries, and network traces to identify root causes of performance degradation
instructions: Provide students with two datasets: traces from a monolithic e-commerce system and equivalent microservices implementation, each handling 10,000 concurrent users during Black Friday simulation. Begin with 15-minute individual examination phase where students review system architecture diagrams and identify key components. Form teams of 3-4 students for collaborative analysis phase (45 minutes). Each team receives identical log files containing: HTTP request/response times, database query execution plans, memory usage patterns, and network latency measurements. Students use provided analysis worksheets to systematically examine: (1) Request flow patterns - trace user checkout process through both systems, (2) Database bottlenecks - identify slow queries and connection pool exhaustion, (3) Service communication overhead - calculate network latency impact in microservices vs. direct method calls in monolithic system, (4) Failure cascade analysis - examine how service failures propagate differently in each architecture. Teams document findings using structured comparison matrices, plotting performance metrics on provided graphs. Final 30 minutes: teams present 5-minute findings to class, focusing on specific bottlenecks discovered and architectural trade-offs identified. Instructor facilitates discussion comparing team findings, highlighting different analytical approaches used. Students submit individual reflection papers (500 words) analyzing which architecture better handles the given load scenario and why, supported by specific evidence from their log analysis.
materials_needed: Two sets of system log files (monolithic and microservices e-commerce applications)
System architecture diagrams for both implementations
Log analysis worksheets with structured comparison matrices
Graph paper or digital graphing tools for plotting performance metrics
Stopwatches or timing applications for presentation management
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification from logs (25 points), (2) Quality of architectural comparison analysis (25 points), (3) Evidence-based reasoning in recommendations (25 points), (4) Clarity of individual reflection demonstrating synthesis of findings (25 points). Students must identify at least 3 specific performance bottlenecks with supporting log evidence and provide architectural reasoning for why each occurs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-highlighted sections in logs showing obvious bottlenecks, offer simplified analysis templates with guided questions. For advanced learners: include additional complexity such as container orchestration logs, provide real-world case studies of major system failures for comparison, challenge them to propose hybrid architectural solutions addressing identified weaknesses.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Survey Results
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same student survey dataset, determining which visualization best communicates key insights. They will justify their evaluation using specific criteria and recommend improvements for less effective visualizations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and scatter plots by applying data visualization principles to assess clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Student Survey Dataset (containing 100 responses about study habits, sleep hours, and GPA) along with three pre-made visualizations: a bar chart showing average study hours by major, a pie chart displaying sleep duration categories, and a scatter plot correlating study hours with GPA. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Have students individually examine each visualization for 3 minutes, taking notes on first impressions and what information each conveys.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Introduce the evaluation criteria: clarity (can viewers quickly understand the message?), accuracy (does the visualization truthfully represent the data?), and purpose alignment (does it serve the intended audience of incoming students?). Students work in pairs to score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Pairs complete the structured evaluation worksheet, ranking the three visualizations from most to least effective. For each ranking, they must provide three specific justifications (e.g., 'The scatter plot effectively shows the positive correlation through clear trend line, uses appropriate axis labels, and avoids misleading scaling').

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair selects the least effective visualization and writes two concrete improvement recommendations with explanations (e.g., 'Replace pie chart with horizontal bar chart because percentages are difficult to compare in pie format').

Step 5 (15 minutes): Conduct gallery walk where pairs post their rankings and justifications. Students place sticky dots next to evaluations they agree with, creating class consensus data.

Conclude with 5-minute whole-class discussion comparing evaluation results and discussing how different audiences might evaluate the same visualizations differently.
materials_needed: Student Survey Dataset (Excel file with 100 sample responses)
Three pre-made visualizations (printed copies or digital display)
Structured Evaluation Worksheet with scoring rubric
Sticky dots for gallery walk voting
Flip chart paper for posting evaluations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (4) Exceptional - provides detailed justifications with specific visualization principles, rankings show deep analysis; (3) Proficient - clear reasoning with some specific examples, logical ranking order; (2) Developing - general comments with limited specific justifications; (1) Beginning - vague reasoning, rankings lack clear logic. Evaluate both individual worksheet responses and quality of improvement recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation criteria definitions with examples (e.g., show sample of misleading vs. clear axis labels). Create sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' For advanced learners: Add fourth criterion of 'innovation' and ask them to redesign the weakest visualization using different chart types or interactive elements.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Survey Results: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze and critique three different visualizations of the same student survey dataset about study habits. They will assess which visualization best communicates key insights and justify their evaluation using established data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, pie chart, scatter plot) by applying data visualization best practices and identifying which most clearly communicates survey insights
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by distributing three printed visualizations of fictional student survey data about daily study hours, preferred subjects, and GPA (bar chart showing study hours by subject, pie chart of subject preferences, scatter plot of study hours vs. GPA). Give students 5 minutes to examine all three individually. Next, introduce the evaluation criteria worksheet with four categories: clarity (Is the message clear?), accuracy (Does it represent data correctly?), design (Are colors/labels appropriate?), and audience (Is it suitable for high school students?). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes to complete the worksheet, rating each visualization 1-5 in each category and writing specific justifications. Then facilitate a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share their highest-rated visualization and defend their choice. Finally, each student individually writes a 3-paragraph evaluation report: paragraph 1 identifies the most effective visualization with overall rating, paragraph 2 explains strengths using specific examples from the criteria, and paragraph 3 suggests one concrete improvement for their chosen visualization. Collect reports as exit tickets. Throughout the activity, emphasize that students must support all judgments with specific evidence from the visualizations and criteria.
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations per student (bar chart, pie chart, scatter plot)
Evaluation criteria worksheet with 4 categories and 1-5 rating scales
Sample student survey dataset description sheet
Blank paper for final evaluation reports
assessment_method: Grade final evaluation reports using 4-point rubric: (4) Clearly identifies most effective visualization with detailed justification using all criteria; (3) Identifies effective visualization with good justification using most criteria; (2) Identifies visualization with basic justification using some criteria; (1) Unclear choice or minimal justification. Look for specific evidence citations and logical reasoning in student explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and highlight one example of good/poor design in each chart. For advanced learners: Ask them to redesign the weakest visualization and explain their design choices, or have them create their own fourth visualization type for comparison.
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Survey Results

title: Design Your Dream City: Linear Programming Transportation Network
description: Students will create an original city transportation optimization problem and develop a complete mathematical solution using linear programming. They will design constraints based on real-world factors like budget, population, and environmental impact, then solve their created problem using graphical and algebraic methods.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original linear programming problem by designing a city transportation scenario with at least 4 realistic constraints and 2 variables
Students will develop a complete mathematical solution through graphical representation, corner point analysis, and optimization verification
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute city planning briefing where students receive their role as transportation consultants. Distribute the City Design Template and explain they must create a transportation network connecting residential areas to business districts. In pairs, students spend 15 minutes brainstorming their city's unique characteristics (population 50,000-200,000, geographic features, budget constraints). Next, students individually spend 25 minutes defining their optimization problem: they must choose 2 transportation modes (buses, trains, bike lanes, etc.) as variables, create an objective function to maximize ridership or minimize cost, and establish exactly 4 constraints including budget ($2-8 million), environmental impact points (≤100), minimum service requirements, and capacity limitations. Students then spend 30 minutes creating their mathematical model, writing inequalities, and graphing on coordinate planes using colored pencils for each constraint. During the solving phase (20 minutes), students identify feasible regions, locate corner points using algebraic methods, and test each point in their objective function. Students conclude by spending 15 minutes preparing a city council presentation poster showing their problem setup, mathematical work, optimal solution, and real-world interpretation. Finally, conduct 5-minute peer presentations where each student presents their transportation solution and receives feedback using the evaluation checklist.
materials_needed: City Design Template worksheet (custom-created)
Graph paper (coordinate plane, 20x20 grid minimum)
Colored pencils or markers (4 different colors)
Scientific calculators
11x17 poster paper for final presentation
City Council Evaluation Checklist handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Problem Creation (original, realistic constraints worth 25 points), Mathematical Accuracy (correct inequalities, graphing, corner point calculations worth 30 points), Solution Process (clear work shown, proper optimization method worth 25 points), and Real-World Application (meaningful interpretation, practical feasibility worth 20 points). Students must earn 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-written constraint examples and a partially completed template with one constraint already graphed. Offer a reference sheet with corner point calculation steps. For advanced learners: challenge them to include integer programming restrictions (whole buses only) or create a 3-variable problem with manual linear algebra solutions. Provide extension research on actual city transportation optimization case studies.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Memorization and Rapid Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and demonstrate rapid recall of the TCP/IP protocol stack layers, their specific functions, and common protocols at each layer. This activity uses spaced repetition and competitive recall to build foundational networking knowledge essential for advanced computer science coursework.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the four TCP/IP protocol stack layers in correct order and identify their specific functions through timed memorization exercises
Students will recognize and match at least 15 common network protocols to their appropriate TCP/IP layers through flashcard drills and competitive recall activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP reference sheet and give students 10 minutes to study silently. The sheet contains: Application Layer (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, DHCP), Transport Layer (TCP, UDP), Internet Layer (IP, ICMP, ARP), and Network Access Layer (Ethernet, WiFi protocols). After study time, collect all materials. Start Round 1: Students work in pairs, alternating as questioner and responder. Questioner asks 'What are the four layers in order?' Responder must answer within 5 seconds. Switch roles and repeat 3 times. Round 2: Individual written recall - students have 2 minutes to write all four layers and their primary functions from memory. Round 3: Protocol matching - display protocol names on screen for 3 seconds each (HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet, DNS, UDP, ICMP, FTP, SMTP, ARP). Students write the correct layer for each protocol. Round 4: Speed competition - call out random protocols, students raise colored cards (red=Application, blue=Transport, green=Internet, yellow=Network Access) within 3 seconds. Track correct responses. Round 5: Final comprehensive recall - students have 5 minutes to write complete TCP/IP stack with all studied protocols correctly categorized. Conclude with immediate feedback and error correction discussion.
materials_needed: TCP/IP protocol stack reference sheets (one per student)
Colored index cards (4 colors per student for layer identification)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projection system for displaying protocols
Answer key for immediate grading
assessment_method: Students earn points as follows: Round 1 verbal recall (2 points for perfect layer sequence), Round 2 written functions (4 points for accurate layer descriptions), Round 3 protocol matching (1 point per correct protocol, 10 total), Round 4 speed cards (1 point per correct rapid response, 15 opportunities), Round 5 comprehensive recall (9 points for complete accurate categorization). Total possible: 30 points. Success threshold: 24+ points (80%). Document individual protocol errors for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic device 'All Transport Internet Network' and allow extended study time with visual diagrams. Create simplified protocol list focusing on HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet initially. For advanced learners: Add OSI model comparison, include additional protocols (SNMP, BGP, IPSec), and challenge them to explain protocol interactions across layers. Consider adding port numbers for Application layer protocols.

title: Interpreting Dimensionality Reduction Manifold Visualizations in t-SNE vs UMAP
description: Students will analyze and compare t-SNE and UMAP dimensionality reduction outputs on the same high-dimensional dataset to understand how different manifold learning algorithms preserve different aspects of data structure. They will interpret clustering patterns, neighborhood preservation, and global structure retention across both methods.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between local and global structure preservation by comparing t-SNE and UMAP visualizations of identical high-dimensional datasets
Students will interpret manifold learning algorithm behavior through systematic analysis of hyperparameter effects on cluster formation and data point relationships
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed dataset (20,000 samples, 784 features) containing MNIST digits with known labels but ask students to work 'blind' initially. Step 1 (15 mins): Students run t-SNE with perplexity values of 5, 30, and 100, generating three 2D scatter plots while recording runtime. Step 2 (15 mins): Students run UMAP with n_neighbors values of 5, 15, and 50, matching the conceptual range of t-SNE perplexity, again recording runtime. Step 3 (20 mins): Students systematically compare visualizations by measuring cluster compactness using silhouette scores, counting distinct visual clusters, and noting relative positions between cluster centers. Step 4 (25 mins): Students write structured comparisons addressing: (a) which algorithm better preserves local neighborhoods evidenced by tight digit groupings, (b) which maintains global structure shown by consistent inter-cluster distances, (c) computational efficiency differences, and (d) hyperparameter sensitivity patterns. Step 5 (15 mins): Reveal true labels and have students color-code their best visualization from each method, then quantify accuracy by calculating adjusted rand index between visual clusters and true digit classes. Students conclude by recommending which method suits exploratory data analysis vs. publication-ready visualizations, justifying with specific evidence from their analysis.
materials_needed: Python environment with scikit-learn, umap-learn, matplotlib, and pandas installed
Pre-processed MNIST dataset (CSV format with 784 pixel columns)
Jupyter notebook template with code cells for t-SNE and UMAP implementation
Timer for runtime measurements
Structured comparison worksheet (digital or physical)
assessment_method: Evaluate based on four criteria: (1) Technical execution - correct implementation of both algorithms with varied hyperparameters (25 points), (2) Quantitative analysis - accurate calculation of silhouette scores and runtime measurements (25 points), (3) Comparative interpretation - demonstrates understanding of local vs global structure preservation with specific visual evidence (30 points), (4) Algorithm recommendation - provides justified recommendation for different use cases based on empirical findings (20 points). Students must submit annotated visualizations plus written analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide code templates with hyperparameter ranges pre-filled, offer interpretation prompts like 'Count the number of distinct clusters you observe' and 'Which visualization would you choose to show someone unfamiliar with your data?' For advanced students: extend analysis to include density-based clustering metrics, experiment with preprocessing techniques (PCA reduction before manifold learning), or compare with additional methods like LLE or Isomap.

title: Analyzing Algorithm Efficiency: Big O Performance Comparison Through Sorting Algorithms
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code implementations, tracing through execution steps, and comparing their Big O performance characteristics. They will create detailed comparison matrices identifying best-case, worst-case, and average-case scenarios for each algorithm.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by tracing through code execution and identifying nested loop patterns and recursive calls
Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through examination of memory allocation patterns in iterative versus divide-and-conquer approaches
instructions:
Begin by distributing three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) in the same programming language to student pairs (10 minutes setup). Each pair receives a worksheet with three identical unsorted arrays of 8 elements: [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90, 88]. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Students manually trace through each algorithm's execution on their assigned array, documenting every comparison and swap operation. They must count total operations and identify when nested loops execute. For merge sort and quicksort, they draw recursion trees showing function calls and returns.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Students analyze the code structure of each algorithm, identifying loop patterns, recursive calls, and memory allocation points. They complete a structured analysis sheet marking: number of nested loops, recursion depth, additional arrays created, and conditional statements that affect execution flow.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Using their traced executions and code analysis, students determine Big O notation for time and space complexity in best, average, and worst cases. They must justify their answers by connecting specific code patterns to complexity classifications (e.g., 'nested for-loops with array length n creates O(n²)').

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Pairs create a comparison matrix plotting all three algorithms against six criteria: best-case time, worst-case time, average-case time, space complexity, stability, and in-place sorting capability. They must provide specific examples of input data that would trigger best and worst-case scenarios.

Conclude with pairs presenting one key insight about when each algorithm would be optimal in real-world applications (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python or Java
Algorithm analysis worksheet with execution tracing tables
Comparison matrix template with six evaluation criteria
Sample array dataset: [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90, 88]
Big O notation reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of manual execution traces with correct operation counts, (2) Correct identification of Big O time/space complexity for all scenarios, (3) Justification quality linking code patterns to complexity analysis, (4) Completed comparison matrix with appropriate real-world application examples. Each criterion worth 25 points. Students must achieve 80% accuracy on complexity identification and provide clear justifications connecting code structure to performance characteristics.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed execution traces for the first few steps of each algorithm and a Big O complexity cheat sheet with common patterns. Pair weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Add challenge questions about hybrid sorting algorithms, ask them to predict performance on larger datasets (n=1000), or have them research and compare additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort using the same analysis framework.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Healthcare Equity Domains
description: Students will critically assess the fairness, bias, and real-world applicability of three different machine learning models trained to predict hospital readmission rates across demographic groups. They will evaluate model performance using multiple metrics, identify ethical concerns, and recommend deployment decisions with detailed justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate machine learning model performance by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, and fairness metrics across protected demographic groups
Students will critique algorithmic bias and ethical implications through systematic comparison of model outcomes and their potential societal impact
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Neural Network) and their performance data on a hospital readmission dataset stratified by race, gender, and age groups. Students receive model outputs including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-scores, AUC-ROC values, and fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) for each subgroup. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze quantitative performance metrics, creating comparison tables and identifying which models perform best overall and within specific demographic groups. They calculate disparate impact ratios and statistical significance of performance differences.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Students evaluate real-world deployment scenarios by examining three case studies: urban hospital, rural clinic, and specialty care center. They assess which model would be most appropriate for each setting, considering patient demographics, resource constraints, and potential consequences of false positives/negatives.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams identify and document ethical concerns, including potential sources of training data bias, feature selection issues, and downstream effects on healthcare access and quality across different populations.

Step 4 (45 minutes): Each team creates a formal recommendation report (2-3 pages) ranking the models for deployment, with detailed justification addressing performance metrics, ethical considerations, and contextual factors. They must explicitly address trade-offs between overall accuracy and fairness.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Teams present 8-minute recommendations to the class, followed by peer questioning and instructor feedback focusing on depth of critical analysis and evidence-based reasoning.
materials_needed: Pre-trained model outputs with performance metrics spreadsheet
Hospital readmission dataset documentation and demographic breakdowns
Three healthcare deployment scenario case study documents
Fairness metrics calculation templates
Access to Python/R with scikit-learn or equivalent libraries
Presentation software and projection capability
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Quantitative analysis accuracy (25 points), depth of ethical evaluation (25 points), quality of contextual reasoning (25 points), and clarity of final recommendation with supporting evidence (25 points). Students must demonstrate sophisticated understanding of trade-offs between competing metrics and articulate nuanced positions on algorithmic fairness.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing fairness metrics calculation examples and guided questions for ethical analysis. Extend advanced learners by requiring additional statistical significance testing, cost-benefit analysis incorporating healthcare economics, or proposing specific model improvement strategies to address identified biases.

title: Design and Implement a Dynamic Stock Portfolio Optimization Algorithm Using Multi-Variable Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will construct an original mathematical model that optimizes stock portfolio allocation under real-world constraints, incorporating risk analysis, expected returns, and market volatility. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then present their algorithm's performance analysis to simulated investment stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 7 class periods (approximately 350 minutes total) plus 6-8 hours independent work
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multi-variable calculus, linear algebra, and probability theory to construct an original portfolio optimization algorithm that maximizes returns while minimizing risk
Students will design and implement a computational solution that incorporates real market constraints and validates their mathematical model through backtesting with historical data
instructions:
**Phase 1 (Days 1-2):** Students form teams of 3-4 and select 8-12 stocks from different sectors using Yahoo Finance or similar platform. Each team downloads 2 years of daily price data and calculates daily returns, mean returns, standard deviations, and correlation matrices using provided Excel templates or Python scripts. Teams must identify and mathematically define at least 5 real-world constraints (e.g., maximum 30% in any sector, minimum 5% cash reserve, transaction costs of 0.1% per trade).

**Phase 2 (Days 3-4):** Teams construct their optimization model by defining the objective function (risk-adjusted return using Sharpe ratio or custom utility function), constraint equations, and decision variables. They must derive the mathematical framework showing partial derivatives for portfolio weights, constraint gradients, and optimality conditions. Teams document their model assumptions and mathematical reasoning in a technical report format.

**Phase 3 (Days 5-6):** Using Python with NumPy/SciPy or MATLAB Optimization Toolbox, teams implement their algorithm and solve for optimal portfolio weights. They must handle numerical challenges like singular matrices or convergence issues. Teams then backtest their strategy against the S&P 500 benchmark using the second year of data, calculating metrics including total return, maximum drawdown, volatility, and Sharpe ratio.

**Phase 4 (Day 7):** Teams prepare 15-minute presentations for a panel of 'investors' (instructor and guest finance professionals if available). Presentations must include mathematical derivations, algorithm performance metrics, risk analysis, and recommendations. Teams defend their methodology during 10-minute Q&A sessions, addressing questions about mathematical assumptions, computational complexity, and real-world applicability.
materials_needed: Access to financial data platform (Yahoo Finance, Bloomberg Terminal, or similar)
Python 3.8+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Matplotlib libraries OR MATLAB with Optimization Toolbox
Historical stock price datasets (provided templates available)
Scientific calculators
Presentation software and projection equipment
Printed constraint specification worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluation using 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Construction (25 points - correctness of objective function, constraint formulation, and theoretical derivations), Implementation Quality (25 points - code functionality, numerical accuracy, error handling), Performance Analysis (25 points - backtesting methodology, statistical significance of results, comparison to benchmarks), Professional Communication (25 points - presentation clarity, defense of mathematical choices, response to technical questions). Teams must submit code, technical report, and presentation slides. Minimum passing requires functional algorithm with documented mathematical framework.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide starter code templates with basic optimization structure, offer guided worksheet for constraint identification, schedule mid-project check-ins for mathematical review. For advanced learners: Challenge with additional constraints like market impact modeling, incorporate stochastic calculus for options hedging, or extend to multi-period dynamic optimization. Consider pairing stronger mathematical students with those having better programming skills.

title: Python Syntax Flash Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements through structured flash card activities and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of Python keywords, operators, and basic syntax structures that students must commit to memory.
learning_objectives: Students will recall Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, return, import, class) by correctly identifying their purposes in code examples
Students will identify Python operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) through visual recognition exercises and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash cards containing 25 essential Python elements (15 minutes setup). Each card shows a Python keyword or operator on one side and its definition/example on the other. Students work in pairs, with Partner A holding cards and Partner B recalling definitions (10 minutes). Partners switch roles for another round (10 minutes). Next, conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall where instructor shows syntax elements on screen and students write down their meanings within 30 seconds per item (15 minutes). Create four teams of 4-6 students each for a competitive recall tournament. Teams take turns identifying randomly selected Python syntax elements projected on screen, earning one point per correct answer (20 minutes). End with individual silent assessment where each student completes a matching worksheet connecting 20 Python syntax elements to their correct definitions (10 minutes). Throughout the activity, emphasize exact spelling and precise terminology. Maintain energetic pace to keep engagement high. Record team scores visibly on whiteboard to maintain competitive atmosphere.
materials_needed: 25 pre-printed flash cards per student pair (Python keywords and operators)
Digital projector or smartboard for displaying syntax elements
Individual matching worksheets (one per student)
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard and markers for scoring
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final individual matching worksheet. During team competition, observe students' verbal responses for correct pronunciation and complete definitions. Award participation points for active engagement during pair work. Create simple rubric: Exemplary (18-20 correct), Proficient (16-17 correct), Developing (14-15 correct), Beginning (below 14 correct).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide visual cue cards with color-coded categories (keywords in blue, operators in red). Allow extra practice time with instructor before team competition. For advanced learners, add challenge cards with more complex syntax like list comprehensions or lambda functions. Encourage advanced students to help facilitate pair work and explain concepts to struggling peers.

title: Interpreting Correlation Matrices and Identifying Feature Relationships in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze a pre-computed correlation matrix from an e-commerce customer dataset to identify strong relationships between numerical features. They will interpret correlation coefficients, distinguish between positive and negative correlations, and explain what these relationships mean for business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by categorizing relationships as weak, moderate, or strong and explaining their business implications
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through guided analysis of feature pairs in customer purchase data
instructions:
Begin by displaying a 6x6 correlation matrix heat map showing relationships between: customer_age, annual_income, time_on_site, pages_viewed, cart_value, and purchase_amount from a fictional e-commerce dataset. Provide students with the correlation matrix as both a heat map visualization and numerical table. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): In pairs, students examine the correlation matrix and identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, writing down the exact coefficient values. They must categorize each relationship as weak (0.0-0.3), moderate (0.3-0.7), or strong (0.7-1.0).

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students select two feature pairs with correlations above 0.6 and write 2-3 sentences explaining what each relationship means in business terms. For example, if cart_value and purchase_amount show r=0.84, they should explain this indicates customers who add more items to their cart typically spend more money.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Present students with three statements mixing correlation and causation (e.g., 'Higher income causes more time spent on the website'). Students must identify which statements incorrectly imply causation and rewrite them to correctly describe correlation only.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students write one paragraph explaining why a business analyst should care about the strongest correlation they identified, including one potential action the business could take based on this relationship. Conclude with a brief class discussion where 3-4 students share their business insights.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix heat map (one per student pair)
Numerical correlation table handout
Correlation strength reference chart (weak/moderate/strong ranges)
Business context worksheet with customer dataset description
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correctly identifies and categorizes correlation strengths, (2) Provides accurate business interpretations of relationships without implying causation, (3) Demonstrates understanding of correlation vs. causation distinction in rewritten statements. Students must score 2/3 points to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example of one correlation interpretation and highlight key vocabulary (positive, negative, strong, moderate). For advanced learners, include additional questions about multicollinearity concerns and ask them to hypothesize about potential confounding variables that might explain observed correlations.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Design Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel installation constraints. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine the optimal solar panel configuration for maximum energy output within budget and space limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a real-world solar energy optimization scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems and interpret solutions within the business context
instructions: Begin by distributing the Solar Panel Optimization Case Study handout detailing GreenTech Solutions' rooftop installation project (10 minutes). Students work in pairs to analyze the scenario: 5000 sq ft rooftop space, $50,000 budget, two panel types (Type A: 250W, $400, 20 sq ft vs Type B: 400W, $750, 35 sq ft), with minimum 80 Type A panels required for grid stability. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Pairs define variables (x = Type A panels, y = Type B panels), formulate the objective function (maximize 250x + 400y watts), and identify all constraints including space (20x + 35y ≤ 5000), budget (400x + 750y ≤ 50000), and minimum requirements (x ≥ 80, y ≥ 0). Phase 2 (25 minutes): Using graph paper and rulers, students plot constraint lines, shade feasible regions, and identify corner points graphically. They calculate objective function values at each vertex to find the optimal solution. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students verify their graphical solution using Excel Solver or online simplex calculators, inputting their formulated constraints and objective function. They document both solutions and compare results. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Pairs prepare a 2-minute presentation summarizing their optimal panel configuration, total wattage output, cost utilization, and space efficiency. Conclude with class discussion comparing different approaches and solutions, emphasizing the practical implications of mathematical optimization in renewable energy planning.
materials_needed: Solar Panel Optimization Case Study handout (1 per student)
Graph paper and colored pencils/markers
Rulers and calculators
Computers with Excel or access to online simplex calculator
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct problem formulation including objective function and all constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate graphical method execution with proper feasible region identification (25 points), (3) Correct simplex method application and solution verification (25 points), (4) Clear presentation of results with business interpretation and comparison between methods (25 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in mathematical calculations and demonstrate understanding of optimization principles in their final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn coordinate axes, offer constraint formulation templates with blanks to fill, and allow use of graphing calculators. Create checkpoint moments after each phase for instructor feedback. For advanced learners: Add sensitivity analysis questions (what if budget increases by 10%?), introduce integer programming concepts, or extend to three-variable problems including maintenance costs. Provide additional optimization scenarios in wind energy or battery storage.

title: Analyzing Attack Vectors in Multi-Layer Network Security Architecture
description: Students will dissect a compromised enterprise network scenario by examining packet captures, system logs, and network topology diagrams to identify vulnerability chains and attack progression patterns. They will trace the attack flow through different network layers and evaluate the effectiveness of existing security controls.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze network packet data and system logs to identify specific attack vectors and their progression through network security layers
Students will evaluate security architecture weaknesses through systematic examination of firewall rules, intrusion detection patterns, and access control failures
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-configured analysis environment containing Wireshark packet captures (3 files: perimeter.pcap, internal.pcap, database.pcap), syslog files from 5 different systems, and network topology diagrams showing DMZ, internal network, and database segments. Students work in pairs and have 20 minutes to familiarize themselves with the scenario documentation describing a financial services company breach. 

In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students open Wireshark and begin with perimeter.pcap, filtering for suspicious traffic patterns using display filters for unusual ports, failed authentication attempts, and data exfiltration indicators. They document initial entry points in a structured analysis template, noting timestamps, source/destination IPs, and protocol anomalies. Simultaneously, they cross-reference firewall logs to identify rule bypasses or misconfigurations.

Phase 2 (60 minutes) involves lateral movement analysis. Students examine internal.pcap for privilege escalation attempts, credential harvesting, and reconnaissance activities. They map attack progression using the provided network diagram, identifying how attackers moved from the DMZ through internal segments. Students analyze Windows Event Logs and Linux auth logs to trace account compromises and unauthorized access patterns.

In Phase 3 (45 minutes), students focus on data exfiltration analysis using database.pcap, identifying SQL injection attempts, database dump activities, and encrypted data transfers. They correlate timing across all three packet captures to construct a complete attack timeline.

Finally (30 minutes), pairs present their findings using a standardized attack chain diagram, identifying each vulnerability exploited, the security controls that failed, and proposing specific remediation measures for each identified weakness.
materials_needed: Wireshark-compatible packet capture files (perimeter.pcap, internal.pcap, database.pcap)
Structured analysis worksheet template with sections for each network layer
Enterprise network topology diagram (PDF) showing firewall placement, VLANs, and security zones
Sample log files: Windows Event Logs (.evtx), Linux syslog files, and firewall logs
Scenario documentation describing the fictional company's infrastructure and incident timeline
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Attack vector identification accuracy (25 points), timeline construction completeness (20 points), security control failure analysis depth (25 points), remediation recommendations feasibility (20 points), and presentation clarity (10 points). Students must identify at least 6 distinct attack techniques, construct an accurate chronological timeline with specific timestamps, and provide technically sound remediation strategies for each identified vulnerability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured Wireshark filters and a partially completed timeline template with key timestamps highlighted. Include a reference sheet of common attack indicators and log entry interpretations. For advanced learners, add encrypted traffic analysis challenges, require them to write custom detection rules for identified attack patterns, or have them perform memory dump analysis using additional forensic tools like Volatility.

title: Evaluating Data Quality Issues in Customer Purchase Dataset
description: Students will critically assess a real customer purchase dataset containing various data quality problems, then judge which issues are most critical to address before analysis. They will create prioritized recommendations for data cleaning based on business impact and analytical reliability.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data quality issues by systematically identifying, categorizing, and ranking problems in a customer dataset
Students will judge the relative importance of different data cleaning approaches through cost-benefit analysis for business decision-making
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'CustomerPurchases_Messy.csv' dataset containing 500 records with intentionally planted issues: missing values (15%), duplicate entries (8%), inconsistent date formats, outliers in purchase amounts, and mixed case in category names. Students work in pairs with laptops and provided data quality checklist template.

**Phase 1 - Issue Identification (15 minutes):** Students systematically examine the dataset using Excel or Google Sheets, documenting every data quality problem they find. They must categorize issues as: Completeness (missing data), Consistency (format variations), Accuracy (outliers/errors), or Validity (impossible values). Each pair records findings on the provided template.

**Phase 2 - Impact Assessment (10 minutes):** Students evaluate each identified issue's potential impact on business analysis by rating severity (1-5 scale) across three dimensions: affects customer segmentation analysis, impacts revenue calculations, and hinders trend identification. They must justify ratings with specific examples from the dataset.

**Phase 3 - Solution Evaluation (15 minutes):** For the top 5 highest-impact issues, students compare different cleaning approaches (deletion vs. imputation vs. correction) by evaluating: time required, data loss risk, and accuracy improvement. They create a prioritized action plan with specific recommendations.

**Phase 4 - Peer Review (10 minutes):** Pairs exchange their recommendations and evaluate another team's approach using the provided peer assessment criteria. They must identify strengths, weaknesses, and suggest improvements in the prioritization logic.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Each pair presents their #1 priority issue and chosen solution to the class, explaining their evaluation criteria and expected business impact.
materials_needed: CustomerPurchases_Messy.csv dataset file (pre-loaded with specific quality issues)
Data Quality Assessment Template (Word/Google Doc with structured tables)
Peer Review Rubric handout
Laptops with Excel or Google Sheets access
Evaluation Criteria Reference Sheet listing business impact factors
assessment_method: Students submit completed assessment templates showing: (1) Comprehensive issue identification with proper categorization (25 points), (2) Justified impact ratings with specific examples (30 points), (3) Logical comparison of cleaning solutions with clear rationale (30 points), (4) Quality of peer feedback demonstrating critical evaluation skills (15 points). Success requires identifying at least 80% of planted issues and providing evidence-based justifications for all priority rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example showing how to evaluate one data quality issue. Give them a smaller 100-record subset initially. For advanced learners: Add a requirement to estimate the statistical impact of each issue on analysis results, or have them propose automated detection rules for each problem type. Consider providing additional datasets from different domains for comparison.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Memory Matrix
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the Big O time complexities for 25 advanced algorithms across different categories (sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, etc.). This foundational knowledge exercise builds the essential computational complexity vocabulary needed for advanced algorithm analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the exact time complexity notation (Big O) for 25 advanced algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions and verbal recitation exercises
Students will identify and recite the space complexity requirements for fundamental data structures through structured memorization drills and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared algorithm reference cards containing 25 algorithms organized into 5 categories: Advanced Sorting (Timsort, Introsort, Radix Sort, Bucket Sort, Counting Sort), Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's), Dynamic Programming (Knapsack variants, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Coin Change), Tree Operations (AVL rotations, Red-Black insertions, B-tree operations, Trie insertions, Heap operations), and String Algorithms (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick, Manacher's). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes studying the cards, focusing on exact Big O notation memorization. Conduct three 10-minute timed recall sessions where students must write down time complexities from memory without references. Between sessions, allow 5-minute review periods. Follow with structured peer quizzing where Partner A shows algorithm names while Partner B recites complexities, then switch roles. Conclude with individual verbal recitation where each student must correctly state 20 out of 25 complexities to the instructor within a 3-minute time limit. Record results immediately and provide instant feedback on incorrect responses.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm reference cards (25 algorithms with time/space complexities)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Individual answer sheets for timed sessions
Scoring rubrics with complexity notations
Whiteboard markers for instructor demonstrations
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final timed verbal recitation to demonstrate mastery. Score based on: Exact Big O notation accuracy (4 points per correct answer), correct identification of best/average/worst case scenarios where applicable (1 bonus point), and completion within 3-minute time limit (5 points). Total possible: 105 points. Passing threshold: 84 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for common patterns (O(n log n) for efficient sorting, O(V²) for basic graph algorithms), allow an additional 1-minute practice session, and group with stronger memorization partners. For advanced learners: Include amortized analysis complexities, require explanation of why each complexity occurs, and challenge them to recall space complexities alongside time complexities for bonus points.

title: Understanding Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Model Performance Decomposition Analysis
description: Students will analyze three pre-trained machine learning models (underfit, optimal, overfit) by decomposing their prediction errors into bias and variance components using bootstrap resampling. They will interpret mathematical relationships between model complexity, training data size, and the fundamental bias-variance tradeoff to understand why model performance behaves predictably across different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the mathematical relationship between bias, variance, and irreducible error by decomposing prediction errors from bootstrap samples of three different model complexities
Students will interpret bias-variance tradeoff patterns through systematic analysis of model performance metrics across varying training set sizes and complexities
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the provided Jupyter notebook containing a synthetic regression dataset (n=1000, polynomial relationship with noise) and three pre-trained models: Ridge regression (α=10, underfit), Ridge regression (α=0.1, optimal), and 15th-degree polynomial (overfit). Students work in pairs with one laptop per pair.

**Phase 1 - Bootstrap Analysis (25 minutes):** Students execute the provided bootstrap function that samples 100 different training sets (80% of data each) and records predictions from all three models on a fixed test set of 200 points. They calculate bias² (squared difference between average prediction and true value), variance (variance of predictions across bootstrap samples), and total error for each test point and model. Students complete the provided analysis template documenting numerical results.

**Phase 2 - Pattern Recognition (20 minutes):** Using the calculated bias and variance matrices, students create three scatter plots (one per model) showing bias² vs variance for each test point. They identify clusters and outliers, then answer guided questions: "Which model shows highest bias?" "Which shows highest variance?" "Where do you observe the optimal tradeoff?" Students annotate their plots with observations.

**Phase 3 - Concept Synthesis (15 minutes):** Students examine provided learning curves showing how bias and variance change as training set size increases from 50 to 800 samples. They write a 200-word explanation connecting their bootstrap findings to these curves, specifically addressing why bias remains constant while variance decreases with more data, and why model complexity affects this relationship. Each pair submits their annotated plots and written explanation.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-configured synthetic dataset and three trained models
Python environment with scikit-learn, numpy, matplotlib, and pandas installed
Bias-variance analysis template worksheet (PDF)
Guided analysis questions handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Numerical accuracy of bias/variance calculations from bootstrap analysis, (2) Correct identification of bias-variance patterns in scatter plots with appropriate annotations, (3) Accurate interpretation of learning curves showing understanding of data size effects, (4) Written explanation demonstrating clear connection between mathematical decomposition and conceptual tradeoff principles. Students must score 3+ on all criteria to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: **Support struggling students:** Provide additional guided questions breaking down each calculation step, offer pre-calculated bias/variance values for verification, and include visual aids showing expected scatter plot patterns. **Extend advanced learners:** Challenge them to modify model hyperparameters and predict resulting bias-variance changes, or analyze how different noise levels in the dataset affect the tradeoff relationship. Provide additional datasets with different underlying functions (sinusoidal, exponential) for comparison analysis.

title: Shopping Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students apply percentage calculation skills to solve real-world shopping scenarios involving discounts, sales tax, and tips. They will work through structured problems using a simulated shopping trip with a fixed budget.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentages by finding discounts, sales tax, and tips in realistic shopping scenarios
Students will apply multi-step percentage problems through budget management decisions in a shopping simulation
instructions: Begin by distributing the Shopping Budget Worksheet and calculator to each student. Give students a scenario: 'You have $100 to spend on back-to-school supplies. You must buy at least 5 items from the provided store catalog.' Display the store catalog on the board showing 15 items with original prices ranging from $8-$35. Announce today's special offers: 20% off clothing, 15% off electronics, and buy-one-get-one 25% off school supplies. Explain that all purchases include 8% sales tax and if they spend over $75, they should calculate a 15% tip for personal shopping assistance. Students work individually for 25 minutes to: (1) Select their 5+ items and record original prices, (2) Calculate applicable discounts for each item, (3) Find subtotal of discounted prices, (4) Calculate 8% sales tax on subtotal, (5) Determine if tip applies and calculate 15% if needed, (6) Find final total and remaining budget. Circulate to check calculations and provide guidance. In the final 10 minutes, have students pair up to compare their shopping lists and verify each other's calculations. Partners should check each percentage calculation step and identify any errors. Conclude by having 2-3 student pairs share their purchases and total costs with the class, explaining their calculation process for one discount and the sales tax.
materials_needed: Shopping Budget Worksheet (1 per student)
Store catalog with 15 items and prices
Basic calculators (1 per student)
Whiteboard or projector for displaying catalog
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct discount calculations, 3 points for accurate sales tax computation, 2 points for proper tip calculation (when applicable), 1 point for staying within budget. Students must achieve 8/10 points to demonstrate proficiency. Observe peer checking discussions for understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference sheet and start them with simpler items (round numbers). Allow use of percentage calculator apps. For advanced learners: Add complexity by introducing compound discounts (additional 5% off already discounted items) or having them compare cost per unit for bulk items.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of different search and sorting algorithms by examining code implementations and performance data. They will decompose each algorithm's structure, compare their efficiency characteristics, and determine optimal use cases for different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort by tracing through code execution and counting operations
Students will compare algorithm performance characteristics through systematic evaluation of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the algorithm analysis worksheet containing pseudocode for linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort. In the first 15 minutes, each group examines one assigned algorithm, tracing through execution with a sample dataset of 8 elements, counting comparison and swap operations at each step. Students document their findings in a structured table showing operation counts for different input scenarios. Next, rotate algorithms every 20 minutes until all groups have analyzed each algorithm. During each rotation, groups build upon previous groups' work, verifying calculations and adding insights. In the analysis phase (25 minutes), groups create comparison charts plotting operation counts against input sizes (n=4, 8, 16, 32) and identify patterns. They categorize each algorithm's Big O notation for time and space complexity. For the final 20 minutes, groups present their findings, explaining which algorithm performs best for: sorted data, reverse-sorted data, random data, and large datasets. Each presentation must include specific operation count examples and justified recommendations for real-world applications like database queries, real-time systems, or memory-constrained environments.
materials_needed: Algorithm analysis worksheet with pseudocode for 4 algorithms
Graph paper or digital graphing tool
Sample datasets (sorted, reverse-sorted, random arrays)
Stopwatch or timer for rotations
Calculators or computers for computation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of operation counting and Big O identification (25%), (2) Quality of algorithm comparison analysis with specific examples (25%), (3) Appropriateness of use-case recommendations with justification (25%), (4) Clear presentation of findings with visual aids (25%). Students must submit completed analysis worksheets and present findings to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled trace tables for the first few steps and highlight key operations to count. Offer algorithm visualization tools or animations to support understanding. For advanced learners, introduce additional algorithms like quicksort or heap sort, or challenge them to analyze space complexity and discuss cache performance implications.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of different search and sorting algorithms by examining code implementations and performance data. They will decompose each algorithm's structure, compare efficiency patterns, and determine optimal use cases for different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort by examining their nested loop structures and recursive calls
Students will compare algorithm performance patterns through systematic evaluation of execution time data across different input sizes
instructions:
Begin by distributing the algorithm analysis worksheet and code samples (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to examine four algorithms: linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort. Each pair receives printed code for all four algorithms and a data table showing execution times for input sizes of 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 elements.

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students analyze each algorithm's code structure, identifying loops, recursive calls, and conditional statements. They document the number of operations relative to input size (n) and predict whether complexity is O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), or O(n²).

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the provided performance data, students create graphs plotting execution time versus input size for each algorithm. They use graph paper or graphing software to visualize the growth patterns.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students compare their theoretical complexity predictions with actual performance graphs. They identify which algorithms show linear growth, quadratic growth, or logarithmic growth patterns, noting any discrepancies between theory and practice.
