Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair completes a comparison matrix, ranking algorithms from most to least efficient for different scenarios: small datasets (n<100), medium datasets (n<10000), and large datasets (n>10000). They justify their rankings using both complexity analysis and performance data.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present one key finding to the class, explaining why a specific algorithm performs better or worse than expected in certain conditions. Conclude with instructor-led discussion connecting complexity analysis to real-world software development decisions.
materials_needed: Printed code samples for linear search, binary search, bubble sort, and merge sort
Algorithm analysis worksheet with structured comparison tables
Performance data spreadsheet showing execution times for different input sizes
Graph paper or access to graphing software (Excel, Google Sheets)
Calculators for complexity calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of algorithm complexity patterns (25 points), (2) Accurate creation and interpretation of performance graphs (25 points), (3) Logical justification of algorithm selection for different scenarios (25 points), (4) Clear explanation of discrepancies between theoretical and actual performance (25 points). Students submit completed worksheets and graphs as deliverables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity cheat sheets showing common patterns (single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²)). Offer pre-drawn graph templates with labeled axes. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms like quicksort or heap sort, ask them to research best-case vs. worst-case scenarios, or have them analyze space complexity in addition to time complexity.
original_title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance

title: Python Data Types Memory Palace - Visual Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) through visual examples and rapid-fire recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for all future Python programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify each of the six basic Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) when shown code examples with 90% accuracy
Students will recall the correct Python data type name when presented with visual value examples through flashcard-style recognition exercises
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Display the Data Type Reference Chart on the main screen showing: int (42, -7, 0), float (3.14, -2.5, 0.0), str ('hello', "world", '123'), bool (True, False), list ([1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b']), dict ({'name': 'John', 'age': 25}). Give each student a set of six colored index cards to create personal reference cards.

**Phase 1 - Reference Creation (10 minutes):** Students copy one data type per colored card: blue for int, green for float, yellow for str, red for bool, orange for list, purple for dict. Each card must include the type name, two code examples, and a simple drawing/symbol they choose to represent that type.

**Phase 2 - Group Drilling (15 minutes):** Project 30 code examples one at a time for 10 seconds each (mix of all six types). Students hold up the matching colored card and shout the data type name in unison. Keep score of class accuracy on whiteboard. Examples include: 'pizza' (str), [10, 20, 30] (list), True (bool), etc.

**Phase 3 - Individual Assessment (10 minutes):** Students work alone with printed worksheet containing 20 code values. They write the data type name next to each example. No reference cards allowed. Collect worksheets for grading.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Review any missed examples as a class. Students create one original example of each data type on back of worksheet as exit ticket.
materials_needed: Data Type Reference Chart (large poster or projected slide)
6 colored index cards per student (blue, green, yellow, red, orange, purple)
Individual assessment worksheet with 20 Python value examples
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard and markers for scoring
assessment_method: Grade individual worksheets using answer key: 18-20 correct = Mastery (90%+), 16-17 correct = Proficient (80-89%), 14-15 correct = Developing (70-79%), below 14 = Needs Support. Additionally, observe student participation during group drilling phase and check exit ticket examples for creativity and accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: **Struggling students:** Provide a simplified reference sheet with only 3 data types initially (int, str, bool), then add others gradually. Allow use of reference cards during assessment. **Advanced students:** Challenge them to identify more complex nested examples like [{'name': 'Alice'}, {'name': 'Bob'}] or distinguish between '42' and 42. Have them create trick examples to challenge classmates.

title: Comparing Data Visualization Types for Customer Purchase Pattern Analysis
description: Students analyze the same customer purchase dataset using three different visualization methods (bar charts, scatter plots, and heatmaps) to understand how different chart types reveal different insights from identical data. They will create interpretations of each visualization and explain which visualization best answers specific business questions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between appropriate visualization types by analyzing customer purchase data through bar charts, scatter plots, and heatmaps
Students will interpret patterns and relationships in data through systematic comparison of visualization outputs and their respective insights
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'CustomerPurchases.csv' dataset containing 500 records with columns: CustomerID, Age, MonthlyIncome, PurchaseAmount, ProductCategory, and PurchaseDate. In the first 15 minutes, students work individually to create three visualizations using provided tools: (1) a grouped bar chart showing average purchase amount by product category and age group (20-30, 31-40, 41-50, 51+), (2) a scatter plot with MonthlyIncome on x-axis and PurchaseAmount on y-axis, colored by ProductCategory, and (3) a heatmap showing correlation between Age, MonthlyIncome, and PurchaseAmount. For the next 20 minutes, students complete the 'Visualization Interpretation Worksheet' with specific prompts: identify the top-spending age group per category from the bar chart, describe the relationship between income and purchase amount from the scatter plot, and list the strongest correlations from the heatmap. In the following 15 minutes, present three business questions: 'Which customer segment should we target for premium products?', 'Is there a relationship between customer income and spending?', and 'What demographic factors predict purchase behavior?' Students must select which visualization best answers each question and write a 2-3 sentence justification. Finally, spend 10 minutes in pairs having students compare their interpretations and discuss any differences in their conclusions, then have 3-4 pairs share their findings with the class.
materials_needed: CustomerPurchases.csv dataset (pre-loaded with 500 customer records)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software installed on computers
Visualization Interpretation Worksheet (printed or digital)
Business Questions handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of data interpretation from each visualization type (12 points total, 4 per chart), (2) Appropriateness of visualization selection for business questions (9 points, 3 per question), (3) Quality of written justifications demonstrating understanding of visualization strengths/limitations (6 points). Students must score 21/27 points (78%) to demonstrate proficiency in understanding visualization applications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made visualization templates with axis labels and provide sentence starters for interpretations ('The bar chart shows that...', 'The scatter plot reveals...'). For advanced learners: Add a fourth visualization type (box plots or violin plots) and include additional questions about statistical distributions and outlier identification. Consider having advanced students create their own business questions that require combining insights from multiple visualizations.

title: Optimizing Packaging Design Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques and linear programming to solve a real-world packaging design problem for a manufacturing company. They will determine optimal dimensions for cylindrical containers while considering material costs, volume constraints, and manufacturing limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply calculus optimization methods to minimize surface area while maximizing volume for cylindrical packaging by setting up and solving derivative equations with constraints
Students will implement linear programming techniques to balance multiple manufacturing constraints through systematic problem-solving and graphical analysis
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: A beverage company needs cylindrical cans with exactly 355ml volume, minimizing aluminum use while considering manufacturing constraints (height between 8-15cm, radius between 2-4cm, material costs $0.02/cm² for sides, $0.03/cm² for top/bottom). 

Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to set up the mathematical model. They must express surface area S = 2πr² + 2πrh as a function of one variable using the volume constraint V = πr²h = 355ml. Guide them to substitute h = 355/(πr²) into the surface area formula.

Step 2 (20 min): Students apply calculus optimization by finding dS/dr, setting equal to zero, and solving for the critical radius value. They must verify this is a minimum using the second derivative test and check that their solution satisfies the manufacturing constraints.

Step 3 (25 min): Introduce additional constraints: maximum production cost of $0.50 per can and minimum structural strength requiring h ≥ 2r. Students create a linear programming model with objective function representing total cost and constraint inequalities. They graph the feasible region and identify corner points.

Step 4 (15 min): Students evaluate their objective function at each corner point to find the optimal solution. They must justify why their solution balances mathematical optimization with practical manufacturing requirements.

Step 5 (10 min): Each pair presents their final dimensions, total cost per can, and material usage, explaining their mathematical reasoning and comparing results with other groups.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (GeoGebra/Desmos)
Graph paper and rulers
Problem scenario handout with specific constraints and cost data
Cylindrical containers of various sizes for physical reference
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: mathematical setup and constraint identification (5 points), correct calculus optimization process (6 points), accurate linear programming implementation (5 points), and clear justification of final solution with manufacturing considerations (4 points). Students must submit written work showing all calculations and a brief presentation defending their optimal design choice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed constraint equations and guide them through the substitution process step-by-step. Offer visual aids showing how surface area changes with radius. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding environmental constraints (recycled material percentages), multiple container sizes simultaneously, or considering discrete manufacturing specifications that require integer programming techniques.

title: Critical Analysis of Distributed System Failure Patterns in Real-World Case Studies
description: Students will examine three major distributed system failures (AWS S3 outage 2017, Facebook outage 2021, and Google Cloud outage 2019) to identify common failure patterns, analyze root causes, and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented solutions. This activity develops critical thinking skills for designing resilient distributed systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by decomposing real-world outage reports into technical components, human factors, and systemic vulnerabilities
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of post-incident remediation strategies through comparative analysis of multiple industry case studies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group one primary case study and providing access to official post-mortem reports. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), groups conduct structured analysis using the provided framework: identify the failure cascade timeline, categorize failure types (hardware, software, configuration, human error), map dependencies that amplified the impact, and extract lessons learned. Students must create a visual failure tree diagram and document their findings in the analysis template. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), groups rotate to review other case studies, taking notes on similarities and differences. During Phase 3 (45 minutes), groups synthesize findings to identify cross-cutting patterns, evaluate which remediation strategies appear most effective across cases, and propose three specific design principles for preventing similar failures. Each group creates a comparative matrix showing failure patterns, root causes, and solution effectiveness ratings. In Phase 4 (30 minutes), groups present their analysis focusing on the most critical patterns identified and defend their remediation strategy rankings. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students individually write about how this analysis would influence their approach to designing a distributed system.
materials_needed: Official post-mortem reports: AWS S3 (Feb 2017), Facebook (Oct 2021), Google Cloud (June 2019)
Failure analysis framework template with structured fields
Digital whiteboard tool (Miro, Mural, or similar) for creating failure tree diagrams
Comparative matrix template for cross-case analysis
Presentation timer and rubric handouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of technical failure analysis - correctly identifies failure cascade and technical root causes (25%), (2) Quality of pattern recognition - identifies meaningful similarities and differences across cases (25%), (3) Critical evaluation of solutions - provides justified rankings of remediation strategy effectiveness with supporting evidence (25%), (4) Visual representation quality - failure tree diagrams accurately represent complex relationships (15%), (5) Presentation clarity - effectively communicates key insights and defends analysis decisions (10%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted sections of post-mortem reports focusing on key technical details, offer sentence starters for analysis template responses, and pair with stronger technical students during group work. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research additional similar incidents, propose novel failure detection mechanisms, or design experiments to test their proposed solutions. Consider assigning them as 'technical consultants' to support other groups while working on extensions.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness: Choosing the Best Chart for Customer Sales Data
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer sales dataset and justify which visualization most effectively communicates key business insights. They will apply evaluation criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness to make their judgment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific criteria including visual clarity, data accuracy, and audience suitability
Students will justify their visualization choice through structured comparison and evidence-based reasoning using provided evaluation rubric
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with three printed visualizations of identical customer sales data: a pie chart showing product categories, a bar chart displaying monthly sales trends, and a scatter plot revealing customer age vs. purchase amount relationships (10 minutes setup). Present the business scenario: 'A retail manager needs to present quarterly performance to executives focusing on which product category to expand.' 

Students work individually to complete the provided evaluation matrix, rating each visualization (1-5 scale) across four criteria: visual clarity (can data be read easily?), data accuracy (are proportions/scales correct?), story effectiveness (does it answer the business question?), and executive appropriateness (suitable for leadership audience?). Allow 15 minutes for individual assessment.

Next, students write a 150-word justification defending their top-ranked visualization choice, citing specific evidence from their evaluation matrix and explaining why their selected chart best serves the business scenario (15 minutes writing time).

Conclude with structured peer sharing: students form groups of 3-4, present their chosen visualization and reasoning to teammates, then discuss areas of agreement and disagreement in their evaluations (15 minutes discussion). Groups identify one key insight about effective visualization selection to share with the full class (5 minutes preparation, 10 minutes class sharing).
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of customer sales data per student
Evaluation matrix worksheet with 1-5 rating scales
Business scenario description handout
Timer for time management
assessment_method: Grade completed evaluation matrices (40% of score) ensuring students rated all criteria with brief explanations. Assess written justifications (40%) using rubric: evidence cited from matrix (10 points), logical reasoning connecting visualization to business need (10 points), clear writing and organization (5 points). Evaluate peer discussion participation (20%) through observation of engagement and contribution quality during group sharing.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing sentence starters for justifications ('This visualization works best because...', 'The data shows...'). Offer one-on-one matrix completion guidance focusing on one criterion at a time. For advanced learners, add challenge questions: 'What modifications would improve your second-choice visualization?' or 'How might different audiences change your selection?'

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Playground with Budget Constraints
description: Students will create an original playground design using geometric principles, scaling, and algebraic optimization. They must work within a specified budget while maximizing play value through strategic mathematical planning and spatial reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric concepts (area, perimeter, volume) with algebraic problem-solving by designing a scale model playground within budget constraints
Students will construct mathematical arguments and justify design decisions through cost-benefit analysis using proportional reasoning and optimization strategies
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the playground design packet containing: lot dimensions (50m × 30m), equipment catalog with prices and dimensions, safety spacing requirements (2m minimum between equipment), and budget limit ($25,000). 

Step 1 (20 min): Teams analyze the equipment catalog, calculating actual dimensions from given scale factors (1:50 scale for models). Students must determine how many of each equipment type fits within safety constraints using area and perimeter calculations.

Step 2 (30 min): Using grid paper, teams create their playground layout to scale. They must calculate total area used, remaining green space, and verify all safety spacing using coordinate geometry principles. Each team creates at least 3 different layout options.

Step 3 (25 min): Teams develop cost equations for each layout option, factoring in base equipment costs plus installation fees (15% of equipment cost) and landscaping ($8 per square meter of remaining space). They must create algebraic expressions to model total costs.

Step 4 (30 min): Using optimization strategies, teams select their final design that maximizes 'play value points' (assigned to each equipment type) while staying within budget. They must show mathematical justification using inequalities and constraint equations.

Step 5 (35 min): Teams build their 3D scale models using provided materials, ensuring accurate proportional representation. All measurements must be calculated and verified using scaling formulas.

Step 6 (20 min): Teams present their designs, explaining mathematical reasoning behind layout choices, cost optimization strategies, and how geometric principles influenced their decisions.
materials_needed: Playground equipment catalog with dimensions and costs (laminated sheets)
Grid paper (1cm squares) and rulers
Cardboard, foam blocks, colored paper for 3D models
Calculators
Digital presentation tool or poster boards
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: Mathematical Accuracy (correct calculations for scaling, area, cost), Design Innovation (creative use of space and equipment selection), Budget Management (stays within constraints with clear cost justification), Mathematical Communication (clear explanation of geometric and algebraic reasoning), and Model Quality (accurate scale representation with proper proportions). Each criterion worth 20 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-calculated area formulas, offer step-by-step calculation templates, and allow use of online scaling calculators. For advanced learners: introduce additional constraints like accessibility requirements, add terrain elevation changes requiring volume calculations, or include time-value analysis for equipment durability and replacement costs.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 20 specific time complexity formulas, their corresponding Big O notations, and the algorithm names that produce each complexity. This intensive recall exercise focuses on advanced algorithmic concepts including amortized analysis and space-time tradeoffs.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations for 20 advanced algorithms by completing timed memory assessments
Students will identify specific complexity formulas (e.g., T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)) and their simplified notations through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the master reference sheet containing 20 algorithm-complexity pairs including: Merge Sort O(n log n), Quicksort worst-case O(n²), Dijkstra's algorithm O((V+E) log V), Floyd-Warshall O(V³), FFT O(n log n), Matrix Chain Multiplication O(n³), Knapsack DP O(nW), Traveling Salesman O(n!), Heap operations O(log n), Hash table average O(1), Red-Black tree operations O(log n), Suffix array construction O(n log n), Convex hull O(n log n), Prime factorization O(√n), Binary search O(log n), Breadth-first search O(V+E), Depth-first search O(V+E), Kruskal's algorithm O(E log V), Union-Find with path compression O(α(n)), and Strassen's matrix multiplication O(n^2.807). Students receive 15 minutes to study the sheet intensively. Remove reference materials and conduct Round 1: display algorithm names for 30 seconds each while students write the exact Big O notation. Round 2: show complexity notations while students recall algorithm names. Round 3: present recurrence relations (e.g., T(n) = T(n-1) + O(1)) for students to identify the resulting complexity. Each round allows 10 seconds per question. Immediately after each round, provide correct answers for self-checking. Conclude with a cumulative assessment where students must achieve 18/20 correct answers across all categories within a 10-minute time limit. Record individual scores and identify patterns in commonly missed items for targeted review.
materials_needed: Master reference sheet with 20 algorithm-complexity pairs
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces (1-20)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector or whiteboard for displaying questions
Red pens for self-grading
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (18/20 correct) on the final cumulative assessment. Grade breakdown: exact notation spelling (50%), correct algorithm identification (30%), accurate recurrence relation recognition (20%). Track completion time as a secondary metric for processing speed evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices (e.g., 'Merge Sort Makes Nice Logs' for O(n log n)), group similar complexities together, and allow color-coding on reference sheets. For advanced learners: include amortized analysis examples, ask them to derive complexities from pseudo-code, and add space complexity requirements alongside time complexity.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Ensemble Models: Understanding SHAP Values vs Permutation Importance
description: Students will analyze and compare different feature importance methodologies (SHAP values, permutation importance, and built-in feature importance) on a gradient boosting model to understand when and why these methods produce different rankings. They will interpret the business implications of these differences using a real-world credit risk dataset.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between global and local feature importance measures by comparing SHAP summary plots with permutation importance rankings on a gradient boosting classifier
Students will interpret the theoretical foundations and practical limitations of different feature importance methods through systematic analysis of model explanations
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained XGBoost model on the German Credit Risk dataset (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives the same trained model but different subsets of test data (stratified by risk categories). Step 1: Students calculate three types of feature importance: built-in XGBoost feature importance (.feature_importances_), permutation importance using scikit-learn's permutation_importance function with 10 repetitions, and SHAP TreeExplainer values for their assigned test subset (45 minutes). Step 2: Teams create side-by-side visualizations comparing the top 10 features from each method, noting ranking differences and magnitude variations (30 minutes). Step 3: Students analyze 5 specific prediction instances using SHAP waterfall plots to understand local vs global importance discrepancies (30 minutes). Step 4: Teams research the mathematical foundations of each method using provided technical papers and create a comparison matrix highlighting computational complexity, interpretability trade-offs, and appropriate use cases (45 minutes). Step 5: Each team presents their findings focusing on one specific feature that ranked differently across methods, explaining the theoretical reasons for the discrepancy and recommending which importance measure a loan officer should trust for decision-making (20 minutes per team). Conclude with instructor-led discussion on the implications for model governance and regulatory compliance in financial services (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-trained XGBoost model on German Credit Risk dataset with pickle file
Jupyter notebooks with SHAP, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries installed
Stratified test data subsets (100-200 samples each) in CSV format
Research papers on SHAP methodology and permutation importance theory
Model performance metrics and baseline comparisons spreadsheet
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Technical accuracy of importance calculations and visualizations (25%), (2) Depth of analysis comparing ranking differences with statistical significance testing (25%), (3) Quality of theoretical explanation linking mathematical foundations to observed differences (30%), (4) Business relevance of recommendations for model deployment and monitoring (20%). Require submission of annotated Jupyter notebook and 10-minute presentation with Q&A.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide code templates with partially completed functions and guided worksheet with specific questions about each importance method. Include visual aids showing the mathematical intuition behind each approach. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement custom SHAP explanations for specific feature interactions, compare results across different model architectures (Random Forest vs XGBoost), or develop automated importance stability metrics for model monitoring pipelines.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Decomposition
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) by examining their code structure, identifying key operations, and comparing their performance characteristics. They will decompose each algorithm's efficiency patterns and justify which algorithm is optimal for different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and dominant operations within each algorithm's structure
Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through systematic comparison of memory usage patterns across bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort implementations
instructions: Begin by distributing three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) to student pairs (15 minutes setup). Students first individually examine each algorithm's structure, marking loops, recursive calls, and key operations with colored pens - use red for loops, blue for recursive calls, green for comparison operations (20 minutes). Next, pairs collaborate to create a complexity analysis table with columns for: Algorithm Name, Best Case Time, Average Case Time, Worst Case Time, Space Complexity, and Key Characteristics (25 minutes). For each algorithm, students must identify the specific code segments responsible for complexity - for example, marking the nested for-loops in bubble sort that create O(n²) behavior, or identifying how merge sort's divide-and-conquer approach creates O(n log n) performance. Students then analyze three different scenarios: sorting 100 already-sorted integers, sorting 10,000 random integers, and sorting 1,000 reverse-ordered integers (20 minutes). They must predict which algorithm performs best for each scenario and explain their reasoning based on the complexity analysis. Finally, pairs present one scenario analysis to the class, defending their algorithm choice with specific complexity evidence (15 minutes presentations). Throughout the activity, emphasize connecting code structure directly to mathematical complexity - students should point to specific lines of code when explaining why bubble sort is O(n²) or why merge sort requires O(n) additional space.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (one set per student pair)
Colored pens or highlighters (red, blue, green for each pair)
Analysis table templates (printed or digital)
Computers with code execution environment (Python, Java, or C++)
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed complexity analysis tables using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all time/space complexities with specific code evidence, (3) Identifies most complexities with adequate justification, (2) Identifies some complexities but lacks clear connection to code structure, (1) Minimal complexity identification or incorrect analysis. Additionally assess scenario predictions for logical reasoning and algorithm selection justification. Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining how specific code constructs (loops, recursion) create complexity patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity analysis sentence starters ('The nested loops in lines X-Y create O(n²) because...') and pre-marked code samples highlighting loop structures. For advanced learners: Add analysis of hybrid algorithms like Timsort, or have them implement modifications to improve specific complexity cases. Provide additional scenarios involving memory-constrained environments or nearly-sorted data patterns.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in High-Stakes Healthcare Applications
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) trained for predicting patient readmission risk, evaluating their suitability for deployment in a real healthcare setting. Students must consider multiple performance metrics, ethical implications, interpretability requirements, and regulatory constraints to make evidence-based recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the appropriateness of different ML algorithms for healthcare prediction tasks by analyzing performance metrics, interpretability trade-offs, and ethical considerations
Students will critique model deployment strategies through comprehensive assessment of bias, fairness, regulatory compliance, and clinical workflow integration
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Provide students with three pre-trained models and a holdout test dataset of 5,000 patient records with demographic data, medical history, and readmission outcomes. Students work in teams of 3-4 to generate predictions and calculate comprehensive performance metrics including AUC-ROC, precision-recall curves, calibration plots, and fairness metrics across demographic subgroups (age, race, gender). Each team member focuses on one model initially, then collaborates on comparative analysis. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams conduct deep-dive evaluation using provided clinical guidelines, FDA regulatory framework documents, and hospital workflow specifications. Students must assess: (1) Model interpretability using SHAP values and feature importance rankings, (2) Fairness evaluation across protected classes using equalized odds and demographic parity, (3) Calibration reliability for different risk thresholds, (4) Computational requirements and integration feasibility. **Phase 3 (45 minutes):** Teams prepare formal recommendations addressing specific deployment scenarios: emergency department triage, discharge planning, and resource allocation. Students must defend their choice of model while acknowledging limitations and proposing monitoring strategies. Each team presents 10-minute recommendations to simulated hospital board (other teams), followed by 5-minute Q&A sessions where peers challenge assumptions and probe decision rationale.
materials_needed: Pre-trained ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) saved as pickle files
Synthetic patient dataset (5,000 records) with readmission labels and demographic attributes
Python environment with scikit-learn, shap, fairlearn, and matplotlib libraries
FDA guidance documents on AI/ML in medical devices
Hospital workflow documentation and clinical decision-making protocols
Model evaluation template spreadsheet with metrics calculation formulas
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Technical analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation and interpretation of performance metrics; Critical reasoning (30 points) - depth of bias analysis, ethical considerations, and limitation acknowledgment; Recommendation quality (25 points) - evidence-based model selection with clear deployment strategy; Peer evaluation performance (20 points) - quality of questions posed during Q&A and ability to defend decisions under scrutiny. Students submit individual reflection papers (500 words) explaining their personal assessment process and how peer feedback influenced their final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation templates with partially completed examples, offer glossary of clinical terms, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create checkpoint meetings at 30-minute intervals to ensure teams stay on track. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as temporal model drift analysis, cost-effectiveness calculations, or multi-objective optimization scenarios. Challenge them to propose novel evaluation metrics specific to healthcare contexts or design A/B testing frameworks for model deployment.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Population Dynamics in Urban Planning
description: Students will synthesize concepts from differential equations, statistics, and optimization to create an original mathematical model predicting population changes in a hypothetical city district over 20 years. They will develop both the theoretical framework and a computational implementation, then present their model to simulate real urban planning decisions.
estimated_duration: 16 hours (spread across 8 class sessions over 2-3 weeks)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original differential equation model incorporating at least three demographic variables (birth rate, death rate, migration) by integrating logistic growth principles with environmental constraints
Students will design a comprehensive validation framework through Monte Carlo simulation and sensitivity analysis to test model robustness under varying parameter conditions
instructions: **Phase 1: Model Design (Days 1-2, 4 hours total)** Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a fictional city district profile including current population (50,000-150,000), geographic constraints, economic indicators, and historical data spanning 10 years. Students first spend 90 minutes researching and selecting mathematical approaches, choosing from differential equations (logistic, Lotka-Volterra variants), discrete models, or hybrid approaches. They must justify their choice in a 500-word technical memo. **Phase 2: Mathematical Framework Development (Days 3-4, 4 hours)** Teams construct their core mathematical model, defining all variables, parameters, and assumptions explicitly. They must incorporate at least three demographic factors and two environmental constraints (housing capacity, resource limits). Students create hand-calculated examples for simplified scenarios and establish boundary conditions. Each team submits model equations with complete variable definitions and parameter estimation methods. **Phase 3: Computational Implementation (Days 5-6, 4 hours)** Using Python or MATLAB, students program their model with graphical output capabilities. They must include parameter input interfaces, multiple scenario testing, and visualization of population trends over time. Code must include comprehensive commenting and error handling for invalid inputs. **Phase 4: Validation and Analysis (Day 7, 2 hours)** Teams conduct sensitivity analysis by varying parameters ±20% and running Monte Carlo simulations with 1000 iterations. They analyze how uncertainty in initial conditions affects long-term predictions and identify critical parameters. **Phase 5: Presentation and Defense (Day 8, 2 hours)** Each team presents their model to the class in a 15-minute formal presentation followed by 5 minutes of peer questioning, defending their mathematical choices and demonstrating model functionality with live scenarios.
materials_needed: Python or MATLAB software access for each student
Pre-prepared city district data packets (demographics, geography, economics) - 8 different fictional scenarios
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Large format paper and markers for model visualization
Access to demographic databases (US Census, UN Population Division)
Presentation equipment (projector, screen, laptops for demonstrations)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and innovation (25 points) - assess equation complexity, variable integration, and theoretical soundness; Computational implementation (20 points) - evaluate code functionality, user interface, and documentation quality; Validation methodology (20 points) - assess sensitivity analysis depth and statistical approach; Model accuracy and realism (15 points) - compare predictions against known demographic principles; Presentation quality (20 points) - evaluate clarity, defense of choices, and response to peer questions. Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery, with partial credit available for each component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide model templates with partially completed differential equations and guided parameter estimation worksheets. Offer daily 15-minute check-ins during Phase 2-3. Create peer mentoring pairs with stronger mathematical students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, age-structured populations, or spatial diffusion models. Encourage exploration of machine learning parameter optimization or comparison with real city data. Provide access to advanced demographic modeling literature and suggest investigation of bifurcation analysis for population equilibrium points.

title: Binary Number System Vocabulary Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall essential binary number system terminology through structured flashcard practice and peer testing. This foundational activity builds the vocabulary needed for understanding how computers store and process data.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and define 12 key binary number system terms including bit, byte, binary digit, decimal, hexadecimal, base-2, base-10, MSB, LSB, nibble, word, and overflow by completing flashcard drills
Students will recall the exact definitions of binary terminology through timed peer quizzing and achieve 90% accuracy on vocabulary matching
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards with 12 binary terminology terms on one side and definitions on the reverse. Give students 15 minutes to study the cards individually, reading each term aloud and its definition twice. Next, pair students and have them take turns testing each other for 10 minutes - one partner shows the term, the other must provide the definition from memory. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes. During Round 1 (5 minutes), allow students to look at definitions if stuck. During Round 2 (5 minutes), no peeking allowed. After peer practice, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire review where you display each term on screen for 10 seconds and students write definitions on their answer sheets. Follow with immediate feedback by reading correct definitions aloud. Conclude with a matching quiz where students draw lines connecting 12 terms to their corresponding definitions within 8 minutes. Collect answer sheets and have students self-check using the answer key displayed on screen. Students must achieve 10/12 correct matches to demonstrate mastery.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards with 12 binary terms and definitions (one set per student)
Answer sheets with matching quiz format
Timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying terms and answer key
Pencils for students
assessment_method: Students complete a 12-item term-to-definition matching quiz and must achieve 10/12 (83%) correct answers. Grade using the provided answer key. Record completion time to identify students who may need additional practice with recall speed.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling learners: Reduce vocabulary set to 8 terms, allow extra study time, or provide visual mnemonics. For advanced learners: Add 4 additional terms (binary coded decimal, two's complement, sign bit, parity bit) and challenge them to create their own memory devices for the definitions.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps in Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-generated correlation heatmap from a customer churn dataset to identify relationships between variables and explain how these correlations inform feature selection decisions. They will practice reading correlation values, recognizing patterns, and connecting statistical relationships to business insights.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing color patterns and numerical values in a heatmap visualization
Students will explain the implications of feature correlations through structured analysis of multicollinearity and predictive relationships
instructions:
Begin by displaying a correlation heatmap generated from a telecommunications customer churn dataset containing 12 features (monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, contract_length, tech_support, online_security, payment_method, internet_service, phone_service, streaming_tv, streaming_movies, senior_citizen). Provide students with printed copies of the heatmap and a correlation interpretation worksheet. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations by examining color intensity and reading exact correlation values from the heatmap cells. They record these values on their worksheet.

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students analyze the correlation between 'monthly_charges' and other features, discussing why certain services might correlate positively or negatively with pricing. They must write explanations connecting statistical relationships to business logic.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Present students with three feature selection scenarios: removing highly correlated features (r > 0.8), identifying features most correlated with churn, and selecting features for a simplified model. Students work in groups of 3-4 to determine which features they would select for each scenario and justify their choices using correlation evidence.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each group presents one scenario solution, explaining how correlation values influenced their feature selection decisions. Other students evaluate whether the explanations demonstrate proper understanding of correlation interpretation and business relevance. Conclude with instructor feedback on common correlation interpretation errors and reinforcement of key concepts.
materials_needed: Printed correlation heatmap (11x17 paper recommended for clarity)
Correlation interpretation worksheet with guided questions
Customer churn dataset documentation with feature descriptions
Colored pencils or markers for annotation
Projector for displaying heatmap to full class
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation values and provides accurate business explanations, (3) Minor errors in interpretation but demonstrates understanding, (2) Some correlation values identified but weak explanations, (1) Significant errors in reading correlations or explanations. Observe group discussions for proper use of terminology (positive/negative correlation, multicollinearity, feature redundancy). Assess final presentations for logical reasoning connecting correlations to feature selection decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation interpretation reference card with ranges (0.7-1.0 strong positive, etc.) and highlight 2-3 obvious correlations to start analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential causation vs correlation issues and discuss how correlation thresholds might vary by industry or use case. Provide additional context about variance inflation factors for multicollinearity assessment.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps in Customer Churn Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze correlation heatmaps from a telecommunications customer dataset to identify relationships between features and explain how these relationships impact churn prediction models. They will distinguish between different types of correlations and their implications for feature selection.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients in heatmaps by identifying strong, moderate, and weak relationships between customer behavior features
Students will explain the implications of multicollinearity through systematic analysis of feature relationships in customer churn datasets
instructions:
Begin by providing each student group (3-4 students) with printed correlation heatmaps from a telecom customer churn dataset containing 15 features (monthly_charges, total_charges, tenure, contract_type, tech_support, etc.). Start with a 5-minute mini-lecture explaining correlation coefficient ranges (-1 to +1) and color coding in heatmaps. 

For the main activity (25 minutes), students work in groups to complete a structured analysis worksheet. They first identify the top 5 strongest positive correlations and top 5 strongest negative correlations, writing the specific coefficient values and feature pairs. Next, they locate all correlations above 0.7 or below -0.7 and mark these as potential multicollinearity concerns. Students then focus on the 'churn' row/column, ranking all features by their correlation strength with the target variable.

In the interpretation phase (15 minutes), groups write 2-3 sentence explanations for each high correlation they identified, connecting the business logic (e.g., why monthly_charges and total_charges are highly correlated). They must also explain what the churn correlations suggest about which features might be most predictive.

Conclude with a 10-minute gallery walk where groups post their findings and rotate to compare interpretations. Each group presents one surprising correlation they discovered to the class. Instructors should emphasize that correlation doesn't imply causation and discuss how these insights inform feature engineering decisions.
materials_needed: Printed correlation heatmaps (one per group of 3-4 students)
Structured analysis worksheets with guided questions
Colored pens/highlighters for marking correlations
Large poster paper for gallery walk findings
Sample telecom churn dataset description sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of correlation strengths and values, (2) Accurate business interpretation of feature relationships, (3) Proper identification of multicollinearity issues, (4) Clear explanation of churn prediction implications. Groups must correctly identify at least 8/10 correlation categories and provide logical business explanations for 3/4 high correlations to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation strength reference card (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7+ strong) and give specific examples of the first correlation interpretation. For advanced learners, provide additional heatmaps from different domains (finance, healthcare) to compare correlation patterns, or challenge them to predict which correlated features should be removed before model training and justify their reasoning.
original_title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps in Customer Churn Analysis

title: Optimizing Wind Farm Layouts Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to solve a real-world wind farm optimization problem. They will determine optimal turbine placement to maximize energy output while satisfying environmental and economic constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize wind turbine spacing by analyzing wind interference patterns and energy output functions
Students will implement linear programming constraints through systematic problem formulation to balance energy production with land use and environmental regulations
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Distribute wind farm data packets containing: topographical maps, wind speed measurements at 12 grid points, turbine specifications (power curve, wake effect radius), and constraint parameters (minimum distances, protected zones). Students work in teams of 3-4. **Phase 2 (45 minutes):** Teams formulate the optimization problem by: (1) defining variables for turbine coordinates (xi, yi), (2) writing the objective function P(x,y) = Σ[power output - wake losses], (3) establishing constraints for minimum separation (√[(xi-xj)² + (yi-yj)²] ≥ dmin), environmental buffers, and budget limits. **Phase 3 (60 minutes):** Students apply calculus techniques: compute partial derivatives ∂P/∂xi and ∂P/∂yi, identify critical points, and use Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization: ∇P = λ∇g where g represents constraint functions. Teams must show all mathematical work and justify each step. **Phase 4 (35 minutes):** Using provided spreadsheet templates, students implement their mathematical solution, input calculated coordinates, and verify constraint satisfaction. Teams generate visual plots showing turbine placement and calculate total expected annual energy output. **Phase 5 (20 minutes):** Each team presents their optimized layout on the smart board, explaining mathematical reasoning and comparing results with other teams' solutions.
materials_needed: Wind farm data packets with topographical maps and wind measurements
Scientific calculators capable of graphing functions
Excel or Google Sheets with optimization solver add-in
Graph paper and colored pencils for layout sketching
Turbine specification sheets with power curves and wake effect formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical formulation (30 points - correct objective function, constraint equations, variable definitions), Calculus application (25 points - accurate partial derivatives, Lagrange multiplier setup, critical point identification), Implementation accuracy (25 points - spreadsheet formulas, constraint verification, numerical results), and Solution justification (20 points - clear explanation of optimization choices and trade-offs).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint templates and step-by-step derivative worksheets. Pair with stronger mathematical peers. For advanced learners: Add dynamic programming elements by including time-varying wind patterns, or introduce stochastic optimization by incorporating uncertainty in wind forecasts. Consider multiple turbine types with different specifications.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Conditions
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort algorithms when operating under artificially imposed memory limitations. They will decompose each algorithm's behavior, compare trade-offs between time and space complexity, and evaluate which algorithm performs optimally under specific constraint scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between memory constraints and algorithmic performance by implementing and profiling three sorting algorithms under controlled memory limitations
Students will differentiate between theoretical and practical algorithm efficiency through empirical testing and comparative performance analysis
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Students work in teams of 2-3. Provide each team with starter code containing basic implementations of quicksort, mergesort, and heapsort in Python. Teams modify each algorithm to track memory usage using the `tracemalloc` module and implement artificial memory limits using custom memory monitoring decorators. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams design and execute controlled experiments testing each algorithm with datasets of varying sizes (1K, 10K, 100K integers) under three memory constraint levels: unrestricted, 50% of optimal, and 25% of optimal memory. Students must document runtime, memory peaks, number of swaps/comparisons, and failure points. **Phase 3 (45 minutes):** Teams analyze collected data using provided visualization templates in Jupyter notebooks, creating performance comparison charts and identifying inflection points where algorithms begin to degrade. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Each team presents a 5-minute analysis defending which algorithm they would recommend for a mobile application with 128MB RAM constraint, supporting their choice with specific data points and algorithmic reasoning.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with tracemalloc, matplotlib, and pandas libraries installed
Jupyter notebook environment or IDE
Pre-generated test datasets (random integers, sorted arrays, reverse-sorted arrays)
Starter code templates with memory monitoring framework
Performance visualization template notebooks
assessment_method: Teams submit a technical report (max 3 pages) containing: (1) Performance comparison tables with specific metrics, (2) Annotated visualizations showing algorithm degradation points, (3) Justified recommendation for memory-constrained environment with supporting evidence. Rubric evaluates data accuracy (25%), depth of algorithmic analysis (35%), quality of comparative reasoning (25%), and clarity of recommendation justification (15%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed data collection scripts and guided analysis questions. Offer algorithm complexity cheat sheets and memory profiling tutorials. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional algorithms (radix sort, bucket sort) or analyze performance with different data patterns (nearly sorted, many duplicates). Encourage investigation of cache performance effects or parallel processing adaptations.

title: Design Your Dream Community: A Linear Programming Urban Planning Challenge
description: Students will create an original urban planning scenario involving resource constraints and multiple objectives, then formulate and solve it using linear programming techniques. They will design both the mathematical model and present their optimal city layout with justifications for their constraints and objective function choices.
estimated_duration: 205 minutes (approximately 3.5 hours or two 90-minute class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original linear programming problem by designing realistic urban planning constraints and creating a mathematical model with at least 3 variables and 5 constraints

Students will synthesize mathematical solutions with practical applications by developing a comprehensive city plan that optimizes their chosen objective function while explaining real-world implications
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a fictional city planning scenario packet containing: population demographics, available land area (1000-1500 acres), budget constraints ($50-75 million), and special requirements (environmental regulations, historical preservation zones). 

Step 1 (30 minutes): Teams brainstorm their city vision and identify decision variables. They must choose exactly 3 land use types from options like residential housing, commercial districts, parks, industrial zones, or educational facilities. Teams define their variables (x₁, x₂, x₃ representing acres allocated to each use).

Step 2 (45 minutes): Teams create their constraint system. They must establish at least 5 realistic constraints including: total land limitation, budget restrictions, zoning requirements, population needs, and environmental regulations. For example: 'Residential housing costs $40,000 per acre, commercial $60,000 per acre' becomes part of budget constraint.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams formulate their objective function. They choose to maximize either community satisfaction points, economic revenue, or environmental sustainability score, creating a weighted formula. Example: Maximize Z = 100x₁ + 150x₂ + 80x₃ (satisfaction points per acre type).

Step 4 (40 minutes): Teams solve their linear programming problem using graphical method or online solver tools, finding optimal allocation values and maximum objective function value.

Step 5 (45 minutes): Teams create visual city maps showing their optimal solution and prepare 8-minute presentations explaining their mathematical model, solution process, and real-world justifications for their design choices.
materials_needed: City planning scenario packets (printed, one per team)
Large poster paper or foam boards
Colored markers and rulers
Graphing calculators or computer access
Linear programming solver software (GeoGebra or online LP calculator)
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model accuracy and complexity (25 points), constraint realism and justification (20 points), correct solution methodology (20 points), visual presentation quality and clarity (20 points), and creative integration of mathematical results with practical urban planning principles (15 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining their constraint derivations and defending their objective function choices during Q&A.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint templates and example objective functions, offer mid-activity check-ins to verify constraint setup before solving. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate integer programming elements (whole building units), add sensitivity analysis to their solutions, or create multiple objective functions and compare results using weighted goal programming techniques.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Memorization Challenge with Network Packet Headers
description: Students memorize and accurately recall the complete TCP/IP protocol stack layers, their specific functions, and the exact field names and byte sizes of TCP and IP packet headers. This foundational knowledge activity prepares students for advanced network programming and security analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five TCP/IP protocol stack layers in correct order and identify their specific functions within 2 minutes
Students will memorize and recite the exact field names, bit positions, and purposes of all TCP header fields and IPv4 header fields through structured repetition exercises
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute presentation displaying the TCP/IP stack: Physical Layer (cables, signals), Data Link Layer (Ethernet frames, MAC addresses), Network Layer (IP routing, addressing), Transport Layer (TCP/UDP ports, reliability), and Application Layer (HTTP, FTP, SMTP protocols). Provide students with blank TCP/IP stack diagrams and header field templates. Conduct Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study provided reference cards showing complete TCP header fields (Source Port 16-bits, Destination Port 16-bits, Sequence Number 32-bits, Acknowledgment Number 32-bits, Header Length 4-bits, Reserved 6-bits, Control Flags 6-bits, Window Size 16-bits, Checksum 16-bits, Urgent Pointer 16-bits, Options variable) and IPv4 header fields (Version 4-bits, Header Length 4-bits, Type of Service 8-bits, Total Length 16-bits, Identification 16-bits, Flags 3-bits, Fragment Offset 13-bits, TTL 8-bits, Protocol 8-bits, Header Checksum 16-bits, Source IP 32-bits, Destination IP 32-bits, Options variable). Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement spaced repetition with 3-minute intervals where students cover references and write complete information from memory. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Partner verification where students quiz each other using provided question sets. Conclude with individual assessment where each student completes blank templates without references within 8-minute time limit.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Stack reference cards (one per student)
TCP Header field specification sheets with bit positions
IPv4 Header field specification sheets with byte layouts
Blank protocol stack diagram templates (3 per student)
Blank header field templates (6 per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Partner quiz question sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on final recall test covering: (1) Complete TCP/IP stack layers in order with one function per layer (25 points), (2) All TCP header field names with correct bit sizes (30 points), (3) All IPv4 header field names with correct bit sizes (30 points), (4) Completion within 8-minute time limit (15 points). Total: 100 points. Partial credit given for field names without correct bit sizes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices ('Please Do Not Take Aspirin' for Physical-Data Link-Network-Transport-Application), use color-coded field groupings, and allow additional 3-minute study periods. For advanced learners: Include IPv6 header fields, add UDP header memorization, or extend to include common port numbers (HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, FTP 21, SMTP 25).

title: Deconstructing Bias in Machine Learning Model Performance Across Demographic Subgroups
description: Students will analyze a pre-trained loan approval model's performance metrics across different demographic groups to understand how algorithmic bias manifests in real-world applications. They will interpret confusion matrices, fairness metrics, and feature importance rankings to comprehend the relationship between data representation, model decisions, and societal impact.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret disparate impact ratios and equalized odds metrics by comparing model performance across protected demographic groups
Students will explain the relationship between training data composition and biased model outcomes through systematic analysis of feature importance and prediction distributions
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a Jupyter notebook containing a pre-trained random forest model for loan approval decisions, along with a holdout test dataset of 10,000 loan applications with demographic information (age, gender, race, income, credit score). In the first 20 minutes, students examine the dataset structure and generate summary statistics for each demographic group, noting differences in approval rates and feature distributions. Next, spend 30 minutes having students calculate and interpret key fairness metrics: disparate impact ratio (approval rate for protected group ÷ approval rate for reference group), equalized odds (difference in true positive rates between groups), and demographic parity (difference in positive prediction rates). During minutes 51-80, students analyze confusion matrices for each demographic subgroup, calculating precision, recall, and F1-scores, then document patterns in false positive and false negative rates. In the following 25 minutes, teams examine feature importance rankings from the model and correlate these with demographic disparities, identifying which features may serve as proxies for protected attributes. Finally, spend 25 minutes having students create a structured analysis document explaining: (1) which demographic groups experience the most bias, (2) how training data composition contributes to these disparities, (3) the business and ethical implications of observed bias patterns, and (4) potential mitigation strategies. Conclude with a 20-minute class discussion where teams present their key findings and debate the trade-offs between different fairness definitions.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib libraries
Pre-trained loan approval model (random forest) saved as pickle file
Synthetic loan dataset (CSV) with 10,000 records including demographic variables
Bias metrics calculation template spreadsheet
Digital whiteboard or shared document for team findings
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate calculation of disparate impact ratio, equalized odds, and demographic parity (25%), (2) Correct interpretation of confusion matrices and performance metrics across groups (25%), (3) Clear explanation of the connection between feature importance and demographic bias (25%), (4) Thoughtful analysis of ethical implications and proposed mitigation strategies (25%). Teams must submit their completed analysis document and present at least two key insights during the class discussion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated summary statistics and a step-by-step formula sheet for bias metrics. Create guided questions like 'Which group has the lowest approval rate?' and 'What does a disparate impact ratio below 0.8 indicate?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional fairness metrics (calibration, individual fairness) or propose algorithmic debiasing techniques like re-weighting or adversarial training. Provide optional readings on fairness-aware machine learning frameworks.

title: Planning a School Pizza Party: Multi-Step Word Problem Application
description: Students will apply their knowledge of multiplication, division, and money calculations to solve a real-world scenario involving planning a pizza party for their class. They will work through multiple interconnected problems to determine quantities needed, calculate costs, and make budget-conscious decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication and division operations to determine food quantities by solving authentic planning scenarios
Students will calculate total costs and make budget decisions through multi-step word problem solving
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' to each student and explaining they are planning a pizza party for 24 students in their class with a $150 budget (10 minutes). Present the scenario: Each student eats 3 slices on average, each pizza has 8 slices and costs $12, drinks cost $18 for a pack that serves 12 students, and paper plates cost $8 for a pack of 50. Students work individually for 15 minutes to solve: How many pizzas are needed? How many drink packs? What will pizzas cost total? What will drinks cost total? What is the remaining budget for extras? After individual work, pair students to compare answers and resolve discrepancies (10 minutes). Circulate to check calculations: 24 students × 3 slices = 72 slices needed, 72 ÷ 8 = 9 pizzas, 9 × $12 = $108 for pizzas, 24 ÷ 12 = 2 drink packs, 2 × $18 = $36 for drinks, 1 pack plates = $8, total spent = $152. Lead whole-class discussion about the budget problem - they're $2 over (10 minutes). Present extension challenge: Students must modify their plan to stay within budget by choosing fewer pizzas, cheaper alternatives, or reducing quantities. Have students present one solution strategy to the class (15 minutes). Conclude by having students write one sentence explaining which math operation was most challenging and why.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Sheet (one per student)
Calculators (optional, but recommended for checking work)
Pencils and erasers
Chart paper for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed planning sheets using a 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct calculations with clear work shown, 3 points for mostly correct with minor errors, 2 points for correct process but calculation mistakes, 1 point for incomplete or incorrect approach. Observe student discussions for mathematical reasoning. Check final budget modification solutions for creativity and mathematical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a formula sheet showing 'total = number × cost per item' and encourage use of manipulatives or drawings to visualize the division problems. Break the problem into smaller chunks, completing one calculation before moving to the next. For advanced learners: Add variables like tax calculations (8% sales tax), comparison shopping with different pizza sizes/prices, or planning for dietary restrictions requiring specialty pizzas at different costs.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition
description: Students will analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort) by examining their code structure, predicting time complexity, and validating predictions through empirical testing. They will decompose each algorithm's performance characteristics and compare efficiency trade-offs across different input scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by examining code structure and identifying nested loops, recursive calls, and iteration patterns
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic performance testing and data visualization of execution times across varying input sizes
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort in Python (15 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students. Each group receives printed code for all three algorithms and data collection worksheets. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Students examine each algorithm's code structure without running it. They identify and document: number of nested loops, recursive function calls, and conditional statements. Students predict time complexity (O(n), O(n log n), O(n²)) for each algorithm based solely on code analysis. Groups record predictions on worksheets with justifications.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Students run each algorithm using provided test datasets of varying sizes (100, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000 elements) on both sorted and random arrays. They measure execution time using Python's time.perf_counter() function and record results in spreadsheets. Students create line graphs plotting input size vs. execution time for each algorithm.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Students analyze their empirical results against initial predictions. They identify which algorithms perform consistently regardless of input order versus those affected by data arrangement. Groups calculate growth rates between data points and match observed patterns to theoretical complexity classes.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents one algorithm analysis to class, explaining code structure findings, empirical results, and any discrepancies between predicted and actual performance. Class discusses optimal algorithm selection for different scenarios.
materials_needed: Pre-written Python files for bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort
Algorithm analysis worksheets with tables for predictions and measurements
Test datasets (CSV files with sorted and randomized integer arrays)
Computers with Python 3.7+ and matplotlib library installed
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets) for data visualization
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of initial complexity predictions with proper justification (25%), (2) Correct implementation of timing measurements and data collection (25%), (3) Quality of performance graphs and trend identification (25%), (4) Analysis comparing empirical results to theoretical complexity with explanation of discrepancies (25%). Students submit completed worksheets, graphs, and written analysis summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity cheat sheet showing common patterns (single loop = O(n), nested loops = O(n²)). Offer pre-formatted spreadsheet templates. For advanced learners: Add analysis of space complexity, investigate best/average/worst case scenarios, or implement hybrid sorting algorithms like Timsort for comparison.

title: Model Selection Tribunal: Evaluating and Defending Machine Learning Approaches for Real-World Business Problems
description: Students critically evaluate three different machine learning models applied to a complex business dataset, then defend their model selection in a structured tribunal format where they must justify their choice against rigorous questioning. This activity simulates real-world data science decision-making where technical merit must be balanced against business constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the performance, interpretability, and business viability of competing machine learning models by analyzing multiple evaluation metrics and presenting evidence-based recommendations
Students will critique model selection decisions through structured peer review and defend their methodology against challenging cross-examination scenarios
instructions: **Phase 1 - Model Analysis (90 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives the same dataset (customer churn prediction with 50,000 records, 25 features) and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network, each with different performance profiles. Teams spend 60 minutes conducting comprehensive model evaluation using provided validation sets. They must analyze: accuracy metrics (precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC), business metrics (cost of false positives/negatives at $500/$200 respectively), interpretability requirements (regulatory compliance), computational costs (inference time <100ms requirement), and model stability (performance across demographic segments). Teams document findings in a structured evaluation matrix and spend 30 minutes preparing their recommendation presentation. **Phase 2 - Tribunal Defense (60 minutes):** Each team presents their model selection (8 minutes max) to a panel of 'stakeholders' (other teams rotating as business executives, compliance officers, and technical architects). Presenters must defend their choice against 5 minutes of challenging questions about trade-offs they made, addressing scenarios like 'What if inference time requirements doubled?' or 'How do you handle the 15% performance gap in the 18-25 demographic?' Each team both presents and serves as questioners. **Phase 3 - Reflection (15 minutes):** Individual written reflection on how their initial choice evolved through the questioning process and what factors proved most critical in model selection.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV format, 50,000 records with ground truth labels)
Three pre-trained model files (Random Forest .pkl, XGBoost .pkl, Neural Network .h5)
Jupyter Notebook template with evaluation framework pre-loaded
Business context document specifying costs, constraints, and regulatory requirements
Model evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Timer for presentation phases
assessment_method: Evaluation based on four components: (1) Technical Analysis Quality (25%) - accuracy and completeness of model evaluation metrics and business impact calculations, (2) Recommendation Justification (30%) - logical reasoning connecting analysis to model choice with explicit trade-off acknowledgment, (3) Defense Performance (25%) - ability to answer challenging questions and adapt position when presented with new constraints, (4) Peer Evaluation (20%) - quality of questions asked during tribunal phases and constructive feedback provided. Rubric includes specific criteria such as 'Identified and quantified at least 3 significant model trade-offs' and 'Successfully defended model choice against minimum 2 major objections.'
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation checklist with specific metrics to calculate and guiding questions for each business constraint.
