title: Budget Planning for a School Event Using Percentage Calculations
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic budget for planning a school dance or fundraiser. They will calculate costs, discounts, taxes, and determine ticket prices needed to break even or make a profit.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine actual costs after discounts and taxes in a real-world budgeting scenario
Students will calculate break-even points and profit margins through systematic application of percentage formulas
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'School Event Planning Worksheet' and price lists to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student is planning either a school dance or bake sale fundraiser with a $500 initial budget. Students must first select 5 essential items from the provided price list (decorations, food, entertainment, etc.). Next, have students calculate the base cost of their selected items using the given prices (10 minutes). Then, students apply the provided discount percentages: 15% off decorations, 10% off food items, and 20% off entertainment. They must show their work calculating the discounted price for each category (15 minutes). After calculating discounted prices, students add 8.5% sales tax to all items except food and calculate their total event cost (10 minutes). In the final phase, students determine how many tickets they need to sell at $8 each to break even, then calculate how many tickets needed to achieve a 25% profit margin (15 minutes). Students must show all percentage calculations using the formula: (part/whole) × 100 = percentage, and demonstrate their understanding by explaining one calculation to a partner (10 minutes). Conclude with students presenting their event budget summary, including total costs, ticket sales needed, and expected profit/loss (15 minutes).
materials_needed: School Event Planning Worksheet (pre-made with item categories and prices)
Calculators (one per student)
Price list handout with 15+ items across different categories
Percentage calculation reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, realistic budget created; (3) Most calculations correct, minor errors in application; (2) Some calculation errors, basic understanding demonstrated; (1) Major calculation errors, incomplete work. Students must correctly calculate at least 4 of 6 required percentages to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide percentage calculation templates and allow use of fraction-to-percentage conversion charts. Pair with stronger math students for peer support. For advanced learners: add complexity by including multiple tax rates, compound discounts, or require them to create alternative budget scenarios with different profit targets.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Product Search
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of different SQL query approaches for an e-commerce product search system. They will examine execution plans, identify performance bottlenecks, and determine the relationship between query structure and resource utilization patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining operator costs, row estimates, and index usage to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient query patterns through systematic comparison of execution statistics and resource consumption metrics
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 students) with access to a pre-populated e-commerce database containing 50,000 products, 100,000 customers, and 250,000 order records. Distribute the analysis worksheet containing 6 different SQL queries that accomplish the same task: finding products by category with price range filtering and customer rating aggregation. Each query uses different approaches (nested subqueries, joins, CTEs, window functions, etc.). Students first execute each query individually using the database management system's query analyzer tool, recording execution time, CPU usage, and I/O statistics in their comparison matrix. Next, they generate and save execution plans for each query, identifying the most expensive operations (table scans, sorts, joins) by examining the graphical or text-based plans. Teams then create a detailed analysis document categorizing each query's performance characteristics: which queries use indexes effectively, which perform unnecessary table scans, and which have optimal join orders. They must identify the top 2 best-performing queries and bottom 2 worst-performing queries, providing specific evidence from execution plans and statistics. Finally, teams prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their findings, including before/after execution plan comparisons and specific recommendations for query optimization. Conclude with a class discussion where teams share their most surprising discovery about query performance patterns.
materials_needed: Pre-populated e-commerce database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server)
Database management software with query execution plan visualization
Query analysis worksheet template with 6 test queries
Performance comparison matrix template
Computers with database client software installed
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate interpretation of execution plans with specific cost metrics identified, (2) Correct identification of performance bottlenecks with supporting evidence, (3) Logical comparison between query approaches with data-driven conclusions, (4) Clear communication of optimization recommendations. Students must submit their completed comparison matrix, written analysis document, and deliver their team presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide execution plan reading guide with common operator symbols explained, offer pre-filled examples for first 2 queries, and pair with stronger database students. For advanced learners: Add index creation/modification tasks, include stored procedure vs. dynamic query analysis, or introduce query hint experimentation to further optimize the best-performing queries.

title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Intervention Strategies
description: Students will construct an original compartmental mathematical model (SEIR variant) to predict disease transmission dynamics in a specific population. They will incorporate real-world intervention strategies, validate their model against historical data, and present policy recommendations based on their mathematical findings.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original differential equation system modeling epidemic spread by selecting appropriate compartments, parameters, and intervention functions for a specific demographic scenario
Students will synthesize mathematical modeling techniques with real-world data validation through computational analysis and statistical comparison methods
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a different demographic scenario (university campus, nursing home, urban neighborhood, or rural community) with specific population characteristics and historical outbreak data. Students spend 45 minutes researching their assigned population's characteristics, contact patterns, and relevant epidemiological parameters using provided databases and research papers. Next, teams design their compartmental model structure (60 minutes), deciding whether to use SEIR, SEIRS, or modified variants, and mathematically formulating their differential equation system. They must justify each compartment, define transition rates, and incorporate at least two intervention strategies (vaccination, social distancing, quarantine, etc.) as time-dependent parameters. Using Python or MATLAB, students implement their model computationally (75 minutes), writing code to solve the differential equation system numerically and generate projection graphs. They calibrate parameters by comparing model outputs to their assigned historical data, adjusting values to minimize residual errors. Teams then conduct sensitivity analysis (45 minutes) by varying key parameters to identify which factors most significantly impact outbreak trajectories. Finally, students prepare a 15-minute presentation (30 minutes preparation) that includes: model equations with parameter justifications, computational results showing intervention effectiveness, validation against historical data with quantified accuracy metrics, and specific policy recommendations for their demographic scenario. During presentations (15 minutes per team plus 5 minutes Q&A), teams must defend their modeling choices and respond to peer critiques about mathematical assumptions and real-world applicability.
materials_needed: Historical epidemic data sets for 4 different demographic scenarios (COVID-19, influenza, or measles outbreaks)
Access to epidemiological research databases (PubMed, CDC reports)
Python with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib libraries OR MATLAB with Simulink
Graphing materials for presentation preparation
Projection system for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model formulation and justification (25 points) - correctness of differential equations, parameter selection, and theoretical grounding; Computational implementation (20 points) - code functionality, numerical accuracy, and appropriate visualization; Data validation and calibration (20 points) - systematic comparison with historical data, quantified accuracy metrics, and parameter adjustment rationale; Intervention analysis (15 points) - realistic implementation of intervention strategies and effectiveness quantification; Presentation and defense (20 points) - clarity of explanation, response to questions, and practical policy recommendations. Students must achieve minimum 15 points in mathematical formulation and 12 points in computational implementation to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation structures for basic SEIR models, offer guided parameter estimation worksheets, and allow use of simplified single-intervention scenarios. Supply debugging assistance for computational implementation and sample code snippets. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, age-structured populations, or spatial transmission patterns. Encourage comparison of multiple model variants (deterministic vs. stochastic) or development of optimization algorithms for intervention timing. Advanced students can also explore machine learning approaches for parameter estimation.

title: Binary Number System Digit Card Recall Challenge
description: Students memorize and practice recalling the first 16 binary numbers (0000 to 1111) and their decimal equivalents using flashcard-style activities. This foundational activity builds essential number system knowledge through repetitive recall exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization and practice activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary conversion reference sheets to each student showing decimal numbers 0-15 with their 4-bit binary equivalents (00-0000, 01-0001, etc.). Allow students 10 minutes to study the sheet silently, encouraging them to use memory techniques like chunking or patterns. Next, organize students into pairs and give each pair a set of 32 double-sided cards: 16 cards showing decimal numbers (0-15) and 16 cards showing binary numbers (0000-1111). Have students place all cards face down and take turns flipping two cards, trying to match decimal numbers with their binary equivalents. When a student makes a correct match, they keep the pair and explain the conversion aloud. Continue until all pairs are matched. After pair work, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session where you display either a decimal or binary number on the board for 5 seconds, and students write the corresponding equivalent on mini whiteboards. Complete three rounds of 8 random numbers each. For the final phase, have students individually complete a written quiz with two columns: Column A lists 10 decimal numbers (0-15) and Column B lists 10 binary numbers. Students draw lines connecting correct pairs within 8 minutes. Review answers immediately as a class, having volunteers explain any challenging conversions.
materials_needed: Binary conversion reference sheets (1 per student)
Double-sided number matching cards (1 set of 32 cards per pair)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (1 per student)
Written quiz worksheets (1 per student)
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 10-point quiz where each correct decimal-to-binary match earns 1 point. Success criteria: 8/10 correct matches (80% accuracy) within the 8-minute time limit. Additionally, observe students during pair activities and award participation points for correct verbal explanations of conversions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a simplified reference card with only numbers 0-7 and allow extra study time. Encourage them to start with patterns (powers of 2). For advanced learners, extend the activity to include 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents alongside binary conversions.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Customer Data Patterns
description: Students will analyze and explain the characteristics of different statistical distributions by examining authentic customer purchase datasets. They will identify distribution types, interpret their properties, and explain what these patterns reveal about customer behavior in business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the characteristics of normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing real customer purchase frequency data and explaining what each pattern indicates about customer segments
Students will distinguish between different distribution types through visual analysis and statistical measures, then explain the business implications of each pattern
instructions: Begin by providing each group of 3-4 students with three different datasets: customer purchase amounts, website visit durations, and product ratings (15 minutes setup). Students first create histograms for each dataset using provided templates or software, spending 20 minutes on visualization. Next, have students examine each histogram and identify: the shape (normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, bimodal), central tendency measures (mean vs median positioning), and spread characteristics (25 minutes analysis phase). In pairs within their groups, students then discuss what each distribution pattern reveals about customer behavior - for example, right-skewed purchase amounts might indicate most customers make small purchases while few make large ones (15 minutes discussion). Each group creates a summary chart comparing the three distributions, noting shape, key statistics (mean, median, standard deviation), and business interpretation (20 minutes documentation). Groups then present one distribution to the class, explaining its characteristics and what it suggests about the underlying customer behavior, with other groups asking clarifying questions about the interpretation (25 minutes presentation phase). Conclude with a brief reflection where students write three key insights about how distribution shapes inform business decision-making (10 minutes individual reflection).
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared datasets (customer purchases CSV, website visits CSV, product ratings CSV) with 500-1000 data points each
Histogram creation templates or access to Excel/Google Sheets
Distribution analysis worksheet with guiding questions
Chart paper and markers for summary creation
Calculator or statistical software access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of distribution shapes and statistical measures (25%), (2) Quality of business interpretation linking distribution characteristics to customer behavior patterns (35%), (3) Clear explanation during group presentation demonstrating understanding of distribution properties (25%), (4) Thoughtful reflection on how distributions inform business decisions (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-labeled distribution examples and sentence starters for business interpretations like 'This right-skewed pattern suggests that most customers...' For advanced learners, introduce concepts like kurtosis, provide additional datasets with unusual patterns, or have them research real company examples where distribution analysis led to business strategy changes. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during the analysis phase.

title: Analyzing Time Complexity Trade-offs in Advanced Data Structure Implementations
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different balanced tree implementations (AVL, Red-Black, and B-trees) by examining their insertion, deletion, and search operations under various load conditions. They will decompose the algorithmic differences and evaluate which implementation provides optimal performance for specific use cases.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity trade-offs between AVL trees, Red-Black trees, and B-trees by examining their rotation mechanisms and rebalancing strategies
Students will evaluate the performance characteristics of each data structure through empirical testing and theoretical complexity analysis
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-implemented balanced tree classes (AVL, Red-Black, B-tree with order 4) in their preferred programming language, each with instrumented methods that count operations. Divide students into teams of 2-3 members. Each team receives three datasets: sparse integers (1000 elements), dense sequential data (10000 elements), and mixed operations dataset (5000 insertions, 3000 deletions, 7000 searches). 

Step 1 (30 minutes): Teams examine the source code for each implementation, focusing on insertion and deletion methods. They must identify and document the key differences in rebalancing strategies, specifically noting rotation counts, tree height maintenance, and node splitting/merging approaches.

Step 2 (45 minutes): Students run performance tests on each dataset, recording execution time, memory usage, and operation counts (rotations, comparisons, node accesses). They must create performance matrices comparing all three structures across the three datasets.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams analyze the collected data to identify patterns. They must calculate the actual time complexity ratios between operations and compare these to theoretical expectations. Students should identify scenarios where each structure performs optimally.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each team presents their analysis, focusing on one specific finding: when and why one structure outperforms the others. They must support their conclusions with both empirical data and theoretical reasoning about the algorithmic differences they identified.
materials_needed: Pre-implemented AVL, Red-Black, and B-tree classes with operation counters
Three standardized datasets (sparse, dense, mixed operations)
Performance measurement framework/timing utilities
Computers with development environment (Java/Python/C++)
Data collection spreadsheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of algorithmic difference identification (25 points) - must correctly identify at least 3 key implementation differences; (2) Quality of empirical analysis (30 points) - includes complete data collection and correct interpretation of performance patterns; (3) Theoretical justification (25 points) - correctly links observed performance to underlying algorithmic properties; (4) Use case recommendations (20 points) - provides specific, justified recommendations for when to use each structure.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided analysis worksheets with specific questions about each algorithm's rebalancing approach. Offer code annotation templates to help identify key differences. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement their own optimized version of one structure or analyze additional structures like Splay trees or Treaps. Provide real-world datasets (database indices, file systems) for more complex analysis.

title: Advanced Design Patterns Memory Challenge: Gang of Four Implementation Recall
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the 23 Gang of Four design patterns, their structural components, and implementation syntax across multiple programming languages. This intensive recall activity tests mastery of advanced software engineering concepts through structured memorization exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the names, categories, and structural components of all 23 Gang of Four design patterns by completing timed memory assessments
Students will identify key implementation syntax and UML diagram elements for Singleton, Factory Method, Observer, and Strategy patterns through visual recognition exercises
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute review session where students study provided reference cards containing all 23 GoF patterns organized by category (Creational: 5 patterns, Structural: 7 patterns, Behavioral: 11 patterns). Each card displays pattern name, intent statement, UML diagram, and Java/Python code skeleton. After review time, collect all materials. 

Round 1 (15 minutes): Distribute blank category sheets. Students must list all pattern names under correct categories within 8 minutes. Allow 2 minutes for self-checking against answer key, then 5 minutes for correction notes. 

Round 2 (20 minutes): Show UML diagram fragments on projector for 30 seconds each. Students identify the pattern name and write the primary intent statement. Cover Singleton, Abstract Factory, Adapter, Composite, Observer, Command, and Strategy patterns. Provide 2 minutes between each diagram for writing responses. 

Round 3 (25 minutes): Code Implementation Recall - Display incomplete code snippets in Java and Python for the four core patterns (Singleton, Factory Method, Observer, Strategy). Students must fill in missing method signatures, key variables, and interface definitions. Allocate 6 minutes per pattern with 1-minute transition periods. 

Conclude with 10-minute reflection where students identify their weakest recall areas and create personalized study lists for improvement.
materials_needed: 23 laminated GoF pattern reference cards with UML diagrams and code examples
Blank categorization worksheets (one per student)
Code snippet worksheets with fill-in-the-blank sections
Digital projector for displaying UML diagrams
Answer keys for immediate feedback
Timer for precise activity pacing
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on pattern name categorization (19/23 correct), 70% accuracy on UML diagram identification (5/7 correct), and 75% accuracy on code completion tasks (3/4 patterns correctly completed) to demonstrate advanced-level recall mastery. Use provided rubric with point deductions for spelling errors in technical terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices for pattern categories and allow reference to simplified pattern summary sheets during Round 2. Advanced learners can complete bonus challenges identifying anti-patterns or suggesting alternative implementations. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger peers during reflection period for collaborative study strategy development.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance vs. Model Explainability in High-Dimensional Healthcare Predictions
description: Students will analyze the critical distinction between feature importance metrics and model explainability methods in a complex healthcare prediction scenario. They will examine how different interpretation techniques can lead to conflicting insights and understand when each approach is most appropriate for stakeholder communication.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between feature importance rankings and SHAP/LIME explanations by comparing outputs from identical random forest models predicting patient readmission risk
Students will interpret the practical implications of model explanation discrepancies through stakeholder persona analysis and communication strategy development
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a trained random forest model predicting 30-day hospital readmission using 47 clinical features. Teams spend 15 minutes examining the model performance metrics (AUC=0.78, precision=0.71, recall=0.65) and the provided feature importance plot showing top 10 features. Next, students execute the SHAP explainer code block to generate waterfall plots for 5 specific patient cases, spending 20 minutes documenting discrepancies between global feature importance and individual SHAP explanations. In the third phase (25 minutes), teams use the LIME explainer on the same 5 patients, creating a comparison matrix showing how LIME local explanations differ from both SHAP values and global importance rankings. Students then receive stakeholder persona cards (hospital administrator, attending physician, data scientist, patient family member) and spend 30 minutes developing explanation strategies for each persona, considering which interpretation method best serves each audience's needs. Teams conclude by creating a decision framework flowchart (20 minutes) that guides when to use feature importance vs. SHAP vs. LIME based on use case requirements, audience technical sophistication, and regulatory constraints. Throughout the activity, students document specific examples where methods contradict each other and hypothesize reasons for these discrepancies, particularly focusing on feature interactions and model behavior in edge cases.
materials_needed: Pre-configured Jupyter notebook with trained random forest model and hospital readmission dataset
SHAP and LIME libraries installed in Python environment
Stakeholder persona cards with detailed role descriptions and decision-making contexts
Comparison matrix templates (digital or printed)
Access to collaborative document platform for team decision frameworks
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy in identifying and documenting specific discrepancies between interpretation methods with quantitative evidence, (2) Quality of stakeholder-appropriate explanation strategies with clear rationale for method selection, (3) Comprehensiveness of decision framework including edge cases and constraints, (4) Depth of analysis in hypothesizing reasons for method contradictions. Success requires teams to identify at least 3 specific discrepancies with numerical evidence and provide appropriate interpretation strategies for all 4 stakeholder types.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions for each analysis phase and pre-populated comparison templates with example entries. Offer additional context about healthcare decision-making and regulatory requirements. For advanced learners, include additional interpretation methods (permutation importance, anchor explanations) and challenge them to develop quantitative metrics for measuring explanation consistency across methods. Provide access to academic papers on explainable AI contradictions for deeper theoretical understanding.

title: Pizza Party Budget Calculator - Applying Multiplication and Division to Real-World Shopping
description: Students will calculate the total cost and required quantities for a class pizza party by applying multiplication and division skills to solve authentic shopping problems. They will work with real menu prices to determine how many pizzas to order and calculate exact costs including tax.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication skills to calculate total costs by multiplying price per item by quantity needed
Students will apply division operations to determine equal portions and cost per student through hands-on budgeting scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pizza menu handouts and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card contains: class size (15-25 students), budget amount ($60-120), and special requirements (vegetarian options, drinks needed, etc.). Students must assume each person eats 2 pizza slices, with 8 slices per pizza. 

Step 1: Students calculate how many pizzas needed by dividing total people by 4 (since 8 slices ÷ 2 slices per person = 4 people per pizza). 

Step 2: Using the menu, students select pizza types and calculate subtotal by multiplying price per pizza by quantity needed. They must include at least one vegetarian option. 

Step 3: Students add 8.5% sales tax by multiplying subtotal by 0.085 and adding to subtotal for final cost. 

Step 4: Students check if total fits within budget. If over budget, they must revise selections and recalculate. 

Step 5: Calculate cost per student by dividing final total by number of students. 

Step 6: Students complete the order form worksheet showing: pizza quantities, itemized costs, tax calculation, total cost, and per-student cost. 

Circulate during work time (15 minutes) to check calculations and provide guidance. Conclude with 2-3 students presenting their solutions, explaining their multiplication and division steps (10 minutes). Emphasize how they applied these operations to solve the real-world problem.
materials_needed: Pizza restaurant menu handouts (showing prices for different pizza sizes and types)
Scenario cards with different class sizes and budgets (one per student)
Pizza Party Order Form worksheets
Calculators (optional for checking work)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed order forms using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correct calculations for pizzas needed, subtotal, tax, and total cost with clear work shown; (3) Minor computational errors but correct application of operations; (2) Correct setup but multiple calculation mistakes; (1) Incorrect application of multiplication/division concepts. Students must achieve level 3 or higher to demonstrate mastery of applying these operations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing which numbers to multiply/divide at each step, or pair with stronger math partners. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including drinks, appetizers, delivery fees, or having them compare costs from multiple restaurants to find the best deal. Consider having them calculate different scenarios (cost if ordering larger pizzas vs. more small pizzas).

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sort Performance
description: Students analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms by examining their time complexity, space complexity, and real-world execution behavior. They will decompose algorithm implementations, compare efficiency patterns across different input sizes, and evaluate which algorithm performs best under specific conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze time and space complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by examining their recursive structures and loop patterns
Students will compare algorithm performance through empirical testing and theoretical analysis to determine optimal use cases
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations in their preferred programming language (Python, Java, or C++). Each implementation should be well-commented but contain no complexity analysis. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students examine each algorithm's structure individually. They identify loops, recursive calls, and memory allocations. Using provided complexity analysis worksheets, they trace through small examples (5-element arrays) to understand execution flow. 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Groups create theoretical complexity predictions. They analyze worst-case, best-case, and average-case scenarios for each algorithm. Students document their reasoning using Big O notation and explain their logic on provided analysis sheets.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Empirical testing phase. Students run each algorithm on provided datasets of varying sizes (100, 1000, 5000, 10000 elements) and input patterns (sorted, reverse-sorted, random). They record execution times using built-in timing functions and memory usage statistics.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Data visualization. Groups create comparison charts plotting execution time vs. input size for each algorithm. They use spreadsheet software or Python matplotlib to generate clear visual representations.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Analysis synthesis. Teams complete comparison matrices identifying when each algorithm excels. They must justify recommendations for specific use cases (small datasets, memory-constrained environments, nearly-sorted data) based on their findings. 

Conclude with 10-minute group presentations where each team shares one key insight about algorithm trade-offs.
materials_needed: Pre-written sorting algorithm implementations in Python/Java/C++
Algorithm complexity analysis worksheets
Test datasets (4 different sizes, 3 different patterns each)
Computers with programming environment and timing libraries
Spreadsheet software or Python with matplotlib
Comparison matrix templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical complexity analysis with correct Big O notation, (2) Quality of empirical data collection and documentation, (3) Appropriateness of algorithm recommendations for given scenarios, (4) Clear explanation of trade-offs between time/space complexity. Students must submit completed worksheets, data visualizations, and written justifications for their recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity analysis examples for simple algorithms like linear search first. Include step-by-step tracing templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze hybrid algorithms like Timsort, or implement optimizations to existing algorithms and measure improvement. Provide additional datasets with edge cases or very large sizes.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Multiple Healthcare Datasets
description: Students will critically assess the validity, reliability, and ethical implications of three different machine learning models predicting patient readmission rates using real healthcare datasets. They will evaluate model performance metrics, identify potential biases, and make evidence-based recommendations for clinical implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML algorithms by comparing performance metrics, bias indicators, and generalizability across diverse patient populations
Students will critique the ethical implications and clinical applicability of predictive models through systematic analysis of fairness metrics and stakeholder impact assessments
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Distribute three pre-trained models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) trained on hospital readmission data from different demographic regions. Provide students with model outputs including: confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, feature importance rankings, and fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) broken down by age, gender, and ethnicity. Students work in teams of 3-4 to independently analyze each model's technical performance using provided evaluation frameworks.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams complete structured evaluation matrices comparing models across six dimensions: predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, interpretability, demographic fairness, clinical actionability, and implementation feasibility. Each dimension uses a 4-point rubric with specific criteria (e.g., AUC >0.85 = 4 points for accuracy). Teams must provide quantitative evidence and qualitative reasoning for each score.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes):** Teams prepare 8-minute presentations defending their recommendation for which model (if any) should be implemented in a clinical setting. Presentations must address: model selection rationale, identified limitations and risks, proposed mitigation strategies for bias/errors, and implementation timeline with success metrics. Include a 2-minute Q&A where other teams challenge assumptions and methodology.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Individual reflection where students write a 500-word critical analysis identifying the most significant limitation they discovered across all models and proposing a data science solution to address it.
materials_needed: Three pre-trained ML models with saved outputs (confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance)
Hospital readmission dataset (MIMIC-III or synthetic equivalent) with demographic variables
Model evaluation framework template with fairness metrics calculations
Presentation rubric and peer evaluation forms
Python/R environment with scikit-learn, fairlearn, and visualization libraries
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Technical analysis accuracy (25 points), Evidence quality and use of metrics (20 points), Critical thinking in bias identification (20 points), Recommendation justification strength (20 points), Presentation clarity and defense of position (15 points). Students must achieve 80+ points and demonstrate ability to identify at least two significant model limitations with proposed solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated fairness metrics and guided questions for each evaluation dimension. Offer model interpretation workshops focusing on reading confusion matrices and ROC curves. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate additional bias metrics (calibration, individual fairness) and consider intersectional bias analysis. Encourage exploration of ensemble approaches or alternative evaluation frameworks like clinical decision curves.

title: Design and Justify a Novel Cryptographic Protocol Using Advanced Number Theory
description: Students will create an original cryptographic encryption/decryption system by synthesizing concepts from modular arithmetic, group theory, and prime number theory. They will develop a complete mathematical framework, implement their protocol, and present a rigorous security analysis to demonstrate its theoretical soundness and practical viability.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original cryptographic protocol by integrating advanced number theory concepts including modular arithmetic, discrete logarithms, and prime factorization properties
Students will construct mathematical proofs through formal verification to demonstrate the security properties and computational complexity of their cryptographic system
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Protocol Design**
Students work in pairs to brainstorm and design their cryptographic system. They must select a mathematical foundation (e.g., elliptic curves, lattice-based problems, or polynomial rings) and define key generation, encryption, and decryption algorithms. Provide each pair with research access to current cryptographic literature. Students document their initial design using mathematical notation, specifying all parameters, operations, and assumptions.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Mathematical Analysis**
Pairs develop formal mathematical proofs for their protocol's security properties. They must prove correctness (decryption recovers original message), analyze computational complexity using Big-O notation, and identify potential vulnerabilities. Students create detailed mathematical documentation including theorem statements, lemmas, and complete proofs using proper mathematical syntax.

**Phase 3 (60 minutes): Implementation and Testing**
Using Python with SymPy library, students implement their protocol with at least 10 test cases demonstrating encryption/decryption cycles. They must handle edge cases, validate input parameters, and measure performance metrics. Code must include comprehensive comments explaining mathematical operations.

**Phase 4 (45 minutes): Peer Review and Presentation**
Each pair presents their protocol to another pair for cryptanalysis. Reviewers attempt to find weaknesses and suggest improvements. Original creators defend their design and incorporate feedback. Session concludes with 5-minute presentations to the entire class highlighting the most innovative aspects of their cryptographic contribution.
materials_needed: Computers with Python 3.8+ and SymPy library installed
Access to mathematical databases (MathSciNet, arXiv.org)
LaTeX editor or equation editor for mathematical notation
Digital whiteboard or presentation software
Cryptographic reference materials and current research papers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of proofs (30 points), originality and sophistication of cryptographic approach (25 points), quality and functionality of implementation with comprehensive testing (25 points), clarity of presentation and ability to defend design choices during peer review (20 points). Deliverables include written mathematical analysis, documented source code, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide templates for proof structure and suggest focusing on modifications of existing protocols rather than completely novel approaches. Offer additional resources on fundamental number theory concepts. For advanced learners: Challenge them to prove resistance against specific attack types (chosen-plaintext, man-in-the-middle) or to optimize their protocol for specific computational constraints like embedded systems or quantum-resistant properties.

title: Programming Language Symbol Matching Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the syntax symbols used in Python programming by matching symbol flashcards with their correct function names and purposes. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for recognizing basic Python operators and punctuation marks.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 15 common Python syntax symbols (=, ==, !=, +, -, *, /, %, (, ), [, ], {, }, :, ;) by matching them to their correct names and functions
Students will recall the purpose of each Python symbol through timed flashcard exercises and verbal recitation
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Print and cut out 45 cards total - 15 symbol cards showing Python operators/punctuation, 15 name cards with terms like 'assignment operator' and 'equals sign', and 15 function cards describing what each symbol does. Arrange students in pairs at desks with space to spread cards. **Round 1 - Symbol to Name Matching (10 minutes):** Give each pair the symbol cards and name cards only. Students work together to match each symbol with its correct name (e.g., '==' matches with 'equality operator'). Instructor circulates to provide immediate feedback. **Round 2 - Add Function Cards (10 minutes):** Introduce the function description cards. Students now create three-card sets: symbol + name + function description (e.g., '==' + 'equality operator' + 'compares two values for equality'). **Round 3 - Individual Recall Test (8 minutes):** Students work individually. Show each symbol card for 5 seconds, students write down both the name and function from memory. **Round 4 - Speed Challenge (5 minutes):** Using only symbol cards, instructor displays each symbol for 3 seconds. Students shout out the name in unison. **Wrap-up (2 minutes):** Students recite the complete list of symbols and names once more as a class.
materials_needed: 45 printed flashcards (3 sets of 15 cards each)
Timer or stopwatch
Answer sheets for individual recall test
Pencils for students
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 12 out of 15 symbols with their names and 10 out of 15 with their functions during the individual recall test. Observe student participation during pair work and group recitation. Use checklist to mark each student's accuracy on symbol recognition and verbal recall performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with only 8 symbols, provide a reference chart during first round, allow extra time during individual testing. For advanced learners: Add 5 additional symbols (+=, -=, *=, /=, //), challenge them to create sentences using multiple symbols, or have them teach struggling peers during pair work.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Real Estate Sales Data
description: Students will analyze actual real estate sales data to identify and explain different types of data distributions (normal, skewed, bimodal). They will interpret what these distribution patterns reveal about market characteristics and make connections between statistical concepts and real-world business implications.
learning_objectives: Students will classify data distributions as normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, or bimodal by examining histograms and summary statistics of housing price data
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through written interpretations connecting statistical concepts to market conditions
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a dataset containing 500 real estate transactions from three different neighborhoods (Dataset A: suburban family area, Dataset B: luxury waterfront, Dataset C: mixed urban district). Students work in pairs for 40 minutes. First 15 minutes: Have students create histograms for house prices in each dataset using provided Excel templates with pre-formatted chart areas. Students calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation using built-in functions. Next 15 minutes: Students examine each histogram and classify the distribution type, noting the relationship between mean and median. They complete a comparison table identifying: distribution shape, central tendency measures, and potential outliers. Final 10 minutes: Students write a 150-word interpretation for each dataset explaining what the distribution pattern suggests about that neighborhood's market characteristics. For example, right-skewed distributions might indicate affordable areas with few luxury properties. Conclude with 10-minute pair sharing where students present one dataset interpretation to another pair and receive feedback on their reasoning.
materials_needed: Three CSV files with 500 real estate records each (price, bedrooms, square footage, neighborhood)
Excel template with pre-formatted histogram charts and summary statistics formulas
Distribution classification worksheet with comparison table
Sample interpretation rubric handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct distribution classification for all three datasets, (2) Accurate calculation of summary statistics, (3) Clear explanation of mean-median relationships, (4) Logical connection between distribution patterns and market characteristics. Success criteria: Students must correctly identify at least 2 out of 3 distribution types and provide reasonable business interpretations with statistical evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a distribution identification flowchart and pre-calculated summary statistics. Offer sentence starters for interpretations like 'The right-skewed distribution suggests...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential causes of bimodal distributions and calculate additional measures like skewness coefficients. Provide bonus dataset with seasonal sales data for time-series distribution analysis.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Scenarios
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to solve complex business problems involving revenue maximization and cost minimization with multiple constraints. They will work through authentic scenarios requiring partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and critical point analysis to determine optimal production levels, pricing strategies, and resource allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivative techniques and Lagrange multipliers to solve multi-variable optimization problems by analyzing realistic business scenarios with budget and resource constraints
Students will implement systematic optimization procedures to determine critical points and verify maximum/minimum solutions through second derivative testing and constraint validation
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct business scenario packets (15 minutes setup). Scenario A: A furniture company optimizing production of chairs and tables with material constraints. Scenario B: A tech startup maximizing subscription revenue with advertising budget limitations. Scenario C: A restaurant chain minimizing food waste while maintaining quality standards across locations. Form groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one scenario (5 minutes). Students must first identify all variables, constraints, and the objective function from the narrative description (20 minutes). Next, they set up the optimization problem using Lagrange multipliers, writing out the gradient equations and constraint equations (25 minutes). Groups then solve the system of equations to find critical points, showing all algebraic steps (35 minutes). Students apply the bordered Hessian test or constraint qualification methods to verify their solutions represent actual maxima or minima (20 minutes). Each group creates a one-page executive summary translating their mathematical results back into business recommendations, including sensitivity analysis of how small changes in constraints affect optimal solutions (25 minutes). Groups rotate stations to examine other scenarios and verify solutions using graphing software like Desmos 3D or GeoGebra (15 minutes). Conclude with whole-class presentations where each group presents their optimization strategy and business recommendations (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Three detailed business scenario packets with numerical data
Graphing calculators or computer access
Desmos 3D Calculator or GeoGebra software
Executive summary template sheets
Whiteboard or flip chart paper for group work
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct identification and setup of optimization problem with constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier method and algebraic solution (35%), (3) Proper verification of critical points using second derivative tests (25%), (4) Clear business interpretation and practical recommendations with sensitivity analysis (15%). Students must demonstrate work for all steps and achieve 70% minimum for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and suggest systematic organization charts for tracking variables. Offer mini-lessons on setting up Lagrangian functions. For advanced learners: Introduce inequality constraints using Kuhn-Tucker conditions, or extend to stochastic optimization with probability distributions. Consider adding time-dependent variables for dynamic optimization problems.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Scenarios: Business Application
description: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization techniques to solve authentic business problems involving resource allocation, profit maximization, and cost minimization. They will work through three progressively complex scenarios requiring mathematical modeling and interpretation of results within business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems by setting up and solving systems of nonlinear equations
Students will demonstrate understanding of optimization theory through interpretation of mathematical solutions in real-world business contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing three business scenario packets (15 minutes setup). Scenario 1: Manufacturing company must maximize profit producing two products with limited labor hours and raw materials. Scenario 2: Marketing department allocating fixed budget across three advertising channels to maximize reach. Scenario 3: Portfolio manager optimizing investment allocation under risk constraints. Students work in pairs for first 20 minutes to read scenarios and identify variables, objective functions, and constraints. Instructor circulates to verify correct problem setup before proceeding. Next 45 minutes: pairs apply Lagrange multiplier method to solve each scenario. They must: (1) Define variables clearly with units, (2) Write objective function and constraint equations, (3) Set up Lagrangian function, (4) Take partial derivatives and set equal to zero, (5) Solve resulting system of equations, (6) Verify solutions satisfy original constraints, (7) Interpret mathematical results in business terms. During final 25 minutes, selected pairs present one scenario solution on whiteboard, explaining mathematical steps and business implications. Other students ask clarifying questions and suggest alternative interpretations. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting mathematical techniques to practical decision-making, emphasizing how optimization theory applies across industries. Conclude with individual 10-minute written reflection on when constrained optimization might be useful in their future careers.
materials_needed: Three printed business scenario packets per student pair
Graphing calculators or laptop computers with mathematical software
Large whiteboard sheets and markers for group presentations
Individual reflection worksheets
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct mathematical setup and variable identification, (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier technique, (3) Valid solution verification and constraint checking, (4) Clear interpretation of results in business context. Successful completion requires scoring 3/4 on each criterion. Additionally assess participation during presentations and quality of career reflection responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide step-by-step Lagrange multiplier template and work through simplified example first. Pair weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: include sensitivity analysis questions asking how solutions change with modified constraints, or add fourth scenario involving inequality constraints requiring Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Scenarios: Business Application
description: Students will apply calculus-based optimization techniques to solve complex business problems involving multiple variables and constraints. They will use Lagrange multipliers and critical point analysis to determine optimal production levels, pricing strategies, and resource allocation for a fictional manufacturing company.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multi-variable calculus optimization methods to determine maximum profit conditions by analyzing production cost and revenue functions with at least three variables
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical modeling of real-world business constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing the "GreenTech Manufacturing" case study packet containing production data, cost functions, and market constraints (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to analyze the scenario where the company produces solar panels with variables: x₁ (standard panels), x₂ (premium panels), x₃ (industrial panels). The profit function P(x₁,x₂,x₃) = 150x₁ + 280x₂ + 450x₃ - 0.5x₁² - 0.3x₂² - 0.2x₃² - 50√(x₁x₂) must be optimized subject to constraints: labor (2x₁ + 4x₂ + 6x₃ ≤ 480), materials (x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ ≤ 200), and storage (x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≤ 120). Step 1: Students identify critical points using partial derivatives (20 minutes). Step 2: Apply Lagrange multiplier method L = P(x₁,x₂,x₃) - λ₁(labor constraint) - λ₂(material constraint) - λ₃(storage constraint) (25 minutes). Step 3: Solve the resulting system of equations using graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (20 minutes). Step 4: Verify solutions using second derivative test and boundary analysis (15 minutes). Step 5: Calculate maximum profit and interpret economic meaning of Lagrange multipliers as shadow prices (10 minutes). Conclude with pairs presenting their optimization strategy and profit projections to the class (15 minutes).
materials_needed: GreenTech Manufacturing case study packets (printed)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Computer access with Wolfram Alpha or GeoGebra
Grid paper and colored pens for constraint visualization
Presentation whiteboards or poster paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct identification and setup of optimization problem with constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier technique with proper mathematical notation (30 points), (3) Correct computational solutions with verification steps shown (25 points), (4) Clear interpretation of results including economic meaning of shadow prices (20 points). Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps plus a 3-minute presentation explaining their optimization strategy and business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-completed constraint setup and focus on computational steps; offer step-by-step Lagrange multiplier template; allow use of online equation solvers with requirement to verify results manually. For advanced learners: Add time-dependent variables creating dynamic optimization problem; introduce inequality constraints requiring Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions; challenge with sensitivity analysis examining how optimal solutions change with constraint modifications.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and calculus optimization techniques to solve a complex manufacturing profit maximization problem with multiple constraints. They will work with realistic cost functions, production limitations, and market demand to determine optimal production quantities and resource allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methodology to solve constrained optimization problems by setting up and solving systems of partial differential equations
Students will implement multi-variable calculus techniques to determine optimal production strategies through analysis of real business constraint scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the case study packet featuring 'TechGadget Manufacturing Corp' which produces smartphones and tablets (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the scenario: profit function P(x,y) = 120x + 200y - 0.02x² - 0.05y² - 0.01xy, where x = smartphones (thousands), y = tablets (thousands). Constraints include: production capacity (2x + 3y ≤ 1800), material costs ($50x + $80y ≤ $60,000), and minimum production requirements (x ≥ 100, y ≥ 50). Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams identify constraint equations, set up the Lagrangian function L(x,y,λ₁,λ₂,λ₃,λ₄), and compute all partial derivatives. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Solve the system of equations ∇L = 0 to find critical points, checking each constraint's binding status. Teams must verify solutions using the bordered Hessian determinant test for constrained optimization. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Calculate maximum profit, interpret economic meaning of Lagrange multipliers (shadow prices), and perform sensitivity analysis by adjusting one constraint by ±10%. Each team creates a executive summary presentation with optimal production quantities, maximum profit value, constraint binding analysis, and managerial recommendations. Instructor circulates providing guidance on partial derivative calculations and constraint interpretation techniques throughout the activity.
materials_needed: TechGadget Manufacturing case study packets (one per team)
Scientific calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Maple)
Graph paper and colored pens for constraint visualization
Executive summary template worksheets
Presentation materials (flipchart paper, markers)
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Correct Lagrangian setup and partial derivatives (25 points), accurate solution of constraint system with proper mathematical notation (35 points), economic interpretation of results and shadow prices (20 points), presentation clarity and business recommendations (20 points). Teams must show all mathematical work and justify constraint binding decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template showing Lagrangian structure, offer step-by-step partial derivative examples, and create constraint visualization aids. For advanced learners: Add inequality constraints requiring KKT conditions, introduce stochastic elements to profit function, or extend to three-product optimization with additional market share constraints.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Scenarios: Business Application
description: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization techniques to solve authentic business problems involving resource allocation, profit maximization, and production planning. They will work through complex scenarios requiring multiple variables and constraints to determine optimal solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methodology to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing real-world business scenarios with multiple variables and constraints
Students will demonstrate the application of partial derivatives and gradient analysis through systematic problem-solving processes involving production, pricing, and resource allocation decisions
instructions:
Begin by distributing three business scenario cards (15 minutes setup). Each scenario involves optimizing a function with 2-3 variables subject to 1-2 constraints: Scenario A - Manufacturing company maximizing profit given material and labor constraints; Scenario B - Delivery service minimizing fuel costs with capacity and time restrictions; Scenario C - Restaurant chain optimizing menu pricing with ingredient cost and demand constraints. 

Form groups of 3-4 students and assign each group one scenario (5 minutes). Students spend 20 minutes reading scenarios and identifying the objective function, constraint equations, and variables. Each group must write these components clearly on their worksheet.

Next, students apply the Lagrange multiplier method (45 minutes). They set up the Lagrangian function L(x,y,λ) = f(x,y) + λ[g(x,y) - c], compute partial derivatives ∂L/∂x, ∂L/∂y, and ∂L/∂λ, then solve the resulting system of equations. Circulate to ensure proper setup and calculation techniques.

Groups then verify their solutions by checking second-order conditions using the bordered Hessian matrix (25 minutes). They must confirm whether their critical point represents a maximum, minimum, or saddle point given the constraint.

Finally, each group presents their solution (15 minutes total - 5 minutes per group), explaining their mathematical process and interpreting results in business context. They must state the optimal values for all variables and explain what this means practically for the business scenario.

Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students compare approaches across different scenarios and identify common challenges in applying optimization techniques.
materials_needed: Three laminated business scenario cards with specific numerical data
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Optimization worksheet templates with guided solution steps
Whiteboard markers and poster paper for group presentations
Access to computer algebra system (Mathematica, Wolfram Alpha, or graphing calculator software)
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct identification of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier methodology including accurate partial derivative calculations (35%), (3) Verification of solution using second-order conditions (25%), (4) Clear interpretation of mathematical results in business context during presentation (15%). Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas, with particular emphasis on showing complete mathematical work and logical problem-solving progression.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated partial derivative templates and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier checklist. Offer simplified scenarios with integer solutions. Pair with stronger mathematical students. For advanced learners: Add inequality constraints requiring Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, introduce scenarios with 3+ variables, or challenge them to solve using alternative methods (substitution, graphical analysis) to compare efficiency and accuracy of different approaches.
