title: Critical Analysis of Database Query Optimization in E-commerce Transaction Systems
description: Students will analyze the performance bottlenecks and optimization strategies in a real-world e-commerce database system by examining query execution plans, identifying inefficiencies, and evaluating multiple optimization approaches. They will dissect complex SQL queries handling customer transactions, inventory management, and reporting to determine root causes of performance issues and assess the trade-offs between different optimization techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex SQL query execution plans by identifying performance bottlenecks, examining index usage patterns, and determining resource consumption metrics in a simulated e-commerce environment
Students will evaluate competing database optimization strategies through comparative analysis of query rewriting techniques, indexing approaches, and architectural decisions
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the 'ShopFast' database schema containing 8 tables (customers, orders, order_items, products, categories, inventory, payments, reviews) and a dataset of 500K+ records. Distribute the performance analysis toolkit including PostgreSQL with pg_stat_statements enabled, pgAdmin, and the query profiling dashboard. In the first 45 minutes, teams examine five pre-written problematic queries: a complex customer lifetime value calculation, a real-time inventory check across multiple warehouses, a monthly sales report with multiple joins, a recommendation engine query, and a fraud detection algorithm. Students must run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on each query, document execution times, identify table scan operations, and map out join strategies. During minutes 45-90, teams analyze the execution plans by categorizing bottlenecks (I/O bound, CPU bound, memory limitations), identifying missing or unused indexes, and examining lock contention patterns. They must complete a detailed bottleneck analysis matrix scoring each issue by impact and frequency. In the final 60 minutes, teams evaluate four different optimization approaches for their assigned primary query: index optimization, query rewriting, partitioning, and caching strategies. They implement each approach, measure performance improvements, and analyze trade-offs including storage overhead, maintenance complexity, and consistency implications. Teams document their findings in a technical analysis report comparing before/after metrics, explaining their reasoning for recommending specific optimizations, and identifying potential negative consequences of each approach.
materials_needed: PostgreSQL database server with ShopFast schema and 500K+ sample records
pgAdmin or similar database management interface
Performance monitoring tools (pg_stat_statements, query profiling dashboard)
Technical analysis report template with bottleneck matrix
Five pre-written problematic SQL queries with baseline performance metrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Query execution plan analysis accuracy (25 points - correctly identifies all major bottlenecks, accurately interprets execution statistics), Bottleneck categorization and prioritization (20 points - systematically classifies issues and ranks by business impact), Optimization strategy evaluation (30 points - thoroughly compares multiple approaches with quantitative evidence), Technical reasoning quality (15 points - demonstrates deep understanding of database internals and trade-offs), Professional documentation (10 points - clear, structured analysis report with supporting data). Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery, with particular emphasis on providing evidence-based recommendations rather than generic solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided worksheet breaking down execution plan reading into smaller steps, offer a glossary of database performance terms, and include sample annotations on one execution plan. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger database students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze query performance across different database engines (PostgreSQL vs MySQL vs MongoDB), investigate advanced optimization techniques like materialized views or query result caching, or extend the analysis to include concurrent user load testing and deadlock detection.

title: Design Your Dream City: Linear Systems Budget Planning Challenge
description: Students will create a comprehensive city development plan by designing and solving original linear systems that represent real-world budget constraints. They must balance competing municipal needs while staying within financial limits, then present their mathematical model and justify their resource allocation decisions.
estimated_duration: 180 minutes (3 hours) - can be split across multiple class periods
learning_objectives: Students will construct original systems of linear equations by analyzing realistic municipal budget scenarios with multiple competing priorities
Students will synthesize mathematical solutions with practical constraints through creating defensible city development proposals that optimize resource allocation
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team a fictional city with specific characteristics (population 50,000-200,000, geographic features, economic base). Provide each team with a base budget of $10-50 million and a list of 8-10 municipal needs (parks, schools, roads, emergency services, utilities, housing, etc.) with associated cost ranges. In the first 30 minutes, teams research and establish specific costs per unit for their chosen city improvements, creating at least 4 variables representing different project types. Next, teams spend 45 minutes developing their constraint equations: they must create one equation for their total budget limit, one for minimum safety requirements (police + fire ≥ 15% of budget), one for infrastructure balance (roads + utilities = 25-35% of budget), and one additional constraint of their choice based on their city's unique needs. During the following 60 minutes, teams solve their system using substitution, elimination, or matrix methods, then verify their solution makes practical sense by checking all constraints. Teams must document their mathematical work clearly and create a visual presentation showing their city layout with budget allocations. In the final 45 minutes, each team presents their 5-minute city proposal, explaining their mathematical model, solution process, and justifying why their resource allocation best serves their city's needs. Other teams ask questions and provide feedback using provided evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: City profile cards with population, geography, and economic data
Municipal services cost reference sheets with realistic price ranges
Graphing calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Large poster paper or digital presentation tools
Colored markers or digital design tools for city layouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy - correct system setup and solution process (25 points), (2) Constraint creativity and realism - thoughtful additional constraints beyond minimum requirements (20 points), (3) Solution justification - clear explanation of why their allocation optimizes city needs (25 points), (4) Presentation quality - clear communication of mathematical reasoning and practical implications (20 points), (5) Peer feedback quality - constructive questions and suggestions during other presentations (10 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide templates showing sample constraint equation formats and offer simplified city profiles with fewer variables (3 instead of 4). Create calculation checkpoints where teacher verifies system setup before students proceed to solving. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include inequality constraints, consider multi-year budget planning with growth projections, or incorporate optimization techniques to maximize specific city outcomes (population growth, sustainability scores, etc.).

title: Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time complexity classifications (Big O notation) for 25 fundamental algorithms across sorting, searching, graph traversal, and dynamic programming categories. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge essential for algorithm analysis and technical interviews.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity notation for 25 standard algorithms including best, average, and worst-case scenarios by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify and state the space complexity classifications for fundamental data structure operations through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-printed algorithm reference cards containing 25 algorithms: Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Radix Sort, Linear Search, Binary Search, Depth-First Search, Breadth-First Search, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, Knapsack Problem, Fibonacci Sequence, Tower of Hanoi, and 11 additional core algorithms. Students have 15 minutes to study the cards, focusing purely on memorizing the time complexity notations (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(n³), O(2ⁿ), O(n!)). Next, collect all reference materials and begin Round 1: instructor calls out algorithm names randomly while students write down the time complexity on their answer sheets (10 minutes, 25 questions). Allow 3 minutes for self-checking against the answer key. Round 2 reverses the process - instructor states a time complexity (e.g., 'O(n log n)') and students list all algorithms matching that complexity (8 minutes). Round 3 involves rapid-fire oral responses where individual students must immediately state the time complexity when an algorithm is called (12 minutes total, 2-3 algorithms per student). Conclude with a cumulative written assessment where students complete a comprehensive matching exercise pairing 25 algorithms with their corresponding time complexities within 10 minutes. Record accuracy scores for each round and provide immediate feedback on commonly missed algorithms.
materials_needed: Pre-printed algorithm reference cards (one set per student)
Answer sheets with numbered lines 1-25
Master answer key for instructor
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard for tracking scores
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final cumulative matching assessment to demonstrate successful recall. Track individual performance across all three rounds using a scoring rubric: Round 1 (40% weight), Round 2 (30% weight), Round 3 (30% weight). Award partial credit for algorithms where students correctly identify the dominant term but miss coefficient details.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices (e.g., 'Bubble sort BUBBLES slowly - O(n²)') and allow color-coded reference cards grouping algorithms by complexity class. Advanced learners should additionally memorize space complexities and be challenged to recall best/average/worst case distinctions for algorithms like Quick Sort where performance varies.

title: Distinguishing Bias Sources in Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Evaluation
description: Students will analyze a complex, real-world machine learning deployment scenario to identify and categorize multiple types of bias occurring at different stages of the ML pipeline. They will demonstrate understanding by mapping specific bias manifestations to their underlying causes and explaining the interconnected nature of algorithmic, data, and human biases in production systems.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between algorithmic bias, selection bias, confirmation bias, and feedback loops by analyzing their manifestations in a multi-stage ML pipeline deployment case study
Students will explain the causal relationships between different bias types through systematic examination of data collection, model training, and deployment phases
instructions: Begin by providing students with a detailed case study of a hiring algorithm deployed by a major tech company, including: original training data demographics, model architecture details, deployment metrics over 18 months, and stakeholder feedback reports (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team member a specific pipeline stage: data collection, preprocessing/feature engineering, model training/validation, and deployment/monitoring. Each student spends 20 minutes independently analyzing their assigned stage, identifying potential bias sources using the provided bias taxonomy reference sheet containing 12 specific bias types with technical definitions. Students then reconvene in teams for 25 minutes to map their findings onto a shared digital bias interaction diagram, using different colors to represent bias types and arrows to show causal relationships. Teams must document at least 8 specific bias instances across all pipeline stages, explaining how biases in earlier stages amplify or interact with later-stage biases. During the final 15 minutes, each team presents their bias interaction diagram to another team, defending their causal relationship mappings and receiving feedback on overlooked connections. Teams conclude by submitting their annotated diagrams with written explanations for each identified bias-to-bias relationship.
materials_needed: Detailed hiring algorithm case study packet (8-10 pages with data tables, model specifications, and outcome metrics)
Bias taxonomy reference sheet with 12 technical bias definitions and examples
Digital diagramming tool access (Miro, Lucidchart, or similar collaborative platform)
Bias interaction diagram template with pipeline stages pre-mapped
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bias identification (minimum 6 of 8 biases correctly identified and categorized), (2) Quality of causal relationship explanations (clear technical reasoning for at least 5 bias interactions), (3) Pipeline-stage integration (evidence of understanding how biases compound across stages), and (4) Technical vocabulary usage (proper application of bias terminology in context). Award full points only when students demonstrate understanding of feedback loops and provide specific, technically sound explanations for bias amplification mechanisms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed bias checklist for each pipeline stage and offer guiding questions like 'How might demographic underrepresentation in training data affect feature importance rankings?' For advanced learners, challenge them to propose specific bias mitigation strategies for each identified bias type and estimate the potential impact of their interventions using quantitative reasoning. Provide additional complexity by introducing edge cases where bias mitigation in one stage might exacerbate bias in another stage.

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis in Web Authentication Systems
description: Students analyze actual code snippets from login systems to identify security vulnerabilities, categorize threat types, and evaluate the potential impact of each weakness. They will examine authentication flows and determine how multiple vulnerabilities compound to create system-wide security risks.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze authentication code samples by identifying specific security vulnerabilities and categorizing them according to OWASP Top 10 classifications
Students will evaluate the severity and interdependencies of multiple security flaws through systematic threat modeling techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided code packet containing 5 different authentication implementations (PHP login script, Node.js JWT handler, Python Flask session manager, Java Spring Security config, and C# ASP.NET authentication). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team to start with a different code sample, rotating every 15 minutes. Students first spend 10 minutes individually reading their assigned code to understand the authentication flow, then 5 minutes discussing findings with teammates. For each code sample, teams must: (1) Create a flowchart mapping the authentication process, (2) Identify and highlight specific vulnerable code lines using colored markers, (3) Classify each vulnerability using OWASP Top 10 categories provided on reference sheets, (4) Rate severity as High/Medium/Low based on potential impact, and (5) Document how vulnerabilities could be chained together for compound attacks. After analyzing all samples, teams spend 20 minutes creating a comparison matrix showing which vulnerability types appear across multiple implementations. Finally, each team presents their findings for one code sample (8 minutes presentation, 2 minutes Q&A), explaining the most critical vulnerability found, demonstrating how it could be exploited, and proposing specific remediation code changes. Display all team matrices simultaneously for cross-comparison during presentations.
materials_needed: Code packet with 5 authentication implementations (printed and digital copies)
OWASP Top 10 reference sheets
Colored highlighters (4 colors per team)
Flowchart template handouts
Vulnerability analysis worksheets
Laptops with code editors for testing fixes
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of vulnerability identification (25% - must find at least 3 real vulnerabilities per code sample), (2) Correct OWASP classification and severity rating (25% - 80%+ accuracy required), (3) Quality of attack chain analysis (25% - demonstrates understanding of how vulnerabilities compound), (4) Presentation clarity and proposed solutions (25% - includes working code fixes). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vulnerability hint cards showing common patterns like SQL injection syntax or weak password hashing. Pair them with stronger students during rotation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research CVE databases for real-world examples of identified vulnerabilities, or implement actual exploits in a sandboxed environment. Consider adding bonus points for identifying subtle logic flaws beyond obvious coding errors.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Production Healthcare Settings
description: Students will critically assess the real-world deployment of a diabetes prediction model by analyzing multiple performance metrics, identifying potential biases, and making evidence-based recommendations for model improvement or replacement. They will evaluate both technical performance and ethical implications of the model's decisions in clinical practice.
estimated_duration: 220 minutes (approximately 3.5 hours across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning models by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, and fairness metrics across demographic subgroups in healthcare contexts
Students will critique model deployment decisions through systematic assessment of bias, interpretability, and clinical impact using established ML evaluation frameworks
instructions:
Begin by distributing the case study materials including: production model performance data from a 6-month deployment of a diabetes risk prediction model, demographic breakdowns of patient populations, and clinical outcome reports. Students work in teams of 3-4. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze provided performance metrics including overall accuracy (87%), precision/recall by demographic groups, AUROC scores, and calibration plots. Students must calculate and interpret fairness metrics (equalized odds, demographic parity) across age, gender, and ethnicity subgroups using provided spreadsheet templates.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Teams evaluate the model's clinical impact by examining false positive/negative rates and their consequences. They review provided clinical scenarios where the model's predictions led to different treatment decisions and assess whether these align with medical best practices.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Students critically assess model interpretability by examining SHAP value outputs and feature importance rankings. They evaluate whether the model's decision-making process is sufficiently transparent for clinical use and identify potentially problematic feature dependencies.

Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams prepare written recommendations addressing: 1) Should this model continue in production? 2) What specific improvements are needed? 3) What additional evaluation metrics should be implemented? 4) How should model monitoring be enhanced?

Step 5 (40 minutes): Teams present 8-minute recommendations followed by 2-minute peer questioning sessions. Other teams use provided evaluation rubrics to assess the thoroughness and validity of recommendations.
materials_needed: Diabetes prediction model performance dataset (CSV format with 6 months of production data)
Clinical outcome reports documenting patient treatments and results
Demographic breakdown spreadsheets with pre-calculated basic metrics
SHAP value visualization outputs and feature importance charts
Fairness metrics calculation templates in Excel/Google Sheets
Clinical decision scenario case studies (PDF document)
Peer evaluation rubrics for final presentations
assessment_method: Students submit a 4-page technical report with sections on: quantitative performance analysis (25%), bias and fairness evaluation (25%), clinical impact assessment (25%), and actionable recommendations (25%). Reports are evaluated using a detailed rubric focusing on depth of analysis, use of appropriate metrics, identification of key issues, and feasibility of recommendations. Peer evaluations of presentations contribute 15% to final score. Success requires demonstrating ability to synthesize multiple evaluation criteria and make nuanced judgments about complex trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided worksheets breaking down fairness metric calculations step-by-step, offer one-on-one sessions to review confusion matrix interpretation, and supply sentence starters for recommendation writing. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research and apply additional fairness metrics not covered in class, evaluate the model against regulatory requirements (FDA guidelines), or design A/B testing protocols for model comparison. Consider providing optional advanced datasets with more complex demographic intersectionalities.

title: Computer Hardware Component Identification and Labeling Activity
description: Students will identify and correctly label the essential components of a desktop computer system by examining physical hardware pieces and matching them to their proper names and functions. This foundational activity builds recognition skills for basic computer architecture vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Students will identify at least 8 essential computer hardware components by examining physical specimens and digital images
Students will recall the correct names and primary functions of CPU, RAM, motherboard, hard drive, power supply, graphics card, optical drive, and cooling fan through hands-on sorting activities
instructions: Begin by arranging students in pairs and distributing one hardware identification worksheet and one set of 10 unlabeled computer components (or high-quality printed photos if physical components unavailable) to each pair. Start with a 5-minute demonstration using a sample motherboard, pointing out and naming each visible component while students observe. Next, give pairs 15 minutes to examine their component set and attempt to match each piece to the corresponding blank spaces on their identification worksheet, which contains component outlines and brief function descriptions. Encourage students to handle components carefully and discuss observations with their partner. After initial matching, conduct a 10-minute guided review session where you hold up each component type and ask pairs to call out the correct name in unison. Provide immediate feedback and correct pronunciation. For the final 10 minutes, have students complete individual exit tickets where they must write the name of each component from memory while viewing unlabeled images. Collect worksheets and exit tickets to assess accuracy. Conclude by having 2-3 volunteer pairs share one interesting observation they made about component size, weight, or appearance that helped them remember the component's identity.
materials_needed: Hardware identification worksheets (one per student pair)
Sets of 10 computer components: CPU, RAM stick, motherboard section, hard drive, power supply, graphics card, optical drive, cooling fan, network card, sound card
Individual exit ticket sheets with unlabeled component images
Magnifying glasses (optional for small component details)
assessment_method: Grade worksheets using a 10-point checklist (1 point per correctly identified component). Success criteria: 80% accuracy (8/10 components correctly identified). Exit tickets provide individual accountability - students must achieve 7/10 correct identifications. Observe pair discussions for engagement and proper handling of components.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing component function hint cards and allowing them to work in groups of three instead of pairs. title: Interpreting Customer Segmentation Results from K-Means Clustering Analysis
description: Students will analyze pre-computed K-means clustering results on customer purchase data to understand what each cluster represents and explain the business implications of the segmentation patterns. They will interpret cluster characteristics by examining centroid values and create actionable business profiles for each customer segment.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret K-means clustering results by analyzing centroid values and cluster statistics to identify distinct customer behavior patterns
Students will explain the business meaning of customer segments through systematic comparison of cluster characteristics and demographic features
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (3-4 students) with a dataset containing 5 customer clusters from a retail company, including cluster centroids for variables: age, annual_income, spending_score, purchase_frequency, and avg_order_value. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the centroid table and identify the highest and lowest values for each variable across clusters, noting patterns in a comparison matrix. Step 2 (20 minutes): For each cluster, students calculate the relative position (high/medium/low) of each centroid value compared to the overall dataset mean, creating a profile summary. Step 3 (25 minutes): Students interpret what each cluster represents by writing 2-3 sentence descriptions of the customer type (e.g., 'high-income frequent buyers' or 'price-conscious occasional shoppers'). Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups create business-focused names for each segment and propose 2 specific marketing strategies per segment based on their characteristics. Step 5 (15 minutes): Students examine cluster sizes and discuss why certain segments might be larger/smaller, considering business implications. Step 6 (10 minutes): Each group presents one cluster interpretation to the class, explaining their reasoning using specific centroid values as evidence.
materials_needed: Customer clustering results dataset with 5 clusters and centroid values
Cluster comparison matrix template (Excel or printed worksheet)
Whiteboard markers and poster paper for group work
Calculator or Excel access for basic computations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of centroid interpretation - correctly identifies high/low values and patterns, (2) Quality of cluster descriptions - uses specific data points to justify customer type labels, (3) Business relevance - proposes realistic marketing strategies aligned with segment characteristics, (4) Evidence-based reasoning - supports conclusions with specific centroid values and statistical comparisons
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example for one cluster showing how to read centroids and translate to business meaning. Offer sentence starters like 'This cluster has high ___ and low ___, which suggests customers who ___.' For advanced learners: challenge them to identify potential overlap between clusters, suggest additional variables that might improve segmentation, or calculate within-cluster variation to assess segment quality.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Trigonometry
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus, trigonometry, and optimization techniques to design an optimal solar panel array layout for a specific geographic location and energy requirement. They will calculate maximum energy output while considering real-world constraints including shadow interference, land area limitations, and seasonal sun angle variations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply optimization techniques using partial derivatives to determine the optimal tilt angle and spacing for solar panels by analyzing trigonometric functions representing sun position throughout the year
Students will implement integration methods to calculate total energy output through systematic application of area calculations and shadow analysis formulas
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute location packets containing latitude coordinates, monthly solar irradiance data, and land constraints (rectangular plot 100m x 150m). Each team receives a different city (Phoenix, Seattle, Miami, Denver). Students set up coordinate systems with panels facing south, defining variables: θ (tilt angle), d (panel spacing), h (panel height 2m), w (panel width 1.65m). **Phase 2 (30 minutes):** Teams apply trigonometric relationships to model shadow length S = h × cot(α), where α is sun elevation angle calculated using α = arcsin(sin(φ)sin(δ) + cos(φ)cos(δ)cos(ω)) with φ=latitude, δ=declination angle, ω=hour angle. Students create shadow interference function determining when adjacent panels cast shadows. **Phase 3 (40 minutes):** Apply optimization by setting up energy function E(θ,d) = (Available_Area/Panel_Area) × Daily_Irradiance × cos(θ-α_optimal) × Shadow_Factor. Students calculate partial derivatives ∂E/∂θ and ∂E/∂d, set equal to zero, solve system of equations using Newton-Raphson method or graphing technology. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Teams integrate their optimal configuration over 12 months using ∫₀³⁶⁵ E(t)dt to calculate annual energy output. Compare results across different cities, analyzing how latitude affects optimal configurations. Present findings with justification of mathematical methods used.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators or computer access with mathematical software (Desmos, GeoGebra, or MATLAB)
Location data packets with latitude, solar irradiance charts, and land constraint specifications
Solar panel specification sheets (dimensions, efficiency ratings)
Grid paper and rulers for initial sketching
Sun angle calculation reference sheets with trigonometric formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical accuracy of optimization setup and derivative calculations (25%), (2) Correct application of trigonometric relationships for shadow and sun angle calculations (25%), (3) Proper implementation of integration for annual energy calculation (25%), (4) Clear presentation of results with mathematical justification and comparison analysis (25%). Students submit calculation worksheets, final optimal configuration diagrams, and 5-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated sun angle tables and shadow length templates, offer step-by-step derivative calculation guides, allow use of numerical optimization tools instead of analytical solutions. For advanced learners: Add complications such as non-rectangular land parcels, multiple panel types with different efficiencies, economic cost-benefit analysis including installation costs, or 3D modeling with varying terrain elevation effects.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Trigonometry: Exercise 1
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus, trigonometry, and optimization techniques to determine the optimal positioning and spacing of solar panels in a real-world installation scenario. They will calculate maximum energy output while considering shadow effects, land constraints, and seasonal sun angle variations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply optimization calculus techniques to maximize solar energy output by determining optimal panel tilt angles and spacing ratios
Students will implement trigonometric functions and shadow calculations through systematic analysis of seasonal sun path variations
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the scenario packet containing: location coordinates (latitude 40.7°N), land dimensions (100m × 60m rectangular plot), panel specifications (2m × 1m panels, 300W capacity), and monthly sun angle data. Each team receives graphing calculators, protractors, and grid paper. **Phase 1 - Mathematical Modeling (45 minutes):** Teams first establish the coordinate system with the land plot origin at southwest corner. Students calculate the sun's elevation angle θ and azimuth angle φ for each month using provided solar position equations. They derive the shadow length formula: L = h/(tan θ) where h is panel height. Teams then develop the energy output function E(α,d) where α is panel tilt angle and d is row spacing distance. **Phase 2 - Constraint Analysis (30 minutes):** Students identify and mathematically express constraints: total panels ≤ (plot area)/(panel footprint including spacing), minimum spacing d ≥ shadow length during winter solstice, 0° ≤ α ≤ 90°. They create inequality expressions for these boundaries. **Phase 3 - Optimization Application (40 minutes):** Teams apply calculus optimization by taking partial derivatives ∂E/∂α = 0 and ∂E/∂d = 0, solving the system while checking constraint boundaries. They use the second derivative test to confirm maximum values. Students calculate total annual energy output and cost-per-watt efficiency. **Presentation Phase (20 minutes):** Each team presents their optimal configuration with mathematical justification, comparing results and explaining variations in approaches.
materials_needed: Solar installation scenario packets with location-specific sun angle data tables
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus CE or equivalent with solar position calculation programs loaded)
Large grid paper (11x17 inches) and engineering rulers
Digital protractors and measuring tools
Solar panel specification sheets with efficiency curves
Laptop/tablet access to Desmos Graphing Calculator or GeoGebra 3D
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical setup and constraint identification (25 points), correct application of optimization techniques with partial derivatives (30 points), accurate trigonometric calculations for shadow analysis (20 points), final solution reasonableness and units (15 points), clear presentation of methodology (10 points). Students must submit their optimization equations, constraint analysis worksheet, and final configuration diagram with calculated annual energy output.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated sun angle tables and shadow length templates, offer step-by-step derivative worksheets, pair with stronger mathematical partners. For advanced learners: Add variables such as panel degradation over time, variable electricity pricing throughout the day, or 3D terrain considerations with slope calculations. Include economic optimization by incorporating installation costs and payback period calculations.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Calculus and Trigonometry: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and trigonometric functions to determine optimal solar panel placement for maximum energy output. They will analyze real-world constraints including shadow effects, seasonal sun angles, and roof dimensions to create an implementation plan for a specific building.
learning_objectives: Students will apply optimization techniques using partial derivatives to maximize solar energy collection by determining optimal panel angles and spacing
Students will implement trigonometric functions and geometric constraints through creating a comprehensive solar array design with mathematical justification
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a specific building profile including roof dimensions, latitude coordinates, and local weather data (15 minutes setup). Students first calculate the sun's elevation angle using θ = arcsin(sin(δ)sin(φ) + cos(δ)cos(φ)cos(h)) where δ is solar declination, φ is latitude, and h is hour angle for their assigned location and season. Next, students determine the optimal tilt angle for panels using β = φ - δ and calculate row spacing to minimize shadows using d = L(cos(β) + sin(β)/tan(α)) where L is panel length, β is tilt angle, and α is sun elevation (45 minutes calculation phase). Teams then apply constrained optimization by setting up the objective function f(x,y) = N(x,y) × P × E where N is number of panels as a function of spacing and arrangement, P is power per panel, and E is efficiency factor. Students use Lagrange multipliers to maximize power output subject to roof area constraints g(x,y) = Ax + By ≤ C where A and B are area coefficients and C is total available space (60 minutes optimization phase). Finally, students create a scaled technical drawing showing panel placement, calculate expected annual energy output in kWh, and prepare a 5-minute presentation justifying their mathematical approach and final design decisions (40 minutes presentation prep). Throughout the activity, circulate to verify calculation accuracy and guide teams struggling with optimization setup.

Solar angle calculation worksheets with trigonometric formulas
Graphing calculators or computers with mathematical software
Grid paper for scaled technical drawings
Solar panel specification sheets with power ratings
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical accuracy of sun angle and optimization calculations (25%), (2) Correct application of constraints and Lagrange multipliers (25%), (3) Feasibility and justification of final design (25%), (4) Quality of technical drawing and energy output projections (25%). Students must demonstrate all calculations and provide written explanations for each optimization decision.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated solar declination values and simplified constraint templates. Offer advanced learners additional challenges such as incorporating battery storage optimization, seasonal efficiency variations, or economic payback period calculations using present value analysis.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive technical analysis of the 2017 Amazon S3 outage by examining system architecture diagrams, error logs, and cascading failure patterns. They will decompose the incident into root causes, identify architectural vulnerabilities, and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented recovery strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real-world incident data and identifying causal relationships between component failures
Students will evaluate architectural design decisions through systematic comparison of pre-incident and post-incident system configurations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with the complete Amazon S3 incident report, system architecture diagrams, timeline data, and sample error logs. Teams spend 45 minutes in Phase 1: Initial Analysis, where they map the failure timeline, identify all affected services, and document the propagation path of failures across system components. In Phase 2: Root Cause Decomposition (60 minutes), teams analyze the billing subsystem removal command that triggered the outage, examine why the restart process took longer than expected, and identify specific architectural dependencies that amplified the impact. They must create visual dependency maps showing service interconnections. Phase 3: Architectural Evaluation (45 minutes) requires teams to compare Amazon's pre-2017 S3 architecture with their post-incident improvements, analyzing partitioning strategies, circuit breaker implementations, and monitoring enhancements. Teams document their findings using structured analysis templates. In Phase 4: Presentation and Critique (30 minutes), each team presents their analysis to the class, focusing on their identified failure patterns and architectural insights. Other teams provide structured peer feedback using evaluation criteria sheets. Conclude with a 15-minute instructor-led discussion synthesizing key insights about distributed system resilience patterns and design principles.
materials_needed: Amazon S3 February 2017 incident report (official AWS post-mortem)
Pre-incident and post-incident S3 architecture diagrams
Sample S3 API error logs from the outage period
Structured analysis templates for documenting findings
Digital whiteboard or diagramming software (Lucidchart/Miro)
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentation assessment
assessment_method: Teams submit written analysis reports (40 points) containing: root cause identification with supporting evidence (10 points), architectural dependency mapping with visual diagrams (15 points), and comparative evaluation of pre/post-incident designs (15 points). Presentation quality and technical accuracy during class discussion (20 points). Peer evaluation of other teams' analyses using provided rubrics (10 points). Total: 70 points. Success requires demonstrating deep understanding of distributed system failure modes and ability to extract actionable architectural insights.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided analysis worksheets with specific questions about each incident phase, offer one-on-one consultation during Phase 2 to help identify failure relationships, and allow extended time for visual diagram creation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research and compare this incident with other major distributed system failures (GitHub 2018, Cloudflare 2019), require them to propose alternative architectural solutions beyond AWS's implemented fixes, or have them create detailed technical presentations suitable for engineering teams.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Student Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same student survey dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key findings. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and scatter plots by applying established visualization criteria to student survey data
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison and written justification of their recommendations
instructions: Begin by distributing the Student Survey Dataset (containing 100 responses about study habits, GPA, and hours studied per week) and three pre-created visualizations of this data: Visualization A (horizontal bar chart showing average study hours by GPA range), Visualization B (pie chart showing distribution of study locations), and Visualization C (scatter plot of study hours vs. GPA with trend line). Provide students with the Visualization Evaluation Rubric containing four criteria: clarity (Is the message immediately clear?), accuracy (Does it correctly represent the data?), appropriateness (Is this the best chart type for this data?), and design quality (Are colors, labels, and formatting effective?). Have students work in pairs for 5 minutes to examine each visualization individually, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses. Next, pairs spend 15 minutes systematically rating each visualization on a 1-4 scale for each criterion, providing specific written evidence for their scores. Students then spend 10 minutes calculating total scores and ranking the visualizations from most to least effective. Each pair writes a 2-paragraph recommendation memo (10 minutes) identifying the best visualization and explaining their reasoning using specific examples from their evaluation. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where pairs share their top choice and one key insight from their evaluation process. The instructor facilitates by asking follow-up questions about conflicting rankings and having students defend their choices.
materials_needed: Student Survey Dataset (Excel file with 100 sample responses)
Three pre-made visualizations (printed handouts or digital files)
Visualization Evaluation Rubric (one per student)
Evaluation worksheets with rating scales
Computers/tablets for viewing digital visualizations (optional)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed rubric worksheets (40 points: 10 points per criterion across 4 categories), recommendation memo quality (40 points: 20 for evidence-based reasoning, 20 for clear communication), and participation in pair discussions and final sharing (20 points). Success criteria: Students score 80% or higher, demonstrate use of specific evidence from visualizations, and provide logical justification for their final ranking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation comments and model one criterion evaluation as a class before independent work. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-rated visualization or to identify additional evaluation criteria not included in the rubric. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support.

title: Design Your Dream House: Area and Perimeter Real-World Application Project
description: Students will create an original house floor plan using specific area and perimeter constraints, then develop a mathematical presentation explaining their design choices. This activity combines geometric concepts with real-world problem-solving and creative design thinking.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original floor plan by applying area and perimeter formulas to meet specific mathematical constraints
Students will create a mathematical justification report through calculating, analyzing, and defending their design choices using geometric principles
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with the scenario: They are junior architects designing a single-story house with a total living space of exactly 1,200 square feet and maximum perimeter of 160 feet due to lot restrictions. Divide class into teams of 2-3 students. Distribute grid paper (1 square = 1 square foot) and project requirements sheet. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams brainstorm room types needed (bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, etc.) and research typical room sizes online using provided tablets. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students sketch initial floor plan designs on grid paper, ensuring each room is properly labeled and dimensioned. They must include at least 5 different rooms with realistic proportions. Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams calculate total area by finding the area of each rectangular room and summing them. They verify the total equals 1,200 sq ft, adjusting room sizes as needed. Step 4 (15 minutes): Students determine the overall perimeter of their house design, ensuring it doesn't exceed 160 feet. Step 5 (30 minutes): Teams create a final clean version of their floor plan on fresh grid paper, adding architectural details like doors and windows. Step 6 (25 minutes): Students prepare a 3-minute presentation including their floor plan poster, area calculations worksheet showing work for each room, perimeter calculation with labeled measurements, and written justification explaining why their design is both mathematically accurate and practically functional.
materials_needed: Grid paper (¼ inch squares, 4 sheets per student)
Rulers and colored pencils/markers
Tablets or computers for room size research
Project requirements handout with constraints
Calculators
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - all area and perimeter calculations correct with work shown; Design Creativity (25%) - original, realistic floor plan with appropriate room proportions; Problem-Solving (25%) - meets all constraints and shows evidence of design iteration; Communication (25%) - clear presentation with mathematical justification. Students must score 3/4 or higher in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn room templates with areas labeled, offer calculation worksheets with area/perimeter formulas visible, pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Add constraints like maximum width/length ratios, include outdoor spaces in calculations, challenge them to optimize for minimum perimeter given the area constraint, or explore irregular shaped rooms using composite area formulas.

title: Deconstructing Model Performance: Understanding Cross-Validation Bias in Temporal Data Scenarios
description: Students will analyze pre-built machine learning models trained on time-series financial data to identify how different cross-validation strategies introduce bias and affect model generalizability. Through systematic comparison of validation approaches, students will demonstrate understanding of temporal data leakage and its impact on model evaluation metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate cross-validation strategies for temporal data by analyzing model performance metrics across different validation schemes
Students will interpret the relationship between data leakage and inflated performance metrics through hands-on examination of financial prediction models
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided Jupyter notebook containing three identical Random Forest models trained on S&P 500 stock price data (2010-2023) using different validation approaches: standard k-fold, time-series split, and stratified k-fold. Form teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Each team receives the same dataset with features including technical indicators, volume metrics, and lagged returns. Students first execute all three model training cells and record the reported accuracy, precision, and recall metrics in the provided comparison table (20 minutes). Next, teams examine the validation splitting visualizations showing how training/test sets are divided temporally, identifying which approach allows future information to leak into past predictions (25 minutes). Students then analyze the feature importance plots and residual distributions for each model, noting discrepancies in which features appear most predictive (30 minutes). Teams calculate the actual forward-looking performance by applying each model to unseen 2024 data provided separately, comparing these results to the reported cross-validation scores (25 minutes). Finally, each team prepares a 5-minute presentation explaining which validation approach produced the most realistic performance estimates and why temporal data requires specialized handling (25 minutes presentation prep, 20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-configured models and S&P 500 dataset (2010-2024)
Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Model performance comparison worksheet (PDF template)
Access to projector/screen for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of problematic validation approach with specific evidence, (2) Correct explanation of temporal data leakage mechanisms, (3) Proper interpretation of performance metric differences between validation methods, (4) Clear articulation of why time-series split produced most realistic results. Award full credit when teams demonstrate understanding that k-fold cross-validation inappropriately uses future data to predict past events.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional visualization showing exact dates in training/test splits and highlight specific examples where future stock prices inform past predictions. Advanced learners can explore additional validation techniques like purged cross-validation or blocked time-series splits, or investigate how different asset classes (bonds, commodities) might require modified approaches to temporal validation.

title: Algorithm Performance Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Decomposition
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their time complexity, space complexity, and behavior under different input conditions. They will decompose each algorithm's structure to identify computational bottlenecks and predict performance patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of sorting algorithms by tracing execution patterns and identifying nested operations
Students will differentiate between best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios through systematic comparison of algorithmic behavior
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in their chosen programming language. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Students trace through each algorithm using a standardized dataset of 8 elements [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90, 88]. They must document step-by-step execution, counting comparisons and swaps for each algorithm. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups analyze the structure of each algorithm by identifying loops, recursive calls, and memory allocation patterns. They complete a provided analysis worksheet categorizing operations as constant, linear, or logarithmic time. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Students test algorithms with three different input scenarios: already sorted array, reverse sorted array, and random array. They record actual execution times and operation counts. Phase 4 (25 minutes): Groups create a comparative analysis chart showing Big O notation for each algorithm's best, average, and worst cases, supported by evidence from their traces and tests. They must explain why certain input conditions trigger worst-case behavior. Phase 5 (15 minutes): Each group presents one key finding about algorithmic trade-offs between time and space complexity to the class.
materials_needed: Pre-written code files for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort
Algorithm analysis worksheet with complexity comparison tables
Computers with IDE/compiler installed
Timer/stopwatch application
Test datasets in three configurations (sorted, reverse, random)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate complexity identification with correct Big O notation, (2) Complete execution traces showing understanding of algorithm flow, (3) Correct categorization of best/average/worst cases with supporting evidence, (4) Clear explanation of trade-offs and performance patterns. Groups must achieve 3/4 points on each criterion for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed trace tables and highlight the connection between nested loops and quadratic complexity. Offer guiding questions like 'How many times does this inner loop execute?' For advanced learners: introduce analysis of hybrid algorithms like Timsort, or challenge them to predict memory usage patterns and cache performance implications.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Selection for Customer Churn Prediction: A Comparative Analysis Activity
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Logistic Regression) for predicting customer churn using a real telecommunications dataset. They will assess model performance, interpretability, and business viability to make a data-driven recommendation for production deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate multiple machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, feature importance, and computational efficiency within a business context
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive comparison of trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and implementation costs
instructions: **Phase 1 (30 mins):** Provide students with the Telco Customer Churn dataset and three pre-trained models with their performance reports. Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze provided confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and feature importance plots for each model. **Phase 2 (45 mins):** Teams create evaluation matrices comparing models across six dimensions: accuracy metrics (precision, recall, F1-score), computational efficiency (training time, prediction speed), interpretability (feature importance clarity, model explainability), implementation complexity (deployment requirements, maintenance needs), business impact (false positive/negative costs), and scalability (performance with larger datasets). **Phase 3 (30 mins):** Each team calculates weighted scores based on provided business priorities: customer retention (40%), operational efficiency (25%), regulatory compliance requiring explainability (20%), and cost constraints (15%). Teams must justify their weighting decisions using business case context. **Phase 4 (45 mins):** Teams prepare 8-minute presentations defending their model recommendation, addressing potential counterarguments, and proposing implementation strategies. **Phase 5 (30 mins):** Peer evaluation session where teams critique other recommendations using structured feedback forms, identifying strengths and weaknesses in evaluation methodologies and business reasoning.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (7,043 records) with preprocessing completed
Three trained model files (.pkl format) with hyperparameter documentation
Performance report spreadsheets containing all evaluation metrics
Business context document outlining company priorities and constraints
Evaluation matrix templates in Excel format
Jupyter notebooks with model loading and prediction code
Peer evaluation rubric forms
assessment_method: Students assessed on: (1) Evaluation Matrix Completion (25%) - comprehensive comparison across all six dimensions with quantitative analysis, (2) Recommendation Report (35%) - written justification including weighted scoring methodology, risk analysis, and implementation plan, (3) Presentation Quality (25%) - clear communication of findings with defense against challenges, (4) Peer Evaluation Participation (15%) - quality of critiques provided to other teams using structured rubric focusing on logical reasoning and evidence-based arguments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation framework templates with partially completed examples and guiding questions for each dimension. Offer mini-tutorials on interpreting ROC curves and confusion matrices. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional evaluation criteria like model fairness metrics, A/B testing considerations, or ensemble method possibilities. Encourage analysis of model uncertainty and confidence intervals in their recommendations.

title: Design a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Emergency Response Systems
description: Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical optimization model that minimizes emergency response times across a city network. They will integrate concepts from graph theory, linear programming, probability theory, and calculus to develop an original algorithmic solution for real-world emergency service deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original multi-variable optimization model by synthesizing graph theory, probability distributions, and linear programming constraints to solve emergency response allocation problems
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical framework through integration of calculus-based optimization, network analysis, and statistical modeling to minimize expected response times
instructions:
Begin with a 15-minute briefing presenting students with authentic city data: population density maps, historical emergency call frequencies, current station locations, and response time statistics. Divide into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives different city layouts (grid-based, radial, or organic street patterns). 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams formulate their optimization problem by defining decision variables (station locations, vehicle allocations), objective function (minimize weighted average response time), and constraints (budget limits, coverage requirements, vehicle capacity). Students must justify their mathematical choices using probability theory for demand modeling and graph theory for network representation.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Construct the complete mathematical model. Teams develop distance functions using Euclidean or Manhattan metrics, incorporate traffic flow using time-dependent weighting functions, and create probability distributions for emergency frequencies based on demographic data. They must derive the optimization equations analytically before implementing computationally.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Implement and solve their model using optimization software (MATLAB, Python with SciPy, or R). Teams run sensitivity analyses by varying budget constraints and service level requirements, documenting how solutions change.

Step 4 (30 minutes): Create a professional presentation including mathematical derivations, computational results, and policy recommendations. Each team presents their unique solution approach, defending their modeling assumptions and comparing results with other teams' approaches.
materials_needed: Real city demographic and geographic datasets (population density, street networks, current emergency service locations)
Computers with optimization software (MATLAB Optimization Toolbox, Python with SciPy/PuLP, or R with ROI package)
Graph paper and mathematical modeling templates
Calculators capable of statistical functions
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of model formulation (25 points), creativity and justification of modeling assumptions (20 points), computational implementation and accuracy (20 points), sensitivity analysis depth and interpretation (15 points), professional presentation quality and defense of methodology (20 points). Students must submit written mathematical derivations, documented code, and executive summary of findings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks with partially completed objective functions and constraint examples. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-station, single-constraint problems first. For advanced learners: Extend to multi-objective optimization including cost minimization and equity considerations, or incorporate dynamic programming for time-dependent routing. Encourage exploration of integer programming formulations or machine learning integration for demand prediction.

title: Programming Language Syntax Memory Match
description: Students will memorize and recall basic syntax elements from three popular programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) through a structured card-matching activity. This foundational exercise builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for coding.
learning_objectives: Students will identify common programming syntax elements (variables, loops, conditionals) by matching code snippets to their correct language
Students will recall basic programming terminology through verbal recitation and written identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made syntax cards to pairs of students (5 minutes setup). Each pair receives 30 cards: 10 cards each for Python, Java, and JavaScript, featuring basic syntax for variables, if-statements, and for-loops. Students first spend 10 minutes studying the cards individually, reading each syntax example aloud and noting the programming language. Next, one student places all cards face-down in a 6x5 grid while their partner looks away (3 minutes). The studying student then attempts to recall and match syntax pairs by flipping two cards at a time, stating the programming language and syntax type before flipping (15 minutes). Partners switch roles and repeat the process (15 minutes). During the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class recall session where you display syntax examples on the projector and students must quickly identify the programming language and syntax type by raising colored cards (red=Python, blue=Java, green=JavaScript). Record correct responses on the board. Conclude with students writing three syntax examples from memory for each language on their individual answer sheets (7 minutes). Circulate throughout all activities to provide immediate feedback and ensure students are verbalizing their responses clearly.
materials_needed: 90 pre-printed syntax cards (30 sets for pairs)
Colored identification cards (red, blue, green) for each student
Individual answer sheets with language sections
Projector or interactive whiteboard
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade individual answer sheets using a 3-point rubric: 3 points for correctly writing syntax examples in all three languages, 2 points for two languages correct, 1 point for one language correct. Observe and record participation during verbal recall activities. Success criteria: 80% of students achieve 2+ points on written assessment and demonstrate active participation in verbal exercises.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide reference sheets with syntax patterns and allow extended study time. Pair weaker students with stronger partners during card activities. For advanced learners, add additional languages (C++, Ruby) or include more complex syntax elements like functions and classes. Consider having advanced students create new cards for the class.

title: Optimizing Hospital Staffing Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world hospital staffing optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, set up objective functions, and use the graphical method to determine optimal nurse scheduling that minimizes costs while meeting patient care requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-constraint optimization problem by translating real-world staffing requirements into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex concepts to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic analysis of feasible regions and corner points
instructions: Begin by distributing the hospital scenario handout describing St. Mary's Hospital's need to schedule full-time (40 hrs/week, $32/hr) and part-time (20 hrs/week, $28/hr) nurses across three shifts. Present the constraints: minimum 180 total nurses needed, at least 60% must be full-time, part-time nurses cannot exceed 80, and total weekly payroll cannot exceed $230,400. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify decision variables (x = full-time nurses, y = part-time nurses) and write the objective function to minimize total cost: C = 1280x + 560y. Next, have pairs spend 20 minutes translating each constraint into mathematical inequalities: x + y ≥ 180, x ≥ 0.6(x + y), y ≤ 80, 1280x + 560y ≤ 230,400, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Provide graph paper and have students spend 25 minutes plotting each constraint line, shading feasible regions, and identifying the bounded feasible region. Students then locate corner points by solving systems of equations where constraint lines intersect: (108, 72), (120, 60), (180, 0), and (100, 80). For the final 20 minutes, students evaluate the objective function at each corner point, determine the minimum cost solution, and verify their answer satisfies all original constraints. Conclude with pairs presenting their optimal solution and cost justification to the class.
materials_needed: Hospital staffing scenario handout with detailed constraints
Graph paper (coordinate grid, 1/4 inch squares)
Graphing calculators or desmos.com access
Colored pencils for shading feasible regions
Linear programming formula reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and all constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphical representation with properly shaded feasible region (25%), (3) Precise identification of corner points through algebraic methods (25%), (4) Correct optimization solution with verification and practical interpretation (25%). Students must submit their graph, calculations, and a brief written explanation of their recommended staffing plan.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-drawn coordinate axes and constraint equation templates. Offer a checkpoint after constraint formulation before graphing begins. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how the solution changes if nurse wages increase by 10%, or extend to integer programming concepts since partial nurses aren't realistic. Consider providing graphing software tutorials for students unfamiliar with technology tools.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 GitLab Database Incident
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive forensic analysis of GitLab's 2017 database deletion incident, examining system architecture decisions, failure cascades, and recovery protocols. They will decompose the incident timeline, evaluate competing hypotheses for root causes, and assess the effectiveness of implemented safeguards.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real-world incident data and identifying causal relationships between architectural decisions and system vulnerabilities
Students will evaluate disaster recovery mechanisms through systematic comparison of backup strategies and their failure modes in high-availability database systems
instructions: Begin by providing students with GitLab's complete incident report, system architecture diagrams, and timeline data (15 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team a specific analysis focus: Team A examines backup system failures, Team B analyzes human factors and procedural breakdowns, Team C evaluates monitoring and alerting gaps, Team D assesses data recovery strategies. Each team spends 45 minutes creating a detailed failure tree analysis, mapping dependencies between system components and identifying critical failure points. Teams must categorize failures as technical, procedural, or design-related, providing evidence from the incident data. Next, conduct a 30-minute cross-examination phase where teams present their preliminary findings and challenge other teams' analyses with probing questions about causation versus correlation. Teams then spend 25 minutes refining their analysis based on peer feedback and creating visual fault diagrams showing failure propagation paths. Finally, each team presents a 10-minute formal analysis including: identified failure patterns, alternative architectural approaches that could have prevented the incident, quantitative risk assessment of their proposed solutions, and specific monitoring metrics that would have provided early warning. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion comparing findings across teams and synthesizing insights about distributed system resilience patterns.
materials_needed: GitLab 2017 incident postmortem report with full timeline
GitLab system architecture diagrams (database replication setup)
Digital whiteboarding tool (Miro, Lucidchart, or similar)
Failure tree analysis template
Access to GitLab's engineering blog posts about the incident
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical accuracy of failure analysis (25 points), depth of causal relationship identification (25 points), quality of alternative solution proposals with justified trade-offs (25 points), effectiveness of visual fault diagrams and evidence synthesis (15 points), peer questioning quality during cross-examination (10 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of at least 5 distinct failure modes and provide quantitative reasoning for proposed improvements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions about specific failure points and pre-structured failure tree templates. Offer additional context about database replication concepts if needed. For advanced learners, challenge them to model the incident using formal methods (Petri nets, state machines) or to design automated chaos engineering tests that would have detected these vulnerabilities proactively.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City Block Using Proportional Reasoning
description: Students will create an original scale model city block by designing buildings, calculating proportional dimensions, and constructing a 3D model while applying geometric principles. This hands-on project integrates measurement, ratio relationships, and spatial reasoning to solve real-world urban planning challenges.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city block layout by applying scale factors and proportional reasoning to create accurate building dimensions
Students will construct a physical 3D model through systematic measurement calculations and geometric shape composition
instructions: Begin with a 15-minute introduction where students examine aerial photos of actual city blocks and discuss architectural features. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives a 24×18 inch base board representing a 400×300 meter city block at 1:2000 scale. Students first sketch their city block design on graph paper, including at least 6 different buildings (residential, commercial, municipal). They must calculate actual building dimensions using the given scale factor, then determine model dimensions. For example, a 40-meter tall building becomes 2 cm in the model. Students create a data table recording: building name, actual dimensions (length, width, height), and model dimensions. Next, teams use cardboard and construction materials to build their structures, measuring carefully with rulers and ensuring proportional accuracy. Buildings must include geometric features like rectangular prisms, triangular roofs, or cylindrical elements. Students add details like roads (scaled width), parking lots, and green spaces. During construction (45 minutes), circulate to check calculations and measurements. Teams then present their city blocks (20 minutes total), explaining their design choices, demonstrating scale calculations for 2-3 buildings, and identifying geometric shapes used. Each presentation should last 3-4 minutes with peer questions. Conclude with a gallery walk where students calculate population density if each building housed specific numbers of people, applying their scale understanding to solve additional problems.
materials_needed: 24×18 inch cardboard base boards (one per team)
Colored cardboard sheets and construction paper
Rulers, protractors, and measuring tapes
Graph paper and pencils
Glue sticks, scissors, and tape
Aerial photos of city blocks for reference
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Mathematical accuracy of scale calculations and measurements (25%), (2) Creative design incorporating required building types and geometric shapes (25%), (3) Construction quality showing proportional relationships (25%), and (4) Clear presentation explaining mathematical reasoning and design decisions (25%). Students must submit their calculation data table and present their model to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-calculated examples for the first building and offering measurement templates. Pair them with stronger math partners for calculation verification. Challenge advanced learners by requiring additional constraints like budget limitations, zoning restrictions, or incorporating more complex geometric shapes like pyramids or hexagonal structures. Provide extension problems involving area calculations or population density optimization.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions and Headers Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific functions, protocols, and header field structures of all four TCP/IP protocol stack layers through systematic drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network protocol architecture that students must have readily accessible for advanced networking courses.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the specific protocols operating at each TCP/IP layer (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) by completing rapid-fire identification exercises
Students will memorize the exact header field names and byte positions for TCP, UDP, IPv4, and Ethernet headers through structured repetition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet containing all four layers with their protocols, functions, and header structures. Give students 15 minutes to study the materials silently. Next, conduct Round 1 (10 minutes): Display layer names one at a time using slides. Students have 30 seconds per layer to write down all protocols operating at that layer (Application: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, DHCP, etc.; Transport: TCP, UDP; Internet: IP, ICMP, ARP; Network Access: Ethernet, WiFi protocols). Collect responses and provide immediate feedback. For Round 2 (15 minutes): Show header diagrams with field names removed. Students must fill in exact field names in correct positions for TCP headers (Source Port, Destination Port, Sequence Number, Acknowledgment Number, Header Length, Reserved, Flags, Window Size, Checksum, Urgent Pointer), UDP headers (Source Port, Destination Port, Length, Checksum), IPv4 headers (Version, IHL, Type of Service, Total Length, Identification, Flags, Fragment Offset, TTL, Protocol, Header Checksum, Source Address, Destination Address), and Ethernet frames (Preamble, Destination MAC, Source MAC, Type/Length, Data, FCS). Time limit: 3 minutes per header type. Round 3 (10 minutes): Rapid-fire verbal quiz where instructor calls out a protocol name and students must immediately state which layer it operates at and name two other protocols from the same layer.
