title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentages to Personal Finance Decisions
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional character. They will calculate discounts, tips, taxes, and savings rates while making informed financial decisions within given constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, taxes, tips, and savings amounts within real-world budget scenarios
Students will implement multi-step percentage problems through systematic budget allocation decisions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the character profile cards and budget worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Each profile contains a monthly income, family size, and special circumstances. Explain that students must create a complete monthly budget using percentage-based calculations for all major categories. 

First, students calculate their after-tax income by applying the given tax percentage (20% for incomes over $3000, 15% for lower incomes). Next, they apply the 50/30/20 budgeting rule: 50% for needs (rent, groceries, utilities), 30% for wants (entertainment, dining out), and 20% for savings and debt payment.

For the needs category, students research and apply local sales tax (8.5%) to grocery budgets and calculate utility costs as 12% of after-tax income. In the wants category, they must calculate restaurant tips at 18% and apply various discount percentages to entertainment purchases (movie tickets 15% off, gym membership 10% off first month).

Students then face three budget challenge scenarios: an unexpected car repair costing 5% of monthly income, a 25% off sale on needed clothing, and an opportunity to increase savings by 3% if they reduce dining out by 20%. They must recalculate their entire budget for each scenario.

Provide calculators and encourage showing all work with clear percentage formulas. Circulate to check calculations and provide hints about decimal-to-percentage conversions. Students complete their final budget presentation on the provided template, showing original budget and all three scenario modifications. Allow time for 2-3 students to present their most challenging calculations to the class.
materials_needed: Character profile cards with income and family details (1 per student)
Budget worksheet templates with percentage calculation spaces
Basic calculators
Local tax rate reference sheet
Scenario challenge cards
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with clear work shown, realistic budget allocations; (3) Most calculations correct with minor errors, generally appropriate allocations; (2) Some calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of percentage application; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Check for proper percentage-to-decimal conversion, accurate multi-step calculations, and logical budget adjustments in challenge scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a percentage calculation reference card with common conversions (10%=0.1, 20%=0.2, etc.) and encourage using the calculator's percentage button. Offer partially completed examples for the first few calculations. For advanced learners, add compound percentage challenges such as calculating interest on savings (1.5% monthly) or comparing percentage-based vs. flat-fee service options. Consider adding investment allocation percentages across different risk categories.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Decomposition
description: Students analyze three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) by examining their code implementations, identifying key operations, and determining their time complexity classifications. They will decompose each algorithm's structure to justify their Big O notation conclusions through systematic analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the computational complexity of sorting algorithms by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and fundamental operations to determine Big O classifications
Students will differentiate between algorithm efficiency patterns through systematic comparison of time complexity behaviors across best, average, and worst-case scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three code implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) to student pairs, ensuring each algorithm is printed on separate sheets with line numbers. Students spend 10 minutes individually reading through all three algorithms, annotating basic operations they identify. Next, pairs work together for 25 minutes using the provided analysis worksheet to systematically examine each algorithm: (1) Count and categorize fundamental operations (comparisons, swaps, recursive calls), (2) Identify loop structures and nesting patterns, (3) Trace through a small dataset example (array of 6 numbers) noting operation counts at each step. For the next 20 minutes, pairs complete the complexity analysis section by determining Big O for best/average/worst cases, showing mathematical reasoning for their conclusions. They must justify why certain operations dominate others and explain how input size affects performance. In the final 15 minutes, each pair presents one algorithm's analysis to another pair, defending their Big O conclusions and discussing scenarios where their assigned algorithm would be preferred. Instructor circulates throughout, prompting deeper analysis with questions like 'What happens when the array is already sorted?' and 'Why does the recursive depth matter here?' Conclude with pairs submitting their completed worksheets containing operation counts, Big O justifications, and scenario recommendations.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort with line numbers
Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with operation counting tables and Big O justification sections
Sample dataset cards (arrays of 6 integers) for tracing exercises
Stopwatches or timers for activity pacing
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all key operations and provides mathematically sound Big O justifications with clear explanations, (3) Identifies most operations with minor errors in complexity analysis, (2) Shows basic understanding but contains significant gaps in reasoning, (1) Incomplete analysis with major misconceptions. Also assess peer presentation quality and ability to defend conclusions during pair-sharing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed worksheet with operation counting started, offer a visual flowchart showing algorithm execution paths, and pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to consider space complexity analysis, analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or research average-case analysis mathematics for quicksort's randomized pivot selection.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Healthcare Disparities
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance and ethical implications of three different machine learning models designed to predict patient readmission rates across diverse demographic groups. They will assess model bias, fairness metrics, and recommend optimal deployment strategies while defending their conclusions with evidence-based arguments.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative performance of multiple ML models by analyzing confusion matrices, ROC curves, and fairness metrics across demographic subgroups
Students will critique model deployment recommendations through systematic bias assessment and ethical impact analysis
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Neural Network) and a healthcare dataset containing patient demographics, medical history, and readmission outcomes (15 minutes setup). Students first spend 45 minutes independently analyzing each model's performance using provided Python notebooks, calculating accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC for overall performance and demographic subgroups (age, race, gender, socioeconomic status). Next, teams collaborate for 60 minutes to evaluate fairness using demographic parity, equalized odds, and individual fairness metrics, identifying which populations each model may disadvantage. During the analysis phase (30 minutes), students must critically assess feature importance, examine prediction disparities across groups, and identify potential sources of algorithmic bias in training data or model architecture. Teams then prepare a 10-minute presentation (45 minutes preparation) where they must defend their choice of the 'best' model for deployment, considering both performance metrics and ethical implications. Each presentation must include: model comparison matrix, bias analysis summary, risk assessment for affected populations, and specific deployment recommendations with mitigation strategies. Conclude with a 30-minute structured debate where teams challenge each other's recommendations, requiring students to defend their evaluation criteria and respond to critiques about overlooked biases or alternative interpretations of the data.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn, aif360 libraries installed
Healthcare readmission dataset (MIMIC-III or synthetic equivalent) with 10,000+ patient records
Three pre-trained ML models saved as pickle files
Evaluation rubric handout with fairness metrics definitions
Presentation template with required analysis sections
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Technical accuracy of performance metrics calculation and interpretation (25%), (2) Depth of bias analysis and identification of affected populations (25%), (3) Quality of evidence used to support model selection and reasoning process (25%), (4) Ability to defend conclusions during Q&A and respond to peer critiques with valid counterarguments (25%). Students must achieve proficient level in all categories, demonstrating they can synthesize technical and ethical considerations to make defensible recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed examples of fairness metric calculations and bias identification templates. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify technical analysis before moving to evaluation phase. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by requiring cost-benefit analysis of false positives/negatives for different demographic groups, or challenge them to propose novel fairness metrics specific to healthcare contexts. Provide additional datasets for extended analysis.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Customer Purchase Datasets
description: Students will analyze real-world e-commerce customer purchase data to identify and explain different distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal) in key business metrics. They will create visual interpretations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of how distribution shapes inform business decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the characteristics of different statistical distributions by analyzing customer purchase amount, frequency, and demographic data from an e-commerce dataset
Students will explain the business implications of distribution patterns through written analysis connecting statistical properties to actionable business insights
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing three datasets: customer purchase amounts (right-skewed), customer ages (normal distribution), and time-between-purchases (bimodal). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Step 1 (20 minutes): Each pair generates histograms, box plots, and summary statistics for all three variables using provided code templates. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students complete a guided worksheet identifying distribution types, noting skewness direction, outliers, and central tendency measures for each variable. Step 3 (25 minutes): Pairs write detailed explanations for each distribution, describing why the business context creates these patterns (e.g., why purchase amounts are right-skewed, why customer ages are normally distributed). Step 4 (20 minutes): Students complete scenario-based questions where they predict how marketing strategies should differ based on each distribution pattern. Instructor circulates, asking probing questions like 'What does this outlier represent?' and 'How would seasonal trends affect this distribution?' Final step: pairs submit completed worksheets with visualizations and written interpretations via learning management system.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-loaded customer datasets (3 CSV files)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Distribution analysis worksheet (PDF with guided questions)
Access to course learning management system for submission
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of distribution types and statistical properties (25%), (2) Quality of visual interpretations and labeling (25%), (3) Depth of written explanations connecting distributions to business context (30%), (4) Logical reasoning in marketing strategy recommendations (20%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide distribution identification flowchart and sentence starters for written explanations. Offer pre-made code snippets for advanced statistical measures. For advanced learners: include additional datasets with multimodal distributions, challenge them to identify potential data collection biases, or ask them to propose hypothesis tests for comparing distributions between customer segments.

title: Optimization Crisis: Designing Cost-Effective Manufacturing Containers
description: Students apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem by determining optimal container dimensions that minimize material costs while meeting volume constraints. They will use Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization to find critical points and verify solutions using second derivative tests.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to optimize multivariable functions subject to equality constraints by solving a container design problem
Students will implement second derivative tests and constraint analysis to verify optimal solutions through systematic mathematical verification processes
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: A manufacturing company needs cylindrical containers with volume exactly 500 cubic inches, where the bottom costs $0.05 per square inch, sides cost $0.03 per square inch, and the top costs $0.02 per square inch. Divide students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes setup). Each team receives the problem handout with cost specifications and must determine optimal radius and height. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams formulate the optimization problem by defining variables (r = radius, h = height), writing the objective function C(r,h) = 0.05πr² + 0.03(2πrh) + 0.02πr², and identifying the constraint g(r,h) = πr²h - 500 = 0. Students must clearly write both functions before proceeding.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams apply the Lagrange multiplier method by computing ∇C = λ∇g, setting up the system of three equations: ∂C/∂r = λ∂g/∂r, ∂C/∂h = λ∂g/∂h, and g(r,h) = 0. Students solve this system algebraically to find critical points.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams verify their solution using the second derivative test for constrained optimization, computing the bordered Hessian matrix and checking the sign of its determinant. They must also verify the constraint is satisfied.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team calculates the minimum cost using their optimal dimensions and creates a visual representation showing their container with labeled dimensions. Teams present their solutions in 2-minute summaries, comparing results and methodologies used.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Wolfram Alpha access)
Problem handout with cost specifications and constraint requirements
Graph paper for sketching container designs
Whiteboard markers for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem setup and function formulation (25 points), correct application of Lagrange multipliers (35 points), proper verification using second derivative test (25 points), and final answer accuracy with units (15 points). Students must show complete algebraic work and achieve r ≈ 3.41 inches, h ≈ 13.64 inches, minimum cost ≈ $4.30 for full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide templates for setting up the Lagrange system and offer hints about substitution strategies. Encourage them to verify constraint satisfaction numerically first. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding a second constraint (surface area limit) or asking them to analyze how the solution changes with different cost ratios. Provide access to graphing tools to visualize the constraint surface and cost function.

title: Critical Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture
description: Students will dissect a provided enterprise web application's three-tier architecture to identify security vulnerabilities across presentation, business logic, and data layers. They will analyze attack vectors, evaluate risk severity using CVSS scoring, and determine the cascading effects of identified vulnerabilities on overall system security.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-tier web application architectures by systematically examining each layer's security implementation and identifying potential attack vectors
Students will evaluate vulnerability interdependencies through comprehensive risk assessment using industry-standard CVSS methodology and threat modeling techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided case study: a fictional e-commerce platform's architecture documentation including network diagrams, code snippets, database schemas, and deployment configurations (15 minutes setup). Organize students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team member a primary focus area: one student analyzes the presentation layer (client-side JavaScript, form validation, session management), another examines the business logic tier (API endpoints, authentication mechanisms, authorization controls), a third investigates the data layer (SQL injection points, encryption implementation, access controls), and the fourth member coordinates cross-layer vulnerability interactions. Students spend 45 minutes conducting individual layer analysis using the provided vulnerability checklist (covering OWASP Top 10, authentication flaws, injection attacks, broken access controls, and cryptographic failures). Each team member documents findings using the standardized vulnerability report template, including vulnerability type, location in code/architecture, potential impact, and CVSS base score calculation. Teams then reconvene for 30 minutes to synthesize findings, mapping how vulnerabilities in one layer could be exploited to compromise other layers. They create a comprehensive attack chain diagram showing potential exploitation paths from initial compromise to full system breach. Finally, teams present their analysis in 10-minute presentations, demonstrating their understanding of vulnerability relationships and system-wide security implications. The instructor facilitates peer feedback sessions where teams challenge each other's findings and suggest additional attack vectors.
materials_needed: Detailed case study packet with architecture diagrams, code samples, and configuration files
OWASP Top 10 vulnerability reference sheets
CVSS v3.1 scoring calculator worksheets
Vulnerability report templates with structured fields
Digital whiteboard or Miro boards for attack chain visualization
Presentation timer and evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: vulnerability identification accuracy (25 points), CVSS scoring precision (20 points), cross-layer impact analysis depth (25 points), attack chain logical flow (20 points), and presentation clarity (10 points). Students must identify minimum 8 distinct vulnerabilities across all three tiers, demonstrate understanding of at least 3 vulnerability interdependencies, and provide mathematically correct CVSS scores for all findings.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing vulnerability hunting checklists with specific line numbers to examine and guided questions for each architecture layer. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as container security analysis, CI/CD pipeline vulnerabilities, or advanced persistent threat scenarios. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger ones within teams and provide real-world CVE examples as reference points.

title: Design a Community Garden: Real-World Area and Perimeter Optimization
description: Students will create an original community garden layout by applying area and perimeter formulas to design garden plots that maximize growing space within given constraints. They will present their designs with mathematical justifications for their choices.
estimated_duration: 100 minutes (can be split across two 50-minute sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design an optimal garden layout by calculating and comparing areas and perimeters of different geometric shapes within specified constraints
Students will create mathematical presentations that justify their design choices through quantitative analysis and problem-solving reasoning
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: Students are landscape designers creating a community garden with a $500 fencing budget ($5 per linear foot, so 100 feet of fencing total). Step 1 (15 minutes): Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with graph paper, calculators, and the design requirements sheet. Explain they must create 4 different garden plots within a rectangular boundary, leaving pathways between plots. Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams brainstorm and sketch initial designs, calculating area and perimeter for each plot shape (rectangles, squares, circles, or combinations). They must show all mathematical work on separate calculation sheets. Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams refine their designs, ensuring total perimeter doesn't exceed 100 feet while maximizing total planting area. They must justify why their chosen shapes are optimal and calculate the cost-effectiveness (area per dollar spent). Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team creates a final presentation poster showing their garden layout, calculations, and written justification. Step 5 (25 minutes): Teams present their designs (3 minutes each), explaining their mathematical reasoning and answering questions from classmates about their optimization choices.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1/4 inch grid, 2 sheets per student)
Scientific calculators
Design requirements handout with constraints
Poster paper (1 per team)
Colored pencils or markers
Rulers and compasses
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations (25%), (2) Creative and practical design meeting all constraints (25%), (3) Clear written justification of optimization choices (25%), and (4) Quality of oral presentation and peer interaction (25%). Students must demonstrate correct formula usage and show all work to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn grid templates with suggested plot locations and area/perimeter formula reference sheets. Pair them with stronger math students. title: Advanced Data Structure Memory Palace: Memorizing Complex Algorithm Time Complexities
description: Students will memorize the exact time and space complexities for 25 advanced algorithms across trees, graphs, and dynamic programming using a systematic memory palace technique. This activity focuses on building instant recall of computational complexity facts that are essential for technical interviews and algorithm selection.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big-O time complexity for 25 advanced algorithms including AVL tree operations, graph traversals, and dynamic programming solutions within 3 seconds per query
Students will identify the space complexity of advanced data structures and their associated algorithms through structured memorization drills
instructions:
Begin by distributing the algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 25 algorithms organized in 5 categories: AVL/Red-Black Trees (5), Graph Algorithms (5), Dynamic Programming (5), Heap Operations (5), and Hash Table Variants (5). Each entry shows algorithm name, average/worst-case time complexity, and space complexity. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students create a physical memory palace using the classroom layout. Assign each of the 5 algorithm categories to specific locations (door, whiteboard, window, teacher's desk, back corner). Students must physically walk to each location and visualize placing the algorithm complexities there.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Implement the Major System mnemonic technique. Students convert Big-O notations to memorable images: O(1)=tea, O(log n)=lynx, O(n)=noah, O(n log n)=noah+lynx, O(n²)=onion, O(2ⁿ)=tunnel. For each algorithm, students create a vivid mental image combining the algorithm's purpose with its complexity image at the designated location.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Conduct three rounds of spaced repetition. Round 1: Students recite all 25 complexities while walking their memory palace route. Round 2: Random spot-checking using flashcards, 30 seconds per student. Round 3: Partner quizzing where students test each other on algorithm names to complexities and vice versa.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Speed assessment. Display algorithm names on screen for 3 seconds each. Students write both time and space complexity. Track accuracy and response time. Students must achieve 80% accuracy to demonstrate successful memorization.
materials_needed: Algorithm complexity reference sheet with 25 advanced algorithms
Major System conversion chart (numbers to consonant sounds)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Flashcards with algorithm names
Assessment sheets for recording complexities
Projector for displaying algorithm names during speed test
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final speed test where algorithm names are displayed for 3 seconds each. Grading rubric: 90-100% correct = A, 80-89% = B, 70-79% = C, below 70% requires remediation. Additionally, assess memory palace effectiveness through a follow-up quiz 24 hours later where students must maintain 75% accuracy to demonstrate retention.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce the algorithm set to 15 most common algorithms and extend memorization time to 25 minutes. Provide pre-made visual associations for Big-O notations. For advanced learners: Include best-case complexities and amortized analysis. Add 10 additional algorithms from advanced topics like suffix trees or network flow. Challenge them to create memory palaces for algorithm implementation details, not just complexities.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Trade-off Through Model Performance Decomposition Analysis
description: Students will analyze pre-trained machine learning models with varying complexity levels to understand how bias and variance components contribute to overall prediction error. They will decompose mean squared error into bias², variance, and irreducible error components using bootstrapped predictions on polynomial regression models of different degrees.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the mathematical relationship between bias, variance, and total error by analyzing decomposed MSE components across model complexity levels
Students will interpret bias-variance trade-off patterns through systematic comparison of bootstrapped prediction distributions from underfitted and overfitted models
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a synthetic dataset (n=200) generated from y = 0.5x³ - 2x² + x + noise, along with pre-coded Python scripts for bias-variance decomposition. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives identical datasets but different polynomial degree ranges (Team 1: degrees 1-5, Team 2: degrees 3-7, Team 3: degrees 5-9). 

Step 1 (20 min): Teams run the provided bootstrap script that trains 1000 models of each polynomial degree on random samples, generating prediction distributions for test points. Students examine the output arrays containing individual model predictions.

Step 2 (25 min): Using the decomposition formulas, teams calculate bias² (squared difference between average prediction and true function), variance (prediction variability across bootstrap samples), and noise components for each model degree. They create visualization plots showing these components versus model complexity.

Step 3 (30 min): Teams analyze their plots to identify the optimal complexity point where total error is minimized. They document specific observations about how bias decreases and variance increases with model complexity, noting the crossover point.

Step 4 (25 min): Conduct cross-team presentations where each team explains their findings. Teams must articulate why their optimal complexity differs and how their degree ranges influenced the trade-off patterns observed.

Step 5 (15 min): Facilitate whole-class discussion comparing results across different complexity ranges, emphasizing how the bias-variance trade-off manifests differently depending on the model space explored.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with NumPy, Scikit-learn, Matplotlib
Pre-generated synthetic polynomial dataset with known ground truth function
Bias-variance decomposition Python script template with bootstrap sampling
Plotting template for visualizing bias², variance, and total error curves
Handout with bias-variance decomposition mathematical formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of bias² values showing understanding that bias decreases with model complexity, (2) Accurate variance calculations demonstrating comprehension that variance increases with complexity, (3) Identification of optimal complexity point with mathematical justification, (4) Clear explanation of trade-off relationship during presentation including why their optimal point differs from other teams. Students submit plots with annotations explaining the mathematical relationship between components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated bias and variance values for one model degree as a reference example, and offer guided questions like 'What happens to the average prediction as we add polynomial terms?' For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them derive the bias-variance decomposition mathematically or apply the analysis to different algorithms (ridge regression, decision trees) to compare how regularization affects the trade-off.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentages and Basic Operations to Real-Life Scenarios
description: Students will create a monthly budget for a fictional teenager by applying percentage calculations, addition, subtraction, and proportion concepts to realistic income and expense scenarios. This hands-on activity connects mathematical operations to practical financial literacy skills.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine savings goals, tax deductions, and expense allocations within a monthly budget scenario
Students will solve multi-step problems involving addition, subtraction, and percentages through creating and balancing a realistic teenage budget
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Teen Budget Scenario' worksheet and calculators to each student (5 minutes). Present the scenario: Students are 16-year-old Alex who earns $400/month from a part-time job. They must plan expenses while saving 15% for a car. Start with guided practice (10 minutes): demonstrate calculating Alex's savings goal ($400 × 0.15 = $60) and available spending money ($400 - $60 = $340). Next, students work in pairs (20 minutes) to complete their budget worksheets. They must allocate remaining $340 across categories: transportation (20%), entertainment (25%), personal items (15%), food/snacks (30%), and miscellaneous (10%). Students calculate dollar amounts for each category, then add specific items within budget limits. For example, if entertainment budget is $85 ($340 × 0.25), they might list: movie tickets ($24), streaming service ($12), arcade visits ($30), leaving $19 remaining. Circulate to check calculations and provide hints. After completion, have pairs present one budget category to the class (10 minutes), explaining their percentage calculations and item choices. Conclude with reflection questions (5 minutes): 'Which percentage was hardest to calculate?' and 'How might this budget change if income increased to $500?' Collect worksheets showing all mathematical work for assessment.
materials_needed: Teen Budget Scenario worksheet (one per student)
Basic calculators (one per student)
Pencils and erasers
Whiteboard markers for demonstrations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct, budget balances exactly, clear mathematical work shown; (3) Minor calculation errors, budget within $5 of target, work mostly shown; (2) Some correct calculations, budget unbalanced but reasonable attempt; (1) Major errors or incomplete work. Also observe pair discussions for understanding of percentage concepts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide percentage calculation reference sheet (15% = 0.15) and encourage use of calculators for all operations. Pair weaker math students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: add complexity by including variable income ($350-$450 depending on hours worked) or introduce concepts like compound interest on savings portion.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance for Healthcare Diagnostic Prediction
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) trained on a healthcare dataset for diagnostic prediction. They will assess model performance using multiple evaluation metrics, identify potential biases, and make justified recommendations for clinical deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, cross-validation results, and statistical significance tests
Students will critique model reliability and ethical implications through bias analysis, fairness assessment, and clinical deployment risk evaluation
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed healthcare dataset (e.g., heart disease diagnosis with 14 features, 1000+ samples) and three pre-trained models with their training code and outputs. In pairs, students spend 30 minutes examining the dataset documentation, noting potential bias sources (demographic representation, feature selection, data collection methods). Next, students analyze model performance over 45 minutes using provided confusion matrices, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and cross-validation scores. They calculate additional metrics not provided (F1-score, specificity, NPV) and perform statistical significance tests between models. During the following 60 minutes, students conduct bias analysis by examining performance across demographic subgroups, identifying disparate impact, and evaluating feature importance for potential discriminatory patterns. They also assess clinical relevance by considering false positive/negative costs in medical contexts. Students then spend 45 minutes creating a comprehensive evaluation report with visualizations comparing all three models across performance, bias, and clinical applicability dimensions. Finally, in 30 minutes, each pair presents their findings to another pair, defending their recommendation for which model (if any) should be deployed in a clinical setting, addressing questions about their evaluation methodology and conclusions.
materials_needed: Pre-processed healthcare dataset (CSV format with documentation)
Three trained ML models with performance outputs (Python pickle files)
Jupyter notebook template with starter code for metrics calculation
Statistical testing reference guide
Clinical decision-making cost matrix template
assessment_method: Students submit a 4-page evaluation report scored on: (1) Comprehensive performance analysis using appropriate metrics (25 points), (2) Thorough bias and fairness assessment with evidence (25 points), (3) Clinical deployment risk analysis with justified reasoning (25 points), (4) Clear recommendation with supporting arguments addressing limitations (25 points). Peer presentation defense adds 10 bonus points for handling questions effectively.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of required metrics to calculate and interpretation guides for each visualization type. Offer pre-calculated demographic breakdowns to focus on analysis rather than data manipulation. For advanced learners, challenge them to propose additional evaluation frameworks, conduct error analysis on misclassified cases, or design A/B testing protocols for model deployment validation.

title: Design and Implement a Novel Cryptographic System Using Advanced Number Theory
description: Students will create an original encryption algorithm by combining modular arithmetic, prime factorization, and linear algebra concepts. They will develop both the mathematical framework and a working implementation, then test its security against common cryptanalytic attacks.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize modular arithmetic, prime number theory, and matrix operations by designing an original encryption algorithm with mathematical proof of functionality
Students will evaluate cryptographic security through systematic vulnerability testing and create comprehensive documentation of their system's strengths and limitations
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 2-3 (20 minutes setup). Each team receives a cryptographic design challenge packet containing three mathematical constraints: their algorithm must incorporate modular exponentiation with primes >1000, utilize at least one 3x3 matrix transformation, and include a key exchange mechanism. 

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams brainstorm and sketch their algorithm design, creating mathematical proofs for encryption/decryption processes. They must document all mathematical operations with formal notation and prove bijective mapping between plaintext and ciphertext spaces. Instructor circulates to verify mathematical rigor.

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Teams implement their algorithm in Python or MATLAB, creating functions for key generation, encryption, and decryption. Code must include comprehensive error handling and documentation. Teams test with provided sample messages and verify perfect decryption accuracy.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Security analysis phase where teams attempt to break each other's algorithms using frequency analysis, brute force estimation, and mathematical attack vectors. Each team documents vulnerabilities discovered in other systems.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams prepare formal presentations including algorithm description, mathematical proofs, implementation demonstration, security analysis results, and proposed improvements. Presentations must include complexity analysis (Big O notation) and comparison to existing cryptographic standards.

Culminating deliverable: Teams submit complete cryptographic system package including mathematical documentation, source code, security analysis report, and 10-minute presentation demonstrating their working system.
materials_needed: Computers with Python 3.8+ or MATLAB R2020b+ installed
Cryptographic design challenge packets (pre-prepared constraint sets)
Access to mathematical reference materials and prime number tables
Large whiteboards or poster paper for algorithm sketching
Sample plaintext messages for testing (provided dataset)
Presentation equipment (projector, screen)
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Mathematical rigor and proof validity (25 points), algorithm originality and complexity (20 points), implementation functionality and code quality (20 points), security analysis depth and accuracy (20 points), presentation clarity and technical communication (15 points). Success requires >80 points with mandatory demonstration of working encryption/decryption cycle.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm template with partial mathematical framework and guided worksheets for modular arithmetic review. Offer simplified constraint options (smaller primes, 2x2 matrices). For advanced learners: Challenge with additional constraints like performance optimization, resistance to quantum attacks, or integration of elliptic curve mathematics. Provide access to academic cryptography papers for inspiration.

title: Programming Language Syntax Elements Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental syntax elements from three major programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) through structured flashcard activities and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds the basic vocabulary needed for future programming tasks.
learning_objectives: Students will identify basic syntax elements (variables, loops, conditionals, functions) in Python, Java, and JavaScript by matching code snippets to language names
Students will recall correct syntax patterns for common programming constructs through structured memorization and repetition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made syntax reference sheets containing 15 essential code patterns for each language (45 total). Give students 10 minutes to study the sheets silently, encouraging them to read each syntax example aloud mentally. Next, organize students into pairs and provide each pair with a set of 45 laminated flashcards - one side showing a programming concept (e.g., 'for loop'), the other showing the correct syntax in one of the three languages. Partner A holds up the concept side while Partner B attempts to recall the exact syntax, then checks the answer. Partners switch roles every 10 cards. After 20 minutes of pair practice, conduct a whole-class 'Lightning Round' where you display syntax snippets on the projector for 10 seconds each, and students write down which language it belongs to on their answer sheets. Include 20 different snippets, mixing all three languages. Conclude with individual practice using the digital quiz platform where students match 30 syntax elements to their corresponding languages within a 15-minute time limit. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact memorization of punctuation, capitalization, and spacing as these are critical in programming.
materials_needed: Pre-printed syntax reference sheets (3 pages per student covering Python, Java, JavaScript basics)
45 laminated flashcards per pair showing programming concepts and syntax
Projector and computer for displaying code snippets
Individual answer sheets for Lightning Round
Access to digital quiz platform (Kahoot, Quizizz, or similar)
Timer for tracking activity segments
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on the digital quiz (24/30 correct matches) and correctly identify at least 16/20 languages during the Lightning Round. Track individual performance through the quiz platform's built-in analytics. Award full points for meeting both benchmarks, partial credit for achieving one benchmark, and requires retake if neither benchmark is met.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted reference sheets with the most common 5 patterns per language marked, allow extended study time, and pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Include additional syntax elements like error handling or object-oriented patterns, challenge them to explain why languages use different syntax for the same concepts, or have them create their own flashcards for advanced topics.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Real-World Datasets
description: Students will analyze three different real-world datasets to identify, classify, and explain the characteristics of various data distributions. Through hands-on exploration using Python and visualization tools, students will demonstrate understanding of how distribution shapes reveal underlying data patterns and inform analysis decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will classify data distributions (normal, skewed, bimodal, uniform) by analyzing histograms, box plots, and summary statistics from three provided datasets
Students will explain the relationship between distribution characteristics and real-world phenomena through written interpretations of each dataset's distribution patterns
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three CSV datasets: customer ages from an e-commerce platform, house prices from a metropolitan area, and test scores from a large university course. Ensure Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn is accessible.

**Phase 1 - Initial Exploration (15 minutes):** Students work individually to load each dataset and generate basic summary statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles) using pandas .describe() function. They create a summary table documenting these statistics for all three datasets.

**Phase 2 - Visualization Creation (20 minutes):** For each dataset, students create three visualizations: histogram with 20 bins, box plot, and kernel density plot. They arrange these in a 3x3 grid using matplotlib subplots for easy comparison across datasets.

**Phase 3 - Pattern Recognition (15 minutes):** Students examine their visualizations and classify each dataset's distribution type (normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, bimodal, or uniform). They document evidence supporting their classification, noting specific features like tail length, peak location, and symmetry.

**Phase 4 - Real-World Connection (15 minutes):** Students write 2-3 sentence explanations for why each dataset exhibits its particular distribution pattern, connecting statistical characteristics to real-world factors (e.g., why house prices might be right-skewed due to luxury properties creating a long tail).

**Wrap-up (10 minutes):** Pairs share one interesting finding with the class, focusing on how distribution shape reveals insights about the underlying phenomenon.
materials_needed: Three pre-selected CSV datasets (customer_ages.csv, house_prices.csv, test_scores.csv)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, and numpy installed
Jupyter notebook template with dataset loading code
Distribution classification reference sheet with visual examples
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed summary statistics table showing accurate calculations, (2) 3x3 visualization grid with properly labeled axes and titles, (3) Distribution classification worksheet with correct categorization and supporting evidence, (4) Written explanations connecting each distribution to real-world factors. Rubric: 4-Excellent (all classifications correct with clear evidence and insightful real-world connections), 3-Proficient (most classifications correct with adequate explanations), 2-Developing (some correct classifications but limited explanations), 1-Beginning (few correct classifications, minimal understanding demonstrated).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a distribution identification flowchart and pre-written code snippets for generating visualizations. Consider pairing with stronger peers during Phase 3. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate skewness and kurtosis values, compare multiple visualization types (violin plots, ridge plots), or identify potential outliers and discuss their impact on distribution interpretation.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Real-World Datasets: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze three different real-world datasets to identify, compare, and explain distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal) using visual and statistical methods. They will demonstrate understanding by categorizing distributions and explaining the business implications of each pattern type.
learning_objectives: Students will classify data distributions as normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, or bimodal by examining histograms, box plots, and summary statistics
Students will explain the practical business implications of different distribution patterns through written analysis of real-world scenarios
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-selected datasets: customer purchase amounts (right-skewed), employee performance scores (normal), and website traffic by hour (bimodal). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students. Each group receives printed summary statistics and accesses datasets via provided links. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups create histograms and box plots for all three datasets using provided software. Students should adjust bin sizes and scales for optimal visualization.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using a distribution classification worksheet, groups examine their visualizations alongside mean, median, mode, and standard deviation values. They categorize each dataset's distribution type and record evidence supporting their classifications.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups complete scenario analysis sheets, connecting each distribution pattern to business decisions. For example, right-skewed purchase data suggests most customers spend little while few spend significantly, impacting marketing strategies.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each group presents one dataset analysis to the class, explaining their classification reasoning and business implications. Other groups provide feedback using peer evaluation forms.

Circulate continuously, asking probing questions like 'What does the relationship between mean and median tell you?' and 'How might this distribution pattern affect business planning?' Ensure groups reference both visual and numerical evidence in their explanations.
materials_needed: Three curated datasets with different distribution patterns (CSV files)
Distribution classification worksheet with visual examples
Business scenario analysis template
R Studio or Python with matplotlib/seaborn installed
Peer evaluation forms
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct distribution classification with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Quality of visualizations with appropriate formatting (25%), (3) Accurate explanation of statistical measures' relationships (25%), (4) Clear articulation of business implications with specific examples (25%). Require written summary plus oral presentation component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide distribution identification flowchart and pre-made code templates for visualizations. Offer visual reference guide showing distribution characteristics. For advanced learners, introduce additional datasets with complex patterns (uniform, exponential) and ask them to research statistical tests for normality (Shapiro-Wilk, Anderson-Darling).
original_title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Real-World Datasets

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Trigonometric Functions
description: Students will apply trigonometric functions and optimization techniques to determine the optimal angle and positioning for solar panels on different roof configurations. They will work with real-world constraints including seasonal sun angles, roof pitch, and energy output calculations to maximize annual energy production.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent) to calculate optimal solar panel angles by analyzing sun elevation angles throughout the year
Students will implement optimization techniques through systematic calculation and comparison of energy output scenarios across multiple panel configurations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and distributing the Solar Panel Optimization Worksheet containing three different house scenarios with varying roof pitches (30°, 45°, 60°). Each team receives a specific geographic location with corresponding seasonal sun angle data. Students start by using trigonometric functions to calculate the angle of incidence between sunlight and potential panel positions for each month. They must apply the cosine law to determine when panels would be perpendicular to sun rays for maximum efficiency. Next, students calculate relative energy output using the formula: Energy Output = Base Output × cos(angle between sun and panel normal). Teams must consider the constraint that panels cannot exceed the roof pitch angle plus 15°. Students then create optimization tables showing monthly energy outputs for 5 different panel angles, applying systematic calculation methods to compare total annual energy production. For each configuration, they must use trigonometric identities to verify their angle calculations and apply the optimization principle to identify the angle producing maximum annual output. Teams plot their results on provided graph paper, creating energy output curves for visual analysis. Finally, students prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their optimal solution with mathematical justification, including cost-benefit analysis using provided installation cost data. Throughout the activity, students must show all trigonometric calculations, apply angle sum and difference formulas where needed, and demonstrate systematic optimization methodology. The instructor circulates to verify calculation accuracy and guide teams toward recognizing the relationship between mathematical optimization and real-world engineering decisions.
materials_needed: Solar Panel Optimization Worksheet with 3 house scenarios
Scientific calculators or tablets with calculator apps
Graph paper and rulers
Seasonal sun angle data sheets for different geographic locations
Installation cost data sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate application of trigonometric functions in calculations (25%), (2) Correct implementation of optimization methodology comparing multiple scenarios (25%), (3) Mathematical justification of final panel angle selection with supporting calculations (25%), (4) Quality of presentation explaining the optimization process and real-world implications (25%). Students must submit calculation worksheets showing all trigonometric work and optimization tables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide trigonometric function reference cards and pre-calculated sun angles for two months as examples. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-angle comparisons before full optimization. For advanced learners: Add variables like panel cost per degree of tilt, shading effects from nearby objects, or optimization across multiple roof faces requiring 3D trigonometric calculations.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Trigonometric Functions: Visual Analysis
description: Students will apply trigonometric functions and optimization techniques to determine the optimal angle and spacing for solar panels in a residential installation. They will use real weather data and geographic coordinates to calculate maximum energy output while considering physical constraints and seasonal variations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions (sine, cosine, tangent) to calculate solar panel angles and shadow lengths by analyzing sun position data throughout the year
Students will implement optimization strategies to maximize energy output through systematic testing of panel configurations using mathematical modeling
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the scenario packet containing: residential lot dimensions (40ft × 60ft), local latitude coordinates, monthly sun angle data, and energy production formulas. Each team receives a different geographic location (Phoenix, Seattle, Miami, or Denver). 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams calculate optimal tilt angles using the formula: Tilt Angle = Latitude + 15° (winter) / Latitude - 15° (summer). Students apply trigonometric functions to determine shadow lengths using L = H × cot(elevation angle), where H is panel height. They must create a data table showing monthly calculations.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using the shadow length calculations, teams determine minimum spacing between panel rows using S = L × cos(azimuth angle) to prevent shading. Students apply the energy formula: E = A × r × H × PR, where A = panel area, r = efficiency rating, H = peak sun hours, PR = performance ratio. They calculate monthly energy output for three different configurations.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams use spreadsheet software to model total annual energy production, applying trigonometric functions to account for seasonal sun path variations. They must test at least 5 different panel arrangements, documenting calculations for each scenario.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Each team presents their optimal configuration, showing mathematical justification using trigonometric calculations. They must defend their solution by demonstrating how they applied optimization principles and explaining trade-offs between maximum energy output and practical installation constraints.
materials_needed: Solar panel scenario packets with geographic data and lot dimensions
Scientific calculators with trigonometric functions
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets)
Graph paper and rulers for scale drawings
Solar energy formula reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct application of trigonometric formulas for angle and shadow calculations (25%), (2) Accurate implementation of optimization strategies with mathematical justification (25%), (3) Proper use of energy production formulas with realistic constraints (25%), (4) Clear presentation of final solution with supporting calculations and rationale (25%). Students must submit calculation worksheets and present solutions to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-completed formula sheets with variable definitions, offer step-by-step calculation templates, and allow use of online trigonometric calculators. For advanced learners: Include additional variables such as temperature coefficients, inverter efficiency losses, and economic analysis using net present value calculations. Consider adding weather variability factors and grid-tie considerations.
original_title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Trigonometric Functions

title: Critical Analysis of Memory Management Vulnerabilities in C/C++ Code Samples
description: Students will systematically analyze provided C/C++ code samples to identify memory management vulnerabilities, classify their types, and evaluate their potential security impact. They will decompose complex buffer overflow scenarios and stack corruption patterns to understand exploitation vectors.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze memory allocation patterns in C/C++ code by identifying heap and stack vulnerabilities using static code analysis techniques
Students will differentiate between various memory management flaws through systematic vulnerability classification and impact assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing five deliberately vulnerable C/C++ code samples (150-300 lines each) containing buffer overflows, use-after-free bugs, double-free errors, and memory leaks. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to perform initial code review using provided vulnerability checklists. Next, demonstrate static analysis tools (Valgrind, AddressSanitizer) for 15 minutes, showing command-line usage and output interpretation. Students then spend 45 minutes running these tools on each code sample, documenting findings in structured analysis sheets that require: vulnerability type identification, affected memory regions, potential exploitation scenarios, and severity ratings (1-10 scale). During the analysis phase, students must trace program execution paths that trigger vulnerabilities, mapping stack frames and heap states at critical points. For each identified vulnerability, students create visual memory diagrams showing before/after states of corruption. In the final 30 minutes, pairs present one complex vulnerability to the class, explaining the root cause, demonstrating the tool output that detected it, and proposing specific remediation strategies. Instructors circulate during analysis time, prompting deeper investigation with questions like 'What happens to adjacent memory regions?' and 'How would an attacker control this input vector?' Students must justify severity ratings by considering factors like remote exploitability, privilege escalation potential, and ease of exploitation.
materials_needed: Five pre-written vulnerable C/C++ code samples with varying complexity levels
Linux virtual machines with GCC, Valgrind, and AddressSanitizer installed
Vulnerability analysis worksheet templates with structured fields
Memory diagram templates for visualization exercises
Access to online CVE database for real-world vulnerability comparison
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of vulnerability identification (25%) - must find at least 80% of planted vulnerabilities, (2) Quality of technical analysis (35%) - demonstrates understanding of memory corruption mechanisms, (3) Effective use of analysis tools (20%) - properly interprets tool output and correlates findings, (4) Clarity of security impact assessment (20%) - provides realistic exploitation scenarios and appropriate severity ratings
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide step-by-step tool usage guides, offer simplified code samples with obvious vulnerabilities, and pair with stronger partners. Use color-coded highlighting to mark suspicious code patterns. For advanced learners: include samples with subtle race conditions, provide access to disassemblers (objdump, IDA Free), challenge them to create proof-of-concept exploits, and encourage analysis of compiler-generated assembly code.

title: Design Your Dream Community: A Quadratic Function Urban Planning Project
description: Students will create an original urban planning proposal for a new community by designing and modeling various structures and systems using quadratic functions. They will construct mathematical models for population growth, park layouts, bridge designs, and water fountains while justifying their design choices through mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will construct multiple quadratic function models by designing realistic urban infrastructure elements including population projections, architectural features, and resource allocation systems
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts through creating a comprehensive community plan that integrates vertex form, standard form, and factored form representations of quadratic functions
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the Urban Planning Design Brief which specifies that each team must create a new community for 5,000-15,000 residents. Each team receives graph paper, calculators, and access to Desmos graphing software. Students spend the first 20 minutes brainstorming their community vision and assigning roles: Lead Planner, Population Analyst, Infrastructure Designer, and Environmental Coordinator. Next, teams spend 40 minutes creating four specific quadratic models: (1) Population growth projection over 20 years using vertex form, (2) Parabolic arch bridge design using standard form with realistic span and height constraints, (3) Water fountain trajectory patterns using factored form showing water arc paths, and (4) Curved park pathway system connecting three key community points. For each model, students must write the equation in at least two different forms, identify key features (vertex, axis of symmetry, intercepts), and explain real-world significance. During the following 30 minutes, teams create their visual presentation using poster paper, incorporating their graphs, equations, and community layout map. They must include a budget analysis showing cost calculations based on their mathematical models. Finally, conduct 25 minutes of team presentations (4-5 minutes each) where teams present their community design, explain their quadratic models, and defend their mathematical choices. Other teams provide feedback using the peer evaluation form focusing on mathematical accuracy and creative application.
materials_needed: Graph paper (5 sheets per student)
Scientific calculators
Access to Desmos Graphing Calculator online
Poster paper (24" x 36")
Colored pencils and markers
Urban Planning Design Brief handout
Peer evaluation forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - correct quadratic equations in multiple forms with proper identification of key features, (2) Creative Application (25%) - innovative and realistic use of quadratic functions in urban planning context, (3) Mathematical Communication (25%) - clear explanations of how each model represents real-world phenomena with proper mathematical vocabulary, (4) Presentation Quality (25%) - organized visual display and effective oral presentation with peer interaction. Students must score 3/4 in each category to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide quadratic function reference sheets with transformation rules, offer pre-made templates for organizing their equations, and allow use of graphing calculator throughout. Pair stronger math students with those needing support within teams. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional mathematical concepts like optimization (finding maximum/minimum values for efficiency), explore piecewise functions for complex designs, or add constraints requiring systems of quadratic inequalities for zoning regulations.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance vs. Practical Significance in A/B Test Results for E-commerce Conversion Optimization
description: Students will analyze real A/B test results from an e-commerce conversion optimization experiment to distinguish between statistical significance and practical business significance. They will interpret confidence intervals, effect sizes, and statistical power while evaluating whether findings warrant implementation decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between statistical significance and practical significance by analyzing A/B test results with varying effect sizes and sample sizes
Students will interpret the business implications of confidence intervals, p-values, and effect sizes through examination of e-commerce conversion data scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared dataset containing A/B test results from three different e-commerce experiments (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to analyze Experiment 1: 'Checkout Button Color Change' with n=50,000 per group, 2.1% vs 2.3% conversion rates, p=0.048. Have them calculate the absolute lift (0.2 percentage points), relative lift (9.5%), and examine the 95% confidence interval [0.002%, 0.398%]. Next, students analyze Experiment 2: 'Product Page Layout' with n=500 per group, 8% vs 12% conversion rates, p=0.089, calculating absolute lift (4 percentage points) and relative lift (50%). For the final 20 minutes, students examine Experiment 3: 'Email Subject Line' with n=100,000 per group, 15.2% vs 15.7% conversion rates, p=0.001. Students must determine which experiments they would recommend implementing, considering: statistical significance (p<0.05), minimum detectable effect thresholds, confidence interval width, and business context provided (implementation costs: $500, $5000, and $100 respectively). Students document their reasoning using the provided decision framework template, specifically addressing why Experiment 2 might be worth implementing despite lacking statistical significance, while Experiment 3 might not warrant implementation despite strong statistical significance. Conclude with pair presentations of their recommendations and reasoning (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-prepared Excel/CSV dataset with three A/B test scenarios including raw conversion data
Business context information sheet detailing implementation costs and company metrics
Decision framework template with sections for statistical measures, business impact, and recommendation
Calculators or laptops with statistical software (R, Python, or Excel)
Confidence interval calculation reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate calculation of effect sizes and confidence intervals (25%), (2) Correct identification of statistical vs practical significance in each scenario (25%), (3) Justified business recommendations incorporating both statistical and practical considerations (35%), (4) Clear articulation of reasoning during presentation including discussion of Type I/II error implications (15%). Students must correctly identify that Experiment 2 shows practical significance without statistical significance, while Experiment 3 shows statistical significance without practical significance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated confidence intervals and focus on interpretation rather than calculation. Offer guiding questions like 'What is the cost per additional conversion?' and 'How confident can we be in this range of effects?' For advanced learners, introduce concepts of statistical power analysis, Bayesian interpretation of results, or multiple testing corrections. Encourage discussion of sequential testing and early stopping rules for A/B tests.

title: Planning a School Garden: Calculating Area and Perimeter for Real Spaces
description: Students will apply their knowledge of area and perimeter calculations to design rectangular garden plots for their school grounds. They will measure actual outdoor spaces, calculate dimensions, and determine fencing and soil requirements using real-world constraints and budget considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate area and perimeter of rectangular spaces by measuring and computing garden plot dimensions for practical landscaping needs
Students will apply mathematical formulas to solve real-world problems through designing functional garden layouts within given constraints
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with measuring tools and worksheets. Take students to a designated outdoor area (school courtyard, unused lawn space, or parking lot section) that measures approximately 20x30 feet. Each team selects and measures a 6x8 foot rectangular section within this space using measuring tapes, ensuring no overlap between team areas. Students record length and width measurements on their worksheets, then return to the classroom. In the classroom phase (15 minutes), teams calculate the area of their garden plot using A = length × width, and determine the perimeter using P = 2(length + width). Next, present the real-world application scenario: students must determine how much topsoil to purchase (soil covers 3 inches deep) and how much fencing is needed for their plot boundaries. Teams calculate soil volume needed by converting their area to cubic feet (area × 0.25 feet depth), then convert to cubic yards by dividing by 27. For fencing, they use their perimeter calculation directly. Provide cost constraints: topsoil costs $45 per cubic yard, fencing costs $8 per linear foot, and each team has a $200 budget. Students must determine if their garden plan fits the budget and, if not, propose modifications to dimensions while maintaining a rectangular shape. Teams present their final calculations, showing original measurements, area, perimeter, material quantities needed, total costs, and any budget adjustments made. Each presentation should include a simple sketch of their proposed garden layout with labeled dimensions.
materials_needed: Measuring tapes (30-foot length minimum)
Garden Planning Worksheets with calculation templates
Calculators
Clipboards for outdoor work
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of measurements and calculations (area, perimeter, volume conversions), (2) Correct application of formulas with proper units, (3) Budget analysis and realistic cost calculations, (4) Clear presentation of solution process and final garden design. Students must show all mathematical work and achieve 80% accuracy on calculations to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing formula reference cards and breaking calculations into smaller steps with checkpoints. Pair them with stronger math partners during measuring phase. For advanced learners, introduce complications like irregular plot shapes, multiple garden sections, or additional factors like walkway space calculations and plant spacing requirements based on geometric patterns.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Performance Decomposition
description: Students will systematically analyze and compare the performance characteristics of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining their time complexity, space requirements, and real-world execution patterns. They will decompose algorithm behavior under different data conditions to identify optimal use cases for each approach.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three search algorithms by systematically measuring performance across varying data sizes and conditions
Students will compare algorithmic trade-offs through structured performance testing and identify optimal algorithm selection criteria for specific scenarios
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute setup where students access the provided Python template containing implementations of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup functions, plus a performance testing framework. Divide students into pairs and assign each pair one of three dataset types: sorted integers (1-10,000), random strings (100-5,000 items), or mixed data with duplicates (500-3,000 items). 

For the next 25 minutes, students execute the analysis protocol: First, run each algorithm on datasets of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 2500, and 5000 items, recording execution time and memory usage. Second, analyze best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios by strategically placing target values at the beginning, middle, and end of datasets. Third, document preprocessing requirements (sorting time for binary search, hash table construction time). 

During minutes 35-50, pairs complete the comparison matrix template, calculating growth rates between dataset sizes, identifying inflection points where one algorithm outperforms another, and noting memory overhead patterns. Students must justify their observations with specific evidence from their test runs.

In the final 15 minutes, conduct a structured gallery walk where each pair presents their findings for their assigned dataset type. Other pairs add sticky note questions and observations. Conclude with a 10-minute debrief where students synthesize findings across all dataset types to create algorithm selection decision trees. Students submit their completed analysis matrices, performance graphs, and recommendation summaries as deliverables.
materials_needed: Python programming environment (IDLE, PyCharm, or online IDE)
Pre-built algorithm implementation template file
Performance testing framework with timing functions
Comparison matrix worksheet (digital or printed)
Dataset generator script for consistent test data
Sticky notes for gallery walk feedback
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of performance measurements and data collection (25%), (2) Quality of algorithmic comparison analysis with specific evidence and calculations (35%), (3) Appropriateness of algorithm recommendations with clear justification (25%), and (4) Identification of trade-offs and edge cases (15%). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining why performance patterns occur, not just documenting what happens.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each analysis step and pre-filled partial data tables. Offer algorithm complexity cheat sheets with Big O notation examples. For advanced learners, extend the activity by adding recursive vs iterative implementations, analyzing cache performance effects, or implementing hybrid search strategies. Provide additional datasets with real-world characteristics (sparse data, frequent duplicates) for deeper analysis.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Healthcare Resource Allocation
description: Students will critically evaluate three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network) trained to predict hospital readmission rates, assessing their ethical implications, business viability, and technical robustness. They will justify which model should be deployed in a real healthcare system by weighing multiple evaluation criteria beyond traditional accuracy metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of competing machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, fairness across demographic groups, and interpretability requirements
Students will critique model deployment decisions through systematic assessment of ethical implications, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder impact in healthcare contexts
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-trained models and their outputs on a holdout dataset containing 5,000 patient records with demographics, medical history, and readmission outcomes. Divide students into teams of 3-4 members (30 minutes setup). Each team receives identical model performance reports, confusion matrices, feature importance plots, and fairness metrics across age, gender, and racial groups.

Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams systematically evaluate each model using the provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: predictive accuracy, fairness/bias, interpretability, computational efficiency, regulatory compliance, and clinical actionability. Students must calculate additional metrics not provided (e.g., positive predictive value for minority groups, calibration scores) using supplied raw predictions.
