Phase 2 (45 minutes): Teams identify critical weaknesses in each model by analyzing edge cases, examining prediction confidence distributions, and assessing performance degradation across patient subgroups. They must document at least three significant concerns per model with supporting evidence.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Each team creates a recommendation memo (max 800 words) justifying their model selection for deployment. The memo must address: primary recommendation with confidence level, ranked evaluation criteria with weights, risk mitigation strategies for identified weaknesses, implementation timeline, and monitoring protocols post-deployment.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Teams present 8-minute recommendations to a mock hospital board (other teams), followed by 4 minutes of critical questioning. Audience members must challenge at least two assumptions or conclusions using evidence from the data.

Conclude with 15-minute debrief discussing how different stakeholder priorities (patients, administrators, clinicians, regulators) influence model evaluation decisions.
materials_needed: Dataset with 5,000 patient records (synthetic data with realistic distributions)
Three pre-trained model outputs with performance reports and visualizations
Model evaluation framework template with scoring rubrics
Python/R environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
Digital presentation platform for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using weighted rubric (100 points total): Technical analysis quality (30 points) - accuracy of calculations, depth of statistical interpretation, identification of model limitations; Critical reasoning (25 points) - logical argument structure, evidence-based conclusions, consideration of multiple perspectives; Ethical evaluation (20 points) - bias assessment, fairness implications, stakeholder impact analysis; Communication (15 points) - clarity of written memo, effectiveness of oral presentation; Peer engagement (10 points) - quality of questions asked, constructive challenges provided during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates for complex metrics, offer guiding questions for each evaluation dimension, and allow extended time for Phase 1 analysis. Create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional evaluation methods (e.g., SHAP analysis, adversarial testing), research current regulatory guidelines (FDA AI/ML guidance), or propose novel fairness metrics relevant to healthcare contexts. Encourage exploration of model ensemble approaches or meta-learning solutions.

title: Design and Construct a Dynamic Optimization System for Multi-Variable Resource Allocation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization framework to solve a complex real-world resource allocation problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will develop both the theoretical model and a functional computational solution, then present their system to industry professionals for feedback.
estimated_duration: 5 weeks (approximately 40-50 hours total student work time)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and optimization theory concepts by designing an original multi-variable optimization model for a complex resource allocation scenario
Students will construct a functional computational implementation of their theoretical model through programming and validate its effectiveness using real-world data sets
instructions: Begin by presenting students with three complex scenarios: hospital resource allocation during emergencies, renewable energy grid optimization, or supply chain distribution networks. Students form teams of 3-4 and select one scenario. Week 1: Teams conduct stakeholder interviews (provided contact list) and research existing solutions, identifying at least 8 variables and 12 constraints. They must justify variable selection using mathematical reasoning and document assumptions. Week 2: Students formulate their optimization problem mathematically, choosing appropriate objective functions (linear, quadratic, or non-linear) and constraint types. They must prove feasibility of their constraint set and demonstrate understanding of duality theory. Week 3: Teams implement their model using Python with optimization libraries (PuLP, SciPy, or Gurobi), creating user interfaces for parameter input. They must include sensitivity analysis features and uncertainty modeling. Week 4: Using provided historical datasets, students validate their models, comparing results against benchmark solutions and conducting statistical significance tests. Week 5: Teams prepare comprehensive presentations including theoretical foundation, computational implementation, validation results, and practical deployment recommendations. Industry professionals attend final presentations and provide feedback using structured evaluation forms. Throughout the project, teams maintain detailed mathematical journals documenting derivations, proofs, and decision rationales.
materials_needed: Access to Python programming environment with optimization libraries (PuLP, SciPy, Gurobi)
Historical datasets for three scenarios (hospital records, energy consumption data, supply chain metrics)
Contact information for industry stakeholders willing to be interviewed
Mathematical computation software (MATLAB, Mathematica, or equivalent)
Presentation technology and screen sharing capabilities for final presentations
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using detailed rubric with five components: Mathematical Rigor (25% - correctness of formulation, proof quality, theoretical understanding), Implementation Quality (25% - code functionality, user interface, computational efficiency), Validation and Analysis (20% - appropriate testing methods, statistical analysis, result interpretation), Innovation and Creativity (15% - novel approaches, creative problem-solving, original insights), and Professional Communication (15% - presentation clarity, stakeholder engagement, documentation quality). Each component scored on 4-point scale with specific criteria. Industry professionals provide additional feedback forms rating practical applicability and deployment feasibility.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template optimization problem structures and guided worksheets for constraint identification. Offer optional review sessions on multivariate calculus and linear algebra fundamentals. For advanced learners, introduce stochastic optimization concepts, machine learning integration possibilities, or multi-objective optimization techniques. Provide additional challenge datasets with increased complexity or encourage exploration of emerging optimization algorithms like genetic algorithms or particle swarm optimization.

title: Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge
description: Students will examine code snippets from Python, Java, and JavaScript to identify and label specific syntax elements such as variables, functions, loops, and conditional statements. This activity builds foundational recognition skills for reading and understanding code structure across multiple programming languages.
learning_objectives: Students will identify common programming syntax elements (variables, functions, loops, conditionals) by examining labeled code snippets from three different languages
Students will recall the purpose and naming conventions of basic programming constructs through guided practice with visual code examples
instructions: Begin by displaying three code snippet handouts face-down on each student's desk along with colored highlighters and the syntax reference sheet. Start with a 5-minute whole-class review using the reference sheet, asking students to read aloud the definitions of variables, functions, loops, and conditional statements. Next, instruct students to flip over the Python code snippet (Handout A) and spend 7 minutes highlighting each syntax element using the color code: yellow for variables, blue for functions, green for loops, pink for conditionals. Circulate during this time to provide individual guidance. After 7 minutes, project the answer key for Handout A and have students self-check their work for 3 minutes, correcting any mistakes with a pen. Repeat this exact process with the Java code snippet (Handout B) and then the JavaScript snippet (Handout C), maintaining the same timing and color-coding system. During the final 8 minutes, conduct a verbal quiz where you point to specific highlighted elements on the projected answer keys and ask individual students to name the syntax type and explain its basic purpose. Students should respond using the exact terminology from their reference sheets. Conclude by having students count their total correct identifications across all three handouts and record this number at the top of their papers.
materials_needed: Three code snippet handouts (Python, Java, JavaScript) with 8-12 syntax elements each
Syntax reference sheet with definitions and examples
Four colored highlighters per student (yellow, blue, green, pink)
Projector or smartboard for displaying answer keys
Black pens for corrections
assessment_method: Students receive 1 point for each correctly identified syntax element across all three handouts (maximum 36 points). Success criteria: 80% accuracy (29/36 points) demonstrates mastery of syntax recognition. Teacher observes during verbal quiz portion, noting students who can correctly name elements and provide basic purpose explanations using reference sheet terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a simplified handout with only 4-6 syntax elements and allow them to work with a partner during highlighting. For advanced learners: Include additional handouts with more complex code featuring nested structures, multiple functions, or advanced syntax elements like classes or exception handling.

title: Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge: Visual Analysis
description: Students will examine code snippets from Python, Java, and JavaScript to identify and recall specific syntax elements such as variable declarations, function definitions, and loop structures. This foundational activity builds recognition of fundamental programming constructs across multiple languages.
learning_objectives: Students will identify basic syntax elements (variables, functions, loops, conditionals) by examining labeled code snippets from three programming languages
Students will recall the correct terminology for fundamental programming constructs through visual recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared syntax identification worksheet containing 15 code snippets (5 from each language: Python, Java, JavaScript). Each snippet is 3-5 lines long and contains one primary syntax element to identify. Give students 2 minutes to examine the reference sheet containing syntax definitions and examples for variables, functions, loops (for/while), if statements, and comments. Explain that they will identify what type of programming construct each snippet represents and which programming language it uses. Students work individually for 15 minutes, writing their answers in the provided answer boxes next to each code snippet. After individual work, pair students for 5 minutes to compare answers and discuss any differences. During this time, circulate to observe student discussions and note common misconceptions. Reconvene the class and project each code snippet on the board. Call on different student pairs to share their identification for each snippet, asking them to explain which visual clues helped them recognize the syntax element and programming language. Provide immediate correction and reinforcement for each answer, highlighting key distinguishing features like Python's indentation, Java's semicolons and braces, and JavaScript's var/let/const keywords. Conclude by having students complete a quick matching exercise where they draw lines connecting syntax examples to their correct terminology and programming language.
materials_needed: Printed syntax identification worksheet with 15 code snippets
Programming syntax reference sheet with definitions and examples
Projector/smartboard for displaying code snippets
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 12 out of 15 syntax elements (80% accuracy) and match programming language for at least 10 out of 15 snippets. Success demonstrated through completed worksheet showing accurate recognition of variables, functions, loops, conditionals, and comments across Python, Java, and JavaScript.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted reference sheet with color-coded syntax elements and allow extended time with reference materials. For advanced learners: Include more complex nested structures and ask them to identify multiple syntax elements within single snippets, or have them create their own examples for classmates to identify.
original_title: Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge

title: Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge: Practical Workshop
description: Students will identify and categorize fundamental programming syntax elements from code snippets in Python. They will practice recognizing variables, operators, keywords, and data types through a structured matching and labeling exercise.
learning_objectives: Students will identify basic Python syntax elements (variables, operators, keywords, data types) by examining provided code snippets
Students will recall the names and purposes of common programming constructs through a guided classification activity
instructions: Begin by distributing the syntax reference sheet and code snippet worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Display the first example on the projector: 'age = 25' and demonstrate how to identify each element (variable name 'age', assignment operator '=', integer data type '25'). Have students work individually through Sheet 1 containing 10 simple code lines, using colored pencils to highlight different syntax types: blue for variables, red for operators, green for keywords, yellow for data types (15 minutes). Circulate to provide individual guidance. Next, students complete Sheet 2 with 15 slightly more complex examples including if statements, loops, and function definitions (20 minutes). For the final phase, pair students to compare their answers and resolve discrepancies using the reference sheet (10 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class review where volunteers identify elements from 3 challenge examples projected on screen, explaining their reasoning (10 minutes). Students must correctly identify at least 80% of elements and provide proper terminology for each syntax component.
materials_needed: Python syntax reference sheet (1 per student)
Code snippet worksheet Set 1 - basic examples (1 per student)
Code snippet worksheet Set 2 - intermediate examples (1 per student)
Colored pencils or highlighters (4 colors per student)
Projector and computer for demonstrations
assessment_method: Collect completed worksheets and grade using a checklist: 1 point for correctly identifying each syntax element type, 1 point for proper terminology usage. Students must achieve 24/30 points (80%) for proficiency. Observe during pair discussions to assess verbal explanation of syntax elements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional examples with partially completed identification, offer one-on-one explanation of the most common elements first. For advanced learners: include bonus challenges with nested functions, list comprehensions, or exception handling syntax to identify more complex elements.
original_title: Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge

title: Interpreting Machine Learning Model Performance Through Cross-Validation Metrics
description: Students analyze and interpret the performance of different machine learning algorithms using cross-validation results and multiple evaluation metrics. They will examine confusion matrices, precision-recall curves, and ROC curves to understand when and why different models succeed or fail on a binary classification problem.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation scores and their standard deviations to assess model stability and generalizability across different algorithms
Students will explain the relationships between precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC metrics through analysis of model performance reports
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing results from 5-fold cross-validation for four different algorithms (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Naive Bayes) trained on a customer churn prediction problem. Each student receives identical printed performance reports showing mean CV scores, standard deviations, confusion matrices, and ROC curves for each model.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to examine the cross-validation scores table. They identify which model has the highest mean accuracy, lowest standard deviation, and best F1-score. They record their observations on the provided worksheet, noting any patterns or surprises.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students analyze the confusion matrices for each model. They calculate and compare the false positive rates and false negative rates, discussing which errors might be more costly in a customer churn scenario. Partners must reach consensus on which model handles false negatives best and document their reasoning.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students examine the ROC curves as a class. The instructor guides discussion about curve interpretation, highlighting how the area under the curve relates to model discrimination ability. Students annotate their curves with threshold trade-offs.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students write a brief recommendation memo selecting the best model for deployment, justifying their choice using specific metric values and business context considerations. They must address at least three different performance metrics in their justification.
materials_needed: Pre-computed cross-validation results dataset (printed reports for each student)
Model performance comparison worksheet template
Colored pens for annotating ROC curves
Calculator or smartphone for metric calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate student worksheets and final recommendation memos using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly interprets all metrics with clear business reasoning, (3) Interprets most metrics accurately with good reasoning, (2) Shows basic understanding with some misinterpretations, (1) Limited understanding of metric relationships. Success requires scoring 3+ points and correctly identifying trade-offs between precision and recall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a metrics reference sheet defining precision, recall, and F1-score with formulas. Encourage them to focus on one model at a time. For advanced learners, introduce additional metrics like Matthews Correlation Coefficient or discuss class imbalance handling techniques. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during Step 2.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Placement Using Quadratic Functions
description: Students apply quadratic function modeling to determine optimal positioning and configuration of solar panels for maximum energy output. They will use real-world constraints including roof dimensions, shading patterns, and seasonal sun angles to create mathematical models and justify their placement decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply quadratic function properties to model solar energy output by analyzing vertex form equations and optimization techniques
Students will construct mathematical arguments to justify optimal solar panel configurations through systematic comparison of multiple quadratic models
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Solar Panel Scenario packet containing three different roof layouts (flat commercial, angled residential, and irregular shape) with specific dimensions and shading data. Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team assigned one roof type initially. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze their roof specifications and identify constraints including usable area, sun exposure hours, and seasonal variations. They record baseline measurements and calculate total available space.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the provided solar output data table, students create quadratic models for energy production based on panel angle (x-axis) versus daily kilowatt-hours (y-axis). They must identify three different potential configurations and write equations in vertex form f(x) = a(x-h)² + k for each setup.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams apply optimization techniques to find maximum energy output points for each configuration. They calculate vertex coordinates, determine practical angle constraints (0° ≤ x ≤ 60°), and evaluate function values at critical points and endpoints.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Students create detailed cost-benefit analyses comparing their three configurations, incorporating panel costs ($200 per unit), installation angles, and projected annual savings. They must justify their final recommendation using mathematical evidence from their quadratic models.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams present their optimal solution to another team with a different roof type, defending their mathematical reasoning and responding to questions about their optimization process.
materials_needed: Solar Panel Scenario packet with 3 roof layouts and constraint data
Solar output data tables with angle/energy measurements
Graphing calculators or Desmos graphing software access
Cost analysis worksheets with current solar panel pricing
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct quadratic model creation with proper vertex form notation, (2) Accurate optimization calculations showing maximum values and constraint applications, (3) Complete cost-benefit analysis with mathematical justification, (4) Clear presentation defending chosen configuration with evidence from models. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing vertex form templates and guided practice finding maximums with simpler quadratic examples first. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints like wind load factors or seasonal efficiency variations requiring piecewise functions. Consider pairing stronger algebra students with those needing support during the modeling phase.

title: Reverse Engineering and Analyzing a Distributed Cache Implementation for Performance Bottlenecks
description: Students will analyze a production-level distributed caching system implementation to identify architectural patterns, performance bottlenecks, and design trade-offs. They will deconstruct the system's components, examine inter-service communication patterns, and evaluate scalability limitations through code analysis and performance profiling data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the architectural components of a distributed caching system by examining source code, configuration files, and system diagrams to identify design patterns and component interactions
Students will evaluate performance bottlenecks and scalability constraints through systematic analysis of profiling data, network latency measurements, and resource utilization metrics
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a complete Redis Cluster implementation including source code, configuration files, and 48-hour performance monitoring data from a simulated e-commerce application. Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the codebase structure, identifying key components including cluster nodes, client libraries, and failover mechanisms. Students create architectural diagrams mapping data flow and component relationships. Step 2 (60 minutes): Using provided performance monitoring data (CPU usage, memory consumption, network I/O, cache hit/miss ratios), students analyze system behavior under different load conditions. They identify performance patterns and bottlenecks using tools like Redis CLI, monitoring dashboards, and log analysis. Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams examine the consistency model implementation, analyzing how the system handles network partitions and node failures. They trace through the source code to understand consensus algorithms and data replication strategies. Step 4 (45 minutes): Students analyze the provided load testing results showing response times under varying concurrent user loads (100, 1000, 10000 users). They identify breaking points and correlate performance degradation with specific system components. Step 5 (30 minutes): Teams prepare analysis reports documenting identified bottlenecks, architectural strengths/weaknesses, and specific code sections responsible for performance limitations. Include quantitative evidence from the monitoring data and specific line references from source code.
materials_needed: Redis Cluster source code repository with complete implementation
48-hour performance monitoring dataset (JSON format with timestamps, metrics)
System architecture documentation and network topology diagrams
Redis CLI and monitoring tools (Redis Insight, Grafana dashboards)
Load testing results with response time distributions
Virtual machines or containers with Redis Cluster deployed
assessment_method: Teams submit a technical analysis report (8-10 pages) containing: (1) Architectural component diagram with detailed annotations (25 points), (2) Performance bottleneck identification with supporting quantitative evidence (30 points), (3) Code-level analysis citing specific functions/methods causing limitations (25 points), (4) Scalability assessment with concrete recommendations (20 points). Rubric evaluates depth of analysis, accuracy of technical conclusions, and quality of evidence supporting claims.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with specific questions about each system component and pre-highlighted code sections to examine. Include performance data visualization templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose specific code optimizations, design alternative architectures, or implement proof-of-concept improvements to identified bottlenecks. Provide additional datasets from different distributed systems (Memcached, Hazelcast) for comparative analysis.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Notation Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the formal mathematical definitions of Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notations along with their corresponding growth rate hierarchies. This activity focuses on precise recall of asymptotic notation definitions and the standard ordering of common complexity functions.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the formal mathematical definitions of O(n), Ω(n), and Θ(n) notations by writing exact symbolic representations with proper quantifiers and variables
Students will identify and recite the hierarchical ordering of 15 standard time complexity functions through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the complexity notation reference sheet containing formal definitions and the standard hierarchy: O(1), O(log log n), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(n³), O(2ⁿ), etc. Students work individually for 20 minutes studying the materials using active recall techniques - covering definitions and testing themselves repeatedly. Next, implement a 15-minute rapid-fire recall session where students rotate through three stations: Station 1 requires writing the complete formal definition of Big O notation including existential quantifiers (∃c>0, ∃n₀>0 such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n≥n₀). Station 2 focuses on Big Omega and Big Theta definitions with identical precision. Station 3 presents complexity functions in random order where students must sequence them from lowest to highest growth rate within 30 seconds per set. Conduct three 5-minute rotation cycles, with students spending exactly 5 minutes at each station before moving clockwise. Follow with a 10-minute individual quiz where students write all three formal definitions from memory and correctly order two sets of 8 complexity functions each. Conclude with immediate peer checking using answer keys, allowing students to identify and mark their specific recall gaps for focused review.
materials_needed: Laminated reference sheets with formal asymptotic notation definitions
Complexity hierarchy charts showing O(1) through O(2ⁿ) functions
Pre-printed quiz sheets with definition prompts and function ordering exercises
Timer/stopwatch for station rotations
Answer keys for peer checking
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on formal definition recall (all three notations with correct mathematical symbols and quantifiers) and 85% accuracy on complexity function ordering. Assessment includes: formal definition completeness (3 points each, 9 total), mathematical notation precision (2 points per definition, 6 total), and correct hierarchical sequencing (1 point per correctly placed function, 16 total). Maximum score: 31 points. Success threshold: 28+ points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide definition templates with partial mathematical symbols filled in, allow extended study time with highlighted key terms, and offer mnemonic devices for function ordering (e.g., 'Constant Logs Never Lie, Never Quadratically Explode'). For advanced learners: include additional complexity classes like O(n!) and O(nⁿ), require explanation of why certain functions don't appear in standard hierarchies, and challenge them to recall average vs. worst-case complexities for specific algorithms.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Ensemble Model Predictions for Healthcare Risk Assessment
description: Students analyze and interpret SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and permutation importance outputs from a Random Forest model predicting patient readmission risk. They will explain how different clinical features contribute to individual predictions and overall model behavior, demonstrating deep understanding of model interpretability concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP waterfall plots and summary plots by explaining how individual features contribute to specific patient risk predictions
Students will differentiate between global and local feature importance through comparative analysis of permutation importance rankings and individual SHAP value distributions
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained Random Forest model for 30-day hospital readmission prediction using the diabetes dataset with features including age, HbA1c levels, number of medications, length of stay, and discharge disposition. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to generate SHAP explanations using the provided Python notebook template. First, they run SHAP TreeExplainer on the entire test set to create summary plots showing global feature importance rankings. Next, they select three specific patient cases (low, medium, high risk) and generate individual SHAP waterfall plots. Students then calculate permutation importance scores using scikit-learn's permutation_importance function with 10 iterations. For the analysis phase (40 minutes), students create a comparative table documenting the top 5 features from both methods, noting ranking differences and explaining why discrepancies occur. They write detailed explanations for each selected patient case, describing how specific feature values (e.g., 'number of medications = 15') push predictions above or below the base rate. Students must identify at least two instances where local SHAP values contradict global importance rankings and provide clinical reasoning for these differences. Finally, they prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their findings to another pair, focusing on actionable insights for healthcare practitioners. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share one surprising finding about feature interactions or importance reversals.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and SHAP libraries installed
Pre-processed diabetes readmission dataset (1000 patient records)
Pre-trained Random Forest model file (.pkl format)
Python notebook template with code scaffolding for SHAP analysis
Patient case study handout with clinical context for selected examples
assessment_method: Evaluate student submissions using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of SHAP plot interpretations (25 points) - correctly identifying direction and magnitude of feature contributions, (2) Quality of global vs. local importance comparison (25 points) - identifying at least 3 meaningful differences with explanations, (3) Clinical reasoning integration (25 points) - connecting feature importance patterns to healthcare domain knowledge, (4) Communication clarity (25 points) - presenting findings with appropriate technical vocabulary and logical flow. Students must achieve 80% (80/100 points) to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional guided questions such as 'Which feature has the largest positive SHAP value for Patient A?' and 'How does this patient's HbA1c level compare to the dataset average?' Offer color-coded interpretation guides for reading SHAP plots. For advanced learners, extend the activity by asking them to investigate feature interactions using SHAP interaction values, or challenge them to propose alternative interpretability methods (LIME, Anchors) and justify when each approach would be most appropriate. Provide additional patient cases with edge cases or unusual feature combinations.

title: Family Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Expenses
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional family of four using percentage calculations to allocate income across essential categories. They will apply percentage increase/decrease concepts to adjust for unexpected expenses and income changes.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by calculating specific amounts for housing, food, transportation, and savings categories
Students will demonstrate percentage increase and decrease concepts through adjusting budget categories when income or expenses change unexpectedly
instructions: Begin by distributing the Family Budget Worksheet and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario provides a family profile with monthly income, family size, and location. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to complete Part 1: calculating basic budget allocations using provided percentage guidelines (30% housing, 15% food, 20% transportation, 10% utilities, 15% miscellaneous, 10% savings). They must show all work using the formula: (percentage ÷ 100) × total income = category amount. Next, introduce Part 2 (15 minutes): students draw a 'Budget Challenge' card containing scenarios like '15% salary increase' or 'car repair costs $800.' They must recalculate affected categories and explain their reasoning in writing. For Part 3 (15 minutes), pair students to compare their solutions and discuss different approaches to handling budget challenges. Each pair creates one recommendation for their assigned family. Conclude with a 5-minute gallery walk where pairs post their final budgets and walk around to view others' solutions, noting creative approaches to budget management.
materials_needed: Family Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Family scenario cards (6 different scenarios)
Budget Challenge cards (12 different challenge scenarios)
Calculators (one per student)
Large poster paper for final recommendations
Markers or colored pencils
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of percentage calculations - all basic allocations correct within $5, (2) Problem-solving approach - shows clear work for challenge scenarios and explains reasoning, (3) Mathematical communication - uses proper percentage terminology and explains process clearly, (4) Real-world application - final recommendations demonstrate understanding of practical budget constraints and family needs.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a percentage calculation reference sheet and pairing them with stronger math partners. Offer a simplified scenario with round numbers ($3000 income vs $2847). For advanced learners, add compound scenarios like 'salary increase AND unexpected medical bills' or have them research actual cost-of-living data for their assigned city to verify budget realism.

title: Database Normalization Analysis: Identifying and Correcting Normal Form Violations
description: Students will analyze a poorly designed database schema containing multiple normalization violations. They will systematically identify specific violations of 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF, then redesign the schema to eliminate redundancy and improve data integrity.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database schemas by identifying specific violations of first, second, and third normal forms using formal normalization rules
Students will decompose unnormalized tables through systematic application of normalization principles to eliminate data redundancy
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'University Course Management' database schema containing a single table with fields: StudentID, StudentName, StudentEmail, CourseID, CourseName, InstructorName, InstructorOffice, Department, Credits, Grade, Semester. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. Step 1 (10 minutes): Students examine the sample data (15 records provided) and identify all functional dependencies using arrow notation (A→B). Step 2 (15 minutes): Students systematically check each normal form. For 1NF, they identify any multi-valued attributes or atomic value violations. For 2NF, they find partial dependencies where non-key attributes depend on part of a composite key. For 3NF, they locate transitive dependencies where non-key attributes depend on other non-key attributes. Students must document each violation with specific field names and explain why it violates the normal form. Step 3 (20 minutes): Students redesign the schema by decomposing the original table into properly normalized tables. They must draw the new schema showing primary keys, foreign keys, and relationships. Each pair creates a final deliverable showing: original schema with violations marked and explained, decomposition process with intermediate steps, and final normalized schema with sample data distributed across the new tables.
materials_needed: Printed 'University Course Management' schema with 15 sample records
Normal form reference sheet with formal definitions
Graph paper or digital diagramming tool (Lucidchart/Draw.io)
Colored pens for marking different types of dependencies
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Functional dependency identification - correctly identifies 8+ dependencies with proper notation, (2) Violation analysis - accurately identifies and explains at least 3 specific normal form violations, (3) Schema decomposition - creates properly normalized tables with correct primary/foreign keys, (4) Data integrity - demonstrates understanding by showing how normalization eliminates specific redundancy issues in the sample data
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed functional dependency list and focus on one normal form at a time. Use color-coding to highlight different types of dependencies. For advanced learners: Extend to BCNF analysis and ask them to consider performance trade-offs of their normalization decisions. Have them analyze query complexity before and after normalization.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Pipeline Architectures for Real-World Business Impact
description: Students will critically evaluate three different end-to-end machine learning pipeline architectures designed to solve the same business problem, assessing their technical merit, business viability, and ethical implications. They will synthesize their analysis into justified recommendations for stakeholder decision-making.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate competing ML pipeline architectures by systematically comparing performance metrics, scalability constraints, and implementation complexity using established evaluation frameworks
Students will critique business and ethical implications of different modeling approaches through structured risk-benefit analysis and stakeholder impact assessment
instructions: **Phase 1: Case Study Setup (45 minutes)** Present students with a realistic business scenario: predicting customer churn for a telecommunications company. Provide three pre-built pipeline architectures: (1) Traditional feature engineering + Random Forest, (2) Deep learning with automated feature extraction, and (3) Ensemble approach combining multiple algorithms. Each pipeline includes documentation, performance metrics on validation data, computational requirements, and implementation timelines. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. **Phase 2: Technical Evaluation (90 minutes)** Teams systematically evaluate each pipeline using provided evaluation matrices covering: model performance (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score), computational efficiency (training time, inference latency, memory usage), scalability (data volume handling, real-time processing capability), maintainability (code complexity, documentation quality, debugging ease), and robustness (performance across different data segments, handling of edge cases). Students document findings in structured comparison tables with supporting evidence. **Phase 3: Business Impact Analysis (60 minutes)** Teams assess business implications including: implementation costs (development time, infrastructure requirements, maintenance overhead), operational risk (system reliability, failure modes, rollback procedures), regulatory compliance (data privacy, model explainability requirements), and stakeholder impact (customer experience, business revenue, employee workflow changes). **Phase 4: Synthesis and Recommendation (45 minutes)** Teams synthesize technical and business evaluations to create ranked recommendations with detailed justifications, identifying optimal solutions for different scenarios (budget-constrained, performance-critical, rapid deployment). Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation with supporting slides and executive summary document.
materials_needed: Three documented ML pipeline codebases with performance benchmarks
Business case study packet with company background and constraints
Evaluation framework templates (technical and business assessment matrices)
Access to Jupyter notebooks or similar development environment
Presentation software and projection capabilities
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: Technical Analysis Depth (thorough evaluation of all technical dimensions with supporting evidence), Business Acumen (realistic assessment of implementation challenges and stakeholder impacts), Critical Thinking Quality (identification of trade-offs, consideration of multiple perspectives, acknowledgment of limitations), and Communication Effectiveness (clear presentation of complex analysis, justified recommendations with actionable next steps). Final deliverables include completed evaluation matrices, executive summary document, and oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation checklists with specific questions to guide analysis, offer one-on-one consultation during evaluation phases, and suggest focusing on fewer evaluation criteria in greater depth. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose hybrid solutions combining strengths of different approaches, conduct additional analysis on edge cases or alternative business scenarios, or research and incorporate cutting-edge evaluation methodologies from recent literature.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Sales Data
description: Students will analyze a provided sales dataset to identify, compare, and explain the characteristics of different statistical distributions found in customer behavior metrics. They will demonstrate understanding by describing how distribution shapes reveal business insights and matching observed patterns to theoretical distribution types.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by examining histograms and summary statistics of customer purchase amounts, return frequencies, and seasonal sales patterns
Students will explain the business implications of distribution characteristics through written interpretation of three different sales metrics
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'RetailMetrics2024.csv' dataset containing 5,000 customer records with purchase_amount, days_between_purchases, and seasonal_sales_score columns. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes using Python/R or Excel to create histograms for each variable and calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation. Next, facilitate a 15-minute partner discussion where students compare their visualizations and identify distribution shapes using provided reference cards showing normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, uniform, and bimodal distributions. During minutes 35-50, students complete the 'Distribution Detective Worksheet' where they match each variable to a distribution type and write 2-3 sentences explaining what each distribution reveals about customer behavior (e.g., 'The right-skewed purchase amount distribution indicates most customers make small purchases, but a few high-value customers significantly impact revenue'). Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where 3-4 student pairs share one insight, focusing on connecting mathematical properties to business meaning. Circulate during individual work to check histogram accuracy and guide students struggling with distribution identification using the shape-comparison strategy.
materials_needed: RetailMetrics2024.csv dataset with 5,000 customer records
Distribution Detective Worksheet (PDF printout)
Statistical distribution reference cards showing 5 distribution types
Python/R/Excel access for each student
Histogram creation guide handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Distribution Detective Worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all three distribution types with accurate, detailed business explanations; (3) Correctly identifies 2-3 distributions with adequate explanations; (2) Correctly identifies 1-2 distributions with basic explanations; (1) Identifies fewer than 2 distributions or provides minimal explanations. Additionally, observe partner discussions for accurate use of statistical vocabulary and logical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide histogram templates with pre-marked bins and offer the 'shape-first, name-second' approach focusing on visual patterns before terminology. For advanced learners, include additional variables like customer_lifetime_value for analysis and challenge them to calculate skewness coefficients to quantify asymmetry. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during the partner discussion phase.

title: Optimizing Urban Water Distribution Networks Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world water distribution optimization problem for a growing city district. They will formulate constraints, define objective functions, and implement the simplex method to determine optimal pipe capacity allocations while minimizing costs and meeting demand requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to model a multi-variable water distribution optimization problem by translating real-world constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method algorithm through systematic tableau operations to determine optimal resource allocation solutions
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Setup (20 minutes)** - Distribute the Water District Scenario handout describing a city expansion requiring water distribution to 4 new neighborhoods with varying demand levels (500, 750, 1200, and 900 thousand gallons daily). Organize students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives different cost coefficients for three pipe types (small: $50/unit, medium: $120/unit, large: $200/unit) and capacity constraints. **Phase 2: Mathematical Formulation (25 minutes)** - Teams identify decision variables (x₁, x₂, x₃ representing quantities of each pipe type), formulate the objective function (minimize total cost), and establish constraints including: minimum flow requirements for each neighborhood, maximum installation capacity per day (80 units), and non-negativity constraints. Students must create at least 6 constraint equations. **Phase 3: Simplex Implementation (35 minutes)** - Using provided simplex tableau templates, teams set up initial tableaux with slack variables. Students perform pivot operations systematically: identify entering variable (most negative coefficient), determine leaving variable (minimum ratio test), and execute row operations to achieve optimal solution. Teams must show all pivot steps with calculations. **Phase 4: Solution Interpretation (15 minutes)** - Teams analyze final tableau to determine optimal pipe quantities, calculate minimum cost, and identify shadow prices for each constraint. **Phase 5: Presentation (25 minutes)** - Each team presents their optimization model, solution process, and recommendations to the class, explaining trade-offs and sensitivity analysis findings.
materials_needed: Water District Scenario handouts with unique cost parameters per team
Pre-formatted simplex tableau worksheets (initial and continuation sheets)
Graphing calculators or laptops with Excel/Google Sheets
Large poster paper and markers for solution presentations
Linear Programming Reference Guide with simplex method steps
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct mathematical formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate execution of simplex method with proper pivot operations shown (35%), (3) Correct interpretation of optimal solution and shadow prices (25%), (4) Clear presentation of recommendations with justification (15%). Students must submit completed tableau worksheets, written solution summary, and deliver 5-minute team presentation. Success requires achieving 3/4 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates with partially completed examples, offer simplex method cheat sheets with step-by-step pivot instructions, and allow use of online simplex calculators for verification after manual completion. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis extensions, challenge them to model additional constraints (environmental impact, installation time windows), or explore integer programming modifications for discrete pipe quantities.

title: Reverse Engineering Security Vulnerabilities in Authentication Systems
description: Students will analyze a deliberately vulnerable authentication system by examining source code, identifying multiple security flaws, and tracing the logical flow that enables each vulnerability. They will then categorize vulnerabilities by severity and propose specific remediation strategies based on their analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze authentication system source code by systematically examining control flow, data validation, and session management to identify security vulnerabilities
Students will differentiate between various vulnerability types through detailed code tracing and impact assessment of SQL injection, session fixation, and privilege escalation flaws
instructions: Begin by providing students with a Node.js/Express authentication system containing 8 deliberately planted vulnerabilities (SQL injection in login, weak session management, missing input validation, privilege escalation, timing attacks, password storage issues, session fixation, and CSRF). Students work in pairs for 180 minutes total. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Students perform static code analysis, reading through login.js, session.js, and user.js files, creating a flow diagram of the authentication process and noting suspicious code patterns. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Students use dynamic analysis by running the application locally, attempting various attack vectors, and documenting which inputs trigger unexpected behaviors. They must trace each successful attack back to specific lines of code and explain the logical flaw. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Students categorize each discovered vulnerability using OWASP Top 10 classifications, assign CVSS scores, and create a prioritized remediation plan with specific code fixes. They must also identify any vulnerabilities they missed by comparing against a provided checklist. Students document findings in a structured security analysis report with code snippets, attack demonstrations, and fix recommendations.
materials_needed: Vulnerable Node.js authentication application (provided GitHub repository)
Local development environment with Node.js 18+, MongoDB, and npm installed
OWASP Top 10 reference guide
CVSS calculator access
Code analysis tools: ESLint security plugin and Snyk CLI
assessment_method: Students submit a security analysis report (40 points) evaluated on: vulnerability identification completeness (15 pts - must find 6/8 vulnerabilities), technical accuracy of code analysis (15 pts), and quality of remediation proposals (10 pts). Live demonstration (10 points) where students show 3 working exploits and explain the underlying code flaws. Rubric includes deductions for incorrect OWASP classifications or incomplete impact analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a code review checklist focusing on input validation and SQL query construction patterns, offer pre-configured debugging environment with console logging enabled. For advanced learners: challenge them to craft automated exploit scripts, analyze the application's compiled bytecode for additional vulnerabilities, or research zero-day attack vectors not covered in OWASP Top 10.

title: Design a Community Garden: Area and Perimeter Optimization Project
description: Students will design an original community garden layout by creating geometric shapes with specific area and perimeter constraints. They will develop mathematical models to optimize space usage and present their designs with detailed calculations and justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original garden design by applying area and perimeter formulas for rectangles, triangles, and circles to meet specified constraints
Students will construct mathematical models through systematic calculation and optimization to justify their design choices
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: students are landscape designers tasked with creating a 500 square meter community garden with a budget allowing for 100 meters of fencing. Distribute design sheets and calculators to individual students (10 minutes). 

Step 1: Students sketch their initial garden layout using at least three different geometric shapes (rectangles for vegetable plots, circles for flower beds, triangles for herb sections). Each shape must be labeled with dimensions (20 minutes).

Step 2: Students calculate the area of each section using appropriate formulas (A = lw, A = πr², A = ½bh) and verify the total area equals exactly 500 m². They must show all work with units (25 minutes).

Step 3: Students determine the perimeter of their entire garden design and calculate required fencing costs at $5 per meter. If over budget, they must redesign sections and recalculate (20 minutes).

Step 4: Students create a second design variation, comparing efficiency by calculating the area-to-perimeter ratio for both designs. They must justify which design better serves the community using mathematical evidence (15 minutes).

Step 5: Students prepare a 3-minute presentation including their final design drawing, calculation summary table, cost analysis, and mathematical justification for their choices (15 minutes preparation).

Conclude with student presentations where peers evaluate designs using the provided rubric criteria (remaining time).
materials_needed: Graph paper or design sheets (1 per student)
Scientific calculators
Rulers and compasses for precise drawings
Colored pencils or markers
Project rubric handouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area and perimeter calculations (25%), (2) Creative and practical design elements (25%), (3) Optimization reasoning and cost analysis (25%), (4) Clear presentation of mathematical justification (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in mathematical accuracy to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing formula reference sheets and breaking calculations into smaller steps with checkpoints. For advanced learners, add constraints like irregular plot boundaries or introduce concepts of maximizing growing space while minimizing maintenance paths. Consider pairing students strategically for peer support during calculation phases.

title: Computer Architecture Components Memory Palace Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific components, specifications, and interconnections of a complex computer system architecture through intensive flashcard drills and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of advanced system components including cache hierarchies, instruction pipelines, and memory subsystems.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the names, functions, and specifications of 50+ computer architecture components by completing timed memorization drills
Students will identify specific CPU instruction pipeline stages and cache hierarchy levels through structured recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Computer Architecture Component Reference Sheet containing 52 specific components (L1/L2/L3 cache specifications, ALU subunits, branch predictors, TLB structures, etc.). Students have 15 minutes to study the sheet silently, focusing on exact names, bit widths, and cycle timings. Next, implement the Memory Palace technique: students spend 10 minutes creating mental associations between components and familiar locations in their home/school. Conduct Round 1 recall test (10 minutes): display component diagrams on screen, students write exact names and one key specification for each of 25 randomly selected components. Provide 5 minutes for students to review missed items using the reference sheet. Execute Round 2 intensive drill (15 minutes): use rapid-fire verbal questioning where students must immediately state the function when given a component name (e.g., 'Branch Target Buffer' → 'Predicts target addresses for indirect branches'). Follow with Round 3 reverse recall (10 minutes): provide functions, students must write exact component names. Conclude with comprehensive assessment (15 minutes): students complete a closed-book worksheet identifying all components in a complex processor block diagram, including cache sizes, pipeline stages, and bus widths. Throughout the activity, maintain strict timing and encourage speed with accuracy.
materials_needed: Computer Architecture Component Reference Sheet (52 items with specifications)
Complex processor block diagram for final assessment
Digital timer/stopwatch
Blank recall worksheets
Answer key with exact specifications
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on the final block diagram identification worksheet, correctly naming at least 44 of 52 components with proper specifications. Grade based on: exact component names (2 points each), correct specifications like bit-width or cycle count (1 point each), and proper placement identification (1 point each). Maximum score: 156 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for complex component names, allow color-coding during study phase, and offer additional 5-minute review periods between rounds. For advanced learners: include additional components from specialized architectures (GPU compute units, vector processing elements), require explanations of component interdependencies, and add timing constraints for professional-level recall speed.

title: Interpreting Complex Machine Learning Model Performance Through Cross-Validation Metrics Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret comprehensive performance metrics from a multi-fold cross-validation study of ensemble models on an imbalanced healthcare dataset. They will explain the relationships between different evaluation metrics and justify model selection decisions based on business constraints and metric trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationships between precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR metrics by analyzing cross-validation results across multiple model architectures
Students will explain the implications of model performance variance across folds through statistical significance testing and confidence interval analysis
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a pre-generated dataset containing 5-fold cross-validation results for Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Neural Network models trained on a medical diagnosis dataset (10,000 samples, 15% positive class). Each student receives identical Excel/CSV files with 15 rows (3 models × 5 folds) and columns for: Model Type, Fold, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, AUC-ROC, AUC-PR, Training Time, and False Positive/Negative counts.

**Phase 1 - Metric Relationships Analysis (25 minutes):** Students create scatter plots comparing precision vs. recall for all model-fold combinations, then calculate Pearson correlation coefficients between F1-score and AUC-PR metrics. They must identify which model shows the most consistent precision-recall trade-off across folds and explain why AUC-ROC might be misleading for this imbalanced dataset.

**Phase 2 - Statistical Significance Testing (30 minutes):** Students perform paired t-tests comparing mean AUC-PR scores between Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models across the 5 folds. They calculate 95% confidence intervals for each model's mean performance and determine if observed differences are statistically significant (α = 0.05). Students must interpret what p-values and confidence interval overlaps mean for model selection.

**Phase 3 - Business Context Integration (25 minutes):** Given a scenario where false negatives cost $50,000 and false positives cost $2,000, students calculate expected cost per prediction for each model using average confusion matrix values. They must justify final model selection by weighing statistical performance, cost implications, and model interpretability requirements. Students document their reasoning in a structured decision matrix format.
materials_needed: Cross-validation results dataset (Excel/CSV format with 15 rows × 10 columns)
Statistical analysis software (Excel with Data Analysis ToolPak, R, or Python)
Graphing capabilities (Excel charts or matplotlib/ggplot2)
Decision matrix template worksheet
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients (25 points), (2) Accurate statistical significance testing with proper p-value interpretation (30 points), (3) Cost-benefit analysis showing correct expected value calculations (25 points), (4) Justified model recommendation addressing all constraints with clear reasoning (20 points). Students must submit scatter plots, t-test results, cost calculations, and 300-word written justification.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide correlation coefficient interpretation guide and t-test calculation templates. Offer decision tree flowchart for systematic model comparison. **Advanced extension:** Add ensemble combination analysis where students determine optimal weighted averaging of top 2 models based on validation performance, or include fairness metrics analysis across demographic subgroups in the dataset.

title: Shopping Mall Floor Plan: Applying Area and Perimeter Calculations
description: Students will create a floor plan for a small shopping mall using given constraints, then calculate the area and perimeter of each store space. They will apply their knowledge of rectangles, squares, and composite shapes to solve real-world spatial problems.
learning_objectives: Students will apply area and perimeter formulas for rectangles and squares by designing store layouts within specific dimensional constraints
Students will calculate total areas and perimeters of composite shapes through measuring and computing their shopping mall floor plan designs
instructions: Begin by distributing grid paper and the 'Mall Design Requirements' handout to each student (5 minutes). Explain that students are architects designing a small shopping mall with exactly 6 stores on a 20×15 grid where each square represents 1 square meter. Read through the constraints together: the mall must include one large anchor store (minimum 40 square meters), two medium stores (15-25 square meters each), three small stores (8-12 square meters each), and walkways that are exactly 2 meters wide connecting all stores. Students work individually to sketch their floor plan, ensuring all stores are rectangular or square shapes (20 minutes). Once designs are complete, students use rulers to verify their grid measurements and calculate the area and perimeter of each individual store, recording results in the provided calculation table (15 minutes). Next, students calculate the total retail space area, total walkway area, and the perimeter of the entire mall exterior (10 minutes). In pairs, students present their designs to a partner, explaining their spatial reasoning and verifying each other's calculations using calculators (15 minutes). Partners check that all constraint requirements are met and mathematical calculations are accurate. Finally, conduct a whole-class gallery walk where students post their designs and walk around to observe different solutions, noting creative approaches to meeting the same constraints (10 minutes). Conclude by having 2-3 students share how they solved the challenge of fitting all required stores while maintaining proper walkway access.
materials_needed: 1cm grid paper (one sheet per student)
Mall Design Requirements handout with constraints listed
Calculation recording table worksheet
Rulers (centimeter measurements)
Calculators
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Design meets all 6 store requirements and walkway specifications, (2) Area calculations are accurate for all stores and total spaces, (3) Perimeter calculations are correct for individual stores and mall exterior, (4) Student can explain their spatial reasoning during partner presentation. Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher with mandatory accuracy on mathematical calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example floor plan and have them focus on calculating areas/perimeters of given shapes before designing their own. For advanced learners: Add constraints like 'stores cannot be longer than 8 meters in any direction' or require them to calculate the cost of flooring at $25 per square meter for stores and $15 per square meter for walkways.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Pipeline Architectures for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will comprehensively evaluate three distinct machine learning pipeline architectures designed to predict customer churn, analyzing their methodological soundness, implementation quality, and business impact. They will synthesize their findings into evidence-based recommendations for production deployment, considering technical performance, interpretability, scalability, and ethical implications.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the methodological rigor of different ML pipeline architectures by systematically analyzing feature engineering approaches, model selection rationale, validation strategies, and bias mitigation techniques

Students will synthesize quantitative performance metrics with qualitative business considerations through comprehensive comparison frameworks that weigh technical accuracy against interpretability, fairness, and operational constraints
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Distribute three pre-built ML pipelines (Pipeline A: Traditional logistic regression with manual feature engineering, Pipeline B: Ensemble methods with automated feature selection, Pipeline C: Deep learning with embedding layers). Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team receiving identical datasets (training: 50,000 customer records, validation: 15,000, test: 10,000) and standardized evaluation criteria sheets. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams systematically execute each pipeline, documenting performance metrics (AUC-ROC, precision/recall, F1-score), computational requirements (training time, memory usage), and interpretability scores using SHAP values. They must identify and document at least three methodological strengths and weaknesses per pipeline, focusing on data preprocessing decisions, hyperparameter optimization approaches, and cross-validation strategies. **Phase 3 (45 minutes):** Teams analyze business impact by calculating expected revenue implications using provided customer lifetime value data ($2,400 average CLV, $50 retention campaign cost). They evaluate fairness metrics across demographic groups using demographic parity and equalized odds measures. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Teams prepare 8-minute presentations defending their pipeline recommendation, addressing a panel of 'stakeholders' (instructor and guest industry professional if possible). Presentations must include quantitative evidence, risk assessment, implementation timeline, and monitoring strategy.
materials_needed: Three pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with distinct ML pipeline architectures
Synthetic customer churn dataset (75,000 records with 23 features including demographics, usage patterns, and service history)
Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, SHAP, fairlearn libraries installed
Evaluation criteria rubric with weighted scoring for technical performance (40%), business impact (30%), methodology (20%), and presentation quality (10%)
Customer lifetime value reference sheet with industry benchmarks
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed evaluation matrix comparing all three pipelines across 15 criteria with numerical scores and written justifications (40 points), (2) Executive summary report (2 pages) with final recommendation including risk mitigation strategies (30 points), (3) Peer evaluation of presentation defending methodology and addressing stakeholder questions (20 points), (4) Individual reflection essay analyzing how different stakeholder priorities (data scientist, product manager, compliance officer) might lead to different pipeline choices (10 points). Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated ability to synthesize technical and business considerations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation framework templates with specific questions for each criterion and sample calculations for business impact metrics. Offer guided worksheet for SHAP interpretation and fairness metric calculation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose hybrid approaches combining strengths of multiple pipelines, conduct sensitivity analysis on key hyperparameters, or design A/B testing framework for production deployment. Encourage exploration of emerging fairness-aware ML techniques.

title: Design and Construct a Predictive Financial Model for Multi-Variable Investment Portfolio Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical model that integrates calculus, probability theory, and linear algebra to optimize investment portfolios under real market constraints. They will develop their own algorithms, validate predictions against historical data, and present defendable investment strategies to simulated stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multivariable calculus, matrix operations, and statistical analysis by constructing an original portfolio optimization algorithm that maximizes expected returns while minimizing risk
Students will design and implement a comprehensive mathematical model through iterative testing, validation, and refinement using real financial datasets spanning multiple market conditions
instructions: Begin by forming teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes). Provide each team with identical datasets containing 5 years of daily stock prices for 20 companies across different sectors, plus corresponding economic indicators (GDP growth, inflation rates, interest rates). Teams first spend 45 minutes exploring the data to identify patterns and correlations using statistical software. Next, students design their unique optimization model (60 minutes): they must mathematically define their objective function incorporating expected return and risk measures, establish at least 5 realistic constraints (budget limitations, diversification requirements, sector allocations), and determine their solution methodology (gradient descent, linear programming, or custom algorithm). During the 90-minute construction phase, teams implement their model using programming tools, creating functions that calculate portfolio weights, expected returns, and risk metrics. They must validate their model by backtesting on historical data from 2018-2020, comparing predicted vs. actual portfolio performance. In the final 45 minutes, teams prepare presentations including: mathematical derivation of their model, justification of chosen constraints and parameters, backtesting results with statistical significance tests, and recommendations for a $1 million investment allocation. Each team presents their model to the class (acting as investment committee) for 8 minutes, followed by 7 minutes of peer questioning focusing on mathematical rigor and practical applicability.
materials_needed: Historical stock price datasets for 20 companies (5-year daily data in CSV format)
Economic indicator datasets (GDP, inflation, interest rates) with corresponding time periods
Computer access with Python/R/MATLAB and relevant libraries (NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, optimization toolboxes)
Statistical software for data analysis and visualization
Presentation software and projection capabilities
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical sophistication and originality of model (25 points), proper integration of multiple mathematical domains (20 points), validation methodology and statistical rigor (20 points), backtesting accuracy and interpretation (15 points), presentation clarity and defense of methodology (10 points), innovation in constraint formulation or solution approach (10 points). Teams must submit written mathematical derivations, documented code, and backtesting results. Success requires demonstrating clear mathematical reasoning, statistically significant backtesting results, and ability to defend methodological choices under peer scrutiny.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template frameworks for common optimization problems and step-by-step guides for implementing basic portfolio theory equations. Offer pre-coded functions for data import and basic statistical calculations. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as transaction costs, short-selling constraints, or behavioral finance factors. Encourage exploration of advanced optimization techniques like genetic algorithms or machine learning integration. Provide optional resources on stochastic calculus and advanced risk measures for students seeking greater mathematical depth.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results to Explain Model Performance Patterns
description: Students will analyze k-fold cross-validation output from three different machine learning models to understand why certain models perform better on specific datasets. They will interpret variance patterns, bias-variance tradeoffs, and explain the relationship between model complexity and generalization performance.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation metrics (mean, standard deviation, fold-wise scores) by comparing performance patterns across linear regression, random forest, and neural network models
Students will explain the relationship between model complexity and performance variance through analysis of cross-validation score distributions and bias-variance indicators
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-computed 10-fold cross-validation results for three models (Linear Regression, Random Forest with 100 trees, Multi-layer Perceptron) trained on a housing price dataset. Display results showing: fold-wise R² scores, mean scores, standard deviations, and training vs. validation score gaps for each model. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to create visual representations of the cross-validation results using box plots or violin plots, plotting the distribution of scores across folds for each model. They should calculate and annotate the coefficient of variation for each model.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Guide students through interpreting patterns by asking specific questions: 'Which model shows the highest variance across folds and why?' 'What does the training-validation gap indicate about overfitting?' Students document their interpretations in a structured worksheet.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students categorize each model's behavior using provided definitions: high bias/low variance, low bias/high variance, or balanced. They must justify their categorization using specific numerical evidence from the cross-validation results.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Pairs present one key insight about why the Random Forest model shows different variance patterns compared to Linear Regression, referencing specific fold scores and relating this to the underlying algorithmic differences.

Conclude with a brief discussion connecting cross-validation interpretation to real-world model selection decisions, emphasizing when high variance might be acceptable versus problematic.
materials_needed: Pre-computed cross-validation results dataset (CSV format with fold-wise scores)
Python environment with matplotlib/seaborn or Excel for visualization
Cross-validation interpretation worksheet with guided questions
Model behavior categorization reference sheet with bias-variance definitions
