assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate calculation and visualization of score distributions (25%), (2) Correct interpretation of variance patterns with numerical evidence (35%), (3) Appropriate categorization of model bias-variance characteristics with justification (25%), (4) Clear explanation of the relationship between algorithmic complexity and cross-validation patterns (15%). Students must achieve level 3 or higher in at least 3 categories to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed box plots and focus on pattern recognition rather than calculation. Offer sentence starters like 'The high standard deviation in Model X suggests...' For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them propose optimal hyperparameters based on the cross-validation patterns or analyze learning curves alongside cross-validation results to deepen bias-variance understanding.

title: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Linear Programming
description: Students apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world traffic optimization problem by modeling intersection constraints, formulating objective functions, and implementing the simplex method. They will analyze traffic data from a four-intersection urban grid to minimize average wait times while satisfying safety and capacity constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to model real-world traffic flow constraints by translating traffic capacity limitations, safety requirements, and timing restrictions into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method to optimize traffic light timing sequences through systematic calculation and interpretation of optimal solutions for urban intersection management
instructions:
Begin by distributing traffic flow data sheets containing hourly vehicle counts for a four-intersection grid (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the scenario: downtown intersections A, B, C, D with given traffic volumes, maximum capacity constraints, and minimum green light duration requirements. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams identify decision variables (green light duration for each direction at each intersection), constraints (minimum/maximum timing limits, total cycle time = 120 seconds, pedestrian crossing requirements), and objective function (minimize total vehicle wait time using provided formula). 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students formulate the complete linear programming model, writing out all constraint inequalities and the objective function. Instructor circulates to verify formulations before proceeding.

Step 3 (35 minutes): Using provided simplex method templates or software tools (Excel Solver/Python), teams solve their optimization problem. They must document each iteration of the simplex tableau or software inputs/outputs.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams interpret their optimal solution, calculating actual wait times, identifying binding constraints, and performing sensitivity analysis on at least two parameters.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their optimal timing solution to the class, explaining their constraint formulation rationale and comparing results with other teams. Instructor facilitates discussion on solution variations and real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Traffic flow data sheets with hourly vehicle counts for four intersections
Linear programming formulation worksheets with constraint templates
Excel with Solver add-in or Python with scipy.optimize installed
Calculators for manual simplex method calculations
Graph paper for plotting feasible regions (if 2-variable simplification used)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation with all constraints and objective function properly identified (25 points), (2) Accurate application of simplex method or software implementation with documented steps (30 points), (3) Correct interpretation of optimal solution including sensitivity analysis (25 points), (4) Clear presentation explaining methodology and real-world implications (20 points). Teams must submit written solution documentation and deliver 5-minute presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint formulation templates and offer a simplified 2-intersection version with graphical solution method. Supply step-by-step simplex method reference cards. For advanced learners: Introduce integer programming constraints for discrete timing intervals, add stochastic elements with variable traffic patterns, or extend to network flow optimization across multiple city blocks with interconnected timing dependencies.

title: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Linear Programming: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world traffic optimization problem for a city intersection network. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the simplex method to determine optimal traffic light timing patterns that minimize overall wait times.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to model traffic flow constraints by translating real-world intersection data into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method to solve multi-variable optimization problems through systematic tableau operations and pivot calculations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the City Traffic Dataset containing traffic volume data for a 4-intersection network during peak hours (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one of four traffic scenarios: morning rush hour, evening rush hour, weekend shopping, or emergency vehicle priority. Each team receives intersection maps showing traffic flow directions, current light timing, and average vehicle counts per minute.

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze their scenario data to identify decision variables (light timing for each direction at each intersection), constraints (minimum green time requirements, maximum cycle length, pedestrian crossing time), and the objective function (minimize total vehicle wait time). Students must write out at least 8 constraint inequalities and define 6-8 decision variables.

Step 2 (35 minutes): Convert the linear programming problem into standard form by introducing slack variables and creating the initial simplex tableau. Teams use graphing calculators or Excel to set up their tableau with all constraints, coefficients, and the objective function row properly formatted.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Apply the simplex method by identifying pivot elements, performing row operations, and iterating until reaching the optimal solution. Teams must show all pivot calculations and tableau transformations step-by-step.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Interpret the final solution by translating optimal values back into practical traffic light timing recommendations. Teams calculate the projected reduction in average wait time and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their solution.

Conclude with team presentations (15 minutes total) where each group presents their optimal timing strategy and projected improvements. Instructor facilitates comparison of different scenarios and discusses real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: City Traffic Dataset handouts (4 different scenarios)
Intersection layout maps with current timing data
Graphing calculators or laptops with Excel/spreadsheet software
Linear programming reference sheets with simplex method steps
Presentation timer and projection screen
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Problem formulation accuracy - correct identification of variables, constraints, and objective function (25%), (2) Mathematical execution - proper simplex method application with correct calculations (35%), (3) Solution interpretation - realistic traffic timing recommendations with justified wait time improvements (25%), (4) Presentation clarity - effective communication of methodology and results (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in mathematical execution to demonstrate proficiency at the apply level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates and simplex method step-by-step checklist. Pair weaker students with stronger teammates for calculations. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including pedestrian crossing optimization, multiple intersection coordination, or sensitivity analysis of the optimal solution. Encourage exploration of software-based linear programming solvers for comparison.
original_title: Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Linear Programming

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis: Dissecting a Multi-Layer Web Application Attack Vector
description: Students will analyze a complex, real-world web application containing multiple interconnected security vulnerabilities to identify attack vectors, trace exploitation paths, and evaluate the cascading impact of security flaws. This activity requires students to examine code, database configurations, and network traffic to understand how individual vulnerabilities combine to create critical security risks.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-layered security vulnerabilities by examining source code, database schemas, and network configurations to identify specific attack vectors and their interdependencies
Students will evaluate the cascading impact of combined security flaws through systematic vulnerability mapping and risk assessment techniques
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the 'VulnShop' vulnerable web application environment (pre-configured Docker container), network packet captures (PCAP files), and source code repository. In the first 45 minutes, students individually examine the provided materials: PHP/JavaScript source code, MySQL database dump, Apache configuration files, and Wireshark packet captures from a simulated attack. Students must document initial observations using the provided vulnerability assessment template. Next, teams collaborate for 60 minutes to map vulnerabilities systematically: identify each security flaw (SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, insecure direct object references, etc.), trace how attackers could chain these vulnerabilities, and analyze the network traffic to understand the actual exploitation sequence. Teams use the provided network diagram and vulnerability matrix spreadsheet to visualize attack paths. In the following 30 minutes, teams prioritize vulnerabilities using CVSS scoring methodology, considering both individual impact and combined exploitation potential. Finally, teams spend 45 minutes preparing a technical presentation that demonstrates one complete attack chain, explains the analysis methodology used, and justifies their risk prioritization decisions. Each team presents their findings in 10-minute presentations, followed by peer questioning sessions where other teams challenge the analysis and propose alternative attack vectors.
materials_needed: VulnShop Docker container with pre-configured vulnerable web application
Wireshark PCAP files containing captured attack traffic
Source code repository (PHP, JavaScript, HTML, SQL files)
Vulnerability assessment template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Network topology diagram of the application infrastructure
CVSS v3.1 calculator and reference guide
Laptops with Docker, Wireshark, and text editors installed
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Vulnerability identification accuracy (25 points - must identify at least 6 of 8 planted vulnerabilities), Attack chain analysis depth (25 points - correctly trace multi-step exploitation paths), Technical analysis quality (25 points - accurate code review and network traffic interpretation), Risk assessment justification (25 points - proper CVSS scoring and impact evaluation). Students must submit their completed vulnerability matrix, annotated code snippets showing specific flaws, and a technical report explaining their most critical attack chain discovery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vulnerability hints worksheet with specific line numbers to examine in source code, and offer guided questions for packet analysis. Create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Include additional zero-day style vulnerabilities requiring deeper analysis, challenge them to develop proof-of-concept exploits, or have them research and present recent CVE examples that match discovered vulnerability patterns.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Model
description: Students will design a scaled city layout using geometric principles, area calculations, and proportional reasoning. They will create both a physical model and mathematical documentation that demonstrates their understanding of measurement, scale, and spatial relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will create a scaled city model by applying geometric principles, area calculations, and proportional reasoning to design functional urban spaces
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts of measurement, scale, and spatial relationships through developing comprehensive planning documentation and cost analysis
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Introduce the challenge: design a city for 50,000 residents on a 2km × 2km plot. Distribute city planning constraint cards (minimum 30% green space, residential areas for population density, commercial zones, transportation networks). Students form teams of 3-4 and select their city theme (eco-friendly, tech hub, historic, etc.). **Phase 2 (40 minutes):** Teams calculate required areas using provided population density standards (residential: 100 people per hectare, commercial: 2% of residential area, schools: 1 per 1,000 residents requiring 2 hectares each). Students create detailed area calculations worksheet showing all mathematical work. Using 1:10,000 scale (1cm = 100m), teams sketch their city layout on grid paper, ensuring all zones fit within the 20cm × 20cm boundary. **Phase 3 (35 minutes):** Teams build 3D models using cardboard, foam blocks, and craft materials. Buildings must be proportionally scaled (average house height = 2mm, office buildings = 5-8mm). Students create legend showing building types and their real-world dimensions. **Phase 4 (25 minutes):** Teams prepare presentation boards including: scaled drawing with calculations, 3D model, population distribution chart, and cost analysis using provided price per square meter data ($200/m² residential, $500/m² commercial). Each team presents their city design explaining mathematical decisions and defending their layout choices to the class acting as city council.
materials_needed: 20cm × 20cm grid paper (1cm squares)
Cardboard pieces, foam blocks, craft materials for building
Rulers, protractors, calculators
City planning constraint cards (pre-printed)
Population density and cost data sheets
Presentation boards or poster paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across: Mathematical Accuracy (calculations correct, scale properly applied), Design Quality (constraints met, logical layout), Documentation (clear showing of work, complete cost analysis), and Presentation (mathematical reasoning explained, design defended). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 in Mathematical Accuracy to demonstrate mastery. Collect calculation worksheets and presentation boards as evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide area calculation templates, offer simplified building shapes (rectangles only), pair with stronger mathematical partner. For advanced learners: add budget constraints requiring optimization, include irregular plot boundaries, challenge them to incorporate mathematical concepts like traffic flow algorithms or population growth projections. Provide calculator access for all students but require showing manual calculation steps.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Model: Exercise 1
description: Students will create an original city layout using geometric principles, proportional reasoning, and algebraic relationships. They will design infrastructure, calculate areas and costs, and present their city plan with mathematical justifications for all design decisions.
estimated_duration: 105 minutes (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric concepts (area, perimeter, angles) and algebraic relationships to create an original city layout with mathematically justified infrastructure decisions
Students will construct cost-benefit models using proportional reasoning and linear equations through the design of public spaces, residential zones, and transportation systems
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute grid paper, calculators, and city planning worksheets. Display the city requirements on the board: minimum 50 square units residential, 20 square units commercial, 15 square units parks, road network connecting all zones, and $500,000 budget constraint.

**Phase 1 - Design Planning (25 minutes):** Students work individually to sketch their city layout on grid paper (1 unit = 1 city block). They must calculate the area of each zone using geometric formulas and ensure all requirements are met. Students create a data table recording zone areas, perimeters, and preliminary cost estimates using provided cost-per-unit rates ($5,000 per residential unit, $8,000 per commercial unit, $3,000 per park unit, $2,000 per road unit).

**Phase 2 - Mathematical Optimization (30 minutes):** Students refine their designs by creating algebraic equations representing total costs and constraints. They must show work for: total area calculations, budget equation (5000r + 8000c + 3000p + 2000d ≤ 500,000), and optimization decisions. Students adjust layouts to maximize citizen happiness points (assigned values for proximity between zones) while staying within budget.

**Phase 3 - Presentation Creation (25 minutes):** Students prepare a 3-minute presentation including: scaled city diagram with labeled dimensions, mathematical calculations sheet showing all area and cost work, written justification explaining how geometric and algebraic principles influenced their design choices, and comparison chart showing their solution versus the minimum requirements.

**Presentations (15 minutes):** Each student presents their city design, highlighting key mathematical decisions and defending their optimization choices to the class.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, minimum 20x20 grid per student)
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils or markers for zone coding
City Planning Worksheet with cost rates and requirements
Rulers for precise measurements
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area calculations, budget constraints met, algebraic work shown), Design Creativity (innovative layout solutions, aesthetic appeal, practical considerations), Mathematical Justification (clear explanations of geometric and algebraic decision-making, optimization reasoning), and Presentation Quality (clear communication of mathematical concepts, professional city diagram, effective time management). Each category worth 25 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn zone templates to trace, offer area calculation reference sheet with common geometric formulas, pair with stronger math partner for peer support. For advanced learners: Add population density constraints requiring ratio calculations, introduce coordinate geometry for precise road planning, challenge to create multiple city variants and compare efficiency using statistical measures.
original_title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Model

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Matrix Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units at each layer of the TCP/IP protocol stack through intensive flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network architecture that students must have instant access to for advanced networking concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact functions of each TCP/IP protocol stack layer (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) by completing timed memory exercises with 95% accuracy
Students will identify specific protocols and their corresponding layers through rapid-fire verbal recitation and written assessments
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet containing all four layers with their functions, protocols, and Protocol Data Units (PDUs). Give students 15 minutes to study the material silently, encouraging them to use memory techniques like acronyms or visualization. Next, collect all reference materials and conduct Phase 1: Layer Functions Recall. Display each layer name on screen for 30 seconds while students write down all functions from memory. Rotate through all four layers twice. In Phase 2: Protocol Placement Challenge, call out specific protocols (HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet, SMTP, UDP, ARP, DNS) and have students write the corresponding layer within 10 seconds per protocol. For Phase 3: PDU Identification, students must match each layer with its correct Protocol Data Unit (Application=Data, Transport=Segment, Internet=Packet, Network Access=Frame) within 2 minutes total. Conclude with Phase 4: Rapid-Fire Verbal Review where students stand and respond to random questions about layer functions, with incorrect answers requiring students to sit down. Continue until only students with perfect recall remain standing. End by redistributing reference sheets for final verification and self-correction of any errors made during the activity.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheets (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projection screen
Answer keys for instructor verification
Blank paper for student responses
assessment_method: Grade students on accuracy of written responses: Layer Functions (40 points - 10 per layer), Protocol Placement (40 points - 5 per protocol), PDU Matching (20 points - 5 per layer). Success criteria: 85/100 points minimum. Track verbal participation in final phase for bonus points. Immediate feedback provided through answer key review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide memory aids like 'All Transport Internet Network' acronym and allow color-coding of different layers. Create simplified function descriptions focusing on key verbs. For advanced learners: Add specific port numbers, include additional protocols like ICMP and DHCP, or require explanation of how data flows between layers during transmission.

title: Deconstructing Bias Propagation in Feature Engineering Pipelines for Credit Risk Models
description: Students will analyze a pre-built credit risk modeling pipeline to identify how demographic biases propagate through feature engineering transformations and compound across multiple preprocessing steps. They will trace bias amplification mechanisms from raw data through engineered features to understand systemic discrimination in automated lending decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will explain how categorical encoding methods (one-hot, target encoding, frequency encoding) differentially amplify demographic biases by analyzing transformation outputs across protected groups
Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between correlation-based feature selection and proxy discrimination through examination of feature correlation matrices and selection algorithms
instructions: Begin with 15 minutes of individual examination of the provided credit dataset (German Credit Data) and preprocessing pipeline code. Students should identify 5 potential bias sources in raw features. Next, form groups of 3-4 students for 45 minutes of collaborative analysis. Each group receives identical Jupyter notebooks with a complete sklearn pipeline including: StandardScaler, target encoder for categorical variables, SelectKBest with f_classif, and RandomForest classifier. Groups must systematically execute each pipeline step, documenting bias metrics (demographic parity difference, equalized odds difference) before and after each transformation. Provide groups with bias calculation functions and visualization templates. Students calculate and plot: (1) approval rate differences by gender/age before and after target encoding, (2) feature importance changes after scaling and selection, (3) correlation heatmaps showing proxy relationships. In the final 25 minutes, groups create annotated visualizations showing bias amplification pathways, specifically documenting how target encoding of 'housing' status amplifies age discrimination and how correlation-based selection retains proxy features while eliminating direct demographic indicators. Each group presents one key finding to demonstrate understanding of bias propagation mechanisms. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting findings to real-world algorithmic discrimination cases.
materials_needed: German Credit Dataset (CSV format)
Pre-configured Jupyter notebooks with sklearn pipeline template
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, seaborn
Bias metrics calculation functions (Python script)
Large format paper for group visualizations
Colored markers for annotation
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of bias metric calculations (25 points), (2) Correct identification of at least 3 bias amplification pathways with mathematical explanations (35 points), (3) Quality of annotated visualizations showing before/after transformations (25 points), (4) Demonstration of understanding through group presentation and peer discussion responses (15 points). Success requires students to correctly explain why target encoding amplifies bias and identify at least one proxy discrimination mechanism.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed bias calculation examples for the first transformation step and guided worksheets with specific questions about each pipeline stage. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose alternative feature engineering approaches that minimize bias propagation and quantify the fairness-accuracy trade-offs using additional metrics like individual fairness measures.

title: Pizza Party Budget Calculator: Applying Percentages and Decimals to Real-World Shopping
description: Students will apply percentage calculations and decimal operations to determine the best pizza deals for a class party within a $50 budget. They will calculate discounts, tax, and tips while comparing multiple pricing scenarios to make informed purchasing decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, tax rates, and tip amounts by working through authentic shopping scenarios
Students will apply decimal operations to compare unit prices and calculate total costs through hands-on budget planning activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the pizza shop price sheets and calculators to each student pair (5 minutes). Project the scenario on the board: 'Plan a pizza party for 24 students with a $50 budget. You must calculate the best deal including 8.5% tax and 15% tip.' Have students work in pairs to examine three different pizza shop options with varying base prices, discount offers, and combo deals (10 minutes). Students must calculate the final cost for each option: first applying any percentage discounts to base prices, then adding 8.5% tax to the discounted subtotal, and finally adding a 15% tip calculated on the pre-tax amount. Circulate to ensure students are showing all calculation steps on their worksheet (15 minutes). Next, have pairs determine how many pizzas they can afford from each shop and calculate the cost per person. They must show work for converting their final totals to per-person costs using decimal division (10 minutes). Students then create a recommendation chart comparing all three options, listing total cost, number of pizzas, and cost per person for each shop (8 minutes). Conclude with pairs presenting their top choice to another pair, explaining their mathematical reasoning and showing their calculation work. Require students to verify each other's percentage and decimal calculations during these mini-presentations (7 minutes). End with a brief whole-class discussion where 2-3 pairs share which shop they selected and why their calculations support this decision.
materials_needed: Pizza shop price sheets (3 different fictional shops with base prices, discount percentages, and combo deals)
Basic calculators (one per student pair)
Budget calculation worksheets with space for showing work
Chart paper or comparison template for final recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate percentage calculations for discounts, tax, and tip (25%), (2) Correct decimal operations for unit pricing and division (25%), (3) Complete showing of mathematical work and steps (25%), (4) Logical recommendation supported by calculations (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in calculations categories to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a calculation steps checklist and allowing use of percentage-to-decimal conversion charts. Offer sentence frames for explaining mathematical reasoning. Extend advanced learners by adding variables like delivery fees, group size changes, or multiple tax rates for comparison shopping across different locations.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Search Functions
description: Students will analyze real-world SQL queries from an e-commerce database to identify performance bottlenecks and explain the relationship between query structure, indexing strategies, and execution time. They will decompose complex queries, examine execution plans, and categorize optimization opportunities.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining query costs, join operations, and index usage to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between efficient and inefficient query patterns through systematic comparison of execution metrics and structural analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with a sample e-commerce database containing 50,000+ product records and 200,000+ customer order records, along with 5 pre-written queries of varying complexity (simple SELECT, JOIN with WHERE, nested subquery, aggregate with GROUP BY, and complex multi-table JOIN). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes. First 20 minutes: Each pair executes all queries using a database management tool (MySQL Workbench or PostgreSQL), recording execution times and examining the automatically generated execution plans. Next 30 minutes: Students create a comparison matrix documenting each query's execution time, number of rows examined, index usage, and join algorithms used. They must identify which queries show 'full table scans' versus 'index seeks' in the execution plans. Following 25 minutes: Pairs analyze the relationship between query structure and performance by categorizing each query as 'efficient,' 'moderately efficient,' or 'inefficient' based on execution metrics, then write explanations for their categorizations citing specific evidence from execution plans. Final 15 minutes: Each pair presents one 'inefficient' query to the class, explaining exactly why it performs poorly by referencing specific elements in the execution plan (table scan operations, high row counts, missing index usage). Instructor facilitates discussion connecting query structure patterns to performance outcomes.
materials_needed: Pre-populated MySQL or PostgreSQL database with e-commerce schema and sample data
Database management software (MySQL Workbench, pgAdmin, or similar)
5 pre-written SQL queries of varying complexity levels
Query analysis worksheet template with comparison matrix
Computers with database software installed
assessment_method: Grade based on completed comparison matrix (40 points: accurate execution metrics and execution plan details), written analysis explanations (40 points: clear identification of performance factors with specific evidence), and quality of verbal presentation (20 points: accurate explanation of bottlenecks with execution plan references). Success criteria: Students correctly identify at least 3 performance bottlenecks, accurately read execution plans to distinguish between index usage types, and provide evidence-based explanations for efficiency categorizations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a sample execution plan analysis with annotations highlighting key performance indicators, and offer a checklist of execution plan elements to examine. For advanced learners: Challenge them to rewrite the inefficient queries with optimization suggestions, or analyze the same queries under different indexing scenarios by adding/removing indexes and comparing results.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Production: A/B Testing Impact Assessment
description: Students will critically evaluate the real-world performance of two competing machine learning models deployed in a simulated e-commerce recommendation system. They will assess model effectiveness using multiple evaluation frameworks, analyze business impact metrics, and provide evidence-based recommendations for model selection and improvement strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative performance of machine learning models by analyzing multiple evaluation metrics including statistical significance, business KPIs, and fairness measures within a production environment context

Students will critique model deployment decisions through systematic assessment of A/B testing results, identifying potential biases, limitations, and recommending actionable improvements based on comprehensive evidence analysis
instructions:
**Phase 1: Dataset Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide students with two datasets: Model A and Model B A/B test results from a simulated e-commerce platform (30,000 user interactions each). Students work in teams of 3-4 to examine the dataset structure, identify key performance indicators, and document initial observations about data quality and completeness.

**Phase 2: Multi-Metric Evaluation Framework (60 minutes)**
Students develop a comprehensive evaluation framework incorporating: (1) Technical metrics - precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC for recommendation accuracy; (2) Business metrics - click-through rate, conversion rate, revenue per user, customer lifetime value; (3) Fairness metrics - demographic parity, equalized odds across user segments. Teams calculate all metrics for both models using provided Python templates in Jupyter notebooks.

**Phase 3: Statistical Significance Testing (30 minutes)**
Conduct chi-square tests for categorical outcomes and t-tests for continuous metrics. Students must determine statistical significance (α = 0.05) and calculate confidence intervals for key performance differences between models.

**Phase 4: Critical Analysis and Bias Assessment (45 minutes)**
Students identify potential sources of bias in the experimental design, analyze performance disparities across demographic groups (age, gender, geographic location), and evaluate the representativeness of the test population compared to the broader user base.

**Phase 5: Strategic Recommendation Report (60 minutes)**
Teams prepare a 10-slide executive presentation including: model performance summary, statistical analysis results, identified risks and limitations, final recommendation with supporting evidence, implementation timeline, and monitoring strategy. Each team presents for 8 minutes followed by 7 minutes of peer questioning and instructor feedback.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with Python 3.8+, pandas, numpy, scipy, sklearn, matplotlib, seaborn
Simulated A/B testing datasets (CSV files) with user demographics, interaction logs, and conversion data
Python code templates for metric calculations and statistical tests
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Evaluation rubric handouts for peer assessment
assessment_method: Students evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation and interpretation of all metrics; Critical Thinking Quality (25 points) - identification of biases, limitations, and alternative explanations; Evidence-Based Reasoning (25 points) - logical connection between data analysis and recommendations; Communication Effectiveness (25 points) - clarity of presentation and response to questions. Peer evaluation contributes 15% of total score through structured feedback forms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated intermediate results and focus evaluation on interpretation rather than computation. Offer guided questions for bias identification and decision frameworks for model selection. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets with missing values requiring imputation strategies, introduce advanced fairness metrics (equalized opportunity, calibration), and challenge them to design follow-up experiments addressing identified limitations.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical model combining graph theory, differential equations, and optimization theory to solve a real-world traffic flow problem. They will design their own traffic network scenario, develop the mathematical framework, and present a comprehensive solution with implementation recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from graph theory, calculus, and linear programming to construct an original mathematical model for traffic optimization by integrating multiple mathematical domains into a cohesive framework
Students will design and justify a novel algorithmic approach to solve their traffic flow model through the creation of computational methods and validation protocols
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Design (45 minutes)** Students work in pairs to create their unique urban traffic scenario. Provide each pair with demographic data sheets for different city types (suburban, metropolitan, industrial). They must define: intersection layouts (minimum 8 nodes), traffic volume patterns, peak hour constraints, and one unique challenge (construction, weather impact, or special events). Students sketch their network and identify 3-4 mathematical constraints. **Phase 2: Model Construction (90 minutes)** Using their scenario, students develop their mathematical framework. They must incorporate: adjacency matrices for network representation, differential equations for traffic flow dynamics (building on fluid dynamics principles), and linear programming for optimization. Provide template worksheets with partial differential equation frameworks they must complete and modify. Students document assumptions, variable definitions, and mathematical relationships. **Phase 3: Solution Development (75 minutes)** Students create their solution algorithm, choosing between analytical methods (Lagrange multipliers, gradient descent) or computational approaches (simplex method, network flow algorithms). They must program their solution using provided MATLAB/Python templates, test with their scenario data, and validate results through sensitivity analysis. **Phase 4: Presentation Creation (30 minutes)** Each pair creates a 10-minute presentation including: problem overview, mathematical model explanation, solution methodology, results analysis, and real-world implementation feasibility. Presentations must include visual aids showing network diagrams, mathematical notation, and computational results.
materials_needed: City demographic data sheets (6 different urban scenarios)
Graph paper and colored pens for network sketching
MATLAB or Python with NumPy/SciPy libraries installed on computers
Mathematical template worksheets with partial differential equation frameworks
Scientific calculators
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Quality (30 points - correct integration of multiple mathematical domains, appropriate assumptions, clear variable definitions), Solution Methodology (25 points - algorithm design, computational implementation, validation approach), Innovation and Creativity (20 points - novel approaches, unique problem aspects, creative constraints), Presentation Quality (15 points - clear explanation, effective visuals, professional delivery), Mathematical Rigor (10 points - proper notation, logical flow, error analysis). Students must achieve minimum 70% in Mathematical Model Quality and Solution Methodology categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional templates with more structured frameworks, offer simplified scenarios with fewer variables, allow use of graphical methods before computational approaches, and provide peer mentoring. For advanced learners: Encourage incorporation of stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or machine learning components. Challenge them to consider dynamic pricing models or autonomous vehicle integration. Provide access to advanced research papers on traffic flow theory.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Networks: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model using graph theory, differential equations, and linear programming to solve real-world urban traffic congestion problems. They will design both the theoretical framework and implement a computational solution with validation against real traffic data.
estimated_duration: 13 hours over 10 days (recommended: 2 weeks with 3-4 sessions per week)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from graph theory, calculus, and optimization theory by constructing an original mathematical model for traffic flow dynamics
Students will develop and justify a complete optimization algorithm through computational implementation and empirical validation using real urban traffic datasets
instructions:
**Phase 1 (Days 1-2, 3 hours):** Students form teams of 3-4 and select a specific urban intersection or network from provided Google Maps traffic data exports. Each team analyzes traffic patterns, identifies 4-5 key variables (vehicle density, signal timing, flow rates, congestion points), and formulates preliminary mathematical relationships. Teams must justify their variable selection using traffic engineering principles and create initial sketches of their network as a weighted directed graph.

**Phase 2 (Days 3-5, 4 hours):** Teams construct their mathematical model by: (1) Defining nodes as intersections and edges as road segments with capacity constraints, (2) Establishing differential equations for traffic flow dynamics using conservation principles, (3) Formulating an objective function to minimize total travel time or maximize throughput, (4) Setting up constraint equations for signal timing, vehicle capacity, and safety margins. Teams document all assumptions and mathematical derivations in LaTeX format.

**Phase 3 (Days 6-8, 4 hours):** Students implement their model computationally using Python with NumPy, SciPy, and NetworkX libraries. They code their optimization algorithm (linear programming, genetic algorithms, or gradient descent), create visualization functions for network flow, and develop sensitivity analysis tools to test parameter variations.

**Phase 4 (Days 9-10, 2 hours):** Teams validate their models against provided real traffic data, calibrate parameters, and refine their solutions. They prepare a comprehensive presentation including: theoretical foundation, mathematical formulation, computational implementation, validation results, and recommendations for traffic management. Final presentations are 15 minutes with 5 minutes Q&A, followed by peer evaluation using provided rubrics.
materials_needed: Real urban traffic datasets (Google Maps API exports or city traffic department data)
Python programming environment with NumPy, SciPy, NetworkX, and Matplotlib libraries
LaTeX editor (Overleaf accounts or local installation)
Graph paper and colored pens for initial network sketching
Access to optimization solver software (CPLEX Academic or Gurobi)
Presentation software and projection capabilities
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model completeness and accuracy (25 points), theoretical justification and assumptions clarity (20 points), computational implementation functionality (20 points), validation methodology and results interpretation (20 points), presentation quality and peer feedback incorporation (15 points). Students submit: complete mathematical derivation document, working Python code with comments, validation report with data analysis, and final presentation slides. Peer evaluations contribute 10% to final score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structures, worked examples of simpler network optimization problems, and additional office hours for mathematical derivation support. Offer pre-selected intersection datasets with cleaner data patterns. For advanced learners: Encourage incorporation of stochastic elements, multi-objective optimization, or machine learning integration. Provide access to more complex urban networks and real-time data feeds. Consider extension to dynamic traffic signal optimization or integration with autonomous vehicle routing algorithms.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Networks

title: Binary Number System Vocabulary and Symbol Recognition Flash Card Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental binary number system terminology and recognize binary notation symbols through structured flash card practice. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for all subsequent computer science topics involving data representation.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the definitions of 15 key binary number system terms (bit, byte, binary digit, base-2, decimal, hexadecimal, MSB, LSB, etc.) with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary number symbols (0, 1) and distinguish them from decimal numbers through rapid recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash card sets to each student (15 cards total). Each card shows a term on one side (e.g., 'bit') and definition on the reverse ('smallest unit of data, can be 0 or 1'). Students work in pairs for 25 minutes total. First 10 minutes: Student A shows terms to Student B, who states definitions aloud. Student A checks accuracy using answer key. Switch roles after 5 minutes. Second 10 minutes: Both students practice rapid symbol recognition using number sequence cards - instructor calls out sequences like '1010' or '23' and students hold up 'BINARY' or 'DECIMAL' cards. Final 5 minutes: Individual quiz where students write definitions for 10 randomly selected terms. Instructor walks around during pair work, noting students who struggle with specific terms. Use timer for each segment to maintain pace. After quiz, review any terms that multiple students missed as whole class discussion.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flash card sets (15 cards per student) with binary terminology
Answer key sheets for student pairs
BINARY/DECIMAL identification cards (2 per student)
Individual quiz sheets with 10 term prompts
Classroom timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade individual quiz out of 10 points (1 point per correct definition). Success criteria: 70% of students score 8/10 or higher. During pair work, use checklist to note which specific terms cause difficulty for remediation planning. Collect completed quiz sheets to identify class-wide knowledge gaps.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide abbreviated definition cards with key words highlighted, allow extra practice time with instructor. For advanced learners: Add 5 bonus terms (nibble, word, dword) or challenge them to create their own flash cards for related networking terminology. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Datasets: Customer Purchase Behavior Analysis
description: Students will analyze three different statistical distributions (normal, skewed, and bimodal) found in customer purchase data to understand how distribution shapes reveal underlying business patterns. They will interpret what each distribution type indicates about customer behavior and make evidence-based explanations about the business implications.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of normal, right-skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing visual patterns in customer purchase histograms and connecting distribution shapes to real business scenarios
Students will explain the relationship between distribution characteristics (mean, median, mode positions) and underlying data generation processes through structured comparison exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-prepared datasets: Dataset A (daily customer spending - normal distribution), Dataset B (customer age at first purchase - right-skewed), and Dataset C (purchase amounts during holiday vs. regular seasons - bimodal). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes total. First 10 minutes: Each pair creates histograms for all three datasets using provided software, noting the shape, center, and spread of each distribution. Next 15 minutes: Using the provided interpretation guide, students identify each distribution type and locate the mean, median, and mode on their histograms. They record observations about the relative positions of these measures. Following 15 minutes: Students complete the 'Distribution Detective' worksheet, answering guided questions about what each distribution shape reveals about customer behavior. For example: 'Why might customer ages be right-skewed?' and 'What business factors could create a bimodal spending pattern?' Final 5 minutes: Each pair shares one key insight about how distribution shape connects to business reality. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting mathematical concepts to practical applications, emphasizing that distribution shapes are not random but reflect underlying processes and behaviors.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets (Customer_Spending_Normal.csv, Customer_Age_Skewed.csv, Purchase_Amounts_Bimodal.csv)
Statistical software access (R Studio, Python with matplotlib, or Excel)
Distribution Interpretation Reference Guide (1-page handout)
Distribution Detective Worksheet (structured question set)
Histogram creation tutorial (quick reference card)
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of all three distribution types with accurate histogram creation, (2) Accurate explanation of mean-median-mode relationships for each distribution type, and (3) Logical connection between distribution shapes and real-world business scenarios with specific examples. Students submit completed worksheets and one histogram per distribution type. Success requires scoring 2/3 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made histograms and focus on interpretation rather than creation; offer sentence starters like 'This right-skewed distribution suggests that most customers...' For advanced learners: Add Dataset D with uniform distribution; challenge them to predict what business scenario might create each distribution type before seeing the data; introduce concepts of outliers and their impact on distribution interpretation.

title: Optimizing Emergency Supply Distribution Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world emergency response scenario where they must optimize the distribution of medical supplies to disaster-affected regions. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the graphical method to find optimal solutions while interpreting results in context.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-variable optimization problem by identifying constraints and objective functions from a real-world scenario
Students will implement the graphical method to determine optimal solutions through systematic plotting and analysis of feasible regions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Emergency Supply Distribution scenario handout (15 minutes). Present students with a disaster relief situation: A relief organization has 480 medical kits and 360 food packages to distribute between two affected regions (Region A and Region B). Region A requires at least 2 medical kits per food package due to injury severity, while Region B needs at least 1 medical kit per food package. Each supply package to Region A costs $50 to deliver, while Region B costs $30 per package. The goal is to minimize total delivery costs while meeting all regional needs and using all available supplies.

Divide students into pairs (5 minutes). Each pair receives graph paper, colored pencils, and calculators. Instruct students to first identify and write down all constraints mathematically (10 minutes): total medical kits (x + y ≤ 480), total food packages (a + b ≤ 360), Region A medical-to-food ratio (x ≥ 2a), Region B ratio (y ≥ b), and non-negativity constraints.

Next, students formulate the objective function to minimize: Cost = 50(x + a) + 30(y + b), where x, a represent medical kits and food packages for Region A, and y, b for Region B (10 minutes).

Students then plot all constraint lines on their coordinate system, clearly marking the feasible region using different colored pencils (20 minutes). They must identify all corner points of the feasible region algebraically by solving systems of linear equations.

Finally, students evaluate the objective function at each corner point to determine the optimal solution (15 minutes). They must write a complete solution statement explaining the optimal distribution strategy and minimum cost, including real-world interpretation of their mathematical results.
materials_needed: Emergency Supply Distribution scenario handout (pre-printed)
Graph paper (coordinate grid, at least 20x20 squares)
Set of colored pencils (minimum 4 colors per pair)
Scientific calculators
Rulers for precise line drawing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct constraint formulation and objective function (25 points), (2) Accurate graphical representation with properly labeled axes and constraint lines (25 points), (3) Precise identification of corner points using algebraic methods (25 points), (4) Correct optimization solution with clear real-world interpretation and cost calculation (25 points). Students must submit their graph, mathematical work, and written solution summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a constraint identification template and offer guided practice with simpler two-variable problems first. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how the solution changes if supply quantities or delivery costs vary by ±10%. Challenge them to solve using the simplex method or add additional constraints like regional population requirements.

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns Through Netflix's Chaos Engineering Case Study
description: Students will dissect Netflix's real-world distributed system architecture and analyze how different failure injection scenarios expose system vulnerabilities. They will examine the relationships between microservice dependencies, identify critical failure points, and evaluate the effectiveness of various resilience patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the cascading failure patterns in distributed microservice architectures by examining Netflix's production incident reports and chaos engineering experiments
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different resilience patterns (circuit breakers, bulkheads, timeouts) through systematic comparison of system behavior under various failure scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with Netflix's public post-mortems from 2019-2023, architectural diagrams of their streaming service, and documented Chaos Monkey experiments. In the first 45 minutes, students individually read and annotate the materials, identifying service dependencies and marking potential failure points on the architecture diagrams using different colored markers for different risk levels. Next, teams spend 60 minutes collaboratively creating a failure dependency matrix, mapping how the failure of each service impacts downstream services, categorizing impacts as: cascading failure, graceful degradation, or isolated failure. Students then analyze three specific chaos experiments: random instance termination, network partition simulation, and database connection exhaustion. For each experiment, teams must trace the failure propagation path, identify which resilience patterns activated, and determine why some services failed while others remained stable. In the following 45 minutes, teams create visual failure trees showing root causes, intermediate effects, and final system impacts for each scenario. Finally, students prepare a 15-minute presentation analyzing the most critical architectural vulnerability they discovered, supported by evidence from the experiments and suggesting specific improvements. Each team presents their findings while other teams provide peer feedback using provided evaluation forms. Conclude with a 20-minute class discussion comparing different teams' analyses and synthesizing key insights about distributed system failure patterns.
materials_needed: Netflix post-mortem reports (2019-2023) - printed copies
Netflix streaming service architecture diagrams - large format prints
Colored markers and sticky notes for annotation
Chaos Monkey experiment documentation and results data
Laptops with draw.io or Lucidchart access for creating failure trees
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate based on four components: (1) Accuracy of failure dependency matrix - correctly identifies 80%+ of critical dependencies and failure propagation paths (25 points), (2) Quality of failure pattern analysis - demonstrates deep understanding of cascading vs. isolated failures with specific evidence (30 points), (3) Visual failure trees - clearly show cause-effect relationships with appropriate technical detail (25 points), (4) Presentation and peer evaluation - effectively communicates findings and provides constructive feedback to peers (20 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled partial dependency matrices with some relationships already mapped, offer glossary of distributed systems terms, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. For advanced learners: challenge them to propose novel chaos experiments, analyze additional Netflix services beyond the core streaming platform, or compare Netflix's approach with other companies' resilience strategies like Amazon or Google.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for Customer Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations created from the same customer satisfaction dataset to determine which best communicates key insights. They will justify their evaluation using established data visualization principles and audience considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar chart, pie chart, and scatter plot) by applying data visualization best practices criteria
Students will judge the appropriateness of visualization choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with three printed visualizations showing customer satisfaction data: a horizontal bar chart showing satisfaction ratings by department, a pie chart of the same data, and a scatter plot comparing satisfaction vs. response time. Give students the evaluation worksheet with criteria categories: clarity, accuracy, audience appropriateness, and visual design principles. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization and complete initial impressions on their worksheet, noting strengths and weaknesses for each criterion. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students discuss their individual assessments and work together to score each visualization on a 1-4 scale for each criterion (4=excellent, 3=good, 2=fair, 1=poor). They must provide written justification for each score.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Pairs calculate total scores and rank the three visualizations from most to least effective. They write a 3-sentence recommendation explaining which visualization they would present to a business manager and why.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their top choice and reasoning. Record responses on board to identify patterns in evaluation criteria that led to different conclusions.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Conclude by having students individually write one key insight they learned about what makes data visualizations effective for business communication.
materials_needed: Three printed customer satisfaction visualizations (one set per student)
Structured evaluation worksheet with 4 criteria categories
Calculators or smartphones for scoring
Whiteboard and markers for class discussion recording
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using rubric: Criterion application (25 points) - scores supported by relevant visualization principles, Justification quality (25 points) - clear reasoning connecting criteria to visual elements, Ranking rationale (25 points) - logical connection between scores and final recommendation, Participation in discussion (25 points) - contributes meaningful insights during pair and class discussions
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with basic visualization principles (avoid 3D charts, use appropriate scales, consider color-blind accessibility). For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-ranked visualization and sketch their proposed changes. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need more support during Step 2.

title: Design and Build a Mathematical Model for a Community Garden Optimization Problem
description: Students will create an original mathematical model to optimize the layout and resource allocation for a community garden project. They will synthesize concepts from geometry, algebra, and linear programming to develop a comprehensive solution that maximizes yield while minimizing costs and addressing real-world constraints.
estimated_duration: 140 minutes (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical optimization model by integrating geometric area calculations, algebraic equations, and constraint-based reasoning to solve a multi-variable community garden problem
Students will design a comprehensive mathematical presentation through visual models, calculations, and justified recommendations that demonstrate synthesis of multiple mathematical concepts
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the Community Garden Challenge packet containing a plot diagram (40ft x 60ft rectangular space), crop data sheets with growth requirements, cost information, and yield projections for 8 different vegetables. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Designer, Cost Analyst, Yield Optimizer, and Presentation Coordinator.

**Phase 1 - Problem Analysis (25 minutes):** Teams analyze the given constraints: minimum 4 crop types, maximum budget of $500, specific spacing requirements for each crop, water access limitations (only 3 irrigation zones possible), and seasonal timing considerations. Students identify variables, create preliminary sketches, and list all mathematical relationships they'll need to model.

**Phase 2 - Model Development (45 minutes):** Students create their mathematical model using coordinate geometry to design the layout, systems of inequalities to represent constraints, and optimization equations to maximize profit or yield. They must calculate areas for each crop section, determine costs for seeds/materials, project harvest yields, and create equations showing the relationships between variables. All work must be documented with clear mathematical notation.

**Phase 3 - Solution Implementation (35 minutes):** Teams solve their model using graphing calculators or spreadsheet software, test multiple scenarios, and select their optimal solution. They create a scaled diagram of their final garden layout with precise measurements and annotations.

**Phase 4 - Presentation Creation (25 minutes):** Students prepare a 5-minute presentation including their mathematical model, solution process, final design with justification, and reflection on real-world applicability. Each team member must present one component of the mathematical work.
materials_needed: Community Garden Challenge packets (1 per team with plot diagrams and data sheets)
Graphing calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Graph paper and rulers for scaled drawings
Colored pencils or markers for garden layout visualization
Presentation materials (poster paper or digital presentation software)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Model Accuracy - correct use of geometric formulas, constraint equations, and optimization methods (25%), (2) Problem-Solving Process - logical approach, appropriate variable identification, and systematic solution method (25%), (3) Solution Justification - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning and real-world relevance (25%), and (4) Creative Integration - originality in model design and innovative synthesis of mathematical concepts (25%). Students submit their mathematical work, scaled garden design, and deliver their team presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed constraint equations and offer guided questions to help identify variables. Consider pairing with stronger math students and provide additional examples of optimization problems. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including seasonal rotation planning, introduce calculus-based optimization methods, or require sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with different constraint values. Encourage exploration of linear programming graphical methods or technology-based solver tools.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Flashcard Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the time and space complexity classifications for 25 advanced algorithms across different domains (graph theory, dynamic programming, string processing, and computational geometry). This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of algorithmic complexity that students must instantly recognize in advanced computer science contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity for 25 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall, KMP string matching, and convex hull algorithms
Students will identify the space complexity classifications for advanced data structures and algorithms through rapid-fire recall exercises
instructions: Begin by providing students with a curated list of 25 advanced algorithms organized into four categories: Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's, Tarjan's SCC), Dynamic Programming (Longest Common Subsequence, Knapsack variants, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Edit Distance), String Processing (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Z-algorithm, Suffix Array construction), and Computational Geometry (Convex Hull, Line Intersection, Closest Pair). Distribute pre-made digital flashcards via Anki or Quizlet, with algorithm names on front and complexity notations on back. Students spend 15 minutes individually studying the flashcards, focusing on exact Big O notations including best, average, and worst-case scenarios where applicable. Next, conduct three rounds of assessment: Round 1 (10 minutes) - students work in pairs, alternating as questioner and responder, cycling through all 25 algorithms twice. Round 2 (10 minutes) - instructor calls out algorithm names randomly while students write complexity on individual whiteboards, holding up answers simultaneously for immediate feedback. Round 3 (15 minutes) - digital quiz where students have 30 seconds per question to select correct time/space complexity from multiple choice options. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify their weakest algorithm categories and create personalized study plans for algorithms they missed.
materials_needed: Pre-loaded Anki or Quizlet flashcard deck with 25 advanced algorithms
Individual whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Digital quiz platform (Kahoot, Poll Everywhere, or Google Forms)
Printed algorithm reference sheet with categories
Timer or stopwatch for timed rounds
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final digital quiz to demonstrate mastery. Track performance across three metrics: individual whiteboard responses (immediate feedback), peer questioning accuracy (partner verification), and final quiz scores. Provide immediate corrective feedback for incorrect responses and require students to verbally state the correct complexity before moving to next question.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce the algorithm set to 15 core algorithms and provide mnemonic devices (e.g., 'Dijkstra Drives Very Fast' for O(V log V)). Offer additional study time with algorithm visualization tools like VisuAlgo. For advanced learners, include amortized complexity analysis for algorithms like dynamic arrays, and challenge them to explain why specific complexities exist rather than just memorizing them.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Model Performance Diagnostics
description: Students will analyze learning curves and cross-validation results from three different machine learning models to understand how bias-variance tradeoff manifests in real model performance. They will interpret diagnostic plots to explain why each model exhibits specific patterns of overfitting or underfitting.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition components by analyzing learning curves, validation curves, and cross-validation score distributions across three different model complexities
Students will explain the relationship between model capacity and generalization error through systematic comparison of training/validation performance gaps
instructions:
Provide students with three pre-trained models: a linear regression (high bias), a decision tree with max_depth=20 (high variance), and a regularized model with optimal hyperparameters (balanced). Each model includes training/validation learning curves, bias-variance decomposition plots, and 10-fold cross-validation results on the same housing price dataset.

Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to examine Model A (linear regression) plots. They identify: final training/validation error gap, learning curve shape, cross-validation score variance, and bias-variance decomposition values. Students record observations in provided template.

Step 2 (15 min): Repeat analysis for Model B (deep decision tree), focusing on same four metrics. Students note differences in curve shapes and error patterns.

Step 3 (15 min): Analyze Model C (regularized model) using identical framework.

Step 4 (20 min): Students create comparison matrix ranking models by bias level, variance level, and expected generalization performance. They write 3-4 sentence explanations for each ranking, citing specific evidence from plots.

Step 5 (15 min): Pairs present one model analysis to class, explaining how the diagnostic plots reveal the bias-variance characteristics. Other students ask clarifying questions about interpretation.

Instructor circulates during Steps 1-4, asking probing questions: 'What does this gap between curves tell you?' 'How does CV score variance relate to model stability?' 'Which bias-variance component dominates here?'
materials_needed: Pre-generated learning curves for three models (provided as PDF handouts)
Bias-variance decomposition plots for each model
Cross-validation results spreadsheet with score distributions
Analysis template worksheet with guided questions
Housing price dataset description and feature information
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using rubric: (1) Correct identification of bias/variance dominance for each model (30 points), (2) Accurate interpretation of learning curve shapes and gaps (25 points), (3) Logical ranking with plot-based evidence (25 points), (4) Clear written explanations using proper terminology (20 points). Success threshold: 75/100 points with no category below 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide definitions card with bias (error from oversimplification) and variance (error from sensitivity to training data variations). Highlight specific plot regions to examine. For advanced learners: Add ensemble model results to compare, or provide bias-variance decomposition code to modify parameters and observe changes in real-time.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Profiling
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by implementing them, measuring their performance with varying data sets, and examining their theoretical vs. actual complexity. They will decompose each algorithm's structure and evaluate trade-offs between different approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity characteristics of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by measuring execution times across datasets of different sizes and compositions
Students will examine the relationship between theoretical Big O notation and actual performance through systematic testing and data visualization
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the starter code template containing three incomplete sorting algorithm implementations and a performance testing framework. Students work in pairs, with each pair receiving a laptop with Python 3.x installed and access to matplotlib library.

**Phase 1 - Implementation (25 minutes):** Students complete the three sorting algorithm implementations using the provided function signatures. Each algorithm must include line-by-line comments explaining the logic. Partners alternate between 'driver' (coding) and 'navigator' (reviewing/suggesting) roles every 10 minutes.

**Phase 2 - Data Collection (20 minutes):** Using the provided testing framework, students run their algorithms on five different dataset configurations: random arrays of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 2000, and 5000 elements. They record execution times in the provided spreadsheet template, running each test three times and calculating averages to account for system variations.

**Phase 3 - Analysis (25 minutes):** Students create performance graphs using matplotlib, plotting array size vs. execution time for each algorithm. They then analyze the curves to identify which algorithms demonstrate O(n²), O(n log n), and hybrid complexity patterns. Students document observations about when quicksort performs poorly (nearly sorted data) and when merge sort maintains consistent performance.

**Phase 4 - Evaluation (10 minutes):** Each pair presents one key insight about algorithm trade-offs to another pair, focusing on specific scenarios where one algorithm outperforms others despite theoretical complexity differences.
materials_needed: Python 3.x installed on computers (one per pair)
Matplotlib and numpy libraries installed
Starter code template file with sorting function signatures
Performance testing framework Python file
Data recording spreadsheet template (digital or printed)
Algorithm complexity reference chart
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Correct implementation of all three sorting algorithms with appropriate commenting (40%), (2) Accurate data collection with proper averaging of test runs (25%), (3) Creation of clear performance visualization graphs (20%), (4) Written analysis identifying complexity patterns and trade-offs with specific examples from their data (15%). Success criteria: Students correctly identify which algorithms exhibit quadratic vs. linearithmic growth patterns and provide at least two specific scenarios where algorithm choice impacts performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pseudocode for each sorting algorithm and pre-filled portions of the most complex algorithm (merge sort). Include debugging tips sheet with common implementation errors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional optimizations (hybrid quicksort with insertion sort for small arrays) or analyze space complexity in addition to time complexity. Provide additional datasets with specific patterns (reverse-sorted, nearly-sorted) to explore worst-case scenarios.

title: Critical Assessment of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems
description: Students will evaluate the effectiveness, ethical implications, and business viability of three different machine learning models designed to predict patient readmission rates. They will analyze model performance metrics, assess potential biases, and make evidence-based recommendations for real-world deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate competing machine learning models by analyzing performance metrics, bias indicators, and interpretability factors to determine optimal deployment strategies
Students will critique the ethical and practical implications of predictive healthcare models through systematic analysis of fairness metrics and stakeholder impact assessments
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Distribute three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Neural Network) with accompanying datasets containing patient demographics, medical history, and readmission outcomes. Students work in teams of 3-4 to calculate and compare: accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and calibration metrics for each model. Provide confusion matrices and feature importance rankings. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams analyze model fairness by computing demographic parity, equalized odds, and individual fairness metrics across age, gender, and socioeconomic groups.
