Students will evaluate architectural trade-offs through systematic comparison of monolithic versus microservices approaches using quantitative metrics and qualitative factors
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with Netflix's public engineering blog posts, architecture diagrams, and the provided case study packet containing system requirements and performance metrics. Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine Netflix's architecture documentation, identifying at least 8 distinct microservices and mapping their interactions using the provided diagramming templates. Students must document data flow, API calls, and dependencies between services like User Service, Recommendation Engine, Video Streaming Service, and Authentication Service. Step 2 (60 minutes): Teams analyze three specific design patterns implemented in the architecture: Circuit Breaker pattern (Hystrix implementation), API Gateway pattern (Zuul), and Service Discovery (Eureka). For each pattern, students must identify the specific problem it solves, map its implementation within Netflix's system, and document failure scenarios it addresses. Step 3 (45 minutes): Using the provided comparison framework, teams evaluate architectural decisions by analyzing trade-offs in five categories: scalability (requests per second capacity), fault tolerance (failure isolation mechanisms), development complexity (team coordination overhead), operational overhead (monitoring and deployment complexity), and cost implications (infrastructure and maintenance). Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams create a comprehensive analysis report including annotated architecture diagrams, pattern implementation analysis, and trade-off evaluation matrix. Each team presents their findings in a 10-minute presentation highlighting their most significant architectural insights and defending their analysis with evidence from the documentation.
materials_needed: Netflix Engineering Blog archive (printed packet with 15-20 selected articles)
Netflix OSS architecture diagrams and technical documentation
Lucidchart or Draw.io accounts for digital diagramming
Architectural pattern reference sheets (Circuit Breaker, API Gateway, Service Discovery)
Trade-off analysis framework template with evaluation criteria
Large format paper (A3) for hand-drawn diagram drafts
Colored markers and sticky notes for collaborative mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Architecture Mapping Accuracy (25 points) - correctly identified services, relationships, and data flows; Design Pattern Analysis (30 points) - accurate pattern identification, implementation understanding, and problem-solution mapping; Trade-off Evaluation (25 points) - comprehensive analysis across all five categories with evidence-based reasoning; Presentation Quality (20 points) - clear communication of insights, effective use of visuals, and ability to defend analysis during Q&A. Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key sections in documentation, offer simplified architecture templates with partial completions, and assign stronger technical students as mentors within teams. Create checkpoint reviews at 30-minute intervals. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional design patterns beyond the required three, research Netflix's chaos engineering practices (Chaos Monkey), or propose alternative architectural solutions for specific bottlenecks they identify. Provide access to additional technical resources like Martin Fowler's microservices articles.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision Making
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which one best supports a specific business decision. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge visualization quality and justify their recommendations with evidence-based reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific criteria including clarity, accuracy, and relevance to business context
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based argumentation
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and distribute the evaluation worksheet and three visualization sets (15 minutes setup). Each set contains the same customer sales data displayed as: a pie chart showing sales by region, a bar chart comparing monthly sales trends, and a scatter plot showing customer age vs. purchase amount. Present the business scenario: 'A retail company needs to decide whether to expand marketing budget in the Northeast region.' Give groups 20 minutes to examine each visualization and rate them using the provided criteria sheet (1-5 scale for: data accuracy, visual clarity, relevance to decision, and professional appearance). Students must document specific strengths and weaknesses for each visualization. Next, facilitate a 15-minute group discussion where each team records their preliminary rankings. Then provide 20 minutes for teams to prepare a 3-minute presentation defending their top choice. During presentations (20 minutes total), other groups score each recommendation using the peer evaluation rubric. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students individually write which visualization they would personally recommend and why, noting if their opinion changed after hearing other arguments. Teachers should circulate during evaluation time, prompting students to justify their ratings with specific visual elements.
materials_needed: Three printed visualization sets per group (9 total visualizations per group)
Evaluation criteria worksheet with 1-5 rating scales
Business scenario handout describing the marketing decision
Peer evaluation rubric for presentations
Individual reflection worksheets
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Systematic application of evaluation criteria with specific evidence (25%), (2) Quality of critical reasoning in identifying strengths/weaknesses (25%), (3) Effectiveness of group presentation and defense of choice (25%), (4) Thoughtful individual reflection demonstrating synthesis of peer feedback (25%). Success requires students to move beyond personal preference to evidence-based evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'The main weakness is...' Advanced learners can be asked to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-rated visualization or consider how different stakeholders might evaluate the same charts differently.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision Making: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different data visualizations of the same dataset to determine which is most effective for a specific business scenario. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and decision-making value of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization techniques by applying established criteria for clarity, accuracy, and business relevance
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning to recommend the most appropriate solution
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-created visualizations of identical sales data: a basic bar chart, a detailed dashboard with multiple metrics, and an infographic-style summary. Each should represent quarterly sales performance across four product categories. Give students the business scenario: 'You are presenting to executives who have 5 minutes to decide which product line needs immediate marketing investment.' 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine each visualization using the provided evaluation rubric covering: data accuracy, visual clarity, cognitive load, and business relevance. They score each visualization 1-4 on each criterion and document specific observations.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students compare their individual assessments and discuss differences in scoring. They must reach consensus on which visualization is most effective and identify three specific strengths and two weaknesses for each option.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Each pair presents their recommendation to another pair, defending their choice with evidence from their evaluation. The listening pair challenges the recommendation with at least two questions about the decision criteria or overlooked factors.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class discussion where pairs share their final recommendations. Create a class tally of choices and discuss patterns in reasoning. Conclude by revealing which visualization actual business executives preferred in a real scenario, discussing any differences between student and professional judgments.
materials_needed: Three printed copies of each visualization per student (9 total per student)
Evaluation rubric handouts with 4-point scales for each criterion
Business scenario description cards
Timer for activity segments
Whiteboard or flipchart for class tally
assessment_method: Grade individual evaluation rubrics for completeness and evidence quality (40%), assess pair consensus documents for depth of analysis and justification (40%), and evaluate participation in peer challenges and class discussion (20%). Success criteria: students provide specific evidence for scores, identify trade-offs between visualization approaches, and articulate clear reasoning for final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'The main weakness I notice is...' For advanced learners: ask them to redesign the weakest visualization to address identified problems, or have them create evaluation criteria for a different business context (emergency response vs. academic research).
original_title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision Making

title: Memory Palace: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Component Memorization
description: Students will memorize the complete TCP/IP protocol stack layers and their associated protocols, standards, and port numbers through structured recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of network protocols that advanced computer science students must know by heart.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all four TCP/IP protocol stack layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) and identify 15 specific protocols within each layer by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recite from memory the standard port numbers for 25 common network services through structured verbal rehearsal sessions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the protocol reference sheets and give students 10 minutes to review silently. Divide class into pairs and assign each pair a specific layer (Application, Transport, Internet, or Network Access). Each pair receives a set of 50 protocol flashcards for their assigned layer. 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to sort flashcards by protocol type, then take turns reading protocol names aloud while partner recites the layer, function, and port number from memory. Switch roles every 5 minutes.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement spaced repetition drill. Display protocol names on screen for 5 seconds each. Students must write down the layer, primary function, and port number (if applicable) within 10 seconds. Complete three rounds, removing correctly answered protocols each round.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Rapid-fire verbal recall. Call out random protocol names; students respond chorally with complete information (layer, function, port). Increase speed each minute.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual assessment. Students complete written quiz listing all protocols by layer, including port numbers, without reference materials. 

Conclude with 5-minute reflection where students identify which protocols they found most difficult to memorize and share memory techniques that worked best.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Stack reference sheets (one per student)
Protocol flashcard sets (50 cards per layer, 4 sets total)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying protocol names
Blank assessment sheets with layer headings pre-printed
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on final written recall test, correctly identifying layer, function, and port number for 45 out of 50 protocols. Award points as follows: Protocol name and layer (2 points each), Function description (3 points), Correct port number (2 points). Maximum 350 points total. Students scoring below 315 points complete additional memorization homework.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory devices (e.g., 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for OSI layers) and allow color-coded reference cards during first two phases. For advanced learners: Include RFC numbers, alternative port numbers, and protocol predecessor/successor relationships. Challenge them to memorize IPv6 protocols and emerging standards.

title: Interpreting Confounding Variables in Observational Studies Through Real Medical Research Cases
description: Students will analyze three published medical observational studies to identify confounding variables and explain how these variables create spurious associations. They will distinguish between correlation and causation by examining how demographic, behavioral, and environmental factors influence study outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between confounding variables and mediating variables by analyzing causal pathways in observational medical studies
Students will interpret how selection bias and unmeasured confounders affect study validity through systematic evaluation of study methodology sections
instructions: Begin by providing students with three real published observational studies: (1) coffee consumption and heart disease, (2) hormone replacement therapy and cardiovascular outcomes, and (3) vitamin supplementation and mortality rates. Form groups of 3-4 students and assign each group one study for 15 minutes of initial review. Students must read the abstract, methodology, and discussion sections carefully. Next, distribute the 'Confounding Variable Analysis Worksheet' containing a causal diagram template. Students spend 20 minutes creating directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) showing relationships between exposure, outcome, and potential confounders. They must identify at least 5 potential confounding variables and classify each as measured/unmeasured in their assigned study. During the following 25 minutes, groups rotate to examine all three studies, comparing how different research teams addressed confounding through statistical methods (stratification, matching, regression adjustment). Students document which confounders were controlled for and which remained unaddressed. In the final 15 minutes, each group presents their most concerning uncontrolled confounder and explains how it could create a spurious association. They must propose one additional data collection strategy that could help address this limitation. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion connecting these examples to broader principles of causal inference in observational research.
materials_needed: Three printed copies of selected observational studies from PubMed
Confounding Variable Analysis Worksheets with DAG templates
Colored pens/markers for creating causal diagrams
Laptops/tablets for accessing study supplementary materials
Whiteboard or flip chart paper for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed DAG diagrams for accuracy of causal relationships (25 points), quality of confounder identification with justification (35 points), and clarity of proposed solutions for unmeasured confounding (25 points). Award 15 points for effective group presentation explaining potential for spurious associations. Use rubric with 'exemplary/proficient/developing/inadequate' categories for each component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed DAG template with 2-3 variables already placed. Offer a reference sheet defining confounding, mediation, and collider bias with simple examples. For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential collider bias or selection bias in addition to confounding, and ask them to critique the statistical methods used for confounder adjustment.

title: Design a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Economic Impact Analysis
description: Students will create an original compartmental mathematical model (SEIR variant) that incorporates both disease transmission dynamics and economic factors. They will develop differential equations, validate their model against real data, and present policy recommendations based on their mathematical analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will design a novel compartmental epidemiological model by integrating differential equations, economic variables, and real-world constraints to predict disease spread and economic impact
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical framework through parameter estimation, sensitivity analysis, and model validation using historical pandemic data
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Each team receives a different historical pandemic dataset (1918 flu, 2009 H1N1, COVID-19 regional data). Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze their assigned dataset to identify key transmission parameters, economic indicators (GDP impact, unemployment rates, business closures), and population demographics. They must document at least 8 quantifiable variables. Step 2 (60 minutes): Students design their base SEIR model by writing the system of differential equations, then innovate by adding 2-3 additional compartments (e.g., hospitalized, economically inactive, vaccinated) and incorporate economic feedback loops where disease spread affects economic activity and vice versa. Step 3 (45 minutes): Using MATLAB, Python, or R, teams implement their model computationally, estimate parameters from their historical data using least-squares fitting or maximum likelihood estimation, and run simulations for various scenarios. Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams perform sensitivity analysis on at least 5 key parameters and validate their model by comparing predictions against withheld test data from their dataset. Step 5 (45 minutes): Each team creates a professional presentation including model equations, parameter justification, simulation results with confidence intervals, economic impact projections, and three specific policy recommendations with mathematical backing. Final presentations are 12 minutes per team with 3 minutes for peer questions.
materials_needed: Historical pandemic datasets (WHO, CDC, World Bank economic data)
MATLAB, Python (SciPy/NumPy), or R with differential equation solvers
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Large format paper for equation development
Access to epidemiological literature database
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and innovation (25 points) - novel model components, correct differential equation formulation; Computational implementation (20 points) - working code, appropriate numerical methods; Data analysis quality (20 points) - parameter estimation, validation against test data; Economic integration (15 points) - realistic economic feedback mechanisms; Communication (20 points) - clear presentation of methods and results, justified policy recommendations. Teams must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template SEIR equations as starting point, offer pre-cleaned datasets, and give guiding questions for economic variable identification. Pair with stronger mathematical teammates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, spatial dynamics, or machine learning parameter optimization. Encourage exploration of age-stratified models or network-based transmission dynamics.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by identifying correct binary sequences from memory
Students will recognize decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire flashcard exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary-decimal flashcards to each student (15 minutes setup). Have students work in pairs, with one partner holding the deck and the other responding. Start with decimal-to-binary practice: Partner A shows a decimal number (0-15), Partner B states the binary equivalent, then Partner A reveals the correct answer on the card's reverse side. Continue for 10 minutes, then switch roles for another 10 minutes. Next, conduct binary-to-decimal practice using the same format for 20 minutes total (10 minutes each partner). After paired practice, transition to individual timed recall (10 minutes). Each student receives a worksheet with 30 random decimal numbers (0-15) and must write binary equivalents within 5 minutes, followed by a 5-minute binary-to-decimal conversion sheet. Conclude with whole-class rapid-fire review (10 minutes): instructor calls out numbers randomly, students respond chorally, then individual volunteers provide answers. Record student response accuracy during this final segment. Throughout the activity, emphasize the pattern recognition (powers of 2: 8-4-2-1) and encourage students to visualize the binary place values. Monitor pair work to ensure both partners participate equally and provide immediate feedback during practice phases.
materials_needed: 32 double-sided flashcards per student (decimal 0-15 on front, binary on back)
Binary conversion practice worksheets (2 per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Pencils for each student
Answer keys for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (12/15 correct) on both timed worksheets to demonstrate mastery. Additionally, observe and record individual responses during the final rapid-fire session using a simple checklist. Successful completion requires consistent correct responses for at least 10 randomly selected numbers during the oral review portion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference chart showing powers of 2 (8-4-2-1) and allow them to use it during initial practice phases. Extend learning for advanced students by including 5-bit numbers (16-31) or introducing hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during partner work.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Memory Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and verbal recitation. This foundational activity builds essential number system recall skills needed for computer science problem-solving.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memory practice and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (decimal on front, binary on back for numbers 0-15). Have students work individually for 10 minutes, cycling through all 16 cards repeatedly, saying both numbers aloud when flipping each card. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 8 minutes - Partner A shows decimal numbers while Partner B states the binary equivalent, then switch roles after 4 minutes. For the group challenge phase (7 minutes), call out random decimal numbers and have students write the binary representation on mini-whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for checking. Create urgency by giving only 10 seconds per number. Conclude with individual assessment (5 minutes): each student receives a worksheet with 10 random decimal numbers from 0-15 and must write the binary equivalent from memory without cards. Walk around during all phases to observe student accuracy and provide immediate correction. Maintain energy by celebrating correct answers and encouraging students who struggle. Record completion rates and accuracy for each phase to track progress.
materials_needed: 16 flashcards per student (decimal 0-15 on front, binary equivalent on back)
Mini-whiteboards and dry-erase markers (1 per student)
Assessment worksheet with 10 decimal numbers per student
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Grade the final worksheet using binary conversion answer key - award 1 point per correct answer (10 points total). Students achieving 8+ points demonstrate mastery. Additionally, observe and record student performance during pair work using quick checkmarks for accuracy rates above/below 80%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-2 reference strip (8-4-2-1) and allow them to point while converting. For advanced learners: extend the range to decimal numbers 16-31 using 5-bit binary, or challenge them to convert in reverse (binary to decimal) during peer quizzing.
original_title: Binary Number Flashcard Memory Challenge

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results to Compare Model Performance
description: Students will analyze and interpret k-fold cross-validation results from three different machine learning models (linear regression, decision tree, random forest) trained on a housing price dataset. They will explain the meaning of performance metrics, identify which model performs best, and justify their conclusions based on variance and bias considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation performance metrics (RMSE, MAE, R²) by analyzing numerical results and explaining what each metric reveals about model quality
Students will compare model performance characteristics through systematic analysis of mean scores, standard deviations, and performance consistency across folds
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared spreadsheet containing 5-fold cross-validation results for three models predicting housing prices. The data should show fold-by-fold RMSE, MAE, and R² values for each model. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to calculate mean and standard deviation for each metric across all models, creating a summary table. Step 2 (20 minutes): Each pair analyzes the results by answering guided questions: 'Which model has the lowest average RMSE and what does this mean?', 'Which model shows the most consistent performance across folds?', 'What does a negative R² in fold 3 of the decision tree indicate?'. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students create visual comparisons using box plots or bar charts showing mean performance with error bars representing standard deviation. Step 4 (20 minutes): Pairs write a 200-word recommendation memo explaining which model they would deploy, addressing both performance quality and consistency. They must reference specific numerical evidence and explain potential business implications of their choice. Step 5 (10 minutes): Class discussion where 3-4 pairs present their recommendations, focusing on how they interpreted the trade-offs between different metrics and consistency considerations.
materials_needed: Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets)
Pre-prepared CSV file with cross-validation results for 3 models across 5 folds
Guided analysis worksheet with interpretation questions
Access to basic plotting tools or graph paper
assessment_method: Evaluate the summary table for accurate calculations (25%), written responses to guided questions demonstrating correct interpretation of metrics (35%), quality of visual comparison showing appropriate representation of variance (20%), and recommendation memo showing synthesis of evidence with business reasoning (20%). Success criteria: correctly identifies best-performing model, explains what RMSE/MAE/R² values mean in context, recognizes high variance issues, and provides evidence-based justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed summary table and definition cards for each metric. Include sentence starters for the recommendation memo. For advanced learners, add questions about statistical significance of performance differences, discuss learning curves, or have them research when each metric type is most appropriate for different business contexts.

title: Optimization in Manufacturing: Minimizing Material Waste for Cylindrical Container Production
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem involving minimizing material costs while maintaining volume constraints. They will use derivatives to find optimal dimensions for cylindrical containers and present cost-benefit analyses to justify their mathematical solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative-based optimization methods to minimize surface area of cylindrical containers by setting up constraint equations and finding critical points
Students will implement mathematical solutions to real-world manufacturing scenarios through systematic problem-solving processes and cost analysis calculations
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: A beverage company needs to manufacture 355mL aluminum cans while minimizing material costs. Distribute the problem worksheet containing material costs ($0.08/cm² for aluminum, $0.12/cm² for top/bottom reinforcement). Students work in pairs for 10 minutes to identify variables and constraints, defining radius (r), height (h), volume constraint (V=355mL), and objective function (minimize surface area). Next, guide students through constraint substitution: from V=πr²h=355, solve for h=355/(πr²). Have students substitute this into surface area formula SA=2πr²+2πrh to create single-variable function SA(r)=2πr²+710π/r. Allow 15 minutes for students to find the derivative: SA'(r)=4πr-710π/r². Students then solve SA'(r)=0 to find critical point: 4πr-710π/r²=0, leading to r³=177.5, so r≈5.62cm and h≈3.57cm. Have pairs calculate total material cost using their optimal dimensions, including reinforcement costs for top and bottom. Students must verify their solution using the second derivative test to confirm minimum. Finally, each pair creates a brief presentation comparing their optimized design to standard can dimensions (r≈3.3cm, h≈10.4cm), calculating percentage savings in material costs. Conclude with 10-minute presentations where pairs justify their mathematical approach and discuss practical manufacturing constraints they might have overlooked.
materials_needed: Problem worksheets with company scenario and material cost data
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Graph paper for sketching functions
Measuring tape and sample cylindrical containers for reference
Presentation materials (whiteboard markers, poster paper)
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct constraint equation setup and variable identification (25%), (2) Accurate derivative calculation and critical point determination (35%), (3) Proper verification using second derivative test (20%), (4) Clear presentation with cost comparison and practical considerations (20%). Students must show all mathematical work and achieve minimum 80% accuracy in calculations for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with constraint equation partially filled, offer step-by-step derivative rules reference sheet, and pair with stronger mathematical partners. For advanced learners: Extend to optimize rectangular boxes, consider multiple material types with different costs, or incorporate shipping constraints that affect height-to-width ratios. Provide real manufacturing data for more complex scenarios.

title: Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing a Multi-Service E-commerce Platform Outage
description: Students analyze a complex system failure scenario involving microservices, databases, and load balancers to identify root causes, cascade effects, and architectural weaknesses. They will dissect system logs, trace failure propagation patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of existing fault tolerance mechanisms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze system architecture vulnerabilities by examining failure propagation patterns across interconnected microservices in a distributed e-commerce platform
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of fault tolerance mechanisms through systematic examination of system logs, monitoring data, and cascade failure sequences
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the complete case study packet containing: system architecture diagram, 500+ lines of timestamped logs from 6 different services, database performance metrics, and load balancer statistics from a 45-minute outage window. In the first 20 minutes, students individually review the timeline and identify potential failure initiation points. Next, teams spend 30 minutes mapping the failure cascade by creating a visual timeline showing how the initial database connection pool exhaustion in the user authentication service propagated to inventory management, payment processing, and recommendation engine services. Students must identify at least 4 distinct failure propagation paths and explain why each service failed. During the following 25 minutes, teams analyze the effectiveness of existing fault tolerance mechanisms by examining circuit breaker logs, retry patterns, and timeout configurations. They should identify which mechanisms worked, which failed, and why. In the final 25 minutes, teams create a comprehensive analysis report documenting: (1) root cause analysis with supporting evidence, (2) failure cascade diagram with timestamps, (3) evaluation of each fault tolerance mechanism's performance, and (4) three specific architectural improvements with technical justification. Teams present their findings in 5-minute presentations, defending their analysis with specific log evidence and technical reasoning.
materials_needed: Complete case study packet with system architecture diagram and failure logs
Digital whiteboard or large paper sheets for failure cascade mapping
Access to log analysis tools or text editors with search functionality
Timing device for structured phases
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of root cause identification with supporting log evidence (25%), (2) Completeness and correctness of failure cascade mapping with proper timestamps (25%), (3) Depth of fault tolerance mechanism analysis with specific examples (25%), (4) Quality of architectural improvement recommendations with technical justification (25%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in identifying the primary root cause and at least 3 of 4 major cascade points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guided questions for each analysis phase and highlight key log entries to examine first. Offer a template for the failure cascade diagram. For advanced learners: include additional services in the architecture, provide monitoring dashboards to analyze, or ask them to design automated detection systems for similar failures.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Model Performance Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret bias-variance decomposition results from multiple machine learning models to understand the fundamental tradeoff affecting model generalization. They will examine numerical outputs, visualizations, and performance metrics to explain how bias and variance contribute to overall prediction error.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition outputs by analyzing numerical results and connecting them to model complexity and dataset characteristics
Students will explain the relationship between bias, variance, and irreducible error through comparative analysis of different algorithm performances
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results from five different models (linear regression, polynomial regression degrees 2, 5, and 10, and random forest) trained on a synthetic dataset with known noise level. Distribute the analysis packet containing: numerical bias-variance tables, learning curves, and scatter plots of predictions vs. true values for each model. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to examine the numerical results table showing bias², variance, noise, and total error for each model. They must identify which model has highest/lowest bias and variance, and calculate the percentage contribution of each component to total error.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the provided visualizations, students analyze the learning curves showing training/validation error vs. training set size for each model. They identify signs of underfitting (high bias) and overfitting (high variance) by examining curve behaviors and gap patterns.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students complete a structured interpretation worksheet requiring them to explain: why linear regression shows high bias/low variance, why degree-10 polynomial shows low bias/high variance, and how random forest balances both components. They must connect mathematical complexity to bias-variance behavior.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs present one model's bias-variance profile to the class, explaining the underlying mechanisms causing observed bias and variance levels. Other students ask clarifying questions about the relationship between model assumptions and decomposition results.

Conclude with a brief discussion connecting bias-variance insights to practical model selection strategies.
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results spreadsheet
Learning curve visualizations for 5 models
Prediction scatter plots for each algorithm
Structured interpretation worksheet with guided questions
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate completed interpretation worksheets using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) correct identification of bias/variance levels from numerical data, (2) accurate explanation of learning curve patterns, (3) clear connection between model complexity and bias-variance behavior, (4) appropriate use of technical vocabulary. Additionally, assess oral presentations for clarity of explanation and accuracy of mechanistic reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a glossary of key terms and a template connecting model characteristics to expected bias-variance patterns. Offer guided questions like 'What happens to bias when model complexity increases?' For advanced learners, include additional decomposition results from ensemble methods or provide raw data to compute their own bias-variance analysis using bootstrap sampling.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-World Shopping
description: Students will create a personal monthly budget using percentage calculations to allocate income across different spending categories. They will then apply percentage discounts and tax calculations to make purchasing decisions within their budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to distribute a given monthly income across housing, food, transportation, and entertainment categories by creating a detailed personal budget
Students will calculate sales tax and discount percentages through simulated shopping scenarios to make informed purchasing decisions
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Monthly Income Cards' (ranging from $1,200-$2,000) randomly to students, ensuring each receives one. Display the budget allocation guidelines on the board: Housing 30%, Food 20%, Transportation 15%, Entertainment 10%, Savings 25%. Students have 10 minutes to calculate their category amounts using these percentages. Next, provide each student with the 'Shopping Scenario Worksheet' containing 8 items with original prices, discount percentages (10%-40% off), and local sales tax rate (8.25%). Students must calculate the final price for each item after applying discounts and adding tax. For the next 15 minutes, students work individually to determine which items they can afford within each budget category. Then form pairs to compare their budgets and purchasing decisions, discussing their mathematical reasoning for 10 minutes. Finally, conduct a whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share one interesting purchasing decision, explaining their percentage calculations. Throughout the activity, circulate to check calculations and provide guidance on percentage formulas (discount = original price × discount rate; final price = discounted price × 1.0825 for tax).
materials_needed: Monthly Income Cards (pre-printed with amounts $1,200-$2,000)
Shopping Scenario Worksheets with 8 items, prices, and discount rates
Calculators (one per student)
Budget allocation guidelines handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Shopping Scenario Worksheets using a 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct percentage calculations (discount and tax) on all 8 items, 3 points for 6-7 correct calculations, 2 points for 4-5 correct, 1 point for 1-3 correct. Additionally, assess budget allocation accuracy: full credit for correctly calculating all 5 budget categories within $5 of exact amounts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a percentage calculation reference sheet showing the formulas step-by-step and allow use of percentage calculators. Offer pre-calculated examples for the first 2 shopping items. For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge: calculate compound interest on their savings amount over 1 year at 3% annual rate, or introduce variable tax rates for different item categories (clothing 0% tax, electronics 8.25% tax).

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Performance Patterns
description: Students analyze the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms by examining execution time data, identifying complexity patterns, and determining optimal use cases. They will dissect timing results to understand how different algorithms behave with varying data sizes and types.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithm performance data by comparing execution times across different input sizes to identify Big O complexity patterns
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency trade-offs through systematic examination of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute setup where students receive three datasets containing execution times for Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, and Quick Sort tested on arrays of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements. Each dataset includes times for sorted, reverse-sorted, and random data. Students work in pairs for the next 25 minutes to create performance graphs plotting array size vs. execution time for each algorithm. They must identify which algorithm performs best under specific conditions and explain why certain algorithms show dramatic time increases while others remain stable. In the following 15 minutes, students examine the code structure of each algorithm, counting nested loops and recursive calls to connect observed performance with theoretical complexity. They then spend 10 minutes categorizing each algorithm's Big O notation (O(n²), O(n log n)) based on their analysis. Students conclude with a 15-minute written analysis answering: Which algorithm would you choose for sorting 50,000 random integers and why? Which performs worst on already-sorted data and what code feature causes this? Teams present their findings in the final 10 minutes, defending their algorithm recommendations with evidence from their data analysis.
materials_needed: Performance dataset spreadsheet with timing data for three sorting algorithms
Graph paper or digital graphing tool (Excel, Google Sheets, or Desmos)
Source code printouts for Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, and Quick Sort
Analysis worksheet with guided questions
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Accurate graph creation showing correct performance trends (25 points), (2) Correct identification of Big O complexity for each algorithm (25 points), (3) Written justification connecting code structure to performance patterns (25 points), (4) Appropriate algorithm recommendation with supporting evidence (25 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining at least two specific reasons why performance differs between algorithms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed graphs with axes labeled and one algorithm plotted as an example. Highlight specific code sections (nested loops) that impact performance. For advanced learners: Include additional algorithms like Heap Sort or challenge them to predict performance on specific data patterns (nearly sorted arrays) and verify predictions against actual results.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and instantly recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 within 3 seconds by using visual flashcard recognition
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire verbal responses
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend 5 minutes allowing students to examine all cards and notice patterns. Next, conduct guided practice where you show decimal numbers on the board and students chorus the binary equivalent, starting with easier numbers (0, 1, 2, 4, 8) that follow clear patterns. After 10 minutes, pair students for partner practice using the flashcards - one partner shows the decimal side while the other responds with the binary representation, switching roles every 2 minutes for 10 minutes total. Follow with individual silent study time where students test themselves using their flashcard set for 8 minutes, focusing on numbers they found challenging. Conclude with a class-wide rapid recognition game where you display random decimal numbers on screen for 5 seconds each, and students write the binary equivalent on their whiteboards, then hold up answers simultaneously. Track which numbers cause the most difficulty across the class. End by having students identify their three most challenging number conversions and repeat those specific flashcards five additional times each. Throughout the activity, emphasize that this is pure memorization work - understanding the conversion process comes later, but automatic recall of these 16 basic conversions will make future binary concepts much easier to grasp.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back (one set per student)
Individual student whiteboards and dry erase markers
Digital presentation screen or projector
Timer or stopwatch
Reference chart showing decimal 0-15 with binary equivalents for instructor use
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly identifying binary equivalents for at least 13 out of 16 decimal numbers (0-15) within 3 seconds each during the final rapid recognition round. Record individual student accuracy rates and note specific numbers requiring additional practice for future review sessions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with just numbers 0-7 and add 8-15 after mastering the first set. Highlight patterns like powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8). For advanced learners: Extend to decimal numbers 16-31 using 5-bit binary representations, or challenge them to recall binary numbers in reverse (show binary, state decimal).

title: Binary Number Flashcard Recognition Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises within 3 seconds per problem
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, with one student showing the decimal side while the partner attempts to state the binary equivalent before checking the answer. Switch roles every 2 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class binary-to-decimal round where you display binary numbers on the projector (start with 0000, 0001, 0010, etc.) and students write decimal answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously after 5 seconds. Record which numbers cause the most difficulty. For the third phase (10 minutes), students work individually with their flashcards, sorting them into 'know immediately' and 'need practice' piles. They should focus intensive practice on their 'need practice' pile, saying each conversion aloud three times. Conclude with a rapid-fire assessment: display 20 random binary numbers (mix of easy and challenging) on slides, giving students 3 seconds each to write answers. Use a timer and change slides automatically. Students self-score by comparing with the answer key provided afterward.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents (one set per student)
Mini whiteboards and markers (one per student)
Projector or interactive whiteboard
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key handout for final assessment
assessment_method: Students must achieve 18/20 correct answers (90%) on the final rapid-fire binary-to-decimal conversion test. Additionally, observe during pair work to ensure students can verbally state at least 12/16 conversions without hesitation. Record individual scores and note specific numbers that require additional practice for homework assignment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with just numbers 0-7 (3-bit) and provide a place-value chart (8-4-2-1 columns) as a reference. Advanced students can extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or practice decimal-to-binary conversions. Provide mnemonic devices like 'double and add' pattern recognition for students who need memory aids.
original_title: Binary Number Flashcard Recognition Challenge

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Machine Learning Models Through Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance plots from three different machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Gradient Boosting) applied to a housing price dataset. They will explain how different algorithms prioritize features differently and justify which features are most reliable predictors based on consistency across models.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings by comparing outputs from three different machine learning algorithms and identifying patterns in feature selection
Students will explain the relationship between feature importance scores and model predictions through structured analysis of visual plots and numerical rankings
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into pairs and distributing the pre-prepared feature importance plots for Random Forest, Logistic Regression (absolute coefficients), and Gradient Boosting models trained on the Boston Housing dataset with 13 features (CRIM, ZN, INDUS, CHAS, NOX, RM, AGE, DIS, RAD, TAX, PTRATIO, B, LSTAT). Each pair receives three bar charts showing feature rankings and a data dictionary explaining each feature. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine each plot individually, listing the top 5 features for each algorithm and noting the importance scores. They record observations in a structured worksheet with columns for each algorithm.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students create a consolidated ranking by identifying features that appear in the top 5 across multiple algorithms. They calculate a simple consensus score by adding ranks across models (lower scores indicate higher consensus importance).

Step 3 (15 minutes): Using the data dictionary, students write explanations for why the top 3 consensus features logically influence housing prices. They must connect feature definitions to real-world housing market factors.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students identify the biggest discrepancy between algorithms (feature ranked high in one model but low in others) and hypothesize why this difference might occur based on how each algorithm works.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Pairs present their top 3 consensus features and biggest discrepancy to another pair, defending their interpretations. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their consensus rankings and reasoning.
materials_needed: Pre-generated feature importance bar charts for Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and Gradient Boosting models (printed or digital)
Boston Housing dataset feature dictionary with clear explanations of all 13 variables
Feature importance analysis worksheet with structured tables for recording rankings
Calculators or computers for computing consensus scores
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of feature rankings extracted from plots (25%), (2) Correct calculation of consensus scores (25%), (3) Quality of real-world explanations connecting features to housing prices with specific examples (30%), (4) Logical hypothesis for algorithm discrepancies that demonstrates understanding of different model behaviors (20%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed example showing how to read one feature importance plot and calculate one consensus score. Highlight the axis labels and provide sentence starters like 'This feature affects housing prices because...' For advanced learners, provide correlation matrix data and ask them to explain why highly correlated features might have different importance rankings, or challenge them to predict which features would be most important for a different target variable like rental prices.

title: Optimization of Renewable Energy Systems Using Calculus
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to design an efficient solar panel array system for a residential building. They will use real-world constraints and data to maximize energy output while minimizing costs through mathematical modeling and analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize solar panel positioning by analyzing multiple variables including angle, spacing, and panel quantity
Students will implement constrained optimization techniques through real-world energy system design scenarios with budget and space limitations
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the scenario packet containing: a residential building blueprint (1,200 sq ft roof), local solar irradiance data, panel specifications (300W panels, $200 each), installation costs ($50 per panel), and constraints (maximum budget $8,000, minimum 2-foot spacing between panels). 

Teams first establish their optimization function by defining variables: panel angle (θ), number of panels (n), and spacing distance (s). They must create the objective function E(θ,n,s) representing total energy output using the formula: E = n × 300W × cos(θ-37°) × irradiance_factor × spacing_efficiency. Next, they establish constraint equations: budget constraint (200n + 50n ≤ 8000), space constraint (panel_area × n + spacing ≤ roof_area), and physical constraints (0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°, s ≥ 2 feet).

Students then apply calculus techniques: compute partial derivatives ∂E/∂θ, ∂E/∂n, ∂E/∂s, set up Lagrangian function L(θ,n,s,λ) = E(θ,n,s) - λ(constraint), and solve the system of equations ∇L = 0. Using graphing calculators or computer software, teams iterate through solutions, checking second derivative test for maximum values.

Finally, teams prepare a technical report including: mathematical model derivation, optimization calculations with work shown, final design specifications (optimal angle, panel quantity, spacing), projected annual energy output, total system cost, and brief justification of their solution. Each team presents their optimized design in a 5-minute presentation, explaining their mathematical reasoning and comparing results with other teams.
materials_needed: Residential building blueprint with roof dimensions
Solar irradiance data table for local geographic region
Solar panel specification sheets (wattage, dimensions, costs)
Graphing calculators or computer access with mathematical software
Technical report template worksheet
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Model Setup (25%) - correct variable definition and objective function; Calculus Application (35%) - proper use of partial derivatives, Lagrangian method, and constraint handling; Solution Accuracy (25%) - mathematically sound optimization with verification; Communication (15%) - clear technical report and presentation. Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculus procedures and produce a feasible design solution.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-written constraint equations and objective function template, offer step-by-step derivative calculation worksheets, pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: add weather variability factors, include maintenance scheduling optimization, or incorporate battery storage system optimization with additional variables and constraints.

title: Dissecting and Analyzing Microservice Architecture Trade-offs in E-commerce Systems
description: Students will analyze a complex e-commerce system's microservice architecture by examining service boundaries, communication patterns, and data consistency models. They will identify architectural bottlenecks, evaluate design decisions against business requirements, and propose evidence-based optimizations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze microservice decomposition strategies by examining service boundaries, coupling levels, and cohesion metrics within a real e-commerce system
Students will evaluate distributed system trade-offs through systematic examination of consistency models, fault tolerance mechanisms, and performance characteristics
instructions: Provide students with a detailed architecture diagram and codebase documentation of a fictional e-commerce platform 'TechMart' containing 12 microservices (User Service, Product Catalog, Inventory, Order Processing, Payment, Shipping, Notification, Analytics, etc.). **Step 1 (20 mins):** Students work in teams of 3-4 to map service dependencies using provided API documentation and database schemas. They create a dependency matrix showing synchronous/asynchronous communications. **Step 2 (25 mins):** Each team analyzes one critical user journey (e.g., 'Complete Purchase Flow') by tracing requests across services, identifying potential failure points, and documenting data consistency requirements at each step. **Step 3 (30 mins):** Teams examine provided performance metrics, error logs, and monitoring data to identify system bottlenecks. They must categorize issues as: network latency, database contention, service overload, or cascade failures. **Step 4 (25 mins):** Students analyze three specific architectural decisions: (a) synchronous vs. asynchronous order processing, (b) shared database vs. database-per-service for inventory, (c) API gateway vs. service mesh for routing. For each decision, they evaluate trade-offs using provided business requirements (99.9% availability, <200ms response time, ACID transactions for payments). **Step 5 (20 mins):** Teams present their analysis findings, focusing on evidence-based reasoning for their bottleneck identification and architectural recommendations.
materials_needed: TechMart system architecture diagram with 12 microservices
API documentation package with 45 endpoints
Simulated performance monitoring dashboard data (Grafana-style metrics)
Database schema documentation for each service
Sample error logs and trace data spanning 30 days
Business requirements specification document
Digital whiteboard tool (Miro/Lucidchart) for dependency mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of dependency mapping and service boundary analysis (25%), (2) Quality of bottleneck identification with supporting evidence from logs/metrics (30%), (3) Depth of trade-off evaluation using specific technical criteria (25%), (4) Soundness of architectural recommendations tied to business requirements (20%). Students submit dependency matrices, bottleneck analysis reports, and trade-off evaluation matrices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled templates for dependency matrices and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer a glossary of microservice patterns and trade-offs. For advanced learners: Include additional challenges like analyzing CAP theorem implications, designing circuit breaker patterns, or proposing event sourcing implementations for specific services.

title: Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Drill
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time complexity classifications for 25 advanced algorithms across sorting, graph traversal, dynamic programming, and string processing categories. This activity focuses on building foundational recall speed for algorithm analysis through structured repetition and systematic categorization.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and state the exact time complexity (Big O notation) for 25 advanced algorithms by completing timed classification exercises
Students will recall specific space complexity requirements for dynamic programming and graph algorithms through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the algorithm reference sheet containing 25 algorithms organized in 5 categories: Advanced Sorting (Radix Sort, Bucket Sort, Counting Sort, Shell Sort, Tim Sort), Graph Algorithms (Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's), Dynamic Programming (Knapsack variants, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Coin Change), String Algorithms (KMP, Rabin-Karp, Boyer-Moore, Aho-Corasick, Suffix Array), and Tree Algorithms (AVL operations, Red-Black tree operations, B-tree operations, Segment tree, Fenwick tree). Students spend 15 minutes studying the reference sheet, focusing on memorizing exact Big O notations for both time and space complexity. Remove reference sheets and conduct Round 1: Present algorithm names on flashcards for 30 seconds each. Students write time complexity on answer sheets. Complete all 25 algorithms without feedback. Round 2: Repeat with 20 seconds per algorithm. Round 3: Final round with 15 seconds per algorithm. After each round, provide correct answers and allow 3 minutes for students to review missed items. Between rounds, students can briefly consult reference sheets for algorithms they missed. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal quiz where students must respond within 10 seconds when algorithm names are called randomly. Record individual response accuracy and speed. The entire sequence should maintain high energy with clear timing announcements and immediate feedback to reinforce correct recall patterns.
materials_needed: Algorithm reference sheet with 25 advanced algorithms and their complexities
Pre-made flashcards with algorithm names
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces for complexity notations
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) in the final 15-second round to demonstrate mastery. Track both accuracy and response time for each student. Award full points for exact Big O notation (e.g., O(V²), O(n log n)), partial credit for correct complexity class but imprecise notation (e.g., 'quadratic' instead of O(V²)). Document persistent errors for individual follow-up.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for common complexity patterns (e.g., 'Double loops = O(n²)'). Allow extended study time with reference sheet between rounds. Pair with stronger students for peer coaching during review periods. For advanced learners: Add worst-case vs. average-case distinctions, include amortized analysis for applicable algorithms, or extend to space complexity requirements. Challenge them to explain why each complexity exists.

title: Pizza Party Fraction Division: Calculating Servings for Real Scenarios
description: Students will solve real-world division problems involving fractions by determining how many servings can be made from given amounts of pizza. They will apply fraction division algorithms to practical scenarios and verify their solutions using visual models.
learning_objectives: Students will apply fraction division algorithms to solve real-world problems involving food portioning and serving calculations
Students will demonstrate fraction division concepts through visual fraction circles and written mathematical procedures
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario cards and fraction circle manipulatives to pairs of students (5 minutes). Each pair receives 3 different pizza party scenarios, such as: 'You have 3¾ pizzas and each person eats ⅝ of a pizza. How many people can you feed?' or 'A recipe calls for 2½ cups of flour, and you have 7⅛ cups. How many batches can you make?' First, students read their scenarios and identify what division problem they need to solve (10 minutes). Next, they use fraction circles to model the problem visually, showing the total amount and the portion size (15 minutes). Then students solve each problem using the standard fraction division algorithm: multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor (15 minutes). They must show all work including converting mixed numbers to improper fractions. Students check their calculated answers against their visual models to verify reasonableness (10 minutes). Finally, pairs present one solved problem to another pair, explaining both their visual model and computational steps (10 minutes). Circulate during work time to check that students are properly converting mixed numbers, correctly identifying reciprocals, and simplifying final answers. Remind students that their final answer should make sense in the context (you can't serve 7.33 people, so discuss rounding appropriately).
materials_needed: Pre-written scenario cards with 9 different real-world fraction division problems
Fraction circle manipulatives (1 set per pair, including halves through tenths)
Worksheet with space for visual models and calculations
Calculators for checking work only
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of division problem from scenario, (2) Accurate visual representation using fraction circles, (3) Proper application of fraction division algorithm with all steps shown, (4) Reasonable final answer with appropriate units/context. Students must demonstrate proficiency in at least 2 of 3 scenarios to meet standard.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide fraction division reference sheet, use simpler scenarios with unit fractions first, and allow extended time with manipulatives. For advanced learners: Include scenarios requiring multiple steps (like calculating leftover amounts) or problems involving three fractions. Consider having them create and solve their own realistic scenarios for classmates.

title: Optimization Problem Solving: Manufacturing Cost Minimization Using Calculus
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving material costs and production constraints. They will construct mathematical models, apply derivative rules, and interpret solutions within business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to minimize manufacturing costs by setting up constraint equations and finding critical points using first and second derivative tests
Students will construct mathematical models from word problems through systematic translation of business constraints into algebraic expressions and calculus functions
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the manufacturing scenario worksheet and graphing calculators. Form pairs with mixed ability levels. **Problem Introduction (10 minutes):** Present the scenario: 'ABC Manufacturing needs to design cylindrical storage tanks with volume 1000 cubic meters. Material costs $15/m² for the curved surface and $25/m² for the top/bottom. Find dimensions that minimize total cost.' Students read and identify given information, constraints, and the optimization goal. **Model Construction (20 minutes):** Students work in pairs to: 1) Define variables (r = radius, h = height), 2) Write the volume constraint equation (πr²h = 1000), 3) Express height in terms of radius (h = 1000/πr²), 4) Write the cost function C(r) = 2πr² × 25 + 2πrh × 15, 5) Substitute to get C(r) in terms of r only. **Optimization Process (25 minutes):** Students apply calculus: 1) Find C'(r) using power rule and chain rule, 2) Set C'(r) = 0 and solve for critical points, 3) Use second derivative test to confirm minimum, 4) Calculate corresponding height and minimum cost. **Solution Verification (10 minutes):** Pairs check their algebra, verify units, and ensure their solution makes practical sense. **Presentation (15 minutes):** Selected pairs present their mathematical model and solution process, explaining each step's business relevance.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario worksheet with cost parameters
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Graph paper for sketching cost functions
Whiteboard markers for pair presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Model Setup (correct constraint and cost function formulation), Calculus Application (accurate derivative calculations and critical point identification), Solution Accuracy (correct final dimensions and minimum cost), Business Interpretation (realistic explanation of results and process). Students submit written work showing all algebraic steps and final verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed constraint equations and derivative formulas. Offer step-by-step derivative calculation guides. For advanced learners: Extend with multiple constraint problems (rectangular boxes with fixed surface area) or add economic factors like production time costs. Challenge them to create their own optimization scenarios.

title: Analyzing Algorithmic Complexity and Optimization Trade-offs in Sorting Algorithm Implementations
description: Students will systematically analyze three different sorting algorithm implementations by examining their time/space complexity characteristics, identifying performance bottlenecks, and evaluating optimization trade-offs. They will decompose algorithm behavior across different input scenarios and synthesize findings into evidence-based recommendations for real-world applications.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity characteristics of QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort implementations by systematically testing performance across varied input conditions
Students will evaluate algorithmic trade-offs through comparative analysis of empirical performance data and theoretical complexity bounds
instructions:
**Phase 1 (30 minutes):** Provide student teams of 2-3 with identical implementations of QuickSort, MergeSort, and HeapSort in Python, along with a performance testing framework. Each team receives datasets of varying characteristics: random arrays (sizes 1K, 10K, 100K), nearly-sorted arrays, reverse-sorted arrays, and arrays with many duplicates. Students first examine the source code for each algorithm, identifying key operations, recursive structures, and memory allocation patterns. They document their initial hypotheses about expected performance characteristics.

**Phase 2 (45 minutes):** Teams execute systematic performance testing using the provided timing framework. They run each algorithm on all dataset types, recording execution times and memory usage. Students plot performance curves and calculate empirical growth rates. Simultaneously, they instrument the code to count key operations (comparisons, swaps, memory allocations) to validate theoretical predictions. Teams maintain detailed data logs with observations about performance variations.

**Phase 3 (30 minutes):** Students analyze their empirical data against theoretical O-notation predictions. They identify discrepancies between theoretical and observed performance, examining factors like cache behavior, pivot selection strategies in QuickSort, and memory allocation overhead in MergeSort. Teams create comparative matrices showing algorithm performance across different input scenarios.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Each team synthesizes findings into evidence-based recommendations for three specific use cases: embedded systems with limited memory, real-time applications requiring predictable performance, and big data processing with massive datasets. They must justify their algorithm selection using their analytical findings and identify potential optimizations or hybrid approaches.
materials_needed: Pre-implemented Python sorting algorithms (QuickSort, MergeSort, HeapSort) with identical interfaces
Performance testing framework with timing and memory profiling capabilities
Structured datasets (random, sorted, reverse-sorted, duplicate-heavy arrays in multiple sizes)
Data analysis templates for recording empirical measurements
Computers with Python 3.8+, matplotlib, and memory_profiler libraries installed
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis and identification of algorithmic characteristics (25%), (2) Quality of empirical testing methodology and data collection (20%), (3) Depth of analysis comparing theoretical vs. observed performance with explanation of discrepancies (25%), (4) Justification quality for algorithm recommendations based on evidence (20%), (5) Clear presentation of findings with appropriate data visualization (10%). Teams submit performance data logs, comparative analysis matrices, and written recommendations document.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with specific questions about code structure, offer pre-calculated theoretical complexity references, and suggest specific metrics to focus on during testing. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement optimizations (e.g., hybrid sorting, better pivot selection), analyze additional algorithms like RadixSort, or extend analysis to parallel computing considerations. Provide optional advanced datasets with pathological cases that expose algorithm weaknesses.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Demographics
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer demographic dataset to determine which visualization best communicates key insights to business stakeholders. They will apply evaluation criteria and justify their recommendations based on clarity, accuracy, and business impact.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific assessment criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for business decision-making
instructions: Begin by distributing the Customer Demographics Dataset (CSV file with 1000 records including age, income, location, purchase history) and three pre-made visualizations of this data: Visualization A (bar chart of age groups vs. average spending), Visualization B (scatter plot of income vs. spending with geographic color coding), and Visualization C (pie chart showing spending distribution by age categories). Give students 5 minutes to individually examine all materials. Form groups of 3-4 students for 25 minutes of collaborative evaluation. Each group receives the 'Visualization Evaluation Framework' handout with four criteria: Data Accuracy (Does the viz correctly represent the data?), Visual Clarity (Is it easy to read and understand?), Business Relevance (Does it answer important business questions?), and Audience Appropriateness (Is it suitable for executives making decisions?). Groups spend 20 minutes systematically evaluating each visualization using the framework, documenting strengths and weaknesses in provided templates. They must identify at least 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses per visualization. In the final 15 minutes, groups prepare a 3-minute presentation ranking the visualizations from most to least effective, with specific evidence supporting their top choice. Each group presents their ranking and justification, with other groups asking clarifying questions. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing different groups' evaluations and identifying common evaluation patterns.
materials_needed: Customer Demographics Dataset (CSV file with 1000 customer records)
Three printed visualizations (A4 size) of the same dataset
Visualization Evaluation Framework handout (4 criteria with rating scales)
Evaluation documentation templates (one per visualization)
Computers/tablets for accessing dataset
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Systematic application of evaluation criteria with specific evidence (25%), (2) Identification of accurate strengths and weaknesses for each visualization (25%), (3) Clear justification for final ranking with business reasoning (25%), and (4) Quality of peer feedback and discussion participation (25%). Students must demonstrate critical thinking by providing at least 6 specific examples of visualization strengths/weaknesses and connect their evaluation to business decision-making needs.
