scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth sample visualization and offer sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'A business leader would find this confusing because...'. For advanced learners, add a challenge to redesign their lowest-ranked visualization and explain what specific changes would improve its effectiveness, or have them consider how different stakeholder audiences (marketing vs. finance teams) might evaluate these visualizations differently.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City Using Geometric Principles
description: Students will create an original scale model city that demonstrates understanding of geometric shapes, proportional reasoning, and area/perimeter calculations. They will design buildings, parks, and streets while applying mathematical concepts to solve real-world spatial problems and justify their design choices using geometric reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original scale model city by applying geometric principles, proportional reasoning, and area/perimeter calculations to create functional urban spaces
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts including similarity, scaling, and geometric properties through designing, building, and presenting a three-dimensional city model
instructions:
SETUP (10 minutes): Distribute materials to groups of 3-4 students. Each group receives a 24x18 inch base board, measuring tools, and construction materials. Present the scenario: 'Your team has been hired as city planners to design a new community on a 1:500 scale where 1 cm = 5 meters.'

PLANNING PHASE (30 minutes): Groups sketch their city layout on grid paper, calculating actual dimensions. They must include: 5 residential buildings (minimum 20m x 15m each), 2 commercial buildings (minimum 30m x 25m each), 1 school (minimum 40m x 30m), 3 parks (total area minimum 2000 square meters), and connecting streets (minimum 8m wide). Students calculate scale dimensions and verify their layout fits within the given space using area and perimeter formulas.

CONSTRUCTION PHASE (45 minutes): Groups build their 3D model using cardboard, foam blocks, and construction materials. Buildings must be proportionally accurate in height (residential: 3 stories = 9m, commercial: 4 stories = 12m, school: 2 stories = 6m). Students continuously measure and adjust to maintain scale accuracy.

DOCUMENTATION (20 minutes): Groups create a mathematical report showing all calculations, scale conversions, and geometric justifications for their design choices. Include area calculations for each zone and total city area utilization.

PRESENTATION (15 minutes): Each group presents their city for 3 minutes, explaining their design rationale, mathematical calculations, and how they solved spatial constraints. Other groups provide feedback using geometric vocabulary.
materials_needed: 24x18 inch foam core or cardboard base boards (1 per group)
Grid paper (1cm squares) and regular paper for planning
Rulers, measuring tapes, and protractors for accurate measurements
Cardboard pieces, foam blocks, colored paper for construction
Calculators for scale conversions and area calculations
Glue sticks, tape, scissors, and colored markers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct scale conversions and calculations (25 points), (2) Design Innovation - creative solutions meeting all requirements (25 points), (3) Construction Quality - proportional, neat 3D model (25 points), (4) Mathematical Communication - clear explanations using proper geometric vocabulary (25 points). Students submit calculation sheets and present orally. Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated dimension conversion charts and templates for basic building shapes. Pair with stronger math students and offer frequent check-ins during planning phase. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including zoning regulations (residential areas must be 500m from commercial), calculating population density, or incorporating advanced shapes like circular parks requiring circumference calculations. Encourage use of CAD software for initial design.

title: Assembly Language Instruction Set Architecture Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the complete x86-64 instruction set categories, register names, and addressing modes through systematic drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity builds foundational knowledge essential for low-level programming and computer architecture understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 16 x86-64 general-purpose registers and their specific naming conventions by completing timed identification exercises

Students will identify the six major instruction categories (data movement, arithmetic, logical, control flow, string, and system) and list 5-7 specific instructions per category through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the x86-64 reference cards to each student and allow 15 minutes for initial study. Create groups of 3-4 students and assign each group one of the six instruction categories. Students spend 20 minutes creating memory aids (mnemonics, acronyms, visual associations) for their assigned category. Next, conduct individual timed recall sessions: display register diagrams on the projector and give students 3 minutes to label all 16 general-purpose registers (RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, RSP, RBP, R8-R15) including their 32-bit, 16-bit, and 8-bit variants. Follow with a 5-minute written exercise where students list instructions for each category without references. Implement a progressive difficulty structure: start with basic registers, advance to instruction categories, then combine with addressing modes (immediate, register, memory, indexed). Use spaced repetition by conducting three separate 2-minute recall rounds with 5-minute study breaks between each round. Conclude with peer verification where students check each other's work against the reference materials. Track individual progress on provided scoring sheets, noting common error patterns for targeted review.
materials_needed: x86-64 instruction set reference cards (one per student)
Blank register diagram worksheets
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector for displaying register diagrams
Individual progress tracking sheets
Answer key with complete instruction listings
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on register identification (14/16 correct) and recall minimum 30 instructions across all categories (5 per category) within time limits. Use provided rubric: 4 points for perfect register recall, 3 points for 85-89% accuracy, 2 points for 75-84%, 1 point for 65-74%. Instruction recall scored separately with 1 point per correctly categorized instruction. Total possible: 50 points (20 for registers, 30 for instructions).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled partial diagrams with every third register completed, extend time limits by 50%, allow reference to simplified instruction subset (20 most common instructions). Create visual memory cards pairing instruction names with simple diagrams. For advanced learners: include instruction flags and condition codes, add addressing mode combinations, require recall of instruction byte encodings for common operations. Challenge them to recall deprecated or specialized instructions beyond the basic set.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Ensemble Model Bias Detection
description: Students will analyze SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and permutation importance outputs from a random forest model trained on a biased hiring dataset to identify which features contribute most to discriminatory predictions. They will interpret complex model explanations to understand how algorithmic bias manifests through feature interactions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP waterfall plots and summary plots by analyzing feature contribution magnitudes and directions to identify bias patterns in hiring decisions
Students will distinguish between local and global feature importance through comparative analysis of SHAP values versus permutation importance rankings
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained random forest model (80% accuracy) on a synthetic hiring dataset containing 15 features including gender, age, university prestige, years of experience, and technical scores. Students work in pairs at computers with Jupyter notebooks containing the model and explanation outputs already generated. First 20 minutes: Students examine the global SHAP summary plot showing feature importance rankings and value distributions. They must identify the top 5 most influential features and document whether each feature's impact appears legitimate or potentially discriminatory. Next 25 minutes: Students analyze 10 individual SHAP waterfall plots for specific predictions, focusing on cases where the model predicted 'hire' vs 'reject'. They compare feature contributions across demographic groups, documenting instances where protected characteristics (gender, age) significantly influenced decisions. Following 20 minutes: Students cross-reference their SHAP findings with permutation importance rankings, noting discrepancies and explaining why certain features might rank differently under each method. They create a comparison table showing the top 10 features under both methods. Final 15 minutes: Each pair presents one specific example of bias they identified, explaining how the SHAP values revealed the discriminatory pattern and proposing which features should be removed or constrained to improve fairness.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded hiring dataset (1000+ samples)
Pre-trained RandomForestClassifier model object
Generated SHAP explainer objects and plots
Permutation importance results dataframe
Bias detection worksheet template
assessment_method: Students submit completed bias detection worksheets containing: (1) Correctly identified top 5 biased features with SHAP value evidence, (2) Accurate interpretation of 3 waterfall plots showing discrimination examples, (3) Comparison table with explanations for SHAP vs permutation importance discrepancies, (4) Actionable recommendations for bias mitigation. Rubric awards 25 points each for accurate feature identification, correct plot interpretation, method comparison, and practical recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions like 'Which features have high absolute SHAP values but shouldn't influence hiring?' and highlight specific regions of plots to analyze. For advanced learners, introduce additional explanation methods (LIME, anchors) or ask them to calculate fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) to quantify the bias they've identified through feature importance analysis.

title: Budget Your Dream Bedroom Makeover
description: Students will apply percentage calculations and decimal operations to plan a bedroom makeover within a $500 budget. They will calculate discounts, sales tax, and determine if their desired items fit within budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine sale prices and tax amounts by working with real-world shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate decimal addition and subtraction through creating and adjusting a detailed budget spreadsheet
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Dream Bedroom Catalog' handout containing 15 furniture and decor items with original prices ranging from $25-$180. Each student receives a budget of exactly $500. Step 1 (10 minutes): Students select 4-6 items they want for their bedroom makeover and record original prices in their budget worksheet. Step 2 (15 minutes): Announce that all items are 15% off this week. Students calculate the sale price for each selected item by finding 15% of the original price, then subtracting from the original price. They must show their work: Sale Price = Original Price - (Original Price × 0.15). Step 3 (10 minutes): Students calculate the subtotal by adding all sale prices using decimal addition. Step 4 (10 minutes): Apply 8.5% sales tax to the subtotal. Students calculate tax amount (Subtotal × 0.085) and add to subtotal for the final total. Step 5 (10 minutes): Students determine if their total exceeds $500. If over budget, they must remove items and recalculate until under budget. If under budget, they can add items or accessories. Step 6 (5 minutes): Students write a reflection explaining their final choices and showing their complete mathematical work. Circulate during each step to check calculations and provide guidance.
materials_needed: Dream Bedroom Catalog handout with 15 items and prices
Budget Planning Worksheet template
Calculators (optional for checking work)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage and decimal calculations correct with clear work shown, final total within budget; (3) Minor calculation errors but process demonstrated correctly; (2) Some calculation errors with partial understanding of process; (1) Major errors in percentage or decimal operations. Students must achieve level 3 or higher to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference card showing the steps (multiply by decimal, subtract from original). Allow use of calculators after attempting by hand. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including different discount rates for different item categories or compound the challenge by adding shipping costs at 6% of subtotal.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Time Complexity Evaluation
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining their code structure, tracing execution paths, and determining Big O notation. They will break down each algorithm's performance characteristics and justify which algorithm is most appropriate for different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of three search algorithms by examining their loop structures, conditional statements, and recursive calls to determine Big O notation
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for each search method
instructions: Begin by distributing three code samples: linear search (iterative), binary search (recursive), and hash table lookup (with collision handling). Give students 10 minutes to read through each algorithm individually. Next, organize students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group one algorithm to analyze first (15 minutes). Groups must identify: (1) the basic operations being counted, (2) how the input size 'n' affects the number of operations, (3) the mathematical relationship between n and operations performed. Each group traces through their algorithm with datasets of sizes 10, 100, and 1000 elements, recording the maximum number of operations needed. After initial analysis, groups rotate to analyze the second algorithm (10 minutes), then the third (10 minutes), building a comparison table of their findings. Groups then spend 15 minutes determining Big O notation for each algorithm's worst-case scenario, documenting their reasoning with specific code line references. Finally, each group presents their analysis (5 minutes per group), explaining which algorithm they would choose for: (a) searching an unsorted array of 1 million elements, (b) searching a sorted array of 1000 elements, (c) performing frequent searches on a stable dataset. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing findings and resolving any discrepancies in Big O determinations.
materials_needed: Printed code samples of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms
Algorithm analysis worksheet with tables for recording operation counts
Calculators or computers for mathematical computations
Whiteboard markers and poster paper for group presentations
Sample datasets of varying sizes (provided as arrays)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of basic operations and loop analysis (25%), (2) Accurate Big O notation determination with mathematical justification (35%), (3) Appropriate algorithm selection for given scenarios with clear reasoning (25%), (4) Quality of group presentation and peer discussion contributions (15%). Students must submit their completed analysis worksheets and provide written justification for each Big O determination.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a Big O reference chart and guide them to focus on the innermost loop first. Offer sentence starters like 'As n increases, the number of operations...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze space complexity as well, or consider the impact of different hash functions on collision rates. Provide additional algorithms like interpolation search for extended analysis.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Deployment Strategies for Real-Time Fraud Detection
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning deployment architectures for a fraud detection system using real performance metrics, cost analysis, and business constraints. They will assess the trade-offs between batch processing, real-time streaming, and hybrid approaches to recommend the optimal solution for a financial services company.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML deployment architectures by analyzing performance metrics, latency requirements, and scalability constraints in a fraud detection context
Students will critique and defend their recommended deployment strategy through comprehensive cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment presentations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4, with each team receiving identical datasets containing 100,000 financial transactions with fraud labels and three pre-trained ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network). Teams spend 20 minutes reviewing the business scenario: a mid-size bank processing 50,000 transactions daily, requiring 99.5% uptime, with fraud detection accuracy >95% and transaction processing latency <200ms. Each team must evaluate three deployment architectures: (1) Batch processing every 15 minutes using Apache Spark, (2) Real-time streaming with Apache Kafka and Docker containers, (3) Hybrid approach combining both. For the next 90 minutes, teams implement simplified versions of each architecture using provided Docker containers and measure key metrics: prediction latency, throughput, resource utilization, and accuracy degradation. They calculate total cost of ownership using provided AWS pricing sheets, considering compute instances, storage, and data transfer costs. Teams document failure scenarios by deliberately introducing system faults (network delays, memory constraints, high transaction volumes) and measuring system behavior. In the final 60 minutes, each team prepares a 10-minute executive presentation defending their recommended architecture, including quantitative performance comparisons, cost projections, risk mitigation strategies, and implementation timeline. Teams must address specific stakeholder concerns: CTO worried about scalability, CFO focused on costs, and Risk Officer concerned about false negatives.
materials_needed: Pre-configured laptop/workstation with Docker and Python environment
Financial transaction dataset (CSV format, 100,000 records)
Three pre-trained ML model files (pickle format)
Docker containers for Kafka, Spark, and monitoring tools
AWS pricing calculator spreadsheet template
Business scenario documentation packet
Performance monitoring dashboard (Grafana/custom)
Presentation template with evaluation criteria
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using rubric with four criteria: (1) Technical Analysis (25%) - accuracy of performance measurements, proper use of monitoring tools, correct cost calculations; (2) Critical Evaluation (30%) - depth of trade-off analysis, identification of failure scenarios, consideration of business constraints; (3) Recommendation Quality (25%) - logical reasoning, evidence-based conclusions, feasibility assessment; (4) Presentation Effectiveness (20%) - clear communication, defense of decisions under questioning, addressing stakeholder concerns. Each criterion scored 1-4 points. Instructor conducts 5-minute Q&A after each presentation, asking probing questions about alternative approaches and edge cases.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step Docker commands cheat sheet, pre-populated cost calculation templates, and example performance metrics interpretation guide. Assign stronger technical students as 'architecture consultants' to help with implementation issues. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional monitoring metrics (memory usage patterns, error rates), consider multi-region deployment scenarios, or evaluate emerging technologies like serverless computing. Provide access to research papers on production ML systems for deeper analysis.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Deployment Strategies for Real-Time Fraud Detection: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate three different ML model deployment architectures (batch processing, real-time streaming, and hybrid) for a credit card fraud detection system. They will assess trade-offs between latency, accuracy, cost, and scalability to recommend the optimal deployment strategy for a financial institution processing 10,000 transactions per minute.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML deployment architectures by analyzing performance metrics, cost implications, and business requirements in a fraud detection context
Students will critique model deployment decisions through systematic comparison of latency, throughput, accuracy degradation, and infrastructure costs across three architectural approaches
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with identical datasets: a pre-trained Random Forest fraud detection model (AUC 0.89), simulated transaction streams (10,000 transactions/minute), and cost matrices for AWS infrastructure components. In the first 45 minutes, each team analyzes one deployment architecture: Team A evaluates batch processing (15-minute intervals), Team B assesses real-time streaming with Apache Kafka/Storm, and Team C examines a hybrid approach combining both. Students must calculate: average detection latency, daily infrastructure costs, model accuracy degradation over time, and system failure impact. During minutes 45-90, teams rotate through all three architectures, documenting performance metrics in provided evaluation matrices. Each architecture includes pre-configured Docker containers with monitoring dashboards showing CPU usage, memory consumption, and processing delays. In minutes 90-120, teams synthesize findings to create recommendation reports addressing: which architecture best serves the business requirement of detecting fraud within 30 seconds while maintaining 95% model accuracy and staying under $5,000 daily infrastructure costs. Teams must justify their recommendations using quantitative evidence from their analysis. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents their 5-minute recommendation with 2 minutes for peer questioning. Presentations must include: numerical comparison tables, identified trade-offs, risk assessments, and implementation timeline estimates. Provide teams with evaluation rubrics emphasizing evidence-based reasoning and consideration of multiple stakeholder perspectives (IT operations, business leaders, compliance officers).
materials_needed: Pre-trained Random Forest fraud detection model (pickle file)
Simulated credit card transaction dataset (100,000 records, CSV format)
Three Docker containers with pre-configured deployment architectures
AWS cost calculator spreadsheet template
Performance metrics tracking worksheet
Infrastructure monitoring dashboard access (Grafana/similar)
Business requirements specification document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Quantitative analysis accuracy (25%) - correct calculation of latency, costs, and performance metrics; (2) Critical evaluation quality (35%) - depth of trade-off analysis and consideration of multiple factors; (3) Recommendation justification (25%) - evidence-based reasoning linking analysis to business requirements; (4) Peer critique engagement (15%) - quality of questions asked during other teams' presentations and responses to feedback on their own recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates with partially completed examples and assign specific roles (data analyst, cost analyst, systems analyst) within teams. Create checkpoint questions every 30 minutes to guide analysis direction. For advanced learners: Introduce additional complexity factors like regulatory compliance requirements (PCI DSS), disaster recovery considerations, or A/B testing capabilities. Challenge them to consider multi-cloud deployment strategies or edge computing implications for global transaction processing.
