title: Design and Validate a Novel Statistical Test for Non-Normal Paired Data
description: Students will create an original statistical hypothesis test specifically designed for paired data that violates normality assumptions. They will develop the mathematical framework, derive critical values, and validate their test through simulation studies comparing it to existing non-parametric alternatives.
learning_objectives: Students will design a novel statistical test by deriving the test statistic distribution and establishing decision rules for paired non-normal data scenarios
Students will construct mathematical proofs for their test's properties through rigorous statistical theory and validate performance characteristics via Monte Carlo simulation
instructions: Begin by having students form teams of 2-3 and spend 15 minutes reviewing limitations of existing tests (paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank) for specific data types. Each team selects a unique scenario: heavy-tailed distributions, discrete ordinal data, or data with systematic measurement error patterns. Over the next 90 minutes, teams develop their test framework: (1) Define the null and alternative hypotheses mathematically (20 min), (2) Derive a test statistic that captures relevant data characteristics, showing all mathematical steps including moment calculations or asymptotic properties (40 min), (3) Establish critical value determination method through theoretical derivation or empirical approximation (30 min). Next, spend 60 minutes implementing their test in R or Python, creating functions that calculate the test statistic and p-values. Teams then design a validation study (45 min) comparing their test to existing methods across different sample sizes (n=10, 25, 50, 100) and effect sizes, running 1000+ simulations per condition. They must calculate Type I error rates under null hypothesis and statistical power under various alternative hypotheses. Finally, teams spend 30 minutes preparing a 10-minute presentation including: mathematical derivation summary, simulation results visualization, and recommendations for when their test should be preferred over alternatives. Conclude with 20 minutes of peer presentations where other teams provide technical feedback and challenge assumptions.
materials_needed: Statistical computing software (R/RStudio or Python with scipy/numpy)
Access to mathematical typesetting (LaTeX or equation editor)
Whiteboard or large paper for mathematical derivations
Graphing materials for simulation result visualization
Timer for presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical rigor of test derivation and theoretical justification, (2) Computational implementation correctness and efficiency, (3) Simulation study design comprehensiveness and statistical validity, (4) Critical analysis of results including honest assessment of test limitations, (5) Quality of mathematical communication in presentation. Students must demonstrate mastery (3+ points) in at least 4/5 areas, with particular emphasis on mathematical creativity and statistical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template frameworks for common test statistic forms and guide them toward simpler scenarios like symmetric distributions. Offer pre-written simulation code structures they can modify. For advanced learners, challenge them to prove asymptotic properties of their test statistic or develop adaptive procedures that adjust based on data characteristics. Encourage exploration of robust estimation techniques or Bayesian interpretations of their test framework.

title: Understanding Feature Selection Impact Through Correlation Matrix Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real-world dataset to understand how different feature selection methods affect model performance. They will interpret correlation matrices and explain the relationships between feature selection decisions and predictive accuracy outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation matrices by identifying multicollinearity patterns and explaining their impact on model performance
Students will compare feature selection outcomes through systematic analysis of three different selection methods on the same dataset
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with the Boston Housing dataset pre-loaded in Jupyter notebooks. In the first 15 minutes, students examine the dataset structure and create a correlation heatmap using seaborn, identifying features with correlation coefficients above 0.7. During minutes 16-30, each group applies three feature selection methods: (1) removing highly correlated features (>0.7 threshold), (2) selecting top 5 features using SelectKBest with f_regression, and (3) using Recursive Feature Elimination with 5 features. For minutes 31-50, groups train simple linear regression models using each feature subset, recording R² scores and RMSE values in a comparison table. In minutes 51-65, students create visualizations comparing the three approaches, plotting actual vs predicted values for each model. Finally, during minutes 66-75, each group prepares a 3-minute explanation of their findings, focusing on why certain feature combinations performed better and how correlation patterns influenced their results. Throughout the activity, students document their observations about which features were consistently selected across methods and hypothesize about the underlying relationships.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, scikit-learn, seaborn, matplotlib installed
Boston Housing dataset (available through scikit-learn)
Comparison table template for recording model performance metrics
Correlation heatmap visualization template
assessment_method: Evaluate student understanding through: (1) Completed comparison table showing accurate R² and RMSE calculations for all three methods, (2) Correctly interpreted correlation matrix with identified high-correlation pairs, (3) Written explanations connecting correlation patterns to feature selection outcomes, and (4) Oral presentation demonstrating understanding of why different methods produced different results. Award full marks for accurate calculations, clear identification of multicollinearity, and logical explanations of performance differences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated correlation matrices and guide them to focus on interpreting values above 0.5. Offer sentence starters like 'When two features are highly correlated, the model...' For advanced learners, challenge them to explore additional selection methods like LASSO regularization or to investigate feature importance rankings. Provide bonus points for students who identify domain-specific reasons why certain features correlate strongly.

title: Optimization of Manufacturing Processes Using Lagrange Multipliers
description: Students will apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving cost minimization and resource constraints. They will work through a complete optimization scenario for a packaging company determining optimal container dimensions while meeting volume requirements and material cost limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing a multi-variable manufacturing scenario with at least two constraints
Students will interpret mathematical solutions within real-world contexts through cost-benefit analysis and feasibility assessment of their optimized solutions
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario handout describing PackCorp's need to design rectangular containers with 500 cubic inch capacity, using materials costing $0.08/sq inch for sides and $0.12/sq inch for top/bottom, with height restrictions between 4-8 inches due to shipping limitations. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: pairs read the scenario, identify variables (length=x, width=y, height=z), write the objective function C(x,y,z) = 0.08(2xz + 2yz) + 0.12(2xy), and list constraints: g₁(x,y,z) = xyz - 500 = 0, g₂(z) = z - 4 ≥ 0, g₃(z) = 8 - z ≥ 0. Next 40 minutes: students set up the Lagrangian L(x,y,z,λ₁,λ₂,λ₃) and solve the system of partial derivatives. They must show all algebraic steps, finding critical points, and checking boundary conditions at z=4 and z=8. Following 20 minutes: pairs calculate the minimum cost for each feasible solution and determine optimal dimensions. Final 10 minutes: each pair presents their optimal dimensions and minimum cost to another pair, explaining why their solution is feasible and cost-effective. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students correctly apply the constraint qualification conditions and properly interpret λ values as shadow prices representing marginal cost changes.
materials_needed: PackCorp Manufacturing Scenario handout with detailed cost structure and constraints
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Mathematica, Maple, or similar)
Grid paper for sketching constraint regions
Solution verification worksheet with checkpoint questions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct formulation of Lagrangian with all constraints (25%), (2) Accurate solution of the system showing all algebraic steps (35%), (3) Proper boundary analysis and feasibility checking (25%), (4) Clear interpretation of results including economic meaning of Lagrange multipliers (15%). Students must submit their complete mathematical work plus a brief written explanation of why their solution optimizes the manufacturing process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed Lagrangian setup and suggest using substitution method first before applying multipliers. Offer a constraint checklist to verify feasibility. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding a third constraint for environmental impact or introducing inequality constraints requiring Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions. Provide additional scenarios with different cost structures or multiple product types.

title: Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in Multi-threaded Applications Using Profiler Data
description: Students will analyze real profiler output from a multi-threaded Java application to identify performance bottlenecks, thread synchronization issues, and memory allocation patterns. They will decompose the profiling data to distinguish between different types of performance problems and their underlying causes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze profiler traces and thread dumps by examining CPU usage patterns, lock contention metrics, and garbage collection statistics to identify specific performance bottlenecks
Students will differentiate between synchronization-related performance issues and algorithmic inefficiencies through systematic examination of profiling data visualizations
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided profiler dataset from a multi-threaded e-commerce application experiencing performance issues (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to examine three data sources: JProfiler CPU sampling data, thread dump analysis, and garbage collection logs. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students analyze the CPU hotspots view to identify the top 10 methods consuming CPU time, categorizing each as either computation-intensive, I/O-bound, or synchronization-related. They must document the percentage of total execution time and thread distribution for each hotspot. Phase 2 (40 minutes) focuses on thread analysis where students examine thread states over time, identifying blocked threads and mapping lock contention points using the profiler's thread timeline view. Students create a dependency graph showing which threads are waiting for which locks. Phase 3 (35 minutes) involves memory analysis where students examine allocation patterns, identifying objects with high allocation rates and correlating these with garbage collection frequency. Students must distinguish between memory leaks and high-churn scenarios. In Phase 4 (20 minutes), students synthesize findings to create a prioritized list of performance issues, ranking them by impact and providing specific evidence from the profiler data. Each pair presents their top 3 findings with supporting metrics to another pair for peer validation (15 minutes). Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing findings across teams and revealing the actual root causes identified by the development team.
materials_needed: JProfiler or VisualVM profiler software installed on student machines
Pre-captured profiler session file (.jps) from multi-threaded application
Thread dump files (.dump format) from the same application session
Garbage collection log files in standard GC format
Analysis worksheet template with data recording tables
Laptop/desktop computers with minimum 8GB RAM
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of CPU hotspots with correct categorization and supporting metrics (25%), (2) Correct analysis of thread synchronization issues with proper identification of deadlock/contention points (30%), (3) Appropriate distinction between memory allocation patterns and accurate correlation with GC behavior (25%), (4) Quality of evidence-based prioritization and clarity of recommendations with quantitative justification (20%). Students submit completed analysis worksheets and a 1-page executive summary of findings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each phase such as 'Which method appears in the top 5 CPU consumers and involves the keyword synchronized?' and offer simplified profiler views with pre-filtered data. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Include additional profiler data from production systems, challenge them to correlate performance issues with business metrics, or have them propose specific code refactoring solutions with estimated performance improvements based on their analysis.

title: Design Your Own Community Budget Allocation Game
description: Students will create an interactive mathematical game that simulates real-world budget allocation decisions for a fictional community. They will integrate percentage calculations, ratio analysis, and graphical data representation while designing engaging gameplay mechanics that teach financial literacy concepts to their peers.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize percentage calculations, ratio analysis, and data visualization by designing an interactive budget allocation game with multiple scenarios and mathematical constraints
Students will construct original mathematical models through creating game rules that incorporate real-world financial decision-making processes and trade-off analysis
instructions: **Phase 1 - Planning (15 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a Community Profile Card containing population data, income statistics, and current budget breakdown for their fictional community (e.g., Riverside Town: 25,000 residents, median income $45,000, current budget $12M). Teams brainstorm their game concept and identify 5-7 budget categories (education, infrastructure, healthcare, public safety, recreation, environmental, emergency fund). **Phase 2 - Mathematical Framework (25 minutes):** Teams create their game's mathematical rules using provided Budget Constraint Template. They must establish: minimum percentage requirements for each category (e.g., education minimum 25%, emergency fund minimum 10%), ratio relationships between categories (e.g., healthcare:public safety ratio cannot exceed 3:1), and consequence formulas for decisions (e.g., insufficient infrastructure funding = -15% community satisfaction score). Teams calculate at least three different budget scenarios showing percentage breakdowns and their mathematical outcomes. **Phase 3 - Game Design (30 minutes):** Using poster board and provided materials, teams create their physical game board with spinner/dice mechanics, decision cards featuring budget dilemmas, and scoring system. They must incorporate their mathematical constraints visually through charts, graphs, or calculation sheets. Teams write clear game instructions including victory conditions and mathematical formulas players must use. **Phase 4 - Testing & Refinement (15 minutes):** Teams conduct quick playtests with another group, gathering feedback on mathematical accuracy and game flow. They revise rules and recalculate examples as needed. **Phase 5 - Presentation (20 minutes):** Each team presents their completed game to the class, demonstrating one round of gameplay while explaining the underlying mathematical concepts and real-world applications of their budget allocation model.
materials_needed: Community Profile Cards (pre-made with demographic and budget data)
Budget Constraint Templates with calculation frameworks
Poster board (11x17 inches minimum)
Colored markers, rulers, calculators
Spinners, dice, or random number generators
Index cards for decision scenarios
Graphing paper and protractors for data visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - correct percentage calculations, ratio relationships, and constraint formulas; Creative Integration (25%) - innovative game mechanics that meaningfully incorporate math concepts; Real-World Application (25%) - realistic budget scenarios and consequences that reflect actual community decisions; Presentation Quality (25%) - clear explanation of mathematical concepts and effective demonstration of gameplay. Students submit their game materials, calculation worksheets, and a one-page reflection explaining their mathematical decision-making process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated percentage conversion charts, offer simplified Community Profile Cards with smaller budget numbers, and assign roles within teams based on strengths (visual designer, calculator, presenter). For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate compound growth formulas for multi-year budget planning, add probability elements for uncertain revenue scenarios, or create digital versions using spreadsheet software with automated calculations and graphical outputs.

title: Designing a Cryptocurrency Exchange Rate Prediction Algorithm Using Multivariable Calculus and Statistical Models
description: Students will synthesize advanced calculus concepts, statistical modeling, and economic principles to construct an original algorithm that predicts cryptocurrency exchange rate fluctuations. They will develop their own mathematical framework combining partial derivatives, optimization theory, and stochastic processes to create a functional prediction model.
estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across multiple class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical algorithm integrating multivariable calculus, linear algebra, and probability theory by developing predictive models for financial market behavior
Students will design and justify a comprehensive mathematical framework through systematic application of optimization techniques, error analysis, and statistical validation methods
instructions: Begin by having students form teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with historical cryptocurrency data spanning 6 months for Bitcoin, Ethereum, and one altcoin of their choice. Teams must first analyze the data to identify key variables affecting price movements using correlation matrices and regression analysis (45 minutes). Next, students design their core algorithm by selecting and combining at least three mathematical approaches: gradient descent optimization, Monte Carlo simulation, moving averages with weighted derivatives, Fourier analysis for cyclical patterns, or Markov chain modeling (90 minutes). They must mathematically justify each component choice using calculus-based reasoning and provide rigorous proofs for any novel combinations. Students then implement their algorithm using Python or MATLAB, creating functions that calculate partial derivatives for multi-factor sensitivity analysis and incorporate stochastic differential equations for volatility modeling (120 minutes). Teams must validate their model by backtesting against reserved data sets and computing confidence intervals using bootstrap methods. Finally, students prepare a formal mathematical presentation (30 minutes) demonstrating their algorithm's theoretical foundation, implementation code, performance metrics (MAE, RMSE, Sharpe ratio), and a critical analysis of limitations including discussion of market efficiency theory and model assumptions.
materials_needed: Historical cryptocurrency price datasets (6+ months, minute-level data)
Python/MATLAB programming environment with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas libraries
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Wolfram Alpha)
Statistical analysis software (R Studio or equivalent)
Presentation software with LaTeX equation support
assessment_method: Evaluate using a detailed rubric: Mathematical rigor and originality of algorithm design (30 points), correct application of multivariable calculus and optimization theory (25 points), quality of statistical validation and error analysis (20 points), functionality and efficiency of code implementation (15 points), clarity of mathematical presentation and defense of methodology (10 points). Students must achieve minimum 80% accuracy in backtesting and demonstrate understanding through oral examination of their mathematical derivations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template code frameworks and guided worksheets for partial derivative calculations. Offer intermediate checkpoints for algorithm component verification. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate machine learning elements like neural networks, explore high-frequency trading implications, or extend their model to predict multiple cryptocurrencies simultaneously using cointegration analysis. Provide additional datasets from forex or stock markets for cross-validation.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Functions for Real-World Resource Allocation
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a complex business scenario involving profit maximization with multiple constraints. They will use Lagrange multipliers and partial derivatives to determine optimal production levels for a manufacturing company with limited resources.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier method to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing a multi-variable profit function with resource limitations
Students will interpret optimization results through economic analysis and make strategic business recommendations based on mathematical findings
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario: TechCorp manufactures tablets (x) and smartphones (y) with profit function P(x,y) = 120x + 80y - 0.5x² - 0.3y² - 0.2xy, subject to constraints: labor (2x + 3y ≤ 240 hours), materials (4x + 2y ≤ 280 units), and non-negativity. Step 1 (15 min): Students work in pairs to set up the Lagrangian function L(x,y,λ,μ) = P(x,y) - λ(2x + 3y - 240) - μ(4x + 2y - 280). Step 2 (20 min): Calculate all partial derivatives and set equal to zero, creating the system of equations. Step 3 (25 min): Solve the system algebraically to find critical points, checking boundary conditions and corner points of the feasible region. Step 4 (15 min): Evaluate the profit function at all candidate points to determine the global maximum. Step 5 (20 min): Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation including: optimal production quantities, maximum profit value, shadow prices (λ and μ values), and interpretation of what happens if constraints change by one unit. Step 6 (15 min): Three randomly selected teams present their solutions. Conclude with whole-class discussion comparing results and discussing the economic significance of shadow prices in resource allocation decisions.
materials_needed: Printed scenario handouts with profit function and constraints
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos, GeoGebra, or Mathematica)
Graph paper for sketching feasible regions
Presentation timer for 3-minute presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Setup (correct Lagrangian formation), Computational Accuracy (solving system of equations), Solution Verification (checking critical points and boundaries), and Business Interpretation (explaining shadow prices and making recommendations). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category and present coherent economic reasoning for their mathematical results.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partial derivative formulas pre-written and offer step-by-step calculation guides. Create mixed-ability pairs and provide graphical representations of the feasible region. For advanced learners: Add a third product variable or introduce integer programming constraints, ask them to analyze sensitivity of the solution to parameter changes, or have them create their own optimization scenarios for classmates.

title: Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Varying Data Conditions
description: Students will systematically analyze the performance characteristics of four sorting algorithms (Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Heap Sort, and Radix Sort) by examining their behavior with different data sets and identifying the algorithmic design factors that cause performance variations. They will deconstruct each algorithm's time and space complexity patterns to determine optimal use cases.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between algorithmic design choices and performance outcomes by comparing execution metrics across four sorting algorithms with six different data conditions
Students will deconstruct the underlying causes of performance variations through systematic examination of each algorithm's computational complexity patterns and memory usage behaviors
instructions:
Begin with a 15-minute setup phase where students access the provided performance testing framework containing pre-implemented versions of Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Heap Sort, and Radix Sort. Students work in pairs to ensure collaborative analysis.

In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students execute each algorithm against six standardized datasets: sorted arrays (10K elements), reverse-sorted arrays (10K elements), random arrays (10K elements), arrays with many duplicates (10K elements), nearly-sorted arrays (10K elements), and small arrays (100 elements). They collect execution time, memory usage, and comparison count metrics using the built-in profiling tools, recording data in the provided analysis spreadsheet.

Phase 2 (30 minutes) focuses on pattern identification. Students create comparative visualizations showing performance trends across data conditions, identifying which algorithms perform best/worst under specific conditions. They must document at least three significant performance patterns they observe.

Phase 3 (45 minutes) requires algorithmic deconstruction. Students examine the source code of each algorithm, mapping specific code structures (recursive calls, partitioning strategies, memory allocation patterns) to the performance patterns they observed. They complete a detailed analysis matrix identifying why each algorithm behaves differently under each data condition.

Conclude with a 15-minute presentation where each pair presents their most significant finding about one algorithm's performance characteristic, supported by both empirical data and algorithmic reasoning. Emphasize connecting implementation details to performance outcomes.
materials_needed: Performance testing framework with implemented sorting algorithms (Python/Java)
Six standardized datasets (provided as data files)
Performance analysis spreadsheet template
Code analysis worksheet with algorithm source code
Computers with programming environment and profiling tools
assessment_method: Students submit completed analysis matrices (40%), performance visualization charts with documented patterns (30%), and algorithmic reasoning explanations linking code structure to performance (30%). Success requires identifying minimum 3 significant patterns, correctly explaining 2 algorithmic design factors causing performance variations, and providing data-supported conclusions about optimal use cases for each algorithm.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each analysis phase and example pattern identification from bubble sort vs selection sort. Extend advanced learners by having them modify algorithm implementations to test hypotheses about performance improvements, or analyze additional algorithms like Tim Sort or Intro Sort for comparison.

title: Memory Palace for Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classifications
description: Students will create and recite from memory a comprehensive classification system for 25 advanced algorithms organized by time and space complexity classes. This activity focuses on memorizing exact complexity notations, algorithm names, and their categorical relationships without requiring implementation or analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact Big O time complexity notation for 25 advanced algorithms including FFT, A*, Dijkstra's, and advanced sorting variants by reciting from memory without reference materials
Students will identify and state the precise space complexity class for each algorithm through structured memory retrieval exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-printed Algorithm Complexity Reference Chart containing 25 algorithms organized in a 5x5 grid by complexity classes (O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(n³), O(2ⁿ), etc.). Give students 15 minutes to study the chart, encouraging them to create mental associations or mnemonic devices. Remove all reference materials. Conduct Round 1 (10 minutes): Call out algorithm names randomly; students must write the exact time complexity notation. Record responses on the tracking sheet. Conduct Round 2 (10 minutes): State a complexity class (e.g., 'O(n log n)'); students list all algorithms in that category from memory. Conduct Round 3 (15 minutes): Present algorithm pairs; students must state which has better/worse time complexity and provide both exact notations. Between each round, allow 3-minute study periods where students can review their errors using the reference chart. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal quiz (5 minutes) where individual students must recite the complete time and space complexity for algorithms called out randomly. Document accuracy rates for each student across all rounds. Students scoring below 80% accuracy receive the reference chart for additional 10-minute memorization before a makeup assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-printed Algorithm Complexity Reference Chart (5x5 grid format)
Student response sheets with algorithm name blanks
Instructor tracking sheet for accuracy recording
Timer/stopwatch
Whiteboard for recording complexity classes during Round 2
assessment_method: Grade based on cumulative accuracy across three rounds: 90-100% accuracy (A), 80-89% (B), 70-79% (C), 60-69% (D). Students must achieve minimum 16/25 correct algorithm-complexity pairings in Round 1, identify at least 3/5 algorithms correctly in each complexity class during Round 2, and answer 7/10 comparison questions correctly in Round 3.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded reference charts grouping similar complexities, allow creation of personal flashcards during study periods, and offer acronym memory aids (e.g., 'Quick Merge Heap' for O(n log n) algorithms). For advanced learners: Include average vs. worst-case complexity distinctions, add 10 additional advanced algorithms (suffix trees, advanced graph algorithms), and require recitation of the specific conditions that affect complexity variations.

title: Interpreting Dimensionality Reduction Trade-offs in High-Dimensional Customer Behavior Data
description: Students will analyze the mathematical and conceptual differences between PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP dimensionality reduction techniques applied to a 47-dimensional customer transaction dataset. They will interpret how each method's underlying assumptions affect the preservation of local versus global data structure and business interpretability.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between variance-based, probability-based, and manifold learning approaches to dimensionality reduction by analyzing their mathematical foundations and comparing visual outputs on identical datasets

Students will interpret the business implications of information loss in each dimensionality reduction technique through systematic comparison of cluster interpretability and feature contribution analysis
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the preprocessed customer transaction dataset (47 features including purchase frequency, average transaction value, product categories, seasonal patterns, etc.) and pre-generated visualizations from PCA, t-SNE (perplexity=30), and UMAP (n_neighbors=15). In the first 20 minutes, students individually examine the three 2D scatter plots and identify visual differences in cluster formation, outlier placement, and data point density. Next, spend 25 minutes having teams analyze the provided mathematical summary sheets explaining each algorithm's objective function: PCA's variance maximization, t-SNE's probability distribution matching, and UMAP's manifold approximation. Students should map each algorithm's mathematical goal to observed visual patterns. During the following 30 minutes, teams complete a structured comparison matrix examining: (1) preservation of global vs. local structure, (2) interpretability of axes, (3) sensitivity to hyperparameters, (4) computational scalability, and (5) business actionability. Provide teams with specific customer personas (high-value loyal customers, seasonal shoppers, etc.) identified through domain expertise, and have them evaluate which dimensionality reduction method best preserves these known business-relevant groupings. In the final 15 minutes, each team presents one key insight about when to choose each method based on business objectives, supported by evidence from their analysis. Conclude with a brief discussion connecting their findings to real-world data science project constraints like computational resources, interpretability requirements, and stakeholder communication needs.
materials_needed: Customer transaction dataset CSV file with 47 preprocessed features (5000 rows)
Pre-generated PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP 2D visualizations in PDF format
Mathematical summary handouts explaining each algorithm's objective function
Structured comparison matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Customer persona reference sheet with known business segments
Laptops with Python/R environment (Jupyter notebooks optional for advanced extension)
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of mathematical concept identification (25%), (2) Quality of visual pattern interpretation linking algorithm properties to observed outputs (30%), (3) Appropriateness of business context recommendations with supporting evidence (30%), (4) Clarity and precision of technical communication during presentations (15%). Success requires demonstrating understanding that PCA preserves global variance structure but loses local relationships, t-SNE excels at local structure preservation but distorts global distances, and UMAP balances both while maintaining computational efficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided questions highlighting specific visual elements to examine (cluster separation, point density, outlier placement) and offer simplified algorithm explanation cards focusing on 'what each method tries to optimize.' For advanced learners, provide access to original code and hyperparameter settings, allowing them to experiment with different parameter values (t-SNE perplexity, UMAP n_neighbors) and analyze how changes affect results. Consider providing additional dimensionality reduction methods (LLE, Isomap) for comparison extension.

title: Budget Your Dream Weekend: Applying Decimal Operations in Real-World Scenarios
description: Students will plan a realistic weekend budget using decimal addition, subtraction, and multiplication to calculate costs for activities, meals, and transportation. They will apply mathematical operations to make spending decisions within a fixed budget constraint.
learning_objectives: Students will apply decimal addition and subtraction by calculating total expenses and remaining budget amounts in a weekend planning scenario
Students will apply decimal multiplication through computing sales tax, tips, and group cost-sharing in authentic spending situations
instructions: Begin by distributing the weekend planning worksheet and announcing that each student has a $75.00 budget for a two-day weekend (15 minutes setup). Present the scenario: students must plan Saturday and Sunday activities including at least one meal out, one entertainment activity, and transportation costs. Display the provided price list on the board or project it, showing realistic local prices with decimals (movie tickets $12.50, pizza slice $3.75, bus fare $2.25, etc.). Students work individually for 25 minutes to select activities and calculate costs using decimal operations. They must show all mathematical work on their worksheet, including adding individual item costs, calculating 8.5% sales tax where applicable, determining 15% tips for restaurant meals, and subtracting running totals from their $75.00 budget. After initial planning, pair students for 10 minutes to compare budgets and check each other's calculations using calculators. Partners must identify any mathematical errors and suggest corrections. Students then have 10 minutes to revise their budgets based on feedback. Conclude with a 15-minute sharing session where volunteers present their weekend plans and explain one complex calculation they performed, such as splitting a $28.75 group dinner among four friends or calculating total cost including tax and tip.
materials_needed: Weekend Planning Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Local Price List handout with decimal prices for 15-20 activities/items
Calculators (one per pair for checking work)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct decimal operations, proper alignment), Problem-Solving Process (shows all work, logical sequence), Budget Constraint (stays within $75 limit), and Real-World Application (realistic choices, appropriate tax/tip calculations). Students must demonstrate at least 80% accuracy in decimal calculations and successfully remain within budget to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a calculation template showing decimal alignment examples and offering a simplified price list with fewer options. Encourage use of estimation strategies before calculating exact amounts. For advanced learners, introduce percentage discounts, group deals, or require planning for multiple people with different budget amounts.

title: Algorithm Performance Analysis: Time Complexity Investigation of Sorting Algorithms
description: Students will analyze and compare the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by examining their code structure, identifying performance bottlenecks, and evaluating empirical runtime data. They will break down each algorithm's recursive calls and loop structures to determine theoretical complexity and validate findings through experimental analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of three sorting algorithms by examining their nested loops, recursive calls, and conditional statements to determine Big O notation
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through systematic comparison of theoretical complexity predictions against empirical runtime measurements across varying input sizes
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (bubble sort, merge sort, quicksort) and a data collection template. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one algorithm to focus on initially (15 minutes setup). 

Phase 1 - Code Structure Analysis (45 minutes): Each team examines their assigned algorithm's source code, identifying and documenting: (1) all loops and their nesting levels, (2) recursive function calls and their frequency, (3) conditional statements affecting execution flow, and (4) operations performed on each data element. Teams create a visual flowchart showing the algorithm's execution path and annotate it with operation counts.

Phase 2 - Theoretical Complexity Determination (30 minutes): Using their code analysis, teams calculate theoretical time complexity by counting operations relative to input size n. They must justify their Big O notation choice with specific evidence from code structure (e.g., 'nested loops create O(n²) because outer loop runs n times, inner loop runs n times for each iteration').

Phase 3 - Empirical Testing (40 minutes): Teams run their algorithm on datasets of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 2500, and 5000 elements, recording execution times in milliseconds. They plot runtime vs. input size graphs and calculate growth rates between data points.

Phase 4 - Cross-Algorithm Analysis (30 minutes): Teams rotate to examine other algorithms' documentation and results. They complete a comparison matrix evaluating best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for all three algorithms.

Phase 5 - Synthesis Presentation (20 minutes): Each team presents their findings, explaining discrepancies between theoretical predictions and empirical results, and recommending optimal algorithm choices for different scenarios.
materials_needed: Pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in chosen programming language
Timer/profiling tool for measuring algorithm execution time
Graphing software or spreadsheet application (Excel, Google Sheets)
Data collection template with sections for code analysis, complexity calculations, and runtime measurements
Test datasets of varying sizes (100, 500, 1000, 2500, 5000 elements)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of Big O notation determination with proper justification from code analysis (25 points), (2) Quality of empirical data collection and graph creation showing clear trends (25 points), (3) Depth of comparative analysis identifying performance trade-offs and use case recommendations (25 points), (4) Clear explanation of relationships between theoretical complexity and observed runtime behavior (25 points). Students must submit their annotated code analysis, completed data tables, runtime graphs, and comparison matrix.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets breaking down complexity analysis into smaller steps, offer pre-labeled code snippets highlighting loops and recursive calls, and pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze memory complexity alongside time complexity, investigate additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or modify existing algorithms to improve performance and re-analyze the impact.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Business Decision Making
description: Students will critically assess three different machine learning approaches applied to a real-world customer churn prediction problem, evaluating their business impact, technical validity, and implementation feasibility. They will then defend their model selection through a structured peer review process and executive summary presentation.
estimated_duration: 7 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of competing ML models by analyzing performance metrics, business constraints, and implementation costs within a realistic business scenario
Students will critique model assumptions and limitations through systematic comparison of Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network approaches using multiple evaluation criteria
instructions:
Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with identical customer churn datasets (10,000+ records) and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network, each achieving 82-87% accuracy. Students receive model performance reports including confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance rankings, training times, and prediction latencies. 

Hour 1-2: Teams analyze each model using provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: predictive accuracy, interpretability, computational efficiency, scalability, business alignment, and implementation complexity. Students complete detailed comparison matrices and identify trade-offs between models.

Hour 3: Teams conduct 'red team' analysis, deliberately seeking weaknesses in each approach by examining edge cases, data drift scenarios, and potential bias issues. They document critical limitations and failure modes for each model.

Hour 4-5: Students prepare executive summaries (2 pages maximum) recommending one model while acknowledging limitations. Summaries must include quantified business impact projections, implementation timeline estimates, and risk mitigation strategies.

Hour 6: Structured peer review sessions where teams present 10-minute recommendations followed by 15-minute challenge sessions. Opposing teams attempt to discredit recommendations using prepared counterarguments. Original teams must defend choices with evidence-based responses.

Final Hour: Teams revise recommendations based on peer feedback and submit final evaluations including: model selection rationale, implementation roadmap, success metrics, and monitoring strategy for production deployment.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV format, 10,000+ records)
Three pre-trained model files with performance reports
Model evaluation framework template with scoring rubrics
Business context document including budget constraints and timeline requirements
Access to Python/R environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
Presentation templates for executive summaries
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis (30 points) - accuracy of performance interpretation and limitation identification; Critical Thinking (25 points) - quality of trade-off analysis and counterargument consideration; Business Judgment (25 points) - alignment with business constraints and realistic implementation planning; Communication (20 points) - clarity of written recommendations and effectiveness in defending positions during peer challenges. Success requires scoring 80+ points with minimum 20 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing evaluation checklist templates and example trade-off analyses from different domains. Offer guided practice in interpreting confusion matrices and ROC curves. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity through ensemble method evaluation, A/B testing design considerations, or ethical AI assessment frameworks. Provide optional deep-dive materials on model explainability techniques and production ML system architecture.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Epidemic Spread with Policy Interventions
description: Students will create an original mathematical model combining differential equations, probability theory, and optimization to predict epidemic spread under various policy scenarios. They will present their model to a panel acting as public health officials, defending their mathematical choices and policy recommendations.
estimated_duration: 390 minutes (spread across 4 class periods over 2 weeks)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from differential equations, probability distributions, and optimization theory by constructing a multi-variable epidemic model with at least three intervention parameters
Students will evaluate and justify their mathematical modeling choices through formal presentation and defense to simulate real-world policy advisory scenarios
instructions:
**Phase 1: Model Construction (Days 1-2, 180 minutes total)**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives a unique demographic dataset (population density, age distribution, mobility patterns) and must construct a modified SEIR model. Begin with the basic structure: dS/dt = -βSI/N, dE/dt = βSI/N - σE, dI/dt = σE - γI, dR/dt = γI. Teams must incorporate at least three policy interventions as controllable parameters: mask mandate effectiveness (reducing β by 15-60%), social distancing compliance (reducing contact rate by 20-80%), and vaccination rate (moving individuals from S to R). Students must justify their parameter ranges using provided research literature. Each team creates their system using Python/MATLAB, solving the differential equation system numerically.

**Phase 2: Optimization and Analysis (Day 3, 120 minutes)**
Teams formulate an optimization problem minimizing total deaths while constraining economic cost (assign monetary values to each intervention). Use Lagrange multipliers or numerical optimization to find optimal policy combinations. Create sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with different constraint values. Generate visualizations showing infection curves under different scenarios.

**Phase 3: Presentation Defense (Day 4, 90 minutes)**
Each team presents 12-minute formal presentations to instructor and guest experts acting as public health board. Include: model assumptions and justifications, mathematical derivation of key equations, optimization results with confidence intervals, policy recommendations with cost-benefit analysis. Panel asks challenging questions about model limitations, parameter sensitivity, and real-world applicability. Teams must defend mathematical rigor and practical feasibility.
materials_needed: Python or MATLAB software with numerical solving packages (scipy.integrate or ode45)
Demographic datasets for 6 different regions (provided as CSV files)
Research literature packet with 15 peer-reviewed papers on epidemic parameters
Economic cost data for policy interventions
Presentation equipment and recording capability
Graphing/visualization libraries (matplotlib, plotly)
assessment_method: Rubric with four components (25% each): 1) Mathematical rigor - correct implementation of differential equations, appropriate parameter justification, valid optimization setup; 2) Model innovation - creative incorporation of realistic factors beyond basic requirements; 3) Analysis quality - thorough sensitivity analysis, appropriate uncertainty quantification, clear interpretation of results; 4) Communication - clear presentation, effective defense of choices, professional response to questions. Each component scored 1-4 scale. Minimum score of 12/16 for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structure with differential equation solver setup, offer optional review session on Lagrange multipliers, allow consultation appointments during construction phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate spatial dynamics using PDEs, add stochastic elements using Monte Carlo methods, or include age-stratified compartments. Consider economic modeling extensions using game theory for compliance behavior.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions that are essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary-decimal flashcards to each student (16 cards total, showing decimal 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary on the other). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, taking turns showing each other the decimal side and stating the binary equivalent aloud. Partner should verify accuracy using the card's reverse side. After initial practice, conduct a whole-class 'popcorn' activity where you display decimal numbers 0-15 randomly on the board and students raise hands to volunteer the binary equivalent. Record correct responses to track participation. Next, reverse the process by showing binary numbers (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.) and asking for decimal equivalents. For the final 15 minutes, implement a 'speed round' where students work individually with their flashcard set, sorting cards into 'know immediately' and 'need more practice' piles. Students must complete one full cycle through all 16 cards in under 60 seconds for the 'mastery' pile. Conclude by having each student write down from memory all 16 binary-decimal pairs on the provided worksheet without referring to cards. Circulate during all activities to provide immediate feedback and correction. Emphasize that this is pure memorization - no calculation methods should be used during recall phases.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 and corresponding 4-bit binary (one set per student)
Whiteboard or projector for displaying numbers
Binary-decimal conversion worksheet for final assessment
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must correctly complete the final written worksheet showing all 16 binary-decimal pairs from memory with 90% accuracy (14/16 correct). Additionally, observe and record student performance during speed rounds - students achieving sub-60 second completion with 90% accuracy demonstrate mastery level recall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pattern recognition hints (powers of 2: 8-4-2-1 positions) and allow extra practice time with a smaller subset (0-7 first). For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents for the same decimal range. Consider mnemonic devices for difficult numbers like 'lucky 13 is 1101'.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recall Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard activities. This foundational exercise builds essential number system knowledge required for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the 4-bit binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will recall binary-to-decimal and decimal-to-binary conversions through timed practice sessions and peer quizzing
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Have students work individually for the first 10 minutes, cycling through all 16 cards, saying each conversion aloud. Instruct them to create two separate piles: 'mastered' for immediate correct answers and 'practice needed' for hesitation or errors. After individual practice, pair students for 15 minutes of peer drilling. Partner A shows the decimal side while Partner B states the binary equivalent, then switch roles and repeat with binary-to-decimal conversions. Partners should track correct/incorrect responses on the provided score sheet. Conduct a 5-minute whole-class rapid-fire session where you call out numbers randomly and students write answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate feedback. Conclude with a 10-minute individual assessment where students complete a worksheet containing 20 mixed conversion problems (10 decimal-to-binary, 10 binary-to-decimal) without reference materials. Walk around during all activities to monitor progress, provide encouragement, and identify students needing additional support. Ensure students understand that binary uses only 0s and 1s, and that each position represents powers of 2 (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s place for 4-bit numbers).
materials_needed: 16 laminated flashcards per student (decimal 0-15 with 4-bit binary equivalents)
Peer practice score sheets (tracking correct/incorrect responses)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Individual assessment worksheet with 20 conversion problems
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (18/20 correct) on the final individual worksheet. Score both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal sections separately. Document peer practice performance using score sheets. Observe and note students who consistently respond correctly during the rapid-fire whiteboard session.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1) and demonstrate the addition method for first few examples. Allow extra individual practice time before peer work. For advanced learners: extend to 8-bit binary numbers (0-255) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to explain the pattern recognition strategies to struggling peers.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Problems
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus techniques to solve authentic business optimization scenarios involving profit maximization and cost minimization. Teams will use partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint analysis to develop comprehensive solutions for three industry-specific cases.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial differentiation and Lagrange multipliers to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing real business scenarios with multiple variables and constraints
Students will implement multivariable optimization techniques through systematic problem-solving protocols to determine maximum profit and minimum cost solutions
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute three business case packets: (1) Manufacturing company maximizing profit with labor/material constraints, (2) Delivery service minimizing fuel costs across multiple routes with time constraints, (3) Restaurant chain optimizing menu pricing with demand elasticity constraints. Each case includes specific numerical data, constraint equations, and company background information.

Teams select one case and spend 20 minutes analyzing the problem structure, identifying decision variables, objective functions, and constraints. They must complete the provided problem analysis template documenting: variables (x₁, x₂, etc.), objective function f(x₁,x₂,...), constraint equations g₁(x₁,x₂,...)=0, and boundary conditions.

Next, teams apply optimization techniques over 40 minutes: calculate first-order partial derivatives, set up Lagrange multiplier equations L=f(x,y)+λg(x,y), solve the resulting system of equations, and verify solutions using second derivative tests. Students must show all mathematical work on provided calculation sheets.

Teams then spend 25 minutes interpreting results in business context: calculate exact profit/cost values, determine sensitivity to constraint changes, and assess practical feasibility of solutions. They complete a business recommendation template addressing implementation strategies and potential limitations.

Finally, each team presents their 5-minute solution to the class (15 minutes total), explaining their mathematical approach, numerical results, and business recommendations. Other teams ask clarifying questions and provide feedback using peer evaluation forms.
materials_needed: Three detailed business case study packets with numerical data
Problem analysis template worksheets
Graphing calculators or laptops with mathematical software (Desmos, Wolfram Alpha)
Large poster paper and markers for calculations
Business recommendation template forms
Peer evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy (40 points) - correct partial derivatives, Lagrange multiplier setup, and solution verification; Problem-solving process (30 points) - systematic approach, clear documentation, and logical progression; Business application (20 points) - realistic interpretation, practical recommendations, and constraint analysis; Presentation quality (10 points) - clear communication of methods and results. Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partial derivative reference sheets and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier examples. Offer intermediate checkpoints where instructor verifies problem setup before proceeding to calculations. For advanced learners, include additional constraints or ask them to analyze how solutions change with modified parameters. Provide alternative cases involving inequality constraints for students who finish early.

title: Distributed System Bottleneck Analysis: Decomposing a Microservices Architecture Performance Crisis
description: Students will analyze a real-world distributed system experiencing performance degradation by examining system logs, metrics, and architecture diagrams to identify bottlenecks, trace dependencies, and determine root causes. They will deconstruct the interactions between microservices to understand how failures cascade through the system.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system performance bottlenecks by correlating log data, metrics, and service dependency maps to identify root causes of system degradation
Students will deconstruct microservices interactions through systematic examination of request flows, database queries, and inter-service communication patterns
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a comprehensive case study packet containing: system architecture diagram of an e-commerce platform with 12 microservices, 48 hours of aggregated log files from all services, Grafana dashboard screenshots showing CPU, memory, and response time metrics, and database query performance reports. Start with a 15-minute briefing explaining the business context: the system handles 50,000+ daily orders but response times have degraded from 200ms to 8+ seconds over the past week. Students spend the first 45 minutes individually examining the materials, creating personal notes on suspicious patterns, anomalies, and potential failure points. Next, teams collaborate for 90 minutes to systematically analyze the data using the provided analysis framework: (1) Map the request flow from user authentication through order completion, (2) Identify services showing abnormal resource consumption or error rates, (3) Correlate timestamp patterns across different service logs to trace cascading failures, (4) Examine database connection pools, query execution times, and lock contentions, (5) Analyze network latency between services and external API calls. Teams then spend 30 minutes creating a visual fault tree diagram showing how issues propagate through the system. Finally, each team presents their 10-minute analysis to the class, defending their root cause hypothesis with specific evidence from the logs and metrics, and proposing targeted solutions that address the underlying architectural weaknesses rather than just symptoms.
materials_needed: Multi-service log file dataset (JSON format, 500MB compressed)
System architecture diagram (Lucidchart or Draw.io format)
Grafana dashboard screenshots (PDF, 20 pages)
Database performance reports (CSV files)
Log analysis tools (ELK stack or Splunk access)
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool for fault tree creation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accuracy of root cause identification (30 points), Quality of evidence correlation across multiple data sources (25 points), Completeness of dependency mapping and failure cascade analysis (20 points), Clarity and logic of fault tree diagram (15 points), Defense of conclusions during presentation with specific log/metric citations (10 points). Teams must identify at least 3 contributing factors and demonstrate understanding of how microservices architectural decisions impact system reliability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed analysis template with guided questions and highlight specific log entries that contain critical clues. Offer a simplified system diagram focusing on 6 core services instead of all 12. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as analyzing the impact of auto-scaling policies, examining circuit breaker patterns, or proposing specific code-level optimizations. Provide access to distributed tracing data (Jaeger/Zipkin) for deeper request flow analysis.

title: Evaluate Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Segmentation Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualization approaches (scatter plot, bar chart, and heatmap) used to display customer segmentation data from an e-commerce dataset. They will judge which visualization best communicates key insights about customer purchasing behaviors and justify their evaluation using specific criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualization techniques by applying clarity, accuracy, and insight communication criteria to customer segmentation displays
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for improving data presentation
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three pre-created visualizations of the same customer segmentation dataset showing customer age, annual spending, and purchase frequency. Display Visualization A (scatter plot with age vs. spending, colored by frequency), Visualization B (grouped bar chart showing average spending by age ranges), and Visualization C (correlation heatmap of all three variables). Give each student the evaluation criteria sheet.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine each visualization and complete an evaluation matrix, rating each visualization (1-5 scale) on: data clarity, ease of interpretation, insight revelation, and visual appeal. They must write 2-3 specific observations for each criterion per visualization.

**Structured Comparison (15 minutes):** Students identify the primary business question each visualization answers best: 'Which customer segments spend most?' 'How do customer characteristics relate?' 'What patterns exist in customer behavior?' They rank visualizations 1-3 for each question with written justification.

**Critical Evaluation (15 minutes):** Students write a 150-word recommendation memo identifying the most effective visualization for a marketing manager's needs. They must cite specific strengths, acknowledge limitations, and suggest one concrete improvement for their chosen visualization.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** In pairs, students share recommendations and challenge each other's reasoning using follow-up questions provided on the worksheet. Partners must identify one point of agreement and one point of disagreement in their evaluations.
materials_needed: Three printed customer segmentation visualizations (A4 size)
Evaluation criteria sheet with 1-5 rating scales
Customer dataset context sheet (variable definitions, business scenario)
Structured comparison worksheet with ranking tables
Peer review question prompts handout
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Systematic use of evaluation criteria with specific evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis between visualizations (25%), (3) Clarity and logic of final recommendation with business justification (25%), (4) Thoughtful peer interaction demonstrating critical thinking (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for evaluation comments ('This visualization shows clearly that...' 'The main weakness is...'). Include a completed sample evaluation for a different dataset. For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to sketch an improved version of their chosen visualization or evaluate a fourth, more complex visualization type like a bubble chart.

title: Design Your Dream Amusement Park: A Quadratic Functions Project
description: Students will design an original amusement park by creating mathematical models for roller coaster paths using quadratic functions. They will construct equations, calculate safety parameters, and present their park design with justifications for all mathematical choices.
estimated_duration: 160 minutes (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct original quadratic function equations by designing roller coaster trajectories that meet specific height and safety constraints
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts of vertex form, intercepts, and domain restrictions through creating a comprehensive amusement park proposal
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a 'Park Development Brief' specifying their assigned plot dimensions (coordinate plane from -20 to 20 on both axes), budget constraints (maximum 5 rides), and safety requirements (minimum ground clearance of 2 units, maximum height of 18 units). 

Students spend 40 minutes in Phase 1: Design Planning. Teams brainstorm ride concepts and sketch preliminary roller coaster paths on coordinate grids. They must identify key points: starting position, maximum height (vertex), ground intersections (x-intercepts), and ending position. Each ride requires at least one quadratic function in vertex form f(x) = a(x-h)² + k.

Phase 2: Mathematical Modeling (50 minutes). Teams create specific quadratic equations for each ride. They must show work calculating the 'a' value using their chosen vertex and one additional point, convert to standard form, find x-intercepts algebraically, and determine the restricted domain for each ride based on park boundaries and safety requirements. Students use graphing calculators to verify equations and create visual representations.

Phase 3: Park Optimization (30 minutes). Teams calculate total park capacity using their ride domains, determine optimal spacing between rides (minimum 3 units apart), and create a cost analysis where different 'a' values represent different construction costs (steeper rides cost more).

Phase 4: Presentation Preparation (25 minutes). Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation including a large-scale coordinate plane display, equation summary sheet, safety verification calculations, and marketing pitch for their park design.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Large coordinate plane poster paper (11x17 minimum)
Colored pencils or markers
Park Development Brief handouts (teacher-created)
Presentation rubric copies
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five categories: Mathematical Accuracy (correct quadratic equations and calculations - 25 points), Creative Application (innovative ride designs that meet constraints - 20 points), Problem-Solving Process (clear work shown for finding vertices, intercepts, and domains - 25 points), Communication (clear presentation with mathematical justification - 20 points), and Collaboration (equal participation and teamwork - 10 points). Total: 100 points. Deliverables include equation worksheet, visual park design, and oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide vertex form template worksheets, offer pre-calculated vertex examples, and allow use of graphing calculator table features to find points. Create partnerships with stronger algebra students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate piecewise functions for complex ride sections, calculate actual physics constraints (velocity/acceleration), or optimize park profit using systems of equations. Provide extension problems involving cubic functions for advanced coaster loops.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Flash Retrieval
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the time and space complexity classifications for 30 advanced algorithms across different domains including graph theory, dynamic programming, and computational geometry. This high-speed retrieval activity strengthens foundational knowledge required for algorithm selection and optimization analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will instantly recall the Big O time complexity notation for 30 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's, Floyd-Warshall, KMP string matching, and convex hull algorithms by responding to algorithm name prompts within 3 seconds
Students will accurately identify space complexity classifications for advanced data structures and algorithms through timed flashcard sessions achieving 90% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made algorithm complexity reference sheet containing 30 algorithms with their time/space complexities. Give students exactly 15 minutes for silent memorization - no discussion allowed. Create digital flashcards using Anki or Quizlet with algorithm names on front, complexity on back. Conduct Round 1: Display algorithm names on screen for 5 seconds each - students write complexities on answer sheets. No talking permitted. Round 2: Reduce display time to 3 seconds per algorithm. Randomize order completely. Round 3: Lightning round at 2 seconds per algorithm with only the most challenging 15 algorithms (Aho-Corasick, suffix array construction, minimum cut algorithms, etc.). Between rounds, allow 2-minute review periods where students can check reference sheets. For the final challenge, call out algorithms randomly and students must stand and shout the complexity - first correct answer wins a point. Track individual scores throughout all rounds. End with 5-minute self-assessment where students identify their weakest algorithm categories and create personal study lists for continued practice.
materials_needed: Printed algorithm complexity reference sheets (30 algorithms with Big O notations)
Digital projector/smart board for displaying algorithm names
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-30
Timer/stopwatch visible to all students
Anki or Quizlet digital flashcard platform access
assessment_method: Score students on accuracy across three timed rounds: Round 1 (5 sec) = 60% weight, Round 2 (3 sec) = 30% weight, Round 3 (2 sec) = 10% weight. Success criteria: 90% accuracy in Round 1, 80% in Round 2, 70% in Round 3. Create individual score tracking sheets. Award mastery level for students achieving 85% overall average across all rounds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet (e.g., 'Dijkstra Visits Every Edge Once' for O(V + E log V)). Allow color-coding of complexity categories during memorization phase. For advanced learners: Add average-case vs worst-case complexity distinctions, include amortized analysis examples, or challenge them to recall the specific constants hidden in Big O notation for certain algorithms.

title: Interpreting Advanced Feature Engineering Techniques in High-Dimensional Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze and interpret the mathematical foundations and practical implications of three advanced feature engineering techniques (polynomial features, target encoding, and dimensionality reduction via PCA) applied to a real customer churn dataset. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining how each technique transforms raw data and impacts model performance through detailed written analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical transformations and business implications of polynomial feature generation, target encoding, and PCA dimensionality reduction by analyzing their effects on a customer churn dataset
Students will explain the trade-offs between model complexity, interpretability, and performance through comparative analysis of feature engineering approaches
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Distribute the preprocessed telecom customer churn dataset (5,000 rows, 15 original features) and three versions of engineered features. Present students with: (a) original dataset, (b) dataset with polynomial features (degree=2) for numeric variables, (c) dataset with target-encoded categorical variables, and (d) dataset reduced to 8 principal components. **Phase 2 (40 minutes):** In pairs, students examine each transformed dataset using provided Jupyter notebooks. They must document: the dimensional changes (original vs transformed), correlation matrices for each version, and sample predictions from pre-trained Random Forest models on each dataset. **Phase 3 (30 minutes):** Students complete individual written responses to guided questions: 'Explain why polynomial features increased dimensionality from 15 to 47 features and identify which original feature combinations contribute most to model performance,' 'Interpret why target encoding reduced categorical variable variance and analyze its impact on model overfitting using the provided validation curves,' and 'Describe how PCA transformation affects feature interpretability and justify whether the 15% accuracy trade-off is acceptable for this business context.' **Phase 4 (20 minutes):** Conduct structured pair-share where students compare their interpretations, focusing on identifying the most appropriate technique for different business scenarios (interpretability-focused vs performance-focused applications).
materials_needed: Telecom customer churn dataset (CSV format, 5,000 rows)
Four pre-processed datasets with different feature engineering approaches
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded data analysis code
Pre-trained Random Forest models with performance metrics
Guided analysis worksheet with specific interpretation questions
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib
assessment_method: Evaluate written responses using 4-point rubric: (4) Accurately explains mathematical transformations AND business implications with specific dataset examples, (3) Correctly interprets most technical concepts with minor gaps in business context, (2) Shows basic understanding but lacks specific examples or contains minor technical errors, (1) Demonstrates limited understanding with significant misconceptions. Success requires scoring 3+ on all three feature engineering technique explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional visual representations of transformation matrices and simplified correlation heatmaps. Offer sentence starters like 'The polynomial transformation increases complexity because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose hybrid approaches combining multiple techniques and estimate computational costs for production implementation at enterprise scale.
