title: Budget Planning for a School Event Using Percentages and Decimals
description: Students will apply their knowledge of percentages, decimals, and basic arithmetic to create a realistic budget for planning a class pizza party. They will calculate costs, apply discounts, determine tax amounts, and make decisions based on budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, tax rates, and budget allocations by working with real-world pricing scenarios
Students will demonstrate decimal operations and rounding skills through creating and adjusting a detailed event budget within given constraints
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planning Sheet' and price lists to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student has a budget of exactly $150 to plan a pizza party for 25 classmates. Students must purchase pizzas, drinks, and paper goods while staying within budget.

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students calculate the base costs by selecting items from the provided price lists. They must choose at least 6 pizzas ($12.99 each), 3 2-liter drinks ($2.49 each), paper plates ($4.99), and napkins ($3.99).

Step 2 (15 minutes): Apply real-world complications. Students calculate a 15% discount on pizza orders over $75, then add 8.25% sales tax to their total. They must show all calculations using proper decimal notation and round to the nearest cent.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students determine if they're over or under budget. If over budget, they must remove items and recalculate. If under budget, they can add dessert options (cookies at $0.75 each or cake for $18.99).

Step 4 (8 minutes): Students complete a reflection sheet explaining their mathematical decisions, showing their percentage and decimal calculations, and justifying their final choices.

Circulate throughout, checking calculations and asking students to explain their reasoning. Remind students to show all work clearly and label their answers with appropriate units (dollars and cents).
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Sheet (1 per student)
Laminated price lists for pizza restaurant, grocery store drinks, and party supplies
Calculators
Reflection worksheet
Pencils and scratch paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate percentage calculations for discount and tax - 25 points, (2) Correct decimal operations and rounding - 25 points, (3) Final budget stays within $150 constraint - 25 points, (4) Clear mathematical reasoning explained in reflection - 25 points. Students must score 70/100 to demonstrate proficiency in applying mathematical operations to real-world contexts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing 'Original Price × 0.15 = Discount Amount' and similar formats. Offer a calculator tutorial for percentage calculations. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including delivery fees, tip calculations (18-20%), or comparing costs from multiple vendors requiring unit rate calculations.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Performance Profiling
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by implementing them, measuring their execution times with different dataset sizes, and examining their time complexity behaviors. They will decompose the algorithmic differences and synthesize findings into performance recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity relationships between bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by measuring execution times across datasets of varying sizes (100, 1000, 10000 elements)
Students will examine algorithmic efficiency patterns through systematic performance profiling and identify the underlying causes of performance differences
instructions:
Begin by providing students with starter code containing three sorting algorithm implementations and a performance testing framework (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair to work on one computer with the provided codebase. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students run the performance testing suite on datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 randomly generated integers. They must record execution times in milliseconds for each algorithm-dataset combination, running each test 5 times and calculating averages to account for system variability.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students analyze the collected timing data by creating performance graphs plotting dataset size (x-axis) versus execution time (y-axis) for each algorithm. They identify growth patterns and compare actual performance against theoretical time complexities (O(n²), O(n log n)).

Step 3 (20 minutes): Students examine the source code of each algorithm, identifying key structural differences that explain performance variations. They must trace through algorithm steps for a small dataset (10 elements) and count comparison operations performed by each algorithm.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs synthesize their analysis into a written recommendation report specifying which algorithm to use for different scenarios: small datasets (n<100), medium datasets (100<n<10000), and large datasets (n>10000). Reports must include quantitative evidence from their testing and qualitative reasoning about algorithmic behavior.

Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share key findings and defend their recommendations using collected evidence.
materials_needed: Computers with Python 3.8+ installed
Starter code package containing bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort implementations
Performance testing framework with timing utilities
Graph paper or digital graphing tool (Excel, Google Sheets)
Data recording worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of performance data collection and calculations (25%), (2) Quality of performance graph creation and pattern identification (25%), (3) Depth of code analysis and explanation of algorithmic differences (25%), (4) Appropriateness and justification of algorithm recommendations (25%). Students must submit timing data tables, performance graphs, code analysis notes, and final recommendation report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed data tables with column headers and sample entries. Offer guiding questions for code analysis ('How many nested loops does each algorithm have?'). For advanced students: Challenge them to test additional scenarios like pre-sorted data, reverse-sorted data, or implement additional algorithms like heap sort for comparison. Encourage investigation of space complexity alongside time complexity.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Selection and Deployment Strategies for Real-World Business Impact
description: Students critically assess multiple machine learning models trained on a customer churn dataset, evaluate their business viability, and make justified recommendations for deployment strategy. They will analyze model performance metrics, computational costs, interpretability requirements, and ethical implications to determine the optimal solution for a specific business context.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the trade-offs between model accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency by comparing at least three different ML algorithms using multiple performance metrics
Students will critique model deployment strategies through comprehensive analysis of business constraints, ethical considerations, and technical infrastructure requirements
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a pre-trained model repository containing: Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, and Neural Network models trained on telecom customer churn data. Each model includes training logs, validation metrics, and computational benchmarks. Students first spend 30 minutes individually reviewing model performance reports (precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, training time, prediction latency). Next, teams collaboratively complete a structured evaluation matrix (45 minutes) scoring each model across six criteria: predictive accuracy, interpretability, computational cost, scalability, maintenance complexity, and fairness metrics. Teams then receive business scenario cards detailing specific constraints: tight budget startup, highly regulated financial institution, or high-volume e-commerce platform. Using these constraints, teams spend 60 minutes developing comprehensive deployment recommendations, including infrastructure requirements, monitoring strategies, and risk mitigation plans. Each team creates a 10-slide presentation justifying their model selection and deployment strategy. During the final 45 minutes, teams present their recommendations (8 minutes each) followed by peer questioning (2 minutes). Instructors facilitate cross-team evaluation using provided peer assessment forms focusing on evidence quality, reasoning depth, and consideration of trade-offs.
materials_needed: Pre-trained ML models with performance logs (Random Forest, XGBoost, Logistic Regression, Neural Network)
Customer churn dataset with 50,000+ records and metadata documentation
Model evaluation matrix template with scoring rubrics
Business scenario constraint cards (3 different contexts)
Peer assessment forms for presentation evaluation
Jupyter Notebook environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib libraries
Presentation software access
assessment_method: Students evaluated using four-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical Analysis - depth of model performance interpretation and metric selection appropriateness, (2) Critical Reasoning - quality of trade-off analysis and evidence-based argumentation, (3) Business Application - alignment of recommendations with scenario constraints and feasibility assessment, (4) Ethical Considerations - identification and mitigation of bias, fairness, and transparency issues, (5) Communication - clarity of presentation and response to peer questions. Final deliverables include completed evaluation matrix, written recommendation report (1000 words), and presentation performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide model interpretation cheat sheets with common metric explanations and business impact examples. Offer structured templates for the evaluation matrix with guiding questions for each criterion. For advanced learners: Include additional models (ensemble methods, deep learning variants) and request analysis of model drift scenarios, A/B testing strategies, or multi-objective optimization approaches. Encourage exploration of advanced fairness metrics and bias detection techniques.

title: Binary Number System Recall Challenge: Identifying Powers of Two
description: Students will memorize and recall the first 12 powers of two (2^0 through 2^11) and their decimal equivalents through flashcard drills and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of binary place values essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal values of powers of two from 2^0 to 2^11 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the corresponding power of two for given decimal values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048) through verbal recitation and written exercises
instructions: Begin by displaying a reference chart showing 2^0 = 1, 2^1 = 2, 2^2 = 4, up through 2^11 = 2048 on the board or projector. Give students 5 minutes to study the chart silently, encouraging them to look for patterns (each value doubles). Remove the chart and distribute physical flashcards with powers of two on one side and decimal values on the other. Have students work in pairs for 10 minutes, taking turns showing cards and testing each other, with the partner providing immediate feedback using the answer key. Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire verbal drill where you call out a power (like '2 to the 5th power') and students must quickly respond with the decimal value (32). Spend 8 minutes on this, ensuring every student participates at least twice. Finally, distribute the written quiz sheet where students must fill in a two-column table: one column lists powers of two, the other lists decimal values with some blanks to complete. Students work individually for 7 minutes to complete both directions - writing decimal values for given powers and writing powers for given decimal values. Collect completed sheets and provide immediate verbal feedback by reading correct answers aloud while students self-check their work.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards (one set per pair) with powers of two on front, decimal values on back
Reference chart poster showing 2^0 through 2^11 with decimal equivalents
Printed quiz sheets with two-column table for individual assessment
Answer key for instructor reference
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (11 out of 12 correct) on the final written quiz to demonstrate mastery. Grade the completed quiz sheets using the provided answer key, marking each correct power-decimal pair. Additionally, observe during pair work and verbal drills to note students who consistently struggle with specific values for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with just the first 8 powers (2^0 to 2^7) and provide a pattern recognition hint sheet showing the doubling sequence. Allow extra study time with the reference chart. For advanced learners, extend the activity to include 2^12 through 2^15, or challenge them to work backwards from decimal values to identify the corresponding powers of two.

title: Interpreting Correlation Patterns in Real-World Dataset Scenarios
description: Students will analyze correlation matrices from three different business scenarios to identify meaningful relationships between variables and distinguish between correlation types. They will practice interpreting correlation coefficients and explaining the practical implications of these relationships in context.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by analyzing three real-world correlation matrices and categorizing relationships as strong, moderate, or weak
Students will distinguish between positive, negative, and spurious correlations through guided analysis of business scenarios involving customer behavior, sales performance, and marketing metrics
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-prepared correlation matrices: (1) E-commerce customer data with variables like page views, time on site, purchase amount, and return frequency, (2) Sales team performance with metrics including calls made, emails sent, meetings scheduled, and revenue generated, and (3) Marketing campaign data with impressions, clicks, conversions, and customer lifetime value. Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group to start with one scenario (15 minutes per scenario, rotating through all three). For each correlation matrix, students must: identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, explain what each correlation means in business context, and flag any relationships that seem surprising or potentially spurious. Provide a correlation interpretation guide showing ranges: 0.7-1.0 (strong), 0.3-0.69 (moderate), 0.1-0.29 (weak). During each 15-minute rotation, students complete a structured worksheet asking: 'What story do these correlations tell about this business?' and 'Which correlations might indicate causation vs. coincidence?' After rotations, conduct a 15-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents one interesting correlation pattern they discovered and explains why it matters for business decision-making. Conclude by having students individually write a 3-sentence summary explaining the difference between correlation strength and business significance.
materials_needed: Three printed correlation matrices (one per business scenario)
Correlation interpretation reference guide handout
Structured analysis worksheet for each scenario
Calculators or smartphones for verification
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correctly identifies correlation strength categories, (2) Provides logical business explanations for relationships, (3) Distinguishes between meaningful and potentially spurious correlations. Success criteria: Students score 2/3 or higher on rubric and demonstrate understanding by correctly explaining at least two correlation patterns during class discussion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional examples of correlation coefficient interpretation and pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. Create a visual correlation strength chart with color coding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential confounding variables that might explain correlations and propose additional data that would strengthen the analysis. Encourage them to calculate partial correlations or suggest experimental designs to test causation.

title: Designing Optimal Solar Panel Arrays Using Trigonometry and Optimization
description: Students will apply trigonometric functions, derivatives, and optimization techniques to design solar panel arrays that maximize energy output throughout the year. They will calculate optimal tilt angles, spacing between rows, and total power generation using real-world constraints and data.
learning_objectives: Students will apply trigonometric functions and their derivatives to model solar irradiance patterns by calculating optimal panel tilt angles for different seasons
Students will apply multivariable optimization techniques to maximize energy output through systematic analysis of panel spacing, shadow effects, and land area constraints
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute setup where students receive site specifications: a rectangular plot (200m × 150m) in Phoenix, Arizona (33.4°N latitude). Distribute solar irradiance data sheets showing monthly sun angles and intensity values. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Engineer (calculations), Data Analyst (spreadsheet work), Design Coordinator (sketches), and Presenter (documentation). 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Students calculate optimal tilt angles using the formula: Optimal tilt = 0.9 × latitude + 23.5° × cos((day of year - 81) × 2π/365). They must determine angles for four key dates: March 21, June 21, September 21, December 21. Using trigonometry, calculate solar elevation angles: sin(elevation) = sin(latitude) × sin(declination) + cos(latitude) × cos(declination) × cos(hour angle). Students plot these on coordinate planes and use calculus to find maximum irradiance points.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Apply shadow analysis using trigonometric relationships. Calculate minimum spacing between panel rows using: D = H / tan(solar elevation), where H is panel height. Students must ensure no shading occurs during peak hours (10 AM - 2 PM) on the winter solstice. Create scaled technical drawings showing panel positions.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Optimize total system output by applying constraint optimization. Given panel dimensions (2m × 1m), calculate maximum number of panels fitting the site while maintaining proper spacing. Use Lagrange multipliers to maximize: Power = Σ(Panel Area × Irradiance × cos(incident angle)) subject to land area and spacing constraints.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams present their final designs with mathematical justifications, comparing seasonal energy outputs and cost-effectiveness ratios.
materials_needed: Solar irradiance data sheets for Phoenix, AZ (monthly values)
Scientific calculators with trigonometric functions
Graph paper and rulers for technical drawings
Laptops with Excel or Google Sheets for optimization calculations
Protractors and compasses for angle measurements
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy (40 points) - correct trigonometric calculations, proper derivative applications, accurate optimization setup; Design feasibility (30 points) - realistic spacing, no shadow conflicts, proper land utilization; Professional presentation (20 points) - clear technical drawings, justified recommendations, effective teamwork; Innovation (10 points) - creative solutions, consideration of additional factors like maintenance access or wind loads.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide trigonometric identity reference sheets and step-by-step calculation templates. Break complex formulas into smaller components and offer guided practice with simpler angles first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate variable-tilt mechanisms, consider economic factors like installation costs and payback periods, or analyze multiple geographic locations simultaneously. Provide additional constraints like local building codes or environmental restrictions.

title: Distributed System Failure Pattern Analysis and Bottleneck Decomposition
description: Students analyze a complex multi-tier web application's system logs, performance metrics, and architecture diagrams to identify failure patterns, diagnose bottlenecks, and decompose the system's critical failure points. They will systematically examine interdependencies between microservices and evaluate cascading failure scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real production logs, trace data, and performance metrics from a multi-tier application
Students will decompose system bottlenecks through systematic evaluation of service dependencies, resource utilization patterns, and critical path analysis
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with a complete distributed system case study package including: system architecture diagram, 48 hours of production logs from 6 microservices, Grafana dashboard screenshots, and incident timeline. Step 1 (45 minutes): Students map service dependencies by creating a detailed dependency graph, identifying synchronous vs asynchronous communication patterns, and marking external dependencies. Step 2 (60 minutes): Using provided log analysis tools, students filter and correlate error patterns across services, focusing on HTTP response codes, timeout patterns, and resource exhaustion indicators. They must identify at least 3 distinct failure modes. Step 3 (45 minutes): Students analyze performance metrics to identify bottlenecks by examining CPU utilization, memory consumption, database query latencies, and network I/O patterns. They create bottleneck severity rankings with supporting data. Step 4 (30 minutes): Teams construct failure scenario trees showing how individual component failures cascade through the system, including probability estimates and impact assessment. Step 5 (60 minutes): Students prepare a technical analysis report documenting their findings with specific evidence from logs/metrics, proposed architectural improvements, and monitoring recommendations. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where other teams provide peer feedback using provided evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: Distributed system case study package with architecture diagrams
Production log files (JSON/XML format) from 6 microservices spanning 48 hours
Grafana dashboard screenshots showing system metrics
Log analysis software (ELK Stack or Splunk)
Network diagram creation tool (Lucidchart or draw.io)
Incident timeline documentation
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of dependency mapping and failure mode identification (25%), (2) Quality of evidence-based bottleneck analysis with supporting metrics (30%), (3) Completeness and logical flow of cascading failure scenarios (25%), (4) Technical depth and feasibility of proposed solutions (20%). Students must identify minimum 3 distinct failure patterns and provide specific log entries/metrics as evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filtered log samples highlighting key error patterns, offer dependency mapping templates, and give guided questions for metric interpretation. For advanced learners: introduce chaos engineering concepts, request quantitative reliability calculations (MTBF/MTTR), and challenge them to design automated failure detection algorithms based on their analysis patterns.

title: Design Your Dream Amusement Park: A Multi-Function Mathematical Model
description: Students will create an original amusement park design by developing mathematical models that incorporate linear, quadratic, and exponential functions to represent ticket pricing, ride capacity, and revenue projections. They will justify their design choices using mathematical reasoning and present their park as a viable business proposal.
estimated_duration: 180 minutes (3 hours) - can be split across multiple class periods
learning_objectives: Students will construct mathematical models using linear, quadratic, and exponential functions by designing realistic amusement park scenarios including pricing structures, ride capacities, and revenue projections
Students will synthesize multiple mathematical concepts through creating a comprehensive business proposal that demonstrates the practical application of functions in real-world contexts
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives the 'Park Design Challenge' packet containing constraints: minimum 8 rides, budget of $50 million, target 5000 daily visitors, and 6-month construction timeline.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams brainstorm their park theme and create initial sketches. They must identify three specific mathematical relationships: ticket pricing strategy (linear function), at least two ride capacity models (quadratic functions showing wait times vs. visitors), and projected monthly revenue growth (exponential function).

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Using graphing calculators and spreadsheet software, students develop their mathematical models. For ticket pricing, they create linear equations considering different visitor demographics. For ride capacity, they model wait times using quadratic functions where x represents hourly visitors and y represents average wait time. For revenue, they develop exponential growth models factoring in seasonal variations and marketing impact.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams create visual presentations including park maps, mathematical graphs with proper labels and scales, and calculated projections for first-year operations. They must show all mathematical work and explain how each function type was chosen for its specific application.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams present 5-minute pitches to the class acting as 'investors.' Presentations must include mathematical justifications for design decisions, demonstrate understanding of function behavior, and address potential limitations of their models. Other teams provide feedback using the provided peer evaluation rubric focusing on mathematical accuracy and real-world applicability.
materials_needed: Park Design Challenge packets (one per team)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Grid paper and colored pencils
Laptops with Excel or Google Sheets access
Presentation materials (poster boards or digital projection capability)
Peer evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of all three function types (25 points), (2) Appropriateness of function selection for each scenario (20 points), (3) Quality of mathematical reasoning and justification (20 points), (4) Creativity and feasibility of overall park design (15 points), (5) Presentation clarity and professional delivery (10 points), (6) Peer collaboration and feedback quality (10 points). Total possible: 100 points. Success requires scoring 70+ points with minimum 3/4 on mathematical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing function template worksheets with partially completed examples and offering one-on-one guidance during Phase 2. Create mixed-ability groups pairing stronger math students with those needing support. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate additional mathematical concepts like trigonometric functions for ride motion patterns or optimization problems for park layout efficiency. Provide extension activities involving calculus applications for maximum revenue calculations.

title: Network Protocol Stack Memory Palace: TCP/IP Layer Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete TCP/IP protocol stack layers, their functions, and associated protocols through systematic repetition and spatial memory techniques. This activity reinforces foundational networking knowledge essential for advanced computer science coursework.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all four TCP/IP protocol stack layers (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) with their specific functions and characteristics through structured memorization drills
Students will identify and list at least 15 specific protocols correctly categorized by their appropriate TCP/IP layer through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet containing all four layers with their functions and protocols. Students have 15 minutes to study the material silently. Next, implement the Memory Palace technique: have students visualize their home layout and assign each TCP/IP layer to a specific room (bedroom=Application Layer, kitchen=Transport Layer, living room=Internet Layer, garage=Network Access Layer). Students spend 10 minutes mentally 'walking' through their house, placing protocols in appropriate rooms while rehearsing layer functions aloud with a partner. Conduct Round 1 assessment: project layer names one at a time, giving students 90 seconds per layer to write down all associated protocols and primary functions from memory. After collecting responses, provide correct answers for self-checking. Implement spaced repetition: students review missed items for 5 minutes, focusing on problem areas identified in Round 1. Execute Round 2 assessment with randomized protocol names displayed - students must identify the correct layer and write one key function. Conclude with rapid-fire verbal quiz: call on individual students to state specific protocol-to-layer mappings within 5 seconds. Document accuracy rates for each student across all three assessment rounds.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet (one per student)
Blank response sheets for assessments
Projector or digital display for protocol names
Timer or stopwatch
Red pens for self-checking
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy across three assessment rounds: (1) Layer-to-protocol mapping with functions, (2) Protocol-to-layer identification, (3) Rapid verbal recall. Success criteria: correctly identify 13+ out of 15 protocols with appropriate layers, accurately state primary function of each layer, complete verbal responses within 5-second time limit with 85% accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory devices (e.g., 'All The Internet Networks' for layer order), allow additional 5-minute review periods between rounds, pair with stronger students for verbal practice. For advanced learners: include OSI model comparison, add subnet mask and port number recall requirements, challenge them to explain protocol interaction between layers during the memory palace walk-through.

title: Pizza Party Budget Calculator: Applying Multiplication and Division to Real-World Planning
description: Students will apply multiplication and division skills to solve a real-world problem by calculating costs, quantities, and portions for a class pizza party. They will work through multi-step word problems using authentic scenarios that require mathematical reasoning and computation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multiplication strategies to calculate total costs and quantities by solving multi-step pizza party planning problems
Students will apply division concepts to determine equal portions and cost per person through hands-on budget calculations
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Pizza Party Planner' worksheet and calculator to each student (5 minutes). Present the scenario: 'Our class of 24 students is planning a pizza party. Large pizzas cost $12 each and feed 6 people. Drinks cost $8 per pack and serve 8 people. Napkins cost $3 per pack of 50.' Have students work in pairs to solve Step 1: Calculate how many pizzas needed (24 ÷ 6 = 4 pizzas) and total pizza cost (4 × $12 = $48). Allow 8 minutes for this step, circulating to check work. For Step 2, students calculate drink requirements (24 ÷ 8 = 3 packs) and cost (3 × $8 = $24), taking 5 minutes. Step 3 involves napkin calculation (24 ÷ 50 = 0.48, so 1 pack needed, costing $3). Give students 3 minutes for this simpler calculation. In Step 4, students find the total party cost ($48 + $24 + $3 = $75) and cost per student ($75 ÷ 24 = $3.13). Allow 7 minutes for final calculations. Conclude with pairs sharing one calculation method with the class, explaining their reasoning (7 minutes). Emphasize how they applied multiplication to find totals and division to find portions and per-person costs.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planner worksheet (one per student)
Basic calculators (one per pair)
Pencils or pens
Chart paper for final presentations (optional)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: 4-Correctly solves all steps with clear work shown; 3-Solves most steps with minor calculation errors; 2-Shows understanding but makes several computational mistakes; 1-Attempts problems but shows limited understanding. Observe pair discussions for mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed worksheet with the first step done as an example, or offer manipulatives like dried beans to represent people/portions. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including tax calculations (8% sales tax), comparing costs from different pizza restaurants, or calculating tips for delivery drivers.

title: Database Schema Vulnerability Analysis and Optimization
description: Students will examine an existing e-commerce database schema containing performance bottlenecks and security vulnerabilities, then analyze the relationships between tables to identify specific issues. They will decompose the schema structure, evaluate indexing strategies, and assess potential SQL injection risks through systematic analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database schema design patterns by identifying normalization violations, redundant relationships, and performance bottlenecks in a real-world e-commerce database
Students will evaluate security vulnerabilities through systematic examination of table structures, field types, and constraint implementations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the provided e-commerce database schema (containing 8 tables: users, products, orders, order_items, categories, reviews, inventory, and payments) along with 15 sample SQL queries that the system commonly executes. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. 

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Students examine the schema diagram and identify all table relationships, primary/foreign keys, and data types. They must document 5 potential normalization issues and 3 missing indexes that could impact performance.

Phase 2 (35 minutes): Provide students with query execution plans for the 15 sample queries. Students analyze which queries show table scans, high cost operations, or inefficient joins. They must rank the top 5 most problematic queries and explain the root cause of each performance issue by tracing through the schema structure.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Students examine the schema for security vulnerabilities by analyzing field constraints, data validation rules, and potential injection points. They must identify at least 3 specific security risks (such as missing input validation on varchar fields, lack of encrypted storage for sensitive data, or insufficient access control structure) and trace how each vulnerability could be exploited through the existing table relationships.

Students complete their analysis by creating a prioritized remediation plan with specific SQL DDL statements for their top 3 findings. Each pair presents their highest-priority finding to the class in a 2-minute explanation.
materials_needed: E-commerce database schema diagram (PDF with 8 interconnected tables)
15 sample SQL queries with execution plans (printed handouts)
Database design reference sheet with normalization rules
SQL injection vulnerability checklist
Laptops with database visualization software (MySQL Workbench or equivalent)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of identified normalization violations and performance bottlenecks (25 points), (2) Quality of query execution plan analysis with specific cost explanations (25 points), (3) Identification of security vulnerabilities with exploitation scenarios (25 points), (4) Prioritized remediation plan with correct SQL syntax (25 points). Students must achieve 70/100 points with at least 15/25 in each category to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed analysis template highlighting the first normalization violation and security risk. Offer a reference chart showing common SQL performance patterns. For advanced learners, include additional complex queries involving subqueries and provide a real database instance to test their proposed schema modifications using actual execution time measurements.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Performance: A Comparative Analysis of Credit Risk Assessment Systems
description: Students critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning approaches (logistic regression, random forest, and neural network) for credit risk assessment using real banking data. They assess model performance across multiple metrics, identify potential biases, and justify recommendations for production deployment.
estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across two class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of three ML models by analyzing precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and fairness metrics across demographic groups
Students will critique model interpretability and business applicability through comprehensive performance analysis and stakeholder impact assessment
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-processed credit dataset (German Credit Data) and three pre-trained models with their prediction outputs and probability scores. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students (45 minutes setup and initial analysis). Each team receives identical model outputs but different stakeholder perspectives: bank executives, risk managers, regulatory compliance officers, or consumer advocates.

Step 1 (60 minutes): Teams calculate and compare standard performance metrics using provided confusion matrices and prediction probabilities. Students must compute precision, recall, F1-score, specificity, and AUC-ROC for each model, creating comparative visualizations.

Step 2 (45 minutes): Conduct fairness analysis by examining model performance across age groups (≤25, 26-60, >60) and gender. Calculate equalized odds, demographic parity, and calibration metrics to identify potential discriminatory patterns.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Analyze model interpretability using provided SHAP values and feature importance rankings. Evaluate which features drive decisions and assess business logic alignment.

Step 4 (60 minutes): Teams prepare detailed evaluation reports addressing: model ranking with justification, identified biases and mitigation strategies, deployment risks from their stakeholder perspective, and specific recommendations with supporting evidence.

Step 5 (45 minutes): Present 8-minute evaluations to class, defending model choice against questions from other stakeholder groups. Include cost-benefit analysis and implementation timeline.

Conclude with 15-minute reflection on evaluation criteria importance and real-world deployment considerations.
materials_needed: German Credit Dataset with 1000 loan records
Pre-trained model outputs (CSV files with predictions and probabilities)
Jupyter notebooks with evaluation metric calculation templates
SHAP analysis results for each model
Stakeholder persona cards with specific priorities and constraints
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, and seaborn
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Quantitative Analysis Accuracy - correct calculation and interpretation of all performance and fairness metrics (25 points), (2) Critical Evaluation Quality - depth of bias identification, limitation analysis, and stakeholder impact assessment (25 points), (3) Justification Strength - evidence-based reasoning for model recommendation with clear trade-off analysis (20 points), (4) Presentation Clarity - effective communication of technical findings to stakeholder audience (15 points), (5) Peer Interaction - quality of questions asked and responses to challenges during presentations (15 points). Minimum 80/100 points indicates successful evaluation competency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation worksheets with formulas and step-by-step examples. Offer one-on-one guidance during Step 1 calculations. Create fairness analysis templates with clear instructions for demographic group filtering. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose additional evaluation metrics (calibration plots, profit curves), conduct cross-validation analysis of model stability, or design A/B testing frameworks for deployment. Encourage exploration of advanced bias mitigation techniques and their trade-offs.

title: Design and Validate a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow
description: Students will construct an original mathematical model using differential equations and graph theory to solve a real-world urban traffic optimization problem. They will create their own traffic network scenario, develop the mathematical framework, and present their solution with validation data.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory by designing an original traffic flow optimization model for a self-created urban intersection scenario
Students will construct and validate a complete mathematical solution through systematic testing, parameter adjustment, and presentation of results with supporting documentation
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Creation (45 minutes)** - Students work individually to design a unique 4-6 intersection urban traffic network. Provide each student with grid paper and traffic flow data templates. They must specify: intersection locations, road capacities (vehicles/minute), peak traffic times, and traffic light timing constraints. Students sketch their network and define 3 optimization objectives (minimize wait time, maximize throughput, reduce emissions). **Phase 2: Mathematical Model Development (90 minutes)** - Students develop their mathematical framework using: (a) Flow conservation equations for each intersection using differential equations, (b) Constraint equations for traffic light timing and road capacity limits, (c) Objective function combining their 3 optimization goals with weighted coefficients. They must show all mathematical derivations and explain variable definitions. **Phase 3: Solution Implementation (60 minutes)** - Using MATLAB or Python, students code their model and run simulations with at least 3 different parameter sets. They must generate: numerical solutions, convergence analysis, and sensitivity testing results. **Phase 4: Validation and Presentation (45 minutes)** - Students create a 10-minute presentation including: problem description, mathematical model explanation, solution methodology, results analysis, and model limitations. They must defend their approach during a 5-minute Q&A session with peers acting as city planning consultants.
materials_needed: Grid paper and rulers for network design
Traffic flow data template sheets
MATLAB or Python software access
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Calculators and reference materials for differential equations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model originality and complexity (25 points), Correct application of mathematical principles (25 points), Implementation quality and computational results (20 points), Presentation clarity and defense of methodology (20 points), Innovation in problem design and solution approach (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made intersection templates and simplified 2-intersection networks, offer step-by-step differential equation setup guides. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multiple vehicle types, or real-time adaptive traffic signals. Provide access to actual city traffic data for enhanced realism.

title: Dissecting Memory Leaks in Multi-threaded C++ Applications Through Static and Dynamic Analysis
description: Students analyze provided buggy C++ code containing multiple memory leak patterns in a multi-threaded environment. They systematically identify leak sources, categorize leak types, and evaluate the effectiveness of different detection tools through comparative analysis of static analyzers versus runtime profilers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex memory leak patterns by systematically examining multi-threaded C++ code using both static analysis tools and dynamic profiling techniques
Students will differentiate between various memory leak categories through detailed code inspection and tool-assisted detection methods
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared C++ project containing a simulated e-commerce backend with intentionally embedded memory leaks (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to first manually examine the codebase, spending 45 minutes creating a preliminary analysis document identifying suspected leak locations using code inspection techniques - focusing on constructor/destructor pairs, new/delete matching, and thread synchronization points. Next, students configure and run Valgrind with Memcheck (20 minutes), documenting all detected leaks with line numbers, leak sizes, and stack traces. Following this, they set up and execute Clang Static Analyzer (15 minutes), comparing its findings against their manual analysis and Valgrind results. Students then use AddressSanitizer with GCC compilation flags (10 minutes) to capture additional runtime leak information. For the analysis phase (60 minutes), students create a comprehensive comparison matrix categorizing each detected leak by type (definite loss, indirect loss, possible loss), severity level, detection method effectiveness, and thread-safety implications. They must trace the execution flow for at least three major leaks, documenting the precise allocation points, intended deallocation points, and failure reasons. Finally, students prepare a 10-minute presentation analyzing the most critical leak, explaining why their chosen detection method was most effective for that specific case, and proposing targeted remediation strategies. Conclude with peer presentations where teams challenge each other's analysis methodologies and findings (30 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-compiled C++ project with embedded memory leaks (teacher-provided)
Linux development environment with GCC, Clang, Valgrind installed
Code analysis worksheet template with comparison matrix
Access to AddressSanitizer and Clang Static Analyzer tools
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of manual leak identification (25%), (2) Correct tool configuration and usage (20%), (3) Depth of comparative analysis between detection methods (30%), (4) Quality of remediation strategies and presentation clarity (25%). Students must identify at least 80% of embedded leaks and correctly categorize leak types to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a guided worksheet with specific line numbers to examine first and step-by-step tool configuration commands. Offer simplified leak patterns in isolated code snippets before tackling the full project. For advanced learners, challenge them to write custom Valgrind suppressions, analyze performance overhead of different detection tools, or propose automated leak detection integration into CI/CD pipelines.

title: Evaluating Data Quality Issues in a Customer Dataset for Business Decision-Making
description: Students will critically assess a real-world customer dataset containing various data quality issues and determine which problems most significantly impact business analytics outcomes. They will rank data quality issues by severity and justify their decisions using established data quality frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data quality issues in a customer dataset by applying completeness, accuracy, consistency, and validity criteria to determine business impact severity
Students will critique different data cleaning approaches through systematic comparison of their effectiveness for specific analytical goals
instructions:
**Phase 1: Dataset Exploration (15 minutes)**
Provide each student with the 'CustomerData_QualityIssues.csv' file containing 500 customer records with intentionally embedded problems (missing phone numbers, inconsistent date formats, duplicate emails, invalid age values). Students individually explore the dataset using Excel or Google Sheets, documenting all quality issues they identify on the provided worksheet.

**Phase 2: Issue Classification (20 minutes)**
Students categorize each identified issue using the four data quality dimensions: Completeness (missing values), Accuracy (incorrect values), Consistency (formatting inconsistencies), and Validity (values outside acceptable ranges). They calculate the percentage of records affected by each issue type and record findings in the classification matrix template.

**Phase 3: Business Impact Assessment (25 minutes)**
Present three business scenarios: 1) Customer segmentation for marketing campaigns, 2) Age-based product recommendations, 3) Contact information for customer service outreach. Students evaluate how each data quality issue would impact these specific use cases, assigning severity scores (1-5 scale) and writing 2-3 sentence justifications for each score.

**Phase 4: Prioritization and Recommendation (15 minutes)**
Students create a ranked priority list of the top 5 data quality issues that require immediate attention, considering both frequency of occurrence and business impact severity. They write a one-paragraph executive summary recommending which issues to address first and why, including estimated effort levels (low/medium/high) for fixing each priority issue.

**Phase 5: Peer Review (10 minutes)**
Pairs of students exchange their priority lists and recommendations, providing written feedback on whether the reasoning is logical and well-supported by evidence from the dataset analysis.
materials_needed: CustomerData_QualityIssues.csv file with 500 customer records containing embedded quality issues
Data Quality Assessment Worksheet template (printable PDF)
Classification Matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Business Scenarios handout describing three use cases
Computers with Excel or Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: 1) Completeness of issue identification (25 points - found at least 8 of 10 embedded issues), 2) Accuracy of business impact assessment (25 points - logical severity scoring with clear justifications), 3) Quality of prioritization reasoning (25 points - priority list demonstrates understanding of frequency vs. impact trade-offs), 4) Clarity of executive recommendation (25 points - actionable summary with realistic effort estimates). Peer feedback quality contributes 10 bonus points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed classification matrix showing 2-3 example issues already categorized. Create a severity scoring guide with specific criteria for each score level. For advanced learners: Add a cost-benefit analysis component where they estimate the business value gained versus effort required for fixing each issue. Challenge them to research and propose specific data validation rules for preventing future quality problems.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Scale Model Community with Mathematical Constraints
description: Students design and construct a mathematically accurate scale model of a small city district, incorporating geometric shapes, proportional relationships, and area/perimeter calculations. They must balance aesthetic choices with mathematical constraints including budget limitations, zoning requirements, and scale accuracy.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original city layout by applying geometric principles, scale factors, and area calculations within specified constraints
Students will construct a physical scale model through systematic application of proportional reasoning and measurement conversion
instructions:
**Phase 1: Planning (20 minutes)** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the City Planning Packet containing: base grid paper (1 cm = 10 meters scale), zoning requirements (residential: 40% of total area, commercial: 35%, parks: 25%), and budget constraints ($50,000 virtual budget with building costs per square meter). Teams brainstorm their city vision and assign roles: Lead Architect, Budget Manager, Measurement Specialist, and Construction Coordinator.

**Phase 2: Mathematical Design (40 minutes)** Students create their city blueprint on grid paper. They must calculate total available area (20cm × 30cm grid = 600 sq cm = 60,000 sq meters at scale), then determine exact areas for each zone using percentages. For each building, students calculate: actual dimensions using scale factor, perimeter for fencing costs, area for construction costs, and verify budget compliance. All calculations must be shown on a separate Mathematics Documentation Sheet.

**Phase 3: Physical Construction (45 minutes)** Using cardboard, rulers, and cutting tools, teams construct their 3D model. Each building must match blueprint dimensions exactly. Students measure and cut pieces, checking measurements twice before cutting. They create different geometric shapes for variety (rectangles, triangles, cylinders for different building types). Parks must include calculated areas for walking paths (perimeter calculations) and green space (area calculations).

**Phase 4: Presentation (15 minutes)** Teams present their city model, explaining three key mathematical decisions, demonstrating how they met zoning requirements, and showing their budget calculations. They must defend their design choices using mathematical reasoning.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 20×30cm sheets)
Cardboard sheets (various colors for different zones)
Rulers and measuring tapes
Scissors and craft knives (supervised use)
Calculators
City Planning Packet with constraints and requirements
Mathematics Documentation Sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (calculations correct, scale properly applied - 25%), Design Innovation (creative use of geometric shapes, thoughtful layout - 25%), Constraint Adherence (meets zoning and budget requirements - 25%), and Communication (clear explanation of mathematical reasoning - 25%). Students submit both physical model and completed Mathematics Documentation Sheet showing all calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated area examples and measurement conversion charts. Offer simplified building templates with dimensions already marked. For advanced learners: Add additional constraints such as traffic flow optimization requiring angle calculations, or incorporate 3D volume calculations for multi-story buildings. Encourage use of more complex geometric shapes like hexagons or trapezoids.

title: Memory Palace: Recalling 25 Essential Design Patterns with Gang of Four Classifications
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall all 23 Gang of Four design patterns plus 2 additional enterprise patterns, organized by their three main categories (Creational, Structural, Behavioral). This intensive recall activity uses spaced repetition and categorization techniques to build foundational pattern recognition essential for advanced software architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 25 design pattern names and correctly classify each into Creational, Structural, or Behavioral categories within 5 minutes
Students will identify the primary intent of each design pattern through structured flashcard memorization and verbal recitation exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 25 design patterns on one side and their classification plus one-sentence intent on the reverse. Spend 10 minutes having students sort physical cards into three piles: Creational (Abstract Factory, Builder, Factory Method, Prototype, Singleton, Dependency Injection), Structural (Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy, MVC), and Behavioral (Chain of Responsibility, Command, Interpreter, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor). After sorting, students work in pairs for 15 minutes using the Leitner spaced repetition system: correctly recalled cards move to pile 2, incorrect cards return to pile 1. Partner A shows pattern name, Partner B states category and intent, then roles switch. Conduct three 5-minute speed rounds where individual students must write all 25 patterns grouped by category from memory. Between rounds, allow 3 minutes for review of missed patterns. For the final assessment, students stand and instructor calls out random pattern names - students must immediately state the category and sit down if incorrect. Continue until only students who correctly identified all called patterns remain standing. Record completion times and accuracy rates for each student.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (25 cards per student) with pattern names and classifications
Timer or stopwatch
Answer sheets with three-column layout for Creational/Structural/Behavioral categories
Red/green index cards for Leitner system sorting
assessment_method: Students must achieve 100% accuracy in categorizing all 25 patterns within the 5-minute final written assessment. Success criteria: correctly spell pattern names, place each in accurate category column, complete within time limit. Partial credit given for 20-24 correct (80%), 15-19 correct (60%). Track individual completion times during standing elimination round as secondary metric.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices (Creational = 'Creating objects', Structural = 'Structuring relationships', Behavioral = 'Behavior between objects') and reduce initial set to 15 core GoF patterns. For advanced learners: add 10 additional enterprise patterns (Repository, Unit of Work, Specification, etc.) and require memorization of pattern problem statements and key participants/collaborations.

title: Understanding Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Analysis of Polynomial Regression Models
description: Students will analyze the relationship between model complexity and prediction error by implementing polynomial regression models of varying degrees and interpreting cross-validation results to understand bias-variance decomposition. Through systematic experimentation with different polynomial orders, students will demonstrate comprehension of how underfitting and overfitting manifest in real prediction scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the bias-variance tradeoff by analyzing cross-validation error curves across polynomial models of different complexities
Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between model flexibility and generalization error through hands-on experimentation with regularization parameters
instructions: Begin by providing students with a synthetic dataset containing 200 points following y = 0.5x³ - 2x² + x + noise (σ=0.3). Students work in pairs using provided Jupyter notebooks pre-loaded with sklearn and visualization libraries. In Phase 1 (25 minutes), each pair fits polynomial regression models of degrees 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, and 15 to the same dataset, recording training MSE for each model. They create a single plot showing all fitted curves overlaid on the original data points. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), students implement 10-fold cross-validation for each polynomial degree, calculating both training and validation MSE. They construct the classic bias-variance plot with model complexity on x-axis and both training/validation error on y-axis. During Phase 3 (20 minutes), pairs examine three critical regions: high bias zone (degrees 1-2), optimal zone (degrees 3-5), and high variance zone (degrees 9-15). They document specific observations about curve behavior, error patterns, and prediction consistency. In Phase 4 (15 minutes), students write a structured interpretation addressing: (1) Why training error decreases monotonically while validation error follows a U-shape, (2) How the gap between training and validation error relates to overfitting, and (3) Which polynomial degree they would select for deployment and why. Conclude with pair presentations of their bias-variance plots and model selection rationale.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Pre-configured notebook with sklearn, numpy, matplotlib, and pandas imported
Synthetic polynomial dataset (CSV file with 200 observations)
Bias-variance analysis worksheet template
Access to shared screen/projector for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of cross-validation implementation and error calculations (25%), (2) Quality and interpretation of bias-variance visualization with proper axis labels and curve identification (25%), (3) Written explanation demonstrating understanding of why validation error exhibits U-shape behavior (25%), and (4) Justification of optimal model selection based on bias-variance tradeoff principles (25%). Students must correctly identify the underfitting region, overfitting region, and optimal complexity zone to demonstrate full understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide code templates with partial implementations and guiding comments for cross-validation loops. Offer visual aids showing theoretical bias-variance curves before the activity. For advanced learners, extend the analysis by implementing Ridge regression with different alpha values, comparing regularized vs. unregularized models, or exploring the bias-variance tradeoff with different noise levels in the dataset.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Real-World Healthcare Scenarios
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) trained on a diabetes prediction dataset by evaluating their performance metrics, ethical implications, and deployment feasibility. They will justify which model should be implemented in a clinical setting based on comprehensive evaluation criteria including accuracy, interpretability, bias, and practical constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, confusion matrices, and ROC curves within a healthcare context
Students will critique the ethical and practical implications of model deployment through systematic assessment of bias, interpretability, and real-world constraints
instructions:
**Phase 1: Dataset and Model Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the Pima Indian Diabetes dataset and three pre-trained models (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) with their outputs. Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze performance metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC for each model. Each team creates comparison tables and visualizes ROC curves using provided Jupyter notebooks.

**Phase 2: Multi-Criteria Evaluation Framework (30 minutes)**
Teams develop evaluation criteria beyond accuracy: interpretability (can doctors understand predictions?), computational efficiency (deployment constraints), bias assessment (performance across demographic groups), and clinical utility (false positive/negative costs). Students weight these criteria based on healthcare priorities.

**Phase 3: Critical Assessment Report (60 minutes)**
Teams complete a structured evaluation matrix scoring each model against their criteria. They must identify potential biases by analyzing model performance across age groups and BMI categories using provided demographic breakdowns. Teams calculate weighted scores and document assumptions.

**Phase 4: Recommendation and Defense (30 minutes)**
Each team presents their model recommendation in a 5-minute pitch to simulate a hospital IT committee meeting. Other teams act as stakeholders (doctors, administrators, patients) and challenge recommendations with prepared questions about model limitations, implementation costs, and ethical concerns.

**Phase 5: Peer Evaluation (15 minutes)**
Students complete peer evaluation forms assessing other teams' reasoning quality, evidence use, and consideration of stakeholder perspectives.
materials_needed: Pima Indian Diabetes dataset with demographic variables
Pre-trained model outputs (Random Forest, SVM, Neural Network) with prediction probabilities
Jupyter notebooks with visualization templates for ROC curves and confusion matrices
Evaluation matrix template spreadsheet
Stakeholder role cards for peer review session
Performance metrics breakdown by demographic groups
assessment_method: Rubric evaluating: (1) Technical accuracy of performance metric interpretation (25%), (2) Quality of evaluation criteria selection and weighting justification (25%), (3) Depth of bias and ethical analysis with specific evidence (25%), (4) Strength of final recommendation with clear reasoning and trade-off acknowledgment (25%). Deliverable: completed evaluation matrix, 2-page recommendation report, and peer evaluation scores. Success requires demonstrating systematic comparison methodology, identifying at least 3 potential deployment challenges, and providing evidence-based justification for model selection.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation criteria checklist, model performance interpretation guide, and sentence starters for recommendation justification. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Include additional models (XGBoost, ensemble methods), require cost-benefit analysis with specific dollar estimates, or add regulatory compliance evaluation (FDA approval considerations). Encourage exploration of model explainability tools like SHAP values.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Statistical Distribution Model for Real-World Phenomena
description: Students will construct an original probability distribution function to model a complex real-world phenomenon of their choice, then rigorously validate their model using mathematical proofs and empirical data analysis. This capstone activity integrates advanced calculus, probability theory, and statistical inference to create novel mathematical contributions.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced probability theory, calculus, and statistical methods by developing an original probability distribution function with complete mathematical justification
Students will evaluate and validate their created distribution through formal mathematical proofs of essential properties and empirical testing against real-world data sets
instructions:
**Phase 1: Phenomenon Selection & Initial Modeling (Week 1, 3 hours)**
Students select a complex real-world phenomenon not well-modeled by standard distributions (e.g., viral social media post engagement patterns, cryptocurrency volatility clusters, or neural spike timing in specific brain regions). They must justify why existing distributions (normal, exponential, Poisson, etc.) are inadequate using statistical goodness-of-fit tests on preliminary data.

**Phase 2: Distribution Construction (Week 2-3, 6 hours)**
Students construct their probability density function f(x) by: (1) Defining the support and parameters based on phenomenon characteristics, (2) Ensuring f(x) ≥ 0 for all x in support, (3) Proving ∫f(x)dx = 1 using calculus techniques, (4) Deriving moment generating function, mean, variance, and higher moments analytically, (5) Investigating limiting behavior and parameter sensitivity.

**Phase 3: Validation & Refinement (Week 4, 4 hours)**
Students collect or source minimum 500 data points of their phenomenon. They estimate parameters using maximum likelihood estimation, implement their distribution in Python/R, perform Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Anderson-Darling tests against empirical data, compare AIC/BIC scores with competing models, and refine their distribution based on diagnostic plots and residual analysis.

**Phase 4: Presentation & Peer Review (Week 5, 2 hours)**
Students prepare 15-minute presentations formatted as conference talks, including motivation, mathematical development, validation results, and potential applications. Peers provide structured feedback using provided rubrics, focusing on mathematical rigor and practical utility.
materials_needed: Statistical software (Python with scipy/numpy/matplotlib or R with specialized packages)
Access to real-world datasets (Kaggle, government databases, or student-collected data)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Maple)
Statistical reference tables and distribution comparison charts
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Students submit a 15-page technical report including: mathematical derivation with complete proofs (30 points), parameter estimation methodology and code (20 points), empirical validation with statistical tests (25 points), comparison with existing models (15 points), and potential applications discussion (10 points). Presentations assessed on clarity of mathematical exposition (15 points) and ability to defend model assumptions during Q&A (10 points). Peer review quality contributes 5 points. Total: 130 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template structure for proofs, suggest starting with modifications of existing distributions rather than completely novel forms, and offer one-on-one sessions for calculus review. For advanced learners: Challenge them to develop multivariate extensions, explore Bayesian parameter estimation, or investigate theoretical properties like infinite divisibility or extreme value behavior. Provide additional datasets for cross-validation across multiple domains.

title: Optimization Engineering Challenge: Designing Cost-Effective Cylindrical Containers
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world industrial problem by designing cylindrical containers that minimize material costs while meeting volume requirements. They will work through the complete optimization process from problem setup to practical implementation recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative-based optimization methods to minimize surface area functions by setting up and solving real-world constraint problems
Students will implement mathematical solutions to engineering scenarios through systematic problem-solving protocols and cost-benefit analysis
instructions:
**Phase 1: Problem Setup (15 minutes)**
Distribute the scenario packet: 'MegaCorp Industries needs cylindrical storage tanks for 500 liters of liquid. Material costs $0.12 per square meter for sides, $0.18 per square meter for bottom (reinforced), and $0.15 per square meter for top.' Students work in teams of 3-4 to identify variables, constraints, and the objective function.

**Phase 2: Mathematical Modeling (25 minutes)**
Teams establish: Volume constraint V = πr²h = 500L = 0.5m³, Surface Area function SA = 2πr² + 2πrh (geometric), Cost function C = 0.18πr² + 0.15πr² + 0.12(2πrh) = 0.33πr² + 0.24πrh (economic). Using the constraint h = 0.5/(πr²), they derive C(r) = 0.33πr² + 0.12/r.

**Phase 3: Optimization Process (30 minutes)**
Teams find C'(r) = 0.66πr - 0.12/r², set equal to zero, and solve: 0.66πr³ = 0.12, yielding r ≈ 0.363m. They verify this is a minimum using the second derivative test: C''(r) = 0.66π + 0.24/r³ > 0. Calculate corresponding h ≈ 1.208m.

**Phase 4: Solution Validation and Presentation (20 minutes)**
Teams calculate total material cost ($0.47), compare with alternative dimensions (provide 2-3 comparison scenarios), and prepare a 3-minute presentation with recommendations including manufacturing feasibility considerations and cost savings projections.
materials_needed: Scenario packet with company specifications and material costs
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system access
Graph paper and rulers for sketching functions
Presentation materials (poster paper or digital presentation tools)
Reference sheet with volume and surface area formulas for cylinders
assessment_method: Teams submit calculation worksheets showing: (1) Correct constraint equation setup (25%), (2) Accurate cost function derivation (25%), (3) Proper application of optimization techniques with correct critical point identification (30%), (4) Valid solution verification and practical recommendations (20%). Presentations assessed on mathematical accuracy and real-world application relevance using provided rubric.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed function setup templates and step-by-step derivative calculation guides. Offer geometric visualization aids showing cylinder components. For advanced learners: Extend to multi-constraint problems (weight limits, shipping dimensions) or compare optimization methods (Lagrange multipliers vs. substitution). Challenge them to incorporate manufacturing tolerances or bulk material pricing tiers.

title: Distributed System Architecture Pattern Analysis: Microservices vs. Monolith Trade-offs
description: Students will analyze the architectural decisions, performance implications, and failure patterns of two existing enterprise applications - one monolithic and one microservices-based. They will decompose system behaviors, examine data flow patterns, and evaluate trade-offs to determine optimal architectural choices for specific business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze system bottlenecks and failure cascades by examining distributed tracing logs and performance metrics from real-world applications
Students will evaluate architectural trade-offs through systematic comparison of scalability patterns, data consistency models, and operational complexity metrics
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with two case study packages: Netflix's microservices architecture documentation and a traditional monolithic e-commerce platform (like early Amazon architecture). Give teams 45 minutes to examine provided materials including system diagrams, performance monitoring dashboards, incident reports, and deployment logs. Each team member should focus on one analysis dimension: scalability patterns, fault tolerance mechanisms, data consistency approaches, or operational overhead metrics. Teams then spend 30 minutes mapping dependencies, identifying single points of failure, and calculating deployment complexity scores using the provided rubric. Next, teams create side-by-side comparison matrices documenting latency patterns, resource utilization, team coordination overhead, and debugging complexity. In the final 45 minutes, teams present 10-minute analyses defending their architectural recommendations for three specific scenarios: startup MVP, high-traffic social platform, and financial trading system. During presentations, other teams challenge assumptions and question trade-off decisions. Conclude with teams submitting detailed technical reports including quantitative comparisons, risk assessments, and context-specific recommendations with supporting evidence from the case studies.
materials_needed: Netflix microservices case study package with system diagrams and monitoring dashboards
Monolithic e-commerce architecture documentation with performance metrics
Sample distributed tracing logs (Jaeger/Zipkin format)
Architectural complexity assessment rubric spreadsheet
Laptops with network access for additional research
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification from logs/metrics (25%), (2) Depth of trade-off analysis with quantitative support (30%), (3) Quality of architectural recommendations with business context justification (25%), (4) Effectiveness of peer challenge responses during presentations (20%). Require submission of comparison matrix and 2-page technical report within 24 hours.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted sections in documentation and guided analysis templates with specific questions. Offer reference sheets explaining common distributed system patterns. For advanced learners, include additional complexity like CAP theorem implications, service mesh configurations, or container orchestration trade-offs. Encourage analysis of emerging patterns like serverless architectures or event-driven systems.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Scale Model with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design and construct a scaled city layout that meets specific population, budget, and geometric requirements. They will integrate proportional reasoning, area calculations, and linear programming concepts to create an optimal urban design plan with accompanying mathematical justification report.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize proportional relationships, area calculations, and optimization concepts by designing a mathematically viable city layout that meets multiple constraints
Students will construct and defend a comprehensive mathematical model through creating detailed budget analyses and geometric proofs for their urban design decisions
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with the city specifications: design a city for 50,000 residents with a $100 million budget on a 10 square mile area (represented by 20cm x 20cm grid paper using 1cm = 0.5 miles scale). Teams receive constraint cards listing required zones: residential (40-60% of area), commercial (15-25%), industrial (10-20%), recreational (8-15%), and transportation (remaining percentage). Each zone has specific costs per square unit and population capacity ratios that students must research from provided data sheets.
