During the 45-minute design phase, students sketch their city layout on grid paper, calculating areas for each zone and ensuring scale accuracy. They must show all mathematical work for area calculations, scale conversions, and budget allocations on separate calculation sheets. Students then use colored pencils to create their final scaled drawing, labeling all zones with dimensions and mathematical annotations.

In the following 30-minute construction phase, teams build a 3D model using cardboard pieces, with building heights determined by population density calculations they must perform. Each building's height represents specific mathematical relationships (residential: 1cm height = 500 people, commercial: 1cm = 200 workers, etc.).

For the final 25-minute presentation phase, teams present their city design explaining: scale factor reasoning, area optimization decisions, budget allocation strategies, and population distribution calculations. They must defend why their design meets all constraints and propose one mathematical improvement for efficiency. Other teams ask mathematical questions about design choices, requiring presenters to show calculations and justify decisions using mathematical reasoning.
materials_needed: 20cm x 20cm grid paper (1 sheet per team)
City planning constraint cards with zone requirements and cost data
Colored pencils or markers (6 colors minimum per team)
Cardboard pieces cut in 2cm x 2cm squares (30 pieces per team)
Calculators
Rulers and protractors
Mathematical calculation worksheet templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of scale calculations, area computations, and budget analysis (25%), (2) Constraint adherence - all zone requirements and budget limits met with supporting calculations (25%), (3) Design creativity and optimization reasoning with mathematical justification (25%), (4) Presentation clarity including defense of mathematical decisions and ability to answer calculation-based questions (25%). Students must submit calculation worksheets, final scaled drawing, and a 1-page mathematical reflection explaining their optimization strategy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide area calculation templates, offer zone percentage calculation sheets with partially completed examples, and assign specific roles (calculator, designer, presenter) within teams. For advanced learners: Add complex constraints like environmental impact coefficients, require geometric efficiency ratios, or challenge them to create algebraic expressions representing their optimization decisions. Provide additional variables such as traffic flow calculations or zoning transition requirements.

title: Memory Palace for Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification
description: Students will memorize and recall the exact time complexity classifications (Big O, Big Theta, Big Omega) for 30 advanced algorithms across different categories using a structured memory palace technique. This activity focuses on building foundational recall of algorithmic complexity patterns that are essential for technical interviews and advanced computer science coursework.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notations for 30 advanced algorithms by constructing and navigating a digital memory palace
Students will memorize the exact space complexity classifications for dynamic programming, graph, and string processing algorithms through systematic repetition and visual association
instructions: Begin by providing students with a curated list of 30 algorithms categorized into: Dynamic Programming (10), Graph Algorithms (10), and Advanced String Processing (10). Each algorithm entry includes its exact time complexity in Big O, Big Theta, and Big Omega notation, plus space complexity. Students spend 15 minutes studying the provided reference sheet containing algorithms like Bellman-Ford O(VE), Floyd-Warshall Θ(V³), Knuth-Morris-Pratt O(n+m), etc. Next, guide students through creating their digital memory palace using the provided template: they assign each algorithm category to a 'room' in their virtual space, then place each algorithm at specific 'locations' within rooms, associating visual cues with complexity notations. For example, Dijkstra's algorithm might be placed at a 'desk' with 'E log V papers' representing O(E log V). Students spend 25 minutes building their palace, creating vivid mental associations between locations and complexity values. Follow with three rounds of progressive recall testing: Round 1 (10 min) - open palace navigation while recalling; Round 2 (10 min) - palace closed, algorithm name given, recall all complexities; Round 3 (15 min) - complexity given, identify possible algorithms. Students record their responses on the provided answer sheets after each round. Conclude with peer verification where partners check each other's recalled complexities against the master reference sheet. Document accuracy percentages for each student across all three rounds.
materials_needed: Digital memory palace template (web-based or app)
Curated algorithm complexity reference sheet (30 algorithms)
Progressive testing answer sheets (3 rounds)
Master answer key for peer verification
Individual laptops or tablets
Timer for each activity phase
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery by scoring 90% or higher on Round 3 recall test (27/30 algorithms correct). Assessment includes: accuracy of Big O notation (30 points), accuracy of space complexity (20 points), speed of recall under 30 seconds per algorithm (10 points). Peer verification must confirm answers match master key. Students failing to reach 90% repeat the memory palace construction with different visual associations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce algorithm set to 20 most common ones, allow extended palace building time (35 min), provide pre-made visual association suggestions. For advanced learners: add average-case complexity analysis, include amortized analysis for applicable algorithms, challenge them to recall algorithm pseudocode along with complexity. Consider pairing strong memorizers with students who need additional support during peer verification phase.

title: Interpreting Statistical Significance in A/B Testing Results with Multiple Hypothesis Corrections
description: Students will analyze real-world A/B testing data from multiple simultaneous experiments to understand the critical distinction between statistical significance and practical significance. They will interpret p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes while applying multiple hypothesis testing corrections to avoid false discoveries.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes by analyzing A/B testing results across 12 simultaneous experiments
Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance through comparative analysis of conversion rate improvements and business impact calculations
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 people) with a dataset containing results from 12 concurrent A/B tests run by a fictional e-commerce company, including sample sizes, conversion rates, confidence intervals, and p-values for each test. In the first 15 minutes, teams examine the raw results and identify which tests show statistical significance at α = 0.05. Next, introduce the multiple comparisons problem: have teams calculate the family-wise error rate (1 - (1-0.05)^12 = 0.46) and discuss why 5-6 'significant' results might be expected by chance alone. During minutes 30-60, teams apply Bonferroni correction (α = 0.05/12 = 0.0042) and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to the p-values, documenting which tests remain significant under each method. In the following 30 minutes, teams calculate effect sizes (Cohen's h) for each test and estimate the business impact using provided revenue-per-conversion data ($23.50 average). Teams must identify tests that are statistically significant but practically insignificant (e.g., 0.1% improvement) versus those that are practically significant but fail statistical tests due to small sample sizes. Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation recommending which 3 tests to implement company-wide, justifying their choices by integrating statistical significance, practical significance, and business impact considerations.
materials_needed: A/B testing dataset with 12 experiments (CSV file with sample sizes, conversion rates, p-values, confidence intervals)
Statistical calculator or Excel/Google Sheets access
Business context document (revenue per conversion, implementation costs)
Multiple hypothesis correction reference sheet with formulas
assessment_method: Teams submit a 2-page technical report containing: (1) corrected p-values using both Bonferroni and FDR methods with calculations shown, (2) effect size calculations for all tests, (3) business impact analysis for top 5 tests, and (4) final recommendations with statistical and business justifications. Rubric awards 25% for correct statistical calculations, 25% for accurate interpretation of significance levels, 25% for business impact analysis, and 25% for integration of statistical and practical considerations in recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a worked example using 3 tests before attempting the full dataset, and offer a calculation template with formulas pre-populated. Advanced learners can explore additional corrections (Holm-Bonferroni, Sidak) or investigate the relationship between sample size and statistical power by calculating required sample sizes for detecting meaningful effect sizes. Consider providing optional reading on sequential testing and early stopping rules for students interested in advanced A/B testing methodologies.

title: Design and Construct an Optimal Distribution Network Using Graph Theory and Linear Programming
description: Students will design a complete distribution network for a multi-regional supply chain by creating an original mathematical model that integrates graph theory, linear programming, and optimization algorithms. They will construct both the theoretical framework and computational solution to minimize costs while meeting real-world constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory concepts with linear programming techniques by designing an original mathematical model for a complex distribution network optimization problem
Students will construct a comprehensive solution framework through developing custom algorithms, implementing computational methods, and creating visual representations of their optimization results
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a complex scenario: a company needs to distribute products from 5 manufacturing plants to 12 regional warehouses, then to 30 retail locations, with varying transportation costs, capacity constraints, and demand requirements. Provide real-world data including: distance matrices, transportation costs per unit per mile, plant production capacities, warehouse storage limits, and retail demand forecasts. Students work in teams of 3-4 for the first 45 minutes to analyze the problem structure and identify mathematical relationships. Each team must first construct a weighted directed graph representing all possible distribution routes, then formulate this as a multi-stage linear programming problem. In the next 90 minutes, teams develop their original optimization model by defining decision variables (flow quantities between each node pair), creating an objective function (minimize total transportation and storage costs), and establishing constraint sets (capacity limits, demand requirements, flow conservation). Teams must then implement their model using programming software, creating custom algorithms to solve their optimization problem. During the final 45 minutes, each team constructs a comprehensive presentation including: their original mathematical formulation, computational implementation code, optimal solution results, sensitivity analysis showing how changes in parameters affect the solution, and visual network diagrams displaying optimal flow patterns. Teams must also design at least two alternative scenarios (such as adding emergency routing or seasonal demand variations) and demonstrate how their model adapts. Conclude with team presentations where each group defends their mathematical choices and demonstrates their working solution.
materials_needed: Laptops with Python/R and optimization libraries (PuLP, Gurobi, or similar)
Graph visualization software (NetworkX, Gephi, or Cytoscape)
Real supply chain dataset with transportation costs and demand data
Large format paper and markers for network diagram sketching
Scientific calculators
Access to linear programming solver software
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model formulation and correctness (25 points), Implementation quality and computational accuracy (25 points), Innovation in problem-solving approach and algorithm design (20 points), Quality of visual representations and network diagrams (15 points), Presentation clarity and defense of mathematical decisions (15 points). Success requires demonstrating a working optimization solution, clear mathematical reasoning, and ability to explain trade-offs in their design choices.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing template code structures and guided worksheets for formulating constraints. Offer intermediate checkpoints where students can verify their graph construction and constraint formulation before proceeding. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as stochastic demand, multi-objective optimization, or dynamic routing scenarios. Provide reference materials on network flow algorithms and encourage exploration of metaheuristic approaches for large-scale problems.

title: Computer Hardware Component Identification Flash Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify 15 essential computer hardware components using visual flash cards and peer-testing activities. This foundational activity helps students recall basic computer parts and their visual appearance before progressing to understanding their functions.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 15 computer hardware components by name when shown visual images with 90% accuracy
Students will recall the correct spelling and capitalization of hardware component names through written flash card responses
instructions: Begin by distributing the hardware component reference sheet containing 15 labeled images: CPU, motherboard, RAM, hard drive, SSD, power supply, graphics card, cooling fan, optical drive, network card, sound card, USB port, HDMI port, ethernet port, and SATA cable. Give students 10 minutes to study the sheet silently, encouraging them to focus on spelling and visual details. Next, provide each student with 15 blank index cards and have them create flash cards with the component image on one side and the name written on the reverse. Allow 15 minutes for card creation. Once complete, pair students and have them test each other using their flash cards for 10 minutes, with Partner A showing images while Partner B identifies components aloud. Switch roles after 5 minutes. For the assessment phase, collect all flash cards and project the 15 component images randomly on the screen. Students write answers on numbered answer sheets, spending 30 seconds per image. Conclude with immediate feedback by displaying correct answers and having students self-score their papers. Students scoring below 13/15 should repeat the study process with remaining time.
materials_needed: Hardware component reference sheet with 15 labeled images (one per student)
Blank index cards (15 per student)
Pencils or pens
Computer projector and screen
Numbered answer sheets (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students complete a 15-question visual identification quiz, writing component names when shown images. Success criteria: 13/15 correct answers (87% accuracy) with proper spelling. Grade using provided answer key, checking for exact spelling matches. Record scores for progress tracking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made flash cards with component names and encourage repetitive practice with a study partner. Create mnemonics for difficult spellings (e.g., 'motherboard holds everything like a mother'). For advanced learners: Add 5 additional components like heat sink, BIOS chip, or expansion slots, or challenge them to identify component manufacturers from images.

title: Interpreting Correlation Matrix Patterns in Customer Behavior Data
description: Students will analyze a pre-built correlation matrix from e-commerce customer data to identify meaningful relationships between variables. They will practice distinguishing between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while explaining the business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3) and explaining their practical significance
Students will explain the business meaning of correlation patterns through written analysis connecting statistical findings to real-world customer behavior scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared correlation matrix heatmap showing relationships between 8 customer variables: age, income, time_on_site, pages_visited, cart_value, purchase_frequency, customer_satisfaction, and loyalty_score. Give students 5 minutes to examine the matrix individually. Next, organize students into pairs and provide the interpretation worksheet. Have pairs spend 15 minutes identifying the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values. Then allocate 10 minutes for pairs to categorize all 28 correlations using the provided strength categories (strong >0.7, moderate 0.3-0.7, weak <0.3). During the next 15 minutes, pairs must select 5 correlations and write business interpretations explaining what each relationship means for customer behavior (e.g., 'The 0.82 correlation between time_on_site and pages_visited suggests engaged users browse more extensively'). For the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their most interesting finding. Conclude by having each pair submit their completed worksheet with correlations categorized and business interpretations written for assessment.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix heatmap (color-coded with coefficient values)
Correlation interpretation worksheet template
Customer variable definitions reference sheet
Correlation strength category guide handout
assessment_method: Evaluate submitted worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of strongest correlations with correct coefficient values, (2) Proper categorization of correlation strengths using provided thresholds, (3) Clear, logical business interpretations that connect statistical findings to customer behavior, (4) Use of appropriate statistical vocabulary in explanations. Each criterion worth 25 points for total of 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example interpretation for one correlation pair and highlight the strongest correlations on their matrix. For advanced learners: Ask them to identify potential confounding variables or discuss why correlation doesn't imply causation for their selected relationships. Consider providing additional context about the data collection methods.

title: Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in Multi-threaded Web Server Architecture
description: Students will examine a provided multi-threaded web server codebase experiencing performance issues under high load. They will systematically analyze thread synchronization patterns, identify bottlenecks, and decompose the relationship between architectural decisions and performance metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze thread synchronization mechanisms and their impact on server performance by examining mutex usage, deadlock potential, and resource contention patterns
Students will differentiate between various performance bottlenecks through systematic profiling data analysis and code structure examination
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided Java web server codebase (ThreadedHTTPServer.java, ConnectionPool.java, RequestHandler.java) and corresponding JProfiler performance reports showing CPU usage, memory allocation, and thread contention under simulated 1000 concurrent requests. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to map out the server's thread architecture using provided UML sequence diagram templates, identifying all synchronization points (synchronized blocks, locks, semaphores). Next, spend 30 minutes having pairs analyze the provided profiling data to identify the top 3 performance bottlenecks, documenting specific line numbers, wait times, and resource utilization percentages. Students then spend 25 minutes examining the relationship between code structure and performance issues by completing a cause-effect analysis matrix linking specific coding patterns (thread pool size, connection handling strategy, shared resource access) to observed performance metrics. In the final 15 minutes, each pair presents their bottleneck analysis to another pair, defending their findings with specific evidence from both code examination and profiling data. Instructor circulates during analysis phases, asking probing questions about thread safety assumptions and synchronization trade-offs.
materials_needed: Multi-threaded Java web server codebase (3 source files)
JProfiler performance reports (PDF format)
UML sequence diagram templates (printed)
Cause-effect analysis matrix worksheets
Computers with Java IDE (IntelliJ IDEA or Eclipse)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of thread architecture mapping with all synchronization points identified, (2) Correct identification of performance bottlenecks with supporting profiling data evidence, (3) Quality of cause-effect analysis linking code patterns to performance issues, (4) Depth of technical reasoning in peer presentation with specific line number references and quantitative performance metrics
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide annotated code snippets highlighting synchronization keywords and offer guiding questions about thread interaction patterns. For advanced learners: Include additional profiling data from different load scenarios (500, 2000, 5000 requests) and challenge them to analyze scalability patterns across multiple performance conditions.

title: Design Your Dream House: Creating a Scale Model with Area and Perimeter Optimization
description: Students will design and create a floor plan for their dream house using coordinate geometry, then build a physical scale model while optimizing room areas within budget constraints. They will apply mathematical concepts including area, perimeter, scale factors, and coordinate plotting to solve real-world design problems.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original house floor plan by applying coordinate geometry, area calculations, and scale factor conversions to design functional living spaces
Students will construct a physical scale model through precise measurements and proportional reasoning while justifying their design choices mathematically
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a 'house budget' of 2,400 square feet total area and design constraints: minimum 4 rooms (bedroom, kitchen, living room, bathroom), each room must be rectangular, and total perimeter cannot exceed 240 feet. Students start by sketching their floor plan on coordinate grid paper (1 unit = 10 feet), plotting vertices of each room and labeling coordinates. They calculate the area of each room using length × width, ensuring the sum equals exactly 2,400 sq ft, and verify the total perimeter stays within limits. Next, students transfer their design to poster board, creating a detailed floor plan with measurements, room labels, and coordinate points marked. They must include a data table showing room dimensions, areas, and perimeter calculations with work shown. For the physical model phase, students convert their floor plan to a 1:100 scale (1 cm = 1 meter in real life) and construct walls using cardboard strips cut to precise scaled measurements. They build the 3D model on a cardboard base, ensuring walls connect properly at plotted coordinates. Students create a presentation poster displaying their original coordinate floor plan, calculation table, scaled measurements, and photos of their 3D model. During the final 15 minutes, students present their designs to the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning for room sizes, coordinate choices, and how they optimized space within the given constraints. Each presentation should include one design challenge they faced and how they solved it mathematically.
materials_needed: Coordinate grid paper (1/4 inch squares)
Cardboard sheets and strips for model building
Rulers and measuring tapes
Calculators
Poster board for presentations
Colored pencils or markers
Glue sticks and scissors
Protractors for measuring angles
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area/perimeter calculations and coordinate plotting (25 points), (2) Creative and functional floor plan design meeting all constraints (25 points), (3) Precision of scale model construction with correct proportions (25 points), (4) Quality of mathematical reasoning in presentation and problem-solving explanation (25 points). Students must submit calculation worksheets, coordinate plots, and completed 3D models.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made coordinate templates with partial room layouts to complete, offer calculation checklists, and pair with stronger math partners. Supply measuring guides and area/perimeter formula reference cards. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring triangular or L-shaped rooms, introduce concepts like cost per square foot optimization, or challenge them to design multi-story houses with stairwell considerations and 3D coordinate systems.

title: Analyzing Database Query Performance and Optimization Strategies
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of different SQL queries on a sample e-commerce database by examining execution plans, identifying bottlenecks, and comparing indexing strategies. They will break down query components to determine which structural elements contribute to performance issues and evaluate the trade-offs between different optimization approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL query execution plans by identifying scan types, join operations, and cost estimates to determine performance bottlenecks
Students will compare the effectiveness of different indexing strategies through systematic performance testing and cost-benefit analysis
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 members) with the pre-loaded 'OnlineStore' database containing 100,000 customer records, 50,000 product records, and 250,000 order records. First, have students execute the baseline query: 'SELECT c.customer_name, p.product_name, o.order_date FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id WHERE o.order_date BETWEEN '2023-01-01' AND '2023-12-31' ORDER BY o.order_date DESC'. Students must capture and document the execution time and examine the query execution plan using EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE commands. Next, teams analyze the execution plan by identifying: table scan methods (full table scan vs index scan), join algorithms used, estimated vs actual row counts, and total query cost. For the analysis phase, students create a structured comparison table examining three scenarios: the original query (no indexes), the same query with a single index on order_date, and the query with composite indexes on (customer_id, order_date) and (product_id). Each scenario requires students to measure execution time, memory usage, and disk I/O operations. Students then systematically break down performance differences by isolating each query component: analyze the WHERE clause filtering efficiency, examine JOIN operation costs, and evaluate the ORDER BY sorting overhead. Finally, teams prepare a detailed analysis report identifying which specific structural elements cause performance degradation, explaining why certain indexes improve performance while others don't, and recommending the optimal indexing strategy with justification based on their data analysis.
materials_needed: Pre-populated 'OnlineStore' database with specified record counts
Database management system with query analysis tools (PostgreSQL, MySQL, or SQL Server)
Performance monitoring worksheet template
Computers with database client software installed
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a rubric scoring: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25 points), (2) Correctness of performance bottleneck identification (25 points), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between indexing strategies (25 points), and (4) Justification of optimization recommendations with supporting data (25 points). Students must submit their analysis report with documented execution times, annotated execution plans, and evidence-based conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a guided worksheet breaking down execution plan symbols and common bottleneck indicators, plus offer one-on-one guidance in interpreting execution costs. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them analyze subquery optimization, explore query hint effects, or examine the impact of different database statistics on query planning.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Public Transportation Networks
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban transportation challenges, incorporating multiple variables, constraints, and objective functions. They will develop both the theoretical framework and computational implementation, then present their model to stakeholders with justification for their design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from linear programming, graph theory, and statistical modeling by constructing an original optimization model for urban transportation networks
Students will design and implement computational algorithms through Python programming to solve their multi-variable optimization problem with realistic constraints
instructions: Begin by providing students with authentic data sets from 3-4 different cities' public transportation systems (ridership data, route maps, operating costs, demographic information). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a different city context. In the first 90 minutes, teams analyze their assigned data to identify key variables (travel time, cost, ridership patterns, equity considerations) and formulate their problem statement. Students must define at least 5 decision variables, 8-10 constraints, and create a multi-objective function balancing efficiency, cost, and accessibility. During the next 120 minutes, teams construct their mathematical model using linear or mixed-integer programming techniques, documenting all assumptions and mathematical relationships. They must create both a theoretical model (written mathematically) and implement it computationally using Python with libraries like PuLP or scipy.optimize. Teams then spend 90 minutes testing their model with their city's data, running sensitivity analyses on key parameters, and validating results against current system performance. Finally, teams prepare a 15-minute presentation for a mock city planning committee (played by other teams and instructor), where they must justify their model design, demonstrate computational results, discuss limitations, and propose implementation strategies. Each team presents while others provide feedback using structured peer evaluation forms focusing on mathematical rigor, practical applicability, and presentation clarity.
materials_needed: Real transportation data sets from 4 different cities (CSV format with ridership, routes, costs)
Computers with Python installed (PuLP, scipy, pandas, matplotlib libraries)
Graph paper and whiteboards for initial model sketching
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentations
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-category rubric (25 points each): 1) Mathematical Model Construction - correctness of formulation, appropriate variable selection, constraint validity; 2) Computational Implementation - working code, appropriate algorithms, sensitivity analysis; 3) Real-world Application - use of authentic data, practical constraints, stakeholder considerations; 4) Communication - clear presentation, defense of choices, professional delivery. Students submit written model documentation, Python code with comments, and reflection on design process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for linear programming setup and starter Python code snippets. Offer mid-process check-ins to validate model formulation before coding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multiple transportation modes, or dynamic routing. Encourage exploration of advanced algorithms like genetic algorithms or machine learning integration.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Public Transportation Networks: Technical Implementation
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization model to solve real-world urban transportation challenges, incorporating multiple constraints and variables. They will develop algorithms, test solutions using programming tools, and present their model with mathematical justification and practical implementation recommendations.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory, linear programming, and statistical analysis to construct a comprehensive transportation optimization model by integrating multiple mathematical domains
Students will design original algorithms and mathematical frameworks through systematic problem decomposition and constraint analysis
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Each team receives a specific city scenario packet containing: population density maps, current transit routes, budget constraints, and ridership data. Teams spend 45 minutes analyzing their scenario and identifying key variables (travel time, cost, capacity, coverage area, environmental impact). Next, students formulate their mathematical model (60 minutes) by: (1) defining decision variables using proper mathematical notation, (2) establishing objective functions (minimize cost, maximize coverage), (3) creating constraint equations for budget, capacity, and geographic limitations, and (4) selecting appropriate solution methods (linear programming, network flow algorithms, or heuristic approaches). Teams then implement their model using Python, MATLAB, or R (90 minutes), writing code to process their data and generate solutions. During implementation, students must document their mathematical reasoning and algorithm choices. Following coding, teams test multiple scenarios (30 minutes) by varying constraints and analyzing sensitivity of solutions. Finally, each team prepares a 15-minute presentation (30 minutes preparation) demonstrating their model, showing mathematical derivations, presenting computational results, and proposing implementation strategies. Presentations include: mathematical model explanation, algorithm flowchart, computational results with visualizations, sensitivity analysis, and real-world feasibility assessment. Conclude with peer evaluation where teams critique each other's mathematical approaches and suggest improvements (20 minutes).
materials_needed: City transportation scenario packets (customized for each team)
Computers with Python/MATLAB/R software installed
Graph paper and mathematical notation reference sheets
Population and ridership datasets in CSV format
Digital mapping tools or GIS software access
Presentation software and projection equipment
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Construction (25 points - correctness of variables, constraints, and objective functions), Algorithm Design and Implementation (25 points - code functionality, efficiency, and documentation), Mathematical Reasoning and Justification (20 points - clarity of derivations and method selection), Solution Quality and Analysis (15 points - feasibility and sensitivity testing), and Presentation and Communication (15 points - clarity of mathematical explanations and practical recommendations). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving at least 80 points overall with minimum 15 points in each Mathematical Model Construction and Algorithm Design categories.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing mathematical model templates and step-by-step algorithm development guides. Offer office hours for debugging code and reviewing mathematical concepts. For advanced learners, introduce stochastic elements (uncertain demand patterns), multi-objective optimization techniques, or machine learning integration for demand prediction. Encourage advanced students to consider dynamic routing problems or incorporate game theory for competitive transit scenarios.
original_title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Public Transportation Networks

title: Binary Number System Memory Palace Creation
description: Students will memorize the decimal values of binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) through creating and practicing with visual memory aids. This foundational knowledge is essential for understanding how computers represent numbers internally.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal values of the first eight binary place values (2^0 through 2^7) without reference materials by using memory techniques
Students will identify the position and corresponding decimal value of each bit in an 8-bit binary number through repeated practice drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the Binary Place Value Reference Sheet to each student (5 minutes). Have students work in pairs to examine the sheet, which shows positions 7-0 from left to right with corresponding decimal values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Instruct students to create physical memory aids using index cards: write one decimal value per card in large numbers (10 minutes). Next, guide students through the 'Powers of Two Chant' - have the entire class recite '1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128' in rhythm while clapping, repeat 5 times (5 minutes). Then conduct individual practice: students arrange their cards in correct order from memory, then flip cards over and recite the sequence. Partner checks accuracy using the reference sheet (10 minutes). Follow with the 'Lightning Round' - call out random positions ('What's position 5?' Answer: 32) and students respond without looking at materials. Start slowly, increase speed gradually (10 minutes). Conclude with the 'Binary Memory Test' - students put away all materials and write the 8 decimal values in correct positional order on a blank sheet. Allow 3 minutes for completion, then have students self-check against the reference sheet and record their score out of 8.
materials_needed: Binary Place Value Reference Sheet (one per student)
Blank index cards (8 per student)
Black markers or pens
Blank paper for final memory test
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students achieve success by scoring 7/8 or higher on the final memory test, correctly writing decimal values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 in proper positional order. Observe during partner practice to identify students who struggle with sequencing. Record individual lightning round response accuracy as formative assessment data.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronyms like 'Cool Hackers Always Program Smart Code Really Fast' for 128-64-32-16-8-4-2-1, allow extra card practice time, or use colored cards for visual learners. For advanced learners: extend to 16-bit values (add 256, 512, 1024, 2048, etc.) or challenge them to tutor struggling peers during partner practice.

title: Binary Number System Memory Palace Creation: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create a visual memory aid by drawing and labeling place values for 8-bit binary numbers. They will memorize the decimal equivalents of each binary position and demonstrate recall through flashcard practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal values of binary place positions (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) by creating a visual memory palace diagram
Students will identify binary place value positions through structured flashcard memorization activities
instructions: Begin by distributing graph paper and colored pencils to each student (5 minutes). Have students draw 8 boxes in a horizontal row, numbering them 0-7 from right to left above each box. In the first row of boxes, students write the binary place values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 (right to left). Below each number, students draw a simple visual symbol to represent that value (1 dot, 2 eyes, 4-leaf clover, 8-legged spider, etc.) using colored pencils (15 minutes). Next, students practice by covering the decimal values and trying to recall them while looking only at their visual symbols (10 minutes). Create pairs for peer testing - one student points to a position while their partner states the decimal value (10 minutes). Students then create individual flashcards using index cards: binary position on one side (e.g., '2^3 position') and decimal value on the other (e.g., '8') for all eight positions (10 minutes). Conclude with individual silent practice using their flashcards, cycling through all eight cards three times, setting aside correctly recalled cards and focusing extra attention on missed ones (10 minutes). Students must demonstrate 100% accuracy on all eight positions during final individual check before completing the activity.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1 sheet per student)
Colored pencils or markers (set per student)
Index cards (8 per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Binary place value reference poster for instructor
assessment_method: Individual oral quiz where instructor points to each binary position (0-7) and student must state correct decimal value within 3 seconds. Success criteria: 8/8 correct responses. Document results on checklist with student names and position-by-position accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-made visual symbol suggestions and allow calculator use to verify powers of 2. Pair with stronger students during peer practice. For advanced learners: extend to 16-bit positions, challenge them to convert simple decimal numbers to binary using their memorized place values, or have them create mnemonic devices to help classmates remember the sequence.
original_title: Binary Number System Memory Palace Creation

title: Interpreting Data Distributions Through Real Estate Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real estate dataset to understand different types of data distributions and their characteristics. They will identify distribution patterns, interpret their meanings, and explain how distribution shapes impact data analysis decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will identify normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by examining histograms and box plots of housing price data
Students will explain the relationship between distribution characteristics and appropriate statistical measures through guided analysis exercises
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a real estate dataset with 1,000+ property records including price, square footage, bedrooms, and neighborhood data (10 minutes setup). First, students create histograms for house prices using matplotlib, adjusting bin sizes from 10 to 50 bins to observe how binning affects distribution appearance (15 minutes). Next, they generate box plots for the same price data and identify outliers, quartiles, and median positions (10 minutes). Students then repeat this process for square footage data and number of bedrooms, creating a total of six visualizations (20 minutes). In pairs, students compare their three histograms side-by-side and classify each as normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, or bimodal, writing brief justifications for their classifications (15 minutes). Each pair then calculates mean vs. median for each variable and discusses why these measures differ based on distribution shape (10 minutes). Students create a summary table documenting distribution type, skewness direction, presence of outliers, and whether mean or median better represents central tendency for each variable (15 minutes). Finally, pairs present one key insight about how distribution shape affects their choice of statistical measures to the class (15 minutes). Throughout the activity, circulate to check that students are correctly interpreting distribution shapes and connecting visual patterns to statistical concepts.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Real estate dataset (CSV file with 1,000+ records)
Pre-written code template with data loading and basic plotting functions
Distribution classification reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed summary tables for correct distribution identification (4 points), appropriate justifications linking visual patterns to distribution types (4 points), and accurate recommendations for mean vs. median usage (4 points). Assess pair presentations for clarity in explaining one statistical insight (3 points). Total: 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using a different variable and highlight key visual cues (tail direction, peak location). Offer sentence starters for justifications. For advanced learners, introduce kurtosis calculations and have them research real-world implications of different distribution types in predictive modeling.

title: Optimization Applications: Designing a Maximum Volume Cylindrical Container with Material Constraints
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving maximizing the volume of a cylindrical container given fixed surface area constraints. They will use derivatives to find critical points and validate their solutions using second derivative tests.
learning_objectives: Students will apply differential calculus optimization methods to determine maximum volume dimensions for a cylindrical container by setting up constraint equations and finding critical points
Students will demonstrate understanding of optimization applications through systematic problem-solving that includes constraint analysis, mathematical modeling, and solution validation
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: A manufacturing company needs to design cylindrical cans with exactly 300 cm² of material (including top and bottom). Students must find dimensions that maximize volume. Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work in pairs to identify variables and constraints. They should define r (radius) and h (height), then write the surface area constraint: 2πr² + 2πrh = 300. Step 2 (15 minutes): Guide students to express volume V = πr²h as a single-variable function by solving the constraint for h: h = (300 - 2πr²)/(2πr), then substituting into volume formula to get V(r) = πr²[(300 - 2πr²)/(2πr)] = (300πr - 2π²r³)/2. Step 3 (20 minutes): Students find dV/dr = (300π - 6π²r²)/2 and set equal to zero. They solve 300π - 6π²r² = 0 to find r = √(50/π) ≈ 3.99 cm. Step 4 (10 minutes): Students verify this is a maximum using the second derivative test: d²V/dr² = -6π²r < 0 when r > 0. Step 5 (15 minutes): Calculate corresponding height h = (300 - 2π(50/π))/(2π√(50/π)) ≈ 7.98 cm and maximum volume V ≈ 398.9 cm³. Step 6 (10 minutes): Students create a summary report showing all work, dimensions, and volume with proper units and validation.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos, GeoGebra)
Printed scenario worksheets with constraint information
Grid paper for sketching functions
Physical cylindrical containers for measurement verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly sets up constraint equation, derives single-variable function, finds critical points, validates maximum, and provides accurate final dimensions; (3) Minor computational errors but demonstrates understanding of optimization process; (2) Sets up problem correctly but makes significant errors in differentiation or solving; (1) Shows some understanding but major conceptual errors in constraint handling or optimization steps. Students submit complete written solutions showing all algebraic steps and final verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with constraint equation already set up, offer step-by-step derivative calculation templates, and allow use of online derivative calculators for verification. For advanced learners: Extend to minimize surface area given fixed volume, explore rectangular box optimization with similar constraints, or investigate how changing total material amount affects optimal dimensions ratio.

title: Distributed System Architecture Analysis: Decomposing Netflix's Microservices Failure Cascade
description: Students analyze a real-world distributed system failure scenario by examining Netflix's 2012 Christmas Eve outage. They will dissect the system architecture, identify failure propagation patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented resilience patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between microservices in a distributed system by mapping service call chains and identifying single points of failure
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of circuit breaker, bulkhead, and timeout patterns through examination of real failure logs and system behavior
instructions:
Begin by providing students with the Netflix Christmas Eve 2012 incident report, system architecture diagrams, and sanitized service logs (30 minutes reading time). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical materials: the incident timeline, service dependency graph, error rate metrics, and response time data. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams create a visual failure propagation map using provided tools. They must identify the root cause service, trace how failures cascaded through dependent services, and mark which services experienced degraded vs. complete failure. Teams annotate their maps with specific timestamps and error rates from the logs.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Students analyze the implemented resilience patterns. They examine code snippets showing circuit breaker configurations, timeout settings, and bulkhead implementations. Teams must identify which patterns worked effectively and which failed, supporting their analysis with specific metrics from the incident data.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Teams evaluate alternative architectural decisions. They propose three specific changes to the system design that could have prevented or mitigated the cascade failure. Each proposal must include: modified service boundaries, different resilience pattern configurations, or infrastructure changes. Teams must justify their recommendations using principles of distributed systems theory.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents their failure analysis and architectural recommendations to the class, followed by peer questioning and instructor feedback on their technical reasoning.
materials_needed: Netflix Christmas Eve 2012 incident report (provided PDF)
Service dependency graph visualization tool (draw.io or Lucidchart)
Sanitized service logs and metrics data (CSV files)
Code snippets showing resilience pattern implementations
Laptops with internet access for research and diagramming
assessment_method: Teams submit: (1) annotated failure propagation diagram with timeline and metrics (25 points), (2) written analysis of resilience pattern effectiveness with supporting evidence from logs (35 points), (3) three justified architectural recommendations with technical rationale (40 points). Rubric evaluates accuracy of failure chain identification, depth of pattern analysis, and feasibility of proposed solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide template diagram with partial service mappings and guiding questions for log analysis. For advanced learners: include additional complexity by providing concurrent incidents from other companies (Amazon S3, GitHub) for comparative analysis and pattern generalization across different system architectures.

title: Evaluating the Reliability of Ice Cream Sales vs. Temperature Data Analysis
description: Students will critically assess a pre-built data analysis comparing ice cream sales to temperature, identifying potential flaws in methodology, data collection, and conclusions. They will judge the validity of claims and recommend improvements to strengthen the analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and reliability of a basic data science analysis by identifying methodological strengths and weaknesses
Students will critique data visualization choices and statistical conclusions through structured peer review and written assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing the sample analysis report containing: a scatter plot of ice cream sales vs. temperature, correlation coefficient (r=0.78), and conclusion stating 'temperature directly causes ice cream sales increases.' Give students 10 minutes to individually read and take notes. Next, provide the evaluation checklist covering: data source credibility, sample size adequacy, visualization clarity, statistical interpretation accuracy, and logical reasoning. In pairs (15 minutes), students use the checklist to systematically evaluate each component, marking 'Strong,' 'Adequate,' or 'Weak' with specific evidence. Have pairs identify the three most significant problems and propose concrete solutions. Conduct a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share their most critical finding. Students then individually complete a written evaluation (20 minutes) addressing: What is the most serious flaw in this analysis? How would you improve the data collection method? Is the causal conclusion justified? Finally, have students rate the overall analysis reliability on a 1-10 scale with justification. Conclude with a 10-minute debrief discussing common evaluation criteria for data science projects and the difference between correlation and causation.
materials_needed: Sample flawed analysis report (1 page per student)
Data analysis evaluation checklist handout
Jupyter notebook or Excel file with the original dataset
Whiteboard or projector for class discussion
assessment_method: Grade individual written evaluations using rubric: Problem identification (25%), Solution quality (25%), Statistical reasoning (25%), Communication clarity (25%). Students must identify at least 2 valid methodological flaws and demonstrate understanding that correlation ≠ causation to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'The data collection is problematic because...' and highlight specific sections to evaluate. For advanced learners: Ask them to redesign the entire study methodology and identify additional variables that should be considered (confounding factors).

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Water Park with Cost Analysis
description: Students will create an original water park design using geometric principles, scaling calculations, and budget constraints. They will construct a physical scale model and present a comprehensive business proposal including area calculations, material costs, and profit projections.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original water park layout by applying geometric formulas for area and perimeter calculations of complex shapes
Students will construct a detailed budget proposal through multi-step percentage calculations, scaling ratios, and linear equation modeling for pricing structures
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a 24"x18" poster board representing a 240m x 180m plot of land. Distribute the constraint cards: budget of $2.5 million, minimum 5 attractions, maximum 40% of land for pools/water features, required 15% for parking, 10% for amenities. **Phase 2 (40 minutes):** Teams sketch their water park design using geometric shapes. They must calculate the actual area of each attraction using scale ratio 1:1000, then determine construction costs using the provided rate sheet ($150/m² for pools, $75/m² for slides, $25/m² for walkways, $50/m² for landscaping). Students create detailed cost spreadsheets showing area calculations, unit costs, and totals. **Phase 3 (35 minutes):** Using cardboard pieces, clay, and craft materials, teams build 3D scale models of their water parks on the poster boards. Models must be proportionally accurate and include labeled attractions with dimensions. **Phase 4 (25 minutes):** Each team presents their design explaining geometric calculations, budget breakdown, and one unique mathematical feature (such as optimizing slide angles using trigonometry or calculating water volume using cylindrical/rectangular prism formulas). Presentations include defending design choices and answering cost-efficiency questions from other teams.
materials_needed: 24"x18" poster board (1 per team)
Constraint requirement cards with budget and land use rules
Construction cost rate sheets with price per square meter
Cardboard pieces, clay, craft sticks, colored paper
Calculators and rulers
Spreadsheet template (digital or printed)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area calculations, scaling, and cost computations), Creative Design (originality, constraint compliance, aesthetic appeal), Model Construction (proportional accuracy, craftsmanship, clear labeling), and Presentation Quality (clear explanation of mathematical processes, defense of design decisions, professional delivery). Each category worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-drawn geometric shape templates and area formula reference cards. Offer calculation checkpoint sheets for step-by-step cost computation guidance. For advanced learners, add challenge constraints like environmental impact calculations using exponential functions or crowd flow optimization using systems of equations. Consider pairing stronger math students with those needing support within teams.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance
description: Students will analyze pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results from multiple ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagging) applied to regression tasks with varying noise levels. They will interpret how ensemble parameters affect the bias-variance trade-off and explain performance differences across different data complexity scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition metrics by analyzing numerical results from ensemble models across different hyperparameter configurations
Students will explain the relationship between ensemble methodology and bias-variance trade-off through comparative analysis of tabulated model performance data
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing bias-variance decomposition results for three datasets (low-noise polynomial, high-noise polynomial, and multi-modal) with results from Random Forest (10, 50, 100 trees), Gradient Boosting (learning rates 0.01, 0.1, 0.3), and Bagging ensembles (5, 25, 50 estimators). Each row contains: model_type, hyperparameter_value, dataset_complexity, bias_squared, variance, noise, total_error, and decomposition_percentage_breakdown. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to examine the data structure and identify patterns. Have them create summary tables showing how bias² and variance change as ensemble size increases for each method on the low-noise dataset.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students analyze cross-method comparisons by calculating the bias-to-variance ratios for each ensemble type at their optimal hyperparameter settings. They should identify which methods are bias-dominated vs. variance-dominated and create comparison charts.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students interpret the impact of dataset complexity by comparing how the same ensemble configurations perform across the three datasets. They should explain why Random Forest with 100 trees shows different bias-variance profiles on high-noise vs. low-noise data.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Pairs present their key findings to adjacent pairs, focusing on explaining one counterintuitive result (e.g., why adding more trees sometimes increases bias). Conclude with whole-class discussion on practical implications for model selection in production environments.
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition CSV file with 270 rows of results
Calculators or spreadsheet software (Excel/Google Sheets)
Printed reference sheet with bias-variance formulas and ensemble method definitions
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of bias-variance trend identification from data (25%), (2) Correctness of cross-method performance explanations (25%), (3) Quality of reasoning about dataset complexity effects (25%), (4) Clarity of interpretation during peer discussions (25%). Students must correctly identify at least 3 key trends and provide sound explanations for ensemble behavior differences to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided calculation templates and highlight specific rows to analyze first. Offer sentence starters like 'When ensemble size increases, I notice that bias...' For advanced learners, include additional decomposition data from neural network ensembles or challenge them to predict performance on unseen dataset types based on the patterns they've identified.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance: Technical Implementation
description: Students will analyze pre-computed bias-variance decomposition results from Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Bagging models applied to regression problems. They will interpret how different ensemble strategies affect the bias-variance tradeoff and explain the mathematical relationships underlying model performance differences.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing numerical outputs and connecting them to ensemble model characteristics across three different algorithms
Students will explain the mathematical relationships between bias, variance, and irreducible error through comparative analysis of ensemble model performance metrics
instructions:
Begin by distributing three datasets containing bias-variance decomposition results for Random Forest (RF), Gradient Boosting (GB), and Bagging models, each tested on identical regression problems with varying noise levels (σ² = 0.1, 0.5, 1.0). Each dataset contains columns: model_type, n_estimators, noise_level, bias², variance, irreducible_error, and total_error. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to create comparative tables showing bias² and variance values for each model type at n_estimators = [10, 50, 100, 200] and noise_level = 0.5. They must calculate the bias-variance ratio (variance/bias²) for each configuration.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students analyze trends by plotting bias² vs. variance for each model type, using n_estimators as color coding. They identify which models are bias-dominated vs. variance-dominated and at what ensemble sizes transitions occur.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students examine the relationship between irreducible error and total error across noise levels. They must explain why Random Forest shows different bias-variance characteristics compared to Gradient Boosting, referencing bootstrap sampling vs. sequential error correction mechanisms.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each pair writes a technical interpretation (200-300 words) explaining: (a) which ensemble method best manages the bias-variance tradeoff under high noise conditions, (b) the mathematical reason why bias² decreases differently across methods, and (c) practical implications for model selection in production environments.

Conclude with pairs presenting one key insight to the class, focusing on counterintuitive findings or practical applications.
materials_needed: Pre-computed bias-variance decomposition CSV files (3 files, ~500 rows each)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Jupyter notebooks with data loading template code
Reference sheet with bias-variance decomposition formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of bias-variance ratio calculations (25 points), (2) Correctness of trend identification in plots with proper axis labeling (25 points), (3) Technical explanation quality demonstrating understanding of ensemble mechanisms (35 points), (4) Mathematical reasoning connecting decomposition components to algorithm characteristics (15 points). Students must achieve 70+ points and correctly identify at least 2 algorithm-specific bias-variance patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made plotting templates and guided questions for each step. Offer a reference table showing expected bias-variance patterns for each algorithm. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets with classification problems using 0-1 loss decomposition, or challenge them to derive theoretical explanations for observed patterns using ensemble theory mathematics.
original_title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze and interpret the bias-variance tradeoff components in different ensemble methods using mathematical decomposition and visualization. They will examine how bagging, boosting, and random forests affect model bias and variance through systematic comparison of prediction error sources.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between bias, variance, and irreducible error by analyzing decomposition formulas across different ensemble algorithms
Students will explain how ensemble methods specifically address bias versus variance components through comparative analysis of bootstrap aggregation and gradient boosting mechanisms
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-trained models on the same regression dataset: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and AdaBoost, along with their prediction outputs on 100 bootstrap samples. In pairs, students first calculate the bias-variance decomposition using the provided formulas: Bias² = (E[f̂(x)] - f(x))², Variance = E[(f̂(x) - E[f̂(x)])²], and Total Error = Bias² + Variance + σ². Students compute these components for each model by: (1) calculating mean predictions across bootstrap samples, (2) computing squared differences between mean predictions and true values (bias²), (3) calculating variance of predictions across samples, and (4) summing components. Next, students create visualization matrices showing bias-variance components for each algorithm across different complexity parameters (max_depth for RF, learning_rate for GB). They then analyze provided learning curves showing training/validation error trajectories and connect these patterns to their bias-variance calculations. Students complete interpretation worksheets comparing: which algorithms primarily reduce bias vs. variance, how ensemble size affects each component, and why certain algorithms show different bias-variance profiles. Finally, pairs present one key insight about how ensemble mechanisms (averaging vs. sequential fitting) create different bias-variance tradeoffs, supported by their numerical analysis. Instructors circulate to verify calculations and guide interpretation of mathematical relationships.
materials_needed: Python environment with scikit-learn, numpy, matplotlib
Pre-trained ensemble models saved as pickle files
Bootstrap sample predictions dataset (CSV format)
Bias-variance calculation worksheet with formulas
Learning curve visualization templates
assessment_method: Evaluate through completed calculation worksheets showing correct bias-variance computations (40%), accuracy of visualizations with proper axis labels and interpretations (30%), and quality of paired presentations demonstrating understanding of ensemble mechanisms' effects on bias-variance components (30%). Success requires mathematical accuracy within 5% of expected values and clear explanations of why different ensemble methods show distinct bias-variance profiles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide step-by-step calculation examples for the first bootstrap sample and pre-formatted visualization code templates. Offer conceptual diagrams showing how bagging reduces variance while boosting reduces bias. For advanced learners, extend analysis to compare bias-variance decomposition across different noise levels in the dataset or examine how feature selection within ensembles affects the decomposition components.
original_title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance

title: Pizza Party Budget Challenge: Applying Decimal Operations
description: Students will plan a class pizza party by calculating costs, quantities, and change using decimal operations. They will apply addition, subtraction, and multiplication of decimals to solve a real-world budgeting problem.
learning_objectives: Students will apply decimal addition and subtraction by calculating total costs and remaining budget amounts in a pizza party planning scenario
Students will apply decimal multiplication through computing costs for multiple quantities of food items and calculating tax amounts
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Pizza Party Planning Worksheet and price menu to each student (5 minutes). Explain that each student has a $75.00 budget to plan a pizza party for 20 classmates. Students must select pizzas, drinks, and desserts while staying within budget and including 8.5% sales tax. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students choose items from the menu, writing quantities and individual prices on their worksheet. They must select at least 4 pizzas, 20 drinks, and 1 dessert option.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students calculate subtotals for each category by multiplying unit prices by quantities. For example: 5 cheese pizzas × $12.75 = $63.75. They show all multiplication work with decimal alignment.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students add all subtotals to find the pre-tax total, demonstrating proper decimal alignment. Example: $63.75 + $18.00 + $8.50 = $90.25.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students calculate 8.5% sales tax by multiplying pre-tax total by 0.085, rounding to nearest cent. They add tax to pre-tax total for final amount.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Students subtract final amount from $75.00 budget to determine if they're over or under budget. If over budget, they must revise their selections and recalculate.

Step 6 (10 minutes): Students pair up to check each other's calculations and discuss their menu choices. Conclude with 2-3 students sharing their final party plans with the class.
materials_needed: Pizza Party Planning Worksheet (one per student)
Laminated price menu with pizza ($12.75-$15.50), drinks ($0.75-$1.25), and desserts ($6.50-$12.00)
Calculators for verification only
Pencils and scratch paper
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with proper decimal alignment and stays within budget; (3) Minor calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of process; (2) Some calculation errors with inconsistent decimal placement; (1) Major errors or incomplete work. Students must show all work for decimal operations and final budget comparison.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing decimal alignment examples and allow calculator use for verification. Pair with stronger math students during Step 6. For advanced learners: Add constraints such as 'must feed 25 people instead of 20' or 'calculate unit cost per person' or include a 15% tip calculation for delivery.

title: Debugging Algorithm Efficiency: Analyzing Sorting Performance Through Code Trace and Complexity Comparison
description: Students will analyze two provided sorting algorithms (bubble sort and merge sort) by tracing through their execution steps, identifying inefficiencies, and comparing their time complexity patterns. They will decompose the algorithms' performance characteristics using concrete data sets and mathematical analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the step-by-step execution patterns of sorting algorithms by manually tracing through bubble sort and merge sort with specific input arrays
Students will compare algorithmic efficiency by examining time complexity relationships and identifying performance bottlenecks through systematic testing
instructions: Begin by providing students with pre-written bubble sort and merge sort implementations and three test arrays: [64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90], [5, 2, 8, 1], and [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (30 minutes): Each pair manually traces through bubble sort execution on the first array, documenting every comparison and swap operation on the provided worksheet. They must record the array state after each complete pass and count total operations. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Repeat the tracing process for merge sort on the same array, documenting the recursive splitting phase and the merging phase separately. Students draw the recursion tree and track comparisons at each merge level. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Run both algorithms on all three test arrays using the provided Python environment, recording actual execution times and operation counts. Students complete a comparison table showing: array size, operations counted manually vs. programmatically, execution time, and space usage observations. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Each pair analyzes their data to identify patterns, noting which algorithm performs better under different conditions (nearly sorted, reverse sorted, random). They must write a brief conclusion explaining why performance differs and predict behavior on larger datasets.
materials_needed: Pre-written Python files containing bubble sort and merge sort implementations with operation counters
Algorithm tracing worksheets with columns for step number, array state, operations performed, and notes
Computers with Python 3.x and timing library access
Calculator for manual complexity calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed tracing worksheets for accuracy (40 points), comparison table completeness and data accuracy (30 points), and written analysis quality showing clear understanding of algorithmic differences (30 points). Success criteria: correctly traced at least 80% of algorithm steps, accurately recorded performance data for all test cases, and provided logical explanations for performance differences with specific examples.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed trace tables with some steps filled in, offer smaller arrays [3, 1, 4] for initial practice, and pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: challenge them to analyze quicksort as a third algorithm, calculate theoretical vs. actual complexity ratios, or modify algorithms to track memory usage patterns alongside time complexity.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different machine learning models' effectiveness for predicting customer churn using real business data. They will evaluate model performance using multiple metrics, assess business impact, and make evidence-based recommendations for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different machine learning algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, business constraints, and implementation feasibility
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic comparison of accuracy, interpretability, and operational requirements
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a customer churn dataset (10,000+ records) and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression, each with different performance characteristics. Students have 15 minutes to examine the dataset structure and business context. Next, allocate 45 minutes for teams to systematically evaluate each model using the provided evaluation framework: (1) Calculate and interpret performance metrics including precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and business-specific metrics like false positive cost ($50 per customer) and false negative cost ($200 lost revenue per churned customer); (2) Assess model interpretability requirements given that marketing teams need to understand prediction reasoning; (3) Evaluate computational requirements and deployment constraints including prediction latency (<100ms) and model retraining frequency. During the next 30 minutes, teams complete a comprehensive model comparison matrix, weighing trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and operational feasibility. Each team then prepares a 10-minute presentation defending their recommended model choice. Conclude with 20 minutes of presentations where teams present their analysis, defend their recommendations against peer questions, and justify why their chosen model best serves the business objectives. Emphasize that there's no single 'correct' answer - evaluation quality and reasoning depth matter most.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset with 10,000+ records (CSV format)
Three pre-trained models with saved predictions and probability scores
Model evaluation framework template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Business context document with cost parameters and deployment requirements
Jupyter notebooks with model performance calculation code
Presentation template for final recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Quantitative Analysis (25%) - accuracy of metric calculations and appropriate metric selection; (2) Critical Thinking (30%) - depth of trade-off analysis and consideration of business constraints; (3) Evidence-Based Reasoning (25%) - quality of justification for model recommendation using data; (4) Communication (20%) - clarity of presentation and ability to defend decisions under questioning.
