Students must submit their completed evaluation matrix and deliver a convincing oral presentation to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated confusion matrices and guided questions about interpreting each metric. Offer a decision tree template to structure their trade-off analysis. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as fairness metrics across customer segments, A/B testing design considerations, or cost-benefit analysis incorporating model maintenance expenses. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers within teams.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Predicting Traffic Flow Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical model combining calculus, statistics, and operations research to optimize traffic flow at a complex intersection. They will develop both the theoretical framework and a computational implementation, then validate their model against real traffic data.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from differential equations, probability theory, and optimization to construct a comprehensive traffic flow model that accounts for variable arrival rates and signal timing
Students will develop and implement a novel algorithm through computational methods to solve their optimization problem and present defendable recommendations for traffic management
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, each assigned specific roles: lead modeler, data analyst, programmer, and presentation coordinator. Provide each team with the intersection layout diagram and 48 hours of traffic count data from the city transportation department. Students start by analyzing the raw data to identify patterns in vehicle arrival rates, peak hours, and directional flows (45 minutes). Next, teams must formulate their mathematical model by defining variables (traffic density ρ, flow rate q, signal phases), establishing relationships using differential equations for traffic flow dynamics, incorporating stochastic elements for arrival distributions, and setting up optimization constraints for signal timing (90 minutes). Teams then implement their model computationally using Python or MATLAB, creating functions for traffic simulation, optimization algorithms, and visualization tools (120 minutes). Following implementation, students validate their model by comparing predictions against reserved test data, calculating error metrics, and refining parameters as needed (60 minutes). Each team prepares a comprehensive presentation including problem statement, mathematical derivation, computational methodology, validation results, and practical recommendations for the city traffic department. During presentations (20 minutes per team), other teams serve as peer reviewers, asking technical questions about model assumptions, mathematical rigor, and real-world applicability. Conclude with teams submitting their complete mathematical documentation, commented code, validation analysis, and a executive summary suitable for municipal traffic engineers.
materials_needed: Real traffic count data from local transportation department (48-hour dataset)
Detailed intersection layout diagrams with lane configurations and signal positions
Computers with Python/MATLAB software and optimization libraries (SciPy, CVX)
Graphing materials for initial data exploration and model sketching
Access to academic databases for traffic flow research papers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a detailed rubric (100 points total): Mathematical rigor and originality of model formulation (25 points), computational implementation quality and documentation (25 points), validation methodology and statistical analysis (20 points), practical applicability and recommendations (15 points), presentation clarity and ability to defend technical decisions (15 points). Students must also submit peer evaluation forms rating other teams' mathematical approaches and provide written feedback on model assumptions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structures, suggest starting with simplified single-lane models before expanding to full intersections, and offer office hours for mathematical concept review. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like pedestrian crossings, emergency vehicle priority, or adaptive signal timing, and encourage exploration of machine learning integration for dynamic parameter adjustment.

title: Binary Number System Flash Card Drill with Visual Verification
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-31 through systematic flash card practice. They will use visual binary blocks to verify their answers and reinforce memory patterns through repetitive recall exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-31 from memory within 5 seconds per number
Students will identify the decimal value of 5-bit binary numbers through flash card recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash cards with decimal numbers 0-31 on one side and their 5-bit binary equivalents on the reverse. Have students work in pairs, with Partner A holding the deck and Partner B as the respondent. Start with numbers 0-15 for the first 10 minutes. Partner A shows a decimal number (e.g., '13'), and Partner B must state the binary equivalent ('01101') within 5 seconds. If incorrect or too slow, Partner A shows the answer and places the card in a 'review' pile. Correct answers go in a 'mastered' pile. After 10 minutes, switch roles and continue with the same number range. For the next 15 minutes, expand to include numbers 16-31, maintaining the same process. During the final 10 minutes, reverse the activity: show binary numbers and have students recall decimal equivalents. Throughout the activity, students should use the provided binary place-value chart (16-8-4-2-1) as reference only when stuck for more than 5 seconds. Encourage students to visualize the binary pattern rather than calculating each time. Track progress by counting cards in each pile. Students must achieve 80% accuracy (24+ correct out of 32) before moving to the next phase.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flash cards with decimal numbers 0-31 and 5-bit binary equivalents
Binary place-value reference chart (16-8-4-2-1 headers)
Timer or stopwatch
Progress tracking sheets for each pair
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly recalling binary equivalents for 26+ decimal numbers (0-31) within 5 seconds each during a final individual quiz. Assessment includes both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal recall. Record accuracy percentage and average response time per student.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with numbers 0-15 only and provide highlighting on the place-value chart. Allow 8-10 seconds initially, then reduce to 5 seconds. For advanced learners, extend to 6-bit numbers (0-63) or include negative numbers using two's complement representation. Consider adding pattern recognition discussions (powers of 2, doubling patterns).

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Marketing Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a marketing campaign dataset to distinguish between correlation and causation by examining relationships between advertising spend, website traffic, and sales conversions. They will identify misleading correlations and explain why certain relationships do not imply causation using statistical evidence and logical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing at least three variable relationships in a marketing dataset and providing written explanations for each distinction
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots to identify spurious relationships through guided analysis of confounding variables
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded marketing dataset containing 500 records with variables: monthly_ad_spend, website_visits, email_opens, social_media_engagement, sales_conversions, and seasonal_index. In pairs, students spend 10 minutes exploring the dataset using provided correlation matrix and scatter plot visualizations. Next, assign each pair one of six specific variable relationships to investigate: (1) ad_spend vs sales_conversions, (2) website_visits vs sales_conversions, (3) email_opens vs social_media_engagement, (4) seasonal_index vs sales_conversions, (5) website_visits vs email_opens, and (6) ad_spend vs social_media_engagement. Students calculate Pearson correlation coefficients using provided calculators and examine corresponding scatter plots for 15 minutes. Then, each pair completes a structured analysis worksheet asking: 'What is the correlation coefficient?', 'Describe the relationship strength', 'Does this relationship suggest causation? Why or why not?', and 'What confounding variables might explain this relationship?'. After 20 minutes of analysis, pairs present their findings in 3-minute presentations to the class. During presentations, other students use a peer evaluation form to identify whether presenters correctly distinguished correlation from causation. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where instructor highlights common misconceptions and reinforces key concepts using student examples. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are interpreting statistical outputs correctly and guide them toward considering alternative explanations for observed relationships.
materials_needed: Marketing dataset CSV file with 500 records pre-loaded on student computers
Correlation matrix printouts for each student pair
Scatter plot visualizations (6 different plots per pair)
Structured analysis worksheet (1 per pair)
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Calculators or spreadsheet software access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) correctly identifies correlation strength AND provides accurate causation assessment with valid alternative explanations; (3) correctly identifies correlation AND causation assessment with minor gaps in reasoning; (2) identifies correlation but shows confusion about causation implications; (1) demonstrates minimal understanding of either correlation or causation concepts. Additionally, assess 3-minute presentations for clear communication of correlation vs causation distinction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide correlation coefficient interpretation guide (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong) and sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests...' and 'However, causation is unlikely because...'. For advanced learners: introduce concepts of partial correlation analysis and challenge them to identify potential mediating variables or suggest controlled experiments that could test causation hypotheses.

title: Optimization Portfolio: Real-World Applications of Linear Programming
description: Students apply linear programming techniques to solve authentic business optimization problems by analyzing constraints, formulating objective functions, and interpreting graphical solutions. They will work with three distinct scenarios: manufacturing resource allocation, transportation logistics, and investment portfolio optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to model complex real-world optimization problems by translating business constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement graphical solution techniques to determine optimal solutions through systematic analysis of feasible regions and corner point evaluation
instructions: Begin by distributing three optimization scenarios (15 minutes): Scenario A - A furniture company with limited wood, labor, and machine time producing chairs and tables; Scenario B - A shipping company minimizing transportation costs between warehouses and retail locations; Scenario C - An investment firm maximizing returns while meeting risk tolerance constraints. Students work in pairs to select one scenario and spend 20 minutes identifying decision variables, constraints, and objective functions. Next, students formulate their mathematical model (25 minutes) by writing the objective function and all constraint inequalities, including non-negativity constraints. They must clearly define variables with units and verify their model with their partner. During the graphical solution phase (35 minutes), students plot constraint lines on coordinate planes, identify the feasible region, and locate corner points. They evaluate the objective function at each corner point to determine the optimal solution. Students then spend 15 minutes interpreting their results in business context, calculating maximum profit/minimum cost, and explaining what the optimal values mean practically. Finally, pairs prepare a 3-minute presentation (10 minutes preparation) summarizing their problem, mathematical model, solution method, and business recommendations.
materials_needed: Three detailed business scenario handouts with specific numerical data
Graphing paper (at least 4 sheets per student)
Colored pencils or markers for constraint line identification
Scientific calculators
Ruler and straightedge for precise graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct mathematical model formulation (25 points) - proper variable definition, accurate constraint writing, appropriate objective function; (2) Accurate graphical solution (25 points) - correct constraint plotting, feasible region identification, corner point calculation; (3) Solution interpretation (25 points) - meaningful business context explanation, practical recommendations; (4) Mathematical communication (25 points) - clear presentation, proper notation, logical reasoning flow.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint identification templates and step-by-step graphing checklists. Offer pre-drawn coordinate grids with appropriate scales. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis questions asking how solutions change with modified constraint values, or provide scenarios requiring slack/surplus variable analysis.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Customer Purchase Patterns
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same e-commerce dataset to determine which best communicates customer purchasing trends. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and actionability of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, scatter plots, and heat maps by applying specific visualization criteria to customer purchase data
Students will critique data visualization choices through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by providing students with three visualizations of identical customer purchase data: a bar chart showing purchases by age group, a scatter plot of age vs. purchase amount, and a heat map displaying purchase patterns by day/hour. Give students 10 minutes to individually examine each visualization. Next, introduce the evaluation framework with four criteria: clarity (Can you understand the message within 10 seconds?), accuracy (Does the visualization honestly represent the data?), completeness (What important information might be missing?), and business value (How actionable are the insights?). Have students work in pairs for 20 minutes to score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, documenting specific evidence for their scores. During this phase, circulate to ensure students are citing concrete examples like 'the heat map's color legend is confusing' or 'the bar chart clearly shows millennials spend most.' For the final 15 minutes, each pair presents their top-ranked visualization to another pair, defending their choice with specific evidence from their evaluation. Students must address one weakness in their chosen visualization and suggest one concrete improvement. Conclude with pairs submitting a one-page evaluation summary ranking all three visualizations with justified reasoning for each criterion score.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of customer purchase data (one bar chart, one scatter plot, one heat map)
Evaluation criteria handout with 1-5 scoring rubric
Timer for activity segments
Blank evaluation worksheets for scoring
assessment_method: Grade the one-page evaluation summary using a rubric: appropriate use of evaluation criteria (25 points), specific evidence cited for scores (25 points), clear ranking with justification (25 points), identification of weaknesses and improvements (25 points). Success requires scoring 80+ points with evidence-based reasoning for all visualization rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'One weakness I notice is...' For advanced learners, add a fifth criterion about audience appropriateness and have them redesign the weakest visualization with specific improvements.

title: Design Your Dream Theme Park: A Mathematical Blueprint Project
description: Students will create a scaled blueprint of an original theme park using coordinate geometry, area calculations, and budget constraints. They will apply multiple mathematical concepts to design rides, pathways, and facilities while justifying their design choices through mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original theme park layout by applying coordinate geometry, scale factors, and area calculations to create a mathematically accurate blueprint
Students will construct a comprehensive budget analysis through percentage calculations, unit rates, and algebraic expressions to justify their design decisions
instructions:
Begin by distributing grid paper and project requirements sheet to each student (15 minutes setup). Explain that students will design a theme park on a 20cm x 20cm grid where each square represents 5 meters in real life. Students must include: 5 rides (each occupying 15-30 grid squares), 3 food courts (10 squares each), 2 gift shops (8 squares each), pathways connecting all areas (2 squares wide), and a parking lot (minimum 100 squares). 

Day 1 (45 minutes): Students sketch initial designs and calculate total areas for each component. They must use coordinate pairs to mark key locations and demonstrate understanding of scale by converting grid measurements to real-world dimensions. 

Day 2 (45 minutes): Students refine blueprints and create a budget spreadsheet. Provide cost parameters: rides cost $2.5 million per grid square, food courts cost $1.8 million per square, gift shops cost $2.2 million per square, pathways cost $0.5 million per square, parking costs $0.3 million per square. Students calculate total project costs and must stay within a $300 million budget. 

Day 3 (30 minutes): Students prepare presentations including their final blueprint, area calculations showing work, coordinate locations of major features, budget breakdown with percentages of total cost per category, and written justification (200 words) explaining how mathematical constraints influenced their design decisions. Each student presents for 3-4 minutes, displaying their blueprint and highlighting one mathematical challenge they overcame.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, minimum 20x20 grid per student)
Colored pencils or markers for blueprints
Calculators
Project requirements handout with cost parameters
Rulers for precise measurements
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Blueprint accuracy and scale usage (25 points), Area calculations with shown work (25 points), Budget calculations and constraint adherence (25 points), Written justification demonstrating mathematical reasoning (15 points), Presentation clarity and mathematical vocabulary usage (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn park perimeters and require only 3 rides instead of 5. Offer calculation templates and check work after each component. For advanced learners: Add constraints like minimum distance requirements between certain features using distance formula, incorporate geometric shapes beyond rectangles, or require profit projections using linear equations based on visitor capacity calculations.

title: Interpreting Advanced A/B Test Results with Multiple Confounding Variables and Statistical Nuances
description: Students will analyze a complex A/B test dataset containing multiple confounding variables, statistical anomalies, and business constraints to demonstrate deep understanding of experimental design principles and statistical interpretation. They will identify why standard statistical significance metrics may be misleading and explain the business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between statistical significance and practical significance by analyzing A/B test results with small effect sizes but large sample sizes
Students will explain how confounding variables (seasonality, user segments, geographic differences) affect experimental validity through systematic analysis of multi-dimensional test data
instructions: Step 1 (15 mins): Provide students with a synthetic e-commerce A/B test dataset containing 500,000 observations with variables: user_id, variant (A/B), conversion_rate, revenue_per_user, signup_date, geographic_region, device_type, and previous_purchases. Include deliberate confounders: Variant B users have 15% more mobile traffic and 20% more international users. Step 2 (25 mins): Students work in pairs to perform initial statistical analysis using Python/R, calculating basic metrics (conversion rates, confidence intervals, p-values). They must document their process in a Jupyter notebook. Step 3 (30 mins): Students identify and quantify confounding variables by creating segmented analyses across device types, regions, and user history. They should discover the mobile/international bias and calculate Simpson's Paradox effects. Step 4 (20 mins): Students interpret business implications by writing a 300-word executive summary explaining why the 0.3% conversion lift (p<0.001) may not justify implementation costs of $50K, considering the confounding factors and 95% confidence interval of [0.1%, 0.5%]. Step 5 (15 mins): Pairs present their findings to another pair, defending their interpretation of statistical vs. practical significance. Step 6 (10 mins): Class discussion on how sample size inflation can create misleading statistical significance in business contexts.
materials_needed: Synthetic A/B test dataset (CSV format, 500K rows) with embedded confounding variables
Jupyter Notebook environment with Python pandas, scipy.stats, and matplotlib libraries
Executive summary template with business context and cost information
Statistical analysis checklist including segmentation requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of all three confounding variables (25 points), (2) Accurate calculation of segmented conversion rates and confidence intervals (25 points), (3) Clear explanation of statistical vs. practical significance with specific numerical justification (25 points), (4) Business recommendation that appropriately weighs statistical findings against implementation costs and confounders (25 points). Students must achieve 80+ points to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions about what variables might differ between groups and a template for segmented analysis. Offer pre-calculated confidence intervals if statistical computation is challenging. For advanced learners: Include additional complexities like time-series effects, multiple testing corrections, or Bayesian interpretation. Challenge them to design follow-up experiments that would eliminate identified confounders.

title: Real-World Percentage Problem Solver: Planning a Birthday Party Budget
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to solve realistic budget planning scenarios for a birthday party. They will calculate discounts, tips, tax, and determine final costs while staying within a given budget constraint.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discounts, tax, and tips by solving multi-step real-world budget problems
Students will demonstrate percentage problem-solving skills through creating and justifying a complete party budget plan
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Birthday Party Budget Challenge' worksheet and calculators to each student. Present the scenario: 'You have $200 to plan a birthday party for 8 people. You must purchase decorations, food, and entertainment while applying various percentage calculations.' 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students read through the price list provided, which includes original prices for party supplies, food items, and activities. Explain that they must calculate final costs after applying given percentages for discounts, sales tax (8.5%), and service tips (15% for catered items).

Step 2 (15 minutes): Working individually, students select items from each category (decorations, food, entertainment) and calculate the actual cost after discounts. For example: balloons originally $12 with 20% off, pizza for 8 people at $45 with 15% tip required.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students calculate 8.5% sales tax on applicable items (excluding services) and add this to their running total. They must show all calculation steps using the percentage formula: (percentage/100) × original amount.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students create their final budget summary, listing each item, original price, percentage applied, calculated amount, and final cost. They must verify their total does not exceed $200.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Pair students to compare budgets and verify each other's percentage calculations. Partners check work using the formula and identify any calculation errors.

Conclude with students presenting one item's complete calculation process to demonstrate their percentage application skills.
materials_needed: Birthday Party Budget Challenge worksheet with price list and percentage scenarios
Basic calculators (one per student)
Pencils and scratch paper
Answer verification checklist for peer review
assessment_method: Students submit completed budget worksheets showing all percentage calculations with work displayed. Grade using 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with clear work shown, budget under $200; (3) Minor calculation errors, process clear; (2) Some correct calculations, unclear work; (1) Major errors or incomplete work. Observe during peer verification for understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage calculation reference card with formulas and examples. Allow use of percentage charts or visual fraction models. For advanced learners: Add compound percentage scenarios (discount then tax) or require comparison of multiple budget options with cost-per-person analysis.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis Through Execution Plan Comparison
description: Students analyze the performance characteristics of different SQL queries by examining execution plans and identifying bottlenecks. They will compare multiple query approaches for the same data retrieval task and determine which implementation is most efficient based on concrete metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze query execution plans by identifying join types, index usage, and cost estimates to determine performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate multiple SQL query implementations through systematic comparison of execution statistics and resource utilization
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a sample database containing three tables: Customers (50,000 records), Orders (200,000 records), and OrderItems (500,000 records). Distribute the Query Analysis Worksheet containing four different SQL queries that retrieve the same business result: total sales per customer in 2023. Query A uses nested subqueries, Query B uses multiple JOINs, Query C uses window functions, and Query D uses a combination of CTEs and JOINs.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to execute each query and capture the execution plan using the database management system's explain plan feature. They record execution time, logical reads, and CPU usage for each query.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the execution plan diagrams, students identify the most expensive operations (table scans, sorts, hash joins) and calculate the percentage cost of each major operation within each query. They document which indexes are being used or ignored.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students create a comparison matrix documenting execution time, resource usage, and complexity metrics for all four queries. They rank queries from most to least efficient based on quantitative data.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each pair presents their findings to another pair, justifying their efficiency ranking with specific evidence from execution plans. They must explain why certain operations are more costly and propose one optimization strategy for the worst-performing query.

Provide the Performance Analysis Template for consistent data collection and ensure all students use the same database instance to maintain result validity.
materials_needed: Pre-populated sample database with Customers, Orders, and OrderItems tables
Query Analysis Worksheet with four SQL variants
Performance Analysis Template spreadsheet
Database management system with execution plan visualization (PostgreSQL, SQL Server, or MySQL)
Computers with database client software installed
assessment_method: Grade completed Performance Analysis Templates using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all major bottlenecks and accurately ranks query efficiency with detailed justification; (3) Identifies most bottlenecks with minor errors in analysis; (2) Shows basic understanding but misses key performance factors; (1) Incomplete analysis with significant errors. Observe pair discussions for evidence of analytical reasoning about query optimization strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a sample execution plan analysis with annotations highlighting key elements to look for (scan vs seek, join algorithms, sort operations). Give them a checklist of performance indicators to examine systematically. For advanced learners, challenge them to write an optimized version of the worst-performing query and predict its execution plan before testing, or analyze the impact of missing indexes on query performance.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Pipeline Bias and Business Impact
description: Students will critically assess a complete machine learning pipeline for a hiring recommendation system, evaluating both technical performance and ethical implications. They will judge the appropriateness of model choices, data preprocessing decisions, and business deployment strategies while proposing evidence-based improvements.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the technical validity and ethical implications of machine learning model choices by analyzing performance metrics across demographic subgroups and assessing fairness constraints
Students will critique business deployment strategies for ML systems through systematic analysis of risk-benefit trade-offs and stakeholder impact assessments
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the 'TechCorp Hiring Algorithm' case study package containing: training dataset (10,000 candidate profiles), preprocessing pipeline code, three competing model implementations (Random Forest, Neural Network, Logistic Regression), validation results, and business deployment proposal. 

Step 1 (45 min): Teams conduct technical evaluation by analyzing model performance across protected characteristics (gender, race, age). Students must calculate disparate impact ratios, equalized odds, and demographic parity metrics for each model. They document findings in evaluation matrices and identify which model exhibits the least bias.

Step 2 (30 min): Teams evaluate data preprocessing decisions by examining feature selection, encoding methods, and handling of missing values. Students assess whether preprocessing steps introduce or amplify bias, particularly around proxy variables for protected characteristics.

Step 3 (45 min): Teams critique the business deployment strategy by analyzing the proposed implementation timeline, monitoring systems, human-in-the-loop processes, and appeal mechanisms. Students evaluate risk mitigation strategies and assess whether proposed safeguards adequately protect against discriminatory outcomes.

Step 4 (30 min): Teams synthesize findings into recommendation reports ranking the three models with detailed justifications. Reports must address technical performance, fairness metrics, business viability, and regulatory compliance considerations.

Step 5 (40 min): Teams present 8-minute evaluations to the class, defending their model selection and deployment recommendations. Other teams provide peer evaluations using structured critique forms focusing on evidence quality, reasoning validity, and consideration of stakeholder impacts.
materials_needed: TechCorp Hiring Algorithm case study package with synthetic dataset (CSV format)
Python/R environment with fairness evaluation libraries (fairlearn, aequitas)
Jupyter notebooks with bias detection templates
Business impact assessment framework handout
Peer evaluation rubric forms
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Technical Analysis Quality (30%) - accuracy of bias calculations, appropriate use of fairness metrics, valid statistical interpretations; (2) Critical Reasoning (35%) - depth of evaluation criteria, quality of evidence-based arguments, consideration of trade-offs; (3) Business Impact Assessment (25%) - realistic stakeholder analysis, practical implementation considerations, regulatory awareness; (4) Communication & Defense (10%) - clear presentation, effective response to peer challenges, professional delivery. Minimum passing requires demonstrating at least 3 different fairness metrics and providing quantitative evidence for all major claims.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide bias calculation templates with partially completed examples, offer guided questions for each evaluation step, and allow extended time for technical analysis. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity with intersectional bias analysis, cost-benefit modeling with different fairness constraints, or evaluation of algorithmic recourse mechanisms. Consider providing real-world case studies of ML bias incidents for additional context.

title: Design and Validate a Multi-Variable Optimization Algorithm for Real-World Supply Chain Management
description: Students will create an original mathematical optimization algorithm to solve a complex supply chain problem involving multiple variables, constraints, and objective functions. They will develop the mathematical model, implement the algorithm, and validate its effectiveness against established methods.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, linear algebra, and optimization theory concepts by designing an original multi-variable optimization algorithm for a real-world logistics problem
Students will construct and justify a comprehensive mathematical model through systematic analysis of constraints, variables, and objective functions while validating their solution methodology
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Definition (45 minutes)** Present students with a complex supply chain scenario: A company must optimize distribution across 8 warehouses, 15 retail locations, with 3 product types, considering shipping costs, storage capacity, demand forecasting, and seasonal variations. Students work in teams of 3-4 to define their specific mathematical model. Each team must identify: decision variables (minimum 12), constraint equations (minimum 8), and objective function components. Teams document their mathematical formulation using LaTeX notation. **Phase 2: Algorithm Development (90 minutes)** Students design their optimization algorithm by selecting and adapting methods such as gradient descent, simplex method, genetic algorithms, or hybrid approaches. They must create detailed pseudocode, prove convergence properties, and establish computational complexity. Teams implement their algorithm in Python using NumPy and SciPy libraries. Code must include error handling, iteration tracking, and solution validation functions. **Phase 3: Testing and Validation (60 minutes)** Students generate test datasets with known optimal solutions to validate their algorithm. They compare performance against established optimization solvers (CPLEX or Gurobi academic versions). Teams must demonstrate their algorithm handles edge cases, constraint violations, and infeasible solutions. **Phase 4: Documentation and Presentation (45 minutes)** Each team creates a technical report (8-10 pages) documenting their mathematical model, algorithm design choices, implementation details, validation results, and computational performance analysis. Teams present 15-minute demonstrations showing their algorithm solving the supply chain problem in real-time.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib libraries installed
Jupyter Notebook environment or PyCharm IDE
Access to CPLEX or Gurobi optimization solvers (academic license)
LaTeX editor or Overleaf accounts for mathematical notation
Pre-generated supply chain datasets with varying complexity levels
Presentation software and projection capabilities
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Formulation (25 points) - correctness of variables, constraints, and objective function; Algorithm Design (25 points) - innovation, theoretical soundness, and computational efficiency; Implementation Quality (20 points) - code functionality, documentation, and error handling; Validation and Testing (15 points) - comprehensive testing approach and performance comparison; Technical Communication (15 points) - clarity of written report and oral presentation. Teams must achieve 80+ points for proficiency, with bonus points awarded for algorithmic innovations that outperform standard solvers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code structure with key function signatures, offer simplified constraint sets, and allow use of existing optimization libraries as building blocks. Supply additional tutorials on mathematical modeling techniques. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, develop parallel processing implementations, or extend to multi-objective optimization. Encourage exploration of machine learning integration for demand prediction components. Provide access to larger, more complex datasets and industrial case studies.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Data Scenarios
description: Students will analyze four different datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation, explaining the underlying mechanisms and potential confounding variables. They will interpret statistical relationships and identify what additional evidence would be needed to establish causal claims.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing scatter plots and correlation coefficients from four different real-world datasets
Students will explain the underlying mechanisms behind statistical relationships through structured interpretation frameworks and peer discussion
instructions: Begin with a 5-minute mini-lecture reviewing correlation coefficients and causation criteria. Divide students into groups of 3-4 and provide each group with printed datasets: Dataset A (ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths), Dataset B (education level vs. income), Dataset C (hours of sleep vs. test scores), and Dataset D (social media usage vs. depression scores). Each dataset includes a scatter plot, correlation coefficient, and basic descriptive statistics. Give groups 20 minutes to work through the structured analysis worksheet for all four datasets. For each dataset, students must: (1) identify the correlation strength and direction, (2) brainstorm possible causal mechanisms, (3) list potential confounding variables, (4) determine if the relationship suggests correlation only or potential causation, and (5) specify what additional data/experiments would strengthen causal claims. After group work, facilitate a 15-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents findings for one dataset. During presentations, other groups can challenge interpretations or suggest alternative explanations. Conclude with a 10-minute individual reflection where students write a paragraph explaining the key differences between correlation and causation using examples from today's activity. Circulate during group work to ensure students are using proper statistical terminology and considering multiple explanations for each relationship.
materials_needed: Four printed dataset packets with scatter plots and correlation statistics
Structured analysis worksheet with 5 interpretation questions per dataset
Whiteboard or projector for group presentations
Individual reflection handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) accurate identification of correlation strength/direction, (2) quality of proposed causal mechanisms, (3) identification of relevant confounding variables, and (4) appropriate conclusions about correlation vs. causation. Individual reflections scored for clear explanation of key concepts and relevant examples. Groups must correctly classify at least 3 of 4 datasets as correlation-only or potential causation to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with correlation interpretation guidelines (e.g., 0.7-1.0 = strong) and a checklist of common confounding variable types. For advanced learners, include a fifth dataset with non-linear relationships or provide actual research papers where they can critique the authors' causal claims. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger peers and provide sentence starters for the reflection activity.

title: Optimizing Water Distribution Network Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world water distribution optimization problem for a municipal system. They will formulate objective functions and constraints, then use the simplex method to determine optimal flow rates through a network of pipes while minimizing pumping costs.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-variable water distribution scenario into standard form with clearly defined objective functions and constraint inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic tableau operations to determine optimal flow rates and minimum cost solutions for infrastructure problems
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute presentation of the scenario: City of Riverside needs to distribute 500,000 gallons/day from 3 pumping stations to 4 districts with varying demands and pumping costs. Provide students with the data sheet containing: pumping capacities (Station A: 200k gal/day at $0.03/gal, Station B: 250k gal/day at $0.025/gal, Station C: 180k gal/day at $0.04/gal), district demands (North: 120k, South: 150k, East: 130k, West: 100k), and pipe capacity constraints between stations and districts. In pairs, students spend 15 minutes identifying decision variables (x₁ through x₁₂ representing flow rates from each station to each district). Next, 20 minutes formulating the objective function (minimize total pumping cost) and all constraints including supply limits, demand requirements, and pipe capacities. Students then convert to standard form by introducing slack variables (15 minutes). Using provided simplex tableau templates, pairs spend 45 minutes executing the simplex method: identifying entering/leaving variables, performing pivot operations, and iterating until reaching optimal solution. Students calculate final flow rates and minimum daily cost. Conclude with 10-minute presentations where each pair explains their optimal distribution strategy and justifies why their solution minimizes costs while meeting all constraints. Instructor facilitates comparison of solutions and discusses real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Water distribution scenario data sheets with pumping costs and district demands
Pre-formatted simplex tableau worksheets with designated spaces for pivot operations
Scientific calculators or Excel with Solver add-in
Network diagram templates showing stations, districts, and pipe connections
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation including all variables, objective function, and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate conversion to standard form with appropriate slack variables (20 points), (3) Proper execution of simplex method with correct pivot operations and tableau progression (35 points), (4) Valid optimal solution with correct flow rates and minimum cost calculation (20 points). Students must show all tableau iterations and justify their final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed constraint equations and highlight the pattern for setting up tableau rows. Offer a checklist for simplex method steps and allow use of online simplex calculators for verification. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how solutions change with 10% demand increases, or extend to include environmental constraints like maximum flow through sensitive areas.

title: Design Your Dream Park: Creating a Scaled Mathematical Model with Budget Constraints
description: Students will design and create a detailed scale model of a community park, applying mathematical concepts including area calculations, scaling, coordinate geometry, and budget optimization. They will synthesize multiple mathematical skills to produce an original design that meets specific constraints and real-world requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original park design by applying area calculations, scaling ratios, and coordinate geometry to produce a mathematically accurate scale model
Students will synthesize budget optimization and geometric principles through designing a functional park layout that maximizes utility within financial constraints
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: students are city planners designing a new 2.4-acre community park with a $150,000 budget (15 minutes setup). Provide teams of 3-4 students with the pricing sheet for park features and constraint requirements. Students must first research and calculate the actual dimensions of their assigned plot shape (rectangular, L-shaped, or triangular) using the given area of 2.4 acres, then determine their scale ratio for the physical model (1:500 recommended). Next, teams spend 20 minutes brainstorming features and creating a rough sketch with coordinates for each element. They then calculate costs for desired features, adjusting their design to stay within budget while maximizing park utility. Students create detailed technical drawings on coordinate grid paper, showing precise measurements and coordinates for each feature (30 minutes). Using cardboard, students construct their 3D scale model, ensuring mathematical accuracy in scaling all elements proportionally (45 minutes). Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their mathematical decisions, cost breakdown, area calculations, and design rationale. During presentations, other teams evaluate designs using the provided rubric. Conclude with a reflection discussion on how mathematical constraints influenced creative decisions and real-world applications of scaling and optimization.
materials_needed: Coordinate grid paper (1cm squares, multiple sheets per team)
Cardboard sheets (8.5x11 and larger), colored paper, scissors, glue sticks
Rulers, protractors, calculators
Park feature pricing sheet with costs per square foot
Design constraint handout specifying requirements (playground, paths, green space percentages)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area calculations and scaling (25 points), (2) Correct application of coordinate geometry in design layout (20 points), (3) Budget optimization showing all calculations and staying within constraints (25 points), (4) Quality and proportional accuracy of physical model (20 points), (5) Clear presentation explaining mathematical reasoning (10 points). Students must show all mathematical work and justify design decisions quantitatively.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated area conversion charts, offer simplified rectangular plots only, and give budget calculation templates. For advanced learners: Include additional constraints like environmental impact costs, require optimization of multiple variables simultaneously, or challenge them to design for irregular terrain with elevation changes requiring volume calculations.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Memorization and Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the seven layers of the OSI model and four layers of the TCP/IP protocol stack, including their specific functions, protocols, and data units. This activity uses structured memorization techniques and rapid-fire identification exercises to build foundational networking knowledge.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all seven OSI model layers and four TCP/IP layers with their corresponding protocols by completing timed identification exercises
Students will memorize the specific data units (bits, frames, packets, segments) and key protocols (HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet) for each layer through structured repetition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the protocol stack reference cards and setting up the digital flashcard system on student devices. Start with a 10-minute guided memorization phase where students use the mnemonic device 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for OSI layers (Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical) and 'Applications Transport Internet Network' for TCP/IP. Have students create their own mnemonic devices and share with partners. Next, conduct three rounds of progressive testing: Round 1 (15 minutes) - students work in pairs with one person showing layer names while the other recalls functions and protocols, then switch roles every 3 minutes. Round 2 (10 minutes) - individual students complete digital flashcards, cycling through all layers until they achieve 90% accuracy on two consecutive attempts. Round 3 (15 minutes) - rapid-fire team competition where teams of 4 students take turns identifying layers, protocols, and data units from instructor prompts, earning points for speed and accuracy. Conclude with a 10-minute individual written recall test where students must list all layers top-to-bottom, identify three protocols per layer, and match data units to appropriate layers without references. Monitor student progress by circulating during pair work, checking digital flashcard completion rates, and recording team competition scores for immediate feedback.
materials_needed: Protocol stack reference cards (laminated, one per student)
Digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet) pre-loaded with protocol stack content
Stopwatch or timer for timed rounds
Whiteboard and markers for team competition scoring
Individual assessment sheets with layer identification templates
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on the final individual written recall test, correctly identifying at least 6/7 OSI layers, 4/4 TCP/IP layers, 15/20 major protocols, and 4/4 data unit types. Additionally, track digital flashcard completion (must achieve 90% accuracy twice) and participation scores during pair work and team competition phases.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-made acronym cards, allow extended time for flashcard practice, and pair with stronger partners during collaboration phases. Create simplified reference sheets focusing on just the four TCP/IP layers initially. For advanced learners: add IPv6 protocols, security layer protocols (SSL/TLS), and require them to explain encapsulation/decapsulation processes at each layer. Challenge them to create alternative mnemonic devices for the class.

title: Interpreting Advanced Ensemble Model Performance Through Multi-Dimensional Bias-Variance Trade-off Analysis
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost) on a high-dimensional dataset with class imbalance. They will interpret how bias-variance decomposition affects model behavior across different data subsets and feature spaces to understand why certain ensemble methods outperform others in specific contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret bias-variance decomposition results by analyzing ensemble model performance patterns across stratified data subsets
Students will explain the relationship between ensemble hyperparameters and bias-variance trade-offs through systematic performance metric comparison
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing the Wine Quality dataset (4,898 samples, 11 features) with artificially induced class imbalance (80% low quality, 20% high quality). Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to implement three ensemble models using scikit-learn: Random Forest (n_estimators=[10,50,100]), Gradient Boosting (learning_rate=[0.01,0.1,1.0]), and AdaBoost (n_estimators=[10,50,100]). Next, spend 25 minutes having students calculate bias-variance decomposition using mlxtend library's bias_variance_decomp function on 5-fold stratified cross-validation. Students must generate performance matrices showing training error, validation error, bias², variance, and noise for each model-hyperparameter combination. During the following 30 minutes, students create visualization plots using matplotlib: (1) bias-variance trade-off curves for each ensemble method, (2) learning curves showing training/validation error convergence, and (3) feature importance heatmaps across different hyperparameter settings. For the final 25 minutes, pairs analyze their results to identify: which ensemble method shows highest bias in low-data regimes, how variance changes with ensemble size, and why certain hyperparameter combinations produce better generalization on imbalanced data. Students document their interpretations in markdown cells, explicitly connecting mathematical bias-variance concepts to observed performance patterns.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pre-installed packages
Python libraries: scikit-learn, mlxtend, matplotlib, pandas, numpy
Wine Quality dataset with induced class imbalance
Bias-variance decomposition template code
assessment_method: Evaluate student success through: (1) Accuracy of bias-variance calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of visualization plots with proper labeling and scaling (25 points), (3) Depth of written interpretation connecting theory to results (30 points), (4) Correct identification of ensemble-specific performance patterns (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining at least two specific instances where bias-variance trade-offs explain observed performance differences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-written code templates for bias-variance decomposition and offer guided questions about interpreting specific plot regions. For advanced learners: extend activity by having them implement custom ensemble methods or analyze bias-variance on additional datasets with different characteristics (text, time-series, or image data).

title: Database Schema Analysis and Optimization Challenge
description: Students will analyze poorly designed database schemas to identify normalization issues, redundancies, and performance bottlenecks. They will systematically examine relationships, dependencies, and query patterns to determine structural problems and propose specific improvements.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database schemas by identifying normalization violations, redundant data, and inefficient relationships using systematic evaluation criteria
Students will differentiate between well-designed and poorly-designed database structures through comparative analysis of multiple schema examples
instructions:
Begin by distributing three database schema diagrams representing an e-commerce system with deliberate design flaws (45 minutes total setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team one schema to analyze first. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams examine their assigned schema using the provided analysis checklist, identifying: (a) tables violating First, Second, or Third Normal Form, (b) redundant data storage, (c) missing or incorrect foreign key relationships, (d) poorly named entities/attributes, and (e) potential performance issues based on common query patterns shown.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams create a detailed findings report documenting each identified issue with specific table/field references, explaining why each problem violates database design principles, and estimating the impact on data integrity and performance.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams rotate to analyze the second schema, comparing their findings with the first. They must categorize problems by severity (critical, moderate, minor) and create a prioritized improvement plan.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Final rotation to the third schema, where teams must complete their analysis in accelerated time, demonstrating mastery of the analytical process.

Step 5 (25 minutes): Each team presents their comparative analysis findings to the class, highlighting the most critical issues across all three schemas and defending their severity rankings with specific evidence.

Conclude with a class discussion comparing team findings and reaching consensus on the most effective analytical approaches for database schema evaluation.
materials_needed: Three printed database schema diagrams (E-R diagrams) with intentional design flaws
Database design analysis checklist handout
Sample query patterns document for each schema
Whiteboard or flip chart paper for team findings
Colored markers for annotation
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of problem identification (40% - correctly identifies 80%+ of planted issues), (2) Quality of analysis reasoning (30% - provides clear explanations linking problems to design principles), (3) Comparative insights (20% - demonstrates understanding of relative severity and patterns across schemas), (4) Professional presentation (10% - clear communication with supporting evidence). Teams must achieve 3+ points in categories 1-2 to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a completed example analysis of a simple two-table schema before the activity. Create reference cards with common normalization violations and their indicators. For advanced learners, include additional challenges like analyzing indexing strategies, considering scalability implications, or proposing specific SQL DDL statements for schema corrections. Encourage advanced students to consider how schema problems would manifest in real application scenarios.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps in Customer Behavior Analysis
description: Students will analyze pre-generated correlation heatmaps from an e-commerce customer dataset to identify relationships between variables like purchase amount, browsing time, and demographics. They will interpret correlation coefficients and explain business implications of different correlation patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by identifying strong, moderate, and weak relationships in customer behavior heatmaps
Students will explain the business significance of feature correlations through structured analysis worksheets and peer discussions
instructions:
Begin by distributing printed correlation heatmaps showing relationships between 8 customer variables (age, income, browsing_time, cart_abandonment_rate, purchase_frequency, avg_purchase_amount, mobile_usage, email_clicks). Provide students with the interpretation guide showing correlation ranges: |r| > 0.7 (strong), 0.3-0.7 (moderate), < 0.3 (weak). 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine the heatmap and complete Part A of the worksheet, identifying the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, writing down the exact coefficient values.

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students complete Part B, categorizing all 28 correlations as strong/moderate/weak and discussing any surprising relationships they notice. Circulate to check their coefficient interpretations.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Groups of 4 tackle Part C, selecting 5 correlations and writing business explanations for each (e.g., 'The 0.68 correlation between income and avg_purchase_amount suggests higher-income customers tend to make larger purchases, indicating potential for premium product targeting').

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each group presents one interesting correlation finding to the class, explaining both the statistical relationship and business implication. 

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conclude with individual reflection where students identify which correlation would be most actionable for marketing strategy and justify their choice in 2-3 sentences.
materials_needed: Printed correlation heatmaps (one per student) showing 8x8 customer variable matrix
Structured analysis worksheet with Parts A-C
Correlation coefficient interpretation reference guide
Colored pens/highlighters for marking heatmaps
assessment_method: Grade worksheets using rubric: Part A - correct identification of strongest correlations (20 points), Part B - accurate categorization of correlation strength (30 points), Part C - clear business explanations linking statistical relationships to actionable insights (40 points), individual reflection quality (10 points). Students must achieve 70% to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example showing how r=0.45 between age and email_clicks represents moderate correlation with business meaning. For advanced learners, add extension questions about causation vs correlation and potential confounding variables. Consider providing simplified 5x5 heatmaps for students needing additional support.

title: Dissecting a Distributed System's Fault Tolerance: Netflix's Microservices Architecture Analysis
description: Students will analyze Netflix's microservices architecture to identify fault tolerance patterns, examine failure propagation scenarios, and evaluate the effectiveness of specific resilience mechanisms. This expert-level activity requires students to break down complex system interactions and assess architectural trade-offs in real-world distributed systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze Netflix's circuit breaker implementation by examining Hystrix code patterns and identifying failure isolation strategies within their microservices ecosystem
Students will evaluate fault tolerance mechanisms through systematic decomposition of service dependencies and failure cascade scenarios in distributed architectures
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with Netflix's public architectural documentation, Hystrix GitHub repository excerpts, and simplified service dependency graphs (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a different failure scenario: database timeout, service overload, network partition, or cascading failures. Students first spend 45 minutes mapping service interactions using provided dependency visualization tools, identifying single points of failure and analyzing data flow patterns. Next, teams examine specific code implementations of circuit breakers, bulkheads, and timeout patterns for 30 minutes, documenting how each pattern prevents failure propagation. During the analysis phase (40 minutes), students trace through their assigned failure scenario, predicting system behavior at each step and identifying which resilience mechanisms activate. Teams create detailed failure timeline diagrams showing: initial trigger, affected services, activated protection mechanisms, and system recovery paths. In the final 30 minutes, teams present their analysis to another team, defending their predictions about system behavior and critiquing the effectiveness of implemented fault tolerance strategies. Conclude with a 20-minute class discussion where teams compare findings across different failure scenarios and identify common architectural patterns.
materials_needed: Netflix architecture documentation packet (Eureka, Hystrix, Zuul components)
Hystrix code samples with circuit breaker implementations
Service dependency mapping software (Lucidchart or Draw.io accounts)
Failure scenario cards with specific technical parameters
Laptops with internet access for code repository browsing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of failure propagation analysis - correctly traces cascading effects through service dependencies, (2) Code pattern recognition - identifies and explains specific fault tolerance implementations, (3) Architectural evaluation - assesses trade-offs and alternative approaches with technical justification, (4) Scenario prediction - provides realistic system behavior predictions with supporting evidence. Students submit annotated dependency diagrams and written analysis reports.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted code sections and guided analysis templates with specific questions. Offer simplified dependency diagrams focusing on 3-4 core services rather than the full ecosystem. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by requiring cost-benefit analysis of fault tolerance mechanisms, comparison with alternative architectural patterns (event sourcing, CQRS), or design of custom resilience strategies for novel failure modes.

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Strategies for Real-World Customer Survey Data
description: Students will assess and critique different data cleaning approaches applied to a messy customer satisfaction survey dataset. They will compare the effectiveness of three pre-implemented cleaning strategies and justify which approach produces the most reliable results for business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different data cleaning methodologies by analyzing their impact on data quality metrics and business insights
Students will critique data preprocessing decisions through systematic comparison of statistical outcomes and visual representations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with the same raw customer survey dataset containing 500 responses with typical data quality issues: missing values (15%), duplicate entries (8%), inconsistent categorical responses, and obvious outliers. Give each group three pre-cleaned versions of this dataset, each processed using different strategies: Strategy A (listwise deletion for missing data, outlier removal), Strategy B (mean imputation, outlier capping), and Strategy C (predictive imputation, outlier retention). Students spend 20 minutes exploring each cleaned dataset using provided Python code templates to generate descriptive statistics, correlation matrices, and basic visualizations. Next, groups spend 30 minutes completing a structured evaluation matrix, rating each strategy on five criteria: data completeness, statistical validity, business interpretability, potential bias introduction, and computational efficiency. They must provide specific evidence from their analysis (e.g., 'Strategy A reduced sample size by 23%, potentially eliminating key customer segments'). Groups then spend 15 minutes preparing a 5-minute presentation defending their choice of best cleaning strategy. During presentations, other groups act as peer reviewers, using provided evaluation sheets to assess the quality of reasoning and evidence presented. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where groups must justify why they would recommend their chosen strategy to a business stakeholder making customer experience decisions.
materials_needed: Raw customer survey CSV file with embedded data quality issues
Three pre-cleaned versions of the dataset using different strategies
Jupyter Notebook templates with data exploration code
Structured evaluation matrix worksheet (printed or digital)
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
Access to Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Thoroughness of data analysis evidence (25%), (2) Quality of criteria-based strategy comparison (25%), (3) Logical reasoning in strategy selection (25%), and (4) Effectiveness of peer critique during presentations (25%). Students must demonstrate specific examples from their analysis and articulate trade-offs between different approaches.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed examples of two comparison criteria and highlight specific cells in the datasets to examine. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional evaluation criteria not provided, or to suggest hybrid approaches combining elements from multiple strategies. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analysts within groups.

title: Design and Build a Community Garden Budget Optimization Model
description: Students will create a comprehensive mathematical model to design an optimal community garden layout while working within budget constraints and space limitations. They will develop original linear programming solutions, create visual representations, and present their optimized designs with mathematical justification.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a linear programming model by defining variables, constraints, and objective functions for a real-world optimization problem
Students will design an original mathematical solution through systematic problem-solving, graphical analysis, and algebraic manipulation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Community Garden Challenge packet containing plot dimensions (50ft x 30ft), budget ($2,500), and crop data including costs, space requirements, and expected yields for 8 different vegetables. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 15 minutes to analyze the scenario and identify key mathematical components.

Next, guide students through defining their optimization problem (25 minutes). Each team must decide their objective function (maximize yield, minimize cost, or maximize profit), define variables for each crop type, and establish at least 5 realistic constraints including budget, space, water requirements, and seasonal limitations. Circulate to ensure teams are setting up proper mathematical notation.

During the model development phase (40 minutes), students create their linear programming system using both algebraic and graphical methods. They must plot constraint lines on coordinate planes, identify feasible regions, and calculate optimal solutions. Provide graphing paper and calculators, encouraging teams to test multiple scenarios.

For the design creation portion (30 minutes), teams translate their mathematical solution into a scaled garden layout drawing. They must show exact measurements, crop placement, and include a detailed budget breakdown that proves their solution satisfies all constraints.

Conclude with team presentations (20 minutes total, 4 minutes per team). Each team presents their garden design, explains their mathematical model, justifies their optimization choice, and demonstrates how their solution meets all requirements. Other teams ask one clarifying question per presentation.
materials_needed: Community Garden Challenge packet with crop data and constraints
Graphing paper (at least 4 sheets per student)
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils or markers for garden layout drawings
Rulers and measuring tools
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical Model Accuracy - correct variable definitions, constraints, and objective function setup (25 points), (2) Solution Quality - proper graphical analysis, feasible solution identification, and optimization calculations (25 points), (3) Design Integration - realistic garden layout that matches mathematical solution with accurate measurements and budget (25 points), (4) Presentation and Justification - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning and defense of design choices (25 points). Teams must score 70+ points to demonstrate proficiency in creating mathematical solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide constraint equation templates and offer one-on-one guidance during variable definition. Consider pairing weaker math students with stronger teammates. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as seasonal rotation planning, multiple budget scenarios, or incorporating quadratic yield functions. Encourage these students to explore sensitivity analysis of their solutions.

title: Advanced Memory Palace: Recalling 32 ARM Assembly Instructions and Their Binary Encodings
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 32 specific ARM assembly instructions along with their corresponding 32-bit binary machine code representations using the memory palace technique. This advanced recall exercise focuses on low-level computer architecture fundamentals that form the foundation for compiler design and embedded systems programming.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact 32-bit binary encoding for 32 specific ARM assembly instructions by constructing and navigating a personalized memory palace
Students will identify the precise opcode, register fields, and immediate value positions within ARM instruction formats through systematic memorization drills
instructions: Begin by providing students with a curated list of 32 ARM assembly instructions including ADD, SUB, MOV, LDR, STR, BEQ, BNE, CMP, AND, ORR, LSL, LSR, PUSH, POP, B, BL, MUL, SDIV, UDIV, ASR, ROR, EOR, BIC, MVN, TST, TEQ, CMN, ADC, SBC, RSB, RSC, and SWI, each with their specific binary encodings for a particular operand configuration. Students must first select a familiar physical location (their home, school building, or neighborhood) to serve as their memory palace. In the first 20 minutes, students map each instruction to a specific location within their chosen space, creating vivid mental associations between the location and both the mnemonic and its binary representation. For example, ADD R1, R2, R3 (binary: 11100000100000010001000000000011) might be placed at their front door, visualized as 'adding' keys to open the door while seeing the binary pattern in the door's window panes. Students spend the next 40 minutes walking through their memory palace repeatedly, both physically drawing floor plans and mentally rehearsing each location-instruction pairing. During the final 30 minutes, students test their recall by having a partner call out random room locations while they respond with both the assembly instruction and complete 32-bit binary encoding. Students must achieve 90% accuracy on both instruction mnemonics and binary codes before proceeding to peer verification, where partners quiz each other using randomized location prompts.
materials_needed: Printed reference sheet with 32 ARM assembly instructions and corresponding 32-bit binary encodings
Blank floor plan templates for mapping memory palace locations
Timer for tracking practice intervals
Answer verification sheets for peer checking
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate 29/32 correct recalls (90% accuracy) of both assembly mnemonics and complete binary encodings when randomly prompted with memory palace locations. Assessment includes: (1) Immediate verbal recall test with partner verification, (2) Written quiz matching 20 randomly selected locations to instruction-binary pairs, (3) Timed challenge requiring recall of all 32 items within 5 minutes. Full credit requires perfect binary accuracy - any bit errors result in partial credit only.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with only 16 instructions, use more familiar/simpler instructions first, allow visual aids during initial practice, and extend practice time by 15 minutes. For advanced learners: Add condition code flags and addressing mode variations, include instruction cycle counts and pipeline effects, or expand to 64 instructions including floating-point operations. Encourage creation of memorable stories connecting adjacent locations in their memory palace.

title: Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Polynomial Regression Visualization
description: Students will analyze and interpret the mathematical relationship between model complexity, bias, and variance by examining polynomial regression models of varying degrees fitted to synthetic datasets. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining how the bias-variance decomposition manifests visually in prediction intervals and loss curves.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the bias-variance tradeoff by analyzing polynomial regression models with degrees 1-15 fitted to noisy sinusoidal data and explaining the relationship between model complexity and generalization error

Students will differentiate between bias and variance components through visual analysis of prediction confidence intervals and mathematical decomposition of mean squared error across multiple bootstrap samples
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with a Jupyter notebook containing pre-generated synthetic dataset: y = sin(2πx) + ε where x ∈ [0,1] and ε ~ N(0,0.3²), with 50 training points and 100 test points. Students work individually for the first 45 minutes, then form pairs for discussion.

Step 1 (15 min): Students fit polynomial regression models of degrees 1, 3, 6, 9, 12, and 15 to the training data using scikit-learn's PolynomialFeatures and LinearRegression. They plot each fitted model alongside the true function and training data.

Step 2 (20 min): For each polynomial degree, students generate 100 bootstrap samples from the training set and fit models to each sample. They calculate and plot the mean prediction and 95% confidence intervals across all bootstrap models for each degree, creating six separate visualization panels.

Step 3 (10 min): Students compute the bias²(x), variance(x), and irreducible error components at 20 evenly spaced test points for each model degree using the bootstrap predictions. They create line plots showing how each component changes with model complexity.
