Step 4 (20 min): In pairs, students write a 300-word interpretation comparing the d=1 (underfit) and d=15 (overfit) models, specifically explaining: (a) why high-bias models show narrow confidence intervals but poor fit, (b) why high-variance models show wide confidence intervals despite appearing to fit training data well, and (c) how the optimal degree (around d=6) balances these components.

Step 5 (15 min): Each pair presents one key insight to the class, focusing on a specific aspect of the bias-variance relationship they observed in their analysis.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Pre-configured notebook with synthetic dataset and plotting templates
scikit-learn, numpy, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries installed
Individual laptops or computer lab access
assessment_method: Grade the 300-word written interpretation using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly explains both bias and variance concepts with specific reference to their plots and numerical results; (3) Explains one concept thoroughly with plot evidence; (2) Shows basic understanding but lacks connection to their specific results; (1) Demonstrates misconceptions about bias-variance relationship. Additionally, evaluate the accuracy of their bias² and variance calculations at three randomly selected test points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed interpretation template with sentence starters like 'The d=1 model shows high bias because...' and 'I can see high variance in the d=15 model when...'. For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them repeat the analysis with different noise levels (σ = 0.1, 0.5) and compare how the optimal complexity changes, or implement the bias-variance decomposition for classification using logistic regression on a binary dataset.

title: Personal Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Expenses
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a young adult scenario using percentage calculations to allocate income across different expense categories. They will apply percentage increase/decrease concepts to adjust their budget based on changing financial circumstances.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by calculating specific dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and savings categories
Students will demonstrate percentage increase and decrease concepts through budget adjustment scenarios involving salary changes and expense modifications
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario cards and budget worksheets to each student (5 minutes). Each student receives a different young adult profile with a specific monthly income ($2,400-$3,600). Display the recommended budget percentages on the board: Housing 30%, Food 15%, Transportation 12%, Entertainment 8%, Savings 10%, Utilities 8%, Miscellaneous 17%. Students first calculate the dollar amount for each category by applying these percentages to their assigned income (15 minutes). They must show their work using the formula: (percentage ÷ 100) × total income = category amount. Next, present three budget adjustment scenarios on slides: 1) 8% salary increase, 2) 15% rent increase, 3) 20% reduction in entertainment spending. For each scenario, students recalculate affected categories and adjust others to maintain a balanced budget (20 minutes). Students must identify which percentage calculations to use (increase: original × 1.08; decrease: original × 0.85) and show all mathematical steps. Have students pair up to verify each other's calculations and discuss their budget decisions (10 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where 3-4 students present their final budgets and explain how percentage changes affected their overall financial plan (10 minutes). Students submit their completed worksheet showing all percentage calculations and final budget allocations.
materials_needed: Young adult scenario cards (12 different profiles with varying incomes)
Personal Budget Calculation worksheets (one per student)
Calculators
Pencils and erasers
Whiteboard or projector for displaying percentage guidelines
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage calculations correct with work shown, realistic budget allocations, accurate adjustment calculations; (3) Most calculations correct with minor errors, logical budget decisions; (2) Some calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of percentage application; (1) Multiple errors or incomplete work. Check for proper use of percentage formulas, accurate decimal/percentage conversions, and reasonable budget adjustments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a percentage calculation reference sheet with step-by-step examples and allow use of calculators throughout. Consider pairing them with stronger math students during verification activity. For advanced learners: Add a fourth scenario involving compound percentage changes (salary increase followed by expense increase) or ask them to create their own realistic scenario with supporting calculations. Provide annual budget conversion challenge (monthly × 12) with tax implications.

title: Evaluating Machine Learning Model Performance for Credit Risk Assessment Using Cross-Industry Standards
description: Students will critically evaluate three different machine learning models (logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting) trained on credit risk data by analyzing performance metrics, business impact, and regulatory compliance. They will defend their model selection through a comprehensive evaluation report addressing technical accuracy, interpretability, and real-world implementation feasibility.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning models by comparing performance metrics, interpretability, and business applicability in a credit risk scenario
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic analysis of bias, fairness, regulatory compliance, and deployment considerations
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-trained models (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting) and a holdout test dataset of 5,000 credit applications with known outcomes. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to generate predictions and calculate performance metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices for each model. Next, spend 30 minutes having teams analyze feature importance and model interpretability using SHAP values or similar explainability tools. Students then spend 25 minutes researching and applying fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds) across protected characteristics like age and gender. Following this technical analysis, dedicate 30 minutes to evaluating business considerations: false positive costs ($500 per rejected good customer), false negative costs ($5,000 per accepted bad customer), model training/maintenance costs, and regulatory requirements (GDPR, Fair Credit Reporting Act). Teams spend 35 minutes creating a comprehensive evaluation matrix weighing technical performance (40%), interpretability (25%), fairness (20%), and business viability (15%). Finally, allocate 40 minutes for teams to prepare and deliver 8-minute presentations defending their recommended model choice, followed by 2 minutes of peer questioning. Conclude with 10 minutes of instructor-led discussion comparing team recommendations and highlighting key evaluation trade-offs.
materials_needed: Pre-trained models saved as pickle files (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting)
Credit risk dataset (CSV format) with 15 features and binary target variable
Jupyter notebook templates with performance metric calculation functions
SHAP or LIME explainability library installed
Fairness evaluation toolkit (AIF360 or Fairlearn)
Presentation slides template with evaluation criteria framework
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Technical analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation and interpretation of all performance metrics; Fairness evaluation (20 points) - proper application of bias detection methods and interpretation; Business impact analysis (25 points) - realistic cost-benefit calculations and regulatory consideration; Model recommendation justification (20 points) - logical defense of choice with evidence-based reasoning; Presentation quality (10 points) - clear communication and response to peer questions. Students must achieve 80+ points to demonstrate mastery of model evaluation at the advanced level.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing metric calculation templates and guided questions for business impact analysis. Offer pre-calculated SHAP values if explainability library installation fails. For advanced learners, introduce additional evaluation dimensions like model robustness testing, adversarial examples, or multi-objective optimization frameworks. Provide extension activities involving ensemble model creation or hyperparameter sensitivity analysis.

title: Design and Defend a Novel Optimization Algorithm for Multi-Variable Real-World Problems
description: Students will create an original optimization algorithm that combines existing mathematical techniques (gradient descent, genetic algorithms, simulated annealing) to solve a complex multi-variable problem of their choice. They will mathematically justify their approach, implement it computationally, and present their methodology to peers for critique and validation.
estimated_duration: 8 weeks (approximately 40-50 hours total student work time)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multiple optimization techniques by designing a hybrid algorithm that addresses specific problem constraints and variables
Students will construct mathematical proofs and computational implementations through iterative testing and refinement of their novel approach
Students will evaluate and defend their algorithm's effectiveness by comparing performance metrics against established optimization methods
instructions: **Phase 1 (Week 1-2):** Students select a real-world optimization problem with 5+ variables (portfolio optimization, supply chain logistics, neural network training, resource allocation). They research existing solutions and identify 2-3 mathematical optimization techniques to potentially combine. Students submit a 2-page problem statement with mathematical formulation including objective function, constraints, and variable definitions. **Phase 2 (Week 3-4):** Students design their hybrid algorithm by mathematically justifying why their combination addresses specific weaknesses in individual methods. They create detailed pseudocode, prove convergence conditions, and establish theoretical time/space complexity bounds. Deliverable: 8-10 page mathematical framework document with formal proofs. **Phase 3 (Week 5-6):** Implementation phase using Python/MATLAB/R where students code their algorithm and test against benchmark datasets. They must include error handling, parameter tuning mechanisms, and performance logging. Students run comparative analysis against at least 2 established algorithms using identical test cases. **Phase 4 (Week 7):** Students prepare 20-minute presentations including: problem motivation (3 min), mathematical foundation (8 min), implementation details (4 min), results comparison (3 min), limitations discussion (2 min). Peer review sessions where students formally critique others' approaches using provided evaluation rubrics. **Phase 5 (Week 8):** Students revise algorithms based on peer feedback, submit final implementation with documentation, and write reflection papers analyzing what they learned about optimization theory and algorithm design.
materials_needed: Access to computational software (Python with NumPy/SciPy, MATLAB, or R)
Benchmark optimization datasets from UCI Machine Learning Repository or similar
Academic database access for research papers on optimization algorithms
Presentation software and classroom projection system
Peer evaluation rubrics for algorithmic assessment
assessment_method: Grading rubric (100 points total): Mathematical rigor and proof correctness (25 points), Algorithm novelty and theoretical justification (25 points), Implementation quality and computational efficiency (20 points), Comparative analysis and statistical validation (15 points), Presentation clarity and peer review participation (15 points). Students must achieve convergent results, demonstrate improvement over baseline methods in at least one metric (speed, accuracy, or memory), and receive passing scores from 3+ peer reviewers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template problem formulations, guided tutorials on optimization fundamentals, and partner them with stronger peers for code review. Offer pre-selected, well-documented problems with existing solution frameworks. For advanced learners: Encourage multi-objective optimization problems, require formal complexity analysis proofs, challenge them to publish-quality documentation, or have them mentor struggling peers. Provide access to advanced optimization literature and suggest novel problem domains.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Production Costs Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques and linear programming constraints to solve a real-world manufacturing cost minimization problem. They will determine optimal production quantities for multiple product lines while considering resource limitations, labor costs, and material constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to minimize production costs by finding critical points in a multi-variable cost function
Students will implement linear programming constraints through systematic algebraic manipulation to determine feasible production regions
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario worksheet describing TechCorp's manufacturing dilemma: producing smartphones (x units) and tablets (y units) with cost function C(x,y) = 0.002x² + 0.003y² + 150x + 200y + 5xy, subject to constraints: 2x + 3y ≤ 1200 (labor hours), x + y ≤ 500 (warehouse capacity), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Form teams of 3-4 students for 90 minutes of collaborative problem-solving. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams calculate partial derivatives ∂C/∂x and ∂C/∂y, then find critical points by setting both equal to zero. Step 2 (25 minutes): Apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to incorporate the inequality constraints, setting up the system: ∇C = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ where g₁ and g₂ represent the constraint functions. Step 3 (25 minutes): Graph the feasible region on coordinate planes, identifying corner points and boundary intersections using algebraic substitution. Step 4 (15 minutes): Evaluate the cost function at all critical points and boundary intersections to determine the absolute minimum. Step 5 (5 minutes): Teams present their optimal solution (x*, y*, minimum cost) with justification. Circulate during work time to check mathematical accuracy and guide teams toward correct application of optimization techniques.
materials_needed: TechCorp Manufacturing Scenario Worksheet (1 per student)
Graphing calculators or Desmos graphing software access
Grid paper for constraint graphing
Scientific calculators for numerical computations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation of partial derivatives and critical points (25%), (2) Proper setup and solution of Lagrangian system (30%), (3) Accurate identification of feasible region and corner points (25%), (4) Correct final optimization result with clear justification (20%). Teams must submit written work showing all algebraic steps and a final presentation slide summarizing their solution.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template showing the first few steps of partial derivative calculation and offer a visual guide for setting up Lagrange multiplier equations. For advanced learners: Extend the problem by adding a third product variable (z) or introduce time-dependent cost functions requiring dynamic optimization techniques. Consider providing sensitivity analysis questions about how optimal solutions change with constraint modifications.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Choices: Restaurant Sales Dashboard Critique
description: Students will critically evaluate three different dashboard designs displaying the same restaurant sales dataset, assessing the effectiveness of visualization choices and data presentation methods. They will judge which dashboard best communicates key business insights and justify their evaluation using data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different chart types (bar charts, pie charts, line graphs) by comparing how well each communicates specific data insights about restaurant performance
Students will critique dashboard design choices through systematic assessment using established data visualization criteria (clarity, accuracy, efficiency, and aesthetics)
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three printed dashboard mockups showing Q3 restaurant sales data: Dashboard A (heavy use of 3D pie charts and bright colors), Dashboard B (clean bar charts and line graphs with muted colors), and Dashboard C (mixed approach with some effective and some poor choices). Provide the evaluation rubric and background context about the restaurant chain needing to identify underperforming locations.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each dashboard independently, completing the provided evaluation matrix. They rate each dashboard (1-5 scale) on four criteria: data clarity (can you quickly identify top/bottom performers?), visual accuracy (do chart choices represent data truthfully?), information efficiency (is cognitive load minimized?), and professional appearance (would this work in a business presentation?).

**Small Group Discussion (10 minutes):** Form groups of 3-4 students to compare individual evaluations. Groups must reach consensus on which dashboard is most effective and identify the top 3 strengths and top 3 weaknesses across all dashboards.

**Presentation and Justification (15 minutes):** Each group presents their verdict to the class in 2 minutes, specifically stating which dashboard they recommend and providing evidence-based reasoning. Groups must reference specific visualization principles (e.g., 'Dashboard B's horizontal bar chart makes it easier to compare revenue across locations than Dashboard A's 3D pie chart').

**Reflection (5 minutes):** Individual written reflection answering: 'What is one visualization mistake you'll avoid in your own work and why?'
materials_needed: Three printed restaurant dashboard mockups (one per student set)
Evaluation matrix worksheet with 4 criteria rating scales
Data visualization principles reference sheet
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Students earn points through: completed evaluation matrix showing ratings and brief justifications for each dashboard (40%), quality of group consensus reasoning and identification of specific strengths/weaknesses (40%), and individual reflection demonstrating understanding of visualization principles (20%). Success requires students to move beyond personal preference to cite specific design principles in their evaluations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation for one dashboard section, highlight specific elements to examine (color choices, chart types, labels). For advanced learners: Ask them to redesign the weakest dashboard section and explain their improvements, or evaluate dashboards from multiple stakeholder perspectives (manager vs. server vs. owner).

title: Design Your Own Board Game: Probability and Expected Value Challenge
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates specific probability scenarios and calculate expected values for game outcomes. They will design game mechanics, create physical prototypes, and present mathematical justifications for their design choices.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original board game by integrating probability concepts including independent events, conditional probability, and expected value calculations
Students will synthesize mathematical reasoning through designing balanced game mechanics and defending their probability-based design decisions
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 (15 minutes setup). Each team receives materials and the constraint sheet specifying their game must include: at least two probability-based decision points, one scenario involving conditional probability, and one element where expected value determines optimal strategy. 

Day 1 (45 minutes): Teams brainstorm game themes and core mechanics. They must sketch their game board and write initial rules. Require teams to identify where probability will be incorporated and submit a one-page proposal including the game's objective, target probability scenarios, and preliminary expected value calculations.

Day 2 (90 minutes): Teams build physical prototypes using provided materials. They must create probability tables for each random element (dice rolls, card draws, spinner outcomes) and calculate theoretical probabilities for winning under different strategies. Circulate to ensure mathematical accuracy and help teams refine calculations.

Day 3 (45 minutes): Teams playtest each other's games, recording actual outcome frequencies to compare with theoretical probabilities. They must document discrepancies and propose rule modifications to achieve desired probability distributions.

Day 4 (60 minutes): Final presentations where each team demonstrates their game, explains the mathematical concepts embedded in their design, presents expected value calculations for different player strategies, and discusses how playtesting results informed their final design. Other teams evaluate games using the provided rubric and ask mathematical questions about design choices.
materials_needed: Poster board or cardboard sheets (11x17 inches minimum)
Colored markers, pencils, rulers
Standard dice, blank dice, spinners, playing cards
Calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Game piece tokens (buttons, coins, small objects)
Constraint specification sheets with mathematical requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Mathematical accuracy of probability calculations and expected value computations, (2) Creative integration of probability concepts into game mechanics, (3) Quality of mathematical reasoning in design justifications, (4) Effectiveness of prototype and playability, (5) Clarity and depth of final presentation including defense of mathematical choices. Students must also submit written documentation showing all calculations and explaining how probability theory influenced each design decision.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide probability calculation templates and example scenarios from familiar games like Monopoly or Yahtzee. Offer pre-made game themes with suggested probability elements. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate multiple probability distributions, Markov chains, or game theory concepts. Encourage analysis of variance in outcomes and statistical significance of playtesting results.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance Rankings in Ensemble Models: Random Forest vs. Gradient Boosting Analysis
description: Students analyze and compare feature importance outputs from Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models on a customer churn dataset to understand how different ensemble algorithms prioritize variables. They will interpret the mathematical foundations behind each importance calculation method and explain discrepancies between rankings.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between Gini-based and permutation importance measures by analyzing their computational differences and interpreting ranking variations across ensemble methods
Students will explain the relationship between model architecture and feature importance calculations through comparative analysis of Random Forest and XGBoost output interpretations
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-processed customer churn dataset (10,000 rows, 15 features) and pre-trained Random Forest and XGBoost models with identical hyperparameters except for algorithm-specific settings. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to generate feature importance plots using both Gini impurity and permutation importance methods for each model, creating four total visualizations using matplotlib and sklearn's feature_importances_ and permutation_importance functions. Next, dedicate 25 minutes for students to create a comparative analysis table documenting the top 5 features from each method, calculating Spearman rank correlation coefficients between the four rankings, and identifying features that show the largest ranking discrepancies (>5 position difference). During the following 30 minutes, pairs research and document the mathematical foundations: Random Forest uses mean decrease in Gini impurity across all trees, while XGBoost employs gain-based importance measuring average information gain from splits. Students must explain why permutation importance (model-agnostic, measuring prediction accuracy decrease when feature values are randomly shuffled) often differs from built-in importance measures. In the final 25 minutes, each pair presents their findings to another pair, specifically addressing: which features are consistently important across all methods, which show high variability, and hypothesizing business reasons for observed patterns in customer churn prediction context.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, sklearn, xgboost, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Pre-processed customer churn dataset (CSV format with categorical variables encoded)
Pre-trained Random Forest and XGBoost model files (.pkl format)
Feature importance analysis template worksheet (PDF)
Access to sklearn documentation and XGBoost feature importance explanations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis tables for accuracy of ranking calculations (25 points), mathematical explanations of importance calculation methods with correct terminology (25 points), identification and business interpretation of ranking discrepancies (25 points), and quality of peer presentation demonstrating understanding of when to trust different importance measures (25 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy on mathematical explanations to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated correlation matrices and guided prompts for mathematical explanations. Include visual flowcharts showing how Gini impurity and permutation importance are calculated. For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them implement SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values for local feature importance and compare with global measures, or analyze feature interactions using partial dependence plots.

title: Database Schema Vulnerability Analysis: Identifying Security Flaws in E-commerce Systems
description: Students will examine a realistic e-commerce database schema containing multiple security vulnerabilities and design flaws. They will systematically identify weaknesses, categorize threats, and prioritize remediation strategies based on risk assessment.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze database schema structures by examining table relationships, field constraints, and access permissions to identify potential security vulnerabilities
Students will evaluate the severity and impact of identified security flaws through systematic threat categorization and risk scoring methodology
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'ShopEasy' database schema documentation (15 minutes setup). The schema includes 8 tables: users, orders, products, payments, admin_logs, customer_reviews, shipping_addresses, and discount_codes. Students work in pairs to examine each table's structure, constraints, and relationships using the provided Entity Relationship Diagram and SQL DDL statements. 

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Students systematically review each table, documenting potential vulnerabilities using the provided analysis worksheet. They should examine: field data types and constraints, primary/foreign key relationships, indexing strategies, and implied access patterns. Common issues to identify include: plaintext password storage, missing input validation constraints, overly permissive field sizes, lack of audit trails, and exposed sensitive data.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Using the CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) framework handout, student pairs categorize each identified vulnerability by severity (Critical, High, Medium, Low) and attack vector (Network, Adjacent, Local, Physical). They complete a risk assessment matrix, considering both likelihood and impact.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Students create a prioritized remediation plan, selecting the top 5 vulnerabilities that pose the greatest risk. For each, they must specify: the exact security flaw, potential attack scenarios, affected user groups, and recommended technical solutions.

Conclude with pairs presenting their highest-priority vulnerability to the class (2 minutes per pair), explaining their analysis methodology and justification for severity ranking. Instructor facilitates discussion comparing different groups' findings and approaches.
materials_needed: ShopEasy database schema documentation packet (ERD + SQL DDL)
Vulnerability analysis worksheet template
CVSS scoring framework reference guide
Risk assessment matrix template
Computers with database visualization software (MySQL Workbench or similar)
assessment_method: Students submit completed vulnerability analysis worksheets and risk assessment matrices (70% of grade). Assessment criteria: identification of at least 6 valid vulnerabilities, accurate CVSS severity classifications, logical prioritization with clear justification, and technical accuracy of proposed solutions. Class presentation quality accounts for 30%, evaluated on clarity of explanation and depth of analysis demonstrated.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a 'vulnerability hints' sheet with general categories to investigate (authentication, authorization, data validation, encryption). Offer example vulnerability analysis for one table as a model. For advanced learners: include additional schema complexity with stored procedures and triggers to analyze, or require students to write actual exploit code demonstrating the vulnerabilities they identify.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Cryptographic Hash Function with Mathematical Proof
description: Students will create an original cryptographic hash function by combining number theory, modular arithmetic, and chaos theory principles. They will mathematically prove key properties of their function and demonstrate its security through collision resistance analysis and computational complexity verification.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced number theory concepts (prime factorization, modular exponentiation, discrete logarithms) by designing a novel hash function algorithm with provable security properties
Students will construct formal mathematical proofs through rigorous analysis demonstrating their hash function's one-wayness, collision resistance, and computational complexity bounds
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 2-3 (45 minutes setup). Each team receives starter code templates and mathematical reference sheets. Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams design their hash function architecture by selecting: (1) a prime modulus p > 2^256, (2) generator elements from multiplicative groups, (3) chaotic map parameters (logistic or tent map coefficients), and (4) bit-mixing operations. Students must document design rationale with mathematical justification for each component choice. Phase 2 (120 minutes): Implementation phase where teams code their hash function in Python, ensuring it processes variable-length inputs and produces fixed 256-bit outputs. They must include extensive comments explaining mathematical operations at each step. Phase 3 (90 minutes): Proof construction phase where teams write formal proofs addressing: (a) preimage resistance using computational hardness assumptions, (b) collision resistance through birthday paradox analysis, and (c) avalanche effect demonstration showing >50% output bit changes for single input bit modifications. Phase 4 (60 minutes): Validation testing where teams run their hash function on standardized test vectors, perform timing analysis on inputs of varying sizes, and attempt to find collisions using brute force methods within computational limits. Teams document all results with statistical analysis. Phase 5 (45 minutes): Peer review where teams exchange implementations, verify proofs, and attempt to break each other's hash functions, documenting any discovered vulnerabilities or proof gaps.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with NumPy, hashlib, and matplotlib libraries installed
Mathematical reference sheets covering modular arithmetic and number theory
Starter code templates with basic I/O structure
Access to computational resources capable of testing hash functions on large datasets
LaTeX editor or mathematical typesetting software for proof documentation
assessment_method: Evaluation using detailed rubric: Hash function design creativity and mathematical soundness (25 points), implementation correctness and efficiency (20 points), formal proof rigor and validity (25 points), experimental validation thoroughness (15 points), and peer review quality and vulnerability analysis (15 points). Success requires achieving collision resistance against 10^6 random trials, sub-linear timing complexity, and mathematically sound proofs verified by instructor review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected prime moduli and generator elements, offer proof templates with guided fill-in-the-blank sections, and allow use of simplified chaotic maps. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate elliptic curve operations, implement quantum-resistant features, or prove additional security properties like semantic security or zero-knowledge compatibility.

title: Python Data Type Memory Palace Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall Python's six fundamental data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) along with their specific syntax examples. Through flashcard creation and peer testing, students will build foundational knowledge essential for Python programming.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) by creating visual flashcards with syntax examples
Students will recall specific Python data type syntax through structured peer testing and self-assessment activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-printed data type reference sheets showing the six Python data types with examples (15 minutes setup). Have students work individually to create physical flashcards using index cards - one data type per card with the type name on front and 2-3 syntax examples on back (20 minutes creation time). Provide specific examples: int (42, -17, 0), float (3.14, -2.5, 0.0), string ('hello', "world", 'Python'), boolean (True, False), list ([1, 2, 3], ['a', 'b'], []), dictionary ({'key': 'value'}, {1: 'one'}, {}). After card creation, pair students for 15 minutes of flashcard drilling where Partner A shows the data type name and Partner B must recite the definition and provide one correct syntax example. Partners switch roles after 7 minutes. Follow with a 10-minute individual quiz where students write all six data types from memory with one example each. Conclude with a class review session (10 minutes) where volunteers share their memorization strategies and instructor clarifies any misconceptions. Circulate continuously during pair work to ensure accuracy and provide immediate feedback on syntax errors.
materials_needed: Index cards (10 cards per student)
Pre-printed Python data type reference sheets
Pencils or pens
Individual quiz sheets with blanks for data types and examples
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade individual quiz sheets using a 12-point rubric (2 points per data type: 1 point for correct type name, 1 point for valid syntax example). Success criteria: 10/12 points (83%) demonstrates adequate memorization. Observe peer testing sessions and award participation points for active engagement and accurate peer feedback.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made flashcards with partial examples to complete, allow extended drilling time, and pair with stronger students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include additional examples like nested lists [1, [2, 3]] or complex dictionaries with multiple data types as values. Consider having them help create a class reference poster.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Real-World Sales Analytics
description: Students will analyze a retail sales dataset to identify and explain different distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal) in customer purchase behaviors. They will interpret what each distribution type reveals about business patterns and make evidence-based conclusions about customer segments.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing histograms and summary statistics of customer purchase data
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through written interpretations connecting statistical observations to real-world scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'RetailSales2023.csv' dataset containing 5,000 customer transactions with variables: transaction_amount, customer_age, items_purchased, and visit_frequency. In the first 15 minutes, students work individually to create histograms for each variable using Python/pandas and matplotlib. They should calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for each distribution. Next, organize students into pairs for 20 minutes to compare their visualizations and identify distribution shapes. Provide the 'Distribution Classification Worksheet' where pairs categorize each variable's distribution and note key characteristics (tail direction, peak count, symmetry). During the following 15 minutes, pairs select one distribution and write a 150-word business interpretation explaining what the pattern reveals about customer behavior. For example, a right-skewed transaction_amount distribution might indicate most customers make small purchases with few high-value buyers. In the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class discussion where three pairs present their interpretations. Display all histograms on the projector and have the class validate or refine the distribution classifications. Students should use specific statistical evidence (mean vs. median relationships, standard deviation values) to support their explanations. Emphasize connecting mathematical observations to practical business insights throughout the activity.
materials_needed: RetailSales2023.csv dataset with 5,000 customer records
Distribution Classification Worksheet (printed copies)
Computers with Python, pandas, and matplotlib installed
Projector for whole-class histogram display
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct histogram creation and statistical calculations (25%), (2) Accurate distribution classification with justification (25%), (3) Quality of business interpretation connecting statistics to real-world meaning (35%), (4) Use of appropriate statistical vocabulary and evidence (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 on all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-made histogram templates and a 'Distribution Characteristics Reference Sheet' with visual examples. Offer sentence starters like 'The right tail indicates...' for interpretations. For advanced learners, introduce additional concepts like kurtosis, provide a second dataset for comparison, or challenge them to suggest business strategies based on their distribution findings.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Real-World Sales Analytics: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze three different sales datasets to identify and explain distribution patterns (normal, skewed, bimodal). They will compare histograms, box plots, and summary statistics to explain what each distribution pattern reveals about underlying business conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of different distribution shapes by analyzing sales data histograms and explaining their business implications
Students will distinguish between normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, and bimodal distributions through hands-on examination of box plots and summary statistics
instructions:
Begin by distributing three pre-prepared datasets: Dataset A (monthly coffee shop sales - normal distribution), Dataset B (luxury car sales - right-skewed), and Dataset C (ice cream sales with seasonal peaks - bimodal). Divide students into groups of 3-4. Each group receives printed summary statistics sheets and access to visualization tools. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups create histograms and box plots for each dataset using provided tools. They record observations about shape, center, and spread on the analysis worksheet.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students examine summary statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles) for each dataset. They complete guided questions comparing these values and noting patterns like mean vs. median relationships in skewed data.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Groups match each distribution type to business scenarios using provided scenario cards. For example, they explain why luxury items typically show right-skewed sales patterns while everyday items follow normal distributions.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents one dataset analysis, explaining the distribution shape, what summary statistics reveal, and real-world factors causing this pattern. Other groups provide feedback using peer evaluation forms.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion connecting distribution patterns to data collection methods and business decision-making. Students record key insights in their reflection journals.
materials_needed: Three curated sales datasets (CSV files) with different distribution patterns
Histogram and box plot creation tool (Excel, Google Sheets, or R)
Pre-calculated summary statistics sheets for each dataset
Distribution pattern analysis worksheets
Business scenario matching cards
Peer evaluation forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of distribution shapes from visual plots, (2) Correct interpretation of summary statistics relationships, (3) Logical explanation of business factors causing distribution patterns, (4) Quality of group presentation including use of appropriate statistical vocabulary. Students must score 3/4 on all criteria to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide distribution identification flowcharts and sentence starters for explanations. Offer one-on-one guidance during Step 2 to reinforce mean vs. median concepts. For advanced learners, introduce concepts of kurtosis and provide additional datasets with outliers to analyze their impact on distribution interpretation.
original_title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Real-World Sales Analytics

title: Distributed System Bottleneck Analysis Using Performance Profiling Data
description: Students analyze real-world performance profiling data from a multi-tier web application to identify system bottlenecks, examine component interactions, and determine root causes of performance degradation. They will decompose complex distributed system behaviors and evaluate the relationships between database queries, API response times, and memory utilization patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze performance bottlenecks in distributed systems by examining profiling data from database, application, and caching layers to identify critical performance constraints
Students will decompose complex system interactions through correlation analysis of CPU utilization, memory consumption, and network latency metrics across multiple system components
instructions:
Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with a dataset containing 7 days of performance metrics from a fictional e-commerce platform experiencing intermittent slowdowns. The dataset includes API response times, database query execution times, Redis cache hit/miss ratios, CPU/memory utilization, and user session data. 

Step 1 (30 minutes): Teams load the dataset into their analysis environment and create initial visualizations of key metrics over time. They must identify at least 3 distinct time periods showing performance anomalies.

Step 2 (45 minutes): Students perform correlation analysis between different metrics to map dependencies. They examine relationships between database query times and API response delays, cache performance and CPU utilization, and user load patterns with system resource consumption.

Step 3 (40 minutes): Teams drill down into the worst-performing 2-hour window, analyzing log entries, query execution plans, and resource allocation patterns. They must trace specific user requests through the system stack to identify where delays occur.

Step 4 (35 minutes): Students create a comprehensive bottleneck analysis report documenting their findings. The report must include: identified bottlenecks ranked by impact severity, evidence supporting each conclusion, component interaction diagrams showing problem areas, and recommended investigation priorities for the development team.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams present their top 2 findings to the class, defending their analysis with specific data points and explaining how they isolated each bottleneck from other system behaviors.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared performance dataset (CSV files with 50,000+ data points)
Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn libraries
Sample distributed system architecture diagram
Performance analysis worksheet template
Access to visualization tools (Grafana or similar dashboard tool)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification - correctly identifies at least 2 major performance constraints with supporting evidence, (2) Quality of correlation analysis - demonstrates clear understanding of component relationships and dependencies, (3) Depth of root cause analysis - traces performance issues to specific system components with logical reasoning, (4) Presentation clarity - effectively communicates findings with appropriate technical detail and data visualization. Students must achieve proficient (3/4) on all criteria to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided analysis questions and pre-built visualization templates focusing on single-metric analysis before moving to correlation studies. Offer one-on-one debugging support for data analysis tools. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity with network topology considerations, provide secondary datasets for comparison analysis, or challenge them to propose specific architectural solutions with performance impact predictions.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Critiquing Chart Effectiveness for COVID-19 Vaccination Trends
description: Students will analyze and critique three different visualizations of the same COVID-19 vaccination dataset using established data visualization principles. They will identify strengths and weaknesses of each chart, then recommend the most effective visualization for a specific audience and purpose.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying visualization design principles and identifying specific strengths and weaknesses
Students will critique data representation choices through systematic comparison of chart types, color schemes, and labeling decisions
instructions: Begin by displaying three pre-prepared visualizations of COVID-19 vaccination rates by age group over 6 months: a cluttered pie chart with poor color choices, a clean line chart with proper labeling, and a bar chart with missing context. Provide students with the 'Data Visualization Evaluation Checklist' containing criteria: clarity, accuracy, audience appropriateness, visual hierarchy, and completeness. In pairs (10 minutes), students examine each visualization and score it 1-5 on each criterion, writing specific evidence for their scores. Next, conduct a whole-class discussion (15 minutes) where pairs share one strength and one weakness they identified for each chart. Record responses on the board, encouraging students to reference specific visual elements. Then, present a scenario: 'You're presenting to healthcare administrators who need to allocate resources.' Students individually (10 minutes) rank the three visualizations from most to least effective for this purpose, writing a 3-sentence justification for their top choice and explaining why they rejected their last choice. Conclude with students submitting their completed checklists and written justifications. Throughout the activity, emphasize that evaluation requires citing specific evidence rather than personal preferences.
materials_needed: Three printed COVID-19 vaccination visualizations (one per student pair)
Data Visualization Evaluation Checklist handout
Scenario description handout
Whiteboard or projector for class discussion
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (4) Provides specific, accurate evidence for all visualization strengths/weaknesses and justifies ranking with clear reasoning; (3) Identifies most strengths/weaknesses with evidence and provides adequate justification; (2) Identifies some issues but lacks specific evidence or weak justification; (1) Minimal identification of issues with little to no supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This chart is unclear because...' and highlight one obvious flaw in each visualization. For advanced learners: Ask them to sketch how they would redesign the weakest visualization and explain their design choices using visualization theory principles.

title: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall specific time and space complexities for 20 advanced data structures and their operations, along with the exact names and characteristics of 15 classic algorithms. This intensive recall activity builds the foundational knowledge necessary for technical interviews and advanced algorithm analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity (best, average, worst case) and space complexity for operations on advanced data structures including B-trees, Red-Black trees, Skip Lists, and Bloom filters within 5 seconds per query

Students will identify and recite the precise algorithmic complexity, space requirements, and key characteristics of advanced algorithms including A*, Dijkstra's, Ford-Fulkerson, and KMP string matching through rapid-fire questioning
instructions: Begin by distributing the comprehensive reference sheet containing 20 data structures (B-tree, Red-Black tree, AVL tree, Skip List, Bloom filter, Trie, Segment tree, Fenwick tree, Disjoint Set, Min/Max Heap, Hash table with chaining/open addressing, Adjacency matrix/list representations) with their complete complexity profiles. Students have 25 minutes for silent memorization using any technique (flashcards, mnemonics, visualization). Next, distribute the algorithm reference sheet covering 15 algorithms: A*, Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal's, Prim's, Ford-Fulkerson, KMP, Rabin-Karp, QuickSort, MergeSort, HeapSort, Radix Sort, Binary Search, and DFS/BFS variants. Allow 20 minutes for memorization. Conduct individual rapid-fire assessment: each student approaches instructor's desk for private 5-minute oral examination. Ask 10 random questions mixing data structure operations and algorithm characteristics. Questions format: 'What is the worst-case time complexity for deletion in a Red-Black tree?' or 'State the space complexity and key invariant of Dijkstra's algorithm.' Students must respond within 5 seconds with complete accuracy. Record responses on provided scoring sheet. After individual assessments, conduct 15-minute group review where students explain memorization strategies and clarify any confusion. Conclude with students creating personal quick-reference cards for future use.
materials_needed: Printed data structure complexity reference sheets (1 per student)
Printed algorithm characteristic reference sheets (1 per student)
Individual assessment scoring sheets for instructor
Timer/stopwatch for response timing
Blank index cards for student reference creation
assessment_method: Individual oral assessment scored on accuracy and speed: 2 points for completely correct answer within 5 seconds, 1 point for correct answer within 10 seconds, 0 points for incorrect/incomplete answers or responses over 10 seconds. Minimum passing score: 16/20 points. Document specific errors for remediation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide color-coded complexity charts and encourage acronym-based memorization techniques. Allow extended 8-second response time during assessment. For advanced learners: include amortized analysis complexities and ask for explanations of why certain complexities occur. Challenge them to recall complexity proofs or provide real-world implementation considerations.

title: Algorithm Complexity Visualization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity notations for 25 advanced data structures and algorithms commonly used in enterprise software development. This intensive recall activity uses spaced repetition and competitive elements to ensure mastery of Big O notation for complex computational scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity (worst, average, best case) for 25 advanced data structures and algorithms by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify the space complexity notation for advanced algorithms including red-black trees, B-trees, and graph traversal algorithms through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared complexity reference sheets containing 25 advanced algorithms: Red-Black Tree operations, AVL Tree rotations, B-Tree insertions/deletions, Dijkstra's algorithm, Floyd-Warshall algorithm, A* pathfinding, Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching, Rabin-Karp algorithm, Segment Tree operations, Fenwick Tree updates, Trie insertions, Suffix Array construction, Topological sorting, Strongly Connected Components (Tarjan's), Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal's and Prim's), Maximum Flow (Ford-Fulkerson), Convex Hull (Graham Scan), Quick Select, Heap operations, Hash Table with collision resolution, Dynamic Programming variants (0/1 Knapsack, Longest Common Subsequence), and Bloom Filter operations. Students have 15 minutes to study the sheet intensively. Remove reference materials and begin Round 1: Display algorithm names one at a time using slides. Students write time complexity (Big O, Big Θ, Big Ω) and space complexity on answer sheets. Allow 45 seconds per algorithm. After completing all 25, provide correct answers for 5-minute review. Conduct Round 2 with algorithms presented in different order, reducing response time to 30 seconds each. For Round 3, present only complexity notations and require students to recall which algorithms match. Advanced variation: Include complexity for specific operations (insertion vs deletion vs search). Track individual scores across rounds to identify improvement patterns. Conclude with peer verification where students exchange papers and verify answers against the master key.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared reference sheet with 25 advanced algorithms and their complexities
Digital presentation slides with algorithm names and complexity notations
Answer sheets with structured tables for time/space complexity entries
Timer or stopwatch for enforcing time limits
Master answer key for instructor verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) in the final recall round to demonstrate mastery. Grade breakdown: Round 1 (40%), Round 2 (35%), Round 3 (25%). Partial credit given for correct Big O notation even if Big Θ or Big Ω are incorrect. Track completion time as secondary metric for identifying students who need additional practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for common patterns (e.g., 'Trees need O(log n) to reach leaves'). Allow use of one 'lifeline' reference check per round. For advanced learners: Include amortized analysis complexities and ask for explanation of why certain algorithms have different best/worst case scenarios. Extend with space-time tradeoff discussions.
original_title: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Memorization Challenge

title: Deconstructing Bias Propagation in Multi-Stage Machine Learning Pipelines
description: Students will analyze a complete ML pipeline from raw data ingestion through model deployment to understand how algorithmic bias compounds at each stage. They will trace specific bias sources through feature engineering, model selection, and evaluation phases using a real-world hiring algorithm case study.
learning_objectives: Students will identify how selection bias, measurement bias, and confirmation bias manifest and propagate through each stage of an ML pipeline by analyzing preprocessing decisions, feature transformations, and evaluation metrics
Students will explain the interconnected relationships between data quality issues, model architecture choices, and fairness outcomes through systematic pipeline decomposition and bias impact mapping
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a complete hiring algorithm pipeline including: raw resume dataset (10,000 samples), preprocessing scripts, feature engineering code, three different model implementations (logistic regression, random forest, neural network), and deployment monitoring logs. Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team one demographic slice to focus on (gender, age, ethnicity, education background). 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the raw data collection process, identifying potential selection biases in job posting locations, application platforms, and historical hiring patterns. Students document their findings using a bias taxonomy worksheet, categorizing each issue by type, severity, and pipeline stage.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Students trace their assigned demographic slice through the feature engineering process, analyzing text preprocessing decisions (keyword weighting, skill extraction algorithms), categorical encoding choices, and dimensionality reduction impacts. They create a bias propagation flowchart showing how initial biases transform and amplify.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams evaluate how different model architectures interact with the biased features, examining training/validation splits, hyperparameter selection criteria, and evaluation metric choices. They calculate fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration) for each model variant.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Students synthesize findings by creating a comprehensive bias impact matrix, mapping specific bias sources to downstream effects and proposing concrete mitigation strategies for each pipeline stage. Teams present their demographic slice analysis to the class, building a complete picture of pipeline-wide bias propagation.
materials_needed: Synthetic hiring dataset with 10,000 resume samples including demographic indicators
Complete ML pipeline codebase (Python/Jupyter notebooks) with preprocessing, training, and evaluation scripts
Bias taxonomy worksheet template with categories for selection, measurement, confirmation, and algorithmic bias
Fairness metrics calculation toolkit (AIF360 or Fairlearn libraries)
Digital whiteboard tool (Miro/Mural) for bias propagation flowchart creation
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Bias identification accuracy - correctly identifies at least 8 distinct bias sources across pipeline stages, (2) Causal reasoning - accurately traces how biases transform and compound through pipeline stages, (3) Quantitative analysis - correctly calculates fairness metrics and interprets results, (4) Solution quality - proposes feasible, stage-specific mitigation strategies with clear implementation steps. Students submit bias impact matrices and present 10-minute team findings. Minimum passing requires 3/4 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide bias detection checklists for each pipeline stage and pre-calculated fairness metrics to focus on interpretation rather than computation. Offer guided questions like 'What assumptions does this preprocessing step make?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to design alternative pipeline architectures that minimize bias propagation, implement differential privacy techniques, or analyze intersectional bias effects across multiple demographic dimensions simultaneously.

title: Grocery Budget Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real Shopping Scenarios
description: Students will apply percentage calculation skills to solve realistic grocery shopping problems involving discounts, tax, and budget constraints. They will use given budgets to make purchasing decisions while calculating sales tax, discount savings, and remaining funds.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine sale prices, tax amounts, and total costs by solving real-world grocery shopping scenarios
Students will calculate budget allocations and remaining balances through multi-step percentage problems involving discounts and taxes
instructions:
Begin by distributing the grocery store flyer and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card contains a specific budget ($50-$150), family size, and shopping mission (weekly groceries, party supplies, etc.). Students must select items from the flyer to meet their family's needs while staying within budget.

Explain the calculation requirements (10 minutes): Students must apply a 7.5% sales tax to all items, calculate savings from any discounts shown on the flyer (10% off produce, 15% off bulk items, etc.), and determine their final total and remaining budget. Provide the calculation worksheet with spaces for itemized lists, discount calculations, tax calculations, and final totals.

Students work independently to complete their shopping lists and calculations (20 minutes). They must show all work for percentage calculations, including: original price × discount percentage = savings amount; (original price - discount) × 1.075 = final price with tax. Circulate to check calculation methods and provide guidance.

Pair students to compare their solutions (8 minutes). Partners check each other's percentage calculations and discuss different item choices within similar budgets. This peer review helps identify calculation errors.

Conclude with whole-class sharing (7 minutes) where 3-4 students present their shopping lists, explain their percentage calculations, and justify how they stayed within budget. Record common calculation strategies on the board for future reference.
materials_needed: Printed grocery store flyer with various discounts and prices
Scenario cards with family budgets and shopping requirements (6-8 different scenarios)
Calculation worksheets with organized spaces for itemized costs
Calculators (1 per student)
Chart paper for recording strategies
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correct percentage calculations for discounts and tax with clear work shown, stays within budget, realistic item selection; (3) Minor calculation errors but demonstrates understanding of percentage application; (2) Some correct calculations but missing steps or budget errors; (1) Significant errors in percentage calculations or unrealistic shopping choices. Check that students show work for at least 3 percentage calculations per worksheet.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation reference card showing percentage formulas and examples, or assign simpler scenarios with round numbers and fewer items. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including comparison shopping between stores, calculating unit prices, or determining the percentage of budget spent on different food categories. Consider providing scenarios with multiple family members having different dietary restrictions requiring more strategic planning.

title: Database Query Performance Analysis: Identifying Bottlenecks in E-commerce Transaction Queries
description: Students will analyze the performance of SQL queries used in an e-commerce database system by examining execution plans, identifying inefficiencies, and categorizing optimization opportunities. This activity develops critical thinking skills for database performance tuning and query optimization strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by interpreting cost metrics, join operations, and index usage patterns to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will categorize query inefficiencies through systematic examination of table scans, missing indexes, and suboptimal join strategies
instructions:
Begin by providing each student team (2-3 members) with the pre-loaded e-commerce database containing 50,000+ product records, 100,000+ customer records, and 500,000+ transaction records. Distribute the worksheet containing 8 problematic SQL queries of varying complexity (simple SELECT with WHERE clauses, complex JOINs with subqueries, aggregate functions with GROUP BY). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams execute each query using the database management system's query analyzer tool and record execution times. Students document initial observations about which queries perform poorly.

Step 2 (20 minutes): For the 3 slowest queries, teams generate and examine execution plans. Students identify specific elements: table scan operations, index seek vs. scan operations, join algorithms used, and estimated vs. actual row counts.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze each problematic query by categorizing issues into four types: missing indexes, inefficient WHERE clause ordering, suboptimal JOIN sequences, or unnecessary subqueries. Students complete the analysis matrix, mapping each query to specific performance issues.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams propose specific optimization strategies for each identified bottleneck, such as creating composite indexes, rewriting subqueries as JOINs, or restructuring WHERE conditions. Students rank optimizations by expected impact.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each team presents one query analysis to the class, explaining their methodology and findings using the execution plan visualization projected on screen.
materials_needed: Pre-loaded MySQL or PostgreSQL e-commerce database with sample data
Database management software with query execution plan capability (MySQL Workbench, pgAdmin, or similar)
Query analysis worksheet with 8 test queries and performance metrics table
Computers with database access for each student team
Projector for execution plan visualization during presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis matrices (40 points): accuracy of bottleneck identification (20 pts), appropriateness of categorization (10 pts), and feasibility of proposed optimizations (10 pts). Assess team presentations (10 points) on clarity of explanation and proper use of technical terminology. Successful completion requires correctly identifying at least 6 out of 8 query issues and providing technically sound optimization strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a sample execution plan analysis for the first query, highlight key metrics to focus on (cost, cardinality, operation types), and offer a checklist of common performance issues. For advanced learners: include queries with more complex optimization challenges (nested subqueries, window functions), ask them to estimate quantitative performance improvements, or have them create additional test queries that demonstrate specific bottleneck patterns.

title: Design and Implement a Machine Learning Algorithm for Predictive Analytics
description: Students will develop an original mathematical framework combining statistical modeling, linear algebra, and calculus optimization to create a functional predictive algorithm. They will construct their own machine learning model from mathematical first principles, implementing gradient descent optimization and validating results through cross-validation techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multivariate calculus, linear algebra, and statistical theory by designing an original gradient descent algorithm for logistic regression
Students will construct a complete mathematical framework through deriving loss functions, implementing matrix operations, and developing validation metrics from foundational principles
instructions:
**Phase 1: Mathematical Foundation (45 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to derive the mathematical components: (1) Define the logistic function σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(-z)) and prove its derivative property σ'(z) = σ(z)(1-σ(z)) using calculus, (2) Construct the likelihood function L(θ) = Π[σ(x_i^T θ)^y_i (1-σ(x_i^T θ))^(1-y_i)] for binary classification, (3) Derive the log-likelihood and its gradient ∇L(θ) using chain rule and matrix calculus. **Phase 2: Algorithm Design (60 minutes)** Teams design their gradient descent implementation: (1) Formulate the update rule θ_(t+1) = θ_t + α∇L(θ_t), (2) Develop convergence criteria using ||∇L(θ)||_2 < ε, (3) Create regularization terms λ||θ||_2^2 to prevent overfitting, (4) Design learning rate scheduling α_t = α_0/(1+βt). **Phase 3: Implementation (90 minutes)** Using Python/R, students code their algorithm from scratch without ML libraries: (1) Implement matrix operations for forward propagation, (2) Code gradient computation using vectorized operations, (3) Build cross-validation framework with k-fold splitting, (4) Create performance metrics (precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC). **Phase 4: Validation (45 minutes)** Test on provided datasets: (1) Compare against scikit-learn's implementation, (2) Analyze convergence behavior through loss plots, (3) Evaluate generalization using validation curves, (4) Document mathematical derivations and computational complexity analysis.
materials_needed: Python/R programming environment with NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib
Three labeled datasets: Iris classification, breast cancer diagnosis, customer churn prediction
Jupyter notebooks or RStudio
Scientific calculators
Graph paper and mathematical notation reference sheets
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Mathematical derivations accuracy (25%) - correct calculus and linear algebra work; Algorithm implementation (25%) - functional code without ML libraries; Performance analysis (25%) - convergence plots, cross-validation results, comparison with standard implementations; Documentation quality (25%) - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning, computational complexity analysis, and interpretation of results. Minimum passing: algorithm achieves >85% accuracy on test datasets with mathematically sound derivations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed gradient calculations and matrix operation templates; offer step-by-step calculus review sessions focusing on chain rule applications. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement L1 regularization (LASSO), develop adaptive learning rates (AdaGrad/Adam), or extend to multinomial classification; encourage exploration of second-order optimization methods like Newton-Raphson or quasi-Newton approaches.

title: Python Data Types Memory Card Matching Activity
description: Students will memorize and identify the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) through a structured card matching game. This foundational activity helps students recall data type names, definitions, and examples before moving to programming applications.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) by matching type names to their definitions with 100% accuracy
Students will identify correct examples of each Python data type through visual recognition exercises within 2 minutes per data type
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Print and cut 18 cards total - 6 cards with data type names (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary), 6 cards with definitions, and 6 cards with code examples. Shuffle all cards and place face-down on tables. Divide class into pairs. **Round 1 - Name to Definition Matching (10 minutes):** Each pair receives 12 cards (names and definitions only). Students flip cards to find matches between data type names and their definitions. When a match is found, students must state the match aloud to their partner. Instructor circulates to verify correct matches. **Round 2 - Adding Examples (10 minutes):** Add the 6 example cards to each pair's set. Students now match triplets: name, definition, and code example. For instance: 'int' + 'whole numbers without decimals' + '42'. **Memorization Phase (8 minutes):** Remove all cards. Give each student a blank worksheet with three columns: Data Type, Definition, Example. Students must fill in all 18 items from memory. **Verification Round (5 minutes):** Students swap worksheets with another pair for peer checking using the original cards as an answer key. **Final Recall Test (7 minutes):** Instructor calls out random data types, and students must immediately respond with both definition and an original example (not from the cards).
materials_needed: 18 printed cards per pair (6 data type names, 6 definitions, 6 code examples)
Blank worksheets with 3-column template (one per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key sheets for peer verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 100% accuracy on the final recall worksheet (6 data types correctly matched to definitions and examples). Peer verification scores are recorded, and instructor conducts spot-checks during the final recall test where students must respond within 10 seconds to demonstrate memorization rather than reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: **Struggling students:** Provide cards with color-coding (same color family for matching sets) and allow extra practice time with just 3 data types initially. Create mnemonic devices ('Boolean = True/False like a light bulb on/off'). **Advanced learners:** Add challenge cards with edge cases (empty lists, nested dictionaries, scientific notation floats) and require them to create original examples using multiple data types in single code statements.

title: Multi-Step Optimization: Designing a Community Solar Farm Layout
description: Students will apply advanced calculus and linear programming concepts to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel placement, cost constraints, and energy output maximization. They will work through complex multi-variable optimization while considering practical engineering constraints and environmental factors.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus techniques including partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize solar panel placement within geometric constraints
Students will implement linear programming methods through systematic constraint analysis to maximize energy output while minimizing installation costs
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing a 500m × 300m rectangular plot with irregular boundary constraints (building shadows, utility easements, and terrain variations marked on grid paper). Students work in teams of 3-4 for 15 minutes to analyze the given parameters: panel dimensions (2m × 1.5m), minimum spacing requirements (0.5m), shadow angles (35° from buildings), cost per panel ($800), energy output formula (E = 250W × cos(θ) × efficiency factor), and terrain slope limitations (maximum 15°). 

Next, teams spend 45 minutes formulating their optimization problem by defining variables (x,y coordinates for each panel, rotation angle θ), writing constraint inequalities for boundaries and spacing, and establishing the objective function combining energy maximization and cost minimization with given weight factors (energy coefficient: 0.7, cost coefficient: 0.3). They must create at least 8 mathematical constraints and justify each one with real-world reasoning.

During the 40-minute solution phase, teams apply calculus methods to find critical points, use the method of Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization, and verify solutions using second derivative tests. They calculate partial derivatives, set up and solve the system of equations, and check boundary conditions. Teams must show all mathematical work and create a scaled diagram of their optimal layout.

Finally, teams spend 20 minutes preparing presentations including: mathematical formulation with all equations clearly labeled, step-by-step solution process, final panel layout diagram with coordinates, calculated maximum energy output, total cost analysis, and sensitivity analysis showing how solution changes with ±10% variation in key parameters. Each team presents their solution in 5 minutes, explaining their mathematical reasoning and comparing results with other teams.
materials_needed: Scenario packets with detailed plot maps on 1cm grid paper
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Computer access with Excel or MATLAB/Python for verification calculations
Large poster paper (24" × 36") and colored markers for final diagrams
Ruler and protractor sets for precise measurements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical formulation accuracy (25 points - correct variables, constraints, objective function), Solution methodology (30 points - proper application of calculus techniques, correct calculations), Real-world application (20 points - justified constraints, practical considerations), Presentation quality (15 points - clear explanation, visual aids), Team collaboration evidence (10 points - equal participation, peer evaluation). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency, with work portfolios including all calculations, peer feedback forms, and reflection essays submitted within 24 hours.
