scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates, offer mini-lessons on Lagrange multipliers during work time, and allow use of online derivative calculators with requirement to explain each step. Create checkpoint sheets for progress monitoring every 20 minutes. For advanced learners: Add complexity with time-varying shadow patterns, introduce integer programming constraints (whole panels only), incorporate weather probability distributions, or extend to 3D optimization with angled mounting systems. Provide research articles on actual solar farm optimization for deeper context.

title: Distributed System Architecture Performance Bottleneck Analysis
description: Students will analyze a complex e-commerce microservices architecture experiencing performance degradation under high load. They will decompose system interactions, identify bottlenecks through trace analysis, and evaluate the cascading effects of component failures on overall system performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system performance by examining service dependencies, latency patterns, and resource utilization metrics across multiple microservices
Students will deconstruct complex system failures through systematic evaluation of distributed tracing data, error logs, and monitoring dashboards
instructions:
Begin by providing each team with the performance crisis scenario: a Black Friday e-commerce platform experiencing 80% increased response times and 15% error rates. Distribute the dataset containing 2 hours of distributed traces from Jaeger, Prometheus metrics, and application logs from 8 microservices (user authentication, product catalog, inventory, payment processing, recommendation engine, shopping cart, order fulfillment, and notification service). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams examine the system architecture diagram and identify service dependencies using the provided service mesh topology. Students document the critical path for a complete user purchase transaction.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using Jaeger UI, students analyze trace spans to identify services with highest P95 latency. They must create a latency distribution chart showing response times for each service and identify the top 3 bottlenecks.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students correlate high-latency traces with Prometheus CPU, memory, and database connection pool metrics. They examine the provided Grafana dashboards to determine resource constraints contributing to performance degradation.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams analyze error logs to identify failure patterns, examining HTTP status codes, database timeouts, and circuit breaker activations. Students map error propagation across service boundaries.

Step 5 (25 minutes): Students synthesize findings into a root cause analysis report, ranking bottlenecks by impact severity and proposing specific architectural improvements (caching strategies, database optimization, horizontal scaling, or circuit breaker tuning).
materials_needed: Jaeger distributed tracing dataset (2GB compressed file with 50,000+ traces)
Prometheus metrics export covering 8 microservices over 2-hour window
Pre-configured Grafana dashboards showing system performance metrics
E-commerce system architecture diagram with service dependency graph
Application log files in JSON format from each microservice
Laptops with Docker containers running Jaeger UI and Grafana
assessment_method: Evaluate deliverable reports using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of bottleneck identification - correctly identifies top 3 performance bottlenecks with supporting trace evidence (25 points), (2) Quality of correlation analysis - demonstrates clear connections between metrics, traces, and errors (25 points), (3) Depth of impact analysis - explains cascading effects and quantifies performance degradation (25 points), (4) Solution feasibility - proposes realistic architectural improvements with technical justification (25 points). Bonus points awarded for identifying non-obvious bottlenecks or innovative optimization strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with specific trace IDs to examine first, and offer simplified Grafana dashboards focusing on key metrics. Include a glossary of distributed systems terminology. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate theoretical throughput limits, model the impact of proposed optimizations using queueing theory, or design a custom monitoring strategy for early bottleneck detection.

title: Design a Mathematical Board Game Using Linear Functions
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates linear functions as the core gameplay mechanism. Players must design game rules, create visual elements, and integrate mathematical concepts where players move along paths determined by linear equations and their graphical representations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize knowledge of linear functions, slope, and graphing by designing an interactive board game that demonstrates these concepts
Students will construct mathematical models through game mechanics that require players to calculate, graph, and interpret linear equations
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with design materials (45 minutes). Students first brainstorm their game concept, deciding on a theme (racing, adventure, business, etc.) and core objective. The game must incorporate at least three linear function elements: players roll dice to determine variables for linear equations (y = mx + b), calculate y-values to determine movement spaces, and encounter special spaces requiring graphing linear functions on provided coordinate grids. 

Next, students create their game board on poster board, designing a path with numbered spaces (minimum 50 spaces) and marking special 'Function Challenge' spaces every 8-10 positions (30 minutes). They must include a coordinate grid section on their board for graphing activities. 

Students then develop their rule set, writing clear instructions that specify: how players generate linear equations using dice or cards, movement calculation procedures, challenge space requirements, and winning conditions (25 minutes). They create game cards with pre-written linear function problems of varying difficulty levels (easy: y = 2x + 1, moderate: y = -3x + 7, challenging: y = 0.5x - 4). 

Groups design and create all game components including player pieces, dice modifications or equation cards, and answer keys for verification (35 minutes). Finally, students test their games by having another group play for 15 minutes, gathering feedback and making necessary adjustments (20 minutes). Each group presents their completed game to the class, explaining their mathematical integration and demonstrating key gameplay mechanics (15 minutes total for all groups).
materials_needed: Poster board (22x28 inches minimum)
Colored markers and pencils
Standard dice (2 per group)
Index cards for game cards
Graph paper sheets
Rulers and protractors
Small objects for game pieces (buttons, coins, etc.)
Calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: Mathematical Accuracy (correct linear function integration, accurate calculations), Game Design Quality (clear rules, functional mechanics, engaging theme), Creative Integration (innovative use of linear functions in gameplay), and Presentation Skills (clear explanation of mathematical concepts, effective demonstration). Students submit their complete game with written rules, answer keys, and a reflection explaining how their design reinforces linear function concepts.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing linear function templates and example game mechanics. Offer pre-made coordinate grids and simplified equation formats (integer coefficients only). For advanced learners, encourage incorporation of systems of linear equations, piecewise functions, or real-world applications like profit/loss scenarios. Provide extension challenges such as creating digital versions or adding statistical probability elements.

title: Advanced Computer Architecture Component Identification and Function Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate memorization of specific CPU microarchitecture components, cache hierarchy specifications, and instruction pipeline stages through rapid-fire identification exercises. This activity focuses on recalling precise technical details of modern processor designs including Intel Core and AMD Zen architectures.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the names and bit-widths of all functional units within superscalar CPU architectures by completing timed component identification tasks
Students will precisely recite cache hierarchy specifications, pipeline stage sequences, and instruction set architecture details through structured memory drills
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Advanced Architecture Reference Sheets containing detailed diagrams of Intel Core i9-12900K and AMD Ryzen 9 5950X microarchitectures (5 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair a computer workstation with the digital flashcard application loaded. 

Round 1 (15 minutes): Display blank CPU block diagrams on the projector. Students must individually write down all component names, including specific functional units (ALU, AGU, load/store units), cache levels with exact sizes (L1I: 32KB, L1D: 32KB, L2: 1MB, L3: shared), and interconnect pathways. No reference materials allowed. Collect sheets after exactly 15 minutes.

Round 2 (10 minutes): Launch the digital flashcard drill. Students take turns with their partner, with one reading cache coherency protocol states (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) while the other recites the complete MESI state transitions from memory. Switch roles every 2 minutes. Monitor pairs to ensure accurate pronunciation of technical terms.

Round 3 (15 minutes): Project instruction pipeline stages for both architectures side-by-side. Students must verbally recite, in sequence, all pipeline stages (Fetch, Decode, Rename, Schedule, Execute, Writeback, Retire) along with the maximum number of instructions that can be processed simultaneously at each stage. Use the provided answer key to verify accuracy immediately.

Conclude with a 5-minute rapid-fire session where students stand and respond to random architecture questions within 3 seconds per question.
materials_needed: Advanced Architecture Reference Sheets with Intel Core i9-12900K and AMD Ryzen 9 5950X detailed block diagrams
Digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet) pre-loaded with 200+ architecture terms
Blank CPU diagram worksheets (2 per student)
Stopwatch or timer application
Projector for displaying architecture diagrams
Laminated answer keys for immediate verification
assessment_method: Students pass by achieving 90% accuracy on component identification (minimum 45/50 components correctly named), successfully completing 8/10 MESI state transitions without hesitation, and correctly reciting complete pipeline sequences for both architectures within 30 seconds each. Use the provided scoring rubric: 3 points per correctly named functional unit, 2 points per accurate cache specification, 5 points for flawless pipeline recitation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices for pipeline stages ('Few Developers Really Struggle Executing Working Recursion') and allow 5-second response time instead of 3. Advanced learners should additionally memorize branch predictor specifications, TLB sizes, and specific instruction latencies. Consider allowing advanced students to attempt ARM Cortex-A78 architecture components as extension material.

title: Analyzing Bias Propagation in Multi-Stage Machine Learning Pipelines
description: Students will examine how statistical bias compounds through feature engineering, model selection, and prediction stages in a real-world credit scoring pipeline. They will trace bias origins, quantify amplification effects, and explain the mathematical relationships between pipeline components and fairness outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will explain how selection bias in training data propagates through feature transformation and model training stages by analyzing correlation matrices and demographic parity metrics at each pipeline stage

Students will interpret the mathematical relationship between algorithmic bias and pipeline architecture through systematic examination of feature importance weights and prediction distributions across protected groups
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a pre-configured Jupyter notebook containing a credit scoring dataset with demographic information and three pipeline variations (basic logistic regression, feature-engineered XGBoost, and ensemble model). In the first 20 minutes, students individually examine the raw dataset documentation and identify potential bias sources, recording demographic distributions and missing data patterns. Next, teams spend 40 minutes systematically running each pipeline stage while calculating fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration) after feature engineering, model training, and final predictions. Students create a bias propagation flowchart showing how initial data imbalances (e.g., 65% male applicants, income disparities) translate into prediction disparities. During the following 30 minutes, teams analyze feature importance scores and correlation matrices to identify which engineered features most amplify demographic differences. Students then examine how ensemble weighting in the third pipeline compounds these effects. In the final 20 minutes, each team presents their bias propagation flowchart to another team, explaining the mathematical connections between pipeline design choices and fairness outcomes. Teams must demonstrate understanding by correctly interpreting why certain pipeline architectures amplify bias while others mitigate it, referencing specific statistical measures and their changes across pipeline stages.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded German Credit Dataset enhanced with synthetic demographic variables
Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, fairlearn, and matplotlib installed
Pipeline template code with three model architectures pre-configured
Bias metrics calculation functions and visualization templates
Digital whiteboard tool (Miro/Jamboard) for flowchart creation
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bias source identification in raw data (4 pts), (2) Correct calculation and interpretation of fairness metrics at each pipeline stage (6 pts), (3) Quality of bias propagation flowchart showing mathematical relationships between stages (6 pts), (4) Clarity of explanation during peer presentation demonstrating understanding of why specific pipeline choices amplify or mitigate bias (4 pts). Teams must achieve 16/20 points with at least 3/4 points in explanation component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed bias propagation template and highlight specific code cells to focus on. Offer guiding questions like 'How does feature scaling affect the correlation between income and approval rates?' For advanced learners, challenge them to propose pipeline modifications that could reduce bias while maintaining predictive performance, requiring them to implement and test their solutions.

title: Analyzing Bias Propagation in Multi-Stage Machine Learning Pipelines: Technical Implementation
description: Students examine how algorithmic bias compounds through interconnected stages of a real-world ML pipeline by tracing data transformations and model decisions. They will interpret bias metrics at each stage and explain how upstream biases amplify downstream outcomes in a credit scoring system.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret demographic parity and equalized odds metrics by analyzing their mathematical relationships across feature engineering, model training, and prediction stages
Students will explain the mechanism of bias amplification through examining how preprocessing decisions affect model fairness outcomes in subsequent pipeline stages
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-built credit scoring pipeline containing four stages: raw data, feature engineering, model training, and final predictions. Distribute the pipeline documentation showing demographic breakdowns and fairness metrics (demographic parity, equalized odds, calibration) calculated at each stage. 

In teams of 3-4, students spend 20 minutes examining Stage 1 data, identifying initial disparities in approval rates across demographic groups. They calculate baseline demographic parity ratios and document findings in provided worksheets. Next, students analyze Stage 2 feature engineering outputs, comparing how correlation-based feature selection affects different demographic groups. They interpret how removing certain features impacts the representation of protected groups in the feature space.

For Stage 3, students examine model training metrics, focusing on how class imbalance correction (SMOTE oversampling) applied unequally across demographics affects equalized odds ratios. They interpret ROC curves stratified by demographic groups and explain differences in false positive/negative rates. Finally, students trace how threshold optimization in Stage 4 compounds previous biases, interpreting calibration plots to understand how prediction confidence varies across groups.

Students complete bias propagation diagrams showing mathematical relationships between stages, annotating how each transformation either mitigates or amplifies disparities. They write explanations connecting preprocessing choices to final fairness outcomes, demonstrating understanding of causal relationships in the pipeline. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where groups explain one specific bias amplification mechanism they identified.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded credit scoring pipeline and datasets
Fairness metrics calculation worksheets with demographic breakdowns
Bias propagation diagram templates
Access to Python libraries: scikit-learn, fairlearn, matplotlib
Pipeline documentation with stage-by-stage metric summaries
assessment_method: Evaluate completed bias propagation diagrams for accuracy of mathematical relationships (40 points), written explanations demonstrating causal understanding of bias amplification mechanisms (40 points), and presentation quality showing clear interpretation of fairness metrics (20 points). Success requires correctly identifying at least 3 bias amplification points and accurately explaining the mathematical relationship between upstream preprocessing and downstream fairness outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed examples of demographic parity calculations for the first stage and guided questions for interpreting ROC curves. Offer visual flowcharts showing pipeline dependencies. For advanced learners, introduce additional fairness metrics (individual fairness, counterfactual fairness) and challenge them to propose specific interventions at each stage with predicted impact calculations.
original_title: Analyzing Bias Propagation in Multi-Stage Machine Learning Pipelines

title: Pizza Party Budget Planning: Applying Percentage Calculations
description: Students will plan a realistic class pizza party by applying percentage calculations to determine costs, taxes, tips, and discounts. They will use real restaurant menus and calculate the total budget needed for their class celebration.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine sales tax, delivery fees, and tip amounts by working with authentic restaurant pricing scenarios
Students will calculate percentage discounts and markups through hands-on budget planning for a class event
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and provide each group with printed pizza restaurant menus and calculators (15 minutes setup). Explain that each group must plan a pizza party for exactly 24 students, with each student eating 2 slices on average, and large pizzas having 8 slices each. Groups calculate they need 6 large pizzas total.

Step 1 (10 minutes): Groups select 6 different pizza varieties from the menu and calculate the subtotal cost. They must show their addition work clearly.

Step 2 (10 minutes): Students apply the local sales tax rate of 8.5% to their subtotal. They must convert the percentage to decimal form (0.085) and multiply, then add this tax amount to their subtotal to get a new total.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Groups apply a 15% tip calculation to their after-tax total (since tips are calculated on the tax-inclusive amount). They show the decimal conversion (0.15) and multiplication process.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Present each group with a different discount scenario: Group A gets 10% off the original subtotal, Group B gets free delivery (saving $3.50), Group C gets a buy-5-get-1-free deal. Groups recalculate their final totals incorporating these discounts.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each group presents their final budget breakdown on the whiteboard, showing original cost, tax calculation, tip calculation, discount applied, and final total. Other groups verify calculations using their calculators.

Conclude by having students compare which group achieved the lowest total cost and discuss how different percentage applications affected their budgets.
materials_needed: Printed pizza restaurant menus (4-5 different menus)
Basic calculators (1 per student)
Worksheet template with calculation spaces
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly applies all percentage calculations with proper decimal conversions and shows complete work; (3) Correctly applies most percentage calculations with minor computational errors; (2) Shows understanding of percentage application but makes several calculation mistakes; (1) Attempts percentage calculations but shows significant misunderstanding of the process. Also assess final budget presentation for accuracy and completeness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide percentage-to-decimal conversion charts and encourage use of the formula 'percentage ÷ 100 = decimal.' Break down multi-step problems into smaller chunks. For advanced learners: Add compound scenarios like 'What if we ordered drinks with 12% markup and applied a group discount?' or have them calculate per-student costs and create different budget tiers.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Search Methods Through Performance Profiling
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of linear search versus binary search algorithms by implementing both methods, measuring their performance with datasets of varying sizes, and creating comparative visualizations. This activity develops critical thinking about algorithm efficiency and trade-offs in real-world applications.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity differences between linear and binary search algorithms by implementing both methods and measuring execution times across datasets of 100, 1000, 10000, and 100000 elements
Students will evaluate the space complexity and preprocessing requirements of each search method through systematic performance testing and data visualization
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and distributing the provided starter code template containing skeleton functions for both search algorithms. In the first 20 minutes, students implement linear_search() and binary_search() functions using the pseudocode references provided. Next, students create four test datasets: sorted integer arrays of sizes 100, 1K, 10K, and 100K elements using the provided data generator script. For the following 30 minutes, students run timed tests by searching for elements at three positions: beginning (index 0), middle, and end of each dataset. They record execution times in the provided spreadsheet template, running each test 10 times and calculating averages. Students then create line graphs plotting dataset size versus average execution time for both algorithms using matplotlib or Excel. In the final 25 minutes, pairs analyze their results by answering guided questions: Which algorithm performs better with larger datasets? How does target element position affect each algorithm? What preprocessing is required for binary search? Students conclude by writing a 200-word analysis comparing theoretical Big O notation (O(n) vs O(log n)) with their empirical results, identifying any discrepancies and explaining real-world implications for database searches, user interfaces, and system performance.
materials_needed: Python development environment (IDLE, PyCharm, or VS Code)
Starter code template with skeleton functions and imports
Data generator script for creating test datasets
Results recording spreadsheet template
Algorithm pseudocode reference sheets
Matplotlib library or Excel for graphing
assessment_method: Grade using rubric (100 points total): Correct algorithm implementations (30 points), accurate data collection with proper timing methodology (25 points), clear comparative graphs with appropriate labels and scales (20 points), written analysis demonstrating understanding of complexity trade-offs and real-world applications (25 points). Students must submit working code, completed data tables, graphs, and written analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed linear search as example, offer debugging checklist, and allow use of simplified 10-element datasets initially. For advanced learners: Add interpolation search implementation, analyze memory usage with memory_profiler library, or extend to compare sorting algorithm complexities (bubble sort vs quicksort vs merge sort).

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Emergency Response Systems
description: Students will create a comprehensive mathematical optimization model that integrates graph theory, probability distributions, and linear programming to solve real-world emergency response allocation problems. They will develop original algorithms and present solutions with complete mathematical justification and computational implementation.
estimated_duration: 315 minutes (5.25 hours) - can be split across multiple sessions
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-objective optimization model incorporating graph theory and stochastic processes by analyzing real emergency response data and constraints
Students will design novel algorithmic solutions through original mathematical proofs and computational implementations using advanced mathematical software
instructions:
Begin by providing students with real emergency response data from a metropolitan area including: hospital locations, ambulance stations, historical call patterns, and traffic data (30 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Modeler, Algorithm Developer, Data Analyst, and Implementation Specialist. 

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the dataset to identify key variables, constraints, and optimization objectives. They must formulate the problem mathematically, defining decision variables, objective functions (minimizing response time while maximizing coverage), and constraints (resource limitations, capacity bounds, regulatory requirements). Students create preliminary mathematical models using systems of equations, probability distributions for demand forecasting, and graph-theoretic representations of the transportation network.

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Teams develop their optimization algorithms, choosing from linear programming, integer programming, heuristic methods, or hybrid approaches. They must provide mathematical proofs for algorithm correctness and complexity analysis. Students implement their solutions using MATLAB, Python with optimization libraries, or R, creating functional code that processes the real data.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Teams validate their models through sensitivity analysis, testing edge cases, and comparing results against current systems. They prepare comprehensive presentations including: problem formulation, mathematical derivations, algorithmic development, computational results, and recommendations for implementation.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents their complete solution to simulate a city council meeting, defending their mathematical choices and responding to technical questions from peers acting as city officials, emergency responders, and budget analysts.
materials_needed: Real emergency response dataset from metropolitan area (CSV format)
MATLAB, Python with SciPy/PuLP libraries, or R with optimization packages
Graph paper and mathematical reference materials
Digital presentation tools and large display screens
Calculators and laptop computers for each team
assessment_method: Evaluate using comprehensive rubric (100 points total): Mathematical Model Formulation (25 points - correctness of variables, constraints, objectives), Algorithm Development (25 points - originality, proof of correctness, complexity analysis), Implementation Quality (20 points - functional code, handles real data, produces valid results), Mathematical Communication (20 points - clear derivations, proper notation, logical flow), Innovation and Feasibility (10 points - creative approaches, practical applicability). Students submit written reports with complete mathematical derivations, documented code, and executive summary for city planners.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template frameworks for model formulation, offer simplified datasets with fewer variables, and supply pseudocode examples for common optimization algorithms. Create checkpoint consultations every 45 minutes to review progress. For advanced learners: Introduce multi-objective optimization techniques, incorporate machine learning for demand prediction, or extend to dynamic/real-time optimization scenarios. Encourage exploration of metaheuristic algorithms or game-theoretic approaches for resource allocation conflicts.

title: Comparing and Contrasting Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning Through Algorithm Classification
description: Students will analyze 12 different machine learning algorithms and classify them as supervised or unsupervised learning approaches. They will then explain the reasoning behind their classifications by identifying key characteristics and comparing the fundamental differences between these two learning paradigms.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms by analyzing algorithm characteristics and data requirements
Students will explain the fundamental differences between supervised and unsupervised learning through structured comparison and classification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Algorithm Classification Worksheet containing 12 algorithm cards (Linear Regression, K-Means Clustering, Decision Trees, Principal Component Analysis, Random Forest, DBSCAN, Support Vector Machines, Hierarchical Clustering, Naive Bayes, Association Rules, Logistic Regression, and Gaussian Mixture Models). Each card includes the algorithm name, a brief description, and sample use cases. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to sort these cards into two piles: 'Supervised Learning' and 'Unsupervised Learning.' During sorting, pairs must document their reasoning for each classification on the worksheet. Next, conduct a 10-minute class discussion where each pair shares their classifications for 2-3 algorithms, explaining their reasoning. Create a master classification chart on the whiteboard, noting any disagreements for further discussion. For the final 20 minutes, students individually complete a comparison matrix worksheet with columns for 'Supervised Learning' and 'Unsupervised Learning' and rows for: 'Data Requirements,' 'Goal/Purpose,' 'Output Type,' 'Evaluation Methods,' and 'Common Applications.' Students fill in each cell with specific characteristics, then write a 3-sentence summary explaining the key difference between the two approaches. Conclude with a 5-minute partner share where students compare their matrices and refine their understanding.
materials_needed: Algorithm Classification Worksheet with 12 pre-made algorithm cards
Comparison Matrix Template (printed for each student)
Whiteboard and markers for class discussion
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 3-point rubric: (1) Algorithm Classification Accuracy - correctly classifies at least 10/12 algorithms with logical reasoning documented; (2) Comparison Matrix Completion - accurately identifies 4/5 key characteristics for each learning type with specific examples; (3) Summary Statement - demonstrates clear understanding of fundamental differences in 3-sentence explanation using proper terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed comparison matrix with 2-3 examples filled in, and offer a word bank of key terms (labeled data, clustering, prediction, pattern discovery). For advanced learners: Add semi-supervised learning as a third category and include more complex algorithms like ensemble methods or deep learning approaches. Consider having advanced students create their own algorithm cards for peer classification.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization for Warehouse Distribution Network
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world logistics problem by determining optimal warehouse locations and inventory levels to minimize total distribution costs. They will work with constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers and analyze the economic implications of their mathematical solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems by finding critical points in multi-variable cost functions with realistic business constraints
Students will implement partial derivative techniques to minimize total distribution costs through systematic mathematical modeling of supply chain variables
instructions: Begin by distributing the warehouse scenario worksheet containing a fictional company with 5 retail locations needing supply from 2-3 potential warehouse sites. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Students analyze the given data including customer demand (D₁-D₅), transportation costs per unit per mile (c), warehouse fixed costs (F₁-F₃), and coordinate locations. They must identify decision variables: warehouse locations (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂), (x₃,y₃) and inventory levels I₁, I₂, I₃. Phase 2 (35 minutes): Students construct the total cost function C = Σ[Fᵢ + cᵢIᵢ + Σⱼ(transportation cost from warehouse i to store j)] subject to constraints: ΣIᵢ ≥ ΣDⱼ (supply meets demand) and Iᵢ ≥ 0. They set up the Lagrangian L = C + λ(constraint). Phase 3 (25 minutes): Students calculate all partial derivatives ∂L/∂xᵢ, ∂L/∂yᵢ, ∂L/∂Iᵢ, ∂L/∂λ and solve the resulting system of equations. They must use the second partial derivative test to verify their critical points represent minima. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Students interpret results by calculating total minimum cost, optimal warehouse coordinates, and optimal inventory distribution, then write a brief business recommendation explaining why their mathematical solution makes economic sense.
materials_needed: Warehouse Distribution Scenario worksheets with specific company data and coordinates
Graphing calculators or computers with mathematical software (Desmos, GeoGebra, or similar)
Grid paper for plotting warehouse locations and store positions
Reference sheets with Lagrange multiplier formulas and second derivative test procedures
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification and setup of cost function with all variables and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier method with all partial derivatives calculated correctly (35%), (3) Proper verification using second derivative test and correct solution of the system (25%), (4) Clear business interpretation connecting mathematical results to practical recommendations (15%). Students must submit their worksheet with all calculations shown plus a written paragraph explaining their final recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template showing the general form of the Lagrangian and highlight which terms represent fixed costs vs. variable costs. Offer a simplified version with only 2 stores and 1 warehouse initially. For advanced learners: Add additional constraints such as warehouse capacity limits, minimum service radius requirements, or time-dependent demand fluctuations. Challenge them to consider the sensitivity analysis by examining how solutions change when transportation costs increase by 10-20%.

title: Critical Analysis of Distributed System Failure Patterns in Netflix's Microservices Architecture
description: Students will forensically examine Netflix's documented system failures from 2019-2022, decompose the root causes across multiple architectural layers, and synthesize failure pattern classifications. This expert-level analysis requires students to dissect complex distributed system interactions and evaluate cascading failure mechanisms in production environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure modes by deconstructing real Netflix outage reports and identifying causal relationships between microservice dependencies
Students will evaluate architectural design decisions through systematic examination of failure propagation patterns and recovery strategies in large-scale systems
instructions: Begin with individual preparation (45 minutes): Each student receives three Netflix outage post-mortems from different years (AWS S3 outage impact 2017, API gateway failures 2019, CDN cascading failures 2021). Students must create failure timeline diagrams mapping service dependencies and identify primary/secondary failure points. Form expert groups of 3-4 students (60 minutes): Groups collaborate to categorize failure patterns using distributed systems taxonomy (Byzantine failures, network partitions, cascading overloads, dependency failures). Each group creates a comprehensive failure analysis matrix documenting: failure trigger, affected services, propagation path, detection time, mitigation strategy, and prevention measures. Groups must identify architectural anti-patterns and propose alternative designs using circuit breaker patterns, bulkhead isolation, or graceful degradation. Transition to presentation phase (90 minutes): Each group presents 15-minute analysis focusing on one specific failure category, followed by 10-minute peer review sessions where other groups challenge assumptions and propose alternative interpretations. Groups must defend their analysis using evidence from system logs, performance metrics, and architectural documentation. Final synthesis (30 minutes): Individual students write executive summaries comparing failure patterns across all cases, ranking architectural vulnerabilities by business impact, and recommending specific design patterns for prevention. Students must justify recommendations using quantitative metrics (MTTR, availability percentages, customer impact data) extracted from the case studies.
materials_needed: Netflix Engineering Blog post-mortem reports (3 specific outage cases)
Digital whiteboard software (Miro or equivalent) for timeline creation
Distributed Systems textbook excerpts on failure patterns
Netflix architecture diagrams and service dependency maps
Laptop computers with internet access for research
assessment_method: Grade based on four components: (1) Failure timeline accuracy and completeness (25 points), (2) Quality of pattern categorization and evidence-based reasoning (30 points), (3) Effectiveness of peer review challenges and defenses during presentations (25 points), (4) Executive summary demonstrating synthesis across cases with quantified recommendations (20 points). Success requires demonstrating deep understanding of distributed systems principles through concrete analysis rather than theoretical knowledge.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing failure pattern templates and guided questions for timeline creation. Offer additional Netflix case studies for reference. For advanced learners, introduce chaos engineering concepts and ask them to design failure injection experiments that would have detected these issues proactively. Provide access to academic papers on distributed systems reliability for deeper theoretical grounding.

title: Evaluating Data Quality and Visualization Choices in Customer Survey Analysis
description: Students will critically assess a pre-analyzed customer satisfaction dataset, evaluating both the data cleaning decisions and visualization choices made by a fictional analyst. They will judge the appropriateness of methods used and recommend improvements based on data science best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate data cleaning decisions by assessing the impact of missing value treatments and outlier handling on dataset integrity
Students will judge the effectiveness of visualization choices through systematic comparison against data communication principles
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Customer Survey Analysis Package' containing: original messy dataset (200 customer responses with 15% missing values, 3 clear outliers), the cleaned dataset, documentation of cleaning steps taken, and 4 visualizations (bar chart of satisfaction ratings, scatter plot of age vs satisfaction, pie chart of product categories, line graph of monthly trends). **Individual Review Phase (15 minutes):** Students examine the original dataset and cleaned version, noting specific cleaning decisions made. They then review each visualization and the analyst's written summary. **Evaluation Worksheet Completion (20 minutes):** Students complete the structured evaluation form rating each cleaning decision (1-5 scale) and each visualization (1-5 scale) with required written justifications. For data cleaning, they assess: appropriateness of missing value method, outlier treatment, and data type conversions. For visualizations, they evaluate: chart type selection, clarity of labels, appropriate use of color, and alignment with the intended message. **Recommendation Development (10 minutes):** Students write 2-3 specific improvement recommendations for both data cleaning and visualization, explaining why their suggested changes would enhance the analysis quality. **Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange evaluation sheets with a partner, discuss their assessments, and note any significant differences in judgment.
materials_needed: Customer Survey Analysis Package (digital files: original dataset CSV, cleaned dataset CSV, cleaning documentation PDF)
Data Quality & Visualization Evaluation Worksheet (printable PDF)
Access to Excel or Google Sheets for data examination
Evaluation rubric handout
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of data quality assessment - correctly identifies strengths/weaknesses in cleaning decisions (25%), (2) Visualization critique quality - demonstrates understanding of effective data communication principles (25%), (3) Justification depth - provides specific, evidence-based reasoning for ratings given (25%), (4) Improvement recommendations - offers actionable, appropriate suggestions with clear explanations (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate proficiency in evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of specific data quality indicators to look for (completeness, consistency, accuracy) and a visual guide showing examples of effective vs. ineffective charts. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets with more complex issues (duplicate records, inconsistent formatting) and ask them to evaluate the statistical appropriateness of any analysis methods used beyond basic descriptive statistics.

title: Design Your Dream City: Linear Function Transportation Network
description: Students create an original city layout using coordinate geometry and design a transportation system using linear functions. They will construct mathematical models that represent real-world transit routes and optimize connections between key city locations.
estimated_duration: 115 minutes (can be split across two class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a coordinate-based city map by placing at least 8 key locations and designing linear function equations that represent efficient transportation routes between them
Students will synthesize slope, y-intercept, and systems of equations concepts through creating an original transit network that minimizes travel distances and transfer points
instructions: Begin by distributing coordinate plane paper and having students work in pairs (5 minutes setup). Students first design their city by plotting 8-10 key locations (hospital, school, mall, airport, etc.) on a coordinate grid with scale 1 unit = 1 kilometer, ensuring points are distributed across all four quadrants (15 minutes). Next, students identify the 5 most important location pairs that need direct transit connections, considering factors like emergency access and daily commute patterns (10 minutes). For each of the 5 connections, students calculate the linear equation in slope-intercept form that represents the most direct route, showing all algebraic work including slope calculation using rise/run formula (25 minutes). Students then create a comprehensive transit map by drawing and labeling all 5 routes on their coordinate plane, using different colors for each line and including the equation directly on each route (15 minutes). To optimize their network, students identify intersection points by solving systems of equations for routes that cross, marking these as transfer stations (20 minutes). Finally, students calculate total network length by finding the distance of each route using the distance formula, then write a 150-word justification explaining their design choices and how their linear functions create an efficient transportation system (15 minutes). Conclude with pairs presenting one route equation and explaining their reasoning to the class (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Coordinate plane paper (4 quadrants, numbered -20 to +20)
Colored pencils or markers (minimum 5 colors)
Scientific calculators
Rulers
City planning reference sheet with common municipal locations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct linear equations and calculations - 25 points), Creative Design (logical city layout and route selection - 20 points), Problem-Solving (effective use of intersections and optimization strategies - 25 points), Communication (clear justification and presentation - 20 points), Professional Presentation (neat, labeled diagram with organized work - 10 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving at least 3/4 points in Mathematical Accuracy and Problem-Solving categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide slope calculation template, offer pre-selected coordinate points, and allow use of graphing software for verification. Pair weaker students with stronger partners and provide step-by-step equation-writing checklist. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate quadratic functions for curved routes, calculate optimal route timing using rate problems, or design a budget constraint requiring cost-per-kilometer analysis. Extension: Create a second transportation mode (subway) using parallel and perpendicular line concepts.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Flash Card Marathon
description: Students will memorize and recall specific Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notations for 25 advanced algorithms and data structure operations. This intensive recall activity focuses on instant recognition of complexity classifications for sophisticated computational procedures including graph algorithms, advanced sorting methods, and complex data structure operations.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the exact time and space complexity notations for 25 advanced algorithms including Dijkstra's algorithm, A* search, and red-black tree operations by completing timed flash card exercises
Students will identify precise Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta classifications for complex data structure operations through rapid-fire verbal recitation sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made flash card deck containing 25 advanced algorithms on one side and their complexity notations on the reverse. Each card includes: algorithm name, brief description, time complexity (best, average, worst case), and space complexity. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes total. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Student A shows algorithm names to Student B, who must recite exact complexity notations including Big O for worst case, Big Omega for best case, and Big Theta for average case where applicable. Cover algorithms like: Dijkstra's shortest path (O(V²) or O(E + V log V) with heap), Bellman-Ford (O(VE)), Floyd-Warshall (O(V³)), A* search (O(b^d)), quicksort variants, merge sort, heap operations, AVL tree rotations, red-black tree insertions, hash table operations with collision resolution, and advanced graph traversals. Phase 2 (15 minutes): Switch roles. Student B quizzes Student A. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Individual speed round using digital timer. Each student goes through entire deck alone, aiming for under 10 seconds per card. Instructor calls time every 30 seconds, students mark their position. Record completion rate and accuracy. Students must state complete notation (e.g., 'time complexity O of E plus V log V, space complexity O of V') not abbreviated forms. Conclude with whole-class rapid-fire session where instructor randomly calls algorithms and students shout out complexities.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flash cards with 25 advanced algorithms and complexity notations
Digital stopwatch or timer app
Algorithm complexity reference sheet for instructor verification
Student progress tracking sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) in final individual speed round and complete deck within 8 minutes. Assessment includes: exact notation recall (3 points each), proper Big O/Omega/Theta usage (2 points each), and speed benchmarks (5 bonus points for sub-6 minute completion). Total possible: 125 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for common patterns (e.g., 'graph algorithms often O(V²) or O(E log V)'), allow reference to complexity hierarchy chart during first round, extend time limits by 25%. For advanced learners: include amortized analysis complexities, add space-time tradeoff variations, challenge them to explain why specific complexities apply, introduce less common algorithms like Johnson's algorithm or persistent data structures.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results and Model Selection Trade-offs in Ensemble Learning
description: Students will analyze and interpret comprehensive cross-validation results from multiple ensemble models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost) applied to a high-dimensional dataset. They will explain the implications of bias-variance trade-offs, overfitting patterns, and computational efficiency considerations when selecting optimal hyperparameters and model architectures.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation metrics (ROC-AUC, precision-recall curves, learning curves) by analyzing variance patterns across folds and explaining their implications for model generalization
Students will explain the relationship between ensemble hyperparameters and bias-variance trade-offs through systematic comparison of validation curves and feature importance distributions
instructions:
Begin by providing students with pre-computed cross-validation results from three ensemble models trained on a customer churn dataset (10,000 samples, 50+ features). Distribute comprehensive results packages including: 5-fold CV scores, validation curves for key hyperparameters (n_estimators, max_depth, learning_rate), learning curves, feature importance rankings, and training times. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine the cross-validation score distributions, calculating mean, standard deviation, and confidence intervals for each model. They identify which model shows highest variance across folds and hypothesize reasons.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students analyze validation curves for Random Forest (n_estimators: 10-500, max_depth: 3-20) and XGBoost (learning_rate: 0.01-0.3, max_depth: 3-10). They must identify optimal hyperparameter ranges and explain overfitting/underfitting patterns by comparing training vs. validation performance trajectories.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams of 4 create comparative analysis matrices examining: (a) computational efficiency vs. performance trade-offs, (b) feature importance stability across CV folds, and (c) learning curve behavior indicating data sufficiency. Each team receives different ensemble configurations to analyze.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams present 3-minute interpretations of their findings, specifically addressing: Why does XGBoost show different bias-variance characteristics than Random Forest? How do hyperparameter choices affect model interpretability? When would computational constraints influence model selection decisions?

Step 5 (10 minutes): Instructor facilitates discussion connecting observations to real-world deployment scenarios, emphasizing production considerations like model updating frequency and inference latency requirements.
materials_needed: Pre-computed CV results dataset (CSV files with 15+ metrics per model)
Jupyter notebooks with visualization code templates
Customer churn dataset documentation with feature descriptions
Validation curve plotting functions (matplotlib/seaborn)
Model comparison matrix templates (Excel/Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Students submit individual written interpretations (500-750 words) addressing: (1) Explanation of CV variance patterns with statistical evidence, (2) Analysis of hyperparameter-performance relationships with specific examples, (3) Justified model selection recommendation considering bias-variance-complexity trade-offs, (4) Discussion of deployment implications. Rubric: Statistical accuracy (25%), Depth of hyperparameter analysis (25%), Model selection justification (25%), Production considerations (25%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide interpretation guide with example phrases for describing validation curves and statistical significance templates. Include glossary of ensemble-specific terms. For advanced learners: Add Bayesian optimization results for comparison, include time-series cross-validation scenarios, or provide multi-objective optimization results considering fairness metrics alongside performance.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Models for Customer Churn Prediction Using Multiple Performance Frameworks
description: Students will critically evaluate and compare three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network) for predicting customer churn using a telecommunications dataset. They will assess model performance using multiple evaluation frameworks including statistical metrics, business impact analysis, and fairness considerations to recommend the optimal solution for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning algorithms by systematically comparing performance metrics, computational requirements, and interpretability trade-offs within a business context
Students will critique model fairness and bias through demographic parity analysis and recommend ethical deployment strategies for the selected algorithm
instructions: Step 1 (30 mins): Provide students with a pre-processed telecommunications customer dataset containing 5,000 records with features including demographics, usage patterns, and service metrics. Students work in teams of 3-4 to explore the dataset and establish baseline understanding of the churn prediction problem. Step 2 (45 mins): Each team implements three models using provided starter code templates: Random Forest (sklearn), XGBoost (xgboost library), and Neural Network (TensorFlow/Keras). Teams must document hyperparameter choices and training procedures. Step 3 (60 mins): Teams calculate comprehensive performance metrics for each model including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and create confusion matrices. They also measure training time, inference speed, and memory usage. Step 4 (45 mins): Conduct business impact analysis by calculating potential revenue loss/savings based on false positives (unnecessary retention efforts costing $50 per customer) and false negatives (lost customers worth $500 annual revenue). Step 5 (30 mins): Perform fairness evaluation by analyzing model predictions across demographic groups (age, gender, region) using demographic parity and equalized odds metrics. Step 6 (45 mins): Teams create comprehensive evaluation matrix comparing all three models across technical performance, business impact, computational efficiency, interpretability, and fairness dimensions. Step 7 (30 mins): Each team presents 10-minute recommendation with supporting evidence, addressing deployment considerations, monitoring strategies, and potential risks.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer dataset (CSV file with 5,000 records, 15 features)
Jupyter Notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Pre-installed libraries: pandas, scikit-learn, xgboost, tensorflow, matplotlib, seaborn
Model evaluation template spreadsheet
Business case scenario document with cost parameters
assessment_method: Students submit a comprehensive evaluation report (8-10 pages) containing: (1) Technical performance comparison table with statistical significance tests (25 points), (2) Business impact analysis with ROI calculations (20 points), (3) Fairness assessment with bias mitigation recommendations (20 points), (4) Final model recommendation with deployment strategy (20 points), (5) Risk assessment and monitoring plan (15 points). Presentations evaluated on clarity of reasoning, evidence quality, and response to questions. Rubric includes criteria for depth of analysis, methodological rigor, and practical applicability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide detailed evaluation metric calculation examples and interpretation guides. Offer pre-built visualization templates for model comparison. Create checkpoint reviews after Steps 3 and 5. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional algorithms (SVM, ensemble methods), conduct cross-validation with different splits, perform feature importance analysis, or explore advanced fairness metrics like individual fairness. Encourage investigation of model explainability using SHAP values or LIME.

title: Designing a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Urban Traffic Flow Management
description: Students will construct an original mathematical model using calculus, linear programming, and statistical analysis to optimize traffic light timing across a simulated city grid. They will develop algorithms, validate their model with real traffic data, and present implementation strategies to address urban congestion problems.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across 3-4 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from multivariable calculus, linear programming, and probability theory by creating an original traffic optimization model that minimizes wait times across multiple intersections
Students will design and justify a comprehensive mathematical solution through iterative testing, data validation, and algorithmic refinement of their traffic management system
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Distribute the urban grid template showing a 4x4 intersection network with provided traffic flow data from morning, afternoon, and evening rush hours. Teams first analyze the baseline data to identify bottlenecks and patterns using statistical methods (45 minutes). Next, students formulate their optimization problem by defining variables (light timing intervals, traffic volume rates, queue lengths), constraints (minimum/maximum light durations, safety requirements, pedestrian crossing times), and objective functions (minimize total wait time, maximize throughput, reduce emissions). This mathematical modeling phase requires 90 minutes. Students then develop their solution algorithm, choosing between linear programming simplex method, gradient descent optimization, or genetic algorithms, justifying their choice based on problem complexity (60 minutes). Implementation follows using Excel Solver, Python optimization libraries, or MATLAB, where teams code their solution and run simulations (75 minutes). Validation occurs by testing the model against provided real-world traffic data from three different cities, calculating improvement percentages and identifying failure cases (45 minutes). Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation including their mathematical formulation, algorithm choice rationale, simulation results, and implementation recommendations for city planners, followed by peer evaluation using provided rubrics (60 minutes total for all presentations).
materials_needed: Urban traffic grid templates with intersection layouts
Real traffic flow datasets from 3 different cities (CSV format)
Access to Excel with Solver add-in or Python with SciPy/PuLP libraries
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Presentation software and projection equipment
Peer evaluation rubrics printed for each student
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model formulation and accuracy (25 points), algorithm selection and implementation (25 points), validation methodology and results analysis (20 points), presentation clarity and professional recommendations (20 points), peer collaboration and process documentation (10 points). Success requires demonstrating measurable improvement over baseline traffic patterns, mathematically sound constraint handling, and realistic implementation considerations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing optimization problem templates and guided questions for constraint identification. Offer algorithm pseudocode examples and debugging checkpoints. For advanced learners, introduce dynamic programming approaches, consider multi-objective optimization with environmental factors, or incorporate machine learning for adaptive traffic prediction. Provide optional extension: compare their model results with actual smart traffic systems from Singapore or Barcelona.

title: Optimization in Manufacturing: Applying Calculus to Minimize Packaging Costs
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and constrained optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem involving minimizing material costs for cylindrical containers. They will use Lagrange multipliers and partial derivatives to determine optimal dimensions while meeting volume requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to minimize surface area of cylindrical packaging given specific volume constraints
Students will implement partial differentiation and critical point analysis through solving authentic manufacturing cost optimization problems
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and distributing the manufacturing scenario packets (15 minutes). Each team receives a different product scenario: Team A (soup cans, 400ml volume), Team B (paint cans, 1 liter volume), Team C (coffee cans, 750ml volume), Team D (motor oil containers, 946ml volume). Students must minimize the surface area function S = 2πr² + 2πrh subject to the volume constraint V = πr²h = constant. First, teams spend 20 minutes setting up their constrained optimization problem, defining variables, and writing the Lagrangian function L(r,h,λ) = 2πr² + 2πrh - λ(πr²h - V). Next, they calculate partial derivatives ∂L/∂r, ∂L/∂h, and ∂L/∂λ, setting each equal to zero (25 minutes). Using graphing calculators or computer algebra systems, teams solve the resulting system of equations to find critical points (20 minutes). They must verify their solution represents a minimum using the second derivative test or by comparing with boundary values (15 minutes). Each team then calculates the actual optimal radius and height for their assigned container volume, determines the minimum surface area, and computes material cost savings compared to a baseline cylindrical design with r = h (20 minutes). Finally, teams prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical work, optimal dimensions, and cost analysis with visual aids (25 minutes). Conclude with team presentations and peer feedback focusing on mathematical accuracy and real-world feasibility (30 minutes).
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario packets (4 different product types with volume specifications)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent) or laptop computers with Desmos/GeoGebra access
Grid paper and rulers for sketching constraint graphs
Material cost data sheets (aluminum, steel, plastic per square meter)
Presentation materials (whiteboards, markers, or digital presentation tools)
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Correct Lagrangian setup (20 points), accurate partial derivative calculations (25 points), proper solution of the system of equations (25 points), verification of minimum condition (15 points), realistic cost analysis with correct units (10 points), and clear mathematical presentation (5 points). Students must show all algebraic steps and provide final answers rounded to 3 decimal places.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide templates for setting up the Lagrangian function and offer guided practice with simpler 2D optimization problems first. Supply reference cards with partial derivative rules. For advanced learners: extend to rectangular box optimization with fixed volume, explore sensitivity analysis by varying the volume constraint, or investigate multi-objective optimization including both material costs and manufacturing complexity.

title: Algorithmic Complexity Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Variants
description: Students analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithm implementations by examining their code structure, tracing execution patterns, and comparing performance characteristics. They will deconstruct each algorithm's recursive calls, loop structures, and memory usage to determine Big O notation and identify optimization opportunities.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of merge sort, quicksort, and heap sort implementations by examining their recursive structures and mathematical recurrence relations
Students will evaluate space complexity trade-offs through detailed memory usage analysis and call stack examination during algorithm execution
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute three code files containing implementations of merge sort, quicksort, and heap sort in the same programming language. Each implementation should include detailed comments and be approximately 30-50 lines. Provide students with complexity analysis worksheets containing sections for: recurrence relations, loop analysis, memory usage tracking, and Big O conclusions.

**Phase 1 - Individual Code Analysis (45 minutes):** Students examine each sorting algorithm independently. For each algorithm, they must: (1) Identify all loops and recursive calls, documenting the input size at each level; (2) Count the number of operations performed at each recursion level or iteration; (3) Write the mathematical recurrence relation (T(n) = ...); (4) Trace through a sample execution with n=8 elements, documenting memory allocation and deallocation; (5) Calculate both time and space complexity using Big O notation.

**Phase 2 - Collaborative Verification (30 minutes):** Students form groups of 3-4 to compare their individual analyses. Each group creates a comparison matrix showing worst-case, average-case, and best-case scenarios for all three algorithms. Groups must reach consensus on their complexity calculations and identify which scenarios favor each algorithm.

**Phase 3 - Critical Evaluation (25 minutes):** Groups present their findings to the class, specifically addressing: (1) Which algorithm performs best for different input sizes and why; (2) Memory usage implications for large datasets; (3) Stability and in-place sorting considerations; (4) Real-world application scenarios where each algorithm would be optimal. Each presentation must include mathematical justification for their complexity calculations.
materials_needed: Three sorting algorithm implementations (merge sort, quicksort, heap sort) in student's programming language
Complexity analysis worksheet templates with sections for recurrence relations and Big O calculations
Sample input datasets of varying sizes (n=8, n=16, n=32) for tracing exercises
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool for group work
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of recurrence relations and Big O calculations (25 points), (2) Correctness of execution tracing and memory analysis (25 points), (3) Quality of algorithm comparison and scenario identification (25 points), (4) Mathematical justification and presentation clarity (25 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in complexity calculations and demonstrate understanding through peer explanations during group work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled recurrence relation templates and guided tracing worksheets with partially completed examples. Offer one-on-one support during individual analysis phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional variants (iterative vs recursive implementations) or extend analysis to hybrid algorithms like Introsort. Encourage exploration of cache performance and practical considerations beyond theoretical complexity.

title: Evaluating Data Cleaning Methods: Coffee Shop Sales Analysis
description: Students will assess the effectiveness of different data cleaning approaches on a messy coffee shop sales dataset. They will compare three pre-cleaned versions of the same dataset and determine which cleaning method produces the most reliable analysis results.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data cleaning strategies by comparing analysis outcomes from three cleaned datasets
Students will critique data cleaning decisions through structured comparison using quality metrics and business impact assessment
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three Excel files: 'Coffee_Sales_Original.xlsx' (with missing values, duplicates, formatting issues), 'Coffee_Sales_Method_A.xlsx', 'Coffee_Sales_Method_B.xlsx', and 'Coffee_Sales_Method_C.xlsx' (each cleaned using different approaches). Provide the 'Data Cleaning Evaluation Worksheet' template.

**Phase 1 - Dataset Exploration (15 minutes):** Students work in pairs to examine the original messy dataset and identify 5-7 specific data quality issues (missing values, inconsistent formatting, duplicates, outliers). They document these issues on their worksheet with specific row/column references.

**Phase 2 - Cleaned Dataset Analysis (25 minutes):** Each pair analyzes all three cleaned versions, documenting how each method addressed the identified issues. They calculate basic statistics (total sales, average transaction value, most popular items) for each cleaned dataset and record results in comparison tables.

**Phase 3 - Method Evaluation (20 minutes):** Using provided criteria (data completeness, business logic preservation, statistical accuracy), students rate each cleaning method on a 1-5 scale with written justifications. They identify which method they would recommend and why, considering trade-offs between data retention and accuracy.

**Phase 4 - Peer Review (10 minutes):** Pairs exchange worksheets with another team to review recommendations and provide feedback on evaluation reasoning.

**Wrap-up (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief presentations where 3-4 pairs share their top-rated method and key evaluation criteria, highlighting different perspectives on the same data.
materials_needed: Coffee_Sales_Original.xlsx (messy dataset with 500 rows)
Three pre-cleaned versions of the dataset using different methods
Data Cleaning Evaluation Worksheet template (Word/PDF)
Computers with Excel or Google Sheets access
Evaluation criteria rubric handout
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate identification of data quality issues in original dataset (25%), (2) Complete analysis of all three cleaning methods with supporting evidence (35%), (3) Clear justification for recommended method using provided criteria (25%), (4) Quality of peer feedback and participation in discussions (15%). Successful completion requires scoring at least 3/4 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of the first 2-3 rows of analysis, offer guided questions for evaluation criteria, and pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose their own fourth cleaning method, calculate additional statistical measures (correlation, variance), or consider how different business contexts might change their recommendations.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City Block with Mathematical Justification
description: Students will create an original scale model of a city block using geometric principles, proportional reasoning, and area/volume calculations. They must mathematically justify all design decisions and demonstrate how their model accurately represents real-world measurements and spatial relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city block layout by applying geometric principles, scale factors, and proportional reasoning to create accurate building dimensions and street layouts
Students will construct a mathematical justification report through detailed calculations of areas, perimeters, volumes, and scale conversions that validate their design choices
instructions:
Step 1 (15 minutes): Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute city planning packets containing: sample city block dimensions (200m × 150m), building type requirements (2 residential, 1 commercial, 1 public building), and zoning restrictions (buildings must occupy 60-75% of available space, minimum 3m between structures). 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams research real building dimensions online and create a planning document listing: chosen scale ratio (1:500 or 1:1000), actual building dimensions, scaled dimensions, and preliminary layout sketch. Instructor circulates to approve scale choices and building selections.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Using graph paper, teams create detailed scale drawings showing: building footprints with labeled dimensions, street layouts, green spaces, and parking areas. All measurements must be calculated and clearly marked. Students must show mathematical work for area calculations and verify their 60-75% space usage requirement.

Step 4 (35 minutes): Teams construct 3D models using cardboard and craft materials. Buildings must reflect accurate scaled heights and proportions. Students create measurement labels showing both scale and actual dimensions for each structure.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams prepare mathematical justification presentations including: scale factor explanation, area/perimeter calculations for each building, total space utilization percentage, and volume calculations for at least two 3D structures. Each team member must present one mathematical component.

Step 6 (15 minutes): Teams present their models and mathematical justifications to the class, explaining design decisions and demonstrating calculation accuracy.
materials_needed: Graph paper (1cm grid)
Cardboard sheets and craft knife
Rulers and measuring tape
Calculators
Laptops/tablets for research
Colored pencils and markers
Glue sticks and tape
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct scale calculations, area/volume computations, and proportional reasoning (25%), (2) Design Creativity - original layout meeting all constraints (20%), (3) Model Construction - accurate 3D representation with proper proportions (25%), (4) Mathematical Justification - clear explanation of all calculations and design decisions (20%), (5) Presentation - effective communication of mathematical reasoning (10%). Students must score 3+ in all categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated building dimension options and scale conversion charts. Offer step-by-step calculation templates and pair with stronger math students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include curved structures, calculate irregular areas, incorporate elevation changes, or add complex geometric features like circular parks or triangular building lots. Encourage use of technology tools for precise calculations.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Sprint
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the specific functions and protocols associated with each layer of the TCP/IP model through structured flashcard drills and timed retrieval practice. This activity focuses on building automatic recall of layer-specific protocols, data units, and primary functions essential for network troubleshooting.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the four layers of the TCP/IP model and their specific protocols (HTTP/HTTPS, TCP/UDP, IP/ICMP, Ethernet) within 30 seconds of prompting
Students will identify the correct data unit names (segments, packets, frames) and primary functions for each TCP/IP layer through rapid-fire questioning exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 32 cards covering TCP/IP layers, protocols, data units, and functions. Students work in pairs for 10 minutes using the Leitner spacing method: correctly recalled cards move to the 'mastered' pile, incorrect cards return to active study pile. Next, conduct a 15-minute individual drilling session where students use the provided digital flashcard app, cycling through randomized questions about layer functions, protocol examples, and data encapsulation terms. Follow with a 10-minute 'speed rounds' phase where Student A reads layer names/protocols from answer sheets while Student B must recall associated functions and data units within 5 seconds per item. Rotate roles after 5 minutes.
