Conclude with a 5-minute individual written recall test where students list all four layers, write three protocols per layer, name the data unit for each layer, and state the primary function of each layer from memory without references. Monitor student pairs during drilling, providing immediate correction for misconceptions about layer boundaries or protocol classifications.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (32 cards per student covering TCP/IP layers, protocols, data units)
Digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet) loaded with TCP/IP protocol stack content
Answer sheets with complete TCP/IP layer breakdown for peer checking
Individual recall test worksheets with structured blanks for layers, protocols, data units, functions
Timer for speed rounds and assessment phases
assessment_method: Grade final recall worksheets using rubric: 4 points for correct layer sequence, 12 points for protocols (3 per layer), 4 points for data unit names, 8 points for layer functions. Minimum 24/28 points indicates mastery. Observe speed round performance noting students who consistently recall information within 5-second timeframe versus those requiring prompting.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic devices ('All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for Application-Presentation-Session-Transport-Network-Data Link-Physical) and reduce protocol requirements to 2 per layer initially. Advanced learners should include port numbers for application protocols, distinguish between connection-oriented vs connectionless protocols, and memorize RFC numbers for major protocols.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Performance Trade-offs in Ensemble Methods
description: Students will analyze and explain the relationships between different feature importance measures across Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost models trained on the same dataset. They will interpret how feature rankings change between methods and explain the implications for model interpretability and business decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings from three different ensemble methods by comparing permutation importance, built-in feature importance, and SHAP values
Students will explain the trade-offs between model complexity and interpretability through systematic analysis of ensemble method characteristics
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained model suite containing Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost classifiers trained on a customer churn dataset with 15 features (demographics, usage patterns, service metrics). Distribute the analysis template containing three sections: Feature Importance Comparison, Model Performance Analysis, and Business Interpretation. In Step 1 (20 minutes), students work individually to extract and document feature importance scores using three methods for each model: built-in feature_importances_, permutation importance from sklearn, and SHAP TreeExplainer values. They must create a comparative ranking table showing top 5 features for each combination. In Step 2 (25 minutes), students analyze performance metrics (AUC-ROC, precision, recall, training time) and model complexity indicators (number of estimators, max depth, learning rate effects). They identify patterns between interpretability and performance trade-offs. In Step 3 (30 minutes), working in pairs, students interpret discrepancies in feature rankings between methods, explaining why certain features rank differently across models (e.g., correlated features, interaction effects, model-specific biases). In Step 4 (25 minutes), pairs prepare a business recommendation memo addressing: which model provides most reliable feature insights, how feature importance stability affects business trust, and recommendations for stakeholder communication. Conclude with 3-minute pair presentations of key findings and business implications.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pre-trained Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and XGBoost models
Customer churn dataset (tabular, 15 features, 5000+ samples)
Analysis template with structured comparison tables
SHAP library and scikit-learn permutation importance modules
Business interpretation memo template
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Accuracy of feature importance extraction and ranking tables (25 points), (2) Correct identification and explanation of ranking discrepancies between methods (30 points), (3) Quality of trade-off analysis linking model complexity to interpretability (25 points), (4) Business memo clarity and actionable recommendations (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining at least 3 specific reasons why feature rankings differ between ensemble methods.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example code snippets for SHAP value extraction and pre-filled partial comparison tables. Offer guiding questions like 'Why might correlated features rank differently in tree-based vs boosting methods?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze feature interactions using SHAP interaction values, compare local vs global explanations, or extend analysis to include LIME explanations for additional perspective.

title: Personal Budget Calculator: Applying Percentage Calculations to Real-Life Expenses
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional young adult by applying percentage calculations to determine spending allocations across different categories. They will use the 50/30/20 budgeting rule to calculate exact dollar amounts for needs, wants, and savings based on a given monthly income.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine budget allocations by converting percentages to dollar amounts using real income scenarios
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage operations through creating and adjusting a comprehensive personal budget spreadsheet
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a scenario card containing a fictional character profile (age 22-25) with a specific monthly after-tax income ranging from $2,800-$4,200. Explain the 50/30/20 rule: 50% for needs (rent, utilities, groceries), 30% for wants (entertainment, dining out), and 20% for savings/debt repayment. Students first calculate these three main category amounts using their character's income. Next, distribute the 'Expense Categories Worksheet' with 12 specific subcategories (rent, utilities, groceries, transportation, phone, insurance, dining out, entertainment, clothing, personal care, emergency savings, retirement savings). Students must allocate their calculated amounts across these subcategories, ensuring totals match their 50/30/20 calculations. For the final 15 minutes, students input their budget into a provided Excel template with formulas that automatically calculate percentages and flag overspending. They must adjust allocations until all categories balance perfectly. Students then present one budget decision to a partner, explaining their percentage calculation and reasoning. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify which calculations were most challenging and write one real-world application they discovered.
materials_needed: Character profile scenario cards (one per student)
Expense Categories Worksheet (printed copies)
Calculators or smartphones with calculator apps
Excel template file: 'Budget_Calculator_Template.xlsx'
Computers or tablets with Excel/Google Sheets access
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of main percentage calculations (50/30/20 from total income) - 25 points, (2) Correct allocation of subcategory amounts that sum to main categories - 25 points, (3) Proper use of Excel formulas and balanced final budget - 25 points, (4) Clear explanation of calculation process during partner sharing - 25 points. Students must achieve 80% accuracy on calculations to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example with a different income amount and highlight the calculation steps. Offer percentage calculation reference cards showing the conversion process (percentage × total = amount). For advanced learners, add complexity by including variable expenses, tax considerations, or comparing different budgeting methods (60/20/20 rule). Encourage them to create additional 'what-if' scenarios with different income levels.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Empirical Testing and Complexity Decomposition
description: Students will analyze and compare the performance characteristics of three sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining their code structure, predicting theoretical complexity, and validating predictions through empirical testing. This activity develops critical thinking about algorithm efficiency and the relationship between theoretical analysis and real-world performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by decomposing their recursive structures and identifying dominant operations within nested loops
Students will evaluate algorithm performance through systematic empirical testing and comparison of theoretical predictions with measured execution times
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-written implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in the chosen programming language (20 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, with each team receiving printed algorithm code and analysis worksheets. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), teams examine each algorithm's structure without running code. They identify: (1) nested loops and recursive calls, (2) dominant operations (comparisons, swaps, array accesses), (3) best/average/worst case scenarios, and (4) theoretical Big-O complexity predictions. Teams document findings on provided analysis sheets with sections for each algorithm. In Phase 2 (40 minutes), teams implement timing tests using provided template code that measures execution time for datasets of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements. They test each algorithm on three data conditions: randomly ordered, already sorted, and reverse sorted arrays. Teams record results in provided data tables and create simple graphs plotting execution time vs. input size. In Phase 3 (30 minutes), teams compare empirical results with theoretical predictions, identifying discrepancies and discussing why certain algorithms perform differently than expected in specific scenarios. Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation highlighting their most significant finding about one algorithm's performance characteristics. Conclude with team presentations and class discussion about the importance of both theoretical and empirical analysis in algorithm selection.
materials_needed: Pre-written sorting algorithm implementations in Python/Java/C++
Algorithm analysis worksheets with structured comparison tables
Timing test template code with random data generators
Graph paper or digital graphing tools
Computers with appropriate programming environment installed
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets (40 points) for accuracy of complexity analysis and quality of empirical data collection. Assess team presentations (30 points) based on clarity of findings and depth of algorithm comparison. Award participation points (30 points) for active engagement during hands-on testing phases and peer discussions. Total: 100 points with rubric emphasizing analytical reasoning over correct answers.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing complexity analysis reference sheets with common patterns (nested loops = O(n²), divide-and-conquer = O(n log n)). Offer guided questions for code examination: 'How many times does this loop execute?' Advanced learners can analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or explore space complexity analysis. Provide optimization challenges: modify quicksort's pivot selection strategy and analyze performance impact.

title: Comparative Evaluation of Machine Learning Pipeline Architectures for Production Deployment
description: Students critically evaluate and compare three distinct machine learning pipeline architectures designed for the same predictive task, assessing their trade-offs in terms of performance, scalability, maintainability, and business impact. They will provide justified recommendations for production deployment based on comprehensive technical and business criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML pipeline architectures by analyzing performance metrics, scalability constraints, and operational requirements in realistic deployment scenarios
Students will critique and justify architectural decisions through systematic comparison of technical trade-offs and business alignment factors
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-built ML pipeline architectures (15 minutes setup): Architecture A (batch processing with Apache Airflow + scikit-learn), Architecture B (real-time streaming with Apache Kafka + MLflow), and Architecture C (serverless with AWS Lambda + containerized models). Each architecture addresses the same customer churn prediction problem but uses different technological approaches.

Students work in teams of 3-4 (120 minutes evaluation phase). Each team receives identical datasets, business requirements documentation, and access to all three pipeline codebases. Teams must systematically evaluate each architecture across six dimensions: prediction accuracy (using provided test datasets), latency performance (measured response times), scalability limits (theoretical and tested), maintenance complexity (code analysis), cost implications (resource usage calculations), and failure resilience (simulated failure scenarios).

Teams document findings in structured evaluation matrices, recording quantitative metrics where possible and qualitative assessments with supporting evidence. They must identify critical trade-offs, such as accuracy vs. latency or scalability vs. cost.

In the synthesis phase (45 minutes), teams prepare recommendations addressing three specific scenarios: a startup with limited resources, an established enterprise with high-volume requirements, and a regulated financial institution with strict compliance needs. Each recommendation must be justified with evidence from their evaluation and explicitly address rejected alternatives.

Conclude with team presentations (60 minutes total, 15 minutes per team including Q&A) where teams defend their architectural recommendations against challenging questions from peers and instructor, focusing on justification of trade-offs and consideration of alternative perspectives.
materials_needed: Three pre-configured ML pipeline environments (Docker containers or cloud instances)
Customer churn dataset (training, validation, and test sets)
Business requirements document with specific SLAs and constraints
Evaluation matrix templates (Excel/Google Sheets)
Access to monitoring tools (Grafana dashboards for performance metrics)
Failure simulation scripts for resilience testing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a detailed rubric (100 points total): Technical analysis depth (25 points - thoroughness of performance testing and architectural understanding), Critical evaluation quality (25 points - identification of meaningful trade-offs and limitations), Justification strength (25 points - evidence-based reasoning and consideration of alternatives), Recommendation appropriateness (25 points - alignment with business scenarios and practical feasibility). Students must submit evaluation matrices, written recommendations (2-3 pages per scenario), and participate in peer Q&A sessions. Success requires scoring 80+ points with no dimension below 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide evaluation checklists with specific metrics to measure, offer guided worksheets for trade-off analysis, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create optional mini-tutorials on pipeline architecture concepts. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose hybrid architectures combining elements from multiple approaches, conduct deeper cost-benefit analyses with real pricing models, or evaluate additional architectures like edge computing solutions. Encourage consideration of emerging technologies and future scalability scenarios.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Decimal Conversion Chart
description: Students will memorize binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and create a reference conversion chart. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal relationships essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization drills and chart construction
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 0=0000, 1=0001, 2=0010, etc.). Conduct a 5-minute introduction explaining that students will memorize these 16 number pairs. Divide class into pairs and have students take turns showing decimal side while partner states binary equivalent, then switch roles. Each pair spends 10 minutes on this initial practice round. Next, distribute blank conversion charts with two columns labeled 'Decimal' and 'Binary.' Students work individually for 8 minutes to fill in all 16 conversions from memory without looking at flashcards. After completion, students check answers against flashcards and mark incorrect responses. Conduct a second 10-minute paired practice session focusing on numbers students missed. For final assessment, give students a fresh blank chart and 5 minutes to complete all conversions. Collect completed charts and have students self-check using answer key projected on screen. Students must achieve 14/16 correct (87.5%) to demonstrate mastery. Those achieving mastery can begin extension activities while others receive additional practice with instructor support.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal 0-15 and corresponding 4-bit binary (one set per pair)
Blank conversion charts with decimal/binary columns (3 per student)
Answer key for projection
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students complete final conversion chart showing all 16 decimal-to-binary conversions (0-15) within 5 minutes. Success criteria: 14/16 correct answers (87.5% accuracy). Grade as Pass/Retry based on meeting threshold. Document specific numbers missed for targeted remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for powers of 2 (1,2,4,8) and highlight patterns like even numbers ending in 0, odd in 1. Create smaller chunks focusing on 0-7 first. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge them to find patterns in binary sequences.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Decimal Conversion Chart: Visual Analysis
description: Students will memorize binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice and reference chart creation. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for binary number system understanding in computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by matching flashcards with 95% accuracy
Students will identify the place values of 4-bit binary positions (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s) through guided chart completion
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made conversion charts with decimal numbers 0-15 in the left column and empty binary columns (8s, 4s, 2s, 1s place values). Students work individually for 15 minutes to complete the chart using the provided reference poster showing binary place values. Next, provide each student with a set of 32 flashcards: 16 cards showing decimal numbers (0-15) and 16 cards showing their corresponding 4-bit binary representations (0000-1111). Students spend 10 minutes arranging cards in matching pairs on their desks, using their completed charts for verification. For the drill phase (15 minutes), students work in pairs with one person holding decimal cards and the other providing binary answers from memory, then switching roles after 7 minutes. Conclude with a 5-minute individual assessment where each student receives 8 random decimal numbers (chosen from 0-15) and must write the correct binary representation without referring to charts or cards. Circulate throughout all phases to monitor progress and provide immediate feedback on errors.
materials_needed: Pre-printed conversion charts (1 per student) with decimal 0-15 and empty binary columns
Laminated flashcard sets with decimal numbers 0-15 and binary equivalents 0000-1111 (1 set per student)
Wall poster showing 4-bit binary place values (8-4-2-1)
Assessment sheets with 8 random decimal numbers for final quiz
Answer keys for instructor verification
assessment_method: Students must correctly write binary representations for 6 out of 8 randomly selected decimal numbers (0-15) on the final quiz to demonstrate mastery. Award 1 point per correct 4-bit binary answer. Additionally, observe pair work to ensure students can verbally recall at least 12 out of 16 conversions during the drill phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with smaller ranges (0-7) and provide partially completed charts with some binary digits filled in. Use colored pencils to highlight place values (8s=red, 4s=blue, etc.). For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider kinesthetic learners by having them physically move between stations with binary representations posted around the room.
original_title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Decimal Conversion Chart

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models: Predicting Customer Churn
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance rankings from a pre-trained Random Forest model used for customer churn prediction. They will examine how different customer attributes contribute to the model's predictions and explain the business implications of these insights.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance scores by ranking and categorizing customer attributes based on their contribution to churn prediction accuracy
Students will explain the relationship between feature importance values and business decision-making through written analysis and peer discussions
instructions: Begin by distributing the customer churn dataset (5 minutes) containing 15 features including demographics, usage patterns, and service metrics. Provide students with the pre-trained Random Forest model output showing feature importance scores ranging from 0.003 to 0.245. In pairs, students first spend 10 minutes examining the feature importance visualization (horizontal bar chart) and identify the top 5 and bottom 5 features. Next, have students categorize the 15 features into three business domains: customer demographics (age, gender, location), usage behavior (monthly minutes, data usage, support calls), and financial factors (monthly charges, total charges, payment method). Working individually for 15 minutes, students calculate the average importance score for each business domain and rank them. Then conduct a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share their domain rankings and hypothesize why certain domains are more predictive. For the final 15 minutes, students write a 200-word interpretation explaining: (1) which specific features most strongly predict churn, (2) why these features might be important from a business perspective, and (3) what actions a company might take based on these insights. Conclude with a 5-minute gallery walk where students review three other interpretations and note one insight they hadn't considered.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset with 15 features (CSV file)
Pre-trained Random Forest feature importance scores (printed handout)
Feature importance visualization (bar chart printout)
Laptops/tablets with Excel or Google Sheets access
Sticky notes for gallery walk
assessment_method: Evaluate the 200-word written interpretation using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of feature identification and ranking (25%), (2) Quality of business reasoning for why features matter (35%), (3) Practicality and specificity of suggested business actions (25%), (4) Use of appropriate data science terminology (15%). Students must correctly identify at least 4 of the top 5 features and provide logical business explanations to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a template with sentence starters like 'The most important feature is ___ because...' and 'This suggests the company should...' For advanced learners, challenge them to research and explain potential biases in the feature importance rankings or suggest additional features that might improve the model's predictive power.

title: Distributed System Failure Pattern Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage
description: Students will analyze the architectural components and cascading failure patterns of the 2017 Amazon S3 outage that brought down major web services. They will examine system dependencies, identify failure propagation mechanisms, and evaluate the effectiveness of different resilience strategies used by affected companies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining real-world outage data and tracing failure propagation through interconnected services
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different fault tolerance mechanisms through comparative analysis of how various companies responded to the same upstream failure
instructions: Begin by providing students with the official AWS post-mortem report, network topology diagrams, and performance monitoring data from the February 28, 2017 S3 outage (30 minutes reading time). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team a different affected service (Netflix, Slack, Trello, or Docker Hub). Each team receives actual error logs, latency graphs, and architectural diagrams for their assigned service. Students spend 45 minutes mapping the dependency chain from S3 to their service, identifying single points of failure using dependency graph analysis tools like Graphviz. They must categorize each failure point as either a design flaw, implementation bug, or operational error. Next, teams analyze their service's response strategy by examining code commits, configuration changes, and communication logs from the incident timeframe (30 minutes). They identify which patterns were used: circuit breakers, bulkheads, timeouts, or graceful degradation. Teams then create a detailed failure timeline showing the exact sequence of cascading failures, measuring the blast radius using quantitative metrics (affected users, downtime duration, revenue impact). In the final 45 minutes, teams present their analysis using a standardized incident analysis framework, comparing their service's resilience approach with the other teams' findings. They must propose three specific architectural changes that would have prevented or mitigated their assigned service's failure, backed by evidence from distributed systems literature and real implementation examples.
materials_needed: AWS S3 official post-mortem report (February 2017)
Network topology diagrams for each assigned service
Historical performance monitoring data and error logs
Graphviz or similar dependency mapping software
Access to GitHub repositories showing incident response commits
Distributed systems resilience pattern reference materials
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of failure chain mapping with at least 80% of critical dependencies identified, (2) Quality of resilience pattern analysis with correct categorization of at least 3 patterns, (3) Quantitative impact analysis with specific metrics and calculations, (4) Feasibility and technical depth of proposed architectural improvements with implementation details and trade-off analysis. Students must submit dependency graphs, timeline visualizations, and a 10-slide technical presentation.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-filled dependency graph templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer reference implementations of common resilience patterns in multiple programming languages. For advanced learners, require additional analysis of economic impact, comparison with similar outages in other cloud providers, and consideration of emerging resilience technologies like chaos engineering or service mesh architectures.

title: Design Your Dream City: Linear Programming Urban Planning Challenge
description: Students will create an original urban planning proposal using linear programming to optimize resource allocation while meeting multiple real-world constraints. They will develop mathematical models, solve optimization problems, and present their city design with supporting calculations and visual representations.
estimated_duration: 95 minutes (can be split across 2 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will formulate original linear programming problems by translating real-world urban planning constraints into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will design comprehensive mathematical solutions through creating graphical representations, calculating optimal vertices, and interpreting results in practical contexts
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Setup (15 minutes)** Present students with the scenario: They are urban planners with a $50 million budget designing a new city district. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives constraint cards showing: minimum housing units (500), minimum commercial spaces (200), maximum land area (100 acres), environmental restrictions, and infrastructure requirements. Teams must decide on their objective function (maximize population, maximize revenue, or minimize environmental impact). **Phase 2: Mathematical Modeling (25 minutes)** Students define variables (x = residential acres, y = commercial acres), write constraint inequalities based on their cards, and formulate their objective function. They must create at least 5 realistic constraints including budget, zoning laws, and resource limitations. Teams record their complete mathematical model on provided templates. **Phase 3: Graphical Solution (20 minutes)** Using graphing paper or GeoGebra, students plot constraint lines, identify feasible region, and locate corner points. They calculate the objective function value at each vertex to find the optimal solution. Students must show all algebraic work for intersection points. **Phase 4: Design Creation (25 minutes)** Based on their optimal solution, teams create a visual city layout using grid paper or digital tools. They must include specific numbers: housing units, commercial buildings, parks, roads, and infrastructure. The design must reflect their mathematical solution precisely. **Phase 5: Presentation Preparation (10 minutes)** Teams prepare 3-minute presentations explaining their mathematical model, solution process, and final city design with justifications for design choices.
materials_needed: Constraint scenario cards (pre-made with specific numerical requirements)
Graphing paper and rulers
GeoGebra software or graphing calculators
Large grid paper or poster board for city design
Colored pencils or markers
Mathematical model template worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy of constraint formulation and objective function (25%), (2) Correctness of graphical solution and vertex calculations (25%), (3) Logical connection between mathematical solution and city design (25%), (4) Quality of presentation and explanation of decision-making process (25%). Students must submit written mathematical work, visual city design, and deliver oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates with blanks to fill in, offer graphing assistance with pre-marked axes, and allow use of online linear programming calculators for verification. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints (whole buildings only), introduce sensitivity analysis by changing one constraint, or require consideration of multi-objective optimization with weighted factors.

title: Deconstructing Bias Sources in Machine Learning Pipeline Components
description: Students will analyze a complete machine learning pipeline to identify and categorize different types of algorithmic bias at each stage. They will examine real-world case studies to understand how bias propagates through data collection, preprocessing, model selection, and deployment phases.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between statistical, historical, representation, and measurement bias by analyzing specific examples within ML pipeline components
Students will interpret the interconnected nature of bias propagation through systematic examination of end-to-end machine learning workflows
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Amazon hiring algorithm case study and the corresponding ML pipeline diagram (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group one pipeline component: data collection, feature engineering, model training, or deployment. Provide each group with the bias identification framework handout containing definitions and detection methods for statistical bias, historical bias, representation bias, measurement bias, aggregation bias, and evaluation bias. 

Students spend 25 minutes analyzing their assigned pipeline component using the provided bias detection checklist. They must identify at least two specific bias types present in their component and document: the bias type, its manifestation, potential causes, and downstream effects on other pipeline components. Groups then create a visual bias map showing how their identified biases connect to other pipeline stages.

Conduct a structured gallery walk (20 minutes) where each group presents their bias map for 4 minutes, followed by 1 minute of clarifying questions. Other groups record connections between presented biases and their own findings on the provided connection tracking sheet.

Conclude with a synthesis phase (15 minutes) where students individually complete a bias propagation diagram, tracing how one specific bias type flows through the entire pipeline. They must explain the compounding effects and identify three critical intervention points where bias could be mitigated. Students submit their completed diagrams with written explanations of bias interconnections and mitigation strategies.
materials_needed: Amazon hiring algorithm case study packet (6 pages per student)
ML pipeline component diagram (poster-size for each group)
Bias identification framework handout with definitions and detection methods
Bias detection checklist with specific criteria for each bias type
Connection tracking sheet for gallery walk documentation
Blank bias propagation diagram template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of bias type identification and categorization (25%), (2) Quality of bias manifestation explanations with specific examples (25%), (3) Demonstration of understanding bias interconnections across pipeline components (25%), (4) Feasibility and specificity of proposed intervention points (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted sections in the case study and sentence starters for bias explanations. Offer a simplified bias checklist focusing on 3 main types instead of 6. For advanced learners, include additional case studies (facial recognition, credit scoring) and challenge them to quantify potential bias impact using provided statistical measures. Encourage them to research recent bias mitigation techniques and evaluate their effectiveness.

title: Budget Planning Challenge: Applying Percentage Calculations to Monthly Expenses
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a college student by applying percentage calculations to determine spending allocations across different expense categories. They will use given income amounts and percentage guidelines to calculate exact dollar amounts for housing, food, transportation, and other expenses.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine specific dollar amounts for budget categories by converting percentages to decimals and multiplying by total income
Students will demonstrate understanding of percentage concepts through creating a balanced monthly budget that totals 100% of available income
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'College Student Budget Worksheet' and scenario cards to each student (5 minutes). Each scenario card contains a different monthly income amount ($1,200, $1,500, or $1,800) and recommended percentage allocations: Housing (40%), Food (20%), Transportation (15%), Entertainment (10%), Savings (10%), and Miscellaneous (5%). Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to calculate exact dollar amounts for each category using their assigned income. They must show their work by writing the calculation process (example: Housing = $1,500 × 0.40 = $600). Next, students verify their calculations by adding all dollar amounts to ensure they equal their total income (5 minutes). In pairs, students then compare their budgets and discuss how different income levels affect spending power in each category (10 minutes). Finally, each student must adjust one category by reducing it by 5 percentage points and redistributing those 5 points to another category, recalculating the affected dollar amounts and explaining their reasoning in writing (10 minutes). The activity concludes with three volunteers sharing their original budget, their adjustment, and justification for the change (5 minutes). Teachers should circulate during individual work time to check calculation methods and provide guidance on decimal conversion if needed.
materials_needed: College Student Budget Worksheet (one per student)
Income scenario cards with different amounts and percentage guidelines
Calculators
Pencils and paper for showing work
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with work shown, budget totals exactly match income, adjustment properly calculated and justified; (3) Most calculations correct, minor arithmetic errors, adjustment attempted; (2) Some calculation errors, basic percentage concept demonstrated; (1) Major calculation errors or incomplete work. Additionally, observe student explanations during pair discussions for understanding of percentage relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet showing percentage-to-decimal conversions (40% = 0.40) and model the first calculation together. For advanced learners: Add a challenge component requiring them to research actual costs in their city and explain whether the percentage guidelines are realistic, or have them create a budget for a different life stage (family with children) using different percentage allocations.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance Across Competing Algorithmic Approaches
description: Students will critically evaluate and defend the selection of optimal machine learning models by comparing performance metrics, bias detection, and business impact across three different algorithmic approaches on a real-world imbalanced dataset. They will present justified recommendations to a simulated stakeholder panel with conflicting priorities.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative strengths and limitations of classification algorithms by systematically comparing performance metrics, computational efficiency, and interpretability trade-offs
Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive bias analysis and stakeholder impact assessment presentations
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Provide teams of 3-4 students with the UCI Credit Card Default dataset and three pre-trained models: Random Forest, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression. Each team receives identical performance reports showing accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and confusion matrices, plus computational training times and feature importance rankings. Students must independently calculate additional metrics including specificity, balanced accuracy, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient using provided formulas and validation datasets.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams conduct bias analysis by evaluating model performance across demographic subgroups (age brackets, gender, education levels) using provided demographic breakdown sheets. They must identify disparate impact ratios and statistical parity differences, then research and document potential fairness implications. Simultaneously, teams analyze business impact scenarios using provided cost matrices: false negatives cost $5000 (loan defaults), false positives cost $200 (lost customers).

**Phase 3 (30 minutes):** Each team prepares a 10-minute stakeholder presentation defending their model selection. They must address three competing priorities: Risk Manager (minimize defaults), Marketing Director (minimize customer rejection), and Ethics Officer (ensure fairness). Teams create visual comparison charts and prepare responses to challenge questions.

**Phase 4 (45 minutes):** Teams present to instructor panel role-playing stakeholders who will challenge decisions with prepared counterarguments. Other teams evaluate presentations using provided peer assessment rubrics focusing on evidence quality, bias consideration, and stakeholder needs balancing.
materials_needed: UCI Credit Card Default dataset with demographic variables
Three pre-trained model performance reports (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, confusion matrices)
Demographic breakdown analysis worksheets
Business cost matrix scenarios document
Peer evaluation rubrics with scoring criteria
Python/R environment with pandas, scikit-learn, and visualization libraries
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Technical Analysis Quality (40%) - accuracy of additional metric calculations, thoroughness of bias analysis, appropriate use of cost-benefit calculations; (2) Critical Evaluation Depth (35%) - quality of algorithm comparison, identification of trade-offs, consideration of limitations and assumptions; (3) Stakeholder Communication (25%) - clarity of recommendation rationale, effective response to challenges, appropriate visualization choices. Rubric uses 4-point scale: Exemplary (demonstrates sophisticated evaluation with nuanced understanding), Proficient (shows solid evaluation skills with minor gaps), Developing (basic evaluation with significant omissions), Inadequate (insufficient evaluation depth).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric calculation templates, bias analysis checklists, and sample stakeholder questions. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify understanding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional fairness metrics (equalized odds, demographic parity), consider ensemble model combinations, or analyze temporal model degradation scenarios. Encourage exploration of emerging bias detection tools and industry case studies.

title: Design and Construct a Predictive Mathematical Model for Urban Traffic Flow Optimization
description: Students will synthesize advanced calculus, statistics, and linear programming concepts to create an original mathematical model that predicts and optimizes traffic flow patterns in a city intersection system. They will present their model with implementation recommendations to a simulated city planning committee.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be spread across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original multi-variable mathematical model incorporating differential equations, probability distributions, and optimization constraints by analyzing real traffic data and urban planning parameters

Students will synthesize advanced mathematical concepts from calculus, statistics, and linear programming through the creation of a comprehensive traffic flow optimization system with practical implementation strategies
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Modeler, Data Analyst, Optimization Specialist, and Presentation Coordinator. Provide each team with real traffic count data from a 4-way intersection over 30 days, including hourly vehicle counts, pedestrian crossings, and accident reports.

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze the dataset to identify patterns, peak hours, and variables affecting traffic flow. Students must create at least three preliminary mathematical relationships using regression analysis and identify key constraints (safety margins, pedestrian crossing times, signal timing limitations).

Phase 2 (120 minutes): Teams construct their comprehensive model by developing a system of differential equations representing traffic flow rates, incorporating probability distributions for arrival patterns, and creating an objective function to minimize total wait time while maximizing safety. Students must justify their choice of mathematical tools and validate their model against historical data.

Phase 3 (90 minutes): Teams optimize their model using linear programming techniques to determine optimal signal timing sequences. They must account for at least five real-world constraints (emergency vehicle priority, pedestrian safety intervals, rush hour adaptations, weather conditions, and special events).

Phase 4 (60 minutes): Each team prepares a 15-minute presentation as if addressing a city planning committee, including model equations, optimization results, implementation timeline, and cost-benefit analysis. Presentations must include visual representations of before/after traffic flow predictions and address potential limitations of their model.
materials_needed: Real traffic count datasets (30 days of hourly data from 4-way intersection)
Statistical analysis software (R, Python with pandas/numpy, or MATLAB)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems
Large format paper and colored markers for model visualization
Access to linear programming solver software
City intersection maps and traffic signal timing specifications
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Construction (25 points) - accuracy of differential equations, appropriate use of probability distributions, and mathematical rigor; Optimization Implementation (25 points) - correct linear programming setup, constraint identification, and solution interpretation; Model Validation (20 points) - testing against historical data and addressing limitations; Practical Implementation (20 points) - realistic constraints, cost considerations, and feasibility analysis; Professional Presentation (10 points) - clarity, mathematical communication, and response to questions. Teams must submit written model documentation and present to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation structures and guide constraint identification through questioning. Offer simplified datasets with fewer variables initially. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, consider multi-intersection networks, or add machine learning components for adaptive signal timing. Provide access to more complex optimization algorithms and real-time traffic simulation software.

title: Programming Language Syntax Symbol Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify fundamental programming symbols used in Python by completing a timed flashcard activity and symbol matching exercise. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for reading and writing basic code structures.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the correct names and functions of 20 basic Python programming symbols (parentheses, brackets, braces, operators, etc.) by completing visual recognition exercises
Students will recall the proper terminology for programming punctuation and operators through structured memorization and testing activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the symbol reference sheet containing 20 fundamental Python symbols: ( ) [ ] { } = == != < > <= >= + - * / % # " ' : ; , . Students have 10 minutes to study this sheet, focusing on symbol names and basic purposes. Next, collect the reference sheets and distribute the blank identification worksheet showing only the symbols without names. Students work individually for 15 minutes to write the correct name next to each symbol (e.g., 'parentheses' next to '( )', 'assignment operator' next to '='). After completion, display the answer key on the projector and have students self-check their responses, circling incorrect answers. For the second phase, conduct a rapid-fire oral review where you display individual symbols on screen for 5 seconds each while students write answers on mini whiteboards and hold them up simultaneously. This allows immediate visual assessment of class understanding. Conclude with a partner quiz where students take turns showing symbols to each other using provided flashcards, with each student attempting to recall all 20 symbols correctly. Partners track correct responses on the provided score sheet. End the session by having students write down the 3-5 symbols they found most challenging for future review.
materials_needed: Python symbol reference sheet (one per student)
Symbol identification worksheet with blank spaces (one per student)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (one set per student)
Symbol flashcards printed on cardstock
Partner score tracking sheets
Computer/projector for displaying symbols
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 16 out of 20 symbols (80%) on the written worksheet to demonstrate mastery. Additional assessment through partner quiz requires accurately recalling at least 15 symbols when shown flashcards. Instructor observes whiteboard responses during rapid-fire section to gauge class-wide understanding and identify students needing additional support.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed worksheet with every other symbol already filled in, or allow them to work with the reference sheet visible for the first attempt. Create mnemonic devices for difficult symbols (e.g., 'curly braces hug the code'). For advanced learners: Include additional symbols like logical operators (and, or, not) or ask them to provide example code snippets using each symbol correctly. Challenge them to explain when each symbol is typically used in programming contexts.

title: Optimization Crisis: Applying Calculus to Design Emergency Water Distribution Systems
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to solve a realistic emergency response scenario. They will optimize the placement and capacity of temporary water distribution centers to minimize total transportation costs while meeting population demands and resource constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative-based optimization methods to minimize cost functions with multiple variables and constraints by solving a multi-stage emergency logistics problem
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques and linear programming algorithms through computational tools to find optimal resource allocation solutions
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing a fictional city map with population density data, existing infrastructure damage reports, and resource availability charts (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Analyst, Computational Specialist, Constraint Manager, and Solution Validator. Present the crisis scenario: A natural disaster has damaged the water infrastructure, and teams must establish 3-5 temporary distribution centers to serve 50,000 residents across 12 districts within 72 hours. Each team receives identical datasets including: population coordinates, daily water requirements (4 gallons/person), transportation costs ($2.50/mile/1000 gallons), and center setup costs ($15,000 fixed + $8/gallon capacity). Teams first identify decision variables (center locations, capacities, service assignments) and formulate the objective function combining transportation and setup costs (45 minutes). Next, they establish constraints: minimum service requirements per district, maximum center capacities (100,000 gallons/day each), budget limit ($180,000), and geographic restrictions (centers cannot be placed in flood zones marked on map). Using provided Excel templates with Solver add-in or Python optimization libraries, teams input their mathematical models and run optimization algorithms (60 minutes). Teams must document three different scenarios: minimum cost solution, maximum service reliability solution, and a balanced compromise solution. Finally, each team presents their optimal solution using provided presentation template, defending their mathematical approach and comparing trade-offs between scenarios (30 minutes presentations, 5 minutes Q&A per team).
materials_needed: Laminated city maps with population density overlays and flood zone markings
Scenario data packets with Excel spreadsheets containing population, cost, and constraint data
Laptops with Excel Solver add-in installed or Python with scipy.optimize library
Scientific calculators as backup computational tools
Presentation template slides with required mathematical documentation sections
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Model Formulation (25 points - correct objective function, complete constraints, appropriate variables), Computational Implementation (25 points - proper use of optimization tools, accurate data input, successful algorithm execution), Solution Analysis (25 points - comparison of scenarios, interpretation of results, identification of trade-offs), and Professional Presentation (25 points - clear mathematical explanations, defense of methodology, response to peer questions). Students must submit their Excel/Python files, written mathematical documentation, and deliver 8-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint templates and guided worksheets breaking down objective function construction into smaller steps. Offer optional tutorial session on Excel Solver basics. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as uncertain demand scenarios requiring stochastic optimization, multiple time periods with dynamic reallocation, or sensitivity analysis on key parameters. Encourage exploration of alternative algorithms like genetic algorithms or simulated annealing.

title: Architectural Analysis of Distributed System Performance Bottlenecks in a Multi-Tier E-commerce Application
description: Students will systematically analyze a complex distributed e-commerce system architecture to identify performance bottlenecks, decompose system interactions, and evaluate the relationships between architectural components and system performance metrics. They will examine load balancer configurations, database sharding strategies, caching layers, and microservice communication patterns to determine root causes of latency issues.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by systematically decomposing component interactions and identifying critical performance bottlenecks using profiling data and architectural diagrams

Students will evaluate the relationships between system design decisions and performance outcomes through detailed examination of monitoring metrics, database queries, and inter-service communication patterns
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with a comprehensive case study packet containing: system architecture diagrams, 7 days of performance monitoring data (CPU, memory, network I/O, database query times), application logs, and user complaint reports about slow checkout processes. Students spend the first 45 minutes individually reviewing all materials and creating personal notes identifying potential problem areas. Next, teams collaborate for 60 minutes to systematically analyze each system layer: presentation tier (load balancer logs, CDN cache hit rates), application tier (microservice response times, API gateway metrics), and data tier (database connection pools, query execution plans, cache miss rates). Teams must create a detailed flow diagram tracing a typical user checkout transaction through all system components, annotating each step with actual performance metrics from the provided data. During the following 30 minutes, teams prioritize identified bottlenecks using impact/effort matrices, considering factors like user experience degradation, system resource utilization, and implementation complexity. Teams then spend 45 minutes developing evidence-based hypotheses about root causes, correlating performance spikes with specific architectural decisions like database partitioning strategies, microservice communication protocols, or caching layer configurations. Finally, each team presents their 10-minute analysis to the class, defending their findings with specific data points and architectural reasoning. Presentations must include: identified bottlenecks ranked by severity, supporting evidence from monitoring data, architectural component relationships that contribute to issues, and technical justification for their prioritization decisions.
materials_needed: Distributed system architecture case study packet with performance data
Application monitoring dashboard screenshots (Grafana/New Relic format)
Database query execution logs and explain plans
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tools (Miro/Lucidchart)
Performance profiling datasets in CSV format
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using detailed rubric: Thoroughness of component analysis (25 points - identifies all major system layers and their interactions), Quality of evidence usage (25 points - cites specific metrics and correlates data patterns with architectural decisions), Accuracy of bottleneck identification (25 points - correctly prioritizes issues based on performance impact), Technical reasoning quality (25 points - demonstrates deep understanding of distributed systems principles and architectural trade-offs). Deliverables include annotated architecture diagrams, prioritized bottleneck analysis report, and peer evaluation of presentation technical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided analysis templates with specific prompting questions for each system tier and sample correlation techniques between metrics and architectural components. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity layers such as container orchestration overhead analysis, cross-region latency considerations, or security scanning impact on performance. Provide reference materials on distributed systems patterns and performance monitoring best practices.

title: Design a Mathematical Board Game for Linear Functions
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates linear functions, slope calculations, and coordinate graphing as core gameplay mechanics. They will develop game rules, design visual components, and test their creation with peers to demonstrate mastery of linear relationships.
estimated_duration: 3 hours (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will design an interactive board game that demonstrates understanding of linear functions by incorporating slope, y-intercept, and coordinate plotting as essential game mechanics
Students will synthesize multiple representations of linear relationships through creating visual game boards, mathematical challenge cards, and strategic gameplay rules
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Explain that each team will create a board game where players must work with linear functions to advance or score points. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams brainstorm their game concept using the provided planning worksheet. They must identify: game objective, how linear functions will be integrated (movement rules, scoring, challenges), target audience, and victory conditions. Examples: racing game where movement distance equals slope calculations, property-buying game with linear pricing models, or adventure game with coordinate-based treasure hunting.

Step 2 (40 minutes): Teams design their game board on poster paper. The board must include a coordinate grid section, spaces that trigger linear function challenges, and visual appeal. Simultaneously, they create 20 challenge cards featuring problems like 'Find the slope between points (2,5) and (6,13)' or 'Graph y = 3x - 4 and move to the y-intercept.'

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams write comprehensive rule sheets including setup instructions, turn sequence, how to use linear functions during play, and winning conditions. Rules must be clear enough for other students to learn quickly.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams create game pieces, dice modifications, or spinners as needed. Provide colored paper, markers, and basic craft supplies.

Step 5 (45 minutes): Game testing round. Each team plays another team's game for 20 minutes, then provides written feedback on mathematical accuracy, clarity of rules, and engagement level. Teams use remaining time to make revisions.

Step 6 (20 minutes): Gallery walk where teams present their final games, explaining how linear functions integrate into gameplay and demonstrating 2-3 example moves or challenges.
materials_needed: Large poster paper or cardboard (1 sheet per team)
Game planning worksheet template
Colored markers, pencils, and rulers
Index cards for challenge cards (20 per team)
Basic craft supplies (scissors, glue sticks, colored paper)
Standard dice and game pieces (optional - teams can create their own)
Peer feedback forms
Calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - linear function problems are correctly solved and appropriately challenging; Game Design (25%) - rules are clear, board is functional and visually appealing; Integration (25%) - linear functions are meaningfully incorporated into core gameplay rather than superficial add-ons; Presentation (25%) - team effectively demonstrates their game and explains mathematical connections. Students also receive peer feedback scores from game testing session. Final deliverables include the physical game, rule sheet, and reflection essay explaining design choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made challenge card templates with partially completed problems, offer linear function reference sheets, and consider pairing with stronger math peers. Create simplified game concept examples focusing on basic slope calculations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate systems of linear equations, piecewise functions, or real-world applications like business profit models. Encourage creation of multiple difficulty levels within their game or digital components using graphing software.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Gradient Boosting Models Using SHAP Values
description: Students will analyze and interpret SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values from a pre-trained XGBoost model to understand how individual features contribute to predictions. They will distinguish between global and local feature importance patterns and explain model behavior for specific instances.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP summary plots and waterfall charts by analyzing feature contribution patterns and identifying the most influential variables in gradient boosting predictions
Students will distinguish between global feature importance and local instance-level explanations through comparative analysis of SHAP visualizations
instructions: Begin by providing students with a Jupyter notebook containing a pre-trained XGBoost model on the Boston Housing dataset with SHAP values already computed (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair 5 specific house instances from the test set. In Step 1 (20 minutes), students examine the SHAP summary plot to identify the top 5 most important features globally and rank them by average absolute SHAP values. They must write a 2-sentence explanation for why each feature logically impacts housing prices. In Step 2 (25 minutes), pairs create SHAP waterfall charts for their assigned instances, documenting how each feature pushes the prediction above or below the base value. They calculate the net positive and negative contributions for each instance. Step 3 (15 minutes) requires students to compare their local explanations with the global importance ranking, identifying at least 2 discrepancies where a globally important feature has minimal impact on their specific instances, or vice versa. In Step 4 (20 minutes), pairs select one instance where the model's prediction seems counterintuitive and write a detailed explanation using SHAP values to justify the model's reasoning. Finally (10 minutes), each pair presents one key insight about the difference between global and local interpretability to the class.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-trained XGBoost model on Boston Housing dataset
Python environment with shap, xgboost, pandas, and matplotlib libraries installed
SHAP values pre-computed and saved for 50 test instances
Data dictionary explaining all housing features
Instance assignment sheet with 5 specific house IDs per pair
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of global feature importance ranking and logical explanations (25 points), (2) Correct calculation and interpretation of local SHAP contributions for assigned instances (30 points), (3) Quality of comparison between global vs. local importance with specific examples of discrepancies (25 points), (4) Depth of explanation for counterintuitive prediction using SHAP reasoning (20 points). Students must achieve 80+ points demonstrating clear understanding of feature contribution interpretation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example with one house instance showing step-by-step SHAP interpretation and highlighting key phrases like 'pushes prediction higher/lower than base value.' Offer a template with sentence starters for explanations. For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential bias or fairness issues revealed by SHAP values, or to propose alternative models based on feature importance insights. Provide additional complex instances with contradictory feature interactions.

title: Personal Budget Planning with Percentages and Decimals
description: Students will create a realistic monthly budget for a fictional teenager using percentage calculations and decimal operations. They will apply their knowledge of converting between percentages, decimals, and fractions to allocate income across different expense categories.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to distribute income across budget categories by creating a personal monthly budget
Students will demonstrate decimal operations through calculating exact dollar amounts for each budget category
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Teen Budget Scenario' worksheet where each student receives a fictional profile (age 16-17, part-time job earning $400-600 monthly). Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to complete Phase 1: Income Analysis. They calculate their monthly take-home pay after a 15% deduction for taxes and savings, converting this percentage to decimal form (0.15) and subtracting from gross income. 

In Phase 2 (25 minutes), students allocate their net income using the provided percentage guidelines: Transportation 25%, Entertainment 20%, Clothing 15%, Food/Snacks 20%, Personal Items 10%, Emergency Fund 10%. Students must convert each percentage to decimal form, multiply by their net income, and record exact dollar amounts rounded to the nearest cent. 

Phase 3 (15 minutes) involves partner work where students compare budgets and verify each other's calculations using calculators. Partners check that all percentages total 100% and that decimal calculations are accurate. 

Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 student pairs present one budget category calculation, explaining their conversion process from percentage to decimal to final dollar amount. Students must justify whether their allocations are realistic and suggest modifications.
materials_needed: Teen Budget Scenario worksheets (6 different fictional profiles)
Budget allocation worksheet with percentage guidelines
Calculators (1 per student)
Percentage-to-decimal conversion reference chart
assessment_method: Evaluate completed budget worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All percentage-to-decimal conversions correct, all calculations accurate, budget totals exactly 100%; (3) Minor calculation errors (1-2), conversions mostly correct; (2) Some calculation errors (3-4), demonstrates partial understanding; (1) Multiple errors, incomplete work. Also assess verbal explanations during partner verification for mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with partially completed conversion tables showing percentage-decimal pairs (25%=0.25, etc.). Give step-by-step calculation templates showing 'multiply by decimal, round to nearest cent.' For advanced learners, add complexity by including irregular expenses, varying monthly incomes, or calculating annual budget projections with 12-month multiplication scenarios.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis Through Performance Profiling
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms by implementing them, measuring their execution times with various input sizes, and decomposing the factors that contribute to their time complexity differences. They will create visual representations of their findings and justify which algorithm performs best under specific conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity behavior of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by measuring execution times across datasets of 100, 1000, and 10000 elements
Students will decompose algorithm performance data through statistical analysis to identify patterns and correlations between input size and execution time
instructions: Begin by providing students with skeleton code files containing the three sorting algorithms with timing measurement functions already integrated. In the first 15 minutes, students work in pairs to complete the missing implementation details for each algorithm. Next, students spend 20 minutes running each algorithm on three pre-generated datasets: random integers (100, 1000, 10000 elements), nearly sorted arrays, and reverse-sorted arrays. They must record execution times in a provided data collection spreadsheet, running each test 5 times and calculating averages. During the following 25 minutes, students create line graphs plotting input size versus execution time for each algorithm, identifying which performs best under different conditions. Students then spend 15 minutes analyzing their graphs to identify linear, quadratic, and logarithmic growth patterns, connecting these observations to theoretical time complexity. In the final 15 minutes, pairs present their findings to another pair, explaining which algorithm they would recommend for: a mobile app sorting user contacts, a database system sorting millions of records, and a real-time game leaderboard. Students must justify their recommendations using specific data points from their analysis and theoretical knowledge of algorithm behavior.
materials_needed: Python IDE or online compiler (Replit/CodePen)
Skeleton code files with timing functions pre-written
Pre-generated test datasets in CSV format (100, 1000, 10000 elements each)
Data collection spreadsheet template
Graph paper or digital graphing tool (Excel/Google Sheets)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed data collection spreadsheets (20 points), accuracy of generated graphs showing correct trends (25 points), written analysis connecting observed performance to theoretical time complexity (30 points), and quality of algorithm recommendations with data-driven justifications (25 points). Success criteria: students correctly identify quadratic growth in bubble sort, logarithmic behavior in merge sort, and can explain why quicksort performance varies with input organization.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed algorithm implementations and focus on data collection and pattern recognition. Offer guiding questions like 'Which line grows steepest?' and 'What happens when input doubles?' For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them analyze space complexity, implement additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), or explore best/worst/average case scenarios with different input distributions.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Prediction
description: Students critically assess three different machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, Neural Network) for predicting hospital readmission risk using real healthcare data. They must justify which model should be deployed in production by evaluating performance metrics, interpretability, computational requirements, and ethical implications.
learning_objectives: Students will critically evaluate competing machine learning models by analyzing multiple performance dimensions including accuracy, fairness, interpretability, and computational efficiency
Students will synthesize quantitative model metrics with qualitative business requirements to justify deployment recommendations through evidence-based argumentation
instructions: Step 1 (30 minutes): Provide teams of 3-4 students with identical datasets containing 50,000 patient records with features like age, diagnosis codes, length of stay, and readmission outcomes. Each team receives pre-trained Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network models with performance outputs including confusion matrices, ROC curves, SHAP values, training times, and prediction latencies. Step 2 (45 minutes): Teams analyze each model using the provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: predictive accuracy (AUC, precision, recall), calibration quality (Brier score, reliability diagrams), fairness across demographic groups (equalized odds, demographic parity), interpretability (SHAP consistency, feature importance stability), computational efficiency (training time, inference speed, memory usage), and robustness (performance on holdout test sets from different hospitals). Step 3 (60 minutes): Teams complete structured evaluation matrices scoring each model (1-5 scale) on all dimensions, then weight these dimensions based on three different deployment scenarios: resource-constrained rural hospital, large urban medical center, and regulatory-heavy insurance application. Step 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents 10-minute recommendations defending their model choice for one assigned scenario, addressing counterarguments about their decision and explaining trade-offs they accepted. Presentations must include quantitative evidence, stakeholder impact analysis, and implementation timeline considerations.
materials_needed: Healthcare dataset with 50,000 anonymized patient records (CSV format)
Three pre-trained models with performance outputs (Python pickle files)
Jupyter notebooks with evaluation code templates
Model evaluation framework rubric (6-dimension scoring matrix)
Presentation template with required sections
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 100-point rubric: quantitative analysis quality (25 points - correct interpretation of metrics, mathematical accuracy), critical reasoning (25 points - logical argumentation, acknowledgment of limitations), stakeholder consideration (20 points - ethical implications, business impact), evidence synthesis (20 points - integration of multiple evaluation dimensions), and presentation clarity (10 points - clear communication of recommendations). Success requires scoring 80+ points with no dimension below 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide metric interpretation guides, offer one-on-one sessions to explain evaluation dimensions, and allow use of evaluation checklists. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose additional evaluation metrics, consider ensemble approaches, or design A/B testing frameworks for deployment. Encourage exploration of model bias detection techniques and regulatory compliance requirements.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Cryptographic Hash Function
description: Students will create an original cryptographic hash function using advanced mathematical principles, then rigorously test its security properties against known attack vectors. This culminates in presenting their algorithm to peers who attempt to break it through mathematical analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize concepts from modular arithmetic, prime number theory, and Boolean algebra to construct an original hash function with specific security requirements
Students will devise comprehensive mathematical proofs and computational tests to validate their algorithm's resistance to collision, preimage, and second preimage attacks
instructions: Begin by having students work in pairs to research three existing hash functions (MD5, SHA-256, and one of their choice) for 45 minutes, documenting their mathematical foundations. Next, each pair designs their original hash function over 90 minutes using these requirements: input domain of arbitrary-length binary strings, fixed 256-bit output, incorporation of at least two number-theoretic operations (modular exponentiation, prime field arithmetic), and one combinatorial transformation (permutation matrices, substitution boxes). Students must document their algorithm using formal mathematical notation and pseudocode. During the third phase (60 minutes), pairs create security proofs addressing: computational complexity analysis showing operations scale appropriately, mathematical argument for avalanche effect (1-bit input change affects 50% of output bits), and theoretical resistance analysis against birthday paradox attacks. In the validation phase (45 minutes), students implement their algorithm computationally, testing on 1000 random inputs to measure actual avalanche effect and collision rates.
