Finally, conduct peer review sessions (30 minutes) where each pair presents their algorithm while others attempt to identify mathematical weaknesses or potential attack vectors. Document all findings, failed attack attempts, and suggested improvements. Conclude with pairs revising their algorithms based on peer feedback and submitting final documentation including complete mathematical specification, security analysis, test results, and reflection on the iterative design process.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Sage)
Programming environment (Python with NumPy/SciPy or equivalent)
Large whiteboards and markers for algorithm visualization
Access to academic databases for cryptography research papers
Hash function testing datasets and benchmark tools
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four components: Mathematical Rigor (25 points - correct use of number theory, formal notation, proof structure), Algorithm Innovation (25 points - originality, complexity, efficiency), Security Analysis (25 points - thoroughness of attack resistance, valid computational complexity arguments), and Peer Review Quality (25 points - ability to identify others' weaknesses, constructive feedback, defense of own work). Minimum passing requires 70/100 points with at least 15/25 in each category.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing templates for mathematical proof structure and pseudocode formatting. Offer simplified number-theoretic building blocks (basic modular arithmetic operations) as starting points. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate elliptic curve mathematics or lattice-based operations, and require formal security proofs using standard cryptographic assumptions (discrete logarithm hardness, factoring difficulty).

title: Binary Number System Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the first 16 binary numbers (0-15) and their decimal equivalents through repetitive practice and flashcard activities. This foundational activity builds essential number system recognition skills needed for understanding computer data representation.
learning_objectives: Students will identify binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed recall exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will recite the powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^7 through verbal repetition and written practice
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary-decimal conversion chart showing numbers 0-15 in both systems. Give students 10 minutes to study the chart silently, encouraging them to look for patterns (even numbers end in 0, powers of 2 have single 1s, etc.). Next, conduct a 5-minute guided recitation where students repeat after you: '0 is 0000, 1 is 0001, 2 is 0010...' through 15. Following this, pair students and distribute flashcard sets. One partner shows the decimal side while the other states the binary equivalent, then they switch roles. Allow 15 minutes for this paired practice. Conduct the first assessment round: display decimal numbers on the board one at a time (2, 7, 11, 4, 13, 9, 1, 15) and have students write binary equivalents on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously. Record which students achieve 7/8 correct. For those needing more practice, repeat the flashcard activity while successful students begin the powers of 2 component. Display the sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and have students chant '2 to the 0 is 1, 2 to the 1 is 2...' five times. Conclude with a final mixed assessment where students write both binary equivalents for given decimals AND decimal values for given powers of 2 exponents. Collect worksheets and check against the answer key for final scoring.
materials_needed: Binary-decimal conversion chart (0-15) - one per student
Binary number flashcard sets (32 cards showing decimal on one side, 4-bit binary on reverse)
Individual student whiteboards and dry erase markers
Powers of 2 reference poster (2^0 through 2^7)
Final assessment worksheet with answer key
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (7/8 correct) on whiteboard recall of decimal-to-binary conversions and 100% accuracy reciting powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^7. Final worksheet scores recorded as: Mastery (90-100%), Developing (70-89%), Beginning (below 70%). Observe during flashcard practice to note students who hesitate more than 3 seconds per conversion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional visual aids showing place values (8-4-2-1 headers), allow reference to fingers for counting in binary, extend practice time to 20 minutes. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or challenge them to find patterns in binary arithmetic (adding 1, doubling numbers).

title: Binary Number System Recall Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured practice and retrieval exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire verbal recitation activities
instructions:
Begin with a 5-minute introduction displaying a reference chart showing decimal numbers 0-15 alongside their 4-bit binary equivalents (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Have students study the chart silently for 3 minutes, encouraging them to identify patterns (even numbers end in 0, powers of 2 have single 1s, etc.). 

Divide the class into pairs and distribute pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers on one side and binary on the reverse. Partner A shows decimal cards while Partner B states the binary equivalent, then they switch roles. Each round lasts 3 minutes with a 1-minute break for self-correction using the reference chart.

Conduct three progressively challenging rounds: Round 1 allows reference chart consultation, Round 2 removes the chart, and Round 3 adds a 5-second time limit per card. After each round, partners mark correct responses on tracking sheets.

Conclude with a whole-class 'Binary Lightning Round' where you call out decimal numbers randomly and students write binary answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously. Cover all numbers 0-15 twice in random order. Record class accuracy rates for each number to identify commonly missed conversions.

End with a 2-minute reflection where students write down the three binary numbers they found most challenging to remember and create personal memory tricks for them.
materials_needed: Reference chart poster showing decimal 0-15 with corresponding 4-bit binary
32 flashcards per pair (16 showing decimal numbers 0-15, 16 showing binary equivalents)
Student tracking sheets with spaces for recording correct/incorrect responses
Mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers (one per student)
Timer for tracking round durations
assessment_method: Success measured by achieving 90% accuracy (14/15 or 15/15 correct) on the final Binary Lightning Round. Track individual student responses on observation sheets, noting specific numbers missed. Students must demonstrate automatic recall without counting or calculation gestures. Provide immediate feedback by showing correct answers after each lightning round question.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by highlighting patterns: all even numbers end in 0, odd numbers end in 1, and powers of 2 (1,2,4,8) contain only one '1'. Provide mnemonic devices like 'Nine = 1001 looks like 9 upside down.' For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (16-31) or challenge them to recall in reverse order. Allow struggling students extra reference chart time and pair them with stronger partners initially.
original_title: Binary Number System Recall Challenge

title: Optimizing Renewable Energy Systems Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving renewable energy allocation. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal energy distribution strategies for a hypothetical smart grid system.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to optimize energy distribution by formulating constraints and objective functions from given renewable energy scenarios
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the renewable energy scenario worksheets containing data for solar, wind, and hydroelectric power sources with associated costs, capacity limits, and demand requirements (10 minutes). Divide students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team a different regional energy grid scenario with specific constraints such as minimum renewable energy percentages, budget limitations, and peak demand periods. Students first spend 20 minutes identifying and defining decision variables (x₁ = solar allocation, x₂ = wind allocation, x₃ = hydro allocation), then formulate the objective function to minimize cost while meeting energy demands. Next, have teams spend 25 minutes writing all constraint inequalities including capacity limits (e.g., x₁ ≤ 500 MW), budget constraints (e.g., 0.12x₁ + 0.08x₂ + 0.15x₃ ≤ 50,000), and regulatory requirements (e.g., x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≥ 800 MW). For the next 30 minutes, students apply the graphical method for two-variable simplified versions, plotting constraint lines and identifying the feasible region on coordinate planes. Then spend 35 minutes using the simplex method or linear programming software to solve the full three-variable problem, documenting each pivot operation and iteration. Finally, dedicate 20 minutes for teams to interpret their solutions, calculate total costs, verify constraint satisfaction, and prepare a brief presentation explaining their optimal energy allocation strategy and its real-world implications for grid management.
materials_needed: Renewable Energy Scenario Worksheets with regional data sets
Graphing paper and rulers for constraint plotting
Scientific calculators or computers with Excel Solver/Python optimization libraries
Linear Programming reference sheets with simplex method steps
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and all constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of graphical method with properly labeled feasible region (25%), (3) Correct implementation of simplex method or software solution with documented steps (25%), and (4) Valid interpretation of results with justified recommendations (25%). Students must submit complete mathematical work, final optimal values, and a one-page analysis of their energy allocation strategy.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing constraint formulation templates and worked examples of similar problems. Offer intermediate checkpoints where students can verify their objective functions before proceeding. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis to examine how changes in energy prices or capacity limits affect optimal solutions, or extend to integer programming constraints for discrete energy unit allocations.

title: Architectural Analysis of Microservices vs. Monolithic E-commerce Systems
description: Students will dissect and compare two real-world e-commerce architectures by analyzing system diagrams, examining failure patterns, and evaluating scalability bottlenecks. Through systematic decomposition of architectural components and data flow patterns, students will identify critical design decisions and their trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze architectural patterns by deconstructing system components, identifying dependencies, and mapping data flows in both microservices and monolithic designs
Students will evaluate system reliability through systematic examination of failure modes, cascading effects, and recovery mechanisms in distributed versus centralized architectures
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with two detailed system architecture diagrams: a monolithic e-commerce platform (showing database, web server, application layers) and an equivalent microservices implementation (showing service mesh, API gateway, individual services, databases). Allocate 45 minutes for initial analysis where students must: (1) Create dependency maps showing how components interact during a typical user purchase flow, (2) Identify single points of failure in each architecture, (3) Trace data consistency mechanisms across both systems. Next, present three realistic failure scenarios (database corruption, network partition, service overload) and give teams 30 minutes to analyze cascading effects in each architecture, documenting how failures propagate and which recovery strategies apply. Have each team create a comparison matrix evaluating: deployment complexity, horizontal scaling capabilities, development team coordination requirements, monitoring complexity, and fault isolation effectiveness. During the final 45 minutes, teams present their architectural analysis to the class, defending their evaluation criteria and conclusions. Require teams to demonstrate deep understanding by explaining: why certain design patterns emerge in each architecture, how data consistency is maintained differently, and what specific technical debt accumulates over time in each approach.
materials_needed: Detailed system architecture diagrams for both monolithic and microservices e-commerce platforms
Failure scenario case studies with specific technical details
Digital collaboration tools (Miro, Lucidchart, or similar) for creating dependency maps
Comparison matrix templates in spreadsheet format
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of component relationship identification (25%), (2) Depth of failure mode analysis with specific technical reasoning (25%), (3) Quality of trade-off evaluation with justified criteria (25%), (4) Clarity of presentation demonstrating systems thinking (25%). Teams must submit their dependency maps, failure analysis documentation, and comparison matrices as deliverables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided question prompts for each analysis phase and simplified architecture diagrams highlighting key components. Offer one-on-one check-ins during the dependency mapping phase. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as containerization considerations, service mesh security implications, or cost analysis including infrastructure and operational overhead.

title: Evaluating the Quality of Data Visualizations for Sales Performance Analysis
description: Students will critically assess and rank three different data visualizations showing the same sales dataset, identifying strengths and weaknesses of each approach. They will justify their evaluation using data visualization best practices and recommend the most effective visualization for a business presentation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different data visualizations by applying established design principles and effectiveness criteria
Students will justify their ranking of visualization quality through written analysis comparing clarity, accuracy, and business impact
instructions:
Begin by displaying three pre-prepared visualizations of the same monthly sales data: a cluttered 3D pie chart with 12 categories, a clean bar chart with clear labels, and a line graph showing trends over time. Provide students with printed copies of all three visualizations and an evaluation rubric covering: data clarity (1-5 scale), visual design principles (1-5 scale), and business usefulness (1-5 scale). 

In the first 15 minutes, have students individually examine each visualization and complete the rubric scoring. Next, spend 20 minutes having students write a 200-word analysis for each visualization, identifying specific strengths and weaknesses (e.g., 'The 3D pie chart obscures actual values due to perspective distortion'). 

For the following 15 minutes, students rank the three visualizations from best to worst and write a 150-word justification explaining their ranking criteria and final recommendation. In pairs, students then spend 10 minutes sharing their rankings and discussing any differences in their evaluations. 

Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where student pairs present conflicting evaluations to the class, defending their positions using specific evidence from the visualizations. The instructor should facilitate by asking probing questions like 'How does the color choice in visualization B affect interpretation?' and 'Which visualization would be most effective for a 5-minute executive presentation?'
materials_needed: Three printed data visualizations (one per student): 3D pie chart, bar chart, and line graph of monthly sales data
Printed evaluation rubric with 3 criteria and 5-point scales
Blank paper for written analysis
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate application of evaluation criteria to each visualization, (2) Quality of written analysis with specific examples, (3) Clear justification for final ranking with evidence, (4) Constructive participation in pair and class discussions. Success requires scoring 3/4 on all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth visualization as a model. Offer sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' or 'The main weakness is...' For advanced learners, ask them to redesign the weakest visualization and explain their design choices, or have them consider how different audiences (executives vs. analysts) might prefer different visualizations.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model City Transportation Network Using Coordinate Geometry
description: Students will design a functional transportation network for a scale model city by creating coordinate-based maps, calculating optimal routes using distance formulas, and constructing physical models with budget constraints. This activity integrates coordinate geometry, optimization, and real-world urban planning principles.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original transportation network layout by applying coordinate geometry concepts including distance formula, midpoint formula, and slope calculations within realistic urban planning constraints
Students will design cost-effective transportation solutions through mathematical modeling of routes, intersections, and connection points while justifying decisions with quantitative analysis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members. Provide each team with a 24×18 inch poster board representing a city grid where 1 inch = 0.5 miles. Distribute the scenario packet containing: population density data for 6 predetermined residential zones, locations of 4 essential services (hospital, school, shopping center, employment district), and a construction budget of $50 million virtual dollars with cost breakdowns ($2M per mile for roads, $8M per subway station, $12M per bridge). 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams establish coordinate system on poster board and plot given locations using provided coordinates. Students must add 3 additional residential zones of their choice, justifying placement using mathematical reasoning about distance and accessibility.

Step 2 (35 minutes): Using distance formula and optimization principles, teams calculate and compare multiple route options between all zones and services. They must create at least 2 alternative network designs, showing all calculations for total distances and construction costs.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams select their optimal design based on mathematical analysis and begin physical construction using colored yarn for roads (red), pipe cleaners for subway lines (blue), and small blocks for stations. All measurements must be precise to scale.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents their network to the class, explaining mathematical reasoning behind route choices, showing cost calculations that stay within budget, and defending their design against peer questions. Presentations must include coordinate calculations, total network length, and cost-benefit analysis comparing their chosen design to alternatives considered.
materials_needed: 24×18 inch poster boards (1 per team)
Scenario packets with population/service location data
Colored yarn in red and blue
Pipe cleaners
Small wooden blocks for stations/intersections
Rulers and protractors
Calculators
Grid paper for calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct distance/slope calculations, coordinate plotting), Design Innovation (creative solutions, justified placement decisions), Budget Management (accurate cost calculations within constraints), and Presentation Quality (clear explanation of mathematical reasoning, defense of design choices). Final deliverables include annotated poster with all calculations shown, written cost analysis, and oral presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide coordinate calculation templates and distance formula reference cards. Consider pre-plotting some locations to reduce initial complexity. For advanced learners: Add constraints like environmental obstacles requiring bridge calculations, introduce traffic flow optimization using weighted distances, or include public transit efficiency ratios in cost-benefit analysis.

title: Shopping Cart Percentage Calculator: Applying Discounts and Tax
description: Students will apply percentage calculations to real-world shopping scenarios by calculating discounts, sales tax, and final totals. They will use their percentage skills to solve multi-step problems involving a simulated online shopping experience.
learning_objectives: Students will apply percentage calculations to determine discount amounts, tax amounts, and final prices in shopping scenarios
Students will demonstrate percentage skills through solving multi-step word problems involving consecutive percentage changes
instructions: Begin by distributing the Shopping Cart Worksheets and calculators to each student (5 minutes). Display the sample problem on the board: 'Original price: $80, 25% discount, 8.5% sales tax on discounted price.' Model the complete solution process, emphasizing the order of operations: calculate discount amount ($20), subtract from original ($60), calculate tax on discounted price ($5.10), add tax to get final total ($65.10). Next, provide each student with their unique Shopping Cart Scenario containing 5 different items with varying original prices, discount percentages, and local tax rates (10 minutes setup). Students work independently to complete their calculations, showing all work for each step: original price, discount calculation, discounted price, tax calculation, and final price. Circulate the room providing individual guidance and checking work in progress (20 minutes). After calculations are complete, have students pair up to verify each other's answers using different colored pens to check their partner's work (10 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where 3-4 students present one of their most challenging problems, explaining their step-by-step process on the board while others verify the accuracy (10 minutes). Collect completed worksheets with all work shown for final assessment.
materials_needed: Shopping Cart Scenario worksheets (unique for each student with 5 items each)
Basic calculators (one per student)
Red and blue pens for peer checking
Whiteboard markers for student presentations
assessment_method: Grade worksheets using 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct final answers with complete work shown, 3 points for correct process with minor calculation errors, 2 points for correct setup with significant errors, 1 point for attempted work with major conceptual errors. Each of the 5 problems worth 4 points (20 points total). Students must achieve 16/20 points (80%) to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a step-by-step reference card showing the exact sequence (1. Calculate discount amount, 2. Subtract discount, 3. Calculate tax on new price, 4. Add tax for final total). For advanced learners: add compound scenarios involving multiple discounts (e.g., 20% store discount plus additional 10% member discount) or include tip calculations on the final amount.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithm Performance Patterns
description: Students will analyze the runtime performance of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort) by examining execution data across varying input sizes. They will identify performance patterns, compare time complexity characteristics, and determine optimal algorithm selection criteria for different scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze algorithm performance data by examining runtime patterns across different input sizes and identifying Big O complexity characteristics
Students will evaluate trade-offs between sorting algorithms through systematic comparison of execution metrics and memory usage patterns
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with pre-generated performance data sheets containing execution times for bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort tested on arrays of sizes 100, 500, 1000, 5000, 10000, and 50000 elements (15 minutes setup). Each dataset includes best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios.

Step 1: Students create performance graphs for each algorithm, plotting input size (x-axis) versus execution time (y-axis) using spreadsheet software. They must generate separate graphs for each test case scenario (25 minutes).

Step 2: Groups analyze growth patterns by calculating the ratio of execution time increases as input size doubles. They document these ratios in a comparison table and identify which algorithms show linear, quadratic, or logarithmic growth patterns (20 minutes).

Step 3: Students examine the data to determine crossover points where one algorithm becomes more efficient than another. They must identify specific input sizes where algorithm preference should change (15 minutes).

Step 4: Each group creates a decision matrix recommending algorithm selection based on input size ranges, memory constraints, and performance requirements. They must justify their recommendations using evidence from their analysis (20 minutes).

Step 5: Groups present their findings in 5-minute presentations, focusing on their decision matrix and supporting evidence. Other groups provide feedback and challenge recommendations (25 minutes).

Conclude with a class discussion comparing different groups' analyses and establishing consensus on algorithm selection criteria.
materials_needed: Pre-generated algorithm performance data sheets (3 algorithms × 6 input sizes × 3 test cases)
Spreadsheet software (Excel, Google Sheets, or LibreOffice Calc)
Graph paper as backup for plotting
Algorithm decision matrix template
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of graph creation and pattern identification (25%), (2) Correctness of growth rate analysis and mathematical reasoning (25%), (3) Quality of algorithm comparison and crossover point identification (25%), (4) Justification strength in decision matrix with evidence-based recommendations (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 or higher in each category, with deliverables including completed graphs, analysis tables, decision matrix, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing graph templates with pre-labeled axes and offering guided questions for pattern recognition ('What happens to execution time when input doubles?'). For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity factors like memory usage analysis, cache performance considerations, or hybrid algorithm evaluation. Provide algorithm pseudocode for students who want to understand implementation details affecting performance.

title: Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Model Architectures for Business Decision Making
description: Students will critically assess three different machine learning approaches (ensemble methods, deep learning, and traditional statistical models) applied to the same business problem using real-world performance metrics, interpretability requirements, and implementation constraints. They will justify their final model recommendation through comprehensive comparative analysis addressing stakeholder concerns.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative strengths and limitations of competing ML model architectures by analyzing performance metrics, computational requirements, and business constraints within a realistic deployment scenario
Students will critique model selection decisions through structured peer review sessions that examine bias, validity, and practical implementation considerations
instructions:
**Phase 1 (90 minutes): Individual Model Analysis**
Provide each student with identical preprocessed customer churn dataset and three pre-trained models: Random Forest ensemble, Neural Network (TensorFlow), and Logistic Regression. Students analyze each model using provided Jupyter notebooks containing performance outputs (confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance plots, training times, memory usage). Students complete standardized evaluation worksheets documenting: accuracy metrics, interpretability scores (1-10 scale with justification), computational resource requirements, and potential bias indicators.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Stakeholder Constraint Integration**
Present business scenario constraints via video briefing: legal team requires model explanations for regulatory compliance, IT department has limited GPU resources, executive team needs 95%+ precision for retention campaigns. Students revise their initial assessments incorporating these real-world limitations, creating weighted scoring matrices that balance technical performance against business requirements.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Peer Critique Sessions**
Arrange students in groups of 3. Each student presents their model recommendation (10 minutes) while others complete structured peer evaluation forms examining: logical reasoning quality, evidence sufficiency, stakeholder consideration completeness, and potential blind spots identification. Groups must reach consensus on strongest recommendation through evidence-based discussion.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Written Justification**
Students individually author final 500-word executive summaries defending their chosen model, explicitly addressing counterarguments raised during peer review and explaining how their solution balances competing priorities.
materials_needed: Preprocessed customer churn dataset (10,000 records, CSV format)
Three pre-trained model files with performance outputs in Jupyter notebooks
Standardized model evaluation worksheets (PDF templates)
Business scenario constraint briefing video (15 minutes)
Structured peer evaluation forms with scoring rubrics
Access to Python environment with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib
assessment_method: Students assessed on: (1) Evaluation worksheet completeness and analytical depth (25 points), (2) Integration of business constraints into technical decisions (25 points), (3) Quality of peer critique feedback and discussion participation (20 points), (4) Executive summary logical argumentation and counterargument addressing (30 points). Final scores require evidence of weighing trade-offs rather than simply identifying 'best' performing model on single metric.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide model evaluation checklist templates and sentence starters for executive summaries. Pair with stronger analytical peers during critique sessions. For advanced learners: Include additional models (XGBoost, SVM) for comparison, require cost-benefit analysis with specific dollar estimates, or add data drift considerations for model maintenance planning.

title: Binary Number System Memory Drill with Visual Cards
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and visual pattern recognition. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 without calculation by using systematic memorization techniques
Students will identify binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8) through repeated visual card matching exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary conversion cards to each student (30 cards total: 15 decimal cards, 15 binary cards). Explain that binary uses only 0s and 1s, with place values of 1, 2, 4, and 8 from right to left. Demonstrate three examples: 5 = 0101, 10 = 1010, 15 = 1111. Have students arrange decimal cards 0-15 in numerical order on their desks (3 minutes). Next, students work in pairs to match each decimal card with its corresponding binary card, using the provided reference sheet initially (8 minutes). Remove reference sheets and have students practice the matching exercise three more times, timing each round (5 minutes per round). Conduct individual recall tests: show each student a decimal number card and have them state the binary equivalent within 5 seconds (2 minutes per student, can be done while others continue practicing). For reinforcement, students create their own memory device or pattern recognition strategy and share with their partner (5 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class rapid-fire review where you call out decimal numbers and students chorus the binary equivalent (3 minutes).
materials_needed: 30 laminated cards per student (15 decimal number cards 0-15, 15 binary equivalent cards)
Binary place value reference sheets (one per pair initially)
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard and markers for demonstrations
assessment_method: Individual recall assessment: Students must correctly state binary equivalents for at least 12 out of 15 decimal numbers (0-15) within 5 seconds each. Record results on checklist. Success criteria: 80% accuracy (12/15 correct) with appropriate response time. Observable behaviors include confident, immediate responses without finger counting or visible calculation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with numbers 0-7 only, provide written place value chart (8-4-2-1), allow pointing to place values while reciting. Use color-coding where each place value has a different color. For advanced learners: Extend to numbers 16-31, introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or challenge them to recall backwards (give binary, state decimal). Create leadership roles where advanced students become 'memory coaches' for struggling peers.

title: Interpreting Model Performance Metrics Through Cross-Validation Results Analysis
description: Students will analyze and interpret the performance of three different machine learning models using cross-validation results displayed in confusion matrices and metric tables. They will explain what the metrics reveal about each model's strengths, weaknesses, and suitability for a specific business problem.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret model performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score) by analyzing cross-validation results from three classification models
Students will explain the relationship between confusion matrix patterns and business implications through structured comparative analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing cross-validation results for three models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, SVM) trained on a customer churn prediction problem. Each student receives identical printouts showing: 5-fold CV confusion matrices, aggregated performance metrics table, and a business context sheet describing the cost of false positives ($50 customer retention effort) versus false negatives ($200 lost customer value). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine Model A (Random Forest) results, calculating average precision, recall, and F1-scores across the 5 folds, then writing 2-3 sentences explaining what these numbers mean in plain language.

Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students compare all three models' metrics, identifying which model has the highest precision, recall, and overall accuracy. They must justify their observations by pointing to specific numbers in the confusion matrices.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students work individually to determine which model best suits the business context, considering the different costs of prediction errors. They write a brief recommendation paragraph citing specific metric values.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Pairs share their recommendations with another pair (groups of 4), discussing any disagreements about model selection and identifying common patterns in their interpretations.

Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 groups present their model recommendations, focusing on how they connected the numerical metrics to business outcomes.
materials_needed: Pre-calculated cross-validation results printouts (5-fold CV confusion matrices for 3 models)
Performance metrics summary table (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score per fold)
Business context information sheet with cost structure
Calculator or smartphone for metric calculations
Worksheet template for recording interpretations and recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 3-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of metric calculations and interpretations (can student correctly identify which model has highest precision/recall), (2) Quality of business reasoning (does recommendation logically connect metrics to costs), (3) Use of evidence (cites specific numbers from results). Success requires scoring 2/3 points in each category. Collect individual worksheets and observe pair discussions for evidence of understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example using a different model, highlight key numbers in the confusion matrices, or offer sentence starters like 'Model A has higher precision because...' For advanced learners: Add questions about statistical significance of differences between models, ask them to calculate confidence intervals for metrics, or have them consider additional metrics like AUC-ROC that aren't provided.

title: Optimizing City Bus Route Networks Using Linear Programming
description: Students apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world transportation optimization problem by determining the optimal bus route configuration for a fictional city. They will use the simplex method to minimize costs while meeting passenger demand constraints across multiple routes and time periods.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-variable transportation scenario into a system of linear inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method through iterative calculations to determine optimal resource allocation for minimizing operational costs
instructions: Begin by distributing the Metro City Transit scenario packets containing passenger demand data for 8 bus routes across 3 time periods (rush hour, midday, evening). Each packet includes: ridership statistics, fuel costs per route mile, driver wage rates, and minimum service requirements. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify decision variables (number of buses per route per time period), constraints (minimum service levels, maximum fleet size of 45 buses, driver availability), and the objective function (minimize total daily operational costs). Next, spend 20 minutes having pairs formulate their linear programming model on provided worksheets, clearly labeling variables as x₁₁, x₁₂, etc. (route i, time period j). Instructor circulates to verify correct constraint formation. For the following 35 minutes, students use graphing calculators or provided Excel templates to implement the simplex method, creating initial tableau and performing pivot operations. They must document each iteration step, showing basis changes and objective function improvements. In the final 15 minutes, pairs interpret their optimal solution, calculating total minimum cost and explaining the practical meaning of their bus allocation recommendations. Students must verify their solution satisfies all original constraints and present one key insight about the trade-offs between service coverage and cost efficiency.
materials_needed: Metro City Transit scenario packets (one per pair)
Linear programming worksheet templates
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent) or laptops with Excel
Simplex method reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct problem formulation with properly defined variables and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate simplex method implementation with documented iterations (35%), (3) Valid optimal solution with constraint verification (25%), and (4) Clear interpretation connecting mathematical results to practical business decisions (15%). Students submit completed worksheets and a one-paragraph analysis of their recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-labeled variable templates and constraint equation starters. Offer a simplified 3-route version of the problem. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by having them explore how solutions change when fleet size increases to 50 buses or fuel costs rise by 15%. Challenge them to add integer programming constraints requiring whole numbers of buses.

title: Reverse Engineering and Security Analysis of a Distributed System Architecture
description: Students will analyze the architecture of a real-world distributed system by examining network traffic, API documentation, and system logs to identify security vulnerabilities and architectural patterns. They will decompose the system's components, evaluate design decisions, and assess the impact of identified vulnerabilities on overall system security.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by decomposing network communication patterns, service dependencies, and data flow between microservices using packet analysis tools and architectural documentation

Students will evaluate security vulnerabilities through systematic examination of authentication mechanisms, data transmission protocols, and access control implementations in multi-tier distributed systems
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a pre-configured virtual environment containing a sample e-commerce distributed system (web frontend, API gateway, user service, product service, payment service, and database). Students receive network packet captures (pcap files), API documentation, Docker Compose files, and sanitized application logs spanning 24 hours of system operation.

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams use Wireshark to analyze network traffic patterns, identifying service-to-service communication protocols, authentication methods, and data serialization formats. Students create a visual architecture diagram mapping all discovered services, their interactions, and communication protocols.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Using provided API documentation and reverse engineering techniques, students analyze authentication flows, session management, and authorization mechanisms. They examine JWT tokens, API keys, and OAuth implementations to understand security boundaries between services.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Teams analyze system logs using ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) to identify error patterns, performance bottlenecks, and potential security incidents. Students correlate log entries across services to trace complete user transactions.

Step 4 (90 minutes): Students systematically evaluate the architecture for security vulnerabilities using OWASP guidelines and distributed system security principles. They assess encryption in transit, service mesh security, container isolation, and database access patterns.

Step 5 (40 minutes): Teams prepare a comprehensive analysis report documenting architectural patterns identified, security vulnerabilities discovered, risk assessments for each vulnerability, and recommended remediation strategies with implementation priorities.
materials_needed: Virtual machines with Ubuntu 20.04 and Docker installed
Pre-deployed distributed e-commerce application (Docker containers)
Wireshark network analysis software
ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for log analysis
Sample network packet captures (pcap files) from 24-hour period
API documentation and OpenAPI specifications
OWASP security testing guidelines reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Architecture diagram accuracy and completeness (25 points), identification and classification of security vulnerabilities (30 points), quality of risk assessment and impact analysis (25 points), feasibility and prioritization of remediation recommendations (20 points). Students submit written reports, architecture diagrams, and present 10-minute findings to simulate security briefings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-labeled network diagrams as templates, offer guided worksheets for vulnerability identification, and supply OWASP checklist with specific questions. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement proof-of-concept exploits in isolated environments, design automated security testing scripts, or propose alternative architectural patterns that address identified vulnerabilities while maintaining system performance requirements.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Beginner Analytics
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same customer sales dataset to determine which chart type best communicates key business insights. They will apply evaluation criteria to judge clarity, accuracy, and appropriateness of each visualization approach.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of bar charts, pie charts, and line graphs by applying specific visualization criteria to a customer sales scenario
Students will critique data presentation choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions: Begin by distributing three printed visualizations of monthly sales data by product category (bar chart, pie chart, line graph) along with the evaluation checklist. Spend 5 minutes explaining that students will act as business consultants determining which chart to recommend to a client. Have students work individually for 15 minutes, using the provided checklist to score each visualization on five criteria: readability (1-5 scale), data accuracy representation (1-5 scale), appropriate chart type for data (yes/no), visual appeal (1-5 scale), and clarity of message (1-5 scale). Students must write 2-3 sentences justifying each score. Next, arrange students in pairs for 10 minutes to compare their individual evaluations and discuss differences in scoring. Each pair must reach consensus on which visualization is most effective and prepare a 1-minute verbal recommendation with three supporting reasons. Conclude with 10 minutes of pair presentations, where each team states their choice and rationale while you record responses on the board. Lead a brief class discussion identifying patterns in the recommendations and common evaluation criteria that emerged across teams.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of identical sales data (bar chart, pie chart, line graph)
Evaluation checklist handout with 5 scoring criteria
Whiteboard or flipchart for recording team recommendations
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade individual evaluation sheets using a 20-point rubric: complete scoring of all three visualizations (6 points), quality of written justifications showing evidence-based reasoning (8 points), participation in pair discussion and consensus-building (3 points), and clear verbal recommendation with supporting rationale (3 points). Success requires 16/20 points minimum.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing sentence starters like 'This chart is effective because...' or 'The main weakness I see is...'. For advanced learners, add a bonus question asking them to suggest specific improvements for the two non-recommended charts or to identify what additional data would strengthen their evaluation.

title: Design Your Dream City: A Geometric Urban Planning Challenge
description: Students will create an original city layout incorporating specific geometric shapes, area calculations, and scale relationships. They will synthesize mathematical concepts including perimeter, area, scaling, and coordinate geometry to design a functional urban environment with detailed mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original city design by applying area and perimeter formulas for composite shapes within specified constraints
Students will synthesize coordinate geometry and scaling principles through creating a proportional map with mathematical documentation
instructions: Begin by distributing grid paper and city planning requirements sheet. Explain that students are urban planners tasked with designing a 10,000 square unit city (Step 1, 5 minutes). Students first sketch their city layout on grid paper where each square represents 100 square units, creating zones for residential (minimum 4,000 sq units), commercial (minimum 2,000 sq units), industrial (minimum 1,500 sq units), and parks/recreation (minimum 2,500 sq units) (Step 2, 15 minutes). Next, students calculate exact areas of each irregularly-shaped zone using composite shape formulas, showing all work on calculation sheets (Step 3, 20 minutes). Students then create a coordinate system overlay, identifying key intersections and landmarks using ordered pairs, and design a transportation grid connecting all zones (Step 4, 15 minutes). For the scaling component, students create a second map at 1:2 scale, calculating new dimensions and verifying proportional relationships (Step 5, 20 minutes). Students design three unique buildings using specific geometric shapes (triangles, rectangles, circles, polygons), calculating perimeter and area for each structure and justifying shape choices based on function (Step 6, 25 minutes). Finally, students prepare a presentation board including both maps, calculation sheets, building designs, and a written reflection explaining how mathematical principles influenced their urban planning decisions (Step 7, 15 minutes). Circulate during work time to check calculations and provide guidance on complex area problems.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 2 sheets per student)
City planning requirements worksheet
Calculation recording sheets
Rulers and protractors
Colored pencils or markers
Scientific calculators
11x17 presentation boards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of area and perimeter calculations (25 points), (2) Correct application of scaling and coordinate geometry (25 points), (3) Creative integration of geometric shapes in building design (25 points), (4) Clear mathematical justification and reflection on design choices (25 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving at least 80% accuracy in calculations and providing complete mathematical reasoning for all design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing area formula reference sheets and breaking composite shapes into simpler rectangles and triangles first. Offer pre-drawn coordinate grids for students having difficulty with plotting. Extend learning for advanced students by adding population density calculations, budget constraints requiring cost-per-square-unit analysis, or incorporating trigonometric concepts for angled streets and triangular lots.

title: Advanced Operating Systems Component Memory Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate precise recall of advanced operating system components, their memory addresses, data structures, and initialization sequences. This intensive memory exercise focuses on low-level OS internals including kernel structures, process control blocks, and memory management unit specifications.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific memory addresses and data structure layouts for kernel components including PCB fields, page table entries, and interrupt vector tables by completing timed recall worksheets
Students will identify precise initialization sequences and system call numbers for advanced OS operations through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Advanced OS Memory Reference Sheet containing 50 critical OS components with their specifications (15 minutes setup). Students have 10 minutes to study the sheet, focusing on: kernel data structures (Process Control Block fields like PID, state, priority, register contexts), memory management components (page table entry bits, TLB structure, virtual memory addresses), interrupt handling (IDT entries, system call numbers 0-399, exception codes), and file system internals (inode structure fields, superblock components, directory entry formats). After study time, collect all reference materials. Distribute the recall assessment containing 40 specific questions requiring exact technical details. Students work individually for 25 minutes answering questions such as: 'List the 12 standard fields in a Process Control Block in order', 'Identify the bit positions for Present, Read/Write, and User/Supervisor flags in x86 page table entries', 'Recall the system call numbers for fork(), execve(), and mmap()', and 'State the exact sequence of steps during context switching'. Provide warning announcements at 15 minutes remaining, 5 minutes remaining, and 1 minute remaining. During the final 10 minutes, conduct immediate peer review where students exchange papers and check answers against the master key, discussing any discrepancies with their partner before final submission.
materials_needed: Advanced OS Memory Reference Sheet (50 components with technical specifications)
Individual recall assessment worksheets (40 specific technical questions)
Master answer key with exact specifications
Stopwatch or timer for precise time management
Whiteboard markers for any clarifying diagrams
assessment_method: Grade based on accuracy of recalled technical details: 36-40 correct answers (90-100% - Advanced mastery), 32-35 correct (80-89% - Proficient recall), 28-31 correct (70-79% - Developing recall), below 28 (below 70% - Needs additional study). Partial credit given only for answers that are technically accurate but incomplete. Full credit requires exact specifications, correct ordering, and precise technical terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide memory palace technique guidance during study time, allow color-coding of related components on reference sheet, offer additional 5-minute study period. For advanced learners: Include bonus questions about OS implementation variations across different architectures, challenge them to explain the reasoning behind specific design choices, or add questions comparing different OS approaches (Linux vs. Windows kernel structures).

title: Interpreting Feature Engineering Impact on Model Performance Through A/B Testing Results
description: Students will analyze real A/B testing data from two machine learning models with different feature engineering approaches to understand how specific feature transformations affect predictive performance. They will interpret confusion matrices, learning curves, and feature importance plots to explain the underlying mechanisms driving performance differences.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between feature engineering techniques and model performance metrics by analyzing comparative A/B testing results across multiple evaluation frameworks
Students will explain the causal mechanisms linking specific feature transformations to changes in precision, recall, and AUC through systematic analysis of model diagnostics
instructions: Begin by providing students with two pre-trained models (Model A: basic features, Model B: engineered features) and their corresponding test results on the same dataset (45 minutes total setup and analysis). Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives: (1) confusion matrices for both models, (2) ROC curves with AUC scores, (3) learning curves showing training/validation performance, (4) feature importance rankings, and (5) sample predictions with confidence intervals. Students spend 15 minutes individually examining the materials, noting key differences in performance metrics. Next, teams collaborate for 20 minutes to map specific feature engineering techniques (polynomial features, interaction terms, normalization, encoding methods) to observed performance changes. They must identify which engineered features contributed most to improvements and hypothesize why. Teams then spend 10 minutes preparing explanations that connect feature transformations to model behavior, focusing on interpretability rather than just metrics. Each team presents 3-minute explanations of their findings, specifically addressing: how feature engineering affected different classes differently, which evaluation metrics were most impacted, and what the learning curves reveal about overfitting/underfitting. Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing team interpretations and highlighting common misconceptions about feature engineering effects.
materials_needed: Pre-trained scikit-learn models (RandomForest with basic vs engineered features) saved as .pkl files
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded confusion matrices, ROC curves, and learning curves
Feature importance visualizations exported as PNG files
Sample dataset (e.g., housing prices with 20+ original features)
Printed handouts showing feature engineering transformations applied to Model B
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of metric interpretation (correctly identifies performance differences and statistical significance), (2) Quality of causal explanations (links specific features to performance changes with valid reasoning), (3) Use of evidence (references multiple evaluation frameworks in explanations), (4) Identification of trade-offs (discusses scenarios where engineered features might not improve performance). Teams must submit written explanations addressing each evaluation criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guided questions about what each metric means and offer simplified feature engineering examples. Create reference sheets showing common feature transformations and their typical effects. For advanced learners: include additional datasets with different characteristics, ask them to propose alternative feature engineering approaches, or have them identify potential biases introduced by feature engineering choices.

title: Shopping Spree Percentage Discount Challenge
description: Students apply percentage calculation skills to real-world shopping scenarios by calculating discounts, taxes, and final prices. They will use their mathematical knowledge to make purchasing decisions within a given budget while comparing multiple discount options.
learning_objectives: Students will calculate percentage discounts and final prices by applying percentage formulas to simulated shopping scenarios
Students will determine the better deal between multiple discount options through systematic comparison of calculated values
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Arrange students in pairs. Distribute the shopping catalog sheets, calculators, and budget cards to each pair. Post the tax rate (8%) prominently on the board. **Phase 1 - Individual Practice (10 minutes):** Each student selects 3 items from the catalog and calculates: original price, discount amount (using given percentage), price after discount, tax amount on discounted price, and final total. Students show all work using the formula: Final Price = (Original Price × (1 - Discount %)) × (1 + Tax %). **Phase 2 - Partner Challenge (15 minutes):** Pairs receive a $200 budget card and must select 5-7 items that maximize their purchases while staying within budget. They encounter items with different discount structures: single percentage discounts (15% off), buy-one-get-one deals (calculate as 50% off second item), and tiered discounts (20% off purchases over $100). Partners must calculate totals for each potential combination and justify their final selection. **Phase 3 - Comparison Task (8 minutes):** Present three scenarios on the board where students choose between: 25% off entire purchase vs. $30 off purchases over $120; 15% off plus free shipping ($8 value) vs. 20% off; Buy 2 get 1 free vs. 30% off all items. Students calculate both options and circle the better deal. **Wrap-up (2 minutes):** Pairs share their most surprising calculation result with the class.
materials_needed: Shopping catalog worksheets with 20+ items and various discount labels
Scientific calculators (1 per student)
Budget scenario cards ($150, $200, $250 amounts)
Comparison scenario worksheets
Answer recording sheets with formula reference
assessment_method: Students submit calculation sheets showing work for all problems with 80% accuracy required for proficiency. Evaluate using 4-point rubric: 4 points for correct formula application and accurate calculations; 3 points for correct process with minor computational errors; 2 points for partially correct method; 1 point for attempted work with major conceptual errors. Check partner justifications for logical reasoning in purchase decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide percentage calculation reference chart and allow extra time with formula sheets. Start with simpler single-discount problems before moving to complex scenarios. For advanced learners: introduce compound discounts (additional 10% off already discounted items) and have them create their own multi-step discount scenarios for classmates to solve.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Evaluation
description: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms (bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort) by examining their code implementations and testing performance with datasets of varying sizes. They will create detailed complexity reports comparing theoretical Big O notation with empirical runtime data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of sorting algorithms by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and identifying worst-case scenarios in code implementations
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency through systematic comparison of theoretical Big O complexity with measured performance data across multiple dataset sizes
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with three Python files containing implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quick sort algorithms, along with a data generation script that creates random integer arrays of sizes 100, 1000, 5000, and 10000 elements. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct static code analysis. Each team member takes responsibility for one algorithm, examining the code line-by-line to identify loops, recursive calls, and conditional statements. Students document their findings on the provided analysis worksheet, determining theoretical time complexity for best, average, and worst-case scenarios, plus space complexity.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Teams run performance tests using the provided timing framework. Students execute each algorithm 5 times per dataset size, recording execution times in milliseconds. They calculate average runtime for each algorithm-dataset combination and plot results on provided graph templates.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Comparative analysis phase. Teams create a comprehensive report comparing theoretical predictions with empirical results. They must identify which algorithm performs best for small vs. large datasets, explain discrepancies between theoretical and actual performance, and analyze when constant factors override Big O predictions.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents one key finding to the class, focusing on a specific insight about algorithm behavior that surprised them or confirmed their theoretical analysis.
materials_needed: Python environment with timing libraries installed
Three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations
Data generation script for creating test arrays
Algorithm analysis worksheets with complexity tables
Graph paper or digital graphing templates
Stopwatch/timing framework code
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of Big O complexity identification in static analysis (25 points), (2) Completeness and accuracy of performance testing data collection (25 points), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between theoretical and empirical results (30 points), (4) Clarity of explanations for performance discrepancies and practical recommendations (20 points). Teams submit analysis worksheets, performance graphs, and written comparative report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide Big O reference sheet with common patterns, offer guided questions for code analysis ('How many times does this loop execute?'), and allow use of pseudocode tracing. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort), implement hybrid approaches, or investigate best-case input scenarios that minimize runtime complexity.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Healthcare Fraud Detection
description: Students will critically assess the appropriateness and effectiveness of different machine learning approaches for detecting healthcare insurance fraud by analyzing model performance metrics, ethical implications, and business constraints. They will justify their final model recommendation through systematic evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and fairness.
estimated_duration: 270 minutes (4.5 hours) - can be split across 2-3 class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the suitability of multiple machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, XGBoost, Neural Networks) for healthcare fraud detection by systematically comparing performance metrics, interpretability requirements, and ethical considerations

Students will critique model selection decisions through comprehensive analysis of confusion matrices, ROC curves, feature importance, and bias detection metrics to recommend the most appropriate solution
instructions: **Phase 1: Dataset Analysis (45 minutes)** - Provide students with a synthetic healthcare claims dataset containing 50,000 records with features like provider specialty, claim amounts, patient demographics, and fraud labels (10% fraud rate). Students work in teams of 3-4 to explore class imbalance, feature distributions, and potential bias indicators. **Phase 2: Model Implementation (90 minutes)** - Each team implements four pre-specified algorithms using provided Python templates in Jupyter notebooks. Students must apply identical preprocessing steps, cross-validation strategies, and hyperparameter tuning approaches. They calculate precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and fairness metrics across demographic groups. **Phase 3: Critical Evaluation Matrix (60 minutes)** - Teams complete a structured evaluation matrix comparing models across six dimensions: predictive performance, computational efficiency, interpretability for regulatory compliance, bias across patient demographics, implementation complexity, and maintenance requirements. Each dimension uses a 5-point scale with specific criteria provided. **Phase 4: Stakeholder Impact Analysis (45 minutes)** - Students analyze how each model choice affects different stakeholders (patients, healthcare providers, insurance companies, regulators) by considering false positive/negative consequences, transparency requirements, and fairness implications. **Phase 5: Final Recommendation (30 minutes)** - Teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their model choice, addressing potential counterarguments, and explaining rejected alternatives with specific evidence from their analysis.
materials_needed: Synthetic healthcare fraud dataset (CSV format, 50,000 records)
Pre-built Python model templates for 4 algorithms
Jupyter notebook environment with scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib, fairlearn libraries
Evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Stakeholder analysis worksheet
Performance metrics calculation guide
assessment_method: Students evaluated using weighted rubric: Model Implementation Accuracy (20%) - correct application of algorithms and metrics calculation; Critical Analysis Depth (30%) - thoroughness of evaluation matrix completion and stakeholder impact assessment; Justification Quality (25%) - evidence-based reasoning for final recommendation with consideration of trade-offs; Presentation Effectiveness (25%) - clear communication of decision rationale and response to peer challenges. Each criterion uses 4-point scale (Exemplary, Proficient, Developing, Inadequate) with specific descriptors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed code snippets for metrics calculation, offer simplified evaluation matrix with guided questions, and assign peer mentors for technical implementation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional algorithms (SVM, ensemble methods), conduct deeper bias analysis using multiple fairness metrics, or propose novel evaluation criteria specific to healthcare context. Consider providing real-world case studies of ML failures in healthcare for additional context.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Healthcare Fraud Detection: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically evaluate three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting) for detecting healthcare insurance fraud using a real-world dataset. They must assess model performance, ethical implications, and business viability to recommend the optimal solution.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple machine learning algorithms by comparing performance metrics, interpretability, and computational requirements in a healthcare fraud detection context
Students will critique the ethical and practical implications of different modeling approaches through structured analysis of bias, fairness, and regulatory compliance considerations
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with the Medicare fraud dataset and three pre-trained models with their performance reports. In the first 30 minutes, teams independently analyze each model's confusion matrix, ROC curves, precision-recall curves, and feature importance rankings. Students must calculate and compare key metrics including sensitivity (crucial for fraud detection), specificity, F1-score, and AUC. Next, spend 45 minutes having teams evaluate non-performance factors: examine each model's interpretability using SHAP values, assess computational costs (training time, prediction latency, memory usage), and research regulatory requirements for healthcare AI systems. Teams then spend 30 minutes conducting ethical evaluation by identifying potential bias sources in the training data, evaluating fairness across different demographic groups using provided demographic breakdowns, and assessing the consequences of false positives (legitimate claims denied) versus false negatives (fraudulent claims approved). In the final 45 minutes, teams synthesize their analysis into a structured recommendation report that ranks the three approaches, justifies their recommendation with specific evidence, identifies implementation risks and mitigation strategies, and proposes success metrics for deployment. Each team presents their 5-minute recommendation to the class, followed by 10 minutes of peer questioning where other teams challenge their reasoning and evidence.
materials_needed: Medicare fraud detection dataset (CMS-1500 claims data with 50,000+ records)
Pre-trained Random Forest, Neural Network, and Gradient Boosting models with saved outputs
Model performance reports including confusion matrices, ROC curves, and SHAP analysis
Jupyter notebooks with model comparison templates
Healthcare AI regulatory guidelines document (FDA, HIPAA requirements)
Demographic breakdown data for bias analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical Analysis - accurate interpretation of performance metrics and statistical significance (25%), (2) Critical Reasoning - depth of analysis comparing trade-offs between models (25%), (3) Ethical Evaluation - identification and assessment of bias, fairness, and regulatory concerns (20%), (4) Evidence-Based Recommendation - quality of justification using specific data and logical reasoning (20%), (5) Professional Communication - clarity and persuasiveness of written report and oral presentation (10%). Students must score 3+ in all categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide interpretation guides for reading ROC curves and confusion matrices, offer sentence starters for ethical analysis ('This model might be biased because...'), and create structured templates for the recommendation report. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them evaluate ensemble methods, conduct cost-benefit analysis with actual dollar amounts, or design A/B testing protocols for model deployment. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger peers and providing mid-activity check-ins.
original_title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Healthcare Fraud Detection

title: Binary Number System Vocabulary and Symbol Recognition Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall the fundamental vocabulary terms and symbols used in binary number systems. Through structured flashcard activities and matching exercises, students will build foundational knowledge of binary terminology that is essential for all future computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the definitions of 10 key binary number system terms (bit, byte, binary digit, base-2, decimal, hexadecimal, MSB, LSB, place value, conversion) by completing flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary symbols (0, 1) and their positional values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) through visual recognition activities
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student (5 minutes). Each set contains 15 cards: 10 vocabulary terms on one side with definitions on the reverse, and 5 symbol cards showing binary positions and their decimal values. 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to study their flashcards, reading each term aloud and then the definition. Instruct them to focus on exact wording of definitions, particularly for 'bit' (binary digit), 'byte' (8 bits), 'MSB' (most significant bit), and 'LSB' (least significant bit).

Phase 2 (10 minutes): Pair students and have them quiz each other. Partner A shows the term, Partner B recites the definition from memory, then they switch roles. Monitor pairs and note students struggling with specific terms.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct whole-class oral quiz. Display terms on projector and call on students randomly to provide definitions. Keep a checklist of correct responses for each student.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Distribute the binary position value worksheet. Students must fill in a table showing positions 0-7, their binary representation (1, 10, 100, etc.), and decimal values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) from memory without references.

Conclude with a 5-minute rapid-fire review where you point to binary symbols on the board and students call out the decimal equivalent.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (15 cards per student)
Binary position value worksheets (one per student)
Projector or whiteboard for displaying terms
Student assessment checklists for instructor
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the final oral quiz (9/10 terms correct) and complete the binary position worksheet with 100% accuracy for positions 0-7. Use the instructor checklist to track individual student performance during partner quizzing. Students who struggle with more than 2 terms during Phase 2 should be flagged for additional practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices (e.g., 'Binary = Two choices: 0 or 1') and allow extra study time with visual aids showing binary patterns. For advanced learners: Extend to positions 8-15 (256, 512, 1024, etc.) and introduce terms like 'nibble' (4 bits) and 'word' (16/32 bits). Consider adding hexadecimal digit recognition (0-9, A-F).

title: Binary Number System Vocabulary and Symbol Recognition Drill: Exercise 1
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental binary number system terminology, symbols, and basic conversion rules through flashcard drills and matching exercises. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary needed for understanding computer data representation.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and define 15 key binary number system terms (bit, byte, binary digit, base-2, etc.) through flashcard recognition exercises
Students will recall the symbols (0, 1) and positional values (powers of 2) used in binary representation by completing timed matching activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student (15 cards per set). Each card has a binary term on one side and definition on the other. Give students 10 minutes to study cards individually, reading each term and definition aloud quietly. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 8 minutes - one student shows the term, partner recites definition from memory, then switch roles. Following partner practice, display the Binary Symbol Chart on the projector showing positions (2^3, 2^2, 2^1, 2^0) and corresponding place values (8, 4, 2, 1). Have students copy this chart into their notebooks and recite it chorally three times. Distribute the Binary Vocabulary Worksheet containing two sections: Section A has 15 fill-in-the-blank definitions, Section B requires students to write the correct power of 2 for each binary position (rightmost through 8th position). Students complete worksheets individually in 12 minutes. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal quiz where you call out terms randomly and students raise hands to provide definitions.
