Call on different students for each term, ensuring all participate. Collect worksheets and flashcards remain with students for continued practice.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (15 cards per student) with binary terms and definitions
Binary Symbol Chart poster or PowerPoint slide
Binary Vocabulary Worksheet (printed copies for each student)
Timer or stopwatch
Projector or interactive whiteboard
assessment_method: Grade worksheets using answer key: Section A (15 points - 1 point per correct definition), Section B (8 points - 1 point per correct power of 2). Observe verbal quiz participation for engagement. Success criteria: 80% accuracy on worksheet (18/23 points) and ability to provide at least one correct definition during verbal quiz.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide worksheet with word bank for Section A and allow use of flashcards during independent work. For advanced learners: Add challenge questions requiring them to convert simple 4-bit binary numbers to decimal using memorized positional values. Create student tutors by pairing advanced students with those needing extra support during partner practice.
original_title: Binary Number System Vocabulary and Symbol Recognition Drill

title: Optimizing Multi-Constraint Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real-world logistics problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will formulate objective functions, identify feasible regions, and determine optimal solutions using both graphical and algebraic methods.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems by formulating constraints and objective functions from real-world scenarios
Students will implement graphical and simplex method solutions through systematic problem-solving procedures to find optimal resource allocation
instructions: Begin by presenting students with the scenario: 'AeroTech Manufacturing produces two drone models - Explorer ($800 profit) and Surveyor ($1200 profit). Constraints: max 40 hours assembly time weekly (Explorer needs 2 hrs, Surveyor needs 4 hrs), max 60 hours testing time (Explorer needs 3 hrs, Surveyor needs 2 hrs), material costs cannot exceed $50,000 weekly (Explorer costs $300, Surveyor costs $500), and minimum 5 Explorers must be produced for contract obligations.' Step 1 (15 mins): Students work in pairs to identify variables (x = Explorers, y = Surveyors) and write the objective function and all constraint inequalities. Step 2 (20 mins): Using graphing calculators or Desmos, students plot constraint lines, identify the feasible region, and mark corner points. They must sketch and label their graph clearly. Step 3 (25 mins): Students calculate exact coordinates of corner points using algebraic methods (substitution/elimination), then evaluate the objective function at each point. Step 4 (15 mins): Students determine the optimal solution, interpret results in business context, and calculate maximum weekly profit. Step 5 (10 mins): Pairs present their solutions to another pair, comparing methods and verifying answers. Instructor circulates continuously, checking constraint formulations and graph accuracy.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos graphing tool
Graph paper (minimum 20x20 grid)
Printed scenario handout with constraint data table
Linear programming formula reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphical representation with labeled feasible region (25%), (3) Precise calculation of corner points and optimal solution (35%), (4) Clear business interpretation and profit calculation (15%). Students must submit graphs, algebraic work, and written explanation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed constraint inequality templates and suggest starting with simpler 2-constraint practice problems. Offer step-by-step graphing checklist. For advanced learners: introduce sensitivity analysis by asking 'how would solution change if assembly time increased to 45 hours?' or extend to three-variable problems requiring simplex tableaux method.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Dashboard Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different sales dashboard visualizations to determine which most effectively communicates key business insights. They will apply data visualization principles to justify their evaluation and provide specific improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying established design principles and business communication criteria
Students will critique dashboard designs through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions:
Begin by displaying three pre-prepared sales dashboards (A, B, C) showing identical quarterly sales data but using different visualization approaches: Dashboard A uses only pie charts and tables, Dashboard B uses bar charts and line graphs, and Dashboard C uses a mix including scatter plots and heat maps. Provide students with a business scenario: 'You are presenting quarterly sales performance to executives who need to quickly identify top-performing regions, seasonal trends, and products requiring attention.' 

Divide students into groups of 3-4. Give each group 15 minutes to individually examine all three dashboards using the provided evaluation checklist covering clarity, accuracy, efficiency, and aesthetic appeal. Students should rate each dashboard 1-5 on each criterion and note specific observations.

Next, spend 20 minutes having groups discuss their individual assessments and reach consensus on rankings. They must identify three specific strengths and three specific weaknesses for each dashboard, citing concrete examples (e.g., 'Dashboard A's pie charts make it difficult to compare Q2 vs Q3 sales volumes').

For the final 15 minutes, each group prepares a 3-minute presentation defending their choice of most effective dashboard. They must explain their reasoning using visualization principles and provide two specific, actionable recommendations for improving their chosen dashboard. Groups present their evaluations, and the class votes on the most convincing argument (not just the most popular dashboard choice).
materials_needed: Three pre-made sales dashboards (printed handouts or digital files)
Evaluation checklist rubric with 4 criteria categories
Business scenario description handout
Presentation timer
Projector or screen for displaying dashboards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: appropriate application of visualization principles (5 points), quality of specific evidence cited (5 points), logical reasoning in comparisons (5 points), and clarity of improvement recommendations (5 points). Students must demonstrate they can distinguish between personal preference and objective effectiveness criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'A specific weakness I notice is...' Advanced learners can be challenged to consider audience-specific factors (executive vs. analyst needs) and suggest alternative visualization types not shown in the original dashboards.

title: Design Your Dream Theme Park: Applied Mathematical Modeling
description: Students will create a scaled mathematical model of an original theme park by integrating geometry, algebra, and statistics. They will develop blueprints, calculate costs, analyze visitor flow patterns, and present their park design with comprehensive mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize geometric principles, algebraic equations, and statistical analysis by designing a mathematically accurate theme park model with scaled measurements and cost projections
Students will construct original mathematical models through creating ride equations, optimizing park layouts, and developing pricing strategies based on data analysis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Distribute the Theme Park Design Packet containing grid paper, measurement constraints, and budget parameters. Each team receives a fictional $50 million budget and must design a park fitting within a 100-acre plot (scale: 1 inch = 50 feet). 

Day 1 (90 minutes): Teams brainstorm and sketch initial park layouts, identifying 5-8 attractions. Students must calculate actual dimensions using scale conversions and create geometric shapes for each attraction area. They research real theme park costs online to establish realistic pricing for rides, facilities, and landscaping.

Day 2 (90 minutes): Students develop mathematical models for three key attractions using algebraic functions (roller coaster height/speed relationships, Ferris wheel rotational motion, carousel circular motion). They create graphs showing these relationships and write equations describing each ride's mathematical properties.

Day 3 (45 minutes): Teams conduct statistical analysis by surveying 20+ peers about preferred attractions, ticket pricing, and visit frequency. They create charts, calculate means/medians, and use this data to justify their design choices and pricing strategies.

Day 4 (90 minutes): Students finalize blueprints on poster board, including scaled measurements, cost breakdowns, mathematical models, and statistical justifications. Each team creates a detailed budget spreadsheet showing construction costs, operational expenses, and projected revenue.

Day 5 (90 minutes): Teams present their theme parks in 8-minute presentations, explaining mathematical reasoning, defending design choices, and answering peer questions about calculations and modeling decisions.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1/4 inch squares)
Poster board (22" x 28")
Colored pencils and markers
Calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Rulers and measuring tools
Theme Park Design Packet with constraints and requirements
Access to internet for research
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (25 points - correct scaling, calculations, and equations), Design Creativity and Feasibility (20 points), Statistical Analysis Integration (20 points - appropriate data collection and interpretation), Budget and Cost Analysis (15 points), Presentation Quality and Mathematical Communication (20 points). Students must demonstrate error rates below 5% in calculations and show clear mathematical reasoning throughout.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing calculation templates, pre-made coordinate grids, and partnering them with stronger math peers. Offer simplified ride options with basic geometric shapes. For advanced learners, introduce calculus concepts for ride optimization, compound interest for financial projections, or probability models for wait times and capacity planning. Provide additional constraints like environmental impact calculations or accessibility requirements.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Class Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity classifications for 25 advanced sorting, graph, and dynamic programming algorithms. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of algorithm complexity analysis that is essential for technical interviews and advanced computer science coursework.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time complexity (best, average, worst case) for 25 advanced algorithms including QuickSort variants, graph traversal algorithms, and dynamic programming solutions by completing timed memorization drills
Students will identify the space complexity requirements for advanced data structures and algorithms through structured flashcard review sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet containing 25 algorithms with their complete complexity analysis (time: best/average/worst case, space complexity, and stability for sorting algorithms). Allow students 15 minutes to study the sheet silently. Next, organize students into pairs and provide each pair with pre-made flashcards - one set showing algorithm names, another showing complexity notations. Students spend 10 minutes in partner drilling: one student shows an algorithm name, partner must recite all complexity metrics within 10 seconds. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes. Following partner practice, conduct three progressive rounds of individual recall testing. Round 1 (10 minutes): Students complete a written worksheet matching 15 algorithms to their time complexities - immediate feedback provided. Round 2 (8 minutes): Verbal rapid-fire round where instructor calls out algorithm names and students raise hands to answer - focus on the 10 most challenging algorithms identified in Round 1. Round 3 (7 minutes): Final comprehensive written assessment covering all 25 algorithms including time complexity, space complexity, and additional properties. Between each round, allow 2-minute review periods where students can re-examine their reference sheets. Conclude with students creating personal 'trouble spot' lists of algorithms they need continued practice with.
materials_needed: Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet with 25 advanced algorithms
Pre-made flashcard sets (algorithm names and complexity notations)
Round 1 matching worksheet with answer key
Round 3 comprehensive assessment form
Timer or stopwatch for each activity segment
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final written assessment covering time complexity, space complexity, and algorithm properties. Award full points for exact notation (e.g., O(n log n), O(n²)), half points for correct complexity class but imprecise notation. Track individual progress through all three rounds to identify improvement patterns and persistent knowledge gaps.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for common complexity patterns (e.g., 'divide and conquer usually means O(n log n)') and group similar algorithms together for chunked learning. Create visual complexity charts showing algorithm families. For advanced learners: extend activity to include amortized analysis, expected vs worst-case scenarios for randomized algorithms, and space-time tradeoffs. Challenge them to explain why specific algorithms have their complexity characteristics.

title: Interpreting Model Performance Trade-offs in High-Dimensional Feature Selection Scenarios
description: Students will analyze and interpret the complex relationships between feature dimensionality, model complexity, and performance metrics across different machine learning algorithms. They will examine real-world scenarios where bias-variance trade-offs manifest differently based on feature selection strategies and dataset characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between curse of dimensionality and model performance by analyzing learning curves across varying feature dimensions (100, 1000, 10000 features)
Students will explain the trade-offs between different regularization techniques (L1, L2, Elastic Net) through comparative analysis of feature selection outcomes on high-dimensional genomics data
instructions: Begin by providing students with three versions of the same genomics dataset: 100 selected features, 1000 features, and 10000 features (30 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one regularization method (L1 Lasso, L2 Ridge, Elastic Net). Students first examine the provided performance matrices showing cross-validation scores, feature selection counts, and computational time across all three feature dimensions (45 minutes analysis). Each team creates interpretation frameworks by plotting learning curves, analyzing feature importance distributions, and calculating stability indices for their assigned regularization method. Teams then rotate through stations to examine other teams' results, recording observations about how different regularization approaches handle the curse of dimensionality (30 minutes rotation). Students reconvene to synthesize findings, focusing on interpreting why certain methods perform better with specific feature dimensions and how bias-variance trade-offs manifest differently. They create comparative interpretation matrices showing when to use each approach based on dataset characteristics (45 minutes synthesis). Finally, teams present 5-minute interpretations of one key insight about feature selection trade-offs, demonstrating understanding of the underlying mathematical relationships without requiring complex calculations. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting interpretations to real-world applications in genomics, finance, and text analytics (30 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Pre-computed results matrices for genomics dataset with performance metrics across three feature dimensions
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded visualization code for learning curves and feature importance plots
Printed interpretation framework templates for systematic analysis
Station rotation worksheets for structured peer analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of interpretation of bias-variance trade-offs in high-dimensional settings (2) Quality of explanations connecting regularization methods to feature selection outcomes (3) Depth of analysis when comparing performance across different dimensionalities (4) Clarity of reasoning when justifying method selection for specific scenarios. Students submit individual reflection papers (500 words) explaining their interpretation of the most significant trade-off discovered.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided interpretation questions and pre-filled partial analysis templates focusing on one feature dimension at a time. Offer vocabulary sheets defining key terms like 'regularization path' and 'feature stability.' For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by including non-linear feature interactions and ensemble method comparisons, or challenge them to interpret results in the context of specific domain knowledge constraints.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Big O Evaluation
description: Students analyze the time and space complexity of three different sorting algorithms by examining their code structure, identifying key operations, and comparing their performance characteristics. They will break down each algorithm to determine Big O notation and predict performance outcomes for different input scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort algorithms by identifying loops, recursive calls, and dominant operations
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios using Big O analysis
instructions: Begin by providing students with printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort (15 minutes setup). Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one algorithm initially. Students spend 20 minutes examining their assigned algorithm's code structure, counting nested loops, identifying recursive patterns, and documenting line-by-line operation counts for small input examples (arrays of 4, 8, 16 elements). Each group creates a visual flowchart showing the algorithm's execution path and marks where the most time-consuming operations occur. Groups then rotate algorithms every 15 minutes, spending time analyzing the remaining two sorting methods using the same systematic approach. During analysis, students complete a structured worksheet with sections for: loop depth counting, recursive call trees (for applicable algorithms), operation counting tables, and preliminary Big O predictions. After analyzing all three algorithms (total 50 minutes), groups reconvene to synthesize findings. They create comparison charts showing time complexity for best/average/worst cases, space complexity requirements, and input size thresholds where each algorithm performs optimally. Groups present 5-minute findings to class, defending their Big O classifications with specific code evidence. Conclude with class discussion comparing theoretical analysis to actual runtime scenarios, addressing when theoretical complexity might not match practical performance.
materials_needed: Printed code implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort with line numbers
Algorithm analysis worksheet templates with operation counting tables
Large poster paper for creating algorithm flowcharts
Colored markers for highlighting code sections
Stopwatch or timer for rotation management
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets for accurate Big O classifications (40%), quality of code structure identification and loop counting (30%), group presentation clarity and evidence-based reasoning (20%), and peer feedback forms rating other groups' algorithm explanations (10%). Success criteria: correctly identify time complexity within one Big O class, provide specific code line references supporting analysis, demonstrate understanding through clear visual representations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed operation counting tables and highlighting key code sections in advance. Offer algorithm complexity reference sheets with common patterns. For advanced learners, introduce analysis of hybrid sorting algorithms like Timsort, or challenge them to propose optimizations for worst-case scenarios. Provide additional algorithms like heap sort or radix sort for extended comparison.

title: Design and Justify a Novel Cryptographic Algorithm Using Advanced Number Theory
description: Students will create an original public-key cryptographic system by synthesizing concepts from modular arithmetic, prime factorization, and elliptic curves. They will develop both the mathematical foundation and practical implementation while analyzing security vulnerabilities and computational complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original cryptographic algorithm by integrating advanced number theory concepts including modular exponentiation, discrete logarithms, and elliptic curve operations
Students will construct a comprehensive security analysis through mathematical proofs, complexity calculations, and vulnerability assessments of their created system
instructions: Begin by having students work in pairs to research three existing cryptographic methods (RSA, Elliptic Curve, Diffie-Hellman) for 45 minutes using provided academic sources. Next, assign each pair to create their hybrid algorithm by combining elements from at least two existing methods or introducing novel mathematical operations (90 minutes). Students must define their key generation process using specific mathematical formulations, create encryption/decryption procedures with step-by-step algorithms, and establish parameter constraints (prime sizes, curve equations, etc.). During the design phase, students document all mathematical assumptions and prove correctness of their encryption/decryption cycle. Following design completion, pairs spend 60 minutes implementing their algorithm in Python, creating functions for key generation, encryption, and decryption with test cases demonstrating functionality. Students then conduct security analysis (45 minutes) by calculating computational complexity using Big O notation, identifying potential attack vectors, and comparing their method's theoretical strength against existing algorithms. Each pair prepares a 15-minute presentation including algorithm overview, mathematical justification, implementation demonstration, security analysis, and practical applications discussion. Conclude with peer evaluation sessions where each pair reviews another team's work, testing implementations and critiquing mathematical rigor. Instructors facilitate discussions on real-world applicability and guide students in identifying areas for algorithmic improvement.
materials_needed: Academic papers on RSA, Elliptic Curve Cryptography, and Discrete Logarithm Problem
Python programming environment with NumPy and SymPy libraries installed
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Wolfram Alpha access)
Presentation software and projector setup
Cryptographic algorithm evaluation rubric templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and correctness of algorithm design (30 points), successful implementation with working code and test cases (25 points), comprehensive security analysis including complexity calculations and vulnerability identification (25 points), clarity and depth of presentation with peer Q&A responses (20 points). Bonus points awarded for novel mathematical insights or practical optimization discoveries.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing algorithm design templates, pre-written helper functions for basic mathematical operations, and guided worksheets for security analysis calculations. For advanced learners, challenge them to implement additional features like digital signatures, optimize for quantum-resistant properties, or conduct comparative benchmarking against professional cryptographic libraries. Provide one-on-one consultations during design phase to ensure mathematical validity.

title: Programming Language Syntax Memory Match Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental syntax elements from three popular programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) through flashcard drills and timed matching exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of basic programming constructs that students must recognize automatically.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize common syntax patterns for variables, loops, and conditionals in Python, Java, and JavaScript by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will recall correct syntax formatting for basic programming constructs through timed matching exercises within 3 minutes per language
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 15 syntax examples per programming language (45 cards total). Each card shows a programming concept on one side (e.g., 'for loop') and correct syntax on the reverse (e.g., 'for i in range(10):'). 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to study flashcards, focusing on one language at a time. They should read each concept aloud, flip the card, and repeat the syntax three times before moving to the next card. Circulate to ensure proper pronunciation of syntax elements.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Pair students and have them quiz each other using the flashcards. Partner A shows the concept side while Partner B recites the syntax from memory. Switch roles every 5 minutes, cycling through all three languages.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Distribute the digital matching worksheet containing scrambled syntax elements and programming concepts. Students must match 45 items (15 per language) within the time limit. Use a timer visible to all students. No collaboration allowed during this phase.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire verbal recall session. Call out programming concepts randomly while students raise hands to provide syntax answers. Award points for correct responses and note common errors for review.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (45 cards per student pair covering Python, Java, JavaScript syntax)
Digital matching worksheet with 45 syntax/concept pairs
Classroom timer or stopwatch
Answer key sheets for peer checking
Whiteboard markers for recording common errors
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (41/45 correct matches) on the digital worksheet within 3 minutes per language section. Track individual performance using a checklist noting: flashcard drill completion, peer quiz participation, matching worksheet score, and verbal recall responses. Award mastery status only when students demonstrate consistent recall across all three assessment components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce to two languages initially and provide syntax reference sheets during first attempt. Create memory aids using color-coding for different languages. For advanced learners, add complexity by including function definitions, class syntax, or error handling constructs. Challenge them to explain syntax differences between languages during peer quiz sessions.

title: Interpreting Statistical Relationships in Customer Churn Analysis Through Correlation Matrix Exploration
description: Students will analyze a customer churn dataset by examining correlation matrices to identify relationships between customer characteristics and churn behavior. They will interpret correlation coefficients and explain which variables are most predictive of customer retention versus departure.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features and churn rates by analyzing patterns in correlation matrices
Students will explain the practical business implications of statistical relationships through written explanations of their findings
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a telecommunications customer churn dataset with 15 variables (tenure, monthly charges, contract type, etc.). In the first 10 minutes, have students run the initial data loading cells and examine the dataset structure using .info() and .describe() methods. Next, guide students through creating a correlation matrix using pandas .corr() function and visualizing it with seaborn's heatmap function (15 minutes). Students should identify correlations above 0.3 and below -0.3 with the 'Churn' variable. For the next 20 minutes, have students work in pairs to interpret three specific relationships: monthly charges vs. churn, contract length vs. churn, and total charges vs. tenure. They must write explanations for each relationship, describing both the statistical strength and business meaning. In the final 15 minutes, each pair presents one relationship to the class, explaining the correlation coefficient value and what it suggests about customer behavior. Students should use phrases like 'moderate positive correlation' or 'weak negative correlation' and connect findings to business decisions like pricing strategies or contract incentives.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib installed
Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV file with 7043 rows, 21 columns)
Pre-written notebook template with data loading code
Correlation interpretation reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correctly identifies correlation coefficients and their directions, (2) Uses appropriate statistical terminology to describe relationship strength, (3) Provides logical business interpretations of correlations, (4) Clearly communicates findings during pair presentation. Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation strength reference chart (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7+ strong) and sentence starters like 'The correlation of X suggests that...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or discuss why correlation doesn't imply causation using specific examples from their analysis.

title: Optimization Crisis: Emergency Resource Allocation Using Linear Programming
description: Students apply linear programming techniques to solve a realistic emergency management scenario involving multiple constraints and competing objectives. They will formulate constraint equations, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal resource allocation strategies for a natural disaster response.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to model real-world emergency resource allocation problems by translating scenario constraints into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal solutions through systematic mathematical analysis and verification
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Emergency Response Scenario handout describing a hurricane aftermath where students must allocate limited helicopters, medical supplies, and personnel across three affected zones with varying needs and accessibility constraints. Each zone has minimum requirement thresholds and maximum capacity limits.

**Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (15 minutes):** Students work in pairs to define decision variables (x₁, x₂, x₃ representing resource units to each zone), identify all constraints from the scenario text, and formulate the objective function (minimize total response time while maximizing lives saved). They must write at least 6 constraint inequalities and justify each mathematical representation.

**Phase 2 - Graphical Analysis (20 minutes):** For the simplified 2-variable version, students plot constraint lines on provided coordinate grids, shade feasible regions, and identify corner points. They must calculate exact coordinates for at least 4 vertices of the feasible region and verify each point satisfies all constraints.

**Phase 3 - Optimization Solution (25 minutes):** Students apply the corner point method to evaluate the objective function at each vertex, determine the optimal solution, and interpret results in the original context. They must show complete calculations and state the final resource allocation with units.

**Phase 4 - Sensitivity Analysis (15 minutes):** Students analyze how the optimal solution changes when one constraint is modified (e.g., 20% more helicopters available) and explain the practical implications for emergency planners.

**Verification & Presentation (10 minutes):** Each pair presents their optimal allocation strategy to another pair, defending their mathematical approach and real-world reasoning. Partners verify calculations using provided solution checker.
materials_needed: Emergency Response Scenario handout with specific numerical constraints
Graphing paper with pre-marked axes (scale 0-100)
Scientific calculators
Linear programming solution verification worksheet
Colored pencils for constraint graphing
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Complete constraint formulation with justifications (25 points), (2) Accurate graphical representation showing feasible region and corner points (25 points), (3) Correct optimal solution with full calculations (30 points), (4) Sensitivity analysis with practical interpretation (20 points). Success criteria: Minimum 80% accuracy in mathematical procedures and clear connection between mathematical results and real-world implications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation template with sentence starters like 'The helicopter constraint is...' and pre-drawn coordinate axes. For advanced learners: Include integer programming constraints (whole helicopters only) requiring modified solution techniques, or extend to 3-variable problem using simplex tableaux method.

title: Distributed System Failure Pattern Analysis: Decomposing the WhatsApp 2021 Global Outage
description: Students will analyze the technical architecture and failure cascade of the October 2021 WhatsApp/Facebook outage by examining BGP routing protocols, DNS dependencies, and microservices architecture. They will decompose the multi-layered failure patterns to identify root causes, propagation mechanisms, and systemic vulnerabilities in large-scale distributed systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between BGP routing, DNS resolution, and application-layer services by tracing failure propagation paths through network topology diagrams
Students will decompose complex system failures into constituent components through systematic examination of logs, architecture diagrams, and timeline correlation analysis
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Distribute the WhatsApp outage case study packet containing: network topology diagrams, BGP routing tables pre/during/post-outage, DNS query logs, internal Facebook engineering blog posts, and external monitoring data from Downdetector and Cloudflare Radar. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams examine the timeline and create a visual failure cascade map. Students must identify the initial trigger (BGP route withdrawal), map the propagation through each system layer (network → DNS → application → user access), and annotate dependencies. Provide colored markers for different failure types: red for complete failures, yellow for degraded performance, blue for recovery actions.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams analyze the technical logs using provided Python scripts to parse BGP announcements and DNS query patterns. Students must identify three specific failure patterns: the BGP route withdrawal mechanism, DNS resolver timeout cascades, and internal tool dependencies that prevented remote recovery. Each team documents their findings in a structured analysis template with evidence citations.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Teams present their failure cascade maps to the class, defending their analysis of root causes versus symptoms. Other teams must challenge assumptions and ask clarifying questions about technical dependencies. Instructor facilitates discussion on systemic design patterns that contributed to the outage severity and duration.
materials_needed: WhatsApp outage case study packet with network diagrams and log excerpts
Large format paper (A3 or flip chart) for failure cascade mapping
Colored markers (red, yellow, blue, black)
Python environment with network analysis libraries (pandas, matplotlib, networkx)
BGP and DNS log parsing scripts (pre-written)
Failure analysis template worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Technical accuracy of failure cascade identification (30 points), evidence-based reasoning linking logs to conclusions (25 points), clarity of dependency mapping and visual representation (20 points), quality of root cause versus symptom differentiation (15 points), and peer discussion contribution and technical questioning (10 points). Teams must submit their annotated failure cascade map and completed analysis template with specific log evidence citations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed failure timeline with key events marked, and offer guiding questions like 'What happens to DNS queries when BGP routes are withdrawn?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose specific architectural changes (circuit breakers, graceful degradation patterns) and analyze similar outages from other major platforms (AWS, Google Cloud) to identify common distributed system anti-patterns.

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Water Park with Budget Constraints
description: Students will create an original scale model water park using geometric principles, algebraic equations, and statistical analysis. They must design attractions within a given budget, calculate materials needed, and present their park with mathematical justifications for all design decisions.
estimated_duration: 3 hours (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a scale model water park by applying geometric scaling, area calculations, and volume formulas to design functional attractions
Students will develop a comprehensive budget analysis through algebraic equations, percentage calculations, and cost-benefit optimization strategies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the scenario: each team receives a $2.5 million budget to design a water park on a 50m × 80m lot, with attractions costing specific amounts per square meter based on type (pools: $800/m², slides: $1200/m², lazy rivers: $600/m², children's areas: $400/m²). Teams spend 20 minutes brainstorming attraction ideas and sketching preliminary layouts on grid paper where 1 square = 2m × 2m real space. Next, students create detailed scale drawings (40 minutes) showing exact dimensions, calculating areas for each attraction type, and determining total costs using algebraic expressions. They must include at least 5 different attraction types and stay within budget constraints. During construction phase (60 minutes), teams build 3D models using provided materials, ensuring mathematical accuracy in scaling (1:100 ratio). Students document their process by creating cost breakdown tables, showing percentage allocation of budget across attraction categories, and calculating capacity using geometric formulas. Teams prepare 8-minute presentations (30 minutes preparation) explaining their mathematical reasoning, cost justifications, and design trade-offs. During presentations (40 minutes total), other teams evaluate designs using provided peer assessment forms focusing on mathematical accuracy and creative problem-solving. Conclude with reflection discussion (15 minutes) where students identify key mathematical concepts used and real-world applications of their learning.
materials_needed: Grid paper (1cm squares, 5 sheets per team)
Cardboard pieces, foam blocks, colored paper for construction
Rulers, protractors, calculators
Budget constraint handouts with cost specifications
Peer evaluation rubrics (printed copies)
Poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: Mathematical Accuracy (correct area/volume calculations, proper scaling, accurate budget analysis), Creative Design (originality, functionality, aesthetic appeal), Problem-Solving Process (documentation of decision-making, optimization strategies), and Presentation Quality (clear mathematical explanations, professional delivery). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving 3/4 or higher in each category. Final deliverables include scale model, detailed cost analysis spreadsheet, and presentation slides with mathematical justifications.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing formula reference sheets, pre-calculated examples of area/volume problems, and partnering with stronger math students. Offer calculation templates and step-by-step cost analysis worksheets. For advanced learners, add complexity by requiring profit projections, incorporating statistical visitor flow analysis, or designing attractions with curved surfaces requiring advanced geometric calculations. Provide extension challenge of optimizing park layout for maximum revenue per square meter.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memory Drill with Network Packet Analysis
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific functions, protocols, and encapsulation processes of each TCP/IP protocol stack layer through structured packet header examination. This activity reinforces foundational networking knowledge essential for advanced network programming and cybersecurity courses.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the four TCP/IP protocol stack layers and their specific functions by analyzing real network packet captures
Students will identify and recite the correct protocols, port numbers, and header fields associated with each layer through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing printed copies of five different network packet captures (HTTP request, HTTPS response, DNS query, FTP transfer, and SMTP email) with headers clearly marked but layer functions removed. Students work individually for the first 15 minutes to label each header section with its corresponding TCP/IP layer (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) and write the primary function of each layer beside it. Provide the master reference sheet after 15 minutes. Students then spend 10 minutes self-checking their work using red pens to mark corrections. Next, conduct a 20-minute rapid-fire oral drill where students stand and you call out either a protocol name (HTTP, TCP, IP, Ethernet), port number (80, 443, 21, 25), or function description. Students must respond within 3 seconds with the correct layer name and one additional fact about that layer. Students who respond incorrectly sit down but can rejoin after correctly answering a follow-up question. For the final 10 minutes, students complete a fill-in-the-blank worksheet listing 25 protocols, port numbers, and layer functions they must complete from memory without references. Collect worksheets immediately upon completion. Throughout the activity, emphasize that this is pure memorization practice - analysis and application will come in subsequent lessons. Maintain a brisk pace to prevent overthinking and encourage automatic recall responses.
materials_needed: 5 printed packet capture samples (HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, FTP, SMTP) with 30 copies each
TCP/IP layer reference sheet master copy
Red pens (30 pieces)
Fill-in-the-blank recall worksheets (30 copies)
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard markers for tracking oral drill responses
assessment_method: Success measured by: (1) Packet labeling accuracy - 80% or higher correct layer identification and function descriptions, (2) Oral drill participation - minimum 5 correct rapid responses before elimination, (3) Final worksheet completion - 20/25 items correctly recalled from memory within time limit. Students achieving all three criteria demonstrate mastery of foundational protocol stack knowledge.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded packet samples where each layer uses different colored highlighting, and allow them to use acronyms (ATIN for Application-Transport-Internet-Network Access). For advanced learners: Include additional protocols like ICMP, DHCP, and BGP in their packet samples, and challenge them to recall specific RFC numbers and header field bit lengths during oral drills.

title: Interpreting Feature Interaction Effects in High-Dimensional Models Using SHAP and Partial Dependence Analysis
description: Students will analyze a complex machine learning model to understand how feature interactions contribute to predictions beyond simple additive effects. They will interpret SHAP interaction values and 2D partial dependence plots to explain non-linear relationships in a real-world dataset with 50+ features.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP interaction matrices to identify the top 5 feature pairs that exhibit the strongest non-additive effects on model predictions
Students will explain feature interaction patterns through analysis of 2D partial dependence plots and connect these findings to domain-specific business implications
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained XGBoost model fitted on the California housing dataset with engineered features (total 52 features including polynomial and interaction terms). Step 1 (15 min): Students load the provided model and test dataset, then generate SHAP values using TreeExplainer for 1000 randomly sampled instances. Step 2 (20 min): Have students create a SHAP interaction matrix heatmap and identify the top 5 feature pairs with highest absolute interaction values. They must document these pairs and their interaction magnitudes. Step 3 (25 min): For each identified pair, students generate 2D partial dependence plots using scikit-learn's PartialDependenceDisplay, setting grid resolution to 20x20 points. They should overlay 200 data points on each plot to show data density. Step 4 (30 min): Students analyze each 2D plot to identify interaction patterns (synergistic, antagonistic, or threshold effects) and write 2-3 sentences explaining how each feature pair jointly influences housing prices. Step 5 (20 min): Students compare their SHAP interaction findings with correlation matrix results to distinguish between linear correlation and non-linear interaction effects. Step 6 (15 min): In pairs, students discuss their findings and prepare a 3-minute explanation of their most significant discovery, connecting the statistical pattern to real-world housing market dynamics.
materials_needed: Pre-trained XGBoost model file (.pkl format) with California housing data
Test dataset CSV file (1000 instances, 52 features)
Python environment with SHAP, scikit-learn, matplotlib, pandas, numpy installed
Jupyter notebook template with code skeleton and data loading functions
assessment_method: Students submit a completed notebook containing: (1) Correctly generated SHAP interaction heatmap with top 5 pairs identified and labeled, (2) Five 2D partial dependence plots with proper titles and data overlays, (3) Written interpretations for each interaction pattern using domain-specific terminology, (4) Comparison table showing correlation vs. interaction values for identified pairs. Rubric: Visualization quality (25%), Correct identification of interactions (30%), Quality of interpretations (35%), Domain connection (10%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional code templates for plot customization and pre-written interpretation sentence starters. Offer reference sheet with common interaction pattern types (synergistic, antagonistic, threshold). For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify interaction effects that contradict domain intuition and research potential explanations, or extend analysis to 3-way interactions using SHAP's higher-order interaction capabilities.

title: Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Runtime Decomposition
description: Students will analyze the time complexity of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup algorithms by examining their code structure, identifying key operations, and comparing their performance characteristics across different input sizes. They will break down each algorithm's runtime behavior to determine Big O classifications.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity of three search algorithms by decomposing their code into fundamental operations and counting iteration patterns
Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic evaluation of worst-case, best-case, and average-case scenarios using Big O notation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Algorithm Analysis Worksheet containing implementations of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup in Python. Form teams of 2-3 students and assign each team one algorithm to start with (rotate every 20 minutes). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine their assigned algorithm's pseudocode and identify the fundamental operations (comparisons, assignments, array accesses). They mark each line of code with operation counts and highlight loops or recursive calls.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams create a table showing how the number of operations changes as input size increases from 10, 100, 1000, to 10,000 elements. They must trace through worst-case scenarios (element not found for linear search, last element for binary search, collision handling for hash tables) and document the maximum operations required.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students graph their operation counts versus input size on provided graph paper, plotting points and drawing trend lines. They identify whether the relationship is linear, logarithmic, or constant.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams rotate to analyze their second algorithm using the same process, then compare findings with their previous analysis. They complete comparison matrices showing relative performance at different input sizes.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Final rotation to third algorithm, followed by whole-class compilation of results. Each team presents their Big O classification for one algorithm, justifying their conclusion by referencing specific code sections and mathematical relationships they identified.

Conclude with teams submitting completed analysis sheets showing operation counts, graphs, and Big O justifications for all three algorithms.
materials_needed: Algorithm Analysis Worksheet with Python implementations of linear search, binary search, and hash table lookup
Graph paper (3 sheets per student)
Calculators
Big O Reference Chart
Colored pencils for graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate submitted analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of fundamental operations in code (25%), (2) Correct calculation of operation counts for different input sizes (25%), (3) Properly constructed graphs showing algorithmic trends (25%), (4) Justified Big O classifications with specific evidence from code analysis (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed operation count tables and highlight the specific lines of code to focus on. Offer sentence starters for Big O justifications. For advanced learners, include additional algorithms (merge sort, quicksort) or ask them to analyze space complexity alongside time complexity. Provide real-world datasets to test their theoretical predictions.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Production: A/B Testing vs Champion-Challenger Framework
description: Students will critically assess two real-world model deployment strategies by analyzing performance metrics, business impact, and implementation trade-offs. They will evaluate conflicting evidence from production data and recommend an optimal deployment approach with detailed justification.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of A/B testing versus champion-challenger deployment strategies by analyzing production performance metrics, statistical significance, and business KPIs
Students will critique model performance evaluation methodologies through systematic assessment of bias, fairness metrics, and long-term sustainability concerns
instructions:
Provide students with two datasets: Dataset A contains 6 months of A/B test results for a recommendation system (50/50 traffic split, CTR, conversion rates, revenue per user). Dataset B shows champion-challenger results for the same period (90/10 split, model accuracy, drift metrics, computational costs). 

Step 1 (45 min): Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze both datasets using provided Jupyter notebooks. They calculate statistical significance, effect sizes, and confidence intervals for key metrics. 

Step 2 (30 min): Teams identify limitations and potential biases in each approach. They examine sample selection bias, seasonal effects, and metric gaming possibilities using provided diagnostic tools.

Step 3 (45 min): Each team creates a comprehensive evaluation matrix comparing both strategies across 8 dimensions: statistical power, business risk, implementation complexity, cost, speed of iteration, user experience impact, long-term learning, and regulatory compliance.

Step 4 (30 min): Teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their recommended approach. They must address three specific stakeholder concerns: engineering team's preference for gradual rollouts, product team's need for rapid iteration, and executive team's risk aversion.

Step 5 (45 min): Present findings to simulated stakeholder panel (instructor + guest industry professional). Other teams serve as peer evaluators using provided scoring rubrics. Include 5-minute Q&A challenging assumptions and methodology.
materials_needed: Two pre-processed datasets (A/B test results CSV, champion-challenger metrics JSON)
Jupyter notebooks with statistical analysis templates
Evaluation matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Video conferencing setup for industry professional participation
Peer evaluation rubric forms
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Technical accuracy of statistical analysis (25 points), (2) Depth of bias identification and methodology critique (25 points), (3) Quality of multi-dimensional evaluation framework (20 points), (4) Strength of evidence-based recommendation and stakeholder consideration (20 points), (5) Professional presentation and defense under questioning (10 points). Minimum 80/100 required for mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide statistical analysis cheat sheets and guided questions for bias identification. Offer optional pre-work session on A/B testing fundamentals. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity with multi-armed bandit comparison, cost-benefit analysis with actual dollar figures, and consideration of ethical AI implications in deployment strategy selection.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Urban Traffic Optimization
description: Students will create an original mathematical model using differential equations and optimization theory to solve real urban traffic flow problems. They will synthesize multiple mathematical concepts including calculus, linear algebra, and probability theory to develop a comprehensive solution that can be implemented by city planners.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize differential equations, optimization algorithms, and statistical modeling to create an original traffic flow management system for a specific urban intersection
Students will construct a comprehensive mathematical framework that integrates multiple advanced concepts to solve authentic transportation engineering problems
instructions: Begin by providing students with real traffic data from 3-4 major city intersections (accident rates, peak flow times, pedestrian counts, signal timing). Working in teams of 3-4, students spend the first 45 minutes analyzing the data to identify key variables and constraints. Next, students spend 60 minutes developing their mathematical framework: they must incorporate at least one system of differential equations for traffic flow dynamics, one optimization function for signal timing, and one probabilistic model for accident prediction. During this phase, circulate to ensure teams are making connections between different mathematical domains. In the following 90 minutes, students use MATLAB or Python to implement their model, creating visual simulations of their proposed traffic management system. They must generate at least three different scenarios (rush hour, normal traffic, emergency situations) and demonstrate how their model adapts. For the final 45 minutes, each team presents their complete model to the class, explaining their mathematical reasoning, showing their simulation results, and defending their design choices against peer questions. Require teams to submit their mathematical derivations, code, simulation outputs, and a 2-page executive summary suitable for city planning officials. Throughout the activity, emphasize that students must justify every mathematical choice with real-world reasoning and demonstrate how their integrated approach improves upon existing traffic management systems.
materials_needed: Real traffic datasets from municipal transportation departments (CSV files with 6 months of data)
MATLAB or Python software with numpy, scipy, and matplotlib libraries installed
Graphing calculators (TI-89 or equivalent)
Large poster paper and markers for mathematical derivations
Access to research databases for traffic engineering literature
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Integration (25% - seamless synthesis of 3+ advanced concepts), Model Innovation (25% - original approach beyond textbook methods), Implementation Quality (25% - functional code with accurate simulations), and Professional Communication (25% - clear presentation suitable for non-mathematicians). Students must demonstrate their model works across all three scenarios and can articulate the mathematical reasoning behind each component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template differential equations and optimization frameworks that they can modify rather than create from scratch. Offer pre-written code snippets for basic traffic flow equations. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate machine learning algorithms for predictive traffic patterns, add economic cost-benefit analysis using advanced calculus, or extend their model to network-wide traffic optimization across multiple intersections using graph theory.

title: Optimization of Manufacturing Production Lines Using Calculus
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus concepts to solve real-world manufacturing optimization problems. They will use partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to determine optimal production rates, resource allocation, and profit maximization for a fictitious electronics manufacturing company.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to determine optimal production quantities that maximize profit given multiple product lines
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems involving limited manufacturing resources and labor constraints
instructions:
Begin by distributing the TechCorp Manufacturing scenario packet containing production cost functions, revenue models, and constraint equations for three product lines (smartphones, tablets, headphones). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Analyst, Calculations Manager, Constraints Specialist, and Presentation Coordinator.

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the given profit function P(x,y,z) = 150x - 2x² + 200y - 3y² + 100z - z² - 50xy + 30xz, where x, y, z represent thousands of units produced monthly for each product. Students calculate partial derivatives ∂P/∂x, ∂P/∂y, ∂P/∂z and find critical points by setting them equal to zero.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Introduce manufacturing constraints: labor hours (8x + 12y + 5z ≤ 10,000), raw materials budget ($20x + $35y + $15z ≤ 50,000), and facility capacity (x + y + z ≤ 800). Teams apply Lagrange multiplier method: ∇P = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ + λ₃∇g₃, solving the resulting system of equations.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Students use graphing calculators or Desmos to verify their analytical solutions and create 3D visualization of the profit function. They evaluate the profit at boundary conditions and compare with interior critical points.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Teams prepare a 2-minute presentation recommending optimal production levels, expected monthly profit, and identifying which constraints are binding. Include sensitivity analysis discussing how profit changes if one constraint is relaxed by 10%.
materials_needed: TechCorp Manufacturing scenario packets (one per team)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Access to Desmos Graphing Calculator online
Engineering paper for detailed calculations
Presentation timer for 2-minute team presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation of partial derivatives and critical points (25 points), (2) Proper setup and solution of Lagrange multiplier system (35 points), (3) Accurate interpretation of results and constraint analysis (25 points), (4) Clear presentation with justified recommendations (15 points). Teams must show all mathematical work and achieve within 5% of the theoretical optimum values.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partial derivative formulas started and constraint equation formats. Offer mini-review sessions on gradient calculations. For advanced learners: Add uncertainty analysis by introducing probabilistic demand functions, or extend to include integer programming constraints where production quantities must be whole numbers. Provide additional scenarios with non-linear constraints.

title: Distributed System Architecture Analysis: Decomposing Netflix's Microservices Fault Tolerance Patterns
description: Students will analyze Netflix's actual microservices architecture by examining their fault tolerance patterns, identifying failure points, and evaluating the effectiveness of their circuit breaker, bulkhead, and timeout strategies. They will deconstruct complex system interactions to understand how architectural decisions impact system reliability and scalability.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system fault tolerance patterns by examining real-world microservices architectures and identifying failure propagation paths
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of circuit breaker, bulkhead, and timeout patterns through systematic decomposition of system interaction diagrams
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with Netflix's public architecture documentation and the Chaos Monkey implementation details (30 minutes setup). Teams first spend 45 minutes mapping Netflix's core services (API Gateway, User Service, Recommendation Engine, Content Delivery, Billing) onto a visual diagram, identifying all inter-service dependencies. Next, students analyze three specific fault tolerance patterns: circuit breakers between recommendation service and user preferences, bulkhead isolation in the content streaming pipeline, and timeout configurations in the payment processing flow (60 minutes). Each team must trace failure scenarios: What happens when the recommendation service fails? How does the circuit breaker prevent cascading failures? Students document their analysis by creating failure tree diagrams showing potential failure points and corresponding mitigation strategies. In the final 45 minutes, teams present their analysis focusing on: 1) Critical failure points they identified, 2) How Netflix's patterns prevent or contain failures, 3) Alternative architectural decisions and their trade-offs, 4) Specific metrics they would monitor to validate pattern effectiveness. Each presentation must include a live demonstration using the provided system simulation tool, showing how removing specific fault tolerance patterns would impact overall system behavior.
materials_needed: Netflix architecture documentation (Microservices: Lessons from Netflix guide)
Chaos Monkey GitHub repository and documentation
System simulation software (Docker containers with simplified Netflix services)
Lucidchart or Draw.io licenses for diagramming
Sample failure scenario datasets
Presentation computers with network access
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using rubric: Accuracy of architectural decomposition (25 points) - correctly identifies service boundaries and dependencies; Depth of pattern analysis (30 points) - demonstrates understanding of how circuit breaker, bulkhead, and timeout patterns function; Quality of failure scenario analysis (25 points) - traces failure propagation accurately and evaluates mitigation effectiveness; Presentation clarity and technical depth (20 points) - explains complex concepts clearly with proper system simulation demonstration. Minimum 70/100 points required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-labeled architectural templates and guided failure scenario worksheets with partially completed examples. Assign specific roles within teams (diagram specialist, pattern analyst, presenter). For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose novel fault tolerance patterns, analyze performance implications using queuing theory, or design automated failure detection algorithms. Provide additional real-world case studies from Uber, Amazon, or Google for comparative analysis.

title: Design a Mathematical Board Game Using Linear Functions and Statistical Analysis
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates linear functions for scoring systems and movement mechanics, then conduct statistical analysis of gameplay outcomes. This activity synthesizes algebraic concepts with data analysis while requiring creative game design principles.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original board game by integrating linear function concepts for scoring mechanisms and player movement systems
Students will develop statistical analysis methods through collecting and interpreting gameplay data from their created games
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives design materials and the project packet outlining requirements. Phase 1 (Day 1, 45 minutes): Teams brainstorm game themes and create initial sketches. They must identify where linear functions will be incorporated - such as scoring formulas based on moves (y = 2x + 10 where x = spaces moved), penalty calculations, or resource accumulation rates. Teams complete a Linear Function Integration Plan documenting at least three specific applications with equations. Phase 2 (Day 2, 60 minutes): Teams construct their physical game boards using poster board, markers, and game pieces. They create rule sheets that explicitly state their linear functions and provide worked examples. Each game must include a data collection sheet for tracking player scores, moves, and outcomes. Phase 3 (Day 3, 45 minutes): Teams playtest their games, recording data from at least 10 complete rounds. They calculate mean scores, determine winning percentages, and create scatter plots showing relationships between variables (moves vs. final score, time played vs. winner margin). Phase 4 (Day 4, 30 minutes): Teams prepare 5-minute presentations showcasing their game, explaining linear function applications, and presenting statistical findings with visual displays. Final submission includes the physical game, rule sheet with mathematical explanations, completed data analysis with graphs, and reflection on how mathematical concepts enhanced gameplay design.
materials_needed: 22x28 inch poster board (1 per team)
Colored markers and pencils
Dice, game pieces, and timers
Graphing paper and calculators
Project requirement packet with Linear Function Integration Plan template
Data collection sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Integration (25%) - accurate use of linear functions with clear equations and examples; Game Functionality (25%) - playable game with coherent rules and engaging mechanics; Statistical Analysis (25%) - complete data collection with appropriate calculations and visual representations; Presentation Quality (25%) - clear explanation of mathematical concepts and professional delivery. Students must demonstrate mastery by correctly applying linear function concepts, conducting valid statistical analysis, and articulating mathematical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing linear function equation templates and sample game mechanics. Offer guided practice with simple scoring systems before complex integration. For advanced learners, encourage incorporation of piecewise functions, systems of equations for multi-player interactions, or advanced statistical measures like standard deviation and correlation coefficients. Provide extension opportunities to create digital versions or analyze probability distributions.

title: TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Rapid Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the specific functions, protocols, and data units at each layer of the TCP/IP protocol stack through intensive flashcard drills and timed identification exercises. This activity reinforces foundational networking knowledge essential for advanced network programming and system administration.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact functions of each TCP/IP protocol stack layer (Application, Transport, Internet, Network Access) by completing timed identification exercises with 95% accuracy
Students will memorize specific protocols, port numbers, and data unit names for each layer through structured flashcard drilling and peer testing
instructions: Begin by providing students with a comprehensive TCP/IP reference sheet containing: Application Layer (HTTP/80, HTTPS/443, FTP/21, SMTP/25, DNS/53, DHCP/67-68), Transport Layer (TCP, UDP, segments/datagrams), Internet Layer (IP, ICMP, ARP, packets), and Network Access Layer (Ethernet, WiFi, frames/bits). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students create digital flashcards using Anki or Quizlet with protocol names on front, layer and port number on back. They must create exactly 20 cards covering key protocols from each layer. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Individual memorization using spaced repetition - students drill flashcards for 10 minutes, then take a 2-minute break, then drill for 8 more minutes. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Pair students for peer testing. Partner A shows protocol name, Partner B must state correct layer, function, and port number within 5 seconds. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Instructor displays random protocol names on projector for 3 seconds each. Students write layer, primary function, and port number on answer sheets. Include 15 protocols total. Phase 5 (5 minutes): Self-scoring using answer key, students calculate accuracy percentage and identify knowledge gaps for future study.
materials_needed: TCP/IP Protocol Reference Sheet (one per student)
Anki or Quizlet account access for each student
Individual answer sheets for final assessment
Projector for displaying protocol names
Timer for paced activities
Answer key for self-scoring
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the final timed protocol identification test (13/15 correct responses). Each response requires correct layer identification, primary function description, and port number. Award 1 point for layer, 1 point for function, 1 point for port number per protocol (45 points total). Additionally, peer testing partnerships must verify successful completion of flashcard drilling phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made flashcard sets and allow extra 2-minute review time before peer testing. Use mnemonic devices like 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' for layer order. For advanced learners: Include additional protocols (SNMP/161, Telnet/23, SSH/22) and require explanation of protocol interactions across layers. Challenge them to identify security implications of each protocol.

title: Deconstructing Feature Engineering Decisions in Production ML Pipeline Case Studies
description: Students analyze three real-world production machine learning pipelines to identify, categorize, and explain the rationale behind specific feature engineering techniques. They will examine how domain knowledge, data characteristics, and business constraints influenced feature transformation choices in different industry contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between different feature engineering techniques (scaling, encoding, transformation, selection) by analyzing their implementation and impact within production ML pipeline case studies
Students will explain the relationship between domain-specific business requirements and feature engineering decisions through comparative analysis of multi-industry ML systems
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute overview of the three case studies: Netflix recommendation system (2019), Uber's demand forecasting (2020), and Airbnb's pricing optimization (2021). Provide students with detailed pipeline documentation, feature transformation code snippets, and performance metrics for each system. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one primary case study for 45 minutes of deep analysis. Students must create a feature engineering decision matrix identifying: (1) each transformation technique used, (2) the original data characteristics that necessitated the transformation, (3) the business/technical rationale, and (4) the measured impact on model performance. Groups then rotate for 20 minutes each to examine the other two case studies, adding comparative notes to their matrix. During analysis, students should identify patterns such as how categorical encoding differs between recommendation vs. pricing systems, or how temporal features are handled differently across domains. In the final 25 minutes, conduct a structured discussion where each group presents one key insight about how domain context influenced feature engineering choices, followed by class identification of universal principles versus domain-specific approaches. Conclude with students individually writing a 300-word synthesis explaining how business constraints and data characteristics should guide feature engineering decisions.
materials_needed: Three detailed ML pipeline case study documents with code snippets
Feature engineering decision matrix template (digital worksheet)
Performance metrics comparison charts for each case study
Jupyter notebooks with anonymized feature transformation examples
Digital collaboration platform (Miro or Jamboard) for group analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate completed decision matrices for accuracy of technique identification (25%), quality of rationale explanations (35%), and depth of comparative insights (25%). Assess individual synthesis papers for demonstration of understanding connections between domain context and feature engineering choices (15%). Success criteria: correctly identifies 80%+ of feature engineering techniques, provides technically accurate rationales, and articulates clear domain-specific vs. universal principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed decision matrix with 2-3 examples filled in and a glossary of feature engineering terms. Offer guiding questions like 'What type of data problem does this transformation solve?' For advanced learners, include additional pipeline performance data and challenge them to hypothesize alternative feature engineering approaches that might improve results, or analyze the computational efficiency trade-offs of different transformation choices.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Differential Equations and Network Theory
description: Students will synthesize concepts from calculus, linear algebra, and graph theory to create an original mathematical model that optimizes traffic flow at a complex urban intersection. They will develop their own system of differential equations, validate it with real-world constraints, and present implementation recommendations to city planners.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original mathematical model incorporating differential equations and network theory by analyzing real urban traffic data and identifying optimization parameters
Students will synthesize multiple mathematical domains (calculus, linear algebra, graph theory) through designing a comprehensive solution to a complex real-world problem
Students will generate novel mathematical relationships and constraints by evaluating traffic flow dynamics, pedestrian patterns, and infrastructure limitations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with traffic data packets containing: hourly vehicle counts, pedestrian crossing times, traffic light timing sequences, and intersection layouts for a specific real urban intersection. Teams spend 45 minutes analyzing the data to identify key variables, constraints, and optimization goals.
