Next, teams develop their mathematical framework (60 minutes): they must create at least 3 differential equations modeling vehicle flow rates, incorporate matrix representations for traffic light states, and apply graph theory to represent intersection topology. Each equation must include at least 5 real-world parameters (vehicle arrival rates, pedestrian crossing delays, turning probabilities, etc.). Teams then validate their models (30 minutes) by testing against provided historical data and adjusting parameters for accuracy within 15% margin. Following validation, teams design implementation strategies (45 minutes), calculating optimal traffic light timing, identifying bottleneck locations, and projecting improvement percentages. Finally, each team prepares a 15-minute presentation (30 minutes preparation) formatted as a city planning committee proposal, including mathematical derivations, visual model representations, cost-benefit analysis, and specific implementation timeline. Presentations occur with teams acting as consultants pitching to 'city officials' (other students and instructor).
materials_needed: Real traffic data sets from 4-6 different urban intersections (vehicle counts, timing data, pedestrian patterns)
Graphing calculators or computer access with mathematical software (MATLAB, Mathematica, or Python with NumPy/SciPy)
Large format paper (11x17) and colored markers for model visualization
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint, Google Slides, or similar)
Traffic engineering reference materials and intersection layout diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical rigor and originality of model (30 points) - assessing equation complexity, parameter integration, and novel approaches; Model validation and accuracy (25 points) - measuring deviation from historical data and adjustment reasoning; Synthesis of mathematical domains (20 points) - evaluating integration of calculus, algebra, and graph theory; Implementation feasibility and recommendations (15 points) - assessing practicality and cost considerations; Presentation clarity and professionalism (10 points) - measuring communication effectiveness and visual aids quality. Students must achieve minimum 24/30 on mathematical rigor to demonstrate mastery at create level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template differential equation frameworks and guided parameter identification worksheets; offer one-on-one consultations during model development phase; allow use of simplified intersection layouts with fewer variables. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements, multiple intersection optimization, or environmental factors (emissions, fuel consumption); encourage exploration of machine learning integration for dynamic parameter adjustment; provide access to more complex real-world datasets including weather and event impacts.

title: Programming Language Syntax Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall basic syntax elements from three major programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript) through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential syntax recognition skills needed before writing any code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify correct syntax for variable declarations, loops, and conditional statements in Python, Java, and JavaScript by completing flashcard drills
Students will recall specific punctuation marks, keywords, and formatting rules for each programming language through timed recognition exercises
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute pre-made flashcard sets containing 30 cards total: 10 cards each for Python, Java, and JavaScript basic syntax elements (variable declaration, if-statements, for-loops, function definitions, comments). Each card shows a concept on front (e.g., 'Python variable declaration') and correct syntax on back (e.g., 'variable_name = value'). **Phase 1 - Individual Study (15 minutes):** Students work alone, cycling through all 30 cards three times. They should say the syntax aloud before flipping each card to check accuracy. Mark cards they miss for extra review. **Phase 2 - Partner Quizzing (10 minutes):** Pair students up. Partner A holds cards and shows only the concept side to Partner B, who must recite the correct syntax from memory. Partners switch roles after 5 minutes. **Phase 3 - Rapid Recall Test (10 minutes):** Display 15 random concepts on screen (5 from each language) one at a time for 30 seconds each. Students write down the correct syntax on their answer sheets without referring to cards. **Phase 4 - Self-Check (5 minutes):** Provide answer key. Students check their responses and calculate accuracy percentage. Record scores for instructor review.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (30 cards per student)
Answer sheets with numbered lines 1-15
Digital timer or stopwatch
Answer key handout
Projector/screen for displaying concepts
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery with 80% accuracy (12/15 correct) on the rapid recall test. Grade based on: syntax accuracy (70%), proper punctuation/capitalization (20%), and completion of all activity phases (10%). Collect answer sheets to verify individual progress and identify common error patterns.
scaffolding_notes: **Support struggling learners:** Reduce to 2 languages instead of 3, provide syntax reference sheet during first attempt, allow 45 seconds per question instead of 30. **Extend advanced learners:** Add complex syntax like nested loops, error handling, or object-oriented concepts; challenge them to write syntax for additional languages like C++ or Ruby; have them create new flashcards for classmates.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs Causation in Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real customer dataset to distinguish between correlation and causation when identifying factors that lead to customer churn. They will examine statistical relationships and explain why certain variables are correlated but not necessarily causal.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing customer churn data and identifying spurious relationships
Students will explain the limitations of correlation analysis through guided interpretation of scatter plots, correlation matrices, and confounding variables
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the telecom customer churn dataset containing 15 variables including monthly charges, contract length, customer service calls, tenure, age, and churn status. Students work in pairs with laptops/tablets.

**Phase 1 - Initial Exploration (15 minutes):** Students calculate correlation coefficients between all variables and churn using provided correlation matrix template. They identify the top 5 variables most strongly correlated with churn and rank them by strength of correlation.

**Phase 2 - Guided Analysis (20 minutes):** Present three pre-selected variable pairs: (1) Ice cream sales vs drowning deaths, (2) Monthly charges vs churn, (3) Customer service calls vs churn. For each pair, students create scatter plots and answer guided questions: 'What is the correlation coefficient?' 'Does this relationship make logical sense?' 'What other factors might explain this relationship?'

**Phase 3 - Critical Thinking (15 minutes):** Students examine the relationship between 'contract length' and 'churn rate.' They discover that customers with month-to-month contracts churn more than yearly contract customers. Using provided prompts, they brainstorm alternative explanations: Does short contract cause churn, or do customers likely to churn choose short contracts?

**Phase 4 - Application (10 minutes):** Students write a brief recommendation memo to a business manager explaining why the company should not assume that reducing monthly charges will decrease churn, despite the strong negative correlation. They must cite at least two potential confounding variables and suggest what additional data would help establish causation.
materials_needed: Telecom customer churn dataset (CSV file with 1000 rows, 15 columns)
Correlation matrix calculation template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Guided analysis worksheet with scatter plot templates
Business memo template (1-page format)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correctly identifies correlation coefficients and ranks variables, (2) Accurately distinguishes correlation from causation in all three examples, (3) Provides logical alternative explanations for contract length relationship, (4) Business memo clearly explains why correlation doesn't imply actionable insights and suggests appropriate next steps for establishing causation
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide correlation coefficient interpretation guide (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7-1.0 strong) and sentence starters for explanations. **Extension for advanced learners:** Have them research and explain Simpson's Paradox using an additional dataset, or calculate partial correlations controlling for a third variable to demonstrate how relationships can change.

title: Optimization in Manufacturing: Applying Calculus to Minimize Production Costs
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving material costs, labor efficiency, and production constraints. They will determine optimal dimensions for packaging design that minimizes total production costs while meeting specific volume requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques to find critical points and determine absolute minimum values by analyzing a multi-variable cost function in a manufacturing context
Students will construct and solve optimization models through systematic problem-solving steps including constraint identification, function formulation, and solution verification
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: A company manufactures cylindrical containers with a required volume of 1000 cubic inches. Material costs $0.15 per square inch for the base and top, $0.08 per square inch for the sides, and there's a fixed setup cost of $50 per production run plus $0.02 per inch of height for specialized tooling. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify all variables and constraints, then individually spend 20 minutes setting up the optimization problem by expressing total cost as a function of radius (r) and height (h), using the volume constraint V = πr²h = 1000 to eliminate one variable. Next, students spend 25 minutes finding the derivative of their cost function, setting it equal to zero, and solving for critical points using algebraic manipulation. They must then verify their solution represents a minimum by applying the second derivative test. In the final 20 minutes, students calculate the exact optimal dimensions, minimum cost, and create a brief written explanation justifying why their solution is economically reasonable. Throughout the activity, circulate to check constraint identification, function setup, differentiation accuracy, and algebraic solving steps.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Printed problem scenario worksheets with company specifications
Graph paper for sketching cost functions
Calculus reference sheets with derivative rules
assessment_method: Grade using a 20-point rubric: constraint identification and variable definition (4 points), correct cost function formulation (5 points), accurate differentiation and critical point calculation (6 points), verification using second derivative test (3 points), and clear written justification of economic reasonableness (2 points). Students must show all algebraic steps and arrive within 5% of the optimal solution.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a template showing the general form of the cost function with blanks to fill in coefficients, and offer hints about substituting h = 1000/(πr²) to create a single-variable function. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding additional constraints such as maximum height restrictions due to shipping limitations, or ask them to analyze how the optimal solution changes if material costs fluctuate by ±20%.

title: Analyzing Concurrency Bugs in Multi-threaded Banking System Code
description: Students will examine a deliberately flawed multi-threaded banking application to identify race conditions, deadlock scenarios, and synchronization failures. They will categorize bug types, trace execution paths, and propose specific fixes for each concurrency issue discovered.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-threaded code execution by systematically tracing thread interleavings and identifying critical sections where race conditions occur
Students will categorize concurrency bugs through detailed code examination and classify them as race conditions, deadlocks, or livelock scenarios
instructions: Provide each student team (2-3 members) with the BankingSystem.java file containing Account, Transaction, and BankManager classes with intentionally embedded concurrency bugs. Begin with a 10-minute code walkthrough where students identify all synchronized blocks, locks, and shared resources. In the analysis phase (45 minutes), students create a detailed bug report using the provided template. They must: 1) Execute the code multiple times to observe inconsistent behaviors, 2) Use thread dump analysis tools to capture deadlock states, 3) Draw thread execution diagrams showing problematic interleavings, 4) For each bug found, document the specific line numbers, affected variables, and failure scenarios. Students should identify at least 5 distinct issues: withdraw/deposit race condition on account balance, deadlock in transfer operations due to lock ordering, lost update problem in transaction logging, ABA problem in balance checking, and improper use of volatile keyword. During the final 20 minutes, teams present one critical bug to the class, demonstrating the failure with specific execution traces and explaining why standard testing might miss the issue. Each presentation must include before/after memory state diagrams and proposed synchronization solutions.
materials_needed: BankingSystem.java source code with embedded concurrency bugs
Bug analysis template with sections for symptoms, root cause, and solutions
Java IDE with debugging capabilities (Eclipse or IntelliJ)
Thread dump analysis tool (jstack or IDE profiler)
Execution trace recording sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Bug identification accuracy (40 points - must find at least 4/5 bugs with correct categorization), execution trace quality (25 points - diagrams clearly show thread interleavings and memory states), root cause analysis depth (20 points - explanations connect code structure to failure modes), and proposed solutions feasibility (15 points - fixes address actual issues without introducing new problems). Require written documentation and successful demonstration of at least one bug reproduction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guided questions about each class method and highlight all synchronized keywords before analysis begins. Offer simplified execution scenarios focusing on two-thread interactions only. For advanced learners: challenge them to estimate the probability of each race condition occurring and analyze performance implications of their proposed fixes. Provide additional scenarios involving atomic operations and lock-free data structures.

title: Evaluating Data Visualizations for Business Decision-Making
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different visualizations of the same sales dataset to determine which best supports a specific business decision. They will apply evaluation criteria including accuracy, clarity, and appropriateness to make and justify their recommendation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different data visualizations by applying specific criteria including data accuracy, visual clarity, and decision-support value
Students will critique visualization choices through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for business contexts
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with the scenario: 'TechStart company needs to decide which product line to expand based on 2023 quarterly sales data.' Give each group three different visualizations of identical sales data: a pie chart showing total sales by product, a line graph showing quarterly trends by product, and a stacked bar chart showing quarterly sales breakdown. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Groups examine each visualization individually, noting what information each conveys clearly and what might be confusing or misleading. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the provided evaluation checklist, groups systematically assess each visualization against four criteria: (1) Data accuracy - does it represent the data correctly? (2) Visual clarity - is it easy to read and understand? (3) Decision relevance - does it help answer the business question? (4) Audience appropriateness - would executives understand it quickly? Groups score each visualization 1-3 on each criterion.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Groups calculate total scores and discuss any discrepancies in their individual assessments, reaching consensus through discussion.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Each group prepares a 2-minute recommendation presentation identifying their chosen visualization and providing three specific reasons why it best supports the expansion decision, citing evidence from their evaluation.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Groups present their recommendations. After each presentation, other groups can ask one clarifying question about the reasoning behind the choice.
materials_needed: Three printed visualizations of identical quarterly sales data (pie chart, line graph, stacked bar chart)
Business scenario handout describing TechStart company's expansion decision
Evaluation checklist with 4 criteria and 1-3 scoring scale
Timer for group activities
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 3-point rubric assessing: (1) Systematic use of evaluation criteria (0-3 points), (2) Quality of evidence cited to support recommendation (0-3 points), (3) Clear justification connecting visualization choice to business decision context (0-3 points). Students demonstrate mastery with 7+ points total and must show evidence-based reasoning in their final recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This visualization is effective because...' and 'The data shows...' For advanced learners, add a challenge: identify one way to improve their chosen visualization and explain what additional data might strengthen the business recommendation. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who need support in evidence-gathering.

title: Design a City Transportation System Using Linear Programming
description: Students will create an original mathematical model for optimizing a city's bus route system using linear programming constraints and objective functions. They will design the transportation network, formulate mathematical equations, and present solutions that minimize cost while maximizing coverage for a fictional city of 50,000 residents.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original linear programming model by defining decision variables, constraints, and objective functions for a real-world transportation optimization problem
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts of inequalities, graphing, and optimization through designing and justifying a complete city bus route system
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute city maps showing 8 residential districts and 5 key destinations (hospital, schools, shopping center, industrial area, government center). Provide constraint cards listing: maximum 6 bus routes, $50,000 daily operating budget, each route costs $8,000/day, minimum 80% population coverage required, maximum 45-minute travel time between any two points. **Phase 1 (25 minutes):** Working in teams of 3-4, students analyze the city layout and identify optimal bus stop locations. They must create decision variables (x₁, x₂, etc. representing each potential route), write the objective function (minimize cost OR maximize coverage), and formulate at least 5 mathematical constraint inequalities based on budget, time, and coverage requirements. **Phase 2 (30 minutes):** Teams graph their constraint system on coordinate planes, identify the feasible region, and determine optimal solutions using corner point method or graphical analysis. Students must show all mathematical work and justify why their solution is optimal. **Phase 3 (20 minutes):** Each team creates a visual presentation showing their final route map, complete mathematical model, solution process, and cost-benefit analysis. **Presentation (25 minutes):** Teams present 3-minute solutions to the class, defending their mathematical choices and explaining how their model addresses real-world constraints. Other students evaluate presentations using peer assessment forms focusing on mathematical accuracy and practical feasibility.
materials_needed: Printed city maps (8.5x11 inch) with residential districts and key locations marked
Constraint requirement cards with budget/coverage specifications
Graphing paper and coordinate plane templates
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils/markers for route mapping
Presentation rubric handouts
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Mathematical accuracy of linear programming model - correct variables, constraints, and objective function (25 points), (2) Quality of graphical solution showing feasible region and optimal point identification (25 points), (3) Practical feasibility of proposed bus route system addressing all given constraints (25 points), (4) Clarity of mathematical reasoning and justification in presentation (25 points). Minimum 70/100 points required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed constraint equations and guided questions for identifying variables. Offer step-by-step graphing guides and allow use of graphing calculators. For advanced learners: Add complexity with multiple objectives (minimize cost AND maximize coverage simultaneously), introduce integer programming constraints (whole number of buses only), or require sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with different budget scenarios.

title: Memory Palace: Recalling TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions and Port Numbers
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific functions of all seven OSI model layers, their corresponding TCP/IP stack equivalents, and 25 critical well-known port numbers. This foundational knowledge activity prepares students for advanced network protocol analysis and troubleshooting.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact functions and protocols of each OSI model layer and TCP/IP stack layer by creating structured memory associations
Students will identify and recite 25 well-known port numbers with their corresponding protocols and services through systematic memorization techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the reference sheet containing OSI layers (Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application) with their TCP/IP equivalents (Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application) and detailed function descriptions. Students have 15 minutes to study using the provided mnemonic device 'Please Do Not Take Sausage Pizza Away' for OSI layers. Next, introduce the critical port numbers list: 20/21 (FTP), 22 (SSH), 23 (Telnet), 25 (SMTP), 53 (DNS), 67/68 (DHCP), 69 (TFTP), 80 (HTTP), 110 (POP3), 119 (NNTP), 123 (NTP), 143 (IMAP), 161/162 (SNMP), 179 (BGP), 389 (LDAP), 443 (HTTPS), 993 (IMAPS), 995 (POP3S). Students create personal memory associations for each port-service pair using the chunking method: group by tens (20s, 60s, 100s, etc.). Provide 20 minutes for memorization using flashcards. Students then work in pairs for 10 minutes, testing each other orally. Cover the reference materials and conduct individual rapid-fire recall sessions where each student has 3 minutes to write down all seven OSI layer functions in order, match them to TCP/IP layers, and list all 25 port numbers with their services. No references allowed during testing. Students must achieve 100% accuracy on layer functions and 90% accuracy on port numbers to demonstrate mastery. Repeat the cycle twice more with 5-minute review periods between attempts.
materials_needed: OSI Model and TCP/IP Stack reference sheet with detailed layer functions
Well-known port numbers reference chart (25 critical ports)
Blank flashcards (50 cards per student)
Timer for structured memorization intervals
Answer key for instructor verification
assessment_method: Students complete three timed written recalls (3 minutes each). Score: OSI layer functions (7 points - must be 100% accurate), TCP/IP mapping (4 points - must be 100% accurate), port numbers with services (25 points - minimum 23/25 correct required). Record improvement across three attempts. Success requires achieving target scores by third attempt.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce port list to 15 most critical ports, provide additional mnemonic devices, allow 5-minute study sessions instead of 3-minute recalls. For advanced learners: add ephemeral port ranges (32768-65535), include less common but important ports (636 LDAPS, 1723 PPTP), require explanations of why certain ports are paired (20/21 FTP data/control).

title: Security Vulnerability Analysis of Web Authentication Systems
description: Students analyze real-world authentication code samples to identify security vulnerabilities, evaluate their potential impact, and categorize threat types. They examine both secure and insecure implementations to understand common attack vectors and defensive patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze authentication code samples by identifying specific security vulnerabilities and explaining their exploitation mechanisms
Students will evaluate the severity and impact of identified vulnerabilities through systematic threat assessment using OWASP guidelines
instructions: Begin by distributing three code samples containing different authentication implementations (15 minutes setup). Sample 1: PHP login with SQL injection vulnerability, Sample 2: JavaScript authentication with client-side validation only, Sample 3: Python Flask implementation with proper security measures. Students work in pairs to examine each code sample systematically. First, they spend 20 minutes per sample identifying potential vulnerabilities by tracing execution flow and noting security concerns. They document findings using the provided vulnerability analysis worksheet, recording line numbers, vulnerability types, and potential attack scenarios. Next, students spend 15 minutes researching each identified vulnerability using OWASP documentation to understand attack methods and impact levels. They then categorize vulnerabilities as High, Medium, or Low severity based on CVSS scoring criteria. In the analysis phase (25 minutes), pairs compare the three implementations, identifying why Sample 3 is more secure and documenting specific defensive techniques used. Students create a vulnerability matrix showing attack type, affected code location, exploitation method, potential damage, and recommended fixes. Finally, each pair presents one critical vulnerability to the class (20 minutes total), explaining the attack vector and demonstrating how an attacker might exploit it using concrete examples.
materials_needed: Three pre-written code samples with embedded vulnerabilities
Vulnerability analysis worksheet template
OWASP Top 10 reference guide
Computers with code editors and web browsers
CVSS scoring calculator access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed vulnerability matrices for accuracy of identified vulnerabilities (40%), correct severity classifications using OWASP criteria (30%), quality of exploitation explanations (20%), and clarity of security recommendations (10%). Successful completion requires identifying at least 70% of embedded vulnerabilities and correctly classifying their severity levels.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with a vulnerability checklist covering common issues (SQL injection, XSS, weak authentication). For advanced learners, include additional samples with subtle timing attacks or cryptographic weaknesses. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during code analysis phases.

title: Critical Evaluation of Predictive Models for Healthcare Risk Assessment
description: Students will critically assess the validity, reliability, and ethical implications of three different machine learning models predicting patient readmission risk. They will evaluate model performance metrics, identify potential biases, and provide justified recommendations for deployment decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple predictive models by analyzing performance metrics, statistical significance, and real-world applicability
Students will critique model fairness and ethical implications through systematic bias detection and impact assessment on different demographic groups
instructions: Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with three pre-trained models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, Neural Network) and their outputs on a hospital readmission dataset containing 10,000 patient records with demographics, medical history, and outcomes. Students spend 30 minutes examining model documentation, training procedures, and initial performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC). Next, students conduct a 45-minute deep-dive analysis using provided confusion matrices, learning curves, and feature importance plots. They must calculate additional metrics like specificity, negative predictive value, and analyze performance across demographic subgroups (age, gender, ethnicity, insurance type). During the following 60 minutes, teams evaluate each model using a structured framework: statistical validity (cross-validation results, overfitting indicators), clinical relevance (false positive/negative costs, interpretability requirements), and ethical considerations (disparate impact ratios, fairness metrics across protected groups). Students then spend 45 minutes preparing a comparative evaluation matrix and written justification. Each team presents their findings in a 10-minute presentation, defending their choice of which model(s) to deploy, reject, or modify. The final 30 minutes involves peer questioning and instructor-led discussion on evaluation criteria prioritization and real-world implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Three pre-trained models with saved outputs and prediction probabilities
Hospital readmission dataset (10,000 records) with demographic variables
Model performance documentation including confusion matrices and ROC curves
Python/R environment with scikit-learn, pandas, and fairness evaluation libraries
Evaluation framework template with bias detection metrics
assessment_method: Grade using rubric evaluating: (1) Technical analysis quality - correct calculation and interpretation of performance metrics (25%), (2) Bias identification - systematic detection of demographic disparities using appropriate statistical tests (25%), (3) Critical reasoning - logical justification of recommendations considering multiple stakeholder perspectives (30%), (4) Evidence synthesis - integration of technical, ethical, and practical considerations into coherent evaluation (20%). Deliverables include completed evaluation matrix, 2-page written recommendation, and presentation performance.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing metric calculation templates and guided questions for bias detection. Offer pre-calculated demographic breakdowns if statistical computation becomes overwhelming. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by including cost-benefit analysis, regulatory compliance requirements, or comparison with published benchmarks. Encourage exploration of advanced fairness metrics like equalized odds or calibration across groups.

title: Design and Validate a Novel Cryptographic Hash Function for Blockchain Applications
description: Students will create an original cryptographic hash function by combining mathematical concepts from number theory, discrete mathematics, and computational complexity. They will implement their function, test its security properties, and present a formal mathematical proof of its collision resistance properties.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across two 2.25-hour sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design an original cryptographic hash function by integrating modular arithmetic, prime number theory, and bit manipulation operations within specified security parameters
Students will construct mathematical proofs demonstrating collision resistance through formal analysis of their function's computational complexity and avalanche effect properties
instructions:
Begin with a 15-minute overview of cryptographic hash function requirements: deterministic output, fixed output size (256 bits), avalanche effect, and collision resistance. Divide students into teams of 2-3. Each team receives a unique prime number p > 10^15 and must incorporate it into their design.

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams design their hash function architecture. They must combine at least three mathematical operations: modular exponentiation using their assigned prime, a custom permutation function based on finite field arithmetic, and bitwise operations (XOR, rotation, substitution). Students document their algorithm with pseudocode and mathematical notation.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Implementation phase using Python. Teams code their hash function, ensuring 256-bit output regardless of input size. They must handle variable-length inputs through padding schemes and implement iterative compression for inputs exceeding block size.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Security analysis. Teams test their function against collision attacks by generating 10,000 random inputs and checking for duplicates. They calculate and document the avalanche effect by measuring bit-change percentages when inputs differ by single bits.

Step 4 (30 minutes): Formal proof construction. Teams write mathematical proofs demonstrating their function's collision resistance, incorporating computational complexity arguments and probability bounds.

Step 5 (60 minutes): Presentations. Each team presents their hash function design, demonstrates live collision testing, and defends their security proof. Other teams attempt to find collisions or identify vulnerabilities.

Conclude with peer evaluation where teams rate others' mathematical rigor, implementation quality, and proof validity using provided rubrics.
materials_needed: Python 3.8+ with NumPy and hashlib libraries installed on each computer
List of unique prime numbers (>10^15) for each team
Cryptographic hash function specification handout
Digital whiteboard software (Miro or Jamboard) for algorithm design
Collision testing dataset with 50,000 pre-generated random strings
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Algorithm Design (25 points - mathematical sophistication, integration of required operations, originality), Implementation Quality (25 points - code correctness, efficiency, proper handling of edge cases), Security Analysis (25 points - thorough collision testing, accurate avalanche effect calculations, vulnerability identification), Mathematical Proof (25 points - logical rigor, proper use of complexity theory, valid probability arguments). Students must score 80+ points for proficiency, with bonus points awarded for discovering collisions in peers' functions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template pseudocode with blank sections to fill, offer pre-written helper functions for modular arithmetic, and allow use of existing cryptographic libraries for comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to prove resistance against birthday attacks, implement side-channel attack protections, or extend their function to support variable output lengths. Provide additional prime numbers for students who finish early to create multiple hash function variants.

title: Python Data Type Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) through flashcard drills and rapid identification exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of data types essential for beginning programming.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and their definitions through memorization exercises
Students will identify specific Python data types when given code examples through visual recognition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made flashcards containing data type names on one side and definitions/examples on the other (5 minutes setup). Have students work in pairs, with Partner A holding flashcards showing only the data type name (int, float, string, boolean, list) while Partner B states the definition and provides one example. Partner A then flips the card to check accuracy. After 8 minutes, partners switch roles for another 8 minutes. Next, display the prepared slideshow containing 20 code examples (one per slide, 30 seconds each). Students must write down the data type for each example on their answer sheet. Examples include: 42 (int), 3.14 (float), 'Hello World' (string), True (boolean), [1, 2, 3] (list). Show each slide for exactly 30 seconds, then advance automatically. After completing all 20 examples, display the answer key slide and have students self-grade their responses. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal review where you call out random examples and students shout out the data type as a class. Record participation and accuracy during this final segment for assessment purposes.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with Python data types (5 cards per pair of students)
PowerPoint slideshow with 20 Python code examples
Answer sheets (one per student)
Answer key handout
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 16 out of 20 data types (80% accuracy) on the slideshow exercise. Grade answer sheets immediately after self-correction. Award participation points for active engagement during flashcard partner work and verbal review. Success criteria: 80% accuracy on written identification plus active participation in both partner and group activities.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with data type definitions during the slideshow activity. Pair weaker students with stronger partners during flashcard work. For advanced learners, include additional data types (tuple, dictionary) on bonus flashcards, or challenge them to create their own examples during partner work.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze a correlation matrix from an e-commerce dataset to identify meaningful relationships between customer demographics and purchasing behaviors. They will explain how different correlation strengths indicate various types of business insights and distinguish between correlation and causation in their interpretations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by categorizing relationships as strong, moderate, or weak and explaining their business implications
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through structured analysis of feature relationships in customer data
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-generated correlation matrix showing relationships between 8 customer variables: age, income, time_on_site, pages_viewed, previous_purchases, cart_abandonment_rate, seasonal_spending, and total_spent. In pairs, students spend 10 minutes examining the matrix and highlighting all correlations with absolute values above 0.5. Next, each pair creates a three-column analysis table: Variable Pair | Correlation Value | Business Interpretation. For 15 minutes, they complete this table for their highlighted correlations, writing 2-3 sentence explanations of what each relationship might mean for business decisions. Following this, pairs spend 10 minutes identifying which correlations might represent causation versus mere correlation, marking each relationship as 'likely causal,' 'possibly causal,' or 'correlation only' with justifications. In the final 15 minutes, conduct a class discussion where 3-4 pairs present their most interesting findings, focusing on one strong positive correlation, one strong negative correlation, and one relationship they believe shows causation. The instructor guides discussion toward common misinterpretations and the importance of domain knowledge in correlation analysis. Students conclude by individually writing a 100-word summary explaining the difference between their strongest correlation finding and their most likely causal relationship.
materials_needed: Pre-generated 8x8 correlation matrix printout (one per pair)
Three-column analysis worksheet template
Highlighters or colored pens
Whiteboard or projector for class discussion
assessment_method: Evaluate the three-column analysis table for accuracy of correlation strength categorization (weak/moderate/strong), quality of business interpretations, and appropriate distinction between correlation and causation. Award points: 40% for correct correlation strength identification, 40% for meaningful business interpretations, 20% for appropriate causation analysis. Individual summary demonstrates understanding of correlation vs. causation distinction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation strength reference guide (0.0-0.3 weak, 0.3-0.7 moderate, 0.7+ strong) and sample business interpretation examples. For advanced learners, include additional variables like customer satisfaction scores or marketing channel data, and challenge them to identify potential confounding variables that might explain apparent correlations.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data: Written Report
description: Students will analyze a correlation matrix of customer demographic and behavioral features to identify meaningful relationships and explain their business implications. They will distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while interpreting the practical significance of these patterns for marketing strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by categorizing relationship strength and explaining directional patterns
Students will explain the business implications of feature correlations through written analysis connecting statistical findings to marketing decisions
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a pre-generated correlation matrix (8x8) showing relationships between customer features: age, income, website_visits, email_opens, purchase_frequency, average_order_value, loyalty_points, and social_media_engagement. Display the correlation matrix as a heatmap using seaborn in Jupyter notebooks. In the first 10 minutes, students individually examine the matrix and identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values. Next, spend 15 minutes in pairs where students compare their findings and discuss what each correlation might mean in business terms. For example, if income correlates 0.73 with average_order_value, what does this suggest about customer segmentation? During the following 20 minutes, students work individually to complete a structured analysis worksheet with three sections: (1) Classification of all 28 correlations as strong (>0.7 or <-0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7 or -0.3 to -0.7), or weak (<0.3 and >-0.3), (2) Selection and explanation of the five most business-relevant correlations, and (3) Identification of one surprising correlation and hypothesis about its cause. Conclude with 10 minutes of whole-class discussion where pairs share one insight about unexpected correlations and their potential business applications. Students must submit their completed worksheet and participate in the discussion to demonstrate understanding.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebooks with pandas and seaborn installed
Pre-generated customer correlation matrix CSV file (8 features, 1000 customer records)
Correlation Analysis Worksheet (printed or digital)
Access to Python environment or Google Colab
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate correlation strength classification (25%), (2) Logical business interpretations with specific examples (35%), (3) Clear explanation of surprising correlation with reasonable hypothesis (25%), (4) Active participation in pair and class discussions (15%). Students must achieve 70% to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet defining correlation strength categories and sample business interpretation examples. Offer sentence starters like 'The correlation between X and Y suggests that customers who...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional features that might strengthen the analysis. Consider providing a second dataset with categorical variables for extended practice with different correlation techniques.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a correlation matrix from customer purchase data to identify meaningful relationships between variables. They will explain how different correlation coefficients indicate the strength and direction of relationships between customer demographics, spending habits, and product preferences.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by classifying relationships as weak, moderate, or strong and explaining their business implications
Students will distinguish between positive and negative correlations through systematic analysis of a customer purchase correlation matrix
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (3-4 students) with a printed correlation matrix showing 8 variables: age, income, years_customer, monthly_spend, discount_usage, loyalty_score, product_categories_purchased, and satisfaction_rating. Start with a 5-minute individual review where students examine the matrix silently and circle any coefficients they find noteworthy. Next, conduct a 10-minute guided walkthrough using the age-income correlation (0.67) as an example, demonstrating how to interpret this as a moderately strong positive relationship and what this means for customer segmentation strategies. Have groups spend 15 minutes completing a structured worksheet where they: (1) identify the three strongest positive correlations and explain what each relationship suggests about customer behavior, (2) find the two strongest negative correlations and hypothesize why these inverse relationships exist, (3) locate three weak correlations (absolute value < 0.3) and discuss why these variables might be relatively independent. During the final 10 minutes, each group presents one surprising or counterintuitive correlation finding to the class, explaining the coefficient value, relationship direction, and potential business implications. Circulate during group work to ensure students are correctly interpreting coefficient magnitudes and signs, prompting them with questions like 'What does a correlation of -0.45 tell us about these two variables?' and 'How might marketing teams use this relationship information?'
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix (8x8) with customer purchase data for each group
Correlation interpretation worksheet with structured questions
Correlation strength reference guide (weak: 0-0.3, moderate: 0.3-0.7, strong: 0.7-1.0)
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of correlation strength categories (25 points), (2) Accurate explanation of positive vs negative relationships (25 points), (3) Logical business interpretations of correlations (25 points), (4) Quality of group presentation and peer discussion (25 points). Students must achieve 18/25 points in categories 1-2 to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded correlation matrix (green for positive, red for negative) and sentence starters like 'A correlation of 0.X indicates...' For advanced learners: Include questions about correlation vs. causation, spurious relationships, and how correlation matrices inform feature selection for machine learning models. Offer additional dataset for independent analysis.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real customer dataset containing 8 variables to identify and explain correlation patterns between features. They will interpret correlation matrices and visualizations to understand relationships between customer demographics, spending habits, and purchase behaviors.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing a correlation matrix and explaining the strength and direction of at least 5 feature relationships
Students will explain the business implications of feature correlations through written analysis connecting statistical findings to customer behavior patterns
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the preprocessed 'customer_purchases.csv' dataset containing 1,000 customer records with variables: age, income, education_years, family_size, annual_spending, purchase_frequency, loyalty_score, and satisfaction_rating. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to load the data into their preferred tool and generate a correlation matrix using built-in functions (pandas.corr() in Python or cor() in R). Next, have students create a correlation heatmap visualization with color coding where values closer to +1/-1 are darker. During minutes 20-35, students identify and document the 3 strongest positive correlations and 3 strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values. For minutes 35-50, pair students to compare findings and discuss potential business reasons behind each correlation pattern. In the final 15 minutes, each pair writes a brief analysis explaining: (1) which correlations make intuitive business sense, (2) which correlations are surprising and why, and (3) one actionable business recommendation based on the strongest correlation found. Circulate during pair work to ensure students are correctly interpreting coefficient magnitudes and distinguishing between correlation strength and business significance.
materials_needed: Preprocessed customer_purchases.csv dataset (1,000 rows, 8 columns)
Computers with Python/pandas or R installed
Correlation coefficient reference sheet showing interpretation ranges
Worksheet template for recording correlation findings
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation identification - correctly identifies strongest positive/negative correlations with precise coefficient values, (2) Interpretation quality - accurately explains what each correlation coefficient means in terms of relationship strength and direction, (3) Business reasoning - provides logical explanations connecting statistical patterns to real customer behaviors, (4) Written analysis - clearly communicates findings with proper statistical terminology and actionable insights.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide showing coefficient ranges (0.7-1.0 = strong, 0.3-0.7 = moderate, 0.1-0.3 = weak) and sentence starters like 'This correlation of X.XX indicates...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or spurious correlations, and ask them to suggest additional data that might strengthen their business recommendations.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data: Written Report
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed customer dataset to identify and interpret correlation patterns between different features. They will explain how various customer characteristics relate to purchase behavior and distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3)
Students will explain the business implications of feature correlations through written analysis of customer behavior patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing the customer_data.csv file containing 1000 customer records with features: age, income, spending_score, purchase_frequency, loyalty_years, and total_spent. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. Step 1 (10 min): Have students load the dataset in Python/Jupyter and generate a correlation matrix using pandas.corr(). Step 2 (15 min): Students create a heatmap visualization using seaborn to display correlations, applying color coding where dark colors indicate strong correlations. Step 3 (10 min): Pairs identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording exact coefficient values. Step 4 (10 min): Students write brief explanations for each identified correlation, describing what the relationship means in business terms. For example, if income and total_spent show 0.85 correlation, they should explain that higher-income customers tend to spend significantly more. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where three pairs share their most surprising correlation finding and explain its potential business impact. Circulate during pair work to ensure students correctly interpret coefficient magnitudes and signs.

Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib installed
Correlation interpretation reference sheet (strong/moderate/weak ranges)
Individual worksheets for recording correlation findings
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct identification of correlation coefficient ranges - 4 points, (2) Accurate business interpretation of at least 4 correlations - 8 points, (3) Proper creation and labeling of correlation heatmap - 4 points, (4) Quality of verbal explanation during class discussion - 4 points. Total: 20 points. Students must achieve 14/20 points to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made code snippets for generating correlation matrices and highlight that coefficients near +1 or -1 indicate strong relationships. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional data collection that might reveal hidden correlations. Encourage discussion of correlation vs. causation distinctions.

description: Students will analyze a customer purchase dataset to identify and explain correlation patterns between different variables. They will distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while explaining the business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and heatmap visualizations by explaining the strength and direction of relationships between customer demographic and purchase behavior variables
Students will differentiate between correlation patterns through systematic analysis of a correlation matrix containing at least 8 variables
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the pre-loaded customer dataset containing 8 variables: age, income, education_years, purchase_frequency, average_order_value, website_time, mobile_app_usage, and customer_satisfaction_score. assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of correlation coefficients with proper categorization by strength, (2) Accurate interpretation of positive/negative relationships, (3) Business explanations that demonstrate understanding without implying causation, (4) Use of appropriate statistical terminology. title: Optimization of Real-World Business Scenarios Using Calculus
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve authentic business optimization problems involving profit maximization and cost minimization. They will work through multi-variable scenarios requiring constraint analysis and interpretation of results within business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques to determine optimal solutions for profit maximization and cost minimization problems by analyzing real business case studies
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems through structured mathematical modeling of business scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct business case studies (manufacturing company profit optimization, delivery route cost minimization, and inventory management optimization). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one case study (15 minutes setup). Each case includes real data: production costs, demand functions, constraint equations, and business context. Students first identify the objective function and constraints from the narrative description, translating business language into mathematical expressions (20 minutes). Next, teams apply appropriate calculus techniques: taking partial derivatives, setting equal to zero, solving systems of equations, and using second derivative tests to confirm maximum/minimum solutions (35 minutes). For constrained problems, students must set up and solve using Lagrange multipliers, showing all algebraic steps. Teams then interpret their mathematical solutions within the business context, calculating specific numerical answers (optimal production quantities, minimum costs, maximum profits) and explaining what these mean for business operations (25 minutes). Each team creates a formal business recommendation report including: problem setup, mathematical solution process, numerical results, and strategic business implications. Teams present 5-minute summaries of their findings to the class, defending their mathematical approach and business interpretations (30 minutes total presentations). Conclude with peer evaluation where teams assess the mathematical accuracy and business reasoning of other groups using provided rubric criteria.
materials_needed: Three detailed business case study packets with real company data
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos/GeoGebra
Flip chart paper and markers for solution presentation
Business recommendation report template
Peer evaluation rubric forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct identification and setup of objective functions and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of calculus techniques with complete mathematical work shown (35%), (3) Correct numerical solutions and verification using second derivative test (25%), (4) Clear business interpretation and practical recommendations (15%). Students submit individual reflection explaining their mathematical reasoning and team collaboration process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed objective function setups and step-by-step derivative calculation guides. Offer simplified single-variable versions of problems before advancing to multi-variable cases. For advanced learners: Include additional constraints requiring more complex Lagrange multiplier applications, or extend to dynamic optimization problems involving time-dependent variables. Provide supplementary cases involving economic elasticity or game theory applications.

title: Analyzing Time and Space Complexity Trade-offs in Advanced Data Structure Implementations
description: Students will dissect and compare multiple implementations of the same abstract data type (priority queue) to analyze the relationship between algorithmic design choices and performance characteristics. They will evaluate how different underlying structures (binary heap, binomial heap, Fibonacci heap) create distinct time/space complexity profiles for various operations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time complexity differences between binary heap, binomial heap, and Fibonacci heap implementations by tracing through decrease-key and extract-min operations step-by-step
Students will evaluate space-time trade-offs through systematic comparison of memory overhead versus operational efficiency across three priority queue variants
instructions:
**Phase 1: Code Analysis Setup (20 minutes)**
Provide students with three working implementations of priority queues: binary heap, binomial heap, and Fibonacci heap. Students work in groups of 3, with each initially focusing on one implementation. They must trace through the provided pseudocode and identify key structural differences, documenting data organization patterns.

**Phase 2: Operation Deconstruction (45 minutes)**
Each student performs detailed analysis of insert, extract-min, and decrease-key operations for their assigned structure. They must create step-by-step execution traces using provided test datasets (20 elements with specific decrease-key sequences). Students document exact number of comparisons, pointer manipulations, and memory allocations for each operation sequence.

**Phase 3: Complexity Matrix Construction (30 minutes)**
Groups reconvene to create a comprehensive comparison matrix. They must analyze worst-case, average-case, and amortized time complexities for each operation across all three structures. Students identify which design decisions (lazy deletion, consolidation timing, node structure) directly impact complexity bounds.

**Phase 4: Trade-off Evaluation (25 minutes)**
Students analyze three real-world scenarios: Dijkstra's algorithm with dense graphs, network routing with frequent priority updates, and task scheduling with mixed operations. For each scenario, they must justify which priority queue implementation provides optimal performance based on operation frequency patterns and memory constraints. Groups present their analysis with supporting complexity calculations and concrete examples of when each structure's trade-offs become advantageous or problematic.
materials_needed: Three complete priority queue implementations (binary heap, binomial heap, Fibonacci heap) with documented pseudocode
Standardized test datasets with 20-element sequences and predefined decrease-key operations
Complexity analysis worksheets with operation counting templates
Digital collaboration platform for matrix construction and group documentation
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric across three dimensions: (1) Accuracy of complexity analysis with correct Big-O notation and mathematical justification, (2) Depth of trade-off evaluation showing understanding of when each structure excels, (3) Quality of scenario-based recommendations with concrete supporting evidence. Students must submit completed comparison matrices, operation trace documentation, and written justifications for scenario-specific implementation choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed trace templates and highlight specific code sections that impact complexity. Offer guided questions about structural differences. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional operations (merge, delete arbitrary element) or consider concurrent access patterns. Encourage exploration of hybrid approaches or modifications that could optimize specific use cases.

title: Design a Real-World Budget Calculator for Teen Financial Independence
description: Students will create a comprehensive budget calculator using algebraic formulas and mathematical modeling to help teenagers plan for moving out of their parents' home. They will research actual costs, develop mathematical relationships, and build a functional tool that incorporates variables like income, expenses, and savings goals.
learning_objectives: Students will construct algebraic equations and inequalities by modeling real-world financial scenarios including income, fixed expenses, variable costs, and savings targets
Students will design a functional budget calculator through systematic application of mathematical operations, percentages, and multi-variable problem solving
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and assign each team a specific scenario: college student, working teenager, or trade school graduate (15 minutes). Each team researches actual costs in your local area for rent, utilities, groceries, transportation, and entertainment using provided websites and local resources (20 minutes). Students then identify mathematical relationships: fixed costs (rent, insurance), variable costs (groceries = base amount + per-person multiplier), and percentage-based calculations (savings = 20% of income, emergency fund = 6 months expenses). Next, teams create their calculator structure by defining input variables (monthly income, number of roommates, transportation type) and output goals (monthly budget breakdown, annual savings, financial readiness score) (25 minutes). Students develop formulas using algebraic expressions: Total_Housing = (Rent + Utilities) ÷ Roommates, Disposable_Income = Income - Fixed_Costs - (Variable_Costs × Usage_Factor), Financial_Health_Score = (Savings_Rate × 40) + (Emergency_Fund_Months × 10). Teams build their calculator using Excel, Google Sheets, or graph paper with clear input sections and automated calculations (45 minutes). Finally, students test their calculator with three different scenarios, document assumptions made, and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their mathematical model and demonstrating how changing variables affects financial outcomes (25 minutes). Each team presents their calculator to another team for peer feedback on accuracy and usability.
materials_needed: Computers or tablets with Excel/Google Sheets access
Internet access for local cost research
Printed local housing/cost data sheets as backup
Calculator for verification
Large poster paper and markers for non-digital option
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: Mathematical Accuracy (correct formulas and calculations), Real-World Application (realistic data and logical assumptions), Tool Functionality (calculator works properly and is user-friendly), and Communication (clear explanation of mathematical reasoning). Students must demonstrate their calculator with live input changes and explain at least 3 algebraic relationships they created.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing formula templates and breaking complex calculations into smaller steps. Offer pre-researched cost data for students who have difficulty with internet research. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate additional variables like inflation rates, tax calculations, or investment growth formulas. Consider pairing stronger math students with those needing support.

title: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Palace
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the time and space complexity classifications of 20 advanced algorithms across different domains (graph theory, dynamic programming, string processing, and machine learning) using spatial memory techniques. This activity focuses on building a comprehensive mental repository of algorithmic complexity facts that serve as foundational knowledge for algorithm selection and optimization tasks.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact time and space complexity notation (Big O, Theta, Omega) for 20 advanced algorithms by constructing and navigating a digital memory palace
Students will identify the worst-case, average-case, and best-case complexity scenarios for each algorithm through structured memorization drills and retrieval practice
instructions: Begin by providing students with the 'Advanced Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet' containing 20 algorithms: Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, A* search, Knuth-Morris-Pratt string matching, Rabin-Karp, suffix array construction, longest common subsequence (LCS), edit distance, knapsack problem variants, quicksort variants, heapsort, mergesort, radix sort, k-means clustering, decision tree construction, neural network backpropagation, Ford-Fulkerson max flow, topological sort, and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree. Students spend 15 minutes creating their digital memory palace using the provided Memory Palace Builder tool, selecting a familiar virtual environment (childhood home, school campus, or favorite building). Next, they systematically place each algorithm at specific locations within their palace, spending 3 minutes per algorithm to create vivid mental associations between the location and the complexity facts. For example, placing Dijkstra's algorithm (O(V²) or O((V+E)log V)) at the front door with visualization of vertices as door locks. Students then complete four 10-minute recall sessions with 5-minute breaks between each session. During recall sessions, they navigate their memory palace virtually and verbally state each algorithm's complexities without reference materials. Instructor monitors using the digital tracking system that records accuracy rates. After each recall session, students review missed items and strengthen weak associations. The session concludes with a rapid-fire recall test where students have 30 seconds to state the time/space complexity for each randomly selected algorithm from the list.
materials_needed: Advanced Algorithm Complexity Reference Sheet (20 algorithms with detailed complexity analysis)
Memory Palace Builder digital tool or VR application
Individual computers or tablets with internet access
Digital timer and tracking spreadsheet for recall accuracy
Printed algorithm flashcards as backup reference material
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (17/20 correct) on the final rapid-fire recall test, correctly stating both time and space complexity for each algorithm. Track improvement using baseline (pre-activity) knowledge test compared to post-activity performance. Award full credit for exact Big O notation, partial credit for correct complexity class but imprecise notation (e.g., 'polynomial' instead of 'O(n²)'). Document retrieval speed - target average response time under 15 seconds per algorithm.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce algorithm set to 12 core algorithms, provide pre-made memory palace templates, and allow reference to complexity 'cheat sheets' during first two recall sessions. Pair with stronger students for peer coaching during palace construction. For advanced learners: expand to 30 algorithms including amortized analysis cases, require explanation of why each complexity occurs, and challenge them to recall complexity proofs or derive complexities for algorithm variations. Encourage creation of multiple memory palaces organized by algorithmic paradigm.

title: SQL Query Performance Analysis and Optimization Workshop
description: Students analyze the execution plans and performance metrics of inefficient SQL queries to identify bottlenecks and propose specific optimization strategies. They will decompose complex queries, examine index usage patterns, and evaluate the trade-offs between different optimization approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze SQL execution plans by examining join operations, index scans, and resource consumption metrics to identify performance bottlenecks
Students will evaluate multiple query optimization strategies through systematic comparison of execution times and resource usage patterns
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a database containing a sample e-commerce schema (customers, orders, products, order_items tables) with 10,000+ records and three deliberately inefficient SQL queries. Students work in pairs using database management tools with query execution plan visualization.

**Phase 1 - Baseline Analysis (15 minutes):** Students execute each provided query and document: execution time, number of rows examined, index usage (or lack thereof), and join methods used. They capture screenshots of execution plans and create a performance baseline table.

**Phase 2 - Query Decomposition (20 minutes):** For each query, students break down the SQL into logical components: WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, GROUP BY operations, and ORDER BY clauses. They identify which operations consume the most resources by analyzing the execution plan tree structure and noting operations with highest cost percentages.

**Phase 3 - Optimization Strategy Development (25 minutes):** Students propose three specific optimization techniques per query (e.g., adding composite indexes, rewriting subqueries as JOINs, eliminating unnecessary ORDER BY clauses). For each proposed change, they predict the expected performance improvement and potential trade-offs.

**Phase 4 - Implementation and Testing (20 minutes):** Students implement their top optimization strategy for each query, re-run performance tests, and compare results to baseline metrics. They document actual vs. predicted improvements.

**Phase 5 - Analysis Report (15 minutes):** Pairs create a structured report comparing original vs. optimized queries, explaining why specific optimizations worked or failed, and identifying patterns across all three queries that indicate broader optimization principles.
materials_needed: MySQL or PostgreSQL database with pre-loaded e-commerce sample data (customers, orders, products, order_items tables)
Three deliberately inefficient SQL queries with different performance issues
Database management tool with execution plan visualization (MySQL Workbench, pgAdmin, or similar)
Performance analysis worksheet template
Computers with database client software installed
assessment_method: Evaluate student pairs using a rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of execution plan interpretation (25 points), (2) Quality of bottleneck identification with specific evidence (25 points), (3) Appropriateness and feasibility of proposed optimizations (25 points), (4) Effectiveness of implemented solutions with quantified improvements (25 points). Students submit performance baseline tables, optimization proposals, test results, and final analysis report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a sample execution plan analysis walkthrough and a checklist of common optimization techniques. Offer guided questions like 'What type of scan is being used?' and 'Are there any missing indexes?' For advanced learners: Include queries with more complex optimization challenges (correlated subqueries, window functions) and ask them to research advanced techniques like query hints or partition pruning. Encourage them to analyze memory usage and I/O patterns in addition to execution time.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Selection for Imbalanced Healthcare Dataset
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of three different machine learning approaches (Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network) on a real-world imbalanced healthcare dataset for predicting patient readmission. They will assess model performance, bias, interpretability, and practical implementation constraints to make evidence-based recommendations for deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the comparative effectiveness of multiple ML algorithms by analyzing performance metrics, bias indicators, and interpretability scores in the context of healthcare decision-making
Students will critique model selection decisions through systematic analysis of trade-offs between accuracy, fairness, interpretability, and computational constraints
instructions:
**Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with the Hospital Readmission dataset (10,000 patients, 15% positive class) and three pre-trained models with their outputs. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives model performance reports, confusion matrices, feature importance rankings, SHAP values, and computational cost metrics for all three models.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (45 minutes):** Each student independently evaluates all three models using the provided evaluation framework: (1) Calculate and interpret precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC, and AUC-PR for each model; (2) Analyze bias metrics including demographic parity and equalized odds across patient age groups and gender; (3) Assess interpretability using SHAP value consistency and feature importance stability; (4) Evaluate computational costs including training time, inference speed, and memory requirements.

**Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (30 minutes):** Teams collaborate to create a comparative analysis matrix ranking each model across four dimensions: predictive performance, fairness, interpretability, and operational feasibility. Teams must identify critical trade-offs and potential failure modes for each approach.

**Phase 3 - Recommendation Development (30 minutes):** Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation recommending one model for deployment, including: (1) Justification based on evaluation criteria; (2) Identification of key limitations and mitigation strategies; (3) Specific monitoring recommendations for production deployment; (4) Ethical considerations for healthcare implementation.

**Phase 4 - Peer Evaluation (20 minutes):** Teams present recommendations while other teams use provided rubric to evaluate the quality of evidence, logical reasoning, and consideration of real-world constraints in each recommendation.
materials_needed: Hospital Readmission dataset (CSV format, 10,000 patient records)
Pre-trained model outputs and performance reports for 3 algorithms
Model evaluation framework worksheet with bias metrics formulas
SHAP visualization outputs and feature importance plots
Peer evaluation rubric for recommendation assessment
Python/R environment with scikit-learn, pandas, and visualization libraries
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Evaluation Framework Application (25 points) - correct calculation and interpretation of performance and bias metrics; (2) Critical Analysis Quality (30 points) - depth of trade-off analysis and identification of model limitations; (3) Recommendation Justification (25 points) - logical reasoning connecting evaluation results to deployment decision; (4) Professional Communication (20 points) - clear presentation of technical findings to stakeholder audience. Minimum passing: 70/100 points with at least 15/25 on evaluation framework application.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide metric calculation templates and interpretation guides for common ML evaluation metrics.
