Offer guided questions for bias analysis ('How might this model perform differently for patients over 65?'). Create decision trees showing how different metric priorities lead to different model choices. **Extensions for advanced learners:** Challenge students to propose ensemble approaches combining multiple models. Ask them to design A/B testing frameworks for production model comparison. Have them evaluate additional fairness metrics like individual fairness or counterfactual fairness.

title: Applying Optimization Techniques to Design a Cost-Efficient Packaging System
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to solve a real-world packaging problem. They will determine optimal dimensions for a shipping box that minimizes material costs while meeting volume constraints and structural requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization techniques to minimize cost functions by analyzing a three-dimensional packaging scenario with multiple constraints
Students will implement partial derivative calculations and critical point analysis through systematic problem-solving steps to determine optimal box dimensions
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario handout: 'ShipSmart Company needs rectangular boxes with 1000 cubic inches volume, costing $0.02/sq inch for sides/bottom and $0.05/sq inch for reinforced top.' Form teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes setup). Each team receives specific additional constraints (weight limits, shipping dimensions, etc.) to differentiate problems. Students first identify variables (length=x, width=y, height=z) and establish the constraint equation xyz=1000. Next, they formulate the cost function C(x,y,z)=0.02(2xy+2xz+2yz)+0.05xy, then substitute z=1000/(xy) to create C(x,y)=0.02(2xy+4000/y+4000/x)+0.05xy. Teams calculate partial derivatives ∂C/∂x and ∂C/∂y, set them equal to zero, and solve the resulting system of equations. Using graphing calculators or computer algebra systems, students verify their critical points and apply the second derivative test to confirm minimum values. Teams then calculate actual dimensions, total cost, and create a visual representation of their optimal box. Finally, each team presents their solution in a 3-minute pitch explaining their mathematical process and justifying why their design minimizes costs. Instructor circulates during work time, checking derivative calculations and guiding teams through algebraic manipulation challenges.
materials_needed: Scenario handout with company specifications and constraint variations
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus CE or equivalent)
Graph paper and rulers for sketching
Computer access to Desmos 3D Calculator or GeoGebra
Presentation materials (whiteboard markers, poster paper)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct constraint identification and function setup (25%), (2) Accurate partial derivative calculations and critical point determination (35%), (3) Proper verification using second derivative test (25%), (4) Clear presentation of final solution with justification (15%). Students must show all mathematical work and achieve minimum 75% accuracy on derivative calculations to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing derivative formula sheets and step-by-step templates for constraint substitution. Offer guided practice with simpler two-variable optimization before tackling the full problem. For advanced learners, add multiple constraints (maximum surface area, minimum height requirements) or extend to cylindrical packaging options requiring trigonometric optimization techniques.

title: Distributed System Failure Point Analysis: Dissecting a Real-World Microservices Architecture
description: Students will examine the architecture of a complex distributed system (Netflix's microservices) and systematically identify potential failure points, cascading failure patterns, and resilience mechanisms. They will create a comprehensive failure analysis report with prioritized recommendations for system hardening.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system architectures by identifying single points of failure, bottlenecks, and vulnerability patterns in a real-world microservices environment
Students will evaluate system resilience mechanisms through detailed examination of circuit breakers, load balancing strategies, and fault tolerance implementations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with Netflix's open-source microservices architecture diagram and accompanying technical documentation. Teams must first spend 45 minutes mapping the complete service dependency graph, identifying all inter-service communication paths, data flow directions, and external dependencies. Next, allocate 60 minutes for systematic failure analysis: teams examine each service node and connection to identify potential failure modes (network partitions, service overload, database failures, cascading timeouts). During this phase, students must categorize failures as: critical (system-wide impact), major (multiple service impact), or minor (isolated service impact). Following this, teams spend 30 minutes analyzing existing resilience mechanisms visible in the architecture (circuit breakers, retry logic, bulkheads, timeouts) and evaluating their effectiveness against identified failure scenarios. In the final 45 minutes, teams create a prioritized remediation plan, ranking the top 5 most critical vulnerabilities and proposing specific technical solutions (implementation of chaos engineering, additional circuit breakers, database replication strategies, etc.). Each team presents their findings in a 10-minute presentation focusing on their highest-priority failure scenario and proposed solution. Conclude with 15 minutes of cross-team discussion comparing different analytical approaches and solution strategies.
materials_needed: Netflix microservices architecture diagram (printed A3 size)
Netflix technical blog posts and documentation packet
Laptops with network analysis tools (Wireshark, draw.io)
Whiteboard and colored markers for dependency mapping
Failure analysis worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Completeness of dependency mapping (25 points), accuracy of failure point identification (30 points), quality of risk categorization and impact analysis (25 points), feasibility and specificity of proposed solutions (20 points). Students must submit their annotated architecture diagram, written failure analysis report, and remediation plan within 24 hours of the activity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed dependency map and a checklist of common distributed system failure patterns to guide their analysis. Advanced learners should be challenged to quantify failure probabilities using reliability engineering calculations and to design automated chaos engineering experiments to validate their identified vulnerabilities.

title: Design Your Dream Amusement Park: Creating Mathematical Models for Roller Coaster Safety
description: Students will design an original amusement park layout and create mathematical models to determine optimal roller coaster specifications including height, speed, and safety parameters. They will synthesize concepts from geometry, algebra, and physics to produce a comprehensive park proposal with mathematical justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize quadratic functions, trigonometry, and geometric principles by designing original roller coaster tracks with mathematically justified safety specifications
Students will construct comprehensive mathematical models through creating budget analyses, capacity calculations, and spatial optimization plans for their amusement park design
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes for team formation and role assignment: lead designer, safety engineer, budget analyst, and presentation coordinator). Distribute the project packet containing grid paper, design requirements, and mathematical formulas. Teams must first brainstorm their park theme and create a scaled layout on grid paper using a 1:500 scale ratio (30 minutes). Next, teams design their signature roller coaster by creating at least three different track sections using quadratic functions, ensuring the maximum height doesn't exceed 150 feet and calculating the theoretical speed at each point using energy conservation principles (45 minutes). Students then develop safety parameters by determining minimum curve radius using centripetal force calculations and establishing safety factors for weight limits (30 minutes). For the budget component, teams calculate construction costs using provided per-foot pricing for different track types, land area costs, and operational expenses (25 minutes). Teams must optimize their park layout to maximize visitor capacity while maintaining 15-foot minimum spacing between attractions using area and perimeter calculations (35 minutes). Finally, students create a visual presentation board showing their park layout, mathematical calculations, safety justifications, and budget breakdown, preparing a 5-minute pitch presentation (40 minutes). Conclude with team presentations where other students evaluate designs using provided peer assessment rubrics.
materials_needed: Large grid paper (11x17 inches, 1/4 inch grid)
Graphing calculators or computer access
Ruler, compass, and protractor sets
Project packet with formulas, pricing sheets, and safety requirements
Colored pencils or markers for design visualization
Poster board for final presentation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of calculations for speed, safety, and budget (25 points), (2) Creative integration of geometric and algebraic concepts in design (20 points), (3) Logical justification of safety parameters and design choices (20 points), (4) Completeness and organization of final presentation (15 points), (5) Effective collaboration and peer feedback quality (10 points), (6) Innovation and feasibility of overall park concept (10 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing calculation templates, step-by-step formula guides, and pairing them with stronger math partners. Offer simplified design requirements focusing on 2-3 main attractions instead of full park layout. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate calculus concepts for optimization problems, add environmental impact calculations, or design rides with more complex mathematical functions like sinusoidal or exponential curves.

title: Budget Your Dream Weekend Trip: Applying Basic Operations and Percentages
description: Students will plan a realistic weekend trip by calculating total costs using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and percentage calculations. They will apply mathematical operations to real-world scenarios involving budgeting, tax calculations, and discount applications.
learning_objectives: Students will apply basic arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) by calculating trip expenses across multiple categories
Students will apply percentage calculations through computing sales tax, tips, and discount amounts in authentic travel scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Dream Weekend Trip Planning Sheet' and calculators to each student. Explain that they have a $500 budget for a 2-day, 1-night trip to a nearby city (15 minutes setup). 

Step 1: Students research and select actual hotel prices online, choosing one hotel and calculating the total cost including 12% tax for one night (10 minutes). 

Step 2: Students plan 6 meals (2 breakfast, 2 lunch, 2 dinner) by finding real restaurant menu prices online or from provided restaurant menus, then calculate a 18% tip for each meal (15 minutes).

Step 3: Students select 3 activities (museums, tours, entertainment) using provided price lists, applying any available discounts (student discounts of 10%, group discounts of 15%, or early bird discounts of 20%) to at least one activity (10 minutes).

Step 4: Students calculate transportation costs by choosing between driving (gas cost: $3.50/gallon, 200 miles total, 25 mpg) or bus tickets ($45 each way per person) (8 minutes).

Step 5: Students add all categories to find their total trip cost, then subtract from their $500 budget to determine remaining funds (7 minutes).

Step 6: If over budget, students must revise their choices and recalculate until they're within the $500 limit (10 minutes).

Conclude with students presenting one calculation to a partner, explaining their mathematical reasoning (5 minutes).
materials_needed: Dream Weekend Trip Planning Sheet (pre-designed template with calculation sections)
Calculator (one per student)
Sample restaurant menus with prices
Activity price list handout
Access to computers/tablets for hotel research
assessment_method: Grade completed planning sheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All calculations correct with clear work shown, stays within budget; (3) Minor calculation errors, stays within budget; (2) Some calculation errors or slightly over budget with revision attempt; (1) Multiple calculation errors or significantly over budget. Check for proper application of percentages for tax, tips, and discounts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a calculation template showing the format for each step (e.g., 'Hotel cost $__ + Tax ($___ × 0.12) = Total $___'). For advanced learners: Add complexity by including currency conversion for international destinations, compound interest calculations for savings needed, or creating budgets for different group sizes.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Deployment Strategies for Real-World Business Impact
description: Students will critically assess and compare three different ML model deployment approaches (batch processing, real-time API, and edge computing) for a provided e-commerce recommendation system case study. They will evaluate trade-offs in performance, cost, scalability, and business value to recommend the optimal deployment strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different ML deployment architectures by analyzing performance metrics, infrastructure costs, and business requirements in a realistic e-commerce scenario
Students will critique and justify deployment decisions through systematic comparison of latency, throughput, maintenance overhead, and ROI implications across multiple implementation approaches
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with a detailed case study packet including: FlexiMart e-commerce platform (50M monthly users), current recommendation system specifications, 6 months of performance data, infrastructure costs, and business KPIs. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. **Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (45 minutes):** Each student independently analyzes one deployment approach using the provided evaluation framework covering: technical performance (latency percentiles, throughput capacity, error rates), operational metrics (deployment complexity, monitoring requirements, failure recovery), cost analysis (infrastructure, maintenance, scaling costs), and business impact (user experience metrics, revenue attribution, A/B test results). Students complete detailed evaluation worksheets with quantitative assessments and qualitative reasoning. **Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (30 minutes):** Teams compile individual analyses, identify key trade-offs, and develop comparison matrices ranking each approach across 12 specific criteria using provided weighted scoring rubric. **Phase 3 - Critical Evaluation (45 minutes):** Teams prepare formal recommendations addressing: primary deployment choice with detailed justification, identification of 3 critical assumptions and their validity, risk assessment including failure scenarios, implementation timeline with resource requirements, and alternative strategies for different business contexts (startup vs. enterprise, different user scales). **Phase 4 - Peer Review (25 minutes):** Teams present 8-minute recommendations followed by structured peer critique sessions using provided evaluation forms focusing on reasoning quality, evidence usage, and consideration of alternatives.
materials_needed: FlexiMart e-commerce case study packet (15 pages) with business context, user data, and technical specifications
Performance dataset (CSV files) containing 6 months of latency, error rates, and cost metrics for each deployment type
Deployment evaluation framework template with weighted scoring criteria
Business impact data including A/B test results, user engagement metrics, and revenue attribution
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded data analysis tools and visualization libraries
Peer evaluation rubrics for structured critique sessions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct interpretation of performance data and cost calculations; Critical Reasoning Quality (25 points) - depth of trade-off analysis and assumption identification; Recommendation Justification (25 points) - logical coherence between evidence and conclusions, consideration of business context; Evidence Integration (15 points) - effective use of quantitative data and case study details; Alternative Consideration (10 points) - acknowledgment and evaluation of competing approaches. Deliverables include completed evaluation worksheets, team comparison matrix, and formal recommendation document (5-7 pages).
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide guided worksheets with specific prompts for each evaluation criterion, offer mini-tutorials on cost calculation methods, and create structured templates for organizing evidence. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers during team formation. **For advanced learners:** Introduce additional complexity by requiring evaluation of hybrid deployment strategies, analysis of edge cases like traffic spikes or system failures, or extension to multi-model deployment scenarios. Challenge them to develop custom evaluation metrics beyond provided framework.

title: Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns Through Multi-Component Architecture Breakdown
description: Students will dissect a complex distributed system failure scenario by examining system logs, network traces, and performance metrics to identify cascading failure patterns and root causes. They will analyze the relationships between microservices, load balancers, databases, and message queues to determine failure propagation mechanisms and system vulnerabilities.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze distributed system failure patterns by examining multi-layer system logs, network traces, and performance metrics to identify root causes and cascading effects
Students will evaluate the relationships between distributed system components through systematic decomposition of failure scenarios and dependency mapping
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a realistic distributed system failure case study including: system architecture diagram, 500+ lines of aggregated logs from 6 different services, network latency graphs, CPU/memory utilization charts, and database query performance data spanning a 2-hour incident window. Students start by spending 20 minutes individually reviewing all materials to understand the system topology. Next, teams collaboratively create a timeline of events by correlating timestamps across different log sources and identifying the sequence of component failures (30 minutes). Teams then map service dependencies by analyzing API calls, database connections, and message queue interactions visible in the logs, creating a dependency graph that shows potential failure propagation paths (25 minutes). Following this, students identify and categorize different types of failures (network partitions, resource exhaustion, cascading timeouts, circuit breaker activations) by examining error patterns and system metrics (30 minutes). Teams analyze the root cause by working backwards from the final system state through the failure cascade, identifying which initial failure triggered subsequent component failures (25 minutes). Finally, each team presents their analysis including: the failure timeline, dependency relationships, failure categorization, root cause identification, and proposed architectural improvements to prevent similar failures (20 minutes per team presentation).
materials_needed: Distributed system architecture diagram with 8-10 microservices
Multi-service log files in JSON format with realistic timestamps and error messages
Network performance monitoring graphs (latency, packet loss, throughput)
System resource utilization charts (CPU, memory, disk I/O) for each service
Database query performance logs with execution times and connection counts
Whiteboard or digital collaboration tool for dependency mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accuracy of failure timeline creation (25 points), Completeness of dependency relationship mapping (25 points), Correct identification and categorization of failure types (20 points), Logical reasoning in root cause analysis with supporting evidence (20 points), Quality of proposed architectural improvements based on analysis findings (10 points). Teams must submit their dependency graph, annotated timeline, and written analysis report along with their presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template timeline with some key events pre-filled, offer a checklist of common distributed system failure patterns to look for, and assign specific log files to individual team members to reduce cognitive load. For advanced learners: Include additional complexity such as multiple concurrent failures, provide incomplete or corrupted log data requiring interpolation, or ask them to estimate the business impact and calculate system availability metrics during the incident.

title: Design Your Dream City: Creating a Mathematical Urban Planning Portfolio
description: Students will create a comprehensive city plan that integrates geometric shapes, area calculations, proportional reasoning, and coordinate geometry. They will design neighborhoods, calculate population density, and create scale drawings while justifying their mathematical decisions through written explanations and visual presentations.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original city layout by applying geometric principles, area formulas, and coordinate geometry to create mathematically accurate maps and building arrangements
Students will construct mathematical justifications for urban planning decisions through calculating population densities, optimizing space usage, and creating proportional scale models
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with large grid paper and city planning requirements (minimum 5 neighborhoods, commercial district, parks totaling 20% of city area, transportation network). Teams spend 15 minutes brainstorming city themes and sketching initial layouts. Next, students create their city on coordinate grids (45 minutes), marking key locations with coordinate pairs and ensuring each neighborhood contains specific geometric shapes (rectangles, circles, triangles) with calculated areas. Students must demonstrate that parks comprise exactly 20% of total city area through written calculations. Following the design phase, teams calculate population density by determining residential area and assigning realistic population numbers per square unit, showing all mathematical work (30 minutes). Students then create a scaled physical model using cardboard, with buildings proportional to their grid drawings - requiring ratio and proportion calculations to convert from 2D to 3D (60 minutes). Finally, teams prepare 8-minute presentations explaining their mathematical choices: coordinate locations of landmarks, area calculations for zoning, population density formulas, geometric shape applications, and scaling ratios used in model construction (30 minutes preparation, 8 minutes per presentation). Throughout the activity, circulate to check mathematical accuracy and push students to explain their reasoning. Conclude with peer feedback sessions where teams evaluate each other's mathematical precision and creative integration of required concepts.
materials_needed: Large coordinate grid paper (1cm squares, 24x36 inches)
Colored pencils and fine-tip markers
Calculators
Cardboard sheets, scissors, and glue sticks for 3D models
Rulers and protractors
City Planning Requirements handout with specific mathematical constraints
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25%) - correct area calculations, coordinate plotting, and density formulas; Creative Integration (25%) - innovative use of geometric shapes and mathematical concepts in design; Communication (25%) - clear explanation of mathematical reasoning in presentation; Collaboration (25%) - effective teamwork and peer feedback quality. Students submit portfolio including: annotated city map with calculations, written justification of design decisions, photos of 3D model with scaling explanations, and reflection on mathematical problem-solving process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide area formula reference sheets, pre-made coordinate grids with helper lines, and calculation templates. Pair with stronger math students and offer one-on-one guidance during calculation phases. For advanced learners: Add constraints like budget limitations requiring cost-per-square-foot calculations, environmental factors requiring statistical analysis, or traffic flow optimization using basic algebraic modeling. Challenge them to research real city planning mathematical principles.

title: Distributed Systems Consensus Algorithm Recognition and Classification
description: Students will memorize and classify the key characteristics, assumptions, and failure models of major consensus algorithms used in distributed systems. This activity focuses on developing precise recall of algorithm properties through systematic categorization and rapid identification exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the specific properties, assumptions, and failure models of Paxos, Raft, PBFT, and HotStuff consensus algorithms through structured memorization exercises
Students will identify consensus algorithm types from given scenario descriptions by matching algorithm characteristics to use case requirements
instructions: Begin by distributing the consensus algorithm reference sheets containing detailed specifications for Paxos, Raft, PBFT, and HotStuff algorithms (15 minutes study time). Students work in pairs to create flashcards covering: algorithm type (CFT/BFT), failure assumptions (crash/Byzantine), message complexity, round complexity, leader requirements, and safety/liveness guarantees. Each pair creates 40 flashcards total (10 per algorithm) with questions on one side and specific answers on the other (20 minutes). Conduct three rounds of rapid-fire recall: Round 1 - students quiz each other using flashcards for 10 minutes, switching every 2 minutes. Round 2 - instructor displays algorithm property combinations on screen for 30 seconds each; students write down the matching algorithm name (15 scenarios, 10 minutes total). Round 3 - scenario-based identification where students receive distributed system requirements (network assumptions, fault tolerance needs, performance constraints) and must identify which consensus algorithm best fits, writing only the algorithm name (10 scenarios, 15 minutes). Between each round, provide 3-minute breaks for students to review their reference materials. Conclude with immediate self-scoring where students check answers against the master key and record their accuracy percentages for each round. Students must achieve 80% accuracy in property recall and 70% accuracy in scenario matching to demonstrate mastery.
materials_needed: Consensus algorithm reference sheets (4 pages covering Paxos, Raft, PBFT, HotStuff)
Blank index cards for flashcard creation (10 cards per student pair)
Scenario description handouts with system requirements
Answer key sheets for self-assessment
Projection system for rapid-fire rounds
assessment_method: Students self-assess using provided answer keys and record scores for three components: flashcard accuracy (40%), property identification accuracy (35%), and scenario matching accuracy (25%). Minimum passing scores are 80% for flashcards, 70% for property identification, and 70% for scenario matching. Instructor spot-checks 25% of student score sheets and conducts brief oral verification with students scoring below thresholds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-made flashcards and allow extended study time with reference materials. Create mnemonics for algorithm properties (e.g., 'Raft Rides Fast' for Raft's efficiency focus). For advanced learners: include additional algorithms like Tendermint or Casper, add questions about algorithm variants and optimizations, or require explanation of why incorrect algorithms don't fit specific scenarios. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during flashcard creation.

title: Design and Build a Mathematical Model for Real Estate Investment Portfolio Optimization
description: Students will create an original multi-variable mathematical model that optimizes real estate investment portfolios under realistic constraints. They will synthesize concepts from linear programming, probability theory, and financial mathematics to develop a comprehensive decision-making framework.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original multi-variable optimization model incorporating at least 8 realistic constraints (zoning laws, budget limits, risk tolerance, market volatility) by integrating linear programming techniques with probability distributions
Students will design a comprehensive mathematical framework that synthesizes calculus-based optimization, statistical analysis, and financial modeling to solve authentic investment decision problems
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a authentic scenario: they have $2.5 million to invest across residential, commercial, and industrial properties in three different metropolitan areas, each with distinct market conditions, appreciation rates, and risk profiles. 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Students research and define their variables (x₁, x₂...x₉ representing investment amounts in each property type/location combination) and establish their objective function (maximize expected 10-year ROI while minimizing portfolio variance). They must incorporate real market data from sources like Zillow, LoopNet, or local MLS systems.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Students construct their constraint system, including: budget constraints (∑xᵢ ≤ 2,500,000), diversification requirements (no single investment >40% of portfolio), minimum investment thresholds, zoning restrictions, and liquidity constraints. Each constraint must be mathematically expressed and economically justified.

Step 3 (75 minutes): Students develop their risk assessment component using probability distributions for market appreciation rates, incorporating correlation coefficients between different property types and geographic regions. They must create expected value calculations and variance formulas for their entire portfolio.

Step 4 (90 minutes): Using software tools, students solve their optimization problem using both graphical methods (for simplified 2-3 variable versions) and computational approaches (Excel Solver, Python scipy.optimize, or MATLAB). They must validate their solutions by testing boundary conditions and performing sensitivity analysis.

Step 5 (60 minutes): Students prepare a professional investment presentation including their mathematical model, solution methodology, optimal portfolio allocation, expected returns with confidence intervals, and risk assessment. They must defend their mathematical choices and demonstrate how changing key parameters affects their recommendations.
materials_needed: Access to real estate market databases (Zillow API, LoopNet, or equivalent)
Spreadsheet software with optimization solver (Excel with Solver add-in or Google Sheets)
Statistical computing environment (Python with scipy/numpy, R, or MATLAB)
Financial calculator or computational software
Presentation software for final deliverable
assessment_method: Students evaluated using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Mathematical rigor - correct formulation of objective function and constraints with appropriate variable definitions (25 points), (2) Model complexity - incorporation of at least 8 realistic constraints with proper mathematical representation (20 points), (3) Statistical integration - appropriate use of probability distributions and risk calculations (20 points), (4) Solution accuracy - correct application of optimization techniques with validation (20 points), (5) Professional communication - clear presentation of methodology and results with economic interpretation (15 points). Minimum passing score: 80/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template constraint frameworks and simplified 3-variable versions focusing on basic linear programming concepts before expanding complexity. Offer guided practice with simpler optimization problems involving 2-3 variables. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate stochastic programming elements, multiple time periods, or integer constraints for property unit purchases. Encourage exploration of more sophisticated risk measures like Value-at-Risk or Conditional Value-at-Risk calculations.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through repetitive practice drills
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (15 minutes setup). Each flashcard set contains 16 cards with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary numbers on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). 

Demonstrate the activity by showing card '7' and revealing '0111', explaining this is memorization practice, not calculation (5 minutes). Have students work in pairs, with Partner A holding cards and Partner B responding. Partner A shows the decimal side for 30 seconds while Partner B states the binary equivalent. If incorrect, Partner A shows the binary side and Partner B repeats it aloud three times. Continue through all 16 cards, then partners switch roles (20 minutes total).

Conduct three rounds with increasing speed: Round 1 allows 10 seconds per card, Round 2 allows 7 seconds, Round 3 allows 5 seconds. Between rounds, give students 3 minutes to study cards individually, focusing on numbers they missed (30 minutes total for all rounds).

Conclude with individual assessment where each student receives a random subset of 8 cards and must provide answers within 5 seconds each. Record results on the provided tracking sheet. End with a 5-minute group discussion where students share memorization strategies that worked best for them.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (16 cards each, one set per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Student tracking sheets for recording accuracy
Answer key for instructors
assessment_method: Individual assessment using 8 randomly selected flashcards with 5-second response time. Success criteria: 7/8 correct answers (87.5% accuracy). Record results on tracking sheets noting specific numbers missed for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with numbers 0-7 only, provide a binary place-value reference card (8-4-2-1), and allow extra study time between rounds. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), challenge them to explain patterns they notice, or have them create flashcards for 6-bit numbers as homework preparation.

title: Optimization Crisis Response: Applying Calculus to Emergency Resource Allocation
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve a realistic emergency management scenario involving resource allocation during a natural disaster. They will use Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization to determine optimal distribution of limited medical supplies across multiple emergency shelters while minimizing total response time.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems by modeling real-world emergency resource allocation scenarios
Students will implement multivariable calculus concepts through systematic analysis of complex logistical problems with multiple constraints and variables
instructions: **Phase 1: Setup (15 minutes)** - Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the emergency scenario packet containing: a regional map with 6 emergency shelters, population data for each shelter, available medical supply quantities (morphine, antibiotics, bandages), transportation constraints, and cost functions. Each team receives identical base data but different priority weightings (elderly populations, critical patients, etc.). **Phase 2: Problem Formulation (25 minutes)** - Teams must first identify decision variables (x₁, x₂, ..., x₆ representing supply allocations to each shelter), write the objective function (minimize weighted response time: f(x₁,...,x₆) = Σᵢ wᵢ·tᵢ·xᵢ where wᵢ are priority weights and tᵢ are transport times), and establish constraints (supply limitations: Σxᵢ ≤ total_supply, non-negativity: xᵢ ≥ 0, minimum requirements: xᵢ ≥ min_needᵢ). **Phase 3: Solution Implementation (35 minutes)** - Using graphing calculators or computer algebra systems, teams apply Lagrange multiplier method: set up L(x,λ) = f(x) + λ·g(x), compute partial derivatives, solve the system ∇L = 0, and verify solutions using second derivative test. Teams must show all mathematical work and justify their approach. **Phase 4: Analysis and Presentation (15 minutes)** - Each team presents their optimal allocation strategy, explains their mathematical reasoning, and compares results with other teams. Discussion focuses on how different priority weightings led to different optimal solutions, demonstrating the real-world complexity of mathematical modeling.
materials_needed: Emergency scenario packet with regional maps and data tables (one per team)
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent) or laptops with computer algebra system software
Large poster paper and markers for solution presentation
Laminated reference sheet with Lagrange multiplier formulas and optimization procedures
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem setup and variable identification (20 points), correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25 points), proper application of Lagrange multiplier technique with shown work (30 points), verification of solution and interpretation of results (15 points), quality of presentation and mathematical communication (10 points). Teams must submit written work showing all calculations and provide oral explanation of their optimization strategy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed objective functions and constraint setups; offer guided practice with simpler 2-variable problems before tackling the full scenario; assign peer mentors within teams. For advanced learners: Introduce additional constraints such as transportation network limitations or time-dependent demand functions; challenge them to solve using alternative methods (graphical analysis, linear programming) and compare efficiency; have them create sensitivity analysis showing how solutions change with different parameter values.

title: Cryptographic Protocol Vulnerability Analysis: Dissecting a Simulated Man-in-the-Middle Attack on TLS Handshake
description: Students will analyze captured network traffic from a simulated TLS handshake attack to identify specific vulnerabilities, trace the attack vectors, and evaluate the effectiveness of different cryptographic countermeasures. This expert-level activity requires students to decompose complex security protocols and distinguish between legitimate and malicious communication patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze TLS handshake packet sequences by examining certificate chains, cipher suites, and key exchange mechanisms to identify protocol weaknesses
Students will differentiate between legitimate and compromised cryptographic exchanges through systematic comparison of network traffic patterns and certificate validation failures
instructions: Begin by distributing three Wireshark capture files: 'legitimate_tls.pcap', 'mitm_attack.pcap', and 'mitm_with_countermeasures.pcap' (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 2-3 students, ensuring each team has access to Wireshark, OpenSSL command-line tools, and the provided analysis worksheet. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams open 'legitimate_tls.pcap' and document the normal TLS 1.3 handshake sequence, recording specific details: ClientHello cipher suites, ServerHello selected parameters, certificate chain length, signature algorithms, and key exchange methods. Students must create a flowchart showing message flow and identify each cryptographic operation. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams analyze 'mitm_attack.pcap', comparing packet-by-packet differences with the legitimate capture. Students must identify: certificate discrepancies (issuer, validity dates, public key fingerprints), cipher suite downgrades, unexpected certificate chain interruptions, and timing anomalies. Using OpenSSL commands, teams extract and verify certificates, documenting validation failures. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Students examine 'mitm_with_countermeasures.pcap' to analyze how certificate pinning, HSTS headers, and certificate transparency logs prevent the attack. Teams must trace how each countermeasure blocks specific attack vectors. Final phase (30 minutes): Teams prepare a technical report documenting their analysis methodology, specific vulnerabilities identified, attack timeline reconstruction, and effectiveness evaluation of each countermeasure, supported by packet-level evidence and cryptographic verification results.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared Wireshark capture files (legitimate_tls.pcap, mitm_attack.pcap, mitm_with_countermeasures.pcap)
Wireshark network analyzer software installed on student computers
OpenSSL command-line tools and certificate analysis utilities
Structured analysis worksheet with packet inspection templates
Access to online certificate transparency log databases
assessment_method: Evaluate technical reports using a 100-point rubric: accurate identification of specific TLS vulnerabilities (25 points), correct interpretation of certificate validation failures (25 points), systematic comparison methodology demonstrating deep protocol understanding (25 points), and comprehensive evaluation of countermeasure effectiveness with supporting cryptographic evidence (25 points). Students must demonstrate expert-level analysis by providing packet numbers, hexadecimal values, and OpenSSL verification output as evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled packet analysis templates highlighting key fields to examine, offer guided walkthroughs of OpenSSL certificate verification commands, and supply reference materials showing normal vs. abnormal TLS patterns. For advanced learners: challenge them to identify additional attack vectors not explicitly mentioned, analyze the cryptographic mathematics behind key exchange vulnerabilities, or research and propose novel detection mechanisms for similar attacks.

title: Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Housing Market Analysis
description: Students will critically assess three different visualizations of the same housing market dataset to determine which most effectively communicates key insights to potential home buyers. They will apply evaluation criteria and justify their recommendations based on data visualization principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data visualizations by applying specific criteria including clarity, accuracy, and audience appropriateness
Students will critique visualization design choices through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three printed visualizations of housing data: a cluttered bar chart with 15+ variables, a clean scatter plot showing price vs. square footage with color-coded neighborhoods, and a misleading pie chart with 3D effects showing price ranges. Give groups the evaluation rubric covering five criteria: data accuracy, visual clarity, audience appropriateness, design principles, and actionability. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine each visualization individually, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses using the rubric. Step 2 (20 minutes): Groups discuss and score each visualization on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, documenting specific evidence for their scores. Step 3 (10 minutes): Groups calculate total scores and rank the three visualizations from most to least effective. Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups prepare a 3-minute presentation defending their top choice, including at least three specific improvements they would make to their selected visualization. Step 5 (15 minutes): Each group presents their recommendation and reasoning. Step 6 (10 minutes): Class discusses patterns in group choices and reflects on which evaluation criteria proved most important for decision-making. Conclude with groups submitting their completed rubrics and a one-paragraph summary of their final recommendation with supporting evidence.
materials_needed: Three printed housing market visualizations per group (A3 or letter size)
Evaluation rubric handouts (one per student)
Calculators or smartphones for scoring
Presentation timer
Flip chart paper and markers for presentation notes
assessment_method: Grade completed rubrics (40% - accuracy of evaluation and evidence quality), presentation delivery (30% - clear reasoning and defense of choice), written recommendation paragraph (30% - logical argument with specific examples). Use 4-point scale: Exemplary (4) - thorough evaluation with detailed evidence; Proficient (3) - solid evaluation with adequate support; Developing (2) - basic evaluation with minimal evidence; Beginning (1) - incomplete evaluation lacking support.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing sentence stems for evaluation comments ('This visualization is effective/ineffective because...'). Pair stronger students with those needing support within groups. For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge: sketch one additional visualization type that would better serve the target audience. Circulate during group work to prompt deeper thinking with questions like 'What evidence supports that claim?' and 'How might a first-time home buyer react to this chart?'

title: Design and Build a Scale Model Community with Mathematical Justification
description: Students will create an original scale model community layout using geometric principles, proportional reasoning, and area calculations. They will design buildings, roads, and public spaces while demonstrating mathematical concepts through detailed calculations and written explanations of their design choices.
estimated_duration: 100 minutes (can be split across 2-3 class periods)
learning_objectives: Students will construct an original scale model community by applying proportional reasoning, area calculations, and geometric principles to create mathematically accurate structures and layouts
Students will synthesize mathematical concepts including scale factors, perimeter, area, and geometric transformations through the design process and defend their choices with quantitative evidence
instructions:
Begin by having students work in pairs to brainstorm their community vision (10 minutes). Provide each pair with a 12"×18" poster board as their base and explain they're designing for a 1:500 scale (1 inch = 500 inches in real life). Students must include at least 8 buildings of different types (residential, commercial, public), 3 roads with specified widths, and 2 recreational spaces. 

In the planning phase (25 minutes), students create a detailed sketch with measurements, calculating actual dimensions of each structure. They must show all mathematical work for converting real-world measurements to scale (e.g., if a house is 2,500 inches long in reality, it should be 5 inches in their model). Students calculate total area usage, ensuring their community uses 60-80% of available space efficiently.

During construction (45 minutes), students build their 3D models using provided materials. Each building must be geometrically accurate with calculated heights, and students must demonstrate understanding of similar figures by creating buildings with proportional dimensions. Roads must connect logically with appropriate widths and angles calculated using protractors.

In the final phase (20 minutes), students create a mathematical portfolio documenting their process. This includes: original calculations showing scale conversions, area calculations for each zone, geometric properties of their buildings (identifying shapes, angles, symmetry), and a written reflection explaining how mathematical concepts influenced their design decisions. Students present their communities to another pair, explaining three specific mathematical decisions they made and why.
materials_needed: 12"×18" poster board (1 per pair)
Cardboard sheets for building construction
Rulers and measuring tapes
Protractors and compasses
Calculators
Graph paper for initial sketching
Colored pencils or markers
Glue sticks and tape
Mathematical portfolio template worksheets
assessment_method: Students will be evaluated using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct scale calculations, area computations, and geometric properties (25 points), (2) Design Innovation - creative problem-solving and original community layout (20 points), (3) Mathematical Justification - clear explanations of mathematical reasoning in portfolio (25 points), (4) Model Construction - accuracy of 3D representation matching calculations (20 points), (5) Presentation - ability to explain mathematical concepts used (10 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide calculation templates with partially completed examples, offer a reference sheet with common real-world building dimensions, and allow use of online scale calculators for verification. Create checkpoint moments every 15 minutes for teacher feedback. For advanced learners: Challenge them to include curved roads requiring trigonometric calculations, incorporate elevation changes with 3D geometric calculations, or add population density requirements that involve statistical reasoning and optimization problems.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Ensemble Models: Random Forest vs Gradient Boosting Comparison
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance outputs from two different ensemble algorithms (Random Forest and XGBoost) applied to the same high-dimensional dataset. They will explain the methodological differences in how each algorithm calculates feature importance and justify why rankings may differ between models.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings from Random Forest and XGBoost models by analyzing permutation importance, gain-based importance, and split-based importance metrics
Students will explain the theoretical differences between ensemble feature importance calculations through comparative analysis of algorithm-specific methodologies
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Setup (15 minutes)** - Provide students with a preprocessed high-dimensional dataset (e.g., medical diagnosis with 50+ features, customer churn with mixed data types). Each student receives identical train/test splits and feature documentation. Students load data using pandas and perform initial exploration using .info(), .describe(), and correlation matrix visualization. **Phase 2: Model Training (25 minutes)** - Students train two models using scikit-learn: RandomForestClassifier with n_estimators=100, max_depth=10, random_state=42, and XGBClassifier with n_estimators=100, max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.1, random_state=42. Students must record training accuracy, validation accuracy, and training time for both models. **Phase 3: Feature Importance Extraction (20 minutes)** - Students extract three types of importance scores: (1) model.feature_importances_ for both algorithms, (2) permutation_importance from sklearn.inspection for both models, (3) XGBoost-specific gain and cover importance using model.get_booster().get_score(). Students create pandas DataFrames ranking features by each importance type. **Phase 4: Comparative Analysis (30 minutes)** - Students generate side-by-side bar plots showing top 15 features for each importance metric. They calculate Spearman rank correlation between Random Forest and XGBoost rankings. Students write 300-word analyses explaining: why Random Forest uses mean decrease impurity vs XGBoost's gradient-based gain, how permutation importance differs from built-in metrics, and which features show consistent vs inconsistent rankings across methods. **Phase 5: Interpretation Report (20 minutes)** - Students select 5 features showing largest ranking differences between algorithms and provide domain-specific explanations for why each algorithm might weight these features differently based on their splitting criteria and ensemble methodology.
materials_needed: High-dimensional tabular dataset (CSV format) with feature documentation
Python environment with scikit-learn, xgboost, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Jupyter notebook template with code skeleton and markdown sections
Feature importance comparison worksheet (PDF template)
assessment_method: Students submit completed Jupyter notebooks with: (1) Correctly generated feature importance rankings for all metrics (20 points), (2) Properly formatted comparative visualizations showing clear differences (25 points), (3) Accurate written explanation of algorithmic differences in importance calculations (30 points), (4) Domain-specific interpretation of 5 discrepant features with methodological justification (25 points). Success criteria: Students must achieve 80% accuracy in explaining why Random Forest's gini-based importance differs from XGBoost's gradient-based gain, and correctly identify at least 3 features where ranking differences exceed 10 positions.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pseudocode templates for feature importance extraction, pre-calculated correlation matrices, and guided questions for each interpretation section. Offer example explanations for 2 discrepant features as models. **For advanced learners:** Add SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) value calculation and comparison, implement custom permutation importance with different perturbation strategies, or extend analysis to include partial dependence plots for top 5 features from each algorithm.

title: Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Sorting Algorithm Performance Comparison
description: Students will analyze the performance characteristics of three different sorting algorithms by examining their time complexity, space complexity, and practical runtime behavior. They will decompose each algorithm's structure, compare efficiency metrics, and determine optimal use cases for different data scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the time and space complexity of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort by tracing through algorithm execution and calculating Big O notation
Students will compare sorting algorithm performance through empirical testing and theoretical analysis to determine optimal applications
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with the starter code containing implementations of bubble sort, merge sort, and quicksort in Python. In Phase 1 (45 minutes), teams will trace through each algorithm using the provided dataset of 10 integers, documenting step-by-step execution in their analysis worksheet. They must count comparisons, swaps, and memory allocations for each algorithm. In Phase 2 (30 minutes), students run timing tests on datasets of sizes 100, 1000, and 5000 elements using the provided test harness, recording execution times in milliseconds. Teams graph their results and identify performance patterns. In Phase 3 (45 minutes), students analyze the theoretical complexity by examining nested loops, recursive calls, and memory usage patterns. They complete complexity analysis charts determining Big O notation for best, average, and worst cases. Finally (25 minutes), teams prepare a 3-minute presentation comparing all three algorithms, recommending which algorithm to use for: nearly sorted data, random data, and memory-constrained environments. Circulate during analysis phases to guide students toward identifying key algorithmic components and ensure accurate complexity calculations.
materials_needed: Python development environment (IDLE, PyCharm, or VS Code)
Starter code file with three sorting algorithm implementations
Algorithm analysis worksheet (PDF template)
Test datasets (100, 1000, 5000 integer arrays in CSV format)
Timing test harness script
Graph paper or digital graphing tool access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate complexity analysis with correct Big O notation for all algorithms (25%), (2) Complete empirical testing data with proper timing measurements and graphs (25%), (3) Logical comparison of algorithms with justified recommendations for different scenarios (25%), (4) Clear presentation demonstrating understanding of trade-offs between algorithms (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide algorithm flowcharts and guided complexity analysis templates with partially completed examples. Offer one-on-one code tracing sessions focusing on counting operations systematically. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (heap sort, radix sort) or implement hybrid sorting approaches. Have them investigate real-world optimizations like Timsort used in Python's built-in sort function.

title: Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Pipeline Design for Business Impact
description: Students will critically assess and compare two complete machine learning pipelines designed to solve the same business problem, evaluating their technical merit, business alignment, and potential real-world impact. They will justify recommendations for pipeline selection and improvement based on comprehensive evaluation criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of machine learning pipeline architectures by analyzing data preprocessing choices, model selection rationale, and validation strategies against business objectives
Students will critique the business impact potential of ML solutions through systematic assessment of scalability, interpretability, ethical considerations, and ROI projections
instructions:
Begin by providing student teams (3-4 members) with two complete ML pipeline documentations for the same business case (e.g., customer churn prediction for a telecom company). Each pipeline should include: raw data samples, preprocessing code, feature engineering approaches, model selection process, validation results, deployment considerations, and business impact projections.

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct independent technical analysis of both pipelines using the provided evaluation framework covering six dimensions: data quality handling, feature engineering sophistication, model appropriateness, validation rigor, scalability design, and interpretability measures. Students document findings in a structured comparison matrix.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Teams perform business impact assessment by evaluating each pipeline against: alignment with stated business objectives, implementation feasibility given organizational constraints, ethical considerations and bias detection, projected ROI calculations, and long-term maintenance requirements. Teams must identify at least three critical strengths and weaknesses per pipeline.

Step 3 (45 minutes): Teams synthesize their technical and business evaluations to make a justified recommendation. They must propose specific improvements to their selected pipeline and defend their choice against potential counterarguments. Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation with visual aids.

Step 4 (60 minutes): Teams present their evaluations and recommendations, followed by 5-minute peer Q&A sessions. Other teams score presentations using provided peer evaluation rubrics. Instructor facilitates discussion on evaluation criteria discrepancies and professional judgment in ML system selection.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Individual reflection where students write a 300-word summary identifying which evaluation criteria they found most challenging to assess and how their perspective on ML pipeline evaluation evolved during the activity.
materials_needed: Two complete ML pipeline documentation packages (code, data samples, validation results, business context)
Structured evaluation framework template with technical and business assessment criteria
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentations
Access to Jupyter notebooks or similar environment for code review
Presentation tools (projector, whiteboard, laptops)
Business case background materials (industry context, organizational constraints)
assessment_method: Evaluation based on: (1) Technical analysis depth and accuracy (25 points) - demonstrated understanding of pipeline components and trade-offs, (2) Business impact assessment quality (25 points) - consideration of real-world constraints and stakeholder needs, (3) Recommendation justification strength (25 points) - logical reasoning and evidence-based arguments, (4) Presentation clarity and peer engagement (15 points), (5) Individual reflection insight (10 points). Students must score minimum 80/100 for proficiency, with specific rubric criteria for each component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions for each evaluation dimension and offer one-on-one consultation during Step 2. Create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger technical students with those having better business acumen. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify subtle biases in training data, propose novel evaluation metrics specific to the business context, or design A/B testing strategies for pipeline comparison in production. Provide additional pipeline variations for extended analysis.

title: Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimal Urban Traffic Flow Network
description: Students will create an original mathematical framework combining graph theory, optimization, and statistical analysis to solve a real-world urban traffic congestion problem. They will develop their own algorithms, validate their model with actual traffic data, and present implementation recommendations to city planners.
estimated_duration: 330 minutes (approximately 5.5 hours across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize graph theory, linear programming, and queuing theory concepts by constructing an original traffic flow optimization model for a specific urban intersection network
Students will formulate novel mathematical algorithms through integration of multiple advanced mathematical domains to solve complex real-world transportation challenges
instructions:
Step 1 (45 min): Students select a real urban area with documented traffic issues using Google Maps traffic data or city transportation websites. They must identify at least 8 interconnected intersections forming a network. Students photograph/screenshot the area and gather rush hour traffic pattern data.

Step 2 (60 min): Working in teams of 3-4, students construct a weighted directed graph representing their chosen network. Vertices represent intersections, edges represent road segments. Students assign weights based on: average travel time, traffic volume capacity, and congestion probability. They must justify all weight assignments with collected data.

Step 3 (90 min): Teams develop their optimization model by combining: (a) shortest path algorithms (modified Dijkstra's), (b) flow conservation constraints using linear programming, and (c) queuing theory for wait time predictions at traffic lights. Students must create original mathematical formulations, not simply apply existing formulas.

Step 4 (75 min): Students implement their model using Python, MATLAB, or similar computational tools. They must code their algorithms from scratch and run simulations comparing current traffic patterns with their optimized solutions. Teams calculate quantitative improvements (reduced travel time, decreased congestion).

Step 5 (60 min): Teams prepare a professional presentation including: mathematical model derivation, algorithm pseudocode, simulation results with visualizations, and specific implementation recommendations for city transportation departments. Each team presents for 15 minutes with Q&A.
materials_needed: Computers with Python/MATLAB/Mathematica software access
Internet access for traffic data collection
Graph paper and colored pens for initial network sketching
Access to real traffic datasets (provided by instructor or city transportation websites)
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluation using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Mathematical Model Originality - novel integration of multiple mathematical domains, (2) Algorithm Development - creation of functional, efficient computational methods, (3) Data Integration - effective use of real-world data to validate and improve model, (4) Implementation Feasibility - practical applicability of recommendations with cost-benefit analysis, (5) Mathematical Rigor - proper use of notation, logical proof structure, and error analysis. Final deliverable includes written technical report (15 pages) and oral presentation. Peer evaluation component included.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template graphs for common intersection types and guided algorithm development worksheets. Offer office hours for debugging code and mathematical derivations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like weather impacts, emergency vehicle routing, or environmental considerations (emissions, noise). Encourage exploration of machine learning integration for predictive traffic modeling.

title: Binary Number Flash Card Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flash card exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the correct binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by matching flash cards with 90% accuracy
Students will recall the decimal value of 4-bit binary numbers through timed recognition exercises within 3 seconds per card
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flash card sets to pairs of students (15 minutes setup). Each set contains 16 cards with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary representations on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for the first 20 minutes, with one student showing the decimal side while the partner states the binary equivalent, then checking the answer. After 10 cards, partners switch roles. Next, conduct a 10-minute individual memorization period where each student silently reviews their complete set, focusing on numbers they found difficult. Follow with a 15-minute speed recognition phase: students work individually, timing themselves as they go through the entire deck showing decimal numbers first, stating binary aloud, then flipping to verify. They record incorrect answers on a tracking sheet. Conclude with a 10-minute partner quiz where students test each other on their weakest numbers identified during speed recognition. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are pronouncing binary numbers correctly (e.g., '0101' as 'zero-one-zero-one' not 'one hundred one') and using proper 4-bit format with leading zeros.
materials_needed: Pre-made flash card sets (one per pair) with decimal 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Individual tracking sheets for recording errors
Timer or stopwatch (classroom timer or phone apps)
Answer key poster for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students complete a final individual recognition test using 10 randomly selected cards from the set. Success criteria: correctly identify 9/10 binary representations within the 3-second time limit. Document results on individual tracking sheets showing improvement from initial attempts to final assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a binary conversion reference chart and allow extra practice time with numbers 0-7 first before advancing to 8-15. For advanced learners: extend activity to include 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider allowing struggling students to work in groups of three for additional peer support during memorization phase.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Performance Metrics Across Different Model Types
description: Students will analyze and interpret k-fold cross-validation results from three different machine learning models (linear regression, decision tree, and random forest) trained on a housing price dataset. They will explain the meaning of performance variations across folds and compare model reliability based on metric distributions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation performance metrics by analyzing variance patterns across k-folds for different model types
Students will explain model reliability and overfitting tendencies through comparison of training vs. validation score distributions
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 people) with a pre-prepared Jupyter notebook containing three trained models on the Boston Housing dataset with 5-fold cross-validation results displayed as box plots and summary statistics tables. In the first 15 minutes, students individually examine the cross-validation scores (RMSE and R²) for each model, noting the mean, standard deviation, and range across folds. Next, spend 20 minutes in teams discussing and documenting answers to guided questions: 'Which model shows the most consistent performance across folds and why?', 'What does high variance in cross-validation scores indicate about a model?', and 'How do the training scores compare to validation scores for each model?' During minutes 36-50, teams create a written interpretation summary explaining which model they would select for production and why, considering both average performance and consistency. They must justify their choice using specific metric values and explain what the cross-validation results reveal about each model's tendency to overfit. In the final 10 minutes, conduct a class discussion where each team presents their model selection decision and reasoning. Instructor facilitates comparison of interpretations and clarifies common misconceptions about cross-validation metrics.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-run cross-validation results and visualizations
Boston Housing dataset (pre-loaded in notebook)
Computers with Python, scikit-learn, pandas, and matplotlib installed
Guided question worksheet (printed or digital)
Answer template for interpretation summary
assessment_method: Evaluate written interpretation summaries using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of performance patterns across models, (2) Accurate explanation of what variance in CV scores indicates, (3) Appropriate comparison of training vs. validation scores, (4) Justified model selection with specific metric references. Participation in team discussion and final presentation accounts for 25% of total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example interpretation for a fourth simple model (e.g., mean baseline) to demonstrate the analysis approach. Offer sentence starters like 'The high standard deviation in Model X indicates...' For advanced learners, include additional datasets with different characteristics or ask them to explain how learning curves would complement the cross-validation analysis.

title: Multi-Variable Calculus Optimization: Designing a Rain Collection System
description: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize the design of a cylindrical rain collection tank with cost constraints. This real-world engineering problem requires students to set up and solve a constrained optimization problem using advanced calculus techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to maximize volume under given material cost constraints by solving a multi-variable optimization problem
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methodology to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic algebraic manipulation and interpretation of results
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: A municipality needs to design cylindrical rain collection tanks where material costs $15 per square meter for the bottom, $10 per square meter for the sides, and $8 per square meter for the top, with a total budget constraint of $5000 per tank. Distribute the problem worksheet and organize students into groups of 3-4. In the first 20 minutes, have students define variables (radius r, height h), write the volume function V(r,h) = πr²h, and establish the constraint function g(r,h) representing total cost. During minutes 21-45, students set up the Lagrange multiplier system: ∇V = λ∇g, systematically computing partial derivatives ∂V/∂r = 2πrh, ∂V/∂h = πr², ∂g/∂r = 30πr, and ∂g/∂h = 10πr². From minutes 46-75, groups solve the resulting system of equations: 2πrh = λ(30πr), πr² = λ(10πr²), and the budget constraint 15πr² + 20πrh = 5000. Students should eliminate λ, solve for the relationship between r and h, then substitute back to find specific values. In the final 25 minutes, have students verify their solution using the second derivative test, calculate the maximum volume achievable, and interpret results in the engineering context. Circulate continuously to check algebraic work and guide students through complex calculations. Conclude with groups presenting their tank dimensions and maximum volume to the class.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Problem worksheet with scenario details and constraint values
Graph paper for sketching level curves
Whiteboard markers for group work stations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct setup of objective and constraint functions (25%), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier methodology with accurate partial derivatives (35%), (3) Accurate algebraic solution and numerical calculations (25%), and (4) Meaningful interpretation of results in engineering context (15%). Students must submit their complete solution process and final tank specifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a template showing the general form of Lagrange multiplier equations and guide them through computing one partial derivative as an example. Offer intermediate checkpoints for verification of constraint function setup. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding a second constraint (maximum height due to zoning laws) or asking them to explore sensitivity analysis by varying the budget constraint and graphing optimal dimensions versus budget.

title: Comparative Analysis of Time Complexity in Sorting Algorithm Implementations
description: Students will analyze the actual runtime performance of three different sorting algorithms (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort) by examining their implementations, predicting theoretical complexities, and comparing empirical results across varying input sizes and data distributions. This activity bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical performance analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between theoretical time complexity and actual runtime performance by comparing predicted versus measured execution times across different sorting algorithms
Students will evaluate algorithm efficiency patterns through systematic testing of sorting implementations with varying input characteristics (size, distribution, ordering)
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4, ensuring each team has access to the provided sorting algorithm implementations. (10 minutes setup)

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Each team receives three pre-written sorting algorithm implementations (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort) with detailed comments. Students must first examine the code structure and identify key operations that contribute to time complexity. They should document their predictions for best-case, average-case, and worst-case scenarios for each algorithm, justifying their analysis based on code examination.

Phase 2 (45 minutes): Teams design and execute systematic performance tests using the provided timing framework. They must test each algorithm with: (a) random arrays of sizes 1000, 10000, 50000, 100000, (b) already-sorted arrays of the same sizes, (c) reverse-sorted arrays, and (d) arrays with many duplicate elements. Students record execution times in milliseconds and organize data in structured tables.

Phase 3 (35 minutes): Using spreadsheet software or Python plotting libraries, teams create comparative visualizations showing runtime growth patterns. They must generate line graphs plotting array size versus execution time for each algorithm, with separate lines for different input types.

Phase 4 (40 minutes): Teams analyze discrepancies between theoretical predictions and empirical results. They must identify specific cases where actual performance deviates from expected complexity bounds and hypothesize reasons (cache effects, implementation details, input characteristics). Final deliverable includes a written analysis report with graphs, data tables, and explanations of findings.
materials_needed: Pre-written sorting algorithm implementations in Python/Java with timing frameworks
