Computers with programming environment (Python/Java IDE)
Spreadsheet software or data visualization libraries (matplotlib, Excel)
Sample dataset generator script for creating test arrays
Performance measurement template with data collection tables
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical complexity analysis (25%), (2) Systematic experimental design and data collection completeness (25%), (3) Quality and clarity of data visualizations (25%), (4) Depth of analysis in explaining performance discrepancies and drawing connections between theory and practice (25%). Teams must submit data tables, graphs, and a 2-page written analysis explaining their findings and conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide complexity analysis reference sheets with step-by-step guidelines for identifying loops and recursive calls. Offer pre-formatted data collection templates and example graph formats. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze additional algorithms (radix sort, counting sort), investigate memory usage patterns, or examine the impact of different programming languages on performance. Encourage exploration of hybrid sorting approaches and their complexity implications.

title: Design a Mathematical Board Game Using Quadratic Functions
description: Students will create an original board game that incorporates quadratic functions as the core gameplay mechanic. They must design game rules, create a physical board, and develop mathematical challenges that require players to solve quadratic equations to advance.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize their understanding of quadratic functions by designing an interactive game that demonstrates real-world applications of parabolic motion and optimization
Students will construct mathematical problems and solutions through developing gameplay mechanics that require quadratic equation solving strategies
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute brainstorming session where students work in pairs to identify real-world scenarios involving quadratic functions (projectile motion, profit optimization, area maximization). Next, spend 15 minutes having pairs share ideas and form groups of 3-4 students with complementary concepts. Groups then spend 20 minutes outlining their game concept, deciding on theme (sports, business, engineering, etc.), board layout, and how quadratic functions will drive gameplay. During the 60-minute creation phase, students simultaneously work on: (1) designing and drawing their board on poster paper with clear paths, spaces, and mathematical challenge zones, (2) writing 15-20 quadratic function problems with varying difficulty levels and complete solution keys, (3) creating game pieces, cards, and rule sheets that explain how solving quadratic equations allows players to move, gain points, or unlock special abilities. Students must include at least three different forms of quadratic equations (standard, vertex, and factored) and specify solution methods (factoring, completing the square, quadratic formula). In the final 30-minutes, each group presents their game by having another group play for 10 minutes while explaining the mathematical concepts, followed by 5 minutes of feedback. Groups must demonstrate how their game reinforces quadratic function concepts and justify their design choices mathematically.
materials_needed: Poster paper (22" x 28")
Colored markers and pencils
Index cards for problem cards
Dice and small game pieces
Calculators
Rulers and compasses
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (problems are correctly written and solved), Creativity (innovative integration of quadratic functions into gameplay), Game Functionality (rules are clear and game is playable), and Mathematical Explanation (can articulate how quadratic concepts drive their game mechanics). Students submit their complete game, problem answer key, and a 1-page reflection explaining their mathematical design choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template boards with pre-marked spaces and a bank of sample quadratic function scenarios. Offer graphic organizers for problem creation and encourage focusing on simpler factoring problems. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate systems of quadratic equations, complex number solutions, or real data from projectile motion experiments to create more sophisticated gameplay mechanics.

title: Memory Palace: Advanced Sorting Algorithm Properties and Time Complexities
description: Students will memorize and recall specific properties, time complexities, space complexities, and stability characteristics of eight advanced sorting algorithms. This activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and verbal recitation to ensure precise retention of technical specifications.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact best-case, average-case, and worst-case time complexities for QuickSort, MergeSort, HeapSort, RadixSort, CountingSort, BucketSort, TimSort, and IntroSort by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify the space complexity, stability, and in-place properties of each algorithm through structured verbal recitation exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made algorithm specification sheets containing eight sorting algorithms with their complete technical properties (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to create digital flashcards using Anki software, with each algorithm requiring exactly 4 cards: one for time complexities, one for space complexity, one for stability/in-place properties, and one for key implementation characteristics like pivot selection or partitioning method. Students spend 25 minutes creating 32 total flashcards with standardized formatting: algorithm name on front, specific property on back using Big-O notation where applicable. Next, students complete three 10-minute spaced repetition sessions using Anki's algorithm, focusing on immediate recall without hesitation. After digital practice, pair students for verbal recitation rounds (20 minutes total). Partner A states an algorithm name, Partner B has 10 seconds to recite all four property categories from memory. Partners alternate through all eight algorithms twice, then switch roles. Conclude with individual written recall test (15 minutes): students receive blank template with algorithm names listed, must fill in all properties without references. Instructor calls out random algorithm-property combinations for spot-checking during final 10 minutes. Emphasize exact terminology: 'O(n log n) average case,' 'stable,' 'not in-place,' etc. Students must achieve 90% accuracy on verbal recitation and 85% on written test to demonstrate mastery.
materials_needed: Pre-printed sorting algorithm specification reference sheets (8 algorithms)
Anki flashcard software installed on student devices
Blank algorithm properties template sheets
Digital timer for recitation rounds
Standardized Big-O notation reference guide
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy during partner verbal recitation (observed by instructor using checklist) and score 85% or higher on final written recall test covering all 32 algorithm properties. Assessment rubric awards 3 points for exact terminology, 2 points for correct concept with minor notation errors, 1 point for partially correct, 0 points for incorrect or missing responses.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing mnemonic devices for each algorithm (e.g., 'QuickSort Quickly Queries: O(n²) worst, O(n log n) average'). Allow extra 5 minutes for flashcard creation and provide pre-filled templates with partial information. For advanced learners, add recursive implementation details, cache performance characteristics, or hybrid algorithm transitions to memorization requirements. Consider audio recordings of correct pronunciations for complex terms.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Bias in Production ML Pipeline Results
description: Students will analyze real-world production machine learning model outputs to understand how feature importance metrics reveal algorithmic bias and model behavior patterns. They will interpret SHAP values, permutation importance, and fairness metrics to explain model decisions and identify potential bias in hiring algorithm results.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and permutation importance scores by analyzing their mathematical foundations and practical implications in model explainability
Students will recognize algorithmic bias patterns through systematic examination of feature importance distributions across protected demographic groups
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a pre-trained hiring decision model dataset containing 10,000 candidate records with features including education, experience, skills scores, age, gender, and ethnicity, along with model predictions and explainability outputs (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (coordinates analysis), Bias Detective (focuses on fairness metrics), Technical Interpreter (explains SHAP mathematics), and Communicator (synthesizes findings). 

In Phase 1 (45 minutes), teams examine global feature importance using three methods: built-in feature_importances_, permutation importance scores, and mean absolute SHAP values. Students must create comparison tables showing rank-ordered features for each method, then explain why rankings differ by connecting mathematical definitions to observed patterns. Teams calculate correlation coefficients between importance rankings and document which features show high variance across methods.

Phase 2 (60 minutes) focuses on local explainability analysis. Students select 20 representative samples (10 hired, 10 rejected) and examine individual SHAP value distributions. They must identify cases where protected attributes (age, gender, ethnicity) contribute significantly to decisions, documenting specific SHAP values and calculating demographic parity differences. Teams create visualization plots showing SHAP value distributions segmented by protected groups.

Phase 3 (45 minutes) requires bias pattern recognition. Students calculate equalized odds ratios, demographic parity metrics, and individual fairness measures across subgroups. They must identify three specific bias patterns, explain the underlying feature importance mechanisms causing bias, and propose technical mitigation strategies. Final deliverable includes a 2-page technical memo explaining model behavior, bias findings, and recommendations using precise statistical language and specific numerical evidence from their analysis.
materials_needed: Pre-processed hiring dataset (CSV format, 10,000 records with 15 features)
Jupyter notebooks with pre-loaded SHAP, scikit-learn, pandas, and matplotlib libraries
Pre-trained Random Forest model (pickle file) with corresponding SHAP explainer object
Fairness metrics calculation template (Python script)
Technical memo template document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Feature importance interpretation accuracy (25 points - correct mathematical explanations of SHAP vs permutation differences), Bias identification precision (30 points - specific numerical evidence of demographic disparities with proper statistical measures), Technical explanation quality (25 points - accurate use of explainability terminology and concepts), Communication clarity (20 points - professional memo format with actionable recommendations). Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated understanding of explainability method differences and identification of at least 2 statistically significant bias patterns with effect sizes >0.1.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide SHAP value interpretation cheat sheet with common patterns, offer pre-calculated demographic parity examples, and allow extended time for Phase 1 completion. Create checkpoint consultations after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement custom fairness metrics, compare model bias across different algorithms (logistic regression vs random forest), or design bias mitigation strategies using adversarial debiasing techniques. Provide access to additional datasets for cross-validation of findings.

title: Budget Your Dream Room: Applying Decimal Operations to Real-World Shopping
description: Students will apply decimal addition, subtraction, and multiplication skills by creating a budget for decorating their dream bedroom with a $500 spending limit. They will calculate costs, determine tax amounts, and make purchasing decisions based on their mathematical calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply decimal addition and subtraction operations by calculating total costs and remaining budget amounts within a room decoration scenario
Students will apply decimal multiplication skills through computing sales tax and discount calculations on furniture and decoration items
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Dream Room Furniture Catalog' (created beforehand with 15-20 items ranging from $12.99 to $149.99) and budget worksheets to each student. Explain that each student has exactly $500.00 to spend and must pay 8.25% sales tax on all purchases. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students browse the catalog and create a wish list of 8-10 items they want for their room, writing item names and prices on their worksheet. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students calculate the subtotal by adding all selected item prices using decimal addition. They must show their work with proper decimal alignment. 

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students calculate 8.25% sales tax by multiplying their subtotal by 0.0825, rounding to the nearest cent. Then they add tax to subtotal for the final total.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students subtract their total from $500.00 to determine remaining budget. If they exceed $500, they must remove items and recalculate.

Step 5 (5 minutes): Students identify one item they could purchase with remaining money and recalculate their final budget.

Circulate during each step to check decimal alignment, computational accuracy, and proper rounding. Provide calculators only after students complete initial calculations by hand. End with 2-3 students sharing their room designs and budget breakdowns with the class.
materials_needed: Dream Room Furniture Catalog (teacher-created with prices in decimal format)
Budget calculation worksheets with organized spaces for each step
Calculators for verification (distributed in final steps only)
Pencils and erasers
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) All decimal calculations correct with proper alignment and rounding, stays within budget; (3) Minor computational errors but proper procedures shown; (2) Some calculation errors with incomplete work shown; (1) Major errors in decimal operations or procedures. Students must achieve level 3 or higher for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a simplified catalog with fewer, round-number prices (like $25.00, $50.00) and reduce required items to 5-6. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including discount percentages (15% off certain items) and require them to determine which discount combination maximizes their purchasing power within the budget.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Practice
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science fundamentals.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid recognition exercises within 3 seconds per conversion
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student (15 minutes setup). Each set contains 16 cards with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and corresponding 4-bit binary representations on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Demonstrate proper flashcard technique: show decimal side, state binary equivalent aloud, flip to verify, sort into 'known' and 'practice needed' piles. Students work individually for 20 minutes using the Leitner system - correctly answered cards move to a separate pile for later review, incorrect cards return to active practice pile. After individual practice, pair students for peer testing (10 minutes). Partner A shows decimal numbers randomly while Partner B provides binary equivalent within 5 seconds. Partners alternate roles every 5 minutes, tracking correct responses on provided score sheets. Conclude with whole-class rapid-fire round (10 minutes) where instructor displays decimal numbers on projector and students write binary equivalents on mini whiteboards, holding up answers simultaneously. Record class accuracy rate on board. Finish with students completing self-assessment rubric rating their confidence level (1-4 scale) for each number 0-15, identifying specific numbers needing additional practice for homework review.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (16 cards per student showing decimal 0-15 and binary equivalents)
Score tracking sheets for peer practice
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Timer or stopwatch
Self-assessment confidence rubric handouts
Projector for whole-class activity
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/16 correct) during peer testing phase and score 80% or higher on final rapid-fire whiteboard round. Track individual progress using score sheets showing improvement from initial practice to final assessment. Award points: 3 points for 90%+ accuracy, 2 points for 75-89%, 1 point for 60-74%, 0 points below 60%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide binary conversion chart reference, start with numbers 0-7 only, allow 10 seconds response time instead of 5. Use color-coding (highlight powers of 2) and encourage counting patterns. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or practice with negative binary representations using two's complement method.

title: Multi-Step Optimization: Designing Cost-Efficient Shipping Networks
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world logistics problem involving minimizing shipping costs across multiple distribution centers. They will use derivatives, constraint optimization, and linear programming concepts to determine optimal warehouse locations and shipping routes.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to minimize total shipping costs by determining optimal warehouse coordinates and capacity allocations
Students will implement constraint optimization techniques through systematic analysis of budget limitations and delivery time requirements in a shipping network scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the shipping network scenario packet to each group of 3-4 students (10 minutes setup). Present the scenario: A company needs to establish 2 new distribution warehouses to serve 8 cities, with given population demands, existing transportation costs per mile, and a $2.5 million budget constraint. Students first identify the objective function (total shipping cost) and constraints (budget, capacity, delivery time) on their worksheet (15 minutes). Next, have students set up the mathematical model using coordinate geometry, where warehouse locations are variables (x₁,y₁) and (x₂,y₂), and they must minimize the sum of distances weighted by shipping volume to each city (25 minutes). Students then apply partial derivatives to find critical points, checking ∂f/∂x₁ = 0, ∂f/∂x₁ = 0, ∂f/∂x₂ = 0, ∂f/∂y₂ = 0, while incorporating the budget constraint using Lagrange multipliers (30 minutes). Have groups use spreadsheet software to test their analytical solutions by creating a cost function model with variable warehouse coordinates, then use Solver add-in to verify their calculus-based results (20 minutes). Students conclude by preparing a 5-minute presentation showing their optimal warehouse locations on the provided regional map, calculated minimum cost, and verification that all constraints are satisfied (15 minutes preparation, 20 minutes presentations). Circulate continuously to ensure proper derivative setup and constraint handling, checking that students correctly apply the distance formula and weight it by shipping volume.
materials_needed: Shipping network scenario packets with city coordinates and demand data
Regional maps with coordinate grid overlay
Scientific calculators
Laptops/tablets with Excel or Google Sheets and Solver add-in
Optimization worksheet templates with constraint spaces
Colored markers for mapping solutions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification and mathematical setup of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Proper application of partial derivatives and Lagrange multiplier method (35%), (3) Accurate computational work and spreadsheet verification (25%), and (4) Clear presentation of solution with justification that constraints are satisfied (15%). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 points in categories 1 and 2 to demonstrate apply-level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written objective function templates and guide them through the first partial derivative step-by-step. Offer a simplified 2-city version before attempting the full 8-city problem. For advanced learners, add complexity by introducing different truck capacities, fuel cost variations, or time-dependent demand fluctuations requiring dynamic optimization approaches.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Circuit Analysis: Comparing Faraday's Law Applications in Real-World Systems
description: Students analyze and compare electromagnetic induction in three different circuit configurations (transformer, generator, and eddy current braking system) to determine how changing magnetic flux produces varying induced EMF patterns. They will decompose complex waveforms and evaluate the efficiency of each system based on their mathematical models.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between magnetic flux change rates and induced EMF by examining oscilloscope data from three different electromagnetic induction systems
Students will evaluate the efficiency and practical applications of electromagnetic induction through quantitative comparison of power losses and energy transfer rates
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection Setup (20 minutes)**
Divide students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three pre-configured electromagnetic induction setups: a step-down transformer (120V to 12V), a hand-crank generator with variable load resistors, and an eddy current braking system with copper disk. Connect oscilloscopes to measure primary/secondary voltages in transformer, generator output voltage, and braking force sensor output. Have students record baseline measurements for 2 minutes at each station, rotating every 7 minutes.

**Phase 2: Variable Analysis (30 minutes)**
Students systematically vary one parameter in each system: transformer load resistance (10Ω, 50Ω, 100Ω), generator crank speed (30, 60, 90 RPM), and copper disk rotation speed (100, 200, 300 RPM). At each setting, record RMS voltage, current, frequency, and phase relationships using digital multimeters and oscilloscopes. Calculate instantaneous power and average power over 30-second intervals.

**Phase 3: Mathematical Modeling (25 minutes)**
Using collected data, students apply Faraday's Law (ε = -dΦ/dt) to create mathematical models for each system. Calculate theoretical vs. measured values for induced EMF, accounting for factors like coil geometry, magnetic field strength, and flux change rates. Use Lenz's Law to explain phase relationships and energy conservation principles.

**Phase 4: Comparative Analysis (25 minutes)**
Create comparison matrices evaluating efficiency (Pout/Pin), frequency response, load sensitivity, and practical applications. Students must identify which system performs best under specific conditions and justify their conclusions using quantitative evidence. Present findings in standardized data sheets with uncertainty analysis.
materials_needed: 3 oscilloscopes with USB data logging capability
Step-down transformer (120V/12V, 2A rating) with variable load bank
Hand-crank generator with tachometer and 10Ω, 50Ω, 100Ω load resistors
Eddy current brake with copper disk, force sensor, and variable speed motor
Digital multimeters (6 units) with RMS capability
LabVIEW or Python data analysis software
Magnetic field strength meters (gaussmeters)
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric: Data accuracy and measurement technique (25 points), mathematical modeling with correct application of Faraday's and Lenz's laws (30 points), comparative analysis with justified conclusions (25 points), uncertainty analysis and error discussion (20 points). Students submit: raw data spreadsheets, calculated theoretical predictions, efficiency comparison matrix, and written analysis identifying optimal applications for each system.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated magnetic field values and simplified data collection templates. Offer guided practice with basic EMF calculations before complex analysis. For advanced learners: Include analysis of harmonic content in waveforms, investigation of core losses in transformer, and design optimization recommendations. Provide additional challenge of predicting system behavior under non-standard conditions.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Comparing Two Password Validation Solutions
description: Students will evaluate and compare two different password validation code implementations by analyzing their security, efficiency, and maintainability. They will create a detailed evaluation report recommending which solution should be adopted for a web application project.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two password validation implementations by analyzing code quality, security vulnerabilities, and performance characteristics
Students will judge the overall effectiveness of each solution through systematic comparison using established software development criteria
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and providing each pair with two password validation code samples (Solution A: basic string checks, Solution B: regex-based with additional security features). Give students 10 minutes to read through both implementations silently. Next, have pairs spend 20 minutes analyzing Solution A using the provided evaluation checklist, examining: functionality correctness (does it validate passwords properly?), security considerations (does it check for common vulnerabilities?), code readability (is it easy to understand?), and performance efficiency (how fast does it execute?). Have them document their findings in the evaluation worksheet. Repeat this 20-minute analysis process for Solution B. Then, students spend 15 minutes directly comparing both solutions side-by-side, rating each criterion on a 1-5 scale and providing written justification for their ratings. For the final 20 minutes, pairs must write a recommendation report (300-400 words) stating which solution they would choose for a production web application and why. The report must include: overall recommendation, three strongest supporting reasons with specific code examples, two potential improvements for their chosen solution, and one risk mitigation strategy. Conclude with 10-minute pair presentations where each team shares their recommendation and key reasoning with the class.
materials_needed: Two password validation code samples (Solution A and Solution B) printed or digital
Code evaluation checklist worksheet
Comparison scoring rubric handout
Access to basic code testing environment or IDE
Timer for time management
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Analysis depth - thoroughly examines each criterion with specific examples, (2) Comparison accuracy - correctly identifies strengths/weaknesses of each solution, (3) Recommendation quality - provides clear, well-justified choice with supporting evidence, (4) Technical understanding - demonstrates comprehension of security, performance, and maintainability concepts. Students must score 3/4 on each criterion to demonstrate mastery of evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example evaluation of a simple 'hello world' function first, offer guiding questions for each evaluation criterion, and allow extended time for analysis. For advanced learners: provide a third, more complex solution to evaluate, ask them to suggest specific code improvements with implementation details, or have them research and apply additional evaluation criteria like scalability or testing coverage.

title: Design and Build a Customer Retention Dashboard for E-commerce Business
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that analyzes customer behavior patterns and generates actionable retention strategies for a fictional e-commerce company. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design custom metrics, and present data-driven recommendations through visual storytelling.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive customer retention dashboard by integrating sales, demographic, and behavioral datasets using advanced visualization techniques
Students will create original business metrics and KPIs through statistical analysis and present strategic recommendations based on their findings
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup and Data Exploration (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three CSV files: customer_transactions.csv (12 months of purchase data), customer_demographics.csv (age, location, acquisition channel), and website_analytics.csv (page views, session duration, bounce rates). Students begin by importing datasets into Tableau or Power BI and performing initial data quality checks, documenting any missing values or anomalies.

**Phase 2: Metric Design and Analysis (60 minutes)**
Teams must create five custom metrics: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), churn probability score, purchase frequency segments, seasonal buying patterns, and channel effectiveness ratios. Students calculate these using appropriate formulas and statistical methods, creating calculated fields in their chosen software. They must justify their metric choices in a brief methodology document.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (75 minutes)**
Students design a 3-panel dashboard: Overview (key metrics and trends), Customer Segments (demographic breakdowns and behavioral clusters), and Retention Strategies (predictive insights and recommendations). Each panel must include interactive filters, drill-down capabilities, and clear data labels. Teams must incorporate at least 6 different chart types and ensure consistent color coding and branding.

**Phase 4: Strategy Development and Presentation (30 minutes)**
Using their dashboard insights, teams develop three specific retention strategies with projected ROI calculations. They prepare a 5-minute presentation highlighting their most compelling findings and actionable recommendations. Presentations must include live dashboard demonstration and defend their analytical approach to audience questions.
materials_needed: Tableau Desktop or Power BI Desktop licenses
Three pre-prepared CSV datasets (customer_transactions.csv, customer_demographics.csv, website_analytics.csv)
Computers with internet access
Presentation setup (projector/screen)
Printed data dictionary and business context handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: Data Integration Quality (seamless joins, proper data types), Metric Innovation (mathematical accuracy, business relevance), Dashboard Design (visual hierarchy, interactivity, user experience), Strategic Insights (depth of analysis, feasibility of recommendations), and Presentation Delivery (clarity, confidence, ability to answer questions). Each criterion worth 20 points for total of 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written SQL queries for complex calculations and dashboard templates with placeholder charts. Offer guided worksheets breaking down CLV calculations step-by-step. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive modeling using trend lines or clustering algorithms, add advanced statistical tests for significance, or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions.

title: PMI Knowledge Area Component Identification Challenge
description: Students will systematically identify and categorize specific project management processes, tools, and deliverables within the 10 PMI Knowledge Areas using real project scenarios. This activity reinforces memorization of advanced PM framework components through structured pattern recognition exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific processes, tools, and deliverables for each of the 10 PMI Knowledge Areas by matching them to complex project scenario elements
Students will identify the correct PMI process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) through categorization of 50 advanced project management components
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared scenario packets and answer sheets to each student (5 minutes). Each packet contains 5 complex project scenarios from different industries (healthcare IT implementation, aerospace product development, financial system integration, construction, and pharmaceutical research). Students work individually for 45 minutes to identify PMI components embedded within each scenario. For each scenario, students must: 1) Identify which of the 10 Knowledge Areas are represented by underlining key phrases, 2) List specific processes from the PMBOK Guide that apply (minimum 3 per scenario), 3) Name specific tools and techniques mentioned or implied (minimum 2 per scenario), 4) Identify deliverables or outputs described (minimum 2 per scenario), and 5) Classify each identified process into its correct process group. Provide students with the PMI Knowledge Areas reference sheet but no process details. After individual work, conduct a 15-minute rapid-fire review where students call out their identifications while you record correct responses on the master answer key projected on screen. Students self-score their work, earning 2 points for correctly identified Knowledge Areas, 3 points for accurate process identification, 2 points for tools/techniques, 2 points for deliverables, and 1 point for correct process group classification. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify their strongest and weakest Knowledge Areas based on their scores.
materials_needed: 5 printed project scenario packets (2 pages each) per student
Individual answer sheets with structured tables for responses
PMI 10 Knowledge Areas reference sheet (1 per student)
Master answer key for instructor projection
Colored pens for self-scoring
Projector and screen for answer review
assessment_method: Students earn points through self-scoring: Knowledge Area identification (10 points max), Process identification (75 points max), Tools/techniques (50 points max), Deliverables (50 points max), Process group classification (25 points max). Success criteria: 70% accuracy overall (147/210 points), with minimum 60% accuracy in each category. Instructor spot-checks 25% of student answer sheets for self-scoring accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide PMBOK Guide process group summary charts and allow use of index tabs on reference materials. Pair with stronger students for peer support during review phase. For advanced learners: Add requirement to identify process interfaces and dependencies between Knowledge Areas, or include identification of specific PMBOK Guide section numbers for each process identified.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Communication: Multi-Stakeholder Impact Analysis
description: Students will analyze a complex organizational crisis case study to understand how different leadership communication approaches impact various stakeholder groups. They will examine the interconnections between leadership decisions, communication strategies, and organizational outcomes through systematic stakeholder impact mapping.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between leadership communication choices and stakeholder responses by examining documented crisis scenarios across multiple organizational levels
Students will differentiate between surface-level communication tactics and underlying leadership principles through comparative analysis of stakeholder impact patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing the Boeing 737 MAX crisis case study packet (20 minutes for individual reading). Divide students into groups of 4, assigning each member a stakeholder role: shareholders, employees, customers, and regulatory bodies. Each student spends 15 minutes identifying how leadership decisions specifically impacted their assigned stakeholder group, documenting evidence from the case materials. Groups then create a visual stakeholder impact map on large paper, with leadership decisions in the center and stakeholder impacts radiating outward, using different colors for each stakeholder type (25 minutes). Next, provide groups with alternative leadership communication scenarios from the same crisis period. Groups analyze how different communication approaches would have created different stakeholder impacts, adding these hypothetical outcomes to their maps using dotted lines (20 minutes). Each group presents their completed map to another group, explaining the cause-and-effect relationships they identified between specific leadership choices and stakeholder outcomes (15 minutes per presentation). Conclude with individual reflection where students write a 300-word analysis identifying three key patterns they discovered about how leadership communication decisions cascade through different organizational stakeholder groups, citing specific evidence from their mapping exercise.
materials_needed: Boeing 737 MAX crisis case study packet (15 pages with timeline, communication transcripts, and stakeholder responses)
Large poster paper (11x17 minimum)
Colored markers (4 different colors per group)
Alternative leadership communication scenario handouts
Stakeholder role description cards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of stakeholder impact identification with specific case evidence, (2) Quality of cause-and-effect connections shown in visual mapping, (3) Depth of analysis in comparing alternative communication approaches, (4) Clarity of pattern recognition in final written reflection. Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying at least 3 specific leadership decisions, explaining their impact on each stakeholder group with evidence, and articulating how different approaches would yield different outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed stakeholder impact template with some connections already drawn. Offer sentence starters for the reflection writing. For advanced learners, add a secondary case study for comparison or require them to identify implicit stakeholder groups (media, suppliers, communities) beyond the four primary roles. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with visual learners within groups.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS by configuring EC2 instances for the web and application tiers, setting up an RDS MySQL database, and implementing S3 for static content storage. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration in a real-world scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier web application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS database, and S3 storage services within AWS console
Students will implement security best practices through proper security group configuration and IAM role assignment for service connectivity
instructions:
**Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Learner Lab access credentials. Students log into AWS Console and verify they're in us-east-1 region. Distribute the provided HTML/PHP application files via shared folder.

**S3 Configuration (20 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-static-[studentname]-[date]'. Upload provided CSS, JavaScript, and image files to the bucket. Configure bucket policy for public read access to static assets. Test access by opening one CSS file URL in browser.

**RDS Setup (25 minutes):** Launch RDS MySQL instance using t3.micro, database name 'webapp_db', master username 'admin', auto-generate password. Configure security group to allow inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from EC2 security group (to be created). Wait for instance to become available, then note endpoint URL.

**EC2 Web Tier (30 minutes):** Launch t3.micro EC2 instance with Amazon Linux 2. Create security group allowing HTTP (80) and SSH (22) from anywhere. In User Data, include script to install Apache and PHP. Connect via SSH, upload provided PHP application files to /var/www/html/. Modify database connection file with RDS endpoint details.

**EC2 Application Tier (20 minutes):** Launch second t3.micro instance for application processing. Configure security group allowing communication from web tier on port 8080. Install required application dependencies and configure service to run on port 8080.

**Integration Testing (15 minutes):** Access web application via EC2 public IP. Test database connectivity by submitting form data. Verify static content loads from S3. Students document their application URL and screenshot successful page load with database interaction.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab access credentials for each student
Pre-built PHP web application files (HTML forms, PHP scripts, CSS)
SQL script for database table creation
Step-by-step reference guide with AWS console screenshots
Computers with web browsers and SSH client capability
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment report containing: (1) Screenshots of each AWS service configuration page, (2) Working application URL with successful form submission demonstration, (3) Architecture diagram showing data flow between S3, EC2, and RDS, (4) Completed troubleshooting log documenting any issues encountered and solutions applied. Rubric: Service configuration (40%), Working application (30%), Architecture understanding (20%), Problem-solving documentation (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates and detailed console navigation screenshots. Offer one-on-one assistance during RDS setup as this is often most challenging. Create checkpoint verification at each major step before proceeding. **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to implement additional features like Auto Scaling Groups, Application Load Balancer, or CloudFront CDN integration. Have them optimize costs by analyzing different instance types and storage classes.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2, RDS, and S3: Practical Workshop
description: Students will configure and deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS, implementing a static website frontend hosted on S3, an EC2 instance running a web server, and an RDS database. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical application of core AWS services in a real-world scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional three-tier web application by configuring EC2 instances, S3 buckets, and RDS databases with proper security groups
Students will implement AWS best practices for web hosting through hands-on configuration of load balancing, security groups, and database connectivity
instructions: **Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access and a simple HTML/PHP contact form template. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-frontend-[studentname]' and enable static website hosting. Upload provided HTML files and configure bucket policy for public read access. Test accessibility via S3 website endpoint. **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Launch an EC2 t2.micro instance with Amazon Linux 2, install Apache and PHP using yum commands. Create security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. Configure Apache to serve dynamic content and test with a simple PHP info page. **Step 3 (15 minutes):** Create RDS MySQL database instance (db.t3.micro) in the same VPC as EC2. Configure security group to allow MySQL traffic (port 3306) only from EC2 security group. Create database schema with a simple 'contacts' table using provided SQL script. **Step 4 (10 minutes):** Modify PHP application on EC2 to connect to RDS database using provided connection code. Test form submission from S3 frontend to EC2 backend, ensuring data is stored in RDS. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Document the complete architecture with screenshots showing each service configuration and test the end-to-end functionality by submitting a contact form entry and verifying database storage.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts for each student
Pre-built HTML contact form template with CSS
PHP backend code template with database connection functions
SQL script for creating contacts table schema
Architecture diagram template for documentation
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment report including: (1) Screenshots of each AWS service configuration (S3 bucket policy, EC2 security groups, RDS instance details) - 40 points, (2) Functional testing evidence showing form submission and database entry verification - 40 points, (3) Completed architecture diagram with proper service connections labeled - 20 points. Success requires all three tiers communicating properly with at least one successful end-to-end transaction documented.
scaffolding_notes: **Struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step CLI commands for database connection testing. Offer troubleshooting checklist for common connectivity issues. **Advanced learners:** Challenge them to add CloudFront distribution for S3 content, implement SSL certificates, or create an Application Load Balancer for multiple EC2 instances. Encourage exploration of CloudFormation templates to automate the deployment process.
original_title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2, RDS, and S3

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Alternative Approaches for Critical Project Risks
description: Students will analyze a real-world project scenario with multiple identified risks and systematically evaluate different risk response strategies. They will deconstruct the effectiveness of various approaches and determine optimal risk response combinations based on project constraints and organizational priorities.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of different risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) by comparing their impact on project objectives within given constraints
Students will differentiate between appropriate risk response combinations through systematic evaluation of cost-benefit trade-offs and resource allocation scenarios
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'TechFlow ERP Implementation' case study packet containing 8 identified project risks with probability/impact ratings and project constraints (45-day timeline, $2.3M budget, 15-person team). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team to analyze risks #1-4 or #5-8. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams read their assigned risks and complete the Risk Response Options Matrix, listing all four possible response strategies for each risk with estimated costs and implementation timeframes.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the provided Decision Criteria Framework, teams analyze each response option against five factors: cost impact, schedule impact, resource requirements, residual risk level, and alignment with organizational risk tolerance. Teams score each option 1-5 on each criterion.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Teams calculate weighted scores using the provided formula and rank response strategies. They must justify eliminating at least one option per risk based on analysis results.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams create their Risk Response Plan Summary, selecting optimal strategies and identifying three potential strategy combinations. They must analyze interdependencies between their assigned risks and explain how their chosen responses affect overall project risk exposure.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Teams present their top-ranked response combination to the class in 3-minute presentations, focusing on their analytical rationale and trade-off justifications.

Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing team approaches and highlighting key analytical insights about risk response strategy selection.
materials_needed: TechFlow ERP Implementation case study packet (8 pages per student)
Risk Response Options Matrix template (1 per student)
Decision Criteria Framework scoring sheet (1 per student)
Risk Response Plan Summary template (1 per team)
Calculators or laptops for weighted scoring calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Options Matrix for thoroughness (25 points), Decision Criteria Framework scoring accuracy and justification quality (35 points), Risk Response Plan Summary strategic reasoning and interdependency analysis (25 points), and presentation clarity of analytical rationale (15 points). Total: 100 points. Success criteria: 80+ points demonstrates proficient analysis skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed matrix examples and decision criteria definitions sheet. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add secondary risk analysis requirement and challenge them to propose hybrid response strategies not listed in standard options. Encourage quantitative risk modeling using Monte Carlo concepts.

title: Comprehensive GA4 Implementation Audit and Strategic Recommendation Report
description: Students will conduct a thorough audit of an existing Google Analytics 4 implementation for a real or simulated e-commerce website, identifying critical gaps, data quality issues, and configuration errors. They will then develop and justify strategic recommendations for optimization based on business objectives and industry best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of GA4 tracking implementation by conducting systematic audits of measurement strategy, event configuration, and data collection accuracy
Students will critique existing analytics setups through comparative analysis against industry benchmarks and recommend prioritized improvements with supporting rationale
instructions: Begin by providing students with access to a GA4 property (demo account or controlled client data) and accompanying business context document outlining company goals, KPIs, and current challenges (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to conduct Phase 1: Technical Audit (60 minutes) - systematically review Enhanced Ecommerce setup, custom event implementation, conversion tracking accuracy, audience definitions, and data stream configuration using the provided audit checklist. They must document 10+ specific findings with screenshots and severity ratings. Phase 2: Strategic Analysis (45 minutes) - students compare current setup against 3 competitor benchmarks (provided), identify gaps in funnel tracking, assess attribution model effectiveness, and evaluate custom dimension usage. Phase 3: Business Impact Assessment (30 minutes) - calculate potential revenue impact of identified issues using provided formulas, prioritize fixes based on implementation effort vs. business value matrix. Phase 4: Recommendation Development (60 minutes) - create detailed action plan with 5 prioritized recommendations, each including implementation steps, resource requirements, success metrics, and timeline. Final Phase: Peer Review (30 minutes) - students exchange reports and provide structured feedback using evaluation criteria, defending their recommendations in 5-minute presentations to simulate client delivery scenarios.
materials_needed: Access to GA4 demo property with e-commerce data spanning 6 months
Business context document with company background, goals, and current KPIs
Technical audit checklist with 25 evaluation criteria
Industry benchmark data for 3 competitor comparison
Revenue impact calculation worksheet with formulas
Recommendation report template with required sections
assessment_method: Grade using detailed rubric: Technical Audit Accuracy (25 points) - correct identification and documentation of implementation issues; Strategic Analysis Depth (25 points) - quality of competitive analysis and gap identification; Business Justification (25 points) - sound reasoning linking technical issues to business impact with quantified estimates; Recommendation Quality (25 points) - feasibility, prioritization logic, and implementation specificity of proposed solutions. Students must achieve 80+ points and successfully defend 2 recommendations during peer review to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided audit walkthroughs for first 2-3 checklist items and offering simplified revenue impact templates. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by requiring custom SQL queries in BigQuery to validate data accuracy, or have them create custom dashboard mockups showing improved reporting capabilities post-implementation.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure spanning three geographically distributed sites with MPLS connectivity, implementing advanced routing protocols, security policies, and high availability features. This capstone activity integrates OSPF, BGP, VPN technologies, network security, and disaster recovery planning into a comprehensive network solution.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, BGP, and MPLS technologies to create a scalable multi-site network architecture with redundant connectivity paths
Students will design comprehensive security policies integrating ASA firewalls, site-to-site VPNs, and access control lists to protect enterprise traffic flows
Students will develop network documentation including logical topology diagrams, IP addressing schemes, and disaster recovery procedures through technical documentation creation
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Architecture Design**
Students work in teams of 3-4 to design a network for fictional company 'TechCorp' with headquarters in New York (500 users), branch offices in Chicago (200 users) and Miami (150 users). Each team receives a requirements document specifying: minimum 99.9% uptime, secure inter-site communication, internet redundancy, and VOIP support. Teams create logical topology diagrams using Visio/Draw.io, design IP addressing using /22 networks for each site, plan OSPF areas (Area 0 backbone, Area 1-3 for sites), and document BGP AS numbers for MPLS provider connectivity.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Physical Implementation**

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: The Three-Body Problem in Astrophysical Contexts
description: Students analyze the complex gravitational interactions in a three-body system by examining the stability and motion patterns of the Jupiter-Sun-Trojan asteroid configuration. They will deconstruct the forces, energy considerations, and orbital mechanics to predict system behavior and identify critical parameters that determine stability.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the gravitational force vectors and net accelerations in a three-body system by calculating individual force components and determining resultant motion patterns
Students will evaluate the energy and momentum conservation principles through systematic examination of kinetic and potential energy changes in Lagrange point configurations
instructions:
Begin with 15 minutes of system setup: Provide each team of 3-4 students with the Jupiter-Sun-Trojan asteroid data package containing masses, initial positions, and velocities. Students designate roles: Force Analyst (calculates gravitational forces), Energy Tracker (monitors kinetic/potential energy), Motion Predictor (analyzes trajectories), and Systems Integrator (synthesizes findings). 

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Students analyze the initial configuration by calculating all pairwise gravitational forces using F = Gm₁m₂/r² for each body pair. The Force Analyst creates vector diagrams showing force directions and magnitudes on each object. Simultaneously, the Energy Tracker calculates initial total system energy using E = ½mv² - Gmm/r for all bodies. 

Phase 2 (40 minutes): Using provided orbital position data at 10-year intervals over 1000 years, students analyze system evolution. The Motion Predictor plots trajectories and identifies periodic vs. chaotic behavior regions. Teams examine how small perturbations in initial conditions affect long-term stability by comparing their baseline case with three provided variant scenarios (±1% mass changes, ±5% position shifts). 

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Students analyze the Lagrange point mechanism by examining why the L4 and L5 points create stable configurations. They deconstruct the balance between centripetal acceleration needs and gravitational force provision, identifying the critical 60-degree angular relationship. The Systems Integrator leads analysis of how gravitational forces from both massive bodies combine to provide exactly the centripetal force needed for circular motion. 

Conclude with 10-minute team presentations of key findings regarding stability criteria and force balance mechanisms.
materials_needed: Jupiter-Sun-Trojan asteroid data package with masses (MJ = 1.898×10²⁷ kg, MS = 1.989×10³⁰ kg, MA = 1.0×10¹⁵ kg), positions, and velocities
Orbital trajectory datasets showing 1000-year evolution with 10-year time steps
Scientific calculators or computational software (Python/MATLAB access preferred)
Vector plotting materials (graph paper, rulers, protractors) or graphing software
Three variant scenario datasets with perturbed initial conditions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of force calculations and vector analysis (25%), (2) Correct application of energy conservation principles with quantitative analysis (25%), (3) Quality of stability analysis including identification of critical parameters (25%), (4) Synthesis of findings into coherent explanation of three-body dynamics (25%). Deliverables include completed calculation worksheets, trajectory analysis graphs, and 5-minute team presentation explaining system behavior and stability mechanisms.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing force calculation templates with partially completed examples and step-by-step energy calculation guides. Offer intermediate checkpoints where teams verify calculations before proceeding. For advanced learners, extend analysis to examine resonance phenomena, provide additional perturbation scenarios to analyze, or challenge them to predict the behavior of unstable Lagrange points (L1, L2, L3). Consider providing access to numerical integration tools for students ready to explore computational approaches.

title: Code Quality Detective: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions
description: Students will analyze and evaluate three different Python functions that solve the same problem, comparing their code quality, readability, and efficiency. They will create a comprehensive evaluation report ranking the functions and justifying their choices using established coding standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different Python function implementations by comparing code readability, efficiency, and adherence to best practices
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic analysis using a provided evaluation framework
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three Python functions (Function A, B, and C) that all calculate the area of a rectangle, but with different coding styles - one well-written with clear variable names and comments, one with poor naming conventions, and one that works but is inefficient. Display these on individual handouts or slides.

**Individual Analysis Phase (15 minutes):** Students work alone to examine each function using the provided evaluation checklist covering: variable naming clarity, code comments, function structure, efficiency, and readability. They take notes on strengths and weaknesses of each function.

**Collaborative Discussion (10 minutes):** In pairs, students share their initial findings and discuss any differences in their evaluations. They must reach consensus on at least two major points for each function.

**Evaluation Report Creation (20 minutes):** Students individually create a written evaluation report that: (1) ranks the three functions from best to worst, (2) provides three specific reasons for their ranking with code examples, (3) suggests two concrete improvements for the lowest-ranked function, and (4) explains which function they would recommend for a beginner programmer and why.

**Peer Review Round (8 minutes):** Students exchange reports with a different partner and provide feedback using a simple checklist: Are rankings clearly justified? Are suggestions specific and actionable? Is the reasoning logical?

**Wrap-up Reflection (2 minutes):** Students write one sentence about what they learned about evaluating code quality that they didn't know before the activity.
materials_needed: Three printed Python function examples (one page per student)
Code evaluation checklist handout
Peer review feedback checklist
Writing materials (paper/digital document)
assessment_method: Evaluate student reports using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate ranking with logical justification (25%), (2) Specific evidence from code examples cited (25%), (3) Practical improvement suggestions provided (25%), (4) Clear recommendation with reasoning for beginner programmers (25%). Success = 3+ points total with at least 2 points in justification category.

title: Code Quality Detective: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions: Practical Workshop
description: Students will analyze and critique three versions of a simple calculator function, comparing their code quality, readability, and efficiency. They will justify their rankings and provide specific improvement recommendations for each version.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of Python functions by comparing code readability, efficiency, and best practices adherence
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic analysis using established coding standards and justify their assessments with specific evidence
instructions: Begin by distributing the three calculator function versions to students (15 minutes setup). Display the evaluation criteria on the board: readability (variable names, comments, structure), functionality (correctness, edge cases), efficiency (unnecessary operations, code length), and best practices (PEP 8 compliance, error handling). Students work individually for 25 minutes to test each function using the provided test cases, then complete the evaluation worksheet ranking the functions from best to worst. Next, organize students into groups of 3-4 for 20 minutes to compare their individual evaluations and reach a group consensus. Each group creates a poster showing their final rankings with supporting evidence. During the final 15 minutes, groups present their top-ranked function choice in a gallery walk format, defending their selection when questioned by peers. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing the different group conclusions and identifying common evaluation criteria that emerged across all groups.

assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of function testing and identification of issues (25%), (2) Quality of justifications with specific code examples (35%), (3) Appropriateness of improvement suggestions (25%), and (4) Participation in group discussion and peer feedback (15%). instructions:

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula and Calculation Sequence Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete mathematical formulas, calculation sequences, and terminology used in Critical Path Method analysis. This intensive recall activity focuses on the precise steps for calculating Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Total Float values using forward and backward pass algorithms.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact mathematical formulas for ES, EF, LS, LF, and Total Float calculations by completing timed formula reproduction exercises
Students will memorize the sequential steps of forward pass and backward pass algorithms through structured repetition and verification activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet containing 15 core formulas (ES = max(EF of predecessors), EF = ES + Duration, etc.) and algorithmic steps. Students have 10 minutes to study silently. Remove reference sheets and conduct Phase 1: Formula Recall (15 minutes) - students individually write all 15 formulas from memory on provided template sheets with designated spaces for each formula type. Phase 2: Algorithm Sequence (10 minutes) - students list the 8-step forward pass sequence and 6-step backward pass sequence in correct chronological order. Phase 3: Terminology Match (10 minutes) - students complete a closed-book matching exercise connecting 20 CPM terms (critical path, slack time, project duration, etc.) to their precise definitions. Phase 4: Verification Round (10 minutes) - redistribute reference sheets for students to self-check their work, marking errors in red ink. Phase 5: Remediation (15 minutes) - students with accuracy below 85% repeat failed sections while others complete advanced terminology exercises with dependencies, leads, and lags. Conclude with immediate verbal spot-checks where instructor randomly calls on students to recite specific formulas or define terms.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheets (1 per student)
Formula Template Worksheets with labeled sections
Algorithm Sequence Recording Sheets
CPM Terminology Matching Worksheets (20 terms/definitions)
Red pens for self-correction
Timer or stopwatch
Advanced terminology extension worksheets
assessment_method: Success measured by accuracy percentages on three components: Formula Recall (85% minimum - 13/15 formulas correct), Algorithm Sequences (100% accuracy required for step order), and Terminology Matching (90% minimum - 18/20 correct matches). Students must achieve all three benchmarks to demonstrate mastery. Document individual scores and identify specific formulas/concepts requiring remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for formula sequences, allow color-coded formula categories, and offer extended study time with visual formula charts. For advanced learners: include complex scheduling formulas (Free Float, Independent Float), PERT probability calculations, and resource-constrained scheduling terminology. Consider pairing strong memorizers with those needing support during verification phase.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership Decision Frameworks Through Historical Case Analysis
description: Students analyze three distinct crisis leadership scenarios from different sectors (military, corporate, non-profit) to identify and compare the underlying decision-making frameworks used by leaders. They will create comprehensive framework maps showing how different leadership approaches influence crisis outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex crisis leadership decisions by identifying the specific decision-making frameworks, stakeholder considerations, and timing factors that influenced outcomes in real-world scenarios
Students will compare competing leadership philosophies through systematic examination of how different leaders approached similar crisis elements across diverse organizational contexts
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Assign each team one crisis scenario: the 2008 financial crisis (Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan Chase), Hurricane Katrina response (General Russel Honoré), and the 2010 Haiti earthquake response (Sean Penn's humanitarian leadership). Provide each team with a comprehensive case study packet containing timeline documents, decision logs, stakeholder communications, and outcome data.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct deep-dive analysis using the provided Crisis Leadership Analysis Template. They must identify: (1) the leader's core decision-making framework, (2) stakeholder prioritization strategies, (3) communication approaches during uncertainty, (4) resource allocation decisions, and (5) adaptation mechanisms when initial strategies failed. Teams document evidence from primary sources to support each identified element.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create visual framework maps using digital mapping tools, showing the interconnections between decision points, stakeholder impacts, and leadership principles. Each map must include specific timestamps, decision rationales, and measurable outcomes.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Structured cross-team analysis session where each team presents their framework map (10 minutes each) followed by facilitated comparison discussions. Teams identify patterns, contradictions, and unique approaches across the three leadership styles. The instructor guides analysis using probing questions about situational factors, organizational constraints, and leadership philosophy differences.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Individual reflection where students complete a structured comparison matrix, rating each leader's approach across five dimensions: stakeholder management, decision speed, communication clarity, resource optimization, and adaptability. Students must provide specific evidence and explain how contextual factors influenced their ratings.
materials_needed: Comprehensive case study packets for Jamie Dimon (2008 financial crisis), General Russel Honoré (Hurricane Katrina), and Sean Penn (Haiti earthquake response)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Template with guided prompts for framework identification
Digital mind-mapping software access (Lucidchart, Miro, or Concept)
Leadership Comparison Matrix worksheet with rating scales and evidence columns
Primary source document collections including meeting transcripts, public statements, and internal communications
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of framework identification with specific evidence citations, (2) Depth of stakeholder analysis showing understanding of competing priorities, (3) Quality of visual framework representation demonstrating clear connections, (4) Sophisticated comparison analysis revealing insights about leadership philosophy differences, (5) Individual reflection matrix showing nuanced understanding of situational leadership factors. Students must score 3/4 on at least four criteria to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key decision points in case studies and offer a partially completed framework template with some elements identified. Consider pairing weaker analytical students with stronger team members during Phase 1. For advanced learners: Add a sixth phase requiring students to synthesize elements from all three approaches into an original crisis leadership framework, with justification for why specific elements were selected from each leader's approach.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2
description: Students will deploy a simple three-tier web application (web server, application server, database) using AWS EC2 instances and configure security groups to control network access. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS concepts including instance types, security groups, and basic networking.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier application architecture by launching and configuring three separate EC2 instances with appropriate instance types
Students will implement security best practices through creating and applying custom security groups with specific inbound/outbound rules
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab credentials or sandbox account access. Ensure students can access the AWS Management Console and have basic familiarity with EC2 dashboard navigation.

**Activity Implementation (35 minutes):** Students work individually to complete the following sequence: 1) Launch three EC2 instances - one t2.micro for web tier (Amazon Linux 2), one t2.micro for application tier (Amazon Linux 2), and one t2.micro for database tier (Amazon Linux 2). 2) Create three custom security groups: 'WebTier-SG' allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) from anywhere, 'AppTier-SG' allowing port 8080 from WebTier-SG only and SSH from anywhere, 'DBTier-SG' allowing port 3306 from AppTier-SG only and SSH from anywhere. 3) Attach appropriate security groups to each instance and verify connectivity rules. 4) SSH into web tier instance and install Apache web server, configure basic HTML page displaying 'Web Tier Active'. 5) Document all instance IDs, security group configurations, and test connectivity between tiers using telnet commands.

**Validation Phase (10 minutes):** Students demonstrate working application by accessing web server via public IP, showing Apache default page, and explaining their security group configuration to instructor or peer.

Computer with web browser and SSH client capability
Provided architecture diagram showing three-tier application structure
Step-by-step checklist handout with port numbers and instance requirements
assessment_method: Students submit screenshot documentation showing: 1) EC2 dashboard with three running instances properly named and tagged, 2) Security groups configuration page showing all three custom security groups with correct rules, 3) Web browser displaying Apache page via public IP, 4) SSH terminal showing successful connection to web tier instance. Rubric awards 25 points each for proper instance deployment, security group configuration, service installation, and documentation completeness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and break activity into smaller 10-minute chunks with checkpoint validations. Consider pair programming approach. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional security measures like key pairs, add load balancer to web tier, or install actual application code (Node.js/PHP) on application tier with database connectivity testing.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a complete web application infrastructure by launching EC2 instances, configuring security groups, and setting up a load balancer. This hands-on activity applies fundamental AWS services to create a scalable, secure web hosting environment.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier web application by launching and configuring EC2 instances with proper security groups and networking
Students will implement high availability through creating and configuring an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic across multiple instances
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access credentials and the provided HTML/CSS sample website files. Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to EC2 Dashboard.

**Instance Deployment (25 minutes):** Students launch two t2.micro EC2 instances in different Availability Zones using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. During launch, they create a new key pair, configure a security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere, and add user data script to install Apache web server and deploy the sample website files.

**Application Configuration (20 minutes):** After instances reach 'running' state, students SSH into each instance to verify Apache installation and customize the default webpage with unique identifiers (Instance 1, Instance 2). They test individual instance access using public IP addresses in web browsers.

**Load Balancer Setup (25 minutes):** Students navigate to EC2 Load Balancers section and create an Application Load Balancer. They configure it to span both Availability Zones, create a target group for HTTP traffic, and register both EC2 instances as targets. Students configure health checks with 30-second intervals.

**Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Students access the load balancer DNS name multiple times, documenting that traffic distributes between instances. They simulate high availability by stopping one instance and confirming the application remains accessible through the load balancer.

**Documentation (10 minutes):** Students capture screenshots of their running infrastructure, record the load balancer URL, and complete a reflection worksheet documenting the architecture components and their interactions.

Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written user data scripts and step-by-step screenshot guides for each AWS console navigation.
