title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Approaches Across Project Scenarios
description: Students analyze three different project scenarios with identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will deconstruct each strategy to identify its components, compare approaches across scenarios, and determine which strategies align best with project constraints and objectives.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by breaking down their components (threat/opportunity type, response category, cost, timeline, and resource requirements) across multiple project contexts
Students will differentiate between risk response effectiveness through systematic comparison of strategy alignment with project constraints, stakeholder priorities, and organizational risk tolerance
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute three project scenario packets: Scenario A (Software implementation project with 6-month timeline), Scenario B (Construction project with weather dependencies), and Scenario C (New product launch with market uncertainties). Each scenario includes 4-5 identified risks with 2-3 proposed response strategies per risk. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each group receives all three scenarios. Students create analysis matrices with columns for: Risk Type, Response Category (Avoid/Mitigate/Transfer/Accept for threats; Exploit/Enhance/Share/Accept for opportunities), Resource Requirements, Cost Impact, Timeline Effect, and Stakeholder Impact. Groups systematically break down each proposed strategy, filling their matrices completely.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups compare strategies across scenarios using guided questions: Which response categories appear most frequently? How do project constraints influence strategy selection? Which strategies show similar patterns across different project types? Students identify 3 key patterns and 2 significant differences.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group selects one risk from each scenario and ranks the proposed response strategies from most to least effective. They must justify rankings using specific criteria: alignment with project objectives, feasibility given constraints, cost-benefit ratio, and stakeholder acceptance likelihood.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Groups present their top-ranked strategy from one scenario, explaining their analysis process and rationale. Other groups provide feedback on analysis completeness and reasoning quality.
materials_needed: Three detailed project scenario packets with risk registers and proposed response strategies
Risk Response Analysis Matrix templates (printed or digital)
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
PMBOK Guide 7th Edition risk management section reference sheets
Evaluation criteria checklist handouts
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis matrices for accuracy and completeness of strategy deconstruction (40 points). Assess comparison analysis for identification of meaningful patterns and differences across scenarios (30 points). Grade strategy rankings and justifications for use of appropriate evaluation criteria and logical reasoning (30 points). Use rubric with criteria: Thorough Analysis (identifies all strategy components), Accurate Comparison (finds valid patterns/differences), Sound Reasoning (justifies rankings with specific evidence).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed matrix examples and guided question prompts for each analysis phase. Offer one-on-one check-ins during Phase 1 to ensure understanding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional evaluation criteria beyond those provided, analyze potential secondary risks created by response strategies, or propose alternative response strategies with full justification.

Each scenario includes 4-5 identified risks with proposed response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept). Teams spend 45 minutes analyzing each scenario using the provided Risk Response Analysis Framework worksheet. For each risk, students must: 1) Identify the chosen response strategy type, 2) Assess strategy appropriateness using the five evaluation criteria (cost-effectiveness, timeline impact, resource availability, stakeholder acceptance, implementation feasibility), 3) Rate each criterion on a 1-5 scale with written justification, 4) Calculate weighted scores based on project priorities, and 5) Recommend alternative strategies where current approaches score below 3.0. During analysis, teams must document their reasoning and identify patterns across scenarios. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents findings for one scenario to the class, highlighting their most significant strategy recommendation change and explaining the analytical reasoning. Other teams provide peer feedback using the structured evaluation form, focusing on the logical consistency of the analysis and evidence quality supporting recommendations.
materials_needed: Three printed project scenario packets with risk registers
Risk Response Analysis Framework worksheets
Evaluation criteria reference sheets with scoring rubrics
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Peer evaluation feedback forms
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Analysis Framework worksheets using a 4-point rubric covering: analytical depth (25%), criterion application accuracy (25%), justification quality (25%), and recommendation feasibility (25%). Each criterion requires specific evidence citations and numerical scoring rationale. Presentations assessed on clarity of analytical process and peer feedback quality.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed example analysis for one risk scenario and highlight key evaluation phrases to use in justifications. Advanced learners can create their own weighting system for evaluation criteria and develop contingency response strategies for their recommended approaches.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Approaches Across Project Scenarios

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Approaches Across Project Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze three different project scenarios with identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will compare the appropriateness of different mitigation approaches and justify alternative strategies based on project constraints and risk characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of risk response strategies by examining their alignment with risk characteristics, project constraints, and organizational priorities
Students will differentiate between appropriate risk response strategies through systematic comparison of mitigation costs, implementation feasibility, and residual risk levels
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the three project scenario handouts: (1) Software implementation with tight deadline, (2) Construction project with weather dependencies, and (3) Product launch with market uncertainty. Each scenario includes 4-5 identified risks with proposed response strategies. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Groups analyze each scenario using the provided Risk Response Analysis Framework. For each risk, students must: identify the risk category (technical, external, organizational, project management), evaluate the proposed response strategy against the four standard responses (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept), assess cost-benefit ratio of the proposed response, and determine if the response aligns with project constraints (budget, timeline, scope). 

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Groups complete a comparative analysis matrix, ranking the effectiveness of each proposed response on a 1-5 scale across five criteria: cost efficiency, implementation speed, residual risk reduction, stakeholder impact, and resource requirements. Students must provide written justification for rankings below 3 or above 4.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): For any response strategies ranked below 3, groups develop alternative approaches and document: specific alternative strategy, implementation steps, resource requirements, expected outcomes, and rationale for why this approach better serves the project.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents their analysis for one scenario, focusing on their lowest-ranked response strategy and proposed alternative. Other groups provide feedback using the peer evaluation checklist provided.
materials_needed: Three printed project scenario handouts with identified risks and proposed responses
Risk Response Analysis Framework worksheet (one per student)
Comparative Analysis Matrix template (one per group)
Peer evaluation checklist
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Analysis Framework worksheets using 4-point rubric covering: accuracy of risk categorization (25%), quality of strategy evaluation against PMI standards (30%), thoroughness of comparative analysis with clear justifications (25%), and feasibility of proposed alternative strategies (20%). Groups must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed sample analysis for one risk scenario and highlight key decision points. Offer guiding questions like 'What project constraint most impacts this response?' For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge to calculate expected monetary value (EMV) for their alternative strategies and consider secondary risk impacts.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Approaches Across Project Scenarios

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Approaches Across Project Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students analyze three distinct project scenarios to compare and contrast the effectiveness of different risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept). They will deconstruct the decision-making rationale behind each strategy selection and evaluate the potential impact on project constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between risk characteristics and appropriate response strategies by examining the probability, impact, and cost factors in real project contexts
Students will compare the effectiveness of different risk response strategies through systematic evaluation of their implications on scope, schedule, budget, and quality
instructions: Begin by dividing the class into teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Distribute three project scenario packets: (1) Software development project with cybersecurity threats, (2) Construction project with weather-related delays, (3) Product launch with supplier reliability issues. Each scenario includes identified risks with probability/impact ratings, budget constraints, and timeline pressures. Teams spend 25 minutes analyzing each scenario using the provided Risk Response Analysis Matrix, identifying which response strategy was chosen and why. Next, teams spend 30 minutes comparing strategies across scenarios, looking for patterns in decision-making criteria. They must identify at least three factors that influenced strategy selection (e.g., risk tolerance, budget availability, timeline flexibility). Teams then prepare a 10-minute presentation analyzing one cross-scenario comparison, explaining why different strategies were optimal for similar risk types in different contexts. During presentations (30 minutes total), other teams use peer evaluation forms to assess the analysis quality. Conclude with a 15-minute debrief where teams share insights about the relationship between project constraints and risk response strategy selection.
materials_needed: Three printed project scenario packets with risk registers
Risk Response Analysis Matrix templates (one per student)
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Peer evaluation forms
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk response strategy identification (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of decision factors (35%), (3) Clear articulation of relationships between project constraints and strategy selection (25%), (4) Use of PMP terminology and concepts (15%). Students must demonstrate understanding of at least 3 decision criteria and correctly identify 80% of optimal strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example analysis for one scenario and highlight key decision factors. Offer sentence starters like 'This strategy was chosen because...' and 'The main difference between scenarios is...'. For advanced learners, add a fourth scenario with ambiguous optimal solutions or ask them to propose alternative strategies with cost-benefit justifications.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation for E-commerce Performance Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions. They will assess the strengths and limitations of each model and justify their recommendation with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-touch, last-touch, data-driven, time-decay) by analyzing conversion path data and ROI metrics across multiple marketing channels
Students will critique attribution model recommendations through systematic comparison of customer journey insights and their impact on marketing budget allocation decisions
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection (20 minutes)**
Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, social media, email, organic search, direct). Students will navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool and export conversion data for the same date range using four different attribution models: First-touch, Last-touch, Data-driven, and Time-decay. They must capture screenshots of the conversion values and channel performance for each model.

**Phase 2: Systematic Analysis (40 minutes)**
Students create a comparative analysis matrix documenting: (1) Total conversions credited to each channel under each model, (2) Revenue attribution differences, (3) Cost-per-acquisition variations, and (4) ROAS calculations for each channel-model combination. They will identify the top 3 performing channels under each attribution model and calculate percentage differences in budget allocation recommendations.

**Phase 3: Critical Evaluation (30 minutes)**
Using the Exploration tool, students will examine customer journey paths to identify patterns in multi-touch conversions. They must evaluate which attribution model best reflects actual customer behavior by analyzing: average time-to-conversion, typical number of touchpoints, and cross-channel interaction patterns. Students will document specific limitations of each model based on the business context.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (20 minutes)**
Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their choice of optimal attribution model for this specific business, including: quantitative justification with specific metrics, identification of model limitations, proposed budget reallocation percentages across channels, and expected impact on overall ROAS. They must address potential counterarguments to their recommendation.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Excel or Google Sheets for analysis matrix creation
Screen capture software or browser screenshot tools
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Calculator for ROAS and percentage calculations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Data Analysis Accuracy - correctly extracts and calculates attribution data across all four models (25%), (2) Critical Evaluation Depth - identifies specific strengths/weaknesses of each model with quantitative support (30%), (3) Strategic Justification - provides compelling business rationale for chosen model with budget impact projections (30%), (4) Counterargument Anticipation - addresses potential criticisms and model limitations proactively (15%). Minimum passing score: 3.0/4.0 overall with no category below 2.5/4.0.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-built analysis matrix template with example calculations for one channel, offer guided practice with Attribution model comparison tool navigation, and supply decision-making framework checklist. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate Conversion Path reports for deeper customer journey analysis, calculate statistical significance of attribution differences, or propose custom attribution model weightings based on business-specific factors.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Architecture with Advanced Security and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure spanning three geographically distributed sites with full redundancy, advanced security policies, and optimized traffic flow. This capstone activity integrates routing protocols, VLANs, security frameworks, and performance optimization to solve real-world networking challenges.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocols by designing an optimal inter-site connectivity solution that ensures sub-200ms latency and 99.9% uptime
Students will construct a comprehensive network security framework through implementing zone-based firewalls, VPN tunneling, and intrusion prevention systems across all network segments
instructions: **Phase 1: Architecture Design (45 minutes)** - Provide students with the scenario: TechCorp needs to connect headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and remote office (50 users) with specific requirements for guest networks, voice traffic prioritization, and secure inter-site communication. Students work in teams of 3-4 to create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes (must use /22 for HQ, /24 for manufacturing, /26 for remote), VLAN segmentation (minimum 5 VLANs per site), and redundant WAN connections. **Phase 2: Configuration Planning (30 minutes)** - Teams develop comprehensive configuration scripts for core switches, routers, and ASA firewalls. They must document OSPF area designs, QoS policies for voice traffic (guarantee 150kbps per phone), and access control lists restricting inter-VLAN communication. **Phase 3: Implementation (90 minutes)** - Students build their network in Packet Tracer, implementing all planned configurations. They must establish site-to-site IPSec VPN tunnels between all locations, configure HSRP for gateway redundancy, and implement port security on access switches. **Phase 4: Testing and Optimization (45 minutes)** - Teams conduct comprehensive testing including failover scenarios, traffic flow analysis, and security penetration testing. They must demonstrate network convergence under 30 seconds during link failures and show proper traffic segmentation between VLANs. **Phase 5: Documentation and Presentation (30 minutes)** - Students create executive summary reports highlighting design decisions, performance metrics, and security implementations, then present solutions to class for peer review.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.2 or newer installed on student computers
TechCorp network requirements specification document (provided template)
Cisco IOS command reference sheets
Network design templates with IP addressing worksheets
Access to Cisco DevNet for configuration examples
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 100-point rubric: Network Architecture Design (25 points - logical topology, appropriate device selection, scalability considerations), Configuration Implementation (35 points - syntax accuracy, security best practices, redundancy implementation), Performance Testing (20 points - meeting latency/uptime requirements, successful failover demonstration), Documentation Quality (20 points - technical accuracy, professional presentation, clear justification of design decisions). Peer evaluation component worth 10% of total grade for presentation feedback.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured templates for basic VLAN and routing setups, offer guided worksheets for IP subnetting calculations, pair with stronger technical partners. For advanced learners: Add requirements for IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate network automation using Python scripts, challenge them to optimize for specific applications like video conferencing or database replication. Instructor should circulate during implementation phase to provide real-time troubleshooting guidance and ensure teams stay on track.

title: Programming Language Syntax Memory Cards Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental syntax elements of Python programming language through a structured flashcard activity. They will practice identifying and reciting basic Python commands, operators, and keywords to build foundational programming vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recite 20 essential Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, etc.) by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recall correct Python syntax patterns for basic programming structures through repetitive matching exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 Python syntax elements on one side and their descriptions/uses on the other. Each student receives an identical set covering: keywords (if, else, elif, for, while, def, return, import, class, try), operators (==, !=, <=, >=, and, or, not), and symbols (:, [], {}, ()). 

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to study their cards, reading each syntax element aloud and its function. Encourage students to create mental associations or mnemonics for difficult items.

Phase 2 (15 minutes): Pair students for reciprocal testing. Partner A shows the syntax element side while Partner B must state its purpose and provide a simple example of usage. They alternate roles every 5 minutes, cycling through all 20 cards.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall session. Display syntax elements on projector for 3 seconds each. Students write down the function/purpose on their answer sheet. Cover all 20 items twice with different ordering.

Phase 4 (5 minutes): Self-assessment phase where students check their answers against the provided answer key and tally correct responses. Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) to demonstrate successful recall.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (one per student, 20 cards each)
Answer sheets for rapid-fire session
Answer key handout
Projector/display screen
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students complete a written recall quiz scoring 16/20 (80%) or higher on syntax identification. Assessment includes: correctly identifying the purpose of displayed Python keywords (10 points), matching operators to their functions (5 points), and recognizing proper use of Python symbols (5 points). Track individual progress through answer sheet collection and partner observation during pair work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce card set to 10 essential items (if, else, for, while, def, ==, !=, :, [], ()) and allow extended study time. Provide visual aids showing syntax in context. For advanced learners: Include additional syntax elements like lambda, yield, with statements, and challenge them to create example code snippets using multiple syntax elements together.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze a correlation heatmap of customer demographic and purchase behavior variables to understand relationships between features. They will practice identifying strong correlations, explaining their business implications, and distinguishing between correlation types in a realistic e-commerce dataset.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features by analyzing color-coded heatmap values and explaining their statistical meaning
Students will distinguish between positive, negative, and weak correlations through systematic examination of correlation matrix patterns
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-generated correlation heatmap of 12 customer variables (age, income, spending_score, purchase_frequency, cart_abandonment_rate, mobile_usage, email_opens, social_media_engagement, loyalty_program_member, average_order_value, product_reviews_written, customer_service_contacts) using a dataset of 5000 customers. Display the heatmap on screen and provide individual printed copies. 

Step 1 (8 minutes): Students work in pairs to examine the heatmap legend and identify the correlation scale (-1 to +1). Have them locate three pairs of variables with correlations above 0.7, three pairs between 0.3-0.6, and three pairs below 0.2. Students record these findings on the provided worksheet with actual correlation values.

Step 2 (12 minutes): Each pair selects one strong positive correlation (>0.6) and one strong negative correlation (<-0.4) from their findings. They must write a 2-3 sentence business interpretation for each relationship, explaining why this correlation might exist and what it suggests about customer behavior.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Pairs examine the diagonal of the heatmap and explain why all values equal 1.0. Then they identify which variables show the weakest overall correlations with other features and hypothesize why these variables might be more independent.

Step 4 (8 minutes): Conduct a class discussion where three pairs share their strongest correlation findings and business interpretations. Other students can agree, disagree, or build upon the explanations.

Step 5 (7 minutes): Individual reflection where each student writes one key insight about correlation interpretation and one question they still have about reading heatmaps.
materials_needed: Pre-generated correlation heatmap (color-printed, one per student)
Correlation interpretation worksheet with recording tables
Customer dataset variable definitions handout
Projector/screen for displaying heatmap
Colored pens/highlighters for marking correlations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 3-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation value identification and categorization (strong/weak/negative), (2) Quality of business interpretations showing understanding of variable relationships, (3) Correct explanation of heatmap features like diagonal values and color coding. Students must achieve 2/3 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation interpretation reference chart with examples (e.g., 0.8 = 'strong positive'). Start them with the most obvious correlations like age-income. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential spurious correlations and discuss when correlation might not imply business causation. Have them suggest additional variables that might strengthen the analysis.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Induction in Multi-Loop Circuit Systems with Variable Parameters
description: Students will systematically analyze complex electromagnetic induction scenarios involving multiple coupled loops with time-varying magnetic fields. They will decompose the system into component interactions, evaluate mutual inductance effects, and predict induced EMF patterns through mathematical modeling and experimental validation.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between changing magnetic flux and induced EMF in multi-loop systems by applying Faraday's law and Lenz's law to predict current directions and magnitudes
Students will examine the interdependence of mutual inductance, self-inductance, and geometric factors through systematic parameter variation and mathematical decomposition
instructions:
Begin with a 15-minute setup where students receive three circular conducting loops of different radii (5cm, 10cm, 15cm), positioned concentrically on a horizontal platform. Place a solenoid beneath the platform connected to an AC power supply with variable frequency (0.1-10 Hz) and amplitude controls. Students work in teams of 3-4, with each member assigned specific measurement responsibilities. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students measure and record baseline parameters - loop resistances using multimeters, exact positioning distances, and solenoid specifications. They calculate theoretical mutual inductance values using M = μ₀πr₁²r₂²/[2(r₁² + r₂² + d²)^(3/2)] for each loop pair.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Systematically vary solenoid frequency from 0.1 to 5 Hz in 0.5 Hz increments while maintaining constant amplitude. Students simultaneously measure induced voltages in all three loops using oscilloscopes, recording peak values, phase relationships, and waveform characteristics. They analyze how frequency affects coupling between loops.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Fix frequency at 2 Hz and vary the vertical distance between solenoid and loops from 2cm to 10cm in 1cm increments. Students analyze how geometric separation affects induced EMF magnitude and phase relationships between loops.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Students create detailed analytical models comparing experimental results with theoretical predictions. They identify discrepancies, propose explanations for deviations (resistance effects, non-ideal coupling, edge effects), and calculate percentage errors for each measurement condition.

Conclude with 10-minute team presentations where groups defend their analytical interpretations and proposed explanations for observed phenomena.
materials_needed: Three conducting loops (copper wire, 5cm, 10cm, 15cm diameter)
Variable frequency AC power supply (0.1-10 Hz, 0-12V output)
Solenoid coil (200 turns, 8cm diameter)
Three digital oscilloscopes with probe sets
Digital multimeters for resistance measurements
Adjustable platform system with centimeter markings
Scientific calculators
Data recording sheets with pre-formatted tables
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point analytical rubric: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations and experimental measurements (25%), (2) Quality of systematic parameter analysis and identification of variable relationships (30%), (3) Depth of explanation for discrepancies between theory and experiment, including proposed physical mechanisms (30%), (4) Clarity and technical accuracy of final analytical presentation (15%). Students must achieve minimum 75% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate clear understanding of mutual inductance effects to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated mutual inductance values and focus on experimental measurement techniques and pattern recognition rather than complex calculations. Offer guided question prompts like 'How does doubling the distance affect the induced voltage?' For advanced learners: Extend analysis to include self-inductance calculations, energy transfer efficiency between loops, and modeling of realistic circuit elements (capacitance, non-linear effects). Challenge them to predict optimal geometric configurations for maximum power transfer.

title: Code Review and Quality Assessment of Simple Calculator Functions
description: Students will evaluate and critique three different implementations of basic calculator functions (add, subtract, multiply, divide) by assessing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will rank the implementations and justify their evaluations using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by analyzing three calculator function implementations against established programming standards
Students will critique different programming approaches through systematic comparison using a structured rubric
instructions: Begin by distributing three printed code samples of calculator functions to each student - Implementation A (clean, well-commented code with error handling), Implementation B (functional but messy code with poor variable names), and Implementation C (overly complex code with unnecessary features). Give students 10 minutes to individually read through all three implementations without discussion. Next, provide the Code Quality Assessment Rubric covering: readability (variable names, comments, formatting), functionality (correctness, edge case handling), efficiency (unnecessary complexity, performance), and maintainability (code structure, reusability). Students spend 20 minutes individually scoring each implementation on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, writing specific justifications for their scores. Form pairs and allow 15 minutes for students to discuss their evaluations and reach consensus on rankings. Each pair creates a one-page summary ranking the three implementations from best to worst, including: overall scores for each implementation, top 3 strengths and weaknesses identified, specific code examples supporting their evaluation, and recommendations for improving the lowest-ranked implementation. Conclude with 10 minutes of whole-class discussion where pairs share their rankings and reasoning, focusing on differences in evaluation criteria prioritization.
materials_needed: Three printed code samples of calculator implementations (different quality levels)
Code Quality Assessment Rubric handouts
Blank evaluation sheets for scoring
Computers or tablets for reference (optional)
assessment_method: Grade the written evaluation summary using a 4-point rubric: (4) Thorough analysis with specific examples and clear justification for rankings; (3) Good analysis with some specific examples and mostly clear reasoning; (2) Basic analysis with limited examples and unclear reasoning; (1) Incomplete analysis with no supporting examples. Observe pair discussions for evidence of evaluation thinking and use of technical terminology.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by highlighting specific lines of code during individual review time and providing sentence starters like 'This code is better because...' Advanced learners can be challenged to suggest specific code refactoring solutions and estimate time required for improvements.

title: Design a Predictive Dashboard for Employee Retention Using Multi-Source Data
description: Students will synthesize HR data, employee surveys, and performance metrics to create an interactive dashboard that predicts employee turnover risk. They will design custom visualizations, develop predictive models, and present actionable insights to stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive predictive analytics dashboard by integrating multiple data sources and applying statistical modeling techniques
Students will synthesize complex HR datasets through custom visualization design and stakeholder-focused narrative development
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Integration (45 minutes)** Provide students with three CSV files: employee_demographics.csv (age, department, tenure), survey_responses.csv (job satisfaction scores, work-life balance ratings), and performance_data.csv (quarterly reviews, promotion history). Students work in teams of 3-4 to clean and merge datasets using Python/Pandas or Excel Power Query. Each team must identify at least 5 data quality issues and document their cleaning decisions. **Phase 2: Exploratory Analysis & Hypothesis Formation (60 minutes)** Teams conduct exploratory data analysis to identify patterns related to employee turnover. They must create at least 3 preliminary visualizations using matplotlib/seaborn or Tableau and formulate 2-3 testable hypotheses about turnover predictors. **Phase 3: Predictive Model Development (75 minutes)** Using their hypotheses, teams build a logistic regression or decision tree model to predict turnover probability. They must split data 70/30 for training/testing, calculate model accuracy, and identify top 3 predictive factors. **Phase 4: Dashboard Creation (90 minutes)** Teams design an interactive dashboard using Tableau, Power BI, or Python Dash containing: risk score by department, individual employee risk ratings, trend analysis over time, and key performance indicators. Dashboard must include filters for department and risk level. **Phase 5: Stakeholder Presentation (30 minutes)** Each team presents their dashboard to simulated HR executives, explaining methodology, insights, and 3 specific retention recommendations with projected impact.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with intentional data quality issues
Tableau/Power BI licenses or Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn
Laptop computers with data analysis software
Presentation projector and screen
Stakeholder role-play instruction sheets for peer evaluators
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Data integration quality and documentation (20 points), statistical model accuracy and interpretation (25 points), dashboard design and interactivity (25 points), insight quality and business relevance (20 points), presentation clarity and recommendations (10 points). Teams submit dashboard files, methodology documentation, and reflection on design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data dictionary templates, sample code snippets for common operations, and checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources (economic indicators, industry benchmarks), implement advanced algorithms (random forest, neural networks), or add predictive confidence intervals to their models.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall specific components, inputs, outputs, and tools from advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, Agile PMI hybrid models, and complex stakeholder management matrices. This high-stakes identification exercise requires precise recall of 150+ specific PM elements across multiple methodologies.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall and identify at least 85% of PRINCE2 processes, management products, and governance structures when presented with scenario-based prompts within 90 seconds per item
Students will memorize and reproduce specific risk assessment matrices, stakeholder influence grids, and earned value management formulas through rapid-fire identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the 150-item master checklist containing specific elements from PRINCE2 (7 processes, 26 management products, 7 principles), Agile-PMI hybrid frameworks (12 Agile practices integrated with PMI knowledge areas), and advanced stakeholder matrices (Power/Interest, Influence/Impact, Salience models). Students have 45 minutes to study materials using provided memory palace worksheets and mnemonic device templates. Next, implement the three-round testing protocol: Round 1 (15 minutes) - Flash card rapid identification where students view element names and must recall their exact definition, inputs, and primary use cases within 90 seconds per card. Round 2 (20 minutes) - Reverse identification where students see definitions/scenarios and must name the specific PM framework element, process, or tool. Round 3 (15 minutes) - Integration recall where students must list all components within a specific framework category (e.g., all PRINCE2 management products, all stakeholder assessment tools) from memory. Use the digital timer for each segment. Students work individually during testing phases but can form study pairs during the initial 45-minute memorization period. Instructors circulate with answer keys, marking correct/incorrect responses immediately. After each round, allow 5 minutes for students to review missed items before proceeding. Conclude with a 10-minute debrief where students identify which memorization techniques were most effective for different types of PM content.
materials_needed: 150-item PM framework component master list with definitions
Digital flashcard deck (Anki or Quizlet) with PRINCE2, Agile-PMI hybrid content
Memory palace worksheet templates
Mnemonic device reference guide for PM terminology
Digital countdown timers (one per student group)
Laminated answer keys for instructors
Stakeholder matrix blank templates for recall exercises
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy across all three testing rounds (128+ correct out of 150 total items). Track performance using the provided scoring matrix: Round 1 worth 40 points, Round 2 worth 35 points, Round 3 worth 25 points. Award partial credit only for responses that include correct framework name and at least two accurate defining characteristics. Immediate feedback provided after each item. Students scoring below 85% must complete remedial memorization assignments before next class.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide color-coded framework maps, reduce initial item count to 100 core elements, allow additional 15 minutes study time, and pair with stronger memorization partner. For advanced learners: add 50 bonus items from emerging PM methodologies (SAFe, LeSS, Design Thinking integration), require explanation of inter-framework relationships, and challenge them to create original mnemonic devices for complex processes.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification Challenge: Exercise 1
description: Students will identify and recall specific components, processes, and artifacts from advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, Agile/Scrum, and PMI's PMBOK through a structured matching and labeling exercise. This activity focuses on precise recall of framework-specific terminology, deliverables, and process sequences.
learning_objectives: Students will identify specific components of PRINCE2, Agile/Scrum, and PMBOK frameworks by matching framework elements to their correct definitions within 90% accuracy
Students will recall the correct sequence of processes within each framework through chronological ordering exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing three color-coded card sets (blue for PRINCE2, green for Agile/Scrum, red for PMBOK) containing 45 cards total - 15 per framework. Each set includes process names, deliverable titles, role definitions, and key artifacts. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes to sort cards by framework without looking at references. Next, provide three large poster boards labeled with each framework name. Students must place cards under correct frameworks and arrange process cards in chronological order. For minutes 21-35, students use the 'Framework Quick Reference Sheets' to verify their placements and make corrections. During minutes 36-45, conduct a gallery walk where students rotate between poster boards, checking others' work and noting discrepancies on provided sticky notes. In the final 10 minutes, facilitate a whole-class discussion to resolve conflicts and confirm correct answers. Students must achieve 90% accuracy in framework identification and 80% accuracy in process sequencing. Record individual scores on the tracking sheet as students complete each section. Emphasize that this is pure recall - no analysis or evaluation is required, only accurate identification and sequencing of memorized framework components.
materials_needed: 135 laminated framework component cards (45 per student set of 3)
Framework Quick Reference Sheets (PMI PMBOK 7th edition, PRINCE2 2017, Scrum Guide 2020)
3 large poster boards per group
Colored sticky notes for corrections
Individual tracking sheets
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Individual scoring based on: Framework identification accuracy (45 points - 1 point per correctly placed card), Process sequencing accuracy (30 points - 2 points per correctly ordered process sequence), Speed bonus (5 points for completion within time limits). Success criteria: minimum 72/80 points (90% framework identification, 80% sequencing). Use provided answer key for immediate verification during gallery walk phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework overview diagrams as visual aids and allow use of color-coding hints on card backs. Pair with stronger students during verification phase. For advanced learners: Add integration cards requiring identification of cross-framework connections and common elements. Include bonus cards with advanced artifacts like risk registers, RACI matrices, and earned value calculations.
original_title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification Challenge

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification Challenge: Written Report
description: Students will systematically identify and recall specific components, artifacts, and terminology from advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, PMI-PMP processes, and Agile/Scrum methodologies. This activity tests precise memorization of framework elements through a structured matching and categorization exercise.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall and identify specific artifacts, roles, and processes from PRINCE2, PMI-PMP, and Agile frameworks by matching terminology to correct framework categories
Students will demonstrate memorization of advanced project management terminology through rapid-fire identification exercises using standardized framework documentation
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared card sets and framework reference sheets to each student (5 minutes setup). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to sort 60 terminology cards into three categories: PRINCE2, PMI-PMP Knowledge Areas, and Scrum/Agile. Cards include specific terms like 'Managing Product Delivery', 'Project Integration Management', 'Definition of Done', 'Business Case', 'Stakeholder Register', and 'Sprint Retrospective'. Students must place each card in the correct framework pile without consulting references. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Using the digital quiz platform, students complete a timed matching exercise where they connect specific project artifacts to their exact framework origins. For example, matching 'Risk Theme' to PRINCE2, 'Burndown Chart' to Scrum, or 'Communications Management Plan' to PMI-PMP. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students participate in a structured recall exercise where they view framework process diagrams with key components blanked out and must fill in missing elements from memory. This includes PRINCE2's seven processes, PMI's five process groups, and Scrum's three roles. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire oral verification where instructor randomly calls on students to define specific advanced terms like 'Tolerance', 'Velocity', 'Work Breakdown Structure', or 'Product Description' and identify their framework association. Record accuracy rates for each student on the provided tracking sheet.
materials_needed: 60 pre-printed terminology cards covering PRINCE2, PMI-PMP, and Scrum frameworks
Digital quiz platform access (Kahoot or Quizizz with pre-loaded questions)
Framework process diagrams with blank components (3 different diagrams per student)
Student tracking sheets for accuracy recording
Timer for each phase
Answer keys for immediate verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy across all four phases to demonstrate mastery. Phase 1: 48/60 cards correctly categorized. Phase 2: 16/20 digital matches correct. Phase 3: 21/25 diagram components accurately recalled. Phase 4: Correctly define and categorize 8/10 randomly selected terms. Provide immediate feedback using answer keys and record individual scores on tracking sheets for progress monitoring.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework summary sheets during Phase 1 only, reduce card sorting to 40 terms focusing on most essential concepts, allow 5 extra minutes per phase. For advanced learners: Add integration challenge requiring explanation of how components work together across frameworks, include hybrid methodology terminology (SAFe, PRINCE2 Agile), require students to identify contradictions or overlaps between framework approaches.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification Challenge: Exercise 3
description: Students will identify and recall specific components, processes, and artifacts from multiple advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, and SAFe. They will demonstrate memorization of framework-specific terminology, roles, and process flows through a comprehensive matching and labeling exercise.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall specific roles, artifacts, and processes from PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, and SAFe frameworks by completing framework component identification tasks
Students will demonstrate memorization of advanced project management terminology through precise matching of definitions to framework-specific concepts
instructions: Begin by distributing three framework reference sheets face-down to each student (5 minutes setup). Students have 10 minutes to review all materials simultaneously. Remove reference sheets and distribute the assessment packet containing: (1) 45 framework component cards with terms like 'Release Train Engineer,' 'Product Backlog Refinement,' 'Managing Product Delivery Process,' without framework labels; (2) Three framework sorting mats labeled PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, and SAFe; (3) Process flow diagrams with 15 blank labels each for the three frameworks. Students work individually for 25 minutes to: sort component cards into correct framework categories, complete process flow diagrams by writing specific process names in sequence order, and match 30 role definitions to exact role titles. In the final 10 minutes, students complete a rapid-fire terminology quiz where they write the framework origin for 20 displayed terms (e.g., 'Epic' - answer: SAFe). Instructor circulates to ensure students are not discussing answers and maintains strict individual work environment. Collect all materials simultaneously at the 50-minute mark.
materials_needed: 45 laminated framework component cards (15 per framework)
Three color-coded framework sorting mats per student
Process flow diagram worksheets (3 per student with 15 blanks each)
30-item role definition matching worksheet
20-question rapid-fire terminology quiz sheet
Framework reference sheets (PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, SAFe summary guides)
assessment_method: Scoring: Component card sorting (45 points, 1 point each), Process flow completion (45 points, 1 point per correct sequence placement), Role matching (30 points, 1 point each), Terminology quiz (20 points, 1 point each). Total: 140 points. Success criteria: 126+ points (90%) demonstrates mastery recall, 112-125 points (80-89%) shows adequate recall, below 112 points requires remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded reference cards during review phase and allow 5 additional minutes. Create memory aids using framework acronyms. For advanced learners: Add integration questions requiring recall of how frameworks complement each other, include lesser-known framework components like PRINCE2's 'Exception Assessment' or SAFe's 'Weighted Shortest Job First' prioritization.

title: Analyzing Leadership Communication Patterns in Crisis Management Case Studies
description: Students will examine authentic crisis leadership scenarios to identify and categorize different communication patterns, decision-making frameworks, and stakeholder engagement strategies. They will demonstrate understanding by mapping how different leadership approaches impact organizational outcomes during high-pressure situations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between leadership communication styles and organizational crisis outcomes by examining three distinct real-world case studies
Students will categorize stakeholder engagement strategies and explain their effectiveness through comparative analysis of leadership decision-making processes
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute three crisis leadership case studies: Tylenol cyanide crisis (Johnson & Johnson, 1982), Southwest Airlines Flight 1380 emergency (2018), and Zoom's privacy crisis response (2020). Each group receives all three cases plus the Leadership Communication Analysis Framework worksheet. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Groups conduct detailed analysis of each case using the provided framework. They must identify: communication timing and channels, stakeholder prioritization decisions, transparency levels, emotional intelligence indicators, and decision-making speed. Students complete structured worksheets for each case, noting specific quotes, actions, and outcomes.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups create comparative analysis charts mapping leadership behaviors against outcomes. They identify patterns across cases, noting which communication approaches correlated with positive vs. negative results. Groups must categorize each leader's approach using established frameworks (transformational, authentic, situational leadership).

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Each group presents one key insight about leadership communication patterns, supported by specific evidence from their analysis. Other groups ask clarifying questions and note additional observations. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting findings to broader leadership theory.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Individual reflection where students write a 300-word synthesis explaining which leadership communication pattern they found most effective and why, referencing specific evidence from all three cases.
materials_needed: Three printed crisis leadership case study packets (Tylenol, Southwest Airlines, Zoom)
Leadership Communication Analysis Framework worksheets
Large poster paper and markers for comparative charts
Digital timer for phase management
Individual reflection worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership behavior identification in case studies (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of patterns (30%), (3) Use of specific evidence to support categorizations (25%), (4) Individual synthesis demonstrating comprehension of effective crisis communication principles (20%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in all categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide highlighted versions of case studies with key leadership moments pre-identified, and offer sentence starters for analysis worksheets. For advanced learners, add a fourth case study (your choice of recent crisis) and require them to predict likely outcomes based on identified patterns before revealing actual results. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who need support.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS using EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will apply core AWS services to deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture. They will configure EC2 instances for the web server, set up an RDS database for data storage, and use S3 for static content hosting while implementing proper security groups and networking.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration principles by launching and configuring web server instances with appropriate security groups and key pairs
Students will implement multi-service integration by connecting EC2 instances to RDS databases and S3 buckets through proper IAM roles and network configurations
instructions: **Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and the pre-built sample web application files (HTML, CSS, PHP connection scripts). Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to the desired region (us-east-1). **Step 1 - S3 Configuration (20 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-static-[studentname]' with public read access enabled. They upload provided CSS, JavaScript, and image files to the bucket, then configure static website hosting and test access via the S3 endpoint URL. **Step 2 - RDS Database Setup (25 minutes):** Students launch a MySQL RDS instance (db.t3.micro) in the default VPC with the identifier 'webapp-database-[studentname]'. They configure the security group to allow inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from the default VPC CIDR block, set master username as 'admin', and record the endpoint URL. Using provided SQL scripts, they connect via MySQL Workbench or command line to create the required database tables. **Step 3 - EC2 Web Server Deployment (30 minutes):** Students launch an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) and configure a security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. After connecting via SSH, they install Apache and PHP using yum commands, then upload the web application files to /var/www/html/. Students modify the database configuration file with their RDS endpoint details and update static content URLs to point to their S3 bucket. **Step 4 - Integration Testing (15 minutes):** Students test the complete application by accessing the EC2 public IP address, verifying that the web page loads with S3-hosted static content and successfully connects to the RDS database by performing create/read operations through the web interface.
materials_needed: AWS account credentials for each student with appropriate IAM permissions
Pre-built sample web application package (HTML, PHP, CSS, JS files)
MySQL database schema and sample data SQL scripts
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
MySQL Workbench or command-line MySQL client
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots and URLs demonstrating: (1) Functional web application accessible via EC2 public IP (25 points), (2) Static content loading from S3 bucket with correct bucket policy configuration (25 points), (3) Database connectivity showing successful data retrieval and insertion through web interface (25 points), (4) Proper security group configurations for all services with principle of least privilege applied (25 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step command scripts for EC2 setup. Create checkpoint verification steps after each major component. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement Auto Scaling Groups, Application Load Balancer, or CloudFront CDN integration. Have them explore VPC creation with custom subnets instead of using default VPC.

title: Project Schedule Variance Analysis and Risk Assessment
description: Students will analyze a failing project's schedule performance data to identify root causes of delays and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed corrective actions. They will decompose schedule variance metrics, compare actual vs. planned performance, and assess the viability of recovery strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze schedule performance index (SPI) and schedule variance (SV) data by examining earned value management reports to identify critical path delays and resource allocation issues
Students will evaluate proposed corrective actions through systematic comparison of implementation costs, timeline impacts, and risk mitigation effectiveness
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Metro Rail Extension Project' case study packet containing: 18-month project timeline, monthly EVM reports showing SPI declining from 1.0 to 0.67, activity network diagram, and resource allocation charts. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Data Analysis (25 minutes):** Teams examine EVM data using the provided analysis worksheet. Students calculate cumulative SV for each reporting period, identify the month when SPI first dropped below 0.9, and map delayed activities to the critical path diagram. They must determine which work packages contribute most significantly to the 6-month delay and analyze resource utilization patterns.

**Phase 2 - Root Cause Investigation (20 minutes):** Using the fishbone diagram template, teams categorize delay causes into: scope changes, resource constraints, external dependencies, and technical challenges. They prioritize causes using impact/frequency matrices and identify interconnected issues.

**Phase 3 - Solution Evaluation (25 minutes):** Teams receive four proposed recovery strategies: fast-tracking, crashing, scope reduction, and resource reallocation. For each strategy, they complete evaluation matrices assessing: cost impact, schedule compression potential, quality risks, and stakeholder acceptance. Teams must rank strategies and justify their top recommendation.

**Phase 4 - Presentation Preparation (15 minutes):** Teams prepare 5-minute presentations summarizing their analysis findings, primary delay causes, and recommended recovery approach with supporting rationale.
materials_needed: Metro Rail Extension Project case study packet (18 pages per team)
EVM Analysis Worksheet templates
Fishbone diagram templates
Strategy Evaluation Matrix handouts
Calculators or laptops with Excel
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of SV/SPI calculations (25 points), correct identification of critical path impacts (25 points), logical root cause categorization with supporting evidence (25 points), and feasibility assessment of recovery strategies with clear ranking criteria (25 points). Teams must show all calculations and provide written justification for their final recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed SPI calculation examples for months 1-3 and a sample root cause analysis for one work package. Offer guiding questions like 'Which activities show the largest variance?' For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring Monte Carlo simulation assessment of recovery strategy success probability, or analysis of secondary schedule impacts on dependent projects.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, then defend their choice of optimal attribution strategy for a specific business scenario. They will analyze conversion path complexity, customer journey patterns, and revenue attribution across multiple touchpoints to make evidence-based strategic recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue attribution discrepancies across a 90-day period

Students will critique attribution model performance through systematic comparison of customer acquisition costs, ROAS calculations, and channel contribution analysis to defend an optimal attribution strategy
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 people) with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retailer. Teams spend the first 30 minutes exploring the Attribution section under Advertising workspace, familiarizing themselves with Model Comparison Tool and Conversion Paths reports. Next, assign each team a specific business scenario card (B2B SaaS with long sales cycles, fast-fashion e-commerce, or subscription box service) that defines their evaluation context, budget constraints, and strategic priorities. During the 45-minute analysis phase, teams must systematically compare all five attribution models by documenting: (1) total conversions and revenue attributed to each channel under each model, (2) percentage variance in attribution between first-click vs. data-driven models for top 5 channels, (3) average customer journey length and touchpoint frequency from Conversion Paths report, and (4) cost-per-acquisition changes when applying different models to their paid media spend data. Teams then spend 30 minutes calculating channel-specific ROAS under each attribution model and identifying which channels would receive budget increases/decreases under each approach. For the final 45-minute evaluation phase, teams must critique each attribution model's strengths and limitations within their assigned business context, considering factors like attribution window appropriateness, cross-device tracking capabilities, and alignment with actual customer behavior patterns. Teams conclude by defending their recommended attribution model through a structured argument that weighs statistical accuracy against actionable insights, supported by specific data points from their analysis.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with multi-channel e-commerce data (6+ months)
Business scenario cards with specific contexts and constraints
Attribution Model Comparison worksheet template
Access to Google Sheets or Excel for calculations
Conversion Path Analysis template
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Data Analysis Accuracy - correct extraction and calculation of attribution metrics across all models (25%), (2) Critical Evaluation Quality - depth of critique regarding each model's appropriateness for their business scenario (30%), (3) Strategic Justification - strength of evidence-based argument defending their recommended attribution approach (30%), and (4) Professional Presentation - clear communication of findings with supporting visualizations (15%). Teams must submit their completed analysis worksheet, calculated ROAS comparisons, and a 2-page strategic recommendation memo.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated channel cost data and a guided worksheet with specific GA4 report navigation steps. Create checkpoint moments at 30-minute intervals where teams can verify their data extraction accuracy. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate Google Ads attribution data and evaluate the impact of different attribution windows (30-day vs 90-day) on their recommendations. Provide additional complexity by asking them to consider data-driven attribution model limitations and propose custom attribution rules.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess each model's impact on marketing budget allocation decisions and defend their recommended attribution strategy through a comprehensive business case presentation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating ROI variations across marketing channels
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis and defend an optimal attribution model selection with quantitative evidence and business justification
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Setup (20 minutes)**
Provide students with access to a demo GA4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, social media, email, organic, display). Students must navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths and export conversion path data for purchases over $100. Next, access the Model comparison report under Attribution settings.

**Phase 2: Attribution Model Analysis (45 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to analyze five attribution models. For each model, they must: (1) Record total conversions and revenue attributed to each channel, (2) Calculate the percentage change in attribution compared to last-click model, (3) Identify which channels gain/lose credit under each model, (4) Calculate cost-per-acquisition for each channel under different models using provided advertising spend data ($10K search, $5K social, $3K display, $2K email).

**Phase 3: Critical Evaluation (30 minutes)**
Students complete an evaluation matrix rating each attribution model (1-5 scale) across criteria: accuracy for business model, alignment with customer journey length, impact on budget optimization, and implementation complexity. They must provide quantitative evidence from their analysis to support each rating.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (25 minutes)**
Each pair prepares a 5-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model. Presentation must include: current model limitations identified through data analysis, projected budget reallocation percentages by channel, expected ROI impact (with calculations), and implementation timeline with potential challenges. Other students act as CMO stakeholders, asking challenging questions about methodology and business implications.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with Enhanced Ecommerce enabled
Sample advertising spend data spreadsheet by channel
Attribution model evaluation matrix template
Access to Google Slides or PowerPoint for presentations
Calculators or Excel for ROI calculations
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across: (1) Technical accuracy of attribution analysis and calculations, (2) Quality of critical evaluation with supporting evidence, (3) Strength of business case and strategic reasoning, (4) Defense of recommendations during Q&A with specific responses to stakeholder concerns. Final deliverable includes completed evaluation matrix, budget reallocation proposal with ROI projections, and peer evaluation of presentation defense.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model comparison cheat sheet explaining when each model is most effective, and offer guided calculation templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate Customer Lifetime Value calculations into their ROI analysis and consider seasonality impacts on attribution effectiveness. Encourage exploration of custom attribution models using GA4's data-driven attribution insights.

Students will critique attribution model limitations and justify strategic recommendations through comprehensive performance analysis using Google Analytics Model Comparison Tool and Conversion Path reports
instructions: Begin by providing students with three Google Analytics demo accounts representing different business types: B2B SaaS (long sales cycle), fast-fashion e-commerce (short cycle), and subscription service (mixed cycle). Students work in teams of 3-4. Step 1 (20 min): Each team accesses Conversions > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool in all three accounts, setting a 90-day lookback window and comparing all five attribution models against the same conversion goal. Step 2 (25 min): Teams extract data for top 10 traffic sources, documenting conversion credits assigned by each model, and calculate percentage differences between models. materials_needed: Three Google Analytics demo accounts with different business models and sufficient historical data
Attribution Model Evaluation Matrix template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Peer evaluation rubric sheets

scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled partial evaluation matrices with example calculations and guided questions for each analysis step. They will assess which attribution model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and make data-driven recommendations for budget reallocation across channels.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business impact of first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models by analyzing multi-channel funnel reports and conversion paths
Students will critique existing marketing channel performance assumptions through comparative attribution analysis and formulate strategic budget redistribution recommendations
instructions:

Students create a comprehensive spreadsheet documenting: conversion values, conversion counts, and cost-per-acquisition for each channel under each model. They then analyze Top Conversion Paths and Assisted Conversions reports to understand customer journey complexity.

They must identify which channels are over/under-credited in last-click attribution, assess the statistical significance of data-driven model recommendations, and examine conversion path length and time lag data to determine model appropriateness for the business type.

**Phase 3 - Strategic Evaluation (25 minutes):** Students create a detailed written evaluation comparing current budget allocation (assumed based on last-click attribution) against optimal allocation suggested by their chosen attribution model. They must justify their selected attribution model using specific data points, calculate potential ROI improvements, identify potential risks of reallocation, and provide implementation timeline recommendations. Final deliverable includes executive summary with specific budget shift percentages and expected performance improvements.
