description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine optimal customer journey analysis approaches. They will assess the business impact of each model and develop strategic recommendations for marketing budget allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of first-touch, last-touch, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue attribution differences
Students will critique attribution model limitations and justify strategic marketing budget recommendations through comprehensive analysis of multi-channel funnel data
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection Setup (20 minutes)**
Students access a provided GA4 property with 6+ months of e-commerce data. Navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution to access Model Comparison tool. Export conversion path data for the same date range using each attribution model: first-touch, last-touch, linear, time-decay, and data-driven. Create a spreadsheet template with columns for Channel, First-Touch Revenue, Last-Touch Revenue, Linear Revenue, Time-Decay Revenue, Data-Driven Revenue, and Variance Analysis.

**Phase 2: Quantitative Analysis (45 minutes)**
Populate the spreadsheet with revenue attribution data from each model. Calculate percentage differences between models for each channel. Identify channels showing highest variance between attribution models (>30% difference). Analyze conversion paths longer than 3 touchpoints to understand customer journey complexity. Document which channels appear undervalued/overvalued in first-touch vs. last-touch models.

**Phase 3: Qualitative Assessment (35 minutes)**
Evaluate each model's alignment with business goals using provided company scenarios (B2B long sales cycle, B2C impulse purchases, etc.). Assess data-driven model reliability by examining confidence intervals and sample size requirements. Identify attribution model blind spots, such as view-through conversions, cross-device tracking limitations, and offline touchpoint exclusion.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation Development (40 minutes)**
Produce a 2-page executive summary recommending optimal attribution model(s) with supporting evidence. Include specific budget reallocation percentages for top 5 channels based on chosen model. Address implementation challenges and propose solutions for identified attribution gaps. Present findings in 5-minute presentations with peer Q&A sessions.
materials_needed: Access to GA4 property with 6+ months e-commerce data
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Business scenario context documents
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of quantitative attribution analysis and variance calculations (25%), (2) Quality of qualitative model assessment demonstrating understanding of business context (25%), (3) Strength of strategic recommendations with clear justification and budget implications (30%), (4) Professional presentation delivery and response to peer questions (20%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all criteria with demonstrated ability to articulate trade-offs between attribution approaches.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated attribution data and focus on interpretation rather than data extraction. Offer guided questions for each evaluation phase. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using GA4's rules-based attribution, incorporate Google Ads data import analysis, or add statistical significance testing of model differences using confidence intervals.
original_title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS Requirements
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure spanning three geographically distributed sites with specific business requirements. They will create original network designs, implement advanced routing protocols, configure comprehensive security policies, and establish quality of service parameters for a fictional company's real-world networking needs.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocols by designing a hierarchical network topology that optimizes traffic flow between corporate headquarters, branch office, and data center locations

Students will construct comprehensive security policies through implementing ASA firewall rules, VPN tunnels, 802.1X authentication, and network access control lists that meet enterprise compliance standards
instructions: Begin by presenting students with the fictional company 'TechGlobal Solutions' business scenario document detailing three sites: HQ (500 users), Branch Office (150 users), and Data Center (50 servers). Students work in teams of 3-4 for 45 minutes to analyze requirements and create initial network diagrams using Visio or Lucidchart. Each team receives different traffic patterns and security constraints to ensure unique solutions. Next, allocate 90 minutes for physical topology design where students must specify exact Cisco equipment models (routers, switches, firewalls), calculate IP addressing schemes using VLSM, and document VLAN segmentation strategies. Require teams to present 10-minute design justifications to the class, defending equipment choices and addressing scalability concerns. Following presentations, students spend 120 minutes in Cisco Packet Tracer implementing their designs. They must configure OSPF areas, establish eBGP peering between sites, implement inter-VLAN routing, and create ASA firewall policies. During implementation, circulate to verify configurations and provide targeted assistance. In the final 60 minutes, teams conduct network testing by simulating traffic flows, testing failover scenarios, and validating security policies. Each team documents configuration commands, network verification outputs, and troubleshooting procedures in a technical implementation guide. Conclude with 15-minute team demonstrations showing working network functionality, security policy enforcement, and QoS traffic prioritization. Require teams to explain how their solution addresses business continuity and future expansion requirements.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software installed on student computers
TechGlobal Solutions business requirements document with network specifications
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart licenses for network diagramming
Cisco equipment specification sheets and pricing guides
Network testing scenario scripts with specific traffic simulation requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - topology efficiency, equipment selection, IP addressing scheme), Technical Implementation (35 points - correct protocol configuration, security policy effectiveness, QoS implementation), Documentation Quality (20 points - configuration accuracy, troubleshooting procedures, technical writing), and Presentation/Justification (20 points - design rationale, business alignment, peer questions handling). Students must demonstrate working network connectivity, successful security policy enforcement, and traffic prioritization to receive full implementation points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured baseline templates with basic routing already established, allowing focus on advanced features and security implementation. Offer reference command sheets for complex configurations and assign stronger technical students as peer mentors within teams. For advanced learners, introduce additional challenges such as implementing MPLS VPNs, configuring network automation using Python scripts, or designing redundant data center architectures with load balancing. Provide access to advanced Cisco documentation and encourage exploration of emerging technologies like SD-WAN integration.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS Requirements: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three sites with BGP routing, MPLS VPN connectivity, comprehensive security policies, and Quality of Service implementation. This capstone activity synthesizes advanced routing protocols, network security, and performance optimization concepts into a real-world network design scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will design a multi-site enterprise network topology by integrating BGP, OSPF, and MPLS technologies while meeting specific business requirements for redundancy and performance
Students will create and implement comprehensive security policies through configuring ASA firewalls, VPN tunnels, and access control lists across the enterprise infrastructure
Students will develop Quality of Service policies by analyzing traffic patterns and implementing traffic shaping, prioritization, and bandwidth allocation strategies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Network Architect, Security Specialist, QoS Engineer, and Implementation Lead. Provide each team with the scenario: TechCorp has headquarters in New York, manufacturing in Dallas, and R&D in Seattle, requiring secure, high-performance connectivity. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze requirements document specifying 500 users in NY, 200 in Dallas, 150 in Seattle, with video conferencing, VoIP, and mission-critical database applications. Students must design network topology using Visio or draw.io, including IP addressing scheme (minimum /22 networks), routing protocols selection, and security zones identification. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, teams build the physical topology with appropriate router/switch models (ISR 4000 series routers, Catalyst 9300 switches, ASA 5500 firewalls). Configure base connectivity including VLANs, trunking, and initial routing. Phase 3 (75 minutes): Implement advanced routing with OSPF areas for internal routing and eBGP for internet connectivity. Configure MPLS VPN between sites using MP-BGP and LDP. Establish redundant paths and verify convergence times. Phase 4 (60 minutes): Deploy security infrastructure including ASA firewall policies, site-to-site VPN tunnels using IPSec, and comprehensive ACLs. Implement network access control and intrusion prevention policies. Phase 5 (45 minutes): Configure QoS policies using MQC (Modular QoS CLI) with traffic classification, marking, queuing, and shaping. Prioritize VoIP (EF), video (AF41), and business-critical data (AF31) while limiting recreational traffic. Phase 6 (30 minutes): Conduct comprehensive testing including connectivity verification, failover testing, security policy validation, and QoS effectiveness measurement using traffic generators.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 network simulation software
TechCorp network requirements specification document
Microsoft Visio or draw.io for topology design
Cisco IOS configuration templates for ISR 4000 series routers
ASA firewall configuration guides and security policy templates
QoS configuration worksheets and traffic classification guides
Network testing and validation checklists
assessment_method: Evaluate using comprehensive rubric (100 points total): Network Design Documentation (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP addressing efficiency, protocol selection justification; Technical Implementation (35 points) - routing convergence, security policy effectiveness, QoS performance metrics; Professional Presentation (20 points) - network diagram clarity, configuration documentation, troubleshooting methodology; Practical Demonstration (20 points) - live network functionality, failover response, security breach prevention, QoS traffic prioritization verification. Students must submit complete network documentation, all device configurations, and demonstrate network functionality under various failure scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-configured base templates for initial device setup and offering checkpoint reviews after each phase. Create reference sheets with common BGP, OSPF, and QoS commands. For advanced learners, add IPv6 dual-stack implementation, SD-WAN overlay configuration, or network automation using Python/Ansible. Pair weaker students with stronger teammates and rotate roles to ensure knowledge transfer. Provide additional scenarios like DDoS attack simulation or branch office expansion for early finishers.
original_title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS Requirements

title: Memory Palace: Core Programming Terms and Definitions Quiz Game
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 fundamental programming terms (variables, loops, functions, etc.) and their exact definitions through flashcard drilling and competitive team quizzing. This foundational vocabulary activity prepares students for writing their first programs by ensuring they can instantly recognize and define key concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact definitions of 20 core programming terms (variable, function, loop, conditional, algorithm, debugging, syntax, compiler, interpreter, array, string, integer, boolean, parameter, argument, method, class, object, library, framework) with 90% accuracy through repeated practice drills
Students will identify programming terms from their definitions and match definitions to terms through timed recall exercises and peer quizzing activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the official term list and definition sheet to each student (5 minutes). Have students create physical flashcards with the term on front and complete definition on back - emphasize writing exactly as provided, not paraphrasing (15 minutes). Conduct individual silent study time where students drill themselves using the 'look, cover, recite, check' method: look at definition, cover it, recite aloud, then check accuracy (10 minutes). Divide class into teams of 4 students each. Run three 5-minute team practice rounds where teammates take turns being quizmaster, asking for definitions of randomly selected terms while others write answers on mini whiteboards (15 minutes total). Conduct formal assessment: project one term at a time on screen for 30 seconds each. Students write the complete definition independently on numbered answer sheets. No talking or materials allowed during assessment (15 minutes). Immediately review correct answers by having different students read definitions aloud while others self-check their papers with red pens (8 minutes). Conclude with reflection where students identify their three most challenging terms to focus on for homework review (2 minutes).
materials_needed: Printed term list with official definitions (one per student)
Blank index cards for flashcards (20 per student)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (one set per team)
Numbered answer sheets for assessment
Red pens for self-checking
Projector/screen for displaying terms during assessment
Timer for managing activity segments
assessment_method: Students must achieve 18/20 correct definitions (90%) on the written recall test to demonstrate mastery. Each definition must include all key components as specified in the official definition sheet. Partial credit given for definitions containing 75% of required elements. Document individual scores and create remediation list for students scoring below 16/20 who need additional practice before moving to application activities.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide definitions with one key word blanked out instead of full recall, allow use of flashcards during team practice rounds, pair with stronger partners during peer quizzing. For advanced learners: challenge them to create example code snippets demonstrating each term, have them explain terms using analogies, or research additional related terminology. Consider providing audio recordings of term pronunciations for ESL students.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Datasets
description: Students will analyze three different real-world datasets to identify, compare, and explain the characteristics of normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions. They will create visual representations and written explanations demonstrating their understanding of how distribution shapes reflect underlying data patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the characteristics of different statistical distributions by analyzing their shape, central tendency, and spread in real-world contexts
Students will explain the relationship between distribution patterns and their practical implications through comparative analysis of multiple datasets
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-selected datasets: employee salaries from a tech company (right-skewed), standardized test scores from a large school district (normal), and customer purchase amounts during a flash sale (bimodal). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group all three datasets. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Have students load the datasets into their analysis environment and create histograms for each dataset using 20-30 bins. Students should save these visualizations and note initial observations about shape.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Guide students to calculate descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation, skewness, kurtosis) for each dataset. They should create a comparison table documenting these values alongside their histogram observations.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students work collaboratively to classify each distribution type and identify key characteristics. They must explain why each dataset exhibits its particular distribution shape by considering the real-world context (e.g., salary caps creating right skew, test design creating normal distribution).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group prepares a brief explanation connecting distribution characteristics to practical implications. For example, explaining why mean vs. median matters for salary reporting, or how bimodal distributions might indicate distinct customer segments.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Groups present one dataset analysis to the class, focusing on the connection between mathematical properties and real-world meaning. Conclude with a class discussion comparing findings across groups.
materials_needed: Three curated CSV datasets (employee salaries, test scores, purchase amounts)
Python/R environment with pandas/dplyr and matplotlib/ggplot2
Jupyter notebooks or RStudio access for each student group
Descriptive statistics reference sheet
Digital whiteboard or presentation tool
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of distribution identification and statistical calculations (40%), (2) Quality of written explanations connecting distribution shape to real-world context (35%), (3) Clarity and insight in group presentation (25%). Students must correctly identify all three distribution types and provide logical explanations for why each dataset exhibits its particular pattern.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written code templates for generating histograms and calculating statistics, offer guiding questions about what each statistic reveals. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest additional statistical tests (normality tests, outlier detection) or explore how sample size affects distribution appearance by analyzing subsets of the data.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Calculus and Trigonometry
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus, trigonometric functions, and optimization techniques to determine the optimal angle and positioning for solar panels to maximize energy output throughout the year. They will work with real weather data and energy consumption patterns to create a comprehensive solar installation proposal.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to determine maximum solar energy output by analyzing functions involving panel angle, seasonal sun position, and geographic location
Students will utilize trigonometric identities and spherical coordinate systems through modeling solar trajectories and calculating incident radiation angles for different times of year
instructions: Begin by distributing the Solar Optimization Data Packet containing: latitude coordinates for 5 different cities, monthly solar declination angles, average daily sunlight hours, and local energy costs. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one city location. Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze the provided solar declination data and establish the function E(θ,t) = I₀ × cos(θ - δ(t)) × h(t) × A × η, where θ is panel tilt angle, δ(t) is seasonal solar declination, h(t) is daylight hours, A is panel area, and η is efficiency coefficient. Step 2 (25 minutes): Students apply partial derivatives to find ∂E/∂θ = 0, solving for optimal tilt angles for each month using the constraint that 0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°. They must show all calculus work including chain rule applications for the composite trigonometric functions. Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams use trigonometric identities to calculate the azimuth angle adjustments needed for maximum morning and afternoon capture, incorporating sin(φ)sin(δ) + cos(φ)cos(δ)cos(h) where φ is latitude and h is hour angle. Step 4 (30 minutes): Students integrate their findings to calculate total annual energy output using definite integrals: ∫₀³⁶⁵ E(θ_opt(t), t)dt, approximating with Riemann sums over monthly intervals. Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams create a final proposal presentation including mathematical justification, optimal angles for each season, expected energy output calculations, and cost-benefit analysis using provided economic data. Each team presents their solution with complete mathematical derivations visible.
materials_needed: Solar Optimization Data Packet with 5 different city coordinates and solar data
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (GeoGebra, Mathematica, or Desmos)
Large poster paper or presentation slides
Protractors and rulers for geometric representations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct application of partial derivatives and optimization techniques (25%), (2) Accurate use of trigonometric functions and identities in solar angle calculations (25%), (3) Proper setup and evaluation of definite integrals for annual energy calculations (25%), (4) Clear mathematical communication and realistic final proposal with justified recommendations (25%). Students must show complete mathematical work and achieve at least 75% accuracy in calculations to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated values for solar declination angles and simplified trigonometric reference sheets. Break optimization into smaller steps with guided practice on simpler single-variable problems first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables such as weather patterns, shading effects, or multiple panel arrays. Have them explore more complex integration techniques or consider economic optimization with time-value of money calculations.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Calculus and Trigonometry: Technical Implementation
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus, trigonometry, and optimization techniques to determine the optimal placement angle and positioning of solar panels for maximum energy efficiency. They will work with real meteorological data and use mathematical modeling to solve a practical engineering problem.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and optimization techniques to maximize solar energy output by determining optimal panel angles and orientations
Students will implement trigonometric functions and vector calculus through analysis of sun position, shadow effects, and energy calculations using real-world constraints
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing meteorological data for a specific city (latitude, average sun hours, seasonal variations) and constraint parameters (roof dimensions, local building codes, budget limitations). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Mathematician, Data Analyst, Model Validator, and Presenter. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the given data and identify key variables affecting solar panel efficiency: sun angle θ, panel tilt angle α, azimuth angle β, seasonal variations, and shading factors. Students must establish the objective function E(α,β,t) representing energy output over time.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Using calculus, students derive the optimization function by applying partial derivatives ∂E/∂α = 0 and ∂E/∂β = 0. They must incorporate trigonometric relationships for sun position: elevation = arcsin(sin(δ)sin(φ) + cos(δ)cos(φ)cos(h)) where δ is solar declination, φ is latitude, and h is hour angle.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams apply constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers to account for physical limitations (roof space, weight restrictions, building codes). Calculate shadow effects using vector projections and determine optimal spacing between panel rows.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Validate results by computing energy output for their optimized configuration versus standard installations using numerical integration. Compare with actual solar installation data provided.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their optimization solution with mathematical justification, highlighting critical decision points and trade-offs. Other teams evaluate solutions using provided peer assessment criteria.
materials_needed: City-specific meteorological data packets (solar irradiance, latitude, seasonal sun charts)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (GeoGebra, Mathematica, or Desmos)
Solar panel specification sheets with efficiency curves
Constraint parameter sheets (building codes, roof dimensions, budget limits)
Peer evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct application of calculus optimization techniques (25%), (2) Accurate use of trigonometric relationships for sun positioning (25%), (3) Proper constraint handling using mathematical methods (25%), (4) Validation of results and mathematical reasoning (25%). Teams must submit their optimization equations, numerical calculations, and a 2-page technical justification explaining their mathematical approach and final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written templates for the objective function and constraint equations with blanks to fill in. Offer step-by-step derivative worksheets and trigonometry reference cards. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity such as time-varying electricity pricing, panel degradation over time, or multiple panel types with different efficiency curves. Challenge them to create 3D visualizations of their optimization surfaces.
original_title: Optimizing Solar Panel Placement Using Calculus and Trigonometry

title: Electromagnetic Field Interaction Analysis in Multi-Component Circuit Systems
description: Students analyze complex electromagnetic field interactions in a three-component circuit system containing capacitors, inductors, and resistors. They examine phase relationships, energy transfer mechanisms, and field coupling effects to determine how electromagnetic fields influence overall circuit behavior and efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic field distributions and their temporal variations by examining vector field plots and calculating energy density distributions in multi-component AC circuits
Students will evaluate the relationship between electromagnetic field coupling and circuit performance through systematic comparison of isolated versus interconnected component behaviors
instructions: Begin by providing student teams (3-4 members) with three circuit configurations: (1) RLC circuit with R=100Ω, L=50mH, C=10μF, (2) coupled inductor system with mutual inductance M=15mH, and (3) parallel plate capacitor array with variable spacing. Students first measure and record voltage, current, and phase data for each circuit operating at frequencies of 500Hz, 1kHz, and 2kHz using oscilloscopes and function generators. Next, teams use COMSOL Multiphysics software to model the 3D electromagnetic field distributions around each component, paying particular attention to electric field lines near capacitors and magnetic field lines around inductors. Students then calculate energy storage in electric fields (U_E = ½εE²) and magnetic fields (U_B = ½μH²/μ₀) at each frequency, creating energy density maps. In the analysis phase, teams identify coupling mechanisms by comparing simulated field overlap regions with measured circuit performance data. Students examine how magnetic flux linkage between components affects overall impedance and how electric field fringing influences capacitive coupling. Teams create detailed field interaction diagrams showing energy flow pathways and identify frequency-dependent coupling strengths. Finally, students prepare technical reports analyzing how field interactions explain observed phase shifts, resonance behavior, and energy transfer efficiency, supported by quantitative field calculations and experimental validation data.
materials_needed: Digital oscilloscopes (100MHz bandwidth minimum)
Function generators with 0.1Hz-10kHz range
RLC circuit components (precision resistors, inductors, capacitors)
COMSOL Multiphysics software with RF module
Digital multimeters with impedance measurement capability
Breadboards and connecting wires
Variable inductor coils for mutual inductance testing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of electromagnetic field calculations and energy density computations (25%), (2) Quality of field interaction analysis and coupling mechanism identification (30%), (3) Integration of experimental data with theoretical field models (25%), (4) Technical report clarity and use of appropriate electromagnetic terminology (20%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in field calculations and demonstrate clear connections between field behavior and circuit performance.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated field templates and guided calculation worksheets with Maxwell equation applications. Offer intermediate checkpoints for field plotting verification. For advanced learners, extend analysis to include relativistic effects in high-frequency circuits, nonlinear field interactions in ferromagnetic materials, or design optimization challenges for minimizing unwanted electromagnetic coupling in sensitive circuits.

title: Bug Fix Solution Evaluation: Comparing and Critiquing Different Approaches
description: Students will evaluate three different code solutions that fix the same bug in a simple calculator program. They will compare the approaches using specific criteria and justify which solution is most effective for a beginner development team.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different bug fix solutions by analyzing code readability, maintainability, and correctness using a structured rubric
Students will critique and rank coding approaches through written justification that demonstrates understanding of code quality principles
instructions: Begin by distributing the Bug Fix Evaluation Worksheet containing a buggy calculator function that incorrectly handles division by zero (5 minutes setup). Present students with three different solutions: Solution A uses a simple if-statement check, Solution B uses try-catch exception handling, and Solution C uses a custom validation function. Have students work individually for 20 minutes to complete the evaluation matrix, scoring each solution (1-5 scale) on four criteria: code readability, error handling effectiveness, maintainability, and beginner-friendliness. Students must provide written justification for each score. Next, form pairs for 15 minutes to compare evaluations and discuss differences in scoring. Each pair must reach consensus on which solution they would recommend for a beginner development team and prepare a 2-minute presentation explaining their choice. Conduct pair presentations (10 minutes total, allowing 30 seconds for questions after each). Conclude with a 5-minute class discussion identifying common evaluation criteria that emerged across all presentations. Students submit their individual evaluation matrices and a final reflection paragraph explaining how their thinking changed (if at all) after peer discussions.
materials_needed: Bug Fix Evaluation Worksheet with buggy calculator code
Three printed code solutions (A, B, C) for each student
Evaluation matrix template with scoring rubric
Timer for time management
assessment_method: Grade using a 20-point rubric: Individual evaluation matrix completeness and justification quality (8 points), appropriate use of evaluation criteria (6 points), pair presentation clarity and reasoning (4 points), final reflection demonstrating critical thinking (2 points). Success requires scoring 16+ points with evidence of comparing solutions rather than just describing them.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guiding questions for each evaluation criteria (e.g., 'Which code would be easier for you to understand in 6 months?'). For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to suggest improvements to their chosen solution or evaluate performance/memory usage implications. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need support during the consensus-building phase.

title: Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard Creation
description: Students will design and build a comprehensive data analysis dashboard that predicts customer churn using real telecommunications data. They will synthesize multiple analytical techniques, create custom visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations based on their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a predictive analytics dashboard by integrating statistical modeling, data visualization, and business intelligence techniques
Students will synthesize customer behavior patterns through exploratory data analysis and create evidence-based retention strategies
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Hypothesis Formation (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the telecommunications customer dataset containing 21 variables (customer demographics, service usage, billing history, churn status). Students work in pairs to explore the dataset using Python/R, identifying key variables that might predict churn. They must document 3 specific hypotheses about churn drivers and create initial exploratory visualizations.

**Phase 2: Model Development (60 minutes)**
Students build and compare two predictive models: logistic regression and random forest. They must split data into 70/30 train/test sets, implement proper cross-validation, and evaluate models using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Students document model performance in a comparison table and select their best-performing model with justification.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students create an interactive dashboard containing: (1) Executive summary with key churn metrics, (2) Customer segmentation visualization showing high-risk groups, (3) Feature importance chart from their selected model, (4) Interactive filters for customer demographics and service types, (5) Predictive risk scoring interface where users can input customer characteristics.

**Phase 4: Business Recommendations (30 minutes)**
Students develop a one-page executive summary with three specific, data-driven recommendations for reducing churn, including estimated impact and implementation timeline. They must reference their model findings and include confidence intervals for their predictions.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV with 7,043 records, 21 variables)
Python with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib libraries OR R with tidyverse, caret packages
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop
Laptop computers with internet access
Executive summary template document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Model Accuracy - proper implementation, validation, and performance metrics (25%), (2) Dashboard Design - clarity, interactivity, and visual appeal (25%), (3) Business Insights - quality and feasibility of recommendations (25%), (4) Technical Documentation - code quality, methodology explanation, and reproducibility (25%). Students must achieve minimum 70% accuracy on test data and include all required dashboard components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written code templates for data loading and basic visualizations, offer guided worksheets for hypothesis formation, and create step-by-step dashboard building tutorials. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement ensemble methods, add real-time prediction capabilities, incorporate additional external datasets (economic indicators, competitor data), or create A/B testing frameworks for their recommendations.

title: Advanced Project Management Methodology Flashcard Marathon
description: Students will systematically memorize and recall advanced project management terminology, formulas, and framework components across multiple methodologies including PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, and PMBOK Guide 7th Edition. This intensive recall exercise builds foundational knowledge for complex project management scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall specific terminology, processes, and components from PRINCE2, PMI-ACP, and PMBOK Guide 7th Edition methodologies by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will demonstrate memorization of earned value management formulas, risk register components, and governance structures through verbal and written recall activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 150 advanced project management terms, formulas, and concepts divided into five categories: PRINCE2 principles and themes (30 cards), PMI-ACP practices and tools (30 cards), PMBOK 7th Edition performance domains (30 cards), Earned Value Management calculations (30 cards), and Risk Management artifacts (30 cards). Students work individually for the first 20 minutes, cycling through all cards and sorting them into 'known' and 'unknown' piles. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 15 minutes using only their 'unknown' cards, with partners providing immediate feedback and corrections. During the third phase (10 minutes), conduct a whole-class rapid-fire session where you randomly call out terms and students must provide definitions within 10 seconds, or vice versa with definitions requiring term identification. Follow with a 10-minute individual review where students re-test themselves on previously 'unknown' cards. Conclude with a 5-minute final sorting where students categorize all cards into 'mastered,' 'partially known,' and 'needs review' piles. Record individual progress on tracking sheets, noting improvement from initial to final sorting. Emphasize speed and accuracy, encouraging students to verbalize answers clearly and completely.
materials_needed: 150 pre-printed flashcards per student covering advanced PM concepts
Individual progress tracking sheets
Digital timer or stopwatch
Answer key reference guide for instructors
Small containers or rubber bands for card organization
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate 80% accuracy on final recall test covering randomly selected 30 cards from their initial 'unknown' pile. Assessment includes: correctly defining 24 out of 30 terms within 10 seconds each, proper recitation of at least 8 out of 10 EVM formulas with variable definitions, and accurate listing of minimum 5 components each for risk registers and PRINCE2 themes. Track progress using before/after comparison of 'known' vs 'unknown' card ratios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce initial card set to 100 cards focusing on core concepts, allow 15-second response time instead of 10, and provide mnemonic device handouts. For advanced learners: add 50 additional cards covering hybrid methodologies and scaling frameworks, require them to create connections between concepts from different methodologies, and challenge them to explain practical applications of memorized formulas.

title: Deconstructing Transformational Leadership Through Crisis Case Study Analysis
description: Students will analyze James Burke's leadership during the 1982 Tylenol crisis to understand how transformational leadership principles manifest in high-stakes decision-making. Through systematic examination of Burke's actions, communications, and strategic choices, students will demonstrate comprehension of transformational leadership's four core components in practice.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and categorize specific examples of idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration by analyzing Burke's documented actions and communications during the crisis

Students will explain the relationship between transformational leadership behaviors and organizational outcomes through structured comparison of pre-crisis, during-crisis, and post-crisis organizational performance metrics
instructions: Begin by distributing the comprehensive Tylenol crisis case study packet containing Burke's speeches, internal memos, press conferences transcripts, and financial data (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 4-5 students, assigning each team member one of the four transformational leadership dimensions plus one member as 'outcomes analyst.' Provide each team with the Transformational Leadership Analysis Matrix template. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Individual team members read the case study and identify 3-4 specific examples of their assigned leadership dimension, citing exact quotes and actions with timestamps/dates. The outcomes analyst charts organizational metrics (stock price, market share, employee retention, public trust surveys) across the timeline. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams reconvene to share findings, completing their matrix by plotting leadership behaviors against organizational outcomes on the provided timeline template. Each behavior must include: the specific action/communication, which transformational dimension it represents, the context/timing, and the measurable organizational impact. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Teams prepare a visual presentation mapping Burke's transformational leadership behaviors to specific crisis outcomes. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents their analysis for 8 minutes, followed by 2 minutes of peer questions focusing on the accuracy of their transformational leadership categorizations and the strength of their behavior-to-outcome connections.
materials_needed: Tylenol Crisis Case Study packet (20-page comprehensive document with timeline)
Transformational Leadership Analysis Matrix template (4x4 grid with outcomes column)
Organizational Performance Data sheets with pre-populated metrics
Flip chart paper and markers for visual presentations
Bass Transformational Leadership Reference Guide handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: Accuracy of transformational leadership dimension identification (5 points - must correctly categorize behaviors using Bass framework), Quality of textual evidence (5 points - specific quotes with proper citation), Logical connection between behaviors and outcomes (5 points - clear causal reasoning), and Presentation clarity (5 points - coherent explanation of analysis). Students must achieve 16/20 points to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a pre-completed example using a different leader, offer definition cards for each transformational dimension, and allow consultation with instructor during individual analysis phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential gaps where Burke could have applied transformational leadership more effectively, or compare his approach to contingency leadership models for the same crisis scenario.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and CloudFront
description: Students will create and deploy a complete static website hosting solution using AWS S3 for storage and CloudFront for content delivery. They will configure bucket policies, enable static website hosting, and set up a global CDN to demonstrate practical cloud deployment skills.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website by configuring S3 bucket hosting settings and uploading web files through the AWS Management Console
Students will implement content delivery optimization through CloudFront distribution setup and domain configuration
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab credentials and a starter HTML/CSS website package (index.html, about.html, style.css, 2 images). Students log into AWS Management Console and verify they're in us-east-1 region.

**S3 Configuration (25 minutes):** Students navigate to S3 service and create a new bucket with a globally unique name (format: firstname-lastname-website-YYYY). They disable 'Block all public access' and acknowledge the warning. Next, they upload all provided website files to the bucket root. Students then enable static website hosting in Properties tab, setting index.html as the index document and creating a simple error.html for 404 errors. They configure the bucket policy using the provided JSON template, replacing the bucket name placeholder with their actual bucket name.

**CloudFront Setup (20 minutes):** Students create a new CloudFront distribution using their S3 bucket as the origin domain. They configure default root object as 'index.html' and select 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' for viewer protocol policy. Students wait for distribution deployment (Status: Deployed) while documenting their S3 website endpoint URL.

**Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Students test both the direct S3 website URL and the CloudFront distribution URL in multiple browsers. They verify all pages load correctly, images display properly, and CSS styling applies. Students document load times from their location and simulate accessing from different geographic regions using browser developer tools. Finally, they intentionally access a non-existent page to verify 404 error handling works correctly.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts with appropriate permissions
Starter website files package (HTML, CSS, images)
Pre-written S3 bucket policy JSON template
Computers with modern web browsers and internet access
Activity worksheet for documenting URLs and test results
assessment_method: Students submit a completed worksheet containing: (1) Working S3 website URL, (2) Working CloudFront distribution URL, (3) Screenshots showing successful page loads from both endpoints, (4) Documentation of bucket policy configuration, (5) Load time comparison between S3 and CloudFront URLs. Success criteria: Both URLs functional, all website elements display correctly, CloudFront shows improved performance metrics, proper error page handling demonstrated.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional visual guides for AWS console navigation and offer pre-configured bucket policy templates. Create troubleshooting checkpoints after each major step. For advanced learners: Challenge them to configure custom domain names, implement additional CloudFront caching behaviors, or add Route 53 DNS configuration. Encourage exploration of S3 versioning and lifecycle policies.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and CloudFront: Exercise 1
description: Students will create and deploy a personal portfolio website using Amazon S3 for hosting and CloudFront for content delivery. They will configure bucket policies, enable static website hosting, and set up a global content delivery network to optimize website performance.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website by configuring Amazon S3 bucket settings and uploading HTML/CSS files
Students will implement content delivery optimization through setting up Amazon CloudFront distribution with custom domain configuration
instructions: **Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Instructor demonstrates AWS Management Console login and provides each student with AWS account credentials. Students log into their AWS accounts and navigate to the S3 service dashboard. **Bucket Creation (15 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a globally unique name (format: portfolio-[lastname]-[mmyy]). They configure the bucket region (US East 1) and disable 'Block all public access' settings. Students then enable static website hosting in bucket properties, setting index.html as the index document. **Content Upload (20 minutes):** Students upload their pre-created portfolio files (index.html, style.css, and one image) to the bucket root directory. They must set object permissions to 'public-read' for each file during upload. Students then create and apply a bucket policy using the provided JSON template to allow public read access to all objects. **Website Testing (10 minutes):** Students access their website using the S3 static website endpoint URL and verify all content loads correctly. They test navigation and image display functionality. **CloudFront Setup (25 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront service and create a new distribution. They configure the origin domain to point to their S3 bucket endpoint, set default root object to 'index.html', and enable compression. Students wait for distribution deployment (10-15 minutes) then test their website using the CloudFront distribution URL. **Documentation (10 minutes):** Students record both S3 and CloudFront URLs in their lab worksheet and answer reflection questions about performance differences and use cases.

Pre-created HTML portfolio files (index.html, style.css, one image file)
Bucket policy JSON template handout

scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide screenshot guides for each AWS console step, pair with more advanced peers, and offer pre-written bucket policy JSON. description: Students will create and deploy a complete static website using AWS S3 for storage and CloudFront for global content delivery. They will apply AWS security best practices by configuring bucket policies and enabling HTTPS distribution.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional static website by configuring S3 bucket hosting and uploading web assets
Students will implement content delivery optimization through CloudFront distribution setup and domain configuration

title: Schedule Compression Technique Analysis for Resource-Constrained Projects
description: Students will analyze a failing project schedule and evaluate the effectiveness of crashing versus fast-tracking techniques. They will examine cost-benefit trade-offs, risk implications, and resource constraints to recommend the optimal schedule compression approach.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the cost-benefit implications of crashing versus fast-tracking by calculating time savings, additional costs, and risk factors for each technique
Students will evaluate schedule compression options through systematic comparison of resource availability, dependency relationships, and stakeholder impact
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Metro Hospital IT Upgrade' case study showing a 6-month project now 8 weeks behind schedule with a fixed deadline. Divide students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Each team receives project documentation including network diagram, resource allocation sheet, and budget constraints. Teams spend 20 minutes reviewing materials and identifying critical path activities that are behind schedule. Next, teams analyze crashing opportunities by calculating cost per day saved for each critical path activity using the provided cost slope data (25 minutes). Simultaneously, they examine fast-tracking possibilities by identifying which activities can be overlapped despite dependencies, noting increased risk and coordination requirements. Teams create a comparison matrix evaluating both techniques across five criteria: time savings potential, additional costs, resource requirements, risk level, and implementation complexity (30 minutes). Each team calculates the optimal combination of techniques to recover the 8-week delay within the remaining budget of $50,000. Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation justifying their recommended approach with quantitative analysis and risk mitigation strategies (20 minutes). During presentations, other teams use provided peer evaluation forms to assess the thoroughness of analysis and feasibility of recommendations (20 minutes). Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing different team approaches and highlighting key decision factors for schedule compression selection (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Metro Hospital IT Upgrade case study packet (network diagram, resource sheets, cost data)
Schedule compression analysis worksheet templates
Calculators or Excel access for cost calculations
Peer evaluation rubrics
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of critical path analysis and time calculations (25%), (2) Completeness of cost-benefit analysis for both techniques (30%), (3) Quality of risk assessment and mitigation strategies (25%), (4) Justification of final recommendation with supporting data (20%). Successful completion requires scoring 3+ points in each category with demonstrated ability to quantify trade-offs between techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed comparison matrix template and step-by-step calculation examples for the first two critical path activities. Advanced learners can be challenged to incorporate Monte Carlo simulation concepts or develop contingency plans for multiple delay scenarios. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing additional support during the analysis phase.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security Policies
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network infrastructure featuring multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, redundancy protocols, and comprehensive security policies. They will create network documentation, implement the design on physical equipment, and validate all functionality through systematic testing.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced Cisco switching and routing configurations through hands-on deployment of VLANs, STP, HSRP, and ACLs on physical equipment
Students will create comprehensive network documentation by developing configuration templates, security policies, and troubleshooting procedures
instructions:
**Phase 1: Requirements Analysis & Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 200 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, IT) requiring network segmentation and security. Students work in teams of 2-3 to analyze requirements and create network topology diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer or Visio. They must design VLAN structure, IP addressing scheme (/24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16), and identify security requirements.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Each team receives access to a lab pod with 2 Cisco Catalyst switches (2960 series), 1 router (2911 series), and 4 PCs. Students configure: VLAN creation and assignment (Data VLAN 10, Voice VLAN 20, Management VLAN 99, Guest VLAN 30), trunk ports with 802.1Q, Spanning Tree Protocol with root bridge election, inter-VLAN routing using router-on-a-stick, HSRP for gateway redundancy, and ACLs restricting inter-departmental access.

**Phase 3: Security Implementation (30 minutes)**
Students implement port security (maximum 2 MAC addresses per port), SSH access with local user authentication, enable logging to syslog server, configure SNMP v3 for monitoring, and create backup configurations.

**Phase 4: Testing & Documentation (45 minutes)**
Teams conduct connectivity testing between VLANs, verify ACL functionality, test failover scenarios, document all configurations with comments, and create network troubleshooting guide with common scenarios and solutions.
materials_needed: 2 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
1 Cisco 2911 router per team
4 Windows PCs with network adapters
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Category 6 Ethernet cables (minimum 12 per team)
Cisco Packet Tracer software license
Putty or SecureCRT terminal software
Network documentation templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with 4 criteria: Network Design (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, security considerations; Implementation Quality (35 points) - configuration accuracy, protocol functionality, redundancy features; Security Implementation (20 points) - ACL effectiveness, access control, monitoring setup; Documentation (20 points) - configuration clarity, troubleshooting procedures, network diagrams. Teams must demonstrate working network with successful ping tests between appropriate VLANs and blocked traffic where ACLs apply. Final deliverable includes network diagram, complete device configurations, and 2-page troubleshooting guide.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured VLAN templates and IP addressing worksheets, assign stronger technical student as team lead, offer checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Add QoS configuration for voice traffic, implement dynamic VLAN assignment using RADIUS, configure EtherChannel link aggregation between switches, add wireless controller integration with guest portal authentication.

description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network infrastructure featuring multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security policies, and redundancy protocols. learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, routing protocols, and security policies by designing a comprehensive network architecture that meets specific business requirements

instructions: **Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)** - Students receive a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 200+ employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest) requiring network segmentation.
