title: Optimizing Pharmaceutical Production: Multi-Variable Calculus in Real-World Manufacturing
description: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to solve a complex pharmaceutical manufacturing optimization problem. They will determine optimal production rates for multiple drug compounds while working within cost, equipment, and regulatory constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial differentiation techniques to analyze multi-variable profit functions in pharmaceutical manufacturing contexts
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems involving production capacity and regulatory compliance limits
instructions: Begin by distributing the PharmaCorp case study packet containing production data for three drug compounds (Alpha, Beta, Gamma) with given profit functions P(x,y,z) = 450x + 320y + 280z - 2x² - 1.5y² - z² - xy - 0.5xz. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 15 minutes analyzing the unconstrained scenario by finding critical points using partial derivatives. Next, introduce three constraints: equipment capacity (2x + 3y + z ≤ 1200), regulatory compliance (x + y ≤ 500), and minimum production quotas (z ≥ 100). Spend 25 minutes having teams set up the Lagrangian function L(x,y,z,λ₁,λ₂,λ₃) and solve the system of equations using matrix methods or computational tools like Wolfram Alpha. Teams must verify their solutions satisfy all constraints and calculate the maximum profit. During the final 15 minutes, each team presents their optimal production strategy (x*, y*, z*) with economic justification. Teams must explain how changing one constraint by 10% would affect their solution using sensitivity analysis. Circulate during work time to ensure proper setup of constraint equations and correct interpretation of Lagrange multiplier values as shadow prices.
materials_needed: PharmaCorp case study packets with profit functions and constraint data
Graphing calculators or laptops with Wolfram Alpha/MATLAB access
Linear algebra reference sheets for matrix operations
Flip chart paper and markers for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: correct setup of Lagrangian (5 points), accurate solution of constraint system (6 points), verification of feasibility and optimality conditions (4 points), economic interpretation of results and shadow prices (3 points), clear presentation with sensitivity analysis (2 points). Students must submit written calculations and present orally.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template worksheets with partially completed Lagrangian setup and remind them to check constraint boundaries systematically. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints like integer programming requirements or ask them to model uncertainty in profit coefficients using stochastic optimization methods.

title: Analyzing Complex Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Source Systems
description: Students will decompose and analyze interference patterns created by multiple coherent wave sources to identify underlying wave parameters and predict resultant amplitudes. They will examine how phase relationships, frequency differences, and spatial arrangements affect the composite wave behavior in both one and two-dimensional systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex interference patterns by deconstructing multi-source wave systems to identify individual wave parameters including amplitude, frequency, and phase relationships
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of different wave sources through mathematical modeling and graphical analysis to predict resultant wave behaviors
instructions:
Begin by providing student teams (3-4 members) with three different interference scenarios: (1) three coherent sound sources with slightly different frequencies creating beats, (2) water wave tank data showing interference from four point sources, and (3) electromagnetic wave interference in a double-slit setup with additional phase-shifting elements. Each team receives raw data sets including amplitude measurements at various points and time intervals. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams use wave analysis software to plot the composite wave patterns and identify key features such as nodes, antinodes, beat frequencies, and standing wave regions. They must create detailed graphs showing both temporal and spatial variations.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Students mathematically decompose the composite patterns by applying superposition principles. They work backwards from the resultant patterns to determine individual source parameters, using Fourier analysis tools to separate frequency components and phase analysis to identify time delays.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams create predictive models by varying one parameter at a time (source separation, phase difference, or amplitude ratios) and calculating expected changes in the interference pattern. They generate theoretical plots for comparison.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Students present their analysis findings, focusing on the relationship between source parameters and resultant patterns. They must explain discrepancies between their theoretical predictions and actual data, considering factors like measurement uncertainty, environmental effects, and non-ideal conditions.

Conclude with teams peer-reviewing each other's mathematical approaches and challenging assumptions made during the decomposition process.
materials_needed: Wave analysis software (MATLAB, Python with SciPy, or similar)
Three different interference data sets with measurement uncertainties
Graphing calculators or computers with plotting capabilities
Fourier analysis tools or software plugins
Reference materials on wave superposition and interference theory
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical accuracy of wave decomposition (25 points), correct identification of source parameters within 5% tolerance (25 points), quality of predictive models and theoretical comparisons (25 points), explanation of discrepancies between theory and data (15 points), and peer presentation effectiveness (10 points). Students must submit detailed calculations, annotated graphs, and written explanations of their analytical process.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing step-by-step mathematical templates for wave superposition calculations and pre-made graph axes with appropriate scales. Offer simplified two-source problems before progressing to multi-source systems. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexities such as non-coherent sources, three-dimensional wave propagation, or relativistic effects in electromagnetic interference. Provide extension problems involving real-world applications like noise cancellation systems or optical interferometry.

title: Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Prone Python Functions
description: Students will critically analyze three intentionally flawed Python functions by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and ranking solutions from best to worst. They will justify their evaluations using specific coding standards and provide detailed improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different Python function implementations by comparing their logic, syntax, and adherence to coding standards
Students will critique code quality through systematic analysis of readability, efficiency, and potential runtime errors
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Code Review Worksheet containing three Python functions that solve the same problem (calculating average of a list) but with different bugs and quality issues: Function A has syntax errors, Function B has logical errors, Function C has poor naming and structure but works. Arrange students in pairs.

**Individual Analysis Phase (15 minutes):** Each student independently examines all three functions, marking bugs with red pen and quality issues with yellow highlighter. Students complete the evaluation matrix, scoring each function (1-5 scale) on: syntax correctness, logical accuracy, readability, and efficiency. They must write specific evidence for each score.

**Pair Discussion Phase (10 minutes):** Partners compare their individual evaluations, discussing disagreements and refining their assessments. They must reach consensus on ranking the functions from best to worst overall quality.

**Justification Phase (8 minutes):** Each pair writes a 100-word justification for their ranking, citing specific examples from the code. They must reference at least two Python coding standards (PEP 8 guidelines provided on worksheet).

**Gallery Walk Evaluation (10 minutes):** Pairs post their rankings and justifications on classroom walls. Students walk around reading others' work, placing sticky dots next to evaluations they find most convincing and well-supported.

**Debrief (7 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion on evaluation criteria. Ask: 'What made some justifications more convincing than others?' Reveal the instructor's expert ranking and reasoning, highlighting how different priorities (working code vs. maintainable code) can lead to different valid evaluations.
materials_needed: Code Review Worksheet with three flawed Python functions
Evaluation matrix handout (1 per student)
PEP 8 coding standards reference sheet
Red and yellow highlighters
Sticky dots for gallery walk
Wall space or whiteboards for posting work
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of bug identification (25% - must find at least 80% of planted errors), (2) Quality of evaluation criteria application (25% - uses specific evidence from code), (3) Justification clarity and logic (25% - reasoning connects evidence to conclusions), (4) Use of coding standards (25% - references at least 2 PEP 8 guidelines appropriately). Students must score 3+ in all categories to demonstrate evaluate-level thinking.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a 'Bug Hunt Checklist' with common Python errors to look for (indentation, syntax, variable names). Give sentence starters for justifications: 'This function is better because...' **For advanced learners:** Add a fourth function with subtle efficiency issues (nested loops). Challenge them to evaluate time/space complexity and suggest algorithmic improvements. Encourage them to consider maintainability and scalability in their evaluations.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard from Raw E-commerce Data
description: Students will create an interactive business intelligence dashboard that predicts customer churn using real e-commerce transaction data. They will design the analytical framework, build predictive models, and construct visualizations that communicate actionable insights to business stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive churn prediction model by integrating multiple data sources and applying machine learning algorithms to identify at-risk customers
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining statistical analysis, data visualization, and business storytelling to present actionable recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Architecture Design (45 minutes)**
Provide teams of 3-4 students with the raw e-commerce dataset containing customer transactions, demographics, and website behavior. Students first spend 15 minutes exploring the data structure and identifying key variables. Next, they create a data pipeline blueprint showing how they will clean, transform, and merge the datasets. Teams document their feature engineering strategy, identifying which metrics they will calculate (recency, frequency, monetary value, engagement scores). Each team presents their 3-minute data strategy to another team for peer feedback.

**Phase 2: Model Development (60 minutes)**
Using their chosen analytics software, students implement their data cleaning pipeline and calculate their engineered features. They then split their data into training/testing sets and build at least two different churn prediction models (e.g., logistic regression and random forest). Students must document model performance metrics and select their final model based on business relevance, not just statistical accuracy. They create customer risk segments (high, medium, low churn probability) and validate these segments make business sense.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students design and build an interactive dashboard with four required components: executive summary with key churn metrics, customer segmentation visualization, individual customer risk profiles, and recommended intervention strategies. The dashboard must include at least three interactive filters and two drill-down capabilities. Teams conclude by preparing a 5-minute stakeholder presentation explaining their methodology, insights, and business recommendations.
materials_needed: E-commerce dataset with 10,000+ customer records including transactions, demographics, and web behavior data (provided as CSV files)
Analytics software access (Tableau, Power BI, or Python with Jupyter notebooks)
Presentation template for stakeholder communication
Model evaluation checklist handout
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed interactive dashboard with all required components (40 points), (2) Technical documentation explaining data pipeline, model selection rationale, and validation approach (30 points), (3) 5-minute stakeholder presentation demonstrating business insights and recommendations (30 points). Rubric evaluates technical accuracy, creative problem-solving, visual design effectiveness, and business relevance of insights.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written code snippets for common data cleaning tasks and a template dashboard structure. Offer guided questions for feature selection. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources, experiment with advanced algorithms (XGBoost, neural networks), or create predictive confidence intervals. Encourage A/B testing simulation for intervention strategies.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard from Raw E-commerce Data: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an interactive analytics dashboard that identifies patterns in customer behavior and predicts churn risk using real e-commerce transaction data. They will design their own analysis framework, build visualizations, and present actionable business recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive data analysis workflow by integrating data cleaning, exploratory analysis, and predictive modeling techniques
Students will create an interactive dashboard through combining statistical analysis with business intelligence visualization tools
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Architecture Design (45 minutes)**
Provide each team with the raw e-commerce dataset containing 10,000 customer records with purchase history, demographics, and engagement metrics. Students first spend 15 minutes exploring the data structure and identifying data quality issues. Next, they design their analysis framework by creating a flowchart showing: data cleaning steps, key metrics to calculate, visualization types needed, and prediction methodology. Teams present their 5-minute design proposals to receive peer feedback.

**Phase 2: Data Pipeline Construction (90 minutes)**
Using their approved framework, students implement their data cleaning pipeline in Python/R, calculating custom metrics like recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) scores, customer lifetime value, and engagement trends. They must document each transformation step and create data validation checkpoints. Students then build their predictive model using logistic regression or decision trees, splitting data 70/30 for training/testing.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Development (75 minutes)**
Teams create interactive dashboards in Tableau/Power BI featuring: customer segmentation scatter plots, churn probability heat maps, trend analysis time series, and key performance indicator cards. Each visualization must include filters for date ranges and customer segments. Students design the dashboard layout prioritizing business user experience and actionable insights.

**Phase 4: Business Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each team delivers a 7-minute presentation demonstrating their dashboard, explaining their methodology, highlighting three key findings, and providing specific retention strategy recommendations with projected impact metrics.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Python/R with pandas, scikit-learn libraries installed
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop licenses
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Flipchart paper and markers for framework design
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: Data Pipeline Quality (20%) - completeness of cleaning and feature engineering; Model Implementation (20%) - appropriate technique selection and validation; Dashboard Design (25%) - visual clarity, interactivity, and user experience; Business Insights (20%) - relevance and actionability of findings; Presentation Quality (15%) - clarity of communication and professional delivery. Students must achieve minimum 3/4 points in each category to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-written code templates for common data cleaning tasks and a dashboard wireframe template. Pair them with stronger technical partners during Phase 2. For advanced learners: challenge them to implement ensemble modeling techniques, create custom calculated fields, or integrate external data sources like demographic census data. Provide additional dataset complexity with missing values and outliers.
original_title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard from Raw E-commerce Data

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Flashcard Marathon
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the 15 essential CPM calculation formulas and their component variables through intensive flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building automatic retrieval of forward pass, backward pass, and float calculations used in advanced project scheduling.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 15 CPM formulas (Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, etc.) with 95% accuracy within 30 seconds per formula
Students will identify and define each variable component (ES, EF, LS, LF, Duration, etc.) in CPM calculations through rapid-fire verbal responses
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made CPM formula flashcards to each student (15 cards total). Each card shows a formula name on front (e.g., 'Early Finish Calculation') and complete formula with variable definitions on back (e.g., 'EF = ES + Duration - 1, where ES = Early Start, Duration = Activity Duration'). 

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually, cycling through all 15 cards, reading formula names aloud and attempting to recite complete formulas before flipping cards. Track successful recalls with checkmarks on recording sheet.

Phase 2 (15 minutes): Partner students for reciprocal drilling. Partner A shows formula name, Partner B has 15 seconds to recite complete formula and define each variable. Partners alternate every 5 minutes. Record accuracy rates.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Conduct instructor-led rapid-fire assessment. Call out formula names randomly; students write complete formulas on whiteboards simultaneously. Display boards for immediate verification. Students must achieve 13/15 correct responses.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Challenge round using complex scenarios. Present network diagrams with missing calculations; students must identify which specific formulas apply and write them from memory. Focus on practical application contexts like 'calculating slack for Resource A' or 'determining critical path timing.'
materials_needed: Pre-printed CPM formula flashcards (15 cards per student)
Individual recording sheets with formula checklist
Small whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each student
Timer/stopwatch
Sample network diagrams for challenge scenarios
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (13/15 formulas correct) on final rapid-fire assessment and complete challenge scenarios within time limits. Grade based on: Formula accuracy (60%), variable definition precision (25%), and speed of recall under 15 seconds per formula (15%). Document individual progress using provided tracking sheets.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for complex formulas (e.g., 'Every Elephant Starts Dancing' for ES + Duration = EF) and allow extended 25-second response time initially. For advanced learners: Include additional formulas for resource-constrained scheduling and cost-time optimization calculations, plus integration challenges combining multiple formula applications.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing Communication Patterns During Organizational Failures
description: Students will analyze real-world crisis leadership cases by examining CEO communication transcripts, press releases, and stakeholder responses to identify underlying leadership theories and approaches. Through systematic comparison of successful versus failed crisis responses, students will demonstrate understanding of adaptive leadership principles and stakeholder management strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will categorize leadership communication strategies used during organizational crises by applying adaptive leadership and situational leadership frameworks to real transcript data
Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective crisis leadership approaches through systematic analysis of stakeholder responses and organizational outcomes
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with the crisis leadership analysis packet containing: transcripts from two contrasting CEO crisis responses (Wells Fargo 2016 vs. Johnson & Johnson Tylenol 1982), stakeholder reaction data, and theoretical framework reference sheets. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct individual case analysis. Each member takes one stakeholder perspective (employees, customers, investors, media) and creates a stakeholder impact matrix identifying specific leader behaviors, communication choices, and resulting stakeholder responses. Students must cite specific transcript quotes and map them to Heifetz's adaptive leadership concepts or Hersey-Blanchard situational leadership models.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams synthesize individual analyses into comparative leadership profiles. Using the provided template, they categorize each leader's approach across five dimensions: problem diagnosis (technical vs. adaptive challenges), communication transparency levels, stakeholder prioritization patterns, decision-making speed, and accountability messaging. Teams must identify at least three concrete examples per dimension.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams prepare visual comparison charts showing leadership theory applications and create hypothesis statements about why different approaches yielded different outcomes. Each team presents their analysis matrix to one other team for peer feedback before final submission.

Conclude with individual reflection where each student writes a 200-word synthesis explaining which leadership theories best explain the observed crisis response patterns and why certain approaches proved more effective for specific stakeholder groups.
materials_needed: Crisis leadership analysis packet with CEO transcript excerpts (Wells Fargo 2016 and Johnson & Johnson Tylenol 1982)
Stakeholder reaction data sheets (news articles, stock prices, employee surveys)
Leadership theory reference sheets (Adaptive Leadership, Situational Leadership models)
Comparative analysis template worksheets
Flip chart paper and markers for visual presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across three criteria: (1) Accuracy of theoretical framework application - correctly maps leader behaviors to specific leadership theories with appropriate citations (40%), (2) Quality of stakeholder analysis - demonstrates clear understanding of how different approaches affected various stakeholder groups with specific evidence (40%), (3) Synthesis depth - draws meaningful connections between leadership theories and crisis outcomes in final reflection (20%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted transcript excerpts focusing on key leadership moments, offer structured sentence starters for theoretical connections, and pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Include additional crisis cases (Boeing 737 Max, Volkswagen emissions), challenge them to identify gaps in existing leadership theories, or have them research long-term organizational outcomes beyond immediate crisis period.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with RDS Database
description: Students will apply AWS cloud fundamentals by deploying a complete web application architecture using EC2 instances for the web tier and RDS for the database tier. They will configure security groups, establish database connectivity, and verify the application functions correctly across multiple AWS services.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration skills by launching and connecting web server instances with proper security group settings
Students will demonstrate RDS database integration by establishing connectivity between EC2 web servers and MySQL database instances through hands-on deployment
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Instructor provides each student with AWS Learner Lab access credentials and a simple PHP web application file (contact form that stores data in MySQL). Ensure students can access AWS Management Console.

**Step 1: Launch RDS Database (15 minutes):** Students navigate to RDS service, click 'Create Database', select MySQL, choose 'Free tier' template. Configure: DB instance identifier 'student-db', master username 'admin', auto-generate password (save it), instance class db.t3.micro, storage 20GB, VPC default, public access 'No', create new security group 'db-security-group', database name 'contacts'.

**Step 2: Configure Database Security Group (10 minutes):** In EC2 console, find 'db-security-group', edit inbound rules, add rule: Type 'MySQL/Aurora', Port 3306, Source 'Custom' with CIDR 10.0.0.0/16.

**Step 3: Launch EC2 Web Server (15 minutes):** Navigate to EC2, launch instance, select Amazon Linux 2 AMI, t2.micro instance, default VPC, auto-assign public IP 'Enable', create new security group 'web-security-group' with HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) from anywhere.

**Step 4: Install Web Server and Deploy Application (20 minutes):** SSH into EC2 instance, install Apache and PHP: 'sudo yum update -y && sudo yum install -y httpd php php-mysql'. Start Apache: 'sudo systemctl start httpd && sudo systemctl enable httpd'. Upload provided PHP application to /var/www/html/, modify database connection string with RDS endpoint.

**Step 5: Test Application (10 minutes):** Access web application via EC2 public IP, submit test contact form, verify data appears in RDS database using MySQL client connection.

**Documentation (5 minutes):** Students screenshot working application and document architecture diagram showing EC2-RDS connection.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab account access for each student
Pre-written PHP contact form application with MySQL database integration
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
MySQL client software for database verification
assessment_method: Success criteria include: (1) Functional web application accessible via public IP (25 points), (2) Successful form submission storing data in RDS database (25 points), (3) Proper security group configurations allowing only necessary traffic (20 points), (4) Architecture diagram accurately depicting EC2-RDS relationship (15 points), (5) Screenshots demonstrating working application and database connectivity (15 points). Students submit screenshots, architecture diagram, and RDS endpoint URL as deliverables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step connection troubleshooting checklist. Create video walkthrough of SSH connection process. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement Auto Scaling Groups, Application Load Balancer, or Multi-AZ RDS deployment. Have them configure CloudWatch monitoring and set up automated backups for RDS instance.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with RDS Database: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a complete web application infrastructure by launching EC2 instances, configuring security groups, and connecting to an RDS MySQL database. This hands-on activity simulates real-world cloud deployment scenarios using AWS Free Tier resources.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web server by launching and configuring an EC2 instance with proper security group settings
Students will establish database connectivity by creating an RDS instance and configuring application-to-database communication through security groups and connection strings
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS account access credentials and a simple PHP web application file (contact-form.php) that connects to MySQL. Students log into AWS Management Console.

**Phase 1 - EC2 Deployment (25 minutes):** Students navigate to EC2 Dashboard and click 'Launch Instance'. Select Amazon Linux 2 AMI (Free Tier eligible), choose t2.micro instance type. In Configure Instance Details, ensure Auto-assign Public IP is enabled. In Configure Security Group, create new security group named 'WebServer-SG' with rules: HTTP (port 80) from 0.0.0.0/0, SSH (port 22) from 0.0.0.0/0, and MySQL/Aurora (port 3306) from 10.0.0.0/8. Launch instance with existing key pair or create new one.

**Phase 2 - Web Server Configuration (20 minutes):** SSH into EC2 instance using provided key pair. Execute commands: 'sudo yum update -y', 'sudo yum install -y httpd php php-mysql', 'sudo systemctl start httpd', 'sudo systemctl enable httpd'. Upload contact-form.php to /var/www/html/ directory using SCP or nano editor.

**Phase 3 - RDS Database Creation (25 minutes):** Navigate to RDS Dashboard, click 'Create Database', select MySQL, choose Free Tier template. Set DB instance identifier as 'webapp-db', master username 'admin', password 'WebApp123!'. In Connectivity section, select same VPC as EC2, choose 'WebServer-SG' security group. Create database and wait for 'Available' status.

**Phase 4 - Application Testing (10 minutes):** Update contact-form.php with RDS endpoint URL, test web application by accessing EC2 public IP address in browser, submit test form data, verify database connectivity through application functionality.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account credentials for each student
Pre-written PHP contact form application file (contact-form.php)
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Key pair file (.pem format) for EC2 access
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate successful deployment through three deliverables: (1) Screenshot of running EC2 instance with correct security group configuration (25 points), (2) Screenshot of RDS database in 'Available' status with proper connectivity settings (25 points), (3) Functional web application accessible via public URL that successfully submits data to database (50 points). Total: 100 points. Instructor will verify each student's public URL functionality and review AWS resource configurations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step command cheat sheet. Pair students with partners for peer support during SSH and command-line activities. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional security measures (restrict SSH to specific IP ranges), add CloudWatch monitoring, or create an Application Load Balancer for high availability. Provide troubleshooting flowchart for common connection issues.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with RDS Database

title: Schedule Compression Technique Analysis: Fast-Track vs. Crash Analysis Workshop
description: Students analyze two real-world project scenarios requiring schedule compression and determine the optimal approach by comparing fast-tracking versus crashing techniques. They will evaluate trade-offs, risks, and resource implications to justify their recommendations through structured analysis frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project schedule compression scenarios by comparing fast-tracking and crashing techniques using cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment matrices
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different schedule compression approaches through systematic examination of resource constraints, dependencies, and quality impacts
instructions:
Begin by distributing two project scenario packets (15 minutes setup). Scenario A: Software development project 3 months behind schedule with fixed go-live date. Scenario B: Construction project facing weather delays with penalty clauses. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, assigning half to each scenario (5 minutes). 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze their assigned scenario using the provided Schedule Compression Analysis Template. They must identify: critical path activities, available resources, budget constraints, quality requirements, and stakeholder expectations. Teams document findings in the template's situational analysis section.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams develop two alternative solutions - one using fast-tracking, another using crashing. For each approach, they complete cost-impact calculations, risk probability matrices (using high/medium/low ratings), and timeline adjustments. They must show specific activities affected, resource additions needed, and potential quality impacts using the comparison worksheet.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams create recommendation matrices scoring each approach against five criteria: cost effectiveness (weighted 25%), schedule improvement (25%), risk level (20%), quality impact (15%), and stakeholder acceptance (15%). They calculate weighted scores and select their recommended approach.

Phase 4 (25 minutes): Team presentations (4 minutes each) where they present their analysis, defend their recommendation, and respond to instructor questions about their reasoning. Other teams provide peer feedback using provided evaluation forms.

Conclude with instructor-led discussion (15 minutes) comparing approaches across scenarios and highlighting key analytical insights about when each technique is most appropriate.
materials_needed: Two detailed project scenario packets with WBS, network diagrams, and resource information
Schedule Compression Analysis Template (Word document with structured sections)
Cost-benefit comparison worksheets with calculation formulas
Risk assessment matrices (Excel templates)
Weighted decision matrix templates
Peer evaluation forms
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
assessment_method: Grade using 100-point rubric: Situational Analysis completeness (20 points), Fast-track solution quality and feasibility (25 points), Crashing solution quality and feasibility (25 points), Recommendation justification with weighted scoring (20 points), and presentation clarity with defense of reasoning (10 points). Students must demonstrate systematic comparison of alternatives and provide quantitative support for recommendations to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of one scenario analysis and offer guided practice with cost calculations. Create mixed-ability teams pairing analytical students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Add third scenario requiring combination of both techniques, or have them develop Monte Carlo simulation models for risk analysis. Provide additional complexity with multi-project portfolio considerations.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics using real e-commerce data, comparing their impact on conversion credit distribution. They will then defend their recommendation for the optimal attribution model based on business objectives and data insights.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based) by analyzing conversion path data and assessing alignment with business goals
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of model outputs and justify alternative approaches based on customer journey patterns
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic channels. Distribute the scenario brief: an online retailer questioning whether their current last-click attribution model accurately represents marketing channel effectiveness. **Phase 1 - Data Extraction (20 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool. They extract conversion data for all available attribution models, focusing on: assisted conversions, conversion value differences, and channel performance variations. Students document findings in provided comparison matrix template. **Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (30 minutes):** Students analyze discrepancies between models, identifying which channels gain/lose credit under different models. They examine top conversion paths in Attribution > Top Conversion Paths, noting average path length and channel interaction patterns. Students calculate percentage differences in channel valuation between models and identify the three most significantly impacted channels. **Phase 3 - Business Context Integration (25 minutes):** Using provided business context (customer lifetime value data, profit margins by channel, marketing spend allocation), students evaluate how each attribution model aligns with stated business objectives. They assess model appropriateness for the 90-day average customer journey length and multi-device usage patterns shown in data. **Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (15 minutes):** Students prepare 5-minute presentations defending their recommended attribution model choice, including: quantitative evidence from analysis, business alignment rationale, implementation considerations, and anticipated impact on marketing budget allocation. Presentations must address potential counterarguments and model limitations.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account access (one per student)
Attribution model comparison matrix template (Excel/Sheets)
Business scenario brief with company objectives and constraints
Customer journey data supplement sheet
Presentation timer and evaluation rubric
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and model comparison (25 points), (2) Depth of critical analysis and insight identification (30 points), (3) Quality of business context integration and strategic thinking (25 points), (4) Strength of recommendation defense and counterargument anticipation (20 points). Success requires scoring 70+ points with evidence-based reasoning throughout.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each analysis phase and offering one-on-one data interpretation sessions. For advanced learners, introduce custom attribution model creation using Google Analytics Intelligence API or challenge them to incorporate cross-device tracking limitations into their analysis. Provide additional complex scenarios involving seasonal businesses or B2B long sales cycles.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network infrastructure for a fictional 500-employee company, incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, network security policies, and Quality of Service configurations. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize advanced Cisco networking concepts into a production-ready solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced Cisco switching and routing configurations through hands-on deployment of VLANs, STP optimization, OSPF routing, and ACL security policies
Students will create comprehensive network documentation and troubleshooting procedures by developing implementation guides and testing protocols
instructions:
**Phase 1 (90 minutes): Network Design and Planning**
Students work in teams of 3-4. Present the scenario: Design network infrastructure for 'TechCorp' with 5 departments (Sales-80 users, Engineering-150 users, HR-25 users, Finance-30 users, IT-15 users) across 3 floors. Each team receives the building floor plan and business requirements document. Teams must create: (1) Logical network topology showing VLAN assignments, (2) Physical topology with switch/router placement, (3) IP addressing scheme using 192.168.0.0/16, (4) VLAN numbering and naming convention. Deliverable: Visio diagram and Excel spreadsheet with all network details.

**Phase 2 (120 minutes): Configuration Implementation**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical lab equipment (3560 switches, 2911 routers), teams implement their designs. Required configurations: (1) Create 5 VLANs with appropriate names and numbers, (2) Configure trunk ports between switches, (3) Implement RSTP for loop prevention, (4) Configure inter-VLAN routing on Layer 3 switch or router, (5) Deploy OSPF routing protocol, (6) Create ACLs restricting HR and Finance access, (7) Configure basic QoS for voice traffic prioritization. Students must document all commands used and verify connectivity between VLANs.

**Phase 3 (60 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Teams create comprehensive testing procedures and execute validation tests: ping tests between VLANs, ACL verification, OSPF neighbor relationships, spanning-tree topology verification. Final deliverable includes: network configuration files, test results documentation, and troubleshooting guide with common issues and solutions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or physical Cisco lab equipment (3560 switches, 2911 routers)
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart for network diagrams
Business requirements document template with TechCorp scenario details
Building floor plan handouts (3-floor layout with cubicle arrangements)
Configuration templates and command reference sheets
Validation testing checklist worksheet
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Network Design Quality (25 points) - logical topology, IP addressing efficiency, scalability; Implementation Accuracy (35 points) - correct VLAN configuration, routing functionality, security policies; Documentation Completeness (25 points) - configuration backup files, testing procedures, troubleshooting guides; Professional Presentation (15 points) - network diagrams clarity, team collaboration, technical communication during final demonstration. Students must achieve 80% connectivity success rate and demonstrate working inter-VLAN communication to pass.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for Struggling Students:** Provide VLAN configuration templates, step-by-step command guides for basic switch setup, pair struggling students with stronger technical teammates, offer additional lab time with instructor guidance. **Advanced Extensions:** Challenge advanced learners to implement HSRP for redundancy, configure dynamic VLAN assignment using RADIUS, add IPv6 dual-stack configuration, implement advanced QoS with traffic shaping policies, or integrate wireless access points with guest network isolation.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS: Practical Workshop
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security policies, and Quality of Service configurations. They will create network documentation, implement the design using Cisco Packet Tracer, and present their solution with justification for all design decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, routing protocols, and security policies by designing a multi-site enterprise network architecture
Students will construct and validate a complete network implementation through hands-on configuration and comprehensive testing procedures
instructions: Begin with a 15-minute scenario briefing: Students receive specifications for a fictional company requiring network infrastructure for 3 departments (Sales-50 users, Engineering-75 users, Management-25 users) across 2 buildings connected via WAN link. Step 1 (45 minutes): Students create detailed network topology diagrams showing physical and logical layouts, IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets, VLAN assignments (Sales-VLAN10, Engineering-VLAN20, Management-VLAN30), and security zones. Step 5 (30 minutes): Students prepare executive summary presentations including network diagrams, cost justifications, security implementation explanations, and disaster recovery considerations. Conclude with 5-minute individual presentations defending design choices.

Network design scenario handout with company specifications

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS: Exercise 2
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology featuring multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, trunk configurations, spanning tree optimization, and quality of service policies. This capstone activity integrates switching, routing, security, and traffic management concepts into a comprehensive network solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a multi-VLAN network architecture by creating detailed topology diagrams with VLAN assignments, IP addressing schemes, and trunk configurations
Students will implement advanced switching and routing protocols through hands-on configuration of VLANs, STP optimization, HSRP, and QoS policies on Cisco equipment
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Network Design and Planning**
Students work in teams of 2-3 to design a network for a fictional 200-employee company with four departments: Sales (50 users), Engineering (75 users), HR (25 users), and Management (50 users). Using Packet Tracer or physical equipment, teams must create a topology featuring: 2 core switches (3560 or higher), 4 access switches (2960 series), 1 multilayer switch for inter-VLAN routing, and 1 router for WAN connectivity. Teams assign VLANs (Sales=VLAN 10, Engineering=VLAN 20, HR=VLAN 30, Management=VLAN 40), design IP addressing using /24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16, and plan trunk links between switches.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Implementation and Configuration**
Teams configure their designed network by: creating VLANs on all switches using 'vlan [number]' and 'name [department]' commands, configuring access ports with 'switchport mode access' and 'switchport access vlan [number]', establishing trunk links using 'switchport mode trunk' and 'switchport trunk allowed vlan [list]', implementing Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol with 'spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst' and priority adjustments, configuring HSRP on multilayer switches for gateway redundancy, and creating basic QoS policies prioritizing Management VLAN traffic.

**Phase 3 (30 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Teams verify connectivity between VLANs using ping tests, document all configurations with 'show run' outputs, create network diagrams showing final topology with IP addresses and VLAN assignments, and prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their design decisions and demonstrating key functionalities.

Students must achieve 80% connectivity success and provide complete configuration documentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with VLAN numbers and IP ranges already assigned, offer command reference sheets with syntax examples, and allow additional consultation time with instructor. title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS: Exercise 3
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network infrastructure incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security protocols, and Quality of Service configurations. This capstone activity synthesizes advanced Cisco networking concepts into a real-world enterprise solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced Cisco configurations through hands-on deployment of VLANs, OSPF routing, port security, and QoS policies on physical equipment
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp needs a network for 200+ employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest) requiring different security levels and bandwidth priorities. Students work in teams of 3-4.

Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams analyze requirements and create network topology using Cisco Packet Tracer or Visio. Must include: hierarchical three-tier design, VLAN segmentation plan, IP addressing scheme using VLSM, equipment specifications (specific Cisco switch/router models), and security zone definitions.

Phase 2 (90 minutes): Physical implementation using provided Cisco equipment. Configure Layer 2 switches with VLANs 10 (Sales), 20 (Engineering), 30 (HR), 99 (Guest), and management VLAN 100. Implement 802.1Q trunking between switches, configure Layer 3 routing using OSPF on Cisco routers, and establish inter-VLAN routing with router-on-a-stick or SVI configuration.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Apply security measures including port security with MAC address limits, implement 802.1X authentication for user devices, configure ACLs restricting inter-departmental access, and enable DHCP snooping and Dynamic ARP Inspection.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Configure QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic (CoS 5), video conferencing (CoS 4), and business-critical applications (CoS 3). Implement traffic shaping and policing on WAN interfaces.

Phase 5 (45 minutes): Testing and documentation. Verify connectivity using ping, traceroute, and show commands. Document all configurations, create network verification matrix, and prepare 10-minute presentation demonstrating functionality.
materials_needed: Cisco Catalyst 2960 or 3560 Layer 2 switches (minimum 2 per team)
Cisco ISR 4000 series routers or equivalent (1 per team)
Ethernet cables (Cat6, various lengths)
Laptop computers with Cisco Packet Tracer installed
Console cables for device configuration
USB-to-serial adapters if needed
Network cable tester
Whiteboard or flip chart paper for topology diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four criteria: Network Design (25 points) - topology appropriateness, IP scheme efficiency, documentation quality; Technical Implementation (35 points) - VLAN configuration accuracy, routing protocol functionality, all devices reachable; Security Implementation (25 points) - ACL effectiveness, port security proper configuration, authentication mechanisms working; QoS and Optimization (15 points) - traffic prioritization functional, bandwidth management configured. Teams must demonstrate live network functionality and submit complete configuration files. Minimum 80% (80/100 points) required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing IP addressing templates and configuration command references. Pair less experienced students with stronger technical partners. For advanced learners, add challenges like implementing HSRP for redundancy, configuring site-to-site VPN tunnels, or integrating wireless access points with controller-based management. Provide Cisco documentation access and encourage use of 'show' and 'debug' commands for troubleshooting.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Drill: Converting Decimal 0-15 to Binary
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0 through 15 through repetitive flashcard practice. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary conversions that are essential for all computer science concepts involving data representation.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by correctly identifying binary equivalents within 3 seconds per number
Students will identify decimal values from their 4-bit binary representations through rapid recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (5 minutes setup). Each card shows a decimal number (0-15) on one side and its 4-bit binary equivalent on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs, with Partner A holding the deck and showing decimal numbers while Partner B states the binary equivalent. Partner A provides immediate feedback using the answer key. Start with numbers 0-7 for the first 10 minutes, drilling each number until the response time is under 3 seconds. Switch roles and repeat for 10 minutes. Next, expand to include numbers 8-15 for another 20 minutes using the same partner rotation. For the final 10 minutes, conduct a reverse drill where Partner A shows binary numbers and Partner B states the decimal equivalent. Throughout the activity, encourage students to use memory aids like 'powers of two' (8-4-2-1 positions) rather than calculation. Monitor pairs and provide immediate correction when students give incorrect answers. Students should achieve 90% accuracy at conversational speed before moving to the next number range.
materials_needed: 16 flashcards per student showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side
Binary equivalents printed on reverse side (4-bit format: 0000-1111)
Answer key sheets for self-checking
Timer or stopwatch for each pair
assessment_method: Conduct individual 2-minute rapid-fire assessments where each student must correctly convert 12 out of 16 random decimal numbers (0-15) to binary within 3 seconds each. Record accuracy percentage and average response time. Students achieving 75% accuracy or higher with sub-3-second response times demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with just numbers 0-7 and provide a powers-of-two reference chart (8-4-2-1). Allow them to point to positions initially before progressing to verbal responses. For advanced learners, extend the range to decimal numbers 16-31 (5-bit binary) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents for the same number set.

title: Optimizing Emergency Response Routes Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world emergency response optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, define objective functions, and use the simplex method to determine optimal ambulance dispatch routes that minimize response time while considering resource limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-constraint emergency response scenario into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic calculations to determine optimal resource allocation for emergency vehicle dispatch
instructions: Begin by distributing the Emergency Response Scenario packet containing a city map with 5 hospitals, 8 emergency locations, and ambulance capacity data (15 minutes). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the scenario where 12 ambulances must be optimally distributed to minimize total response time while respecting hospital capacity limits and fuel constraints. In Phase 1 (25 minutes), teams identify decision variables (number of ambulances assigned to each hospital-emergency route), formulate the objective function (minimize sum of distance × ambulances for all routes), and write constraint inequalities for hospital capacity (≤4 ambulances each), fuel limits (total distance ≤500 miles), and emergency coverage requirements (each emergency location must have ≥1 assigned ambulance). Phase 2 (40 minutes) involves setting up the initial simplex tableau with slack variables and implementing iterative calculations. Students must show all pivot operations, ratio tests, and optimality checks. Teams create a detailed solution matrix showing entering/leaving variables for each iteration. In Phase 3 (20 minutes), students interpret their final tableau to determine the optimal ambulance distribution and calculate the minimum total response time. Each team prepares a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical formulation, key simplex iterations, and final resource allocation with justification. Circulate continuously to check constraint formulations and simplex calculations, providing hints for pivot selection when needed.
materials_needed: Emergency Response Scenario packet with city map and data tables
Simplex method calculation worksheets with pre-formatted tableaux
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for constraint plotting
Presentation timer and flip chart paper
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation (25 points - correct identification of variables, objective function, and all constraints), Simplex method execution (40 points - accurate tableau setup, correct pivot operations, proper ratio tests), Solution interpretation (20 points - optimal values identified, practical meaning explained), Presentation quality (15 points - clear mathematical communication, justified recommendations). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in simplex calculations and correctly identify the optimal solution to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint identification templates and pre-completed first simplex iteration. Offer visual aids showing pivot selection rules. For advanced learners: Add sensitivity analysis component asking how solution changes with different hospital capacities, or extend to integer programming version requiring whole ambulances only. Provide dual problem formulation as an additional challenge.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Brake System Analysis: Comparing Theoretical Models with Real-World Performance
description: Students will analyze the electromagnetic braking system of a maglev train by deconstructing the relationship between induced EMF, eddy currents, and braking force. They will evaluate discrepancies between theoretical calculations and experimental data to identify factors affecting system efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between conductor velocity, magnetic field strength, and induced EMF by examining electromagnetic brake performance data across varying operational parameters
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of theoretical models through systematic comparison of calculated versus measured braking forces in eddy current brake systems
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a dataset containing velocity profiles, magnetic field measurements, and braking force recordings from an electromagnetic brake test apparatus. In the first 20 minutes, teams examine the raw data to identify three distinct operational phases: initial acceleration, constant velocity, and electromagnetic braking phases. Students calculate theoretical induced EMF using Faraday's law (EMF = -dΦ/dt) for each data point during the braking phase, assuming a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the conductor motion. Next, teams spend 30 minutes determining theoretical eddy current magnitudes using Ohm's law, incorporating the conductor's resistivity and geometric factors provided in the material specifications sheet. Students then calculate expected braking forces using F = BIL relationships, where B is magnetic field strength, I is induced current, and L is conductor length in the field. During the following 25 minutes, teams create comparative graphs plotting theoretical versus experimental braking forces against time, velocity, and position. Students identify systematic deviations between theoretical predictions and measured values, particularly noting non-linear relationships at high velocities. In the analysis phase (35 minutes), teams investigate potential sources of discrepancy including: skin effect at varying frequencies, magnetic field non-uniformities, temperature-dependent resistivity changes, and mechanical factors like air resistance. Students quantify the percentage error between theoretical and experimental values across different velocity ranges. Finally, teams prepare a technical analysis report documenting their findings, including error analysis, identification of dominant physical effects causing model limitations, and recommendations for improving theoretical predictions. Each team presents their most significant finding regarding model accuracy limitations.
materials_needed: Electromagnetic brake performance dataset (Excel file with velocity, magnetic field, and force measurements)
Material properties specification sheet (conductivity, dimensions, temperature coefficients)
Graphing software (Excel, Python, or MATLAB)
Scientific calculators
Electromagnetic induction reference equations sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations using Faraday's and Ohm's laws (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis identifying specific discrepancies and their magnitudes (30%), (3) Depth of investigation into physical factors causing model limitations (25%), and (4) Technical communication in written report and presentation clarity (20%). Success requires identifying at least three significant factors affecting model accuracy and quantifying errors within 15% of instructor solutions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided calculation worksheets with partially completed EMF calculations and highlight specific data ranges to analyze first. Offer additional reference materials explaining skin effect and temperature dependence. For advanced learners, provide supplementary datasets from different conductor materials or introduce frequency-domain analysis of eddy current effects, challenging them to develop improved theoretical models incorporating non-linear effects.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in Simple JavaScript Functions
description: Students will evaluate three different approaches to fixing a broken JavaScript calculator function by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will critique each solution using established coding standards and justify which approach is most appropriate for a beginner development team.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different JavaScript bug fix implementations by applying code quality criteria including readability, efficiency, and maintainability
Students will critique coding solutions through systematic analysis using a structured evaluation framework and defend their recommendations with evidence-based reasoning
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a handout containing: (1) Original broken calculator function that incorrectly handles division by zero and string inputs, (2) Three different 'fixed' versions labeled Solution A, B, and C, (3) Code evaluation checklist covering readability, error handling, efficiency, and best practices. **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students work independently to test each solution mentally/on paper, rating each criterion on the checklist (1-5 scale) and writing 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning for each solution. **Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their evaluations, focusing on areas where they rated solutions differently. Partners must provide evidence from the code to support their positions. **Class Evaluation (15 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion where volunteer pairs present which solution they recommend and why. Create a class tally of preferences on the board. Address common misconceptions about code quality. **Individual Reflection (10 minutes):** Students write a final 100-word recommendation memo to a 'junior developer' explaining which solution to implement, including at least two specific code examples as evidence and one potential improvement suggestion.
materials_needed: Printed handout with original buggy JavaScript function and three solution versions
Code evaluation checklist rubric (printed)
Computers/laptops for students to test code (optional but recommended)
Whiteboard/projector for class discussion
assessment_method: Evaluate final recommendation memos using rubric: (1) Clear position stated with specific solution choice (20 points), (2) Two concrete code examples cited as evidence (30 points), (3) Demonstrates understanding of code quality principles through accurate critique (30 points), (4) Provides constructive improvement suggestion (20 points). Observe peer discussions for evidence of analytical reasoning and use of technical vocabulary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled evaluation checklist with 1-2 criteria already completed as examples, pair with stronger analytical thinkers during peer discussion phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional bugs not mentioned in the original problem, or ask them to propose a fourth solution that combines the best elements of the given options.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn using real e-commerce data, incorporating multiple analysis techniques and presenting actionable business insights. They will synthesize descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and data visualization to deliver a comprehensive business intelligence solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a predictive analytics workflow by integrating data cleaning, exploratory analysis, and machine learning modeling techniques
Students will construct an interactive business dashboard through combining statistical insights with compelling visualizations that drive decision-making
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the e-commerce customer dataset containing 12 months of transaction history, customer demographics, and engagement metrics (2,500+ records). Students have 90 minutes to complete this activity.

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Data Exploration and Hypothesis Formation
Students examine the dataset structure, identify missing values, and formulate three specific hypotheses about factors contributing to customer churn. They must document data quality issues and create a data cleaning plan. Each team assigns roles: Data Engineer (cleaning), Analyst (exploration), Modeler (predictions), and Presenter (dashboard design).

Phase 2 (35 minutes): Analysis and Model Development
Teams clean their data according to their plan, then conduct exploratory data analysis focusing on their hypotheses. They calculate key metrics (customer lifetime value, purchase frequency, engagement scores) and build a simple logistic regression model to predict churn probability. Students must identify the top 5 predictive factors and validate their model using a 70/30 train-test split.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Dashboard Creation and Business Recommendations
Using their analysis results, teams create an interactive dashboard containing: churn probability distribution, key driver analysis, customer segmentation by risk level, and trend visualizations. The dashboard must include at least three actionable business recommendations with supporting data evidence. Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their methodology and insights.

Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure teams are progressing through each phase and provide guidance on technical challenges without solving problems directly.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with transaction, demographic, and engagement data)
Laptops with Python/R installed (pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib/seaborn libraries)
Tableau Public or Power BI accounts for dashboard creation
Data dictionary and variable explanation sheet
Presentation timer and projection capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Data methodology - appropriate cleaning and analysis techniques (25%), (2) Model validity - logical approach to churn prediction with reasonable accuracy metrics (25%), (3) Dashboard design - clear visualizations that effectively communicate insights (25%), and (4) Business recommendations - actionable suggestions supported by data evidence (25%). Teams must submit their dashboard file, analysis code, and a one-page executive summary. Bonus points awarded for creative visualizations or advanced statistical techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code for data cleaning and basic visualizations, offer guided questions to structure their analysis, and suggest focusing on 2-3 key variables rather than the full dataset. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement ensemble modeling techniques, create customer lifetime value predictions, or incorporate external data sources. Encourage advanced teams to mentor struggling groups during Phase 2. Provide statistical reference sheets and offer optional mini-tutorials on advanced visualization techniques.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an interactive analytical dashboard that predicts customer churn using historical data, implementing multiple visualization types and statistical models. estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-layered predictive analytics dashboard by integrating data preprocessing, statistical modeling, and interactive visualizations
Students will synthesize customer behavior patterns through advanced data analysis techniques to generate actionable business recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Foundation (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the telecom customer dataset containing 20 variables (customer demographics, service usage, billing history, churn status). Students work in pairs to first examine data quality, identifying missing values, outliers, and data types. They must document 5 data quality issues and propose solutions.

**Phase 2: Exploratory Analysis Design (60 minutes)**
Students create an analysis plan targeting churn prediction. They must identify 8-10 key variables for analysis and design specific visualizations: correlation heatmap for numeric variables, demographic breakdowns by churn status, service usage patterns, and billing trend analysis. Each pair sketches their dashboard layout on paper before coding.

**Phase 3: Statistical Modeling (75 minutes)**
Using Python/R, students implement logistic regression and decision tree models to predict churn probability. They must split data 70/30 for training/testing, calculate model accuracy, precision, and recall metrics. Students document which variables most strongly predict churn and interpret coefficients/feature importance.

**Phase 4: Dashboard Construction (90 minutes)**
Students build interactive dashboards using Tableau/Power BI/Plotly Dash containing: customer segment filters, churn probability distributions, top risk factors visualization, and a customer lookup tool showing individual churn risk scores. **Phase 5: Business Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each pair presents their dashboard to the class as if presenting to company executives, highlighting 3 key insights about customer churn patterns and providing 4 specific, data-driven recommendations for reducing churn rates.
materials_needed: Telecom customer churn dataset (CSV file with 7,043 records, 20+ variables)
Python/R with pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib/seaborn libraries installed

Presentation projection capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across 5 dimensions: Data Quality Assessment (identifies issues, proposes solutions), Statistical Analysis (appropriate model selection, correct interpretation of metrics), Dashboard Design (functionality, interactivity, visual appeal), Business Insights (relevance, specificity of recommendations), and Presentation Quality (clarity, professional delivery). Each dimension weighted equally for 100 total points. Students must achieve 75+ points and demonstrate working dashboard functionality during live presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data cleaning templates and code snippets for basic visualizations. Offer simplified dashboard requirements (4 charts minimum vs 6). title: PRINCE2 Process Model Component Identification Challenge
description: Students will systematically identify and memorize the 39 management products across PRINCE2's seven process groups through structured recall exercises. This activity focuses on accurate recognition of deliverables, reports, and registers within each process without requiring analysis or application.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 39 PRINCE2 management products by matching them to their correct process groups within 90% accuracy
Students will identify the specific purpose and classification (plan, report, register, or log) of each management product through progressive disclosure exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the PRINCE2 Process Reference Cards face-down to each student (10 minutes setup). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to complete the Management Products Matrix, filling in as many of the 39 products as they can recall from memory across the seven processes (Starting up, Directing, Initiating, Controlling a Stage, Managing Product Delivery, Managing Stage Boundary, Closing). Provide 3 minutes per process group. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Arrange students in pairs. Partner A uses the reference cards to quiz Partner B on products from randomly selected processes, then switch roles after 10 minutes. Partners must state the product name and its classification (plan/report/register/log). Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire class review where instructor calls out a process name and students must immediately write down all associated management products within 60 seconds per process. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Students individually complete the verification checklist, checking off each of the 39 products they can now recall without assistance. Conclude with students highlighting any products they still cannot recall for focused review.
