PRINCE2 Process Reference Cards (laminated, one set per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Individual verification checklists
Red and green highlighter pens
assessment_method: Students complete a final individual recall test listing all 39 management products under correct process headings within 15 minutes. Success criteria: 90% accuracy (35/39 products correctly placed). Award full points for exact product names and correct process placement. Deduct 0.5 points for spelling errors, 1 point for incorrect process placement, 1 point for missing products.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide the first letter of each management product name and allow use of acronyms (PID for Project Initiation Documentation). Group products by type first (all plans together, then reports, etc.) before sorting by process. For advanced learners: Add requirement to state which role is responsible for creating each product and identify interdependencies between products across processes.

title: Deconstructing Transformational Leadership Through Multi-Perspective Crisis Analysis
description: Students will analyze a complex organizational crisis through the lens of transformational leadership theory, examining how different leadership dimensions manifested across multiple stakeholders. They will demonstrate understanding by mapping specific leader behaviors to the four components of transformational leadership and explaining the interconnections between these dimensions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between the four components of transformational leadership (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration) by categorizing specific leader behaviors from a real crisis scenario
Students will explain the relationships between transformational leadership dimensions through structured analysis of stakeholder perspectives and outcomes
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Netflix leadership crisis case study (Reed Hastings' 2011 Qwikster decision) along with the Transformational Leadership Analysis Framework handout. Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member a stakeholder role: employees, customers, investors, and board members. 

Phase 1 (20 minutes): Individual preparation where each student reads the case and identifies 8-10 specific leadership behaviors or decisions, noting direct quotes and actions from their assigned stakeholder's perspective. Students use the framework to tentatively categorize these behaviors under the four transformational leadership components.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Within groups, members present their findings sequentially (5 minutes each), focusing on how Hastings' behaviors aligned or conflicted with transformational leadership principles from their stakeholder's viewpoint. The group recorder captures all behaviors on the large analysis matrix poster.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Groups collaborate to identify patterns and contradictions across stakeholder perspectives. They must reach consensus on classifying 12 key behaviors into the four transformational categories, noting where behaviors might overlap multiple categories.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Groups create a visual concept map showing the relationships between the four transformational leadership components as demonstrated in this crisis. They must include at least 6 connecting arrows with explanatory labels showing how components reinforced or undermined each other.

Phase 5 (15 minutes): Gallery walk where groups examine other teams' matrices and concept maps, using sticky notes to pose questions or offer alternative interpretations. Conclude with whole-class discussion addressing the most significant discrepancies in categorization and the implications for understanding transformational leadership complexity.
materials_needed: Netflix Qwikster crisis case study (3-page detailed scenario with stakeholder quotes)
Transformational Leadership Analysis Framework handout with component definitions
Large poster paper (11x17) with pre-drawn analysis matrix
Colored markers (4 colors per group)
Sticky notes (multiple colors)
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of behavior categorization into transformational leadership components (40%), (2) Quality of explanations for stakeholder perspective differences (30%), (3) Depth of relationship mapping between leadership dimensions in concept map (20%), (4) Engagement in peer review and discussion phases (10%). Success requires demonstrating understanding that transformational leadership components are interconnected and context-dependent, not isolated behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted case study excerpts and sentence starters for categorization explanations. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers during group work. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify where Hastings' approach deviated from pure transformational leadership toward other models, and to propose alternative leadership responses for each stakeholder group. Provide supplementary mini-cases showing contrasting leadership approaches to similar crises.

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and CloudFront
description: Students will create a complete static website hosting solution by configuring an S3 bucket for web hosting and implementing CloudFront distribution for global content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical application of AWS core services for real-world web deployment scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website by configuring S3 bucket policies and enabling static website hosting features
Students will implement content delivery optimization through setting up and configuring a CloudFront distribution with custom domain settings
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and a starter HTML/CSS website package containing index.html, error.html, and a styles folder with 2-3 CSS files. Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to S3 service.

**S3 Configuration (25 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a globally unique name following DNS naming conventions. Upload website files maintaining folder structure. Navigate to bucket Properties tab and enable Static Website Hosting, setting index.html as index document and error.html as error document. In Permissions tab, disable Block Public Access settings and add bucket policy allowing public read access to all objects. Test website functionality using the S3 endpoint URL.

**CloudFront Implementation (20 minutes):** Navigate to CloudFront service and create new distribution. Set S3 bucket as origin domain, configure default root object as index.html, and enable compression. Set cache behaviors for CSS files with longer TTL values. Deploy distribution and wait for status to change from 'In Progress' to 'Deployed'.

**Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Test website accessibility through CloudFront domain name. Verify CSS styling loads correctly and error page displays for non-existent URLs. Document both S3 and CloudFront URLs, comparing load times and noting geographical distribution benefits.

**Documentation (5 minutes):** Students complete deployment checklist including bucket name, policy configuration, CloudFront distribution ID, and both access URLs with timestamp of successful deployment.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account credentials for each student
Pre-built static website package (HTML, CSS, image files)
Deployment checklist template
AWS S3 bucket policy JSON template
assessment_method: Students must successfully demonstrate: (1) Functional website accessible via S3 endpoint (25 points), (2) Working CloudFront distribution with proper caching configuration (35 points), (3) Correct bucket security policy implementation (25 points), (4) Completed documentation with all required URLs and configuration details (15 points). Total: 100 points with 70+ indicating successful mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written bucket policy JSON and CloudFront configuration screenshots for reference. Create checkpoint validation after each major step. For advanced learners: Add custom domain configuration using Route 53, implement multiple cache behaviors for different file types, or add Lambda@Edge function for basic authentication.

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website Using Amazon S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create a complete static website hosting solution by configuring Amazon S3 buckets for web hosting and implementing CloudFront CDN for global content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration while building a real-world web hosting architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will apply S3 bucket configuration principles by setting up static website hosting with proper permissions and policies
Students will implement CloudFront distribution setup through connecting their S3-hosted website to AWS's global CDN network
instructions:
**Preparation (5 minutes):** Ensure all students have AWS Free Tier accounts and provide the sample HTML/CSS files (index.html, error.html, style.css). Display the reference architecture diagram showing S3-CloudFront integration.

**Part 1 - S3 Setup (20 minutes):** Students log into AWS Console and navigate to S3. They create a new bucket with a globally unique name (suggest using 'website-[their-initials]-[date]' format). In bucket properties, they enable static website hosting, set index.html as the index document and error.html as the error document. Students then upload their provided HTML/CSS files to the bucket root. Next, they configure bucket permissions by disabling 'Block all public access' and adding a bucket policy (provide template) that allows public read access to all objects.

**Part 2 - CloudFront Distribution (15 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront service and create a new distribution. They select their S3 bucket as the origin domain, configure the default cache behavior to redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and set the default root object to 'index.html'. After creation, students copy the CloudFront distribution domain name.

**Part 3 - Testing and Verification (10 minutes):** Students test both the S3 website endpoint and CloudFront URL in browsers, verify HTTPS functionality, and document the different response times. They submit a simple report with both URLs and a screenshot showing successful page loads.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Class discussion on observed performance differences and cost implications of using CloudFront versus S3-only hosting.

Sample website files (index.html, error.html, style.css)
Bucket policy JSON template
Architecture reference diagram
Computers with internet access and modern web browsers

Success criteria: both URLs functional, HTTPS working, and demonstrable understanding of performance differences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written bucket policies and step-by-step screenshots for bucket permission settings. Create troubleshooting guide for common issues like 403 errors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to add custom error pages, implement cache invalidation, or configure custom domain names. instructions: **Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Instructor provides each student with AWS account credentials and a starter portfolio template containing index.html, about.html, contact.html, and styles.css files. Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to S3 service. **S3 Configuration (25 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a globally unique name following format 'portfolio-[lastname]-[random4digits]'. They configure bucket for static website hosting by enabling the feature in Properties tab, setting index.html as index document and error.html as error document. They test the website using the S3 endpoint URL provided in the static website hosting configuration. **CloudFront Setup (20 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront service and create a new distribution. They configure the origin domain to point to their S3 bucket's website endpoint (not the bucket itself), set default root object to 'index.html', and enable compression. Students configure caching behavior to allow GET and HEAD methods, set TTL values (min: 0, default: 86400, max: 31536000), and enable query string forwarding. **Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** After CloudFront deployment completes (typically 15-20 minutes), students test their website using the CloudFront distribution URL. title: Risk Register Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Evaluation
description: Students will analyze a real-world project risk register to identify risk patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of existing mitigation strategies, and categorize risks by their potential impact on project triple constraints. This activity develops critical analytical skills needed for effective risk management in project environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies and patterns by examining probability-impact relationships across different risk categories in a project risk register
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of current risk response strategies through systematic assessment of mitigation approaches against PMI risk management best practices
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the sample construction project risk register containing 25 identified risks with current mitigation strategies. Each team receives colored markers, analysis worksheets, and PMI risk management reference sheets. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams categorize all 25 risks using the provided risk breakdown structure template, sorting by technical, external, organizational, and project management categories. They create a visual risk map plotting probability vs. impact on the provided grid.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students analyze risk interdependencies by identifying which risks could trigger others, drawing connection lines on their risk map. They must identify at least 5 risk relationships and document the cascading effects.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate each existing mitigation strategy against PMI's four risk response strategies (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept). They assess effectiveness using the provided scoring rubric (1-5 scale) and identify gaps in current approaches.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team develops three alternative mitigation strategies for the highest-priority risks, considering cost-benefit analysis and resource constraints provided in the scenario.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams present their analysis findings to the class, focusing on identified patterns, ineffective current strategies, and proposed improvements. Other teams provide peer feedback using structured evaluation forms.
materials_needed: Sample construction project risk register (25 risks with current mitigation strategies)
Risk breakdown structure template worksheets
Probability-impact grid charts (large format)
PMI risk management reference sheets
Colored markers and sticky notes
Scoring rubric for strategy effectiveness
Peer evaluation forms
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization and mapping (25%), (2) Quality of interdependency analysis with supporting rationale (25%), (3) Thoroughness of mitigation strategy evaluation using PMI criteria (30%), (4) Feasibility and innovation of proposed alternative strategies (20%). Teams must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example of 3 risks as a model and offer one-on-one guidance during Step 2. Advanced learners can be challenged to conduct quantitative risk analysis using expected monetary value calculations and create risk response contingency plans with specific triggers and timelines.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Routing Protocols
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF, HSRP, and advanced security features. They will create network documentation, implement the design on physical/virtual equipment, and validate all services are functioning correctly.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, routing protocols, and security policies by designing a comprehensive enterprise network architecture
Students will construct and validate a fully functional multi-VLAN network through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers
instructions:
Phase 1 - Design (90 minutes): Students work in teams of 2-3 to create network requirements for a fictional 200-employee company with 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest). They must design a topology using Cisco Packet Tracer showing: 3 VLANs for departments plus management VLAN, 2 Layer 3 switches with HSRP for redundancy, OSPF routing between distribution layers, port security and 802.1X authentication, and DHCP scoping per VLAN. Teams document IP addressing schemes, VLAN assignments, and security policies in a formal network design document.

Phase 2 - Implementation (120 minutes): Using physical Cisco 2960 switches and 2911 routers (or GNS3/EVE-NG), teams configure their designed network. Step-by-step: Configure VLANs and trunk ports on access switches, implement HSRP on distribution switches with priority settings, configure OSPF areas and redistribute connected networks, set up DHCP pools with appropriate exclusions and options, implement port security with sticky MAC addresses, configure basic 802.1X with local users, and establish inter-VLAN routing with ACLs for department isolation.

Phase 3 - Testing & Documentation (60 minutes): Teams conduct comprehensive testing including ping tests between VLANs, DHCP lease verification, HSRP failover testing, OSPF convergence validation, and security policy verification. They document all configurations, create network diagrams showing actual vs. planned implementation, and prepare a 10-minute presentation demonstrating network functionality. Each team presents their solution, explaining design decisions and demonstrating key features like VLAN isolation, redundancy failover, and security enforcement.
materials_needed: Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches (2 per team) or equivalent virtual switches
Cisco 2911 ISR routers (2 per team) or GNS3/EVE-NG simulation
Console cables and USB-to-Serial adapters
Ethernet patch cables (minimum 8 per team)
Cisco Packet Tracer software for initial design
Network documentation templates and IP address planning worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four components: Network Design Document (25%) - completeness of topology, IP addressing scheme, security policies; Implementation Quality (35%) - successful VLAN configuration, routing protocol operation, redundancy implementation; Testing & Validation (25%) - comprehensive testing procedures, problem identification and resolution; Professional Presentation (15%) - clear explanation of design decisions, demonstration of network features, response to technical questions. Success requires 80% minimum score with all VLANs operational, HSRP failover functional, and inter-VLAN routing with ACLs working correctly.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic switch/router configurations, offer additional guided practice with individual VLAN and routing protocol labs, create troubleshooting checklists for common configuration errors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like EtherChannel link aggregation, advanced OSPF features (area types, route summarization), integration with external BGP routing, or advanced security features like RADIUS authentication and dynamic VLAN assignment.

title: Python Syntax Flashcard Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements including keywords, operators, and basic statement structures. They will use digital flashcards and participate in rapid-fire recall exercises to demonstrate mastery of core Python vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recall 20 essential Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, etc.) by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recognize and name Python operators (+, -, *, /, ==, !=, <, >) and their symbols through visual identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made Anki flashcard deck containing 30 Python syntax cards. Students spend 15 minutes individually studying the cards, cycling through keywords (front shows keyword, back shows definition/example), operators (front shows symbol, back shows name and function), and basic syntax structures (front shows code snippet, back shows explanation). After individual study, pair students for 10 minutes of mutual testing using the same flashcards. Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session: display Python code snippets on the projector with missing keywords or operators highlighted in yellow. Students have 10 seconds to write down the missing element on their answer sheet. Complete 15 different code examples covering variables, loops, conditionals, and functions. For the final 10 minutes, students complete an individual written quiz where they must fill in blanks for 20 Python syntax elements in context. Provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers and having students self-score their quizzes using the provided answer key.
materials_needed: Pre-made Anki flashcard deck with 30 Python syntax cards
Projector and computer for displaying code snippets
Individual answer sheets with numbered blanks (1-15)
Written quiz handouts with 20 fill-in-the-blank Python code examples
Answer key printouts for self-scoring
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final written quiz to demonstrate successful recall. Additionally, observe student performance during rapid-fire recall session, noting response speed and accuracy. Use checklist rubric: Excellent (18-20 correct), Proficient (16-17 correct), Developing (13-15 correct), Beginning (below 13 correct).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference sheet with Python keywords grouped by category (control flow, data types, etc.) and allow extra study time. For advanced learners: include additional flashcards with more complex syntax like list comprehensions, lambda functions, and exception handling keywords. Consider pairing strong students with those needing support during partner practice.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance and Model Performance Trade-offs in Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance scores from three different machine learning models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, XGBoost) trained on customer churn data. They will explain why different models prioritize different features and discuss the business implications of these interpretations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings across multiple models by comparing coefficient values, permutation importance, and SHAP values
Students will explain model performance trade-offs through analyzing precision-recall curves and confusion matrices in the context of business costs
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-trained model outputs showing feature importance rankings for all three algorithms (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group one primary model to focus on initially. Students first spend 20 minutes individually examining their assigned model's feature importance scores, identifying the top 5 most important features and writing brief explanations for why each feature might be predictive of churn. Next, groups reconvene to create a shared interpretation document, discussing discrepancies in individual interpretations and reaching consensus (25 minutes). Groups then rotate stations to examine the other two models' outputs, spending 15 minutes at each station to document how feature rankings differ. In the final 30 minutes, each group presents a 5-minute summary comparing all three models, specifically addressing: (1) which features appear consistently important across models, (2) which features show high variance in importance rankings, and (3) what these differences suggest about each algorithm's decision-making approach. Groups must conclude with specific business recommendations about which model to deploy based on interpretability versus performance trade-offs. Instructor facilitates discussions between presentations, prompting students to justify their reasoning and challenge assumptions about feature relationships.
materials_needed: Pre-trained model outputs with feature importance scores (CSV files)
Customer churn dataset documentation with feature descriptions
Model performance metrics sheets (accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score)
Jupyter notebooks or printed feature importance visualizations
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of feature importance interpretation (25%), (2) Quality of cross-model comparisons with specific examples (25%), (3) Logical connection between technical findings and business recommendations (25%), (4) Use of appropriate data science terminology in explanations (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying at least 3 meaningful differences between models and providing evidence-based business justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a feature importance interpretation template with sentence starters like 'This feature ranks highly because...' and 'The business impact of this feature is...'. Include a glossary of key terms (coefficient, permutation importance, SHAP). For advanced learners, provide additional model diagnostics like partial dependence plots and ask them to explain non-linear relationships or feature interactions that might explain ranking differences.

title: Optimization of Packaging Costs Using Calculus: Real-World Business Case Study
description: Students apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve a realistic business problem involving minimizing packaging costs for a shipping company. They will use partial derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization to determine optimal box dimensions and material allocation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to minimize packaging costs by constructing mathematical models from real business constraints
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic algebraic manipulation and verification of solutions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the case study packet describing 'EcoShip Solutions,' a company needing to minimize cardboard costs while maintaining specific volume requirements and structural integrity constraints. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to analyze the problem parameters: boxes must hold 1000 cubic inches, cardboard costs $0.02 per square inch, and bottom reinforcement requires double-thickness material costing $0.035 per square inch. 

Next, guide students through a 25-minute modeling phase where they define variables (length=x, width=y, height=z), establish the volume constraint (xyz = 1000), and construct the cost function C(x,y,z) = 0.02(2xy + 2xz + 2yz) + 0.015xy for the reinforced bottom. Students must show all mathematical setup work on their solution sheets.

During the 35-minute solution phase, teams apply Lagrange multipliers to minimize C subject to the volume constraint. They calculate partial derivatives ∇C and ∇g (where g(x,y,z) = xyz - 1000), set up the system ∇C = λ∇g, and solve the resulting equations algebraically. Instructor circulates to check intermediate steps and provide targeted hints.

In the final 15-minute verification phase, students confirm their solution satisfies the constraint, verify it's a minimum using the second derivative test or border analysis, and calculate the total minimum cost. Teams prepare a brief summary showing optimal dimensions and cost savings compared to a standard 10×10×10 cube design.
materials_needed: EcoShip Solutions case study packets (1 per student)
Graphing calculators or laptops with mathematical software (Desmos, GeoGebra, or similar)
Solution recording sheets with guided framework
Whiteboard space or large paper sheets for team calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct mathematical model setup with appropriate variables and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier technique with proper partial derivatives (35%), (3) Complete algebraic solution with verification steps (25%), and (4) Correct interpretation and business context application (15%). Students submit individual solution sheets plus one team summary report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template sheets with partially completed constraint equations and remind them that z can be expressed as 1000/(xy). Offer a checkpoint after the modeling phase to verify correct setup. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding material waste constraints (15% waste factor) or multiple box size options with different volume requirements to create a more complex optimization scenario.

title: Analyzing Circuit Failure Modes in Multi-Stage Amplifier Networks
description: Students will systematically analyze a malfunctioning three-stage BJT amplifier circuit by examining voltage and current measurements at key nodes to identify failure modes and trace the cascade effects through the circuit stages. This activity requires students to break down complex circuit behavior into component-level analysis and synthesize findings to determine root causes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-stage amplifier circuit failures by systematically examining DC bias conditions, AC signal paths, and component interdependencies to identify root causes of malfunction
Students will differentiate between various failure modes (open circuits, short circuits, component degradation) through interpretation of voltage/current measurement data and signal flow analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the circuit schematic showing a three-stage common-emitter BJT amplifier with measured voltages at 15 test points under fault conditions. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (20 min): Students examine the provided measurements and compare them to expected values from their reference chart. They must identify which measurements indicate abnormal operation and mark these on their schematic. Phase 2 (25 min): For each abnormal measurement, students trace backwards through the circuit to identify possible component failures that could cause these readings. They create a fault tree diagram showing potential causes. Phase 3 (25 min): Students analyze the interaction between stages - how a fault in stage 1 affects stages 2 and 3. They must distinguish between primary failures (actual component faults) and secondary effects (downstream impacts). Phase 4 (15 min): Students synthesize their analysis to propose the most likely failure scenario, ranking possibilities by probability and providing technical justification. They must explain why other possibilities are less likely. Phase 5 (5 min): Each pair presents their conclusion in 2 minutes, defending their analysis against instructor challenges about alternative explanations.
materials_needed: Three-stage BJT amplifier schematic with 15 labeled test points
Data sheet showing measured voltages/currents at each test point under fault condition
Reference chart showing expected normal operating values for each test point
Blank fault tree diagram template
BJT characteristic curves and component datasheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of abnormal measurement identification (25%), (2) Quality of fault tree analysis showing systematic breakdown of possible causes (30%), (3) Correct analysis of inter-stage interactions and cascade effects (25%), (4) Logical synthesis and ranking of failure scenarios with technical justification (20%). Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guiding questions for each phase ('What should the base voltage be for Q2?' 'If R3 is open, how would this affect subsequent stages?'). For advanced learners: Add frequency response considerations and ask them to predict how the identified faults would affect AC performance at different frequencies. Provide additional fault scenarios with multiple simultaneous failures.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing a Simple Calculator Program
description: Students will evaluate a pre-written Python calculator program by identifying bugs, security issues, and code quality problems. They will justify their assessments using established coding standards and provide ranked recommendations for improvement.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the functionality and reliability of a Python calculator program by testing edge cases and identifying logical errors
Students will critique code quality and maintainability through systematic assessment using PEP 8 standards and best practices
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the buggy calculator.py file containing a basic calculator with intentional issues including: division by zero handling, input validation problems, unclear variable names, missing comments, and inconsistent formatting. Also distribute the Code Review Checklist handout.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students work independently to:
1. Run the program and test it with various inputs (positive/negative numbers, zero, non-numeric input, large numbers)
2. Read through the code line-by-line using the provided checklist
3. Document findings in three categories: Functionality Issues, Code Quality Issues, and Security/Safety Concerns
4. For each issue found, students must note the line number and explain why it's problematic

**Evaluation and Ranking Phase (15 minutes):** Students create a prioritized list of the top 5 issues they found, ranking them from most critical to least critical. For each issue, they must:
- Explain their reasoning for the priority ranking
- Suggest a specific solution
- Estimate the difficulty of fixing it (Easy/Medium/Hard)

**Peer Review Phase (15 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their findings and discuss any discrepancies in their evaluations. They should focus on defending their priority rankings and learning from issues they might have missed.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief whole-class discussion where 2-3 pairs share their highest priority issue and justification.
materials_needed: calculator.py file with intentional bugs (division by zero, poor variable names, missing input validation)
Code Review Checklist handout (covering functionality, readability, efficiency, error handling)
Computers with Python installed
Finding Documentation Template (table for recording line numbers, issues, and solutions)
assessment_method: Students submit their completed Finding Documentation Template showing: (1) At least 4 legitimate issues identified with correct line numbers (40%), (2) Clear explanations of why each issue is problematic (30%), (3) Logical priority ranking with solid justifications (20%), (4) Realistic and specific solutions proposed (10%). Success requires finding major functional bugs and demonstrating understanding of code quality principles.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide guided testing scenarios ("try entering 'abc' when prompted for a number") and highlight specific code sections to examine. **For advanced students:** Challenge them to also evaluate code efficiency, suggest refactoring opportunities, or propose additional features while maintaining code quality. Consider providing a second, more complex program to review.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing a Simple Calculator Program: Practical Workshop
description: Students will evaluate a pre-written Python calculator program by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and ranking different implementation approaches. This activity develops critical thinking skills for code assessment and quality judgment.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the functionality and efficiency of a Python calculator program by systematically testing inputs and analyzing code structure
Students will critique multiple code implementations through structured comparison using established programming principles
instructions:
Begin by distributing three different Python calculator implementations (provided as starter code) to each student pair. Each implementation contains 2-3 deliberate issues: one has logic errors, one has poor variable naming, and one has inefficient code structure but works correctly. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually examine Implementation A, testing it with at least 5 different input combinations including edge cases (division by zero, negative numbers, decimals). They document any bugs found and rate the code readability on a 1-5 scale with justification.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Repeat the process with Implementation B, using the same test cases for consistency. Students note differences in approach and identify strengths/weaknesses compared to Implementation A.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Examine Implementation C using identical testing methodology. Students complete a comparison chart ranking all three implementations across four criteria: functionality, readability, efficiency, and error handling.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Student pairs discuss their findings and must reach consensus on which implementation they would recommend for a beginner programmer to study, providing three specific reasons for their choice.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each pair presents their recommendation to another pair, defending their choice when challenged. Groups then submit a one-page evaluation report ranking the implementations with evidence-based justifications for each ranking decision.
materials_needed: Three Python calculator implementations (provided as .py files)
Code evaluation rubric handout
Comparison chart template (digital or printed)
Access to Python IDE or online Python interpreter
Test case worksheet with suggested inputs
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 20-point rubric: Testing thoroughness (5 points), Bug identification accuracy (5 points), Ranking justification quality (5 points), Use of programming principles in evaluation (3 points), Peer discussion participation (2 points). Students must identify at least 80% of planted issues and provide evidence-based reasoning for their final ranking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a code-reading checklist and pre-written test cases with expected outputs. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific code improvements for each implementation and estimate the relative performance impact of different approaches using Big O notation concepts.
original_title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing a Simple Calculator Program

title: Creating a Predictive Sales Dashboard with Multi-Source Data Integration
description: Students will design and build an interactive dashboard that integrates customer demographics, historical sales data, and seasonal trends to predict quarterly sales performance. They will synthesize multiple datasets, create original visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations based on their analytical findings.
learning_objectives: Students will create an integrated data model by combining at least three disparate datasets using appropriate join methods and data transformation techniques
Students will design original predictive visualizations through the development of interactive dashboard components that forecast sales trends and identify key performance drivers
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Preparation (45 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: customer_demographics.csv (500 records), sales_history.csv (2000 transactions), and seasonal_trends.csv (36 months). Students work in pairs to examine data structure using Excel or Google Sheets, identifying primary keys and data quality issues. They must document 5 data cleaning steps needed and create a data dictionary with field definitions.

**Phase 2: Integration & Modeling (60 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students import all three datasets and create relationships between tables. They must perform left joins to combine customer data with sales history, then incorporate seasonal adjustments. Students calculate new metrics: customer lifetime value, seasonal multipliers, and growth rates. Each pair creates 2 calculated fields showing quarterly projections.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students design a 4-panel dashboard including: 1) Sales forecast timeline with confidence intervals, 2) Top customer segments heatmap, 3) Seasonal performance comparison charts, and 4) KPI cards showing predicted vs. actual performance. Dashboard must include 3 interactive filters (date range, product category, customer segment) and consistent color coding.

**Phase 4: Business Insights (30 minutes)**
Pairs write a 2-page executive summary identifying 3 specific business recommendations based on their analysis. They must justify each recommendation with specific data points from their dashboard and quantify potential impact (revenue/percentage changes).
materials_needed: Three prepared CSV datasets (customer_demographics.csv, sales_history.csv, seasonal_trends.csv)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Computers with internet access for software download
Executive summary template document
Data dictionary worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across 5 criteria: Data Integration Quality (correct joins, clean data handling), Dashboard Functionality (all interactive elements work, professional design), Analytical Accuracy (calculations correct, appropriate chart types), Business Insight Quality (specific, data-supported recommendations), and Presentation Clarity (clear navigation, consistent formatting). Students submit dashboard file plus executive summary. Minimum passing: 12/20 points with no category scoring below 2/4.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide join relationship diagram template and pre-written calculated field examples. Offer step-by-step video tutorials for basic dashboard creation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external economic data, create statistical confidence intervals for predictions, or build drill-through functionality between dashboard panels. Provide dataset with intentional data quality issues for additional complexity.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific mathematical formulas, terminology, and calculation sequences used in Critical Path Method analysis. This high-stakes recall activity focuses on advanced CPM concepts including float calculations, crashing formulas, and resource leveling equations that practicing project managers must know by heart.
learning_objectives: Students will recall from memory the exact mathematical formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), and Late Finish (LF) calculations by completing timed formula reconstruction exercises

Students will identify and name the precise components of advanced CPM terminology including Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, and Project Float through rapid-fire definition matching activities
instructions: Begin by distributing blank CPM formula reference sheets to each student (5 minutes setup). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to fill in 25 missing formula components from memory, including ES = max(EF of predecessors), EF = ES + Duration, LS = LF - Duration, LF = min(LS of successors), Total Float = LS - ES, Free Float = min(ES of successors) - EF, and cost-crashing formulas. No notes or references permitted. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire terminology drill where instructor calls out advanced CPM terms (Critical Path, Dummy Activity, Node Slack, Resource Smoothing, Fast Tracking, Crashing) and students must write precise definitions within 30 seconds per term. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Present students with 15 complex project network diagrams containing multiple paths, merge points, and resource constraints. Students must identify and list all critical path sequences, calculate total project duration, and determine which activities have zero float - all from memory without performing calculations on paper. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Students self-check answers using provided answer key, marking incorrect responses in red. Instructor circulates to verify completion and identify students requiring additional memorization support. Conclude with 5-minute group recitation of the five most critical CPM formulas in unison.
materials_needed: Blank CPM formula reference sheets (one per student)
15 pre-designed complex network diagrams with solutions
Digital timer visible to all students
Red pens for self-assessment
CPM formula answer key sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on formula completion (20/25 components correct), 90% accuracy on terminology definitions (minimum 13/15 terms correct), and correctly identify all critical paths in at least 12/15 network diagrams. Document individual scores on provided tracking sheet and note students scoring below thresholds for remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (EELS: Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish) and allow 15 extra seconds per terminology question. For advanced learners: Add complex resource-constrained scheduling formulas and multi-project portfolio CPM calculations. Consider pairing strong students with those needing support during self-check phase.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing Decision-Making Frameworks Through Multi-Stakeholder Lens
description: Students will analyze complex crisis leadership decisions by examining the same scenario from multiple stakeholder perspectives, identifying underlying leadership frameworks, and explaining how different theoretical models influence decision-making processes. This expert-level activity requires students to synthesize multiple leadership theories while demonstrating deep comprehension of stakeholder dynamics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze crisis leadership decisions by comparing and contrasting how three different leadership frameworks (transformational, situational, and servant leadership) would approach the same multi-stakeholder scenario
Students will explain the interconnections between stakeholder perspectives and leadership decision-making processes through structured analytical frameworks
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 6, with each group receiving the 'TechCorp Data Breach Crisis' case study (15 minutes setup). Within each group, create three pairs: each pair receives one leadership framework card (transformational, situational, or servant leadership) containing key principles and decision-making characteristics. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each pair analyzes the crisis scenario through their assigned framework lens, documenting on the provided analysis template: (a) immediate priorities this framework would establish, (b) stakeholder engagement approach, (c) communication strategy rationale, and (d) long-term recovery decisions. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Pairs rotate to review other frameworks' analyses, using colored pens to annotate similarities, differences, and potential conflicts between approaches on sticky notes. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Groups reconvene to create a comprehensive stakeholder impact matrix, mapping how each leadership framework's decisions would affect customers, employees, shareholders, regulators, and community partners differently. Groups must identify and explain at least three critical decision points where frameworks diverge significantly. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Each group presents their matrix to another group, explaining the theoretical foundations behind framework differences and justifying why certain stakeholder impacts occur. Conclude with individual reflection journals (15 minutes) where students explain which framework elements they would combine and why, demonstrating understanding of leadership theory integration.
materials_needed: TechCorp Data Breach Crisis case study (2-page detailed scenario)
Leadership framework reference cards (transformational, situational, servant leadership)
Stakeholder impact matrix templates (11x17 paper)
Analysis documentation templates
Colored pens/markers for annotation
Sticky notes in three colors
Individual reflection journal templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of framework application (25%) - correctly identifies and applies leadership principles, (2) Depth of stakeholder analysis (25%) - demonstrates understanding of multi-perspective impacts, (3) Quality of comparative analysis (25%) - clearly explains differences and similarities between frameworks with specific examples, (4) Synthesis and justification (25%) - provides reasoned explanations for framework integration decisions. Collect group matrices, observation notes during presentations, and individual reflection journals for comprehensive assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework application examples from simpler scenarios before the activity, create reference sheets with guiding questions for each analysis phase, and allow extended time for template completion. For advanced learners: Add complexity by introducing ethical dilemma elements, requiring integration of additional leadership theories (authentic, adaptive leadership), or having them develop original crisis scenarios for peer groups to analyze using the same process.

title: Deploy and Configure a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS
description: Students will implement a complete three-tier web application architecture using AWS services including EC2, RDS, and Application Load Balancer. They will configure security groups, deploy application code, and establish database connectivity to create a functional web application accessible from the internet.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier web application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS database, and load balancer components on AWS
Students will implement proper security configurations through creating and applying security groups with appropriate port rules and access controls
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Instructor provides each student with AWS Learner Lab access credentials and a simple PHP web application code package containing connection scripts. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify access to EC2, RDS, and VPC services.

**Phase 1 - Database Layer (25 minutes):** Students navigate to RDS service and launch a MySQL database instance using t3.micro class with the following specifications: database name 'webapp', master username 'admin', password 'TempPass123!', publicly accessible disabled, and default VPC. While RDS provisions, students create a security group named 'database-sg' allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from source '10.0.0.0/16'.

**Phase 2 - Application Layer (30 minutes):** Students launch two EC2 instances (Amazon Linux 2, t2.micro) in different availability zones, naming them 'WebServer-1' and 'WebServer-2'. They create security group 'webserver-sg' allowing HTTP (port 80) from anywhere and SSH (port 22) from their IP. Students SSH into each instance, install Apache and PHP using 'sudo yum install -y httpd php php-mysqli', upload provided application files to /var/www/html/, and modify database connection strings with RDS endpoint information.

**Phase 3 - Load Balancer Layer (20 minutes):** Students create an Application Load Balancer named 'webapp-alb' using security group 'alb-sg' (HTTP port 80 from anywhere). They configure target group 'webapp-targets' with health check path '/health.php', register both EC2 instances as targets, and verify healthy status.

**Phase 4 - Testing (15 minutes):** Students access the load balancer DNS name in browser, verify application loads correctly, test database connectivity by submitting form data, and confirm load balancing by stopping one instance and verifying continued availability.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab account access for each student
Pre-built PHP web application package with database connection scripts
Step-by-step worksheet with RDS endpoint recording space
Computer with SSH client and web browser
Network connectivity confirmation checklist
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate: (1) Functional web application accessible via load balancer URL with working database connectivity (40 points), (2) Properly configured security groups with correct port rules and source restrictions (30 points), (3) Load balancing functionality proven by instance failover test (20 points), (4) Clean resource documentation showing all component relationships (10 points). Instructor verifies each component through AWS console review and application testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and database connection string examples. Create checkpoint verification at each phase before proceeding. For advanced learners: Add CloudWatch monitoring setup, implement auto-scaling groups, or configure SSL certificates with Route 53 custom domain. Provide troubleshooting decision tree for common connectivity issues.

title: Deploy and Configure a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply AWS fundamentals by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture using EC2, RDS, and S3. This hands-on activity requires students to configure security groups, launch instances, set up a MySQL database, and establish proper networking connections between all components.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration principles by launching and connecting web server and application server instances with proper security group settings
Students will implement AWS database services by creating and configuring an RDS MySQL instance and establishing secure connections from application servers
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Learner Lab credentials and the sample PHP application files (contact form with database connectivity). Students log into AWS Management Console and download application files to local machine.

**Phase 1 - Storage Tier (15 minutes):** Students create S3 bucket named 'webstatic-[studentname]-[date]', upload CSS and image files from provided application package, and configure bucket for static website hosting with public read permissions.

**Phase 2 - Database Tier (20 minutes):** Students navigate to RDS service and create MySQL database instance (db.t3.micro) named 'webapp-db'. Configure database with username 'admin', password 'WebApp123!', and create security group 'db-sg' allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from application tier subnet only.

**Phase 3 - Application Tier (25 minutes):** Students launch EC2 instance (t2.micro) with Amazon Linux 2, install Apache and PHP using provided installation script, and create security group 'app-sg' allowing HTTP (port 80) from web tier and SSH (port 22) from their IP. Upload PHP application files and configure database connection string with RDS endpoint.

**Phase 4 - Web Tier (20 minutes):** Students launch second EC2 instance for web server, configure Apache as reverse proxy, create security group 'web-sg' allowing HTTP from internet (0.0.0.0/0), and configure proxy rules to forward dynamic requests to application server.

**Testing Phase (10 minutes):** Students test complete application by submitting contact form, verifying data storage in RDS using provided SQL queries, and confirming static assets load from S3.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab access credentials for each student
Sample PHP contact form application with database connectivity code
Apache/PHP installation script for Amazon Linux 2
SQL test queries for database verification
Architecture diagram template for documentation
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Running web application with successful form submission, (2) RDS database query results displaying submitted data, (3) S3 bucket configuration with uploaded static files, (4) Security group configurations for all three tiers. Grading rubric: Application functionality (40%), proper security group configuration (30%), correct inter-tier communication (20%), documentation quality (10%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step SSH connection guides. Create checkpoint verification at each phase before proceeding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement auto-scaling groups, load balancers, or CloudFormation templates for infrastructure as code. Encourage exploration of CloudWatch monitoring and SNS notifications.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS

title: Deploy and Configure a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS: Team Exercise
description: Students will apply AWS services knowledge by deploying a complete three-tier web application using EC2, RDS, and S3. They will configure security groups, launch database instances, and establish connectivity between application layers to create a functioning web application accessible from the internet.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration skills by launching and configuring web server instances with proper security group settings
Students will apply database deployment principles by creating and connecting an RDS MySQL instance to their web application tier
instructions: Begin by having students access their AWS Management Console and create a new VPC with public and private subnets (10 minutes). Next, students launch an EC2 instance (t2.micro) in the public subnet, selecting Amazon Linux 2 AMI and creating a new key pair for SSH access (15 minutes). Students then configure security groups: one for the web tier allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) from anywhere, and another for the database tier allowing MySQL (port 3306) only from the web security group (10 minutes). In the private subnet, students create an RDS MySQL instance (db.t3.micro) with the database security group, noting the endpoint URL and credentials (20 minutes). Students SSH into their EC2 instance and install Apache web server and PHP using yum package manager (10 minutes). They then create a simple PHP application that connects to the RDS database, displays a connection status, and allows basic data insertion into a 'users' table (25 minutes). Students upload static assets (CSS, images) to an S3 bucket with public read permissions and modify their PHP application to reference these S3-hosted assets (15 minutes). Finally, students test their complete application by accessing the public IP address of their EC2 instance, verifying database connectivity, data insertion functionality, and proper loading of S3-hosted static content (15 minutes). Throughout the activity, students document their configuration choices and troubleshoot any connectivity issues between tiers.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account for each student
Pre-written PHP application code template with database connection functions
Sample static assets (CSS file and 2-3 images) for S3 upload
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Step-by-step configuration checklist handout

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis Using Project Scenario Decomposition
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario to identify risk interdependencies and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will break down the scenario into component risks, examine cause-and-effect relationships, and assess the alignment between risk characteristics and chosen response strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationships between multiple project risks by mapping cause-and-effect chains and identifying risk interdependencies within a realistic project scenario
Students will evaluate the appropriateness of risk response strategies through systematic comparison of risk characteristics against PMI's four response categories (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept)
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'TechFlow ERP Implementation' case study containing 8 interconnected project risks and their proposed response strategies (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a workspace with flip chart paper. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams create a risk interdependency map by placing each risk on a sticky note and drawing arrows to show cause-and-effect relationships, labeling arrow strength as High/Medium/Low impact. Phase 2 (30 minutes): For each risk, teams complete the Risk Analysis Matrix worksheet, categorizing each risk by probability (1-5 scale), impact (1-5 scale), and controllability (High/Medium/Low). They then evaluate whether the proposed response strategy (avoid/transfer/mitigate/accept) matches the risk characteristics using the PMI Risk Response Decision Tree provided. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams identify and document three specific misalignments between risk characteristics and proposed responses, explaining why current strategies are inappropriate and recommending alternative approaches with justification. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents their most critical misalignment finding to the class, explaining their analysis process and alternative recommendation. Instructor facilitates brief Q&A after each presentation, focusing on analysis methodology rather than answers.
materials_needed: TechFlow ERP Implementation case study (2-page handout with 8 risks and proposed responses)
Risk Analysis Matrix worksheet (1 page per team)
PMI Risk Response Decision Tree reference sheet
Flip chart paper and colored markers
Sticky notes (different colors for different risk categories)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Risk interdependency mapping completeness and accuracy (25%), (2) Systematic application of analysis framework to categorize risks (25%), (3) Quality of reasoning in identifying strategy misalignments with specific evidence (30%), (4) Clarity and logic in presenting alternative recommendations (20%). Students must identify at least 2 legitimate misalignments with sound justification to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of first risk analysis and emphasize using the decision tree systematically for each risk. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens if this risk occurs?' and 'Can we control this risk's likelihood?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify risk interactions using probability mathematics and develop integrated response strategies that address multiple related risks simultaneously.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis Using Project Scenario Decomposition: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario to identify risk categories, evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies, and determine which responses align with project constraints. This activity develops critical thinking skills for risk management decision-making in real project environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by categorizing threats and opportunities and evaluating strategy alignment with project objectives
Students will differentiate between risk response types through systematic comparison of strategy effectiveness and resource requirements
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Software Implementation Project' case study handout containing 12 identified risks with proposed response strategies, project constraints, and stakeholder priorities. Form teams of 3-4 students. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Each team reads the case study and creates a risk categorization matrix, sorting the 12 risks into threat categories (technical, organizational, external, project management) and opportunity categories (cost savings, schedule acceleration, scope enhancement). **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Teams analyze each proposed response strategy using the provided evaluation framework: identify whether each response is avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept, exploit, enhance, share, or accept; assess resource requirements (high/medium/low); evaluate alignment with project constraints (budget, timeline, quality standards). **Step 3 (15 minutes):** Teams identify conflicts between proposed strategies and project constraints, documenting specific examples where responses may create secondary risks or resource conflicts. **Step 4 (20 minutes):** Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation recommending modifications to 3 risk response strategies, justifying changes based on their analysis. **Step 5 (15 minutes):** Each team presents their recommendations while other teams provide feedback using the peer evaluation form. Instructor facilitates discussion on strategy trade-offs and decision-making rationale.
materials_needed: Software Implementation Project case study handout (2 pages per student)
Risk categorization matrix template
Risk response evaluation framework handout
Peer evaluation forms
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed risk categorization matrices (40 points: accuracy of risk categorization, completeness of strategy analysis). Assess presentation quality (35 points: clarity of reasoning, justification of recommendations, use of PMP terminology). Review peer evaluation forms for constructive feedback (25 points: specific examples, professional critique). Success criteria: 80% accuracy in risk categorization, clear identification of at least 2 strategy conflicts, and evidence-based recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of one risk analysis and offer the 'Risk Response Decision Tree' job aid. Encourage them to focus on 2-3 most obvious risks first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify risk impacts using probability/impact matrices and calculate expected monetary values for their recommended strategy changes. Have them consider stakeholder risk tolerances in their analysis.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Effectiveness Evaluation for E-commerce Conversion Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions. They will assess the strengths and limitations of each model and justify their recommended attribution strategy for specific business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, linear, time-decay, position-based) by analyzing conversion path data and assessing impact on marketing channel performance metrics
Students will critique and justify the selection of optimal attribution models through comprehensive analysis of customer journey complexity, business goals, and marketing channel effectiveness data
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Setup (20 minutes)** - Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active (paid search, social media, email, direct, organic search, display advertising). Students access Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths and Model comparison tool. **Phase 2: Baseline Analysis (30 minutes)** - Students document current attribution model settings and extract conversion data for each marketing channel under the existing model. They create a baseline performance spreadsheet showing conversions, revenue, and cost-per-acquisition for each channel. **Phase 3: Multi-Model Comparison (45 minutes)** - Using the Model comparison tool, students systematically apply each of the six attribution models to the same conversion data. They document how conversion credits shift between channels under each model, noting percentage changes in attributed conversions and revenue for each channel. Students calculate the variance in ROI rankings across models. **Phase 4: Customer Journey Analysis (35 minutes)** - Students examine conversion paths of varying lengths (1-touch vs. multi-touch journeys) using the Top conversion paths report. They identify patterns in customer behavior, average path length, and time to conversion. Students correlate these patterns with attribution model appropriateness. **Phase 5: Critical Evaluation (40 minutes)** - Students create a comprehensive evaluation matrix rating each attribution model against criteria: accuracy for business type, actionability for budget decisions, technical feasibility, and alignment with customer journey reality. They write detailed justifications for their assessments, citing specific data points from their analysis. **Phase 6: Strategic Recommendation (30 minutes)** - Students prepare a final recommendation report selecting the optimal attribution model for the business scenario, including implementation timeline, expected impact on marketing decisions, and potential limitations of their chosen approach.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled and 6+ months of multi-channel conversion data
Excel or Google Sheets template for attribution model comparison analysis
Attribution model evaluation matrix template with weighted scoring criteria
Access to GA4 Reports > Advertising > Attribution section and Model comparison tool
assessment_method: Students submit a comprehensive attribution strategy report (3-4 pages) including: (1) Data-driven comparison table showing quantitative differences between attribution models (25 points), (2) Critical analysis of each model's strengths/weaknesses with specific evidence from the GA4 data (30 points), (3) Justified final recommendation with implementation strategy and expected business impact (25 points), (4) Professional presentation of findings with clear data visualizations and executive summary (20 points). Rubric emphasizes depth of analysis, use of specific GA4 metrics, and quality of strategic reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled comparison templates and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer simplified scenarios focusing on 3-4 attribution models instead of all six. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution insights, cross-platform attribution analysis including offline conversions, and integration with Google Ads attribution modeling. Challenge them to propose A/B testing methodologies for attribution model validation.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Effectiveness Evaluation for E-commerce Conversion Optimization: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing real e-commerce data across multiple scenarios. They will assess which attribution model provides the most accurate insights for specific business objectives and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of at least four different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay) by comparing conversion data patterns and business impact metrics
Students will critique attribution model limitations through analysis of customer journey complexity and recommend optimal models for specific e-commerce scenarios
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Ensure Multi-Channel Funnel reports are available. Divide students into groups of 3-4.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Each group extracts conversion data using four attribution models: last-click, first-click, linear, and time-decay. Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool, select 'Conversions' as the conversion type, and export data for each model. They must document: total conversions per channel, conversion value, and cost-per-acquisition for each attribution model.

**Phase 2 - Scenario Analysis (30 minutes):** Present three business scenarios: (1) Brand awareness campaign evaluation, (2) Performance marketing ROI optimization, (3) Customer lifetime value improvement. Groups analyze how each attribution model would influence budget allocation decisions for each scenario, calculating percentage differences in channel performance rankings.

**Phase 3 - Critical Evaluation (25 minutes):** Students identify limitations of each model by examining customer journey length data from Path Length reports and analyzing assisted conversions. They must document at least three specific weaknesses per model and provide evidence from the data.

**Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (20 minutes):** Groups develop specific recommendations matching attribution models to business scenarios, including implementation timelines and success metrics. Final deliverable includes a 2-page analysis with quantitative justification and risk assessment for each recommendation.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Access to Multi-Channel Funnel reports with 6+ months of data
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel) for data analysis
Three specific business scenario handouts
Attribution Model Comparison worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data accuracy and completeness (25 points), Attribution model limitation identification with evidence (25 points), Scenario-specific recommendations with quantitative justification (30 points), Critical analysis depth and business insight quality (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of at least 3 attribution model weaknesses and provide specific percentage-based evidence for their recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each attribution model analysis. Create step-by-step navigation screenshots for accessing reports. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using data-driven attribution, incorporate Google Ads integration analysis, and add statistical significance testing requirements for their recommendations.
