title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with BGP Routing and Security Policies
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, BGP peering, and comprehensive security policies. They will create detailed network documentation and present their design rationale to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, BGP routing protocols, and access control lists to design a scalable enterprise network infrastructure
Students will evaluate and justify network design decisions through comprehensive documentation and stakeholder presentations
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Network Design Planning**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the enterprise scenario: A 500-employee company with HR, Finance, Engineering, and Guest networks requiring segmentation and internet connectivity through dual ISPs. Teams analyze requirements and sketch initial topology designs including IP addressing schemes, VLAN assignments, and BGP AS numbers.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Physical Implementation**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment, teams configure their designed network. Students must implement: 4 VLANs (VLAN 10-HR, 20-Finance, 30-Engineering, 40-Guest), configure trunk ports between switches, establish HSRP for gateway redundancy, configure OSPF for internal routing, and establish eBGP peering with two simulated ISPs (AS 65001, 65002). Each team member takes responsibility for specific components: Switch/VLAN configuration, routing protocols, security policies, or documentation.

**Phase 3 (30 minutes): Security Implementation**
Implement access control lists restricting inter-VLAN communication (HR cannot access Engineering, Guest isolated from internal networks), configure port security on access ports, and establish SSH access with encrypted passwords on all devices.

**Phase 4 (45 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Conduct comprehensive connectivity testing using ping, traceroute, and show commands. Document all configurations, create network diagrams with IP addressing tables, and prepare 10-minute presentations explaining design decisions, security rationale, and redundancy mechanisms.

**Phase 5 (60 minutes): Stakeholder Presentations**
Teams present their solutions to simulated executives (instructor and peer evaluators), defending design choices and answering technical questions about scalability, security, and cost considerations.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or physical Cisco routers (2841 or higher)
Cisco switches (2960 series minimum, 4 per team)
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Ethernet cables (minimum 12 per team)
Enterprise network requirements document template
Network documentation templates (topology diagrams, IP addressing sheets)
Laptops with terminal emulation software (PuTTY or similar)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network functionality and connectivity (30 points), proper VLAN and BGP configuration (25 points), security implementation effectiveness (20 points), documentation quality and completeness (15 points), presentation clarity and technical accuracy (10 points). Students must demonstrate working inter-VLAN routing, successful BGP convergence, and functional ACLs through live testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic switch/router settings and IP addressing hints. Offer configuration checklists for each protocol. For advanced learners: Add complexity with route redistribution between OSPF and BGP, implement QoS policies for voice traffic simulation, or configure advanced security features like 802.1X port authentication. Encourage advanced teams to implement IPv6 dual-stack configuration.

title: Optimization in Real-World Packaging: Maximizing Volume with Material Constraints
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a realistic packaging problem for a fictional company. They will use derivatives to find maximum volumes while working within material cost constraints and manufacturing limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative-based optimization methods to determine maximum volume configurations for rectangular packaging by setting up and solving constraint equations
Students will implement multi-variable calculus techniques through systematic analysis of cost-benefit scenarios in manufacturing contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet: students represent packaging engineers for 'EcoBox Solutions' tasked with designing optimal shipping containers. Each student receives specific constraints: total material budget of $2.40 per box, cardboard costs $0.15 per square foot, and boxes must have rectangular bases with length twice the width. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students set up the problem by defining variables (w=width, l=2w=length, h=height), establishing the surface area formula SA=2(wl+wh+lh)=2(2w²+3wh), and creating the cost constraint equation 0.15×SA=2.40. Step 2 (20 minutes): Students solve for height in terms of width: h=(16-4w²)/(3w), then establish the volume function V(w)=2w²×h=2w²×(16-4w²)/(3w)=(32w-8w³)/3. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students find the derivative V'(w)=(32-24w²)/3, set equal to zero, and solve to get w=√(4/3)≈1.155 feet. Step 4 (20 minutes): Students verify this is a maximum using the second derivative test V''(w)=-16w, calculate optimal dimensions (w≈1.155 ft, l≈2.31 ft, h≈1.73 ft), and determine maximum volume ≈4.62 cubic feet. Step 5 (10 minutes): Students create a brief presentation slide showing their optimization process, final dimensions, and maximum volume with cost verification.
materials_needed: Scenario packet with EcoBox Solutions company brief and constraint specifications
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos/GeoGebra)
Graph paper for sketching functions
Digital presentation platform (Google Slides/PowerPoint)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly sets up constraint equations, properly applies optimization techniques, accurately calculates dimensions and maximum volume; (3) Minor computational errors but demonstrates understanding of optimization process; (2) Sets up problem correctly but makes significant calculation mistakes; (1) Incomplete problem setup or major conceptual errors. Students must submit written work showing all steps plus presentation slide.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed constraint equation setup and encourage graphing V(w) to visualize the maximum. For advanced learners: extend to cylindrical containers or add additional constraints like minimum base area requirements. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during Step 2-3.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Field Interference Patterns in Multi-Source Wave Systems
description: Students will dissect complex electromagnetic interference patterns created by multiple coherent sources to identify individual wave characteristics and predict field strength variations. This activity requires students to decompose superposition effects and analyze how phase relationships, frequency differences, and spatial geometry affect resultant field patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic interference patterns by decomposing multi-source wave systems into component waves and identifying phase relationships, amplitude contributions, and frequency effects
Students will evaluate field strength variations through systematic examination of constructive and destructive interference zones using mathematical modeling and experimental data correlation
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a complex interference pattern dataset from a 4-source electromagnetic wave system (frequencies: 2.4 GHz, 2.41 GHz, 2.42 GHz, and 2.43 GHz). Students receive field strength measurements at 400 grid points across a 2m × 2m detection plane. Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams plot the raw interference pattern using provided software and identify regions of maximum and minimum field strength. They must mark at least 12 interference maxima and 12 minima on their plots. Step 2 (35 minutes): Students systematically analyze the pattern by calculating theoretical positions for two-source interference between each possible pair of sources (6 combinations total). They create overlay maps showing where each pair's interference patterns would produce maxima and minima. Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams examine frequency beating effects by identifying regions where close-frequency sources (2.4-2.41 GHz and 2.42-2.43 GHz) create temporal amplitude variations. They must calculate beat frequencies and correlate with measured field oscillations. Step 4 (25 minutes): Students decompose the overall pattern by determining relative phase shifts between sources. Using mathematical analysis, they work backward from interference positions to determine initial phase relationships. Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams validate their analysis by predicting field strength at 20 previously unmeasured test points and comparing with provided verification data. Final step (15 minutes): Each team presents their decomposition analysis, explaining how individual source characteristics combine to create the observed complex pattern.
materials_needed: Electromagnetic field strength dataset (400 measurement points) for 4-source system
MATLAB or Python with numpy/matplotlib libraries
Graph paper and colored pencils for manual plotting
Scientific calculators
Verification dataset with 20 additional measurement points
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of interference maxima/minima identification (25%), (2) Correctness of two-source pair analysis and theoretical calculations (30%), (3) Beat frequency analysis and phase shift determination (25%), (4) Prediction accuracy for verification points - must achieve >80% accuracy within ±5% tolerance (20%). Students must also provide written justification for their decomposition methodology and explain discrepancies between theoretical and measured values.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed calculations and focus initially on just two sources before expanding to four. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-source patterns first. For advanced learners: Include additional complications such as source amplitude variations, non-coherent noise components, or 3D field analysis. Challenge them to determine source positions from interference patterns alone or analyze polarization effects.

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Three Calculator Implementations
description: Students will analyze and evaluate three different implementations of a basic calculator program, assessing code quality, maintainability, and best practices. They will create a detailed comparison report ranking the implementations and justifying their evaluation with specific evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three calculator code implementations by analyzing readability, efficiency, and adherence to coding standards
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison using established quality criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three pre-written calculator programs (Implementation A: well-structured with clear variable names and comments; Implementation B: functional but poorly formatted with cryptic variable names; Implementation C: over-engineered with unnecessary complexity). Each program performs basic arithmetic operations but demonstrates different coding approaches.

**Individual Analysis Phase (25 minutes):** Students examine each implementation using the provided evaluation checklist covering: variable naming conventions, code organization, comment quality, error handling, and overall readability. They must score each criterion on a 1-5 scale and document specific examples from the code.

**Comparison Matrix Creation (15 minutes):** Students create a side-by-side comparison table showing strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. They must identify at least 3 specific strengths and 3 weaknesses per implementation with line number references.

**Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Students rank the three implementations from best to worst, writing a 200-word justification explaining their ranking decisions. They must reference specific code examples and connect their evaluation to real-world software development consequences.

**Peer Review (15 minutes):** In pairs, students share their rankings and justifications, discussing differences in their evaluations. They must identify at least one insight they gained from their partner's analysis.

**Final Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write 2-3 sentences explaining which evaluation criteria they found most important and why, connecting to professional software development contexts.
materials_needed: Three pre-written calculator programs (A, B, C) in same programming language
Code quality evaluation checklist handout
Comparison matrix template worksheet
Access to code editor or printed code copies
assessment_method: Grade using rubric with four components: (1) Completeness of evaluation checklist (25 points) - all criteria scored with evidence, (2) Quality of comparison matrix (25 points) - specific strengths/weaknesses identified with line references, (3) Ranking justification (35 points) - clear reasoning connecting code quality to practical impacts, (4) Professional communication (15 points) - clear writing and proper use of technical terminology. Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide sentence starters for justifications ("Implementation X is superior because...", "The main weakness of Implementation Y is..."). Highlight 2-3 specific code sections in each implementation to focus analysis. **Extension for advanced learners:** Ask them to rewrite the worst-ranked implementation to address identified weaknesses, or evaluate additional criteria like performance optimization and security considerations.

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Three Calculator Implementations: Practical Workshop
description: Students will analyze and evaluate three different JavaScript calculator implementations with varying code quality levels. They will assess each version against established coding standards and justify their quality rankings through written evaluations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three JavaScript calculator implementations by comparing them against established coding standards for readability, maintainability, and functionality
Students will critique code quality through systematic analysis and defend their quality rankings with specific evidence from the code examples
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-written JavaScript calculator implementations labeled Version A, B, and C (15 minutes setup). Version A should demonstrate excellent practices (clear variable names, proper commenting, modular functions, error handling). Version B should show mediocre quality (some good practices mixed with poor ones like inconsistent naming, minimal comments). Version C should exhibit poor practices (unclear variable names like 'x', 'y', no comments, one massive function, no error handling). 

Divide students into pairs and distribute the Code Quality Evaluation Worksheet containing criteria: readability (variable naming, code structure), maintainability (comments, function organization), functionality (error handling, edge cases), and efficiency (redundant code, optimal solutions). Each pair spends 20 minutes examining all three versions, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses for each criterion.

Next, pairs complete individual evaluation forms (15 minutes), ranking the three implementations from best to worst and providing written justifications citing specific code examples. For instance, they might write: 'Version A ranks highest because functions like calculateSum() use descriptive names while Version C uses unclear names like func1().'

Conclude with pair presentations (20 minutes total, 3-4 minutes per pair). Each pair presents their rankings and one key piece of evidence for their top and bottom choices. Facilitate brief discussions when pairs disagree on rankings, encouraging them to defend their evaluations with specific code references.
materials_needed: Three JavaScript calculator implementations (Version A, B, C) printed or digitally shared
Code Quality Evaluation Worksheet with assessment criteria
Individual evaluation forms for ranking and justification
Computers or tablets for viewing code (if shared digitally)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Excellent - correctly identifies quality differences, provides specific code examples, clear justifications; (3) Proficient - identifies most quality issues, adequate examples, sound reasoning; (2) Developing - identifies some issues, limited examples, basic reasoning; (1) Beginning - minimal quality recognition, vague examples, unclear reasoning. Grade based on written evaluation forms and presentation quality.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a completed example evaluation of a simple 'Hello World' program showing good vs. poor practices. Highlight specific code snippets during the activity and ask guiding questions like 'What makes this variable name helpful?' For advanced learners, add a fourth implementation with subtle quality issues or ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-ranked version.
original_title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Three Calculator Implementations

title: Design a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Business Growth
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior and demographics to provide actionable business recommendations. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and present strategic insights to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive customer segmentation model by analyzing transactional, demographic, and behavioral data using statistical clustering techniques
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining multiple visualization types that communicate customer insights to non-technical business stakeholders
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Preparation (45 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: customer_transactions.csv (6 months of purchase data), customer_demographics.csv (age, location, acquisition channel), and website_behavior.csv (page views, session duration, bounce rates). Students work in pairs to load data into their chosen tool, identify data quality issues, and create a master dataset by joining tables on customer_id. They must document 5 data quality issues found and their solutions.

**Phase 2: Segmentation Analysis (60 minutes)**
Students calculate RFM metrics (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value) for each customer and perform K-means clustering with 4-6 segments. They must justify their chosen number of clusters using elbow method or silhouette analysis. Each segment should be profiled with at least 5 distinguishing characteristics (average order value, preferred product categories, geographic distribution, etc.).

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Using their analysis, students design a 3-page interactive dashboard: Overview page (key metrics, segment distribution pie chart), Segment Deep-dive page (filterable tables, demographic breakdowns, behavioral patterns), and Business Impact page (revenue contribution by segment, growth opportunities). Dashboard must include at least 6 different visualization types and 3 interactive filters.

**Phase 4: Strategy Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each pair presents their dashboard to another pair acting as business stakeholders, delivering 3 specific marketing recommendations based on their segmentation with projected ROI estimates.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with realistic e-commerce data (500+ customer records)
Tableau Public, Power BI, or Python with Plotly/Streamlit installed on computers
Presentation template with business context and company background
Clustering analysis reference sheet with K-means algorithm explanation
assessment_method: Students submit dashboard files and written report (1000 words) documenting methodology, segment profiles, and business recommendations. Rubric evaluates: Data preparation quality (25%), Statistical rigor of segmentation (25%), Dashboard design and interactivity (25%), Business insight quality and feasibility (25%). Peer feedback forms assess presentation clarity and persuasiveness of recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code for data joining and K-means clustering, offer pre-made color palettes for visualizations, and give guiding questions for each analysis step. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional clustering algorithms (hierarchical, DBSCAN), add predictive elements (customer lifetime value, churn probability), or create automated reporting features with scheduled data refreshes.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Calculation Formula Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 essential Critical Path Method terms, definitions, and mathematical formulas through intensive flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This foundational knowledge enables precise application of CPM techniques in complex project scheduling scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all CPM terminology including Early Start (ES), Late Start (LS), Early Finish (EF), Late Finish (LF), Total Float, and Free Float definitions within 30 seconds per term
Students will memorize and recite the exact mathematical formulas for forward pass, backward pass, and float calculations through structured repetition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM terminology reference sheet containing 25 terms with definitions and 8 calculation formulas. Students have 20 minutes to study independently using any memorization technique. Next, implement the progressive recall protocol: Round 1 (15 minutes) - students work in pairs with provided flashcards, alternating as questioner and responder, covering all 25 terms twice. Round 2 (10 minutes) - individual silent review focusing on missed items from Round 1. Round 3 (20 minutes) - rotate partners and repeat flashcard exercise, but now include formula recitation where students must write formulas from memory on mini-whiteboards. Round 4 (15 minutes) - final individual assessment where students complete the terminology matching worksheet and formula recall quiz without references. Monitor student progress by circulating and noting common errors. Conclude with immediate feedback session where correct answers are displayed and students self-check their work, identifying specific terms requiring additional practice.
materials_needed: CPM terminology reference sheet with 25 key terms and definitions
Pre-made flashcard set (50 cards: 25 terms, 25 definitions)
Mini-whiteboards and dry erase markers (one per student)
CPM formula reference sheet with 8 calculation formulas
Terminology matching worksheet (assessment version)
Digital timer for each round
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (23/25 terms correct) on the final terminology matching quiz and correctly write 7/8 formulas with proper variable notation. Award points as follows: Term-definition matching (75 points, 3 per correct match), Formula accuracy (25 points, 3-4 points per formula based on complexity). Record individual scores and identify students scoring below 85% for additional practice sessions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide abbreviated study sheet with only 15 core terms, allow additional 10-minute review period, and permit use of pneumonic devices written on index cards. For advanced learners: add 10 supplementary terms related to resource leveling and crashing techniques, require explanation of when each formula applies in project contexts, and challenge them to create original memory aids for classmates.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Philosophy: Comparative Analysis of Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Management Case Studies
description: Students will analyze two contrasting leadership approaches by examining how transformational and transactional leaders respond to organizational crises. Through systematic comparison of real-world case studies, students will demonstrate deep understanding of these leadership philosophies and their underlying principles.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership philosophies by identifying specific behavioral indicators and decision-making patterns in crisis scenarios
Students will interpret the underlying motivational theories and power structures through systematic analysis of leader-follower interactions during organizational challenges
instructions: Begin by distributing two detailed case studies: Southwest Airlines' response to 9/11 (transformational - Herb Kelleher) and General Motors' 2008 financial crisis response (transactional - Rick Wagoner). Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to read both cases, highlighting leader behaviors, communication patterns, and decision-making processes. Next, provide the Leadership Philosophy Analysis Matrix template with columns for 'Leadership Behavior,' 'Underlying Philosophy,' 'Follower Response,' and 'Outcome Impact.' Students spend 30 minutes categorizing evidence from both cases into transformational vs. transactional frameworks, identifying specific examples of inspirational motivation vs. contingent rewards, intellectual stimulation vs. management by exception, and individualized consideration vs. passive leadership. During the analysis phase, students must cite specific quotes and actions from leaders, connecting them to Bass's Four I's of transformational leadership or Burns' transactional leadership components. In the final 25 minutes, pairs present their comparative analysis to another pair, defending their categorizations with textual evidence. Each group must identify at least three distinct philosophical differences and explain how these differences manifested in crisis response strategies. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where groups share one surprising insight about how leadership philosophy directly influenced organizational outcomes during crisis periods.
materials_needed: Southwest Airlines 9/11 response case study (3-page printed version)
General Motors 2008 crisis case study (3-page printed version)
Leadership Philosophy Analysis Matrix template (digital or printed)
Bass's Transformational Leadership reference sheet
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Analysis Matrix for accuracy in categorizing behaviors (40%), quality of textual evidence cited (30%), and depth of philosophical connections made (30%). Students must correctly identify minimum 6 leadership behaviors per case study and demonstrate understanding by explaining the 'why' behind each categorization with specific theoretical connections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed matrix with 2-3 examples already categorized and explained. For advanced learners, add a third case study (hybrid leadership style) and require them to identify elements that don't fit neatly into either category, pushing them toward situational leadership understanding.

title: Risk Register Comparative Analysis: Examining Risk Response Strategy Effectiveness Across Project Phases
description: Students will analyze three different risk registers from construction projects at varying phases (initiation, execution, closing) to identify patterns in risk response strategies and evaluate their appropriateness. They will deconstruct the relationship between risk characteristics, project phase constraints, and selected mitigation approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective risk response strategies by examining real-world risk registers and categorizing responses based on PMBOK risk management principles
Students will analyze the correlation between project phase characteristics and risk response selection through systematic comparison of risk treatment approaches across project lifecycles
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three anonymized construction project risk registers labeled 'Project A-Initiation,' 'Project B-Execution,' and 'Project C-Closing.' Each register contains 8-12 risks with identified responses. Organize students into teams of 3-4.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student individually reviews all three registers, using the provided analysis worksheet to categorize each risk response as Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, or Accept. Students note response appropriateness on a 1-5 scale with justification.

**Phase 2 - Team Comparison (20 minutes):** Teams consolidate individual findings using the comparison matrix template. They identify: (1) Most common response types per project phase, (2) Instances where response type seems mismatched to risk severity/probability, (3) Patterns in stakeholder involvement across phases.

**Phase 3 - Cross-Phase Analysis (15 minutes):** Teams complete the 'Phase Constraints Impact Chart,' analyzing how project phase limitations (budget availability, timeline pressure, stakeholder engagement) influenced response selection. They must cite specific examples from the registers.

**Phase 4 - Synthesis Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents their top 3 insights about risk response patterns, highlighting one example of excellent strategy alignment and one example of poor strategy selection. Teams must reference specific risks and justify alternatives for poorly selected responses.

**Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates discussion on how project phase characteristics should influence risk response strategy selection, connecting findings to PMBOK risk management process integration.
materials_needed: Three authentic construction project risk registers (8-12 risks each, different project phases)
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet (individual)
Team Comparison Matrix Template
Phase Constraints Impact Chart
PMBOK Risk Response Strategy Reference Sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk response categorization (25%), (2) Quality of cross-phase pattern identification with specific examples (30%), (3) Appropriateness of alternative response recommendations (25%), (4) Integration of PMBOK principles in analysis (20%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in at least 3 categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide risk response decision tree flowchart and highlight 2-3 obvious examples in each register before independent work. For advanced learners: Add fourth register with international project requiring cultural/regulatory considerations, or ask them to create cost-benefit analysis for their recommended alternative responses.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Analysis: Evaluating E-commerce Conversion Path Effectiveness
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 by analyzing multi-channel conversion paths for an e-commerce business. They will assess which attribution model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by comparing conversion path analysis results and ROI calculations
Students will critique current marketing channel performance through cross-referencing attribution reports with audience behavior data to make evidence-based budget reallocation recommendations
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Collection (20 minutes)** Students access provided GA4 demo account or instructor-shared view-only account with 6+ months of e-commerce data. Navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths. Export data for 90-day period showing assisted conversions, top conversion paths, and channel interaction patterns. Switch between attribution models (Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison) and screenshot key metrics for each model. **Phase 2: Analysis Setup (25 minutes)** Create comparison spreadsheet with columns for each attribution model showing: channel-specific conversion values, cost-per-acquisition, return-on-ad-spend (ROAS), and assisted conversion rates. Calculate the variance in credit allocation between models for top 5 traffic channels. Cross-reference with Audience reports (Demographics, Interests) to identify which channels drive highest-value customer segments. **Phase 3: Critical Evaluation (35 minutes)** Students work in pairs to evaluate each attribution model's strengths/weaknesses for this specific business context. Consider factors: customer journey length (Advertising > Attribution > Path length), seasonal patterns (Reports > Life cycle > Acquisition > Traffic acquisition with date comparisons), and profit margins by product category. Identify which model most accurately reflects actual customer behavior patterns and provides most actionable insights for marketing budget decisions. **Phase 4: Recommendation Development (25 minutes)** Prepare 3-slide presentation defending chosen attribution model with: quantitative comparison showing percentage differences in channel valuation, specific budget reallocation recommendations with projected ROI impact, and identified limitations/assumptions of chosen model. **Phase 5: Peer Review (15 minutes)** Present findings to another pair, defend model choice against questioning, and provide feedback on peers' analysis methodology and evidence quality.
materials_needed: GA4 account with 6+ months e-commerce data (demo account or instructor-provided access)
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for analysis
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
Calculator for ROI computations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Data accuracy and completeness of attribution model comparison (25%), (2) Quality of critical analysis considering business context and customer behavior patterns (35%), (3) Evidence-based justification for recommended attribution model with quantitative support (25%), (4) Identification and acknowledgment of chosen model's limitations and assumptions (15%). Successful completion requires demonstrating clear understanding of how different models impact channel valuation and providing actionable, defensible recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled comparison template with sample calculations and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer attribution model 'cheat sheet' explaining when each model works best. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models, analyze micro-conversions alongside macro-conversions, or evaluate attribution for different customer segments separately. Encourage integration of external data sources (ad spend from platforms, profit margins) for more sophisticated analysis.

title: Interpreting Confusion Matrices for Multi-Class Classification Problems
description: Students will analyze pre-generated confusion matrices from three different machine learning models to understand model performance patterns and identify specific classification errors. They will compare precision, recall, and F1-scores across classes to explain which model performs best for different business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret confusion matrix patterns by identifying true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives for each class in a multi-class classification problem
Students will explain the relationship between confusion matrix values and performance metrics through calculating and comparing precision, recall, and F1-scores across different models
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-prepared confusion matrices for a customer churn prediction problem with four classes: 'Loyal', 'At-Risk', 'Lost', and 'New' customers (15 minutes setup). Organize students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group one confusion matrix initially. Have students spend 20 minutes examining their assigned matrix, identifying the diagonal (correct predictions) and off-diagonal elements (misclassifications), and noting which classes are most frequently confused with each other. Next, provide the formula sheet for precision, recall, and F1-score calculations. Students calculate these metrics for each class in their assigned matrix (25 minutes). Rotate the matrices so each group analyzes all three models (30 minutes total for remaining two matrices). During the final 25 minutes, groups create a comparison chart ranking the three models for each class and overall performance. Each group presents their findings in a 3-minute summary, explaining which model they would recommend for: (1) minimizing false negatives for 'At-Risk' customers, (2) maximizing overall accuracy, and (3) balanced performance across all classes. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion connecting confusion matrix patterns to real-world business implications of different types of classification errors.
materials_needed: Three printed 4x4 confusion matrices with different performance patterns
Formula reference sheet for precision, recall, and F1-score calculations
Calculators or laptops with calculator function
Comparison chart template (paper or digital)
Whiteboard or projector for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of classification patterns in confusion matrices (25%), (2) Accurate calculation of precision, recall, and F1-scores for at least 2 classes per matrix (35%), (3) Appropriate model selection reasoning for each business scenario (25%), and (4) Clear explanation of the relationship between matrix values and business impact (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in calculation accuracy and 2/4 points in all other areas to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a worked example using a 2x2 confusion matrix before moving to 4x4 matrices, and highlight one row/column at a time when calculating metrics. Create reference cards showing the precision formula with highlighted numerator/denominator for each class. For advanced learners, introduce weighted averages for overall metrics, discuss class imbalance implications, or have them suggest additional evaluation metrics like ROC curves. Provide a real dataset excerpt so advanced students can connect matrix patterns to actual customer behaviors.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Arrays Using Linear Programming and Calculus
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques and multivariable calculus to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel placement on irregularly shaped rooftops. They will work with constraints, objective functions, and shadow calculations to maximize energy output while considering budget and structural limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to maximize solar energy output by formulating constraint equations and objective functions from real building specifications
Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques through partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to determine optimal panel positioning under shadow constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing rooftop blueprints showing irregular building shapes with dimensions, structural load limits, and obstacle locations (chimneys, vents). Students work in teams of 3-4. In the first 20 minutes, teams analyze their assigned building data to identify: available surface area, structural weight capacity (kg/m²), budget constraints ($15,000-$25,000), and shading obstacles. Next, spend 30 minutes having students establish variables: let x₁, x₂, x₃ represent number of panels in different roof sections, define P(x,y,t) as power output function accounting for sun angle over time t, and create constraint inequalities for weight (Σwᵢxᵢ ≤ Wₘₐₓ), budget (Σcᵢxᵢ ≤ B), and area limitations. During minutes 50-80, students formulate the optimization problem: maximize P(x₁,x₂,x₃,t) = Σηᵢ·Aᵢ·I(t)·cos(θᵢ(t))·(1-shadow_factor) subject to their established constraints. For minutes 80-110, teams apply the simplex method or use graphical analysis for 2-variable cases, then use calculus to find critical points by setting ∂P/∂xᵢ = 0 and applying second derivative tests. In the final 30 minutes, students calculate actual energy output predictions, total system cost, payback period, and create a visual layout showing optimal panel placement. Each team presents their solution showing mathematical work, final configuration diagram, and economic justification.
materials_needed: Building blueprint packets with 5 different rooftop layouts and specifications
Solar panel specification sheets (efficiency ratings, dimensions, costs, weights)
Graphing calculators or computer access with optimization software (Excel Solver or Python)
Sun path diagrams and shadow calculation worksheets
Large grid paper for scale drawings
assessment_method: Teams submit a technical report (40 points) containing: properly formulated constraint equations (10 pts), correct objective function with shadow calculations (10 pts), accurate mathematical solution process (10 pts), and realistic final recommendations (10 pts). Oral presentations (20 points) demonstrate understanding of optimization methods used and ability to defend mathematical choices. Peer evaluation forms (10 points) assess collaboration and mathematical communication within teams.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide constraint equation templates, offer simplified 2-variable versions focusing on area and budget only, and supply shadow calculation lookup tables. For advanced learners: introduce time-dependent optimization requiring integration over seasonal sun paths, add maintenance scheduling variables, or incorporate battery storage optimization as additional variables requiring dynamic programming approaches.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Using Thevenin Equivalent Analysis
description: Students will systematically analyze a complex multi-loop DC circuit with multiple voltage sources and resistive components to identify which component failure caused observed voltage discrepancies. They will deconstruct the circuit using Thevenin equivalent analysis and compare theoretical predictions with experimental data to isolate the faulty component.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex multi-loop circuits by applying Thevenin equivalent circuit principles to simplify and isolate individual component contributions
Students will evaluate experimental voltage measurements against theoretical calculations through systematic component-by-component failure analysis
instructions: Begin by providing each student group with a pre-built circuit containing 6 resistors (ranging from 100Ω to 1kΩ), 3 DC voltage sources (5V, 9V, 12V), and measurement data showing unexpected voltage readings at three test points. Students have 20 minutes to measure actual voltages using digital multimeters at the designated nodes. Next, instruct students to create Thevenin equivalent circuits for each test point by removing the load resistor and calculating equivalent resistance (15 minutes of calculations). Students must then determine the open-circuit voltage for each Thevenin equivalent using nodal analysis or mesh current methods (25 minutes). Following calculations, students systematically test their Thevenin models by reconnecting loads and comparing predicted voltages with both their measurements and the provided 'faulty' data (20 minutes). During the analysis phase (30 minutes), students identify discrepancies between their Thevenin predictions and the given faulty measurements, then hypothesize which component failure (open circuit, short circuit, or resistance change) could explain each discrepancy. Students test their hypotheses by temporarily modifying their physical circuit to simulate suspected failures and observing if the voltage patterns match the original faulty data. Finally, groups present their analysis methodology and conclusions, explaining how Thevenin equivalent analysis helped isolate the specific component failure location and type (15 minutes per group presentation).
materials_needed: Pre-constructed breadboard circuits with 6 resistors (100Ω, 220Ω, 330Ω, 470Ω, 680Ω, 1kΩ)
Three DC power supplies (5V, 9V, 12V) or battery packs
Digital multimeters (one per group of 2-3 students)
Circuit failure scenario data sheets with 'measured' faulty voltages
Graph paper and scientific calculators
Jumper wires and spare resistors for testing failure hypotheses
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of Thevenin equivalent calculations (25 points), (2) Systematic comparison methodology between theoretical and experimental data (25 points), (3) Logical reasoning in identifying component failure type and location (30 points), (4) Quality of experimental verification of failure hypothesis (20 points). Students must submit calculation worksheets, hypothesis testing data, and final component failure diagnosis with supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed Thevenin calculation templates and guide them to focus on one test point initially. Offer hint cards suggesting specific failure types to consider (open, short, 50% resistance change). For advanced learners, introduce frequency-dependent components or ask them to design a diagnostic protocol for identifying multiple simultaneous component failures. Encourage advanced students to consider measurement uncertainty and tolerance effects in their analysis.

title: Design and Build a Customer Retention Dashboard for an E-commerce Business
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard from raw e-commerce data to identify customer retention patterns and develop data-driven recommendations for business improvement. This capstone activity combines data cleaning, statistical analysis, and visualization design to produce a comprehensive business intelligence tool.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer transaction data by designing custom metrics and creating interactive visualizations that reveal retention patterns
Students will construct evidence-based business recommendations through statistical analysis and present findings via a professional dashboard interface
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Preparation (45 minutes)**

Provide students with the 'EcommerceTransactions.csv' dataset containing 10,000 customer records with fields: CustomerID, OrderDate, OrderValue, ProductCategory, and CustomerAcquisitionDate. Students work individually to import data into Tableau or Power BI, then clean the dataset by removing duplicates, handling null values, and creating calculated fields for: customer lifetime value, days since last purchase, purchase frequency, and customer tenure.

**Phase 2: Metric Design (30 minutes)**

Students define and calculate three custom retention metrics: 30-day repeat purchase rate, customer cohort retention curves, and churn risk scoring based on recency/frequency analysis. They must document their metric definitions in a shared spreadsheet and validate calculations with sample customers.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (60 minutes)**

Using their chosen BI tool, students build a 4-panel dashboard containing: (1) executive summary KPIs showing overall retention rates, (2) cohort analysis heatmap displaying monthly retention by acquisition cohort, (3) customer segmentation scatter plot with lifetime value vs. purchase frequency, and (4) at-risk customer identification table with actionable contact priorities. Each panel must include interactive filters for date range and product category.

**Phase 4: Business Recommendations (30 minutes)**

Students analyze their dashboard findings to develop three specific, data-supported recommendations for improving customer retention. They create a final slide within the dashboard summarizing key insights, proposed interventions, and expected impact metrics. Each recommendation must reference specific data points from their analysis.
materials_needed: EcommerceTransactions.csv dataset (provided by instructor)
Tableau Desktop or Microsoft Power BI (student licenses)
Laptops/computers with internet access
Dashboard template rubric handout
Shared Google Spreadsheet for metric definitions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data cleaning and calculated fields (25 points), Custom metric accuracy and documentation (20 points), Dashboard design and interactivity (25 points), Visual clarity and professional presentation (15 points), Business recommendations quality and data support (15 points). Students submit dashboard files plus a 2-page executive summary. Bonus points awarded for creative insights or advanced statistical techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated field formulas and dashboard wireframe templates. Offer 15-minute checkpoint consultations after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate statistical significance testing, predictive modeling elements, or advanced visualizations like survival curves. Provide access to supplementary datasets for cross-validation of findings.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate recall of advanced Critical Path Method formulas and terminology by completing timed identification exercises using real project network diagrams. This activity focuses on memorizing and retrieving specific CPM calculations including Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Float calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), and Total Float by completing formula identification cards within 90 seconds per formula
Students will identify specific CPM terminology definitions through rapid-fire recall exercises using authentic project scheduling scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet face-down to each student (5 minutes setup). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Display a project network diagram on the projector showing activities A through J with durations. Students have 2 minutes to study the diagram, then remove it from view. Provide each student with a CPM Formula Worksheet containing 10 blank formula templates (ES = ?, EF = ?, LS = ?, LF = ?, TF = ?). Students must fill in the complete formulas from memory within 8 minutes. No reference materials allowed. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire terminology recall using flashcards. Display terms like 'Critical Path,' 'Resource Leveling,' 'Schedule Compression,' 'Fast Tracking,' and 'Crashing' for 5 seconds each. Students write definitions on individual whiteboards and hold up answers simultaneously. Cover 25 terms total. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Memory verification round where students self-check their Phase 1 formulas against the reference sheet, marking correct/incorrect answers. Record individual scores on the tracking sheet. Conclude with a 5-minute group recitation where the class states each formula aloud in unison three times to reinforce memory consolidation.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet (1 per student)
Project network diagram printout (A through J activities)
CPM Formula Worksheet with 10 blank templates
Individual whiteboards and dry-erase markers
CPM terminology flashcards (25 cards)
Student score tracking sheet
Timer/stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (8/10) on formula recall and 70% accuracy (18/25) on terminology definitions to demonstrate mastery. Use the provided scoring rubric: Formula Section (50 points) - 5 points per correct formula; Terminology Section (50 points) - 2 points per correct definition. Record completion time for each phase. Students scoring below threshold receive immediate remediation using the reference materials.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for formula sequences (e.g., 'Every Smart Leader Thinks Forward' for ES-EF-LS-LF-TF). Allow additional 30 seconds per formula during Phase 1. For advanced learners: Add complex scenarios requiring formula application with multiple predecessors and successors. Include advanced concepts like Free Float and Independent Float calculations.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Recall Challenge: Technical Implementation
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the 16 essential CPM formulas and their variable definitions used in advanced project scheduling analysis. This high-stakes recall activity tests retention of complex mathematical relationships critical for PMP certification and professional practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 16 Critical Path Method formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF, etc.) by completing timed formula reconstruction exercises without reference materials
Students will identify and define 48 specific CPM variable abbreviations (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF, D, etc.) through rapid-fire terminology matching activities
instructions: Begin by distributing Formula Reference Sheets face-down to each student. Explain that they have 15 minutes to study the 16 CPM formulas and 48 variable definitions silently. After study time, collect all reference materials. Distribute the CPM Formula Recall Worksheet containing 16 incomplete formulas with missing components (e.g., 'EF = ES + ___' or '___ = LF - LS'). Students have exactly 20 minutes to complete all formulas from memory. Next, project the Variable Definition Quiz on screen, showing abbreviations one at a time for 10 seconds each (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF, D, etc.). Students write the complete definition for each abbreviation. After 48 terms, conduct immediate peer checking using answer keys. Students mark correct/incorrect responses and calculate their accuracy percentage. Finally, identify students scoring below 80% for immediate remediation using color-coded formula cards. Have high-scoring students (90%+) serve as peer tutors for struggling learners. Conclude with a verbal rapid-fire round where you call out scenarios and students shout back the appropriate formula name.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheets (16 formulas with definitions) - one per student
CPM Formula Recall Worksheets with blanks - one per student
Variable Definition Answer Keys - one per student
Color-coded formula cards for remediation
Digital timer/stopwatch
Projector for displaying variable abbreviations
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (13/16 correct) on formula completion and 85% accuracy (41/48 correct) on variable definitions. Grade using provided answer key with exact formula syntax required. Award full points only for precise mathematical notation and complete variable definitions matching provided standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded formula families (time calculations=blue, float calculations=green). Use pneumonic devices like 'Early Start + Duration = Early Finish.' For advanced learners: Challenge them to explain when each formula applies in real project scenarios or derive formulas for complex network situations with multiple constraints.
original_title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Recall Challenge

title: Analyzing Leadership Paradoxes Through Multi-Stakeholder Impact Mapping
description: Students will examine and interpret complex leadership paradoxes by analyzing how contradictory leadership decisions affect different organizational stakeholders. Through detailed case study analysis, students will demonstrate understanding of how paradoxical leadership behaviors can simultaneously create positive and negative outcomes across multiple organizational levels.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the underlying tensions in paradoxical leadership decisions by mapping stakeholder impacts across organizational hierarchies
Students will explain how competing leadership demands create systemic trade-offs through comprehensive multi-dimensional analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing the Netflix leadership case study featuring Reed Hastings' 2011 Qwikster decision and the 2018 culture memo controversy (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, ensuring diverse professional backgrounds per team. Each team receives a large poster board and colored markers. Step 1: Teams spend 20 minutes identifying and listing all stakeholders mentioned or implied in both scenarios (employees, shareholders, customers, competitors, media, board members, etc.). Step 2: Create a stakeholder impact matrix by drawing a large grid with stakeholders on the Y-axis and the two leadership decisions on the X-axis (15 minutes). Step 3: For each stakeholder-decision intersection, teams spend 30 minutes analyzing and documenting both positive and negative impacts using specific evidence from the case, color-coding positive impacts in green and negative impacts in red. Step 4: Teams identify and circle paradoxical outcomes where the same leadership action created opposing effects for the same stakeholder or similar effects for opposing stakeholders (20 minutes). Step 5: Each team presents their completed matrix to the class, spending 5 minutes explaining their three most significant paradoxical findings and how these paradoxes reflect competing leadership demands (20 minutes total for all presentations). Step 6: Conclude with individual reflection where each student writes a 200-word summary explaining how understanding these paradoxes changes their interpretation of effective leadership in complex organizational contexts (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Netflix leadership case study packet (Qwikster decision and culture memo)
Large poster boards (one per team)
Colored markers (green, red, black, blue)
Individual reflection worksheets
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed stakeholder impact matrices using a 4-point rubric: stakeholder identification completeness (25%), impact analysis accuracy and evidence use (35%), paradox recognition and explanation (25%), individual reflection quality demonstrating comprehension (15%). Success requires identifying minimum 8 stakeholders, documenting at least 3 clear paradoxical outcomes with specific evidence, and articulating nuanced understanding in reflection.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a stakeholder identification starter list and impact analysis sentence stems ('This decision helped/harmed [stakeholder] because...'). For advanced learners, add complexity by requiring analysis of long-term vs. short-term paradoxical effects and connection to specific leadership theories. Consider pairing students with complementary analytical strengths within teams.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis Through Project Scenario Breakdown
description: Students will analyze a complex construction project scenario to identify risk categories, evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk responses, and determine interdependencies between risk mitigation strategies. This activity develops critical thinking skills for real-world project risk management decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by categorizing risks into technical, external, organizational, and project management types and evaluating the appropriateness of avoid, transfer, mitigate, and accept strategies
Students will examine risk interdependencies through systematic mapping of how individual risk responses impact other project constraints and stakeholder interests
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 members (5 minutes). Distribute the Metropolitan Hospital Expansion Project case study, which includes 12 identified risks with proposed response strategies. Each group receives different colored sticky notes and a large poster template with four quadrants labeled: Technical Risks, External Risks, Organizational Risks, and Project Management Risks (5 minutes setup). 

Students first individually read the case study and identify all risks mentioned, writing each on a sticky note (10 minutes). Groups then collaborate to categorize each risk into the appropriate quadrant on their poster, discussing disagreements until consensus is reached (15 minutes). 

Next, groups analyze each proposed risk response strategy using the provided evaluation matrix. For each risk, they must: identify whether the response strategy (avoid/transfer/mitigate/accept) is appropriate given the risk probability and impact, determine if the response creates secondary risks, calculate the cost-benefit ratio using provided budget data, and assess alignment with project constraints (25 minutes). 

Groups create a risk interdependency map by drawing connection lines between risks that influence each other, using different colored lines for positive and negative correlations (15 minutes). Each group prepares a 5-minute presentation highlighting their three most critical findings about inappropriate risk responses or overlooked interdependencies (10 minutes preparation). 

Groups present their analysis in round-robin format, with other groups providing one question or challenge per presentation (20 minutes total). Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing group findings and introducing additional industry examples (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Metropolitan Hospital Expansion Project case study handout (12 pages with risk register)
Risk Response Evaluation Matrix template (Excel spreadsheet with probability/impact calculations)
Large poster paper with pre-drawn quadrant template
Colored sticky notes (4 colors per group)
Colored markers for interdependency mapping
Timer for presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization (25%), (2) Quality of risk response analysis with specific justifications (35%), (3) Identification of at least 5 meaningful risk interdependencies with clear explanations (25%), and (4) Presentation clarity and peer engagement (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in categories 1-3 to demonstrate analyze-level competency.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a partially completed risk categorization example and sentence starters for analysis ('This response strategy is inappropriate because...'). For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by asking them to propose alternative response strategies with cost estimates and timeline impacts, or analyze how risk responses might differ across project phases.

title: Critical Evaluation of Multi-Channel Attribution Models for E-commerce Campaign Optimization
description: Students will critically analyze and evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce conversion data. They will assess which attribution model provides the most accurate insights for budget allocation decisions and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating attribution discrepancies across channels
Students will critique existing campaign performance interpretations through comparative analysis of attribution model outputs and defend optimal budget reallocation strategies
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with at least 500 conversions across multiple channels (paid search, social, email, direct, organic). Students work individually. **Step 1 (20 minutes):** Navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. Students must extract conversion and revenue data for the same date range using all five attribution models, documenting results in provided spreadsheet template with specific metrics: total conversions, conversion value, cost per conversion, and ROAS for each channel. **Step 2 (25 minutes):** Calculate percentage variance between last-click (baseline) and each alternative model for every channel. Identify the three channels with highest attribution discrepancies and analyze the conversion path reports to understand customer journey patterns causing these differences. **Step 3 (30 minutes):** Using the Conversion Paths report, examine the top 10 conversion sequences. Students must evaluate which attribution model most accurately reflects the actual customer decision-making process based on touchpoint frequency, sequence patterns, and time between interactions. **Step 4 (35 minutes):** Create a detailed budget reallocation proposal comparing current spend (based on last-click attribution) with recommended spend under their chosen optimal attribution model. Include projected ROI improvements, risk assessment, and implementation timeline. Students must defend their choice with at least three quantitative metrics and address potential counterarguments.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 property with 6+ months e-commerce data
Attribution analysis spreadsheet template with pre-formatted calculation fields
Campaign budget and cost data spreadsheet
Access to Google Ads account linked to GA4 property
assessment_method: Students submit a 3-page executive summary with: (1) Data analysis section showing attribution model comparison with accurate calculations (30 points), (2) Critical evaluation section identifying optimal attribution model with justified reasoning using conversion path evidence (40 points), (3) Budget reallocation strategy with ROI projections and risk mitigation (30 points). Rubric evaluates data accuracy, depth of critical analysis, strength of evidence-based arguments, and feasibility of recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated variance formulas and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer example conversion path interpretations. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution modeling exercise using Google Analytics Intelligence API, or add competitive analysis component comparing attribution insights across multiple industries.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Redundancy and Security
description: Students will architect a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites with redundant WAN connections, implement OSPF routing with area design, configure VLANs with inter-VLAN routing, and establish site-to-site VPN connectivity. This capstone project integrates routing protocols, switching technologies, security implementations, and network optimization strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable three-site enterprise network topology by creating detailed network diagrams, IP addressing schemes, and VLAN segmentation plans that meet specific business requirements

Students will implement advanced routing and switching configurations through hands-on configuration of OSPF multi-area design, HSRP redundancy, 802.1Q trunking, and IPSec VPN tunnels using Cisco equipment
instructions:
**Phase 1 (90 minutes): Network Design & Planning**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with the business scenario: Company ABC needs to connect headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and remote office (50 users). Each site requires guest network isolation, server farm access, and redundant internet connectivity. Teams must create: (1) Physical and logical network topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, (2) Complete IP addressing scheme using /16 network with VLSM, (3) OSPF area design with area 0 at headquarters, (4) VLAN design with naming conventions and purposes, (5) Security policy including ACLs and VPN requirements.

**Phase 2 (120 minutes): Implementation in Packet Tracer**
Teams build their designed network using Cisco Packet Tracer with minimum equipment: 6 routers (2901 series), 6 switches (2960 series), and appropriate end devices. Configure OSPF routing with proper area assignments and authentication. Implement VLANs across all sites with 802.1Q trunking. Configure HSRP on distribution switches for gateway redundancy. Establish site-to-site IPSec VPN tunnels between all locations. Create and apply standard and extended ACLs for security requirements.

**Phase 3 (60 minutes): Testing & Documentation**
Conduct comprehensive connectivity testing using ping, traceroute, and show commands to verify all network services. Document all router and switch configurations with comments explaining each section. Create network verification report showing routing tables, VLAN assignments, and VPN tunnel status. Prepare 10-minute presentation explaining design decisions, implementation challenges, and solutions deployed.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version)
Network diagramming software (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart)
Business requirements document template
IP address planning worksheet
Cisco IOS command reference sheets
Laptops/computers with sufficient processing power
Projector for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - topology appropriateness, IP scheme efficiency, OSPF area logic; Implementation Accuracy (35 points) - correct configurations, full connectivity, security measures; Documentation (20 points) - configuration comments, verification reports, design rationale; Presentation (20 points) - technical accuracy, problem-solving explanations, team coordination. Success criteria: All inter-site connectivity functional, VPN tunnels established, VLANs properly segmented, OSPF convergence under 30 seconds, ACLs blocking unauthorized traffic while permitting required services.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured baseline templates with basic connectivity, offer checkpoint reviews after each phase, pair with stronger technical partners, provide additional command syntax references. For advanced learners: Add requirements for BGP external routing, implement QoS policies, configure SNMP monitoring, design disaster recovery scenarios, optimize convergence times through advanced OSPF features like LSA filtering and area summarization.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Redundancy and Security: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure spanning multiple geographic sites with redundant WAN connections, VLAN segmentation, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity integrates routing protocols, switching technologies, network security, and disaster recovery planning into a realistic business scenario.
estimated_duration: 5.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes, VLAN structures, and redundant pathways

Students will implement advanced Cisco technologies through hands-on configuration of OSPF routing, HSRP redundancy, inter-VLAN routing, and ASA firewall policies to meet enterprise-level performance and security standards
instructions:
**Phase 1: Requirements Analysis (45 minutes)** - Present students with GlobalTech Corp scenario: headquarters in Dallas (500 users), branch offices in Chicago (150 users) and Miami (100 users), requiring secure inter-site communication, guest network isolation, and 99.9% uptime SLA. Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze requirements and create initial network design documents including subnet calculations for /22 network 192.168.0.0, VLAN planning (data, voice, guest, management), and equipment specifications.

**Phase 2: Topology Design (60 minutes)** - Using Cisco Packet Tracer, teams create detailed network topology featuring dual ISP connections at headquarters, MPLS primary/broadband backup WAN links, Cisco 2960 access switches, 3560 distribution switches, and 4331 routers at each site. Students must document IP addressing schemes, VLAN assignments, and create logical network diagrams showing Layer 2/3 boundaries.

**Phase 3: Core Configuration (90 minutes)** - Teams configure OSPF routing with area design (Area 0 at HQ, Area 1-2 for branches), implement HSRP for gateway redundancy using virtual IP addresses, configure inter-VLAN routing with SVIs, and establish VTP domains for VLAN propagation. Each team member specializes in one site's configuration while maintaining coordination.

**Phase 4: Security Implementation (75 minutes)** - Configure Cisco ASA firewalls with inside/outside/DMZ zones, implement access control lists restricting inter-VLAN communication, establish site-to-site VPN tunnels using IPSec, and configure port security on access switches. Teams create security policy documents detailing firewall rules and access restrictions.

**Phase 5: Testing and Documentation (60 minutes)** - Execute comprehensive testing including ping/traceroute verification, failover testing by disabling primary links, security validation through unauthorized access attempts, and performance testing with traffic generators. Teams create final documentation packages including configuration files, network diagrams, IP address spreadsheets, and operational procedures manual.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version) installed on lab computers
GlobalTech Corp business scenario handout with detailed requirements
Network documentation templates (topology diagrams, IP address tables, security policies)
Access to physical Cisco lab equipment: 2960 switches, 4331 routers, ASA 5506-X firewalls (minimum 3 sets for team rotation)
Ethernet cables, console cables, and USB-to-serial adapters
IP subnet calculator reference sheets
assessment_method: Teams submit comprehensive network design portfolio (40 points) including annotated topology diagrams, complete configuration files, and operational documentation. Live demonstration and defense (35 points) where teams present their solution and answer technical questions about design decisions. Practical functionality testing (25 points) evaluated through instructor-led verification of connectivity, redundancy failover, security policies, and performance benchmarks. Rubric includes technical accuracy, design scalability, security implementation, documentation quality, and professional presentation delivery.
scaffolding_notes: **Supporting Struggling Students**: Provide pre-configured baseline templates with partial OSPF and VLAN configurations, offer one-on-one troubleshooting sessions during configuration phases, create checkpoint reviews after each phase with instructor feedback. **Extending Advanced Learners**: Challenge teams to implement QoS policies for voice traffic prioritization, configure dynamic routing redistribution between OSPF and EIGRP, add wireless controller integration with guest portal authentication, implement network monitoring with SNMP and syslog servers, or design IPv6 dual-stack implementation alongside IPv4.
