title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Redundancy and Security: Practical Workshop
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three geographically distributed sites with redundant WAN connections, advanced routing protocols, network segmentation, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity integrates OSPF, EIGRP, BGP, VLANs, ACLs, VPN technologies, and Quality of Service implementations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) and switching technologies to create a scalable multi-site network architecture that meets specified business requirements
Students will design and implement comprehensive security policies including ACLs, VPN tunnels, and network segmentation through hands-on configuration and testing of Cisco devices
instructions:
**Phase 1 (90 minutes): Network Design and Planning**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a business scenario: Company ABC needs to connect headquarters (200 users), manufacturing site (150 users), and remote office (50 users) with specific requirements including voice traffic prioritization, guest network isolation, and secure inter-site communication. Teams must create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes (using VLSM), equipment placement, redundant paths, and security zones. Teams document their design rationale, including routing protocol selection, VLAN segmentation strategy, and security policy framework.

**Phase 2 (120 minutes): Physical Implementation**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical lab equipment (3 routers, 6 switches per team), students configure their designed network. Begin with basic device setup: hostname, passwords, and interface addressing. Implement OSPF for internal routing within each site, EIGRP for inter-site communication, and BGP for external connectivity simulation. Configure VLANs for network segmentation (management, users, voice, guest), implement trunking between switches, and establish inter-VLAN routing. Create site-to-site VPN tunnels using IPSec, implement QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic, and configure comprehensive ACLs restricting inter-VLAN and external access.

**Phase 3 (60 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Teams systematically test all network functionality: ping tests between all sites and VLANs, verify routing table convergence, test failover scenarios by disabling primary links, validate ACL effectiveness by attempting blocked connections, and demonstrate QoS implementation through bandwidth utilization tests. Document all configurations with running-config exports, create network troubleshooting procedures, and prepare a 10-minute presentation explaining their architectural decisions and demonstrating key network functions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version) or physical Cisco lab equipment
3 Cisco ISR routers (2900 series or equivalent) per team
6 Cisco Catalyst switches (2960 series or equivalent) per team
Console cables and crossover/straight-through Ethernet cables
Network design templates and IP addressing worksheets
Business requirement specification documents for each team scenario
assessment_method: Evaluation based on four components: Network Design Document (25%) - assessed for technical accuracy, scalability, and security considerations; Implementation Quality (40%) - verified through live demonstration of all required features and protocols; Testing Documentation (20%) - completeness of test procedures and results validation; Presentation (15%) - clarity of architectural explanation and demonstration of advanced features. Success criteria include: all three sites can communicate with sub-second convergence, VPN tunnels are established and functional, QoS policies demonstrate measurable traffic prioritization, ACLs effectively segment network access, and failover scenarios work within 30 seconds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic device settings, offer simplified network topologies with fewer redundant paths, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create checkpoint reviews after each major configuration section. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate network automation using Python scripts, implement advanced security features like 802.1X authentication, or design disaster recovery procedures. Encourage optimization challenges such as minimizing convergence times or maximizing bandwidth utilization efficiency.

title: Python Data Type Memory Challenge: Flashcard Classification Drill
description: Students memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list) and their characteristics through a structured flashcard activity. Students will identify data types from code examples and match type names with their definitions and example values.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the names of Python's five basic data types (int, float, str, bool, list) by completing timed flashcard rounds
Students will identify specific data type examples through visual recognition of code syntax patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student (5 minutes setup). Each set contains 25 cards: 5 definition cards, 5 example cards, 5 syntax pattern cards, 5 use case cards, and 5 memory trick cards for each data type. Start with Round 1: Definition Recall (8 minutes). Students work individually, cycling through definition cards, stating the data type name aloud when shown characteristics like 'whole numbers, positive or negative.' Round 2: Example Recognition (8 minutes). Display code examples on the board one at a time: x = 42, name = 'Alice', prices = [1.99, 2.50]. Students hold up corresponding data type name cards simultaneously. Record participation points. Round 3: Speed Matching (10 minutes). In pairs, students lay out all 25 cards face down in a 5x5 grid. Player 1 flips two cards, attempting to match a data type name with its example (int with 42). Successful matches earn the pair. Switch turns until all matches found. Round 4: Recall Quiz (4 minutes). Project 10 mixed examples on screen. Students write data type names on individual whiteboards, revealing answers simultaneously for immediate feedback. End with whole-class chanting of 'int-float-string-boolean-list' three times while pointing to posted visual aids showing each type's icon.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (25 cards per student)
Individual mini whiteboards and dry erase markers
Projector/screen for displaying code examples
Data type reference poster with visual icons
Timer/stopwatch for rounds
assessment_method: Students earn points through: Round 2 participation (2 points per correct card raise, 10 total), Round 3 pair matching completion (5 points for finishing), Round 4 quiz accuracy (1 point per correct answer, 10 total). Success criteria: 20/25 points demonstrates mastery. Record scores on checklist for immediate feedback.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by pairing them with stronger partners during Round 3, providing a reference sheet with data type definitions visible throughout activity. For advanced learners, add challenge cards featuring edge cases like empty lists [] or negative numbers, and introduce compound data types (dict, tuple) as bonus content.

title: Optimization Analysis for Urban Transit System Design
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world urban planning problem involving bus route efficiency. They will use Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization to minimize travel time while maximizing coverage within budget limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing a multi-variable urban transit scenario with realistic constraints
Students will demonstrate optimization problem-solving skills through systematic mathematical modeling of complex real-world transportation logistics
instructions: Begin by distributing the Urban Transit Challenge packet containing a city grid map, population density data, and budget constraints (10 minutes). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the scenario: a city needs to optimize 5 bus routes covering 20 neighborhoods with varying population densities, where each route costs $50,000 annually and must serve at least 1,000 residents daily. Teams first identify decision variables (route locations x₁, x₂, ...x₅ and y₁, y₂, ...y₅), objective function (minimize average travel time T = Σ(distance × population)/total population), and constraints (budget: Σcosts ≤ $250,000, coverage: each route serves ≥1,000 residents, geographic: routes must connect existing infrastructure points). Next, teams set up the Lagrangian function L(x,y,λ,μ) incorporating all constraints (20 minutes). Students then calculate partial derivatives and solve the system of equations using provided computation sheets, showing all algebraic steps (25 minutes). Teams verify their solutions by checking constraint satisfaction and calculating the optimized total travel time. Finally, each team presents their optimal route configuration using the city map, explaining their mathematical reasoning and comparing results with other teams' solutions (15 minutes). Instructor circulates throughout, providing guidance on Lagrangian setup and derivative calculations while ensuring teams show complete mathematical work rather than relying solely on computational tools.
materials_needed: Urban Transit Challenge packet with city grid map and population data
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Large format city maps for presentation (11x17 inches)
Colored markers for route drawing
Lagrangian computation worksheets with partial derivative templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate setup and solution of Lagrangian system with proper calculus techniques (40%), (3) Verification of constraint satisfaction and mathematical reasoning (20%), (4) Clear presentation of optimized solution with justification (15%). Teams must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and present their final route design.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled variable identification sheets and step-by-step Lagrangian setup templates; pair with stronger mathematical teammates; offer mini-lessons on partial derivative review. For advanced learners: introduce additional constraints such as environmental impact factors, peak/off-peak timing variables, or extend to 3D optimization with elevation considerations; challenge them to solve using alternative optimization methods for comparison.

title: Analyzing Multi-Loop Circuit Performance Under Varying Load Conditions
description: Students will systematically analyze a complex three-loop circuit containing resistors, capacitors, and inductors to determine how component failures and load variations affect current distribution and power dissipation. They will decompose the circuit behavior using multiple analytical methods and synthesize findings to predict system reliability.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze current and voltage relationships in multi-loop circuits by applying Kirchhoff's laws, mesh analysis, and nodal analysis to compare results across different analytical approaches
Students will evaluate circuit performance degradation through systematic examination of component tolerance effects and failure modes on overall system behavior
instructions:
**Phase 1: Circuit Analysis Setup (15 min)**
Provide students with a three-loop RLC circuit schematic containing: Loop 1 (12V source, 100Ω resistor, 10mH inductor), Loop 2 (220Ω resistor, 47μF capacitor in series), Loop 3 (330Ω load resistor, 22μF capacitor in parallel). Students work in pairs to identify all nodes, meshes, and component relationships.

**Phase 2: Multi-Method Analysis (45 min)**
Students must solve the circuit using three different methods: (1) Kirchhoff's voltage/current laws with simultaneous equations, (2) mesh current analysis, and (3) nodal voltage analysis. For each method, they calculate steady-state and transient responses at f=60Hz. Students document each step in their analysis worksheet and compare results for consistency.

**Phase 3: Component Variation Analysis (30 min)**
Students systematically vary each component value by ±20% (resistor tolerance) and ±10% (reactive components) to analyze sensitivity. They create a data table showing how current magnitude and phase shift change in each loop for every component variation. Students must identify which components most critically affect circuit performance.

**Phase 4: Failure Mode Analysis (20 min)**
Students simulate component failures: open circuits (capacitor failure), short circuits (resistor failure), and changed inductance values. For each failure scenario, they predict the effect on remaining circuit elements and verify through calculation.

**Phase 5: Synthesis and Recommendations (10 min)**
Pairs synthesize their analysis to rank components by criticality and propose design modifications to improve circuit robustness. They must justify recommendations using quantitative data from their analysis.
materials_needed: Multi-loop RLC circuit schematic with specified component values
Scientific calculators with complex number capabilities
Analysis worksheet templates with pre-formatted data tables
SPICE circuit simulation software (LTSpice or equivalent)
Graph paper for phasor diagrams
assessment_method: Students submit completed analysis worksheets showing all three solution methods with numerical verification (40 points). Evaluate accuracy of component sensitivity analysis data tables (30 points). Assess quality of failure mode predictions with supporting calculations (20 points). Grade final recommendations based on quantitative justification and feasibility (10 points). Success criteria: >85% accuracy in calculations, consistent results across all three methods, and evidence-based component criticality ranking.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide completed examples of each analytical method for a simpler two-loop circuit. Offer calculation checkpoints after each phase. Supply complex number operation reference sheets. **Extension for advanced learners:** Add frequency-dependent analysis requiring students to examine circuit behavior across 10Hz-10kHz range. Include impedance matching calculations for maximum power transfer. Challenge students to design component value modifications that optimize circuit Q-factor while maintaining performance specifications.

title: Code Quality Comparison: Evaluating Two Solutions to a Shopping Cart Bug
description: Students will analyze and evaluate two different code solutions that fix the same shopping cart quantity bug. They will assess code quality, maintainability, and efficiency to determine which solution is superior and justify their recommendation with evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of two code solutions by analyzing readability, efficiency, and maintainability criteria
Students will justify their recommendation for the superior solution through structured comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Shopping Cart Bug Scenario' handout containing: original buggy code that allows negative quantities, Solution A (input validation approach), and Solution B (absolute value approach). Display the evaluation criteria on board: Readability, Maintainability, Error Handling, and User Experience.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine both solutions and complete the 'Code Evaluation Matrix' worksheet. For each solution, they rate 1-5 on each criterion and write 2-3 sentences explaining their rating. They must identify at least 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses per solution.

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their evaluations. Partners must discuss any rating differences of 2+ points and attempt to reach consensus on the most important factors for this specific bug fix.

**Written Recommendation (15 minutes):** Students write a 200-word recommendation memo addressed to a 'Senior Developer.' The memo must: state their chosen solution, provide 3 specific reasons with code examples, acknowledge 1 limitation of their choice, and explain why it's still superior.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion where 3-4 students present their recommendations. Focus on how different priorities (quick fix vs. long-term maintenance) might influence the evaluation.

**Reflection (5 minutes):** Students complete exit ticket: 'What's one evaluation criterion you didn't initially consider that emerged during discussion?'
materials_needed: Shopping Cart Bug Scenario handout with original code and two solutions
Code Evaluation Matrix worksheet template
Evaluation criteria reference sheet
Exit ticket slips
assessment_method: Grade the recommendation memo using 4-point rubric: Clear position statement (1 pt), Three evidence-based reasons with code references (3 pts), Acknowledgment of solution limitations (1 pt), Professional memo format and grammar (1 pt). Observe peer discussions for evidence of criterion-based reasoning vs. personal preference.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence stems like 'This solution is more readable because...' and highlight key differences in the code with comments. For advanced learners: Add a third solution with exception handling and ask them to evaluate all three, or have them consider performance implications with large datasets.

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Business Strategy
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will synthesize multiple data sources, develop custom metrics, and design visualizations to support business decision-making for an e-commerce company.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying RFM analysis techniques to transactional data and creating distinct customer personas
Students will design an interactive business dashboard through combining statistical analysis, data visualization, and strategic recommendations for targeted marketing campaigns
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Preparation (20 minutes)**
Provide students with a simulated e-commerce dataset containing 10,000+ customer transactions over 2 years, including customer ID, purchase date, product category, and order value. Students work in pairs to clean and explore the data using Excel or Tableau. They must identify data quality issues, handle missing values, and create calculated fields for days since last purchase, purchase frequency, and total monetary value per customer.

**Phase 2: RFM Analysis Development (35 minutes)**
Students calculate RFM scores by creating quintile rankings (1-5) for each dimension. They develop a scoring rubric where Recency measures days since last purchase (lower = better), Frequency counts total purchases (higher = better), and Monetary sums total spending (higher = better). Students then combine scores to create customer segments like 'Champions' (555), 'Loyal Customers' (X4X-X5X), 'At Risk' (2XX-3XX), and 'Lost Customers' (1XX).

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (40 minutes)**
Using their chosen tool, students design a 4-panel dashboard including: (1) Customer segment distribution pie chart, (2) RFM score scatter plot matrix, (3) Revenue contribution by segment bar chart, and (4) Time-series trend of segment migration. Each visualization must include interactive filters for date range and product category.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendations (25 minutes)**
Students create a one-page executive summary identifying the top 3 customer segments by value, proposing specific marketing strategies for each segment (email frequency, discount levels, product recommendations), and estimating potential revenue impact. They must justify recommendations using dashboard insights and include 2-3 KPIs to measure campaign success.
materials_needed: Simulated e-commerce transaction dataset (CSV format, 10,000+ records)
Tableau Public, Power BI, or Excel with Power Query
RFM analysis scoring template worksheet
Executive summary template (Word document)
Access to computers with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Data accuracy and RFM calculations (25%), (2) Dashboard design and interactivity (30%), (3) Quality and feasibility of strategic recommendations (30%), and (4) Professional presentation and documentation (15%). Students must submit their dashboard file, executive summary, and present findings in 3-minute pitches. Success requires accurate segment identification, functional interactive elements, and data-driven business recommendations with measurable outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM score examples, offer dashboard wireframe templates, and create guided calculation worksheets. Pair weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables (customer acquisition cost, lifetime value predictions), create predictive models for segment migration, or develop A/B testing frameworks for their recommendations. Encourage integration of external market research or competitor analysis.

title: Interactive Customer Segmentation Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations for different customer segments.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive RFM analysis model by integrating transactional data, demographic information, and behavioral metrics to create distinct customer segments

Dashboard design checklist handout
Presentation rubric for peer evaluation

title: Critical Path Dependencies Matrix: Memorizing Sequential Task Relationships
description: Students memorize and accurately recall complex task dependencies, predecessor-successor relationships, and critical path sequences from a multi-phase software development project scenario. They demonstrate recall through rapid identification of dependency chains without reference materials.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize 25 specific task dependencies and their sequential relationships within a critical path network by completing timed recall exercises
Students will identify and recite predecessor-successor task pairs from memory through structured questioning protocols
instructions: Begin by distributing the Software Development Project Dependencies Chart containing 25 interconnected tasks (Requirements Gathering → System Design → Database Schema Creation, etc.). Students have 15 minutes to study the complete dependency matrix, focusing on memorizing which tasks must precede others and identifying the three possible critical paths. During study time, encourage students to create mental associations and use the provided mnemonic devices (e.g., 'RSD-DB' for Requirements-System Design-Database). After study period, collect all materials. Conduct Phase 1 testing: call out task names randomly and require students to immediately state all predecessor tasks from memory within 10 seconds per response. Record accuracy on tracking sheets. Phase 2: present 10 scenario cards describing project situations (e.g., 'Database testing reveals critical errors'). Students must recite from memory which subsequent tasks will be delayed and identify if the critical path is affected. Phase 3: rapid-fire critical path identification where students must verbally trace the longest path through the network within 90 seconds. Repeat the entire cycle three times with different questioning sequences to ensure retention. Students failing to achieve 80% accuracy repeat the study-test cycle. Document individual performance on provided score sheets, noting specific dependency pairs causing difficulty.
materials_needed: Software Development Project Dependencies Chart (25 tasks with interconnections)
Mnemonic device reference cards
10 scenario situation cards
Individual tracking score sheets
Stopwatch/timer
Answer key with all dependency relationships
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy across three testing phases: (1) Predecessor identification - correctly name predecessors for 20/25 tasks within time limits, (2) Impact analysis - accurately identify affected subsequent tasks for 8/10 scenario cards, (3) Critical path recitation - correctly trace at least 2/3 critical paths within 90 seconds. Track errors by dependency type and provide remediation for students scoring below threshold.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide color-coded dependency charts, reduce initial memorization set to 15 tasks, allow 15-second response time, and offer additional mnemonic device training. For advanced learners: add resource constraint dependencies, include float time calculations from memory, introduce multiple concurrent project scenarios, and require memorization of task duration estimates alongside dependencies.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: Analyzing Real-World Tensions in Executive Decision-Making
description: Students will analyze authentic case studies of senior executives facing paradoxical leadership situations (e.g., being decisive yet collaborative, maintaining stability while driving change). Through structured comparative analysis, students will demonstrate deep understanding of how effective leaders navigate inherent contradictions in complex organizational contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between surface-level leadership challenges and underlying paradoxical tensions by analyzing multi-layered case studies of C-suite decision-making scenarios
Students will categorize various leadership paradoxes and explain their interconnected nature through systematic comparison of executive responses across different industry contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing three complex case studies featuring different leadership paradoxes: Reed Hastings (Netflix) balancing freedom with accountability, Satya Nadella (Microsoft) maintaining competitive edge while fostering collaboration, and Mary Barra (GM) preserving tradition while driving innovation (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one primary case and two secondary cases for comparison. Students spend 45 minutes conducting deep case analysis using the provided 'Paradox Mapping Framework' worksheet, identifying: (1) the core paradoxical tension, (2) immediate symptoms vs. root contradictions, (3) stakeholder perspectives creating the paradox, (4) short-term and long-term implications of different approaches, and (5) the leader's actual resolution strategy. Teams then create a visual 'Paradox Navigation Map' showing how their primary leader's approach connects to broader leadership theory (20 minutes). During the presentation phase (30 minutes total), each team presents their primary case analysis (5 minutes), followed by structured peer questioning where other teams identify similar/contrasting patterns from their cases (3 minutes discussion per team). Conclude with a facilitated synthesis discussion (15 minutes) where students collectively categorize the paradoxes into broader leadership frameworks (competing values, dialectical thinking, both/and leadership) and articulate how understanding these tensions differs from simply recognizing leadership challenges.
materials_needed: Three detailed case studies (4-5 pages each) with financial data, stakeholder quotes, and timeline of decisions
Paradox Mapping Framework worksheet with guided analysis prompts
Large format paper (A3/11x17) and colored markers for visual mapping
Digital timer for session management
Leadership theory reference sheets covering competing values framework and dialectical leadership concepts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy in identifying core paradoxical tensions vs. surface problems (25%), (2) Depth of analysis connecting leader behaviors to theoretical frameworks (25%), (3) Quality of comparative insights across cases showing pattern recognition (25%), (4) Sophistication of synthesis demonstrating understanding of paradox as inherent leadership reality rather than problem to solve (25%). Success criteria: Students score 3+ on all dimensions, demonstrate ability to explain why paradoxes cannot be permanently resolved, and articulate specific leadership behaviors that embrace rather than eliminate tensions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions focusing on one paradox dimension at a time, offer sentence starters for analysis ('This creates tension because...', 'The leader balanced this by...'). For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify meta-paradoxes (paradoxes about managing paradoxes) and connect findings to neuroscience research on cognitive complexity. Consider providing additional cases from different cultural contexts to explore how cultural values influence paradox navigation.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS
description: Students will deploy a complete three-tier web application (presentation, application, and database layers) using AWS services including EC2, RDS, and Elastic Load Balancer. They will configure security groups, establish database connections, and test the deployed application to demonstrate practical cloud architecture implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier architecture by launching EC2 instances, creating an RDS database, and configuring an Application Load Balancer
Students will implement AWS security best practices through configuring security groups with appropriate inbound/outbound rules for each tier
instructions:
**Phase 1: Environment Setup (20 minutes)**
1. Students log into AWS Management Console using provided sandbox accounts
2. Navigate to EC2 dashboard and select the us-east-1 region
3. Create a new Key Pair named 'webapp-keypair' and download the .pem file

**Phase 2: Database Tier Creation (25 minutes)**
1. Navigate to RDS service and click 'Create Database'
2. Select MySQL engine, choose 'Free tier' template
3. Set DB instance identifier as 'webapp-db', master username as 'admin', password as 'WebApp123!'
4. Configure VPC security group named 'db-security-group' allowing inbound MySQL/Aurora (port 3306) from anywhere
5. Click 'Create Database' and wait for status to show 'Available'

**Phase 3: Application Tier Deployment (30 minutes)**
1. Launch 2 EC2 instances using Amazon Linux 2 AMI (t2.micro)
2. Create security group 'app-security-group' allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) from anywhere
3. In User Data section, paste provided script that installs Apache, PHP, and connects to RDS
4. Tag instances as 'WebApp-Server-1' and 'WebApp-Server-2'

**Phase 4: Load Balancer Configuration (20 minutes)**
1. Navigate to EC2 Load Balancers and create Application Load Balancer
2. Name it 'webapp-alb', select internet-facing scheme
3. Add both EC2 instances to target group 'webapp-targets'
4. Configure health check path as '/health.php'

**Phase 5: Testing and Validation (15 minutes)**
1. Access load balancer DNS name in browser to verify application loads
2. Stop one EC2 instance to test high availability
3. Document the complete architecture with IP addresses and connection details
materials_needed: AWS sandbox accounts with EC2, RDS, and ELB permissions
Pre-written PHP application code with database connection script
User data script for automatic Apache/PHP installation
Architecture diagram template for documentation
Computers with web browsers and SSH clients
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Screenshot of functioning web application accessed via load balancer URL (25 points), (2) Completed architecture diagram showing all components and their relationships (25 points), (3) Security group configuration screenshots demonstrating proper port restrictions (25 points), (4) Written reflection explaining how each AWS service contributes to application scalability and availability (25 points). Success criteria: Application must be accessible via load balancer, remain functional when one server is stopped, and demonstrate secure database connectivity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step screenshots for each AWS console navigation. Create troubleshooting checklist for common issues like security group misconfigurations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like CloudWatch monitoring, auto-scaling groups, or multi-availability zone deployment. Encourage exploration of cost optimization through reserved instances or spot instances.

instructions:
**Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access credentials. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify they can access EC2, RDS, and S3 services. Distribute the sample PHP web application code (a simple task manager that connects to MySQL database).

**Implementation Phase (45 minutes):** Students begin by creating an S3 bucket named 'student-[lastname]-webapp-assets' and uploading provided CSS/image files. Next, they launch an EC2 t2.micro instance running Amazon Linux 2, ensuring to create a new key pair and configure security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. While EC2 launches, students create an RDS MySQL t3.micro instance with database name 'taskmanager', noting the endpoint URL. After EC2 is running, students SSH into the instance, install Apache and PHP, then upload and configure the web application code to connect to their RDS instance. **Step 5 - Application Integration (15 minutes):** Students modify the database connection strings in the PHP code to point to their RDS endpoint, upload the application files to the EC2 instance, and test full functionality including database writes and S3 file uploads.

**Step 6 - Verification Testing (10 minutes):** Students access their application via the public IP, create test database entries, upload files to S3, and verify all three tiers communicate properly.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and Advanced Security Policies
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) technology. They will create custom security policies, implement Quality of Service (QoS) configurations, and establish redundant routing protocols to ensure high availability and optimal performance.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize DMVPN Phase 3 implementation with EIGRP routing and IPSec encryption by configuring hub-and-spoke topology with spoke-to-spoke communication
Students will design comprehensive network security policies through integration of zone-based firewalls, access control lists, and certificate-based authentication
Students will construct advanced QoS frameworks incorporating traffic shaping, priority queuing, and bandwidth allocation policies across WAN links
instructions: Begin by providing each team with three Cisco ISR 4000 series routers and network topology diagrams showing Site A (headquarters), Site B (manufacturing), and Site C (remote office). Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze business requirements document specifying 500 headquarters users, 200 manufacturing users, and 50 remote users, then create detailed network design including IP addressing scheme using VLSM, DMVPN tunnel architecture, and traffic flow diagrams. Step 2 (60 minutes): Configure DMVPN hub router at headquarters with NHRP, mGRE tunnels, and IPSec profiles, then establish spoke routers with dynamic tunnel registration and Phase 3 spoke-to-spoke capabilities. Step 3 (45 minutes): Implement EIGRP routing protocol with named configuration, configure route summarization at site boundaries, and establish authentication using key chains. Step 4 (30 minutes): Design and deploy zone-based firewall policies allowing specific inter-site traffic while blocking unauthorized access, create custom class maps and policy maps for different user groups. Step 5 (40 minutes): Configure hierarchical QoS policies with Low Latency Queuing (LLQ) for voice traffic, guaranteed bandwidth for critical applications, and traffic shaping for non-essential services. Step 6 (20 minutes): Conduct comprehensive testing including failover scenarios, traffic prioritization verification, and security policy validation using packet capture analysis and show commands documentation.
materials_needed: Nine Cisco ISR 4331 routers with appropriate licensing
Cisco Packet Tracer Advanced or GNS3 with IOS images
Network topology templates and business requirements documentation
Certificate authority setup for IPSec authentication
Traffic generation tools (iPerf3 or similar)
Wireshark for packet analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate using comprehensive rubric: Network design documentation (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, security considerations; Implementation quality (35 points) - DMVPN functionality, routing convergence, QoS effectiveness verified through performance metrics; Security implementation (25 points) - firewall policies, encryption strength, access control effectiveness; Documentation and troubleshooting (15 points) - configuration backups, testing procedures, problem resolution methodology. Students must demonstrate working spoke-to-spoke communication, sub-second failover times, and successful traffic prioritization under load testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured basic router templates with fundamental settings, offer DMVPN configuration checklists with specific command sequences, and assign peer mentors for complex troubleshooting. For advanced learners: Extend activity by implementing IPv6 dual-stack configuration, adding SD-WAN overlay comparisons, integrating network automation using Python and NETCONF, or designing disaster recovery scenarios with geographic redundancy requirements.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and Advanced Security Policies: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) technology. They will integrate advanced routing protocols, implement comprehensive security policies, and create detailed network documentation with troubleshooting procedures.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed implementation plans with DMVPN Phase 2 architecture
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco technologies through configuring EIGRP over DMVPN, implementing zone-based firewalls, and establishing QoS policies across the WAN infrastructure
instructions: **Phase 1: Planning (45 minutes)** - Provide teams of 3-4 students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp has headquarters in New York (500 users), manufacturing in Dallas (200 users), and R&D in Seattle (100 users). Students analyze provided traffic patterns, security requirements, and budget constraints. Teams create network diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes (using 10.0.0.0/8), DMVPN hub-and-spoke design with headquarters as hub, and identify required Cisco equipment models. **Phase 2: Configuration (90 minutes)** - Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 with ISR 4000 series routers, students configure: DMVPN Phase 2 with mGRE tunnels, NHRP authentication using pre-shared keys, EIGRP routing over tunnel interfaces with proper network statements, and IPSec profiles with AES-256 encryption. Students implement zone-based firewalls with DMZ zones for servers, create QoS policies prioritizing VoIP traffic (30% bandwidth allocation), and configure NTP synchronization. **Phase 3: Testing & Documentation (45 minutes)** - Teams verify connectivity using extended ping tests between all sites, demonstrate spoke-to-spoke communication bypassing hub, capture and analyze tunnel establishment packets using built-in packet capture tools, and create comprehensive documentation including configuration backups, network diagrams with IP assignments, troubleshooting flowcharts for common DMVPN issues, and performance baseline measurements. Students present 10-minute demonstrations showing successful inter-site communication and explaining their design decisions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 with ISR 4000 router images
Network diagramming software (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart)
TechCorp business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Cisco IOS command reference guides
Laptops/workstations with administrative privileges
assessment_method: Evaluation based on four components: (1) Network design quality (25%) - topology scalability, IP addressing efficiency, security consideration integration; (2) Configuration accuracy (35%) - functional DMVPN tunnels, proper routing convergence, successful QoS implementation; (3) Testing validation (25%) - comprehensive connectivity verification, packet capture analysis, performance metrics documentation; (4) Professional documentation (15%) - complete configuration backups, clear network diagrams, detailed troubleshooting procedures. Students must achieve 80% functionality threshold with all sites communicating and security policies operational.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide DMVPN configuration templates with key parameters highlighted, offer step-by-step EIGRP configuration checklists, and assign peer mentors for troubleshooting support. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase to ensure progress. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement DMVPN Phase 3 for optimal routing, integrate additional security features like IPS signatures, design redundant hub architecture, or implement advanced QoS with traffic shaping and policing policies. Encourage exploration of SD-WAN concepts as network evolution.
original_title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and Advanced Security Policies

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and Advanced Security Policies: Practical Workshop
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution spanning three geographic locations using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) technology. They will integrate advanced routing protocols, implement comprehensive security policies, and create detailed network documentation including disaster recovery procedures.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by integrating DMVPN Phase 3, EIGRP routing, and zone-based firewall policies to meet specific business requirements
Students will create comprehensive network implementation documentation through hands-on configuration and testing of hub-and-spoke VPN connectivity with spoke-to-spoke tunnels
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Design and Planning**
Students receive a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with headquarters in Dallas and branch offices in Miami and Seattle, requiring secure inter-site communication for 500+ users. Working in teams of 2-3, students must design the complete network architecture using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3. They create network diagrams showing IP addressing schemes (using 10.0.0.0/8), DMVPN tunnel interfaces, and security zones.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Core Configuration**
Students configure three Cisco ISR 4000 series routers as hub (Dallas) and spokes (Miami/Seattle). Begin with basic interface configuration and EIGRP routing (AS 100). Configure DMVPN hub with tunnel interface 0, using 172.16.1.1/24 for the tunnel network. Implement NHS (Next Hop Server) and NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) settings. Configure spoke sites with static NHRP mapping to hub and dynamic spoke-to-spoke resolution.

**Phase 3 (75 minutes): Advanced Features and Security**
Implement IPSec encryption using IKEv2 with AES-256 encryption and SHA-256 hashing. Configure zone-based firewall policies allowing specific traffic between sites while blocking unauthorized access. Create three security zones: INSIDE, OUTSIDE, and VPN with appropriate class-maps and policy-maps. Test connectivity using extended ping tests and verify tunnel establishment with 'show dmvpn' commands.

**Phase 4 (45 minutes): Documentation and Presentation**
Teams create comprehensive documentation including configuration files, IP address tables, troubleshooting guides, and disaster recovery procedures. Prepare 10-minute presentations demonstrating network functionality and explaining design decisions.

Computers with minimum 8GB RAM for network simulation

Success criteria include: all three sites can communicate securely, spoke-to-spoke tunnels establish dynamically, firewall policies block unauthorized traffic while permitting business applications, and documentation follows industry standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic interface settings and IP addressing completed. Offer checkpoint verification sheets for each configuration phase. Create troubleshooting flowcharts for common DMVPN issues. title: Python Data Type Memory Palace: Building Visual Flashcard Collections
description: Students create and use visual flashcards to memorize the eight fundamental Python data types, their definitions, and syntax examples. They will organize these cards into a systematic memory collection and practice active recall through structured review sessions.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the eight fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, tuple, dict, set) by creating and reviewing visual flashcards
Students will identify correct syntax examples for each Python data type through systematic flashcard practice sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing 8 blank index cards to each student and displaying the Python data types reference sheet. Students spend 15 minutes creating one flashcard per data type: front side shows the data type name in large letters, back side includes definition, one syntax example, and a simple visual symbol they choose. For example, 'int' card might show 'Integer - whole numbers, positive or negative' with example 'x = 42' and a symbol of building blocks. After creation, students pair up for 10 minutes to quiz each other using the cards, with Partner A showing data type names while Partner B provides definitions and examples. Switch roles after 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class 'rapid fire' session where you call out data types and students hold up cards, then provide verbal definitions. Follow with reverse practice: show syntax examples on screen (like 'name = "Alice"') and students identify the data type by holding up correct cards. Conclude with individual silent review where each student sorts their cards into 'confident' and 'needs practice' piles. Students who finish early can create additional example cards for their challenging data types. End with students storing cards in provided envelopes labeled with their names for future review sessions.
materials_needed: 8 blank index cards per student
Colored pens or markers (at least 4 colors per student)
Python Data Types Reference Sheet (printed handout)
Small envelopes for card storage (one per student)
Projector/screen for displaying syntax examples
assessment_method: Check each student's completed set of 8 flashcards for accuracy of definitions and syntax examples (1 point per correct card). Observe pair practice sessions and award participation points for active engagement. Conduct final quick assessment by randomly selecting 3 cards from each student and asking them to recite the information without looking at the back.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written definition templates with blanks to fill in, and pair them with stronger partners during practice. Advanced learners can add multiple syntax examples per card, include common error examples, or create additional cards for complex data structures like nested lists or dictionary methods.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real Customer Data Patterns
description: Students will analyze three different statistical distributions (normal, skewed, and bimodal) using actual e-commerce customer purchase data. They will identify distribution characteristics, explain what each pattern reveals about customer behavior, and predict business implications through guided interpretation exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will classify statistical distributions by examining histograms, box plots, and summary statistics from customer transaction datasets
Students will explain the business meaning behind distribution patterns through structured analysis of central tendency, spread, and shape characteristics
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-prepared datasets: Dataset A (customer ages - normal distribution), Dataset B (purchase amounts - right-skewed), and Dataset C (customer satisfaction scores - bimodal). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Each pair creates histograms and box plots for all three datasets using provided Python scripts, calculating mean, median, mode, and standard deviation. Second 15 minutes: Using the Distribution Analysis Worksheet, students identify each distribution type and list three observable characteristics (shape, central tendency relationship, outlier presence). Third 15 minutes: Students write brief explanations connecting each distribution pattern to customer behavior - for example, explaining why purchase amounts are right-skewed (most customers spend little, few spend much) or what bimodal satisfaction scores might indicate (two distinct customer segments). Final segment: Each pair presents one dataset interpretation to another pair, explaining their reasoning. Instructor circulates throughout, asking probing questions like 'What would happen to the mean if we removed the top 5% of purchases?' and 'How might marketing strategies differ for each customer segment represented in the bimodal data?' Students document their analysis and peer discussions in a structured reflection template.
materials_needed: Three pre-cleaned CSV datasets with customer data (ages, purchases, satisfaction)
Laptop/computer with Python and pandas, matplotlib libraries installed
Distribution Analysis Worksheet (printed handout)
Reflection template (digital or printed)
assessment_method: Grade completed Distribution Analysis Worksheets using rubric: Correct distribution identification (25 points), accurate characteristic descriptions (25 points), logical business interpretations (25 points), quality of peer explanation (25 points). Success indicator: 80% of students correctly identify at least 2 of 3 distributions and provide reasonable business explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide histogram templates with distribution type examples posted on wall, offer sentence starters like 'This distribution suggests customers tend to...' For advanced learners: challenge them to propose statistical tests to confirm their distribution classifications or suggest data collection methods to verify their business hypotheses.

title: Optimizing Manufacturing Production: Real-World Linear Programming Application
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex manufacturing optimization problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will use graphical methods and the simplex algorithm to determine optimal production levels that maximize profit while adhering to resource limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve a multi-variable optimization problem by setting up objective functions and constraint equations from real manufacturing data
Students will implement both graphical and algebraic solution techniques to determine optimal production strategies through systematic constraint analysis
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the manufacturing scenario handout describing XYZ Electronics producing smartphones and tablets with specific profit margins ($120 smartphones, $180 tablets). Present constraint data: 480 hours assembly time, 240 hours testing time, 1000 component sets available. **Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (15 minutes):** Students work in pairs to define variables (x = smartphones, y = tablets), write the objective function (Maximize P = 120x + 180y), and translate constraints into inequalities (2x + 3y ≤ 480 for assembly, x + 2y ≤ 240 for testing, x + y ≤ 1000 for components, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0). **Phase 2 - Graphical Solution (25 minutes):** Using graphing calculators or Desmos, students plot constraint lines, identify the feasible region, and locate corner points. They must calculate exact coordinates for each vertex of the feasible region polygon. **Phase 3 - Optimization (20 minutes):** Students evaluate the objective function at each corner point, identify the optimal solution, and calculate maximum profit. They must show all arithmetic calculations explicitly. **Phase 4 - Verification (15 minutes):** Students verify their solution using the simplex method or linear programming software (Excel Solver), comparing results and explaining any discrepancies. **Wrap-up (15 minutes):** Each pair presents their optimal production strategy, stating how many units of each product to manufacture and the resulting profit, while explaining the binding constraints that limit further profit increases.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario handout with XYZ Electronics case study
Graphing calculators or computers with Desmos access
Graph paper with coordinate grids
Excel or Google Sheets with Solver add-in
Linear programming formula reference sheet
assessment_method: Students submit a complete solution report including: (1) Correctly formulated objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate graphical representation with labeled feasible region (25 points), (3) Correct identification of corner points with coordinates (20 points), (4) Accurate calculation of optimal solution and maximum profit (20 points), (5) Verification using secondary method with explanation of results (10 points). Success requires 80% accuracy across all components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn coordinate axes, offer constraint inequality templates, and give step-by-step graphing checklist. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints (whole units only), introduce sensitivity analysis to determine how constraint changes affect optimal solutions, or extend to three-variable problems requiring algebraic methods only.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting
description: Students receive broken complex circuits with multiple failure points and must systematically analyze voltage, current, and resistance relationships to identify all failure modes. They will decompose the circuit into functional blocks, predict expected values, and determine the cascade effects of component failures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-component circuit failures by systematically measuring electrical parameters and comparing them to theoretical predictions
Students will evaluate the interdependence of circuit elements through fault isolation techniques and failure mode analysis
instructions:
Begin by providing each team of 2-3 students with a pre-constructed circuit board containing 8-12 components including resistors, capacitors, transistors, and op-amps, with 2-3 deliberately introduced faults (open circuits, short circuits, or damaged components). Give students the original circuit schematic and expected performance specifications. 

Step 1 (15 min): Students must first analyze the intended circuit function by calculating theoretical voltage and current values at 6 designated test points using Kirchhoff's laws and component specifications. They record these predictions in a structured data table.

Step 2 (25 min): Using multimeters and oscilloscopes, students systematically measure actual values at each test point, documenting deviations from theoretical predictions. They must follow a structured troubleshooting protocol: measure supply voltages first, then DC bias points, then AC signal levels.

Step 3 (20 min): Students analyze their data to identify failure patterns by comparing measured vs. expected values. They must determine which components are functioning outside specifications and hypothesize failure modes (open, short, drift, etc.).

Step 4 (15 min): Teams create a failure analysis report identifying each faulty component, explaining how each failure affects downstream circuit behavior, and predicting the cascade effects. They must use component-level analysis to explain why specific voltage/current relationships changed.

Step 5 (10 min): Students present their analysis to another team for peer verification, defending their conclusions with quantitative evidence and circuit theory principles.
materials_needed: Pre-built circuit boards with introduced faults (one per team)
Original circuit schematics with component values and specifications
Digital multimeters with current measurement capability
Dual-channel oscilloscopes with probe sets
DC power supplies (0-15V variable)
Function generators for AC signal injection
Component datasheets and reference materials
Structured troubleshooting worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations (25%), (2) Systematic measurement methodology (20%), (3) Correct identification of faulty components (25%), (4) Analysis of failure mode effects and circuit interactions (20%), (5) Quality of evidence-based reasoning in final report (10%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in fault identification and demonstrate clear understanding of how component failures propagate through the circuit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guidance on systematic measurement sequences and offer pre-calculated theoretical values for verification. Create simplified circuits with single failure points initially. For advanced learners: Introduce frequency-dependent failures, temperature effects, or require students to design test procedures for intermittent faults. Challenge them to predict failure probabilities and design redundancy solutions.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting: Exercise 1
description: Students analyze complex DC circuits with intentionally introduced faults to identify failure points and predict system behavior. They systematically examine voltage and current relationships across components to isolate defective elements and explain the cascade effects on overall circuit performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between component failures and overall circuit behavior by systematically measuring and comparing theoretical versus actual voltage/current values
Students will evaluate the cascade effects of individual component failures through logical deduction and quantitative analysis of circuit measurements
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a pre-built circuit board containing 6-8 components (resistors, capacitors, diodes) with one deliberately faulty component (open resistor, shorted capacitor, or reversed diode). Do not reveal which component is faulty. Students first spend 15 minutes calculating expected voltage and current values at each test point using circuit analysis techniques (Kirchhoff's laws, voltage dividers). Next, they systematically measure actual values using multimeters, recording data in a structured table with columns for: component location, expected voltage, measured voltage, expected current, measured current, and deviation percentage. Students then spend 20 minutes analyzing discrepancies between theoretical and measured values, identifying patterns that suggest failure modes. They must isolate the faulty component by testing individual elements and explain how the failure propagates through the circuit using current flow diagrams. Teams create a fault analysis report documenting: (1) systematic measurement approach, (2) comparison analysis showing deviation calculations, (3) logical reasoning chain leading to fault identification, (4) explanation of how the specific failure affects downstream components, and (5) proposed repair strategy with predicted post-repair behavior. Conclude with 10-minute team presentations where groups explain their analytical process and defend their conclusions to peers who can challenge their reasoning.
materials_needed: Pre-built circuit boards with intentionally faulty components (different faults per team)
Digital multimeters with voltage, current, and resistance measurement capabilities
Circuit schematic diagrams matching the physical boards
Component specification sheets with tolerance values
Structured data recording worksheets
Graph paper for current flow diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: systematic measurement approach (25 points), accuracy of theoretical calculations (20 points), quality of deviation analysis with proper calculations (25 points), correct fault identification with supporting evidence (20 points), and clarity of failure propagation explanation with diagrams (10 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in fault identification and demonstrate logical reasoning chains connecting measurements to conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide measurement sequence flowcharts and partially completed data tables with some expected values pre-calculated. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to current when resistance increases?' For advanced learners, introduce multiple simultaneous faults or ask them to predict failure probability based on component stress analysis and temperature effects on component values.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting: Exercise 2
description: Students will analyze complex DC circuits with intentional component failures to identify root causes and predict system behavior. They will decompose circuit problems using Kirchhoff's laws, Ohm's law, and voltage divider principles to distinguish between normal operation and failure modes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-loop DC circuits by systematically applying Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws to identify which specific components are causing abnormal behavior
Students will differentiate between open circuit, short circuit, and component degradation failures through comparison of theoretical calculations with measured circuit behavior
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 2-3 students with a pre-built breadboard circuit containing 4-5 resistors, 2 voltage sources, and 3-4 measurement points, with one intentionally faulty component (open resistor, shorted connection, or degraded resistor with 50% higher resistance). Students first spend 15 minutes calculating expected voltages and currents at each measurement point assuming all components are functioning normally, using nodal analysis or mesh current methods. Next, students measure actual voltages and currents using digital multimeters for 10 minutes, recording data in a structured table comparing predicted vs. actual values. In the analysis phase (20 minutes), teams must identify discrepancies exceeding 10% tolerance and hypothesize which component is faulty based on the deviation patterns. Students then isolate and test individual components using multimeter resistance measurements to confirm their hypothesis. Finally, teams spend 15 minutes creating a diagnostic flowchart showing their analytical process and explaining how the specific failure mode (open, short, or degradation) created the observed voltage/current deviations throughout the circuit. Each team presents their findings in a 5-minute summary, explaining their systematic approach and the physics principles that enabled them to locate the fault.
materials_needed: Pre-built breadboard circuits with intentional faults (one per team)
Digital multimeters with voltage, current, and resistance measurement capabilities
Circuit schematic diagrams showing component values and measurement points
Data recording sheets with predicted vs. actual measurement tables
Replacement components for verification testing
assessment_method: Grade based on 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of initial theoretical calculations using circuit analysis principles, (2) Quality of systematic troubleshooting methodology and logical reasoning process, (3) Correct identification of faulty component with supporting evidence, (4) Clear explanation of how failure mode physics created observed symptoms. Each criterion worth 25 points for 100-point total.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing voltage divider calculation templates and step-by-step Kirchhoff's law application guides. For advanced learners, introduce AC circuits with reactive components or provide circuits with multiple simultaneous faults requiring more sophisticated analysis techniques.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting: Exercise 3
description: Students analyze deliberately sabotaged complex circuits containing resistors, capacitors, and inductors to identify failure modes and predict system behavior. They systematically break down circuit responses using oscilloscope data and theoretical calculations to isolate component failures.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex RLC circuit behavior by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental oscilloscope measurements to identify component failures
Students will evaluate the relative impact of different component failures through systematic elimination and frequency response analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-built circuits (30 minutes setup). Each team of 3 students receives one 'mystery circuit' containing a deliberate component failure (open resistor, shorted capacitor, or altered inductor value). Students first spend 15 minutes deriving the theoretical transfer function for their assigned circuit topology, calculating expected resonant frequency, damping coefficient, and amplitude response. Next, students connect their circuit to the function generator and oscilloscope, taking measurements at 10 specific frequencies spanning 100Hz to 10kHz (20 minutes). They plot experimental frequency response data and overlay their theoretical predictions (15 minutes). Students then systematically analyze discrepancies between theory and experiment, forming hypotheses about which component has failed and how (20 minutes). Using multimeters, students test individual components to verify their hypothesis (10 minutes). Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their analytical process: theoretical calculations, experimental data comparison, failure hypothesis, and verification results. During presentations, other teams evaluate the logical consistency of the analytical approach and identify alternative explanations for observed discrepancies (30 minutes total for all presentations). Conclude with a class discussion comparing different failure modes and their signatures in frequency response data (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-built RLC circuits with deliberate component failures (one per team of 3)
Function generators and oscilloscopes (one set per team)
Digital multimeters with component testing capability
Semi-log graph paper or graphing software
Scientific calculators
Component specification sheets for reference values
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Theoretical calculations accuracy (25%), experimental methodology and data quality (25%), logical analysis connecting theory to observations (30%), identification of correct failure mode with supporting evidence (20%). Success requires correctly identifying the failed component and explaining how experimental deviations led to this conclusion.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with partially completed calculation templates and suggest specific frequency ranges to focus measurements. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them analyze temperature effects or predict long-term reliability based on failure mode. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger partners for calculation verification.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze complex RC and RLC circuits with intentionally introduced faults to identify failure points and predict system behavior. They will decompose circuit responses, compare theoretical predictions with measured data, and determine root causes of performance deviations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze circuit component failures by systematically examining voltage, current, and impedance relationships across multiple measurement points
Students will differentiate between normal and abnormal circuit behavior through comparative analysis of theoretical calculations versus experimental measurements
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with a pre-constructed circuit board containing an RLC circuit with one unknown fault (open resistor, shorted capacitor, or degraded inductor). Teams receive 15 minutes to examine the circuit schematic and calculate expected values for voltage, current, and phase relationships at 5 designated test points using given component values. Next, teams spend 20 minutes making actual measurements using multimeters and oscilloscopes, recording data in a structured analysis table. During the following 25 minutes, students must systematically compare measured versus calculated values, identifying discrepancies and forming hypotheses about potential failure modes. Teams then spend 15 minutes testing their hypotheses by making additional targeted measurements at suspected failure points. In the final 20 minutes, each team presents their analysis methodology, shows their data comparison charts, identifies the specific component failure, and explains how this failure propagates through the circuit to cause the observed symptoms. Instructor facilitates discussion by asking probing questions about alternative failure modes and validation methods. Students must document their complete analytical process, including initial calculations, measurement procedures, hypothesis formation, and verification steps in a technical report format.
materials_needed: Pre-fabricated RLC circuit boards with hidden component failures (one per team)
Digital multimeters with AC/DC capability
Dual-channel oscilloscopes with probe sets
Function generators (1-100 kHz range)
Circuit analysis worksheets with measurement tables
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations and systematic measurement approach (25%), (2) Quality of data analysis and identification of discrepancies (30%), (3) Logical reasoning in hypothesis formation and testing methodology (25%), (4) Correct identification of failed component with supporting evidence (20%). Students must submit completed analysis worksheets and deliver 3-minute team presentations demonstrating their analytical process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided calculation templates and suggest specific measurement sequences. Offer hints about which parameters change most dramatically with each type of component failure. For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify the degree of component degradation, predict circuit lifetime, or analyze temperature effects on the failure mode. Consider having them design diagnostic procedures for similar circuits.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting

title: Code Review Evaluation: Comparing Three Simple Calculator Implementations
description: Students will evaluate three pre-written Python calculator programs by analyzing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will rank the implementations and justify their evaluation using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three calculator code implementations by applying software development criteria including readability, functionality, and error handling
Students will critique and rank code quality through systematic comparison using a provided evaluation framework
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three Python calculator code samples (provided as separate files: calc_a.py, calc_b.py, calc_c.py) to each student. Each implementation performs basic arithmetic but varies in code quality, structure, and features. Provide the Code Evaluation Checklist handout.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students test each calculator program and complete the evaluation checklist for all three implementations. They assess: (1) Code readability (variable names, comments, structure), (2) Functionality (does it work correctly for all operations), (3) Error handling (what happens with invalid input), (4) User experience (clear prompts, helpful output), and (5) Code efficiency (unnecessary complexity, redundant code).

**Ranking and Justification (15 minutes):** Students rank the three implementations from best (1) to worst (3) and write a 150-word justification explaining their ranking decision. They must reference specific examples from the code and connect their observations to software development principles.

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** In pairs, students share their rankings and justifications, discussing any disagreements and explaining their reasoning. Partners can challenge each other's evaluations with specific evidence.

**Wrap-up Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write a brief reflection identifying which evaluation criterion they found most important and why, connecting this to real-world software development practices.
materials_needed: Three Python calculator implementations (calc_a.py, calc_b.py, calc_c.py)
Code Evaluation Checklist handout with scoring criteria
Computers with Python installed or online Python interpreter access
Ranking and Justification worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed evaluation checklists (40 points - 8 points per criterion across 3 implementations), ranking justification quality (30 points - must include specific examples and clear reasoning), and peer discussion participation (30 points - active engagement and evidence-based arguments). Success criteria: Students provide specific code examples in justifications, apply all five evaluation criteria consistently, and demonstrate understanding of code quality principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example evaluations of a fourth calculator implementation and highlight specific code snippets that demonstrate good/poor practices. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific code improvements for the lowest-ranked implementation or evaluate additional criteria like scalability and maintainability.

title: Design and Build a Municipal Budget Dashboard for City Council Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard using real municipal budget data to help city council members visualize spending patterns and make informed budget allocation decisions. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design appropriate visualizations, and present actionable insights through their custom dashboard.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an interactive dashboard by integrating multiple municipal datasets and designing appropriate visualizations for non-technical stakeholders
Students will formulate data-driven budget recommendations through analysis of spending trends, demographic data, and service utilization metrics
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide teams of 3-4 students with datasets including: 5-year municipal budget records, census demographic data, and service utilization metrics (parks, libraries, public safety calls). Each team receives a different mid-sized city's data. **Phase 1 - Data Integration (45 minutes):** Students clean and merge datasets, identifying key relationships between budget allocations and community outcomes. They must document data quality issues and create standardized metrics for comparison across departments. **Phase 2 - Dashboard Design (60 minutes):** Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students create 4-6 interactive visualizations showing: budget trends over time, per-capita spending by service area, correlation between spending and service utilization, and demographic impact analysis. Dashboard must include filters for year, department, and neighborhood if applicable. **Phase 3 - Insight Development (30 minutes):** Teams analyze their visualizations to identify 3 specific budget optimization opportunities, such as underutilized services, inequitable resource distribution, or efficiency improvements. **Phase 4 - Stakeholder Presentation (20 minutes):** Each team presents their dashboard to simulated city council members (other students), delivering a 5-minute presentation highlighting key findings and budget recommendations. Council members ask questions and vote on most compelling proposals.
materials_needed: Municipal budget CSV files (5 years of data per city)
US Census demographic data extracts
Service utilization datasets (police calls, library visits, park usage)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Presentation display capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four criteria: (1) Data Integration Quality - accurate merging and cleaning with documented processes (25 points), (2) Dashboard Design - appropriate chart types, clear navigation, and professional appearance (25 points), (3) Analytical Insights - evidence-based recommendations with supporting data (25 points), (4) Stakeholder Communication - clear presentation with effective response to questions (25 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
