title: PMI Process Group and Knowledge Area Matrix Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMBOK Guide's 49 project management processes organized across 5 process groups and 10 knowledge areas. This intensive recall activity requires students to demonstrate mastery of the foundational framework that underpins all advanced project management practices.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all 49 PMBOK processes by identifying their correct process group and knowledge area placement within 90 seconds per matrix quadrant
Students will demonstrate memorization of process sequencing through rapid-fire verbal recitation of process names, inputs, and primary outputs
instructions: Begin by distributing blank 5x10 matrix templates with process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) as columns and knowledge areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) as rows. Students receive 10 minutes to study a completed reference matrix showing all 49 processes in their correct positions. Remove reference materials and start the memorization challenge with Phase 1: Matrix Completion (15 minutes). Students must fill in all 49 process names in correct matrix positions. Processes include complex items like 'Develop Project Management Plan' (Integration/Planning), 'Control Procurements' (Procurement/Monitoring & Controlling), and 'Close Project or Phase' (Integration/Closing). Phase 2: Speed Recall (20 minutes). Call out random knowledge areas; students have 30 seconds to verbally list all processes within that area in correct process group sequence. Phase 3: Reverse Challenge (15 minutes). State a process name; students must immediately identify its process group and knowledge area intersection. Phase 4: Critical Path Verification (10 minutes). Students must identify which processes have mandatory dependencies and recall their typical sequencing order. Conclude with peer verification where partners check each other's completed matrices against master key. Document individual completion times and accuracy percentages for each phase.
materials_needed: Blank 5x10 matrix templates (2 per student)
PMBOK Guide 49-process reference chart
Digital timer/stopwatch
Master answer key with process descriptions
Red pens for peer checking
assessment_method: Success measured by: Matrix completion accuracy (minimum 45/49 processes correctly placed = 92%), Speed recall performance (minimum 7/10 knowledge areas completed within time limit), Reverse challenge accuracy (minimum 80% correct process group/knowledge area identification), Overall completion time tracking for remediation identification
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing process group definitions card and allowing 5 additional minutes for initial study. Create mnemonic devices for knowledge area sequences. For advanced learners, add process input/output memorization component and require identification of ITTOs (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) for selected processes.

title: Multi-Perspective Leadership Crisis Analysis: Understanding Situational Leadership Through Stakeholder Lens Mapping
description: Students will analyze a complex organizational crisis scenario through the perspectives of five different stakeholder groups to demonstrate understanding of situational leadership theory. They will map how effective leadership responses must adapt based on follower readiness levels and situational demands.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between directive, coaching, supporting, and delegating leadership styles by analyzing their appropriateness for different stakeholder groups during a crisis scenario
Students will interpret the relationship between follower development levels and required leadership approaches through systematic stakeholder perspective mapping
instructions:
Begin by providing students with the 'MediTech Product Recall Crisis' case study (a fictional pharmaceutical company facing a contaminated batch recall affecting 50,000 patients). Divide the class into teams of 5, with each member assigned one stakeholder perspective: Board of Directors, Manufacturing Team, Customer Service Representatives, Regulatory Affairs Team, and Media Relations Team. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Individual team members read the case study and complete their assigned 'Stakeholder Readiness Assessment Matrix,' rating their group's competence (technical skills) and commitment (motivation/confidence) on scales of 1-4 for handling this crisis. They also identify their stakeholder group's primary concerns and information needs.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams reconvene and each member presents their stakeholder analysis. Using the provided 'Situational Leadership Mapping Template,' teams plot each stakeholder group on the readiness matrix and determine the most appropriate leadership style (S1-Directing, S2-Coaching, S3-Supporting, S4-Delegating) for the CEO to use with each group.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Teams develop specific leadership communication strategies for each stakeholder group, writing sample communication scripts that demonstrate understanding of how leadership approach must vary. For example, highly directive communication for overwhelmed customer service reps versus collaborative consultation with experienced regulatory affairs specialists.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Teams present their stakeholder maps and rationale to the class, explaining why different leadership styles are required for different groups within the same crisis situation. Conclude with reflection on how this demonstrates that effective leadership requires understanding follower needs rather than applying one-size-fits-all approaches.
materials_needed: MediTech Product Recall Crisis case study (2-page document)
Stakeholder Readiness Assessment Matrix worksheets (5 different versions)
Situational Leadership Mapping Template (large format poster)
Colored markers or pens for mapping
Sample Communication Scripts template
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate application of situational leadership theory to stakeholder analysis (25%), (2) Quality of readiness level justifications with specific evidence from case study (25%), (3) Appropriateness of leadership style selections with clear rationale (25%), (4) Demonstration of understanding that leadership must adapt to follower characteristics through communication examples (25%). Successful completion requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the 'Leadership Style Quick Reference Guide' with behavior examples for each quadrant and sentence starters for justifications. Offer additional coaching during Step 1 to help identify concrete evidence of competence/commitment levels. For advanced learners, add complexity by having them consider how leadership approaches might evolve as the crisis progresses and stakeholder readiness levels change over time.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront
description: Students will create and deploy a functional static website using AWS S3 for hosting and CloudFront for content delivery. learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website by configuring AWS S3 bucket policies and enabling static website hosting features
Students will implement a content delivery network through AWS CloudFront distribution setup and domain configuration
instructions: **Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and the starter website files (index.html, style.css, script.js, and 2-3 image files). Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to S3 service. **Bucket Creation (15 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with naming convention 'firstname-lastname-static-site-[date]'. They must uncheck 'Block all public access' and acknowledge the warning. In Properties tab, students enable 'Static website hosting', set index.html as index document, and note the endpoint URL. **File Upload (10 minutes):** Students upload all website files to the bucket root directory, ensuring 'Grant public-read access' is selected during upload. They test the static website endpoint URL in a browser to verify basic functionality. **CloudFront Setup (20 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront service and create a new distribution. Students configure default root object as 'index.html' and create distribution. **Testing Phase (10 minutes):** Once CloudFront status shows 'Deployed', students access their website via the CloudFront domain name and test loading speed from different geographic locations using online tools. **Documentation (10 minutes):** Students record both S3 endpoint URL and CloudFront URL, document configuration choices made, and screenshot successful deployment showing website loading with CloudFront URL in address bar.

Pre-built static website files (HTML, CSS, JS, images)
Web browser with internet access
Geographic speed testing tool (GTmetrix or WebPageTest)

scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step screenshot guide for S3 bucket policy configuration and offer pre-configured CloudFront settings template. Rubric: URLs functional (40%), correct configuration screenshots (30%), performance analysis (20%), cache behavior understanding (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide pre-written bucket policies and step-by-step screenshots. Pair struggling students with more advanced peers. Create troubleshooting guide for common errors like bucket naming conflicts and permission issues. **Advanced extensions:** Configure custom domain with Route 53, implement Lambda@Edge function for basic authentication, set up automated deployment using AWS CLI, or configure multiple CloudFront behaviors for different file types.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create and deploy a simple static website using AWS S3 for storage and CloudFront for content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates fundamental AWS services integration by building a real-world web hosting solution.
learning_objectives: Students will apply S3 bucket configuration principles by creating a static website with proper permissions and policies
Students will implement CloudFront distribution setup through connecting it to their S3 bucket for global content delivery
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Instructor verifies all students have AWS Free Tier accounts and provides sample HTML/CSS files (index.html, error.html, style.css). Students organize files in a local folder named 'my-website'.

**Phase 1 - S3 Setup (15 minutes):** Students log into AWS Console and navigate to S3. They create a new bucket with a globally unique name (format: 'student-name-website-2024'). Students enable static website hosting in bucket properties, setting index.html as index document and error.html as error document. They upload all website files to the bucket root directory.

**Phase 2 - Configure Permissions (10 minutes):** Students modify bucket policy to allow public read access by adding the provided JSON policy template (instructor provides specific policy). They test the website using the S3 static website endpoint URL provided in bucket properties.

**Phase 3 - CloudFront Integration (15 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront console and create a new distribution. They select their S3 bucket as origin domain, configure default root object as 'index.html', and set price class to 'Use Only US, Canada and Europe'. Students wait for distribution deployment (5-10 minutes) then test access via CloudFront URL.

**Phase 4 - Validation (5 minutes):** Students document both S3 and CloudFront URLs, verify website loads from both endpoints, and submit URLs via learning management system. Instructor spot-checks deployments by visiting submitted URLs.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account for each student
Sample website files (index.html, error.html, style.css)
S3 bucket policy JSON template
Computers with internet access and modern web browsers
assessment_method: Students submit: 1) Working S3 static website URL, 2) Working CloudFront distribution URL, 3) Screenshot showing CloudFront distribution status as 'Deployed'. Success criteria: Both URLs display the website correctly, CloudFront URL shows improved loading performance, and bucket policy allows public access without compromising security.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step screenshots and pair them with successful peers. Pre-create bucket policy templates with clear placeholders. For advanced learners: Challenge them to add custom domain names, implement HTTPS certificates, or set up multiple environments (dev/prod) with different configurations.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create and deploy a personal portfolio website to AWS S3, then configure CloudFront for global content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services while building practical cloud deployment skills.

title: Deploy a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply AWS S3 and CloudFront services to host and distribute a static website with global content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical cloud hosting implementation using core AWS services.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website by configuring AWS S3 bucket settings and uploading web content files
Students will implement content distribution through creating and configuring a CloudFront distribution for global website access
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and the starter website files (index.html, style.css, and one image file). Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to S3 service.

**S3 Configuration (25 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a unique name (format: firstname-lastname-website-YYYY). They configure bucket settings by disabling 'Block all public access' and acknowledging the warning. Next, students upload their website files to the bucket root directory. They then enable static website hosting in bucket properties, setting index.html as the index document and error.html as the error document. Students apply a bucket policy (provided template) to make objects publicly readable.

**CloudFront Setup (20 minutes):** Students navigate to CloudFront service and create a new distribution. They set the origin domain to their S3 bucket's static website endpoint (not the bucket itself). Students configure default cache behavior settings: viewer protocol policy to 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS', allowed HTTP methods to 'GET, HEAD', and cache TTL to 300 seconds. They leave other settings as default and create the distribution.

**Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Students test their S3 website URL first to ensure basic functionality. They then wait for CloudFront deployment (5-10 minutes) and test the CloudFront distribution URL. Students verify that both HTTP and HTTPS requests work, and document both URLs in their submission form.

**Documentation (10 minutes):** Students complete a structured worksheet documenting their S3 bucket name, website endpoint URL, CloudFront distribution ID, and final website URL, plus answer three reflection questions about the services used.
materials_needed: AWS account credentials for each student (IAM users with S3 and CloudFront permissions)
Starter website files package (index.html, style.css, sample image)
S3 bucket policy template document
Submission worksheet template
Computers with internet access and modern web browsers
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheet with: (1) Working S3 static website URL (25 points), (2) Functional CloudFront distribution URL with HTTPS enabled (35 points), (3) Correct documentation of AWS resource names and IDs (20 points), (4) Accurate responses to reflection questions about service purposes and benefits (20 points). Total: 100 points. Success criteria: Website accessible via both S3 and CloudFront URLs, proper HTTPS redirect functionality, and demonstration of understanding through written responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide screenshot-based visual guides for each AWS console step, assign peer partners for collaboration, and offer pre-configured bucket policy text for copy-paste. Create a troubleshooting checklist for common issues like bucket naming conflicts and public access settings. title: Deploy a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create and deploy a static website to AWS S3 with global content delivery through CloudFront. This hands-on activity applies core AWS services to solve a real-world web hosting scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS S3 bucket configuration by creating a static website with proper permissions and hosting settings
Students will implement AWS CloudFront distribution through connecting S3 bucket to a global CDN for optimized content delivery
instructions:
Begin by having students log into AWS Management Console using provided lab accounts (10 minutes). Students work individually to complete the following steps:

3. Configure Static Website Hosting (15 minutes): Access bucket Properties tab, enable Static Website Hosting, set index.html as index document, save configuration, and note the endpoint URL.

5. Test S3 Website (5 minutes): Access website using S3 endpoint URL to verify functionality.

6. Create CloudFront Distribution (20 minutes): Navigate to CloudFront service, create distribution, set S3 website endpoint as origin domain, configure default cache behavior, set price class to 'Use Only US, Canada and Europe', and deploy distribution.

7. Final Testing (10 minutes): After distribution status changes to 'Deployed' (5-10 minutes), access website using CloudFront domain name and verify improved loading through global CDN.

Students document their S3 bucket URL and CloudFront distribution domain for submission.

title: Risk Impact Analysis: Deconstructing Project Failure Scenarios
description: Students will analyze a complex project case study to identify interconnected risks, examine their relationships, and evaluate the cascading effects of risk events on project constraints. They will deconstruct a failed project scenario to determine root causes and analyze how different risk response strategies could have altered outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies by mapping cause-and-effect relationships between identified risks in a software development project scenario
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of existing risk response strategies through systematic comparison of planned versus actual risk impacts on schedule, budget, and scope
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'DataFlow Mobile App Project' case study packet containing project charter, risk register with 15 identified risks, timeline with actual events, and budget variance reports. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Risk Analyst (focuses on technical risks), Stakeholder Analyst (focuses on communication/resource risks), Timeline Analyst (focuses on schedule impacts), and Integration Lead (synthesizes findings). 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each team member individually reads the case study and creates a preliminary risk categorization using the provided Risk Analysis Worksheet. Students identify which risks materialized, when they occurred, and initial impact assessment.

Phase 2 (35 minutes): Teams collaborate to create a Risk Relationship Map using sticky notes on flip chart paper. Place each materialized risk in chronological order, then use different colored arrows to show: direct causation (red), contributing factors (yellow), and amplifying effects (blue). Teams must identify at least 3 risk chains where one risk triggered multiple others.

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Using the Risk Impact Analysis Template, teams evaluate each risk chain by calculating cumulative schedule delays, budget impacts, and scope changes. Teams analyze whether the original risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) were appropriate and propose alternative responses.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Teams present their most significant risk chain analysis to the class, explaining the interconnections and defending their alternative response strategy recommendations. Each presentation limited to 4 minutes with 2 minutes for peer questions.
materials_needed: DataFlow Mobile App Project case study packet (6 pages per student)
Risk Analysis Worksheet template (1 per student)
Risk Impact Analysis Template (1 per team)
Flip chart paper and colored sticky notes
Red, yellow, and blue markers for relationship mapping
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using Risk Analysis Rubric with four criteria: Risk Identification Accuracy (25% - correctly identified 80%+ of materialized risks), Relationship Mapping Quality (30% - demonstrated clear cause-effect chains with appropriate categorization), Impact Analysis Depth (25% - provided quantified analysis of schedule/budget/scope impacts), and Alternative Strategy Justification (20% - proposed feasible alternative responses with clear rationale). Teams scoring 85%+ demonstrate mastery of risk analysis skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed Risk Relationship Map showing 2-3 risk connections as examples, and offer guiding questions like 'What happened immediately after this risk occurred?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify probability impacts using Monte Carlo concepts or analyze how different project management methodologies (Agile vs. Waterfall) might have changed risk profiles. Provide additional complexity by asking them to create risk response contingency plans.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Effectiveness Analysis and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing real e-commerce data across multiple customer touchpoints. They will critique current attribution strategies and develop evidence-based recommendations for optimizing marketing spend allocation based on customer journey analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models by analyzing conversion path data from a provided Google Analytics account

Students will critique existing marketing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of revenue attribution discrepancies across different models and formulate strategic recommendations for budget reallocation
instructions:
Begin by providing students access to a Google Analytics demo account with 6+ months of e-commerce data (instructor sets up Google Analytics Demo Account access 24 hours prior). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical datasets but different marketing scenarios (high social media spend, high paid search spend, etc.). 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. They extract data for all available attribution models, focusing on revenue and conversion metrics for their assigned channel mix.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the Top Conversion Paths report, teams analyze the 20 most common customer journey patterns, documenting touchpoint sequences and identifying which channels appear most frequently in assisted vs. last-click positions.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams calculate revenue attribution differences between models, creating a spreadsheet showing percentage variance in channel value attribution. They must identify which channels are most over/under-valued by last-click attribution compared to data-driven models.

Step 4 (35 minutes): Teams develop a critical evaluation framework assessing each attribution model against criteria: accuracy for their scenario, actionability for marketing decisions, and business impact potential. They must cite specific data points and conversion path examples.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Teams create strategic recommendations including specific budget reallocation percentages, attribution model selection with detailed justification, and implementation timeline. Final deliverable is a 10-slide presentation with executive summary, data analysis, model critique, and actionable recommendations.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account access credentials for each team
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Marketing scenario assignments (prepared by instructor with different channel spend profiles)
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Attribution model evaluation framework template
assessment_method: Teams are evaluated using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Data accuracy and extraction completeness (20%), (2) Critical analysis depth of attribution model limitations (25%), (3) Quality of evidence supporting recommendations (20%), (4) Strategic thinking and business applicability (20%), (5) Presentation clarity and professional delivery (15%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions, demonstrating ability to identify at least 3 significant attribution discrepancies, provide 5+ specific recommendations with quantified impact, and deliver compelling business case for proposed changes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer attribution model comparison cheat sheet with key strengths/weaknesses. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources, create custom channel groupings, or develop ROI projections for their recommendations. Consider adding competitive analysis component using similar industry benchmarks.

title: Python Data Type Identification Card Matching Game
description: Students will memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) by matching data type names with their definitions and examples through a structured card-based activity. This foundational exercise builds essential vocabulary recognition needed before writing any Python code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) by matching names to definitions with 90% accuracy
Students will recall specific examples of each Python data type through a timed card matching exercise
instructions: Begin by preparing three sets of laminated cards: Set A contains data type names (int, float, string, boolean, list), Set B contains definitions, and Set C contains code examples. Distribute one complete set to each pair of students. Start with a 5-minute instructor demonstration using oversized cards at the front of the class, showing how 'int' matches with 'whole numbers without decimals' and the example '42'. Have students arrange their Set A cards in a row on their desks. Read aloud each definition from the answer key while students hold up the corresponding Set B definition card - this creates active recall practice. Next, students work in pairs for 10 minutes to match all three sets correctly: name cards, definition cards, and example cards should form complete triplets. Circulate to provide immediate feedback and correction. For the final 8 minutes, conduct a speed round where you call out either a definition or example, and students must quickly hold up the correct data type name card. Keep score for motivation. Conclude with a 2-minute reflection where each pair states one data type and its definition aloud to the class. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact terminology - 'integer' not 'number', 'string' not 'text' - to build precise technical vocabulary that matches Python documentation.
materials_needed: Laminated card sets (15 cards per set: 5 names, 5 definitions, 5 examples)
Answer key with correct matches for instructor reference
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard markers for tracking speed round scores
assessment_method: Students must correctly match all 5 data types to definitions (5 points) and examples (5 points) for a total of 10 points. During the speed round, award 1 point per correct identification. Success criteria: 8/10 points on matching exercise and 70% accuracy during speed identification rounds. Document results on a simple checklist with student names.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with only 3 data types (int, string, boolean) and add complexity gradually. Provide a reference sheet with data type names visible. For advanced learners, include additional data types like tuple and dictionary, or have them create their own example cards with more complex code snippets like nested lists or mathematical expressions.

title: Optimization in Engineering Design: Maximizing Solar Panel Efficiency
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving solar panel placement and efficiency. They will use derivatives to find maximum energy output while considering physical constraints and cost factors.
learning_objectives: Students will apply first and second derivative tests to determine optimal angles and configurations for solar panel installations by analyzing energy output functions
Students will implement constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers to maximize solar energy production through multi-variable calculus techniques
instructions: Begin by distributing the solar panel specification sheets and energy output formulas (15 minutes setup). Present the scenario: A residential client wants to install solar panels on a south-facing roof with dimensions 20m × 12m, with a budget of $25,000. Students work in pairs to model the energy output function E(θ,n) = n × 300 × cos(θ-37°) × 8.5 × 0.85, where θ is tilt angle, n is number of panels, and consider constraints: panel cost ($800 each), installation angle limitations (15°-60°), and roof space (each panel: 2m × 1m). First, students find the derivative dE/dθ and solve dE/dθ = 0 to determine optimal tilt angle (20 minutes). Next, they use the second derivative test to confirm this is a maximum. Then, students apply constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers for the cost constraint g(θ,n) = 800n - 25,000 ≤ 0 and space constraint h(n) = 2n - 120 ≤ 0 (30 minutes). Students must calculate ∇E = λ∇g + μ∇h and solve the system of equations. Finally, they verify their solution using graphing technology, plot the energy function, and prepare a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical work and final recommendation including total energy output, payback period, and sensitivity analysis for ±5° angle variations (25 minutes presentation prep, 20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Solar panel specification sheets with efficiency ratings and dimensions
Graphing calculators or Desmos/GeoGebra access
Constraint optimization formula reference sheet
Graph paper and rulers for sketching functions
Presentation materials (poster paper or laptops for slides)
assessment_method: Students submit written solutions showing: (1) Correct derivative calculations and critical point identification (25 points), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier method with complete algebraic work (35 points), (3) Verification using technology with accurate graphs (20 points), (4) Clear presentation of final recommendations with mathematical justification (20 points). Success criteria: 80% accuracy in mathematical procedures, correct identification of optimal values within 5% of theoretical maximum, and logical presentation of engineering recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed derivative worksheets and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier templates. Offer one-on-one support during calculation phases. For advanced learners: Add weather variability factors requiring integration over seasonal data, or include multiple roof orientations requiring 3D optimization. Encourage exploration of economic factors like electricity rates and government incentives in their optimization model.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Complex Pendulum-Spring-Damper System
description: Students will decompose and analyze the energy transformations occurring in a compound physical system consisting of a pendulum with an attached spring and magnetic damping. They will identify energy loss mechanisms, quantify energy conversions, and evaluate the relative contributions of different damping forces throughout the motion cycle.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the instantaneous energy distribution between kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, and dissipated energy by examining position, velocity, and force data at specific time intervals
Students will evaluate the relative significance of different damping mechanisms through mathematical modeling and experimental data comparison
instructions:
Begin by setting up the compound pendulum system with a 1-meter rod, 500g mass, attached spring (k=20 N/m), and magnetic damper. Position motion sensors and force sensors at key locations. Students work in teams of 3-4. (15 minutes setup)

First, students observe one complete damped oscillation cycle and identify all energy transformation points, creating a preliminary energy flow diagram. They must identify at least 5 distinct energy states and 3 damping mechanisms. (20 minutes)

Next, teams collect quantitative data using Logger Pro software, recording position, velocity, spring compression, and magnetic field strength at 0.1-second intervals for 60 seconds of motion. Students calculate instantaneous kinetic energy (½mv²), gravitational potential energy (mgh), and elastic potential energy (½kx²) for each data point. (25 minutes)

Teams then create detailed energy vs. time graphs for each energy type and calculate the rate of energy dissipation by finding the derivative of total mechanical energy. They must identify which damping mechanism (air resistance, magnetic, or friction) dominates at different amplitude ranges by comparing theoretical predictions with measured energy loss rates. (30 minutes)

Finally, students modify one system parameter (spring constant, damping strength, or initial amplitude) and predict how this affects energy distribution. They test their predictions experimentally and analyze discrepancies between predicted and observed results. (25 minutes)

Conclude with team presentations of their energy analysis, focusing on quantitative comparisons and identified system inefficiencies. Each team presents their most surprising finding about energy behavior in the system. (15 minutes)
materials_needed: Compound pendulum apparatus with 1-meter rod and 500g mass
Helical spring with spring constant k=20 N/m
Magnetic damping system with adjustable field strength
Vernier motion sensors and force sensors
Logger Pro data acquisition software
Graphing calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
Protractors and meter sticks for initial measurements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of energy calculations with less than 5% error in mathematical computations (25 points), (2) Completeness of energy transformation identification - must identify all major energy states and transitions (25 points), (3) Quality of analysis comparing theoretical vs. experimental damping rates with supported conclusions (30 points), (4) Effectiveness of modified system predictions and experimental validation with clear reasoning (20 points). Students submit individual reflection papers analyzing their team's findings and personal understanding of energy system complexity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide energy calculation templates, pre-made data tables, and guided questions for each analysis step. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive differential equations governing the system behavior, incorporate rotational kinetic energy calculations, or analyze frequency-dependent damping effects. Provide additional complex systems (coupled oscillators) for extended analysis.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Password Validation Function Quality
description: Students will evaluate three different implementations of a password validation function by analyzing code quality, security practices, and effectiveness. They will rank the implementations and justify their decisions using specific criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different password validation implementations by analyzing code readability, security practices, and functional completeness
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison using established software quality criteria
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-written password validation functions in Python (Function A: basic length check only; Function B: comprehensive validation with clear variable names and comments; Function C: overly complex with nested conditions and poor naming). Give students 10 minutes to individually read through all three functions without discussion. Next, introduce the evaluation criteria checklist: code readability (variable names, comments, structure), security effectiveness (checks for length, uppercase, lowercase, numbers, special characters), and maintainability (simplicity, logical flow, error handling). Have students spend 15 minutes independently scoring each function on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, then calculate total scores. Form groups of 3-4 students for 20 minutes to compare their individual evaluations, discuss discrepancies, and reach consensus on rankings with written justifications. Each group creates a one-page evaluation report ranking the functions from best to worst, with specific evidence from the code supporting their decisions. Groups present their rankings and reasoning to the class (3 minutes per group), followed by instructor-led discussion about evaluation differences and professional code review practices. Conclude with students writing individual reflection paragraphs about which evaluation criteria they found most important and why.
materials_needed: Three pre-written password validation functions (printed handouts)
Code evaluation criteria checklist (printed)
Scoring sheets for individual evaluation
Whiteboard or projector for group presentations
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade based on individual scoring accuracy (25%), quality of group evaluation report with specific evidence and clear reasoning (50%), and individual reflection paragraph demonstrating understanding of evaluation criteria importance (25%). Success criteria: correctly identifies security weaknesses, uses specific code examples as evidence, provides logical justification for rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide highlighted examples of good vs. poor variable naming and point out specific security features to look for. For advanced learners, ask them to suggest specific code improvements for the lowest-ranked function or introduce additional criteria like performance considerations and code reusability.

title: PMBOK Guide Knowledge Area Integration Mapping Challenge
description: Students will recall and identify the 49 specific processes within the PMBOK Guide's 10 Knowledge Areas and map them to their corresponding Process Groups. This advanced memorization activity reinforces the foundational framework that underlies all project management methodology.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the 49 PMBOK processes by name and correctly associate each with its designated Knowledge Area within 90% accuracy
Students will identify the Process Group classification for each PMBOK process through rapid-fire recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing blank Process Integration Matrices (10x5 grid with Knowledge Areas as rows and Process Groups as columns) and process name cards to each student. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to place all 49 process cards into the correct matrix positions from memory, starting with processes they're most confident about. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Students form pairs to cross-check their matrices, discussing any discrepancies without consulting reference materials. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire verbal quiz where instructor calls out a Knowledge Area and students must recite all associated processes within 30 seconds per area. Rotate through different students for each Knowledge Area. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Reverse challenge - instructor states a process name and students must immediately identify both the Knowledge Area and Process Group. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Final verification using master reference sheet where students self-correct their matrices and calculate accuracy percentages. Throughout the activity, emphasize speed and accuracy to reinforce automatic recall rather than analytical thinking.
materials_needed: 49 laminated process name cards per student (e.g., 'Develop Project Charter', 'Plan Scope Management')
Blank 10x5 Process Integration Matrix worksheets
PMBOK Process Groups and Knowledge Areas master reference sheets
Timer/stopwatch
Red and green pens for self-correction
assessment_method: Success measured by final matrix accuracy score (Advanced: 90-100%, Proficient: 80-89%, Developing: 70-79%). Additional points awarded for rapid-fire recall speed (correctly naming 4+ processes within 30-second Knowledge Area challenges). Students submit completed matrices with self-calculated accuracy percentages and instructor spot-checks 25% for verification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide Knowledge Area definition cards as memory triggers and allow them to start with just Integration and Scope Management processes. For advanced learners: add ITTOs (Inputs, Tools/Techniques, Outputs) identification challenge or require them to explain the logical flow between processes within each Knowledge Area while maintaining memorization focus.

title: Situational Leadership Model Analysis Through Crisis Decision Points
description: Students will analyze complex organizational crisis scenarios to identify how effective leaders adapted their leadership styles using Hersey-Blanchard's Situational Leadership Model. They will demonstrate understanding by categorizing follower readiness levels and explaining the rationale behind leadership style transitions during critical decision points.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between the four situational leadership styles (S1-S4) by analyzing leader behaviors during documented organizational crises
Students will interpret the relationship between follower development levels (D1-D4) and appropriate leadership responses through case study examination
instructions:
Begin by distributing four detailed crisis case studies (20 minutes): Netflix's content strategy pivot (2007-2012), Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982), Airbnb's COVID-19 response (2020), and Starbucks' racial bias incident response (2018). Each case includes timeline, stakeholder profiles, and leader decision points marked as 'Critical Moments A-D.' 

Divide students into expert groups of 4-5, assigning each group one case study (5 minutes setup). Groups spend 45 minutes analyzing their case using the provided Situational Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet. They must: identify follower competence and commitment levels at each critical moment, determine which leadership style (Directing, Coaching, Supporting, or Delegating) was used, evaluate style appropriateness, and predict alternative outcomes with different approaches.

Next, reorganize into 'jigsaw' groups with one expert from each case study (10 minutes transition). In these mixed groups of 4, each expert presents their analysis using the structured 8-minute presentation template: 2 minutes context, 4 minutes critical moment analysis with Situational Leadership mapping, 2 minutes lessons learned (30 minutes total presentations).

Conclude with individual reflection where students complete a comparative analysis matrix, identifying patterns across all four cases about when and why leadership styles should shift during organizational stress (15 minutes). Students must cite specific evidence from cases to support their style-situation matches.

assessment_method: Evaluate completed Situational Leadership Analysis Framework worksheets using 4-point rubric assessing: accurate identification of follower development levels (25%), correct matching of leadership styles to situations (25%), quality of evidence-based reasoning (25%), and insightful alternative scenario predictions (25%). scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide leadership style decision trees and follower assessment checklists. Offer sentence starters for analysis explanations. title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront
description: Students will create a complete static website hosting solution by configuring AWS S3 buckets for storage and AWS CloudFront for content delivery. They will apply AWS security best practices and demonstrate understanding of cloud architecture by implementing a real-world web hosting scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS S3 bucket configuration principles by creating and securing a static website hosting environment with proper permissions and policies
Students will implement AWS CloudFront distribution setup through hands-on configuration of caching, SSL certificates, and custom domain integration
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Learner Lab credentials or free tier account. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify access to S3 and CloudFront services. Distribute the sample HTML/CSS files (index.html, error.html, styles.css) containing a simple portfolio website template.

**S3 Configuration (20 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket with a globally unique name following format 'student-name-static-site-2024'. They enable static website hosting in bucket properties, set index.html as index document and error.html as error document. Students upload provided website files, ensuring public read access by configuring bucket policy using provided JSON template. They test the S3 website endpoint URL to verify basic functionality.

**CloudFront Setup (25 minutes):** Students create a CloudFront distribution with their S3 bucket as origin. They configure default cache behavior, set price class to 'Use Only US, Canada and Europe', and enable compression. Students create a custom error page configuration for 404 errors. They wait for distribution deployment (15-20 minutes) while documenting their architecture diagram.

**Security Implementation (10 minutes):** Students modify S3 bucket policy to restrict direct access and only allow CloudFront origin access control. They verify the S3 endpoint returns access denied while CloudFront URL serves content properly.

**Testing and Documentation (10 minutes):** Students test website loading speed from CloudFront URL, verify custom error pages work, and complete a deployment checklist documenting all configuration settings, URLs, and security measures implemented.
materials_needed: AWS account credentials (Learner Lab or Free Tier)
Sample website files (index.html, error.html, styles.css)
S3 bucket policy JSON template
Architecture diagram template
Deployment checklist worksheet
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Working CloudFront URL demonstrating functional website (40 points), (2) Completed architecture diagram showing S3-CloudFront relationship (20 points), (3) Screenshot evidence of proper security configuration with S3 direct access blocked (20 points), (4) Deployment checklist with all configuration details documented (20 points). Success criteria: Website loads via CloudFront URL, S3 direct access is properly restricted, custom error pages function correctly, and documentation is complete and accurate.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured bucket policy templates and step-by-step screenshot guides. Pair students for peer support during CloudFront deployment waiting time. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement custom SSL certificates, add multiple origins, configure cache invalidation policies, or integrate with Route 53 for custom domain names. Provide troubleshooting flowchart for common configuration errors.

description: Students will apply AWS S3 bucket configuration and CloudFront distribution setup to deploy a functional static website. They will implement proper security settings, configure custom domain routing, and optimize content delivery through hands-on practice with real AWS services.

instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and a starter website package containing index.html, error.html, CSS file, and 3 images. Students should log into AWS Management Console and navigate to S3 service.

They must enable static website hosting in bucket properties, set index.html as index document and error.html as error document. Students upload all website files maintaining folder structure, then configure bucket policy using provided JSON template to allow public read access to objects.

Students deploy the distribution and note the CloudFront domain name.

**Phase 4 - Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Students test both S3 website endpoint and CloudFront distribution URL in browsers, verify images load correctly, and test error page by accessing non-existent URLs. They document response times and note geographic distribution benefits.
materials_needed: AWS account credentials for each student
Pre-built HTML website package (index.html, error.html, 2-3 image files)
S3 bucket policy JSON template
Student worksheet for documenting URLs and testing results
Web browsers for testing
assessment_method: Students submit a completed worksheet containing: (1) S3 bucket name and website endpoint URL, (2) CloudFront distribution domain name, (3) Screenshots of working website from both S3 and CloudFront URLs, (4) Screenshot of successful error page display, (5) Brief comparison of load times between S3 and CloudFront access. Rubric: Complete deployment (40%), Proper configuration screenshots (30%), Functional testing evidence (20%), Load time analysis (10%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step screenshots of each AWS console screen and pre-written bucket policy with clear placeholder indicators. Create checkpoint verifications after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement custom domain names using Route 53, add custom error pages for different HTTP status codes, or configure CloudFront cache behaviors for different file types with varying TTL settings.

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website Using AWS S3 and CloudFront: Practical Workshop
description: Students will apply AWS S3 and CloudFront services to host and distribute a static website. They will configure bucket policies, enable static website hosting, and set up a content delivery network to optimize global access.
learning_objectives: Students will apply S3 bucket configuration principles to deploy a functional static website by uploading HTML files and configuring public access settings
Students will implement CloudFront distribution settings to optimize website performance through hands-on CDN configuration and testing
instructions:
**Pre-activity Setup (5 minutes):** Instructor demonstrates AWS Management Console navigation and provides students with prepared HTML files (index.html with basic content, error.html for 404 pages). Students log into AWS Free Tier accounts.

**Phase 1 - S3 Bucket Creation (15 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a globally unique name following format 'website-[lastname]-[randomnumber]'. They select US East (N. Virginia) region, disable 'Block all public access', and acknowledge the warning about public access.

**Phase 2 - Website Configuration (20 minutes):** Students upload provided HTML files to their bucket root. They navigate to bucket Properties tab, scroll to 'Static website hosting', enable it, and set index.html as index document and error.html as error document. Students copy the bucket website endpoint URL for testing.

**Phase 3 - Bucket Policy Application (15 minutes):** In the Permissions tab, students add a bucket policy using provided JSON template, replacing 'BUCKET-NAME' with their actual bucket name. The policy allows public read access to all objects. Students test website accessibility using the endpoint URL.

**Phase 4 - CloudFront Distribution (20 minutes):** Students create a CloudFront distribution, setting origin domain to their S3 bucket website endpoint (not the bucket itself). They configure default root object as 'index.html', select price class 'Use Only US, Canada and Europe', and deploy. Students note the distribution domain name.

**Phase 5 - Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** After CloudFront deployment completes, students access their website through both S3 endpoint and CloudFront domain, documenting load times and testing from different geographic locations using online tools.

Rubric: Complete functionality (40%), Proper configuration screenshots (30%), Performance comparison (20%), Reflection quality (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide step-by-step screenshot guide, pair with stronger peers, offer pre-filled bucket policy templates with highlighted areas to modify. **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to add custom domain using Route 53, implement HTTPS certificate via Certificate Manager, or configure cache behaviors for different file types. title: Risk Register Impact Analysis: Comparing Qualitative vs. Quantitative Assessment Methods
description: Students will analyze a real-world project risk register to compare the effectiveness of qualitative versus quantitative risk assessment methodologies. They will break down risk components, evaluate assessment accuracy, and determine which method provides better decision-making insights for specific risk types.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk assessment data by comparing qualitative probability/impact ratings against quantitative monetary values and statistical probabilities
Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of each risk assessment method through systematic examination of risk register entries and their business context
instructions: **Phase 1 (15 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the IT Infrastructure Upgrade project risk register containing 12 identified risks with both qualitative (High/Medium/Low probability and impact) and quantitative data (monetary impact ranges, percentage probabilities). Each team receives analysis worksheets and calculators. **Phase 2 (25 minutes):** Teams examine each risk entry, focusing on three specific risks assigned to them: 'Legacy System Integration Failure,' 'Vendor Delivery Delays,' and 'Budget Overrun Due to Scope Creep.' For each risk, they complete comparison matrices analyzing: (1) How qualitative rankings translate to quantitative values, (2) Which method better captures stakeholder concerns, (3) Which provides clearer prioritization guidance. **Phase 3 (20 minutes):** Teams calculate Expected Monetary Value (EMV) for their assigned risks using provided formulas, then compare EMV rankings against qualitative priority rankings. They identify discrepancies and analyze root causes using the provided decision tree templates. **Phase 4 (15 minutes):** Teams prepare 3-minute presentations highlighting their key findings: which assessment method they recommend for each risk type and why, supported by specific data from their analysis. **Phase 5 (10 minutes):** Class discussion where teams share insights and instructor facilitates comparison of different teams' conclusions about assessment method effectiveness.
materials_needed: Pre-populated IT Infrastructure Upgrade project risk register (Excel format)
Risk Analysis Comparison Worksheet (printed template)
EMV calculation reference sheet with formulas
Decision tree templates
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of EMV calculations (25%), (2) Quality of method comparison analysis with specific examples (35%), (3) Logical justification for recommended assessment approaches (25%), (4) Clear presentation of findings with data support (15%). Students must identify at least 2 specific scenarios where qualitative and quantitative methods yield different prioritizations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide EMV calculation examples and step-by-step guidance sheets. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose hybrid assessment approaches or analyze additional risks beyond the assigned three. Provide Monte Carlo simulation data for deeper quantitative analysis.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Critical Evaluation and Business Impact Assessment
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess business impact by comparing conversion credit distribution across marketing channels and make strategic recommendations for budget reallocation based on their analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and quantifying discrepancies in channel performance metrics
Students will critique current marketing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and defend budget reallocation recommendations with statistical evidence
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection Setup (20 minutes)**

Students access Google Analytics 4 demo account or provided case study dataset. Navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. Configure date range to previous 90 days and select primary conversion event (purchases). Export baseline data showing conversions and revenue by channel under last-click attribution.

**Phase 2: Multi-Model Analysis (45 minutes)**

Systematically analyze each attribution model: Switch between last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven models. For each model, record: total conversions by channel, revenue attribution percentages, and conversion value changes. Create comparison matrix documenting how each channel's performance varies across models. Calculate percentage differences in attribution for each marketing channel (paid search, social media, email, display, direct).

**Phase 3: Customer Journey Investigation (30 minutes)**

Navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Top conversion paths. Analyze actual customer journeys leading to conversions. Identify patterns: average path length, most common channel sequences, and time between touchpoints. Document insights about customer behavior that explain attribution model differences.

**Phase 4: Critical Evaluation Report (45 minutes)**

Produce written evaluation addressing: Which attribution model most accurately reflects customer behavior patterns? What are the limitations of each model for this business type? How would adopting different models impact marketing budget allocation? Provide specific recommendations with quantified financial impact projections. Include methodology critique discussing potential data biases and measurement limitations.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 access (demo account or instructor-provided dataset)
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data comparison matrices
Calculator for percentage change calculations
Attribution model comparison template (instructor-provided)
Business case study context document with marketing spend data
assessment_method: Rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and calculations (25 points), (2) Depth of attribution model comparison and statistical analysis (30 points), (3) Quality of critical evaluation and identification of model limitations (25 points), (4) Strength of business recommendations with supporting evidence (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of when each model is appropriate and provide budget reallocation recommendations with projected ROI impact.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data collection templates and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer example attribution scenarios with clear cause-effect relationships. For advanced learners: Include analysis of assisted conversions, cross-device tracking implications, and custom attribution model creation. Challenge them to incorporate external factors (seasonality, competitor activity) into their evaluation framework.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using traditional MPLS, Internet VPN, and SD-WAN technologies. They will create network diagrams, implement routing protocols, configure security policies, and establish redundant connectivity while optimizing traffic flow based on application requirements.
estimated_duration: 420 minutes (7 hours) - can be split across multiple lab sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced routing protocols (EIGRP, OSPF, BGP) with SD-WAN overlay technologies by designing a hybrid WAN architecture that meets specific business requirements
Students will construct comprehensive network security policies through implementation of zone-based firewalls, VPN tunnels, and application-aware routing policies
instructions: Begin with a 30-minute briefing presenting the scenario: Company ABC needs to connect headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and remote office (50 users) with specific SLA requirements for voice, video, and data traffic. Students work in teams of 2-3. Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams create detailed network topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes (/24 subnets minimum), device models (ISR 4000 series routers, Catalyst 9000 switches), and connection types. They must document bandwidth requirements, failover scenarios, and traffic prioritization policies. Phase 2 (120 minutes): Using Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) or physical equipment, students configure base Layer 3 connectivity between sites using OSPF as the IGP and BGP for external connections. They implement VRF-Lite for traffic segmentation between departments. Phase 3 (90 minutes): Students deploy SD-WAN controllers (vManage, vSmart, vBond) and configure vEdge routers at each site, establishing secure fabric connectivity with OMP routing. Phase 4 (60 minutes): Teams create and apply centralized policies for application routing, security zones, and QoS marking. They must demonstrate traffic steering based on application type (Office 365 direct internet, ERP through MPLS, backup traffic via Internet VPN). Phase 5 (30 minutes): Students conduct failover testing, documenting convergence times and traffic behavior during link failures. Final deliverable includes complete configuration files, network documentation, and 10-minute presentation demonstrating network functionality.
materials_needed: Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) license or physical lab with 6x ISR 4331 routers, 3x Catalyst 9300 switches
SD-WAN software licenses (vManage, vSmart, vBond controllers, vEdge images)
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart licenses for network diagramming
Network requirements document template with SLA specifications
Traffic generation tools (iPerf3, Ostinato) for testing
assessment_method: Evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points - topology accuracy, IP addressing, device selection justification), Configuration Implementation (35 points - functional routing, SD-WAN fabric establishment, policy application), Security Implementation (20 points - zone-based firewall rules, VPN configuration, access control), Testing and Validation (20 points - failover demonstration, performance metrics, troubleshooting documentation). Students must successfully demonstrate end-to-end connectivity, policy enforcement, and failover scenarios during live evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic IP addressing and offer checkpoint reviews after each phase. Create troubleshooting flowcharts for common SD-WAN deployment issues. For advanced learners: Add requirements for multi-homed Internet connections, implement advanced security features like intrusion prevention, or integrate with cloud services (AWS/Azure ExpressRoute). Consider adding network automation components using Python scripts for configuration deployment.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN Integration: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using traditional MPLS, internet VPN, and SD-WAN technologies. They will create network diagrams, implement routing protocols, configure security policies, and establish redundant connectivity while optimizing for cost and performance.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, BGP, and EIGRP routing protocols by designing a hierarchical network topology that supports 500+ users across multiple sites
Students will create a comprehensive SD-WAN deployment through configuring Cisco Viptela controllers, edge devices, and policy frameworks for traffic optimization
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (90 minutes)**
Students work in teams of 3-4 to design a network for fictional company 'GlobalTech Corp' with headquarters (200 users), manufacturing site (150 users), and branch office (100 users). Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, create detailed network topology diagrams including IP addressing schemes (use 10.0.0.0/8 private addressing), VLAN segmentation for departments, and WAN connectivity options. Document bandwidth requirements: HQ needs 100Mbps internet + 50Mbps MPLS, manufacturing needs 50Mbps internet + 20Mbps MPLS, branch needs 25Mbps internet backup.

**Phase 2: Core Infrastructure Implementation (120 minutes)**
Configure three Cisco ISR 4000 series routers as site gateways. Implement OSPF area 0 for HQ, area 1 for manufacturing, area 2 for branch office. Configure BGP peering with simulated ISP (AS 65001) using private AS numbers 65100-65102 for each site. Set up GRE tunnels between sites as MPLS backup. Configure Catalyst 9300 switches with VLANs: VLAN 10 (management), VLAN 20 (users), VLAN 30 (servers), VLAN 40 (guest). Implement STP rapid-PVST+ and configure trunk links with proper native VLAN settings.

**Phase 3: SD-WAN Overlay (90 minutes)**
Deploy Cisco SD-WAN solution using vManage controller (simulate with dedicated VM), vSmart policy controller, and vBond orchestrator. Configure vEdge routers at each site with templates for interface configuration, routing policies, and security settings. Create application-aware routing policies prioritizing voice traffic over MPLS and web traffic over internet connections. Implement centralized security policies including zone-based firewalls and intrusion prevention.

**Phase 4: Testing and Optimization (60 minutes)**
Execute comprehensive testing plan including failover scenarios, traffic optimization verification, and security policy validation. Document network performance metrics and create troubleshooting procedures for common failure scenarios.

VMware Workstation/VirtualBox with Windows 10 VMs for SD-WAN controllers
Cisco SD-WAN simulation lab files or DevNet sandbox access

Performance testing tools (iperf3, Wireshark)
assessment_method: Students submit comprehensive network documentation package including: (1) Detailed topology diagrams with IP addressing schemes (25 points), (2) Complete device configurations with comments explaining design decisions (30 points), (3) SD-WAN policy configuration files and templates (25 points), (4) Testing results documentation with performance metrics and failover verification (20 points). Rubric evaluates technical accuracy, design scalability, security implementation, and documentation quality. Peer review component where teams present solutions and critique others' designs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates for router/switch configurations and step-by-step SD-WAN setup guides. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate network automation using Python/Ansible, or implement advanced QoS policies with DSCP marking and traffic shaping. Provide access to Cisco DevNet learning labs for additional hands-on practice with real equipment.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN Integration: Exercise 2
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three geographically distributed sites, incorporating SD-WAN technology, redundant connections, and advanced security policies.
