title: Programming Language Syntax Elements Memory Match
description: Students will memorize and identify fundamental syntax elements from three common programming languages (Python, Java, and JavaScript) through a structured flashcard and matching activity. This foundational exercise builds essential recall skills for basic programming constructs that students will use throughout their coding journey.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the correct syntax for common programming constructs (variables, loops, conditionals, functions) in Python, Java, and JavaScript by completing flashcard drills with 85% accuracy
Students will identify which programming language uses specific syntax patterns through a timed matching exercise
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute pre-made flashcard sets to each student containing 36 cards - 12 syntax examples each for Python, Java, and JavaScript. Include variable declarations, for loops, if statements, and function definitions for each language. Also provide answer sheets with language identification keys.

**Phase 1 - Individual Study (15 minutes):** Students examine flashcards showing code snippets on one side and language identification plus explanation on the reverse. They study each card for 30 seconds, reading the syntax aloud quietly, then flipping to verify the language and construct type. Students cycle through all 36 cards twice, setting aside any they find challenging.

**Phase 2 - Self-Testing (10 minutes):** Students look only at the code snippet side and attempt to identify: (1) which programming language it represents, and (2) what programming construct it demonstrates. They check answers immediately and create a separate pile of incorrectly identified cards for additional review.

**Phase 3 - Partner Verification (8 minutes):** Pair students to quiz each other using the cards they initially found difficult. Partner A shows code snippets to Partner B, who must state the language and construct type within 5 seconds. Partners switch roles after 4 minutes.

**Assessment Activity (12 minutes):** Present 20 mixed syntax examples via projection screen. Students write answers on response sheets, identifying both the programming language and construct type for each example. Display each example for 15 seconds before advancing to the next.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (36 cards per student) with Python, Java, and JavaScript syntax examples
Answer verification sheets with correct language and construct identifications
Individual response sheets for final assessment
Digital projector or smartboard for displaying assessment examples
Timer for pacing activities
assessment_method: Grade final response sheets using provided answer key. Success criteria: 85% accuracy (17/20 correct) on language identification and 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on construct type identification. Award full credit for meeting both criteria, partial credit for meeting one criterion, and require remediation for students below both thresholds.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce flashcard set to 24 cards (focus on just Python and Java initially) and provide syntax reference sheets during study phase. For advanced learners: Add additional languages like C++ or include more complex constructs such as classes, exception handling, or lambda functions. Consider having advanced students create their own flashcards for newer syntax elements.

title: Interpreting Customer Churn Patterns Through Exploratory Data Analysis Visualizations
description: Students will analyze a customer churn dataset by examining correlation matrices, distribution plots, and feature relationships to explain why customers leave a telecommunications service. They will interpret statistical visualizations to identify key patterns and articulate data-driven insights about customer behavior.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients and heatmaps by explaining the strength and direction of relationships between customer features and churn rates
Students will explain customer churn patterns through systematic analysis of distribution plots, box plots, and categorical breakdowns
instructions: Begin by distributing the Telco Customer Churn dataset (available on Kaggle) and have students work in pairs. Provide each pair with a Jupyter notebook template containing pre-loaded data and empty code cells. Students spend the first 15 minutes exploring the dataset structure using df.info() and df.describe() commands, documenting their observations about data types, missing values, and basic statistics. Next, guide students through creating a correlation matrix heatmap using seaborn, focusing on numerical features like tenure, monthly charges, and total charges against the churn target variable. Students must interpret correlation values above 0.3 or below -0.3, explaining what these relationships mean in business context. For the next 20 minutes, students create distribution plots comparing churned vs. non-churned customers across key features like contract type, payment method, and internet service type. They use matplotlib and seaborn to generate side-by-side histograms and box plots. During this phase, circulate to ensure students are labeling axes properly and calculating summary statistics. In the final 15 minutes, each pair writes a brief interpretation summary identifying the top 3 factors most strongly associated with customer churn, supported by specific statistical evidence from their visualizations. Students must cite exact correlation values, median differences, or percentage breakdowns in their explanations. Conclude with 2-3 pairs presenting one key insight to the class, explaining both the statistical evidence and the business implication.
materials_needed: Telco Customer Churn dataset (CSV file)
Jupyter notebook template with data loading code
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Laptop or computer for each student pair
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate interpretation of correlation coefficients with correct directional language, (2) Proper explanation of distribution differences using specific statistical measures, (3) Clear articulation of business implications from statistical patterns, (4) Quality of visual analysis including appropriate chart selection and interpretation. Students must submit their annotated notebook and written summary identifying 3 key churn factors with supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide showing how to translate numerical values into descriptive language (e.g., 0.4 = moderate positive relationship). Offer sentence starters like 'The correlation between X and churn is ___, which suggests that customers with higher X values are ___ likely to churn.' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify interaction effects between variables or calculate effect sizes for categorical differences using Cohen's d or similar metrics.

title: Optimization Analysis: Designing a Solar Panel Array for Maximum Energy Output
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem by determining the optimal dimensions and positioning of solar panels to maximize energy collection while working within physical and budgetary constraints. This activity integrates derivative applications, constraint optimization, and mathematical modeling.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to determine maximum energy output by analyzing solar panel positioning and dimensions within given constraints
Students will construct and solve optimization models through systematic application of Lagrange multipliers and critical point analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing a residential rooftop layout (40ft × 25ft) with obstacles marked, solar panel specifications, and cost constraints ($15,000 budget). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Calculator, Constraint Analyst, Model Validator, and Presentation Coordinator. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the given data including solar irradiance function I(θ,φ) = 800cos²(θ)sin(φ) watts/m², where θ is tilt angle and φ is azimuth angle, panel dimensions (1.2m × 2.0m), cost per panel ($250), and installation constraints. Students must identify all variables and constraints.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Teams formulate the optimization problem by defining the objective function for total energy output E = n × I(θ,φ) × A × efficiency, where n is number of panels, A is panel area, and efficiency = 0.18. Students establish constraints: budget constraint (250n ≤ 15,000), space constraint (panel area × n ≤ available roof area), and physical constraints (0° ≤ θ ≤ 60°, 0° ≤ φ ≤ 180°).

Step 3 (40 minutes): Apply optimization techniques using Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization. Students calculate partial derivatives, set up the Lagrangian L = E - λ₁(budget constraint) - λ₂(space constraint), solve the system of equations ∇L = 0, and verify solutions using second derivative test.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams validate their solutions by checking boundary conditions, testing corner cases, and calculating actual energy output values. Use graphing calculators or computer algebra systems to verify critical points.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their optimal configuration including number of panels, positioning angles, total cost, and maximum daily energy output in kWh.
materials_needed: Scenario packets with rooftop blueprints and solar specifications
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Computer access with Desmos Graphing Calculator or Mathematica
Measurement tools (rulers, protractors) for blueprint analysis
Presentation materials (whiteboards, markers)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical setup and constraint identification (25 points), correct application of Lagrange multiplier method (30 points), accurate calculations and solution verification (25 points), and clear presentation of final optimization solution with justification (20 points). Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed Lagrangian setup and guide them through the first constraint application. Offer step-by-step derivative calculation templates. For advanced learners: Add time-dependent variables (seasonal sun angle changes) or introduce economic factors like energy payback calculations over 20 years. Consider additional constraints like wind load limitations or shading effects between panels.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Induction Patterns in Multi-Loop Circuit Systems
description: Students will decompose complex electromagnetic induction scenarios involving multiple conducting loops at varying distances and orientations. They will analyze how changing magnetic fields create different induced EMF patterns and distinguish between self-inductance and mutual inductance effects in coupled circuit systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between magnetic flux changes and induced EMF by examining multi-loop configurations with varying geometric parameters
Students will distinguish between self-inductance and mutual inductance contributions through systematic comparison of isolated versus coupled loop behaviors
instructions:
Begin by providing each team with three scenarios: (1) Two parallel circular loops 5cm apart with varying current in primary loop, (2) Two perpendicular square loops sharing a common center, (3) Three coaxial circular loops of different radii in series. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 90 minutes total.

Step 1 (20 min): Teams calculate theoretical magnetic flux through each loop using Biot-Savart law and geometric relationships. Provide current functions: I₁(t) = 2sin(10t) A for scenario 1, step function 0→3A for scenario 2, and exponential decay I(t) = 5e^(-2t) A for scenario 3.

Step 2 (25 min): Using Faraday's law, calculate induced EMF in each loop. Students must identify which EMF components arise from self-inductance versus mutual inductance by systematically 'turning off' coupling between loops in their calculations.

Step 3 (25 min): Teams use circuit simulation software (LTSpice or equivalent) to model each scenario, comparing simulated EMF values with theoretical calculations. Require screenshots showing voltage-time graphs for each loop.

Step 4 (20 min): Analyze discrepancies between theory and simulation. Students must identify whether differences arise from: resistance effects, non-ideal geometry assumptions, or numerical approximation limitations. Create comparison tables showing percent differences and proposed explanations.

Conclude with 5-minute team presentations highlighting their most significant analytical insight about inductance coupling effects, supported by quantitative evidence from their calculations and simulations.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators capable of complex trigonometric functions
Computers with LTSpice or equivalent circuit simulation software installed
Printed scenario worksheets with specific loop dimensions and current functions
Graph paper for sketching magnetic field line patterns
Digital presentation setup for final team presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Theoretical calculations accuracy (25%) - correct application of Biot-Savart and Faraday's laws, (2) Self/mutual inductance distinction (30%) - clear identification and quantification of coupling effects, (3) Simulation analysis quality (25%) - meaningful comparison between theory and simulation with valid explanations for discrepancies, (4) Analytical reasoning (20%) - depth of insight in identifying key physical principles governing the coupling behaviors. Require submission of calculation worksheets, simulation screenshots, and comparison tables.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step Biot-Savart calculation templates and pre-built LTSpice circuit files requiring only parameter modifications. Offer geometric visualization aids showing magnetic field line sketches. For advanced learners: Add fourth scenario involving non-coplanar loops with complex 3D geometry, or extend to analyze frequency-dependent coupling effects using AC analysis tools. Encourage investigation of practical applications like transformer design or wireless charging systems.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Three Password Validation Functions
description: Students will analyze and critique three different password validation functions written in Python, evaluating their effectiveness, security, readability, and performance. They will rank the functions from best to worst and justify their decisions using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of existing code by applying readability, security, and performance criteria to three password validation functions
Students will critique programming implementations through systematic analysis and provide evidence-based rankings with written justifications
instructions: Begin by displaying three pre-written password validation functions (provided below) on the projector or shared screen. Distribute printed copies to each student along with the evaluation worksheet. Explain that students have 25 minutes to individually analyze each function using the provided criteria checklist: readability (variable names, comments, structure), security (password requirements, vulnerability protection), performance (efficiency, unnecessary operations), and maintainability (code organization, ease of modification). Students should take notes on each function's strengths and weaknesses using the worksheet sections. After individual analysis, students rank the three functions from 1 (best) to 3 (worst) and write a 150-word justification explaining their ranking decisions with specific examples from the code. In the final 10 minutes, facilitate a class discussion where 4-5 students share their rankings and reasoning. Record different rankings on the board and highlight where students identified different strengths/weaknesses in the same code. Function A uses basic string methods with clear variable names but limited security. Function B implements comprehensive security checks but has poor readability. Function C balances security and readability but contains performance inefficiencies. Provide these functions as handouts with line numbers for easy reference during discussion.
materials_needed: Printed copies of three password validation functions (Function A, B, and C)
Code evaluation worksheet with criteria checklist and ranking sections
Projector or shared screen for displaying code
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of code strengths/weaknesses in each function using provided criteria (40%), (2) Logical ranking with clear justification citing specific code examples (40%), (3) Quality of written explanation demonstrating evaluation reasoning (20%). Students must identify at least 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses per function and provide code line references in their justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth simple function showing how to identify strengths/weaknesses and write justifications. Pair them with stronger students during discussion. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific code improvements for their lowest-ranked function and explain how those changes would address identified weaknesses. Challenge them to consider additional evaluation criteria like error handling or user experience.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Three Password Validation Functions: Comparative Study
description: Students will critically analyze and compare three different JavaScript password validation functions to determine which implementation is most effective. They will evaluate each function against security, readability, and performance criteria to make a justified recommendation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three password validation code implementations by analyzing their security effectiveness, code readability, and performance characteristics
Students will justify their selection of the best implementation through written assessment using specific technical criteria and evidence-based reasoning
instructions: Begin by distributing the three pre-written JavaScript password validation functions (Function A uses basic string methods, Function B uses regular expressions, Function C uses a hybrid approach with multiple validation steps). Give students 10 minutes to individually read through all three functions and make initial notes about what each does. Next, provide the evaluation criteria sheet covering: Security (Does it check length, special characters, numbers, mixed case?), Readability (Is the code easy to understand and maintain?), and Performance (How efficient is the execution?). Have students spend 25 minutes working in pairs to systematically evaluate each function against these criteria, filling out the comparison matrix worksheet. They should test each function with 5 provided sample passwords (weak, medium, strong examples) and record the results. For the next 15 minutes, pairs must write a 200-word recommendation report stating which function they would choose for a real application and why, citing specific evidence from their testing. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where 3-4 pairs present their recommendations, highlighting any disagreements and the reasoning behind different choices. Students submit their completed comparison matrix and recommendation report as individual assessments.
materials_needed: Three pre-written JavaScript password validation functions (printed handouts)
Evaluation criteria rubric sheet
Password comparison matrix worksheet
Sample password test cases (5 examples)
Computer/browser with JavaScript console or CodePen access
assessment_method: Grade the comparison matrix (40 points) for accuracy of technical analysis and the recommendation report (60 points) using a rubric that scores: technical accuracy of evaluation (25 points), quality of evidence cited (20 points), clarity of reasoning (15 points). Success criteria: Students must identify at least 2 strengths and 1 weakness per function, correctly test all sample passwords, and provide specific technical justification for their final recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed comparison matrix with 1-2 examples filled in, and offer sentence starters for the recommendation report. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional evaluation criteria (like accessibility or user experience) or to suggest specific code improvements for their chosen function.

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Sales Data
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will develop their own segmentation criteria, design visualizations, and present actionable business recommendations based on their analytical findings.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive customer segmentation strategy by applying RFM analysis methodology to real e-commerce transaction data
Students will create an interactive dashboard with original visualizations through combining multiple data analysis and visualization techniques
instructions: Begin by providing students with a dataset containing 6 months of e-commerce transactions (customer ID, purchase date, order value, product categories). In the first 30 minutes, students work individually to explore the data structure and identify data quality issues using Excel or Python/pandas. Next, form teams of 3-4 students who will spend 45 minutes calculating RFM scores: Recency (days since last purchase), Frequency (number of transactions), and Monetary (total spend per customer). Teams must establish their own scoring criteria (1-5 scale) and justify their thresholds based on data distribution analysis. During the following 60 minutes, students create customer segments by combining RFM scores into meaningful groups (e.g., Champions, Loyal Customers, At Risk, Cannot Lose Them). They must name each segment and define characteristics using statistical summaries. For the next 90 minutes, teams build an interactive dashboard using Tableau, Power BI, or Python (matplotlib/plotly) featuring: a segment overview chart, RFM score distributions, customer lifecycle analysis, and segment-specific metrics. The dashboard must include filters for date ranges and product categories. In the final 45 minutes, each team presents their dashboard to the class, explaining their segmentation logic, key insights discovered, and three specific marketing recommendations for each customer segment. Presentations should demonstrate dashboard interactivity and defend analytical choices made during the process.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV format, 10,000+ records)
Computers with Excel, Tableau/Power BI, or Python environment
Projector for team presentations
RFM analysis reference guide handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data exploration and cleaning (20 points), RFM calculation accuracy and methodology justification (25 points), dashboard design and functionality (25 points), quality of insights and business recommendations (20 points), presentation clarity and defense of analytical decisions (10 points). Students submit dashboard files and a 2-page methodology report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM score examples and dashboard templates with basic structure. Offer simplified dataset with fewer variables. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables (product preferences, seasonality), implement machine learning clustering algorithms, or create predictive models for customer lifetime value.

Students will construct an interactive dashboard through combining statistical analysis, data visualization, and business intelligence tools
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 people) with the e-commerce dataset containing customer transactions from the past 2 years. In the first 30 minutes, teams analyze the data structure and brainstorm segmentation approaches, documenting their strategy in a planning template. Next, spend 45 minutes having students design their RFM scoring system: they must define recency periods (0-365 days), frequency brackets (1-50+ orders), and monetary value ranges ($0-$10,000+), then create weighted scoring formulas. During the following 60 minutes, students implement their segmentation logic using Python/Pandas or Excel, calculating RFM scores for each customer and assigning segment labels (Champions, Loyal Customers, At Risk, etc.). They must validate their segments by spot-checking 10 random customers and adjusting criteria if needed. In the next 45 minutes, teams build their dashboard using Tableau, Power BI, or Python visualization libraries, creating at least 4 charts: segment distribution pie chart, average monetary value by segment bar chart, customer lifecycle scatter plot, and trend analysis line chart. Instructors should circulate during implementation phases, checking progress every 15 minutes and providing technical support as needed.

RFM Analysis Planning Template (Word document)
Laptops with Python/Pandas OR Excel OR Tableau/Power BI installed
Dashboard presentation template
Printed RFM scoring reference guide
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical Implementation (40 points - correct RFM calculations, functional dashboard, appropriate visualizations), Design Quality (30 points - clear layout, effective color schemes, intuitive navigation), Business Insight (20 points - logical segmentation criteria, actionable recommendations, trend identification), and Presentation (10 points - clear explanation of methodology, confident delivery, responds to questions). title: PMI-PMP Knowledge Area Terminology Speed Recall Challenge
description: Students memorize and rapidly recall 150+ advanced project management terms, formulas, and definitions from all ten PMI knowledge areas. They compete in timed rounds to demonstrate mastery of complex PM vocabulary essential for professional certification.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions for 150 advanced PMI terminology terms including EVM formulas, risk assessment techniques, and quality management concepts within 10 seconds per term
Students will identify correct PMI knowledge area classifications for complex project management processes through rapid-fire verbal responses
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared deck of 150 terminology cards covering all ten PMI knowledge areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder Management). Each card contains an advanced term on one side (e.g., 'Schedule Performance Index', 'Monte Carlo Analysis', 'Analogous Estimating') and complete definition plus knowledge area on reverse. Students receive 20 minutes for individual memorization using any technique (flashcards, mnemonics, grouping by knowledge area). Next, arrange students in groups of 4-5 with one designated scorekeeper per group. Round 1 (15 minutes): One student draws a card and reads the term aloud; the active participant has 10 seconds to provide the complete definition. Award 2 points for perfect definitions, 1 point for partially correct answers. Rotate roles after every 5 cards. Round 2 (10 minutes): Speed classification round where students must identify which PMI knowledge area each term belongs to within 5 seconds. Award 1 point per correct classification. Round 3 (15 minutes): Formula recall challenge focusing specifically on Earned Value Management calculations (PV, EV, AC, CV, SV, CPI, SPI, EAC, ETC, TCPI). Students must recite exact formulas and explain what each acronym represents. Award 3 points for complete formula plus explanation. Conclude with individual reflection where each student writes down their three weakest terminology areas for targeted review. Post group scores on whiteboard and recognize top performers.
materials_needed: 150 professionally printed terminology flashcards covering all PMI knowledge areas
Digital timer with audible alerts
Scoring sheets with point tracking grids
Whiteboard and markers for scorekeeping
PMI PMBOK Guide 7th Edition (reference copies)
assessment_method: Students must achieve minimum 70% accuracy across all three rounds (105/150 total possible points) to demonstrate satisfactory recall mastery. Track individual scores for: Round 1 definitions (max 60 points), Round 2 classifications (max 30 points), Round 3 formulas (max 60 points). Award mastery certificates to students scoring 85% or higher. Document specific terminology gaps for each student to guide future study priorities.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide abbreviated 75-card deck focusing on most essential terms, extend response time to 15 seconds, allow use of knowledge area reference sheets during Round 2. For advanced learners: Include additional 50 cards with emerging PM methodologies (Agile, Scrum Master terminology), require students to provide real-world application examples with definitions, challenge them to create original mnemonics for complex formulas to teach struggling peers.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing Multi-Stakeholder Decision-Making Through the 2008 Financial Crisis
description: Students will analyze complex leadership decisions during the 2008 financial crisis by examining primary source materials from government officials, banking executives, and regulatory agencies. They will identify and explain the competing leadership philosophies, stakeholder pressures, and decision-making frameworks that influenced critical policy responses during this period.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and crisis leadership approaches by analyzing documented decision-making processes of key figures during the 2008 financial crisis

Students will explain the relationship between stakeholder influence, organizational constraints, and leadership decision-making through detailed examination of primary source testimonies and policy documents
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into research teams of 4-5 members, assigning each team one key leader: Ben Bernanke (Federal Reserve), Henry Paulson (Treasury Secretary), Jamie Dimon (JPMorgan Chase), Dick Fuld (Lehman Brothers), or Sheila Bair (FDIC). Provide each team with a curated document packet containing Congressional testimonies, internal memos, interview transcripts, and policy announcements from their assigned leader during September-December 2008. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct deep-dive analysis using the provided Leadership Decision Matrix template, identifying: (1) stated leadership philosophy/approach, (2) key stakeholder groups influencing decisions, (3) organizational constraints faced, (4) communication strategies employed, and (5) decision-making timeline and rationale. Students must cite specific quotes and document references for each matrix element.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create a visual leadership profile poster displaying their analysis, including a decision-tree diagram showing how their leader's philosophy translated into specific actions, and a stakeholder influence map showing competing pressures.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Conduct structured comparison sessions where teams present their findings in 8-minute rotations, with audience members completing comparison worksheets identifying similarities and differences in leadership approaches. Facilitate whole-group discussion focusing on how different leadership styles emerged under identical crisis conditions, and why certain approaches succeeded or failed given organizational contexts.
materials_needed: Curated primary source document packets (5 different sets, 15-20 pages each)
Leadership Decision Matrix templates (digital or printed)
Large poster paper and colored markers
Comparison worksheets for audience analysis
Timer for structured rotations
Access to projector/screen for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point analytical rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership style identification with specific textual evidence (25%), (2) Depth of stakeholder influence analysis with documented examples (25%), (3) Quality of visual representation showing clear connections between philosophy and actions (25%), (4) Sophistication of comparative analysis demonstrating understanding of contextual factors influencing leadership effectiveness (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by providing at least 3 specific examples from primary sources for each rubric category.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted key passages in documents and offering leadership style definition cards as reference tools. For advanced learners, include additional challenge documents such as international regulatory responses or provide access to recorded interviews for deeper analysis. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those who need support in document interpretation.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Comparing Proactive vs. Reactive Project Management Approaches
description: Students will analyze two complete risk registers from similar construction projects to identify patterns in risk identification, assessment, and response strategies. They will differentiate between proactive and reactive risk management approaches and evaluate their impact on project outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk identification patterns by comparing two complete risk registers to distinguish between proactive and reactive risk management approaches
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies through systematic examination of risk probability, impact ratings, and mitigation plans
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute Case A (Westfield Office Complex) and Case B (Downtown Retail Center) risk registers, each containing 25+ identified risks with probability/impact ratings, risk scores, and response strategies. Provide the Risk Analysis Comparison Template with sections for: Risk Categories, Timing of Identification, Response Strategy Types, and Outcome Predictions. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams examine Case A risk register, categorizing risks by PMI standard categories (scope, schedule, cost, quality, resource, stakeholder). Students identify when each risk was likely identified (planning vs. execution phase) based on risk descriptions and specificity levels. 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams repeat analysis for Case B, noting differences in risk granularity, assessment depth, and response sophistication. Students calculate average risk scores per category and identify patterns in mitigation vs. acceptance strategies.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Using provided project outcome data (final cost variance, schedule performance index, quality metrics), teams analyze correlation between risk management approach and project success. Students complete comparison matrix identifying specific examples of proactive planning (detailed contingency plans, early stakeholder engagement) vs. reactive responses (generic mitigation, late identification).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about how risk identification timing affects response effectiveness, supported by specific examples from both cases. Conclude with instructor-led discussion connecting analysis to PMI risk management knowledge area standards.
materials_needed: Case A: Westfield Office Complex Risk Register (25 risks with ratings)
Case B: Downtown Retail Center Risk Register (25 risks with ratings)
Risk Analysis Comparison Template (Excel/PDF)
Project outcome summary sheets for both cases
PMI Risk Management Process reference guide
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison templates using 4-point rubric: Risk Categorization Accuracy (25%), Pattern Identification Quality (25%), Evidence-Based Analysis (25%), Response Strategy Evaluation (25%). Successful completion requires identifying at least 3 distinct differences between approaches with specific supporting examples and accurate correlation between risk management quality and project outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled risk category examples and highlight 2-3 obvious proactive vs. reactive examples to build pattern recognition. For advanced learners: Add challenge question requiring students to redesign Case B's reactive risks as proactive entries, including specific prevention strategies and earlier identification triggers. Consider providing Monte Carlo simulation data for quantitative risk analysis extension.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, comparing last-click, first-click, linear, and data-driven attribution models. They will assess which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and make strategic budget reallocation recommendations based on their analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of four attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and identifying model-specific insights that impact marketing strategy decisions
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer journey touchpoints and justify budget reallocation recommendations with quantitative evidence
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Setup (20 minutes)** - Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic sources. Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison and configure a custom date range. They must export attribution data for display ads, paid search, organic search, social media, and email campaigns showing conversions and conversion value under each of the four attribution models. **Phase 2: Quantitative Analysis (45 minutes)** - Students create a comparative spreadsheet calculating the percentage difference in attributed conversions and revenue between models for each channel. They must identify which channels gain/lose credit under different models and calculate the potential budget impact if shifting from last-click to data-driven attribution. Students document at least 5 specific insights where attribution models show significant variance (>20% difference). **Phase 3: Qualitative Evaluation (30 minutes)** - Using the Model comparison tool's conversion paths report, students analyze actual customer journeys to identify patterns. They must evaluate model accuracy by examining path length, time lag data, and assisted conversions. Students assess whether the data-driven model's machine learning approach provides more realistic credit distribution than rule-based models. **Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (25 minutes)** - Students prepare a 2-page executive summary recommending one attribution model with specific budget reallocation percentages across channels. The recommendation must address model limitations, implementation timeline, and expected ROI impact based on their analysis.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Access to GA4 Attribution reports and Model comparison tool
Executive summary template document
assessment_method: Students submit their comparative analysis spreadsheet (25 points) and executive summary (75 points). Rubric evaluates: accuracy of model comparison calculations, depth of attribution model critique, quality of evidence supporting recommendations, identification of model limitations, and feasibility of proposed budget changes. Success requires demonstrating understanding that different models serve different strategic purposes and no single model is universally superior.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-built spreadsheet templates with formulas and focus analysis on 2-3 channels only. Offer guided questions like 'Which model gives social media the most credit and why?' Advanced learners should incorporate seasonality analysis, calculate statistical significance of model differences, and propose A/B testing frameworks for validating attribution model changes in live campaigns.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for optimizing marketing budget allocation across channels and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and comparing ROI calculations across paid search, social media, and email marketing channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through systematic comparison of model outputs and formulate evidence-based recommendations for marketing budget reallocation
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active. Students work individually with laptops/computers.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students navigate to GA4 > Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison. They must extract key metrics (conversions, revenue, ROAS) for paid search, social media, email, and organic search across all five attribution models. Students create a comparison spreadsheet documenting: channel performance rankings under each model, revenue attribution differences, and conversion volume variations.

**Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (30 minutes):** Students analyze discrepancies between models, identifying which channels gain/lose credit under different approaches. They calculate percentage differences in attributed revenue between models and determine statistical significance of variations. Students must identify three specific instances where model choice would lead to different strategic decisions.

**Phase 3 - Business Context Evaluation (25 minutes):** Provide students with additional context: company sells B2B software with 45-day average consideration cycle, limited annual marketing budget of $500K, and goal to increase enterprise client acquisitions by 25%. Students evaluate which attribution model best aligns with business objectives and customer journey characteristics.

**Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (20 minutes):** Students prepare a structured recommendation including: chosen attribution model with three supporting arguments, specific budget reallocation percentages across channels, potential risks/limitations of their choice, and success metrics to monitor post-implementation. Each recommendation must include quantitative justification from their GA4 analysis.
materials_needed: GA4 demo account with 6+ months multi-channel e-commerce data
Laptop/computer with internet access for each student
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets access
Business context scenario document (B2B software company profile)
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
assessment_method: Students submit a 2-page strategic memo evaluated using a 4-point rubric: Data Analysis Quality (25% - accuracy of GA4 data extraction and statistical interpretation), Critical Evaluation (30% - depth of model comparison and identification of business implications), Strategic Reasoning (30% - logic and feasibility of recommendations with quantitative support), Professional Communication (15% - clarity and structure of memo format). Success requires scoring 3+ on all criteria with specific GA4 evidence cited.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide GA4 navigation guide with screenshots, offer data collection template with pre-filled headers, and give access to worked example using different industry data. **Extension for advanced learners:** Add custom conversion events analysis, require statistical significance testing using confidence intervals, or include cross-device attribution considerations and privacy impact assessment for iOS 14.5+ changes.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics attribution models using real e-commerce data, comparing last-click, first-click, linear, and data-driven attribution models. learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the performance differences between attribution models by analyzing conversion paths and ROI metrics across multiple marketing channels
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and recommend optimal models based on business context
instructions:

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess how each model impacts budget allocation decisions and provide strategic recommendations for optimal attribution strategy implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business impact of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies in GA4
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and defend their recommended attribution approach with quantitative evidence
instructions: Step 1 (15 min): Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display advertising). Students access Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. Step 2 (30 min): Students generate attribution comparison reports for each model (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) focusing on three key metrics: conversion volume, conversion value, and return on ad spend (ROAS) by channel. They export data to Google Sheets for analysis. Step 3 (45 min): Students calculate percentage differences between models for each channel, identifying which channels gain/lose attribution credit under different models. They must analyze at least 20 conversion paths using the 'Top conversion paths' report to understand customer journey complexity. Step 4 (30 min): Students evaluate business impact by calculating budget reallocation scenarios - if $50,000 monthly ad budget were distributed based on each attribution model's channel valuations. Step 5 (60 min): Students create comprehensive evaluation reports including: attribution model comparison matrix, channel performance variance analysis, customer journey complexity assessment, and strategic recommendation with implementation timeline. Step 6 (30 min): Peer review presentations where students defend their chosen attribution strategy against challenges from classmates, requiring justification with specific data points and business reasoning.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Google Sheets or Excel for data analysis
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Sample $50,000 monthly advertising budget scenario worksheet
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Data analysis accuracy - correct calculation of attribution differences and statistical significance, (2) Critical evaluation depth - thorough assessment of each model's strengths/weaknesses with specific examples, (3) Strategic reasoning - logical connection between data insights and business recommendations, (4) Peer defense performance - ability to justify recommendations and respond to critiques with evidence. Final deliverable: 8-page analytical report plus 10-minute presentation defense.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model definition sheet, pre-calculated example using sample data, and guided worksheet with specific questions for each analysis step. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution setup, integration with Google Ads conversion tracking, and multi-touch attribution impact on customer lifetime value calculations. Consider adding cross-device tracking complexity analysis.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Exercise 4
description: Students will critically analyze three different attribution models (Last Click, First Click, and Data-Driven) using real Google Analytics 4 data from an e-commerce site. They will evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of each model and make evidence-based recommendations for optimal attribution strategy based on specific business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across Last Click, First Click, and Data-Driven models
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer journey complexity and recommend optimal attribution strategies for specific business contexts
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection (15 minutes)**
Provide each student with access to a shared GA4 demo account or dataset containing 3 months of e-commerce data. Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths and export data showing the same conversions under all three attribution models (Last Click, First Click, Data-Driven). They must capture screenshots of attribution comparison reports showing revenue differences between models.

**Phase 2: Quantitative Analysis (25 minutes)**
Students create a comparison matrix in Excel/Google Sheets calculating percentage differences in attributed revenue between models. They identify the top 5 channels with the greatest attribution discrepancies and calculate the dollar impact of choosing one model over another. Students must document at least 3 specific examples where attribution models tell completely different stories about channel performance.

**Phase 3: Customer Journey Mapping (20 minutes)**
Using the Top Conversion Paths report, students analyze 10 high-value conversion paths (minimum 3 touchpoints each). They categorize paths by complexity (simple: 1-3 touchpoints, moderate: 4-6 touchpoints, complex: 7+ touchpoints) and evaluate which attribution model best reflects actual customer behavior for each category.

**Phase 4: Business Context Evaluation (25 minutes)**
Students receive three business scenario cards: (1) Performance marketing agency focused on paid search, (2) Brand-focused company prioritizing awareness campaigns, (3) Multi-channel retailer with long sales cycles. For each scenario, they must evaluate which attribution model aligns with business goals and justify their reasoning using specific data points from their analysis.

**Phase 5: Strategic Recommendation (15 minutes)**
Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their attribution model recommendation for one assigned business scenario, including potential implementation challenges and measurement limitations they identified.
materials_needed: Access to Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce data
Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Business scenario cards (3 different contexts)
Attribution comparison report templates
Screen recording software for capturing GA4 reports
assessment_method: Students submit a written analysis (500 words) plus Excel workbook showing: (1) Quantitative comparison of attribution models with calculated revenue impacts, (2) Critical evaluation of each model's strengths/weaknesses with specific examples, (3) Evidence-based recommendation for assigned business scenario with implementation considerations, (4) Identification of at least 2 potential biases or limitations in their chosen model. Rubric awards points for data accuracy (25%), depth of critical analysis (35%), quality of business justification (25%), and recognition of model limitations (15%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-populated comparison templates and guided questions for each analysis phase. Create a checklist of required data points to collect. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose custom attribution models or analyze attribution at the product category level. Have them research and incorporate external attribution methodologies like Marketing Mix Modeling for comparison.

description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, comparing the effectiveness of data-driven, first-click, last-click, and linear attribution models. They will then defend their recommended attribution strategy through a comprehensive business case presentation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of four different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue impact metrics in Google Analytics 4
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer journey complexity and business context alignment
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Analysis Setup (20 minutes)**
Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. Have them configure four attribution models: Data-driven, First-click, Last-click, and Linear attribution, filtering data for the past 90 days with minimum 100 conversions per channel.

**Phase 2: Quantitative Evaluation (45 minutes)**
Students extract key metrics for each attribution model: total conversions, conversion value, cost-per-acquisition, and return on ad spend (ROAS) across paid search, social media, email, and display channels. They must create a comparison matrix documenting percentage differences in attribution credit between models, identifying which channels gain/lose credit under each model. Students then analyze the Path Length and Time Lag reports to understand customer journey complexity.

**Phase 3: Business Context Analysis (30 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional business scenario: B2B SaaS company with 45-day average sales cycle, high customer lifetime value ($2,400), and mixed online/offline touchpoints. Students must evaluate how well each attribution model aligns with this business reality, considering factors like sales cycle length, touchpoint complexity, and business objectives.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (25 minutes)**
Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice. They must address three key areas: quantitative evidence from their analysis, business context alignment, and anticipated implementation challenges. Include specific budget reallocation recommendations between channels based on their chosen model.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce data
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for analysis matrix
Business scenario handout with company context
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Attribution model comparison template worksheet

Students must demonstrate clear understanding of each model's strengths/limitations and provide specific budget reallocation percentages.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer attribution model definition reference cards. For advanced learners: Include additional challenge of evaluating custom attribution models or incorporating offline conversion data. Have them consider statistical significance testing for attribution differences and advanced path analysis techniques.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Exercise 6
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing real e-commerce data across multiple customer journey scenarios. They will assess the strengths and limitations of each model and defend their recommendation for the optimal attribution strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and position-based attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating revenue attribution differences
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey scenarios and defend evidence-based recommendations for attribution model selection
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with Google Analytics demo account access and three pre-selected e-commerce datasets representing different business models: B2B SaaS (long sales cycle), fashion retail (seasonal/impulse buying), and subscription service (recurring revenue). Create groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one dataset.

**Phase 1 - Data Analysis (45 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool. They must extract data for all five attribution models over a 6-month period, documenting: total conversions, conversion value, average days to conversion, and top 5 conversion paths. Students create spreadsheets comparing how each model attributes revenue to different channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct).

**Phase 2 - Scenario Evaluation (30 minutes):** Present three business scenarios with different objectives: maximizing customer acquisition, optimizing marketing budget allocation, and improving customer lifetime value. Students evaluate which attribution model best serves each scenario using their data analysis, considering factors like customer behavior patterns, channel performance variations, and business goals alignment.

**Phase 3 - Critical Assessment (25 minutes):** Students identify limitations of their recommended models by analyzing outlier conversion paths, seasonal variations, and cross-device tracking gaps. They must address potential biases and data accuracy issues in their chosen attribution approach.

**Phase 4 - Presentation and Defense (30 minutes):** Each group presents their attribution model recommendation with supporting evidence, including projected impact on budget allocation and expected ROI changes. Other groups challenge recommendations through structured questioning, requiring presenters to defend their analysis methodology and address counterarguments.

Three curated datasets representing different business models (B2B SaaS, fashion retail, subscription service)
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel)
Presentation software for final recommendations
Scenario handouts with specific business objectives and constraints
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Data analysis accuracy and completeness (25 points), quality of attribution model comparison with quantitative evidence (25 points), logical reasoning in scenario-based recommendations (25 points), and defense of methodology during peer challenges (25 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of attribution model limitations and provide specific ROI projections to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model comparison template with key metrics pre-identified and guided questions for each evaluation criterion. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify data extraction accuracy. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models using Google Analytics Intelligence API or evaluate attribution across multiple Google Analytics properties. Encourage analysis of attribution model impact on marketing automation workflows.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Security Policies
description: Students will create a comprehensive enterprise network design incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, security policies, and redundancy protocols. They will physically configure Cisco switches and routers to implement their custom network architecture while documenting all configurations and security measures.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco switching and routing protocols through hands-on configuration of VLANs, STP, HSRP, and access control lists on physical hardware
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp has 150 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest) requiring network segmentation and security (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 2-3 to complete this 4-phase project. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Design network topology using Packet Tracer or Visio, creating logical diagrams showing VLAN assignments, IP subnetting (using /24 networks), trunk links, and router placement. Include redundancy planning with dual switches. Phase 2 (60 minutes): Configure physical Cisco 2960 switches - create VLANs 10 (Sales), 20 (Engineering), 30 (HR), 40 (Guest), configure trunk ports between switches, implement STP with designated root bridge, and assign access ports to appropriate VLANs. Phase 3 (75 minutes): Configure Cisco 2911 router with subinterfaces for inter-VLAN routing, implement HSRP for gateway redundancy, configure DHCP pools for each VLAN, and create ACLs restricting Guest VLAN access to internet only while blocking internal resources. Phase 4 (45 minutes): Test connectivity between VLANs, verify ACL functionality using ping and telnet tests, document all configurations with 'show running-config' outputs, and create network troubleshooting procedures. Each team presents their solution explaining design decisions and demonstrating functionality (30 minutes total). Instructor circulates during configuration phases, checking progress and providing guidance on complex CLI commands.
materials_needed: 2 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
1 Cisco 2911 ISR router per team
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Ethernet cables (Cat5e/6) - minimum 8 per team
Laptops with terminal emulation software (PuTTY/SecureCRT)
Cisco Packet Tracer or Microsoft Visio for design phase
Network design template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Network design documentation (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP addressing scheme, VLAN planning; Configuration implementation (40 points) - successful VLAN creation, trunk configuration, inter-VLAN routing, HSRP setup; Security implementation (20 points) - ACL effectiveness, proper access restrictions; Presentation and troubleshooting (15 points) - clear explanation of design decisions, demonstration of network functionality, response to instructor testing scenarios
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured IP addressing templates and step-by-step CLI command reference sheets. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Add OSPF dynamic routing between multiple routers, implement port security features, configure VPN tunnels for remote access, or integrate wireless controllers with guest network isolation. Consider adding network monitoring with SNMP configuration.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Security Policies: Practical Workshop
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF, access control lists, and network security policies. They will create network documentation and present their design rationale to simulate real-world network deployment scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network architecture by analyzing business requirements and creating logical topology diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced Cisco switching and routing configurations through hands-on device programming using VLANs, OSPF, ACLs, and port security features
instructions:
**Phase 1: Requirements Analysis & Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp has 200 employees across 4 departments (HR-25 users, Finance-40 users, Engineering-100 users, Management-35 users) requiring network segmentation and security policies. Students work in teams of 2-3 to create network requirements documents and logical topology diagrams using network design software.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment (2 switches, 1 router, 4 PCs), students configure: VLAN creation and assignment (VLAN 10-HR, 20-Finance, 30-Engineering, 40-Management), trunk ports between switches, router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing with subinterfaces, OSPF routing protocol configuration, and ACLs restricting inter-departmental access based on security policies.

**Phase 3: Security Implementation (30 minutes)**
Students implement port security on access ports, configure DHCP snooping, enable storm control, and create management ACLs for administrative access.

**Phase 4: Testing & Documentation (30 minutes)**
Conduct connectivity testing between VLANs, verify ACL functionality, document all IP addresses and VLAN assignments, and create troubleshooting procedures.

**Phase 5: Presentation (15 minutes per team)**
Teams present their network design, demonstrate functionality, explain security policy decisions, and answer technical questions from peers and instructor.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or 2 Cisco Catalyst switches and 1 ISR router
4 computers or laptops for end devices
Console cables and Ethernet patch cables
Network topology design software (Visio, Lucidchart, or Draw.io)
Company scenario handout with specific business requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP addressing scheme, security policy rationale; Technical Implementation (40 points) - VLAN configuration, routing protocols, ACL functionality, security features; Testing & Verification (20 points) - connectivity tests, troubleshooting documentation; Presentation Quality (15 points) - technical explanation, problem-solving approach, peer question responses. Students must achieve 80% functionality on live network demonstration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured basic switch settings, offer VLAN configuration templates, and assign peer mentors for troubleshooting support. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Add HSRP redundancy configuration, implement dynamic VLAN assignment, configure network monitoring with SNMP, or integrate wireless access points with guest network isolation.
