title: Binary Number System Memorization and Recognition Drill
description: Students will memorize and practice recalling binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic repetition and flashcard exercises. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for binary-decimal conversion needed in computer systems understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 from memory within 3 seconds per number by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through structured recognition exercises using visual cards and digital tools
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary conversion reference chart showing decimal numbers 0-15 with their 4-bit binary equivalents (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Give students 10 minutes to study the chart silently, encouraging them to look for patterns like how each position represents powers of 2. After study time, collect the charts and conduct a 15-minute guided practice session where you display each decimal number on the projector for 5 seconds while students write the binary equivalent on their answer sheets. Immediately show the correct answer and have students self-check. Next, reverse the process by showing binary numbers and having students write decimal equivalents. Following guided practice, pair students and distribute physical flashcards with decimal numbers on one side and binary on the reverse. Partner A shows decimal numbers to Partner B, who must state the binary equivalent within 3 seconds. Partners switch roles after 10 cards. Conduct three rounds with different card sets. Conclude with an individual 5-minute timed quiz where students convert 20 decimal numbers (0-15, with some repeats) to binary without reference materials. Students must achieve 80% accuracy to demonstrate mastery. Record completion times and accuracy rates for each student.
materials_needed: Binary conversion reference chart (one per student)
Physical flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 (two sets per pair)
Individual answer sheets for guided practice
Stopwatch or timer
Projector for displaying numbers
Final quiz sheets with 20 decimal-to-binary problems
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final timed quiz to demonstrate mastery. Additional assessment through observation during partner practice, noting fluency and confidence. Create a simple rubric: Mastery (16-20 correct, under 4 minutes), Developing (12-15 correct), Beginning (below 12 correct). Record both accuracy and completion time for progress tracking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the powers-of-2 breakdown (8-4-2-1 positions) written above each binary digit and allow extended study time with the reference chart. Consider pairing them with stronger students during partner practice. For advanced learners, extend to 8-bit numbers (0-255) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Challenge fast finishers to work backwards from binary to decimal or create their own flashcards for larger numbers.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Machine Learning Models Using Real Estate Data
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance scores from a pre-trained Random Forest model predicting house prices. They will explain how different features contribute to predictions and identify potential biases or data quality issues revealed through feature importance analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance coefficients from tree-based models by ranking and explaining the relative contribution of each variable to model predictions
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation in feature importance through guided analysis of housing market variables and their relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing 15 housing features (square footage, number of bedrooms, neighborhood income, school ratings, etc.) and corresponding feature importance scores from a trained Random Forest model (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group a different subset of 5 features to analyze deeply. Students first rank all 15 features by importance score and create a horizontal bar chart visualization (20 minutes). Next, each group focuses on their assigned features, researching why these might be important for house price prediction and identifying potential confounding variables or data collection biases (25 minutes). Groups then examine feature correlations using a provided correlation matrix to identify highly correlated feature pairs and discuss whether high importance might be due to multicollinearity (20 minutes). Each group prepares a 3-minute presentation explaining: (1) their assigned features' importance scores in context, (2) one potential bias or data quality concern, and (3) one business recommendation based on their findings (15 minutes preparation). Groups present their findings while other students take notes on a provided template, asking clarifying questions about interpretations (20 minutes presentations). Conclude with a whole-class discussion comparing findings across feature groups and identifying common themes about model interpretability challenges (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-processed real estate dataset with 15 features and 500+ housing records
Feature importance scores output from trained Random Forest model
Correlation matrix spreadsheet or visualization
Laptops/tablets with Excel or Google Sheets access
Presentation template with guided questions
Note-taking template for peer presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of feature importance ranking and chart creation (25%), (2) Quality of explanations for why features matter in housing context (25%), (3) Identification of at least one valid bias/data quality concern (25%), (4) Clarity of business recommendation supported by evidence (25%). Students submit group charts, written explanations, and individual reflection on one new insight about model interpretability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence stems like 'This feature is important because...' and 'A potential bias could be...' Advanced learners can calculate partial dependence plots for their assigned features or research alternative feature importance methods (permutation importance, SHAP values). Consider pairing students with complementary strengths in statistics and domain knowledge.

title: Analyzing Energy Transfer Mechanisms in a Multi-Stage Rube Goldberg Machine
description: Students will analyze a complex Rube Goldberg machine video to identify, categorize, and evaluate the efficiency of energy transformations at each stage. They will create detailed energy flow diagrams and calculate theoretical vs. actual energy losses to determine optimization points.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze energy transformation pathways by identifying and categorizing each conversion stage in a multi-step mechanical system
Students will evaluate energy transfer efficiency through quantitative calculations comparing theoretical and observed energy losses at each conversion point
instructions:
Begin by showing students a 3-minute Rube Goldberg machine video (suggested: OK Go 'This Too Shall Pass' or similar complex machine). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives the analysis worksheet and accesses the video on individual devices for detailed examination. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams watch the video multiple times, pausing to identify each distinct energy transformation. Students must catalog at least 12 different transformation stages, noting the time stamp, objects involved, and energy types (kinetic, potential gravitational, potential elastic, thermal, sound, etc.).

Step 2 (20 minutes): For each identified transformation, students create detailed energy flow diagrams showing input energy type, conversion mechanism, output energy type, and estimated energy losses. They must use standardized physics symbols and include vector arrows indicating energy flow direction.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams select 5 transformations for quantitative analysis. Using provided mass estimates and measured distances/times from video analysis, students calculate theoretical energy values and compare with observed outcomes. They must identify energy loss mechanisms (friction, air resistance, sound production, heat generation) and estimate efficiency percentages.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team identifies the three least efficient transformations and proposes specific modifications to improve energy transfer efficiency. Proposals must include sketches and brief calculations showing expected improvement percentages.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Teams present their most significant finding to the class, focusing on one unexpected energy loss mechanism they discovered and their proposed optimization solution.
materials_needed: High-resolution Rube Goldberg machine video (3-4 minutes, complex multi-stage)
Individual devices/tablets for video replay and analysis
Energy transformation analysis worksheets with standardized physics symbols
Digital calipers or rulers for screen measurements
Scientific calculators
Stopwatches or video analysis software with frame-by-frame capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Identification accuracy - correctly identifies and categorizes 12+ energy transformations with proper physics terminology; (2) Quantitative analysis - performs accurate calculations for 5 transformations with correct units and significant figures; (3) Critical evaluation - identifies specific energy loss mechanisms and provides feasible optimization solutions with supporting calculations; (4) Energy flow diagrams - creates clear, accurate diagrams using proper physics symbols and conventions. Each criterion worth 25 points for total 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-identified list of first 5 transformations and energy types reference sheet. Offer simplified calculation templates with step-by-step formulas. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze rotational kinetic energy transformations and calculate moments of inertia for complex objects. Have them research real-world applications where similar energy cascades occur (hydroelectric systems, mechanical watches).

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Two Calculator Solutions
description: Students will critically evaluate two different calculator program implementations by analyzing code quality, identifying strengths and weaknesses, and justifying which solution is superior. This activity develops evaluation skills by comparing real code examples against established programming principles.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of two calculator programs by analyzing readability, functionality, and maintainability using a structured rubric
Students will justify their selection of the superior code solution through written analysis comparing specific code characteristics and programming best practices
instructions: Begin by providing each student with two printed calculator programs (Solution A: poorly written with no comments, inconsistent naming, and nested if-statements; Solution B: well-structured with clear variable names, comments, and modular functions). Give students 10 minutes to individually read through both solutions and test them using the provided test cases. Next, distribute the Code Quality Evaluation Checklist covering: variable naming conventions, code comments and documentation, function organization, error handling, and code efficiency. Have students spend 20 minutes systematically evaluating each solution against the checklist, marking scores from 1-5 for each criterion. In pairs, students discuss their findings for 15 minutes, comparing scores and reasoning. Each student then completes a written evaluation report (15 minutes) that includes: numerical scores for each criterion, identification of three specific strengths and three weaknesses for each solution, and a final recommendation with justification for which solution is superior. Students must cite specific code examples in their reasoning. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where volunteer pairs share their recommendations and defend their choices. The instructor should guide discussion toward recognizing that while both programs produce correct mathematical results, Solution B demonstrates superior software development practices essential for real-world applications.
materials_needed: Two printed calculator program solutions (one poorly written, one well-structured)
Code Quality Evaluation Checklist with 1-5 scoring rubric
Set of 8 test cases for calculator functions
Evaluation Report Template worksheet
assessment_method: Grade the written evaluation reports using a 20-point rubric: accurate scoring of code quality criteria (8 points), identification of specific strengths/weaknesses with code examples (8 points), clear justification for final recommendation (4 points). Success requires scoring 16+ points and correctly identifying that the well-structured solution is superior despite both programs functioning correctly.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide highlighted code sections and guiding questions like 'What makes this variable name clear/unclear?' For advanced learners, add a third solution with moderate quality and ask them to rank all three, or have them suggest specific code improvements for the weaker solution.

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Marketing Strategy
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value). They will design visualization strategies, implement data transformations, and present actionable marketing recommendations based on their segmentation model.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive RFM segmentation model by applying statistical analysis techniques to customer transaction data
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining multiple visualization types that communicate customer insights to business stakeholders
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Model Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the e-commerce dataset containing customer transactions over 12 months. Students work in pairs to explore the data structure and calculate RFM metrics. They must define scoring criteria for each dimension (1-5 scale) and create customer segments (Champions, Loyal Customers, At Risk, etc.). Students document their segmentation logic and rationale.

**Phase 2: Dashboard Construction (90 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students build their dashboard with required components: customer segment distribution chart, RFM score scatter plots, revenue by segment bar chart, and customer journey timeline. They must implement interactive filters for date ranges and segment selection. Students apply color coding consistently and ensure all charts update dynamically based on filter selections.

**Phase 3: Marketing Strategy Development (30 minutes)**
For each customer segment, students develop specific marketing recommendations including campaign types, messaging approaches, and budget allocation percentages. They must justify recommendations using data insights from their dashboard and calculate potential ROI for each strategy.

**Phase 4: Stakeholder Presentation (15 minutes per pair)**
Students present their dashboard to the class acting as marketing executives, demonstrating interactive features and explaining their segmentation approach. They must answer questions about methodology choices and defend their marketing recommendations using dashboard insights.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer transaction dataset (CSV file with CustomerID, PurchaseDate, TransactionAmount, ProductCategory)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software access
Marketing strategy template worksheet
Presentation timer and evaluation forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Technical accuracy of RFM calculations and segmentation logic, (2) Dashboard design quality including visual hierarchy and interactivity, (3) Marketing strategy relevance and data-driven justification, (4) Presentation clarity and stakeholder engagement, (5) Ability to answer technical questions about methodology. Each criterion worth 20 points for total of 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide RFM calculation templates and dashboard wireframe examples. Offer additional guidance on statistical quartile calculations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive elements like customer lifetime value or churn probability, and to implement advanced dashboard features like drill-down capabilities or automated insights.

title: Interactive Customer Segmentation Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior patterns and develops targeted marketing recommendations. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualization frameworks, and construct actionable business insights for stakeholder presentation.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive customer segmentation model by analyzing transactional data patterns, demographic information, and behavioral metrics to identify distinct customer groups

Students will construct an interactive dashboard through data visualization tools that presents segmentation insights and generates specific marketing strategy recommendations for each customer segment
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Data Exploration and Strategy Design**
Provide students with the e-commerce dataset containing customer transactions, demographics, and website behavior. In pairs, students examine the data structure and brainstorm segmentation approaches. They must identify 3-5 key variables for segmentation (e.g., purchase frequency, average order value, product categories, seasonal patterns). Students create a segmentation strategy document outlining their approach and rationale.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Data Analysis and Segmentation Creation**
Using Excel or Tableau, students clean and transform the data, calculating derived metrics like customer lifetime value, recency of purchases, and category preferences. They apply clustering techniques or create rule-based segments, testing different combinations until they identify 4-6 distinct customer segments. Each segment must be named and characterized with specific behavioral traits.

**Phase 3 (75 minutes): Dashboard Construction**
Students design and build an interactive dashboard featuring segment visualizations, key performance indicators for each group, and comparison charts. The dashboard must include filters for time periods and product categories, with clear visual hierarchy and professional formatting.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Marketing Strategy Development**
For each identified segment, students develop specific marketing recommendations including preferred communication channels, promotional strategies, product recommendations, and budget allocation suggestions. They create a summary slide deck for stakeholder presentation.

**Phase 5 (20 minutes): Peer Review and Refinement**
Pairs exchange dashboards for feedback on clarity, insights, and recommendations, then make final refinements based on peer input.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records including CustomerID, TransactionDate, ProductCategory, OrderValue, Demographics)
Microsoft Excel with Data Analysis Toolpak or Tableau Desktop/Public
Segmentation strategy template worksheet
Dashboard design checklist rubric
Computers with internet access for research
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Interactive dashboard file demonstrating clear segmentation with 4-6 distinct groups, (2) Marketing strategy document with specific recommendations per segment, (3) 5-minute presentation to class. Rubric evaluates: data analysis accuracy (25%), dashboard design and interactivity (25%), insight quality and business relevance (25%), marketing recommendations specificity (15%), presentation clarity (10%). Success requires identifying statistically distinct segments with actionable characteristics and creating professional-grade visualizations with clear business value.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-defined segmentation variables and step-by-step Excel formulas. Offer template dashboard layouts and example marketing strategies from similar industries. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive elements (future purchase probability), use advanced clustering algorithms, or integrate external market research data. Consider adding competitor analysis component or A/B testing recommendations for their proposed strategies.
original_title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Marketing Strategy

title: Interactive Customer Segmentation Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and develop actionable marketing recommendations for different customer segments.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying RFM analysis to transactional data and creating distinct customer personas
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining multiple visualization types that effectively communicates segmentation insights to business stakeholders
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a dataset containing 12 months of e-commerce transactions (customer ID, purchase date, order value, product categories). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Data preparation phase. Students clean the dataset, handle missing values, and calculate RFM metrics for each customer: days since last purchase (Recency), total number of orders (Frequency), and total spend (Monetary value). They create quintile rankings (1-5) for each RFM component.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Segmentation creation. Students combine RFM scores to create customer segments (e.g., Champions: 5-5-5, At Risk: 2-3-3, New Customers: 5-1-1). They must define at least 6 distinct segments with clear business meanings and calculate segment sizes.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Dashboard design and construction. Using Tableau or Power BI, students build an interactive dashboard containing: a segment overview with customer counts and revenue contribution, RFM score distribution charts, segment comparison tables, and at least two drill-down capabilities (by time period or product category).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Strategy development. For each segment, students write specific marketing recommendations (budget allocation, communication frequency, promotional strategies) supported by their data analysis. They must justify recommendations with specific metrics from their analysis.

Teachers circulate to provide technical support and ensure students are interpreting business context correctly. Each pair presents their dashboard and recommendations in a 3-minute showcase, focusing on one 'priority segment' they identified.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI Desktop software
Computers with minimum 8GB RAM
Customer segmentation reference guide handout
Business context briefing document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Technical execution (dashboard functionality, data accuracy, visual design clarity - 25%), Analytical depth (segment definition logic, RFM implementation correctness - 25%), Business application (marketing recommendations specificity and data-driven justification - 25%), and Presentation clarity (dashboard storytelling, stakeholder communication effectiveness - 25%). Students submit dashboard file plus 2-page strategy memo.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM templates and segment definition examples. Offer step-by-step video tutorials for dashboard creation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables (geography, seasonality), implement predictive elements (customer lifetime value), or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Provide additional datasets for cross-validation of their segmentation approach.
original_title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Marketing Strategy

title: Interactive Customer Segmentation Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior and demographics, then develop targeted marketing recommendations. This activity combines data visualization, statistical analysis, and business strategy to solve a real-world marketing challenge.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying clustering algorithms to transactional and demographic data
Students will design an interactive dashboard through integrating multiple visualization techniques to communicate insights to business stakeholders
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a synthetic e-commerce dataset containing 2,000 customer records including demographics (age, location, income), purchase history (frequency, monetary value, recency), and product categories. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to explore the dataset structure and identify key variables for segmentation.

Next, guide students through creating customer segments using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) combined with demographic clustering. Students spend 45 minutes building their segmentation model, applying K-means clustering with 4-6 segments, and validating cluster quality using silhouette scores and business logic.

For dashboard creation (60 minutes), students use Tableau or Power BI to build interactive visualizations including: segment overview charts, customer journey heatmaps, geographic distribution maps, and profitability analysis by segment. Each dashboard must include filters for time periods, product categories, and demographic slicing.

Students then develop targeted marketing strategies (30 minutes) for each segment, creating specific campaign recommendations with budget allocations, channel preferences, and expected ROI projections. They must justify their strategies using insights from their dashboard.

Conclude with 15-minute peer presentations where each pair demonstrates their dashboard functionality and presents one detailed marketing strategy. Audience members evaluate dashboards using provided criteria and ask clarifying questions about methodology and business recommendations.
materials_needed: Synthetic e-commerce customer dataset (CSV format with 2,000 records)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI licenses/accounts for each student pair
Marketing strategy template worksheet
Laptop/desktop computers with internet access
Presentation display system for final demonstrations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Technical execution - correct implementation of clustering algorithms and statistical validation (25%), (2) Dashboard design - clarity, interactivity, and visual appeal of dashboard elements (30%), (3) Business insights - quality and feasibility of marketing recommendations with supporting data (30%), (4) Presentation - clear communication of methodology and findings to business audience (15%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM scores and suggest starting with 3 clear segments (high, medium, low value). Offer dashboard templates with basic chart structures. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive elements like customer lifetime value or churn probability, and experiment with advanced clustering techniques like hierarchical clustering or DBSCAN. Encourage integration of external data sources like seasonality trends.

title: PMI Framework and Methodology Terminology Mastery Challenge
description: Students will complete a comprehensive terminology recall exercise focusing on advanced PMI-based project management frameworks, processes, and knowledge area definitions. This activity reinforces memorization of critical PM vocabulary and standard definitions used in professional certification contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions of 50+ advanced PMI terminology terms by completing timed flashcard exercises and definition matching activities
Students will identify correct PMI process group classifications and knowledge area categorizations through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the PMI Terminology Reference Sheet containing 75 advanced terms from PMBOK Guide 7th Edition (15 minutes setup). Students work individually using the three-phase recall method. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Students review all terms silently, creating mental associations. Provide colored highlighters for students to mark difficulty levels - green (confident), yellow (uncertain), red (need focus). Phase 2 (25 minutes): Implement the 'Term Tennis' drill where instructor calls out a definition and students must write the corresponding term within 30 seconds. Cover 40 terms total, including: earned value management formulas (CPI, SPI, EAC, BAC), risk management processes (qualitative vs quantitative analysis), procurement contract types (CPFF, FPIF, T&M), and agile-hybrid terminology (product owner, sprint retrospective, backlog refinement). Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students complete a rapid-fire matching exercise connecting 25 processes to their correct knowledge areas and process groups. Use timer projections to maintain urgency. Conclude with individual self-assessment where students identify their weakest terminology categories for targeted review. Instructor circulates continuously, noting students who struggle with specific terminology clusters for follow-up support.
materials_needed: PMI Terminology Reference Sheet (75 terms with definitions)
Colored highlighters (green, yellow, red)
Term Tennis answer sheets (pre-printed templates)
Process-to-Knowledge Area matching worksheets
Digital timer with projection capability
PMBOK Guide 7th Edition terminology appendix
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on the final matching exercise (20/25 correct matches) and demonstrate recall of at least 35/40 terms during Term Tennis drill. Assessment includes: immediate scoring of matching worksheet, instructor observation checklist tracking individual participation during Term Tennis, and student self-assessment reflection identifying 5 strongest and 5 weakest terminology areas with specific examples.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory devices (example: CPI = Cost Performance Index = 'Can Project Improve'), allow additional 15 seconds during Term Tennis, and pair with stronger students for peer explanation. For advanced learners: challenge them to explain term applications in real project scenarios, have them create original memory devices for complex terms, and assign them as peer tutors during individual review time.

title: Deconstructing Transformational Leadership Through Crisis Decision Analysis
description: Students will analyze real corporate crisis scenarios to understand how transformational leadership behaviors manifest differently from transactional approaches during high-stakes decision-making. Through comparative case study analysis, students will identify and categorize specific leadership behaviors using established transformational leadership frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing documented decisions and communications during three major corporate crises

Students will classify specific leader actions using Bass's Four I's framework (Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration) through structured case study examination
instructions: Begin by distributing three crisis case study packets: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982), Starbucks' racial bias incident response (2018), and Airbnb's discrimination crisis management (2016). Each packet contains 4-6 primary source documents including CEO statements, internal memos, and employee communications. Divide students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group one case study for 25 minutes of initial analysis. Provide each group with the Bass Transformational Leadership Analysis Matrix - a structured worksheet with four quadrants representing the Four I's, plus a fifth section for transactional behaviors. Students must extract specific quotes, decisions, and actions from their assigned case, categorizing each piece of evidence into the appropriate framework component. After initial analysis, rotate groups so each examines all three cases for 15 minutes each, building comparative insights. During rotations, groups use colored sticky notes to add their observations to wall-mounted case study charts. In the final 20 minutes, reconvene for structured comparison discussion. Display all three cases simultaneously using prepared comparison templates on whiteboards or large displays. Guide students through systematic comparison: 'Looking at Idealized Influence, what specific behaviors did you observe in each case? How did the context influence the expression of this leadership dimension?' Repeat this process for each of the Four I's, then examine transactional elements. Conclude by having each group present one key insight about how transformational leadership adapts to crisis contexts while maintaining core characteristics.
materials_needed: Three case study packets with 4-6 primary source documents each (printed)
Bass Transformational Leadership Analysis Matrix worksheets (one per student)
Colored sticky notes (4 colors minimum)
Large poster paper or whiteboard space for each case study
Comparison template charts for final discussion
Timer for rotation management
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Analysis Matrix worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Accurately categorizes 8+ leadership behaviors with specific textual evidence and clear rationale; (3) Categorizes 6-7 behaviors with adequate evidence; (2) Categorizes 4-5 behaviors with limited evidence; (1) Categorizes fewer than 4 behaviors or lacks supporting evidence. Additionally, assess participation in final comparison discussion through observation checklist focusing on ability to articulate distinctions between leadership styles and provide cross-case insights.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted versions of case study documents focusing on key leader statements and decisions. Include a reference sheet with definitions and examples of each Four I's component. For advanced learners: Add a sixth analysis category requiring them to identify situational leadership adaptations and evaluate effectiveness of chosen approaches. Encourage them to research additional primary sources beyond provided materials and consider alternative leadership frameworks for comparison.

title: Critical Path Method vs. Critical Chain Analysis: Comparing Schedule Compression Techniques
description: Students will analyze two different project schedules using Critical Path Method (CPM) and Critical Chain Project Management (CCPM) approaches to determine which technique is more appropriate for specific project constraints. They will examine resource dependencies, buffer placement, and compression strategies to make evidence-based recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the differences between CPM and CCPM scheduling approaches by comparing their application to identical project scenarios
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different schedule compression techniques through systematic examination of resource constraints and buffer strategies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and distributing the Project Alpha case study materials (30 minutes total). Each pair receives identical project data including: 15 activities with durations, dependencies, and resource requirements. In Phase 1 (15 minutes), one student in each pair creates a CPM network diagram identifying the critical path, total float, and free float for each activity. Simultaneously, the partner develops a CCPM schedule for the same project, placing feeding buffers and a project buffer while considering resource constraints. In Phase 2 (10 minutes), pairs analyze both schedules side-by-side using the provided comparison worksheet. They must identify: (1) duration differences between approaches, (2) resource leveling impacts, (3) risk mitigation strategies in each method, and (4) buffer utilization effectiveness. During Phase 3 (15 minutes), each pair completes a decision matrix evaluating both approaches against five weighted criteria: schedule predictability (25%), resource optimization (20%), risk management (20%), stakeholder communication clarity (15%), and implementation complexity (20%). They must justify their scoring with specific evidence from their analysis. In Phase 4 (20 minutes), pairs present their findings to another pair, defending their recommendation for which approach better suits Project Alpha's constraints. The receiving pair challenges assumptions and asks clarifying questions about buffer calculations and resource dependencies. Finally, each pair submits their completed comparison worksheet and decision matrix with a 200-word executive summary explaining their recommended approach and three key supporting rationales.
materials_needed: Project Alpha case study packet (15 activities with dependencies and resource assignments)
CPM network diagram template sheets
CCPM schedule template with buffer calculation guide
Schedule comparison analysis worksheet
Decision matrix evaluation form with weighted criteria
Calculators or Microsoft Project software access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accurate CPM analysis with correct critical path identification (25 points), proper CCPM schedule with appropriate buffer placement (25 points), thorough comparison identifying 4+ key differences with supporting evidence (25 points), completed decision matrix with justified scoring rationale (15 points), and executive summary with clear recommendation backed by analytical reasoning (10 points). Students must achieve 70+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated activity early/late start times and a partially completed network diagram. Offer a checklist for buffer calculation steps in CCPM. For advanced learners, introduce Monte Carlo simulation concepts for buffer sizing or add scope change scenarios requiring schedule reanalysis. Consider providing industry-specific examples (construction vs. software development) for additional complexity.

title: Strategic Attribution Model Evaluation and Business Impact Assessment
description: Students critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine which model most accurately represents customer journey value. They will assess the business implications of model selection on marketing budget allocation and ROI calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, linear) by analyzing conversion path reports and comparing revenue attribution accuracy
Students will assess the strategic business impact of attribution model selection through ROI variance analysis and budget reallocation recommendations
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide each team of 3-4 students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic sources. Students access Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. **Phase 1 - Data Analysis (45 minutes):** Teams examine conversion paths for purchases over $500, documenting touchpoint sequences in provided spreadsheet. They run model comparison reports for: first-click, last-click, data-driven, and linear attribution, recording revenue attribution differences for each traffic source (Google Ads, Facebook, Email, Organic Search). Students calculate percentage variance between models for each channel. **Phase 2 - Business Context Integration (30 minutes):** Teams receive fictional company brief including current marketing spend allocation ($50K monthly across channels) and average customer lifetime value data. Using attribution variance data, they calculate potential ROI differences and identify overvalued/undervalued channels under current last-click model. **Phase 3 - Strategic Evaluation (30 minutes):** Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice, including: quantified business impact analysis, specific budget reallocation recommendations with dollar amounts, implementation timeline, and potential risks/limitations. **Presentation & Peer Review (40 minutes):** Teams present findings while others complete evaluation matrices scoring recommendations on data accuracy, business viability, and implementation feasibility.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce data
Attribution analysis worksheet template
Fictional company marketing brief document
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
Presentation timer and scoring sheets
assessment_method: Evaluation based on: attribution model comparison accuracy (25 points), business impact calculations correctness (25 points), strategic recommendation quality and feasibility (30 points), presentation clarity and defense of position (20 points). Peer evaluations contribute 15% to final score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model comparison cheat sheet and guided calculation templates. For advanced learners: Include cross-device attribution analysis and custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution insights. Offer additional complexity by incorporating offline conversion data integration scenarios.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network Infrastructure with Advanced Routing Protocols
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology featuring multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF protocol implementation, and network security policies. They will create both the logical network design and physical implementation using Cisco equipment, then validate functionality through comprehensive testing scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, OSPF routing, and access control principles by designing a scalable enterprise network architecture that meets specific business requirements
Students will construct and validate a fully functional multi-site network infrastructure through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers with documented security policies
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp has 3 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR) across 2 locations requiring secure network segmentation. Students work in teams of 2-3 for 4 hours total. 

Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams create detailed network diagrams using Visio or Packet Tracer, defining IP addressing schemes (must use /24 subnets), VLAN assignments (Sales=VLAN 10, Engineering=VLAN 20, HR=VLAN 30), and OSPF area designs. Include firewall placement and trunk configurations between switches.

Phase 2 (90 minutes): Configure physical equipment starting with base switch configurations. Teams must create VLANs, assign ports to appropriate VLANs, configure trunk ports with 802.1Q encapsulation, and implement VLAN interface IP addressing. Document all commands used.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Configure OSPF routing protocol on routers, establishing area 0 as backbone and area 1 for remote site. Implement inter-VLAN routing using Layer 3 switches or router-on-a-stick configuration. Configure HSRP for gateway redundancy.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Implement security measures including port security (maximum 2 MAC addresses per port), DHCP snooping, and basic ACLs restricting HR VLAN access to specific servers only.

Phase 5 (30 minutes): Conduct comprehensive testing using ping, traceroute, and show commands to verify connectivity, routing tables, and VLAN functionality. Teams must demonstrate successful inter-VLAN communication and proper traffic isolation.
materials_needed: 3 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
2 Cisco ISR 4000 series routers per team
Category 6 Ethernet cables (12 per team)
Console cables for configuration
Laptops with PuTTY or SecureCRT installed
Microsoft Visio or Cisco Packet Tracer software
Network documentation templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network design documentation (25 points) - logical topology, IP scheme correctness, security considerations. Configuration accuracy (30 points) - proper VLAN setup, OSPF implementation, ACL functionality. Functionality demonstration (25 points) - successful inter-VLAN routing, connectivity tests, redundancy verification. Professional documentation (20 points) - command logs, troubleshooting notes, network diagrams with proper labeling. Teams must present their working network and explain design decisions to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured IP addressing templates and basic VLAN configuration examples. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase with instructor verification. Pair weaker students with strong technical partners. For advanced learners: Add requirements for QoS implementation, VPN tunneling between sites, or advanced OSPF features like route summarization and stub areas. Challenge them to implement network monitoring using SNMP or implement IPv6 dual-stack configuration.

title: Memory Palace for Python Keywords and Operators
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 essential Python keywords and operators by creating flashcards and participating in structured recall exercises. This foundational activity ensures students can identify and name basic Python syntax elements before writing code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 20 fundamental Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, import, return, True, False, None, and, or, not, in, is, try, except, break, continue, pass) by matching them to their written forms
Students will recall the names and symbols of 8 basic Python operators (+, -, *, /, //, %, **, ==) through timed flashcard exercises
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute pre-made keyword reference sheets containing 20 Python keywords and 8 operators with definitions. Have students arrange desks for individual work with space to spread flashcards. **Activity Phase 1 (15 minutes):** Students create physical flashcards using index cards - keyword/operator on front, definition on back. Instructor circulates to verify accuracy and spelling. Students then spend 5 minutes in silent self-study, reading through all cards. **Activity Phase 2 (15 minutes):** Pair students randomly. Partner A shows keyword/operator side, Partner B states the definition from memory. Switch roles every 2 minutes (instructor times). Partners check accuracy against reference sheet and mark incorrect responses on tracking sheet. **Activity Phase 3 (10 minutes):** Conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall. Instructor displays keyword/operator on projector for 3 seconds. Students write definition on response sheet. Cover all 28 items once. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students self-check answers against reference sheet and calculate their accuracy percentage. Collect response sheets and tracking sheets for assessment.
materials_needed: Blank index cards (30 per student)
Pre-printed Python keyword/operator reference sheets
Individual response sheets with numbered lines 1-28
Partner tracking sheets
Projector or smartboard for displaying items
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Success measured by accuracy on final recall test: 85%+ correct (24/28) = proficient, 75-84% correct (21-23/28) = developing, below 75% (20 or fewer) = needs support. Review partner tracking sheets to identify specific keywords causing difficulty. Collect and spot-check 5 flashcard sets per class for completeness and accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial set to 15 most common items (if, else, for, while, def, +, -, *, /, ==), provide pre-made flashcards, allow extra 5 minutes for self-study. For advanced learners: Add 10 additional keywords (lambda, yield, assert, global, nonlocal, with, as, from, finally, elif) and challenge them to create mnemonics or memory tricks to share with struggling peers.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fix Quality in Simple Calculator Functions
description: Students evaluate three different programmer solutions to fix bugs in basic calculator functions (add, subtract, multiply, divide). They assess code quality, identify strengths and weaknesses, and rank solutions using specific evaluation criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and correctness using a structured rubric
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison of error handling, edge cases, and code documentation quality
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with three printed code samples showing different approaches to fixing division-by-zero and invalid input bugs in a simple calculator program. Display the evaluation rubric on the board with four criteria: Correctness (25%), Error Handling (25%), Code Readability (25%), and Edge Case Coverage (25%). **Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine each solution independently, testing the logic mentally with sample inputs (10÷0, 5÷2, 'abc'+3). They complete an evaluation worksheet scoring each solution 1-4 on each criterion and writing brief justifications. **Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their initial evaluations, discussing disagreements and sharing insights they missed. **Final Ranking (10 minutes):** Students individually rank the three solutions from best to worst, writing a 3-sentence justification explaining their top choice and why they rejected their lowest-ranked option. **Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion where students share their rankings and reasoning, highlighting different valid perspectives on what makes code 'better.'
materials_needed: Three printed code samples per student (Solutions A, B, C)
Evaluation worksheet with scoring rubric
Sample test cases sheet (normal inputs, edge cases, invalid inputs)
Basic calculators for students to verify mathematical results
assessment_method: Grade evaluation worksheets (60%) for appropriate use of criteria and clear justifications, plus final ranking explanations (40%) for logical reasoning. Success criteria: Students must identify at least 2 specific strengths and 1 weakness per solution, apply all 4 rubric criteria consistently, and provide evidence-based justification for their final ranking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guiding questions like 'What happens if someone enters zero as the second number?' and highlight specific lines to examine. For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to suggest one specific improvement for each solution and explain how it would enhance the code quality.

title: Advanced Project Management Methodology Recall Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate recall of complex project management frameworks, methodologies, and their specific components through a structured memorization and retrieval exercise. This activity focuses on recalling detailed elements of advanced PM methodologies including PRINCE2, PMI's PMBOK Guide processes, and Agile frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the 47 project management processes from PMBOK Guide 7th edition by categorizing them into their correct process groups and knowledge areas
Students will identify and recite the seven principles and seven themes of PRINCE2 methodology through structured memory exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing blank process mapping templates to each student (5 minutes). Project the master reference chart showing PMBOK's 5 process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) and 10 knowledge areas on the board for 3 minutes only, then remove it. Students must now recall and fill in all 47 processes in their correct intersections on the template grid (15 minutes). Next, provide students with PRINCE2 methodology cards - each card contains one principle or theme without labels. Students must sort these 14 cards into two groups (principles vs. themes) and recite them in correct order (10 minutes). For the third phase, display a mixed list of 30 project management terms from various methodologies (Scrum ceremonies, PRINCE2 roles, PMBOK artifacts, SAFe components) for 2 minutes. Remove the list and have students write down as many terms as possible, grouped by methodology (12 minutes). Finally, conduct rapid-fire verbal recall rounds where students must state the correct number of elements in various PM frameworks (e.g., 'How many Scrum events are there?' Answer: 5) (10 minutes). Students work individually throughout but can verify answers in pairs during the final 5 minutes before submission.
materials_needed: Blank PMBOK process mapping templates (49 cells: 5x10 grid plus process groups)
PRINCE2 methodology cards (14 cards with principles and themes)
Mixed PM terminology reference sheets
Timer or stopwatch
Master answer keys for instructor verification
assessment_method: Score based on accuracy: PMBOK grid (47 points - 1 per correct process placement), PRINCE2 sorting (14 points - 1 per correct categorization), terminology recall (30 points maximum), rapid-fire responses (10 points). Passing score: 75/101 points (74%). Partial credit given for correct terms in wrong categories. Document specific errors for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide process group headers filled in, reduce terminology list to 20 items, allow 30 seconds extra per rapid-fire question. For advanced learners: Add requirement to include brief purpose statements for each recalled process, include additional methodologies (SAFe, Crystal), challenge them to recall processes in numerical order by PMBOK numbering system.

title: Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Theory Comparative Analysis Through CEO Case Studies
description: Students will analyze real-world CEO leadership behaviors through the lens of Bass's Full Range Leadership Model to distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership approaches. They will categorize specific leadership actions and explain how different theoretical components manifest in executive decision-making scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing documented CEO actions across four transformational dimensions (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration) and three transactional dimensions (contingent reward, management-by-exception active, management-by-exception passive)
Students will interpret how leadership theory applies to real-world scenarios through systematic categorization of 20+ specific executive behaviors using Bass's Full Range Leadership Model framework
instructions: Step 1 (10 minutes): Distribute the Bass Full Range Leadership Model reference sheet and three CEO case study packets: Satya Nadella (Microsoft transformation 2014-2018), Howard Schultz (Starbucks turnaround 2008-2017), and Jack Welch (General Electric 1981-2001). Each packet contains 8-10 documented leadership actions with specific quotes and decisions. Step 2 (15 minutes): In groups of 3-4, students review the theoretical framework, focusing on the seven leadership dimensions. Instructor clarifies any definitional questions about idealized influence (role modeling), inspirational motivation (vision articulation), intellectual stimulation (encouraging innovation), individualized consideration (mentoring), contingent reward (performance-based recognition), management-by-exception active (monitoring for problems), and management-by-exception passive (intervening only when problems become serious). Step 3 (45 minutes): Each group analyzes one CEO case, creating a detailed categorization matrix. For each documented leadership action, students must: identify which theoretical dimension it represents, provide specific textual evidence, and write a 2-3 sentence explanation of why this behavior fits the chosen category. Groups use the provided analysis template with columns for 'Leadership Action,' 'Theoretical Category,' 'Evidence Quote,' and 'Justification.' Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups present their analysis matrices to the class, highlighting 3-4 most clear examples of transformational behaviors and 2-3 examples of transactional behaviors from their assigned CEO. Other groups ask clarifying questions and suggest alternative categorizations. Step 5 (10 minutes): Instructor leads synthesis discussion comparing patterns across all three leaders, emphasizing how the same theoretical frameworks apply differently across industries and contexts.
materials_needed: Bass Full Range Leadership Model reference sheet with dimension definitions
Three CEO case study packets (8-10 documented actions each)
Leadership behavior categorization matrix template
Flipchart paper and markers for group presentations
Timer for activity pacing
assessment_method: Evaluate completed categorization matrices using 4-point rubric: (4) Accurately categorizes 90%+ behaviors with clear theoretical justification and specific evidence; (3) Accurately categorizes 75-89% behaviors with adequate justification; (2) Accurately categorizes 60-74% behaviors with minimal justification; (1) Categorizes <60% behaviors accurately or lacks theoretical justification. Additionally assess presentation quality based on clarity of examples and ability to defend categorization choices during Q&A.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of 2-3 leadership actions already categorized with full justification as models. Create small reference cards with key phrases for each theoretical dimension. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify behaviors that span multiple categories or represent hybrid approaches. Ask them to evaluate which leadership style was most effective for each CEO's specific organizational context and why.

title: Project Schedule Variance Analysis and Recovery Strategy Development
description: Students will analyze a troubled project's schedule performance data to identify root causes of delays and compare alternative recovery strategies. They will examine earned value metrics, critical path impacts, and resource constraints to recommend the most viable corrective action plan.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze schedule variance data using earned value management metrics (SV, SPI, ETC) to identify specific performance issues and their underlying causes
Students will compare three different schedule recovery strategies through cost-benefit analysis and risk assessment to determine optimal corrective actions
instructions: **Phase 1 - Data Analysis (20 minutes):** Distribute the XYZ Software Implementation Project case study containing: baseline schedule (50 activities), actual progress through week 16, earned value data, and resource utilization reports. Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives printed copies of the Gantt chart, EVM dashboard, and resource calendars. Teams first calculate current Schedule Variance (SV = EV - PV) and Schedule Performance Index (SPI = EV/PV) for each work package. Using the critical path analysis template, they identify which delayed activities impact the critical path versus those with float remaining. **Phase 2 - Root Cause Analysis (15 minutes):** Teams examine resource allocation data, change request logs, and dependency relationships to determine why specific activities are behind schedule. They categorize causes into: resource constraints, scope changes, external dependencies, or estimation errors. Each cause must be supported with specific evidence from the case data. **Phase 3 - Strategy Development (25 minutes):** Teams evaluate three pre-defined recovery options: (A) Fast-tracking by parallelizing testing phases, (B) Crashing by adding 2 senior developers, (C) Scope reduction by deferring 3 non-critical features. Using the decision matrix template, teams analyze each option across criteria: cost impact, schedule improvement, quality risk, and stakeholder acceptance. They must calculate the cost per day saved and assess probability of success. **Phase 4 - Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents their 5-minute recommendation using the standard template: current situation analysis, root causes identified, strategy comparison results, and final recommendation with implementation steps.
materials_needed: XYZ Software Implementation Project case study packet (12 pages per team)
Earned Value Management calculation templates
Critical path analysis worksheets
Decision matrix evaluation forms
Scientific calculators
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Teams earn points using this rubric: Schedule variance calculations accuracy (25 points), root cause analysis depth and evidence quality (25 points), strategy comparison thoroughness including quantitative analysis (30 points), and recommendation justification with implementation feasibility (20 points). Instructor observes team discussions for participation grades and reviews completed worksheets for technical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide completed SV/SPI calculations for first 3 work packages as examples, offer laminated formula reference cards, and assign mixed-ability teams with designated roles. For advanced learners: add Monte Carlo simulation requirements for risk analysis, require consideration of resource leveling constraints, or challenge them to develop a fourth hybrid recovery strategy combining elements from the given options.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing Protocols
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF, BGP, and network security policies. They will create original network documentation, implement the design using Cisco Packet Tracer, and present a comprehensive network proposal including redundancy and scalability considerations.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original enterprise network topology by integrating VLANs, OSPF areas, BGP routing, and security policies to meet specific business requirements
Students will create comprehensive network documentation through producing detailed network diagrams, IP addressing schemes, and configuration templates
instructions:
**Phase 1: Requirements Analysis (30 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 200 employees across 3 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR) requiring secure network segmentation and internet connectivity through two ISPs. Students must identify network requirements including VLAN segmentation, IP addressing, routing protocols, and security needs.

**Phase 2: Network Design (60 minutes)**
Students create original network topology using drawing software, defining: 4 VLANs (Management, Sales, Engineering, HR), OSPF single-area design, BGP configuration for dual-homed internet connectivity, and Layer 3 switch for inter-VLAN routing. They must develop a custom IP addressing scheme using 10.0.0.0/16 with proper subnetting for each VLAN and include redundancy planning.

**Phase 3: Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer, students build their designed topology with minimum 2 Layer 3 switches, 4 Layer 2 switches, 2 routers for internet simulation, and 12 end devices. They configure VLANs and trunking, implement OSPF routing, establish BGP peering with simulated ISPs, and create inter-VLAN routing with ACLs for security.

**Phase 4: Documentation and Testing (45 minutes)**
Students create network documentation including topology diagram with IP addresses, complete device configurations, VLAN and routing tables, and connectivity test results. They must verify full connectivity between VLANs through routing protocols and document troubleshooting procedures.

**Phase 5: Presentation (30 minutes)**
Students present their network design in 8-minute presentations covering design rationale, implementation challenges, security considerations, and scalability recommendations for future growth.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version)
Network diagramming software (Visio, Draw.io, or Lucidchart)
TechCorp business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Cisco IOS command reference sheets
Presentation software (PowerPoint or Google Slides)
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Network Design Quality (25 points) - topology correctness, scalability, redundancy; Technical Implementation (35 points) - working VLANs, OSPF/BGP configuration, inter-VLAN routing, security ACLs; Documentation Quality (25 points) - professional diagrams, complete configurations, IP addressing scheme; Presentation (15 points) - technical accuracy, design justification, scalability planning. Success criteria: Minimum 80% overall score with functioning network demonstrating full inter-VLAN connectivity and proper routing protocol operation.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students**: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic switch/router configurations, offer VLAN configuration checklists, and pair with stronger peers for Phase 3 implementation. Consider allowing simplified topology with fewer VLANs. **For advanced learners**: Challenge them to implement additional features such as HSRP/VRRP for gateway redundancy, QoS policies for voice traffic prioritization, or EtherChannel link aggregation. Encourage exploration of IPv6 dual-stack implementation or advanced BGP features like route filtering and communities.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing Protocols: Practical Workshop
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology featuring multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF and EIGRP protocols, and redundancy mechanisms. They will create network documentation, implement the solution in Packet Tracer, and present their design rationale to simulate real-world network deployment scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, routing protocols, and redundancy concepts by designing a scalable enterprise network architecture that meets specific business requirements
Students will construct a fully functional multi-site network implementation through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers with comprehensive testing and documentation
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp needs a network for 3 buildings (200, 150, and 100 employees respectively) with departments requiring network segmentation. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives identical requirements: Sales VLAN (10), Engineering VLAN (20), HR VLAN (30), Guest VLAN (99), plus server farm and DMZ segments. Students spend the first 30 minutes analyzing requirements and sketching their topology on whiteboards, identifying switch placement, router locations, and VLAN assignments. Next, teams create detailed IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16, ensuring logical addressing that supports future growth. For the following 90 minutes, students build their networks in Cisco Packet Tracer, configuring Layer 2 switches with VLANs and trunking, Layer 3 switches or routers for inter-VLAN routing, OSPF for internal routing between buildings, EIGRP for WAN connections, and HSRP/VRRP for gateway redundancy. Teams must implement access control lists restricting inter-departmental access, configure port security on access ports, and establish spanning tree protocol for loop prevention. The final 45 minutes involve comprehensive testing using ping tests between all VLANs, traceroute verification of routing paths, and failover testing by shutting down primary links. Students document their configurations, create network diagrams using Visio or draw.io, and prepare 10-minute presentations explaining their design decisions, addressing scalability, security considerations, and troubleshooting approaches. Each presentation includes a live demonstration of their working network and response to instructor-posed 'what-if' scenarios.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software installed on student computers
Company scenario handouts with specific network requirements
Whiteboards and markers for initial topology planning
Network diagramming software access (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart)
Presentation display capability (projector/smart board)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - logical topology, appropriate device selection, scalable IP addressing; Implementation Accuracy (25 points) - correct VLAN configurations, functioning routing protocols, successful inter-VLAN communication; Security Implementation (20 points) - appropriate ACLs, port security, network segmentation; Documentation Quality (15 points) - clear network diagrams, complete configuration backups, professional presentation; Problem-Solving Demonstration (15 points) - successful troubleshooting during testing phase, thoughtful responses to scenario questions during presentation
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic switch/router settings, offer step-by-step VLAN configuration checklists, and pair with stronger teammates. Create 'help stations' with common configuration commands posted. For advanced learners: Add complexity with BGP routing to simulate ISP connections, implement advanced security features like 802.1X authentication, or integrate wireless controllers with guest network isolation. Challenge them to optimize routing metrics and implement Quality of Service policies.

Students will evaluate and justify their network design choices through comprehensive documentation and peer presentation sessions

Presentation projector/screen for demonstrations
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentations

learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, OSPF routing, and HSRP redundancy concepts by designing a scalable enterprise network topology from scratch

learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable enterprise network architecture by integrating VLANs, dynamic routing protocols (OSPF/BGP), and redundancy mechanisms to meet specific business requirements

instructions:
