title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation and Optimization Recommendations
description: Students will critically evaluate two competing e-commerce websites' Google Analytics implementations and measurement strategies. They will assess the effectiveness of each approach against business objectives and provide evidence-based recommendations for optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics measurement frameworks by comparing conversion tracking, goal configuration, and attribution models across two e-commerce case studies
Students will judge the quality of analytics implementation strategies through systematic assessment using industry best practices and ROI impact analysis
instructions:
**Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with two detailed case studies of e-commerce websites (Company A: subscription-based software, Company B: retail fashion). Each case includes screenshots of their GA4 setup, including: conversion events, audience definitions, attribution settings, custom dimensions, and 6-month performance data. Students work in pairs.

**Phase 1 - Analysis (45 minutes):** Students systematically evaluate each company's analytics approach using the provided evaluation framework covering: 1) Goal alignment with business objectives, 2) Conversion tracking completeness, 3) Attribution model appropriateness, 4) Audience segmentation effectiveness, 5) Custom dimension usage, and 6) Data quality and accuracy. They complete detailed comparison matrices scoring each area on a 1-10 scale with written justifications.

**Phase 2 - Critical Assessment (30 minutes):** Pairs identify strengths, weaknesses, and gaps in each implementation. They calculate potential revenue impact using provided formulas and benchmark data. Students must defend their assessments with specific GA4 metrics and industry standards.

**Phase 3 - Recommendations (45 minutes):** Students develop prioritized optimization recommendations for the weaker-performing company, including specific GA4 configuration changes, new tracking implementations, and expected ROI improvements. They create a 10-slide presentation with implementation timeline and success metrics.

**Presentation and Peer Review (25 minutes):** Each pair presents their evaluation and recommendations (5 minutes), followed by peer questioning and instructor feedback focusing on analytical rigor and practical feasibility.
materials_needed: Two comprehensive e-commerce case study packets with GA4 screenshots and performance data
Analytics evaluation framework rubric handout
Industry benchmark data sheets
ROI calculation templates and formulas
Access to presentation software
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: 1) Comparison matrix completeness and accuracy (25 points), 2) Quality of critical analysis with supporting evidence (30 points), 3) Feasibility and impact potential of recommendations (25 points), 4) Presentation clarity and defense of conclusions (20 points). Rubric includes specific criteria for advanced-level evaluation skills including use of multiple assessment criteria, consideration of alternative solutions, and evidence-based reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each evaluation criterion and example calculations. Offer mid-activity check-ins to review analysis progress. For advanced learners: Add third case study for comparison, require cost-benefit analysis of recommendations, or include competitive benchmarking component. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling pairs during analysis phase.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Architecture with BGP and MPLS Integration
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three geographic sites with BGP routing, MPLS connectivity, and redundant failover mechanisms. This capstone activity requires synthesizing advanced routing protocols, WAN technologies, and network security principles into a cohesive, production-ready design.
estimated_duration: 450 minutes (7.5 hours) - can be spread across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by integrating BGP, OSPF, and MPLS technologies with documented justifications for protocol selections
Students will create comprehensive network configurations through hands-on implementation of routers, switches, and security policies across simulated enterprise sites
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Network Architect, Routing Specialist, Security Engineer, and Documentation Lead. Provide each team with the scenario: TechCorp requires connectivity between headquarters (New York), manufacturing facility (Chicago), and data center (Dallas) with specific requirements: 99.9% uptime, secure inter-site communication, load balancing, and disaster recovery capabilities.

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze requirements and create detailed network diagrams using Visio or Lucidchart, specifying IP addressing schemes (using /24 subnets from 10.1.0.0/16), VLAN segmentation for departments, BGP AS numbers, and MPLS provider integration points. Each site must support 500+ users with separate VLANs for Management, Users, Servers, and Guest networks.

Phase 2 (180 minutes): Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, teams build the physical topology with ISR 4000 routers, Catalyst 9300 switches, and ASA firewalls. Configure OSPF within each site (Area 0 for HQ, Area 1 for Chicago, Area 2 for Dallas), establish iBGP between sites using AS 65001, and implement MPLS VPN connectivity through simulated service provider cloud (AS 65000). Include redundant links with HSRP/VRRP for gateway redundancy.

Phase 3 (120 minutes): Implement security policies including access control lists restricting inter-VLAN communication, VPN tunnels for remote access, and network address translation. Configure quality of service (QoS) policies prioritizing voice and critical business applications. Test connectivity using ping, traceroute, and bandwidth verification tools.

Phase 4 (60 minutes): Document complete configuration files, create network maintenance procedures, and prepare 10-minute presentations demonstrating working network functionality and explaining design decisions to simulate presenting to executive stakeholders.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 simulation software with IOS images
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart for network diagramming
Cisco IOS configuration reference guides and command sheets
Laptops/workstations with minimum 8GB RAM for network simulation
Network requirements specification document template
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
assessment_method: Evaluate using weighted rubric: Network Design Documentation (25%) - accuracy of topology diagrams, IP addressing, and protocol selection justifications; Configuration Implementation (35%) - functional routing between sites, proper VLAN segmentation, security policies; Network Testing (20%) - demonstrated connectivity, failover scenarios, performance metrics; Professional Presentation (20%) - clear explanation of design decisions, demonstration of working network, response to technical questions. Students must achieve 80% overall with minimum 70% in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing IP addressing templates, sample BGP configuration snippets, and troubleshooting flowcharts. Pair weaker students with stronger teammates and conduct mid-activity check-ins. For advanced learners, add complexity by requiring IPv6 dual-stack implementation, advanced QoS with traffic shaping, or integration of SD-WAN concepts. Provide additional challenges like simulating link failures and demonstrating automatic failover mechanisms.

title: Python Data Type Classification Memory Match
description: Students will memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and their characteristics through a structured card matching activity. This foundational exercise helps students build essential vocabulary recognition needed for programming success.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and identify their correct names when shown examples
Students will recognize data type characteristics by matching type names with their definitions and example values
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Print and cut the provided card sets - one set contains 15 data type name cards (3 cards each for int, float, string, boolean, list) and another set contains 15 matching cards with definitions and examples. Arrange students in pairs at tables.

**Phase 1 - Study Period (8 minutes):** Give each pair one complete set of matched cards laid out face-up. Students spend 4 minutes studying the pairs, reading aloud to each other: 'int means integer - whole numbers like 5, -3, 100.' Then flip all cards face-down and spend 4 minutes testing each other by pointing to cards and having their partner guess.

**Phase 2 - Memory Challenge (12 minutes):** Collect study materials. Give each pair a shuffled deck of all 30 cards face-down. Students take turns flipping two cards, trying to match data type names with their corresponding definitions/examples. When they find a match, they must state aloud: 'Float matches with decimal numbers like 3.14' before keeping the pair. Continue until all matches are found.

**Phase 3 - Speed Recall (10 minutes):** Call out random examples ('True', '42', 'Hello', '[1,2,3]', '3.14') and have students write down the correct data type name on their answer sheet. Complete 15 examples total, pausing 20 seconds between each. Students check answers using the reference cards.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students complete exit ticket listing all five data types from memory and one example of each.
materials_needed: Pre-printed card sets (30 cards per pair - 15 data type names, 15 definitions/examples)
Student answer sheets for speed recall phase
Exit tickets with blanks for 5 data types and examples
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Success measured by: (1) Accuracy during Phase 2 matching - pairs should achieve 80% correct matches within time limit, (2) Speed recall phase - minimum 12/15 correct identifications, (3) Exit ticket completion - all 5 data types named correctly with at least 4/5 appropriate examples provided
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide reference sheet with data types during Phase 2, reduce speed recall to 10 items, allow collaborative completion of exit ticket. For advanced learners: Add complex data types (tuple, dictionary), include type conversion examples, challenge them to create their own example values for each type during the activity

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Estate Market Analysis
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed real estate dataset to distinguish between correlational and causal relationships among housing variables. Through guided exploration, they will interpret correlation matrices and identify common fallacies in data interpretation.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing correlation coefficients in a real estate dataset and explaining why strong correlations do not imply causal relationships
Students will interpret correlation matrices through systematic examination of variable relationships and identification of spurious correlations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the housing dataset (CSV file with 1000+ records including variables: house price, square footage, number of bedrooms, age of house, neighborhood crime rate, proximity to schools, and local ice cream shop density). Students work in pairs with laptops/computers. 

Step 1 (15 min): Have students load the dataset and generate a correlation matrix using provided Python/R template code. They should identify the three strongest positive and negative correlations, recording exact correlation coefficients.

Step 2 (20 min): Present students with pre-made scatter plots of key variable pairs. They must interpret what each correlation means practically (e.g., 'as square footage increases, price tends to increase') and classify each relationship as 'likely causal,' 'likely spurious,' or 'unclear causation.'

Step 3 (25 min): Introduce the surprising finding: ice cream shop density correlates positively (r=0.73) with house prices. Students discuss in pairs why this correlation exists, then share hypotheses. Guide them toward understanding confounding variables (both ice cream shops and expensive houses cluster in affluent, walkable neighborhoods).

Step 4 (15 min): Present three additional correlation scenarios from the dataset. Students must explain each correlation and identify potential confounding variables or third factors that could explain the relationship without direct causation.

Step 5 (10 min): Each pair completes a structured worksheet identifying one spurious correlation, one likely causal relationship, and explaining the key differences between correlation strength and causal evidence.
materials_needed: Pre-processed real estate CSV dataset with 1000+ housing records
Python or R template code for correlation matrix generation
Pre-made scatter plots for key variable relationships
Correlation interpretation worksheet (printable PDF)
Laptops/computers with data analysis software installed
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of spurious vs. likely causal correlations, (2) Accurate explanation of why correlation ≠ causation with specific examples, (3) Proper interpretation of correlation coefficients and their practical meaning, (4) Identification of plausible confounding variables. Students must score 3/4 points to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a correlation strength reference chart (weak: 0.1-0.3, moderate: 0.3-0.7, strong: 0.7+) and sentence starters for explanations. Create simplified datasets with fewer variables if needed. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose controlled experiments that could test causal hypotheses, or introduce partial correlation analysis to control for confounding variables.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Production Functions Using Lagrange Multipliers
description: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve complex resource allocation problems in manufacturing contexts. They will work with realistic production functions involving labor, capital, and material constraints to determine optimal production strategies that maximize profit while meeting specific operational limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methodology to optimize multi-variable production functions by setting up and solving constrained optimization problems with three variables and two constraints
Students will implement partial derivative calculations and constraint analysis through systematic algebraic manipulation to determine economically viable production solutions
instructions:
Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario worksheets and organizing students into pairs (5 minutes). Present the core problem: A electronics company produces smartphones with production function P(L,K,M) = 2.5L^0.4K^0.3M^0.3, where L=labor hours, K=capital investment ($1000s), M=raw materials (kg). The company has budget constraint 15L + 25K + 8M = 12000 and production quota constraint P(L,K,M) ≥ 180 units. Students must find the optimal allocation that minimizes total cost while meeting the production requirement.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students set up the Lagrangian function L(L,K,M,λ,μ) incorporating both constraints. They must identify which constraint is the objective function and which are limitations.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Students calculate all five partial derivatives (∂L/∂L, ∂L/∂K, ∂L/∂M, ∂L/∂λ, ∂L/∂μ) and set them equal to zero. Circulate to verify mathematical setup and catch early errors.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Students solve the resulting system of five equations with five unknowns using substitution method. Provide algebraic manipulation hints as needed, focusing on isolating lambda and mu terms first.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students verify their solution by substituting back into original constraints and calculating the minimum cost. They must also check second-order conditions to confirm this is indeed a minimum.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present their optimal resource allocation (L*, K*, M*) and minimum cost to the class, explaining their solution strategy and any computational challenges encountered.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario worksheets with production function P(L,K,M) = 2.5L^0.4K^0.3M^0.3
Scientific calculators capable of fractional exponents
Graph paper for sketching constraint boundaries
Whiteboard space for each pair to work through algebraic steps
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct Lagrangian setup with proper constraint identification (25 points), (2) Accurate calculation of all five partial derivatives (30 points), (3) Systematic solution of the 5x5 equation system (30 points), (4) Verification of solution and economic interpretation of results (15 points). Students must achieve minimum 70 points (28/40) to demonstrate proficiency in applying Lagrange multiplier techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template showing general Lagrangian form L(x,y,z,λ,μ) = f(x,y,z) + λg(x,y,z) + μh(x,y,z) and guide them through partial derivative rules for composite functions. For advanced learners: Extend the problem by adding a third constraint (environmental regulation limiting total resource usage) or ask them to analyze how the optimal solution changes with different budget levels using sensitivity analysis.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems
description: Students will systematically analyze complex interference patterns created by variable multi-slit configurations to determine how slit width, spacing, and number affect the resulting diffraction envelope and interference fringes. Through quantitative analysis of experimental data and theoretical predictions, students will decompose the overall pattern into its constituent single-slit diffraction and multi-slit interference components.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between slit parameters (width, separation, number) and resulting interference patterns by comparing experimental measurements with theoretical calculations
Students will decompose complex multi-slit interference patterns through systematic examination of intensity distributions, fringe spacing, and envelope modulation
instructions: **Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Arrange students in groups of 3-4. Each group receives a laser pointer (650nm), variable multi-slit apparatus (2, 3, 4, and 5 slits with adjustable width 0.02-0.10mm and spacing 0.1-0.5mm), white screen, rulers, and intensity measurement app. Position laser 2m from slit apparatus, screen 3m from slits. **Data Collection Phase (45 minutes):** Groups systematically collect data for 12 different configurations: Start with double-slit (width=0.04mm, spacing=0.2mm), measure and record intensity at 20 positions across central 10cm of pattern using light meter app. Repeat for triple-slit, quadruple-slit, and quintuple-slit with same parameters. Then vary slit width to 0.06mm and 0.08mm, repeating measurements for each configuration. Students photograph each pattern and create intensity vs. position graphs. **Analysis Phase (30 minutes):** Using provided theoretical formulas, students calculate expected intensity patterns for each configuration. They identify: (1) individual slit diffraction envelope, (2) multi-slit interference pattern, (3) missing orders where diffraction minima coincide with interference maxima. Students create overlay plots comparing experimental and theoretical data. **Synthesis Phase (20 minutes):** Groups analyze how increasing slit number affects: fringe sharpness, secondary maxima intensity, and overall pattern complexity. They determine the mathematical relationship between slit width ratio and missing order positions. **Presentation Phase (15 minutes):** Each group presents one key finding about the relationship between physical parameters and pattern characteristics, supported by quantitative evidence from their analysis.
materials_needed: 650nm laser pointers (one per group)
Variable multi-slit diffraction apparatus with 2-5 adjustable slits
Light intensity measurement smartphone app (e.g., Light Meter Pro)
2-meter measuring sticks and rulers
White projection screens
Graphing software or graphing calculators
Theoretical intensity formula reference sheets
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Complete data tables with experimental measurements for all 12 configurations (25 points), (2) Overlay graphs comparing experimental vs. theoretical intensity patterns with percent error calculations (30 points), (3) Written analysis identifying three specific relationships between slit parameters and pattern characteristics with quantitative evidence (30 points), (4) Accurate identification and explanation of at least two missing orders in their patterns (15 points). Success criteria: <10% average error between experimental and theoretical values, correct identification of diffraction envelope effects, and clear articulation of parameter relationships.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-made data collection templates, offer simplified 2-slit analysis first, and give guided questions for identifying pattern features. Consider pairing with stronger students and providing step-by-step calculation examples. **For advanced students:** Challenge them to predict and verify patterns for non-uniform slit spacings, analyze the Fourier transform relationship between aperture function and diffraction pattern, or investigate how coherence length affects pattern visibility with different laser sources.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems: Exercise 1
description: Students will decompose complex interference patterns from double and triple-slit experiments to identify individual wave contributions and predict how systematic changes affect the overall pattern. This activity requires students to differentiate between various interference phenomena and synthesize their understanding of wave superposition principles.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-slit interference patterns by decomposing them into constituent single-slit and double-slit components using mathematical modeling and graphical analysis
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of different interference mechanisms through quantitative comparison of experimental data with theoretical predictions
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with experimental data sets showing intensity patterns for single-slit, double-slit, and triple-slit configurations using identical slit widths (0.02 mm) and separations (0.1 mm) with 632.8 nm laser light. Students first plot all three data sets on the same graph using graphing software, identifying key features like primary maxima positions, secondary maxima, and envelope functions (20 minutes). Next, teams must decompose the triple-slit pattern by overlaying theoretical predictions: they calculate the expected single-slit envelope function using I = I₀[sin(β)/β]² where β = πa sin(θ)/λ, then determine the multi-beam interference factor using appropriate phase relationships (25 minutes). Students then analyze discrepancies between their theoretical model and experimental data, identifying sources of error and limitations in their assumptions (15 minutes). Each team creates a comprehensive analysis report documenting their mathematical decomposition, graphical comparisons, and error analysis. Finally, teams present their findings to the class, defending their analytical approach and conclusions (20 minutes presentations). Throughout the activity, students must justify their choice of analysis methods and explain how each interference mechanism contributes to the overall observed pattern.
materials_needed: Experimental data sets for single, double, and triple-slit interference patterns (digital files)
Graphing software (Origin, MATLAB, or Python with matplotlib)
Scientific calculators
Large format paper for hand calculations and sketches
Digital presentation tools
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Mathematical accuracy of decomposition calculations (25%), (2) Quality of graphical analysis and proper identification of interference components (25%), (3) Depth of error analysis and identification of physical limitations (25%), (4) Clarity of reasoning in presentation and defense of analytical approach (25%). Success requires demonstrating quantitative agreement within 15% between theoretical predictions and experimental data, plus clear articulation of assumptions made.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide templates for calculations and guided questions about which physical principles apply at each step. Offer pre-made graphs with key features highlighted. For advanced learners, extend to analyzing 4-slit or 5-slit patterns, or challenge them to predict how changing wavelength or slit parameters would modify their analysis. Consider having advanced students mentor struggling teams during the calculation phase.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Slit Diffraction Systems: Exercise 2
description: Students will analyze complex interference patterns created by double-slit and triple-slit configurations using laser diffraction data. They will decompose the patterns into component waves, examine phase relationships, and predict how systematic changes to slit parameters affect the resulting interference fringes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-slit interference patterns by identifying individual wave components and their phase relationships using quantitative measurements
Students will examine the mathematical relationship between slit separation, wavelength, and fringe spacing through systematic data comparison across multiple experimental configurations
instructions:
Begin by setting up three laser diffraction stations with identical 650nm red laser pointers: Station A (double-slit, d=0.25mm), Station B (double-slit, d=0.50mm), and Station C (triple-slit, d=0.25mm). Position screens 2 meters from each aperture. Divide students into teams of 3-4, rotating every 15 minutes between stations.

At each station, students measure and record: central maximum width, positions of first five bright fringes on each side, positions of first three dark fringes, and overall pattern envelope width. They photograph each pattern with rulers for scale reference.

After data collection (45 minutes), teams analyze their measurements using spreadsheet software. They calculate fringe spacing (Δy), compare measured values to theoretical predictions using y = mλL/d, and determine percent error for each configuration. Students then overlay intensity graphs from all three stations to identify how slit number and separation affect pattern characteristics.

For the synthesis phase, students examine phase diagrams showing wave superposition at specific screen positions. They identify constructive and destructive interference points, relating phase differences to path length differences between slits. Teams create vector diagrams showing amplitude and phase relationships for at least three different screen positions.

Finally, students predict interference patterns for two new configurations: quadruple-slit with d=0.25mm and double-slit with d=0.75mm. They sketch expected patterns, calculate first five maximum positions, and justify their predictions using wave theory principles. Teams present one prediction to the class with supporting calculations.
materials_needed: Three 650nm red laser pointers with safety goggles
Double-slit apertures: 0.25mm and 0.50mm spacing
Triple-slit aperture: 0.25mm spacing
White screens or projection paper
Metric rulers and measuring tape
Digital cameras or smartphones
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets)
Protractors for vector diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 100-point rubric: Data collection accuracy (25 points) - measurements within 5% of theoretical values; Mathematical analysis (30 points) - correct application of interference equations and error calculations; Pattern interpretation (25 points) - accurate identification of wave components and phase relationships; Prediction quality (20 points) - logical reasoning and correct theoretical application for novel configurations. Require submission of data tables, calculation worksheets, annotated photographs, and one-page prediction summary.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-labeled data collection templates and step-by-step calculation guides with sample problems. Offer measurement assistance and encourage peer collaboration during data collection. For advanced learners, extend the activity by introducing polarization effects, analyzing white light diffraction patterns, or examining Fresnel diffraction theory. Challenge high achievers to derive intensity equations for multi-slit systems or investigate applications in spectroscopy.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program
description: Students will evaluate three different approaches to fixing bugs in a basic calculator program by analyzing code quality, testing effectiveness, and implementation decisions. They will justify which solution best addresses the identified issues and meets software development standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code readability, functionality, and testing coverage
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison using established software quality criteria
instructions: Begin by providing each student with a printed packet containing: the original buggy calculator code (15 lines with 3 specific bugs), three different student-submitted fixes (Fix A, B, and C), and a code evaluation checklist. Spend 5 minutes explaining that they are acting as senior developers reviewing junior programmer solutions. Students work individually for 25 minutes to: (1) Read the original code and identify the three bugs (division by zero error, incorrect operator precedence, missing input validation), (2) Examine each fix attempt and test it mentally with provided test cases, (3) Complete the evaluation checklist rating each fix on functionality (does it work?), code quality (is it readable and maintainable?), error handling (does it prevent crashes?), and efficiency (is it unnecessarily complex?). After individual analysis, pair students for 10 minutes to compare their evaluations and discuss differences. Each student then writes a 150-word recommendation memo identifying their chosen best fix and providing three specific justifications. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where volunteers share their recommendations and reasoning. The instructor should prepare Fix A (partial solution), Fix B (complete but messy solution), and Fix C (elegant complete solution) to ensure meaningful comparison differences.
materials_needed: Printed code packets with original buggy calculator program
Three different bug fix solutions (Fix A, B, C) printed separately
Code evaluation checklist/rubric handout
Test cases sheet with 8 calculator scenarios
Blank paper for recommendation memo
assessment_method: Grade recommendation memos using rubric: Correct bug identification (25 points), accurate evaluation of each fix's strengths/weaknesses (45 points), clear justification for chosen solution with specific examples (20 points), professional memo format and grammar (10 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted versions showing where each bug occurs and offer guided questions like 'What happens when someone enters zero as the second number?' For advanced learners: Include a fourth solution with subtle security issues, or ask them to write an improved version combining the best elements from all three fixes.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate three different solutions to fix bugs in a basic Python calculator program. They will analyze each solution's effectiveness, justify their reasoning, and recommend the best approach based on code quality, maintainability, and functionality criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by comparing code quality, readability, and functionality using established programming criteria
Students will judge the merits of programming solutions through systematic analysis and provide evidence-based recommendations for implementation
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the buggy calculator code and three solution files to each student. Display evaluation criteria on the board: functionality (does it work?), code readability (clear variable names, comments), error handling (manages invalid input), and maintainability (easy to modify later). **Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine the original buggy code that fails when dividing by zero and crashes with non-numeric input. They then analyze Solution A (basic try-catch block), Solution B (input validation with user-friendly error messages), and Solution C (comprehensive error handling with logging). For each solution, students complete an evaluation matrix rating each criterion on a 1-5 scale with written justification. **Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their evaluations and discuss disagreements. Students must defend their ratings with specific code examples. **Final Recommendation (10 minutes):** Each student writes a 150-word recommendation memo identifying the best solution, explaining why it's superior to the alternatives, and noting any potential drawbacks. **Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Randomly select 4-5 students to share their recommendations. Discuss how different priorities (beginner-friendly vs. professional standards) might influence solution choice.
materials_needed: Buggy Python calculator code file (calc_buggy.py)
Three solution files (solution_a.py, solution_b.py, solution_c.py)
Evaluation criteria rubric handout
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Computers with Python installed or online Python interpreter access
assessment_method: Grade the evaluation matrix (40%) and recommendation memo (60%). Matrix scored on: accurate functionality assessment (10 points), appropriate readability ratings with examples (10 points), correct error handling evaluation (10 points), realistic maintainability judgments (10 points). Memo scored on: clear solution ranking with justification (20 points), specific evidence from code analysis (20 points), acknowledgment of trade-offs or limitations (20 points).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed evaluation matrix with 1-2 criteria already filled in as examples. Highlight specific code sections to focus on. For advanced learners: Add a fourth criterion about performance/efficiency, or ask them to propose their own improved solution combining the best elements from all three approaches.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Exercise 2
description: Students will evaluate three different bug fix solutions for a broken Python calculator program by analyzing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will justify their choice of the best solution and provide constructive feedback on all approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code functionality, readability, and adherence to programming best practices
Students will justify their selection of the optimal solution through structured comparison criteria and written reasoning
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with the original broken calculator code that has three specific bugs: division by zero error, incorrect order of operations, and missing input validation. Present three different 'developer solutions' that fix these issues using varying approaches (basic fix, intermediate with error handling, advanced with comprehensive validation). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students individually test each solution by running the code with provided test cases, documenting which bugs each solution addresses and any remaining issues. 

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the evaluation matrix worksheet, students score each solution on five criteria: functionality (does it work?), code readability, error handling, user experience, and maintainability. Each criterion uses a 1-5 scale with specific descriptors provided.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students write a 200-word justification explaining which solution they would recommend for production use, citing specific evidence from their testing and evaluation matrix. They must address why they rejected the other two solutions.

Step 4 (10 minutes): In pairs, students share their recommendations and discuss any differences in their evaluations, focusing on the reasoning behind their choices rather than trying to reach consensus.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Facilitate a brief class discussion where 2-3 student pairs share interesting points of disagreement and their resolution strategies. Emphasize that different solutions may be optimal depending on project requirements and constraints.
materials_needed: Broken calculator Python code file (calculator_buggy.py)
Three solution files (solution_basic.py, solution_intermediate.py, solution_advanced.py)
Evaluation matrix worksheet with 5 criteria and 1-5 scoring rubrics
Test cases document with 10 specific calculator inputs to try
Python IDE or online Python environment (Repl.it, PyCharm, or VS Code)
assessment_method: Grade the completed evaluation matrix (40 points) and written justification (60 points). Matrix scoring: award full points if students provide specific evidence for each score. Justification rubric: 20 points for clear recommendation with reasoning, 20 points for specific code examples cited, 20 points for addressing weaknesses of rejected solutions. Success criteria: Students score 80+ points and demonstrate ability to use concrete evidence rather than personal preference in their evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation for one criterion, offer sentence starters for the justification ('I recommend Solution X because...', 'The main weakness of Solution Y is...'). For advanced learners: Add a bonus question asking them to propose a fourth solution that combines the best elements of all three, or have them evaluate the solutions' performance and memory efficiency in addition to the basic criteria.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Exercise 3
description: Students will evaluate three different approaches to fixing bugs in a basic Python calculator program. They will analyze each solution's effectiveness, efficiency, and code quality to determine which fix is most appropriate and justify their reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code quality, functionality, and maintainability criteria
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a buggy Python calculator program that has division by zero errors and input validation issues. Give them three different 'student solutions' that fix these bugs using different approaches: Try-except blocks, if-statement validation, and input sanitization. **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students first run each solution to test functionality, then complete an evaluation worksheet rating each approach on: correctness (does it work?), readability (is code clear?), efficiency (performance), and maintainability (easy to modify?). They use a 1-5 scale with written justification for each rating. **Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discussing differences in their ratings and reasoning. They must reach consensus on which solution is 'best' overall. **Class Presentation (15 minutes):** Three pairs present their chosen solution, explaining their evaluation criteria and defending their choice. Other students can challenge their reasoning with evidence from the code. **Reflection (5 minutes):** Students individually write a brief reflection on what makes code 'good' beyond just working correctly, identifying which evaluation criteria they found most important and why.
materials_needed: Buggy calculator Python program (provided starter code)
Three pre-written 'student solutions' with different fix approaches
Code evaluation worksheet with rating criteria
Computers with Python installed or online Python environment access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of functional testing (20 points) - did they correctly identify which solutions work? (2) Quality of evaluation criteria application (30 points) - appropriate use of readability, efficiency, maintainability standards (3) Justification quality (30 points) - evidence-based reasoning for ratings and final choice (4) Peer discussion contribution (20 points) - meaningful participation in pair work and class discussion
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of specific items to look for when testing (edge cases, error messages, user experience). Give sentence starters for justifications like 'This solution is better because...' For advanced students: Have them identify additional bugs not addressed by any solution, or ask them to propose a fourth solution combining the best elements of all three approaches.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Practical Workshop
description: Students will evaluate three different proposed solutions to fix bugs in a basic Python calculator program. They will assess each solution's correctness, efficiency, and code quality using established criteria and justify their recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different debugging approaches by analyzing code solutions against correctness, efficiency, and maintainability criteria
Students will critique multiple programming solutions through systematic comparison and provide justified recommendations for implementation
instructions: Begin by providing students with a buggy Python calculator program containing three specific errors: division by zero not handled, invalid input crashes the program, and incorrect order of operations. Present three different 'developer solutions' that fix these bugs using varying approaches (basic try-catch, comprehensive input validation, or object-oriented restructure). Organize students into pairs and give them 15 minutes to test each solution using the provided test cases. Have them document which test cases pass/fail for each solution in the evaluation worksheet. Next, students spend 20 minutes analyzing each solution using the provided rubric covering: correctness (does it fix all bugs?), code readability (clear variable names, comments), efficiency (unnecessary complexity), and maintainability (easy to modify/extend). Students then spend 10 minutes ranking the three solutions from best to worst, writing 2-3 sentence justifications for each ranking decision. Finally, conduct a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share their top-ranked solution and defend their choice. Other students can challenge rankings by citing specific rubric criteria. Conclude by revealing which solution was actually implemented by the 'development team' and discuss why evaluation skills matter in real software development scenarios.
materials_needed: Buggy calculator Python program file (calculator_buggy.py)
Three solution files (solution_a.py, solution_b.py, solution_c.py)
Test cases document with 10 specific input scenarios
Code evaluation rubric worksheet
Computers with Python installed
assessment_method: Grade completed evaluation worksheets using a 20-point rubric: testing documentation (5 points), criterion-based analysis quality (10 points), ranking justifications (5 points). Success requires students to identify at least 80% of the differences between solutions and provide evidence-based reasoning for their final rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed evaluation worksheet with sample analysis for one solution. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens when you input text instead of numbers?' Advanced learners can propose their own fourth solution and evaluate it against the original three, or create additional test cases to further differentiate the solutions.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification and Matching Exercise
description: Students will memorize and accurately identify 50+ specific components across multiple advanced project management frameworks (PMBOK 7th Edition, PRINCE2, Agile/Scrum, and Lean Six Sigma). Through intensive flashcard drilling and timed matching exercises, students will demonstrate precise recall of framework elements, their definitions, and correct categorizations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific process groups, knowledge areas, and artifacts from PMBOK 7th Edition, PRINCE2, Scrum, and Lean Six Sigma frameworks by achieving 90% accuracy on timed identification tests
Students will memorize exact definitions and categorizations of 50+ project management terms through structured repetition and matching exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-prepared component cards containing 52 project management elements (13 from each framework: PMBOK 7th Edition performance domains and principles, PRINCE2 themes and processes, Scrum events and artifacts, Lean Six Sigma DMAIC phases and tools). Students work in pairs, with one partner holding definition cards and the other holding framework/category cards. 

Round 1 (15 minutes): Partner A reads definitions aloud while Partner B identifies the specific term and its originating framework. Record correct responses on tracking sheets. Switch roles after 7.5 minutes. 

Round 2 (10 minutes): Distribute the large wall-mounted framework matrices (four 3x4 grids labeled with framework categories). Students must physically place laminated component cards in correct matrix positions within 8 minutes. Instructor announces one framework at a time, allowing 2 minutes per framework. 

Round 3 (10 minutes): Individual rapid-fire recall test using the digital presentation slides. Display component names for 5 seconds each while students write the framework name and category on answer sheets. Cover all 52 components without repetition. 

Round 4 (10 minutes): Peer verification phase where students exchange answer sheets and use the master key to grade their partner's responses. Students must identify and discuss any discrepancies with their partner before final scoring. 

Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify their weakest framework area and select 10 specific components for additional study using the provided digital flashcard links.
materials_needed: 52 laminated component definition cards (13 per framework)
52 laminated framework/category identification cards
4 large wall-mounted framework matrices (poster-sized)
Individual tracking sheets with scoring rubrics
Digital presentation slides with component names
Master answer key with correct framework categorizations
Timer/stopwatch
Access to Anki or Quizlet digital flashcard sets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (47/52 correct) on the individual rapid-fire test to demonstrate mastery. Track performance using the provided scoring rubric: 47-52 correct = Advanced recall mastery, 42-46 = Proficient recall, 37-41 = Developing recall, below 37 = Requires additional memorization practice. Document specific missed components for targeted remediation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial card set to 26 components (top 6-7 from each framework), provide mnemonic device handouts, and allow use of color-coded category hints during Round 2. For advanced learners: Add 20 additional components from advanced frameworks (SAFe, Crystal, XP methodologies), require them to create original mnemonics for their weakest areas, and challenge them to achieve 100% accuracy in under 6 minutes during the rapid-fire round.

title: Decoding Leadership Paradoxes: Situational Analysis of Contradictory Leadership Behaviors
description: Students analyze complex real-world leadership scenarios where successful leaders demonstrate seemingly contradictory behaviors (e.g., being both decisive and collaborative). They will identify the underlying situational factors that explain these paradoxes and demonstrate understanding of contextual leadership theory.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between surface-level contradictions and contextual leadership adaptations by analyzing multi-dimensional case scenarios involving leadership paradoxes
Students will explain the relationship between situational variables and leadership behavior choices through systematic deconstruction of paradoxical leadership decisions
instructions: Begin by distributing three complex leadership case studies featuring paradoxical behaviors: Case A (CEO who micromanages new hires but gives complete autonomy to veterans), Case B (military leader who shows vulnerability during crisis briefings but maintains strict authority in operations), and Case C (nonprofit director who makes unilateral budget cuts while expanding democratic decision-making processes). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to identify the apparent contradictions in each case, writing them on provided analysis sheets with specific behavioral examples. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Form groups of 4 students. Each group receives the 'Situational Context Framework' worksheet containing categories: stakeholder variables, temporal pressures, organizational culture, task complexity, and risk factors. Groups systematically analyze one assigned case, mapping contradictory behaviors against these contextual variables. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Groups rotate to examine remaining cases, building on previous groups' analysis by adding new insights in different colored pens. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents their 'paradox resolution' for one case, explaining how situational factors justify the seemingly contradictory leadership approaches. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students write a synthesis statement explaining how contextual leadership theory resolves apparent contradictions, using specific examples from all three cases. Instructor circulates throughout, prompting deeper analysis with questions like 'What situational factor most strongly influences this behavior?' and 'How might this same leader behave differently if X variable changed?'
materials_needed: Three detailed leadership paradox case studies (2-3 pages each)
Individual analysis worksheets with contradiction identification tables
Situational Context Framework worksheets with defined categories
Colored pens (3 different colors per group)
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy in identifying contradictory behaviors with specific examples, (2) Depth of situational analysis using framework categories, (3) Quality of explanation linking context to behavior choices, (4) Synthesis statement demonstrating understanding of paradox resolution. Students must score 3/4 on all criteria, with particular emphasis on providing evidence-based explanations rather than superficial observations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example analysis of a simpler leadership paradox before the activity. Offer sentence starters like 'This behavior appears contradictory because...but when considering [situational factor], it makes sense because...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify additional paradoxes within the cases and predict how leaders might behave in modified scenarios with different contextual variables.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application Using EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will apply core AWS services to build a complete web application infrastructure by launching EC2 instances, setting up an RDS database, and configuring S3 storage. This hands-on activity demonstrates real-world cloud architecture patterns through guided implementation of a three-tier application stack.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 service knowledge by launching and configuring web server instances with proper security groups and key pairs
Students will demonstrate understanding of AWS service integration through connecting EC2 instances to RDS databases and S3 storage buckets
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access credentials and ensure they can log into the AWS Management Console. Share the provided HTML/PHP sample application files via learning management system.

**Phase 1 - S3 Configuration (15 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'student-[lastname]-webapp-assets' in us-east-1 region. They upload the provided CSS and image files, configure bucket for static website hosting, and set appropriate public read permissions using bucket policies.

**Phase 2 - RDS Database Setup (20 minutes):** Students launch a MySQL RDS instance (db.t3.micro) with the identifier 'webapp-db-[student-id]'. They configure the database in the default VPC, create security group 'webapp-db-sg' allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from EC2 security group only. Students record the RDS endpoint URL for later use.

**Phase 3 - EC2 Web Server Deployment (25 minutes):** Students launch an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) with a new security group 'webapp-web-sg' allowing HTTP (80) and SSH (22) traffic. They connect via EC2 Instance Connect, install Apache and PHP using yum package manager, and configure the web server to start automatically.

**Phase 4 - Application Integration (15 minutes):** Students modify the provided PHP configuration file with their RDS endpoint, upload application files to /var/www/html/, and test the complete application by accessing the EC2 public IP address. They verify database connectivity and S3 asset loading through browser testing.

**Documentation Phase (10 minutes):** Students capture screenshots of their running application and document the architecture components in a simple diagram showing the connections between S3, EC2, and RDS services.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab account credentials for each student
Sample PHP web application files (index.php, config.php, styles.css)
Pre-created sample images for S3 upload
Architecture diagram template
Step-by-step checklist handout
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment checklist showing completion of each phase (25 points), screenshots of functioning web application displaying database content and S3-hosted images (50 points), and a labeled architecture diagram identifying the three AWS services and their connections (25 points). Success criteria includes: application loads without errors, displays dynamic content from RDS, shows images served from S3, and diagram accurately represents the deployed architecture.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and detailed CLI commands for software installation. Create troubleshooting guide covering common issues like security group misconfigurations and database connection errors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like CloudFront CDN for S3 assets, Application Load Balancer for high availability, or automated deployment using AWS CLI scripts.

title: E-commerce Analytics Performance Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models and ROI Optimization Strategies
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of an e-commerce website's Google Analytics implementation, critically assess the effectiveness of different attribution models, and provide data-driven recommendations for optimization. They will analyze real conversion data across multiple channels and justify their proposed changes using advanced GA4 metrics and reporting features.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue impact across paid search, organic, social, and email channels

Students will critique existing goal configurations and Enhanced Ecommerce tracking implementation through systematic analysis of funnel performance, product performance reports, and checkout behavior data
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retail business. Students have 90 minutes to complete their audit. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool and export data comparing all available attribution models for the past 90 days. They must calculate the percentage difference in attributed conversions and revenue between models for each channel. Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the Explore section, students create a custom funnel analysis examining the checkout process, identifying the top 3 drop-off points and calculating abandonment rates for each step. They must segment this data by traffic source and device category. Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the Monetization > Ecommerce purchases report, identifying the top 10 products by revenue and the bottom 10 by conversion rate. They must cross-reference this with the Product performance report to identify optimization opportunities. Step 4 (20 minutes): Students prepare a executive summary presentation including: their evaluation of which attribution model most accurately reflects customer behavior (with 3 supporting data points), their assessment of the current conversion funnel effectiveness (including 2 specific improvement recommendations), and their judgment on product performance optimization priorities (ranking top 5 actions by potential ROI impact). Each team presents their findings in the final 15 minutes, defending their recommendations with specific GA4 data points and metrics.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Individual laptops/computers with Chrome browser
Google Sheets or Excel for data analysis and calculations
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
Provided GA4 reference guide with attribution model definitions
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Attribution Model Evaluation (30 points) - accuracy of calculations, depth of cross-channel analysis, and quality of model recommendation with supporting evidence; Conversion Funnel Critique (30 points) - identification of key drop-off points, segmentation analysis depth, and feasibility of improvement recommendations; Product Performance Assessment (25 points) - correlation analysis between metrics, prioritization logic, and ROI potential justification; Presentation Quality (15 points) - clarity of data visualization, strength of argumentation, and ability to defend recommendations during Q&A.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template worksheet with pre-formatted tables for data collection and calculation formulas already set up. Offer guided questions like 'Which channel shows the biggest difference between first-click and last-click attribution?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate custom dimensions analysis, cohort behavior evaluation, or predictive metrics. Encourage use of GA4's machine learning insights and comparison with Google Ads attribution data for paid channels.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing and Security Features
description: Students will create a comprehensive enterprise network topology from scratch, implementing VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF dynamic routing, and advanced security features including ACLs and port security. This capstone activity integrates multiple Cisco technologies to solve a real-world business networking scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize VLAN segmentation, OSPF routing protocols, and security policies by designing a complete enterprise network topology for a multi-department organization
Students will create and implement advanced Cisco configurations through hands-on router and switch programming using CLI commands and validation testing
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**

Provide students with the business scenario: A 200-employee company with HR, Finance, IT, and Guest departments requiring network segmentation and controlled inter-department communication. Students work in teams of 2-3 to design their network topology on paper, including IP addressing schemes, VLAN assignments, and security requirements.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**

Students configure their assigned Packet Tracer simulation or physical lab equipment. Begin with basic device initialization: set hostnames, enable passwords, and console security. Next, create VLANs on switches (VLAN 10-HR, VLAN 20-Finance, VLAN 30-IT, VLAN 99-Management) and assign ports to appropriate VLANs. Configure trunk links between switches using 802.1Q encapsulation.

**Phase 3: Advanced Configuration (75 minutes)**

Implement inter-VLAN routing using router-on-a-stick or Layer 3 switching. Configure OSPF routing protocol between multiple routers with proper area assignments. Create and apply extended ACLs to restrict Finance VLAN access to HR resources while allowing IT full network access. Implement port security on access ports with maximum MAC addresses and violation actions.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (30 minutes)**

Verify connectivity using ping tests, show commands, and traceroute between VLANs. Document all configurations, IP schemes, and security policies in a network diagram with annotations. Demonstrate successful implementation to instructor with live testing scenarios.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software with premium device access
Physical lab equipment: 3 Cisco routers (2811 or higher), 4 Cisco switches (2960 series), Ethernet cables
Network design templates and IP addressing worksheets
Business scenario handout with specific departmental requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Network Design (25%) - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, security planning; Technical Implementation (40%) - correct VLAN configuration, OSPF setup, ACL functionality; Testing & Troubleshooting (25%) - successful connectivity demonstrations, proper use of show commands; Documentation (10%) - clear network diagrams, configuration backup files, security policy documentation. Students must achieve 80% minimum with working inter-VLAN communication and functional security policies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic device settings and step-by-step configuration checklists. Offer one-on-one troubleshooting sessions focusing on command syntax. For advanced learners: Add WAN connectivity with frame relay or MPLS, implement dynamic NAT/PAT, configure VTP for VLAN management, or add wireless controller integration with guest network isolation.

title: Binary Number Memory Drill with Visual Flashcards
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 using digital flashcards and peer quizzing. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary-decimal conversions through repetitive practice and visual association.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 from memory within 3 seconds per number
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through flashcard recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary conversion reference chart to each student and allow 5 minutes for silent review. Display the digital flashcard presentation on the main screen, starting with decimal number 0 and its binary equivalent 0000. Have students repeat aloud '0 equals 0000' three times in unison. Continue this pattern through all 16 numbers (0-15), spending 1 minute on each number with choral repetition. After completing the full sequence, divide students into pairs and give each pair one set of physical flashcards. Partner A holds up a decimal number card while Partner B states the binary equivalent from memory within 5 seconds. If incorrect, Partner A shows the answer and both students repeat the correct pairing three times. Partners complete 8 cards each, then switch roles for the remaining 8 cards. During the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class speed drill where you display random decimal numbers on screen and students write binary answers on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously. Call on students who answer correctly to reinforce success. End by having each student complete the exit ticket quiz containing 8 randomly selected decimal-to-binary conversions. Collect exit tickets to assess individual recall accuracy before students leave.
materials_needed: Binary conversion reference chart (0-15) printed for each student
Digital flashcard presentation with decimal and binary pairs
Physical flashcard sets (32 cards per pair: 16 decimal, 16 binary)
Individual whiteboards and dry erase markers
Exit ticket quiz sheets with 8 decimal-to-binary problems
assessment_method: Grade exit tickets using a simple checklist: 8/8 correct = mastery achieved, 6-7/8 correct = approaching mastery, 5 or fewer correct = needs additional practice. Record completion rates and accuracy scores. Observe during pair work for students struggling with recall speed or accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a place-value chart (8-4-2-1) and allow them to use finger counting during initial practice. Pair them with stronger students during partner work. For advanced learners, extend the activity to include 5-bit numbers (16-31) or introduce binary-to-decimal conversion challenges.

title: Optimization Design Challenge: Maximizing Solar Panel Efficiency Through Calculus
description: Students apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving solar panel placement and energy efficiency. They will use partial derivatives, constraint optimization, and numerical methods to determine optimal panel angles and spacing for maximum energy output.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems by determining optimal solar panel configurations within physical and budgetary constraints
Students will implement partial differentiation and critical point analysis through real-world energy efficiency calculations involving multiple variables
instructions: Begin by providing each team with the scenario packet containing specifications for a 100m² rooftop solar installation with a $50,000 budget. Students receive data sheets with solar irradiance values, panel efficiency curves, and cost matrices. In the first 30 minutes, teams analyze the constraint equations: budget constraint (200x + 150y ≤ 50,000 where x = premium panels, y = standard panels), space constraint (2.5x + 2.0y ≤ 40 panels), and the energy function E(x,y,θ,d) = efficiency × irradiance × cos(θ-37°) × spacing_factor, where θ is panel angle and d is inter-panel distance. During minutes 31-60, students set up the Lagrangian L = E(x,y,θ,d) + λ₁(budget constraint) + λ₂(space constraint) and calculate partial derivatives ∂L/∂x, ∂L/∂y, ∂L/∂θ, ∂L/∂d, ∂L/∂λ₁, ∂L/∂λ₂. In the next 45 minutes, teams solve the system of six equations to find critical points, using provided Python/MATLAB templates to handle the numerical computation. They must verify solutions using the bordered Hessian determinant test for constrained optimization. The final 45 minutes involve calculating actual energy output using their optimal values, creating a technical report with mathematical justification, and preparing a 5-minute presentation showing their optimization process, final panel configuration, projected annual energy output, and sensitivity analysis for one variable.
materials_needed: Solar installation scenario packets with technical specifications and cost data
Graphing calculators or computer access with Python/MATLAB
Pre-written code templates for numerical optimization solving
Solar irradiance data tables for local geographic coordinates
Technical report template with required mathematical sections
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: correct setup of Lagrangian and constraint equations (25 points), accurate calculation of partial derivatives (25 points), proper application of optimization solution methods (25 points), realistic final energy output calculations with units (15 points), and clear mathematical communication in technical report (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with partially completed Lagrangian setups and step-by-step derivative calculation guides. Offer advanced learners additional constraints such as seasonal angle adjustments, shading analysis using trigonometric optimization, or economic optimization including time-value of money calculations with exponential functions.

title: Optimization Design Challenge: Maximizing Solar Panel Efficiency Through Calculus: Exercise 1
description: Students apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve a real-world engineering problem involving solar panel placement and efficiency. They will use derivatives, constraint optimization, and geometric modeling to determine optimal angles and positioning for maximum energy output.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize solar panel positioning by analyzing efficiency functions with multiple constraints
Students will implement calculus-based optimization techniques through solving authentic engineering problems involving geometric constraints and trigonometric relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the solar panel scenario packet containing efficiency data tables, geographic parameters (latitude 42°N), and seasonal sun angle charts (15 minutes setup). Divide students into engineering teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Engineer (coordinates solution approach), Data Analyst (manages calculations), Design Specialist (handles geometric constraints), and Quality Controller (verifies mathematical accuracy). Present the challenge: Design a solar panel array for a rectangular rooftop (40m × 25m) to maximize annual energy output, considering panel tilt angle θ, azimuth angle φ, spacing between rows to prevent shadowing, and local building codes requiring 2m clearance from roof edges. Students first establish the efficiency function E(θ,φ,s) where s represents spacing, incorporating provided efficiency curves and shading calculations (30 minutes). Teams then identify constraints: 0° ≤ θ ≤ 90°, -90° ≤ φ ≤ 90°, minimum spacing s ≥ h/tan(solar elevation), and total array must fit within roof boundaries. Using calculus techniques, students find critical points by setting partial derivatives equal to zero: ∂E/∂θ = 0, ∂E/∂φ = 0, ∂E/∂s = 0, then apply the second derivative test to confirm maximum values (45 minutes). Teams use Lagrange multipliers to handle geometric constraints and verify solutions satisfy boundary conditions. Finally, students calculate total annual energy output, create technical drawings showing optimal panel layout, and prepare 5-minute presentations defending their mathematical approach and final design recommendations (30 minutes presentation prep, 20 minutes presentations).
materials_needed: Solar efficiency data tables with seasonal variations
Scientific calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Wolfram Alpha)
Graph paper and technical drawing templates
Digital presentation tools (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
Protractors and rulers for geometric verification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Mathematical Accuracy (25% - correct application of partial derivatives and optimization techniques), Constraint Handling (25% - proper use of Lagrange multipliers and boundary analysis), Solution Validation (25% - verification through second derivative test and practical feasibility), and Communication (25% - clear presentation of methodology and results). Students submit calculation worksheets, technical drawings, and deliver team presentations for comprehensive evaluation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated efficiency functions and step-by-step derivative templates, offer one-on-one coaching during constraint identification phase. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including economic optimization (cost per kWh), seasonal variations in electricity pricing, or extend to 3D optimization including panel height variations. Provide additional real-world constraints like wind load calculations or maintenance accessibility requirements.
