title: Risk Impact Matrix Analysis: Comparing Project Risk Management Strategies
description: Students will analyze three different project scenarios by examining their risk registers and comparing the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will deconstruct risk assessment decisions and evaluate the appropriateness of risk mitigation approaches across varying project contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk probability and impact assessments by deconstructing completed risk registers from three different project types
Students will compare risk response strategies through systematic evaluation of mitigation effectiveness across construction, IT, and pharmaceutical project scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute three pre-prepared project case studies: a hospital construction project, a software migration project, and a drug development project, each containing completed risk registers with 8-10 identified risks, probability/impact ratings, and selected response strategies. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each group examines all three risk registers and creates a comparative analysis chart identifying patterns in risk assessment methodologies. Students must identify which risks were rated similarly across projects despite different contexts and question whether the probability/impact scores are justified based on project type. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups focus on risk response strategies, analyzing why certain approaches (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) were chosen for specific risks. They must identify at least two instances where they disagree with the selected response strategy and propose alternatives with justification. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group prepares a presentation highlighting their most significant finding about inconsistencies or questionable decisions across the three projects. Phase 4 (30 minutes): Groups present their 5-minute analyses, followed by instructor-led discussion connecting findings to PMI's risk management standards. Conclude with individual reflection where each student writes a one-paragraph summary identifying which project demonstrated the most effective risk management approach and why.
materials_needed: Three detailed project case studies with completed risk registers (printed packets)
Risk analysis comparison template worksheets
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
PMI Risk Management Standard reference sheets
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk assessment analysis - identifies valid concerns about probability/impact ratings; (2) Quality of comparative analysis - draws meaningful connections between different project contexts; (3) Justification of alternative risk responses - provides sound reasoning based on PMI standards; (4) Presentation clarity - effectively communicates key findings with specific examples from the case studies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided analysis worksheet with specific questions about each risk category and prompts for comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate expected monetary value for quantifiable risks and propose entirely different risk breakdown structures for one of the projects. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers within groups.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation for E-commerce Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data scenarios. They will analyze customer journey data, compare attribution model outcomes, and make strategic recommendations for budget allocation across marketing channels.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business impact of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, and linear) by analyzing conversion path reports and ROI metrics
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of channel performance data and justify optimal model selection for specific business scenarios
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three distinct e-commerce datasets in GA4 demo accounts, each representing different business models: subscription service, high-ticket retail, and impulse purchase products. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to familiarize themselves with each dataset's conversion paths using Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths.

Next, have teams spend 45 minutes analyzing each attribution model's impact on channel valuation. Students navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool, selecting different lookback windows (30, 60, 90 days) and comparing how each model attributes conversions to paid search, display, social, email, and organic channels. They must document conversion value differences and calculate percentage variance between models for each channel.

For the evaluation phase (60 minutes), teams assess which attribution model best serves each business scenario by examining: customer purchase cycles, average order values, typical conversion timeframes, and marketing channel costs. Students use the Data-driven attribution insights report to understand actual customer behavior patterns and compare these findings against simpler attribution models.

Students then create a 10-minute presentation defending their attribution model recommendation for one assigned business scenario. They must address model limitations, potential revenue impact of their choice, and specific implementation considerations. Include peer evaluation where teams score presentations using provided criteria.

Conclude with a 15-minute debrief where teams discuss how their recommendations might change with different business objectives (brand awareness vs. direct response) or budget constraints.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo accounts with e-commerce tracking enabled
Three prepared datasets representing different business models
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
Peer evaluation rubric sheets
Presentation timer/projection setup
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data interpretation from GA4 reports (25%), (2) Quality of attribution model analysis including quantitative comparison (30%), (3) Strength of business justification and strategic reasoning (30%), (4) Identification of model limitations and implementation considerations (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category and demonstrate clear understanding of how attribution model choice impacts marketing budget allocation decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled comparison tables and guided questions for each attribution model. Offer additional support in interpreting conversion path visualizations. For advanced learners, include custom attribution model creation using GA4's rule-based attribution or challenge them to incorporate external cost data to calculate true ROAS under different models. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those needing support in data interpretation.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing and Security
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three geographically distributed sites with BGP, OSPF, MPLS, and comprehensive security policies. They will create network documentation, implement redundancy protocols, and establish monitoring systems for a fictional company with specific business requirements.
estimated_duration: 255 minutes (4.25 hours) - can be split across multiple class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by analyzing business requirements and implementing hierarchical network models with appropriate routing protocols
Students will create comprehensive network security policies through the integration of firewalls, VPNs, ACLs, and network segmentation strategies
Students will develop network monitoring and documentation systems by implementing SNMP, syslog, and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Requirements Analysis & Design**

Provide students with a fictional company scenario: GlobalTech Corp needs connectivity between headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and R&D facility (100 users). Each site requires guest access, server farms, and executive subnets. Students work in teams of 3-4 to create network topology diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3.

**Phase 2 (120 minutes): Implementation**

Students configure their designed network using virtual Cisco routers and switches. They must implement: OSPF for internal routing, BGP for inter-site connectivity, HSRP for gateway redundancy, VLANs with 802.1Q trunking, site-to-site VPN tunnels, and layered security with ACLs and zone-based firewalls. Each team member takes responsibility for one site's configuration.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Testing & Documentation**

Teams conduct comprehensive connectivity testing between all sites, verify redundancy failover scenarios, and create detailed documentation including IP addressing tables, routing tables, and security policy matrices. They must demonstrate end-to-end connectivity while maintaining security segmentation.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Presentation & Peer Review**

Each team presents their solution to the class, explaining design decisions and demonstrating key features. Other teams evaluate solutions using provided peer assessment rubrics focusing on scalability, security, and implementation quality.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.0+ or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images
Computers with minimum 8GB RAM for network simulation
GlobalTech Corp business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Network documentation templates (topology diagrams, IP addressing sheets)
Peer assessment rubrics
Presentation equipment (projector/screen)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design (25 points) - topology appropriateness, scalability, documentation quality; Technical Implementation (40 points) - correct protocol configuration, security implementation, redundancy setup; Testing & Validation (20 points) - comprehensive connectivity tests, failover demonstrations; Presentation (15 points) - clear explanation of design decisions, professional delivery, peer feedback quality. Students submit network configuration files, documentation packet, and reflection essay on design trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students**: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic connectivity, offer checkpoint reviews after each phase, create reference cards with common Cisco commands, pair weaker students with stronger team members for mentoring. **Extensions for advanced learners**: Add requirements for QoS implementation across WAN links, integrate network automation using Python scripts, implement advanced security features like 802.1X authentication, design disaster recovery protocols, or add IPv6 dual-stack configuration throughout the network.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Analysis: Comparing Faraday's Law Applications in Power Generation Systems
description: Students will analyze and compare electromagnetic induction mechanisms in three different power generation systems (hydroelectric, wind, and bicycle dynamo) by examining magnetic flux changes, induced EMF calculations, and energy conversion efficiency. They will decompose complex electromagnetic relationships to identify key variables affecting power output and evaluate design trade-offs.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between magnetic flux change and induced EMF by calculating and comparing power outputs across three different generator configurations
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different electromagnetic induction designs through quantitative analysis of efficiency factors and systematic comparison of energy conversion mechanisms
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with three generator scenarios: a hydroelectric turbine (B=0.8T, 500-turn coil, radius=2m, rotation=120rpm), a wind turbine (B=0.6T, 800-turn coil, radius=1.5m, rotation=45rpm), and a bicycle dynamo (B=1.2T, 200-turn coil, radius=0.05m, rotation=300rpm). Students first calculate the magnetic flux for each system using Φ=NBA·cos(ωt), then determine the induced EMF using Faraday's law (ε = -dΦ/dt = NBAω·sin(ωt)) for maximum values (30 minutes calculation phase). Next, teams analyze power output using P=ε²/R (assume R=10Ω for each system) and create comparative data tables showing EMF, power, and efficiency relationships (25 minutes). Teams then identify and rank the three most significant variables affecting power output in each system by examining how changes in magnetic field strength, coil geometry, and rotational speed impact results (20 minutes analysis). Finally, students evaluate design trade-offs by analyzing why each system uses different parameter combinations despite following identical physical principles, considering practical constraints like size, cost, and environmental factors (25 minutes synthesis). Each team presents their quantitative analysis and design evaluation conclusions to the class (15 minutes per team presentations).
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or laptops with calculation software
Generator scenario specification sheets with technical parameters
Data analysis worksheets with comparison tables
Whiteboard markers and presentation materials
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy in EMF and power calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of comparative analysis identifying key variables and their quantitative impacts (25 points), (3) Depth of design trade-off evaluation with specific evidence from calculations (25 points), (4) Clear presentation of analytical reasoning and conclusions (25 points). Students must demonstrate all calculations, provide ranked variable importance with justification, and present coherent analysis connecting mathematical results to practical design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step calculation templates and check mathematical work at each phase before proceeding. Offer guiding questions like 'Which variable appears in both the numerator and denominator?' For advanced learners: Extend analysis to include AC/DC conversion losses, introduce variable load resistance scenarios, or analyze harmonic content in non-sinusoidal flux changes. Consider adding economic cost-benefit analysis incorporating materials and maintenance factors.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Two Student-Written Calculator Functions
description: Students will critically analyze and compare two different implementations of a basic calculator function, evaluating their code quality, efficiency, and maintainability. They will create a detailed evaluation report ranking the solutions and providing specific improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by analyzing readability, efficiency, and maintainability of two calculator function implementations
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison using established coding standards and best practices
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a handout containing two versions of a simple calculator function that performs addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Version A uses clear variable names, proper commenting, and error handling. Version B has unclear variable names, no comments, and minimal error checking. Both functions work correctly but differ significantly in quality.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine both code samples using the provided evaluation checklist covering: variable naming conventions, code comments, error handling, function structure, and readability. They must score each criterion on a 1-5 scale and write brief justifications.

**Comparison Activity (15 minutes):** Students create a side-by-side comparison table listing strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. They must identify at least 3 specific differences and explain how these differences impact code maintainability and user experience.

**Evaluation Report (15 minutes):** Students write a 200-word evaluation report that: 1) Ranks the two implementations from best to worst, 2) Provides evidence-based reasoning for their ranking using specific code examples, 3) Suggests 2-3 concrete improvements for the lower-ranked solution.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange reports with a partner and provide feedback on the evaluation criteria used and conclusions reached. Partners must identify whether the evaluation is thorough and well-supported.

**Wrap-up Discussion (5 minutes):** Instructor leads brief discussion on common evaluation findings and reinforces key code quality principles identified by students.
materials_needed: Printed handout with two calculator function code samples
Code evaluation checklist rubric
Comparison table template
Writing materials or computers for report writing
assessment_method: Grade evaluation reports using 4-point rubric: (4) Comprehensive analysis with specific examples and well-justified ranking, (3) Good analysis with adequate supporting evidence, (2) Basic analysis with some supporting details, (1) Minimal analysis with little evidence. Success requires scoring 3 or higher with clear identification of at least 5 quality differences and logical ranking justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions for each evaluation criterion and offer one-on-one code walkthrough. For advanced learners: Include a third, more complex code sample with subtle issues like inefficient algorithms or security vulnerabilities. Encourage them to research industry-standard code quality tools and metrics.

title: Design a Custom Data Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard from scratch using real local business data to help owners make strategic decisions. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and develop actionable recommendations based on their analytical findings.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an interactive dashboard by integrating at least three different data sources and creating five distinct visualization types
Students will formulate data-driven business recommendations through comprehensive analysis of trends, correlations, and outliers in real-world datasets
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Planning (30 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to select a local business type (restaurant, retail store, or service provider). Provide each pair with three CSV datasets: sales transactions (6 months), customer demographics, and external factors (weather, local events, economic indicators). Students spend 15 minutes exploring the data structure and identifying key variables, then create a project plan outlining their dashboard's target audience, key questions to answer, and preliminary visualization ideas.

**Phase 2: Data Preparation (45 minutes)**
Using Excel or Google Sheets, students clean and merge their datasets. They must handle missing values, create calculated fields (monthly sales growth, customer lifetime value, seasonal trends), and establish relationships between datasets. Students document their data cleaning decisions in a shared worksheet.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (60 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop, students build their dashboard with mandatory components: one time-series chart, one geographic visualization, one comparison chart, one correlation analysis, and one key performance indicator display. Each visualization must include appropriate filters and interactive elements. Students must use consistent color schemes and clear labeling.

**Phase 4: Analysis & Recommendations (30 minutes)**
Students analyze their completed dashboard to identify three specific business insights and develop corresponding actionable recommendations. They prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their methodology, key findings, and suggested actions for business improvement.

**Phase 5: Peer Review & Refinement (15 minutes)**
Pairs rotate to review two other dashboards, providing feedback using a structured checklist covering clarity, functionality, and insight quality. Students have 10 minutes to implement one suggested improvement before final submission.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets per student pair (sales, demographics, external factors)
Computers with Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop installed
Peer review checklist worksheets
Project planning template sheets
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration (25 points - accuracy of merging, calculated fields), Visualization Design (30 points - appropriate chart types, interactivity, aesthetics), Business Insights (25 points - depth of analysis, relevance of findings), Recommendations (20 points - specificity, feasibility, data support). Students submit their dashboard file, documentation worksheet, and recorded 5-minute presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data cleaning templates and step-by-step visualization guides. Pair with stronger analytical partners. Offer simplified datasets with fewer variables. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced analytics (forecasting, clustering), use APIs for real-time data, or create mobile-responsive dashboards. Encourage exploration of advanced Tableau/Power BI features like calculated parameters or custom visualizations.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Recall Challenge
description: Students will systematically recall and identify advanced Critical Path Method terminology, calculation formulas, and network diagram symbols through a timed multi-stage recall exercise. This activity tests memorization of complex CPM concepts including float calculations, crashing techniques, and resource leveling terminology.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific CPM terminology including Early Start (ES), Late Start (LS), Early Finish (EF), Late Finish (LF), Total Float, and Free Float definitions by completing terminology matching exercises
Students will identify CPM network diagram symbols, arrow notation conventions, and critical path marking standards through visual recognition tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Recall Worksheet containing three sections. In Section A (8 minutes), students must write definitions for 20 advanced CPM terms including Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, Interfering Float, Critical Activity, Near-Critical Activity, Resource Leveling, Resource Smoothing, Activity Crashing, and Project Crashing. Provide no reference materials. In Section B (7 minutes), display 15 network diagram symbols on screen for 30 seconds each. Students must identify each symbol (activity nodes, dummy activities, merge points, burst points, milestones) and write the correct terminology. Use a timer and announce each transition. In Section C (10 minutes), present 10 CPM calculation scenarios showing partially completed forward and backward pass calculations. Students must recall and write the correct formulas for ES, EF, LS, LF, Total Float (LF-EF or LS-ES), and Free Float calculations without performing actual calculations. After 25 minutes total, immediately collect worksheets. Conduct a 10-minute rapid-fire review where students call out answers while you display correct responses on screen. Track individual student accuracy rates for each section on your assessment rubric.
materials_needed: CPM Recall Worksheet with three distinct sections (one per student)
Digital timer with audible alerts
PowerPoint presentation with 15 network diagram symbols
Answer key with complete terminology definitions and formulas
Assessment tracking sheet with student names and scoring columns
assessment_method: Score each section separately: Section A (20 points - 1 point per correct definition), Section B (15 points - 1 point per correctly identified symbol), Section C (10 points - 1 point per correct formula). Total possible: 45 points. Success criteria: 38+ points (85%) indicates mastery of CPM terminology recall. Record accuracy rates by section to identify specific knowledge gaps for individual students.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide acronym memory aids (ES-EF-LS-LF sequence) before starting and allow them to use the first 2 minutes to write key acronyms. For advanced learners, add a bonus section requiring recall of Monte Carlo simulation terminology, PERT probability formulas, and Earned Value Management integration points with CPM calculations.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Recall Challenge: Technical Implementation
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific components, symbols, and mathematical relationships used in Critical Path Method network diagrams. This advanced memorization activity focuses on the precise terminology, calculation formulas, and diagrammatic conventions essential for CPM analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 12 standard CPM network diagram components (nodes, arrows, dummy activities, etc.) and their exact symbolic representations within 90 seconds
Students will recite the complete forward pass and backward pass calculation formulas through rapid-fire verbal assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Reference Sheet containing 12 critical components: activity nodes (circles), activity arrows, dummy activities (dashed lines), early start (ES), early finish (EF), late start (LS), late finish (LF), total float formula (LS-ES or LF-EF), free float formula (ES of successor - EF of predecessor), forward pass formula (EF = ES + Duration), backward pass formula (LS = LF - Duration), and critical path definition (zero float activities). Give students 15 minutes to study using any memorization technique. Next, conduct Round 1: Symbol Recognition - display 12 blank CPM diagram symbols on screen, students write component names in 3 minutes. Round 2: Formula Recall - students write all 5 mathematical formulas from memory in 4 minutes. Round 3: Verbal Speed Test - individually quiz each student to recite all components in under 90 seconds. Round 4: Blind Diagram Labeling - provide unlabeled CPM network, students must correctly label all ES, EF, LS, LF values and identify critical path within 8 minutes using memorized formulas. Conclude with peer verification where partners check each other's recalled information against reference sheet. Document individual student completion times and accuracy rates for each round.
materials_needed: CPM Reference Sheet with 12 standardized components and symbols
Blank CPM network diagram templates (minimum 8 activities)
Digital timer/stopwatch
Microsoft Project or Lucidchart software access
Individual student tracking sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 100% accuracy in symbol recognition, 95% accuracy in formula recall, complete verbal recitation in under 90 seconds, and correctly label 90% of diagram components. Award points: Symbol Recognition (25 points), Formula Recall (25 points), Speed Test (30 points), Diagram Labeling (20 points). Total possible: 100 points. Minimum passing score: 85 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for formula sequences, allow color-coding of different component types, extend memorization time to 20 minutes, and permit one reference card during initial rounds. For advanced learners: add resource leveling terminology, include cost-time trade-off formulas, require explanation of when to use free vs. total float, and challenge them to mentor struggling peers during verification phase.
original_title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Recall Challenge

title: Deconstructing Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Response Analysis
description: Students analyze real organizational crisis scenarios to distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership approaches, examining how different leadership styles manifest in high-stakes decision-making contexts. They will identify specific behavioral indicators and predict outcomes based on leadership theory frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing documented leader responses during organizational crises
Students will explain the relationship between leadership style and organizational outcomes through systematic case study examination
instructions: Begin by distributing three detailed crisis scenarios (20 minutes): (1) Tesla's 2018 production challenges under Elon Musk, (2) Southwest Airlines' operational meltdown in December 2022, and (3) Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis response in 1982. Each scenario includes timeline, stakeholder communications, decision-making processes, and outcomes. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one scenario. Teams spend 30 minutes reading and highlighting evidence of leadership behaviors using provided coding sheets with transformational indicators (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence) and transactional indicators (contingent rewards, management-by-exception, corrective actions). Next, teams create a leadership behavior matrix (25 minutes) plotting identified behaviors on a transformational-transactional spectrum with specific quotes and actions as evidence. Teams then rotate stations (15 minutes each, 45 minutes total) to examine the other two scenarios, adding observations to comparison charts. In the final phase (30 minutes), teams present their analysis using the 'Evidence-Theory-Prediction' framework: presenting concrete behavioral evidence, connecting to leadership theory, and predicting alternative outcomes if different leadership styles were applied. Conclude with a whole-class discussion mapping common patterns across all three crises.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis scenario packets (4-6 pages each) with leader quotes, timeline, and outcome data
Leadership behavior coding sheets with transformational/transactional indicators checklist
Leadership behavior matrix templates (printed on 11x17 paper)
Colored highlighters (4 colors per team)
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed leadership behavior matrices for accuracy of behavior identification (40%), quality of textual evidence cited (30%), and depth of theory-to-practice connections (30%). Use rubric with ratings: Expert (correctly identifies 8+ behaviors with strong evidence), Proficient (6-7 behaviors with adequate evidence), Developing (4-5 behaviors with weak evidence), Beginning (fewer than 4 behaviors identified).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted scenario excerpts focusing on 3-4 clear leadership moments, and offer sentence starters like 'This demonstrates transformational leadership because...' For advanced learners, add complexity by requiring analysis of follower responses and organizational culture factors, or having them identify hybrid approaches that blend both leadership styles.

title: Deconstructing Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Response Analysis: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze real-world crisis leadership scenarios to distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership approaches. They will examine authentic leader communications, decision-making patterns, and stakeholder engagement strategies to demonstrate deep understanding of these contrasting leadership paradigms.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing authentic crisis response communications from three different organizational leaders
Students will explain the contextual effectiveness of each leadership approach through systematic evaluation of leader actions against established theoretical frameworks
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 4-5 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute three crisis scenario packets: (1) Jacinda Ardern's COVID-19 response communications, (2) Jamie Dimon's 2008 financial crisis leadership at JPMorgan Chase, and (3) Satya Nadella's Microsoft cultural transformation during competitive threats. Each packet contains 5-7 authentic artifacts: video transcripts, internal memos, public statements, and employee testimonials. Teams rotate through stations every 25 minutes, spending focused time with each scenario. At each station, teams complete a structured analysis worksheet identifying specific leader behaviors, mapping them to Bass's Four I's of transformational leadership (Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration) or transactional elements (Contingent Reward, Management by Exception). Students must cite specific textual evidence and timestamp video references. During the final 45 minutes, teams create a comparative matrix on large format paper, plotting each leader's approach across situational variables: crisis urgency, stakeholder diversity, organizational culture, and long-term vs. short-term focus. Teams present their 8-minute findings to the class, defending their classifications with evidence. Conclude with a 15-minute instructor-led discussion connecting patterns to theoretical frameworks, highlighting how situational factors influence leadership approach effectiveness.
materials_needed: Three crisis scenario packets with printed transcripts and artifact collections
Laptop/tablet stations with video clips and timestamps
Structured analysis worksheets with Bass's transformational leadership framework
Large format paper (24x36 inches) and colored markers for matrix creation
Timer for station rotations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of behavior identification and theoretical mapping (25%), (2) Quality of textual evidence and specific citations (25%), (3) Depth of comparative analysis in final matrix (25%), (4) Clarity of oral presentation and defense of classifications (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category, demonstrating ability to distinguish leadership approaches with supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted key phrases in scenarios and a checklist of transformational/transactional indicators. Pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners, add a fourth complex scenario (hybrid leadership) and require them to propose situational modifications that might change each leader's optimal approach. Encourage advanced students to facilitate peer discussions during rotations.
original_title: Deconstructing Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Response Analysis

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN Implementation
description: Students will architect and implement a comprehensive enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using SD-WAN technology, OSPF routing, and redundant WAN connections. This capstone activity integrates advanced routing protocols, security policies, and network optimization techniques into a production-ready deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will design a complete multi-site network topology by integrating OSPF areas, VLAN segmentation, and SD-WAN policies to meet specific business requirements
Students will create and deploy network configurations through hands-on implementation of routing protocols, security policies, and traffic optimization on Cisco equipment
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Architecture Design**
Provide students with the scenario: Global manufacturing company with headquarters (500 users), regional office (200 users), and remote facility (50 users). Students work in teams of 2-3 to design network topology using draw.io or Visio. Requirements include: redundant WAN connections, guest/corporate network separation, QoS for VoIP traffic, and centralized internet breakout. Teams must document IP addressing scheme using /24 subnets from 172.16.0.0/16, OSPF area assignments (Area 0 at HQ, Area 1 and 2 at branches), and VLAN design with separate VLANs for management, users, servers, and guest access.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): SD-WAN Policy Creation**
Using Cisco vManage simulator, students configure centralized policies. Create device templates for vEdge routers at each site with specific interface configurations, OSPF settings, and security policies. Design application-aware routing policies prioritizing business-critical applications over broadband, with VoIP traffic receiving highest priority. Implement security policies including zone-based firewall rules and URL filtering for guest networks.

**Phase 3 (120 minutes): Implementation and Testing**
Deploy configurations to physical Cisco ISR 4000 series routers or GNS3 simulation. Configure OSPF routing with proper area assignments, establish IPsec tunnels between sites, and implement QoS policies. Students must demonstrate connectivity between all sites, verify OSPF neighbor relationships, test failover scenarios by disconnecting primary WAN links, and validate QoS implementation using traffic generators.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Documentation and Presentation**
Teams create technical documentation including network diagrams, configuration files, IP address tables, and troubleshooting procedures. Present 10-minute solution overview highlighting design decisions, security implementations, and performance optimizations to class.
materials_needed: Cisco ISR 4000 series routers (6 units) or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images
Cisco vManage SD-WAN management platform access or simulation
Network cables, console cables, and managed switches
Draw.io or Microsoft Visio for network diagramming
Traffic generation tools (iPerf3 or similar)
Packet capture software (Wireshark)
Laboratory scenario handout with business requirements
assessment_method: Evaluate using weighted rubric: Network Design (25%) - topology meets requirements, proper IP addressing, logical VLAN structure; Implementation (35%) - working configurations, successful routing, proper security policies; Testing and Validation (20%) - demonstrated connectivity, failover testing, QoS verification; Documentation (15%) - complete technical documentation, clear diagrams, configuration backups; Presentation (5%) - clear explanation of design decisions and implementation choices. Teams must achieve minimum 80% functionality in connectivity testing and demonstrate at least two failover scenarios successfully.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-configured base templates, offer guided worksheets for IP addressing calculations, pair with stronger technical partners, and allow reference to previous lab configurations. For advanced learners: add additional requirements such as implementing DMVPN as backup, integrating with cloud services (AWS/Azure), adding network automation using Python/Ansible, or implementing advanced security features like Cisco Umbrella integration and detailed network analytics.

title: Optimizing Urban Transit Routes Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving urban bus route planning. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal solutions for minimizing transit costs while meeting service requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-constraint transit optimization scenario into a system of linear inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement graphical and simplex methods to solve optimization problems through systematic mathematical analysis of feasible regions and vertex evaluation
instructions: Begin by distributing the Urban Transit Challenge packet containing a fictional city's transit data (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to analyze the scenario: Metro City needs to optimize two bus routes (Route A: downtown-airport, Route B: residential-university) with constraints including budget limits ($50,000 weekly), driver availability (120 hours), fuel consumption (800 gallons), and minimum service requirements (Route A: 40 trips, Route B: 30 trips). Each Route A trip costs $180 and uses 3 hours labor/6 gallons fuel; Route B costs $120 with 2 hours labor/4 gallons fuel. Step 1 (20 minutes): Students identify decision variables (x = Route A trips, y = Route B trips) and formulate all constraints as linear inequalities. Step 2 (25 minutes): Create the objective function to minimize total cost (180x + 120y) and graph the feasible region using coordinate planes with properly scaled axes. Step 3 (30 minutes): Identify corner points of the feasible region through algebraic intersection calculations. Step 4 (20 minutes): Evaluate the objective function at each vertex to determine the optimal solution. Step 5 (15 minutes): Interpret results in context, explaining the practical meaning of the optimal number of trips for each route. Circulate continuously, checking constraint formulations and graphing accuracy. Conclude with pairs presenting their optimal solutions and justifications to the class (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Urban Transit Challenge scenario packets (one per pair)
Graphing paper with 1/4-inch grid
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils for constraint boundary graphing
Digital graphing software (Desmos or GeoGebra) access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct constraint formulation and objective function identification (25%), (2) Accurate graphical representation of feasible region with properly labeled axes and boundaries (25%), (3) Precise mathematical calculation of vertex coordinates and objective function evaluation (25%), (4) Clear interpretation of optimal solution with practical context explanation (25%). Students submit their complete solution worksheet showing all algebraic work and final recommendation memo.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-labeled constraint templates and step-by-step graphing guides with partially completed examples. Offer constraint identification practice problems before the main activity. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking 'what-if' questions about parameter changes, or extend to three-variable problems requiring simplex tableau methods. Provide additional constraints like vehicle capacity limits or environmental restrictions.

title: Electromagnetic Interference Analysis in Multi-Circuit Systems
description: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic interference patterns between three coupled circuits operating at different frequencies. They will decompose the interference mechanisms, evaluate crosstalk effects, and determine optimal shielding configurations using both theoretical calculations and simulation data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic coupling mechanisms by decomposing mutual inductance, capacitive coupling, and radiative interference in a three-circuit system
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different shielding configurations through systematic comparison of signal-to-noise ratios and crosstalk measurements
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the pre-constructed circuit board containing three parallel transmission lines: a 1 MHz oscillator circuit, a 10 MHz digital clock circuit, and a sensitive 100 kHz analog measurement circuit. Students first spend 15 minutes using oscilloscopes to measure baseline signals from each circuit operating independently. Next, they activate all three circuits simultaneously and spend 20 minutes documenting interference patterns, measuring amplitude changes, harmonic distortion, and timing jitter in the analog circuit. Using provided equations for mutual inductance (M = k√(L₁L₂)) and capacitive coupling, students calculate theoretical coupling coefficients between each circuit pair over 25 minutes. They then systematically test four shielding configurations: no shielding, grounded metal barriers between circuits, ferrite core placement, and twisted-pair wiring modifications. For each configuration, students record quantitative measurements including crosstalk voltage levels, frequency spectrum analysis, and signal degradation percentages over 30 minutes. Students analyze their data by creating comparison matrices showing coupling strength versus frequency separation, identifying which coupling mechanism dominates at different frequency ranges. Finally, they spend 20 minutes developing design recommendations for minimizing interference, supporting their conclusions with calculated coupling ratios and measured improvement factors. Teams present their analysis methodology and shielding effectiveness rankings, explaining the physical principles underlying their observations and comparing theoretical predictions with experimental results.
materials_needed: Pre-built three-circuit PCB with 1 MHz, 10 MHz, and 100 kHz circuits
Digital oscilloscope with 4 channels and FFT capability
Grounded metal shielding strips (6 pieces per team)
Ferrite cores (assorted sizes, 10 pieces per team)
Twisted-pair wire sections for circuit modifications
Mutual inductance calculation reference sheets
Data recording templates with measurement matrices
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of coupling mechanism identification and quantitative calculations (25%), (2) Systematic methodology in testing shielding configurations with proper controls (25%), (3) Quality of data analysis including frequency-dependent trends and theoretical-experimental comparisons (25%), and (4) Technical justification of design recommendations with supporting evidence (25%). Students must submit completed data matrices, calculation worksheets, and a 2-page technical analysis report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guided calculation templates with partially completed mutual inductance examples and highlight specific oscilloscope settings for consistent measurements. Offer advanced learners additional challenges such as calculating skin depth effects in shielding materials, analyzing transmission line impedance matching, or investigating ground loop interference patterns. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support for data collection phases.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Python Calculator Functions
description: Students will evaluate and critique three different Python calculator implementations by analyzing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will rank the solutions, justify their evaluations, and provide specific improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three Python calculator implementations by analyzing code structure, readability, and adherence to best practices
Students will critique and rank code solutions through systematic assessment using established software quality criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three pre-written Python calculator scripts (labeled A, B, C) to each student. Each script performs basic arithmetic operations but with varying quality levels: Script A has good structure and documentation, Script B has functional code but poor naming and no comments, Script C has bugs and security issues (eval() usage). Provide the Code Quality Evaluation Checklist handout.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students examine each script against the checklist criteria: functionality, code readability, variable naming, comments/documentation, error handling, and security considerations. They test each calculator by running the code and noting any issues or bugs. Students complete the evaluation matrix, scoring each script on a 1-5 scale for each criterion.

**Ranking and Justification Phase (10 minutes):** Based on their analysis, students rank the three scripts from best to worst overall quality. They write a 2-3 sentence justification for their ranking, citing specific evidence from their evaluation matrix.

**Improvement Recommendations (10 minutes):** For the lowest-ranked script, students identify the three most critical issues and write specific, actionable improvement suggestions (e.g., 'Replace eval() function with if-elif statements for security' rather than 'improve security').

**Peer Validation (10 minutes):** Students pair up and compare their rankings and justifications. They discuss any major differences in their evaluations and can revise their assessments if convinced by their partner's reasoning.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief class discussion on common evaluation patterns and most frequently identified issues.
materials_needed: Three pre-written Python calculator scripts (A, B, C) printed or in digital format
Code Quality Evaluation Checklist handout
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Computers with Python installed for code testing
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation matrices, ranking justifications, and improvement recommendations. Grade using rubric: Thorough analysis of all scripts (30%), accurate identification of code issues (25%), logical ranking with clear justification (25%), specific and actionable improvement suggestions (20%). Success criteria: Students identify at least 4 distinct quality differences between scripts and provide evidence-based rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional examples of good vs. poor code practices, offer guided questions for each evaluation criterion, or allow them to work with a partner during analysis phase. For advanced learners: Ask them to rewrite the poorest script incorporating their suggestions, or have them create additional evaluation criteria related to performance or maintainability.

title: Decoding Crisis Leadership Communication: Multi-Stakeholder Message Analysis Workshop
description: Students analyze authentic crisis leadership communications across different stakeholder groups to understand how effective leaders adapt their messaging strategies. They will examine tone, content emphasis, timing, and channel selection to comprehend the complexity of crisis communication leadership.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the strategic communication choices made by crisis leaders by analyzing authentic multi-stakeholder messages from the same crisis event
Students will explain the relationship between leadership communication strategies and stakeholder needs through comparative analysis of message adaptations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 4-5 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with a crisis leadership case packet containing 6-8 authentic communications from the same crisis event (e.g., Johnson & Johnson Tylenol crisis, United Airlines dragging incident, or recent corporate data breach). Each packet should include messages to employees, customers, media, investors, regulators, and community members. Teams spend 45 minutes analyzing communications using the provided matrix framework, categorizing each message by: audience type, primary message goal, emotional tone, level of detail provided, accountability language used, and communication channel selected. During analysis, students must identify patterns in how the leader modified approach for different stakeholders while maintaining message consistency. Next, conduct 30-minute structured discussions where each team presents their findings on one stakeholder group, explaining why the leader made specific communication choices. Teams must connect their observations to crisis leadership theory, identifying evidence of transformational vs. transactional approaches, stakeholder prioritization strategies, and reputation management techniques. Finally, spend 20 minutes having teams create a visual stakeholder communication map showing how the crisis leader's message strategy flowed across different audiences, highlighting areas of message alignment and adaptation. Conclude with teams presenting their maps and explaining the leadership communication strategy they identified.
materials_needed: Crisis communication packet with 6-8 authentic messages per team (printed copies)
Message analysis matrix worksheet with stakeholder categories
Large format paper or digital collaboration tool for mapping
Colored markers or digital annotation tools
Crisis leadership theory reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of message categorization and pattern identification (25%), (2) Quality of explanations connecting communication choices to leadership theory (30%), (3) Depth of stakeholder analysis and relationship understanding (25%), (4) Clarity and insight in visual communication map and presentation (20%). Success requires demonstrating understanding of how crisis leaders strategically adapt communications while maintaining core message integrity.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing sentence starters for analysis ('The leader chose this tone because...', 'This message differs from others by...'). Offer communication theory quick-reference guides with key concepts highlighted. For advanced learners, add comparison element by providing communications from a second crisis leader handling similar situation, requiring students to evaluate effectiveness of different approaches and recommend improvements.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Mitigation Approaches
description: Students will analyze and compare risk response strategies across three different project scenarios to identify patterns, evaluate effectiveness, and determine optimal mitigation approaches. This activity develops critical thinking skills for selecting appropriate risk management strategies based on project context and constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between project characteristics and optimal risk response strategies by comparing mitigation approaches across three distinct project types
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies through systematic comparison of cost, timeline impact, and success probability metrics
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute the three project scenario packets: IT system implementation, construction project, and pharmaceutical product launch. Each scenario includes identical risk categories (technical, resource, regulatory, market) but different project contexts and constraints. Teams spend 20 minutes individually reviewing each scenario's proposed risk response strategies, noting the chosen approach (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and supporting rationale. Next, teams create a comparative analysis matrix (25 minutes) plotting each risk response against criteria: cost impact (1-5 scale), implementation complexity (1-5 scale), timeline effect (days), and success probability (percentage). Teams must identify at least three patterns across scenarios, such as 'high-budget projects favor transfer strategies' or 'tight timelines increase acceptance of residual risks.' During the analysis phase (20 minutes), teams examine why similar risks received different responses across projects, focusing on contextual factors like budget constraints, stakeholder risk tolerance, and regulatory requirements. Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation (15 minutes prep time) highlighting their top three insights about risk response selection patterns. Conclude with team presentations (20 minutes total) followed by instructor-led discussion connecting findings to PMI's risk management framework and real-world application principles.
materials_needed: Three detailed project scenario packets with risk registers and response strategies
Risk response analysis matrix template (Excel or printed)
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Timer or stopwatch for time management
PMI Risk Management Standard reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of comparative analysis matrix completion, (2) Quality of pattern identification with specific examples, (3) Depth of contextual reasoning for risk response differences, (4) Clear communication of insights during presentation. Award full points when teams identify 3+ valid patterns, provide quantitative comparisons, and connect findings to project constraints.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling teams by providing guiding questions like 'What project factors might influence choosing transfer over mitigation?' and offering partially completed matrix examples. Extend learning for advanced students by asking them to propose alternative risk responses for one scenario and justify their recommendations using quantitative risk analysis techniques.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Audit and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of attribution models for an e-commerce website using Google Analytics 4, comparing first-click, last-click, linear, and data-driven models. They will analyze the impact on conversion reporting, budget allocation decisions, and provide strategic recommendations for optimal attribution model selection based on business objectives and customer journey complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and assessing their impact on campaign performance metrics in GA4
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of model outputs and defend their recommended attribution approach using data-driven evidence
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to GA4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store) or prepared dataset. Students work individually with instructor guidance. **Step 1 (30 minutes):** Navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison. Students extract data for the last 90 days comparing First-click, Last-click, Linear, and Data-driven attribution models. Record conversions, conversion value, and CPA for each model across Google Ads, Facebook, Email, and Organic channels. **Step 2 (45 minutes):** Access Advertising > Attribution > Conversion Paths to analyze typical customer journeys. Students identify average path length, most common channel sequences, and time-to-conversion patterns. Document findings showing how different touchpoints contribute to conversions. **Step 3 (30 minutes):** Calculate percentage differences in attributed conversions between models for each channel. Determine which channels would receive more/less budget allocation under each attribution model. Create comparison matrix showing impact on ROAS calculations. **Step 4 (60 minutes):** Research the business context (B2B vs B2C, purchase cycle length, average order value, customer lifetime value). Students prepare formal recommendation report including: current attribution gaps, model comparison analysis, recommended attribution strategy with justification, implementation timeline, and expected impact on marketing decisions. **Presentation (30 minutes):** Students present 10-minute recommendations to class, defending their choice against alternative models and addressing peer challenges.
materials_needed: GA4 Demo Account access or prepared e-commerce dataset
Excel or Google Sheets for calculations and data organization
Attribution Model Comparison Template (provided)
Business context briefing document for the analyzed website
Presentation software (Google Slides/PowerPoint)
assessment_method: Students evaluated using detailed rubric: Data Analysis Accuracy (25%) - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences; Critical Evaluation (30%) - depth of model comparison and identification of strengths/weaknesses; Strategic Reasoning (25%) - quality of justification for recommended attribution model; Business Application (20%) - consideration of business context and implementation feasibility. Deliverables include completed comparison matrix, written recommendation report (1000 words), and peer-evaluated presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled templates with sample calculations, offer guided practice with simpler 2-model comparisons first, and pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation, cross-platform attribution analysis incorporating offline conversions, or integration with Google Ads bidding strategy recommendations. Provide additional datasets from different industry verticals for broader analysis.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Audit and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of different attribution models using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4, analyzing their impact on conversion attribution and ROI calculations. They will then develop strategic recommendations for optimizing attribution settings based on business objectives and customer journey complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data-driven, first-click, last-click, and position-based attribution models by comparing conversion attribution discrepancies across a 6-month dataset
Students will critique current attribution model performance through comprehensive ROI impact analysis and justify strategic recommendations for model optimization
instructions: Begin by providing each student with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data (instructor should set up demo accounts 24 hours prior). Select date range: exactly 6 months prior to current date. Ensure enhanced e-commerce tracking is enabled in the dataset view. ANALYSIS PHASE (75 min): Step 1 - Students extract conversion data for identical date ranges using four attribution models: data-driven, first-click, last-click, and position-based. Attribution Analysis Spreadsheet Template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Executive Summary Template (Word/Google Docs)
Laptops with internet access
Projector for pair presentations
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Data accuracy in extracting attribution metrics (25%), (2) Mathematical precision in variance and ROI calculations (20%), (3) Quality of business insights connecting attribution differences to strategic implications (25%), (4) Justification strength using quantitative evidence for recommendations (20%), (5) Professional presentation and defense of findings (10%).
