title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Systematic Diagnostic Decomposition
description: Students receive a complex DC circuit with multiple parallel and series branches containing unknown component failures. They must systematically analyze voltage and current measurements to identify which specific components have failed and determine the exact nature of each failure (open circuit, short circuit, or altered resistance).
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex circuit behaviors by systematically comparing theoretical predictions with experimental measurements to isolate component failures
Students will evaluate the interdependent relationships between circuit elements through methodical voltage and current analysis across multiple nodes and branches
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-constructed circuits (15 minutes setup). Each circuit contains 6-8 resistors in mixed series-parallel configuration with 2-3 intentionally damaged components. Provide students with multimeters and the original circuit schematic showing intended component values. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes following this sequence: (1) Calculate expected voltage drops and currents for each branch assuming all components function normally (20 minutes). (2) Systematically measure actual voltages across each component and currents through each branch, recording data in provided analysis sheets (25 minutes). (3) Compare measured values to theoretical predictions, identifying discrepancies greater than 10% tolerance (15 minutes). (4) For each discrepancy, analyze whether the deviation indicates open circuit (infinite resistance), short circuit (zero resistance), or component degradation (altered resistance value) by examining voltage/current relationships (20 minutes). (5) Create a diagnostic flowchart showing their logical reasoning process for isolating each failure (10 minutes). Instructor circulates continuously, asking probing questions about student reasoning without providing direct answers. Conclude with 5-minute pair presentations of their failure analysis and diagnostic methodology.
materials_needed: Pre-constructed DC circuits with intentional component failures (one per student pair)
Digital multimeters with voltage and current measurement capability
Circuit schematics showing original component specifications
Structured data collection worksheets
Graphing paper for diagnostic flowcharts
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations (25%), (2) Systematic measurement methodology and data quality (25%), (3) Correct identification of failed components and failure types (35%), (4) Logical coherence of diagnostic reasoning process demonstrated in flowchart and verbal explanation (15%). Students must identify at least 80% of component failures correctly and demonstrate sound analytical reasoning to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed calculation templates and guided measurement sequence cards. Suggest starting with simpler circuit sections before tackling complex parallel branches. For advanced learners: Add frequency-dependent components (capacitors/inductors) or require students to predict how failures would affect circuit behavior under different load conditions. Encourage development of general diagnostic algorithms applicable to any circuit topology.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Comparing Two Beginner Calculator Programs
description: Students will evaluate two pre-written calculator programs by assessing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will justify their recommendations using specific evaluation criteria and provide detailed feedback for improvement.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two calculator programs by analyzing code structure, functionality, and adherence to programming best practices
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for code improvement
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute printed copies of two calculator programs - Program A (clean, well-commented code with proper variable names) and Program B (functional but messy code with poor naming and no comments). Provide evaluation rubric covering: functionality, readability, commenting, variable naming, and code structure.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students first test both programs using provided test cases (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and edge cases like division by zero). They document which tests pass/fail for each program. Next, they analyze code quality using the rubric, scoring each program on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and writing specific evidence for their scores.

**Comparison Phase (15 minutes):** Students create a side-by-side comparison table highlighting strengths and weaknesses of each program. They identify at least 3 specific improvements for the weaker program and explain why one program is superior overall.

**Recommendation Phase (10 minutes):** Students write a 150-word recommendation memo to a hypothetical project manager, stating which program should be selected for production use. They must justify their choice with specific examples from their analysis and propose concrete next steps.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange recommendations with a partner and provide feedback on the quality of evidence and reasoning used in the evaluation.
materials_needed: Printed copies of Calculator Program A (clean version)
Printed copies of Calculator Program B (messy version)
Code evaluation rubric handout
Test cases worksheet with expected outputs
Comparison table template
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Accuracy of functionality testing (25%), Quality of code analysis with specific evidence (35%), Completeness of comparison table (20%), and Strength of written recommendation with justification (20%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all rubric criteria and identifying at least 80% of the intentional code quality issues.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted examples of good vs. poor code practices and sentence starters for evaluation statements. For advanced learners: Add a third program with subtle security vulnerabilities to evaluate, or have them propose specific code refactoring solutions with before/after examples.

title: Deconstructing Transformational Leadership: Multi-Perspective Case Analysis of Crisis Decision-Making
description: Students will analyze complex organizational crisis scenarios through the lens of transformational leadership theory, examining how leaders' behaviors align with or deviate from the four dimensions of transformational leadership. They will demonstrate deep understanding by explaining the underlying mechanisms and interconnections between idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration in real-world contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between the four dimensions of transformational leadership (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration) by categorizing specific leader behaviors from crisis case studies
Students will explain the causal relationships between transformational leadership behaviors and organizational outcomes through systematic analysis of multi-stakeholder perspectives
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Theranos crisis case study packet containing CEO communications, board meeting transcripts, employee testimonials, and investor statements (15 minutes setup). Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member a stakeholder role: employee, investor, board member, and customer. Each student receives role-specific supplementary materials and a transformational leadership framework reference sheet.

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Individual analysis where each student examines the case through their assigned stakeholder lens, identifying 8-10 specific leadership behaviors and categorizing them using the four transformational leadership dimensions. Students complete a behavior mapping worksheet, noting evidence and stakeholder impact for each behavior.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Groups reconvene for structured discussion using the 'Round Robin Evidence Sharing' protocol. Each stakeholder presents their findings for 5 minutes while others take notes on a comparison matrix. Groups must identify contradictions between stakeholder perspectives and explain why the same behavior might be perceived differently.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Groups create a 'Leadership Dimension Impact Map' showing how each transformational leadership dimension (or its absence) created cascading effects throughout the organization. They must draw arrows showing causal relationships and write brief explanations for each connection.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Gallery walk where groups post their impact maps and provide peer feedback using structured feedback forms focusing on accuracy of dimension identification, strength of evidence, and clarity of causal explanations.
materials_needed: Theranos crisis case study packet (4-page document with CEO emails, board transcripts, employee testimonials, investor statements)
Transformational leadership framework reference sheets (1 per student)
Behavior mapping worksheets with pre-formatted tables
Stakeholder role cards with specific perspective guidelines
Large poster paper for impact mapping
Colored markers and sticky notes
Peer feedback forms with evaluation criteria
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of behavior categorization within transformational leadership dimensions (25%), (2) Quality of evidence cited from case materials (25%), (3) Clarity of explanations for causal relationships between leadership behaviors and outcomes (30%), (4) Integration of multiple stakeholder perspectives in final analysis (20%). Students must correctly identify at least 6/8 behaviors, cite specific evidence for each claim, and demonstrate understanding of interconnections between dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted case excerpts with potential behaviors marked, offer sentence starters for causal explanations ('This behavior led to... because...'), and create simplified dimension definition cards with examples. For advanced learners: Add competing leadership theories (authentic, servant leadership) for comparative analysis, require them to identify implicit leadership behaviors not explicitly stated in the case, or ask them to predict long-term organizational culture impacts based on observed patterns.

title: Critical Path Risk Impact Analysis: Comparing Mitigation Strategies
description: Students will analyze a construction project's critical path activities to identify vulnerability patterns and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk mitigation strategies. They will compare time-based versus resource-based mitigation approaches and determine which combination provides optimal project protection.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze critical path activities by examining their interdependencies, float calculations, and risk exposure levels to identify the three highest-impact vulnerability points
Students will compare competing risk mitigation strategies through cost-benefit analysis and timeline impact assessment to recommend the most effective approach
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 18-month office building construction project network diagram with 45 activities, including duration, predecessor relationships, and early/late start dates (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Risk Analyst, Schedule Analyst, Cost Analyst, and Strategy Coordinator. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams calculate total float for all activities and identify the complete critical path. Using the provided risk register with 23 identified risks, students map risks to specific critical path activities, analyzing which activities have multiple risk exposures and calculating potential schedule impact using the probability × impact matrix.

Step 2 (30 minutes): Present three pre-developed mitigation strategy scenarios: Strategy A (resource leveling and activity crashing), Strategy B (schedule buffering and parallel work streams), and Strategy C (vendor diversification and contingency planning). Teams analyze each strategy's impact on the critical path by recalculating durations, costs, and risk probability reductions.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams create a comparative analysis matrix evaluating each strategy across five criteria: schedule impact, cost increase, risk reduction effectiveness, implementation complexity, and stakeholder acceptance. They must justify their scoring using specific calculations and project data.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents their recommended hybrid approach combining elements from multiple strategies, defending their choice with quantitative analysis and explaining how their solution addresses the top three critical path vulnerabilities identified in Step 1.
materials_needed: Construction project network diagram with activity details spreadsheet
Risk register template with probability/impact ratings
Three detailed mitigation strategy scenario descriptions
Comparative analysis matrix template
Calculators or laptops with Excel/Project software access
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Critical path analysis accuracy (25 points), risk-activity mapping completeness (20 points), strategy comparison depth and mathematical accuracy (25 points), recommendation justification quality (20 points), and presentation clarity (10 points). Require submission of completed analysis matrices and calculation worksheets showing float computations and revised schedules.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a sample critical path calculation for the first 5 activities and offering a risk mapping template with guided questions. For advanced learners, add Monte Carlo simulation requirements or introduce resource constraint complications that require optimization analysis beyond basic critical path method.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Comparative Analysis and Recommendation
description: Students will analyze conversion data across different attribution models in Google Analytics to evaluate their impact on marketing budget allocation decisions. They will critique the effectiveness of various models and justify their recommendation for optimal attribution strategy based on business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based) by analyzing their impact on conversion credit distribution across marketing channels
Students will critique attribution model performance through comparative analysis of ROI calculations and justify their strategic recommendations for budget reallocation
instructions: Begin by providing students with three Google Analytics demo accounts containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multi-channel funnels enabled. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students (20 minutes setup). Each team receives a different business scenario: B2B SaaS (long sales cycle), e-commerce fashion retailer (seasonal), or local service business (location-based). Students first navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool and export data for all five attribution models. They must analyze how conversion values and channel performance rankings change across models, calculating percentage differences in attributed conversions for each channel (45 minutes analysis). Next, teams evaluate ROI implications by applying their company's average profit margins to determine budget reallocation recommendations, creating a comparison matrix showing how each model would influence spending decisions (30 minutes calculations). Teams then assess which attribution model best aligns with their assigned business scenario's customer journey characteristics, considering factors like sales cycle length, touchpoint complexity, and strategic marketing goals (25 minutes evaluation). Finally, each team presents their findings using a standardized template: current attribution model critique, comparative analysis results, recommended model with justification, and proposed budget reallocation strategy with projected impact calculations (40 minutes presentations, 8 minutes per team). Conclude with peer evaluation where teams score each other's recommendations using provided criteria (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo accounts with Multi-Channel Funnels enabled (3 different business types)
Business scenario handouts with company context and profit margin data
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Presentation rubric for peer evaluation
Laptops with internet access and Google Analytics access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of attribution model analysis and calculations (25%), (2) Quality of critical evaluation comparing model effectiveness (25%), (3) Justification strength for recommended attribution model (25%), (4) Feasibility and logic of budget reallocation strategy (25%). Students must demonstrate clear understanding of each model's methodology, provide quantitative evidence for their critique, and connect recommendations to business context.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled calculation templates and attribution model decision tree flowchart. Pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using Google Analytics Intelligence API, or analysis of cross-device tracking impact on attribution accuracy. Encourage consideration of offline conversion tracking integration.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site MPLS VPN Network with Advanced Security and QoS
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete MPLS VPN solution connecting three geographically distributed sites with varying traffic requirements. They will implement advanced routing protocols, security policies, and quality of service configurations while documenting their design decisions and troubleshooting methodologies.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive MPLS VPN topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes, VLAN structures, and routing protocol selections
Students will implement advanced BGP route reflector configurations, OSPF area designs, and LDP label distribution through hands-on router configuration and verification testing
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with a scenario packet containing: Company ABC with headquarters (200 users), manufacturing site (150 users), and branch office (50 users) requiring secure inter-site communication. Students must create detailed network topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, including: PE/CE router placement, MPLS cloud representation, IP addressing plan using /24 subnets from 10.0.0.0/16, VLAN assignments for different departments, and BGP AS number allocation.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using GNS3 with Cisco IOSv routers, students configure: 6 routers total (2 PE routers, 3 CE routers, 1 route reflector), OSPF Area 0 in MPLS backbone with authentication, MP-BGP VPNv4 address family configurations, Route Distinguishers (RD) and Route Targets (RT) for VPN separation, and LDP label distribution protocol. Students must document every CLI command used and create verification scripts.

**Phase 3: Security and QoS Integration (60 minutes)**
Implement advanced features: IPSec VPN backup tunnels for redundancy, Access Control Lists restricting inter-departmental traffic, QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic (30% bandwidth) and critical data (50% bandwidth), and SNMP monitoring with custom OIDs for traffic analysis.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)**
Conduct comprehensive testing: ping/traceroute between all sites, bandwidth utilization tests using iperf, failover testing by shutting down primary links, and security validation by attempting unauthorized access. Create professional network documentation including configuration backups, troubleshooting runbooks, and network monitoring procedures.
materials_needed: GNS3 network simulator with Cisco IOSv images
Visio or draw.io for network diagramming
Scenario packets with business requirements
Access to iperf traffic generation tools
Network documentation templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points - topology accuracy, IP addressing efficiency, protocol selection justification), Implementation Quality (35 points - configuration correctness, security implementation, QoS policies), Testing Results (25 points - connectivity verification, performance metrics, failover procedures), and Professional Presentation (15 points - documentation clarity, troubleshooting procedures, team collaboration). Students must demonstrate working network connectivity and explain design decisions during 10-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base router templates and step-by-step configuration guides for basic MPLS setup. Offer additional lab time for hands-on practice with individual coaching. For advanced learners: Add complexity with multi-vendor interoperability (Juniper/Cisco), implement advanced BGP communities for traffic engineering, or integrate SD-WAN overlay technologies. Encourage exploration of network automation using Python and NETCONF/RESTCONF APIs.

title: Optimizing Warehouse Operations Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world warehouse optimization problem involving multiple constraints. They will formulate objective functions, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal solutions using both graphical and algebraic methods.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to optimize a multi-variable warehouse inventory problem by constructing constraint inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to determine optimal solutions through systematic problem-solving procedures
instructions:
Begin by distributing the warehouse scenario: 'MegaStore has 10,000 sq ft of storage and $50,000 budget. Product A requires 4 sq ft, costs $20, profits $8. Product B requires 6 sq ft, costs $35, profits $12. Labor constraints limit to 800 total items.' (15 minutes)

Students work in pairs to define variables (x = Product A quantity, y = Product B quantity) and formulate constraints: 4x + 6y ≤ 10,000 (space), 20x + 35y ≤ 50,000 (budget), x + y ≤ 800 (labor), x,y ≥ 0. The objective function is maximize P = 8x + 12y. (20 minutes)

Using graphing paper, students plot all constraint lines, shade feasible regions, and identify corner points. They must calculate exact intersection coordinates algebraically: solve systems like 4x + 6y = 10,000 and x + y = 800 simultaneously. (25 minutes)

Next, students evaluate the objective function P = 8x + 12y at each corner point: (0,0), (800,0), (200,600), (0,800), and (0,1428.57). They identify which point yields maximum profit while remaining feasible. (15 minutes)

For verification, students apply the simplex method using provided tableau templates. They perform pivot operations systematically, identifying entering/leaving variables until reaching optimality. (30 minutes)

Finally, pairs prepare 3-minute presentations explaining their optimal solution, including units of each product, maximum profit, and which constraints are binding. They must justify why their solution is superior to alternative corner points. (20 minutes)

Conclude with whole-class discussion comparing solutions and discussing sensitivity analysis: how would solutions change if storage increased to 12,000 sq ft? (15 minutes)
materials_needed: Warehouse optimization scenario handout
Graph paper (coordinate plane with 50x50 grid minimum)
Simplex tableau templates
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils for constraint graphing
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (4) Correct constraint formulation and objective function; (3) Accurate graphical solution with proper corner point identification; (2) Correct simplex method application with valid pivot operations; (1) Clear presentation with justified optimal solution and profit calculation. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency. Submit written work showing all calculations and final presentation notes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn coordinate axes and constraint equation templates. Offer step-by-step simplex method checklist. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints (products must be whole numbers) requiring branch-and-bound method. Include sensitivity analysis calculations for changing constraint parameters. Provide three-variable extension problem with advertising budget allocation.

title: Electromagnetic Wave Interference Pattern Analysis in Multi-Layer Thin Films
description: Students will analyze complex interference patterns in multi-layer optical thin films by decomposing wave interactions at each interface and evaluating how material properties affect overall transmission and reflection spectra. They will break down the system into component interactions to predict and explain observed optical phenomena.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic wave behavior by decomposing complex multi-layer interference into individual interface interactions and phase relationships
Students will evaluate the relationship between material optical properties and resultant interference patterns through systematic comparison of theoretical predictions with experimental spectra
instructions: Begin by providing students with experimental transmission/reflection spectra for three different multi-layer thin film systems: a two-layer anti-reflective coating (SiO2/TiO2 on glass), a three-layer optical filter, and a distributed Bragg reflector with 5 periods. Students work in groups of 3-4 for 20 minutes to examine the spectra and identify key features (minima, maxima, periodicity, bandwidth). Next, distribute material property data sheets containing refractive indices, extinction coefficients, and layer thicknesses for each system. Over 45 minutes, students must decompose each system by: (1) Drawing ray diagrams showing all significant wave paths and reflections at each interface, (2) Calculating phase differences for each reflected/transmitted ray using optical path lengths, (3) Applying Fresnel equations to determine amplitude coefficients at each boundary, and (4) Constructing phasor diagrams to show vector addition of all wave components. Students then spend 30 minutes using transfer matrix method calculations to predict theoretical spectra, comparing amplitude and phase at each wavelength. In the final 25 minutes, groups create detailed analysis reports comparing their theoretical predictions with experimental data, identifying discrepancies and explaining physical causes (material dispersion, surface roughness, measurement limitations). Each group presents one key finding to the class, focusing on how specific material or geometric parameters control the interference behavior.
materials_needed: Experimental optical spectra datasets (transmission/reflection vs wavelength)
Material property reference sheets with refractive index data
Scientific calculators or MATLAB/Python access
Graphing paper and colored pens for phasor diagrams
Fresnel equation reference cards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of phase and amplitude calculations at interfaces (25%), (2) Completeness of wave path decomposition and ray diagrams (25%), (3) Quality of theoretical vs. experimental comparison with quantified discrepancies (25%), and (4) Physical reasoning in explaining system behavior and parameter effects (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in at least three categories to demonstrate analyze-level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed phasor diagrams and step-by-step calculation templates for the first few interfaces. Offer wavelength-specific worked examples showing phase calculations. For advanced learners, introduce polarization effects, oblique incidence analysis, or challenge them to optimize layer thicknesses for specific spectral requirements using their analytical framework.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Basic Python Calculator Programs
description: Students will evaluate and critique three pre-written Python calculator programs with different approaches and quality levels. They will identify strengths, weaknesses, and make recommendations for improvement while defending their assessments with specific evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and effectiveness of basic Python programs by analyzing code structure, functionality, and best practices
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic code review and provide evidence-based recommendations for improvement
instructions: Begin by distributing three different Python calculator programs (provided as printed handouts and digital files): Program A uses functions with proper error handling, Program B uses basic sequential code with minimal validation, and Program C uses classes but has logical errors. Give students 10 minutes to run each program and test functionality using the provided test cases (addition, subtraction, division by zero, invalid input). Next, students work individually for 25 minutes to complete the evaluation worksheet, rating each program on a 1-5 scale across four criteria: code readability, error handling, user experience, and code organization. They must provide specific evidence from the code to justify each rating. Students then write a 2-paragraph recommendation for which program they would choose as the best foundation for further development, citing specific code examples and explaining their reasoning. In the final 15 minutes, facilitate a class discussion where 4-5 students share their top choice and key evidence, while others can agree or disagree with specific justifications. Conclude by revealing which program was written by a professional developer and discuss how their evaluations compared to industry standards.
materials_needed: Three Python calculator programs (printed and digital copies)
Code evaluation worksheet with 1-5 rating scales
List of 8 specific test cases to run on each program
Computers with Python installed
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of functionality testing and identification of bugs/features, (2) Quality of evidence cited from code to support ratings, (3) Logical reasoning in final program recommendation with specific examples, (4) Ability to articulate and defend evaluation criteria during class discussion. Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in three categories to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a code annotation guide highlighting where to look for functions, error handling, and user prompts. Pair them with stronger peers during testing phase. For advanced learners, add a fourth program with more complex features and ask them to suggest specific code improvements with example implementations. Provide sentence starters like 'This program is superior because...' and 'The evidence I see in the code is...'

title: PMI Knowledge Area Critical Component Identification Challenge
description: Students will systematically recall and identify critical components, processes, and artifacts within each of the 10 PMI Knowledge Areas. This advanced memory drill prepares students for PMP certification and reinforces comprehensive project management framework understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific processes, inputs, outputs, and tools for each of the 10 PMI Knowledge Areas by completing structured identification matrices
Students will identify critical artifacts and deliverables associated with advanced project management practices through timed recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the PMI Knowledge Area Matrix worksheets and setting up individual workstations with reference prohibition signs. Announce that students have 45 minutes to complete the identification challenge without consulting any materials. Start with a 5-minute orientation where you display the 10 Knowledge Areas on the board: Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, and Stakeholder Management. Instruct students to fill in Column 1 with the specific number of processes in each Knowledge Area (Integration=7, Scope=6, etc.). For the next 15 minutes, students complete Column 2 by listing the specific process names within each Knowledge Area (e.g., for Integration: Develop Project Charter, Develop Project Management Plan, Direct and Manage Project Work, etc.). During minutes 20-35, students tackle Column 3, identifying 2-3 key inputs and outputs for each process group within the Knowledge Areas. In the final 10 minutes, students complete Column 4 by recalling specific tools and techniques associated with advanced processes like Earned Value Management formulas (CV=EV-AC, SV=EV-PV), risk analysis methods (Monte Carlo, Decision Trees), and quality management tools (Control Charts, Fishbone Diagrams). Circulate during the activity to ensure no reference materials are being used and provide time warnings at 30, 15, and 5-minute intervals. Conclude with immediate peer verification using official PMI reference sheets.
materials_needed: PMI Knowledge Area Matrix worksheets (4-column format)
Official PMBOK Guide reference sheets for verification
Individual workspace signs stating 'No Reference Materials'
Digital timer with audible alerts
Colored pens for peer verification phase
assessment_method: Grade using point allocation: Column 1 (Knowledge Area process counts) = 20 points, Column 2 (Process names) = 40 points, Column 3 (Key inputs/outputs) = 25 points, Column 4 (Tools/techniques) = 15 points. Minimum 80% accuracy required for mastery. Deduct points for reference material violations. Peer verification must show 90% agreement with official PMBOK standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the first 2-3 processes in each Knowledge Area as starter prompts and allow an additional 10 minutes. Advanced learners should include ITTOs (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) for at least 15 processes and incorporate Agile/hybrid methodology variations. Consider grouping advanced students to tackle additional complexity like process interdependencies.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: A Multi-Theory Analysis of Contemporary Leadership Dilemmas
description: Students will analyze complex, real-world leadership scenarios through the lens of multiple advanced leadership theories to demonstrate deep understanding of how different theoretical frameworks interpret the same leadership challenges. They will deconstruct paradoxical leadership situations where competing theories offer conflicting guidance.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between servant leadership, transformational leadership, and authentic leadership frameworks by applying each theory's core principles to identical complex scenarios
Students will interpret the underlying assumptions and philosophical foundations of competing leadership theories through structured comparative analysis of paradoxical leadership dilemmas
instructions: Begin by distributing three identical complex leadership scenarios involving ethical dilemmas, cultural conflicts, and stakeholder tensions (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 4-5, with each group receiving detailed theoretical frameworks for servant leadership (Greenleaf), transformational leadership (Bass & Avolio), and authentic leadership (George & Sims). Each group selects one scenario and assigns theory specialists: one student becomes the 'servant leadership advocate,' another the 'transformational leadership advocate,' and a third the 'authentic leadership advocate,' with remaining members serving as 'synthesis analysts.' Theory advocates spend 25 minutes developing their theoretical lens analysis using provided academic sources, identifying how their assigned theory would interpret the leader's challenges, predict outcomes, and recommend actions. During the 30-minute structured debate phase, advocates present their theory's perspective while synthesis analysts document conflicts, overlaps, and gaps between theories. Groups then spend 20 minutes creating a visual framework mapping where theories align, diverge, and create paradoxes. Each group presents their 8-minute analysis to the class, specifically highlighting moments where theories contradict each other and explaining why these contradictions exist based on each theory's foundational assumptions. Conclude with a 15-minute reflection where students individually write about which theoretical contradictions surprised them and how understanding these paradoxes changes their leadership comprehension.
materials_needed: Three pre-written complex leadership scenarios (2 pages each) involving multinational team conflicts
Theoretical framework summary sheets for servant, transformational, and authentic leadership theories
Academic article excerpts from Greenleaf, Bass, Avolio, George, and Sims
Large poster paper and colored markers for visual framework creation
Digital timer for structured debate segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate application of theoretical principles to scenarios (25%), (2) Clear articulation of theoretical contradictions with specific examples (30%), (3) Quality of visual framework showing theory intersections and divergences (25%), (4) Individual reflection demonstrating metacognitive understanding of how paradoxes deepen leadership comprehension (20%). Success requires students to identify at least 3 specific theoretical contradictions and explain their root causes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide theory comparison templates with sentence starters like 'According to servant leadership, this situation requires...' and 'This creates a paradox because transformational leadership suggests...' For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by adding situational leadership or complexity leadership theory as a fourth lens, or challenge them to propose resolution strategies for theoretical paradoxes.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Deconstructing Project Threats and Opportunities
description: Students will analyze a complex software development project's risk register to identify patterns in risk categories, evaluate risk response strategies, and determine the effectiveness of risk mitigation approaches. They will break down interconnected risks and assess their cumulative impact on project objectives.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies within a project risk register by mapping cause-and-effect relationships between identified threats and opportunities
Students will evaluate the appropriateness of selected risk response strategies through systematic comparison against PMI risk management best practices
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (5 minutes). Distribute the pre-prepared risk register containing 15 risks from a fictional e-commerce platform development project, including probability/impact ratings, risk owners, and proposed responses. Each team receives the same risk register plus analysis worksheets.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams categorize all risks using the provided risk breakdown structure template, identifying technical, external, organizational, and project management risks. They must justify their categorizations in writing.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the risk interdependency mapping worksheet, teams identify and diagram relationships between risks. They draw connection lines between related risks and label each connection with the type of relationship (trigger, amplify, mitigate, or compete for resources).

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the appropriateness of each risk response strategy (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) by completing the strategy evaluation matrix. For each risk, they must assess whether the chosen response aligns with the risk's probability, impact, and cost of response, then recommend changes where appropriate.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams calculate the cumulative risk exposure by analyzing how interconnected risks could compound project impact. They identify the three highest-priority risk clusters and propose integrated response approaches.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each team presents one key finding about risk interdependencies and one recommendation for improving the risk response strategy to the class.

Instructor circulates throughout, asking probing questions about team reasoning and ensuring teams support their analyses with specific evidence from the risk register.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared 15-item risk register for e-commerce platform project (printed copies)
Risk breakdown structure template worksheets
Risk interdependency mapping worksheets with connection symbols legend
Strategy evaluation matrix templates
Calculators or laptops for risk exposure calculations
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization with clear justifications (25 points), (2) Completeness and logic of interdependency mapping with correctly identified relationships (30 points), (3) Quality of risk response strategy analysis with specific PMI-based recommendations (30 points), (4) Mathematical accuracy of cumulative risk calculations and priority ranking (15 points). Teams must submit completed worksheets and present findings. Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example of risk interdependency mapping and offer a checklist of questions to guide strategy evaluation. For advanced learners: Add secondary risks that might emerge from proposed risk responses and ask them to develop contingency plans. Consider providing additional risk scenarios for extended analysis or asking them to create their own risk register for peer team analysis.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation: Critiquing Multi-Channel Attribution Models
description: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) for a multi-channel e-commerce business. They will analyze real conversion path data, assess each model's impact on budget allocation decisions, and defend their recommended attribution strategy through a comprehensive business case.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the validity and business impact of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating channel performance variations across models
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through systematic comparison of ROI calculations and defend alternative approaches with evidence-based recommendations
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with a dataset containing 6 months of multi-channel conversion data from Google Analytics 4, including organic search, paid search, social media, email, and display advertising touchpoints. Include monthly advertising spend by channel ($50K total budget). Divide class into teams of 3-4.

**Phase 1 - Data Analysis (45 minutes):** Teams import the dataset into Google Analytics Intelligence or Google Sheets. Students calculate conversions and revenue attribution for each channel using all five attribution models. They must create comparison tables showing how attribution changes affect calculated ROAS (Return on Ad Spend) for each channel. Teams document which channels gain/lose credit under each model and quantify the differences.

**Phase 2 - Business Impact Assessment (30 minutes):** Using their attribution calculations, teams determine how budget allocation would change under each model if optimizing for 4:1 minimum ROAS. They calculate the financial impact of budget shifts and identify which attribution model would result in the highest projected total revenue based on historical performance data.

**Phase 3 - Strategy Evaluation (25 minutes):** Teams evaluate each attribution model against three criteria: accuracy for business type, actionability for marketing decisions, and alignment with customer behavior patterns evident in the data. They must identify limitations and potential biases in each approach.

**Phase 4 - Presentation (30 minutes):** Each team presents their recommended attribution model with supporting evidence, addresses potential counterarguments, and defends their budget reallocation strategy. Other teams provide peer evaluation using provided criteria.
materials_needed: Multi-channel e-commerce conversion dataset (6 months, 500+ conversions)
Google Analytics 4 demo account with Model Comparison Tool access
Budget allocation worksheet template with ROAS calculations
Attribution model evaluation rubric
Google Sheets or Excel for data manipulation
assessment_method: Teams submit a 4-page executive summary defending their chosen attribution model (40 points). Evaluation criteria: thoroughness of data analysis (10 pts), validity of business reasoning (10 pts), quality of counterargument responses (10 pts), and clarity of recommendation rationale (10 pts). Peer evaluation scores from presentations contribute 20 points. Minimum 32/60 points required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution calculation templates and guiding questions for each evaluation criterion. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify data analysis accuracy. For advanced learners: Include customer lifetime value data to evaluate long-term attribution impact, or add complications like offline conversion data integration. Provide access to Google Analytics Attribution API for automated analysis.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation: Critiquing Multi-Channel Attribution Models: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically evaluate three different attribution models (last-click, first-click, and data-driven) for a real e-commerce business scenario. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model effectiveness, and defend their recommended attribution strategy based on specific business objectives and customer journey data.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing multi-channel funnel reports and conversion path data in Google Analytics
Students will critique attribution model selection through developing evidence-based recommendations that align with specific e-commerce business goals
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a fictional online retailer. Distribute the business scenario packet including: company background, marketing channel spend ($50K total across Google Ads, Facebook, email, organic search), quarterly revenue targets, and current attribution model (last-click). **Individual Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Top Conversion Paths and Model Comparison Tool. They must extract data for all three attribution models, focusing on: conversion volume differences, revenue attribution changes per channel, and assisted conversion rates. Students create comparison tables documenting how each model redistributes credit across channels. **Evaluation Framework Application (30 minutes):** Using provided evaluation criteria (business goal alignment, data accuracy, actionability, fairness to channels), students score each attribution model on a 1-5 scale with written justifications. They must identify which channels are over/under-credited in each model and calculate potential budget reallocation impacts. **Recommendation Development (25 minutes):** Students write a 500-word executive summary defending their chosen attribution model. Must include: quantified impact on channel performance assessment, specific budget redistribution recommendations, implementation timeline, and anticipated challenges. **Peer Review (15 minutes):** Students exchange recommendations and provide structured feedback using the evaluation rubric, identifying strengths and weaknesses in peers' analytical reasoning. **Presentation (20 minutes):** Selected students present conflicting recommendations, defending their choices against peer challenges in a structured debate format.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account access (Merchandise Store)
Business scenario packet with company background and marketing spend data
Attribution model evaluation framework rubric
Spreadsheet template for data comparison tables
Peer review feedback forms
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Data extraction accuracy (20 points), attribution model analysis depth (25 points), evaluation criteria application (20 points), recommendation quality and business alignment (25 points), peer review quality (10 points). Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated ability to justify model selection using quantitative data and clear business rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each attribution model analysis. Offer one-on-one review sessions during the evaluation phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value data, propose custom attribution model modifications, or analyze attribution model performance across different product categories within the same dataset.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation: Critiquing Multi-Channel Attribution Models: Business Application
description: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 for a multi-channel e-commerce campaign. They will analyze real conversion data, critique current attribution settings, and provide evidence-based recommendations for optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models by analyzing cross-channel conversion paths and ROI data for an e-commerce business
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of first-click, last-click, data-driven, and position-based models using actual campaign performance metrics
instructions: Begin by providing students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic sources (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display ads). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students (20 minutes setup). Each team receives identical datasets but focuses on different product categories. Step 1: Students navigate to GA4 > Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths and export conversion path data for their assigned product category (15 minutes). Step 2: Teams analyze the 'Top conversion paths' report, identifying the most common multi-touch customer journeys and calculating the average path length and time to conversion (25 minutes). Step 3: Using the Attribution comparison tool, students compare revenue attribution across all four attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, position-based) for their product category, documenting percentage differences in channel credit allocation (30 minutes). Step 4: Teams examine the Model comparison report to identify which channels are over/under-credited under different models, focusing on channels with >20% attribution variance (20 minutes). Step 5: Students calculate ROAS (Return on Ad Spend) for each paid channel under each attribution model using the formula: (Revenue attributed to channel ÷ Channel cost) × 100 (25 minutes). Step 6: Teams create a comprehensive evaluation report that critiques the current attribution model, identifies its strengths/weaknesses for their product category, and provides three specific, data-backed recommendations for attribution optimization. The report must include quantitative evidence supporting each recommendation (45 minutes). Step 7: Teams present their findings in 8-minute presentations, defending their recommendations against peer questions (40 minutes total).
materials_needed: Access to GA4 demo account with e-commerce data (Universal Analytics Demo Store or similar)
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets) for calculations
Attribution comparison template with ROAS calculation formulas
Channel cost data spreadsheet for ROAS calculations
Evaluation report template with rubric criteria
assessment_method: Students submit a written evaluation report (40% of grade) containing: quantitative analysis of attribution model performance, identification of 3 specific model weaknesses with data evidence, 3 optimization recommendations with projected impact calculations. Presentation performance (35% of grade) evaluated on: clarity of recommendations, use of data to support arguments, ability to defend choices during Q&A. Peer evaluation of presentation content and delivery (25% of grade). Success criteria: Students must demonstrate >15% variance identification between attribution models, provide ROAS calculations for all paid channels, and offer recommendations that address specific business objectives with measurable outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated channel cost data and step-by-step GA4 navigation screenshots. Offer attribution model comparison template with formula examples. Create checkpoint reviews after Steps 3 and 5. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) into their attribution analysis, analyze attribution by device/geography segments, or propose custom attribution models. Provide access to Google Analytics Intelligence API for automated insights comparison.
original_title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation: Critiquing Multi-Channel Attribution Models

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and QoS for a Fictional Company
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution for a multi-location business, implementing Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) for site connectivity and Quality of Service (QoS) policies for traffic prioritization. They will create original network documentation, security policies, and troubleshooting procedures.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable DMVPN hub-and-spoke architecture by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network topology diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco technologies through configuring OSPF routing, DMVPN Phase 3, and class-based QoS policies on physical or virtual Cisco routers
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Design Creation**
Students work individually to design a network for 'TechCorp Industries' with 1 headquarters and 4 branch offices. Provide the business requirements document specifying 200 HQ users, 50 users per branch, video conferencing needs, and VoIP requirements. Students must create: (1) Physical and logical topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, (2) Complete IP addressing scheme using VLSM with /24 networks, (3) DMVPN tunnel design with hub at HQ, (4) QoS policy document prioritizing voice > video > data traffic.

**Phase 2 (120 minutes): Implementation and Configuration**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 with actual IOS images, students build their designed network. They configure: (1) Basic router interfaces and OSPF Area 0, (2) DMVPN Phase 3 with NHRP, mGRE tunnels, and IPSec encryption, (3) QoS class-maps and policy-maps implementing LLQ for voice and CBWFQ for other traffic, (4) NAT/PAT on branch routers for internet access. Students must document all configuration commands in a structured lab report.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Students verify connectivity between all sites using ping, traceroute, and show commands. They generate traffic using Packet Tracer's simulation mode to demonstrate QoS functionality. Final deliverables include: network diagrams, complete router configurations, verification screenshots showing DMVPN neighbor relationships and QoS statistics, and a troubleshooting guide with common issues and solutions. Students present their solution in 5-minute presentations explaining design decisions and demonstrating network functionality.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.0 or higher (or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images)
TechCorp Industries business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Network diagramming software (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart)
Computers with administrative access for software installation
DMVPN configuration template and QoS command reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, documentation completeness), Technical Implementation (40 points - DMVPN functionality, QoS configuration accuracy, routing convergence), Verification and Testing (20 points - connectivity tests, traffic flow analysis, troubleshooting procedures), Professional Presentation (15 points - clear explanations, design rationale, time management). Students must achieve 80% on technical implementation and demonstrate working inter-site connectivity to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide DMVPN configuration templates with key commands highlighted, offer one-on-one troubleshooting sessions during implementation phase, and allow use of simplified 3-site topology. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack requirement, implement DMVPN Phase 2 spoke-to-spoke tunnels, integrate advanced QoS features like traffic shaping and policing, or add redundant hub routers with load balancing.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Visual Analysis and Statistical Summaries
description: Students will analyze three different datasets with varying distribution shapes (normal, skewed, bimodal) to interpret how distribution characteristics affect data interpretation and decision-making. They will explain the relationship between visual patterns and statistical measures to demonstrate understanding of data distribution concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of different distribution shapes by analyzing histograms, box plots, and statistical summaries to explain data characteristics
Students will distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate statistical measures through comparison of mean, median, and mode across different distribution types
instructions: Begin by providing students with three pre-prepared datasets: Dataset A (normally distributed customer satisfaction scores), Dataset B (right-skewed income data), and Dataset C (bimodal exam scores from two different class sections). Have students work in pairs at computers for 45 minutes. First 15 minutes: Students create histograms and box plots for each dataset using provided Python/R code templates, focusing on observing visual patterns rather than coding. Next 15 minutes: Students calculate and record mean, median, mode, standard deviation, and quartiles for each dataset using built-in statistical functions. Following 10 minutes: Pairs analyze their results by answering guided questions: 'What shape does each distribution have?', 'Which measure of central tendency best represents each dataset and why?', 'What story does each distribution tell about the underlying population?' Final 5 minutes: Each pair writes a brief interpretation paragraph for one assigned dataset, explaining what the distribution pattern reveals about the data context (customer behavior, income inequality, or class performance differences). Circulate during work time to ensure students are connecting visual patterns to numerical summaries rather than just calculating values. Conclude with 3-4 pairs sharing their interpretations, emphasizing how distribution shape influences which statistics are most meaningful and reliable for decision-making.
materials_needed: Three prepared datasets in CSV format (customer_satisfaction.csv, income_data.csv, exam_scores.csv)
Python/R environment with pandas/matplotlib or equivalent statistical packages
Guided analysis worksheet with specific questions for each dataset
Statistical summary template for recording calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of distribution shapes from visual plots, (2) Accurate explanation of why specific measures of central tendency are most appropriate for each dataset type, (3) Clear interpretation paragraph connecting statistical findings to real-world context. Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining reasoning rather than just providing correct calculations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide distribution shape reference cards with visual examples and pre-filled statistical summary tables to focus on interpretation rather than calculation. Offer sentence starters like 'This distribution shows...' and 'The best measure of center is... because...'. For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict what additional variables might create these distribution patterns, calculate confidence intervals, or identify potential outliers and their impact on statistical measures.

title: Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming with Real Constraints
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex manufacturing optimization problem involving multiple products, resource constraints, and profit maximization. They will formulate the mathematical model, graph feasible regions, and implement the simplex method to determine optimal production quantities for a fictional electronics company.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a real-world manufacturing scenario into a mathematical model with objective function and constraints
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to solve multi-variable optimization problems through systematic computational procedures
instructions: Begin by distributing the manufacturing scenario: TechCorp produces smartphones and tablets with limited assembly time (480 hours/week), testing time (240 hours/week), and materials budget ($50,000/week). Smartphones require 2 hours assembly, 1 hour testing, costs $150 in materials, and profit $200. Tablets require 3 hours assembly, 2 hours testing, cost $250 in materials, and profit $300. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to formulate the linear program: define variables (x = smartphones, y = tablets), write objective function (maximize 200x + 300y), and establish constraints (2x + 3y ≤ 480, x + 2y ≤ 240, 150x + 250y ≤ 50,000, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0). Next, spend 25 minutes having students graph the feasible region on provided coordinate paper, identifying corner points by solving systems of equations at constraint intersections. Students then apply the corner point theorem, evaluating the objective function at each vertex: (0,0), (0,160), (240,0), (120,80), and (200,40). For the final 15 minutes, students use provided simplex method templates to verify their graphical solution, setting up the initial tableau and performing pivot operations. Each pair must document their mathematical work, justify their optimal solution, and calculate maximum weekly profit. Conclude with pairs presenting their optimal production strategy and profit calculation to the class.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario handout with TechCorp problem details
Coordinate graph paper with axes scaled 0-300
Simplex method tableau templates
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Ruler and colored pencils for constraint graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correct formulation of all constraints and objective function, accurate graphical solution with properly identified corner points, correct simplex implementation, and optimal solution of 120 smartphones and 80 tablets with $48,000 profit; (3) Minor computational errors but correct methodology; (2) Correct setup but significant calculation mistakes; (1) Incomplete formulation or major conceptual errors. Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and final production recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-drawn constraint lines and focus on substitution method for finding intersections. Offer step-by-step simplex operation guides. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how profit margins or constraint changes affect the optimal solution, or add integer programming restrictions requiring whole unit production.

title: Analyzing Multi-Physics Coupling in Electromagnetic Brake Systems Through Component Breakdown
description: Students will systematically decompose the electromagnetic braking process in high-speed trains into constituent physics principles and analyze the interdependent relationships between electromagnetic induction, thermodynamics, and mechanical dynamics. They will identify critical coupling points where multiple physics domains interact and evaluate how changes in one domain cascade through the system.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the electromagnetic braking system by decomposing it into electromagnetic, thermal, and mechanical subsystems and identifying their interaction mechanisms
Students will differentiate between primary and secondary physics effects through systematic cause-and-effect mapping of the braking process timeline
instructions: Begin with 15 minutes of individual analysis where each student examines the provided electromagnetic brake schematic and real-world performance data from a high-speed train braking event. Students identify and list all observable physics phenomena in chronological order during the 0-10 second braking sequence. Next, organize students into groups of 3-4 for 25 minutes to create a multi-layer systems diagram. Layer 1 maps electromagnetic effects (eddy current formation, magnetic field changes, induced EMF). Layer 2 maps thermal effects (Joule heating, heat dissipation, thermal expansion). Layer 3 maps mechanical effects (force generation, deceleration, vibration). Groups must draw connecting arrows between layers showing cause-and-effect relationships and label each connection with the governing physics principle. During the final 20 minutes, groups present their diagrams while other groups challenge their analysis by asking 'What if' questions: 'What if ambient temperature increases by 40°C?' or 'What if the conductor material changes from aluminum to copper?' Presenting groups must trace through their diagram to predict system behavior changes. Conclude with 10 minutes where each student writes a brief analysis identifying which coupling point they consider most critical to system performance and justify their reasoning using quantitative relationships from their diagram.
materials_needed: High-resolution schematic of electromagnetic brake system with component labels
Real braking performance dataset (velocity, current, temperature vs. time) from train manufacturer
Large format paper (A2 size) for system diagrams
Colored markers or pens for different physics domains
Digital timer for time management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Completeness of physics phenomena identification (20%), (2) Accuracy of cause-and-effect relationships between domains (30%), (3) Quality of justification for critical coupling point selection (25%), and (4) Depth of response to 'What if' scenario challenges (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding of at least 8 distinct physics principles and correctly identify minimum 5 inter-domain connections to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed template with some phenomena pre-identified and guiding questions for each layer. Offer a reference sheet with relevant equations (Faraday's law, Joule heating, Newton's laws). For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by providing data from different brake designs (linear motor brakes, friction brakes) and challenge them to analyze comparative system efficiency and identify optimization opportunities through their multi-physics analysis.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug-Fixed Solutions
description: Students will critically evaluate two different solutions to a common programming bug, comparing their effectiveness, readability, and maintainability. They will then justify their choice of the superior solution using specific software quality criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two bug-fix solutions by applying code quality criteria including readability, efficiency, and maintainability
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the bug scenario handout containing a simple Python function with an off-by-one error in a list iteration, plus two different corrected versions (Solution A uses range(len(list)), Solution B uses enumerate()). Provide the evaluation checklist with 5 criteria: correctness, readability, efficiency, maintainability, and best practices.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine both solutions, testing them mentally with sample inputs to verify correctness. They complete the evaluation matrix, rating each solution (1-5 scale) on all five criteria with written justification for each rating.

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discussing any rating differences and sharing their reasoning. They must reach consensus on which solution is superior overall.

**Written Justification (15 minutes):** Each student writes a 200-word evaluation summary stating their final choice and defending it with specific evidence from the code. They must address at least three evaluation criteria and explain why their chosen solution would be better for a team development environment.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion where 3-4 students share their conclusions. Focus on the reasoning process rather than the 'correct' answer, highlighting different valid perspectives on code quality trade-offs.
materials_needed: Bug scenario handout with original buggy code
Two solution versions printed on separate sheets
Code evaluation criteria checklist
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Python interpreter access (optional for testing)
assessment_method: Evaluate students' written justifications using a 4-point rubric: (4) Uses 4+ criteria with detailed evidence and clear reasoning; (3) Uses 3 criteria with good evidence and sound reasoning; (2) Uses 2-3 criteria with some evidence but weak reasoning; (1) Uses fewer than 2 criteria or lacks supporting evidence. Students must demonstrate critical thinking beyond simple preference statements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guiding questions for each evaluation criterion (e.g., 'Which code would be easier for a new team member to understand?'). For advanced learners: Add a third solution using list comprehension and ask them to evaluate all three, or have them identify additional evaluation criteria beyond the provided checklist.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework and Methodology Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall specific elements, phases, and terminology from advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, SAFe, and Critical Chain Project Management. Through rapid-fire identification exercises, students will demonstrate mastery of complex PM methodologies and their distinguishing characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific phases, gates, and deliverables from PRINCE2, SAFe, and Critical Chain Project Management methodologies by completing timed identification exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify advanced project management terms, acronyms, and framework-specific terminology through structured memorization drills and peer testing activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the Advanced PM Framework Reference Sheet containing 150 specific terms, phases, and concepts from PRINCE2 (50 items), SAFe Scaled Agile (50 items), and Critical Chain Project Management (50 items). Allow students 20 minutes for silent study using any memorization technique. Next, organize students into groups of 4 and assign each group one methodology to focus on intensively for 10 minutes. Conduct Round 1: Flash Card Lightning Round (15 minutes) where students rotate through three stations, spending 5 minutes at each methodology station. At each station, display digital flash cards showing definitions, and students must write the corresponding term within 15 seconds per card. Move to Round 2: Peer Challenge Phase (20 minutes) where students pair up with someone from a different methodology group. Partners alternate asking each other to define terms, identify phases in correct sequence, or explain specific framework components. Award one point per correct response. Conclude with Round 3: Master Recall Assessment (10 minutes) where all students individually complete a comprehensive identification worksheet containing 30 mixed questions across all three methodologies. Questions include: 'List the seven PRINCE2 themes in order,' 'Identify the four SAFe core values,' and 'Define buffer management in Critical Chain methodology.' Students have 45 seconds maximum per question. Collect all worksheets for scoring and provide immediate verbal feedback on common missed items.
materials_needed: Advanced PM Framework Reference Sheet (150 terms across 3 methodologies)
Digital flash card presentation system or printed flash cards
Individual worksheets for final assessment
Timer/stopwatch for each station
Scoring sheets for peer challenge phase
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (27/30 correct) on the final Master Recall Assessment worksheet. Award points as follows: Framework phases in correct sequence (3 points each), accurate term definitions (2 points each), correct acronym identification (1 point each). Peer challenge scores contribute 20% to overall activity grade. Provide immediate feedback highlighting specific missed concepts requiring additional memorization.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling learners: Provide color-coded reference sheets grouping similar concepts, allow use of pneumonic devices during study time, and pair with stronger peers during challenge phase. For advanced learners: Add integration questions requiring recall of how frameworks complement each other, include less common methodology variations (PRINCE2 Agile, SAFe Portfolio level), and challenge them to create their own flash cards for additional frameworks like PMBOK Guide processes.

title: Comparative Analysis of Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership in Crisis Management
description: Students will analyze and compare two distinct leadership approaches by examining real crisis management scenarios from Fortune 500 companies. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying key behavioral patterns, decision-making frameworks, and stakeholder communication strategies that distinguish transformational from transactional leadership during organizational crises.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing documented crisis management responses from two contrasting organizational leaders
Students will explain the relationship between leadership style and crisis outcomes through structured comparative analysis using the Full Range Leadership Model framework
instructions: Begin by distributing two detailed case study packets: Johnson & Johnson's 1982 Tylenol crisis (transformational approach) and Wells Fargo's 2016 fake accounts scandal response (transactional approach). Provide students with the Full Range Leadership Model analysis framework sheet containing specific behavioral indicators for each leadership style. In pairs, students spend 25 minutes reading and annotating their assigned case study, identifying specific quotes, decisions, and actions that demonstrate either transformational behaviors (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence) or transactional behaviors (contingent reward, management by exception, laissez-faire tendencies). Next, pairs create a detailed comparison matrix on provided templates, plotting identified behaviors against the framework criteria and noting specific evidence from the cases. During the final 20 minutes, each pair presents their matrix to another pair, explaining their reasoning for categorizing specific leadership behaviors and discussing how each approach influenced stakeholder trust, employee morale, and long-term organizational reputation. Conclude with pairs submitting completed analysis matrices containing at least 8 specific behavioral examples per case study, with direct quotes and clear connections to leadership theory components.
materials_needed: Johnson & Johnson Tylenol Crisis case study packet (4-page detailed timeline with stakeholder communications)
Wells Fargo fake accounts scandal case study packet (4-page detailed timeline with leadership responses)
Full Range Leadership Model framework analysis sheet with behavioral indicator checklists
Comparison matrix template (2-column chart with theory alignment rows)
Highlighters in two different colors for annotation
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership behavior identification (8+ specific examples per case), (2) Correct application of Full Range Leadership Model categories with theoretical justification, (3) Quality of textual evidence with direct quotes supporting classifications, (4) Clear articulation of connections between leadership style and crisis outcomes. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted key passages and a partially completed matrix example. Offer a leadership behavior definition sheet with simplified language. For advanced learners, add a third case study option (Southwest Airlines post-9/11 response) and require integration of additional leadership theories such as authentic leadership or servant leadership principles. Encourage advanced students to identify hybrid approaches that blend both styles.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2 and RDS
