assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of correlation calculations, (2) Quality of causal vs. correlational reasoning with specific examples, (3) Identification of confounding variables and alternative explanations, (4) Clear communication in presentation. Students must score 3/4 on reasoning and communication sections to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This correlation might be explained by...' and 'A confounding variable could be...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to research actual studies about similar relationships or design experiments that could test causation. Offer additional complex scenarios with multiple interacting variables.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Collision Systems: Momentum and Energy Conservation Breakdown
description: Students will systematically analyze complex collision scenarios involving three or more objects by decomposing momentum and energy conservation principles. They will identify which conservation laws apply under different conditions and explain discrepancies between theoretical predictions and real-world measurements.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-body collision systems by separating momentum conservation from energy conservation and identifying when each principle applies
Students will evaluate experimental collision data through systematic comparison with theoretical predictions to identify sources of energy loss
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with three collision scenarios: (1) three steel balls on air track with known masses and initial velocities, (2) a pendulum striking two stationary balls of different materials, and (3) video analysis of car crash test involving multiple vehicles. 

Step 1 (15 min): Students calculate theoretical outcomes using conservation of momentum for each scenario, showing all vector components and assuming perfectly elastic collisions. They must create momentum diagrams before and after collision.

Step 2 (20 min): Students analyze provided experimental data or video measurements, calculating actual final velocities and directions. They plot momentum vectors graphically and calculate percentage differences from theoretical values.

Step 3 (25 min): Students systematically examine energy conservation by calculating initial kinetic energy, final kinetic energy, and energy 'lost' for each collision. They must identify specific mechanisms of energy dissipation (sound, heat, deformation) and rank scenarios by efficiency.

Step 4 (20 min): Groups create comparative analysis charts showing when momentum conservation holds versus when energy conservation breaks down. They must propose modifications to make each collision more elastic and predict quantitative improvements.

Step 5 (15 min): Each group presents one collision analysis, defending their identification of dominant energy loss mechanisms and explaining why momentum remained conserved while kinetic energy did not. Other groups challenge conclusions with evidence-based questions.
materials_needed: Three collision scenario data sets with precise measurements
Air track collision video or simulation software
Multi-vehicle crash test footage with velocity/acceleration data
Graphing calculators or computers with plotting software
Large poster paper for momentum vector diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of momentum calculations and vector analysis, (2) Identification and quantification of energy loss mechanisms, (3) Quality of comparative analysis between scenarios, (4) Logical reasoning in explaining conservation law applications. Students must achieve 3/4 in each category and demonstrate understanding through peer questioning responses.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing momentum calculation templates and suggesting they start with 2D collisions before 3D analysis. For advanced learners, introduce coefficient of restitution calculations and challenge them to predict collision outcomes for different material combinations or impact angles.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradigms Through Cross-Cultural Crisis Response Analysis
description: Students will analyze and compare how transformational, servant, and authentic leadership paradigms manifest differently across Eastern and Western cultures during organizational crises. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying core theoretical distinctions and explaining cultural adaptations of leadership frameworks through structured case analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, servant, and authentic leadership paradigms by analyzing their theoretical foundations and identifying distinguishing characteristics within crisis scenarios
Students will explain how cultural contexts influence leadership paradigm implementation through comparative analysis of Eastern and Western organizational responses
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute individual review period where students examine three provided crisis case studies: Toyota's 2010 recall crisis (Japanese context), Patagonia's supply chain ethical crisis (American context), and Tata Group's Mumbai attacks response (Indian context). Distribute the Leadership Paradigm Analysis Matrix to each student. 

Form groups of 4-5 students for 45 minutes of collaborative analysis. Each group receives one case study and must identify evidence of transformational leadership (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence), servant leadership (stewardship, empathy, healing, community building), and authentic leadership (self-awareness, transparency, ethical perspective, balanced processing) within their assigned crisis response. Groups must complete the matrix by citing specific leader behaviors, decisions, and communications that exemplify each paradigm, then analyze how cultural values (individualism vs. collectivism, power distance, uncertainty avoidance) shaped the leadership approach.

Conduct 30 minutes of structured presentations where each group presents their findings using the paradigm matrix. Other groups complete peer evaluation forms, identifying which leadership theories they observe and questioning cultural interpretations. During presentations, groups must explain why certain paradigm elements were emphasized or de-emphasized based on cultural context.

Conclude with 15 minutes of guided reflection where students individually complete synthesis worksheets comparing all three cases, identifying patterns in how different cultures prioritize leadership paradigm elements during crises, and articulating their understanding of theoretical distinctions between the three leadership approaches.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis case studies (Toyota 2010, Patagonia supply chain, Tata Mumbai attacks)
Leadership Paradigm Analysis Matrix worksheets
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Individual synthesis reflection worksheets
Flipchart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Paradigm Analysis Matrix (40 points: 10 points each for accurate identification of transformational, servant, authentic leadership elements, plus 10 points for cultural analysis). Assess presentation quality (30 points: clarity of paradigm distinctions, cultural context explanation, evidence citation). Review individual synthesis worksheets (30 points: comparative analysis accuracy, theoretical understanding demonstration, personal reflection depth). Use rubric with criteria: Exemplary (demonstrates nuanced understanding of paradigm differences), Proficient (identifies key distinctions with minor gaps), Developing (basic understanding with significant misconceptions).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide leadership paradigm definition cards with key characteristics highlighted, and offer guided questions for case analysis. Create mixed-ability groups pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners, add complexity by asking them to identify hybrid leadership approaches or propose alternative paradigms that might be more culturally appropriate. Provide additional mini-cases for extended analysis and encourage critical evaluation of Western leadership theory applicability in non-Western contexts.

title: Risk Register Interdependency Analysis for Software Development Project
description: Students will analyze a complex software development project's risk register to identify interconnected risks, categorize risk relationships, and evaluate how risk responses might create cascading effects. This activity develops critical thinking skills needed for comprehensive risk management planning.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies by mapping cause-and-effect relationships between identified project risks using dependency matrices
Students will differentiate between primary, secondary, and tertiary risk impacts through systematic categorization and impact pathway tracing
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-populated risk register containing 15 risks for a mobile app development project, including technical risks (API integration failures, security vulnerabilities), resource risks (key developer unavailability, budget overruns), and external risks (regulatory changes, vendor delays). Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to read through each risk and its initial impact assessment. Step 2 (20 minutes): In pairs, students create a risk interdependency matrix using the provided template, marking relationships as 'Causes' (C), 'Amplifies' (A), or 'Mitigates' (M) between each risk pair. Step 3 (25 minutes): Pairs analyze their completed matrix to identify risk clusters - groups of 3+ interconnected risks that could create cascading failures. They must document at least 2 risk clusters with written explanations of the failure pathways. Step 4 (15 minutes): Students examine the provided risk response strategies and identify which responses might inadvertently trigger other risks or create new dependencies. Step 5 (10 minutes): Each pair presents one risk cluster to the class, explaining the interdependency chain and recommending integrated response strategies. Instructor facilitates discussion on how traditional single-risk responses fail in complex scenarios. Conclude with reflection on how this analysis would influence their overall risk management approach and contingency planning priorities.
materials_needed: Pre-populated risk register spreadsheet for mobile app project (15 identified risks with descriptions)
Risk interdependency matrix template (15x15 grid with risk names)
Risk response strategy reference sheet
Flipchart paper and markers for cluster visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate completed interdependency matrices for accuracy of relationship identification (40 points), quality of risk cluster analysis with clear pathway explanations (35 points), and appropriateness of integrated response recommendations (25 points). Use rubric scoring: Excellent (shows complex multi-level dependencies), Proficient (identifies direct dependencies), Developing (basic connections only).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed matrix showing 3-4 example relationships and offer guiding questions like 'If this risk occurs, which other risks become more likely?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify dependency strength using probability multipliers and create risk heat maps showing cascade probability paths.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Comparative Analysis and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (Last Click, First Click, Linear, Time-Decay, and Data-Driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and defend their strategic recommendation with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across a 90-day period
Students will critique the business impact of attribution model selection through comparative analysis of channel performance metrics and ROI calculations
instructions: Begin by providing students access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account with at least 90 days of e-commerce data. Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison. Have them select all five attribution models (Last Click, First Click, Linear, Time-Decay, Data-Driven) and apply a 90-day lookback window. Students must document conversion and revenue differences for each major channel (Paid Search, Organic Search, Social Media, Email, Direct). Next, spend 30 minutes having students calculate percentage variance in attributed revenue between models for each channel, identifying which channels gain or lose credit under different models. Students then analyze the Conversion Paths report for 15 minutes to understand typical customer journey length and touchpoint frequency. For the evaluation phase (45 minutes), students must assess three scenarios: B2B software company with long sales cycles, fast-fashion retailer with impulse purchases, and subscription service with trial periods. They evaluate which attribution model best serves each business type's needs, considering customer behavior patterns, budget allocation implications, and measurement accuracy. Students conclude by preparing a 10-minute presentation defending their attribution model recommendation for one scenario, including quantitative evidence, potential limitations, and implementation considerations. Require students to address counterarguments and explain why rejected models are insufficient.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account access with e-commerce tracking enabled
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel) for calculations
Three business scenario briefing documents (B2B software, fast-fashion, subscription service)
Attribution model comparison template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation of attribution differences and variance percentages; Critical Evaluation (30 points) - depth of model comparison and identification of strengths/weaknesses; Strategic Reasoning (25 points) - logical connection between business scenarios and model selection; Evidence-Based Defense (20 points) - use of quantitative data to support recommendations and address counterarguments. Students must achieve 80+ points demonstrating advanced evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated variance examples and guided question prompts like 'How does customer journey length affect model choice?' For advanced learners, introduce custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven modeling or challenge them to evaluate attribution models' impact on marketing mix modeling and incrementality testing.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Comparative Analysis and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, comparing their impact on marketing channel performance assessment. They will then defend their recommended attribution strategy through a comprehensive business case presentation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of at least four different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by analyzing conversion path data and assessing each model's impact on channel ROI calculations
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and formulate evidence-based recommendations for optimal marketing budget allocation
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, social media, email, display, organic search). In Phase 1 (45 minutes), students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison tool and systematically document conversion values, conversion counts, and channel performance under each attribution model. They must create a comparison matrix showing percentage differences in attributed conversions per channel across models. In Phase 2 (60 minutes), teams analyze Multi-Channel Funnel reports to identify typical customer journey patterns, calculating average path length, time lag between touchpoints, and most common conversion paths. They must screenshot and annotate at least 5 representative customer journeys. Phase 3 (45 minutes) requires teams to evaluate business context by reviewing provided company scenarios (B2B software vs. fast fashion retailer vs. luxury goods), determining which attribution model best aligns with each business type's sales cycle and customer behavior. In Phase 4 (30 minutes), teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their attribution model recommendation, including: quantitative impact analysis showing budget reallocation amounts, risk assessment of switching models, implementation timeline, and expected ROI changes. Each presentation must address potential stakeholder objections and include specific GA4 configuration steps for implementing their recommended approach.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with 6+ months e-commerce data
Three distinct business scenario handouts (B2B, fast fashion, luxury goods)
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Presentation software (Google Slides/PowerPoint)
Calculator or Excel for ROI calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accuracy of data extraction and calculations (25 points), depth of attribution model analysis showing understanding of strengths/weaknesses (25 points), quality of business case logic connecting model choice to company context (25 points), presentation effectiveness including defense of recommendations and stakeholder objection handling (25 points). Success requires teams to demonstrate quantifiable differences between models, justify recommendations with specific data points, and show mastery of GA4's attribution reporting interface.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed comparison matrix template and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify data extraction accuracy. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models using GA4's data-driven attribution insights, calculate statistical significance of performance differences, or propose A/B testing frameworks for validating attribution model changes in live environments.
original_title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Comparative Analysis and Strategic Recommendation

title: Python Syntax Flashcard Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements including keywords, operators, and basic function structures through structured flashcard exercises. This activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for Python programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify 25 core Python keywords (if, else, for, while, def, class, etc.) and their spelling by completing timed flashcard rounds
Students will recall the correct syntax format for 10 basic Python structures (function definition, if statement, for loop, etc.) through written reproduction exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 35 Python syntax elements divided into three categories: keywords (15 cards), operators (10 cards), and basic structures (10 cards). Each card shows a Python element on one side and its purpose/example on the other. Start with a 5-minute individual study period where students review all cards silently. Next, conduct Round 1 (10 minutes): students work in pairs, testing each other on keyword recognition only. One student shows the definition side, partner must recall the exact keyword spelling. Switch roles every 2 minutes, tracking correct responses on provided score sheets. For Round 2 (10 minutes): focus on operators using the same partner format. Students must identify symbols (+, -, ==, !=, etc.) when given their function descriptions. Round 3 (15 minutes): tackle basic structures where students must write the correct syntax format when given a description (e.g., 'How do you define a function that takes two parameters?'). Conclude with a 10-minute individual assessment where each student completes a worksheet containing 20 random items from all three categories. Students must provide answers without referring to cards. Record individual scores and identify areas needing reinforcement for future lessons.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (35 cards per student pair)
Score tracking sheets (one per student)
Individual assessment worksheets (20 questions each)
Timer or stopwatch
Pencils or pens for writing responses
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final individual worksheet to demonstrate successful memorization. Grade based on: keyword spelling accuracy (40%), operator symbol recognition (30%), and basic syntax structure format (30%). Provide immediate feedback by reviewing answers as a class after completion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: start with smaller card sets (10-15 items) and extend practice time by 5 minutes per round. Provide visual aids showing syntax examples on the classroom board. For advanced learners: add 10 additional cards with more complex Python structures (list comprehensions, lambda functions) and challenge them to create their own flashcards for advanced topics.

title: Understanding Data Distribution Patterns Through Visual Analysis of Real Estate Datasets
description: Students will analyze and interpret different types of data distributions using a real estate pricing dataset. They will identify distribution patterns, explain their characteristics, and connect these patterns to real-world business implications through guided visual analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will identify normal, skewed, and bimodal distribution patterns by examining histograms and box plots of housing price data
Students will explain the relationship between distribution shape and central tendency measures through comparative analysis of mean, median, and mode values
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a housing dataset with 5,000 records including price, square footage, number of bedrooms, and neighborhood data (10 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and assign each pair one of four variables to analyze: house prices, square footage, bedrooms, or days on market. Students first create histograms using matplotlib with 20 bins, then generate corresponding box plots and calculate descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, standard deviation) for their assigned variable (25 minutes). Next, each pair examines their visualizations to identify the distribution shape (normal, left-skewed, right-skewed, or bimodal) and documents three specific observations about the pattern, such as presence of outliers, tail direction, or multiple peaks (15 minutes). Students then research and write a 2-paragraph explanation connecting their distribution findings to real estate market conditions, addressing questions like: Why might house prices show right skewage? What business decisions could be affected by this distribution pattern? (20 minutes). Finally, pairs present their variable analysis to another pair, explaining their distribution type, showing their visualizations, and discussing business implications while the listening pair asks clarifying questions and provides feedback using the provided peer evaluation form (15 minutes). Conclude with a whole-class discussion where each group shares one key insight about how distribution shape affects data interpretation in business contexts (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Pre-cleaned real estate dataset (CSV file with 5,000 records)
Distribution identification reference sheet with visual examples
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Computers or laptops for each student pair
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of distribution type with visual evidence (25%), (2) Accurate calculation and interpretation of descriptive statistics (25%), (3) Quality of written explanation connecting distribution patterns to business context with specific examples (30%), (4) Clear verbal presentation demonstrating understanding of concepts and ability to answer peer questions (20%). Students must score 3/4 or higher on each criterion to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a distribution identification flowchart and pre-written sentence starters for business explanations. Offer one-on-one guidance during visualization creation and encourage them to focus on obvious patterns first. For advanced learners, challenge them to perform additional analysis such as comparing distributions across different neighborhoods, conducting normality tests, or exploring transformation techniques to normalize skewed data. Provide extension questions about sampling bias and data collection methods.

title: Quantum Tunneling Analysis: Deconstructing Wave Function Behavior at Potential Barriers
description: Students will analyze quantum tunneling probability data from three different barrier configurations to identify the relationship between transmission coefficients and barrier parameters. They will deconstruct wave function components before and after barriers to explain how particle energy, barrier width, and barrier height independently influence tunneling phenomena.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze transmission coefficient data by comparing wave function amplitudes across varying barrier widths and heights to identify exponential decay relationships
Students will differentiate between classical and quantum mechanical predictions through systematic examination of particle behavior at potential energy barriers below classical thresholds
instructions: Begin by providing students with three datasets containing transmission coefficients (T) for electrons encountering rectangular potential barriers: Dataset A (varying barrier width: 0.5-5.0 nm, constant height: 2.0 eV), Dataset B (varying barrier height: 1.0-4.0 eV, constant width: 2.0 nm), and Dataset C (constant parameters with varying incident electron energy: 0.5-1.8 eV). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning each team one primary dataset and access to all three for comparison. In the first 20 minutes, teams create semi-logarithmic plots of transmission coefficient versus their assigned variable using graphing software. Next, spend 25 minutes having students calculate the slope of their ln(T) vs. parameter plots and determine the characteristic decay length or energy scale. Teams then analyze the wave function components by examining provided amplitude ratios (A_reflected/A_incident and A_transmitted/A_incident) for five specific cases from their dataset. During the following 30 minutes, students must identify which classical physics predictions fail by comparing their quantum results to classical over-the-barrier calculations, documenting specific discrepancies. In the final 25 minutes, teams prepare a comparative analysis presentation identifying how each parameter (width, height, energy) influences the exponential relationship T ∝ exp(-2κx), where κ depends on barrier properties. Teams must explicitly connect their mathematical findings to physical wave function behavior, explaining why tunneling decreases exponentially with certain parameters while showing threshold behavior with others.
materials_needed: Three pre-calculated datasets with transmission coefficients and wave function amplitudes
Graphing software (Python with matplotlib, Excel, or Origin Pro)
Scientific calculators
Large format paper for presentation preparation
Access to quantum mechanics reference materials
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of exponential relationships from graph analysis (25%), (2) Accurate calculation and interpretation of decay parameters (25%), (3) Clear differentiation between classical and quantum predictions with specific examples (25%), (4) Synthesis of findings across all three datasets to explain parameter dependencies (25%). Students must submit their graphs, calculations, and a 2-page written analysis comparing their findings across datasets.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-formatted graph templates and guiding questions for each calculation step. Offer a reference sheet with the key equations (κ = √(2m(V-E))/ℏ) and unit conversions. For advanced learners, extend the activity by having them predict tunneling behavior for asymmetric barriers or calculate resonant tunneling conditions for double-barrier systems using the same analytical approach.

title: Evaluating Code Quality: Peer Review of Basic Calculator Functions
description: Students will critically assess and compare two different implementations of basic calculator functions (add, subtract, multiply, divide) written by their peers. They will evaluate code quality using established criteria including readability, efficiency, error handling, and adherence to coding standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of peer-written calculator functions by applying a structured rubric covering readability, functionality, and best practices
Students will critique different coding approaches through systematic comparison and provide constructive feedback with specific improvement recommendations
instructions: Begin by having students work in pairs. Provide each pair with two pre-written calculator function implementations (Implementation A and Implementation B) that perform the same basic operations but use different approaches - one clean and well-structured, one with common beginner issues like poor variable names, no error handling, and inconsistent formatting. Give students the Code Quality Evaluation Checklist containing 12 specific criteria: variable naming clarity, function documentation, error handling for division by zero, code formatting consistency, appropriate data types, input validation, meaningful comments, function modularity, code efficiency, adherence to naming conventions, proper return statements, and overall readability. Students spend 15 minutes individually examining both implementations, then 20 minutes discussing their findings with their partner. They must complete the evaluation checklist for both implementations, assign scores (1-3 scale) for each criterion, and write a one-paragraph justification for which implementation is superior. Next, pairs spend 10 minutes creating a prioritized list of three specific improvements for the weaker implementation, including exact code suggestions. Finally, conduct a 15-minute class discussion where 3-4 pairs present their evaluations, focusing on criteria where implementations scored differently. Conclude by having students reflect on how this evaluation process will improve their own coding practices.
materials_needed: Two pre-written calculator function implementations (printed or digital)
Code Quality Evaluation Checklist with 12 specific criteria
Scoring sheets with 1-3 rating scale
Computers or tablets for students to reference code
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of code quality identification - correctly identifies 8+ issues from checklist, (2) Quality of comparison - provides specific evidence for scoring decisions, (3) Improvement recommendations - suggests 3 actionable, technically sound improvements, (4) Justification clarity - written paragraph demonstrates understanding of code quality principles with specific examples from the implementations
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a simple 'hello world' function first, and allow them to work in groups of 3 instead of pairs. Highlight 2-3 most obvious differences between implementations before they begin. For advanced learners, provide a third implementation with subtle issues like inefficient algorithms or security vulnerabilities, and ask them to research and propose alternative coding patterns or frameworks that could improve all implementations.

title: Design a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Marketing Strategy
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard analyzing customer purchasing patterns to develop targeted marketing recommendations. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and construct actionable business insights for an e-commerce company's quarterly marketing strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive customer segmentation analysis by integrating sales, demographic, and behavioral data using statistical clustering methods
Students will construct an interactive dashboard with data visualizations through combining descriptive statistics, trend analysis, and predictive insights to support marketing decision-making
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Data Integration and Exploration**
Provide students with three CSV datasets: customer_transactions.csv (6 months of purchase data), customer_demographics.csv (age, location, income), and website_behavior.csv (page views, session duration, bounce rates). Students work in pairs to merge datasets using customer_ID as the primary key in Excel or Tableau. They must identify and document at least 5 data quality issues (missing values, duplicates, outliers) and create a data cleaning protocol.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Segmentation Analysis Creation**
Using their cleaned dataset, students perform RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value) to identify 4-6 distinct customer segments. They calculate percentiles for each RFM component, assign scores (1-5 scale), and use pivot tables or clustering algorithms to group customers. Students must name each segment (e.g., 'High-Value Loyalists', 'At-Risk Champions') and write 2-3 sentence behavioral profiles for each group.

**Phase 3 (75 minutes): Dashboard Construction**
Students design a 4-panel interactive dashboard showing: (1) segment size and revenue contribution pie charts, (2) RFM score distributions as histograms, (3) geographic heat map of segment locations, and (4) trend lines showing segment performance over the 6-month period. Each visualization must include clear titles, axis labels, legends, and color-coding consistent across panels.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Strategic Recommendations**
Based on their analysis, students create a one-page executive summary with 3-4 specific marketing recommendations per segment, including suggested communication channels, promotional strategies, and budget allocation percentages. They must justify each recommendation with specific data points from their dashboard.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with realistic e-commerce data (customer_transactions.csv, customer_demographics.csv, website_behavior.csv)
Microsoft Excel with Data Analysis Toolpak enabled OR Tableau Public accounts
Executive summary template document
Color printer access for final dashboard prints
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data integration and cleaning accuracy (20 points), RFM segmentation methodology and mathematical correctness (25 points), dashboard design quality including visual hierarchy and interactivity (25 points), strategic recommendations specificity and data-driven justification (20 points), professional presentation and documentation clarity (10 points). Students submit their dashboard file, executive summary, and a 2-minute recorded explanation of their key findings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step RFM calculation worksheets and dashboard templates with pre-formatted layouts. Offer mini-tutorials on pivot tables and basic statistical functions. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive analytics using customer lifetime value calculations, add statistical significance testing for segment differences, or create automated dashboard refresh capabilities using API connections.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 advanced CPM terminology definitions, mathematical formulas, and calculation sequences used in complex project scheduling scenarios. This intensive recall activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of sophisticated project management concepts including float calculations, resource leveling terminology, and Monte Carlo simulation parameters.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the precise definitions of 25 advanced CPM terms including Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, Resource Leveling, and Critical Chain by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will memorize the exact mathematical formulas for Early Start, Late Start, Early Finish, Late Finish, and float calculations through structured repetition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM terminology reference sheet containing 25 advanced terms with definitions, formulas, and acronyms. Students have 15 minutes to study silently. Next, implement Phase 1: Flashcard Drilling (20 minutes). Students work in pairs using provided flashcards. Partner A reads the term/formula prompt while Partner B provides the complete definition or calculation sequence. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 2: Speed Recall Test (10 minutes). Display terms individually on screen for 15 seconds each. Students write complete definitions on answer sheets without consulting materials. Phase 3: Formula Reconstruction (15 minutes). Present scenario-based problems requiring specific formulas. Students must write out the exact formula name, mathematical expression, and variable definitions from memory. For example: 'Calculate Total Float for Activity D' requires students to recall 'Total Float = Late Start - Early Start OR Late Finish - Early Finish' plus define each variable. Phase 4: Verification Round (10 minutes). Students exchange papers and grade using the answer key. Immediate feedback is provided for incorrect responses. Students must verbally state three incorrectly answered items to their partner with correct definitions before concluding.
materials_needed: CPM terminology reference sheet with 25 advanced terms and formulas
Pre-made flashcard set (50 cards: 25 terms, 25 definitions)
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces 1-25
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor verification
Projector/screen for displaying speed recall prompts
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the speed recall test and 100% accuracy on formula reconstruction to demonstrate mastery. Grade using provided answer key. Document specific missed items for individual remediation. Success criteria: correct spelling of technical terms, complete mathematical formulas with proper notation, and accurate variable definitions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory aids (e.g., PERT = Program Evaluation Review Technique) and allow extended study time. Create visual diagrams connecting related terms. For advanced learners: add integration challenges requiring students to explain relationships between terms or apply formulas to multi-step calculations. Include bonus terminology from Agile-hybrid methodologies.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge: Technical Implementation
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 advanced CPM terminology terms, mathematical formulas, and their precise definitions through intensive flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational memory of complex project scheduling concepts essential for advanced project management practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact definitions of 25 advanced CPM terms including Early Start (ES), Late Start (LS), Early Finish (EF), Late Finish (LF), Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, and Interfering Float by completing timed memory exercises

Students will memorize and recite the four fundamental CPM calculation formulas (ES=max(EF of predecessors), EF=ES+Duration, LF=min(LS of successors), LS=LF-Duration) through repetitive drill practice
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 25 CPM terms on one side and definitions/formulas on the reverse. Students work individually for the first 15 minutes, cycling through all cards using the 'look-cover-recall-check' method: examine the term, cover the definition, attempt to recite it verbatim, then verify accuracy. After individual practice, pair students and conduct 10 minutes of partner drilling where one student shows the term while the other recites the definition, alternating roles every 2-3 minutes. Conduct the first timed recall test (5 minutes): project 25 terms randomly on screen, students write definitions on provided answer sheets. Allow 10 minutes for students to review missed items using flashcards. Repeat the timed test with the same terms in different order. For the final challenge (8 minutes), display 10 project network scenarios where students must write the correct CPM formula and identify which timing calculation applies. Conclude with immediate feedback session where instructor reads correct answers aloud and students self-score using provided answer keys. Record individual scores for each testing round to track improvement.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (25 cards per student) with CPM terminology
Answer sheets with numbered spaces 1-25 for definitions
Timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying terms and network diagrams
Answer keys for self-scoring
Score tracking sheets for each student
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final timed recall test and 70% accuracy (7/10 correct) on formula application scenarios. Assessment includes exact definition matching (partial credit not awarded), correct formula identification, and proper mathematical notation. Track improvement between first and second timed tests as secondary success indicator.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce initial flashcard set to 15 most critical terms and provide definition sentence starters or keyword hints. Allow additional 2-3 minutes on timed tests. For advanced learners, include 10 additional complex terms (Resource Leveling, Schedule Compression, Fast Tracking) and require them to create original network diagrams demonstrating each formula application.
original_title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge: Exercise 2
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 advanced Critical Path Method terms, formulas, and network diagramming symbols through structured flashcard drilling and rapid-fire recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of CPM calculations including forward pass, backward pass, and float calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the definitions of 25 advanced CPM terms (Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, Interfering Float) with 95% accuracy through timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify and recite the four core CPM calculation formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF) and three float calculation formulas through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM terminology reference sheet containing 25 terms with definitions and 7 formulas. Give students 15 minutes to study silently. Next, organize students into pairs and provide each pair with a set of 32 double-sided flashcards (25 terminology cards, 7 formula cards). Partner A holds cards showing terms/formula names while Partner B recites definitions/complete formulas from memory. Partners alternate every 5 minutes for 20 minutes total. Then conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session: display term/formula names on screen for 10 seconds each while students write complete definitions/formulas on individual response sheets. Include terms like 'Hammock Activity,' 'Resource Leveling,' 'Schedule Compression,' and 'Critical Chain Method.' For formulas, test Early Start (ES = Maximum EF of predecessors), Early Finish (EF = ES + Duration), Late Finish (LF = Minimum LS of successors), Late Start (LS = LF - Duration), Total Float (TF = LS - ES or LF - EF), Free Float (FF = Minimum ES of successors - EF), and Independent Float (IF = Minimum ES of successors - Maximum EF of predecessors - Duration). Conclude with individual silent review where students identify their three weakest recall areas and spend 10 minutes creating personal memory aids (mnemonics, diagrams, or associations) for those specific terms/formulas.
materials_needed: CPM terminology reference sheet (25 advanced terms with definitions)
Set of 32 laminated flashcards per student pair
Individual response sheets with numbered lines 1-32
Digital timer visible to all students
Projector/screen for displaying terms during rapid-fire session
assessment_method: Grade individual response sheets using binary scoring (1 point for completely correct definition/formula, 0 points for incomplete/incorrect). Success criteria: 90% accuracy (29/32 points) for advanced level. Track common errors and provide immediate feedback. Award bonus points for perfect recall of the three most complex formulas (Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronyms for formula sequences (EELS: Early Start, Early Finish, Late Finish, Late Start) and allow color-coded flashcards grouping related concepts. For advanced learners: add 10 bonus terms related to resource-constrained scheduling and PERT methodology, or challenge them to explain the logical relationships between float calculations.
original_title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge: Technical Implementation
description: Students will recall and accurately identify 40+ specific CPM terminology definitions, mathematical formulas, and calculation components through a structured memory assessment. This activity focuses on memorizing the foundational vocabulary and computational elements essential for advanced project scheduling analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will recall CPM terminology including ES, EF, LS, LF, total float, free float, critical path, and backward/forward pass definitions by completing timed recall exercises
Students will remember specific CPM calculation formulas and their variable components through systematic memorization and rapid retrieval practice
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Reference Sheet containing 42 key terms and 8 calculation formulas. Give students 15 minutes to study the sheet silently, encouraging them to use personal memorization techniques (flashcards, acronyms, repetition). After study time, collect all reference materials. Divide class into pairs for the first recall round (10 minutes): Partner A reads term numbers from the Master List while Partner B provides definitions and formulas from memory. Partners switch roles halfway through. Next, conduct individual written recall (20 minutes): Students complete the CPM Memory Assessment Form with three sections - Section A: Define 25 terminology items (1 point each), Section B: Write 8 complete formulas with variable explanations (3 points each), Section C: Identify which formula applies to 9 given scenarios (2 points each). Finally, facilitate immediate peer checking (10 minutes): redistribute reference sheets and have students grade their partner's assessment using the provided answer key. Students mark incorrect responses and calculate total scores out of 67 points. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify their three weakest recall areas and commit to specific review strategies.
materials_needed: CPM Reference Sheet with 42 terms and 8 formulas (one per student)
CPM Memory Assessment Form with three sections (one per student)
Master Term List numbered 1-42 for partner practice
Answer Key with complete definitions and formulas
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery with 80% accuracy (54/67 points) on the written recall assessment. Grade breakdown: Section A definitions (25 points) - accept paraphrased answers that capture core meaning; Section B formulas (24 points) - require exact mathematical notation and all variables identified; Section C scenario identification (18 points) - must match precise formula to situation. Document students scoring below 80% for additional memorization practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory aids (ESLF for Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish), allow color-coding during study time, and offer additional 5-minute review before assessment. For advanced learners: challenge them to create original mnemonics for complex formulas, explain terminology connections to partners, or identify real-world applications for each term during reflection period.

title: Dissecting Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Case Study Analysis
description: Students will analyze real organizational crisis scenarios to differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership approaches, identifying specific behavioral indicators and their contextual effectiveness. This expert-level activity requires deep comprehension of leadership theory nuances and their practical manifestations in high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by categorizing specific leader actions from authentic crisis scenarios into theoretical frameworks
Students will interpret the contextual effectiveness of different leadership approaches through systematic analysis of organizational outcomes and follower responses
instructions:
Begin by distributing three detailed case studies of organizational crises: Southwest Airlines' response to the 2018 engine failure incident, Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis management (1982), and Wells Fargo's account fraud scandal response (2016). Each case study should include direct quotes from leaders, specific actions taken, timeline of decisions, and measurable outcomes. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to read one assigned case study, highlighting leadership behaviors and decisions. Provide a structured analysis template with columns for 'Leader Action/Statement,' 'Transformational Indicators,' 'Transactional Indicators,' and 'Evidence/Rationale.' 

Step 2 (25 minutes): Form expert groups of 4-5 students who analyzed the same case. Groups collaborate to complete a comprehensive analysis matrix, identifying patterns and debating classifications. They must reach consensus on at least 10 specific leadership behaviors, providing textual evidence for each categorization.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Reorganize into mixed groups with one expert from each case study. Each expert presents their case analysis while others take notes on a comparison chart, identifying similarities and differences across crisis contexts.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Mixed groups synthesize findings to create a 'Leadership Approach Effectiveness Scale' ranking each case study's leadership response from most to least effective, justifying rankings with specific evidence linking leadership style to organizational outcomes.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Groups present their effectiveness rankings to the class, defending their rationale through reference to specific transformational/transactional behaviors and measurable results.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis leadership case studies with primary source quotes and outcome data
Structured analysis template worksheet with leadership behavior categorization columns
Comparison chart handout for cross-case analysis
Digital timer for activity transitions
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis matrices for accuracy of transformational/transactional categorizations (40 points), quality of textual evidence provided (30 points), and logical justification in effectiveness rankings (30 points). Award full points when students correctly identify at least 8/10 leadership behaviors, provide specific quotes or actions as evidence, and demonstrate clear understanding of contextual factors influencing leadership effectiveness.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a reference sheet with key transformational indicators (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence) and transactional indicators (contingent reward, management by exception, laissez-faire tendencies). For advanced learners, add a reflection component requiring them to predict how different leadership approaches might have altered crisis outcomes, incorporating additional leadership theories like situational or authentic leadership.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Construction Project Case Study
description: Students will analyze a construction project's risk register and evaluate the effectiveness of selected risk response strategies. They will examine the relationship between risk characteristics, response strategies, and project constraints to determine optimal risk management approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by examining their alignment with risk probability, impact, and project constraints within a construction project scenario
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of risk mitigation approaches through systematic comparison of strategy outcomes against project success criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Riverside Mall Construction Project case study packet containing: project charter, risk register with 15 identified risks, current response strategies, and project constraints. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Risk Categorization (15 minutes):** Each team categorizes the 15 risks using the provided probability/impact matrix. Students must justify placement of each risk in high, medium, or low priority categories based on quantitative data provided (cost impacts, schedule delays, quality metrics).

**Phase 2 - Strategy Analysis (25 minutes):** Teams analyze the current response strategies for the 8 highest-priority risks. Using the provided analysis template, students examine: (1) Strategy type (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept), (2) Cost-benefit ratio, (3) Feasibility given project constraints, (4) Secondary risk creation, (5) Timeline impact. Teams must identify at least 3 strategy-risk misalignments.

**Phase 3 - Alternative Strategy Development (20 minutes):** For identified misalignments, teams develop alternative response strategies. Each alternative must include: specific actions, resource requirements, timeline, success metrics, and rationale for why it better addresses the risk characteristics.

**Phase 4 - Presentation Preparation (10 minutes):** Teams prepare 3-minute presentations focusing on their most critical finding: one poorly-aligned strategy and their improved alternative.

**Phase 5 - Team Presentations (15 minutes):** Each team presents their analysis. Other teams score presentations using the provided peer evaluation rubric focusing on analytical depth and strategy justification.
materials_needed: Riverside Mall Construction Project case study packets (1 per student)
Risk probability/impact matrix templates
Risk response strategy analysis worksheets
Peer evaluation rubrics
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Students submit completed analysis worksheets showing risk categorization rationale, strategy evaluation matrices, and alternative strategy proposals. Grading rubric: Risk categorization accuracy (25%), strategy analysis depth (35%), alternative strategy quality (25%), presentation clarity (15%). Success criteria: Correctly categorize 6/8 high-priority risks, identify valid strategy misalignments with supporting evidence, propose feasible alternatives with quantified benefits.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide risk analysis decision tree flowchart, offer examples of well-analyzed vs. poorly-analyzed risks, assign stronger analytical thinkers as team leads. **Advanced extension:** Challenge advanced students to conduct Monte Carlo risk analysis using provided probability distributions, or analyze cross-risk dependencies and portfolio effects of strategy changes.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Construction Project Case Study: Exercise 1
description: Students will analyze a construction project's risk register to evaluate the appropriateness of selected risk response strategies. They will examine risk-response alignment, identify gaps in strategy selection, and recommend improvements based on PMI risk management principles.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze existing risk response strategies by evaluating their alignment with risk characteristics, project constraints, and organizational capabilities
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk response selections through systematic comparison against PMI risk management criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Downtown Office Complex construction project case study containing: project overview, 15-item risk register with probability/impact ratings, current response strategies, and budget/timeline constraints. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student reviews the risk register independently, focusing on 3-4 assigned risks. Students complete the Risk Response Analysis Worksheet, evaluating: (1) alignment between risk type and chosen strategy, (2) feasibility given project constraints, (3) cost-effectiveness of response, and (4) potential secondary risks created.

**Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (20 minutes):** Teams compile individual analyses, discussing discrepancies in evaluation. Teams identify the three most problematic risk-response pairings and prepare evidence-based justifications using PMI risk response strategy criteria (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept for threats; exploit, enhance, share, accept for opportunities).

**Phase 3 - Strategy Redesign (15 minutes):** For each problematic pairing identified, teams develop alternative response strategies, specifying: new strategy type, implementation approach, resource requirements, timeline, and success metrics. Teams must reference specific PMI knowledge area interactions (cost, schedule, quality, scope).

**Phase 4 - Peer Review (10 minutes):** Teams rotate and review another team's analysis using the provided peer evaluation checklist, focusing on logical reasoning, PMI principle application, and feasibility of recommendations.
materials_needed: Downtown Office Complex case study packet (6 pages per student)
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet template
PMI Risk Response Strategy reference sheet
Peer evaluation checklist
Flipchart paper and markers for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Analysis Worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of strategy-risk alignment analysis (25%), (2) Quality of evidence supporting problematic pairings (25%), (3) Feasibility and PMI-compliance of alternative strategies (30%), (4) Integration of cost/schedule/scope considerations (20%). Successful completion requires 3.0/4.0 average with no category below 2.0.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide PMI risk response decision tree flowchart and worked example of one risk analysis. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers during team phase. **Extension for advanced learners:** Add quantitative risk analysis component requiring Monte Carlo simulation interpretation, or include stakeholder influence matrix requiring communication strategy integration.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Construction Project Case Study

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation: Comparing Multi-Touch Attribution Models for ROI Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce Google Analytics data to determine which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value. They will assess the business impact of each model and recommend an optimal attribution strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue attribution discrepancies in Google Analytics
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer lifetime value calculations and channel performance metrics
instructions: Begin by providing students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display ads). In pairs, students first spend 15 minutes exploring the Advertising > Attribution section to familiarize themselves with available attribution models. Next, have each pair select a specific product category and spend 30 minutes extracting conversion data using each of the five attribution models, recording revenue attributed to each channel in a provided spreadsheet template. Students then calculate the percentage difference in attributed revenue between models for each channel, identifying which channels gain or lose credit under different models. During the following 25 minutes, pairs analyze the Model Comparison Tool to understand how attribution changes affect calculated ROAS for each marketing channel. Students must then spend 20 minutes researching the typical customer journey length for their chosen product category using the Path Length and Time Lag reports. In the final 30 minutes, each pair creates a presentation evaluating which attribution model most accurately reflects their product category's customer behavior, justifying their recommendation with specific data points including: average days to conversion, typical touchpoints before purchase, revenue variance between models, and impact on budget allocation decisions. Presentations should include specific scenarios where their recommended model would lead to different strategic decisions compared to default last-click attribution.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Attribution analysis spreadsheet template with pre-built formulas
Laptop/computer with internet access for each student pair
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
Customer journey research worksheet with guiding questions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Data accuracy - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences across all five models, (2) Critical analysis - identification of at least 3 specific limitations of current attribution model and 2 advantages of recommended model, (3) Business justification - clear connection between attribution choice and budget allocation decisions with quantified impact, (4) Evidence quality - use of specific GA4 reports and metrics to support recommendations with actual percentage differences and conversion data
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-selected product categories with obvious attribution patterns and guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps. Advanced learners can incorporate custom conversion events, analyze attribution for different user segments, or build custom attribution models using the Data-Driven Attribution insights. Consider pairing analytical students with those stronger in presentation skills.

title: Python Data Types Memory Card Match
description: Students will memorize and recall the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) and their corresponding example values through a structured card matching activity. This foundational exercise builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) by matching type names to their definitions
Students will recall correct syntax examples for each Python data type through repeated exposure and memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made card sets to pairs of students (5 minutes). Each set contains 12 cards: 6 data type name cards (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) and 6 example cards (42, 3.14, 'Hello', True, [1,2,3], {'key':'value'}). Have students lay all cards face-up on their desk. Instructor demonstrates the first match by pairing 'int' with '42', explaining that integers are whole numbers. Students then take turns finding matches, with their partner confirming correctness using the provided answer key (10 minutes). Once all pairs are matched, shuffle cards and repeat the process with cards face-down for memory challenge (8 minutes). Students must state the data type name and provide the definition when flipping cards ('This is int - it stores whole numbers'). Conduct a final round where students race to sort scrambled cards into correct type-example pairs within 3 minutes (5 minutes). End with individual quick-fire recall where instructor shows example values on screen and students write down the corresponding data type name (7 minutes). Collect answer sheets for assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-printed card sets (12 cards per pair of students)
Answer key sheets for student pairs
Timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for final recall activity
Individual answer sheets for assessment
assessment_method: Success measured by: (1) Correct matching during card activities (observable), (2) Accurate verbal definitions when stating matches (80% accuracy required), (3) Final written recall quiz scoring 5/6 or better on data type identification. Create simple checklist rubric: Excellent (6/6 correct), Proficient (5/6 correct), Developing (3-4/6 correct), Beginning (0-2/6 correct).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide cards with color-coding (warm colors for numbers, cool colors for text-based types) and include memory aids on cards ('int = integer = whole number'). For advanced learners: Add challenge cards with complex examples (nested lists, multiple data types) or have them create their own example cards for bonus data types like tuples or sets.

title: Multi-Variable Optimization: Designing Profitable Manufacturing Operations
description: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem involving profit maximization under resource constraints. They will implement mathematical models using both analytical and computational methods to determine optimal production levels for a multi-product factory.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methodology to solve constrained optimization problems by setting up and solving systems of nonlinear equations with three variables and two constraints
Students will implement optimization algorithms through computational tools to verify analytical solutions and analyze sensitivity to parameter changes
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario worksheet: 'Zenith Manufacturing produces smartphones (x) and tablets (y) with profit functions P(x,y) = 120x + 80y - 0.5x² - 0.3y² - 0.2xy, subject to material constraint 3x + 2y ≤ 1200 and labor constraint 2x + 4y ≤ 1600.' Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Students set up the Lagrangian L(x,y,λ₁,λ₂) and derive the system of equations by taking partial derivatives. Instructor circulates to verify correct setup before proceeding. Next 30 minutes: Students solve the 4×4 system analytically, finding critical points and testing constraint boundaries. They must show all algebraic steps on provided solution sheets. Following 25 minutes: Using Python/MATLAB, students implement the scipy.optimize.minimize function with constraints, inputting their analytical setup. They generate 3D surface plots showing the objective function and constraint boundaries. Final 15 minutes: Students compare analytical and computational results, calculate maximum profit, and determine optimal production quantities. They must document any discrepancies and explain economic interpretation of Lagrange multipliers (shadow prices). Each pair submits: handwritten analytical solution, printed code with outputs, and one-page executive summary with production recommendations.
materials_needed: Zenith Manufacturing scenario worksheets (one per pair)
Graph paper and calculators
Computers with Python/MATLAB and optimization libraries installed
Lagrange multiplier reference sheet with derivative formulas
assessment_method: Grade using 100-point rubric: Correct Lagrangian setup (20 points), accurate analytical solution with clear algebraic steps (30 points), properly implemented computational verification with correct syntax (25 points), accurate final answers within 5% tolerance (15 points), clear economic interpretation of results and shadow prices (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed Lagrangian setup and system of equations template. Offer pre-written code skeleton with comments indicating where to input their mathematical expressions. For advanced learners: Add third constraint (storage capacity) requiring 3 Lagrange multipliers, or extend to dynamic optimization over multiple time periods with inventory considerations.

title: Analyzing Energy Loss Mechanisms in Real-World Pendulum Systems
description: Students will analyze video recordings of different pendulum systems to identify, quantify, and compare multiple energy dissipation mechanisms. They will decompose complex damping behaviors into constituent components and evaluate the relative significance of each mechanism.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze real pendulum motion data by identifying and quantifying at least three distinct energy loss mechanisms (air resistance, friction, string flexibility) from amplitude decay patterns
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of different damping mechanisms through mathematical modeling and comparison of theoretical predictions with experimental observations
instructions: Begin by distributing high-speed video recordings (240 fps, 5-minute duration) of four different pendulum setups: simple pendulum in air, pendulum in viscous fluid, pendulum with flexible string, and pendulum with bearing friction. Students work in teams of 3-4. First 20 minutes: Teams use video analysis software to extract position vs. time data, creating amplitude envelope graphs for each system. Next 30 minutes: Students identify distinct mathematical patterns in amplitude decay (exponential, power law, linear) and hypothesize underlying physical mechanisms. They must justify each hypothesis with specific evidence from their data. Following 40 minutes: Teams develop mathematical models for each identified mechanism using provided differential equation templates. They fit their models to experimental data using least-squares regression, calculating R² values and residual analysis. Next 25 minutes: Students create comparative analysis charts showing the relative strength of each damping mechanism across all four systems, ranking mechanisms by energy dissipation rate. Final 25 minutes: Each team presents their analysis to another team, defending their mechanism identification and quantitative conclusions. Teams must address challenges to their interpretations and revise conclusions if warranted based on peer feedback.
materials_needed: Four high-speed video files of different pendulum systems (provided as .mp4 files)
Tracker video analysis software (free download)
Graphing calculators or laptops with Excel/Python
Differential equation reference sheet for damping mechanisms
Data analysis worksheet with guided questions
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Mechanism identification accuracy - correctly identifies 3+ physical mechanisms with proper justification (25%), (2) Mathematical modeling precision - appropriate equations with R² > 0.85 for data fits (30%), (3) Quantitative analysis depth - calculates and compares damping coefficients with correct units and uncertainty (25%), (4) Synthesis quality - ranks mechanisms by significance with supporting evidence and addresses limitations (20%)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-loaded data files and guided worksheets with partially completed calculations. Offer mechanism identification hints after 15 minutes if needed. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive damping equations from first principles, incorporate temperature effects on viscosity, or analyze coupling between multiple mechanisms simultaneously.

title: Code Review Showdown: Evaluating Bug Fixes in HTML/CSS Website Projects
description: Students will critically evaluate and rank three different bug fix solutions for common HTML/CSS website issues, then justify their choice based on code quality criteria. This activity develops critical thinking skills for assessing code effectiveness, maintainability, and best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different HTML/CSS bug fix solutions by analyzing code quality, browser compatibility, and maintainability factors
Students will critique peer solutions through structured code review techniques and defend their rankings using software development best practices
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Broken Website' starter files containing a simple 3-page portfolio site with three deliberate bugs: misaligned navigation menu, broken responsive layout on mobile, and incorrect color contrast. Provide three pre-written solution sets (Solution A, B, C) that fix these bugs using different approaches - one optimal solution, one functional but messy solution, and one over-engineered solution.

**Individual Analysis Phase (15 minutes):** Students open each solution in their code editor and browser, testing functionality across desktop and mobile views. They complete the provided evaluation matrix, scoring each solution (1-5 scale) on four criteria: code readability, browser compatibility, performance impact, and maintainability. Students must write specific evidence for each score.

**Peer Discussion Phase (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their evaluations and discuss discrepancies. Partners must reach consensus on which solution ranks highest overall and identify the top three strengths and weaknesses across all solutions.

**Justification Phase (10 minutes):** Each pair writes a 100-word recommendation memo explaining their chosen solution, addressing why it's superior to alternatives and what improvements could still be made. They must reference specific code examples and development principles.

**Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor reveals which solution was intended as 'optimal' and facilitates discussion on evaluation criteria importance, real-world code review processes, and how different project contexts might change solution rankings.
materials_needed: Broken website starter files (HTML, CSS, image assets)
Three pre-written solution sets (HTML/CSS files)
Code evaluation matrix worksheet
Code editor (VS Code, Sublime Text, or similar)
Web browser for testing
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Evaluation Matrix Completion - accurate scoring with specific evidence for each criterion, (2) Peer Consensus - demonstrates compromise and collaborative analysis, (3) Justification Quality - uses technical vocabulary and references concrete code examples, (4) Critical Thinking - identifies trade-offs between solutions and considers context factors. Full points require defending choices with development principles rather than personal preference.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a 'Code Quality Checklist' with specific items to look for (indentation consistency, semantic HTML tags, CSS organization). Pair them with stronger technical partners. **For advanced learners:** Add a fourth 'mystery solution' they must create themselves, or have them evaluate solutions for accessibility compliance using screen reader testing. Consider adding time pressure to simulate real code review deadlines.

title: Design a Personalized Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Sales Data
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using real e-commerce transaction data. They will design custom metrics, develop visualization strategies, and present actionable business recommendations based on their analytical framework.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer transaction patterns by developing a multi-dimensional segmentation model using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value)
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through combining statistical analysis, data visualization, and business intelligence tools to communicate insights effectively
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with a CSV dataset containing 6 months of e-commerce transactions (customer_id, purchase_date, order_value, product_category, quantity). Students access Tableau Public or Power BI and open a new project.

**Phase 1 - Data Exploration (20 minutes):** Students import data and create initial exploratory visualizations to identify data quality issues, outliers, and basic patterns. They document 3 key observations about customer behavior in a shared worksheet.

**Phase 2 - Segmentation Development (30 minutes):** Students calculate RFM scores for each customer: Recency (days since last purchase), Frequency (number of purchases), and Monetary value (total spent). They create quartile-based scoring (1-4 scale) for each dimension and combine scores to form customer segments (e.g., Champions: 4-4-4, At Risk: 2-2-3).

**Phase 3 - Dashboard Creation (25 minutes):** Students design a 4-panel dashboard including: (1) Customer segment distribution pie chart, (2) Average order value by segment bar chart, (3) Purchase frequency timeline, and (4) Top product categories per segment. Each visualization must include interactive filters for date range and product category.
