**Phase 4 - Business Recommendations (15 minutes):** Students create a summary card within their dashboard listing 3 specific marketing strategies for their highest-value segment and 2 retention strategies for at-risk customers, supported by their data analysis.

**Presentation (10 minutes):** Students export their dashboard as PDF and submit via learning management system with a 200-word reflection on their segmentation approach and key insights discovered.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV format with 1000+ records)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI (free versions acceptable)
Computer with internet access
Shared Google Sheet for initial observations
Dashboard submission template
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Data accuracy and RFM calculations (25 points), Dashboard design and interactivity (25 points), Visual clarity and professional appearance (20 points), Business recommendations quality and data support (20 points), Reflection depth and analytical thinking (10 points). Students must achieve 70+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide RFM calculation templates and pre-built dashboard wireframes. Offer one-on-one guidance during Phase 2. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional segmentation variables (geographic, seasonal patterns) or experiment with clustering algorithms (K-means) for comparison with RFM approach.

title: Critical Path Method Terminology and Formula Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 25 advanced CPM-specific terms, formulas, and acronyms through structured repetition and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of complex project scheduling concepts including float calculations, network analysis terminology, and critical path identification rules.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact definitions of 25 advanced CPM terms (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF, IF, critical path, near-critical path, etc.) by completing timed flashcard exercises with 95% accuracy
Students will memorize and reproduce CPM calculation formulas (Early Start, Late Finish, Total Float, Free Float) through structured practice sessions and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM terminology reference sheet containing 25 terms with definitions and 8 key formulas. Give students 15 minutes for initial review and note-taking. Next, implement a three-phase recall system: Phase 1 (10 minutes) - Students work in pairs using provided flashcards, alternating between questioner and responder, covering terms 1-12. Phase 2 (10 minutes) - Switch pairs and cover terms 13-25 plus formulas, with partners checking accuracy against answer key. Phase 3 (15 minutes) - Individual timed recall test where students write definitions for randomly selected 15 terms and reproduce 5 formulas from memory within time limit. During each phase, circulate to monitor pronunciation of acronyms (ES = Early Start, not 'es') and verify students are using exact wording from definitions, not paraphrasing. For formula practice, require students to write out variable meanings (ES = Early Start time) alongside mathematical expressions. Conclude with immediate feedback session where correct answers are displayed, and students self-score their recall accuracy. Record individual scores for tracking memorization progress across multiple sessions.
materials_needed: CPM terminology reference sheet with 25 advanced terms and definitions
Set of 33 double-sided flashcards per pair (terms + formulas)
Answer key sheets for peer checking
Individual recall test sheets with blank spaces for 15 terms + 5 formulas
Stopwatch or timer for each phase
Scoring rubric with point allocations
assessment_method: Students must achieve 95% accuracy (24/25 terms correct, exact wording required) on final individual recall test. Formula reproduction must include correct mathematical notation and variable definitions. Partial credit: 0.5 points for definitions with minor word variations but correct core meaning. Track progress using individual score sheets across multiple sessions until mastery threshold reached.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic device examples (ES comes before EF chronologically) and reduce initial term count to 15. Create color-coded flashcards grouping related concepts. For advanced learners: Add 10 supplementary terms from PMBOK Guide Chapter 6, include exception cases for formula applications, and require explanation of when each formula type is most applicable in real project scenarios.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing the Tylenol Murders Response Framework
description: Students will analyze Johnson & Johnson's crisis leadership response during the 1982 Tylenol murders case to understand how effective crisis leadership principles manifest in real-world scenarios. They will systematically examine leadership decisions, communication strategies, and stakeholder management approaches to identify transferable crisis leadership frameworks.
estimated_duration: 220 minutes (3 hours 40 minutes) over two class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will categorize specific crisis leadership behaviors demonstrated by J&J executives by mapping actions to established crisis management theories (Coombs' SCCT, Bennis' Leadership Competencies)

Students will interpret the relationship between transparent communication strategies and stakeholder trust maintenance through detailed analysis of press releases, internal memos, and public statements from the Tylenol crisis
instructions: Begin by distributing the Tylenol Crisis Leadership Analysis Packet containing chronological timeline, key decision points, stakeholder map, and primary source documents (45 minutes total prep). Divide students into teams of 4-5, assigning each team a specific stakeholder perspective: consumers, employees, shareholders, regulatory bodies, or media. Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams examine provided materials using the Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet, identifying 8-10 specific leadership decisions made by CEO James Burke and his team. Students must categorize each decision using the provided theoretical frameworks and rate effectiveness on a 1-5 scale with written justification. Phase 2 (45 minutes): Teams create a visual stakeholder impact map showing how each leadership decision affected their assigned stakeholder group, using color-coding for positive/negative/neutral impacts and including direct quotes from source materials as evidence. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Conduct structured gallery walk where teams rotate through other groups' stakeholder maps, adding sticky note observations about leadership pattern consistencies across stakeholder groups. Phase 4 (40 minutes): Facilitate whole-group synthesis discussion using prepared discussion prompts: 'What leadership behaviors appeared across all stakeholder interactions?' and 'Which theoretical frameworks best explain Burke's decision-making pattern?' Students must reference specific evidence from their analysis. Conclude with individual reflection where each student writes a 200-word summary identifying three transferable crisis leadership principles and explaining how they would apply one principle to their current/future leadership context.
materials_needed: Tylenol Crisis Leadership Analysis Packet (timeline, decision matrix, primary source documents)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet with theoretical frameworks
Stakeholder impact map templates (large format paper)
Colored markers/pens for visual mapping
Sticky notes for gallery walk feedback
Discussion prompt cards for facilitation
assessment_method: Evaluate using three-part rubric: (1) Analysis accuracy - teams correctly identify and categorize 6+ leadership decisions with appropriate theoretical frameworks (40 points); (2) Evidence integration - stakeholder maps include minimum 8 direct quotes/specific examples with clear impact explanations (35 points); (3) Synthesis demonstration - individual reflections show understanding of transferable principles with specific, realistic application examples (25 points). Total: 100 points. Observe group discussions for understanding depth through student use of leadership vocabulary and cross-references to case evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key decisions in source materials and sentence starters for theoretical framework categorization ('This decision demonstrates [theory] because...'). For advanced learners: Add comparative element by providing brief overview of other crisis cases (Exxon Valdez, Wells Fargo) and challenge them to identify what made J&J's approach uniquely effective. Consider providing additional theoretical frameworks (Transformational Leadership, Authentic Leadership) for deeper analysis layers.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for Construction Project Scenarios
description: Students will examine three construction project risk scenarios and analyze the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will break down each scenario to identify risk triggers, evaluate response options, and determine optimal mitigation approaches based on project constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk scenarios by deconstructing risk events, probability factors, and potential impacts within construction project contexts
Students will evaluate risk response strategies through systematic comparison of avoid, mitigate, transfer, and accept approaches for given scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the three construction project scenarios: Scenario A (Weather delays affecting foundation work), Scenario B (Key subcontractor bankruptcy during framing phase), and Scenario C (Material cost escalation for steel components). Each team receives all scenarios plus the Risk Analysis Worksheet. For the first 20 minutes, teams work individually on Scenario A, using the worksheet to: 1) Identify primary and secondary risks, 2) Assess probability (1-5 scale) and impact (1-5 scale), 3) Calculate risk scores, 4) List all possible response strategies for each risk. During minutes 21-40, teams analyze response strategies by mapping each against project constraints (budget, schedule, quality, scope) and ranking effectiveness. In minutes 41-50, teams select their recommended response strategy and document justification including cost-benefit analysis. Repeat this process for Scenarios B and C (50 minutes total). In the final 20 minutes, conduct gallery walk presentations where each team posts their analysis sheets and explains their reasoning for one scenario to the class. Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing different teams' approaches and highlighting analysis patterns.
materials_needed: Three detailed construction project risk scenarios (printed handouts)
Risk Analysis Worksheet template with probability/impact matrix
Flipchart paper for presentations
Colored markers for analysis mapping
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: 1) Risk identification completeness (identifies 4+ risks per scenario), 2) Analysis depth (provides quantitative probability/impact scores with justification), 3) Strategy evaluation quality (compares 3+ response options with clear criteria), 4) Recommendation rationale (links strategy choice to specific project constraints and provides cost-benefit reasoning). Teams must demonstrate analysis rather than simply listing options.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide risk identification prompts and sample probability/impact calculations from similar scenarios. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add secondary risk analysis (risks created by response strategies) and require integration of multiple response strategies into comprehensive risk management plans. Challenge them to consider stakeholder impact variations.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for Construction Project Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze pre-defined construction project scenarios to identify risk categories and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will then compare their analysis with actual project outcomes to assess decision-making quality.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze given project risk scenarios by categorizing risks using the PMBOK risk breakdown structure and determining appropriate response strategies
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of risk response strategies through comparative analysis of predicted outcomes versus actual project results
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the Construction Project Risk Analysis packet containing three real-world scenarios: Airport Terminal Expansion, Highway Bridge Construction, and Commercial Building Project. Each scenario includes initial risk assessments, chosen response strategies, and actual outcomes with budget/schedule impacts. Teams spend 20 minutes on Phase 1: Risk Categorization - classify each identified risk using PMBOK's technical, external, organizational, and project management categories, then plot risks on probability/impact matrices. In Phase 2 (25 minutes): Strategy Evaluation - teams analyze whether the chosen risk response (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) was optimal for each risk's category and severity level. They must justify alternative strategies using PMI principles. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Outcome Analysis - compare actual project results with predicted outcomes, identifying where risk responses succeeded or failed and calculating cost/schedule variance attributed to risk management decisions. Teams create a summary chart showing risk category, original strategy, recommended strategy, and variance impact. Final 15 minutes: each team presents their analysis of one scenario, highlighting the most critical insight about risk response effectiveness. Instructor facilitates discussion on patterns across scenarios and alignment with PMI risk management framework.
materials_needed: Construction Project Risk Analysis packet (3 scenarios with data sheets)
PMBOK Risk Breakdown Structure reference chart
Probability/Impact matrix templates
Risk Response Strategy comparison worksheet
Calculators for variance analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 20-point rubric: Risk categorization accuracy (5 points), strategy evaluation depth and PMI alignment (7 points), variance analysis calculations (4 points), and quality of recommendations with justification (4 points). Observe team discussions for understanding of risk interdependencies and strategic thinking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed examples of risk categorization for the first 2-3 risks in each scenario. Offer a decision tree template for strategy selection. For advanced learners, add secondary risk analysis requirements and ask them to propose hybrid response strategies combining multiple approaches.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for Construction Project Scenarios

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Optimization Audit
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data scenarios. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model limitations, and provide strategic recommendations for attribution model selection based on business objectives and customer journey complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business relevance of Last Click, First Click, Linear, and Data-Driven attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue attribution discrepancies

Students will critique current attribution model configurations through comparative analysis of multi-channel funnel data and recommend optimized attribution strategies for specific business scenarios
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Analysis Setup (15 minutes)**

Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic sources. Students work in pairs to navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison. Have them select a date range of the last 90 days and ensure all available channels are included (Organic Search, Paid Search, Social, Email, Direct, Display).

**Phase 2: Attribution Model Comparison (25 minutes)**

Students systematically document conversion and revenue data for each attribution model: Last Click, First Click, Linear, Time Decay, Position-Based, and Data-Driven. They create a comparison matrix showing how each model attributes the same conversions differently. Require students to identify the three largest discrepancies between models and calculate percentage differences in attribution.

**Phase 3: Conversion Path Analysis (20 minutes)**

Using the Path Analysis report, students examine actual customer journeys for high-value conversions (>$500). They analyze path length, touchpoint sequences, and time between interactions. Students must identify patterns where different attribution models would dramatically impact channel performance evaluation.

**Phase 4: Critical Evaluation and Recommendation (25 minutes)**

Students prepare a written evaluation addressing: (1) Which attribution model most accurately reflects the customer journey based on path analysis evidence, (2) Specific limitations of each model for this business type, (3) How model choice would impact budget allocation decisions, and (4) Recommended attribution strategy with justification. Each pair presents their findings in a 3-minute summary to the class.
materials_needed: GA4 demo account with multi-channel e-commerce data (Google Merchandise Store or similar)
Attribution Model Comparison worksheet template
Access to Google Analytics 4 interface
Spreadsheet software for calculations
Timer for presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and calculations (25%), (2) Depth of attribution model analysis and identification of limitations (30%), (3) Quality of evidence-based recommendations with clear business rationale (30%), (4) Clear articulation of evaluation criteria and logical reasoning (15%). Students must demonstrate understanding of when each model is most/least appropriate and provide specific examples from the data.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps and pre-filled example calculations. Offer additional support in interpreting conversion path visualizations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate seasonality factors, create custom attribution models using GA4's rule-based attribution, or analyze the statistical significance of attribution differences using confidence intervals.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Campus Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise campus network from scratch, incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, HSRP redundancy, port security, and network access control. This capstone activity synthesizes advanced switching, routing, and security concepts into a real-world network deployment scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced switching configurations through hands-on configuration of VLANs, STP optimization, port security, and 802.1X authentication
Students will construct redundant routing solutions by configuring HSRP, load balancing, and failover mechanisms across multiple distribution layer switches
instructions: Begin by distributing the fictional company scenario (TechCorp with 200 employees across 4 departments requiring network segmentation). Students work in teams of 2-3 to first spend 45 minutes designing their network topology on paper, including VLAN assignments, IP subnetting (/24 networks from 192.168.0.0/16), and equipment placement. Each team receives access to a lab pod with 4 Cisco 2960 switches, 2 Cisco 3560 distribution switches, and 1 Cisco 4331 router. In the next 2 hours, teams configure their access layer switches with appropriate VLANs (Sales-VLAN 10, Engineering-VLAN 20, HR-VLAN 30, Guest-VLAN 40), implement spanning tree portfast and BPDU guard on access ports, and configure port security with maximum 2 MAC addresses per port. Following this, teams spend 90 minutes configuring trunking between switches using 802.1Q, setting up VLAN interfaces on distribution switches for inter-VLAN routing, and implementing HSRP for gateway redundancy with preemption enabled. The final 90 minutes involves configuring 802.1X authentication using a RADIUS server simulation, implementing access control lists to restrict inter-VLAN communication based on business rules, and testing all connectivity scenarios. Teams document their configurations using 'show run' outputs and create a network verification checklist. Conclude with 30-minute team presentations where each group demonstrates their working network, explains design decisions, and performs live troubleshooting of an instructor-introduced failure scenario.
materials_needed: Cisco 2960 switches (4 per team)
Cisco 3560 distribution switches (2 per team)
Cisco 4331 router (1 per team)
Ethernet cables (CAT6, various lengths)
Laptop/PC with terminal emulation software (PuTTY or SecureCRT)
TechCorp business requirements document
Network documentation templates
RADIUS server simulator software
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network design documentation (25 points - topology accuracy, IP addressing scheme, VLAN planning), Technical implementation (50 points - working VLANs, successful inter-VLAN routing, HSRP functionality, port security active, 802.1X authentication operational), Problem-solving demonstration (15 points - successful resolution of instructor-introduced network failure), Professional presentation (10 points - clear explanation of design rationale and configuration choices). Teams must demonstrate full connectivity between all VLANs through the designated gateway, show active HSRP status, and prove port security is blocking unauthorized devices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured baseline templates with basic VLAN structure, offer guided worksheets for IP subnetting calculations, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create checkpoint milestones every 45 minutes with instructor verification before proceeding. For advanced learners: Add complexity with QoS configuration for voice VLANs, implement EtherChannel link aggregation between distribution switches, configure SNMP monitoring, or add IPv6 dual-stack implementation. Encourage advanced teams to implement network automation using Python scripts for configuration deployment.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Drill: Variables and Data Types
description: Students will memorize and recall the correct syntax for declaring variables and identifying data types in Python through structured flashcard practice. This foundational activity builds essential recall skills for basic programming constructs that students must know automatically before applying them in coding tasks.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the correct syntax for declaring integer, string, float, and boolean variables in Python by completing flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the appropriate data type for given values through visual recognition drills and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to pairs of students (15 minutes setup). Each set contains 20 cards with Python variable declarations on one side and explanations on the reverse. Pair students and assign roles: 'Questioner' and 'Responder.' The Questioner shows cards displaying values like '42', 'Hello World', '3.14', 'True' and asks 'What data type?' and 'How do you declare a variable with this value?' The Responder must state the data type (integer, string, float, boolean) and provide correct syntax (e.g., 'age = 42'). After 10 minutes, students switch roles. In the final 15 minutes, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire round where you display values on the projector and students write answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously. Record correct responses for each student. Students must achieve 18/20 correct responses to demonstrate mastery. Provide immediate correction for wrong answers, having the class repeat the correct syntax three times aloud. End with students reciting the four data types and their declaration patterns in unison.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (20 cards each, 1 set per pair)
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers (1 per student)
Projector/screen for whole-class activity
Student tracking sheet for recording scores
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify data types and write proper variable declaration syntax for 18 out of 20 examples during the final rapid-fire assessment. Track individual responses using the scoring sheet. Award full points for exact syntax matches (including proper use of quotes, assignment operators, and variable naming conventions).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference card with the four data types and example syntax visible throughout the activity. Pair them with stronger partners initially. For advanced learners, include additional cards with complex data types (lists, dictionaries) or require them to explain why certain variable names are invalid according to Python naming conventions.

title: Analyzing Multi-Path Interference Patterns in Double-Slit Experiments with Variable Parameters
description: Students will systematically analyze how wavelength, slit separation, and screen distance affect interference patterns in Young's double-slit experiment. They will decompose experimental data to identify individual contributions of each parameter and synthesize findings to predict optimal conditions for specific fringe visibility requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between experimental parameters (wavelength, slit separation, screen distance) and resulting interference patterns by systematically varying one parameter while controlling others
Students will differentiate between the effects of coherence length and geometric factors on fringe visibility through quantitative comparison of multiple data sets
instructions: Begin with 15 minutes of data collection setup. Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: data collector, parameter controller, pattern analyzer, and calculations specialist. Provide each team with pre-collected interference pattern images from 12 different experimental configurations (3 wavelengths: 450nm, 550nm, 650nm; 2 slit separations: 0.1mm, 0.3mm; 2 screen distances: 1m, 2m). Students spend 30 minutes measuring fringe spacing using ImageJ software, recording at least 10 measurements per pattern and calculating standard deviations. Next, dedicate 25 minutes to systematic parameter analysis: teams create three separate graphs plotting fringe spacing vs. each parameter while holding others constant. They must identify linear relationships and calculate slopes with uncertainties. Following this, allocate 20 minutes for visibility analysis: students calculate fringe visibility (Vmax-Vmin)/(Vmax+Vmin) for each pattern and correlate with coherence parameters. In the final 30 minutes, teams analyze discrepancies between theoretical predictions (λD/d formula) and experimental results, identifying systematic errors and their sources. Each team creates a comprehensive analysis report including error propagation calculations, parameter sensitivity analysis, and recommendations for optimizing experimental conditions for maximum fringe visibility. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations of their most significant finding regarding parameter interdependence.
materials_needed: 12 high-resolution digital images of double-slit interference patterns with known parameters
ImageJ software installed on computers (one per team)
Millimeter rulers and digital calipers for screen measurements
Scientific calculators or laptops with Excel/Python for error analysis
Pre-formatted data collection sheets with parameter tables
Graph paper and colored pencils for manual plotting backup
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of fringe spacing measurements with proper error analysis (25%), (2) Quality of parameter relationship identification and graphical analysis with trend lines and R-squared values (30%), (3) Depth of systematic error analysis and theoretical comparison including percent discrepancies (25%), (4) Synthesis of findings into coherent optimization recommendations with quantitative justification (20%). Successful completion requires R-squared values >0.95 for parameter relationships, error bars on all measurements, and identification of at least 3 sources of systematic error with quantitative impact assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step ImageJ tutorials, pre-made Excel templates with error propagation formulas, and guiding questions for each analysis section. Offer checkpoint conferences after each major section. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like finite slit width effects, analyze non-uniform illumination impacts, or design experiments to test coherence length limitations. Provide access to more complex interference patterns with multiple wavelengths or partially coherent sources.

title: Bug Report Quality Assessment and Ranking Activity
description: Students will evaluate and rank a collection of real bug reports from different quality levels, defending their rankings based on established criteria. This activity develops critical evaluation skills for assessing software documentation quality and communication effectiveness in development workflows.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate bug report quality by applying industry-standard criteria including reproducibility, clarity, and completeness
Students will critique and rank multiple bug reports through systematic comparison and evidence-based justification
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet containing 6 anonymized bug reports of varying quality levels (2 excellent, 2 poor, 2 average) from real GitHub issues or bug tracking systems. Provide the Bug Report Quality Rubric with 5 criteria: Problem Description Clarity, Steps to Reproduce, Expected vs Actual Results, Environment Details, and Overall Usefulness. **Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students read each bug report and score it using the rubric (1-4 scale per criterion). They calculate total scores and write brief justification notes for each report, identifying specific strengths and weaknesses. **Ranking Phase (10 minutes):** Students rank all 6 reports from best (#1) to worst (#6) based on their evaluation scores, then select their top choice and bottom choice for detailed analysis. **Pair Discussion (15 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their rankings, discussing disagreements and defending their choices using specific examples from the reports. They must reach consensus on the best and worst reports. **Presentation (15 minutes):** Each pair presents their consensus choices to the class, explaining why their selected 'best' report exemplifies quality bug reporting and why their 'worst' report fails to meet professional standards. **Reflection (10 minutes):** Students individually write a summary of lessons learned about what makes bug reports effective or ineffective for developers.
materials_needed: Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet with 6 real anonymized bug reports
Bug Report Quality Rubric handout with 5 evaluation criteria
Individual scoring sheets for students
Projector/screen for pair presentations
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Completed rubric scoring for all 6 reports with written justifications (40 points), (2) Quality of evidence-based arguments during pair discussions - observed participation (20 points), (3) Clarity and reasoning in pair presentation defending best/worst choices (25 points), (4) Individual reflection summary demonstrating understanding of effective bug reporting principles (15 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of one additional bug report to model the process. Offer sentence starters for justifications like 'This report is effective because...' or 'The main weakness is...'. For advanced learners: Challenge them to rewrite the worst-ranked bug report to meet professional standards, or research the actual resolution of one report to evaluate if the original report provided sufficient information for debugging.

title: Bug Report Quality Assessment and Ranking Activity: Written Report
description: Students will evaluate and rank five real bug reports from different quality levels, justify their rankings based on established criteria, and propose improvements. This activity develops critical evaluation skills for identifying what makes effective bug documentation in software development.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate bug report quality by analyzing completeness, clarity, and reproducibility using industry-standard criteria
Students will justify their quality rankings through written explanations that demonstrate understanding of effective bug reporting practices
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet containing five anonymized bug reports labeled A-E, ranging from excellent to poor quality. Each report should be 1-2 paragraphs describing different software issues (e.g., login failure, UI display problem, crash on mobile app, search function error, payment processing bug). Provide the evaluation criteria checklist covering: problem description clarity, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual behavior, environment details, and severity assessment.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students read each bug report and score them using the provided 1-5 scale checklist. They must identify specific strengths and weaknesses for each report, noting missing information, unclear descriptions, or exemplary details.

**Ranking Phase (10 minutes):** Students rank the five reports from best (1) to worst (5) and write a 2-3 sentence justification for their top and bottom choices, citing specific examples from the reports.

**Small Group Discussion (15 minutes):** Form groups of 3-4 students to compare rankings and justifications. Groups must reach consensus on the top 2 and bottom 2 reports, preparing to share their reasoning with the class.

**Improvement Task (15 minutes):** Each group selects the worst-ranked bug report and rewrites it to meet professional standards, adding missing information and improving clarity.

**Class Sharing (10 minutes):** Groups present their consensus rankings and share their improved bug report, explaining what changes they made and why these improvements matter for development teams.
materials_needed: Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet with 5 sample reports (A-E)
Evaluation Criteria Checklist (laminated reference cards)
Blank paper for rewriting bug reports
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade using a 20-point rubric: Individual ranking accuracy (5 points - comparing to expert rankings), written justifications showing criteria application (8 points), group collaboration and consensus building (3 points), and quality of bug report improvement (4 points). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying at least 3 specific strengths/weaknesses across all reports.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by highlighting one clear example of good vs poor bug reporting before the activity begins. Provide sentence starters for justifications: 'This report is effective because...' or 'This report lacks...' For advanced learners, add a bonus task to create evaluation criteria for a specialized domain (mobile apps, web accessibility, or API testing) and re-evaluate one report using their custom criteria.
original_title: Bug Report Quality Assessment and Ranking Activity

title: Design a Customer Retention Dashboard for E-commerce Analytics
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that analyzes customer behavior patterns and designs actionable retention strategies for an e-commerce business. They will synthesize multiple data sources to build comprehensive visualizations and develop data-driven recommendations for improving customer lifetime value.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer transaction data, demographic information, and behavioral metrics by creating an integrated analytical framework that identifies retention opportunities
Students will design interactive visualizations and actionable business recommendations through dashboard creation and strategic presentation of key performance indicators
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each team of 3-4 students with the sample e-commerce dataset containing 12 months of customer transactions, demographics, and website interaction data. Students access Tableau Public or Power BI and create new project workspace.

**Phase 1 - Data Exploration & Integration (40 minutes):** Students import all three data files and perform initial data quality assessment. They identify missing values, outliers, and data inconsistencies. Teams create calculated fields for: customer lifetime value (CLV), recency-frequency-monetary (RFM) scores, churn probability indicators, and seasonal purchase patterns. Students document data cleaning decisions and create data dictionary.

**Phase 2 - Dashboard Design (60 minutes):** Teams design 4-panel dashboard layout: (1) Customer segmentation visualization using RFM analysis with interactive filters, (2) Churn risk heatmap showing at-risk customer segments, (3) Revenue trend analysis with seasonal decomposition, (4) Customer journey funnel with drop-off points identified. Students implement interactive elements including date range selectors, customer segment filters, and drill-down capabilities for detailed customer profiles.

**Phase 3 - Strategy Development (30 minutes):** Based on dashboard insights, teams formulate three specific retention strategies with projected ROI calculations. Students create executive summary slide identifying top 3 actionable recommendations with supporting data evidence, target customer segments, and implementation timeline.

**Presentation & Peer Review (20 minutes):** Each team presents 5-minute dashboard walkthrough and retention strategy recommendations. Audience completes peer evaluation rubric focusing on data visualization clarity, analytical depth, and business recommendation feasibility.
materials_needed: Sample e-commerce dataset (transactions.csv, customers.csv, web_analytics.csv)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI access
Laptop/computer with internet connection
Peer evaluation rubric handouts
Dashboard design template guide
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Data integration completeness and accuracy of calculated metrics (25%), (2) Dashboard design effectiveness including visual hierarchy and interactivity (25%), (3) Analytical insight quality demonstrating pattern recognition and statistical understanding (20%), (4) Business recommendation feasibility with supporting quantitative evidence (20%), (5) Presentation clarity and professional communication (10%). Students submit dashboard file, data dictionary, and executive summary document.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM score formulas and dashboard wireframe templates. Offer guided worksheet for identifying key metrics. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate predictive modeling elements, create customer segmentation using clustering algorithms, or design A/B testing framework for retention strategies. Provide additional datasets for cross-industry comparison analysis.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Memory Matrix Challenge
description: Students memorize and accurately recall complex project management frameworks, methodologies, and their specific components through systematic retrieval practice. This activity tests retention of advanced PM concepts including PRINCE2 processes, Agile ceremonies, risk response strategies, and stakeholder analysis matrices.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the seven PRINCE2 processes and their 26 sub-processes by completing timed memory retrieval exercises

Students will identify and recite specific components of advanced PM frameworks including Scrum events, risk response types, and stakeholder power-interest grid classifications through structured recall activities
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute individual study period where students review provided reference cards containing: PRINCE2's 7 processes with sub-processes, Scrum's 5 events with timeboxes, 4 risk response strategies with examples, and stakeholder analysis grid with 9 classifications. Remove all materials after study time. Distribute blank framework templates and set a 15-minute timer for Phase 1: students complete PRINCE2 process hierarchy from memory, filling in main processes and their sub-processes. Collect papers and redistribute fresh templates for Phase 2: 10-minute Scrum ceremony recall, where students list each ceremony, its participants, duration, and primary purpose. Phase 3 involves 8 minutes to complete risk response matrix, matching strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) with appropriate scenario examples. Final phase requires 7 minutes to recreate stakeholder power-interest grid with all 9 quadrant labels and recommended management strategies. After completion, students pair up for 10-minute peer verification using answer keys. Partners check accuracy and calculate scores using provided rubric. Conclude with 5-minute class discussion identifying most commonly forgotten elements and memory techniques that worked best.
materials_needed: PRINCE2 reference cards with 7 processes and 26 sub-processes
Scrum ceremony reference sheets with timeboxes and participants
Risk response strategy cards with scenario examples
Stakeholder analysis grid templates (blank and answer key versions)
Digital timers or stopwatch applications
Scoring rubric sheets for peer assessment
assessment_method: Peer-assessed scoring using 4-point rubric: PRINCE2 section (40 points - 2 points per main process, 1 point per sub-process), Scrum ceremonies (20 points - 4 points per complete ceremony entry), Risk responses (20 points - 5 points per strategy with example), Stakeholder grid (20 points - 2 points per quadrant plus management strategy). Minimum 70% (70/100 points) indicates successful recall mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory aids (e.g., 'Directed Planning Controls Managing Product Boundaries Close' for PRINCE2) and allow color-coded reference cards during study phase. Advanced learners can add integration points between frameworks or create their own memory palace explanations. Consider allowing struggling students extra 2-3 minutes per phase or providing partially completed templates as starting scaffolds.

title: Deconstructing Adaptive Leadership Through Crisis Decision Analysis
description: Students will analyze real-world organizational crisis scenarios to understand how adaptive leadership principles differ from technical leadership approaches. They will examine leader behaviors, decision-making processes, and stakeholder responses to distinguish between adaptive challenges requiring new learning versus technical problems with known solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between adaptive and technical leadership challenges by analyzing three documented organizational crisis cases and categorizing leader responses
Students will interpret the relationship between adaptive leadership behaviors and organizational outcomes through systematic comparison of leadership communication patterns and stakeholder reactions
instructions: Begin by distributing three detailed crisis case studies (15 minutes): Netflix's shift from DVD to streaming (2007-2012), Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis response (1982), and Kodak's digital transformation failure (1990s-2010s). Each case study should be 2-3 pages with leader quotes, timeline of decisions, and stakeholder responses documented. Divide students into groups of 4-5, assigning each group one primary case to analyze deeply (5 minutes). Provide each group with the Adaptive Leadership Analysis Framework handout containing Heifetz and Linsky's key principles: identifying adaptive vs. technical challenges, getting on the balcony, regulating distress, maintaining disciplined attention, giving work back to people, and protecting voices of leadership. Groups spend 45 minutes completing their analysis worksheet, which requires them to: (1) categorize each major decision as adaptive or technical with justification, (2) identify specific leader behaviors that demonstrate 'getting on the balcony' perspective, (3) analyze how leaders regulated organizational distress during uncertainty, and (4) evaluate stakeholder response patterns. After analysis, groups rotate through 15-minute stations where they present findings to peers from other case studies (45 minutes total). Each presenting group explains their case's adaptive challenges, highlights 2-3 critical leadership moments, and facilitates discussion about why certain approaches succeeded or failed. Conclude with 20-minute whole-class synthesis where students identify common patterns across all three cases, discussing how adaptive leadership principles manifested differently based on organizational culture, industry context, and crisis severity.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (Netflix, Johnson & Johnson, Kodak) with leader quotes and timelines
Adaptive Leadership Analysis Framework handout based on Heifetz and Linsky's model
Analysis worksheet with structured comparison tables
Flip chart paper and markers for station presentations
Timer for rotation management
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy in distinguishing adaptive vs. technical challenges with specific evidence (25%), (2) Depth of analysis connecting leader behaviors to theoretical frameworks (25%), (3) Quality of cross-case pattern recognition during synthesis discussion (25%), (4) Effectiveness of peer teaching during station presentations including clear explanations and facilitated discussion (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by providing at least two specific examples from their case study for each adaptive leadership principle discussed.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a pre-filled example analysis of one leadership decision to model the thinking process. Offer guiding questions like 'What new learning was required here?' and 'How did uncertainty affect stakeholder behavior?' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify additional leadership frameworks (transformational, servant, authentic) present in their cases and explain how these interact with adaptive leadership principles. Provide supplementary readings on complexity theory and organizational change for deeper analysis.

title: Risk Impact Matrix Analysis for Multi-Project Portfolio Scenario
description: Students will analyze a complex multi-project scenario containing 15 identified risks across three interconnected projects. They will deconstruct the risk relationships, categorize impacts, and synthesize findings to recommend prioritized risk response strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies between multiple projects by mapping cause-effect relationships and identifying cascading impacts
Students will differentiate between direct and indirect risk impacts through systematic examination of project constraints and stakeholder effects
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'TechCorp Digital Transformation Portfolio' case study packet containing three project summaries (ERP Implementation, Mobile App Development, Data Center Migration) and a master risk register with 15 pre-identified risks. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team one primary project focus while requiring analysis of all three projects.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams read the case study and complete the Risk Categorization Worksheet, sorting the 15 risks into technical, organizational, external, and project management categories. Each risk must be justified with specific evidence from the case.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using the provided Risk Impact Matrix template, teams plot each risk based on probability (1-5 scale) and impact severity (1-5 scale). Teams must examine four impact dimensions: schedule, budget, scope, and quality, assigning weighted scores for their primary project.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Teams identify and map risk interdependencies using the Relationship Analysis Grid. They must find at least 5 instances where risks from different projects could trigger or amplify each other, documenting the connection type (trigger, amplify, or mitigate).

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams analyze the completed matrix to identify patterns and create a prioritized action plan. They must justify why their top 3 risks require immediate attention and propose specific response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept) with concrete implementation steps.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their top 3 priority risks and proposed responses to the class, explaining their analytical reasoning. Other teams provide feedback using the peer evaluation checklist.

Conclude with a 10-minute instructor-led discussion comparing team findings and highlighting analysis techniques that led to different conclusions.
materials_needed: TechCorp Digital Transformation Portfolio case study packet (3 pages per student)
Risk Categorization Worksheet templates
5x5 Risk Impact Matrix templates with weighted scoring guide
Relationship Analysis Grid templates
Peer evaluation checklists
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Logical placement of risks on impact matrix with clear probability/impact justification (30%), (3) Quality of interdependency analysis showing understanding of cross-project relationships (25%), (4) Feasibility and specificity of recommended response strategies (20%). Teams must score 3+ in all categories to demonstrate proficiency at the analyze level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of 2-3 risks to demonstrate the analysis process. Offer guiding questions like 'What would happen to Project B if this risk occurs in Project A?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to quantify potential financial impacts using the provided cost data and to develop contingency plans for their top risks. Consider assigning them as peer mentors to support other teams.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Effectiveness Evaluation for E-commerce Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing real e-commerce conversion data across multiple marketing channels. They will assess which attribution model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions and justify their recommendations with data-driven evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and position-based attribution models by comparing conversion credit distribution across paid search, social media, email, and display campaigns

Students will critique attribution model performance through analyzing customer journey complexity, campaign ROI variations, and budget allocation implications to recommend optimal measurement strategies
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to Google Analytics Demo Account (Google Merchandise Store) and distribute the Attribution Analysis Worksheet. Students work in pairs to ensure peer discussion and validation of findings.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. They must extract conversion data for the past 90 days across all five attribution models (Last Interaction, First Interaction, Linear, Time-Decay, Position-Based). Students record: total conversions, conversion value, and channel-specific attribution percentages for Paid Search, Organic Search, Social Network, Email, and Display channels.

**Phase 2 - Channel Impact Analysis (30 minutes):** For each attribution model, students calculate the percentage change in conversion credit for each channel compared to last-click attribution. They identify which channels gain/lose the most credit under different models and document patterns in customer journey complexity using the Top Conversion Paths report.

**Phase 3 - ROI Impact Assessment (25 minutes):** Students analyze how attribution model choice affects calculated ROI for each channel by cross-referencing cost data from Acquisition > All Traffic > Channels report. They must identify which channels would receive budget increases/decreases under each model.

**Phase 4 - Critical Evaluation (40 minutes):** Student pairs evaluate each attribution model against three criteria: alignment with actual customer behavior, actionability for marketing decisions, and business impact accuracy. They must select the most effective attribution model for this e-commerce business and prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their choice with specific data points and strategic implications.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account access (Google Merchandise Store)
Attribution Analysis Worksheet with data collection templates
Laptops/computers with internet access
Calculator or spreadsheet software for ROI calculations
Presentation timer for final recommendations
assessment_method: Students submit completed Attribution Analysis Worksheet (40 points) and deliver 5-minute presentations (60 points). Evaluation criteria include: accuracy of data extraction (20%), depth of multi-model comparison analysis (25%), quality of ROI impact assessment (25%), and strength of final recommendation justification with supporting evidence (30%). Presentations must include specific conversion percentages, channel impact calculations, and clear business rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide screenshot guides for navigating Google Analytics interface and pre-filled calculation examples for the first attribution model comparison. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate seasonal trends analysis, create custom attribution models using Google Analytics Intelligence API, or evaluate attribution model effectiveness across different product categories within the same dataset.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Drill with Decimal Conversion
description: Students will memorize binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through systematic flashcard practice and recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential number system knowledge needed for all computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the 4-bit binary representations for decimal numbers 0-15 within 3 seconds per number through flashcard drilling
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through timed recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend 5 minutes having students examine all cards simultaneously, reading both sides aloud. Next, conduct instructor-led drilling: hold up decimal numbers randomly while students call out binary equivalents in unison for 10 minutes. Then reverse the process, showing binary numbers for students to identify decimal equivalents for another 10 minutes. Pair students for partner practice (15 minutes): one partner shows cards while the other responds within 3 seconds, then switch roles after 7 minutes. Create four groups for competitive relay races (10 minutes): first student in each line converts a number, tags next teammate, continues until all 16 numbers are completed correctly. Conclude with individual silent quiz (10 minutes): students write binary equivalents for randomly ordered decimal numbers 0-15 on provided worksheet. Circulate continuously during partner and group work to provide immediate feedback and ensure proper binary notation format (always 4 digits with leading zeros where needed).
materials_needed: 16 pre-made flashcards per student (decimal 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back)
Individual quiz worksheets with decimal numbers 0-15 in random order
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for immediate checking
assessment_method: Students must correctly recall 14 out of 16 binary conversions on the final individual quiz within the 10-minute time limit. Each answer must use proper 4-bit format with leading zeros. Award full points for 14-16 correct, partial credit for 11-13 correct, needs improvement for fewer than 11 correct.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-two reference chart (8-4-2-1) and allow extra practice with numbers 0-7 first. Pair with stronger partners initially. For advanced learners: extend to 8-bit numbers (0-255) or include hexadecimal equivalents on flashcard backs for triple conversion practice.

title: Interpreting Data Quality Issues in Real-World Customer Datasets
description: Students will analyze a provided customer transaction dataset containing various data quality issues to identify, categorize, and explain the impact of missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies. They will create a comprehensive data quality assessment report demonstrating their understanding of how different types of data problems affect analysis outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will classify different types of data quality issues (missing values, outliers, duplicates, inconsistencies) by examining patterns in a customer transaction dataset
Students will explain the potential impact of specific data quality problems through written analysis connecting issues to business decision-making scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared customer dataset (CSV file with 5,000 records containing intentionally introduced data quality issues). Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. First 15 minutes: Students load the dataset using pandas and perform initial exploration using .info(), .describe(), and .head() functions to get familiar with the structure. Next 30 minutes: Using a provided checklist, students systematically examine each column for missing values (using .isnull().sum()), duplicate records (.duplicated()), and basic statistics to identify potential outliers. They document findings in the provided template. Following 25 minutes: Students use visualization tools (matplotlib/seaborn) to create histograms and box plots for numerical columns, identifying and marking obvious outliers and unusual distributions. For categorical columns, they examine value_counts() to spot inconsistencies in formatting or unexpected categories. Next 15 minutes: Students categorize each identified issue using the provided classification system (Type A: Missing data, Type B: Outliers, Type C: Inconsistencies, Type D: Duplicates) and record the count and percentage of affected records. Final 5 minutes: Students complete their data quality report template, writing 2-3 sentences explaining how each major issue type they found could impact customer segmentation analysis or sales forecasting.
materials_needed: Customer transaction dataset CSV file (pre-prepared with data quality issues)
Data quality assessment template worksheet
Data quality issue classification reference sheet
Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Data quality checklist handout
assessment_method: Evaluate completed data quality reports using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of at least 80% of planted data quality issues, (2) Correct classification of issues into provided categories, (3) Appropriate use of statistical measures and visualizations to support findings, (4) Clear explanations of business impact with specific examples. Students must achieve at least 3/4 points on each criterion to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions for each analysis step and offer a partially completed example report showing proper formatting. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose specific data cleaning strategies for each issue type they identify and estimate the potential improvement in data reliability after cleaning. Provide additional datasets with more subtle quality issues.

title: Multi-Body Gravitational System Analysis: Deconstructing the Earth-Moon-Sun Tidal Force Problem
description: Students will analyze the complex gravitational interactions in the Earth-Moon-Sun system to determine the relative contributions of each celestial body to Earth's tidal phenomena. They will decompose vector forces, evaluate competing gravitational influences, and assess how orbital mechanics create spring and neap tide patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the differential gravitational forces between Moon-Earth and Sun-Earth systems by calculating force ratios and examining geometric relationships during different lunar phases
Students will decompose complex three-body gravitational interactions through vector analysis to determine the net tidal force magnitude and direction at specific Earth locations
instructions: Begin by providing students with precise orbital data: Earth-Moon distance (3.84×10⁸ m), Earth-Sun distance (1.50×10¹¹ m), lunar mass (7.35×10²² kg), solar mass (1.99×10³⁰ kg), and Earth's radius (6.37×10⁶ m). Divide students into groups of 3-4. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each group calculates gravitational force per unit mass at Earth's surface for both Moon and Sun using F/m = GM/r². Students must show work for both the near-side and far-side of Earth relative to each celestial body. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups create vector diagrams showing gravitational forces during four lunar phase configurations: new moon, first quarter, full moon, third quarter. They must calculate the net differential force (tidal force) by subtracting Earth's center gravitational acceleration from surface point accelerations. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Students analyze their calculations to determine when constructive interference (spring tides) and destructive interference (neap tides) occur. They must explain why lunar tidal forces are ~2.2 times stronger than solar tidal forces despite the Sun's greater mass. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents one specific case (assigned lunar phase) explaining the force geometry and resulting tidal prediction. Groups must defend their vector analysis and mathematical reasoning when questioned by peers. Instructor circulates continuously, checking calculations and probing conceptual understanding through Socratic questioning.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or laptops with calculation software
Large format graph paper or digital graphing tools
Colored pens/pencils for vector diagrams
Astronomical data reference sheet with precise values
Protractors for measuring angles in vector diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical accuracy of force calculations and differential analysis, (2) Correct vector decomposition and geometric reasoning, (3) Logical analysis connecting force relationships to tidal phenomena, (4) Clear explanation of interference patterns and phase-dependent effects. Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas, with particular emphasis on showing complete mathematical work and providing physics-based justifications for their conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn coordinate systems and force magnitude templates. Break vector addition into x and y components explicitly. For advanced learners: Add elliptical orbit corrections, include Earth's rotation effects, or analyze tidal forces on other planets' moon systems. Consider having advanced students calculate actual tidal bulge heights using elastic deformation principles.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fixes in Simple Calculator Functions
description: Students will evaluate three different programmer solutions to fix bugs in basic calculator functions, comparing their effectiveness, efficiency, and code quality. They will justify their rankings and provide specific recommendations for improvement.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code quality, readability, and functionality using established criteria
Students will critique multiple programming solutions through systematic comparison and provide justified recommendations for best practices
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three printed code samples showing different fixes for a calculator's division function that originally crashed when dividing by zero. Each solution uses a different approach: Solution A uses try-catch exception handling, Solution B uses if-statement validation, and Solution C returns a special error code. Provide students with the evaluation criteria sheet.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each solution independently, testing the logic mentally and noting strengths/weaknesses on their worksheet. They should consider: Does it prevent crashes? Is the code readable? How does it handle edge cases? Is it maintainable?

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to discuss their initial evaluations. Partners should challenge each other's reasoning and refine their assessments.

**Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Each student ranks the three solutions from best to worst, writing a 3-sentence justification for their top choice and a 2-sentence explanation for why their lowest-ranked solution is inadequate.

**Class Comparison (10 minutes):** Create a class tally of rankings on the whiteboard. Select 3-4 students with different rankings to present their justifications (1 minute each).

**Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write one specific improvement they would make to their lowest-ranked solution and explain why this change would be beneficial.
materials_needed: Three printed code samples showing different bug fix approaches
Evaluation criteria worksheet with code quality rubric
Student response sheets for rankings and justifications
Whiteboard and markers for class tally
assessment_method: Evaluate student response sheets using a 3-point rubric: (3) Comprehensive evaluation with clear criteria application and well-reasoned justifications; (2) Adequate evaluation with some criteria application and basic justifications; (1) Limited evaluation with unclear reasoning. Success requires students to reference at least 3 evaluation criteria and provide specific examples from the code.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each criterion (e.g., 'What happens if the user enters 0 as the second number?'). For advanced learners: Add a fourth solution with more complex error handling and ask them to propose their own alternative solution with justification.

title: Deconstructing Multi-Stakeholder Leadership Crisis: The Boeing 737 MAX Analysis
description: Students will analyze the complex leadership decisions during the Boeing 737 MAX crisis by examining multiple stakeholder perspectives and identifying the underlying leadership theories that influenced critical decision-making processes. This expert-level activity requires students to synthesize technical, ethical, and organizational leadership concepts within a real-world catastrophic failure scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and authentic leadership approaches by analyzing documented leadership behaviors during the Boeing 737 MAX crisis timeline

Students will interpret the interplay between organizational culture, stakeholder pressure, and leadership decision-making through systematic examination of primary source materials and stakeholder testimonies
instructions:
Begin by distributing the curated document packet containing: congressional hearing transcripts, internal Boeing emails, FAA communications, and pilot union statements from 2016-2020. Form teams of 4 students, assigning each member a stakeholder role: Boeing executives, FAA regulators, airline customers, and pilot representatives. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each team member individually reviews all materials through their assigned stakeholder lens, creating a chronological timeline of critical leadership decisions and identifying specific leadership theories demonstrated. Students must cite specific quotes and actions as evidence.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Within teams, members present their stakeholder analysis while others take structured notes using the provided conflict matrix template. Teams must identify where different leadership approaches created stakeholder conflicts and where alignment existed.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams synthesize findings into a comprehensive leadership analysis addressing: Which leadership theories dominated decision-making at each crisis stage? How did competing stakeholder pressures influence leadership authenticity? What leadership blind spots contributed to the crisis escalation?

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Teams present 8-minute findings to the class, focusing on their most significant insights about leadership complexity in multi-stakeholder environments. Other teams provide structured peer feedback using the evaluation rubric.

Conclude with individual reflection: students write a 300-word analysis identifying which leadership concepts they now understand differently and which stakeholder perspective most challenged their initial assumptions.
materials_needed: Curated Boeing 737 MAX document packet (congressional transcripts, emails, FAA communications)
Stakeholder role assignment cards with specific focus questions
Conflict matrix template for tracking stakeholder tensions
Leadership theory reference sheet (transformational, transactional, authentic, servant leadership)
Presentation evaluation rubric
Digital timer and presentation equipment
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification and application of leadership theories with specific textual evidence (25%), (2) Depth of stakeholder perspective analysis showing understanding of competing pressures (25%), (3) Quality of synthesis demonstrating comprehension of leadership complexity (25%), (4) Clarity of individual reflection showing evolved understanding (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each dimension.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted key passages and leadership theory definition cards with concrete examples. For advanced learners, add supplementary materials about board governance and introduce complexity leadership theory. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those needing support during Phase 2 synthesis. Provide sentence starters for reflection writing: 'Initially I believed...but now I understand...' and 'The most challenging aspect was understanding how...'

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Evaluating Triple Constraint Trade-offs
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies by examining their impact on scope, schedule, and budget constraints. They will deconstruct the relationships between risk responses and project objectives to recommend optimal mitigation approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationships between risk response strategies and triple constraint impacts by comparing quantitative effects across scope, schedule, and budget dimensions
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response approaches through systematic assessment of cost-benefit ratios and strategic alignment with project objectives
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Software Implementation Project' case study containing 8 identified risks with probability/impact ratings and 3 proposed response strategies per risk (24 total strategies). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team 4 risks to analyze deeply. Students spend 15 minutes individually reading the case and completing the Risk Response Analysis Worksheet, identifying how each assigned strategy affects scope (features/quality), schedule (timeline/milestones), and budget (direct costs/resource allocation). Next, teams collaborate for 25 minutes using the Triple Constraint Impact Matrix template to plot each response strategy's effects, calculating weighted impact scores using the provided formula: (Scope Impact × 0.4) + (Schedule Impact × 0.3) + (Budget Impact × 0.3). Teams then spend 20 minutes evaluating strategy effectiveness by ranking responses for each risk using criteria: cost-benefit ratio, feasibility, alignment with project priorities, and residual risk level. Each team creates a summary recommendation slide identifying their top 2 response strategies per assigned risk with quantitative justification. During the final 25 minutes, teams present findings in 4-minute rotations while other teams use peer evaluation forms to assess analysis quality. Conclude with a 10-minute instructor-led discussion comparing team recommendations and highlighting key analytical insights about risk response trade-offs.
materials_needed: Software Implementation Project case study handout (2 pages)
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet template
Triple Constraint Impact Matrix Excel template
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
Flip chart paper and markers for summary presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of triple constraint impact calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of strategy effectiveness analysis with supporting rationale (25 points), (3) Appropriateness of final recommendations with quantitative justification (25 points), (4) Peer presentation clarity and professional delivery (25 points). Successful completion requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion and demonstrating clear understanding of risk-constraint relationships through mathematical analysis and logical reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the completed first risk analysis as an example and offer simplified impact scoring (1-3 scale instead of 1-5). Create mixed-ability teams pairing analytical students with those needing support. For advanced learners, add secondary constraints analysis (quality, resources, stakeholder satisfaction) and require Monte Carlo simulation consideration for probability-weighted outcomes. Provide additional case complexity by introducing interdependent risks requiring portfolio-level analysis.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation and Optimization Audit
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of three different e-commerce businesses' Google Analytics implementations by analyzing their conversion funnel performance, goal configuration, and attribution modeling strategies. They will create comprehensive audit reports with prioritized improvement recommendations based on business impact and implementation feasibility.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics goal configurations and conversion tracking setups by conducting comparative analysis across multiple e-commerce case studies
Students will assess the appropriateness of attribution models and measurement frameworks through systematic evaluation of business objectives alignment and data accuracy
instructions: **Phase 1: Case Study Distribution (15 minutes)** Provide each student team of 3-4 members with three anonymized e-commerce case studies containing: GA4 screenshots of conversion paths, goal configurations, attribution model settings, audience definitions, and 6-month performance data. Each case represents different business models (subscription, marketplace, direct-to-consumer). **Phase 2: Individual Analysis (45 minutes)** Students independently examine each case study using the provided evaluation framework covering: conversion funnel effectiveness (analyzing drop-off rates and micro-conversions), goal hierarchy appropriateness (revenue goals vs engagement goals alignment), attribution model selection rationale (first-click vs data-driven vs linear model performance), audience segmentation strategy effectiveness, and custom event tracking implementation quality. Students document findings using the structured analysis template, noting strengths, weaknesses, and data gaps. **Phase 3: Collaborative Evaluation (30 minutes)** Teams reconvene to compare individual analyses and reach consensus on rankings. They must evaluate which case study demonstrates: most effective conversion tracking strategy, best attribution model selection for business type, and most actionable audience segmentation approach. Teams prepare evidence-based justifications for their rankings. **Phase 4: Optimization Recommendations (45 minutes)** For the lowest-performing case study, teams develop a detailed improvement plan including: three high-priority technical fixes with implementation timelines, revised goal configuration strategy with specific metrics, alternative attribution model recommendation with expected impact quantification, and enhanced audience segmentation proposal with targeting rationale. **Phase 5: Peer Review and Defense (30 minutes)** Teams present their evaluations and recommendations to another team for peer review, defending their analytical approach and improvement strategies through structured Q&A sessions.
materials_needed: Three detailed e-commerce case study packets with GA4 screenshots and performance data
Structured evaluation framework template with weighted scoring criteria
Analysis documentation worksheets with comparative ranking matrices
Access to Google Analytics Demo Account for reference verification
Peer review feedback forms with technical assessment criteria
