assessment_method: Students evaluated using weighted rubric: Analytical rigor (30% - depth of conversion funnel analysis, attribution model evaluation accuracy, audience segmentation assessment quality), Critical evaluation skills (25% - evidence-based ranking justification, comparative analysis thoroughness, identification of measurement gaps), Strategic recommendations (25% - feasibility of proposed solutions, business impact prioritization, technical implementation understanding), Professional presentation (20% - clear communication of findings, effective defense of methodology, constructive peer feedback provision). Deliverables include completed evaluation matrices, optimization recommendation report, and peer review assessments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions for each evaluation criterion, offer GA4 interface navigation support, and create checkpoint reviews after each analysis phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced GA4 features evaluation (Enhanced Ecommerce events, custom dimensions effectiveness), cross-platform attribution analysis, and ROI calculations for their optimization recommendations. Provide supplementary case study with complex multi-channel attribution scenarios.

title: Python Data Type Memory Cards Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the five fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list) and their defining characteristics through a structured flashcard activity. This foundational knowledge-building exercise uses spaced repetition and peer quizzing to solidify basic programming concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the five fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list) by correctly naming each type when shown example values
Students will recall the key characteristics of each Python data type through verbal explanation during peer quizzing sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard templates to each student (15 cards total: 3 cards per data type). Have students create their own flashcard set by writing the data type name on one side and 2-3 example values plus one key characteristic on the reverse. For integers: write 'int' on front, '42, -7, 0' and 'whole numbers only' on back. For floats: write 'float' on front, '3.14, -2.5, 0.0' and 'numbers with decimal points' on back. Continue this pattern for strings ('Hello', 'Python', '' - text in quotes), booleans (True, False - logical values only), and lists ([1,2,3], ['a','b'], [] - ordered collections in brackets). Allow 20 minutes for card creation. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other for 15 minutes using their completed cards. Partner A shows the data type name, Partner B must state two examples and the key characteristic, then roles reverse. Conclude with a whole-class rapid-fire recall session where the instructor displays random Python values on the projector (like 'Hello World', 3.14159, True, [1,2,3,4]) and students must shout out the correct data type. Keep score and celebrate correct responses to maintain engagement.
materials_needed: Blank index cards (15 per student)
Black ink pens or pencils
Projector or interactive whiteboard
Pre-written list of 20 diverse Python values for final quiz
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric per data type (15 points total): 3 points for correctly naming the data type AND providing accurate examples AND stating the key characteristic; 2 points for correct naming plus one additional element; 1 point for correct data type identification only. Students must score 12/15 points (80%) to demonstrate successful memorization. Document performance during peer quizzing and final rapid-fire session.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide completed example cards for one data type as a model and allow them to work with a study buddy during creation time. Consider reducing the requirement to 2 cards per data type instead of 3. For advanced learners, add complex data types like dictionaries and tuples, or have them create cards with edge cases (empty strings, negative floats, nested lists) to deepen their understanding.

title: Optimization Analysis for Real-World Business Scenarios Using Calculus
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve authentic business optimization problems involving profit maximization and cost minimization. They will analyze multi-variable scenarios, determine critical points, and interpret results within realistic business constraints to make data-driven recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques and critical point analysis to optimize profit functions in realistic business scenarios with given constraints
Students will implement second derivative tests and boundary analysis to validate optimization solutions and interpret results within business contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct business scenario packets (15 minutes setup). Each scenario includes: a tech startup's pricing strategy with demand function P(x) = 120 - 0.5x and cost function C(x) = 2000 + 30x + 0.1x²; a manufacturing company's production optimization with revenue R(x,y) = 80x + 60y - 2x² - y² - xy and constraint x + 2y ≤ 40; and a delivery service's route efficiency problem with time function T(d) = 0.02d² - 1.5d + 45 for distance d. Form groups of 3-4 students, ensuring mixed ability levels (5 minutes). Students first individually read their assigned scenario and identify the objective function, constraints, and business context (10 minutes). Groups then collaborate to set up the optimization problem mathematically, taking derivatives and finding critical points using appropriate techniques—single-variable calculus for scenario 1, Lagrange multipliers for scenario 2, and constraint analysis for scenario 3 (25 minutes). Next, groups apply second derivative tests or border analysis to verify maximum/minimum solutions and check endpoint conditions (15 minutes). Students must then interpret their mathematical results within the business context, calculating specific values (optimal price, production levels, or route distances) and explaining the practical meaning (20 minutes). Finally, each group prepares a 5-minute presentation showing their mathematical work, optimal solution, and business recommendation with justification (15 minutes preparation, 15 minutes presentations). Circulate continuously to check mathematical accuracy and push students to connect abstract results to real business implications.
materials_needed: Three printed business scenario packets with specific functions and constraints
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos/GeoGebra
Large poster paper or whiteboard space for group work
Presentation timer and evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Mathematical accuracy of derivative calculations and critical point identification, (2) Correct application of optimization techniques and verification methods, (3) Accurate interpretation of results within business context, and (4) Quality of business recommendations with mathematical justification. Students must achieve proficiency in all four areas, with specific point deductions for computational errors, incomplete verification, or failure to connect mathematical results to practical business decisions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing derivative formula reference sheets and step-by-step optimization flowcharts. Offer simplified single-variable versions of problems initially. For advanced learners, add additional constraints like budget limitations or market competition factors, require sensitivity analysis of their solutions, or challenge them to create their own business optimization scenario for peers to solve.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Analysis: Decomposing Faraday's Law in Multi-Coil Generator Systems
description: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic induction scenarios involving multiple rotating coils in non-uniform magnetic fields. They will break down the system components, examine how geometric and temporal variables affect induced EMF, and evaluate the relative contributions of different physical parameters to total power output.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between coil geometry, rotation speed, and magnetic field strength by decomposing Faraday's law into component variables and calculating individual contributions to total EMF
Students will evaluate competing design parameters in multi-coil generator systems through systematic comparison of power output under varying conditions
instructions: Begin by distributing the multi-coil generator scenario worksheet featuring three different coil configurations (50-turn circular coil radius 0.15m, 80-turn square coil side 0.12m, 30-turn rectangular coil 0.10m × 0.20m) rotating at different angular velocities (100, 150, 200 rad/s) in a non-uniform magnetic field B(r) = 0.8 - 0.2r² Tesla. Students work in groups of 3-4 for 90 minutes total. First 20 minutes: Each group analyzes the given data set, identifying all variables affecting EMF and sketching magnetic flux vs. time graphs for each coil. Minutes 21-45: Groups calculate instantaneous EMF for each coil using ε = -dΦ/dt, breaking down the calculation into geometric factors (area, turns) and kinematic factors (angular velocity, field variation). They must show how each variable contributes to the total EMF expression. Minutes 46-70: Groups compare power outputs P = ε²/R (assuming resistance R = 2.5Ω for all coils) and create ranking matrices showing which design parameters most significantly impact performance. They analyze trade-offs between coil size, turn density, and rotational speed. Minutes 71-85: Groups prepare 3-minute presentations explaining their analysis methodology and defending their conclusions about optimal generator design. Final 5 minutes: Class votes on most convincing analysis approach. Throughout the activity, instructor circulates to ensure groups are properly decomposing the complex EMF equation rather than simply plugging numbers into formulas.
materials_needed: Multi-coil generator scenario worksheets with specific geometric and kinematic parameters
Scientific calculators with trigonometric functions
Graph paper or digital graphing software (Desmos/GeoGebra)
Presentation timer and voting materials
assessment_method: Students submit individual analysis reports (due next class) showing: (1) Complete mathematical decomposition of EMF equations with each variable's contribution clearly identified (25 points), (2) Comparative analysis table ranking design parameters by impact magnitude with quantitative justification (25 points), (3) Written evaluation of trade-offs between competing design choices with specific numerical evidence (25 points), (4) Quality of group presentation demonstrating clear analytical reasoning (25 points). Success requires students to move beyond calculation to show understanding of how component variables interact within the larger electromagnetic system.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide EMF equation template with blanks to fill in specific variables, and offer guided questions about which terms change with each parameter. For advanced learners: Add complexity by introducing coil resistance variation with temperature or considering eddy current losses in realistic materials. Provide extension problems involving optimization calculus to find maximum power conditions.

title: Code Review Challenge: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program
description: Students will critically evaluate three different bug fix solutions for a basic calculator program by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and correctness. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluation using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by comparing code readability, performance, and maintainability using a structured rubric
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic analysis of syntax, logic flow, and adherence to coding best practices
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario handout describing a calculator program with a division-by-zero bug (5 minutes). Present three different fix solutions: Solution A uses try-catch exception handling, Solution B uses if-statement validation, and Solution C uses a combination approach with user prompts. Organize students into pairs and provide each pair with the evaluation worksheet containing five criteria: correctness, code readability, error handling effectiveness, user experience, and maintainability (10 minutes). 

Students spend 25 minutes analyzing each solution against the five criteria, rating each on a 1-5 scale and writing 2-3 sentence justifications for each rating. They must identify specific code elements that support their scores, such as variable naming conventions, comment quality, and logical structure. 

Next, pairs rank the three solutions from best to worst and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their top choice (15 minutes). During presentations, other students use peer evaluation forms to assess the quality of reasoning presented (15 minutes). 

Conclude with a class discussion where students defend their rankings when challenged by peers, requiring them to reference specific code examples and development principles. The instructor facilitates by asking probing questions like 'What would happen if this code were maintained by a different programmer?' and 'How would this solution perform with 1000 users?' (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Printed scenario handout with calculator bug description and three solution codes
Evaluation worksheet with 5-point rating scales for each criterion
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Timer for activity segments
Whiteboard or projector for displaying code solutions
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Completeness of criteria analysis with specific code references (25%), (2) Quality of written justifications showing understanding of development principles (25%), (3) Logical ranking with clear reasoning (25%), and (4) Effective defense of choices during discussion using evidence (25%). Students must score 3/4 or higher on each dimension to demonstrate proficiency in evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of one solution showing proper justification format and specific code references. Offer sentence starters like 'This solution is effective because...' and 'The code quality could be improved by...'. For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge to propose their own fourth solution and evaluate how it compares to the original three, or have them consider additional criteria like memory usage and testing requirements.

title: Design a Municipal Budget Dashboard for City Council Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard analyzing 5-year municipal budget trends to identify spending patterns and develop recommendations for budget reallocation. This culminating project requires students to synthesize multiple datasets, design visualizations, and present actionable insights to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive data dashboard by integrating multiple municipal budget datasets and creating interactive visualizations that reveal spending trends across departments
Students will construct evidence-based budget recommendations through statistical analysis and present findings in a stakeholder-ready format
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration (45 minutes)**
Provide each team of 3-4 students with five CSV files containing municipal budget data (2019-2023) including: general fund, capital projects, personnel costs, infrastructure spending, and revenue sources. Students begin by importing datasets into Excel/Google Sheets, identifying data quality issues (missing values, formatting inconsistencies), and creating a master dataset with standardized categories.

**Phase 2: Analysis Framework Development (60 minutes)**
Students develop three research questions about budget allocation effectiveness (e.g., "Which departments show the most volatile spending patterns?" "How has infrastructure investment correlated with population growth?"). They calculate year-over-year percentage changes, identify top 3 spending categories per department, and perform correlation analysis between revenue sources and expenditure patterns.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (90 minutes)**
Using provided dashboard template, students create five interactive charts: (1) Multi-year spending trend line graph by department, (2) Budget allocation pie chart with year selector, (3) Revenue vs. expenditure scatter plot, (4) Department comparison bar chart showing efficiency metrics, (5) Geographic heat map of capital project spending. Each visualization must include title, axis labels, data source citation, and interactive filtering capability.

**Phase 4: Recommendation Development (45 minutes)**
Based on dashboard insights, teams formulate three specific budget recommendations with supporting evidence, projected impact, and implementation timeline. Students prepare 5-minute presentations targeting city council audience, including dashboard demonstration and Q&A preparation.

**Phase 5: Peer Review and Refinement (30 minutes)**
Teams rotate through stations reviewing other dashboards using provided rubric, offering feedback on clarity, accuracy, and recommendation feasibility. Students incorporate feedback and finalize deliverables.
materials_needed: 5 municipal budget CSV datasets (2019-2023) per team
Excel or Google Sheets with charting capabilities
Dashboard template with pre-formatted layout sections
Budget analysis worksheet with calculation formulas
Presentation rubric and peer feedback forms
Projector/screen for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (20 points - completeness, accuracy of data cleaning), Dashboard Design (30 points - visual clarity, interactivity, professional appearance), Statistical Analysis (25 points - appropriate calculations, trend identification, correlation analysis), Recommendations (15 points - evidence-based, specificity, feasibility), Presentation Skills (10 points - clarity, time management, stakeholder focus). Minimum 70 points required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned sample dataset and step-by-step calculation guides. Offer dashboard templates with partially completed examples. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets (demographic, economic indicators) for more sophisticated analysis. Challenge them to incorporate predictive modeling or cost-benefit analysis. Encourage exploration of advanced visualization tools like Tableau Public.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: Multi-Framework Analysis of Complex Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three authentic leadership paradox scenarios using multiple theoretical frameworks to demonstrate comprehensive understanding of how different leadership models interpret the same complex situations. They will create comparative framework matrices showing how transformational, situational, and authentic leadership theories would explain leader behaviors and outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret complex leadership paradoxes by applying transformational, situational, and authentic leadership frameworks to the same scenarios
Students will distinguish between different theoretical explanations through systematic comparative analysis of framework predictions and outcomes
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4, ensuring each group has access to leadership theory reference materials. Distribute the three pre-selected paradox scenarios: (1) A CEO who increases profits while implementing massive layoffs but maintains high employee loyalty, (2) A military leader who disobeys direct orders to save civilian lives and receives both court-martial and hero status, (3) A nonprofit director who uses deceptive fundraising tactics to fund legitimate charitable work. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each group receives a structured analysis template with three columns for each leadership framework. Students must identify key leadership behaviors, predict outcomes according to each theory, and explain why each framework would interpret the leader's actions differently. Provide guiding questions: 'What would transformational leadership theory predict about follower responses?' 'How does situational leadership explain the leader's adaptive choices?' 'Which aspects align with authentic leadership principles?'

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups create visual comparison matrices showing where frameworks agree, conflict, or remain silent about each scenario. They must identify specific theoretical constructs (charismatic influence, contextual adaptation, self-awareness) and map them to observed behaviors.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Structured gallery walk where groups rotate through other teams' analyses, using provided feedback forms to note insights, challenge interpretations, and identify gaps in theoretical application. Conclude with whole-group synthesis discussion focusing on framework limitations and complementary explanations.
materials_needed: Three detailed leadership paradox case studies (2-3 pages each)
Leadership theory quick-reference sheets covering transformational, situational, and authentic leadership
Structured analysis templates with framework comparison matrices
Large poster paper or digital collaboration platform access
Peer feedback forms for gallery walk assessment
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis matrices using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of theoretical application (25%), (2) Depth of comparative analysis between frameworks (25%), (3) Quality of evidence linking theory to scenario behaviors (25%), (4) Identification of framework limitations and complementary insights (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category, demonstrated through precise use of theoretical vocabulary and clear logical connections between framework predictions and observed outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing theory application examples from simpler scenarios and sentence starters for comparative analysis. Offer framework decision trees to guide theoretical selection. Extend advanced learners by adding servant leadership or complexity leadership frameworks to their analysis, or asking them to propose hybrid theoretical explanations for the paradoxes.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Evaluating Multi-Project Portfolio Decisions
description: Students will analyze real project scenarios to evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) across multiple interconnected projects. They will break down complex risk situations, compare alternative approaches, and justify optimal response combinations based on organizational constraints and project dependencies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between risk response strategies and project constraints by evaluating three interconnected project scenarios with competing resource demands
Students will differentiate between appropriate risk response strategies through systematic comparison of cost, timeline, and stakeholder impact factors
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the 'TechCorp Portfolio Case Study' containing three interconnected software projects: Project Alpha (mobile app, $2M budget, 12 months), Project Beta (data migration, $800K, 8 months), and Project Gamma (cloud infrastructure, $1.5M, 10 months). Each project has 4-6 identified risks with current response strategies already implemented. Teams receive constraint cards showing limited budget reserves ($400K total), shared development team of 15 people, and fixed go-live date for all projects. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams create a risk interdependency matrix, mapping how risks in one project affect others. Step 2 (25 minutes): For each risk, teams analyze the current response strategy by examining three factors: resource allocation efficiency, timeline impact, and stakeholder satisfaction scores provided in the case materials. Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams identify problematic response combinations where current strategies conflict or suboptimize portfolio outcomes. Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams develop alternative response strategy combinations for the three most critical risks, documenting trade-offs using a structured comparison template. Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their top recommendation with quantified justification. Step 6 (20 minutes): Each team presents while others complete peer evaluation forms rating the analysis depth and justification quality.
materials_needed: TechCorp Portfolio Case Study packets (3 pages per team)
Risk interdependency matrix templates (1 per team)
Response strategy comparison templates (3 per team)
Constraint reference cards showing budget/resource limits
Peer evaluation forms (1 per student)
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk interdependency analysis (25%), (2) Depth of strategy evaluation using provided criteria (30%), (3) Quality of alternative strategy justification with quantified trade-offs (30%), and (4) Clarity of presentation and peer interaction (15%). Successful completion requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category, demonstrating ability to break down complex multi-project scenarios and support recommendations with systematic analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of one risk's analysis and offer guiding questions for each analysis step. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add a secondary challenge requiring them to propose risk response strategies for budget scenarios reduced by 20%, or ask them to mentor other teams during the analysis phases while completing additional complexity factors.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, then defend their choice of optimal attribution model for a specific business scenario. This advanced activity requires students to analyze conversion paths, assess model limitations, and justify strategic decisions based on data-driven insights.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by analyzing conversion path reports and ROI impact for an e-commerce case study
Students will critique the limitations and biases of each attribution model through comparative analysis of campaign performance metrics across multiple touchpoints
instructions:
Begin by providing students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, social media, email, display, organic). Students work individually for the first 90 minutes, then in pairs for discussion and refinement.

Step 1 (30 minutes): Students navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution and examine the Model Comparison tool. They must document baseline metrics for each attribution model: conversion value, conversion count, and ROAS for each marketing channel.

Step 2 (45 minutes): Using the Conversion Paths report under Reports > Advertising > Attribution, students analyze the customer journey data. They identify the average path length, most common conversion sequences, and time lag between touchpoints. Students create a matrix comparing how each attribution model credits conversions differently for the top 5 conversion paths.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Students calculate the budget reallocation implications by determining how marketing spend would shift under each model, assuming a $100,000 monthly budget distributed based on attributed conversion value.

Step 4 (45 minutes): In pairs, students debate which attribution model best serves the business objectives provided in the case study (either brand awareness focus, direct response focus, or balanced growth). Each pair must prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their chosen model.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Pairs present their recommendations, with the class voting on the most compelling argument based on data support, consideration of model limitations, and business alignment.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with multi-channel e-commerce data
Business scenario case study handout with company objectives
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
Laptops/computers with internet access
Presentation timer for final presentations
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and calculations from GA4 reports (25%), (2) Depth of critical analysis comparing model strengths/weaknesses with specific examples (30%), (3) Quality of business justification linking model choice to company objectives (25%), (4) Presentation clarity and defense against peer questions (20%). Students must achieve proficient or above in all categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled data tables and guided questions for each attribution model. Offer a checklist of key metrics to examine and sample business reasoning statements. For advanced learners, introduce custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution insights, or have them analyze attribution across different product categories or customer segments within the same dataset.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing conversion paths across multiple marketing channels. They will assess the strengths and limitations of each model and defend their recommendation for optimal attribution strategy based on specific business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of at least four different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based) by analyzing their impact on channel performance metrics and ROI calculations
Students will judge the appropriateness of attribution models through comprehensive analysis of customer journey data and business context to formulate data-driven strategic recommendations
instructions:
Begin by providing students with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display advertising). Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. Have them select a date range covering the full 6-month period and compare all five attribution models simultaneously. Students must document conversion values, conversion counts, and channel rankings under each model in a provided data collection template.

Next, spend 30 minutes having students analyze the Top Conversion Paths report to understand typical customer journey lengths and touchpoint sequences. They should identify patterns such as average path length, most common first and last interactions, and channel combinations that lead to highest-value conversions. Provide three distinct business scenarios (B2B software with long sales cycles, fast-fashion e-commerce with impulse purchases, and local service business with relationship-based sales).

For the evaluation phase (40 minutes), students must assess each attribution model's appropriateness for each business scenario. They should consider factors including sales cycle length, average order value, customer lifetime value, marketing budget allocation across channels, and business objectives. Students must identify specific weaknesses in their current attribution approach and quantify the potential impact of switching models on budget allocation decisions.

Conclude with 20 minutes for students to prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their attribution model recommendation for one assigned business scenario. They must present their analysis to another pair, justify their choice using specific data points, address potential counterarguments, and explain implementation implications for marketing strategy and budget allocation.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account with multi-channel e-commerce data
Data collection template spreadsheet with attribution model comparison charts
Three detailed business scenario case study documents
Presentation template with evaluation criteria framework
Access to computers with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and interpretation from attribution reports (25%), (2) Depth of critical analysis comparing model strengths/weaknesses (30%), (3) Quality of justification linking attribution choice to business context (25%), (4) Ability to defend recommendation and address counterarguments during peer presentation (20%). Students must achieve proficient or higher in all categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a step-by-step navigation guide with screenshots for accessing attribution reports, and offer a structured analysis framework with guiding questions for each evaluation criterion. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models, analyze data-driven attribution insights, or calculate the financial impact of attribution model changes on marketing ROI across different customer segments.
original_title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and Strategic Recommendation

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN and Zero Trust Security Architecture
description: Students will architect and implement a comprehensive enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using SD-WAN technology, incorporating zero trust security principles, QoS policies, and redundant connectivity. This capstone project requires integration of routing protocols, security frameworks, and modern networking paradigms into a fully functional business network.
estimated_duration: 5.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a complete enterprise network topology by integrating OSPF/BGP routing, SD-WAN overlay, and zero trust security principles across multiple sites
Students will create comprehensive network documentation through detailed configuration files, network diagrams, and implementation procedures that meet industry standards
instructions: **Phase 1: Network Design (90 minutes)** - Divide students into teams of 3-4. Present the scenario: Company headquarters in New York, manufacturing site in Dallas, and sales office in Seattle, each requiring specific bandwidth allocations and security policies. Teams must create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, specifying device models, IP addressing schemes (using /24 subnets from 10.0.0.0/16), VLAN designs, and WAN connectivity options. Each site requires redundant internet connections and internal segmentation for users, servers, and IoT devices. **Phase 2: Configuration Development (120 minutes)** - Teams develop complete device configurations including: OSPF areas with proper LSA filtering, BGP peering for redundant ISP connections, Cisco SD-WAN vEdge router configurations with application-aware routing policies, ASA firewall rules implementing zero trust micro-segmentation, and QoS policies prioritizing voice (30%), video (25%), business-critical applications (25%), and best effort (20%). **Phase 3: Implementation and Testing (90 minutes)** - Deploy configurations in simulation environment, verify connectivity using ping, traceroute, and show commands, test failover scenarios by disabling primary links, validate QoS implementation using traffic generators, and document all verification steps with screenshots and command outputs. **Phase 4: Presentation (30 minutes)** - Teams present their solution including architecture justification, security implementation, and troubleshooting procedures to the class, simulating a client presentation format.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.2 or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images
Network diagram templates (Visio or Lucidchart access)
Scenario documentation packet with specific business requirements
Configuration template library for reference
Traffic generation tools (built into Packet Tracer or external tools for GNS3)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: Network Design (25%) - topology correctness, scalability, redundancy; Configuration Quality (30%) - syntax accuracy, best practices, security implementation; Documentation (25%) - completeness, clarity, professional formatting; Presentation (20%) - technical accuracy, business justification, problem-solving approach. Students must achieve minimum 3/4 in each category and demonstrate successful end-to-end connectivity with all failover scenarios working correctly.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-configured base templates and step-by-step configuration checklists. Offer intermediate checkpoints where instructor reviews progress and provides feedback. For advanced learners, add requirements for IPv6 dual-stack implementation, automation using Python/Ansible scripts, or integration with cloud services. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support and provide reference materials including Cisco documentation links and command quick-reference guides.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Drill: Variable Declaration Patterns
description: Students will memorize and recall the exact syntax patterns for declaring variables in five common programming languages (Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, and C#). Through repetitive flashcard drills and timed recall exercises, students will build foundational knowledge of basic programming syntax that they can retrieve instantly when coding.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the correct variable declaration syntax for integers, strings, and booleans in Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, and C# by matching syntax patterns to language names with 90% accuracy
Students will recall from memory the specific keywords, symbols, and formatting rules for variable declarations through structured flashcard practice and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-made flashcard sets to students, with each set containing 15 cards showing variable declaration examples (3 data types × 5 languages). Spend 5 minutes having students examine all cards in pairs, reading aloud each syntax pattern. Next, conduct a 10-minute guided practice where you display each programming language name on the board and students must call out the correct variable declaration syntax for an integer variable. Follow this with 15 minutes of individual flashcard practice where students flip through their deck, attempting to recall the syntax before checking the answer. Students should separate cards into 'mastered' and 'needs practice' piles. Conduct a 5-minute partner quiz where Student A shows the language name and data type (e.g., 'Java - string variable'), and Student B must recite the exact syntax (e.g., 'String variableName = value;'). Partners switch roles halfway through. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class rapid-fire session where you call out random combinations of language and data type, and students write the syntax on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate feedback. Record which students consistently demonstrate accurate recall for assessment purposes.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (15 cards per student) showing variable declaration syntax
Mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers (1 per student)
Timer or stopwatch
Projector/whiteboard for displaying language names
Student tracking sheet for recording accuracy rates
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (13/15 correct responses) during the final rapid-fire whiteboard session. Track individual performance using a checklist marking correct/incorrect for each syntax pattern tested. Students who miss more than 2 syntax patterns require additional practice sessions. Award full credit for exact syntax including proper capitalization, semicolons, and bracket placement.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce the number of languages to 3 (Python, Java, JavaScript) and provide a reference sheet during initial practice. Create color-coded cards grouping similar syntax patterns. For advanced learners, add array declarations and constant variable syntax, or include additional languages like Ruby or Swift. Consider having advanced students create their own flashcards for additional programming concepts.

title: Multi-Criteria Optimization: Designing an Efficient Solar Panel Array
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques and calculus optimization to design a solar panel array that maximizes energy output while minimizing cost and land usage. They will work with real constraint equations and use both graphical and analytical methods to find optimal solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve a three-variable optimization problem involving solar panel placement constraints
Students will implement calculus-based optimization techniques to determine optimal panel angles and spacing through derivative analysis and constraint equations
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Solar Array Design Challenge packet containing: cost per panel ($450), energy output formula (E = 250cos²θ × d⁻⁰·³ watts where θ is tilt angle, d is inter-panel distance), land constraint (maximum 10,000 m²), and minimum energy requirement (50kW). Form teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams establish their constraint equations. Have students define variables: n = number of panels, θ = tilt angle (15°-60°), d = spacing distance (2-8 meters). They must write inequality constraints: total area ≤ 10,000m², total energy ≥ 50,000W, cost ≤ $100,000, and 15° ≤ θ ≤ 60°. Students graph the feasible region on provided coordinate paper using the first two constraints.

Phase 2 (35 minutes): Teams apply the simplex method to find corner points of the feasible region, then calculate energy output for each corner point using the given formula. Simultaneously, they use calculus to optimize the energy function: take partial derivatives ∂E/∂θ and ∂E/∂d, set equal to zero, and solve the resulting system. Students must show all algebraic steps and verify second derivative test for maximum/minimum.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Teams use Excel or Desmos to verify their analytical solutions graphically. They plot the energy function surface over the feasible region and identify the optimal point. Finally, teams prepare a 2-minute presentation showing their optimal configuration: number of panels, tilt angle, spacing, total cost, energy output, and land usage.

Conclude with team presentations (15 minutes) where each group states their optimal solution and explains one key mathematical technique they used.
materials_needed: Solar Array Design Challenge packet (pre-printed with all constraint data and formulas)
Graphing paper with coordinate grids (minimum 20×20 squares)
Scientific calculators with trigonometric functions
Computers/tablets with Excel or Desmos graphing calculator access
Presentation timer for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct constraint equation setup (25 points), (2) Accurate application of simplex method with all corner points identified (25 points), (3) Proper use of partial derivatives with correct optimization solution (30 points), (4) Verification through graphical analysis matches analytical solution within 5% tolerance (20 points). Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps and their final optimal values.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a constraint equation template with variables pre-defined, and offer a step-by-step partial derivative worksheet. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger mathematical partners. For advanced learners: Add a second optimization objective (minimize environmental impact) requiring multi-objective optimization techniques, or introduce integer programming constraints where panel numbers must be whole numbers.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: The Three-Body Problem Case Study
description: Students will dissect the complex dynamics of the Earth-Moon-Sun system by analyzing gravitational interactions, identifying perturbations, and evaluating the stability of Lagrange points. They will break down how each celestial body influences the others and determine which factors dominate under different conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the competing gravitational forces in the Earth-Moon-Sun system by calculating force ratios at different orbital positions and identifying dominant interactions
Students will evaluate the stability characteristics of Lagrange points through mathematical modeling and graphical analysis of potential energy surfaces
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute setup where students form groups of 3-4 and receive printed orbital data sheets containing Earth-Moon-Sun distances, masses, and velocities at 8 key orbital positions throughout one month. Each group designates roles: Calculator (mathematical analysis), Modeler (software visualization), Analyst (pattern identification), and Presenter (synthesis communication). 

For the first 30 minutes, students calculate gravitational force vectors between all three bodies at each orbital position using F = Gm₁m₂/r². They create force diagrams showing how the Sun's pull on the Moon varies as Earth-Moon distance changes, identifying when tidal forces are maximum. Students then calculate the ratio of Solar-to-Terrestrial gravitational influence on the Moon at apogee versus perigee.

Next, spend 25 minutes using computational tools (Mathematica, Python, or provided simulation software) to model the restricted three-body problem. Students input real astronomical data and generate trajectory plots for test masses placed near the five Lagrange points. They analyze which points show bounded versus unbounded motion when perturbed.

In the final 20 minutes, groups examine their force calculations and simulation results to identify: (1) which gravitational interactions dominate during different lunar phases, (2) why only L4 and L5 Lagrange points remain stable, and (3) how solar perturbations affect lunar orbital eccentricity. Each group prepares a 3-minute presentation explaining one key finding with supporting mathematical evidence and visual representations from their analysis.
materials_needed: Earth-Moon-Sun orbital data sheets with 8 monthly positions
Scientific calculators or laptops
Computational software (Mathematica, Python with matplotlib, or online three-body simulator)
Large format paper for force vector diagrams
Colored pencils for vector representation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical Accuracy - correct force calculations and ratios, (2) Pattern Recognition - identification of dominant interactions at different positions, (3) Stability Analysis - accurate interpretation of Lagrange point behavior from simulations, (4) Synthesis Quality - clear explanation of how multiple gravitational sources create complex dynamics. Award points for quantitative evidence supporting conclusions and accurate use of physics terminology.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed force calculation templates and step-by-step software tutorials. Offer advanced learners extension challenges like analyzing asteroid capture at Lagrange points or calculating libration periods around stable points. Provide intermediate checkpoints every 20 minutes where groups can verify calculations with instructor before proceeding.

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Function Implementation Approaches
description: Students will evaluate and compare three different implementations of the same function to determine which approach is most effective. They will analyze code readability, efficiency, and maintainability using established criteria and justify their selection with evidence-based reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different code implementations by applying readability, efficiency, and maintainability criteria to determine the most effective solution
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison and justify their recommendations with specific evidence from code analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the evaluation worksheet and three code implementations of a 'calculateGPA' function written in Python. Each implementation produces the same output but uses different approaches: Implementation A uses a simple loop, Implementation B uses list comprehension, and Implementation C uses a nested function with error handling. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually read all three implementations and run them using the provided test cases to verify they produce identical outputs. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the evaluation criteria checklist, students analyze each implementation across four dimensions: readability (variable names, comments, structure), efficiency (number of operations, memory usage), maintainability (ease of modification, error handling), and beginner-friendliness (complexity level, learning curve). Students score each implementation 1-5 on each criterion.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students calculate weighted scores using the provided formula (readability 30%, efficiency 25%, maintainability 25%, beginner-friendliness 20%) and rank the implementations.

Step 4 (15 minutes): In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss differences in their evaluations. They must provide specific code examples to support their judgments.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each pair presents their top choice to another pair, defending their selection with evidence from their analysis. The receiving pair challenges the recommendation by asking clarifying questions about specific evaluation criteria.

Step 6 (10 minutes): Students individually write a 150-word recommendation memo stating which implementation they would choose for a beginner programming course, including three specific reasons supported by code examples.
materials_needed: Three printed Python code implementations of calculateGPA function
Evaluation criteria checklist with 1-5 scoring rubric
Sample test cases with expected outputs
Calculators for weighted scoring
Recommendation memo template
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation worksheets with numerical scores and justifications, plus recommendation memo. Assess using rubric: appropriate use of evaluation criteria (25%), accurate analysis with code examples (30%), logical justification of ranking (25%), quality of written recommendation (20%). Success requires scoring 16/20 points with evidence-based reasoning for all judgments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example evaluation of a different function and highlight key phrases for justifications. Pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: add a fifth criterion (scalability) and ask them to modify the lowest-ranked implementation to address its weaknesses, then re-evaluate their changes.

title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMI Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK) matrix, including all 49 project management processes categorized by 10 knowledge areas and 5 process groups. This intensive memorization activity builds foundational recall essential for advanced project management practice and PMP certification preparation.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes by their exact names and categorize each within the correct knowledge area and process group intersection through timed recall exercises
Students will identify and recite the specific inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for 15 critical processes through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing blank 10x5 matrix templates with knowledge areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) listed vertically and process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) horizontally. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study the completed reference matrix, using chunking techniques to group related processes. Encourage mnemonic devices and visualization. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Remove reference materials. Students complete blank matrices in pairs, with partners checking accuracy using provided answer keys. Rotate partnerships every 5 minutes to prevent dependency. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct individual speed rounds where each student must fill a blank matrix within 8 minutes. Track completion time and accuracy percentage. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Select 15 critical processes (provided list includes Plan Schedule Management, Control Costs, Manage Quality, etc.). Students must recite from memory the specific ITTO (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) elements for each process when called upon randomly. Use rapid-fire questioning format. Phase 5 (5 minutes): Final verification round where students self-assess their completed matrices against the master key, calculating accuracy percentages and identifying knowledge gaps for future study.
materials_needed: Blank PMBOK matrix templates (10x5 grid, one per student plus extras)
Complete PMBOK 7th Edition process matrix reference sheets
ITTO reference cards for 15 critical processes
Digital timer with audible alerts
Red pens for self-assessment marking
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the final matrix completion (44/49 processes correctly placed) within the 8-minute time limit. ITTO recall assessment requires correct identification of at least 2 inputs, 2 tools/techniques, and 2 outputs for each of the 15 critical processes when questioned. Provide immediate feedback with percentage scores and specific error identification for remediation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made acronym cards (e.g., 'I SCREAM' for Integration knowledge area processes) and allow additional 2-minute time extensions initially. Create color-coded matrices grouping similar processes. For advanced learners: Add challenge round requiring recall of process interdependencies and predecessor/successor relationships. Include memorization of specific page references from PMBOK Guide for each process.

title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Memorization Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMI Project Management Process Groups and Knowledge Areas matrix, including all 49 individual processes with their exact names and classifications. This foundational knowledge exercise prepares students for advanced project management certification and real-world application.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 10 PMI Knowledge Areas and their associated processes by completing timed identification exercises without reference materials
Students will identify the correct Process Group classification for each of the 49 PMI processes through systematic memorization and retrieval practice
instructions: Begin by providing students with the complete PMI Process Groups and Knowledge Areas matrix (5 Process Groups × 10 Knowledge Areas = 49 processes). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study the matrix, focusing on memorizing process names, spellings, and their exact placement. Emphasize critical processes like 'Develop Project Management Plan' (Planning/Integration) and 'Control Quality' (Monitoring & Controlling/Quality). Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement spaced repetition using flashcards. Students work in pairs, with one person showing Knowledge Area cards while the partner recites all associated processes and their Process Groups. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct individual timed recall sessions. Provide blank matrix templates where students must fill in all 49 processes within 12 minutes. No reference materials allowed. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Verification and correction phase. Students exchange papers and check answers against the master matrix. Mark incorrect spellings, misplaced processes, and omissions. Students must achieve 90% accuracy (44/49 correct) to pass. Phase 5 (5 minutes): Immediate retry for students below threshold, focusing on their specific error patterns identified in Phase 4.
materials_needed: PMI PMBOK Guide 7th Edition Process Groups and Knowledge Areas matrix (printed copies)
Blank matrix templates (2 copies per student)
Process flashcards with Knowledge Areas on front, processes on back
Timer/stopwatch for timed exercises
Red pens for peer correction
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (44 out of 49 processes correct) on the blank matrix completion within 12 minutes. Scoring criteria: 1 point for correct process name in correct Knowledge Area/Process Group intersection, 0.5 points deducted for spelling errors, 0 points for wrong placement or omission. Final scores recorded as Pass (90%+) or Retry Required (<90%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for each Knowledge Area (e.g., 'I Can Stop Problems Really Quickly' for Integration processes). Break memorization into chunks of 2-3 Knowledge Areas at a time. For advanced learners: Add process input/output memorization, require recall of process definitions, or include process sequencing dependencies within each Knowledge Area.
original_title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Memorization Challenge

title: Deconstructing Leadership Failure: Analyzing the Theranos Case Through Multiple Theoretical Frameworks
description: Students will analyze the Theranos leadership crisis by applying three distinct leadership theories (transformational, ethical, and authentic leadership) to understand how leadership failures manifest across different theoretical perspectives. This expert-level analysis requires synthesizing complex theoretical knowledge with real-world case evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational, ethical, and authentic leadership theories by identifying specific theoretical components violated in the Theranos case
Students will interpret leadership failure patterns through comparative analysis of how each theoretical framework explains different aspects of the crisis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5, assigning each group one of three leadership theories: transformational leadership (Bass & Riggio), ethical leadership (Brown & Treviño), or authentic leadership (Avolio & Gardner). Provide each group with the comprehensive Theranos case study materials and their assigned theory's core research articles (20 minutes reading time). 

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Groups create a detailed analysis matrix identifying specific instances where Elizabeth Holmes' leadership violated their assigned theory's core principles. They must cite specific case evidence and connect it to theoretical concepts using academic terminology. Each violation must include: the theoretical principle, the contradicting behavior/decision, specific evidence from the case, and the theoretical explanation for why this constitutes a leadership failure.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Groups rotate through 'theory stations' where they examine the other groups' analyses, adding insights about how their assigned theory would additionally explain the leadership failures identified by other frameworks. This creates cross-theoretical understanding.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group presents a 5-minute synthesis explaining how their theory uniquely contributes to understanding the Theranos leadership failure, highlighting aspects that other theories might miss or under-emphasize.

Conclude with a 15-minute instructor-led discussion comparing how each theoretical lens reveals different dimensions of leadership failure, emphasizing that expert-level leadership understanding requires multi-theoretical perspective-taking.
materials_needed: Theranos comprehensive case study (John Carreyrou's 'Bad Blood' excerpts and SEC documents)
Bass & Riggio transformational leadership theory summary and key research articles
Brown & Treviño ethical leadership framework and measurement scales
Avolio & Gardner authentic leadership theory and core components
Analysis matrix templates with theory-specific prompting questions
Flipchart paper and markers for station rotations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric measuring: (1) Theoretical accuracy - correct identification and application of theory components (25%), (2) Evidence integration - specific, relevant case connections to theoretical violations (25%), (3) Comparative analysis - ability to distinguish how different theories explain different failure aspects (25%), (4) Synthesis quality - demonstrates understanding of multi-theoretical perspective value (25%). Students must achieve proficient level (3/4) on all criteria, with at least advanced (4/4) on two criteria for expert-level understanding demonstration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide theory application templates with specific prompting questions and case study sections pre-highlighted for relevant evidence. Offer leadership theory comparison charts showing key differences. For advanced learners, challenge them to identify theoretical gaps or contradictions, propose integration of additional leadership theories (servant, adaptive leadership), or develop original theoretical insights about leadership failure patterns that emerge from cross-theoretical analysis.

title: Programming Vocabulary Flashcard Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental programming terminology through structured flashcard practice and peer testing. This activity focuses on building essential vocabulary recognition for basic programming concepts including data types, operators, and control structures.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and define 20 essential programming terms including variables, integers, strings, loops, and functions by completing flashcard memorization exercises
Students will recall the correct definitions of programming vocabulary terms through timed peer quizzing activities with 80% accuracy
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets containing 20 fundamental programming terms (variables, integer, string, boolean, loop, function, array, conditional, syntax, algorithm, debugging, compiler, variable declaration, assignment operator, comparison operator, iteration, parameter, argument, return value, and comment). Each flashcard shows the term on one side and definition on the reverse. 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to study their flashcards using the 'look-cover-recall' method. They read the term, study the definition for 10 seconds, cover it, then attempt to recite the definition aloud. They repeat this process for each card, cycling through the entire set three times.

Phase 2 (10 minutes): Pair students and have them take turns as 'quizzer' and 'responder.' The quizzer shows only the term side of each flashcard while the responder provides the definition. Partners switch roles after completing all 20 cards once.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Conduct a whole-class rapid-fire review where you display terms on the board and students write definitions on paper within 30 seconds per term. Select 10 terms randomly from the original 20.

Phase 4 (5 minutes): Students self-assess by checking their written definitions against the official flashcard definitions, marking correct and incorrect responses for personal tracking.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (one per student, 20 cards each)
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projector for displaying terms
Paper and pencils for written responses
Answer key with official definitions
assessment_method: Students receive credit based on their Phase 3 written quiz performance (80% = 16/20 correct definitions) and completion of all four phases. Use a simple checklist rubric: Full Credit (16+ correct definitions + participated in all phases), Partial Credit (12-15 correct definitions + participated in all phases), Needs Improvement (below 12 correct or incomplete participation).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce flashcard set to 15 most essential terms, provide definition sentence starters, or allow open-book reference during peer quizzing. For advanced learners: Add 10 additional intermediate terms (polymorphism, recursion, scope, etc.), require them to create original example sentences using each term, or have them create new flashcards for next class.

title: Optimizing Manufacturing Efficiency Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will formulate objective functions, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal solutions using both graphical and algebraic methods.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-variable manufacturing scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal production quantities that maximize profit while respecting resource limitations
instructions:
Begin by presenting the scenario: TechCorp manufactures two products (smartphones and tablets) with limited resources (assembly time: 480 hours/week, testing time: 240 hours/week, raw materials: $50,000/week). Smartphones require 2 hours assembly, 1.5 hours testing, $80 materials, and yield $200 profit. Tablets require 3 hours assembly, 1 hour testing, $120 materials, and yield $300 profit. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students work in pairs to identify decision variables (x = smartphones, y = tablets) and write the objective function (Maximize P = 200x + 300y). 

Step 2 (20 minutes): Have students formulate constraints: 2x + 3y ≤ 480 (assembly), 1.5x + y ≤ 240 (testing), 80x + 120y ≤ 50,000 (materials), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. 

Step 3 (25 minutes): Students graph the feasible region on coordinate planes, finding intersection points of constraint lines. They must identify corner points: (0,0), (0,160), (120,80), (160,0), and (0,416.67) but check feasibility against all constraints. 

Step 4 (20 minutes): Students evaluate the objective function at each feasible corner point to determine the optimal solution. They should find the maximum occurs at (120,80) yielding P = $48,000. 

Step 5 (15 minutes): Students verify their solution using sensitivity analysis, determining how changes in constraints affect the optimal solution. 

Step 6 (10 minutes): Pairs present their optimal production plan and justify their mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: Graph paper or coordinate plane worksheets
Graphing calculators or GeoGebra software access
Printed scenario handouts with constraint data
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint line graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphical representation of feasible region with labeled corner points (25%), (3) Correct calculation of optimal solution with verification (35%), (4) Clear mathematical communication and justification of results (15%). Students must submit their graphs, calculations, and a written recommendation memo.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint inequality templates and step-by-step graphing guides. Offer additional practice with simpler two-constraint problems first. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis questions like 'What happens if assembly time increases by 10%?' or extend to three-variable problems requiring simplex tableau method.

title: Analyzing Multi-Variable Factors in Projectile Motion Through Experimental Data Decomposition
description: Students analyze real experimental data from projectile motion trials with varying launch angles, initial velocities, and air resistance conditions. They decompose the motion into component vectors, identify patterns in trajectory deviations, and determine which variables most significantly impact range and flight time accuracy.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relative impact of launch angle, initial velocity, and air resistance on projectile motion accuracy by examining multi-variable experimental datasets
Students will decompose complex projectile trajectories into component motions through mathematical separation of kinematic variables and error analysis
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4. Distribute Dataset A containing 60 projectile motion trials with recorded launch angles (15°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 75°), initial velocities (10-50 m/s), and air resistance coefficients (0, 0.1, 0.3 kg/m). Each team receives different target distances (50m, 100m, 150m). Step 1 (20 min): Students plot actual vs. theoretical trajectories using provided graphing software, identifying systematic deviations. Step 2 (25 min): Teams calculate horizontal and vertical velocity components for each trial, then determine percentage errors between experimental and theoretical values. Step 3 (30 min): Students create correlation matrices analyzing relationships between input variables (angle, velocity, air resistance) and outcome variables (range accuracy, flight time, maximum height). Step 4 (20 min): Teams identify which variable combinations produce <5% error from theoretical predictions and which exceed 20% error. Step 5 (25 min): Students generate heat maps showing optimal parameter combinations for their assigned target distances. Step 6 (15 min): Each team presents their analysis, explaining which factors most critically affect accuracy and why certain angle-velocity combinations perform better under specific air resistance conditions. Conclude with teams comparing findings across different target distances.
materials_needed: Experimental projectile motion dataset with 60+ trials (CSV format)
Graphing software (Excel, Python matplotlib, or similar)
Scientific calculators
Correlation analysis templates
Heat map generation software or graph paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of component velocity calculations and error analysis (25%), (2) Quality of correlation analysis identifying key variable relationships (25%), (3) Correct interpretation of data patterns and deviation explanations (30%), (4) Clear presentation of optimal parameter combinations with scientific reasoning (20%). Students must demonstrate understanding of how each variable independently and collectively affects projectile motion accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated theoretical values and focus on pattern recognition rather than complex calculations. Offer guiding questions like 'Which trials had the largest range errors?' For advanced learners: Include additional variables like projectile mass variations or crosswind effects, and ask them to develop predictive models for untested parameter combinations.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Reporting Systems for a Small Business
description: Students will evaluate three different bug tracking systems (GitHub Issues, Trello, and Jira) by analyzing their features, usability, and suitability for a fictional small software company. They will create a detailed recommendation report justifying their choice based on specific evaluation criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three bug tracking systems by comparing features, pricing, and usability against established criteria to determine the best solution for a specific business context
Students will critique the strengths and weaknesses of different software tools through hands-on exploration and systematic comparison analysis
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 2-3. Provide each group with the scenario: 'DevStart Solutions is a 5-person software company building mobile apps. They need a bug tracking system that costs under $50/month, integrates with their existing tools (Slack, VS Code), and is easy for non-technical clients to use when reporting bugs.' 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups create evaluation criteria weighted by importance (cost 20%, ease of use 30%, integration capabilities 25%, reporting features 25%). 

Step 2 (45 minutes): Each group explores all three platforms using provided demo accounts. They must create a sample bug report in each system, test integration features, and document user interface observations using the provided evaluation worksheet.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Groups complete comparison matrices, rating each platform 1-5 on their established criteria. They calculate weighted scores and identify the top choice.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each group creates a 2-page recommendation report including: executive summary, detailed comparison table, pros/cons analysis, final recommendation with justification, and implementation timeline.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Groups present 5-minute recommendations to the class, defending their choice against questions about alternative options and addressing potential weaknesses in their selection.
materials_needed: Demo accounts for GitHub Issues, Trello, and Jira
Evaluation worksheet template with comparison matrix
Business scenario handout with company requirements
Computers with internet access
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Completeness of evaluation criteria (25%) - all platforms thoroughly tested, (2) Quality of analysis (30%) - logical reasoning and evidence-based conclusions, (3) Justification strength (25%) - clear defense of choice with consideration of alternatives, (4) Professional presentation (20%) - clear communication and response to questions. Students must score 3/4 in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made evaluation criteria and guided questions for each platform exploration. Offer templates for the comparison matrix. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research additional tools (Asana, Monday.com) or consider advanced features like API capabilities, custom workflows, and scalability for company growth.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Memory Matrix
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific formulas, calculations, and terminology used in Critical Path Method analysis for complex project scheduling. This activity focuses on precise retention of forward pass, backward pass, and float calculation formulas through structured repetition and testing.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), and Late Finish (LF) calculations by completing timed formula identification exercises
Students will identify and define all CPM terminology including Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, and Critical Path through systematic memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet containing 12 core formulas (ES = max EF of predecessors, EF = ES + Duration, LF = min LS of successors, LS = LF - Duration, Total Float = LF - EF or LS - ES, Free Float = min ES of successors - EF, etc.). Students have 15 minutes to study the sheet intensively. Remove reference sheets and conduct Round 1: Display 8 incomplete formulas on screen (e.g., 'Total Float = __ - __ or __ - __'). Students write complete formulas in 5 minutes. Collect responses and immediately provide correct answers. Redistribute reference sheets for 10 additional minutes of focused study. Conduct Round 2: Present 15 definition prompts (e.g., 'The calculation that determines the latest an activity can start without delaying the project'). Students write corresponding terms and formulas in 8 minutes. After collecting responses, facilitate 5-minute peer checking session where students compare answers with partners. Conclude with Round 3: Rapid-fire oral quiz where individual students must state specific formula components when given scenarios (e.g., 'Activity B has predecessors A and C. A's EF is 5, C's EF is 8. What is B's ES and what formula did you use?'). Each student answers 2-3 questions maximum. Record accuracy rates for each student across all three rounds.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet (printed, one per student)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for displaying incomplete formulas
Individual response sheets (3 different versions for each round)
Answer key with all 12 formulas and 20 key definitions
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy across all three rounds to demonstrate mastery. Round 1: 8 formula completions (6.8/8 required). Round 2: 15 term/formula identifications (12.75/15 required). Round 3: Individual oral responses graded as correct/incorrect with immediate feedback. Track cumulative scores and require additional practice sessions for students scoring below 85% threshold.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded formula sheets grouping related calculations, extend study time by 5 minutes between rounds, and allow use of mnemonic devices during memorization. For advanced learners: Include additional complex formulas like Resource-Constrained Critical Path calculations, add time pressure reduction challenges, and require explanation of when each formula variant should be applied in different project contexts.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Comparative Analysis of Executive Decision-Making Frameworks
description: Students will analyze and compare how different CEOs applied contrasting leadership theories during major organizational crises, identifying the underlying decision-making frameworks and their outcomes. This activity develops deep comprehension of how theoretical leadership models manifest in high-stakes real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, situational, and authentic leadership approaches by analyzing their application in three documented crisis scenarios
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership theory and practical decision-making outcomes through structured case comparison methodology
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4.
