Distribute three detailed crisis case studies: Reed Hastings (Netflix) during the Qwikster transition crisis (2011), Mary Barra (GM) during the ignition switch recall crisis (2014), and Brian Chesky (Airbnb) during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis (2020). Each group receives identical materials including crisis timelines, leadership decision documentation, and theoretical framework reference sheets covering transformational, situational, and authentic leadership models. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Groups conduct parallel analysis of all three cases, using provided analytical matrices to map specific leader behaviors against theoretical frameworks. Students must identify at least 5 concrete decisions per leader and categorize them by leadership approach, noting supporting evidence from documented statements, actions, and outcomes.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups create comparative visualization charts showing how each leader's approach evolved throughout their crisis timeline. They must identify patterns in decision-making speed, stakeholder communication style, and adaptation strategies.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Each group presents their findings to two other groups in rotation, defending their theoretical classifications with specific evidence. Listeners challenge interpretations and suggest alternative framework applications.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Groups synthesize feedback and finalize their analysis reports, including a section on contextual factors that influenced each leader's approach selection. Conclude with individual reflection submissions on which theoretical framework proved most adaptable across different crisis contexts.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis case study packets with primary source documentation
Leadership theory reference sheets (transformational, situational, authentic leadership)
Analytical matrix templates for behavior mapping
Large format paper for visualization charts
Colored markers or digital presentation tools
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical framework identification with specific behavioral evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing pattern recognition across cases (25%), (3) Depth of interpretation regarding context-theory relationships (25%), (4) Clarity and defense of classifications during peer presentations (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly linking at least 12 of 15 total leadership decisions to appropriate theoretical frameworks with supporting rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted key decision points in cases and simplified theory comparison charts. Offer sentence starters for analysis statements. For advanced learners, include additional micro-decisions within each crisis and challenge them to identify hybrid approaches or theory limitations. Provide supplementary readings on contingency leadership theory for deeper analysis.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with Security Groups
description: Students will launch an EC2 instance, configure security groups for web traffic, and deploy a simple web application to demonstrate practical cloud server management. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS concepts through real-world application deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web server by launching and configuring an AWS EC2 instance with appropriate security settings
Students will apply security group rules through creating custom inbound/outbound traffic policies for web applications
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute demonstration of the AWS Management Console interface. Divide students into pairs and provide each team with AWS Academy Learner Lab credentials. Students first navigate to EC2 Dashboard and click 'Launch Instance'. Guide them to select Amazon Linux 2 AMI (free tier) and t2.micro instance type. In Step 3 (Configure Instance), students add this User Data script in Advanced Details: '#!/bin/bash yum update -y yum install -y httpd systemctl start httpd systemctl enable httpd echo "

Hello from [Student Name]'s Server

" > /var/www/html/index.html'. For Step 6 (Security Groups), students create new security group named '[TeamName]-WebServer-SG' with rules: SSH (port 22) from My IP, and HTTP (port 80) from Anywhere. Students launch instance and wait 5 minutes for initialization. They then test deployment by accessing the public IP address in browser to verify their custom webpage displays. Next, students modify security groups by temporarily removing HTTP rule, testing access (should fail), then re-adding rule to confirm functionality returns. Finally, teams document their instance details including Instance ID, Public IP, Security Group settings, and take screenshots of successful webpage and security group configurations. Conclude with 15-minute peer review where teams present their deployed applications and security configurations.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts with EC2 access
Computers with web browsers and internet access
Provided User Data script template for web server installation
Worksheet for documenting instance configurations and IP addresses
assessment_method: Success measured by functional checklist: (1) EC2 instance running with correct AMI/instance type (25%), (2) Custom security group with proper HTTP/SSH rules (25%), (3) Web application accessible via public IP showing personalized content (25%), (4) Completed documentation worksheet with screenshots and configuration details (25%). Students must demonstrate live webpage access to instructor for full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written User Data scripts and step-by-step screenshot guide for security group creation. Create 'buddy system' pairing advanced students with beginners. For advanced learners: Add challenges like configuring custom ports, implementing HTTPS with self-signed certificates, or deploying applications from GitHub repositories using additional User Data commands.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, HSRP redundancy, port security, and DHCP services. This capstone activity requires students to create original network designs that meet specific business requirements while implementing advanced Cisco technologies.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed implementation plans with IP addressing schemes and security policies
Students will create a fully functional enterprise network through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers using advanced protocols including HSRP, VTP, and 802.1Q trunking
instructions: **Phase 1: Design (45 minutes)** - Present students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 200 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, IT) requiring network segmentation and redundancy. Students work in pairs to create network diagrams using draw.io, defining: VLAN structure (minimum 4 VLANs plus management), IP addressing scheme using /24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16, redundant gateway design with HSRP, and security requirements document. **Phase 2: Physical Setup (30 minutes)** - Each pair receives 2 Cisco 2960 switches, 2 Cisco 2911 routers, and 4 PCs. Students cable their topology according to their design, ensuring trunk links between switches and routers for HSRP implementation. **Phase 3: Configuration (90 minutes)** - Students configure switch VLANs, trunking (802.1Q), and VTP domain. Next, configure inter-VLAN routing on both routers with HSRP for gateway redundancy (Router 1 priority 110, Router 2 priority 100). Implement port security on access ports (maximum 2 MAC addresses, violation mode restrict). Configure DHCP pools for each VLAN on the primary router with appropriate exclusions. **Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (30 minutes)** - Students test connectivity between VLANs, verify HSRP failover by disconnecting primary router, confirm port security by connecting unauthorized device, and document all configurations with 'show run' outputs. Create troubleshooting log showing resolution of any connectivity issues encountered.
materials_needed: 2 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per student pair
2 Cisco ISR 2911 routers per student pair
4 Windows/Linux PCs for endpoint testing
Ethernet cables (8 per pair: 4 access, 2 trunk, 2 router interconnect)
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Packet Tracer or GNS3 software as backup environment
Network diagram template (draw.io or Visio)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Network Design (25%) - logical VLAN segmentation, proper IP addressing, HSRP implementation plan; Configuration Accuracy (40%) - all VLANs functional, HSRP working with proper priorities, port security active, DHCP distributing addresses; Testing Documentation (20%) - comprehensive connectivity tests, successful HSRP failover demonstration, port security violation evidence; Professional Documentation (15%) - complete configuration backups, network diagram accuracy, troubleshooting log quality. Students must achieve 85% overall with no category below 70% to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured VLAN templates and IP addressing worksheets, allow use of Packet Tracer for initial design validation before physical implementation, pair with stronger students for peer mentoring. For advanced learners: Add OSPF routing protocol between routers, implement ACLs for inter-VLAN security policies, configure SNMP monitoring, or add wireless controller integration with guest VLAN isolation. Provide Cisco documentation references rather than step-by-step commands to encourage independent problem-solving.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, spanning tree protocol, HSRP redundancy, and advanced security features. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize multiple networking concepts into a cohesive, production-ready network design.
learning_objectives: Students will design a multi-VLAN network topology with redundant paths by creating detailed network diagrams and IP addressing schemes that meet specific business requirements
Students will implement advanced Cisco switching and routing protocols through hands-on configuration of VLANs, STP, HSRP, and security features on physical or simulated equipment
instructions: Begin by providing students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp needs a network for 200 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest) with specific security and redundancy requirements. Students work in teams of 2-3. Phase 1 (60 minutes): Teams create a comprehensive network design including: physical topology diagram showing 4 switches and 2 routers in redundant configuration, VLAN assignment plan (Sales-VLAN10, Engineering-VLAN20, HR-VLAN30, Guest-VLAN40), IP addressing scheme using 192.168.0.0/16 with appropriate subnetting, and security requirements matrix. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment, teams implement their design by configuring VLANs on access switches, setting up trunk links between switches, configuring Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol with designated root bridges, implementing inter-VLAN routing on Layer 3 switches, setting up HSRP for gateway redundancy with primary/backup roles, and applying port security, DHCP snooping, and access control lists. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Teams test connectivity between VLANs, verify redundancy by simulating link failures, document all configurations with running-config exports, and create a network maintenance guide. Each team presents their solution in a 10-minute presentation demonstrating live network functionality and explaining design decisions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or physical lab with 4 Cisco switches (2960 or higher) and 2 routers (2911 or higher)
Network topology templates and IP addressing worksheets
Company scenario handout with specific business requirements
Configuration checklists and verification command reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, security plan completeness), Technical Implementation (40 points - correct VLAN configuration, working inter-VLAN routing, functional redundancy protocols, effective security measures), Testing and Verification (20 points - connectivity tests pass, redundancy demonstration successful, performance metrics documented), Professional Presentation (15 points - clear explanation of design choices, effective demonstration of network functionality, quality of maintenance documentation)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates, offer guided worksheets for IP addressing calculations, and allow use of simplified topology with fewer VLANs. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Add Quality of Service (QoS) configuration requirements, implement dynamic routing protocols (OSPF/EIGRP), incorporate wireless access points with controller-based management, or add network monitoring with SNMP configuration.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy: Exercise 2
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, HSRP redundancy, port security, and DHCP services. They will create network documentation, implement the design using Cisco Packet Tracer, and present their solution addressing specific business requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network architecture by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco technologies through configuring switches, routers, HSRP, VLANs, and security features in a simulated enterprise environment
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Present students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp needs a network for 200+ employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest). Distribute requirement sheets specifying: VLAN segregation needed, guest network isolation, redundant gateway requirement, and security policies. Students test connectivity between VLANs, verify HSRP failover functionality, and confirm port security violations trigger properly.

**Phase 3 (30 minutes):** Teams prepare 10-minute presentations including network diagram overview, VLAN design rationale, IP addressing scheme explanation, HSRP configuration demonstration, security implementation details, and troubleshooting scenarios they resolved. Each presentation must include a live demonstration of failover testing and inter-VLAN communication verification.

Business requirement handout with TechCorp scenario details
Network diagramming software (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart access)
HSRP configuration reference guide
Presentation projection system

Minimum 3.0 average required for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide VLAN configuration templates, offer pre-configured base topology, assign peer mentors for Phase 2 implementation. title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Redundancy: Exercise 3
description: Students will design a complete enterprise network topology from scratch, implementing VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, HSRP redundancy, and advanced security features. They will create network documentation, configure all devices, and troubleshoot connectivity issues to demonstrate mastery of enterprise networking concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable enterprise network topology by integrating VLANs, redundant gateways, and security policies based on business requirements
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco technologies through hands-on configuration of switches, routers, and security features in a simulated enterprise environment
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: 'TechCorp has 200 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest) requiring network segmentation and redundancy.' Students work in teams of 2-3 to create a network topology diagram using Packet Tracer, including: minimum 3 switches in a hierarchical design, 2 routers for HSRP redundancy, 4 VLANs with appropriate subnetting (use 192.168.0.0/22), and security zones with ACL requirements.

**Phase 2: Device Configuration (90 minutes)**
Students implement their design in Packet Tracer: Configure VLANs on all switches with appropriate port assignments, set up trunk links with 802.1Q encapsulation, implement STP with manual root bridge selection, configure inter-VLAN routing using router-on-a-stick, establish HSRP between routers (Virtual IP: 192.168.0.1), and create extended ACLs to restrict inter-VLAN communication (HR VLAN cannot access Engineering, Guest VLAN restricted to internet only).

Teams create comprehensive network documentation including IP addressing scheme, VLAN assignments, ACL policies, and configuration commands used. Test connectivity between all VLANs, verify HSRP failover by shutting down primary router, confirm ACL restrictions are working, and document all test results with screenshots.

**Phase 4: Presentation (15 minutes per team)**
Each team presents their network design, demonstrates live configurations, explains design decisions and security implementations, and answers instructor questions about troubleshooting scenarios.

Pre-created company scenario handout with specific requirements

Evaluation rubric printouts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - topology appropriateness, scalability, documentation clarity; Technical Implementation (40 points) - correct VLAN configuration, working HSRP, functional ACLs, proper subnetting; Problem-Solving Skills (20 points) - troubleshooting approach, configuration efficiency; Presentation Quality (15 points) - technical explanation accuracy, ability to answer questions. Students must achieve 80% minimum score and demonstrate live failover functionality to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic switch/router setup, offer VLAN configuration cheat sheets, pair with stronger technical partners. For advanced learners: Add requirements for OSPF routing protocol implementation, integrate wireless access points with WPA2-Enterprise, implement port security with MAC address limiting, or add network monitoring with SNMP configuration. Provide additional scenarios with more complex ACL requirements.

title: Optimizing Package Delivery Routes Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world logistics optimization problem by formulating constraints, creating objective functions, and using the simplex method to find optimal delivery routes. This activity integrates multiple mathematical concepts including systems of inequalities, optimization theory, and matrix operations to solve a complex multi-variable problem.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to formulate a delivery optimization problem by translating real-world constraints into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will execute the simplex method algorithm to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic pivot operations and tableau manipulations
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the logistics scenario: 'Metro Delivery Company has 3 distribution centers (A, B, C) and must deliver to 4 zones with specific capacity, cost, and time constraints.' Provide constraint data sheets showing vehicle capacities (Center A: 200 packages/day, B: 150 packages/day, C: 180 packages/day), delivery costs per zone, and minimum delivery requirements per zone. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (25 minutes):** Teams define decision variables (x₁₁, x₁₂... representing packages from center i to zone j), write the objective function to minimize total delivery costs, and formulate constraint inequalities for capacity limits and demand requirements. Students must identify at least 7 constraints including non-negativity conditions.

**Phase 2 - Simplex Method Application (35 minutes):** Using provided simplex tableau templates, teams convert their problem to standard form by adding slack variables, create the initial tableau, and perform pivot operations. Students must show each iteration step, identify entering/leaving variables, and calculate new tableau values. Provide calculators and encourage systematic checking of arithmetic.

**Phase 3 - Solution Interpretation (15 minutes):** Teams identify the optimal solution from their final tableau, calculate total minimum cost, and determine exact package allocations for each center-to-zone route. Students prepare a brief presentation of their optimization strategy and results.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Teams present key findings, compare optimal solutions across groups, and discuss real-world applications of linear programming in logistics, manufacturing, and resource management.
materials_needed: Logistics scenario handout with specific numerical constraints and costs
Simplex tableau templates (printed worksheets)
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for constraint visualization
Presentation boards or large paper sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Problem formulation accuracy - correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints (25%), (2) Simplex method execution - proper tableau setup and pivot operations (35%), (3) Solution accuracy - correct optimal values and cost calculation (25%), (4) Real-world interpretation - logical explanation of results and business implications (15%). Students must submit completed tableaux showing all iteration steps and a written summary of their optimal delivery strategy.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide partially completed constraint equations as examples, offer a step-by-step pivot operation checklist, and assign stronger math students as peer tutors within teams. Consider allowing use of linear programming software for verification after manual calculations. **Extension for advanced learners:** Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking students to determine how changes in capacity or costs affect the optimal solution, or add integer programming constraints requiring whole vehicle assignments.

title: Code Review Showdown: Evaluating Bug-Prone JavaScript Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written JavaScript functions containing common beginner errors and security vulnerabilities. They will rank code samples from best to worst, justify their decisions, and propose specific improvements using established coding standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate JavaScript code quality by analyzing syntax errors, logic flaws, and security vulnerabilities against industry best practices
Students will critique and rank multiple code implementations through systematic comparison using a provided evaluation rubric
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into pairs. Distribute printed Code Review Packet containing 5 JavaScript functions (each solving the same problem: user input validation) with varying quality levels. Provide Code Quality Rubric handout.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student silently reviews all 5 code samples, identifying specific issues using the rubric categories: syntax correctness, logic flow, security practices, readability, and efficiency. Students mark problems directly on printouts and take notes.

**Pair Discussion (15 minutes):** Partners compare findings and collaborate to rank the 5 functions from highest to lowest quality. They must reach consensus and document 3 specific reasons for each ranking decision.

**Evaluation Report (20 minutes):** Pairs complete a structured evaluation form for each function, including: overall quality score (1-10), top 3 strengths, top 3 weaknesses, security risk level (high/medium/low), and specific improvement recommendations with line numbers.

**Gallery Walk Presentations (15 minutes):** Each pair posts their rankings on classroom walls. Students circulate to view other teams' evaluations, noting major disagreements or insights.

**Debrief Discussion (10 minutes):** Instructor reveals the 'expert rankings' and facilitates discussion about evaluation criteria differences, common blind spots in code review, and real-world implications of code quality decisions.
materials_needed: Code Review Packet with 5 pre-written JavaScript functions (printed)
Code Quality Evaluation Rubric handout
Structured Evaluation Forms (one per code sample)
Large sticky notes for gallery walk
Markers or pens
assessment_method: Grade evaluation forms using 4-point scale: 4=Identifies all major issues and provides specific, actionable improvements; 3=Identifies most issues with good improvement suggestions; 2=Identifies some issues but improvements are vague; 1=Misses major issues or provides irrelevant feedback. Minimum passing: correctly identify at least 70% of planted errors and rank highest/lowest quality samples accurately.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted copies marking where to look for specific error types, offer one-on-one guidance during individual analysis phase. For advanced learners: Include additional functions with subtle performance issues or design pattern problems, ask them to research and propose alternative implementation approaches using different coding paradigms.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard with Actionable Insights
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn using real e-commerce data, combining multiple analytical techniques to generate business recommendations. They will synthesize descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and data visualization to produce a comprehensive decision-support tool for business stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-layered analytical dashboard by integrating exploratory data analysis, predictive modeling, and interactive visualizations
Students will synthesize statistical insights and machine learning predictions through creating actionable business recommendations with supporting data evidence
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Preparation (20 minutes)** Provide students with the Kaggle E-commerce Customer Dataset containing 5,000 records with variables including customer demographics, purchase history, website behavior, and churn status. Students import data into Tableau/Power BI and perform initial cleaning: handle missing values, create calculated fields for customer lifetime value and days since last purchase. **Phase 2: Exploratory Analysis Creation (25 minutes)** Students build 4 foundational visualizations: customer segmentation scatter plot (CLV vs. purchase frequency), churn rate by demographic heatmap, time-series trend of monthly churn rates, and correlation matrix of behavioral factors. Each visualization must include appropriate filters and formatting. **Phase 3: Predictive Model Integration (30 minutes)** Using the dataset's features, students create a simple logistic regression model in Excel/Google Sheets or import pre-calculated churn probability scores. They build a risk scoring system categorizing customers into High (>70%), Medium (30-70%), and Low (<30%) churn risk segments. **Phase 4: Dashboard Assembly (35 minutes)** Students combine all elements into a single interactive dashboard featuring: executive summary with key metrics, customer risk segmentation table with drill-down capability, predictive insights panel showing top churn indicators, and recommendation engine suggesting retention strategies for each risk segment. **Phase 5: Business Recommendations (10 minutes)** Students create a one-page executive summary documenting three specific, data-driven retention strategies with projected ROI calculations based on their analysis.
materials_needed: E-commerce Customer Dataset (CSV file with 5,000+ records)
Tableau Public, Power BI Desktop, or Google Data Studio access
Laptops/computers with internet connectivity
Dashboard template worksheet for organization
Executive summary template (provided)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Technical execution - dashboard functionality, visual design, and data accuracy (25%), (2) Analytical depth - appropriate use of statistical methods and model interpretation (25%), (3) Business insight quality - relevance and feasibility of recommendations (25%), (4) Dashboard usability - intuitive navigation and stakeholder-appropriate design (15%), (5) Executive summary clarity - concise communication of key findings and ROI projections (10%). Students must demonstrate working dashboard functionality and present 3-minute pitch to simulated business stakeholders.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-built dashboard template with placeholder charts that need data connections and formatting. Offer step-by-step video tutorials for basic Tableau/Power BI functions. Create peer partnerships for technical troubleshooting. **For advanced students:** Challenge them to incorporate additional external datasets (economic indicators, competitor data), implement advanced statistical techniques (decision trees, clustering), or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Encourage A/B testing framework design for recommendation validation.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard with Actionable Insights: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn using real e-commerce data, incorporating multiple visualization types and statistical models. They will design their own analytical framework, build predictive models, and present actionable business recommendations through a comprehensive dashboard interface.
learning_objectives: Students will design a complete analytical framework for customer churn prediction by combining exploratory data analysis, statistical modeling, and interactive visualizations
Students will create an original dashboard interface that synthesizes multiple data sources and presents actionable business insights through custom visualizations and predictive analytics
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Framework Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the e-commerce customer dataset containing 12 months of transaction data, customer demographics, and engagement metrics. Students work in pairs to explore the data using Python/Pandas, identifying key variables that might predict churn (customers with no purchases in last 90 days). They must create their own analytical framework by defining churn criteria, selecting 5-7 key predictor variables, and sketching their dashboard layout on paper.

**Phase 2: Model Development (60 minutes)**
Students build and compare three different predictive models: logistic regression, decision tree, and random forest using scikit-learn. They must evaluate model performance using confusion matrices, ROC curves, and accuracy metrics. Students document which model performs best and why, then create feature importance rankings to understand which factors most influence churn.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (90 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students design and build an interactive dashboard with five required components: (1) executive summary with key churn statistics, (2) customer segmentation visualization, (3) predictive model results with confidence intervals, (4) trend analysis showing churn patterns over time, and (5) actionable recommendations panel. Dashboard must include at least three interactive filters and two drill-down capabilities.

**Phase 4: Business Insights & Presentation Prep (30 minutes)**
Students prepare a 5-minute presentation focusing on their top 3 business recommendations based on their analysis. They must justify each recommendation using specific data points from their dashboard and estimate potential revenue impact of implementing their suggestions.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset with 10,000+ records (CSV format)

Create checkpoint reviews after each phase with instructor feedback. description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn risk and generates specific business recommendations using real e-commerce data. learning_objectives: Students will design a predictive analytics dashboard by integrating multiple data sources, calculating churn probability scores, and creating interactive visualizations

instructions:

title: PMI-ACP Agile Practice Standards Memorization Challenge
description: Students will systematically memorize and recall 50 specific Agile practice standards from the PMI Agile Certified Practitioner (PMI-ACP) framework using spaced repetition flashcards. This activity focuses on exact recall of practice definitions, associated knowledge and skills areas, and their corresponding Agile methodologies.
estimated_duration: 45 minutes per session, recommend 5 sessions over 2 weeks
learning_objectives: Students will recall verbatim definitions of all 50 PMI-ACP practice standards by completing timed flashcard sessions with 95% accuracy
Students will identify the correct knowledge and skills area for each practice standard through rapid-fire matching exercises
instructions: Begin by providing students with a master list of 50 PMI-ACP practice standards organized into seven knowledge and skills areas: Agile Principles and Mindset (7 practices), Value-driven Delivery (8 practices), Stakeholder Engagement (5 practices), Team Performance (8 practices), Adaptive Planning (7 practices), Problem Detection and Resolution (7 practices), and Continuous Improvement (8 practices). Students create physical flashcards with practice names on front and exact PMI definitions on back, including associated methodology tags (Scrum, Kanban, XP, etc.). Implement a structured 45-minute session: Minutes 1-15, students review all 50 cards individually, reading aloud three times each. Minutes 16-25, pair students for reciprocal testing using the Leitner system - correctly recalled cards move to 'mastered' pile, incorrect cards return to 'review' pile. Minutes 26-35, conduct rapid-fire individual assessment where instructor calls out practice names and students must state complete definition within 15 seconds. Minutes 36-40, students complete written matching exercise connecting each practice to its knowledge area without reference materials. Final 5 minutes involves self-assessment where students identify their three weakest areas for focused review. Track individual progress using a digital spreadsheet showing daily accuracy rates for each knowledge area. Students must achieve 95% accuracy on all seven categories before advancing to application-level activities.
materials_needed: PMI-ACP Practice Standards Reference Guide (printed copies)
Blank index cards (100 per student)
Digital timer/stopwatch
Individual progress tracking spreadsheets
Matching exercise worksheets (pre-printed)
assessment_method: Students complete a comprehensive recall test requiring exact verbatim recitation of randomly selected practice definitions (minimum 40 out of 50 practices). Assessment includes: definition accuracy (70%), methodology association accuracy (20%), and knowledge area classification (10%). Passing score is 95% overall with no knowledge area below 90%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling learners, reduce initial load to 25 practices focusing on three knowledge areas, and allow reference to root words during definitions. Advanced learners should additionally memorize historical context for each practice's development and cross-reference similarities between methodologies. Provide mnemonic device worksheets for complex definitions and allow audio recording for auditory learners.

title: Deconstructing Paradoxical Leadership Tensions Through Multi-Stakeholder Case Analysis
description: Students will analyze complex organizational case studies to identify and explain inherent leadership paradoxes (exploration vs. exploitation, autonomy vs. control, cooperation vs. competition). Through systematic stakeholder mapping and tension identification, students will demonstrate deep understanding of how effective leaders navigate competing demands simultaneously rather than choosing binary solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between surface-level management problems and underlying paradoxical tensions by systematically analyzing multi-stakeholder organizational scenarios
Students will explain the interconnected nature of leadership paradoxes through detailed stakeholder impact mapping and tension relationship diagrams
instructions: Begin by distributing three complex case studies featuring different paradoxical leadership scenarios: Netflix's culture of freedom/responsibility, Amazon's customer obsession/cost leadership, and Patagonia's profit/purpose tensions. Divide students into groups of 4-5, assigning each group one case study for 20 minutes of initial analysis. Provide the Paradox Analysis Framework handout containing four analytical steps: (1) Stakeholder identification and mapping, (2) Competing demand extraction, (3) Tension relationship diagramming, and (4) Leadership response categorization. During the analysis phase, students must identify at least 5 distinct stakeholder groups, extract 3-4 competing organizational demands, and create visual tension maps showing how paradoxes interconnect rather than exist in isolation. After analysis, each group presents their findings using the provided template, spending 8 minutes explaining their paradox map and 4 minutes demonstrating how the leader's actions addressed multiple tensions simultaneously. During presentations, non-presenting groups complete peer evaluation forms rating the depth of paradox identification and accuracy of stakeholder impact analysis. Conclude with a 15-minute facilitated discussion comparing paradox patterns across all three cases, focusing on how expert leaders reframe either-or thinking into both-and approaches. Document key insights on a shared digital whiteboard, categorizing findings by paradox type (learning, organizing, performing, belonging) and leadership response strategies.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (Netflix, Amazon, Patagonia leadership scenarios)
Paradox Analysis Framework handout with four-step methodology
Large poster paper and colored markers for tension mapping
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Digital whiteboard access (Miro or Mural)
Presentation template with required analysis sections
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Stakeholder identification completeness and accuracy (25%), (2) Paradox extraction depth showing competing tensions rather than simple problems (35%), (3) Visual tension mapping demonstrating interconnected relationships (25%), and (4) Explanation quality showing understanding of both-and vs. either-or leadership approaches (15%). Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories, with particular emphasis on distinguishing paradoxical tensions from standard business trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-populated stakeholder templates and guiding questions for paradox identification ('What does this stakeholder want that conflicts with others?'). For advanced learners, challenge them to identify second-order paradoxes (paradoxes created by resolving first-order tensions) and connect findings to specific paradoxical leadership theories (Lewis, Schad, Smith frameworks). Provide vocabulary support sheets defining key terms like 'dynamic equilibrium' and 'transcendent integration.'

title: Risk Register Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Comparison
description: Students will analyze three different project risk registers from various industries to identify patterns in risk categorization, probability-impact relationships, and mitigation strategies. They will then compare the effectiveness of different risk response approaches and justify which strategies would be most appropriate for each identified risk.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk probability and impact matrices by examining the relationship between risk ratings and proposed response strategies across multiple project contexts
Students will differentiate between risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) through systematic comparison of real-world risk register examples
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes for setup). Distribute three pre-prepared risk registers: one from an IT software implementation project, one from a construction project, and one from a pharmaceutical product launch. Each register should contain 8-10 risks with varying probability/impact ratings and different response strategies. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze each risk register individually, identifying how risks are categorized (technical, external, organizational, project management) and examining the consistency between probability-impact ratings and chosen response strategies. Students use the provided analysis worksheet to document patterns.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Teams compare response strategies across all three registers, focusing on similar risk types (e.g., resource unavailability, regulatory changes, technology failures). They must identify where different projects chose different response strategies for similar risks and analyze why these differences might be justified based on project context.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Each team selects three risks where they believe the original response strategy was suboptimal. They must justify their analysis using PMI risk management principles and propose alternative strategies, explaining how project context (budget, timeline, industry regulations) influenced their recommendations.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams present one risk analysis to the class, explaining their reasoning for recommending a different response strategy. Other teams can challenge their analysis, creating discussion about risk response trade-offs.

Conclude with instructor-led debrief highlighting key patterns students identified and connecting findings to PMI's risk management framework.
materials_needed: Three realistic project risk registers (8-10 risks each) from different industries
Risk analysis worksheet template with sections for categorization, P-I matrix evaluation, and strategy comparison
PMI Risk Management Process Group reference sheet
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization and P-I relationship analysis, (2) Quality of cross-project strategy comparisons with specific examples, (3) Justification strength for alternative strategies using PMI principles, (4) Demonstration of understanding context factors influencing risk response selection. Each criterion worth 25 points for 100-point total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example analysis of one risk to demonstrate expected depth and PMI terminology usage. Offer a risk response strategy decision tree as reference. For advanced learners, add a fourth risk register from an international project requiring consideration of cultural and regulatory complexity, or ask them to create secondary risk analyses for their proposed alternative strategies.

title: Risk Register Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Comparison: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze three different project risk registers from varying industry contexts to identify patterns, evaluate risk assessment consistency, and compare mitigation strategies. They will then synthesize findings to recommend improvements for risk management processes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk probability and impact ratings across multiple project contexts by comparing assessment methodologies and identifying inconsistencies
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different risk mitigation strategies through systematic comparison of risk register entries and their outcomes
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Provide each team with three anonymized risk registers from different industries (construction, IT software development, pharmaceutical research). Ensure each register contains 15-20 risks with probability/impact scores, mitigation strategies, and outcome status.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student examines one assigned risk register, creating a summary matrix identifying: (1) most common risk categories, (2) probability/impact assessment patterns, (3) types of mitigation strategies used, and (4) success rate of implemented strategies.

**Phase 2 - Team Comparison (20 minutes):** Teams combine individual analyses to create a comparative analysis chart. Students identify: differences in risk scoring methodologies, variations in mitigation approach effectiveness, industry-specific risk patterns, and gaps in risk identification or response strategies.

**Phase 3 - Critical Evaluation (15 minutes):** Teams analyze why certain mitigation strategies succeeded or failed by examining: resource allocation patterns, timeline considerations, stakeholder involvement levels, and monitoring frequency. They identify best practices and problematic approaches.

**Phase 4 - Synthesis and Recommendations (10 minutes):** Each team develops three specific, actionable recommendations for improving risk management processes based on their cross-project analysis. Recommendations must address assessment consistency, mitigation strategy selection, or monitoring improvements.

**Presentation (15 minutes):** Teams present their key findings and top recommendation to the class, explaining their analytical reasoning and supporting evidence from the risk registers.

Risk analysis comparison template/worksheet
Flip chart paper and markers for team presentations
PMI Risk Management Standard reference guide
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk pattern identification (25%), (2) Depth of comparative analysis between industries (25%), (3) Quality of critical evaluation of mitigation strategies (25%), (4) Specificity and feasibility of improvement recommendations (25%). Teams must demonstrate analytical reasoning with specific evidence from risk registers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide analysis template with guided questions for each phase. Offer examples of what constitutes 'patterns' in risk data. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify root causes behind industry differences and propose integrated risk management frameworks that could work across multiple project types.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Measurement Framework Effectiveness
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of an existing e-commerce website's Google Analytics implementation, critically assessing the measurement framework's alignment with business objectives and providing strategic recommendations. They will analyze tracking setup, goal configuration, attribution models, and reporting effectiveness to determine overall measurement maturity.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of Google Analytics measurement frameworks by conducting systematic audits of tracking implementation, goal configuration, and attribution modeling against established e-commerce best practices
Students will critique existing analytics strategies through comparative analysis of multiple measurement approaches and justify recommendations for optimization based on business impact potential
instructions: Begin by assigning students to teams of 3-4, providing each team with access credentials to a demo e-commerce Google Analytics account (or case study dataset). In the first 30 minutes, teams conduct initial reconnaissance: examining account structure, property setup, view configuration, and basic tracking implementation using the GA debugger and Tag Assistant. Next, spend 45 minutes on deep measurement audit: students evaluate goal setup effectiveness by analyzing conversion funnel logic, assess e-commerce tracking completeness (product performance, checkout behavior, transaction data), and examine attribution model appropriateness for the business model. During the following 30 minutes, teams perform comparative analysis using GA Intelligence insights and benchmarking data to evaluate performance against industry standards. Students then spend 45 minutes developing strategic recommendations: prioritizing measurement gaps, proposing specific configuration changes, and creating implementation timelines with expected impact metrics. In the final 30 minutes, each team presents their audit findings to the class, defending their evaluation criteria and justifying their strategic recommendations. Other teams provide peer feedback using structured evaluation forms. Instructors facilitate discussion on evaluation methodology differences and strategic thinking quality.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account access (Universal Analytics and GA4)
Google Tag Assistant browser extension
GA Debugger Chrome extension
E-commerce Analytics Audit Template spreadsheet
Industry benchmark data sheets
Peer evaluation rubrics (printed)
assessment_method: Students submit a written audit report (15 points) containing executive summary, detailed findings with evidence screenshots, strategic recommendations with justification, and implementation roadmap. Oral presentation evaluated on clarity of evaluation criteria, depth of analysis, and quality of strategic reasoning (10 points). Peer evaluation scores on feedback quality and professional critique delivery (5 points). Total: 30 points using detailed rubric measuring analytical rigor, strategic thinking, and professional communication.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with structured audit checklists and example evaluation criteria. Offer mid-activity check-ins to guide analysis direction. For advanced learners, introduce complex scenarios like multi-channel attribution challenges or advanced segment analysis requirements. Provide additional datasets from different industries for comparative evaluation practice.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise WAN Architecture with DMVPN and SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise WAN solution connecting four geographically distributed sites using DMVPN Phase 3 with SD-WAN overlay for traffic optimization. They will create original network designs, implement advanced routing protocols, and develop comprehensive security policies while considering real-world constraints like bandwidth costs and application requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize DMVPN Phase 3, OSPF, and BGP technologies by designing a scalable hub-and-spoke WAN architecture that supports dynamic spoke-to-spoke communication
Students will construct an integrated SD-WAN solution through hands-on configuration of application-aware routing policies and centralized management systems
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team a fictional enterprise scenario with specific requirements (provided scenario cards include company size, application types, budget constraints, and compliance needs). In the first 45 minutes, teams analyze requirements and create original network topology diagrams using Visio or Lucidchart, determining hub placement, spoke configurations, and tunnel designs. They must justify their architectural decisions in writing, addressing scalability, redundancy, and cost considerations. Next, spend 90 minutes in the lab where each team configures their designed solution using Cisco VIRL/CML or physical equipment. Students configure hub routers with DMVPN Phase 3, implement OSPF within DMVPN cloud, establish eBGP peering with service providers, and configure spoke routers with dynamic routing. During the following 60 minutes, teams integrate SD-WAN functionality by configuring application classification policies, setting up centralized policy management through vManage (or Packet Tracer SD-WAN simulation), and implementing traffic steering based on application requirements and link performance. In the final 45 minutes, each team presents their complete solution to the class, demonstrating live network functionality, explaining design rationale, and conducting a simulated failure scenario to show network resilience. Presentations must include network diagrams, configuration snippets, monitoring dashboards, and a cost-benefit analysis comparing their solution to alternatives.
materials_needed: Cisco VIRL/CML licenses or Packet Tracer with SD-WAN support
Network topology design software (Visio, Lucidchart, or draw.io)
Enterprise scenario requirement cards (pre-created by instructor)
Cisco ISR 4000 series routers or equivalent virtual instances
Access to Cisco SD-WAN documentation and configuration guides
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - topology appropriateness, scalability considerations, and documentation clarity; Technical Implementation (35 points) - correct DMVPN configuration, routing protocol functionality, and SD-WAN policy implementation; Problem-Solving and Innovation (20 points) - creative solutions to constraints and effective troubleshooting; Presentation and Communication (20 points) - clear explanation of design decisions and professional delivery. Students must demonstrate working connectivity between all sites and show application traffic following configured SD-WAN policies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide configuration templates with partial commands filled in, assign them simpler scenarios with fewer sites, and pair them with stronger technical partners while ensuring they contribute to design decisions. Create checkpoint guides for each major configuration section. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integration with cloud providers (AWS/Azure), or implementation of advanced security features like FlexVPN. Challenge them to optimize for specific KPIs like latency reduction or bandwidth efficiency.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Diagnostic Decomposition
description: Students systematically analyze a malfunctioning complex circuit containing resistors, capacitors, and inductors by breaking down voltage and current measurements at specific nodes. They identify which components are causing the circuit to deviate from theoretical predictions and determine the underlying failure mechanisms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex RLC circuit behavior by systematically examining voltage-current relationships at each circuit node to isolate component failures
Students will differentiate between theoretical and measured circuit parameters through quantitative comparison of impedance calculations versus experimental data
instructions: Begin by providing student teams of 2-3 with a pre-built RLC circuit containing one deliberately faulty component (resistor with 50% higher resistance, capacitor with 20% reduced capacitance, or inductor with damaged core). Give teams the theoretical circuit diagram showing intended component values and expected node voltages at 1kHz AC input. Students first calculate theoretical impedances and predicted voltage drops across each component using complex number analysis. Next, teams measure actual voltage amplitudes and phase angles at each circuit node using oscilloscopes, recording data in a systematic troubleshooting table. They calculate actual component impedances from their measurements using Z = V/I relationships. Students then compare measured versus theoretical values, identifying which component shows the largest percentage deviation. For the suspect component, they analyze whether the deviation pattern matches known failure modes (resistance drift, capacitance loss, inductance change). Teams create a diagnostic flowchart showing their analytical process: theoretical calculations → systematic measurements → impedance comparisons → failure mode identification. Finally, they physically remove and test the suspect component with a component analyzer to verify their analytical conclusion. Each team presents their analysis process, highlighting how they isolated the failure through systematic decomposition rather than random testing.
materials_needed: Pre-built RLC circuits with one faulty component per team
Digital oscilloscopes with dual-channel capability
Function generators (1kHz sine wave output)
Component analyzers (LCR meters)
Circuit diagrams with theoretical component values
Scientific calculators or computers with complex number capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of theoretical impedance calculations (25%), (2) Systematic measurement procedure and data quality (25%), (3) Logical analysis comparing theoretical vs. measured values (25%), (4) Correct identification of faulty component with justified reasoning (25%). Students must show mathematical work, measurement data tables, and analytical reasoning process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide impedance calculation templates and measurement sequence checklists. Offer guided practice with known-good circuits first. For advanced learners: Include circuits with multiple subtle faults, require analysis of temperature effects on component values, or challenge them to predict component lifetime based on failure patterns.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Detection and Fix Recommendations
description: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different code review approaches by analyzing pre-written code samples with intentional bugs and assessing the quality of peer-generated bug reports and fix suggestions. They will then defend their evaluations using established code quality criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different debugging approaches by comparing peer-generated bug reports against established code quality standards
Students will critique and rank fix recommendations through systematic analysis using a provided evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Provide each group with the same set of 5 Python code snippets (each 10-15 lines) containing common beginner errors: syntax errors, logic errors, variable naming issues, missing error handling, and inefficient loops. In Phase 1 (20 minutes), each group reviews all code snippets and creates bug reports listing: identified issues, severity level (critical/major/minor), and proposed fixes. Groups document their findings on the provided template sheets. In Phase 2 (15 minutes), rotate the bug reports so each group receives another group's analysis. Using the Code Quality Evaluation Checklist, groups assess the completeness and accuracy of the received bug reports. They score each report on: thoroughness of bug identification (0-4 points), appropriateness of severity ratings (0-3 points), and quality of proposed solutions (0-3 points). In Phase 3 (20 minutes), groups create a ranking of all reviewed bug reports from most to least effective, providing written justification for their top and bottom choices. They must reference specific evaluation criteria and provide evidence from the code examples. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents their #1 ranked report and explains their reasoning.
materials_needed: 5 printed Python code snippets with intentional bugs (one set per group)
Bug Report Template sheets
Code Quality Evaluation Checklist handout
Ranking and Justification worksheet
Answer key with correct bug identification for instructor reference
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric on: (1) Accuracy of their evaluation scores compared to instructor answer key (3 points), (2) Quality of written justifications demonstrating use of evaluation criteria (3 points), and (3) Participation in defending rankings during class discussion (2 points). Students must score 6/8 points to demonstrate proficient evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the Code Quality Checklist early and highlight 2-3 key criteria to focus on initially. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger peers within groups. For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge: have them evaluate whether the original code snippets represent realistic beginner mistakes and suggest improvements to make the exercise more authentic.

title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete mapping of all 49 PMBOK Guide processes across the 10 Knowledge Areas and 5 Process Groups. This intensive recall activity focuses on precise process naming, correct Knowledge Area classification, and accurate Process Group placement using a systematic memorization and testing approach.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK Guide process names with 100% accuracy by completing timed written assessments
Students will identify the correct Knowledge Area and Process Group for each of the 49 processes through structured matrix completion exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the blank 10x5 matrix template with Knowledge Areas listed vertically (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) and Process Groups horizontally (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing). Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study the complete filled matrix, using chunking techniques to group processes by Knowledge Area first, then by Process Group. Encourage mnemonic devices and pattern recognition. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Remove reference materials. Students complete the first recall attempt on a fresh blank matrix, writing full process names in correct intersections. Phase 3 (5 minutes): Peer checking using answer key - partners mark errors and identify knowledge gaps. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Second study period focusing specifically on missed processes, with emphasis on exact wording (e.g., 'Develop Project Management Plan' vs 'Create Project Management Plan'). Phase 5 (10 minutes): Final assessment using a randomized list of 25 processes where students must write the corresponding Knowledge Area and Process Group. Phase 6 (5 minutes): Self-scoring and reflection on improvement areas. Instructor circulates throughout, noting common error patterns and providing immediate feedback on process name precision.
materials_needed: Blank 10x5 PMBOK matrix templates (3 per student)
Complete PMBOK Process Matrix answer key (laminated for reuse)
Randomized process list assessment sheets
Red pens for peer correction
Timer for each phase
assessment_method: Success measured by final assessment score: 90-100% = Mastery (22-25 correct), 80-89% = Proficient (20-21 correct), 70-79% = Developing (17-19 correct), Below 70% = Needs Remediation. Track improvement from attempt 1 to final assessment. Document specific error patterns (wrong Knowledge Area, wrong Process Group, incorrect process naming) for targeted follow-up instruction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled partial matrices with 50% of processes completed, focus on one Knowledge Area at a time, or allow use of acronym hints. For advanced learners: Add process input/output recall, include ITTOs (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) identification, or require explanation of process relationships and dependencies between Knowledge Areas.

title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Recall Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete 49-process PMBOK mapping across all 10 Knowledge Areas and 5 Process Groups. This intensive recall activity focuses on building foundational memory of the Project Management Institute's standardized framework through systematic repetition and verification exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes by accurately placing each process name within its correct Knowledge Area and Process Group intersection
Students will identify specific process inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for 15 selected high-stakes processes through timed memory assessments
instructions: Begin by distributing blank 10x5 grid templates with Knowledge Areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) as rows and Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) as columns. Students have 5 minutes to study the complete filled matrix provided as reference material. Remove reference materials and give students 20 minutes to fill in all 49 process names in correct intersections using only memory. After completion, redistribute reference materials for self-checking and marking incorrect placements in red. Conduct second round: provide 15 pre-selected critical processes (Plan Schedule Management, Control Quality, Manage Stakeholder Engagement, etc.) on individual cards. Students have 3 minutes per process to write down 3 specific inputs, 3 tools/techniques, and 3 outputs from memory on provided templates. Rotate cards every 3 minutes until all 15 processes completed. Final verification phase: students exchange papers and grade using provided answer keys. Record accuracy percentages for both matrix completion and process detail recall. Conclude with 10-minute group discussion identifying most commonly missed processes and memory strategies that worked best.
materials_needed: Blank 10x5 Knowledge Area/Process Group grid templates (one per student)
Complete PMBOK process matrix reference sheets
15 laminated process name cards for rotation exercise
Process input/tools/output recording templates
Detailed answer keys for all 15 selected processes
Red marking pens for self-correction
Timer or stopwatch for time management
assessment_method: Success measured by: Matrix completion accuracy (85%+ processes placed correctly = proficient, 95%+ = advanced). Process detail recall scored as percentage correct across all ITTOs with 70%+ inputs/outputs correct and 60%+ tools/techniques correct indicating mastery. Document individual accuracy rates and identify specific knowledge gaps for remediation.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing Knowledge Area acronym memory devices (I-S-S-C-Q-R-C-R-P-S) and allowing them to complete matrix in 2-3 stages rather than all at once. For advanced learners, add challenge round requiring recall of process sequence dependencies and critical path relationships between processes within each Knowledge Area.
original_title: PMI Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Recall Challenge

title: Deconstructing Leadership Philosophy Through Crisis Decision Analysis
description: Students will analyze real corporate crisis scenarios to identify and explain how different leadership philosophies (transformational, servant, authentic, and situational) manifest in executive decision-making patterns. This expert-level activity requires students to demonstrate deep comprehension of leadership theory application in high-stakes environments.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, servant, authentic, and situational leadership philosophies by analyzing documented executive decisions during organizational crises
Students will explain the relationship between leadership philosophy and decision-making patterns through comparative analysis of three distinct crisis scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 4, assigning each member one leadership philosophy (transformational, servant, authentic, situational). Distribute the three crisis case packets: Tesla's 2018 production crisis, Johnson & Johnson's 1982 Tylenol crisis, and Wells Fargo's 2016 account fraud scandal. Each packet contains executive quotes, decision timelines, stakeholder communications, and outcome data. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Individual students analyze all three cases through their assigned leadership philosophy lens, identifying specific decisions, communications, and actions that align with or contradict their philosophy. They must document evidence using the provided analysis template, noting decision speed, stakeholder prioritization, communication tone, and resource allocation patterns. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups reconvene to create a comparative matrix mapping each crisis response against all four leadership philosophies. Students must reach consensus on which philosophy best explains each leader's approach, supporting their conclusions with specific textual evidence. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group presents their matrix to the class, explaining their reasoning for philosophical alignment and identifying moments where leaders exhibited mixed or evolving philosophical approaches. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students individually write a synthesis paragraph explaining how leadership philosophy influences crisis decision-making patterns.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis case study packets (Tesla 2018, J&J 1982, Wells Fargo 2016)
Leadership philosophy reference sheets with key characteristics
Decision analysis templates with evidence documentation sections
Large format paper for group matrix creation
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of philosophical identification with specific evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of distinctions between philosophies (25%), (3) Depth of explanation connecting philosophy to decision patterns (25%), (4) Synthesis paragraph demonstrating comprehension of philosophy-practice relationship (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing philosophy quick-reference cards with decision-making indicators and sample questions for evidence analysis. For advanced learners, add a extension requiring them to predict how an unassigned fifth philosophy (transformative or complexity leadership) would have approached one crisis scenario, supporting predictions with theoretical justification.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Philosophy Through Crisis Decision Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze three distinct leadership philosophies (transformational, servant, and authentic leadership) by examining how leaders with different approaches responded to the same organizational crisis. They will identify underlying philosophical principles and explain how these worldviews shaped specific decision-making patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational, servant, and authentic leadership philosophies by analyzing real crisis response decisions from three different organizational leaders

Students will explain how underlying leadership worldviews influence tactical decision-making through systematic comparison of communication patterns, stakeholder prioritization, and resource allocation choices
instructions: Begin by distributing three case study packets, each containing 8-10 pages of primary source materials (emails, press releases, internal memos, recorded statements) from different CEOs who led their organizations through the 2020 COVID-19 business disruptions. Assign Case A (Transformational - Marc Benioff/Salesforce), Case B (Servant Leadership - Cheryl Sandberg/Meta), and Case C (Authentic Leadership - Satya Nadella/Microsoft). Form groups of 6 students, with 2 students per case. Give groups 45 minutes to read and complete individual analysis worksheets identifying: (1) three key decisions made, (2) stakeholder groups prioritized, (3) communication tone/language patterns, (4) resource allocation choices, and (5) stated rationale for decisions. After individual analysis, students share findings within their group for 15 minutes. Next, provide each group with a leadership philosophy comparison matrix handout containing core principles of each leadership style (transformational focuses on inspiration and vision, servant prioritizes follower growth, authentic emphasizes self-awareness and transparency). Groups spend 30 minutes mapping their case study findings to philosophical principles, identifying which leadership style each CEO demonstrated and providing specific evidence. Finally, conduct a 20-minute whole-class discussion where each group presents their analysis, explaining how they connected observed behaviors to underlying philosophical frameworks. Students must justify their classifications using specific quotes and decisions from the source materials.
materials_needed: Three case study packets with primary source documents from Salesforce, Meta, and Microsoft COVID-19 responses
Individual analysis worksheets with 5 reflection questions
Leadership philosophy comparison matrix handouts
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric measuring: (1) Accuracy of philosophical identification with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Quality of connections between observed behaviors and leadership principles (35%), (3) Use of specific textual evidence from primary sources (25%), and (4) Clarity of explanation during group presentation (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a pre-filled example analysis of one decision using a fourth case study. Highlight key phrases in source documents that indicate philosophical orientation. For advanced learners, add a synthesis question asking them to predict how each leader would handle a different crisis scenario based on their identified philosophical framework.
original_title: Deconstructing Leadership Philosophy Through Crisis Decision Analysis

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website on AWS S3 with CloudFront Distribution
description: Students will create and deploy a complete static website hosting solution using AWS S3 buckets and CloudFront CDN. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical application of core AWS services for web hosting while implementing security best practices and performance optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional static website by configuring AWS S3 bucket policies and static website hosting settings
Students will implement content delivery optimization through creating and configuring an AWS CloudFront distribution with custom domain settings
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access credentials and a pre-built HTML/CSS website folder containing index.html, error.html, and assets folder with 2-3 images. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify they can access S3 and CloudFront services.

**S3 Configuration (25 minutes):** Students create a new S3 bucket with a globally unique name following format 'studentname-static-website-[timestamp]'. They upload all website files maintaining folder structure, then enable static website hosting in bucket properties, specifying index.html as index document and error.html as error document. Next, they configure bucket policy for public read access using provided JSON template, replacing bucket name placeholder with their actual bucket name.

**CloudFront Setup (20 minutes):** Students create CloudFront distribution using their S3 bucket as origin domain. They configure default root object as 'index.html', set price class to 'Use Only US, Canada and Europe', and enable compression. Students wait for distribution deployment status to change from 'In Progress' to 'Deployed' (typically 10-15 minutes).

**Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Students test website accessibility using both S3 website endpoint and CloudFront distribution URL. They verify all pages load correctly, images display properly, and error page appears when accessing non-existent URLs. Students document both URLs and test load times using browser developer tools, comparing S3 direct access versus CloudFront delivery performance.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab account for each student
Pre-built static website files (HTML, CSS, images) in downloadable zip format
S3 bucket policy JSON template with placeholder for bucket name
Instruction handout with AWS console navigation screenshots
assessment_method: Students submit a completion checklist documenting: (1) S3 bucket name and website endpoint URL, (2) CloudFront distribution domain name, (3) Screenshots showing successful website loading from both endpoints, (4) Performance comparison data showing load times, (5) Screenshot of bucket policy configuration. Success criteria: website loads completely from both URLs, CloudFront shows faster load times than direct S3 access, all navigation links function properly.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional screenshots of each AWS console step and pair with more experienced peers. Create troubleshooting guide covering common issues like bucket naming conflicts and policy syntax errors. For advanced learners: Add custom domain configuration using Route 53, implement HTTPS certificate using AWS Certificate Manager, or add custom error pages for different HTTP status codes.

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website on AWS S3 with CloudFront Distribution: Practical Workshop
description: Students will create a complete static website hosting solution by configuring AWS S3 buckets, uploading web content, and setting up CloudFront distribution for global content delivery. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical application of core AWS services for web hosting.
learning_objectives: Students will apply S3 bucket configuration principles by creating a static website hosting environment with proper permissions and policies
Students will implement CloudFront distribution setup through connecting S3 origins and configuring caching behaviors for optimized content delivery
instructions:
**Phase 1: Environment Setup (15 minutes)**
Students access AWS Management Console using provided sandbox accounts. Instructor demonstrates navigating to S3 service and explains the interface layout. Students create a uniquely named bucket following naming convention: 'studentname-website-yyyy' where yyyy is current year.

**Phase 2: S3 Configuration (20 minutes)**
Students enable static website hosting in bucket properties, setting index.html as index document and error.html as error document.
