Configure bucket policy for public read access using provided JSON template. Students modify the template by replacing 'BUCKET-NAME' placeholder with their actual bucket name. Upload provided HTML files (index.html, about.html, styles.css, error.html) using drag-and-drop interface.

**Phase 3: Website Testing (10 minutes)**
Students access the S3 website endpoint URL to verify basic functionality. Test navigation between pages and confirm CSS styling loads correctly. Document the S3 website URL for comparison with CloudFront URL later.

**Phase 4: CloudFront Setup (25 minutes)**
Navigate to CloudFront service and create new distribution. Set origin domain to S3 bucket website endpoint (not the bucket itself). Configure default cache behavior with 'Redirect HTTP to HTTPS' viewer protocol policy. Set default root object as 'index.html'. Students wait for distribution deployment (status changes from 'In Progress' to 'Deployed').

**Phase 5: Final Testing and Documentation (10 minutes)**
Access website via CloudFront distribution domain name. Compare loading speeds between S3 direct access and CloudFront distribution. Students complete deployment worksheet documenting both URLs, configuration choices, and observed performance differences.
materials_needed: AWS sandbox accounts with S3 and CloudFront permissions
Pre-built HTML website files package (index.html, about.html, styles.css, error.html)
S3 bucket policy JSON template document
Deployment tracking worksheet
AWS Management Console access via web browsers
assessment_method: Success measured by functional website accessible via CloudFront URL (40 points), correctly configured S3 bucket with public access (30 points), completed deployment worksheet with both URLs and performance observations (20 points), and proper bucket naming convention followed (10 points). Students must demonstrate website loads via HTTPS through CloudFront distribution and submit screenshot evidence of working site.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled bucket policy templates with only bucket name to modify, offer one-on-one guidance during CloudFront setup phase, and create visual checklist for each configuration step. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement custom error pages, configure multiple cache behaviors for different file types, or add custom domain names with SSL certificates. Provide troubleshooting guide for common issues like bucket policy syntax errors and CloudFront propagation delays.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website on AWS S3 with CloudFront Distribution

title: Risk Register Analysis: Comparing Risk Response Strategies Across Project Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three different project risk registers to identify patterns in risk categorization, evaluate the effectiveness of selected response strategies, and determine optimal risk management approaches. They will break down complex risk scenarios to understand the relationship between risk characteristics and appropriate mitigation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by comparing threat and opportunity management approaches across three distinct project types (construction, IT implementation, pharmaceutical development)
Students will evaluate risk prioritization decisions through systematic examination of probability-impact matrices and their alignment with project constraints and objectives
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute three different risk registers: Project A (office building construction), Project B (ERP system implementation), and Project C (clinical trial management). Each register contains 15-20 risks with varying probability/impact ratings, response strategies, and ownership assignments.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student examines one risk register, identifying: (1) distribution of risks across PMI risk categories (technical, external, organizational, project management), (2) relationship between risk rating and selected response strategy (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept for threats; exploit, enhance, share, accept for opportunities), and (3) patterns in risk ownership assignments.

**Phase 2 - Team Comparison (20 minutes):** Teams create a comparative analysis matrix displaying: risk category distributions, response strategy frequencies, average implementation costs, and timeline impacts across all three projects. Students must identify at least three significant differences and two similarities between projects.

**Phase 3 - Strategy Evaluation (15 minutes):** Teams analyze whether response strategies align with project characteristics. For example, evaluate why construction projects might favor 'transfer' strategies while IT projects prefer 'mitigate' approaches. Students must cite specific examples from the registers.

**Phase 4 - Recommendations (10 minutes):** Each team selects one poorly managed risk from each register and proposes alternative response strategies, justifying their recommendations based on project context, constraints, and risk characteristics.
materials_needed: Three realistic project risk registers (15-20 risks each) in spreadsheet format
Blank comparative analysis matrix templates
PMI Risk Management Process Guide reference sheets
Laptops or tablets for teams
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization analysis (25%), (2) Quality of strategy-to-context alignment evaluation (30%), (3) Depth of comparative insights between projects (25%), (4) Feasibility and justification of alternative recommendations (20%). Teams must submit their analysis matrix and present one key finding to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed analysis matrix with 2-3 examples filled in, and offer a checklist of questions to guide their evaluation process. For advanced learners: Add a fourth risk register from a different industry and ask them to predict risk patterns before analysis, or have them create secondary risk assessments for their recommended response strategies.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Dynamics in the Jupiter-Io-Europa System
description: Students will decompose the complex three-body gravitational system of Jupiter, Io, and Europa to analyze how tidal forces and orbital resonances create observable phenomena. They will examine real orbital data to identify patterns and evaluate the relative contributions of different gravitational interactions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the hierarchical structure of gravitational forces in the Jupiter-Io-Europa system by calculating force magnitudes and examining their directional relationships
Students will evaluate the cause-and-effect relationships between orbital resonances and tidal heating through systematic comparison of theoretical predictions with observational data
instructions: Begin by distributing the Jupiter system orbital data spreadsheet containing 6 months of position data for Io and Europa at 12-hour intervals. Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes to plot the orbital positions and identify any patterns in the orbital periods. Next, guide students through calculating the gravitational force vectors: Have them compute Jupiter's gravitational force on each moon using F = GMm/r², then calculate the moon-to-moon gravitational forces at closest approach, conjunction, and opposition positions. Students should create force diagrams showing all three gravitational interactions at these key orbital configurations. For the third phase (30 minutes), students analyze the 2:1 orbital resonance by examining how Io completes exactly 2 orbits for every 1 Europa orbit. They should plot the relative positions over time and identify when the moons align. Have them calculate the tidal force gradient using F_tidal = 2GMmΔr/r³ for both moons and compare these values. In the final analysis phase (25 minutes), students must connect their calculations to real phenomena: They should examine provided volcanic activity data from Io and correlate eruption patterns with orbital position relative to Jupiter and Europa. Students create a comprehensive analysis report explaining how the gravitational hierarchy (Jupiter >> Europa on Io >> Io on Europa) creates the observed tidal heating patterns. Conclude with pairs presenting their force analysis diagrams and defending their conclusions about which gravitational interactions most significantly influence each moon's behavior.
materials_needed: Jupiter system orbital data spreadsheet (6 months of Io/Europa positions)
Io volcanic activity database printouts
Scientific calculators or laptops with Excel/Python
Large format paper for force vector diagrams
Colored pens/markers for vector representations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of gravitational force calculations (25%), (2) Quality of force vector diagrams showing proper scaling and directions (25%), (3) Correct identification and explanation of orbital resonance patterns (25%), (4) Logical connection between calculated forces and observed phenomena with evidence-based reasoning (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed force calculation template and highlight the key orbital positions to analyze first. Offer a concept map showing the relationships between tidal forces, orbital mechanics, and geological activity. For advanced learners, extend the analysis to include perturbation effects on orbital eccentricity and challenge them to predict future volcanic activity patterns based on upcoming orbital configurations.

title: Comparative Analysis of Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Historical Crisis Case Studies
description: Students will conduct an in-depth comparative analysis of how transformational and transactional leadership approaches were applied during three major historical crises. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying key characteristics, explaining the rationale behind leadership decisions, and interpreting the contextual factors that influenced leadership effectiveness.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership characteristics by analyzing the decision-making patterns and communication strategies of leaders during the 2008 Financial Crisis, COVID-19 pandemic, and 9/11 terrorist attacks
Students will interpret the relationship between situational context and leadership effectiveness through structured comparison matrices and evidence-based explanations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Assign each team one of three crisis scenarios: 2008 Financial Crisis (focusing on leaders like Ben Bernanke, Timothy Geithner), COVID-19 pandemic (focusing on leaders like Jacinda Ardern, Andrew Cuomo), or 9/11 attacks (focusing on leaders like Rudy Giuliani, George W. Bush). Provide each team with their crisis leadership packet containing 8-10 pre-selected primary sources including speeches, interviews, policy documents, and contemporary news articles. Teams spend 45 minutes conducting initial analysis using the provided Leadership Characteristics Matrix, identifying and documenting specific examples of transformational behaviors (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence) versus transactional behaviors (contingent rewards, management by exception, corrective actions). Next, teams create a detailed comparison chart (30 minutes) showing how their assigned leaders demonstrated each leadership type, including direct quotes and specific actions as evidence. In the final phase (60 minutes), teams present their findings in a structured 8-minute presentation followed by 4 minutes of cross-examination from other teams. During presentations, non-presenting teams complete peer evaluation forms focusing on accuracy of leadership type identification and quality of supporting evidence. Conclude with a 20-minute facilitated discussion where students synthesize patterns across all three crises, identifying when each leadership type was most effective and explaining the contextual factors that influenced leadership success or failure.
materials_needed: Leadership Characteristics Matrix template (laminated copies)
Crisis Leadership Document Packets (one per scenario, 8-10 sources each)
Presentation timer and projection equipment
Peer evaluation forms
Flip chart paper and markers for comparison charts
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy in identifying transformational vs. transactional leadership characteristics (25%), (2) Quality and relevance of evidence provided from primary sources (25%), (3) Depth of explanation regarding contextual factors influencing leadership effectiveness (25%), (4) Clarity and organization of comparative analysis during presentation (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category, demonstrating clear understanding through specific examples and coherent explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example matrix from a different crisis and offer guided questions for source analysis. Create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger analytical thinkers with developing students. For advanced learners, add a requirement to propose alternative leadership approaches and predict different outcomes, or include analysis of cultural differences in leadership responses across different countries during the same crisis.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for Multi-Phase Construction Project
description: Students analyze a complex construction project's risk register to differentiate between risk response strategies, evaluate their appropriateness for specific risk scenarios, and assess potential conflicts between responses across project phases. They will deconstruct the decision-making rationale behind each strategy selection.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by examining their alignment with risk characteristics, project constraints, and stakeholder priorities in a multi-phase construction scenario
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk response selections through systematic evaluation of strategy effectiveness and resource allocation conflicts
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute the Riverside Bridge Construction risk register containing 20 identified risks across three project phases: foundation, superstructure, and finishing. Each risk entry includes probability/impact ratings, current response strategy, assigned owner, budget allocation, and timeline dependencies. Teams receive analysis worksheets with four columns: Risk ID, Current Strategy, Strategy Rationale Analysis, and Alternative Recommendation. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams systematically examine each risk entry, identifying whether the assigned response strategy (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) aligns with the risk's probability/impact profile. Students must justify their analysis using PMI risk management principles, noting specific misalignments such as high-impact risks being accepted without justification or low-probability risks receiving expensive mitigation strategies. 

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams analyze cross-phase dependencies, identifying where risk responses in one phase create conflicts or inefficiencies in subsequent phases. For example, they might discover that transferring weather delay risk in the foundation phase conflicts with the mitigation strategy for the same risk type in the superstructure phase. 

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Each team presents their three most critical findings to the class, explaining their analytical reasoning and proposing alternative response strategies. Other teams provide peer feedback using the provided evaluation criteria. 

Conclude with a 10-minute instructor debrief highlighting common analytical patterns and reinforcing key risk response selection principles.
materials_needed: Riverside Bridge Construction risk register (20 risks with detailed scenarios)
Risk Response Analysis worksheets (4-column format)
PMI Risk Response Strategy reference cards
Probability/Impact matrix templates
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of strategy-to-risk alignment analysis (25%), (2) Quality of justification using PMI principles (25%), (3) Identification of cross-phase conflicts and dependencies (25%), (4) Viability and rationale of alternative recommendations (25%). Teams must correctly analyze at least 15 of 20 risks and identify minimum 3 cross-phase conflicts to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example analysis for the first 2 risks and offer strategy selection flowcharts. Advanced learners can be challenged to calculate ROI for their alternative strategies and consider secondary risk impacts. Pair weaker analytical thinkers with stronger team members and provide additional coaching during Phase 1.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Analysis and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real Google Analytics 4 data from an e-commerce website. They will assess how each model impacts conversion credit distribution across marketing channels and provide strategic recommendations for optimizing marketing budget allocation based on their analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and assessing their impact on channel performance metrics in Google Analytics 4
Students will critique existing marketing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of model outputs and defend budget reallocation recommendations with data-driven evidence
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Collection (20 minutes)** Students access the provided GA4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store) and navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths. They export 90-day conversion path data including all touchpoints for purchases over $100. Next, they access Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool and generate reports comparing all five attribution models for the same time period. Students screenshot key metrics and export data tables. **Phase 2: Comparative Analysis (45 minutes)** Working in pairs, students create a comprehensive comparison matrix documenting how each attribution model assigns conversion credit across channels (Organic Search, Paid Search, Social, Email, Direct). They calculate percentage differences in attributed conversions and revenue for each channel between models, identifying which channels gain/lose credit under different models. Students must document at least 3 significant discrepancies (>15% difference) between model outputs. **Phase 3: Business Context Integration (25 minutes)** Students research the provided fictional company scenario: B2B SaaS company with 6-month sales cycles, high customer lifetime value ($5,000 average), and current 40% budget allocation to last-click attributed channels. They analyze how attribution model choice affects ROI calculations and budget decisions. **Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (30 minutes)** Each pair prepares a 5-minute presentation defending their chosen attribution model and proposing specific budget reallocations. They must address potential stakeholder objections and quantify expected impact on overall marketing efficiency. Presentations include model comparison visuals, budget reallocation proposals with percentage changes, and ROI projections.
materials_needed: Access to Google Analytics 4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store)
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel)
Fictional B2B SaaS company scenario document with current marketing spend breakdown
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
Comparison matrix template with attribution model columns
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and analysis from GA4 (25%), (2) Depth of comparative evaluation showing understanding of model strengths/weaknesses (25%), (3) Quality of strategic reasoning connecting analysis to business recommendations (25%), (4) Defense of recommendations addressing potential counterarguments (15%), (5) Professional presentation of findings with clear data visualizations (10%). Minimum passing requires demonstrating accurate model comparison, identifying at least 3 significant attribution discrepancies, and providing quantified budget recommendations with supporting rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled comparison matrix template with example calculations, offer guided questions for each analysis phase, and allow access to GA4 navigation cheat sheet. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase to ensure data collection accuracy. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value calculations into their model evaluation, analyze attribution in relation to customer journey stage, or propose custom attribution model parameters. Encourage integration of additional GA4 reports like User Acquisition and Traffic Acquisition for deeper channel analysis.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Classification Models
description: Students will analyze pre-trained Random Forest models to understand how different features contribute to classification decisions. They will compare feature importance rankings across different datasets and explain the practical implications of these rankings for real-world decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance scores from Random Forest models by ranking features and explaining their relative contributions to model predictions
Students will compare feature importance patterns across different classification problems through structured analysis of visualization outputs
instructions: Begin by organizing students into pairs and distributing the prepared Jupyter notebook containing three pre-trained Random Forest models: customer churn prediction, loan approval, and medical diagnosis. Each model includes feature importance visualizations and raw importance scores. In the first 15 minutes, students individually examine Model 1 (customer churn), identifying the top 5 most important features and writing one-sentence explanations for why each feature might be predictive of customer churn. Next, pairs spend 20 minutes collaboratively analyzing all three models, creating a comparison table that lists the top 3 features for each model and categorizing them as 'demographic,' 'behavioral,' or 'financial' variables. During this phase, students must also identify any features that appear important across multiple models and hypothesize why. In the following 15 minutes, each pair selects one model and writes a 150-word business recommendation explaining how stakeholders should prioritize their data collection efforts based on the feature importance rankings. Students must justify their recommendations by connecting feature importance scores to actionable business decisions. Finally, spend 10 minutes having three pairs present their business recommendations while other students ask clarifying questions about the connection between statistical importance and practical significance. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are distinguishing between correlation and causation when interpreting feature importance.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with three pre-trained Random Forest models and visualization code
Dataset documentation explaining each feature's meaning
Comparison table template (digital or printed)
Access to Python environment with scikit-learn and matplotlib
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of feature ranking identification and explanations, (2) Quality of cross-model comparisons and pattern recognition, (3) Appropriateness of business recommendations linked to importance scores, (4) Demonstration of understanding the difference between statistical importance and practical significance during discussions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example for one model showing proper explanation format and business connection. Offer guiding questions like 'What does a high importance score tell us about this feature's role in predictions?' For advanced learners, include a fourth model with categorical features and challenge them to explain why tree-based importance might differ from permutation importance, or have them calculate and compare Shapley values for the same models.

title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Propulsion Systems Using Tsiolkovsky's Equation
description: Students will dissect the performance characteristics of real multi-stage rockets by analyzing thrust-to-weight ratios, specific impulse variations, and mass fraction optimization. They will compare theoretical predictions using Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation with actual flight data from historical missions to identify design trade-offs and engineering constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between mass ratios, specific impulse, and delta-v requirements by deconstructing multi-stage rocket configurations and comparing theoretical calculations with real mission data
Students will evaluate the engineering trade-offs in rocket design through systematic examination of propellant types, staging sequences, and payload capacity constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing data packets containing specifications for three historical rockets: Saturn V, Falcon Heavy, and Ariane 5, including stage masses, propellant types, specific impulse values, and mission profiles (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning each team one rocket system. Students first calculate theoretical delta-v for each stage using Tsiolkovsky's equation (Δv = ve × ln(m0/mf)), where ve is exhaust velocity derived from specific impulse data (45 minutes). Next, teams analyze actual flight telemetry data provided, plotting velocity profiles and comparing with their theoretical calculations, identifying discrepancies and proposing explanations for differences such as gravity losses, drag, and steering losses (60 minutes). Teams then examine design decisions by calculating mass fractions for each stage and evaluating how propellant choice (RP-1/LOX vs LH2/LOX) affects performance parameters. They must identify at least three specific trade-offs between payload capacity, cost, and performance (45 minutes). Each team creates a comparative analysis matrix showing how their assigned rocket optimizes different parameters compared to the others. Finally, teams present 8-minute analyses highlighting their rocket's design philosophy, quantified performance characteristics, and critical engineering compromises, followed by peer questioning focused on alternative design approaches (40 minutes). Conclude with individual reflection essays analyzing how staging optimization principles could apply to theoretical Mars mission architectures.
materials_needed: Historical rocket specification data sheets (Saturn V, Falcon Heavy, Ariane 5)
Flight telemetry datasets with velocity-time profiles
Scientific calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Graph paper and plotting materials
Tsiolkovsky equation reference sheets with unit conversions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of Tsiolkovsky calculations and proper unit conversions (25%), (2) Quality of analysis comparing theoretical vs. actual performance with justified explanations for discrepancies (35%), (3) Identification and evaluation of at least three specific engineering trade-offs with quantitative support (25%), (4) Clarity of presentation and depth of responses to peer questions (15%). Students must achieve level 3 or higher in all categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide step-by-step calculation templates and pre-made unit conversion charts. Offer guiding questions like 'How does specific impulse relate to exhaust velocity?' and 'What factors might cause real performance to differ from ideal calculations?' For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate gravitational losses into their calculations and analyze how different launch trajectories affect overall mission efficiency. Provide additional data on engine throttling and variable specific impulse for deeper analysis.

title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Propulsion Systems Using Tsiolkovsky's Equation: Exercise 1
description: Students will decompose the complex physics of multi-stage rocket systems by analyzing real NASA mission data. They will examine how mass ratios, specific impulse, and staging configurations affect overall mission delta-v requirements and identify optimal design parameters.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between rocket mass ratios, specific impulse, and achievable delta-v by applying Tsiolkovsky's equation to multi-stage systems
Students will examine real mission profiles to identify critical design trade-offs through comparative analysis of different staging strategies
instructions: Begin by distributing NASA mission data packets for Saturn V (Apollo 11), Falcon Heavy, and Delta IV Heavy rockets, including stage masses, fuel types, and specific impulse values. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to extract key parameters and organize data into provided spreadsheet templates. Next, demonstrate the multi-stage rocket equation derivation on the board, showing how Tsiolkovsky's equation applies iteratively: Δv_total = v_e1×ln(m0/m1) + v_e2×ln(m1/m2) + v_e3×ln(m2/m3). Students then spend 40 minutes calculating theoretical delta-v for each rocket system, comparing results with actual mission requirements (Low Earth Orbit: 9.4 km/s, Geostationary Transfer: 10.1 km/s, Trans-lunar injection: 11.1 km/s). During the analysis phase (30 minutes), teams create comparison charts examining: mass ratio efficiency (wet mass/dry mass per stage), propellant selection impact on specific impulse, and staging sequence effects on payload capacity. Teams identify which design elements contribute most significantly to mission success by calculating sensitivity ratios (% change in performance per % change in parameter). Finally, each team prepares a 5-minute presentation analyzing one rocket's optimization strategy, highlighting the most critical engineering trade-offs discovered. Conclude with a class discussion comparing findings and identifying common design principles across different mission profiles.
materials_needed: NASA rocket specification data sheets (Saturn V, Falcon Heavy, Delta IV Heavy)
Scientific calculators or laptop computers
Pre-formatted Excel/Google Sheets templates with rocket equation formulas
Mission delta-v requirement reference charts
Graph paper and colored pens for data visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate application of multi-stage rocket equations with correct mathematical procedures, (2) Thorough analysis of mass ratio and specific impulse relationships with quantitative evidence, (3) Clear identification of design trade-offs with supporting calculations, (4) Effective presentation of findings with logical conclusions. Students must achieve 75% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate understanding of at least 3 major design trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with partially completed calculation templates and rocket equation reference cards. Offer guided practice with single-stage examples before multi-stage analysis. For advanced learners, introduce gravitational losses, atmospheric drag effects, and optimization using Lagrange multipliers. Consider pairing stronger math students with those needing calculation support.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Propulsion Systems Using Tsiolkovsky's Equation

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner JavaScript Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written JavaScript functions by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and providing specific improvement recommendations. This activity develops their ability to judge code effectiveness and apply best practices in a structured evaluation process.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and correctness of JavaScript functions by systematically analyzing code structure, logic, and adherence to best practices
Students will assess debugging solutions through peer review and provide justified recommendations for code improvements
instructions: Begin by distributing the Code Review Worksheet containing three JavaScript functions: a simple calculator function with subtle bugs, a name formatter with style issues, and a password validator with logic errors. Each function includes 8-12 lines of code appropriate for beginners. Give students 5 minutes to read through all three functions without making changes. Next, have students work individually for 25 minutes using the provided evaluation checklist. They must identify and document: syntax errors, logical mistakes, variable naming issues, and opportunities for improvement. For each issue found, students must explain why it's problematic and suggest a specific fix. After individual analysis, pair students for 15 minutes to compare findings and discuss their evaluations. Partners should reach consensus on the most critical issues and prioritize fixes. Each pair then presents their top 3 findings for one assigned function to the class (10 minutes total). During presentations, other students can add additional observations. Finally, reveal the 'expert solutions' and have students self-assess their evaluation accuracy using the provided answer key. Students complete a reflection form rating their confidence in identifying different types of code issues and noting which evaluation criteria they found most challenging to apply.
materials_needed: Code Review Worksheet with 3 buggy JavaScript functions
Evaluation checklist covering syntax, logic, style, and best practices
Expert solution answer key with explanations
Individual reflection form
Computers with text editors or online JavaScript environment
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Issue Identification (40%) - correctly identifies bugs and problems; Quality Assessment (30%) - evaluates code style and best practices; Improvement Recommendations (20%) - provides specific, actionable suggestions; Justification (10%) - explains reasoning for evaluations. Success criteria: identifies at least 70% of intentional issues, provides clear explanations for findings, and offers realistic improvement suggestions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example evaluation of a simple function, offer guided questions like 'Does this variable name clearly indicate its purpose?' and allow use of JavaScript documentation. For advanced learners: include additional functions with more complex issues, ask them to rewrite functions implementing their suggestions, or have them create evaluation criteria for advanced concepts like performance optimization.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner JavaScript Functions: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written JavaScript functions by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and ranking solutions from best to worst. They will justify their evaluations using established coding standards and provide improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different JavaScript function implementations by comparing their efficiency, readability, and correctness against coding best practices
Students will critique code quality through systematic analysis of syntax, logic, and adherence to naming conventions
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Code Review Packet' containing three JavaScript functions that solve the same problem (calculating average of an array) with varying quality levels. Function A has syntax errors and poor naming, Function B is functional but inefficient, and Function C follows best practices. Students work individually with computers/tablets to test code.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each function and complete the evaluation worksheet. They must: (1) Test each function with provided sample inputs, (2) Identify any bugs or errors, (3) Rate readability on a 1-5 scale with justification, (4) Check for proper variable naming and commenting, (5) Assess efficiency and logic flow.

**Phase 2 - Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Students rank the three functions from best (1) to worst (3) and write a 3-sentence justification for their ranking. They must reference specific criteria: functionality, readability, efficiency, and adherence to JavaScript conventions.

**Phase 3 - Peer Discussion (8 minutes):** Pair students to compare rankings and discuss disagreements. Each pair must reach consensus on the ranking order and prepare one improvement suggestion for the worst-ranked function.

**Phase 4 - Class Debrief (7 minutes):** Conduct whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their rankings and reasoning. Record common evaluation criteria on the board. Conclude by revealing the 'expert ranking' and discussing any surprising insights about code quality assessment.
materials_needed: Code Review Packet with 3 JavaScript functions printed for each student
Evaluation worksheet template
Computers/tablets with JavaScript console or online code editor (repl.it, CodePen)
Sample test inputs document
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate bug identification in all functions (25%), (2) Logical ranking with clear justification referencing at least 3 evaluation criteria (35%), (3) Quality of improvement suggestions showing understanding of best practices (25%), (4) Active participation in peer discussion and ability to defend evaluation choices (15%). Students must correctly identify the major syntax error and rank functions appropriately to pass.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide a checklist of specific items to look for (syntax errors, variable names, comments, logic flow). Pair struggling students with stronger peers during discussion phase. Offer simplified evaluation criteria focusing on 'Does it work?' and 'Is it readable?' **Extension for advanced learners:** Ask them to rewrite the worst function to demonstrate best practices, or evaluate additional criteria like memory usage and scalability. Have them create their own problematic function for classmates to evaluate.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner JavaScript Functions

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Business Growth
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary value). They will synthesize multiple data sources, design custom visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations for targeted marketing strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive RFM customer segmentation model by analyzing transactional data patterns and creating weighted scoring algorithms
Students will design an interactive dashboard interface through combining multiple visualization types that communicate customer insights to business stakeholders
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Preparation (20 minutes)**
Provide students with a simulated e-commerce dataset containing customer transactions from the past 18 months (CustomerID, OrderDate, OrderValue, ProductCategory). Students begin by cleaning the dataset, identifying missing values, and calculating three key metrics per customer: days since last purchase (Recency), total number of purchases (Frequency), and average order value (Monetary). They must document their data cleaning decisions in a methodology log.

**Phase 2: Segmentation Model Creation (25 minutes)**
Students develop their RFM scoring system by creating quintile rankings (1-5 scale) for each metric, then combining scores to form customer segments. They must justify their weighting decisions and create at least 5 distinct customer personas (e.g., 'Champions', 'At-Risk', 'New Customers'). Each segment requires a written profile describing characteristics and recommended marketing approaches.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Design and Construction (35 minutes)**
Using their chosen visualization tool, students build an interactive dashboard featuring: a customer segment overview chart, RFM score distributions, revenue contribution by segment, and trend analysis over time. The dashboard must include filters for date ranges and product categories, plus hover-over details for individual customer information.

**Phase 4: Business Strategy Development (15 minutes)**
Students conclude by creating a one-page executive summary with three specific, data-driven marketing recommendations. Each recommendation must reference specific customer segments, include projected ROI estimates, and propose success metrics for campaign evaluation.
materials_needed: Simulated e-commerce transaction dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Tableau Desktop, Power BI, or Python with Plotly/Dash libraries
Customer segmentation template worksheet
Executive summary presentation template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Data methodology accuracy and documentation (20 points), (2) Segmentation model logic and statistical validity (25 points), (3) Dashboard functionality and visual design clarity (25 points), (4) Business insights depth and actionability (20 points), (5) Professional presentation and communication (10 points). Students must achieve minimum 70% to demonstrate proficiency in creating analytical solutions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing RFM calculation formulas and sample segmentation criteria. Offer pre-built dashboard templates with placeholder charts they can customize. For advanced learners, challenge them to incorporate additional variables (geographic data, product preferences) or implement machine learning clustering algorithms (K-means) to validate their manual segmentation approach.

title: Interactive Customer Segmentation Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior, demographics, and engagement metrics using real e-commerce data. They will design original analytical frameworks, develop custom visualizations, and present strategic recommendations for targeted marketing campaigns.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multiple data sources (sales, demographics, web analytics) by creating an integrated customer segmentation model with at least 4 distinct segments
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through combining advanced visualization techniques with business intelligence principles to support executive decision-making
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration & Exploration (45 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: customer_transactions.csv (6 months of purchase data), customer_demographics.csv (age, location, acquisition channel), and engagement_metrics.csv (email opens, website visits, social media interactions). Students work in pairs to load data into Tableau/Power BI and perform initial quality assessment. They must identify and document at least 5 data quality issues and propose solutions.

**Phase 2: Segmentation Framework Design (30 minutes)**
Each pair develops their original customer segmentation framework by combining RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) with demographic and engagement variables. Students must define 4-6 customer segments with specific criteria (e.g., 'High-Value Millennials: customers aged 25-35, spending >$500/month, high social media engagement'). They sketch their dashboard layout on paper, planning 6-8 visualizations.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (60 minutes)**
Using their chosen BI tool, students build interactive dashboards featuring: customer segment overview (pie/donut chart), geographic distribution (map), purchase behavior trends (time series), and segment comparison matrix (heatmap). Each visualization must include filters for date range, product category, and acquisition channel. Students create calculated fields for segment classification and key metrics.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendations (30 minutes)**
Pairs develop 3 specific marketing strategies targeting their identified segments, including budget allocation recommendations, channel preferences, and expected ROI projections. They prepare 5-minute presentations with supporting data evidence from their dashboards.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with 1000+ customer records
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Laptops/computers with internet access
Presentation timer and projector for final presentations
Dashboard design template worksheet (paper-based planning tool)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Data Integration Quality - proper joins, data cleaning documentation, handling of missing values; (2) Segmentation Logic - mathematical rigor of RFM calculations, meaningful segment definitions, clear differentiation criteria; (3) Dashboard Design - visual hierarchy, interactivity functionality, professional appearance, mobile responsiveness; (4) Business Impact - actionable recommendations, ROI justification, strategic alignment with business goals. Each component weighted equally for 100-point total score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written SQL queries for data cleaning, offer segment definition templates, and allow use of dashboard gallery examples for inspiration. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate machine learning clustering algorithms (K-means), create predictive lifetime value models, or integrate external data sources like social media APIs. Consider pairing stronger technical students with those having stronger business acumen.
original_title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Business Growth

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Component Identification and Terminology Mastery
description: Students will identify and recall specific components, terminology, and relationships within advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, Agile-Waterfall hybrid models, and Program Management Office (PMO) governance structures. This activity focuses on memorizing and recognizing complex project management elements that practicing professionals must know instantly.
learning_objectives: Students will identify all seven PRINCE2 processes, their 26 specific activities, and associated management products by completing a comprehensive framework mapping exercise
Students will recall specific terminology, acronyms, and definitions for 45 advanced project management concepts through structured memorization and rapid-response testing
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute individual study period where students review provided reference sheets containing PRINCE2 processes (Starting Up, Initiating, Directing, Controlling a Stage, Managing Product Delivery, Managing Stage Boundaries, Closing), PMO governance levels (Strategic, Tactical, Operational), and Agile-Hybrid terminology. Distribute laminated card sets containing 45 terms on one side and definitions on reverse. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes using spaced repetition technique: Partner A shows term cards, Partner B provides definition and context, then roles reverse every 5 minutes. Next, conduct a 20-minute structured identification exercise where students complete a detailed framework diagram, labeling all PRINCE2 process inputs, outputs, and decision points without references. Follow with a 15-minute rapid-fire terminology quiz where students have 30 seconds per question to write definitions for randomly selected terms. Conclude with 10 minutes of peer verification where students check each other's framework diagrams against master answer key and discuss any discrepancies. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact terminology usage and precise component relationships as these are critical for professional certification exams and workplace communication.
materials_needed: Laminated terminology flash cards (45 cards per pair)
PRINCE2 framework reference sheets
Blank framework diagram templates
Digital timer for rapid-fire sections
Master answer keys for verification
PMO governance structure charts
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on framework diagram labeling (40 components correctly identified and placed) and 85% accuracy on terminology definitions (38 out of 45 terms correctly defined with key elements included). Assessment includes peer verification checkpoints and instructor spot-checks during rapid-response segments.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide acronym memory devices (e.g., PRINCE2's 'Starting Up' = SU) and allow color-coding of related framework components. Advanced learners can integrate additional frameworks like SAFe or identify cross-framework terminology overlaps. Consider providing audio recordings of terms for auditory learners and allow kinesthetic learners to physically arrange framework component cards.

title: Crisis Leadership Decision-Making Framework Analysis Through Historical Case Comparison
description: Students will analyze and compare the decision-making frameworks used by three different leaders during major organizational crises, identifying patterns in their approaches and explaining the underlying leadership theories that guided their actions. This expert-level activity requires deep comprehension of multiple leadership models and their real-world applications.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the decision-making processes of crisis leaders by mapping their actions to established leadership theories (transformational, authentic, adaptive leadership)
Students will explain the relationship between leadership communication strategies and stakeholder outcomes through comparative analysis of three historical crisis scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing three detailed crisis case studies (20 minutes): 1) Reed Hastings during Netflix's 2011 Qwikster backlash, 2) Cheryl Sandberg managing Facebook's 2016 election interference crisis, and 3) Andy Jassy leading Amazon Web Services' 2017 S3 outage response. Students work in groups of 4-5, with each group receiving identical materials but different analysis templates. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each group member becomes an 'expert' on one case study, reading thoroughly and completing a leadership analysis worksheet identifying: decision timeline, stakeholder communication approach, team mobilization tactics, and recovery strategies. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups reconvene for expert sharing, where each member presents their case analysis while others take structured notes on a comparison matrix. Phase 3 (40 minutes): Groups collaborate to identify patterns across all three cases, categorizing leadership behaviors using provided theory reference sheets (transformational, authentic, adaptive, servant leadership frameworks). They must explain why certain approaches worked or failed in each context. Phase 4 (25 minutes): Each group creates a visual framework diagram showing how the three leaders' approaches align with or diverge from established leadership theories, including specific quotes and decisions as evidence. Groups present their frameworks in a gallery walk format, with rotating 5-minute presentations to other groups.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (8-10 pages each) with timeline, stakeholder maps, and outcome data
Leadership theory reference sheets covering transformational, authentic, adaptive, and servant leadership models
Structured comparison matrix worksheets
Large poster paper and colored markers for framework diagrams
Individual leadership analysis worksheets with guided questions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership theory application to case details (25%), (2) Quality of cross-case pattern identification with specific evidence (25%), (3) Clarity of explanation for why certain leadership approaches succeeded/failed in context (25%), (4) Visual framework coherence and presentation effectiveness (25%). Collect both individual worksheets and group framework diagrams. Observe group discussions for depth of theoretical understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key sections in case studies and sentence starters for analysis worksheets. Include a leadership theory matching activity as warm-up. For advanced learners: Add a fourth case study with ambiguous outcomes, require integration of additional leadership theories (situational, complexity leadership), or have them develop crisis leadership recommendations for a novel scenario based on their analysis.

title: Critical Path Analysis and Schedule Compression Trade-off Evaluation
description: Students will analyze a project network diagram to identify the critical path, evaluate the impact of potential delays, and systematically compare crashing versus fast-tracking strategies for schedule compression. This activity develops skills in schedule analysis and risk-based decision making for project managers.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project network diagrams by identifying critical paths, calculating float values, and determining schedule compression opportunities using forward/backward pass calculations
Students will evaluate trade-offs between crashing and fast-tracking strategies through systematic comparison of cost, risk, and timeline impacts on project deliverables
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Software Implementation Project' network diagram showing 15 activities with durations, dependencies, and resource costs. Form teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives analysis worksheets and calculators. **Phase 1 - Critical Path Analysis (20 minutes):** Teams perform forward and backward pass calculations to determine early start/finish and late start/finish dates for all activities. Students identify the critical path and calculate total float for non-critical activities. Teams must document their calculations showing ES, EF, LS, LF for each activity node. **Phase 2 - Impact Analysis (15 minutes):** Present teams with three delay scenarios: Activity B delayed 3 days, Activity F delayed 2 days, Activity J delayed 4 days. Teams analyze which delays impact the critical path and calculate new project completion dates. Students must justify their reasoning with mathematical evidence. **Phase 3 - Compression Strategy Evaluation (25 minutes):** Teams evaluate compression options to recover lost time: crashing (reducing activity duration by adding resources) versus fast-tracking (running activities in parallel). Provide cost data for crashing each activity and risk ratings for fast-tracking parallel activities. Teams complete a comparison matrix weighing factors: additional cost, schedule reduction, resource requirements, quality risks, and stakeholder impact. **Presentation Phase (15 minutes):** Each team presents their recommended strategy with supporting analysis. Teams must defend their choice against questions about alternative approaches and implementation challenges.
materials_needed: Pre-designed network diagram with 15 activities showing AON format with durations and dependencies
Activity cost and resource data sheets for crashing analysis
Risk assessment matrices for fast-tracking evaluation
Critical path analysis worksheets with calculation templates
Comparison matrix templates for strategy evaluation
Calculators or computers with project management software access
assessment_method: Grade using rubric with four components: (1) Critical path calculations accuracy (25 points) - all ES/EF/LS/LF values correct and critical path properly identified, (2) Impact analysis quality (25 points) - correct delay impact calculations with clear reasoning, (3) Strategy comparison thoroughness (25 points) - systematic evaluation of crashing vs fast-tracking with quantified trade-offs, (4) Recommendation justification (25 points) - evidence-based strategy selection with consideration of multiple factors and stakeholder needs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed calculation templates with first few activities solved, offer step-by-step calculation guides, and pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Add Monte Carlo simulation requirements for schedule risk analysis, include resource leveling considerations, or require evaluation of multiple compression combinations with optimization recommendations.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation Development
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for specific business scenarios and defend their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI discrepancies across paid search, display, and social media channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and formulate evidence-based recommendations for budget reallocation
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active. Students start by navigating to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. Have them export data for the past 90 days comparing all five attribution models across three specific channel groupings: Paid Search, Display Advertising, and Social Network. Students must document conversion values, conversion counts, and cost-per-acquisition differences between models, creating a comprehensive spreadsheet analysis. Next, teams examine the Top Conversion Paths report to identify the three most common customer journey patterns, noting average days to conversion and touchpoint frequency. They then access the Time Lag and Path Length reports to understand customer behavior patterns. Using this data, teams must evaluate each attribution model's strengths and weaknesses for their assigned business scenario (provided case studies include: B2B SaaS with long sales cycles, fast-fashion e-commerce, and subscription meal delivery). Teams calculate the potential budget impact of switching from last-click to their recommended model, showing specific dollar amounts that would shift between channels. Finally, each team prepares a 15-minute presentation defending their chosen attribution model with quantitative evidence, addressing potential counterarguments, and providing specific implementation recommendations including timeline and expected ROI changes. Presentations must include before/after budget allocation charts and risk assessment analysis.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Enhanced Ecommerce demo account access for each team
Three distinct business scenario case study packets
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel) for data analysis
Presentation software for final deliverables
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 100-point rubric: Data Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct extraction and calculation of attribution model differences; Critical Evaluation (25 points) - thorough assessment of each model's appropriateness for business context; Strategic Reasoning (25 points) - logical defense of chosen model with quantitative support; Implementation Plan (25 points) - realistic timeline, budget impact calculations, and risk mitigation strategies. Peer evaluation component where teams score each other's presentations adds 10% bonus potential.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-populated data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer mid-activity check-ins after data collection phase. For advanced learners, add custom attribution modeling requirements using Google Analytics Intelligence API or require integration of offline conversion data. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those needing support during team formation.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation Development: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine optimal customer journey tracking strategies. They will assess the effectiveness of various attribution models and develop evidence-based recommendations for improving conversion attribution accuracy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, linear) by analyzing conversion path data and identifying attribution discrepancies across channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of model performance metrics and develop strategic recommendations for attribution model optimization
instructions: **Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple traffic sources (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical datasets but different business scenarios (B2B SaaS, retail fashion, subscription service). **Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Teams navigate to GA4 Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. Students must: 1) Export conversion data for each attribution model (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based, data-driven) 2) Calculate percentage differences in attributed conversions between models for each channel 3) Identify which channels gain/lose attribution credit under different models 4) Document conversion path length patterns and typical customer journey duration 5) Analyze revenue attribution variations across models using the Revenue attribution report. **Evaluation Phase (30 minutes):** Teams create comparison matrices showing: conversion volume changes, revenue attribution shifts, cost-per-acquisition variations per channel, and statistical significance of differences. Students must identify model limitations by examining edge cases where attribution fails or provides misleading insights. **Recommendation Development (20 minutes):** Each team develops a 5-slide presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice, including: primary and backup model selections, implementation timeline, expected business impact metrics, and monitoring strategies for model performance validation.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Business scenario descriptions for each team (provided handouts)
GA4 Attribution Models reference guide
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: Data Analysis Accuracy (25% - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences), Critical Evaluation Quality (30% - depth of model comparison and limitation identification), Recommendation Justification (30% - evidence-based reasoning and business alignment), and Presentation Clarity (15% - clear communication of findings and strategic rationale). Minimum passing score: 3.0/4.0 with no category below 2.5.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided worksheet for model comparison calculations. Offer reference examples of strong vs. weak attribution analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value considerations, propose custom attribution model parameters, or analyze cross-device attribution challenges. Provide access to additional GA4 features like Audience Overlap reports for deeper insights.
original_title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation Development

title: Binary Number Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recognition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid recognition exercises within 30 seconds per problem
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student, with decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Spend 5 minutes explaining the flashcard format and demonstrating proper use. Have students work individually for 15 minutes in self-paced study mode, flipping through cards and testing themselves on both decimal-to-binary and binary-to-decimal conversions. Encourage students to separate cards into 'known' and 'needs practice' piles. After individual study, pair students for 10 minutes of partner drilling, where one student shows the decimal side while the partner states the binary equivalent, then switch roles. Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire session for 8 minutes: display decimal numbers on the board for 10 seconds each while students write binary answers on mini whiteboards, then reveal correct answers immediately. Follow with reverse practice showing binary numbers for decimal identification. Conclude with a 7-minute individual quiz where students complete a worksheet with 16 mixed conversion problems (8 decimal-to-binary, 8 binary-to-decimal) without flashcards. Walk around during all activities to monitor progress and provide immediate feedback. Emphasize that students should focus on memorization rather than calculation methods during this activity.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcard sets (16 cards each showing decimal 0-15 with 4-bit binary on reverse)
Mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each student
Binary-decimal conversion quiz worksheet (16 problems)
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Grade the final quiz worksheet using a simple checklist: 14-16 correct answers (90%+) = Proficient recall achieved, 11-13 correct (70-85%) = Developing recall needs continued practice, below 11 correct = Beginning level requires reteaching. Observe during partner work for participation and accuracy, noting students who struggle with specific number ranges for targeted follow-up.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling learners: Reduce initial set to numbers 0-7, provide a place-value chart showing 8-4-2-1 positions, and allow extra individual study time. For advanced students: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), introduce hexadecimal equivalents on card backs, or challenge them to help tutor struggling peers during partner work.

title: Interpreting Statistical Summaries from Box Plots and Histograms
description: Students will analyze a real dataset containing housing prices using both box plots and histograms to identify distribution patterns, outliers, and central tendencies. They will then explain how different visualization methods reveal different aspects of the same data and make data-driven conclusions about housing market trends.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret distribution characteristics (skewness, outliers, central tendency) by analyzing box plots and histograms of housing price data
Students will explain the relationship between statistical measures and visual representations through comparative analysis of multiple visualization types
instructions:
Begin by providing each student pair with the Boston Housing dataset (available via scikit-learn) pre-loaded in Jupyter notebooks with basic exploratory code already written. Students should have pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries imported. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students examine the provided box plot of median home values and write down three observations about the data distribution, specifically noting the median line position, whisker lengths, and any visible outliers beyond the whiskers.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students create a histogram of the same housing price data using matplotlib, experimenting with bin sizes of 10, 20, and 50 bins. They document how changing bin size affects their interpretation of the distribution shape and identify which bin size best reveals the data patterns.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Working in pairs, students compare their box plot observations with histogram findings, specifically addressing: Does the box plot median align with the histogram's peak? How do outliers appear differently in each visualization? What distribution shape (normal, skewed left/right) is evident?

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students analyze a second variable (e.g., crime rate) using the same dual-visualization approach, applying their developed interpretation skills to identify patterns and outliers.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each pair writes a 2-paragraph summary explaining which visualization better reveals different aspects of the data and provides three specific data-driven insights about Boston housing patterns that could inform real estate decisions.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, seaborn installed
Boston Housing dataset from scikit-learn
Pre-written starter code with data loading and basic box plot
Worksheet template for recording observations and comparisons
assessment_method: Students submit their completed Jupyter notebook with both visualizations and written 2-paragraph analysis. Grade using rubric: Correct identification of distribution characteristics (25%), Accurate comparison between visualization types (25%), Appropriate histogram bin size selection with justification (25%), Clear data-driven insights with supporting evidence (25%). Success requires scoring 80% or higher across all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of specific elements to look for in each visualization (median location, outlier count, distribution symmetry). Offer sentence starters for analysis paragraphs. For advanced learners, introduce additional statistical measures like IQR calculations or challenge them to create subplots comparing multiple variables simultaneously, or explore violin plots as a combination approach.

title: Optimizing Container Design Using Calculus and Constraints
description: Students will apply differential calculus and Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world optimization problem involving the design of cylindrical shipping containers. They will determine optimal dimensions to minimize material costs while meeting volume and structural constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a multi-constraint engineering problem by setting up and solving systems of equations involving partial derivatives
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods through systematic problem-solving steps to find optimal solutions under real-world constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario handout describing ShipCo's need for cylindrical containers with 500 cubic meter capacity, where material costs $8/m² for cylindrical walls and $12/m² for top/bottom circles, with height restrictions of 2-4 meters due to warehouse limitations. Form pairs and assign each team to work through the problem systematically. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students define variables (radius r, height h), write the volume constraint equation (πr²h = 500), and express the cost function C = 16πr² + 8πrh in terms of one variable using substitution. Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams find the critical points by taking the derivative of C(r) and setting it equal to zero, then solve for the optimal radius. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students verify their solution satisfies the height constraint by calculating h = 500/(πr²) and checking if 2 ≤ h ≤ 4. Step 4 (10 minutes): Teams apply the Lagrange multiplier method as verification, setting up L(r,h,λ) = 16πr² + 8πrh + λ(πr²h - 500) and solving the system of partial derivatives. Step 5 (15 minutes): Students calculate the minimum cost and create a brief presentation showing their mathematical work and final recommendations. Circulate continuously to check equation setup, derivative calculations, and constraint verification. Conclude with 3-4 team presentations (10 minutes total) comparing solutions and discussing practical implications.
materials_needed: ShipCo container optimization scenario handouts
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos/GeoGebra)
Graph paper and rulers
Whiteboard markers for team workspace boards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct setup of constraint equation and objective function (25%), (2) Accurate application of calculus optimization techniques including proper derivatives (35%), (3) Verification that solution satisfies all given constraints (25%), and (4) Clear mathematical communication in final presentation (15%). Students must show complete mathematical work and arrive at radius ≈ 3.17m, height ≈ 5.02m to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and guide them through the substitution process step-by-step. Offer derivative calculation templates and encourage use of technology to verify algebraic work. For advanced learners: Extend the problem by adding a third constraint (weight limitations) or asking them to investigate how the optimal solution changes with different cost ratios for materials.

title: Analyzing Multi-Phase Circuit Failures in Complex RLC Networks
description: Students analyze a malfunctioning three-phase RLC circuit by decomposing complex impedance relationships, identifying failure points through phasor analysis, and evaluating the cascading effects on power distribution. They must distinguish between normal operating conditions and fault scenarios using both analytical methods and simulation data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex impedance relationships in three-phase RLC circuits by decomposing phasor diagrams and calculating phase angle deviations from theoretical values
Students will evaluate circuit failure modes through systematic comparison of measured versus predicted voltage/current relationships across multiple network nodes
instructions: Begin by distributing the circuit schematic showing a three-phase RLC network with specified component values (R=50Ω, L=0.2H, C=100μF per phase) and measured data from 12 test points. Students work in teams of 3-4 for 20 minutes to calculate theoretical impedance values for each phase at 60Hz, creating phasor diagrams for normal operation. Next, provide oscilloscope traces and multimeter readings showing actual circuit behavior with clear anomalies. Teams spend 25 minutes analyzing discrepancies by: (1) calculating actual impedance from measured V/I ratios, (2) identifying which components deviate from specifications, (3) mapping voltage drops across each circuit element, and (4) determining power factor changes. Using MATLAB/Simulink or similar software, teams spend 30 minutes modeling both the theoretical circuit and fault conditions, running simulations to verify their analytical findings. Each team creates a fault analysis report identifying: primary failure location, secondary effects on other phases, calculated vs. measured impedance matrices, and power distribution impacts. Teams present 10-minute analyses explaining their reasoning process, showing phasor diagrams comparing normal vs. fault conditions, and defending their conclusions using quantitative evidence. Conclude with 15 minutes of peer evaluation where teams critique each other's analytical approaches and propose alternative diagnostic methods.
materials_needed: Three-phase RLC circuit schematic with component specifications
Oscilloscope trace printouts showing voltage/current waveforms at 12 test points
Multimeter measurement data sheets with complex impedance values
MATLAB/Simulink software access or equivalent circuit simulation tool
Scientific calculators capable of complex number operations
Large format paper for phasor diagram construction
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of theoretical impedance calculations and phasor constructions (25%), (2) Correctness of fault identification and supporting quantitative analysis (30%), (3) Quality of simulation model and verification process (25%), (4) Clarity of reasoning in oral presentation and defense of conclusions (20%). Students must achieve 75% accuracy in calculations and correctly identify the primary fault location to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed phasor diagrams and impedance calculation templates. Offer guided questions: 'Which phase shows the largest impedance deviation?' and 'How does capacitor failure affect phase relationships?' For advanced learners, introduce harmonic analysis of the fault conditions, require calculation of sequence components (positive, negative, zero), or challenge them to predict fault progression over time with component aging models.

title: Code Quality Audit: Evaluating and Ranking Simple Python Functions
description: Students will critically assess and rank three different implementations of the same basic Python function based on code quality criteria. They will justify their rankings using specific evidence and provide improvement recommendations for each implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three Python function implementations by applying code quality criteria including readability, efficiency, and maintainability
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and evidence-based ranking with written justifications
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a worksheet containing three different implementations of a function that calculates the average of numbers in a list.
