Label them Implementation A, B, and C. Include a code quality checklist covering: variable naming, comments/documentation, code structure, error handling, and efficiency.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each implementation using the checklist, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses. They should identify specific lines or elements that demonstrate good or poor practices.

**Ranking Activity (10 minutes):** Students rank the three implementations from best (1) to worst (3) based on overall code quality. They must write 2-3 sentences justifying each ranking decision using specific examples from the code.

**Peer Discussion (8 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and justifications. They discuss any disagreements and may revise their rankings based on peer insights.

**Individual Reflection (7 minutes):** Students complete a reflection form identifying: (1) the most important code quality factor they discovered, (2) one specific improvement they would make to the lowest-ranked implementation, and (3) one coding practice they will apply in their own future work.

**Materials Distribution:** Ensure each student receives the worksheet with all three code implementations printed clearly, the code quality checklist, and the reflection form before beginning.
materials_needed: Worksheet with three Python function implementations (printed or digital)
Code quality assessment checklist
Ranking justification template
Individual reflection form
Computers/tablets if using digital format
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Completion of quality checklist for all three implementations (30%), (2) Clear ranking with specific, evidence-based justifications citing actual code elements (50%), (3) Thoughtful reflection demonstrating understanding of code quality principles (20%). Success requires identifying at least 2 specific strengths/weaknesses per implementation and providing concrete examples.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a partially completed example analysis of one implementation, highlight specific code lines to focus on, or pair with stronger students during discussion. **For advanced students:** Add a fourth implementation with more complex issues, ask them to rewrite the poorest implementation, or have them create their own improved version incorporating best practices from all three examples.

title: Design a Data-Driven Business Intelligence Dashboard for Local Restaurant Performance
description: Students will synthesize multi-source restaurant data to create an original interactive dashboard that identifies performance patterns and generates actionable business recommendations. They will combine sales, customer feedback, and operational data to design visualizations that tell a cohesive story about restaurant performance trends.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an interactive dashboard by integrating at least three different data sources and creating five distinct visualization types that reveal business insights
Students will generate original business recommendations through systematic analysis of data patterns and present findings using professional data storytelling techniques
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration (45 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: monthly sales data (12 months), customer review scores (rating, sentiment, date), and operational metrics (staff hours, inventory costs, customer wait times). Students work in pairs to clean and merge datasets using Excel or Google Sheets, identifying common fields (dates, location IDs) for joining. They must document data quality issues found and cleaning steps taken.

**Phase 2: Dashboard Design (60 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students create an interactive dashboard with mandatory elements: 1) Time-series chart showing sales trends with seasonal annotations, 2) Correlation scatter plot between customer satisfaction and revenue, 3) Geographic heat map if multiple locations exist, 4) KPI cards showing key metrics, 5) Filter controls for date ranges and categories. Each visualization must include proper titles, axis labels, and color schemes that enhance readability.

**Phase 3: Insight Generation (30 minutes)**
Students analyze their completed dashboard to identify three specific business insights (e.g., 'Saturday dinner sales drop 23% when wait times exceed 25 minutes'). They must support each insight with specific data evidence and propose one actionable recommendation per insight.

**Phase 4: Presentation (15 minutes)**
Pairs present their dashboard live, walking through their design choices, key findings, and business recommendations in exactly 5 minutes, followed by peer questions. Emphasize data storytelling: start with business context, reveal insights progressively, and conclude with clear next steps for restaurant management.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV files: restaurant sales data (monthly), customer reviews dataset, operational metrics file
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI (free versions)
Computers with internet access
Presentation timer/stopwatch
Dashboard design checklist handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: Data Integration Quality (proper cleaning, successful joins), Dashboard Design (visual hierarchy, interactivity, professional appearance), Analytical Rigor (insight validity, evidence support), Business Application (recommendation feasibility, strategic thinking), and Presentation Skills (clarity, time management, storytelling). Each criterion worth 20 points. Students must achieve 70+ points and include all mandatory visualization types to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data integration templates showing join examples, offer pre-made color palettes, and give insight starter phrases like 'When X increases, Y tends to...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data (weather, local events), create calculated fields for advanced metrics (customer lifetime value, profit margins), or build predictive trend lines. Provide one-on-one technical support during Phase 2 for software difficulties.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Identification and Recitation
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific formulas, terminology, and calculation components used in Critical Path Method analysis. This activity focuses on building foundational recall of CPM mathematical relationships including Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Float calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recite the six core CPM formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF, Total Float, Free Float) with 100% precision using standardized notation
Students will identify and define 15 specific CPM terminology components through rapid-fire recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet containing the six formulas without definitions (15 minutes setup). Students work individually to create memorization aids using the provided index cards, writing one formula per card with standardized notation: ES = maximum EF of predecessors, EF = ES + Duration, LF = minimum LS of successors, LS = LF - Duration, Total Float = LF - EF or LS - ES, Free Float = minimum ES of successors - EF. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Students use spaced repetition technique, reviewing cards every 3 minutes, then 5 minutes, then 7 minutes. Phase 2 (15 minutes): Pair students for cross-testing where Partner A shows formula name, Partner B recites complete formula from memory, then switch roles. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Conduct whole-class rapid-fire session where instructor calls out scenarios like 'Activity has ES=5, Duration=3, what is EF?' Students write answers on whiteboards simultaneously and display. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual silent quiz where each student writes all six formulas from memory with correct mathematical notation. Conclude with group recitation of all formulas in sequence (5 minutes). Students must achieve 100% accuracy on formula notation and mathematical relationships.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet (without explanations) - 1 per student
Index cards (6 per student) for formula memorization
Individual whiteboards and dry erase markers
Timer for spaced repetition intervals
Pre-written scenario cards for instructor prompting
assessment_method: Individual written quiz requiring students to write all six CPM formulas with correct notation (6 points). Oral recitation accuracy during pair work (peer assessment checklist worth 4 points). Whiteboard response accuracy during rapid-fire session (10 scenario responses worth 1 point each). Success criteria: 18/20 points minimum, with mandatory 100% accuracy on final formula writing quiz.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices sheet (Every Student Eats Food, Late Students Leave Fast) and allow formula cards reference during first two phases. Use color-coding for different formula types (green for early times, red for late times, blue for float). For advanced learners: Add precedence diagramming method (PDM) relationship formulas (SS, SF, FF, FS with leads/lags) and challenge them to create memory palace techniques to teach struggling peers.

title: Deconstructing Multi-Dimensional Leadership Crisis Decision Frameworks
description: Students will analyze three authentic organizational crisis scenarios by mapping the leadership decision-making frameworks employed, identifying the underlying theoretical models, and explaining how different leadership approaches influenced stakeholder outcomes. This expert-level activity requires students to demonstrate deep comprehension of complex leadership theories in high-stakes contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, situational, and ethical leadership frameworks by analyzing their application in authentic crisis management scenarios
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership decision-making models and stakeholder impact through systematic case study deconstruction
instructions: Begin by distributing three detailed crisis case studies: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol recall (1982), Wells Fargo's account fraud scandal (2016), and Patagonia's supply chain transparency initiative (2011). Each case should be 3-4 pages with leadership decisions, timeline, and outcomes clearly documented. Form teams of 4 students and assign each team one primary case for 90 minutes of deep analysis. Provide each team with the Leadership Framework Analysis Template containing sections for: decision timeline mapping, theoretical framework identification, stakeholder impact matrix, and leadership approach classification. During the first 30 minutes, teams read their assigned case individually and complete preliminary framework identification worksheets. For the next 45 minutes, teams collaborate to populate the analysis template, specifically identifying which leadership theories (transformational, transactional, servant, authentic, situational) are evident in executive decisions. Teams must cite specific textual evidence and map decisions to theoretical constructs. In the final 15 minutes, teams prepare a 5-minute presentation summarizing their framework analysis. Following team work, conduct 15-minute presentations where each team presents their findings while other teams complete comparative analysis worksheets, noting similarities and differences in leadership approaches across the three crisis scenarios. Conclude with a 20-minute facilitated discussion where students synthesize patterns across cases and explain how different theoretical frameworks produced varying stakeholder outcomes.
materials_needed: Three authentic crisis case studies (Johnson & Johnson Tylenol, Wells Fargo fraud, Patagonia transparency)
Leadership Framework Analysis Template (digital or printed)
Preliminary framework identification worksheets
Comparative analysis worksheets for peer evaluation
Leadership theory reference sheets with key characteristics
Timer and presentation technology
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Framework Analysis Templates using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of 3+ leadership theories with textual evidence, (2) Clear explanation of decision-framework connections, (3) Comprehensive stakeholder impact analysis, (4) Synthesis quality during presentations. Students must score 3/4 on all categories to demonstrate understanding. Additionally, assess comparative analysis worksheets for accurate pattern recognition across cases.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-populated decision timeline templates and leadership theory characteristic cards for reference matching. Offer sentence starters for framework explanations. For advanced learners, include additional complexity by requiring analysis of cultural context factors and ethical framework integration. Provide supplementary cases for extended analysis and ask them to identify hybrid leadership approaches not clearly fitting single theoretical models.

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will configure and deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS, connecting an EC2 web server to an RDS database and S3 storage bucket. This hands-on activity demonstrates real-world cloud deployment scenarios using core AWS services.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS databases, and S3 buckets with proper security groups
Students will establish secure connections between AWS services through hands-on configuration of VPC networking and IAM roles
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS Free Tier account access and shares the sample PHP web application code via GitHub link. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify they can access EC2, RDS, and S3 services.

**Phase 1 - S3 Configuration (20 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-assets-[studentID]' with public read access for static files. Upload provided CSS, JavaScript, and image files. Configure bucket policy for web access and test file accessibility via browser.

**Phase 2 - RDS Database Setup (25 minutes):** Launch MySQL RDS instance (db.t3.micro) with specific configuration: database name 'webappdb', master username 'admin', auto-generated password. Create security group allowing inbound traffic on port 3306 from EC2 security group (to be created). Wait for database to become available and note the endpoint URL.

**Phase 3 - EC2 Web Server Deployment (30 minutes):** Launch Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) with Apache and PHP pre-installed via user data script provided. Create security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. Connect via EC2 Instance Connect and download the web application code. Configure database connection settings using RDS endpoint.

**Phase 4 - Integration Testing (15 minutes):** Modify application configuration file with S3 bucket name and RDS connection details. Test complete application functionality: user registration, file upload to S3, and data retrieval from RDS. Document the public IP address and verify all three tiers communicate successfully.

**Students work individually but can consult peers for troubleshooting. Instructor circulates to verify security group configurations and connection strings.**
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account for each student
Sample PHP web application code repository (GitHub link)
Pre-written user data script for EC2 Apache/PHP installation
Configuration template with placeholder values for database and S3 connections
Network diagram showing three-tier architecture
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment report containing: (1) Screenshots of running application with timestamp, (2) AWS resource summary showing all three services configured, (3) Public URL of working application, (4) Brief explanation of how data flows between tiers. Rubric: Complete functionality (40%), proper security group configuration (30%), successful service integration (20%), documentation quality (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step connection troubleshooting checklist. Offer one-on-one assistance during RDS setup as this is typically the most challenging phase. **For advanced students:** Challenge them to implement HTTPS with SSL certificate, add CloudWatch monitoring, or create an Application Load Balancer for high availability. Encourage exploration of infrastructure-as-code using CloudFormation templates.

title: Schedule Variance Analysis and Root Cause Investigation
description: Students will analyze a project's schedule performance data to identify variance patterns and investigate underlying causes. They will decompose schedule metrics, examine critical path impacts, and differentiate between symptoms and root causes using systematic analytical techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze schedule variance data by calculating SV, SPI, and forecasting metrics to identify performance trends and problem areas
Students will differentiate between schedule variance symptoms and root causes through structured cause-and-effect analysis and critical path examination
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Phoenix Software Implementation' case study packet containing: baseline schedule (24 activities), actual progress data through month 4, earned value metrics, and resource allocation charts. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Data Analysis (20 minutes):** Teams calculate Schedule Variance (SV = EV - PV) and Schedule Performance Index (SPI = EV/PV) for each work package. Students create a variance tracking table identifying which activities show SV > 10% deviation from baseline. Teams plot SPI trends over the 4-month period and identify the three most problematic work packages.

**Phase 2 - Critical Path Impact Assessment (15 minutes):** Using the provided network diagram, teams trace how identified variances affect the critical path. Students determine if delays are on critical path activities or have float available. Teams calculate potential project completion date using current SPI trend (EAC schedule = BAC/SPI).

**Phase 3 - Root Cause Investigation (25 minutes):** For the top 3 problematic activities, teams use the provided fishbone diagram template to categorize potential causes under: Resources, Methods, Materials, Environment, and Management. Students analyze provided interview excerpts from team leads, vendor correspondence, and resource utilization reports to distinguish between symptoms (what happened) and root causes (why it happened).

**Phase 4 - Analysis Synthesis (10 minutes):** Teams create a one-page executive summary ranking root causes by impact severity and likelihood, supported by quantitative evidence from their calculations. Include recommended corrective actions with rationale.

**Debrief (10 minutes):** Teams present their top root cause with supporting analysis. Instructor facilitates discussion on analysis methodology effectiveness.
materials_needed: Phoenix Software Implementation case study packet (baseline schedule, progress data, network diagram)
Earned Value calculation worksheets
Fishbone diagram templates
Interview excerpts and vendor correspondence documents
Calculators or Excel access
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheets using rubric: Calculation accuracy (25 points), Critical path analysis correctness (25 points), Root cause differentiation quality (30 points), Evidence-based reasoning (20 points). Minimum 70/100 for proficiency. Observe team discussions for analytical thinking process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed SV/SPI calculation examples for first two activities, offer guided questions for root cause identification ('Is this something that happened or something that caused it to happen?'). For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring Monte Carlo simulation for schedule forecasting, or analysis of resource leveling impacts on critical path.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN, QoS, and Security Integration
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) with integrated Quality of Service (QoS) policies and comprehensive security measures. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize advanced routing, VPN, security, and traffic management concepts into a fully functional network design.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable DMVPN Phase 3 topology by creating network diagrams, IP addressing schemes, and configuration templates that support 500+ users across three sites
Students will implement integrated QoS policies through DSCP marking, traffic shaping, and priority queuing to ensure voice and video traffic meets SLA requirements of <150ms latency
Students will construct a comprehensive security framework by deploying Zone-Based Firewalls, IPSec encryption, and access control lists that achieve 99.9% threat mitigation
instructions:
Phase 1 (60 minutes): Students work in teams of 2-3 to design the network topology. Provide each team with the scenario: Company HQ in New York (200 users), Branch 1 in Chicago (150 users), Branch 2 in Dallas (100 users), with requirements for voice/video conferencing, file servers, and internet access. Teams must create detailed network diagrams using Visio/draw.io showing DMVPN hub-and-spoke with spoke-to-spoke tunnels, OSPF routing areas, and security zones. They must design a hierarchical IP addressing scheme using /24 subnets minimum, document VLAN assignments, and specify hardware requirements (router models, interface types, bandwidth requirements).

Phase 2 (90 minutes): Using GNS3 or Packet Tracer with Cisco ISR 4000 series routers, teams configure the DMVPN Phase 3 topology. Start with hub router (HQ) configuration: enable DMVPN interface, configure NHRP, set up IPSec profiles with AES-256 encryption. Configure spoke routers with dynamic tunnel interfaces and NHRP shortcuts. Implement OSPF area design with area 0 at HQ and area 1, 2 for branches. Verify full mesh reachability using ping and traceroute between all sites.

Phase 3 (75 minutes): Implement comprehensive QoS policies. Configure DSCP marking for voice (EF), video (AF41), and data traffic classes. Set up Low Latency Queuing (LLQ) with voice priority queue limited to 33% bandwidth. Apply traffic shaping on WAN interfaces with guaranteed minimums: voice 128kbps, video 512kbps, critical data 256kbps. Test using traffic generators and verify latency measurements.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Deploy security measures including Zone-Based Firewall with DMZ, LAN, and WAN zones. Configure inspect policies for HTTP, HTTPS, SSH traffic. Implement access control lists restricting inter-branch communication to specific protocols. Set up logging and SNMP monitoring. Final testing includes security penetration attempts and performance validation under load.
materials_needed: GNS3 network simulation software with Cisco ISR 4331 router images
Microsoft Visio or Draw.io for network diagram creation
Cisco IOS XE configuration reference guides
Network traffic generator tools (iPerf3, D-ITG)
Wireshark packet capture software
Pre-configured scenario requirement sheets with SLA specifications
assessment_method: Teams submit: (1) Complete network design documentation including topology diagrams, IP addressing tables, and hardware specifications (25 points), (2) Functional GNS3/Packet Tracer network file with all configurations (35 points), (3) QoS performance test results showing latency <150ms for voice traffic and bandwidth allocation compliance (20 points), (4) Security audit report demonstrating firewall rule effectiveness and access control validation (20 points). Instructor evaluates using live network demonstration where teams must troubleshoot induced failures and explain design decisions. Minimum 80% functionality required for passing grade.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base router templates with basic interface and routing setup, offer checkpoint reviews after each phase, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create configuration checklists and command reference sheets specific to DMVPN and QoS. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate network automation using Python/Ansible for configuration deployment, implement advanced security features like IPS and advanced malware protection, or design redundant hub architecture with load balancing.

title: Design and Build a Multi-Source Sales Performance Dashboard
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard by combining data from three different sources (CSV sales data, JSON customer demographics, and API weather data) to analyze how weather patterns impact regional sales performance. They will design custom visualizations and provide actionable business recommendations based on their integrated analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize data from multiple heterogeneous sources (CSV, JSON, API) by designing and implementing data integration workflows using Python pandas and requests libraries
Students will create an interactive business dashboard through constructing custom visualizations and developing automated reporting features using Plotly Dash framework
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Architecture Design (45 minutes)**
Students work in pairs to sketch their dashboard wireframe on paper, identifying which visualizations will answer the business question: 'How does weather affect regional sales performance?' Provide each pair with sample datasets: sales_data.csv (10,000 records with date, region, product, revenue), customer_demographics.json (5,000 customer profiles with location data), and OpenWeatherMap API documentation. Students must plan their data integration strategy, identifying common fields (date, location) and required transformations.

**Phase 2: Data Integration Implementation (60 minutes)**
Using Jupyter notebooks, students write Python code to: (1) Load and clean the CSV sales data using pandas, handling missing values and standardizing date formats; (2) Parse the JSON customer file and merge it with sales data on customer_id; (3) Create a function to fetch historical weather data from OpenWeatherMap API for each sales region and date range; (4) Design and implement a unified dataset combining all three sources, ensuring proper data types and consistent geographic coding.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students build their interactive dashboard using Plotly Dash, implementing: (1) A time-series chart showing sales trends with weather overlay (temperature/precipitation); (2) A geographic heat map displaying sales performance by region; (3) Interactive filters for date range, product category, and weather conditions; (4) Summary statistics cards showing correlation coefficients between weather variables and sales metrics; (5) A downloadable report feature that generates PDF summaries.

**Phase 4: Business Insights Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each pair demonstrates their dashboard to another pair, explaining their design decisions and presenting three specific business recommendations based on their weather-sales correlation analysis.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with Python 3.8+
Required Python libraries: pandas, requests, plotly, dash, numpy
Sample datasets: sales_data.csv, customer_demographics.json
OpenWeatherMap API key (free tier)
Graph paper for wireframe sketching
Presentation timer for final demos
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (30 points) - correct merging, API implementation, data cleaning; Dashboard Functionality (35 points) - working interactive elements, appropriate visualizations, user experience; Business Insights (25 points) - clear recommendations supported by data, correlation analysis accuracy; Code Quality (10 points) - documentation, error handling, efficiency. Students submit their Jupyter notebook, dashboard URL, and a 2-page business report with recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written API connection code and detailed pandas merge examples. Create checkpoint questions after each phase to verify understanding. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional data sources (social media sentiment, competitor pricing), implement machine learning predictions for future sales, or add advanced statistical analysis features like confidence intervals and hypothesis testing to their correlations.

title: PMBOK Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Memorization Challenge
description: Students will systematically memorize and recall the complete PMBOK Guide's 49 project management processes organized across 10 Knowledge Areas and 5 Process Groups. This intensive recall activity builds foundational memory of the PMI framework essential for advanced project management practice.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all 49 PMBOK processes by matching each process to its correct Knowledge Area and Process Group within 90 seconds
Students will identify specific ITTO (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) categories for 20 randomly selected processes through timed flashcard drills
instructions: Step 1 (10 min): Distribute the blank PMBOK Process Matrix template with 10 Knowledge Areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) as rows and 5 Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) as columns. Students receive a randomized list of all 49 processes to place correctly. Step 2 (15 min): Working individually, students fill the matrix from memory, placing each process in its exact intersection point. No reference materials allowed. Step 3 (10 min): Students self-check using the official PMBOK answer key, marking incorrect placements in red. Step 4 (20 min): For processes missed, students create physical flashcards with process name on front, Knowledge Area/Process Group location plus one key ITTO element on back. Step 5 (15 min): Paired speed drilling - Partner A shows process names, Partner B must state location within 5 seconds, then switch roles. Step 6 (10 min): Final individual assessment - complete fresh blank matrix within 90 seconds, achieving 90% accuracy minimum. Instructor times each student individually and records completion rates.
materials_needed: Blank PMBOK Process Matrix templates (2 per student)
Randomized process name cards (49 processes)
Official PMBOK Process Matrix answer key
Blank index cards for flashcards (20 per student)
Red pens for self-correction
Digital stopwatch or timer app
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (44/49 processes correct) on final timed matrix completion within 90 seconds. Grade breakdown: 90-100% accuracy = A, 80-89% = B, 70-79% = C, below 70% requires remediation. Document specific processes missed for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students should focus on memorizing one Knowledge Area at a time, starting with Integration Management (7 processes). Provide mnemonic devices for Process Groups (I-P-E-M-C). Advanced learners should additionally memorize primary inputs/outputs for each process and practice drawing the matrix from complete memory within 60 seconds.

title: Multi-Dimensional Leadership Style Analysis Through Crisis Decision Mapping
description: Students will analyze complex leadership decisions made during organizational crises by examining multiple leadership theories simultaneously and identifying the interconnections between different leadership approaches. This expert-level activity requires students to demonstrate deep understanding by synthesizing how situational, transformational, and adaptive leadership theories interact in real crisis scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the intersection of situational, transformational, and adaptive leadership theories by deconstructing crisis leadership decisions using a multi-dimensional framework
Students will demonstrate understanding of leadership complexity through creating detailed decision maps that illustrate how different leadership approaches complement or conflict with each other
instructions: Begin by providing students with three detailed crisis case studies (15 minutes reading time): a corporate data breach, a hospital during pandemic surge, and a military unit under fire. Divide class into expert groups of 4-5 students, assigning each group one case study. Each group receives a large format decision mapping template with three overlapping circles representing situational leadership (task vs. relationship focus), transformational leadership (inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration, idealized influence), and adaptive leadership (technical vs. adaptive challenges, experimentation, distributed leadership). Students spend 45 minutes analyzing their assigned case, identifying specific leader decisions and plotting them within the appropriate sections of the overlapping circles. Critical decisions that demonstrate multiple leadership approaches simultaneously must be placed in intersection zones with detailed justifications. Groups then create a 10-minute presentation explaining their most complex intersection point—where all three leadership theories converge. During presentations (30 minutes total), listening groups use structured observation sheets to identify additional intersections the presenting group may have missed. Conclude with a 15-minute whole-class synthesis where students compare patterns across all three crisis scenarios, specifically focusing on which leadership theory intersections appear most frequently during crisis decision-making and why certain combinations prove more effective than others.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis case studies (2-3 pages each) with specific leader decisions documented
Large format tri-circle Venn diagram templates (11x17 paper minimum)
Colored markers or sticky notes for categorizing decisions
Structured observation sheets for peer feedback during presentations
Timer for managing activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed decision maps using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership theory application (25%), (2) Quality of justification for intersection placements (30%), (3) Identification of complex multi-theory convergence points (25%), and (4) Synthesis of cross-case patterns during discussion (20%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly placing at least 8 leadership decisions, providing theoretical justification for 3+ intersection points, and identifying 2+ patterns across different crisis contexts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case study sections focusing on clear leadership decisions and offer simplified decision mapping templates with guided questions. For advanced learners, add a fourth leadership theory circle (servant leadership or authentic leadership) and require analysis of cultural context factors that might influence leadership theory effectiveness. Consider providing theory reference sheets for struggling students while challenging advanced students to identify theory limitations or contradictions.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Audit and Recommendation
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 for an e-commerce website, analyzing their impact on conversion credit distribution and ROI calculations. They will critically assess model effectiveness and provide data-driven recommendations for attribution strategy optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of data-driven, last-click, first-click, and position-based attribution models by comparing conversion value distributions and channel performance metrics
Students will critique current attribution strategies through systematic analysis of customer journey data and provide justified recommendations for model selection based on business objectives
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, display, social, email, organic). Students work individually with provided spreadsheet templates for data collection.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. They extract conversion data for each attribution model (data-driven, last-click, first-click, position-based) across all channels, recording: total conversions, conversion value, cost-per-acquisition, and ROAS. Students document findings in provided comparison matrix, noting significant variations (>15% difference) between models.

**Phase 2 - Journey Analysis (30 minutes):** Using the Path Analysis report under Explore, students analyze top 10 conversion paths, identifying average touchpoints-to-conversion and most common channel sequences. They evaluate which attribution model most accurately reflects observed customer behavior patterns, documenting evidence with specific path examples and statistical summaries.

**Phase 3 - Business Impact Assessment (25 minutes):** Students calculate budget reallocation scenarios under each model, determining potential ROI changes if marketing spend shifted based on different attribution insights. They identify channels that would gain/lose budget (>20% change) and estimate financial impact using provided cost and revenue data.

**Phase 4 - Strategic Recommendation (30 minutes):** Students prepare a formal recommendation memo (500 words) selecting the optimal attribution model, providing three key justifications supported by their analysis. They must address implementation timeline, expected business impact, and measurement success metrics. Final recommendations include specific next steps and potential risks.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce data (Universal Analytics Demo Account or similar)
Attribution comparison spreadsheet template with pre-formatted tables
Customer journey analysis worksheet
Sample marketing cost data by channel
Business recommendation memo template
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Data accuracy and completeness (25 points), depth of attribution model analysis with specific evidence (25 points), quality of customer journey insights with supporting data (20 points), strength of business justification and feasibility of recommendations (20 points), professional presentation and clear communication (10 points). Students must achieve 80+ points demonstrating mastery-level evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: **Support strategies:** Provide guided practice with attribution comparison tool navigation, offer pre-populated data collection templates, and supply sample analysis questions for journey evaluation. **Advanced extensions:** Challenge high-performing students to incorporate external factors (seasonality, competitive analysis), design custom attribution models using GA4's data export, or present recommendations with projected quarterly performance forecasts and A/B testing frameworks.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-Site MPLS VPN Network with QoS and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise MPLS VPN solution connecting three geographically distributed sites with full redundancy, quality of service policies, and security measures. This capstone activity synthesizes advanced routing protocols, VPN technologies, and network optimization techniques into a production-ready network design.
learning_objectives: Students will create a comprehensive MPLS VPN network topology by integrating BGP, OSPF, and LDP protocols across provider and customer equipment
Students will design and implement advanced QoS policies through traffic classification, queuing mechanisms, and bandwidth allocation strategies
Students will construct network redundancy solutions by deploying dual-homed connections and failover mechanisms
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Students work in teams of 3-4 to design their MPLS network topology. Provide each team with a business scenario packet containing: headquarters (500 users), branch office A (150 users), and branch office B (75 users). Teams must create detailed network diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets from 10.x.0.0/16 allocation, MPLS label distribution paths, and redundant link requirements.

**Phase 2: Equipment Configuration (90 minutes)**
Using GNS3 with Cisco IOS images, teams configure six routers: two provider edge (PE) routers, two provider (P) routers, and two customer edge (CE) routers per site. Students must establish OSPF area 0 in provider core, implement MP-BGP for VPNv4 route exchange, configure VRF instances for customer separation, and establish LDP for label distribution. Each configuration must include loopback interfaces for router identification and MPLS-enabled interfaces.

**Phase 3: QoS Implementation (60 minutes)**
Teams create class-maps identifying voice (DSCP EF), video (DSCP AF41), and data traffic (default). Configure policy-maps with priority queuing for voice (30% bandwidth), class-based weighted fair queuing for video (40% bandwidth), and remaining bandwidth for data. Apply service policies on all customer-facing interfaces and verify traffic classification using traffic generators.

**Phase 4: Redundancy and Testing (45 minutes)**
Implement link redundancy using HSRP on customer networks and configure fast reroute mechanisms in MPLS core. Test failover scenarios by systematically disconnecting primary paths and measuring convergence times. Document all failure scenarios and recovery procedures in technical reports.
materials_needed: GNS3 network simulation software with Cisco IOS 15.x router images
Microsoft Visio or Draw.io for network topology creation
TrafGen traffic generation software for QoS testing
Wireshark for packet analysis and verification
Business scenario packets with detailed requirements per team
assessment_method: Evaluation based on four components: Network topology design documentation (25%) - assessed for technical accuracy, scalability, and adherence to best practices; Working MPLS VPN configuration (35%) - verified through end-to-end connectivity tests and routing table analysis; QoS implementation effectiveness (25%) - measured through traffic prioritization tests and bandwidth utilization reports; Redundancy and failover performance (15%) - evaluated on convergence times under 30 seconds and successful traffic rerouting. Each team presents their solution with live demonstrations and submits complete configuration files with detailed technical documentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic OSPF and interface configurations, offer step-by-step MPLS configuration guides, and pair with stronger team members for peer support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features such as MPLS Traffic Engineering with RSVP-TE, IPv6 VPN services (6VPE), or integrate SD-WAN concepts with traditional MPLS. Provide access to additional router instances for more complex topologies and encourage exploration of automation tools like Ansible for configuration management.

title: Optimizing Community Garden Layout Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving maximizing crop yield in a community garden subject to multiple constraints. They will formulate the problem mathematically, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal solutions using the corner point method.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-variable optimization problem by translating real-world constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will determine optimal solutions through systematic evaluation of corner points and interpretation of results in practical context
instructions: Begin by distributing the Community Garden Scenario handout (15 minutes). Students work in pairs to read the scenario: A 1000 m² community garden needs to allocate space between tomatoes (x) and lettuce (y) to maximize profit. Constraints include: minimum 100 m² for tomatoes, minimum 150 m² for lettuce, total area ≤ 1000 m², labor hours ≤ 80 (tomatoes need 0.1 h/m², lettuce needs 0.05 h/m²), and water requirements ≤ 200 L/day (tomatoes need 0.3 L/m², lettuce needs 0.1 L/m²). Profit: tomatoes $8/m², lettuce $5/m². Step 1 (20 minutes): Pairs formulate the objective function and all constraint inequalities, writing them clearly on worksheets. Step 2 (25 minutes): Using graphing paper, students plot each constraint line and shade the feasible region. Instructor circulates to verify correct boundary lines and shading. Step 3 (20 minutes): Students identify all corner points of the feasible region by solving systems of equations where constraint lines intersect. Step 4 (15 minutes): Evaluate the objective function at each corner point and determine the optimal solution. Step 5 (15 minutes): Pairs write a 2-paragraph recommendation memo explaining their optimal allocation and expected profit, justifying why this solution is mathematically optimal.
materials_needed: Community Garden Scenario handout with specific numerical data
Linear programming worksheet template with spaces for constraints and calculations
Graph paper (at least 20x20 grid)
Calculators
Rulers and colored pencils for graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct formulation of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphing of feasible region with proper shading (25%), (3) Correct identification and calculation of corner points (25%), (4) Accurate optimization solution and clear written explanation (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn axes with scale marks, offer constraint inequality examples, and give a corner point calculation template. For advanced learners: Add a second optimization scenario with 3 variables requiring algebraic solution methods, or introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how the solution changes if profit margins increase by 20%.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Analysis: Deconstructing Real-World Generator Systems
description: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic induction scenarios by deconstructing multi-component generator systems and examining how changing magnetic flux produces electrical output. They will break down the relationships between mechanical input, magnetic field variations, and electrical power generation in wind turbine and hydroelectric generator configurations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the cause-and-effect relationships between rotational mechanics, magnetic field changes, and induced EMF by deconstructing generator system components and their interactions
Students will examine the efficiency factors in electromagnetic induction systems through comparative analysis of real-world generator data and theoretical calculations
instructions: Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4, providing each team with generator system diagrams and performance data sheets (15 minutes setup). Present two scenarios: a 2.5 MW wind turbine generator and a 500 MW hydroelectric generator, each with detailed specifications including rotor dimensions, magnetic field strengths, rotation speeds, and power outputs. Students first spend 20 minutes individually examining the provided data to identify key variables affecting electromagnetic induction in each system. Next, teams collaborate for 45 minutes to create analytical breakdowns using the provided worksheets. They must: 1) Calculate theoretical EMF using Faraday's law for both systems, 2) Identify and quantify three major efficiency loss factors in each generator type, 3) Analyze why the hydroelectric generator produces more power per rotation than the wind turbine, and 4) Determine the optimal rotation speed ranges for maximum power output. Teams then spend 25 minutes creating comparison matrices that highlight how coil design, magnetic field strength, and rotational velocity contribute differently to power generation in each system. Each team presents their analysis for 10 minutes, focusing on the most significant factor affecting efficiency in each generator type. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where teams defend their efficiency rankings and propose design modifications to improve performance. Provide calculation sheets with Faraday's law applications and efficiency formulas as reference materials throughout the activity.
materials_needed: Wind turbine generator technical specification sheets with coil dimensions, magnetic field data, and performance curves
Hydroelectric generator system diagrams with rotor specifications and power output data
Scientific calculators capable of trigonometric functions
Analysis worksheets with guided calculation templates for EMF and efficiency determinations
Comparison matrix templates for organizing analytical findings
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of EMF calculations using Faraday's law (25%), (2) Identification and quantification of efficiency factors with supporting evidence (30%), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between generator types with clear reasoning (25%), (4) Justification of design modification proposals based on electromagnetic principles (20%). Students must demonstrate calculations, provide evidence-based conclusions, and present coherent analysis of component relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled calculation templates with Faraday's law steps and offer one-on-one guidance during individual analysis time. Supply additional worked examples showing EMF calculations for similar generators. For advanced learners, introduce three-phase generator analysis, challenge them to calculate power losses due to eddy currents and hysteresis, or have them design optimal coil configurations for specific environmental conditions. Provide supplementary data on generator maintenance costs and environmental factors affecting performance.

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Three Password Validation Functions
description: Students will analyze and compare three different implementations of password validation functions written in Python. They will evaluate each function's code quality, efficiency, and adherence to best practices, then justify their ranking of the implementations from best to worst.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three password validation functions by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and adherence to coding standards
Students will justify their assessment of code quality through written explanations comparing strengths and weaknesses of each implementation
instructions: Begin by distributing the three password validation functions (provided as separate code files: version_a.py, version_b.py, version_c.py). Each function performs the same task but uses different coding approaches. Give students 10 minutes to read through all three implementations without making judgments yet. Next, provide the evaluation criteria checklist covering: code readability (variable names, comments, structure), efficiency (unnecessary loops, redundant operations), best practices (function length, error handling, input validation), and maintainability (ease of modification, clear logic flow). Have students work individually for 25 minutes to complete the evaluation matrix, scoring each function on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and writing specific examples to support their scores. Students should then spend 15 minutes ranking the three functions from best to worst overall, writing a 3-4 sentence justification for their ranking that references specific code examples. In the final 15 minutes, facilitate a class discussion where students share their rankings and justifications, focusing on areas where opinions differ. Encourage students to defend their evaluations using concrete evidence from the code. Conclude by revealing that all three functions were written by different experience levels (junior, mid-level, senior developers) and discuss how code quality evolves with experience.
materials_needed: Three Python files containing different password validation implementations
Evaluation criteria checklist handout
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Computers with Python installed or code viewing capability
assessment_method: Grade based on completed evaluation matrix (40%), quality of written justification with specific code examples (40%), and participation in class discussion defending their evaluation (20%). Success criteria: students provide specific code examples for each score, demonstrate understanding of coding best practices, and can articulate clear reasoning for their final ranking.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional examples of good vs. poor code quality and pair them with stronger students during discussion. For advanced learners: challenge them to rewrite the worst-ranked function to improve its quality, or have them evaluate additional criteria like security vulnerabilities or performance optimization opportunities.

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard with Actionable Business Recommendations
description: Students will create an original customer segmentation analysis by designing their own analytical framework, building interactive visualizations, and developing strategic business recommendations. This activity combines statistical analysis with business intelligence to solve real-world marketing challenges.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying clustering algorithms and creating custom analytical frameworks
Students will synthesize data insights into actionable business strategies through interactive dashboard design and executive-level recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Framework Design (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with the e-commerce customer dataset containing purchase history, demographics, and behavioral metrics. Teams first spend 20 minutes examining the raw data and brainstorming which customer characteristics might drive segmentation (RFM analysis, geographic patterns, product preferences, etc.). Each team must then create their own unique analytical framework by selecting 4-6 key variables and hypothesizing how these will reveal distinct customer segments. Teams document their framework rationale in a one-page strategy brief.

**Phase 2: Analysis and Segmentation (60 minutes)**
Using their chosen framework, teams perform exploratory data analysis to validate their variable selections. They clean and prepare their data, then apply K-means clustering with 3-5 segments. Teams must justify their cluster number choice using elbow method and silhouette analysis. Each team creates statistical profiles for their segments, calculating means, medians, and key differentiators for each variable. Teams name their segments based on behavioral characteristics (e.g., "Budget Browsers," "Premium Loyalists").

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Teams build interactive dashboards using Tableau or Power BI, incorporating: segment size visualization, key metric comparisons across segments, geographic distribution maps, and purchase behavior trends. Each dashboard must include at least one drill-down capability and filtering options. Teams create a "Segment Spotlight" feature allowing users to click on any segment for detailed profiles.

**Phase 4: Business Strategy Development (30 minutes)**
Final phase requires teams to develop three specific, measurable marketing strategies for their highest-value segment, including targeted messaging, channel recommendations, and success metrics. Teams prepare 5-minute executive presentations combining their dashboard demonstration with strategic recommendations.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records including demographics, purchase history, website behavior)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop licenses
Statistical software access (Python/R or Excel with Analysis Toolpak)
Presentation template for executive summary
Laptops with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Framework originality and justification (20 points), statistical analysis accuracy and cluster validation (25 points), dashboard functionality and design quality (25 points), business recommendations specificity and feasibility (20 points), presentation clarity and professional delivery (10 points). Each team submits their dashboard file, statistical analysis documentation, and strategic recommendations document.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-selected variable combinations and step-by-step clustering tutorials. Offer dashboard templates with basic structure. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced techniques like hierarchical clustering comparison, predictive modeling for customer lifetime value, or A/B testing simulation for their recommended strategies. Encourage integration of external data sources.

title: PMI Knowledge Area Terminology Rapid Recall Challenge
description: Students memorize and rapidly recall 150+ specific project management terms, formulas, and acronyms across all 10 PMI Knowledge Areas. This intensive memorization activity prepares students for advanced certification exams by building foundational vocabulary recall speed and accuracy.
estimated_duration: 5 days x 30-45 minutes per session (total: 150-225 minutes)
learning_objectives: Students will memorize 150 project management terms, definitions, and formulas from the PMBOK Guide by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will recall specific PMI Knowledge Area terminology with 90% accuracy through structured repetition exercises
instructions: Day 1: Distribute the master terminology list containing 15 terms per Knowledge Area (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder). Students create physical flashcards with term/acronym on front, complete definition and Knowledge Area on back. Spend 45 minutes creating cards in groups of 3-4, with each student responsible for 2-3 Knowledge Areas. Day 2-4: Implement spaced repetition sessions. Begin each 30-minute session with individual silent review (10 minutes), followed by paired testing where partners quiz each other (15 minutes), ending with whole-class rapid-fire recall (5 minutes). Track missed terms on individual error logs. Day 5: Conduct final assessment using digital quiz platform. Present 75 randomized terms for 60 seconds each. Students must write complete definition and identify correct Knowledge Area. Immediately following digital quiz, conduct verbal speed round where instructor calls out terms and students shout definitions. Repeat any missed terms three times as a class. Conclude with students organizing all flashcards into Knowledge Area stacks and performing final self-assessment by going through each stack without looking at backs first.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition terminology reference sheets (pre-compiled by instructor)
200 blank index cards per student
Individual error tracking worksheets
Digital quiz platform (Kahoot, Quizizz, or LMS quiz tool)
Timer/stopwatch for paced activities
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (135/150 terms) on final digital quiz within time limits. Grade breakdown: Digital quiz accuracy (70%), peer testing participation documented on tracking sheets (20%), flashcard quality and completeness check (10%). Provide immediate retesting opportunity for students scoring below 85%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial load to 10 terms per Knowledge Area and provide pre-made definition templates with key words missing. Create study buddy partnerships with stronger students. For advanced learners: Add process group classifications to each term, include related formulas and calculation examples, require students to create scenario-based memory devices connecting multiple terms.

title: Deconstructing Strategic Leadership Decision-Making Through Crisis Simulation Analysis
description: Students will analyze a multi-layered organizational crisis simulation to understand how strategic leadership principles manifest in high-stakes decision-making environments. They will examine the interconnected relationships between stakeholder management, resource allocation, communication strategies, and ethical considerations within complex leadership scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between tactical and strategic leadership responses by analyzing decision points in a crisis simulation involving multiple stakeholder groups
Students will interpret the underlying leadership theories and frameworks through systematic deconstruction of executive decision-making processes during organizational uncertainty
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'MedTech Corp Crisis' case study packet, which details a pharmaceutical company facing simultaneous FDA investigation, product recall, and whistleblower allegations (15 minutes for individual reading). Divide students into analysis teams of 4-5 members, assigning each team a specific leadership lens: transformational leadership theory, stakeholder theory, ethical leadership framework, or crisis management theory (5 minutes setup). Each team receives a detailed timeline of CEO decisions made during the 90-day crisis period, including internal memos, public statements, board communications, and resource allocation documents. Teams spend 45 minutes mapping each leadership decision against their assigned theoretical framework, identifying specific examples of how the theory manifests in practice. They must create a visual decision tree showing cause-and-effect relationships between leadership choices and organizational outcomes. During the analysis phase, teams use structured worksheets to categorize decisions as strategic vs. tactical, identify stakeholder impacts, and trace decision rationale through supporting documents. Next, conduct a 30-minute rotating gallery walk where teams present their frameworks to others, explaining how their theoretical lens reveals different aspects of the leadership approach. Conclude with a 20-minute synthesis discussion where teams identify overlapping patterns and contradictions between frameworks, focusing on how different leadership theories complement or conflict when applied to the same situation.
materials_needed: MedTech Corp Crisis case study packet (12-page document with timeline, memos, and financial data)
Leadership framework reference sheets for each theory
Large format paper (A3/11x17) for decision tree mapping
Colored markers and sticky notes for visual analysis
Structured analysis worksheets with prompting questions
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification and explanation of theoretical concepts within real decisions (25%), (2) Quality of cause-effect relationships mapped in decision trees (25%), (3) Depth of analysis in distinguishing strategic vs tactical choices (25%), and (4) Synthesis quality during cross-framework discussions showing understanding of theory integration (25%). Success requires demonstrating comprehension of how leadership theories translate into observable behaviors and measurable outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing decision-tracking templates with pre-identified key decision points and theory definition cards with specific behavioral indicators. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by asking them to identify missing leadership approaches or propose alternative theoretical frameworks that might better explain observed behaviors. Consider providing supplementary mini-cases showing contrasting leadership approaches to similar crises.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Deconstructing Project Failure Scenarios
description: Students will analyze real project failure case studies to identify missed risk response opportunities and evaluate the effectiveness of implemented risk strategies. They will break down complex project scenarios to determine causal relationships between risk events and project outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project failure scenarios by identifying specific risk events and categorizing them according to PMBOK risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept)
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of existing risk responses through systematic comparison of planned versus actual outcomes in documented project cases
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the Denver International Airport Baggage System case study packet to each team, ensuring each student receives the timeline, budget data, and stakeholder communication logs. Teams spend 20 minutes reading and highlighting key risk events chronologically. Next, provide each team with the Risk Analysis Matrix template containing columns for: Risk Event, Risk Category, Planned Response, Actual Response, Impact Level, and Effectiveness Rating. Teams spend 30 minutes identifying and documenting at least 8 distinct risk events from the case study, filling out all matrix columns. During the analysis phase (25 minutes), teams must classify each risk response using PMBOK categories and rate effectiveness on a 1-5 scale with written justification. Teams then create a visual cause-and-effect diagram showing how individual risk events cascaded into project failure (20 minutes). Each team presents their top 3 most critical risk response failures to the class (15 minutes total), explaining what alternative strategies could have been implemented. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion comparing findings across teams and identifying common patterns in risk response effectiveness.
materials_needed: Denver International Airport Baggage System case study packet (6-page document with timeline, budget, and communications)
Risk Analysis Matrix template (Excel or printed worksheet)
Flipchart paper and colored markers for cause-and-effect diagrams
PMBOK Risk Response Strategy reference sheet
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Analysis Matrix for accuracy of risk categorization (25 points), quality of effectiveness ratings with justifications (25 points), visual cause-and-effect diagram showing clear connections (25 points), and team presentation demonstrating understanding of alternative strategies (25 points). Students must correctly identify at least 6 of 8 major risk events and provide evidence-based effectiveness ratings to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case study versions with risk events marked and offer a partially completed matrix template. Advanced learners can be challenged to calculate quantitative risk impact using provided budget data and create probability-impact matrices. Consider pairing weaker analytical students with stronger team members and provide additional PMBOK reference materials for complex risk scenarios.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Impact Assessment and Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance differences between Google Analytics' default last-click attribution and alternative attribution models using real e-commerce data. They will assess conversion path complexity, revenue attribution variations, and provide strategic recommendations for optimal attribution model selection based on business context and customer journey patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across multiple touchpoints
Students will critique attribution model limitations through systematic comparison of customer journey complexity and provide evidence-based recommendations for model optimization
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Students work individually with provided demo accounts or instructor-shared view access.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (20 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. They must extract conversion and revenue data for the same date range using four models: Last click, First click, Linear, and Data-driven. Students create a spreadsheet documenting: total conversions, revenue attributed, and percentage differences for each channel across all four models.

**Phase 2 - Path Analysis (25 minutes):** Using the Attribution > Conversion paths report, students analyze the top 20 conversion paths by frequency. They categorize paths by complexity (1 touchpoint, 2-3 touchpoints, 4+ touchpoints) and identify which channels most frequently appear in multi-touch journeys. Students calculate the percentage of conversions that involve multiple touchpoints versus single-touch conversions.

**Phase 3 - Critical Evaluation (30 minutes):** Students create a comparative analysis matrix evaluating each attribution model's strengths and weaknesses for this specific business. They must consider: customer journey length, channel interaction patterns, business objectives, and revenue impact differences. Students identify which channels are most over/under-credited in the default last-click model.

**Phase 4 - Strategic Recommendation (25 minutes):** Based on their analysis, students prepare a written recommendation memo (500-700 words) proposing the optimal attribution model for this business, including implementation timeline, expected impact on marketing budget allocation, and potential challenges. The memo must include specific data points from their analysis as supporting evidence.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with 6+ months e-commerce data
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets)
Attribution model comparison template worksheet
Business context briefing document describing company goals and marketing strategy
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed data analysis spreadsheet with attribution model comparisons (25 points), (2) Conversion path complexity analysis with categorization (25 points), (3) Strategic recommendation memo with supporting evidence (50 points). Rubric evaluates data accuracy, depth of analysis, quality of critique regarding model limitations, feasibility of recommendations, and use of specific GA4 data to support conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled templates with column headers and sample calculations. Offer guided questions for each analysis phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate seasonality analysis, calculate statistical significance of attribution differences, or create custom channel groupings. Provide additional complexity by asking them to consider cross-device tracking implications on attribution accuracy.

title: Programming Language Vocabulary Flashcard Creation and Drill
description: Students will create digital flashcards for 20 fundamental programming terms and definitions, then practice recalling these terms through structured drilling exercises. This activity builds essential vocabulary foundation for beginning programmers learning their first programming language.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and define 20 fundamental programming vocabulary terms including variable, loop, function, array, and boolean by creating accurate digital flashcards
Students will recall programming terminology definitions with 85% accuracy through timed flashcard practice sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-selected list of 20 programming terms: variable, integer, string, boolean, array, loop, function, parameter, argument, conditional, algorithm, syntax, compiler, debugging, IDE, object, class, method, recursion, and iteration. Have students work individually for the first 15 minutes to research each term using provided textbook resources and create digital flashcards using Quizlet or Anki. Each flashcard must include the term on one side and a complete definition plus one code example on the reverse side. Circulate to verify accuracy and provide immediate feedback. After creation, pair students for 10 minutes of reciprocal drilling where Partner A shows terms to Partner B, who must provide definitions, then switch roles. Next, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire review for 5 minutes where you display random terms on the projector and students write definitions on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for quick assessment. Conclude with individual timed practice using their digital flashcards for 10 minutes, where students cycle through all 20 terms at least twice, marking any terms they struggle to recall instantly. Students must log their accuracy rate and identify the 5 most challenging terms for additional study. End by having students write these 5 difficult terms and definitions three times each in their programming journals to reinforce memory through repetition.
materials_needed: Pre-printed list of 20 programming vocabulary terms
Student devices with internet access
Quizlet or Anki flashcard application accounts
Programming textbook or reference materials
Mini whiteboards and markers
Projector for whole-class review
Programming journals or notebooks
Timer for timed activities
assessment_method: Evaluate students based on: (1) Flashcard quality checklist - each card has accurate definition and relevant code example (40 points), (2) Partner drilling participation observation using behavior checklist (20 points), (3) Mini whiteboard accuracy during rapid-fire review - minimum 15/20 correct (20 points), (4) Final timed practice accuracy rate logged by student - target 85% or 17/20 correct (20 points). Total possible: 100 points. Students scoring below 70% must complete additional practice sessions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed flashcard templates with definition frameworks to fill in, allow use of visual aids or diagrams on flashcards, extend time limits for all activities, and pair with stronger students during partner drilling. For advanced learners: Require additional programming terms (25-30 total), include multiple code examples per term, add related terms or synonyms to flashcards, and challenge them to explain terms using analogies or real-world connections during partner work.

title: Analyzing Multi-Mode Heat Transfer in a Thermos Flask Design Challenge
description: Students will analyze the heat transfer mechanisms in commercial thermos flask designs by quantifying conduction, convection, and radiation losses. They will deconstruct thermal protection strategies and propose design modifications based on their analysis of heat transfer coefficients and material properties.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relative contributions of conduction, convection, and radiation heat transfer modes in a thermos flask system by calculating heat loss rates and identifying dominant mechanisms
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of thermal insulation strategies through quantitative comparison of heat transfer coefficients and material thermal properties
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a disassembled thermos flask, thermal imaging camera access, and temperature probes. In the first 30 minutes, students measure initial temperatures of hot water (80°C) in both the intact thermos and a control glass beaker, recording data every 5 minutes for thermal decay curves. Next, students disassemble their thermos flask completely, photographing and sketching each component while identifying materials (stainless steel, vacuum space, reflective coating, plastic cap). During minutes 30-60, teams calculate conduction heat transfer through the cap and base using Fourier's law, measuring material thickness and looking up thermal conductivity values. For minutes 60-90, students use thermal imaging to identify heat loss pathways and quantify surface temperatures, then calculate radiation heat transfer using the Stefan-Boltzmann equation for both inner and outer surface temperatures. In minutes 90-120, teams analyze convection currents in the air gap (if vacuum is compromised) by observing temperature gradients and calculating natural convection coefficients. Students then create a comprehensive heat transfer analysis chart showing calculated heat loss rates for each mechanism (W/K) and determine which mode dominates. Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation proposing three specific design modifications with quantitative justifications, such as improved vacuum maintenance, alternative reflective coatings, or modified geometric configurations. Each modification must include calculated predicted performance improvements.
materials_needed: Disassemblable thermos flask (one per team of 3-4 students)
Thermal imaging camera or infrared thermometer
Digital temperature probes with data logging capability
Hot water source (80°C)
Glass beaker for control experiment
Calipers for measuring material thickness
Thermal conductivity reference tables or database access
Graphing calculator or laptop with spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of heat transfer calculations for all three modes (25%), (2) Correct identification and quantification of dominant heat transfer mechanisms (25%), (3) Quality of thermal imaging analysis and temperature gradient interpretation (25%), and (4) Feasibility and quantitative justification of proposed design modifications (25%). Students must submit calculation worksheets, thermal analysis charts, and deliver oral presentations with peer evaluation components.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated thermal conductivity values and simplified heat transfer equations with unit guidance. Offer step-by-step calculation templates and encourage focus on one heat transfer mode at a time. For advanced learners, introduce transient heat transfer analysis using lumped capacitance methods, challenge them to model vacuum degradation over time, or have them research advanced insulation materials like aerogels with cost-benefit analysis.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions for a Simple Calculator App
