materials_needed: Pre-populated risk register spreadsheet with 15 software project risks (both qualitative and quantitative data included)
Risk comparison matrix template (printed or digital)
Laptops/tablets for teams
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of discrepancy identification between assessment methods (25%), (2) Quality of analysis explaining why discrepancies exist (25%), (3) Justification strength for recommended assessment approach per risk (25%), (4) Individual reflection demonstrating understanding of contextual decision factors (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions like 'What stakeholder would care more about dollar amounts versus probability ratings?' and highlight 2-3 obvious discrepancies to start their analysis. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by asking them to propose hybrid assessment approaches or consider how organizational risk tolerance affects method selection.
original_title: Risk Register Impact Analysis: Comparing Qualitative vs Quantitative Assessment Methods

title: Risk Register Impact Analysis: Comparing Qualitative vs Quantitative Assessment Methods: Business Application
description: Students will analyze a real project scenario's risk register by comparing outcomes from qualitative and quantitative risk assessment methods. They will examine how different assessment approaches affect project decision-making and resource allocation priorities.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of qualitative vs quantitative risk assessment methods by evaluating their impact on project resource allocation decisions
Students will differentiate between risk assessment approaches through systematic comparison of probability-impact matrices and expected monetary value calculations
instructions: Step 1 (10 min): Divide students into teams of 3-4. Distribute the 'Construction Project Risk Scenario' handout containing 12 identified risks for a $2M office building project, including initial risk descriptions and stakeholder concerns. Step 2 (20 min): Each team receives identical risk data but splits into two sub-groups. Sub-group A performs qualitative analysis using probability-impact matrix (1-5 scale) and creates risk ranking. Sub-group B performs quantitative analysis using provided cost/schedule impact data to calculate Expected Monetary Value (EMV) for each risk. Provide teams with calculators and EMV formula reference sheets. Step 3 (15 min): Sub-groups reconvene to compare their risk priority rankings. Teams document discrepancies in a comparison matrix, noting where qualitative high-priority risks differ from quantitative high-EMV risks. Step 4 (20 min): Teams analyze three specific scenarios: limited contingency budget ($50K), compressed schedule (20% reduction), and stakeholder risk tolerance changes. For each scenario, teams determine which assessment method provides more actionable guidance and justify their reasoning with specific examples. Step 5 (15 min): Each team presents their analysis of one scenario, explaining which risks they would prioritize and why their chosen assessment method is more appropriate for that context. Other teams provide feedback using structured peer evaluation forms focusing on analytical reasoning quality.
materials_needed: Construction Project Risk Scenario handout with 12 detailed risks
Probability-Impact Matrix template (1-5 scale)
EMV calculation reference sheet with formulas
Risk comparison matrix worksheet
Calculators
Peer evaluation forms
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using rubric with 4 criteria (25 points each): (1) Accuracy of risk calculations and rankings, (2) Quality of comparative analysis between methods, (3) Justification strength for scenario-based decisions, (4) Clear articulation of method appropriateness. Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated understanding of when each assessment method provides superior project management value.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing completed examples of 2 risks with both assessment methods shown. Offer step-by-step EMV calculation guides and probability-impact matrix anchoring examples. For advanced learners, add Monte Carlo simulation concepts or require integration of secondary risk factors like risk interdependencies and timing considerations.
original_title: Risk Register Impact Analysis: Comparing Qualitative vs Quantitative Assessment Methods

title: E-commerce Analytics Performance Audit and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate two competing e-commerce websites' Google Analytics performance data to assess their digital marketing effectiveness. They will synthesize findings to recommend which business model demonstrates superior customer acquisition and retention strategies based on comprehensive analytics metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different e-commerce conversion funnels by analyzing Google Analytics data including goal completion rates, assisted conversions, and attribution modeling reports
Students will critique and compare customer lifetime value strategies through detailed analysis of cohort reports, user retention metrics, and revenue attribution across multiple touchpoints
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with anonymized Google Analytics data exports from two competing e-commerce sites (Company A: subscription model, Company B: one-time purchase model). Teams access pre-configured Google Analytics demo accounts with 12 months of data. **Phase 2 (60 minutes):** Teams conduct comprehensive analysis using specific reports: Multi-Channel Funnels > Assisted Conversions, Audience > Cohort Analysis, Conversions > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool, and Enhanced E-commerce > Shopping Behavior Analysis. Students must calculate customer acquisition cost (CAC), lifetime value (LTV), and return on ad spend (ROAS) for both companies using provided Excel templates with embedded formulas. **Phase 3 (45 minutes):** Teams evaluate data quality and limitations by examining sampling rates, data accuracy indicators, and identifying potential tracking gaps using the Account > Property > Data Quality reports. They must document at least 3 data reliability concerns per company. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their choice of superior business model, incorporating specific metrics as evidence and addressing potential counterarguments from opposing viewpoints.**
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo accounts with e-commerce tracking enabled
Pre-exported CSV files containing 12 months of traffic and conversion data
Excel template with CAC/LTV calculation formulas
Presentation template with required slide structure
Access to Google Slides or PowerPoint
Evaluation rubric handouts
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of metric calculations and data interpretation (25%), (2) Quality of evidence supporting business model recommendation (25%), (3) Critical assessment of data limitations and potential biases (20%), (4) Coherence of strategic recommendations aligned with analytics insights (20%), (5) Professional presentation delivery and response to questions (10%). Minimum passing score: 3.0/4.0 overall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheet with specific report navigation steps and metric definition glossary. Assign stronger analytics students as 'data mentors' within teams. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced segments, custom calculated metrics, or predictive analysis using Google Analytics Intelligence features. Encourage exploration of Data Studio integration for advanced visualization.

title: Binary Number Memory Drill with Visual Pattern Cards
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 using visual pattern cards and structured repetition exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions through systematic practice.
learning_objectives: Students will memorize the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will recall binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8) through visual pattern recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made binary conversion cards to each student - one set showing decimal numbers 0-15 on front with corresponding 4-bit binary on back (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Have students work in pairs for 5 minutes examining all cards simultaneously, encouraging them to identify visual patterns (odd numbers end in 1, multiples of 4 have specific patterns). Next, conduct a whole-class recitation where students chant the place values from right to left: '1, 2, 4, 8' three times while holding up corresponding fingers. For the main drill (15 minutes), student pairs take turns as flashcard holder and responder. The holder shows decimal numbers in random order, and responder must state the binary equivalent within 3 seconds. Switch roles every 2 minutes, cycling through all 16 numbers twice per role. During practice, circulate to correct errors immediately and ensure proper 4-bit format (leading zeros included). Conclude with individual assessment: display decimal numbers 3, 7, 10, 12, 15 on screen for 10 seconds each. Students write binary equivalents on paper without consultation. Finally, have students create their own mnemonic device for remembering that 8=1000, 4=0100, 2=0010, 1=0001, writing it on the back of their assessment sheet.
materials_needed: Pre-printed binary conversion cards (16 cards per student showing 0-15 decimal to 4-bit binary)
Blank paper for final assessment
Projector/screen for displaying assessment numbers
Timer or stopwatch for 3-second intervals
assessment_method: Students must correctly write binary equivalents for 5 given decimal numbers (3, 7, 10, 12, 15) within 10 seconds each. Success criteria: 4/5 correct answers with proper 4-bit formatting including leading zeros. Award 2 points per correct answer, 1 point if correct but missing leading zero.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a place value reference card (8-4-2-1) and start with powers of 2 only (1, 2, 4, 8). For advanced learners: extend to 8-bit binary (0-255 range) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Allow struggling students extra time during assessment and provide verbal encouragement during partner drills.

title: Optimization Portfolio: Real-World Calculus Applications in Business and Engineering
description: Students will apply differential calculus techniques to solve three complex optimization problems from different professional contexts. They will demonstrate mastery by constructing complete mathematical models, performing calculations, and presenting justified solutions with economic or engineering interpretations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply first and second derivative tests to determine optimal solutions for multivariable business profit maximization problems by constructing and solving complete mathematical models
Students will implement constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers to solve engineering design problems through systematic problem-solving methodology
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Distribute three problem scenarios: (1) A manufacturing company optimizing rectangular packaging to minimize material costs while maintaining 500 cubic inch volume, (2) A tech startup maximizing revenue function R(x,y) = 120x + 80y - 2x² - y² - xy with budget constraint 3x + 2y ≤ 100, and (3) An engineering firm designing cylindrical storage tanks to maximize volume with surface area limitations. Organize students into groups of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Mathematician, Model Constructor, Solution Validator, and Presenter.

**Problem-Solving Phase (45 minutes):** Each group tackles all three problems sequentially. For Problem 1, students must set up the optimization equation V = lwh = 500, express surface area S = 2lw + 2lh + 2wh, take partial derivatives, and solve the system. For Problem 2, they apply Lagrange multiplier method: ∇R = λ∇g where g(x,y) = 3x + 2y - 100. For Problem 3, students optimize V = πr²h subject to surface area constraint S = 2πr² + 2πrh = constant. Students must show all derivative calculations, critical point identification, second derivative tests for verification, and provide units with final answers.

**Validation Phase (15 minutes):** Groups cross-check solutions using graphing calculators or Desmos to verify critical points and confirm maximum/minimum nature. They calculate actual numerical values and verify constraint satisfaction.

**Presentation Phase (20 minutes):** Each group presents one problem solution on whiteboard, explaining mathematical reasoning, showing verification steps, and interpreting results in professional context (e.g., 'The optimal package dimensions reduce material costs by 23% while maintaining required volume').
materials_needed: Three printed problem scenario packets per group
Graphing calculators (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)
Access to Desmos Graphing Calculator online
Whiteboard markers and large format paper
Scientific calculators as backup
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Mathematical Setup and Modeling (25 points) - correct equations and constraints; Calculation Accuracy (30 points) - proper derivative techniques and algebraic manipulation; Solution Verification (25 points) - second derivative tests and constraint checking; Professional Interpretation (20 points) - meaningful context explanation and units. Each group submits written solutions and presents one problem. Individual accountability through random questioning during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for Struggling Students:** Provide derivative formula reference sheets, offer guiding questions ('What quantity are we maximizing?', 'What are our constraints?'), and allow peer tutoring within groups. Create checkpoint moments after setup phase for instructor feedback. **Advanced Extensions:** Challenge advanced learners with sensitivity analysis questions ('How does optimal solution change if volume requirement increases to 600 cubic inches?'), introduce economic interpretation of Lagrange multipliers as shadow prices, or add time-dependent optimization problems requiring chain rule applications.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions
description: Students will critically evaluate three different bug fix solutions for the same JavaScript function by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and maintainability. They will justify their choice of the best solution using established coding principles and provide detailed feedback using a structured evaluation framework.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different bug fix approaches by comparing their adherence to clean code principles, performance implications, and long-term maintainability
Students will critique code solutions through systematic analysis using a structured rubric that assesses readability, efficiency, and correctness
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Code Evaluation Worksheet containing a buggy JavaScript function that calculates shipping costs with three proposed fixes (Solution A: quick patch, Solution B: refactored approach, Solution C: over-engineered solution). Each solution correctly fixes the bug but uses different approaches.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students work independently to examine each solution against five criteria: correctness, readability, performance, maintainability, and adherence to best practices. They score each solution 1-4 on each criterion and write 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning for each score.

**Comparative Evaluation (15 minutes):** Students complete a comparison matrix ranking the three solutions from best to worst overall. They must identify the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and write a 100-word justification for their top choice, citing specific code examples and explaining how their chosen solution balances the competing factors.

**Peer Review Phase (10 minutes):** In pairs, students share their evaluations and discuss any disagreements in scoring or ranking. They document one insight gained from their partner's perspective.

**Final Recommendation (10 minutes):** Each student writes a brief recommendation memo to a hypothetical senior developer, stating which solution should be implemented and why, including potential risks or considerations for their chosen approach.
materials_needed: Code Evaluation Worksheet with buggy function and three fix solutions
Evaluation rubric with 5 criteria and 4-point scale
Comparison matrix template
Access to code editor or IDE for testing solutions
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 20-point rubric: Quality of individual criterion scoring (8 points), justification depth and use of specific examples (6 points), logical ranking with clear reasoning (4 points), and professional communication in final recommendation (2 points). Success requires scoring 16+/20 points with demonstrated ability to cite specific code elements in evaluations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of one criterion before starting, and offer guiding questions for each evaluation criterion. For advanced learners: Add a fourth solution with subtle security implications, or ask them to propose and evaluate their own alternative fix using the same framework.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate three different bug fix solutions for a simple calculator program by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and potential side effects. They will justify their choice of the best solution through structured peer discussions and written assessments.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by comparing code readability, performance impact, and maintainability using established criteria
Students will critique peer solutions through structured code review sessions and defend their evaluation decisions with specific technical evidence
instructions: Begin by distributing three different solutions to a calculator division-by-zero bug (15 minutes setup). Each solution uses a different approach: try-catch exception handling, if-statement validation, or input sanitization. Students work in pairs to analyze each solution using the provided evaluation criteria sheet covering readability (1-5 scale), maintainability (1-5 scale), performance impact (low/medium/high), and potential edge cases missed. Pairs spend 20 minutes examining each solution, filling out evaluation matrices, and identifying pros/cons. Next, conduct a structured peer review session (25 minutes) where each pair presents their top-ranked solution to another pair, defending their choice with specific code examples and criteria scores. The listening pair challenges the evaluation using counter-arguments and alternative perspectives. Rotate so all pairs both present and critique. Finally, students individually write a 200-word justification (15 minutes) explaining which solution they would implement in production, addressing potential stakeholder concerns (end-users, maintenance team, performance requirements). Conclude with a brief class discussion (10 minutes) where volunteers share how peer feedback influenced their final evaluation. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students reference specific code lines and use technical vocabulary when making evaluative statements.
materials_needed: Three printed code solutions for calculator division-by-zero bug (different approaches)
Code evaluation criteria rubric sheets
Sample calculator program with the original bug
Computers with code editor (VS Code or similar)
Timer for structured rotations
assessment_method: Evaluate students using: (1) Completed evaluation matrices showing numerical scores and specific evidence for each criterion (40 points), (2) Peer review participation rubric measuring quality of technical arguments and respectful challenging of ideas (30 points), (3) Individual written justification demonstrating synthesis of multiple perspectives and stakeholder considerations (30 points). Success criteria: Students score solutions using consistent logic, provide code-specific evidence, and acknowledge trade-offs in their final recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This solution is more maintainable because...' and highlight specific code lines to analyze. Pair weaker students with stronger partners initially. For advanced learners: Add complexity by asking them to consider additional criteria like security implications, scalability, or industry coding standards. Challenge them to propose hybrid solutions combining elements from multiple approaches.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate three different solutions to a common programming bug, analyzing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluations using established coding standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different bug fix implementations by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and adherence to best practices
Students will critique programming solutions through structured comparison using a provided evaluation framework
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Shopping Cart Bug Scenario' handout containing a simple e-commerce cart function with a quantity calculation error, plus three different student-submitted fixes labeled Solution A, B, and C. Provide the 'Code Evaluation Checklist' with criteria: correctness, readability, efficiency, and maintainability. **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each solution independently, testing the logic mentally or on paper, and scoring each solution (1-4 scale) on the four criteria. They must write 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning for each score. **Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discussing disagreements and refining their assessments. Partners don't need to reach consensus but should understand different perspectives. **Ranking Activity (10 minutes):** Each student individually ranks the three solutions from best to worst, writing a 100-word justification that references specific code elements and evaluation criteria. **Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates discussion by polling student rankings, highlighting common evaluation points, and revealing which solution was written by a senior developer (Solution B), discussing why professional code might differ from student expectations.
materials_needed: Shopping Cart Bug Scenario handout with 3 solution variants
Code Evaluation Checklist with 4-point rubric
Lined paper for written justifications
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Grade the written ranking justifications using a 3-point rubric: (3) Uses specific code examples and addresses at least 3 evaluation criteria with clear reasoning, (2) References code elements and addresses 2 criteria with adequate reasoning, (1) General comments with minimal specific analysis. Observe pair discussions for participation and use of technical vocabulary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed evaluation table and highlight specific lines to examine in each solution. For advanced learners: Add a bonus question asking them to write an improved fourth solution or identify security considerations not addressed in any solution.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fix Solutions

title: Design and Build a Predictive Sales Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that analyzes historical sales data to predict future trends and generate actionable business recommendations. They will design data visualizations, build predictive models, and present insights that could influence real business decisions.
estimated_duration: 4 hours (can be split across 2-3 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multiple data analysis techniques by combining descriptive statistics, trend analysis, and basic forecasting to create a comprehensive business intelligence tool
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through integrating data cleaning, visualization design, and predictive modeling to solve authentic business problems
instructions:
**Phase 1: Setup & Data Exploration (45 minutes)**
Provide each team of 3-4 students with a dataset containing 2 years of monthly sales data for a fictional local business (include columns: date, product_category, sales_amount, customer_count, marketing_spend, season). Students begin by importing data into Tableau Public and conducting exploratory analysis to identify patterns, outliers, and seasonal trends. They must document 5 key insights about the business performance.

**Phase 2: Dashboard Design Planning (30 minutes)**
Teams sketch their dashboard layout on paper, deciding which visualizations will best tell the data story. They must plan: 1 time-series chart showing sales trends, 1 comparative analysis of product categories, 1 correlation analysis between marketing spend and sales, and 1 forecasting visualization. Each team assigns roles: Data Analyst (focuses on calculations), Visualization Designer (charts and aesthetics), and Business Strategist (interprets insights).

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (90 minutes)**
Students build their interactive dashboard in Tableau Public. They create calculated fields for growth rates, moving averages, and seasonal adjustments. Teams implement filters allowing users to explore data by time period and product category. They add trend lines and basic forecasting using Tableau's built-in prediction tools to project next quarter's sales.

**Phase 4: Business Recommendations (45 minutes)**
Each team develops 3 specific, data-driven recommendations for the business owner based on their analysis. They create a summary slide within their dashboard explaining their methodology and confidence levels in predictions.

**Phase 5: Peer Review & Presentation (30 minutes)**
Teams present their dashboards to another team for feedback using provided evaluation criteria, then make final refinements before submission.
materials_needed: Sample sales dataset (CSV file with 24 months of data including sales, marketing, and customer metrics)
Computers/tablets with internet access for Tableau Public
Large paper sheets and markers for dashboard sketching
Peer evaluation rubric handout
Business scenario background document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: Data Analysis Quality (accuracy of insights, appropriate statistical measures), Dashboard Design (visual clarity, interactivity, professional appearance), Predictive Modeling (appropriate forecasting method, realistic projections), and Business Application (actionable recommendations, understanding of business context). Students submit their published Tableau dashboard link plus a 2-page written summary of methodology and recommendations. Peer feedback forms contribute 20% to final grade.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide dashboard template with placeholder charts and step-by-step Tableau tutorial videos. Offer simplified dataset with clearer patterns. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data (economic indicators, competitor analysis) or implement more sophisticated forecasting methods. Encourage exploration of advanced Tableau features like parameters and calculated fields for what-if scenarios.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Sales Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that combines multiple data sources to predict quarterly sales trends for a fictional local retail business. They will design data collection frameworks, build analytical models, and present actionable insights through visualizations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer transaction data, seasonal patterns, and economic indicators by designing a comprehensive predictive model using statistical forecasting methods
Students will construct an interactive business intelligence dashboard through integration of data visualization tools and written executive summary recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Architecture Design (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three CSV datasets: 2-year transaction history (15,000 records), local economic indicators (unemployment, population growth), and competitor pricing data. Teams spend 15 minutes exploring data structure and quality issues using Excel/Google Sheets. Next, teams create a data integration plan documenting which variables to combine, how to handle missing values, and what new calculated fields to generate (revenue per customer, seasonal adjustment factors, price elasticity measures).

**Phase 2: Predictive Model Construction (60 minutes)**
Using provided Tableau Public or Power BI templates, teams build forecasting models. First 20 minutes: clean and merge datasets, creating master analysis table. Next 25 minutes: construct trend analysis using moving averages and seasonal decomposition to identify quarterly patterns. Final 15 minutes: apply linear regression or exponential smoothing to generate 6-month sales predictions with confidence intervals.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Teams design executive dashboard with exactly four components: historical performance summary chart, predictive model visualization showing forecast vs. actual trends, key performance indicator cards (projected revenue, customer growth rate, inventory turnover), and interactive filter allowing users to adjust assumptions (economic conditions, marketing spend, competitor actions). Include data source documentation and methodology explanations.

**Phase 4: Business Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each team presents 5-minute pitch to simulated business owner, demonstrating dashboard functionality and providing three specific strategic recommendations based on their analysis. Include discussion of model limitations and data quality concerns.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets per team (transaction_history.csv, economic_indicators.csv, competitor_data.csv)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Laptops/computers with spreadsheet software
Dashboard template file with basic formatting structure
Business scenario handout describing fictional retail company context
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Data integration quality and methodology documentation (25 points), statistical model accuracy and appropriate technique selection (30 points), dashboard design clarity and interactivity functionality (25 points), business presentation quality and actionable recommendations (20 points). Students submit dashboard file, written methodology report (500 words), and peer evaluation forms rating team collaboration.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing data cleaning checklist template and step-by-step forecasting formula guide. Offer optional 15-minute mini-lesson on statistical concepts during Phase 2. For advanced learners, provide additional dataset (social media sentiment data) and challenge them to incorporate external API data source or advanced machine learning algorithms like ARIMA modeling.
original_title: Design and Build a Predictive Sales Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Identification and Recall Challenge
description: Students will systematically identify and recall specific elements of complex Critical Path Method network diagrams, including activity dependencies, float calculations, and critical path components. This advanced recall activity requires memorization and recognition of sophisticated project scheduling terminology and mathematical relationships within realistic project scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the precise definitions of forward pass, backward pass, early start, early finish, late start, and late finish by accurately identifying these components in complex network diagrams within 90 seconds per diagram
Students will recognize and name all critical path determination rules, float calculation formulas, and network diagram symbols through rapid-fire identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing laminated sets of 12 complex CPM network diagrams featuring 15-20 activities each, representing realistic construction, IT implementation, and pharmaceutical development projects. Each diagram contains deliberately mislabeled or missing components. Students work individually for the first 20 minutes, using provided reference sheets to identify: (1) all critical path activities by name and sequence, (2) activities with total float greater than zero, (3) free float vs. total float distinctions for specified activities, and (4) early/late start-finish calculations for marked nodes. After individual work, form pairs for 15 minutes where Partner A shows Partner B a diagram and asks rapid-fire questions: 'What's the early start of Activity J?' 'Which activities have zero total float?' 'What's the formula for free float?' Partner B must respond within 10 seconds before switching roles. In the final 10 minutes, conduct a whole-class rapid recall session where you project diagrams for 30 seconds each while students write down: the critical path sequence, total project duration, and three activities with the highest total float. Use a timer visibly displayed throughout all phases. Provide immediate confirmation of correct answers after each diagram. Students must achieve 80% accuracy on component identification and recall specific CPM formulas verbatim without reference materials.
materials_needed: 12 laminated CPM network diagrams (different colors for each project type)
CPM terminology reference sheets (1 per student)
Digital timer with large display
Answer key sheets for instructors
Individual response sheets with pre-formatted answer spaces
Projector for whole-class rapid recall session
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify 80% of critical path components, recall CPM formulas with 100% accuracy (exact wording required), and complete rapid-fire partner questioning with 75% correct responses within time limits. Track performance using provided checklist rubric with specific point allocations: Component identification (40 points), formula recall (35 points), rapid response accuracy (25 points). Minimum passing score: 80/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide color-coded diagrams where critical path activities are highlighted in red, and offer formula cards with missing words to fill in rather than complete recall. Advanced learners receive additional diagrams with resource constraints, multiple critical paths, and must recall advanced concepts like resource leveling terminology and crashing cost calculations. Consider allowing struggling students extra 30 seconds for rapid-fire responses.

title: Deconstructing Transformational vs. Transactional Leadership Through Crisis Response Case Analysis
description: Students will analyze and differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership approaches by examining real CEO responses during the 2008 financial crisis. They will identify specific behaviors, communication patterns, and decision-making frameworks that exemplify each leadership style through structured case comparison.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership characteristics by analyzing documented CEO behaviors during crisis situations
Students will interpret the underlying motivational strategies and communication approaches through systematic comparison of leadership artifacts
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and providing each pair with two contrasting CEO case studies: Jamie Dimon (JPMorgan Chase) representing transformational leadership and John Thain (Merrill Lynch) representing transactional leadership during 2008-2009. Give students 20 minutes to individually read their assigned materials, including transcripts of shareholder calls, internal memos, and media interviews. Next, provide the 'Leadership Behavior Analysis Matrix' worksheet with specific categories: vision communication, employee motivation tactics, decision-making transparency, change management approach, and stakeholder engagement style. Students spend 25 minutes working in pairs to complete the matrix, identifying and categorizing specific quotes, actions, and decisions from each CEO. Then facilitate a 15-minute structured comparison where each pair maps their findings onto the transformational-transactional leadership spectrum using the provided sliding scale template. Students must justify placement with specific evidence and explain how each behavior aligns with theoretical frameworks (Bass & Avolio's model). Conclude with a 10-minute gallery walk where pairs post their completed spectrums and observe others' analyses, noting convergent and divergent interpretations. Finally, conduct a 15-minute debrief discussion focusing on the nuanced differences between leadership styles and their contextual effectiveness during crisis situations.
materials_needed: Two comprehensive CEO case study packets (8-10 pages each) with crisis response documentation
Leadership Behavior Analysis Matrix worksheets (one per pair)
Transformational-Transactional Leadership Spectrum templates with sliding scale
Colored markers or pens for matrix completion
Large poster paper for gallery walk display
Bass & Avolio theoretical framework reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Behavior Analysis Matrices using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) accuracy of behavior categorization with specific textual evidence, (2) depth of analysis connecting behaviors to theoretical frameworks, (3) quality of justification for spectrum placement, and (4) demonstration of understanding through peer discussion contributions. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted key passages in case studies and sentence starters for matrix completion ('This demonstrates transformational leadership because...'). For advanced learners, include additional CEO examples (Richard Fuld, Vikram Pandit) for expanded comparison and ask them to identify hybrid leadership approaches that don't fit neatly into either category.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application Using AWS EC2 and S3
description: Students will deploy a static website to AWS S3 and configure an EC2 instance to serve dynamic content. They will apply AWS security groups, IAM roles, and storage configurations to create a functional web application with both static and dynamic components.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website to AWS S3 by configuring bucket policies and static website hosting settings
Students will configure an EC2 instance to serve dynamic content through proper security group setup and application deployment
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab credentials and access to a pre-built HTML/CSS website template and a simple Node.js application file. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify access to EC2 and S3 services.

**Phase 1 - S3 Static Website (25 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket with a unique name following naming conventions (studentname-website-bucket-YYYY). They upload the provided HTML, CSS, and image files to the bucket, then enable static website hosting in bucket properties. Students configure bucket policy to allow public read access using the provided JSON template, then test the static website URL.

**Phase 2 - EC2 Dynamic Component (30 minutes):** Students launch a t2.micro Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance using the provided AMI. They create a new security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere. After instance launch, students connect via EC2 Instance Connect and install Node.js using provided commands. They upload and configure the Node.js application to run on port 80, then start the service.

**Phase 3 - Integration and Testing (15 minutes):** Students modify their static website to include AJAX calls to their EC2 instance's public IP address. They update the S3 bucket with the modified files and test both static content delivery and dynamic API responses. Students document both URLs and demonstrate functionality by showing different responses from the dynamic component.

**Wrap-up (10 minutes):** Students screenshot their working application, note their resource URLs, and properly terminate EC2 instances to avoid charges.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts for each student
Pre-built HTML/CSS website template with index.html, styles.css, and sample images
Simple Node.js application file (express server with basic API endpoints)
S3 bucket policy JSON template for public read access
Step-by-step command reference sheet for EC2 setup and Node.js installation
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) S3 bucket configuration with static website hosting enabled, (2) EC2 instance running with correct security group settings, (3) functional website displaying static content, (4) successful API call returning dynamic data from EC2, and (5) AWS resource cleanup completion. Rubric awards 20 points each for correct S3 setup, EC2 configuration, static site functionality, dynamic integration, and proper resource management.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written security group rules and bucket policies to copy-paste, offer one-on-one screen sharing for AWS console navigation, and create a troubleshooting checklist for common errors. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement HTTPS using CloudFront, add a custom domain using Route 53, or create an RDS database connection for the dynamic component. Provide AWS CLI commands as an alternative to console-based deployment.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application Using AWS EC2 and S3: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a static website to AWS S3 and configure an EC2 instance to serve a dynamic web application. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration and basic cloud deployment workflows.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a static website to AWS S3 by configuring bucket policies and enabling static website hosting
Students will configure an EC2 instance to host a web application through security group setup, SSH connection, and web server installation
instructions:
**Phase 1: S3 Static Website (25 minutes)**
1. Have students log into AWS Management Console using provided lab accounts
2. Navigate to S3 service and create a new bucket with naming convention: 'student-website-[lastname]-[date]'
3. Upload provided HTML files (index.html, style.css, image folder) to the bucket
4. Configure bucket for static website hosting: Properties → Static website hosting → Enable
5. Set index.html as index document and error.html as error document
6. Modify bucket policy using provided JSON template to allow public read access
7. Test website accessibility using the S3 endpoint URL

**Phase 2: EC2 Web Server Setup (35 minutes)**
1. Launch new EC2 instance: Amazon Linux 2, t2.micro, create new key pair
2. Configure security group to allow HTTP (port 80), HTTPS (port 443), and SSH (port 22) access
3. Download and save the key pair file to designated folder
4. Connect to EC2 instance using SSH (provide platform-specific connection commands)
5. Install Apache web server: 'sudo yum update -y' then 'sudo yum install httpd -y'
6. Start Apache service: 'sudo systemctl start httpd' and enable auto-start: 'sudo systemctl enable httpd'
7. Upload provided PHP application files to /var/www/html/ directory using SCP
8. Test application by accessing EC2 public IP address in browser
9. Document both URLs (S3 and EC2) in provided worksheet with screenshots
materials_needed: AWS lab accounts with IAM permissions for S3 and EC2
Pre-built HTML/CSS files for static website
Sample PHP web application files
Student worksheet template for documenting URLs and configurations
Platform-specific SSH client instructions (Windows/Mac/Linux)
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheet containing: (1) Working S3 static website URL with screenshot, (2) Working EC2 web application URL with screenshot, (3) Documented security group configurations, (4) Reflection on differences between S3 and EC2 hosting. Rubric: URLs functional (40%), screenshots included (20%), security configurations documented (25%), reflection quality (15%)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured bucket policy JSON and step-by-step SSH connection videos. Create troubleshooting checklist for common errors (security group misconfiguration, file permissions). For advanced learners: Add CloudFront CDN setup for S3 website, implement SSL certificates, or configure auto-scaling groups for EC2 instances. Provide additional challenges like setting up RDS database integration.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application Using AWS EC2 and S3

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three different project scenarios to identify risk patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of chosen risk response strategies, and determine optimal alternative approaches. They will break down complex risk situations to understand the relationship between risk categories, response strategies, and project constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of risk response strategies by comparing their impact across three distinct project scenarios with different constraints
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk responses through systematic evaluation of strategy alignment with risk characteristics and project context
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute the three project scenario packets: (1) Software implementation with tight deadline, (2) Construction project with weather dependencies, (3) Product launch with regulatory approval requirements. Each scenario includes 8-10 identified risks with currently assigned response strategies (accept, avoid, mitigate, transfer). **Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student independently reviews all three scenarios, creating a comparison matrix that categorizes risks by type (technical, external, organizational, project management) and maps current response strategies. Students must identify at least 2 risks per scenario where the chosen strategy appears misaligned with risk characteristics. **Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (20 minutes):** Teams consolidate individual findings, focusing on patterns across scenarios. They must reach consensus on: Which risks show poor strategy-risk alignment and why? What common factors make certain strategies more effective in specific contexts? How do project constraints (time, budget, scope, quality) influence optimal strategy selection? **Phase 3 - Alternative Strategy Development (15 minutes):** For each identified misalignment, teams develop alternative response strategies with specific justification based on risk probability, impact, and project constraints. Teams must consider secondary risks that might emerge from their proposed changes. **Phase 4 - Cross-Team Validation (10 minutes):** Teams pair up to present their top 3 strategy recommendations to another team, receiving feedback on feasibility and completeness of their analysis.
materials_needed: Three detailed project scenario packets with risk registers
Risk response strategy reference sheets (PMBOK definitions)
Risk analysis comparison matrix templates (printed)
Flip chart paper and markers for team presentations
Timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization and pattern identification (25%), (2) Quality of strategy-alignment analysis with specific justification (35%), (3) Feasibility and creativity of alternative strategies proposed (25%), (4) Evidence of systematic comparison across scenarios rather than isolated analysis (15%). Teams must submit completed comparison matrices and alternative strategy proposals with rationale.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide risk categorization hints in Phase 1, offer sentence starters for justification statements, assign stronger analytical thinkers as team leads. **Advanced extension:** Challenge high-performing teams to quantify risk exposure changes with their proposed strategies, or analyze how their recommendations would change if project priorities shifted (e.g., time becomes less critical, budget constraints tighten).

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students analyze three different project scenarios to identify risk patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of chosen risk response strategies, and determine which projects have the most robust risk management approaches. This activity develops critical thinking skills for real-world PMP risk management decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies across multiple project scenarios by identifying patterns, gaps, and effectiveness indicators
Students will evaluate and compare risk management approaches through systematic assessment criteria and justify their recommendations
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute three project scenario packets (Software Migration Project, Construction Project, Marketing Campaign Project) to each team, along with the Risk Analysis Worksheet. Each scenario contains 8-10 identified risks with corresponding response strategies.

**Individual Review (15 minutes):** Each student independently reads all three scenarios and completes Part 1 of the worksheet, categorizing each risk response strategy (Accept, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate) and noting initial observations about strategy appropriateness.

**Team Analysis Phase (25 minutes):** Teams collaborate to complete Part 2, systematically analyzing each project using provided criteria: strategy alignment with risk severity, cost-effectiveness, timeline impact, and stakeholder considerations. Students must identify at least 3 strengths and 3 weaknesses per project's risk approach.

**Comparative Evaluation (20 minutes):** Teams rank the three projects from most to least effective risk management approach using the provided scoring rubric (1-5 scale across 6 dimensions). They must provide written justification for rankings and identify 2-3 specific improvements for the lowest-ranked project.

**Team Presentations (15 minutes):** Each team presents their top-ranked project choice with 3 key supporting arguments. Other teams can challenge reasoning with questions. Instructor facilitates discussion on varying perspectives and real-world applications.

**Debrief (5 minutes):** Class discusses common patterns identified across scenarios and how this analysis process applies to actual PMP exam situations and professional practice.
materials_needed: Three printed project scenario packets with risk registers
Risk Analysis Worksheet (2 pages per student)
Scoring rubric handout
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
Timer for activity phases
assessment_method: Grade completed Risk Analysis Worksheets using 4-point rubric: Strategy Categorization Accuracy (25%), Quality of Strengths/Weaknesses Analysis (35%), Ranking Justification Logic (25%), Team Presentation Clarity (15%). Students must demonstrate clear reasoning connecting risk characteristics to strategy appropriateness and show understanding of PMP risk management principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide strategy definition cards and encourage them to focus on one project initially before comparing. For advanced learners: Challenge them to propose alternative strategies for identified weaknesses and calculate potential cost impacts. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during team formation.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Scenarios

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Scenarios: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze three different project scenarios with varying risk profiles and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will break down each scenario's risk factors, compare response approaches, and determine which strategies are most appropriate for each project context.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) by examining their application across three distinct project scenarios
Students will differentiate between appropriate risk responses through systematic comparison of strategy effectiveness and resource implications
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the three project scenario handouts: Software Implementation (high technical risk), Construction Project (high safety/weather risks), and Product Launch (high market/competitive risks). Each scenario includes 5-6 specific risks with attempted response strategies. 

Phase 1 (20 minutes): Each group analyzes one scenario first, using the Risk Analysis Framework worksheet to categorize each risk by type, probability, and impact. Students identify which of the four response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) was used for each risk and document the rationale.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Groups rotate to analyze the second and third scenarios, comparing how similar risk types are handled differently across projects. They complete a comparison matrix showing which strategies work best for technical vs. external vs. market risks.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Groups present their analysis to the class, specifically explaining: (1) Which risk response was most/least effective in each scenario and why, (2) How project context influenced strategy selection, (3) What alternative responses they would recommend. Other groups provide feedback using the peer evaluation form.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion connecting findings to PMI's risk management framework, highlighting patterns in strategy selection based on risk categories and project constraints.
materials_needed: Three project scenario handouts (2 pages each) with embedded risk situations
Risk Analysis Framework worksheets with categorization tables
Risk Response Comparison Matrix template
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Analysis Framework worksheets (40% - accuracy of risk categorization and strategy identification), Comparison Matrix quality (30% - depth of cross-scenario analysis and justification), and presentation effectiveness (30% - clarity of analysis explanation and alternative recommendations). Use 4-point rubric: Exemplary (demonstrates sophisticated analysis with clear justifications), Proficient (accurate analysis with adequate explanations), Developing (basic analysis with limited justification), Beginning (incomplete or inaccurate analysis).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of one risk analysis and strategy evaluation. Include definition cards for each risk response strategy. For advanced learners: Add a fourth scenario involving international project complexities, or have them create risk response cost-benefit analyses with numerical estimates.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Scenarios

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Audit and Optimization Strategy
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and position-based) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for specific business scenarios and develop data-driven recommendations for attribution strategy optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business relevance of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI metrics across multiple marketing channels

Students will critique the limitations of current attribution settings through comparative analysis and develop strategic recommendations for model selection based on business objectives and customer journey characteristics
instructions: Begin by providing each student with access to a demo Google Analytics 4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, social media, email, display, organic search). Students work individually for 90 minutes. First 30 minutes: Students navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution and examine the Model Comparison report. They must document conversion values, conversion counts, and channel performance across all five attribution models, creating a comparative spreadsheet with percentage differences between models. Next 30 minutes: Students analyze the Top Conversion Paths report to identify common customer journey patterns, noting path length, time lag, and channel sequences for the top 20 conversion paths. They calculate the average path length and identify which channels most frequently appear as first-touch, mid-funnel, and last-touch interactions. Final 30 minutes: Students prepare a detailed written evaluation (500-750 words) addressing three scenarios: (1) which attribution model they would recommend for a business focused on customer acquisition, (2) which model best serves retention-focused campaigns, and (3) how they would modify attribution windows based on the observed customer journey data. Students must justify each recommendation using specific data points from their analysis and explain potential limitations or biases in their chosen models.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel)
Attribution model comparison template
Business scenario case study documents
assessment_method: Evaluate submissions using a 4-point rubric: (1) Data accuracy and completeness of attribution model comparison (25%), (2) Quality of customer journey pattern analysis with specific metrics and insights (25%), (3) Strategic reasoning and justification for model recommendations across three business scenarios (35%), (4) Recognition and articulation of attribution model limitations and potential biases (15%). Students must demonstrate understanding by citing specific data points and explaining cause-effect relationships between attribution choices and business outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps and pre-formatted data collection tables. Include prompting questions like 'Which channel shows the biggest difference between first-click and last-click attribution?' For advanced learners, challenge them to calculate custom attribution weights based on channel performance data or to propose data collection improvements that would enhance attribution accuracy. Provide additional scenarios involving offline conversions or cross-device tracking challenges.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Infrastructure with Advanced Security and QoS Policies
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network spanning three geographically distributed sites with interconnected LANs, WANs, VPNs, and advanced services. They will create original network designs incorporating OSPF routing, VLAN segmentation, firewall policies, and Quality of Service configurations to meet specific business requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize enterprise networking concepts by designing an original multi-site network topology that integrates routing protocols, VLANs, security policies, and QoS mechanisms
Students will construct and validate a fully functional network implementation through hands-on configuration of Cisco routers, switches, and security appliances using industry-standard protocols
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (90 minutes)**

Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives a fictional company scenario requiring network infrastructure for headquarters (500 users), branch office (150 users), and data center (50 servers). Teams must create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes, VLAN designs, and device placement.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (180 minutes)**

Teams build their networks using provided Cisco equipment. Start with basic Layer 2 switching configuration, implementing VLANs for different departments (Finance: VLAN 10, HR: VLAN 20, IT: VLAN 30). Configure trunk ports between switches and access ports for end devices. Next, implement Layer 3 routing using OSPF protocol across all three sites, ensuring full connectivity between locations.

**Phase 3: Advanced Services Configuration (120 minutes)**

Implement security policies using Access Control Lists (ACLs) to restrict inter-VLAN communication based on business rules. Configure site-to-site VPN tunnels using IPSec between headquarters and branch office. Establish QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic over data traffic, implementing traffic shaping and policing.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (60 minutes)**

Conduct comprehensive testing including ping tests, traceroute verification, VPN connectivity validation, and QoS performance measurement. Create network documentation including configuration backups, IP address tables, and troubleshooting procedures. Present final implementation to class with live demonstrations of key features.
materials_needed: Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches (minimum 3 per team)
Cisco ISR 4000 series routers (minimum 3 per team)
Cisco ASA 5500 series firewalls (1 per team)
Cat6 Ethernet cables (20 per team)
Cisco Packet Tracer software licenses
Laptop computers with console cables
Network documentation templates
assessment_method: Evaluation using 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - logical topology, proper IP subnetting, appropriate device selection; Implementation Accuracy (35 points) - correct VLAN configuration, successful OSPF routing, functional VPN tunnels; Security and QoS Configuration (25 points) - effective ACL policies, working QoS implementation; Documentation and Presentation (15 points) - complete network diagrams, configuration backups, clear troubleshooting procedures. Teams must demonstrate live network functionality with ping tests between all sites and successful traffic prioritization.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic IP addressing completed, offer step-by-step configuration checklists for each protocol, assign peer mentors from advanced students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like network monitoring using SNMP, redundancy protocols (HSRP/VRRP), or wireless controller integration. Provide access to advanced Cisco documentation and encourage exploration of emerging technologies like SD-WAN concepts.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Functions for Real-World Business Scenarios
description: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve complex optimization problems involving production constraints, budget limitations, and resource allocation. They will work through authentic business cases requiring multi-step calculus applications and interpret their mathematical solutions in economic contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to optimize multi-variable functions subject to multiple constraints by solving three distinct business optimization scenarios

Students will implement partial differentiation and constraint analysis techniques through systematic problem-solving protocols to determine maximum profit, minimum cost, and optimal resource allocation
instructions: Begin by distributing three business scenario packets to teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Each packet contains: a manufacturing company needing to maximize profit with labor/material constraints, a logistics firm minimizing transportation costs with capacity limits, and a tech startup optimizing server allocation with budget restrictions. Students first spend 20 minutes analyzing their assigned scenario, identifying the objective function, constraint equations, and relevant variables. Next, they systematically apply the Lagrange multiplier method: setting up the Lagrangian function, computing partial derivatives, solving the system of equations, and verifying critical points using the bordered Hessian test (45 minutes). During this phase, circulate to ensure proper mathematical notation and computational accuracy. Students then interpret their mathematical results in business terms, calculating actual dollar amounts, resource quantities, and efficiency metrics (25 minutes). Each team presents their complete solution to another team, explaining both mathematical procedures and business implications (20 minutes per presentation). Conclude with teams rotating through all three scenarios, comparing optimization strategies and identifying patterns in constraint-handling techniques. Emphasize the connection between mathematical critical points and real-world decision-making throughout the activity.
materials_needed: Three detailed business scenario packets with specific numerical data
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica/Wolfram Alpha access)
Large format paper for detailed mathematical work
Economic context reference sheets with profit/cost terminology
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct setup of Lagrangian functions and constraint identification, (2) Accurate computation of partial derivatives and critical point solutions, (3) Proper verification using second-order conditions, (4) Clear interpretation of mathematical results in business context. Students must submit complete written solutions showing all algebraic steps, plus a one-page executive summary explaining their recommendations to business stakeholders.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide template worksheets with partially completed Lagrangian setups and step-by-step derivative computation guides. Offer additional practice with simpler two-variable, single-constraint problems before attempting full scenarios. For advanced learners, introduce inequality constraints using Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions, or challenge them to modify scenarios by adding additional realistic constraints like environmental regulations or market demand fluctuations.

title: Analyzing Energy Dissipation Mechanisms in Multi-Stage Collision Systems
description: Students will decompose a complex three-car collision scenario to identify and quantify different energy dissipation mechanisms. They will examine how momentum conservation and energy loss interact across multiple collision phases, distinguishing between elastic deformation, plastic deformation, friction, and sound energy losses.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-stage collision dynamics by decomposing momentum and energy changes across each collision phase to identify predominant dissipation mechanisms
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of different energy loss pathways through quantitative comparison of calculated versus observed kinetic energy changes
instructions:
**Phase 1 (15 min):** Distribute collision scenario data showing three cars (masses: 1200kg, 1500kg, 800kg) with initial velocities, intermediate velocities after first collision, and final velocities after second collision. Include coefficient of restitution values, skid marks data, and decibel measurements. Students work in groups of 3-4 to map the collision sequence chronologically.

**Phase 2 (25 min):** Each group creates a detailed energy flow diagram identifying: kinetic energy at each stage, potential elastic energy storage during deformation, energy lost to permanent deformation, frictional heating during skidding, and acoustic energy release. Students calculate actual values using provided formulas for each mechanism. They must justify why certain mechanisms dominate in each collision phase.

**Phase 3 (20 min):** Groups analyze discrepancies between theoretical momentum conservation calculations and actual measured outcomes. They identify which energy dissipation mechanisms account for observed differences and rank them by magnitude of energy loss. Students create a quantitative breakdown showing percentage contribution of each dissipation pathway.

**Phase 4 (15 min):** Teams present their analysis to another group, defending their identification of primary versus secondary energy loss mechanisms. They must explain how different collision characteristics (head-on vs. glancing, speeds involved, vehicle construction) influence which dissipation pathways dominate the energy budget.
materials_needed: Multi-stage collision data packets with masses, velocities, and collision parameters
Scientific calculators or tablets with calculation software
Large format paper for energy flow diagrams
Reference sheets with energy dissipation formulas (elastic potential, friction work, acoustic power)
Colored markers for diagram creation
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of energy calculations for each dissipation mechanism (25%), (2) Correct identification and ranking of primary vs secondary energy loss pathways (30%), (3) Quality of reasoning linking collision characteristics to dominant dissipation mechanisms (25%), (4) Clear justification of discrepancies between theoretical and observed outcomes (20%). Students submit calculated energy budgets and written analysis defending their mechanism hierarchy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made energy flow diagram templates and step-by-step calculation worksheets for each dissipation type. Offer guiding questions about which mechanisms typically dominate at high vs low speeds. For advanced learners: Include rotational kinetic energy components, ask them to predict how different vehicle materials would alter the dissipation hierarchy, or have them design experiments to isolate individual mechanisms.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Tracking Solutions for Small Development Teams
description: Students will critically evaluate three different bug tracking software solutions by analyzing their features, usability, and suitability for a hypothetical 5-person development team. They will create justified recommendations based on specific criteria and present their findings through a comparative analysis report.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug tracking tools by analyzing feature sets, user interfaces, and integration capabilities against predetermined criteria
Students will critique the suitability of software solutions through hands-on testing and systematic comparison of strengths and weaknesses
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 2-3. Provide each group with the scenario: 'TechStart Solutions, a 5-person web development team, needs a bug tracking system for their e-commerce projects. They have a $200/month budget, need GitHub integration, and require mobile access.' Give groups 15 minutes to familiarize themselves with the evaluation criteria checklist: cost-effectiveness (25%), ease of use (25%), integration capabilities (20%), mobile accessibility (15%), and reporting features (15%). Next, assign each group to test three specific tools: Jira, GitHub Issues, and Linear. Allocate 45 minutes for hands-on exploration where students create sample projects, add test bugs, assign tasks, and navigate interfaces. During testing, students must complete the provided evaluation matrix, scoring each tool (1-5 scale) against all criteria and documenting specific evidence for their scores. Following the testing phase, give groups 30 minutes to analyze their findings, calculate weighted scores, and identify the top recommendation with two alternative options. Students must justify their rankings by citing specific examples from their testing experience. Finally, each group presents their 5-minute recommendation to the class, explaining their methodology, key findings, and final recommendation with supporting rationale. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion comparing different groups' conclusions and reasoning approaches.
materials_needed: Computers/laptops with internet access (one per 2-3 students)
Evaluation criteria checklist handout
Pre-made evaluation matrix template (digital or print)
Access to free trials/accounts for Jira, GitHub, and Linear
TechStart Solutions company scenario handout
Timer for time management
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Systematic use of evaluation criteria with documented evidence (25 points), (2) Quality of comparative analysis and logical reasoning (25 points), (3) Appropriateness and justification of final recommendation (25 points), (4) Professional presentation of findings with clear supporting examples (25 points). Students must submit their completed evaluation matrix and present their findings to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided questions for each tool ('How many clicks to create a bug report?' 'Can you access this on mobile?') and offer a sample evaluation for one criterion. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring them to consider scalability for team growth, evaluate API documentation quality, or research actual pricing for enterprise features beyond the basic requirements.

title: Project Management Framework Components Rapid Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall specific components, artifacts, and terminology from major project management frameworks including PMBOK Guide knowledge areas, PRINCE2 themes, and Agile ceremonies. This intensive memorization activity builds foundational knowledge essential for advanced project management practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 10 PMBOK Guide knowledge areas and their 49 processes by completing timed retrieval exercises within 90% accuracy
Students will identify specific project artifacts, roles, and ceremonies from PMBOK, PRINCE2, and Scrum frameworks through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the framework reference sheets containing PMBOK's 10 knowledge areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) with their 49 processes, PRINCE2's 7 themes and 7 processes, and Scrum's 5 events and 3 artifacts. Students have 20 minutes to study materials silently. Next, collect all reference materials and begin Round 1: PMBOK Knowledge Areas. Display each knowledge area name for 30 seconds while students write all associated processes from memory. Continue through all 10 areas. Round 2 focuses on PRINCE2 components. Call out each of the 7 themes (Business Case, Organization, Quality, Plans, Risk, Change, Progress) and students list associated activities and artifacts within 2 minutes per theme. Round 3 covers Scrum framework recall. Students have 5 minutes to list all events (Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective), artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment), and roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Development Team) with their specific purposes. Conduct immediate peer checking using answer keys. Students exchange papers and mark correct responses. Follow with a rapid-fire verbal quiz where individuals stand and answer specific questions about framework components until they miss one, then sit down. Top 3 remaining students receive recognition. Conclude with individual reflection where students identify their weakest areas for future study focus.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 6th Edition process reference sheets (1 per student)
PRINCE2 methodology summary handouts with themes and processes
Scrum framework component cards with definitions
Timer or stopwatch
Answer keys for peer checking
Blank paper for student responses
assessment_method: Grade based on accuracy percentages: 90-100% = Excellent recall (A), 80-89% = Good recall (B), 70-79% = Satisfactory recall (C), Below 70% = Needs improvement. Assess across three rounds with weighted scoring: PMBOK processes (50%), PRINCE2 themes (25%), Scrum components (25%). Track individual improvement from initial study phase to final rapid-fire round.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (e.g., 'I Simply Schedule Cost-Quality Resources Communicating Risk Procurement to Stakeholders' for PMBOK). Allow struggling learners to work in pairs during initial study phase. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring them to recall process inputs/outputs or explain interconnections between frameworks. Challenge high performers to create their own memory devices for classmates.

title: Deconstructing Multi-Stakeholder Leadership Crisis Decisions Through Cross-Cultural Case Analysis
description: Students will analyze complex leadership decisions made during multi-stakeholder organizational crises by examining three real-world cases from different cultural contexts. They will identify underlying leadership theories, decision-making frameworks, and cultural influences that shaped executive responses to demonstrate deep comprehension of advanced leadership principles in practice.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the application of transformational, situational, and authentic leadership theories by analyzing executive decision-making patterns across three documented organizational crises

Students will explain the influence of cultural dimensions (power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individualism-collectivism) on leadership approaches through comparative case study examination and structured discussion protocols
instructions:
Begin by distributing three detailed case studies: Toyota's 2010 recall crisis (Japanese context), Wells Fargo's 2016 fake accounts scandal (American context), and Volkswagen's 2015 emissions scandal (German context).
