Provide each student with a structured analysis template containing sections for stakeholder mapping, decision chronology, leadership theory identification, and cultural factor analysis. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Students work individually to read all three cases and complete preliminary analysis templates, focusing on identifying specific leadership behaviors, stakeholder responses, and decision outcomes. They must document at least 5 specific leadership actions per case with supporting evidence from the text.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member to be the 'expert' on one case plus comparative analysis role. Expert members present their case analysis focusing on leadership theory applications, while the comparative analyst identifies patterns across all three cases related to cultural influences.

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Groups create visual concept maps connecting leadership theories to specific decisions, using different colors to represent cultural influences. Maps must include: decision trees showing alternative paths leaders could have taken, theory labels with specific definitions, and cultural dimension indicators.

Phase 4 (30 minutes): Gallery walk where groups examine other teams' concept maps, adding sticky note questions and observations. Conclude with whole-class discussion synthesizing key insights about how cultural context shapes leadership theory application in crisis situations.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (Toyota 2010, Wells Fargo 2016, Volkswagen 2015) with 8-10 pages each including timeline, stakeholder profiles, and outcome data
Structured analysis templates with sections for leadership theory identification, cultural dimension assessment, and decision evaluation
Large poster paper (11x17 minimum) and colored markers for concept mapping
Sticky notes in three different colors for gallery walk feedback
Leadership theory reference sheets including transformational, situational, authentic, and servant leadership frameworks
Hofstede's cultural dimensions summary cards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership theory identification and application (25%) - must correctly identify at least 2 theories per case with specific behavioral evidence; (2) Depth of cultural analysis (25%) - demonstrates understanding of how cultural dimensions influenced decisions; (3) Quality of comparative connections (25%) - draws meaningful parallels and contrasts across cases; (4) Concept map clarity and theoretical integration (25%) - visually represents complex relationships between theories, decisions, and cultural factors. Students must score 3/4 or higher on each dimension to demonstrate mastery-level understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted case excerpts focusing on key leadership moments, offer sentence starters for analysis templates, and pair with stronger analytical thinkers during group work. Create theory identification checklists with specific behavioral indicators. For advanced learners: Add fourth case study from emerging economy context, require integration of additional leadership theories (complexity leadership, adaptive leadership), and challenge them to develop alternative decision scenarios with predicted outcomes based on different theoretical approaches.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Identifying Response Strategy Misalignments in IT Infrastructure Project
description: Students will analyze a comprehensive risk register from a failed IT infrastructure project to identify misaligned risk response strategies and categorize risks by impact patterns. They will deconstruct the relationship between risk categories, probability-impact ratings, and chosen response strategies to determine critical decision-making flaws.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategy alignments by examining the relationship between risk probability-impact ratings and selected mitigation approaches in a real project scenario
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk categorizations through systematic evaluation of technical, organizational, and external risk factors
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (5 minutes). Distribute the 25-item IT infrastructure project risk register containing deliberately misaligned response strategies. Each team receives the same register showing risks for server migration, network security, and staff training components. Students first individually review the register for 10 minutes, noting initial observations. Teams then systematically analyze each risk entry using the provided analysis framework: 1) Examine risk probability and impact ratings (15 minutes), 2) Evaluate whether the chosen response strategy (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) aligns with the P×I matrix positioning (20 minutes), 3) Identify risks that should be recategorized based on their descriptions and business context (15 minutes), 4) Create a corrected response strategy matrix showing recommended changes (15 minutes). Teams document findings in the structured analysis template, noting specific misalignments and providing justifications for corrections. Each team presents their top 5 critical misalignments to the class (3 minutes per team), explaining their analytical reasoning. Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing team findings and highlighting common analysis patterns (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-designed IT infrastructure project risk register (25 risks with intentional strategy misalignments)
Risk analysis framework handout with P×I matrix guidelines
Structured analysis template worksheet
Whiteboard or flip chart paper for team presentations
Colored pens/markers for matrix creation
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of misalignment identification (25%), (2) Quality of analytical reasoning and justifications (35%), (3) Appropriate use of PMP risk management terminology (20%), (4) Effectiveness of corrected strategy recommendations (20%). Teams must identify at least 15 of 20 planted misalignments and provide sound justification for 80% of their corrections to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed sample analysis of 3 risks before the activity and assign stronger analytical thinkers as team leaders. For advanced learners, add a secondary challenge requiring them to estimate potential cost impacts of the misaligned strategies and calculate risk exposure values. Consider providing additional context about the fictitious company's risk tolerance levels for deeper analysis.

title: Programming Vocabulary Flash Card Memory Challenge
description: Students will create and use flash cards to memorize 20 fundamental programming terms and their definitions. They will practice recall through structured partner activities and complete a final identification quiz to demonstrate their retention of key computer science vocabulary.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the definitions of 20 fundamental programming terms (variable, loop, function, array, string, integer, boolean, algorithm, debugging, syntax, compiler, IDE, object, class, method, parameter, argument, return, conditional, iteration) through flash card practice
Students will identify programming vocabulary terms when given their definitions through verbal and written recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared vocabulary list containing 20 programming terms with definitions. Give students 15 minutes to create physical flash cards using index cards - term on one side, definition on the other. Demonstrate proper card creation with the first term 'variable' as an example. Next, pair students and have them spend 20 minutes using the 'drill and practice' method: Partner A shows the term, Partner B recites the definition from memory, then they switch roles after 10 terms. Circulate to monitor accuracy and pronunciation. After partner practice, conduct a whole-class 'Around the Room' activity for 10 minutes where you show a definition on the projector and students must quickly identify the correct term by raising hands. Call on different students for each term to ensure participation. Finally, administer a 10-minute written quiz where students match 15 randomly selected terms to their definitions. Collect flash cards to review student-created definitions for accuracy. End with a 5-minute reflection where students write down the three terms they found most challenging to remember and explain why.
materials_needed: Index cards (at least 20 per student)
Pre-prepared vocabulary list with 20 programming terms and definitions
Projector or interactive whiteboard
Printed quiz sheets with matching exercise
Pencils or pens for students
assessment_method: Students must score at least 80% (12/15 correct) on the matching quiz to demonstrate successful recall. Additionally, evaluate flash card quality using a 3-point rubric: 3 points for accurate definitions and clear handwriting, 2 points for mostly accurate with minor errors, 1 point for multiple errors or illegible writing. Observe partner practice sessions and award participation points for active engagement and correct verbal responses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-made flash cards with definitions and have them focus on recognition rather than creation. Allow them to use visual cues or mnemonics. For advanced learners, challenge them to create example code snippets or real-world analogies for each term on the back of their cards, and have them explain connections between related terms like 'parameter' and 'argument'.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Matrices for Customer Churn Prediction
description: Students will analyze a pre-calculated correlation matrix from a telecom customer dataset to identify key relationships between customer features and churn behavior. They will interpret correlation coefficients and explain how these relationships inform feature selection decisions for machine learning models.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer features and churn rates by analyzing numerical values and explaining their business significance
Students will classify feature relationships as strong, moderate, or weak correlations through systematic evaluation of correlation matrix values
instructions: Begin by distributing the telecom customer correlation matrix heatmap (15x15 features) showing relationships between variables like monthly_charges, total_charges, contract_length, customer_service_calls, and churn_label. In pairs, students spend 10 minutes examining the matrix to identify the 5 highest positive and 5 highest negative correlations with the churn_label column. Next, provide the correlation interpretation guide: |r| > 0.7 (strong), 0.3-0.7 (moderate), 0.1-0.3 (weak), <0.1 (negligible). Students categorize their identified correlations using this scale and write 2-3 sentence explanations for each relationship's business meaning. For example, if monthly_charges shows r=0.65 with churn, they should explain this indicates customers with higher bills are moderately more likely to leave. After 20 minutes of analysis, facilitate a 15-minute class discussion where each pair shares one surprising correlation they discovered. Students must justify why the relationship makes business sense or propose hypotheses for unexpected correlations. Conclude by having students individually complete a reflection worksheet ranking the top 3 features they would prioritize for a churn prediction model based on correlation strength and business logic, providing written rationale for each choice.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix heatmap (one per pair of students)
Correlation interpretation reference guide handout
Individual reflection worksheet with ranking template
Calculators or access to basic computing tools
assessment_method: Grade individual reflection worksheets using rubric: Accurate correlation classification (30%), Clear business interpretation explanations (40%), Logical feature prioritization with justification (30%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in correlation categorization and provide coherent business explanations to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, highlight 2-3 obvious correlations first and provide sentence starters like 'This correlation suggests that customers who _____ are more/less likely to churn because _____.' For advanced learners, introduce concepts of spurious correlations and ask them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional features that might strengthen weak correlations.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions
description: Students will critically assess three pre-written Python functions that solve the same problem (calculating grade averages) but with different code quality levels. They will apply coding best practices criteria to rank the functions and justify their evaluation with specific evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate Python function quality by applying readability, efficiency, and maintainability criteria to rank three code samples
Students will critique programming solutions through structured comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for code improvements
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Code Evaluation Worksheet containing three Python functions (Function A: clean, well-documented code; Function B: functional but messy; Function C: poor variable names, no comments). Post the evaluation criteria on the board: Readability (variable names, comments), Structure (proper indentation, logical flow), and Functionality (works correctly, handles edge cases).

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each function individually, testing them with the provided sample inputs (normal grades, empty list, grades with decimals). They complete the analysis table, rating each function 1-5 on the three criteria and noting specific examples.

**Ranking Phase (10 minutes):** Students rank the functions from best (1) to worst (3) overall code quality. They must write a 3-sentence justification for their top choice and bottom choice, citing specific code examples.

**Peer Review (8 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss disagreements. They identify at least two specific improvements for the lowest-ranked function.

**Class Discussion (7 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class sharing of rankings with student-provided evidence. Create a class consensus ranking on the board, highlighting the most compelling justifications students provided.

**Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write three key takeaways about what makes code 'good quality' based on their evaluation experience.
materials_needed: Code Evaluation Worksheet with three Python functions
Sample test inputs sheet (3 different grade lists)
Evaluation criteria rubric handout
Access to Python interpreter or online Python compiler
Whiteboard or projection screen
assessment_method: Grade the completed evaluation worksheet using a 4-point rubric: (4) Accurate functionality testing with correct rankings and detailed justifications citing specific code examples; (3) Mostly accurate testing with clear rankings and adequate justifications; (2) Some testing completed with basic rankings but limited justification; (1) Incomplete testing or rankings without supporting evidence. Focus on quality of evidence provided rather than specific ranking choices.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a partially completed analysis table with one function already evaluated as an example. Offer sentence starters for justifications like 'Function X is best because...' and 'The code shows good/poor quality when...' **For advanced students:** Add a fourth, more complex function with subtle issues, or ask them to rewrite the worst function to demonstrate their evaluation criteria in practice.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written Python functions for readability, efficiency, and best practices. They will compare multiple solutions to the same problem and justify which implementation is superior based on established coding standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate Python function implementations by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and adherence to PEP 8 standards
Students will critique multiple coding solutions through systematic comparison using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: Begin by providing students with three different Python functions that solve the same problem: calculating the average of a list of numbers. Function A uses clear variable names and proper spacing, Function B has poor naming and no comments, and Function C includes error handling and documentation. Give students 10 minutes to individually examine each function using the provided evaluation checklist covering: variable naming, code comments, error handling, efficiency, and PEP 8 compliance. Next, have students work in pairs for 15 minutes to discuss their individual assessments and complete a comparison matrix ranking each function from 1-3 in each category. Each pair must then write a 2-paragraph justification explaining which function is best overall and why, citing specific examples from the code. During the final 15 minutes, facilitate a whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their conclusions. Record differing opinions on the board and guide students to understand that evaluation criteria can be weighted differently based on context (beginner readability vs. production efficiency). Conclude by having each student submit their individual evaluation checklist and pair justification as exit tickets.
materials_needed: Three pre-written Python functions solving the same problem (printed handouts)
Code evaluation checklist template (one per student)
Comparison matrix worksheet (one per pair)
Computers with Python interpreter for testing code if needed
assessment_method: Grade based on completion of evaluation checklist (40%), quality of pair justification paragraph with specific code examples (40%), and participation in class discussion (20%). Success criteria: Students identify at least 3 specific differences between functions and provide evidence-based reasoning for their rankings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth simple function first. Highlight one obvious difference between functions to get them started. For advanced learners, ask them to rewrite the worst function to make it better, or provide additional functions with more subtle differences to evaluate.
original_title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner Python Functions

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard for a Fictional SaaS Company
description: Students will create an interactive analytical dashboard that predicts customer churn risk by synthesizing multiple data sources, developing custom metrics, and designing visualizations for executive decision-making. They will construct both the analytical framework and present actionable business recommendations based on their findings.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive churn prediction model by integrating customer usage data, demographic information, and behavioral patterns using statistical analysis techniques
Students will create an interactive dashboard through data visualization tools that communicates risk factors and actionable insights to non-technical stakeholders
instructions: Begin by providing each team (3-4 students) with three CSV datasets: customer_demographics.csv (500 records with age, plan_type, signup_date), usage_metrics.csv (monthly login frequency, feature usage, support tickets), and churn_history.csv (12-month historical churn outcomes). Students start by conducting exploratory data analysis for 30 minutes, identifying data quality issues and potential predictive variables. Next, teams spend 45 minutes cleaning and merging datasets, creating new calculated fields such as 'days_since_last_login', 'support_ticket_trend', and 'feature_adoption_score'. In the third phase (60 minutes), students develop their churn risk scoring methodology by testing correlations between variables and historical churn outcomes, then create risk categories (Low, Medium, High, Critical). During the dashboard creation phase (90 minutes), teams build interactive visualizations showing current customer risk distribution, key risk factors, and drill-down capabilities by customer segment. Students must include at least 5 different chart types and implement filtering functionality. In the final 45 minutes, teams prepare a 5-minute executive presentation explaining their methodology, key findings (minimum 3 actionable insights), and recommended intervention strategies for high-risk customers. Each team presents their dashboard live, demonstrating interactivity and answering questions about their analytical choices. Instructors circulate throughout, providing technical guidance and challenging assumptions about variable selection and business logic.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with realistic SaaS customer data
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop installed on computers
Laptops/computers with Excel or Google Sheets access
Presentation projector and screen
Printed dataset documentation sheets describing variable definitions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration & Cleaning (25 points - accuracy of joins, handling missing data, appropriate calculated fields), Analytical Methodology (25 points - logical risk scoring approach, statistical validity, variable selection rationale), Dashboard Design (25 points - visual clarity, interactivity, appropriate chart selection, professional appearance), Business Communication (25 points - actionable insights, executive-level presentation, clear recommendations, ability to answer methodology questions). Students submit both their dashboard file and a 2-page methodology summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of required calculated fields and suggested chart types; offer pre-written SQL queries for complex joins; pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement predictive modeling using regression analysis; require advanced statistical measures like confidence intervals; ask them to create automated alert systems for new high-risk customers; encourage incorporation of external data sources like industry benchmarks.

title: Leadership Philosophy Deconstruction and Comparative Analysis
description: Students will analyze and compare the underlying philosophical foundations of three distinct leadership approaches through structured case study examination. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying core assumptions, contextual factors, and theoretical underpinnings that drive different leadership behaviors in complex organizational scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, servant, and authentic leadership philosophies by analyzing their foundational principles, key assumptions, and practical applications in real-world scenarios
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership context, organizational culture, and philosophical approach through systematic comparison of case studies
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 (15 minutes setup). Assign each group one of three leadership case studies: a transformational leader managing organizational change, a servant leader in a nonprofit crisis, and an authentic leader navigating ethical dilemmas. Provide each group with their case study packet containing background information, leader quotes, stakeholder perspectives, and outcome data.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Groups conduct deep analysis using the provided Leadership Philosophy Analysis Framework. They must identify: (1) the leader's core beliefs about human nature and motivation, (2) their assumptions about power and influence, (3) their approach to decision-making and stakeholder engagement, and (4) how context shaped their leadership choices. Groups document findings on structured worksheets with specific evidence citations.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Rotate groups through three analysis stations, spending 10 minutes at each. At each station, they examine artifacts (interview transcripts, organizational documents, performance metrics) from the other two leadership cases, taking notes on similarities and differences.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Groups create comparative analysis charts mapping all three leadership approaches across six dimensions: view of followers, source of influence, decision-making style, communication patterns, change approach, and success metrics. They must provide specific textual evidence for each mapping decision.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Gallery walk where groups post their analysis charts and conduct peer review using provided feedback forms focusing on accuracy of philosophical identification and strength of supporting evidence.
materials_needed: Three detailed leadership case study packets (5-7 pages each) with primary source quotes and contextual data
Leadership Philosophy Analysis Framework worksheets
Artifact packets for rotation stations (interview transcripts, policy documents, performance reports)
Large format paper for comparative analysis charts
Colored markers and sticky notes
Peer feedback forms with specific evaluation criteria
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of philosophical identification with specific evidence citations (25%), (2) Depth of comparative analysis showing understanding of nuanced differences (30%), (3) Quality of contextual interpretation linking environment to leadership approach (25%), and (4) Use of discipline-specific terminology and frameworks (20%). Students must demonstrate understanding through written analysis charts and verbal explanations during gallery walk.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a pre-completed example analysis of a fourth leadership case and offer guided questioning prompts at each phase. Create mixed-ability groups pairing stronger analytical thinkers with developing students. For advanced learners, add a synthesis challenge requiring them to design a hybrid leadership approach combining elements from all three philosophies, with justification for when each component would be most effective.

title: Project Schedule Variance Analysis and Risk Impact Assessment
description: Students will analyze a real-world project schedule with multiple critical path delays and budget variances to identify root causes, assess risk impacts, and differentiate between schedule compression techniques. This activity requires students to examine earned value management data and make strategic recommendations for project recovery.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project schedule variances by examining critical path dependencies, resource constraints, and earned value metrics to identify primary delay causes
Students will differentiate between crashing and fast-tracking techniques through comparative analysis of cost-benefit scenarios and risk implications for schedule recovery
instructions:
Step 1 (15 minutes): Distribute the 'TechFlow ERP Implementation' case study packet containing: project network diagram with 25 activities, baseline vs. actual schedule data, earned value report showing SV of -$45K and CV of -$23K, and resource allocation matrix. Students work in teams of 3-4.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Teams analyze the critical path using the provided network diagram, identifying activities currently behind schedule. They must calculate float for non-critical activities and determine which delays are impacting project completion date. Teams document findings on the Analysis Worksheet, specifically identifying: current critical path duration (baseline vs. actual), activities with negative float, and resource over-allocations.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Using the earned value data, teams calculate SPI (Schedule Performance Index) and CPI (Cost Performance Index), then analyze what these metrics reveal about project performance trends. Teams must identify whether delays are due to productivity issues, scope changes, resource constraints, or external dependencies by examining the provided activity status reports.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Teams develop two alternative recovery scenarios: one using crashing techniques and another using fast-tracking. For each scenario, they must analyze: additional costs, new risk exposures, resource requirements, and impact on project quality. Teams complete the 'Recovery Options Matrix' comparing both approaches.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each team presents their analysis findings and recommended recovery approach to the class, justifying their choice based on risk tolerance, budget constraints, and stakeholder priorities. Other teams provide peer feedback using the provided evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: TechFlow ERP Implementation case study packet (network diagram, schedule data, EV report)
Analysis Worksheet template with sections for critical path analysis and variance calculations
Recovery Options Matrix template for comparing crashing vs. fast-tracking scenarios
Calculators or Excel access for EVM calculations
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 100-point rubric: Critical Path Analysis accuracy (25 points), EVM calculations and interpretation (25 points), Root cause identification with supporting evidence (25 points), Recovery scenario analysis showing understanding of crashing vs. fast-tracking trade-offs (25 points). Students must achieve 70% to demonstrate proficiency in schedule analysis techniques.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed critical path diagram and EVM calculation template with formulas pre-populated. Offer a reference sheet with common delay causes and recovery technique definitions. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring Monte Carlo simulation analysis of schedule risks or asking them to develop a communication plan for stakeholders explaining the delay impacts and recovery options.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess conversion path complexity, revenue attribution accuracy, and provide strategic recommendations for optimal model selection based on business objectives and customer journey patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the performance effectiveness of multiple attribution models by analyzing conversion paths, revenue distribution, and channel impact discrepancies in GA4's Model Comparison Tool

Students will critique attribution model limitations through systematic comparison of customer journey data and formulate evidence-based recommendations for model selection aligned with specific business scenarios
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to a GA4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multi-channel conversion paths. Students work in pairs and access Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison tool. **Phase 1 - Data Collection (45 minutes):** Students configure the Model Comparison tool to analyze all five attribution models simultaneously, focusing on: (1) Total conversions and revenue for each model, (2) Channel-specific attribution differences using the 'Conversion paths' dimension, (3) Time-to-conversion patterns in the 'Path length' report. They must document numerical differences between models, identify which channels gain/lose attribution under each model, and screenshot key discrepancies. **Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (60 minutes):** Students create a comparative analysis matrix evaluating each model against criteria: accuracy for long vs. short conversion cycles, alignment with assisted vs. direct conversions, representation of upper/middle/lower funnel activities, and bias toward specific channel types. They must identify scenarios where each model fails to represent true customer behavior. **Phase 3 - Business Context Evaluation (30 minutes):** Present three business scenarios: (A) SaaS company with 45-day consideration cycles, (B) Fashion retailer with seasonal campaigns, (C) B2B services with committee-based decisions. Students must evaluate which attribution model best serves each scenario's strategic needs. **Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (30 minutes):** Students prepare a formal recommendation report including: selected attribution model with justification, identified limitations and mitigation strategies, implementation timeline, and success metrics for model performance monitoring.
materials_needed: GA4 property with minimum 6 months e-commerce data including multi-channel conversion paths
Google Sheets template for attribution model comparison matrix
Business scenario case study documents (3 different company profiles)
Access to GA4 Model Comparison tool with Editor permissions
assessment_method: Students submit a 3-page strategic recommendation report evaluated on: (1) Quantitative analysis accuracy - correct identification of attribution differences with supporting data (25 points), (2) Critical evaluation depth - thorough assessment of each model's strengths/weaknesses with specific examples (30 points), (3) Business alignment - logical connection between model selection and business scenario requirements (25 points), (4) Implementation feasibility - realistic timeline and success metrics (20 points). Peer evaluation component where pairs critique another team's recommendations using provided rubric.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide pre-filled comparison matrix templates with guided questions, offer model-specific analysis checklists, and create step-by-step GA4 navigation guides with screenshots. **Advanced extension:** Challenge advanced learners to incorporate Google Analytics Intelligence API data, evaluate custom attribution models using machine learning insights, or develop attribution model A/B testing frameworks with statistical significance calculations.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model performance against business objectives, and present strategic recommendations for optimal attribution model selection.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of six different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies in Google Analytics 4
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis and justify optimal model selection based on specific business scenarios and customer journey complexity
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to Google Analytics 4 demo account or real e-commerce data with minimum 3-month transaction history. Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team receives a different business scenario (subscription service, seasonal retailer, B2B software, luxury goods). **Phase 1 - Data Collection (45 minutes):** Students navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison. They extract conversion and revenue data for all six attribution models, focusing on: assisted conversions, conversion lag time, path length distribution, and channel performance variations. Teams document findings in provided spreadsheet template with screenshots. **Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (60 minutes):** Using collected data, students calculate percentage differences between models, identify channels most affected by model choice, and map findings to customer journey characteristics. They research industry benchmarks and compare their data against established conversion path patterns. **Phase 3 - Business Impact Assessment (45 minutes):** Teams evaluate how each attribution model aligns with their assigned business scenario's objectives, budget allocation needs, and customer behavior patterns. They assess potential budget redistribution impacts and ROI implications. **Phase 4 - Strategic Recommendation (30 minutes):** Students prepare 10-minute presentations defending their recommended attribution model choice, including implementation timeline, expected challenges, and success metrics. They must address counterarguments and alternative approaches.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 access (demo account or real data with 3+ months history)
Attribution analysis spreadsheet template with calculation formulas
Business scenario descriptions (4 different e-commerce types)
Industry benchmark data sheets for attribution models
Presentation template with evaluation criteria sections
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Data collection accuracy and completeness (25 points), analytical depth and model comparison quality (30 points), business scenario alignment and strategic thinking (25 points), presentation quality and defense of recommendations (20 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of attribution limitations, provide quantitative justification for choices, and address implementation feasibility.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided analysis worksheets with specific questions for each attribution model, offer one-on-one data interpretation sessions, and create simplified business scenarios. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution modeling challenges, require integration with Google Ads data, add cross-platform attribution considerations, or request development of hybrid attribution approaches with weighted model combinations.
original_title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce Google Analytics data. They will analyze conversion paths, assess each model's impact on channel performance metrics, and provide strategic recommendations for optimal budget allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five attribution models by comparing conversion credit distribution and ROI calculations across paid search, display, email, and social channels
Students will critique attribution model limitations through multi-touch conversion path analysis and recommend the most appropriate model for specific business scenarios
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Students first spend 15 minutes exploring the Multi-Channel Funnels reports to understand the conversion landscape. Next, teams navigate to Attribution > Model Comparison Tool and systematically analyze each attribution model over the past 90 days. For each model, students must document: (1) total conversions attributed to each channel, (2) conversion value per channel, (3) cost-per-acquisition changes, and (4) ROAS variations. Teams create a comparative matrix showing percentage differences between models for each metric. In the analysis phase (45 minutes), students examine specific conversion paths in the Top Conversion Paths report, identifying patterns where attribution models show significant disagreement. They must select 5 high-value conversion paths and trace how each attribution model assigns credit differently. Students then research the business context (seasonal campaigns, product launches, promotional periods) that might explain conversion patterns. For evaluation, teams spend 30 minutes developing weighted criteria for model selection, considering factors like business goals, campaign types, customer journey length, and data availability. Finally, each team prepares a 10-minute presentation recommending one primary attribution model and one secondary model for different scenarios, supported by quantitative evidence and qualitative reasoning about customer behavior implications.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account access with Enhanced Ecommerce enabled
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data comparison matrix
Campaign context document with promotional calendar and business objectives
Attribution model evaluation worksheet template
Presentation software (PowerPoint/Google Slides)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct extraction and calculation of attribution metrics; Critical Evaluation (30 points) - depth of analysis comparing model strengths/weaknesses with specific examples; Strategic Reasoning (25 points) - logical connection between business context and model recommendations; Presentation Quality (20 points) - clear communication of findings and actionable recommendations. Students must achieve 80+ points demonstrating mastery-level evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each attribution model analysis step. Create checkpoint reviews after data collection and analysis phases. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources (Google Ads, Facebook Ads) to evaluate cross-platform attribution discrepancies, or analyze attribution model performance across different product categories or customer segments within the same dataset.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Infrastructure with SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network solution spanning three geographical sites with headquarters, branch office, and data center locations. They will integrate software-defined WAN (SD-WAN) technology, implement advanced routing protocols, and establish comprehensive security policies while ensuring high availability and optimal performance across the infrastructure.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by integrating OSPF, BGP, and SD-WAN technologies to meet specific business requirements
Students will create comprehensive network security policies through implementation of advanced firewall rules, VPN configurations, and network segmentation strategies
Students will develop network monitoring and troubleshooting procedures by establishing SNMP monitoring, configuring syslog servers, and creating automated backup solutions
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Design and Planning**
Students work in teams of 2-3 to analyze the provided business scenario: a financial services company requiring connectivity between New York HQ (500 users), Chicago branch (150 users), and Dallas data center (50 servers). Begin by creating detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets from 10.0.0.0/16, VLAN assignments (Management: VLAN 10, Users: VLAN 20, Servers: VLAN 30, Guest: VLAN 40), and equipment placement. Document bandwidth requirements (HQ-DC: 1Gbps, HQ-Branch: 100Mbps) and redundancy needs.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Core Infrastructure Implementation**
Configure three Cisco ISR 4000 series routers as site gateways, implementing OSPF Area 0 for internal routing and eBGP (AS 65001-65003) for inter-site communication. Set up Cisco Catalyst 9300 switches at each site with trunk ports, access ports, and spanning tree protocol. Configure VLANs and inter-VLAN routing using SVIs. Establish primary and backup WAN connections using MPLS and broadband internet.

**Phase 3 (75 minutes): SD-WAN and Security Implementation**
Deploy Cisco vEdge routers running SD-WAN software, creating overlay tunnels between sites with dynamic path selection based on application requirements. Configure traffic policies prioritizing voice (CoS 5), video conferencing (CoS 4), and business-critical applications (CoS 3). Implement site-to-site IPSec VPN tunnels with AES-256 encryption and establish clientless SSL VPN access for remote users. Configure zone-based firewalls with DMZ, Inside, and Outside security zones.

**Phase 4 (45 minutes): Monitoring and Documentation**
Set up SNMP v3 monitoring targeting CPU utilization, interface statistics, and memory usage. Configure centralized syslog server collecting logs from all network devices. Create automated configuration backup scripts running daily. Document all configurations, create network topology diagrams, and prepare troubleshooting runbooks with common scenarios and resolution steps.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer Advanced version or EVE-NG with Cisco IOS images
Business scenario documentation with requirements specification
Network diagramming software (Visio, Draw.io, or Lucidchart)
Configuration templates for ISR 4000, Catalyst 9300, and vEdge devices
IP addressing worksheets and VLAN planning templates
Security policy template documents
assessment_method: Evaluate using comprehensive rubric: Network Design (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, equipment selection appropriateness; Implementation (35 points) - configuration correctness, protocol convergence, connectivity testing results; Security (20 points) - firewall rule effectiveness, VPN functionality, access control implementation; Documentation (20 points) - diagram completeness, configuration backup procedures, troubleshooting guide quality. Students must demonstrate full end-to-end connectivity, successful failover scenarios, and present their solution defending design decisions to instructor panel.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with partial configurations, offer guided configuration checklists for each protocol, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create troubleshooting flowcharts for common connectivity issues. For advanced learners: Add requirements for QoS implementation with custom traffic classes, integration of wireless controllers with centralized authentication, implementation of network automation using Python scripts, and advanced security features like intrusion prevention systems and network access control.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Infrastructure with SD-WAN Integration: Exercise 1
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using traditional WAN and SD-WAN technologies. They will create original network designs, implement advanced routing protocols, configure security policies, and establish redundant connectivity while documenting their custom solution architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, BGP, and EIGRP routing protocols by designing a hierarchical network topology that optimizes traffic flow across multiple autonomous systems
Students will construct an original SD-WAN solution through hands-on configuration of Cisco vEdge routers and vManage orchestration platform
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Architecture Design (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 2-3. Each team receives a fictional company scenario with three sites: headquarters (500 users), branch office (150 users), and data center (50 servers). Students must create original network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes, VLAN segmentation, and routing protocol selection. Teams document bandwidth requirements, redundancy paths, and security zones.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using Cisco ISR 4000 series routers and Catalyst 9300 switches, teams build their designed topology. Configure OSPF as the IGP for intra-site routing, establish eBGP peering between sites, and implement HSRP for gateway redundancy. Set up VLANs 10 (Users), 20 (Servers), 30 (Management) with appropriate inter-VLAN routing. Configure access control lists restricting server VLAN access to specific protocols only.

**Phase 3: SD-WAN Integration (75 minutes)**
Deploy Cisco SD-WAN solution using vEdge 1000 routers. Configure vManage controller with custom policies prioritizing voice traffic over MPLS links and data traffic over internet connections. Establish IPsec tunnels between all sites, implement application-aware routing policies, and configure centralized security policies. Create custom SLA classes monitoring latency, jitter, and packet loss.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (30 minutes)**
Execute comprehensive testing including failover scenarios, traffic prioritization verification, and security policy validation. Document configuration commands, network diagrams, and troubleshooting procedures in a professional network implementation guide.
materials_needed: 6x Cisco ISR 4331 routers with security license
9x Cisco Catalyst 9300-24P switches
3x Cisco vEdge 1000 routers
Cisco SD-WAN vManage controller (VM)
Cisco Packet Tracer software
Console cables and laptops for each team
Pre-configured MPLS simulation environment
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: Network Design Originality (25%) - innovative topology solutions and justified technology choices; Technical Implementation (35%) - successful configuration of all protocols with zero downtime during failover testing; SD-WAN Integration (25%) - functional policy-based routing with measurable QoS improvements; Professional Documentation (15%) - complete configuration backup, network diagrams, and troubleshooting guide meeting industry standards. Students must demonstrate live network functionality and explain design decisions during 10-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic OSPF configuration and simplified SD-WAN policies. Offer guided worksheets with specific CLI commands and configuration checkpoints. For advanced learners: Challenge them to integrate additional technologies like DMVPN, implement zero-touch provisioning, or design disaster recovery procedures. Encourage exploration of automation using Python scripts for configuration deployment.
original_title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Infrastructure with SD-WAN Integration

title: Portfolio Optimization Using Linear Programming: Real Estate Investment Analysis
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a complex real estate investment portfolio optimization problem with multiple constraints. They will formulate objective functions, identify feasible regions, and use the simplex method to determine optimal investment allocations across different property types.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve multi-variable optimization problems by formulating constraints and objective functions from real-world scenarios
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal solutions through systematic mathematical analysis of feasible regions
instructions:
Step 1 (15 minutes): Distribute the Real Estate Investment Scenario handout. Students work in pairs to analyze a case where they must allocate $2 million across residential properties (R), commercial properties (C), and industrial properties (I) with constraints: R + C + I ≤ 2000 (budget in thousands), R ≥ 400 (minimum residential requirement), C ≤ 800 (commercial limit due to market saturation), I ≥ 200 (industrial minimum), and R + I ≥ 1000 (combined residential/industrial requirement). The objective function maximizes monthly rental income: 12R + 18C + 15I.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students identify and write all constraints in standard form, then plot the feasible region on provided coordinate planes. They must clearly label all constraint lines, identify corner points, and shade the feasible region accurately.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Using the corner point method, students evaluate the objective function at each vertex of the feasible region. They must show all calculations explicitly and create a comparison table of corner points versus objective function values.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students verify their graphical solution using the simplex method tableau, completing at least two iterations to demonstrate understanding of pivot operations and optimality conditions.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present their optimal investment allocation to the class, justifying their mathematical approach and interpreting the economic meaning of their solution, including shadow prices for binding constraints.
materials_needed: Real Estate Investment Scenario handout with specific numerical constraints
Graph paper with pre-drawn coordinate axes (scale 0-2000)
Scientific calculators
Simplex method tableau worksheets
Colored pencils for constraint line identification
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct constraint formulation and feasible region identification (25%), (2) Accurate corner point calculations and objective function evaluation (35%), (3) Proper simplex method implementation with correct pivot operations (25%), (4) Clear interpretation of optimal solution with economic reasoning (15%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in mathematical calculations and demonstrate understanding of when solutions are optimal.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates and pre-calculated first simplex tableau. Offer graphing assistance by providing constraint equations in slope-intercept form. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking them to determine how changes in rental rates affect optimal allocation, or add integer constraints requiring whole numbers of properties.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Electromagnetic Wave Interference Patterns in Thin Film Coatings
description: Students will analyze complex interference patterns produced by electromagnetic waves in multi-layered thin film systems to determine optimal coating thickness for specific optical applications. They will decompose the wave interactions at each interface and synthesize their findings to predict anti-reflective coating performance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the phase relationships and amplitude changes of electromagnetic waves at multiple interfaces by calculating reflection and transmission coefficients for each boundary
Students will decompose complex interference patterns through mathematical modeling to determine how film thickness, refractive index, and wavelength affect overall reflectance
instructions:
Step 1 (15 min): Provide student teams of 3-4 with experimental reflectance vs. wavelength data for three different thin film coating systems: single-layer MgF₂, double-layer MgF₂/ZnS, and triple-layer TiO₂/SiO₂/MgF₂ on glass substrates. Each dataset shows reflectance curves from 400-700nm wavelength range.

Step 2 (25 min): Students analyze the interference minima and maxima positions in each dataset. They must identify the relationship between film thickness and destructive interference conditions using the equation 2nt cos θ = mλ, where n is refractive index, t is thickness, θ is refraction angle, m is interference order, and λ is wavelength. Students calculate individual layer thicknesses from the interference patterns.

Step 3 (30 min): Using provided refractive index values (MgF₂: 1.38, ZnS: 2.35, SiO₂: 1.46, TiO₂: 2.4), students apply the matrix method to model wave propagation through each multilayer system. They calculate the characteristic matrices for each layer and multiply them to find total system reflectance at 550nm wavelength.

Step 4 (20 min): Students analyze how each additional layer contributes to overall anti-reflective performance by comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data. They must identify which wavelengths show optimal interference (minimum reflectance) and explain the physical mechanisms causing broader spectral coverage in multilayer systems.

Step 5 (15 min): Teams present their analysis of one coating system, explaining how layer sequence and thickness ratios create specific interference conditions for different wavelength ranges.
materials_needed: Experimental reflectance vs. wavelength datasets (3 different coating systems)
Scientific calculators or MATLAB/Python access
Refractive index reference table for coating materials
Graph paper or plotting software
Matrix multiplication reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of thickness calculations from interference patterns (25%), (2) Correct application of matrix method for multilayer analysis (30%), (3) Quality of physical explanation connecting layer properties to interference behavior (25%), (4) Analysis of experimental vs. theoretical agreement and identification of discrepancies (20%). Students must show all mathematical work and provide written explanations for each calculated value.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step matrix multiplication examples and pre-calculated values for the first layer. Offer guided questions like 'What happens to wave phase when n₂ > n₁?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to optimize coating design for specific applications (e.g., solar cells, camera lenses) or analyze the effects of non-normal incidence angles on coating performance.

title: Evaluating Code Quality: Debugging and Refactoring Assessment
description: Students will analyze three provided code samples with intentional bugs and poor practices, evaluate their quality using a structured checklist, and justify which code requires the most urgent attention. This activity develops critical thinking skills for identifying problematic code patterns and prioritizing fixes in real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by systematically applying readability, functionality, and maintainability criteria to identify critical issues
Students will assess the relative severity of programming problems through comparative analysis and evidence-based reasoning
instructions: Begin by distributing three code samples (Sample A: basic calculator with logic errors, Sample B: user registration form with security vulnerabilities, Sample C: data sorting function with performance issues). Give students 5 minutes to read through all samples without making changes. Provide the evaluation checklist covering: syntax errors, logical correctness, security considerations, code readability, performance efficiency, and maintainability. Students work individually for 20 minutes, scoring each code sample (1-5 scale) on all criteria and documenting specific issues found. Next, students write a 3-paragraph analysis: paragraph 1 summarizes findings for each sample, paragraph 2 compares the three samples identifying the most problematic, paragraph 3 justifies their ranking with specific evidence from the code. Form groups of 3-4 students for 15 minutes to discuss their evaluations and reach consensus on which code needs immediate attention. Each group creates a prioritized action plan listing the top 5 fixes across all samples. Groups present their findings in 3-minute presentations, explaining their reasoning and defending their prioritization choices. Conclude with a class discussion comparing different groups' evaluations and the reasoning behind their decisions.
materials_needed: Three printed code samples with intentional flaws (Python or Java)
Code quality evaluation checklist handout
Presentation timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or flip chart for group presentations
assessment_method: Grade based on: individual evaluation accuracy (40% - correct identification of major issues), written analysis quality (35% - clear reasoning and evidence), group presentation effectiveness (25% - logical prioritization and defense of choices). Use rubric: Excellent (identifies 80%+ issues, provides detailed justification), Good (identifies 60-79% issues, adequate reasoning), Needs Improvement (identifies <60% issues, weak justification).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional examples of each evaluation criteria before starting, allow pair work during individual analysis phase. For advanced learners: add a fourth code sample with subtle architectural issues, require them to suggest specific refactoring solutions rather than just identifying problems, have them research and propose alternative algorithms for performance issues.

title: Design and Build a Real Estate Investment Dashboard from Scratch
description: Students will create an interactive data analysis dashboard to evaluate residential property investments using real market data. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design custom visualizations, and develop actionable investment recommendations with supporting analytical frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize property listing data, demographic information, and market trends by designing an integrated analytical framework that identifies optimal investment opportunities
Students will construct interactive visualizations and automated decision-support tools through dashboard development that enables dynamic property comparison and risk assessment
instructions: **Phase 1 (30 minutes): Data Architecture Design** - Provide each team of 3-4 students with three datasets: property listings (500+ homes with price, size, location), neighborhood demographics (income, population, schools), and 5-year market trends (price appreciation, rental rates). Students sketch their dashboard layout on paper, identifying 5-7 key metrics they'll track and how datasets will connect. **Phase 2 (45 minutes): Data Integration & Cleaning** - Teams import datasets into their chosen platform and create merged datasets. They must identify and resolve at least 3 data quality issues (missing values, inconsistent formatting, outliers) and document their cleaning decisions. **Phase 3 (60 minutes): Custom Analytics Creation** - Students develop 3 original calculated metrics (e.g., price-per-square-foot ratios, neighborhood appreciation scores, rental yield predictions) and create algorithms to rank properties. They must justify their mathematical approaches and weight different factors. **Phase 4 (45 minutes): Interactive Dashboard Assembly** - Teams build their dashboard with minimum requirements: 4 different chart types, 2 interactive filters, 1 map visualization, and 1 summary scorecard. Each visualization must tell part of their investment story. **Phase 5 (30 minutes): Decision Framework Implementation** - Students create an automated recommendation engine within their dashboard that flags top 10 investment opportunities based on their custom scoring system, including risk assessments and expected ROI calculations.
materials_needed: Curated real estate dataset (CSV format) with 500+ property listings including price, square footage, bedrooms, location coordinates
Demographics dataset with zip code-level income, education, and population data
Historical market trends dataset with 5-year price and rental data by neighborhood
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software access for each student team
Laptop computers with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across 5 dimensions: (1) Data Integration Quality - accuracy of joins and data cleaning documentation, (2) Analytical Innovation - originality and mathematical soundness of custom metrics, (3) Dashboard Design - visual clarity, interactivity, and user experience, (4) Investment Logic - coherence of recommendation framework and risk assessment, (5) Technical Implementation - functionality of filters, calculations, and automated features. Each team presents 10-minute dashboard demonstrations with Q&A. Final deliverable includes dashboard file, data dictionary, and 2-page methodology report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written SQL queries for common data joins and a template dashboard structure with placeholder charts. Offer guided worksheets for calculating basic real estate metrics like cap rates and price appreciation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external APIs (school ratings, crime data, economic indicators), implement machine learning prediction models within their dashboard, or create mobile-responsive versions. Provide access to additional datasets like property tax records or zoning information.

title: PMBOK Guide Knowledge Area Artifact Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall specific project management artifacts, templates, and deliverables associated with each of the ten PMBOK Guide knowledge areas. Through a timed identification exercise, they will demonstrate mastery of 150+ standard project management documents and their correct knowledge area classifications.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the complete list of 47 project management processes and identify their corresponding knowledge areas within 90 seconds per process
Students will memorize and list a minimum of 15 specific artifacts, templates, or deliverables for each of the ten PMBOK knowledge areas through rapid-fire recall exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared artifact reference sheets containing 150 project management documents (15 per knowledge area). Give students 45 minutes to study and memorize the associations using any method they prefer. After study time, collect all materials. Conduct Round 1: Display 50 randomly selected artifact names on slides, showing each for 15 seconds. Students write the correct knowledge area on their answer sheet. Conduct Round 2: Call out knowledge area names and give students 60 seconds to write down as many associated artifacts as they can recall from memory. Rotate through all 10 knowledge areas. Conduct Round 3: Present 25 real project scenarios (e.g., 'The project manager needs to document lessons learned from a failed vendor relationship'). Students must identify which specific artifact should be used and its knowledge area within 30 seconds per scenario. After each round, provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers. Students self-score using the provided answer key. Record individual scores on the class tracking sheet. Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where students identify their weakest knowledge areas and plan targeted review strategies for missed items.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared artifact reference sheets (10 knowledge areas × 15 artifacts each)
PowerPoint slides with 50 random artifact names for Round 1
Timer/stopwatch visible to all students
Answer sheets with numbered lines for each round
Complete answer key with all correct associations
25 realistic project scenario cards for Round 3
Individual score tracking sheets for each student
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (120/150 correct) across all three rounds combined to demonstrate mastery. Round 1: 2 points per correct knowledge area identification (100 points possible). Round 2: 1 point per correctly recalled artifact (150 points possible). Round 3: 3 points per scenario (artifact + knowledge area both correct, 75 points possible). Total possible: 325 points. Mastery threshold: 260 points (80%). Track individual knowledge area weaknesses for remediation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded reference sheets where each knowledge area has a distinct color, reduce initial memorization load to 10 artifacts per area, and allow note cards during Round 1 only. For advanced learners: Include 25 additional PRINCE2 and Agile framework artifacts, require them to identify overlapping artifacts between knowledge areas, and challenge them to explain why certain artifacts belong to specific knowledge areas during the reflection period.

title: Decoding Leadership Styles Through Crisis Decision Analysis
description: Students will analyze authentic crisis decision-making scenarios from Fortune 500 CEOs to identify and differentiate between transformational, transactional, and servant leadership approaches. They will examine the underlying motivations, communication patterns, and decision-making frameworks that characterize each leadership style.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational, transactional, and servant leadership styles by analyzing real CEO crisis responses and identifying specific behavioral indicators
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership philosophy and decision-making outcomes through systematic case study examination
instructions: Begin by distributing three anonymized crisis scenario packets (20 minutes setup). Each packet contains: CEO's actual email to employees, board meeting transcript excerpts, media interview clips, and subsequent company performance data. Divide students into groups of 4, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (coordinates discussion), Evidence Collector (tracks specific quotes/behaviors), Style Identifier (matches behaviors to leadership theories), and Outcome Evaluator (analyzes results). Groups spend 45 minutes analyzing their assigned scenario using the provided Leadership Style Matrix worksheet, which requires them to: (1) identify 8-10 specific leader behaviors/statements, (2) categorize each behavior according to leadership theory characteristics, (3) determine the dominant leadership style with supporting evidence, (4) predict outcomes based on style-situation alignment. After analysis, conduct structured rotations where each group presents their findings to two other groups (15 minutes per presentation, 45 minutes total). During presentations, listening groups must complete a Peer Analysis Form identifying areas of agreement/disagreement with the presenting group's style classification. Conclude with a 30-minute whole-class debrief where groups reveal the actual CEO identities and compare their analyses to documented leadership assessments of these leaders. Students must justify any discrepancies between their analysis and established leadership profiles.
materials_needed: Three anonymized CEO crisis scenario packets with supporting documents
Leadership Style Matrix worksheet with behavioral indicators checklist
Peer Analysis Forms for cross-group evaluation
Timer for structured rotations
Whiteboard or digital display for final reveal and comparison
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Style Matrix worksheets using 4-point rubric: Evidence Quality (specific, relevant behavioral examples cited), Theoretical Application (accurate matching of behaviors to leadership styles), Justification Depth (logical reasoning connecting evidence to conclusions), and Peer Interaction (quality of questions and feedback during rotations). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category and correctly identify the dominant leadership style with minimum 6 supporting evidence points.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with a pre-filled example analysis of a fourth scenario and highlighted key behavioral indicators reference sheet. For advanced learners, add a synthesis component requiring them to design hybrid leadership approaches combining elements from multiple styles, or analyze how cultural context might influence leadership style effectiveness in each scenario.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Compound Pendulum System with Damping
description: Students will decompose the complex motion of a physical pendulum into its constituent energy components and analyze how different damping mechanisms affect energy transformation rates. They will create detailed energy flow diagrams and quantitatively compare theoretical predictions with experimental data to identify sources of energy dissipation.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interconversion between gravitational potential, rotational kinetic, and translational kinetic energy in a compound pendulum by constructing mathematical models and energy-time graphs
Students will examine the relationship between damping coefficients and energy dissipation rates through systematic comparison of experimental data with theoretical decay models
instructions:
Begin by setting up three identical compound pendulums (meter sticks with masses attached at different positions) with varying damping conditions: air resistance only, magnetic eddy current damping, and friction damping at the pivot. Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team analyzing one pendulum system for 20 minutes, then rotating to compare systems. 

For each system, students first measure physical parameters: moment of inertia (calculated from mass distribution), center of mass location, and damping coefficient (from preliminary free oscillation tests). Using motion sensors and data acquisition software, they record angular position, velocity, and acceleration for 10 complete oscillation cycles.

Next, students calculate instantaneous energy values at 0.1-second intervals: gravitational potential energy (mgh relative to lowest point), rotational kinetic energy (½Iω²), and total mechanical energy. They create detailed spreadsheets showing energy transformations and plot energy vs. time graphs for each component.

Students then analyze energy dissipation patterns by fitting exponential decay curves to total energy data, extracting decay constants, and comparing with theoretical predictions based on damping type. They identify discrepancies between measured and predicted values, hypothesizing about additional energy loss mechanisms.

Finally, teams create comprehensive energy flow diagrams showing quantitative energy transfers, including percentages lost to each damping mechanism. They present 5-minute analyses comparing all three systems, explaining why different damping types produce different energy decay patterns and identifying which theoretical model best fits each experimental condition.
materials_needed: Three meter sticks with adjustable mass clamps
Magnetic damping apparatus with adjustable field strength
Friction damping pivot with adjustable tension
Rotary motion sensors with 0.1° resolution
Data acquisition software (LabVIEW or equivalent)
Digital scales accurate to 0.1g
Stopwatches
Graphing software (Excel with curve-fitting capability)
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of energy calculations and mathematical modeling (25%), (2) Quality of energy flow diagrams with correct quantitative relationships (25%), (3) Depth of analysis comparing experimental data to theoretical predictions with specific explanations for discrepancies (30%), (4) Clarity of presentation demonstrating understanding of energy transformation principles across different damping conditions (20%). Students must achieve level 3 or higher in at least 3 categories to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated moment of inertia values and energy calculation templates. Offer guided practice in curve-fitting techniques before the main activity. For advanced learners, challenge them to derive damping coefficients from first principles, incorporate temperature effects on air resistance, or analyze nonlinear damping behaviors. Provide additional pendulum configurations (different mass distributions) for extended investigation.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Compound Pendulum System with Damping: Comparative Study
description: Students will decompose the complex motion of a physical pendulum with air resistance into its constituent energy components and analyze how energy flows between kinetic, potential, and dissipated forms. They will use experimental data and theoretical models to identify discrepancies and evaluate the validity of different damping models.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the energy transformation pathways in a damped physical pendulum by separating rotational kinetic, gravitational potential, and dissipated energy components from experimental motion data
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different damping models (linear vs. quadratic air resistance) through systematic comparison of predicted versus observed energy dissipation rates
instructions: **Phase 1 (15 min):** Set up the physical pendulum using a uniform rod suspended at a point 1/4 of its length from one end. Install motion sensors to record angular position vs. time. Students work in teams of 3-4, with roles assigned: data collector, theoretical calculator, graph analyst, and model evaluator. **Phase 2 (20 min):** Release the pendulum from 45° and record motion for 60 seconds. Simultaneously, students calculate theoretical values assuming no damping, linear damping (F = -bv), and quadratic damping (F = -cv²). Use the rod's measured mass (0.5 kg), length (1 m), and moment of inertia to establish baseline energy calculations. **Phase 3 (30 min):** Students analyze the experimental data by plotting total mechanical energy vs. time and identifying the rate of energy loss. They must separate the instantaneous energy into: rotational kinetic energy (½Iω²), gravitational potential energy (mgh where h depends on angular position), and cumulative dissipated energy (initial total energy minus current total energy). **Phase 4 (25 min):** Compare experimental energy dissipation curves with predictions from both damping models. Students must identify which segments of the motion (large vs. small amplitude oscillations) better fit each model and explain the physical reasons for discrepancies. They create overlay graphs showing experimental data, linear model predictions, and quadratic model predictions. **Phase 5 (10 min):** Teams present their analysis conclusions, specifically addressing: at what amplitude does the damping transition from quadratic-dominated to linear-dominated behavior, and what percentage of initial energy remains after 10 oscillations compared to theoretical predictions.
materials_needed: Uniform metal rod (1 meter length, 0.5 kg mass)
Adjustable suspension clamp with low-friction bearing
Digital motion sensor or smartphone with gyroscope app
Computer with data analysis software (Excel or Python)
Protractor for initial angle measurement
Stopwatch
Digital scale for mass verification
assessment_method: Students submit a comprehensive analysis report including: (1) Correctly calculated theoretical energy values for all three models with proper equations (25 points), (2) Accurate experimental energy separation graphs with labeled axes and uncertainty bars (25 points), (3) Quantitative comparison between models using R² correlation values or chi-squared analysis (25 points), (4) Physics-based explanation of when and why each damping model applies, supported by experimental evidence (25 points).
