Success requires achieving >80% accuracy in energy calculations and demonstrating clear understanding of model limitations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated moment of inertia formulas and energy equation templates. Offer guided practice with simpler systems (mass on spring) first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate bearing friction as an additional damping mechanism, or analyze how pendulum bob shape affects air resistance coefficients. Provide access to curve-fitting algorithms to determine optimal damping coefficients.
original_title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Compound Pendulum System with Damping

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Tracker Application Implementations
description: Students will critically evaluate two different implementations of a simple bug tracking application by analyzing code quality, functionality, and design decisions. They will create detailed evaluation reports comparing the strengths and weaknesses of each solution and recommend which implementation should be adopted for production use.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality and functionality by systematically analyzing two bug tracker implementations against established criteria
Students will judge the relative merits of different programming approaches through structured comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by distributing the evaluation materials and forming pairs (10 minutes). Each pair receives two working implementations of a bug tracker application: Implementation A (uses basic HTML forms with JavaScript validation) and Implementation B (uses a simple Python Flask backend with HTML frontend). Provide students with the evaluation criteria checklist covering: code readability, functionality completeness, error handling, user experience, and maintainability.

Students spend 45 minutes examining both implementations. They must run each application, test core features (add bug, view bugs, mark as resolved), and review the source code. They document their findings using the provided evaluation worksheet, noting specific examples and evidence for each criterion.

Next, pairs spend 30 minutes creating a comparison matrix scoring each implementation (1-5 scale) on the five criteria. They must justify each score with specific code examples or functionality observations. Students then write a 300-word recommendation report stating which implementation they would choose for production use and why.

Conclude with 15-minute pair presentations where each team shares their recommendation and key supporting evidence. Other students ask clarifying questions about the evaluation process and reasoning. Instructor facilitates discussion about different evaluation outcomes and the importance of systematic assessment in software development decisions.
materials_needed: Two pre-built bug tracker applications (Implementation A: HTML/JavaScript, Implementation B: Python Flask)
Code evaluation criteria checklist
Evaluation worksheet templates
Comparison matrix template
Computers with web browsers and Python installed
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Thoroughness of code analysis with specific examples, (2) Quality of comparative reasoning with evidence, (3) Clarity and logic of final recommendation, (4) Appropriate use of evaluation criteria. Students submit completed worksheets, comparison matrices, and recommendation reports. Peer feedback forms completed during presentations provide additional assessment data.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guided questions for each evaluation criterion and sentence starters for the recommendation report. Pair stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners, add security assessment criteria and ask them to identify specific code improvements for the weaker implementation. Provide code commenting guides for students unfamiliar with reading others' code.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework and Methodology Recall Challenge
description: Students will systematically recall and match complex project management frameworks, methodologies, and their specific components through a timed, multi-stage identification exercise. This activity tests retention of advanced PM knowledge including Agile ceremonies, risk management processes, and quality assurance frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately identify and recall specific components of advanced project management frameworks (PRINCE2, PMI, Agile, Lean Six Sigma) by matching methodology elements to their correct framework within 90% accuracy
Students will demonstrate recall of complex project management terminology and processes through rapid-fire identification exercises covering 50+ advanced concepts
instructions: Begin by distributing the prepared card sets to each student - one deck contains 60 project management concept cards (blue), another contains 60 definition/process cards (yellow). Students have 3 minutes to review all cards without matching. Remove cards and project the first slide showing 15 scrambled PM concepts (e.g., 'Sprint Retrospective,' 'RACI Matrix,' 'Monte Carlo Analysis,' 'Ishikawa Diagram'). Students write the correct methodology/framework for each concept in 4 minutes. Next, display 20 partial process descriptions (e.g., 'This ceremony occurs at the end of each iteration to reflect on team performance...'). Students must complete the process name and identify which framework it belongs to in 5 minutes. For the third round, show 15 advanced acronyms (e.g., 'DMAIC,' 'ITIL,' 'SCRUM') and students recall the full expansion plus primary application in 3 minutes. Finally, conduct a rapid-fire oral round where you read 20 definitions aloud, and students write only the specific term being defined in 30 seconds each. Collect all response sheets immediately after each round. No collaboration or reference materials permitted. Provide immediate feedback after each round by displaying correct answers and briefly explaining any concepts with low accuracy rates.
materials_needed: Pre-printed card sets (120 cards per student: 60 concept cards, 60 definition cards)
PowerPoint presentation with 4 timed slides containing PM concepts, processes, acronyms
Answer sheets with numbered sections (1-15, 1-20, 1-15, 1-20)
Timer/stopwatch visible to all students
Answer key with explanations for instructor reference
assessment_method: Grade each round separately: Round 1 (15 points), Round 2 (20 points), Round 3 (15 points), Round 4 (20 points). Total possible: 70 points. Success criteria: 85% (59+ points) demonstrates advanced recall mastery, 70-84% (49-58 points) shows proficient recall, below 70% requires remediation. Track specific error patterns (e.g., Agile vs. Scrum confusion) for targeted review.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a methodology reference sheet with major frameworks listed (no details) before starting. For advanced learners: Add bonus questions requiring recall of historical context or creator names for each methodology. Consider allowing high performers to peer-tutor during review phases.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Communication: Analyzing Multi-Stakeholder Response Strategies
description: Students will analyze and interpret complex leadership communication patterns during organizational crises by examining authentic case studies from multiple stakeholder perspectives. Through systematic deconstruction of leader messages, timing, and channels, students will demonstrate understanding of how effective crisis leadership communication differs across audiences and contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the underlying strategic rationale behind crisis communication decisions by analyzing message content, timing, and channel selection across three stakeholder groups
Students will distinguish between effective and ineffective crisis leadership communication patterns through comparative analysis of authentic organizational crisis responses
instructions: Begin by distributing the Wells Fargo 2016 account fraud crisis communication package containing CEO statements, employee memos, customer communications, and regulatory responses (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 4-5, assigning each team one stakeholder perspective: employees, customers, regulators, investors, or media. Each team receives the complete communication timeline but focuses analysis on messages directed to their assigned stakeholder group. Teams spend 45 minutes systematically analyzing their assigned communications using the provided Crisis Communication Analysis Framework, documenting: message timing relative to crisis events, emotional tone and language choices, specific promises or commitments made, communication channels selected, and apparent strategic intent. Teams then rotate stations for 20 minutes each, reviewing other teams' stakeholder-focused analyses and noting patterns, contradictions, or gaps between different stakeholder messages. During rotation, teams complete the Cross-Stakeholder Comparison Matrix, identifying where leadership communication was consistent versus contradictory across audiences. In the final 30 minutes, facilitate a structured debrief where each team presents one key insight about how leadership communication strategy varied by stakeholder, supported by specific textual evidence. Record insights on a shared digital board, then guide discussion on patterns that distinguish effective crisis leadership communication from ineffective approaches. Conclude by having students individually complete a reflection synthesis identifying three principles of effective crisis communication leadership they extracted from the analysis.
materials_needed: Wells Fargo 2016 crisis communication timeline packet (chronological compilation of all stakeholder communications)
Crisis Communication Analysis Framework worksheet (structured template with analysis categories)
Cross-Stakeholder Comparison Matrix template
Digital collaboration board (Miro, Jamboard, or similar)
Rotation station markers and timers
assessment_method: Evaluate teams' completed Analysis Framework worksheets for depth of interpretation (40%), accuracy of Cross-Stakeholder Comparison Matrix entries with supporting evidence (35%), and quality of individual reflection synthesis demonstrating understanding of crisis communication principles (25%). Use 4-point rubric assessing: identification of strategic intent, use of textual evidence, recognition of stakeholder-specific patterns, and articulation of leadership communication principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions for each analysis category and highlight key sections in communication examples. Pair stronger analytical students with those needing support during rotation activities. For advanced learners, add secondary crisis case (Target 2013 breach) for comparative analysis and challenge them to identify industry-specific communication patterns. Provide sentence stems for reflection synthesis to support clear articulation of insights.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real Estate Data: A Pattern Recognition Workshop
description: Students will analyze histograms and box plots of housing price data from three different neighborhoods to identify distribution patterns and explain what these patterns reveal about market characteristics. They will practice distinguishing between normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions while connecting statistical concepts to real-world business implications.
learning_objectives: Students will classify distribution types (normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, bimodal) by examining histogram shapes and box plot characteristics in housing price datasets
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through written analysis connecting statistical observations to market conditions
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing housing prices from three neighborhoods: Downtown (luxury market), Suburbs (middle-class), and University District (mixed student/family housing). Each group receives printed histograms and box plots for all three areas plus a data interpretation worksheet.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students examine the Downtown neighborhood visualizations first. Guide them to identify the distribution shape by looking at histogram symmetry, tail length, and peak location. Have them mark key features on the box plot: median position, quartile spacing, and outlier presence. Students record observations on their worksheet.

Step 2 (15 minutes): Repeat the analysis process for Suburbs and University District data. Students should notice the Suburbs showing normal distribution, Downtown displaying right-skew with outliers, and University District exhibiting bimodal patterns.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Groups complete the interpretation section, explaining why each neighborhood shows its particular distribution pattern. For example, Downtown's right-skew suggests most properties are moderately priced with some luxury outliers. University District's bimodal pattern indicates two distinct market segments (student housing vs. family homes).

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents one neighborhood analysis to the class, explaining both the statistical characteristics they identified and the real-world factors causing these patterns. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting statistical concepts to market dynamics.

Conclude with a brief reflection where students identify which distribution type would be most challenging for pricing predictions and why.
materials_needed: Pre-generated housing price dataset with 3 neighborhoods (CSV file)
Printed histogram and box plot visualizations for each neighborhood
Data interpretation worksheets with guided questions
Calculators or laptops with basic statistical software
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification of distribution types (25%), (2) Accurate description of statistical features like skewness and outliers (25%), (3) Logical explanation of business implications (35%), (4) Clear presentation and use of statistical vocabulary (15%). Students must correctly identify at least 2 out of 3 distribution types and provide reasonable business explanations to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a distribution identification cheat sheet with visual examples of each type and key questions like 'Where is the peak?' and 'Which tail is longer?'. Offer sentence starters for business explanations such as 'This skewed pattern suggests...' For advanced learners, introduce additional concepts like kurtosis or ask them to predict how seasonal factors might change these distributions. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during group work.

title: Analyzing Multi-Path Interference Patterns in Advanced Optical Systems
description: Students will decompose complex interference patterns from a three-slit optical setup to identify individual wave contributions and predict pattern modifications. They will examine how phase relationships between multiple coherent sources create composite interference effects and distinguish between contributions from different slit pairs.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex three-slit interference patterns by separating individual two-slit contributions and identifying their phase relationships
Students will examine the relationship between slit separation parameters and resultant intensity distributions through quantitative pattern decomposition
instructions:
Begin by setting up three parallel slits with separations d₁₂ = 0.5mm, d₂₃ = 0.3mm, and d₁₃ = 0.8mm, positioned 2 meters from a projection screen. Illuminate with 632.8nm laser light and capture the resulting interference pattern using a digital camera with linear sensor array. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to collect intensity data at 50 points across a 10cm screen section, recording pixel intensities in spreadsheet format.

Next, students spend 25 minutes performing mathematical analysis. They must calculate theoretical two-slit patterns for each slit pair (1-2, 2-3, 1-3) using I = I₀cos²(πd sin θ/λ), where θ represents angular position. Using graphing software, they overlay these three theoretical curves and compare with experimental data, identifying constructive and destructive interference locations.

During the following 20 minutes, students modify the setup by blocking slit 2, then slit 1, collecting new data sets. They analyze how removing each slit affects the overall pattern, comparing actual results with predictions made during theoretical analysis. Students must identify which interference maxima disappear and explain the physical reasoning.

For the final 15 minutes, students predict intensity patterns for modified configurations: doubling d₁₂ while maintaining other separations, and rotating the entire slit assembly 5 degrees. They justify predictions using phasor diagram analysis, showing vector addition of three wave contributions at specific screen positions. Students present findings through annotated graphs showing experimental data, theoretical predictions, and percentage deviations at critical points.
materials_needed: 632.8nm HeNe laser with beam expander
Three-slit apparatus with micrometer adjustments (slit width ~0.05mm)
2-meter optical bench with adjustable screen mount
Digital camera with macro lens and linear CCD capability
Computer with Excel/MATLAB and graphing software
Optical power meter for intensity calibration
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of experimental data collection and theoretical calculations (25%), (2) Quality of pattern decomposition showing individual slit-pair contributions (30%), (3) Correctness of predictions for modified configurations with physical justification (25%), (4) Analysis of discrepancies between theory and experiment with error source identification (20%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in intensity predictions and correctly identify at least 4 specific interference features.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated intensity templates for two-slit cases and guided worksheets with specific angular positions marked. Offer additional practice with phasor diagrams using interactive simulations. For advanced learners, extend analysis to include slit width effects using sinc function modulation, or analyze non-uniform slit spacing patterns. Consider adding polarization analysis for students completing early.

title: Analyzing Multi-Path Interference Patterns in Advanced Optical Systems: Exercise 1
description: Students will decompose complex interference patterns from multi-slit and grating systems to identify individual wave contributions and predict how systematic modifications affect the overall pattern. They will examine real experimental data to distinguish between theoretical predictions and practical limitations in optical systems.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex interference patterns by decomposing them into constituent wave components and identifying the physical parameters responsible for specific pattern features
Students will evaluate the relationship between theoretical wave superposition models and experimental results through systematic comparison of predicted versus observed intensity distributions
instructions: Begin by distributing three sets of experimental interference data: single-slit, double-slit, and 6-slit diffraction patterns, each measured at 632.8 nm wavelength with varying slit widths and separations. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to plot intensity vs. position data using graphing software and identify key pattern characteristics (primary maxima locations, secondary peaks, intensity ratios, envelope shapes). Next, provide theoretical equations for each configuration and have students spend 20 minutes calculating expected patterns using the given experimental parameters (slit width a=50μm, separation d=200μm, screen distance L=2m). Students must create overlay plots comparing theoretical curves with experimental data. During the following 25 minutes, students systematically analyze discrepancies by examining: (1) how finite slit width affects the envelope function, (2) why experimental secondary maxima have lower intensities than predicted, (3) how slight variations in slit spacing create asymmetries in the pattern. Provide a data set where one parameter is intentionally altered (slit separation increased by 10%) and have students identify which parameter changed by reverse-engineering from the pattern shift. Students spend 15 minutes documenting their analysis methodology and conclusions. Conclude with 10-minute pair presentations where each team explains one specific discrepancy between theory and experiment, identifying the physical cause and proposing experimental improvements to minimize the deviation.
materials_needed: Three datasets of experimental interference patterns (CSV files with intensity vs position data)
Graphing software (Python/matplotlib, Excel, or Origin)
Theoretical interference equation reference sheets
Scientific calculators or computers with mathematical software
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of pattern features and parameter extraction (25%), (2) Correct application of theoretical models and calculation accuracy (25%), (3) Thorough analysis of theory-experiment discrepancies with valid physical explanations (30%), (4) Clear presentation of findings with appropriate use of technical terminology (20%). Students must submit overlay plots, analysis documentation, and deliver 3-minute presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide partially completed calculation templates and highlight specific pattern features to analyze first. Offer guiding questions like 'How does the envelope shape relate to single-slit diffraction?' Advanced learners can extend by analyzing polarization effects in the data or modeling coherence length limitations on fringe visibility.
original_title: Analyzing Multi-Path Interference Patterns in Advanced Optical Systems

title: Code Review Comparison: Evaluating Two JavaScript Function Implementations
description: Students will evaluate and compare two different JavaScript functions that solve the same problem, analyzing their efficiency, readability, and maintainability. They will justify which implementation is superior and propose specific improvements for both versions.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two JavaScript function implementations by analyzing code quality, performance, and maintainability criteria
Students will justify their selection of the superior implementation through structured comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions: Begin by distributing the Code Review Worksheet containing two JavaScript functions (Function A and Function B) that both calculate the average of numbers in an array, but use different approaches. Function A uses a for loop with manual sum calculation, while Function B uses the reduce() method. Give students 10 minutes to individually read both functions and make initial notes. Next, have students work in pairs for 20 minutes to complete the evaluation matrix, scoring each function on five criteria: readability (1-5), efficiency (1-5), maintainability (1-5), error handling (1-5), and beginner-friendliness (1-5). Students must provide written justification for each score. During the following 15 minutes, pairs should write a 3-4 sentence recommendation paragraph stating which function they would choose for a beginner programming tutorial and why. In the final 15 minutes, conduct a class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their recommendations and defend their choices. The instructor should facilitate debate by asking probing questions like 'How did you weigh readability versus efficiency?' and 'What evidence supports your maintainability score?' Conclude by having each pair submit their completed evaluation matrix and recommendation paragraph. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are providing specific evidence from the code rather than general statements.
materials_needed: Code Review Worksheet with two JavaScript functions printed for each student
Evaluation criteria matrix handout
Computers or tablets for students to test code snippets (optional)
Whiteboard or projector for displaying functions during discussion
assessment_method: Grade using a 20-point rubric: Evaluation matrix completion with justifications (8 points), quality of evidence cited from code (6 points), recommendation paragraph with clear reasoning (4 points), and participation in class discussion (2 points). Success requires scoring 16+ points total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist of specific code elements to examine (variable names, loop structure, built-in methods used). Offer sentence starters like 'This function is more readable because...' For advanced learners, add a third criterion asking them to evaluate memory usage and provide alternative implementations with trade-off analysis.

title: Customer Segmentation Dashboard Creation Using Sales Transaction Data
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior patterns using RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis. They will synthesize transaction data, develop customer personas, and design visual storytelling elements to communicate business insights to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying RFM analysis techniques to raw transaction data
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through combining statistical analysis, data visualization, and business storytelling principles
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with a dataset containing 12 months of customer transaction records (customer_id, purchase_date, order_value, product_category). Teams spend 15 minutes exploring the data structure and identifying data quality issues. Next, students calculate RFM metrics: Recency (days since last purchase), Frequency (total number of purchases), and Monetary value (total spending) for each customer (30 minutes). Using quartile-based scoring (1-4 scale), teams assign RFM scores and create customer segments such as 'Champions' (high RFM), 'At-Risk' (high monetary, low recency), and 'New Customers' (high recency, low frequency/monetary). Students then develop 3-5 distinct customer personas with detailed profiles including demographics, purchasing patterns, and recommended marketing strategies (45 minutes). Using Tableau or Power BI, teams create an interactive dashboard featuring: segment overview with customer counts and revenue contribution, trend analysis showing segment evolution over time, geographic distribution maps, and actionable recommendations panel (90 minutes). Teams conclude by preparing a 10-minute presentation positioning themselves as data consultants presenting to company executives, explaining methodology, key insights, and strategic recommendations. Each dashboard must include filters for date ranges and product categories, at least 5 different visualization types, and clear executive summary with 3 specific business recommendations. Instructors circulate during work time, checking RFM calculations and providing feedback on visualization clarity and business relevance.
materials_needed: Customer transaction dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI licenses for each team
Computers with sufficient processing power for data analysis
RFM analysis calculation template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Customer persona template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric scoring dashboard technical accuracy (25 points: correct RFM calculations, appropriate segmentation), visual design effectiveness (25 points: clarity, interactivity, professional appearance), business insight quality (25 points: actionable recommendations, strategic thinking), and presentation delivery (25 points: clear communication, executive-level messaging). Students submit dashboard files, calculation worksheets, and written executive summary. Peer evaluation component where teams rate others' dashboards for usability and insight value.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-calculated RFM score examples, offer dashboard template with basic layout structure, and pair with stronger analytical teammates. For advanced learners: challenge them to incorporate additional variables (product preferences, seasonal patterns), use advanced clustering algorithms (K-means), or create predictive models for customer lifetime value. Provide optional advanced datasets with additional customer attributes for deeper segmentation analysis.

title: Advanced Project Management Terminology and Framework Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 50 advanced project management terms, processes, and framework components through intensive spaced repetition exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of complex PM concepts including earned value management formulas, risk register components, and PMBOK knowledge area interdependencies.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall 45 out of 50 advanced project management terms, formulas, and framework components by completing timed flashcard exercises and verbal recitation drills
Students will identify specific PMBOK process inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs through structured memory matching activities within 90 seconds per process group
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-prepared flashcard sets containing 50 advanced PM concepts (10 cards each for: EVM formulas with variables, risk register mandatory fields, PMBOK process group flows, critical path method components, and quality management tools). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes using the Leitner spaced repetition method - correctly recalled cards move to pile 2, incorrect cards remain in pile 1. After initial review, conduct Round 1: individual timed recall (3 minutes) where students write definitions for 15 randomly selected terms. Provide 2-minute discussion break for peer clarification. Round 2: verbal speed recall where Student A shows term, Student B has 10 seconds to provide definition, then roles switch. Continue for 20 terms each. Round 3: advanced application recall where instructor calls out scenarios ('Calculate Schedule Performance Index when...') and students must recall exact formula and variable definitions within 15 seconds. Record responses on provided tracking sheets. Final assessment involves individual written recall test of 25 randomly selected items from the original 50, completed in 10 minutes with no reference materials. Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) to demonstrate mastery. Conclude with group verbal review of most challenging terms for reinforcement.
materials_needed: 50 pre-made flashcards with advanced PM terms (EVM formulas, PMBOK processes, risk components, etc.)
Individual tracking sheets for recording student progress
Timer or stopwatch for timed exercises
Final assessment sheets with 25 randomized questions
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (20/25 correct) on the final written recall assessment completed within 10 minutes. Track progress using provided sheets during paired activities. Award full credit for meeting accuracy threshold, partial credit (70%) for 16-19 correct answers, and requires remediation for scores below 16/25.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, reduce initial flashcard set to 35 terms and allow 15 seconds instead of 10 for verbal recall. Provide mnemonic device examples for complex formulas (SPI = EV/PV = 'Earned Value Per Planned Value'). For advanced learners, add bonus challenge requiring recall of formula derivations and real-world application contexts. Consider providing audio recordings of terms for auditory learners during initial memorization phase.

title: Advanced Project Management Terminology and Framework Recall Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 50 advanced project management terms, methodologies, and framework components through structured repetition and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building a solid foundation of PM vocabulary essential for professional certification and advanced practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions of 50 advanced project management terms including PMBOK processes, Agile ceremonies, and risk management concepts through flashcard-based study sessions
Students will identify and name all components of the Project Management Knowledge Areas, Process Groups, and key Agile/Scrum artifacts through structured memory exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the curated list of 50 advanced PM terms covering PMBOK 6th Edition knowledge areas, Agile/Scrum terminology, and risk management concepts. Students spend 20 minutes creating physical or digital flashcards with term on front, complete definition and example on back. Terms include: Monte Carlo Analysis, Critical Chain Method, Product Backlog Refinement, Definition of Done, Earned Value Management, Fast-tracking, Resource Leveling, etc. Next, conduct three 10-minute spaced repetition rounds: Round 1 - students review all 50 cards individually; Round 2 - pair students to quiz each other on 25 cards each; Round 3 - rotate pairs and focus on previously missed terms. Follow with a 15-minute rapid-fire recall test where instructor displays terms on screen for 10 seconds each, students write definitions. Conclude with a 10-minute group verification session where students compare answers and discuss any discrepancies. Track individual progress using a checklist format where students mark terms they've mastered versus those needing additional review.
materials_needed: Curated list of 50 advanced PM terms with official definitions
Blank index cards or access to digital flashcard app (Anki/Quizlet)
Timer/stopwatch
Projection screen for rapid-fire testing
Individual progress tracking sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (45/50 terms) on the final rapid-fire recall test. Assessment includes: correct definition (2 points), appropriate context/example (1 point), spelling accuracy (1 point) per term. Partial credit given for definitions that capture main concept but lack precision. Track progress through individual checklists and peer verification during group sessions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce initial set to 25 terms, provide visual memory aids, allow audio recordings of definitions. For advanced learners: add 25 additional terms from PMI-ACP or PfMP frameworks, require students to create original contextual examples, challenge them to identify relationships between terms and explain how they interconnect within project lifecycles.
original_title: Advanced Project Management Terminology and Framework Recall Challenge

title: Dissecting Leadership Communication Failures: A Multi-Stakeholder Analysis
description: Students will analyze a complex organizational crisis by examining leaked internal communications, public statements, and stakeholder reactions to demonstrate understanding of how leadership communication cascades through organizational levels. They will map the disconnects between intended messages and received interpretations across different stakeholder groups.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the underlying leadership communication strategies by analyzing authentic artifacts from a documented organizational crisis
Students will explain the multi-directional impact of leadership messaging through systematic stakeholder perspective mapping
instructions: Step 1 (15 mins): Distribute the Wells Fargo 2016 fake accounts scandal case packet containing: CEO John Stumpf's internal memo to employees, his Congressional testimony transcript, three customer complaint letters, two employee whistleblower interviews, and stock analyst reports. Students work in groups of 4, with each member assigned a stakeholder role: employees, customers, investors, and regulators. Step 2 (25 mins): Each student individually analyzes all documents through their assigned stakeholder lens, completing a 'Communication Impact Matrix' that identifies: key messages received, emotional tone perceived, credibility assessment, and trust implications. They must cite specific phrases from documents as evidence. Step 3 (30 mins): Groups reconvene to share findings. The 'employee' perspective student presents first, followed by customer, investor, then regulator perspectives. Other group members take notes on disconnects and contradictions between stakeholder interpretations of the same communications. Step 4 (20 mins): Groups create a visual 'Leadership Communication Cascade Map' showing how Stumpf's intended messages transformed as they moved through organizational layers and external channels. They must identify at least three specific points where message distortion occurred and explain the leadership communication principles that were violated. Step 5 (15 mins): Each group presents their cascade map to the class, highlighting their most significant insight about leadership communication complexity.
materials_needed: Wells Fargo crisis case packet with 8 authentic documents per student
Communication Impact Matrix worksheets (pre-formatted)
Large poster paper for cascade mapping
Colored markers for visual mapping
Stakeholder role assignment cards
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of stakeholder perspective analysis with specific textual evidence (25%), (2) Identification of communication disconnects between stakeholder groups (25%), (3) Quality of leadership communication principles explanations (25%), (4) Visual cascade map clarity and insight depth (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by explaining rather than just identifying patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed Communication Impact Matrix with example entries and guiding questions for each stakeholder perspective. For advanced learners: Add a sixth document (board meeting minutes) and challenge them to propose three specific alternative communication strategies Stumpf could have employed, with predicted stakeholder responses.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with S3 Storage
description: Students will deploy a simple web application on an EC2 instance and configure it to store and retrieve static files from an S3 bucket. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration and basic cloud architecture principles.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web application by launching and configuring an AWS EC2 instance with proper security groups
Students will integrate AWS S3 storage through configuring the web application to upload and serve static files from an S3 bucket
instructions: Begin by having students log into AWS Management Console using provided sandbox accounts (15 minutes setup). Step 1: Students create an S3 bucket with a unique name following naming conventions (bucket-firstname-lastname-webapp), enable public read access, and upload a sample image file. Step 2: Launch an EC2 t2.micro instance using Amazon Linux 2 AMI, creating a new key pair for SSH access and configuring security group to allow HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) traffic from anywhere. Step 3: Connect to EC2 instance via SSH or EC2 Instance Connect, install Apache web server using 'sudo yum update && sudo yum install httpd', and start the service. Step 4: Create a simple HTML file at /var/www/html/index.html that displays student name and includes an image tag pointing to their S3 bucket object URL. Step 5: Install AWS CLI on the instance, configure credentials using IAM user access keys, and modify the HTML to include a file upload form. Step 6: Create a simple PHP script that handles file uploads to S3 using AWS SDK, testing the complete upload/display functionality. Step 7: Students document their architecture by creating a simple diagram showing EC2, S3, and data flow connections. Throughout the activity, emphasize proper security practices including least-privilege IAM policies and secure key management. Conclude with students demonstrating their working application to peers and explaining the AWS services integration.
materials_needed: AWS sandbox accounts with EC2 and S3 permissions for each student
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or built-in terminal for Mac/Linux)
Provided HTML template and PHP code snippets
Sample image files for testing uploads
AWS architecture diagram template
assessment_method: Students must demonstrate a working web application accessible via public EC2 IP address that successfully displays content from S3 bucket. Evaluation rubric includes: EC2 instance properly configured and accessible (25 points), S3 bucket created with correct permissions and file uploads working (25 points), web application displays S3 content correctly (25 points), architecture diagram accurately represents their implementation (15 points), and proper security group configuration demonstrated (10 points). Students submit EC2 public IP, S3 bucket name, and architecture diagram.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written code snippets and step-by-step screenshots for each AWS console action. Offer one-on-one troubleshooting for SSH connection issues. For advanced learners, challenge them to implement additional features like multiple file types, CloudFront CDN integration, or automated deployment using user data scripts. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing extra support during the EC2 configuration phase.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with S3 Storage: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a simple web application on an AWS EC2 instance and configure it to serve static assets from an S3 bucket. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration and basic cloud deployment practices.
learning_objectives: Students will apply EC2 instance configuration skills by launching, connecting to, and installing a web server on a virtual machine
Students will implement S3 bucket integration through uploading static files and configuring proper access permissions for web serving
instructions:
**Pre-class Setup (5 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS account credentials or ensures students have AWS Free Tier accounts activated. Share the sample HTML/CSS files and simple Python Flask application code via learning management system.

**Phase 1 - EC2 Setup (20 minutes):** Students log into AWS Console and navigate to EC2 Dashboard. Launch a t2.micro Amazon Linux 2 instance using the quick launch wizard. Select 'Create new key pair' and download the .pem file. Configure security group to allow HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) traffic from anywhere. Connect to instance using EC2 Instance Connect or SSH client. Install Python3, pip, and Flask using: `sudo yum update -y`, `sudo yum install python3 -y`, `pip3 install flask`.

**Phase 2 - S3 Configuration (15 minutes):** Create new S3 bucket with globally unique name following naming conventions. Upload provided CSS, JavaScript, and image files to bucket. Configure bucket policy for public read access to static assets. Enable static website hosting and note the endpoint URL.

**Phase 3 - Application Deployment (15 minutes):** Upload Flask application code to EC2 instance using nano editor or SCP. Modify application configuration to reference S3 bucket URLs for static assets. Start Flask application using `python3 app.py --host=0.0.0.0 --port=80` with sudo privileges. Test application accessibility via EC2 public IP address.

**Phase 4 - Verification and Documentation (10 minutes):** Access deployed application through web browser, verify static assets load from S3, take screenshots of working application, document AWS resource costs in provided worksheet.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account credentials for each student
Sample Flask web application code (app.py)
Static web assets package (CSS, JS, images)
AWS deployment worksheet template
Computers with web browsers and SSH capability
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Running EC2 instance in AWS Console, (2) S3 bucket with uploaded files and public access configuration, (3) Working web application accessed via public IP, (4) Completed cost estimation worksheet. Rubric awards 25 points each for successful EC2 deployment, S3 configuration, application functionality, and cost documentation accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for Struggling Students:** Provide pre-configured security group settings and step-by-step screenshot guide. Pair struggling students with more experienced peers. Offer alternative connection methods (Instance Connect vs SSH). **Extensions for Advanced Learners:** Configure custom domain using Route 53, implement CloudFront CDN for S3 assets, add RDS database integration, or set up Application Load Balancer for high availability.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with S3 Storage

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Critical Path Impact Assessment
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies on project timeline, budget, and scope. They will deconstruct the relationships between risk events, response strategies, and their cascading effects on project constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between risk response strategies and project constraints by evaluating cause-and-effect relationships in a multi-risk scenario
Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective risk response strategies through systematic comparison of their impact on critical path activities
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'MegaTech Software Implementation' case study packet containing: project network diagram (15 activities), risk register (8 identified risks), and proposed response strategies matrix. Form teams of 3-4 students. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Each team examines the network diagram to identify the critical path and calculate total float for non-critical activities. Teams must document critical path sequence and duration. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Teams analyze each risk's potential impact on critical path activities using the probability-impact matrix provided. They categorize risks as 'critical path affecting' or 'non-critical path affecting' and justify classifications. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate the four proposed risk response strategies (accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid) for the three highest-priority risks. Using the analysis worksheet, they assess each strategy's: cost-effectiveness, timeline impact, resource requirements, and secondary risk creation. Teams must identify which responses create new risks or dependencies. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation recommending the optimal risk response combination, supporting their choice with quantitative analysis from phases 2-3. Presentations must include: revised critical path duration, budget impact calculations, and justification for rejecting alternative strategies. Conclude with 10-minute debrief focusing on how teams' analytical processes differed and what factors most influenced their strategy selection.
materials_needed: MegaTech case study packet with network diagram and risk register
Probability-Impact matrix template (1 per team)
Risk response analysis worksheets (1 per student)
Calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of critical path identification and calculations (25%), (2) Quality of risk-impact analysis with clear cause-effect reasoning (30%), (3) Depth of risk response strategy evaluation including cost-benefit analysis (30%), (4) Strength of final recommendations with supporting quantitative evidence (15%). Teams must submit completed analysis worksheets and deliver presentations to receive full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed critical path example from different project and offer risk analysis sentence starters ('This risk affects the critical path because...'). For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring Monte Carlo simulation estimates for schedule impacts or asking them to develop contingency response plans for their recommended strategies.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Audit and Recommendation Report
description: Students will critically evaluate three different attribution models (First Touch, Last Touch, and Time Decay) using real e-commerce data to determine optimal budget allocation across marketing channels. They will assess each model's strengths and weaknesses, then justify their recommended attribution strategy with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating ROI variations across First Touch, Last Touch, and Time Decay models
Students will critique attribution model limitations through systematic comparison of customer journey scenarios and justify optimal marketing budget reallocation decisions
instructions: **Phase 1: Data Setup (20 minutes)** - Provide students with Google Analytics demo account access containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multi-channel funnels enabled. Students work in pairs to navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool. Have them select three attribution models: First Interaction, Last Interaction, and Time Decay (7-day half-life). Export conversion and revenue data for Organic Search, Paid Search, Display, Social, and Email channels. **Phase 2: Quantitative Analysis (45 minutes)** - Students calculate conversion rate and ROAS differences between models for each channel. Create spreadsheet comparing: attributed conversions, revenue per channel, cost per acquisition variations, and percentage differences between models. Identify which channels gain/lose attribution credit under each model. **Phase 3: Critical Evaluation (30 minutes)** - Analyze three provided customer journey scenarios (short sales cycle B2C, long consideration B2B, and repeat purchase scenarios). Students evaluate which attribution model best represents true customer behavior for each scenario, considering business context, typical customer journey length, and marketing objectives. **Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation (35 minutes)** - Develop written recommendation report including: chosen attribution model with quantitative justification, proposed budget reallocation across channels (with percentage changes), identified model limitations and mitigation strategies, and implementation timeline. Present 5-minute verbal summary defending model choice against instructor challenges about alternative scenarios.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account with Multi-Channel Funnels data
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets
Three customer journey scenario case studies (provided)
Current marketing budget allocation data by channel
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
assessment_method: Rubric scoring (100 points total): Quantitative analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct calculations and data interpretation; Critical evaluation depth (30 points) - thorough assessment of model strengths/weaknesses with specific examples; Recommendation quality (25 points) - well-justified model selection with clear reasoning; Defense presentation (20 points) - ability to address counterarguments and demonstrate deep understanding. Success requires scoring 80+ points with no category below 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students**: Provide step-by-step screenshot guide for navigating Multi-Channel Funnels, offer calculation templates with formulas pre-built, schedule 10-minute check-ins during analysis phase. **Extension for advanced learners**: Include custom attribution model creation using Google Analytics Intelligence API, analyze attribution across device types, or incorporate offline conversion data. Challenge them to build monte carlo simulation of attribution uncertainty.

title: Basic Data Type Identification and Classification Flash Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and identify the five fundamental data types in Python (integer, float, string, boolean, list) through a structured flash card activity. This activity helps students build essential foundational knowledge needed before writing any code.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list) and their characteristics by completing flash card exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify specific examples of each data type through visual recognition activities and verbal recitation
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flash cards to each student - one set contains data type names (int, float, str, bool, list) and the other contains 20 example values (4 examples per type: integers like 42, -7; floats like 3.14, -0.5; strings like 'Hello', 'Python'; booleans True, False; lists like [1,2,3], ['a','b']). 

Step 1 (5 minutes): Students work individually to study the definition cards, reading aloud each data type name and its key characteristic (int = whole numbers, float = decimal numbers, str = text in quotes, bool = True/False values, list = items in square brackets separated by commas).

Step 2 (10 minutes): Pair students up. One partner shows an example card (like '3.14') while the other must quickly name the data type ('float'). Partners alternate roles, cycling through all 20 example cards twice.

Step 3 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class rapid-fire rounds. Display examples on the board one at a time. Students hold up fingers (1=int, 2=float, 3=str, 4=bool, 5=list) to indicate their answer. Provide immediate feedback and correction.

Step 4 (10 minutes): Individual quiz - students complete a matching worksheet connecting 15 new examples to their corresponding data types. Examples include: 100 (int), 'Computer Science' (str), [10, 20, 30] (list), False (bool), 2.718 (float).

Conclude by having students create their own example for each data type and share with a neighbor for verification.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flash cards with data type definitions (5 cards per student)
Pre-printed flash cards with example values (20 cards per student)
Individual matching quiz worksheets
Whiteboard or projector for class examples
Answer key for immediate feedback
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (13/15 correct) on the final matching worksheet. Additionally, observe student responses during the rapid-fire finger voting - students should demonstrate consistent correct identification of at least 80% of examples shown. Collect worksheets for individual scoring and provide immediate verbal feedback during pair work.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reference sheet with visual cues (quotes around strings, decimal points in floats, square brackets for lists). Allow extra study time with definition cards. For advanced learners: Introduce edge cases like empty lists [], negative numbers, or multi-word strings. Have them create tricky examples to challenge classmates.

title: Comparative Analysis of Quantum Tunneling in Different Potential Barriers Using Wave Function Decomposition
description: Students will analyze and compare wave function behavior across three distinct potential barrier configurations (rectangular, triangular, and parabolic) to determine how barrier shape affects tunneling probability and transmission coefficients. They will decompose complex wave functions into component parts and evaluate the physical significance of each component in the tunneling process.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze wave function continuity and boundary conditions by systematically examining the mathematical relationships between incident, reflected, and transmitted wave components across different barrier geometries
Students will evaluate the relationship between barrier shape and tunneling probability through quantitative comparison of transmission coefficients and qualitative analysis of wave function behavior
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-calculated wave function datasets representing electron tunneling through 2 eV barriers of different shapes: rectangular (width 0.5 nm), triangular (base 0.5 nm), and parabolic (width 0.5 nm at base). Form groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one barrier type initially. Students spend 15 minutes plotting their assigned wave function using provided graphing software, identifying distinct regions: approach zone, barrier interior, and transmission zone. Next, students calculate transmission coefficients using T = |ψ_transmitted|²/|ψ_incident|² at five different electron energies (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.8, 1.9 eV). During the following 20 minutes, groups rotate to analyze the second barrier type, repeating calculations and plotting. After another rotation (15 minutes), groups complete analysis of the third barrier type. Students then spend 25 minutes creating comparative data tables and graphs showing transmission coefficient versus electron energy for all three barriers. Finally, groups prepare 10-minute presentations analyzing: (1) how wave function amplitude and phase change within each barrier type, (2) which barrier geometry allows maximum tunneling at each energy level, (3) physical explanations for observed differences using quantum mechanical principles, and (4) predictions for barrier performance at energies not tested. Conclude with 15 minutes of presentations where each group presents findings and receives peer feedback using structured evaluation forms.
materials_needed: Three pre-calculated wave function datasets (rectangular, triangular, parabolic barriers)
Graphing software (MATLAB, Python with matplotlib, or Desmos)
Scientific calculators
Data analysis worksheets with calculation templates
Peer evaluation rubrics for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of transmission coefficient calculations (25%), (2) Quality of wave function analysis and identification of key features (25%), (3) Depth of comparative analysis between barrier types with physical reasoning (30%), (4) Clarity and scientific accuracy of presentation including predictions and conclusions (20%). Students must achieve minimum 3/4 points in categories 2 and 3 to demonstrate analyze-level proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide completed sample calculations for one energy level and barrier type, offer guided questions for wave function interpretation, and pair with stronger peers during rotations. For advanced learners: challenge them to derive analytical expressions for transmission coefficients, investigate barrier combinations, or analyze the effect of changing barrier height while maintaining constant shape ratios.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Comparing Two JavaScript Function Implementations
description: Students evaluate two different JavaScript functions that solve the same problem by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will justify their choice of the superior implementation using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two JavaScript function implementations by analyzing readability, efficiency, and adherence to coding standards
Students will justify their assessment of code quality through written comparison using industry-standard evaluation criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a handout containing two JavaScript functions that calculate the sum of even numbers in an array (Function A uses a for loop with if statements, Function B uses filter and reduce methods). Include a evaluation criteria checklist covering: readability, efficiency, maintainability, and coding standards.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine both functions line-by-line, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses using the provided criteria. They should test both functions mentally with sample inputs [2,4,6,8] and identify any potential issues.

**Evaluation Process (20 minutes):** Students complete a structured comparison worksheet rating each function (1-5 scale) on the four criteria. They must provide specific evidence from the code to support each rating, citing exact line numbers and explaining their reasoning.

**Written Justification (15 minutes):** Students write a 150-word recommendation memo stating which function they would approve for production use. The memo must include: their final choice, three specific reasons supporting their decision, and one improvement suggestion for their chosen function.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange memos with a partner and provide feedback using a peer evaluation checklist, focusing on whether the justification is well-supported by evidence from the code analysis.
materials_needed: Printed handout with two JavaScript functions solving the same problem
Code evaluation criteria checklist (readability, efficiency, maintainability, standards)
Structured comparison worksheet with rating scales
Peer evaluation checklist for memo review
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of code strengths/weaknesses with specific examples, (2) Appropriate use of evaluation criteria with justified ratings, (3) Clear written recommendation with evidence-based reasoning, (4) Professional memo format and grammar. Success = 3/4 points minimum.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a partially completed comparison worksheet with one example evaluation. For advanced learners, add a third function using recursion and ask them to evaluate all three, or have them identify security vulnerabilities in addition to the standard criteria.

title: Design and Build a Customer Behavior Dashboard for E-commerce Decision Making
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that transforms raw e-commerce transaction data into actionable business insights. They will design visualizations, calculate key metrics, and present data-driven recommendations to stakeholders using real customer purchase patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive analytical framework by identifying key performance indicators, selecting appropriate visualization types, and structuring data workflows for e-commerce business intelligence
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through data cleaning, metric calculation, and visualization creation that enables stakeholder decision-making
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Framework Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the sample e-commerce dataset containing 2,000+ transactions with fields: customer_id, purchase_date, product_category, purchase_amount, customer_age, geography, and marketing_channel. Students work in pairs to explore the dataset using Excel/Google Sheets, identifying data quality issues and brainstorming 5-7 business questions their dashboard should answer (e.g., 'Which customer segments generate highest lifetime value?'). They create a dashboard wireframe sketch showing planned layout, chart types, and key metrics.

**Phase 2: Data Preparation & Metric Development (60 minutes)**
Students clean the dataset by handling missing values, standardizing formats, and creating calculated fields. They must develop at least 4 key metrics: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV), Average Order Value (AOV), Customer Acquisition Cost by channel, and Monthly Recurring Revenue. Using pivot tables and formulas, they aggregate data by relevant dimensions (time periods, customer segments, product categories).

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (90 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students build their interactive dashboard with minimum requirements: 2 time-series charts showing trends, 1 geographic visualization, 2 categorical comparison charts, and 1 customer segmentation analysis. Each visualization must include appropriate filters, clear titles, and color coding. Students add text boxes explaining insights and recommendations.

**Phase 4: Stakeholder Presentation (30 minutes)**
Pairs present their dashboard to another pair (acting as business stakeholders), delivering a 5-minute pitch highlighting 3 key insights and 2 specific business recommendations. Presenters must defend their design choices and answer questions about methodology and conclusions.
materials_needed: Sample e-commerce transaction dataset (CSV file with 2,000+ records)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for initial data exploration
Dashboard wireframe template worksheet
Access to computers with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Completed interactive dashboard file, (2) Written executive summary (500 words) explaining key insights and business recommendations, (3) Peer evaluation form rating other teams' presentations. Rubric evaluates: Data accuracy and cleaning (25%), Visualization design and interactivity (30%), Business insight quality (25%), and Presentation clarity (20%). Success criteria: Dashboard loads without errors, displays minimum required visualizations, provides at least 3 data-supported insights, and includes actionable recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned dataset option and dashboard template with basic chart structures. Offer guided worksheet with specific formulas for key metrics. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets (marketing campaign data, customer surveys) for deeper analysis. Challenge them to incorporate predictive elements like customer churn probability or sales forecasting using trend analysis.

title: PMI Knowledge Area Critical Path Components Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete hierarchical structure of all 10 PMI Knowledge Areas, including their 49 constituent processes, exact process group classifications, and specific ITTO (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) categories. This intensive recall activity prepares students for advanced PMP certification scenarios requiring instant process identification.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMI processes by name and correctly classify each within their respective Knowledge Area and Process Group through timed written assessments
Students will identify specific ITTO categories for each process through systematic memorization drills and peer verification exercises
instructions: Begin with 15 minutes of individual study using provided PMI process charts. Students must silently memorize the complete hierarchy: 10 Knowledge Areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder), their 49 processes, and Process Group classifications (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing). After study time, conduct Round 1: Knowledge Area Recall (10 minutes) - students write all 10 Knowledge Areas from memory, no references allowed. Check answers immediately using answer keys. Round 2: Process Classification (15 minutes) - display random process names on screen for 30 seconds each. Students must write the correct Knowledge Area and Process Group for each of 20 processes. Round 3: ITTO Speed Challenge (20 minutes) - provide process names, students must list 3 specific inputs, 3 tools/techniques, and 3 outputs for 10 selected processes within 2 minutes per process. Use timer for each round. Round 4: Peer Verification (15 minutes) - students pair up, one reads process names while partner recites classifications without notes. Switch roles after 7 minutes. Conclude with comprehensive written assessment (25 minutes) covering all memorized content. Students must achieve 80% accuracy on final assessment to demonstrate mastery. Provide immediate feedback using prepared answer sheets after each round.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition process charts (1 per student)
Laminated answer keys for instructor verification
Digital timer/stopwatch
Pre-prepared PowerPoint slides with random process names
Final assessment sheets with 50 recall questions
Red pens for immediate grading
assessment_method: Students must score 80% or higher on the final 50-question written assessment covering: Knowledge Area identification (20%), Process-to-Knowledge Area matching (30%), Process Group classification (25%), and ITTO component recall (25%). Track individual progress through each round using provided scoring sheets. Award full credit only for exact terminology matching PMBOK standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide acronym memory devices (e.g., 'I Should Schedule Cost Quality Resources Communication Risk Procurement Stakeholders') and allow 5 additional minutes during study phase. Create simplified process groups color-coding system. For advanced learners: add bonus questions requiring recall of process sequence dependencies and critical path relationships between Knowledge Areas. Challenge them to identify which processes are most frequently tested on PMP exams.

title: Decoding Multi-Stakeholder Crisis Leadership: The Organizational Triangle Analysis
description: Students will analyze complex crisis leadership scenarios involving three competing stakeholder groups to understand how effective leaders balance conflicting demands and maintain organizational cohesion. This activity requires students to demonstrate deep comprehension of stakeholder management theory, crisis communication principles, and adaptive leadership frameworks through systematic analysis of real-world cases.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the underlying tensions between competing stakeholder interests (employees, shareholders, customers) in crisis situations by mapping power dynamics and conflicting priorities using stakeholder analysis frameworks
Students will explain how transformational leadership principles manifest differently across various crisis contexts through comparative analysis of three distinct organizational crises
instructions:
**Phase 1: Case Distribution & Individual Analysis (25 minutes)**
Distribute three crisis scenarios: Tech company data breach affecting customer privacy, Manufacturing plant closure impacting local community, Financial services merger creating employee uncertainty. Students work individually, spending 8 minutes per case using the provided Stakeholder Power-Interest Grid template. They must identify primary stakeholders, map their power levels (high/medium/low) and interest intensity, then document specific conflicting demands each group places on leadership.

**Phase 2: Triangle Mapping Exercise (20 minutes)**
Students create visual 'Organizational Triangle' diagrams for each scenario, placing the three primary stakeholder groups at triangle vertices. Along each triangle edge, they write the specific tensions between stakeholder pairs (e.g., employee job security vs. shareholder cost reduction). At the triangle center, they identify the leader's central challenge and document evidence of transformational vs. transactional leadership approaches used.

**Phase 3: Cross-Case Pattern Analysis (30 minutes)**
In groups of 4, students compare their individual analyses to identify recurring patterns across all three scenarios. Using the Adaptive Leadership Framework handout, they must categorize leader behaviors into technical vs. adaptive challenges, document which stakeholder communication strategies proved most effective, and explain why certain leadership approaches succeeded or failed in each context.

**Phase 4: Synthesis & Justification (15 minutes)**
Each group prepares a 3-minute presentation explaining one key insight about how expert leaders navigate stakeholder triangulation during crises, supported by specific evidence from all three cases.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis leadership case studies (2 pages each) with stakeholder background information
Stakeholder Power-Interest Grid templates (one per student)
Adaptive Leadership Framework reference sheets
Large paper sheets for triangle mapping diagrams
Colored markers or pens for visual mapping
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of stakeholder identification and power mapping (25%), (2) Depth of tension analysis between competing groups (25%), (3) Correct application of leadership theory to explain leader behaviors (25%), (4) Quality of cross-case pattern recognition and evidence-based conclusions (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ points in each category, demonstrating comprehensive understanding rather than surface-level observations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled stakeholder examples for the first scenario and guided questions for tension identification. For advanced learners: Add a fourth stakeholder group (regulatory bodies) to increase complexity, or require them to propose alternative leadership strategies with theoretical justification. Consider pairing analytical thinkers with visual learners during group phases.

title: Risk Register Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Decomposition
description: Students will analyze a complex project risk register from a software implementation project, breaking down risk interdependencies and evaluating the effectiveness of proposed mitigation strategies. They will identify gaps in risk responses and recommend improvements based on PMI risk management principles.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies and cascade effects by examining a multi-layered risk register and mapping cause-and-effect relationships between identified risks
Students will evaluate the adequacy of risk response strategies through systematic assessment against PMI risk management framework criteria
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the provided risk register containing 15 risks from a fictional ERP implementation project, including probability/impact ratings, risk owners, and current mitigation strategies. Form teams of 3-4 students. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Each team creates a risk interdependency map using sticky notes and flipchart paper. Students identify which risks could trigger or amplify other risks, drawing connection lines and labeling relationship types (causal, correlational, or conditional). **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Teams analyze each risk response strategy using the provided evaluation matrix with criteria: cost-effectiveness, feasibility, timeline alignment, stakeholder impact, and residual risk level. Rate each strategy 1-5 on each criterion. **Step 3 (15 minutes):** Identify the three highest-priority gaps where current mitigation strategies are inadequate (total scores below 15). For each gap, teams must specify: what makes the current strategy insufficient, which PMI risk response strategy would be more appropriate (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept), and specific implementation recommendations. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation focusing on their most critical finding: the risk with the most dangerous interdependencies and their recommended strategy revision. **Step 5 (15 minutes):** Each team presents while others complete peer evaluation forms, noting whether the analysis correctly identified risk relationships and whether recommendations align with PMI principles.
materials_needed: Pre-built ERP implementation risk register (15 risks with current strategies)
Risk evaluation matrix template with 5 criteria
Large flipchart paper and colored sticky notes
PMI risk response strategy reference sheet
Peer evaluation forms with specific criteria checklist
assessment_method: Teams submit their completed risk interdependency map (25 points), evaluation matrix with scores and justifications (35 points), and three gap analysis reports with specific recommendations (40 points). Success criteria: correctly identified at least 8 risk interdependencies, properly applied PMI risk response categories, and provided actionable recommendations with clear implementation steps.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a partially completed interdependency map showing 3 example connections and offer guiding questions for each evaluation criterion. For advanced learners: challenge them to quantify the potential cost impact of risk cascades and develop contingency plans for their top 2 recommendations, including trigger conditions and escalation procedures.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Recommendation Engine
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, position-based, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model performance against business objectives, and develop evidence-based recommendations for optimal attribution strategy implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of six attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating revenue attribution discrepancies across channels
Students will critique current attribution strategies through systematic comparison of model performance metrics and business impact assessment
Students will synthesize findings into actionable recommendations by weighing model accuracy, business goals, and implementation feasibility
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection Setup (20 minutes)**
Students access provided Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool. Export data for all six attribution models showing channel performance, conversion values, and conversion counts. Create Excel workbook with separate tabs for each model's data.

**Phase 2: Quantitative Analysis (45 minutes)**
Calculate percentage variance in revenue attribution between models for each marketing channel (paid search, organic, email, social, display). Identify channels with highest attribution volatility (>30% variance between models). Create visualization comparing conversion paths length and time-to-conversion across models. Document three key statistical findings per model with supporting data.

**Phase 3: Business Context Evaluation (30 minutes)**
Analyze provided business scenario documents detailing company's marketing objectives, budget allocation, and customer journey complexity. Map each attribution model's strengths/weaknesses against business requirements. Score each model (1-5 scale) across criteria: accuracy for business model, implementation complexity, actionability of insights, and alignment with marketing goals.

**Phase 4: Strategic Recommendation Development (25 minutes)**
