Synthesize analysis into comprehensive recommendation report. Include: primary attribution model recommendation with justification, secondary model for comparison purposes, implementation timeline, expected impact on marketing decisions, and potential limitations. Support recommendations with minimum five data points from analysis and explicit connections to business objectives.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets access
Business scenario document packet (3-4 pages detailing company context)
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Access to Google Analytics Model Comparison Tool
assessment_method: Students submit comprehensive evaluation report (1500-2000 words) including: quantitative analysis section with calculations and visualizations (25 points), critical evaluation of each model's business fit (25 points), evidence-based recommendation with implementation plan (35 points), and quality of data interpretation and professional presentation (15 points). Rubric emphasizes depth of analysis, use of specific GA metrics, and connection between data insights and business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide attribution model comparison checklist, offer simplified business scenarios, and give template for organizing quantitative findings. For advanced learners: introduce custom attribution modeling concepts, require analysis of seasonal attribution variations, or add competitive analysis component comparing attribution strategies across industries. Consider pairing students with different GA experience levels for peer support.

title: Optimizing Municipal Water Distribution Systems Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving water distribution to multiple city districts. They will use the simplex method and graphical analysis to minimize pumping costs while meeting demand constraints and system capacity limits.
learning_objectives: Students will apply the simplex method to solve multi-variable linear programming problems by manually executing tableau iterations for a 4-variable water distribution scenario
Students will implement constraint analysis and sensitivity testing through systematic evaluation of changing demand parameters in municipal infrastructure planning
instructions: Begin by distributing the Water Distribution Challenge packet containing a map of Metro City with 6 districts, current demand data, and pumping station specifications (5 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Lead Analyst (manages constraints), Cost Calculator (tracks objective function), Solution Validator (checks feasibility), and Systems Engineer (interprets results). Present the scenario: Metro City must distribute water from 3 pumping stations to 6 districts with varying hourly costs ($0.12-$0.28 per 1000 gallons) and capacity limits (2000-5000 gallons/hour per station). Students first identify decision variables (x₁, x₂, x₃ representing flow rates from each station), then formulate the objective function to minimize total pumping costs: Min Z = 0.12x₁ + 0.21x₂ + 0.28x₃. Next, teams establish constraints: demand requirements (≥15,000 gallons/hour total), individual station capacities, and non-negativity conditions (20 minutes). Using provided simplex tableau templates, students manually solve the linear program, performing pivot operations and tracking iterations until reaching optimality (45 minutes). Teams then conduct sensitivity analysis by adjusting demand upward by 10% and resolving to determine cost impacts (25 minutes). Finally, each team prepares a 5-minute presentation showing their optimal solution, total minimum cost, station utilization rates, and recommendations for handling increased demand scenarios (15 minutes presentations, 5 minutes feedback per team).
materials_needed: Metro City Water Distribution Challenge packet with district map and data tables
Simplex method tableau worksheets (3 per team)
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for constraint visualization
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Stopwatch for timing iterations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation accuracy (25 points) - correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints; Simplex method execution (35 points) - proper tableau setup, accurate pivot operations, and convergence to optimal solution; Sensitivity analysis (20 points) - systematic parameter adjustment and impact interpretation; Team presentation (20 points) - clear communication of results and practical recommendations. Students must achieve minimum 70% in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-formatted constraint templates and checkpoint guidance after each tableau iteration. Offer graphical method option for 2-variable simplified version. For advanced learners: Introduce integer programming constraints (whole-number pump operations only), add environmental impact coefficients to create multi-objective optimization, or incorporate time-varying demand patterns requiring dynamic programming extensions.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Wave Propagation Through Multi-Layer Dielectric Media Using Transfer Matrix Method
description: Students will analyze the transmission and reflection coefficients of electromagnetic waves passing through complex multi-layer dielectric structures. They will decompose the wave interactions at each interface and synthesize the overall system response using matrix formalism.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic wave behavior at dielectric interfaces by applying boundary conditions and calculating reflection/transmission coefficients for each layer transition
Students will evaluate the cumulative effects of multiple interfaces through systematic application of transfer matrix methodology to predict overall system transmission
instructions: Begin by providing students with a specific three-layer dielectric system: air (n₁=1.0) → glass (n₂=1.5, thickness=2.0mm) → oil (n₃=1.3, thickness=0.5mm) → water (n₄=1.33). Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to calculate individual interface reflection coefficients using r₁₂=(n₁-n₂)/(n₁+n₂) for each boundary. Next, have them spend 25 minutes deriving the characteristic matrix for each layer using M=[cos(β), i*sin(β)/η; i*η*sin(β), cos(β)] where β=2πnd/λ and η is impedance. For the analysis phase (30 minutes), students multiply the matrices in sequence and extract overall transmission coefficient T=1/M₁₁. They must then analyze how transmission varies with wavelength by calculating T for λ=400nm, 550nm, and 700nm. Have students plot their results and identify wavelength-dependent features. In the final 15 minutes, pairs compare results with adjacent groups and analyze discrepancies. Students must identify which interfaces contribute most to reflection losses and explain the physical mechanisms causing wavelength selectivity. Conclude with each pair presenting one key insight about how layer thickness affects spectral response.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators with complex number capability
Graph paper or plotting software (Excel/Python)
Reference sheet with refractive index values and formulas
Ruler for precise graph construction
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation of individual interface coefficients (25%), (2) Proper matrix multiplication and overall transmission derivation (35%), (3) Accurate wavelength-dependent analysis with correct physical interpretation (25%), (4) Clear identification of dominant loss mechanisms and spectral features (15%). Students must submit calculations, graphs, and written analysis of physical mechanisms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide worked example for two-layer system first, offer step-by-step calculation template, and allow use of computational tools for matrix operations. For advanced learners: Extend to analyze oblique incidence effects, investigate anti-reflection coating optimization, or explore applications in optical filter design. Consider providing real experimental data for comparison.

title: Code Quality Evaluation: Comparing Two Basic Calculator Implementations
description: Students will analyze and evaluate two different implementations of a simple calculator program, comparing their code quality, readability, and maintainability. They will create a detailed evaluation report justifying which implementation is superior and why.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by analyzing readability, structure, and best practices in two calculator implementations
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison using established coding standards
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with two pre-written calculator programs (Calculator A and Calculator B) that perform basic arithmetic operations (+, -, *, /) but use different coding approaches. Calculator A should demonstrate good practices (clear variable names, comments, proper indentation, error handling) while Calculator B should have poor practices (unclear names, no comments, inconsistent formatting, no error handling).

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students examine both programs and complete an evaluation worksheet covering: variable naming conventions, code organization, comment quality, error handling, and overall readability. They rate each aspect on a 1-5 scale with written justifications.

**Comparison Matrix Creation (15 minutes):** Students create a side-by-side comparison table listing strengths and weaknesses of each implementation. They must identify at least 3 strengths and 3 weaknesses for each program.

**Evaluation Report Writing (25 minutes):** Students write a 300-word evaluation report recommending which calculator implementation a development team should adopt. The report must include: overall assessment, specific evidence supporting their choice, and at least two concrete improvement suggestions for their chosen implementation.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students exchange reports with a partner and provide feedback on the quality of reasoning and evidence presented.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Facilitate discussion where students defend their choices and explain their evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: Two pre-written calculator programs (Calculator A and Calculator B) in Python or Java
Code evaluation worksheet template
Comparison matrix template
Computers with text editors or IDEs installed
assessment_method: Grade the evaluation reports using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of code analysis (identifies specific good/poor practices), (2) Quality of evidence (uses concrete examples from code), (3) Clarity of recommendation (makes clear choice with solid reasoning), (4) Writing quality (clear, organized, professional). Students must score 3/4 in each category to demonstrate mastery of evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a checklist of specific code quality factors to look for (variable names, indentation, comments, etc.) and sentence starters for the evaluation report. For advanced learners: Ask them to also evaluate performance efficiency, suggest specific refactoring techniques, or compare the code against industry style guides like PEP 8 for Python.

title: Design and Build a COVID-19 Impact Dashboard for Local Business Recovery
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard that combines multiple datasets to tell the story of COVID-19's impact on local businesses and recovery patterns. They will synthesize economic, health, and demographic data to develop actionable insights for city planners and business owners.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive data visualization dashboard by integrating at least three different datasets related to COVID-19 business impacts
Students will construct data-driven recommendations through statistical analysis and create narrative explanations that connect quantitative findings to real-world policy implications
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Planning (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team selects a specific city or region and gathers three required datasets: (1) business closure/reopening data from local government sources, (2) unemployment statistics from Bureau of Labor Statistics, and (3) demographic data from Census Bureau. Teams create a project charter defining their target audience (city council, chamber of commerce, etc.), key research questions, and dashboard objectives.

**Phase 2: Data Cleaning & Integration (60 minutes)**
Using provided Python template in Jupyter Notebook, teams clean datasets by handling missing values, standardizing date formats, and merging tables on common geographic identifiers. Students document data quality issues and cleaning decisions in markdown cells. Each team must create at least one calculated field (e.g., recovery rate, impact severity index) that combines variables from multiple datasets.

**Phase 3: Analysis & Insight Development (75 minutes)**
Teams conduct exploratory data analysis using pandas and matplotlib to identify trends, correlations, and outliers. They must perform at least two statistical tests (correlation analysis, t-test, or regression) to validate their observations. Students create 5-7 preliminary visualizations and select the 3-4 most compelling for their dashboard.

**Phase 4: Dashboard Creation (90 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, teams build interactive dashboards with filtering capabilities, hover tooltips, and linked visualizations. Dashboard must include: executive summary panel, time-series trend analysis, geographic comparison view, and recommendations section with specific, measurable policy suggestions supported by their data analysis.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook with Python (pandas, matplotlib, seaborn libraries)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI (free versions)
Access to data sources: COVID-19 business impact datasets, BLS unemployment data, Census demographic data
Project charter template document
Rubric handout with dashboard design criteria
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Data Integration Quality - successful merging of 3+ datasets with proper cleaning documentation, (2) Statistical Analysis Rigor - appropriate use of statistical methods with correct interpretation, (3) Dashboard Design Excellence - clear navigation, effective visualizations, professional appearance, (4) Insight Quality - actionable recommendations supported by evidence, (5) Presentation Clarity - ability to explain methodology and defend conclusions during 10-minute team presentations. Each dimension weighted equally for final score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned sample datasets and step-by-step video tutorials for basic dashboard functions. Offer template analysis questions and visualization examples. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate machine learning predictions, add advanced statistical modeling (regression analysis), or create multiple dashboard versions for different stakeholder audiences. Encourage use of advanced Tableau features like calculated fields and dashboard actions.

title: Design and Build a COVID-19 Impact Dashboard for Local Business Recovery: Visual Analysis
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that combines multiple data sources to analyze and visualize COVID-19's impact on local businesses. They will design their own analytical framework, create custom metrics, and build a presentation tool for city council recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive analytical framework by integrating at least three different data sources and designing custom KPIs to measure business recovery patterns
Students will develop an interactive dashboard through data visualization tools that tells a cohesive story about local economic recovery with actionable insights
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes):** Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with the starter datasets: local business license data (2019-2023), unemployment statistics by zip code, and Google mobility reports. Teams spend 20 minutes exploring data structure and quality, documenting data limitations and gaps. Next 25 minutes: teams brainstorm and document their analytical approach, defining 4-5 custom metrics they will create (e.g., 'Business Recovery Index,' 'Neighborhood Resilience Score'). **Phase 2 (90 minutes):** Students clean and merge datasets using their chosen tools. They must create at least two calculated fields that don't exist in raw data. Teams document their data transformation decisions and create a data dictionary. **Phase 3 (75 minutes):** Using Tableau, Power BI, or similar tools, students build their dashboard with minimum requirements: one trend analysis, one geographic visualization, one comparative analysis, and one predictive insight. Dashboard must include interactive filters and clear narrative flow. **Phase 4 (30 minutes):** Teams prepare 5-minute presentations positioning themselves as data consultants presenting to city council. They must include methodology explanation, key findings, and three specific policy recommendations supported by their analysis.
materials_needed: Curated COVID-19 business impact datasets (Excel/CSV format)
Local unemployment and demographic data files
Google mobility reports for target geographic area
Access to Tableau Public, Power BI, or Google Data Studio
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Data analysis guide template with evaluation criteria
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five dimensions: Data Integration Quality (20%) - accuracy of merges and data cleaning; Analytical Innovation (25%) - creativity and validity of custom metrics; Dashboard Design (20%) - visual clarity and interactive functionality; Insight Quality (25%) - depth of analysis and actionable recommendations; Presentation Effectiveness (10%) - clear communication of methodology and findings. Students submit dashboard file, data documentation, and reflection memo explaining design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data merge templates and pre-calculated metric examples. Offer guided worksheet for dashboard layout planning. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external APIs, create forecasting models, or build multiple scenario analyses. Consider allowing advanced students to source additional datasets independently.
original_title: Design and Build a COVID-19 Impact Dashboard for Local Business Recovery

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and rapidly recall the 23 essential formulas, definitions, and calculation components used in Critical Path Method scheduling analysis. This activity uses spaced repetition flashcards and timed recall exercises to build foundational knowledge for advanced project scheduling calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all CPM formula components (ES, EF, LS, LF, Float, Duration) and their mathematical relationships within 30 seconds per formula set
Students will identify and state the correct sequence of CPM calculation steps through rapid-fire verbal recitation exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet containing 23 key formulas (Early Start = max EF of predecessors, Early Finish = ES + Duration, etc.). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes using the '3-2-1' memorization method: 3 minutes studying one formula set, 2 minutes partner testing without looking, 1 minute immediate review of errors. Rotate through all formula sets twice. Next, conduct 15 minutes of 'Speed Recall Rounds' where instructor calls out scenarios ('Calculate Late Start for Activity D') and students must write the correct formula and variable definitions within 45 seconds. Use a digital timer displayed prominently. For the final 20 minutes, implement 'Formula Relay Racing': teams of 4 students line up, instructor presents a network diagram on screen, first student identifies Early Start calculations needed, second student states the formula, third student identifies required inputs, fourth student verifies the mathematical relationship. Award points for accuracy and speed. Rotate team positions after each scenario. Present 8 different network scenarios of increasing complexity. Record individual accuracy rates on tracking sheets throughout all activities.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet (23 formulas printed on cardstock)
Digital countdown timer with large display
8 pre-drawn network diagrams with activity durations
Individual tracking sheets for accuracy scoring
Whiteboard markers and small whiteboards for each student
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on final speed recall test covering all 23 formula components. Assessment includes: (1) Written quiz - match 15 formulas to their correct applications within 10 minutes, (2) Verbal recitation - state complete CPM calculation sequence without reference materials, (3) Formula identification - given 5 project scenarios, identify which CPM formulas apply. Track individual performance using provided scoring rubric: 4 points for immediate correct recall, 3 points for correct with hesitation, 2 points for correct after prompting, 1 point for incorrect.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial formula set to 12 core formulas, provide mnemonic devices ('Early Start = Earliest predecessor Finishes'), use color-coded formula cards by calculation type. For advanced learners: Add resource leveling formulas, include probabilistic scheduling (PERT) formula variations, challenge them to create original mnemonic devices for classmates. Consider pairing advanced students with struggling ones during partner practice phases.

title: Analyzing Leadership Style Impacts Through Multi-Perspective Case Deconstruction
description: Students will systematically analyze how different leadership styles create cascading organizational effects by examining a complex business crisis from multiple stakeholder perspectives. This expert-level activity requires students to demonstrate deep understanding of leadership theory applications and their interconnected consequences across organizational levels.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between specific leadership behaviors and organizational outcomes by deconstructing a multi-layered crisis scenario using established leadership frameworks
Students will explain the cascading effects of leadership decisions through systematic evaluation of stakeholder impact patterns and theoretical alignment
instructions: Begin by distributing the Netflix 2011 Qwikster crisis case study materials to teams of 4 students. Assign each team member a specific stakeholder lens: Board/Investors, Middle Management, Frontline Employees, and Customers. Allow 20 minutes for individual reading and initial analysis using the provided leadership theory reference sheet (transformational, transactional, authentic, servant leadership frameworks). Each student must identify 3 specific leadership behaviors exhibited by Reed Hastings and categorize them using the frameworks. Next, conduct 30-minute team discussions where each member presents their stakeholder perspective analysis, focusing on how identified leadership behaviors impacted their assigned group. Teams must create a visual mapping showing connections between leadership behaviors and stakeholder impacts using the provided digital collaboration tool. During the final 25 minutes, facilitate whole-class presentations where 3 randomly selected teams present their analysis maps. Each presenting team must explain: (1) which leadership style dominated Hastings' approach, (2) how this style created specific positive/negative cascading effects, and (3) what alternative leadership behaviors could have produced different outcomes. Non-presenting teams submit written peer evaluations identifying one insight they gained about leadership style impacts. Conclude with a 10-minute instructor-led synthesis highlighting patterns across team analyses and connecting findings to broader leadership principles.
materials_needed: Netflix Qwikster crisis case study packet (8 pages per student)
Leadership theory reference sheet with behavioral indicators
Digital collaboration platform access (Miro, Jamboard, or Padlet)
Peer evaluation forms
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership behavior identification and theoretical categorization (25%), (2) Depth of stakeholder impact analysis with specific examples (25%), (3) Quality of visual mapping showing clear connections between behaviors and outcomes (25%), (4) Sophistication of alternative solutions proposed with theoretical justification (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly linking at least 2 leadership theories to specific case behaviors and explaining 3 cascading organizational effects.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted case study versions and leadership behavior prompt questions. Offer sentence starters for impact analysis. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by requiring integration of situational leadership theory or analysis of cultural/industry context factors. Provide extension readings on crisis leadership for deeper exploration.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Comparing Impact Assessment Methods Across Project Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three different project risk registers to compare how various risk assessment methodologies (qualitative vs. quantitative) impact project decision-making. They will deconstruct each approach to identify strengths, weaknesses, and situational appropriateness of different risk evaluation techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of qualitative versus quantitative risk assessment methods by comparing their application across three distinct project scenarios
Students will differentiate between appropriate risk response strategies through systematic examination of risk probability, impact, and organizational context
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute the three risk register case studies: (1) Software Development Project using qualitative 5x5 probability/impact matrix, (2) Construction Project using quantitative Expected Monetary Value (EMV), and (3) Marketing Campaign using hybrid qualitative-quantitative approach. Provide analysis worksheets and ensure each team has access to calculators or laptops.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Each team member takes one risk register and completes individual analysis using the provided worksheet. Students identify: risk identification methods used, assessment techniques applied, response strategies selected, and overall risk exposure calculation methods. They must document at least 5 specific observations about their assigned methodology's approach.

**Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (15 minutes):** Team members present their individual findings to teammates. Teams complete comparative analysis matrix, plotting each methodology against criteria: accuracy of risk quantification, resource requirements for assessment, stakeholder communication effectiveness, and decision-making support quality. Teams must reach consensus on ranking each method (1-3) for each criterion.

**Phase 3 - Scenario Application (15 minutes):** Present teams with a new project scenario (pharmaceutical product launch). Teams must analyze which risk assessment methodology would be most appropriate and justify their recommendation using evidence from their comparative analysis. They prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their choice and supporting rationale.

**Presentation and Debrief (20 minutes):** Each team presents their methodology recommendation. Instructor facilitates discussion on situational factors that influence risk assessment method selection, highlighting PMI standards alignment.
materials_needed: Three printed risk register case studies (Software, Construction, Marketing projects)
Individual analysis worksheets with structured observation prompts
Team comparative analysis matrix template
New scenario handout (pharmaceutical product launch)
Calculators or laptops for EMV calculations
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of individual risk methodology analysis (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis with specific evidence cited (30%), (3) Appropriateness of methodology recommendation with clear justification (30%), and (4) Effective use of PMP terminology and concepts (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion, demonstrating ability to analyze rather than simply describe risk management approaches.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided analysis questions for each risk register and definition sheet for technical terms. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring cost-benefit analysis of implementing each methodology and identification of hybrid approaches that could combine strengths of different methods. Encourage exploration of industry-specific risk assessment variations.

title: Comprehensive E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation and Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of an existing e-commerce website's Google Analytics implementation by analyzing real performance data, identifying strategic gaps, and developing evidence-based recommendations for improvement. They will assess both technical setup and business intelligence utilization to determine ROI optimization opportunities.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of current Google Analytics tracking implementation by conducting a comprehensive audit of goals, events, and conversion funnels against industry best practices

Students will synthesize quantitative performance data and qualitative user behavior insights to formulate strategic recommendations for improving e-commerce conversion rates and customer lifetime value
instructions:
Begin by providing students with access to a demo e-commerce Google Analytics account (or case study dataset) containing 6 months of performance data. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical data but will focus on different business scenarios (B2B vs B2C, seasonal vs year-round, mobile-first vs desktop-focused). 

Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct technical audit using provided checklist, examining goal setup, Enhanced Ecommerce tracking, attribution models, audience segmentation, and custom dimensions. Students document gaps between current implementation and Google Analytics 4 best practices.

Step 2 (60 minutes): Teams analyze performance data focusing on acquisition channels, user behavior flow, product performance, and revenue attribution. Students must identify top 3 conversion optimization opportunities using data visualization tools and statistical significance testing.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate current attribution model effectiveness by comparing last-click, first-click, linear, and data-driven attribution results. Students assess which model provides most actionable insights for their assigned business scenario.

Step 4 (45 minutes): Teams synthesize findings into strategic recommendations, prioritizing initiatives by potential ROI impact, implementation difficulty, and resource requirements. Students must justify recommendations using specific metrics and benchmarks.

Step 5 (30 minutes): Each team presents 8-minute recommendations to class, followed by peer evaluation using structured feedback forms focusing on data interpretation accuracy, strategic thinking, and feasibility assessment.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce data or comprehensive case study dataset
Technical audit checklist template with 25+ evaluation criteria
Data visualization software (Google Data Studio or Tableau)
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Business scenario assignment cards with specific context details
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 100-point rubric: Technical audit completeness and accuracy (25 points), data analysis depth and statistical rigor (25 points), strategic recommendation quality and feasibility (25 points), presentation clarity and peer feedback incorporation (15 points), and professional deliverable formatting (10 points). Peer evaluations contribute 20% of final score.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with guided analysis templates and sample calculations for key metrics. Offer mid-activity checkpoint consultations to verify analysis direction. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity through multi-channel attribution modeling, customer lifetime value calculations, or competitive benchmarking requirements. Consider pairing analytics beginners with experienced students within teams.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Campus Network with OSPF and Advanced Security Policies
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise campus network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF dynamic routing, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize advanced networking concepts into a functional, secure network infrastructure that meets specific business requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced routing protocols and security policies through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers using CLI commands
Students will validate network functionality by creating comprehensive testing procedures and troubleshooting scenarios
instructions: **Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)** - Provide students with a fictional company scenario requiring 6 departments across 3 floors. Students work in pairs to create a network topology diagram using Visio or Packet Tracer, designing VLANs for each department (Sales, HR, IT, Finance, Guest, Management), calculating subnets using VLSM for 500+ total hosts, and documenting OSPF area assignments. **Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)** - Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment (3 Layer 3 switches, 2 routers), students configure VLANs and trunk ports on switches, implement inter-VLAN routing using SVI interfaces, configure OSPF routing with proper area design (Area 0 backbone, Area 1 for departments), and apply port security limiting MAC addresses to 2 per port. **Phase 3: Security Implementation (60 minutes)** - Students create and apply ACLs restricting Guest VLAN access to internet only, implement SSH access with encrypted passwords on all devices, configure DHCP snooping and ARP inspection on access ports, and establish NTP synchronization across all network devices. **Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)** - Students verify connectivity between all VLANs using ping and traceroute, test ACL functionality by attempting blocked connections, generate OSPF neighbor tables and routing tables as evidence, and create a final network documentation package including configurations, IP addressing tables, and security policy summaries.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or 3 Cisco Catalyst 3560 switches
2 Cisco ISR 4000 series routers (if using physical equipment)
Ethernet cables (Cat 6) - minimum 12 cables
Console cables for device access
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart for network diagrams
Network documentation templates (IP addressing worksheets)
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Network topology diagram with VLSM calculations (25 points), (2) Complete device configurations exported as .txt files (30 points), (3) Screenshot evidence of successful ping tests between VLANs and OSPF neighbor relationships (25 points), (4) Security verification showing ACL logs and SSH connectivity (20 points). Rubric evaluates technical accuracy, adherence to best practices, completeness of documentation, and demonstration of working network functionality.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide IP addressing calculation worksheets, OSPF configuration templates, and step-by-step CLI command guides. Allow use of pre-configured base templates in Packet Tracer. **Extensions for advanced learners:** Add BGP configuration for external routing, implement QoS policies for voice traffic prioritization, configure HSRP for gateway redundancy, or add wireless controller integration with guest portal authentication.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Game
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and speed recognition activities. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid-fire recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, with one partner showing decimal numbers while the other recalls the binary equivalent, then switching roles after 7 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class 'Binary Bingo' game where each student receives a 4x4 grid filled with random decimal numbers 0-15. Call out binary numbers (e.g., '1010') and students must identify the decimal equivalent (10) and mark it on their grid. Continue until someone achieves four in a row. For the final 10 minutes, implement a 'Lightning Round' where students stand and you rapidly display binary numbers on the projector screen for 3 seconds each. Students who correctly identify the decimal equivalent remain standing, while incorrect answers sit down. The last 2-3 students standing win. Throughout all activities, emphasize that students should visualize the place values (8-4-2-1) to aid memorization. Circulate during pair work to identify students struggling with specific numbers and provide individual coaching on place value breakdown.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Binary Bingo cards (4x4 grids with random decimal numbers 0-15)
Computer/projector for displaying binary numbers
Markers or chips for Bingo cards
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/15 correct) on a final 2-minute speed quiz where they write binary equivalents for randomly ordered decimal numbers 0-15. Track participation during Lightning Round - students who remain standing for at least 8 correct answers demonstrate mastery. Observe pair work interactions and note students who consistently hesitate beyond 5 seconds per conversion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a place value chart (8-4-2-1) and start with numbers 0-7 only, gradually adding 8-15. Create memory aids like 'nine is 1001 - bookends of 1s around two zeros.' For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need support during flashcard practice.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Healthcare Datasets
description: Students will analyze authentic healthcare datasets to distinguish between correlation and causation by examining statistical relationships and identifying confounding variables. They will interpret scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and study design elements to explain why strong correlations may not indicate causal relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing three healthcare datasets with varying degrees of statistical relationships
Students will interpret correlation coefficients and scatter plots through guided examination of confounding variables and alternative explanations
instructions:
Begin by providing each student team (3-4 members) with three pre-loaded Jupyter notebooks containing healthcare datasets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths by month, (2) Number of hospitals vs. mortality rate by city, and (3) Smoking vs. lung cancer rates with age controls. Start with a 10-minute mini-lecture reviewing correlation coefficient ranges (-1 to +1) and scatter plot interpretation. 

For the first 20 minutes, teams work through Dataset 1, calculating Pearson correlation coefficients using pandas.corr() and creating scatter plots with matplotlib. Students record the correlation strength and initially hypothesize about causation. Then introduce the concept of lurking variables - guide them to consider seasonal temperature as the confounding factor.

During minutes 20-40, teams analyze Dataset 2, again calculating correlations and plotting relationships. This time, facilitate discovery that cities with more hospitals often have higher populations and more severe cases, making hospitals a marker of healthcare demand rather than a cause of mortality.

In the final 25 minutes, examine Dataset 3 which shows genuine causation supported by controlled study design. Students compare correlation coefficients across age groups and examine how the relationship remains consistent when controlling for confounding variables.

Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where each team presents one dataset, explaining their correlation findings and whether causation can be inferred. Teams must provide specific evidence from their analysis and identify at least two alternative explanations for each correlation.
materials_needed: Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with healthcare variables
Laptop/computer access for each student team
Correlation interpretation reference sheet
Digital whiteboard or presentation screen
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficients, (2) Accurate identification of confounding variables in at least 2/3 datasets, (3) Clear articulation of why correlation ≠ causation with specific examples, (4) Quality of alternative explanations provided during presentation. Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide correlation coefficient interpretation charts and sentence starters like 'This correlation might be explained by...' Advanced learners can explore partial correlation analysis using scipy.stats or investigate additional datasets with multiple confounding variables. Consider pairing weaker statistics students with stronger peers during team formation.

title: Analyzing Complex Circuit Behavior Using Kirchhoff's Laws and Thevenin Equivalent Analysis
description: Students will decompose a multi-loop DC circuit containing dependent sources into component relationships and systematically analyze voltage/current distributions. They will then synthesize their findings by determining the Thevenin equivalent circuit and comparing predicted versus measured behaviors.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependent relationships between voltages and currents in a complex multi-loop circuit by applying Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws systematically
Students will examine the validity of circuit simplification techniques through comparison of Thevenin equivalent predictions with original circuit measurements
instructions:
Begin by distributing the circuit schematic containing two independent voltage sources (12V and 8V), one current-controlled voltage source (2i₁), four resistors (R₁=100Ω, R₂=220Ω, R₃=330Ω, R₄=470Ω), and three distinct loops. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. 

Step 1 (20 min): Have students identify all nodes, loops, and branch currents, then write the complete set of KVL and KCL equations without solving. They must justify their choice of current directions and loop orientations.

Step 2 (25 min): Students solve the system of equations using matrix methods to find all branch currents and node voltages. They must show intermediate steps and verify their solution satisfies all original equations.

Step 3 (20 min): Students physically construct the circuit using breadboard and measure actual voltages/currents using multimeters. They record discrepancies between theoretical and measured values, identifying potential sources of error.

Step 4 (15 min): Students determine the Thevenin equivalent circuit as seen from terminals across R₄, calculating VTH and RTH analytically.

Step 5 (10 min): Students replace the original circuit with their calculated Thevenin equivalent and measure the current through R₄, comparing this with both their original theoretical calculation and original circuit measurement. They must explain any discrepancies and assess which method provides most reliable results for practical circuit analysis.
materials_needed: Circuit schematic with specified component values
Breadboard and connecting wires
Resistors: 100Ω, 220Ω, 330Ω, 470Ω (±5% tolerance)
DC power supplies (12V and 8V adjustable)
Digital multimeters (voltage and current measurement)
Current-controlled voltage source or op-amp circuit equivalent
Scientific calculator or computer with matrix calculation capability
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correctness of KVL/KCL equation setup (25 points), (2) Accuracy of mathematical solution with clear methodology (25 points), (3) Quality of experimental measurements and error analysis (25 points), (4) Validity of Thevenin analysis and comparison conclusions (25 points). Students must submit completed calculations, measurement data tables, and written analysis of discrepancies between methods.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template matrices for equation organization and step-by-step Thevenin calculation worksheet. Review dependent source analysis separately if needed. For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict how results would change with ±20% component tolerance variations, or extend analysis to include AC steady-state behavior with reactive components.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Analytics Dashboard for Student Retention
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts student dropout risk using synthetic university enrollment data. They will design their own analytical framework, select appropriate visualizations, and present actionable insights to stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multiple data analysis techniques by combining descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and predictive modeling into a comprehensive analytical framework
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through strategic selection and integration of visualizations that communicate complex patterns to non-technical stakeholders
instructions:
Begin by providing teams of 3-4 students with a synthetic dataset containing 5,000 student records including demographics, academic performance, engagement metrics, and retention outcomes. (15 minutes setup)

Phase 1 - Framework Design (45 minutes): Teams brainstorm and document their analytical approach by identifying 3-5 key research questions about student retention, selecting relevant variables, and sketching their intended dashboard layout on paper. Each team presents their framework to another team for feedback.

Phase 2 - Data Exploration (60 minutes): Students perform exploratory data analysis using their chosen tool, calculating summary statistics, identifying missing data patterns, and discovering correlations. They must document at least three surprising findings and explain their potential impact on retention prediction.

Phase 3 - Model Development (75 minutes): Teams create a predictive model using logistic regression or decision trees, splitting data into training/testing sets, evaluating model performance using accuracy and confusion matrices, and identifying the top 5 most important predictive factors.

Phase 4 - Dashboard Construction (90 minutes): Students build their interactive dashboard incorporating: executive summary with key metrics, risk factor visualization showing top predictors, student segmentation charts, prediction accuracy display, and actionable recommendations panel. All visualizations must include appropriate titles, labels, and color coding.

Phase 5 - Stakeholder Presentation (30 minutes): Each team delivers a 7-minute presentation to simulated university administrators, explaining their methodology, demonstrating dashboard functionality, and providing three specific intervention recommendations with supporting evidence.
materials_needed: Synthetic student dataset (CSV file with 5000 records, 15 variables)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software
Large paper sheets and markers for framework sketching
Projection equipment for presentations
Stakeholder persona cards (Dean, Academic Advisor, IT Director)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Dashboard functionality and design (25 points), analytical rigor and model accuracy (25 points), insight quality and business relevance (25 points), presentation clarity and stakeholder focus (25 points). Students must achieve minimum 15 points in each category and demonstrate working dashboard interactivity.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students with pre-made data analysis templates and step-by-step dashboard building guides. Provide advanced learners with additional datasets for cross-validation or challenge them to implement advanced features like drill-down capabilities and automated alerting systems.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Recognition and Terminology Recall
description: Students will systematically identify and recall specific elements, terminology, and calculation components within complex Critical Path Method network diagrams. This activity focuses on accurate recognition and definition of advanced CPM concepts including forward pass, backward pass, total float, free float, and critical activities.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and correctly label all CPM network diagram components including early start (ES), early finish (EF), late start (LS), late finish (LF), and activity durations by examining provided complex project networks
Students will recall and accurately define 15 specific CPM terminology terms through structured flashcard exercises and verbal recitation drills
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-drawn CPM network diagrams featuring 12-15 interconnected activities with partially completed time calculations (5 minutes setup). Provide each student with a CPM terminology reference sheet face-down initially. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to identify and circle all ES, EF, LS, LF values visible on their diagram, then label empty nodes with the correct abbreviations. They must also identify the critical path by highlighting it in red. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Flip reference sheets and conduct rapid-fire terminology recall. Call out definitions while students write corresponding terms (e.g., 'The amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting project completion' - answer: Total Float). Phase 3 (10 minutes): Students pair up to quiz each other using provided flashcards containing 15 advanced CPM terms including: precedence relationships, dummy activities, crash duration, crash cost, resource leveling, fast tracking, crashing, schedule compression, activity-on-node (AON), activity-on-arrow (AOA). Phase 4 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class verification where students call out components they identified on their diagrams while instructor confirms accuracy on projected master diagram.
materials_needed: Pre-printed CPM network diagrams (one per student) with 12-15 activities and partial calculations
CPM terminology reference sheets with 15 advanced terms and definitions
Laminated flashcards with CPM terms and definitions (one set per pair)
Red highlighting pens for critical path marking
Projector for displaying master diagram solution
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy on diagram component identification (correctly label minimum 12 of 15 ES/EF/LS/LF values and identify critical path) and demonstrate 85% accuracy on terminology recall (correctly define minimum 13 of 15 terms during flashcard exercises). Instructor uses checklist to track individual student responses during pair work and records accuracy scores for both diagram analysis and term definitions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded diagrams where different calculation types use different colors, and offer abbreviated terminology cards with only 10 key terms. For advanced learners: Add resource-constrained network diagrams requiring identification of resource conflicts, and include terms related to Monte Carlo simulation and PERT analysis. Consider providing blank network templates for students to practice drawing their own diagrams.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Communication Patterns in Crisis Scenarios
description: Students will analyze authentic leadership communication artifacts from three different crisis scenarios (corporate, military, and nonprofit contexts) to identify and classify distinct leadership communication patterns, approaches, and their underlying theoretical frameworks. This activity develops deep comprehension of how leadership theory translates into practice across diverse high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and adaptive leadership communication strategies by analyzing real crisis communication transcripts and identifying specific linguistic and structural patterns

Students will interpret the relationship between situational context variables and leadership approach selection through systematic comparison of leader responses across three distinct crisis scenarios
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5, ensuring each group has access to the digital case study packet containing: (1) Tylenol poisoning crisis - James Burke's internal and external communications, (2) Apollo 13 mission - Gene Kranz's mission control communications, and (3) Hurricane Katrina response - Red Cross leadership communications. Provide each group with the Leadership Communication Analysis Framework handout.

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each group member individually reviews one complete communication set, using the analysis framework to identify: communication tone and style, decision-making patterns, stakeholder engagement approaches, and emotional regulation strategies. Students mark specific textual evidence and timestamp references.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Group members share their individual analyses, creating a collaborative comparison matrix on the provided template. Groups identify patterns, contradictions, and unique approaches across the three scenarios.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Groups classify each leader's dominant approach using Goleman's leadership styles framework, providing specific textual evidence for their classifications. They must identify at least three distinct communication patterns per leader.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Groups prepare a 3-minute presentation summarizing their key findings, focusing on how contextual factors influenced leadership communication choices. Each presentation must include one surprising insight and one practical application.

Phase 5 (15 minutes): Groups present findings, followed by instructor-facilitated discussion connecting observations to leadership theory frameworks covered in previous sessions.
materials_needed: Digital case study packet with timestamped transcripts and video clips from three crisis scenarios
Leadership Communication Analysis Framework handout with structured analysis prompts
Comparison matrix template (digital or print)
Goleman's Six Leadership Styles reference sheet
Presentation timer and projection capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of pattern identification with specific textual evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of contextual influences (25%), (3) Correct application of theoretical frameworks to real examples (25%), (4) Synthesis demonstrated through insights connecting theory to practice (25%). Students must achieve proficiency in at least 3 categories to demonstrate understanding-level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key passages and guiding questions for each communication example. Consider pairing with stronger analytical peers. For advanced learners: Add a fourth crisis scenario requiring independent analysis, or challenge them to identify additional theoretical frameworks beyond those provided. Encourage connections to current events or personal leadership experiences.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for ROI Optimization
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive audit of an e-commerce website's Google Analytics setup, critically evaluate the effectiveness of current attribution models against business objectives, and defend their recommended attribution strategy changes. This activity requires students to synthesize technical GA knowledge with business strategy to make data-driven recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of current attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and comparing multi-channel funnel reports against stated business objectives

Students will critique existing Google Analytics configuration decisions through systematic assessment of goal setup, audience segmentation, and channel groupings to identify optimization opportunities
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Data Collection & Initial Assessment**
Provide students with access to a demo Google Analytics account for a fictional e-commerce business (or create realistic sample reports). Students work in pairs to document the current setup: attribution model in use, conversion goals configured, audience segments defined, and channel groupings. They export key reports including Multi-Channel Funnels > Assisted Conversions, Attribution > Model Comparison Tool, and Conversions > Goals Overview for the past 90 days.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Critical Analysis**
Students analyze the exported data to identify patterns and discrepancies. They must evaluate whether the current attribution model aligns with the customer journey length (using Time Lag and Path Length reports), assess if channel performance metrics support or contradict the business's marketing spend allocation, and identify potential attribution bias affecting decision-making. Students create a findings matrix documenting strengths, weaknesses, and gaps in the current approach.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Strategy Development**
Based on their analysis, student pairs develop alternative attribution model recommendations. They must justify their choices using specific data points, calculate potential impact on reported ROI for each marketing channel, and identify implementation requirements (custom channels, goal modifications, audience adjustments).

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Peer Review & Defense**
Pairs present their recommendations to another team for critical review. The reviewing team challenges assumptions, questions methodology, and suggests alternatives. Presenting teams must defend their recommendations with evidence and acknowledge limitations in their approach.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Sample business brief with marketing objectives and budget allocation
Data export templates for Multi-Channel Funnels and Attribution reports
Evaluation matrix template for documenting findings
Presentation template for recommendations
assessment_method: Students submit a 3-page executive summary with: (1) Current state assessment with specific data citations (25 points), (2) Critical evaluation of attribution model effectiveness with quantified impact analysis (35 points), (3) Justified recommendations with implementation roadmap (25 points), (4) Acknowledgment of limitations and potential risks (15 points). Peer review quality and defense during presentation contribute additional 10 points. Rubric emphasizes use of specific GA metrics, logical reasoning, and business impact quantification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheets with specific GA report locations and sample calculation formulas. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Introduce custom attribution modeling concepts, require integration of Google Ads data, or add competitive analysis component using similar GA setups. Offer access to advanced segments and custom dimensions for deeper analysis.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for ROI Optimization: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate three different attribution models (last-click, first-click, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data from Google Analytics 4, comparing their effectiveness in measuring campaign ROI. They will assess the strengths and limitations of each model and recommend the optimal attribution strategy for a specific business scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and comparing revenue attribution across channels
Students will critique current attribution strategies through systematic analysis of customer journey data and business impact metrics
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to Google Analytics 4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store) or prepared dataset exports. Distribute three business scenarios: B2B SaaS (long sales cycle), fast fashion retailer (short cycle), and luxury goods (research-heavy). Students work in teams of 3-4, each assigned one scenario. **Phase 1 - Data Collection (20 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison in GA4. They must extract conversion and revenue data for the past 3 months across all three attribution models (last-click, first-click, data-driven). Record data for paid search, display, social media, and email channels in provided spreadsheet template. **Phase 2 - Comparative Analysis (25 minutes):** Teams calculate percentage differences in attributed conversions and revenue between models for each channel. They identify which channels gain/lose credit under each model and analyze the customer journey length and touchpoint patterns using Path Analysis reports. **Phase 3 - Business Context Evaluation (20 minutes):** Students evaluate each attribution model against their assigned business scenario, considering factors like sales cycle length, average order value, customer acquisition cost, and marketing budget allocation. They must identify potential over/under-investment in channels based on different attribution models. **Phase 4 - Strategic Recommendation (15 minutes):** Teams prepare 5-minute presentations defending their recommended attribution model, including specific implementation timeline, expected impact on marketing spend allocation, and key performance indicators for measuring success.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account access or prepared data exports
Attribution analysis spreadsheet template with pre-formatted calculations
Three detailed business scenario handouts with company background and marketing objectives
Presentation template with evaluation criteria framework
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using rubric (100 points total): Data accuracy and completeness (25 points), depth of comparative analysis with specific metrics (25 points), quality of business context integration and scenario alignment (25 points), strength of recommendation justification with implementation details (25 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of attribution model limitations and provide quantified impact projections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation screenshots and pre-identified key metrics to focus on. Include decision-making framework checklist. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional factors like view-through conversions, cross-device tracking limitations, or privacy regulation impacts. Have them calculate statistical confidence intervals for their recommendations.
original_title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for ROI Optimization

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for ROI Optimization: Business Application
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics for a real e-commerce business scenario. They will analyze three months of multi-channel funnel data, assess the impact of different attribution models on marketing budget allocation decisions, and defend their recommended attribution strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, position-based) by analyzing their impact on conversion credit distribution and ROI calculations
Students will critique existing marketing channel performance interpretations through comparative analysis of attribution model outputs and justify optimal budget reallocation strategies
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Analysis Setup (20 minutes)**

Provide students with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 3 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Students work in pairs to navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool.

**Phase 2: Attribution Model Comparison (40 minutes)**

Students systematically analyze each attribution model by: (1) Recording conversion values and channel performance rankings under each model, (2) Calculating percentage differences in attributed conversions between models for each channel, (3) Identifying which channels gain/lose credit most dramatically when switching models, (4) Documenting how customer journey length affects model selection.

**Phase 3: Business Impact Assessment (30 minutes)**

Using provided marketing channel costs ($50,000 total monthly budget distributed as: Paid Search 40%, Social Media 25%, Email 20%, Display 15%), students calculate ROI under each attribution model and determine how budget reallocation would change based on model choice.

**Phase 4: Strategic Evaluation and Defense (40 minutes)**

Students prepare a 10-minute presentation evaluating: (1) Which attribution model most accurately reflects customer behavior patterns in the data, (2) Potential risks and benefits of adopting their recommended model, (3) How their choice would change marketing spend allocation, (4) Defense against counterarguments for alternative models. Each pair presents to another pair, followed by structured debate on model selection rationale.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Spreadsheet template for attribution model comparison data
Marketing budget allocation worksheet with channel costs
Customer journey mapping template
Presentation template for strategy defense
assessment_method: Students evaluated using rubric (100 points total): Data Analysis Accuracy (25 points - correct calculation of attribution differences), Critical Evaluation Quality (30 points - depth of analysis on model appropriateness), Strategic Reasoning (25 points - logical connection between data insights and budget recommendations), Defense Presentation (20 points - ability to justify choices and respond to challenges). Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated ability to defend model selection against peer critique.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data comparison tables and guided questions for each analysis step. Create checkpoint reviews after each phase. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using Google Analytics, analysis of view-through conversions, and consideration of offline conversion importing. Challenge them to incorporate statistical significance testing of attribution model differences.
original_title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for ROI Optimization

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise WAN Solution with SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise WAN infrastructure connecting three geographically distributed sites using traditional MPLS, broadband backup links, and Cisco SD-WAN overlay technology. They will create comprehensive network documentation, security policies, and traffic engineering schemes while implementing Quality of Service prioritization for critical business applications.
learning_objectives: Students will design a resilient multi-site WAN architecture by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network topology diagrams with OSPF routing, MPLS connectivity, and SD-WAN overlay implementation
Students will construct complete router configurations through hands-on CLI implementation including BGP peering, IPSec tunnels, QoS policies, and centralized policy management using Cisco vManage
instructions: Begin with a 45-minute planning phase where students analyze the provided business scenario: Company XYZ requires connectivity between headquarters (500 users), branch office (150 users), and data center (hosting critical applications). Students work in teams of 3-4 to create detailed network diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes (using /24 subnets from 10.10.0.0/16), VLAN assignments, and routing protocols. Next, conduct a 90-minute configuration phase using Cisco VIRL or EVE-NG simulation environment. Each team configures three ISR 4000 series routers as site edge devices, implementing OSPF Area 0 for internal routing, eBGP peering with service provider (AS 65001), and establishing IPSec site-to-site tunnels as backup connectivity. Students then spend 60 minutes implementing SD-WAN overlay using vEdge routers, creating centralized policies in vManage for application-aware routing, directing voice traffic over MPLS and bulk data over broadband links. The final 75-minute phase involves comprehensive testing and documentation. Teams verify end-to-end connectivity using extended ping tests, trace routing between all sites, and traffic flow validation using built-in packet capture tools. Students create executive summary reports documenting network performance metrics, failover scenarios, and cost-benefit analysis comparing traditional WAN versus SD-WAN implementation. Each team presents their solution in a 10-minute presentation highlighting design decisions, challenges encountered, and lessons learned. Instructors circulate during configuration phases to provide guidance on complex CLI syntax and troubleshoot connectivity issues.
materials_needed: Cisco VIRL or EVE-NG network simulation software with ISR 4000 and vEdge router images
Business requirements document template with specific application requirements and SLA metrics
Network documentation templates including topology diagrams, IP address allocation sheets, and configuration checklists
Access to Cisco vManage sandbox environment or simulation equivalent
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - topology accuracy, IP addressing scheme, protocol selection), Configuration Implementation (35 points - working OSPF/BGP, successful IPSec tunnels, functional SD-WAN policies), Testing and Validation (20 points - comprehensive connectivity tests, performance measurements, failover demonstrations), and Professional Documentation (20 points - clear network diagrams, complete configuration backup files, executive summary quality). Students must achieve 80% minimum score with all sites maintaining full connectivity under normal and failure scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured base templates with basic IP addressing and interface configurations, allowing focus on advanced routing and SD-WAN concepts. Offer step-by-step configuration guides for complex BGP and IPSec implementations. For advanced learners, introduce additional challenges such as implementing DMVPN for branch-to-branch communication, integrating Cisco DNA Center for policy management, or designing multi-tenant segmentation using VRF-Lite technology. Provide access to Cisco documentation and online learning modules for independent research.

title: Programming Terminology Memory Palace Card Match
description: Students will memorize and recall 20 fundamental programming terms and their exact definitions through a physical card-matching activity. This activity focuses on building foundational vocabulary essential for beginning programmers.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recall the exact definitions of 20 basic programming terms including variable, function, loop, array, and boolean by matching term cards to definition cards
Students will demonstrate memorization of programming vocabulary through verbal recitation and written recall exercises
instructions:
Begin by preparing 40 cards: 20 with programming terms (variable, function, loop, array, boolean, string, integer, algorithm, debugging, compiler, syntax, parameter, argument, return, conditional, iteration, object, class, method, library) and 20 with their corresponding definitions. Shuffle both sets separately. Divide students into pairs and give each pair one complete set of shuffled cards. 

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students spread all cards face-up on their desks and work together to match each term with its correct definition. Circulate to provide immediate feedback and corrections. Once pairs successfully match all 20 terms, have them read each match aloud to their partner.

Phase 2 (8 minutes): Students flip all definition cards face-down, keeping only term cards visible. Partner A picks a term card and must recite the definition from memory. Partner B checks the corresponding definition card for accuracy. They alternate roles until all terms are covered.

Phase 3 (7 minutes): Remove all cards. Give each student a blank worksheet listing the 20 terms. Students must write the complete definition for each term from memory within the time limit. No collaboration allowed during this phase.

Conclude with a whole-class review where volunteers share definitions for randomly selected terms. Correct any misconceptions immediately and have the class repeat correct definitions in unison for reinforcement.
materials_needed: 40 index cards per pair (20 terms, 20 definitions)
Printed definition reference sheet for instructor
Blank recall worksheets with 20 programming terms listed
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must correctly write definitions for at least 16 out of 20 terms (80% accuracy) on the final recall worksheet. Award full points for definitions that include key components and use precise terminology. Partial credit given for definitions missing minor details but demonstrating core understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide visual cues or first letters of key words in definitions. Allow extended time during recall phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to create example code snippets demonstrating each term or provide additional advanced terms like polymorphism, inheritance, or recursion for extra practice.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance Rankings in Machine Learning Models
description: Students will analyze and compare feature importance outputs from different machine learning algorithms to understand how models prioritize variables. They will interpret the rankings and explain the business implications of these findings using a real estate pricing dataset.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance scores from Random Forest and Linear Regression models by ranking variables and explaining their relative contributions to predictions
Students will compare feature importance patterns across different algorithms through systematic analysis of coefficient values and ranking differences
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a trained Random Forest and Linear Regression model on the Boston Housing dataset (15 minutes setup). Students work in pairs to complete four sequential tasks. First, they extract feature importance scores from both models and create side-by-side comparison tables showing feature names, importance scores, and rankings (20 minutes). Second, they identify the top 5 most important features for each model and calculate ranking differences between algorithms (15 minutes). Third, students create two horizontal bar charts visualizing feature importance scores for each model, ensuring proper labeling and sorting by importance (25 minutes). Fourth, they write a 200-word interpretation explaining why certain features rank differently between models, connecting findings to real estate domain knowledge (e.g., why location features might be weighted differently by tree-based vs linear models). Students must address three specific questions: Which features show the largest ranking differences? What algorithmic properties might explain these differences? How would these insights inform feature selection for a real estate pricing application? Conclude with pair presentations where each team shares one key insight about feature ranking differences (20 minutes). Instructors circulate during analysis phases, ensuring students focus on interpretation rather than just calculation.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook with pre-trained Random Forest and Linear Regression models on Boston Housing dataset
Python environment with scikit-learn, pandas, and matplotlib installed
Feature importance extraction code templates
Comparison table worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate extraction and ranking of feature importance scores (25%), (2) Correct identification of ranking differences between models (25%), (3) Quality of visualizations with proper labeling and formatting (25%), (4) Written interpretation demonstrating understanding of why algorithms produce different rankings and business implications (25%).
