Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled comparison tables with partial data and guided questions about specific features. Offer sentence starters for interpretations like 'Random Forest ranks X higher because...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate correlation between feature rankings, research additional feature importance methods (SHAP, permutation importance), or analyze feature interactions that might explain ranking differences.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Business Scenarios Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques and linear programming to solve real-world business problems involving profit maximization and resource allocation. They will work through three progressively complex scenarios requiring them to set up constraint systems, find critical points, and interpret solutions in business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization methods to determine maximum profit points by setting up Lagrangian functions with business constraints
Students will implement linear programming techniques to solve resource allocation problems through graphical and simplex methods
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute the three business scenario packets: (1) Manufacturing company with two products and material constraints, (2) Restaurant chain optimizing menu items with labor and ingredient limits, (3) Investment portfolio with risk-return constraints. Each team receives calculators, graphing materials, and digital access to optimization software. **Phase 2 (40 minutes):** Teams work through Scenario 1 together. They must: identify decision variables (x, y), write the objective function for profit maximization, establish constraint inequalities from given resource limits, graph the feasible region, and find corner points using substitution method. Instructor circulates to verify constraint setup and mathematical accuracy. **Phase 3 (35 minutes):** Teams tackle Scenario 2 independently, now applying Lagrange multipliers for the constrained optimization problem. They calculate partial derivatives, set up the Lagrangian L(x,y,λ) = f(x,y) - λg(x,y), solve the system of equations ∇L = 0, and verify using second derivative test. **Phase 4 (25 minutes):** Teams present their solution approach for Scenario 3 to another team, explaining their mathematical reasoning and business interpretation. They must justify why their solution is optimal and discuss sensitivity analysis implications. **Phase 5 (15 minutes):** Whole-class debrief where teams share which optimization method worked best for each scenario type and common pitfalls encountered.
materials_needed: Three printed business scenario packets with specific numerical data
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent)
Graph paper and colored pencils for feasible region plotting
GeoGebra or Desmos online graphing access
Linear programming solver software or Excel Solver add-in
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct mathematical setup of objective functions and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of optimization techniques with proper notation (35%), (3) Valid interpretation of mathematical results in business context (25%), (4) Clear communication of solution process during peer presentation (15%). Students submit written work showing all calculations and final business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint identification templates and step-by-step Lagrangian setup guides. Pair with stronger mathematical teammates initially. For advanced learners: Add integer programming constraints or introduce dual problem analysis. Challenge them to create sensitivity analysis graphs showing how optimal solutions change with parameter variations.

title: Analyzing Quantum Tunneling Probability Distributions in Multi-Barrier Systems
description: Students will analyze transmission coefficient data from simulated quantum tunneling experiments through double and triple barrier systems. They will decompose complex probability distributions, identify resonance conditions, and examine how barrier parameters affect tunneling characteristics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze transmission probability patterns by identifying resonance peaks and their relationship to barrier spacing in multi-barrier quantum systems
Students will examine the relationship between barrier height, width, and particle energy through systematic comparison of probability distribution curves
instructions: Begin by distributing the quantum tunneling simulation dataset containing transmission coefficients for electrons (mass = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) through double and triple rectangular barriers with varying parameters. Students work in pairs using graphing software to plot transmission probability T versus particle energy E for three scenarios: (1) double barriers with d=2nm spacing, heights V₁=V₂=1.5eV, widths w₁=w₂=0.5nm, (2) same system with d=4nm spacing, and (3) triple barrier system with identical 1.0eV barriers separated by 1.5nm gaps. In the first 45 minutes, students create overlaid plots for scenarios 1-2, identifying and marking all resonance peaks where T>0.8. They calculate the energy differences between consecutive peaks and determine if spacing follows the relationship ΔE ∝ 1/d². Next, students analyze scenario 3 by comparing peak positions to single-barrier calculations, identifying which peaks correspond to single-well resonances versus multi-well coupling effects. They examine peak widths (full-width half-maximum) and correlate narrow peaks with longer particle dwell times using the time-energy uncertainty principle. In the final 30 minutes, students create a comparative analysis chart showing how barrier separation affects: peak spacing, maximum transmission values, and the number of resonances within 0-3eV range. They must identify at least two instances where increased barrier separation leads to peak splitting and explain this using quantum interference principles.
materials_needed: Quantum tunneling simulation dataset (CSV files with E vs T data for 3 scenarios)
Graphing software (Origin, MATLAB, or Python with matplotlib)
Scientific calculators
Analysis worksheet template with guided questions
assessment_method: Evaluate students on: (1) Accurate identification of resonance peaks (±0.05eV precision) - 30 points, (2) Correct calculation and verification of ΔE ∝ 1/d² relationship within 15% theoretical value - 25 points, (3) Proper distinction between single-well and multi-well resonances with physical explanations - 25 points, (4) Analysis of peak width trends with quantitative supporting data - 20 points. Students submit annotated graphs and completed analysis worksheets.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-marked example peaks on the first dataset and give specific energy ranges to focus analysis. Offer a reference sheet with key quantum tunneling formulas. For advanced learners, include additional datasets with asymmetric barriers or challenge them to predict transmission patterns for a four-barrier system using their derived relationships. Provide supplementary questions about temperature effects on tunneling probability.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Password Validation Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate three different password validation code samples by analyzing their functionality, security practices, and code quality. They will rank the solutions and provide detailed justifications for their evaluation decisions using established coding criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate password validation code implementations by assessing functionality, security, readability, and efficiency using a structured rubric
Students will justify their ranking decisions through written analysis that compares code quality across multiple criteria
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-written password validation functions (15 minutes setup). Each function should validate passwords with different approaches: Function A uses basic length checking, Function B includes complexity requirements but has security flaws, and Function C implements comprehensive validation with proper security practices but complex syntax. Provide students with the evaluation rubric covering four criteria: Functionality (Does it work correctly?), Security (Are passwords properly protected?), Readability (Is the code easy to understand?), and Efficiency (Does it perform well?). Students work individually for 25 minutes to test each function with sample inputs, trace through the code logic, and score each function on a 1-4 scale per criterion. They must document specific evidence for each score (e.g., 'Function B scores 2/4 on security because passwords are stored in plain text on line 12'). Next, students rank the three functions from best to worst overall and write a 200-word justification explaining their ranking decision, addressing trade-offs between criteria. In the final 15 minutes, facilitate a class discussion where 3-4 students share their rankings and reasoning. Conclude by revealing which function represents industry best practices and discussing why evaluation skills matter in professional development.
materials_needed: Three pre-written password validation functions (printed or digital)
Code evaluation rubric handout
Sample password test cases (weak, medium, strong passwords)
Computers or tablets for code testing
Visual Studio Code or online code editor (repl.it)
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Accurate scoring of each function using the rubric with specific evidence cited (40 points), (2) Logical ranking decision that reflects their scoring (20 points), (3) Written justification that addresses trade-offs and demonstrates critical thinking (30 points), (4) Participation in class discussion with thoughtful contributions (10 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation for one criterion to model the process, offer sentence starters for justifications ('Function X is better because...'), and allow pair work for initial code analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to suggest specific code improvements for each function, research additional security vulnerabilities, or evaluate a fourth function with edge cases.

title: Design a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Analytics
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations for targeted marketing strategies.
estimated_duration: 3.5 hours (can be split across two class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will create a comprehensive customer segmentation model by applying RFM analysis techniques to real e-commerce transaction data
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining data visualization principles with business intelligence tools to communicate insights effectively
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with a dataset containing 12 months of e-commerce transactions (customer_id, purchase_date, order_value, product_category). Step 1 (45 minutes): Teams calculate RFM metrics - Recency (days since last purchase), Frequency (number of transactions), and Monetary (total spending). Students must clean data, handle missing values, and create calculated fields. Step 2 (60 minutes): Using Excel, Tableau, or Power BI, students create RFM scores by ranking customers into quintiles (1-5) for each dimension, then combine scores to form segments like 'Champions' (555), 'At Risk' (155), etc. Step 3 (45 minutes): Design dashboard layout with four key visualizations: customer segment distribution (donut chart), RFM score scatter plots, segment profitability analysis (bar chart), and customer lifecycle timeline. Include interactive filters for date ranges and product categories. Step 4 (30 minutes): Develop three specific marketing recommendations per segment, including budget allocation suggestions and expected ROI metrics. Step 5 (20 minutes): Create executive summary slide with key insights, segment sizes, and revenue impact projections. Teams present 5-minute dashboard demonstrations focusing on business value and actionable insights.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Data visualization software (Tableau Public, Power BI Desktop, or Excel)
Laptops/computers with internet access
RFM analysis template spreadsheet
Business case study handout with company background
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Data accuracy and RFM calculations (25%), (2) Dashboard design and visualization effectiveness (25%), (3) Business insight quality and marketing recommendations (30%), (4) Presentation clarity and professional delivery (20%). Require submission of dashboard file, executive summary document, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-calculated RFM formulas and dashboard templates. Offer advanced learners additional datasets to create comparative analyses or machine learning clustering validation. Include data dictionary and RFM interpretation guide. Consider pairing strong analytical students with those having design skills.

title: PMBOK Guide Process Group and Knowledge Area Matrix Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete mapping of all 49 PMBOK processes across the five process groups and ten knowledge areas. This advanced recall exercise requires students to demonstrate precise knowledge of process classifications and their interconnections within the project management framework.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes and their exact placement within the process group/knowledge area matrix by completing timed recall exercises
Students will identify specific process inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs through structured memorization drills and verification activities
instructions: Begin by distributing blank PMBOK Process Group/Knowledge Area matrices to each student (5x10 grid with headers only). Provide students with 10 minutes to study the complete filled matrix using their PMBOK guides or reference materials. After study time, collect all reference materials and have students attempt to fill in all 49 processes in their correct positions within 15 minutes. Next, pair students and have them quiz each other using the process verification cards for 20 minutes - one student draws a card showing a process name, the other must state its process group, knowledge area, and recite three key inputs/outputs from memory. Rotate roles every 5 minutes. For the final phase, conduct a class-wide rapid-fire recall session where you call out either a process group/knowledge area intersection (e.g., 'Planning/Scope Management') and students must immediately respond with the correct processes, or call out a process name and students respond with its classification. Students earn points for correct, immediate responses. Conclude with individual reflection where students identify which processes they struggled to recall and create personal memory aids. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact terminology and spelling as found in PMBOK Guide 7th edition.
materials_needed: Blank PMBOK Process Group/Knowledge Area matrix templates (one per student)
Complete PMBOK Process matrix reference sheets
Process verification cards with process names and key details
PMBOK Guide 7th edition or digital access
Timer/stopwatch
Scoring sheets for rapid-fire round
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (39/49 processes) in correct matrix placement and demonstrate ability to recall key inputs/outputs for at least 35 processes during peer verification. Final assessment includes rapid-fire round where students must respond correctly to 15/20 callouts within 3 seconds each.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic device examples and allow color-coding of process groups during initial study. Suggest focusing on one knowledge area at a time. For advanced learners, add requirements to recall specific page numbers, include process purpose statements, or identify predecessor/successor process relationships within project phases.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Failure: Crisis Response Analysis Through the Challenger Disaster Case Study
description: Students will analyze the multi-layered leadership failures that contributed to the 1986 Challenger Space Shuttle disaster by examining decision-making processes, communication breakdowns, and organizational culture dynamics. Through systematic deconstruction of primary source materials, students will demonstrate understanding of how leadership theories apply to real-world crisis situations.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing NASA leadership communications and decisions during the 24 hours preceding the Challenger launch

Students will explain the relationship between organizational culture and leadership effectiveness through comparative analysis of Rogers Commission testimony from different hierarchical levels at NASA and Morton Thiokol
instructions: Begin by dividing students into research teams of 3-4 members, assigning each team a specific leadership perspective: NASA Management, Morton Thiokol Engineers, Flight Crew Leadership, or Political/Public Pressure Leadership. Provide each team with their specialized document packet containing transcripts, memos, and testimony relevant to their assigned perspective. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct deep-dive analysis using the provided Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet, identifying specific examples of leadership behaviors, decision-making patterns, and communication styles within their assigned perspective. Students must categorize each leadership action using established leadership theories (transformational, servant, situational, etc.) and document evidence with direct quotes and timestamps. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create a visual timeline mapping their leadership perspective's critical decisions and communications, highlighting moments where leadership theory principles were either applied effectively or violated. Phase 3 (60 minutes): Conduct structured roundtable discussion where each team presents their perspective's leadership analysis for 10 minutes, followed by 5 minutes of cross-examination from other teams. Facilitate synthesis discussion focusing on how different leadership approaches at various organizational levels contributed to the disaster. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Individual reflection where students complete a written comparison identifying at least three specific leadership theory applications they observed across different organizational levels and explain how alternative leadership approaches might have changed outcomes.
materials_needed: Rogers Commission Report excerpts organized by leadership perspective (4 different document packets)
Audio transcripts of NASA/Morton Thiokol teleconference from January 27, 1986
Leadership Analysis Framework worksheets with theory reference guide
Timeline template sheets and colored markers
Individual reflection questionnaire forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification and categorization of leadership behaviors using proper theoretical frameworks (25%), (2) Quality of evidence selection with specific quotes and examples (25%), (3) Depth of analysis connecting leadership actions to organizational outcomes (25%), (4) Individual reflection demonstrating synthesis across perspectives and alternative solution thinking (25%). Students must achieve at least 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing leadership theory quick-reference cards with key characteristics and examples. Offer sentence starters for analysis such as 'This decision reflects transformational leadership because...' For advanced learners, provide supplementary materials about similar organizational disasters (Columbia, Deepwater Horizon) for comparative analysis and ask them to develop leadership intervention strategies that could prevent similar failures.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for Revenue Optimization
description: Students will critically analyze real e-commerce Google Analytics data using three different attribution models (last-click, first-click, and data-driven) to evaluate which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation. They will create a comprehensive audit report with strategic recommendations for marketing channel optimization based on their comparative analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by comparing conversion paths and ROI metrics across paid search, organic, social, and email channels
Students will critique existing marketing measurement strategies through systematic analysis of multi-channel funnel reports and customer journey data
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection Setup (45 minutes)**
Provide students with access to a demo Google Analytics 4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Students work in pairs to navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison. Have them export data for three attribution models: last-click, first-click, and data-driven, filtering for conversions >$50 to focus on high-value transactions.

**Phase 2: Comparative Analysis (60 minutes)**
Students create a spreadsheet comparing the three models across five metrics: total conversions, conversion value, cost per acquisition (CPA), return on ad spend (ROAS), and assisted conversions. They must calculate percentage differences between models for each channel (paid search, display, social, email, organic) and identify which channels show the greatest variance in attribution credit.

**Phase 3: Customer Journey Evaluation (45 minutes)**
Using the Multi-Channel Funnels > Top Conversion Paths report, students analyze the 10 most common conversion paths, documenting average path length and time to conversion. They evaluate which attribution model best reflects the actual customer journey complexity and touchpoint influence.

**Phase 4: Strategic Audit Report (90 minutes)**
Students compile a 3-page audit report containing: (1) Executive summary with primary findings, (2) Detailed comparison table with visual charts showing attribution differences, (3) Strategic recommendations for budget reallocation across channels, (4) Implementation timeline with specific percentage shifts in spending, and (5) Success metrics for measuring the impact of recommended changes. Each recommendation must include specific rationale tied to their data analysis.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets access
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
Sample e-commerce dataset with 6+ months of multi-channel data
Audit report template with required sections
assessment_method: Rubric evaluating: (1) Data accuracy and completeness of attribution comparisons (25 points), (2) Quality of critical analysis identifying strengths/weaknesses of each model (30 points), (3) Feasibility and specificity of strategic recommendations with clear budget allocation percentages (25 points), (4) Professional presentation and clear communication of complex findings (20 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by achieving 80+ points and presenting one key recommendation to class with supporting data visualization.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data tables and guide them through the first attribution model comparison step-by-step. Offer sentence starters for analysis sections. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional GA4 reports like User Acquisition cohort analysis or predictive metrics, and to create custom calculated fields for more sophisticated ROI analysis. Encourage exploration of position-based or time-decay attribution models for deeper evaluation.

title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for Revenue Optimization: Business Application
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three different attribution models (first-click, last-click, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess the business impact of each model and present evidence-based recommendations for optimal attribution strategy implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey touchpoints and recommend optimal models based on business context
instructions: **Setup Phase (20 minutes):** Provide students with access to GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retailer. Students work in pairs to access the Advertising > Attribution section. **Analysis Phase (60 minutes):** Step 1: Students extract attribution comparison reports for the three models, focusing on revenue attribution by channel (Google Ads, Facebook, Email, Organic Search, Direct). Step 2: They analyze conversion path length data in the User Acquisition reports, documenting average touchpoints before conversion. Step 3: Students examine the Model Comparison Tool to identify the largest attribution discrepancies between models, specifically noting which channels gain/lose credit. Step 4: Using the Funnel Exploration report, they map typical customer journeys and identify critical touchpoints. **Evaluation Phase (40 minutes):** Step 5: Students calculate ROI differences for each channel under different attribution models using provided CPM/CPC data. Step 6: They assess business context factors (sales cycle length, average order value, customer lifetime value) to determine model appropriateness. **Presentation Phase (30 minutes):** Students create a 5-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice, including implementation timeline and expected business impact. Each pair presents to another pair for peer evaluation using provided criteria.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Spreadsheet template with CPM/CPC cost data for attribution ROI calculations
Attribution model comparison worksheet with guided analysis framework
Presentation template with required evaluation criteria sections
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and interpretation (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis between attribution models (30%), (3) Strength of evidence supporting final recommendation (25%), (4) Business context integration and implementation feasibility (20%). Deliverables include completed analysis worksheet, ROI calculations spreadsheet, and recorded presentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-populated data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer attribution model decision tree flowchart. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution settings, integrate Google Ads conversion import analysis, and require consideration of cross-device tracking implications.
original_title: E-commerce Analytics Strategy Audit: Evaluating Multi-Channel Attribution Models for Revenue Optimization

title: Design and Implement a Scalable Multi-Campus Enterprise Network with Advanced Security Policies
description: Students will architect a complete enterprise network solution for a fictional company with three geographically distributed campuses, implementing advanced routing protocols, security policies, and redundancy mechanisms. They will create detailed network diagrams, configuration files, and operational procedures that demonstrate mastery of complex Cisco networking concepts.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across multiple class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocols to create an optimal inter-campus routing strategy for a multi-site enterprise environment
Students will design comprehensive security policies integrating VLANs, ACLs, VPN tunnels, and firewall rules to protect critical network segments while maintaining operational efficiency
instructions: **Phase 1: Requirements Analysis (45 minutes)** - Present students with a detailed business scenario: TechCorp has headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and R&D facility (150 users) across three cities. Each site requires specific network segments for employees, guests, servers, and IoT devices. Students must identify bandwidth requirements, security zones, and redundancy needs. **Phase 2: Network Architecture Design (90 minutes)** - Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, students create detailed network topologies for each campus showing core, distribution, and access layers. They must select appropriate Cisco switch and router models, plan IP addressing schemes using VLSM, and design inter-site connectivity using MPLS or site-to-site VPNs. Include redundant paths and specify routing protocols for each network segment. **Phase 3: Configuration Implementation (120 minutes)** - Students develop complete configuration files for all network devices including: OSPF/EIGRP routing with proper area design, VLANs with 802.1Q trunking, spanning tree optimization, ACLs for security zones, VPN configurations for remote access, and QoS policies for voice/video traffic. Each configuration must include detailed comments explaining design decisions. **Phase 4: Security Policy Creation (60 minutes)** - Design comprehensive security policies including firewall rules, intrusion prevention guidelines, network access control procedures, and incident response protocols. Create user authentication systems using 802.1X and RADIUS integration. **Phase 5: Documentation and Presentation (45 minutes)** - Compile professional network documentation including physical/logical diagrams, IP address management spreadsheets, configuration backup procedures, and operational runbooks. Present solution to class with justification for all major design decisions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 network simulation software
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart for network diagramming
TechCorp business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Cisco IOS configuration reference guides
Network design templates and IP addressing worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Architecture Design (25 points) - logical topology, appropriate device selection, scalable IP addressing; Configuration Quality (30 points) - syntactically correct, well-commented, implements all requirements; Security Implementation (25 points) - comprehensive policies, proper segmentation, defense-in-depth; Documentation and Presentation (20 points) - professional diagrams, clear explanations, convincing justification of design choices. Students must demonstrate working configurations through simulation testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured starter templates, break complex configurations into smaller modules, offer one-on-one troubleshooting sessions, and allow use of configuration generators with explanation requirements. For advanced learners: Add requirements for IPv6 dual-stack implementation, software-defined networking concepts, network automation using Python scripts, or integration with cloud services like AWS Direct Connect.

title: Python Data Type Memory Palace: Building Mental Maps of Basic Data Types
description: Students will memorize the five fundamental Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and their defining characteristics through visual association and structured recall practice. This foundational knowledge activity prepares students for hands-on programming by ensuring automatic recognition of data type properties.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and state their primary characteristics by completing flashcard drills and verbal recitation exercises
Students will identify correct syntax examples for each data type through matching activities and recognition quizzes
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute printed data type reference cards to each student. Project the master chart showing: int (whole numbers, no quotes), float (decimal numbers), string (text in quotes), boolean (True/False), list (items in square brackets). **Phase 1 - Initial Exposure (10 minutes):** Read aloud each data type name and definition while students repeat in unison. Have students trace over the syntax examples on their cards with colored pencils - blue for numbers, red for text, green for lists. **Phase 2 - Memory Reinforcement (15 minutes):** Conduct rapid-fire recall sessions. Call out a data type name; students must immediately shout back its key characteristic (e.g., 'String!' → 'Text in quotes!'). Repeat 3 rounds, increasing speed each time. Then reverse: show syntax examples on screen, students identify the data type. **Phase 3 - Visual Association (10 minutes):** Students draw simple icons next to each data type on their cards (calculator for int/float, speech bubble for string, checkmark for boolean, shopping list for list). **Phase 4 - Peer Testing (8 minutes):** Partner students. One reads data type names from shuffled cards, partner recites characteristics and syntax from memory. Switch roles after 4 minutes. **Closure (2 minutes):** Final whole-class choral recitation of all five data types with characteristics.
materials_needed: Printed reference cards with data type names and syntax examples (one per student)
Colored pencils or markers (blue, red, green)
Projector/screen for displaying examples
Timer for pacing activities
assessment_method: Students must achieve 100% accuracy on a 10-question identification quiz: 5 questions naming data types from syntax examples, 5 questions stating key characteristics when given type names. Observe during peer testing for immediate feedback. Record completion of visual association drawings as participation points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pneumonic devices ('Strings have quotation wings', 'Lists live in square brackets'). Allow reference to visual icons during initial quiz attempts. For advanced learners: Add complex examples like nested lists or scientific notation floats. Challenge them to create their own memory aids for classmates.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Marketing Dataset
description: Students will analyze a marketing campaign dataset containing customer demographics, ad spend, and sales data to distinguish between correlational and causal relationships. They will create visual interpretations and explanations of why certain statistical relationships do not imply causation.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing at least three variable pairs in a marketing dataset and explaining the underlying mechanisms
Students will interpret scatter plots and correlation coefficients through identifying confounding variables and proposing alternative explanations for observed relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-loaded Jupyter notebook containing a marketing dataset with 1,000 customer records including age, income, education level, ad impressions, click-through rates, and purchase amounts (15 minutes setup). Form pairs and assign each pair three specific variable combinations: (1) ad impressions vs. purchases, (2) customer age vs. purchase amount, and (3) education level vs. click-through rate. Students first calculate Pearson correlation coefficients using pandas.corr() and create scatter plots using matplotlib for each pair (25 minutes). Next, each pair examines their correlation results and brainstorms at least two potential confounding variables for each relationship, documenting these in a shared Google Doc template with columns for 'Variables,' 'Correlation Value,' 'Potential Confounders,' and 'Alternative Explanations' (20 minutes). Students then research one additional external factor (like seasonal trends, economic conditions, or demographic preferences) that could influence their strongest correlation and write a 3-sentence explanation of how this factor might create a spurious relationship (15 minutes). Conclude with pair presentations where each team shows their strongest correlation plot, states the coefficient, and explains why this relationship likely does NOT represent direct causation, offering their alternative explanation (20 minutes). During presentations, listening pairs must ask one clarifying question about confounding variables or suggest an additional alternative explanation.
materials_needed: Jupyter notebook environment with pandas, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Pre-loaded marketing_data.csv file with 1,000 customer records
Google Doc template with analysis columns
Projector for student presentations
Handout with correlation interpretation guidelines (-1 to +1 scale)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate correlation calculation and visualization (25%), (2) Identification of at least 2 relevant confounding variables per relationship (35%), (3) Clear written explanation distinguishing correlation from causation with external research (25%), (4) Effective presentation with response to peer questions (15%). Success requires scoring 3+ points total with no category scoring 0.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a worked example using ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths with temperature as the confounding variable. Offer sentence starters like 'This correlation exists because...' and 'A third factor that influences both variables is...' For advanced learners, challenge them to propose a controlled experiment design that could test for actual causation, or have them explore partial correlation analysis to control for one confounding variable.

title: Optimizing Emergency Vehicle Routes Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving emergency vehicle dispatch. They will analyze traffic patterns, calculate optimal routes considering multiple constraints, and determine resource allocation for maximum efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to minimize emergency response time by optimizing vehicle routes under fuel and distance constraints
Students will implement linear programming methods through graphical analysis and simplex method to maximize coverage area while minimizing operational costs
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a city grid map showing 6 emergency stations and 15 incident locations with varying priority levels (5 minutes setup). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives identical datasets including: traffic speed matrices for different time periods, fuel consumption rates, vehicle capacity constraints, and incident priority weights.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze the constraint equations and identify decision variables (number of vehicles from each station, route selections). They must formulate the objective function to minimize total weighted response time.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using calculus techniques, students find critical points by taking partial derivatives of the objective function with respect to each decision variable. They apply Lagrange multipliers to handle constraints (fuel limits: 50 gallons per vehicle, maximum 3 vehicles per station).

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams set up the linear programming problem in standard form, identifying feasible regions through graphical method for simplified 2-variable cases, then extend to full problem using simplex tableau method.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Students use Excel Solver or similar software to verify their analytical solutions and perform sensitivity analysis on key parameters.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Each team presents their optimal solution, including total response time, resource allocation, and cost analysis. They must justify mathematical methods used and explain how their solution handles real-world constraints.

Instructor circulates during work time, checking mathematical setup and computational accuracy. Provide hints for teams struggling with constraint formulation or derivative calculations.
materials_needed: City grid maps with marked emergency stations and incident locations (printed copies)
Traffic speed and incident priority data sheets for each team
Graphing paper and colored pencils for feasible region plotting
Calculators or computers with Excel/optimization software access
Lagrange multiplier reference sheet with step-by-step procedure
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Correct mathematical formulation of objective function and constraints (25 points), (2) Accurate application of partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers (25 points), (3) Proper setup and solution of linear programming problem (25 points), (4) Verification of results using software tools (15 points), (5) Quality of final presentation and justification of approach (10 points). Students must submit written work showing all calculations and a brief report explaining their optimization strategy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide templates for constraint equation setup and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier worksheets. Offer simplified version with only 3 stations and 8 incidents. For advanced learners: Add dynamic traffic conditions requiring time-dependent optimization, or introduce integer programming constraints (vehicles must be whole numbers). Challenge them to consider multi-objective optimization balancing response time against fuel costs.

title: Comparative Analysis of Energy Dissipation Mechanisms in Damped Oscillatory Systems
description: Students analyze real experimental data from three different damped oscillatory systems (pendulum, spring-mass, and RLC circuit) to identify patterns in energy dissipation, compare damping coefficients, and evaluate the effectiveness of theoretical models. They will decompose complex oscillatory behavior into constituent components and synthesize findings into a comprehensive analysis report.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze experimental data from three damped oscillatory systems by calculating damping coefficients, decay constants, and energy dissipation rates to identify systematic patterns across different physical domains
Students will compare theoretical predictions with experimental results through quantitative error analysis and determine the validity limits of simplified damping models
instructions: Begin by distributing three datasets to student pairs: underdamped pendulum motion (amplitude vs. time), damped spring-mass system (displacement vs. time), and RLC circuit (voltage vs. time). Each dataset contains 200+ data points spanning 10-15 oscillation periods. Students first import data into Excel/Python and create time-series plots with logarithmic amplitude scales. Next, they calculate the logarithmic decrement δ = ln(A_n/A_(n+1)) for consecutive amplitude peaks, determining average values and standard deviations. Using δ, students compute damping ratios (ζ = δ/√(4π² + δ²)) and quality factors (Q = π/δ) for each system. They then fit exponential decay envelopes (A(t) = A₀e^(-γt)) to amplitude data using least-squares regression, extracting decay constants γ. Students calculate theoretical predictions using given system parameters (mass, spring constant, resistance values) and compare with experimental values through percent error analysis. For energy analysis, they plot total mechanical/electrical energy versus time and determine energy dissipation rates (dE/dt). Students create comparative tables showing damping parameters across all three systems, identifying which system exhibits the strongest/weakest damping. Finally, they analyze residual plots from their curve fits to assess model validity and identify systematic deviations. The activity concludes with students writing a 2-page technical analysis comparing damping mechanisms, discussing physical origins of energy loss in each system, and evaluating when simple exponential models fail.
materials_needed: Three experimental datasets (CSV files): damped pendulum, spring-mass system, and RLC circuit data
Excel or Python with NumPy/Matplotlib libraries
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for manual calculations verification
System parameter reference sheets (masses, spring constants, resistance values)
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Data analysis accuracy (25 points) - correct calculation of damping parameters with proper error analysis; Comparative analysis (25 points) - meaningful comparison of damping mechanisms across systems with quantitative support; Model evaluation (25 points) - thorough assessment of theoretical vs. experimental agreement with residual analysis; Technical communication (25 points) - clear presentation of methods, results, and conclusions in professional format. Students must achieve 80% accuracy in parameter calculations and demonstrate understanding of physical mechanisms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step calculation templates and pre-made Excel formulas for logarithmic decrement. Offer guided practice with one dataset before independent analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive theoretical damping expressions from first principles, analyze frequency-dependent damping effects, or investigate nonlinear damping models. Provide additional datasets with critical damping or variable damping coefficients.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes and Code Improvements
description: Students will critically evaluate three different code solutions to the same programming problem, assessing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will rank the solutions and provide detailed justifications for their evaluations using established coding criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by analyzing readability, efficiency, and maintainability of three different programming solutions
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison using a structured rubric and provide ranked recommendations
instructions: Begin by distributing three code samples that solve the same problem (calculating compound interest) but with varying quality levels - one well-written, one with minor issues, and one with significant problems. Provide students with the Code Quality Evaluation Checklist containing criteria: functionality (does it work correctly?), readability (clear variable names, comments, structure), efficiency (unnecessary loops, redundant code), and best practices (proper error handling, input validation). Students work individually for 25 minutes to test each code sample, document bugs or issues found, and rate each solution on a 1-10 scale for each criterion. They must write 2-3 sentences justifying each rating. Next, students rank the three solutions from best to worst and write a one-paragraph recommendation explaining which code they would approve for production use and why. In the final 10 minutes, facilitate a class discussion where students share their rankings and justifications, focusing on disagreements to highlight different evaluation perspectives. Students submit their completed evaluation forms with ratings, justifications, rankings, and recommendations.
materials_needed: Three code samples solving compound interest calculation (different quality levels)
Code Quality Evaluation Checklist handout
Computer with code editor/IDE for each student
Sample input data for testing the code
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric: Thorough testing (25 points) - student identified major bugs and tested edge cases; Criteria application (25 points) - accurate ratings with clear justifications for each criterion; Ranking logic (25 points) - logical ranking with well-supported reasoning; Professional recommendation (25 points) - practical, detailed recommendation with specific examples from code analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of one code evaluation and highlight specific things to look for in each criterion category. For advanced learners: Add a fifth task requiring them to rewrite the worst code sample with improvements, or evaluate additional criteria like security vulnerabilities and scalability concerns.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes and Code Improvements: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate three different code solutions to the same problem, identifying strengths, weaknesses, and potential issues in each approach. They will then rank the solutions and justify their decisions using established coding principles and best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and effectiveness of different code solutions by applying coding standards, readability principles, and performance considerations
Students will critique and rank programming approaches through systematic analysis of functionality, maintainability, and efficiency factors
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three different Python solutions to a simple calculator function that adds two numbers and handles basic error cases. Each solution has different approaches: Solution A uses basic if-statements, Solution B uses try-except blocks, Solution C uses input validation with custom error messages. Display solutions on screen or distribute printed copies.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each solution using the provided evaluation checklist covering: functionality (does it work correctly?), readability (is code clear and well-commented?), error handling (how does it manage invalid inputs?), and maintainability (how easy would it be to modify?). Students take notes on strengths and weaknesses for each solution.

**Evaluation and Ranking (10 minutes):** Students complete an evaluation matrix, scoring each solution 1-5 on the four criteria. They calculate total scores and rank solutions from best (1st) to worst (3rd). Students write 2-3 sentences justifying their top choice.

**Peer Discussion (8 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss differences. They must defend their choices using specific examples from the code.

**Class Debrief (7 minutes):** Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion where 3-4 students share their top choice and reasoning. Class votes on overall best solution and discusses why evaluation criteria matter in real software development.
materials_needed: Three printed code solutions (one per student)
Evaluation checklist handout with 4 criteria
Evaluation matrix worksheet
Projector/screen for displaying code
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation matrix with scores and written justification. Rubric: Accurate functionality assessment (25%), thoughtful readability analysis (25%), appropriate error handling evaluation (25%), clear justification with specific examples (25%). Success requires scoring at least 3/4 points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for justifications and highlight 1-2 obvious differences between solutions. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific improvements for their lowest-ranked solution or consider additional criteria like performance or security implications.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes and Code Improvements

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Identification
description: Students will identify and recall specific components, symbols, and terminology used in Critical Path Method network diagrams through a systematic visual recognition exercise. This activity focuses on memorizing the precise definitions and visual representations of advanced CPM elements including forward pass calculations, backward pass calculations, and float types.
learning_objectives: Students will identify all CPM network diagram symbols and their precise meanings by matching visual components to their technical definitions
Students will recall specific CPM terminology and calculation formulas through structured memorization exercises using flashcard methodology
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Master Reference Sheet and 50 pre-prepared flashcards to each student (15 minutes setup). Phase 1 (25 minutes): Students work individually to study the reference sheet, focusing on memorizing 15 key CPM components: Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, Critical Path, Activity Duration, Precedence Relationships, Forward Pass Formula, Backward Pass Formula, Node numbering conventions, Dummy Activities, and Activity-on-Node vs Activity-on-Arrow notation. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Students use flashcards in pairs, with one student showing the visual symbol or term while the partner recalls the exact definition. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Individual silent review where students create their own mental associations for each component. Phase 4 (25 minutes): Instructor displays 20 different CPM network diagram segments on screen, each showing for 30 seconds. Students must write down the specific name and function of highlighted components. Include complex elements like multiple predecessor relationships, float calculations, and critical path identification. No discussion allowed during this phase. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Students self-check answers using the master reference sheet and record their accuracy score.
materials_needed: CPM Master Reference Sheet (laminated, one per student)
Set of 50 CPM component flashcards per student
Digital projector for displaying network diagrams
Pre-prepared PowerPoint with 20 CPM diagram segments
Individual answer sheets with numbered spaces 1-20
Timer for controlling flashcard rotations
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (17/20 correct) on the visual identification test to demonstrate mastery. Assessment based on: (1) Correct identification of CPM symbols and notation (40 points), (2) Accurate recall of technical definitions (30 points), (3) Proper recognition of calculation formulas and their components (30 points). Instructor conducts spot-checks during flashcard phase, awarding participation points for active engagement and peer teaching behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional 15-minute pre-activity session with basic CPM terminology review, allow use of reference sheet during first 10 identification questions, pair with stronger students during flashcard phase. For advanced learners: Include additional 10 complex network scenarios with resource leveling and project crashing elements, challenge them to identify optimization opportunities in displayed diagrams, assign peer tutoring roles during flashcard activities.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradigm Shifts: Analyzing the Evolution from Command-Control to Adaptive Leadership
description: Students will analyze complex leadership case studies involving organizational paradigm shifts to understand how different leadership theories manifest in crisis situations. They will demonstrate comprehension by mapping theoretical frameworks to real-world leadership decisions and explaining the underlying principles that drive adaptive versus traditional leadership approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between command-control and adaptive leadership paradigms by analyzing specific decision-making processes in three crisis leadership scenarios
Students will explain the underlying theoretical principles of transformational, servant, and adaptive leadership through systematic comparison of leader behaviors and organizational outcomes
instructions: Begin by distributing three complex leadership case studies: Netflix's transformation under Reed Hastings (2007-2012), Jacinda Ardern's COVID-19 response (2020-2021), and General Stanley McChrystal's military reform in Iraq (2003-2008). Form groups of 3-4 students, assigning each group one primary case study for deep analysis (45 minutes). Each group receives a Leadership Paradigm Analysis Framework template with four sections: Context Analysis, Decision Mapping, Theoretical Alignment, and Paradigm Identification. Students first spend 15 minutes individually reading their assigned case, highlighting specific leadership decisions, communication patterns, and organizational responses. Next, groups collaborate for 30 minutes to complete the framework template, identifying where the leader's actions align with specific theoretical models (transformational, servant, adaptive, authentic leadership). Groups must provide textual evidence for each theoretical connection and explain why certain approaches were chosen over others. Following analysis, conduct a structured gallery walk (20 minutes) where each group posts their completed frameworks and rotates to examine others' work, taking notes on commonalities and differences. Conclude with a facilitated discussion (15 minutes) where groups present one key insight about how their leader navigated paradigm shifts, specifically addressing what theoretical principles guided major decisions and how context influenced leadership approach selection.
materials_needed: Three printed case study packets (Netflix transformation, Ardern COVID response, McChrystal military reform)
Leadership Paradigm Analysis Framework templates (one per student)
Large poster paper for gallery walk displays
Colored markers and sticky notes
Timer for activity transitions
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Paradigm Analysis Frameworks using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of theoretical alignment (25%) - correctly identifies and explains 2-3 leadership theories evident in the case; (2) Quality of evidence (25%) - provides specific, relevant textual support for theoretical connections; (3) Depth of paradigm analysis (25%) - demonstrates clear understanding of how leader shifted between or combined different approaches; (4) Articulation of principles (25%) - explains underlying theoretical principles that guided leadership decisions with proper terminology and conceptual clarity.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a pre-completed example using a simpler case study and offer a leadership theory reference sheet with key characteristics of each model. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger theoretical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add a synthesis requirement to identify emerging leadership paradigms not covered in traditional theories, or have them create their own theoretical framework based on patterns observed across all three cases. Provide additional complex cases for extended analysis.

title: Risk Response Strategy Gap Analysis Using PMBOK Framework
description: Students will examine a troubled project scenario to identify gaps between implemented risk responses and PMBOK best practices. They will break down existing risk management approaches, compare them against standard methodologies, and determine which components are missing or inadequate.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze existing risk response strategies by comparing them against PMBOK Guide risk management processes to identify implementation gaps
Students will examine the relationship between risk categories, response types, and project outcomes through systematic evaluation of a case study scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Metro Transit Expansion Project' case study packet (15 minutes reading time). This case describes a $45M transit project experiencing schedule delays, budget overruns, and stakeholder conflicts. Students work in groups of 3-4. Step 1 (20 minutes): Each group creates a risk register template with columns for Risk ID, Category, Probability, Impact, Risk Score, and Current Response. Groups extract 8-10 risks from the case study and populate their register. Step 2 (25 minutes): Using PMBOK risk response strategies (Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate, Accept for threats; Exploit, Share, Enhance, Accept for opportunities), groups categorize each current response and identify which PMBOK strategy it represents. Many responses will be incomplete or incorrectly categorized. Step 3 (20 minutes): Groups conduct gap analysis by comparing current responses against PMBOK best practices. They document gaps using a provided template with columns for 'Current Approach,' 'PMBOK Standard,' and 'Gap Identified.' Step 4 (15 minutes): Each group presents one critical gap to the class, explaining why the current approach is inadequate and which PMBOK principle is violated. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting gaps to project problems described in the case. Step 5 (10 minutes): Individual reflection where students write three key insights about how proper risk response alignment prevents project issues.
materials_needed: Metro Transit Expansion Project case study packet (6 pages)
Risk register template worksheets
Gap analysis template handouts
PMBOK risk response strategy reference sheets
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed gap analysis templates using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies 6+ gaps with accurate PMBOK connections, (3) Identifies 4-5 gaps with mostly accurate connections, (2) Identifies 2-3 gaps with some accuracy, (1) Identifies fewer than 2 gaps or major inaccuracies. Individual reflection responses assessed for depth of insight connecting risk management gaps to project outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of first 2 risks in register, highlight key phrases in case study that indicate risk responses, offer PMBOK quick-reference cards. For advanced learners: Challenge them to calculate risk exposure values, identify secondary risks created by inadequate responses, or develop corrective action plans with timelines and resource requirements.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Campus Network with Inter-VLAN Routing and Redundancy
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise campus network topology featuring multiple VLANs, redundant links, spanning tree protocol, and router-on-a-stick inter-VLAN routing. This capstone activity synthesizes switching, routing, and network design principles into a functional business network solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a hierarchical campus network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with VLAN segmentation
Students will implement inter-VLAN routing and redundancy protocols through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers in a simulated enterprise environment
instructions: Begin with a 15-minute business scenario briefing: students receive requirements for AcmeCorp's 3-building campus needing separate VLANs for HR (10 users), Finance (15 users), IT (8 users), and Guest network (50 users), plus server VLAN. Divide into teams of 2-3 students. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams create detailed network topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying VLAN IDs (HR-VLAN 10, Finance-VLAN 20, IT-VLAN 30, Guest-VLAN 40, Server-VLAN 50), IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets, switch hierarchy with core/distribution/access layers, and redundant uplinks. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment, configure the core multilayer switch with VLANs and SVI interfaces, set up trunk ports between switches with 802.1Q encapsulation, configure access ports for each VLAN, implement RSTP for loop prevention, and configure router subinterfaces for inter-VLAN routing using 802.1Q tagging. Phase 3 (30 minutes): Test connectivity between VLANs, verify spanning tree operation with show spanning-tree commands, document all IP assignments and VLAN mappings, and create a troubleshooting guide. Teams present their working network topology and demonstrate inter-VLAN communication, explaining their design decisions for redundancy and segmentation.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or 4 Cisco switches (2960 series) and 1 router (2900 series) per team
Network diagramming software (Visio, draw.io, or Lucidchart)
Ethernet cables and console cables for physical equipment
Business requirements handout with AcmeCorp scenario details
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network design diagram completeness and accuracy (25 points), successful VLAN configuration and trunk setup (25 points), working inter-VLAN routing with proper IP addressing (25 points), redundancy implementation with spanning tree (15 points), and presentation quality with troubleshooting documentation (10 points). Students must demonstrate ping connectivity between all VLANs and explain their spanning tree root bridge placement.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing VLAN configuration templates and step-by-step router subinterface examples. Offer IP addressing worksheets with pre-calculated subnets. For advanced learners, add challenges like implementing VTP (VLAN Trunking Protocol), configuring port security, adding ACLs to restrict inter-VLAN traffic, or implementing EtherChannel for link aggregation. Provide quick reference cards with essential show commands for verification.

title: Binary Number System Identification and Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 to 1111 (0-15) through structured practice and testing. This foundational activity builds essential number system recognition skills needed for all computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the decimal equivalent of any 4-bit binary number (0000-1111) within 5 seconds by memorizing the conversion patterns
Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and peer testing
instructions: Begin by distributing the binary-decimal conversion chart showing 4-bit binary numbers 0000-1111 with their decimal equivalents 0-15. Give students 10 minutes to study the chart silently, encouraging them to look for patterns (like how each bit position represents powers of 2: 8-4-2-1). Next, conduct a 15-minute guided practice session where you display binary numbers on the board and students call out decimal equivalents in unison, starting with obvious patterns (0000=0, 1111=15) then moving to systematic practice. Pair students for 10 minutes of flashcard practice using the provided cards - one partner shows a binary number, the other states the decimal equivalent, then they switch roles. Follow with 5 minutes of individual silent review time. Conclude with a 10-minute assessment where students individually complete a worksheet identifying 16 binary numbers in random order. Students must write only the decimal equivalent next to each binary number. Walk around during assessment to observe student confidence and accuracy. Record completion times to gauge memorization strength.
materials_needed: Laminated binary-decimal conversion chart (4-bit numbers 0000-1111)
Set of 32 flashcards per pair (16 binary, 16 decimal equivalents)
Individual assessment worksheet with 16 binary numbers in random order
Stopwatch or timer
Whiteboard markers for instructor demonstrations
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 14 out of 16 binary-to-decimal conversions on the individual worksheet within the 10-minute time limit. Success criteria: 87.5% accuracy (14/16 correct) demonstrating solid memorization. Track response time during peer practice - target is 5 seconds or less per conversion. Use completion checklist to mark: speed (fast/medium/slow), accuracy (high/medium/low), and confidence level observed.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: highlight the 8-4-2-1 pattern on their charts, start with numbers containing only one '1' bit (0001, 0010, 0100, 1000), then combine patterns. Provide additional practice focusing on just 0000-0111 first. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or challenge them to convert backwards from decimal to binary without reference materials.

title: Interpreting A/B Test Results Through Statistical Significance Analysis
description: Students will analyze real A/B test data from an e-commerce website conversion experiment to determine statistical significance and interpret business implications. They will examine p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes to understand when results are actionable versus inconclusive.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret statistical significance by analyzing p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes from A/B test datasets
Students will distinguish between statistically significant and practically significant results through guided analysis of conversion rate experiments
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared dataset containing 14 days of A/B test results comparing two website checkout button designs (Version A: 2,847 visitors, 142 conversions; Version B: 2,901 visitors, 174 conversions). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. First 15 minutes: Have students calculate basic conversion rates for each version and hypothesize which performed better. Next 15 minutes: Guide students through calculating the z-test statistic using the provided formula sheet, determining the p-value, and constructing 95% confidence intervals for the difference in conversion rates. Students use calculators or Excel for computations. Following 10 minutes: Students interpret their statistical results by answering guided questions: 'Is p < 0.05?', 'What does the confidence interval tell us?', 'Does it include zero?' Final 5 minutes: Students determine practical significance by calculating the absolute difference in conversion rates and estimating potential revenue impact using provided average order value ($67). Instructor circulates throughout, checking calculations and clarifying interpretation questions. Students document findings on the structured worksheet, noting both statistical conclusions and business recommendations. Conclude with 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their interpretations and explain their reasoning for recommending implementation or further testing.
materials_needed: A/B test dataset printout with visitor and conversion numbers
Statistical formula reference sheet with z-test and confidence interval formulas
Structured analysis worksheet with guided questions
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
Average order value and business context information sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct calculation of conversion rates and z-statistic, (2) Accurate interpretation of p-value and statistical significance, (3) Proper construction and interpretation of confidence intervals, (4) Appropriate distinction between statistical and practical significance with justified business recommendation. Students must achieve 3/4 points to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed calculation examples from a similar dataset and highlight key interpretation phrases ('p < 0.05 means...', 'confidence interval including zero suggests...'). Offer step-by-step calculation templates. For advanced learners: Introduce concepts of statistical power, Type I/II errors, or have them design follow-up experiments. Provide additional datasets with different sample sizes to explore how this affects significance testing.

title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Propulsion Systems Through Mission Profile Decomposition
description: Students will dissect the SpaceX Falcon Heavy's three-stage propulsion system by analyzing thrust-to-weight ratios, specific impulse variations, and fuel consumption patterns across different mission phases. They will break down complex rocket equations to determine optimal staging sequences and identify design trade-offs between payload capacity and mission efficiency.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-stage rocket propulsion systems by decomposing the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for each stage and calculating cumulative delta-v requirements
Students will evaluate propulsion efficiency trade-offs through systematic comparison of specific impulse values, thrust profiles, and mass ratios across different staging configurations
instructions: Begin by distributing the Falcon Heavy technical specification sheets and mission profile data (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Propulsion Analyst, Staging Sequence Specialist, Mass Budget Calculator, and Mission Efficiency Evaluator. Each team receives identical datasets but different mission scenarios (GTO, Mars transfer, or lunar insertion). Students first spend 20 minutes individually calculating basic parameters: initial mass ratios, stage-specific delta-v contributions, and burn duration for their assigned mission using provided formulas. Next, teams collaborate for 45 minutes to create a comprehensive staging analysis chart, plotting thrust-to-weight ratio versus time, identifying critical transition points between stages, and calculating total mission delta-v requirements. Teams must justify why certain engines (Merlin 1D vs. Merlin Vacuum) are used at specific stages by analyzing their performance characteristics. During the final 30 minutes, each team presents their findings using the provided analysis template, explaining how propulsion system design choices impact mission success probability. Teams must identify at least three design trade-offs and propose one alternative staging configuration, supporting their recommendations with quantitative analysis. Instructor circulates during collaborative work, asking probing questions about assumption validity and encouraging deeper investigation of anomalous results.
materials_needed: Falcon Heavy technical specification sheets with engine performance data
Mission profile datasets (delta-v requirements, payload masses, orbital parameters)
Scientific calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Large format paper for creating staging analysis charts
Tsiolkovsky equation reference sheets with derivations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of mathematical calculations and proper application of rocket equations (25%), (2) Quality of staging sequence analysis and identification of transition points (25%), (3) Depth of trade-off analysis with supporting quantitative evidence (25%), (4) Clarity of alternative design proposal with justified recommendations (25%). Students must achieve proficiency in all categories, demonstrating correct use of physics principles and logical reasoning in their propulsion system analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated mass ratios and focus on conceptual relationships between variables. Offer step-by-step calculation worksheets and encourage peer tutoring within teams. For advanced learners, introduce atmospheric drag considerations, variable specific impulse calculations, or challenge them to optimize staging for multiple mission profiles simultaneously. Provide additional datasets from other launch vehicles for comparative analysis.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Password Validation Functions
description: Students will evaluate and compare three different password validation function implementations by analyzing their security effectiveness, code quality, and adherence to best practices. They will rank the implementations and justify their evaluation using specific criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three password validation implementations by comparing their security measures, code readability, and error handling against established criteria
Students will justify their ranking of code implementations through written analysis that demonstrates understanding of secure coding principles
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a printed handout containing three password validation functions written in Python (Function A: basic length check only, Function B: comprehensive validation with regex and multiple criteria, Function C: moderate validation with some security flaws). Include evaluation criteria sheet listing: security strength (40%), code readability (25%), error handling (20%), and efficiency (15%). **Individual Analysis (25 minutes):** Students examine each function independently, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses using the provided criteria. They must identify at least 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses per function, writing specific examples from the code. **Evaluation Process (15 minutes):** Students score each function on a 1-10 scale for each criterion, calculate weighted totals, and rank functions 1st, 2nd, 3rd. They must write a 3-sentence justification for their top choice and bottom choice. **Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare rankings and discuss one major disagreement in their evaluations. **Reflection (5 minutes):** Individual writing: 'What surprised you most about evaluating code quality?' and 'Which criterion was hardest to judge and why?'
materials_needed: Printed handout with 3 password validation functions (Python code)
Evaluation criteria checklist with weightings
Calculator or smartphone for weighted scoring
Lined paper for notes and justifications
assessment_method: Grade based on: Completeness of analysis notes (25%), accuracy of criterion application (35%), quality of written justifications with specific examples (30%), and participation in peer discussion (10%). Success = correctly identifying major security flaw in Function C, ranking Function B highest for security, and providing code-specific examples in justifications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Highlight one example strength/weakness in Function A to model analysis depth. Provide sentence starters like 'This function is secure because...' For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific code improvements for their lowest-ranked function and consider additional criteria like maintainability or performance optimization.

title: Design a Business Intelligence Dashboard for Local Coffee Shop Chain
description: Students will create an interactive business intelligence dashboard by synthesizing sales, customer, and inventory data from a fictional 3-location coffee shop chain.
