They will design visualizations, establish KPIs, and build actionable recommendations for business growth using real-world data analysis principles.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive BI dashboard by integrating multiple data sources and creating meaningful visualizations that reveal business insights
Students will formulate data-driven business recommendations through systematic analysis of sales patterns, customer behavior, and operational metrics
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide each student with three CSV files: daily_sales.csv (6 months of transaction data), customer_data.csv (loyalty program information), and inventory_costs.csv (product costs and margins). Students access Tableau Public or Power BI (free versions). **Phase 1 - Data Integration (30 minutes):** Students import all three datasets and create relationships between tables using common fields (store_id, product_id, customer_id). They clean data by removing duplicates, handling missing values, and standardizing date formats. **Phase 2 - KPI Development (25 minutes):** Students identify and calculate five key business metrics: daily revenue by location, customer retention rate, profit margins by product category, peak sales hours, and average transaction value. They create calculated fields for metrics not directly available in raw data. **Phase 3 - Dashboard Design (40 minutes):** Students design a single-page dashboard containing: revenue trend line chart, location comparison bar chart, product performance heat map, customer segment pie chart, and hourly sales pattern chart. Each visualization must include filters for date range and location. **Phase 4 - Insights & Recommendations (20 minutes):** Students analyze their dashboard to identify three specific business opportunities (e.g., underperforming locations, optimal staffing hours, high-margin product promotion opportunities) and document these findings in a summary text box on their dashboard. **Presentation (15 minutes):** Students export their dashboard as PDF and present one key finding to the class in 60 seconds, explaining both the data pattern they discovered and their recommended business action.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV files with realistic coffee shop data (daily_sales.csv, customer_data.csv, inventory_costs.csv)
Computers with internet access
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI (free versions)
Data dictionary handout explaining field definitions
Dashboard design checklist template
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: Data Integration (correctly joined tables, clean data) - 25%, KPI Accuracy (proper calculations, relevant metrics) - 25%, Dashboard Design (clear visualizations, effective filters, professional layout) - 30%, Business Insights (logical conclusions, actionable recommendations, evidence-based reasoning) - 20%. Students submit PDF export of dashboard plus 200-word reflection on their analytical process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step screenshot guide for software navigation and pre-written SQL queries for complex calculations. Offer template dashboard layout showing optimal chart placement. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets (weather data, competitor pricing) to create more sophisticated analysis. Challenge them to implement statistical forecasting or cluster analysis for customer segmentation. Pair struggling students with advanced peers for peer mentoring during Phase 2.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Term and Formula Identification Challenge
description: Students will identify and recall specific CPM terminology, formulas, and calculation components through a timed recognition exercise using complex project network diagrams. This activity focuses on memorizing the precise vocabulary and mathematical relationships essential for advanced project scheduling analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will identify all 15 core CPM terms (Early Start, Late Start, Early Finish, Late Finish, Total Float, Free Float, Critical Path, Forward Pass, Backward Pass, Activity Duration, Precedence Relationship, Network Logic, Resource Leveling, Schedule Compression, and Crash Cost) by matching them to their exact definitions within 90% accuracy

Students will recall the four fundamental CPM calculation formulas (ES + Duration = EF, LF - Duration = LS, LS - ES = Total Float, and Crash Cost per Day = (Crash Cost - Normal Cost)/(Normal Duration - Crash Duration)) through formula reconstruction exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Network Diagram packet containing three complex project networks (25-30 activities each) and the CPM Reference Sheet with blanked-out terms and formulas. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to complete the CPM terminology matching exercise, connecting 15 technical terms to their precise definitions. No collaboration allowed. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Present students with four incomplete CPM formulas on worksheets. They must fill in missing variables, operators, and complete formula structures from memory. Provide the formula categories (Early/Late calculations, Float calculations, Crash analysis) but not the actual formulas. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Using the provided network diagrams, students identify and label specific diagram components without performing calculations - only recognizing and naming elements like 'critical path activities,' 'float situations,' 'merge points,' and 'burst points.' Students circle and label 20 specific network features across all three diagrams. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Rapid-fire oral review where instructor calls out scenarios and students shout out the appropriate CPM term or formula component. Rotate through all students systematically. Collect all materials immediately after completion to prevent reference during assessment.
materials_needed: CPM Network Diagram packet with 3 complex project networks (printed, one per student)
CPM Terminology Matching worksheet with 15 terms and definitions (scrambled)
Formula Reconstruction worksheet with 4 incomplete CPM formulas
CPM Reference Answer Key for instructor verification
Timer or stopwatch for phase management
Red pens for immediate self-checking activities
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on terminology matching (14/15 correct), 100% accuracy on formula reconstruction (4/4 formulas complete with correct variables and operators), and 85% accuracy on network diagram component identification (17/20 elements correctly labeled). Use immediate peer checking with answer keys, followed by instructor spot-checking of 25% of student work. Record individual scores on CPM Recall Assessment tracking sheet with specific breakdowns by activity phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide CPM terminology flashcards for 5-minute pre-activity review and allow them to use a partially completed reference sheet during Phase 1. For advanced learners: Add a bonus round requiring recall of advanced CPM concepts like 'hammock activities,' 'lag relationships,' and 'schedule risk analysis terms.' Provide additional complex network diagrams with resource constraints and multiple calendar scenarios for extended identification practice.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Communication: Analyzing Executive Response Strategies During Organizational Failures
description: Students will analyze and compare three real-world crisis communication strategies used by different organizational leaders during major corporate failures. They will identify underlying leadership theories, communication frameworks, and decision-making models demonstrated in each case to understand how theoretical leadership concepts manifest in high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and authentic leadership approaches by analyzing specific communication choices made during organizational crises
Students will classify crisis communication strategies using established frameworks (Situational Crisis Communication Theory, Stakeholder Theory) through comparative case analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing three crisis case packets: Tylenol cyanide crisis (1982), Wells Fargo account fraud scandal (2016), and Boeing 737 MAX crashes (2018-2019). Each packet contains CEO statements, press releases, internal memos, and stakeholder responses. Divide class into teams of 4-5 students, assigning each team one primary case for 90 minutes of deep analysis. Teams must complete a structured analysis worksheet identifying: (1) specific leadership behaviors exhibited, (2) communication timing and channels used, (3) stakeholder groups addressed, (4) underlying leadership theory demonstrated, and (5) alignment with crisis communication best practices. After individual case analysis, conduct a 60-minute 'expert panel' session where each team presents their case findings in 15-minute segments, followed by 5-minute Q&A periods. During presentations, non-presenting teams complete comparison matrices, noting similarities and differences in leadership approaches. Conclude with a 30-minute facilitated discussion where teams identify patterns across all three cases, connecting observed behaviors to specific leadership theories (transformational vs. transactional leadership, authentic leadership principles, stakeholder theory applications). Students must support all observations with specific textual evidence from the case materials and cite relevant leadership theory concepts from assigned readings.
materials_needed: Three comprehensive crisis case study packets with primary source documents
Structured analysis worksheets with theory identification frameworks
Comparison matrix templates for cross-case analysis
Digital presentation setup (projector, screen, laptop connections)
Leadership theory reference sheets with key concepts and definitions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: accurate identification and explanation of leadership theories demonstrated (30 points), quality of textual evidence supporting analysis (25 points), effectiveness of comparative analysis across cases (25 points), and clarity of connections between observed behaviors and theoretical frameworks (20 points). Students must submit completed analysis worksheets and comparison matrices as deliverables.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-highlighted case excerpts showing clear leadership behaviors and theory connection guides with explicit examples. For advanced learners, add a fourth case study (Facebook Cambridge Analytica) and require integration of additional leadership theories (servant leadership, ethical leadership models). Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who need support during team analysis phases.

title: Project Schedule Risk Impact Analysis: Critical Path vs Float Management
description: Students will analyze a complex project schedule network diagram to identify critical path dependencies, evaluate the impact of potential delays on project milestones, and develop risk mitigation strategies. They will decompose schedule relationships to determine which activities pose the greatest risk to project completion dates.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze critical path method (CPM) calculations by examining activity dependencies, float values, and resource constraints in a multi-phase construction project scenario
Students will evaluate schedule risk impacts through systematic comparison of baseline vs. compressed schedule scenarios and their effects on project deliverables
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the Metro Office Building construction project schedule containing 45 activities across 5 phases: Foundation, Structure, MEP, Interior, and Closeout. Each team receives printed network diagrams, activity duration tables, and resource allocation charts. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams calculate the critical path using forward and backward pass methods, identifying early start/finish and late start/finish dates for each activity. They must document all calculations showing work for at least 15 key activities spanning multiple phases.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Present three risk scenarios via sealed envelopes: Scenario A (concrete delivery delayed 5 days), Scenario B (electrical inspection fails requiring 3-day rework), Scenario C (interior materials arrive 7 days late). Teams analyze how each scenario impacts their calculated critical path and overall project completion.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams create a risk impact matrix comparing original schedule against all three scenarios. They must identify which activities shift to/from critical path status, calculate new project durations, and determine float consumption patterns. Teams document their analysis using provided templates showing before/after Gantt charts.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team develops three specific mitigation strategies per scenario, considering resource reallocation, schedule compression techniques (crashing vs fast-tracking), and contingency planning. Teams must justify their recommendations using quantitative analysis from their calculations.

Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where each group explains their critical path analysis, demonstrates scenario impact calculations, and defends their mitigation strategies to the class.
materials_needed: Metro Office Building project network diagram printouts (1 per team)
Activity duration and resource tables spreadsheet
Risk impact analysis template worksheets
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
Sealed scenario envelopes with risk descriptions
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Critical path calculations accuracy (25 points), scenario impact analysis completeness (25 points), mitigation strategy feasibility and justification (25 points), team presentation clarity and defense of analysis (25 points). Students must demonstrate correct CPM formulas, show mathematical work, and provide evidence-based reasoning for all recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide CPM calculation reference sheets and work through the first 3-4 activity calculations as a guided example. Consider pairing weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Add resource-constrained scheduling analysis and require Monte Carlo simulation discussion for uncertainty quantification. Challenge them to propose alternative project delivery methods that could reduce overall risk exposure.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Effectiveness Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation and create strategic recommendations for marketing teams.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI metrics across paid search, social media, and email campaigns
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer journey complexity and recommend optimal models for different business scenarios
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels. Students work individually initially, then in pairs for peer review. **Step 1 (20 minutes):** Navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison. Students export conversion data for the same date range using all five attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven). They must document conversion values, conversion counts, and ROAS for paid search, Facebook ads, email campaigns, and organic social. **Step 2 (25 minutes):** Analyze conversion path length and touchpoint complexity using Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths. Students identify patterns: What percentage of conversions involve 1, 2-3, 4-5, or 6+ touchpoints? Which channels appear most frequently in multi-touch journeys? **Step 3 (30 minutes):** Calculate the variance in channel performance across models. Students create a comparison matrix showing how each channel's attributed conversion value changes between models, calculating percentage differences and identifying which channels gain/lose credit most dramatically. **Step 4 (25 minutes):** Evaluate business context by reviewing Monetization > Ecommerce purchases to understand average order value, customer lifetime value segments, and seasonal patterns. **Step 5 (30 minutes):** Synthesize findings into strategic recommendations. Students must justify which attribution model(s) to use for budget allocation decisions, identify model limitations, and propose testing strategies for validation.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with multi-channel e-commerce data
Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Strategic recommendation report template
assessment_method: Students submit a 2-page strategic report with data visualizations evaluated on: (1) Accuracy of attribution model comparisons and calculations (25%), (2) Depth of critical evaluation of each model's strengths/weaknesses (30%), (3) Quality of business context integration and scenario-specific recommendations (25%), (4) Justification of recommended testing and validation approaches (20%). Peer review feedback on recommendations constitutes additional formative assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-populated data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis step. Offer one-on-one sessions to review GA4 navigation basics. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer cohort analysis, evaluate statistical significance of attribution differences, or propose custom attribution model parameters using machine learning principles.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise network solution spanning three geographical sites with SD-WAN connectivity, incorporating advanced routing protocols, security policies, and failover mechanisms. This capstone activity integrates OSPF, BGP, VPN technologies, and Cisco SD-WAN to solve a real-world business scenario.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive multi-site network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes, VLAN segmentation, and routing protocols
Students will implement SD-WAN policies and security configurations through hands-on configuration of Cisco vEdge routers and vManage orchestration platform
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: TechCorp requires connectivity between headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and remote office (50 users) with specific SLA requirements. Phase 1 (60 minutes): Students work in teams of 3-4 to design the complete network architecture. They must create detailed Visio diagrams showing physical and logical topologies, develop IP addressing schemes using VLSM, plan OSPF areas and BGP AS configurations, and define SD-WAN policies for traffic prioritization. Each team presents their design for peer review and instructor feedback. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Using GNS3 or Cisco VIRL, teams implement their designs on virtual infrastructure. They configure Cisco ISR 4000 series routers as CPE devices, deploy vEdge routers for SD-WAN functionality, establish OSPF routing within sites and BGP between sites, implement IPSec VPN tunnels as underlay, and configure SD-WAN overlay policies in vManage. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams must simulate network failures and demonstrate automatic failover capabilities. They document configuration files, create network monitoring dashboards, and prepare a final presentation showing traffic flows, failover scenarios, and performance metrics. Each team presents their working solution, demonstrating connectivity tests, failover mechanisms, and explaining design decisions to address specific business requirements.
materials_needed: GNS3 or Cisco VIRL simulation software with Cisco IOS XE images
Cisco SD-WAN simulator or VIRL SD-WAN images (vEdge, vManage, vSmart)
Microsoft Visio or Lucidchart for network diagrams
Laptops with minimum 16GB RAM for running multiple virtual devices
Business scenario handout with specific SLA and security requirements
assessment_method: Teams are evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points - topology accuracy, IP scheme efficiency, protocol selection justification), Implementation Quality (35 points - configuration correctness, SD-WAN policy effectiveness, security implementation), Demonstration (25 points - successful connectivity tests, failover functionality, troubleshooting skills), and Presentation (15 points - technical communication, design rationale, business alignment). Deliverables include network diagrams, configuration files, testing documentation, and 15-minute presentation with live demonstration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured templates for basic router configurations and simplified topology options focusing on dual-site connectivity. Offer guided worksheets for IP addressing calculations and OSPF area planning. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like QoS marking and queuing, integrate network automation using Python scripts, or add security services like Cisco Umbrella integration. Encourage exploration of advanced SD-WAN features like application-aware routing and centralized policy management.

title: Optimizing Delivery Routes Using Linear Programming Techniques
description: Students will apply linear programming methods to solve a real-world logistics problem by formulating constraints, creating objective functions, and using the simplex method to find optimal delivery routes for a multi-stop transportation scenario. This activity bridges theoretical mathematical concepts with practical business applications.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a complex multi-variable delivery optimization problem into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic calculation to determine optimal resource allocation for minimizing transportation costs
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packets containing a delivery company's data: 5 distribution centers, 8 delivery destinations, vehicle capacities, fuel costs per mile, and time constraints (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Lead Mathematician (manages calculations), Constraint Analyst (identifies limitations), Objective Function Designer (formulates goals), and Solution Validator (checks work). Teams spend 25 minutes analyzing the scenario to identify decision variables (x₁, x₂, etc. representing routes), formulate the objective function (minimize total cost = fuel costs + time penalties), and establish constraints (vehicle capacity ≤ 2000kg, total time ≤ 8 hours, non-negativity constraints). Next, teams spend 45 minutes applying the simplex method manually, creating initial tableaux, performing pivot operations, and iterating toward optimal solutions. Provide simplex method reference sheets and encourage systematic documentation of each iteration. Teams then spend 20 minutes validating their solutions by substituting values back into original constraints and calculating total costs. Finally, conduct 15-minute team presentations where each group explains their formulation approach, demonstrates key simplex iterations, and justifies their optimal solution. Instructor circulates continuously, providing guidance on mathematical procedures and ensuring proper constraint identification.
materials_needed: Delivery scenario data packets (one per team)
Simplex method reference sheets with pivot operation rules
Graph paper for tableau construction
Scientific calculators
Presentation boards or flip chart paper
Markers and rulers
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Problem formulation accuracy (25 points - correct identification of variables, constraints, and objective function), Simplex method execution (35 points - proper tableau setup, accurate pivot operations, correct iterations), Solution validation (20 points - verification through substitution, cost calculation accuracy), and Team presentation quality (20 points - clear explanation of methodology, mathematical reasoning, and final recommendations). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in constraint formulation and demonstrate at least 3 correct simplex iterations to meet proficiency standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled constraint templates, offer guided practice with 2-variable problems before the main activity, and assign peer tutors within teams. Create checkpoint moments every 15 minutes for progress verification. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis questions, challenge them to consider integer programming constraints, or add stochastic elements like variable fuel prices. Provide extension scenarios with additional delivery locations or multiple vehicle types requiring more complex constraint systems.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Circuit Analysis: Comparing Faraday's Law Applications in Generator vs. Transformer Systems
description: Students will analyze and compare electromagnetic induction phenomena in two different circuit configurations by examining magnetic flux changes, induced EMF calculations, and energy transfer mechanisms. They will deconstruct the underlying physics principles to explain why each system produces different electrical outputs despite following the same fundamental law.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between magnetic flux change rate and induced EMF by comparing quantitative data from generator and transformer circuits
Students will evaluate energy conversion efficiency through systematic examination of input mechanical energy versus electrical output in both systems
instructions: Begin by dividing students into pairs and providing each team with pre-recorded oscilloscope data from both a hand-crank generator and a step-up transformer (turns ratio 1:5). Phase 1 (15 min): Students examine Generator Dataset A showing EMF output vs. rotation frequency (5 data points from 1-10 Hz) and calculate induced EMF using ε = -N(dΦ/dt) = -NBA(2πf)cos(2πft). They must identify the relationship between mechanical input frequency and peak voltage output. Phase 2 (20 min): Students analyze Transformer Dataset B showing primary current/voltage and secondary voltage measurements with varying AC input frequencies (50-500 Hz). They calculate theoretical vs. actual voltage ratios and determine efficiency losses. Phase 3 (15 min): Using provided magnetic field strength values (B = 0.05 T for generator, B = 0.12 T for transformer core), coil specifications (generator: 200 turns, 0.04 m² area; transformer: primary 100 turns, secondary 500 turns), students create comparative analysis charts showing EMF prediction vs. measured values. Phase 4 (20 min): Teams construct cause-effect diagrams identifying why energy losses occur differently in each system (mechanical friction in generator vs. core losses in transformer). Final Phase (10 min): Each pair presents one key insight about how magnetic flux change mechanisms differ between rotational and stationary coil systems.
materials_needed: Pre-recorded oscilloscope datasets (Generator Dataset A and Transformer Dataset B)
Scientific calculators
Graph paper and colored pencils
Magnetic field strength reference cards
Circuit specification sheets with coil parameters
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate EMF calculations with proper Faraday's Law application (25%), (2) Correct identification of flux change differences between systems (25%), (3) Quantitative efficiency analysis with supporting evidence (25%), (4) Logical cause-effect reasoning for energy loss mechanisms (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide EMF calculation templates with partially completed formulas and highlight key variables in datasets. For advanced learners: Include additional dataset with variable load resistance values and challenge them to analyze power transfer optimization using impedance matching principles.

title: Creating a Multi-Variable Predictive Dashboard for Local Housing Market Trends
description: Students will design and build an interactive data dashboard that predicts housing prices using multiple variables from real estate datasets. They will synthesize economic indicators, demographic data, and property features to create original visualizations and predictive models that tell a compelling story about their local housing market.
learning_objectives: Students will create an original predictive model by integrating at least 4 different data sources and applying multiple statistical techniques to forecast housing prices
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining data visualization principles, statistical analysis, and storytelling to communicate insights to non-technical stakeholders
instructions: Begin by having students form teams of 2-3 and select a specific metropolitan area for analysis (15 minutes). Provide access to the curated datasets including Zillow housing data, Census demographic information, local employment statistics, and mortgage rate histories. Students first spend 45 minutes exploring and cleaning their chosen datasets, identifying at least 4 key variables that might influence housing prices (square footage, neighborhood income, school ratings, proximity to transit). Next, guide them through creating exploratory visualizations using their chosen tool - scatter plots showing relationships between variables, time series showing price trends, and geographic heat maps showing price distributions (30 minutes). Students then develop their predictive model by testing at least two different approaches: linear regression and one advanced method like random forest or neural networks, comparing accuracy metrics (45 minutes). For dashboard creation, students design 3-4 interactive visualizations that allow users to filter by date range, price range, and neighborhood, ensuring each chart serves a specific analytical purpose (60 minutes). Students must include a 'prediction tool' where users can input property characteristics and receive estimated prices. Finally, teams prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining their methodology, key findings, and demonstrating their dashboard's functionality (30 minutes). Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are documenting their data sources, transformation steps, and analytical decisions for reproducibility.
materials_needed: Real estate dataset (Zillow API or pre-downloaded CSV files)
US Census demographic data by ZIP code
Local employment/economic indicator datasets
Data analysis software (Python with Pandas/Plotly, R with Shiny, or Tableau)
Computers with internet access
Project template worksheet for documentation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (25 points - appropriate data sources, proper cleaning, logical variable selection), Statistical Methodology (25 points - correct model implementation, appropriate technique selection, accuracy metrics), Dashboard Design (25 points - user interface clarity, interactivity functionality, visual appeal), and Communication (25 points - clear insights presentation, technical accuracy, stakeholder-appropriate language). Students submit their dashboard files, documented code, and a 2-page methodology report explaining their analytical choices and limitations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-cleaned starter datasets, offer template code snippets for common operations, and suggest focusing on linear regression before attempting advanced models. Create checkpoint moments every 30 minutes for progress review. For advanced learners: encourage incorporation of external APIs for real-time data, implementation of multiple prediction models with ensemble methods, or addition of advanced features like confidence intervals and sensitivity analysis. Provide access to additional datasets like crime statistics or environmental factors.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Diagram Component Recognition Challenge
description: Students will identify and recall specific components, symbols, and terminology used in Critical Path Method network diagrams through a structured recognition exercise. This activity focuses on memorizing the precise definitions and visual representations of advanced CPM elements including activity-on-node vs. activity-on-arrow notation, float calculations, and critical path indicators.
learning_objectives: Students will identify all 15 standard CPM network diagram symbols and notation elements by matching them to their precise technical definitions within 90% accuracy
Students will recall the specific formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), and Total Float calculations through written reproduction from memory
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Symbol Recognition Sheet containing 15 unlabeled network diagram elements (forward pass arrows, backward pass arrows, activity nodes, dummy activities, critical path highlighting, etc.). Students work individually for 20 minutes to match each symbol with its correct terminology from a provided definition bank. Next, display 8 complex network diagram segments on the projector, each showing different scenarios (critical activities, non-critical activities, multiple paths, etc.). Students have 3 minutes per diagram to write down all visible CPM components they can identify on their answer sheets. Following this, conduct a rapid-fire oral recall session where students must recite the five float calculation formulas when shown only the formula abbreviations (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF). Finally, present 12 real project network diagrams from various industries (construction, software, manufacturing) and have students circle and label every CPM element they can recognize within 15 minutes. Conclude with students creating a personal reference card listing all 15 symbols, 5 formulas, and 8 key CPM terminology definitions from memory. Throughout the activity, emphasize exact terminology usage and precise symbol recognition rather than calculation or analysis.
materials_needed: CPM Symbol Recognition Sheet with 15 network diagram elements
Definition bank handout with 20 technical terms
8 projected network diagram segments
12 industry-specific network diagrams (printed)
Blank reference cards (3x5 inches)
Red pens for self-checking
Answer key with precise definitions
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on symbol-definition matching (14/15 correct), successfully identify at least 85% of CPM components in projected diagrams, recite all 5 formulas with correct variable definitions, and complete reference cards with 100% accurate terminology. Use provided rubric: 4 points for perfect symbol recognition, 3 points for formula recall accuracy, 2 points for diagram component identification speed, 1 point for reference card completeness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed symbol sheet with 5 answers filled in, and allow use of color-coded reference materials during the first round. Offer additional practice with simplified 3-activity network diagrams. For advanced learners, include resource leveling symbols, precedence diagramming method (PDM) relationship types (SS, SF, FF), and lag/lead time notations. Challenge them to identify components in hand-drawn versus software-generated diagrams.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Multi-Perspective Analysis of the 2008 Financial Crisis Response
description: Students will analyze and compare the leadership approaches of three key figures during the 2008 financial crisis (Ben Bernanke, Hank Paulson, and Timothy Geithner) to understand how different leadership styles and decision-making frameworks influence crisis management outcomes. Through systematic examination of primary sources and stakeholder perspectives, students will demonstrate comprehension of adaptive leadership principles in high-stakes environments.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between adaptive and technical leadership approaches by analyzing specific decisions made by financial crisis leaders through documented evidence and stakeholder testimonies

Students will interpret the relationship between leadership communication strategies and stakeholder confidence through comparative analysis of public statements, congressional testimonies, and market responses during September-December 2008
instructions:
Begin with a 10-minute overview of the September 2008 timeline (Lehman collapse through TARP passage). Divide students into groups of 3, assigning each member one leader to focus on: Bernanke (Federal Reserve Chair), Paulson (Treasury Secretary), or Geithner (NY Fed President). Provide each student with their leader's testimony packet and crisis timeline. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Individual analysis using the provided Leadership Decision Matrix. Students identify 3 critical decisions their assigned leader made, categorizing each as adaptive (requiring learning/experimentation) or technical (applying known solutions). For each decision, students document: the specific action taken, stated rationale, immediate stakeholder reactions, and measurable outcomes within 30 days.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Within groups, students present their findings using the structured comparison template. They must explain their leader's dominant style, provide evidence for their categorizations, and identify moments when their leader shifted approaches. Groups complete a comparative analysis chart showing how all three leaders handled similar challenges (bank bailouts, public communication, congressional relations).

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Groups prepare a 3-minute presentation answering: 'Which leadership approach was most effective for maintaining financial system stability, and why?' They must reference specific evidence and acknowledge limitations of their analysis. Conclude with 10 minutes of structured peer feedback using the evaluation criteria rubric.
materials_needed: Primary source packet: Congressional testimonies from Bernanke, Paulson, and Geithner (September-December 2008)
Leadership Decision Matrix worksheet with adaptive/technical categorization framework
Crisis timeline handout with key dates, market indicators, and policy announcements
Structured comparison template for group analysis phase
Evaluation criteria rubric for peer assessment
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Leadership Decision Matrix worksheets for accuracy of categorizations and quality of evidence (40%). Assess group comparative analysis charts for thoroughness and insight (35%). Score final presentations using provided rubric focusing on evidence-based reasoning and acknowledgment of complexity (25%). Success requires students to correctly identify at least 2 of 3 leadership approaches as adaptive vs. technical and provide specific, accurate evidence from primary sources.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key passages in testimonies and a decision categorization example using a non-crisis leadership scenario. Offer sentence starters for analysis statements. For advanced learners: Include additional stakeholder perspectives (bank CEOs, international finance ministers) and challenge them to identify second-order effects of leadership decisions on global markets. Provide extension questions about alternative leadership approaches that could have been employed.

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS by configuring EC2 instances for the web tier, setting up an RDS database for the data tier, and using S3 for static content storage. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS services integration and best practices for scalable application deployment.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional three-tier web application by configuring EC2, RDS, and S3 services within the AWS Management Console
Students will implement AWS security best practices through proper security group configuration and IAM role assignment for service communication
instructions: Begin with students logging into their AWS Free Tier accounts and navigating to the EC2 Dashboard (5 minutes). First, have students create a security group named 'WebTier-SG' allowing HTTP (port 80), HTTPS (port 443), and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere, then create a second security group 'DatabaseTier-SG' allowing MySQL (port 3306) access only from the WebTier-SG group (10 minutes). Next, students launch a t2.micro EC2 instance using Amazon Linux 2 AMI, attach the WebTier-SG security group, and create a new key pair for SSH access (10 minutes). While the instance launches, students navigate to RDS and create a t3.micro MySQL database instance in the same availability zone, using the DatabaseTier-SG security group, with database name 'webapp_db', username 'admin', and a secure password they document (15 minutes). Students then create an S3 bucket with a unique name following the naming convention 'studentname-webapp-assets-[random number]' and upload provided CSS and image files, enabling public read access on these objects (10 minutes). Once the EC2 instance is running, students SSH into it and install Apache web server using 'sudo yum update -y' and 'sudo yum install -y httpd php php-mysql' (10 minutes). Students then create a simple PHP web page that connects to their RDS database and displays a connection status, referencing the S3-hosted CSS file for styling (15 minutes). Finally, students test their application by accessing the EC2 public IP address in a browser and verify all three tiers are functioning correctly (10 minutes). Students document their application's public URL, RDS endpoint, and S3 bucket URL as deliverables.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier account for each student
Sample CSS file and web assets provided by instructor
PHP web application template with database connection code
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or terminal for Mac/Linux)
Activity worksheet for documenting AWS resource details
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Running EC2 instance with correct security groups (25 points), (2) Accessible web application displaying database connection status (25 points), (3) S3 bucket with uploaded assets and public access configured (25 points), (4) Completed worksheet with all AWS resource URLs and configuration details (25 points). Bonus points awarded for implementing additional security measures like restricting SSH access to specific IP addresses.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step screenshots for each AWS console navigation. Offer one-on-one SSH troubleshooting support as this is often a stumbling block. For advanced learners, challenge them to implement an Application Load Balancer, set up CloudWatch monitoring, or configure automatic database backups. Provide extension activities like implementing SSL certificates or setting up a CDN with CloudFront.

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3: Team Exercise
description: Students will apply AWS cloud fundamentals by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture. They will configure EC2 instances for the web tier, set up an RDS database for the data tier, and use S3 for static content hosting, demonstrating practical cloud deployment skills.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS databases, and S3 buckets within AWS console
Students will apply AWS security best practices through proper VPC setup, security groups configuration, and IAM role assignment
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS Academy Learner Lab access credentials and a simple PHP web application code package containing index.php, config.php, and sample CSS files.

**Phase 1 - Infrastructure Setup (25 minutes):** Students log into AWS console and create a new VPC with public and private subnets. They launch a t2.micro EC2 instance in the public subnet, selecting Amazon Linux 2 AMI. Students configure security groups allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from their IP address only.

**Phase 2 - Database Configuration (20 minutes):** Students create an RDS MySQL database instance (t3.micro) in the private subnet with a specific database name 'webapp_db'. They configure the database security group to allow MySQL traffic (port 3306) only from the EC2 security group. Students record database endpoint and credentials.

**Phase 3 - Storage Setup (15 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket with a unique name, upload provided CSS and image files, and configure the bucket for static website hosting with public read access for web assets only.

**Phase 4 - Application Deployment (20 minutes):** Students SSH into their EC2 instance, install Apache and PHP using yum commands. They upload the provided PHP application files, modify config.php with their RDS endpoint details, and update HTML to reference S3-hosted static assets.

**Phase 5 - Testing and Documentation (10 minutes):** Students test their application by accessing the EC2 public IP address, verify database connectivity by submitting test data, and document their architecture with screenshots showing all three tiers functioning together.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts for each student
Pre-built PHP web application package (index.php, config.php, style.css, sample images)
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Architecture diagram template for documentation
Step-by-step checklist handout with specific AWS configuration parameters
assessment_method: Students submit a completion report containing: (1) Screenshots of functioning web application with visible URL, (2) AWS console screenshots showing EC2, RDS, and S3 resources properly configured, (3) Completed architecture diagram labeling all components, (4) Written reflection identifying one security improvement they implemented. Success criteria: All three tiers operational, proper security group configuration, successful database connection test, and accurate documentation. Grading rubric: Functionality (40%), Security Configuration (30%), Documentation (20%), Reflection (10%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and database connection string examples. Create checkpoint validation after each phase before proceeding. Offer peer partnering for troubleshooting. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like auto-scaling groups, load balancers, or CloudFront CDN integration. Encourage exploration of Infrastructure as Code using CloudFormation templates for their deployed architecture.

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3: Team Exercise
description: Students will apply AWS cloud services knowledge by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture. They will configure EC2 instances for the web server, set up an RDS database, and implement S3 for static file storage, demonstrating practical cloud deployment skills.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration principles by launching and configuring a web server instance with proper security groups and key pairs
Students will implement multi-service AWS architecture through connecting EC2, RDS, and S3 services to create a functional web application
instructions:
**Phase 1: Environment Setup (15 minutes)**
Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab credentials. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify access to EC2, RDS, and S3 services in us-east-1 region. Distribute the sample PHP web application files (contact form with database integration) via shared folder.

**Phase 2: S3 Static Storage Setup (20 minutes)**
Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-static-[student-initials]-[date]'. Configure bucket for static website hosting, upload CSS and image files from provided assets folder. Set appropriate public read permissions for static files only. Test access to static files via S3 URL.

**Phase 3: RDS Database Configuration (25 minutes)**
Students launch MySQL RDS instance (db.t3.micro) with database name 'webapp_db'. Configure security group allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from EC2 security group only. Record database endpoint URL. Using provided SQL script, create 'contacts' table with fields: id, name, email, message, timestamp.

**Phase 4: EC2 Web Server Deployment (35 minutes)**
Launch Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) with security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22). SSH into instance and install Apache, PHP, and MySQL client using yum package manager. Upload provided PHP application files to /var/www/html/. Configure database connection parameters in config.php file using RDS endpoint. Modify application to reference S3 URLs for static assets. Start Apache service and enable auto-start.

**Phase 5: Integration Testing (15 minutes)**
Students test complete application by submitting contact form entries through web browser using EC2 public IP address. Verify data appears in RDS database using MySQL client. Confirm static files load correctly from S3. Document any connection issues and troubleshoot using AWS CloudWatch logs.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts with $100 credit limit
Sample PHP web application files (contact form, config template, CSS, images)
SQL database creation script for contacts table
Student worksheet with configuration parameters template
AWS CLI reference guide for basic commands
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Functional web form accessible via EC2 public IP, (2) Database query results showing submitted form data in RDS, (3) S3 bucket contents with static files, (4) Architecture diagram labeling all services and connections. Rubric: Functional application (40%), proper service configuration (30%), security best practices implementation (20%), documentation quality (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates, offer debugging checklist for common connection issues, pair struggling students with successful peers for troubleshooting. Create video walkthrough for SSH key setup and file transfer processes. **Extensions for advanced students:** Implement CloudFront CDN for S3 assets, add Application Load Balancer for high availability, configure CloudWatch monitoring dashboards, implement automated backups using AWS Backup service.
original_title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3: Team Exercise
description: Students will apply AWS cloud fundamentals by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture. They will configure EC2 instances for the web tier, set up RDS for the database tier, and use S3 for static content storage, demonstrating practical cloud deployment skills.
learning_objectives: Students will apply AWS EC2 configuration concepts by launching and configuring web server instances with proper security groups and key pairs
Students will implement multi-tier architecture principles through connecting EC2 instances to RDS databases and S3 storage buckets
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS account credentials and confirms students can access AWS Console. Distribute the sample HTML/PHP application files and database schema script via shared folder.

**Phase 1 - S3 Setup (15 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'webapp-static-[studentname]' with public read access. They upload provided CSS, JavaScript, and image files, then test accessibility via bucket URL. Students record the S3 bucket URL for later use.

**Phase 2 - RDS Configuration (20 minutes):** Students launch a MySQL RDS instance (t3.micro) named 'webapp-db' in the default VPC. They configure security groups to allow MySQL traffic (port 3306) from EC2 instances only. Using the provided connection details, students connect via MySQL Workbench and execute the provided schema script to create tables.

**Phase 3 - EC2 Deployment (25 minutes):** Students launch an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) and install Apache/PHP. They modify the provided PHP application code to include their specific RDS endpoint and S3 bucket URLs. Students configure security groups allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access, then upload application files via SCP.

**Phase 4 - Integration Testing (10 minutes):** Students access their web application via EC2 public IP, test database connectivity by submitting form data, and verify static assets load from S3. They document any connection issues and troubleshoot using CloudWatch logs.

**Deliverable Creation (5 minutes):** Students capture screenshots of working application, create architecture diagram showing all three tiers, and submit AWS resource URLs for verification.
materials_needed: AWS account with appropriate permissions (EC2, RDS, S3, CloudWatch)
Sample PHP web application files with database connection code
MySQL database schema creation script
MySQL Workbench or equivalent database client software
SSH client (PuTTY for Windows or terminal for Mac/Linux)
assessment_method: Students submit: 1) Screenshot showing functional web application with data retrieval from RDS (25 points), 2) Architecture diagram labeling all AWS services and connections (25 points), 3) List of AWS resource URLs (EC2 public IP, RDS endpoint, S3 bucket URL) for instructor verification (25 points), 4) Brief reflection describing one challenge encountered and how they resolved it (25 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step connection troubleshooting checklist. Offer pair programming option for PHP configuration. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement auto-scaling groups, add CloudFront CDN for S3 content, or configure RDS multi-AZ deployment. Provide additional scenarios like adding ElastiCache or implementing infrastructure as code using CloudFormation templates.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Approaches Across Project Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three different project scenarios to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of various risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept). They will examine the relationship between risk characteristics, project constraints, and optimal response selection to determine which strategies are most appropriate for specific risk situations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of different risk response strategies by comparing their application across three distinct project scenarios with varying constraints and risk profiles
Students will evaluate the relationship between risk characteristics (probability, impact, timing) and response strategy selection through systematic comparison and justification of their choices
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute the three project scenario packets: Scenario A (Software Implementation with tight budget), Scenario B (Construction project with regulatory constraints), and Scenario C (Product launch with market uncertainties). Each scenario contains 5 identified risks with detailed probability/impact assessments and project constraint information.

Phase 1 (30 minutes): Each group analyzes all three scenarios independently. For each risk in each scenario, students must: (1) identify which of the four response strategies would be most appropriate, (2) explain why other strategies would be less effective, (3) consider how project constraints influence their choice, and (4) estimate resource requirements for their chosen response.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Groups create a comparative analysis matrix showing their recommended responses across all scenarios. They must identify patterns in their decision-making and note where similar risks required different responses due to varying project contexts.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group presents one scenario's analysis to the class, focusing on their most challenging risk response decision. Other groups provide feedback and alternative perspectives.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Instructor-led debrief discussing common patterns, decision criteria, and how project context influences risk response selection. Students complete individual reflection sheets analyzing differences between their initial instincts and final group decisions.
materials_needed: Three detailed project scenario packets with risk registers (printed)
Risk response strategy reference sheets
Comparative analysis matrix templates (digital or printed)
Individual reflection worksheets
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk response strategy selection with clear justification (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of contextual factors (25%), (3) Depth of reasoning in explaining why alternative strategies were rejected (25%), (4) Individual reflection demonstrating analytical thinking about decision-making process (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ points in each category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a decision tree template showing key questions for each response strategy selection. Offer one-on-one guidance during Phase 1 analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify hybrid response strategies or propose modifications to the given project constraints that would change their response recommendations. Encourage them to calculate ROI for their response strategies.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and Quality of Service
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure supporting multiple VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security policies, and QoS prioritization. This capstone activity integrates switching, routing, security, and network optimization concepts into a functional business-ready solution.
estimated_duration: 5.5 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive network topology with VLANs, trunking, and routing protocols by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed implementation plans
Students will create advanced security configurations including ACLs, port security, and DHCP snooping through hands-on device configuration and testing
Students will implement Quality of Service policies for voice, video, and data traffic by configuring traffic classification, marking, and queuing mechanisms
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario requiring network redesign for 200 employees across 4 departments (Finance, HR, Engineering, Guest). Phase 1 (60 minutes): Students work in teams of 3-4 to design network topology using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3. They must create VLAN assignments (Finance VLAN 10, HR VLAN 20, Engineering VLAN 30, Guest VLAN 40), determine IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets, select appropriate Cisco switch and router models, and document trunk links and access ports. Phase 2 (90 minutes): Teams configure physical or simulated devices including creating VLANs on switches, configuring trunk ports with 802.1Q encapsulation, setting up DHCP pools for each VLAN, implementing inter-VLAN routing using router-on-a-stick or SVI configuration, and establishing OSPF routing between multiple switches. Phase 3 (75 minutes): Implement security measures including standard and extended ACLs restricting inter-departmental access, port security limiting MAC addresses per port, DHCP snooping on untrusted ports, and SSH configuration for secure management. Phase 4 (60 minutes): Configure QoS policies including voice VLAN configuration for IP phones, traffic classification using DSCP markings, priority queuing for voice traffic, and bandwidth allocation for different traffic types. Phase 5 (45 minutes): Teams conduct comprehensive testing including connectivity verification between VLANs, security policy validation, QoS effectiveness measurement, and documentation of all configurations with detailed network diagrams.
materials_needed: Cisco Catalyst 2960 or 3560 switches (minimum 3 per team)
Cisco ISR 2911 or 4321 routers (1 per team)
Cisco IP phones 7940 or 8841 (2 per team)
Ethernet cables (Cat6, various lengths)
Laptop computers with terminal emulation software (PuTTY or SecureCRT)
Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 simulation software
Network documentation templates and IP address planning worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design (25 points) - topology accuracy, VLAN planning, IP addressing scheme; Configuration Implementation (35 points) - correct VLAN creation, trunking, routing protocols, all devices reachable; Security Implementation (20 points) - functional ACLs, port security, secure management access; QoS Configuration (15 points) - voice VLAN setup, traffic prioritization, bandwidth management; Documentation (5 points) - complete network diagrams, configuration backups, testing results. Students must demonstrate full connectivity, security policy enforcement, and QoS functionality through live testing scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured baseline templates with basic VLAN structure, offer configuration checklists with step-by-step verification commands, assign peer mentors from advanced students, and break complex configurations into smaller validated segments. For advanced learners: Add redundancy requirements using spanning tree protocols, implement advanced security features like 802.1X authentication, configure dynamic routing protocols across multiple sites, integrate wireless access points with controller-based management, or add network monitoring using SNMP and NetFlow analysis.

title: Engineering Cost Optimization Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a multi-constraint engineering design problem involving cost minimization for a renewable energy system. They will formulate constraints, identify decision variables, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to find optimal solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methodology to formulate a real-world engineering optimization problem by identifying decision variables, objective functions, and constraints
Students will implement both graphical and algebraic solution methods to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions:
Begin with 10 minutes of problem presentation: provide the scenario where students are renewable energy consultants tasked with minimizing installation costs for a hybrid solar-wind farm. Distribute the problem sheet specifying: minimum 500 MW total capacity, solar panels cost $2000/MW with 8-hour daily generation, wind turbines cost $3500/MW with 12-hour daily generation, land constraints (max 200 solar units, max 150 wind units), and minimum daily energy requirements of 4000 MWh. 

Next 20 minutes: students work in pairs to formulate the linear programming model. They must define decision variables (x = solar units, y = wind units), write the objective function (minimize 2000x + 3500y), and establish constraints including capacity, energy output, and non-negativity requirements. Circulate to verify correct mathematical formulation.

Following 25 minutes: students apply the graphical method by plotting constraint lines on provided coordinate grids, identifying the feasible region, and locating corner points. They must calculate objective function values at each vertex to determine the optimal solution.

Final 25 minutes: introduce simplex tableau method using provided templates. Students convert their problem to standard form, create initial tableau, and perform pivot operations to reach optimality. They must verify their graphical solution matches the simplex result.

Conclude with 10 minutes of solution comparison where pairs present their optimal mix and justify their mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: Engineering optimization problem sheets (one per student pair)
Graph paper with pre-drawn coordinate systems
Simplex tableau templates
Scientific calculators
Rulers and colored pencils for constraint graphing
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct problem formulation including all variables and constraints (25%), (2) Accurate graphical solution with properly identified feasible region and optimal point (25%), (3) Correct simplex method implementation with accurate tableau operations (30%), (4) Clear mathematical communication and justification of final solution (20%). Students must submit written work showing all calculations and a brief explanation of their optimization strategy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide constraint formulation templates with partially completed examples, offer step-by-step graphical method checklists, and allow calculator use for arithmetic operations. For advanced learners: introduce sensitivity analysis by asking them to determine how cost coefficients could change while maintaining the same optimal solution, or extend to integer programming constraints requiring whole number solutions.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in Simple Calculator Functions
description: Students evaluate three different approaches to fixing a buggy calculator function by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will critique each solution and justify their ranking of which fix is most appropriate for production use.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different bug fix implementations by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and maintainability using established coding standards
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison of multiple approaches to the same problem
instructions:
Begin by providing students with a simple JavaScript calculator function containing a division-by-zero bug and three different proposed fixes (15 minutes setup). Display the original buggy function on screen: a basic calculator that crashes when dividing by zero. Present three fix approaches: Fix A (simple if-statement returning 'Error'), Fix B (try-catch block with console logging), and Fix C (input validation with user-friendly error object). 

Divide students into groups of 3-4 and give each group printed copies of all code samples (5 minutes). Each group spends 20 minutes analyzing the fixes using the provided evaluation criteria sheet covering: code readability, error handling approach, user experience, maintainability, and performance impact. Students must score each fix on a 1-5 scale for each criterion and provide written justification.

Next, groups spend 10 minutes ranking the three fixes from best to worst, creating a one-page summary explaining their decision with specific code examples. During the final 15 minutes, each group presents their ranking and justification to the class (2 minutes per group), followed by instructor-led discussion comparing different group conclusions. 

Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students individually write which evaluation criteria they found most important and why, connecting to real-world software development scenarios.
materials_needed: Printed code samples showing original bug and three fixes (one set per group)
Evaluation criteria checklist handouts
Computers/laptops with web browser for testing code samples
Projector for displaying code and group presentations
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade based on completed evaluation matrix (40%), quality of written justification with specific examples (35%), and participation in group presentation (25%). Success criteria: students must use at least 4 of 5 evaluation criteria, provide specific code references in justifications, and demonstrate understanding that multiple solutions can be valid depending on context.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide sentence starters for justifications and highlight specific lines to focus on in each code sample. For advanced learners: ask them to propose a fourth solution and evaluate how their approach compares to the given options, or consider additional criteria like security implications and scalability.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula and Calculation Component Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific mathematical formulas, variance calculations, and statistical parameters used in Critical Path Method scheduling under uncertainty. This advanced recall activity focuses on the precise mathematical components of PERT/CPM analysis including forward pass, backward pass, and probability distribution calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), Late Finish (LF), and Total Float calculations by completing timed formula reproduction exercises

Students will identify and recite the specific statistical formulas for PERT time estimation including optimistic, pessimistic, most likely time calculations and standard deviation formulas through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet containing 15 critical formulas including ES = max(EF of predecessors), EF = ES + Duration, LS = LF - Duration, LF = min(LS of successors), Total Float = LF - EF, PERT Expected Time = (O + 4M + P)/6, PERT Variance = ((P-O)/6)², Project Variance = sum of critical path activity variances, Standard Deviation = √Project Variance, and Z-score = (Target Date - Expected Date)/Project Standard Deviation. Allow students 20 minutes to study these formulas intensively using active memorization techniques. Next, collect all reference materials and conduct Round 1: Basic Formula Recall (10 minutes) - project 10 formula prompts one at a time (e.g., 'Formula for Early Finish?') and have students write complete formulas on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate verification. Record individual scores. Conduct Round 2: Application Context Recall (15 minutes) - present specific project scenarios (e.g., 'Activity A has ES=5, Duration=8, what is the EF formula and calculation?') requiring students to recall both formula and computational process. Finally, implement Round 3: Advanced Integration Recall (15 minutes) - display complex network diagrams requiring students to identify which specific formulas apply to calculate critical path duration, project completion probability, and schedule compression impacts. Students must write the exact formula sequence needed without performing calculations. Conclude with immediate feedback session reviewing any commonly missed formulas and having students repeat incorrect responses three times aloud.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet with 15 specific mathematical formulas
Individual dry-erase whiteboards and markers for each student
Digital timer with audible alerts
Pre-prepared PowerPoint slides with formula prompts and network diagrams
Score tracking sheets for instructor use
Sample project network diagrams with 8-12 activities showing dependencies
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (13/15 formulas correct) across all three rounds to demonstrate mastery. Score using binary marking (correct formula = 1 point, incorrect/incomplete = 0 points). Assess formula accuracy including correct mathematical notation, proper variable placement, and complete expression. Track individual performance on score sheets noting specific formulas missed for targeted remediation. Successful completion requires accurate recall of core CPM formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF, Total Float), PERT statistical formulas (expected time, variance, standard deviation), and project-level calculations (critical path probability, Z-score analysis).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for formula recall (e.g., 'Early Start = Maximum Early Finish of predecessors' becomes 'ES = Max EF pred'), allow use of partial reference sheets showing variable definitions only, and implement peer tutoring pairs during study phase. For advanced learners: Extend activity by requiring recall of resource-constrained scheduling formulas, earned value management equations (CV, SV, CPI, SPI), and Monte Carlo simulation parameters. Challenge advanced students to recite formulas for schedule compression techniques including crashing cost calculations and fast-tracking risk assessment metrics.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: A Case Analysis of Contradictory Leadership Demands
description: Students will analyze complex leadership scenarios that present inherent contradictions and paradoxes, identifying how effective leaders navigate competing demands. Through systematic examination of real-world cases, students will demonstrate understanding of leadership paradoxes by explaining the underlying tensions and rationale behind seemingly contradictory leadership decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the nature of leadership paradoxes by identifying and categorizing contradictory demands in complex organizational scenarios
Students will interpret leadership decision-making rationale through systematic analysis of how leaders balance competing organizational tensions
instructions: Begin by distributing three pre-selected case studies featuring leadership paradoxes (15 minutes setup). Case 1: A CEO who promotes collaboration while making unilateral strategic decisions. Case 2: A military leader who demonstrates both compassion and ruthless discipline. Case 3: A nonprofit director who pursues growth while maintaining mission authenticity. Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning each team one case initially (5 minutes). Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams use the provided Paradox Analysis Framework to dissect their assigned case. They must identify the specific contradictory demands, map stakeholder perspectives, and explain why both sides of the paradox are necessary. Teams document findings on structured worksheets, noting evidence from the case that supports each paradoxical element. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Implement a 'jigsaw' rotation where one member from each team moves to analyze a second case with new teammates, bringing insights from their original case. This creates mixed groups with diverse case experience. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams synthesize findings across all cases using a comparative matrix, identifying patterns in how leaders manage paradoxes. They must explain three universal principles for navigating leadership contradictions, supported by specific evidence from the cases. Phase 4 (25 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about leadership paradoxes to the class, explaining their reasoning and connecting to broader leadership theory. Conclude with individual reflection writing (10 minutes) where students explain which paradox they found most challenging to understand and why.
materials_needed: Three detailed leadership paradox case studies (2-3 pages each)
Paradox Analysis Framework worksheets with guided questions
Comparative Analysis Matrix templates
Flipchart paper and markers for group work
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of paradox identification and explanation (25%), (2) Quality of evidence used to support analysis (25%), (3) Depth of understanding demonstrated in comparative synthesis (25%), and (4) Clarity of reasoning in explaining leadership decision-making rationale (25%). Success requires students to correctly identify at least 2 paradoxes per case, provide specific textual evidence, and articulate logical explanations for contradictory leadership behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for analysis questions and offer a completed example using a simple leadership scenario. Create mixed-ability teams and assign specific roles (evidence finder, pattern identifier, presenter). For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional paradoxes not obvious in the cases, connect findings to specific leadership theories (transformational, situational, etc.), or analyze how cultural context might influence paradox navigation.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application on AWS using EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will deploy a complete three-tier web application architecture on AWS by configuring EC2 instances for the web and application tiers, setting up an RDS database, and implementing S3 for static file storage. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS service integration and basic cloud architecture principles.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS database, and S3 bucket with proper security groups and networking
Students will demonstrate AWS service integration through implementing a functional web application that connects frontend, backend, and database components
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with AWS Academy Learner Lab access and a simple PHP/MySQL contact form application code (available via GitHub link). Ensure students can access the AWS Management Console.

**Step 1 - S3 Configuration (15 minutes):** Students create an S3 bucket named 'student-[lastname]-webapp-assets', upload provided CSS and image files, configure bucket for static website hosting, and set appropriate public read permissions using bucket policy template.

**Step 2 - RDS Database Setup (20 minutes):** Students launch a MySQL RDS instance (db.t3.micro) in the default VPC, configure security group to allow MySQL traffic (port 3306) from EC2 security group, note down endpoint URL, and create database credentials (username: admin, password: StudentPass123!).

**Step 3 - EC2 Web Server Deployment (25 minutes):** Students launch Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro), configure security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) traffic, connect via EC2 Instance Connect, install Apache and PHP using provided yum commands, download application code from GitHub, and modify database connection settings in config.php file using nano editor.
