**Step 4 - Application Configuration (15 minutes):** Students update the application's config file with their RDS endpoint, S3 bucket URL for static assets, test database connectivity using provided MySQL commands, and create the contacts table using provided SQL schema.

**Step 5 - Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Students access their application via EC2 public IP address, submit test contact form entries, verify data appears in RDS database, and confirm static assets load from S3 bucket.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts with $100 credit limit
GitHub repository with PHP contact form application code
Provided SQL schema file for contacts table
Security group configuration templates
S3 bucket policy JSON template
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Functional web application running on EC2 with public IP, (2) RDS instance status page showing 'Available', (3) S3 bucket contents with uploaded static files, (4) MySQL query results showing submitted contact form data, (5) AWS billing dashboard showing resource usage. Rubric: Complete deployment (40%), Proper security configuration (25%), Functional application with database connectivity (25%), Documentation quality (10%).
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates, offer command cheat sheets for Linux/MySQL operations, pair with stronger technical students, provide video walkthrough of EC2 connection process. **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to implement SSL certificates, add CloudFront CDN for S3 assets, create custom VPC with public/private subnets, implement Auto Scaling groups, or add CloudWatch monitoring and alarms.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Conversion Chart Creation
description: Students will memorize binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through repetitive drilling and create a personal reference chart. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, with one partner showing the decimal side while the other states the binary equivalent, then switching roles every 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers on the board for 5 seconds each, and students write binary equivalents on individual whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate feedback. After 10 minutes of whole-class drilling, students individually complete a blank conversion chart template with decimal numbers 0-15 in the left column and empty binary column on the right. They must fill in all binary equivalents from memory without referring to flashcards. Once completed, students check their charts against the answer key and correct any errors using red ink. Finally, students create their own personalized reference chart on cardstock, decorating it with colors or patterns to aid memorization, focusing extra attention on numbers they missed during the memory exercise. Conclude with a rapid-fire verbal quiz where students stand and sit down if they cannot immediately answer when called upon.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Individual whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each student
Blank conversion chart template (printed worksheets)
Answer key for binary conversions 0-15
Colored pencils or markers
Cardstock paper for final reference charts
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/15 correct) on the completed conversion chart filled from memory. Additionally, assess participation during pair work and responsiveness during rapid-fire verbal quiz. Award full credit for charts showing 14-15 correct conversions, partial credit for 11-13 correct, and require remediation for fewer than 11 correct answers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, allow them to use the pattern method (powers of 2: 8-4-2-1) written at the top of their chart and provide extra practice with smaller ranges (0-7 first). Advanced learners can extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or practice hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need support during partner drilling.

title: Interpreting Cross-Validation Results to Compare Machine Learning Model Performance
description: Students will analyze and interpret k-fold cross-validation output from three different classification algorithms (Decision Tree, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) trained on a customer churn dataset. They will explain the meaning of performance metrics and justify which model performs best based on the validation results.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret cross-validation scores and variability measures by analyzing mean accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores across folds for multiple algorithms
Students will explain the significance of performance differences through comparing standard deviations and identifying potential overfitting or underfitting patterns
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-prepared dataset containing cross-validation results from three models: Decision Tree (5-fold CV results: accuracy=[0.82, 0.79, 0.85, 0.81, 0.83], precision=[0.78, 0.74, 0.81, 0.77, 0.79], recall=[0.85, 0.82, 0.89, 0.84, 0.87]), Random Forest (accuracy=[0.87, 0.88, 0.86, 0.89, 0.87], precision=[0.84, 0.85, 0.83, 0.86, 0.84], recall=[0.89, 0.91, 0.88, 0.92, 0.89]), and Logistic Regression (accuracy=[0.79, 0.81, 0.78, 0.80, 0.79], precision=[0.82, 0.84, 0.81, 0.83, 0.82], recall=[0.76, 0.78, 0.75, 0.77, 0.76]). Step 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually to calculate mean and standard deviation for each metric per model using provided Excel template or Python notebook. Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students create a comparison table ranking models by each metric and discuss which standard deviation values indicate more reliable performance. Step 3 (10 minutes): Students individually write a 150-word interpretation explaining: (a) which model they would recommend and why, (b) what the standard deviation tells them about model stability, (c) potential trade-offs between precision and recall for each model. Step 4 (10 minutes): Facilitate whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their recommendations and reasoning, highlighting how different business contexts (cost of false positives vs false negatives) might influence model selection.
materials_needed: Pre-formatted Excel spreadsheet with cross-validation results data
Python Jupyter notebook template with pandas DataFrames (alternative to Excel)
Model comparison table worksheet template
Calculator or computer access for statistical calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate students' written interpretations using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct calculation of means and standard deviations, (2) Appropriate ranking and selection of best model with justification, (3) Accurate explanation of what standard deviation indicates about model reliability, (4) Clear articulation of precision-recall trade-offs. Full credit requires addressing all four components with technically accurate explanations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed calculation examples for the first model and a sentence starter template for the written interpretation. Pair weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners: Ask them to research and explain additional metrics like AUC-ROC, discuss confidence intervals for the means, or consider how cross-validation strategy (k-fold vs stratified) might impact results interpretation.

title: Multi-Variable Calculus: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Placement Using Lagrange Multipliers
description: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world optimization problem involving the placement of solar panels on an irregularly shaped rooftop. They will work with constraint functions, partial derivatives, and interpret their mathematical solutions in practical terms.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier techniques to solve constrained optimization problems by setting up and solving systems of partial derivative equations
Students will implement multi-variable calculus concepts through solving realistic engineering scenarios involving multiple constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing the rooftop blueprints and solar panel specifications (15 minutes setup). Present the scenario: A building has an L-shaped rooftop with dimensions given by the constraint g(x,y) = x² + 2y² - 100 ≤ 0, and students must maximize solar energy output f(x,y) = 8x + 6y - 0.1x² - 0.05y² subject to this constraint and a budget constraint h(x,y) = 200x + 150y - 12000 ≤ 0. Step 1 (20 minutes): Students work in pairs to identify the objective function and constraint equations, then set up the Lagrangian L(x,y,λ,μ) = f(x,y) - λg(x,y) - μh(x,y). Step 2 (25 minutes): Calculate partial derivatives ∂L/∂x, ∂L/∂y, ∂L/∂λ, ∂L/∂μ and set equal to zero, creating a system of four equations. Step 3 (30 minutes): Solve the system using substitution or matrix methods, checking boundary conditions and corner cases. Step 4 (20 minutes): Evaluate critical points using the bordered Hessian to confirm maximum values. Step 5 (15 minutes): Interpret results by calculating actual solar panel quantities, total cost, and expected energy output. Students must present their solution showing mathematical work, practical implementation plan, and justification for why their solution satisfies both constraints. Circulate during work time to check derivative calculations and system-solving approaches.
materials_needed: L-shaped rooftop blueprint handouts with coordinate system
Solar panel specification sheets with cost and energy output data
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Mathematica/Maple)
Graph paper and rulers
Bordered Hessian reference sheet
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct setup of Lagrangian and constraint identification (25 points), (2) Accurate calculation of partial derivatives and system setup (30 points), (3) Proper solution of the system and critical point analysis (25 points), (4) Realistic interpretation and practical implementation plan (20 points). Students must submit written work showing all mathematical steps plus a 2-minute oral presentation of their final recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed Lagrangian setup and derivative templates, offer step-by-step derivative calculation guides, and pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Add a third constraint involving panel tilt angles, require sensitivity analysis for parameter changes, or extend to 3D optimization with panel height variables. Consider providing online graphing tools to visualize constraint regions.

title: Code Review Evaluation: Assessing Bug Fix Quality and Best Practices
description: Students will evaluate three different code solutions that fix the same simple bug, analyzing code quality, readability, and adherence to best practices. They will rank the solutions and provide detailed justifications using established criteria for good programming practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three bug fix solutions by comparing code quality, readability, and maintainability using a structured rubric
Students will critique programming approaches through written analysis that identifies strengths, weaknesses, and improvement recommendations
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a simple Python function containing a clear bug (e.g., an off-by-one error in a loop that processes a list). Display three different corrected versions: Solution A uses a quick fix with minimal changes, Solution B refactors for better readability, and Solution C adds error handling and documentation. Provide students with an evaluation rubric covering four criteria: correctness (does it fix the bug?), readability (clear variable names, logical structure), maintainability (easy to modify later), and best practices (proper error handling, documentation). Give students 15 minutes to individually examine each solution, testing them mentally or with provided sample inputs. Next, have students spend 10 minutes ranking the solutions from best to worst, writing 2-3 sentences justifying each ranking decision. In pairs, students spend 10 minutes comparing their rankings and discussing differences in their evaluations. Finally, conduct a 10-minute class discussion where pairs share their top-ranked solution and reasoning. Conclude by revealing expert consensus on the ranking with explanations, allowing students to reflect on how their evaluation process compared to professional standards.
materials_needed: Printed handout with original buggy code and three solutions
Code evaluation rubric with 4-point scale for each criterion
Sample test inputs for students to trace through solutions
Projector or whiteboard for class discussion
assessment_method: Evaluate student ranking sheets for: (1) Correct identification of the bug fix in each solution (3 points), (2) Appropriate use of evaluation criteria from rubric (4 points), (3) Clear written justifications for rankings (3 points). Total: 10 points. Look for evidence that students can distinguish between working code and quality code.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a different code snippet before the activity. Offer guiding questions like 'Which solution would be easier for another programmer to understand?' For advanced learners: Add a fourth solution with a subtle performance improvement and ask them to consider efficiency as an additional criterion, or have them write their own improved solution.

title: Customer Retention Dashboard Creation with Predictive Insights
description: Students will design and build a comprehensive customer retention dashboard using real e-commerce data, incorporating multiple visualization types and predictive analytics. They will synthesize customer behavior patterns, churn indicators, and revenue metrics to create an actionable business intelligence tool with recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will create an interactive customer retention dashboard by integrating multiple data sources and visualization techniques to display key performance indicators
Students will develop predictive churn models through statistical analysis and generate strategic business recommendations based on their findings
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with the e-commerce dataset containing 18 months of customer transaction data (customer_id, purchase_date, order_value, product_category, customer_acquisition_date). In the first 30 minutes, teams explore the dataset using Excel/Google Sheets to identify data quality issues and create a data cleaning plan. Next, students spend 45 minutes in Tableau/Power BI creating their dashboard foundation: import cleaned data, establish relationships between tables, and create calculated fields for customer lifetime value, days since last purchase, and purchase frequency. During the following 60 minutes, teams build five specific visualizations: (1) customer segmentation scatter plot showing recency vs. frequency, (2) monthly cohort retention heatmap, (3) revenue trend line with churn overlay, (4) product category performance bar chart, and (5) at-risk customer identification table. In the next 30 minutes, students apply predictive analytics by creating a simple churn probability score using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) and adding conditional formatting to highlight high-risk segments. Teams then spend 45 minutes developing three specific business recommendations based on their dashboard insights, focusing on retention strategies for different customer segments. Finally, in the last 30 minutes, each team presents their dashboard to the class, demonstrating interactivity features and explaining their methodology for identifying at-risk customers and proposed retention interventions.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV format, 10,000+ records)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop licenses
Laptops/computers with internet access
Digital presentation platform (Zoom screen share or projector)
Dashboard evaluation rubric handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data cleaning and preparation (20 points), Dashboard design and functionality (30 points), Visualization accuracy and clarity (25 points), Predictive analysis implementation (15 points), Business recommendations quality (10 points). Students submit their dashboard file plus a 2-page written report explaining their churn prediction methodology and retention strategy recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned dataset option and dashboard template with placeholder visualizations to modify. Offer step-by-step video tutorials for basic Tableau/Power BI functions. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources (economic indicators, seasonality), implement advanced statistical models (logistic regression), or create automated alert systems for when customers enter high-risk categories.

title: Situational Leadership Model Analysis Through Critical Incident Mapping
description: Students will analyze complex leadership scenarios using Hersey-Blanchard's Situational Leadership II model to identify optimal leadership styles based on follower development levels. They will map critical incidents from authentic case studies to demonstrate deep understanding of the relationship between directive and supportive behaviors across different situational contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between the four situational leadership styles (S1-S4) by analyzing follower competence and commitment levels in multi-layered organizational scenarios
Students will interpret the dynamic relationship between directive and supportive leadership behaviors through systematic evaluation of real-world critical incidents
instructions: Begin by distributing the Harvard Business Review case study 'Turnaround at the Preston Plant' and the Situational Leadership II diagnostic matrix. Form teams of 3-4 students, ensuring mix of experience levels. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each team reads the case study and identifies 6-8 critical leadership moments where the plant manager must adapt their approach. Students use highlighters to mark directive behaviors (yellow) and supportive behaviors (green) throughout the text. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams complete the SL-II matrix for each critical incident, plotting follower development levels (D1-D4) against leadership styles (S1-S4). They must provide specific textual evidence for each classification, noting follower competence indicators (skills, knowledge, experience) and commitment indicators (confidence, motivation, morale). Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams create a visual timeline showing leadership style transitions, identifying where mismatches occurred between follower needs and leadership approach. They annotate each transition with rationale and potential alternative approaches. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Teams prepare 3-minute presentations focusing on one critical mismatch, explaining the gap between actual and optimal leadership style using SL-II terminology and framework principles.
materials_needed: Harvard Business Review case study 'Turnaround at the Preston Plant' (print copies)
Situational Leadership II diagnostic matrix handouts
Yellow and green highlighters for each student
Large poster paper for timeline creation
Colored markers or pens for visual mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification and classification of follower development levels with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Correct matching of appropriate leadership styles to situations with clear rationale (25%), (3) Quality of visual timeline showing understanding of dynamic leadership adaptation (25%), (4) Demonstration of SL-II vocabulary and concept integration in presentation (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ on all categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted examples of directive vs. supportive behaviors and a completed sample matrix for one scenario. Create reference cards with D1-D4 and S1-S4 definitions. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring analysis of cultural factors, power distance considerations, or integration with additional leadership theories like transformational leadership or LMX theory.

title: Risk Register Variance Analysis: Comparing Planned vs. Actual Risk Impacts
description: Students will analyze a completed project's risk register to identify discrepancies between planned risk responses and actual outcomes. They will decompose the effectiveness of risk management strategies and determine which factors contributed to successful or failed risk mitigation.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response effectiveness by comparing planned mitigation strategies against actual project outcomes using variance analysis techniques
Students will differentiate between successful and unsuccessful risk management approaches through systematic examination of risk register data and impact measurements
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the case study materials containing a software development project's initial risk register (25 identified risks) and the final project report showing actual outcomes. Each team receives printed risk register templates, highlighters, and calculators.

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams examine the initial risk register, identifying the top 10 highest probability×impact risks. Students highlight these risks and note the planned response strategies (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept).

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the final project report, teams track what actually happened to each of the 10 risks. They complete a variance analysis worksheet, calculating the difference between predicted impact (time/cost) and actual impact. Teams categorize each risk outcome as: better than expected, as expected, or worse than expected.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Teams analyze patterns by grouping risks by response strategy type and examining which strategies were most/least effective. They identify three specific factors that contributed to successful risk management and three factors that led to failures.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team creates a visual comparison chart showing planned vs. actual impacts for their top 5 risk variances. They prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their analysis of why certain risk responses succeeded or failed.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Teams present findings to the class, focusing on their identified success/failure factors. Instructor facilitates discussion on common patterns across teams and connects findings to PMI risk management best practices.
materials_needed: Software development project case study with initial risk register (25 risks)
Final project report showing actual outcomes and lessons learned
Risk variance analysis worksheet templates
Colored highlighters (3 colors per team)
Calculators
Flip chart paper and markers for visual charts
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of variance calculations (25%), (2) Quality of pattern analysis and factor identification (35%), (3) Logical connections between risk strategies and outcomes (25%), and (4) Clarity of visual presentation and explanations (15%). Students must correctly identify at least 8/10 risk outcomes and provide evidence-based reasoning for 2+ success factors and 2+ failure factors to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example of variance analysis for 2 risks and offer a structured template with guided questions. Pair weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. For advanced learners, challenge them to calculate risk exposure changes, suggest alternative response strategies for failed risks, and analyze secondary risks that emerged. Provide additional complex projects for extended analysis.

title: Cross-Platform Attribution Model Analysis and Business Impact Assessment
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, comparing last-click, first-click, linear, and data-driven attribution models. They will analyze discrepancies between models and make evidence-based recommendations for optimal attribution strategy based on business context and customer journey complexity.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business relevance of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across a 90-day period
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of model performance metrics and justify optimal attribution approaches for specific business scenarios
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Setup (45 minutes)**
Provide students with access to a demo GA4 property containing e-commerce data spanning 90 days. Students must navigate to Reports > Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison and configure four attribution models: Last Click, First Click, Linear, and Data-Driven. They should export conversion and revenue data for each model, focusing on three specific conversion events: purchases, newsletter signups, and demo requests. Students create a comparative data table documenting total conversions, revenue attributed, and average order value for each model.

**Phase 2: Cross-Channel Analysis (60 minutes)**
Using the Attribution > Conversion Paths report, students examine customer journeys exceeding 7 days with 3+ touchpoints. They must identify the top 5 conversion paths by volume and analyze how attribution differs across models for these specific paths. Students document channel performance variations, noting which channels gain/lose attribution credit under different models. They should pay particular attention to assisted conversions vs. last-click conversions for paid search, social media, and email campaigns.

**Phase 3: Business Context Integration (45 minutes)**
Students receive three business scenario cards: (1) B2B SaaS with 45-day average sales cycle, (2) Fast-fashion e-commerce with impulse purchases, (3) Luxury goods retailer with extensive research phase. For each scenario, they must evaluate which attribution model best reflects the actual customer decision-making process and business objectives. Students create justification matrices weighing factors like sales cycle length, average customer lifetime value, marketing budget allocation needs, and campaign optimization requirements.

**Phase 4: Recommendation Synthesis (30 minutes)**
Students prepare executive summary presentations defending their attribution model recommendations for each business scenario, including quantitative evidence from their GA4 analysis and qualitative reasoning based on customer behavior patterns.
materials_needed: Access to Google Analytics 4 demo account with 90+ days of e-commerce data
Google Sheets or Excel for data compilation and analysis
Three printed business scenario cards with company profiles and objectives
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and model comparison calculations, (2) Depth of cross-channel attribution analysis with specific examples, (3) Quality of business context integration showing understanding of customer journey implications, (4) Evidence-based justification for attribution model recommendations with quantitative support, (5) Professional presentation of findings with clear executive summary. Students must score 3+ on all criteria, with particular emphasis on demonstrating critical evaluation skills through identification of model limitations and trade-offs.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-populated data collection templates with column headers and sample entries. Offer guided questions for each analysis phase (e.g., 'Which channels show the biggest difference between first-click and last-click attribution?'). Create step-by-step navigation screenshots for accessing GA4 reports. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional metrics like time decay analysis, create custom attribution models using GA4's data-driven insights, or analyze attribution differences across device categories and geographic segments. Encourage integration of external factors like seasonality or competitive landscape impacts.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing and Security
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete enterprise network infrastructure incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF, access control lists, and network security policies. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize advanced Cisco networking concepts into a functional, secure network design that meets specific business requirements.
estimated_duration: 4 hours (240 minutes) across two lab sessions
learning_objectives: Students will create a comprehensive network topology design incorporating VLANs, OSPF routing, and security policies by analyzing given business requirements and constraints
Students will implement and configure advanced Cisco networking features including trunk ports, STP, ACLs, and DHCP services through hands-on lab construction
Students will develop network documentation and troubleshooting procedures by creating detailed configuration guides and testing protocols
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: 'TechCorp has 3 departments (Sales-50 users, Engineering-30 users, Management-15 users) across 2 floors requiring secure, segmented network access with internet connectivity.' Students work in teams of 2-3 to design the network topology using Cisco Packet Tracer, determining VLAN assignments (Sales-VLAN 10, Engineering-VLAN 20, Management-VLAN 30), IP addressing schemes using /24 subnets, and switch/router placement. **Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Students configure actual Cisco equipment: Set up 2 Cisco 2960 switches and 1 Cisco 2911 router. Configure VLANs on switches, establish trunk links between switches using 802.1Q, configure router-on-a-stick for inter-VLAN routing with subinterfaces, implement OSPF routing protocol, and configure DHCP pools for each VLAN. **Phase 3: Security Implementation (60 minutes)**
Implement access control lists: Create standard ACLs blocking inter-departmental traffic except Management-to-all access, configure extended ACLs restricting specific protocols, implement port security on access ports, and configure SSH access with encrypted passwords. **Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)**
Conduct connectivity tests between VLANs, verify DHCP assignments, test ACL restrictions, document all configurations with running-config exports, create network diagrams with IP addressing tables, and develop troubleshooting procedures for common issues.
materials_needed: 2 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
1 Cisco 2911 router per team
6 Ethernet cables (Cat5e/Cat6)
3 computers/laptops for end devices
Cisco Packet Tracer software
Console cables for device configuration
Network documentation templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design (25 points) - correct topology, appropriate VLAN segmentation, proper IP addressing; Implementation (35 points) - functional VLAN configuration, successful inter-VLAN routing, working DHCP; Security Configuration (25 points) - properly functioning ACLs, port security implementation, secure management access; Documentation (15 points) - complete configuration backup, accurate network diagrams, clear troubleshooting procedures. Students must demonstrate working connectivity between appropriate VLANs and blocked communication where ACLs are applied.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic VLAN structure, offer configuration command reference sheets, and pair with stronger technical partners. Create checkpoint assessments after each phase. For advanced learners: Add requirements for dynamic routing protocols (EIGRP), implement VTP for VLAN management, configure QoS policies for voice traffic, or integrate wireless access points with controller-based management. Encourage exploration of advanced security features like 802.1X authentication.

title: Interpreting Correlation Matrices in Customer Behavior Analysis
description: Students analyze a pre-built correlation matrix from an e-commerce dataset to identify relationships between customer variables and explain their business implications. They will interpret correlation coefficients and distinguish between strong, moderate, and weak relationships while connecting findings to real-world marketing strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3) and explaining their direction
Students will explain business implications of variable relationships through written analysis connecting correlation findings to customer behavior patterns
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided correlation matrix heat map showing relationships between 8 customer variables: age, income, website_time, pages_viewed, purchase_frequency, average_order_value, email_opens, and customer_satisfaction (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs and provide the interpretation worksheet. In Step 1 (20 minutes), students identify and record the five strongest positive correlations and five strongest negative correlations from the matrix, writing the exact coefficient values. In Step 2 (25 minutes), pairs categorize each identified relationship as strong, moderate, or weak using the provided classification system, then write one-sentence explanations for why each relationship makes logical sense. For Step 3 (30 minutes), students select three correlations and write detailed business interpretations explaining how a marketing manager could use each insight, specifying concrete actions like targeted campaigns or website improvements. In Step 4 (15 minutes), pairs identify one surprising or counterintuitive correlation from the matrix and hypothesize two possible explanations for why it exists. Conclude with a 15-minute gallery walk where pairs post their most interesting finding and walk around to view others' discoveries, followed by brief whole-class discussion of common patterns identified across all groups.
materials_needed: Printed correlation matrix heat map (one per pair)
Correlation interpretation worksheet with coefficient classification guide
Calculators or laptops for verification
Chart paper and markers for gallery walk
Sample customer dataset description sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of correlation identification and classification (25%), (2) Quality of logical explanations for relationships (25%), (3) Depth and specificity of business implications (35%), and (4) Creativity and reasoning in explaining surprising correlations (15%). Students must correctly identify correlation strength categories and provide actionable business insights to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example using two variables and highlight the correlation matrix diagonal and symmetry properties. Give advanced learners additional challenges: calculate partial correlations, identify potential confounding variables, or research industry benchmarks for comparison. Consider providing correlation strength reference cards and business context sheets for different industries.

title: Optimization Problem Solving: Designing a Maximum Volume Container
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world packaging problem by finding the dimensions that maximize the volume of an open-top box constructed from a rectangular sheet of material. They will use derivatives, critical points, and constraint analysis to determine the optimal solution and justify their mathematical reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques and critical point analysis to solve constrained optimization problems by determining maximum volume dimensions for a container design
Students will construct mathematical models from real-world constraints and validate solutions through both analytical and graphical methods
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario: A manufacturing company needs to create open-top rectangular boxes from 20×30 inch sheets of cardboard by cutting identical squares from each corner and folding up the sides. Students work in pairs for 90 minutes total. Phase 1 (20 minutes): Students sketch the problem, identify the constraint (fixed sheet size), and establish variables. They should define x as the side length of cut squares and express length, width, and height in terms of x. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Students derive the volume function V(x) = x(20-2x)(30-2x) and determine the practical domain (0 < x < 10). Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students find the derivative V'(x), set it equal to zero, and solve the resulting quadratic equation. They must identify critical points and use the second derivative test to confirm maximum volume. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Students calculate exact dimensions and maximum volume, then verify their solution makes physical sense by checking boundary conditions at x = 0 and x = 10. Each pair creates a detailed solution report showing all algebraic steps, derivative calculations, and final dimensions with units. Conclude with pairs presenting their optimal dimensions and comparing solutions for accuracy.
materials_needed: 20×30 inch rectangular cardboard sheets (one per pair)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos/GeoGebra)
Rulers and scissors for physical verification
Graph paper for sketching functions
Solution report template worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct mathematical model setup and constraint identification (25%), (2) Accurate derivative calculation and critical point determination (35%), (3) Proper application of optimization tests and solution validation (25%), (4) Clear mathematical communication and justification of final answer (15%). Students must show complete algebraic work and arrive at x ≈ 3.33 inches for maximum volume of approximately 889.63 cubic inches.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide the volume function formula and guide them through the first few steps of differentiation using the product rule. Offer a step-by-step derivative calculation template. For advanced learners: Extend the problem by having them optimize for minimum surface area given a fixed volume constraint, or analyze how the optimal solution changes with different initial sheet dimensions using parametric analysis.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference Patterns in Multi-Frequency Circuit Systems
description: Students will decompose complex electromagnetic interference (EMI) data from a multi-component electronic circuit to identify interference sources, distinguish between conducted and radiated emissions, and evaluate the effectiveness of different shielding strategies. This activity requires students to break down spectral analysis data and correlate it with circuit topology and component behavior.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic spectrum data by identifying frequency signatures, harmonics, and interference patterns to determine primary EMI sources in complex circuits
Students will evaluate the relationship between circuit design parameters and EMI characteristics through systematic comparison of multiple circuit configurations
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with EMI spectrum analyzer data from three different circuit configurations: (1) unshielded switching power supply with digital processor, (2) same circuit with partial shielding, and (3) fully shielded version with additional filtering. Students receive printed frequency domain plots (10 Hz to 1 GHz) and corresponding time-domain oscilloscope traces. In the first 20 minutes, teams examine the spectral data to identify distinct frequency peaks, noting amplitude levels and bandwidth characteristics. They must categorize emissions as fundamental frequencies, harmonics, or intermodulation products. Next, students spend 25 minutes correlating identified frequencies with known switching frequencies (125 kHz power supply, 16 MHz processor clock) and their harmonics using provided component specifications. They create a frequency map showing which circuit elements generate which spectral components. During the following 30 minutes, teams compare the three circuit configurations, analyzing how shielding and filtering affect different frequency ranges. They must identify which mitigation strategies are most effective for specific frequency bands and explain the physics behind the attenuation mechanisms. Students then spend 20 minutes evaluating compliance with FCC Part 15 limits by overlaying regulatory masks on their data and identifying which configurations pass or fail at specific frequencies. Finally, teams spend 15 minutes preparing a technical analysis summary documenting their methodology, key findings about EMI sources, and recommendations for design improvements. Throughout the activity, instructors circulate to ensure students are properly interpreting logarithmic scales, understanding dB measurements, and making accurate frequency-to-source correlations.
materials_needed: EMI spectrum analyzer printouts (3 configurations × 4-6 teams)
Oscilloscope time-domain traces corresponding to spectrum data
Circuit schematic diagrams with component specifications
FCC Part 15 regulatory limit templates (overlay sheets)
Scientific calculators
Graph paper and colored pencils for frequency mapping
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of frequency identification and source correlation (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis between circuit configurations (30%), (3) Correctness of regulatory compliance evaluation (25%), and (4) Technical justification of mitigation strategy effectiveness (20%). Students must submit their frequency maps, comparative analysis charts, and written technical summary. Look for proper use of EMI terminology, accurate mathematical relationships between fundamental and harmonic frequencies, and evidence-based conclusions about shielding effectiveness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a frequency identification worksheet with the first 2-3 peaks already labeled as examples, and offer a step-by-step checklist for comparing configurations. Include a reference sheet with common EMI terminology and dB calculation formulas. For advanced learners, provide additional spectral data from circuits with spread-spectrum clocking or advanced filtering techniques, and challenge them to predict EMI characteristics for a fourth unlabeled circuit configuration. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during the correlation phase.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Analytics Dashboard for Customer Churn Prevention
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn risk using real e-commerce data. They will combine multiple analytical techniques, design visualizations, and develop actionable business recommendations in a comprehensive deliverable.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer behavior patterns by integrating multiple data sources and creating predictive models for churn identification
Students will construct an interactive analytical dashboard through visualization design that communicates risk factors and business recommendations to stakeholders
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration & Exploration (45 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: customer_demographics.csv, transaction_history.csv, and support_tickets.csv. Students work in pairs to merge datasets using customer_id as the key. They must identify and document at least 5 potential churn indicators (e.g., declining purchase frequency, increased support tickets, account age). Students create a master dataset with engineered features like 'days_since_last_purchase' and 'average_monthly_spend'.

**Phase 2: Predictive Model Development (60 minutes)**
Using their integrated dataset, students build a logistic regression model to predict churn probability. They must split data 70/30 for training/testing, create binary churn labels based on 90+ days of inactivity, and validate model performance using confusion matrices. Students document feature importance and model accuracy metrics.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students design a 4-panel dashboard in Tableau/Power BI: (1) Executive summary with key churn metrics, (2) Customer segmentation heat map showing risk levels, (3) Trend analysis of churn drivers over time, (4) Individual customer risk profiles with drill-down capability. Each panel must include interactive filters for date ranges and customer segments.

**Phase 4: Business Recommendation Development (30 minutes)**
Based on their analysis, students create a one-page executive brief with three specific, data-driven recommendations for reducing churn. Each recommendation must include expected impact metrics and implementation timeline. Students prepare a 5-minute presentation of their dashboard and recommendations.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets (customer_demographics.csv, transaction_history.csv, support_tickets.csv)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop licenses
Excel or Python/R for data preparation
Presentation template for executive brief
Laptops with internet connectivity
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-category rubric: (1) Data Integration Quality - accurate merging with meaningful feature engineering (25 points), (2) Model Development - appropriate methodology with documented validation (25 points), (3) Dashboard Design - clear, interactive visualizations with business relevance (30 points), (4) Business Recommendations - actionable insights supported by data evidence (20 points). Students submit dashboard files, executive brief, and present findings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data dictionary with variable definitions, offer pre-written SQL queries for common joins, and supply dashboard wireframe templates. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement multiple model types (random forest, neural networks), add real-time data simulation features, or incorporate external economic indicators that might influence churn patterns.

title: Deploy a Multi-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2 and RDS
description: Students will apply AWS cloud fundamentals by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture consisting of a web server, application server, and database. This hands-on activity requires students to configure EC2 instances, set up an RDS database, and establish proper security groups to create a functional cloud-based application.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier web application by configuring EC2 instances and RDS database services in AWS
Students will implement proper security configurations through creating and managing security groups for web and database tiers
instructions:
**Pre-Setup (5 minutes):** Ensure all students have AWS Educate accounts activated and can access the AWS Management Console. Provide the sample PHP web application code (simple inventory management system) via shared folder.

**Phase 1: Database Tier Setup (20 minutes):** Students log into AWS Console and navigate to RDS. Guide them to create a MySQL database instance: select 'MySQL', choose 't3.micro' instance type, set database name as 'inventory_db', create master username 'admin' with password 'Student123!'. Configure security group 'db-security-group' allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from web tier only.

**Phase 2: Web Tier Deployment (25 minutes):** Navigate to EC2 Dashboard. Launch new instance using Amazon Linux 2 AMI, select t2.micro instance type. Create security group 'web-security-group' allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. In User Data section, students paste provided bootstrap script that installs Apache, PHP, and MySQL client. Launch instance and note public IP address.

**Phase 3: Application Configuration (15 minutes):** SSH into EC2 instance using provided key pair. Students upload the PHP application files to /var/www/html/ directory. Edit database connection file (config.php) to include RDS endpoint, database name, and credentials. Test database connectivity using MySQL client.

**Phase 4: Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Access web application through EC2 public IP address in browser. Students should successfully view the inventory interface, add sample data, and verify data persistence by refreshing the page. Document the complete application URL and take screenshots of working application.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students submit their deployed application URLs and architecture diagrams showing the connection between EC2 and RDS components.
materials_needed: AWS Educate accounts for each student
Pre-written PHP inventory management application code
Bootstrap script for EC2 user data configuration
AWS EC2 key pair file (.pem) for SSH access
Architecture diagram template for documentation
assessment_method: Students will be evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Database deployment and configuration (25 points), EC2 instance setup with proper security groups (25 points), successful application deployment and database connectivity (30 points), functional web interface with data persistence (20 points). Success criteria include: accessible web application via public URL, ability to add/view data through web interface, proper security group configurations preventing unauthorized access, and completed architecture documentation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and detailed screenshots of each AWS console step. Create checkpoint verification guides after each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like auto-scaling groups, load balancers, or multi-AZ database deployment. Encourage exploration of CloudWatch monitoring and cost optimization techniques.

title: Project Schedule Compression Analysis: Crashing vs. Fast Tracking Trade-offs
description: Students will analyze a delayed construction project scenario and evaluate the effectiveness of different schedule compression techniques. They will examine cost-benefit trade-offs, risk implications, and resource constraints to determine optimal compression strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the cost-benefit implications of crashing versus fast tracking techniques by comparing quantitative data from a construction project scenario
Students will evaluate risk factors and resource constraints through systematic examination of schedule compression alternatives and their interdependencies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes). Distribute the 'Riverside Community Center Construction Project' case study packet containing: original 18-month project schedule with 45 activities, current status showing 3-month delay, cost data for crashing each activity, and resource availability constraints. Each team receives different stakeholder perspectives (client, contractor, subcontractor, or regulatory body). Phase 1 (30 minutes): Teams analyze the current project status using the provided Gantt chart and identify critical path activities. They must calculate the cost per day saved for each crashable activity and identify potential fast tracking opportunities between dependent phases. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Teams develop three alternative compression scenarios: pure crashing approach, pure fast tracking approach, and hybrid approach. For each scenario, they calculate total additional costs, time savings, and identify introduced risks using the provided risk assessment matrix. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams complete a comparative analysis worksheet evaluating each scenario against five criteria: total cost impact, schedule reduction achieved, risk level introduced, resource feasibility, and stakeholder acceptance from their assigned perspective. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents their recommended approach in 3 minutes, justifying their choice with quantitative analysis and addressing potential objections from other stakeholder perspectives.
materials_needed: Riverside Community Center Construction Project case study packets (one per team)
Microsoft Project file or printed Gantt charts showing current project status
Schedule compression analysis worksheets with cost-benefit comparison tables
Risk assessment matrix templates with probability/impact scales
Calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of critical path identification and cost calculations (25%), (2) Quality of risk analysis for each compression technique (25%), (3) Logical reasoning in comparative analysis between alternatives (25%), (4) Integration of stakeholder perspective in final recommendation with supporting evidence (25%). Students must demonstrate quantitative analysis and provide at least three specific justifications for their chosen approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide critical path highlighting on Gantt charts and cost calculation examples for first two activities. For advanced learners: Add resource leveling constraints and require Monte Carlo simulation discussion for risk quantification. Consider pairing analytical students with those stronger in presentation skills within teams.

title: Multi-Platform Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Recommendation Report
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real Google Analytics 4 data from multiple traffic sources. They will assess which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and defend their recommendation with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative effectiveness of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution differences across paid search, social media, and email campaigns

Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer lifetime value, conversion lag time, and channel interaction patterns to formulate evidence-based recommendations
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active. Ensure students can access the Attribution section under Advertising. **Step 1 (20 minutes):** Students export attribution comparison reports for all five models, focusing on campaigns from Google Ads, Facebook Ads, and email marketing. They must capture data for: total conversions, conversion value, cost per acquisition, and return on ad spend (ROAS) for each channel under each model. **Step 2 (25 minutes):** Using the Model Comparison Tool, students analyze the percentage difference in attributed conversions between models for each channel. They calculate the variance coefficient to determine which channels show the highest attribution volatility. **Step 3 (30 minutes):** Students examine conversion path reports to identify average touchpoints before conversion, time lag patterns, and cross-channel interaction sequences. They must document at least 10 specific customer journey patterns that reveal attribution model limitations. **Step 4 (45 minutes):** Students create a comprehensive evaluation matrix scoring each attribution model (1-5 scale) across six criteria: accuracy for their business model, channel fairness, data requirements, implementation complexity, decision-making utility, and alignment with customer behavior patterns. **Step 5 (30 minutes):** Students prepare a executive summary recommending one primary attribution model with a secondary backup model, including projected budget reallocation percentages across channels and expected ROI impact over 12 months.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis and matrix creation
Access to Google Ads and Facebook Ads sample campaign data
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Executive report template with predefined sections
assessment_method: Students submit a 3-page executive report with data appendix. Grading rubric (100 points): Data accuracy and completeness (25 points), depth of attribution model analysis with specific examples (25 points), quality of evaluation criteria and scoring rationale (20 points), strength of recommendation with quantitative justification (20 points), professional presentation and actionable insights (10 points). Success requires demonstrating clear understanding of attribution model trade-offs with specific numerical evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled evaluation matrix template with criteria definitions and scoring guidance. Offer guided worksheet breaking down each attribution model's strengths/weaknesses. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value calculations, seasonal adjustments, or custom attribution model proposals using Google Analytics Intelligence API data.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security Policies
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise network infrastructure incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, DHCP services, and advanced security policies. They will create network documentation, configure multiple Cisco devices, and validate network functionality through comprehensive testing scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced networking configurations through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches and routers with security policies and testing protocols
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Students receive a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 150 employees across 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Guest). Begin by having students analyze requirements and create a network topology using Packet Tracer or Visio. They must design 4 VLANs with appropriate subnetting using 192.168.0.0/22 address space, plan trunk links, and document security requirements.

**Phase 2: Equipment Setup (30 minutes)**
Provide each team with 2 Cisco 2960 switches, 1 Cisco 2911 router, and necessary cables. Students physically cable devices according to their topology, ensuring proper trunk connections between switches and router-on-a-stick configuration for inter-VLAN routing.

**Phase 3: Configuration Implementation (90 minutes)**
Students configure VLANs (Sales-VLAN10, Engineering-VLAN20, HR-VLAN30, Guest-VLAN40) on switches with appropriate access and trunk ports. On the router, they configure sub-interfaces for each VLAN with DHCP pools, implement access control lists restricting HR and Guest network access, and configure port security on switches. Each configuration command must be documented with explanations.

**Phase 4: Security Policy Implementation (45 minutes)**
Students implement advanced security features including: port security with MAC address limiting, DHCP snooping to prevent rogue DHCP servers, dynamic ARP inspection, and storm control. They must also configure SSH access with local user authentication and disable unnecessary services.

**Phase 5: Testing and Validation (30 minutes)**
Conduct comprehensive testing using ping tests between VLANs, verify DHCP functionality, test ACL restrictions, and validate security policies. Students document all test results and troubleshoot any connectivity issues.
materials_needed: 2 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
1 Cisco 2911 router per team
6 Ethernet cables per team
2 console cables per team
Laptops with PuTTY or SecureCRT installed
Network topology worksheet templates
Cisco Packet Tracer (backup/simulation option)
assessment_method: Evaluation based on four deliverables: (1) Network design document with topology diagram and IP addressing scheme (25 points), (2) Complete device configurations saved as text files with command explanations (35 points), (3) Successful demonstration of network functionality including inter-VLAN communication and security policy enforcement (25 points), (4) Professional network documentation including test results and troubleshooting log (15 points). Students must achieve 80% functionality testing to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured VLAN templates and step-by-step command references. Pair weaker students with stronger partners and offer additional instructor check-ins during configuration phases. For advanced learners: Add OSPF routing between multiple routers, implement VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP), configure EtherChannel link aggregation, or integrate wireless access points with guest network isolation.

title: Programming Language Syntax Memory Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall basic syntax elements from three programming languages (Python, Java, C++) through interactive flashcard activities and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed before any coding practice can begin.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and recall 15 fundamental programming syntax elements (keywords, operators, data types) across Python, Java, and C++ by completing flashcard drills with 85% accuracy
Students will demonstrate memorization of basic programming vocabulary through rapid-fire verbal responses and written syntax matching exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcard sets to each student containing 45 cards total (15 syntax elements × 3 languages). Each card shows a programming concept on one side (e.g., 'integer variable declaration') and the corresponding syntax on the reverse (Python: 'x = 5', Java: 'int x = 5;', C++: 'int x = 5;'). 

Minutes 1-15: Students work individually studying their flashcard set, focusing on memorizing exact syntax spelling and punctuation. Circulate to ensure students are actively reading both sides and testing themselves.

Minutes 16-25: Pair students and have them quiz each other using the 'concept-to-syntax' direction. Partner A reads the concept, Partner B must provide all three language syntaxes from memory. Switch roles every 5 minutes.

Minutes 26-35: Conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall session. Display programming concepts on projector one at a time for 10 seconds each. Students write down syntax for all three languages on provided answer sheets. No looking at flashcards allowed.

Minutes 36-40: Immediate self-scoring using answer key. Students count correct responses out of 45 total possible (15 concepts × 3 languages). Record scores for assessment purposes.

Minutes 41-45: Brief reflection where students identify their three weakest syntax areas and create a personal study list for homework review.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets (45 cards per student covering Python, Java, C++ syntax)
Answer sheets with numbered blanks (1-45)
Answer key handouts for self-scoring
Projector/screen for displaying programming concepts
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy (38/45 correct responses) on the timed recall exercise to demonstrate successful memorization. Grade based on: Syntax accuracy (20 points), Spelling/punctuation precision (15 points), Completion of all 45 items (10 points). Observe during pair work for engagement and correct flashcard usage.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by allowing them to focus on just 2 languages initially or providing syntax pattern sheets highlighting common structures. For advanced learners, add complexity by including function syntax, loop structures, or having them create additional flashcards for advanced concepts like exception handling or object instantiation.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Dataset Comparisons
description: Students will analyze and compare the statistical distributions of three different variables from a housing prices dataset to understand how data shape and spread affect analytical conclusions. They will create visual comparisons and write interpretive summaries explaining what each distribution reveals about the underlying phenomena.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the meaning of different distribution shapes (normal, skewed, bimodal) by analyzing housing price variables and explaining their real-world implications
Students will compare statistical measures (mean, median, standard deviation) across multiple distributions through guided analysis and written explanations
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the prepared housing dataset containing price, square footage, and number of bedrooms variables (5 minutes setup). Students work individually to create histograms for all three variables using their chosen tool, ensuring bins are appropriately sized for meaningful interpretation (15 minutes). Next, students calculate and record the mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for each variable in their analysis worksheet (10 minutes). In pairs, students examine their three distributions and discuss: Which variable shows the most skewness? Why might this occur in real estate data? Which distribution is closest to normal? (10 minutes discussion). Each student then writes a 200-word interpretation comparing the three distributions, addressing: the shape characteristics of each distribution, what the measures of central tendency reveal about typical housing characteristics, and how the spread/variability differs between variables and what this means for potential buyers or analysts (15 minutes writing). Conclude with a class discussion where 3-4 pairs share one key insight about how distribution shape affects data interpretation in real estate contexts (10 minutes). Students submit their histograms, calculations worksheet, and written interpretation for assessment.
materials_needed: Housing prices dataset (CSV file with 500+ records containing price, sqft, bedrooms columns)
Statistical analysis software (R, Python with pandas/matplotlib, or Excel)
Distribution analysis worksheet template
Computers/tablets for each student
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of histogram creation and statistical calculations (25%), (2) Correct identification of distribution shapes and characteristics (25%), (3) Quality of real-world interpretation connecting statistical properties to housing market phenomena (35%), (4) Clear comparison between the three variables with specific evidence (15%). Success criteria: Students score 3/4 or higher on each rubric component.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made histogram templates and a checklist of distribution characteristics to identify. Offer guiding questions like 'What does it mean when mean > median?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential outliers, calculate skewness coefficients, or predict how seasonal factors might affect these distributions. Consider providing additional variables (location, age of house) for extended analysis.

title: Optimizing Urban Food Truck Routes Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving food truck route planning in an urban environment. They will formulate constraints, create objective functions, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal solutions for maximizing daily profit while meeting operational constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-constraint food truck routing scenario into mathematical inequalities and objective functions
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to solve optimization problems involving at least 4 variables and 6 constraints
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Setup (15 minutes)** Distribute the Urban Food Truck Scenario handout containing: daily operating costs, profit margins per location type (business district: $180/day, university campus: $150/day, residential area: $120/day, park venue: $200/day), time constraints (8-hour operating day), fuel costs between locations, and regulatory restrictions (maximum 2 hours per location, minimum 1 hour service time). Students work in pairs to identify decision variables (time spent at each location type). **Phase 2: Mathematical Formulation (25 minutes)** Students formulate the linear programming model by: (1) defining variables x₁, x₂, x₃, x₄ representing hours at each location type, (2) creating the objective function: Maximize P = 180x₁ + 150x₂ + 120x₃ + 200x₄, (3) establishing constraints including time limitation (x₁ + x₂ + x₃ + x₄ ≤ 8), individual location limits (0 ≤ xᵢ ≤ 2 for all i), minimum service requirements (xᵢ ≥ 1 or xᵢ = 0), and fuel cost limitations. **Phase 3: Solution Implementation (35 minutes)** For 2-variable simplified version, students use graphical method plotting feasible region and finding corner points. For full 4-variable problem, students apply simplex algorithm using provided templates, creating initial tableau and performing pivot operations. **Phase 4: Analysis and Validation (15 minutes)** Students verify their solution by substituting values back into original constraints, calculate maximum daily profit, and compare different scenario outcomes. Each pair presents their optimal route schedule and justifies their mathematical approach.
materials_needed: Urban Food Truck Scenario handout with specific profit/cost data
Graph paper and rulers for graphical method
Simplex algorithm template worksheets
Scientific calculators
Excel or linear programming software (LINDO/Solver) access
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation with all variables and constraints identified (25 points), (2) Accurate mathematical execution of chosen solution method with clear work shown (35 points), (3) Correct final answer with proper units and interpretation (25 points), (4) Valid solution verification and business context explanation (15 points). Students must submit completed worksheet showing all mathematical steps plus a 2-paragraph written explanation of their optimal route recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled constraint templates and guide them through the first two constraints as examples. Offer graphical method option for simplified 2-variable version before attempting full problem. For advanced learners: Include sensitivity analysis component asking how solution changes with ±20% profit variations, or add integer programming constraints requiring whole-hour decisions only. Provide additional scenarios with conflicting objectives (profit vs. customer satisfaction).

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference Patterns in Multi-Wave Systems
description: Students will decompose complex electromagnetic interference patterns into constituent wave components and evaluate how phase relationships, amplitude ratios, and frequency differences create observable interference phenomena. They will analyze real-world data from radio telescope observations to identify multiple signal sources and their interaction patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic wave interference patterns by decomposing multi-source signals into individual wave components using Fourier analysis techniques

Students will evaluate the relationship between wave parameters (amplitude, frequency, phase) and resulting interference patterns through quantitative comparison of theoretical predictions with observational data
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with a dataset containing 30 minutes of radio telescope observations showing interference between a pulsar signal, background cosmic radiation, and terrestrial radio interference. In the first 45 minutes, teams use MATLAB or Python to plot the raw signal data and identify at least three distinct frequency components through visual inspection of the time-domain and frequency-domain representations. Students must create power spectral density plots and identify peak frequencies within ±0.1 Hz accuracy. During the next 60 minutes, teams apply Fast Fourier Transform analysis to isolate individual wave components, determining the amplitude, frequency, and initial phase of each identified signal. They must calculate theoretical interference patterns for each pair of identified waves using superposition principles, showing all mathematical work for constructive and destructive interference conditions. In the following 45 minutes, students compare their theoretical predictions with the actual observed interference patterns by overlaying calculated waveforms onto the original data using plotting software. They must quantify the accuracy of their analysis by calculating root-mean-square error between predicted and observed amplitudes at 100 evenly-spaced time points. Finally, teams spend 30 minutes preparing a technical analysis report documenting their wave decomposition methodology, mathematical calculations, and accuracy assessment. Each team presents their findings in a 10-minute presentation, defending their analytical approach and discussing sources of error in their wave parameter determinations.
materials_needed: Radio telescope interference dataset (CSV format with time-stamped amplitude measurements)
MATLAB software or Python with NumPy/SciPy libraries installed on computers
Graphing calculators for verification calculations
Technical report template with required analysis sections
Projection system for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Wave identification accuracy (25 points - must identify all major frequency components within ±5% of actual values), mathematical analysis quality (30 points - correct application of superposition and Fourier analysis with proper units and significant figures), theoretical-experimental comparison (25 points - quantitative error analysis with RMS calculations), and technical communication (20 points - clear presentation of methodology and results with appropriate scientific terminology)
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-written MATLAB/Python code templates for FFT analysis and offering guided practice with simpler two-wave interference examples. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them account for Doppler shift effects in the pulsar signal or analyze polarization-dependent interference patterns. Provide reference sheets with key electromagnetic wave equations and Fourier analysis formulas.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Implementations
description: Students will critically evaluate three different implementations of a basic calculator program using established software quality criteria. They will assess code readability, functionality, efficiency, and maintainability to determine which implementation best meets professional standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different code implementations by applying specific quality criteria (readability, functionality, efficiency, maintainability)
Students will judge the relative merits of programming approaches through structured comparison and written justification
instructions: Begin by distributing the Code Evaluation Worksheet and three calculator implementations (Implementation A: well-structured with clear variable names and comments; Implementation B: functional but poorly formatted with cryptic variable names; Implementation C: over-engineered with unnecessary complexity). Give students 10 minutes to individually review all three implementations, running each program to test basic operations (+, -, *, /) with sample inputs (12+5, 20-8, 6*4, 15/3). Next, have students spend 20 minutes completing the evaluation matrix, rating each implementation on a 1-5 scale across four criteria: Code Readability (variable names, comments, formatting), Functionality (correct calculations, error handling), Efficiency (unnecessary code, performance), and Maintainability (ease of modification, code organization). For each rating, students must provide specific evidence from the code. Then, students work in pairs for 15 minutes to compare their evaluations and discuss discrepancies, reaching consensus on ratings where possible. Finally, each pair presents their top-ranked implementation in a 3-minute presentation, explaining their reasoning using specific code examples. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion identifying common evaluation patterns and establishing class consensus on quality indicators.
materials_needed: Three pre-written calculator implementations in Python or JavaScript
Code Evaluation Worksheet with rating matrix
Computers with appropriate IDE/text editor installed
Sample test cases handout (12+5, 20-8, 6*4, 15/3, edge cases)
assessment_method: Grade using rubric: Evaluation Matrix Completion (40% - accurate ratings with specific textual evidence), Pair Consensus Process (20% - productive discussion and compromise), Presentation Quality (25% - clear justification with code examples), Participation in Final Discussion (15% - meaningful contributions to class consensus building)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation for one criterion before starting. Offer sentence starters like 'This code is readable because...' For advanced learners: Add a fifth implementation with subtle bugs to identify, or ask them to propose specific improvements to the lowest-rated implementation.

title: Project Management Methodology Framework Terminology Identification Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately identify 75 specific terms, acronyms, and definitions from five major project management methodologies (Waterfall, Agile, Scrum, PRINCE2, and Lean Six Sigma).
