This advanced recall activity uses spaced repetition and rapid-fire identification techniques to build foundational vocabulary mastery.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific terminology and acronyms from five project management methodologies with 90% accuracy through timed identification exercises
Students will memorize precise definitions of 75 advanced project management terms through systematic flashcard drilling and peer testing
instructions: Begin by distributing the master terminology list containing 15 terms from each methodology (75 total), including complex terms like 'Definition of Done,' 'RACI Matrix,' 'Critical Chain Method,' and 'DMAIC.' Students spend 20 minutes reviewing the list silently, using highlighters to mark unfamiliar terms. Next, pair students and provide each pair with pre-made flashcards containing terms on one side and definitions on the other. Partners alternate as questioner and responder, cycling through all 75 cards twice (15 minutes). Implement Round 1: Display terms on screen for 10 seconds each while students write the methodology and brief definition on answer sheets. Cover all 75 terms in random order (25 minutes). Follow with Round 2: Show only definitions while students identify the specific term and methodology (20 minutes). Conclude with Round 3: Rapid-fire verbal quiz where instructor calls out terms and students shout back the methodology, or vice versa. Students who answer incorrectly sit down; continue until 3-5 students remain standing (10 minutes). Throughout the activity, maintain high energy and pace to prevent memorization fatigue.
materials_needed: Master terminology list with 75 PM terms across 5 methodologies
Pre-printed flashcard sets (one per student pair)
PowerPoint slides with terms and definitions
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-75
Colored highlighters for each student
Timer for each round
assessment_method: Grade based on written answer sheets from Rounds 1-2, requiring 90% accuracy (68/75 correct) for full credit. Award participation points for Round 3 performance. Use checklist rubric: Full Credit (68+ correct, active participation), Partial Credit (55-67 correct), Needs Improvement (<55 correct). Collect answer sheets immediately after each round to prevent correction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide the methodology list as a word bank and allow consultation during Round 1. Create study groups for pre-activity review sessions. For advanced learners, require them to provide real-world application examples for terms they answer correctly, or challenge them to identify which methodology would be most appropriate for given project scenarios.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Multi-Perspective Analysis of Executive Decision-Making Under Pressure
description: Students analyze authentic crisis leadership scenarios from multiple theoretical frameworks simultaneously, examining how different leadership models explain the same executive decisions. They synthesize their understanding by mapping decision patterns across transformational, situational, and adaptive leadership theories.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, situational, and adaptive leadership approaches by analyzing the same crisis leadership decisions through each theoretical lens
Students will interpret the underlying assumptions and decision-making processes of crisis leaders through systematic comparison of competing leadership frameworks
instructions: Begin by distributing three authentic crisis leadership case studies: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982), Captain Chesley Sullenberger's Hudson River landing (2009), and Jacinda Ardern's Christchurch response (2019). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one case study. Provide each team with three theoretical framework analysis templates: one for transformational leadership (focusing on idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration), one for situational leadership (examining leader behavior adaptation based on follower readiness), and one for adaptive leadership (analyzing technical vs. adaptive challenges, regulation of distress, and experimental solutions). Teams spend 45 minutes completing all three templates for their assigned case, identifying specific leader behaviors, decisions, and communication patterns that align with each theory. Next, conduct a structured gallery walk where teams rotate through stations, spending 15 minutes at each station examining other teams' analyses. Students use sticky notes to add observations about patterns they notice across different cases and theories. Reconvene teams for 20 minutes to create a synthesis matrix comparing how each theory explains crisis leadership effectiveness, noting convergences and divergences. Teams prepare 8-minute presentations highlighting their most significant insights about which theoretical lens best explains their case study's leadership decisions and why. Conclude with a 15-minute facilitated discussion where teams defend their theoretical choice while responding to challenges from peers who analyzed the same decisions through different lenses.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis leadership case studies with decision timelines and outcome data
Theoretical framework analysis templates for transformational, situational, and adaptive leadership
Large poster paper for synthesis matrices
Colored sticky notes for gallery walk observations
Presentation timer and evaluation rubrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) accuracy of theoretical application to case details (25%), (2) depth of analysis comparing leader behaviors across frameworks (30%), (3) quality of synthesis identifying patterns and contradictions (25%), and (4) ability to justify theoretical choice with evidence during presentations and peer discussions (20%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly identifying at least 3 specific examples per theory and articulating 2 meaningful comparisons between frameworks.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed analysis templates with 1-2 examples filled in, and offer guiding questions like 'What specific words did the leader use that show inspirational motivation?' For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by asking them to identify limitations of each theoretical framework and propose hybrid approaches that might better explain the leadership decisions.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on EC2 with Load Balancing
description: Students will deploy a simple web application across multiple EC2 instances and implement an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS services including EC2, Security Groups, and Elastic Load Balancing through practical application.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a web application on multiple EC2 instances by configuring user data scripts and security groups
Students will implement traffic distribution through creating and configuring an Application Load Balancer with health checks
instructions: Begin by having students log into their AWS Management Console and navigate to the EC2 dashboard (5 minutes). Students will first create a security group named 'WebApp-SG' allowing inbound HTTP traffic on port 80 from anywhere (0.0.0.0/0) and SSH on port 22 from their IP address (10 minutes). Next, students launch two t2.micro EC2 instances in different availability zones within the same region, using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. In the user data section, students paste a provided script that installs Apache web server and creates a simple HTML page displaying the instance ID (15 minutes). After instances are running, students verify both web servers are accessible by visiting their public IP addresses in a browser (5 minutes). Students then create an Application Load Balancer in the EC2 console, selecting 'internet-facing' scheme and mapping it to the same subnets as their instances (10 minutes). They create a target group named 'WebApp-Targets' with HTTP protocol on port 80, register both EC2 instances, and attach this target group to their load balancer (15 minutes). Students configure health check settings with a 30-second interval and '/index.html' as the health check path (5 minutes). Finally, students test the load balancer by accessing its DNS name multiple times and observing traffic distribution between instances by noting different instance IDs displayed (10 minutes). Students document their load balancer DNS name and screenshot successful page loads showing different instance IDs.
materials_needed: AWS account with appropriate IAM permissions for EC2 and ELB services
Pre-written user data script for Apache installation and HTML page creation
Web browser for testing applications
Document or spreadsheet for recording DNS names and observations
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Two running EC2 instances in different AZs, (2) Both instances accessible via individual public IPs, (3) Application Load Balancer status as 'active', (4) Target group showing both instances as 'healthy', (5) Load balancer DNS successfully serving pages from both instances (evidenced by different instance IDs). Award points: 4 points for each screenshot requirement met (20 total), plus 5 points for written reflection on load balancing benefits.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a checklist template and pre-configured security group settings. Offer one-on-one guidance during user data script entry. For advanced learners, add challenges like implementing SSL certificates, creating custom health check pages, or setting up Auto Scaling groups to work with the load balancer.

title: Project Risk Response Strategy Analysis and Optimization
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will examine the relationships between risks, assess resource allocation decisions, and determine optimal response combinations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of different risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) by examining their impact on project constraints and objectives
Students will evaluate risk response combinations through systematic comparison of cost-benefit trade-offs and resource optimization scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the 'Metro Transit Expansion Project' case study packet containing 12 identified risks with current response strategies and project constraints (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a colored worksheet packet. Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze each risk using the provided Risk Response Analysis Matrix, rating current strategies on effectiveness (1-5 scale) against cost, timeline impact, and residual risk level. Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the Resource Allocation Spreadsheet, teams calculate total costs for current response strategies and compare against the $2.3M risk budget. They must identify which responses exceed budget constraints and create priority rankings. Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams develop alternative response combinations by switching strategies for 4-6 risks, documenting their rationale using the Strategy Justification Template. They must address interdependencies between risks R-3 (permit delays) and R-7 (weather impacts). Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents their top 3 strategy modifications to the class using the provided presentation template, explaining trade-off decisions. Conclude with instructor-led discussion comparing team approaches and revealing the actual project outcomes (10 minutes). Teams must submit completed analysis matrices, revised resource allocation sheets, and written justifications for evaluation.
materials_needed: Metro Transit Expansion Project case study packets (1 per student)
Risk Response Analysis Matrix templates (1 per team)
Resource Allocation Spreadsheet (Excel file on shared drive)
Strategy Justification Template (Word document)
Colored worksheet packets (different color per team)
Laptop/tablet access for spreadsheet calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk-response effectiveness analysis (25 points), (2) Mathematical precision in resource allocation calculations (20 points), (3) Quality of alternative strategy justifications with evidence (25 points), (4) Identification and explanation of risk interdependencies (20 points), (5) Professional presentation of findings (10 points). Teams must achieve 70+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example for risks R-1 and R-2, offer calculation check-in at 15-minute mark, and pair with stronger analytical team members. For advanced learners: Add secondary risk analysis requirement, challenge to optimize within 80% of budget constraint, or include qualitative risk factors like stakeholder satisfaction in their evaluation matrix.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Business Impact Assessment
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing a real e-commerce dataset, comparing last-click, first-click, linear, and data-driven attribution models. They will assess each model's business implications and defend their recommendation for optimal attribution strategy based on specific business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of four different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating revenue attribution discrepancies of at least 15% between models
Students will critique attribution model limitations through systematic comparison of customer journey complexity against model assumptions and business context
instructions: **Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with Google Analytics demo account access containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (paid search, organic, social, email, direct). Students work in pairs and receive three business scenario cards: B2B SaaS (long consideration), Fashion Retail (impulse purchases), and Financial Services (high-value, research-intensive). **Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool. They must extract data for all four attribution models, documenting: conversion volume changes, revenue attribution shifts by channel, and average time-to-conversion differences. Students create a comparative matrix showing percentage changes in channel performance between models. **Evaluation Phase (30 minutes):** For their assigned business scenario, students evaluate each model against five criteria: alignment with customer behavior, marketing budget allocation accuracy, campaign optimization potential, technical implementation complexity, and business stakeholder comprehension. They must identify specific limitations (e.g., data-driven model requiring sufficient conversion volume) and rank models using weighted scoring. **Recommendation Phase (20 minutes):** Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model, including three supporting data points, two major limitations acknowledgments, and implementation timeline with success metrics. They must address potential stakeholder objections and provide fallback options.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Business scenario cards (B2B SaaS, Fashion Retail, Financial Services)
Attribution Model Comparison Template spreadsheet
Evaluation criteria rubric handout
Laptops with internet access
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Data Analysis Accuracy - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences (25 points), (2) Critical Evaluation - systematic assessment using all five criteria with specific examples (30 points), (3) Business Justification - logical reasoning connecting model choice to business context with supporting evidence (25 points), (4) Limitation Acknowledgment - identification of at least two significant model constraints with mitigation strategies (20 points). Minimum passing score: 75/100.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-populated data extraction templates and guided questions for each evaluation criterion. Offer mid-activity check-ins at 30-minute mark. For advanced learners: challenge them to propose custom attribution model modifications, calculate statistical significance of attribution differences, or evaluate cross-device tracking implications. Provide additional datasets from different industries for extended analysis.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Business Impact Assessment: Exercise 1
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value. They will then defend their recommendation to stakeholders through a comprehensive business case analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of first-click, last-click, data-driven, and linear attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and revenue attribution discrepancies across a 90-day period
Students will critique the business implications of attribution model selection through cost-per-acquisition analysis and budget reallocation recommendations for paid media channels
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with access to a GA4 property containing at least 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Students first spend 20 minutes in the Attribution section under Advertising, examining the Model Comparison report. They must document conversion counts and revenue totals for each attribution model across all channels, creating a comparative spreadsheet. Next, students spend 30 minutes analyzing the Conversion Paths report to identify common multi-touch customer journeys, noting the average path length and time lag between first interaction and conversion. In the third phase (25 minutes), teams calculate the percentage difference in attributed conversions and revenue between models for each channel, identifying which channels gain or lose credit under different models. Students then spend 35 minutes researching the business context by examining channel costs in Google Ads (if available) or using provided cost data to calculate cost-per-acquisition under each model. Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their chosen attribution model, including specific budget reallocation recommendations and projected ROI impact. Each team must address potential counterarguments and explain how their choice aligns with business objectives such as customer lifetime value or brand awareness goals.
materials_needed: GA4 property with 6+ months e-commerce data and multiple traffic sources
Spreadsheet software (Google Sheets or Excel)
Channel cost data or Google Ads account access
Presentation software
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data analysis and mathematical calculations (25%), (2) Quality of business reasoning and stakeholder consideration (30%), (3) Strength of argument defense and counterargument addressing (25%), (4) Practical feasibility and specificity of recommendations (20%). Students must demonstrate clear understanding of attribution model mechanics and provide specific dollar amounts for budget shifts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-filled data collection templates and guiding questions for each analysis step. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify data extraction accuracy. For advanced learners, introduce custom attribution models or cross-platform attribution challenges using Google Analytics Intelligence API queries to export data for deeper statistical analysis.
original_title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Business Impact Assessment

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Infrastructure with Advanced Security and QoS Requirements
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network solution spanning three geographic sites with interconnected VLANs, advanced routing protocols, comprehensive security policies, and quality of service implementations. This capstone activity integrates all major Cisco networking concepts into a real-world business scenario requiring original network design decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocols to create an optimized multi-site network topology that meets specific business requirements for redundancy and performance

Students will design original VLAN segmentation schemes and security policies through integration of ACLs, VPNs, and firewall configurations to protect critical business data across multiple network segments
instructions:
**Phase 1 (60 minutes): Network Requirements Analysis and Design**
Provide teams with the fictional company 'TechCorp Global' scenario: headquarters in New York (500 users), manufacturing site in Texas (200 users), and R&D facility in California (100 users). Each team receives identical business requirements documents specifying: executive VLAN needs 10Mbps guaranteed bandwidth, manufacturing floor requires isolated network with 24/7 uptime, R&D needs secure file transfer capabilities, and all sites must have redundant internet connections.

Students begin by analyzing requirements and sketching their initial network topology on whiteboards, identifying required Cisco device types, IP addressing schemes, and VLAN structures. Instructor circulates to ensure teams understand business constraints and technical limitations.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Packet Tracer Implementation**
Teams transfer their designs into Cisco Packet Tracer, configuring routers (2811 or 2901), switches (2960), and security appliances (ASA 5505). Students must implement: OSPF for internal routing between NY and Texas, EIGRP for NY-California connection, BGP for internet connectivity, inter-VLAN routing with specific subnet allocations, site-to-site VPN tunnels between all locations, and QoS policies ensuring executive traffic priority.

**Phase 3 (45 minutes): Testing and Documentation**
Teams conduct comprehensive connectivity testing using ping, traceroute, and show commands to verify all requirements. Students create network diagrams with IP addressing tables and configuration summaries. Each team prepares a 10-minute presentation defending their design choices and demonstrating successful implementation through live packet captures showing traffic flow between sites.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version) installed on lab computers
TechCorp Global business requirements document (provided by instructor)
Whiteboards and markers for initial topology sketching
Network documentation templates
Stopwatch for timing presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using 100-point rubric: Network topology design appropriateness (25 points), successful configuration implementation verified through working connectivity tests (30 points), security policy effectiveness demonstrated through controlled access testing (20 points), QoS implementation showing measurable bandwidth allocation (15 points), and professional presentation quality with clear justification of design decisions (10 points). Students must achieve 80% for mastery demonstration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured router templates with basic settings and offer checkpoint reviews after each phase. Create reference sheets with essential command syntax for OSPF, EIGRP, and VPN configurations. For advanced learners: Add requirements for network automation using Python scripts, implement advanced security features like IPS policies, or require cost analysis comparing different ISP connectivity options with justification for choices.

title: Interpreting Machine Learning Model Performance Metrics Dashboard
description: Students will analyze a pre-built dashboard containing performance metrics from three different classification models (logistic regression, random forest, decision tree) trained on a customer churn dataset. They will interpret confusion matrices, ROC curves, and precision-recall metrics to determine which model performs best for different business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret confusion matrices, ROC-AUC scores, and precision-recall curves by analyzing their components and explaining what each metric reveals about model performance
Students will compare multiple machine learning models through systematic evaluation of their performance metrics in different business contexts
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (2-3 students) with the prepared dashboard containing metrics from three models trained on customer churn data. Spend 5 minutes explaining the business context: a telecom company wants to predict which customers will cancel their service. In Phase 1 (15 minutes), students examine Model A's metrics individually, writing down their interpretation of: the confusion matrix values (true positives, false positives, etc.), the ROC curve shape and AUC score meaning, and the precision-recall trade-off shown in the PR curve. In Phase 2 (20 minutes), groups rotate through three stations, spending 6-7 minutes at each, analyzing Models B and C using the same framework. At each station, they complete a structured comparison worksheet noting accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC values. In Phase 3 (15 minutes), groups synthesize their findings to answer: 'Which model would you recommend if the business priority is minimizing false positives (avoiding unnecessary retention campaigns)?' and 'Which model if the priority is minimizing false negatives (catching all potential churners)?' Finally (10 minutes), each group presents their recommendation for one scenario to the class, justifying their choice with specific metric values and business reasoning.
materials_needed: Pre-built Tableau or Power BI dashboard with confusion matrices, ROC curves, and PR curves for 3 models
Model comparison worksheet template with metric interpretation guides
Customer churn dataset context sheet explaining business scenario
Laptops or tablets for accessing dashboard
Flip chart paper and markers for final presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate interpretation of individual metrics (confusion matrix components, AUC meaning, precision/recall trade-offs), (2) Correct comparison between models using quantitative evidence, (3) Appropriate model selection justified by business context, and (4) Clear communication of reasoning in final presentation. Students must correctly interpret at least 3 of 4 key metrics and provide business-appropriate justification to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a metric interpretation reference card with formulas and business meanings. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to customers in each quadrant of the confusion matrix?' For advanced learners, add complexity by introducing cost-sensitive evaluation (assign dollar costs to false positives vs false negatives) or ask them to identify potential data quality issues that might affect model performance.

title: Real Estate Investment Portfolio Optimization Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a multi-constraint real estate investment problem. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal investment allocations across residential, commercial, and industrial properties.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a real-world investment scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement both graphical and simplex methods to solve optimization problems and interpret results within the business context
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the investment scenario packet containing: $2M budget, three property types (residential 8% ROI, commercial 12% ROI, industrial 15% ROI), minimum investment requirements (20% residential, 15% commercial), maximum risk exposure (40% industrial), and liquidity constraints (60% must be in residential + commercial). Students work in pairs with graphing paper and calculators.

**Phase 1 - Problem Formulation (25 minutes):** Students define variables (x₁=residential, x₂=commercial, x₃=industrial investment amounts), write the objective function to maximize ROI, and identify all constraints including budget, minimum investment percentages, maximum risk exposure, and non-negativity. They must write each constraint as a linear inequality.

**Phase 2 - Graphical Solution (30 minutes):** For the two-variable case (combining commercial and industrial as one variable), students plot constraint boundaries on coordinate planes, identify the feasible region, and locate corner points. They evaluate the objective function at each vertex to find the optimal solution.

**Phase 3 - Simplex Method (35 minutes):** Students convert inequalities to equalities using slack variables, set up the initial simplex tableau, and perform pivot operations. They continue iterations until reaching the optimal solution, documenting each tableau step.

**Phase 4 - Analysis and Presentation (20 minutes):** Pairs calculate the maximum ROI, determine exact investment amounts for each property type, and prepare a 3-minute presentation explaining their solution strategy and business recommendations. Each pair presents their optimal portfolio allocation and justifies their mathematical approach.
materials_needed: Real estate investment scenario packets (one per pair)
Graphing paper and rulers
Scientific calculators
Simplex tableau templates
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation with all constraints identified (25%), (2) Accurate graphical solution with properly plotted feasible region (25%), (3) Correct simplex method implementation with documented steps (30%), (4) Clear interpretation of results and business recommendations (20%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint templates and worked examples of similar problems. Offer graphing assistance by pre-plotting axes and scales. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how solutions change with different ROI rates or budget constraints. Challenge them to solve using computer software and compare manual calculations.

title: Electromagnetic Induction Circuit Analysis: Dissecting Faraday's Law in Complex Multi-Loop Systems
description: Students analyze a complex electromagnetic induction scenario involving multiple conducting loops, varying magnetic fields, and mutual inductance. They decompose the system to determine individual EMF contributions, current distributions, and energy dissipation patterns using Faraday's law, Lenz's law, and Kirchhoff's rules.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the electromagnetic induction effects in multi-loop circuits by systematically applying Faraday's law to each loop and examining the interdependence of induced EMFs
Students will decompose complex induction problems through systematic identification of flux linkages, current pathways, and energy transfer mechanisms in coupled circuits
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a detailed schematic showing three concentric rectangular conducting loops (inner: 5cm×3cm, middle: 10cm×6cm, outer: 15cm×9cm) positioned in a time-varying magnetic field B(t) = 0.2sin(377t) Tesla, perpendicular to the loop planes. Each loop has specified resistance (R₁=2Ω, R₂=5Ω, R₃=8Ω) and mutual inductance coefficients provided in a matrix. Step 1 (20 min): Students individually calculate the flux through each loop as a function of time, accounting for the area differences and field uniformity. Step 2 (25 min): Working in pairs, students apply Faraday's law to determine the EMF induced in each loop, carefully noting the sign conventions and directions using Lenz's law. Step 3 (30 min): Teams analyze the circuit connectivity, determining whether loops are in series, parallel, or have mutual coupling, then apply Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws to solve for current in each loop. Step 4 (25 min): Students calculate instantaneous and average power dissipated in each resistor, and analyze energy flow between loops through mutual inductance. Step 5 (20 min): Each team presents their systematic approach, highlighting how they decomposed the complex system into manageable components and identified key physical relationships. During analysis, students must justify their choice of coordinate systems, explain their sign conventions, and validate results using energy conservation principles.
materials_needed: Multi-loop circuit schematics with specific dimensions and component values
Scientific calculators with trigonometric functions
Mutual inductance coefficient matrices for each loop configuration
Large whiteboards and markers for circuit analysis
Digital simulation software (PhET Circuit Construction Kit or equivalent)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct application of Faraday's law with proper sign conventions (25%), (2) Systematic circuit analysis using Kirchhoff's laws with clear justification of assumptions (25%), (3) Accurate calculation of currents and power distributions with dimensional analysis (25%), (4) Clear explanation of physical reasoning and identification of energy transfer mechanisms (25%). Students must submit detailed calculations, annotated circuit diagrams, and a brief reflection on their analytical approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step calculation templates, review flux calculation fundamentals, and offer simplified two-loop practice problems. For advanced learners: Include capacitive elements in the circuits, ask them to analyze frequency-dependent behavior, or challenge them to design loop configurations that optimize power transfer efficiency.

title: Code Quality Audit: Evaluating Beginner JavaScript Functions
description: Students will critically assess three pre-written JavaScript functions of varying quality, identifying strengths and weaknesses in code structure, efficiency, and best practices. They will rank the functions from best to worst and justify their evaluations using specific criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate JavaScript code quality by analyzing readability, efficiency, and adherence to coding standards
Students will justify their assessment of code samples through written critiques using established evaluation criteria
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Code Evaluation Worksheet containing three JavaScript functions that solve the same problem (calculating the sum of numbers in an array) but with different approaches and quality levels. Function A uses clear variable names, proper comments, and efficient logic. Function B has poor variable names, no comments, but correct logic. Function C has good structure but contains a logical error and inefficiency. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually read all three functions and run them in a provided online JavaScript editor to observe outputs. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Using the provided evaluation checklist covering readability (variable names, comments), functionality (correct output, handles edge cases), and efficiency (unnecessary loops, optimal approach), students score each function on a 1-5 scale for each criterion. 

Step 3 (10 minutes): Students rank the three functions from best (1) to worst (3) and write a 2-3 sentence justification for each ranking, citing specific examples from the code. 

Step 4 (10 minutes): In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss differences, focusing on their reasoning rather than trying to reach consensus. 

Step 5 (10 minutes): Conduct a class discussion where volunteer pairs share one significant difference in their evaluations and explain their reasoning. Instructor facilitates discussion about how different priorities (readability vs. efficiency) can lead to different valid evaluations.
materials_needed: Code Evaluation Worksheet with 3 JavaScript functions
Evaluation criteria checklist handout
Access to online JavaScript editor (JSFiddle or CodePen)
Computers or tablets for each student
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation worksheets showing numerical scores for each criterion, final rankings (1-3), and written justifications. Success criteria: correctly identifies at least 2 strengths and 2 weaknesses across all functions, provides rankings with logical reasoning based on stated criteria, and demonstrates understanding that code evaluation involves trade-offs between different quality factors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth sample function, highlight key code sections with colored annotations, or allow them to work with a partner throughout. For advanced learners: Add a fourth function with more complex issues, ask them to rewrite the worst function to address identified problems, or have them create their own evaluation criteria for additional code aspects like maintainability.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing Decision-Making Frameworks Through Historical Case Studies
description: Students will analyze three distinct crisis leadership scenarios from different industries and time periods to identify underlying leadership frameworks and decision-making patterns. They will compare and contrast how leaders navigated uncertainty, stakeholder pressures, and resource constraints to demonstrate understanding of crisis leadership principles.
learning_objectives: Students will explain the relationship between leadership decision-making frameworks and crisis outcomes by analyzing documented leadership choices across three historical scenarios
Students will interpret the impact of situational factors on leadership effectiveness through structured comparison of crisis response strategies
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5 and assigning each group one of three pre-selected crisis scenarios: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982), Captain Chesley Sullenberger's Hudson River landing (2009), or Jacinda Ardern's Christchurch shooting response (2019). Provide each group with a comprehensive case study packet containing timeline documents, stakeholder statements, media coverage, and post-crisis interviews. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Groups conduct deep-dive analysis using the provided Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet, identifying: (1) key decision points and timing, (2) stakeholder communication strategies, (3) resource allocation choices, (4) team coordination methods, and (5) long-term consequence management. Students must cite specific evidence from documents for each framework element.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Each group creates a visual leadership decision map showing the chronological flow of critical choices, marking decision-making triggers, information sources consulted, and alternative options considered but rejected. 

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Conduct structured inter-group presentations where each group has 12 minutes to present their analysis, followed by 3 minutes of targeted questions from other groups focusing on framework application differences.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Facilitate whole-class synthesis discussion using guided questions: 'What patterns emerged across different crisis contexts?', 'How did situational factors influence framework effectiveness?', and 'Which leadership principles remained constant despite varying circumstances?' Students individually complete exit reflection capturing three key insights about crisis leadership frameworks.
materials_needed: Three comprehensive crisis case study packets (15-20 pages each with primary source documents)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheets (one per student)
Large poster paper and colored markers for decision mapping
Digital timer for phase management
Individual reflection sheets for exit activity
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of framework element identification with cited evidence (25%), (2) Quality of decision mapping showing clear cause-effect relationships (25%), (3) Depth of comparative analysis during presentations demonstrating understanding of contextual factors (30%), (4) Individual reflection showing synthesis of leadership principles across scenarios (20%). Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed framework worksheets with 2-3 examples filled in and offering guiding questions for document analysis. For advanced learners, provide additional contemporary crisis scenarios for comparison or challenge them to identify potential alternative frameworks not covered in the primary analysis. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who excel at visual representation.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancing
description: Students will deploy a complete web application infrastructure using AWS EC2 instances, configure an Application Load Balancer, and implement basic security groups. This hands-on activity demonstrates practical cloud deployment skills by having students build a scalable web architecture from scratch.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier web application by launching and configuring EC2 instances across multiple availability zones
Students will implement load balancing and security controls through AWS Application Load Balancer and Security Groups configuration
instructions: **Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Learner Lab credentials and ensure they can access the AWS Management Console. Students should have the provided HTML/PHP sample application files downloaded locally. **Step 1 - Launch Web Servers (15 minutes):** Students launch two t2.micro EC2 instances in different availability zones using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. During launch, they must configure User Data scripts to install Apache web server and deploy the sample application. Key configuration: select default VPC, create new security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access. **Step 2 - Configure Application (10 minutes):** After instances are running, students SSH into each instance to verify web server installation and upload custom application files via SCP or direct editing. They must modify index.php to display the instance ID and availability zone for identification purposes. **Step 3 - Create Load Balancer (15 minutes):** Students create an Application Load Balancer in the EC2 console, selecting all available subnets. They configure a target group with health check path '/index.php' and register both EC2 instances as targets. Load balancer security group must allow HTTP traffic from anywhere. **Step 4 - Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Students test the complete setup by accessing the load balancer DNS name multiple times, verifying traffic distribution between instances. They must document response differences showing requests hitting different servers. **Final Documentation (5 minutes):** Students capture screenshots of their architecture diagram from the EC2 dashboard and record load balancer DNS name and target health status.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab access credentials for each student
Sample PHP web application files (index.php, style.css)
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows, Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Architecture diagram template for documentation
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment report containing: (1) Screenshots of running EC2 instances in different AZs (25 points), (2) Load balancer configuration showing healthy targets (25 points), (3) Evidence of successful load balancing with different server responses (25 points), (4) Completed architecture diagram with all components labeled (15 points), (5) Cost estimation using AWS Pricing Calculator (10 points). Success requires functional load balancer distributing traffic between healthy web servers.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written User Data scripts and step-by-step screenshot guides for each AWS console interaction. Create troubleshooting checklist for common issues (security group rules, health check failures). For advanced learners: Add RDS database tier, implement auto-scaling group, or configure SSL certificates. Encourage exploration of CloudFormation templates to automate the deployment process.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancing: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a complete web application infrastructure using AWS EC2 instances, configure an Application Load Balancer, and implement basic security groups. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS concepts by building a real-world scalable web architecture.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional two-tier web application by launching and configuring multiple EC2 instances with proper security groups
Students will implement load balancing and high availability through configuring an Application Load Balancer with health checks
instructions:
**Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access or sandbox account with $25 credit limit. Students log into AWS Management Console and navigate to EC2 dashboard. Create a new key pair named 'weblab-key' and download the .pem file.

**Instance Deployment (25 minutes):** Launch two t2.micro EC2 instances in different availability zones using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. Configure security group 'web-sg' allowing inbound HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) from anywhere. In User Data field, paste provided bash script that installs Apache and creates a simple HTML page displaying the instance ID. Tag instances as 'WebServer-1' and 'WebServer-2'.

**Load Balancer Configuration (20 minutes):** Navigate to Load Balancers section and create Application Load Balancer named 'web-alb'. Configure listener on port 80, select both availability zones where instances are running. Create target group 'web-targets' with HTTP health check on '/' path. Register both EC2 instances to target group.

**Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Wait for target health checks to pass (healthy status). Access load balancer DNS name in browser multiple times to verify traffic distribution between instances. SSH into one instance and stop Apache service, then refresh browser to confirm load balancer routes traffic only to healthy instance. Restart Apache and verify both instances receive traffic again.

**Documentation (10 minutes):** Students complete provided worksheet documenting their architecture diagram, load balancer DNS name, and answers to reflection questions about scalability and fault tolerance.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts or AWS Free Tier accounts
Pre-written Apache installation script for User Data
Architecture documentation worksheet template
Web browser for testing load balancer functionality
assessment_method: Students submit completed worksheet with architecture diagram (20 points), functioning load balancer DNS name that demonstrates traffic distribution (30 points), correct security group configuration screenshot (25 points), and written responses to three reflection questions about high availability concepts (25 points). Pass threshold: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step screenshots for load balancer creation. Pair students for peer support during SSH testing phase. For advanced students: Add challenge to implement Auto Scaling Group with launch template, or configure HTTPS listener with self-signed certificate. Provide additional scenarios for testing failover with different failure types.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancing

title: Risk Register Analysis and Response Strategy Evaluation
description: Students will analyze a complex project risk register to identify risk interdependencies, evaluate the effectiveness of proposed response strategies, and categorize risks by their potential impact on project triple constraints. This activity develops critical analytical skills needed for risk management in real-world project scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies and cascading effects by examining relationships between multiple identified project risks
Students will evaluate the appropriateness and effectiveness of risk response strategies through systematic assessment of mitigation, transfer, acceptance, and avoidance approaches
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute the pre-prepared risk register containing 15-20 risks from a fictional enterprise software implementation project, including risks related to scope creep, vendor delays, resource availability, regulatory changes, and technical integration challenges. Each team receives identical risk registers with columns for Risk ID, Description, Probability, Impact, Risk Score, Current Response Strategy, and Owner.

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze each risk's potential relationships with other risks in the register. Students must identify at least 5 risk interdependencies and map how one risk could trigger or amplify others. They create a visual risk relationship diagram showing primary, secondary, and tertiary risk connections.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate each proposed risk response strategy against PMI's four response categories (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept). Students must assess whether the assigned strategy is optimal by considering cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and alignment with project constraints. They document 3-5 recommendations for strategy improvements with specific justifications.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each team presents their most critical finding - either the most dangerous risk interdependency chain or their strongest recommendation for strategy modification. Presentations are limited to 3 minutes per team with 1 minute for peer questions.

Conclude with a 10-minute debrief where instructor highlights common analytical patterns and connects findings to real-world project management scenarios.
materials_needed: Pre-prepared risk register spreadsheet (digital or printed copies)
Blank flip chart paper or digital collaboration tool (Miro, Jamboard)
Colored markers or digital drawing tools
Presentation timer
PMI Risk Response Strategy reference guide
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk interdependency identification (25%), (2) Quality of risk response strategy evaluation with supporting rationale (35%), (3) Clarity and professionalism of visual risk mapping (20%), (4) Effectiveness of verbal presentation and peer engagement (20%). Teams must identify minimum 5 valid interdependencies and provide 3 well-justified strategy recommendations to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed risk relationship template and strategy evaluation checklist with guided questions. Advanced learners should quantify risk impacts using expected monetary value calculations and propose alternative risk monitoring approaches. Consider pairing analytical thinkers with visual learners to balance team strengths.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with BGP Failover and Security Policies
description: Students will architect and deploy a complete multi-site enterprise network infrastructure incorporating BGP routing, redundant WAN connections, VLAN segmentation, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity requires synthesizing advanced routing protocols, network security, and high-availability design principles into a functional enterprise solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network topology by integrating BGP routing, OSPF, and VLAN technologies with redundant failover mechanisms
Students will implement comprehensive network security policies through configuring ACLs, firewall rules, and network access control across multiple network segments
Students will create detailed network documentation and disaster recovery procedures by developing configuration templates, network diagrams, and troubleshooting guides
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Architecture Design (90 minutes)**
Students work in teams of 3-4 to design a network for a fictional company with headquarters and two branch offices. Each team receives a business requirements document specifying 500+ users, compliance requirements (PCI DSS), and uptime goals (99.9%). Teams must create logical and physical topology diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specify all IP addressing schemes using VLSM, design BGP AS numbering and routing policies, and plan security zones with appropriate access controls.

**Phase 2: Configuration Development (120 minutes)**
Using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3, teams build their network topology with minimum equipment: 3 ISR 4000 series routers, 6 Catalyst 3850 switches, 2 ASA 5516-X firewalls, and 50+ end devices. Students configure BGP peering between sites with route filtering, implement OSPF as IGP with area design, create VLANs for different departments (Sales, Finance, IT, Guest), establish inter-VLAN routing with security policies, configure redundant WAN links with automatic failover, and implement network access control using 802.1X.

**Phase 3: Testing and Documentation (60 minutes)**
Teams conduct comprehensive testing including connectivity verification between all sites and VLANs, BGP failover simulation by disabling primary links, security policy validation through unauthorized access attempts, and performance testing with traffic generators. Teams document all configurations in standardized templates, create network troubleshooting procedures, develop change management processes, and prepare a 10-minute presentation demonstrating network functionality and security features.

**Phase 4: Peer Review and Optimization (30 minutes)**
Teams rotate to review other implementations, identifying potential improvements in security, scalability, or efficiency. Final optimization based on peer feedback is implemented before final assessment.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.0+ or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images
Microsoft Visio or draw.io for network diagrams
Business requirements document template with specific technical constraints
Network configuration documentation templates
Computers with minimum 8GB RAM for network simulation
Access to Cisco documentation and configuration guides
assessment_method: Assessment using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - topology scalability, IP addressing efficiency, security architecture; Technical Implementation (35 points) - BGP configuration accuracy, VLAN implementation, security policies, failover functionality; Documentation Quality (20 points) - configuration templates, network diagrams, troubleshooting procedures; Presentation and Defense (20 points) - demonstration of network features, response to technical questions, peer review quality. Students must achieve 80% minimum score with all critical security features functioning correctly.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic connectivity established, offer checkpoint reviews after each phase with specific feedback, create configuration checklists for complex protocols like BGP, and pair with stronger technical partners. For advanced learners: Add requirements for IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate network automation using Python scripts, implement advanced security features like IPS and network analytics, or design multi-vendor interoperability scenarios. Provide access to Cisco Learning Labs for additional hands-on practice with real equipment.

title: Computer System Components Memory Match and Label
description: Students will memorize and identify the six essential components of a computer system through visual recognition activities. They will practice recalling component names, locations, and basic functions using physical flashcards and computer diagrams.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the names and locations of six basic computer components (CPU, RAM, hard drive, motherboard, power supply, graphics card) by matching visual images to component names
Students will identify each component's primary function through guided memorization exercises and verbal recitation
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made component flashcards (images on one side, names on the other) to pairs of students. Spend 5 minutes having students examine cards together, saying component names aloud while viewing images. Next, display a large computer system diagram on the projector with numbered but unlabeled components. Students work individually for 10 minutes to write component names next to each number on their worksheet, referring to flashcards as needed. Collect worksheets and review answers as a class, having students repeat each component name three times chorally. For the matching activity, shuffle and redistribute flashcards image-side up across desks. Call out component names randomly while students race to find and hold up the correct image card. Award one point per correct identification. In the final 10 minutes, project unlabeled computer photos and have students write all six component names from memory on exit tickets. Circulate to ensure students are actively participating in each memorization phase and provide individual pronunciation help as needed.
materials_needed: 36 laminated flashcards (6 components × 6 pairs of students) with component images and names
Large computer system diagram poster or projector slide
Component identification worksheets (one per student)
Exit ticket templates
Pencils or pens for each student
assessment_method: Students demonstrate mastery by correctly identifying at least 5 out of 6 components on the exit ticket from memory, spelling component names with no more than one letter error per word, and achieving 70% accuracy during the flashcard matching activity. Use observation checklist to track individual participation during choral repetition.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling learners by providing mnemonic devices (CPU = Computer's Processing Unit) and allowing extended flashcard reference time. For advanced students, add challenge components like network cards or optical drives, or have them explain component interactions beyond basic functions.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Predictive Model Selection
description: Students will analyze correlation heatmaps from a housing price dataset to identify multicollinearity issues and explain which features should be retained or removed for model building. This activity develops critical interpretation skills for feature engineering decisions in machine learning workflows.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients in heatmaps by identifying strong positive/negative relationships and explaining their implications for model performance
Students will distinguish between beneficial correlations (feature-target) and problematic correlations (feature-feature multicollinearity) through systematic heatmap analysis
instructions:
Begin by providing each student group with a pre-generated correlation heatmap from the Boston Housing dataset containing 13 features plus the target variable (median home value). Display the heatmap using a diverging color scale (-1 to +1) with clear numerical labels. 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students individually examine the heatmap and identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording the feature pairs and exact correlation values. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): In pairs, students categorize correlations into two types: feature-to-target correlations (potentially useful for prediction) and feature-to-feature correlations above |0.7| (potential multicollinearity issues). They create a two-column table listing these relationships. 

Step 3 (20 minutes): Each pair writes explanations for why high feature-to-feature correlations can harm model performance, specifically addressing redundant information and coefficient instability. They then propose which features to remove from correlated pairs, justifying their choices based on domain knowledge and correlation strength with the target variable. 

Step 4 (10 minutes): Pairs present one multicollinearity case to the class, explaining their feature removal decision. The instructor facilitates discussion about alternative approaches like principal component analysis or regularization techniques. 

Provide students with a reference sheet defining correlation strength thresholds: weak (0-0.3), moderate (0.3-0.7), strong (0.7-1.0).
materials_needed: Boston Housing dataset correlation heatmap (printed color copies or digital display)
Correlation strength reference sheet
Analysis worksheet with two-column table template
Python/R environment with seaborn or corrplot libraries (if generating live heatmaps)
assessment_method: Evaluate student pairs' two-column correlation categorization table (40% - must correctly identify at least 4 feature-feature correlations >|0.7|), written explanations of multicollinearity impacts (40% - must mention redundant information AND coefficient instability), and feature removal justifications (20% - must reference both target correlation strength and domain reasoning). Use a 4-point rubric: Excellent (demonstrates complete understanding), Proficient (minor gaps), Developing (major conceptual errors), Inadequate (fails to demonstrate understanding).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed correlation table with 2-3 examples already filled in, and offer sentence starters like 'High correlation between X and Y means...' For advanced learners, introduce variance inflation factor (VIF) calculations as a numerical alternative to visual heatmap analysis, or challenge them to propose regularization techniques (Ridge/Lasso) as alternatives to feature removal.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configurations Using Calculus and Linear Programming
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel placement on irregularly-shaped rooftops. They will determine optimal panel configurations to maximize energy output while satisfying physical and budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to optimize solar panel positioning by analyzing shadow patterns and energy output functions
Students will implement linear programming constraints and objective functions through systematic mathematical modeling of real-world resource allocation problems
instructions: Begin by distributing the rooftop blueprint packets containing three different building layouts (L-shaped, rectangular with obstacles, and triangular). Students work in teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Each team receives a different rooftop configuration to ensure varied solutions. Introduce the scenario: A solar installation company needs to maximize kilowatt-hour output while staying within a $50,000 budget, considering panel costs ($800 each), installation constraints (minimum 3-foot spacing), and seasonal shadow patterns. Teams first establish their coordinate system by placing the origin at the building's southwest corner and measuring all dimensions in feet (20 minutes). Next, students develop the objective function by creating equations for daily energy output E(x,y,θ) where (x,y) represents panel positions and θ represents tilt angle, incorporating provided solar irradiance data and shadow-casting formulas (25 minutes). Students then identify and mathematically express all constraints: budget inequality (800n ≤ 50,000), spacing requirements (distance between panels ≥ 3 feet), boundary conditions (panels must fit within rooftop), and shadow constraints using trigonometric functions for neighboring panels and rooftop obstacles (30 minutes). Using graphing calculators or MATLAB, teams apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to find critical points of their constrained optimization problem, computing partial derivatives and solving the resulting system of equations (40 minutes). Finally, students verify their solutions by checking second-derivative tests for maxima and testing boundary conditions, then calculate the total projected annual energy output and cost breakdown for their optimal configuration (20 minutes). Each team presents their mathematical model, solution process, and final panel layout with energy projections.
materials_needed: Rooftop blueprint packets with scaled drawings (3 different layouts per class)
Solar irradiance data tables for different months and panel angles
Graphing calculators or computers with MATLAB/GeoGebra access
Grid paper and rulers for manual calculations and sketching
Solar panel specification sheets with dimensions and cost data
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical model setup and objective function formulation (25 points), correct identification and expression of all constraints (20 points), proper application of optimization techniques including Lagrange multipliers (25 points), accuracy of calculations and solution verification (20 points), and presentation clarity with justification of final design decisions (10 points). Teams must submit their mathematical work, final panel layout diagram, and energy/cost analysis spreadsheet.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint templates and guide them through setting up the first few partial derivatives. Offer simplified rooftop shapes (rectangular only) and reduce the number of variables by fixing panel orientation. For advanced learners, add complexity by including seasonal optimization (different configurations for summer/winter), battery storage optimization decisions, or multi-objective optimization considering both cost and environmental impact. Provide additional real-world constraints like wind load calculations or electrical grid connection requirements.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Collision Dynamics Through Video Analysis and Energy-Momentum Conservation
description: Students will analyze real-world collision footage to decompose complex multi-body interactions, examining how momentum and energy conservation principles apply differently across elastic, inelastic, and explosive collision scenarios. They will identify systematic patterns in energy transformations and momentum transfers to evaluate the validity of theoretical predictions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-body collision systems by decomposing momentum vectors and energy transformations to identify conservation principle violations and their physical causes

Students will evaluate the relationship between collision elasticity and energy dissipation through quantitative comparison of before/after kinetic energy calculations across different collision types
instructions:
Begin by distributing high-speed collision videos (3 types: elastic ball collisions, car crashes, explosive separations) and providing students with Tracker video analysis software on computers. Form groups of 3-4 students, with each group analyzing one collision type initially (20 minutes setup). 

Step 1 (30 minutes): Students calibrate their videos using known reference objects, then track the position-time data for each object involved in their assigned collision. They must identify at least 3 objects in each collision and track motion for 2 seconds before and after impact.

Step 2 (40 minutes): Using spreadsheet calculations, students determine velocity vectors immediately before and after collision for each object. They calculate total system momentum in both x and y directions, then compute percentage momentum conservation error. Students must also calculate individual and total kinetic energies before and after collision.

Step 3 (35 minutes): Groups rotate to analyze a second collision type, comparing momentum conservation accuracy and energy loss patterns. They create comparative data tables and identify which collision characteristics (mass ratios, impact angles, material properties) most strongly correlate with momentum conservation violations.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Students synthesize findings by creating cause-effect diagrams linking collision parameters to conservation principle adherence. They must propose specific physical mechanisms explaining energy dissipation in each collision type and predict momentum conservation accuracy for untested scenarios.

Conclude with groups presenting their most significant analytical finding and one testable hypothesis about collision behavior to the class (15 minutes).
materials_needed: High-speed collision videos (3 different types: elastic spheres, vehicle crashes, explosive separations)
Computers with Tracker video analysis software installed
Spreadsheet software (Excel or Google Sheets)
Calculators
Printed data collection templates with momentum/energy calculation formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of momentum vector calculations and conservation analysis (25%), (2) Quality of energy transformation identification and quantification (25%), (3) Depth of cause-effect relationships identified between collision parameters and conservation violations (25%), (4) Validity and testability of proposed hypotheses for predicting collision outcomes (25%). Students must achieve proficient level (3/4) in all categories, demonstrating quantitative analysis with less than 5% calculation errors.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-calibrated videos and step-by-step calculation templates with sample calculations completed. Offer vector decomposition review sheets and momentum conservation checkpoint questions. Extend advanced learners by providing complex 3D collision videos requiring 3-dimensional momentum analysis, or challenge them to derive collision outcome prediction equations from their empirical relationships. Consider pairing stronger physics students with those needing support during calculation phases.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program
description: Students will evaluate three different bug fix solutions for a broken calculator program by assessing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will justify their rankings and provide detailed feedback using established code review criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different bug fix approaches by analyzing code quality, functionality, and maintainability against established criteria
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic code review practices and provide justified recommendations for implementation
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Broken Calculator Scenario' handout containing: (1) original buggy calculator code with addition and division functions that crash on invalid input, (2) three different student-submitted bug fixes labeled Solution A, B, and C, and (3) the Code Review Evaluation Sheet. Explain that they are junior developers reviewing peer submissions.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each solution against four criteria: (1) Does it fix the bug completely? (2) Is the code readable and well-commented? (3) Does it handle edge cases properly? (4) Does it follow coding best practices? They score each solution 1-4 points per criteria and take notes.

**Evaluation and Ranking (10 minutes):** Students calculate total scores, rank solutions from best to worst, and write a 2-3 sentence justification for their top choice. They must identify at least one strength and one weakness for each solution.

**Peer Discussion (8 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and defend their choices. They must reach consensus on which solution they would recommend for production deployment.

**Reflection Documentation (7 minutes):** Students complete the evaluation report by writing specific feedback for each solution author, including what they did well and what should be improved. They conclude with their final recommendation and reasoning.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief whole-class discussion on common evaluation patterns and the importance of systematic code review in professional development.
materials_needed: Broken Calculator Scenario handout with original buggy code
Three pre-written bug fix solutions (Solution A: basic fix, Solution B: comprehensive with error handling, Solution C: over-engineered solution)
Code Review Evaluation Sheet with scoring rubric
Computers with text editors or printed code samples
assessment_method: Students submit completed Code Review Evaluation Sheets scored on: (1) Accurate identification of bugs and fixes (25 points), (2) Appropriate use of evaluation criteria with evidence (30 points), (3) Clear justification for rankings with specific examples (25 points), (4) Constructive feedback with actionable suggestions (20 points). Success requires 70+ points and demonstrating ability to evaluate code beyond just 'it works' to include quality factors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth solution and highlight specific phrases to use in technical feedback. Create a checklist version of criteria with yes/no questions. For advanced learners: Add security and performance evaluation criteria, or have them suggest alternative solutions and evaluate their own approaches against the provided ones.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Practical Workshop
description: Students will evaluate three different bug fix solutions for a broken JavaScript calculator, assessing code quality, efficiency, and maintainability. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluation using established coding criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different code solutions by comparing their effectiveness, readability, and adherence to coding standards
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic assessment using a provided evaluation framework
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the broken calculator code and three bug fix solutions to each student. Display the evaluation criteria poster prominently. **Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine the original buggy calculator code that fails when dividing by zero and produces incorrect results for decimal operations. They then review Solution A (basic if-statement fix), Solution B (comprehensive error handling with try-catch), and Solution C (object-oriented approach with validation methods). Students use the provided evaluation worksheet to score each solution on a 1-5 scale across four criteria: functionality, code readability, efficiency, and maintainability. **Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pair students to compare their individual rankings and discuss their reasoning. Each pair must reach consensus on the best solution. **Group Presentation (15 minutes):** Call on 4-5 pairs to present their top choice and defend their decision in 2 minutes each. Record rankings on the whiteboard. **Reflection and Debrief (10 minutes):** Lead discussion on evaluation patterns, highlighting how different priorities (beginner-friendly vs. enterprise-ready) influence assessment. Students complete exit ticket identifying one strength and one weakness they discovered in their evaluation process.
materials_needed: Printed handout with buggy calculator code and three fix solutions
Code evaluation worksheet with 1-5 scoring rubric
Evaluation criteria poster (functionality, readability, efficiency, maintainability)
Computers with JavaScript environment or code editor
Exit ticket template
assessment_method: Grade completed evaluation worksheets using rubric: thorough analysis of each solution (40 points), clear justification for rankings (30 points), accurate identification of code strengths/weaknesses (20 points), participation in peer discussion and presentation (10 points). Students must demonstrate understanding of evaluation criteria through specific examples from the code.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This solution is better because...' and highlight specific code lines to examine. Offer simplified evaluation focusing on just functionality and readability. For advanced learners: Include additional solutions with different programming paradigms, ask them to suggest improvements to existing solutions, or have them create evaluation criteria for security considerations.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program: Exercise 2
description: Students will analyze and evaluate three different code solutions that fix bugs in a basic calculator program. They will assess each solution's quality, efficiency, and maintainability, then rank them with detailed justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different debugging approaches by comparing code quality, readability, and performance metrics
Students will critique multiple programming solutions through systematic analysis using established software quality criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with a buggy calculator program that has three specific issues: division by zero crashes the program, negative number inputs cause incorrect results, and decimal calculations round incorrectly. Also provide three different 'fixed' versions of the code, each taking a different approach to solving these bugs.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students work alone to test each fixed version using a provided test case list (10 calculations including edge cases). They document which bugs each version fixes, note any remaining issues, and evaluate code readability by counting lines of code, commenting quality, and variable naming clarity.

**Evaluation Framework Application (15 minutes):** Students use a provided rubric to score each solution on five criteria: correctness (does it fix all bugs?), efficiency (performance and resource usage), maintainability (code clarity and documentation), robustness (handles edge cases), and user experience (error messages and interface).
