Each criterion is scored 1-5 points.

**Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Students rank the three solutions from best to worst, writing a 150-word justification that references specific code examples and rubric scores. They must identify the single biggest strength and weakness of their top-ranked solution.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare rankings and discuss differences in evaluation, focusing on how different priorities (speed vs. readability, etc.) influenced their decisions.
materials_needed: Original buggy calculator program (Python or JavaScript file)
Three fixed versions of the calculator program
Test case worksheet with 10 specific calculations to run
Code evaluation rubric with 5 criteria and scoring guidelines
Computers with appropriate programming environment installed
assessment_method: Grade students on: (1) Completion of testing worksheet showing they ran all test cases (25 points), (2) Accurate application of rubric with numerical scores for each solution (35 points), (3) Quality of written justification that uses specific evidence from code and testing (40 points). Success = 70+ points with clear reasoning that demonstrates understanding of software quality principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a sample evaluation of a fourth code solution as an example, highlight key sections of code to focus on, and offer sentence starters for the justification writing. For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to write their own improved solution, or evaluate solutions using additional criteria like security considerations and scalability potential.
original_title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in a Simple Calculator Program

title: PMI Knowledge Area Integration Framework Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMI Knowledge Area framework including all 49 project management processes, their respective process groups, and specific inputs/outputs. This advanced recall activity focuses on the intricate details of how processes interconnect across the ten knowledge areas through shared deliverables and information flows.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMI project management processes by correctly identifying their knowledge area and process group classification within 90 seconds per process
Students will identify specific process inputs and outputs through rapid-fire recall exercises targeting the 600+ documented process elements
instructions: Begin by distributing the PMI Process Map template (10 knowledge areas × 5 process groups grid) to each student. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study the complete framework using the PMBOK Guide reference sheets, focusing on memorizing process names, locations, and three key inputs/outputs per process. Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement spaced repetition drill - call out a process name every 30 seconds, students must write the knowledge area and process group on their answer sheet. Cover all 49 processes twice. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Reverse recall challenge - announce a knowledge area and process group intersection, students must name the process(es) that belong there. Phase 4 (20 minutes): Input/Output rapid recall - display process names on screen for 10 seconds each, students write three specific inputs and three outputs from memory. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Integration connections recall - present key deliverables (Project Charter, WBS, Risk Register, etc.) and students list all processes that use this item as input or produce it as output. Conclude with peer verification where students check each other's answers against the official PMBOK reference.
materials_needed: PMI Process Map blank template (10×5 grid)
PMBOK Guide 7th Edition reference sheets
Digital timer/stopwatch
Process Input/Output reference cards
Answer sheets with numbered lines (1-49)
Projector/screen for displaying process names
assessment_method: Score based on accuracy: Process identification (2 points × 49 = 98 points), Input/Output recall (1 point per correct item, maximum 294 points), Integration connections (2 points per correct process linkage, maximum 40 points). Total possible: 432 points. Success criteria: 85% accuracy (367+ points) demonstrates advanced-level recall mastery of PMI framework details.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (IIPMO for process groups), allow them to start with one knowledge area at a time, and give 45 seconds instead of 30 for initial rounds. For advanced learners: Add process sequence dependencies, require them to identify critical path relationships between processes, or include agile/hybrid process variations from PMBOK 7th edition.

title: PMI Knowledge Area Integration Framework Recall Challenge: Team Exercise
description: Students will systematically recall and demonstrate their memorization of the 10 PMI Knowledge Areas and their 49 associated processes across 5 process groups. This intensive recall activity tests advanced knowledge of PMBOK Guide framework integration points and process interdependencies.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 10 PMI Knowledge Areas and their corresponding 49 processes by completing a timed matrix mapping exercise
Students will identify specific ITTO (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) elements for 15 selected processes through structured recall cards
instructions: Begin by distributing blank PMI Process Group/Knowledge Area matrix templates (5x10 grid). Students have 20 minutes to fill in all 49 process names in their correct intersections without references. After completion, distribute 15 pre-selected ITTO recall cards covering processes from different knowledge areas (e.g., Develop Project Charter, Plan Risk Management, Control Procurements). Each card shows only the process name - students must write from memory: 3 key inputs, 3 tools/techniques, and 3 outputs for each process. Allow 25 minutes for ITTO completion. During the final 10 minutes, conduct rapid-fire verbal verification where students state the knowledge area for randomly called processes. For the integration challenge, present 5 process dependency scenarios (e.g., 'Which process must complete before Define Activities can begin?') requiring students to recall specific process sequences. Maintain strict no-reference policy throughout. Record individual completion times and accuracy rates. Conclude with immediate answer key review, having students mark their own work and calculate accuracy percentages for matrix completion (target: 90%+) and ITTO recall (target: 80%+).
materials_needed: Blank PMI Process Group/Knowledge Area matrix templates (one per student)
Pre-designed ITTO recall cards for 15 specific processes
Process dependency scenario question sheets
Complete PMBOK Guide answer keys for immediate verification
Stopwatches or timer applications
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery with 90%+ accuracy on process matrix placement (44/49 processes correct), 80%+ accuracy on ITTO components (36/45 elements correct across 15 processes), and 100% accuracy on process dependency sequencing (5/5 scenarios correct). Partial credit awarded: matrix 2 points per correct process, ITTO 1 point per correct element, dependencies 4 points each.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide knowledge area headers as hints, allow matrix completion in 25 minutes instead of 20, reduce ITTO cards to 10 processes. For advanced learners: add process integration questions requiring recall of cross-knowledge area dependencies, include questions about agile/hybrid process adaptations, challenge with PMBOK 7th edition performance domain connections.
original_title: PMI Knowledge Area Integration Framework Recall Challenge

title: Multi-Perspective Leadership Crisis Analysis: Understanding Stakeholder Impact Dynamics
description: Students analyze a complex organizational crisis through the lens of different stakeholder groups to understand how leadership decisions create cascading effects across multiple constituencies. They will demonstrate comprehension by mapping cause-and-effect relationships and explaining the rationale behind competing stakeholder perspectives.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interconnected consequences of leadership decisions by mapping stakeholder impact chains across at least four different constituency groups
Students will demonstrate understanding of leadership complexity through written explanations of how single decisions create multiple, sometimes conflicting, outcomes for different stakeholders
instructions:
Begin by presenting the Boeing 737 MAX crisis case study, providing students with a 2-page background document detailing the timeline from design decisions through grounding (10 minutes reading time). Divide students into groups of 4-5, assigning each group member a specific stakeholder identity: airline executives, pilots/crew, passengers/families, Boeing shareholders, and regulatory officials. Provide each student with a stakeholder profile sheet containing specific concerns, constraints, and success metrics for their assigned role. 

Phase 1 (20 minutes): Individual stakeholder analysis where each student identifies 3-4 key leadership decisions from the crisis and analyzes their specific impact on their assigned stakeholder group, documenting immediate and long-term consequences. 

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Round-robin sharing within groups where each stakeholder presents their perspective on the same leadership decisions, while others take notes on conflicting viewpoints and overlapping concerns. 

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Collaborative creation of a stakeholder impact web on large poster paper, using different colored markers for each stakeholder group to trace how leadership decisions created ripple effects across constituencies. Groups must identify at least three decision points where stakeholder interests directly conflicted. 

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents their stakeholder web to the class, specifically explaining two examples where they now understand why effective leadership required balancing competing interests, and one example where leadership failed to anticipate cross-stakeholder consequences. Conclude with groups posting webs around room for gallery walk comparison of different groups' interpretations.
materials_needed: Boeing 737 MAX crisis case study packet (2 pages per student)
Stakeholder profile sheets for 5 different constituencies
Large poster paper (1 sheet per group)
Colored markers (5 different colors per group)
Sticky notes for additional observations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of stakeholder impact identification (25%), (2) Clear explanation of cause-effect relationships between leadership decisions and stakeholder outcomes (35%), (3) Demonstration of understanding multiple perspectives on same decisions (25%), and (4) Quality of visual stakeholder web showing interconnections (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher in each category, with written reflection submitted within 48 hours explaining two key insights about leadership complexity gained through the multi-stakeholder analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'This leadership decision impacted my stakeholder group by...' and 'The long-term consequence was...' For advanced learners, add a sixth stakeholder (government officials or media) and require them to identify second-order effects where stakeholder reactions created additional leadership challenges. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who struggle with cause-effect reasoning during the collaborative web creation phase.

title: Critical Path Analysis: Deconstructing Schedule Compression Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three different project schedule scenarios to identify critical path impacts when schedule compression techniques (crashing and fast-tracking) are applied. They will compare the effectiveness, risks, and cost implications of each approach to determine optimal compression strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze critical path changes by comparing baseline schedules with compressed alternatives using precedence diagramming method
Students will differentiate between crashing and fast-tracking impacts through systematic evaluation of cost, risk, and schedule trade-offs
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute three project scenarios: Software Implementation (45 activities), Construction Project (38 activities), and Product Launch (52 activities). Each scenario includes network diagram, activity durations, costs, and resource requirements. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Baseline Analysis (20 minutes):** Teams identify the critical path for each scenario using forward and backward pass calculations. Document critical activities, total project duration, and float for non-critical activities. Create visual network diagrams highlighting critical paths in red.

**Phase 2 - Compression Analysis (30 minutes):** For each scenario, teams analyze provided compression options: Scenario 1 offers 3 crashing options and 2 fast-tracking options; Scenario 2 offers 4 crashing and 3 fast-tracking options; Scenario 3 offers 2 crashing and 4 fast-tracking options. Calculate new critical paths, project durations, additional costs, and identify newly introduced risks for each compression alternative.

**Phase 3 - Comparative Evaluation (20 minutes):** Teams complete analysis matrices comparing compression options across five criteria: schedule reduction achieved, cost increase, risk level (1-5 scale), implementation complexity, and stakeholder impact. Teams must justify ratings with specific evidence from calculations.

**Phase 4 - Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents their recommended compression strategy for one assigned scenario, defending their choice with quantitative analysis and risk assessment. Other teams challenge recommendations through structured questioning.
materials_needed: Three detailed project scenarios with network diagrams and activity data sheets
Critical path calculation worksheets with forward/backward pass templates
Compression analysis matrices (Excel templates or printed forms)
Colored pens/highlighters for network diagram marking
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across four dimensions: (1) Accuracy of critical path calculations and compression impact analysis (40%), (2) Quality of comparative evaluation with justified criteria ratings (25%), (3) Logical reasoning in final recommendations with supporting evidence (25%), (4) Effective communication during presentation and peer questioning (10%). Teams must achieve 3/4 points in calculation accuracy to pass.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide critical path calculation example walkthrough, offer templates with partially completed calculations, pair weaker students with stronger analytical thinkers. **Advanced extension:** Add resource leveling constraints requiring teams to consider resource availability when analyzing compression options, or introduce multiple compression combinations requiring optimization analysis.

title: Comprehensive GA4 Implementation Audit and Strategic Recommendations
description: Students will conduct a thorough evaluation of an existing Google Analytics 4 implementation by analyzing tracking accuracy, data quality, and business alignment. They will then create prioritized recommendations for optimization and present their findings with supporting evidence and implementation roadmaps.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate GA4 tracking implementation quality by conducting systematic audits of data collection, event configuration, and conversion tracking accuracy
Students will assess the strategic value of current analytics setup through gap analysis between business objectives and available reporting capabilities
instructions: Begin by providing student teams (2-3 people) with access to a demo GA4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Teams spend 45 minutes conducting initial exploration using the provided audit checklist covering: tracking code implementation verification, enhanced e-commerce setup validation, custom event configuration review, audience definition assessment, and conversion tracking accuracy check. Next, teams spend 60 minutes performing quantitative analysis by comparing GA4 data against provided baseline metrics from Google Tag Manager Debug Console logs and identifying discrepancies in transaction tracking, event parameter consistency, and user journey completeness. Students then spend 45 minutes evaluating strategic alignment by mapping current tracking capabilities against provided business objectives document, identifying missing KPIs, assessing data visualization effectiveness in existing reports, and reviewing attribution model appropriateness. Following analysis, teams spend 75 minutes developing comprehensive recommendations including priority-ranked implementation fixes, cost-benefit analysis for each recommendation, realistic timelines for implementation, and potential risks or challenges. Finally, teams present 15-minute findings to the class, defending their prioritization decisions and responding to peer questions about their evaluation criteria and recommended solutions.
materials_needed: Shared GA4 demo property access with realistic e-commerce data
Google Tag Manager Debug Console reference logs
Business objectives and KPI requirements document
GA4 implementation audit checklist template
Presentation software access
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric covering: audit thoroughness and accuracy (25%), quality of quantitative analysis and evidence (25%), strategic thinking in recommendations (25%), and presentation clarity with peer Q&A responses (25%). Success requires identifying at least 8 implementation issues, providing data-driven justification for top 3 priorities, and demonstrating clear understanding of business impact.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students with guided audit checklist walkthroughs and sample discrepancy identification examples. Extend advanced learners by requesting custom calculated metrics creation and advanced segment analysis to support their recommendations.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with SD-WAN and Security Integration
description: Students will architect and deploy a comprehensive enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using SD-WAN technology, integrated security policies, and redundant connectivity. This capstone project synthesizes advanced routing, security, and modern networking technologies into a production-ready design with full documentation and disaster recovery procedures.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize advanced networking concepts by designing a multi-site enterprise topology incorporating OSPF, BGP, SD-WAN, and security policies within a simulated production environment
Students will construct comprehensive network documentation and implementation procedures through creation of network diagrams, configuration templates, and disaster recovery playbooks
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (90 minutes)**
Students work in teams of 3-4 to design a network for fictional company 'GlobalTech Inc.' with headquarters in New York (500 users), manufacturing site in Chicago (200 users), and R&D facility in Seattle (100 users). Each team receives identical requirements: 99.9% uptime SLA, support for voice/video traffic, secure remote access, and compliance with SOX regulations. Teams must create detailed network topology diagrams using Visio or Lucidchart, specifying all device models, interface assignments, IP addressing schemes using VLSM, and redundancy mechanisms.

**Phase 2: Configuration Development (120 minutes)**
Using GNS3 or Cisco Modeling Labs, teams build their designed topology with Cisco ISR 4000 series routers, Catalyst 9000 switches, and ASA 5500 firewalls. Students configure OSPF as IGP within each site, eBGP between sites and service providers, implement SD-WAN using Cisco Viptela controllers for overlay connectivity, and establish IPsec tunnels for backup connectivity. Each site requires three VLANs (Data, Voice, Management) with appropriate QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic.

**Phase 3: Security Implementation (60 minutes)**
Teams configure zone-based firewalls, implement 802.1X authentication for wired access, establish site-to-site VPN tunnels, and create access control lists restricting inter-VLAN communication based on business requirements. Students must demonstrate understanding of defense-in-depth principles by implementing security at multiple network layers.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (90 minutes)**
Teams conduct comprehensive testing including connectivity verification between all sites, failover testing by simulating link failures, QoS validation using traffic generators, and security policy verification through penetration testing scenarios. Students create complete documentation package including configuration files, network diagrams, IP address spreadsheets, and step-by-step disaster recovery procedures.
materials_needed: Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) or GNS3 with Cisco IOS images (ISR 4000, Catalyst 9000, ASA 5500)
Network diagramming software (Visio, Lucidchart, or Draw.io)
Project requirements document with GlobalTech Inc. specifications
IP address planning worksheets and VLSM calculators
Configuration template library for common Cisco features
assessment_method: Teams submit complete project portfolio (40% weight) including network diagrams, configuration files, and documentation. Live demonstration (35% weight) requires teams to explain design decisions, demonstrate network functionality, and perform failover scenarios while answering technical questions. Peer evaluation (25% weight) assesses individual contributions using structured rubric covering technical accuracy, design rationale, implementation quality, and professional presentation. Success criteria: Network achieves 100% connectivity between sites, demonstrates automatic failover within 30 seconds, QoS policies show measurable voice traffic prioritization, and security policies prevent unauthorized access attempts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-configured base templates with basic connectivity and step-by-step configuration guides for complex features like SD-WAN. Assign specific roles within teams (routing specialist, security specialist, documentation lead) to ensure balanced participation. Advanced learners can extend the project by implementing IPv6 dual-stack configuration, advanced QoS features like traffic shaping, or integration with cloud services using AWS/Azure virtual gateways. Provide troubleshooting decision trees and common error resolution guides for independent problem-solving.

title: Programming Language Syntax Matching Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental programming syntax elements by matching code snippets with their correct language identifiers. This activity builds foundational recognition skills for common programming languages through repetitive visual matching exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall basic syntax patterns for five common programming languages (Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, HTML) by correctly identifying code snippets
Students will memorize key language-specific syntax elements through structured flashcard matching activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-printed syntax reference cards showing 25 code snippets (5 per language) without language labels. Each card displays one syntax element: variable declarations, function definitions, loops, conditionals, or comments. Post five large language identifier signs (Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, HTML) around the classroom. Give students 10 minutes to study a master reference sheet showing all syntax patterns with correct language labels. Remove reference sheets and explain the matching challenge: students must physically move around the room and sort their assigned 5 random cards under the correct language signs. Allow 15 minutes for sorting while circulating to observe student choices without providing feedback. After sorting, reveal correct answers by displaying the master reference sheet again. Students check their placements and record their accuracy scores. Conduct a 10-minute group review where students explain one syntax difference they noticed between languages. Redistribute cards ensuring each student receives different snippets, then repeat the entire sorting process for round two. Conclude with students writing down three syntax patterns they found most challenging to remember and creating personal memory aids for these patterns.
materials_needed: 125 pre-printed syntax snippet cards (25 unique snippets × 5 copies)
5 large language identifier signs with stands
Master reference answer sheet (1 per student)
Individual score tracking sheets
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students receive 1 point for each correctly placed syntax card (maximum 5 points per round, 10 points total). Success criteria: 70% accuracy (7/10 points) demonstrates adequate recall. Track individual progress through score sheets and observe student explanations during group review for verbal recall demonstration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide cards with subtle visual hints (color-coded borders) and allow extended study time with reference sheets. Pair struggling students with stronger peers during review discussions. For advanced learners: include more complex syntax examples like object-oriented concepts or provide unlabeled mixed-language code blocks to separate into distinct languages.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Customer Churn Prediction Models
description: Students analyze and interpret feature importance outputs from three different machine learning models (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, and XGBoost) trained on a customer churn dataset. They will explain why different models prioritize different features and translate technical findings into business recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance rankings from multiple ML models by analyzing coefficient values, permutation importance scores, and SHAP values to identify key predictors
Students will explain the business significance of feature rankings through written analysis comparing model interpretations and their real-world implications
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-trained model outputs showing feature importance rankings for all three models on the telecommunications customer churn dataset (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4. Each group receives identical datasets containing: feature importance scores, model performance metrics, and feature descriptions with business context. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students examine the top 10 features from each model, creating a comparison table noting similarities and differences in rankings. They should identify which features appear consistently important across models and which vary significantly.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Groups analyze why specific features rank differently across models. Provide guiding questions: 'Why might Random Forest rank contract_length higher than Logistic Regression?' 'What does it mean when XGBoost heavily weights monthly_charges but Random Forest doesn't?' Students research each algorithm's feature selection tendencies using provided reference materials.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Groups translate technical findings into business insights. They write a 2-page memo addressing: Which customer characteristics most reliably predict churn? What conflicting signals do the models provide? How would they prioritize retention strategies based on these findings? Include specific feature values and thresholds where relevant.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each group presents their key finding to the class, focusing on one major discrepancy between models and their business interpretation. Other groups ask clarifying questions about the technical reasoning.

Conclude with instructor-led discussion connecting interpretations to model selection decisions in production environments (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-trained model outputs (Random Forest, Logistic Regression, XGBoost feature importance scores)
Customer churn dataset with 15 features and business context descriptions
Model performance comparison sheet (accuracy, precision, recall for each model)
Algorithm reference guide explaining how each model calculates feature importance
Business memo template with specific sections for technical findings and recommendations
assessment_method: Evaluate the 2-page business memo using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of technical interpretation - correctly identifies and explains feature importance differences, (2) Quality of business reasoning - logically connects technical findings to customer behavior insights, (3) Clarity of recommendations - provides specific, actionable strategies based on feature analysis, (4) Use of evidence - supports claims with specific feature values and model comparisons. Additionally, assess group presentation for clear explanation of one model discrepancy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for memo sections ('The most consistent predictor across all models is... because...') and a completed example using a different dataset. Create a feature importance interpretation flowchart showing how to move from technical scores to business meaning. For advanced learners: Include SHAP value plots for deeper interpretation, ask them to recommend which model to deploy based on feature interpretability needs, or have them identify potential bias issues in feature selection.

title: Optimization Crisis: Designing Emergency Supply Routes Using Calculus
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world emergency logistics problem. They will determine optimal supply routes and resource allocation for disaster relief operations using constrained optimization methods and Lagrange multipliers.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to minimize transportation costs and delivery time in a disaster relief scenario by setting up and solving constrained optimization problems
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic mathematical modeling of real-world constraints
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the Emergency Response Scenario packet containing a map with 8 affected towns, 3 supply depots, road conditions, and resource requirements. Form teams of 3-4 students. Each team receives calculators, graphing software access, and constraint worksheets. **Phase 1 - Problem Modeling (25 minutes):** Teams analyze the scenario and identify variables: x₁, x₂, x₃ (supplies from each depot), and constraints (budget=$500,000, fuel=10,000 gallons, time≤48 hours). Students must formulate the objective function to minimize total cost C(x₁,x₂,x₃) = 15x₁ + 22x₂ + 18x₃ subject to given constraints. **Phase 2 - Mathematical Solution (35 minutes):** Teams apply Lagrange multiplier method: ∇f = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ + λ₃∇g₃. Students must show all partial derivatives, solve the system of equations, and verify solutions satisfy KKT conditions. **Phase 3 - Verification and Analysis (25 minutes):** Teams use graphing software to visualize the constraint region and verify their analytical solution. They must check boundary conditions and confirm their solution is indeed a minimum. **Phase 4 - Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents their optimal allocation plan, showing mathematical work, explaining why their solution minimizes costs while meeting all constraints, and discussing the practical implications of their mathematical decisions.
materials_needed: Emergency Response Scenario packets with maps and data tables
Graphing calculators or computer access to Desmos/GeoGebra
Constraint worksheets with pre-formatted equation templates
Large poster paper for final presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem setup and constraint identification (25 points), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier method with complete mathematical work (35 points), (3) Verification of solution using graphical methods and boundary analysis (25 points), (4) Clear presentation explaining mathematical reasoning and real-world implications (15 points). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint equations and step-by-step Lagrange multiplier templates. Offer guided practice with simpler 2-variable problems first. For advanced learners: Add additional constraints (vehicle capacity limits, driver availability) requiring integer programming concepts. Challenge them to consider sensitivity analysis - how solutions change with small constraint modifications.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in Multi-Stage Projectile Motion with Air Resistance
description: Students will analyze the complex energy transformations occurring during projectile motion through varying atmospheric densities, breaking down how mechanical energy converts between kinetic, potential, and thermal forms. They will examine real trajectory data to identify inefficiencies and predict optimal launch parameters for maximum range.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between air density, drag forces, and energy dissipation by comparing theoretical parabolic trajectories with actual projectile paths through computational modeling
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different launch angles and velocities through systematic decomposition of energy transformation rates at multiple trajectory points
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with trajectory data sets from projectile launches at different altitudes (sea level, 3000m, 6000m elevation). Each data set contains position coordinates, velocities, and timestamps at 0.1-second intervals for a 2kg projectile launched at 45° with initial velocity of 50 m/s. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams calculate kinetic energy, potential energy, and total mechanical energy at each data point using provided spreadsheet templates. Students must show calculations for the first three points manually before using formulas.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Using Python or Excel, teams create energy vs. time graphs for all three altitude scenarios. They must identify where energy losses occur and calculate the rate of energy dissipation (dE/dt) at five specific trajectory points: launch, 25% peak height, peak height, 75% descent, and impact.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams analyze drag coefficient variations by comparing actual energy losses to theoretical calculations using drag equations. They must determine how air density affects energy transformation efficiency and create a comparative analysis chart showing energy loss percentages.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Using their analysis, teams predict optimal launch parameters for maximum range at each altitude, justifying their predictions with energy transformation data. They must present their findings using energy diagrams showing the breakdown of energy at critical trajectory points.

Conclude with teams presenting their analysis to the class, focusing on how atmospheric conditions affect energy transformation patterns and projectile efficiency.
materials_needed: Three trajectory data sets (CSV files with position, velocity, time data)
Computers with Excel or Python/Jupyter notebooks
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for energy diagrams
Air density reference charts
Drag coefficient formula reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of energy calculations and graphs (25%), (2) Depth of drag force analysis and identification of energy loss patterns (30%), (3) Quality of predictions with supporting energy transformation evidence (25%), (4) Clarity of energy diagrams and presentation of findings (20%). Teams must submit spreadsheet calculations, comparative analysis charts, and written justifications for optimal launch parameters.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed sample calculations for the first two data points and pre-formatted graph templates. Offer guiding questions like 'Where do you see the steepest energy loss?' Advanced learners can investigate additional factors like projectile rotation effects or analyze trajectories with varying projectile masses and shapes to determine how object characteristics affect energy transformation patterns.

title: Bug Report Evaluation and Priority Assessment Challenge
description: Students will critically evaluate authentic bug reports from a fictional e-commerce website to determine their validity, severity, and development priority. They will justify their assessments by analyzing user impact, technical feasibility, and business value to make informed triage decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the credibility and completeness of bug reports by analyzing reproduction steps, error descriptions, and supporting evidence
Students will critique and rank bug priorities through systematic assessment of user impact, technical severity, and business consequences
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet containing 8 realistic bug reports for 'ShopEasy' e-commerce site (15 minutes setup). Each report includes: title, description, steps to reproduce, expected vs actual behavior, screenshots, user environment, and reporter credentials. 

Students work individually for 45 minutes to complete three evaluation phases: Phase 1 - Validity Assessment (15 minutes): Students mark each report as 'Valid Bug,' 'Invalid/User Error,' or 'Needs More Information,' providing 2-3 sentence justifications citing specific evidence from reports. Phase 2 - Severity Classification (15 minutes): For valid bugs only, students assign severity levels (Critical, High, Medium, Low) using provided criteria matrix considering factors like data loss risk, feature functionality, and user workflow impact. Phase 3 - Priority Ranking (15 minutes): Students create a numbered priority list of all valid bugs, writing brief explanations for their top 3 and bottom 3 choices.

Conduct 20-minute peer review sessions where students compare assessments in pairs, discussing discrepancies and refining their reasoning. Facilitate 15-minute whole-class discussion where volunteers present their most controversial decisions, defending their evaluations against peer challenges. Conclude with 5-minute reflection where students identify the most difficult evaluation decision and explain what additional information would have helped their assessment process.
materials_needed: Bug Report Evaluation Worksheet with 8 sample reports
Severity Classification Criteria Matrix handout
Priority Ranking Template sheet
Computers or tablets for digital worksheet access (optional)
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Validity justifications demonstrate logical reasoning with specific evidence citations, (2) Severity assignments align with provided criteria and show understanding of user impact, (3) Priority rankings reflect balanced consideration of multiple factors with clear explanations, (4) Peer discussion contributions show ability to defend decisions and incorporate feedback constructively. Students must achieve satisfactory ratings in all four areas.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a completed example for the first bug report and offering guiding questions like 'What would happen if this bug affected 1000 users?' For advanced learners, add complexity by including duplicate reports requiring identification of redundancies, or provide additional context about upcoming product releases that might influence priority decisions.

title: PMI-PMP Critical Path Method Terminology Mastery Challenge
description: Students will demonstrate precise recall of 50 advanced Critical Path Method (CPM) terms, definitions, and calculation formulas through a progressive elimination challenge. This activity focuses on memorizing complex project scheduling terminology essential for PMP certification and advanced project management practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific CPM terminology including Early Start (ES), Late Start (LS), Early Finish (EF), Late Finish (LF), Total Float, and Free Float by matching terms to exact definitions within 3 seconds per item
Students will recite from memory the precise mathematical formulas for forward pass, backward pass, and float calculations through rapid-fire verbal assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM terminology reference sheet containing 50 terms with definitions and formulas. Allow students 20 minutes to study and memorize content using any preferred method (flashcards, repetition, mnemonics). Create teams of 4 students each. Round 1 (15 minutes): Display term on screen for 3 seconds. Teams write definition on whiteboards simultaneously. Award 1 point for exact matches to reference definitions. Eliminate teams scoring below 70% after 20 questions. Round 2 (10 minutes): Surviving teams face formula recall. Instructor states scenario: 'Activity A has duration 5 days, ES=3.' Teams must write complete formula and calculate EF within 30 seconds. Award 2 points per correct formula and calculation. Round 3 (10 minutes): Individual lightning round for remaining team members. Instructor rapidly calls out terms; students must provide exact definitions within 5 seconds. Students eliminated after two incorrect responses. Final phase (5 minutes): Last 3 students face complex scenario requiring recall of multiple interconnected formulas. Present network diagram with 6 activities; students must recite step-by-step CPM calculation process including all formula components. Winner demonstrates perfect recall of terminology, definitions, and mathematical relationships without reference materials.
materials_needed: CPM terminology reference sheet with 50 advanced terms and definitions
Mathematical formulas handout for ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF calculations
Individual whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each team
Digital timer for precise time management
Sample network diagrams for final challenge scenarios
PowerPoint presentation with terms displayed for 3-second intervals
assessment_method: Award points using precise rubric: Round 1 - 1 point per exact definition match (70% minimum to advance); Round 2 - 2 points for correct formula + accurate calculation (80% minimum); Round 3 - Individual elimination based on 5-second response time and accuracy; Final assessment through comprehensive scenario requiring perfect recall of 6+ interconnected formulas and terminology without reference materials
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing acronym memory devices (SELF for Start-Early, Start-Late, Finish-Early, Finish-Late) and color-coded formula cards during study period. For advanced learners, introduce resource-constrained scheduling terminology and precedence diagramming method variations. Allow peer tutoring during initial study phase and provide additional complex network scenarios for extended practice.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership Frameworks Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis
description: Students will analyze the 2008 financial crisis leadership decisions through three distinct theoretical frameworks (transformational, authentic, and adaptive leadership) to demonstrate comprehensive understanding of how different leadership models interpret and respond to the same crisis scenario. This expert-level activity requires students to differentiate between competing leadership theories and explain their underlying assumptions about effective crisis management.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, authentic, and adaptive leadership frameworks by analyzing specific leader behaviors during the 2008 financial crisis through each theoretical lens
Students will explain the fundamental assumptions and decision-making processes of each leadership model through comparative analysis of crisis response strategies
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 6, then subdivide each group into three pairs. Distribute the comprehensive case study packet containing documented decisions, communications, and outcomes from leaders including Ben Bernanke (Federal Reserve), Timothy Geithner (Treasury), and Jamie Dimon (JPMorgan Chase) during September-December 2008. Assign each pair within a group one leadership framework: transformational (focusing on inspirational motivation and intellectual stimulation), authentic (emphasizing self-awareness and moral perspective), or adaptive (concentrating on adaptive challenges and learning). Give pairs 45 minutes to analyze their assigned leaders' actions exclusively through their framework lens, identifying specific behaviors, decisions, and communications that exemplify their theory. They must document at least 8 concrete examples with timestamps and explain how each demonstrates their framework's core principles. After individual analysis, reunite groups of 6 for 30-minute structured discussions where each pair presents their findings using the provided comparison template. Groups must identify overlaps, contradictions, and gaps between frameworks when analyzing identical leadership moments. Finally, conduct 20-minute cross-group presentations where one group presents their multi-framework analysis while others provide feedback using the evaluation criteria sheet, focusing on accuracy of framework application and depth of comparative insights.
materials_needed: Comprehensive 2008 financial crisis case study packet (15 pages with timeline and leader profiles)
Leadership framework reference sheets for transformational, authentic, and adaptive theories
Structured comparison template with analysis prompts
Evaluation criteria sheets for peer feedback
Flipchart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Framework accuracy - correct identification and application of each theory's core principles (25%), (2) Evidence quality - specific, relevant examples with clear connections to theoretical concepts (25%), (3) Comparative analysis - identification of meaningful similarities, differences, and contradictions between frameworks (25%), (4) Synthesis demonstration - clear articulation of how different frameworks lead to different interpretations of identical leadership situations (25%). Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted case study sections that clearly demonstrate each framework and offering sentence starters for analysis statements. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by requiring them to identify limitations of each framework and propose hybrid approaches that combine elements from multiple theories. Provide leadership theory quick-reference cards for students unfamiliar with framework terminology.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for Multi-Project Portfolio
description: Students will analyze three interconnected project scenarios to identify risk interdependencies and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will deconstruct complex risk situations to determine optimal resource allocation and timeline adjustments across the portfolio.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk interdependencies between multiple projects by examining cause-and-effect relationships and identifying cascade failure points
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of risk response strategies through systematic comparison of cost-benefit ratios and resource allocation impacts
instructions:
Begin by organizing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute the Portfolio Risk Scenario packet containing three interconnected construction projects: a hospital expansion, adjacent parking structure, and utility relocation project. Each project has 5-7 identified risks with proposed response strategies and budget allocations. 

Step 1 (25 minutes): Teams examine each project individually, creating risk breakdown structures and identifying primary vs. secondary risks using the provided risk register templates. Students must categorize each risk by PMBOK knowledge area and determine probability/impact ratings.

Step 2 (35 minutes): Teams map risk interdependencies across all three projects using the relationship matrix worksheet. They must identify at least 6 cross-project risk connections and analyze how risks in one project trigger or amplify risks in others. Teams document their findings using the provided interdependency mapping template.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams evaluate the proposed risk response strategies for effectiveness by calculating risk exposure reduction, analyzing resource conflicts between competing strategies, and identifying gaps in the current approach. They must use the cost-benefit analysis template to compare alternative strategies.

Step 4 (25 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation recommending strategy modifications, including specific budget reallocations and timeline adjustments. Each team presents their analysis to the class, defending their recommendations with quantitative evidence from their worksheets.
materials_needed: Portfolio Risk Scenario packet (3 project descriptions with risk registers)
Risk interdependency mapping templates (relationship matrix worksheets)
Cost-benefit analysis calculation templates with formulas
Flip chart paper and colored markers for presentations
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk interdependency identification (25 points - must identify minimum 6 valid connections), (2) Quality of cost-benefit calculations (25 points - correct formulas and realistic assumptions), (3) Logical reasoning in strategy evaluation (25 points - evidence-based recommendations), (4) Presentation clarity and defense of recommendations (25 points - clear communication with quantitative support). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed interdependency matrices and guide them through the first cost-benefit calculation as an example. Offer risk categorization reference sheets with PMBOK knowledge areas. For advanced learners: Add a fourth project to increase complexity, require Monte Carlo simulation analysis, or ask them to develop contingency plans for their top 3 recommended strategies.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Dataset Analysis
description: Students will analyze a real-world dataset containing variables with strong correlations to distinguish between correlation and causation relationships. They will examine ice cream sales and drowning incidents data to understand why correlation does not imply causation and identify confounding variables.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between correlation and causation by analyzing correlation coefficients and identifying confounding variables in a real dataset
Students will interpret statistical relationships through guided examination of scatterplots, correlation matrices, and temporal data patterns
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'Summer Safety Dataset' containing monthly data for ice cream sales, drowning incidents, temperature, and pool attendance across 24 months (15 minutes setup). Have students work in pairs to first calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between ice cream sales and drowning incidents using Excel or Google Sheets CORREL function (10 minutes). Students should discover a strong positive correlation (r ≈ 0.85). Next, instruct pairs to create a scatterplot of these two variables and discuss what they observe (10 minutes). Facilitate a brief whole-class discussion where students share their correlation findings and initial interpretations (5 minutes). Then provide guided questions: 'Does this mean ice cream causes drowning?' and 'What other factors might explain this relationship?' (5 minutes). Have students examine the temperature variable by creating additional scatterplots showing temperature vs. ice cream sales and temperature vs. drowning incidents (15 minutes). Students should calculate these correlations and note that temperature correlates strongly with both variables. Conclude with pairs completing a structured worksheet where they identify temperature as the confounding variable, explain the true causal relationships (temperature → increased swimming → more drownings; temperature → higher ice cream demand), and provide one additional example of correlation without causation from their own experience (10 minutes). End with a gallery walk where pairs post their explanations and examples (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Summer Safety Dataset (CSV file with 24 months of ice cream sales, drowning incidents, temperature, and pool attendance data)
Excel or Google Sheets access for each student pair
Correlation vs. Causation Analysis Worksheet
Chart paper and markers for gallery walk
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies confounding variable, accurately explains all causal relationships, provides relevant personal example; (3) Identifies confounding variable, explains most relationships correctly; (2) Shows partial understanding of correlation vs. causation concept; (1) Demonstrates minimal understanding. Also observe pair discussions for evidence of reasoning about statistical relationships.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed correlation matrix and guide them through the first scatterplot creation step-by-step. Offer sentence stems like 'The real cause of both variables is...' For advanced learners, challenge them to research and analyze a more complex dataset with multiple potential confounding variables, or have them explore partial correlations to control for the confounding variable mathematically.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Dataset Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze pre-selected datasets with known correlation patterns to distinguish between correlation and causation scenarios. They will explain the underlying factors that create spurious correlations and identify confounding variables that affect data interpretation.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing three distinct real-world datasets and explaining the underlying mechanisms
Students will identify confounding variables and spurious correlations through guided dataset exploration and peer discussion
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and providing each group with three datasets: (1) ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths by month, (2) number of firefighters vs. fire damage costs, and (3) hours of TV watching vs. life expectancy by country. Give groups 15 minutes to calculate correlation coefficients using provided spreadsheet templates with pre-built formulas. Next, have each group create scatter plots for all three datasets and identify which show positive, negative, or no correlation (10 minutes). Then conduct a 20-minute guided analysis where groups discuss each dataset: For dataset 1, guide them to identify temperature/season as the confounding variable. For dataset 2, help them recognize that fire severity determines both variables. For dataset 3, introduce economic development as a lurking variable. Have groups complete a structured worksheet asking: 'What is the correlation coefficient?', 'Does correlation imply causation here?', 'What other variables might explain this relationship?', and 'Can you think of a plausible causal mechanism?' Conclude with a 15-minute gallery walk where each group presents one dataset analysis to the class, explaining why the correlation does or does not indicate causation. During presentations, encourage other groups to ask clarifying questions about alternative explanations.
materials_needed: Three pre-loaded Excel/Google Sheets files with correlation datasets
Printed analysis worksheets with guided questions
Calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
Chart paper and markers for presentations
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strength AND causation status AND explains confounding variables with specific examples; (3) Correctly identifies correlation and causation with minor explanation gaps; (2) Identifies correlation but struggles with causation reasoning; (1) Shows minimal understanding of correlation-causation distinction. Also assess verbal explanations during presentations for clarity and use of appropriate terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'The correlation is ___ but causation is unlikely because ___' and offer additional examples of obvious non-causal correlations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to research and propose statistical methods to test for causation (like controlled experiments or instrumental variables) and find additional examples of spurious correlations in their field of interest.
original_title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real Dataset Analysis

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Arrays Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel installation constraints. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use graphical and algebraic methods to determine optimal solutions for maximizing energy output within budget and space limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-constraint optimization problem by translating real-world solar energy scenarios into mathematical models
Students will implement graphical and simplex methods to determine optimal resource allocation through systematic analysis of feasible regions and corner point evaluation
instructions:
Begin by distributing the scenario packets containing three different property layouts with varying constraints (45 minutes total setup and individual work). Each student receives a property diagram showing available roof space, shading patterns, and budget limitations. Students must determine the optimal mix of two solar panel types: Type A (200W, $300, 2m²) and Type B (350W, $500, 3.5m²). 

Step 1 (10 minutes): Students identify decision variables (x = number of Type A panels, y = number of Type B panels) and formulate the objective function to maximize total wattage: P = 200x + 350y. 

Step 2 (15 minutes): Students translate given constraints into linear inequalities. For example: Budget constraint (300x + 500y ≤ 15000), space constraint (2x + 3.5y ≤ 80), and non-negativity constraints (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0). 

Step 3 (10 minutes): Using graph paper, students plot constraint lines and identify the feasible region by shading the area satisfying all constraints simultaneously. 

Step 4 (10 minutes): Students locate corner points of the feasible region through intersection calculations and evaluate the objective function at each vertex to determine the optimal solution. They must show all algebraic work for intersection points and objective function evaluations, then verify their graphical solution using the corner point theorem.
materials_needed: Property scenario packets with floor plans and constraint data (3 different scenarios)
Graph paper with 1cm grid squares
Scientific calculators
Colored pencils for constraint line identification
Linear programming solution verification worksheet
assessment_method: Students submit completed optimization worksheets showing: (1) Correct mathematical formulation (25 points), (2) Accurate graphical representation with properly labeled axes and constraints (25 points), (3) Precise corner point calculations with algebraic work shown (25 points), and (4) Correct identification and justification of optimal solution including units and real-world interpretation (25 points). Partial credit awarded for systematic approaches even with computational errors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-drawn coordinate axes and constraint equation templates. Offer step-by-step checkpoint sheets breaking down the graphing process. For advanced learners, introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how the optimal solution changes with ±10% variations in panel costs or a third panel type with different specifications. Provide extension problems involving integer programming constraints.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in a Multi-Stage Pendulum-Spring System
description: Students will decompose the complex motion of a compound pendulum-spring system into distinct phases and analyze how gravitational potential, kinetic, and elastic potential energies transform throughout the complete oscillation cycle. They will identify energy dissipation mechanisms and quantify the efficiency of energy transfer between different forms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the energy transformation patterns in a compound pendulum-spring system by creating detailed energy-time graphs for each phase of motion
Students will examine the relationship between theoretical and experimental energy values through systematic data collection and mathematical modeling
instructions: Begin by setting up the compound pendulum system: attach a 500g mass to a 0.8m string, then connect a spring (k=50 N/m) between the mass and a fixed point 0.3m below the pivot. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Phase 1 (15 min): Teams predict and sketch expected energy transformations on provided templates, identifying critical transition points where one energy form dominates. Phase 2 (25 min): Using high-speed cameras or motion sensors, teams record 10 complete oscillation cycles, measuring position, velocity, and spring compression at 0.1-second intervals. Phase 3 (30 min): Students calculate gravitational PE (mgh), kinetic energy (½mv²), and elastic PE (½kx²) for each data point, creating three separate energy-time graphs using graphing software. Phase 4 (20 min): Teams analyze their graphs to identify: (a) points of maximum/minimum for each energy type, (b) phase relationships between energy transformations, (c) total energy changes indicating dissipation, and (d) coupling effects between pendulum and spring motions. Phase 5 (15 min): Compare experimental results with theoretical predictions, calculating percentage differences and identifying systematic versus random errors. Teams present one key insight about energy coupling or dissipation patterns discovered through their analysis.
materials_needed: Compound pendulum apparatus (string, 500g mass, spring with k=50 N/m, mounting hardware)
High-speed camera or motion sensor system
Digital scale and measuring tape
Graphing software (Logger Pro, Excel, or Python)
Energy transformation analysis worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of energy calculations and graph construction (25%), (2) Quality of phase-by-phase energy analysis identifying transition points (30%), (3) Depth of comparison between theoretical and experimental results with error analysis (25%), (4) Clarity of conclusions about energy coupling mechanisms and dissipation sources (20%). Students must submit graphs, calculations, and a 2-page analysis report.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated templates with partially completed energy equations and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer simplified systems (pendulum-only first) before adding spring complexity. For advanced learners, introduce damping coefficients, analyze frequency coupling between pendulum and spring modes, or investigate non-linear effects at large amplitudes using Lagrangian mechanics.

title: Code Review Challenge: Evaluating Buggy Login Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate three different Python login function implementations that contain various bugs and security issues. They will rank the functions from best to worst, justify their rankings, and provide specific improvement recommendations for each implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and security of Python login functions by analyzing code structure, identifying bugs, and assessing security vulnerabilities
Students will justify their code quality rankings through written explanations that demonstrate understanding of best practices in authentication systems
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the handout containing three Python login functions labeled A, B, and C. Each function has different issues: Function A has logic errors and poor variable naming, Function B has security vulnerabilities like plain-text password storage, and Function C has syntax errors and missing error handling. Provide students with the evaluation criteria checklist covering functionality, security, readability, and error handling.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine each function independently, testing them mentally or on paper against sample inputs. They identify specific problems, rate each function on a 1-5 scale across the four criteria, and take detailed notes on their findings.

**Ranking and Justification (15 minutes):** Students rank the three functions from best (1) to worst (3) overall quality. They write a 2-3 sentence justification for each ranking, citing specific code examples and explaining how identified issues impact the function's effectiveness.

**Improvement Recommendations (15 minutes):** For each function, students write 2-3 specific, actionable recommendations for improvement. These must be concrete changes (e.g., 'Hash passwords using bcrypt library' rather than 'improve security').

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare rankings and justifications. They must defend their evaluations and identify any overlooked issues in their partner's analysis.

**Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion of rankings, common issues identified, and best practices for login function implementation.
materials_needed: Handout with three buggy Python login functions (A, B, C)
Code evaluation criteria checklist
Ranking and justification worksheet
Pen/pencil for written analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies all major issues, provides clear ranking justification with specific examples, offers actionable improvements; (3) Identifies most issues, adequate justification with some examples; (2) Identifies some issues, basic justification; (1) Minimal issue identification, weak or missing justification. Students must achieve level 3 or higher on all three functions to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a 'bug hunting checklist' with specific questions like 'Does the function handle empty inputs?' and 'Are passwords stored securely?' For advanced learners: Add a bonus task to rewrite the worst function with proper implementation, or analyze additional security considerations like rate limiting and session management.

title: Design and Build a Customer Segmentation Dashboard for E-commerce Analytics
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary). They will design the analytical framework, process raw transaction data, and build visualizations that provide actionable business insights.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a complete RFM segmentation model by analyzing customer transaction patterns and creating meaningful behavioral categories
Students will design an interactive dashboard through combining multiple visualization techniques that communicate customer insights to business stakeholders
instructions:
**Setup (15 minutes):** Provide each student with a CSV dataset containing 6 months of e-commerce transactions (customer_id, purchase_date, order_value, product_category). Students work individually using Excel/Google Sheets or Tableau/Power BI.

**Phase 1 - Data Preparation (45 minutes):** Students clean the dataset by removing duplicates, handling missing values, and creating calculated fields for days since last purchase, total purchase frequency, and total monetary value per customer. They must document their data cleaning decisions in a separate sheet.

**Phase 2 - RFM Analysis Creation (60 minutes):** Students calculate RFM scores by creating quintile rankings (1-5 scale) for each dimension. They then combine scores to create customer segments (e.g., Champions: 5-5-5, At-Risk: 2-2-3). Students must create at least 8 distinct segments with business-relevant names.

**Phase 3 - Dashboard Construction (90 minutes):** Students design a 4-panel dashboard including: (1) segment distribution pie chart, (2) RFM score scatter plots with color-coding, (3) revenue contribution by segment bar chart, and (4) customer lifecycle stage funnel. Each visualization must include interactive filters for date ranges and product categories.

**Phase 4 - Business Recommendations (30 minutes):** Students write a 500-word executive summary identifying the top 3 customer segments, explaining their characteristics, and proposing specific marketing strategies for each segment. They must justify recommendations using dashboard insights.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV with 10,000+ records)
Excel/Google Sheets or Tableau/Power BI software access
RFM analysis template worksheet
Dashboard design requirements checklist
Executive summary template document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data preparation and RFM calculations (25 points), Dashboard design and functionality (35 points), Visual clarity and professional presentation (20 points), Business insights and actionable recommendations (20 points). Students must submit their working dashboard file plus executive summary. Success requires accurate segmentation logic, functional interactivity, and data-driven business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM formulas and dashboard templates with placeholder charts. Offer guided practice with a smaller sample dataset first. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables (geographic data, seasonal trends), create predictive elements (customer lifetime value), or build automated refresh capabilities for real-time data updates.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: A Multi-Framework Analysis Activity
description: Students analyze complex leadership paradoxes through the lens of three different leadership theories to demonstrate deep understanding of how theoretical frameworks shape interpretation of leadership challenges. This expert-level activity requires students to synthesize knowledge across multiple leadership models and explain how each framework reveals different aspects of the same leadership dilemma.
learning_objectives: Students will explain how transformational, situational, and authentic leadership theories interpret the same leadership paradox by creating detailed comparative analyses
Students will demonstrate understanding of theoretical frameworks' core principles through systematic application to complex, real-world leadership scenarios
instructions: Begin by presenting students with three pre-selected leadership paradoxes: 1) A CEO who must simultaneously cut costs and invest in innovation, 2) A military commander balancing mission success with soldier welfare, and 3) A nonprofit director choosing between organizational growth and mission purity. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Each group selects one paradox and receives three theory reference sheets: Transformational Leadership (Bass & Riggio), Situational Leadership (Hersey-Blanchard), and Authentic Leadership (George & Sims). Groups spend 45 minutes analyzing their chosen paradox through each theoretical lens, documenting: what each theory identifies as the core challenge, what leadership behaviors each theory would recommend, what outcomes each theory would prioritize, and where the theories align or conflict. Students create a structured comparison matrix with these four dimensions as rows and the three theories as columns. Next, groups prepare 8-minute presentations explaining their paradox and demonstrating how each theory 'sees' the situation differently (30 minutes preparation). During presentations (24 minutes total), listening groups complete reflection sheets identifying which theoretical interpretation they found most compelling and why. Conclude with 15-minute debrief where instructor highlights patterns across presentations and addresses misconceptions about theory application.
materials_needed: Three leadership paradox scenario handouts (one page each)
Theory reference sheets for Bass & Riggio Transformational Leadership model
Theory reference sheets for Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model
Theory reference sheets for George & Sims Authentic Leadership model
Comparison matrix templates (printed worksheets)
Presentation reflection sheets for audience members
Timer for managing presentation segments
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using 4-point rubric assessing: accuracy of theory application (25%), depth of analysis showing understanding of theoretical nuances (25%), quality of comparisons identifying meaningful similarities/differences (25%), and clarity of explanations demonstrating comprehension (25%). Additionally assess presentation delivery for coherent explanation of how each theory interprets the paradox differently.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide sentence starters like 'Transformational leadership theory would view this challenge as...' and 'The key difference between these approaches is...' For advanced learners, add a synthesis requirement asking them to propose a hybrid approach combining insights from all three theories, or challenge them to identify limitations each theory has when applied to their paradox.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Strategic Recommendation Report
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real Google Analytics 4 data from an e-commerce website. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the relative effectiveness of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating ROI variance across marketing channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and defend alternative approaches using statistical evidence
instructions: Begin by providing students access to a GA4 property with at least 6 months of e-commerce data containing multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct). Students work in pairs for 20 minutes to extract attribution reports for the same date range using each of the five models available in GA4's Attribution section. Next, students spend 30 minutes calculating the attribution percentage difference for each channel across models, identifying which channels gain or lose credit most dramatically. In the following 40 minutes, students must research the business context: average customer lifetime value, typical sales cycles, and campaign costs from provided budget sheets. They then spend 45 minutes creating a comparative analysis matrix showing how each attribution model would influence budget allocation decisions, calculating potential ROI changes if budgets shifted by 20% based on each model's insights. Students conclude by spending 35 minutes writing a strategic recommendation memo (500 words) that evaluates all five models, identifies the optimal model for this specific business scenario, and provides three specific budget reallocation recommendations with projected impact calculations. The final 10 minutes involves peer review using the provided evaluation checklist.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Marketing budget spreadsheet with channel costs and performance metrics
Attribution model comparison template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Strategic recommendation memo template
Peer evaluation checklist with scoring criteria
assessment_method: Students submit a strategic memo evaluated on four criteria using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of attribution data extraction and calculations (25%), (2) Depth of comparative analysis between models with specific examples (30%), (3) Quality of business justification for recommended model selection (30%), and (4) Feasibility and specificity of budget reallocation recommendations with ROI projections (15%). Passing requires scoring 3+ on all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated attribution percentages and focus evaluation on interpretation rather than calculation. Offer guiding questions like 'Which channels benefit most from last-click attribution and why?' Advanced learners should incorporate seasonality analysis and create custom attribution models using GA4's conversion paths report, then evaluate their custom model against the five standard options.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real Customer Data: Identifying Patterns and Business Implications
description: Students will analyze three different statistical distributions found in an e-commerce customer dataset to understand their characteristics and business meanings. They will interpret histograms, calculate key statistics, and explain what each distribution pattern reveals about customer behavior.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the shape, central tendency, and variability of normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing customer purchase data visualizations
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution patterns through structured comparison of customer spending, session duration, and purchase frequency data
instructions: Begin by distributing the provided dataset containing 1000 customer records with three variables: purchase_amount (normal distribution), session_duration (right-skewed), and days_between_purchases (bimodal). Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. Step 1 (10 min): Each pair generates histograms for all three variables using provided Python code templates, adjusting bin sizes to clearly show distribution shapes. Step 2 (15 min): Students calculate and record mean, median, mode, standard deviation, and range for each variable using the statistics summary sheet.
