They must identify which measures of central tendency are most appropriate for each distribution type. Step 3 (15 min): Using the interpretation guide, pairs analyze each histogram to classify distribution shapes (normal, right-skewed, bimodal) and identify key characteristics like outliers, peaks, and symmetry. Step 4 (5 min): Students complete the business interpretation worksheet, explaining what each distribution pattern suggests about customer segments and behavior patterns. For example, bimodal purchase frequency might indicate distinct customer types (frequent vs. occasional buyers). Instructor circulates to check progress and provide hints using the scaffolding question prompts. Final step involves pairs sharing one key insight with the class during a 10-minute discussion where instructor connects findings to real-world data science applications in customer analytics and business decision-making.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV file with 1000 records)
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and numpy installed
Pre-written Python code templates for generating histograms
Statistics summary recording sheet (printed handout)
Distribution interpretation guide with visual examples
Business implications worksheet
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct identification of all three distribution types, (2) Accurate calculation of descriptive statistics with appropriate measures highlighted, (3) Clear explanation of distribution characteristics using proper statistical vocabulary, (4) Logical connection between distribution patterns and business insights. Students must achieve at least 3/4 points on each criterion. Collect completed worksheets and review histogram outputs for technical accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions like 'Where is the peak located?' and 'Are the tails equal length?' Offer pre-calculated statistics to focus on interpretation rather than computation. For advanced learners, include additional variables (customer_age, product_categories) and ask them to hypothesize reasons for observed patterns or suggest follow-up analyses. Provide optional extension activity connecting distributions to appropriate statistical tests.

title: Optimization of Manufacturing Container Design Using Calculus
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem by designing a cylindrical container that minimizes material costs while meeting volume constraints. They will use derivatives, Lagrange multipliers, and constraint optimization to find the optimal dimensions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to minimize surface area given volume constraints by setting up and solving the Lagrangian system
Students will demonstrate understanding of constraint optimization through systematic problem-solving of a manufacturing cost scenario
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario: 'TechCorp needs cylindrical containers holding exactly 500 cubic inches, minimizing aluminum usage.' Form teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). Each team receives constraint sheets showing volume V = πr²h = 500 and surface area S = 2πr² + 2πrh. Students first identify variables (r = radius, h = height) and write the objective function to minimize surface area (15 minutes). Next, teams solve for h in terms of r using the volume constraint: h = 500/(πr²), then substitute into surface area equation to get S(r) = 2πr² + 1000/r (20 minutes). Students then find the critical points by taking the derivative S'(r) = 4πr - 1000/r² and setting equal to zero (15 minutes). Teams solve 4πr³ = 1000 to find r = ∛(250/π) ≈ 4.31 inches, then calculate corresponding height h ≈ 8.62 inches (15 minutes). Students verify this is a minimum using the second derivative test: S''(r) = 4π + 2000/r³ > 0 (10 minutes). Finally, teams calculate the minimum surface area and create a brief presentation showing their mathematical work and explaining why this solution minimizes material costs (25 minutes). Conclude with team presentations (2-3 minutes each) where students justify their optimization approach and discuss real-world applications.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Printed scenario sheets with company background and specifications
Constraint reference cards showing volume and surface area formulas
Graph paper for sketching functions
Whiteboard markers and presentation boards for team solutions
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct setup of constraint equation and objective function (25%), (2) Accurate calculus procedures including derivatives and critical point identification (35%), (3) Verification of minimum using second derivative test (25%), (4) Clear mathematical communication in presentation with real-world interpretation (15%). Students must show complete mathematical work and explain each optimization step.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint equations and guide through first derivative step-by-step. Offer formula sheets with common optimization patterns. For advanced learners: Extend to compare cylindrical vs. rectangular container efficiency, or add material thickness considerations requiring more complex constraints. Challenge them to optimize for shipping efficiency by adding transportation cost factors.

title: Customer Segmentation Dashboard Creation from E-commerce Transaction Data
description: Students will design and build an interactive dashboard that segments customers based on purchasing behavior using real e-commerce transaction data. They will synthesize multiple analytical techniques to create actionable business insights and present recommendations through data visualization.
learning_objectives: Students will create a comprehensive customer segmentation model by combining RFM analysis (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) with clustering algorithms using transaction data
Students will design an interactive dashboard that synthesizes multiple data analysis techniques to generate actionable business recommendations for marketing strategy
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Preparation (20 minutes)**
Provide each team of 3-4 students with a CSV file containing 12 months of e-commerce transaction data (customer ID, purchase date, product category, purchase amount). Students clean the data by removing duplicates, handling missing values, and creating calculated fields for days since last purchase, total purchase frequency, and total monetary value per customer.

**Phase 2: Analysis Design (30 minutes)**
Teams develop their analytical framework by: (1) Creating RFM scores for each customer using quintile rankings, (2) Applying K-means clustering to identify 4-5 distinct customer segments, (3) Calculating key metrics for each segment including average order value, purchase frequency, and customer lifetime value estimates. Students document their methodology choices and rationale.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (40 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students build an interactive dashboard containing: (1) A scatter plot matrix showing RFM relationships with cluster color-coding, (2) Segment comparison charts displaying key metrics, (3) Interactive filters for time period and product category, (4) A summary table with segment characteristics and recommended marketing actions. Each visualization must include clear titles, labels, and business context.

**Phase 4: Business Recommendations (20 minutes)**
Teams create a one-page executive summary that names each customer segment (e.g., "Loyal Champions," "At-Risk Customers"), describes their characteristics, and provides specific, actionable marketing recommendations with expected outcomes. Students must justify recommendations using their data analysis findings.
materials_needed: E-commerce transaction dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI Desktop software
Excel or Google Sheets for initial data cleaning
Template executive summary document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Technical execution - correct RFM calculations and clustering implementation (25%), (2) Dashboard design - clear visualizations with appropriate interactivity (25%), (3) Business insight quality - logical segment naming and characteristics identification (25%), (4) Recommendation validity - specific, data-supported marketing actions with measurable outcomes (25%). Students submit dashboard files, methodology documentation, and executive summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated RFM scores and focus on visualization creation and interpretation. Offer template dashboard layouts and guided questions for business recommendations. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables (seasonality, product preferences), experiment with alternative clustering algorithms, or create predictive models for customer churn within segments. Provide access to larger datasets or multiple product categories for more complex analysis.

title: Project Management Knowledge Integration Framework (PMKIF) Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMBOK Guide's 49 project management processes across 10 knowledge areas and 5 process groups. This intensive recall activity requires students to demonstrate mastery of the intricate relationships between processes, their inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs without reference materials.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes with their corresponding knowledge area and process group classifications by completing timed verbal recitation exercises
Students will identify specific inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for each of the 10 integration management processes through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute preparation phase where students review their PMBOK process maps silently. Divide the class into groups of 4 students each. Assign each group one of the 10 knowledge areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder). Within each group, students rotate through four stations: Process Naming (5 minutes), Input Identification (7 minutes), Tools/Techniques Recall (7 minutes), and Output Enumeration (6 minutes). At the Process Naming station, one student calls out a knowledge area and process group intersection, and the partner must name all applicable processes. At Input Identification, students must list the primary inputs for each process in their assigned knowledge area without consulting materials. The Tools/Techniques station requires students to recall at least three specific tools or techniques for each process. At the Output Enumeration station, students must identify all outputs for each process, including documents, deliverables, and updates. After 25 minutes of station rotations, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire session where random students are called to identify processes based on specific scenarios (10 minutes). Conclude with a 5-minute individual written verification where each student lists all processes in their assigned knowledge area with complete ITTO (Inputs, Tools/Techniques, Outputs) information.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition process maps (one per student for prep only)
Station rotation timer or stopwatch
Knowledge area assignment cards
Blank ITTO worksheets for final verification
Scenario cards for rapid-fire session
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the final written ITTO verification sheet for their assigned knowledge area. Verbal participation during station rotations is assessed using a 3-point scale: 3=immediate accurate recall, 2=accurate recall with brief hesitation, 1=inaccurate or significantly delayed response. Rapid-fire scenario responses are marked as correct/incorrect with immediate feedback provided.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide mnemonic device handouts and allow them to focus on just the process names before adding ITTO details. Advanced learners should be challenged to explain the logical flow between processes and identify which outputs from one process serve as inputs to others. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during station rotations.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: Multi-Framework Analysis of Transformational vs. Transactional Approaches
description: Students will analyze complex leadership scenarios through multiple theoretical lenses to understand the paradoxical nature of effective leadership. They will compare and contrast transformational and transactional leadership frameworks while examining how context influences leadership effectiveness.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between transformational and transactional leadership behaviors by analyzing authentic case studies using Bass's Full Range Leadership Model
Students will explain the contextual factors that determine leadership effectiveness through systematic comparison of leadership approaches across different organizational scenarios
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5, assigning each group one of five pre-selected leadership scenarios: crisis management at Johnson & Johnson (Tylenol crisis), Steve Jobs' return to Apple, military leadership in Afghanistan, healthcare transformation during COVID-19, or educational leadership during remote learning transitions. Provide each group with their scenario packet containing detailed background information, stakeholder perspectives, and outcome data (15 minutes setup). Groups first individually read and annotate their scenarios using the provided analysis template, identifying specific leader behaviors and decisions (20 minutes). Next, groups collaboratively map identified behaviors onto Bass's Full Range Leadership Model grid, categorizing each behavior as transformational (idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration) or transactional (contingent reward, management-by-exception active/passive) or laissez-faire (25 minutes). Groups then analyze contextual factors using the Situational Leadership framework, examining follower readiness, task complexity, organizational culture, and external pressures (20 minutes). Each group creates a visual comparison matrix showing how the same leader demonstrated both transformational and transactional behaviors depending on context, noting apparent contradictions and explaining why both approaches were necessary (25 minutes). Groups present their 8-minute analysis to the class, highlighting three key paradoxes they discovered and explaining how context influenced leadership approach selection (40 minutes total presentations). Conclude with a whole-class discussion synthesizing patterns across all scenarios, focusing on when leaders successfully balanced competing demands and when they failed to adapt their approach (15 minutes).
materials_needed: Five detailed leadership scenario packets (15-20 pages each) with background, stakeholder interviews, timeline, and outcomes
Bass's Full Range Leadership Model reference sheets and behavior categorization templates
Large poster paper and colored markers for creating visual matrices
Digital presentation tools (laptops/tablets) for group presentations
Contextual analysis framework handouts with guiding questions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of behavior categorization using leadership frameworks (25%), (2) Quality of contextual analysis and identification of situational factors (25%), (3) Depth of paradox identification and explanation of competing demands (30%), (4) Clarity of presentation and synthesis of insights (20%). Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories, demonstrating clear understanding of how leadership approaches must adapt to context while maintaining consistency in core principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted scenario sections and sentence starters for analysis templates. Offer additional examples of transformational vs. transactional behaviors before group work begins. For advanced learners, include supplementary readings on authentic leadership and ethical decision-making frameworks, challenging them to identify instances where leaders faced moral dilemmas requiring paradoxical approaches. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who excel at visual presentation skills.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis and Optimization for Construction Project Delays
description: Students will analyze a construction project's risk register containing weather, supply chain, and regulatory risks to evaluate the effectiveness of current response strategies. They will decompose each risk response strategy, assess alignment with organizational constraints, and recommend optimizations based on cost-benefit analysis and risk interdependencies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of existing risk response strategies by examining their alignment with project constraints, budget limitations, and timeline requirements
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk response choices through systematic evaluation of risk probability, impact, and organizational risk tolerance
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Metro Bridge Construction Project case study packet containing a risk register with 8 identified risks and current response strategies (15 minutes setup). Divide students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Risk Analyst, Strategy Evaluator, Cost Analyst, and Timeline Coordinator. Each team receives the project parameters: $2.8M budget, 18-month timeline, and organizational risk tolerance matrix.

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze each risk entry, breaking down the current response strategy into its component parts. Students must identify whether each response follows avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept approaches, then map these against the project's triple constraint (scope, time, cost). Teams complete the Risk Response Analysis Worksheet, documenting their findings for each of the 8 risks.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Students evaluate strategy effectiveness by applying the provided decision criteria matrix. They must assess each response strategy against five factors: cost efficiency (weighted 25%), timeline impact (weighted 30%), resource availability (weighted 20%), stakeholder acceptance (weighted 15%), and implementation complexity (weighted 10%). Teams calculate weighted scores and identify the three lowest-performing strategies.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): For the three identified weak strategies, teams develop alternative approaches. Students must justify their recommendations using PMI risk management principles, considering risk interdependencies and secondary risks. Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation summarizing their analysis findings and strategic recommendations.

Conclude with team presentations (30 minutes total, 5 minutes per team plus Q&A), where other teams provide peer feedback using the provided evaluation criteria checklist.
materials_needed: Metro Bridge Construction Project case study packet with risk register
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet (Excel template)
Decision Criteria Matrix with weighted factors
Organizational Risk Tolerance Matrix handout
PMI Risk Response Strategy reference guide
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Evaluation criteria checklist for peer assessment
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Analysis Worksheets using a 4-point rubric: Accurate strategy categorization (25%), Thorough constraint analysis (25%), Justified effectiveness evaluation with weighted calculations (30%), and Quality of alternative recommendations with PMI alignment (20%). Presentations assessed on clarity of analysis rationale and peer feedback quality. Minimum passing score: 3.0/4.0 overall with no category below 2.5.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example analysis for the first risk entry, offer one-on-one consultation during Phase 2 calculations, and supply risk response strategy decision tree flowchart. For advanced learners: Add secondary risk analysis requirement, include Monte Carlo simulation consideration for quantitative risks, and challenge them to develop contingency response plans for their recommended strategies.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Impact Assessment and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the performance differences between Google Analytics' default Last Click attribution model and alternative attribution models (First Click, Linear, Time Decay, Position Based) using real e-commerce data. They will assess the strategic implications of each model and defend their recommendation for optimal attribution strategy based on business objectives and customer journey characteristics.
estimated_duration: 5 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution discrepancies across at least three different models
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comprehensive analysis of multi-channel funnel reports and justify strategic recommendations based on business context
instructions: Begin by providing students access to Google Analytics demo account or prepared dataset containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multi-channel conversion paths (30 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to navigate to Conversions > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. First, teams export conversion and revenue data for identical date ranges using Last Click, First Click, Linear, Time Decay, and Position Based models (45 minutes). Next, students create comparative analysis charts showing percentage differences in channel attribution across models, identifying which channels gain/lose credit under different models (60 minutes). Teams then examine Multi-Channel Funnel reports under Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Top Conversion Paths to understand typical customer journey patterns and path length distributions (45 minutes). Using this data, students must evaluate each attribution model's alignment with observed customer behavior patterns and business objectives. Teams prepare 15-minute presentations defending their recommended attribution strategy, addressing three critical evaluation criteria: accuracy in representing customer journey influence, alignment with marketing campaign objectives, and actionability for budget allocation decisions (90 minutes preparation). During presentations, teams must justify why their chosen model best serves the business while acknowledging limitations and potential biases. Conclude with peer evaluation where teams score each other's recommendations using provided rubric focusing on depth of analysis, evidence quality, and strategic reasoning (30 minutes).
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account access or prepared GA dataset with e-commerce tracking
Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis and visualization
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Attribution model evaluation rubric handout
Business context scenario document describing company objectives and marketing mix
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Technical Analysis - accurate data extraction and mathematical comparison of attribution models (25%), (2) Critical Evaluation - depth of analysis regarding model strengths/weaknesses and bias identification (30%), (3) Strategic Reasoning - quality of business justification and alignment with objectives (30%), (4) Defense and Critique - ability to respond to questions and evaluate peer recommendations (15%). Students submit data analysis spreadsheet, presentation slides, and peer evaluation forms.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-built data extraction templates and guided analysis worksheets with specific questions to answer. Offer attribution model comparison cheat sheet explaining when each model works best. For advanced learners: challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models or Data-Driven Attribution analysis, evaluate cross-device tracking implications, or propose A/B testing methodology for attribution model validation.

title: Analyzing Complex Circuit Failures Using Kirchhoff's Laws and Component Behavior
description: Students analyze a multi-loop circuit with deliberately introduced component failures to identify the faulty elements and predict system behavior. They must decompose the circuit systematically, apply Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws, and correlate theoretical predictions with measured data to isolate failure modes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex multi-loop circuits by systematically applying Kirchhoff's laws to identify inconsistencies between theoretical and measured values
Students will differentiate between various component failure modes through comparative analysis of voltage, current, and resistance measurements across multiple circuit nodes
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-built breadboard circuits (30 minutes setup time) containing 3-4 loops with resistors, capacitors, and one deliberately faulty component per circuit (open resistor, short circuit, or degraded capacitor). Students work in pairs and receive identical circuit diagrams but different failure scenarios. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students calculate theoretical voltage and current values at 8 designated test points using Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) and current law (KCL), assuming all components are functioning normally. They must show mesh current equations and nodal voltage calculations. Step 2 (20 minutes): Using digital multimeters, students measure actual voltage and current at each test point, recording values in a data comparison table alongside theoretical predictions. Step 3 (25 minutes): Students analyze discrepancies between theoretical and measured values, identifying which Kirchhoff law violations indicate specific failure types. They must examine: voltage drops that don't sum to zero around loops (KVL violations), current imbalances at nodes (KCL violations), and abnormal resistance readings. Step 4 (15 minutes): Students predict the exact component failure and its location, then verify by component replacement or isolation testing. Step 5 (10 minutes): Pairs present their analysis methodology and failure identification to another pair, explaining their reasoning process and mathematical verification steps.
materials_needed: Pre-built breadboard circuits with mixed components (resistors 100Ω-1kΩ, capacitors 10μF-100μF)
Digital multimeters with voltage, current, and resistance measurement capability
Circuit diagrams with 8 labeled test points and component values
Deliberately faulty components (open resistors, wire jumpers for shorts, degraded capacitors)
Data recording sheets with theoretical vs. measured value tables
assessment_method: Students submit analysis worksheets showing: (1) Complete Kirchhoff law calculations with correct mesh/nodal equations (25 points), (2) Systematic data collection with proper measurement techniques (20 points), (3) Logical identification of law violations and failure correlation (30 points), (4) Correct failure prediction with mathematical justification (20 points), (5) Clear explanation of analysis methodology to peers (5 points). Success requires 80% accuracy in calculations and correct failure identification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed mesh current equations and highlight specific test points to focus analysis. Offer guided questions like 'Which loop shows the largest KVL violation?' For advanced learners: Introduce multiple simultaneous failures, add reactive components with AC analysis, or require frequency-dependent failure characterization using oscilloscopes and function generators.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Beginner JavaScript Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written JavaScript functions for readability, functionality, and best practices. They will use established coding standards to judge code quality and provide detailed feedback with improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate JavaScript function quality by applying industry coding standards and best practices criteria
Students will critique code effectiveness through systematic analysis of readability, functionality, and maintainability factors
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Code Evaluation Worksheet and three printed JavaScript function examples (15 minutes setup). Introduce the evaluation criteria: functionality (does it work?), readability (clear variable names, proper indentation), efficiency (unnecessary code), and best practices (proper commenting, consistent naming). Demonstrate the evaluation process using a sample function on the board, showing how to score each criterion 1-5 and write specific feedback (10 minutes). 

Students work individually to evaluate Function A using the provided checklist, spending 15 minutes analyzing each criterion and writing 2-3 sentences of justification for their scores. They must identify at least two specific strengths and two areas for improvement. Next, students evaluate Function B (15 minutes) and Function C (15 minutes) using the same process.

After individual evaluation, pair students to compare their assessments of Function C (10 minutes). They must discuss scoring differences and reach consensus on the most critical improvement needed. Each pair writes one paragraph defending their final recommendation.

Conclude with a class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their evaluations of Function C, explaining their reasoning (15 minutes). Display the functions on screen for reference. Students submit their individual evaluation sheets and the pair's consensus paragraph.
materials_needed: Code Evaluation Worksheet with 1-5 scoring rubric for each criterion
Three printed JavaScript function examples of varying quality levels
Sample function for demonstration (printed and digital for projection)
Computers or tablets for students to view code clearly
assessment_method: Grade using a 20-point rubric: accurate functionality assessment (5 points), identification of readability issues (5 points), appropriate efficiency evaluation (5 points), quality of written justifications with specific examples (5 points). Success requires scoring 16+ points and identifying at least 75% of the deliberate code quality issues embedded in the examples.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation and highlight key phrases like 'unclear variable names' or 'missing comments.' Pair them with stronger evaluators. For advanced learners, add a fourth function with subtle security issues or ask them to rewrite one function incorporating their suggestions, then evaluate their own revision.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula Components Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the specific mathematical formulas, terminology, and calculation sequences used in Critical Path Method analysis for complex project scheduling. This activity focuses on perfect recall of CPM computational elements including Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Float calculations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all six CPM calculation formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, FF) with 100% accuracy by completing timed formula reproduction exercises
Students will identify and define 15 specific CPM terminology terms through rapid-fire flashcard sessions and written recall assessments
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute individual study period where students review provided CPM formula reference sheets containing: Early Start (ES = Maximum EF of predecessors), Early Finish (EF = ES + Duration), Late Finish (LF = Minimum LS of successors), Late Start (LS = LF - Duration), Total Float (TF = LS - ES or LF - EF), and Free Float (FF = Minimum ES of successors - EF). Next, conduct three 5-minute timed recall rounds. Round 1: Students write all six formulas from memory on blank paper without references. Round 2: Present 15 CPM terms (critical path, forward pass, backward pass, dummy activity, crash duration, etc.) via digital flashcards; students write definitions. Round 3: Show incomplete formulas with missing variables; students fill blanks. After each round, provide 2 minutes for self-checking against answer keys. Follow with partner verification where students quiz each other using instructor-provided question cards. Conclude with a 10-minute individual written assessment requiring students to reproduce all formulas and define key terms without any aids. Document results immediately using the provided scoring rubric.
materials_needed: CPM formula reference sheets (one per student)
Blank paper for recall exercises
Digital timer/stopwatch
CPM terminology flashcards (physical or digital)
Partner quiz question cards
Answer keys for self-checking
Individual assessment forms
Scoring rubric sheets
assessment_method: Use a 100-point rubric: Formula accuracy (60 points - 10 points per correct formula with proper notation), Terminology definitions (30 points - 2 points per accurate definition), Speed of recall (10 points - bonus points for completing within time limits). Success criteria: 85% overall score with minimum 80% on formula accuracy section. Track individual performance on each round to identify specific knowledge gaps.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for formula sequences, allow color-coding of formula components, and offer additional 5-minute review periods between rounds. Create formula pattern recognition sheets showing visual relationships. For advanced learners: Add complex multi-predecessor scenarios, introduce resource-constrained formulas, and challenge them to explain formula derivations. Provide real project network diagrams for formula application context.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: The Challenger Disaster Decision-Making Analysis
description: Students will analyze the complex leadership dynamics and decision-making processes that led to the 1986 Challenger Space Shuttle disaster. Through systematic examination of primary documents, organizational charts, and testimony transcripts, students will demonstrate understanding of how leadership failures cascade through organizational hierarchies and identify specific breakdowns in communication, risk assessment, and ethical decision-making.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the multi-layered leadership failures by mapping decision points, stakeholder influences, and communication breakdowns across NASA's organizational structure during the Challenger launch decision
Students will demonstrate understanding of crisis leadership principles through systematic comparison of actual leadership behaviors against established crisis management frameworks
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into research teams of 4-5 members, assigning each team a specific organizational level: NASA Senior Leadership, Shuttle Program Management, Engineering Teams (Morton Thiokol), Launch Decision Committee, and External Pressures/Political Influences. Provide each team with their designated document packet containing primary sources: internal memos, meeting transcripts, organizational charts, technical reports, and testimony excerpts from the Rogers Commission Report. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct deep-dive analysis of their assigned organizational level, identifying key leaders, their stated positions, decision-making authority, and communication patterns. Students must create a detailed timeline of critical decisions and map stakeholder relationships using the provided organizational analysis template. 

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Each team presents their findings using a standardized 6-minute presentation format covering: leadership structure, critical decisions made, communication gaps identified, and pressure points influencing decisions. Other teams take structured notes using the cross-reference matrix provided.

Phase 3 (35 minutes): Conduct a whole-class synthesis session where teams collaboratively construct a comprehensive leadership failure map on the wall-mounted timeline. Students must identify interconnections between organizational levels, pinpoint cascade failure points, and categorize leadership breakdowns using the Crisis Leadership Framework (provided reference sheet). 

Conclude with individual reflection where each student completes a structured analysis comparing the identified leadership failures against three established crisis leadership models: Kouzes-Posner Leadership Challenge, Heifetz Adaptive Leadership, and Bennis Crisis Leadership Competencies.
materials_needed: Rogers Commission Report excerpts organized by organizational level (5 document packets)
NASA organizational charts from 1985-1986
Organizational analysis templates with stakeholder mapping grids
Cross-reference matrix worksheets for note-taking
Wall-mounted timeline template (10-foot paper roll)
Crisis Leadership Framework reference sheets (Kouzes-Posner, Heifetz, Bennis models)
Colored sticky notes and markers for mapping exercise
assessment_method: Students will be evaluated using a 4-point analytical rubric measuring: (1) Accuracy of organizational relationship mapping (25 points), (2) Depth of leadership failure identification with specific evidence citations (30 points), (3) Quality of cross-organizational connection analysis (25 points), and (4) Theoretical framework application in individual reflection (20 points). Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstration of understanding through accurate identification of at least 8 specific leadership breakdown points and clear articulation of how failures cascaded across organizational boundaries.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted key passages in documents and sentence starters for analysis templates. Create role-specific guiding questions that break down complex organizational relationships. For advanced learners, add supplementary materials comparing Challenger to other organizational disasters (Columbia, Deepwater Horizon) and challenge them to develop predictive indicators for similar leadership failures. Consider providing additional primary sources from Congressional hearings for extended analysis.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Multi-Project Portfolios
description: Students will analyze and compare risk response strategies across three different project scenarios to identify patterns, evaluate effectiveness, and determine optimal approaches. They will examine how project context, constraints, and stakeholder priorities influence risk management decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategies by comparing their effectiveness across different project contexts and constraints
Students will evaluate the relationship between project characteristics and optimal risk management approaches through systematic comparison of three case scenarios
instructions: Begin with 5-minute individual review where each student examines three provided project case studies: a software development project (6-month timeline, $500K budget), a construction project (18-month timeline, $2M budget), and a marketing campaign (3-month timeline, $150K budget). Each case includes identical risk categories but different response strategies. Next, form groups of 3-4 students for 25-minute collaborative analysis phase. Groups create a comparison matrix examining: risk tolerance levels, resource allocation for risk responses, stakeholder impact considerations, and timeline constraints. Students must identify why different strategies were chosen for similar risks across projects. During 15-minute synthesis phase, groups analyze patterns and develop hypotheses about optimal risk response selection criteria. Each group then presents 5-minute findings focusing on: most significant differences in approach, underlying factors driving strategy selection, and recommendations for future project risk planning. Conclude with 10-minute class discussion where groups share insights and instructor facilitates analysis of cross-cutting themes. Students document individual reflections on how project context shapes risk management decisions.
materials_needed: Three detailed project case studies with risk registers and response strategies
Risk response comparison matrix template (Excel or printed worksheet)
Flip chart paper and markers for group presentations
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: accuracy of pattern identification (25%), quality of analysis connecting project context to risk strategies (35%), effectiveness of group comparison matrix (25%), and depth of individual reflection (15%). Success requires identifying at least 4 distinct patterns and providing evidence-based explanations for strategy differences.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guiding questions for each risk category and highlighting key contextual factors to examine. For advanced learners, add challenge of proposing alternative strategies and justifying improvements, or analyzing how cultural and geographical factors might influence risk response selection.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Audit and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 for a real e-commerce business case. They will analyze customer journey data, compare attribution models' impact on marketing budget allocation decisions, and defend their recommended attribution strategy with data-driven arguments.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of multiple attribution models (first-click, last-click, data-driven, position-based) by analyzing their impact on conversion credit distribution and marketing ROI calculations

Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey complexity and recommend optimal attribution frameworks based on business objectives and data patterns
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a demo GA4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retailer (or use Google Merchandise Store demo). Students work in pairs and receive a business brief outlining current marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display ads) and budget allocation concerns.

**Phase 1 - Data Analysis (45 minutes):** Students navigate to GA4's Attribution section and export conversion path reports for each attribution model. They must document: (1) top 5 converting paths for each model, (2) channel credit distribution percentages, (3) revenue attribution differences exceeding $10,000 between models, and (4) average customer journey length and touchpoint complexity.

**Phase 2 - Comparative Evaluation (30 minutes):** Using provided budget allocation spreadsheet template, students calculate how each attribution model would influence marketing spend recommendations. They must identify which channels gain/lose budget under each model and quantify the differences. Students then analyze customer journey reports to determine if attribution results align with actual user behavior patterns.

**Phase 3 - Strategic Recommendation (35 minutes):** Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their chosen attribution model. They must address: (1) business context alignment, (2) customer journey complexity considerations, (3) potential budget reallocation impacts, (4) limitations of their chosen model, and (5) implementation timeline. Each pair presents to another pair for peer evaluation using provided rubric.
materials_needed: GA4 demo account access with e-commerce data (Google Merchandise Store or instructor-created)
Business scenario brief document with current marketing mix and budget constraints
Excel/Google Sheets budget allocation calculation template
Attribution model comparison worksheet
Peer evaluation rubric for presentations
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) completed attribution analysis worksheet with data justifications (40 points), (2) budget impact calculations with clear methodology (30 points), (3) written strategic recommendation memo (500-750 words) defending chosen attribution model with specific data citations (30 points). Rubric evaluates data accuracy, depth of analysis, logical reasoning, consideration of business context, and acknowledgment of model limitations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps and data interpretation prompts. Create checkpoint conversations at each phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources, consider cross-device tracking implications, or propose custom attribution model parameters. Encourage analysis of statistical significance in model differences.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with DMVPN and Advanced Security
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise network solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN), BGP routing, and advanced security features. This capstone activity requires synthesizing knowledge of routing protocols, VPN technologies, QoS implementation, and network security to create a production-ready network design.
estimated_duration: 540 minutes (9 hours, typically spread across 3 class sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-site network architecture by integrating DMVPN Phase 3, BGP routing, and hierarchical network design principles
Students will implement advanced security policies through configuring zone-based firewalls, IPSec encryption, and network access control across the enterprise infrastructure
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members, assigning roles: Network Architect, Security Engineer, Routing Specialist, and QoS Engineer. Provide each team with the business requirements document specifying three sites (HQ with 500 users, Branch A with 150 users, Branch B with 75 users) requiring secure connectivity, voice/video traffic prioritization, and guest network isolation.

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams create detailed network diagrams using Visio or draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes using VLSM, VLAN segmentation plans, and equipment placement. Students must justify their design choices in writing, addressing scalability, redundancy, and security requirements.

Phase 2 (180 minutes): Using GNS3 or Cisco Modeling Labs, teams build their network topology with actual Cisco router and switch images. Configure DMVPN hub at headquarters with two spokes, implement EIGRP as underlay routing protocol, and establish BGP peering between sites for specific route advertisements.

Phase 3 (120 minutes): Implement security policies including zone-based firewall rules, configure IPSec encryption parameters for DMVPN tunnels, and create separate VRFs for guest networks. Students must document all configuration commands and create network security policies.

Phase 4 (90 minutes): Configure QoS policies for voice, video, and data traffic classification using DSCP markings and implement traffic shaping on WAN interfaces. Test connectivity between all sites and verify traffic prioritization using packet captures.

Phase 5 (60 minutes): Teams present their complete solution, demonstrating network functionality, explaining security implementations, and defending design decisions to simulated executive stakeholders. Include network documentation, configuration backups, and disaster recovery procedures.
materials_needed: GNS3 or Cisco Modeling Labs software with Cisco IOS router images (ISR 4000 series)
Cisco Catalyst switch images (9300 series) for each team
Business requirements document template with specific traffic patterns and security policies
Visio or draw.io access for network diagramming
Wireshark for packet analysis and QoS verification
High-performance computers capable of running multiple virtual network devices
assessment_method: Evaluate using a comprehensive rubric (100 points total): Network Design Documentation (25 points - accuracy of IP addressing, VLAN design, and topology diagrams), Technical Implementation (40 points - successful DMVPN configuration, routing protocol operation, and security policy deployment), QoS Configuration (15 points - proper traffic classification and bandwidth allocation), Professional Presentation (10 points - clear communication of technical concepts), and Innovation/Optimization (10 points - creative solutions exceeding minimum requirements). Students must demonstrate working connectivity between all sites, successful traffic prioritization, and secure guest network isolation to pass.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-configured base router templates and step-by-step DMVPN configuration guides. Offer intermediate checkpoints where teams can validate their progress with instructor guidance. For advanced learners, introduce additional challenges such as implementing MPLS Layer 3 VPNs as an alternative solution, adding IPv6 dual-stack configuration, or integrating SD-WAN concepts with traditional routing protocols. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing additional support within each team.

title: Optimizing Warehouse Distribution Networks Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world warehouse distribution optimization problem. They will formulate constraints, set up objective functions, and use the simplex method to minimize transportation costs while meeting supply and demand requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation by converting a multi-warehouse distribution scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method through systematic tableau operations to find optimal shipping quantities that minimize total costs
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Distribute the warehouse scenario worksheet featuring 3 warehouses supplying 4 retail stores with given supply capacities (W1: 200 units, W2: 150 units, W3: 180 units) and store demands (S1: 120 units, S2: 90 units, S3: 140 units, S4: 180 units). Provide per-unit shipping costs matrix between each warehouse-store pair. **Phase 1 (25 minutes):** Working in pairs, students identify decision variables (xij = units shipped from warehouse i to store j), formulate supply constraints (∑xij ≤ supply capacity for each warehouse), demand constraints (∑xij ≥ demand for each store), and create the objective function (minimize total shipping cost). **Phase 2 (35 minutes):** Students convert their formulation into standard form by adding slack variables and setting up the initial simplex tableau. They identify entering and leaving variables using the most negative coefficient rule and minimum ratio test. **Phase 3 (40 minutes):** Students perform pivot operations systematically, updating tableau entries using the formula: new_entry = old_entry - (pivot_column_entry × pivot_row_entry)/pivot_element. They continue iterations until all objective function coefficients are non-negative. **Phase 4 (15 minutes):** Teams interpret their optimal solution, identifying shipping quantities for each route and calculating minimum total cost. They verify their solution satisfies all constraints and prepare a brief presentation of their distribution strategy.
materials_needed: Warehouse distribution scenario worksheet with supply/demand data
Shipping cost matrix table (3×4 grid with specific dollar amounts)
Simplex tableau templates (printed or digital spreadsheet)
Calculators or computers with Excel/Google Sheets access
Graph paper for constraint plotting (optional verification)
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct problem formulation with all constraints and objective function properly stated (25 points), (2) Accurate simplex tableau setup and pivot operations with minimal computational errors (35 points), (3) Correct optimal solution identification and cost calculation (25 points), (4) Clear interpretation and business reasoning for the distribution strategy (15 points). Students must achieve 80% (80/100 points) for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed constraint templates and guide through first pivot operation step-by-step. Offer constraint graphing as visual aid for 2-variable subset problems. For advanced learners: Introduce sensitivity analysis by asking how optimal solution changes with 10% increase in warehouse capacity, or add integer programming constraints requiring whole-number shipments. Provide degeneracy scenarios for additional complexity.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in a Double-Slit Experiment to Determine Light Wavelength
description: Students will collect experimental data from a laser double-slit setup and analyze the interference pattern to calculate the wavelength of unknown laser light. They will decompose the relationship between slit separation, screen distance, and fringe spacing to evaluate measurement uncertainty and compare theoretical predictions with experimental results.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the geometric relationships in double-slit interference by measuring fringe spacing and calculating wavelength using Young's equation
Students will examine sources of experimental error through statistical analysis of multiple measurements and uncertainty propagation calculations
instructions: Begin by setting up the laser double-slit apparatus with the laser 2 meters from the screen and double-slit slide positioned 10 cm from the laser (ensure room is darkened). Students work in pairs to collect data over 45 minutes. First, students measure and record the slit separation 'd' using the provided micrometer (typically 0.04-0.08 mm). Next, they precisely measure the distance 'L' from the slits to the screen using a meter stick. Students then photograph the interference pattern and use the ruler placed against the screen for scale reference. Using ImageJ software or printed photographs with rulers, students measure the distance between 10 consecutive bright fringes and divide by 10 to get average fringe spacing 'y'. They repeat this measurement for 5 different sets of fringes across the pattern. Students calculate wavelength using λ = dy/L for each measurement set, then determine the mean wavelength and standard deviation. They compare their result to the known laser wavelength (typically 632.8 nm for HeNe or 650 nm for diode lasers). For error analysis, students identify three major sources of uncertainty: slit separation measurement (±0.002 mm), distance measurement (±2 mm), and fringe spacing measurement (±0.1 mm). Using partial derivatives, they calculate the total uncertainty in wavelength: δλ/λ = √[(δd/d)² + (δy/y)² + (δL/L)²]. Finally, students create a data table showing individual calculations, statistical analysis, and error propagation, concluding with a comparison of their experimental wavelength range to the theoretical value.
materials_needed: HeNe or diode laser (632.8 nm or 650 nm)
Double-slit slides with known separations (0.04-0.08 mm)
White projection screen or wall
Meter sticks and rulers with mm markings
Digital camera or smartphone
Micrometer or calipers (0.01 mm precision)
ImageJ software or printed ruler for measurements
Scientific calculators
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Data Collection - accurate measurement of all variables with proper significant figures and multiple trials (25%), (2) Mathematical Analysis - correct application of Young's equation and statistical calculations (25%), (3) Error Analysis - identification of uncertainty sources and proper propagation calculations (25%), (4) Scientific Reasoning - logical comparison of experimental results to theoretical values with justified conclusions about accuracy (25%). Students must achieve wavelength within 10% of actual value with properly calculated uncertainties.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated slit separations and focus on fringe measurement techniques; offer guided worksheets with partially completed error propagation formulas. For advanced learners: Challenge them to analyze how changing slit separation affects measurement precision, investigate the relationship between fringe visibility and slit width, or extend to analyzing circular aperture diffraction patterns. Provide troubleshooting guide for common setup issues like laser alignment and focus problems.

title: Evaluating Code Review Quality: Assessing Pull Request Feedback Effectiveness
description: Students will analyze and judge the quality of code review comments on GitHub pull requests, determining which feedback is most valuable for improving code quality. They will assess reviewer comments against established code review criteria and rank feedback from most to least helpful.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code review comments by analyzing their specificity, constructiveness, and alignment with software development best practices
Students will critique the effectiveness of peer feedback through systematic comparison against established code review standards
instructions: Begin by providing each student with printed copies of three GitHub pull request conversations (15 minutes setup). Each PR should contain 4-6 review comments of varying quality - some excellent (specific, actionable, references standards), some poor (vague, unconstructive, personal attacks), and some mediocre (partially helpful but incomplete). First, students individually spend 20 minutes reading through all three PRs and the associated review comments. Next, distribute the 'Code Review Quality Rubric' containing five criteria: specificity of feedback, constructiveness of tone, reference to coding standards, actionability of suggestions, and focus on code rather than coder. Students then spend 25 minutes scoring each comment (1-4 scale) against these criteria and writing 2-3 sentence justifications for their scores. Following individual assessment, organize students into pairs for 15 minutes to compare their evaluations and discuss discrepancies in scoring. Each pair must reach consensus on the top 3 most valuable comments across all PRs and identify the 2 least helpful comments, providing written rationale. Finally, conduct a 10-minute whole-class discussion where pairs share their top-rated comments and explain their reasoning. Conclude by having each student write a brief reflection on what makes code review feedback effective and how they would improve the poorest-quality comments they evaluated.
materials_needed: Printed copies of 3 GitHub pull request conversations with review comments
Code Review Quality Rubric handout
Evaluation scoring sheets
Computers or tablets for accessing GitHub (optional for visual reference)
assessment_method: Grade based on completed scoring rubric with justifications (40%), quality of consensus rationale with partner (30%), participation in class discussion (15%), and final reflection demonstrating understanding of effective code review principles (15%). Success criteria: scores align with instructor rubric within 1 point, written justifications cite specific examples, and reflection identifies at least 3 key principles of quality code reviews.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example evaluation of one comment before starting, highlight key phrases in the rubric, and pair with stronger partners. For advanced learners: include pull requests with more subtle quality differences, ask them to rewrite poor comments to demonstrate improvement, or have them evaluate reviews in programming languages they're less familiar with to focus purely on review quality principles.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Decision-Making Models Through Crisis Case Analysis
description: Students will analyze real organizational crisis scenarios to identify and explain the underlying leadership decision-making models used by executives. Through structured case dissection, students will demonstrate understanding of how different leadership frameworks (transformational, situational, servant leadership) manifest in high-stakes decision-making processes.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and situational leadership models by identifying specific behavioral indicators within documented crisis responses
Students will explain the relationship between leadership decision-making frameworks and organizational outcomes through systematic case analysis and evidence mapping
instructions:
Begin by distributing three complex crisis case studies: Tylenol poisoning crisis (Johnson & Johnson, 1982), Wells Fargo account fraud scandal (2016), and Patagonia's political activism stance (2016-present). Divide class into teams of 4-5 students, assigning each team one case study. Provide teams with the Leadership Decision-Making Analysis Framework worksheet containing four sections: Decision Context, Leadership Behaviors Observed, Framework Identification, and Impact Analysis. 

During the 45-minute analysis phase, teams must: 1) Map the timeline of key leadership decisions, 2) Extract specific quotes and actions from leaders, 3) Match observed behaviors to theoretical frameworks using the provided Leadership Behavior Checklist, and 4) Trace decision outcomes to specific leadership approaches. Circulate between teams, prompting deeper analysis with questions like 'What evidence supports your framework identification?' and 'How do you explain seemingly contradictory leadership behaviors?'

For the presentation phase (30 minutes total), each team presents for 8 minutes using the structured template: 2 minutes crisis overview, 4 minutes framework analysis with specific evidence, 2 minutes outcome correlation. Other teams use peer evaluation forms to assess the strength of evidence presented. Conclude with a 15-minute facilitated discussion where teams identify patterns across cases and explain why certain leadership approaches proved more effective in specific crisis contexts.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (Johnson & Johnson Tylenol, Wells Fargo fraud, Patagonia activism)
Leadership Decision-Making Analysis Framework worksheets
Leadership Behavior Checklist reference sheets
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Digital timer for time management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: 1) Accuracy of framework identification with specific textual evidence (25%), 2) Quality of behavior-to-theory connections with clear explanations (35%), 3) Depth of outcome analysis linking leadership choices to results (25%), and 4) Presentation clarity and peer engagement (15%). Students must score 3/4 on framework identification and behavior connections to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case excerpts and a behavior-matching exercise before full analysis. Offer sentence starters like 'The evidence for transformational leadership includes...' Advanced learners should analyze contradictory leadership behaviors within single cases and propose hybrid model explanations. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those needing support during evidence mapping phase.

title: Critical Path vs. Resource-Constrained Schedule Analysis
description: Students will analyze a multi-project scenario to differentiate between critical path scheduling and resource-constrained scheduling impacts. They will examine how resource limitations affect project timelines and identify the root causes of schedule variances in complex project environments.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the differences between critical path method outcomes and resource-constrained schedules by comparing two versions of the same project timeline
Students will examine resource allocation conflicts and their cascading effects through systematic evaluation of project dependencies and resource assignments
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Software Implementation Project' case study containing: initial project network diagram with 15 activities, duration estimates, predecessor relationships, and resource requirements for 4 specialist roles (2 developers, 1 database admin, 1 systems analyst). Also provide the completed CPM schedule showing 42-day duration.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students first review the CPM schedule results and identify the critical path activities. Then, using the resource availability constraints (developers available only 50% time due to maintenance duties, database admin shared across 3 projects, systems analyst available full-time), students manually trace through the schedule to identify resource conflicts. They document conflicts on the provided worksheet, noting which activities cannot start as scheduled due to resource unavailability.

**Phase 2 - Comparative Analysis (20 minutes):** In pairs, students create a resource-constrained schedule using the template provided. They must reschedule conflicted activities, calculate new early start/finish dates, and identify the new critical path. Students then complete a comparison matrix analyzing: original vs. new project duration, critical path changes, resource utilization rates, and risk impact on key milestones.

**Phase 3 - Root Cause Analysis (15 minutes):** Pairs analyze three provided variance scenarios where projects exceeded planned duration. Using the 5-Why technique worksheet, they trace each delay back to either poor resource planning, unrealistic CPM assumptions, or external factors. Students categorize each root cause as preventable through better resource management or unavoidable external constraints.

**Debrief (5 minutes):** Teams present one key insight about when CPM alone is insufficient for realistic project planning.
materials_needed: Software Implementation Project case study packet (network diagram, activity list, resource requirements)
Completed CPM schedule reference sheet
Resource constraint worksheet with conflict tracking table
Resource-constrained schedule template with Gantt chart format
Comparison matrix template (Excel or printed)
5-Why analysis worksheet for three variance scenarios
assessment_method: Evaluate student pairs on: (1) Accuracy of resource conflict identification (25 points - must identify at least 6 of 8 conflicts), (2) Correctness of resource-constrained schedule calculations (35 points - early start/finish dates within 1 day tolerance), (3) Quality of comparative analysis matrix completion (25 points - addresses all four comparison categories with specific data), (4) Root cause analysis depth (15 points - traces at least 2 scenarios to actionable root causes using 5-Why methodology). Success threshold: 75/100 points demonstrating analytical thinking beyond surface-level schedule adjustments.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a partially completed resource conflict worksheet with the first 3 conflicts pre-identified as examples. Include a reference card showing step-by-step resource-constrained scheduling calculations. Pair struggling students with stronger partners who can explain their reasoning process. **For advanced learners:** Add a third analysis phase where they recommend specific resource management strategies (resource leveling, crashing, or outsourcing options) with cost-benefit calculations. Challenge them to identify which activities could be fast-tracked without additional resource conflicts.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Optimization Strategy
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data scenarios. They will assess data-driven attribution versus rules-based models and defend their recommended attribution strategy for specific business contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business impact of data-driven attribution versus last-click, first-click, and linear attribution models by analyzing conversion path reports and ROI calculations

Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and defend optimized attribution recommendations based on business objectives and data limitations
instructions: **Phase 1 (20 minutes):** Provide students with three realistic business scenarios: (A) SaaS company with 90-day consideration cycle, (B) fashion e-commerce with seasonal campaigns, (C) B2B service with multi-touchpoint sales process. Students access provided GA4 demo accounts with 6 months of conversion data for each scenario. **Phase 2 (40 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool in GA4. They must export attribution comparison reports for each scenario, documenting conversions and revenue attributed under each model (data-driven, last-click, first-click, linear, time-decay, position-based). Students calculate percentage differences in channel performance rankings and revenue attribution between models. **Phase 3 (35 minutes):** Using the Path analysis report under Advertising > Attribution, students analyze top conversion paths for each business type. They identify patterns in customer journey length, touchpoint diversity, and channel interaction sequences. Students must document at least 5 key insights about customer behavior patterns for each scenario. **Phase 4 (45 minutes):** Students create comprehensive evaluation reports comparing attribution models' strengths/weaknesses for each business context. They must justify which attribution model best serves each business's goals, considering factors like: campaign optimization needs, budget allocation accuracy, customer journey complexity, and data volume requirements. **Phase 5 (20 minutes):** Teams present 5-minute recommendations to class, defending their attribution strategy choices with specific data evidence and addressing potential counterarguments about their model selection.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo accounts with e-commerce data (3 different business types)
GA4 Attribution reports access permissions
Excel or Google Sheets for calculations
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Business scenario handouts with company context and objectives
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Data analysis accuracy - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences (25%), (2) Critical evaluation depth - thorough comparison of model strengths/limitations with specific examples (30%), (3) Business context application - appropriate model recommendations aligned with business objectives (25%), (4) Defense of recommendations - ability to justify choices and address counterarguments with data evidence (20%)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model comparison checklist and guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps. Offer pre-calculated examples of attribution differences. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation exercise using GA4's data-driven attribution insights, and challenge them to identify attribution model limitations in cross-device tracking scenarios.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS Architecture
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network spanning three geographic sites with EIGRP routing, site-to-site VPN tunnels, role-based access control, and traffic prioritization. They will create comprehensive network documentation and present their design rationale to stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 6 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize EIGRP routing protocols, VPN technologies, and VLAN segmentation by designing a scalable multi-site network architecture that meets specific business requirements
Students will evaluate and implement advanced security policies and QoS mechanisms through hands-on configuration of Cisco ASA firewalls and router-based traffic shaping
instructions:
Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: GlobalTech Corp needs to connect their headquarters (500 users), manufacturing site (200 users), and remote office (50 users) with specific requirements for guest access, voice traffic prioritization, and departmental isolation. Divide students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Network Architect, Security Specialist, QoS Engineer, and Documentation Lead.

Phase 1 (90 minutes): Teams analyze requirements and create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3. They must design IP addressing schemes using VLSM, plan EIGRP areas, specify hardware requirements, and identify security zones. Each team presents their initial design for peer review.

Phase 2 (180 minutes): Using physical Cisco equipment or advanced simulation, teams implement their designs. Configure three routers as site gateways with EIGRP routing, establish IPSec site-to-site VPN tunnels between all locations, create VLANs for different departments (Sales, Engineering, Guest), implement inter-VLAN routing with access control lists, and configure QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic and limiting guest bandwidth.

Phase 3 (60 minutes): Teams test connectivity between all sites, verify VPN tunnel establishment, demonstrate VLAN isolation, test QoS implementation by generating different traffic types, and document all configurations with justifications.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team delivers a 10-minute stakeholder presentation explaining their design decisions, demonstrating network functionality, and defending their security and QoS implementations. Other teams act as executives asking technical and business questions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer or GNS3 network simulation software
Three Cisco ISR 4000 series routers with security license
Six Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches
Ethernet cables and console cables
Laptops/computers for configuration and documentation
Network requirements specification document template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - addressing scheme efficiency, scalability, documentation clarity), Implementation Accuracy (35 points - correct EIGRP configuration, successful VPN establishment, proper VLAN setup, functional ACLs), QoS and Security Implementation (25 points - appropriate traffic policies, security zone configuration, access restrictions), and Stakeholder Presentation (15 points - technical accuracy, business justification, response to questions). Students must achieve 80% functionality in live network testing to pass.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-configured base templates and IP addressing worksheets. Offer intermediate checkpoints with instructor verification before proceeding to next phase. For advanced learners, add requirements for BGP routing to simulate ISP connections, implement certificate-based VPN authentication, or integrate wireless controller configuration for guest access.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Scenarios
description: Students will analyze three pre-selected datasets with different correlation patterns to distinguish between correlation and causation. They will examine scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and contextual information to explain why strong correlations may or may not indicate causal relationships.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing correlation coefficients and scatter plots from three distinct real-world datasets
Students will explain the limitations of correlation analysis through written justifications that identify potential confounding variables and alternative explanations
instructions: Begin by distributing three dataset scenarios: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning incidents (r=0.85), (2) Education spending vs. test scores by state (r=0.72), and (3) Shoe size vs. reading ability in elementary students (r=0.89). Provide each student with printed scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and brief contextual descriptions. In the first 15 minutes, have students work individually to calculate and verify the correlation strength using the provided data tables. Next, organize students into groups of 3-4 for 25 minutes to discuss each scenario. Each group receives a structured worksheet with questions: 'What does the correlation coefficient tell us?', 'What alternative explanations could account for this relationship?', 'What additional data would help determine causation?', and 'Can you identify potential confounding variables?' Groups must complete the worksheet with specific examples for each dataset. During the final 20 minutes, conduct a whole-class discussion where each group presents their analysis of one scenario. Focus on having students articulate why Dataset 1 shows spurious correlation (both increase in summer), Dataset 2 shows potential causation with confounds (socioeconomic factors), and Dataset 3 demonstrates a lurking variable (age affects both variables). Conclude by having students individually write a 3-sentence summary explaining when correlation suggests causation versus when it doesn't, using examples from the activity.
materials_needed: Three printed datasets with scatter plots and correlation coefficients
Structured analysis worksheet (one per group)
Calculators or laptop access for correlation verification
Whiteboard markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation strength AND provides accurate alternative explanations with specific confounding variables; (3) Identifies correlation strength with mostly accurate explanations; (2) Basic understanding shown but explanations lack specificity; (1) Confusion between correlation and causation evident. Also assess individual summary statements for clear articulation of the distinction.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a 'Correlation Analysis Checklist' with prompts like 'Look for a third variable that affects both' and 'Consider the data collection context.' For advanced learners, introduce Simpson's Paradox examples or have them research additional real-world correlation/causation cases to present to the class.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Dataset Scenarios: Visual Analysis
description: Students will analyze three pre-selected datasets containing different correlation patterns to distinguish between correlation and causation relationships. They will create visual interpretations and provide evidence-based explanations for why certain correlations do not imply causal relationships.
