They sort cards into three piles: immediate recall (under 3 seconds), delayed recall (3-8 seconds), and no recall (over 8 seconds or incorrect). Phase 2 (15 minutes): Partner students for cross-drilling. Partner A reads terms while Partner B provides definitions and knowledge area classifications. Switch roles every 5 minutes. Phase 3 (10 minutes): Conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall session. Display random PMBOK terms on projector for 5 seconds each. Students write knowledge area and brief definition on response sheets. Include advanced terminology such as 'progressive elaboration,' 'rolling wave planning,' 'parametric estimating,' and 'critical chain method.' Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual assessment quiz covering 25 randomly selected terms from all knowledge areas. Students must provide exact knowledge area and core definition within 30-second time limits per question.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcard sets covering all 49 PMBOK processes with definitions
Advanced PM terminology cards (100 key terms with definitions)
Digital timer/stopwatch for each pair
Response sheets for individual assessment
Projector for whole-class recall session
PMBOK Guide 7th Edition reference sheets
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy on the final 25-term quiz within time constraints. Evaluation criteria: Correct knowledge area identification (40%), accurate core definition (40%), completion within time limit (20%). Peer observation checklist during partner drilling phase assessing recall speed and accuracy.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide knowledge area color-coding system and reduce initial term sets to 5 processes per knowledge area. Offer audio recordings of terms and definitions for auditory learners. For advanced learners: Add ITTOs (Inputs, Tools & Techniques, Outputs) for each process and include terminology from Agile Practice Guide and other PMI standards. Challenge them to recall process sequence within knowledge areas.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancer
description: Students will apply AWS cloud fundamentals by deploying a simple web application across multiple EC2 instances and implementing an Application Load Balancer for high availability. This hands-on activity reinforces core AWS services through practical implementation of a scalable web infrastructure.
learning_objectives: Students will apply EC2 instance configuration skills by launching and customizing two web servers with unique content in different availability zones
Students will implement load balancing concepts through creating and configuring an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic between their EC2 instances
instructions: **Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS account credentials and ensure they can access the AWS Management Console. Students should have the provided HTML template files downloaded locally. **Step 1 - Launch EC2 Instances (15 minutes):** Students navigate to EC2 Dashboard and launch two t2.micro instances using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. They must select different availability zones (e.g., us-east-1a and us-east-1b) and create a security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere. **Step 2 - Configure Web Servers (20 minutes):** Using EC2 Instance Connect, students access each instance via browser-based SSH. They install Apache web server using 'sudo yum update -y' followed by 'sudo yum install -y httpd'. Students start the service with 'sudo systemctl start httpd' and enable auto-start with 'sudo systemctl enable httpd'. They then create custom index.html files in /var/www/html/ directory - Server 1 displays 'Hello from Server 1 in AZ-A' and Server 2 displays 'Hello from Server 2 in AZ-B'. **Step 3 - Create Load Balancer (20 minutes):** In EC2 Dashboard, students navigate to Load Balancers and create an Application Load Balancer. They configure it as internet-facing, select both availability zones where their instances reside, use the same security group as EC2 instances, create a new target group named 'web-servers', and register both EC2 instances as targets. **Step 4 - Testing and Validation (10 minutes):** Students access the load balancer DNS name multiple times and document that traffic alternates between servers, demonstrating successful load distribution.
materials_needed: AWS account with EC2 and ELB permissions for each student
Pre-created HTML template files with server identification placeholders
AWS Management Console access via web browser
Student worksheet for documenting DNS names and testing results
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Two running EC2 instances in different AZs, (2) Custom web pages displaying from each server, (3) Load balancer configuration page, (4) Evidence of traffic distribution by showing different server responses when accessing the load balancer URL. Rubric: EC2 deployment (25 points), web server configuration (25 points), load balancer setup (25 points), successful traffic distribution (25 points).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written commands in a reference sheet and pair them with more confident peers. Create checkpoints after each major step with instructor verification. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement health checks, add auto-scaling groups, or configure SSL certificates. Provide additional scenarios like simulating server failure to test load balancer behavior.

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancer: Practical Workshop
description: Students will deploy a simple web application across multiple AWS EC2 instances and configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration and basic cloud architecture principles.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a web application on multiple EC2 instances by launching instances, installing web servers, and uploading application files
Students will configure an Application Load Balancer through the AWS Console to distribute traffic across their EC2 instances and verify proper load distribution
instructions:
**Preparation (5 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS account access and shares the sample HTML application files. Students log into AWS Console and navigate to EC2 dashboard.

**Phase 1 - Launch EC2 Instances (15 minutes):** Students launch two t2.micro EC2 instances using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. Configure security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere. Use the same key pair for both instances. Tag instances as 'WebServer-1' and 'WebServer-2'.

**Phase 2 - Install Web Server (20 minutes):** SSH into each instance separately. Install Apache web server using 'sudo yum install httpd -y' and start service with 'sudo systemctl start httpd'. Create unique index.html files on each server displaying the server name (e.g., 'Hello from WebServer-1'). Test by accessing each instance's public IP in browser.

**Phase 3 - Create Load Balancer (15 minutes):** Navigate to EC2 Load Balancers section. Create Application Load Balancer named 'MyWebAppLB' with internet-facing scheme. Select all available subnets. Use existing security group allowing HTTP traffic. Create target group named 'WebServerTargets' with HTTP protocol on port 80.

**Phase 4 - Configure and Test (10 minutes):** Register both EC2 instances to target group. Wait for health checks to show 'healthy' status. Access load balancer DNS name multiple times in browser, refreshing to observe traffic distribution between servers. Document which server responds to each request.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students terminate EC2 instances and delete load balancer to avoid charges. Submit screenshots showing successful load balancing.
materials_needed: AWS account with EC2 and ELB permissions for each student
Sample HTML application files with server identification
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Web browser for testing
Provided EC2 key pair file (.pem)
assessment_method: Students submit a document containing: (1) Screenshots of both EC2 instances running with unique web pages (20 points), (2) Screenshot of Application Load Balancer configuration showing healthy targets (25 points), (3) Screenshots demonstrating load balancer distributing requests to different servers (30 points), (4) Brief explanation of observed load balancing behavior (15 points), (5) Confirmation of resource cleanup (10 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written HTML files and SSH command cheat sheet. Pair students for peer support during SSH configuration. For advanced learners: Add CloudWatch monitoring to observe traffic metrics, implement health check customization, or configure SSL termination on the load balancer. Consider adding auto-scaling groups as an extension activity.
original_title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancer

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Recommendation Framework
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics attribution models by analyzing real e-commerce conversion data across multiple touchpoints. They will assess the business impact of each model and provide strategic recommendations for optimal attribution model selection based on specific business scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business relevance of Last Click, First Click, Linear, Time-Decay, and Data-Driven attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution differences
Students will assess the strategic implications of attribution model selection through comparative analysis of customer journey insights and ROI calculations across different marketing channels
instructions: Begin by providing each student group (3-4 members) with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active (15 minutes setup). Students first navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model Comparison tool and extract conversion and revenue data for all five attribution models, documenting findings in the provided analysis template (30 minutes). Next, students examine the Top Conversion Paths report under Advertising > Attribution to identify the most common customer journey patterns, noting path length, channel sequence, and time to conversion (25 minutes). Groups then calculate the percentage difference in attributed conversions and revenue between models for each channel, identifying which channels gain or lose credit under different models (20 minutes). Students analyze three provided business scenarios: a brand awareness-focused company, a direct-response retailer, and a B2B service provider with long sales cycles. For each scenario, groups must evaluate which attribution model best aligns with business goals, considering factors like sales cycle length, marketing strategy, and budget allocation needs (40 minutes). Finally, each group prepares a formal recommendation memo addressing a specific business stakeholder, defending their attribution model choice with quantitative evidence from the data analysis, potential implementation challenges, and expected impact on marketing budget allocation (30 minutes). Groups present their findings in 8-minute presentations, with peers evaluating recommendations using provided criteria sheets focusing on data accuracy, strategic alignment, and implementation feasibility.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Attribution Model Analysis Template (Excel/Google Sheets)
Three detailed business scenario descriptions with company backgrounds
Peer evaluation criteria sheets for presentations
Access to Google Slides or PowerPoint for final presentations
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 100-point rubric: Data Analysis Accuracy (25 points) - correct extraction and calculation of attribution differences; Critical Evaluation (30 points) - depth of analysis comparing model strengths/weaknesses for different scenarios; Strategic Recommendation Quality (25 points) - logical reasoning connecting data insights to business decisions; Presentation and Defense (20 points) - clear communication and ability to respond to peer questions. Success requires scoring 80+ points with demonstrated ability to identify meaningful attribution differences and provide actionable business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide pre-filled data extraction templates with formulas, offer guided questions for each analysis section, and allow extended time for navigation training. For advanced learners: introduce custom attribution modeling concepts, require additional analysis using Exploration reports, challenge them to identify data quality issues or suggest GA4 configuration improvements. Consider pairing weaker technical students with stronger ones while ensuring all members contribute to strategic analysis components.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Verification
description: Students will memorize and recall binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice. They will demonstrate their recall ability by converting decimal numbers to binary and vice versa without calculation aids.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify correct decimal-to-binary conversions through verbal recitation and written verification activities
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the other (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.). Have students work in pairs for 15 minutes, with one student showing the decimal side while the partner states the binary equivalent, then checking the answer. Partners switch roles every 5 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers on the projector and students write binary answers on mini whiteboards, holding them up simultaneously for immediate feedback. Spend 10 minutes on decimal-to-binary conversions (numbers 0-15 randomly presented), then 10 minutes on binary-to-decimal conversions. For the final 10 minutes, have students complete an individual worksheet with 20 mixed conversion problems (10 decimal-to-binary, 10 binary-to-decimal) without referring to flashcards. Walk around to provide immediate feedback and mark correct answers. Students must achieve 80% accuracy to demonstrate mastery. Create a reference chart on the board showing all 16 conversions that remains visible throughout the partner practice but gets covered during individual assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Mini whiteboards and dry erase markers for each student
Individual assessment worksheets with 20 conversion problems
Digital projector or document camera
Reference chart poster showing decimal 0-15 and binary equivalents
assessment_method: Students must achieve 16/20 correct answers (80%) on the final individual worksheet. Grade using answer key: 1 point per correct conversion. Track completion time - mastery level students finish in under 8 minutes. Document which specific numbers students consistently miss for remediation planning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a powers-of-2 reference strip (8-4-2-1) and allow extra practice time with flashcards. For advanced learners: extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during partner practice.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformation Inefficiencies in Multi-Stage Mechanical Systems
description: Students will dissect a complex mechanical system (compound pulley with inclined plane) to identify energy losses at each transformation stage and determine which physical principles account for measured inefficiencies. They will use experimental data to differentiate between theoretical predictions and real-world performance limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze energy transformation pathways by quantifying mechanical energy losses at each stage of a compound pulley-inclined plane system
Students will differentiate between theoretical and experimental efficiency values through systematic comparison of calculated versus measured energy outputs
instructions: Begin by providing each group with a pre-assembled compound pulley system (2 fixed, 1 movable pulley) connected to a 30° inclined plane with a 2kg mass. Students first calculate theoretical mechanical advantage (MA = 4) and expected efficiency assuming no friction. Next, students measure actual forces using spring scales at three points: input force at rope, tension in final pulley cable, and force required to lift mass directly up the incline. Record 5 trials of each measurement. Students then calculate work input (force × distance pulled) and work output (weight × height lifted) for the complete system. Using energy bar charts, students map energy transformations: chemical (human) → kinetic (rope/pulleys) → gravitational potential (lifted mass) + thermal (friction losses). Students identify loss mechanisms by comparing subsystem efficiencies: isolate pulley system efficiency by measuring input/output forces with mass on horizontal surface, then isolate inclined plane efficiency using direct measurements. Calculate percentage energy loss for each subsystem and overall system. Students create detailed energy flow diagrams showing quantified losses at each transformation point. Finally, students analyze which design modifications would most significantly improve overall efficiency by examining the relative contribution of each loss mechanism. Groups present their analysis including calculated vs. measured efficiency values, identified loss mechanisms with supporting evidence, and ranked improvement recommendations with quantitative justifications.
materials_needed: Compound pulley system with 2 fixed and 1 movable pulley
Adjustable inclined plane set to 30° angle
2kg calibrated mass
3 spring scales (0-20N range)
Measuring tape or meter stick
Digital stopwatch
Calculator or computer with spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of experimental measurements and calculations (25%), (2) Completeness of energy transformation analysis with quantified losses (25%), (3) Quality of comparison between theoretical vs. experimental results with explanations for discrepancies (25%), (4) Depth of improvement recommendations with quantitative support (25%). Success requires identification of at least 3 distinct energy loss mechanisms with calculated percentages within 10% of expected values.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-drawn energy bar chart templates and calculation worksheets with partially completed examples. Offer guiding questions like 'Where might energy be lost between the rope and pulley contact?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive mathematical relationships between friction coefficients and measured efficiency losses, or investigate how pulley radius affects mechanical advantage and efficiency trade-offs.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformation Inefficiencies in Multi-Stage Mechanical Systems: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze a complex mechanical system (compound pulley with inclined plane) to identify specific sources of energy loss and quantify the contribution of each inefficiency type. They will decompose theoretical versus actual energy transformations to determine where and why mechanical advantage is reduced.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze energy flow pathways in a multi-component mechanical system by calculating theoretical versus measured values at each transformation stage
Students will differentiate between various sources of energy loss through systematic examination of friction, deformation, and heat generation data
instructions: Begin by setting up the apparatus: mount a compound pulley system (minimum 4 pulleys) connected to a 30-degree inclined plane with a 2kg mass. Install force sensors at three measurement points: input force location, intermediate pulley junction, and final load point. Connect temperature sensors to pulley axles and the inclined plane surface. Divide students into teams of 3-4. Each team receives data collection sheets with pre-calculated theoretical values for mechanical advantage (MA), velocity ratios, and energy efficiency. Students first operate the system at slow, medium, and fast speeds, recording input force, output force, displacement distances, time intervals, and temperature changes at all sensor locations. Next, teams calculate actual mechanical advantage for each speed and compare with theoretical MA of 8:1 for their specific pulley configuration. Students then analyze force sensor data to identify where energy losses occur by calculating work input at each stage versus work output. They must determine the percentage of energy lost to: bearing friction in pulleys, sliding friction on inclined plane, rope stretch/deformation, and heat generation (using temperature data and specific heat calculations). Teams create energy flow diagrams showing quantified losses at each transformation point. Finally, students propose three specific modifications to reduce energy losses and predict the new system efficiency, supporting their predictions with physics principles and calculations from their analysis.
materials_needed: Compound pulley system with minimum 4 pulleys and mounting framework
30-degree adjustable inclined plane with smooth and rough surface options
Set of masses (500g, 1kg, 2kg, 5kg)
Digital force sensors (3 per group) with data logging capability
Infrared temperature sensors (4 per group)
Stopwatches and meter sticks
Data analysis software (Logger Pro or equivalent)
Pre-calculated theoretical values worksheet for system specifications
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of energy loss calculations at each system stage (25 points), (2) Quality of analysis identifying specific inefficiency sources with supporting data (25 points), (3) Logical reasoning in proposed system improvements with physics justification (25 points), (4) Precision in comparing theoretical vs. actual mechanical advantage across different operating speeds (25 points). Students submit energy flow diagrams, calculation sheets, and written analysis of inefficiency sources.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide partially completed energy flow diagrams and guide them to focus on one energy transformation at a time. Offer calculation templates with units clearly labeled. For advanced learners: challenge them to analyze angular momentum effects in pulley rotation, investigate non-linear friction relationships at different speeds, or design optimal pulley arrangements using their inefficiency data to maximize overall system efficiency.
original_title: Analyzing Energy Transformation Inefficiencies in Multi-Stage Mechanical Systems

title: Code Review and Improvement Recommendations for Basic Calculator Functions
description: Students will evaluate pre-written calculator functions by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and providing specific improvement recommendations. This activity develops critical thinking skills for code analysis and quality assessment in a beginner-friendly context.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the correctness and efficiency of basic calculator functions by analyzing provided code samples and identifying specific errors or improvements
Students will critique programming practices through systematic code review using a structured evaluation checklist
instructions: Begin by distributing three intentionally flawed calculator function code samples (addition, subtraction, multiplication) written in Python to each student pair. Provide the Code Evaluation Checklist covering functionality, readability, error handling, and efficiency. In pairs, students spend 15 minutes testing each function using the provided test cases, documenting which tests pass/fail. Next, students spend 20 minutes systematically evaluating each function against the checklist criteria, rating each aspect as 'Good,' 'Needs Improvement,' or 'Poor' with written justifications. Students then spend 15 minutes writing specific improvement recommendations for each function, including corrected code snippets for identified bugs. Finally, pairs spend 10 minutes presenting their evaluation of one assigned function to another pair, explaining their findings and recommendations. Conclude with a 5-minute whole-class discussion where each pair shares their most significant finding. Instructor circulates throughout, asking probing questions like 'What evidence supports your rating?' and 'How would you prioritize these improvements?' Document student reasoning and provide immediate feedback on evaluation accuracy.
materials_needed: Three Python calculator function files with intentional bugs (.py files)
Code Evaluation Checklist handout with 12 specific criteria
Test cases document with expected inputs/outputs for each function
Evaluation worksheet template for recording findings
Python IDE or online Python interpreter (repl.it or similar)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of bug identification (25%), (2) Quality of evidence-based reasoning (25%), (3) Appropriateness of improvement recommendations (25%), (4) Clarity of written explanations (25%). Students must identify at least 2/3 intentional bugs and provide specific, actionable recommendations to achieve proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example evaluation of a simple 'Hello World' function and pair them with stronger partners. Offer sentence starters like 'This code fails because...' and 'I would improve this by...'. For advanced learners: Include additional functions with subtle logic errors, ask them to suggest alternative implementation approaches, or have them create test cases for edge conditions not covered in the provided materials.

title: Design and Build a Personal Finance Dashboard for College Students
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard that analyzes spending patterns and budget optimization for college students using real financial data. They will design visualizations, implement filtering mechanisms, and develop actionable financial recommendations based on their analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will construct an interactive dashboard with at least 5 different visualization types by integrating multiple data sources and implementing user controls
Students will synthesize financial data patterns to generate three specific, evidence-based budget recommendations through statistical analysis and trend identification
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Preparation (30 minutes)**
Provide students with a dataset containing 6 months of anonymized college student financial transactions (1,500+ records) including categories: food, transportation, entertainment, textbooks, utilities, and income sources. Students work in pairs to clean the data by identifying outliers, standardizing category names, and creating calculated fields for monthly totals and percentage breakdowns.

**Phase 2: Dashboard Design & Planning (20 minutes)**
Students sketch their dashboard layout on paper, deciding on 5 required visualizations: spending trends over time, category breakdown pie chart, income vs. expenses comparison, monthly budget variance analysis, and one custom visualization of their choice. They must plan interactive filters for date ranges and spending categories.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Construction (60 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students build their dashboard following their design. They create calculated fields for budget variance (actual vs. recommended spending), implement dropdown filters for month/category selection, and ensure all visualizations update dynamically. Each visualization must include appropriate titles, axis labels, and color coding.

**Phase 4: Analysis & Recommendations (25 minutes)**
Students analyze their completed dashboard to identify three spending patterns and create corresponding recommendations. They must support each recommendation with specific data points (percentages, dollar amounts, trends) and explain the analytical method used to reach their conclusion.

**Phase 5: Presentation Preparation (15 minutes)**
Pairs prepare a 3-minute presentation demonstrating their dashboard functionality and presenting their top recommendation with supporting evidence.
materials_needed: Anonymized college student financial dataset (CSV format, 1,500+ transaction records)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI software access
Computers with internet connectivity
Sketching paper and pencils for initial design
Sample budget guidelines handout for college students
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Dashboard Functionality (25%) - all 5 visualizations working with proper interactivity; Data Accuracy (20%) - correct calculations and clean data handling; Design Quality (20%) - clear, professional layout with appropriate chart types; Analysis Depth (25%) - three well-supported recommendations with specific data evidence; Presentation (10%) - clear demonstration and explanation. Students must score 3/4 or higher in each category to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide dashboard template with pre-built layout and guided calculation formulas; offer one-on-one software tutorials during construction phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources (local cost of living), add predictive analytics for future spending, or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Provide access to advanced visualization techniques like heat maps or waterfall charts.

title: PMBOK Guide Knowledge Area Components Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall all 49 processes within the 10 PMBOK Guide knowledge areas and their corresponding process groups through structured flashcard drills and timed recall exercises. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of the Project Management Institute's standard framework that practicing project managers must know by heart.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all 49 PMBOK processes and their corresponding knowledge areas within 90 seconds by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will correctly identify which of the 5 process groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) each process belongs to through rapid-fire verbal quizzing
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the complete PMBOK Process Map reference sheet showing all 10 knowledge areas and 49 processes. Give students 15 minutes to study the document silently, encouraging them to create mental associations or mnemonics. Next, distribute pre-made digital flashcards using Anki software, with process names on one side and knowledge area + process group on the reverse. Students spend 20 minutes in individual drill mode, cycling through all 49 cards at least twice. Form pairs for peer testing: Partner A reads a process name, Partner B must state the knowledge area and process group within 5 seconds. Switch roles every 10 processes. Conduct three rounds of this peer testing (15 minutes total). Follow with a whole-class rapid-fire session where you call out random process names and students raise colored cards: blue for Initiating, green for Planning, yellow for Executing, red for Monitoring & Controlling, orange for Closing. Complete 25 random processes in this format. Conclude with individual written recall test: students have 8 minutes to list as many of the 49 processes as possible, organized by knowledge area. No reference materials allowed during testing phase. Immediately after, provide answer key for self-checking and identify gaps for further study.
materials_needed: PMBOK Process Map reference sheets (1 per student)
Anki flashcard software installed on devices/tablets
Pre-loaded PMBOK process flashcard deck file
Colored index cards (5 colors: blue, green, yellow, red, orange)
Timer/stopwatch
Answer key sheets for self-assessment
assessment_method: Success measured by final written recall test: 90-100% accuracy (44-49 processes correctly listed) = Mastery; 80-89% accuracy (39-43 processes) = Proficient; 70-79% accuracy (34-38 processes) = Developing; Below 70% = Needs Additional Study. Processes must be spelled correctly and placed in appropriate knowledge areas. Partial credit given for correct knowledge area placement even if process name is slightly incorrect.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory aids (e.g., 'I People Can Make Dreams' for Integration knowledge area processes). Allow extended study time and reduce initial target to 35 processes. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring them to also recall key inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for each process, or have them create and lead the peer testing rounds for other students.

title: Crisis Leadership Decision Architecture Analysis
description: Students will examine three real-world organizational crisis scenarios to identify and differentiate between the underlying leadership decision-making frameworks, cognitive biases, and stakeholder management approaches used by leaders. They will demonstrate understanding by mapping decision pathways and explaining the rationale behind leadership choices during high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex crisis leadership scenarios by identifying decision-making frameworks, cognitive processes, and stakeholder considerations within authentic organizational contexts
Students will differentiate between various crisis leadership approaches through systematic comparison of decision architectures and their underlying theoretical foundations
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 members (10 minutes setup). Distribute three detailed crisis case studies: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982), BP's Deepwater Horizon response (2010), and Airbnb's pandemic pivot (2020). Each group receives identical materials including timeline documents, stakeholder maps, and decision outcome data. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Groups conduct parallel analysis of all three cases using the provided Decision Architecture Template. Students must identify: (1) the leader's primary decision-making framework (rational, intuitive, or bounded rationality), (2) evidence of specific cognitive biases (confirmation bias, anchoring, availability heuristic), (3) stakeholder prioritization patterns, and (4) communication strategy evolution. Groups document evidence using direct quotes from leadership statements and specific actions taken within 72-hour windows.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Using the Comparative Analysis Matrix, groups systematically compare the three leadership approaches across six dimensions: speed of response, transparency level, stakeholder engagement, resource allocation, communication consistency, and long-term strategic alignment. Students must provide specific examples and metrics where available.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Groups create visual Decision Pathway Maps showing how each leader's cognitive process led to specific outcomes. Maps must include decision points, information inputs, stakeholder influences, and feedback loops. Students prepare 3-minute presentations explaining one key insight about how leadership understanding of crisis dynamics shaped their decision architecture.

Final Phase (20 minutes): Facilitated discussion where groups share insights while instructor records patterns on whiteboard, focusing on how different leadership mental models produce different organizational responses to similar crisis pressures.
materials_needed: Three detailed crisis case study packets with primary source documents
Decision Architecture Template worksheets
Comparative Analysis Matrix handouts
Large poster paper for Decision Pathway Maps
Colored markers and sticky notes
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of framework identification with supporting evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing clear differentiation between approaches (25%), (3) Completeness and clarity of Decision Pathway Maps demonstrating process understanding (25%), (4) Depth of insight in explaining how leadership cognition influenced crisis outcomes (25%). Success requires scoring 3/4 on all dimensions with specific evidence cited from case materials.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted key passages in case studies and offer simplified Decision Architecture Template with guided prompts. Consider pairing with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify additional theoretical frameworks not provided in templates, research subsequent leadership decisions by the same leaders in different contexts, or develop predictive models for crisis leadership effectiveness based on their analysis patterns.

title: Deploy and Configure a Two-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with RDS
description: Students will apply core AWS services to build a functional two-tier web application architecture. They will deploy a web server on EC2, create an RDS MySQL database, and configure the connection between tiers using security groups and VPC settings.
learning_objectives: Students will apply EC2 instance configuration skills by launching, securing, and connecting to a web server instance running a PHP application
Students will apply RDS database management by creating a MySQL database instance and establishing secure connectivity with the web tier through proper security group configuration
instructions: **Pre-activity Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Academy Learner Lab access and a simple PHP contact form application code (available via GitHub link). **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Students launch an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance (t2.micro) in the default VPC, selecting the existing key pair provided by instructor. They must tag the instance with 'Name: [StudentName]-WebServer' and 'Environment: Learning'. **Step 2 (20 minutes):** Students connect to their EC2 instance via SSH and install Apache web server and PHP using yum package manager. They download the provided PHP application code, place it in /var/www/html/, and start the Apache service. Students verify the web application loads by accessing the public IP address. **Step 3 (25 minutes):** Students create an RDS MySQL database instance (db.t3.micro) named 'contactdb' with master username 'admin' and a secure password. They must place it in the default DB subnet group and create a new security group called '[StudentName]-DB-SG' allowing inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) only from their web server's security group. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Students modify their web server's security group to allow inbound HTTP (port 80) from anywhere and SSH (port 22) from their IP only. They update the PHP application's database configuration file with the RDS endpoint, username, and password. **Step 5 (10 minutes):** Students test the complete application by submitting data through the web form and verifying it's stored in the RDS database using MySQL command line connection from the EC2 instance.
materials_needed: AWS Academy Learner Lab accounts with $100 credit limit per student
Pre-built PHP contact form application with MySQL backend (GitHub repository link)
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows, Terminal for Mac/Linux)
Instructor-provided EC2 key pair file (.pem format)
Database connection testing SQL script
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) Running EC2 instance with correct tags, (2) Web application loading in browser, (3) RDS instance status as 'Available', (4) Security group configurations for both web and database tiers, (5) Successful form submission with data visible in database query results. Rubric: EC2 deployment and configuration (25 points), RDS setup and connectivity (25 points), Security group configuration (25 points), End-to-end application functionality (25 points). Pass threshold: 75/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step command cheat sheet for Linux commands. Offer one-on-one troubleshooting for SSH connectivity issues. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like Auto Scaling Groups, Application Load Balancer, or Multi-AZ RDS deployment. Encourage exploration of CloudFormation templates to automate the deployment process.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Evaluating Multi-Project Portfolio Scenarios
description: Students will analyze complex project scenarios containing multiple interconnected risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will deconstruct risk relationships, assess strategy alignment with organizational objectives, and determine optimal response combinations.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between project risks by mapping cause-and-effect relationships within a multi-project portfolio scenario
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies through systematic comparison against PMI risk management principles and organizational constraints
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (10 minutes setup). Distribute the Portfolio Risk Scenario packet containing three interconnected projects with 15 identified risks and 12 proposed response strategies. Each team receives identical materials but different organizational constraint cards (budget limitations, resource availability, timeline pressures). 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams create a risk interdependency matrix, identifying how risks across the three projects influence each other. Students must categorize each risk relationship as: direct impact, indirect impact, or cascade trigger. They document their analysis on the provided matrix template, noting risk probability changes when other risks occur.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams analyze each proposed risk response strategy against PMI's four response categories (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept). Using the strategy evaluation worksheet, they assess each response for: appropriateness to risk type, cost-effectiveness within their assigned constraints, implementation feasibility, and potential secondary risks created. Teams must provide written justification for each evaluation.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams synthesize their analysis to recommend an optimal combination of 8 response strategies from the original 12 options. They must demonstrate how their selected strategies address risk interdependencies while respecting organizational constraints. Final recommendations are documented on the decision matrix template with supporting rationale.

Conclude with team presentations (15 minutes total, 3-4 minutes per team) where groups present their top 3 strategic recommendations and defend their analytical reasoning. Other teams provide peer feedback using the provided evaluation criteria checklist.
materials_needed: Portfolio Risk Scenario packet (3 projects, 15 risks, 12 response strategies)
Risk Interdependency Matrix template (Excel or printed worksheet)
Strategy Evaluation Worksheet with PMI criteria columns
Organizational Constraint Cards (4 different scenarios)
Decision Matrix Template for final recommendations
Peer Evaluation Checklist
Flipchart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Grade using a 100-point rubric: Risk interdependency analysis accuracy (25 points), strategy evaluation thoroughness and PMI alignment (35 points), synthesis quality and constraint consideration (25 points), presentation clarity and peer feedback quality (15 points). Success criteria: 80+ points demonstrates proficient analysis skills, with all risk relationships accurately identified and strategy evaluations showing clear PMI principle application.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed sample of 3 risk relationships and 2 strategy evaluations as reference examples. Offer mid-activity check-ins at 20 and 40-minute marks. For advanced learners: add secondary challenge of calculating risk monetary impact changes based on their strategy selections, or require them to propose 2 alternative strategies not included in the original 12 options.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Critical Assessment for E-commerce Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data to determine which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value. They will defend their recommendations through comprehensive analysis of conversion paths, channel performance, and business impact metrics.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models by comparing data-driven, last-click, and first-click models against actual e-commerce conversion data
Students will justify their attribution model recommendations through systematic analysis of multi-touch conversion paths and ROI calculations across paid search, social media, and email channels
instructions: Begin by providing students with access to a GA4 property containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels active. Students work in teams of 3-4. Step 1 (20 minutes): Each team accesses Reports > Advertising > Attribution and examines the Model Comparison Tool, documenting conversion values across data-driven, last-click, first-click, linear, and time-decay models for paid search, social, and email channels. Step 2 (30 minutes): Teams navigate to Explore > Path Exploration to analyze actual customer conversion paths, identifying common multi-touch sequences and calculating the average path length and time to conversion. Step 3 (25 minutes): Using the Attribution tool's conversion credit analysis, teams calculate ROI differences for each channel under different models, noting which channels gain or lose attribution credit. Step 4 (40 minutes): Teams evaluate business context by reviewing campaign costs in linked Google Ads data and email marketing spend, then determine which attribution model most accurately reflects true channel performance based on customer behavior patterns observed. Step 5 (45 minutes): Each team prepares a formal recommendation presentation defending their chosen attribution model, including specific evidence from path analysis, ROI calculations, and business impact projections. Teams must address potential counterarguments and explain implementation implications for budget allocation across channels.
materials_needed: GA4 property with 6+ months e-commerce data and multiple active marketing channels
Google Ads account linked to GA4 (for cost data)
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
Spreadsheet software for ROI calculations
Access to campaign cost data for email marketing
assessment_method: Teams evaluated using rubric covering: 1) Accuracy of attribution model data extraction and analysis (25%), 2) Quality of conversion path interpretation and insights (25%), 3) Soundness of ROI calculations and business logic (25%), 4) Strength of recommendation defense and counterargument addressing (25%). Deliverables include completed analysis worksheet, ROI calculation spreadsheet, and 10-minute presentation with Q&A defense.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model comparison template with guided questions and pre-calculated examples. Offer additional practice with Path Exploration navigation. For advanced learners: Include analysis of custom attribution models, seasonality impact assessment, and cross-device conversion path evaluation. Challenge them to propose attribution model A/B testing methodology.

title: Interpreting Confusion Matrix Results for Multi-Class Classification Problems
description: Students will analyze pre-generated confusion matrices from three different machine learning models to interpret performance metrics and explain which model performs best for specific business scenarios. This activity develops understanding of model evaluation beyond simple accuracy scores.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret confusion matrix components (true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives) by calculating precision, recall, and F1-scores for each class in a multi-class problem
Students will explain model performance differences through comparative analysis of confusion matrices and justify model selection based on business context
instructions: Begin by distributing three confusion matrices from models predicting customer churn categories (Low Risk, Medium Risk, High Risk) along with the business scenario worksheet. In the first 10 minutes, have students work individually to examine Matrix A and calculate precision, recall, and F1-score for each of the three classes using the provided formulas. Next, organize students into pairs for 15 minutes to compare their calculations and repeat the process for Matrices B and C. During the following 20 minutes, pairs should complete the interpretation worksheet, identifying which model has the highest precision for High Risk customers, which has the best overall recall, and which shows the most balanced performance across all classes. Then present three business scenarios: (1) a company wanting to minimize false alarms to avoid annoying loyal customers, (2) a company that cannot afford to miss any high-risk churners, and (3) a company needing balanced performance across all risk categories. Give pairs 15 minutes to match each scenario with the most appropriate model and write a 2-3 sentence justification for their choice. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where each pair presents one scenario-model pairing and explains their reasoning, while you facilitate discussion about trade-offs between different performance metrics.
materials_needed: Three printed confusion matrices (5x5 tables) for models A, B, and C
Business scenario worksheet with calculation templates
Calculators or laptops with basic calculator function
Formula reference sheet for precision, recall, and F1-score calculations
assessment_method: Grade the completed worksheet using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate calculations of all precision, recall, F1-scores (40%), (2) Correct identification of best-performing model for each metric (30%), (3) Appropriate model-scenario matching with clear business reasoning (30%). Students must achieve 75% accuracy on calculations and provide logical justifications for scenario matching to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a worked example using a 2x2 confusion matrix before starting the activity and offer a step-by-step calculation guide. Create mixed-ability pairs to encourage peer support. For advanced learners, add questions about ROC curves, ask them to calculate macro and micro-averaged F1-scores, or have them propose additional business scenarios where different metrics would be prioritized.

title: Optimization Application: Designing a Water Treatment Plant Distribution System
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to design a cost-effective water distribution system for a municipal treatment plant. They must determine optimal pipe diameters, pump locations, and flow rates while considering real-world constraints including budget limitations, environmental regulations, and service requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constrained optimization methods to minimize total system costs while meeting flow rate and pressure requirements across multiple distribution points
Students will implement partial derivative techniques and gradient analysis through solving a complex engineering optimization problem with multiple variables and constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing the scenario packet containing a city map with 8 service zones, population data, elevation changes, and cost tables for different pipe materials (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a different budget constraint ($2M, $2.5M, or $3M). Students first identify decision variables: pipe diameters (d₁-d₈), pump capacities (P₁-P₃), and flow rates (Q₁-Q₈). Next, they formulate the objective function: Total Cost = Σ(pipe costs + pumping costs + maintenance costs) subject to constraints including flow conservation equations, minimum pressure requirements (≥30 psi at each zone), and maximum velocity limits (≤8 ft/sec). Teams then apply calculus optimization: set up the Lagrangian function L(d,P,Q,λ) incorporating all constraints with multipliers, compute partial derivatives ∂L/∂dᵢ = 0, ∂L/∂Pⱼ = 0, ∂L/∂Qₖ = 0, and solve the resulting system using provided software tools or numerical methods. Students must verify their solution satisfies all physical constraints and compare costs across different design alternatives. Finally, each team prepares a technical report documenting their mathematical approach, solution methodology, optimal design parameters, and cost analysis. Teams present their solutions, explaining how they handled trade-offs between pipe sizing costs and pumping energy costs.
materials_needed: City water distribution scenario packet with maps, population data, and elevation profiles
Cost tables for PVC, steel, and ductile iron pipes (per diameter and length)
Pump specification sheets with cost and energy consumption data
Scientific calculators or computer access with MATLAB/Python optimization libraries
Engineering paper and technical report template
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical formulation accuracy (25 points) - correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints; Solution methodology (30 points) - proper application of Lagrange multipliers and optimization techniques; Constraint verification (20 points) - demonstration that solution meets all physical and regulatory requirements; Technical communication (25 points) - clarity of mathematical notation, logical presentation, and engineering justification of design decisions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled constraint equation templates and guide them through setting up one Lagrangian term before independent work. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify mathematical setup before solving. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including pipe network loops requiring Hardy Cross method, seasonal demand variations, or environmental impact constraints requiring multi-objective optimization techniques.

title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Propulsion Systems Using Energy and Momentum Conservation
description: Students will examine and break down the complex physics of multi-stage rocket launches by analyzing energy transformations, momentum conservation, and mass variations at each stage separation. They will deconstruct real mission data to identify the underlying physical principles and evaluate the efficiency of different staging strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between variable mass systems and momentum conservation by examining rocket equation derivations and stage separation data
Students will evaluate energy transformation patterns in multi-stage rockets through quantitative comparison of kinetic, potential, and chemical energy changes
instructions:
Begin by distributing the SpaceX Falcon Heavy mission data packet containing mass specifications, velocity profiles, and altitude data for each stage (15 minutes setup). Divide students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group a specific mission phase: Stage 1 separation, Stage 2 ignition, or payload deployment. Each group receives the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation (Δv = ve ln(m0/mf)) and energy analysis worksheets.

Students first identify all relevant variables in their assigned phase, including initial mass (m0), final mass (mf), exhaust velocity (ve), and gravitational potential energy changes (20 minutes). They must distinguish between the rocket's changing mass due to fuel consumption versus stage separation events.

Next, groups calculate the theoretical velocity change using the rocket equation and compare it to actual mission data, identifying discrepancies and analyzing potential causes such as atmospheric drag, gravitational losses, or engine inefficiencies (25 minutes). They create energy flow diagrams showing chemical potential energy conversion to kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy, and thermal losses.

Groups then examine the momentum transfer during stage separation, calculating the momentum of discarded stages versus remaining rocket components. They analyze why multi-stage designs are more efficient than single-stage rockets by comparing the mass ratios and velocity increments (20 minutes).

Finally, each group presents their phase analysis to the class, explaining the dominant physical principles and inefficiencies they identified. The class collectively reconstructs the complete mission profile, identifying transition points where different physics concepts become dominant (15 minutes). Groups must defend their analysis when questioned by peers about their assumptions or calculations.
materials_needed: SpaceX Falcon Heavy mission data packets with mass, velocity, and altitude profiles
Scientific calculators or laptops with spreadsheet software
Rocket equation reference sheets and energy transformation worksheets
Graph paper and colored pens for energy flow diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct application of conservation laws with appropriate variable identification, (2) Accurate quantitative analysis with proper units and significant figures, (3) Clear identification of energy transformation pathways and inefficiencies, (4) Logical reasoning in comparing theoretical predictions to actual data with plausible explanations for discrepancies. Students must submit their calculations, energy diagrams, and a 200-word reflection on the dominant physics principle in their assigned phase.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated exhaust velocities and simplified mass ratios, focusing on conceptual understanding over complex calculations. Offer guiding questions like 'What happens to the rocket's acceleration as fuel is consumed?' For advanced learners, introduce relativistic effects for high-velocity stages or challenge them to optimize staging strategies by varying mass ratios and analyzing trade-offs between payload capacity and mission requirements.

title: Evaluating Simple Calculator Code: Bug Detection and Solution Assessment
description: Students will analyze three different implementations of a basic calculator program to identify bugs, assess code quality, and determine which solution best meets given requirements. They will justify their evaluations using specific criteria and provide improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different calculator implementations by identifying bugs, assessing code readability, and comparing functionality against specified requirements
Students will judge the quality of programming solutions through systematic analysis using a provided rubric and defend their conclusions with evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with three printed code samples of simple calculator programs (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division). Each implementation has different issues: Code A has syntax errors, Code B has logical errors but runs, Code C is well-written but missing one required function. Also distribute the requirements checklist and evaluation rubric.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students examine each code sample independently, using the requirements checklist to test functionality. They must: 1) Identify and mark any syntax or logical errors, 2) Rate code readability on the rubric (1-4 scale), 3) Check off which requirements each solution meets, 4) Note any security or efficiency concerns, 5) Test the logic mentally with sample inputs (2+3, 10-5, 6×4, 8÷2).

**Evaluation Phase (15 minutes):** Students complete the evaluation worksheet, ranking the three solutions from best to worst. They must justify their rankings with specific evidence from their analysis. For each solution, they write 2-3 sentences explaining strengths and weaknesses, and provide one concrete improvement suggestion.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations. They discuss differences in rankings and must reach consensus on which solution they would recommend for a beginning programmer to study, providing three supporting reasons.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Pairs share their final recommendations with the class, explaining their top choice and one key improvement they suggested.
materials_needed: Three printed calculator code samples (deliberately containing different types of errors)
Requirements checklist worksheet with 6 specific functionality requirements
Code evaluation rubric with criteria for readability, functionality, and efficiency
Individual evaluation worksheet with ranking sections and justification prompts
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric assessing: 1) Accuracy of bug identification (4 points - finds all major issues), 2) Quality of justification (4 points - uses specific evidence from code), 3) Appropriateness of improvement suggestions (4 points - suggestions are actionable and relevant), 4) Participation in peer discussion (4 points - contributes meaningfully to consensus). Success requires scoring 12/16 points minimum.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a bug-hunting checklist with specific items to look for (missing semicolons, variable names, etc.) and highlight line numbers where issues exist. **For advanced students:** Add a fourth code sample with subtle algorithmic efficiency issues, or ask them to write pseudocode for their recommended improvements. **Additional support:** Create pairs strategically mixing confidence levels during peer review phase.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Comparative Analysis of Authentic Leadership Failures and Recoveries
description: Students will analyze real leadership crisis scenarios by comparing failed versus successful crisis responses to identify underlying leadership principles and decision-making frameworks. This expert-level activity requires students to demonstrate deep understanding of situational leadership theory, stakeholder management, and ethical decision-making under pressure.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective crisis leadership approaches by analyzing documented leadership decisions across multiple authentic case studies
Students will classify leadership responses according to established crisis leadership frameworks through structured comparative analysis matrices
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 (15 minutes setup). Distribute case study packets containing three paired scenarios: each pair includes one leadership crisis failure and one success from similar contexts (e.g., corporate data breaches, natural disaster responses, organizational restructuring). Teams receive: Wells Fargo account scandal vs. Johnson & Johnson Tylenol crisis; Boeing 737 MAX response vs. Southwest Airlines Flight 1380 response; and Yahoo data breach response vs. Equifax post-breach recovery strategy. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze each scenario using the provided Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework, documenting: stakeholder identification and prioritization, communication strategies and timing, decision-making processes, resource allocation, and ethical considerations. Students complete structured comparison matrices for each paired scenario, identifying specific leadership behaviors, decision points, and outcomes.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams synthesize findings across all three pairs to identify patterns. They create a comprehensive analysis document outlining: five critical success factors for crisis leadership, three common failure patterns, and recommendations for crisis leadership preparation. 

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams present their key findings to the class, focusing on one specific leadership principle they identified, supported by evidence from their analysis. Other teams provide feedback using the peer evaluation rubric, identifying strengths in analysis and areas for deeper exploration.
materials_needed: Crisis Leadership Case Study Packet (6 detailed scenarios with timeline, stakeholder maps, and outcome data)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework template with guided questions
Comparative Analysis Matrix worksheets
Peer Evaluation Rubric forms
Access to business databases for additional research (Bloomberg, Harvard Business Review case studies)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership principle identification and application (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis with specific evidence (30%), (3) Depth of understanding demonstrated in synthesis across multiple cases (25%), (4) Clarity and persuasiveness of presentation with peer feedback integration (20%). Success criteria: Students must identify at least 3 distinct leadership principles, provide specific behavioral evidence from cases, and demonstrate understanding of situational factors affecting leadership effectiveness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guided questions within the analysis framework and pair them with stronger analytical thinkers. Offer mid-activity check-ins to ensure understanding of framework application. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify contradictory evidence, explore cultural/industry context factors, or research additional cases that challenge their initial conclusions. Provide access to academic leadership theory articles for deeper theoretical connections.

title: Critical Path Analysis: Identifying Schedule Compression Opportunities in Construction Projects
description: Students will analyze a multi-phase construction project network diagram to identify the critical path, evaluate schedule compression techniques, and determine the optimal combination of crashing and fast-tracking strategies. They will examine trade-offs between cost, risk, and time reduction while maintaining project quality standards.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project network diagrams by identifying critical and near-critical paths using forward and backward pass calculations
Students will evaluate schedule compression alternatives through systematic comparison of crashing costs, fast-tracking risks, and resource optimization strategies
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Riverside Office Complex' project case study containing a 25-activity network diagram with duration, cost, and resource data. Form teams of 3-4 students. Provide each team with calculators, colored pens, and analysis worksheets.

**Phase 1 - Critical Path Identification (20 minutes):** Teams perform forward pass calculations starting from project initiation, recording Early Start (ES) and Early Finish (EF) for each activity. Then conduct backward pass from project completion, calculating Late Start (LS) and Late Finish (LF). Students identify the critical path by finding activities with zero total float (ES=LS and EF=LF). Mark critical activities in red on the network diagram.

**Phase 2 - Compression Analysis (25 minutes):** Using provided cost-per-day crash data, teams calculate the crash cost per day saved for each critical path activity. Simultaneously, they identify potential fast-tracking opportunities by analyzing predecessor relationships and associated risks (rework probability, quality impact scores). Create a comparison matrix ranking options by cost-effectiveness and risk level.

**Phase 3 - Strategy Development (15 minutes):** Teams develop an optimal 30-day schedule compression plan combining crashing and fast-tracking. They must justify their selection using quantitative analysis (crash costs, risk scores) and qualitative factors (resource availability, stakeholder impact). Document assumptions and create a revised network diagram.

**Presentation & Peer Review (15 minutes):** Each team presents their 5-minute solution, highlighting critical path analysis accuracy, compression strategy rationale, and cost-benefit calculations. Other teams provide structured feedback using the provided evaluation checklist.
materials_needed: Riverside Office Complex case study packet with network diagram and activity data sheets
Critical path analysis worksheets with calculation templates
Colored pens (red, blue, green) for diagram marking
Calculators or laptops with Excel
Flip chart paper for presenting revised network diagrams
Peer evaluation checklists
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Critical Path Identification accuracy (25 points - correct ES, EF, LS, LF calculations and path identification), Compression Analysis quality (35 points - accurate crash cost calculations, thorough fast-tracking risk assessment, comprehensive option comparison), Strategy Justification strength (25 points - logical decision-making process, quantitative support, realistic assumptions), and Professional Communication (15 points - clear presentation, effective visual aids, constructive peer feedback). Students must achieve 80+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a partially completed forward pass example and a step-by-step calculation guide. Pair with stronger analytical partners and offer instructor check-ins after each phase. **For advanced learners:** Add resource leveling constraints requiring analysis of resource conflicts and provide Monte Carlo simulation data for incorporating schedule uncertainty. Challenge them to develop contingency plans for high-risk fast-tracking decisions.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and ROI Optimization Assessment
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics by analyzing real e-commerce data across multiple marketing channels. They will assess which attribution model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and make strategic recommendations for budget reallocation based on their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the accuracy and business impact of first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models by comparing conversion values and channel performance metrics
Students will critique current marketing spend allocation through systematic analysis of multi-channel funnel reports and recommend evidence-based budget optimization strategies
instructions:
**Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with at least 5 marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, display). Students work individually on laptops with GA access.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students navigate to Conversions > Attribution > Model Comparison Tool. They must extract and document conversion values, conversion counts, and cost-per-acquisition for each of the five attribution models across all available channels. Students create a comparison matrix showing percentage differences between models for each channel.

**Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (30 minutes):** Using the Multi-Channel Funnel reports, students analyze customer journey patterns, identifying which channels serve as initiators, assisters, and closers. They must evaluate which attribution model most accurately reflects actual customer behavior patterns by examining top conversion paths and time lag reports.

**Phase 3 - Strategic Assessment (35 minutes):** Students assess current marketing spend allocation (provided as supplementary data) against attribution insights. They must identify overvalued and undervalued channels, calculate potential ROI improvements, and evaluate risks associated with budget reallocation recommendations.

**Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (30 minutes):** Students prepare a executive summary presenting their chosen attribution model with justification, three specific budget reallocation recommendations with projected impact percentages, and implementation timeline with success metrics for measuring effectiveness.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Laptops/computers with internet access
Supplementary marketing spend data spreadsheet
Attribution model comparison template worksheet
Executive summary template document
assessment_method: Students submit executive summary reports evaluated using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of attribution model analysis with supporting GA data (25%), (2) Quality of critical evaluation comparing model effectiveness with specific examples (25%), (3) Strategic soundness of budget recommendations with quantified projections (25%), (4) Professional presentation of findings with clear justification for chosen attribution approach (25%). Minimum passing requires demonstrating accurate data extraction, identifying at least two significant attribution differences, and providing three actionable recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled data extraction templates and guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer one-on-one navigation support during initial GA exploration. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using Google Analytics Intelligence API, incorporate statistical significance testing of attribution differences, or add competitive analysis component using similar attribution methodologies.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-VLAN Campus Network with Advanced Security and QoS Implementation
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise campus network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security policies, and Quality of Service (QoS) configurations. This capstone activity requires students to synthesize multiple networking concepts into a cohesive, production-ready network design that addresses real-world business requirements.
estimated_duration: 4.5 hours (270 minutes) spread across 2-3 class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network architecture by analyzing given business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement advanced routing protocols, security access control lists, and QoS policies through hands-on configuration of Cisco devices in a simulated enterprise environment
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp needs a new campus network supporting 500+ users across 4 departments (Engineering, Sales, HR, Guest) with specific security and performance requirements. Step 1 (45 minutes): Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze requirements and create comprehensive network design documentation including logical topology diagrams, VLAN planning (minimum 6 VLANs including management and DMZ), IP addressing scheme using VLSM, and equipment specifications. Step 2 (90 minutes): Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical lab equipment, teams configure their designed network implementing: Layer 2 switching with VTP, STP optimization, and port security; Layer 3 routing using OSPF with multiple areas; inter-VLAN routing via router-on-a-stick or SVI configuration. Step 3 (60 minutes): Implement advanced security features including standard and extended ACLs for inter-department traffic control, DHCP snooping and DAI for Layer 2 security, and basic firewall rules on edge devices. Step 4 (45 minutes): Configure QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic (highest), video conferencing (high), business applications (medium), and internet browsing (low) using classification, marking, and queuing mechanisms. Step 5 (30 minutes): Conduct comprehensive testing including connectivity verification between all VLANs, security policy validation by attempting blocked connections, QoS effectiveness testing using traffic generators, and network convergence testing by simulating link failures. Document all configurations and create troubleshooting procedures for common issues.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software (latest version) or physical lab with 4 Cisco switches (2960 series), 2 routers (ISR 4000 series), and connecting cables
Network design templates and business requirement specification documents
IP address planning worksheets and VLSM calculation tools
Traffic generation software for QoS testing (OSTINATO or similar)
Network documentation templates for configuration backup and procedures
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network design documentation quality and feasibility (25 points), successful implementation of all required features with proper configuration syntax (35 points), security policy effectiveness demonstrated through testing scenarios (20 points), QoS implementation with measurable traffic prioritization (15 points), and professional presentation of final network with troubleshooting documentation (5 points). Teams must demonstrate live network functionality and defend design decisions during 10-minute presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic connectivity established, offer configuration checklists for each technology component, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. Create optional guided practice labs for individual technologies before integration. For advanced learners: Add requirements for IPv6 dual-stack implementation, advanced routing features like route redistribution and policy-based routing, network automation using Python scripts, or integration with wireless controllers and access points. Challenge them to optimize for specific metrics like convergence time or bandwidth utilization.

title: Python Data Types Memory Card Matching Game
description: Students will memorize and recall the six fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) and their corresponding example values through a structured card matching activity. This kinesthetic learning approach helps beginners build essential foundational knowledge needed for all Python programming.
learning_objectives: Students will identify all six fundamental Python data types (int, float, str, bool, list, dict) by matching data type names with their correct definitions
Students will recall specific example values for each Python data type through repeated practice with flashcard exercises
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Create 24 index cards - 6 cards with data type names (int, float, str, bool, list, dict), 6 cards with definitions, and 12 cards with example values (2 examples per type).
