Shuffle all cards and place face-down on desks. **Round 1 (15 minutes):** Students work in pairs. Each pair receives one complete set of 24 cards. Students spread cards face-down in a 4x6 grid. Taking turns, each student flips two cards trying to match data type names with their definitions (int matches 'whole numbers', float matches 'decimal numbers', etc.). When a match is found, students must verbally state the match before keeping the cards. Continue until all name-definition pairs are matched. **Round 2 (15 minutes):** Reset with cards showing data type names and example values only (18 cards total). Students now match data type names with example values (int matches '42' and '-7', str matches 'hello' and 'Python', etc.). **Round 3 (10 minutes):** Quick recall test - instructor calls out a data type name, students must immediately write down the definition and two example values. **Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students create their own memory aid by writing all six data types, definitions, and examples on a reference sheet they can keep.
materials_needed: Index cards (24 per pair of students)
Black markers for writing cards
Printed data type reference sheet template
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key for instructor verification
assessment_method: Students must correctly match at least 5 out of 6 data type-definition pairs and 10 out of 12 example values to achieve mastery. Final assessment through quick recall test where students score 1 point for correct definition and 1 point for each correct example (maximum 18 points, passing score 15/18).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce to 4 data types initially (int, str, bool, list) and provide visual cues with color-coded cards. For advanced learners: Add complex data types (tuple, set) and require students to create original examples or identify invalid examples mixed into the cards.

title: Python Data Types Memory Card Matching Game: Practical Workshop
description: Students will memorize and recall the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) and their corresponding example values through a structured card matching activity. This hands-on game reinforces fundamental programming concepts through repetitive practice and peer interaction.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the five basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list) by matching data type names with correct example values
Students will recall Python data type syntax and formatting rules through repeated card matching exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing one set of 20 pre-made cards to each group of 3-4 students (10 cards show data type names: int, float, string, boolean, list - with 2 copies each; 10 cards show example values: 42, -17, 3.14, -0.5, 'hello', "Python", True, False, [1,2,3], ['a','b']). Have students shuffle all cards and place them face-down in a 4x5 grid on their desk. 

Explain the rules: players take turns flipping two cards, attempting to match a data type with a correct example. When a match is found, the player keeps the pair and takes another turn. If no match, cards are flipped back face-down and the next player goes. Before keeping any pair, the student must verbally state the data type name and explain why the example represents that type (e.g., "This is an integer because 42 is a whole number with no decimal point").

Circulate during the 15-minute game period, listening to explanations and correcting misconceptions immediately. Stop play every 5 minutes to have groups recite all five data types in unison. After the matching game ends, conduct a 5-minute rapid-fire recall session where you display example values on the projector and students write down the corresponding data type on their worksheet.

Conclude with each student completing a solo memory quiz: present 10 Python values (mix of all five data types) and have them write the correct data type name beside each value within 3 minutes. Collect worksheets for immediate assessment.
materials_needed: Pre-made card sets (20 cards per group of 3-4 students)
Individual worksheets with 10 practice problems
Projector or smartboard for displaying examples
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must score 8/10 or higher on the final solo memory quiz to demonstrate mastery. During card matching, observe and document whether students can correctly verbalize data type explanations. Award full credit for accurate identification and partial credit for correct data type with unclear explanation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with data type definitions and allow them to use it during the first round only. For advanced learners, introduce additional data types (tuple, dictionary) or ask them to create their own example values for each category during extended practice time.
original_title: Python Data Types Memory Card Matching Game

title: Interpreting Customer Churn Analysis Results from Different Machine Learning Models
description: Students will analyze and interpret the outputs from three different machine learning models (logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting) trained on a customer churn dataset. They will compare model performance metrics, explain feature importance rankings, and articulate the business implications of each model's predictions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret confusion matrices, ROC curves, and feature importance plots by analyzing numerical outputs and visual representations from three different ML models
Students will explain the relationship between model performance metrics (precision, recall, F1-score) and business decision-making through structured comparison exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared model results packet containing confusion matrices, classification reports, ROC curves, and feature importance plots for all three models trained on the telecom churn dataset. In pairs, students spend 15 minutes examining the logistic regression results first, completing the 'Model Interpretation Worksheet' sections 1-3 which ask them to identify the true positive rate, explain what a precision of 0.73 means in business terms, and rank the top 5 most important features. Next, pairs spend 20 minutes comparing all three models using the worksheet's comparison matrix, filling in performance metrics and noting which model has the highest recall and why this matters for churn prediction. During the following 15 minutes, each pair selects one model they would recommend to the business stakeholder and prepares a 2-minute explanation focusing on the trade-offs between false positives (wasted retention efforts) and false negatives (lost customers). In the final 20 minutes, pairs present their recommendations while the instructor facilitates discussion about why different pairs might choose different models based on business priorities. Throughout the activity, students must reference specific numbers from the model outputs and connect technical metrics to real-world consequences. The instructor circulates during pair work to check that students are correctly reading the confusion matrices and can explain what feature importance scores represent in practical terms.
materials_needed: Pre-generated model results packet (3 pages per student) with confusion matrices, ROC curves, and feature importance plots
Model Interpretation Worksheet with structured comparison sections
Telecom customer churn dataset description sheet explaining features like 'monthly_charges' and 'contract_type'
Calculators or laptops for metric calculations
assessment_method: Grade completed worksheets using rubric: 4 points for correctly interpreting confusion matrix values, 4 points for accurately explaining precision/recall in business context, 4 points for logical model recommendation with supporting evidence from metrics, 3 points for clear presentation connecting technical results to business impact. Total: 15 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a 'metrics cheat sheet' defining precision as TP/(TP+FP) with business translation examples. Highlight key numbers in the results packet. For advanced students: include additional metrics like AUC scores and ask them to calculate cost-benefit analysis assuming $100 cost per retention campaign and $500 value per retained customer.

title: Code Review and Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate three different implementations of basic calculator functions (add, subtract, multiply, divide) written by fictional developers. They will assess code quality, identify strengths and weaknesses, and rank the implementations based on established criteria including readability, efficiency, error handling, and best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different code implementations by applying specific quality criteria and providing justified rankings
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic analysis of code structure, documentation, and functionality
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with three printed code samples (Implementation A, B, and C) of calculator functions in their chosen beginner language (Python recommended). Each implementation should have different strengths/weaknesses: A) well-documented but inefficient, B) efficient but poorly named variables, C) good structure but missing error handling. Give students the evaluation rubric with four criteria: Code Readability (25%), Functionality (25%), Error Handling (25%), and Best Practices (25%).

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine each implementation independently, taking notes on strengths and weaknesses for each criterion. They test the code mentally or on paper with sample inputs (5+3, 10÷0, 7-2, 4×6) to assess functionality and error handling.

**Scoring and Ranking (10 minutes):** Students assign scores (1-4 scale) for each criterion per implementation, calculate total scores, and rank implementations from best to worst. They must write 2-3 sentence justifications for their rankings.

**Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss differences in evaluation. They must defend their choices using specific evidence from the code.

**Final Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write which implementation they would recommend for a beginner programmer to study and why, demonstrating their ability to evaluate code for educational value.
materials_needed: Three printed code implementation samples (Implementation A, B, C)
Code evaluation rubric handout with 4 criteria
Sample test cases worksheet (5 mathematical problems including edge cases)
Individual scoring sheet with 1-4 scale ratings
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Completion of scoring rubric with justified numerical ratings for each criterion, (2) Written ranking with specific evidence-based justifications, (3) Quality of final recommendation showing synthesis of evaluation criteria. Success criteria: Students identify at least 2 specific strengths and 2 weaknesses per implementation, provide logical ranking based on rubric scores, and demonstrate understanding of code quality principles in their recommendation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example evaluation of one criterion for Implementation A, offer sentence starters for justifications ('This code is better because...', 'The main weakness is...'). For advanced students: Add a fourth implementation with subtle bugs to evaluate, ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-ranked implementation, or have them create their own evaluation criteria beyond the provided rubric.

title: Code Review and Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Functions: Practical Workshop
description: Students will critically evaluate pre-written calculator function code samples by applying coding standards, identifying bugs, and recommending improvements. They will compare different implementations and justify which version demonstrates better software development practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality of basic Python functions by applying established coding standards and identifying logical errors
Students will critique different code implementations through systematic comparison using a structured rubric
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Calculator Code Review Packet' containing three different implementations of basic calculator functions (add, subtract, multiply, divide). Each implementation has intentional issues: Version A has poor variable naming and no comments, Version B has logical errors in division function, Version C has good structure but inefficient code. **Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students use the provided 'Code Quality Checklist' to evaluate each version across five criteria: readability, functionality, error handling, efficiency, and documentation. They must identify specific problems, mark line numbers, and rate each criterion on a 1-4 scale. **Pair Discussion (15 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their evaluations, discuss disagreements, and refine their assessments. Each pair must reach consensus on which version is best overall. **Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Students individually rank all three versions from best to worst and write a 100-word justification explaining their ranking based on evidence from their analysis. **Class Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates discussion where pairs share their rankings and reasoning. Students must defend their choices using specific examples from the code.
materials_needed: Calculator Code Review Packet with 3 Python code versions (printed or digital)
Code Quality Checklist rubric handout
Computers with Python IDE or code viewer
Evaluation worksheet for student responses
assessment_method: Students submit completed evaluation worksheets showing: (1) Detailed analysis of each code version with specific line references, (2) Numerical ratings for each quality criterion with brief explanations, (3) Final ranking with 100-word written justification using evidence from their analysis. Success criteria: Identifies at least 3 specific issues per code version, provides accurate functionality assessment, and justification demonstrates clear reasoning based on coding standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example evaluation of a simple 'hello world' function first, highlight specific lines to focus on, offer sentence starters for justifications. For advanced learners: Include additional code samples with more complex issues, ask them to suggest specific code improvements, or have them create their own 'good vs. poor' code examples for peer evaluation.
original_title: Code Review and Quality Assessment: Evaluating Simple Calculator Functions

title: Adaptive Leadership Framework Analysis Through Crisis Case Deconstruction
description: Students will analyze real organizational crisis scenarios through the lens of Heifetz's Adaptive Leadership model, identifying technical vs. adaptive challenges and explaining how leaders navigate the productive zone of disequilibrium. This activity develops deep comprehension of adaptive leadership principles by examining authentic leadership decisions during organizational transformation.
learning_objectives: Students will distinguish between technical problems and adaptive challenges by categorizing specific leadership decisions from three crisis case studies
Students will explain the relationship between productive disequilibrium and adaptive change through detailed analysis of leader behaviors and organizational responses
instructions:
Begin by distributing three detailed crisis case studies (Netflix's pivot from DVD to streaming, IBM's transformation under Lou Gerstner, and Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis response). Provide students with the Adaptive Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet containing four analytical categories: Challenge Type Identification, Disequilibrium Management, Stakeholder Response Patterns, and Leadership Intervention Strategies.

Step 1 (20 minutes): Students work individually to read one assigned case study and complete initial framework analysis, identifying at least 5 specific examples of technical problems versus adaptive challenges within their case.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Form expert groups of 3-4 students who analyzed the same case. Groups collaborate to refine their analysis, reaching consensus on challenge categorization and documenting evidence for each framework component. Each group creates a visual mapping showing the progression from disequilibrium to adaptation.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Reorganize into mixed groups containing one expert from each case study. Students present their case analysis using the framework, explaining how their assigned leader managed productive disequilibrium and facilitated organizational adaptation. Other group members ask clarifying questions and identify patterns across cases.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each mixed group synthesizes findings by creating a comparative chart highlighting commonalities and differences in adaptive leadership approaches across all three crisis scenarios. Groups identify three key principles that effective adaptive leaders consistently demonstrate when managing organizational transformation.
materials_needed: Three detailed case study packets (Netflix transformation, IBM turnaround, Tylenol crisis)
Adaptive Leadership Analysis Framework worksheets
Large poster paper and colored markers for visual mapping
Digital timer for activity transitions
Comparative analysis template sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy in distinguishing technical vs. adaptive challenges (25%), (2) Quality of evidence supporting framework analysis (25%), (3) Depth of explanation regarding disequilibrium management strategies (25%), and (4) Synthesis quality in comparative analysis and principle identification (25%). Students must demonstrate understanding by providing specific textual evidence and explaining cause-effect relationships between leadership actions and organizational outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted case study excerpts and sentence starters for framework analysis. Offer advanced learners additional complexity by introducing competing leadership theories (transformational, authentic leadership) for comparative analysis. Consider pairing English language learners with strong verbal processors during group discussions.

title: E-commerce Attribution Model Performance Evaluation and Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data from Google Analytics 4. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model performance against business objectives, and provide strategic recommendations for optimal attribution model selection.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and calculating revenue attribution differences of at least 15% between models
Students will critique attribution model performance through comparative analysis of customer journey data and defend their strategic recommendations using quantitative evidence from GA4 reports
instructions: **Setup (10 minutes):** Provide students with access to GA4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store) or prepared dataset containing 90 days of e-commerce data with multi-channel conversion paths. Ensure students can access Attribution > Model Comparison and Advertising > Attribution reports. **Phase 1 - Data Collection (25 minutes):** Students extract attribution data by: 1) Navigating to Attribution > Model Comparison, 2) Setting date range to last 90 days, 3) Comparing all five attribution models simultaneously, 4) Recording conversions and revenue for each model in provided spreadsheet template, 5) Documenting top 10 conversion paths from Attribution > Conversion Paths report. **Phase 2 - Analysis (30 minutes):** Students calculate: 1) Percentage revenue difference between each model and last-click baseline, 2) Channel performance variations across models, 3) Average conversion path length and time-to-conversion, 4) Revenue-per-conversion for each attribution approach. **Phase 3 - Business Context Integration (20 minutes):** Provide business scenario: 'Company has 45-day average consideration period, focuses on customer lifetime value, and runs integrated campaigns across paid search, display, and social media.' Students must evaluate which attribution model best serves these objectives. **Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (25 minutes):** Students create executive summary including: 1) Quantitative comparison table, 2) Model strengths/weaknesses analysis, 3) Primary recommendation with justification, 4) Implementation timeline and success metrics, 5) Potential challenges and mitigation strategies. **Presentation (10 minutes):** Students present 3-minute recommendations to class, defending their choice against peer questions.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account access (Google Merchandise Store)
Attribution analysis spreadsheet template with pre-built formulas
Business scenario handout with company objectives and constraints
Executive summary template with required sections
Laptops/computers with internet access
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 100-point rubric: Data accuracy and completeness (25 points) - correctly extracted and calculated attribution metrics; Analysis depth (25 points) - identified significant patterns and model differences with supporting evidence; Business alignment (25 points) - recommendation clearly connects to stated business objectives with logical reasoning; Professional presentation (25 points) - clear executive summary format with defendable conclusions. Success requires minimum 80% score and ability to justify recommendation when challenged by instructor questions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step GA4 navigation screenshots, pre-populate spreadsheet with sample calculations, offer simplified business scenario focusing on single objective. For advanced learners: Include custom attribution model creation using GA4's data-driven attribution settings, require statistical significance testing of results, add competitive analysis component comparing attribution strategies across industries, challenge them to propose A/B testing framework for attribution model validation.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drilling with Partner Verification
description: Students will memorize decimal-to-binary conversions for numbers 0-31 through structured flashcard practice and peer testing. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of binary representations essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-31 by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify binary place values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16) through structured memorization exercises and peer verification
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-31 on one side and binary equivalents on the other. Pair students and assign roles: 'Learner' and 'Tester.' **Round 1 - Individual Study (10 minutes):** Learners study cards independently, focusing on numbers 0-15 first. They should cover the binary side and attempt to recall each conversion, then flip to verify. Encourage students to identify patterns (powers of 2). **Round 2 - Partner Testing (8 minutes):** Testers show decimal numbers in random order. Learners have 5 seconds per card to state the binary equivalent. Testers mark correct/incorrect responses on tracking sheet. Focus only on numbers 0-15. **Round 3 - Expanded Practice (10 minutes):** Repeat individual study with full set (0-31). Students should group difficult numbers separately for extra attention. **Round 4 - Full Assessment (10 minutes):** Partners switch roles. New learners attempt all 32 conversions while being timed and scored. **Wrap-up (2 minutes):** Students record their scores and identify three numbers they found most challenging for additional practice. Partners briefly discuss patterns they noticed (e.g., powers of 2, doubling patterns).
materials_needed: 32 pre-printed flashcards with decimal numbers 0-31 on front, binary equivalents on back
Tracking sheets for recording correct/incorrect responses
Timer or stopwatch for each pair
Pencils for scoring
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (29/32 correct) on the final partner test within 3 minutes. Track individual scores on recording sheet. Success criteria: correctly state binary equivalent within 5-second time limit per card. Record specific numbers missed for targeted remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with only numbers 0-15, provide binary place value reference chart (16-8-4-2-1), and extend time limits to 8 seconds per card. For advanced learners: Include hexadecimal equivalents on back of cards, reduce time limit to 3 seconds per card, or extend range to 0-63.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Behavior Data
description: Students will analyze a pre-processed customer dataset to identify and interpret correlation patterns between demographic features and purchase behavior. They will create correlation matrices, distinguish between different correlation strengths, and explain the business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer demographic variables and purchase amounts by analyzing correlation matrices and explaining the strength and direction of relationships
Students will distinguish between spurious and meaningful correlations through guided analysis of feature relationships in customer behavior data
instructions: Begin by providing each student with the 'customer_behavior.csv' dataset containing 1000 records with features: age, income, education_years, family_size, and monthly_purchase_amount. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. Step 1 (10 min): Students load the dataset in Jupyter Notebook and use pandas.corr() to generate a correlation matrix, then create a heatmap using seaborn. Step 2 (15 min): Students identify the three strongest positive correlations and three strongest negative correlations, recording the exact coefficient values and variable pairs in their analysis worksheet. Step 3 (15 min): Using the provided correlation interpretation guide (weak: 0-0.3, moderate: 0.3-0.7, strong: 0.7-1.0), students categorize each identified correlation and write 2-3 sentences explaining what each relationship means in business terms. Step 4 (5 min): Students compare their findings with another pair, discussing any discrepancies in interpretation. Instructor circulates to check correlation calculations and guide discussions about causation vs. correlation. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where pairs share one surprising correlation they discovered and explain its potential business significance.
materials_needed: customer_behavior.csv dataset (provided via LMS)
Jupyter Notebook with pandas, seaborn, matplotlib pre-installed
Correlation Analysis Worksheet (PDF handout)
Correlation Interpretation Reference Guide
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct correlation coefficient identification (25%), (2) Accurate strength categorization using provided ranges (25%), (3) Clear business interpretation of relationships (35%), (4) Distinction between correlation types with reasoning (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide correlation coefficient lookup table and sentence starters like 'When [variable] increases, [variable] tends to...' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional data collection that might reveal causation. Consider providing partial correlation analysis as an extension.

title: Optimizing Municipal Water Distribution Network Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world municipal water distribution problem, determining optimal flow rates and pump operations to minimize costs while meeting demand constraints. They will use both graphical and algebraic methods to validate their solutions and interpret results in the context of city infrastructure planning.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-variable optimization problem by translating real-world water distribution constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the simplex method and graphical analysis through systematic problem-solving to determine optimal resource allocation in municipal infrastructure
instructions: Begin by distributing the Municipal Water Authority case study packet containing a city map with 6 districts, current water demand data, pump capacity specifications, and operational cost structures (15 minutes setup). Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze the scenario where they must determine optimal water flow from 3 treatment plants to 6 districts while minimizing pumping costs and meeting minimum pressure requirements. Each team first identifies decision variables (flow rates from each plant to each district), formulates the objective function (minimize total pumping costs = 0.12x₁ + 0.15x₂ + 0.18x₃ + operational costs), and establishes constraints (demand requirements: x₁ + x₂ + x₃ ≥ district demand; capacity limits: plant output ≤ maximum capacity; pressure maintenance: flow combinations must maintain 40+ PSI). Teams spend 25 minutes setting up their linear programming model, then 30 minutes solving using graphical method for simplified 2-variable version and Excel Solver for full problem. Students must create a feasible region graph, identify corner points, evaluate the objective function at each vertex, and determine the optimal solution. Next, teams spend 20 minutes interpreting results by calculating total daily costs, determining which plants operate at capacity, and identifying bottlenecks in the distribution network. Finally, students prepare a 10-minute presentation recommending their optimal solution to the 'city council' (class), including cost-benefit analysis and addressing potential implementation challenges such as equipment upgrades or demand fluctuations.
materials_needed: Municipal Water Authority case study packets with city maps and data tables
Graph paper and colored pencils for feasible region plotting
Laptops with Excel and Solver add-in installed
Scientific calculators
Presentation materials (flip chart paper, markers)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical formulation accuracy (25 points - correct identification of variables, objective function, and constraints), Solution methodology (30 points - proper application of graphical and algebraic methods), Computational accuracy (20 points - correct optimal values and cost calculations), Real-world interpretation (15 points - meaningful analysis of results in municipal context), and Professional presentation (10 points - clear communication of recommendations with supporting evidence)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed constraint matrix and guided worksheet breaking down the formulation process into smaller steps. Offer visual aids showing the relationship between mathematical constraints and physical infrastructure limitations. For advanced learners, introduce integer programming extensions (pumps can only operate at discrete levels), sensitivity analysis to determine how demand changes affect optimal solutions, or multi-objective optimization considering both cost and environmental impact. Provide additional scenarios with different city layouts or seasonal demand variations.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures Through Diagnostic Troubleshooting
description: Students analyze complex circuit diagrams containing intentional design flaws and component failures to identify root causes of system malfunctions. They will deconstruct circuit behavior, examine component interactions, and determine which specific elements are causing observed symptoms.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-loop circuits with mixed AC/DC components by systematically examining voltage, current, and power relationships at each node
Students will differentiate between circuit design flaws and component failures through comparative analysis of theoretical versus measured circuit behavior
instructions:
Begin by distributing three different circuit diagrams (15 minutes setup): Circuit A contains a short circuit in a parallel branch, Circuit B has an incorrectly rated capacitor causing phase issues, and Circuit C has a faulty transistor in an amplification stage. Provide each team of 3-4 students with multimeters, function generators, and breadboard components. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Students first calculate theoretical values for voltage, current, and power at 8 designated test points using Kirchhoff's laws, Ohm's law, and AC circuit analysis. They must show all calculations and create expected value tables.

Phase 2 (60 minutes): Teams build their assigned circuit and measure actual values at the same test points. They record discrepancies between theoretical and measured values, noting any unusual behavior (excessive heat, unexpected voltage drops, distorted waveforms).

Phase 3 (30 minutes): Students analyze their data by creating comparison charts and identifying patterns in the discrepancies. They must determine whether issues stem from design flaws, component failures, or measurement errors.

Phase 4 (45 minutes): Each team presents their analysis to the class, explaining their diagnostic process, supporting evidence, and proposed solutions. Other teams ask probing questions about methodology and conclusions.

Conclude with a 15-minute debrief where students compare their analytical approaches and discuss how different failure modes manifest in circuit behavior.
materials_needed: Three pre-designed circuit diagrams with intentional flaws
Digital multimeters (one per team)
Function generators with oscilloscope capability
Breadboards and standard electronic components (resistors, capacitors, transistors)
Circuit analysis software (LTSpice or equivalent)
Comparison chart templates
assessment_method: Grade using a 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Accuracy of theoretical calculations and systematic approach (25%), (2) Quality of experimental data collection and measurement techniques (25%), (3) Logical analysis connecting discrepancies to root causes with supporting evidence (30%), (4) Clear presentation of diagnostic reasoning and proposed solutions (20%). Students must correctly identify the specific failure mode and provide quantitative evidence supporting their conclusion.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide step-by-step calculation templates and highlight which circuit laws apply to each analysis step. Offer additional practice with simpler single-loop circuits first. For advanced learners, introduce multiple simultaneous failures or ask them to design diagnostic test procedures for circuits they haven't seen before. Encourage use of circuit simulation software to verify their theoretical predictions.

title: Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Fixing Solutions
description: Students will evaluate and compare three different solutions to a simple programming problem, identifying the most effective approach based on readability, efficiency, and correctness criteria. They will justify their choice through written analysis and peer discussion.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different code solutions by analyzing their correctness, readability, and efficiency using established criteria
Students will justify their evaluation decisions through structured written reasoning and defend their choices in peer discussions
instructions: Begin by displaying three different Python solutions to calculate the sum of even numbers from 1 to 100 on the board or projector. Solution A uses a for loop with modulo operator, Solution B uses list comprehension, and Solution C uses a while loop with increment by 2. Give students 5 minutes to read through all three solutions individually. Distribute the evaluation worksheet with three criteria sections: Correctness (Does it work? Are there bugs?), Readability (Is it easy to understand?), and Efficiency (How fast/memory-efficient is it?). Have students spend 15 minutes independently scoring each solution on a 1-5 scale for each criterion, writing 2-3 sentence justifications for each score. Next, arrange students in groups of 3-4 to compare their evaluations for 10 minutes, discussing differences in their scoring. Each group must reach consensus on which solution is 'best overall' and prepare a 2-minute presentation explaining their reasoning. Groups present their findings (12 minutes total), after which facilitate a 8-minute whole-class discussion about evaluation criteria and how different priorities (speed vs. readability) might change their conclusions. Conclude by having students individually write a 100-word reflection on what makes code 'good' and how evaluation criteria might change based on project context.
materials_needed: Three pre-written Python code solutions printed or displayed
Code evaluation worksheet with scoring rubric
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or projector for displaying code
Paper for student reflections
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Evaluation Quality (scored each solution appropriately with clear reasoning), Justification Depth (provided specific examples from code to support scores), Peer Collaboration (actively participated in group consensus-building), and Critical Thinking (reflection demonstrates understanding of context-dependent evaluation). Each category worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide guiding questions like 'What happens if you trace through this code step by step?' and 'Which variable names help you understand the purpose?' For advanced learners, add a fourth solution with intentional bugs or ask them to consider additional criteria like maintainability or scalability.

title: Creating a Multi-Source Customer Segmentation Dashboard with Predictive Recommendations
description: Students will design and build an interactive business intelligence dashboard that combines customer transaction data, demographic information, and behavioral analytics to create distinct customer segments. They will develop actionable marketing recommendations based on their segmentation analysis and present findings through data visualizations.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer transaction data, demographic profiles, and behavioral metrics by creating a comprehensive segmentation model using clustering algorithms
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through data visualization tools that communicates customer insights and generates specific business recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration (45 minutes)**
Provide student teams of 3-4 with three separate CSV datasets: customer_transactions.csv (purchase history, amounts, frequency), customer_demographics.csv (age, location, income brackets), and customer_behavior.csv (website clicks, email opens, social media engagement). Students must first examine data quality, identify missing values, and create a unified customer dataset by matching customer IDs across all three sources. Have them document data cleaning decisions and create a data dictionary.

**Phase 2: Segmentation Development (60 minutes)**
Using their integrated dataset, students perform exploratory data analysis to identify patterns. They must create at least 4 distinct customer segments using K-means clustering or similar techniques, considering variables like purchase frequency, average order value, engagement scores, and demographic factors. Students name each segment (e.g., 'Budget-Conscious Millennials', 'High-Value Loyalists') and write detailed personas describing typical customers in each group.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students build an interactive dashboard using Tableau, Power BI, or similar tools. Required components include: segment size comparison charts, geographic distribution maps, revenue contribution by segment, behavioral pattern visualizations, and trend analysis over time. Each visualization must include clear titles, appropriate color schemes, and interactive filters allowing users to drill down into specific segments.

**Phase 4: Recommendation Development (30 minutes)**
Teams develop 3-5 specific, actionable marketing recommendations for each customer segment, supported by their data analysis. Recommendations must include target channels, messaging themes, promotional strategies, and expected outcomes with quantified goals.
materials_needed: Three pre-prepared CSV datasets with customer data (transactions, demographics, behavior)
Tableau Public, Power BI Desktop, or Google Data Studio access
Excel or Google Sheets for data cleaning
Presentation template for final recommendations
Sample business context document describing the fictional company
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (20 points - completeness, accuracy of joins, cleaning documentation), Segmentation Analysis (25 points - statistical validity, meaningful segments, clear personas), Dashboard Design (30 points - visual clarity, interactivity, professional appearance), Business Recommendations (20 points - specificity, data support, feasibility), and Presentation Quality (5 points - clarity, time management). Students submit their cleaned dataset, dashboard file, and a 2-page executive summary of findings and recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned sample data and dashboard templates with placeholder visualizations to modify. Offer guided worksheets for persona development and recommendation frameworks. For advanced learners: Include additional datasets (seasonal trends, competitor data) and challenge them to incorporate predictive modeling elements like customer lifetime value calculations or churn prediction scores into their segmentation approach.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Components Recall Challenge
description: Students will systematically recall and identify specific components, processes, and terminology from advanced project management frameworks including PRINCE2, Agile-Waterfall hybrid models, and PMI's Program Management Standard. This activity tests detailed memorization of complex methodologies through structured retrieval exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the seven principles, seven themes, and seven processes of PRINCE2 methodology by completing timed identification exercises
Students will identify specific roles, artifacts, and governance structures across multiple advanced PM frameworks through systematic memory retrieval tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the framework component cards face-down to each student (15 minutes setup). Students work individually for the first phase. Start with Round 1 (20 minutes): Display partial framework diagrams on screen showing PRINCE2, SAFe, and PMI Program Management structures with key components removed. Students must write down the missing elements from memory - including specific role titles (e.g., 'Senior Supplier,' 'Release Train Engineer'), process names (e.g., 'Managing Product Delivery,' 'Innovation and Planning Iteration'), and artifact types (e.g., 'Program Benefits Management Plan,' 'Definition of Done'). Round 2 (15 minutes): Flash terminology cards for 5 seconds each - students write definitions for 30 advanced terms like 'Epic Hypothesis Statement,' 'PRINCE2 Exception Report,' 'Program Roadmap,' and 'SAFe DevOps transformation patterns.' Round 3 (20 minutes): Present scrambled process flows from different methodologies. Students must sequence 45 specific steps correctly across three frameworks and identify which framework each belongs to. Final phase (10 minutes): Students self-check answers using provided answer keys, marking correct responses. Instructor reviews common errors and clarifies frequently missed components. No discussion or collaboration allowed until the checking phase to ensure pure recall assessment.
materials_needed: Laminated framework component cards with 150+ specific elements
Digital presentation slides with incomplete PRINCE2, SAFe, and PMI diagrams
Printed answer sheets with numbered spaces for 45 responses
Timer/stopwatch for each round
Comprehensive answer keys with exact terminology
Projector/screen for displaying framework diagrams
assessment_method: Students earn points based on exact terminology accuracy: 2 points for completely correct responses (exact spelling and context), 1 point for substantially correct responses with minor errors, 0 points for incorrect/missing responses. Success criteria: 80% accuracy (72/90 possible points) demonstrates mastery of advanced framework recall. Track specific error patterns across PRINCE2 principles vs. processes, SAFe roles vs. ceremonies, and PMI artifacts vs. deliverables for targeted remediation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework summary sheets 24 hours before activity and allow use of one 'reference card' during Round 1 only. For advanced learners: Add bonus round requiring recall of specific page numbers or section references from PMBOK Guide 7th edition and PRINCE2 manual for key concepts. Consider adding integration questions asking them to recall which frameworks share similar concepts under different names.

title: Deconstructing Multi-Stakeholder Crisis Leadership: A Comparative Decision Analysis
description: Students analyze and compare leadership decisions made during three different organizational crises, examining how situational factors, stakeholder pressures, and leadership theories influenced decision-making processes. Through systematic comparison, students demonstrate understanding of how leadership principles adapt across complex, high-stakes scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between competing leadership approaches by analyzing decision patterns across three crisis scenarios involving different stakeholder configurations
Students will interpret the relationship between situational leadership variables and decision outcomes through structured comparative analysis of crisis response strategies
instructions: Begin by providing students with three detailed crisis case studies: a pharmaceutical company product recall (multiple regulatory bodies), a tech company data breach (customers, investors, government), and a manufacturing plant closure (employees, community, shareholders). Each case study should be 2-3 pages with identical formatting: situation overview, key stakeholders, timeline of decisions, and outcomes. Divide students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group all three cases. Provide the Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework template with five dimensions: stakeholder prioritization patterns, communication timing and channels, resource allocation decisions, risk mitigation strategies, and leadership style adaptations. Students spend 40 minutes individually reading cases and completing initial framework notes. Groups then collaborate for 60 minutes, creating a comparative analysis matrix that identifies patterns, contradictions, and situational variables across the three scenarios. Each group prepares a 10-minute presentation focusing on two key insights: which leadership theories best explain the observed decision patterns, and how stakeholder complexity influenced leadership adaptations. During presentations, non-presenting groups use a structured peer evaluation form rating clarity of analysis, depth of theoretical connections, and quality of evidence from cases. Conclude with a 15-minute facilitated discussion where students synthesize common leadership principles that transcend specific crisis contexts while identifying situation-specific adaptations.
materials_needed: Three standardized crisis case studies (2-3 pages each)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework template (digital or printed)
Comparative analysis matrix template
Peer evaluation forms for presentations
Timer for time management
Projection capability for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparative analysis matrices using a 4-point rubric assessing: accuracy of pattern identification across cases (25%), appropriate application of leadership theories to explain decisions (30%), quality of stakeholder impact analysis (25%), and depth of situational variable recognition (20%). Presentations assessed on clarity of insights and use of evidence. Minimum passing requires demonstrating understanding in at least 3 of 4 rubric areas.
scaffolding_notes: Provide struggling students with pre-highlighted key decisions in each case study and sentence starters for framework responses. For advanced learners, add a fourth mini-case as a prediction exercise where they apply identified patterns to forecast leadership decisions in a new scenario. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who excel at presentation skills.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Alternative Mitigation Approaches for IT Infrastructure Project
description: Students will analyze a complex IT infrastructure project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will break down the relationships between risks, assess the appropriateness of proposed response strategies, and justify their analytical conclusions using PMP risk management principles.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of risk response strategies by examining their alignment with risk characteristics, project constraints, and organizational capabilities
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk response choices through systematic evaluation of strategy-risk relationships and cost-benefit considerations
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'CloudTech Migration Project' case study containing 8 identified risks with corresponding risk response strategies already proposed by a fictional project team. Each risk includes probability/impact ratings, risk triggers, and 2-3 alternative response strategies.

**Individual Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students work individually to complete the Risk Response Analysis Matrix template. For each of the 8 risks, they must: (1) Identify which response strategy category (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) each proposed option represents, (2) Analyze why each strategy does/doesn't align with the risk's probability and impact levels, (3) Examine resource requirements and constraints for each option, (4) Evaluate potential secondary risks created by each response.

**Peer Review Phase (15 minutes):** Students pair up and compare their individual analyses. Each pair must identify at least 3 instances where they disagreed on strategy appropriateness and discuss the reasoning behind their evaluations. They should focus on analyzing the logical connections between risk characteristics and response strategy selection.

**Group Synthesis (15 minutes):** Pairs join into groups of 4-6 to create a consensus ranking of the 8 risks from 'best response strategy alignment' to 'poorest response strategy alignment.' Groups must provide analytical justification for their top and bottom rankings, citing specific PMP risk response principles.

**Presentation & Critique (20 minutes):** Each group presents their #1 best-aligned and #1 worst-aligned risk response, explaining their analytical reasoning. Other groups provide constructive critique by identifying additional factors that should be considered in the analysis or alternative interpretations of the risk-response relationship.

**Debrief (10 minutes):** Instructor facilitates discussion on common analytical patterns observed across groups and reinforces key principles for evaluating risk response strategy appropriateness in real projects.
materials_needed: CloudTech Migration Project case study handout (2 pages per student)
Risk Response Analysis Matrix template (1 page per student)
Flipchart paper and markers for group work
PMP Risk Management Process reference sheet
Timer for activity phases
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Analysis Matrix using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accurate categorization of response strategies (25%), (2) Quality of alignment analysis between risk characteristics and responses (35%), (3) Identification of secondary risks and resource constraints (25%), (4) Logical justification of recommendations using PMP principles (15%). Successful completion requires scoring 3+ points in categories 2 and 4, demonstrating analytical thinking rather than simple recall.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example for one risk showing the analytical process. Create reference cards with key questions to ask when evaluating each response strategy type. For advanced learners: Add quantitative analysis component requiring students to calculate expected monetary value for each response option, or introduce enterprise risk management considerations that span multiple projects.

title: Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Decimal Conversion
description: Students will memorize binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice and timed recall exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recognition of basic binary patterns essential for computer science understanding.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through repeated practice drills
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for the first 10 minutes, with one partner showing the decimal side while the other attempts to state the binary equivalent before checking the answer. Partners switch roles every 2 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers on the board for 5 seconds each, and students write the binary equivalent on their answer sheets. Cover numbers 0-15 in random order twice (10 minutes total). For the final phase, reverse the process by showing binary numbers and having students write the decimal equivalents. Provide immediate feedback after each number by revealing the correct answer. Students should track their correct responses on a personal score sheet. Conclude with a 5-minute individual practice session where students use the flashcards independently, focusing on numbers they missed during group activities. Throughout the activity, emphasize the patterns (powers of 2) but focus primarily on memorization rather than calculation strategies.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 and 4-bit binary equivalents
Whiteboard or projector for displaying numbers
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-32
Personal score tracking sheets
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (14/15 or better) on the final individual practice round. Collect answer sheets from the timed drills and score based on correct binary-to-decimal and decimal-to-binary conversions. Award full credit for exact matches only (including leading zeros for binary numbers). Observe student participation during partner work and note students who struggle with specific number patterns.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, start with powers of 2 only (1, 2, 4, 8) before introducing other numbers, and provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1 place values). For advanced learners, extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents. Consider pairing stronger students with those who need more support during partner activities.

title: Analyzing Energy Transformations in Complex Pendulum Systems with Air Resistance
description: Students will decompose and examine the energy transformations in a compound pendulum system under varying air resistance conditions. They will analyze experimental data to identify energy loss mechanisms and quantify the relationship between system parameters and energy dissipation rates.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the energy transformation patterns in a compound pendulum system by examining position, velocity, and acceleration data over multiple oscillation cycles
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of different energy dissipation mechanisms through systematic comparison of theoretical predictions with experimental measurements
instructions:
Begin by setting up three identical compound pendulums (physical pendulums with distributed mass) with different air resistance configurations: one in normal air, one with a lightweight streamlined weight, and one with a high-drag surface attachment. Install motion sensors to capture position data at 100 Hz sampling rate. Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team analyzing one pendulum system for 45 minutes, then rotating stations. 

Step 1 (15 min): Teams calibrate sensors and release pendulums from identical 30-degree angles, recording 50 complete oscillations. Students must identify the system's moment of inertia, center of mass location, and initial mechanical energy.

Step 2 (20 min): Using Logger Pro or similar software, students create position vs. time graphs, then generate velocity and acceleration plots through differentiation. They calculate instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for every 10th data point across the oscillation sequence.

Step 3 (25 min): Students construct energy vs. time plots for all three energy forms (kinetic, potential, total mechanical) and identify patterns in energy loss rates. They must calculate the exponential decay constant for amplitude reduction and determine the Q-factor (quality factor) for each system.

Step 4 (20 min): Teams analyze their data to separate energy losses due to air resistance from other dissipation mechanisms (bearing friction, internal damping). They create comparative graphs showing energy loss rates vs. oscillation number for all three pendulum configurations.

Step 5 (15 min): Students prepare a technical analysis report documenting their findings, including mathematical relationships between drag coefficients and energy dissipation rates, supported by quantitative evidence from their measurements.
materials_needed: Three identical compound pendulums with adjustable mass distributions
Motion sensors with 100+ Hz sampling capability (Vernier or PASCO)
Streamlined weight attachments and high-drag surface materials
Logger Pro or equivalent data analysis software
Digital protractors for initial angle measurement
Precision balance for mass measurements
assessment_method: Students submit a technical analysis report (1000 words) containing: (1) Quantitative comparison of energy decay constants between systems (25 points), (2) Mathematical derivation linking experimental Q-factors to theoretical damping models (25 points), (3) Graphical analysis showing energy transformation patterns with error analysis (25 points), (4) Evidence-based conclusions about relative importance of different dissipation mechanisms (25 points). Rubric emphasizes accuracy of calculations, depth of physical reasoning, and quality of experimental analysis.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated moment of inertia values and template spreadsheets for energy calculations. Offer guided practice with simpler harmonic oscillator data before compound pendulum analysis. For advanced learners: Challenge them to develop mathematical models predicting energy loss rates from first principles, or investigate non-linear effects at large amplitudes. Encourage exploration of phase space plots and advanced damping models.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Tracker Application Solutions
description: Students will evaluate and compare three different beginner-level bug tracker application implementations using specific software quality criteria. They will assess code readability, functionality, and maintainability to determine which solution best meets professional development standards.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three bug tracker code implementations by applying a structured quality assessment rubric covering readability, functionality, and maintainability
Students will critique coding practices through systematic comparison and provide justified recommendations for code improvement
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 2-3. Provide each group with three pre-written bug tracker applications (30-50 lines each) - one well-written, one poorly formatted, and one with logical issues. Give students the Code Quality Assessment Sheet with criteria: Variable Naming (clear/unclear), Code Organization (logical structure), Comments (helpful/missing), Functionality (works/has bugs), and Error Handling (present/absent). 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine Code Sample A, testing it in the provided IDE and rating each criterion on a 1-5 scale with written justification. Step 2 (15 minutes): Repeat process for Code Sample B. Step 3 (15 minutes): Repeat for Code Sample C. Step 4 (20 minutes): Groups complete comparison matrix, ranking the three solutions from best to worst overall quality. They must provide three specific reasons for their top choice and identify two concrete improvements for their lowest-ranked solution. 

Step 5 (15 minutes): Each group presents their top-ranked solution to the class, explaining their evaluation criteria and defending their choice. Other groups can challenge decisions with evidence from the code. Conclude with instructor revealing which sample represents industry-standard code and discussing how student evaluations aligned with professional standards.
materials_needed: Three pre-written bug tracker code samples (different quality levels)
Code Quality Assessment Sheet template (printable PDF)
Computer/laptop with Python or JavaScript IDE for each group
Comparison matrix worksheet
Timer for activities
assessment_method: Grade based on completed assessment sheets (40%), quality of written justifications for ratings (30%), accuracy of final ranking with supporting evidence (20%), and participation in group presentation defending choices (10%). Success criteria: Students provide specific code examples to support ratings, identify at least 3 concrete quality differences between samples, and demonstrate understanding by defending their evaluation during peer discussions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide example evaluations for first 2-3 criteria, highlight specific lines of code to examine, offer sentence starters like 'This code is better because...' For advanced learners: Add additional criteria like performance efficiency, security considerations, or scalability. Challenge them to suggest specific refactoring techniques and estimate time required for improvements.

title: Customer Churn Prevention Dashboard Design Challenge
description: Students will design and build a comprehensive analytical dashboard that predicts customer churn risk using real telecommunications data. They will create original data visualizations, develop predictive models, and present actionable business recommendations to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-layered analytical dashboard by integrating descriptive statistics, predictive modeling, and interactive visualizations
Students will synthesize customer behavior patterns through exploratory data analysis to generate original business intelligence recommendations
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Data Exploration & Problem Framing**
Provide student teams (3-4 members) with the telecommunications customer dataset containing 20 variables including monthly charges, contract type, tenure, and churn status. Teams spend 30 minutes conducting exploratory data analysis using Python/R to identify key patterns. They must document 3 preliminary hypotheses about churn drivers and create basic summary statistics. Final 15 minutes: teams present their hypotheses to class for peer feedback.

**Phase 2 (90 minutes): Dashboard Architecture Design**
Teams sketch their dashboard layout on whiteboards, defining 4 required sections: Executive Summary (KPIs), Risk Segmentation (customer categories), Predictive Model Results, and Action Items. They must specify which visualizations will appear in each section and justify their choices. Instructor circulates to approve designs before teams proceed to building phase.

**Phase 3 (120 minutes): Dashboard Construction**
Using Tableau/Power BI, teams build their dashboards implementing their approved designs. Required elements: interactive filters, at least 5 different chart types, calculated fields for churn probability scores, and color-coding for risk levels. Teams must also create a simple logistic regression model to generate churn probability scores for integration.

**Phase 4 (30 minutes): Stakeholder Presentation**
Each team delivers a 5-minute presentation to simulated telecom executives (played by instructor and guest participants), demonstrating their dashboard functionality and presenting 3 specific retention strategies based on their analysis. Q&A follows each presentation.
materials_needed: Telecommunications customer churn dataset (CSV format with 7,043 records)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI licenses for each team
Python/R environment with pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn libraries
Whiteboard and markers for each team
Laptops/computers with internet access
Presentation projector and screen
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across 5 dimensions: Technical Implementation (dashboard functionality, model accuracy), Design Quality (visual clarity, user experience), Business Insight (actionable recommendations, data interpretation), Presentation Skills (clarity, stakeholder engagement), and Collaboration (equal participation, peer feedback quality). Each dimension weighted equally for 100 total points. Students submit dashboard files, analysis code, and written executive summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide dashboard template with pre-built sections to modify rather than create from scratch. Offer guided worksheets for hypothesis generation and model building steps. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources (economic indicators, competitor analysis) or implement advanced ML algorithms (random forest, gradient boosting). Encourage A/B testing simulation features in their dashboards.

title: PMI-ACP Agile Framework Terminology Mastery Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall 75+ specific terminology and definitions from advanced agile project management frameworks including SAFe, LeSS, and Nexus. This high-stakes recall exercise prepares students for professional certification exams and real-world agile transformations.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions of 25 SAFe terminology items, 25 LeSS framework terms, and 25 Nexus scaling terms by completing timed flashcard sessions
Students will identify exact acronym expansions and their contextual meanings through structured memorization drills covering PI Planning, ART synchronization, and scaled retrospectives
instructions: Begin by distributing the curated terminology bank containing 75 terms across three categories: SAFe (Solution Train, Program Increment, Agile Release Train, etc.), LeSS (Overall Retrospective, Sprint Planning One, Area Product Owner, etc.), and Nexus (Integration Team, Nexus Sprint Planning, Cross-Team Refinement, etc.). Students work individually for the first 20 minutes using spaced repetition flashcards, cycling through each term 3 times minimum. Next, conduct three 8-minute speed rounds where students write definitions from memory - one round per framework. Provide immediate feedback after each round, highlighting commonly missed terms. Follow with 15 minutes of peer quizzing in pairs, where partners alternate asking for definitions and acronym expansions. Students must achieve 90% accuracy on definitions and 95% accuracy on acronym expansions. Conclude with a 10-minute individual assessment where students complete a terminology matching exercise containing 30 randomly selected terms from the master bank. Record scores immediately and identify students requiring remediation. Provide correction sheets showing exact definitions for any missed items.
materials_needed: PMI-ACP certified terminology bank with 75 pre-selected terms and official definitions
Digital flashcard application (Anki or Quizlet) with spaced repetition algorithm
Printed terminology matching worksheets with answer keys
Timer for speed rounds
Score tracking sheets for individual progress monitoring
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (68/75 terms) on final terminology matching assessment. Evaluation includes: exact definition recall (40 points), acronym expansion accuracy (30 points), and contextual usage identification (30 points). Partial credit not awarded - definitions must be precisely memorized as per PMI standards.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide mnemonic devices for complex terms, allow additional 10-minute review period, and offer color-coded category cards. For advanced learners: include 25 additional terms from DevOps integration and portfolio management, require creation of interconnection maps between framework terminologies, and challenge them to identify overlapping concepts across all three frameworks.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes: Multi-Perspective Crisis Analysis
description: Students will analyze real-world leadership paradoxes through multiple theoretical lenses to demonstrate deep understanding of competing leadership frameworks. They will examine how different leadership theories explain contradictory decisions made by the same leader during a complex organizational crisis.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between competing leadership theories by analyzing how transformational, situational, and authentic leadership frameworks interpret the same leadership decisions
Students will synthesize multiple theoretical perspectives through structured comparison matrices that reveal inherent contradictions in leadership approaches
instructions: Begin by distributing the Netflix leadership crisis case study (Reed Hastings' 2011 Qwikster decision and reversal) along with three theoretical framework summary sheets. Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member a specific role: Transformational Leadership Analyst, Situational Leadership Analyst, Authentic Leadership Analyst, and Synthesis Coordinator. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Individual specialists spend 20 minutes analyzing Hastings' decisions through their assigned theoretical lens, completing the provided analysis template with specific evidence from the case. They must identify 5 specific leadership behaviors and explain how their theory interprets each action. The Synthesis Coordinator prepares the comparison matrix template during this time. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Specialists present their analyses to their group (7 minutes each), while the Coordinator maps contradictions and alignments on the matrix. The group identifies at least 3 major paradoxes where theories completely contradict each other's interpretation of the same leadership behavior. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Groups prepare a 5-minute presentation focusing on one major paradox, explaining why competent leadership theories reach opposite conclusions about the same decision. Phase 4 (25 minutes): Group presentations with 2 minutes for clarifying questions after each presentation. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion identifying patterns across all paradoxes presented.
materials_needed: Netflix/Qwikster crisis case study packet (8 pages per student)
Transformational Leadership theory summary sheet with key principles
Situational Leadership theory summary sheet with decision matrix
Authentic Leadership theory summary sheet with core dimensions
Individual analysis template with evidence collection grid
Group synthesis matrix template (large format poster paper)
Colored markers for matrix coding
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of theoretical application (25%) - correct use of framework terminology and principles, (2) Evidence quality (25%) - specific, relevant case details supporting analysis, (3) Paradox identification (25%) - clear articulation of contradictions between theories, (4) Synthesis depth (25%) - demonstration of understanding why theories conflict. Students must score 3+ in all categories, with particular emphasis on their ability to explain theoretical contradictions without dismissing any framework as 'wrong.'
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide theory application examples from a different business case before starting, create sentence stems for analysis templates ('According to transformational leadership theory, this decision demonstrates...'). For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring integration of power-distance cultural dimensions or stakeholder theory considerations. Encourage them to propose resolution strategies for the theoretical paradoxes they identify.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Comparing Risk Response Strategies Across Project Phases
description: Students will analyze a comprehensive risk register from a software development project and systematically compare the effectiveness of different risk response strategies across project phases. They will examine how risk priorities shift and evaluate the appropriateness of chosen mitigation approaches.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk register entries by examining the relationship between risk probability, impact, and timing across project lifecycle phases
Students will compare risk response strategies through systematic evaluation of avoid, mitigate, transfer, and accept approaches for similar risk categories
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the pre-populated risk register containing 20 risks from a 12-month software development project, with entries spanning initiation through closure phases. Provide the risk response strategy reference sheet and comparison matrix template. Form teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Risk Categorization (15 minutes):** Teams sort risks into the four main categories (technical, organizational, external, project management) and identify which project phase each risk was most critical. Students mark risks on the provided project timeline template.

**Phase 2 - Strategy Analysis (20 minutes):** For each risk category, teams analyze the chosen response strategy by examining: (1) alignment between risk impact/probability scores and selected strategy, (2) cost-effectiveness of the response, (3) timing of implementation relative to project phase. Teams complete the comparison matrix showing strategy patterns.

**Phase 3 - Cross-Phase Comparison (15 minutes):** Students identify risks that appear in multiple phases and analyze how response strategies evolved. They examine whether strategies appropriately shifted as project progressed and risks materialized or diminished.

**Phase 4 - Alternative Strategy Evaluation (20 minutes):** Teams select 5 high-priority risks and propose alternative response strategies, justifying their recommendations using PMI risk management principles. They must address why their alternative would be more effective than the original choice.

**Presentation & Debrief (10 minutes):** Each team presents one key insight about risk response strategy effectiveness, highlighting patterns they discovered across project phases.
materials_needed: Pre-populated risk register spreadsheet with 20 detailed risk entries
Risk response strategy reference sheet (PMI-based)
Comparison matrix template (Excel or printed)
Project timeline template showing all 5 process groups
Laptops or tablets for digital analysis
assessment_method: Evaluate completed comparison matrices using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization and phase mapping, (2) Depth of strategy analysis with specific justifications, (3) Quality of cross-phase comparisons showing understanding of risk evolution, (4) Feasibility and PMI-alignment of proposed alternative strategies. Students must demonstrate analysis through specific examples and quantitative reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide risk analysis flowchart and sentence starters for justifications. Assign specific roles within teams (risk categorizer, strategy analyzer, timeline mapper). For advanced learners: Add secondary risks that could emerge from proposed response strategies and require cost-benefit analysis using provided budget constraints.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise WAN Solution with DMVPN and QoS
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise WAN solution connecting three geographically distributed sites using Dynamic Multipoint VPN (DMVPN) Phase 3 with integrated Quality of Service (QoS) policies. This capstone activity requires synthesizing advanced routing protocols, security frameworks, and traffic management to create a production-ready network infrastructure.
learning_objectives: Students will create a comprehensive network architecture diagram incorporating DMVPN hub-and-spoke topology with spoke-to-spoke communication by analyzing business requirements and traffic patterns
Students will implement advanced DMVPN Phase 3 configuration with EIGRP routing and IPSec encryption through hands-on router configuration and testing
Students will design custom QoS policies with traffic classification, marking, and queuing mechanisms by evaluating application priorities and bandwidth constraints
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Students work in teams of 2-3 to analyze provided business requirements: headquarters with 200 users, branch office A with 50 users, branch office B with 75 users, requiring voice, video, and data traffic prioritization. Teams create detailed network topology diagrams using draw.io, specifying IP addressing schemes (using 10.0.0.0/8 with proper subnetting), DMVPN tunnel interfaces, and hub/spoke relationships.

**Phase 2: Configuration Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using GNS3 with Cisco IOSv routers, students configure the hub router (HQ) with DMVPN tunnel interface, NHRP server settings, and EIGRP AS 100. Configure two spoke routers with DMVPN clients, NHRP clients, and appropriate routing. Implement IPSec profiles with AES 256 encryption and SHA-256 authentication.
