Verify spoke-to-spoke communication bypasses hub (Phase 3 functionality).

**Phase 3: QoS Policy Creation (60 minutes)**
Develop class-maps for voice (EF), video (AF41), business-critical data (AF31), and default traffic. Create policy-maps with appropriate bandwidth allocations: voice 20%, video 30%, business data 25%, default 25%. Apply hierarchical QoS with parent policy for tunnel bandwidth shaping and child policy for classification. Configure DSCP marking and priority queuing.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)**
Perform comprehensive testing using ping, traceroute, and traffic generation tools. Verify QoS functionality with different traffic types. Create final documentation including configuration files, testing results, and troubleshooting procedures. Present 10-minute demonstration to instructor showing spoke-to-spoke connectivity and QoS policy enforcement.
materials_needed: GNS3 network simulator software with Cisco IOSv images (15.6 or higher)
Draw.io or Visio for network diagrams
Computers with minimum 8GB RAM and virtualization support
Pre-configured business requirements document with traffic specifications
QoS testing tools (iperf3, Ostinato traffic generator)
Cisco IOS command reference guides
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points total): Network design accuracy and completeness (25 points), DMVPN configuration functionality with proper Phase 3 implementation (30 points), QoS policy effectiveness and proper traffic handling (25 points), documentation quality and professional presentation (20 points). Success criteria include: all sites can communicate directly (spoke-to-spoke), voice traffic receives priority treatment under congestion, and configuration survives router reload testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base router configurations with interfaces and basic IP addressing completed. Offer step-by-step DMVPN configuration templates and QoS policy examples. Create checkpoint milestones for each phase. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack implementation, integrate with external BGP routing, implement redundant hub configuration for high availability, or add advanced security features like certificate-based authentication. Encourage optimization of EIGRP metrics and advanced QoS features like CBWFQ and LLQ combinations.

title: Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models: A Comparative Analysis Activity
description: Students will analyze and interpret feature importance outputs from a Random Forest classifier trained on a customer churn dataset. They will compare different importance metrics and explain how each feature contributes to model predictions in business terms.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret feature importance scores from Random Forest models by analyzing Gini importance and permutation importance outputs
Students will explain the practical business implications of feature rankings through written analysis and peer discussion
instructions: Begin by providing students with a pre-trained Random Forest model on a telecommunications customer churn dataset containing 15 features (monthly charges, contract type, tenure, etc.). In pairs, students spend 15 minutes examining two feature importance visualizations: a bar chart showing Gini importance scores and another showing permutation importance scores. Each pair receives a worksheet with the model's confusion matrix (accuracy: 82%) and feature descriptions. Students first individually rank the top 5 most important features from each method, noting any differences between the two approaches. Next, pairs discuss their rankings for 10 minutes, focusing on why certain features might rank differently between methods. Students then spend 20 minutes writing a brief analysis explaining: (1) which three features are most critical for predicting churn according to both methods, (2) one significant difference between the two importance rankings and a possible explanation, and (3) specific business recommendations based on the top features (e.g., 'Monthly charges ranks #1, suggesting pricing strategy review'). Finally, conduct a 15-minute class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their key findings. Instructor facilitates by asking probing questions about the reliability of different importance measures and how feature interactions might affect interpretations. Conclude by having students submit their written analysis and participate in a brief exit ticket identifying one insight about feature importance interpretation.
materials_needed: Pre-trained Random Forest model file (.pkl format)
Customer churn dataset (CSV with 15 features, 1000+ rows)
Feature importance visualization charts (2 per pair)
Analysis worksheet template with confusion matrix
Jupyter notebook environment with scikit-learn installed
assessment_method: Written analysis graded on 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of top features from both methods (25%), (2) Clear explanation of differences between importance measures (25%), (3) Relevant business recommendations tied to specific features (25%), (4) Quality of reasoning and use of technical vocabulary (25%). Participation in discussions assessed through observation checklist.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed analysis template with sentence starters like 'The most important feature is X because...' and a glossary of key terms. For advanced learners: Include additional importance metrics (SHAP values) and ask them to critique the model's limitations or suggest alternative approaches for feature selection.

title: Optimization Design Challenge: Maximizing Profit for a Custom Manufacturing Company
description: Students will apply calculus optimization techniques to solve a real-world business problem involving multiple constraints. They will determine optimal production quantities, pricing strategies, and resource allocation to maximize profit for a fictional manufacturing company producing custom electronics cases.
learning_objectives: Students will apply differential calculus optimization methods to determine maximum profit points by setting up and solving systems of equations with multiple variables and constraints
Students will implement the Lagrange multiplier method to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical analysis of production scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the business scenario packet describing 'TechCase Solutions,' a company producing three types of phone cases with different profit margins, material costs, and labor requirements. Students work in pairs to analyze the given data: Type A cases ($12 profit, 2 hours labor, $8 materials), Type B cases ($18 profit, 3 hours labor, $12 materials), Type C cases ($25 profit, 4 hours labor, $15 materials). The company has 480 labor hours weekly and $2400 materials budget, with market demand constraints of maximum 60 Type A, 40 Type B, and 30 Type C cases weekly. Students must first establish the objective function P(x,y,z) = 12x + 18y + 25z and identify all constraints as inequalities. Next, they apply the method of Lagrange multipliers to find critical points, testing corner points of the feasible region using the simplex method approach. Students create a systematic table showing all feasible combinations and calculate profit for each scenario. They must then verify their solution by taking partial derivatives and confirming the optimality conditions are satisfied. In the final 30 minutes, pairs present their optimal production plan, including exact quantities of each case type, total expected profit, and complete resource utilization. Each presentation must include the mathematical justification showing why their solution represents a true maximum rather than a local optimum or saddle point.
materials_needed: TechCase Solutions business scenario packet (pre-printed with company data and constraints)
Graphing calculators or laptop computers with mathematical software (GeoGebra or Desmos)
Grid paper for constraint graphing and feasible region mapping
Formula reference sheets containing Lagrange multiplier method steps
assessment_method: Students are evaluated using a 20-point rubric: correct objective function setup (4 points), accurate constraint identification and mathematical representation (4 points), proper application of Lagrange multiplier method with shown work (6 points), verification of optimality through derivative testing (3 points), and clear presentation of final solution with business interpretation (3 points). Full credit requires exact numerical answers and complete mathematical justification.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed constraint table and guided worksheet breaking down the Lagrange multiplier method into smaller steps. Offer visual aids showing the geometric interpretation of constraints. For advanced learners, extend the problem by adding seasonal demand variations, introducing integer programming constraints, or requiring sensitivity analysis showing how profit changes with small constraint modifications.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Source Acoustic Systems
description: Students will analyze complex wave interference patterns generated by multiple acoustic sources to determine source characteristics and predict resultant wave behavior. They will decompose superimposed waveforms and evaluate the relationship between source parameters and interference outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-source wave interference patterns by identifying individual source contributions and calculating phase relationships between overlapping waves
Students will evaluate the impact of varying source frequencies, amplitudes, and positions through systematic decomposition of complex waveform data
instructions:
Begin by providing student teams (3-4 members) with three datasets containing acoustic measurements from different multi-speaker configurations: Dataset A (2 sources, same frequency), Dataset B (3 sources, harmonic frequencies), and Dataset C (4 sources, inharmonic frequencies). Each dataset includes time-domain waveforms, frequency spectra, and spatial measurement positions. 

Step 1 (20 min): Students analyze Dataset A by plotting the resultant waveform and identifying constructive/destructive interference points. They must calculate the phase difference between sources and predict the interference pattern using wave superposition principles.

Step 2 (25 min): For Dataset B, students decompose the complex waveform into individual frequency components using Fourier analysis tools. They identify each source's contribution and analyze how harmonic relationships create beating patterns and amplitude modulation.

Step 3 (30 min): Students tackle Dataset C by applying vector addition of waves, considering both amplitude and phase for each frequency component. They must determine the number of sources, estimate individual source parameters, and predict the interference pattern at unmeasured positions.

Step 4 (15 min): Teams create a systematic comparison chart analyzing how source separation distance, frequency relationships, and amplitude ratios affect the resultant interference patterns across all three datasets.

Step 5 (20 min): Each team presents their analysis of one dataset to the class, defending their parameter calculations and predictions. Other teams evaluate the analysis accuracy and suggest alternative interpretations.

Throughout the activity, students use computational tools for waveform analysis while applying theoretical principles of wave superposition, phase relationships, and spatial interference patterns.
materials_needed: Three pre-recorded acoustic interference datasets with measurement metadata
MATLAB, Python with NumPy/SciPy, or equivalent computational analysis software
Graphing calculators or computer access for each student team
Wave analysis worksheet templates with calculation spaces
Digital projector for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of phase relationship calculations and source parameter identification (25%), (2) Correct application of superposition principles and mathematical analysis (25%), (3) Quality of predictions for unmeasured positions with justification (25%), (4) Clear presentation of findings with defense of analytical choices (25%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate logical reasoning in their interference pattern explanations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing reference cards with key wave equations and step-by-step calculation templates. Offer simplified two-source examples for initial practice. For advanced learners, introduce Doppler effects in moving source scenarios or challenge them to design optimal speaker configurations for specific interference goals. Consider pairing strong analytical students with those needing mathematical support.

title: Code Quality Inspector: Evaluating Simple Python Functions
description: Students will act as code reviewers to evaluate three pre-written Python functions for beginners, assessing code quality, functionality, and best practices. They will rank the functions from best to worst and provide detailed justifications for their evaluations using a structured rubric.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate Python function quality by analyzing code readability, efficiency, and adherence to naming conventions
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and ranking with written justification
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the 'Code Inspector Worksheet' containing three Python functions that solve the same problem (calculating area of a rectangle) but with varying quality levels. Function A uses poor variable names (a, b), lacks comments, and has inconsistent spacing. Function B has decent structure but verbose variable names and unnecessary complexity. Function C follows best practices with clear names, comments, and clean formatting.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students evaluate each function using the provided 4-point rubric covering: readability (variable names, comments), functionality (correctness, efficiency), and style (formatting, Python conventions). They score each function 1-4 in each category and write 2-3 sentences explaining their reasoning.

**Ranking and Justification (10 minutes):** Students rank the three functions from best (1) to worst (3) and write a paragraph justifying their ranking. They must reference specific code elements and explain which criteria were most important in their decision.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** In pairs, students share their rankings and discuss differences in their evaluations. They identify at least one insight they gained from their partner's perspective.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Facilitate whole-class discussion where students defend their top choice and explain evaluation criteria. Record common themes about what makes code 'good' on the board.
materials_needed: Code Inspector Worksheet with three Python functions
Evaluation rubric (4-point scale for readability, functionality, style)
Computers with Python interpreter or online Python editor
Answer key with sample evaluations for instructor reference
assessment_method: Grade based on completion of rubric scores with justifications (40%), quality of written ranking explanation showing specific evidence (40%), and participation in peer/class discussions (20%). Success criteria: Student provides specific examples from code to support evaluations and demonstrates understanding of code quality principles.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This function is better because...' and highlight specific lines to evaluate. For advanced learners: Add a fourth function with subtle bugs or ask them to rewrite the worst function following best practices. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during peer review.

title: Advanced Project Management Methodology Terminology Mastery Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall 50 advanced project management terms, acronyms, and definitions from multiple methodologies (PMI, PRINCE2, Agile, Lean Six Sigma) through structured flashcard drilling and timed recall exercises. This activity builds foundational vocabulary essential for advanced project management certification and practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific definitions for 50 advanced project management terms across PMI, PRINCE2, Agile, and Lean Six Sigma methodologies by achieving 90% accuracy on verbal and written recall tests
Students will identify and state the correct acronym expansions and contextual applications for 25 advanced PM abbreviations through rapid-fire questioning sessions
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared terminology list containing 50 advanced PM terms with definitions (10 minutes). Students work in pairs to create physical flashcards, writing the term on one side and complete definition plus methodology source on the reverse (15 minutes). Conduct Round 1: Partner drilling where Student A shows terms to Student B for 8 minutes, then switch roles for 8 minutes. Document incorrect responses on tracking sheets. Round 2: Instructor-led rapid-fire questioning where students stand and must correctly define terms within 10 seconds or sit down; continue until 3 students remain standing (12 minutes). Round 3: Written recall test where students write definitions for 20 randomly selected terms from the list within 15 minutes. Round 4: Acronym speed challenge where instructor calls out abbreviations (WBS, EVM, RACI, etc.) and students write full expansions and brief context (10 minutes). Conclude with peer verification of written responses using answer keys, with students marking their own papers and calculating accuracy percentages (7 minutes). Record individual scores on master tracking sheet for progress monitoring.
materials_needed: Pre-printed list of 50 advanced PM terms with official definitions from PMI PMBOK, PRINCE2 manual, Scrum Guide, and Lean Six Sigma references
Blank index cards (100 per student pair)
Individual tracking sheets for incorrect responses
Master answer key with acceptable definition variations
Stopwatch or timer
Individual score recording sheets
assessment_method: Success measured by: (1) 90% accuracy on 20-term written recall test, (2) Ability to remain standing for minimum 15 questions in rapid-fire round, (3) 100% accuracy on acronym expansions for at least 20 of 25 terms, (4) Peer verification confirms definitions match acceptable variations in answer key. Students achieving all four criteria demonstrate mastery; those meeting 3/4 criteria show proficiency; 2/4 indicates need for additional practice.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial term count to 35, provide definition stems or first letters as hints, allow 15 seconds instead of 10 in rapid-fire round. Pair with stronger partners for drilling sessions. For advanced learners: Add 25 bonus terms from specialized areas (risk management, earned value formulas, advanced scheduling techniques), require them to create original example scenarios for each term, challenge them to identify methodology conflicts or overlapping definitions.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Decision-Making: The Challenger Space Shuttle Crisis Analysis
description: Students will analyze primary source documents and testimony from the 1986 Challenger disaster to understand how organizational hierarchy, communication breakdowns, and leadership decision-making processes contributed to the tragedy. Through systematic examination of documented exchanges between NASA leadership and Morton Thiokol engineers, students will demonstrate understanding of complex leadership dynamics under pressure.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the relationship between organizational structure and communication effectiveness by analyzing documented exchanges between NASA administrators and engineering teams during the Challenger launch decision process

Students will explain how leadership cognitive biases and external pressures influence critical decision-making through systematic examination of pre-launch meeting transcripts and executive testimonies
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Challenger case study packet containing: Rogers Commission Report excerpts (pages 82-95), Morton Thiokol teleconference transcript from January 27, 1986, and NASA administrator testimonies. Divide students into groups of 4-5, assigning roles: Lead Analyst, Timeline Coordinator, Communication Tracker, Decision Mapper, and Synthesis Reporter. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Each group receives identical document sets. Students individually read assigned sections using the provided Leadership Decision Analysis Framework, identifying: (1) key decision points, (2) information flow patterns, (3) authority structures, and (4) pressure points. Students annotate documents using color-coded highlighting: blue for technical concerns, red for schedule pressures, green for hierarchical communications, yellow for dissenting voices.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Within groups, the Timeline Coordinator creates a visual timeline of events, while the Communication Tracker maps information flow between organizational levels. The Decision Mapper identifies critical choice points and alternatives considered. The Lead Analyst synthesizes patterns of leadership behavior, focusing on how leaders processed conflicting information.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Groups construct a leadership decision-making model showing how external pressures (political, schedule, budgetary) intersected with internal dynamics (hierarchy, expertise, communication channels). Using the provided template, groups identify specific leadership failures and explain the underlying organizational and psychological factors.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Each Synthesis Reporter presents their group's analysis to the class, focusing on one key leadership lesson. Other groups provide feedback using the peer assessment criteria, identifying additional insights or alternative interpretations of the evidence presented.
materials_needed: Challenger case study packet with Rogers Commission Report excerpts (pages 82-95)
Morton Thiokol teleconference transcript from January 27, 1986
NASA administrator testimony transcripts (Larry Mulloy, George Hardy)
Leadership Decision Analysis Framework worksheet
Color-coded highlighter sets (4 colors per student)
Large format timeline template sheets
Organizational mapping templates
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Students submit individual reflection papers (500 words) demonstrating understanding by: (1) explaining three specific leadership decision-making failures with supporting evidence from documents, (2) interpreting how organizational hierarchy affected information flow using concrete examples, (3) connecting the case analysis to broader leadership principles. Rubric evaluates: accuracy of document interpretation (25%), depth of leadership concept explanation (35%), quality of evidence-based reasoning (25%), and synthesis of multiple perspectives (15%). Group presentations assessed on clarity of analysis and use of specific textual evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted sample documents showing examples of each annotation type, and offer structured sentence starters for analysis statements. Create mixed-ability groups pairing stronger analytical students with those needing support. For advanced learners, provide additional primary sources (Allan McDonald's engineer testimony, Richard Feynman's investigation notes) and challenge them to develop alternative decision-making frameworks. Consider providing video testimony clips for visual learners who struggle with text-heavy analysis.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Identifying Risk Response Strategy Misalignments
description: Students analyze a complex project risk register to identify inconsistencies between risk ratings, response strategies, and resource allocations. They will decompose risk management decisions to determine which responses are inappropriate for given risk characteristics and stakeholder contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk response strategy selections by examining the relationship between risk probability, impact, and chosen mitigation approaches within a multi-stakeholder project environment
Students will differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate risk responses through systematic evaluation of risk categories, organizational constraints, and strategic alignment
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute the TechCorp ERP Implementation Risk Register containing 15 risks with varying probability/impact ratings, assigned owners, response strategies, and budget allocations. Each team receives analysis worksheets and access to PMI risk management guidelines. **Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student independently reviews 5 assigned risks, documenting: (1) Risk category and characteristics, (2) Stakeholder impact assessment, (3) Current response strategy evaluation, (4) Resource allocation appropriateness. Students use the provided analysis framework to score each element 1-5. **Phase 2 - Team Synthesis (20 minutes):** Teams consolidate individual findings, identifying patterns and discrepancies. They create a priority matrix plotting 'severity of misalignment' vs 'implementation difficulty' for each problematic risk response. Teams must reach consensus on top 5 misaligned responses using evidence from the register. **Phase 3 - Root Cause Analysis (15 minutes):** For each identified misalignment, teams analyze underlying causes: organizational constraints, stakeholder conflicts, resource limitations, or strategy selection errors. They document cause-effect relationships using fishbone diagrams. **Phase 4 - Solution Development (10 minutes):** Teams propose alternative response strategies for the 3 most critical misalignments, considering project constraints and stakeholder interests. Solutions must include rationale, resource implications, and implementation timeline. **Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents one critical misalignment, their analysis methodology, and proposed solution to the class for peer feedback.
materials_needed: TechCorp ERP Risk Register spreadsheet with 15 pre-populated risks
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet template
PMI Risk Management Standard reference sheets
Fishbone diagram templates
Priority matrix plotting sheets
Laptops/tablets for teams
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of misalignment identification (25%), (2) Quality of cause-effect analysis with supporting evidence (25%), (3) Appropriateness of alternative response strategies considering project constraints (25%), (4) Clear presentation of analytical reasoning process (25%). Teams must identify at least 3 legitimate misalignments with documented rationale to meet proficiency threshold.
scaffolding_notes: **Support for struggling students:** Provide risk response decision tree flowchart and worked example of one risk analysis. Assign stronger analytical thinkers as team leads. Offer mid-activity check-ins during Phase 2. **Extensions for advanced learners:** Add secondary stakeholder impact analysis requirement, include quantitative risk modeling calculations, or require cost-benefit analysis of proposed alternatives with NPV calculations.

title: Comprehensive E-commerce Analytics Strategy Evaluation and Optimization Recommendations
description: Students will critically evaluate a real e-commerce website's Google Analytics implementation and conversion funnel performance, then develop and justify strategic optimization recommendations. They will assess data accuracy, measurement strategy effectiveness, and business impact potential of proposed changes.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of an e-commerce site's Google Analytics setup by analyzing tracking implementation, goal configuration, and data quality metrics
Students will critique current conversion funnel performance through multi-dimensional analysis of user behavior data and recommend strategic improvements with ROI projections
instructions:
**Phase 1: Site Selection and Initial Audit (45 minutes)**
Assign students individual e-commerce websites from a pre-approved list (ensure GA access via demo accounts). Students begin by conducting a comprehensive tracking audit: examining Enhanced Ecommerce implementation, goal setup accuracy, audience segmentation logic, and attribution model selection. They document findings in a structured audit template, noting tracking gaps, measurement inconsistencies, and data quality issues.

**Phase 2: Performance Analysis (60 minutes)**
Students dive deep into 6-month performance data, analyzing conversion funnels across multiple dimensions: device types, traffic sources, geographic regions, and customer segments. They identify drop-off points, calculate conversion rates by segment, assess customer lifetime value patterns, and evaluate the effectiveness of current marketing channels. Students must justify their analytical approach and explain why specific metrics were prioritized.

**Phase 3: Critical Evaluation and Strategy Development (75 minutes)**
Using their findings, students evaluate the overall analytics strategy against industry benchmarks and best practices. They identify three critical improvement areas and develop specific, actionable recommendations with projected impact estimates. Each recommendation must include implementation timeline, resource requirements, success metrics, and potential ROI calculations. Students prepare a executive-level presentation defending their strategic choices.

**Phase 4: Peer Review and Defense (30 minutes)**
Students present their findings to peer evaluators who challenge assumptions, question methodology, and assess recommendation feasibility. Presenters must defend their evaluation criteria and justify why their recommendations would deliver superior business outcomes compared to alternative approaches.
materials_needed: Access to Google Analytics demo accounts with e-commerce data
Pre-selected list of 15-20 e-commerce websites with varying complexity levels
Google Analytics audit template with 25+ checkpoint criteria
Industry benchmark data sheets for e-commerce KPIs
ROI calculation spreadsheet templates
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
assessment_method: Students evaluated on four-part rubric (25 points each): 1) Audit thoroughness and accuracy of technical assessment, 2) Quality of data analysis and insight generation, 3) Strategic thinking demonstrated in recommendations with realistic ROI projections, 4) Defense of methodology and ability to address peer challenges. Final deliverable includes 15-slide presentation plus detailed implementation roadmap. Success requires scoring 85+ points and defending at least 2 of 3 peer challenges effectively.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guided audit checklist with specific GA reports to examine, offer mid-activity check-ins for methodology validation, and pair with stronger analytical partners during peer review. For advanced learners: challenge them to incorporate Google Analytics Intelligence insights, compare multiple attribution models, or develop custom segment strategies. Provide access to Google Tag Manager for students ready to evaluate technical implementation complexity.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network with Advanced Routing Protocols and Security Policies
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network infrastructure spanning three geographic sites, implementing OSPF routing, EIGRP redistribution, VPN connectivity, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity integrates advanced routing protocols, network security, and troubleshooting methodologies to solve real-world networking challenges.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF multi-area design principles with EIGRP routing to create an optimal network topology that supports 500+ users across three sites
Students will construct IPSec site-to-site VPN tunnels and implement zone-based firewall policies through hands-on configuration and testing
Students will evaluate network performance metrics and design redundancy solutions by analyzing traffic patterns and implementing failover mechanisms
instructions: **Phase 1 - Network Architecture Design (45 minutes):** Students work in teams of 3-4 to design a network topology for a fictional company with headquarters (200 users), manufacturing site (150 users), and remote office (100 users). Each team receives a requirements document specifying bandwidth needs, security requirements, and budget constraints. Students create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, defining IP addressing schemes using VLSM, identifying OSPF areas, and planning EIGRP autonomous systems. Teams must justify router placement, switch hierarchy, and redundancy paths. **Phase 2 - Core Configuration (90 minutes):** Using physical Cisco equipment or GNS3 simulation, students configure their designed network. Each team member takes responsibility for one site's configuration. Students implement OSPF multi-area routing with proper area types (backbone, standard, stub), configure EIGRP with load balancing and variance settings, and establish route redistribution between protocols using route-maps for traffic engineering. All configurations must include proper interface descriptions, logging, and SNMP community strings. **Phase 3 - Security Implementation (60 minutes):** Students configure IPSec site-to-site VPNs between all locations using pre-shared keys and AES encryption. Implement zone-based firewalls on border routers with specific policies allowing HTTP/HTTPS traffic while blocking P2P applications. Configure AAA authentication using local user databases and establish SSH access with privilege levels. **Phase 4 - Testing and Documentation (45 minutes):** Teams conduct comprehensive connectivity testing using ping, traceroute, and show commands to verify routing tables and VPN status. Students create network documentation including configuration backups, IP address spreadsheets, and troubleshooting procedures. Present solutions to class with live demonstrations of failover scenarios by disconnecting primary links.
materials_needed: 3 Cisco ISR 4000 series routers per team (or GNS3 with appropriate IOS images)
6 Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
Ethernet cables (straight-through and crossover)
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Cisco Packet Tracer software
Network requirements specification document template
Laptop computers with terminal emulation software (PuTTY or SecureCRT)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - topology efficiency, IP addressing scheme, protocol selection justification), Configuration Accuracy (35 points - working OSPF/EIGRP routing, successful VPN establishment, proper security policies), Documentation Completeness (20 points - network diagrams, configuration files, testing results), Troubleshooting Demonstration (20 points - ability to identify and resolve connectivity issues during live testing). Teams must achieve 80% functionality for passing grade, with bonus points awarded for implementing advanced features like QoS policies or IPv6 dual-stack configuration.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic interface configurations and IP addressing completed. Create checkpoint worksheets for each phase to ensure progress. Pair weaker students with stronger teammates and assign specific, well-defined tasks. For advanced learners: Add complexity by requiring BGP peering with simulated ISP, implementing MPLS VPN between sites, or creating network automation scripts using Python and Netmiko. Challenge them to optimize convergence times and implement advanced security features like certificate-based VPN authentication.

title: Binary Number System Memory Palace Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the decimal equivalents of binary numbers 0000 to 1111 (0-15) through guided repetition and flashcard exercises. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-to-decimal conversions essential for computer science fundamentals.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) by completing timed flashcard drills with 90% accuracy
Students will identify and recite the powers of 2 from 2^0 to 2^7 through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) on one side and decimal equivalents (0-15) on the reverse. Start with a 5-minute instructor-led demonstration where you show each binary number and have students chant the decimal equivalent in unison. Next, pair students and give each pair one complete set of 16 flashcards. Partner A shows the binary side while Partner B states the decimal equivalent, then they switch roles. Each partner completes one full cycle through all 16 cards (8 minutes total). After partner practice, conduct individual timed trials. Each student receives a worksheet with 16 binary numbers in random order and has exactly 2 minutes to write decimal equivalents. Collect worksheets and immediately review answers aloud, having students self-check their work. For reinforcement, display a powers-of-2 chart (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) and have students recite it three times as a group. Conclude with a second individual quiz using a different random order of the same 16 binary numbers. Students who score below 14/16 (87.5%) receive additional flashcard sets to take home for extra practice. Record all scores for progress tracking.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards showing 4-bit binary numbers (0000-1111) with decimal equivalents on reverse - one set per student pair
Individual quiz worksheets with 16 randomized 4-bit binary numbers - two different versions per student
Powers of 2 reference chart (visible to whole class)
Timer or stopwatch
Answer key sheets for instructors
assessment_method: Success measured by individual timed quiz scores: 16/16 correct = Mastery (100%), 14-15/16 = Proficient (87.5-93.75%), 12-13/16 = Developing (75-81.25%), below 12/16 = Needs Support. Students must achieve 14/16 or higher on the final quiz to demonstrate successful recall. Document improvement between first and second quiz attempts.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide visual aids showing place values (8-4-2-1 headers), allow use of finger counting methods, or start with 3-bit numbers first. Create mnemonic devices for common patterns (like 1010 = 10, 1100 = 12). For advanced learners: Extend to 8-bit binary numbers (00000000-11111111), introduce hexadecimal equivalents, or challenge them to convert decimal back to binary.

title: Multi-Variable Calculus Application: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration
description: Students will apply partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers to solve a real-world optimization problem involving solar panel placement on irregularly shaped rooftops. They will determine optimal panel configurations while considering geometric constraints, shadow effects, and cost-efficiency ratios.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial derivatives and critical point analysis to optimize solar panel placement by constructing and solving multivariable functions with geometric constraints
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier techniques to maximize energy output through systematic constraint optimization of irregular surface areas
instructions: Begin with 10 minutes of setup: Distribute rooftop blueprints (3 different irregular shapes per group) and solar panel specification sheets. Form groups of 3-4 students, assigning roles: lead mathematician, constraint analyst, and solution validator. Phase 1 (25 minutes): Each group analyzes their assigned rooftop shape, identifying key variables: panel dimensions (x,y), tilt angles (θ), spacing distances (d), and shadow interference zones. Students must establish the objective function E(x,y,θ,d) representing total energy output, incorporating efficiency coefficients provided in specification sheets. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups identify and mathematically express constraints: rooftop boundary equations, minimum spacing requirements (d ≥ 2.5 meters), maximum tilt angles (θ ≤ 45°), and municipal height restrictions. Students set up the Lagrange multiplier system: ∇E = λ∇g + μ∇h where g and h represent primary constraints. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Students solve the system algebraically, finding critical points through partial differentiation. They must verify solutions using the second derivative test and boundary analysis. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Groups calculate actual energy output values, cost analysis, and create scaled diagrams showing optimal panel placement. Final 10 minutes: Each group presents one key finding, explaining their mathematical reasoning and real-world implications. Instructor circulates continuously, providing targeted hints for algebraic manipulation and constraint formulation difficulties.
materials_needed: Irregularly shaped rooftop blueprints (9 different designs, scaled 1:100)
Solar panel specification sheets with efficiency coefficients and dimensional data
Graphing calculators or laptops with mathematical software (Mathematica/MATLAB)
Large grid paper for scaled diagrams
Constraint reference cards with municipal building codes
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct objective function formulation with appropriate variables and coefficients (25%), (2) Accurate constraint identification and mathematical expression (25%), (3) Proper application of Lagrange multipliers and algebraic solution methods (30%), (4) Verification of solutions and practical interpretation of results (20%). Students must submit handwritten work showing all partial derivatives, critical point calculations, and final optimized configuration diagrams.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written constraint templates and objective function frameworks, offer intermediate check-points every 15 minutes, and supply reference cards with partial derivative rules. For advanced learners: Introduce additional constraints like wind load factors, seasonal sun angle variations, or economic depreciation models requiring time-dependent optimization. Encourage exploration of numerical methods when analytical solutions become intractable.

title: Analyzing Wave Interference Patterns in Multi-Source Systems
description: Students analyze complex wave interference patterns from multiple coherent sources to determine source configurations, phase relationships, and predict intensity distributions. They decompose superposition effects to identify individual wave contributions and their interactions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-source wave interference patterns by identifying nodal lines, maxima locations, and phase relationships to determine source configurations
Students will evaluate the contributions of individual wave sources through mathematical decomposition of complex superposition patterns
instructions: Begin by providing students with three interference pattern datasets: Pattern A (2 in-phase sources), Pattern B (3 sources with varying phases), and Pattern C (4 sources in square configuration). Form groups of 3-4 students and assign each group one primary pattern. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students map the interference pattern on coordinate grids, identifying and marking all nodal lines, intensity maxima, and minima locations with precise coordinates. Step 2 (20 minutes): Using path difference calculations, students determine the wavelength by measuring distances between adjacent maxima along specific reference lines. They must show calculations for at least three different measurement locations to verify consistency. Step 3 (25 minutes): Students analyze the symmetry of the pattern to deduce the number of sources and their spatial arrangement. They sketch the probable source configuration and justify their reasoning using geometric principles of wave propagation. Step 4 (20 minutes): For each identified source, students calculate relative phase differences by examining how nodal lines shift from expected positions for in-phase sources. They create phase diagrams showing the relationship between all sources. Step 5 (15 minutes): Students predict the intensity at five specified test points by vector addition of amplitudes from all sources, showing complete mathematical work. Step 6 (10 minutes): Groups rotate to examine other patterns and verify their analytical methods work across different configurations. Final step (15 minutes): Each group presents their analysis for one pattern, defending their conclusions about source number, positions, phases, and predicted intensities.
materials_needed: Three sets of printed wave interference pattern data on coordinate grids
Rulers and protractors for precise measurements
Graphing calculators or computers with mathematical software
Colored pencils for marking different wave contributions
Large format paper for creating source configuration diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of wavelength determination from measurements (25%), (2) Correctness of source configuration identification with geometric justification (25%), (3) Mathematical precision in phase difference calculations and vector addition (30%), and (4) Quality of predictions with verification against actual pattern data (20%). Students must achieve 85% accuracy in mathematical calculations and correctly identify source arrangements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide templates with partially completed coordinate systems and guided calculation sheets showing the first few steps. Offer reference cards with key wave interference equations. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by providing patterns with amplitude variations between sources or ask them to design source configurations that would produce specific desired interference patterns.

title: Code Review Showdown: Evaluating Bug-Prone Python Functions
description: Students will critically evaluate three pre-written Python functions that contain common beginner mistakes and logical errors. They will rank the functions from best to worst, justify their evaluations using specific coding principles, and propose concrete improvements for each function.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and functionality of Python code by analyzing syntax errors, logical flaws, and adherence to coding best practices
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and ranking based on predetermined quality criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Function Evaluation Worksheet' containing three Python functions: a temperature converter with mixed data types, a password validator with incomplete logic, and a list sorter with infinite loop potential. Display evaluation criteria on the board: functionality, readability, error handling, and efficiency.

**Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine each function independently, testing them mentally or on paper. They identify specific issues like syntax errors, logical flaws, poor variable naming, and missing edge cases. Students document problems using the provided error-tracking template.

**Ranking Phase (10 minutes):** Students rank the three functions from 1 (best) to 3 (worst) based on overall code quality. They must write a 2-3 sentence justification for each ranking, citing specific examples from the code.

**Peer Discussion (8 minutes):** In pairs, students compare their rankings and justifications. They must defend their choices and consider alternative perspectives. If rankings differ, pairs negotiate to reach consensus or agree to disagree with documented reasoning.

**Improvement Proposals (10 minutes):** Each student selects the worst-ranked function and writes specific, actionable improvements. They must propose at least three concrete changes: fix syntax/logic errors, improve variable names, and add error handling.

**Gallery Walk Validation (7 minutes):** Students post their rankings and improvements around the room. They conduct a silent gallery walk, placing sticky dots next to evaluations they agree with, creating a class consensus visualization.
materials_needed: Function Evaluation Worksheet with 3 buggy Python functions
Error-tracking template handout
Evaluation criteria reference sheet
Colored sticky dots for voting
Large paper sheets for posting work
assessment_method: Students earn points through a 4-category rubric: Issue Identification (4 points - finds 80%+ of errors), Ranking Justification (3 points - provides specific, code-based reasoning), Improvement Quality (3 points - suggests feasible, technical solutions), and Peer Engagement (2 points - actively participates in discussions). Total: 12 points. Success threshold: 9+ points.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a 'Common Python Errors Checklist' with syntax patterns to look for. Pair weaker students with stronger peers during discussion phase. For advanced learners, add a bonus challenge: propose alternative algorithms or discuss time complexity improvements. Consider providing a Python interpreter for students who want to test code execution.

title: Project Management Knowledge Acronym Rapid Recall Championship
description: Students participate in a timed, competitive recall exercise to memorize and instantly recognize 45 advanced project management acronyms, methodologies, and certification standards. This high-speed knowledge retrieval activity reinforces foundational PM terminology essential for advanced practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall definitions of 45 advanced project management acronyms within 3 seconds per item through rapid-fire flashcard drilling
Students will identify specific PM methodologies, tools, and standards by memorizing their abbreviated forms and full expansions through competitive team exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the Master Acronym List containing 45 advanced PM terms (e.g., RACI, PMBOK, PRINCE2, SAFe, ITIL, SLA, KPI, ROI, NPV, IRR, EVM, CPI, SPI, BAC, EAC, VAC, WBS, OBS, RBS, RAM, SWOT, PEST, MoSCoW, SMART, PDCA, DMAIC, etc.). Allow students 20 minutes for individual silent memorization using any preferred technique. Form teams of 4-5 students each. Round 1 (15 minutes): Flash acronyms on screen for 3 seconds each. Teams write full expansions and brief definitions on answer sheets. Round 2 (10 minutes): Reverse format - show full terms, teams write acronyms. Round 3 (15 minutes): Lightning round - verbal rapid-fire where one team member from each group stands, instructor calls acronym, first to correctly expand and define scores points. Rotate team representatives every 5 questions. Round 4 (10 minutes): Challenge round - show complex project scenarios, teams identify which 3-5 acronyms are most relevant. Maintain scoring throughout all rounds. Deduct points for incorrect answers to discourage guessing. Conclude with team rankings and individual spot-checks where random students must demonstrate mastery of 10 randomly selected acronyms. Award certificates to top-performing teams and individuals who achieve 90%+ accuracy.
materials_needed: Master Acronym List with 45 PM terms, definitions, and contexts
Digital presentation slides with timer functionality
Answer sheets with numbered spaces (4 different versions for each round)
Stopwatch or presentation timer
Scoring sheets for each team
Recognition certificates or small prizes for winners
assessment_method: Success measured by: Team scores across 4 rounds (40 points), individual final quiz achieving 36/40 correct answers (90%), verbal demonstration of 8/10 randomly selected acronyms with complete definitions, and completion time under 3 seconds per item during lightning rounds
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing acronym category sheets (financial, scheduling, quality, risk, etc.) and mnemonic device examples. Pair weaker students with stronger teammates. For advanced learners, add bonus questions about acronym origins, alternative meanings in different industries, or require integration of multiple acronyms in scenario responses.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Response: Analyzing the 2008 Financial Crisis Executive Communications
description: Students will analyze and compare actual crisis communications from three major financial institution CEOs during the 2008 financial crisis to understand how different leadership communication strategies impact stakeholder trust and organizational outcomes. They will identify patterns in messaging, timing, and audience targeting to comprehend the relationship between crisis leadership theory and real-world application.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze authentic crisis leadership communications by identifying specific theoretical frameworks (transformational, situational, authentic leadership) demonstrated in CEO statements and press releases during the 2008 financial crisis

Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective crisis leadership strategies through systematic comparison of communication timing, message framing, and stakeholder engagement approaches
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group one of three financial institutions: Lehman Brothers (Dick Fuld), JPMorgan Chase (Jamie Dimon), or Goldman Sachs (Lloyd Blankfein). Provide each group with a chronological packet containing 6-8 authentic documents: CEO letters to shareholders, press releases, congressional testimony excerpts, and internal memos from September 2008 to March 2009. Give students 45 minutes to read through materials and complete the Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheet, which requires them to: (1) identify three specific leadership theories evident in their CEO's approach, (2) categorize communications by primary audience (employees, shareholders, regulators, public), (3) map the evolution of messaging tone from pre-crisis to post-crisis, and (4) extract five direct quotes that exemplify crisis leadership principles. After individual group analysis, conduct a structured comparison session where each group presents their findings using a standardized template projected on screen. Groups have 8 minutes each to present their CEO's approach, followed by 5 minutes of guided questioning from other groups using provided question stems. Conclude with a 20-minute facilitated discussion where students identify cross-cutting patterns and connect observed behaviors to crisis leadership literature. Document insights on a shared digital board, organizing findings into 'Effective Practices,' 'Missed Opportunities,' and 'Theoretical Implications' categories.
materials_needed: Chronological document packets for each CEO (6-8 documents per packet, printed)
Crisis Leadership Analysis Framework worksheets
Digital projection system for presentations
Shared digital whiteboard platform (Miro or Jamboard)
Question stem cards for peer questioning
Timer for session management
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Analysis Framework worksheets using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of leadership theories with specific textual evidence, (2) Clear categorization of audience-targeted communications, (3) Logical mapping of message evolution with timeline accuracy, (4) Quality of extracted quotes demonstrating crisis leadership principles. Additionally, assess participation in group presentations and peer questioning for depth of comparative analysis and ability to synthesize patterns across different leadership approaches.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing a leadership theory reference sheet with key characteristics and examples. Offer sentence starters for analysis statements and encourage them to focus on 2-3 theories initially. For advanced learners, provide additional materials including media coverage and stock price data to analyze external perceptions and market responses. Challenge them to propose alternative communication strategies and predict potential outcomes using leadership theory predictions.

title: Comprehensive Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation and Optimization Strategy
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce data in Google Analytics 4. They will assess which model provides the most accurate representation of customer journey value and develop strategic recommendations for attribution optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI discrepancies across paid search, social media, and email marketing channels

Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer lifetime value, conversion lag time, and channel interaction patterns to formulate data-driven optimization recommendations
instructions: **Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide each student team (2-3 people) with access to a shared Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retailer. Ensure students can access Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison and Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths reports. **Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Students export attribution comparison data for the following models: First-click, Last-click, Linear, Time-decay, and Data-driven (if available). For each model, they must calculate: (1) Total attributed conversions by channel, (2) Cost per acquisition differences of ±20% or more between models, (3) Revenue attribution variations exceeding $10,000. Students create a comparison matrix documenting how each model values the customer journey differently, focusing on channels with the highest attribution discrepancies. **Evaluation Phase (30 minutes):** Teams analyze conversion path reports to identify: (1) Average path length for high-value customers (>$200 orders), (2) Time lag between first interaction and conversion, (3) Most common channel sequences leading to conversion. Students must identify which attribution model best reflects these behavioral patterns and justify their reasoning with specific data points. **Recommendation Phase (25 minutes):** Each team develops a strategic recommendation document addressing: (1) Which attribution model to implement and why, (2) Specific budget reallocation recommendations between channels based on their analysis, (3) Three specific testing strategies to validate their chosen model's effectiveness, including success metrics and timeframes. **Presentation Phase (15 minutes):** Teams present their findings in 3-minute pitches, defending their attribution model choice against instructor challenges about edge cases and implementation complexity.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with 6+ months of multi-channel e-commerce data
Google Sheets or Excel for data analysis and matrix creation
Access to Advertising > Attribution reports in GA4
Presentation software (Google Slides/PowerPoint) for final recommendations
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points): Data accuracy and completeness in attribution comparison matrix (25 points), Quality of behavioral pattern analysis from conversion paths (25 points), Logical reasoning and evidence support for chosen attribution model (30 points), Strategic feasibility and specificity of budget reallocation recommendations (20 points). Students must demonstrate mastery by identifying attribution discrepancies >15% between models and providing quantitative justification for their strategic choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-formatted comparison templates and guide them to focus on 3 main channels initially. Offer guiding questions like 'Which channels show the biggest difference between first-click and last-click attribution?' For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value calculations, seasonal attribution variations, or cross-device journey analysis. Encourage exploration of custom attribution models using GA4's data-driven attribution insights.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Dynamic Routing and Security Policies
description: Students will architect and configure a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, OSPF dynamic routing, and comprehensive security policies. This capstone activity requires synthesizing advanced Cisco networking concepts to create a functional, scalable network infrastructure that meets specific business requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive network topology by integrating VLANs, routing protocols, and security measures to meet defined enterprise requirements
Students will implement advanced Cisco IOS configurations through hands-on router and switch programming using industry-standard commands and best practices
Students will evaluate network performance and security through systematic testing and validation of all implemented services
instructions: **Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)** - Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp with 4 departments (Sales, Engineering, HR, Finance) across 3 buildings requiring secure inter-department communication. Students work in teams of 2-3 to create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying: VLAN assignments (Sales-VLAN10, Engineering-VLAN20, HR-VLAN30, Finance-VLAN40), IP addressing schemes using 192.168.0.0/16 with appropriate subnetting, router placement for inter-VLAN routing, OSPF areas configuration, and security policies including ACLs for department isolation. **Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)** - Teams configure actual Cisco equipment: 3 x 2960 switches, 2 x 1941 routers. Step-by-step implementation: (1) Configure VLANs on all switches using 'vlan [number]' and 'name [department]' commands, (2) Assign switch ports to VLANs using 'switchport access vlan [number]', (3) Configure trunk links between switches with 'switchport mode trunk', (4) Set up router-on-a-stick configuration for inter-VLAN routing using subinterfaces, (5) Implement OSPF routing with 'router ospf 1' and appropriate network statements, (6) Create and apply ACLs using 'access-list [number]' commands to restrict cross-department traffic. **Phase 3: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)** - Teams conduct comprehensive testing: ping tests between VLANs, OSPF neighbor verification using 'show ip ospf neighbor', ACL functionality validation, and create detailed configuration documentation with troubleshooting logs.
materials_needed: 3 x Cisco Catalyst 2960 switches per team
2 x Cisco 1941 routers per team
Ethernet cables (12 per team)
Console cables for configuration
Cisco Packet Tracer software
PCs for testing connectivity (4 per team)
Network requirement specification document
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Network topology diagram with detailed annotations (25 points), (2) Complete router and switch configuration files with proper documentation (35 points), (3) Comprehensive testing report showing successful ping tests, routing table outputs, and ACL verification (25 points), (4) Troubleshooting log documenting any issues encountered and resolution methods (15 points). Instructor conducts live demonstration where teams explain their design decisions and demonstrate network functionality.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide VLAN configuration templates and command reference sheets, assign peer mentors from advanced students, break complex tasks into smaller checkpoints with instructor verification. For advanced learners: Add complexity with redundant links requiring STP configuration, implement QoS policies for voice traffic simulation, configure port security and DHCP snooping, or integrate wireless access points with guest network isolation.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Circuit Failures: Systematic Troubleshooting of Complex RLC Networks
description: Students will systematically analyze a malfunctioning three-branch RLC circuit by decomposing complex impedance relationships, identifying component failure patterns, and evaluating the cascading effects on circuit behavior. They will differentiate between multiple possible failure modes and determine root causes through quantitative analysis.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex RLC circuit behavior by systematically decomposing impedance contributions and identifying component-specific failure signatures
Students will evaluate multiple failure hypotheses through comparative analysis of theoretical predictions versus measured circuit responses
instructions: Begin by providing each group with a pre-built RLC circuit containing three parallel branches: Branch 1 (10Ω resistor + 100mH inductor), Branch 2 (20Ω resistor + 47µF capacitor), and Branch 3 (15Ω resistor only). Secretly introduce one failure in each circuit: either a 50% increase in one component's value, a short circuit, or an open circuit. Give students 15 minutes to measure and record voltage/current at five specific test points using multimeters and function generators set to 1kHz. Next, have students spend 20 minutes calculating theoretical values for each branch assuming all components are functional, using complex impedance analysis. They must show phasor diagrams and calculate expected phase relationships. In the following 25 minutes, students systematically compare measured versus theoretical values, creating a failure analysis matrix that examines each component's potential contribution to discrepancies. They should analyze: magnitude deviations, phase shift anomalies, and frequency response patterns. Students then formulate three specific hypotheses about which component failed and how, ranking them by probability based on quantitative evidence. During the final 15 minutes, groups present their analysis to another group, defending their primary hypothesis using impedance calculations, phasor relationships, and measurement data. The receiving group must critique the analysis and suggest alternative interpretations. Conclude with revealing actual failures and having students reflect on analysis accuracy.
materials_needed: Pre-built RLC circuits with intentional component failures (one per group of 3-4 students)
Digital multimeters with AC capability
Function generators (1kHz sine wave output)
Oscilloscopes for phase measurement
Component value reference sheets
Failure analysis matrix worksheets
Scientific calculators or tablets with complex number capability
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Mathematical analysis accuracy - correct impedance calculations and phasor diagrams (25%), (2) Systematic comparison methodology - organized data analysis and logical hypothesis formation (30%), (3) Evidence-based reasoning - quality of support for failure identification using quantitative data (30%), (4) Peer critique quality - depth of analysis during group presentations and ability to identify alternative explanations (15%). Students must submit their failure analysis matrix and mathematical work for individual assessment.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide impedance calculation templates and guide them through the first branch analysis as an example. Offer a structured hypothesis testing checklist. For advanced learners: Challenge them to predict how the identified failure would affect circuit behavior at different frequencies (100Hz, 10kHz) and to propose specific component replacement strategies that would optimize overall circuit performance.

title: Code Quality Assessment: Evaluating Two Beginner Python Solutions
description: Students will analyze and compare two different Python solutions to the same basic problem, evaluating which implementation is better based on specific software quality criteria. They will justify their assessment using evidence-based reasoning about code readability, efficiency, and maintainability.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate two Python code solutions by applying readability, efficiency, and maintainability criteria to determine the superior implementation
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison and provide written justification for their assessment
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the handout containing two Python solutions for calculating the sum of even numbers from 1 to 20. Solution A uses a for loop with if statements, while Solution B uses list comprehension with the sum() function. Provide the evaluation criteria sheet listing: readability (variable names, comments, structure), efficiency (number of operations, memory usage), and maintainability (ease of modification, code length). **Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Students examine both solutions, running each in their Python environment to verify functionality. They complete the comparison worksheet, rating each solution (1-5 scale) on the three criteria and noting specific evidence. **Pair Discussion (10 minutes):** Students pair up to compare their initial assessments, discussing differences in their ratings and sharing observations about each solution's strengths and weaknesses. **Written Evaluation (15 minutes):** Each student writes a 150-200 word assessment stating which solution is superior and why. They must reference at least two specific examples from the code and address all three evaluation criteria. **Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Volunteers share their conclusions while the instructor facilitates discussion about different valid perspectives and the importance of context in code evaluation. **Reflection (5 minutes):** Students write three key insights about what makes code 'good' based on this evaluation exercise.
materials_needed: Handout with two Python solutions for sum of even numbers problem
Evaluation criteria reference sheet (readability, efficiency, maintainability definitions)
Comparison worksheet template
Python environment (IDLE, online interpreter, or IDE)
Writing materials or document editor
assessment_method: Grade the written evaluation using this rubric: Clear position statement (2 points), specific code examples cited (3 points), addresses all three criteria (3 points), logical reasoning and evidence (2 points). Observe pair discussions for engagement and use of technical vocabulary. Success = 8/10 points minimum, with evidence-based reasoning and specific code references.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'Solution A is more readable because...' and highlight specific code lines to analyze. Create a checklist of evaluation questions. For advanced learners: Ask them to consider additional criteria like scalability or error handling, or have them suggest improvements to both solutions. Provide a third, more complex solution for additional comparison.

title: PMI Knowledge Area Integration Mapping Challenge
description: Students will recall and accurately identify specific processes, inputs, outputs, and tools across all ten PMI knowledge areas through a comprehensive matching and sequencing exercise. This activity reinforces memorization of the PMBOK Guide's process framework and prepares students for advanced project management certification.
learning_objectives: Students will recall specific process names, inputs, outputs, and tools for each of the 49 project management processes by completing targeted matching exercises
Students will identify the correct knowledge area and process group classification for each project management process through systematic categorization tasks
instructions:
Begin by distributing the prepared card sets to teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes setup). Each team receives 147 process cards (49 processes × 3 cards each: one showing process name, one showing 2-3 key inputs, one showing 2-3 key outputs), 30 tool/technique cards, 10 knowledge area headers, and 5 process group headers. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams must first sort all process cards by knowledge area, placing them under correct headers (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder). Instructor circulates with master answer key, providing immediate feedback when teams complete each knowledge area section.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Within each knowledge area, teams arrange processes by process group sequence (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing). Teams must match input and output cards to their corresponding process name cards, creating complete process triplets.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Teams select appropriate tool/technique cards for each process, placing them alongside the process triplets. Each process should have 1-3 relevant tools attached.

Final verification (10 minutes): Teams perform peer review with adjacent team, checking accuracy using provided verification sheets. Instructor conducts spot-checks on 10 randomly selected processes per team, focusing on complete accuracy of process-input-output-tool combinations.
materials_needed: 147 pre-printed process cards (color-coded: white for process names, blue for inputs, green for outputs)
30 laminated tool/technique cards with brief descriptions
15 knowledge area and process group header cards per team
Master answer key with complete PMBOK process mapping
Verification checklists for peer review
Large table space (minimum 4ft x 6ft per team)
assessment_method: Teams earn points based on accuracy: 2 points per correctly placed process in knowledge area (98 points max), 2 points per correct process group placement (98 points max), 3 points per accurate input-output-process match (294 points max), 1 point per appropriate tool selection (49 points max). Minimum passing score: 441/539 points (82%). Individual accountability ensured through random questioning where each team member must explain rationale for 3 randomly selected process mappings.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide knowledge area reference sheets with process counts per area, allow consultation of PMBOK index during Phase 1 only, assign strongest team member as 'process group specialist.' For advanced learners: Add constraint cards requiring teams to identify process dependencies and information flow between processes, challenge them to identify which processes are most frequently tailored or omitted in agile environments, require explanation of why certain inputs become outputs in subsequent processes.

title: Deconstructing Adaptive Leadership Responses to Organizational Crisis
description: Students analyze authentic leadership communication artifacts from three major organizational crises to identify and explain the underlying adaptive leadership principles, distinguishing between technical and adaptive challenges in each response. This expert-level activity requires deep comprehension of Heifetz's Adaptive Leadership Theory and its practical applications.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between technical problems and adaptive challenges by analyzing real leadership responses to organizational crises and categorizing specific decisions within Heifetz's framework
Students will explain the relationship between adaptive leadership behaviors and stakeholder outcomes through detailed interpretation of multi-modal leadership communications during crisis periods
instructions: Begin by distributing three crisis case study packets: Tylenol poisoning crisis (1982), Wells Fargo account fraud scandal (2016), and Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccine pause (2021). Each packet contains CEO communications, board statements, employee memos, and media interviews spanning 30-60 days. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one primary case plus access to comparison materials. Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams conduct systematic artifact analysis using the provided Adaptive Leadership Diagnostic Framework worksheet. Students must identify and highlight specific textual evidence of: getting on the balcony behaviors, identifying adaptive vs. technical elements, regulating distress mechanisms, maintaining disciplined attention strategies, and giving work back to stakeholders. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create visual mapping displays showing the timeline of adaptive leadership decisions, noting inflection points where leaders shifted between technical solutions and adaptive interventions. Phase 3 (45 minutes): Structured cross-case analysis where each team presents their primary case findings to other teams, followed by guided comparison discussions focusing on pattern recognition across different crisis types, industries, and stakeholder configurations. Conclude with individual reflection journals where students synthesize insights about how adaptive leadership principles manifest differently across contexts while maintaining core theoretical consistency.
materials_needed: Three comprehensive crisis case study packets with primary source documents
Adaptive Leadership Diagnostic Framework worksheets (laminated for reuse)
Large format poster paper and colored markers for visual mapping
Digital timer and presentation remote
Individual reflection journal templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: accuracy of technical vs. adaptive challenge identification (25%), quality of textual evidence selection and annotation (25%), depth of cross-case pattern analysis in presentations (25%), and sophistication of theoretical synthesis in reflection journals (25%). Success requires demonstrating nuanced understanding of how adaptive leadership principles operate across varied organizational contexts.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing pre-highlighted sample artifacts showing clear examples of adaptive vs. technical responses, and offer sentence starters for reflection journals. Extend advanced learners by challenging them to identify limitations or gaps in leaders' adaptive approaches and propose alternative interventions using additional adaptive leadership frameworks from Northouse or Yukl.

title: Risk Register Analysis: Categorizing and Prioritizing Project Risks Using PMBOK Framework
description: Students will analyze a comprehensive risk register from a software implementation project, categorize risks using RBS (Risk Breakdown Structure), and prioritize them using probability-impact matrices. This activity develops critical skills in risk pattern recognition and stakeholder impact assessment.
learning_objectives: Students will categorize 15 identified project risks by analyzing risk characteristics and mapping them to appropriate RBS categories (technical, organizational, external, project management)
