assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct application of conservation laws to each collision phase (25%), (2) Accurate energy loss calculations and collision type classifications (25%), (3) Quality of discrepancy analysis linking theoretical deviations to real-world factors (30%), (4) Presentation clarity and response to peer questions (20%). Students must demonstrate quantitative reasoning and show all calculation steps with proper uncertainty propagation.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide momentum/energy calculation templates and encourage focus on two-body interactions before tackling three-body systems. Offer guiding questions like 'What forces act during collision?' For advanced learners: Introduce rotational kinetic energy considerations, challenge them to propose experimental designs for testing their hypotheses, or have them analyze collision data with larger uncertainties requiring statistical analysis methods.

title: Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Fix Solutions
description: Students will critically evaluate three different solutions to the same JavaScript bug, assessing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluation using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different bug-fix approaches by analyzing code quality, readability, and performance metrics
Students will critique coding solutions through structured peer review using industry-standard evaluation criteria
instructions: Begin by presenting students with a simple JavaScript function containing a common array manipulation bug (15 minutes setup). Display the buggy function that attempts to remove duplicates from an array but fails with certain edge cases. Provide three pre-written 'student solutions' - Solution A (overly complex but works), Solution B (elegant and efficient), and Solution C (partially correct with remaining bugs). Form pairs and give each pair printed copies of all three solutions with line numbers. Students spend 20 minutes individually analyzing each solution using the provided evaluation checklist: correctness (does it fix the original bug?), edge case handling, code readability, performance efficiency, and adherence to JavaScript best practices. After individual analysis, pairs discuss their findings for 15 minutes, comparing notes and reaching consensus. Each pair then completes a ranking worksheet, ordering the solutions from best to worst and writing 2-3 sentences justifying each ranking decision. Conclude with a 15-minute class discussion where pairs share their rankings. Reveal the 'instructor's expert evaluation' and discuss why Solution B represents industry best practices, highlighting specific elements like proper variable naming, efficient algorithm choice, and comprehensive edge case handling.
materials_needed: Printed code solution sheets (3 solutions per student pair)
Code evaluation checklist handouts
Solution ranking worksheets
Projector/screen for displaying original buggy code
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade completed ranking worksheets using rubric: Correct identification of bugs/fixes (25 points), quality of justification reasoning (25 points), use of technical vocabulary (20 points), evidence of systematic evaluation process (20 points), participation in pair discussion (10 points). Minimum 70/100 points indicates successful evaluation skills.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide additional guiding questions on evaluation checklist and allow extra discussion time with instructor. For advanced learners: Add a fourth 'mystery solution' written in a different programming paradigm, or ask them to write their own improved solution and defend it against the provided options.

title: Design and Build a Data Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive data dashboard from scratch using real business data to solve a specific operational challenge. They will synthesize multiple data sources, design visualizations, and present actionable recommendations to simulated business stakeholders.
estimated_duration: 210 minutes (3.5 hours) - can be split across 2-3 class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will construct an interactive data dashboard by integrating at least three different data sources and applying appropriate visualization techniques
Students will formulate data-driven business recommendations through systematic analysis and synthesis of quantitative and qualitative insights
instructions: **Phase 1: Problem Definition (30 minutes)** - Assign students to teams of 3-4. Provide each team with a business scenario packet containing: a local restaurant's 6-month sales data (CSV), customer review data (JSON), and competitor pricing data (Excel). Teams select one of three challenges: increasing weekend revenue, reducing food waste, or improving customer satisfaction scores. **Phase 2: Data Integration (45 minutes)** - Students use Tableau Public or Power BI to import and clean their datasets. They must identify and document at least 5 data quality issues (missing values, inconsistent formats, outliers) and apply appropriate cleaning techniques. Instructor circulates to check data connection success. **Phase 3: Dashboard Design (60 minutes)** - Teams create a 4-panel dashboard including: trend analysis over time, comparative analysis (competitors/periods), geographic or demographic breakdown, and key performance indicators. Each visualization must include interactive filters and clear titles. Students sketch their dashboard layout on paper before building digitally. **Phase 4: Insight Generation (30 minutes)** - Teams analyze their dashboard to identify 3 specific, actionable insights. They must support each insight with quantitative evidence and estimate potential business impact (revenue/cost). **Phase 5: Presentation (45 minutes)** - Each team presents their dashboard live to the class (acting as business owners) in 6-minute presentations followed by 2 minutes of questions. Presentations must include problem context, methodology, key findings, and specific recommendations with implementation timelines.
materials_needed: Sample business datasets (sales_data.csv, reviews.json, competitor_pricing.xlsx)
Business scenario packets with company background and challenges
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI Desktop (free versions)
Computers with internet access
Projection system for presentations
Dashboard design template worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across five dimensions: (1) Data Integration Quality - proper cleaning, combining multiple sources, documentation of process; (2) Dashboard Design - visual clarity, interactivity, professional appearance; (3) Analytical Rigor - appropriate statistical methods, valid conclusions, quantified insights; (4) Business Relevance - actionable recommendations, realistic implementation, clear value proposition; (5) Presentation Skills - clear communication, effective use of visuals, professional delivery. Each dimension worth 20 points. Students also submit their dashboard file and a 1-page methodology summary.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned practice datasets and dashboard templates with placeholder charts. Offer guided worksheets for each phase with specific prompts. Pair weaker technical students with stronger ones. For advanced learners: Provide additional datasets (social media, weather, economic indicators) for more complex analysis. Challenge them to incorporate predictive modeling or statistical significance testing. Encourage use of advanced features like calculated fields and custom visualizations.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Components Identification Challenge
description: Students will recall and identify specific components, processes, and terminology from advanced project management frameworks including PMBOK 6th Edition knowledge areas, Agile ceremonies, and risk management categories. This rapid-fire identification activity tests retention of complex PM methodologies and their interconnected elements.
learning_objectives: Students will identify specific PMBOK 6th Edition knowledge areas, process groups, and their associated inputs/outputs by matching terminology to definitions within timed constraints
Students will recall advanced project management concepts including risk categories, stakeholder analysis matrices, and Agile/Scrum ceremonies through structured identification exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing laminated card sets to teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes setup). Each set contains 120 cards: 60 term cards (blue) featuring advanced PM concepts like 'Monte Carlo Analysis,' 'Analogous Estimating,' 'Sprint Retrospective,' and 60 definition cards (white) with precise descriptions. Explain the three-round structure (5 minutes). Round 1 (15 minutes): Teams sort blue cards into five PMBOK knowledge area categories (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Risk Management) without referring to definitions. Round 2 (20 minutes): Teams match 30 selected term cards to their corresponding definition cards, focusing on advanced techniques like Earned Value Management formulas, Critical Chain Method, and Kanban principles. Round 3 (10 minutes): Rapid recall quiz where instructor calls out scenarios ('Calculate Schedule Performance Index when EV=800, PV=1000') and teams hold up the correct term card ('SPI = 0.8' card). Between rounds, allow 3-minute team discussion periods. Rotate facilitator role within teams each round. Record team scores on whiteboard after each round. Conclude with 5-minute debrief where teams identify their most challenging knowledge area gaps.
materials_needed: Laminated card sets (120 cards per team: 60 blue term cards, 60 white definition cards)
Digital timer with audible alerts
Whiteboard and markers for scoring
Answer key sheets for instructors
Table tents for team identification
assessment_method: Score teams using point system: Round 1 (2 points per correctly categorized term, maximum 120 points), Round 2 (3 points per correct match, maximum 90 points), Round 3 (5 points per correct rapid response, maximum 50 points). Success criteria: Teams achieving 180+ total points demonstrate advanced-level retention. Individual assessment through post-activity quiz requiring students to define 10 randomly selected terms with 80% accuracy threshold.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide reference sheets with knowledge area frameworks and allow consultation during Round 1 only. Create mixed-ability teams pairing strong and developing students. For advanced learners: Add bonus challenge cards featuring PMI-ACP and PfMP concepts, introduce penalty system for incorrect rapid responses, or require teams to create original scenario examples using selected terms.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Philosophy: Analyzing Contrasting Executive Decision-Making Frameworks
description: Students will analyze and compare the underlying leadership philosophies of two contrasting Fortune 500 CEOs by examining their documented decision-making processes during organizational crises. They will identify key philosophical differences and explain how these frameworks influence strategic outcomes.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and transactional leadership philosophies by analyzing documented crisis management decisions of contrasting CEOs
Students will explain the relationship between leadership philosophy and organizational outcomes through systematic comparison of executive decision-making frameworks
instructions: Begin by providing students with comprehensive case study packets containing documented decisions, public statements, and strategic communications from two contrasting CEOs during major organizational crises (e.g., Satya Nadella's cultural transformation at Microsoft vs. Jack Welch's restructuring at GE). Divide class into teams of 3-4 students, ensuring diverse perspectives in each group. Phase 1 (30 minutes): Each team receives both case study packets and spends 15 minutes per case identifying specific evidence of each leader's core philosophical assumptions about people, change, and organizational purpose. Students must extract direct quotes and cite specific actions as evidence. Phase 2 (25 minutes): Teams create a comparative analysis matrix mapping each leader's philosophy across five dimensions: view of human motivation, approach to change management, communication style, risk tolerance, and stakeholder prioritization. Teams must categorize each leader's approach using established leadership theory frameworks (transformational, transactional, servant, authentic leadership models). Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams prepare a 5-minute presentation explaining how each leader's philosophical framework directly influenced their crisis management outcomes. Presentations must include specific cause-and-effect relationships between philosophical beliefs and strategic decisions, supported by quantifiable organizational results where available. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Teams present findings while other groups take structured notes using a provided comparison worksheet. Conclude with whole-class discussion identifying patterns and implications for leadership effectiveness in different organizational contexts.
materials_needed: Comprehensive case study packets for two contrasting Fortune 500 CEOs with documented crisis decisions
Comparative analysis matrix templates (printed worksheets)
Leadership theory reference sheets with key frameworks defined
Presentation timer and evaluation sheets for peer assessment
Whiteboard or digital presentation tools for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of philosophical framework identification with appropriate citations (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing clear understanding of differences (30%), (3) Logical explanation of philosophy-outcome relationships with specific evidence (30%), (4) Effective use of leadership theory vocabulary and concepts (15%). Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly categorizing each leader's approach and providing at least three specific examples of how philosophical differences led to different strategic choices.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case study sections focusing on key decisions and include guided questions for each analysis phase. Offer leadership theory concept maps showing relationships between different frameworks. For advanced learners, include additional CEO examples for broader comparison and challenge them to identify hybrid approaches or philosophical evolution over time. Provide optional extension reading on cultural context influences on leadership philosophy.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Traditional vs. Agile Approaches
description: Students will analyze two different project scenarios to examine how risk response strategies differ between traditional waterfall and agile project management approaches. They will deconstruct the effectiveness of various risk responses and justify which strategies are most appropriate for each methodology.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the effectiveness of different risk response strategies (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) by comparing their application in waterfall versus agile project contexts
Students will differentiate between proactive and reactive risk management approaches through systematic evaluation of real project scenarios
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute Case Study A (traditional software implementation) and Case Study B (agile mobile app development) to all teams. Each case includes 8 identified risks with proposed response strategies. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze Case Study A, creating a risk response matrix that categorizes each response as avoid/transfer/mitigate/accept and evaluates appropriateness using criteria: cost-effectiveness, timeline impact, and stakeholder acceptance. Teams must identify which responses are proactive vs. reactive.

Phase 2 (25 minutes): Teams repeat the analysis for Case Study B, noting how agile principles (iterative development, frequent feedback, adaptive planning) influence risk response selection.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Teams create a comparative analysis chart identifying: 1) Which risks appear in both scenarios but require different responses, 2) How response timing differs between methodologies, 3) Three specific examples where the same risk requires opposite strategies (e.g., scope change risks).

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about methodology-specific risk responses to the class, supporting their analysis with evidence from the cases.

Instructor circulates during analysis phases, asking probing questions like 'Why would this mitigation strategy fail in an agile environment?' and 'What assumptions about project predictability drive this response choice?'
materials_needed: Case Study A: Enterprise ERP Implementation (2-page document with 8 risks and proposed responses)
Case Study B: Agile Mobile Banking App Development (2-page document with 8 risks and proposed responses)
Risk Response Analysis Template (Excel or PDF worksheet)
Flip chart paper and markers for comparative analysis charts
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Risk Response Matrix for accuracy of categorization (20 points), quality of appropriateness justifications using provided criteria (30 points), and depth of comparative analysis showing methodology-specific insights (30 points). Assess team presentation for clarity of insight and supporting evidence (20 points). Use provided rubric with 4 performance levels: Exemplary, Proficient, Developing, Inadequate.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed matrix example and question prompts like 'How does iteration frequency affect this risk?' For advanced learners, add a third mini-case involving hybrid methodology or ask them to propose alternative responses not mentioned in the cases. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who have practical project experience.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Traditional vs. Agile Approaches: Comparative Study
description: Students will analyze two different project scenarios and compare how risk response strategies differ between traditional waterfall and agile project management approaches. They will examine the effectiveness of various risk mitigation techniques and justify their strategic choices based on project context.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between project methodology and risk response strategy selection by comparing identical risks across waterfall and agile contexts
Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies through systematic comparison of cost, timeline, and stakeholder impact factors
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Distribute two identical project scenarios: developing a customer portal system using (1) traditional waterfall methodology with 18-month timeline, and (2) agile methodology with 6 two-week sprints. Each scenario contains 8 pre-identified risks including technical integration challenges, resource availability, scope creep, and regulatory compliance issues. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams analyze each scenario separately, identifying appropriate risk response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) for each risk. They must document their reasoning using the provided analysis template, considering factors like project phase flexibility, stakeholder communication frequency, budget constraints, and change management capabilities.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create a comparative analysis matrix showing how the same risks require different response strategies based on methodology. They must identify at least 3 specific differences and explain the underlying reasons using PMP risk management principles.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each team presents one risk comparison to the class, defending their strategic choices and responding to peer questions. Teams must reference specific PMBoK risk management processes and tools in their justification.

Conclude with a 10-minute reflection where teams identify patterns in how project methodology influences risk strategy selection and document key insights for future application.
materials_needed: Two detailed project scenario handouts (4 pages each)
Risk analysis template with evaluation criteria matrix
PMBoK Guide risk management process reference sheet
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of risk response strategy selection (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis with specific examples (25%), (3) Use of PMBoK terminology and concepts (25%), (4) Clarity of reasoning and justification (25%). Teams must demonstrate understanding of at least 6 out of 8 risk scenarios and provide methodologically sound rationale for strategy differences.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example of one risk analysis and encourage focus on 4-5 risks rather than all 8. Advanced learners should incorporate quantitative risk analysis techniques and consider secondary risks created by their chosen response strategies. Offer additional scenarios involving hybrid methodologies for extension activities.
original_title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Traditional vs. Agile Approaches

title: Critical Evaluation of Multi-Channel Attribution Models for E-commerce Conversion Optimization
description: Students will critically assess the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 for a real e-commerce business case. They will analyze conflicting data interpretations across models and make evidence-based recommendations for budget allocation and marketing strategy adjustments.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the validity and limitations of first-click, last-click, linear, and data-driven attribution models by analyzing their impact on conversion credit distribution across marketing channels
Students will critique existing attribution model choices through comparative analysis of ROI calculations and justify alternative approaches based on business context and customer journey complexity
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection (45 minutes)**
Provide students with GA4 demo account access or prepared datasets showing 6-month e-commerce performance across channels (Google Ads, Facebook, Email, Organic Search, Direct). Students work in teams of 3-4. Each team accesses Attribution > Model Comparison Tool and exports conversion data under each attribution model (first-click, last-click, linear, data-driven, time-decay). They must document channel performance metrics including conversion value, conversion count, and cost data for each model.

**Phase 2: Critical Analysis (60 minutes)**
Teams create comparison matrices showing how each attribution model redistributes conversion credit differently. Students must identify the biggest discrepancies between models (minimum 3 significant variations) and research the underlying algorithmic reasons. They analyze customer journey data in Exploration > Path Exploration to understand typical conversion paths and journey length. Teams must critique each model's assumptions against actual customer behavior patterns observed in the data.

**Phase 3: Business Impact Assessment (45 minutes)**
Using provided cost-per-acquisition data for each channel, teams calculate ROI under each attribution model. They must identify which channels would receive budget increases/decreases under each model and quantify the potential impact (minimum $50,000 annual budget reallocation). Teams evaluate the business context (provided case study parameters: B2B vs B2C, consideration period, average order value) to determine model appropriateness.

**Phase 4: Recommendation Presentation (30 minutes)**
Each team presents 8-minute recommendations defending their chosen attribution model with specific evidence, addressing model limitations, and proposing implementation timeline with success metrics.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account access or pre-exported attribution datasets
E-commerce case study scenarios with business context details
Channel cost data spreadsheet (CPC, CPM, email costs)
Presentation software (Google Slides/PowerPoint)
Attribution model comparison template worksheet
assessment_method: Teams evaluated on: 1) Accuracy of data interpretation (25%) - correctly identifying attribution differences and calculating ROI impacts, 2) Depth of critical analysis (30%) - demonstrating understanding of model limitations and biases, 3) Quality of business justification (25%) - aligning model choice with business context and customer behavior, 4) Presentation clarity and evidence use (20%) - effectively communicating recommendations with supporting data. Rubric includes specific benchmarks: identifying minimum 3 significant attribution discrepancies, calculating accurate ROI variations, addressing at least 2 model limitations, and providing quantified budget impact projections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide attribution model definition sheets and guided worksheet for ROI calculations. Offer mid-activity check-ins to verify data extraction accuracy. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate GA4 Exploration reports for deeper customer journey analysis, consider custom attribution models, or evaluate attribution modeling impact on customer lifetime value calculations. Provide additional datasets from different industries for comparative analysis.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Inter-VLAN Routing and Security Policies
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise network solution featuring multiple VLANs, Layer 3 routing, DHCP services, and access control lists. They will create network documentation, configure Cisco switches and routers from scratch, and validate their design through comprehensive testing protocols.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network topology by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will implement inter-VLAN routing and security policies through hands-on configuration of Cisco switches, routers, and access control mechanisms
instructions: **Phase 1 (45 minutes): Network Design** Students work in teams of 2-3 to analyze a provided business scenario (200-employee company with HR, Finance, IT, and Guest departments). Teams create: (1) Logical network topology using draw.io or Visio, (2) VLAN assignment table, (3) IP addressing scheme using /24 subnets from 192.168.0.0/16, and (4) Security requirements matrix. **Phase 2 (90 minutes): Physical Implementation** Using Cisco Packet Tracer or physical equipment (2 x 2960 switches, 1 x 1941 router), teams configure: (1) VLANs 10, 20, 30, 40 on switches with appropriate naming, (2) Trunk links between switches using 802.1Q, (3) Router-on-a-stick configuration for inter-VLAN routing, (4) DHCP pools for each VLAN on the router, and (5) Access control lists restricting HR VLAN from accessing other departments. **Phase 3 (30 minutes): Testing and Documentation** Teams execute testing protocol: ping tests between VLANs, DHCP functionality verification, ACL effectiveness testing, and create a final configuration backup. Submit network diagram, configuration files, and test results documentation. Instructor circulates providing guidance on CLI syntax and troubleshooting connection issues.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer software or physical lab with 2 x Catalyst 2960 switches and 1 x ISR 1941 router
Network design software (draw.io, Visio, or similar)
Business scenario handout with department requirements and user counts
Configuration template worksheets
Console cables and laptops for physical lab access
assessment_method: Rubric-based evaluation (100 points): Network design accuracy and scalability (25 points), Correct VLAN and trunk configuration (20 points), Functional inter-VLAN routing with DHCP (25 points), Working ACL implementation (15 points), Professional documentation and testing results (15 points). Students must demonstrate live network functionality and explain configuration choices during 10-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured router templates with partial commands, offer command reference sheets with common IOS syntax, and assign peer mentors from advanced students. For advanced learners: Add OSPF routing between multiple routers, implement VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP), configure port security features, or integrate wireless access points with guest network isolation.

title: Binary Number System Recall Challenge: Converting Decimal 0-15
description: Students memorize and practice recalling the binary representations of decimal numbers 0 through 15. Through repetitive flashcard drills and timed recall exercises, students build automatic recognition of these fundamental binary-decimal conversions.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 from memory within 3 seconds per number
Students will identify the decimal equivalent of 4-bit binary numbers through rapid recognition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Have students work in pairs for the first 15 minutes, taking turns showing the decimal side while their partner states the binary equivalent, then checking the answer. Encourage students to use the cards repeatedly, focusing on numbers they find most challenging. After pair practice, conduct a whole-class drill where you display decimal numbers 0-15 randomly on the board or projector, giving students 10 seconds to write the binary equivalent on individual whiteboards. Record which students answer correctly for each number. Next, reverse the process by showing binary numbers (0000, 0001, 0010, etc.) and having students write the decimal equivalent. Conclude with a individual timed challenge: students receive a worksheet with 20 random decimal numbers (0-15) and must write binary equivalents within 5 minutes. Provide immediate feedback by displaying correct answers. End the session by having students identify their three most challenging number pairs and write them on sticky notes for homework review. Emphasize that this foundational knowledge will support upcoming lessons on larger binary numbers and binary arithmetic operations.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back (one set per student pair)
Individual mini whiteboards and dry-erase markers for each student
Printed worksheet with 20 random decimal numbers (0-15) for final assessment
Projector or board for displaying numbers during class drills
Sticky notes for students to record challenging pairs
assessment_method: Students must achieve 80% accuracy (16/20 correct) on the final timed worksheet within 5 minutes. Track individual performance during class drills using a checklist showing each student's correct responses for numbers 0-15. Award full credit for meeting the 80% threshold, partial credit for 60-79% accuracy, and require additional practice for below 60%.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference chart showing the place values (8-4-2-1) and allow them to use finger counting initially. Create additional practice sheets focusing only on numbers 0-7 before progressing to 8-15. For advanced learners: extend the activity to include decimal numbers 16-31 (5-bit binary) or introduce hexadecimal equivalents alongside binary representations.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Heatmaps for Customer Behavior Analysis
description: Students will analyze a correlation heatmap showing relationships between customer demographic and behavioral variables to identify meaningful patterns and potential multicollinearity issues. They will practice interpreting correlation coefficients and explaining their business implications in the context of customer segmentation.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between customer variables by analyzing color-coded values in a heatmap and explaining their statistical significance
Students will classify variable relationships as positive, negative, or negligible correlations through systematic examination of coefficient magnitudes and directions
instructions: Begin by displaying a pre-generated correlation heatmap showing relationships between 8-10 customer variables (age, income, purchase_frequency, time_on_site, cart_abandonment_rate, email_opens, social_media_engagement, customer_lifetime_value). Distribute printed copies and provide 5 minutes for individual observation. Form pairs and give each pair a structured analysis worksheet with three sections: Strong Correlations (|r| > 0.7), Moderate Correlations (0.3 < |r| < 0.7), and Weak Correlations (|r| < 0.3). Students spend 15 minutes identifying and categorizing at least 12 variable pairs, writing the exact correlation coefficient and whether it's positive or negative. Next, pairs select their 5 strongest correlations and spend 10 minutes writing business interpretations for each (e.g., 'Income and customer_lifetime_value show r=0.84, suggesting higher-income customers tend to have significantly greater long-term value'). In the final 10 minutes, pairs identify potential multicollinearity concerns by finding variable clusters with multiple strong intercorrelations and explain why this might problematic for predictive modeling. Each pair submits their completed worksheet with categorized correlations, business interpretations, and multicollinearity assessment. Conclude with 5-minute whole-class discussion where 2-3 pairs share their most surprising findings.
materials_needed: Pre-generated customer behavior correlation heatmap (printed and digital versions)
Structured analysis worksheets with three correlation strength categories
Calculator or correlation coefficient reference guide
Projector/screen for displaying heatmap
assessment_method: Grade submitted worksheets using rubric: Correct correlation categorization (30 points - 2 points per correctly categorized pair), accurate business interpretations (40 points - 8 points per interpretation showing clear understanding of relationship direction and strength), multicollinearity identification (20 points for identifying clustered variables), professional communication (10 points for clear, specific language)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation strength reference card and sentence starters like 'The correlation between X and Y is [strength] and [direction], which means...' For advanced learners, ask them to propose specific business actions based on their findings and identify which correlations might be spurious or require further investigation.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: Breaking Down the Three-Body Problem
description: Students will analyze the complex gravitational interactions in a three-body system by decomposing force vectors, identifying equilibrium points, and evaluating system stability. They will examine how small perturbations in initial conditions lead to chaotic behavior in celestial mechanics.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze gravitational force vectors in a three-body system by decomposing each body's net force into component influences from the other two bodies
Students will evaluate system stability through identification of Lagrange points and analysis of perturbation effects on orbital trajectories
instructions: Begin by distributing the Earth-Moon-Sun system data sheets containing masses, distances, and initial velocity vectors (15 minutes setup). Form groups of 3-4 students, with each group receiving different initial condition scenarios. Step 1: Students calculate gravitational forces between each pair of bodies using F = Gm₁m₂/r², creating force vector diagrams for each body at t=0 (25 minutes). Step 2: Groups analyze the net acceleration vectors and predict initial motion directions, documenting their reasoning with mathematical justification (20 minutes). Step 3: Using provided simulation software (Universe Sandbox or equivalent), students run their scenarios for 10 orbital periods, recording position data at regular intervals (30 minutes). Step 4: Students analyze discrepancies between their predictions and simulation results, identifying which gravitational interactions they initially underestimated or overlooked (25 minutes). Step 5: Groups systematically vary one parameter (mass, distance, or velocity) by 1%, 5%, and 10%, running new simulations to analyze sensitivity to initial conditions (35 minutes). Step 6: Students identify and analyze the five Lagrange points in their system, calculating the equilibrium conditions and testing stability by introducing small perturbations (40 minutes). Step 7: Groups create comprehensive analysis reports comparing theoretical predictions with simulation results, explaining sources of complexity and presenting evidence for chaotic vs. stable regions (30 minutes). Conclude with presentations where each group defends their analysis of why three-body systems exhibit fundamentally different behavior than two-body systems (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Three-body system data sheets with Earth-Moon-Sun parameters
Scientific calculators or computers with computational software
Universe Sandbox or equivalent gravitational simulation software
Graph paper and vector drawing tools
Data recording templates for position/velocity tracking
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of force calculations and vector decomposition (25%), (2) Quality of analysis comparing predictions to simulation results with quantitative evidence (30%), (3) Depth of evaluation regarding system sensitivity and chaos identification (25%), (4) Clarity of written analysis report and oral defense of conclusions (20%). Success requires demonstrating understanding of how individual gravitational interactions combine to create emergent system behaviors.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated force magnitudes and focus on vector addition; offer guided worksheets for Lagrange point identification. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive analytical approximations for restricted three-body problems or analyze real asteroid systems at Jupiter's Lagrange points; extend to four-body systems or investigate historical solutions like Euler's collinear configuration.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Dashboard for Customer Churn Analysis
description: Students will synthesize customer data patterns to design an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn risk. They will create original visualizations, develop actionable business recommendations, and present their analytical framework to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize customer behavioral data by creating an integrated predictive dashboard with at least 4 interactive visualizations
Students will construct evidence-based business recommendations through statistical analysis and trend identification
Students will design an original analytical framework by combining multiple data sources and presenting actionable insights
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Framework Design (45 minutes)**

Provide students with the customer churn dataset containing 12 months of data (demographics, usage patterns, support tickets, billing history). Students work in teams of 3-4 to explore the dataset using Excel/Google Sheets initially. Each team identifies 5-7 key variables they believe influence churn and creates a hypothesis statement about customer retention patterns.

**Phase 2: Dashboard Construction (90 minutes)**

Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students build their predictive dashboard with specific requirements: (1) Overview KPI panel showing current churn rate, at-risk customers, and revenue impact, (2) Customer segmentation visualization showing behavioral clusters, (3) Trend analysis chart displaying churn patterns over time, (4) Risk scoring visualization highlighting high-risk customer profiles, (5) Interactive filters for demographics, service tiers, and time periods. Students must ensure all visualizations connect logically and tell a cohesive story.

**Phase 3: Insights Development (30 minutes)**

Teams analyze their dashboard outputs to identify the top 3 factors driving churn and develop specific, measurable recommendations for reducing customer attrition. They must quantify potential impact (e.g., "Implementing proactive outreach to customers with >5 support tickets could retain 15% more customers monthly").

**Phase 4: Stakeholder Presentation (45 minutes)**

Each team presents their dashboard live to the class (acting as company executives) in 8-minute presentations. They must demonstrate dashboard functionality, explain their analytical approach, defend their insights with data evidence, and respond to challenging questions about methodology and business viability.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV format with 2000+ records, 15+ variables)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI access for each student
Laptops/computers with internet connectivity
Presentation display/projector
Evaluation rubric handouts
Timer for presentation sessions
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Dashboard Design Quality (25 points - visual clarity, interactivity, technical execution), Analytical Rigor (25 points - appropriate statistical methods, data accuracy, logical reasoning), Business Insight Quality (25 points - actionable recommendations, quantified impact, feasibility), Presentation Effectiveness (25 points - clarity, stakeholder engagement, question handling). Students must score 70+ points to demonstrate proficiency at the create level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide dashboard template with pre-built basic charts they can modify, offer data interpretation guides with sample insights, pair with stronger analytical partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external data sources, build predictive models using calculated fields, create executive summary reports with statistical confidence intervals, or develop A/B testing frameworks for their recommendations.

title: PMI Risk Register Terminology Speed Recall Challenge
description: Students will rapidly recall and match 50 advanced project management terms from PMI's risk management knowledge areas with their precise definitions. This high-intensity activity tests memorization of complex terminology including risk response strategies, quantitative analysis methods, and specialized risk assessment techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will recall 45+ advanced PMI risk management terms and their exact definitions within 15 minutes through rapid-fire matching exercises
Students will identify specific risk response strategy definitions (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept, exploit, enhance, share) through timed recognition tasks
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-prepared term cards face-down to each student (50 terms total). Set up the digital timer for 15 minutes and display it prominently. Students work individually for the first 10 minutes, flipping cards one at a time and writing the corresponding definition on their answer sheet. Terms include: Monte Carlo simulation, Expected Monetary Value (EMV), Probability-Impact Matrix, Secondary Risk, Residual Risk, Risk Appetite, Risk Tolerance, Tornado Diagram, Decision Tree Analysis, and 41 others from PMI's risk management processes. After 10 minutes, announce a 2-minute partner verification phase where students can discuss uncertain answers with their neighbor. During the final 3 minutes, conduct rapid-fire verbal checks by calling out 10 random terms and having students shout out key definition components. Record participation and accuracy on the tracking sheet. Conclude by having students self-score using the provided answer key, marking correct matches with green ink and incorrect ones with red ink. Students must achieve 90% accuracy (45/50 correct) to demonstrate mastery of advanced PM terminology recall.
materials_needed: 50 laminated term cards with advanced PMI risk management vocabulary
Individual answer sheets with numbered lines 1-50
Digital countdown timer with audio alerts
Answer key with complete definitions
Green and red ink pens for self-scoring
Student tracking sheet for instructor use
assessment_method: Students achieve mastery by correctly matching 45+ terms (90%) within the time limit. Assessment includes: immediate self-scoring using answer key (40 points), participation in rapid-fire verbal section (5 points), and completion of reflection question identifying their 3 weakest terminology areas (5 points). Maximum score: 50 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a reference sheet with the first letter of each definition and allow an additional 3 minutes. For advanced learners: challenge them to create original sentences using 5 terms correctly in context, or have them lead the rapid-fire section by calling out terms to classmates.

title: Multi-Attribution Model Performance Audit for E-commerce Conversion Optimization
description: Students will conduct a comprehensive evaluation of different attribution models within Google Analytics 4 to determine the most effective model for a specific e-commerce business scenario. They will analyze conversion paths, assess model accuracy against business goals, and provide strategic recommendations for attribution model selection.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of different GA4 attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, data-driven) by analyzing conversion path data and comparing model outputs against specific business KPIs
Students will critique attribution model performance through systematic analysis of customer journey complexity, campaign ROI variations, and conversion value discrepancies across models
instructions: Begin by providing each student team (2-3 members) with access to a GA4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Students first spend 30 minutes exploring the Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool to familiarize themselves with available attribution models. Next, teams analyze conversion paths by navigating to Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths, filtering for transactions with 2+ touchpoints over the past 90 days. Students document path complexity patterns and identify the top 10 most common conversion sequences. In the third phase (45 minutes), teams systematically compare all five attribution models using the Model comparison report, focusing on three specific metrics: conversion value, conversion count, and ROAS for each traffic source/medium combination. Students must create a comparative matrix showing percentage differences between models for their top 5 traffic sources. During the analysis phase (60 minutes), teams evaluate each model's alignment with the provided business scenario (subscription-based vs. impulse purchase business model), considering factors like typical customer decision timeline, average order value patterns, and marketing channel investment strategy. Teams then assess model reliability by examining data-driven model thresholds and statistical significance indicators. Finally, students prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice, including specific implementation timeline, expected impact on campaign optimization decisions, and potential limitations. Each presentation must include supporting data visualizations exported from GA4 and address at least two potential counterarguments to their recommendation.
materials_needed: GA4 demo account access with e-commerce tracking enabled
Business scenario handout (subscription vs impulse purchase company profiles)
Attribution model comparison template spreadsheet
Google Slides or PowerPoint for presentations
Screen recording software for capturing GA4 navigation
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Thoroughness of data analysis - evidence of exploring all five attribution models with quantitative support (25%), (2) Quality of evaluation criteria - demonstrates understanding of business context alignment and model limitations (25%), (3) Strength of recommendation justification - provides compelling evidence-based argument with consideration of counterpoints (25%), (4) Presentation clarity and use of GA4 data visualizations to support conclusions (25%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a guided worksheet with specific GA4 navigation steps and key questions to answer at each analysis stage. Offer mid-activity check-ins to review their comparative matrix before moving to evaluation phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate custom conversion events, analyze seasonal attribution patterns, or evaluate the impact of iOS 14.5+ privacy changes on attribution model accuracy. Encourage exploration of GA4's machine learning insights panel for additional context.

title: Optimization Challenge: Designing Maximum-Volume Packaging for Real Products
description: Students apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to solve authentic packaging design problems for actual consumer products. They will use Lagrange multipliers and constraint analysis to maximize volume while adhering to real-world manufacturing constraints including material costs, shipping dimensions, and regulatory requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems by analyzing real packaging scenarios with multiple variables and constraints
Students will implement calculus-based optimization strategies through systematic problem-solving processes involving partial derivatives, constraint equations, and critical point analysis
instructions: Begin by distributing product specification sheets containing real packaging scenarios (cereal boxes, beverage containers, or shipping cartons) with given constraints such as surface area limits, material costs per square unit, and shipping pallet dimensions. Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to analyze their assigned scenario and identify all variables, objective functions, and constraints. Next, demonstrate the systematic approach using one example: define variables (length=x, width=y, height=z), establish the objective function (Volume = xyz), and write constraint equations (surface area: 2xy + 2xz + 2yz ≤ maximum allowed). Have students spend 25 minutes setting up their Lagrange function L(x,y,z,λ) = xyz + λ(constraint - surface area limit) and computing partial derivatives. Circulate to verify setups before proceeding. Students then solve the system of equations by setting ∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y = ∂L/∂z = ∂L/∂λ = 0, spending 30 minutes on algebraic manipulation and solution verification. Require students to check second-order conditions using the bordered Hessian matrix to confirm maximum points. In the final 20 minutes, pairs calculate final dimensions, maximum volume, and material costs, then create a brief presentation slide showing their optimal design with justification. Each pair presents their solution for 3 minutes, explaining their constraint interpretation, mathematical approach, and practical feasibility of their optimized packaging design.
materials_needed: Product specification sheets with real packaging constraints (5-6 different scenarios)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Maple, or online tools)
Grid paper and rulers for sketching
Presentation slides template or poster paper
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct identification and setup of optimization problem with constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier methodology including proper partial derivatives (35%), (3) Correct algebraic solution and verification using second-order conditions (25%), and (4) Clear presentation of results with practical interpretation and feasibility analysis (15%). Students must show all mathematical work and provide final dimensions with units.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint equations and guide them through the first few partial derivative calculations. Offer a step-by-step checklist for the Lagrange multiplier process. For advanced learners, introduce additional constraints such as environmental regulations, stackability requirements, or multiple material types with different costs, requiring more sophisticated optimization techniques and consideration of integer programming elements.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Collision Systems: Energy Transfer and Conservation Breakdown
description: Students will analyze complex multi-body collision scenarios using high-speed video data to examine energy conservation violations and identify the underlying physical mechanisms. They will decompose collision sequences into phases and evaluate the relative contributions of elastic, inelastic, and rotational energy components.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze multi-body collision data by identifying energy transfer mechanisms and quantifying conservation law violations in real-world scenarios
Students will examine the relationships between collision geometry, material properties, and energy dissipation through systematic data interpretation and mathematical modeling
instructions: Begin by providing student teams of 3-4 with high-speed video footage (1000+ fps) of a three-ball collision system where Ball A strikes Ball B, which then impacts Ball C. Students receive position-time data extracted from the video at 2ms intervals. Step 1 (15 min): Teams calculate velocities for each ball in 10ms segments before, during, and after each collision phase using kinematic equations. Step 2 (20 min): Students compute translational kinetic energy for each ball at key time intervals and create energy-time graphs for the entire system. Step 3 (25 min): Teams analyze the energy data to identify where and when energy is lost, calculating the percentage of energy dissipated in each collision phase. They must distinguish between energy losses due to deformation, friction, sound, and rotational motion. Step 4 (30 min): Students examine collision angles and contact times to determine how geometric factors influence energy transfer efficiency. They calculate coefficients of restitution for each collision pair and analyze deviations from ideal elastic behavior. Step 5 (20 min): Teams create a comprehensive analysis report documenting energy flow diagrams, identifying the primary mechanisms of energy dissipation, and proposing modifications to minimize energy losses. Step 6 (15 min): Groups present their findings, comparing energy loss mechanisms and discussing how their analysis could inform engineering applications like automotive safety or sports equipment design.
materials_needed: High-speed collision video files (minimum 1000 fps)
Extracted position-time data spreadsheets with 2ms time intervals
Scientific calculators or computational software (Python/MATLAB)
Graph paper or digital graphing tools
Ball mass and diameter specifications
Coefficient of restitution reference tables
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of kinematic calculations and energy computations (25%), (2) Quality of energy loss analysis and mechanism identification (30%), (3) Depth of geometric factor analysis and coefficient calculations (25%), (4) Clarity and scientific reasoning in final report and presentation (20%). Students must demonstrate quantitative analysis with less than 5% computational error and identify at least three distinct energy dissipation mechanisms with supporting evidence.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated velocity data for the first collision and energy calculation templates. Offer guided practice with two-body collisions before advancing to three-body systems. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate rotational energy analysis, model air resistance effects, or predict collision outcomes for different ball materials using their derived relationships. Provide access to more complex collision scenarios involving different mass ratios.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes and Best Practices
description: Students will critically evaluate three different code solutions to a simple calculator bug, assessing code quality, effectiveness, and adherence to best practices. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluations using specific software development criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate different code solutions by analyzing their effectiveness, readability, and maintainability using established coding standards
Students will critique programming approaches through systematic comparison and provide evidence-based recommendations for code improvements
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with three printed code samples (Solution A, B, and C) that fix the same bug in a basic calculator function - specifically a division by zero error. Each solution uses different approaches: try-catch blocks, if-statements, and input validation. Also provide the evaluation rubric sheet.

**Individual Analysis (20 minutes):** Students examine each code solution and complete an evaluation matrix, rating each solution (1-5 scale) on: code readability, error handling effectiveness, performance impact, maintainability, and adherence to naming conventions. They must write specific evidence for each rating in the provided spaces.

**Ranking and Justification (15 minutes):** Students rank the three solutions from best to worst and write a 150-word justification explaining their ranking. They must reference at least three specific code elements (variable names, logic structure, error messages, etc.) and explain how each solution would perform in a real application.

**Peer Review (15 minutes):** Pair students to compare their rankings and justifications. Each student presents their top choice to their partner, explaining two strengths and one potential improvement. Partners ask clarifying questions about the evaluation criteria used.

**Class Discussion (10 minutes):** Facilitate a brief discussion where 3-4 students share which solution they ranked highest and one key factor that influenced their decision. Record the class consensus on the whiteboard and highlight common evaluation criteria mentioned.
materials_needed: Three printed code solution samples (one page each) showing different approaches to fixing division by zero
Evaluation matrix worksheet with rating scales and evidence boxes
Assessment rubric handout with coding standards criteria
Pens/pencils for annotations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed evaluation matrices for appropriate use of criteria (25 points), written justifications for evidence-based reasoning and specific code references (35 points), and peer review participation demonstrating critical thinking (15 points). Success requires ratings supported by specific code examples and justifications that reference at least three evaluation criteria with clear reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a completed example evaluation of a fourth code sample and highlight key phrases to look for in code quality. Offer a checklist of specific items to examine in each solution. For advanced learners, add a bonus task to write two specific code improvements for their lowest-ranked solution, or have them evaluate the solutions' security implications and scalability potential.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Analytics Dashboard for Customer Churn
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn using real e-commerce data, combining statistical analysis, visualization design, and business storytelling. They will design their own analytical framework, build predictive models, and present actionable insights through a custom dashboard interface.
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize multiple data sources and analytical techniques by creating an original predictive model for customer behavior patterns
Students will design and construct an interactive business dashboard through integration of statistical analysis, data visualization, and user experience principles
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Exploration & Framework Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with the e-commerce dataset containing customer demographics, purchase history, and engagement metrics. Students work in pairs to explore the data using Python/Jupyter notebooks, identifying key variables that might predict churn. They must create their own analytical framework by defining churn criteria (e.g., no purchase in 6 months), selecting relevant features, and hypothesizing relationships. Students document their approach in a structured analysis plan.

**Phase 2: Model Development (60 minutes)**
Students build and compare at least two predictive models (e.g., logistic regression, random forest) using scikit-learn. They must engineer new features, handle missing data, and evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics. Each pair creates a model comparison matrix documenting accuracy, precision, recall, and business interpretability. Students select their best-performing model and extract key insights about churn drivers.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Using Tableau or Power BI, students design and build an interactive dashboard containing: (1) executive summary with key churn statistics, (2) customer segmentation analysis with risk scoring, (3) predictive model results with confidence intervals, and (4) actionable recommendations panel. The dashboard must include at least 5 interactive elements (filters, drill-downs, hover details) and follow business presentation standards with clear titles, legends, and professional formatting.

**Phase 4: Business Presentation (30 minutes)**
Pairs present their dashboards in 5-minute business pitches to simulated executives (other student pairs), explaining their methodology, key findings, and specific recommendations for reducing churn. Presenters must justify their analytical choices and respond to questions about model limitations and implementation feasibility.
materials_needed: E-commerce customer dataset (CSV format with 10,000+ records including demographics, purchase history, engagement metrics)
Computers with Python, Jupyter notebooks, pandas, scikit-learn, and matplotlib installed
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software access
Business presentation template with required dashboard sections
Model evaluation worksheet for documenting performance metrics
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Technical Implementation (40 points) - model accuracy, feature engineering, code quality; Dashboard Design (30 points) - visual clarity, interactivity, professional presentation; Business Communication (20 points) - actionable insights, clear recommendations, effective presentation; Analytical Reasoning (10 points) - methodology justification, limitation awareness. Students submit Jupyter notebook, dashboard file, and 2-page executive summary. Peer evaluations during presentations contribute 15% of total score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-written code templates for basic model implementation, offer guided worksheets for feature selection, and create dashboard wireframe examples. Pair weaker technical students with stronger partners. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement ensemble methods, create custom metrics for business impact, add statistical significance testing, or build real-time data refresh capabilities. Encourage exploration of advanced visualization techniques like cohort analysis or customer journey mapping.

title: Advanced Project Management Methodology and Framework Recall Challenge
description: Students demonstrate their ability to accurately recall and identify specific elements of advanced project management methodologies including PMI knowledge areas, PRINCE2 principles, Agile ceremonies, and risk management frameworks. This rapid-recall activity tests memorization of critical PM terminology, processes, and framework components essential for advanced practice.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall and identify all 10 PMI knowledge areas and their 49 sub-processes by completing timed matching exercises
Students will correctly recite the 7 PRINCE2 principles and 4 integrated elements through structured verbal assessment protocols
instructions: Begin by distributing the comprehensive recall worksheets containing 150 advanced PM terms, processes, and framework elements (15 minutes setup). Divide students into pairs for peer verification. Round 1 (20 minutes): Students complete Section A covering PMI's 10 knowledge areas - they must write all knowledge areas from memory, then match 25 specific processes to correct knowledge areas without references. Round 2 (15 minutes): Students tackle Section B on PRINCE2 methodology, recalling all 7 principles (continued business justification, learn from experience, defined roles/responsibilities, manage by stages, manage by exception, focus on products, tailor to suit environment) and identifying 4 integrated elements (principles, themes, processes, project environment). Round 3 (20 minutes): Advanced risk management recall where students list 15 specific risk response strategies across avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept categories, plus recall Monte Carlo simulation steps and Expected Monetary Value calculation components. Round 4 (15 minutes): Agile framework recall covering all Scrum ceremonies (Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective) with specific timeboxes, participants, and outcomes. Partners verify answers using provided answer keys. Conclude with individual reflection (5 minutes) where students identify knowledge gaps for further study. Instructor circulates continuously, noting students struggling with specific frameworks for targeted remediation.
materials_needed: 150-item advanced PM terminology recall worksheet (printed, 2 pages per student)
Comprehensive answer keys for peer verification (1 per pair)
Digital timer/stopwatch visible to all students
PMI PMBOK 7th edition quick reference cards (backup for struggling students)
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy across all four recall rounds (128/150 items correct) to demonstrate mastery. Assessment includes: Section A - 35 items (knowledge areas + process matching), Section B - 40 items (PRINCE2 components), Section C - 45 items (risk management elements), Section D - 30 items (Agile ceremonies). Peer verification provides immediate feedback. Instructor spot-checks 20% of papers for verification accuracy. Students scoring below 85% receive targeted remediation assignments focusing on their weakest framework areas.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide PMI and PRINCE2 quick reference cards after first attempt, allow additional 5 minutes per section, pair with high-performing students for peer support. For advanced learners: Add bonus section requiring recall of specific PMBOK page references, include hybrid methodology components (SAFe, Disciplined Agile), challenge them to create mnemonics for complex processes to share with struggling peers.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership: Analyzing Multi-Stakeholder Communication Strategies Through Real-World Case Studies
description: Students will analyze authentic crisis leadership scenarios by examining how leaders balanced competing stakeholder interests, adapted communication styles, and made strategic decisions under pressure. Through structured case study analysis, students will demonstrate understanding of adaptive leadership principles and stakeholder management complexities.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective crisis communication strategies by analyzing leader responses across multiple stakeholder groups in documented organizational crises
Students will explain the relationship between situational leadership adaptations and stakeholder outcomes through comparative analysis of leader decision-making frameworks
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 4-5 members (15 minutes setup). Provide each team with a comprehensive crisis case study packet containing: timeline of events, stakeholder communication artifacts (emails, press releases, internal memos), financial data, and outcome metrics. Assign each team member a specific stakeholder perspective to champion: employees, customers, investors, regulators, and community. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Individual stakeholder analysis. Each team member examines all communication materials from their assigned stakeholder's viewpoint, documenting: what messages the leader sent, when communications occurred, what channels were used, and how their stakeholder group likely perceived each message. Students complete a stakeholder impact matrix rating leader effectiveness on a 1-5 scale with evidence.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Team synthesis meeting. Members present their stakeholder analyses, identifying conflicts between stakeholder needs and how the leader prioritized competing demands. Teams create a visual timeline showing communication sequences and stakeholder reactions.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Cross-case comparison. Teams rotate to review other teams' completed analyses, noting patterns in leadership approaches across different crisis types. Each team identifies three critical leadership principles that emerge across cases.

Phase 4 (25 minutes): Structured debrief. Teams present one key insight about how effective crisis leaders balance stakeholder tensions, supported by specific evidence from their case analysis. Instructor facilitates discussion connecting observations to adaptive leadership theory and situational communication models.
materials_needed: 6-8 detailed crisis leadership case study packets (15-20 pages each) with authentic communication artifacts
Stakeholder impact matrix templates (digital or printed)
Large format paper or digital collaboration boards for timeline creation
Case rotation tracking sheets
Access to presentation display capability
assessment_method: Evaluate completed stakeholder impact matrices for evidence quality and analytical depth (40% of grade). Assess team timeline visualizations for accuracy and insight identification (30% of grade). Score final presentations using rubric measuring: use of specific evidence, connection to leadership concepts, and quality of cross-case insights (30% of grade). Success criteria: students provide at least 3 specific examples per stakeholder perspective, identify minimum 2 stakeholder conflicts with supporting evidence, and articulate leadership principles using course terminology.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide stakeholder analysis question prompts and example evidence citations. Create template sentences for connecting observations to leadership concepts. For advanced learners: add secondary sources about crisis leadership theory to compare against case observations, or assign facilitation of cross-team discussions during rotation phase. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who excel at presentation skills within teams.

title: Comparative E-commerce Attribution Model Analysis and Strategic Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models (first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven) using real e-commerce conversion data in Google Analytics. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for a specific business scenario and defend their recommendation with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of five different attribution models by analyzing their impact on channel performance metrics and ROI calculations
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of conversion paths and justify an optimal model selection for a given business context
instructions: **Setup Phase (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data from a multi-channel retailer. Students work in pairs and receive a business brief detailing the company's marketing objectives, budget constraints, and current attribution model concerns. **Analysis Phase (45 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Model comparison tool. They must configure comparisons between all five attribution models, focusing on: (1) Revenue differences across paid search, social media, email, and display channels, (2) Conversion path length analysis using the Top Conversion Paths report, (3) Time lag analysis between first interaction and conversion. Students document quantitative findings in a provided analysis template, calculating percentage differences in attributed conversions and revenue for each channel under different models. **Evaluation Phase (30 minutes):** Students assess model performance against three criteria: alignment with business goals, accuracy in reflecting customer journey complexity, and actionability for budget allocation decisions. They must identify strengths and limitations of each model using specific data points from their analysis. **Recommendation Phase (20 minutes):** Students prepare a 5-minute presentation defending their chosen attribution model. The recommendation must include: quantified impact on marketing spend allocation, specific implementation timeline, and anticipated challenges. **Peer Review Phase (15 minutes):** Each pair presents to another pair, receiving structured feedback on the strength of their evidence and logical reasoning.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Business scenario brief document with company background and objectives
Attribution analysis template spreadsheet
Evaluation criteria rubric handout
Presentation timer and feedback forms
assessment_method: Students evaluated using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Accuracy of data interpretation and calculations (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis between models (25%), (3) Strength of justification for recommended model using quantitative evidence (30%), (4) Consideration of implementation challenges and business context (20%). Successful completion requires scoring 3+ on all criteria and presenting clear ROI impact projections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured custom reports showing attribution comparisons and guided question prompts for each analysis step. Consider pairing with stronger analytics students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate customer lifetime value considerations, analyze attribution by device category, or propose custom attribution model weighting based on their findings.

title: Design and Implement a Resilient Multi-Site Enterprise Network Architecture with Disaster Recovery
description: Students will architect, configure, and deploy a comprehensive enterprise network spanning three geographically distributed sites with full redundancy, automated failover mechanisms, and disaster recovery capabilities. They will create original network designs, implement advanced routing protocols, and develop custom monitoring solutions to ensure 99.9% uptime requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will design an original multi-site enterprise network topology by integrating OSPF, BGP, HSRP, and MPLS technologies to meet specific business continuity requirements
Students will create custom network automation scripts and monitoring dashboards through Python programming and SNMP implementation to proactively manage network health
instructions: Begin by forming teams of 3-4 students (15 minutes). Each team receives a detailed business scenario: a financial services company requiring three connected sites (headquarters, data center, branch office) with zero-tolerance for downtime. Students start by creating original network diagrams using Packet Tracer or GNS3, incorporating redundant WAN links, backup power considerations, and traffic flow analysis (60 minutes). Next, teams physically configure Cisco routers and switches: implement OSPF areas with proper summarization, establish eBGP peering between sites, configure HSRP for gateway redundancy, and set up EtherChannel for link aggregation (120 minutes). Students then develop Python scripts using Netmiko library to automate configuration backups and monitor interface statistics via SNMP (45 minutes). Teams create custom dashboards displaying real-time network metrics, bandwidth utilization, and automated alerts for threshold violations (30 minutes). Finally, conduct disaster recovery testing by systematically failing primary links, power sources, and routing protocols while documenting failover times and recovery procedures (45 minutes). Students present their complete solution including network diagrams, configuration files, automation scripts, monitoring dashboards, and disaster recovery documentation to simulate a board presentation (30 minutes per team). Conclude with peer evaluation where teams attempt to break each other's networks through controlled failure scenarios (45 minutes).
materials_needed: 6 Cisco 2900 series routers per team
4 Cisco Catalyst 3560 switches per team
Ethernet cables (Cat6, various lengths)
Serial cables for WAN simulation
Laptops with GNS3/Packet Tracer, Python 3.x, and SSH clients installed
Network monitoring software (PRTG or SolarWinds trial versions)
Cisco IOS licensing for advanced features
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Innovation (25 points) - originality of topology, proper addressing schemes, scalability considerations; Technical Implementation (30 points) - correct protocol configuration, redundancy mechanisms, security measures; Automation Quality (20 points) - script functionality, error handling, code documentation; Disaster Recovery Effectiveness (15 points) - failover speed, recovery procedures, documentation completeness; Professional Presentation (10 points) - technical communication, business justification, peer feedback incorporation. Students must demonstrate live network functionality, explain design decisions, and successfully recover from induced failures within specified time limits.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates, step-by-step configuration guides, and assign them to teams with stronger technical members. Offer additional lab time for hands-on practice with individual protocols before integration.
