For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement SD-WAN concepts, integrate network security appliances, or develop machine learning algorithms for predictive network maintenance. Encourage exploration of emerging technologies like intent-based networking or network function virtualization.

title: Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns in Real Estate Price Analysis
description: Students will analyze a dataset of residential property sales to identify and explain distribution patterns, outliers, and relationships between variables. They will create multiple visualizations and write explanations demonstrating their understanding of how data characteristics affect analytical conclusions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret distribution shapes, central tendencies, and variability in housing price data by analyzing histograms, box plots, and summary statistics
Students will explain the relationship between property features and price distributions through comparative analysis of categorical and numerical variables
instructions:
Begin by providing each student with the same cleaned dataset containing 500 residential property records with variables: price, bedrooms, bathrooms, square_footage, lot_size, year_built, neighborhood, and property_type. 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Students load the dataset and generate basic summary statistics using describe() function. They identify the range, mean, median, and standard deviation for price and square_footage variables.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Students create three visualizations: (1) histogram of property prices with 20 bins, (2) box plot of prices by neighborhood (limit to top 5 neighborhoods by count), and (3) scatter plot of square_footage vs price. They must include appropriate titles, axis labels, and legends.

Step 3 (15 minutes): Working in pairs, students examine their visualizations and identify: distribution shape (normal, skewed, bimodal), presence of outliers, and any obvious patterns or clusters in the data.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each pair writes a 200-word interpretation report addressing: (1) What the price distribution reveals about the housing market, (2) How neighborhood affects price patterns, (3) The strength and direction of the relationship between size and price, and (4) Which properties might be considered outliers and why.

Step 5 (10 minutes): Three volunteer pairs present one key finding to the class, explaining how their visualization supports their conclusion. Instructor facilitates discussion about different interpretations of the same patterns.
materials_needed: Cleaned CSV dataset with 500 residential property records
Python environment with pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn installed
Jupyter notebook template with data loading code
Handout defining distribution terminology (skewness, outliers, correlation)
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of summary statistics calculation (20 points), (2) Quality of visualizations with proper formatting and labels (30 points), (3) Correctness of pattern identification in written report (30 points), (4) Logical reasoning connecting data characteristics to real-world implications (20 points). Students must correctly identify distribution shape and at least two meaningful patterns to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template code for generating visualizations and a checklist of patterns to look for. Pair them with stronger peers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to create additional visualizations (violin plots, correlation heatmaps) or segment analysis by property type. Encourage them to research neighborhood characteristics to explain price patterns.

title: Optimizing Multi-Variable Production Functions for Manufacturing Efficiency
description: Students will apply partial derivatives and constrained optimization techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing problem. They will determine optimal resource allocation to maximize production output while operating within budget and capacity constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply partial differentiation techniques to analyze multi-variable production functions by calculating marginal products and rates of change
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical procedures
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute setup where students receive their manufacturing scenario packet containing a Cobb-Douglas production function P(L,K) = 20L^0.6K^0.4 representing weekly output based on labor hours (L) and capital investment (K), along with constraints: budget limit 2L + 5K ≤ 1000 and minimum production requirement P ≥ 500. Form teams of 3-4 students for 15 minutes to analyze the scenario and identify variables, constraints, and objectives. Next, spend 25 minutes on Phase 1 where teams calculate partial derivatives ∂P/∂L and ∂P/∂K to determine marginal productivity rates, then interpret these values in business context by explaining what happens to production when labor or capital increases by one unit. In Phase 2 (35 minutes), students set up the Lagrangian function L(L,K,λ) = 20L^0.6K^0.4 - λ(2L + 5K - 1000) and solve the system of equations by taking partial derivatives and setting equal to zero. They must show all algebraic steps to find critical points. During Phase 3 (20 minutes), teams verify their solution satisfies all constraints, calculate the maximum production value, and prepare a business recommendation memo explaining optimal labor hours, capital investment, expected weekly output, and justification using mathematical analysis. Conclude with 15-minute team presentations where each group presents their optimal solution and mathematical reasoning to the class.
materials_needed: Manufacturing scenario packets with specific production function and constraints
Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Graph paper and rulers for sketching constraint regions
Business memo template worksheets
Access to computer algebra system (optional: Desmos, GeoGebra, or Wolfram Alpha)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Correct calculation of partial derivatives and setup of optimization problem (25%), (2) Accurate application of Lagrange multiplier method with complete algebraic work (35%), (3) Verification of constraints and interpretation of results in business context (25%), (4) Quality of mathematical communication in presentation and written memo (15%). Students must demonstrate all work and achieve 70% for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide step-by-step Lagrange multiplier template with partially completed equations and offer hints about constraint substitution methods. Advanced learners can explore sensitivity analysis by investigating how optimal solutions change with different budget limits or add additional constraints like maximum labor hours. Consider providing graphing tools to visualize constraint regions for visual learners.

title: Analyzing Multi-Physics Coupling in a Thermoelectric Generator Through Energy Flow Decomposition
description: Students will dissect the complex energy conversion mechanisms in a thermoelectric generator by analyzing the interplay between thermal, electrical, and materials physics. They will decompose experimental data to isolate and quantify the competing effects of Seebeck voltage generation, Joule heating, thermal conduction, and Thomson heating.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the thermodynamic efficiency of a thermoelectric device by separating and quantifying irreversible losses from each coupled physical process using experimental voltage and temperature data
Students will evaluate the relative contributions of Seebeck, Peltier, and Thomson effects through systematic manipulation of boundary conditions and mathematical decomposition of measured parameters
instructions: Begin by providing each team with a bismuth telluride thermoelectric module, two precision thermocouples, a variable load resistor (0-100Ω), hot and cold water baths, and data acquisition software. In the first 20 minutes, teams establish steady-state conditions with ΔT = 40K between hot and cold sides, measuring open-circuit voltage and internal resistance. Next, students systematically vary the load resistance in 10Ω increments from 0-100Ω, recording voltage, current, hot-side temperature, and cold-side temperature at each point (30 minutes). During data collection, students must maintain constant bath temperatures within ±0.5K. In the analysis phase (45 minutes), teams create I-V characteristic curves and calculate power output, then use the measured data to separate total heat flow into: (1) Seebeck-generated EMF component, (2) Joule heating losses (I²R), (3) thermal conduction losses (kΔT/L), and (4) Thomson heating effects. Students apply the coupled thermoelectric equations: Q_h = αTI + 0.5I²R + K(T_h-T_c) and Q_c = αT_cI - 0.5I²R + K(T_h-T_c), solving simultaneously to extract material properties α (Seebeck coefficient), R (electrical resistance), and K (thermal conductance). Finally, teams construct energy flow diagrams showing quantified energy paths and calculate the theoretical maximum efficiency using extracted parameters compared to measured efficiency. Each team presents their decomposition analysis, identifying which physical process dominates energy losses at different operating points.
materials_needed: Bismuth telluride thermoelectric modules (40mm x 40mm)
Type-K thermocouple probes with 0.1K resolution
Variable decade resistor box (0-100Ω, 5W rating)
Controlled temperature water baths (±0.5K stability)
Digital multimeters with data logging capability
LabVIEW or Python data acquisition software
Thermal interface paste
Aluminum heat sink blocks
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Complete I-V and power curves with uncertainty analysis (25 points), (2) Mathematical decomposition showing separated energy terms with derived material properties α, R, K within 15% of literature values (35 points), (3) Energy flow diagram quantifying each loss mechanism (25 points), (4) Analysis comparing theoretical vs. measured efficiency with explanation of discrepancies (15 points). Grading emphasizes accuracy of physical reasoning in separating coupled effects rather than perfect numerical results.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-derived thermoelectric equations and template spreadsheets with guided calculation cells. Offer intermediate checkpoints for I-V curve shape and temperature stability before proceeding to analysis. For advanced learners, challenge them to include temperature-dependent material properties, analyze figure-of-merit optimization, or investigate Thomson effect contributions which are often neglected in introductory treatments.

title: Design a Predictive Customer Churn Dashboard with Actionable Insights
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that predicts customer churn for a fictional subscription service using real data patterns. They will combine multiple analytical techniques to design visualizations and develop specific business recommendations based on their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive predictive analytics dashboard by integrating customer behavior data, churn probability models, and interactive visualizations
Students will synthesize data insights to formulate specific, evidence-based business strategies through written recommendations and presentation materials
instructions:
**Phase 1 (45 minutes): Data Exploration and Model Design**
Provide students with a customer dataset containing 12 months of subscription data (customer_id, signup_date, monthly_charges, contract_length, support_tickets, usage_hours, payment_method, churn_status). Students work in pairs to explore the dataset using Excel or Google Sheets, identifying 3-4 key variables that correlate with churn. They calculate churn rates by segment (e.g., contract type, price tier) and create a simple scoring model assigning risk points to different customer characteristics.

**Phase 2 (60 minutes): Dashboard Creation**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students design a 4-panel dashboard: (1) Overall churn metrics and trends, (2) Customer segmentation analysis with risk scores, (3) Predictive model showing high-risk customers, and (4) Financial impact visualization showing revenue at risk. Each panel must include interactive filters for contract type, tenure, and monthly charges. Students must incorporate at least two different chart types (bar charts, scatter plots, heat maps, or line graphs).

**Phase 3 (30 minutes): Strategy Development**
Based on their analysis, students develop three specific intervention strategies targeting different risk segments. Each strategy must include: target customer criteria, proposed action, expected outcome metrics, and implementation timeline. They create a one-page executive summary with supporting data visualizations.

**Phase 4 (15 minutes): Peer Review**
Pairs rotate to review two other dashboards, providing feedback using a structured form focusing on data accuracy, visual clarity, and business relevance of recommendations.
materials_needed: Customer churn dataset (CSV file with 1000+ records)
Computers with Tableau Public or Power BI access
Dashboard evaluation rubric handouts
Executive summary template document
Peer review feedback forms
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Dashboard functionality and design (40 points) - includes accurate calculations, appropriate visualizations, and interactive features; Data analysis quality (30 points) - correct identification of churn patterns and risk segmentation; Business recommendations (20 points) - specificity, feasibility, and data support; Presentation clarity (10 points) - professional formatting and clear communication. Students must achieve 70+ points to demonstrate proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated churn rates by segment and a dashboard template with placeholder charts. Offer guided questions for pattern identification. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate additional variables like customer lifetime value, create cohort analysis, or develop ROI calculations for their proposed interventions. Provide access to more complex datasets with multiple product lines.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Communication: A Multi-Perspective Analysis of Organizational Response Strategies
description: Students will analyze authentic crisis communication from three different organizational leaders during the same industry-wide crisis, comparing their strategic approaches, stakeholder messaging, and underlying leadership philosophies. This activity develops deep comprehension of how different leadership styles manifest in high-stakes communication decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and servant leadership approaches by analyzing specific crisis communication artifacts and identifying characteristic language patterns, decision frameworks, and stakeholder prioritization strategies

Students will interpret the relationship between organizational culture and leadership communication style through comparative analysis of tone, transparency levels, and accountability messaging across three case studies
instructions: Begin by distributing three crisis communication packages to student teams of 4-5 members (20 minutes setup). Each package contains: CEO statement, employee memo, customer communication, and media interview transcript from different companies responding to the 2021 supply chain crisis (Amazon, Patagonia, and General Motors selected for distinct leadership approaches). Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams rotate through three analysis stations, spending 15 minutes at each. Station A focuses on 'Language and Tone Analysis' where students identify specific word choices, emotional appeals, and communication formality levels. Station B examines 'Stakeholder Prioritization' by mapping which groups (employees, customers, investors, community) receive primary attention in each leader's messaging. Station C analyzes 'Accountability and Transparency Levels' by categorizing statements as deflecting, acknowledging, or accepting full responsibility. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams create a comparative matrix documenting their findings across all three leaders, identifying patterns that align with specific leadership theories from course readings. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Each team presents one key insight about how leadership philosophy directly influenced communication strategy, providing specific textual evidence. Instructor facilitates connections between observations and theoretical frameworks including Kouzes-Posner, Bass's transformational leadership model, and Greenleaf's servant leadership principles. Conclude with 10-minute reflection on which approach would be most effective in students' own organizational contexts.
materials_needed: Three crisis communication document packets (printed, 4 pages each)
Analysis worksheet templates for each station
Large poster paper and markers for matrix creation
Access to course readings on leadership theories
Timer for station rotations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership theory identification with specific textual evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of differences between approaches (30%), (3) Connection between leadership philosophy and communication strategy with concrete examples (25%), (4) Participation in station rotations and final presentation clarity (20%). Success requires demonstrating comprehension of how theoretical leadership concepts manifest in real-world crisis scenarios.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing leadership theory reference sheets at each station and highlighting key phrases in communication samples. For advanced learners, add a fourth analysis dimension examining cultural context and industry norms, or have them research follow-up communications to analyze consistency over time. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with peers who excel at presentation skills.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Performance Audit and Optimization Recommendations
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics 4 using real e-commerce data, comparing first-click, last-click, data-driven, and position-based models. They will assess which model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation and make evidence-based recommendations for attribution strategy optimization.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the performance and limitations of four different attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI metrics across multiple marketing channels
Students will critique existing attribution strategies through comparative analysis of customer journey data and formulate data-driven recommendations for attribution model selection
instructions:
**Setup (15 minutes):** Provide students with access to a Google Analytics 4 demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data with multiple marketing channels (organic search, paid search, social media, email, direct, display). Ensure Attribution settings show data for all four models: first-click, last-click, data-driven, and position-based.

**Phase 1 - Data Collection (30 minutes):** Students navigate to Advertising > Attribution > Conversion paths and Model comparison reports. They must extract key metrics for each attribution model: total conversions, conversion value, cost-per-acquisition, and channel contribution percentages. Students create a comparison matrix documenting how each model attributes credit to the five highest-performing channels.

**Phase 2 - Critical Analysis (45 minutes):** Working in pairs, students analyze discrepancies between models, identifying which channels gain/lose attribution credit under different models. They examine specific conversion paths (minimum 20 paths) to understand why attribution varies. Students must identify three specific scenarios where each model would be most/least appropriate based on business goals and customer behavior patterns.

**Phase 3 - Strategic Evaluation (30 minutes):** Students evaluate the business impact of each model by calculating budget reallocation scenarios. They determine which model would lead to optimal ROI if budget decisions were based solely on that attribution method. Students must consider factors like touchpoint timing, channel interaction effects, and campaign objectives.

**Phase 4 - Recommendation Development (20 minutes):** Each pair creates a formal recommendation report justifying their chosen attribution model with specific evidence from their analysis, including potential risks and implementation considerations.
materials_needed: Google Analytics 4 demo account with e-commerce tracking enabled
Excel or Google Sheets for data analysis
Access to Attribution reports with 6+ months of multi-channel data
Conversion path data showing minimum 500 completed conversions
Cost data imported for paid channels
assessment_method: Students submit a 2-page recommendation report evaluated on: (1) Accuracy of data extraction and metric calculations (25%), (2) Depth of comparative analysis between attribution models (30%), (3) Quality of evidence used to support recommendations (25%), (4) Consideration of business context and implementation challenges (20%). Rubric includes specific criteria for identifying attribution discrepancies, explaining customer journey implications, and providing actionable optimization strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a template matrix for data collection and guiding questions for each analysis phase. Offer pre-selected conversion paths to analyze if students have difficulty navigating reports. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate custom attribution models or analyze attribution in conjunction with audience segments. Encourage exploration of cross-device attribution challenges and privacy implications of different models.

title: Analyzing Multi-Stage Rocket Performance Through Energy and Momentum Conservation
description: Students will decompose a three-stage rocket launch scenario into distinct phases and analyze the energy transformations and momentum changes at each stage separation. They will evaluate the efficiency of each stage and determine optimal mass ratios using real SpaceX Falcon Heavy data.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the momentum conservation during stage separations by calculating velocity changes and comparing theoretical predictions with actual telemetry data
Students will evaluate energy efficiency across rocket stages through systematic examination of kinetic, potential, and chemical energy transformations at each separation event
instructions: Begin with 15 minutes of data distribution - provide each team of 3-4 students with SpaceX Falcon Heavy telemetry data showing altitude, velocity, and mass at three separation events (boosters, first stage, fairing). Students first spend 20 minutes individually examining the data to identify the three distinct phases and noting velocity/altitude changes. Next, teams collaborate for 45 minutes to create detailed energy-momentum analysis charts. Each team assigns one member to analyze momentum conservation (calculating impulse and velocity changes), one to track kinetic energy transformations, one to examine potential energy changes with orbital mechanics, and one to estimate propellant chemical energy conversion efficiency. Teams must create quantitative comparisons between theoretical predictions using rocket equations and actual telemetry values. During the 30-minute analysis phase, students identify discrepancies between theoretical and actual values, hypothesize causes (atmospheric drag, engine throttling, gravitational losses), and calculate percentage errors. Teams then spend 25 minutes preparing technical presentations with visual data representations. Each team presents their 8-minute analysis to the class, focusing on one specific aspect: momentum conservation accuracy, energy transformation efficiency, or discrepancy explanations. Conclude with 15 minutes of peer evaluation where teams critique each other's analysis methods and conclusions using provided evaluation criteria.
materials_needed: SpaceX Falcon Heavy mission telemetry dataset (CSV format with time, altitude, velocity, mass data)
Scientific calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
Large format graph paper or digital graphing tools
Rocket equation reference sheets with standard atmospheric and gravitational parameters
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of momentum calculations and theoretical comparisons (25%), (2) Correctness of energy transformation analysis with proper unit conversions (25%), (3) Quality of discrepancy identification and scientific reasoning for differences between theoretical and actual values (25%), (4) Clarity of visual data presentation and peer presentation delivery (25%). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculations and provide at least three scientifically valid explanations for theoretical-actual discrepancies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-calculated intermediate values and step-by-step calculation templates focusing on one stage only. Offer dimensional analysis worksheets and common unit conversion references. For advanced learners, extend analysis to include orbital mechanics calculations, compare with other rocket systems (Saturn V, Artemis SLS), or investigate optimization strategies for mass ratios and engine-specific impulse values.

title: Code Review Quality Assessment: Evaluating Bug Fixes in Simple Python Functions
description: Students will evaluate the quality and correctness of three different bug fix solutions for a broken Python calculator function. They will assess each solution against established criteria and justify their selection of the best fix with detailed reasoning.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different bug fix solutions by analyzing code correctness, readability, and efficiency against established quality criteria
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic comparison and provide justified recommendations for implementation
instructions: Begin by providing students with a broken Python calculator function that has an obvious division-by-zero error and poor variable naming (15 minutes setup). Present three pre-written 'student solutions' that fix the bug in different ways: Solution A uses basic try/except, Solution B uses conditional checking, and Solution C uses both techniques but with overly complex logic. Give students the evaluation criteria sheet covering: correctness (does it work?), readability (clear variable names, comments), efficiency (minimal unnecessary code), and error handling (appropriate user feedback). Students work individually for 25 minutes to test each solution using provided test cases, document pros/cons in a comparison table, and rate each solution 1-10 on each criterion. They must write 2-3 sentences justifying each rating. In the final 15 minutes, students write a one-paragraph recommendation explaining which solution they would choose for production code and why, addressing potential counterarguments. Circulate during individual work to ensure students are testing code properly and using specific examples in their evaluations rather than vague statements.
materials_needed: Pre-written broken Python calculator function with test cases
Three different bug fix solutions (printed or digital)
Evaluation criteria rubric sheet
Python IDE or online compiler access
Comparison table template
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Testing accuracy (did they correctly identify what works), Criteria application (systematic use of all four criteria with specific examples), Justification quality (clear reasoning with evidence), and Professional recommendation (addresses trade-offs and considers real-world context). Students must score 3/4 on at least 3 categories to demonstrate evaluation mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters like 'This solution handles errors by...' and model evaluating one criterion for the first solution together. For advanced learners: Add a fourth solution with subtle security issues or ask them to propose their own improved solution incorporating the best elements from all three versions.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis
description: Students analyze complex leadership scenarios involving inherent paradoxes (e.g., empowerment vs. accountability) by examining the same situation through multiple theoretical lenses. They demonstrate understanding by identifying contradictory forces leaders must balance and explaining how different leadership theories interpret these tensions.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and explain leadership paradoxes by analyzing real-world scenarios through at least three different theoretical frameworks

Students will demonstrate understanding of leadership complexity through detailed comparison of how transformational, servant, and situational leadership theories interpret the same paradoxical situation
instructions: Provide each student with the 'MedTech Crisis Leadership Case' (a detailed scenario about a healthcare technology company CEO managing simultaneous demands for innovation speed and regulatory compliance during a pandemic). Students work individually for 15 minutes to read and annotate the case, identifying key decision points and stakeholder tensions. Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member one of four theoretical lenses: Transformational Leadership (Bass), Servant Leadership (Greenleaf), Situational Leadership (Hersey-Blanchard), and Authentic Leadership (George). Each student spends 20 minutes analyzing the CEO's decisions through their assigned theory, documenting on a structured analysis template how their theory would interpret the leader's choices regarding: 1) balancing employee autonomy with crisis control, 2) managing transparent communication vs. maintaining confidence, 3) prioritizing stakeholder needs during resource scarcity. Groups then engage in a 25-minute structured discussion where each member presents their theoretical interpretation for 5 minutes, followed by group identification of paradoxes that emerge when comparing perspectives. Finally, groups create a visual paradox map showing contradictory leadership demands and how each theory suggests resolving tensions. Groups present their 3-minute paradox maps to the class, focusing on explaining rather than defending their theoretical interpretations.
materials_needed: MedTech Crisis Leadership Case study (3-page detailed scenario)
Leadership Theory Analysis Template (structured worksheet)
Large poster paper or digital collaboration tool (Miro/Jamboard)
Colored markers or digital annotation tools
Theory reference cards with key principles for each framework
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: 1) Accurate application of theoretical frameworks to case details (25%), 2) Clear identification of at least 3 leadership paradoxes with specific examples (30%), 3) Thoughtful explanation of how different theories interpret the same leadership behaviors (25%), 4) Quality of visual paradox map showing understanding of competing demands (20%). Success demonstrated through written analysis templates and oral explanations during presentations.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing theory summary cards with guiding questions for case analysis and pairing them with stronger theoretical thinkers during group work. For advanced learners, add a synthesis challenge: propose an integrated approach that combines insights from multiple theories to navigate identified paradoxes, requiring them to create original frameworks rather than just applying existing ones.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis: Written Report
description: Students will analyze complex leadership scenarios containing inherent paradoxes by examining them through multiple theoretical frameworks. They will demonstrate understanding by explaining how different leadership theories would interpret the same situation and identifying the underlying tensions leaders must navigate.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, situational, and authentic leadership approaches by analyzing their application to a single complex organizational crisis scenario
Students will interpret leadership paradoxes through systematic comparison of how three distinct theoretical frameworks would address competing organizational demands
instructions: Begin by distributing the Netflix leadership crisis case study (Reed Hastings' 2011 Qwikster decision) to teams of 4 students. Each team receives three theoretical framework cards: Transformational Leadership (Bass), Situational Leadership (Hersey-Blanchard), and Authentic Leadership (George). Phase 1 (20 minutes): Teams read the case and identify key leadership decisions, stakeholder conflicts, and paradoxes present. They create a timeline of critical decision points on large paper. Phase 2 (45 minutes): Assign each team member one framework plus one person as 'synthesizer.' Framework analysts spend 15 minutes individually analyzing how their assigned theory would explain Hastings' decisions, noting strengths and blind spots. Next, each analyst presents their 5-minute theoretical interpretation to teammates, focusing on what their framework reveals and what it misses. The synthesizer takes notes on contradictions and overlaps. Phase 3 (25 minutes): Teams collaborate to create a visual matrix showing how each framework interprets three specific leadership paradoxes from the case (innovation vs. stability, transparency vs. strategic secrecy, speed vs. consensus). Phase 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents one paradox analysis to the class, explaining how the three frameworks offer different but valid interpretations of the same leadership challenge. Instructor facilitates discussion on why expert leaders need multiple theoretical lenses.
materials_needed: Netflix Qwikster crisis case study (2-page detailed version)
Three theoretical framework reference cards per team
Large paper sheets (11x17) for timeline creation
Colored markers or pens
Digital timer for phase management
assessment_method: Evaluate teams using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of theoretical application - correctly identifies 2-3 key principles from each framework, (2) Paradox identification - articulates specific tensions with supporting evidence, (3) Comparative analysis - explains how frameworks complement/contradict each other with examples, (4) Synthesis quality - demonstrates understanding that expert leadership requires navigating theoretical tensions rather than choosing single approaches
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework summary sheets with 3-4 key questions each theory would ask about the case. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify a fourth leadership theory that might offer additional insights, or ask them to facilitate cross-team discussions during presentations. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with visual learners for optimal team composition.
original_title: Deconstructing Leadership Paradoxes Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis

title: Deploy and Configure a Web Application on AWS EC2 with Load Balancing
description: Students will deploy a simple web application across multiple EC2 instances and configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS services integration and basic cloud architecture principles.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a web application on multiple EC2 instances by launching instances, installing web servers, and uploading application files
Students will configure an Application Load Balancer to distribute traffic across EC2 instances through the AWS Management Console
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute demonstration of the AWS Management Console navigation. Distribute pre-written HTML files containing a simple web application with unique identifiers for each instance. Students work individually, following these steps: (1) Launch two t2.micro EC2 instances in different availability zones using Amazon Linux 2 AMI, ensuring security groups allow HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) traffic (15 minutes). (2) Connect to each instance via EC2 Instance Connect and install Apache web server using 'sudo yum update -y' and 'sudo yum install httpd -y', then start the service with 'sudo systemctl start httpd' (10 minutes). (3) Upload the provided HTML files to each instance's /var/www/html/ directory, ensuring each instance displays a unique page identifier (10 minutes). (4) Create an Application Load Balancer in the EC2 console, selecting the appropriate VPC and subnets that match the instance locations (10 minutes). (5) Configure a target group with health checks, add both EC2 instances as targets, and attach to the load balancer (15 minutes). (6) Test the deployment by accessing the load balancer's DNS name multiple times, documenting which instance responds to each request (10 minutes). Instructor circulates to provide individual support and verify configurations. Conclude with a 5-minute group discussion comparing results and troubleshooting common issues.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier accounts for each student (set up prior to class)
Pre-written HTML files with unique instance identifiers
Step-by-step handout with AWS console screenshots
Computers with internet access and modern web browsers
assessment_method: Students submit screenshots showing: (1) two running EC2 instances in different AZs, (2) successful Apache test pages with unique identifiers, (3) configured load balancer with healthy targets, and (4) documentation of load balancer distributing requests between instances. Award points: EC2 setup (25%), web server configuration (25%), load balancer creation (25%), traffic distribution demonstration (25%).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide additional console navigation support and pre-configured security groups. Create a troubleshooting checklist for common issues like security group misconfigurations or failed health checks. For advanced learners: challenge them to implement sticky sessions, add auto-scaling groups, or configure HTTPS with SSL certificates.

title: Project Schedule Network Diagram Analysis: Critical Path and Float Calculation
description: Students will analyze a complex project schedule network diagram to identify multiple critical paths, calculate total and free float for non-critical activities, and evaluate the impact of potential schedule compression scenarios. This activity develops advanced schedule analysis skills essential for PMP practitioners.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project network diagrams by identifying all critical paths and calculating float values for each activity using the Critical Path Method
Students will evaluate schedule compression alternatives through systematic comparison of crashing versus fast-tracking impacts on project timeline and resources
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-drawn network diagram showing a software development project with 15 activities, including parallel paths and dummy activities (10 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Schedule Analyst (leads calculations), Risk Assessor (evaluates compression impacts), and Resource Coordinator (tracks resource implications). Students first perform forward pass calculations to determine Early Start and Early Finish dates for all activities, working left to right through the network (15 minutes). Next, conduct backward pass calculations to establish Late Start and Late Finish dates, working right to left from the project completion node (15 minutes). Calculate Total Float (LS-ES or LF-EF) and Free Float (ES of successor - EF of current activity) for each non-critical activity (10 minutes). Identify and highlight all critical paths where Total Float equals zero - this project contains two critical paths (10 minutes). Teams then receive three schedule compression scenarios: reduce project duration by 2 weeks, 4 weeks, or 6 weeks. For each scenario, analyze which activities to crash (add resources) versus fast-track (overlap activities), calculating the cost and risk implications provided in the resource cost table (20 minutes). Document findings in the provided analysis template, including original critical path(s), float calculations, recommended compression strategy for each scenario, and justification for choices (15 minutes). Conclude with team presentations where each group explains their compression recommendations and defends their analysis against questions from other teams (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Pre-drawn project network diagram with 15 activities (printed copies)
Activity duration and resource cost reference table
Schedule analysis worksheet template
Calculators or Excel spreadsheet access
Colored pens/highlighters for marking critical paths
Flip chart paper for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Accurate forward/backward pass calculations (25 points), correct identification of all critical paths (20 points), accurate float calculations for non-critical activities (20 points), logical analysis of compression scenarios with cost-benefit justification (25 points), and clear presentation with defense of recommendations (10 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate understanding of schedule compression trade-offs to meet proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a partially completed calculation worksheet with the first 3 activities solved as examples, and offer a quick reference card with CPM formulas. Advanced learners can be challenged to calculate Free Float for activities with multiple successors, analyze the impact of schedule compression on project quality metrics, or propose alternative network logic to reduce critical path length without adding resources.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Evaluation for E-commerce Campaign Optimization
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different Google Analytics attribution models using real e-commerce data scenarios. They will assess which attribution model provides the most actionable insights for budget allocation decisions and justify their recommendations with quantitative evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and ROI metrics
Students will critique attribution model limitations through comparative analysis of customer journey scenarios and recommend optimal models for specific business contexts
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Analysis Setup (15 minutes)**
Provide students with three pre-configured Google Analytics demo accounts representing different business types: B2B SaaS (long sales cycle), fashion e-commerce (impulse purchases), and subscription service (trial-to-paid conversion). Students work in teams of 3-4, with each team assigned one business scenario.

**Phase 2: Attribution Model Comparison (30 minutes)**
Students navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool in their assigned GA account. They must extract and record conversion data for a 90-day period across all five attribution models (First Interaction, Last Interaction, Linear, Time-Decay, Data-Driven). Teams create a comparison matrix documenting: total conversions, conversion value, cost-per-acquisition, and channel performance rankings for each model.

**Phase 3: Conversion Path Analysis (25 minutes)**
Using the Top Conversion Paths report, teams identify the three most common customer journey patterns. They analyze how each attribution model distributes credit across touchpoints in these journeys and calculate the percentage difference in channel valuation between models. Teams must document which channels gain/lose credit under each model.

**Phase 4: Business Impact Assessment (35 minutes)**
Teams evaluate which attribution model would lead to optimal budget allocation for their assigned business type. They must consider customer behavior patterns, sales cycle length, and marketing objectives. Teams prepare a formal recommendation memo (500 words) defending their chosen model with specific data points, addressing model limitations, and proposing implementation strategy.

**Phase 5: Peer Evaluation (15 minutes)**
Teams present their recommendations to groups assigned different business scenarios. Peer evaluators use provided rubric to assess the logical reasoning, data usage, and feasibility of recommendations.
materials_needed: Google Analytics demo accounts with Multi-Channel Funnel data enabled
Attribution model comparison worksheet template
Business context briefing sheets (B2B SaaS, e-commerce, subscription)
Peer evaluation rubric forms
Computers with internet access and spreadsheet software
assessment_method: Students evaluated on: (1) Data extraction accuracy and completeness (25 points) - correctly recording metrics from all attribution models, (2) Analytical reasoning quality (35 points) - logical evaluation of model strengths/weaknesses with supporting evidence, (3) Business application appropriateness (25 points) - recommendation alignment with business context and customer behavior, (4) Peer evaluation participation (15 points) - quality of feedback provided to other teams using rubric criteria
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step navigation screenshots for accessing GA reports, offer simplified comparison template with guided questions, and pair with stronger analytics students. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external cost data, create custom attribution models using GA4's Data-Driven Attribution API, or analyze attribution differences across device categories and geographic segments.

title: Programming Language Syntax Elements Memory Card Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the basic syntax elements of Python programming language through a structured flashcard activity and verbal quiz. This activity focuses on building foundational recall of essential programming vocabulary and symbols before students begin writing code.
learning_objectives: Students will identify and name 15 fundamental Python syntax elements (keywords, operators, symbols) through flashcard memorization
Students will recall the correct spelling and purpose of basic Python programming terms during a timed verbal assessment
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards containing 15 essential Python elements: print(), input(), if, else, elif, for, while, def, return, +, -, *, /, =, ==, !=, <, >, and, or. Give students 15 minutes to study the cards individually, reading each term aloud and examining its visual appearance. Next, have students work in pairs for 10 minutes, taking turns showing the front of cards (with term names hidden) while their partner attempts to name the element. Partners should provide immediate correction and encouragement. After pair work, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire recall session lasting 8 minutes where you display enlarged versions of the syntax elements on screen for 3 seconds each, and students write down the names on provided answer sheets. Follow this with a 7-minute partner quiz where Student A shows 8 random cards to Student B, who must correctly name each element within 5 seconds. Partners then switch roles. Conclude with a 5-minute reflection where students identify their three most challenging elements and write them three times each on paper while saying the names aloud.
materials_needed: Pre-printed flashcards with 15 Python syntax elements (one set per student)
Digital presentation slides with enlarged syntax elements
Answer sheets for written recall activity
Timer or stopwatch
Reflection worksheets
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify 12 out of 15 syntax elements during the partner quiz phase (80% accuracy). Assessment includes: written answer sheets from the rapid-fire session (5 points), partner quiz observation checklist (10 points), and completed reflection worksheet showing effort to practice challenging terms (5 points). Total: 20 points possible.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide cards with visual cues or color-coding, allow extra study time, pair with supportive partners. For advanced learners: include additional elements like list brackets [], dictionary braces {}, or compound operators +=, -=. Consider adding pronunciation practice for students with language learning needs.

title: Optimization Analysis for Packaging Design: Maximizing Volume with Constraint Applications
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus and constraint optimization techniques to solve a real-world packaging problem. They will determine optimal dimensions for a custom shipping container while considering material cost limitations and structural requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multiplier methods to optimize container volume by incorporating material cost and surface area constraints
Students will demonstrate multivariable calculus concepts through systematic analysis of critical points and boundary conditions in practical packaging scenarios
instructions:
Begin with 10-minute setup: distribute materials and organize students into teams of 3-4. Present the scenario: 'EcoShip Company needs rectangular shipping containers with maximum volume, but material costs limit surface area to 24 square meters, and structural requirements mandate that length must be at least 1.5 times the width.' 

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams define variables (l=length, w=width, h=height) and establish the objective function V(l,w,h) = lwh and constraints g₁: 2lw + 2lh + 2wh = 24 and g₂: l ≥ 1.5w. Students must write these mathematically before proceeding.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Apply Lagrange multiplier method. Teams calculate ∇V = λ₁∇g₁ + λ₂∇g₂ and solve the system: ∂V/∂l = λ₁∂g₁/∂l, ∂V/∂w = λ₁∂g₁/∂w, ∂V/∂h = λ₁∂g₁/∂h, plus constraint equations. Instructor circulates to verify setup before teams proceed to calculations.

Step 3 (20 minutes): Teams solve for critical points, testing cases where l = 1.5w (constraint boundary) and interior solutions. Calculate specific numerical values for optimal dimensions.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Verify solutions using second derivative test or comparing function values at critical points and boundary conditions. Teams must justify why their solution represents a maximum.

Step 5 (15 minutes): Present findings with visual representation showing the optimal container dimensions, maximum volume achieved, and verification that all constraints are satisfied. Include cost analysis showing material usage efficiency.
materials_needed: Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Desmos/GeoGebra)
Large grid paper for constraint visualization
Lagrange multiplier reference sheet with formula templates
Physical rectangular containers of various dimensions for visualization
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct mathematical setup of objective function and constraints (25%), (2) Proper application of Lagrange multiplier method with accurate calculations (35%), (3) Verification of optimal solution using appropriate tests (25%), (4) Clear presentation of final dimensions with practical interpretation (15%). Successful completion requires all constraint conditions satisfied and maximum volume verified mathematically.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed Lagrange setup templates and encouraging verification of each calculation step with neighbors. For advanced learners, extend by adding additional constraints (weight limits, shipping regulations) or exploring sensitivity analysis of how optimal dimensions change with different surface area budgets. Provide geometric intuition by having students sketch level curves of the volume function.

title: Code Quality Detective: Evaluating Bug-Prone vs. Clean Code Samples
description: Students will analyze and compare two versions of the same simple program (a basic calculator) to evaluate code quality, identify potential issues, and justify which version is more maintainable. This activity develops critical evaluation skills by examining real code examples with common beginner mistakes versus best practices.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate code quality by systematically comparing two program versions using established criteria (readability, functionality, maintainability)
Students will justify their assessment of which code sample is superior through written analysis citing specific examples and potential consequences
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide students with two printed code samples of a basic calculator program - Version A (poorly written with issues like no comments, inconsistent naming, repeated code, magic numbers) and Version B (clean code with proper naming, comments, functions, constants). Each student works individually with a provided evaluation checklist.

**Analysis Phase (20 minutes):** Students examine both versions using the checklist covering: variable naming clarity, code organization, presence of comments, error handling, code duplication, and readability. They must identify specific examples of problems in Version A and improvements in Version B, writing notes directly on the printed code.

**Evaluation Phase (15 minutes):** Students complete an evaluation form ranking each version (1-5 scale) across six criteria, then write a 150-word justification explaining which version they would choose for a real project and why. They must cite at least three specific code examples to support their decision.

**Peer Review (10 minutes):** Students pair up to share their evaluations and discuss any disagreements in their assessments. Partners initial each other's work to confirm the peer review occurred.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Instructor facilitates brief whole-class discussion asking 2-3 students to share their most surprising discovery about code quality differences.
materials_needed: Printed code samples (Version A and Version B calculator programs)
Code evaluation checklist handout
Evaluation form with rating scales and justification space
Pens/pencils for annotation
assessment_method: Grade the evaluation form using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification of code quality issues in both versions, (2) Appropriate use of evaluation criteria from checklist, (3) Clear justification with specific code examples cited, (4) Logical reasoning connecting code quality to real-world consequences. Each component worth 25 points for 100 total points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed example evaluation of the first few lines of code to model the process. For advanced learners: Include a third code sample with subtle issues (like inefficient algorithms) and ask them to rank all three versions with additional criteria like performance and scalability.

title: Design a Predictive Analytics Dashboard for Local Business Decision-Making
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that combines multiple data sources to predict customer behavior patterns for a local business scenario. They will synthesize sales data, demographic information, and seasonal trends to develop actionable business recommendations with visual analytics.
learning_objectives: Students will construct a comprehensive predictive analytics dashboard by integrating multiple datasets and applying forecasting techniques to real-world business scenarios
Students will synthesize data visualization principles, statistical modeling, and business intelligence concepts through the creation of an interactive decision-support tool
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Collection & Preparation (30 minutes)**
Provide students with three CSV files: 'coffee_shop_sales.csv' (2 years of daily sales), 'local_demographics.csv' (neighborhood population data), and 'weather_events.csv' (historical weather patterns). Students work in pairs to clean and merge datasets using Excel/Google Sheets, identifying missing values and data inconsistencies. They must document their data cleaning decisions in a shared worksheet.

**Phase 2: Analysis & Modeling (45 minutes)**
Using Tableau Public or Power BI, students create calculated fields to identify seasonal trends, customer peak hours, and correlation between weather and sales. They must generate at least three predictive insights: monthly sales forecasts, optimal staffing recommendations, and inventory suggestions. Students apply moving averages and trend analysis to create forecasting models.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (60 minutes)**
Students design an interactive dashboard containing: executive summary with KPI cards, sales trend visualization with filters by date/product, predictive charts showing 3-month forecasts, and a recommendations panel with specific actions. The dashboard must include at least 4 interactive elements (filters, parameters, or drill-down features) and follow data visualization best practices with consistent color schemes and clear labeling.

**Phase 4: Business Presentation (15 minutes)**
Each pair presents their dashboard to the class, explaining their methodology, key findings, and specific business recommendations. They must defend their analytical choices and respond to questions about data limitations and forecast accuracy.
materials_needed: Three prepared CSV datasets (coffee_shop_sales.csv, local_demographics.csv, weather_events.csv)
Tableau Public or Microsoft Power BI (free versions)
Computers with internet access
Dashboard design template/checklist handout
Business scenario description document
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (25 points - accuracy of data cleaning and merging), Analytical Rigor (25 points - appropriate statistical methods and forecasting techniques), Dashboard Design (25 points - visual clarity, interactivity, and user experience), Business Relevance (25 points - actionable insights and practical recommendations). Students submit their dashboard file and a 2-page methodology report detailing their analytical approach and limitations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned sample datasets and step-by-step Tableau tutorial videos. Offer dashboard wireframe templates and checklist of required elements. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate external APIs (weather services), apply advanced statistical models (regression analysis), or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Encourage integration of machine learning algorithms for more sophisticated predictions.

title: Advanced PMI Knowledge Areas and Process Groups Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall all 49 project management processes from the PMBOK Guide, their corresponding knowledge areas, and process group classifications. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge essential for advanced project management certification and practice.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes by name and correctly classify each into its corresponding knowledge area and process group within 90% accuracy
Students will identify specific process inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for 25 designated high-priority processes through structured memorization exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the PMBOK Process Reference Matrix to each student (15 minutes setup). Students work individually for Phase 1: Give students 45 minutes to study the complete matrix using the provided memory palace worksheet, where they create mental associations between processes and their classifications. Encourage students to use the acronym sheets and visualization cards provided. Phase 2 (30 minutes): Implement progressive testing rounds. Round 1 - students write all 49 process names from memory (10 minutes). Round 2 - match each process to correct knowledge area using provided answer sheets (10 minutes). Round 3 - classify processes into initiating, planning, executing, monitoring/controlling, or closing groups (10 minutes). Phase 3 (25 minutes): Partner drill sessions where Student A calls out a knowledge area, and Student B must recite all processes within that area, then switch roles. Phase 4 (20 minutes): Final comprehensive assessment where students complete the blank PMBOK matrix without references. Instructor circulates throughout, providing immediate feedback and clarification. End with 10-minute debrief where students identify their strongest and weakest knowledge areas for future study focus.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 7th Edition Process Reference Matrix (1 per student)
Memory palace creation worksheets with visual templates
Laminated process classification answer sheets
Knowledge area acronym reference cards
Blank assessment matrices for final testing
Timer/stopwatch for timed rounds
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy (44/49 processes) on final blank matrix completion. Grade breakdown: Process names correct (40%), Knowledge area classification (30%), Process group classification (30%). Document individual process gaps for remediation planning. Provide immediate scoring using answer key overlay sheets.
scaffolding_notes: Struggling students receive color-coded process cards grouped by knowledge area and additional 15 minutes study time with mnemonic device handouts. Advanced learners extend activity by memorizing key inputs/outputs for critical path processes and can peer-tutor during partner sessions. Provide audio recordings of process names for auditory learners.

title: Leadership Theory Integration Analysis: Comparing Transformational and Servant Leadership in Crisis Management
description: Students will analyze and compare transformational and servant leadership theories by examining authentic crisis management scenarios from Fortune 500 companies. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying theoretical principles, explaining their interconnections, and interpreting how different leadership approaches influence organizational outcomes during high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational and servant leadership theories by analyzing their core principles and identifying specific behavioral indicators in real-world crisis scenarios
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership theory and organizational outcomes through comparative analysis of documented leadership responses during corporate crises
instructions: Begin by distributing two detailed case studies: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis (1982) under James Burke's leadership and Southwest Airlines' post-9/11 response under Herb Kelleher's leadership (20 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning half the teams to analyze Burke through a transformational leadership lens and half to analyze Kelleher through a servant leadership lens. Provide each team with a theoretical framework handout containing: Bass's Four I's of Transformational Leadership (Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individual Consideration) or Greenleaf's Servant Leadership principles (Listening, Empathy, Healing, Awareness, Persuasion, Conceptualization, Foresight, Stewardship, Growth, Community Building). Teams spend 45 minutes mapping specific leader behaviors from their case to theoretical constructs, creating evidence tables with direct quotes and documented actions. Next, conduct a structured academic debate format: transformational teams present their analysis (8 minutes), servant leadership teams present theirs (8 minutes), followed by cross-examination rounds where teams ask clarifying questions about theoretical applications (15 minutes total). Teams then collaborate in mixed groups (one transformational analyst + one servant leadership analyst) to create comparison matrices identifying overlaps, contradictions, and unique aspects of each approach (25 minutes). Conclude with individual reflection essays where students explain which theoretical framework better explains effective crisis leadership and justify their reasoning using evidence from both cases (20 minutes).
materials_needed: Detailed case study packets: Johnson & Johnson Tylenol Crisis (1982) with timeline, leadership communications, and outcome data
Detailed case study packets: Southwest Airlines post-9/11 crisis response with documented leadership decisions and financial impacts
Transformational Leadership framework handout with Bass's Four I's definitions and behavioral indicators
Servant Leadership framework handout with Greenleaf's ten principles and assessment criteria
Evidence mapping templates with columns for 'Leader Behavior,' 'Supporting Quote/Data,' and 'Theoretical Connection'
Comparison matrix templates with rows for each leadership principle and columns for similarities/differences
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of theoretical identification - correctly matches 80%+ of leader behaviors to appropriate theoretical constructs; (2) Quality of evidence - uses specific, relevant quotes and data to support theoretical connections; (3) Depth of comparison - identifies at least 3 meaningful similarities and 3 significant differences between approaches; (4) Justified interpretation - final reflection demonstrates clear understanding of how theoretical frameworks explain leadership effectiveness with logical reasoning supported by case evidence. Students must score 3+ on all criteria to demonstrate understanding level mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-highlighted case studies with key leadership behaviors marked, offer sentence starters for theoretical connections ('This behavior demonstrates [theory] because...'), and allow extended time for evidence mapping. For advanced learners: Add a third leadership theory (authentic or adaptive leadership) for triangulated analysis, require them to identify limitations of each theoretical framework, or have them research additional crisis leadership examples to test theoretical applications beyond provided cases.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis for IT Software Implementation Project
description: Students will analyze a realistic IT project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the appropriateness of proposed risk response strategies. They will dissect the relationship between risk characteristics and chosen responses, then recommend alternative strategies with detailed justifications.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the alignment between risk characteristics (probability, impact, category) and proposed response strategies by evaluating five specific project risks using PMI's risk response framework
Students will differentiate between effective and ineffective risk response strategies through systematic comparison of alternatives using cost-benefit analysis principles
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'CloudTech ERP Implementation' case study packet containing: project overview, risk register with 8 identified risks, and current response strategies. Form teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes). Each team receives a different colored packet to prevent copying. Teams spend 15 minutes reading and discussing the scenario to ensure comprehension. 

Next, teams select 5 risks from the register and complete the Risk Response Analysis Matrix on provided templates (25 minutes). For each selected risk, students must: identify risk category (technical, organizational, external, project management), assess probability/impact ratings, evaluate the proposed response strategy's appropriateness, and calculate rough cost estimates for implementation. 

Teams then brainstorm and document 2-3 alternative response strategies for their most critical risk (15 minutes). They must justify why alternatives might be more effective, considering factors like cost, timeline impact, resource availability, and organizational constraints. 

During the analysis phase (20 minutes), teams create a comparison chart ranking all response options (original plus alternatives) using weighted criteria: implementation cost (25%), effectiveness in reducing risk exposure (35%), resource requirements (20%), and alignment with project constraints (20%). 

Finally, each team presents their analysis for one high-priority risk to the class (3 minutes per team, 15 minutes total). Presentations must include: risk description, critique of original strategy, recommended alternative, and supporting rationale. Other teams provide feedback using the peer evaluation form, focusing on thoroughness of analysis and quality of justification.
materials_needed: CloudTech ERP Implementation case study packets (color-coded by team)
Risk Response Analysis Matrix templates (printed)
Weighted criteria comparison chart templates
Peer evaluation forms
Calculators or laptops for cost calculations
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Grade using 100-point rubric: Risk Analysis Accuracy (30 points - correct identification of risk characteristics and appropriate use of PMI terminology), Strategy Evaluation Quality (25 points - depth of critique with specific examples and clear reasoning), Alternative Solutions (25 points - creativity, feasibility, and alignment with project constraints), Presentation Clarity (20 points - organized delivery, professional communication, effective use of time). Students must score 70+ points to demonstrate analyze-level competency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide a completed example of risk analysis for one scenario risk, offer PMI risk response strategy reference sheet, and allow extra 5 minutes for case study review. For advanced learners: add requirement to consider secondary risks created by their proposed responses, calculate expected monetary value (EMV) for alternatives, or analyze interdependencies between selected risks and their response strategies.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise Network Architecture with Advanced Services
description: Students will create a comprehensive network design for a fictional multi-site enterprise, implementing advanced routing protocols, security policies, and network services. They will build and configure the entire network infrastructure using Cisco Packet Tracer, then present their design decisions and demonstrate functionality through comprehensive testing scenarios.
estimated_duration: 420 minutes (7 hours) - can be delivered across 3-4 class sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocols to create an optimal inter-site connectivity solution for a complex enterprise topology
Students will construct a complete network security framework by integrating VLANs, ACLs, VPNs, and firewall policies across multiple geographic locations
Students will evaluate and justify their architectural choices through comprehensive network documentation and live demonstration of critical business scenarios
instructions: **Phase 1: Requirements Analysis (45 minutes)** - Present students with a detailed business scenario: TechCorp has headquarters in New York (500 users), branch offices in Chicago (200 users) and Miami (150 users), plus a data center in Dallas. Provide specific requirements: each site needs 3 VLANs (Sales, Engineering, Management), secure inter-site communication, redundant WAN connections, guest network access, and cloud connectivity. Students work in teams of 3-4 to analyze requirements and create initial design sketches. **Phase 2: Network Architecture Design (90 minutes)** - Teams use Visio or draw.io to create detailed network diagrams showing physical and logical topologies. They must specify router models (ISR 4000 series for sites, ASR 1000 for data center), switch models (Catalyst 9300 series), IP addressing schemes using appropriate subnets, OSPF areas design with area 0 as backbone, EIGRP implementation for internal routing, eBGP for ISP connections, and VPN tunnels between sites. Students document routing protocol selection rationale and create IP addressing tables. **Phase 3: Implementation in Packet Tracer (180 minutes)** - Teams build their complete network in Cisco Packet Tracer, configuring all devices according to their design. This includes basic device configuration with hostnames, passwords, and management IPs; VLAN creation and trunk configuration on switches; OSPF configuration with proper area assignments and network statements; inter-VLAN routing using SVIs or router-on-a-stick; ACL implementation for security policies; site-to-site VPN configuration using IPSec; and DHCP services configuration. **Phase 4: Testing and Validation (60 minutes)** - Teams execute comprehensive testing scenarios including end-to-end connectivity tests between all sites and VLANs, routing table verification and convergence testing, security policy validation by attempting unauthorized access, VPN tunnel functionality verification, and network failure simulation with recovery testing. **Phase 5: Documentation and Presentation (45 minutes)** - Teams prepare executive summary documents and deliver 10-minute presentations explaining their design rationale, demonstrating key functionalities, and justifying technology choices.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer (latest version) installed on student computers
Microsoft Visio or draw.io access for network diagramming
TechCorp business requirements document (instructor-provided)
Cisco IOS command reference guides
Network documentation templates
Presentation equipment (projector, screen, audio)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points) - logical topology, appropriate technology selection, scalability considerations; Implementation Accuracy (30 points) - correct device configurations, functional routing protocols, working security policies; Testing Thoroughness (20 points) - comprehensive test scenarios, proper validation methods, failure recovery demonstration; Documentation Quality (15 points) - complete IP addressing tables, clear diagrams, executive summary; Presentation Effectiveness (10 points) - technical accuracy, design justification, demonstration skills. Students must achieve connectivity between all sites, demonstrate security policy enforcement, and show VPN functionality to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with basic device settings, offer step-by-step OSPF configuration guides, create simplified testing checklists, and allow extended time for implementation phase. For advanced learners: Add requirements for QoS implementation across WAN links, incorporate IPv6 dual-stack configuration, require implementation of network automation using Python scripts, add advanced security features like 802.1X authentication, and challenge them to optimize routing with traffic engineering principles.

title: Binary Number Flashcard Memory Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall the binary representations of decimal numbers 0-15 through structured flashcard practice. This foundational activity builds automatic recall of basic binary-decimal conversions essential for computer science concepts.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the binary representation of decimal numbers 0-15 by completing timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
Students will identify decimal equivalents of 4-bit binary numbers through structured memorization practice
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards showing decimal numbers 0-15 on one side and their 4-bit binary equivalents on the reverse (e.g., 5 = 0101, 12 = 1100). Students work in pairs for the first 15 minutes, with one partner showing decimal numbers while the other states the binary equivalent, then switching roles after 7 minutes. Next, conduct a whole-class round-robin where each student must quickly state one binary conversion when called upon, cycling through the room twice (10 minutes). For the final 10 minutes, students complete individual silent practice using the flashcards, sorting them into 'mastered' and 'needs practice' piles. Conclude with a rapid-fire assessment where students write binary equivalents for 10 randomly selected decimal numbers (0-15) in 3 minutes. Throughout the activity, emphasize that students should visualize the 4-bit pattern and practice saying conversions aloud to strengthen memory pathways. Monitor student pairs during practice, providing immediate correction for errors and encouraging students to repeat correct answers three times to reinforce memorization.
materials_needed: Pre-made flashcards with decimal numbers 0-15 on front, 4-bit binary on back (one set per student pair)
Timer or stopwatch
Individual assessment sheets with 10 blank decimal-to-binary conversion problems
Answer key for instructor reference
assessment_method: Students must achieve 9/10 correct answers (90%) on the final 3-minute written assessment of decimal-to-binary conversions. Award full credit for correct 4-bit binary representations (including leading zeros), partial credit for correct binary digits in wrong positions, and document specific number combinations that students struggle with for future practice sessions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Start with numbers 0-7 only, provide a powers-of-2 reference chart (8-4-2-1), and allow extra practice time with visual aids. For advanced learners: Extend to 5-bit numbers (0-31), introduce binary-to-decimal reverse practice, or challenge them to tutor struggling classmates while practicing 8-bit conversions independently.

title: Optimization Engineering Challenge: Designing Maximum Volume Packaging Solutions
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to solve real-world packaging constraints by determining dimensions that maximize volume while meeting specific material and cost limitations. They will work with composite functions, derivatives, and constraint equations to design optimal cylindrical and rectangular packaging solutions.
learning_objectives: Students will apply single and multivariable calculus optimization methods to maximize volume functions subject to surface area and cost constraints
Students will implement derivative techniques and critical point analysis through solving authentic packaging design problems with multiple variables and constraints
instructions: Begin by distributing three distinct packaging scenarios to student teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes setup). Scenario A: Design a cylindrical can using exactly 300 cm² of material to maximize volume. Scenario B: Create a rectangular box with square base where material costs $0.02/cm² for the base and $0.01/cm² for sides, with a $2.50 budget to maximize volume.
