Scenario C: Design a cylindrical container with hemispherical ends using 500 cm² total surface area. Students first identify the constraint equation and objective function for their scenario (20 minutes). Next, they set up the optimization problem by expressing volume as a function of one variable using the constraint to eliminate other variables (25 minutes). Teams then find critical points by taking derivatives and setting equal to zero, showing all algebraic steps (30 minutes). They must verify their solution represents a maximum using the second derivative test or boundary analysis (20 minutes). Finally, students calculate the exact dimensions and maximum volume, then create a visual representation showing their container design with labeled dimensions (25 minutes). Each team presents their solution method and final design to the class, explaining how they verified their answer represents the true maximum (15 minutes per team). Instructor circulates continuously, checking mathematical setup and providing hints for algebraic manipulation difficulties.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or graphing calculators
Graph paper and rulers
Scenario handouts with specific constraint parameters
Presentation boards or digital presentation software
Colored pencils or markers for technical drawings
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric evaluating: (1) Correct identification and setup of constraint/objective functions (25%), (2) Accurate derivative calculations and critical point determination (25%), (3) Proper verification that solution is maximum using second derivative or boundary analysis (25%), (4) Clear presentation of final dimensions with units and visual representation (25%). Students must show complete algebraic work and explain reasoning for full credit.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with constraint equation partially set up, offer one-on-one guidance during derivative calculation step, and suggest checking work using graphing calculator. For advanced learners: Add additional constraints like minimum height requirements, extend to optimization with Lagrange multipliers, or challenge them to solve all three scenarios and compare methods.

title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Anomaly Analysis: Investigating Stellar Classification Discrepancies
description: Students analyze real spectroscopic data from three mystery stars to identify inconsistencies between their apparent visual classification and their actual spectral properties. They must deconstruct the relationship between temperature, luminosity, and spectral lines to resolve classification conflicts and propose explanations for anomalous readings.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze spectroscopic data by comparing peak wavelengths, absorption line patterns, and intensity distributions to determine actual stellar temperatures and compositions

Students will evaluate conflicting observational evidence through systematic examination of Wien's displacement law, Stefan-Boltzmann relationships, and spectral line analysis to identify measurement errors or exotic stellar phenomena
instructions: **Setup (5 min):** Distribute three sets of real stellar spectra data (downloadable from SDSS database) labeled as 'Star A: Suspected M-dwarf,' 'Star B: Suspected G-type,' and 'Star C: Suspected O-type.' Provide each student with printed spectra graphs, data tables showing photometric magnitudes, and analysis worksheets. **Phase 1 (20 min):** Students individually calculate the peak wavelength for each star using provided intensity vs. wavelength data, then apply Wien's displacement law (λmax = 2.898×10⁻³ m·K / T) to determine surface temperatures. They must show all calculations and compare results to expected temperatures for the suspected classifications. **Phase 2 (25 min):** Students analyze absorption line patterns by measuring equivalent widths of hydrogen Balmer lines, helium lines, and metal absorption features. Using provided reference charts, they determine actual spectral types based on line strength ratios. **Phase 3 (30 min):** In pairs, students create comparison matrices identifying discrepancies between calculated temperatures, observed spectral features, and initial classifications. They must propose three possible explanations for each anomaly (examples: binary companion, interstellar reddening, evolved star phase, measurement error). **Phase 4 (15 min):** Student pairs present their most compelling anomaly explanation to the class, defending their analysis with quantitative evidence. **Wrap-up (5 min):** Instructor reveals actual stellar identities and confirms which anomalies represent real astrophysical phenomena versus observational challenges.
materials_needed: Three authentic stellar spectra datasets from Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) with deliberately mismatched initial classifications
Scientific calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
Printed reference charts for stellar spectral classification standards
Blank analysis worksheets with calculation templates for Wien's law and Stefan-Boltzmann applications
Colored pencils for marking different spectral line types
assessment_method: Grade based on: (1) Accuracy of temperature calculations using Wien's law (25 points), (2) Correct identification of spectral line patterns and resulting classifications (30 points), (3) Quality of discrepancy analysis showing clear comparison between expected and observed properties (25 points), (4) Feasibility and scientific reasoning of proposed explanations for anomalies (20 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in calculations and demonstrate logical reasoning connecting quantitative analysis to qualitative conclusions.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated peak wavelength values and focus on applying Wien's law formula. Offer simplified spectral line identification charts with only the most prominent features highlighted. For advanced students: Include additional challenge of estimating stellar distances using apparent vs. absolute magnitude relationships, or analyzing potential binary star orbital mechanics if that explains the anomalies. Provide access to more sophisticated analysis software like IRAF or Python astronomy libraries.

title: Decoding Leadership Paradoxes: Multi-Framework Analysis of Complex Executive Decisions
description: Students analyze a complex, real-world leadership crisis through the lens of five competing leadership frameworks to understand how different theoretical perspectives can lead to conflicting but equally valid interpretations. This activity demonstrates the nuanced nature of leadership theory application in ambiguous, high-stakes situations.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between competing leadership frameworks by analyzing how each would interpret the same complex leadership scenario differently
Students will synthesize multiple theoretical perspectives through structured comparison matrices to demonstrate understanding of framework limitations and complementary insights
instructions: Begin by presenting the case study: Netflix CEO Reed Hastings' 2011 Qwikster decision and subsequent reversal within 23 days, including stock price drop, customer backlash, and internal team dynamics (10 minutes). Divide students into five expert groups of 3-4 members, assigning each group one leadership framework: Transformational Leadership Theory, Situational Leadership Model, Authentic Leadership Theory, Complexity Leadership Theory, and Servant Leadership Framework. Provide each group with a framework analysis template containing specific theoretical components and guiding questions. Groups spend 25 minutes analyzing Hastings' decisions through their assigned lens, identifying: key leadership behaviors exhibited, theoretical predictions vs. actual outcomes, framework strengths in explaining the situation, and framework blind spots. Next, create new mixed groups with one expert from each framework group (15 minutes setup). These integration groups spend 30 minutes completing a comparative analysis matrix, documenting where frameworks align, contradict, or complement each other regarding Hastings' approach. Each integration group presents a 5-minute synthesis highlighting the most significant theoretical tensions and insights discovered. Conclude with a 15-minute facilitated discussion on implications for practicing leaders when theoretical frameworks provide conflicting guidance.
materials_needed: Netflix Qwikster case study packet with timeline, financial data, and stakeholder quotes
Framework Analysis Templates (5 different versions with theory-specific prompts)
Comparative Analysis Matrix worksheets
Digital timer for time management
Flipchart paper and markers for group presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of framework application - correct identification and application of theoretical components, (2) Depth of analysis - evidence of understanding framework nuances and limitations, (3) Synthesis quality - ability to articulate meaningful connections and contradictions between frameworks, (4) Critical insight - demonstration of understanding that leadership situations often require multiple theoretical lenses. Success requires scoring 3+ in all categories.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide framework summary cards with key concepts and sample application questions. Assign stronger students as group facilitators and provide additional 'challenge questions' that push analysis beyond surface level. For advanced learners, include supplementary reading on leadership paradox theory and ask them to propose a meta-framework that reconciles contradictory insights.

title: Deploy and Configure a Multi-Tier Web Application on AWS EC2 with Auto Scaling
description: Students will deploy a complete three-tier web application (web server, application server, database) across multiple AWS EC2 instances and configure auto scaling groups to handle traffic variations. This hands-on activity applies core AWS concepts including EC2 instance management, security groups, load balancing, and auto scaling policies.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a multi-tier application architecture by launching and configuring EC2 instances for web, application, and database tiers
Students will implement auto scaling and load balancing through AWS services to ensure application availability and performance
instructions:
**Pre-Activity Setup (10 minutes):** Instructor provides AWS Learner Lab credentials and a simple Node.js application package with database connection scripts. Students log into AWS Management Console and verify access to EC2, RDS, and Auto Scaling services.

**Phase 1 - Database Tier (20 minutes):** Students launch an Amazon RDS MySQL instance using t3.micro class in the default VPC. Configure security group to allow inbound MySQL traffic (port 3306) from application tier subnet. Students must record the RDS endpoint URL for later configuration.

**Phase 2 - Application Tier (25 minutes):** Launch two EC2 instances (t2.micro) using Amazon Linux 2 AMI. Install Node.js and upload the provided application code via SCP. Configure environment variables to connect to the RDS database using the recorded endpoint. Create an Application Load Balancer targeting both instances on port 3000. Test connectivity between tiers.

**Phase 3 - Web Tier (20 minutes):** Launch an EC2 instance for Nginx web server. Configure Nginx as a reverse proxy to forward requests to the Application Load Balancer. Create security groups allowing HTTP/HTTPS traffic from internet to web tier, and application traffic between web and app tiers.

**Phase 4 - Auto Scaling Implementation (25 minutes):** Create an AMI from one configured application server. Build a launch template using this AMI. Set up an Auto Scaling Group with minimum 2, maximum 5 instances. Configure scaling policies based on CPU utilization (scale out at 70%, scale in at 30%). Register the Auto Scaling Group with the existing load balancer.

**Phase 5 - Testing and Validation (15 minutes):** Generate load using provided stress testing script. Monitor CloudWatch metrics to observe scaling events. Verify application remains accessible during scaling operations.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab account credentials for each student
Pre-built Node.js application package with database connection code
Load testing script (Apache Bench or similar)
Architecture diagram template for documentation
Security group configuration worksheet
assessment_method: Students submit a completed architecture diagram showing all deployed resources, security group configurations, and auto scaling policies. Assessment rubric includes: (1) All three tiers properly deployed and communicating (25 points), (2) Auto scaling group correctly configured with appropriate policies (25 points), (3) Load balancer distributing traffic effectively (20 points), (4) Security groups follow principle of least privilege (20 points), (5) Application remains available during load testing (10 points). Students must demonstrate working application and explain scaling behavior during brief individual check-ins.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and detailed networking diagrams. Offer step-by-step command sheets for SSH connections and software installation. Create checkpoint sheets for each phase completion. For advanced students: Challenge them to implement additional features like CloudWatch alarms, SNS notifications for scaling events, or multi-AZ deployment. Encourage exploration of different instance types and cost optimization strategies.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Evaluating Mitigation vs. Transfer Decisions
description: Students analyze three real-world project scenarios to determine the most appropriate risk response strategies by examining risk probability, impact, organizational capacity, and cost-benefit trade-offs. They will deconstruct existing risk response decisions and justify alternative approaches using PMP risk management frameworks.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk characteristics (probability, impact, detectability) to determine optimal response strategies by comparing mitigation, transfer, acceptance, and avoidance options
Students will examine organizational constraints and project context factors through systematic evaluation of resource availability, risk tolerance, and strategic alignment
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Distribute the three case study packets: 'Software Implementation Delay Risk,' 'Supply Chain Disruption Risk,' and 'Regulatory Compliance Risk.' Each packet contains risk register excerpts, organizational context, budget constraints, and current response strategies. **Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student independently reviews all three cases, completing the Risk Response Analysis Worksheet. They identify: risk category, probability/impact ratings, current response strategy, organizational risk tolerance level, and available resources. **Phase 2 - Team Deliberation (25 minutes):** Teams discuss each case systematically. For Case 1, teams analyze why the current mitigation strategy may be insufficient given the 40% probability and high impact rating. They examine whether risk transfer through insurance or vendor agreements would be more cost-effective. For Case 2, teams evaluate the supply chain risk transfer strategy, analyzing whether the $50K insurance premium is justified against potential $200K impact. For Case 3, teams assess the current acceptance strategy for regulatory risk, determining if active mitigation through compliance consulting would better serve the organization's risk-averse profile. **Phase 3 - Strategy Recommendation (15 minutes):** Teams complete the Strategy Comparison Matrix, documenting their recommended response strategy for each case with specific rationale addressing: cost-benefit analysis, alignment with organizational risk tolerance, resource requirements, and timeline implications. **Presentation (15 minutes):** Each team presents one case analysis, defending their recommended strategy against instructor challenges about implementation feasibility and alternative approaches.
materials_needed: Three printed case study packets with risk registers and organizational profiles
Risk Response Analysis Worksheet (Excel template)
Strategy Comparison Matrix template
PMP Risk Management Process Guide reference sheet
Calculators or laptops for cost-benefit calculations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk characteristic identification (25%), (2) Quality of strategy analysis considering organizational constraints (35%), (3) Justification strength using PMP frameworks and quantitative reasoning (25%), (4) Professional presentation and defense of recommendations (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 or higher on each criterion with demonstrated use of probability-impact analysis and clear cost-benefit reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example of risk analysis for a simple scenario, offer risk probability/impact calculation templates, and assign roles within teams (analyst, calculator, presenter). For advanced learners: Introduce secondary risk considerations, require Monte Carlo simulation estimates, or add stakeholder communication strategy requirements to their recommendations.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Drill: Python Fundamentals
description: Students will memorize and recall basic Python syntax elements through structured flashcard activities. They will identify and recite fundamental programming constructs including data types, operators, and basic statement structures.
learning_objectives: Students will recall Python syntax for variable declaration, print statements, and basic operators by completing timed flashcard exercises
Students will identify correct Python data type syntax (strings, integers, floats, booleans) through visual recognition activities
instructions:
Begin by distributing pre-made flashcards to each student (30 cards total). Each card shows a Python concept on one side (e.g., 'How do you print text?') and the syntax on the reverse (e.g., 'print("Hello World")'). 

Phase 1 (10 minutes): Students work individually, cycling through all cards twice. They read the concept, attempt to recall the syntax, then flip to verify. Mark cards they answered incorrectly for focused review.

Phase 2 (8 minutes): Pair students up. Partner A shows concept side to Partner B, who states the syntax aloud. Partner A confirms correctness. Switch roles every 15 cards. 

Phase 3 (7 minutes): Conduct whole-class rapid-fire recall. Display concepts on projector screen for 10 seconds each. Students write syntax on individual whiteboards and hold up simultaneously. Instructor provides immediate verbal confirmation of correct answers.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Individual assessment quiz. Students receive worksheet with 15 syntax questions (e.g., 'Write the Python code to create a variable named age with value 25'). No reference materials allowed. Students must complete from memory only.

Conclude with brief review of commonly missed items identified during the quiz phase.
materials_needed: 30 pre-made Python syntax flashcards per student
Individual mini-whiteboards and markers
Projector and screen for displaying concepts
Printed assessment worksheets (15 questions each)
Timer for tracking phase durations
assessment_method: Grade the final 15-question syntax worksheet using binary scoring (1 point for completely correct syntax, 0 for incorrect/incomplete). Success criteria: 12/15 correct answers (80%) demonstrates adequate recall of fundamental Python syntax elements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a reduced set of 20 flashcards focusing on most essential syntax (variables, print, basic math). Allow them to use cards as reference during first half of assessment. For advanced learners: Include additional flashcards covering list comprehensions, dictionary syntax, and function definitions. Challenge them to create their own flashcards for advanced topics.

title: Interpreting Correlation Patterns in Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze a correlation matrix from an e-commerce dataset to identify meaningful relationships between customer demographics and purchasing behaviors. They will differentiate between strong, moderate, and weak correlations while explaining the practical business implications of their findings.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients by categorizing relationships as strong (>0.7), moderate (0.3-0.7), or weak (<0.3) and explaining their statistical meaning
Students will explain the business implications of correlation patterns through written analysis connecting statistical findings to real-world customer behavior
instructions: Begin by distributing the pre-calculated correlation matrix showing relationships between 8 variables: customer age, income, time_on_site, pages_viewed, previous_purchases, cart_abandonment_rate, seasonal_purchases, and total_spend (15 minutes setup). Organize students into pairs and provide the interpretation worksheet. In Phase 1 (20 minutes), students examine the correlation matrix and identify all correlation coefficients above 0.5 or below -0.5, recording these in their worksheet table with classifications (strong positive, moderate positive, moderate negative, etc.). In Phase 2 (25 minutes), pairs select their three most interesting correlations and write 2-3 sentence explanations for each, addressing: What does this correlation tell us about customer behavior? Why might this relationship exist? What business decisions could this inform? During Phase 3 (15 minutes), each pair presents one correlation finding to another pair, practicing verbal explanation of their interpretation. Conclude with a 10-minute whole-class discussion where 3-4 pairs share their most surprising finding. Throughout the activity, circulate to ensure students are correctly interpreting coefficient magnitudes and signs, and guide them toward meaningful business insights rather than just statistical descriptions.
materials_needed: Pre-calculated 8x8 correlation matrix printout (one per student)
Correlation interpretation worksheet with classification table
Correlation strength reference chart (weak/moderate/strong ranges)
Sample business context description of the e-commerce dataset
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 3-point rubric: (1) Accurate identification and classification of correlation strengths, (2) Clear explanation of what correlations mean in statistical terms, (3) Relevant connection to business implications. Students must correctly classify 6/8 correlations and provide coherent explanations for their three selected relationships to demonstrate understanding.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example of one correlation interpretation and highlight key phrases like 'as X increases, Y tends to increase.' For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or question whether correlation implies causation in their selected relationships. Consider providing additional context about data collection methods.

title: Optimizing Multi-Modal Transportation Networks Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world transportation logistics problem involving multiple shipping methods, constraints, and cost optimization. They will formulate objective functions, identify constraints, and use the simplex method to find optimal solutions for a company's distribution strategy.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming formulation techniques to convert a multi-modal transportation scenario into mathematical constraints and objective functions
Students will implement the simplex method to solve complex optimization problems through systematic algebraic manipulation and interpretation of results
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: MegaCorp needs to ship 10,000 units from 3 warehouses to 4 distribution centers using trucks, trains, and planes, each with different costs and capacity limits. Distribute the detailed problem packet containing specific warehouse capacities (W1: 3000, W2: 4000, W3: 3000), distribution center demands (D1: 2500, D2: 2000, D3: 3000, D4: 2500), and cost matrices for each transportation mode. Form teams of 3-4 students and assign roles: Lead Analyst (formulates constraints), Cost Optimizer (develops objective function), Solution Manager (applies simplex method), and Results Interpreter (analyzes feasibility and sensitivity). Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams identify decision variables (x_ijk representing units shipped from warehouse i to destination j via mode k), formulate the objective function minimizing total cost, and write constraint inequalities for supply limits, demand requirements, and transportation capacity restrictions. Phase 2 (35 minutes): Convert the problem to standard form, create initial simplex tableau, and systematically perform pivot operations. Students must show all algebraic steps and maintain organized tableaux. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Interpret optimal solution, calculate total minimum cost, verify constraint satisfaction, and conduct sensitivity analysis on key parameters. Teams document their complete solution process and prepare a 3-minute presentation of their optimization strategy and results.
materials_needed: Multi-modal transportation problem packets with specific numerical data
Graphing calculators or computers with Excel/linear programming software
Simplex tableau worksheets with pre-formatted grids
Flip chart paper and markers for solution presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Correct problem formulation (25 points) - accurate identification of variables, constraints, and objective function; Simplex method execution (35 points) - proper tableau setup, correct pivot operations, and algebraic accuracy; Solution interpretation (25 points) - feasibility verification, cost calculation, and sensitivity analysis; Mathematical communication (15 points) - clear notation, organized work, and logical presentation of results.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide constraint formulation templates and worked examples of similar 2-warehouse problems; offer simplex method reference cards with pivot selection rules. For advanced learners: Introduce additional constraints like environmental impact factors or driver hour regulations; challenge them to solve using dual simplex method or analyze multiple objective functions simultaneously.

title: Multi-Variable Circuit Analysis: Decomposing Complex DC Networks Using Nodal and Mesh Methods
description: Students will systematically break down a complex 12-node DC circuit with multiple voltage sources, current sources, and resistive elements. They will compare and contrast the efficiency of nodal versus mesh analysis methods by examining the mathematical structure and computational complexity of each approach.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the mathematical relationships between circuit topology and solution complexity by comparing the number of equations generated in nodal versus mesh analysis for the same network

Students will deconstruct a multi-source DC circuit into component subsystems through systematic application of Kirchhoff's laws and examine how different analysis methods reveal distinct aspects of current and voltage distributions
instructions: Begin by distributing the complex circuit diagram containing 12 nodes, 3 independent voltage sources (5V, 12V, -8V), 2 current sources (3A, 1.5A), and 15 resistors ranging from 2Ω to 50Ω (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3 students, assigning roles: Circuit Mapper (identifies nodes/meshes), Equation Builder (sets up mathematical systems), and Solution Validator (checks units and reasonableness). Phase 1 (25 minutes): Teams analyze circuit topology, identifying essential nodes for nodal analysis and independent meshes for mesh analysis. Document the decision-making process for reference node selection and mesh current directions. Phase 2 (35 minutes): Simultaneously solve using both methods - one team member develops the nodal equation system while another creates the mesh equation system. Use MATLAB or similar software to solve the resulting linear systems. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Compare solutions for consistency, analyzing discrepancies if any exist. Calculate power dissipated in each resistor using results from both methods. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Teams prepare a comparative analysis examining: (a) number of unknowns in each method, (b) complexity of resulting equations, (c) computational efficiency, and (d) which method provides more intuitive insight into circuit behavior. Conclude with 10-minute team presentations highlighting their analytical findings and method preferences with technical justification.
materials_needed: Complex 12-node circuit diagram with component values labeled
MATLAB or GNU Octave software access
Scientific calculators
Graph paper for circuit redrawing and equation setup
Digital multimeter simulation software (optional: LTSpice for verification)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Circuit topology analysis accuracy (25 points), correctness of nodal equations (20 points), correctness of mesh equations (20 points), solution validation and cross-checking (15 points), comparative analysis depth and technical reasoning (15 points), presentation clarity and technical communication (5 points). Students must achieve >80% accuracy in both solution methods and demonstrate clear understanding of when each method is preferable.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a simplified 6-node version first, offer equation setup templates, and pair with stronger peers. Create step-by-step checklist for systematic node/mesh identification. For advanced learners: Introduce dependent sources, ask them to derive general rules for method selection based on circuit topology, or challenge them to solve using modified nodal analysis including voltage source treatment.

title: PMBOK Guide Knowledge Area and Process Group Matrix Recall Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete mapping of all 49 project management processes across the 10 Knowledge Areas and 5 Process Groups as defined in PMBOK Guide 7th Edition. This intensive recall activity strengthens foundational knowledge essential for advanced project management practice and PMP certification preparation.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK processes and their exact placement within the Knowledge Area-Process Group matrix with 95% accuracy through timed retrieval exercises
Students will identify specific process inputs, tools/techniques, and outputs for 15 critical processes through structured memorization drills
instructions: Begin by distributing blank 10x5 matrix templates with Knowledge Areas (Integration, Scope, Schedule, Cost, Quality, Resource, Communications, Risk, Procurement, Stakeholder) listed vertically and Process Groups (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing) horizontally. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Students study the complete filled matrix, using color-coding techniques where each Knowledge Area has a distinct color. Encourage active reading aloud and visualization techniques. Phase 2 (10 minutes): Remove reference materials. Students complete blank matrices individually, filling in all 49 processes in their correct positions. Phase 3 (20 minutes): Conduct rapid-fire verbal quizzing where instructor calls out specific Knowledge Area-Process Group intersections (e.g., 'Risk Management, Planning Process Group') and students must immediately respond with all applicable processes. Rotate through all students systematically. Phase 4 (15 minutes): Advanced recall challenge - instructor provides process names randomly, students must state the Knowledge Area, Process Group, plus one key input and one key output for that process. Phase 5 (10 minutes): Peer verification where students exchange completed matrices and check accuracy against master reference, marking errors for focused review. Conclude with individual reflection on areas requiring additional memorization practice.
materials_needed: Blank Knowledge Area-Process Group matrix templates (2 per student)
PMBOK Guide 7th Edition reference charts
Colored pens/highlighters (10 different colors)
Digital timer or stopwatch
Master answer key for verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 95% accuracy (maximum 2-3 errors) on completed matrix within time limit. Verbal responses during rapid-fire quizzing scored as correct/incorrect with 80% minimum threshold. Advanced recall challenge requires accurate identification of Knowledge Area, Process Group, plus one input and output for 12 out of 15 randomly selected processes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide mnemonic devices for each Knowledge Area, start with fewer processes (focus on Integration Management first), allow additional study time with audio recordings of process names. For advanced learners: Include ITTOs (Inputs, Tools/Techniques, Outputs) recall for all processes, add enterprise environmental factors and organizational process assets connections, incorporate process sequencing and dependency relationships.

title: Decoding Leadership Paradoxes Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis
description: Students analyze complex leadership scenarios containing inherent paradoxes (e.g., confidence vs. humility, stability vs. change) by examining multiple stakeholder perspectives. They demonstrate understanding by explaining how different leadership theories account for contradictory behaviors and outcomes within the same leadership situation.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret contradictory leadership behaviors within complex organizational scenarios by applying multiple leadership theoretical frameworks simultaneously
Students will explain how situational variables influence the effectiveness of paradoxical leadership approaches through structured stakeholder analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Netflix leadership case study featuring Reed Hastings' decision-making during the Qwikster crisis (2011). Form groups of 4 students, assigning each member a specific stakeholder role: Board Director, Senior Manager, Customer Representative, and Industry Analyst. Provide each group with theory reference sheets covering Transformational Leadership, Situational Leadership, and Paradoxical Leadership frameworks. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Individual stakeholders read the case and complete their assigned stakeholder analysis worksheet, identifying leadership behaviors that appear contradictory from their perspective. Each stakeholder must document specific examples where Hastings demonstrated both sides of three leadership paradoxes: confidence/humility, control/empowerment, and stability/change.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups convene to share stakeholder perspectives. Using the provided comparison matrix template, they map contradictory behaviors against the three leadership theories, noting where theories align or conflict in explaining the same behavior. Groups must reach consensus on why certain paradoxical behaviors were effective or ineffective for different stakeholders.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Each group creates a visual leadership paradox map showing how the same leadership decision created positive outcomes for some stakeholders while creating negative outcomes for others. They must include theory-based explanations for these differential impacts.

Phase 4 (15 minutes): Groups present their paradox maps to the class, specifically explaining how their understanding of leadership complexity evolved through the multi-perspective analysis. Conclude with individual reflection journals where students synthesize their understanding of how leadership effectiveness depends on stakeholder context and theoretical lens.
materials_needed: Netflix-Qwikster case study (detailed 4-page version)
Stakeholder analysis worksheets (4 different versions)
Leadership theory reference sheets (Transformational, Situational, Paradoxical)
Comparison matrix templates
Large poster paper for visual mapping
Colored markers and sticky notes
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of stakeholder perspective analysis (25%), (2) Correct application of leadership theories to explain paradoxes (35%), (3) Quality of synthesis in paradox mapping showing interconnections (25%), (4) Depth of reflection demonstrating evolved understanding of leadership complexity (15%). Success requires students to identify at least 6 contradictory behaviors, correctly apply all three theories, and articulate how the same leadership action can be simultaneously effective and ineffective.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case excerpts showing obvious contradictions and theory definition cards with guiding questions. Offer sentence starters for analysis worksheets. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by including Authentic Leadership theory and requiring them to facilitate cross-group discussions. Provide extension activity involving creation of their own paradoxical leadership scenario based on current business cases.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis and Optimization
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario with multiple identified risks and evaluate the effectiveness of proposed risk response strategies. They will deconstruct the relationships between risks, assess the appropriateness of chosen response strategies, and recommend strategic improvements based on project constraints and objectives.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the alignment between risk categories and response strategies by examining cause-and-effect relationships within a multi-risk project environment
Students will evaluate the cost-benefit effectiveness of risk response strategies through systematic comparison of resource allocation and risk mitigation outcomes
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'Metro Transit Expansion Project' case study containing 12 identified risks across technical, organizational, and external categories, along with proposed response strategies and budget constraints (10 minutes). Organize students into groups of 3-4, assigning each group a different stakeholder perspective (project sponsor, technical lead, community relations manager, or finance director). Each group receives a risk analysis worksheet with evaluation criteria matrix. 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Groups analyze each risk using the probability-impact matrix provided, then categorize the proposed responses (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and evaluate appropriateness for each risk level. Students must identify at least three instances where response strategies may be misaligned with risk severity or project objectives.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Groups conduct cost-benefit analysis of the top 6 highest-priority risks, calculating residual risk levels after proposed responses and determining resource allocation efficiency. They must justify why certain responses may be over-engineered or insufficient given budget constraints of $2.3M for risk responses.

Phase 3 (20 minutes): Groups prepare evidence-based recommendations for optimizing the overall risk response strategy, identifying interdependencies between risks that weren't addressed in original plan, and proposing alternative strategies that better align with their stakeholder perspective while maintaining overall project viability.

Conclude with 15-minute stakeholder presentations where each group presents their top 3 strategic recommendations with supporting analysis, followed by cross-examination from other stakeholder groups to simulate real project governance discussions.
materials_needed: Metro Transit Expansion Project case study packet (4 pages per student)
Risk Analysis Worksheet with probability-impact matrix template
Cost-benefit calculation spreadsheet template
Stakeholder role description cards
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk-response alignment analysis (25%), (2) Quality of cost-benefit calculations and reasoning (25%), (3) Evidence-based justification for strategic recommendations (25%), and (4) Integration of stakeholder perspective in decision-making rationale (25%). Students must demonstrate clear cause-effect reasoning and cite specific data points from case study to achieve proficient level.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide completed example analysis for 2 sample risks and highlight key decision criteria. Offer guided questions worksheet focusing on 'what factors make this response appropriate/inappropriate?' For advanced learners: Add secondary stakeholder concerns (environmental impact, political considerations) and require integration of qualitative risk factors beyond standard probability-impact calculations.

title: Programming Language Syntax Flash Card Drill
description: Students will memorize and recall fundamental Python syntax elements through structured flash card practice. This activity focuses on building automatic recognition of basic programming constructs including variable declarations, print statements, and basic operators.
learning_objectives: Students will recall correct Python syntax for variable assignment, print statements, and arithmetic operators by practicing with digital flash cards
Students will identify proper Python syntax elements through timed recognition exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing pre-made digital flash cards using Anki or Quizlet containing 25 essential Python syntax elements (Step 1, 5 minutes). Have students create accounts and access the shared deck titled 'Python Basics Syntax.' Demonstrate proper flash card technique: read the prompt aloud, attempt to recall the answer within 3 seconds, reveal the answer, and mark confidence level (Step 2, 5 minutes). Students work individually through the complete deck once, focusing on variable assignments (x = 5), print statements (print('Hello')), arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /), comparison operators (==, !=, <, >), and basic string operations (Step 3, 15 minutes). After the initial round, students identify cards marked as 'difficult' and create a focused review pile (Step 4, 5 minutes). Conduct three timed practice rounds: Round 1 focuses on missed items only (5 minutes), Round 2 reviews the complete deck with 2-second time limits (8 minutes), and Round 3 involves random sampling of 10 cards for speed recall (2 minutes). Conclude with partner verification where students quiz each other using 5 randomly selected cards from the deck, with partners checking accuracy against the provided answer key (Step 5, 10 minutes). Document progress by having students record their accuracy percentage and identify their three most challenging syntax elements on the provided tracking sheet.
materials_needed: Digital devices (tablets, laptops, or smartphones) with internet access
Pre-created Anki or Quizlet deck: 'Python Basics Syntax' with 25 cards
Printed answer key for partner verification
Student progress tracking sheets
Timer or stopwatch
assessment_method: Success measured by 80% accuracy rate on final 10-card random quiz and completion of progress tracking sheet. Students must correctly recall syntax within 3-second time limit. Partner verification confirms accuracy through cross-checking with answer key.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: reduce deck to 15 cards focusing on variables and print statements only, extend time limits to 5 seconds. For advanced learners: add 10 additional cards covering conditional statements (if/else) and create personal mnemonics for complex syntax patterns.

title: Analyzing Quantum Tunneling Probability Variations in Multi-Barrier Semiconductor Heterostructures
description: Students will analyze transmission coefficient data from quantum tunneling simulations across different barrier configurations in semiconductor heterostructures. They will decompose complex wave function interactions and evaluate how barrier width, height, and spacing affect tunneling probability in resonant tunneling diodes.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze quantum tunneling transmission coefficients by comparing wave function behavior across multiple barrier configurations and identifying resonance conditions
Students will evaluate the relationship between barrier parameters and tunneling probability through systematic examination of semiconductor heterostructure simulations
instructions: Begin by distributing three datasets containing transmission coefficient versus electron energy plots for different AlGaAs/GaAs heterostructure configurations: single barrier (3nm), double barrier with 2nm spacing, and double barrier with 5nm spacing. Students work in groups of 3-4 for 20 minutes to examine each dataset, identifying peak positions, widths, and maximum transmission values. Next, provide students with the corresponding wave function probability density plots for each configuration at three specific energies: below resonance, at resonance, and above resonance (15 minutes). Each group creates a comparative analysis table documenting: barrier penetration depth, standing wave patterns in quantum wells, and phase relationships between incident and transmitted waves. For 25 minutes, groups use the time-independent Schrödinger equation solution templates to calculate theoretical transmission coefficients for their assigned configuration, comparing results with simulation data. Students must identify discrepancies and propose physical explanations. In the final 30 minutes, each group presents their analysis of how barrier spacing affects: resonance energy positions, peak sharpness (quality factor), and off-resonance transmission probability. Groups must explain their findings using quantum mechanical principles including wave interference, bound state formation, and tunneling decay length. Conclude with a 10-minute class discussion where groups synthesize findings to predict optimal heterostructure design for resonant tunneling diode applications.
materials_needed: Three datasets of transmission coefficient vs energy plots (AlGaAs/GaAs configurations)
Wave function probability density plots at specified energies
Schrödinger equation solution templates with barrier parameters
Scientific calculators or MATLAB/Python access
Graph paper and colored pens for analysis diagrams
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate identification of resonance conditions and peak characteristics (25%), (2) Correct analysis of wave function behavior and phase relationships (25%), (3) Valid comparison between theoretical calculations and simulation data with physical explanations for discrepancies (30%), (4) Clear presentation connecting barrier parameters to tunneling probability with quantum mechanical reasoning (20%)
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-labeled energy diagrams showing barrier positions and offer guided questions about wave behavior at interfaces. Supply formula sheets with key equations highlighted. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by providing temperature-dependent data or asking them to predict I-V characteristics from their transmission analysis. Encourage exploration of three-barrier systems or consideration of scattering effects.

title: Design and Build a Customer Churn Prediction Dashboard with Actionable Business Recommendations
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that combines statistical analysis, data visualization, and predictive modeling to identify at-risk customers. They will develop original business intervention strategies based on their analytical findings and present actionable recommendations to stakeholders.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive analytical framework by integrating descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and predictive modeling techniques to identify customer churn patterns
Students will construct an interactive dashboard through data visualization tools that communicates complex analytical findings to non-technical business stakeholders
instructions: Begin by providing each team with the sample customer dataset containing 12 months of transaction data, demographics, and engagement metrics (30 minutes setup). Teams first conduct exploratory data analysis using Excel or Python to identify key variables correlating with customer churn, calculating retention rates, average customer lifetime value, and engagement trends by customer segments. Next, students clean the dataset by handling missing values, creating derived variables (recency, frequency, monetary scores), and standardizing data formats (45 minutes). Students then build a predictive model using logistic regression or decision trees to score customers by churn probability, validating model accuracy with train/test splits (60 minutes). Using Tableau, Power BI, or similar tools, teams create an interactive dashboard featuring: churn probability by customer segment, key risk factors visualization, monthly trend analysis, and customer drill-down capability (90 minutes). Students must design three specific business intervention strategies (email campaigns, loyalty programs, personalized offers) based on their analytical insights, including implementation timelines and success metrics. Each strategy should target different risk segments identified in their analysis. Teams prepare a 10-minute stakeholder presentation explaining their methodology, key findings, dashboard functionality, and recommended actions with expected ROI calculations. Conclude with peer feedback sessions where teams evaluate each other's dashboards for clarity, analytical rigor, and business applicability using provided rubric criteria (30 minutes).
materials_needed: Customer transaction dataset (CSV file with 1000+ records, 15+ variables)
Excel or Python/Pandas for data analysis
Tableau Public, Power BI, or Google Data Studio for dashboard creation
Presentation software (PowerPoint, Google Slides)
Rubric handout for peer evaluation
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric across five criteria: (1) Data analysis thoroughness and accuracy of statistical calculations, (2) Predictive model implementation and validation methodology, (3) Dashboard design effectiveness including interactivity and visual clarity, (4) Business recommendations specificity and feasibility with clear ROI projections, (5) Stakeholder presentation quality and ability to translate technical findings into business language. Each criterion worth 20 points. Students must achieve 70+ points for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide data analysis templates with guided formulas, offer dashboard wireframe examples, and create checkpoint sessions after each major phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced modeling techniques (ensemble methods, feature engineering), add real-time data refresh capabilities, or develop A/B testing frameworks for intervention strategies. Consider pairing stronger analytical students with those having better business acumen.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Terminology Speed Recall Challenge
description: Students will rapidly identify and recall specific terminology, processes, and components from advanced project management frameworks including PMBOK 7th Edition, PRINCE2, and Agile/Scrum methodologies. This high-intensity recall activity tests memorization of complex project management concepts through structured retrieval practice.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall specific terminology from PMBOK 7th Edition performance domains, PRINCE2 themes, and Scrum artifacts within 5-second time limits
Students will identify correct definitions for advanced project management concepts through rapid-fire terminology matching exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the 150-item terminology bank covering PMBOK 7th Edition (50 terms), PRINCE2 methodology (50 terms), and Scrum/Agile frameworks (50 terms). Give students 15 minutes to review all terms silently. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Set up three rotation stations: Station 1 focuses on PMBOK terms (performance domains, project life cycles, tailoring considerations), Station 2 covers PRINCE2 elements (themes like organization, quality, risk; processes like initiating, directing, managing), and Station 3 addresses Scrum/Agile terminology (sprint artifacts, ceremonies, roles). At each station, display term definitions on screen for 5 seconds while teams write the corresponding term. Include complex concepts like 'predictive life cycle tailoring,' 'PRINCE2 exception management process,' and 'Scrum retrospective facilitation techniques.' Teams rotate every 12 minutes, spending exactly 4 minutes per terminology category at each station. After rotations, conduct rapid-fire oral recall where individual students must provide definitions when given terms, with 5-second response limits. Record correct responses on tracking sheets. Conclude with teams self-checking answers against provided answer keys, calculating accuracy percentages for each framework category.
materials_needed: 150-item terminology bank with PMBOK 7th Edition, PRINCE2, and Scrum terms printed on handouts
Digital timer with audible alerts
Three large displays or projectors for station-based definition presentations
Answer key sheets for each framework category
Individual response tracking sheets for scoring
assessment_method: Students must achieve 85% accuracy across all three framework categories (minimum 43/50 correct responses per framework). Assess through: (1) Written station responses scored against answer keys, (2) Individual oral recall performance with 5-second time limits, (3) Team accuracy calculations for each framework section. Track individual progress using response sheets showing correct/incorrect answers per terminology category.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide framework-specific glossary cards during review period, allow 7-second response time instead of 5 seconds, pair with stronger students during team rotations. For advanced learners: Add integration questions requiring recall of relationships between frameworks, include obscure terminology from PMI standards beyond PMBOK, challenge them to explain contextual applications of recalled terms within 10-second limits.

title: Leadership Theory Integration Matrix: Analyzing Multi-Dimensional Leadership Approaches
description: Students will analyze complex leadership scenarios through the lens of multiple leadership theories simultaneously, creating integration matrices that demonstrate deep comprehension of how different theoretical frameworks complement, contradict, or synthesize with each other. This expert-level activity requires students to move beyond single-theory application to sophisticated multi-theory interpretation.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret complex organizational leadership challenges by systematically applying and comparing five distinct leadership theories (Transformational, Servant Leadership, Situational Leadership, Leader-Member Exchange, and Authentic Leadership) within structured analytical matrices

Students will demonstrate comprehensive understanding of theoretical relationships by identifying convergences, divergences, and synthesis opportunities between leadership frameworks through detailed comparative analysis
instructions:
Begin by distributing the pre-selected case study packet containing three complex organizational scenarios: a healthcare system merger, a tech startup scaling crisis, and a non-profit leadership succession challenge. Form teams of 4-5 students with mixed leadership experience levels. Each team receives five theory reference sheets with key principles, assumptions, and applications clearly outlined. 

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams create a 5x3 matrix (five theories x three scenarios) on large poster paper. For each cell, students must identify specific theory applications, predicted outcomes, and potential limitations for that scenario. Encourage deep discussion about why certain theories may be more or less applicable.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams complete a secondary analysis layer by identifying integration opportunities - marking cells where theories complement each other with green dots, where they conflict with red dots, and where they could synthesize into hybrid approaches with yellow dots. Students must provide written justification for each marking.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Conduct structured gallery walks where teams rotate through other matrices, adding sticky note questions or alternative interpretations. Each team must engage with at least three other matrices, focusing on areas where their analysis differed significantly.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Teams reconvene to revise their original matrix based on peer feedback and new insights. They prepare a 3-minute presentation highlighting their most significant theoretical integration discovery and one area where multiple theories failed to adequately address the leadership challenge.
materials_needed: Three complex organizational case study packets (6-8 pages each)
Five laminated leadership theory reference sheets per team
Large poster paper (24x36 inches) and colored markers
Colored dot stickers (green, red, yellow) - 30 of each color per team
Small sticky notes for peer feedback
Timer and presentation easel
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric across four dimensions: (1) Theoretical Accuracy - correct application of theory principles and concepts, (2) Integration Sophistication - quality of cross-theory analysis and synthesis identification, (3) Critical Analysis Depth - evidence of moving beyond surface-level application to nuanced interpretation, and (4) Collaborative Engagement - meaningful contribution to team discussions and peer feedback process. Students must demonstrate mastery (3-4 points) in at least three dimensions, with specific evidence documented through matrix annotations, peer feedback quality, and presentation insights.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide theory application templates with guiding questions and encourage them to focus on 2-3 theories initially before expanding. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers during matrix creation. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify gaps where existing theories fall short and propose theoretical extensions or entirely new frameworks. Encourage them to facilitate peer discussions and serve as theory consultants for other teams during gallery walks.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Threat and Opportunity Management Approaches
description: Students will analyze a complex project scenario to identify risks and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will compare and contrast threat mitigation approaches versus opportunity enhancement strategies, determining optimal responses based on project constraints and organizational risk tolerance.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project risk scenarios by categorizing threats and opportunities and evaluating appropriate response strategies within budget and schedule constraints
Students will differentiate between risk response strategies through systematic comparison of strategy effectiveness, cost-benefit ratios, and alignment with project objectives
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute the 'Metro Transit App Development' case study containing 12 identified risks (6 threats, 6 opportunities) with project parameters: $2.5M budget, 18-month timeline, regulatory compliance requirements. Step 1 (15 minutes): Each group analyzes the risk register, categorizing each risk by probability/impact matrix position and determining whether it's a threat or opportunity. Step 2 (20 minutes): For each risk, groups must identify all applicable response strategies from the four threat responses (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and four opportunity responses (exploit, enhance, share, accept). Step 3 (25 minutes): Groups create a comparison matrix analyzing each potential response strategy against three criteria: implementation cost, timeline impact, and probability of success. They must calculate a weighted score for each strategy using provided weighting factors (cost: 40%, timeline: 35%, success probability: 25%). Step 4 (15 minutes): Groups select their top 3 recommended strategies for threats and top 3 for opportunities, justifying selections based on their analysis. Step 5 (20 minutes): Each group presents one threat and one opportunity analysis to the class, explaining their reasoning and defending their strategy choices. Other groups provide feedback using the 'PMI Challenge Protocol' - identifying strengths (Plus), areas for improvement (Minus), and questions (Interesting).
materials_needed: Metro Transit App Development case study packet (3 pages per student)
Risk Response Strategy Comparison Matrix template (Excel spreadsheet)
Probability/Impact Matrix reference sheet
PMI Challenge Protocol feedback forms
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of risk categorization and P/I matrix placement (25%), (2) Completeness and logic of strategy comparison analysis (35%), (3) Quality of justification for selected strategies with supporting evidence (25%), (4) Effective use of PMP terminology and concepts (15%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category to demonstrate mastery.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed comparison matrix with 2-3 examples filled in, and offer a risk response strategy quick-reference card. For advanced learners: Add a secondary challenge requiring them to develop contingency plans for their top-ranked strategies and calculate expected monetary value for quantifiable risks. Consider pairing stronger analytical thinkers with students who excel at presentation skills.

title: Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Real Estate Data
description: Students will analyze a real estate dataset to interpret correlation matrices and explain the relationships between property features. They will distinguish between correlation and causation while identifying which features most strongly predict property values.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret correlation coefficients between housing features by analyzing a correlation matrix and explaining the strength and direction of relationships
Students will distinguish between correlation and causation through guided analysis of real estate property relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the Boston Housing dataset (or similar real estate data) containing 13 features including median home value, crime rate, number of rooms, age of property, and distance to employment centers. Students work in pairs for 45 minutes. First, have students spend 10 minutes exploring the dataset structure using pandas.describe() and pandas.info() to understand variable types and ranges. Next, students create a correlation matrix using pandas.corr() and visualize it with seaborn.heatmap(), spending 15 minutes identifying the strongest positive and negative correlations. In the analysis phase (15 minutes), students select three feature pairs with correlations above 0.7 or below -0.7 and write explanations for why these relationships exist, considering real-world housing market factors. Students must then identify one strong correlation that likely represents causation versus one that represents mere association, providing justification. Finally, spend 5 minutes having each pair share one surprising correlation they discovered and their interpretation. Instructor should circulate during analysis, prompting students with questions like 'What does a correlation of -0.74 tell us about the relationship?' and 'Could this relationship work in reverse?'
materials_needed: Boston Housing dataset (CSV file)
Jupyter Notebook environment with pandas, seaborn, and matplotlib installed
Correlation interpretation reference sheet with coefficient ranges
Laptops or computers with Python environment
assessment_method: Evaluate students using a 3-point rubric: (1) Correct interpretation of correlation coefficient values and signs, (2) Logical explanations connecting correlations to real-world housing factors, (3) Accurate distinction between correlation and causation examples. Students submit written responses identifying their three strongest correlations with explanations, plus one causation vs. correlation comparison.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a correlation interpretation guide (e.g., 0.7-1.0 = strong positive) and sentence starters like 'This positive correlation suggests...' For advanced learners, challenge them to identify potential confounding variables or suggest additional data that might explain unexpected correlations. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support.

title: Optimizing Manufacturing Costs Using Linear Programming
description: Students will apply linear programming techniques to solve a real-world manufacturing optimization problem involving multiple constraints and variables. They will formulate objective functions, graph feasible regions, and determine optimal production quantities to maximize profit while meeting resource limitations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply linear programming methods to formulate and solve a multi-variable optimization problem by translating business constraints into mathematical inequalities
Students will implement the graphical method and simplex algorithm to determine optimal solutions through systematic mathematical analysis
instructions: Begin by presenting the scenario: TechWidget Manufacturing produces two products (smartphones and tablets) with limited resources. Distribute the problem sheet showing: smartphones yield $150 profit each, tablets $200 each; assembly requires 2 hours per smartphone, 3 hours per tablet (480 hours available weekly); testing needs 1 hour per smartphone, 2 hours per tablet (300 hours available); materials cost $100 per smartphone, $180 per tablet ($25,000 budget). Students work in pairs for 15 minutes to identify variables (x=smartphones, y=tablets) and write the objective function (maximize P=150x+200y). Next, have pairs spend 20 minutes formulating constraint inequalities: 2x+3y≤480 (assembly), x+2y≤300 (testing), 100x+180y≤25000 (budget), x≥0, y≥0. Using graphing software, students plot constraints and identify the feasible region (25 minutes). They must find intersection points by solving systems of equations algebraically. In the final 30 minutes, students evaluate the objective function at each vertex of the feasible region, identify the optimal solution, and interpret results in business context. Each pair submits a complete solution showing: constraint formulation, graphed feasible region with labeled vertices, calculated profit at each vertex, and a written recommendation stating optimal production quantities with maximum profit.
materials_needed: Problem scenario handout with manufacturing data
Graph paper or graphing software (GeoGebra or Desmos)
Scientific calculators
Constraint inequality reference sheet
assessment_method: Evaluate submissions using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct variable definition and objective function formulation, (2) Accurate constraint inequalities and feasible region identification, (3) Precise vertex calculations and profit evaluations, (4) Clear business interpretation and optimal solution recommendation. Each criterion worth 25 points for 100 total.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-written constraint templates with blanks to fill in coefficients, and offer a step-by-step vertex-finding checklist. Advanced learners can extend the problem by adding a third product variable, incorporating integer constraints, or analyzing sensitivity to parameter changes in the profit coefficients.

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems: The Three-Body Problem with Earth-Moon-Satellite Dynamics
description: Students will decompose complex gravitational interactions in a three-body system by examining how Earth, Moon, and an artificial satellite influence each other's motion. They will analyze force vectors, potential energy landscapes, and stability conditions to predict orbital behavior and identify Lagrange points.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the gravitational force contributions from multiple massive bodies by decomposing vector components and calculating net forces at specific positions
Students will examine the relationship between potential energy surfaces and orbital stability through mathematical modeling and graphical interpretation
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 and providing each team with the scenario: a 1000 kg communication satellite positioned at various points in the Earth-Moon system. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams calculate gravitational forces from both Earth (M_E = 5.97×10^24 kg) and Moon (M_M = 7.35×10^22 kg) on the satellite at five predetermined positions along the Earth-Moon line, including the L1 Lagrange point (approximately 326,000 km from Earth). Students must decompose forces into x and y components using vector analysis.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using provided potential energy equation U = -GM_E*m/r_E - GM_M*m/r_M, teams create a potential energy map by calculating values at a 10×10 grid of positions in the Earth-Moon plane. They plot equipotential contours using graphing software or manual calculation.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams analyze their force and energy data to identify regions of equilibrium, stability, and instability. They must explain why certain positions allow stable orbits while others lead to ejection or collision. Students examine how the effective potential (including centrifugal force) creates 'hills' and 'valleys' that govern satellite motion.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Each team presents one specific position analysis, explaining the force balance, energy considerations, and predicted satellite behavior. They must justify whether a satellite placed at that position with zero initial velocity would remain stable, oscillate, or escape the system.
materials_needed: Scientific calculators or computers with spreadsheet software
Graph paper and colored pencils for contour plotting
Reference sheet with Earth-Moon system parameters (masses, separation distance of 384,400 km)
Coordinate grid templates showing Earth-Moon system to scale
Vector analysis reference formulas
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Accuracy of gravitational force calculations and vector decomposition, (2) Correct application of potential energy concepts and contour interpretation, (3) Quality of stability analysis linking forces to orbital behavior, (4) Clear explanation of physical reasoning in presentations. Students must demonstrate understanding by correctly predicting satellite motion at untested positions.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing partially completed force calculation templates and suggesting they start with positions along the Earth-Moon line before attempting off-axis points. For advanced learners, introduce perturbation analysis around equilibrium points or challenge them to find approximate positions of L4 and L5 Lagrange points using their potential energy maps.

title: Code Review Comparison: Evaluating Bug Detection Approaches
description: Students will analyze and compare the effectiveness of two different code review methods by examining their ability to identify bugs in a simple Python calculator program. They will evaluate which approach yields better results for beginner programmers and justify their conclusions with evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the effectiveness of checklist-based versus open-ended code review methods by comparing bug detection rates and quality of feedback
Students will critique the strengths and weaknesses of each review approach through systematic analysis of review outcomes and recommendation formulation
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with a printed copy of a 30-line Python calculator program containing 5 intentional bugs (syntax error, logic error, edge case handling, variable naming issue, and missing input validation). Also provide two code review instruction sheets: Method A (checklist with 8 specific items to check) and Method B (open-ended instructions to 'find any issues').

**Phase 1 - Dual Review Process (20 minutes):** Students work individually to review the same code twice using both methods. First, spend 10 minutes using Method A (checklist approach), documenting found issues on the provided form. Then, spend 10 minutes using Method B (open-ended approach) on a fresh copy, without referring to previous findings. Students record all discoveries separately for each method.

**Phase 2 - Effectiveness Analysis (15 minutes):** Students create a comparison table analyzing: (1) number of bugs found by each method, (2) time to find each bug, (3) accuracy of bug descriptions, and (4) false positives identified. They calculate percentages and note which method felt more systematic or intuitive.

**Phase 3 - Evaluation and Recommendation (15 minutes):** Using their data, students write a 200-word evaluation answering: Which method is more effective for beginners and why? What are the trade-offs? They must support their conclusion with specific evidence from their analysis and provide a recommendation for new programmers, including suggested improvements to their preferred method.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students submit their comparison tables and written evaluations. Brief class discussion on patterns observed across different students' findings.
materials_needed: Printed Python calculator code with 5 embedded bugs (one per student)
Method A instruction sheet with 8-item review checklist
Method B instruction sheet with open-ended review guidelines
Comparison table template
Timer or stopwatch for each student
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: (1) Completeness of bug detection analysis with specific counts and percentages, (2) Quality of method comparison showing clear understanding of trade-offs, (3) Strength of evidence-based conclusion with data support, (4) Practicality and feasibility of final recommendation for beginner programmers. Each criterion worth 25 points for total of 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a partially completed comparison table template and sentence starters for the evaluation paragraph. For advanced learners: Add a third phase where they design an improved hybrid method combining strengths of both approaches, then test it on a second code sample to validate their hypothesis.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula and Terminology Precision Drill
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific formulas, calculations, and technical terminology used in Critical Path Method analysis for complex project scheduling. This activity focuses on precise retention of mathematical relationships, float calculations, and duration compression techniques.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the exact formulas for Early Start (ES), Early Finish (EF), Late Start (LS), and Late Finish (LF) calculations by completing timed calculation sequences
Students will identify specific CPM terminology including Total Float, Free Float, Independent Float, and Interfering Float through rapid-fire definition matching exercises
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Cards to each student (5 minutes). Have students work individually to memorize the four core formulas: ES = Maximum EF of predecessors, EF = ES + Duration, LF = Minimum LS of successors, LS = LF - Duration. Students spend 15 minutes using spaced repetition flashcards, covering the formula, attempting to write it from memory, then checking accuracy. Next, introduce the Float Formula Cards: Total Float = LS - ES = LF - EF, Free Float = ES(successor) - EF(current), Independent Float = ES(successor) - LF(current) - Duration. Students practice these for 10 minutes using the same cover-and-recall method. Following memorization, conduct a rapid-fire terminology drill where you display project network scenarios on screen for 30 seconds each. Students must write down the appropriate calculation setup (not solve) for scenarios like 'Activity B has ES=5, Duration=3, find EF' or 'Activity X has LS=12, ES=8, calculate Total Float.' Complete 15 scenarios total. Finish with a partner verification round (10 minutes) where Student A states a formula or definition while Student B validates accuracy using the reference cards. Rotate roles after each item. Conclude with individual written recall quiz containing 20 fill-in-the-blank formula components and 10 terminology definitions, completed without reference materials in 15 minutes.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Cards (laminated, one set per student)
Float Formula Reference Cards with visual diagrams
Digital timer or stopwatch
Projector/screen for scenario display
Pre-prepared network diagram scenarios (15 different cases)
Written recall quiz sheets (30 questions each)
assessment_method: Success measured by 90% accuracy on the final written recall quiz, with specific scoring: CPM formulas (40 points - 2 points per formula component), Float calculations (30 points - 3 points per formula), Terminology definitions (30 points - 3 points per definition). Partner verification checklist confirms mutual accuracy during practice rounds. Time requirements: all formulas recalled within 30 seconds each during partner testing.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded formula cards where each variable (ES, EF, LS, LF) has consistent colors across all formulas. Create pneumonic devices like 'Early Start = Maximum Early Finish of Previous tasks.' For advanced learners: Add resource-constrained scheduling formulas and crash cost calculations (Cost slope = (Crash Cost - Normal Cost)/(Normal Duration - Crash Duration)). Include precedence diagramming method (PDM) relationship calculations for Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start with lag times.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Triple Constraint Impacts
description: Students will analyze different risk response strategies for a given project scenario by examining their impacts on scope, schedule, and cost constraints. They will compare the effectiveness of multiple response options and justify their recommendations based on project priorities and stakeholder requirements.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationships between different risk response strategies (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) and their impacts on project triple constraints by evaluating quantitative and qualitative data
