Students will compare the effectiveness of multiple risk response options through systematic evaluation using decision matrices and cost-benefit analysis
instructions: **Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the 'Software Implementation Project' case study packet containing: project charter, WBS excerpt, schedule baseline, budget summary, and three identified high-impact risks. Form teams of 3-4 students. **Step 1 (15 minutes):** Teams read the case study and identify the current project constraints and priorities. Each team member takes notes on one constraint (scope, schedule, cost, plus quality). **Step 2 (25 minutes):** For each of the three risks provided, teams brainstorm 2-3 different response strategies. Using the provided analysis template, they document: strategy type, implementation steps, resource requirements, timeline, and predicted impact on each constraint (using scale of -3 to +3). **Step 3 (20 minutes):** Teams complete the decision matrix worksheet, weighing each response option against criteria: cost of implementation, probability of success, impact on stakeholder satisfaction, and alignment with project priorities. Calculate weighted scores for each option. **Step 4 (15 minutes):** Teams prepare a 3-minute presentation summarizing their top recommendation for each risk, including quantitative justification and implementation timeline. **Step 5 (20 minutes):** Each team presents one risk analysis. Other teams ask clarifying questions and challenge assumptions using the provided peer evaluation checklist.
materials_needed: Software Implementation Project case study packet (4 pages)
Risk Response Analysis Template worksheets
Decision Matrix Evaluation sheets with weighted criteria
Peer Evaluation Checklist forms
Calculators or laptops with Excel access
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate completed Decision Matrix worksheets using 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of constraint impact predictions with clear reasoning, (2) Appropriate weighting of decision criteria based on project context, (3) Mathematical accuracy in scoring calculations, (4) Quality of justification linking quantitative analysis to final recommendations. Peer evaluations contribute 20% to final score.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed decision matrix examples and constraint impact reference guide. Assign stronger analytical thinkers as team leads. For advanced learners: Add secondary risks triggered by response strategies, require sensitivity analysis showing impact of changing constraint priorities, or include stakeholder influence-interest analysis in decision criteria.

title: Design and Deploy a Multi-VLAN Enterprise Network with Advanced Security and QoS Policies
description: Students will architect and implement a complete enterprise network topology incorporating VLANs, inter-VLAN routing, advanced security configurations, and Quality of Service policies. This culminating project requires students to synthesize knowledge of switching, routing, security, and network optimization to create a production-ready network solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable multi-VLAN network architecture by analyzing business requirements and creating detailed network diagrams with IP addressing schemes
Students will configure advanced Cisco switching and routing protocols through hands-on implementation of VLANs, STP, OSPF, and access control lists
Students will develop comprehensive network security policies by implementing port security, 802.1X authentication, and firewall rules
Students will create Quality of Service configurations through traffic classification and bandwidth management policies
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario requiring network segmentation for 4 departments (Finance, HR, Engineering, Guest). Students work in teams of 2-3 to create network topology diagrams using Packet Tracer, defining VLAN structure, IP subnetting (using /24 networks from 192.168.0.0/16), and device placement. Each team must justify their design choices in a 10-minute presentation.

**Phase 2: Physical Implementation (90 minutes)**
Using Cisco 2960 switches and 1941 routers, teams build their designed topology. Configure VLANs 10 (Finance), 20 (HR), 30 (Engineering), 99 (Guest), and 100 (Management). Implement trunk links between switches using 802.1Q encapsulation. Configure inter-VLAN routing using router-on-a-stick or SVI methods. Set up OSPF routing protocol with area 0 configuration.

**Phase 3: Security Configuration (60 minutes)**
Implement port security limiting MAC addresses to 2 per access port with violation mode restrict. Configure standard and extended ACLs preventing Finance VLAN from accessing HR VLAN, blocking Guest VLAN from internal networks except web traffic. Set up SSH access with local user authentication and disable Telnet. Configure DHCP snooping on access ports.

**Phase 4: QoS Implementation (45 minutes)**
Create traffic classes prioritizing VoIP traffic (if applicable), limiting Guest VLAN bandwidth to 10Mbps, and ensuring Finance VLAN receives guaranteed 50Mbps minimum bandwidth. Implement traffic policing and shaping policies.

**Phase 5: Testing and Documentation (30 minutes)**
Conduct connectivity tests between VLANs, verify security policies block unauthorized traffic, and document all configurations with running-config exports and network verification commands.
materials_needed: Cisco 2960 switches (minimum 2 per team)
Cisco 1941 routers (1 per team)
CAT5e/6 Ethernet cables (8-10 per team)
Console cables and USB-to-serial adapters
Laptops/PCs with PuTTY or SecureCRT installed
Cisco Packet Tracer software
Network topology template worksheets
IP address planning worksheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Documentation (25 points) - topology accuracy, IP scheme correctness, design justification; Configuration Implementation (40 points) - VLAN functionality, routing protocols, trunk configuration; Security Implementation (20 points) - ACL effectiveness, port security operation, management access; QoS Policies (10 points) - traffic classification and bandwidth management; Documentation Quality (5 points) - configuration exports and verification screenshots. Teams must demonstrate working network with ping tests, show security policies blocking traffic, and present final running configurations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates with partial VLAN configurations and step-by-step command references. Pair weaker students with stronger technical partners. Offer additional lab time for practice with basic switching commands. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement EtherChannel link aggregation, HSRP redundancy protocols, or integrate wireless access points with controller-based management. Have them create Python scripts for automated configuration deployment using Netmiko library.

title: Optimizing Solar Panel Array Layout Using Calculus and Geometric Constraints
description: Students will apply multivariable calculus optimization techniques to design an efficient solar panel array layout for a real building rooftop. They will work with actual building dimensions, shadow constraints, and cost functions to determine the optimal panel placement that maximizes energy output while minimizing installation costs.
learning_objectives: Students will apply Lagrange multipliers and constraint optimization to solve a real-world energy optimization problem involving multiple variables and geometric constraints
Students will implement derivative-based optimization techniques through systematic analysis of cost-benefit functions in renewable energy contexts
instructions: Begin by distributing building specification sheets containing actual rooftop dimensions, obstacle locations, and local solar irradiance data (15 minutes setup). Organize students into teams of 3-4, assigning roles: Lead Mathematician (calculus computations), Geometric Analyst (constraint mapping), Cost Engineer (economic calculations), and Project Coordinator (synthesis and presentation). Teams receive identical building specs: 40m × 25m rectangular rooftop with two 3m × 4m HVAC units and one 2m × 6m stairwell access. Each standard solar panel measures 2m × 1m with 300W capacity. Students must establish their objective function combining energy output (revenue) and installation costs, considering that panels cannot be placed within 1.5m of obstacles or roof edges due to maintenance access requirements. Teams spend 45 minutes deriving constraint equations, mapping feasible installation zones, and setting up the optimization problem using variables for panel quantity (n), spacing between rows (s), and tilt angle (θ). Next, students apply calculus optimization techniques, computing partial derivatives of their objective function and using constraint methods to find critical points (35 minutes). They must verify their solutions represent true maxima through second derivative testing. Teams then validate their mathematical solutions by creating scaled diagrams showing exact panel placement coordinates and calculating total system specifications. Finally, each team presents their optimized design in 8-minute presentations, defending their mathematical approach and comparing energy output projections. Conclude with peer evaluation where teams critique each other's constraint handling and mathematical rigor.
materials_needed: Building specification sheets with rooftop dimensions and obstacle locations
Solar panel technical specification sheets (dimensions, wattage, cost data)
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system access
Large grid paper or CAD software for layout diagrams
Local solar irradiance data tables
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Mathematical setup and constraint identification (25 points), correct application of optimization techniques and calculus procedures (30 points), accuracy of final numerical solutions (20 points), quality of geometric layout validation (15 points), and presentation clarity with mathematical justification (10 points). Students must submit written calculations, final layout diagrams with coordinates, and energy/cost projections.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide constraint equation templates and guide them through the first few partial derivative calculations. Offer intermediate checkpoints to verify their objective function setup before proceeding to optimization. For advanced learners, introduce additional real-world complexities such as varying panel orientations, seasonal shadow analysis, or integration of battery storage optimization into their mathematical model.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference in Circuit Design: Multi-Variable Impact Assessment
description: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic interference (EMI) patterns in multi-component electronic circuits by examining frequency domain data, component positioning, and shielding effectiveness. They will deconstruct the relationships between circuit design parameters and EMI signatures to identify critical interference pathways and propose evidence-based mitigation strategies.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the causal relationships between circuit component placement, operating frequencies, and EMI patterns by systematically examining spectral data and geometric configurations
Students will deconstruct complex EMI scenarios through comparative analysis of shielded versus unshielded circuit configurations and their corresponding frequency response characteristics
instructions:
Begin by distributing three different circuit board designs (PCB layouts A, B, C) along with corresponding EMI spectral analysis data sets covering 10 MHz to 1 GHz range. Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning each team one primary circuit design. 

Step 1 (20 minutes): Teams examine their assigned PCB layout and identify all active components, trace routing patterns, ground plane configurations, and any existing shielding elements. Students create a component interaction map showing potential coupling pathways.

Step 2 (25 minutes): Using the provided spectral data, teams identify peak interference frequencies and correlate these with component switching frequencies, harmonics, and clock signals. Students must calculate theoretical harmonic frequencies for comparison with measured data.

Step 3 (30 minutes): Teams analyze the spatial relationships between high-EMI components and sensitive circuits, measuring trace lengths, calculating coupling coefficients, and identifying near-field/far-field interference zones using provided electromagnetic field strength measurements.

Step 4 (20 minutes): Each team examines comparative data from the other two circuit designs, identifying design patterns that correlate with higher or lower EMI signatures. Students create a matrix comparing design parameters versus EMI performance metrics.

Step 5 (25 minutes): Teams synthesize their analysis into a technical assessment report identifying the three most critical EMI pathways in their assigned design, supported by quantitative evidence from spectral and spatial analysis. They must propose specific design modifications with predicted EMI reduction percentages based on theoretical calculations.
materials_needed: Three different PCB layout diagrams with component specifications and dimensions
EMI spectral analysis datasets (CSV format, 10 MHz - 1 GHz) for each PCB design
Electromagnetic field strength measurement data at multiple test points
Scientific calculators or computer access for harmonic frequency calculations
Graph paper and colored pens for creating component interaction maps
Digital calipers or rulers for measuring trace lengths and component spacing
assessment_method: Evaluate technical reports using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of frequency correlation analysis and harmonic calculations (25 points), (2) Quality of spatial relationship analysis and coupling pathway identification (25 points), (3) Depth of comparative design analysis with quantitative evidence (25 points), (4) Technical soundness and feasibility of proposed design modifications with supporting calculations (25 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide electromagnetic coupling coefficient formulas and worked examples of harmonic frequency calculations. Create guided worksheets with partially completed component interaction maps. For advanced learners: Include additional variables such as temperature effects on EMI, substrate material properties, and advanced shielding effectiveness calculations. Challenge them to model EMI reduction using transmission line theory and Maxwell's equations.

title: Design and Build a Predictive Dashboard for Local Business Performance
description: Students will create an interactive analytical dashboard that combines multiple data sources to predict quarterly business performance for a local retail scenario. They will synthesize sales, demographic, and economic data to develop actionable business recommendations through data visualization and predictive modeling.
estimated_duration: 3.5 hours (can be split across multiple sessions)
learning_objectives: Students will construct a multi-source data pipeline by integrating sales transactions, demographic census data, and economic indicators into a unified analytical framework
Students will design predictive visualizations and automated alerts through creating an interactive dashboard that forecasts quarterly revenue trends and identifies risk factors
instructions:
**Phase 1: Data Integration (45 minutes)**
Divide students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three CSV datasets: fictional retail sales data (2 years, 10,000+ transactions), local demographic data, and economic indicators. Students must first examine data quality using Python pandas, identifying missing values, outliers, and inconsistencies. Teams create a data cleaning protocol document, then merge datasets using customer zip codes as primary keys. Each team develops a standardized schema with consistent date formats, categorical encodings, and normalized numerical scales.

**Phase 2: Analytical Framework Development (60 minutes)**
Teams design their analytical approach by defining 3-5 key performance indicators (KPIs) relevant to retail success. Using Tableau or Power BI, students create calculated fields for metrics like customer lifetime value, seasonal adjustment factors, and market penetration rates. They must establish baseline performance benchmarks from historical data and identify at least three external factors that correlate with sales performance. Teams document their analytical reasoning and create data dictionaries explaining each calculated metric.

**Phase 3: Dashboard Creation (75 minutes)**
Students build interactive dashboards featuring: time-series visualizations with trend forecasting, geographic heat maps showing performance by location, customer segmentation analysis with behavioral insights, and alert systems for performance thresholds. Dashboards must include dropdown filters, drill-down capabilities, and automated refresh schedules. Teams create user personas (store manager, regional director, marketing analyst) and customize dashboard views for each role's decision-making needs.

**Phase 4: Validation and Presentation (30 minutes)**
Teams test dashboard functionality, validate predictions against holdout data, and prepare 5-minute presentations demonstrating their solution. Each presentation must include business problem definition, data methodology, key insights discovered, and three specific actionable recommendations with projected ROI calculations.
materials_needed: Three prepared CSV datasets per team (sales transactions, demographics, economic indicators)
Tableau Desktop or Power BI licenses for each student
Python environment with pandas, numpy, matplotlib libraries installed
Computers with dual monitors (recommended for dashboard development)
Business scenario handout with company background and objectives
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data Integration Quality (25 points - completeness, accuracy, documentation), Analytical Framework (25 points - KPI relevance, statistical validity, methodology), Dashboard Design (30 points - functionality, user experience, visual clarity), Business Insights (20 points - actionable recommendations, ROI justification, presentation quality). Students submit: final dashboard file, data processing code, methodology documentation, and recorded presentation. Peer evaluation component includes teams testing each other's dashboards for usability.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-cleaned sample datasets, template dashboard layouts, and step-by-step video tutorials for basic Tableau/Power BI functions. Assign peer mentors within teams for technical support. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate machine learning algorithms for more sophisticated predictions, add real-time data streaming capabilities, or develop mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Provide access to additional datasets (weather, competitor pricing) for more complex analysis.

title: Decoding Leadership Paradoxes: Analyzing Competing Demands in Complex Organizations
description: Students will analyze real-world leadership paradoxes through case study examination, identifying and explaining how expert leaders navigate competing organizational demands. They will demonstrate understanding by categorizing paradox types and explaining the underlying tensions that create leadership dilemmas.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex leadership paradoxes by examining multi-stakeholder case studies and identifying the competing organizational demands that create leadership tensions
Students will explain the relationship between leadership paradoxes and organizational effectiveness through structured comparison of paradox resolution strategies
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Harvard Business Review case study 'Netflix: Managing Paradoxes of Innovation' and three additional paradox scenarios (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, ensuring mix of experience levels. Each team receives a different paradox category: Innovation vs. Efficiency, Autonomy vs. Control, Competition vs. Collaboration, or Short-term vs. Long-term thinking.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams read their assigned case and complete the Paradox Analysis Framework worksheet. They must identify: (a) the specific competing demands, (b) stakeholder perspectives on each side, (c) potential consequences of choosing either extreme, and (d) how the leader attempted resolution. Teams use the provided tension mapping template to visualize the paradox dynamics.

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams rotate through gallery walk stations, spending 7 minutes at each paradox display. At each station, they complete reflection prompts: 'How does this paradox relate to your assigned paradox?' and 'What patterns do you notice in resolution approaches?' Teams document insights on sticky notes.

Phase 3 (25 minutes): Return to original teams for synthesis discussion. Teams complete the Paradox Integration Matrix, plotting all four paradox types on dimensions of 'Stakeholder Impact' vs. 'Time Sensitivity.' They prepare 3-minute explanations of their matrix placement reasoning.

Phase 4 (20 minutes): Each team presents their matrix and explains one key insight about how expert leaders think differently about paradoxes compared to novice leaders. Other teams ask clarifying questions and note connections to their own analyses.
materials_needed: Netflix case study and 3 additional leadership paradox scenarios (printed)
Paradox Analysis Framework worksheets
Tension mapping templates with sticky notes
Large poster paper and markers for gallery walk displays
Paradox Integration Matrix handouts
Timer for rotation management
assessment_method: Evaluate using the Paradox Understanding Rubric (4-point scale): (1) Accuracy of paradox identification and stakeholder analysis, (2) Quality of explanation linking competing demands to organizational outcomes, (3) Sophistication of pattern recognition across different paradox types, (4) Clarity of reasoning in matrix placement and presentation. Success requires scoring 3+ on all dimensions, demonstrating ability to explain rather than merely identify paradox elements.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide paradox identification checklist and sentence starters for analysis framework. Pair with stronger analytical thinkers during gallery walk. For advanced learners: Challenge them to identify meta-paradoxes (paradoxes about managing paradoxes) and connect to leadership theory frameworks like complexity leadership or dynamic capabilities. Encourage them to facilitate discussions during rotations.

title: Deploy a Three-Tier Web Application Using AWS EC2, RDS, and S3
description: Students will apply AWS core services knowledge by deploying a complete three-tier web application architecture. They will configure EC2 instances for the web tier, set up an RDS database for the data tier, and use S3 for static content storage, demonstrating real-world cloud application deployment skills.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional three-tier web application by configuring EC2 instances, RDS databases, and S3 buckets with proper security groups
Students will apply AWS networking and security best practices through implementing VPC subnets, security groups, and IAM roles for their application stack
instructions:
**Setup Phase (10 minutes):** Provide each student with AWS Learner Lab access credentials and a pre-written simple PHP web application code (blog application with user registration). Students log into AWS Management Console and verify their lab environment has $100 credit limit.

**Tier 1 - Data Layer (25 minutes):** Students create an RDS MySQL database instance: navigate to RDS service, select 'Create Database', choose MySQL 8.0, select 'Free Tier' template, name database 'webapp-db', set master username 'admin' with password 'WebApp123!'. Configure VPC security group to allow inbound traffic on port 3306 from EC2 security group (to be created). Wait for database status to show 'Available'.

**Tier 2 - Application Layer (30 minutes):** Students launch EC2 instance: select Amazon Linux 2 AMI, t2.micro instance type, configure in default VPC with auto-assign public IP enabled. Create new security group 'web-sg' allowing HTTP (port 80), HTTPS (port 443), and SSH (port 22) from anywhere. Launch instance with existing key pair or create new one. SSH into instance, install Apache and PHP using 'sudo yum install -y httpd php php-mysql', start Apache service, and upload the provided PHP application code to /var/www/html/.

**Tier 3 - Presentation Layer (20 minutes):** Students create S3 bucket for static assets: navigate to S3, create bucket with unique name 'webapp-static-[studentID]', upload provided CSS and image files, configure bucket policy for public read access to static files. Update PHP application configuration file with RDS endpoint and S3 bucket URL.

**Testing Phase (15 minutes):** Students access their web application via EC2 public IP address, test user registration functionality to verify database connectivity, and confirm images load from S3 bucket. Document the complete application URL and take screenshots of working application.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab accounts with $100 credit for each student
Pre-written PHP blog application with database schema (provided as downloadable zip file)
Static web assets (CSS files, placeholder images) for S3 upload
Step-by-step worksheet with RDS endpoint and S3 URL recording sections
SSH key pair files or instructions for generating new ones
assessment_method: Students submit a deployment report including: (1) Screenshots of running web application showing successful user registration and image loading (40 points), (2) AWS architecture diagram showing all three tiers with security groups documented (30 points), (3) Completed worksheet with RDS endpoint, S3 bucket URL, and EC2 public IP recorded (20 points), (4) Reflection paragraph describing one challenge faced and how they resolved it (10 points). Total: 100 points. Success criteria: Application must be publicly accessible and demonstrate database connectivity.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide pre-configured security group templates and detailed screenshots of each AWS console step. Assign peer mentors who completed the task successfully. Create a troubleshooting checklist for common issues (security group misconfigurations, database connection errors). **For advanced learners:** Challenge them to implement additional features: configure Application Load Balancer for high availability, set up CloudWatch monitoring with custom alarms, or implement auto-scaling groups. Provide bonus points for implementing HTTPS with SSL certificates or database read replicas.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Comparing Threat vs. Opportunity Management Approaches
description: Students will analyze real project scenarios to differentiate between risk response strategies for threats versus opportunities, examining the effectiveness and appropriateness of each strategy type. They will deconstruct complex risk situations to identify optimal response approaches based on project constraints and stakeholder impact.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze project risk scenarios by categorizing threats and opportunities and evaluating the appropriateness of specific response strategies (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept vs. exploit, enhance, share, accept)
Students will examine the relationship between risk response strategies and project success factors through systematic comparison of strategy outcomes and resource allocation decisions
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (5 minutes). Distribute the Risk Scenario Analysis Worksheet containing 8 detailed project scenarios - 4 focusing on threats and 4 on opportunities. Each scenario includes project context, stakeholder information, budget constraints, and timeline pressures.

Phase 1 (20 minutes): Teams analyze each scenario individually, identifying whether each situation represents a threat or opportunity, then selecting the most appropriate response strategy from the four options available for each type. Students must document their reasoning using the provided decision matrix that weighs factors like cost, timeline impact, stakeholder acceptance, and technical feasibility.

Phase 2 (15 minutes): Teams compare their threat response strategies against their opportunity response strategies, creating a visual comparison chart that highlights key differences in approach, resource allocation, and stakeholder communication requirements. They must identify at least three fundamental differences between how threats and opportunities should be managed.

Phase 3 (10 minutes): Each team presents one threat scenario and one opportunity scenario to the class, explaining their chosen response strategy and justifying why alternative strategies were rejected. During presentations, non-presenting teams use evaluation forms to assess whether the presented strategies align with PMI best practices.

Conclude with a 5-minute debrief where teams identify common patterns in effective risk response selection and discuss how organizational risk tolerance might influence strategy choices. Teams submit their completed worksheets and comparison charts for individual assessment.
materials_needed: Risk Scenario Analysis Worksheet (8 scenarios with project details)
Decision Matrix Template (Excel or printed format)
Visual Comparison Chart Template
Peer Evaluation Forms
PMI Risk Management Process Reference Guide
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct identification of threats vs. opportunities (25%), (2) Appropriate strategy selection with sound justification (35%), (3) Quality of comparative analysis between threat and opportunity approaches (25%), (4) Clarity and accuracy of presentation and peer feedback (15%). Success requires scoring 3/4 on all criteria, demonstrating clear understanding of when and why to apply specific risk response strategies.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a decision tree flowchart that guides strategy selection based on risk probability and impact levels. Offer additional examples of each response strategy type with clear outcomes. For advanced learners, introduce secondary risk considerations and ask them to develop contingency response plans for their primary strategies. Encourage analysis of how response strategies might change based on different organizational maturity levels.

title: Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation Through Real-World Case Study Analysis
description: Students analyze three pre-selected data scenarios to distinguish between correlation and causation, explaining the underlying mechanisms and identifying potential confounding variables. They will demonstrate understanding by categorizing relationships and justifying their reasoning using statistical evidence.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between correlation and causation by analyzing real-world datasets and identifying the presence or absence of causal mechanisms
Students will explain the role of confounding variables through structured case study examination and peer discussion
instructions:
Begin by dividing students into groups of 3-4. Distribute three case study packets: (1) Ice cream sales vs. drowning deaths, (2) Education level vs. income, and (3) Social media usage vs. depression scores. Each packet contains a scatter plot, correlation coefficient, and brief context description. 

Phase 1 (15 minutes): Groups examine Case Study 1 individually, using the provided analysis framework with questions: What is the correlation strength? What causal relationship might people assume? What alternative explanations exist? Students record responses on the structured worksheet.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Rotate through Cases 2 and 3 using the same framework. For each case, students must: identify the correlation coefficient interpretation, propose at least two possible causal explanations, list three potential confounding variables, and classify the relationship as 'likely causal,' 'spurious correlation,' or 'unclear/needs more data.'

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Groups create a summary chart comparing all three cases, highlighting key differences in their reasoning. They must justify why some correlations suggest causation while others don't.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Conduct gallery walk where groups post their charts and examine others' reasoning. Conclude with whole-class discussion identifying common patterns and misconceptions. Instructor facilitates by asking: 'What additional data would strengthen causal claims?' and 'Which confounding variables were most commonly overlooked?'
materials_needed: Three printed case study packets with scatter plots and correlation data
Structured analysis worksheets with guiding questions
Large poster paper for summary charts
Colored markers or pens
Timer for activity phases
assessment_method: Evaluate completed worksheets using 4-point rubric: (4) Correctly identifies correlation vs causation in all cases with comprehensive confounding variable analysis, (3) Correctly identifies most relationships with adequate explanations, (2) Shows partial understanding with some misconceptions, (1) Demonstrates minimal grasp of concepts. Additionally, assess oral contributions during gallery walk for depth of reasoning.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide additional prompting questions like 'What else might be happening during summer months?' for the ice cream case. Offer a word bank of potential confounding variables. For advanced learners, introduce Bradford Hill criteria for causation or have them research additional confounding variables using laptops. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during group work.

title: Optimization in Urban Planning: Applying Calculus to Design Efficient City Transit Systems
description: Students will apply advanced calculus concepts including derivatives, optimization, and constraint analysis to solve a real-world urban planning problem. They will determine optimal bus route spacing and frequency to minimize citizen travel time while operating within budget constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will apply derivative techniques and optimization methods to minimize multi-variable cost functions in a realistic urban transit scenario
Students will implement Lagrange multiplier methods to solve constrained optimization problems through systematic mathematical modeling
instructions:
Begin by distributing the urban planning scenario packet containing a simplified city grid (15x10 blocks), population density data, and budget constraints ($2.5M annual operating budget, $50K per bus route setup, $180K annual cost per bus). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a different neighborhood district.

Step 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze their assigned district's population data and identify key transit demand points (schools, shopping centers, residential clusters). Students must plot these on their grid and calculate population-weighted distances.

Step 2 (20 minutes): Introduce the mathematical model. Total citizen travel time T = Σ(population_i × distance_to_nearest_stop_i) + Σ(waiting_time_j × users_per_stop_j). Students set up this function using their district data, incorporating the constraint that total annual cost ≤ $2.5M.

Step 3 (25 minutes): Teams apply calculus optimization techniques. They must take partial derivatives with respect to number of routes (n) and bus frequency (f), then use Lagrange multipliers to handle the budget constraint. Students solve the system: ∇T = λ∇g where g represents the budget constraint.

Step 4 (15 minutes): Teams calculate optimal solutions and verify results by testing edge cases (±10% variations in their optimal values). They must show that their solution produces lower total travel time than alternative configurations.

Step 5 (20 minutes): Each team presents their optimal transit design to the class, defending their mathematical approach and demonstrating how their solution balances efficiency with budget constraints. Other teams peer-review calculations and challenge assumptions.
materials_needed: Urban planning scenario packets with city grids and population data
Graphing calculators or computer algebra system (Mathematica/Maple)
Large format graph paper (11x17 inches)
Colored markers for route mapping
Digital presentation tools (projector, laptops)
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric: (1) Correct setup of optimization problem with appropriate constraints (25%), (2) Accurate application of calculus techniques including partial derivatives and Lagrange multipliers (30%), (3) Valid mathematical solution with proper verification steps (25%), (4) Clear presentation defending methodology and results (20%). Students must submit written calculations and deliver 5-minute team presentations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide template worksheets with partially completed derivative setups and constraint equations. Offer one-on-one coaching during Step 2 to ensure proper function setup. For advanced learners: Add complexity by including multiple vehicle types (buses vs. light rail) with different cost structures, or incorporate time-varying demand patterns requiring dynamic optimization approaches.

title: Evaluating Code Quality: Simple Calculator Function Assessment
description: Students will critically assess three different implementations of a basic calculator function by analyzing code quality, efficiency, and best practices. They will rank the solutions and justify their evaluations using specific programming criteria.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate three different code implementations by comparing their readability, efficiency, and adherence to coding standards
Students will critique programming solutions through systematic analysis using a structured evaluation framework
instructions: 1. SETUP (5 minutes): Distribute the handout containing three different implementations of a simple calculator function that performs addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Each implementation has different strengths and weaknesses (Implementation A: clean but inefficient, Implementation B: efficient but poorly documented, Implementation C: well-balanced). 2. INDIVIDUAL ANALYSIS (15 minutes): Students examine each implementation using the provided evaluation checklist covering: code readability (variable names, formatting), functionality (does it work correctly), error handling (division by zero, invalid inputs), efficiency (unnecessary operations), and documentation (comments, clarity). Students take notes on strengths and weaknesses for each version. 3. RANKING EXERCISE (10 minutes): Students rank the three implementations from best to worst, writing a 2-3 sentence justification for each ranking decision. They must reference specific code elements and explain their reasoning using programming terminology. 4. PEER DISCUSSION (8 minutes): In pairs, students compare their rankings and discuss differences in their evaluations. They must defend their choices using evidence from the code. 5. CLASS DEBRIEF (7 minutes): Instructor facilitates whole-class discussion where students share their top-ranked choice and one key criterion that influenced their decision. Record different perspectives on the board to show how evaluation criteria can vary based on context and priorities.
materials_needed: Printed handout with three calculator function implementations
Code evaluation checklist/rubric
Pen/pencil for note-taking
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate students based on: (1) Completion of evaluation checklist with specific evidence cited (40%), (2) Quality of ranking justifications showing clear reasoning and use of programming terminology (40%), (3) Active participation in peer discussions and ability to defend choices with code-based evidence (20%). Look for students identifying concrete issues like variable naming, logical errors, or missing error handling.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide sentence starters for justifications ('This implementation is better because...') and highlight specific lines of code to examine first. For advanced learners: Ask them to suggest specific improvements for the lowest-ranked implementation or consider additional evaluation criteria like maintainability or scalability.

title: Project Management Knowledge Framework Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the complete PMBOK Guide's 49 project management processes organized by 10 knowledge areas and 5 process groups. This intensive recall activity builds foundational knowledge essential for advanced project management practice and PMP certification preparation.
learning_objectives: Students will recall all 49 PMBOK project management processes by correctly matching each process to its corresponding knowledge area and process group within 90 seconds
Students will identify the complete list of 10 knowledge areas and 5 process groups through rapid-fire verbal recitation with 100% accuracy
instructions: Begin by distributing the PMBOK Process Reference Matrix to each student for 15-minute intensive study period - no talking allowed. Students should use active memorization techniques like chunking processes by knowledge area first, then by process group. After study time, collect all materials. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students. Round 1 (10 minutes): Display knowledge area names one at a time on screen for 30 seconds each. Teams write down all processes they recall for that knowledge area. Award 2 points per correct process, deduct 1 point for incorrect processes. Round 2 (10 minutes): Display process group names (Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring & Controlling, Closing). Teams have 2 minutes per process group to list all processes belonging to that group. Same scoring system applies. Round 3 (15 minutes): Lightning round - instructor calls out random process names, teams must immediately shout the correct knowledge area AND process group. First correct team gets 3 points. Continue until all 49 processes are covered. Round 4 (10 minutes): Each team selects one member to verbally recite all 10 knowledge areas in correct PMBOK order, then all 5 process groups in chronological order. Perfect recitation earns 10 bonus points. Conclude with immediate score tabulation and winner announcement. Provide correct answer sheet for self-checking missed items.
materials_needed: PMBOK Guide 49 Process Reference Matrix (one per student)
Projection screen/smartboard for displaying categories
Stopwatch/timer
Scoresheets for each team
Complete answer key with all processes organized by knowledge area and process group
assessment_method: Team scoring based on accuracy: 90-100% = Mastery Level, 80-89% = Proficient, 70-79% = Developing, Below 70% = Needs Improvement. Individual assessment through post-activity quiz requiring students to correctly place 20 randomly selected processes into proper knowledge area and process group matrix within 10 minutes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide acronym memory devices (e.g., 'I Properly Execute Many Changes' for process groups) and allow color-coded reference cards during practice rounds. For advanced learners: Add bonus challenges requiring recall of key inputs/outputs for each process or identification of process interdependencies across knowledge areas.

title: Leadership Style Impact Analysis: Decoding Situational Leadership Effectiveness Through Case Study Comparison
description: Students will analyze complex organizational scenarios to identify how different leadership styles (directive, coaching, supporting, delegating) impact team performance and employee engagement. Through structured case study comparison, they will demonstrate understanding of situational leadership theory by explaining why specific approaches succeed or fail in given contexts.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between the four situational leadership styles by analyzing their application in complex organizational scenarios and explaining the rationale behind each approach
Students will interpret the relationship between leadership style effectiveness and situational variables through systematic case study comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions: Begin by providing students with four detailed case studies (15 minutes reading time), each featuring the same crisis scenario—a product launch delay—but with leaders employing different situational leadership styles. Case A shows directive leadership with explicit commands and close supervision. Case B demonstrates coaching leadership with explanation and guidance. Case C illustrates supporting leadership with collaborative problem-solving. Case D presents delegating leadership with autonomy and minimal oversight. Each case includes identical team composition: 2 experienced developers, 2 new hires, 1 project manager. Divide students into groups of 4, assigning each member one case study (20 minutes individual analysis). Students complete a structured analysis worksheet identifying: leadership behaviors observed, decision-making processes, communication patterns, team responses, and outcome indicators. During individual work, circulate to ensure students are extracting specific evidence rather than making general observations. Next, groups reconvene to share findings using a comparison matrix (25 minutes). Each student presents their case while others record comparative data on leadership approaches, team reactions, and effectiveness indicators. Groups must reach consensus on which approach was most effective and justify their reasoning with specific evidence from the cases. Finally, conduct whole-class discussion (15 minutes) where each group presents their conclusion and supporting rationale. Facilitate analysis of why certain styles worked better, connecting student observations to situational leadership theory principles without explicitly teaching the theory—students should demonstrate understanding through their comparative analysis.
materials_needed: Four detailed case studies (2-3 pages each) featuring identical scenarios with different leadership approaches
Structured analysis worksheets with specific observation categories
Comparison matrix templates for group work
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accuracy of leadership style identification with specific behavioral evidence (25%), (2) Quality of comparative analysis showing understanding of situational factors (25%), (3) Logical reasoning connecting leadership approach to outcomes with supporting details (25%), (4) Demonstration of understanding through group discussion contributions and final justification (25%). Success requires students to cite specific evidence, make accurate comparisons, and explain causational relationships between leadership style and effectiveness.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: provide guiding questions on worksheets such as 'What specific words or actions show how this leader makes decisions?' and 'How did team members respond differently in each scenario?' For advanced learners: add complexity by including discussion of cultural factors, team development stages, or asking them to predict how each leadership style would perform if the scenario variables changed (different team experience levels, different crisis types).

title: Risk Response Strategy Matrix Analysis for Complex IT Project Scenarios
description: Students will analyze multi-layered project risk scenarios to determine optimal risk response strategies by examining risk probability, impact, and interdependencies. They will deconstruct complex risk situations and evaluate the effectiveness of different response combinations across project constraints.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk scenarios by decomposing multiple risk factors and their cascading effects on project objectives
Students will evaluate competing risk response strategies through systematic comparison of costs, benefits, and implementation feasibility
instructions:
Begin by distributing the 'CloudTech Implementation Project' case study packet to teams of 3-4 students (10 minutes setup). Each team receives identical scenario materials including project charter, stakeholder matrix, and initial risk register with 12 identified risks. Students first individually read and annotate the case study, highlighting risk interconnections (15 minutes). 

Next, teams collaborate to create a Risk Interdependency Map using provided templates, plotting how risks influence each other using arrows and impact ratings (20 minutes). Teams then analyze each risk using the provided Decision Matrix Template, scoring risks on probability (1-5), impact on scope/time/cost/quality (1-5 each), and detectability (1-5). 

For the core analysis phase, teams evaluate three pre-defined risk response strategy combinations: 'Aggressive Mitigation,' 'Balanced Portfolio,' and 'Accept and Monitor.' Using the Strategy Evaluation Worksheet, teams analyze each approach by calculating total response costs, residual risk scores, and implementation complexity ratings (25 minutes).

Teams document their analysis in a structured report template covering: risk prioritization rationale, strategy comparison matrix, recommended approach with justification, and implementation timeline. Each team presents their 5-minute analysis to another team, defending their chosen strategy and responding to challenge questions (20 minutes peer review).

Conclude with instructor-led debrief where teams share key insights about risk interdependencies and strategy trade-offs, connecting findings to PMI risk management principles (15 minutes).
materials_needed: CloudTech Implementation Project case study packet (4 pages per student)
Risk Interdependency Map template sheets (11x17 paper)
Decision Matrix Template worksheets
Strategy Evaluation Worksheet (Excel or printed)
Colored pens/markers for mapping
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Risk interdependency identification completeness and accuracy, (2) Strategy analysis depth using quantitative and qualitative factors, (3) Justification quality with PMI framework alignment, (4) Professional presentation during peer review. Collect team analysis reports and individual reflection sheets rating contribution to team analysis process.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide risk analysis checklist with guiding questions and example interdependency relationships from different project domain. Pair weaker analytical thinkers with stronger team members for initial case study review. For advanced learners: Add constraint requiring consideration of organizational risk appetite and stakeholder risk tolerance variations, or introduce dynamic risk scenarios where probability/impact changes mid-project.

title: Multi-Channel Attribution Model Analysis and Business Recommendation
description: Students will critically evaluate the effectiveness of different attribution models in Google Analytics using real e-commerce data to determine optimal customer journey tracking. They will analyze first-click, last-click, linear, time-decay, and data-driven attribution models to make evidence-based recommendations for marketing budget allocation.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the strengths and limitations of five attribution models by analyzing conversion path data and revenue attribution differences across paid search, social media, and email channels
Students will critique current attribution strategies through comparative analysis and defend alternative approaches using statistical evidence from Google Analytics reports
instructions: Begin by providing each team of 3-4 students with access to a Google Analytics demo account containing 6 months of e-commerce data. Students first navigate to Conversions > Multi-Channel Funnels > Model Comparison Tool and configure it to compare all five attribution models (first interaction, last interaction, linear, time decay, data-driven) across three key channels: paid search, email, and social network. They spend 20 minutes extracting data on conversion values, conversion counts, and conversion rate differences between models. Next, students analyze the Top Conversion Paths report to identify the most common customer journey sequences, noting path length and time lag patterns. In pairs within their teams, students then evaluate which attribution model most accurately reflects their assigned business scenario (provided case studies include B2B SaaS, fashion e-commerce, and subscription service). Teams spend 45 minutes creating a comprehensive evaluation matrix comparing each model's treatment of assisted conversions, direct traffic, and cross-device behavior. Students must identify at least three significant discrepancies between models and explain the business implications. Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation defending their recommended attribution model choice, including specific evidence from the data analysis, projected impact on marketing spend allocation, and potential limitations of their recommendation. Each presentation must address how their choice affects campaign optimization decisions and budget distribution across the three analyzed channels.
materials_needed: Google Analytics Demo Account access (Merchandise Store)
Attribution Model Evaluation Template (provided spreadsheet)
Business scenario case study handouts (3 different industries)
Laptops/computers with internet access
Presentation software (Google Slides or PowerPoint)
assessment_method: Rubric scoring: Data extraction accuracy (25%), critical analysis quality of model differences (30%), evidence-based reasoning in recommendations (25%), presentation clarity and defense of position (20%). Teams must demonstrate understanding by answering challenge questions about their recommendation's impact on marketing ROI and identifying two potential negative consequences of their chosen approach.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided worksheet with specific GA navigation steps and pre-populated data tables to fill. For advanced learners: Add custom attribution modeling analysis using Google Analytics Intelligence API or challenge them to incorporate external data sources like advertising cost data to calculate true ROAS under different attribution scenarios.

title: Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real Customer Purchase Data
description: Students will analyze actual e-commerce customer purchase data to understand the characteristics and implications of different statistical distributions. They will interpret histograms, calculate distribution parameters, and explain how distribution shapes inform business decisions.
learning_objectives: Students will interpret the shape, central tendency, and spread of normal, skewed, and bimodal distributions by analyzing customer purchase amount data
Students will explain the business implications of different distribution characteristics through written justifications connecting statistical patterns to marketing strategies
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Provide each student with the prepared dataset containing 1,000 customer purchase records with columns: customer_id, purchase_amount, product_category, and purchase_date. Distribute the analysis worksheet and ensure students can access Python/R or Excel.

**Phase 1 - Data Exploration (15 minutes):** Students create histograms for purchase_amount data across three product categories (electronics, clothing, books). They calculate mean, median, mode, and standard deviation for each category using provided formulas or built-in functions.

**Phase 2 - Distribution Analysis (20 minutes):** Students identify distribution types (normal, right-skewed, left-skewed, bimodal) for each category by examining histogram shapes. They complete a comparison table noting: peak location, tail direction, mean vs. median relationship, and outlier presence. Students use the provided distribution identification flowchart as reference.

**Phase 3 - Business Interpretation (15 minutes):** Students write 2-3 sentence explanations for each distribution, addressing: What does this shape tell us about customer behavior? How might this inform pricing strategies? What marketing approaches would be most effective? They reference specific statistical measures to support their interpretations.

**Wrap-up (5 minutes):** Students share one key insight about how distribution shape impacts business decisions. Instructor facilitates brief discussion connecting statistical understanding to data-driven decision making.
materials_needed: Curated e-commerce dataset (CSV file with 1,000 records)
Analysis worksheet with calculation templates
Distribution identification flowchart reference sheet
Computer with Excel, Python, or R access
Graphing capability (software or graphing calculator)
assessment_method: Evaluate completed analysis worksheet using rubric: (1) Correct distribution identification for all three categories (30 points), (2) Accurate calculation of statistical measures within 5% margin (25 points), (3) Clear business interpretations that logically connect statistical patterns to practical implications (35 points), (4) Proper histogram construction with labeled axes and appropriate bin sizes (10 points). Minimum passing score: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-calculated statistical measures and focus on interpretation tasks. Offer sentence starters like 'This right-skewed distribution suggests that most customers...' For advanced learners: Include additional analysis of seasonal trends, correlation between categories, or confidence interval calculations. Encourage exploration of kurtosis and its business implications.

title: Optimizing Real Estate Investment Returns Using Derivative Analysis
description: Students apply calculus optimization techniques to analyze a realistic real estate investment scenario, determining optimal property purchase timing and rental pricing strategies. They will use derivative analysis to maximize profit functions while considering market constraints and economic variables.
learning_objectives: Students will apply first and second derivative tests to determine maximum profit points in multi-variable real estate investment functions
Students will implement constraint optimization using Lagrange multipliers to solve bounded real estate market problems with budget limitations
instructions: Begin by distributing the Real Estate Investment Portfolio handout containing three property scenarios with different market conditions (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students, assigning roles: Lead Analyst, Market Researcher, Financial Calculator, and Presenter. Each team receives a specific city market dataset with variables including property appreciation rates (2-8% annually), rental demand functions, maintenance costs, and interest rates. Students first establish profit functions P(x,t) where x represents purchase price and t represents time to hold before selling. They must incorporate rental income R(t) = -0.2t² + 15t + 800, maintenance costs M(t) = 50t + 200, and appreciation A(t) = 0.03t² + 0.05t. Teams spend 25 minutes deriving the complete profit function, then apply first derivative tests to find critical points. Using graphing calculators or Desmos, they plot functions and verify maximum points using second derivative tests (20 minutes). Next, introduce budget constraints: maximum investment of $400,000 and minimum expected ROI of 12%. Students apply Lagrange multiplier method to optimize within these constraints (30 minutes). Teams calculate optimal purchase timing, holding period, and expected returns, creating a one-page investment recommendation. Final 15 minutes involve team presentations of solutions, comparing strategies across different market scenarios and justifying mathematical reasoning behind recommendations.
materials_needed: Real Estate Investment Portfolio handouts with market data for 6 different cities
Graphing calculators (TI-84 or equivalent) or laptops with Desmos access
Constraint optimization formula reference sheets
Financial calculator or spreadsheet software access
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric: (1) Correct derivation of profit function incorporating all variables (25%), (2) Accurate application of derivative tests with proper mathematical notation (25%), (3) Correct implementation of Lagrange multipliers for constrained optimization (25%), (4) Clear presentation of investment strategy with mathematical justification (25%). Students must show all calculus work and achieve minimum 75% accuracy in mathematical computations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-completed profit function templates and derivative formula cards. Offer checkpoint consultations after each major step. For advanced learners, introduce additional variables like tax implications, inflation rates, or stochastic market volatility models requiring partial differential equations. Consider adding risk analysis using standard deviation calculations.

title: Analyzing Electromagnetic Interference in Multi-Frequency Circuit Systems
description: Students will analyze complex electromagnetic interference patterns in circuits containing multiple frequency sources by decomposing signal data and identifying causal relationships. They will evaluate how different circuit components contribute to interference and predict system behavior under varying conditions.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze electromagnetic interference patterns by decomposing multi-frequency signal data and identifying the contributions of individual circuit components
Students will evaluate the causal relationships between circuit parameters and interference magnitude through systematic comparison of experimental datasets
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4. Provide each team with three datasets containing voltage measurements from identical RLC circuits operating at different frequencies (10 kHz, 50 kHz, 100 kHz) with known interference sources. Students first spend 20 minutes examining the raw data using oscilloscope software to identify anomalous patterns and frequency components. Next, teams use FFT analysis tools to decompose each signal into constituent frequencies, creating frequency domain plots for all three datasets. Students then spend 30 minutes comparing the decomposed signals, identifying which frequency components appear consistently across datasets versus those unique to specific configurations. Teams must calculate the interference amplitude at each frequency and correlate these values with the known circuit parameters (resistance values, capacitor ESR, inductor core material). Following analysis, students create a comprehensive comparison matrix showing interference magnitude versus frequency and circuit parameters. Each team then predicts interference patterns for two hypothetical scenarios: adding a 75 kHz source and replacing ceramic capacitors with tantalum ones. Students must justify their predictions using evidence from their analysis. Teams present their findings in 10-minute presentations, explaining their analytical process, key correlations discovered, and prediction methodology. Conclude with peer evaluation where teams critique each other's analytical approaches and prediction validity.
materials_needed: Three pre-recorded oscilloscope datasets (CSV format) showing RLC circuit interference at 10kHz, 50kHz, 100kHz
Circuit schematics with component specifications for each dataset
MATLAB or Python with SciPy for FFT analysis
Computers with oscilloscope simulation software (LTSpice or equivalent)
Spreadsheet software for creating comparison matrices
Projection equipment for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: FFT analysis accuracy and interpretation (25 points), identification of interference patterns and correlations (25 points), quality of comparative analysis between datasets (20 points), validity and justification of predictions (20 points), presentation clarity and peer interaction (10 points). Success requires correctly identifying at least 80% of significant interference frequencies, establishing valid correlations between circuit parameters and interference magnitude, and making predictions consistent with electromagnetic theory.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-made FFT plots and focus on pattern recognition rather than signal processing. Offer guided questions about which frequencies show highest interference and why. For advanced learners, introduce additional complexity by having them consider parasitic effects, propose circuit modifications to minimize interference, or analyze the phase relationships between interfering signals. Provide reference materials on electromagnetic compatibility principles for deeper theoretical connections.

title: Evaluating Password Validation Functions: Security vs. Usability Trade-offs
description: Students will critically assess three different password validation code implementations by analyzing their security effectiveness, user experience impact, and maintainability. They will rank the implementations and justify their evaluation using specific criteria and real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate password validation implementations by analyzing security strength, usability factors, and code quality metrics
Students will critique software design decisions through structured comparison and evidence-based reasoning
instructions:
Begin by providing students with three pre-written password validation functions (15 minutes setup): Function A (basic length check only), Function B (comprehensive rules with strict requirements), and Function C (moderate rules with user feedback). Divide students into groups of 3-4 and assign each group a evaluation worksheet with criteria matrix including Security Level (0-10), User Experience (0-10), Code Maintainability (0-10), and Performance Impact (0-10). 

Students spend 20 minutes testing each function with a provided set of 15 sample passwords ranging from weak ('123') to complex ('MyP@ssw0rd2024!'). They document which passwords pass/fail for each function and note any error messages. Next, students spend 15 minutes reviewing the source code for each function, identifying potential security vulnerabilities, code complexity, and maintenance issues. 

In the evaluation phase (25 minutes), groups complete their criteria matrix, scoring each function and providing written justification for scores. They must consider real-world scenarios like user frustration, security breaches, and development costs. Each group then ranks the three functions from best to worst overall implementation. 

Conclude with 15-minute group presentations where each team presents their ranking with supporting evidence, followed by class discussion comparing different evaluation approaches and highlighting trade-off decisions in software development.
materials_needed: Three pre-written password validation functions in Python or JavaScript
Set of 15 test passwords (weak to strong examples)
Evaluation criteria matrix worksheet
Computers with code editor or online coding environment
Timer for activity segments
assessment_method: Grade using rubric with four components: Accurate testing results (25%), thorough code analysis identifying specific issues (25%), justified scoring with clear reasoning (30%), and quality of final ranking with supporting evidence (20%). Students must demonstrate evaluation skills by providing specific examples and trade-off reasoning rather than general statements.
scaffolding_notes: Support struggling students by providing guiding questions for each evaluation criteria and examples of what to look for in code analysis. For advanced learners, add additional criteria like accessibility compliance, internationalization support, or integration complexity. Consider pairing stronger students with those needing support during the analysis phase.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Components and Dependencies Memorization Challenge
description: Students will memorize and accurately recall the specific components, formulas, and dependency relationships within Critical Path Method analysis. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge of CPM terminology, calculation elements, and network diagram symbols that are essential for advanced project scheduling.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall the four time calculations (ES, EF, LS, LF) and their specific formulas used in Critical Path Method analysis by completing timed recall exercises
Students will identify and name the six types of task dependencies (FS, SS, FF, SF and their lag/lead variations) through visual symbol recognition drills
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Component Reference Sheet containing 24 critical elements: 4 time calculations with formulas, 6 dependency types with symbols, 8 network diagram components, and 6 float calculation terms. Students have 15 minutes to study this material silently. Remove reference sheets and conduct Round 1: Project instructor displays 12 time calculation scenarios on slides (3 minutes per slide). Students write the correct formula and abbreviation for each scenario (ES=Early Start, EF=Early Finish, etc.). Round 2: Show 15 network diagram symbols for 30 seconds each. Students must write the dependency type and any lag/lead indicators. Round 3: Present 18 definition prompts verbally (e.g., 'The amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project end date'). Students write the exact CPM term (Total Float, Free Float, etc.). After each round, students self-check using answer keys. Conduct immediate review of missed items. Final challenge: Students must recreate the complete CPM formula sheet from memory within 10 minutes, including all abbreviations, formulas, and dependency symbols. Pair students to verify accuracy using the original reference sheet.
materials_needed: CPM Component Reference Sheet (24 elements with definitions and formulas)
Digital slides with time calculation scenarios and network symbols
Answer keys for each round
Blank formula recreation sheets
Timer/stopwatch
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the final formula sheet recreation (22/24 elements correct) and score 80% or higher on each of the three timed rounds. Assessment includes: correct spelling of all CPM terminology, accurate mathematical formulas with proper variables, and precise drawing of dependency symbols with directional arrows.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide color-coded reference sheets grouping related concepts, allow 20-minute initial study time, and permit one 'hint card' during final recreation. For advanced learners: Add complex dependency combinations (SS+3, FF-2), include resource leveling terms, and challenge them to create their own CPM scenario problems for peer testing.

title: Deconstructing Crisis Leadership Through Multi-Perspective Case Analysis
description: Students analyze the 2010 Chilean mine rescue leadership decisions through the lenses of three different leadership theories, comparing how each framework explains the same critical decisions. They create detailed theory-to-action mappings that demonstrate deep understanding of how leadership models manifest in high-stakes scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, situational, and adaptive leadership approaches by mapping specific leader behaviors from the Chilean mine rescue to corresponding theoretical frameworks

Students will interpret the effectiveness of different leadership decisions through systematic comparison of how three leadership theories would predict and evaluate the same crisis management choices
instructions: Begin by providing students with a detailed 4-page case study of the 2010 Chilean mine rescue, focusing on decisions made by Mining Minister Laurence Golborne, rescue coordinator André Sougarret, and shift supervisor Luis Urzúa (15 minutes reading time). Divide class into groups of 3, assigning each member one leadership theory: transformational leadership (Bass & Riggio), situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard), and adaptive leadership (Heifetz). Each student spends 20 minutes individually identifying 5 specific leadership decisions from the case and analyzing them through their assigned theoretical lens using a provided analysis template with columns for: decision made, theoretical explanation, predicted outcomes, and theory-specific evaluation criteria. Students then reconvene in their groups for 30 minutes to compare their analyses of the same 5 decisions, noting where theories align, conflict, or offer complementary insights. Each group creates a visual comparison matrix showing how each theory interprets the same leadership moments differently. Groups spend 15 minutes preparing a 5-minute presentation highlighting their most significant theoretical divergence and convergence. During presentations (25 minutes total), other groups use a peer evaluation form to assess the accuracy of theoretical applications. Conclude with a 10-minute instructor-led discussion connecting patterns across all group findings to broader leadership understanding principles.
materials_needed: 4-page Chilean mine rescue case study with timeline of leadership decisions
Leadership theory reference sheets for transformational, situational, and adaptive leadership
Decision analysis template with pre-formatted columns
Visual comparison matrix template (digital or poster-sized paper)
Peer evaluation rubric for theoretical accuracy
Presentation timer
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 20-point rubric: theoretical accuracy (5 points per theory application), quality of comparative analysis between theories (5 points), and identification of leadership decision impacts (5 points). Students must correctly apply at least 4 of 5 leadership theory concepts to specific case decisions, demonstrate clear understanding of theoretical differences through comparative statements, and provide evidence-based evaluations of leadership effectiveness using theory-specific criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide pre-highlighted case study sections and sentence starters for theoretical connections ('This decision reflects transformational leadership because...'). For advanced learners, add a fourth leadership theory (servant leadership) and require them to identify gaps where no theory adequately explains observed behaviors, proposing theoretical extensions or combinations.

title: Deploy and Configure a Static Website Using Amazon S3 with Custom Domain
description: Students will create and deploy a complete static website using Amazon S3 bucket hosting, configure proper permissions, and connect a custom domain name. This hands-on activity demonstrates core AWS storage and web hosting concepts through practical implementation.
learning_objectives: Students will apply S3 bucket configuration principles by creating a static website hosting environment with proper permissions and policies
Students will implement DNS routing through Route 53 by connecting a custom domain to their S3-hosted website
instructions: **Phase 1: Setup (15 minutes)** - Distribute AWS account credentials and ensure students can access AWS Management Console. Have students create a project folder with provided HTML/CSS template files (index.html, error.html, styles.css). **Phase 2: S3 Bucket Creation (20 minutes)** - Guide students to create an S3 bucket with their name-website format (e.g., john-portfolio-website). Emphasize bucket naming requirements: globally unique, lowercase, no spaces. Students enable static website hosting in bucket properties, set index.html as index document and error.html as error document. **Phase 3: Content Upload and Permissions (25 minutes)** - Students upload their HTML/CSS files to the bucket root. Configure bucket policy for public read access using provided JSON template. Students must modify the bucket name in the policy JSON to match their bucket. Test initial website URL provided by S3. **Phase 4: Domain Configuration (30 minutes)** - In Route 53, students register a subdomain using the provided shared domain (e.g., john.classproject.com). Create an A record alias pointing to their S3 website endpoint. Wait for DNS propagation (2-5 minutes) and test custom domain access. **Phase 5: Verification and Documentation (10 minutes)** - Students complete verification checklist: website loads via S3 URL, custom domain works, all pages display correctly, CSS styling applied. Submit screenshot showing website loaded via custom domain and AWS console showing bucket configuration.
materials_needed: AWS Free Tier accounts (pre-created for students)
Starter website files: index.html, error.html, styles.css templates
Bucket policy JSON template document
Shared domain for Route 53 subdomain creation (e.g., classproject.com)
Verification checklist handout
assessment_method: Students submit: (1) Screenshot of working website via custom domain URL, (2) Screenshot of S3 bucket showing static website hosting enabled, (3) Screenshot of Route 53 record set configuration. Rubric: Website accessible via custom domain (40 points), proper S3 configuration visible (30 points), all template content displays correctly (20 points), completed within time limit (10 points). Pass threshold: 70/100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide step-by-step screenshot guide for S3 console navigation, offer pre-configured bucket policy with clear instructions on what to modify. For advanced learners: Challenge them to add CloudFront distribution for CDN, implement multiple pages with navigation, or add custom error pages with styling. Pair struggling students with successful peers for peer assistance during DNS configuration phase.

title: Risk Response Strategy Analysis: Evaluating Trade-offs in Project Risk Management
description: Students analyze a complex project scenario with multiple interconnected risks and evaluate the effectiveness of different risk response strategies. They will break down the relationships between risks, assess the impact of various mitigation approaches, and justify their strategic recommendations based on project constraints and objectives.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the interdependencies between project risks by mapping cause-and-effect relationships and identifying cascading failure points
Students will evaluate competing risk response strategies through systematic comparison of cost, schedule, scope, and stakeholder impact trade-offs
instructions:
