learning_objectives: Students will design a scalable enterprise network topology by analyzing business requirements and implementing hierarchical network architecture across multiple sites
Students will synthesize advanced Cisco technologies through configuring OSPF routing, HSRP redundancy, site-to-site VPNs, and multi-layer security policies in an integrated network solution
instructions:
**Phase 1: Network Design (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp requires network connectivity between headquarters (200 users), branch office (75 users), and data center (50 servers). Students work in teams of 2-3 to create detailed network diagrams using Cisco Packet Tracer, specifying IP addressing schemes using VLSM, VLAN segmentation for departments (Sales, Engineering, Finance, Guest), and redundant paths between sites.

**Phase 2: Core Infrastructure Implementation (90 minutes)**
Students configure the network backbone using Cisco routers (ISR 4000 series) and switches (Catalyst 9000 series) in Packet Tracer. Begin with basic device configuration including hostnames, passwords, and SSH access. Implement OSPF routing protocol with proper area design (Area 0 backbone, Area 1 for branch, Area 2 for data center). Configure inter-VLAN routing using SVIs on multilayer switches. Set up HSRP for gateway redundancy at each site with proper priority and preemption settings.

**Phase 3: Security and VPN Implementation (60 minutes)**
Establish site-to-site IPSec VPN tunnels between all locations using pre-shared keys and proper encryption parameters (AES-256, SHA-256). Configure access control lists to restrict traffic between VLANs according to security policies (Engineering cannot access Finance VLAN, Guest network isolated). Implement port security on access switches with violation actions. Configure DHCP services with appropriate scopes for each VLAN.

**Phase 4: Testing and Documentation (45 minutes)**
Conduct comprehensive connectivity testing between all sites and VLANs. Verify redundancy by simulating link failures and confirming automatic failover. Create detailed configuration documentation including IP addressing tables, VLAN assignments, and security policy matrix. Present solution to class with justification for design decisions.
materials_needed: Cisco Packet Tracer 8.2 or newer installed on student computers
TechCorp network requirements document (instructor-provided scenario)
Network diagram templates and IP addressing worksheets
Access to Cisco documentation and configuration guides
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Network Design Quality (25 points - logical topology, proper addressing, redundancy planning), Configuration Accuracy (35 points - correct OSPF, HSRP, VPN, and security settings), Functionality Testing (25 points - full connectivity, redundancy verification, security policy enforcement), and Documentation Quality (15 points - complete configuration records, clear diagrams, professional presentation). Students must achieve 80% functionality with no critical security vulnerabilities to pass.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured basic device settings and step-by-step OSPF configuration templates. Break complex tasks into smaller checkpoints with instructor verification. For advanced learners: Add requirements for QoS implementation, network monitoring with SNMP, or integration with wireless controllers. Encourage optimization of routing metrics and advanced security features like 802.1X authentication.

title: Python Data Types Memory Challenge
description: Students will memorize and recall the six fundamental Python data types through flashcard creation and rapid-fire identification exercises. This foundational activity builds essential vocabulary recognition needed for programming in Python.
learning_objectives: Students will identify the six basic Python data types (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary) by name when shown code examples
Students will recall the correct Python data type names through timed flashcard exercises with 90% accuracy
instructions: Begin by displaying six code examples on the board, each representing a different Python data type: x = 42 (int), y = 3.14 (float), name = 'Alice' (string), is_valid = True (boolean), colors = ['red', 'blue'] (list), and person = {'age': 25} (dictionary). Spend 5 minutes explaining each example while students take notes. Next, distribute blank index cards and have students create flashcards with the code example on one side and the data type name on the other (15 minutes). Students should create one card per data type, writing clearly in large letters. Once cards are complete, pair students and have them quiz each other using their flashcards for 10 minutes, taking turns showing the code side while their partner identifies the data type. For the final assessment, conduct a whole-class rapid-fire round where you display random code examples on the projector for 5 seconds each, and students write down the data type name on paper. Complete 12 examples total (2 of each type in random order). Between each example, give students 10 seconds to write their answer before moving to the next slide. Conclude by having students self-check their answers against the correct responses you provide.
materials_needed: Blank index cards (6 per student)
Colored pens or markers for students
Computer with projector for displaying code examples
Pre-prepared PowerPoint slides with 12 Python code examples
Answer sheets for final assessment
assessment_method: Students must correctly identify at least 10 out of 12 data types (83% accuracy) during the rapid-fire assessment. Grade the written answer sheets immediately and provide individual feedback. Award full credit for exact spelling of data type names (int, float, string, boolean, list, dictionary).
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students, provide a reference sheet with the six data type names visible during practice rounds. Allow them extra review time with flashcards before the final assessment. For advanced learners, include additional examples with nested data structures like lists containing dictionaries, and challenge them to identify both the outer and inner data types.

title: Optimizing Emergency Response Routes Using Calculus of Variations
description: Students will apply the calculus of variations to determine optimal emergency vehicle routes through urban environments with varying terrain and traffic conditions. They will solve Euler-Lagrange equations to minimize travel time while considering real-world constraints such as road capacity, elevation changes, and traffic density patterns.
learning_objectives: Students will apply the Euler-Lagrange equation to solve for optimal path functions by formulating and solving brachistochrone-type problems in emergency response scenarios
Students will implement calculus of variations principles through computational analysis of multi-constraint optimization problems involving time-critical transportation routes
instructions: Begin by distributing the Emergency Response Scenario packet containing three city maps with elevation contours, traffic density heat maps, and hospital locations (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3-4 students and assign each team a specific emergency type (cardiac, trauma, fire response). Students first establish their objective functional by defining travel time as an integral involving velocity constraints, elevation penalties, and traffic multipliers - provide the general form: I[y] = ∫[t1 to t2] F(x,y,y')dt where F incorporates terrain difficulty factor α(x,y), traffic density β(x,y), and vehicle speed limitations (20 minutes). Next, teams derive their specific Euler-Lagrange equation: d/dx(∂F/∂y') - ∂F/∂y = 0, substituting their emergency vehicle parameters and constraint functions (25 minutes). Using provided MATLAB templates, students discretize their differential equations and implement numerical solutions using finite difference methods, plotting multiple potential routes (30 minutes coding phase). Teams then validate their theoretical solutions by comparing computational results with their analytical predictions, identifying discrepancies and adjusting boundary conditions (20 minutes analysis). Each team presents their optimal route solution, explaining how calculus of variations principles led to their path selection, demonstrating the trade-offs between direct distance and constraint penalties (15 minutes per team presentation). Conclude with peer evaluation where teams assess each other's mathematical rigor and practical feasibility using provided rubric sheets (10 minutes).
materials_needed: Emergency Response Scenario packets with 3 detailed city maps including elevation and traffic data
MATLAB software with Optimization Toolbox installed on student computers
Pre-coded MATLAB templates for Euler-Lagrange equation solving
Scientific calculators
Rubric evaluation sheets for peer assessment
Large format paper for route sketching and mathematical work
assessment_method: Evaluate using 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct formulation of objective functional with appropriate constraint integration (25%), (2) Accurate derivation and solution of Euler-Lagrange equation (30%), (3) Proper implementation of numerical methods with validated computational results (25%), (4) Clear presentation demonstrating understanding of optimization trade-offs and real-world applicability (20%). Students must submit their mathematical derivations, MATLAB code with comments, and a 2-page technical summary explaining their route selection rationale.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide partially completed Euler-Lagrange derivations with key steps highlighted, offer simplified scenarios with single constraints first, and pair with stronger mathematical peers. For advanced learners: Introduce additional constraints like fuel optimization, multiple vehicle coordination, or dynamic traffic conditions; challenge them to incorporate stochastic elements or develop sensitivity analysis for their solutions.

title: Analyzing Multi-Component Electrical Circuit Failures Through Systematic Troubleshooting
description: Students will systematically analyze a complex electrical circuit with multiple intentional faults to identify failure points and their cascading effects. They will decompose the circuit behavior, distinguish between primary and secondary failures, and evaluate the interconnected relationships between circuit components.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze complex circuit behavior by systematically measuring and comparing theoretical versus actual voltage, current, and power values at specific nodes and branches
Students will differentiate between primary circuit failures and secondary effects through logical elimination of variables and component isolation techniques
instructions: Begin by providing each group of 3-4 students with a pre-built circuit board containing: two voltage dividers, an RC low-pass filter, an LED indicator circuit, and a transistor amplifier stage, with 2-3 intentional faults (such as open resistors, reversed diodes, or incorrect capacitor values). Give students 15 minutes to examine the circuit schematic and predict expected behavior at 8 designated test points. Next, have students spend 25 minutes systematically measuring actual values using multimeters and oscilloscopes, recording data in a structured analysis table comparing predicted vs. actual readings. During the third phase (20 minutes), students must isolate circuit sections by disconnecting specific components and re-measuring to determine which faults are primary causes versus secondary effects. For example, if an LED fails to illuminate, students should measure voltage across the LED, then the current-limiting resistor, then trace back through the circuit systematically. Students must document their reasoning process, creating a fault tree diagram showing the logical progression of their analysis. In the final 15 minutes, groups present their findings to the class, explaining their systematic approach and justifying why they identified specific components as faulty. Each group must defend their analysis method and explain how they distinguished correlation from causation in component interactions.
materials_needed: Pre-built circuit boards with 2-3 intentional faults per board
Circuit schematic diagrams with 8 labeled test points
Digital multimeters (1 per group)
Oscilloscopes with probes
Component isolation tools (jumper wires, alligator clips)
Structured data collection worksheets
Fault tree diagram templates
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Systematic measurement approach - students follow logical sequence and document all readings, (2) Analytical reasoning - students correctly distinguish primary faults from secondary effects with evidence, (3) Circuit decomposition - students effectively isolate subsections to test hypotheses, (4) Technical communication - students accurately use electrical terminology and justify conclusions with measured data. Success requires scoring 3+ on all criteria.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide guided measurement sequence cards showing exactly which test points to measure first, and offer simplified circuits with only one fault. For advanced learners: Add time-varying faults using temperature-sensitive components or intermittent connections, and require students to propose circuit modifications that would prevent the identified failure modes.

title: Code Review Battle: Evaluating Bug-Prone JavaScript Functions
description: Students analyze and critique three deliberately flawed JavaScript functions by identifying bugs, assessing code quality, and ranking solutions from worst to best. They must justify their evaluations using specific programming principles and provide improvement recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will evaluate the quality and correctness of JavaScript functions by systematically identifying bugs, security issues, and style violations
Students will critique multiple code solutions through comparative analysis and rank them based on efficiency, readability, and maintainability criteria
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the Code Review Worksheet containing three JavaScript functions that calculate user age from birthdate - each with different types of flaws (syntax errors, logic bugs, security vulnerabilities, poor naming). Organize students into pairs.

**Phase 1 - Individual Analysis (15 minutes):** Each student independently examines all three functions using the provided checklist: syntax correctness, logic accuracy, variable naming, error handling, and security considerations. Students mark identified issues directly on their worksheet and rate each function on a 1-10 scale.

**Phase 2 - Peer Discussion (10 minutes):** Pairs compare their findings, debate disagreements, and must reach consensus on ranking the functions from worst (#1) to best (#3). They document their reasoning using the evaluation criteria.

**Phase 3 - Justification Writing (15 minutes):** Each pair writes a 150-word evaluation report explaining their ranking decision. Report must include: specific bugs found, assessment of code readability, performance considerations, and two concrete improvement suggestions for the worst-ranked function.

**Phase 4 - Gallery Walk Evaluation (10 minutes):** Pairs post their rankings and justifications around the room. Students vote on which evaluation report is most thorough and convincing, practicing peer assessment skills.

**Debrief (5 minutes):** Instructor reveals the 'official' ranking based on professional standards and discusses how student evaluations compared. Highlight common evaluation criteria students missed and reinforce the importance of systematic code review practices.
materials_needed: Code Review Worksheet with 3 flawed JavaScript functions
Evaluation criteria checklist printout
Sticky notes for voting
Answer key with detailed bug explanations
assessment_method: Grade using 4-point rubric: Bug Identification (4 points - finds 6+ issues, 3 points - finds 4-5 issues, 2 points - finds 2-3 issues, 1 point - finds 0-1 issues), Ranking Justification (4 points - clear reasoning with specific examples, 2 points - general reasoning, 1 point - minimal justification), and Improvement Suggestions (2 points - actionable and specific, 1 point - vague or incorrect). Total: 10 points. Success = 7+ points.
scaffolding_notes: **For struggling students:** Provide a detailed bug-hunting checklist with specific questions like 'Are all variables declared?' and 'Does the function handle invalid inputs?' Pair weaker students with stronger peers. **For advanced learners:** Add a fourth function with subtle performance issues and ask them to evaluate computational complexity. Challenge them to rewrite the worst function demonstrating best practices.

title: Advanced Project Management Framework Recognition and Terminology Mastery Assessment
description: Students will memorize and recall specific terminology, formulas, and framework components from advanced project management methodologies including PMBOK Guide processes, Agile ceremonies, and risk management calculations. This activity focuses on building foundational knowledge recall for complex PM concepts through structured memorization and rapid retrieval exercises.
learning_objectives: Students will accurately recall all 49 PMBOK Guide process names with their corresponding knowledge areas and process groups within 45 seconds per process by completing timed flashcard drills
Students will precisely recite critical path method formulas, earned value management calculations, and risk probability impact matrix classifications through structured memorization exercises
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Advanced PM Knowledge Cards deck containing 120 cards covering: PMBOK processes (49 cards), Agile/Scrum terminology (25 cards), Risk Management formulas (20 cards), Quality Management tools (15 cards), and Stakeholder Analysis frameworks (11 cards). 

Phase 1 (25 minutes): Students work individually studying cards using the Leitner Box method. Provide each student with 5 labeled boxes (Daily, Every 2 Days, Weekly, Bi-weekly, Monthly). Students start all cards in Box 1, moving correctly recalled cards to Box 2 and keeping missed cards in Box 1. Continue cycling through boxes based on recall accuracy.

Phase 2 (20 minutes): Implement rapid-fire recall sessions. Call out specific prompts: 'Name the 5 process groups in order,' 'Recite the Earned Value formulas for CPI, SPI, and EAC,' 'List all Scrum ceremonies with time-boxes.' Students must respond within 10 seconds. Record accuracy rates on the tracking sheet.

Phase 3 (15 minutes): Conduct peer-to-peer verification rounds. Pair students and have them quiz each other using randomized card selections. Each student must correctly recall 25 random items from their partner's selection. Partners verify answers using the provided answer key and mark accuracy on individual scorecards.

Phase 4 (10 minutes): Complete the Advanced PM Terminology Speed Test - a written assessment requiring students to fill in 50 blanks covering critical formulas, process definitions, and framework components within the time limit.
materials_needed: Advanced PM Knowledge Cards deck (120 cards per student)
5 labeled Leitner boxes per student
Individual tracking sheets with accuracy recording grids
Comprehensive answer key with exact terminology
Advanced PM Terminology Speed Test worksheets
Digital timer/stopwatch
Individual scorecards for peer verification
assessment_method: Students must achieve 90% accuracy on the Speed Test (45/50 correct answers) and demonstrate 85% recall accuracy during rapid-fire sessions (17/20 correct responses within time limits). Assessment includes: written test scores, timed verbal recall accuracy rates, and peer verification results. Partial credit not awarded - responses must be exactly correct including proper spelling and complete formulas.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Reduce initial card deck to 60 essential items, extend response time to 15 seconds, and provide mnemonic device reference sheets. Create study partnerships with stronger students for additional practice sessions. For advanced learners: Add integration challenges requiring recall of how frameworks connect, include advanced certifications terminology (PgMP, PfMP), and require explanation of when to apply specific tools within 30-second responses.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Failures: Crisis Decision-Making Analysis
description: Students will analyze complex leadership failures during organizational crises by examining decision-making patterns, stakeholder impacts, and systemic factors. They will demonstrate understanding by identifying recurring failure patterns across multiple real-world cases and explaining the underlying leadership principles that were violated.
learning_objectives: Students will categorize specific leadership decision-making failures by analyzing documented crisis responses across three distinct organizational contexts
Students will explain the relationship between leadership communication strategies and stakeholder trust erosion through comparative case study examination
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 4-5 members (15 minutes setup). Assign each team one of five pre-selected leadership failure cases: Wells Fargo account scandal (2016), Boeing 737 MAX crisis (2018-2019), Theranos fraud (2015-2018), Volkswagen emissions scandal (2015), or WeWork IPO collapse (2019). Provide each team with a standardized case packet containing: timeline of events, key leader statements/communications, financial impact data, stakeholder reactions, and regulatory responses. Teams spend 45 minutes conducting structured analysis using the provided Leadership Failure Analysis Framework, which requires them to: (1) map the decision-making process at three critical junctures, (2) identify which stakeholder groups were impacted and how, (3) categorize the leadership failures using Kouzes-Posner's Five Practices framework violations, and (4) trace the communication strategy evolution throughout the crisis. After analysis, teams rotate through gallery walk stations (20 minutes) to examine other teams' analyses, noting patterns and differences. Conclude with 25-minute structured discussion where each team presents one key insight about recurring failure patterns, while instructor facilitates identification of cross-case themes such as ethical blind spots, communication transparency failures, and accountability avoidance. Students individually complete a synthesis reflection identifying three universal leadership principles violated across multiple cases.
materials_needed: Five standardized case study packets with primary source documents
Leadership Failure Analysis Framework worksheets
Large poster paper and markers for gallery walk displays
Digital timer for rotation management
Kouzes-Posner Five Practices reference sheets
assessment_method: Evaluate using three components: (1) Completed analysis frameworks demonstrating accurate categorization of failures and stakeholder impacts (40%), (2) Quality of cross-case pattern identification during gallery walk discussions, assessed through peer observation forms (30%), (3) Individual synthesis reflection showing clear explanation of violated leadership principles with specific evidence from multiple cases (30%). Success requires accurate use of leadership terminology, evidence-based conclusions, and demonstration of understanding connections between leadership decisions and organizational outcomes.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide highlighted case packets with key decision points pre-marked, offer additional examples of Kouzes-Posner framework applications, and assign peer mentors within teams. For advanced learners: Include additional stakeholder perspective documents (employee testimonials, customer impact stories), challenge them to identify potential alternative decision paths leaders could have taken, and ask them to facilitate small group discussions during gallery walk rotations.

title: Deploy a Two-Tier Web Application on AWS Using EC2 and RDS
description: Students will apply AWS fundamentals by deploying a complete web application infrastructure consisting of an EC2 web server and RDS database. This hands-on activity demonstrates real-world cloud architecture implementation using AWS services.
learning_objectives: Students will deploy a functional web application by configuring EC2 instances and RDS databases using AWS Management Console
Students will implement security best practices through proper configuration of security groups and database access controls
instructions: Begin with a 10-minute demonstration of the AWS Management Console navigation. Students work individually with provided AWS Learner Lab accounts. Step 1 (15 minutes): Students launch an Amazon EC2 t2.micro instance running Amazon Linux 2, selecting the default VPC and enabling auto-assign public IP. They must create a new security group allowing HTTP (port 80) and SSH (port 22) access from anywhere. Step 2 (20 minutes): Students create an Amazon RDS MySQL database instance (db.t3.micro) in the same VPC, creating a new subnet group spanning two availability zones. They configure a new security group allowing MySQL access (port 3306) only from the EC2 security group created earlier. Step 3 (15 minutes): Students connect to their EC2 instance via SSH using the provided key pair, install Apache web server and PHP using yum package manager, and start the web service. Step 4 (20 minutes): Students download and configure a provided PHP sample application that connects to their RDS database, updating the database connection string with their RDS endpoint. Step 5 (10 minutes): Students test their application by accessing the public IP address in a browser and verifying database connectivity by submitting a simple form that writes to the database. Instructor circulates to provide individual assistance and verify each student's progress at each checkpoint.
materials_needed: AWS Learner Lab accounts with $100 credit for each student
Pre-written PHP sample application with database connection code
SSH client software (PuTTY for Windows or Terminal for Mac/Linux)
AWS EC2 key pair file (.pem format) provided to students
assessment_method: Students demonstrate successful completion by showing: 1) Running web application accessible via public URL (40 points), 2) Functional database connectivity with data persistence (30 points), 3) Properly configured security groups with least-privilege access (20 points), 4) Screenshot documentation of AWS resources in Management Console (10 points). Instructor uses checklist to verify each component during lab walkthrough.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured security group templates and step-by-step command reference sheet for Linux commands. Pair students with technical difficulties with more advanced peers. For advanced learners: Challenge them to implement additional features like auto-scaling groups, load balancers, or multi-AZ RDS deployment. Provide extension activity to configure CloudWatch monitoring and set up billing alerts.

title: Project Risk Register Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Evaluation
description: Students will analyze a provided project risk register containing 12 identified risks, evaluate the effectiveness of existing mitigation strategies, and determine which risks require revised response plans. This activity develops critical thinking skills for risk management processes outlined in the PMBOK Guide.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze risk probability and impact ratings by examining quantitative and qualitative data to identify inconsistencies in risk prioritization
Students will evaluate the adequacy of current risk response strategies through systematic comparison against PMBOK risk response types and project constraints
instructions:
**Setup (5 minutes):** Distribute the standardized risk register spreadsheet containing 12 risks from a software implementation project, including risk ID, description, probability (1-5), impact (1-5), risk score, assigned owner, current mitigation strategy, and status updates. Divide class into teams of 3-4 students.

**Phase 1 - Risk Analysis (20 minutes):** Teams examine each risk entry and identify: (1) risks with probability/impact ratings that seem inconsistent with the description, (2) risks missing critical information, and (3) the top 5 risks based on calculated risk scores. Students must document their findings on the provided analysis worksheet.

**Phase 2 - Strategy Evaluation (25 minutes):** For each of the top 5 identified risks, teams evaluate the current mitigation strategy by: (1) categorizing it as avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept, (2) assessing whether the strategy appropriately matches the risk type and project constraints, (3) identifying gaps in the response plan, and (4) determining if the assigned risk owner has appropriate authority and expertise.

**Phase 3 - Recommendations (15 minutes):** Teams prepare a priority-ranked list of 3 risks requiring immediate attention, with specific justification for why current strategies are inadequate. Each recommendation must include the proposed response type change and implementation approach.

**Presentation (10 minutes):** Each team presents their top priority risk and proposed solution change to the class for peer feedback.
materials_needed: Pre-populated risk register Excel spreadsheet with 12 sample risks
Risk analysis worksheet template (PDF)
PMBOK risk response strategy reference sheet
Laptops or tablets for teams
Flip chart paper and markers for presentations
assessment_method: Teams submit completed analysis worksheets evaluated on: (1) Accuracy of risk prioritization with clear mathematical justification (25 points), (2) Quality of strategy evaluation showing understanding of risk response types (35 points), (3) Feasibility and specificity of recommendations with implementation details (25 points), (4) Professional presentation of findings with peer Q&A responses (15 points). Total: 100 points.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide a completed example analysis for one sample risk and create mixed-ability teams pairing stronger students with those needing support. For advanced learners: Add secondary risks and risk interdependencies to analyze, or require Monte Carlo simulation calculations for quantitative risk analysis of their top recommendations.

title: Design and Implement a Multi-Site Enterprise WAN Architecture with SD-WAN Integration
description: Students will architect a complete enterprise WAN solution connecting four geographically distributed sites using traditional MPLS, backup internet circuits, and SD-WAN overlay technology. They will create detailed network diagrams, configure routing protocols, implement QoS policies, and establish secure tunnels while documenting their design decisions and troubleshooting procedures.
estimated_duration: 5.25 hours (315 minutes) spread across multiple sessions
learning_objectives: Students will synthesize MPLS, BGP, OSPF, and SD-WAN technologies by designing a resilient multi-site WAN architecture that meets specific business requirements
Students will construct comprehensive network documentation through creating implementation guides, configuration templates, and disaster recovery procedures
instructions:
**Phase 1: Requirements Analysis (45 minutes)**
Provide students with a fictional company scenario: TechCorp has headquarters in New York (500 users), regional offices in Chicago (200 users), Denver (150 users), and Los Angeles (300 users). Students must analyze bandwidth requirements, application priorities, and budget constraints ($50K monthly). Have them document traffic flows, identify critical applications (VoIP, video conferencing, ERP), and establish SLA requirements.

**Phase 2: Architecture Design (90 minutes)**
Students create detailed network topology using Visio or draw.io, incorporating Cisco ISR 4000 series routers, ASA firewalls, and Catalyst switches. They must design MPLS topology with PE-CE connections, plan IP addressing using /24 subnets for each site, and integrate Cisco SD-WAN (vEdge routers) as overlay. Require BGP configuration for internet circuits and OSPF for internal routing.

**Phase 3: Configuration Development (120 minutes)**
Using GNS3 or Cisco Modeling Labs, students build scaled-down lab environment and configure actual devices. They must implement MPLS VRF configurations, establish SD-WAN fabric with vManage orchestrator, configure QoS policies prioritizing voice traffic, and set up IPSec tunnels for backup connectivity. Include HSRP configuration for gateway redundancy.

**Phase 4: Documentation and Testing (60 minutes)**
Students create implementation runbook with step-by-step procedures, develop troubleshooting guide with common failure scenarios, and design monitoring dashboard showing circuit utilization and application performance. They must simulate link failures and document failover behavior, then present their solution to the class explaining design rationale and trade-offs made.
materials_needed: GNS3 or Cisco Modeling Labs (CML) software with Cisco IOS images
Microsoft Visio or draw.io for network diagrams
Cisco SD-WAN simulator or sandbox environment
Sample company requirements document template
Access to Cisco documentation and configuration guides
assessment_method: Evaluate using rubric with four components: Architecture Design (25 points) - logical topology, proper technology selection, scalability considerations; Technical Implementation (30 points) - working configurations, proper protocol selection, security measures; Documentation Quality (25 points) - clarity, completeness, professional formatting; Problem-solving Demonstration (20 points) - troubleshooting scenarios, failure analysis, optimization recommendations. Students must achieve 80% minimum with working lab demonstration required.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-configured base templates, offer one-on-one lab time, and create simplified three-site version. Supply configuration examples for complex protocols like BGP and MPLS. For advanced learners: Add IPv6 dual-stack requirements, implement advanced SD-WAN policies with application-aware routing, integrate with cloud providers (AWS/Azure), or add network automation using Python scripts and NETCONF/RESTCONF APIs.

title: Optimizing Stadium Seating Revenue Using Quadratic Functions
description: Students will apply quadratic optimization techniques to solve a real-world stadium pricing problem by determining the ticket price that maximizes revenue. They will work with demand functions, revenue equations, and calculus-based optimization methods to make data-driven business recommendations.
learning_objectives: Students will apply quadratic optimization techniques to determine maximum revenue points by setting up and solving real-world pricing scenarios
Students will construct and manipulate quadratic revenue functions through systematic analysis of demand-price relationships
instructions: Begin by distributing the stadium scenario packet containing historical attendance and pricing data for Metro Stadium (capacity 45,000). Students work in teams of 3-4. Phase 1 (15 minutes): Teams analyze the data table showing that when tickets cost $20, attendance is 40,000, and for every $5 price increase, attendance drops by 2,500. Students must identify the linear demand function A(p) = 40,000 - 500(p-20). Phase 2 (20 minutes): Teams construct the revenue function R(p) = p × A(p) and expand it to standard quadratic form R(p) = -500p² + 50,000p. They must show all algebraic steps on poster paper. Phase 3 (15 minutes): Students apply three different optimization methods: completing the square, using the vertex formula p = -b/2a, and taking the derivative R'(p) = 0. All three methods must yield p = $50. Phase 4 (10 minutes): Teams calculate maximum revenue ($1,250,000) and optimal attendance (27,500) using their derived price point. Phase 5 (20 minutes): Students create a comprehensive business presentation including the quadratic graph with labeled vertex, domain restrictions (price must be positive, attendance cannot exceed capacity), and sensitivity analysis showing revenue changes for ±$5 price variations. Each team presents their findings with mathematical justification for exactly 3 minutes, followed by peer questioning.
materials_needed: Stadium pricing scenario packet with historical data tables
Graphing calculators or Desmos access on tablets/computers
Large poster paper and markers for function work
Business presentation template handout
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric covering: (1) Correct demand function derivation (25%), (2) Accurate revenue function construction and algebraic manipulation (25%), (3) Successful application of all three optimization methods with consistent results (30%), (4) Professional presentation with clear mathematical reasoning and appropriate business context (20%). Students must achieve 3/4 points in each category for proficiency.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-completed data organization tables and guided practice with simpler linear demand scenarios. Offer step-by-step optimization method cards as references. For advanced learners: Extend to piecewise functions for different seating sections, incorporate cost functions for profit optimization, or analyze multiple constraint scenarios (weather impacts, competitor pricing).

title: Analyzing Multi-Body Gravitational Systems Using Phase Space Diagrams
description: Students will decompose complex three-body gravitational problems by analyzing phase space trajectories and energy distributions. They will examine how initial conditions affect orbital stability and identify critical points where systems transition between stable and chaotic behavior.
learning_objectives: Students will analyze the relationship between initial velocity vectors and orbital stability by constructing phase space diagrams for restricted three-body problems
Students will differentiate between regular and chaotic motion patterns through systematic examination of Poincaré sections and energy surface topology
instructions:
Begin by distributing the Earth-Moon-spacecraft scenario datasets containing 12 different initial conditions (15 minutes setup). Form teams of 3 students, assigning roles: Data Analyst (processes numerical solutions), Visualizer (creates phase space plots), and Theorist (applies conservation laws). Each team receives identical gravitational parameters but different initial spacecraft positions and velocities.

Phase 1 (45 minutes): Teams import their assigned dataset into Python/MATLAB and generate 6D phase space projections (x, y, vx, vy for spacecraft motion). Students plot position coordinates against corresponding velocities, creating four 2D phase portraits. The Data Analyst calculates total energy and angular momentum at 100 time intervals, while the Visualizer maps trajectory crossings through the y=0 plane (Poincaré section).

Phase 2 (30 minutes): Teams analyze their phase portraits to identify: periodic orbits (closed curves), quasi-periodic motion (nested tori), and chaotic regions (scattered points). The Theorist correlates energy fluctuations with trajectory stability, examining whether energy conservation holds within numerical precision (±0.1%).

Phase 3 (45 minutes): Teams compare results across all 12 initial conditions, categorizing each as stable, marginally stable, or chaotic based on maximum Lyapunov exponent calculations. Students create a stability map plotting initial velocity magnitude versus angle, identifying boundaries between motion types.

Concluding synthesis (30 minutes): Each team presents their stability analysis, explaining how phase space structure reveals underlying dynamical behavior. Teams must justify their classification criteria and predict long-term evolution for borderline cases.
materials_needed: Pre-computed three-body orbital datasets (12 CSV files with position/velocity time series)
Python with matplotlib/numpy or MATLAB with plotting toolbox
Phase space analysis worksheet with energy/momentum calculation templates
Digital projector for team presentations
assessment_method: Evaluate based on: (1) Accuracy of phase space diagram construction (25 points), (2) Correct identification of motion types using quantitative criteria (30 points), (3) Quality of stability boundary analysis with supporting calculations (30 points), (4) Clear explanation of phase space-dynamics connection in final presentation (15 points). Students must achieve >80% accuracy in classifying orbital stability and demonstrate understanding of conservation law violations as chaos indicators.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-made plotting templates and guided worksheets with specific calculation steps. Offer simplified 2-body cases first to build intuition. For advanced learners: Challenge them to derive analytical approximations for stability boundaries near Lagrange points, or extend analysis to include relativistic corrections for Mercury-like orbits.

title: Design a Predictive Analytics Dashboard for Customer Churn Prevention
description: Students will create an interactive dashboard that combines multiple data analysis techniques to predict and prevent customer churn for a fictional subscription service. They will synthesize statistical analysis, visualization design, and business strategy into a comprehensive analytical solution.
learning_objectives: Students will design a comprehensive predictive analytics dashboard by integrating multiple data sources and statistical models to solve a real-world business problem
Students will create actionable business recommendations through systematic analysis of customer behavior patterns and churn indicators
instructions: Begin by dividing students into teams of 3-4 members (15 minutes). Provide each team with the fictional 'StreamFlix' dataset containing 12 months of customer data including demographics, usage patterns, payment history, and support interactions. Teams first spend 30 minutes exploring the dataset to identify potential churn indicators using descriptive statistics and correlation analysis. Next, students develop predictive models using logistic regression or decision trees (45 minutes), testing at least two different approaches and comparing accuracy metrics. Teams then design their dashboard layout on paper, identifying 5-7 key visualizations that tell a coherent story about churn risk (20 minutes). Using Tableau or Power BI, students build their interactive dashboard incorporating: a churn risk score distribution, customer segmentation analysis, timeline of churn patterns, and at-risk customer identification tool (90 minutes). Students must include drill-down capabilities and filtering options. Finally, teams prepare a 10-minute presentation explaining their methodology, key findings, and specific business recommendations for reducing churn by at least 15%. Each presentation should include a live dashboard demonstration and defend their analytical choices. Conclude with peer feedback sessions where teams evaluate each other's dashboards using provided criteria sheets (30 minutes).
materials_needed: StreamFlix customer dataset (CSV file with 10,000+ records)
Tableau Public or Power BI Desktop software
Laptops/computers with internet access
Dashboard evaluation rubric handouts
Flip chart paper and markers for planning
Presentation timer and projection equipment
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 100-point rubric: Data exploration and model development (25 points), dashboard design and functionality (30 points), visual storytelling and clarity (20 points), business recommendations quality (15 points), and presentation delivery (10 points). Students must achieve 80% accuracy in their predictive model, include at least 5 interactive visualizations, and provide 3 specific, data-driven business recommendations.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-identified churn indicators list and dashboard template with placeholder visualizations. Offer one-on-one guidance during model development phase. For advanced learners: Challenge them to incorporate advanced techniques like customer lifetime value calculations, implement real-time data refresh capabilities, or create mobile-responsive dashboard versions. Provide additional datasets for cross-validation.

title: Critical Path Method (CPM) Formula and Network Diagram Component Identification Challenge
description: Students will identify and recall specific formulas, terminology, and network diagram components used in Critical Path Method calculations. This intensive recall activity focuses on memorizing the precise mathematical formulas for Early Start, Early Finish, Late Start, Late Finish, and Total Float calculations along with recognizing standard CPM notation symbols.
learning_objectives: Students will recall the five core CPM calculation formulas (ES, EF, LS, LF, TF) by completing timed formula identification exercises with 95% accuracy
Students will identify standard CPM network diagram symbols and notation through visual recognition activities using authentic project scheduling scenarios
instructions: Begin by distributing the CPM Formula Reference Sheet face-down to all students (5 minutes setup). Divide class into pairs and provide each pair with one set of 25 CPM Component Flashcards and one CPM Network Diagram Sample. Round 1 (15 minutes): Students work individually to complete the 'CPM Formula Fill-in-the-Blank' worksheet without references. They must write the complete formulas for: Early Start (ES = Maximum EF of predecessors), Early Finish (EF = ES + Duration), Late Finish (LF = Minimum LS of successors), Late Start (LS = LF - Duration), and Total Float (TF = LS - ES or LF - EF). Round 2 (20 minutes): Using flashcards, partners quiz each other on CPM terminology including: critical path, dummy activity, forward pass, backward pass, slack time, precedence relationships (FS, SS, FF, SF), and milestone symbols. One partner shows the term, the other provides the definition. Round 3 (15 minutes): Students examine the network diagram sample and identify 15 specific components: activity nodes, duration values, dependency arrows, critical path highlighted in red, early start/finish times, late start/finish times, float calculations, project start node, project end node, and resource assignments. They must circle each component and label it correctly on their worksheet. Conclude with rapid-fire verbal quiz (10 minutes) where instructor calls out scenarios and students shout the appropriate formula or term.
materials_needed: CPM Formula Reference Sheet (1 per student)
Set of 25 CPM Component Flashcards (1 set per pair)
CPM Network Diagram Sample with 15+ identifiable components (1 per student)
CPM Formula Fill-in-the-Blank worksheet (1 per student)
Stopwatch or timer
Red markers for highlighting critical paths
assessment_method: Grade students on three deliverables: (1) Formula worksheet completion with 19/20 formulas correct for full points, (2) Network diagram component identification with 13/15 components correctly labeled, (3) Partner quiz performance tracked on peer evaluation form showing 80%+ accuracy on terminology definitions. Use provided answer key for immediate feedback and award participation points for engagement during rapid-fire quiz.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide the CPM Formula Reference Sheet during Round 1 and allow extra 5 minutes per round. Create simplified flashcards with only 15 core terms instead of 25. For advanced learners: Add complex scenarios requiring formula application in multi-path networks, include resource-constrained scheduling terminology, and challenge them to identify advanced concepts like leads, lags, and hammock activities in bonus network diagrams.

title: Deconstructing Leadership Crisis Communication: A Multi-Framework Analysis of Executive Responses
description: Students will analyze authentic crisis communication statements from three different CEOs using established leadership communication frameworks to identify underlying leadership philosophies and decision-making patterns. This activity develops deep comprehension of how leadership theory manifests in high-stakes, real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will differentiate between transformational, transactional, and servant leadership approaches by analyzing CEO crisis communication statements through Kouzes & Posner's Five Practices framework
Students will interpret the relationship between organizational values and leadership decision-making through systematic comparison of executive messaging during parallel crisis situations
instructions: Begin by dividing students into groups of 4-5. Distribute three crisis communication case packets: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol recall (James Burke), Wells Fargo account scandal (John Stumpf), and Patagonia's supply chain crisis (Yvon Chouinard). Each packet contains the CEO's public statements, internal memos, and stakeholder responses. Step 1 (25 minutes): Groups read all three cases and create initial impressions using the provided Leadership Philosophy Identification Matrix. Step 2 (35 minutes): Apply Kouzes & Posner's Five Practices (Model the Way, Inspire Shared Vision, Challenge the Process, Enable Others to Act, Encourage the Heart) to each CEO's response. Students complete detailed analysis sheets rating each practice on a 1-5 scale with specific textual evidence. Step 3 (20 minutes): Map each leader's approach onto the Leadership Styles Spectrum (directive, supportive, participative, achievement-oriented) and identify primary and secondary styles exhibited. Step 4 (30 minutes): Create comparison matrices identifying patterns in decision-making speed, stakeholder prioritization, accountability language, and future-focused messaging. Step 5 (25 minutes): Groups prepare 8-minute presentations using the provided template: leadership style identification, framework application evidence, crisis response effectiveness analysis, and organizational culture implications. Each group presents one case in-depth while briefly comparing to the other two.
materials_needed: Three crisis communication case study packets with primary source documents
Leadership Philosophy Identification Matrix worksheets
Kouzes & Posner Five Practices analysis sheets
Leadership Styles Spectrum mapping templates
Comparison matrix templates (Excel or printed versions)
Digital presentation template with required sections
assessment_method: Evaluate using a 4-point rubric assessing: (1) Accurate framework application with specific textual evidence, (2) Clear differentiation between leadership approaches with nuanced analysis, (3) Logical connections drawn between leadership theory and practical outcomes, (4) Quality of comparative analysis demonstrating pattern recognition across cases. Students submit completed analysis sheets and deliver group presentations. Minimum 80% accuracy required on framework applications.
scaffolding_notes: For struggling students: Provide pre-filled examples for one CEO using each framework, offer sentence starters for analysis statements, and allow extended time for case reading. For advanced learners: Add Situational Leadership Theory as a fourth analytical lens, require integration of organizational behavior concepts like psychological safety, and challenge them to predict alternative outcomes under different leadership approaches.
